Harvest when the papery husk has dried to tan-brown and the golden berry inside detaches easily. Fallen fruits left in their husks on the ground remain fresh for several weeks.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in extremely acidic, well-drained soil; Gulf Coast requires 200–300 chill hours, lower than rabbiteye varieties but slightly higher than Sharpblue. Excellent choice for zone 8–9 gardens on the Gulf Coast. Plant with O'Neal, Sharpblue, or Emerald for cross-pollination.
directions: Prepare acidic soil to pH 4.5–5.0 before planting; Gulf Coast is a Southern highbush blueberry developed jointly by the USDA and the University of Florida and released in 1987, specifically bred for the lower-chill coastal regions of the Gulf South including Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle. It requires 200–300 chill hours and produces reliable crops where northern highbush varieties fail to fruit. Berries are medium-large, blue, firm, with a dry scar and good sweet flavor that develops best with warm, sunny ripening conditions. The plant has a naturally spreading habit and is fairly tolerant of the heavy clay soils found in coastal areas if drainage is adequate — raised beds work excellently. Gulf Coast is also noted for tolerance of the wet winters common on the Gulf Coast, as long as roots are not waterlogged for extended periods. An excellent variety to pair with Climax rabbiteye blueberry to extend season: Gulf Coast ripens 2–3 weeks before Climax begins.

plant_note: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in early spring in very acidic soil; half-high types excel in zones 3–5 where standard highbush varieties suffer winter dieback.
directions: Half-high blueberries are crosses between highbush and lowbush species, combining the large-berry quality of highbush with the extreme cold hardiness of lowbush — cultivars such as 'Northblue', 'Northcountry', and 'Polaris' survive to -35°F when snow-covered. Maintain soil pH between 4.5 and 5.0 and mulch heavily with pine bark or sawdust. Cross-pollination between two compatible cultivars improves berry size and total yield. Pruning is minimal for the first five years; thereafter remove the thickest, oldest canes each late winter to encourage fresh productive wood.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger; provide a very sturdy trellis or pergola capable of holding hundreds of pounds of vine.
directions: Hardy kiwi vines are dioecious — plant one male vine for every 6–8 female vines or choose a self-fertile cultivar such as 'Issai'. The vines can take 4–7 years to bear fruit but become very productive once established, requiring a pergola or heavy-gauge trellis rated to hold at least 200 lbs. Prune to a permanent framework of main arms and renewal spurs each late winter, cutting lateral shoots back to 2–4 buds. Harvest when smooth, grape-sized fruits yield slightly to pressure and taste sweet.

plant_note: Plant two compatible cultivars (cross-pollination required) in spring in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 2–7; Haskap (Honeyberry, Blue Honeysuckle) is an exceptionally cold-hardy edible honeysuckle shrub from the boreal forests of Siberia, Japan, and northern North America — one of the first fruits to ripen in spring, producing elongated, dark blue-purple berries with complex blueberry-raspberry-elderberry flavor used fresh, frozen, and in jams.
directions: Plant Haskap in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; always plant two or more compatible cultivars for cross-pollination; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; berries ripen 2–3 weeks before strawberries and should be harvested promptly. Lonicera caerulea var. edulis and its cultivated selections (Honeyberry or Haskap) represent one of the hardiest edible shrubs in cultivation — tolerating temperatures to -40°F or below in adapted varieties, and withstanding late spring frosts during bloom thanks to early-season cold-hardiness of the flowers. Two compatible cultivars are essential for reliable fruiting, as the species is largely self-incompatible; many named Canadian and Japanese breeding program selections are available for pairing. The elongated, dark blue-black berries are nutritionally similar to blueberries but with a distinctly more complex flavor — sweet-tart with blueberry, raspberry, and elderberry undertones and a pleasant tartness. The shrubs are extremely long-lived (50+ years), begin bearing in year 2–3 after planting, and require minimal pruning beyond removing deadwood. Excellent for northern gardens where blueberries struggle, and the extremely early ripening season makes them valuable for extending the fresh-fruit season.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in wet to moist soil along stream banks, pond margins, or low wet areas; hazel alder tolerates periodic flooding and establishes quickly when planted in consistently wet ground.
directions: Plant in consistently wet, moist-to-saturated soil along stream edges, pond margins, or low wet areas in full sun to partial shade; hazel alder is a multi-stemmed native shrub or small tree that thrives where few plants can, colonizing eroded stream banks and stabilizing them with a dense fibrous root system. Like other alders it hosts nitrogen-fixing Frankia bacteria in root nodules, enriching surrounding soil and supporting the broader riparian plant community. Reddish-purple male catkins emerge as early as February before any leaves appear, providing critical early-season pollen for queen bumblebees and other overwintered insects. The persistent woody seed cones persist through winter and are eaten by redpolls, goldfinches, and other seed-eating birds.

plant_note: Set rooted cuttings in spring into moist, fertile soil at the base of a sturdy fence, arbor, or large tree; plant in a location that receives at least a few hours of direct sun to encourage fruiting, and water well through the first growing season.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into moist, organically rich soil at the base of a large, sturdy support structure, watering thoroughly and mulching to retain moisture through the first growing season while the root system establishes. Heartleaf peppervine is a vigorous deciduous vine native to floodplain forests and bottomland thickets of the southeastern US, recognized by its broad, bold, heart-shaped leaves and the showy clusters of small berries that ripen from green through turquoise to blue-black in fall, providing an important food source for mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and other songbirds. This large-scale native vine is well suited to covering fences, large arbors, and the trunks of substantial trees in moist, lowland sites where vigorous growth is desired and space is not limiting. Once established on fertile, consistently moist soil, it requires no supplemental care and will cover its support structure rapidly; direct new growth as needed to keep the vine on its intended structure.

plant_note: Set dormant canes early spring while soil is workable, before bud break.
directions: Plant 'Heritage' canes in well-drained loam enriched with compost, spacing them 2-3 feet apart in rows. This reliable everbearing (primocane) variety fruits on first-year canes in late summer and again the following early summer. For a single heavy fall crop, mow all canes to the ground each late winter. Provide a trellis or T-post support and keep beds mulched to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Higgins is a female-flowered (pistillate) variety that requires a perfect-flowered pollinator vine nearby. Plant within 50 feet of Ison, Triumph, or another perfect-flowered variety. In zone 9 Higgins ripens in August–September. The very large fruit size makes it one of the most impressive muscadines at the market and fresh-eating table.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil and provide a pollinator vine; Higgins is a Georgia Experiment Station-released muscadine variety renowned for producing fruits of extraordinary size — large white (bronze-skinned) muscadines reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter, among the very largest in the muscadine world. The large, pale bronze-gold fruits have a sweet, rich, floral muscadine flavor and a tender skin that makes fresh eating considerably more pleasant than older tough-skinned varieties. Higgins is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the impressive fruit size creates visual impact at farmers' markets and U-pick operations. As a female-flowered (pistillate) variety, Higgins requires a perfect-flowered pollinator nearby — without cross-pollination the vine sets little or no fruit. Plant alongside Ison, Triumph, or another self-fertile muscadine for reliable production. In zone 9 the long, warm summer provides ideal conditions for the large fruits to develop to their full potential size.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root or container stock in early spring once soil is workable; fall planting is possible in zones 6–8.
directions: Blueberries require acidic soil with a pH of 4.5–5.5; amend with elemental sulfur and use acidic mulch such as pine bark or wood chips 3–4 in deep. Plant at least two cultivars for cross-pollination and better fruit set. Prune out old canes older than 6 years at the base each late winter to stimulate productive new wood. Harvest when berries turn deep blue and detach with minimal resistance, typically 7–10 days after color change.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in cool-summer climates in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; gooseberries perform poorly in hot, humid summer climates and need afternoon shade and reliable soil moisture where summers are warm.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun where summers are cool; mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune to an open framework each winter to ease harvest among the thorny stems. Hinnomaki Red is a Finnish-bred gooseberry cultivar prized for combining reliable productivity, good mildew resistance, and outstanding fruit quality — the medium-sized berries ripen from green to a deep red-burgundy with a rich, sweet-tart flavor considered among the best of any gooseberry for fresh eating out of hand, as well as excellent for pies, jams, and fools. The compact, upright bush is more manageable and less sprawling than many older gooseberry varieties, and its Nordic breeding gives it strong cold hardiness alongside dependable disease resistance in cool, humid summer climates. Best suited to northern gardens with cool summers; in hot, humid zones the plant struggles with heat stress and powdery mildew regardless of afternoon shade. Zone 3–7.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring.
directions: 'Hinnonmaki Red' is a hardy Finnish gooseberry with dark-red, aromatic berries that are tart when green for cooking and sweet when fully ripe for dessert. It shows good mildew resistance and thrives in cool, moist conditions. Grow in full sun to partial shade in rich, well-drained soil and mulch to keep the roots cool. Prune to an open-centered bush in winter, removing crossing and low branches, and wear gloves when harvesting the thorny stems.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; hoary blueberry grows naturally at higher elevations in the southern Appalachians in moist acidic forest understory and open heath balds.
directions: Plant in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; hoary blueberry is a native Appalachian species of high-elevation heath and forest understory communities, distinguished by its distinctly hairy (hoary) twigs and leaf undersides — the fine hairs give new growth and undersides a grayish, woolly appearance. The plant is closely related to rabbiteye blueberry but adapted to cooler, higher-elevation sites. The blue-black berries are edible and well-flavored. In the garden, it performs well in moist, acidic shade conditions that suit other ericaceous plants like rhododendron and mountain laurel. An excellent native for the acid woodland garden in zones 5–8.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade to partial sun; hobblebush requires consistently moist conditions and cool summer temperatures and performs poorly in sites with hot, dry summers or direct afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, allowing generous spacing for the broad, arching form; hobblebush requires cool summer temperatures and consistent moisture, and is best suited to northern gardens or high-elevation sites where summer heat is moderate. Viburnum lantanoides produces large, heart-shaped leaves on low-arching branches that root where they contact the ground — the source of the name 'hobblebush,' as the rooted stems can trip unwary woodland walkers — and bears flat-topped clusters of showy white flowers in April and May followed by berries that ripen from red to black and attract thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Fall foliage color is among the most dramatic of any native shrub, turning rich crimson to claret-red in September, making hobblebush a multi-season standout for shaded northern woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; plant at least two different cultivars for cross-pollination, as most cultivars are self-infertile.
directions: Plant two or more different cultivars for cross-pollination in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full sun; honeyberry is an edible-fruited honeysuckle native to boreal regions of Russia, Japan, and Canada that produces sweet-tart blue berries resembling elongated blueberries in late spring — the first fresh fruit of the season in cold climates. Plants tolerate temperatures to -40°F and the flowers survive spring frosts to -8°F. Fruit is borne on second-year wood, so avoid heavy pruning in the first three years. Cultivars 'Tundra', 'Indigo Gem', and 'Borealis' are among the most productive for North American gardens.

plant_note: Plant two or more compatible cultivars in early spring for cross-pollination; haskap blooms very early and needs a matching early-blooming partner.
directions: Honeyberries are among the earliest fruits to ripen — often 2–3 weeks before strawberries — and flowers can survive temperatures as low as -4°F, making them ideal for short-season climates. Two compatible cultivars from the same breeding group must be planted for cross-pollination. Minimal pruning is needed for the first 5 years; thereafter, remove a few of the oldest, thickest canes annually to renew. Harvest when berries are entirely blue-purple inside (cut one open to check), as color alone can be misleading.

common_name: Illini Hardy Blackberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Erect Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in early to mid-spring after the coldest weather has passed; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, ripening mid-to-late season.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5). Illini Hardy is an erect, thorny blackberry developed at the University of Illinois specifically for reliable cane survival in cold northern winters where most blackberry varieties suffer significant winterkill, tolerating temperatures well below zero without winter cane protection. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening mid-to-late season with good yields once established. Because the canes are self-supporting and very cold-tolerant, Illini Hardy is a dependable choice for northern growers who want blackberries without the trellising and winter mulching that tender varieties require. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 6-8 per plant to keep the planting productive and manageable.

plant_note: Plant bare-root in fall or early spring; seed requires 60–90 days cold-moist stratification for germination; plant male and female shrubs for reliable fruiting as plants are dioecious.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Indian plum is a Pacific Northwest native deciduous shrub prized for being one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small clusters of fragrant white flowers appear in February or March before leaves emerge, often while snow is still on the ground, providing an invaluable nectar source for early bees and hummingbirds. Small oval drupes (like tiny olives) ripen to blue-black with a single large stone; the flavor is astringent and bitter raw but palatable to birds and was eaten sparingly by many Native peoples. An excellent choice for wildlife habitat gardens, riparian buffers, and native plant landscapes in the Pacific Northwest and northern California.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring.
directions: 'Invicta' is a heavy-cropping green culinary gooseberry with outstanding resistance to American gooseberry mildew. The vigorous, spreading, and notably spiny bush yields large pale-green berries excellent for pies, jams, and preserves. Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil and space generously for airflow. Prune to an open goblet each winter to ease harvest among the sharp thorns and shorten leading shoots to encourage fruiting spurs.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Ison is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine that does not require a pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; the vigorous vines can spread 20–30 feet. In zone 9 Ison ripens in late August–September. Prune heavily in late winter to encourage productive new growth.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ison is one of the most widely planted muscadine varieties in the Southeast, selected by Ison's Nursery in Georgia for its combination of very large, sweet, black-bronze-skinned fruits and self-fertility — the perfect-flowered habit means a single Ison vine sets full crops without requiring a separate pollinator vine. The large, round to slightly oval fruits ripen to deep bronze-black with a rich, sweet, complex muscadine flavor and relatively low tannin compared to older varieties. Ison is used for fresh eating, juice, wine, and muscadine jelly, where the large fruit size and good juice content are advantageous. The vine is vigorous and productive once established, with crops of 30–60 pounds per mature vine in good growing conditions. Unlike some muscadine varieties that have a thick, tough skin, Ison's skin is more tender and the slip-skin characteristic less pronounced, making fresh eating more pleasant.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Issai is the only commonly available self-fertile Actinidia arguta cultivar, producing fruit without a separate male vine — an important practical advantage for gardeners with space for only one vine. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola; Issai is less vigorous than most hardy kiwi vines but still requires substantial support. In zone 9 it ripens in September–October.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Issai is a Japanese-selected cultivar of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) notable for being reliably self-fertile — unlike the species, which requires separate male and female vines for fruit production, Issai is a self-pollinating selection that sets fruit as a single plant. The small, smooth-skinned, grape-sized kiwiberry fruits ripen in September–October to a dark green with a delicate strawberry-kiwi flavor — eaten whole without peeling, unlike fuzzy kiwis (Actinidia deliciosa) that require peeling. Hardy kiwi fruits are considerably smaller than supermarket fuzzy kiwis but have a thin, edible skin and a sweet, complex, tropical flavor. Issai is less vigorous than most Actinidia arguta plants — a compact 15–20 foot climber rather than the 40+ foot sprawl of standard hardy kiwi — making it more manageable in garden settings. In zone 9 the vines experience mild winters and may have reduced dormancy; provide some shading in the hottest zones.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container canes in spring on a trellis in well-drained soil; note that Japanese wineberry is invasive in parts of the eastern U.S. — check local regulations before planting.
directions: Japanese wineberry is an Asian Rubus species with distinctive red glandular-hairy canes that are ornamentally attractive year-round. It fruits on floricanes in mid-to-late summer, bearing translucent orange-red to deep ruby berries enclosed in a sticky calyx that opens at ripeness — a feature that helps distinguish ripe from unripe fruit and reduces bird predation. Cut all fruited floricanes to the ground after harvest and thin primocanes to 4–6 per hill for next year's crop. The species naturalizes aggressively in disturbed areas in the eastern U.S. and is considered invasive in several states; confirm legality before planting.

common_name: Jersey Blueberry (Classic Northern Highbush Blueberry, New Jersey Standard Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Jersey requires cross-pollination — plant with a compatible highbush variety such as Bluecrop, Duke, or Blueray for reliable fruit set and heavier yields; Jersey is a late-season highbush variety ripening in August in most of the Northeast, extending the fresh blueberry season after early and mid-season varieties have finished.
directions: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil amended with peat moss or pine bark; maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.2 for healthy growth and production; mulch heavily with pine bark or acid wood chips; fertilize with ammonium sulfate in early spring; Jersey ripens in August (late season) producing large, firm, light blue berries with a mild, sweet flavor and excellent storage quality. Jersey blueberry is one of the oldest and most historically important highbush blueberry varieties in American commercial and home garden production — developed by Frederick Coville at the USDA Beltsville Agricultural Research Center in 1928 from deliberate crosses with wild Vaccinium corymbosum selections from the Atlantic coastal plain. Jersey was one of the first named highbush blueberry varieties released and became the cornerstone of the New Jersey commercial blueberry industry (the first commercial blueberry industry in the United States), for which it was specifically developed. For several decades, Jersey was essentially THE commercial highbush blueberry of the American East Coast, dominating production in New Jersey, Michigan, and the other blueberry-producing states before the development of newer varieties with earlier ripening or larger fruit. Despite its age (nearly 100 years of commercial production), Jersey remains popular for several reasons: its late-season ripening (August) extends the fresh blueberry window after most other varieties have finished, its very large, firm, light blue berries store and ship exceptionally well (better than softer-berried varieties), and its mild, sweet flavor is reliable and consistent. Jersey is considered somewhat milder in flavor than Bluecrop or Elliott but produces reliably in a wide range of conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or rooted tip layers in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Jewel black raspberry is more heat-tolerant than red raspberry but still struggles in the hottest zone 9 summers. It is best suited to zone 9a or the cooler parts of zone 9b. The floricane crop ripens May–June in zone 9, ahead of peak summer heat, making June the primary harvest window.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Jewel is a Cornell University-released black raspberry (Rubus occidentalis) — an entirely distinct species from red raspberries with a different flavor, deeper color, and more intense aromatic character. Black raspberries produce jet-black, hollow drupes with an intensely rich, complex, wine-like flavor that differs dramatically from the lighter, brighter flavor of red raspberries — the dark color indicates very high anthocyanin content, among the highest of any commonly grown berry. Black raspberry flavor is described as a deep, earthy, complex fruitiness with more tannin and less overt sweetness than red raspberries, making them outstanding for jams, pies, syrup, black raspberry ice cream (a regional specialty in the Ohio River Valley), and liqueurs. Jewel is the leading commercial black raspberry variety, selected for large, firm fruits and good resistance to anthracnose disease. In zone 9 the June ripening precedes peak summer heat, making black raspberry production more feasible than red raspberry in warm climates.

common_name: Jewel Strawberry (Mid-Season June-Bearer, Premier New York Strawberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as soil is workable; Jewel is a Cornell University-developed mid-season June-bearing strawberry that has become the dominant commercial strawberry in New York State and is widely grown throughout the Northeast for its exceptional large-fruited, highly flavorful berries and outstanding performance in humid northeastern growing conditions.
directions: Plant in early spring; Jewel is a high-yielding, large-fruited mid-season June-bearer that peaks about 5–7 days after Earliglow; berries have excellent fresh flavor and store and process better than many June-bearers; remove flowers the first year; the plants are vigorous and winter-hardy in zones 3–7 with straw mulch. Jewel strawberry is a Cornell University-developed variety (released 1985) that became the dominant commercial and farm-stand strawberry in New York State and one of the most important strawberries in the northeastern United States. Cornell's New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva bred Jewel specifically for northeastern growing conditions — the humid, cool summers and reliable winter cold of New York — and the variety's success reflects that targeted development: it performs exceptionally in zones 4–7 humid northeastern conditions where some varieties from drier or warmer climates show reduced vigor or disease problems. The berries are large to very large, consistently well-shaped, dark red throughout with outstanding fresh flavor — considered by many northeastern tasters to combine the best attributes of Earliglow flavor with Allstar size. Jewel is noted for holding flavor and firmness well across a range of weather conditions, producing consistently good berries even in the hot, humid spells that sometimes degrade the quality of other varieties during ripening. It is vigorous enough to be productive for 3–4 years in a well-managed bed, somewhat longer than many modern varieties. The standard strawberry at many northeastern U-pick farms and roadside stands.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. John produces heavier crops when cross-pollinated with Adams or another elderberry variety. In zone 9 it flowers in May–June and produces ripe berries in July–August. John is a vigorous spreader by root suckers in moist soils; mow around the planting to control spread.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to periodically wet soil; John is a named American elderberry cultivar selected at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva as part of the New York State elderberry improvement program — the same program that produced the widely-grown Adams cultivar. John was selected as a pollinator companion for Adams, producing profuse flowers slightly earlier than Adams to ensure cross-pollination during the Adams flowering period. The vigorous, upright shrub produces large, flattened flower corymbs (elderflower clusters) with abundant small white flowers in early summer, followed by heavy clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late summer. John is particularly valued in mixed elderberry plantings where it improves Adams yields through cross-pollination; the two varieties are the most common pairing in eastern American elderberry plantings. In zone 9 both elderberry flowers and berries are produced abundantly in favorable moist conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 8 plant January–March. Josephine is a fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry that in zone 8 begins ripening its fall primocane crop in late August–September. For a single large fall crop, mow all canes to the ground in late winter; for two crops per season, leave floricanes for an early summer crop followed by the fall primocane harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Josephine is a Cornell University fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry selected for exceptional fruit quality — widely considered to have the finest flavor of any fall-bearing raspberry released by the Cornell small fruit breeding program, with very large, conical, bright red berries and a sweet, complex, intensely raspberry-flavored aroma and taste that rivals the best summer-bearing varieties. The primocane-fruiting habit provides a late-season crop in August–October from first-year canes, avoiding the May–June crowded harvest season when many other soft fruits are also ripe. The berries are soft and best for fresh eating or immediate processing — Josephine is not a commercial shipping variety, but for home garden fresh eating it represents the highest quality among fall-bearing raspberries. The vigorous, productive canes grow 4–6 feet tall and the plants are reliably productive once established, returning annually from the root system.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; jostaberry is self-fertile and a single plant will produce fruit.
directions: Jostaberry is a thornless hybrid of black currant and gooseberry, combining the vigor and disease resistance of both parents with a flavor profile between the two. It is significantly larger and more vigorous than either parent, and is notably resistant to gooseberry mildew and currant big bud mite. Prune as you would a black currant — remove one-third of the oldest canes each late winter to stimulate new productive growth. Harvest in mid-summer when berries have turned from red to very dark purple-black and developed a sweet, slightly musky flavor; verify local Ribes restrictions before planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Ken's Red is a female cultivar and requires a male hardy kiwi vine within pollinating range for fruit set. Provide a very sturdy trellis, fence, or pergola, since mature vines are vigorous and heavy once fruiting.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis or arbor. Ken's Red is a female hardy kiwi cultivar originating in New Zealand, distinguished from most other Actinidia arguta selections by its attractive reddish-purple fruit skin and red-blushed flesh near the skin, in addition to the sweet, tangy flavor typical of hardy kiwi. The smooth skin means the small, grape-sized fruit can be eaten whole without peeling, and its distinctive red coloring makes it a visually striking choice for a home fruit planting or farmers-market crop. Like all Actinidia arguta, it is dioecious and needs a separate male vine nearby to ensure good pollination and a full fruit set. A flavorful, ornamental option for gardeners who want something visually distinct from standard green-fleshed hardy kiwi, zone 4–8.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter through early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Kiowa is thorned, so wear heavy gloves during planting and all subsequent pruning. Space 4 feet apart in rows.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; Kiowa is a thorned, erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 1996 as part of the same breeding program that produced Natchez and Ouachita. It is distinguished principally by its extraordinary berry size — among the largest of any blackberry variety, often exceeding 10–14 grams per fruit — and its exceptionally long harvest season that can extend 6–8 weeks through June and July in zone 8–9. Flavor is sweet and complex. The upright, thorned canes are self-supporting and vigorous, producing heavily. Kiowa shows good adaptability to the South and mid-South, performing well in humid, hot climates where some varieties decline. The principal trade-off is the thorns — unavoidable when harvesting and pruning — but many growers consider this worthwhile for the combination of size, yield, and long season. Prune fruited floricanes to ground level after the last berries are harvested; tip primocanes at 36–42 inches in summer to promote lateral branching.

plant_note: Plant after last frost with a very sturdy pergola or trellis; self-fertile cultivars such as 'Issai' are suitable for single-plant planting.
directions: Kiwiberry is a compact-fruited selection of hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) grown specifically for smooth-skinned, grape-sized fruits that are eaten whole without peeling — they have the same flavor as standard kiwifruit but ripen 3–4 weeks earlier. Self-fertile cultivars such as 'Issai' and 'Ken's Red' allow single-plant production, but yields are higher when a male pollenizer is present. The extremely vigorous vines require a heavy-gauge trellis or pergola capable of bearing hundreds of pounds of vine and fruit; prune hard each dormant season to renewal spurs. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and taste sweet with no starchiness.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Koralle is self-fertile and, like other lingonberry cultivars, can produce two crops per year — a smaller summer crop and a larger fall crop.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions. Koralle is a classic Dutch-bred lingonberry cultivar, one of the earliest widely distributed named lingonberry selections and still valued for its heavy, reliable fruit production and vigorous, dense, low-growing habit. The glossy evergreen foliage forms an attractive year-round groundcover, topped with clusters of small white to pale pink bell-shaped spring flowers followed by bright red, tart berries used in Scandinavian-style jams, sauces, and preserves. Because lingonberries thrive in acidic soil and tolerate shade better than most fruiting shrubs, Koralle makes an excellent edible groundcover planted beneath blueberries, azaleas, or pines where soil is already acidic. Shear plants back lightly every few years to rejuvenate growth and maintain a dense, productive mat.

subcategory: East Asian compact edible mulberry shrub-tree
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 5–9; Korean Mulberry (Morus australis) is a compact, multi-stemmed mulberry native to Korea, Japan, China, and the Himalayas — smaller than White or Red Mulberry — bearing abundant small to medium, very sweet, juicy black-purple mulberries relished by birds and people, and with a long history of use in East Asian traditional medicine.
directions: Plant Morus australis in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment, then reduce as the plant is drought-tolerant once established; prune in winter to shape and control size; harvest berries as they ripen and turn deep purple-black, as they stain readily. Korean Mulberry is the smallest-growing of the commonly cultivated mulberry species — typically maturing as a large multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 5–15 feet tall — making it better suited to smaller gardens than the more vigorous White Mulberry (Morus alba) or American Red Mulberry (Morus rubra). The abundant small to medium berries are very sweet and richly flavored, ripening over several weeks in early to midsummer; birds are strongly attracted to fruiting trees so netting may be needed for a full harvest. In East Asian traditional medicine systems, the berries (sang shen), leaves (sang ye), bark (sang bai pi), and twigs (sang zhi) are all used in herbal preparations for treating conditions ranging from hypertension and diabetes to tinnitus and gray hair. The leaves are used for silkworm (Bombyx mori) cultivation like other mulberry species. Compact enough for container growing in large pots; prune annually to maintain size and maximize fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Krewer is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release valued for ripening late in the season, extending the fresh blueberry harvest window well past most other Southern cultivars. Plant with Brightwell, Premier, or Climax for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Krewer is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry selected for its notably late ripening window, extending the fresh Southern blueberry harvest into midsummer after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, a valuable trait for home gardeners and market growers wanting to spread out the harvest season. The vigorous, productive bushes bear medium to large berries with good flavor and firmness. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Krewer requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other, choosing early- and mid-season partners to spread bloom timing and further extend the overall harvest. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

common_name: Lane Muscadine Grape (Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Lane is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine released by the University of Georgia and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Lane is a modern University of Georgia muscadine release valued for its very large, glossy black berries with a thinner, more tender skin than many older black muscadines, along with sweet, richly flavored flesh well suited to fresh eating. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, ripening in the mid-to-late season, and its improved skin quality and berry size have made it a popular choice for both home gardens and u-pick plantings across the Gulf South. Keep vines well watered during fruit development for the best berry size, and thin overcrowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid weather.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Late Fry is self-fertile and, true to its name, ripens near the very end of the muscadine season, extending harvest well past earlier black varieties like Cowart.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Late Fry is a University of Arkansas release bred as a black-fruited counterpart to the popular bronze variety Fry, producing very large, glossy black berries with the same thin skin and high sugar content that made Fry a favorite for fresh eating. It is self-fertile and ripens late in the season, filling out the tail end of the muscadine harvest after earlier black varieties are finished. Vigor and disease resistance are good across the humid Gulf South. Because it is one of the last muscadines to ripen, protect ripening clusters from birds and other wildlife, which concentrate on the few varieties still fruiting late in the season.

common_name: Leatherleaf Mahonia (Chinese Mahonia, Leatherleaf Oregon Grape)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in well-drained, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf mahonia is one of the toughest shade shrubs and tolerates dry shade under trees once established. The spiny leaflets make handling difficult — wear gloves.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf mahonia is a bold architectural evergreen shrub with some of the most striking foliage in the shade garden — stiff, upright canes bearing enormous compound leaves (18–24 inches) of dark, holly-like leaflets with viciously spiny edges that create a dramatic tropical effect in the deepest shade. Fragrant yellow flowers appear in winter in drooping grape-like clusters, followed by powdery blue-purple berries in spring that are edible (tart, used for jelly and wine). It is one of the few large shrubs that truly thrives in deep, dry shade — an outstanding barrier plant and shade specimen. NOTE: Mahonia bealei is listed as invasive in several southeastern states including Texas and Georgia — check local invasive species lists before planting; the native alternative Mahonia trifoliolata (agarita) is an excellent substitute in Texas.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; Leikora is a female fruiting cultivar requiring a male pollinator such as 'Pollmix' or 'Hergo-M' within 50–100 feet for fruit set. One male plant can pollinate 6–8 female plants. Sea buckthorn tolerates poor, sandy, gravelly soils — it is one of the most nutrient-poor-soil-tolerant fruiting shrubs due to its nitrogen-fixing root nodules. Avoid planting in wet or clay soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-fertile soil — sandy, rocky, and coastal soils are ideal; Leikora is a German-selected female sea buckthorn cultivar bred for commercial berry production, selected at the Bundesanstalt für Züchtungsforschung as one of the heaviest-bearing named female cultivars with large, bright orange-yellow berries that ripen in August–September in dense clusters along the stems. Sea buckthorn berries contain extraordinary concentrations of vitamin C (up to 15 times that of oranges), vitamin E, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids — the nutritional profile has driven substantial commercial interest in sea buckthorn juice, oil capsules, and skincare products. The tart, acidic, tropical-citrus flavor of the fresh berries makes them challenging to eat raw but outstanding processed into juice (often blended with apple or honey to moderate acidity), jam, wine, and dietary supplements. Leikora is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant shrub adapted to harsh, exposed sites where few other fruiting plants survive.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early to midsummer, or plant rooted container stock in spring; site at forest margins or on structures with dappled light, as this species naturally inhabits the woodland edge rather than open, exposed positions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, loamy to rocky soil in part shade to full sun along a trellis, fence, or forest edge; Limber Honeysuckle is a native twining vine found across northern and central North America from Quebec to British Columbia and south into the Ozarks and Appalachians, scrambling up shrubs and small trees along forest margins where it is an important nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds during their spring and early-summer residency. The flowers range from orange-yellow to red and appear in May–June in clustered whorls at the stem tips, followed by translucent red to orange berries in late summer that are eaten by thrushes, vireos, and other woodland songbirds. Like Lonicera prolifera, it has perfoliate leaves near the stem tips where the uppermost pair of leaves fuse into a disk, though in this species the leaves beneath the flower clusters are typically distinctly bluish-green. It is non-invasive and well-behaved in the garden, rarely exceeding 15 feet, making it one of the best native vine choices for small to medium trellises in northern gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted plugs or divisions in early spring in acidic, well-drained soil; also useful as a groundcover under acid-loving shrubs.
directions: Lingonberries require acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) and perform well as an ornamental groundcover in zones 2–7. They produce two crops per year — a smaller crop in midsummer and a larger one in fall. Minimal pruning is needed; shear plants to 3–4 in every few years to rejuvenate. Harvest when berries are deep red and slightly tart; they store well refrigerated and are traditionally used in Scandinavian preserves and sauces.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings in early spring after last frost; provide a sturdy T-trellis at planting since canes reach 8–10 ft.
directions: Loganberry, a natural hybrid of blackberry and raspberry discovered in California in the 1880s, produces long, dark red, tart berries that are excellent for jams and wine. Train the vigorous trailing canes on a two- or three-wire trellis, weaving new primocanes along the wires during the growing season. After the summer harvest, cut all floricanes that bore fruit to the ground and secure the new primocanes in their place. The thornless 'LY59' strain is preferred for home gardens; in borderline zones, lay canes down and mulch after leaf drop.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: Lowbush blueberries require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0) and spread by underground rhizomes to form colonies. Manage in a two-year cycle: mow or burn half the planting to the ground each year so alternating sections produce a full crop annually. Harvest in midsummer when berries are deep blue-purple and sweet. Drought-tolerant once established, but irrigation during fruit fill improves berry size.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in late winter to early spring; in zone 7–9 plant December–February. Magnolia is self-fertile and does not require a separate male pollinator — unlike many muscadine varieties that carry only pistillate (female) flowers, Magnolia has perfect flowers (both male and female). Space vines 10–15 feet apart on a trellis system; the 4-arm Kniffin system is standard for muscadines in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Magnolia is a USDA-developed self-fertile bronze muscadine grape, bearing medium to large bronze-to-copper-colored fruits with a mild, sweet flavor and thin, tender skin — one of the more elegant-tasting muscadine varieties for fresh eating, without the strongly musky, foxy character of older selections. The perfect-flowered Magnolia vine can pollinate female-only varieties like Carlos and Fry planted nearby, making it doubly useful as a multi-variety vineyard anchor. Fruits ripen in late August to September in most zone 8–9 plantings, later than some early-season varieties. The vines are vigorous and productive, typically yielding 15–20 pounds per vine at maturity. Train on a 4-wire trellis system, prune back to 2–3 buds per spur in late winter, and fertilize lightly in early spring.

plant_note: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; maqui is dioecious — plant both male and female shrubs for fruit production, or purchase self-fertile cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; maqui berry is a Chilean native shrub prized for its small, intensely purple-black berries with the highest reported anthocyanin content of any known berry — significantly higher than acai, blueberries, or pomegranates, giving it extraordinary antioxidant properties. The berries have a pleasant sweet-tart flavor with herbal overtones; they are eaten fresh, made into juice, jams, and wine, and used extensively in Mapuche traditional medicine. It grows naturally in the coastal and Andean ranges of Chile and Argentina, tolerating mild frost, and adapts to a Mediterranean climate with dry summers. An emerging superfood crop with increasing commercial cultivation in Chile.

plant_note: Plant in early spring once soil is workable; elderberries fruit best with a second variety nearby for pollination.
directions: Marge is a prolific European elderberry prized for heavy yields of dark berries used in syrups, jams, and wine. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil and keep it well watered, as elderberries are shallow-rooted and thirsty. Fruit set improves dramatically with a second, different elderberry variety planted nearby for cross-pollination. Prune out the oldest canes each late winter to keep the plant vigorous and productive. Always cook the berries before eating, since raw fruit and other plant parts can cause stomach upset.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or tip-rooted canes in early spring as soon as soil is workable, with a T-trellis capable of handling 8-ft canes installed at the same time.
directions: Marionberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (Chehalem x Olallie) developed by Oregon State University and is the most widely grown blackberry in the Pacific Northwest, prized for its deep, complex, slightly tart flavor. The thorny, vigorous canes must be trained along a two-wire trellis; weave new primocanes along the lower wire during the summer and tie them to the upper wire the following spring. After the mid-summer harvest, remove all fruited floricanes at the base and train the new primocanes into their place. Marionberries are sensitive to freezes below about 10°F; in colder areas, protect canes over winter.

common_name: Mars Seedless Grape (Cold-Hardy Disease-Resistant Blue Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant dormant, rooted vines in early spring in well-drained soil; Mars is self-fertile, compact, and well suited to a small arbor, patio trellis, or single-wire fence rather than a full commercial vineyard trellis.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor. Bred at the University of Arkansas breeding program and released in the 1970s, Mars combines good disease resistance with genuinely seedless, blue-black berries and a sweet, fruity, slip-skin flavor reminiscent of Concord but milder. Its compact vine habit and strong resistance to common grape diseases make it far easier to grow without a heavy spray program than European wine grapes, especially in humid climates. Prune hard each winter to a few renewal spurs on permanent cordons, and thin crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size and air circulation.

plant_note: Plant after last frost in full sun with a trellis or fence; roots are cold-hardy to zone 6 and re-sprout from the roots each spring.
directions: Maypop (Passiflora incarnata) is a North American native passionflower that is cold-hardy to zone 6, distinguishing it clearly from the tropical Passiflora edulis (passionfruit). The ornamental lavender flowers are stunning and the egg-sized yellow-green fruits have sweet, aromatic pulp similar to tropical passionfruit. Plants die back to the roots in zone 6–7 winters and re-sprout vigorously in late spring — do not remove the crown before new growth appears. Plant cross-pollinators nearby (more than one plant) for reliable fruit set. Harvest when fruits turn yellowish-green and fall or detach easily.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring; Meader is a male cultivar grown solely to pollinate female hardy kiwi vines (such as Anna, Geneva, or Ken's Red) — it produces no fruit itself. One male vine can pollinate several female vines within about 30–50 feet.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, on a sturdy permanent trellis; site centrally within pollinating distance of the female vines it is meant to serve. Meader is a male hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) cultivar selected by Professor Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire, prized specifically for its exceptional cold hardiness — among the most cold-tolerant hardy kiwi selections available, able to survive winter conditions that damage or kill less hardy male cultivars. As a male vine, it produces abundant flowers but no fruit; its sole purpose in the garden is to provide pollen for nearby female cultivars, and because Actinidia arguta is dioecious, at least one male vine is essential wherever female vines are grown for fruit. Its outstanding hardiness makes it the standard pollinator choice for northern hardy kiwi plantings, ensuring the pollinator survives winters that a female cultivar chosen for fruit quality alone might not, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown stock in spring in moist to well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican elderberry establishes rapidly and may produce its first berry clusters within one to two years of planting. Hardwood cuttings taken in winter root reliably in moist potting mix or directly in the ground. For heaviest fruit set, plant at least two individuals of different seed origins to encourage cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moderately moist soil; Mexican elderberry is more drought-tolerant than eastern common elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established and adapts well to the neutral to alkaline soils of the Southwest, California foothills, and the intermountain West. Sambucus mexicana (syn. Sambucus nigra subsp. cerulea) is the native elderberry of California, the Southwest, and the Pacific Northwest mountains, forming a large, fast-growing, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with massive, flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) of creamy-white blossoms in late spring that are irresistible to native bees, butterflies, and beneficial insects. The flowers are followed by heavy drooping clusters of small, powdery-blue to blue-black berries in late summer — excellent for elderberry syrup, jelly, wine, and traditional medicine. CAUTION: cook berries before eating; raw berries, bark, and leaves contain cyanogenic glycosides. An outstanding wildlife plant — the berries are consumed by dozens of bird species including waxwings, robins, and thrushes.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), fertile soil in part shade; miracle berry is a West African rain forest understory shrub that requires acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist conditions similar to blueberries — it cannot tolerate alkaline water or soil and performs best in acidic, non-chlorinated water.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in part shade; water with rainwater or filtered water — chlorinated tap water and alkaline water damage the plant. Synsepalum dulcificum (miracle berry or miracle fruit) is a West African evergreen shrub that produces the most remarkable edible berry in the botanical world: small (1-inch), red, olive-shaped berries containing a glycoprotein called miraculin, which temporarily binds to sour taste receptors on the tongue and causes sour, acidic foods to taste intensely sweet for 30–60 minutes after eating a single berry. The berries themselves have virtually no sugar content and a bland flavor — the effect is entirely on taste perception, not on the food itself. After eating a miracle berry, lemons taste like lemon candy, vinegar tastes sweet, sour cream becomes sweet cream, and Tabasco sauce tastes like hot doughnut glaze. Miracle berry parties (where participants eat the berry and sample unusual flavor combinations) have become a culinary novelty. The plant is native to West African rain forest understory and requires the same acidic, humus-rich, moist, part-shade conditions as blueberries — it is extremely pH-sensitive and will decline rapidly in alkaline soil or water. In zone 10–12, it can be grown outdoors; in zone 8–9, best in a pot brought indoors in winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall; mock strawberry is extremely adaptable and will colonize partial to full shade under trees where few groundcovers thrive. It spreads by runners similar to regular strawberry and can cover large areas quickly.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained to moderately moist, average soil — mock strawberry is one of the most shade-tolerant edible groundcovers available for difficult spots under trees. It spreads vigorously by runners, forming a dense weed-suppressing carpet of trifoliate leaves studded with small yellow flowers from spring through fall followed by round, bright red berries. The fruits are edible and safe but mild and nearly tasteless compared to true strawberries — they lack the complex aroma that makes true strawberry irresistible. They are best used in jams or flavored beverages rather than eaten fresh. The plant does well in lawn edges, woodland paths, and shaded slopes where it outcompetes many weeds while providing interest through yellow flowers and bright fruit. May naturalize aggressively; divide to control spread.

common_name: Monterey Strawberry (Day-Neutral UC Davis Heavy-Fruiting Strawberry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or plugs in fall (September–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring through fall harvest; Monterey is a day-neutral variety that produces fruit continuously throughout the growing season rather than in a single concentrated June crop. In zone 9, plant October–November for harvest beginning March–April and continuing until heat stops production in June, then resuming when temperatures cool in September–October. Beds typically remain productive for 2–3 seasons before renewal.
directions: Plant bare-root or plugs in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil; mulch with straw to maintain moisture and keep fruit off the soil. Monterey is a day-neutral strawberry developed by the University of California at Davis and released in 2009 by plant breeders Douglas Shaw and Kirk Larson — a variety bred to combine the high-productivity and large berry size of California commercial strawberries with the continuous-production advantage of day-neutral types. Day-neutral strawberries (unlike traditional June-bearing types) produce fruit throughout the growing season regardless of day length — triggered to bloom and fruit by temperature rather than day length. This gives Monterey a very long harvest window in zone 8–10, where it can produce from early spring through late fall with a summer break during the hottest months. The berries are large (1–1.5 inch diameter), firm, and very flavorful — significantly more aromatic and sweet than many commercial varieties, though with the large size that makes them visually attractive. Monterey was developed for California coast conditions (mild summers, year-round production) and performs exceptionally well in Gulf Coast fall and spring conditions that mimic coastal California temperatures.

common_name: Montgomery Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Mid-Season Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Montgomery is a vigorous, productive rabbiteye blueberry cultivar bred for reliable mid-season production and good fruit quality in Southern growing conditions. Plant with a different rabbiteye cultivar for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Montgomery is a vigorous rabbiteye blueberry cultivar developed for Southern growing conditions, producing a reliable mid-season crop of medium to large, firm berries with good flavor. The bushes are notably vigorous and productive, establishing quickly and bearing well once mature, making Montgomery a dependable choice for filling out a mid-season harvest window alongside earlier and later rabbiteye selections. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, it requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Take hardwood cuttings in late winter or softwood cuttings in early summer and root in well-drained propagation mix; plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — multicaulis mulberry is vigorous and begins fruiting within two to three years of establishment.
directions: Propagate from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter and root in a well-drained propagation mix under plastic film, or take semi-softwood cuttings in early summer; plant rooted cuttings out in spring after the last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Multicaulis mulberry is a vigorous, large-leaved variety of white mulberry selected in China for its enormous leaves — up to 12 inches long — that historically supported the silk industry; in the food garden it channels that same vigor into abundant, sweet white to pale-pink berries that ripen weeks ahead of most mulberries. The tree tolerates a wide range of soils including clay, heat, and urban conditions, and once established is drought-resilient while performing best with consistent moisture during fruiting. Harvest berries over several weeks as they ripen unevenly, spreading a sheet beneath the canopy and shaking branches gently to collect ripe fruit.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, coastal soil in full sun to part shade; muntries is a low-growing, ground-hugging Australian native groundcover shrub from the coastal heathlands and mallee scrub of South Australia and western Victoria — producing small, round, green to purple-red berries with an apple-spice flavor four times higher in antioxidants than blueberries by weight.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly, coastal-type soil in full sun to part shade; drought-tolerant once established; avoid clay or poorly drained soils. Kunzea pomifera (muntries, emu apple, or native cranberry) is a prostrate, ground-hugging Australian native shrub from the coastal heathlands, mallee scrub, and sand dunes of South Australia and western Victoria — one of the most remarkable and underappreciated Australian native food plants. The plant spreads slowly as a low (6–18 inch), dense, aromatic groundcover with tiny, dark-green leaves and small white bottlebrush-like flowers, eventually producing clusters of small (1/4–1/2 inch), round berries that ripen from green to red-purple in late summer. The berries have a unique, complex, sweet-spicy flavor combining apple, cinnamon, and a subtle eucalyptus note — quite unlike any other berry. Nutritionally, muntries are exceptional: ORAC (antioxidant) values four times higher than blueberries by weight, with high vitamin C, flavonoids, and polyphenols. Aboriginal Australians historically ate muntries extensively as a major food source across the southern Australian coast. In the modern Australian native food industry, muntries are used in jams, sauces, ice creams, and gourmet berry products, and are increasingly available from specialty nurseries. As a garden plant, muntries serves as an excellent low-maintenance native groundcover that also produces an edible crop.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in early spring; use self-fertile cultivars or plant one male ('bronze') vine per 4–6 female vines.
directions: Muscadine grapes are native to the southeastern U.S. and far more heat- and disease-resistant than European or labrusca types. Train to a single trunk with two permanent lateral cordons on a high-wire trellis at 5–6 ft; spur-prune cordons each dormant season to 2–3 bud spurs spaced 4–6 in apart. Many cultivars are not self-fertile, so check pollination requirements before purchasing. Harvest by shaking or hand-picking individual berries when they reach full color and slip easily from the skin.

plant_note: Plant runners or divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; musk strawberry is unique among strawberries in performing well in dappled or partial shade — a valuable trait for woodland or shaded garden situations where other strawberries fruit poorly.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; musk strawberry is a European native species and one of the most historically important cultivated strawberries before the modern hybrid garden strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) replaced it in the 19th century. The medium-sized fruits have an intense, musky-aromatic fragrance far more complex and perfumed than modern strawberry varieties — often described as combining strawberry with pineapple and rose. The plant uniquely tolerates partial shade, making it one of the few berry crops for understory or semi-shaded settings. Most cultivated plants are of a single sex (plants were traditionally vegetatively propagated), so both male and female plants must be obtained for fruiting. 'Capron Royal' and 'Profumata di Tortona' are heritage Italian cultivars. The berries are soft and must be eaten immediately after harvest.

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for Gulf Coast gardens; Mysore raspberry fruits primarily in cool weather — fall through spring — making it the ideal raspberry for zone 9–10 where temperate raspberries fail in summer heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Mysore raspberry is the premier fruiting bramble for subtropical gardens — the only raspberry-type fruit that thrives and produces abundantly in zone 9–10 conditions where standard raspberries fail from summer heat and disease. Native to the hills of South Asia, it produces arching, thorny canes 5–8 feet tall with attractive silver-backed leaves and large clusters of small, dark-red to black berries with an intense raspberry flavor from October through April. Unlike temperate raspberries, it fruits on second-year canes (floricanes) but in a warm-climate evergreen pattern. Cut canes to the ground after fruiting; the plant regrows vigorously. It can be invasive outside cultivation where conditions suit it — avoid planting near natural areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted runners in spring in moist, acidic, peaty soil; requires cool summer temperatures and will not thrive where summers are hot.
directions: The nagoonberry (arctic raspberry) is a low-growing, rhizomatous Rubus native to Alaska, Scandinavia, and northern Russia, bearing small, deep rose-red berries in early summer that are considered among the finest-flavored wild berries in the boreal world — exceptionally fragrant, rich, and complex. Plants require cool, moist, acidic bog or tundra-edge conditions (pH 4.5–5.5) and cool summer temperatures; they will not survive heat and are rarely successful south of zone 5 except at high elevations. Propagate by dividing rhizomes in early spring. The Finnish-bred cultivar 'Mespi' (a nagoonberry x Arctic raspberry hybrid) shows improved yield and adaptability while retaining the outstanding flavor of the wild species.

plant_note: Plant two or more plants for cross-pollination in early spring; extremely adaptable to cold, dry, or alkaline sites.
directions: Nanking cherry is one of the hardiest fruiting shrubs available, reliably surviving temperatures below -40°F and tolerating poor, dry, or alkaline soils. The abundant small red cherries ripen in early summer and have a sweet, slightly tart flavor excellent for jams, juices, and fresh eating. Two or more plants are needed for cross-pollination; plants flower very early in spring and may need frost protection of blossoms in zones 3–4 during cold snaps. Prune after harvest to remove dead wood and open the canopy; the shrub is generally very healthy with minimal pest and disease problems.

plant_note: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; nannyberry is one of the most shade-tolerant native viburnums and grows naturally as a large shrub or small tree at the edges of moist woodlands and thickets.
directions: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; nannyberry is one of the most shade-tolerant native viburnums and grows naturally as a large shrub or small tree at the edges of moist woodlands and thickets. Viburnum lentago is a large native viburnum of the northeastern and central United States, producing shiny, deeply veined, finely toothed leaves and flat-topped clusters of creamy-white flowers in late spring that are outstanding for native bees; the abundant, blue-black, berry-like drupes in fall and winter provide critical food for migrating and overwintering songbirds — particularly cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes — and are also edible for humans, with a sweet, date-raisin flavor when fully ripe. The fall foliage turns rich wine-red to purplish-red; the plant often sends up suckers and gradually forms a thicket.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun in spring; natal plum is salt-tolerant and thrives in coastal conditions, making it ideal for Gulf Coast landscapes.
directions: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; natal plum is a South African native shrub with glossy, dark-green, oval leaves armed with forked spines, fragrant white flowers like large jasmine blooms, and cranberry-sized red to deep-crimson fruits that are among the finest edible berries available in zone 9–11 landscapes. The fruit has a rich, sweet, somewhat cranberry-like flavor and is excellent for jams, jellies, juices, and fresh eating. Plants bloom and fruit nearly year-round in frost-free climates. Salt-tolerant, drought-resistant, and excellent as a security hedge or coastal planting. Note: only the ripe red fruits are edible — all other plant parts including unripe fruits are toxic.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; in zone 9 February–March planting gives canes the longest establishment season. Space 3–4 feet apart in rows 8–10 feet apart. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, typically May–June in zones 8–9.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5); Natchez is a semi-erect, thornless blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2007, widely considered one of the finest named varieties for the Gulf Coast and mid-South. It is the earliest-ripening major thornless variety, typically producing its first berries in late May to early June in zones 8–9 — a full 2–3 weeks before Ouachita and other Arkansas releases. Berries are very large (9–12 grams), elongated, jet-black, sweet, and aromatic with excellent fresh-eating quality. Yields are high, and the self-supporting semi-erect canes need only minimal trellising. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select 4–6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for next year's crop. Natchez is susceptible to double-blossom rosette disease in areas with high disease pressure; avoid overhead irrigation. In zone 9a, provide afternoon shade or plant on a north-facing slope to reduce heat stress during fruiting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown canes in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 plant December–February. Navaho is erect and self-supporting — tip new canes at 3–4 feet in midsummer to encourage branching and maximize fruiting wood the following year. Remove old canes to the ground after harvest. Chill hour requirement is approximately 400–500 hours (viable in most of zone 9). Navaho ripens in late June, about 2 weeks after Arapaho, providing a sequential harvest window when both varieties are planted.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Navaho is a thornless erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas fruit breeding program and released in 1988. The large, glossy, jet-black berries are among the sweetest of any commercial blackberry variety — significantly sweeter than most thorned varieties and with a more balanced sweet-tart flavor than the extremely tart early-season varieties. The high sugar content and mild, pleasant flavor make Navaho berries exceptional for fresh eating without added sugar and for preserves where reduced sugar is desired. The thornless, erect habit makes harvesting unusually practical: no thorns to navigate and no extensive trellis infrastructure required. Navaho produces mid-to-late season, ripening in late June–July in zone 9, providing fruit after the earlier erect varieties have finished and extending the fresh blackberry season. The firm berries have good post-harvest shelf life, remaining harvestable for several days without softening if kept cool.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger eases.
directions: 'Navaho' is an erect, thornless blackberry that produces firm, very sweet berries with excellent shelf life on self-supporting canes. Because it grows upright it needs little or no trellising, though a single wire helps in windy sites. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep suckers thinned to maintain a manageable hedgerow. Prune out fruited floricanes each fall and tip new primocanes to encourage branching.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in early spring; in zone 8 plant February–March. Nero is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator. The shrub is adaptable to a wide range of soils including poorly drained or wet sites where most fruiting shrubs fail. Nero suckers moderately and can form a small colony in suitable conditions — mow around the planting to control spread.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist soil — tolerates periodic wet feet better than most fruiting shrubs; Nero is a Czech-selected black chokeberry cultivar widely used in European commercial aronia production, selected for slightly more compact growth habit than Viking with comparable or superior berry yield relative to plant size. The medium to large, round, blue-black to jet-black berries ripen in late August–September with the characteristic high-tannin, astringent flavor of the species — intensely purple when juiced and among the highest known plant sources of anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins. Nero is the most widely grown aronia variety in European commercial production, where aronia juice and concentrate are major products. The compact, upright-to-rounded shrub fits well into mixed border plantings and provides four-season interest with spring flower clusters, glossy summer foliage, heavy late-summer berry crops, and outstanding fall color.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Nesbitt is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; ripens mid-season, typically late August in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood on a two-wire trellis or arbor. Nesbitt is a University of Georgia-released muscadine selected for its combination of very large, deep purple-black fruit, vigorous productive vines, and reliable self-fertility, making it a popular home-garden choice that needs no separate pollinator vine. The fruit has a thin, tender skin for a muscadine, sweet juicy flesh, and good flavor for fresh eating, with fruit size among the largest of the widely grown self-fertile varieties. The vigorous vine bears heavily once established and holds its crop well, tolerating the humid, disease-prone conditions of Gulf South summers better than bunch grapes. A dependable, high-yielding choice for a home muscadine arbor in zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant in spring; heat-tolerant dewberry-raspberry hybrid.
directions: The nessberry is an old dewberry-raspberry cross developed for the hot South, producing dark, wine-red berries with a sprightly flavor. Its trailing canes benefit from a low trellis and adapt well to heat and heavier soils where standard raspberries struggle. Plant in full sun in well-drained ground and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Remove spent floricanes after the summer crop and train fresh primocanes for the following season.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Noble is self-fertile and mid-to-late season (September in zone 9). One of the best black muscadines for wine, juice, and jelly production due to its very high anthocyanin and resveratrol content.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Noble is a black-skinned muscadine released by North Carolina State University in 1971 and named for James Noble, an early muscadine researcher. It is the standard against which black muscadine wine varieties are measured: the deep purple-black berries are extraordinarily high in anthocyanins, resveratrol, and other polyphenols that give muscadine wine and juice its distinctive deep color and purported health benefits. Flavor is rich, musky, and complex — more intensely flavored than bronze varieties — producing deep-colored wine, juice, and jelly with earthy, berry notes. Fresh-eating quality is good but not as mild as bronze types; the thick skin and seeds are more pronounced. Noble is self-fertile and produces consistently high yields even as a single vine. Its exceptional disease resistance and adaptability make it one of the best black muscadines for the humid Gulf South. Harvest when berries are fully black and yield easily to gentle pressure.

common_name: Northblue Blueberry (Half-High Cold-Hardy Highbush Blueberry, Northern Half-High)
