plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, organic-rich soil in full sun; Northblue is a University of Minnesota-developed half-high blueberry variety with exceptional cold-hardiness (to -30°F or colder when established and mulched) specifically for zones 3–5 where standard highbush varieties suffer severe winter dieback; plant with Northcountry, Northsky, or Polaris for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.2) with excellent drainage; mulch with pine bark 3–4 inches deep to protect roots and maintain moisture; fertilize with acidifying fertilizer (ammonium sulfate) in spring; Northblue ripens mid-season (July in Minnesota and Wisconsin) producing large, dark blue berries with excellent highbush flavor — larger and better-flavored than lowbush but hardier than standard highbush. Northblue blueberry is one of the University of Minnesota-developed half-high blueberry varieties that transformed blueberry growing in zones 3–5 of the upper Midwest, making reliable blueberry production possible in climates where standard highbush varieties (which are typically hardy only to about -20°F with snow cover) suffered severe dieback or winter-killed entirely. The half-high blueberries were developed by crossing standard highbush Vaccinium corymbosum (for berry size and quality) with the ultra-cold-hardy native lowbush blueberry Vaccinium angustifolium (for hardiness) — and Northblue represents one of the earliest and most successful results of this breeding work. Northblue plants grow 2–3 feet tall — intermediate between lowbush (6–18 inches) and highbush (4–6 feet) — and produce large, dark blue berries with a distinctly better flavor and larger size than wild lowbush berries, closer to highbush quality. The combination of cold-hardiness to -35°F (with some snow cover and mulching), compact size, and genuinely good fruit quality (not just acceptable — actually good by highbush standards) makes Northblue one of the most important blueberry varieties for cold-climate gardeners. Cross-pollination with another half-high variety (Northcountry, Northsky, Polaris) is required for best fruit set.

common_name: Northcountry Blueberry (Half-High Minnesota Cold-Hardy Blueberry, Twin Cities Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.2), well-drained, organic-rich soil in full sun; Northcountry is a University of Minnesota half-high blueberry with extreme cold-hardiness (to -30°F) designed for zones 3–5; plant with Northblue, Northsky, or Polaris for cross-pollination; the compact plants (2–3 feet) are particularly suited to small gardens and landscaping in cold climates.
directions: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.2); mulch heavily; fertilize lightly with ammonium sulfate; Northcountry ripens slightly earlier than Northblue (late June to early July in Minnesota), making it valuable for extending the blueberry season from the beginning; berries are medium-sized, sky-blue, with a mild but pleasant flavor and good sweetness; the plants have attractive red-orange fall color. Northcountry blueberry is a companion half-high variety to Northblue from the same University of Minnesota breeding program, released together as a pair that complements Northblue's mid-season ripening with an earlier season (typically ripening 1–2 weeks before Northblue). The pairing of Northcountry (early) with Northblue (mid) or Northsky (late) is the standard recommendation from University of Minnesota Extension for home blueberry plantings in zones 3–5, providing a 3–4 week fresh blueberry season from one combined planting. The cross-pollination between these varieties also improves fruit set on both plants. Northcountry plants grow slightly more compact than Northblue (typically 24–36 inches rather than 36–48 inches), with a dense, mounded habit that makes them particularly attractive as landscape shrubs in addition to their edible fruit value. The berries are medium-sized (slightly smaller than Northblue), sky-blue in color, with a good sweet-mild flavor and good shelf life for a half-high variety. The extreme cold-hardiness — tested to -30°F with snow cover — and early ripening season make Northcountry one of the most important blueberry varieties for northern Minnesota, North Dakota, and other severe cold-climate gardening situations.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall after removing the waxy outer coating by rubbing in coarse sand or washing with a mild solvent, then allow natural cold stratification over winter; northern bayberry tolerates poor, sandy, acidic soil and salt spray, making it an outstanding native for coastal and disturbed sites.
directions: Sow seeds in fall after rubbing away the waxy seed coating, or provide a 60–90 day cold stratification period before spring sowing; northern bayberry grows naturally in coastal dunes, sandy thickets, and open woods from Newfoundland to North Carolina and thrives in lean, acidic, sandy or loamy soils with excellent drainage. This nitrogen-fixing native is highly tolerant of salt spray, wind, and drought, making it an exceptional choice for coastal landscapes and difficult sites where more refined shrubs fail. The aromatic, blue-gray waxy berries cluster tightly along the branches and persist into winter, historically rendered for bayberry candles; in the garden they provide excellent winter interest and food for birds such as yellow-rumped warblers. Northern bayberry spreads slowly by root suckers to form naturalistic colonies and requires both male and female plants for berry production.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring into dry, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; ideal as a low ground-covering berry plant for thin-soiled banks and barrens.
directions: Northern Dewberry is a low-trailing native of dry, open, sandy or rocky ground and thin-soiled barrens throughout eastern North America, distinguished from upright blackberries by its prostrate, creeping canes that root at the tips to form low, dense, ground-covering mats. Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring into dry, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing plants 2 to 3 feet apart; individual canes will trail and root freely to expand coverage over a wide area. White flowers appear in spring and ripen into sweet, black, aggregate drupes in late May to June, making Northern Dewberry one of the earliest-fruiting native brambles and a critical early-summer food source for bluebirds, mockingbirds, towhees, and box turtles. This species excels in sandy, infertile, full-sun sites where taller brambles and most garden fruits cannot survive, making it a uniquely useful edible ground cover for difficult dry spots.

plant_note: Plant canes in early spring while dormant.
directions: Nova is a hardy, disease-resistant red raspberry that stands up to harsh winters and yields firm, flavorful berries. Plant dormant canes in early spring in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow airflow and easy picking. Provide a trellis or support to keep the fruiting canes upright. This summer-bearing type fruits on second-year canes, so remove spent floricanes after harvest while leaving new primocanes for next season. Mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Ochlockonee is a low-chill (about 400-450 hours), late-ripening rabbiteye that extends the harvest season and needs another rabbiteye cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily to keep roots cool and moist through the long southern summer. Ochlockonee is a University of Florida-released rabbiteye blueberry named for the Ochlockonee River in the Florida Panhandle, valued for ripening late in the season, after most other rabbiteye cultivars have finished, which lets home growers stretch fresh blueberry harvest into July. The vigorous, upright bush produces firm, medium-to-large, good-flavored berries in heavy clusters, and its low chill requirement makes it well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South. Fertilize lightly with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again after harvest, and remove old, unproductive canes each winter to keep the bush renewing vigorous fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full to partial sun; odorless bayberry is a coastal plain specialist that naturally inhabits wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bay swamps and performs best in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full to partial sun; odorless bayberry is a coastal plain specialist that naturally inhabits wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bay swamps and performs best in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions. Myrica heterophylla is a semi-evergreen to evergreen native bayberry of the southeastern coastal plain, closely related to wax myrtle but lacking the characteristic aromatic fragrance; it produces similar small waxy berries that attract overwintering songbirds and provides dense cover in wet to moist habitats where few other shrubs thrive. This species is an excellent choice for rain gardens, wet swales, and pond margins in the Southeast, where its compact form and wildlife value make it a workhorse of native planting designs.

plant_note: Plant in spring in mild-winter regions; needs a long growing season.
directions: The olallieberry is a trailing blackberry hybrid (a cross involving loganberry and youngberry parentage) popular along the California coast for its rich, sweet-tart flavor. Its long, sprawling canes must be trained onto a trellis and are best separated by fruiting year for easier pruning. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with regular irrigation through the dry season. Prune out fruited canes after the early-summer harvest and tie in the new canes for next year.

common_name: Onslow Rabbiteye Blueberry (Vigorous Productive Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Onslow is a North Carolina-released rabbiteye blueberry noted for strong vigor and heavy, reliable production. Plant with a different rabbiteye cultivar for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Onslow is a rabbiteye blueberry cultivar released for the Southeast, valued for exceptional plant vigor and consistently heavy production of medium to large, good-flavored berries. Its strong growth makes it well suited to establishing a productive planting relatively quickly, and it performs reliably across the range of soil conditions typical of Southern blueberry patches, provided the acidic, well-drained requirements common to all rabbiteye types are met. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Onslow requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; thrives in dry shade where few other fruiting shrubs succeed.
directions: Oregon grape is a native Pacific Northwest evergreen shrub with holly-like spiny leaves that produces clusters of tart, powder-blue berries in midsummer — one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant edible-fruiting shrubs available. The berries are too tart to eat fresh in quantity but are excellent for jellies, syrups, and wine when sweetened; they are high in berberine, a compound with traditional medicinal use. Plant in groups of three or more for best cross-pollination and fruit set. Prune by removing the oldest, leggiest canes at the base every few years to encourage compact, multi-stemmed growth.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; oriental photinia establishes readily and is quite drought-tolerant once rooted, but consistent moisture in the first season promotes faster establishment and stronger flowering the following spring.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; oriental photinia is adaptable to a range of soil types and is notably more disease-resistant than the commonly planted red-tipped photinia. Photinia villosa is a deciduous shrub or small tree from East Asia offering outstanding multi-season interest: flat clusters of small white flowers appear in spring, followed by persistent bright red berries that last well into winter, and the foliage turns a brilliant red-orange in autumn that rivals the best fall color of any shrub in the temperate garden. Birds, particularly thrushes and waxwings, relish the persistent berries through late winter, making this an excellent choice for a wildlife-supporting mixed shrub border.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Osage is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry with a relatively compact habit compared to other erect varieties. In zone 9 it ripens in late May–June, one of the earlier erect thornless blackberries. Prune fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes on a two-wire trellis system.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Osage is a University of Arkansas-released thornless semi-erect blackberry selected for early ripening (among the first thornless erect blackberries to ripen in June in zone 9) and exceptional flavor — rated by Arkansas evaluators as the best-flavored of their thornless erect releases, with a rich, sweet, complex blackberry flavor and balanced sugar-to-acid ratio that surpasses the milder flavor of some other University of Arkansas varieties. The large berries are firm, glossy, and jet-black with excellent shelf life after harvest. The early ripening of Osage is a meaningful advantage in zone 9 where the blackberry harvest window can be shortened by early summer heat — getting the bulk of the crop in late May to mid-June avoids the worst of the heat. In zone 9 Osage is planted alongside mid-season varieties like Apache to extend the harvest over a longer period.

common_name: Osceola Blueberry (Southern Highbush Large-Berry Low-Chill Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in early spring in highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-amended, well-drained soil; blueberries require acidic conditions and will fail quickly in alkaline soils. In zone 9, Osceola requires only 150–200 chilling hours (hours below 45°F), making it reliable where northern varieties fail from insufficient winter chill. Plant 2 or more varieties for cross-pollination and improved yields. Osceola ripens May–June in zone 9. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain soil acidity.
directions: Plant in highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil; acidify if necessary with sulfur or peat moss. Mulch with pine bark or pine straw. Osceola is a southern highbush blueberry developed in Florida through the University of Florida breeding program — a hybrid of northern highbush (Vaccinium corymbosum) and the native southern rabbit-eye relative (Vaccinium darrowi) that produces a plant adapted to the warm, humid conditions and low chilling hours of the Gulf South. The challenge of growing blueberries in the Deep South is chilling requirement: most northern highbush varieties need 800–1,200 hours below 45°F per winter to break dormancy and fruit properly, a requirement never met in zone 8–10 winters where chilling hours typically run 150–400. Osceola and other southern highbush varieties were specifically bred for low chilling requirements (150–200 hours), allowing reliable fruiting in zone 8–10 where northern varieties fail. Osceola produces large, firm, high-quality berries with excellent flavor — among the largest of the southern highbush varieties — ripening mid-season (May–June in zone 9). It is one of the most widely planted commercial and home garden blueberries in Florida and along the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter through early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March for maximum establishment. Ouachita sets fruit in its second year, typically June in zone 8–9, slightly later than Natchez.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained acidic soil; Ouachita is a thornless, semi-erect blackberry developed by the University of Arkansas and released in 2003 — one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in the mid-South and Gulf Coast because of its outstanding combination of productivity, fruit quality, and disease resistance. Berries are medium-large (7–9 grams), glossy black, firm, and mildly sweet with a pleasant balanced flavor and small seeds. Yields are among the highest of any named blackberry variety, and the plants show good resistance to orange rust and anthracnose — a meaningful advantage in the humid South. Canes are self-supporting but benefit from a simple T-trellis for row plantings. Prune floricanes to the ground immediately after harvest; thin primocanes to 4–6 per plant and tip at 36 inches in late summer to encourage lateral branching that will carry next year's fruit. Ouachita's mid-season ripening (about 2 weeks after Natchez) makes it an excellent partner variety for an extended harvest window.

plant_note: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda dogwood is shade-tolerant and adaptable but is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker disease — provide good air circulation and avoid injuring the bark.
directions: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; pagoda dogwood is shade-tolerant and adaptable but is susceptible to dogwood borers and golden canker disease — provide good air circulation and avoid injuring the bark. Cornus alternifolia is the only native eastern dogwood with alternate (rather than opposite) leaves, and it produces one of the most distinctive and elegant branching patterns of any native tree — distinctly horizontal, tiered layers of branches that create a pagoda-like architectural silhouette outstanding in winter; its small, fragrant, flat-topped white flower clusters are followed by showy blue-black berries on red pedicels that are consumed by dozens of migrating bird species. Four-season interest: layered winter form, white spring flowers, summer fruit, and red-purple fall foliage.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in zones 9–11; in cooler zones grow in large containers and overwinter indoors.
directions: Passionfruit is a vigorous, tendril-climbing vine requiring a sturdy wire trellis or fence. Train the main stem vertically and allow lateral shoots to drape horizontally from the top — these laterals bear the flowers and fruit. Prune heavily after fruiting to rejuvenate the vine and maintain productive growth. Harvest when the fruit skin begins to wrinkle and the fruit falls or detaches easily; purple cultivars are generally more cold-tolerant than yellow types.

plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns in early spring with crowns level at the soil surface; must be grown near standard red strawberries for adequate pollination.
directions: Pineberry is a white-fruited strawberry cultivar (largely derived from the South American species Fragaria chiloensis crossed with F. x ananassa) that produces pale cream-white berries with red achenes and a distinctive pineapple-like aroma when fully ripe. Pineberries have low self-fertility and require a red-fruiting strawberry variety planted nearby as a pollinator for adequate fruit set. Grow exactly as you would a june-bearing or everbearing strawberry, removing blossoms the first season to build root strength. Harvest when berries are white to pale pink with red seeds and give off a sweet pineapple fragrance.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; grows well alongside red and white currants with identical cultural requirements.
directions: Pink currants are naturally occurring or selected mutations of red currant (Ribes rubrum) producing pale rose-pink to blush-colored berries that are milder and sweeter than the typical red forms — popular cultivars include 'Pink Champagne' and 'Gloire de Sablons'. Culture is identical to red currant: plant in cool, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0–6.5 and prune each late winter to retain 8–12 mixed-age canes, removing any older than 5 years. The translucent pink strigs are ornamentally striking and ripen slightly earlier than most red currants. Check state Ribes restrictions before ordering.

plant_note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: 'Pink Lemonade' is an ornamental rabbiteye-type hybrid bearing translucent pink berries with a mild, sweet flavor that deepen in color as they ripen. It offers attractive white-pink spring blooms and fiery fall foliage in addition to novelty fruit. Grow in full sun in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5) kept evenly moist with a pine-bark or pine-needle mulch. Yields improve with a second blueberry variety nearby for cross-pollination; prune lightly after the third year to renew fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Pixwell holds its berries away from the thorny stems on longer stalks, making harvest noticeably easier than many gooseberry cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in hot climates. Pixwell was bred specifically to make gooseberry picking less painful, holding its pale green, ripening-to-pink berries on longer stems that dangle clear of the thorny branches, unlike older cultivars whose fruit clusters tightly among the spines. The berries have the classic tart gooseberry flavor, excellent for pies, preserves, and sauces, and the plant is vigorous, cold-hardy, and self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator. Prune out wood older than three years each dormant season to keep the bush productive, and site with some afternoon shade in warmer climates, since gooseberries generally prefer cooler growing conditions than the Deep South provides.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Polana is a primocane (fall-bearing) raspberry that in zone 9 produces a fall crop on first-year canes in September–November — potentially the only practical raspberry crop in the warmest zone 9 areas, as the fall primocane season occurs during cooler fall temperatures. Mow or cut all canes to the ground in late winter for a single annual fall crop.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Polana is a Polish-bred, fall-bearing (primocane) raspberry producing its main crop on first-year canes in autumn — earlier than most other fall-bearing varieties, beginning to ripen in August–September in most climates. The earlier fall ripening is a significant advantage because it means more of the crop matures before winter freezes end the season in northern areas, and in zone 9 the earlier ripening of Polana compared to later fall-bearing types like Heritage means the crop starts before the hottest September weather. The firm, conical, dark red berries have excellent flavor — well-balanced sweet-tart with rich raspberry aroma. Polana is one of the most productive fall-bearing varieties per area; the compact, self-supporting primocane habit (no trellis needed) makes it practical for small gardens. In zone 9 fall raspberries are more reliably successful than summer varieties because the October ripening occurs in cooler conditions.

plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Ponca's upright, thornless canes need only a simple support and produce an unusually sweet, small-seeded berry prized for fresh eating.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the upright canes onto a simple two-wire trellis for support. Released by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Ponca is one of the newer thornless erect blackberry cultivars, notable for exceptionally high sugar content and small seed size that give it outstanding fresh-eating flavor compared to older, tarter cultivars. The compact, upright canes need less trellising than sprawling semi-erect types, and the plant produces a concentrated harvest over a relatively short picking window in early summer. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to make room for the canes that will fruit the following season.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; Poorman is a classic American gooseberry hybrid bred for milder flavor and fewer, softer thorns than European gooseberry types.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch and reduce mildew pressure). Poorman is a long-cultivated American gooseberry hybrid, valued for combining good disease resistance with berries that are sweeter and milder than many European gooseberry cultivars, making them pleasant for fresh eating as well as pies, jams, and preserves. The medium-sized fruit ripens from green to a rosy red-pink blush, and the bush, while still thorny like most gooseberries, is comparatively less vicious to harvest from than many older European types. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on both old and new wood; prune out the oldest canes each winter and thin crowded growth to improve air circulation, since gooseberries are prone to powdery mildew in humid, poorly ventilated plantings. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately wet soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw requires a male pollinator nearby for berry production — one male plant will pollinate up to three female plants.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw holly is a multi-season native shrub that blooms with small white flowers in spring attractive to native bees, then develops abundant bright-orange to red berries that ripen in fall and persist through winter to provide critical food for cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other frugivorous birds. A male pollinator must be planted nearby for fruiting; nurseries often sell named female selections (Warren's Red, Council Fire) paired with a male. Tolerates the periodic flooding and clay soils common to Gulf Coast lowland sites. Exceptional as a wildlife garden shrub, in rain gardens, and along creek margins.

common_name: Powder Blue Rabbiteye Blueberry (Late-Season Heavy-Bearing Gulf South Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant nursery-grown rooted cuttings in fall or spring in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil amended with generous amounts of pine bark, peat moss, or acidic compost; rabbiteye blueberries are among the most heat and drought-tolerant blueberries for zone 7–9. Powder Blue requires cross-pollination from a second rabbiteye variety (Brightwell, Tifblue, Premier, or Climax) for good fruit set; plant at least two different rabbiteye varieties. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw. Powder Blue is a late-season rabbiteye ripening in July in the Gulf South — after earlier varieties like Climax and Premier — extending the total blueberry harvest window by 3–4 weeks.
directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained, organically rich soil at the same depth as the nursery container; mulch 4–6 inches deep with pine bark or pine straw to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Do not fertilize with standard garden fertilizers — use acid-specific fertilizers (ammonium sulfate or azalea/camellia formulas). Powder Blue is a rabbiteye blueberry (Vaccinium virgatum, formerly classified as V. ashei) released in 1978 by North Carolina State University — one of the most widely planted and highest-yielding rabbiteye varieties across the Southeast. Rabbiteye blueberries are the blueberry species native to the Gulf South — the wild Vaccinium virgatum grows naturally throughout the coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana — and they are dramatically better adapted to the heat, humidity, and acidic sandy soils of the Gulf South than the northern highbush blueberries that dominate the commercial blueberry market. Powder Blue produces very large berries for a rabbiteye — medium-firm, light blue (giving the variety its name), with a mild, sweet flavor. The late-season ripening (July in zone 8–9) means Powder Blue fills the end of the Gulf South blueberry season after earlier-ripening varieties have peaked, extending the household fresh blueberry window into midsummer. Established rabbiteye plantings (plants reach bearing age in 3–5 years and can remain productive for 30–50 years) are highly cost-effective long-term investments for Gulf South home fruit gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for best establishment before summer heat. Powderblue blooms late-mid season and cross-pollinates best with Brightwell, Tifblue, or Climax — plant at least two varieties within 50 feet for maximum fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Powderblue is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry valued for its vigorous, upright, disease-resistant growth habit and dependable, heavy production of firm, small-to-medium, powder-blue berries with excellent shelf life and a mild, sweet flavor well suited to both fresh eating and freezing. It ripens mid-to-late season, several weeks after Climax and Premier, helping extend the rabbiteye harvest window into July in most Gulf Coast plantings. The upright, vigorous canes tend to sucker less than some rabbiteye varieties, keeping the planting tidier, and the bush shows good tolerance of the humid, disease-prone conditions typical of southeastern summers. Mulch heavily with pine bark, maintain consistent moisture through fruit development, and fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer at bloom and again after harvest. Zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant during dormancy (December–February in zone 9) in highly acidic soil; Premier requires 400–500 chill hours. Plant with Climax or Brightwell for cross-pollination; Premier's early-mid season ripening (late May to June) extends the harvest begun by early Climax.
directions: Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.0) amended with pine bark, peat, or sulfur; Premier is an early-to-mid-season rabbiteye blueberry released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1978, valued particularly for its very large berry size — among the largest of the rabbiteye types — and excellent fresh-eating flavor. Berries are light blue, mild, sweet, and ripen from late May through June in zone 8–9. The spreading, vigorous plant is one of the more open-canopied rabbiteye varieties, giving better air circulation that reduces disease problems. Premier is a perennial favorite for u-pick operations and home gardens in the Gulf Coast South because the large berries are showy and harvest quickly. Fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or cottonseed meal) in early spring and again in late spring; avoid high-nitrogen applications after July. Prune to remove crossing branches and old unproductive wood after the third year of growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February. Premier is an early-ripening rabbiteye variety that begins bearing in late May–early June, among the first rabbiteyes to ripen in zone 9. Plant with Brightwell, Climax, or Tifblue for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil amended with pine bark in full sun; Premier is the standard early-season rabbiteye blueberry for zone 7–9, producing large, light blue, mildly flavored berries beginning in late May in most Gulf Coast plantings — up to 3 weeks before mid-season varieties. The upright, vigorous shrubs can reach 8–10 feet with age and are among the most productive of the early-season rabbiteyes. The berries have a larger size than most other early varieties but a thinner skin than mid-season types; harvest promptly after coloring to prevent skin softening. Premier has a chilling requirement of approximately 350 hours, making it reliable in zone 8–9 without the risk of premature bloom during January warm spells. Cross-pollinates well with Brightwell, Climax, Centurion, and Tifblue.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Prima Donna requires approximately 300–400 chill hours, suitable for zone 9a and the warmer parts of zone 9b. Cross-pollinate with another low-to-mid-chill southern highbush variety. In zone 9 it ripens in May–June.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Prima Donna is a southern highbush blueberry selected by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery for its combination of high fruit quality and strong plant vigor in warm-climate conditions. The medium-large berries are firm, flavorful, and sweet with a pleasant balance of sugar and acid that makes them superior for fresh eating. Prima Donna's primary advantage is a high-quality, consistent fruit that stores and ships better than softer varieties — the firm texture retains quality for 2–3 weeks under refrigeration, significantly longer than some other southern varieties. In zone 9 home gardens this means less pressure to consume the harvest immediately after picking. Prima Donna is popular in commercial pick-your-own operations in the Southeast precisely because the firm berries withstand handling by customers without bruising. The plant habit is vigorous and upright, producing good yields without excessive vegetative growth.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Prime-Ark 45 is a primocane-fruiting thorny erect blackberry that produces a fall primocane crop in August–September and a spring floricane crop in May–June in zone 9. Despite its thorns, the very large, high-quality fruit makes it worth the harvesting inconvenience. Provide sturdy trellis support for the heavy primocanes.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Prime-Ark 45 is the premier primocane-fruiting blackberry for the Southeast from the University of Arkansas, producing very large (among the biggest primocane-fruiting blackberries), firm, sweet, intensely flavored berries on both first-year (summer) and second-year (spring) canes. The fruit quality is significantly higher than earlier primocane blackberry releases — larger, firmer, sweeter berries that are excellent for fresh eating and hold well after harvest. Prime-Ark 45 is thorny, unlike the thornless Prime-Jan, but the superior fruit quality compensates for the harvesting difficulty. The number '45' in the name refers to internal University of Arkansas breeding program designation. In zone 9 the fall primocane crop matures in August–September when few other berries are available, providing fresh blackberries in a season gap that no other easily-grown small fruit fills. The spring floricane crop in May–June follows the standard blackberry season timing.

plant_note: Plant in spring; primocane-fruiting so it can crop the first year.
directions: 'Prime-Ark Freedom' is the first thornless primocane-fruiting blackberry, capable of bearing very large berries on first-year canes. It offers an early summer crop on floricanes and a late-summer-to-fall crop on new primocanes. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, and support the canes on a trellis in windy locations. In hot climates the fall crop yields the sweetest fruit when temperatures moderate; soft-tip the primocanes to boost lateral fruiting.

common_name: Prime-Ark Traveler Blackberry (Thornless Machine-Harvestable Primocane Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; as a primocane-fruiting type, Prime-Ark Traveler can produce a fall crop on new canes the same year it is planted, in addition to the following year's traditional summer crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and provide a sturdy trellis, since this vigorous primocane-fruiting cultivar produces fruit on first-year canes in addition to the traditional second-year floricane crop. Bred by the University of Arkansas specifically for firmness that withstands mechanical harvesting and shipping, Prime-Ark Traveler also performs well as a home-garden thornless blackberry, producing a first crop on primocanes in late summer and fall in addition to the normal early-summer floricane harvest. Because it fruits on both first- and second-year wood, pruning decisions affect which crop you prioritize: cutting all canes to the ground in winter sacrifices the floricane crop but still allows a fall primocane harvest, while leaving some canes standing provides both crops.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Prime-Jan is a primocane-fruiting variety — it produces fruit on first-year canes (primocanes) in addition to second-year floricanes. In zone 9 the primocane crop ripens August–September and the floricane crop in May–June, providing two distinct harvest periods. Erect habit requires no trellis.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Prime-Jan is a University of Arkansas thornless erect blackberry notable for its primocane-fruiting (fall-bearing) character — unlike conventional blackberries that produce fruit only on second-year canes (floricanes), Prime-Jan produces fruit on first-year canes in late summer and fall (August–September) as well as a conventional floricane crop in spring (May–June). This dual-cropping habit provides two distinct harvest windows per season, approximately doubling the period of fresh blackberry production from a single planting. The primocane crop in late summer fills the gap between the spring blackberry season and fall, when no other thornless erect blackberries are producing. In zone 9 both crops ripen reliably, and the late-summer primocane crop avoids the rush of the spring berry season when many other fruits are also ripe. The fruit quality is comparable to other University of Arkansas erect varieties — medium to large, sweet-tart, jet-black berries with good flavor.

plant_note: Plant in cool to mild climates (zone 8–10) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with support for climbing; Purple Apple Berry is a delicate Australian native twining vine from cool, moist forests of Victoria, Tasmania, and New South Wales bearing nodding, pale-yellow to greenish flowers followed by deep-purple, oblong berries eaten by Aboriginal Australians as bush tucker — one of few Australian native fruits suited to temperate and mild cool-temperate climates.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with a trellis, fence, or shrub as support; Billardiera longiflora is a light, delicate twiner that does not require heavy support — it weaves through shrubs naturally and benefits from an organic mulch layer to keep the root zone cool and moist. Billardiera longiflora (Purple Apple Berry or Climbing Blueberry) is a dainty, evergreen, twining vine native to cool, moist forests and mountain gullies of Tasmania, Victoria, South Australia, and New South Wales, where it climbs through the understory layer on fences and shrubs to produce small, nodding, narrowly bell-shaped, pale greenish-yellow to cream flowers in spring and early summer, followed in autumn by oblong, shiny, deep-purple berries roughly the size and shape of a large olive. The berries are entirely edible and were a prized bush food of southeastern Aboriginal peoples — sweet, slightly glutinous, with a mild, pleasant flavor reminiscent of a mild grape-berry combination. Billardiera longiflora is well-suited to cool-temperate and mild-temperate gardens in zones 8–10, thriving in sheltered, partially shaded positions in moist, well-drained, organically enriched soil. An excellent choice for cool-climate cottage gardens, shaded fences, and native wildlife gardens attracting insects and small birds.

plant_note: Plant rooted cane tips or divisions in early spring; dewberry is the trailing, low-growing, first-ripening blackberry type native to eastern North America — it thrives in partial shade, open woodland edges, and dry, sandy soils that challenge cultivated blackberries.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, acidic soil; northern dewberry is a trailing native blackberry that runs along the ground rather than forming erect canes, with individual canes spreading 3–6 feet from the crown. It is among the first bramble fruits to ripen in summer — often a full month before other blackberries — producing glossy, deep black, juicy, intensely sweet-tart fruits excellent for fresh eating and preserves. The trailing habit makes it suitable for slopes, embankments, and naturalized woodland edges; it thrives under open forest canopy where cultivated blackberries would languish. Unlike erect blackberries it does not sucker aggressively but can spread by cane-tip rooting. The canes have sharp prickles; wear gloves for harvest and management.

plant_note: Plant divisions or bare-root stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; tolerates more shade than most Rubus species — ideal for woodland edges.
directions: Purple-flowering raspberry is a thornless native North American Rubus producing large, showy rose-purple flowers attractive to pollinators followed by broad, flat, raspberry-like fruits in midsummer. The berries are edible but dry and seedy — more appealing to wildlife than humans — making this species primarily grown as an ornamental fruiting shrub for naturalizing woodland edges and native plantings. It spreads vigorously by root suckering and can colonize large areas; control spread by removing suckers as needed at the perimeter. No trellising is required; prune out older, dying canes to the ground in late winter to encourage fresh, vigorous shoots.

common_name: Quinault Strawberry (Day-Neutral Everbearing Pacific Northwest Strawberry)
plant_note: Plant in spring after last frost in full sun; Quinault is a day-neutral everbearing variety that produces crops in spring and fall (rather than a single June-bearing crop) and is particularly valued for its ability to produce fruit on brand-new plants in the same year of planting — an advantage for gardeners who want strawberries without waiting through an entire season before harvesting.
directions: Plant in spring in a rich, well-prepared bed; do not remove flowers from Quinault in the first year — as a day-neutral type it will produce fruit on new plants; allow fall runners to fill in the bed for subsequent seasons; remove runners in summer to redirect energy to fruit production. Quinault strawberry is a Washington State University-developed day-neutral (everbearing) variety (released 1967) that produces fruit regardless of day length, yielding crops in spring, mid-summer (briefly), and fall rather than the concentrated June-bearing harvest of standard varieties. This fruiting pattern is genuinely different from both June-bearing (single spring crop) and older everbearing (two main crops, spring and fall) varieties — true day-neutral varieties like Quinault produce small but continuous fruit throughout the growing season whenever temperatures are moderate (below 80°F). The practical implication for home gardeners is that Quinault plants bear fruit in their first growing season from spring plantings, providing immediate gratification without waiting through an entire growing year before harvesting. This first-year fruiting makes Quinault a particularly good variety for children's gardens, community gardens, and impatient gardeners. The variety was developed at Washington State University for Pacific Northwest conditions (mild, cool summers), where it has been widely grown since its release. The berries are large, red, and soft with a sweet flavor similar to alpine strawberries — best for fresh eating rather than processing.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Rebel requires approximately 500–600 chill hours, suitable for zone 9a and the upper part of zone 9b. Cross-pollinate with another mid-chill variety for best production. In zone 9 Rebel ripens in May–June and produces large, high-quality fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Rebel is a southern highbush blueberry developed by Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, released specifically for its combination of very large fruit size and excellent flavor — the berries are among the largest available in southern highbush blueberries, and their rich, sweet-tart, complex flavor rivals northern highbush varieties that are not adapted to zone 9 conditions. The vigorous, productive plant produces heavy crops of these exceptional large-caliber berries with a firm texture that holds up well in packing, shipping, and storage. Rebel's fruit quality has made it popular among commercial pick-your-own operations in the Southeast where premium large berries command top prices. In zone 9 home gardens it provides exceptional fresh eating quality — the large berries are satisfying to pick and eat fresh from the bush. Cross-pollinate with Flordablue, Biloxi, or Windsor for maximum crop set.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; adapts to a wide range of soils including wet, poorly drained sites.
directions: Red chokeberry (Aronia arbutifolia) is a taller, more upright native shrub than its black-fruited relative, bearing bright red berries that ripen in fall and persist well into winter, providing exceptional wildlife food and four-season ornamental interest. The berries are intensely astringent fresh but soften after frost and are suitable for jellies, juices, and wines with added sweetener. The cultivar 'Brilliantissima' is widely grown for its especially vibrant fall foliage and heavy fruit set. Prune oldest canes to the ground every 3–4 years to control suckering and maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring as soon as soil is workable.
directions: Red currants fruit heavily on spurs of wood two years old and older; prune each late winter to keep 8–12 canes of mixed ages and remove any cane older than 5 years. They tolerate more shade than most fruits and appreciate afternoon shelter in hot climates. Harvest entire strigs (clusters) when berries are uniformly bright red and slightly translucent. Check state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Red Elderberry is more shade-tolerant than American Elderberry. The raw berries are mildly toxic and cause nausea — cook thoroughly before any culinary use, or grow primarily as a wildlife plant.
directions: Red Elderberry is a fast-growing native shrub of cool, moist forests, rocky slopes, talus, and ravines across the northern United States and Canada, valued for its dramatic pyramid-shaped white flower clusters in spring and vivid red berry clusters in early summer that ripen weeks before American Elderberry. The berries are relished by over 50 species of birds including thrushes, waxwings, grouse, and tanagers, making Red Elderberry among the most important native berry shrubs for wildlife in northern gardens. Unlike the closely related American Elderberry, Red Elderberry berries are mildly toxic when eaten raw due to cyanogenic glycosides and should be cooked before any culinary use; fully cooked berries have been used for jams, wines, and syrups in both traditional and modern kitchens. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Elderberry is more shade-tolerant than American Elderberry and thrives at cool woodland edges and in dappled understory light.

plant_note: Plant in spring in very acidic, humus-rich soil or on decaying conifer wood; native to the Pacific Northwest understory and tolerates deep shade.
directions: Red huckleberry is a Pacific Northwest native that naturally colonizes rotting conifer stumps and logs, requiring extremely acidic conditions (pH 4.0–5.0) and excellent drainage with abundant organic matter. The bright scarlet berries ripen in summer and are tart — excellent for jams, syrups, and pies — and are an important wildlife food for birds and bears. Established plants spread slowly by rhizomes and require minimal pruning; remove only dead or crossing branches in late winter. Difficult to transplant as a wild specimen; use nursery-grown container stock for best results.

common_name: Red Lake Currant (Classic American Red Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; Red Lake is a University of Minnesota release and one of the most widely planted red currant cultivars in North America.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. Red Lake is a classic American red currant, released by the University of Minnesota in the 1930s and long the standard home-garden red currant, valued for its long, uniform strigs (clusters) of large, bright red, tart-sweet berries that are self-fertile and productive without a second bush. Fruit is excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking, and the tart flavor mellows somewhat with full ripeness. Because red currants fruit on spurs of older wood rather than new growth, prune to an open, vase-shaped framework in winter and remove wood older than three years to keep the bush productive. Net the bushes at ripening, since birds find currants highly attractive.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; red mulberry grows naturally along stream banks, woodland edges, and moist bottomland and tolerates partial shade better than most fruit trees.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the red mulberry is the only mulberry native to eastern North America and produces berries superior in flavor and nutrition to the introduced white mulberry — richer, more complex, and deeply red to black when fully ripe. It is an ecologically critical plant, providing fruit for hundreds of wildlife species at a critical early-summer period. The berries are edible fresh or made into pies, jams, wine, and dried fruit; harvest is best done by spreading a tarp and shaking the branches, as berries stain everything they touch. Red mulberry is distinguished from white mulberry by its leaves, which are rough on the upper surface (smooth in white mulberry). It unfortunately hybridizes readily with the invasive white mulberry where the two grow together, threatening the genetic integrity of pure wild populations; purchasing certified native red mulberry trees from reputable nurseries is important.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring; in zone 7 plant February–March. Red Pearl is self-fertile and produces two crops per year — a primary crop in late summer (August) and a second crop in fall (September–October). Plant in very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) similar to blueberry culture. The low creeping habit makes Red Pearl excellent as an edible groundcover under acid-loving trees and shrubs.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil similar to blueberry growing conditions; Red Pearl is a Dutch-selected lingonberry (Vaccinium vitis-idaea) cultivar renowned as one of the most productive named varieties, producing two crops of bright red berries per season rather than the single crop of most species plants — the first crop ripens in August and the second in October, significantly extending the fresh lingonberry harvest. The glossy, bright scarlet berries have the characteristic lingonberry flavor: tart, slightly bitter, and astringent when raw, transforming into the quintessential lingonberry jam flavor when sweetened and cooked. Lingonberry jam is the traditional accompaniment to meatballs and other Scandinavian dishes and is a major commercial product in northern Europe. The low-growing, evergreen, spreading habit makes Red Pearl an excellent edible groundcover for shady acidic spots under blueberries, azaleas, rhododendrons, and pines where few other fruiting plants thrive. Spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a dense carpet.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Regent is self-fertile but cross-pollination with another Amelanchier alnifolia cultivar improves fruit set. The compact habit makes Regent outstanding for small gardens, foundation plantings, and edible landscape uses where full-size Amelanchier trees are too large.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Regent is a compact, dwarf saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia) selected by South Dakota State University, producing a shrub typically 3–5 feet tall rather than the 8–12 foot height of standard saskatoon varieties — making it the most practical Amelanchier for small residential gardens, containers, and formal edible landscape plantings where size is a constraint. The sweet, blueberry-like berries ripen in June–July in clusters of 5–10 and are among the most delicious of any native North American fruit — eaten fresh, made into pies, jams, and wine, or dried like raisins. The flavor is richer and sweeter than blueberry with almond-like notes from the tiny edible seeds. Regent blooms very early in spring (March–April in zone 9), providing one of the first nectar sources for bees and early pollinators. The white flower clusters, attractive summer foliage, and orange-to-red fall color make Regent exceptional as an edible ornamental.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Regent is a compact shrub-form saskatoon serviceberry selected specifically for heavy production of sweet, juicy fruit on a size manageable for home gardens and hedgerows.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Regent is a compact selection of saskatoon serviceberry, bred specifically as a fruiting shrub rather than a landscape specimen tree, producing heavy crops of sweet, blueberry-like berries on a manageable-sized bush well suited to home orchards, hedgerows, and edible landscaping. It shares the white spring flowers and good fall color of its tree-form relatives but stays considerably smaller, making it easier to net against birds and to harvest by hand. It is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and low-maintenance, needing only occasional removal of the oldest stems to keep the planting vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; Rosborough was bred specifically for hot, humid Gulf South conditions and has thorns, unlike many modern thornless cultivars.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the semi-erect canes onto a sturdy trellis. Developed by the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program, Rosborough was selected specifically for reliable performance in the hot, humid conditions of Texas and the Gulf South, producing good yields of medium-to-large, flavorful berries in early-to-mid summer. It has thorns, unlike many newer cultivars, but its regional heat tolerance and disease resistance have made it a long-standing favorite among Gulf Coast growers who prioritize proven regional performance over the novelty of thornlessness. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest each year to keep the planting vigorous and productive.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring.
directions: 'Rovada' is a late-season red currant that bears exceptionally long strigs of bright, uniform berries prized for jelly and fresh use. It flowers late, escaping frost, and crops reliably even in cooler summers. Unlike black currants, red currants fruit on spurs of older wood, so prune to an open goblet framework and shorten new growth in winter. Grow in partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch, and net the bushes to protect ripe fruit from birds.

plant_note: Plant early spring; keep away from wild brambles to limit disease.
directions: 'Royalty' is a hybrid of red and black raspberry yielding large, richly flavored purple berries excellent for jam and baking. The tall, sturdy canes do not sucker as aggressively as red types and are best tip-pruned in summer to encourage lateral branching. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and remove old floricanes after fruiting. Plant at least 300 feet from wild or black raspberries to reduce viral disease pressure.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; running serviceberry spreads by stolons to form low, attractive colonies and is excellent for erosion control on shaded slopes.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; running serviceberry is the low-growing, colony-forming native serviceberry of the northeastern US and Appalachians, spreading by stolons to form attractive low thickets 1–3 feet tall on rocky slopes, woodland edges, and open forests. Like all serviceberries, it produces masses of white flowers in early spring that are an important nectar and pollen source for early-emerging native bees, followed by sweet, blueberry-like June berries in early summer that are excellent fresh, dried, or cooked into pies and preserves. The low, suckering habit makes it more useful as a shade-tolerant groundcover or erosion control plant than as a specimen shrub. It colors brilliantly orange-red in fall. An ideal native edible shrub for shaded slopes, woodland edges, and low-maintenance natural landscapes in the Northeast and Appalachians.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; russet buffaloberry is a native Canadian and northern US shrub — one of the most cold-hardy native berry shrubs on the continent — producing red-orange to yellow, translucent, bitter berries that are edible only after frost or cooking; its unique saponin content was traditionally exploited by indigenous peoples to whip the berries into a frothy 'Indian ice cream' or 'soopalallie.'
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established; the plant fixes nitrogen through Frankia bacterial symbiosis. Shepherdia canadensis (russet buffaloberry or soopalallie) is a deciduous native shrub of Canada, Alaska, and the northern United States — one of the most cold-hardy native fruiting shrubs on the continent, thriving in zone 2–6 conditions where few fruiting plants survive. The plant produces small (1/4-inch), translucent, red-orange to yellow, elliptic berries in summer that are bitter and astringent when eaten raw due to saponin content, but become edible after frost or cooking. The most famous traditional use is as 'sxusem' or 'soopalallie' (in Chinook jargon) — the indigenous peoples of British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest whipped the raw berries with water to produce a frothy, bright-red, bitter-sweet foam similar to meringue, traditionally sweetened with berries or honey and eaten as 'Indian ice cream.' The high saponin content is what enables the foam to form — the same compounds that make dish soap foam. The berries are also used for jelly, syrup, and beverages. Shephaerdia canadensis is a dioecious nitrogen-fixer (requires separate male and female plants, and fixes nitrogen through Frankia actinorrhizal symbiosis), making it valuable in cold-climate food forest systems as a soil-building shrub with an edible berry crop.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter, or cold-stratify seeds for 60–90 days before spring sowing; plant in lean, dry, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun — russet buffaloberry fixes nitrogen via root nodules and thrives in poor soils where other fruiting shrubs struggle.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly in the garden or cold-stratify for 60–90 days before planting in spring; plant in dry, rocky, or sandy soil with excellent drainage in full sun, as russet buffaloberry naturally colonizes forest edges, rocky slopes, and open woodlands from Alaska to the northeastern United States. This dioecious nitrogen-fixer requires both male and female plants to produce its small, tart red berries, which ripen in midsummer. The berries were a prized food source for many indigenous peoples and can be whipped with a small amount of water and a touch of sweetener into a stable foam traditionally called 'sxusem' or Indian ice cream. Established plants are extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once rooted, making russet buffaloberry an excellent low-maintenance native for challenging northern and high-altitude sites.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, strongly acidic, well-drained soil under conifer canopy.
directions: Salal is an evergreen native shrub of the Pacific Northwest coast, found beneath conifers from central California to Alaska, where it forms dense thickets on acidic, well-drained forest soils. The dark blue-purple berries are similar in size to a blueberry but have mealy, mildly sweet flesh and were an important food source for coastal Indigenous peoples, eaten fresh or dried into cakes. Salal is propagated by division or from container-grown nursery stock; seed germination is slow and unreliable. The glossy foliage is commercially valuable in the floral trade, and home growers can cut leathery stems for arrangements without harming the plant.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich soil; salmonberry naturalizes readily in Pacific Northwest conditions.
directions: Salmonberry is a Pacific Northwest native shrub that thrives in moist to wet, shaded sites along streams and forest edges, making it one of the few fruiting canes suitable for boggy ground. Fruits ripen very early — often in May or June — in shades from yellow-orange to deep red-salmon, with a mild, slightly bland flavor best suited to fresh eating or jams. Thin old canes to the ground each year after fruiting to maintain vigor, as the plant spreads by rhizomes and can form dense thickets. Wildlife value is extremely high; berries attract birds and bears within days of ripening.

common_name: San Andreas Strawberry (UC Davis Day-Neutral Everbearing with Excellent Summer Flavor)
plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns or transplants in fall (October–November) in zone 9 for a winter-to-spring production season; San Andreas is a day-neutral variety that initiates flowers regardless of day length, allowing production outside the standard June-bearing window. In zone 9, fall planting produces the best results: plants establish during the mild winter, begin producing January–February, and continue through May before summer heat ends the season. Day-neutral strawberries do not require the cold vernalization that June-bearers need; they produce continuously through spring and may produce lightly in fall as well. Plant at the correct depth — crown at soil level, not buried. San Andreas was released by the University of California Davis strawberry breeding program and has become one of the most widely planted day-neutral strawberry varieties in commercial production in California.
directions: Plant crowns with crown at soil surface; mulch with straw. Pick when fully red. San Andreas Strawberry was released by the University of California Davis strawberry breeding program around 2009 as part of a sequence of day-neutral variety releases (Albion, Seascape, San Andreas, Monterey) that established UC Davis as the primary source of commercial day-neutral strawberry genetics in North America. The UC Davis program, which has produced many of the most important commercial strawberry varieties in the world over the past several decades, focused San Andreas specifically for improved performance in California's commercial production regions — the Watsonville and Salinas Valley coastal areas that produce the majority of California's fresh-market strawberries. Day-neutral varieties (also called everbearing in older terminology) distinguish themselves from June-bearing types by initiating flower production regardless of day length: standard June-bearers require specific short-day conditions to trigger flowering, restricting their production season, while day-neutral varieties flower whenever temperatures are favorable (roughly 35–85°F). San Andreas produces medium to large, conical fruits with bright red skin, firm flesh, and excellent sweet flavor with good acid balance — qualities that place it at the premium end of commercial strawberry flavor, closer to the flavor of Albion than many other commercial varieties. The skin is moderately firm, allowing several days of shelf life after harvest, and the flesh is red throughout without the white core common in lower-quality commercial varieties. For zone 9 fall-winter planting, San Andreas's day-neutral character and good heat tolerance make it one of the better choices for a productive winter-through-spring strawberry season.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; excellent for coastal plain sites and old fields where other blackberries fail.
directions: Sand Blackberry is a low-growing native blackberry of dry, sandy, acidic open ground across the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas, identified by its broadly wedge-shaped leaflets with distinctive white-felted undersides. Plant rooted cuttings in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 3 to 5 feet apart to allow for natural spreading by root sprouts into a dense, wildlife-supporting thicket. White flowers appear in spring on second-year canes, followed by small but sweet, glossy black drupes in early summer that are excellent for jams, pies, and fresh eating. Remove spent floricanes after harvest each season and allow vigorous new primocanes to develop; this species is far more drought-tolerant than Rubus allegheniensis or R. argutus and thrives where heavier soils would cause root rot.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in well-drained, sandy, or gravelly soil; sand cherry excels on poor, droughty sites where other stone fruits fail.
directions: Sand cherry is a small, sprawling native North American shrub bearing small dark purple to black cherries in midsummer with a flavor ranging from pleasantly tart to bitter depending on provenance and ripeness stage. The fruits are consumed fresh, dried, or processed into pemmican and preserves and were an important food source for Plains Indigenous peoples. The plant is extraordinarily cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, spreading by root suckers to form low thickets excellent for erosion control. Harvest when berries are fully dark and soft; cross-pollination between multiple plants improves fruit set significantly.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full shade to partial sun; dwarf smilax is a coastal plain specialist adapted to the dry, shady conditions beneath longleaf pine and live oak canopies where few other evergreen groundcovers thrive.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full shade to partial sun; dwarf smilax is a coastal plain specialist adapted to the dry, shady conditions beneath longleaf pine and live oak canopies where few other evergreen groundcovers thrive. Smilax pumila is a low, trailing, spiny evergreen vine native to the pinelands and oak hammocks of the southeastern coastal plain, producing attractive glossy foliage that remains green through winter and showy clusters of bright red berries in late winter and early spring when wildlife food is scarce — making it exceptionally valuable for birds and small mammals during the hungry gap. Use it as a weed-suppressing groundcover under open-canopied native trees, where it will spread gradually into dense mats that require virtually no maintenance once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted tip-cuttings in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; sawtooth blackberry spreads by root suckers and tip-rooting canes and can colonize disturbed areas aggressively. Best managed by keeping within defined areas — mowing around the perimeter in spring controls spread.
directions: Plant divisions or rooted tip-cuttings in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; sawtooth blackberry is one of the most common and widespread native blackberries of the eastern and southeastern US — a vigorous, thorny-caned shrub with large, deeply sawtooth-toothed compound leaves and masses of white flowers in spring followed by sweet-tart black drupelets in midsummer. One of several eastern blackberry species (along with Rubus allegheniensis and others) forming the backbone of wild blackberry patches in woodlands, old fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas from New England to Florida. The fruit is sweet-tart and excellent for fresh eating, jams, cobblers, and pies. In the natural garden, sawtooth blackberry forms important wildlife thickets — the thorny canes provide nesting sites and escape cover for songbirds, rabbits, and ground-nesting animals; the berries feed more than 100 species of birds and mammals. More tolerant of partial shade and moist soils than many other native blackberries.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, fertile soil; Scotia is not self-fertile and should be planted with another elderberry cultivar such as Adams or York nearby for cross-pollination and full fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; elderberries tolerate wet sites better than most fruiting shrubs and are well suited to low or seasonally damp spots in the garden. Scotia is a Nova Scotia-origin American elderberry selection valued for its very early ripening and large, showy fruit clusters of small, dark purple-black berries, borne on a vigorous, suckering shrub. Berries must be cooked before eating, as raw elderberries and other plant parts contain compounds that can cause stomach upset; ripe, cooked fruit is traditionally made into syrup, jelly, wine, and pie, and the broad, flat flower clusters can also be used fresh or dried for elderflower cordial and fritters. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew the shrub, since elderberries fruit best on relatively young wood, and cut the whole planting back hard every few years to keep it a manageable size.

plant_note: Plant one male plant for every 5–7 female plants in early spring; sea buckthorn is wind-pollinated and needs close proximity between sexes.
directions: Sea buckthorn is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing shrub that thrives in poor, dry, sandy soils where most fruits struggle. It is dioecious and requires male plants for pollination — one male per 5–7 females; sex is not identifiable until first flowering, so purchase sexed plants. The tiny berries are borne directly on the branches in dense clusters and are difficult to harvest without damaging the plant; a common approach is to cut fruiting branches in fall and strip berries indoors or by freezing and shaking. The tart, orange berries are extremely high in vitamin C.

plant_note: Set crowns in early spring; day-neutral so it fruits the first season.
directions: 'Seascape' is a day-neutral strawberry that produces large, firm, sweet berries continuously from late spring through fall regardless of day length. Set crowns at soil level so the growing point is neither buried nor exposed, spacing plants about a foot apart in raised beds or containers. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist with drip irrigation and straw mulch. Pinch off early flowers for the first few weeks after planting to build strong plants, then allow continuous fruiting.

common_name: Sequoia Strawberry (California Large-Fruited Heat-Tolerant Winter Strawberry)
plant_note: In zones 8–10 (California, Gulf Coast), plant dormant crowns or plugs in fall (September–November) for late winter to spring harvest; Sequoia is a California-developed University of California variety that has been grown in California since the 1950s and remains one of the most widely planted strawberries in mild-winter, warm-climate gardens for its ability to produce very large, flavorful berries under warm conditions where northeastern varieties perform poorly.
directions: In warm climates (zones 8–10), plant in fall for a spring harvest; in cooler climates plant in early spring; Sequoia produces very large, sweet berries with tender flesh that is best consumed fresh — it has less firmness than modern commercial varieties, making it ideal for home gardens where immediate consumption is the goal rather than shipping. Sequoia strawberry is a University of California variety (released 1953) that became one of the most widely planted strawberries in California commercial production in the mid-20th century and has remained popular in California and mild-winter gardens for its large, intensely flavored berries that represent the ideal of the fresh-eating home garden strawberry. The variety was developed by Dr. Harold Thomas at UC Riverside specifically for California's mild-winter, warm-spring growing conditions — conditions very different from the cool, humid eastern states where most strawberry varieties were bred. Sequoia produces berries that are exceptionally large (often double the diameter of standard varieties), vivid red, with a characteristic deep sweetness and complex strawberry fragrance that makes them among the most intensely flavored of any readily available variety. The flesh is somewhat soft — Sequoia berries bruise easily and have short shelf life (2–3 days maximum), which is why this variety essentially disappeared from commercial production as the industry shifted toward firmer-berried shipping varieties — but this same softness contributes to the intense, yielding, jam-like texture that makes Sequoia exceptional for fresh eating. For zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardens, Sequoia performs well as a fall-planted winter strawberry, producing its harvest in late February through April before summer heat arrives.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring while still dormant; fall planting works well in zones 5–8.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–7.0) in full to partial sun; serviceberry tolerates wet sites and woodland edges better than most fruiting shrubs. No cross-pollinator is required, though planting two or more selections increases yield. Fruits ripen in late spring to early June, turning from red to deep purple-blue when fully sweet — birds will compete for them, so netting is advisable. Prune crossing or crowded stems in late winter to maintain an open, multi-stemmed form and remove root suckers to control spread.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to wet, well-drained to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; shadblow serviceberry is a native multi-stemmed deciduous shrub or small tree of wetlands, streambanks, and moist woodland edges throughout the Northeast — named for the shad fish that run upstream when it flowers in earliest spring, producing spectacular clouds of white flowers followed by sweet, blueberry-like berries in early summer.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; shadblow tolerates wet, poorly drained sites better than most Amelanchier species — excellent for rain gardens, streambanks, and moist woodland edges. Amelanchier canadensis (shadblow serviceberry or downy serviceberry) is one of the most widespread native Amelanchier species of the eastern United States, growing naturally in bogs, streambanks, wet woods, and swampy thickets from Maine to Georgia and inland to the Great Lakes. The plant flowers in earliest spring — often the first woody plant to bloom, sometimes even before forsythia — with spectacular clusters of pure white, 5-petaled flowers on bare branches that open as the leaves begin to emerge. The flowers are followed in June by small (1/3-inch), round, purple-black to dark blue-purple berries with a mild, sweet, almond-apple flavor distinctly different from blueberries — produced abundantly enough that a mature shrub can yield several quarts of fruit. The berries are excellent fresh, in pies, jams, pancake syrup, and anywhere blueberries are used. The name 'shadblow' (also written shad-bush or shad-blow) derives from the colonial observation that the tree bloomed when alewife and shad fish began running up rivers from the sea — a reliable calendar indicator for early spring fishing. Notable for better tolerance of wet soils than smooth serviceberry (A. laevis).

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, very acidic soil in winter through early spring; Sharpblue requires only 150–200 chill hours, the lowest requirement of any major blueberry cultivar, making it one of the very few blueberries that perform in zone 9b–10. Plant with O'Neal, Gulf Coast, or Misty for cross-pollination.
