directions: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.5) amended with peat or composted pine bark; Sharpblue is a Southern highbush blueberry developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program and released in 1976 as one of the first cultivars specifically bred for extremely low-chill environments — it requires only 150–200 chill hours and thrives in zone 9–10 where rabbiteye varieties often fail to fruit consistently. This makes it particularly valuable for gardeners in coastal zone 9b, south Florida, and similar climates where winter chill accumulation is marginal. Berries are medium-sized, dark blue, very flavorful and aromatic — quality rivals highbush varieties grown in cooler climates. The plant is slightly tender and may be damaged by hard freezes below 15°F, though it recovers quickly. It is nearly evergreen in frost-free areas and can produce two crops per year in very warm locations. An excellent container blueberry for patios in the deep South.

common_name: Shawnee Blackberry (University of Arkansas Large Late-Season Thorned Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root canes or rooted tip cuttings in late winter or spring; Shawnee is an erect, thorned blackberry producing canes 5–7 feet tall that benefit from a T-trellis for support of the heavy fruit load. In zone 9, plant January–February; canes fruit in their second year (first-year canes are vegetative; second-year floricanes bear fruit in June–July then die back). Shawnee ripens in late June–July in zone 9 — 1–2 weeks after earlier erect varieties — extending the harvest window. The thorns on Shawnee are significant and protective gloves are needed for pruning and harvest.
directions: Plant bare-root canes 3–4 feet apart in rows 8–10 feet apart; tip-prune new canes at 3–4 feet in summer to encourage lateral branching. After fruiting, remove second-year (fruited) canes at ground level. Shawnee is a University of Arkansas erect blackberry released in 1985 — part of the legendary Arkansas blackberry breeding program led by Dr. James N. Moore that produced the majority of the blackberry varieties grown commercially and in home gardens across the eastern United States. The Arkansas program's systematic approach to blackberry improvement — selecting for large fruit size, good flavor, and erect cane habit suitable for mechanical harvesting — transformed blackberry production from a minor cottage-scale enterprise to a significant commercial crop. Shawnee produces very large, firm, glossy black berries (among the largest of the Arkansas releases in its era) with excellent flavor — described as rich and sweet with good balance, not overly tart. The late-season ripening of Shawnee means the fruits develop during the hottest part of the Gulf South summer (June–July in zone 9), and adequate irrigation during fruit development is important to maintain size and quality. The erect cane habit (no sprawling) makes Shawnee manageable in home gardens with a simple 2-wire T-trellis at 3 and 5 feet, providing a contained, productive planting in moderate space.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. Shiny Blueberry is a low-growing colony-forming blueberry that spreads by rhizome; plant multiple plants or named varieties of the same type for better cross-pollination and heavier fruiting.
directions: Shiny Blueberry is the low-growing native blueberry of the Florida peninsula and southeastern coastal plain, native to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained flatwoods, scrub, and longleaf pine savannas from South Carolina to Florida and west to Mississippi, forming dense, rhizome-spreading colonies under open, sunny conditions. The small, glossy, dark green leaves are evergreen in zones 8–9, giving the plant its common name, and the small, sweet, dark blue berries ripen in spring — earlier than most other blueberries — providing fruit for birds and gardeners alike. Unlike the taller highbush blueberries, Shiny Blueberry is a groundcover-scale plant that works well as an edible lawn substitute in acidic, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; it requires the same highly acidic soil conditions as all blueberries and benefits from cross-pollination with additional plants for heavy fruiting. Excellent for edible native landscape designs in the lower South.

plant_note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; silky dogwood grows naturally in streamside thickets, wet meadows, and pond margins and is one of the best native shrubs for stabilizing stream banks and rain gardens.
directions: Plant container or balled stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; silky dogwood grows naturally in streamside thickets, wet meadows, and pond margins and is one of the best native shrubs for stabilizing stream banks and rain gardens. Cornus amomum is a loosely branched, multi-stemmed native shrub with soft, somewhat silky-haired leaves, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in June that are outstanding for native bees and small butterflies, and blue-black berry-like drupes in fall that are among the most heavily consumed native fruits by migrating songbirds — particularly wood thrushes, robins, and waxwings; the red-purple winter stems provide dormant season interest. Plant in groupings for best berry production and wildlife impact.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late fall or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; plant one male per three to four female plants for fruit production. Buffaloberry fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility.
directions: Root hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; silver buffaloberry is a spiny, thicket-forming native shrub of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain West with distinctive silvery-gray foliage and clusters of brilliant orange-red to red berries that ripen in summer and fall. The plant is dioecious — male and female flowers appear on separate plants — so both sexes must be planted for fruit production. Berries are tart but edible, historically used by Plains nations to make pemmican and sauce for buffalo meat (hence the name). Plants fix nitrogen through root nodules, tolerate extreme cold, drought, alkaline soils, and salt — among the most rugged food-producing shrubs for difficult Great Plains conditions. Excellent wildlife hedge.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall in well-drained, sandy, strongly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; small black blueberry is native to the sandy pine flatwoods and longleaf pine savannas of the Gulf Coastal Plain and requires the infertile, acidic, well-drained conditions of that habitat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, strongly acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), lean soil in partial shade to full sun; small black blueberry is a dwarf, spreading native vaccinium of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine flatwoods, closely associated with longleaf pine habitat. The small, very dark blue-black berries ripen in early summer and, while tiny, are intensely flavored and sweet — eaten fresh or used in preserves and baked goods in the traditional Southern way. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form low colonies and provides important food for dozens of bird species. In the native range, it grows in the precise habitat type (sandy, dry, very acidic) that is among the most threatened ecosystems in North America. An excellent species for naturalized longleaf pine ecosystem restoration in the Gulf Coastal Plain.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; viburnum nudum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites and thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, and low areas where standing water occasionally occurs.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; viburnum nudum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites and thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, and low areas where standing water occasionally occurs. Viburnum nudum produces one of the most spectacular fall berry displays of any native shrub: the abundant berry clusters transition through pink, rose, blue, and finally blue-black as individual berries ripen at different times in September and October, creating a multi-colored cluster that is breathtaking and irresistible to migrating songbirds; the berries are consumed within days of full ripeness by cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and dozens of other species. The glossy, semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage turns rich burgundy-red in fall; white, fragrant flower clusters in May attract native bees.

plant_note: Plant tip-rooted cuttings in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun; southern dewberry is a trailing species that tips-root naturally wherever the cane touches soil. It grows in dry, sandy, disturbed areas, road banks, and open pine flatwoods of the Southeast.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; southern dewberry is a trailing or low-arching native bramble of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, producing large, juicy, black berries in late spring that are among the most flavorful of any native Rubus. The berries are excellent for eating fresh, preserving, and making wine and cobblers. The trailing canes root where they touch the soil, naturally colonizing disturbed, sandy, open habitats. Unlike upright blackberries, the low, trailing canes of dewberry are less showy but provide excellent wildlife value — the berries are consumed by birds, small mammals, and box turtles. In zone 9a, dewberry is one of the first fruits to ripen in spring (typically April–May), well before blackberries and blueberries.

plant_note: Plant in early spring in very acidic, well-drained soil; low-chill cultivars such as 'Sunshine Blue' or 'O'Neal' are essential in mild-winter climates.
directions: Southern highbush blueberries are interspecific hybrids bred for low chill-hour requirements (150–500 hours below 45°F), making them the only highbush-type blueberry suitable for Gulf Coast, Florida, and mild-winter California climates. Maintain soil pH at 4.5–5.5 with pine bark mulch and acidifying fertilizers; do not use lime. Plant two or more cultivars for cross-pollination and improved fruit size. Prune lightly for the first three years, then begin removing the oldest, least productive canes each late winter to stimulate vigorous new wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Southern Home is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine; train onto an arbor or pergola where its ornamental, deeply lobed foliage can be shown off along with its fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy arbor or pergola, where the vine doubles as an ornamental landscape feature. Southern Home is a distinctive interspecific hybrid between muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) and traditional bunch grape (Vitis vinifera), bred at the University of Georgia specifically for its uniquely ornamental, deeply lobed, almost oak-leaf-shaped foliage that sets it visually apart from the simple rounded leaves of standard muscadine varieties, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for a decorative fruiting arbor. The self-fertile vine produces medium-sized, black, muscadine-flavored fruit in loose bunches more reminiscent of a traditional grape cluster than the typical loose, few-berried muscadine set, and it carries good resistance to Pierce's disease inherited from its muscadine parentage — a critical advantage over standard bunch grapes in the humid Gulf South and Southeast, where Pierce's disease kills most vinifera and many hybrid grapes outright. An excellent choice for gardeners who want both fruit and ornamental landscape value from the same vine, zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Southland is self-fertile and ripens mid-season in the Gulf South, a reliable middle-of-the-pack variety to fill out the harvest window between early and late black muscadines.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and train onto a wire trellis or arbor. Southland is a University of Georgia release valued for its large, dark reddish-black berries with a thin skin and sweet, rich muscadine flavor good for fresh eating as well as juice and wine. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and consistently productive, with solid disease resistance across the humid Gulf South. Mid-season ripening makes Southland a dependable companion to earlier black varieties like Cowart and later ones like Ison, spreading harvest over a longer window. Prune annually in late winter while dormant to renewal spurs to keep the vine productive and manageable on the trellis.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained, organically rich soil; Southland has an unusually low chill requirement for a red raspberry, allowing it to break dormancy and fruit reliably in mild southern winters where most red raspberries fail to set a crop.
directions: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil in full sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest parts of zone 9, and mulch well to keep roots cool. Southland is one of the few red raspberry cultivars bred specifically for adaptation to mild southern winters, with a low chilling-hour requirement that lets it flower and fruit where standard northern raspberries decline within a season or two from insufficient winter chill. It produces a light-to-moderate crop of medium-sized, sweet-tart red berries in late spring, with some plants also producing a smaller fall crop on primocanes. Yields are modest compared with northern raspberry cultivars grown in their ideal climate, but Southland remains one of the more dependable options for gardeners in zone 8-9 who want to try growing red raspberries. Prune out spent floricanes after harvest and thin new canes to maintain airflow and reduce disease in humid conditions.

common_name: Springhigh Southern Highbush Blueberry (Ultra-Early Low-Chill Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring in acidic, well-drained soil; Springhigh has a very low chill requirement of around 150-200 hours and is among the earliest-ripening southern highbush blueberries, well suited to zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun, and pair with another early-blooming southern highbush variety for best pollination and fruit set. Developed by the University of Florida's blueberry breeding program, Springhigh was selected for an unusually low chilling requirement that lets it flower and fruit reliably in the mild winters of the Deep South, where many northern blueberry types fail to break dormancy evenly. It ripens very early in the season, often the first blueberry to color up in the garden, giving growers a jump on the market and on fresh eating alike. Keep soil consistently moist during bloom and fruit development, since southern highbush types have shallow root systems that dry out quickly in sandy Gulf Coast soils.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded location. Seeds exhibit double dormancy and require a warm period followed by cold stratification; propagation by cuttings is more reliable.
directions: Plant in partial shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Squashberry is native to the understory of boreal and subarctic forests and performs best where it receives filtered light or morning sun with afternoon shade. Maintain even soil moisture, especially during summer, by applying a generous layer of organic mulch around the root zone. Clusters of translucent orange-red berries ripen in late summer and were historically harvested by indigenous peoples of the north for fresh eating, jam, and pemmican. Propagate by softwood cuttings taken in early summer, treated with rooting hormone and kept in a humid environment; division of established clumps in early spring is also effective.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for best establishment before summer heat. Star is one of the lowest-chill southern highbush blueberries (approximately 200 hours), making it highly reliable across zone 8–9 and into zone 10a. Self-fertile but production improves with a nearby SHB cross-pollinator such as Sharpblue, O'Neal, or Misty.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat in full sun; Star is a University of Florida/IFAS-released southern highbush blueberry selected specifically for very low chilling requirements (approximately 200 hours below 45°F), making it one of the best choices for zone 8–9 gardens where chilling is variable from year to year. The large, firm, excellent-flavored berries ripen in May–June in most Gulf Coast plantings, earlier than rabbiteye varieties and with superior berry size and flavor. Unlike rabbiteye blueberries, Star is self-fertile and will produce a reasonable crop without a cross-pollinator, though yields are maximized with one nearby. The more compact, upright habit (4–6 feet tall versus 8–10 feet for mature rabbiteye) makes Star better suited to smaller gardens and container plantings. Maintain consistent moisture through the production season, as SHB types are more sensitive to drought than rabbiteye.

plant_note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, keeping the crown level with the soil surface.
directions: Plant bare-root crowns in spring with the crown at soil level, setting runners into a matted-row system 12–18 in apart. Pinch all blossoms the first year to build root vigor; harvest begins the following June when berries are uniformly red and pull easily from the stem. Renovate beds immediately after harvest by mowing foliage to 3–4 in and thinning plants to 4–6 per square foot. Mulch crowns with straw in fall in zones 4 and colder.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, well-drained to poorly drained, fertile soil in zone 5–9; Sugarberry (Southern Hackberry) is a large, fast-growing native bottomland tree of the southeastern United States — widespread from Virginia to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas — producing abundant small, reddish-orange to black berries eaten by at least 25 bird species and a wide range of mammals, and one of the most valuable native wildlife trees of the South.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Celtis laevigata is an exceptionally adaptable native tree tolerating periodic flooding, clay soils, silt, calcareous substrates, and seasonal drought once established — one of the few large trees naturally adapted to Gulf Coast bottomland conditions. Celtis laevigata (Sugarberry or Southern Hackberry) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous native tree of the southeastern United States, ranging from the coastal plain of Virginia and Maryland south through Florida and west to Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas — a dominant tree of river bottomlands, floodplains, moist woodland slopes, and disturbed sites across the South. The common name 'Sugarberry' references the small, round, thin-skinned, reddish-orange to dark-purple to black fruits (technically drupes) that ripen in late summer and fall — sweet, date-raisin-like in flavor, tiny but edible and historically eaten by indigenous peoples across its range. The wildlife value is extraordinary: the berries are consumed by at least 25–30 bird species including mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, wood thrushes, bluebirds, and yellow-rumped warblers, and by raccoons, opossums, foxes, and white-tailed deer. As a native habitat tree, Sugarberry also supports the larvae of several butterfly species including the Hackberry Emperor (Asterocampa celtis) and Tawny Emperor (A. clyton), whose caterpillars feed exclusively on Celtis foliage. An outstanding choice for native wildlife plantings, riparian buffers, and restoration plantings in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Sugargate is self-fertile (perfect-flowered) and does not require a separate pollinator vine, though it is a lighter producer than some varieties and benefits from attentive pruning and fertility to maximize yield.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune to a well-spaced fruiting framework each winter. Sugargate is a University of Georgia-released black muscadine grown almost entirely for exceptional fresh-eating quality — its large, tender-skinned fruit carries the highest sugar content and richest, sweetest flavor of any widely planted muscadine cultivar, making it a favorite among home growers and muscadine enthusiasts who prioritize taste over yield. The vine is somewhat less vigorous and productive than heavier-bearing varieties like Nesbitt or Supreme, so it is often planted as a specialty dessert selection alongside a more prolific cultivar rather than as the sole vine in a planting. Give it full sun, good drainage, and attentive care to get the best from its outstanding flavor, zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Summer raspberries fruit on floricanes — canes produced in year one that overwinter and bear fruit the following summer. After harvest, cut all fruited floricanes to the ground and thin new primocanes to 4–6 per linear foot for best airflow. Support canes on a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft. Harvest when berries pull cleanly from the plug with no resistance, typically over 3–4 weeks in early summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Summit requires approximately 400–500 chill hours — suitable for zone 9a but marginal for warmer zone 9b areas. Cross-pollinate with another mid-range chill southern highbush variety. In zone 9 it ripens in late May–June.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Summit is a southern highbush blueberry released by the University of Georgia for its outstanding combination of large, flavorful berries and good disease resistance to the humid-summer conditions of the Southeast. The large, firm, dark blue berries have excellent flavor — sweet and complex with good sugar-to-acid balance — and a dry scar that reduces the tendency to leak after picking, improving storage quality. Summit is specifically bred for disease resistance to mummy berry (Monilinia vaccinia-corymbosi) and to stem blight, which are the primary fungal diseases limiting blueberry production in the humid Gulf South. This disease package makes Summit particularly valuable in zone 9 conditions where wet summers favor fungal diseases. The mid-season ripening (late May–June) slots Summit between the earliest varieties and the latest-season types, contributing to an extended home harvest season when planted with Biloxi, Flordablue, and Windsor.

plant_note: Plant in spring; well suited to containers and mild-winter areas.
directions: 'Sunshine Blue' is a compact, semi-dwarf southern highbush blueberry that is self-fertile and needs only about 150 chill hours, making it ideal for warm regions and pots. It tolerates a slightly higher soil pH than most blueberries but still performs best in acidic, well-drained media. Grow in full sun, water consistently, and feed with an acid-formulated fertilizer during the growing season. Its tidy habit and showy pink-to-white flowers make it a productive ornamental for patios and small gardens.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Supreme is a female-flowered (pistillate) variety requiring a perfect-flowered pollinator vine within 50 feet. Plant with Ison, Triumph, or another self-fertile variety. In zone 9 Supreme ripens September–October, among the latest-ripening muscadines, extending the fresh muscadine season well into fall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with a perfect-flowered pollinator vine; Supreme is a USDA-released dark (black-skinned) muscadine producing the largest black-skinned fruits of any commercially available muscadine variety — round to slightly oval berries reaching 1.5–2 inches in diameter with deep blue-black to jet-black skin and rich, deeply flavored, sweet-tart purple flesh. The combination of very large fruit size, deep color, and late ripening (September–October in zone 9) makes Supreme particularly valuable for extending the fresh muscadine season after most other varieties have finished. The deep color indicates high anthocyanin content and the associated antioxidant capacity that has made muscadine grapes a focus of nutritional research. Supreme is primarily a fresh-eating variety; the very large individual berry size and attractive appearance make it outstanding for fresh market and U-pick use. As a pistillate variety, it requires a self-fertile pollinator nearby for any fruit production.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp fly honeysuckle grows naturally in boggy, moist, shrubby areas and at the margins of fens, bogs, and wet meadows across the northern US and Canada.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp fly honeysuckle is a native shrub honeysuckle of northern boggy habitats — a deciduous shrub with paired, yellowish-white flowers in late spring and attractive paired red berries in summer. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle vine (Lonicera japonica), this is a well-behaved native shrub that does not spread aggressively. The berries, while not favored as human food, are consumed by numerous bird species in summer and early fall. The shrub provides nesting structure for a variety of native birds in boggy habitats. An excellent native choice for consistently moist to wet, acidic, partially shaded sites in the cold-hardy northern zones 2–6.

plant_note: In zone 9, plant dormant crowns in October–November for harvest December–March; Sweet Charlie is an early-season variety that begins fruiting before Chandler, producing its first ripe berries in December in zone 9a–9b. Ideal for home gardens and farmers' markets where the earliest strawberries command premium prices.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with crown at soil level in well-drained, amended beds in full sun; Sweet Charlie is a short-day strawberry cultivar released by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences in 1992, bred specifically for warm climates and the production systems of the Gulf South and Florida. It consistently ranks as one of the earliest and sweetest commercial strawberries in Florida and the Gulf South — often the first variety to ripen by 2–3 weeks over Chandler, with exceptional flavor characterized by very high sugar content and intensely sweet berry aroma. The medium-sized fruits are softer than Chandler (limiting shelf life for commercial distribution) but deliver superior fresh-eating flavor — the classic choice for local farmers' markets and u-pick operations where fruit is eaten the same day. Sweet Charlie is popular with home gardeners who prefer flavor over shipping durability. It shows good tolerance of Florida's warm winters and performs well in zone 9 planted on the October–November schedule. Manage irrigation carefully — overwatering increases disease; underwatering reduces berry size.

common_name: Sweet Jenny Muscadine Grape (Very Large Black Self-Fertile Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Sweet Jenny is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine released by the University of Georgia breeding program and does not require a separate pollinator vine.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Sweet Jenny is a University of Georgia muscadine release notable for producing some of the largest fruit of any black muscadine cultivar, with sweet, mild-flavored flesh and a skin tender enough for easy fresh eating rather than just juice or wine. The self-fertile vine is vigorous, productive, and ripens over an extended mid-to-late season window, making it a favorite for home gardeners who want big, showy fruit without needing a second pollinator vine. Water consistently during fruit sizing for the largest berries, and thin crowded shoots in summer to improve air circulation and reduce fruit rot in humid Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or October–November. Sweet Scarlet goumi is self-fertile but produces more heavily with another goumi nearby for cross-pollination. In zone 9 it bears fruit earlier (May–June) than in northern climates. The nitrogen-fixing root nodules improve soil fertility over time — a useful attribute in poor soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — poor and lean soils are acceptable as the nitrogen-fixing roots improve fertility over time; Sweet Scarlet Goumi is a named cultivar of the Japanese goumi bush (Elaeagnus multiflora), a nitrogen-fixing shrub producing clusters of small, oval, bright scarlet-red berries with silvery speckles — the appearance is immediately distinctive and unlike any common North American fruit. The ripe berries have a tart-sweet, astringent flavor similar to a cranberry crossed with a sour cherry, with resinous notes and a unique aromatic quality. The astringency decreases and sweetness increases as the berries ripen fully in late May–June. Goumi berries are high in lycopene (the red carotenoid), vitamins A and C, and contain higher protein than most berries. They are eaten fresh when fully ripe, made into jams, juices, and wine, or dried. Sweet Scarlet is specifically selected for sweeter fruit than many other goumi selections. As an Elaeagnus species, the shrub fixes nitrogen and is an excellent companion plant near fruit trees in a food forest design.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root vines in early spring; install a sturdy trellis or arbor before planting.
directions: Table grapes require a robust trellis capable of supporting 15–30 lbs of fruit per vine; the two-wire Kniffin system or a pergola are common choices. Train a permanent trunk and 2–4 fruiting arms during the first 3 years; thereafter, annual dormant pruning should remove 90% of the previous year's growth, leaving spurs or canes with 2–4 buds each. Thin clusters after fruit set to improve berry size and airflow. Harvest when berries reach full color, the tendrils nearest the cluster have dried, and sugar is confirmed by taste.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Tara is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) bronze muscadine and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; ripens early-to-mid season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Tara is a University of Georgia-released bronze muscadine grown for its consistently high fruit quality — large, uniform, golden-bronze berries with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a relatively tender skin — combined with a self-fertile, productive vine that bears reliably without a separate pollinator variety. It ripens earlier in the season than many bronze muscadines, extending the harvest window when planted alongside later-ripening varieties, and the fruit holds well on the vine without excessive cracking or splitting in humid weather. Widely recommended for both fresh eating and home winemaking, Tara is a strong choice for a Gulf South home muscadine planting, zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant rooted tip cuttings or bare-root canes in early spring and install a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft at the same time.
directions: Tayberry is a Scottish-bred hybrid (blackberry x raspberry) with long, conical, deep purple-red berries that ripen in mid-summer; the flavor is richer and sweeter than loganberry. Train the long trailing canes fan-style along wires, keeping current-year primocanes separate from fruiting floricanes to simplify post-harvest cleanup. After harvest, remove all fruited canes to the ground and tie in the new primocanes. In zone 5–6, protect canes over winter by detaching them from wires and covering with straw mulch or a frost-cloth tunnel.

common_name: Texas Elderberry (Mexican Elder, Blue Elderberry, Tapiro)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas Elderberry establishes readily and grows quickly in warm, humid conditions. Cuttings root easily in water or moist soil in warm weather — the simplest propagation method. Plant at least 2 plants of different seed origins for better cross-pollination and heavier fruit set. Hardwood cuttings taken in winter also root reliably. Unlike Common Elderberry (S. canadensis), Texas Elderberry is adapted to the heat and alkaline soils of Central and South Texas.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil; Texas Elderberry adapts to a wide range of soil types from sandy loam to limestone caliche, and is more drought-tolerant than the Eastern Common Elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) once established. Sambucus mexicana (also listed as S. nigra subsp. canadensis var. mexicana and S. caerulea in western references) is the native elderberry of Texas, the Desert Southwest, Mexico, and Central America, ranging from the western Edwards Plateau of Texas through the Rio Grande Valley. It overlaps geographically with S. canadensis to the east but is adapted to the more alkaline, hotter, drier conditions of central and south Texas and the Mexican highlands. The plant produces large, flat-topped clusters of small, creamy-white flowers (excellent nectar source for native bees and butterflies) followed by clusters of small, blue-black to dark purple berries similar to common elderberry. The berries ripen in late summer–fall and are used to make elderberry wine, juice, jelly, and the traditional folk medicine elderberry syrup for immune support. CAUTION: Raw berries, bark, leaves, and roots contain cyanogenic glycosides — cook berries thoroughly before consumption; do not eat raw.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Thiessen is one of the earliest-ripening named saskatoon cultivars and is self-fertile, though cross-pollination improves fruit set. The large, upright shrub-to-small-tree form requires more space than compact types like Regent; allow 8–12 feet between plants for good air circulation and full sunlight to minimize powdery mildew.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Thiessen is a named saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia) cultivar selected in Alberta, Canada, widely regarded as one of the best-flavored named saskatoon varieties with very large berries (among the largest of any named cultivar) and a sweet, rich, complex flavor with prominent almond notes from the edible seeds. The very large, round, dark purple-blue berries ripen in early to mid-June — among the earliest of the named cultivars, making Thiessen valuable for extending the fresh fruit season into late spring when few other fruits are available. The upright, vigorous shrub can reach 12–14 feet in height at maturity, forming a small multi-stemmed tree form. Thiessen is popular in commercial saskatoon orchards in the Canadian Prairie provinces, where the saskatoon berry industry produces fruit for fresh market, U-pick, frozen, dried, and processed products. The species is among the most cold-hardy edible fruits in cultivation, surviving temperatures below -40°F.

plant_note: Plant root divisions or container-grown plants in early spring in partial shade with moist, well-drained soil.
directions: Thimbleberry is a large-leafed, thornless native Rubus that thrives along woodland edges and mountain slopes from Alaska to Mexico, tolerating more shade than almost any other fruiting cane. The soft, bright red berries resemble a wide, shallow thimble and have a delicate, sweet flavor but are extremely fragile — they must be eaten or processed within hours of harvest. Propagate by dividing root clumps in spring; seed germination is erratic and requires cold stratification. Allow the plant to naturalize in a semi-wild planting rather than managing it as a formal fruiting cane.

plant_note: Set out dormant plants in early spring once soil can be worked.
directions: Prime-Ark Freedom is a thornless, primocane-fruiting blackberry that bears large, sweet berries on first-year canes, giving a summer crop that can extend into fall. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and provide a trellis or support for the vigorous canes. Because it fruits on new wood, you can mow floricanes to the ground in late winter for a single heavy late-season crop, or leave them for two harvests. Keep soil evenly moist during fruit development and mulch to suppress weeds. Feed in early spring with a balanced fertilizer.

plant_note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic, well-drained soil; Tifblue requires 400–600 chill hours and a cross-pollinating companion (Climax, Premier, Brightwell) for reliable production. It is not self-fruitful. Late-season (July–August in zone 8–9) ripening extends the blueberry harvest past all other rabbiteye varieties.
directions: Amend soil to pH 4.5–5.0 with peat or sulfur before planting; Tifblue is a rabbiteye blueberry developed by the Georgia Experiment Station (Tifton, Georgia) and released in 1955, becoming the most widely planted rabbiteye blueberry variety in the world for most of the 20th century. Though newer varieties (Climax, Premier, Brightwell) have larger or earlier-ripening fruit, Tifblue maintains a loyal following as the definitive late-season rabbiteye: its berries ripen in late July through August in zone 8–9, extending the blueberry season 4–6 weeks past early varieties. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, mildly sweet, with a firm texture that makes them excellent for shipping, freezing, and baking where texture is important. Tifblue is also one of the most important pollinators for other rabbiteye varieties, its abundant, late-season pollen highly compatible with Fry and other non-self-fertile varieties. Plants are vigorous, productive, and cold-hardy for a rabbiteye (surviving 10–15°F without significant damage in established plants). As a historical benchmark variety and reliable late-season producer, Tifblue remains valuable in zone 7–9 blueberry plantings.

plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8–9 plant December–February. Tifblue is a mid-to-late season variety that requires cross-pollination with an early-season variety (Premier, Climax) for maximum fruit set. Its larger chilling requirement (500–600 hours) compared to other rabbiteyes makes it slightly less suited to zone 9a's mild winters than Premier or Brightwell.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun; Tifblue was the rabbiteye blueberry standard for decades — a large, vigorous, upright shrub with good berries and excellent adaptability. Released by the USDA-ARS Tifton, Georgia station, it produces medium to large, light blue, firm, mild-flavored berries in late June to July, extending the harvest season after early and mid-season varieties have finished. The berries have excellent shelf life due to their firm texture. However, Tifblue's higher chilling requirement (500–600 hours) makes it a less reliable choice in the warmer parts of zone 8–9 where chilling hours may not accumulate sufficiently in mild winters. Best suited to zone 6–8 where more consistent chilling ensures reliable bloom and full fruit set.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or October–November. Tillamook is self-fertile but cross-pollination with Sweet Scarlet or another goumi variety improves fruit set. In zone 9 it bears in May–June. The shrub is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean soils due to nitrogen fixation by root nodules.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-moderately-fertile soil — avoid over-fertilizing as excess nitrogen suppresses fruit production in this nitrogen-fixing shrub; Tillamook is a Raintree Nursery-selected goumi cultivar known for producing larger, sweeter fruit than most other goumi selections, with a berry size approaching that of a small cherry and a flavor noticeably sweeter and more pleasant for fresh eating than the more astringent wild-type goumi. The large, bright scarlet to deep red berries ripen with the distinctive silvery speckle pattern characteristic of Elaeagnus species, and the mature ripe fruit has a sweet-tart flavor with less of the mouth-puckering tannin that makes less-ripe goumi berries challenging to eat raw. Tillamook was selected from plants grown at Raintree Nursery in Morton, Washington — a Pacific Northwest selection that nonetheless performs well in zone 9 given its cold hardiness and drought tolerance. Like all goumi, it fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility for neighboring plants in a permaculture or food forest context.

plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring; in zone 8-9 plant December-February for best establishment. Titan is a University of Georgia rabbiteye release known for producing the largest berries of any commercial rabbiteye cultivar, on vigorous, upright, productive bushes. Plant with Brightwell, Premier, or Climax for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained sandy or loamy soil with pine bark amendment in full sun. Titan is a University of Georgia-released rabbiteye blueberry celebrated for producing exceptionally large berries, among the biggest of any rabbiteye cultivar available, with good firmness and a pleasant, mild sweet-tart flavor that makes for an impressive fresh-eating harvest. The vigorous, upright bushes are productive and ripen mid-to-late in the rabbiteye season, extending the harvest window when paired with earlier cultivars like Alapaha or Premier. Like all rabbiteye blueberries, Titan requires cross-pollination from a different rabbiteye cultivar to set a full crop, so plant at least two different varieties within 50-100 feet of each other. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, moisture-retentive soil rabbiteye blueberries need, and avoid soils with a pH above 5.5, which causes chlorosis and poor growth. Prune out old, unproductive canes each winter to encourage vigorous new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant bushes autumn to early spring.
directions: 'Titania' is a vigorous, disease-resistant black currant valued for strong resistance to white pine blister rust and mildew. It produces long strigs of large, glossy berries over an extended ripening window, making harvest easier. Grow in full sun to light shade in fertile, moisture-retentive soil enriched with compost. Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer in spring and prune out the oldest quarter of the wood each dormant season to keep the bush productive.

common_name: Top Hat Blueberry (Dwarf Container Blueberry, Patio Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) well-drained soil or in large containers (15+ gallons) filled with peat-based acidic mix; Top Hat is a true dwarf blueberry (18–24 inches tall) that grows well in containers on patios, decks, and balconies — the only named blueberry variety that is genuinely practical for container culture in small spaces without requiring large raised beds; plant two for cross-pollination since Top Hat is not reliably self-fruitful.
directions: Plant in highly acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5–5.5) or containers filled with peat-based mix; fertilize with acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or azalea fertilizer) in early spring; Top Hat requires two plants for best pollination and fruit set; berries ripen mid-season (July in zones 5–6) — medium-sized, sweet, and flavorful; does not need pruning for first 4–5 years. Top Hat is the most widely grown dwarf container blueberry and the standard recommendation from extension services for gardeners wanting to grow blueberries in containers, small raised beds, or on patios where the 4–6 foot size of standard highbush varieties is impractical. The variety is a University of Michigan-developed dwarf highbush × lowbush half-high cross that was specifically selected for its unusually compact habit — plants grow only 18–24 inches tall and wide, far smaller than either highbush (4–6 feet) or lowbush (6–12 inches, spreads widely). This intermediate compact size makes Top Hat ideal for large container culture in a way that no other named blueberry variety achieves: large enough to be productive, small enough to manage easily in a 15–20 gallon container, and cold-hardy enough to survive winters outdoors in zones 4–7 on a patio or protected corner. The berries are medium-sized, deep blue, and well-flavored for a half-high type — sweeter and more aromatic than wild lowbush berries and with good quality comparable to standard highbush varieties. The plants are also attractive ornamentally: brilliant red fall foliage makes Top Hat an attractive container plant throughout the growing season. One of the most important blueberry introductions specifically designed for urban and suburban small-space gardening.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant September–November for best establishment during the cool rainy season. Toyon is drought-tolerant once established and should be watered minimally after the first year — summer irrigation encourages root disease. It is adapted to California's Mediterranean climate with dry summers and winter rainfall; the Gulf Coast's year-round rainfall requires excellent drainage and minimal watering once established.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in extremely well-drained, lean soil — avoid summer irrigation once established; Toyon (California Holly, Christmas Berry) is a large, handsome, evergreen shrub native to California chaparral and oak woodland, producing spectacular clusters of brilliant red to orange-red berries in November–January — the traditional holiday decoration plant of coastal California and the plant thought to have inspired the name 'Hollywood.' The berries have a slightly bitter, astringent flavor when raw but become edible and pleasant when fully ripe and soft after frost or light cooking; indigenous Californians ate them roasted, fermented into cider, or dried. The white flower clusters in summer attract bees, and the winter berries support mockingbirds, waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds through the season when few other fruiting plants are active. Toyon is one of the most ornamentally rewarding California natives for gardens in the dry western zones and Mediterranean climates; its tolerance of the Gulf Coast requires excellent drainage and restrained irrigation.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns or plugs in early spring; Tribute is a day-neutral (everbearing) cultivar that flowers and fruits continuously through the growing season regardless of day length, rather than producing one concentrated June crop.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; remove the first flush of flowers after planting to strengthen the plant before letting it fruit. Tribute is a USDA-released day-neutral strawberry cultivar, valued for producing a steady, moderate harvest of medium-large, firm, well-flavored berries from late spring through fall rather than a single concentrated June crop, extending the home strawberry season significantly compared with traditional June-bearing types. It shows good resistance to several common strawberry diseases, including red stele and verticillium wilt, making it a dependable choice in a range of soil conditions. Because day-neutral types put continuous energy into fruiting rather than runner production, they produce fewer runners than June-bearers, and removing flowers for the first several weeks after planting helps establish a stronger root system for sustained production through the season.

plant_note: Plant after last hard frost in spring; provide a strong trellis.
directions: 'Triple Crown' is a thornless semi-erect blackberry famed for high yields of large, sweet, glossy-black fruit in mid to late summer. Train the vigorous canes onto a sturdy T-trellis and tip the primocanes at about four feet to promote fruiting laterals. Grow in full sun in deep, well-drained soil with consistent summer moisture during ripening. Remove spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to make room for next year's fruiting wood.

plant_note: Plant dormant crowns or plugs in early spring; Tristar is a day-neutral (everbearing) cultivar that flowers and fruits continuously through the growing season, well suited to containers and small raised beds because of its compact habit.
directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; remove the first flush of flowers after planting to strengthen the plant before letting it fruit. Tristar is a USDA-released day-neutral strawberry cultivar bred alongside Tribute, valued for its compact, tidy plant habit and continuous production of small-to-medium, sweet, glossy red berries from late spring through fall, making it a favorite for hanging baskets, containers, and small raised beds where a sprawling June-bearer would be impractical. It shows good disease resistance for a day-neutral type, including tolerance to red stele root rot, and its everbearing habit means a small planting can supply a steady trickle of fresh berries all season rather than one large harvest. Pinch off runners as they form to keep the plant's energy focused on fruit production rather than spreading.

plant_note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Triumph is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine that sets good crops without a pollinator but benefits from cross-pollination. In zone 9 it ripens in late August–September. Train on a sturdy trellis; the vigorous vines require heavy winter pruning to produce the next season's crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Triumph is a bronze-skinned (white) muscadine grape selected by the University of Georgia for large, sweet, bronze-gold fruits with an exceptionally sweet flavor and low acidity — one of the sweetest muscadine varieties available and a benchmark for fresh-eating quality among bronze muscadines. The large, round fruits (1–1.25 inches) ripen to a deep bronze-gold color and have a thin, tender skin with less of the tough slip-skin character that makes some muscadine varieties less appealing for fresh eating. The sweet, mild, slightly floral flavor with classic muscadine aromatic notes makes Triumph outstanding for fresh eating, and the golden color produces beautiful pale-gold juice and jelly. Triumph is a self-fertile (perfect-flowered) variety that sets crops reliably without a pollinator. In zone 9 the vine is vigorous and productive; provide generous spacing (20+ feet) for the mature vine's spread.

plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in early spring on a trellis; tummelberry is more cold-hardy than tayberry and better suited to short-season northern gardens.
directions: The tummelberry is a Scottish-bred Rubus hybrid developed at the Scottish Crop Research Institute from a tayberry cross, selected specifically for greater cold hardiness and easier mechanical harvest than its parent. It produces large, dark red to maroon conical berries slightly smaller than tayberries in midsummer with a rich, aromatic flavor well suited to preserves, juices, and desserts. Train the long, semi-trailing canes on a two-wire trellis at 3 and 5 ft, fruiting on second-year floricanes; cut all fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes for the following year. It is substantially hardier than tayberry and performs reliably in zones 4–5 with minimal winter protection.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a two-wire trellis. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, typically ripening early in the blackberry season.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Tupy is a vigorous, thorny, erect blackberry developed by the Brazilian agricultural research agency EMBRAPA from Arkansas breeding lines, and it has become one of the most widely planted commercial blackberries in warm-climate regions of Latin America because of its exceptional heat tolerance and productivity under conditions too warm for many U.S.-bred varieties. Berries are large, glossy black, firm, and tart-sweet, ripening early in the season with a long harvest window and heavy yields. Because canes are thorny, plan for careful pruning and picking; remove fruited floricanes after harvest and tie in 4-6 vigorous new primocanes per plant for the following year. Tupy tolerates the intense heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast better than many thornless northern-bred varieties, making it a strong choice for zone 9-10 growers.

plant_note: Plant dormant, container-grown bushes in late winter to early spring in highly acidic soil; Vernon ripens mid-season and needs another rabbiteye cultivar such as Climax or Tifblue nearby for cross-pollination and full fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark and mulched heavily to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool. Vernon is a mid-season rabbiteye blueberry bred for the Gulf South, producing an upright, vigorous, productive bush with firm, well-flavored, medium-to-large berries that hold well on the bush without excessive splitting in humid weather. It fills the harvest gap between early cultivars like Climax and later ones like Tifblue or Ochlockonee, giving home orchards a steadier, more extended supply of fresh fruit. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and again lightly after harvest, avoid high-nitrogen feeding late in the season, and prune out old canes each winter to maintain strong annual production.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in early spring; in zone 8 plant February–March. Viking aronia is self-fertile and produces good crops without a cross-pollinator, though yields improve with another aronia variety nearby. The vigorous shrub tolerates wet, poorly drained soils that would kill most fruiting shrubs — a significant advantage in low-lying garden areas.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist or periodically wet soil; Viking is a Scandinavian-selected cultivar of black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) developed for maximum berry production, selected in Sweden for its very heavy crop load of large, dark purple-black berries on an upright, vigorous shrub. The berries ripen in late August–September and are among the most tannin-rich, astringent fruits in cultivation when eaten raw — the name 'chokeberry' derives from this mouth-puckering astringency. Processed into juice, syrup, wine, jam, or dried, the astringency mellows and the extraordinarily high anthocyanin and polyphenol content — among the highest of any commonly grown fruit — makes aronia products popular as nutritional supplements and functional foods. Viking is one of the highest-yielding aronia cultivars per area, producing 10–20 pounds per mature shrub. The shrub also provides excellent ornamental value with white flower clusters in spring and brilliant orange-to-red fall foliage.

plant_note: Plant dormant canes or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Von is a thorny, trailing blackberry that requires a sturdy trellis or fence for support. It ripens earlier than most erect varieties — May–June in zone 9. Prune fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train the long, flexible primocanes on horizontal wires.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Von is a trailing (dewberry-type) blackberry selected by the University of Georgia specifically for the Gulf Coast and Deep South, with exceptional heat tolerance and disease resistance suited to the humid conditions of the lower South. Unlike the erect University of Arkansas varieties that were developed for upland conditions, Von was selected specifically for performance in the hot, humid, rainy conditions of coastal Georgia, the Florida panhandle, and Gulf Coast zone 9. The large, sweet, flavorful berries ripen in May–June in zone 9, earlier than most erect varieties. Von requires a trellis or fence to support its trailing, vining habit, but the trailing type has the advantage of naturally positioning the fruiting lateral branches where they receive maximum sun exposure. Disease resistance to orange rust and rosette disease is an important selection criterion in zone 9 where these diseases can be serious problems for susceptible trailing blackberry varieties.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wax myrtle is highly adaptable and tolerates poor, sandy, wet, or salty soils, making it one of the most versatile native evergreens for the Southeast.
directions: Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wax myrtle is highly adaptable and tolerates poor, sandy, wet, or salty soils and thrives in coastal and inland settings alike. Myrica cerifera is a fast-growing, aromatic, nitrogen-fixing native evergreen shrub or small tree of the Southeast, valued for its densely branched form that provides excellent year-round cover, nesting habitat, and foraging sites for wildlife; the distinctive blue-gray, waxy-coated berries produced in dense clusters along the stems attract over 40 bird species including yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, and bluebirds. Plant in groupings to form evergreen screens or wildlife hedgerows, and allow the plant to grow to its natural multi-stemmed form for maximum habitat value.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 8–11; White Cross Berry is a drought-tolerant African savanna shrub or small tree with distinctive bicolor (green above, white/silver beneath) leaves bearing small, yellow star-shaped flowers and round, reddish-orange to dark-brown edible berries eaten across sub-Saharan Africa as a bush food and used medicinally.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, average to poor soil; Grewia bicolor is highly drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry and semi-arid conditions — once established it requires little or no supplemental water in warm arid and semi-arid climates. Grewia bicolor (White Cross Berry or Crossberry) is a thorny, much-branched shrub or small tree native to the dry, open savannas, bushveld, and semi-arid woodland of sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal east through Ethiopia and south through East Africa to South Africa and Mozambique — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important shrubs of African savanna ecosystems. The distinctive bicolor leaves — deep green and glossy above, densely silver-white hairy and felted beneath — give the plant a shimmering two-tone appearance in the breeze. Small, 5-petaled, yellow or cream star-shaped flowers are borne prolifically from the leaf axils in summer, followed by round to oblong, 2–4-lobed berries — ripening from green through reddish-orange to dark brown or black — that are sweet-mucilaginous, edible raw or dried, and important bush food across the plant's range. The berries are browsed by elephants, giraffes, and many antelope species, and are eaten by indigenous peoples dried as a sweetener or fermented into beer. The roots and bark carry extensive traditional medicinal uses across sub-Saharan Africa for fevers, diarrhea, and sexually transmitted infections. An excellent drought-tolerant, wildlife-attracting shrub for hot, dry, sunny gardens in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring; white currants perform well trained as a cordon against a north- or east-facing wall.
directions: White currant is a yellow-fruited mutation of red currant sharing identical cultivation requirements: it fruits most heavily on spurs of two-year-old and older wood. The translucent, ivory-white berries are sweeter and milder than red currants and are prized for elegant fresh-eating and jellies. Prune each late winter to maintain 8–12 canes of mixed ages, removing canes older than 5 years. Harvest entire strigs when berries have turned fully translucent white-golden and taste sweet; check local Ribes restrictions before purchasing.

plant_note: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings or container shrubs in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; white currant is the mildest-flavored of the currants, with translucent, pearl-like berries that are sweet enough to eat fresh.
directions: Plant rooted hardwood cuttings or container-grown shrubs in fall or very early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white currant fruits best with some afternoon shade in warm climates and benefits from a cross-pollinator though it is largely self-fertile. Ribes sativum in its white-fruited forms (often grouped with R. rubrum) produces distinctive, translucent, pearl-white to pale-pink berries with a milder, less tart flavor than red currants, making them more suitable for fresh eating and elegant as a garnish on desserts; they are excellent for jelly, wine, and as a decoration for cakes and pastries. White currant is one of the most attractive of all fruiting shrubs when in fruit — the translucent clusters catch the light beautifully. 'Blanka', 'Primus', and 'White Versailles' are classic cultivars available from specialty nurseries.

common_name: White Pearl Currant (Sweet Pale-Fruited Ornamental Currant)
plant_note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; White Pearl is a white-fruited currant, a color form of the red currant species, notable for milder, sweeter flavor than most red currants.
directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. White Pearl is a white currant cultivar, a translucent, pale ivory-colored color form of the red currant species that lacks the anthocyanin pigment giving red currants their color, resulting in a noticeably milder, sweeter flavor with less tartness — a trait that makes white currants especially good for fresh eating out of hand rather than only for jelly and cooking. The long, drooping strigs of pearly, translucent berries are also strikingly ornamental against the green foliage. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on spurs of older wood like other red-type currants, so prune to an open framework in winter and remove the oldest wood to maintain vigor. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil in zone 8–11; White Stinkwood is a large, graceful, fast-growing native shade tree of South Africa and eastern Africa, widely planted across the region as a street, park, and garden tree for its elegant, weeping form, light-filtering canopy, and excellent wildlife value — producing abundant small, yellow-orange to reddish drupes eaten by birds and small mammals.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile to average soil; Celtis africana is drought tolerant once established, growing well in a wide range of soils including clay, rocky, and alkaline soils typical of the South African highveld and bushveld — water regularly only in the first year of establishment. Celtis africana (White Stinkwood, Witstinkhout) is a large, graceful, fast-growing deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the forests, river margins, and bush-margins of South Africa (particularly the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Limpopo, and Mpumalanga) and extending north through East Africa. The English common name 'stinkwood' refers to the smell of freshly cut wood — the dried wood does not smell strongly and is actually a fine-grained, attractive timber used for furniture and flooring in South Africa (though far less valuable than the true 'Black Stinkwood,' Ocotea bullata). Celtis africana is one of South Africa's most popular garden shade trees: fast-growing, with an elegant, slightly weeping branch structure, fine-textured, lime-green foliage that provides deep shade, and outstanding wildlife value — the small, round, yellow-orange to red-black fruits are eagerly eaten by many fruit-eating birds including barbets, mousebirds, bulbuls, and starlings. The tree supports many butterfly species and is larval host plant for the Charaxes butterfly group.

plant_note: Transplant rooted runners in spring or fall; pin runner tips to moist soil and cut free when rooted. Easiest to establish from rooted plugs or runners rather than seed.
directions: Plant rooted runners in moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this native species is one parent of the cultivated strawberry and produces intensely flavorful small red fruits that surpass commercial strawberries in taste, though not in size. The plant spreads vigorously by runners to form a dense groundcover that suppresses weeds and tolerates moderate foot traffic. Fruits are borne in late spring through early summer; birds, chipmunks, and turtles compete for the harvest so a loose barrier net may be needed. Divide or thin the planting every 2–3 years by removing older central crowns and retaining the vigorous outer runners.

plant_note: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; willow-leaved sea buckthorn is dioecious — plant at least one male per five or six females to ensure pollination and fruit production; it grows naturally along Himalayan river valleys and tolerates poor, gravelly, or stony soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean soil — willow-leaved sea buckthorn tolerates poor, gravelly, or stony ground and is highly drought-tolerant once established, making it a superb windbreak tree for cold, exposed sites. Cold-stratify seeds for 30–60 days before sowing in early spring, or sow fresh seed in fall for natural stratification. Because the species is dioecious, include at least one male tree for every five to six female trees to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set; the dense orange berry clusters ripen in late summer to autumn and are extraordinarily rich in vitamin C, carotenoids, and omega-7 fatty acids. Larger and more tree-like than common sea buckthorn (H. rhamnoides), it can reach 30 feet, providing significant shade and windbreak value while producing a heavy fruit crop.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in fall or early spring; in zone 9 plant October–February. Windsor requires 500–600 chill hours and is best suited for the colder areas of zone 9a where winter temperatures regularly provide adequate chilling. It is not recommended for zone 9b or warmer zones. Cross-pollination with another variety is beneficial for maximum yield.
directions: Plant in full sun in very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), organically rich, well-drained, sandy soil; Windsor is a southern highbush blueberry requiring 500–600 chill hours — more than the ultra-low-chill varieties like Flordablue and Biloxi, but still significantly less than northern varieties that require 800–1,200 hours. This intermediate chill requirement makes Windsor suitable for zone 9a where winters typically provide 500–700 chill hours but unsuitable for the warmer zone 9b areas. The advantage of Windsor's higher chill requirement is higher fruit quality — the berries are larger, firmer, darker, and more flavorful than very-low-chill varieties, with the rich, complex blueberry flavor that intensifies with more winter dormancy. Windsor was developed to provide the best possible fruit quality while still meeting the reduced chill requirements of the upper Gulf Coast. The midseason ripening (May–June in zone 9) follows the earliest varieties and provides an extended blueberry harvest season when planted alongside Biloxi or Flordablue.

plant_note: Plant grafted or own-rooted dormant vines in early spring on a well-drained slope with good air drainage.
directions: Wine grapes thrive in lean, well-drained soils with a pH of 5.5–6.5 and perform best on slopes with excellent air circulation to reduce disease pressure. Establish a vertical shoot positioning (VSP) trellis with catch wires at 4 and 5 ft above the cordon wire. Rigorous dormant pruning — leaving only 30–60 buds per vine depending on vigor — is essential for fruit quality. Harvest timing is cultivar- and use-specific; measure Brix (sugar) with a refractometer and monitor seed color and berry flavor.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or transplants in early spring; note that wineberry is invasive in much of the eastern U.S., so check local regulations before planting.
directions: Wineberry, native to Japan and China, produces small, brilliant red, jewel-like drupes with a sweet, delicate flavor; it is grown for fruit production in Asia and has naturalized extensively in the eastern U.S. and should be grown only in contained settings or where legal. The canes are covered in red glandular hairs and tip-root readily, so remove spent canes promptly and clear any rooted tips. Harvest when berries are uniformly bright red and detach easily from the sticky calyx — they do not ripen after picking and must be used within 1–2 days. Pruning follows the same floricane/primocane cycle as standard raspberries.

common_name: Winterthur Viburnum (Compact Possumhaw with Multi-Season Berry Color)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Winterthur is a compact possumhaw viburnum selection with berries that shift through pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen, all often visible on the same cluster at once.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites, including rain gardens and pond margins. Winterthur is a compact selection of native possumhaw viburnum producing showy clusters of berries that pass through a striking sequence of pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen in late summer and fall, often displaying several colors on the same cluster at once, in addition to attractive burgundy-red fall foliage. Its smaller stature compared to the species fits typical residential borders better, and planting a second unrelated clone nearby improves the reliability and abundance of berry set.

common_name: Womack Blackberry (Texas A&M Heat-Tolerant Thorny Blackberry)
plant_note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring; space 3-4 feet apart in rows 8-10 feet apart on a trellis. Fruiting occurs in the second year from planting, ripening in the main-season window in zones 8-9.
directions: Plant dormant canes 1-2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0-6.5) and train onto a two-wire trellis. Womack is an erect, thorny blackberry released from the Texas A&M blackberry breeding program and bred specifically to withstand the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Texas and the western Gulf South. It produces medium to large, firm, sweet-tart berries with good flavor and holds up well to summer heat that causes softer varieties to decline in quality. As an older Texas A&M release, it is a dependable, disease-tolerant option where more modern thornless varieties struggle with heat stress. Prune out fruited floricanes after harvest and select vigorous new primocanes to tie in for next year's crop; wear heavy gloves when working the thorny canes.

common_name: Woodard Rabbiteye Blueberry (Classic Large-Berried Southern Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant in late winter to early spring in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Woodard needs a compatible rabbiteye pollinator such as Climax or Tifblue nearby for good fruit set.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. One of the older, longer-established rabbiteye blueberry cultivars, Woodard is valued for its unusually large, soft-textured, mild-flavored berries that ripen in early-to-mid season, a bit ahead of many later rabbiteye types. The bushes are moderately vigorous and productive, though the soft fruit texture makes it better suited to fresh home use and processing than commercial shipping. Keep soil consistently moist through bloom and fruit development, and mulch well to conserve moisture and maintain the acidic soil conditions blueberries require.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root stock in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil; worcesterberry is very thorny — wear heavy gloves when handling.
directions: The worcesterberry is a North American species of gooseberry (Ribes divaricatum) sometimes grown as a productive alternative to European gooseberries because it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and American gooseberry mildew. The small, dark purple-black berries resemble currants more than typical gooseberries and ripen in midsummer with a tart, rich flavor excellent for jams and pies. Prune to an open-vase structure each late winter, keeping 8–10 canes of mixed ages. Verify state restrictions on Ribes planting before ordering, as some states still restrict the genus.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Wyldewood produces heavier crops with cross-pollination from another elderberry variety nearby. In zone 9 it produces abundant flowers in May–June and ripe fruit clusters in July–August. Elderberries spread by root suckers in suitable conditions; manage spread with mowing around plantings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil; Wyldewood is a named American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) cultivar developed from wild selections in Oklahoma by the Oklahoma State University extension program, selected for extraordinary production of large, dense berry clusters — corymbs up to 10–14 inches across with hundreds of small, dark purple-black berries per cluster. Wyldewood is considered one of the highest-yielding American elderberry cultivars, with mature plants producing 12–20 pounds or more of fruit clusters annually. The berries are used for elderberry syrup (widely used as an immune-support supplement), elderflower and elderberry liqueurs and wines, jams, pies, and lemonade. Raw elderberries contain very small amounts of cyanogenic compounds and should not be eaten raw in large quantities; cooking neutralizes these compounds. Wyldewood is specifically bred for Oklahoma and surrounding regions and performs excellently throughout zone 9 conditions.

scientific_name: Rubus caesius x idaeus x ursinus hybrid
plant_note: Plant bare-root canes in spring on a sturdy two- or three-wire trellis; youngberry is a trailing type requiring support and grows best in warm, humid climates.
directions: The youngberry is a dewberry hybrid developed in Louisiana in the early 1900s by B.M. Young, producing very large, dark maroon-purple berries with a high juice content and sweet-tart flavor excellent for wine, juice, and pies. Culture is similar to boysenberry: train long, trailing canes on a T-trellis at 3 and 5 ft, fruiting on second-year floricanes; after harvest, cut all fruited canes to the ground and tie new primocanes in their place. The plants are less cold-hardy than standard blackberries and benefit from cane protection or mulching in zone 6 winters. Harvest when berries turn uniformly dark purple-black and release easily from the plug.

plant_note: Sow in early spring around the last frost date, or in late summer 6–8 weeks before first frost to allow fall establishment.
directions: Inoculate seed with Medicago-specific rhizobium and broadcast at 15–20 lb per acre (about 1/4 oz per 100 sq ft), raking seed to 1/4 in depth into a firm, well-prepared seedbed with pH 6.5–7.0. Alfalfa fixes 100–200 lb of nitrogen per acre per year once established and deep taproots (up to 6 ft) break hardpan and mine subsoil minerals. Terminate by mowing at early bloom stage — typically every 30–40 days in summer — before the first killing frost; turning it under releases a large pulse of nitrogen. In perennial plantings, allow one cutting to go to seed to rejuvenate the stand every two or three years.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained to seasonally wet, alkaline to neutral, clay-loam to sandy loam, lean to average soil in full sun; alkali sacaton is the most alkaline- and salt-tolerant of the native southwestern bunchgrasses, growing on saline flats, alkali playas, and seasonally flooded bottomlands where most grasses cannot survive.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained to seasonally wet, alkaline to neutral, clay-loam to sandy loam, lean to average soil in full sun; alkali sacaton is one of the most ecologically important and visually striking native grasses of the arid and semi-arid Southwest — a large, coarse bunchgrass producing massive, open, airy panicles (up to 20 inches long) of extraordinarily fine-textured, wind-trembling seed clusters that light up golden in morning and evening light. The enormous panicle creates one of the most beautiful seed head effects of any native grass — a luminous, cloud-like mass of fine-branched flower stalks hovering above the blue-green foliage in summer.
