The primary ecological niche is alkaline, saline, and seasonally flooded low-lying sites — alkali flats, salt meadows, river floodplains, and irrigation-influenced soils — where its exceptional tolerance for salt and alkali makes it the dominant or sole grass. An outstanding ornamental grass for challenging alkaline soils of the arid West. Very fast-germinating and establishing from seed. Related to prairie dropseed (S. heterolepis) but much larger.

plant_note: Broadcast seed in early spring as soon as soils can be worked, or frost-seed in late winter; alsike clover is one of the few clovers that establishes well in wet, acidic, or poorly drained soils where red and white clover fail. Inoculate seed with Rhizobium leguminosarum trifolii.
directions: Broadcast seed at 6–8 lbs per acre in early spring in full sun onto a firm, moist seedbed; alsike clover tolerates wet, poorly drained, and moderately acidic soils (pH as low as 5.5) where red clover and white clover fail to persist, making it the preferred clover for heavy-clay, low-lying, or seasonally flooded areas. Trifolium hybridum produces erect to ascending stems with smooth trifoliate leaves and distinctive pink-and-white bicolor flower heads that are exceptionally attractive to honeybees and are considered one of the best bee plants among the clovers; it is a natural hybrid species named for its intermediate characteristics between red and white clover. It is shorter-lived than red clover in persistently dry soils but outperforms all other clovers on wet, cold, or acidic ground. Fixes 80–160 lbs N/acre and is widely used in cool, wet northern and Pacific Northwest cover crop mixes.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; scarify seeds lightly for more uniform germination. Inoculate with Aeschynomene-specific Bradyrhizobium inoculant for nitrogen fixation in soils where the plant has not grown before.
directions: A native annual legume of moist, open, disturbed habitats, roadsides, and wet meadows in the southeastern US and throughout tropical America, producing delicate, sensitive pinnate leaves and clusters of small yellow, brownish-red-veined pea flowers from summer through fall. The jointed seed pods break apart at the segments at maturity — a characteristic trait that gives the plant the common name 'joint-vetch' — and the seeds are relished by mourning doves, quail, and other seed-eating birds, making this an excellent wildlife food plot legume for warm climates. Direct sow after last frost in moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; inoculate with Aeschynomene-specific Bradyrhizobium to maximize nitrogen fixation in new planting sites. It tolerates periodic flooding and is well adapted to the wet, disturbed margins of ponds and seasonal wet areas throughout zones 7-11.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks before first fall frost; germinates and establishes faster than perennial ryegrass and can be interseeded into standing late-season crops.
directions: Broadcast seed at 20–25 lb per acre (about 1/2 oz per 100 sq ft) onto a prepared surface and rake to 1/4 in depth; annual ryegrass has one of the fastest establishment rates of all cool-season grasses, providing rapid erosion control and weed suppression. The dense, fibrous root system scavenges residual nitrogen effectively, locking it up over winter to prevent leaching. Terminate in early spring before it joints and sets seed — once headed, it becomes very difficult to kill without herbicide or repeated tillage. Mow to 2–3 in and till, or use a roller-crimper at boot stage for no-till termination; allow residue 2–3 weeks to break down before planting.

plant_note: Sow in fall in mild-winter regions for late-season biomass and nitrogen.
directions: Inoculate with clover rhizobia and broadcast at about 0.2-0.3 lb per 1,000 sq ft onto a firm seedbed, covering no deeper than 0.25 inch. Arrowleaf clover is a reseeding annual legume of the southern United States that produces high biomass and fixes nitrogen well into late spring. It is later maturing than crimson clover, extending the window of living cover and pollinator bloom. Terminate by mowing at early to mid bloom, then incorporate or leave residue as mulch. Allowing a portion to set seed lets the stand reseed naturally for the following season.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in fall; in zone 9 sow October–November. Australian Winter Pea is cold-hardy to about 10–15°F once established and is one of the most reliable cool-season leguminous cover crops for the Gulf South — it establishes in fall, grows slowly through winter, and produces a large flush of biomass in late winter and early spring before being terminated ahead of the spring garden. Inoculate with hairy vetch-type Rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Terminate by mowing or rolling when pods begin to form.
directions: Broadcast 40–80 lbs per acre (or 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft) into prepared soil in fall; Australian Winter Pea (Lathyrus hirsutus) is a vining, annual cool-season legume used as a winter cover crop and green manure throughout the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and mid-South. It is one of the few leguminous cover crops that establishes reliably in Gulf Coast fall conditions, tolerating the warm early-fall temperatures that prevent hairy vetch from establishing and the occasional winter cold snaps that kill crimson clover. The sprawling, twining vines produce a dense, weed-suppressing mat through winter and a large flush of nitrogen-rich biomass in late winter–early spring. When inoculated with the correct Rhizobium strain, it fixes 50–100 lbs of nitrogen per acre. Australian Winter Pea is sometimes called hairy vetchling or Caley pea; it is not edible and should not be confused with edible garden peas. Terminate by mowing or rolling 3–4 weeks before the next crop to allow residue to decompose and release nitrogen.

plant_note: Sow in early fall, often mixed with a cereal, so vines establish before frost.
directions: Inoculate seed with pea-vetch rhizobia and drill at 1.5-2 inches deep or broadcast at about 2-4 lb per 1,000 sq ft into a firm seedbed. Austrian winter pea is a viny legume that fixes substantial nitrogen and is frequently sown with cereal rye or oats for support and biomass. It overwinters in mild climates and resumes vigorous vining growth in spring. Terminate by mowing or crimping at early flowering when nitrogen fixation peaks, then incorporate or leave as mulch. The residue releases nitrogen quickly, benefiting a following heavy-feeding vegetable crop.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill after all frost danger has passed into warm soil in full sun; bahiagrass germinates slowly and unevenly, and stands often take a full season to fully establish, but once rooted it forms a durable, low-maintenance, deep-rooted sod that persists for years.
directions: Broadcast seed at 15–20 lb/acre into warm, well-prepared soil in full sun; slow to establish but exceptionally drought-tolerant, low-input, and persistent once rooted, thanks to a deep, extensive root system. Bahiagrass is a warm-season perennial grass widely planted across the Gulf South and Southeast as a durable pasture, hay, and erosion-control grass, particularly valued on poor, sandy, or infertile soils where few other forage grasses perform reliably. Its deep, tough root system makes it one of the most drought-resistant pasture grasses available in the region, and its low fertility requirements and tolerance of close, continuous grazing have made it a standard choice for Gulf Coast livestock pasture for decades. The characteristic seed heads, forked into a distinctive V or Y shape, are a recognizable feature of bahiagrass pastures throughout summer and fall. A tough, low-maintenance, long-lived grass for Gulf South pasture, roadside, or erosion-control plantings, zone 7–10.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before frost; balansa clover is exceptionally flood- and waterlogging-tolerant, making it ideal for wet, low-lying spots.
directions: Broadcast tiny seed at 2–4 lb/acre (due to its small seed size) onto a firm, moist seedbed; balansa clover establishes quickly and tolerates prolonged waterlogging that would kill crimson or Persian clover. It hollows out a rapid canopy that suppresses winter weeds while fixing nitrogen throughout the cool season. Terminate at early bloom by mowing or rolling for the best nitrogen contribution and easiest residue breakdown. Excellent choice for poorly drained field margins or orchard middles that receive runoff.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil in early spring or fall; tolerates light frost.
directions: Barley is a fast-establishing cereal grain used as a soil-building cover crop, sprouting grain, and livestock feed. Drill or broadcast the seed into cool, firm soil in early spring or fall and rake it in for good contact. It germinates quickly, tolerates light frost, and produces abundant biomass that suppresses weeds and protects bare ground. Mow or turn under the growth before it heads out to return organic matter, or let it mature if harvesting grain.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in zone 7–9 for a winter nitrogen-fixing cover crop; barrel medic germinates in cool autumn soil and grows through mild winters, producing hard seeds that remain dormant in the soil for years and regenerate the stand without reseeding. Scarify or acid-treat seed to improve germination if using non-fresh seed.
directions: Broadcast seed in fall on prepared, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; barrel medic is a Mediterranean annual legume that has become one of the most important self-seeding winter cover crops in warm-winter climates. The seed pods are distinctive barrel- or snail-shaped spirals with spines — an adaptation for animal dispersal. Many seeds develop a hard seed coat and remain viable in the soil for decades, creating a persistent seed bank that regenerates the cover without annual reseeding — a 'hard-seeded' trait extremely valuable in dryland farming. The plant is also the primary model organism in legume biology research (like Arabidopsis for broadleaf plants), so it is among the best-characterized plants in science. Fixes substantial nitrogen for warm-season crops that follow. In zone 9, sow September–October for winter cover; the stand dies out by late spring when soil warms.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, clay-loam to sandy loam, average soil in full sun; basin wildrye tolerates highly alkaline, saline, and even seasonally wet soils better than most native grasses. An excellent large grass for difficult alkaline or saline situations in the Great Basin and Rocky Mountain West.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, clay-loam to sandy loam, average soil in full sun; basin wildrye is one of the largest and most robust native bunchgrasses of the Great Basin and intermountain West — a cool-season grass forming massive, upright clumps of blue-gray-green foliage and tall, erect seed stalks rising 4–6 feet tall. The broad, blue-gray, arching leaves are ornamentally striking, resembling 'blue oat grass' but at a dramatically larger scale. Native to sagebrush steppe, salt desert shrubland, and alkaline flats throughout the Great Basin from eastern California to Wyoming and Colorado. Exceptional tolerance of alkaline and saline soils — one of the best native grasses for revegetating saline, alkaline, or disturbed soils in the Great Basin where other grasses struggle. Provides critical winter cover and forage for deer, elk, and pronghorn under deep snow. An outstanding large ornamental grass for bold landscape use in appropriate dry western gardens — the blue-gray foliage and massive clumps create a strong architectural statement. Provides excellent erosion control on steep, dry, alkaline banks.

common_name: Beach Jack Bean (Bay Bean, Seaside Jack Bean, Coastal Jack Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, sandy, coastal soil; Canavalia rosea is the standard beach-stabilizing, nitrogen-fixing legume of tropical coastlines worldwide and the default choice for establishing live cover on coastal dunes, sand flats, and disturbed coastal ground in zone 9-12. The large, showy pink to rose-purple flowers are produced continuously through the warm months and are attractive to large native bees. The large (3–5 inch) flat beans are TOXIC when raw and should not be eaten without extensive preparation — this is a cover crop and coastal stabilizer, not a culinary bean. Non-toxic external contact.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, sandy, coastal soil — Beach Jack Bean is one of the most drought and salt tolerant leguminous plants available, thriving in the harsh conditions of coastal dunes, beach margins, and sandy disturbed ground where most other plants fail to establish. Canavalia rosea is a vigorous, perennial, trailing to sprawling vine in the Fabaceae family with a circumtropical distribution on the coastlines of both hemispheres, naturally occurring on beaches from Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts through the Caribbean, Mexico, Central and South America, tropical Africa, India, Southeast Asia, and Australia — one of the most cosmopolitan coastal plants in the world. The plant produces trifoliate leaves with large, oval, dark-green leaflets on trailing stems that spread across the sand surface, rooting at nodes to form a dense, stabilizing mat 12–18 inches deep. Through the warm months, erect flower racemes emerge bearing 5–15 large (1-inch), showy flowers in bright rose-pink to purple-pink — among the most ornamental of any legume flower. The flowers attract large carpenter bees and other native bees. After flowering, large, flat, rigid pods 3–5 inches long develop containing the large, kidney-shaped seeds. Beach Jack Bean fixes nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis and adds organic matter as stems root and die, steadily improving poor coastal soils. The beans contain toxic alkaloids (canavanine) and are poisonous when raw — not for culinary use without extensive processing. An outstanding, low-maintenance native legume for coastal dune stabilization and cover cropping in zone 9-12.

plant_note: Broadcast seed after last frost when soils have warmed to at least 60°F; berseem clover grows quickly and can reach first cutting in as little as 45 days. In zones 9–10, sow in fall or late winter for a warm-season winter annual.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 15–20 lbs per acre after last frost into a firm, moist seedbed in full sun; berseem clover is a fast-maturing annual clover originating from the Nile Valley and Mediterranean region and is widely grown as a high-quality warm-season cover crop and forage throughout the southern United States. It produces high-quality, high-protein biomass that can be cut multiple times (cutting regrowth encourages multiple harvests) and is considered superior forage to most other clovers for livestock and poultry because it does not cause bloat. Inoculate seed with Rhizobium leguminosarum trifolii for nitrogen fixation; fixes 80–150 lbs N/acre in a single season. Berseem clover is frost-sensitive and dies at 28°F, making termination easy in northern gardens by the first hard frost, with no need for mechanical destruction of the stand.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, sandy, acidic to neutral, nutrient-poor soil in full sun; bird's-foot is one of the few nitrogen-fixing legumes adapted to strongly acidic, nutrient-deficient sandy soils where most legumes fail.
directions: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, sandy, acidic to neutral (pH 4.5–6.5), nutrient-poor soil in full sun; bird's-foot is a specialist of nutrient-poor, acidic, sandy soils and will not thrive in rich, heavy, or alkaline conditions. Ornithopus perpusillus is a small, delicate European annual legume of heathlands, sandy roadsides, and acid grasslands; it produces pinnate leaves on prostrate stems and tiny, pink-and-white, pea-like flowers followed by distinctive, curved, bird's-foot-shaped seed pods in spring and early summer. As a cover crop, it is invaluable for improving sandy, acid soils where other leguminous cover crops cannot establish; it fixes nitrogen, improves soil organic matter, and can be used as a low-growing, self-seeding living mulch in acid-soil crops such as blueberries and azaleas. Self-seeds freely in favorable sandy, acid conditions.

plant_note: Broadcast seed in early spring on a firm, weed-free seedbed; bird's-foot trefoil establishes slowly in its first season but becomes persistent and competitive once rooted. Inoculate seed with Rhizobium loti; do not cover seed more than 1/4 inch as seedlings are small and lack vigor to emerge from depth.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 4–6 lbs per acre in early spring on a firm, moist seedbed; bird's-foot trefoil is a creeping to semi-erect perennial legume that tolerates a wider range of difficult soil conditions than most clovers, including moderately acidic soils (pH 5.5–7.5), poorly drained or wet sites, and low-fertility soils, making it extremely useful for establishing cover and fixing nitrogen on disturbed, marginal, or problem sites. Lotus corniculatus produces cheerful clusters of yellow and orange pea flowers from late spring through fall that are excellent for pollinators, particularly bumblebees; the clusters of seed pods resemble a bird's foot or claw, giving rise to the common name. It is widely used in meadow mixes, roadsides, and erosion control seedings but can spread aggressively and become invasive in some native plant communities in North America — avoid planting near intact native grasslands or meadows. Does not cause bloat in livestock and fixes 50–100 lbs N/acre annually.

plant_note: Sow in early spring; establishes slowly but becomes a persistent, non-bloating perennial legume ideal for slopes and orchard floors.
directions: Inoculate seed with Mesorhizobium loti and broadcast at 5–8 lb/acre onto a firm, weed-free seedbed; seedling vigor is slow, so suppress weed competition aggressively in the establishment year. Once established, birdsfoot trefoil is drought-tolerant and persists on shallow, acidic, or gravelly soils where alfalfa fails. It fixes moderate nitrogen, flowers bright yellow, and does not cause bloat in livestock — a key advantage over true clovers. Mow or graze periodically to prevent it from going rank and woody but allow it to flower at least once per season to feed pollinators.

plant_note: Sow in early-to-mid fall when soil temperatures are between 50-65°F. Inoculate with a Biserrula-specific rhizobium strain (Group F in Australia) before sowing — standard clover inoculants are not effective. Sow shallowly at 3-6 lb per acre on clay-loam or heavier soils.
directions: Biserrula is best suited to heavier-textured, alkaline to neutral clay-loam soils where serradella does not perform well, tolerating pH levels up to 8.0 and providing reliable nitrogen fixation even under moderate drought. Sow in fall using seed inoculated with the correct Biserrula-specific rhizobium group, as general-purpose legume inoculants will not form effective nodules. Its deep taproot improves compacted or waterlogged soils over successive seasons, making it a strong rotational choice before cereal crops. The hard seed coat gives biserrula a significant soil seed-bank advantage — allow pods to mature and shatter naturally every second or third year to replenish the seed bank for low-input, self-regenerating pasture or cover-crop systems.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky, lean soil in full sun; black grama is a desert grassland native adapted to the hottest, driest conditions of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran desert grasslands and requires excellent drainage and full sun. Extremely drought tolerant once established.
directions: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky, lean soil in full sun; black grama is one of the most important and characteristic native grasses of the Chihuahuan Desert grassland — the dominant grass of desert grasslands from western Texas and southern New Mexico through Arizona into Sonora and Chihuahua. The name 'black grama' comes from the characteristic dark woolly hairs (eriopo = woolly-footed) at the nodes of the stolons. A warm-season grass that spreads by stolons to form a low, sod-like turf in dry desert conditions. Extremely important as a livestock forage grass in the Chihuahuan Desert and a key indicator of healthy desert grassland condition — when overgrazing leads to shrub encroachment (mesquite or creosote) replacing the grass, black grama is typically the first native grass to disappear and one of the last to recover. Highly drought tolerant, essentially requiring no supplemental irrigation in appropriate desert climates. An essential component of Chihuahuan Desert and desert grassland restoration planting mixes.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before frost; black oat produces more biomass and stronger allelopathy than common oats and is the preferred cover in no-till systems.
directions: Broadcast seed at 40–60 lb/acre and cover to 1 in depth in fall; black oat (Avena strigosa) is widely used in Brazilian no-till systems for its exceptional allelopathic residue that suppresses weeds well into the following season. It winter-kills in zones colder than 5, creating a ready-made mulch mat without any tillage needed. In milder climates it overwinters and can be roll-crimped in spring when fully headed out to create a thick residue layer for direct transplanting through. Combine with a legume such as hairy vetch or crimson clover to add a nitrogen component to the mulch.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in moist, sandy or loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; lightly scarify seeds before sowing for more reliable germination.
directions: Bladderpod Sesbania is a native annual legume of moist coastal plain habitats, ditches, and wet roadsides from Virginia to Texas, growing 4 to 8 feet tall with pinnate leaves and small, yellow, pea-like flowers in summer that are visited by native bumblebees. Its most distinctive feature is the inflated, papery, bladder-like seed pods that develop in late summer and rattle audibly when dry, making it easy to identify at maturity. Like other Sesbania species it fixes atmospheric nitrogen, building soil fertility in low, wet areas where most conventional cover crops fail to thrive. Direct sow lightly scarified seeds after the last frost in moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil, and mow plants to the ground before pods ripen fully to prevent excessive self-seeding the following year.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; blue wild rye is one of the most shade-tolerant native bunchgrasses of western North America, naturally growing under open canopy oak woodland, mixed forest edges, and shaded slopes where few grasses survive.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average, loamy or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; blue wild rye is a cool-season native bunchgrass widely distributed across western North America from Alaska through California, the Rocky Mountains, and into the Great Plains — one of the very few native grasses that can establish and persist under the partial shade of oak woodland, mixed forest edges, and shaded north-facing slopes. The bluish-green (glaucous) foliage is distinctly attractive and gives the species its common name. The tall, nodding seed heads are produced in early summer. An outstanding native grass for shaded wildflower meadow projects, oak woodland understory plantings, and difficult shaded sites where most grasses and groundcovers struggle. Valued for erosion control on partially shaded slopes. Self-sows modestly in appropriate conditions. Matures early and becomes summer-dormant in drier areas, going dormant in summer and greening again with fall rains — a cool-season grass cycle typical of western grassland species.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Brazilian stylo is the most widely grown tropical pasture and cover crop legume in the world, used across Australia, Africa, and Southeast Asia to improve nitrogen-depleted tropical soils and as a protein-rich, drought-tolerant component of tropical pasture systems.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 2–5 lbs per acre in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; inoculate with appropriate Rhizobium before sowing. Stylosanthes guianensis (Brazilian stylo or common stylosanthes) is a semi-erect to sprawling South American tropical legume that has become one of the most globally important tropical cover crops, pasture species, and soil improvement plants. It is grown extensively throughout northern Australia (where it was introduced as a pasture legume), sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia to improve nitrogen-depleted, acidic, infertile tropical soils. The plant fixes significant quantities of nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with specific Rhizobium strains, makes excellent protein-rich grazing for livestock, and builds organic matter over time. Stylosanthes is notably tolerant of low-fertility, acidic soils and drought — it thrives on marginal lands where few other legumes survive. Dozens of improved cultivars have been selected for disease resistance (especially anthracnose), yield, and adaptation to different soil types and rainfall patterns. In garden use in zone 9–12, it functions as an outstanding summer green manure on poor, sandy, acidic soils — sow in spring, incorporate at flowering in 60–90 days before planting a food crop.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer to early fall in average, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; incorporate into the soil as green manure when stems are in bud stage (before flowering) for best biofumigant effect — the glucosinolates in the tissues break down to isothiocyanates that suppress soil pathogens and nematodes.
directions: Direct sow in late summer to early fall in average, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; incorporate into the soil as green manure when stems are in bud stage (before flowering) for best biofumigant effect — the glucosinolates in the tissues break down to isothiocyanates that suppress soil pathogens and nematodes. Brassica juncea is a fast-growing, cold-tolerant annual Brassica crop used as both a culinary mustard (the seeds are ground for prepared mustard) and an important cover crop for biofumigation, organic weed suppression, and green manure; high-glucosinolate varieties are specifically bred for maximum biofumigant effect against root-knot nematodes, Fusarium, Verticillium, and other soil pathogens, and may reduce pathogen pressure by 30–80% compared to untreated controls. The flowers provide excellent early-spring nectar for bumblebees before spring crops are established; allow a portion of the stand to flower when using primarily for pollinator benefit rather than biofumigation.

plant_note: Direct sow at 20–25 lbs per acre (or 1/2 lb per 1,000 sq ft) on prepared soil in warm weather; brown top millet is one of the fastest-establishing summer annuals for warm soils — germination and early cover are often visible within 5–7 days.
directions: Brown top millet is the most popular warm-season cover crop grain for wildlife food plots and dove fields across the southeastern United States, producing abundant, small-seeded seed heads in 50–70 days that are consumed avidly by mourning doves, bobwhite quail, mourning doves, and more than 30 other species of wild birds — it is essentially the standard seed for managed dove hunting fields in the Gulf South. As a summer annual, it establishes extremely rapidly in warm soil, provides quick weed suppression through its rapid canopy closure, and produces excellent biomass for soil organic matter after incorporation; it is also used as an emergency crop cover on eroded or disturbed soils where quick establishment is critical. Sow in June or early July for peak seed production by August–September for dove season; for cover crop biomass, incorporate into the soil after seed set when stalks are still green for maximum nitrogen and organic matter contribution. Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established — among the most reliable summer cover crops for the hot, dry conditions of the Gulf Coast in July–August.

common_name: Browntop Millet (Gulf South Dove and Quail Wildlife Food Plot Warm-Season Annual Grass)
plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed at 15–20 lbs/acre (or 1 lb per 1,000 sq ft) on a prepared seedbed after last frost; browntop millet is extremely fast-growing and can be planted as late as August in the Gulf South for fall dove season. In zone 9, plant April–August for seed production in August–October when dove season typically opens. Browntop millet germinates and establishes rapidly even on poor, sandy soils — it is one of the most drought-tolerant warm-season grasses for the Southeast. The plant reaches maturity and sets seed within 60–75 days of planting, making it practical for quick establishment when the growing window is short.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 15–20 lbs per acre on a loosened seedbed; no need to cover more than 0.25 inch deep. Browntop millet establishes readily with minimal care. Browntop Millet (Urochloa ramosa, formerly classified as Brachiaria ramosa and Panicum ramosum) is a warm-season annual grass that is one of the most important wildlife food plot plants in the Gulf South and Southeast — planted extensively by hunters, wildlife managers, and conservation farmers specifically for dove, quail, turkey, and songbird feed, as the small seeds are highly palatable to ground-feeding birds. The common name 'browntop' refers to the characteristic brown color of the mature seed heads, which develop in dense, spreading panicles atop the slender stems. Browntop millet's key attributes for food plot and cover crop use are its speed (60–75 days from planting to seed maturity — among the fastest of any annual forage grass), drought tolerance (established plants survive extended dry periods on poor sandy soils), and reliable seed set (the plant produces abundant small seeds per plant across a wide range of soil conditions). In addition to wildlife value, browntop millet is an effective short-season summer cover crop that suppresses weeds and adds organic matter when tilled under; it self-seeds readily and may naturalize as a volunteer in subsequent seasons. Native to India and tropical Asia, browntop has naturalized throughout the warm southeastern United States.

plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed; grows quickly in warm soil.
directions: Broadcast buckwheat seed onto worked soil once frost danger has passed and rake in lightly for good contact. It germinates within a week and races to flower in about a month, smothering weeds and drawing in bees. Mow or turn it under at first bloom to add green matter and free up phosphorus for the next crop. Succession-sow every few weeks through summer for continuous soil coverage, but never let a stand fully set seed unless you want volunteers.

plant_note: Broadcast seed on warm soil after frost; it grows fast and is easily killed by cold.
directions: Buckwheat is a fast-growing warm-season cover crop that smothers weeds, attracts pollinators, and improves soil when turned under. Broadcast seed densely onto raked soil after the last frost and rake in lightly; it germinates within a few days. Mow or till it in at flowering, before seeds set, to prevent unwanted reseeding and to add organic matter. It thrives in poor soils and needs little water, making it an easy short-term summer cover between crops.

plant_note: Direct sow or allow to self-seed in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; burclover is a Mediterranean annual legume that volunteers readily in Gulf Coast lawns and gardens, acting as a winter-active nitrogen fixer before dying back in summer heat.
directions: Broadcast seeds in fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; burclover requires little management and often self-seeds prolifically once established. Medicago polymorpha (burclover or California burclover) is a small, sprawling, Mediterranean annual legume that has naturalized widely throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain, California, and mild-winter regions of North America. In zone 9 lawns and gardens, it is often considered a volunteer ground cover — germinating with fall rains, growing through the mild winter as a low, clover-like plant with small, three-part leaves and tiny yellow flowers, fixing nitrogen symbiotically with soil rhizobia, and dying back naturally when summer heat arrives. The seeds are distinctive small, spiny burs that adhere to clothing and animal fur. While sometimes considered a weedy nuisance, burclover is increasingly recognized as a useful volunteer cover crop and winter ground cover for no-till and regenerative gardeners: it adds nitrogen, prevents winter erosion, and dies back naturally without tillage. It tolerates drought, alkaline soil, and poor fertility well — making it especially useful in challenging sites.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; bush muhly grows naturally beneath desert shrubs and in rocky desert washes in the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts, often found sheltering under desert shrubs (mesquite, acacia, creosote). Extremely heat and drought tolerant once established.
directions: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; bush muhly is one of the most distinctive and graceful native grasses of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts — a wiry-stemmed, fine-leaved bunchgrass with a uniquely open, spreading, almost shrubby growth habit (unlike the tight tufts of most other grasses) and feathery, airy, purple-tinged flower and seed panicles that are extremely ornamental in late summer and fall. The open, branching, almost woody-at-the-base stems spread outward and become partially supported by nearby desert shrubs, earning the common name 'bush muhly.' In the autumn flowering and seeding season, the fine-textured purple-pink panicles create a misty, ethereal effect highly attractive in ornamental and naturalistic plantings. One of the best native ornamental grasses for the hot, dry Southwest garden — deer-resistant, drought-tolerant, extremely heat-hardy. Widely used in desert-adapted landscape plantings in Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas. A favorite of hummingbirds for the purple-flowering form.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; button medic is a winter annual in warm climates (zones 7–10) and should be sown in September–October to overwinter as a productive cover crop.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; button medic is a winter annual in warm climates (zones 7–10) and should be sown in September–October to overwinter as a productive cover crop. Medicago orbicularis is a Mediterranean annual member of the medic family named for its distinctive flat, circular, button-like seed pods — a single coil instead of the multiple-coiled pods of barrel medic (M. truncatula); it is a fast-establishing winter annual cover crop well-suited to Mediterranean climates and the mild winters of the Gulf Coast. It fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis, produces excellent bee forage from its small yellow flowers in early spring, and dies naturally as temperatures warm, leaving a nitrogen-rich mulch that can be incorporated as green manure before spring planting; it reseeds readily in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Sow in early fall for Southeast US; Cahaba White Vetch establishes readily and is one of the best vetches for the warm-winter Southeast where hairy vetch may be less reliable.
directions: Drill or broadcast at 25–35 lbs per acre in early fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Cahaba White Vetch is a common vetch selection developed specifically for the southeastern United States, offering faster establishment, better tolerance of mild winters, and more consistent performance than hairy vetch in zones 7–9. It fixes substantial nitrogen (50–100 lbs per acre in a good stand), produces good biomass for soil incorporation, and the white to pale lavender flowers provide late-winter nectar for early bees. Mow or disk before pods form to preserve nitrogen and prevent volunteers; the flat-lying growth habit makes it an excellent smother crop for winter weed suppression.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; calopo is a fast-growing, vining South American legume cover crop widely used as an understory nitrogen-fixing groundcover in rubber, oil palm, and cacao plantations across Southeast Asia — it covers the soil rapidly, suppresses weeds, and fixes substantial nitrogen.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 3–5 lbs per acre in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; calopo establishes quickly and smothers weeds as a living mulch. Calopogonium mucunoides (calopo or calopogonium) is a trailing and twining annual vine legume from South America that has become one of the most important tropical plantation cover crops in Southeast Asia, particularly Indonesia and Malaysia. It is grown as an understory cover crop beneath rubber trees (Hevea brasiliensis) and oil palms (Elaeis guineensis), where it rapidly covers bare soil between tree rows, fixing nitrogen from the atmosphere through root nodule bacteria, suppressing weeds, preventing soil erosion during tropical monsoon rains, and building soil organic matter as it dies and decomposes. The vine produces attractive, soft-hairy, trifoliate leaves and small, blue-purple flowers; it sprawls to 3–6 feet, rooting at nodes to form a continuous groundcover. It is suited for areas that receive moderate to high rainfall and prefer partial shade as found under plantation canopy. Calopo can be incorporated as a green manure at flowering for maximum nitrogen benefit. A staple of tropical sustainable agriculture that is little-known in North American horticulture.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for natural cold stratification over winter, or cold-stratify seed for 30–60 days and sow in early spring; seed requires scarification (nicking or hot-water soak) plus cold stratification to break dormancy. Best results come from fall sowing directly into a prepared seedbed or native meadow area.
directions: Sow scarified and cold-stratified seed in fall or early spring in full sun in well-drained to moderately moist, loamy to sandy soil; Canada milk vetch is a native North American perennial legume of prairies, open woodlands, stream banks, and disturbed areas from the Atlantic coast west to the Rocky Mountains, making it an excellent choice for prairie restoration, native meadow establishment, and pollinator habitat seedings across much of the country. Astragalus canadensis produces upright stems 2–4 feet tall clad in pinnately compound leaves, topped in summer with dense, cylindrical spikes of cream to greenish-white pea flowers that attract hummingbirds, bumblebees, and a variety of native bees; it spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeds to form colonies. As a native legume, it supports specialist native bee species that depend on Astragalus pollen and provides high-protein forage for deer and other wildlife; it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through Mesorhizobium symbiosis and is well adapted to the droughts and extreme temperature swings of prairie and plains environments. Requires patience — establish slowly in year one but become robust and competitive by year two.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by rubbing on sandpaper, then sow in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, lean soil; Canada milkvetch spreads by rhizomes and also self-seeds to form drifts over time in prairie and meadow conditions. Inoculate with Astragalus-specific rhizobium for best nodulation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Canada milkvetch is one of the most ecologically important native prairie legumes of eastern and central North America, fixing substantial atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule associations and providing critical pollen and nectar for bumble bees (particularly the federally threatened rusty-patched bumble bee) through the dense spikes of pale cream to yellowish flowers in summer. The plant spreads by rhizomes to form loose colonies — a beneficial trait in prairie restoration but something to manage in formal borders. The inflated seed pods are distinctive and attractive in dried arrangements. Unlike many astragalus species, Canada milkvetch is non-toxic to livestock and wildlife. An underused native alternative to introduced legume cover crops for prairie-style and meadow plantings.

plant_note: Fall or early spring sowing suits this cool-season native grass; benefits from cold stratification.
directions: Sow Canada wild rye in fall or early spring, pressing seed into contact with bare soil no more than a quarter inch deep. This fast-establishing native cool-season grass is a favorite nurse crop, holding slopes against erosion while slower prairie species take hold. Its arching, feathery seed heads feed birds and add graceful movement to naturalized plantings. Water during establishment, then let it fend for itself as a hardy, largely maintenance-free perennial.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 4–8 weeks before the first hard frost so plants establish a strong rosette before winter; winter canola overwinters as a low rosette and resumes rapid growth and flowering in spring, typically terminated or harvested in late spring.
directions: Drill seed 1/2–1 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; establish well before hard frost, since a strong rosette is essential for winter survival. Canola is a low-erucic-acid cultivated form of Brassica napus, grown both as an oilseed cash crop and as a deep-taprooted cover crop that scavenges nitrogen, breaks up compacted subsoil, and adds substantial organic matter ahead of a following summer crop. In spring, the overwintered rosette bolts rapidly and produces tall stems topped with abundant small yellow flowers that are highly attractive to honeybees and other pollinators during an otherwise thin nectar period, making it a valuable dual-purpose planting for growers interested in both soil building and pollinator forage. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or incorporation before or at flowering if grown strictly as a cover crop, since the residue becomes fibrous and slow to break down once the plant sets seed. Zone 5–9.

common_name: Caribbean Stylo (Carib Stylo, Hamata Stylosanthes, Pencil Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow in full sun in lean, well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil; Stylosanthes hamata is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-adapted legume groundcovers for zone 9-12, widely used throughout the Caribbean and tropical Americas for range improvement, erosion control, and nitrogen fixation in poor, dry, sandy soils where most other groundcovers fail to establish. Very low growing (6–18 inches), it spreads laterally and self-seeds freely. The small yellow-orange pea flowers are produced almost continuously through the warm months and attract small native bees. In zone 9, the plant may be killed by hard frosts but often reseeds itself the following spring in appropriate conditions.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any lean, well-drained, sandy, or gravelly soil — Caribbean Stylo establishes readily in poor, dry conditions and is one of the most useful, low-maintenance leguminous groundcovers available for zone 9-12 landscapes with challenging, infertile, dry soils. Stylosanthes hamata is a low-growing, semi-erect, annual to perennial herbaceous legume in the Fabaceae family (tribe Aeschynomeneae) native to the Caribbean, Mexico, Central and South America — widely distributed through the tropical Americas in open, sunny, dry, disturbed grassland and savanna habitats. The plant produces slender, branching stems bearing small, trifoliate leaves with narrow leaflets and, through the warm months, tiny (0.25-inch) yellow to orange-yellow flowers in small clusters. As a legume, Stylosanthes hamata fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis, steadily improving the fertility of poor, sandy soils over time. Widely used in tropical range management and pasture improvement throughout the Caribbean, Australia, and tropical Africa for its ability to establish in degraded, dry, sandy range land where more demanding forages will not survive. In zone 9-12 ornamental gardens, Caribbean Stylo serves as a drought-tolerant, nitrogen-fixing groundcover for difficult, sunny, dry areas — roadsides, slopes, and sandy fills — and produces a season-long display of small yellow flowers attractive to native bees and small pollinators. Self-seeds freely to maintain coverage. Non-toxic.

common_name: Centro (Trailing Centro, Common Butterfly Pea Vine)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; centro is a trailing, twining tropical South American legume cover crop widely used in tropical pasture improvement and as a soil-covering, nitrogen-fixing companion plant in tropical plantation agriculture — it is distinct from Clitoria ternatea (blue butterfly pea) despite a similar common name.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 3–5 lbs per acre in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; centro establishes a persistent perennial groundcover in the tropics. Centrosema pubescens (centro or trailing centro) is a sprawling, twining legume vine from tropical South America that has been introduced throughout the tropics as a versatile cover crop and pasture improvement plant. It is widely established in Australia, Southeast Asia, and Africa as a component of improved tropical pastures, where it provides high-protein forage and fixes nitrogen alongside tropical grasses. The plant produces trifoliate leaves and attractive lavender-to-white butterfly-shaped flowers (similar in appearance to those of Clitoria ternatea but botanically distinct — Centrosema is a different genus). As a cover crop in tropical zone 10–12 gardens and plantations, centro is perennial and persistent, forming a trailing groundcover that suppresses weeds and continuously fixes nitrogen through the warm season. It tolerates moderate shade under tree canopies and can be grown in mixed plantings. Seed should be inoculated with appropriate Bradyrhizobium strains before sowing for best nitrogen fixation.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed in early to mid-fall into a firm, weed-free seedbed. Works well on thin, stony, or alkaline soils where other legumes struggle.
directions: Sow seed directly into a firm seedbed in early fall at a rate of 40-60 lbs per acre, covering seed 1-2 inches deep. Chickling vetch establishes a deep taproot that breaks up compacted layers and scavenges nutrients from subsoil. Terminate before or at flowering in spring by mowing or rolling to maximize nitrogen release to the following crop. Avoid allowing seed to mature and shatter, as the plant can self-sow aggressively in subsequent seasons.

plant_note: Inoculate seeds with appropriate Rhizobium bacteria before sowing in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cicer milkvetch requires the specific inoculant (cowpea group will NOT work) to fix nitrogen effectively. It is slow to establish in year one but becomes very productive in years 2–3. It spreads aggressively by rhizomes and may outcompete other cover crop species in mixed stands.
directions: Direct-sow (properly inoculated) in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cicer milkvetch is a perennial legume from Europe and western Asia that has been developed as a drought-tolerant, cold-hardy perennial cover crop and forage plant for the northern Great Plains and intermountain West, where its ability to persist for many years without reseeding offers major advantages over annual cover crop legumes. It fixes nitrogen through rhizobial symbiosis, spreads by rhizomes to form dense, weed-suppressing stands, and tolerates drought and alkaline soils that defeat most legume cover crops. The small, cream-white to pale-yellow pea flowers attract bumblebees and native bees. Unlike many legumes that are annual or biennial, cicer milkvetch can persist and actively fix nitrogen for 10–15 years in appropriate conditions. It is used extensively for rangeland improvement, roadside erosion control, and perennial cover in dryland farming systems of the West. The seed requires a specific Rhizobium inoculant strain to achieve effective nitrogen fixation — purchase and apply the correct inoculant at planting.

common_name: Common Bermudagrass (Warm-Season Sun-Loving Turf and Pasture Grass)
plant_note: Direct sow hulled bermudagrass seed at 1–2 lbs/1000 sq ft in late spring when soil is consistently above 65°F; use a drop spreader for even distribution and drag or rake lightly to achieve 0.125 inch coverage. In zone 9, seed April–June. Bermudagrass can also be established by sprigs or sod of improved hybrid varieties (Tifway 419, Tifblair, Celebration) that do not produce viable seed. Common bermudagrass from seed is less uniform but less expensive than hybrid types.
directions: Broadcast hulled seed at 1–2 lbs per 1,000 sq ft and rake lightly; maintain consistent moisture during germination. Mow at 0.5–1.5 inches for turf use. Common bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) is one of the most widely grown warm-season grasses in the world — an aggressive, fine-textured perennial grass that forms dense turf and pasture cover throughout the southern United States, where it is both the most important utility grass and the most problematic weed in garden beds. The same aggressive stolon-and-rhizome growth habit that makes bermudagrass an excellent erosion-control, pasture, and athletic turf grass also makes it notoriously difficult to eradicate from garden beds where it has established — a practical reality every Gulf South gardener learns quickly. Bermudagrass requires full sun (will not persist in shade), tolerates heat, drought, and heavy foot traffic better than almost any other grass, recovers rapidly from damage and wear, and goes straw-brown dormant during winter but greens up again reliably in spring. The key distinction between common bermudagrass (from seed) and hybrid bermudagrasses (Tifway 419, Celebration, Latitude 36, etc.) is that common types are more variable in texture and quality, while improved hybrids offer finer texture, denser growth, and better disease resistance but must be established vegetatively.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; a fast summer cover crop terminated before it sets seed.
directions: A fast-growing warm-season cover crop that smothers weeds, scavenges phosphorus, and improves soil health even in poor ground. Broadcast or drill seed after the last frost onto a firm, moist seedbed and rake in lightly. It grows quickly and blooms within a month, attracting pollinators and beneficial insects. Mow or cut it down at first flower before seed sets to prevent volunteers, then leave the residue as a nutrient-rich mulch.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 8–9) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy soil in full sun; oats are one of the most widely used cool-season cover crops in the South and Mid-Atlantic — fast-establishing, winter-hardy (though killed by hard freezes below 10–20°F, leaving behind weed-suppressing mulch), and excellent for building organic matter before spring planting.
directions: Broadcast or drill at 2–3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in fall; mow or incorporate in spring before planting summer crops. Avena sativa (common oat or cereal oat) is one of the world's most important cereal grain crops and one of the most widely used cool-season cover crops across North America. As a grain crop, oats are distinguished by their extraordinarily high soluble fiber (beta-glucan) content, which has been clinically demonstrated to reduce LDL cholesterol — making oat consumption one of the most evidence-based dietary interventions for cardiovascular health. Steel-cut oats, rolled oats, and oat flour are kitchen staples worldwide. As a cover crop in zone 6–10, oats are outstanding for fall planting: they establish quickly in cool weather, grow vigorously to 2–4 feet, suppress weeds effectively through the winter, and are either winter-killed by hard freezes (leaving a weed-suppressing mulch that requires no tillage to terminate — a self-terminating cover crop) or mowed down in spring before summer planting. Oats also scavenge residual soil nitrogen, preventing leaching over winter. In zone 8–9, oats typically winter-kill at temperatures below 15–20°F, providing a built-in termination; in milder areas, mow or incorporate before heading. Mix with hairy vetch or field peas for a nitrogen-fixing, carbon-building combination cover crop.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost; common vetch is slightly more cold-tolerant than crimson clover and grows in poorer soils than hairy vetch.
directions: Sow inoculated seed at 40–50 lb per acre (about 1 oz per 20 sq ft) in fall, raking to 1/2 in depth; common vetch tolerates sandy, low-fertility soils where hairy vetch may struggle and establishes a climbing, vining habit that benefits from a grass companion for support. It fixes 80–120 lb of nitrogen per acre over winter and spring and is easier to terminate than hairy vetch because the vines are thinner and dry down faster. Mow at early bloom before pods swell to prevent reseeding; the narrow tendriled stems break down readily and release nitrogen within 2–3 weeks.

common_name: Creeping Tick Trefoil (Beggar Weed, Creeping Tick Clover)
plant_note: Broadcast seeds in spring or early summer in well-drained, sandy to loamy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; creeping tick trefoil is a naturalized warm-season legume that volunteers readily in Gulf Coast lawns, pastures, and disturbed areas, fixing nitrogen and providing ground cover through summer months.
directions: Broadcast seeds in spring in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; established plants spread by creeping stems and self-seeding. Desmodium incanum (creeping tick trefoil or beggar weed) is a low-growing, sprawling, tropical and subtropical legume that has naturalized widely across the Gulf Coastal Plain, Florida, and the Caribbean — commonly seen as a lawn 'weed' in zone 9 but increasingly recognized as a valuable warm-season nitrogen-fixing groundcover and cover crop for challenging sites. The plant produces small, clover-like, three-leaflet leaves on trailing stems and small, pink to lavender pea-like flowers in loose racemes from spring through fall, followed by flat seed pods with small segments that adhere to clothing and fur (the 'beggar weed' or 'tick' name). As a low-input cover crop, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root symbiosis, tolerates drought and poor soil, and provides pollinator support with its small flowers. In tropical and subtropical pasture systems, it is used as a legume component of grass-legume mixtures for soil improvement. Note: the sticky seed pods make it unsuitable near recreation areas where clothing contamination is unwanted.

plant_note: Broadcast seed in late summer to early fall (6–4 weeks before first frost) in zones 6–10; in zone 5, sow earlier in late summer to allow sufficient establishment before hard frost. Inoculate seed with Rhizobium leguminosarum trifolii for maximum nitrogen fixation.
directions: Broadcast seed in late summer or early fall onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in full sun at 15–25 lbs per acre; crimson clover germinates rapidly in warm fall soil and overwinters as a low rosette, then bolts to produce spectacular, elongated, bright-crimson flower heads in spring that are exceptionally attractive to honeybees, bumble bees, and many species of native bees. Terminate by mowing or tillage in spring before or at early bloom to maximize the nitrogen credit to the following crop; the stand naturally winterkills above zone 6 and can be managed as a spring-terminated annual in zones 7–9. Fixes 75–200 lbs of atmospheric nitrogen per acre depending on stand density and termination timing, making it one of the highest nitrogen-fixing annual cover crops available. Do not allow seed set before incorporation or it will become a weedy reseeder in subsequent crops.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to fall for overwintering, or early spring in cold regions.
directions: Crimson clover is a nitrogen-fixing legume cover crop that enriches soil and produces showy crimson flowers loved by bees. Broadcast seed onto prepared soil in fall for overwintering or in early spring, raking in lightly for good contact. Let it grow to bloom, then mow and turn it under a few weeks before planting to release nitrogen and add organic matter. Distinct from perennial red clover, it grows quickly and is easy to incorporate into rotations.

plant_note: Scarify or soak seed overnight before direct sowing in spring into any well-drained, sunny site; inoculate with appropriate Rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. WARNING: Crown vetch is listed as invasive in numerous US states and should not be planted near natural areas, woodland edges, or native plant communities.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil — crown vetch is exceptionally adaptable to poor, dry, rocky, or compacted soils and requires virtually no maintenance once established; it was widely planted for highway slope stabilization and erosion control throughout the 20th century and is extremely effective at holding disturbed soil. The dense, spreading mats of pinnate foliage bear clusters of small pink-and-white pea flowers throughout summer that are attractive to bees. INVASIVE WARNING: Crown vetch spreads aggressively by both rhizome and seed and is now listed as invasive or a noxious weed in many US states, where it smothers native vegetation in woodland margins, old fields, and natural areas. Do not plant within a quarter mile of natural areas, forest edges, or native plant communities. Consider native alternatives for erosion control such as Virginia wild rye (Elymus virginicus), wild ginger (Asarum canadense), or prairie dropseed (Sporobolus heterolepis).

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; crown vetch spreads aggressively by rhizomes and self-seeding — excellent for erosion control on steep slopes but invasive in natural areas in some states.
directions: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; scarify seeds by nicking or soaking overnight to improve germination, and inoculate with Rhizobium leguminosarum for maximum nitrogen fixation. Coronilla varia is a European leguminous perennial widely planted in North America for highway and railroad bank erosion control due to its vigorous spreading habit, nitrogen fixation, and drought tolerance; it produces pinnate leaves on sprawling, vining stems and clusters of pink-to-white, pea-like flowers from late spring through summer. It is highly invasive in natural areas in much of the US and should NOT be planted near natural habitats; it is best restricted to permanently disturbed, high-maintenance sites such as highway cuts and steep slopes where its aggressive spreading is an asset. Fixes 75–150 lb N/acre when well-established.

plant_note: Sow in spring or early fall; a hardy perennial ground cover.
directions: Scatter Dutch white clover thinly over raked soil in spring or early fall and press in for good seed-to-soil contact, keeping the surface moist until it sprouts. This low-growing perennial legume spreads by creeping stems to form a durable living ground cover that fixes nitrogen and crowds out weeds. It thrives as a lawn companion, orchard understory, or pathway cover and tolerates light foot traffic. Mow occasionally to keep it tidy and encourage dense growth.

common_name: Dwarf Essex Rape (Winter Forage Brassica Cover Crop, Classic Deer Food Plot Variety)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer/early fall (August–September in zone 9) for fall-winter production; Dwarf Essex Rape germinates rapidly in warm-to-cool soil and establishes quickly, reaching palatable size for deer and livestock in 45–60 days. In zone 9, plant August–September for October through February grazing. The plant is a brassica (related to cabbage and turnip) and produces abundant, nutrient-rich foliage that becomes more palatable after the first frost sweetens the leaves — brassicas convert starches to sugars in response to cold, which significantly improves palatability. At 45–60 days, the established plants produce a dense canopy of dark green leaves eaten heavily by deer; after initial grazing, plants regrow and continue producing through winter. Dwarf Essex Rape is not a perennial — it completes its life cycle in one season and must be reseeded annually.
directions: Broadcast at 5–7 lbs/acre (2–3 lbs/1000 sq ft) in late summer; expect first grazing in 45–60 days. Dwarf Essex Rape (Brassica napus 'Dwarf Essex') is one of the foundational winter forage and cover crop brassica varieties, widely used in food plot management, livestock grazing, and cool-season cover crop systems throughout the southeastern United States. 'Rape' refers to the crop group (from Latin rapa, meaning turnip), of which canola is the most commercially prominent member; Dwarf Essex is a forage-type selection rather than an oilseed type, producing abundant leaf biomass at a shorter, more compact height (18–30 inches) compared to standard rape varieties (which can exceed 4 feet). The 'Dwarf Essex' selection specifically was identified for its compact growth, good palatability, high leaf-to-stem ratio (important for forage quality), and rapid establishment that suits deer food plot and winter cover crop applications. In the Gulf South, Dwarf Essex Rape fills an important niche in winter rotation schedules: it establishes rapidly in late summer when heat is still present, provides rapidly-available winter forage in the critical October–December period when natural browse quality declines, and continues producing through mild Gulf South winters. The combination of rapid establishment, high nutritional value, palatability after frost, and minimal input requirements has made Dwarf Essex Rape one of the most widely planted cool-season food plot varieties in the southeastern United States for several decades.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–June. Egyptian Riverhemp is a fast-growing, warm-season legume used as a green manure, forage crop, and soil improvement cover crop in tropical and subtropical regions. Scarify seeds (nick seed coat or soak in hot water for 30 minutes) to improve germination rate from the naturally hard seed coat. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, inoculate seed with appropriate Rhizobium inoculant before planting for maximum N-fixation. Plants grow extremely fast — reaching 6–10 feet in 60–90 days in zone 9 — making rapid canopy cover and high biomass production for incorporation or cutting. Chop and incorporate into soil before seed set to prevent naturalization; it is potentially invasive in wetlands.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in moist to moderately well-drained, low-fertility soil — Sesbania sesban is adapted to waterlogged, flooded, and poor soils where most other cover crops fail; inoculate seed with appropriate Rhizobium before planting; Egyptian Riverhemp is one of the fastest-growing and most productive warm-season nitrogen-fixing cover crops available for tropical and subtropical climates — capable of producing 5–10 tons of dry biomass per acre per season and fixing 100–200 pounds of nitrogen per acre when properly inoculated, making it among the most efficient green manure crops for improving depleted soils in zone 9 and the tropical belt. The rapid growth rate — reaching 6–10 feet in 60–90 days — produces a dense, shading canopy that suppresses weeds effectively while simultaneously building organic matter and fixing atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Rhizobium bacteria. The combination of nitrogen fixation, rapid biomass production, weed suppression, and adaptation to waterlogged and flooded soils that defeat other cover crops makes Sesbania sesban one of the most valuable green manure crops for difficult, wet, low-fertility subtropical soils. Chop and incorporate the green material 60–90 days after sowing, before seed set — the succulent stems and leaves decompose rapidly, releasing nitrogen and organic matter into the soil within 2–4 weeks of incorporation.

common_name: Elbon Rye (Gulf South Winter Cover Crop Rye, Nematode-Suppressive Annual)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall; Elbon rye germinates readily in cool soil (even 34°F) and grows vigorously through Gulf South winters when other cover crops falter. In zone 9, plant September–November for a December–March growing period. Elbon is notable for being developed specifically for the Gulf South's mild winters — unlike northern-adapted rye varieties that may over-winter poorly or behave differently in zone 9's warm-enough winters, Elbon was selected for performance in Louisiana, Texas, and neighboring states. Elbon rye releases glucosinolates as the biomass breaks down, which have demonstrated nematode-suppressive effects — making Elbon a valuable cover crop in rotation before susceptible crops like tomatoes and peppers in zone 9 nematode-management programs. Terminate by rolling, mowing, or incorporation 2–3 weeks before planting the following crop.
directions: Broadcast seed at 100–120 lbs/acre (1.5–2 lbs/1000 sq ft) in fall; mow or roll-crimp before spring vegetable planting. Elbon Rye is a cultivar of cereal rye (Secale cereale) that was developed at Texas A&M University specifically for performance in the Gulf Coast and mid-South region — a region where most northern rye varieties were developed for colder conditions and where Elbon performs more consistently under mild-winter Gulf South conditions. Cereal rye is one of the most cold-tolerant cover crops available, germinating in temperatures as low as 34°F and growing slowly but continuously through cool winters, making it one of the few cover crops that can provide meaningful biomass accumulation during Gulf South winters. Elbon's specific adaptation to southern latitudes — earlier tillering, better performance under mild winter temperatures, and good late-winter biomass accumulation — makes it the preferred cereal rye variety in Texas and Louisiana extension service cover crop recommendations. The dense, fibrous root system of Elbon rye provides significant soil structure benefits: deep roots break up compacted layers, capture and hold nitrogen leached from soil by winter rains, and add substantial organic matter when incorporated. The aboveground biomass acts as a mulch that suppresses weeds, moderates soil temperature, and reduces erosion. The nematode-suppressive properties, documented particularly against root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.), make Elbon rye particularly valuable as a pre-tomato or pre-pepper cover crop in zone 9 where nematode pressure is a significant yield-limiting factor.

plant_note: Sow in fall as a winter annual in mild climates or spring in cold climates; emmer is a hulled wheat requiring special threshing or purchase of pre-hulled grain for milling — factor this into production planning.
directions: Drill or broadcast at 90–120 lbs per acre in fall for winter growth or early spring in cold climates in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; emmer wheat (the farro medio of Italian cuisine) is one of humanity's oldest cultivated grains, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent around 10,000 BC and still grown in Ethiopia, Italy, and the Near East where it is prized for a nutty, complex flavor and high nutritional value including higher protein and fiber than modern wheat. It is a hulled grain — the hull adheres tightly and must be removed by specialized processing; purchase pre-hulled or 'pearled' emmer for cooking, or grow it as an attractive ornamental grain. Highly disease-resistant, drought-tolerant, and productive on poor, rocky soils where modern wheat struggles.

plant_note: Sow in late spring or summer; it is more heat tolerant than other mustards.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.25-0.5 lb per 1,000 sq ft and rake to cover roughly 0.25 inch deep in warm soil. Ethiopian mustard is more heat and drought tolerant than white or brown mustard, making it useful for summer biofumigation windows. Its high glucosinolate content suppresses nematodes and soilborne pathogens when the biomass is chopped and incorporated. Mow or flail at early flowering and immediately work the residue into moist soil, then irrigate or roll to seal the surface. Wait two to three weeks before planting a sensitive crop into the treated bed.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or fall in mild climates; cold hardy to the low twenties.
directions: Inoculate with faba-bean rhizobia and sow large seed 2-3 inches deep at about 4-6 inches apart in rows or broadcast heavily. Faba beans are upright legumes that fix large amounts of nitrogen and improve soil structure with their sturdy taproots. They tolerate cool weather and wet soils, making them a strong early-spring green manure in temperate gardens. Terminate by mowing or cutting at early flowering when nitrogen fixation is greatest, then incorporate the succulent stems into the soil. Allow two to three weeks for decomposition before planting a following crop.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 9) in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Austrian winter pea is a fast-growing, winter-hardy cover crop that fixes 60–150 lbs nitrogen per acre and creates substantial biomass for spring incorporation.
directions: Broadcast or drill seeds in fall at 2–4 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; inoculate seeds with rhizobium inoculant before planting for maximum nitrogen fixation. Pisum sativum ssp. arvense (Austrian winter pea or field pea) is one of the premier cool-season cover crops for the Gulf South and Southeast — a winter-annual legume that germinates quickly in fall, grows vigorously through the mild zone 9 winter, and can be terminated and incorporated in spring to release 100 lbs or more of biologically fixed nitrogen per acre as green manure. Unlike garden peas, field peas are grown for soil improvement rather than harvest (though young shoots and pods are edible). They are commonly mixed with cereal rye or oats as a winter cover-crop cocktail: the pea climbs the grain stems, which support the vines; the grain adds carbon while the pea adds nitrogen; together they create a thick, weed-suppressing, moisture-retaining cover. Terminate by mowing or rolling before flowering if retaining seed is a concern. In zone 9, fall sowing from September through November is ideal; the plants may succumb to hard freezes below 18°F but survive typical zone 9 winters with ease.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep in fall 6–10 weeks before first frost, or in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost; field pea requires cool soil (below 65°F) to germinate well and performs best as a fall-sown winter annual in the Gulf South.
directions: Field pea (Austrian winter pea) is the premier cool-season legume cover crop for the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, providing rapid establishment, heavy nitrogen fixation, and excellent biomass production during the mild Gulf South winter when most cover crops struggle. Planted in fall, it overwinters as a cold-hardy vine, fixes 50–150 pounds of atmospheric nitrogen per acre, and produces 2–4 tons of organic matter per acre by the time it is terminated in spring — a nitrogen contribution equivalent to a full pre-plant fertilizer application that is released slowly as the biomass decomposes. The trailing vines suppress winter weeds effectively and the purple-pink flowers attract native bees in late winter and spring when few other plants are blooming; the tender vine tips are edible by humans, livestock, and wildlife. In zone 8–10, field peas can be planted as early as September for maximum winter biomass; terminate by mowing or rolling in spring 2–4 weeks before planting summer crops to allow nitrogen release.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before frost in fall, or in earliest spring; nitrogen-fixing and edible tender shoots.
directions: Sow inoculated seed about 1 in deep, often mixed with oats or rye for support. The vines fix nitrogen and produce edible pea shoots you can harvest before turning the crop under. Terminate at flowering for the best nitrogen contribution.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed in early to mid-fall into a prepared seedbed; the crop overwinters as a rosette and resumes rapid growth in early spring.
directions: Field Pennycress is a fast-growing winter annual cover crop naturalized throughout North America, valued for its ability to establish quickly in cool fall soils, suppress weeds through dense canopy coverage, and provide some of the earliest spring pollen and nectar available to emerging bees when almost nothing else is blooming. It is also being actively developed by University of Minnesota researchers as a high-oil oilseed crop for sustainable aviation fuel and other bioproducts, making it a cover crop with commercial upside potential. Sow seed in fall by broadcasting at 5-8 lb per acre into a firm seedbed; the plants overwinter as low rosettes and bolt to flower in April-May before ceasing growth. Terminate by mowing or rolling before seed set if you want to prevent naturalization, or allow some seed set to encourage re-establishment the following fall.

common_name: Florida Beggarweed (Twisted Desmodium, Beggarweed, Tick Trefoil)
plant_note: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, sandy to loamy soil; Florida Beggarweed grows naturally in sandy, sunny, disturbed ground throughout the Gulf Coast and Southeast and will often establish from wild seed in garden areas — it is frequently encountered as a beneficial volunteer rather than a planted crop. As a native annual legume, it fixes nitrogen, provides wildlife habitat (seeds eaten by quail and doves), and produces nectar for pollinators. The flat, segmented seed pods attach to clothing and animal fur (the 'beggar' quality) — plant away from high-traffic walkways.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, lean soil — Florida Beggarweed establishes most vigorously in open, sunny, sandy conditions and is a natural component of zone 8-12 Gulf Coast gardens that forms spontaneously in appropriate conditions. Desmodium tortuosum is a tall, annual to biennial legume native to Florida, the Gulf Coast states, the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central America in the Fabaceae family — one of the most ecologically valuable and practically useful native legumes for zone 8-12 gardens, historically grown as a 'forage crop' and soil-improving summer green manure throughout the southeastern US and recognized increasingly as a valuable native plant for wildlife and pollinator gardens. The plant produces upright, branching stems 3–6 feet tall with trifoliate leaves and, in summer and fall, clusters of small, typical legume flowers in pink to rose-purple that attract native bees, honeybees, and butterflies. As a legume, Florida Beggarweed fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis, improving sandy, depleted soils over the growing season. The flat, segmented seed pods ('loments') that mature in fall readily attach to animal fur and clothing — dispersing seeds wide and far, which explains the plant's wide natural distribution and common name. The seeds are an important wildlife food source — consumed heavily by bobwhite quail, doves, wild turkeys, and seed-eating songbirds throughout the fall and winter. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; the deep taproot loosens compacted soil.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.1-0.2 lb per 1,000 sq ft onto a firm, weed-free seedbed and rake to a shallow 0.25 inch depth. Forage chicory is a deep-rooted perennial that mines nutrients from the subsoil, breaks up compaction, and provides mineral-rich forage and pollinator bloom when allowed to flower. It establishes as a rosette the first year and bolts in following seasons. Manage as a living cover by mowing to prevent flowering, or terminate by tillage or cutting the crown below the soil surface. Because it is persistent, mow or till before seed set to keep it from spreading beyond the intended area.

plant_note: Sow in late summer so plants bulk up before cold weather slows growth.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.2-0.4 lb per 1,000 sq ft and rake to cover 0.25 inch deep in a firm, fertile seedbed. Forage kale produces large amounts of leafy biomass and a fibrous root system that scavenges nitrogen and improves soil structure. It is very cold hardy and stays green well into winter, providing living cover and weed suppression during the cool season. Terminate by mowing or grazing before it bolts in spring, then incorporate the residue with light tillage. In colder zones repeated hard freezes may winterkill the crop, easing termination.

plant_note: Sow 6–10 weeks before first frost; produces a large, soil-penetrating taproot that winter-kills in cold climates, leaving a decomposed channel.
directions: Broadcast seed at 8–10 lb/acre or drill at 6–7 lb/acre and cover to 1/4 in depth; forage radish emerges quickly and develops a taproot up to 18 in deep that fractures compacted subsoil and scavenges nitrates before they leach. In USDA zones 5 and colder the taproot reliably winter-kills, leaving a hollow channel that improves spring drainage and air porosity. Where winters are mild, mow the rosette before it bolts in spring to avoid a weedy seed bank. The decomposing roots have a pungent sulfur smell for 1–2 weeks after freeze-kill — this is normal.

plant_note: Sow after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F; drill or broadcast into a well-prepared seedbed for maximum biomass production before mowing or grazing.
