directions: Drill seed 3/4–1 inch deep into warm, fertile soil in full sun; forage sorghum grows taller and leafier than grain sorghum or sorghum-sudangrass hybrids, commonly reaching 8–15 feet, and is grown specifically for maximum tonnage as silage, green chop, or hay rather than grain or a fast-terminating cover. It is deeply drought-tolerant once established thanks to an extensive root system, making it valuable for building organic matter and suppressing weeds in hot, dry summer conditions where many other warm-season cover crops struggle. Mow or graze at 3–4 feet to encourage tillering and repeated cutting, and allow several weeks for the heavy residue to break down before planting a following crop into it. Note that young, frost-stressed, or drought-stunted sorghum can accumulate prussic acid (cyanogenic compounds) and should not be grazed immediately after a frost or severe drought stress — wait several days and check tissue before turning out livestock.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast after last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; forage-type soybean varieties are bred for maximum leafy biomass and re-growth after grazing or mowing rather than for grain yield.
directions: Drill inoculated seed 1–1.5 inches deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; forage soybean grows quickly into a dense, leafy, nitrogen-fixing summer cover, producing substantially more biomass and better regrowth after cutting or grazing than standard grain soybean varieties, which are bred to concentrate resources into seed rather than leaf and stem growth. It is widely used as a high-protein warm-season grazing and hay crop, as a deer and wildlife food-plot planting, and as a soil-building green manure that can be mowed and incorporated multiple times through the summer before a fall cover crop or cash crop follows. Its rapid growth and dense canopy also suppress weeds effectively during the hottest part of the growing season. A productive, multi-purpose warm-season legume for pasture, wildlife, or soil-building use, zone 4–10.

plant_note: Sow 6–10 weeks before first frost; forage turnip produces heavy leaf canopy that smothers weeds and a fleshy taproot that winterkills to release nutrients.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 1–2 lb/acre and cover to 1/4 in depth; forage turnip is faster-maturing and less prone to overwintering than oilseed radish, making it a reliable fall cover where a quick canopy is needed. It scavenges residual nitrogen and suppresses winter annual weeds under its broad leaves. The bulbous root winter-kills in hard frost zones and decomposes rapidly, releasing stored nutrients at planting time. In mild climates it may overwinter and bolt in spring — mow before flowering to prevent volunteer seedlings in subsequent crops.

plant_note: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm before sowing this heat-loving annual.
directions: Broadcast at roughly 0.5-1 lb per 1,000 sq ft and rake to cover about 0.5 inch deep in warm, firm soil. Foxtail millet is exceptionally drought tolerant and matures quickly, making it ideal for filling short summer windows between cash crops. Its fibrous roots improve soil tilth while the dense canopy shades out weeds. Mow before the seed heads harden to prevent reseeding, then incorporate or leave the residue as surface mulch. In cold regions frost will terminate any remaining plants at season's end.

plant_note: Direct-sow in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; French honeysuckle is a Mediterranean biennial that is sown in fall, overwinters as a rosette (surviving light freezes to about 15°F), and flowers in spring. In mild climates (zone 7+) it performs reliably as a cool-season cover crop and winter green manure. It fixes nitrogen abundantly and the fragrant flowers are outstanding bee forage.
directions: Direct-sow in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; French honeysuckle is a biennial Mediterranean legume grown both as a cover crop and as an ornamental, producing brilliant crimson-red, intensely fragrant pea flowers in late spring — striking enough that it was a highly fashionable cottage garden flower in 17th and 18th century Europe, prized for its intense sweet fragrance and vivid color. Known as 'sulla' in Italy and the Mediterranean, it is an important forage crop for sheep and cattle in Mediterranean countries. As a cover crop it fixes substantial nitrogen, tolerates alkaline and chalky soils, and provides outstanding early-spring bee forage with its fragrant nectar-rich flowers. The foliage is ornamental, with broadly pinnate, blue-green leaves. It is outstanding for zones 6–9 as a fall-sown winter annual or biennial that flowers in late spring and then is tilled in as green manure before summer vegetables are planted. More ornamental than most cover crops, it can be grown in flower borders as well as vegetable gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or clay-loam, lean soil in full sun; galleta grass spreads readily by rhizomes once established, forming a dense sod. Can be difficult to establish from seed — seeding into moist seed beds immediately after rains or irrigation gives best results.
directions: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or clay-loam, lean soil in full sun; galleta grass is the dominant sod-forming native grass of the Colorado Plateau, Navajo Nation lands, and Great Basin desert — the characteristic grass of the wide, flat, hard, often alkaline or clay-rich desert floors and mesa tops of the intermountain West. Spreads aggressively by rhizomes to form dense, low-growing turf that suppresses weeds and resists erosion on dry, hard-packed ground. The wiry, stiff stems and semi-rolled leaves are adaptations to the extreme drought, cold, wind, and alkaline conditions of the Colorado Plateau. An essential component of Great Basin desert restoration seed mixes for reclaiming disturbed desert soils, roadsides, and mine spoils. The deep rhizome network provides exceptional erosion control on dry, exposed slopes. Highly important as forage for livestock, pronghorn, and mule deer across the vast piñon-juniper and sagebrush rangelands.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; giant wild rye is one of the most shade-tolerant of the large native grasses of the West Coast — growing naturally under oak woodland canopies and in partial shade of chaparral margins along the California coast and foothills.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; giant wild rye is the largest and most dramatic of the native California bunchgrasses — a massive, clump-forming cool-season grass from the coastal bluffs, oak woodlands, and chaparral margins of California and Baja California. Producing broad, blue-gray-green leaves and towering seed stalks 6–8 feet tall in early summer, it creates an impressive, architectural presence in the landscape. One of the few large native grasses tolerating partial shade — growing naturally under the dappled canopy of coast live oak and blue oak woodlands. The cultivar 'Canyon Prince' (a dwarf, silver-blue form selected from Santa Cruz Island) is widely grown in California native plant gardens for its compact size and striking silver-blue foliage color. Extremely drought tolerant once established — summer-dormant in dry-summer California climates. An essential large ornamental grass for California native plant gardens, coastal bluff restorations, and dry-shade situations under oaks where conventional grasses and groundcovers struggle.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zone 9) or very early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; camelina is a cool-season oilseed brassica relative that germinates in near-freezing temperatures, grows rapidly, and matures a seed crop in 75–110 days — useful as a short-season winter annual oilseed or cover crop.
directions: Broadcast or drill seeds at 0.25–0.5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; camelina establishes rapidly and needs little management. Camelina sativa (gold of pleasure or false flax) is an ancient European oilseed crop from the brassica family — known to have been cultivated in Europe since the Bronze Age — that is experiencing a significant agricultural renaissance as a low-input winter cover crop, biofuel feedstock, and omega-3-rich nutritional oil. The seeds contain 35–40% oil with an exceptionally high omega-3 fatty acid content (35–40% linolenic acid) and an unusually long shelf life due to naturally high vitamin E (tocopherol) content; the oil is gaining recognition as a culinary and nutritional product. As a cover crop, camelina is notable for its extreme cold-hardiness (germinates above 35°F), exceptional drought tolerance, and ability to grow in poor, lean soils where most crops struggle. It is one of the few cover crops that can be grown in dry, high-altitude, or marginal soils as a productive cash crop or green manure. The small, shiny, golden-brown seeds are harvested in summer when the seed pods turn golden-tan.

common_name: Graza Radish (Multi-Branching Grazing and Tillage Radish Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow 6-10 weeks before first frost; Graza is an Australian-bred forage radish cultivar with a multi-branched, shallower root system than daikon-type tillage radishes, producing abundant leafy forage suited to grazing as well as soil-building.
directions: Broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep in late summer to early fall; Graza was bred in Australia specifically for dual use as livestock forage and a soil-building cover crop, with a more branched, fibrous root system than single-taproot daikon-type tillage radishes, along with abundant, fast-growing leafy top growth well suited to grazing or mowing for biomass. Its extensive root network still provides meaningful soil loosening and organic matter benefits, though with less of the single deep-drilling taproot effect of dedicated tillage radish cultivars like Groundhog. In zones cold enough for a hard freeze, the roots die back over winter, releasing captured nutrients as they decompose. In milder zones where the plant survives, mow or graze before it flowers and sets seed to prevent it becoming a volunteer weed in the following crop.

plant_note: Broadcast in spring in moist, acidic, wet meadow or bog edge soil; greater birdsfoot trefoil is specifically adapted to wet, peaty, acidic conditions where common birdsfoot trefoil (L. corniculatus) does poorly. Inoculate with appropriate Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. loti for good nitrogen fixation.
directions: Broadcast seed in wet to moist, acidic, peaty or heavy clay soils in full sun; greater birdsfoot trefoil fills the ecological niche of a legume adapted to wet, acidic, low-fertility conditions — exactly the situation where most other leguminous cover crops fail due to poor drainage or low pH. Unlike common birdsfoot trefoil (L. corniculatus) which prefers well-drained soil and neutral to alkaline pH, this species grows naturally in bogs, wet meadows, pond margins, and flushes with pH as low as 5.0. The yellow flowers in summer attract bumblebees and are important in semi-natural wet meadows. Fixes nitrogen even in poorly aerated, waterlogged soils where rhizobium populations are typically suppressed. Valuable for naturalizing wet, difficult areas as a nitrogen-building groundcover.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost when soil is warm; amaranth loves heat.
directions: Direct sow green garnet amaranth after the last frost into warm soil, barely covering the tiny seeds. Thin plants for grain heads or grow densely and cut young leaves as a spinach-like green or microgreen. This heat- and drought-tolerant heirloom shrugs off poor soil, producing tall stalks topped with feathery green seed heads that mature to gluten-free grain. Harvest seed when heads shatter easily and dry thoroughly before storing.

common_name: Groundhog Radish (Deep-Tillage Forage Radish Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow 6-10 weeks before first frost; Groundhog is a forage radish cultivar bred for an especially large, deep taproot that drills through compacted soil layers more aggressively than standard daikon-type tillage radish.
directions: Broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep in late summer to early fall; Groundhog is a forage radish cultivar selected for producing an especially large, thick, deeply penetrating taproot, even more aggressive at breaking through plow pans and compacted subsoil layers than standard daikon-type tillage radish. The huge root can grow a foot or more deep, drilling channels that improve water infiltration and root penetration for the following crop, while scavenging and holding nitrogen that would otherwise leach away over winter. In zones cold enough for a hard freeze, the roots die and rot in place over winter, leaving open channels and releasing captured nutrients as they decompose, so no spring tillage or herbicide termination is needed. In milder zones where the radish survives, mow before it flowers and sets seed to prevent it becoming a volunteer weed in the following crop.

plant_note: Sow after last frost in hot, dry climates; exceptional drought tolerance makes this the best legume cover for arid Southwest summers.
directions: Direct-sow inoculated seed 1 in deep at 20–30 lb/acre into warm, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed; guar is native to arid Asia and thrives in sandy, alkaline soils with limited irrigation. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and produces significant biomass even in drought conditions, making it invaluable in the semi-arid Southwest and high plains. Terminate by mowing at early pod formation before seed fully hardens; the dense residue builds organic matter in soils chronically short of it. Avoid waterlogged sites — standing water causes rapid root rot.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; hairy grama is one of the most drought-tolerant native grasses of the Great Plains and Southwest, tolerating more rocky and shallow soils than blue grama and extending into drier, rockier habitats.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; hairy grama is closely related to blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis) and often grows with it across the shortgrass prairies, mixed-grass prairies, and desert grasslands of the Great Plains and Southwest. Distinguished from blue grama by the conspicuous long awns (bristles) projecting beyond the tips of the seed head spikelets, giving the seed head a hairy or bushy appearance (hence 'hirsuta' = hairy). Like blue grama, the seed heads are held horizontally — parallel to the ground rather than upright — in the characteristic grama-grass posture. More tolerant of rocky, shallow, gravelly, and disturbed soils than blue grama, often colonizing road cuts, eroded slopes, and rocky outcrops where blue grama struggles. Important warm-season grass for dryland seed mixes, native lawn conversions, and erosion control on dry, rocky slopes across the Great Plains and Southwest. Highly palatable to livestock and deer when green.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds after last frost once soil warms above 70°F; hairy indigo establishes best on sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and benefits from inoculation with appropriate Indigofera rhizobia before planting.
directions: Hairy indigo is a tropical legume that has been widely used as a summer cover crop and green manure in Florida and the Gulf Coast region since the early 20th century, when it was introduced as a low-input nitrogen source for sandy, infertile soils typical of the Gulf Coastal Plain where cool-season legumes cannot grow. It fixes atmospheric nitrogen at rates of 60–100 pounds per acre, produces dense biomass that suppresses summer weeds, and tolerates the heat, drought, and low-fertility sandy soils of Gulf South gardens and fields that challenge other cover crops in the summer months. The small, pink to purple flowers attract native bees throughout the growing season, and established plants are very drought resistant once rooted, requiring no irrigation on well-drained sands. In organic vegetable gardens and orchards in zone 8–11, use hairy indigo as a summer understory cover crop between rows or in fallow beds July–September to build organic matter and nitrogen before fall vegetable planting; terminate by mowing or tilling 3–4 weeks before fall planting.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer to fall (August–October depending on zone) at 30–60 lb/acre (or 1–2 oz per 100 sq ft) in well-drained to moderately moist, average soil in full sun; always mix with a cereal grain companion (winter rye or oats at 50–70 lb/acre) to provide trellis support, and inoculate seed with vetch-type Rhizobium before sowing.
directions: Direct sow in late summer to fall (August–October depending on zone) at 30–60 lb/acre (or 1–2 oz per 100 sq ft) in well-drained to moderately moist, average soil in full sun; always mix with a cereal grain companion (winter rye or oats at 50–70 lb/acre) to provide trellis support, and inoculate seed with vetch-type Rhizobium before sowing. Vicia villosa (hairy vetch) is the workhorse of winter cover crops, capable of fixing 80–200 lb of nitrogen per acre per season and surviving winter temperatures to -15°F (-26°C) when well established; it has a vining, hairy habit and produces spectacular spikes of small, two-toned purple-and-white pea flowers in spring that are extremely attractive to bumblebees before termination. It is one of the best cover crops for building organic matter and suppressing spring weeds; terminate by crimping or incorporation at early bloom before pods set to maximize nitrogen release and prevent volunteer seedling problems in subsequent seasons.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast 4-6 weeks before the first killing frost to allow establishment before winter dormancy. Frequently seeded with a cereal rye companion to provide a trellis for the vining stems.
directions: Sow at 30-40 lbs per acre when grown alone, or 15-20 lbs per acre when mixed with a cereal rye companion, drilling seed 1-1.5 inches deep. Hairy vetch overwinters and resumes rapid growth in spring, producing a dense mat of biomass that can fix 80-200 lbs of nitrogen per acre by termination. Roll-crimp or mow the stand at 50% bloom in spring to create a thick weed-suppressing mulch for no-till cash crop transplanting or direct seeding. Manage carefully and terminate before seed set to prevent the plant from becoming a persistent weed in subsequent crops.

plant_note: Scarify or nick seeds before sowing to break the hard seed coat and improve germination; sow after last frost directly in place in moist to moderately moist soil.
directions: Hemp Sesbania is one of the fastest-growing native annuals in North America, capable of reaching 6 to 12 feet in a single warm season with long, pinnate leaves and small, yellow, pea-like flowers that attract native bees from summer through fall. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it builds soil fertility and produces exceptional biomass for use as a green manure when mowed or turned under before seed set. Scarify seeds by nicking or scuffing the seed coat before direct sowing after the last frost in moist, open ground in full sun. Cut or mow plants to the ground before seed pods ripen to prevent prolific self-seeding; incorporate the cut material into the soil as a rich green manure.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist to seasonally wet, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to sandy loam soil in full sun; hemp sesbania is a fast-growing tropical legume used as a summer green manure crop in South and Southeast Asian paddy rice systems — it grows rapidly, fixes large amounts of nitrogen, and is incorporated before rice planting to enrich the soil.
directions: Broadcast or drill seeds in warm, moist soil in full sun at 3–5 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; incorporate into the soil as a green manure before flowering for maximum nitrogen benefit. Sesbania cannabina (dhaincha or hemp sesbania) is a fast-growing, tropical Asian legume used as one of the most important green manure and cover crop species in paddy rice farming systems across South and Southeast Asia. In Bangladesh, India, and Southeast Asia, dhaincha is sown in flooded or waterlogged paddies before the rice crop — a location where most cover crops cannot survive, but where dhaincha thrives in saturated conditions. It grows to 4–6 feet in 60–90 days, fixing substantial nitrogen through root symbiosis with Rhizobium bacteria, and is then incorporated into the flooded paddy soil as a nitrogen-rich green manure that significantly reduces the need for synthetic fertilizers in rice production. The plant is also notable for fiber extraction — the stems yield strong, durable bast fiber (hence 'hemp sesbania') historically used for rope, jute bags, and paper production in South Asia. As a garden cover crop in zone 8–12, it is outstanding for wet, poorly drained, nitrogen-deficient soils where other legumes cannot grow.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; horseshoe vetch is a chalk and limestone grassland specialist and the sole larval food plant of the adonis blue and chalk hill blue butterflies.
directions: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, calcareous (chalky or limey) soil in full sun; horseshoe vetch is specialized for thin, alkaline soils and will not thrive on acidic or heavy soils — it is a chalk grassland plant in the truest sense. Hippocrepis comosa is a low-growing, mat-forming European native perennial legume of chalk and limestone grasslands, producing dense, pinnate foliage and clusters of bright-yellow, pea-like flowers in late spring that attract numerous butterfly species; its distinctive seed pods are shaped like a series of horseshoes connected in a chain, giving rise to the common name. It is the larval food plant of the adonis blue (Polyommatus bellargus) and chalk hill blue (Polyommatus coridon) butterflies and is a key component of chalk grassland restoration seed mixtures; it fixes nitrogen in thin, nutrient-poor, alkaline soils where most other nitrogen-fixers cannot compete.

plant_note: Drill in early to mid-fall on alkaline or calcareous soils where hairy vetch may underperform. Inoculate seed with the appropriate pea-vetch Rhizobium group before sowing.
directions: Drill seed 1-2 inches deep in early fall at 30-50 lbs per acre, applying a pea-vetch inoculant to ensure effective nitrogen fixation on soils with no prior vetch history. Hungarian vetch is particularly well suited to the alkaline, high-pH soils of continental European-style climates and performs reliably under conditions that limit other vetches. Terminate the stand in spring by mowing or incorporation before seed set to maximize nitrogen credit to the following crop. The pale pink to white flowers attract early-season pollinators before the crop is turned in.

plant_note: Scarify or nick seeds before sowing in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Illinois bundle-flower is drought-tolerant and fixes nitrogen as a legume. It is very slow to germinate and establish — patience is required in the first season. Once established, it is long-lived and increasingly productive. The seeds contain 38% crude protein, among the highest of any native prairie plant.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Illinois bundle-flower is a native prairie legume found throughout the central United States that is attracting significant interest as a perennial grain crop — its seeds contain approximately 38% crude protein, making them among the most protein-rich of any native plant, and researchers at the Land Institute and elsewhere have been working to develop it as a domesticated perennial grain crop that would not require annual tillage. The plant produces dense, spherical, mimosa-like flower heads of tiny white flowers on upright stems, followed by bundles of curved seed pods that give rise to the common names. As a deep-rooted prairie legume, it fixes nitrogen and is highly drought-tolerant — evolved to thrive in the droughty Great Plains climate. It is also ornamentally attractive: the finely divided, sensitive-plant-like foliage closes in response to touch, the spherical flower heads are interesting, and the seed bundles are ornamental in the fall garden. An important plant for native prairie restoration and an emerging candidate for sustainable grain agriculture.

plant_note: Scarify seed and broadcast or drill in spring into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in full sun; Illinois bundleflower establishes slowly in its first year while building a deep taproot, then persists as a long-lived perennial stand for many years.
directions: Sow scarified, inoculated seed in a firm seedbed in full sun; drought-tolerant once established thanks to a deep taproot, and tolerant of a wide range of soils including heavier clays. Illinois bundleflower is a native tallgrass prairie legume valued in restoration seed mixes, pasture improvement, and wildlife food plots for its combination of nitrogen fixation, high forage protein content, and excellent seed production — the distinctive round, bristly seed clusters (which give the plant its common name) are heavily used by upland game birds and songbirds through fall and winter. Fine, fern-like, mimosa-type foliage and small white puffball flowers in summer make it an attractive addition to a native prairie or pollinator planting as well as a working forage legume, and once established it persists and reseeds reliably for many years without replanting. A useful, multi-purpose native perennial for pasture, restoration, or wildlife plantings in zone 4–9.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; tolerates saturated and periodically flooded conditions far better than most legumes. Inoculate with Aeschynomene-specific Bradyrhizobium; stem nodules form naturally in waterlogged conditions without inoculant in established paddy systems.
directions: A pantropical annual legume native to India and widely naturalized in the southeastern US and throughout tropical regions, recognized by its sensitive pinnate leaves that fold when touched or shaded — a trait that earns it the common name 'shyleaf' — and small, yellow, red-veined pea flowers that appear from summer through fall. Unlike most legumes, it forms nitrogen-fixing nodules on its stems as well as its roots, and these stem nodules function effectively even in flooded, waterlogged paddy soils, making it a foundational nitrogen-fixing component of traditional Asian and African rice-based farming systems. Direct sow after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and inoculate with Aeschynomene-specific Bradyrhizobium in new sites; it establishes readily in poorly drained areas where other cover crop legumes fail. An excellent nitrogen-fixing cover crop for low, wet areas, rain gardens, and flooded margins in zones 8-11.

plant_note: Sow in late summer or early fall in a prepared seedbed; fall-sown plants establish root systems through winter and produce more vigorous growth in spring. Spring sowing is possible but fall planting gives better first-year establishment.
directions: Sow at 8-12 lbs per acre (or approx. 1 oz per 100 sq ft) in prepared, well-drained soil in late summer; intermediate wheatgrass is a perennial cool-season grass that has been developed into the commercial grain crop Kernza by the Land Institute, representing a breakthrough in sustainable agriculture — a grain crop that doesn't need to be replanted annually, builds soil carbon, prevents erosion year-round with its deep roots, and requires far less water and fertilizer than annual wheat. The grain can be used in baking, beer, pasta, and cereals with a mild, slightly sweet flavor. Grain yield peaks in years 2-4 then gradually declines; the stand can be maintained for 5-7 years with proper management. An excellent demonstration plant for regenerative agriculture principles in larger garden plots.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in warm soil after last frost; in zone 9 plant April–August for summer cover cropping. Iron and Clay germinates and establishes rapidly in warm soil and is drought-tolerant once established — making it the standard summer cover crop throughout the Gulf South where summers are too hot and dry for most other leguminous covers. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or tilling before pods fully set to prevent reseeding.
directions: Broadcast 50–100 lbs of seed per acre (or 3–4 oz per 100 sq ft for garden use) into prepared, warm soil in full sun; Iron and Clay cowpea is the standard warm-season leguminous cover crop for the Gulf South and mid-Atlantic, valued for rapid establishment, exceptional heat and drought tolerance, vigorous weed suppression, and the ability to fix 100–150 lbs of nitrogen per acre when properly inoculated with rhizobium. The rambling vines spread 2–3 feet and form a dense ground cover that shades out weeds and prevents erosion during the fallow period between summer and fall crops. Inoculate seed with cowpea-specific Bradyrhizobium inoculant before planting for maximum nitrogen fixation. Terminate by mowing and incorporating 3–4 weeks before the next crop; the decomposing vines release nitrogen gradually for the following crop. Iron and Clay cowpea also provides excellent wildlife food plot value, attracting white-tailed deer, quail, and doves.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant warm-season cover-crop legumes.
directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed at 40–50 lb per acre (about 1 oz per 25 sq ft), 1/2 in deep in warm, well-drained soil; cowpeas germinate and grow rapidly, fixing 100–150 lb of nitrogen per acre while suppressing summer weeds with their spreading vines. The crop tolerates sandy, infertile, and slightly acidic soils where most legumes struggle. Terminate by mowing at early pod stage before seeds mature to prevent volunteer plants; large amounts of vine biomass decompose quickly in warm weather. Pairs well with sorghum-sudangrass for a combined legume-grass summer cover.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow April–July. Iron and Clay is a hybrid between iron cowpea and clay cowpea — producing a vigorous, drought-resistant, fast-covering warm-season cover crop that is one of the most widely planted summer cover crops in the Gulf South and Southeast US. It is primarily used for deer food plots, summer cover, erosion control on disturbed soils, and green manure preceding fall vegetable plantings. Inoculate seed with cowpea Rhizobium inoculant for maximum nitrogen fixation. The spreading vines can reach 18–24 inches tall and cover the ground rapidly, suppressing summer weeds effectively. Mow or disk and incorporate before seed set if naturalizing is not desired. Excellent summer deer forage — often planted in wildlife food plots.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed in full sun in any well-drained to moderately drained soil — Iron and Clay Pea adapts to poor, sandy, low-fertility soils where other cover crops struggle; inoculate with cowpea Rhizobium for maximum nitrogen fixation; Iron and Clay Pea is a hybrid cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) cover crop that is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, rapid-covering warm-season green manures available for Gulf South summer use — producing a dense, weed-suppressing ground cover within 4–6 weeks of germination and fixing 100–200 pounds of nitrogen per acre per season when properly inoculated with Rhizobium. The exceptional heat and drought tolerance of Iron and Clay allows it to establish and cover ground through the peak of Gulf South summer (June–September) when soil temperatures, dry spells, and heat stress defeat other cover crops and leave bare soil exposed to erosion and weed pressure. As a wildlife food plot crop, Iron and Clay Pea is one of the most widely planted warm-season forages for white-tailed deer in the Southeast — the highly palatable vines and pods providing high-protein forage through summer and early fall. For zone 9 vegetable gardeners, Iron and Clay sown in June–July and incorporated in September–October provides both summer weed suppression and a substantial nitrogen boost for fall vegetable plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil temperature reaches 68°F or warmer; jack bean is a tropical legume that requires a long, warm growing season of at least 4–5 months and performs best in zone 9–12 where the season allows full pod and seed development.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, low- to moderate-fertility soil in full sun 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm; jack bean is a vigorous tropical legume grown throughout the humid tropics and subtropics as a cover crop, green manure, and food legume. The large, upright to semi-climbing plants produce conspicuous rose-purple flowers followed by flat, strap-like pods 8–14 inches long containing large white seeds used in soups, stews, and curries in parts of Africa, Central America, and Southeast Asia — caution: seeds are toxic unless thoroughly cooked due to the alkaloid canavanine and must be boiled in multiple changes of water before eating. As a cover crop, jack bean fixes significant atmospheric nitrogen, smothers weeds with its dense foliage, and tolerates poor, acid, and lateritic soils that challenge other legumes. Terminate as a cover crop by mowing or incorporation at early pod set to maximize the nitrogen benefit to subsequent crops.

plant_note: Broadcast seed on a firm seedbed at or just after last frost; widely available through wildlife management suppliers; consider native Lespedeza species where habitat restoration is the goal.
directions: Broadcast seed on a firm, raked seedbed at or just after the last frost date, pressing lightly into contact with the soil surface without deep burial. Japanese lespedeza produces low-growing, branching stems with small trifoliate leaves and tiny pink-purple flowers in late summer, adapting readily to poor, dry, and acidic soils where improved clovers and vetches struggle to persist. The high seed yield makes it one of the most widely used wildlife food plot legumes in the eastern US, with quail, dove, and deer all utilizing the seeds and foliage heavily. Where native habitat restoration is the priority, the true native lespedezas — including Lespedeza capitata and Lespedeza virginica — are strongly preferred over this naturalized introduction.

plant_note: Sow into warm soil after the last frost when soil reaches at least 60 F.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.5-1 lb per 1,000 sq ft onto a moist seedbed and rake lightly to cover 0.25-0.5 inch deep. Japanese millet germinates fast in warm soil and tolerates temporarily wet or flooded ground better than most summer cover crops. It produces abundant biomass in as little as six to eight weeks and can be used to smother summer weeds in fallow beds. Terminate by mowing before seed set to avoid volunteers, then incorporate residue or leave as mulch. Frost will kill the crop, providing free termination ahead of fall or spring plantings.

plant_note: Sow in fall for winter growth in mild climates; Khorasan is a large-kerneled free-threshing durum relative that can be stored and milled without special hulling equipment — it is easier to process than emmer.
directions: Drill or broadcast at 100–120 lbs per acre in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile to poor soil; Khorasan wheat (trademarked as KAMUT® when meeting specific organic and quality standards) is an ancient durum wheat relative from the Fertile Crescent region, producing very large kernels twice the size of modern wheat with a distinctive buttery, nutty flavor and higher protein (17–18%), selenium, zinc, and magnesium content than common wheat. A free-threshing grain (unlike emmer or einkorn), it processes easily with standard equipment. Tall, stately plants with long beards are ornamental in the garden. Grows well on dryland and lower-fertility soils and is notably drought-tolerant; many people with wheat sensitivities (not celiac) report tolerating Khorasan better than modern wheat.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; kidney vetch is a key native European wildflower meadow plant and the sole larval food plant of the small blue butterfly.
directions: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, calcareous soil in full sun; kidney vetch is adapted to thin, chalky, limey soils where it excels as a nitrogen fixer and wildflower meadow component. Anthyllis vulneraria is a European native perennial legume of chalk grasslands, limestone pavements, and coastal cliffs, producing distinctive heads of densely clustered, woolly, tubular flowers in shades of yellow, cream, orange, pink, and red depending on subspecies; it is one of the most ornamentally variable native wildflowers of European calcareous grasslands. It is a key component of chalk and limestone wildflower meadow seed mixtures, fixes nitrogen in poor soils, and is the sole larval food plant of the small blue butterfly (Cupido minimus). Outstanding for establishing species-rich wildflower turf on thin, alkaline soils.

plant_note: Broadcast seed on a firm, raked seedbed at or just after last frost; no seed covering needed as light aids germination.
directions: Broadcast scarified seed on a firm, raked seedbed in spring at or just after the last frost date, pressing lightly into contact with the soil but not burying deeply. Korean lespedeza produces small trifoliate leaves and tiny pink-purple pea flowers from late summer through fall, followed by single-seeded pods that are heavily consumed by bobwhite quail, wild turkey, and mourning dove. It is more drought-tolerant and better adapted to poor, acidic, infertile soils than crimson clover or hairy vetch, making it a reliable warm-season legume for thin or degraded pastures. Turn it under before seed set if using as a nitrogen-fixing green manure, or leave standing through winter for maximum wildlife benefit.

plant_note: Sow in spring; slow to establish but forms a long-lived rhizomatous stand.
directions: Inoculate with the specific kura clover rhizobia strain and broadcast at about 0.2-0.4 lb per 1,000 sq ft into a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 0.25 inch deep. Kura clover establishes slowly during its first year because it invests heavily in rhizomes, but once established it forms a persistent living mulch. Its spreading roots fix nitrogen and provide erosion control and pollinator forage for many years. Manage rather than fully terminate it by mowing or suppressing with strip tillage so it regrows between cash crops. For complete removal, repeated tillage or cultivation is required because of its vigorous rhizomes.

plant_note: Sow after last frost in warm soil; an exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant warm-season legume cover from Africa.
directions: Plant inoculated seed 1 in deep after soil temperatures exceed 65°F; lablab vines grow vigorously and can climb trellises or sprawl as a smothering ground cover. It fixes up to 200 lb N/acre equivalent under good conditions and tolerates low-fertility and mildly saline soils where cowpea struggles. Terminate by mowing or chopping at early pod set; raw mature pods contain toxic lectins, so the foliage should not be eaten without cooking. In frost-free zones it can be managed as a short-lived perennial ground cover.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant from March through July. Lablab grows vigorously as a summer cover crop and can also be trellised as an ornamental, bearing purple flowers and glossy purple-black pods that are edible when young. It fixes nitrogen and smothers weeds effectively.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil warms; lablab establishes quickly and vines aggressively — provide a strong trellis or fence for ornamental plantings, or let it sprawl as a ground cover in cover-crop beds. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most other legumes, making it ideal for summer cover-cropping in the Deep South where other legumes fail. Young pods and leaves are edible after cooking (raw pods contain low levels of cyanogenic glycosides), and the dried seeds are a staple pulse in Africa and South Asia. Till in at flowering for maximum green manure nitrogen contribution to the soil.

plant_note: Broadcast sow in spring or fall; seeds germinate best in darkness and cool soil.
directions: Broadcast lacy phacelia seed in spring or fall and rake it in lightly, as the seed needs darkness to germinate. This fast-growing cover crop improves soil structure, reduces erosion, and produces bell-shaped violet flowers on curled fiddlehead clusters that are magnets for bees and beneficial insects. Mow or turn it under before it sets seed if you want to prevent self-sowing, or let a patch bloom to feed pollinators. It tolerates poor soils and needs little water once established.

plant_note: Broadcast on a firm, well-prepared seedbed in early fall or early spring; Ladino clover establishes a persistent, spreading perennial stand and tolerates wetter soils than most clovers, making it a good choice for low, moist ground.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed at 2–4 lb/acre on a firm, weed-free seedbed no more than 1/4 inch deep; Ladino clover is a giant-type selection of white clover (Trifolium repens), bred for substantially larger leaves, taller growth, and heavier biomass and forage yield than common white or Dutch white clover, while retaining the same low, spreading, stoloniferous habit and strong nitrogen-fixing ability. It tolerates wetter soils and heavier grazing or mowing pressure than many other clovers, and its persistent perennial nature means a single planting can provide years of nitrogen-fixing groundcover, pollinator forage, and high-quality grazing without replanting. Widely used in permanent pasture mixes and as a living mulch between rows of perennial crops, it also draws heavy honeybee traffic during its long bloom period. A productive, versatile perennial legume for pasture, orchard understory, or long-term soil building, zone 4–9.

plant_note: Sow in fall for best performance; lana woolypod vetch establishes quickly and fixes nitrogen through winter; inoculate with appropriate Rhizobium; often mixed with oats or cereal rye for a combined cover crop.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 20–30 lbs per acre (or mix 10 lbs vetch with 40 lbs cereal rye) in early fall in well-drained to average soil; lana woolypod vetch is a smooth-leafed variety of woolypod vetch developed at UC Davis, with less hairiness than hairy vetch (Vicia villosa) and greater heat tolerance, making it better suited to California valleys and Gulf Coast winters. It fixes 80–150 lbs of nitrogen per acre in a good stand, produces abundant biomass for soil incorporation, and smothers winter weeds effectively. Mow and incorporate at early bloom (before pods form) for maximum nitrogen release. The attractive purple-blue flowers support foraging bees through late winter.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; leadtree is an extremely fast-growing tropical legume tree that is important in tropical agroforestry as a nitrogen fixer and green manure crop, but is invasive in Florida and many tropical regions — check local regulations before planting.
directions: Scarify seeds and sow in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; leadtree grows extremely rapidly and fixes large amounts of nitrogen. IMPORTANT: Leucaena leucocephala is listed as invasive in Florida, Hawaii, and many tropical regions — do not plant near natural areas or waterways. Leucaena leucocephala (leadtree or wild tamarind) is a Central American tropical legume tree of extraordinary importance in global tropical agriculture — ranked among the most useful trees in the world for nitrogen fixation (fixing up to 500 lbs of nitrogen per acre per year), fast biomass production for green manure, livestock fodder, fuel wood, and erosion control in tropical agroforestry systems across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. It grows extraordinarily fast (to 15–20 feet in a year) in poor, dry soils and is highly drought-tolerant once established. Young leaves, seeds, and pods are edible as a vegetable in some cuisines; however, a toxic alkaloid (mimosine) limits consumption quantities. The tree is listed as invasive in Florida and Hawaii where it crowds out native vegetation in disturbed areas. In tropical agricultural systems, its nitrogen-fixing capacity and drought tolerance make it a key component of alley cropping systems and organic farming in the humid tropics.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline, low-fertility soil in full sun; scarify seed lightly and inoculate with medic-type Rhizobium before sowing; little burr medic self-seeds prolifically in suitable conditions and can maintain itself without reseeding in dryland farming systems.
directions: Direct sow in fall in dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline, low-fertility soil in full sun; scarify seed lightly and inoculate with medic-type Rhizobium before sowing; little burr medic self-seeds prolifically in suitable conditions and can maintain itself without reseeding in dryland farming systems. Medicago minima is a prostrate, hairy annual medic native to dry, disturbed, sandy soils of the Mediterranean region and widely naturalized throughout the dryland regions of the world; it produces tiny, yellow, pea-like flowers and distinctive spiny, coiled seed pods with hooked spines (burrs) that aid in seed dispersal, and fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium root nodules in poor, thin, sandy soils where clover and alfalfa struggle. It is particularly useful as a self-reseeding annual cover crop in dryland farming systems, sandy coastal gardens, and dry herb garden paths where its low, prostrate habit and nitrogen-fixing ability improve soil fertility with minimal water input.

plant_note: Sow in late summer 6–10 weeks before first fall frost, or in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Mammoth is a single-cut, late-maturing type of red clover that produces the largest plant mass and highest nitrogen fixation of the standard red clovers.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 10–12 lbs per acre (1 lb per 1,000 sq ft) onto a firm, weed-free seedbed; inoculate with clover rhizobia for reliable nitrogen fixation in new ground. Mammoth Red Clover is a large, late-maturing single-cut type that produces more biomass per planting than standard medium red clover, reaching 3–4 feet in height and fixing 80–200 lbs of nitrogen per acre when properly inoculated; it is best terminated at early bloom for maximum nitrogen availability to the following crop. The large, showy magenta flower heads are outstanding for pollinators — a diverse range of native bees, bumble bees, and honey bees work the blooms heavily. In the South, sow in fall as a winter annual that overwinters, blooms in spring, and is terminated before summer cash crops go in.

subcategory: Southern African drought-tolerant edible tuber legume
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or in warm soil in full sun in sandy, well-drained, nutrient-poor soil in zone 9–12; Marama Bean (Morama Bean, Gemsbok Bean) is a perennial, tuberous-rooted wild legume from the Kalahari and Namib desert regions of Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa — a trailing vine developing an enormous edible storage tuber (sometimes reaching 100 kg in old plants) and producing flat woody pods with 2–3 large seeds with outstanding nutritional content: 30–35% protein and 40% fat, comparable to soybeans and peanuts combined.
directions: Direct sow Marama Bean in sandy, well-drained, nutrient-poor soil in full sun after last frost or year-round in zone 10–12; minimal fertilization needed; plants develop a large taproot tuber — do not disturb; harvest seeds when pods dry; water only during establishment. Tylosema esculentum is one of the most nutritionally remarkable wild legumes known — its seeds contain approximately 30–35% protein and 38–40% fat, making them nutritionally comparable to combining soybean and peanut in a single seed. For the San (Bushman) and other indigenous peoples of the Kalahari, marama beans have been a critical dry-season protein and fat source for thousands of years — seeds are boiled, roasted, or ground into a nutritious paste or flour, and the seeds can also be roasted to produce a beverage resembling coffee. The massive underground tuber (technically a massive swollen hypocotyl) accumulates water and carbohydrates over decades — older plants may develop tubers weighing 50–100 kg — and the water-rich flesh has historically provided emergency moisture in the desert. The trailing stems and attractive round leaves grow across sandy desert soils and fix nitrogen through root nodules. Under cultivation in well-drained, sunny garden conditions in zone 9–12, marama bean provides a drought-tolerant ground cover and nitrogen fixer while producing protein-rich seeds. Of serious interest to researchers as a potential drought-tolerant protein crop for arid regions facing food insecurity.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; mesa dropseed grows naturally on dry, open desert mesas, sandy plains, and desert grassland of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts and Great Basin transition zones. Extremely heat and drought tolerant — requires no supplemental irrigation in appropriate climates.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; mesa dropseed is a medium-sized warm-season bunchgrass of desert mesas and sandy desert grasslands from the Texas Panhandle and New Mexico through Arizona and into the Great Basin — one of the characteristic dropseed grasses (Sporobolus) of the hot, dry southwestern lowlands. The airy, open, finely branched panicles are ornamental and distinctive. 'Dropseed' refers to the characteristic of the genus where the tiny, shiny seeds fall (drop) as soon as they are ripe, spreading quickly around the parent plant. An important forage grass for pronghorn, desert mule deer, and livestock on desert ranges. One of the better grasses for very hot, dry, sandy desert-grassland restoration planting mixes across the Southwest. Related to prairie dropseed (S. heterolepis, of the northern prairies) but adapted to much hotter, drier conditions. Fast-germinating and establishing from seed in appropriate warm, dry conditions.

common_name: Napier Grass (Elephant Grass, Uganda Grass, Merker Grass)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (sections with 2–3 nodes) horizontally or at an angle in moist soil after soil warms to 65°F; napier grass is a tropical perennial killed by hard frost but grows with extraordinary vigor in zones 9–11, producing 20–40 tons of dry biomass per acre per year and forming dense stands that exclude all weeds — the single most productive warm-season biomass plant available for tropical and subtropical climates.
directions: Plant stem cuttings 3–4 inches deep at 2–3 foot spacing; napier grass establishes rapidly and reaches cutting height of 3–5 feet within 60–90 days; cut or chop-and-drop as green mulch every 6–8 weeks during growing season to maintain tender regrowth and prevent woodiness; use as chop-and-drop mulch for tropical garden beds or incorporate as green manure. Napier grass (Pennisetum purpureum) is arguably the most productive tropical biomass grass in the world — a C4 perennial native to sub-Saharan Africa (the Napier Valley region of Kenya) that has been planted throughout the humid tropics for fodder, green manure, and more recently as a dedicated biomass energy crop. Under optimal tropical conditions it can produce more than 40 tons of dry biomass per acre per year — a yield surpassed by few plants on earth — while requiring minimal inputs once established. In zone 9a and the Gulf Coast, Napier grass performs as a vigorous warm-season perennial from spring through late fall, dying back after the first frost but typically regrowing from established root crowns unless soil temperatures drop below about 20°F for extended periods. It is used in permaculture and tropical market gardens as a chop-and-drop biomass plant: the tall stems are cut every 6–8 weeks and the chopped material laid as mulch or incorporated as high-carbon green manure. The dense, fibrous root system accumulates significant organic matter in the soil over multiple seasons. New dwarf varieties ('Mott' dwarf napier) are available for smaller gardens. Note: classified as potentially invasive in Hawaii and Florida — check local guidelines before planting near natural areas.

common_name: Narrow-Leaf Lupin (Blue Lupin, Australian Sweet Lupin)
plant_note: In zones 7–9 sow in fall 4–8 weeks before first frost; in zones 3–6 sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; narrow-leaf lupin is more frost-hardy than white lupin (tolerates -10°C) and better adapted to sandy, acidic soils (pH 4.5–7.0) where white lupin and most legumes fail; the most important grain lupin species in Australia, where it transformed dryland wheat farming as a rotation crop.
directions: Broadcast or drill at 60–100 lbs per acre (1.5–2.5 lbs per 1000 sq ft); inoculate with Bradyrhizobium lupini Group G specifically matched to this species; narrow-leaf lupin is more drought-tolerant than white lupin once established and is excellent for poor sandy soils; terminate at early bloom by mowing and incorporating to release 80–140 lbs N/acre. Narrow-leaf lupin (Lupinus angustifolius) is the dominant commercial grain lupin species in Australia, where it was transformed by the breeding work of John Gladstones at the University of Western Australia into a major crop that revolutionized dryland wheat farming — the introduction of sweet, low-alkaloid varieties in the 1960s and 1970s enabled farmers in western Australia to use lupins as a grain legume rotation crop, building soil fertility in the highly acidic, phosphorus-deficient sands of the Australian wheat belt. Australia now produces the majority of the world's grain lupins, with Lupinus angustifolius representing 95% of production. As a cover crop in American gardens and small farms, narrow-leaf lupin excels in the same difficult conditions: acidic, sandy, infertile soils where clovers, vetch, and peas struggle to establish. It fixes 80–140 lbs N/acre with proper inoculation, produces substantial biomass, and its deep taproot improves soil structure. The flowers are blue to pale violet-blue on erect stems — attractive enough to serve double duty as an ornamental.

common_name: Nitro Radish (Nitrogen-Scavenging Forage Radish Cover Crop)
plant_note: Sow 6-10 weeks before first frost; Nitro is a forage radish cultivar bred for rapid fall growth and aggressive nitrogen scavenging, capturing residual soil nitrogen in its foliage and root before winter leaching losses occur.
directions: Broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep in late summer to early fall; Nitro is a forage radish cultivar bred for exceptionally fast fall growth and strong nitrogen-scavenging ability, rapidly taking up residual soil nitrogen left over from a previous crop's fertilization before fall and winter rains can leach it below the root zone. The large taproot also breaks through compacted soil layers, improving structure and water infiltration for the following crop. In zones cold enough for a hard freeze, the roots die and rot in place over winter, releasing the captured nitrogen back into the topsoil in plant-available form as they decompose, timed to benefit a spring-planted crop. In milder zones where the radish survives, mow before it flowers and sets seed to prevent it becoming a volunteer weed in the following crop.

plant_note: Sow early spring or late summer for a quick cool-season cover.
directions: Broadcast oat seed over worked soil in early spring or six to eight weeks before your first fall frost and rake in about half an inch. Fast, dense growth shades out weeds and its fibrous roots hold soil against erosion and winter rains. In cold zones the crop reliably winter-kills, leaving a soft mulch that is easy to plant into come spring. It also builds plenty of organic matter when turned under while still green.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost; oats winter-kill below about 10°F, leaving a ready-to-plant mat of residue in spring without tillage.
directions: Broadcast seed at 50–80 lb per acre (about 1 oz per 30 sq ft) and rake to 1/2 in depth; oats establish quickly and produce substantial biomass before being killed by hard freezes. Their winter-killed residue lies flat as a weed-suppressing mulch that is easy to plant or transplant through in spring without additional termination work. Often mixed with field peas or hairy vetch to add nitrogen to the primarily carbonaceous grass residue. In mild-winter regions (zones 8–9), oats may overwinter and require mowing to terminate before spring planting.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill 6–10 weeks before the first fall frost into a well-prepared seedbed; oilseed radish grows quickly and, in USDA zone 5 and colder, reliably winter-kills, leaving surface residue and a decomposing root channel by spring.
directions: Broadcast seed at 8–12 lb/acre and lightly incorporate into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; oilseed radish germinates and grows rapidly, producing a vigorous rosette of large leaves over a long, thick taproot. Bred as a fast-biomass, high-glucosinolate type within the same species as tillage/forage radish, it is especially valued for biofumigation — as the roots and residue break down, they release natural sulfur compounds that can suppress certain soilborne pathogens and nematodes, in addition to the physical benefits of a deep taproot that fractures compacted soil layers and scavenges leachable nitrogen before winter. In mild-winter climates the rosette can survive and bolt in spring; mow before flowering to prevent an unwanted seed bank. The decomposing roots produce a strong sulfurous smell for a week or two after a hard freeze — this is normal and passes as residue breaks down.

plant_note: Sow six to eight weeks before frost so plants form a strong rosette to overwinter.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.25-0.5 lb per 1,000 sq ft and rake to cover 0.25-0.5 inch deep in a firm seedbed. Winter-type oilseed rape develops a deep taproot that breaks up compacted subsoil and scavenges nitrogen and sulfur. Overwintering plants bolt and flower in spring, providing early forage for pollinators if allowed to bloom. Terminate by mowing at early flowering before pods set, then incorporate the residue with tillage. Allow two to three weeks of breakdown before planting the following crop to avoid nitrogen tie-up.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade; orchardgrass tolerates more shade than most pasture grasses, giving it its name from traditional use in the dappled light of orchard alleys.
directions: Drill seed 1/4–1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to partial shade; establishes quickly and tolerates more shade than nearly any other common pasture or cover crop grass, a trait reflected in its name from long use as groundcover beneath orchard trees. Orchardgrass is a deep-rooted, long-lived, cool-season bunchgrass widely used across temperate North America as a high-quality hay and pasture grass, valued for its rapid spring growth, good regrowth after cutting or grazing, and reasonable drought tolerance once its root system is established. As a cover crop, it forms a dense, persistent sod useful for erosion control on slopes and waterways, and its shade tolerance makes it one of the few grasses well suited to groundcover beneath widely spaced fruit or nut trees, where full-sun grasses like bermudagrass or bahiagrass struggle. A versatile, shade-tolerant perennial grass for pasture, hay, or orchard-floor groundcover, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Scarify seeds and direct sow in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; panicled tick trefoil grows naturally in dry to moderately moist open woodlands, woodland edges, and old fields throughout eastern North America.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun at woodland edges and in naturalized plantings; panicled tick trefoil is one of the most important native wildflower legumes of the eastern woodland edge — a tall, erect perennial with trifoliate leaves and loose, elongated panicles of small pink to lavender pea flowers in late summer. The plant is critically important as a host plant for Eastern tailed-blue, silver-spotted skipper, and several other butterfly and moth species that are specialists of native legumes. The jointed seed pods break into small, sticky segments (the 'ticks' that give the genus its name) and cling tenaciously to clothing and animal fur — an effective dispersal strategy that makes some people view the plant as a nuisance. In naturalistic gardens and wildlife corridors, it is an outstanding wildflower that seeds itself through open, lightly shaded areas without becoming aggressive in well-maintained beds.

plant_note: Sow after last frost in warm soil; the most heat- and drought-tolerant warm-season cover grass, thriving in Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1/2 in deep into warm soil; pearl millet germinates and establishes faster than sorghum-sudangrass in sandy, low-fertility soils. It produces large amounts of biomass for smothering weeds and building organic matter, and tolerate short dry spells without wilting like corn or sorghum can. Mow or terminate before seed heads mature to prevent unwanted reseeding. Mix with cowpeas for a combined nitrogen-fixing and biomass cover.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; pearl millet is the world's most drought-tolerant cereal grain — it thrives where maize, sorghum, and other grains fail — and is an outstanding summer cover crop for hot, dry, sandy soil in zone 7–12 where it grows to 6–8 feet, fixes atmospheric carbon, suppresses weeds, and improves soil structure.
directions: Direct sow at 10–20 lbs per acre in warm, well-drained, lean soil in full sun; mow or incorporate when 50–60% heading for maximum biomass. Cenchrus americanus (pearl millet or bajra, formerly Pennisetum glaucum) is the world's most drought-tolerant cereal grain crop — an ancient African cultigen domesticated in the Sahel region over 3,000 years ago and now the primary staple grain for hundreds of millions of people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Pearl millet thrives under extremely high temperatures (up to 110°F), very low and erratic rainfall (8–20 inches annually), and highly infertile, sandy soils — growing successfully where maize, sorghum, and virtually any other grain crop cannot produce. The grain (bajra in India, the primary use) is ground into flour for flatbreads (bajra roti) and porridges; the nutritional profile is excellent (higher in protein, iron, and zinc than maize or sorghum). As a cover crop in zone 7–12, pearl millet is outstanding for hot, dry, sandy, infertile soils where most summer cover crops fail — it grows to 6–8 feet rapidly, produces enormous biomass to incorporate as organic matter, suppresses weeds completely, and requires essentially no inputs. It is also an important wildlife food and game food-plot crop for white-tailed deer, quail, and dove.

common_name: Pensacola Bahia Grass (Gulf South Drought-Tolerant Lawn and Pasture Grass)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed at 5–10 lbs/1000 sq ft in late spring when soil is consistently above 65°F; scratch seed into soil with a rake or slit-seeder for good soil contact. Pensacola Bahia germinates slowly (2–4 weeks) and establishes slowly — expect a full season before a complete stand develops. In zone 9, seed April–June for establishment by fall. Pensacola Bahia goes semi-dormant and may brown during cold winters but recovers reliably in spring.
directions: Sow scarified seed at 5–10 lbs per 1,000 sq ft after last frost when soil is warm; keep moist during the slow 2–4 week germination period. Pensacola Bahia is the standard low-maintenance lawn and pasture grass for the Gulf South coastal plain — a cultivar of bahia grass (Paspalum notatum) selected for improved cold tolerance, germination, and lawn quality over the common 'Argentine' type. Bahia grass is unique among Gulf South turf grasses for its extraordinary drought and heat tolerance combined with extremely low input requirements: it grows vigorously in poor, sandy, acidic soils with minimal fertilization, outcompetes many weeds once established, and maintains reasonable appearance through Gulf South summers with little supplemental irrigation. The deep, extensive root system (roots reach 6–8 feet deep) explains the drought tolerance — the roots access soil moisture well below what shallow-rooted turf grasses can reach. Pensacola is a narrower-leaf, more attractive form than common bahia grass, making it more acceptable for residential lawn use while retaining the toughness of the species. The grass is a fixture throughout Florida, coastal Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, where it covers millions of acres of utility areas, roadsides, pastures, and low-maintenance residential lawns.

common_name: Peredovik Sunflower (Russian Oilseed Sunflower, Standard Wildlife and Food Plot Variety)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in zone 9 (April–May), or midsummer (July) for a fall crop. Peredovik produces single-headed sunflowers on tall, upright stems (5–7 feet) with seed heads 6–8 inches in diameter packed with small, oilseed-type black or black-striped seeds. The small oilseed-type seed (smaller than confection sunflower varieties) is higher in oil content than large-seeded types, making it particularly attractive to songbirds, doves, and deer. Plant at higher density than confection sunflowers (6–8 inch spacing) to maximize seed heads per acre in food plot applications. Peredovik can be direct-harvested for bird feed or left standing as a wildlife food source. In zone 9's warm climate, Peredovik thrives with excellent drought tolerance once established — well-suited to dry summer conditions without irrigation.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 6–12 inches for maximum seed heads. Leave standing for wildlife or harvest heads when seeds are dry and firm. Peredovik is a Russian oilseed sunflower variety that was introduced to North America from the Soviet Union and became the standard oilseed sunflower for both commercial oilseed production and wildlife food plot planting across the United States. The name Peredovik (meaning 'leader' or 'front-runner' in Russian) reflects the variety's status in Soviet agricultural programs where sunflower was a major oilseed crop for domestic vegetable oil production. Peredovik produces the small, dark (black or black-and-gray-striped) seeds characteristic of oilseed sunflowers — smaller than confection-type sunflower seeds grown for direct human consumption, but with a higher percentage of oil per seed, a thin shell that wildlife and songbirds can crack easily, and a nutrient density that makes them preferred by many seed-eating birds over larger-seeded confection types. The variety's value for wildlife habitat and food plot management in the Gulf South and across the US has made it by far the most commonly planted sunflower variety in food plot and wildlife habitat seed mixes. For zone 9 gardeners interested in supporting native bird populations, Peredovik planted in a sunny corner of the garden or in a dedicated wildlife patch provides enormous nutritional value to mourning doves, goldfinches, house finches, northern cardinals, and many migratory sparrow species during fall migration. The plants also provide insect habitat and the tall stalks support overwintering insects beneficial for garden pest control.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; perennial horsegram is an East African legume used as a drought-tolerant, perennial tropical pasture cover crop in Queensland, Australia and across Africa and Southeast Asia — it excels in low-rainfall, infertile, acidic conditions where other tropical legumes cannot establish.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarify seed or soak 24 hours before planting. Macrotyloma axillare (perennial horsegram or axillaris) is an East African legume that has been widely adopted as a drought-tolerant, perennial tropical pasture cover crop in Queensland, Australia, where it was introduced and extensively trialed as a low-maintenance, nitrogen-fixing component of improved subtropical pastures. The cultivar 'Archer' was selected in Australia for superior persistence, drought tolerance, and productivity in dry subtropical conditions. Unlike annual tropical cover crops, perennial horsegram persists in the soil from one season to the next, regrowth from the root crown after dry-season dormancy — providing a permanent nitrogen-fixing cover without annual replanting costs. It is notably tolerant of acid, infertile, low-phosphorus soils where other legumes fail to establish. The plant produces twining stems with small trifoliate leaves and inconspicuous cream-colored flowers. In zone 9–12 gardens, it is an excellent choice for permanent cover under fruit trees on lean, acidic soil, where it builds fertility year by year without intervention.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sprigs in late spring once soil is warm; establishment is slow the first season but the stand fills in by year 2.
directions: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 in deep in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil; perennial peanut tolerates poor, acidic soils typical of Gulf Coast landscapes. Establishment is slow the first year but the low, dense mat fixes nitrogen and crowds out weeds without mowing once established. It can be used as a lawn alternative, orchard under-planting, or living mulch in vegetable corridors. In zones 8–9 the top may freeze back in hard winters but the rhizomes resprout reliably from below ground.

common_name: Perennial Peanut (Pinto Peanut, Rhizoma Perennial Peanut, Ornamental Peanut)
plant_note: Plant sprigs (vegetative divisions) or sod plugs in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Arachis pintoi is one of the most popular and proven low-maintenance groundcovers for zone 8b-11, especially throughout Florida and the Gulf Coast where it has been widely used for decades as lawn alternative, median strip groundcover, and landscape cover. Spreads by rhizomes and stolons; mow occasionally to keep tidy. Drought-tolerant once established. Fixes nitrogen from the air, improving soil over time. The small yellow peanut-shaped flowers are decorative. Suppresses weeds effectively in established beds.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil — Perennial Peanut is one of the most adaptable and low-maintenance groundcovers for Gulf Coast zone 8b-11, establishing in a wide range of soil types and requiring minimal inputs once established. Arachis pintoi is a stoloniferous, mat-forming, perennial legume native to Brazil and Bolivia in the Fabaceae family, introduced to Florida and the Gulf Coast in the 1930s and now one of the most widely used ornamental groundcovers in the region. The plant produces a dense, attractive, low mat of 4-leaflet compound leaves (like a clover leaf) from creeping stolons and rhizomes, and throughout the warm months produces small (0.5-inch), bright golden-yellow, peanut-shaped flowers at the tips of short upright stems. As a legume, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Rhizobium bacteria, improving soil fertility over time — making it doubly valuable as both an ornamental groundcover and a nitrogen-contributing cover crop when incorporated into garden beds. The plant spreads steadily but is not considered invasive. In zone 8b-9, established plants die back to the roots in hard freezes but regrow vigorously in spring. A true perennial in zone 9b-11, requiring no replanting. One of the finest groundcovers for hot, humid Gulf Coast landscapes. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early fall; perennial ryegrass establishes fastest of all cool-season grasses and forms dense sod for erosion control.
directions: Broadcast seed at 20–30 lb/acre and rake lightly to 1/4 in depth; perennial ryegrass germinates in 5–7 days at optimal temperatures and establishes the fastest ground cover of any cool-season grass, making it excellent for emergency erosion control or orchard middles. It can be used as a short-rotation annual cover in cold winters (zones 3–5) or managed as a persistent sod in mild climates. Terminate before planting vegetables by aggressive mowing followed by solarization or herbicide; perennial ryegrass regrows readily from crowns and requires thorough kill. Mix with red or white clover for a nitrogen-fixing living mulch under fruit trees.

common_name: Perennial Soybean (Glycine, Soja Bean, Wight's Perennial Soybean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in any well-drained soil with good air circulation; Neonotonia wightii is a vigorously climbing, twining vine that needs support or space to sprawl — control by mowing before seed set to prevent unwanted spread. It is a prolific nitrogen fixer when properly inoculated with appropriate Bradyrhizobium strains. In zone 9, the tops are killed by frost but root crowns often survive and resprout in spring. Use as a summer biomass crop mowed into garden beds before fall planting, or as a trellis cover crop to fix nitrogen while creating summer shade. Check local invasive status.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil with support for climbing — Perennial Soybean is a vigorous, twining vine that grows rapidly in warm conditions and fixes large quantities of atmospheric nitrogen, making it one of the most productive leguminous cover crops for zone 9-12. Neonotonia wightii (formerly Glycine wightii, Glycine javanica) is a perennial, twining legume vine native to sub-Saharan Africa in the Fabaceae family — the same tribe (Phaseoleae) and general lineage as the commercial soybean (Glycine max), hence the common name 'Perennial Soybean,' though not directly edible as a food crop. The plant produces trifoliate leaves on twining stems that climb vigorously over other vegetation, fences, and trellises, and produces small (0.25-inch), lavender-purple flowers in axillary racemes through the warm months — the flowers attracting bees and small pollinators. As a legume, it forms root nodules with nitrogen-fixing Bradyrhizobium bacteria, fixing significant quantities of atmospheric nitrogen. Neonotonia wightii has been extensively used in tropical and subtropical agriculture as a high-biomass forage crop (the foliage is highly nutritious for livestock) and as a cover crop and living mulch in commercial plantations (coffee, citrus, macadamia) throughout the tropics to fix nitrogen and suppress weeds. In zone 9 home gardens, it is best used as a summer biomass-building cover to improve soil before mowing and incorporating before fall vegetable planting. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Broadcast seed at 8–12 pounds per acre in late summer or early fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian clover is winter-hardy to about 20°F, making it a useful winter annual in zones 7–9 where it overwinters and provides early spring nitrogen to following crops.
directions: Broadcast seed in late summer or early fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian clover is a Mediterranean annual clover widely used as a winter cover crop in mild-winter zones 7–9 where it establishes in fall, overwinters successfully, and produces a significant nitrogen-fixing spring flush before being incorporated as a green manure ahead of warm-season transplants. The distinctive pink-to-purple flowers open in the distinctive 'upside down' (resupinate) orientation that gives the species its name and common name. It is considered one of the best annual clovers for the winter-cover-crop niche in Gulf Coast and southeastern gardens — more productive and earlier-maturing than many other clovers in mild winters. Mow or till under at early flowering to maximize nitrogen release to following crops. Excellent as a nurse crop for cool-season vegetables.

plant_note: Sow 2–6 weeks before last spring frost, or in early fall in mild climates; flowers arrive in about 6 weeks and are among the best for attracting bees.
directions: Broadcast tiny seed at 3–5 lb per acre (a light dusting per 100 sq ft) on the surface of a firm, moist seedbed without covering, as seed needs light to germinate; rake in very lightly if birds are a problem. Phacelia establishes quickly in cool soil, outcompeting many weeds with dense, ferny foliage that also conserves soil moisture. The blue-purple flowers are exceptional for beneficial insects and bees — allow partial bloom before mowing to maximize pollinator benefit. Terminate by mowing just as the last flowers fade; it decomposes rapidly and leaves no allelopathic residue.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in warm soil after last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; phasey bean germinates readily without scarification and establishes quickly in warm, humid conditions — ideal for summer cover cropping in the Gulf South.
directions: Phasey bean is a fast-growing tropical American legume that has become one of the most widely used summer cover crops in Hawaii and the Gulf Coast, valued for its rapid establishment, vigorous nitrogen fixation, heat and humidity tolerance, and ability to grow as a self-reseeding annual in frost-free areas of zone 9–11.
