The plant produces small, attractive red-purple flowers on erect, trifoliate-leaved stems throughout summer, with long, slender seed pods containing multiple seeds; it naturally reseeds in zone 9 and south, making it a long-term self-perpetuating cover crop in orchards, landscape beds, and permanent native plantings. As a legume, it inoculates easily with cowpea rhizobia and fixes 50–80 pounds of nitrogen per acre; its moderate height keeps it manageable as an understory cover beneath small fruit trees and shrub rows. Used extensively in no-till and reduced-tillage systems as a living mulch terminated by mowing in fall before cool-season crops are established.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; plains lovegrass grows naturally in dry, open grasslands, sandy plains, and rocky desert slopes of the Southern Plains and Southwest. Excellent as an ornamental grass for hot, dry, full-sun locations.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, sandy or loamy, lean soil in full sun; plains lovegrass is a medium-sized, warm-season native bunchgrass of the Southern Plains and Chihuahuan Desert transition zone, producing delicate, extremely fine-textured, open, and airy panicles of tiny flowers and seeds from mid-summer through fall. The seed panicles create a misty, diaphanous effect — a haze of fine purple-pink to silvery seed heads floating above the grass clumps. The 'lovegrass' common name (shared by many Eragrostis species) references the delicate, romantic quality of the seed heads. Provides important food for doves, sparrows, and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter. Distinguished from the non-native weeping lovegrass (E. curvula) by its native origin, finer texture, and less weeping, more upright form. An excellent native ornamental grass for hot, dry, full-sun gardens and naturalistic prairie plantings in the southern plains states and Southwest.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after soil warms (68°F+) in moist to wet, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy soil in full sun; prickly sesban (dhaincha) is one of the most important green manure and cover crop plants of tropical and subtropical rice farming systems — extraordinarily fast-growing (up to 1 inch per day), nitrogen-fixing (80–120 lbs N/acre), and tolerant of waterlogged, flooded, and saline soils that most cover crops cannot handle.
directions: Broadcast or drill at 20–30 lbs/acre in full sun in moist to waterlogged conditions; incorporate or chop-and-drop before seed set to prevent naturalization; do not allow to seed down in sensitive wetland areas. Sesbania bispinosa (prickly sesban or dhaincha) is one of the most important green manure and cover crop species in tropical Asian rice farming systems — a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing annual legume widely used across India, Bangladesh, Thailand, and the Philippines as a pre-rice or in-rice green manure crop. The plant's growth speed is remarkable: under warm, wet conditions it can add over an inch of height per day, reaching 4–8 feet in just 60–75 days from seeding. Its nitrogen fixation is similarly impressive, with reported values of 80–120 lbs of N per acre in a single growing cycle — equivalent to substantial synthetic fertilizer applications. Prickly sesban is uniquely adapted to waterlogged and flooded conditions that most cover crops cannot tolerate — making it the standard choice for pre-flooding cover crops in paddy rice systems, where it can be grown, then incorporated into the field before flooding for transplanted rice. It also tolerates moderately saline soils better than most legumes. The 'prickly' in the name refers to spines on the seed pods. In zone 8–12, dhaincha is an excellent summer cover crop for warm, moist gardens; cut before flowering to use as a soil amendment.

common_name: Purple Tephrosia (Wild Indigo, Fish Poison Plant, Wild Hog Weed)
plant_note: Direct sow in full sun in any lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; Tephrosia purpurea is a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing, drought-tolerant shrubby legume native to tropical Asia, widely naturalized throughout the Gulf Coast and Caribbean, and an important larval host plant for the Ceraunus Blue butterfly (Hemiargus ceraunus) throughout zone 9-12. It grows naturally in disturbed, sandy, open ground and establishes rapidly in poor soils. The small pink to purple flowers are produced prolifically from spring through fall. CAUTION: Tephrosia purpurea contains rotenone and related toxins and is poisonous to fish and mildly toxic to mammals if consumed in quantity — do not plant near fish ponds or allow livestock to graze.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any lean, well-drained, sandy soil — Purple Tephrosia establishes readily in poor, disturbed, sandy soils and is one of the most drought-tolerant and ecologically valuable small legumes for zone 9-12, functioning as a nitrogen fixer, butterfly larval host, and pollinator plant simultaneously. Tephrosia purpurea is a low, spreading, semi-woody annual to short-lived perennial shrub in the Fabaceae family (tribe Millettieae) native to tropical Asia, Africa, and Australia, now naturalized throughout the Caribbean, Florida, and the Gulf Coast in open, disturbed, sunny habitats. The plant produces upright to spreading stems bearing pinnately compound leaves of 9–17 pairs of narrow, oblong, gray-green leaflets, and through the warm months produces numerous small (0.3–0.5 inch) pink to rosy-purple typical legume flowers in axillary and terminal racemes — modest individually but produced in sufficient quantity to provide a continuous, soft display through the growing season. As a legume, Tephrosia purpurea fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis and improves sandy, depleted soils over time. Its ecological role as a larval host plant for the Ceraunus Blue butterfly (Hemiargus ceraunus) throughout south Florida and the Caribbean makes it particularly valuable for butterfly gardens in zone 9b-12, where this small, brilliant blue butterfly seeks out Tephrosia for egg-laying. The plant also contains rotenone-related compounds that were historically used as a fish poison and mild insecticide — do not plant near fish ponds.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; purple three-awn grows naturally in hot, dry, open desert grassland, rocky slopes, and sandy plains throughout the Southwest and Southern Plains. Very drought tolerant — essentially no supplemental irrigation needed after establishment in appropriate climates.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; purple three-awn is the most widespread of the Aristida (three-awn) grasses of the western half of North America — a small to medium-sized warm-season bunchgrass named for the three awns (bristle-like extensions) on each seed that give the panicle its distinctive appearance. The purple-tinted seed heads in summer and fall are ornamental in mass plantings, creating a haze of fine purple-red color over large areas of desert grassland. An important native grass of the Chihuahuan Desert grassland, Sonoran Desert margins, and Southern Plains, often occurring in disturbed, degraded, or overgrazed soils where more palatable native grasses have been lost. Despite its common occurrence in disturbed sites, it is a valuable native for erosion control on dry, rocky, sandy slopes where more demanding species are difficult to establish. Three-awn grass seeds have been problematic for livestock and dogs — the sharp, twisted awns can penetrate skin and cause injury.

plant_note: Sow in fall in mild-winter regions; it is less cold hardy than hairy vetch.
directions: Inoculate with vetch-pea rhizobia and broadcast at about 1-2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, raking to cover 1 inch deep. Purple vetch is a fast-growing annual legume best suited to mild-winter climates where it fixes nitrogen through the cool season. It climbs readily, so pairing it with a cereal companion improves standability and biomass. Terminate by mowing or crimping at early bloom before viable seed forms to prevent weedy volunteers. Incorporate the succulent residue or leave it as a nitrogen-rich mulch two to three weeks before planting.

plant_note: Sow in late summer to early fall for quick fall cover that scavenges nutrients.
directions: Broadcast at about 0.25-0.5 lb per 1,000 sq ft and rake to cover 0.25 inch deep in a moist seedbed. This fast-growing brassica establishes quickly, forming a fibrous root mat that takes up excess nitrogen and reduces leaching over winter. It is less cold hardy than oilseed rape and often winterkills in colder regions, providing free termination. Where it survives, mow at early flowering and incorporate the residue two to three weeks before planting. The rapid canopy closure also smothers fall-germinating weeds.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost, or frost-seed in late winter; short-lived perennial that fixes nitrogen and blooms its second year.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a prepared bed at 8–10 lb per acre, raking to 1/4 in depth; red clover tolerates slightly acidic soils and moderate shade better than most legume cover crops. It overwinters in zones 4 and warmer and puts on vigorous growth in early spring, often topping 2 ft before bloom. Terminate at early flower stage — before the first florets open to brown — to capture maximum fixed nitrogen of 80–150 lb per acre. A second flush of growth often follows mowing, allowing a second cut of biomass before final incorporation.

plant_note: Broadcast seed at 2–4 lbs per acre into a well-prepared seedbed when soil reaches 65°F; Rhodes grass establishes quickly and can tolerate a wide range of soils including alkaline and saline conditions; it is a valuable summer cover crop and forage grass for zones 8–11, providing fast ground cover, erosion control, and organic matter accumulation in the hot-season window when cool-season cover crops are not viable.
directions: Broadcast seed at 2–4 lbs per acre and lightly rake; Rhodes grass can also spread via stolons once established; graze, mow, or chop-and-drop at 18–24 inch height before heading; drought-tolerant once established but grows fastest with adequate moisture in summer; terminate before seed set to prevent reseeding. Rhodes grass (Chloris gayana) is a warm-season perennial grass native to tropical and subtropical Africa that has been widely naturalized throughout the world's warm regions as a drought-tolerant forage and cover crop grass. Named for Cecil John Rhodes, the colonial-era mining magnate who popularized it across southern Africa in the late 19th century, it is now one of the most widely grown tropical forage grasses in the world, valued for its ability to establish quickly on poor, dry, alkaline, and even mildly saline soils where more demanding grasses fail. In the Gulf South and zone 8–11 regions, Rhodes grass fills the summer cover crop window when cool-season legumes (crimson clover, winter peas) have been terminated and summer heat makes establishment of new cool-season species impractical. It provides rapid ground cover to prevent erosion and weed establishment, accumulates organic matter through root turnover, and can be mowed and incorporated as green manure before a fall garden planting. The grass produces attractive finger-like seed heads that are ornamental. Somewhat drought-tolerant once established, persisting on as little as 12–15 inches of annual rainfall. Note: can become naturalized in warm regions — mow before seed set if invasive potential is a concern.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or clay soil in full sun; ring muhly grows naturally in dry, rocky, desert grassland and piñon-juniper woodland soils of the Southwest at 3,500–7,000 feet elevation. Extremely drought tolerant once established, requiring essentially no supplemental water in appropriate climates.
directions: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or clay soil in full sun; ring muhly is a low, tufted, fine-leaved native bunchgrass of dry southwestern desert grassland and piñon-juniper woodland, producing wiry, thread-like leaves and delicate, airy seed panicles. Named for the 'fairy ring' pattern that develops as old clumps die out in the center while continuing to grow at the outer rim — over many years, a single plant produces an ever-expanding ring of grass that leaves a bare center, similar to the fairy rings of mushrooms. The rings can reach 2–4 feet in diameter in old, undisturbed specimens. The fine, wiry texture and extremely low water needs make ring muhly an excellent ornamental groundcover grass for hot, rocky, dry southwestern garden settings. An excellent low-maintenance native grass for piñon-juniper landscaping, xeriscape rock gardens, and restoration plantings in the Colorado Plateau, New Mexico, and Arizona mountain foothills.

plant_note: Sow in fall in California and similar Mediterranean climates for winter growth; rose clover is a winter annual that must establish before temperatures drop below 25°F; inoculate seed with Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar. trifolii before sowing.
directions: Broadcast seed in fall at 8–12 lbs per acre into a firm seedbed in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; rose clover is a Mediterranean annual clover widely used in California, Texas, and the Pacific Northwest as a winter cover crop and pasture legume, valued especially for its tolerance of dry, poor, acidic soils where other clovers fail. It fixes significant amounts of atmospheric nitrogen, reseeds itself reliably from hard seed, and is exceptionally drought-tolerant through its summer dormant period as seeds await fall rains. The fuzzy rose-pink to red flower heads attract bees. Mow or turn under at early bloom for maximum nitrogen contribution before the seeds mature.

plant_note: Sow in early spring; the deep taproot exploits subsoil moisture and breaks compaction.
directions: Sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep at about 0.5-1 lb per 1,000 sq ft into warm, well-drained soil after the ground can be worked. Safflower develops a strong taproot that penetrates several feet, breaking up compacted subsoil and drawing up moisture and nutrients from depth. It is highly drought tolerant, making it a useful soil-building cover for dry sites and rotations. Terminate by mowing before the spiny flower heads mature, since the bracts become sharp and seed can volunteer. Incorporate the residue or leave it as surface mulch to protect the soil and improve organic matter.

plant_note: Sow direct in early spring in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, chalky or limey soil in full sun; sainfoin requires good drainage and calcareous soil — it will not thrive on acid, waterlogged, or clay-heavy ground. Sow seed-in-pod (hulled or unhulled) at 25–40 lbs per acre.
directions: Sow direct in early spring at 25–40 lbs per acre (seed-in-pod) in well-drained, calcareous, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; sainfoin is a deep-rooted perennial legume from the Eurasian steppes and chalk grasslands that is exceptional for dry, poor, chalky, and limestone soils where most other legumes perform poorly. Onobrychis viciifolia produces upright, pinnate-leafed stems and striking spikes of vivid rose-pink, veined, pea-like flowers from late spring through summer that are among the most attractive of any cover crop and are magnets for bumblebees and honeybees; the name 'sainfoin' means 'healthy hay' in French, reflecting its long history as premium livestock forage. Unlike most legumes, sainfoin does not cause bloat in ruminants due to its condensed tannin content, making it particularly valuable as pasture in extensive livestock systems. Sainfoin fixes atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis and the deep taproot mines subsoil nutrients, breaking up hardpan; it is very drought tolerant once established and thrives on thin, stony calcareous soils.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; scorpion senna is a useful nitrogen-fixing shrub for dry, alkaline bank stabilization and wildlife habitat in zones 7–10.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; scorpion senna tolerates poor, rocky soils and drought once established and is excellent for dry bank stabilization and wildlife habitat in warm climates. Coronilla emerus (Hippocrepis emerus) is a deciduous to semi-evergreen European native shrub in the pea family producing wiry, green stems with pinnate leaves and clusters of bright-yellow flowers with bronze markings from spring through summer followed by distinctive, elongated, segmented seed pods resembling a scorpion's tail; it is a useful nitrogen-fixing shrub for poor, dry, alkaline soils in zones 7–10. The flowers attract butterflies and bees; the shrub provides nesting cover for birds; it is naturalizing and somewhat invasive in warm, dry climates where conditions suit it. Useful as a medium-height groundcover for dry, sunny banks and slopes.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sensitive partridge pea self-sows prolifically in appropriate open, disturbed conditions and naturalizes readily in sandy roadsides, old fields, and sunny groundcover beds.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sensitive partridge pea is a smaller relative of the showy partridge pea (C. fasciculata) that shares the same remarkable leaf sensitivity — the pinnate, compound leaves immediately fold closed when touched or disturbed, re-opening within minutes. The bright yellow flowers, smaller than partridge pea but produced in similar abundance, provide pollen for a number of native bees including specialist Chamaecrista bees that depend specifically on the pea flowers. It grows in the driest, most disturbed sandy and rocky soils across eastern North America, where it is one of the pioneering native annuals that colonizes bare, sunny ground. The seeds are consumed by quail and other ground-feeding birds. An easy self-seeding native annual for adding nitrogen fixation and wildlife value to dry, sunny, sandy garden areas with minimal intervention.

plant_note: Broadcast scarified seed on a firm, well-prepared seedbed in early to mid spring; sericea lespedeza establishes slowly in its first year but forms a deep-rooted, long-lived stand once settled. It spreads readily by reseeding and can become difficult to remove — plant only where a persistent, deep-rooted legume is genuinely wanted, and check local status before planting, as some states regulate it as a noxious weed.
directions: Broadcast scarified, inoculated seed on a firm seedbed in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant and well adapted to poor, acidic, eroded, or infertile soils once its deep taproot is established. Sericea lespedeza is a warm-season perennial legume long used across the South for erosion control on cut slopes and marginal land, as a nitrogen-fixing soil builder, and as wildlife food-plot forage valued by deer, quail, and turkey for its late-summer seed and leguminous browse. Its deep root system makes it exceptionally drought-hardy and long persisting once established, continuing to produce for a decade or more without reseeding on a well-managed site. Because it spreads aggressively by seed and can outcompete native vegetation in unmanaged settings, it is best confined to dedicated forage or reclamation plantings rather than mixed cover-crop rotations, and mowing before seed set helps limit unwanted spread. Zone 5–9.

plant_note: Sow in fall when soils cool below 75°F. Inoculate seed with the appropriate Ornithopus-specific rhizobium inoculant before sowing, especially in fields where serradella has not been grown before. Broadcast or drill seed shallowly at 10-15 lb per acre into a firm seedbed.
directions: Serradella thrives in sandy, acidic soils with a pH of 4.5-6.5 where clovers and vetches often fail — lime the field sparingly if at all, as this legume is adapted to low-fertility, low-pH conditions. Sow seed shallowly (no deeper than 0.5 inch) in fall, using rhizobium-inoculated seed to ensure effective nitrogen fixation. The crop establishes slowly but produces good biomass through winter and spring, fixing 50-100 lb of nitrogen per acre by the time it is incorporated or mowed before planting summer crops. In orchards and vineyards, allow it to reseed naturally in fall for a low-maintenance, self-renewing ground cover.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 70°F; sesbania germinates and establishes extremely rapidly and can grow 6–8 feet in a single season. Terminate by mowing or incorporating before it sets seed to prevent naturalization.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed in warm, moist soil; sesbania is one of the fastest-growing nitrogen-fixing legumes in the world, capable of producing 4–6 tons of organic matter per acre in a single season in warm climates. In South Asia it is the premier green manure for flooded rice paddies, incorporated at tillage to supply nitrogen equivalent to 100+ lbs/acre urea. For Gulf Coast home gardeners it is a superb summer cover crop that grows rapidly in the intense summer heat when cool-season covers are impossible and provides deep-rooted biomass for improving heavy clay soils. Terminate by mowing when 3–4 feet tall and allow residue to decompose before planting fall vegetables. Tolerates temporary flooding and poor soils.

subcategory: tropical warm-season cover crop and ornamental
plant_note: Direct sow in spring after soil warms in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; showy rattlebox is a fast-growing tropical annual legume cover crop used for nitrogen fixation and nematode suppression in warm-season rotation systems — particularly effective against root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species); IMPORTANT: toxic to horses, cattle, pigs, and poultry due to pyrrolizidine alkaloids in seeds and foliage — do NOT use as forage or in areas accessible to livestock.
directions: Broadcast or drill in warm season in full sun; incorporate before seed set; CAUTION: toxic to livestock — do not use as forage; effective nematode suppression cover crop. Crotalaria spectabilis (showy rattlebox or ornamental crotalaria) is a tropical annual legume native to Asia and Africa, naturalized across warm regions worldwide, and widely used in tropical and subtropical cover cropping systems for two important soil health benefits: nitrogen fixation (60–100 lbs N/acre) and nematode suppression. The plant's nematode-suppressing properties are its most important agronomic feature: C. spectabilis is one of the most effective non-chemical tools for managing root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species) — a devastating pest of vegetables, strawberries, and ornamentals in sandy soils of the Gulf South and tropical regions. The plant produces compounds that are toxic to nematode larvae, dramatically reducing nematode populations when grown for one season and incorporated into the soil. The plant is also ornamentally attractive: tall (3–5 feet), with bright-yellow, butterfly-like flower spikes and interesting inflated seed pods that rattle when dry (the genus name Crotalaria means 'rattle'). IMPORTANT CAUTION: The seeds and foliage contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids that are toxic to horses, cattle, pigs, and poultry — causing liver damage and death. Use only in areas inaccessible to livestock, or as a summer cover crop terminated before animals access the field.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky, acidic to slightly acid soil in full sun; sidebeak pencilflower is adapted to nutrient-poor, well-drained, acidic sandy soils and will decline in heavy, moist, or fertilized conditions.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; sidebeak pencilflower is a diminutive native perennial legume of dry, sandy pinelands, sandhills, and rocky acidic outcrops across the southeastern Coastal Plain. The genus name (Stylosanthes = 'stalk-flower') refers to the unusual structure of the flower, in which the petals are carried on a long, narrow floral tube or 'beak.' The tiny yellow flowers are produced throughout summer and fall, providing pollen and nectar for small native bees. This is one of the few leguminous plants native to the nutrient-poor sandy soils of the longleaf pine ecosystem, where it fixes nitrogen under conditions that would challenge most legumes. The wiry, semi-prostrate stems form a low, spreading mat that can serve as a drought-tolerant groundcover in dry, acidic, sandy conditions. Grows naturally in the same habitats as gopher tortoises in the Southeast.

common_name: Siratro (Purple Bush Bean, Phasey Bean, Purplebush)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in any well-drained soil; Macroptilium atropurpureum establishes rapidly and fixes nitrogen from the air through root nodule bacteria. In zone 9, it often grows as a short-lived perennial — the tops may freeze back but roots and lower stems survive and resprout. Use as a living mulch between rows, a summer cover crop to mow and incorporate before fall planting, or an erosion-control cover on disturbed areas. Excellent nectar source for butterflies and small native bees. Somewhat invasive outside agricultural use in tropical areas — avoid planting near natural areas.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil — Siratro is one of the most drought-tolerant tropical legume cover crops available and establishes vigorously in hot, dry conditions where many other cover crops fail. Macroptilium atropurpureum is a twining, semi-erect to climbing legume native to Mexico, Central America, and South America in the Fabaceae family, widely used throughout the tropical and subtropical world as a cover crop, forage crop, and nitrogen-fixing groundcover. The plant produces trifoliate leaves (three broad leaflets, the middle one often lobed) on trailing to climbing stems that spread across the ground or climb on adjacent vegetation. Through the warm months, the plants produce clusters of small, vivid dark reddish-purple to maroon-red, butterfly-shaped (papilionaceous) flowers that are attractive to butterflies, native bees, and small pollinators. As a legume, Siratro fixes significant quantities of atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis with Bradyrhizobium bacteria, enriching the soil over the growing season. The dried, hay-form foliage is used as a high-protein livestock fodder in tropical agriculture. In zone 9 home gardens, Siratro is used as a summer living mulch between vegetable beds, as an annual cover to improve soil before fall crops, and as a wildflower-adjacent ornamental ground layer. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; scarify or nick seeds to improve germination rates. Inoculate with appropriate Bradyrhizobium for maximum nitrogen fixation. Mow or incorporate into soil before seed set to prevent prolific self-seeding.
directions: An upright warm-season annual legume naturalized throughout the southeastern US and tropical regions worldwide, producing trifoliate leaves and tall racemes of bright yellow, pea-like flowers from late summer through fall, followed by inflated seed pods that rattle audibly when ripe. Scarify or nick seeds before direct sowing after last frost to speed germination; inoculate with Bradyrhizobium for best nitrogen-fixation results in new planting sites. As a nitrogen-fixing cover crop and green manure, it builds soil fertility rapidly in warm, well-drained, full-sun beds in zones 8-11. Mow or till under before seed set — all parts, especially the seeds, contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids that are toxic to livestock and humans if ingested.

common_name: Soil Builder Peas and Oats Cover Crop
plant_note: Broadcast in spring or late summer to build and protect soil.
directions: Broadcast this field pea and oat mix densely over prepared soil in spring or late summer, then rake in and water. The fast-growing combination adds organic matter and nutrients while shading out weeds. Pea plants fix nitrogen and the oats provide structure and biomass, together conditioning even rough ground such as former lawns and vacant lots. Let the stand grow until flowering, then cut and turn it under a few weeks before planting your main crop. The oats often winterkill in cold regions, leaving an easy-to-manage mulch.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March through June. Sorghum-sudangrass hybrids can be planted through July for late-summer cover. Sorghum is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant of all summer crops, making it ideal for the Texas and Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1–1.5 inches deep in a wide range of soils including heavy clays and infertile ground; sorghum establishes a deep root system that loosens compacted subsoil and mines deeply-held nutrients. As a summer cover crop it suppresses weeds aggressively and builds organic matter; mow or disk before seed heads shatter to prevent volunteers. As a grain crop the seed heads can be harvested for bird feed, home brewing (sorghum is the base grain for many African and Asian fermented beverages), or ground into gluten-free flour. The juice squeezed from sweet sorghum stalks is boiled down to sorghum molasses, a traditional Southern sweetener. Beware allelopathic compounds released by sorghum residues — delay direct-seeding small-seeded crops for 3–4 weeks after incorporation.

scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor × Sorghum bicolor var. sudanense
plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; produces massive biomass for weed suppression and soil building.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed 3/4 in deep into warm soil; sorghum-sudangrass hybrids germinate and grow aggressively, reaching 6–8 feet before termination. The dense canopy suppresses even aggressive perennial weeds, and allelopathic root exudates further inhibit weed germination. Mow to 4–6 in to encourage regrowth and additional tillering before final termination; allow residue 2–3 weeks to partially break down before transplanting into it. Avoid planting in soybean rotations immediately after, as the sorghum-family residue can briefly stunt legume establishment.

plant_note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep at 4–6 pounds per 1,000 square feet in warm (65°F+) soil in full sun; sorghum-sudangrass is extremely aggressive in good conditions and can grow 1–2 inches per day in peak summer heat. Terminate with a roller-crimper, tillage, or mowing at or before anthesis.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil (65°F minimum) in full sun after last frost; sorghum-sudangrass is the premier summer cover crop for the South and Gulf Coast, producing more biomass per day than any other cover crop in hot weather — 6–12 feet of lush growth that smothers weeds, suppresses nematodes, builds organic matter rapidly, and breaks up compacted soil with its fibrous root system. The allelopathic root exudates suppress germination of subsequent crops if incorporated when immature; allow residue to fully decompose before planting a following crop. Mow or roll at boot stage (before flowering) to maximize biomass and prevent unwanted reseeding. An outstanding choice for filling the fallow summer season in zone 8–11 gardens, breaking pest and disease cycles between cash crops, and adding large quantities of organic matter to difficult clay or compacted soils.

scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor × Sorghum bicolor var. drummondii
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; sow at 30–40 lbs/acre or broadcast and rake in for home garden use. Sorghum-sudangrass is the ideal summer cover crop for the Gulf South (zone 8–10) where cool-season covers like crimson clover or winter rye die in summer heat. Mow at 3–4 feet tall before heading to prevent seed set and stimulate regrowth; can be mowed 2–3 times per season for maximum biomass. Incorporate 2–3 weeks before planting fall crops to allow decomposition.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed after last frost at 4–6 lbs per 1,000 sq ft; mow at 3–4 feet before heading to stimulate regrowth. Incorporate or mow and compost 2–3 weeks before planting fall crops. Sorghum-sudangrass hybrid (sometimes sold as 'sudex' or 'sordan') is the most important summer annual cover crop for warm-climate gardens in zones 7–10 — the warm-season counterpart to winter rye or winter cover crop mixes that die when summer heat arrives. The hybrid is produced by crossing grain sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) with sudangrass (a variety of the same species), resulting in a vigorous, fast-growing, heat-tolerant grass that can produce 4,000–6,000 lbs of dry matter per acre in a single season. For the Gulf South garden, sorghum-sudangrass solves the challenging 'summer fallow' problem: from June through September, heat and humidity make most vegetable production difficult, and bare soil is subject to erosion, compaction, weed invasion, and nutrient leaching. A sorghum-sudangrass cover fills that window with living roots (suppressing nematodes through allelopathic compounds), dense canopy (shading out weeds), and substantial organic matter that improves soil tilth for fall planting. The roots reach 6–8 feet deep, breaking through hardpan and improving drainage in compacted soils.

plant_note: Sow in late summer 6–10 weeks before first fall frost for a frost-killed winter cover in zones 4–8; the oat plant is killed by temperatures below 20°F, making it a convenient 'mow-free' winter cover that lies flat and decomposes naturally without spring tillage.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed at 2–3 oz per 100 sq ft onto a well-prepared, lightly raked bed in late summer or early fall; germination is rapid in cool soil and the oat establishes quickly, outcompeting late-season weeds. Spring oat is one of the most versatile and widely used cool-season cover crops because it is killed by hard frost (below 20°F) without any action by the gardener, leaving a mat of dead mulch that protects bare soil through winter and decomposes quickly in spring with minimal residue management; it also mixes exceptionally well with hairy vetch or crimson clover, providing a physical trellis for the climbing legume while the legume fixes nitrogen. For warm climates (zones 8–11) sow in early spring as a short-term summer smother crop between vegetable beds.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked for a fast summer smother crop.
directions: Broadcast or drill at roughly 2-3 lb per 1,000 sq ft into a firm seedbed and rake to cover about 1 inch deep. Spring oats germinate quickly in cool soil and produce dense biomass that outcompetes weeds and captures nitrogen. Unlike winter oats, spring oats will not survive hard freezes, which makes winterkill a convenient no-till termination in cold climates. In mild areas terminate by mowing before seed heads form, then incorporate or leave residue as surface mulch. Follow with a nitrogen-fixing legume to balance the carbon added by the grass residue.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for best germination in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or clay-loam, lean soil in full sun; squirreltail is a pioneer grass that germinates most readily in cool weather (fall or early spring), establishing quickly in disturbed, dry soils where other grasses fail. An excellent early colonizer for erosion control on dry, rocky, alkaline sites.
directions: Direct sow in fall for best germination in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky, sandy or clay-loam, lean soil in full sun; squirreltail is a small, cool-season native bunchgrass named for its distinctive seed heads — the very long, spreading, diverging awns (bristles) on each spikelet create a seed head resembling a squirrel's bushy tail. When the seed heads mature and dry, the awns spread outward dramatically, making the plant immediately distinctive and ornamental. One of the most widely distributed native grasses of the arid West — found from the Great Basin and Mojave Desert through the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains on dry, rocky, alkaline soils, often in disturbed areas, rocky road cuts, and desert flats. One of the most important pioneer and restoration grasses for the arid West because it germinates early in cool weather, establishes fast in poor, dry soils, and outcompetes invasive annual grasses (cheatgrass, medusahead) in some conditions. An essential component of Great Basin and Intermountain West restoration seed mixes. The spreading awns act as effective natural seed dispersal mechanisms — attaching to fur, feathers, and clothing.

common_name: St. Augustine Grass (Gulf Coast Standard Warm-Season Lawn Grass)
plant_note: Establish from sod, plugs, or sprigs (not from seed, as no commercially viable seed is available); plant when soil temperature is consistently above 70°F. In zone 9, plant April–August for best establishment before fall. Mow at 3–4 inches (do not scalp — St. Augustine cannot recover from severe mowing that removes the green leaf tissue). Water deeply 2–3 times per week during establishment; once established, 1 inch per week is usually sufficient in the Gulf South.
directions: Install sod or plant plugs (12 inches apart) in spring through midsummer; keep consistently moist for 4–6 weeks during establishment. Mow at 3–4 inches; never remove more than one-third of the leaf blade at once. St. Augustine grass (Stenotaphrum secundatum) is the dominant lawn grass of the Gulf Coast region — the standard residential, commercial, and golf course rough grass of Florida, coastal Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia below zone 8. No other turfgrass matches St. Augustine for shade tolerance among warm-season grasses: it remains acceptably dense under moderate tree canopy where bermudagrass, zoysia, and bahia grass would fail from insufficient light — a critical advantage in the mature tree-shaded residential lots common throughout the Gulf South. The coarse-textured, broad-bladed leaves produce a lush, deep green lawn appearance that is visually distinct from the finer textures of bermuda or zoysia. St. Augustine spreads aggressively by above-ground stolons (runners), quickly filling gaps when plugs are installed correctly. The primary maintenance challenges are chinch bugs (a significant pest throughout the Gulf South), gray leaf spot (a fungal disease that can defoliate in warm, humid conditions), and susceptibility to cold injury below 20°F. Varieties like 'Floratam,' 'Raleigh,' 'Palmetto,' and 'Seville' offer different compromises of cold tolerance, shade tolerance, and disease resistance.

plant_note: Direct sow at 3–5 lb/acre (or ½ oz per 100 sq ft) in spring in moist to wet, heavy clay or loamy soil; inoculate seed with clover-type Rhizobium before sowing and scarify lightly if seed coat is hard.
directions: Direct sow at 3–5 lb/acre (or ½ oz per 100 sq ft) in spring in moist to wet, heavy clay or loamy soil; inoculate seed with clover-type Rhizobium before sowing and scarify lightly if seed coat is hard. Trifolium fragiferum is a low-growing, creeping perennial clover distinguished from other clovers by its unusual inflated, strawberry-like fruiting heads that give the plant its common name; it is exceptionally tolerant of waterlogging, saline soils, and heavy clay — soil conditions that defeat most other clovers — making it the best clover for coastal areas, tidal influence, and problem wet spots. As a perennial nitrogen-fixing cover crop, it establishes a persistent ground cover that can be mowed and left in place for years, fixing atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium root nodules. It is excellent for living mulch systems, riparian buffer strips, and orchard understories on poorly drained land.

plant_note: Sow 6–10 weeks before first frost in mild-winter climates; uniquely reseeds itself by burying its own seed pods underground.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed at 15–20 lb/acre onto a well-prepared seedbed in late summer to early fall; subterranean clover tolerates poorly drained and acidic soils better than most annual clovers. The prostrate stems root at nodes and the spent flower heads push seed capsules into the soil surface, allowing the stand to self-reseed year after year without replanting. It fixes moderate nitrogen and forms a dense mat that suppresses winter and spring weeds. Mow or graze lightly in late winter to stimulate pod development, then allow to dry before any tillage.

plant_note: Direct-sow after soil is thoroughly warm (above 60°F) in spring or early summer; sudangrass grows very rapidly in hot conditions and should be mowed or tilled when it reaches 18–24 inches to prevent it from setting seed and to stimulate branching. For summer cover crop use in hot climates like the Gulf Coast, it is ideal — it germinates and establishes in June heat that kills cool-season cover crops.
directions: Direct-sow in warm, well-drained soil after soil temperatures exceed 60°F; sudangrass is the premier warm-season summer cover crop for the South and Gulf Coast, growing rapidly in the intense summer heat that kills cool-season cover crops like crimson clover and winter rye — it can gain 6–8 inches per week in hot conditions. The dense root system breaks up compacted soil, and the rapidly decomposing residue adds significant organic matter. Mow when 18–24 inches tall (before heading) to encourage dense regrowth and prevent seed set. It produces allelopathic compounds that suppress some weed seeds — incorporate into the soil 2–4 weeks before planting vegetables to allow the allelopathic effect to dissipate. Sudangrass x sorghum hybrids ('BMR' or 'brown midrib' types) break down faster in the soil than standard varieties and are preferred where rapid residue decomposition is needed. An outstanding solution for the summer fallow period in zone 7–11 vegetable gardens where nothing else grows quickly enough in the heat.

plant_note: Sow after last frost once soil is consistently warm; a standout warm-season nitrogen fixer and nematode suppressor for zone 9–11.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed 1/2 in deep into warm, well-drained soil after danger of frost has passed. Sunn hemp grows rapidly — up to 6 feet in two months — and fixes 100–200 lb of nitrogen per acre while suppressing root-knot nematodes through root exudates. Terminate by mowing at first bloom (roughly 60–70 days) before seed set, since mature plants become woody and slow to decompose. Do not plant where livestock can graze, as the foliage contains alkaloids toxic to most grazing animals.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 6–8 weeks before the first hard frost, or in early spring, into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to light shade; tall fescue establishes a dense, deep-rooted sod that persists for many years once mature.
directions: Drill seed 1/4–1/2 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun to light shade; tolerates more shade than most pasture and cover crop grasses, making it useful under widely spaced orchard trees. Tall fescue is a deep-rooted, cool-season perennial grass widely used across the transition zone and upper South as a persistent pasture and hay grass, valued for its tolerance of heavy grazing, foot traffic, drought, and a wide range of soil conditions once established. As a cover crop, it forms a dense, long-lived sod that provides excellent erosion control on slopes, waterways, and orchard alleys, and its deep root system builds soil structure and organic matter over time. Older common tall fescue varieties carry a fungal endophyte that can cause toxicity issues in grazing livestock — endophyte-free or novel-endophyte cultivars are recommended where livestock grazing is intended. A tough, versatile, long-lived grass for permanent pasture, erosion control, or shaded orchard groundcover, zone 4–8.

plant_note: In mild-winter climates (zones 7–9), sow in early autumn for overwintering and spring bloom. In colder zones, direct-sow in earliest spring as soon as the soil can be worked, as seeds germinate well in cool conditions and seedlings tolerate frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in fall or early spring into well-drained soil; soaking seeds overnight before planting improves germination rates. Provide twiggy brush, netting, or a trellis for the tendriling stems to climb, or let the vine sprawl as a ground cover to suppress weeds. Tangier pea is highly attractive to bumblebees and other native pollinators and will fix substantial nitrogen when inoculated with a legume inoculant before sowing. Mow or turn the vines into the soil when flowering peaks or pods begin to set to capture maximum nitrogen benefit for the following crop.

plant_note: Direct-sow as early as possible in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Tartary buckwheat tolerates cool soil temperatures and light frosts that would damage common buckwheat and is significantly more cold-tolerant at germination. It matures quickly and can be sown as a succession cover crop in fall in mild climates. Historically grown at high altitudes in the Himalayas and Tibet where common buckwheat fails.
directions: Direct-sow in well-drained, average to lean soil in early spring or fall; Tartary buckwheat is a cool-tolerant relative of common buckwheat native to the high-altitude plateaus of the Himalayas, Tibet, and Yunnan, grown for 4,000 years as a grain crop in conditions too cold and harsh for most cereals. It differs from common buckwheat in germinating at lower temperatures, tolerating light frosts, and having significantly higher concentrations of rutin (a bioflavonoid with antioxidant properties) — up to 100 times more rutin than common buckwheat. In Bhutan, Nepal, and Tibet, Tartary buckwheat flour is used to make traditional foods such as Bhutan's staple 'puta' noodles. As a cover crop, it establishes rapidly, suppresses weeds through dense canopy and allelopathic root exudates, and its residue breaks down quickly in the soil. More tolerant of cold and more adaptable to cool, wet climates than common buckwheat. An excellent cool-season cover crop for spring or fall use in zone 2–9.

plant_note: Sow 6–10 weeks before first frost; the deep taproot breaks up compacted soil and winter-kills in cold zones.
directions: Broadcast seed about 1/2 in deep in late summer; the thick taproot drills deep and shatters compaction. In cold-winter areas it dies and rots in place, leaving channels and released nutrients. Where it survives, mow before it flowers to prevent seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow in late spring in very well-drained to seasonally wet, slightly alkaline to neutral, heavy clay or fine sandy loam soil in full sun; tobosa grass grows naturally in Chihuahuan Desert playas (dry lake beds) and swales that receive concentrated runoff, adapting to both extreme drought between rains and brief periodic flooding.
directions: Direct sow in late spring in very well-drained to seasonally wet, slightly alkaline to neutral, heavy clay or fine sandy loam soil in full sun; tobosa grass is the dominant warm-season grass of the Chihuahuan Desert playa flats and desert swales — the wide, flat, internally-draining dry lake beds and seasonally wet depressions of the Chihuahuan Desert from west Texas to southern New Mexico and northern Chihuahua. A coarse, stiff, rhizomatous warm-season grass that forms distinctive, dense, nearly pure-stand tobosa flats on heavy clay soils that flood briefly after summer monsoon rains and then dry completely. The stiff, curling leaves are unpalatable to livestock when dry and mature, but the green growth after summer rains is important forage. Very tolerant of the extreme conditions of playa-flat habitats — alternating drought, heat, and brief flooding on dense, shrinking-and-cracking Vertisol clay soils. An essential species for the restoration of degraded Chihuahuan Desert grassland playa habitats. More heat-tolerant than galleta grass, extending into the hotter Chihuahuan and Sonoran desert zones.

plant_note: Sow 4–6 weeks before first frost in fall; combines the cold-hardiness of rye with the palatability and residue quality of wheat.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed at 60–90 lb/acre and cover to 1 in depth in fall; triticale is a wheat-rye hybrid that is nearly as cold-hardy as cereal rye but produces softer, lower-lignin residue that breaks down faster in spring. It scavenges soil nitrogen over winter and produces abundant biomass for weed suppression and organic matter. Terminate in early spring at the jointing stage (before the seed head emerges from the boot) by rolling, flail-mowing, or tillage; residue breaks down within 3–4 weeks in warm spring conditions. Pairs well with hairy vetch to combine nitrogen fixation with grass biomass.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil in full sun; tropical kudzu (Pueraria phaseoloides) is a Southeast Asian vine legume — the agricultural workhorse cover crop of tropical rubber and oil palm plantations worldwide, fixing large amounts of nitrogen and forming a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover; it is biologically distinct from the invasive kudzu (P. montana) of the southeastern United States.
directions: Direct sow in warm, moderately fertile, moist soil in full sun; inoculate seed with Bradyrhizobium before planting; plant in contained areas as the vine can spread aggressively. Pueraria phaseoloides (tropical kudzu or puero) is a Southeast Asian legume vine and the dominant cover crop species in tropical rubber (Hevea) and oil palm (Elaeis) plantation agriculture throughout Malaysia, Indonesia, and across equatorial Asia and Africa. It was deliberately introduced throughout the tropics as the premier nitrogen-fixing, weed-suppressing, soil-protecting cover crop for plantation agriculture — where it forms a continuous 12–24 inch deep groundcover between tree rows that prevents soil erosion during heavy monsoon rains, fixes 100–300 lbs of nitrogen per acre per year, and builds organic matter as older plant material decomposes. Tropical kudzu is biologically distinct from the invasive kudzu of the eastern United States (P. montana var. lobata) — it lacks the tremendous invasive vigor of its relative, though it does spread readily in favorable tropical conditions and should be managed responsibly. The plant produces attractive large, trifoliate leaves and purple flowers similar to common kudzu. Of all tropical nitrogen-fixing cover crops, puero is arguably the most widely used and most agronomically important globally.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill seed in early spring 2–6 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall; inoculate with the correct Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar viciae inoculant before sowing for maximum nitrogen fixation, and mix with a support grass such as oats or rye to provide climbing structure and prevent lodging.
directions: Broadcast seed at 1–2 lb per 1,000 sq ft into a raked seedbed, or drill at 1/2 inch depth, ideally inoculated and mixed with a companion grass (oats, rye, or timothy) that gives the scrambling stems something to climb; tufted vetch is a widely naturalized perennial of meadows, hedgerows, and field margins across the Northern Hemisphere that produces long racemes of densely packed blue-purple flowers from late spring through summer, making it highly valuable to bees, bumblebees, and other long-tongued pollinators. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it can fix 100–150 lb of nitrogen per acre per year when well inoculated; it can be cut and incorporated into soil at early flowering for a green manure benefit, or left to bloom and seed for wildlife habitat and naturalized meadow plantings. Note that tufted vetch can spread aggressively in favorable conditions and is considered weedy in some regions — monitor spread and remove seed heads if naturalization is not desired.

plant_note: Sow after last frost; velvet bean is the most aggressive warm-season smothering cover legume, capable of blanketing 100+ sq ft per plant.
directions: Plant large seeds 1–2 in deep at 40–60 lb/acre (or 12 in apart in garden rows) after the soil is consistently warm; velvet bean vines scramble aggressively over weeds, fixing up to 400 lb N/acre equivalent while out-competing even nutsedge and Bermuda grass. All plant parts carry stinging trichomes — wear long sleeves and gloves when handling. Terminate by mowing or machete-chopping at flowering, then incorporate for a massive nitrogen and organic-matter boost. The hard, shiny seeds require scarification or a 24-hour soak before planting to improve germination.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep at 6–12 inch spacing after soil warms to 70°F in full sun; velvet bean is extremely vigorous and will climb aggressively over other plants — plant where aggressive spread and dense shading are acceptable. The seed pods are covered with irritating hairs; handle with gloves.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms in full sun — velvet bean is one of the most powerful warm-season cover crops and green manures in the tropics and subtropics, producing prodigious quantities of nitrogen-rich biomass in hot, humid conditions while smothering weeds under its dense, vining canopy. It fixes 150–300 pounds of nitrogen per acre and adds enormous quantities of organic matter when turned in. In zone 9–11 it can be used as a summer cover crop between spring and fall garden rotations. The seed pods and leaves are covered with fine silica hairs that cause severe itching on contact; handle all plant parts with gloves. The seeds (roasted and processed to remove L-DOPA) are eaten as a pulse in tropical regions. L-DOPA from mucuna seeds is also studied as a source of the Parkinson's disease medication. An extremely effective but aggressive cover crop suited to tropical and subtropical climates.

plant_note: Direct sow at 20-30 lb/acre (or broadcast thickly) after last frost on warm, moist, well-drained soil; scarify seeds to hasten germination. Incorporate as green manure before seed set to prevent self-seeding and avoid seed toxicity risks to livestock.
directions: A tropical annual legume with distinctive wedge-shaped, retuse-tipped simple leaves and upright racemes of bright yellow pea flowers from late summer through fall; native to tropical Asia and Africa, it is one of the most widely grown cover crop legumes in subtropical and tropical agriculture globally. Direct sow after last frost at high seeding rates on warm, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; scarify seeds to improve germination and inoculate with Bradyrhizobium for maximum nitrogen fixation. It establishes rapidly and suppresses weeds effectively, making it a productive green manure in Hawaii, Florida, and tropical farming systems. Incorporate into the soil before seed set, as all plant parts — especially the seeds — are toxic to livestock and humans due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid content.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; weeping lovegrass is extremely drought tolerant and is used extensively for erosion control on dry, lean banks, roadsides, and disturbed areas in the Southeast and Southwest. Can be invasive in some areas — check local status.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; weeping lovegrass is a South African perennial grass introduced to the US as an erosion control and forage grass for dry, poor soils, producing attractive, arching, fine-textured foliage and delicate, pendulous flower and seed clusters in summer that give the plant its 'weeping' common name. It has naturalized widely in the Southwest and Southeast, becoming invasive in some dryland habitats including Texas grasslands and southeastern pine flatwoods where it outcompetes native grasses. Despite its invasive risk in some regions, it remains valuable for immediate stabilization of disturbed, dry, eroded slopes where native grasses are slow to establish. Check local invasive status before planting in the Southwest or Southeast — in some states it is listed as invasive. In the driest parts of the Southwest where alternatives are scarce, it provides rapid, long-term erosion control.

plant_note: Sow winter wheat in fall for overwintering or spring wheat in early spring.
directions: Sow wheat by broadcasting or drilling into prepared soil about one inch deep, either in autumn for an overwintering cover or in early spring. Winter wheat establishes roots before dormancy, protecting soil through the cold months and greening up quickly when temperatures rise. As a cover crop, turn it under before it heads out to add organic matter, or let it ripen to a golden head for grain, wheatgrass, or microgreens. Keep evenly moist during establishment for a uniform stand.

plant_note: Frost-seed onto bare or thin ground in late winter to early spring; the freeze-thaw cycle works seed into the soil surface naturally.
directions: Broadcast inoculated seed at 1/4–1/2 lb per 1,000 sq ft onto a lightly raked surface; the tiny seed needs good soil contact but should not be covered more than 1/4 in. White clover spreads by stolons to form a dense living mulch that fixes nitrogen and feeds beneficial insects with nectar-rich flowers. Mow periodically to prevent flowering from shading out adjacent crops, or allow it to bloom freely when used as a pollinator corridor. In annual vegetable beds, turn the stand under in early spring and wait 2–3 weeks before planting so the nitrogen flush is available to the next crop.

common_name: White Lead Tree (Jumbie Bean, Koa Haole, River Tamarind)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds after last frost in full sun in well-drained soil; White Lead Tree germinates readily and grows rapidly once established. Scarify seeds by nicking or soaking in hot water (180°F) for 10 minutes, then cooling overnight. In zone 9a, treat as a warm-season annual or fast-growing cover crop; it may survive mild winters in zone 9b. CAUTION: This species is listed as invasive in many tropical and subtropical regions — do not plant near natural areas, riverbanks, or wild lands where it can escape.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in any well-drained soil; White Lead Tree is extremely adaptable — tolerating drought, alkaline and acid soils, and nutrient-poor conditions where other nitrogen-fixing legumes fail. Leucaena leucocephala is a fast-growing multi-purpose tropical legume tree native to Central America that has been one of the world's most widely planted agroforestry species for nitrogen fixation, animal fodder, green manure, and biomass production in the humid tropics. Its extensive root system fixes atmospheric nitrogen, dramatically improving poor soils. Young leaves, seeds, and pods contain high protein and are used as livestock fodder; young seeds and leaves are consumed as a vegetable in Mexico and some Asian countries, though the amino acid mimosine limits safe consumption to modest amounts. INVASIVE NOTE: Leucaena leucocephala is considered one of the world's 100 worst invasive species by the IUCN and has naturalized aggressively in Hawaii, Florida, and other tropical/subtropical regions — escape into natural areas is a serious concern. Use only in contained garden settings and manage carefully to prevent spreading.

common_name: White Lupin (Lupino Bianco, Egyptian Lupin, Grain Lupin)
plant_note: In zones 7–10, sow in fall 4–8 weeks before first frost for overwintering as a green manure; in zones 3–6 sow in early spring as soon as soil reaches 40°F; inoculate seed with Bradyrhizobium lupini before sowing for best nitrogen fixation; white lupin is the highest-yielding nitrogen fixer among the grain lupins, fixing 100–180 lbs N/acre under good conditions.
directions: Broadcast or drill at 80–120 lbs per acre (about 2–3 lbs per 1000 sq ft) in a firm, well-drained seedbed; white lupin prefers neutral to slightly alkaline, well-drained soil and will not tolerate waterlogged or highly acidic conditions; inoculate with the correct Bradyrhizobium strain, as standard clover or pea inoculant does not work for lupins; terminate by mowing and incorporating at early-to-mid bloom for maximum nitrogen return. White lupin (Lupinus albus) is the most widely cultivated of the grain lupin species, with a history of cultivation in the Mediterranean region and Near East stretching back to at least 3,000 years — depicted in Egyptian hieroglyphs and grown throughout the Roman Empire as both human food and soil-improving green manure. It is the highest-nitrogen-fixing species among the cultivated lupins, capable of fixing 100–180 lbs of atmospheric nitrogen per acre under optimal conditions with proper Bradyrhizobium inoculation, making it one of the most effective winter legume cover crops for building fertility in depleted soils. The seeds of traditional varieties are high in alkaloids (quinolizidine alkaloids) that make them bitter and potentially toxic without processing — ancient Romans soaked them in running water for days to remove the bitterness. Modern 'sweet' varieties (very low alkaloid content) have been developed for food use and are the primary commercial grain lupin in the European and Australian food markets. As a cover crop, both sweet and bitter varieties are equally valuable for nitrogen fixation and biomass. White lupin outperforms most other winter legumes in producing deep taproots (3–5 feet) that break up subsoil compaction while also contributing organic matter from the extensive root system.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 8–9) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; white lupine is an ancient Mediterranean grain and green manure legume — one of the oldest cultivated plants in Europe — grown for centuries as both a high-protein food crop and a nitrogen-fixing soil improvement cover crop; modern 'sweet' (low-alkaloid) varieties are preferred for both food and cover crop use.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in fall; incorporate as green manure at early flowering for maximum nitrogen benefit. Lupinus albus (white lupine or field lupin) is an ancient Mediterranean grain legume — one of the oldest cultivated plants in Europe, documented in Greek and Roman agriculture, long grown both as a protein-rich food grain and as a soil-improving green manure. White lupine is currently experiencing a significant agricultural revival as a European protein crop: the seeds are approximately 38–42% protein (comparable to soybean), 8–13% oil with favorable omega-3 fatty acid ratios, and contain significant dietary fiber. 'Sweet lupine' varieties with very low alkaloid content are used in Europe to produce lupine flour, lupine 'milk,' lupine tofu-analogue products, and as a high-protein additive in bread, pasta, and snack foods — an emerging alternative to soy protein that is rapidly growing in European food markets. As a cover crop in zone 6–10, white lupine is an outstanding cool-season nitrogen fixer and organic matter builder on poor, acidic, sandy soils where other legumes struggle; it has deep taproots that break up compacted subsoil. In zone 8–9, plant in fall for late-winter flowering; incorporate before flowering for the best nitrogen benefit.

plant_note: Sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost, or in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; a fast-growing brassica smother crop with biofumigant properties.
directions: Broadcast seed at 8–10 lb per acre (about 1/4 oz per 100 sq ft) onto a firm seedbed, raking to 1/4 in depth; mustard germinates in cold soil within days and establishes an aggressive canopy that smothers weeds. When chopped and incorporated at early flower stage, the glucosinolates in the tissue break down into biofumigant compounds that suppress soil-borne pathogens and weed seeds — a technique called biofumigation. Mow and immediately till to a 4–6 in depth, then water and tarp the bed for 2 weeks to trap fumigant gases. Terminate before it sets seed, as mustard reseeds abundantly and can become a weed.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer 6–8 weeks before frost; a biennial that fixes up to 150 lb N/acre in its second year.
directions: Scarify or inoculate seed with Rhizobium meliloti, then broadcast at 10–15 lb/acre and cover lightly; white sweet clover tolerates alkaline, poor soils where other clovers fail. The plant forms a taproot in year one and overwinters to bloom prolifically in year two, fixing enormous nitrogen and feeding pollinators. Terminate in year two at early bud stage before stems become woody; chop and incorporate so the high-coumarin stems have several weeks to break down before planting. Avoid using freshly mowed green residue as mulch around brassicas, as coumarin can temporarily inhibit germination.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; best suited to Gulf Coast and tropical zones 8-11 where long frost-free summers allow full maturity.
directions: Direct sow in warm, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil after the last frost date when soil temperature is consistently above 70 degrees F, covering seed to about one-half inch depth. Wild bushbean establishes quickly and produces upright racemes of striking dark purple-red pea flowers from summer through fall, followed by long, narrow, cylindrical seed pods; the vigorous growth and prolific nitrogen fixation make it a valued green manure and livestock forage crop in Gulf Coast organic farming systems. It is much less cold-tolerant than hairy vetch and will not survive frost, so it must be turned under before the first fall freeze or allowed to reseed naturally in frost-free areas. Inoculate with appropriate cowpea-type Rhizobium for maximum nitrogen fixation on first plantings in new ground.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast in early fall on sandy, dry, or calcareous soils. Best suited to Mediterranean-climate regions with mild, wet winters and dry summers.
directions: Drill seed 1-2 inches deep in early fall at 40-60 lbs per acre, preferably inoculating with the appropriate Rhizobium strain if wing pea has not been grown in the field before. The distinctive winged stems form a low, interlocking canopy that suppresses winter weeds effectively. Allow the stand to fix nitrogen through the winter and terminate in spring before full seed set. Wing pea performs best where drainage is good; avoid waterlogged or heavy clay soils.

plant_note: Plant in early to mid fall so plants establish crowns before winter dormancy.
directions: Drill or broadcast at 2-3 lb per 1,000 sq ft about 1 inch deep into a firm, well-drained seedbed. Winter barley tolerates drought and saline soils better than other cereals and releases allelopathic compounds that suppress weeds. It is less cold hardy than rye or wheat, so it performs best in USDA zones 6 and warmer. Terminate in spring by mowing or crimping at the boot stage before pollen shed, then incorporate or leave as mulch. Barley residue breaks down faster than rye, allowing earlier planting of the succeeding crop.

plant_note: Sow from 6 weeks before to just after first frost; the most cold-hardy cover crop, germinating in near-freezing soil.
directions: Broadcast seed at about 1/2 in depth in fall; it germinates in cold soil when little else will. It scavenges leftover nitrogen and smothers weeds over winter, then puts on fast spring growth. Mow and turn under 2–3 weeks before planting, as its residue briefly suppresses small seeds.

plant_note: Drill or broadcast 4-6 weeks before hard freeze so plants tiller before dormancy.
directions: Sow at 60-120 lb per acre or about 2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, drilling 1-1.5 inches deep or broadcasting onto a firm, moist seedbed. Winter wheat overwinters as a rosette, resumes growth in spring, and scavenges residual soil nitrogen while suppressing weeds. It is easier to terminate than cereal rye, making it a good choice for gardeners. Terminate in spring by mowing at the boot to early-flowering stage, then incorporate with tillage or crimp and leave residue as mulch. Allow two to three weeks of decomposition before planting the following crop.

plant_note: Sow in early fall; it matures earlier than common hairy vetch.
directions: Inoculate seed and drill or broadcast at about 1-2 lb per 1,000 sq ft, covering to 1 inch deep in a firm seedbed. Woolly pod vetch is an early-maturing relative of hairy vetch that fixes nitrogen and produces dense sprawling growth. Its earlier flowering makes it easier to terminate ahead of spring planting than standard hairy vetch. Mow or roller-crimp at early bloom for effective no-till kill, then plant into the residue mat. Because it can reseed, terminate before pods harden to limit volunteers in future crops.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; no scarification is typically necessary but nicking hard seeds speeds germination. Incorporate as green manure before seed set to prevent self-seeding and protect livestock.
directions: A tropical annual legume covered in soft, spreading hairs, with trifoliate leaves and short racemes of small yellow pea flowers followed by distinctively woolly, inflated seed pods that rattle when ripe; naturalized widely across the southeastern US coastal plain in disturbed, open, moist to dry ground. Direct sow after last frost in warm, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil — it tolerates low-fertility sandy soils well and fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis. As a warm-season cover crop in tropical and subtropical gardens and fields, it establishes readily from seed with little input and builds organic matter effectively when tilled under as green manure. Like all Crotalaria species, the seeds contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids toxic to livestock and humans — always incorporate before seed set and keep animals away from flowering or seeding plants.

plant_note: Broadcast or drill in early fall beneath orchards or vineyards, or into stubble after summer harvest. Widely adapted to California's Central Valley and coastal valleys as a low-input winter cover.
directions: Sow at 30-50 lbs per acre by broadcasting into a rough seedbed or drilling 1-1.5 inches deep in early fall, inoculating seed with a pea-vetch Rhizobium strain for maximum nitrogen fixation. Woollypod vetch establishes a thick, vining canopy over winter that outcompetes annual weeds and protects bare soil from erosion in California's rainy season. Mow or roll the stand in spring at early to full bloom to release fixed nitrogen and create a surface mulch that conserves moisture ahead of summer crops. This species handles dry spells better than hairy vetch, making it a reliable choice for drier dryland and low-rainfall irrigated systems.

common_name: Wrens Abruzzi Rye (Early-Maturing Southern Winter Cereal Rye)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall; Wrens Abruzzi is one of the most widely grown cereal rye cover crop cultivars in the South, valued for earlier fall growth and earlier spring maturity than many other rye varieties, letting it be terminated and the ground replanted sooner.
directions: Broadcast seed at 100-120 lbs/acre (1.5-2 lbs/1000 sq ft) in fall; mow or roll-crimp before spring vegetable planting. Wrens Abruzzi is one of the most popular and widely available cereal rye cover crop cultivars in the southeastern United States, selected for vigorous fall establishment and notably earlier spring maturity than many other rye varieties, which lets growers terminate it and get the following crop planted sooner in spring. Like other cereal ryes, it germinates in cool soil down to the mid-30s Fahrenheit and grows steadily through winter, providing substantial biomass, deep rooting that improves soil structure, effective weed suppression, and erosion control on fallow ground during the cool season. Its dense root system scavenges and holds nitrogen that would otherwise leach away over winter, releasing it back to the soil as the residue breaks down after termination. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or incorporation two to three weeks before planting the following crop to allow residue to begin breaking down and to avoid allelopathic effects on small-seeded crops planted too soon after termination.

common_name: Yellow Lupin (European Yellow Lupin, Gelbe Lupine)
plant_note: Sow in spring as soon as soil can be worked in zones 3–7; or in early fall in zones 7–9; yellow lupin is the most acid-tolerant of the grain lupins (grows well at pH 4.5–6.5) and the most cold-hardy, tolerating frost to -12°C in the vegetative stage; its primary use in European agriculture is as a green manure and forage crop on the lightest, most acidic, most infertile sandy soils where few other crops succeed.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed at 80–120 lbs per acre into light, acidic, sandy soils with good drainage; yellow lupin is uniquely adapted to pH 4.5–6.5 soils where white and narrow-leaf lupins struggle; inoculate with Bradyrhizobium lupini Group A; the aromatic yellow flowers attract bees; terminate at early bloom when biomass is maximum and nitrogen content is highest. Yellow lupin (Lupinus luteus) is the most cold-hardy and most acid-tolerant of the three main grain lupin species, native to the Mediterranean coastal regions of Portugal, Spain, and Morocco, where it grows on the poorest, most acidic, driest sandy soils. In European agriculture, particularly in Germany, Poland, and the Baltic states, yellow lupin has been grown for centuries as the standard green manure crop for reclaiming heathlands and sandy 'bad lands' — soils so acid, infertile, and droughty that even rye struggles. The species' extraordinary tolerance of acid conditions (pH 4.5 being optimal, with acceptable performance to pH 4.0) makes it uniquely valuable for the poorest sandy soils in the American Southeast and Pacific Northwest where soil pH is challenging. The seeds of traditional varieties are very high in bitter alkaloids (even more so than white lupin) and require special sweet cultivars for food use; in Germany sweet-lupin breeding in the early 20th century produced commercial yellow lupin varieties that have been grown as animal feed. As a cover crop, yellow lupin fixes 80–130 lbs N/acre and produces enough biomass to significantly improve soil organic matter on very poor soils. The distinctive fragrant yellow flowers are genuinely attractive in bloom.

common_name: Yellow Serradella / Bird's-foot Trefoil Cover Crop
plant_note: Sow in fall as temperatures begin to drop. Like serradella, yellow serradella requires inoculation with a specific Ornithopus rhizobium strain for effective nitrogen fixation. Broadcast onto a prepared, weed-free seedbed and lightly incorporate or roll to ensure good seed-to-soil contact.
directions: Direct sow yellow serradella in fall at 8-12 lb per acre into sandy or loamy, well-drained soils with a pH of 5.0-7.0, using rhizobium-inoculated seed for reliable nitrogen fixation. It is slightly better adapted to neutral to mildly acidic soils than common serradella, making it a useful choice for a broader range of Mediterranean-climate growing conditions. The compressed, segmented pods shatter and reseed readily at maturity, so allow pods to ripen fully before mowing if natural reseeding is desired for the following season. Terminate by mowing or incorporating before pod shatter to prevent volunteer problems ahead of summer cash crops.

plant_note: Direct-sow in early spring or late summer; behaves like white sweet clover but is slightly shorter and prefers drier soils.
directions: Scarify hard-coated seed before sowing to improve germination, and inoculate with Sinorhizobium meliloti for reliable nitrogen fixation in new plantings. Broadcast at 10–12 lb/acre and press lightly into a firm seedbed; yellow sweet clover is more drought-tolerant than most clovers and establishes well on thin, calcareous soils. It overwinters as a rosette and bolts to bloom in spring of the second year; terminate at early bud for maximum N contribution. Allow 3–4 weeks between incorporation and planting to let allelopathic coumarin compounds dissipate.

common_name: Aaron Caladium (Large White Sun-Tolerant Strap-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Aaron is one of the most sun-tolerant caladium varieties — it tolerates 3–5 hours of direct morning sun without bleaching or burning, expanding its usefulness to lightly shaded positions.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Aaron is one of the oldest, most commercially important, and most reliably grown white caladium varieties — a large strap-leaf type producing elongated, lance-to-heart-shaped leaves with near-white to cream-white leaf surfaces and contrasting green margins, creating a clean, elegant, white-and-green color combination that is among the most versatile in shade garden design. Unlike many white caladiums that require deep shade, Aaron's strap-leaf form and leaf cuticle characteristics give it exceptional sun tolerance — Aaron can be planted in positions receiving 3–5 hours of direct morning sun without the bleaching, edge-burn, or leaf collapse that afflicts most large-leaved white fancy caladiums. This higher sun tolerance makes Aaron useful in transition zones between full shade and partial sun where white color is desired but deep-shade caladiums would stretch and underperform. The white coloration brightens dark shade positions dramatically and creates an elegant effect in formal garden beds, containers, and mass plantings along shaded foundations. Aaron remains one of the most widely produced commercial caladium varieties because of its reliable performance, good tuber production, vigorous growth, and consistent white color. In zone 9, Aaron produces its best growth and color during the warm season from May through October. Combine with 'Burning Heart' for bold red-and-white contrast in shade beds.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in virtually any soil in shade; Abraham-Isaac-Jacob is extraordinarily adaptable and will succeed in dry shade, wet shade, heavy clay, or sandy soil — conditions that defeat most shade groundcovers. It is slow to establish in the first year but spreads reliably thereafter by underground rhizomes.
