directions: Plant in virtually any moist to dry soil in full to part shade; Abraham-Isaac-Jacob is a robust, large-leafed borage-family perennial from Turkey and the Caucasus that has earned a dedicated following among shade gardeners for one exceptional quality: it will cover dry shade under large deciduous trees where almost nothing else grows, spreading steadily by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat of enormous, rough-textured, heart-shaped leaves reaching 12–18 inches across on mature plants. In very early spring — February or March — clusters of small, intensely blue, reflexed flowers emerge on bare stems before the foliage appears, giving the unusual appearance of flowers seemingly floating above bare ground. The common name 'Abraham-Isaac-Jacob' describes the three-color pattern of the buds (purple), open flowers (blue), and spent flowers (pink), all visible simultaneously on the nodding flower cluster, similar to Pulmonaria. After flowering, the bold, tropical-looking foliage expands to dominate and cool the ground beneath trees for the rest of the season. An outstanding solution for the most difficult dry-shade situations.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring after all frost danger has passed, in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. In zones 8–9, Abyssinian Banana must be treated as a large annual or overwintered indoors; dig and pot the plant before frost and store in a frost-free location.
directions: Abyssinian Banana is the most dramatic of the ornamental bananas, native to the highland forests of Ethiopia and East Africa and grown worldwide as a bold tropical accent plant for its colossal size and the extraordinary visual impact of its enormous leaves — reaching up to 10 feet long with striking red midribs on deep green blades — that create an instant tropical atmosphere wherever they are planted. Unlike true bananas (Musa species), Abyssinian Banana is monocarpic, meaning each trunk (pseudostem) flowers once after 3–10 years and then dies; unlike rhizomatous bananas it does not produce pups from the base, and in Ethiopia the starchy corm and pseudostem are fermented to produce enset (a culturally crucial food for over 20 million people) rather than relying on the fruit for food. In zones 9b–11 it persists as a perennial; in zones 8–9 it is typically grown as an impressive annual or dug and stored frost-free for the winter. Provide the richest, most moisture-retentive soil available, regular fertilization, and full sun for maximum leaf size.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Impatiens walleriana is susceptible to impatiens downy mildew (IDM), which has devastated impatiens plantings across North America since 2011 — if IDM has been a problem in your area, consider New Guinea impatiens or SunPatiens (Impatiens hawkeri types) instead, which are resistant to IDM. The Accent series has demonstrated good performance when planted in well-drained conditions with good air circulation. Do not overhead water.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Accent Red Impatiens is part of the Accent series of Impatiens walleriana — the standard, traditional shade-flowering annual that has been the top-selling bedding plant in North America for decades due to its unmatched ability to produce continuous, vivid color in deep shade conditions where virtually no other flowering annual will bloom adequately. The compact, mounded habit, brilliant scarlet-red flowers, and vigorous production without deadheading made the Accent series the industry benchmark for impatiens performance. Impatiens walleriana (busy Lizzie) is the defining shade bedding plant for beds under trees, north-facing foundations, and deeply shaded borders — its natural woodland origin (East African highlands) gives it genuine shade tolerance rather than the partial-shade preference of most 'shade plants'. The continuous, prolific bloom and brilliant color saturation in true shade conditions remains a standard that few plants can match.

common_name: Acoma Crape Myrtle (Weeping White Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Acoma's gracefully weeping branch habit spreads wider than it grows tall, so allow ample lateral space when siting it.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Acoma is a distinctive weeping, semi-dwarf National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle with pure white flower clusters produced from summer into fall on gracefully arching branches, a growth habit unusual among crape myrtles that gives it strong specimen and accent value. Like its sibling cultivars it shows good resistance to powdery mildew and develops attractive mottled, exfoliating bark with maturity. Its spreading, weeping form makes it well suited as a small specimen tree, container planting, or bank cover where the arching branches can be shown off. Remove root suckers and prune only lightly to shape rather than heavily topping the plant.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; acuminate epimedium spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover. It is one of the largest-flowered epimediums and produces unusually long, graceful flower spurs.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; acuminate epimedium is a Chinese species prized among epimedium collectors for its exceptionally long, elegant flower spurs — among the longest of any epimedium species — which give the flowers a dramatic, almost exotic appearance in the spring garden. The flowers come in combinations of white, purple, and pale violet with contrasting inner petals, and the unusually long curved spurs trail beneath like the limbs of a spider or a shuttlecock in flight. The foliage is semi-evergreen, with new leaves emerging with attractive bronze-red tints in spring before maturing to glossy green. More shade-tolerant than many epimediums and reliably drought-tolerant once established under trees. A superb epimedium species for the woodland garden and difficult dry-shade conditions.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Adagio is the most popular dwarf miscanthus selection and is particularly well-suited to smaller residential gardens where the full-size maiden grass cultivars would overwhelm the space.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Adagio is a compact dwarf miscanthus cultivar reaching only 3–4 feet — roughly half the size of standard maiden grass — making it one of the few miscanthus cultivars truly appropriate for small gardens, residential foundation plantings, and mixed borders without dominating surrounding plants. The narrow, fine-textured, silvery-green blades have a thin white midrib, giving the plant a delicate, refined appearance that belies its toughness and heat tolerance. In late summer, Adagio produces proportionally large, showy, silver-pink plumes that appear at about the height of the foliage mass, creating a beautiful late-season display that lasts well into winter. The compact size and early bloom time (earlier than most miscanthus — often blooming in late August in zone 9) make Adagio one of the most ornamentally productive miscanthus selections for the Gulf South, where the late-blooming miscanthus often do not flower before the first frost. Fall color transitions through golden-yellow. Excellent for mass planting, specimen use, or as a soft backdrop for autumn-blooming perennials. Cut back to 6 inches in February in zone 9 before new growth begins.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups (rooted offsets) in spring in well-drained, sandy to gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; Adam's Needle is the most cold-hardy and widely adaptable yucca native to the eastern United States, thriving across a remarkably broad range from zone 4 through zone 11 and performing in a wider range of climates than any other commonly grown yucca.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; avoid clay soils or any location where water collects; once established, Adam's Needle is extremely drought-tolerant and virtually care-free; remove spent flower stalks after blooming; propagate from pups that form at the base of mature rosettes. Adam's Needle (Yucca filamentosa) is the most widespread and commonly grown yucca in American horticulture — native to the sandy coastal plains and dry inland areas of the southeastern United States from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Mississippi — and the standard garden yucca against which other species are compared. The species is named for its most distinctive leaf characteristic: along each leaf margin run numerous fine, thread-like fibers (filaments) that curl loosely and peel away from the leaf edge, giving the plant a distinctive fringe of white curling threads that is unique among commonly grown yuccas and easily visible in the field. The rosette of stiff, blue-green, sword-shaped leaves (2–3 feet long) grows slowly for 3–5 years before sending up a spectacular 4–8 foot flower spike bearing dozens to hundreds of nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers with a sweet fragrance — one of the most dramatic summer flowering events in the native plant garden. The yucca moth (Tegeticula yuccasella) is the sole pollinator, with a mutualistic relationship unique in the plant-pollinator world: female yucca moths deliberately pack pollen onto the yucca stigma, then lay eggs in the ovary, and the larvae feed on some of the developing seeds — leaving enough viable seeds for yucca reproduction. Named cultivars include 'Color Guard' (yellow-striped leaves) and 'Bright Edge' (gold-margined leaves).

common_name: Adolphe Audusson Camellia (Deep Red Camellia japonica)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Adolphe Audusson is one of the most vigorous japonica cultivars and can become a large shrub or small tree over many years in zone 9 — allow adequate space at planting.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Adolphe Audusson is a classic, vigorous Camellia japonica cultivar valued for one of the deepest, richest red flower colors available in japonica camellias — a vivid blood-red to deep crimson-red in large, semi-double flowers with a prominent central cluster of golden-yellow stamens that creates a striking color contrast. The bold, saturated red flower color and large flower size make it one of the most eye-catching camellia selections for winter color in the shaded garden. Introduced in France in 1877 and still widely grown, Adolphe Audusson is a vigorous grower that develops into a large shrub or small tree in zone 9 conditions, with upright growth to 7–14 feet and dense, dark-green, glossy evergreen foliage. It blooms in mid-season (December through February in zone 9), with peak bloom typically in January. The bold red flower color provides exceptional cut-flower value — the flowers last well in arrangements. 'Adolphe Audusson Variegated' is a sport with red flowers marked with white streaks and spots; 'Adolphe Audusson Special' has darker red, more formal double flowers. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil; apply sulfur-based acidifying fertilizer if soil pH drifts above 6.5.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, rocky or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; tolerates caliche and desert soils well.
directions: Adonis Blazingstar is a slender, much-branched native perennial of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and adjacent Mexico, growing on dry, rocky, calcareous or sandy desert hills and open slopes in the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert regions. Unlike its white-flowered Great Plains relatives, it produces numerous bright yellow to orange-yellow, 5-petaled flowers 1 to 1.5 inches across on airy, much-forked stems, blooming freely from spring through fall and opening in the afternoon and evening hours rather than strictly at night. The lighter, daytime-accessible blooms attract a broader range of native bees and butterfly visitors than the nocturnal Mentzelia species, making it a highly productive pollinator plant across a long season. Direct sow in fall in extremely lean, rocky or sandy, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; an outstanding xeriscape perennial for Texas Hill Country and Chihuahuan Desert native gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; dislikes root disturbance from transplanting.
directions: 'African Bride' bears dramatic white blooms with contrasting near-black centers atop airy, threadlike foliage. Direct sow in place because love-in-a-mist resents transplanting once its taproot forms. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil and thin seedlings for good airflow. After flowering, papery, dark-tinged seed pods develop that are excellent in fresh and dried arrangements. It self-sows readily, returning year after year in the garden.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in fall; African cornflag is a vigorous naturalizer in zones 8b–10, spreading freely by cormlets to form large colonies on slopes and roadsides. In zone 8 it may need light mulch protection in cold winters. Plant in areas where spread is welcome or where colonies can be naturalized.
directions: Plant corms in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; African cornflag is a vigorous South African corm in the iris family producing upright, sword-like fans of pleated, bright-green leaves and, in late winter and early spring (January–March), strongly arching flowering spikes bearing numerous, bright orange-red to scarlet tubular flowers that are powerfully attractive to hummingbirds and sunbirds. The flowers are curved and tubular — adapted for long-billed bird pollinators — and appear in great abundance on established colonies. It naturalizes freely in zones 8b–11 by producing abundant cormlets, spreading on sunny hillsides and roadsides in California, the Gulf Coast, and other warm-winter climates to form spectacular stands of winter-to-spring color. The variety 'Duckitt's Yellow' produces clear yellow flowers and is more restrained in spread. Outstanding for naturalizing on difficult slopes, sunny banks, and low-maintenance areas where a self-sustaining winter color display is desired.

plant_note: Plant tubers just below the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; African cyclamen flowers in autumn before or with the leaves and goes summer dormant. It is similar to C. hederifolium but larger in all parts — larger tuber, larger leaves, larger flowers — and slightly less cold-hardy. In zone 9 it can remain in the ground year-round; protect the tuber from hard frost in colder zones. The large tubers can reach 12 inches across in very old plants.
directions: Plant tubers near the soil surface in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; African cyclamen is essentially a larger, more tender version of the familiar C. hederifolium — producing in autumn (September–November) before or with the leaves, pink to deep rose-pink, reflexed-petaled cyclamen flowers of the typical shuttlecock form, fragrant, and the characteristic ivy-shaped, attractively marbled and silver-patterned leaves that follow and persist through winter and spring before the plant goes summer dormant. What distinguishes C. africanum is scale: the flowers are larger than those of C. hederifolium, the marbled, silver-zoned leaves are larger, and the tubers of old plants can reach extraordinary dimensions — dinner plate-sized, flat-topped, brownish-gray corms that have been in the ground for decades and represent some of the most massive of all hardy bulbs. Native to the woodlands and scrubland of Algeria and Tunisia, it is marginally less cold-hardy than C. hederifolium, thriving in zones 8–11 and making it an outstanding candidate for the Gulf Coast and California shade garden where C. hederifolium can be inconsistent. Outstanding under the dry shade of large trees in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained germination mix; seedlings grow quickly and should be potted on before becoming root-bound. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil as soon as the risk of hard frost has passed; osteospermum thrives in cool weather and slows during peak summer heat. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage continuous bloom and pinch stem tips to promote branching early in the season. In zones 9–11 it may survive as a short-lived perennial; take stem cuttings in late summer to perpetuate favorite selections.

common_name: African Daisy (Freeway Daisy, Trailing African Daisy)
plant_note: Plant container transplants in spring or fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; trailing African daisy is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and is one of the most successful perennial groundcovers for sunny, dry slopes and roadside banks in California and the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; trailing African daisy establishes best in fall or early spring and becomes drought-tolerant once rooted. Osteospermum fruticosum (trailing African daisy or freeway daisy) is a sprawling, mat-forming perennial producing cheerful white, lavender, or purple ray flowers (1.5–2 inches across) with blue-purple disk centers in enormous profusion from fall through spring, with some blooms year-round in mild climates; blooming peaks in late winter and spring when the mat literally disappears under flowers. This South African native was heavily planted along California freeways beginning in the 1960s, giving rise to its common name 'freeway daisy'; it is now widely naturalized in coastal California. In zones 9–11, it performs as a perennial groundcover for hot, sunny, dry slopes, road banks, and xeric garden borders where its trailing stems quickly form a weed-suppressing mat. It does not tolerate frost below about 25°F but rebounds rapidly from light damage. Shear or mow hard after the main bloom flush to encourage compact regrowth and repeat bloom.

common_name: African False Lily of the Valley (Little White Soldiers)
plant_note: Divide offset bulblets or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade in spring; African false lily of the valley thrives in conditions of consistent shade and moisture that simulate its forest-floor native habitat. It goes semi-dormant in winter with reduced watering but is never fully deciduous in mild climates. Excellent for deep shade where bulbs that need more light would fail.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; African false lily of the valley is a South African forest-floor bulb prized for two qualities — its shade tolerance (making it one of the few true bulbs that thrives in deep shade) and the attractive dark-spotted pattern of its leaves (the species epithet maculata means 'spotted'). The broadly oval, smooth, dark-green leaves are irregularly decorated with darker green to bronze-purple spots and blotches that give each leaf a painted, dappled quality reminiscent of certain Pulmonaria or Arum species. In late spring through summer it produces dense, upright racemes of small, white, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers similar in form to lily of the valley but upright rather than pendant. The small, crowded, bright-white flowers create a cheerful, clean display. It spreads by producing numerous small offset bulblets, quickly forming a tight, spreading colony in favorable conditions. An outstanding choice for zones 9–11 where a shade-tolerant, spotted-leaved, white-flowering bulb groundcover is needed under dense tree canopy.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost in a warm, sunny spot.
directions: Sow African flake daisy directly after the last frost, barely covering the seed in a sunny, well-drained bed. These cheerful yellow blooms with purple centers open on compact, fine-foliaged plants that shrug off heat and drought. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display going through the warm months. Perfect for water-wise borders and containers, it asks for little more than sun and sharp drainage.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; African iris blooms most profusely in full sun but tolerates partial shade well. Avoid deadheading spent flower stalks — the branching stems continue to produce new flower buds from the same stalk for months.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; African iris is one of the most practical and reliable perennials for zone 8–11 landscapes, earning its common name 'fortnight lily' because it blooms in cycles roughly every two weeks throughout the warm season. The elegant white flowers with yellow and purple markings closely resemble true iris flowers but are produced on branching stalks that continue reblooming without deadheading — the spent blooms drop cleanly without the need for any grooming. The clumping, strap-like, evergreen leaves provide bold, attractive foliage year-round. It is exceptionally drought, heat, salt, and poor-soil tolerant once established, performing equally well in coastal and inland gardens. Divide congested clumps every 4–5 years in spring. A closely related species, Dietes bicolor (yellow African iris), produces pale yellow flowers with purple spots and is similarly adaptable. An outstanding low-maintenance perennial for mass plantings, borders, and water-wise landscapes.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; agapanthus blooms most freely when root-bound and when the bulb-like roots can see some light — avoid deep planting and unnecessary disturbance, as established clumps bloom most reliably when left undivided.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; African lily is a South African evergreen perennial that has become one of the most widely planted flowering perennials in warm-climate gardens worldwide — producing large, round, elegant, spherical flower heads of 20–40 individual, tubular, funnel-shaped, bright blue to violet-blue or white flowers on strong, upright, 2–4-foot stems above broad rosettes of glossy, strap-shaped, dark-green, evergreen leaves, blooming in summer (June–August). The spherical blue flower heads are among the most refined and beautifully structured of any summer-blooming perennial and associate superbly with white and yellow flowers. Agapanthus praecox (syn. A. orientalis) is the largest and most common species in cultivation, forming substantial clumps that flower most freely when moderately crowded and root-bound; excessive division reduces flowering. Tolerates partial shade, clay soil, coastal salt spray, and moderate drought once established. The deciduous species (A. campanulatus, A. caulescens) are hardier (to zone 6) but less evergreen; A. praecox is evergreen but limited to zone 8–12.

common_name: African Lily (Blue Lily of the Nile, Agapanthus)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; agapanthus is one of the best-performing perennials for Gulf Coast summer gardens — heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and producing a stunning display of blue or white trumpet flowers in July–September.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; bloom is best after mild crowding — do not divide too frequently. Agapanthus africanus (African blue lily or lily of the Nile) is a classic South African perennial that has become one of the most widely grown ornamental plants in warm, Mediterranean, and subtropical climates worldwide — producing bold clumps of long, strap-shaped, arching, dark-green evergreen leaves topped by tall (18–36 inch) stems bearing large, spherical umbels of 20–50 tubular, blue-violet to white flowers in July–September. The flower heads, 4–8 inches across and resembling a blue fireworks burst, are a stunning feature in summer borders when most other perennials have passed their peak. Agapanthus is remarkably adaptable once established — tolerating heat, drought, poor soils, and coastal salt spray — and practically maintenance-free. Flower color ranges from deep violet-blue through pale lavender to pure white; the blue forms are the most commonly grown. The plant is also outstanding as a container subject, performing reliably when somewhat pot-bound. CAUTION: All parts are mildly toxic if ingested; sap may irritate skin.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; African mahogany grows naturally in the Sahel and savanna belt of West Africa in seasonally dry, tropical conditions and is more drought-tolerant than the American mahoganies once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–12; African mahogany is a West African timber and shade tree in the Meliaceae family (same family as American mahogany), widely planted in tropical and subtropical regions for shade and timber. The pinnate compound leaves create a dense canopy that provides excellent shade. The reddish-brown wood is harder than West Indian mahogany but less prized in fine furniture; it is extensively used in flooring, general construction, and plywood production in Africa. In south Florida, African mahogany is widely planted as a fast-growing street and shade tree, developing a large, spreading crown that provides dense summer shade. More salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant than American mahogany and faster-growing, making it practical for large-scale urban tree planting in zone 10 coastal Florida.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sow no earlier than 6 weeks before last frost, as large-seeded transplants tend to become rootbound quickly.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sow no earlier than 6 weeks before last frost, as large-seeded transplants tend to become rootbound quickly. Tagetes erecta is the tall, large-flowered marigold with enormous double pompom flower heads 3–4 inches across in brilliant yellow, orange, and cream — sacred to the goddess Xochiquetzal in Aztec culture and still used extensively in Mexican Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos) festivals, where millions of flowers are harvested annually. The petals are edible and have a mild, spicy, slightly citrusy flavor; dried petals are used to color butter, cheese, and poultry feed (providing the beta-carotene that gives egg yolks their golden color in commercial farming). It is the most important commercial cut marigold species; choose large transplant sizes in spring as they establish quickly.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–June. Polly performs best as a container plant in zone 9, where it can be moved indoors during the rare cold snaps. In the warmest zone 9 areas it may survive as an in-ground perennial in a sheltered, heavily mulched location. Provide very bright indirect light or early morning sun with afternoon shade — direct summer sun bleaches and burns the dramatic dark leaves. Maintain high humidity (mist frequently or place on a humidity tray). In zone 9's warm, humid summers, Polly can be grown outdoors in deep shade for the summer season.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but well-aerated soil — Alocasia require moisture but are sensitive to root rot in poorly drained or overly wet conditions; African Mask Alocasia (Polly) is a compact cultivar of Alocasia x amazonica, an Aroid hybrid of unknown tropical Southeast Asian species parentage, producing dramatically dark, arrow-shaped to elongated, deeply lobed leaves with prominent, contrasting, chalk-white primary and secondary veins against near-black to deep forest-green leaf surfaces. The high-contrast white vein pattern on the dark leaf — which does indeed have an unsettling resemblance to decorative African masks — is one of the most striking and dramatic foliage effects possible in a houseplant or shade garden specimen. The 'Polly' selection is a more compact form (18–24 inches) than the larger-growing Alocasia x amazonica species, making it more practical for container use and indoor cultivation. Each leaf is simultaneously a botanical and artistic object — the precise geometry of the veining pattern and the glossy, slightly undulating dark green leaf surface create an effect that is more designed than any human art and more dramatic than almost any other commonly grown plant.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep soil; African Rosewood is a large, deciduous West African savanna tree of great commercial and ecological importance — its heartwood is one of the most internationally traded and threatened tropical timbers, prized for furniture and instruments — and it bears brilliant yellow pea-family flowers in terminal clusters before leaf-out in the dry season.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil; Pterocarpus erinaceus is a drought-adapted savanna tree that requires excellent drainage and tolerates seasonal dry periods — avoid waterlogged sites and heavy clay soils. Pterocarpus erinaceus (African Rosewood, Vène, or Kosso) is a large, deciduous legume tree native to the open savanna, guinea woodland, and dry forest zones of West Africa from Senegal east through the Sudan-Sahel zone to Ethiopia, a member of the Fabaceae family and one of the continent's most economically significant and critically over-exploited timber trees. The heartwood is dense, durable, deep reddish-brown to rose-red with interlocked grain — superficially resembling Asian rosewoods (Dalbergia spp.) — and has been the subject of massive illegal logging and export particularly to China and East Asia in the 21st century for furniture manufacture, resulting in international CITES trade regulation. Before logging, trees produce spectacular, dense, terminal clusters of deep-yellow pea-family flowers in the dry season on leafless branches. The tree is a critical component of the West African parkland agroforestry system where it is retained in farmers' fields for shade, nitrogen fixation, fodder, and traditional medicine (the red-staining bark gum is used medicinally across West Africa). A valuable shade and nitrogen-fixing tree for tropical agroforestry systems where large specimens can be grown sustainably.

common_name: African Trumpet Tree (Magnificent Fernandoa, Yellow African Trumpet)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Fernandoa magnifica is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting. The tree is relatively fast-growing and can begin blooming within 3–5 years from seed. The enormous clusters of large yellow-orange trumpet flowers make it one of the most impressive African ornamental trees for tropical landscapes. Semi-deciduous — it briefly drops leaves before the main spring bloom. Drought-tolerant once established on well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — African Trumpet Tree is drought-tolerant once established and grows vigorously in the well-drained, sandy soils of tropical coastal landscapes. Fernandoa magnifica is a medium-sized, semi-deciduous flowering tree from eastern tropical Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Zimbabwe) in the Bignoniaceae family, belonging to the same remarkable family that gave horticulture Jacaranda, Tabebuia, Catalpa, and Bignonia. The tree produces large, pinnately compound leaves and bears its flowers in massive, terminal, many-flowered panicles at the tips of the branches: each individual flower is a large (2–3 inch), funnel to broadly trumpet-shaped bloom in vivid yellow-orange to orange, with five spreading, frilled petal lobes and a slightly darker orange interior. When a Fernandoa magnifica flowers — typically in spring, often producing the display on leafless or partially leafless branches — the sheer density and size of the flower clusters is extraordinary, covering the branch tips in orange-yellow bloom. The species is a significant ornamental tree in tropical East African gardens and in tropical botanical collections worldwide, considered one of the finest flowering trees of the African continent in terms of bloom impact. Underused in zone 10-11 US tropical landscapes compared to its merit.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun in spring; African tulip tree grows very rapidly — often reaching 20 feet within a few years of planting — and begins producing flowers within 3–5 years from seed. It is considered invasive in Hawaii, parts of Florida, and many Pacific Island nations where it has escaped cultivation and displaced native vegetation in disturbed forest areas.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; African tulip tree (fountain tree, fireball) is a large, fast-growing West African tropical tree of the bignonia family (Bignoniaceae) that produces one of the most spectacular and instantly recognizable flower displays of any tropical tree — large, upright, cup-shaped, terminal clusters of 10–20 large, flared, bright scarlet-orange to crimson flowers with yellow-edged petals are produced at the branch tips year-round in zone 10–12 tropical climates, creating a constant flaming-red display from a distance. The flower buds hold water — a trait used by children in the native range who squeeze the buds to squirt water — and are visited by sunbirds and bats as pollinators. The tree grows rapidly to 40–50 feet with a dense, spreading canopy, making it an effective but large shade tree. It has become invasive in Hawaii, Pacific island nations, and parts of tropical Florida, where it spreads aggressively by wind-borne seeds into disturbed forest areas — check local regulations before planting.

plant_note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix or water; African violets propagate easily from leaf cuttings with petiole attached, inserted into moist mix at 45 degrees — new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4–8 weeks. In zone 11–12 they can grow outdoors in deep shade and high humidity.
directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow as a houseplant in bright indirect light — never direct sun — in slightly acidic, well-drained, slightly moist potting mix: African violet is the world's most popular flowering houseplant, grown by millions indoors for its rosettes of soft, velvety, dark green leaves and year-round clusters of flowers in purple, violet, lavender, pink, white, and bicolor combinations. The keys to success are bright indirect light (east or north window in summer; south or west in winter), bottom-watering or careful top-watering that avoids wetting the crown and leaves, and consistently moist but not waterlogged, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) potting mix with good aeration. Feed every 4 weeks with a balanced fertilizer formulated for African violets. The genus was recently reclassified from Saintpaulia to Streptocarpus; thousands of named cultivars are available through the African Violet Society of America.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; African wild iris is remarkably drought-tolerant once established but benefits from regular watering during the first growing season — do not cut the flower stalks after blooming, as the same stalks rebloom for multiple years, and removing them sacrifices future flowering.
directions: Plant rhizomes or container specimens in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; African wild iris is a South African rhizomatous perennial of the iris family (Iridaceae) that is one of the most reliable, long-lived, and drought-tolerant evergreen perennials for Gulf Coast and warm-climate gardens, producing large, white, six-petaled flowers 3–4 inches across with bright-yellow and blue-violet marks at the petal bases on tall, branching, flat, fan-like stems from spring through early summer and intermittently at other seasons. The plant's most unusual feature is that it reblooms on the same persistent flower stems for multiple years — so the stems should never be removed after blooming, as the following season's flowers emerge from the same stalk. The fans of sword-shaped, dark-green, evergreen leaves are ornamental year-round and the plant spreads slowly into large, weed-suppressing clumps. Extremely adaptable to heat, drought, alkaline soil, and coastal conditions; an outstanding low-maintenance evergreen perennial for zone 8–11 public and residential landscapes, often seen lining roads and medians throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; agave-leaf sea holly is evergreen in mild winters and forms an impressive, large rosette of leaves that requires substantial space. The flower stems are summer-produced on previous year's growth, and the spent stems should be cut back after seeding. More cold-tolerant than expected for an Argentine species.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; agave-leaf sea holly is a large-scale Argentine eryngium that earns its common name through its remarkable foliage — the basal leaves are broad, strap-shaped, toothed along the margin with spine-tipped teeth, and arranged in a bold rosette that closely resembles a medium-sized agave in form and architecture. This agave-like rosette, in glossy, bright green, provides architectural structure throughout the year. In summer, tall, branching flower scapes emerge from the center carrying numerous small, pale-green to whitish, typical eryngium flower heads (each a rounded bur of spiky bracts above a domed disc) — smaller and less colorful than the metallic-blue European sea hollies but collectively impressive for their number and the height of the scapes. The whole plant creates a bold, architectural structure in the garden — a rosette of agave-like leaves at ground level sending up flowering stalks to 5–6 feet. Outstanding as an architectural specimen or back-of-border plant in drought-tolerant, Mediterranean-climate, or prairie-style gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow dust-fine seed on the surface of moist starting mix without covering — light is essential for germination. Ageratum produces fluffy, powder-puff blooms that attract butterflies and beneficial insects. Shear plants back lightly when flowering slows or plants become leggy to promote a fresh flush of bloom. Consistent moisture is important, as dry conditions cause the plants to stop flowering.

common_name: Aimee Gardenia (Very Large Flower Exhibition Gardenia from Louisiana)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade; 'Aimee Yoshiba' produces some of the largest gardenia flowers available — flowers can reach 4–5 inches across, making individual blooms among the most spectacular of any gardenia.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0) soil in partial shade to morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Aimee (also known as 'Aimee Yoshiba') is a Louisiana-associated gardenia cultivar producing some of the largest flowers of any commonly grown Gardenia jasminoides — individual blooms reaching 4–5 inches across with many rows of creamy white, wavy, overlapping petals that create a full, formal double flower of extraordinary refinement. The flowers open creamy white and age to a warm ivory-yellow, with the same intense, classic gardenia fragrance that has made gardenias the most beloved fragrant landscape shrub in the American South. 'Aimee' grows as a vigorous, upright-spreading shrub to 5–7 feet in typical Gulf South gardens, larger and more open in habit than compact cultivars like 'Radicans' or 'Chuck Hayes'. The spring bloom (April–June) is the primary season, often with sporadic rebloom in fall if conditions are favorable. As with all Gardenia jasminoides, 'Aimee' requires strongly acidic soil for healthy growth — iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves with green veins) is the primary symptom of insufficient acidity, corrected with sulfur soil acidification and acid-forming fertilizers. The large flower size and outstanding fragrance make 'Aimee' the preferred gardenia for cut flower use, where a single bloom can fragrance a room for several days.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to part shade; ajuga is one of the most reliable and ornamental groundcovers for shaded areas under trees and along shaded borders, spreading by stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; space 12–18 inches apart and allow to spread. Ajuga reptans (bugleweed or carpet bugleweed) is one of the most widely grown and adaptable shade groundcovers in temperate gardens — a European native that spreads by horizontal stolons to form a dense, 4-to-6-inch-tall, weed-suppressing carpet of rosettes, producing spectacular spikes of small, tubular, blue-violet (or pink, white, or cream in cultivars) flowers in April–May that are important early-season nectar sources for native bees and bumble bees. The foliage is the primary season-long attraction: many cultivars offer striking leaf colors from dark bronze-purple ('Catlin's Giant,' 'Burgundy Glow') to variegated cream and pink ('Burgundy Glow') to metallic chocolate ('Black Scallop'). Ajuga thrives in the difficult dry-shade conditions under large trees where other groundcovers struggle. It is essentially maintenance-free once established, spreading moderately (not invasively) by stolons. In zone 9, it performs best in shade with consistent moisture and may go partially dormant in the hottest, driest summers; crown rot can occur in hot, humid conditions — ensure good air circulation.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, humus-rich, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade; Alabama azalea is a shallow-rooted woodland plant that requires well-drained, acidic soil and cannot tolerate alkaline, compacted, or waterlogged conditions.
directions: Alabama azalea is a rare native deciduous azalea endemic to the limestone cedar glades and sandy, acidic woodlands of central Alabama and adjacent states — one of the most sweetly fragrant of all native azaleas, its white to creamy-white flowers with yellow-orange blotches emit a delicate, spicy-sweet fragrance reminiscent of lemony honey that fills the woodland in spring. It blooms in April after the piedmont azalea but before leaves emerge, producing large, showy clusters of flowers at a time when the garden's background is still relatively bare. Alabama azalea is adapted to the warm, humid climate of the upper Gulf Coastal Plain, tolerating zone 9 summers better than most native azaleas of eastern North America — an important advantage for Gulf Coast native gardens where heat and humidity defeat many Rhododendron species. In acidic woodland gardens and under tall pines, plant in combination with native groundcovers like Carex, Pachysandra procumbens, and native ferns for an authentic Alabama woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade. Alabama Snow-Wreath is a critically rare Alabama endemic and should only be sourced from nurseries that propagate their own cuttings.
directions: Alabama Snow-Wreath is one of the rarest native shrubs in North America, a monotypic genus (the only species in its genus) restricted in the wild to a handful of limestone bluffs and rocky river slopes in northwestern Alabama and a very few widely scattered natural populations in other southeastern states. In April and May it produces a cloud of unusual, feathery, white, petal-less flowers — the 'petals' are entirely absent, and the display comes entirely from numerous long white stamens — giving the shrub an airy, ethereal appearance reminiscent of its common name. An adaptable plant in cultivation that grows well in partial shade in a wide range of soils from dry and rocky to moderately moist, Alabama Snow-Wreath is easy to propagate from cuttings and is increasingly available from specialty native plant nurseries. Never collect from wild populations — purchase only from nurseries that propagate their own plants from cultivated stock.

common_name: Alabama Sunrise Heucherella (Bright Gold-to-Red Seasonal Color-Change Heucherella)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alabama Sunrise changes color dramatically through the season, emerging bright gold in spring and deepening toward orange-red as temperatures cool in fall.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, with mulch to keep roots cool. Alabama Sunrise is a heucherella cultivar grown chiefly for its dramatic seasonal color transformation, unfurling bright gold-yellow leaves with red veining in spring that gradually shift toward warm orange and finally deep red-bronze tones as the weather cools in fall, giving the planting a constantly changing look through the growing season. Like other heucherella it spreads gradually to form a groundcover-like patch, combining the colorful foliage of heuchera with the vigorous habit of foamflower, and produces modest sprays of small white flowers in late spring that are secondary to its foliage display. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Alabama Sunset Coleus (Classic Orange-Red Heirloom Sun Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Alabama Sunset is a classic heirloom coleus cultivar with warm orange-red leaves veined in maroon and edged in chartreuse, a longtime favorite sun-tolerant selection for bold summer foliage color.
directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Alabama Sunset is a classic, long-popular coleus cultivar bearing warm orange-red leaves marked with darker maroon veining and a bright chartreuse-green edge, a fiery, autumnal color combination that has kept it a garden favorite for decades. It tolerates considerably more direct sun than traditional shade coleus, making it a versatile choice for both sunny mixed borders and shadier spots, though the richest, most saturated coloring develops with some protection from the most intense afternoon sun in zone 9. The vigorous, upright, well-branched plants provide season-long color without relying on flowers, which should be pinched off as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage. Pinch growing tips periodically through the season to maintain a dense, bushy habit and prevent the plant from becoming leggy.

plant_note: Start indoors; cold-moist stratification improves germination.
directions: 'Alan's Pride' is a first-year-flowering coneflower with unusual zesty lime-green blooms on graceful 2-foot stems. Start seed indoors and give it a period of cold-moist stratification to break dormancy and improve germination. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where it becomes drought tolerant once established. The blooms draw bees and butterflies, and leaving seed heads standing feeds finches into fall and winter. Divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow after frost; needs light to germinate.
directions: 'Alaska' is a classic, long-lived Shasta daisy bearing large 3-inch white flowers with sunny yellow centers from summer into fall. Press seed onto the surface since it needs light to germinate, and keep it evenly moist until sprouts appear. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil for the sturdiest, most floriferous plants. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering, and the long stems make excellent cut flowers. Divide clumps every two to three years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost; resents transplanting.
directions: 'Alaska' nasturtium stands out for its cream-and-green marbled foliage that stays showy even between the bright, edible flowers. Direct sow the large seeds where they are to grow, as nasturtiums dislike having their roots disturbed. Grow in full sun to part shade in lean soil, since overly rich ground produces leaves at the expense of blooms. Both the peppery flowers and leaves are edible and make a colorful garnish. This compact, bushy type is well suited to containers and bed edges.

common_name: Alba Plena Camellia (White Formal Double Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Alba Plena is one of the earliest-blooming japonica camellias — November through January in zone 9 — so site away from frost pockets where early-season cold snaps could damage open flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Alba Plena is one of the oldest and most historically significant Camellia japonica cultivars in cultivation — an early-season white camellia with perfectly formed, large, formal double flowers in pure white with tightly spiraled, overlapping petals arranged in a geometrically precise rosette pattern of extraordinary elegance. The pure white flowers are exceptional for formal garden compositions, white-themed borders, and cut-flower use — few winter-blooming plants can rival the pristine beauty of fully open Alba Plena flowers. In zone 9, it blooms from November through January, making it one of the earliest reliable winter blooms in the Southern garden. The vigorous, upright growth to 5–12 feet produces dense, glossy dark-green foliage that provides excellent year-round screening and foundation value. Alba Plena was introduced to Western cultivation from China in 1792 and has been grown in Southern American gardens since the early nineteenth century — one of the most historically long-cultivated garden plants in the South. Early bloom season means open flowers may occasionally be damaged by hard frosts in zone 9 winters; siting under the canopy of overhead trees provides some protection. Maintain acidic soil pH with periodic applications of acidic fertilizer and deep organic mulch.

plant_note: Plant in spring once ground is workable. Best established in consistently moist to wet soil; boggy sites are ideal. This dioecious shrub requires both male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in partial shade in reliably moist to boggy soil, mimicking its natural habitat along streambanks and in swampy woods. Dig a hole at least twice the width of the root ball and amend heavy clay with organic matter to improve moisture retention. Water deeply and consistently through the first two growing seasons to establish a strong root system. Berries attract birds in fall; plant at least one male and one female for fruit set.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Aleppo pine is a Mediterranean dryland pine adapted to hot, dry, alkaline conditions and thin limestone or sandy soils. One of the most drought-tolerant pines for hot, dry climates in zones 8–10.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Aleppo pine is the most drought-tolerant and widely distributed pine of the Mediterranean Basin, covering rocky, thin limestone and sandy soils around the sea from Spain to Turkey. In California and the Southwest US, it has been planted for over a century as a tough, drought-tolerant pine for hot, dry, alkaline conditions where most other pines fail. The light gray-green to blue-green paired needles and the open, slightly irregular crown give it a soft, Mediterranean character. Old trees develop a picturesque, wind-sculpted silhouette with distinctive sinuous, upswept branches. The small, asymmetric, orange-brown cones are persistent and add winter interest. Well-suited to the dry, alkaline conditions of California's interior valleys, the Southwest, and the alkaline calcareous soils of the Hill Country and Edwards Plateau of Texas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil under dry shade; this Algerian species is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and thrives beneath the root canopy of large trees where few other groundcovers survive.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full to partial shade, where its glossy, bronze-tinted heart-shaped leaves form a weed-suppressing mat through vigorous rhizomatous spread. Bright yellow flowers emerge in early spring before the foliage hardens, offering one of the earliest color displays in the shaded garden. Unlike most epimediums, E. perralderianum is semi-evergreen and retains attractive foliage well into winter, especially in milder parts of its hardiness range. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to showcase the spring flower display; once established, this species is among the most drought- and root-competition-tolerant of all groundcovers.

common_name: Algerian Ivy (Canary Island Ivy, Canariensis Ivy)
plant_note: Root cuttings or plant container transplants in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Algerian ivy is more heat and drought tolerant than English ivy and a better choice for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast shade gardens. It can also be grown as a trailing vine for containers.
directions: Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Algerian ivy is the superior ivy for Gulf Coast zone 7–10 gardens — larger-leaved, more heat tolerant, and more drought tolerant than English ivy, making it better suited to the summer conditions of the Gulf South. The leaves are 3–8 inches across, rich glossy green (sometimes with a reddish tint in winter), and distinctly larger than the familiar English ivy. The variegated form 'Gloire de Marengo' has silvery gray-green leaves with creamy white margins and is one of the most beautiful of all shade vines. Like English ivy it can climb by aerial roots and spreads vigorously as a groundcover, but has a less aggressive spreading habit than English ivy and is less likely to invade natural areas. Still, plant with care and keep away from forest edges.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alice is a large-growing cultivar — allow 6–8 feet in all directions at planting time to avoid future overcrowding.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Alice oakleaf hydrangea is an outstanding cultivar selected and named for Alice Recknagel Ireys, a distinguished American landscape architect, by Michael Dirr at the University of Georgia — the plant's finest characteristics reflecting the horticultural standards of its namesake. Alice produces exceptionally large, upright panicle flower clusters — sometimes reaching 14 inches long — that are among the biggest of any oakleaf hydrangea cultivar, creating a spectacular mid-May to June display in zone 9 gardens. The individual flowers open pure white and age gradually to a beautiful soft rose-pink, creating clusters that simultaneously show white and pink tones. The foliage is large, bold, and deeply lobed with the characteristic oak-leaf silhouette, turning rich burgundy-red in autumn in zone 9. Alice grows vigorously to 6–10 feet tall and equally wide, making it an outstanding large-scale specimen, naturalizing under trees, or massing for a bold woodland effect. The peeling cinnamon-brown bark is ornamental in winter. Alice received the Award of Garden Merit from the Royal Horticultural Society, confirming its outstanding ornamental performance.

common_name: Alice du Pont Mandevilla (Classic Vigorous Pink Mandevilla)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil and air are warm, training the twining vine onto a trellis, arbor, or fence; Alice du Pont is one of the oldest and most vigorous mandevilla cultivars, producing large, clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers over glossy foliage.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a trellis, arbor, or other support able to accommodate a vigorous twining vine. Alice du Pont is a long-established classic mandevilla cultivar, valued for producing large, glossy, deep green leaves and abundant clear pink, trumpet-shaped flowers continuously from late spring through fall, with a naturally vigorous, fast-climbing habit compared to some of the more compact modern mandevilla series. It thrives in the heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer, needing only regular water and monthly fertilizing during active growth. In zone 9a it typically dies back after a hard freeze but often regrows from the roots in a mild winter; in colder zones it is best grown as a container plant brought indoors or treated as an annual.

common_name: All Gold Forest Grass (Golden Japanese Hakone Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; All Gold develops vivid chartreuse-yellow color in bright partial shade — deep shade causes the foliage to revert toward green, while direct sun scorches the delicate leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; All Gold is the all-golden form of the celebrated Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra) — a graceful, slow-growing, clump-forming grass producing cascading, arching, narrow leaves in a warm chartreuse-yellow to golden color that creates a luminous glow effect in the shade garden. The warm golden color of All Gold is even more vivid than the striped 'Aureola' cultivar — because all the leaf tissue is chartreuse-gold rather than striped, the overall color effect is bolder and more uniform. The gently cascading, arching habit creates the effect of flowing water tumbling down a slope, making Japanese forest grass one of the most graceful and unique ornamental plants available for the partial-shade garden. All Gold is slow to establish but gradually forms expanding clumps that become increasingly impressive with each year. The warm gold color lights up dark shade garden corners and combines beautifully with the cool blue of hostas and the burgundy tones of Japanese painted ferns and heucheras. In zone 9, All Gold performs in bright indirect shade — on the north or east side of structures, under high-canopied pines, or at the edge of tree canopies where filtered light predominates. Consistent moisture and humus-rich, acidic soil are essential; the plant will not tolerate drought or alkaline clay without amendment.

common_name: Allee Lacebark Elm (Texas A&M Drought-Tolerant Shade Tree)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Allee was selected by Texas A&M for its uniform vase-shaped form, striking exfoliating bark, and excellent heat and drought tolerance for southern shade tree use.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Allee is a lacebark elm cultivar selected and introduced by Texas A&M University for its uniform, vase-shaped growth habit, resembling the classic silhouette of American elm without the vulnerability to Dutch elm disease that devastated that species. Its most striking feature is the beautifully mottled, exfoliating bark in patches of gray, green, orange, and brown that develops as the tree matures, giving significant year-round ornamental interest even in winter. It is highly tolerant of heat, drought, and the alkaline, compacted soils common in urban and suburban Southern landscapes, requiring only routine structural pruning while young to establish strong branch angles for a long-lived, storm-resistant shade tree.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in wet to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; allegheny monkey flower grows in standing shallow water and saturated soils along stream banks, pond margins, and wet meadows. Seeds are tiny — surface sow without covering.
directions: Surface sow on moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil at pond margins, stream banks, and rain garden edges in partial shade to full sun; allegheny monkey flower is a native perennial of wet streambanks and pond edges across most of eastern North America, producing bright lavender-blue tubular flowers with distinctive two-lobed lips that give the plant a fanciful face resembling a grinning monkey — the whimsical origin of the common name shared across the Mimulus genus. The square stems are typical of the mint family to which it belongs. It grows in standing water up to 2 inches deep and in perpetually saturated soils at pond edges, making it excellent for naturalistic water garden margins. An important nectar plant for bumblebees and hummingbirds. Blooms from early summer into fall with consistent moisture. Self-sows freely along muddy stream banks. Excellent for naturalizing wet sites where its spreading colonies create a vivid blue summer display.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; Allegheny spurge is slower to spread than Japanese pachysandra but far more beautiful, with ornamentally mottled foliage.
directions: Plant divisions or container specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Allegheny spurge is the native North American alternative to the ubiquitous Japanese pachysandra, producing semi-evergreen to evergreen mats of large, attractively silver-mottled leaves that are significantly more ornamental than the plain green of P. terminalis. The lightly fragrant, white to pink flower spikes emerge at ground level in early spring before the new leaves expand, adding a subtle bonus to the elegant foliage. It spreads more slowly than its Japanese counterpart but colonizes effectively over 3–5 years in suitable conditions. Extremely useful for naturalizing dry to moist, heavily shaded areas in zone 4–9 gardens, including the Gulf South where it handles summer heat better than expected for a woodland native.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native marginal aquatic perennial
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in full sun to partial shade in shallow water or permanently wet soil in zone 8–12; Alligator Flag (Fire-Flag) is a tall, dramatic, native marginal aquatic perennial found throughout the Gulf Coast, Caribbean, and tropical Americas — producing bold, canna-like foliage on tall stems reaching 6–8 feet and loose, zig-zagging racemes of small violet-purple flowers beloved by ruby-throated hummingbirds.
directions: Plant Thalia geniculata rhizome divisions in moist to wet soil or in the shallow margins of ponds in full sun to partial shade; space plants 3–5 feet apart and allow to form clumps; divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and spread to new areas. Alligator Flag is one of the most striking native marginal aquatics of the Gulf Coast and is an important wildlife plant throughout its natural range from the southeastern United States through the Caribbean and Central America into South America. The bold, upright, canna-like leaves create a dramatic vertical accent at the water's edge; the tall, arching, zigzag-jointed flower stalks bear small but intricate violet-blue flowers that are a magnet for hummingbirds throughout the warm season. In Gulf Coast gardens (zone 8–10), Alligator Flag can become a large, clump-forming colony in bog gardens, pond margins, and low wet areas; the foliage dies back to the rhizome after frost in zone 8–9 but re-emerges reliably in spring. Seeds develop in nutlet-like capsules and are relished by waterfowl. An excellent choice for naturalizing wet swales, retention pond edges, and rain gardens throughout the coastal South.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; alligator juniper is highly drought tolerant once established, growing naturally on dry, rocky mountain slopes and canyon walls of the Southwest at 4,500–8,000 feet elevation.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; alligator juniper is unmistakable — the only juniper with distinctive, deeply checkered, rectangular bark plates that perfectly resemble the textured, scaly skin of an alligator, making it one of the most easily identified conifers in the field. Native to the rocky, dry mountain slopes of southeastern Arizona, New Mexico, western Texas, and northern Mexico (the sky island mountain ranges and the Sierra Madre foothills) at mid-to-high elevations. One of the longer-lived junipers, with ancient specimens estimated at 500–1,000 years old. The blue-glaucous, berry-like seed cones are larger than most junipers. One of the drought-toughest conifers for the desert Southwest and Chihuahuan Desert transition zone — an excellent landscape tree for hot, dry, rocky sites where nearly nothing else survives. The dramatic bark texture makes it one of the most distinctive ornamental trees for dry southwestern landscapes.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in wet, acidic, mucky to sandy, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a water feature or in a rain garden; Alligator Lily requires consistently wet to waterlogged soil and will not tolerate drought. Divide bulb clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Alligator Lily is a Florida endemic spider-lily found in wet flatwoods, freshwater marshes, and wet prairie margins of south and central Florida, producing elegant white flowers with reflexed petals and a distinctive fringed central cup (corona) characteristic of the Hymenocallis genus. Rare in cultivation despite being well suited to wet gardens, pond margins, and water features, Alligator Lily is a true South Florida native restricted to the peninsula and not found naturally anywhere else in the world. Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in wet, acidic, mucky to sandy, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade near a water feature or rain garden; established clumps multiply steadily through bulb offsets to form impressive colonies in appropriate wet conditions. Alligator Lily is intolerant of drought and requires consistently moist to wet soil — it performs best in natural pond margins, wet flatwood restoration plantings, and South Florida water gardens.

plant_note: Surface sow; needs light to germinate.
directions: This pastel blend of sweet alyssum forms low, spreading mounds smothered in tiny, honey-scented flowers. Sow on the soil surface and press in gently, since the seed needs light to sprout, and keep it moist until established. Grow in full sun to part shade along borders, in rock gardens, or cascading from containers. The fragrant blooms attract beneficial pollinators throughout the cool season. Shear plants back lightly if they slow in summer heat to encourage a fresh flush of bloom.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring or plant divisions in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; alpine rock cress is one of the finest early-spring rock garden plants, covering itself in pure-white (or pink in cultivars) flowers before most other plants have emerged.
directions: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun, or plant divisions in spring or fall; alpine rock cress requires excellent drainage — plants will rot in wet or waterlogged soil especially in winter. Arabis alpina is a mat-forming European alpine perennial in the mustard family, producing rosettes of grayish-green, slightly hairy leaves and in early spring covering itself completely in pure-white, 4-petaled flowers in dense racemes that create a solid mat of white from March through May — one of the most reliable and spectacular early-spring groundcovers for rock gardens, walls, and sunny banks. The pink-flowered cultivar 'Rosea' and semi-double 'Flore Pleno' are popular alternatives; all are excellent for spilling over walls and between rocks. Shear lightly after blooming to keep compact and encourage fresh growth.

plant_note: Divide established clumps carefully in early fall after flowering, ensuring each section has healthy roots and a rosette of leaves. Replant immediately in a gritty, humus-rich, well-drained mix in a cool, lightly shaded position such as a trough or rock garden. Protect from winter wet with a pane of glass rather than mulch, which can cause crown rot.
directions: Alpine snowbell demands excellent drainage and cool, consistently moist conditions; plant in a trough, raised bed, or rock garden crevice filled with a mix of gritty sand, pea gravel, and leaf mold. Choose a position with morning sun and afternoon shade, or dappled light, to replicate its high-altitude habitat. Divide established clumps after flowering in fall to propagate, handling the shallow roots with care and replanting immediately. Winter wet is the primary threat to survival — shelter plants with a pane of glass over winter if prolonged wet spells are typical in your climate.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; alpine wallflower is a perennial species from the Iberian Peninsula that is longer-lived than common wallflower (E. cheiri) in well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to slightly neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; alpine wallflower requires excellent drainage and is best propagated from cuttings annually as it tends to become woody and die out in the center after 2–3 years. Erysimum linifolium is a Spanish native perennial wallflower with narrow, linear, gray-green leaves (giving it the name "flat-leaved") and produces a long, extended succession of fragrant, lavender-purple to mauve flowers in terminal clusters from spring through summer; it blooms for several months if the spent flower clusters are regularly removed. The cultivar 'Bowles' Mauve' (formerly attributed to this species but now considered a complex hybrid) is one of the longest-blooming of all perennial wallflowers, flowering nearly year-round in mild climates and making it one of the most popular of all perennial wallflowers in UK gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in moist to consistently moist, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, sandy or rocky subalpine soil in partial shade to full sun; alpine wintergreen requires cool summer temperatures and strongly acidic conditions and is best suited to Pacific Northwest, Rocky Mountain, and upper Midwest gardens.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained, peaty or sandy-rocky subalpine soil in partial shade to full sun; alpine wintergreen requires cool summer temperatures and good winter snow cover to perform at its best. Gaultheria humifusa is a mat-forming, evergreen sub-shrub of rocky subalpine and alpine slopes throughout the western mountains of North America from Alaska to California and New Mexico, producing a dense, low carpet of tiny, rounded, dark-green, slightly aromatic leaves — similar to the familiar eastern G. procumbens but much lower-growing — with small white urn-shaped flowers tucked among the leaves in summer, followed by small red, mildly wintergreen-flavored berries in late summer and fall. It is a superb groundcover for acidic rock gardens, alpine gardens, and under rhododendrons or conifers in cool-climate gardens. The berries are attractive to birds and safe for human consumption in small quantities. Not suitable for warm-climate gardens — it requires cold winters and mild summers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade along stream banks or at the margins of ponds; golden saxifrage requires consistent moisture and will not tolerate drought.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; alternate-leaved golden saxifrage forms dense, low, spreading mats along stream banks, seeps, and woodland spring margins and requires consistently high moisture — it will not survive drought. Chrysosplenium alternifolium is a diminutive, 3–6-inch-tall European and Asian native groundcover in the saxifrage family with small, rounded, kidney-shaped, toothed leaves and clusters of tiny, chartreuse-yellow to golden flowers surrounded by brightly colored, leaf-like bracts in early spring, creating a cheerful carpet of yellow-green along shaded, wet stream margins. It is uncommon in cultivation but is increasingly sought by shade and water garden enthusiasts for its ability to create a lush, moss-like carpet in the wettest, shadiest spots where other groundcovers fail; in North America it occurs natively in the far north.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich potting mix in partial shade; aluminum plant prefers consistently moist but never waterlogged soil — it is sensitive to drought (leaves collapse quickly) but equally sensitive to root rot in compacted or consistently wet media.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; aluminum plant is a Vietnamese shade perennial of the nettle family (Urticaceae) — one of the most easily grown and most instantly recognizable small tropical foliage plants — whose oval, quilted, dark-green leaves are distinctively marked with four elevated, raised, silver-white, metallic panels between the leaf veins that catch light and create a three-dimensional, embossed, hammered-aluminum effect on the leaf surface. The silver patterning is so striking and consistent that the plant is immediately recognizable even at a distance. It grows as a compact, bushy, somewhat succulent-stemmed mound and is among the most tolerant of lower indoor light levels of any tropical foliage plant, thriving in bright-shade to moderate-shade conditions where many other variegated plants would lose their markings. As an outdoor plant in zone 10–12, it forms a low mounding groundcover in shade gardens. Tip-pinch regularly to maintain compact, bushy growth — plants left unpinched become tall and lanky within a few months. Propagates trivially easily from stem cuttings rooted in water.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall with the neck and top half of the bulb above soil level in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 8–10 amaryllis naturalize in the ground and bloom reliably each winter-spring without the 6–8 week dry rest period required for potted indoor forcing.
directions: Plant bulbs with the top half exposed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; amaryllis (correctly Hippeastrum) is one of the most spectacularly beautiful of all bulbous plants, producing massive trumpet-shaped flowers 6–8 inches across in brilliant red, pink, white, coral, salmon, or bicolor striped patterns on hollow, leafless stalks 18–24 inches tall. In zone 8–10 amaryllis naturalizes beautifully in the garden, blooming each January through April without any special treatment — simply plant the bulbs in fall, fertilize lightly in fall and early spring, and allow the foliage to die back naturally each summer. Gulf Coast gardens are famous for spectacular outdoor amaryllis displays along entry walks and in foundation plantings. The large clumps multiply year by year to create a more impressive display. Indoor forcing in pots requires a 6–8 week dry rest period at cool temperatures before returning to warmth and water.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; needs light and cool soil.
directions: 'Amazing Grey' produces one-of-a-kind crepe-paper blooms in smoky lavender-grey tones, bred over many years from the Mother of Pearl blend. Scatter the tiny seed on the surface in early spring or fall, as it needs light and cool soil to germinate, and do not cover it. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where it is quite drought tolerant. Because it resents transplanting, always direct sow where it is to bloom. Let some flowers form seed pods and it will happily self-sow for future seasons.

common_name: Amazon Lily (Eucharis Lily, White Amazon Lily, Madonna Lily of the Tropics)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil or potting mix; Amazon Lily cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 50°F. Unlike most bulbs, it prefers consistent moisture year-round and only needs a brief 4–6 week dry spell to trigger blooming. Grow in groupings for best display — single bulbs rarely bloom as freely as established clumps. In zone 9, container culture allows flexibility. Keep the bulb top at soil level. Propagate by separating offsets. All parts toxic.
