Asclepias asperula is a low, spreading native milkweed of the Southwest and Gulf Coast from Kansas and Oklahoma south through Texas and into New Mexico, growing in dry prairies, rocky hillsides, and open roadsides; it produces clusters of distinctive greenish-white flowers with purple to maroon markings from April through June, held at or just above the sprawling, rough-textured foliage — the curved, horn-like follicle pods that split to release silky-plumed seeds inspired the common name. It is one of the earliest-blooming milkweeds in its range and is a critical early-season host plant for monarch butterfly larvae and an important nectar source for migrating monarchs in spring; queen butterflies also use it as a larval host. Once established in appropriate lean, dry conditions, antelope horns milkweed is exceptionally drought-tolerant, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free — avoid rich soils or regular irrigation, which will shorten its life.

common_name: Antenna Orchid (Trigger Orchid, Scorpion Orchid, Antennifera Restrepia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered light in small pots of fine bark or sphagnum moss-bark mix in a cool to intermediate location; Restrepia antennifera is a cool-growing orchid from high-altitude Colombian cloud forests (5,000–9,000 feet) that prefers cooler temperatures (day 65–75°F, night 50–60°F). Excellent terrarium orchid — the small size and preference for high humidity (70%+) make it ideal for enclosed humid conditions. The leaves produce plantlets (keikis) at the leaf tips that can be detached and rooted. Blooms sequentially through most of the year. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered light in cool, humid conditions — Antenna Orchid is a miniature cloud forest orchid that grows most happily in the cool, high-humidity conditions of a terrarium or cool shaded porch and will decline in hot, dry summer conditions. Restrepia antennifera is a tiny, sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to the high-altitude cloud forests of Colombia and Venezuela in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most popular miniature orchids for terrarium culture for the extraordinary appearance of its flowers. The plant is very small — barely 4–8 inches tall — with a single, broadly oval, thick, leathery leaf per stem. But the flowers produced from the leaf base are visually extraordinary: the two lateral sepals are broad, fused along their inner margins into a single, deflexed 'synsepal' structure in yellow-orange to orange-red with contrasting purple-red veining and spotting — forming the lower visible portion of the flower. The two upper petals are highly modified into extremely long, thin, thread-like structures terminating in slightly thickened, warty, club-shaped tips — the 'antennae' that give the plant its common name and that wave gently in air movement. The lip is small and attached to the moveable column in a trigger mechanism related to pollinator deception. Restrepia antennifera produces flowers sequentially from the same leaf nodes, providing months of bloom from a small plant. An outstanding miniature orchid for terrarium culture. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Anthony Waterer blooms on new wood — shear to 6–8 inches in late winter or very early spring to stimulate maximum new growth and flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Anthony Waterer is the classic carmine-rose Japanese spiraea cultivar — one of the oldest and most widely grown selections of Spiraea japonica, introduced before 1884 and still among the most popular compact summer-blooming shrubs in American horticulture. The flat-topped, 3–4 inch flower clusters are a rich carmine-rose to deep rose-pink color from June through August (in zone 7–8), with peak bloom lasting 4–6 weeks followed by scattered repeat bloom if sheared lightly after the first flush. As with all Japanese spiraea cultivars, Anthony Waterer blooms on new wood — shear the entire plant hard to 6–8 inches in late winter or very early spring to stimulate vigorous new growth and produce the densest possible flower coverage. An established plant that is not sheared becomes leggy and produces fewer flowers; annual hard pruning is the most important maintenance practice for this species. Anthony Waterer grows to 3–4 feet tall and wide with a neat, rounded, mounding form that requires virtually no pruning to maintain shape beyond the annual renewal shearing. The new growth often emerges with distinctive cream and pink variegation, maturing to green. The plant is exceptionally adaptable — tolerating clay soil, heat, drought, and urban conditions throughout zone 9.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, chunky, humus-rich, acidic epiphytic mix (orchid bark, perlite, and peat) in bright indirect light or deep shade; anthurium roots require excellent air circulation and will rot in dense, waterlogged soil. Keep roots slightly elevated if possible for best drainage.
directions: Plant in chunky, well-drained epiphytic mix in bright indirect light to deep shade — anthurium produces some of the most striking and long-lasting of all tropical flowers, with waxy, heart-shaped spathes in red, pink, white, coral, or burgundy surrounding a contrasting spadix, each spathe remaining attractive for 2–3 months. It is one of the most popular tropical houseplants worldwide and the most important cut flower in Hawaii's floriculture industry. As a garden plant in zone 10–12, it thrives in the deep shade of trees and covered patios, exactly where little else grows. The glossy, dark green leaves are themselves ornamental. It is sensitive to direct sun (which burns the leaves), overwatering, and temperatures below 55°F. In zone 9a it is an outstanding container plant for shaded patios, wintering indoors. Keep soil moderately moist and fertilize lightly every 6 weeks.

common_name: Apeldoorn Tulip (Classic Large Red Darwin Hybrid Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Apeldoorn is one of the most widely planted Darwin hybrid tulips, known for large flowers on sturdy, tall stems that hold up well to wind and rain.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Apeldoorn is a classic Darwin hybrid tulip, a group bred for extra-large flowers on strong, tall stems, producing bright, clear scarlet-red blooms that have made it one of the most commercially planted tulip cultivars in the world for mass displays and cut flowers. Darwin hybrids like Apeldoorn also tend to perennialize somewhat better than many other tulip types in climates with adequate winter chill, though in mild-winter zone 8-9 gardens they are still usually most reliable treated as a fresh fall planting.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into moist, rocky, slightly acidic soil in a partial-shade woodland setting; firm seed lightly into surface as light aids germination.
directions: Campanula divaricata is a delicate native bellflower of the Appalachian Mountains and upper Piedmont, producing airy, branching stems covered in tiny (1/3-inch), nodding, pale lavender-blue bells from July through September that are excellent for long-season color in shaded rock gardens. It grows in moist to dry rocky woodland slopes and cliff bases in slightly acidic soil. Bees and butterflies work the flowers for nectar. Self-seeds moderately without becoming invasive; combine with ferns, coral bells, and native gingers for a layered shade garden.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; Appalachian bugbane has a very restricted natural range in shaded gorges and moist ravines in the central Appalachians (TN, NC, KY, AL) and is a rare but stunning native for large shaded gardens.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Appalachian bugbane (formerly Cimicifuga rubifolia) has a very restricted natural range in shaded gorges, moist ravines, and rich mesic slopes in Tennessee, North Carolina, Kentucky, and Alabama, making it one of the rarest and most conservation-significant native garden plants. It is closely related to the widely grown Actaea racemosa (black cohosh) and produces similar dramatic, arching, bottle-brush spikes of tiny white flowers on stems 4–6 feet tall in late summer and fall above bold, compound foliage, but is distinguished by its leaf shape — the leaflets are broader and more coarsely toothed, resembling those of a raspberry, hence the species name rubifolia. It is a magnificent specimen plant for large, shaded native gardens; purchase only nursery-propagated stock and never collect from the wild, as natural populations are small and threatened. Long-lived and deer-resistant once established.

plant_note: Plant rhizome/corm divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland or meadow soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian bunchflower grows naturally in rich mountain woodlands and moist mountain meadows and tolerates more shade than M. virginicum.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Appalachian bunchflower (Melanthium hybridum) is closely related to Virginia bunchflower (M. virginicum) but differs in growing primarily in rich, moist Appalachian mountain woodlands and forest margins rather than coastal plain wet meadows, and in bearing leaves that are somewhat wider and more variable — the name 'hybridum' reflects the morphological variability of the species rather than hybrid origin. It produces the same stately, grass-clump form and tall summer flowering stems 3–5 feet tall topped with large panicles of cream-to-greenish-white flowers that age purple, providing a dramatic vertical accent in the shaded native garden. Less commercially available than M. virginicum but worth seeking from Appalachian native plant nurseries for its superior shade tolerance and ornamental appeal in forested garden settings. All parts are toxic; handle with gloves.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Appalachian sedge is slow to establish but very long-lived once settled — allow 1–2 growing seasons for full establishment and spreading. It naturalizes readily from seed in suitable conditions, forming expanding clumps that can eventually replace turf grass in shaded areas. In zone 9 it performs as a reliable, low-growing, semi-evergreen to evergreen ground cover. Unlike many sedges that require moist soil, Appalachian sedge tolerates dry shade under mature trees — one of its most valuable practical attributes.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained to dry, moderately fertile to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Appalachian sedge is native to dry woodland habitats and tolerates the difficult conditions of dry shade under mature trees; Appalachian sedge is a fine-textured, low-growing native sedge endemic to the Appalachian region and extending through the Gulf South, providing an ecologically appropriate, low-maintenance alternative to lawn grass or imported ground covers in shaded landscapes. The narrow, arching, bright green to yellow-green leaves form a low, graceful, grass-like mound 6–10 inches high that spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding to form a naturalistic, weed-suppressing ground cover under trees. As a native species adapted to the woodland understory of the Southeastern United States, Appalachian sedge supports native invertebrates and serves as a host plant for several native skipper butterflies, contributing ecological function along with aesthetic value. Unlike turf grass, Appalachian sedge requires no mowing, very little fertilization, and tolerates the dry shade and root competition under mature trees that eliminates conventional lawn alternatives — its primary competitive advantage as a practical garden plant. The low-growing, flowing texture provides a natural woodland floor aesthetic compatible with native shade tree and shrub plantings.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Appalachian Spring is the most disease-resistant Cornus florida cultivar — specifically selected for resistance to dogwood anthracnose (Discula destructiva), the devastating fungal disease that has killed millions of dogwood trees in the eastern US.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Appalachian Spring is the most significant disease-resistant flowering dogwood cultivar ever introduced — selected from wild dogwood populations in the Appalachian Mountains specifically for its outstanding resistance to dogwood anthracnose (Discula destructiva), the fungal disease that since the 1970s has killed millions of wild dogwood trees across the eastern United States and continues to devastate unresistant trees in humid forest conditions. Dogwood anthracnose causes branch dieback, water-soaked lesions, and can kill an entire tree within 2–3 years of infection — it is the primary reason dogwood populations have declined so dramatically in eastern American forests. Appalachian Spring was selected by the US National Arboretum through a program specifically aimed at finding anthracnose-resistant genotypes among surviving wild populations where the disease had been established for decades. The flower display is classic white Cornus florida — large, four-bracted, pure white flowers in March through April — combined with the full suite of ornamental qualities: excellent fall red color, attractive horizontal branching, and fall red berries for wildlife. In zone 9, Appalachian Spring performs similarly to other Cornus florida cultivars but offers insurance against the anthracnose that has become more of a concern in humid Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions very carefully in fall in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, undisturbed forest soil in deep shade; Appalachian twayblade depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi for establishment and is essentially impossible to grow without these fungal partners present in the native soil. Only plant in existing undisturbed woodland with intact organic duff layer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, undisturbed woodland soil in deep shade with an intact organic duff layer; Appalachian twayblade is a diminutive native terrestrial orchid of cool, shaded, moist forest floors in the Appalachians and adjacent regions. The plant is distinguished by a single pair of opposite, rounded leaves (hence 'twayblade' — two-blade) at the base of a slender stem bearing tiny greenish flowers. Like all native terrestrial orchids, it depends entirely on specific soil fungi (mycorrhizae) for survival and cannot be successfully grown in sterilized or amended potting soil. The plant's best use in the landscape is simply protecting existing populations in undisturbed woodland rather than attempting cultivation. Listed in some states as a species of conservation concern due to woodland habitat loss. Grow only from ethically sourced, nursery-propagated stock.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist shade; cold stratification over winter improves germination. Plants bloom in their second year.
directions: Appendaged Waterleaf is a native biennial or short-lived perennial of the waterleaf family, found in moist, shaded deciduous woodlands and rich floodplain forests across the eastern and central United States. In its first year it produces a rosette of large, pinnately lobed, soft-hairy leaves often decorated with pale whitish mottling; in the second year it sends up branched stems topped with rounded clusters of tubular, pale lavender to white flowers with conspicuously long-exserted stamens that give the blooms a feathery, soft appearance in spring. Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, and allow the colony to self-sow for a self-sustaining planting. It is an underused native for shaded wild gardens and woodland restoration plantings in zones 3-8.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost; prefers cool growing conditions.
directions: Sow Apricot Beauty calendula a quarter inch deep around the last frost, as cool soil suits germination. This heirloom pot marigold bears soft semi-double blooms in apricot, peach, and pale-gold tones on tidy plants. The edible, medicinal petals are lovely in salads and herbal preparations. Deadhead often to extend bloom, and expect a fresh flush as autumn cools.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 4 weeks early.
directions: 'Apricotta' is an award-winning cosmos with soft apricot-pink blooms centered in yellow on tall, sturdy stems ideal for cutting. Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors about a month early, barely covering the seed. Grow in full sun in average to lean soil, as rich ground produces foliage rather than flowers. It is drought tolerant once established and blooms prolifically from midsummer to frost. Deadhead or cut regularly to keep the plants flowering and to attract bees and butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; aquatic milkweed grows naturally in swamp forests, streambanks, and floodplain margins across the Gulf Coastal Plain. In zone 9, it may remain semi-evergreen in mild winters.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; aquatic milkweed is the only native milkweed in North America adapted to the forested swamp conditions of the Gulf Coastal Plain — growing naturally in the shade of bottomland forests, swamp edges, and along bayous and sluggish streams from Florida to Texas and north to Illinois. Unlike most milkweeds that demand dry, sunny conditions, this species thrives in wet, partially shaded sites where it provides monarch butterfly larval habitat in habitats otherwise lacking milkweed. The tiny white flowers in rounded clusters are delicate and fragrant. As a monarch host plant, it is critically important because it blooms in two seasons — spring and fall — aligning with monarch migration and breeding in the Gulf South. An outstanding zone 9a milkweed for shaded, wet areas and streamside gardens where no other milkweed will thrive.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; in zones below 10, grow in containers and bring indoors before first frost.
directions: Root cuttings in moist sand/perlite mix in summer heat or plant container specimens in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Arabian jasmine is the national flower of the Philippines and the primary source of the jasmine scent used in perfumes and jasmine tea — the double-flowered form 'Grand Duke of Tuscany' is especially fragrant, with blooms that intensify their perfume at night. Plants bloom intermittently throughout the warm season and can be trained as vines on a trellis or grown as shrubs. Fertilize monthly during active growth with a balanced fertilizer. In zone 9 grow against a warm south-facing wall and protect from hard freezes; in zone 8 and colder grow in containers. Harvest flowers in the morning for the strongest fragrance.

common_name: Arabian Star of Bethlehem (Black-Centered Star Flower)
plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Arabian star of Bethlehem grows in late winter through spring, blooms in late spring, then goes summer dormant. In zones 7b–10 it can remain in the ground through summer dormancy with withheld water; lift and store dry in colder zones. An excellent cut flower with long vase life.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Arabian star of Bethlehem is one of the most distinctive and fragrant spring-blooming bulbs — a Mediterranean and North African native producing in late spring (May–June), tall, upright scapes bearing a raceme of large (2 inch), pure-white, six-petaled, cup-shaped flowers each with a dramatic, prominent, dark, blue-black to jet-black ovary at the center — a shining black jewel at the heart of each snow-white flower creating a startling, bold contrast of white and black that gives the blooms an immediately recognizable and distinctive appearance unlike any other common spring bulb. The fragrance is sweet and noticeable, particularly in the evening. The flowers are excellent cut flowers with exceptional vase life of 2–3 weeks, making this a valuable bulb for cutting gardens. The large, broad, strap-shaped leaves are present from autumn through late spring, then die back in summer dormancy. Outstanding in zones 7b–10 where it can remain in the ground as a perennial; in zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens it naturalizes effectively. A superb, slightly unusual spring-flowering bulb for the cutting garden.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings after all frost danger has passed into well-drained, full-sun soil.
directions: Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer and root them in a well-draining mix before transplanting to a permanent site in spring. This fast-growing coastal shrub thrives in sandy, poor soils and tolerates salt spray, making it ideal for seaside gardens in warm zones. The aromatic gray-green trifoliate leaves and purple flower spikes appear through summer and have long been used in Asian herbal traditions for their fragrant essential oils. In borderline zones 8-9, plant against a south-facing wall and mulch the base heavily to protect the crown through cold snaps.

common_name: Archduke Charles Rose (Color-Changing Antique China Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Archduke Charles is an antique China rose introduced around 1837, valued in Gulf South gardens for blooms that darken from pink to deep crimson as they age and for the class's characteristic heat and disease tolerance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced around 1837, Archduke Charles is a classic China rose whose fully double blooms open pale pink at the petal edges with deep rose-red centers, then darken dramatically toward crimson-purple as they age in warm weather, so a single well-established bush can show several bloom colors simultaneously. Like other China roses it flowers almost without pause from spring through the first hard frost and carries strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, thriving in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South with minimal spray input. The rounded, bushy shrub works well massed, in mixed borders, or as an informal low hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or weak wood; hard pruning is unnecessary and reduces flowering, since China roses bloom continuously on both old and new growth.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and replant immediately in wet, cold-climate shade. Well-suited to northern and high-elevation gardens where other groundcovers struggle.
directions: Establish divisions in spring in deep shade or heavy shade with consistently wet or waterlogged soil. This native species thrives at the margins of cold streams, bogs, and seeps in northern gardens. It spreads at a moderate pace by rhizomes, forming dense weed-suppressing colonies useful for stabilizing moist, shaded banks. Far less aggressive than its European relative, it makes a manageable groundcover for cold-climate woodland gardens.

common_name: Areca Palm (Butterfly Palm, Golden Cane Palm, Madagascar Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Areca Palm is frost-sensitive (damaged below 32°F) and should be planted in zone 10-11 for outdoor landscape use, or grown in large containers in zone 9. In zone 9, use as a large container specimen on the patio from spring through fall, moving to a greenhouse or heated space in winter. Areca Palm is chlorine-sensitive — use filtered or collected rainwater in hard water areas, and avoid over-fertilizing with fluoride-containing formulations.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Areca Palm prefers consistently moist conditions and will develop yellowing fronds (potassium deficiency) in the alkaline soils common across the Gulf Coast — acidify soil with sulfur and use palm-formulated fertilizer containing micronutrients. Dypsis lutescens (formerly Chrysalidocarpus lutescens) is the most widely sold palm in the US nursery trade and one of the most commonly planted landscape palms in zone 10-11 Florida, Texas, and Gulf South landscapes — the graceful, arching, feathery fronds on cane-like yellow-green stems form magnificent multi-stemmed clumps reaching 15–25 feet. The yellow-green color of the stems (giving 'Golden Cane Palm' its name) and the softly arching frond tips that sway in the slightest breeze create an exceptionally elegant tropical effect. Native to Madagascar, where it is now endangered in the wild due to habitat loss, Areca Palm has become one of the world's most cultivated ornamental palms. The NASA Clean Air Study ranked it as one of the best air-purifying plants, removing xylene, toluene, and formaldehyde from indoor air. Non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring 2–3 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, gritty to loamy soil in zone 7–10; Argentine Rain Lily is a summer-blooming South American bulb from the grasslands of Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil — producing beautiful, large (for the genus), nodding, funnel-shaped, rose-pink flowers on 12-inch stems within days of a soaking summer rain, with each flower held at a characteristic 45-degree angle that distinguishes Habranthus from Zephyranthes.
directions: Plant Habranthus robustus bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; bulbs perform best with a dry dormant period in late spring followed by a good soaking (simulating monsoon rains) to trigger flowering; clumps multiply over time and bloom most profusely when slightly crowded. Argentine Rain Lily is the largest-flowered and most robust species in the Habranthus genus — a group of summer-rain-triggered bulbs closely related to Zephyranthes but distinguished by the characteristic nodding, angled flower posture (held at roughly 45 degrees) rather than upright. Flowers emerge in impressive flushes within 24–72 hours of a summer downpour, creating a breathtaking display: 3–4 inch, rose-pink to pale-pink funnel-shaped flowers with a golden-yellow center, held on slender stems above narrow, rush-like leaves. Exceptionally easy to grow and reliably perennial throughout zone 7–10, including the Gulf Coast where summer rains naturally trigger perfect bloom cycles. Bulbs naturalize readily in lawn edges, rock gardens, and raised beds; they naturalize particularly well in Texas and the Gulf South where the summer rain/dry pattern matches their native South American prairie climate. Divide crowded clumps every 3–4 years and replant offsets to spread.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Argentine trumpet vine tolerates partial shade more successfully than most Bignonia family vines and produces acceptable flower display in the filtered light of open tree canopy — one of the better shade-tolerant flowering vines for zone 8–11.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Argentine trumpet vine (lavender trumpet vine) is a South American evergreen or semi-evergreen vine of the bignonia family that produces clusters of large, flared, trumpet-shaped, soft-lavender to pale-lilac and white flowers with violet-purple striping and veining on the throat in spring (April–May) and intermittently through the year, creating a refined and graceful floral display above its dense, glossy, dark-green, tendril-climbing foliage. The soft, delicate lavender-lilac color and the large, attractive, trumpet flower form give it a more elegant and less brash appearance than orange or red trumpet vines. It is notably more shade-tolerant than most Bignoniaceae vines and can bloom acceptably in partial-shade positions — a valuable attribute for the shadier garden where most large flowering vines fail. Hardy to approximately 20°F in zone 8, it is one of the more cold-tolerant of the tropical trumpet vine family. Excellent trained on arbors, fences, and large trellises in zone 8–11. May be invasive in some warm, moist climates — monitor for naturalization near natural areas.

common_name: Argentine Trumpet Vine (Garrocha Tecoma, Red Esperanza)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Tecoma garrocha is cold-hardy to zone 7-8 (20–25°F) — more cold-tolerant than T. stans. It grows as a large sprawling shrub or small tree in zone 9. The long, tubular flowers are outstanding hummingbird attractants. Prune by one-third in late winter to shape and stimulate new flowering stems. Can be trained as a small tree with staking. The orange-red flower color is somewhat different from yellow-flowered T. stans, offering a warmer-toned alternative. Propagate from stem cuttings or seed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Tecoma garrocha grows most vigorously in full sun and will produce fewer flowers and become leggy in shade. Tecoma garrocha is a large, fast-growing, semi-deciduous shrub or small tree native to Argentina and Bolivia in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the commonly grown Yellow Bells (T. stans) but with distinctly orange-red to coral-red tubular flowers rather than yellow — a color difference with significant ornamental consequence. The plant produces compound leaves of several lance-shaped leaflets and bears its trumpet-shaped flowers in terminal clusters throughout the warm months from spring through fall, with a particularly prolific bloom in summer and early fall. The long, tubular, orange-red flowers are extraordinary hummingbird attractants — the nectar-rich, hummingbird-adapted flower form and vivid color ensures a continuous parade of hummingbirds in zone 9 gardens where this shrub is planted. Unlike many tropical-looking flowering shrubs, Tecoma garrocha is genuinely cold-hardy — cold-hardy to zone 7-8, surviving temperatures to 20°F — one of the most cold-hardy of the Tecoma species. This cold tolerance combined with its spectacular hummingbird value and long bloom season makes T. garrocha one of the most underused and undervalued ornamental shrubs for zone 8-9 Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Direct sow on bare, sandy soil in fall; nick or soak seeds overnight before sowing to encourage germination and winter-into-spring bloom.
directions: Arizona Lupine is a vivid native annual of sandy desert flats, bajadas, and dry washes across southern Arizona, the Mojave and Sonoran deserts of California, and adjacent Mexico, producing silky-haired palmate foliage and dense spikes of deep magenta-pink to rose-purple flowers from February through April. It is one of the most spectacular wildflowers of the Colorado Desert during superbloom years, blanketing open sandy ground with color. Direct sow in fall on bare, dry, sandy or gravelly, freely draining soil in full sun; nick or soak seeds beforehand to improve germination rates. This species does not transplant well and should be established in place, where it will self-sow reliably in subsequent seasons once it has set seed.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, rocky, calcareous, very well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Arizona Marina is a native perennial legume of dry, rocky, calcareous hills and canyon walls in Arizona, New Mexico, and adjacent northern Mexico. It produces woody-based, branching stems with small, pinnate, gland-dotted leaves and short racemes of relatively large blue-violet pea flowers marked with a striking yellow keel spot, blooming from summer through fall. Scarify seeds lightly before fall direct sow into dry, rocky, calcareous, very well-drained soil in full sun; no supplemental irrigation is needed once the plant is established. An ecologically appropriate and underused native legume, Arizona Marina is well suited to Chihuahuan Desert and Arizona xeriscape gardens where lean, alkaline soils and summer drought are the norm.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Arizona Red Shades blooms heavily in its first year and becomes more floriferous as the clump matures. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering, or leave some seed heads for bird food in fall. In zone 9 provide excellent drainage — gaillardia is more likely to die from wet roots in hot weather than from the heat itself. The plants bloom most heavily in spring and fall with reduced flowering in the hottest summer weeks.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, slightly acidic to neutral soil — blanket flowers demand excellent drainage and suffer in rich, moist soils; Arizona Red Shades is an All-America Selections award-winning perennial gaillardia (blanket flower) from the Arizona series, selected for compact habit (12–18 inches) and exceptional heat and drought tolerance. The rich, warm flowers in deep red, terra-cotta, russet, and burgundy shades with yellow tips reflect the sunset colors of the American Southwest that gaillardia's native habitat inspired. The blanket flower name comes from the plant's resemblance to Native American woven blanket patterns, as well as its tendency to spread and 'blanket' dry garden areas. The extremely long bloom season (from late spring through fall frost), outstanding drought tolerance once established, and attraction to butterflies and beneficial insects make Arizona Red Shades one of the most practical low-maintenance perennials for sunny, dry garden locations. Unlike many perennials, it is heat-adapted rather than merely heat-tolerant — performing magnificently in summer conditions that challenge less heat-adapted plants.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or start from seed August–September for fall bloom. Arizona Sun is an All-America Selections winner selected for compact, non-flopping form (8–12 inches rather than the 18–24 inch height of standard Gaillardia x grandiflora). The compact form is more floriferous and longer-lasting in garden performance than standard selections. Gaillardia requires excellent drainage — it is extremely susceptible to root rot in wet, heavy soils. Deadhead to extend bloom; allow some heads to mature for seed if naturalization is desired. In zone 9 it blooms most heavily in spring (March–May) and fall (October–November).
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil — Arizona Sun Blanket Flower demands the same excellent drainage and lean, dry conditions as its prairie native parent species; Arizona Sun is an All-America Selections award-winning compact selection of Blanket Flower (Gaillardia x grandiflora), producing the classic Gaillardia flower — a large, single, daisy-form flower with bright red to orange-red ray petals tipped with yellow, surrounding a prominent rust-red central dome of disc florets — at a compact, non-flopping scale that makes it practical for the front of sunny borders, container culture, and mass planting. The vivid red-and-yellow bicolor combination of Gaillardia flowers is one of the most intense and saturated warm-color combinations available from any perennial flower, creating a bold, cheerful display through the spring and fall bloom seasons in zone 9. Gaillardia's native prairie origin (G. pulchella is native across much of the Central and Southern US) means natural adaptation to the lean, dry, hot conditions of zone 9 summers — thriving in conditions that would stress or kill less drought-adapted perennials. The combination of vivid color, native adaptation, extreme drought tolerance, and compact habit makes Arizona Sun one of the most useful and reliable compact perennials for sunny, dry zone 9 situations.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Arkansas beardtongue is a small, slender native penstemon of the south-central US excellent for limestone glades, rocky prairies, and sunny native plant gardens in zones 5–9.
directions: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, calcareous or rocky soil in full sun; Arkansas beardtongue requires excellent drainage and is adapted to the thin, rocky, alkaline limestone glades and prairies of the Ozarks and Ouachitas. Penstemon arkansanus is a small, delicate native penstemon of rocky, limestone glades, cedars barrens, and rocky prairies in Arkansas, Missouri, Oklahoma, and adjacent states; it produces narrow, linear leaves and slender spikes of small, white to pale-lavender, tubular flowers with a slightly two-lipped structure from April through June. Though small and often overlooked, it is a tough, adaptable native perennial for dry, calcareous soils in zones 5–9 where it naturalizes and self-seeds in favorable, well-drained spots; it is an excellent early-season native bee plant.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on calcareous or limestone-derived soils; cold exposure over winter aids germination.
directions: A native ironweed of moist, open, calcareous prairies, limestone glades, and stream margin meadows in Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Missouri, bearing clusters of deep purple-violet composite flowers in late summer and fall on upright stems with narrow, lance-shaped, rough leaves. More compact and tolerant of calcareous soils than Vernonia missurica, making it especially well suited to prairie restorations on limestone-derived substrates. Grow in moist, average to slightly alkaline, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; direct sow in fall. An outstanding late-season nectar source for monarchs and native bees.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in well-drained, dry, sandy, acidic, lean soil in full sun; Arkansas oak is an uncommon red-group oak of dry, sandy pinelands and upland scrub of the lower Mississippi River valley and Gulf Coastal Plain. It is adapted to sandy, infertile, dry, acidic conditions.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, dry, sandy, acidic, infertile soil in full sun; Arkansas oak is a relatively uncommon, small-statured oak of the red oak group naturally restricted to dry, sandy, acidic soils in the Gulf Coastal Plain and lower Mississippi River valley, primarily in Arkansas, Louisiana, and Texas. The leaves are variable in shape, sometimes entire, sometimes shallowly lobed, with a distinctive blue-green upper surface from which the common name 'bluejack' derives. A small tree, rarely exceeding 25 feet, it grows naturally in sandy pinelands and upland scrub alongside longleaf pine. The small acorns are eaten by deer and turkeys. An uncommon and undervalued native tree for dry, sandy, acidic sites in the Gulf South where its modest size and adaptability to infertile conditions make it appropriate for naturalistic woodland gardens and pine savanna restoration.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike most clematis, Armand clematis is evergreen with leathery leaves and blooms very early in spring on the previous year's growth, so any pruning needed to control its size should happen right after flowering, not in late winter.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence able to support a large, vigorous evergreen vine. Native to China, Armand clematis is unusual among clematis for its leathery, glossy, evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure, and for its very early spring bloom of small, intensely fragrant white star-shaped flowers produced in such abundance that a mature vine can perfume an entire section of garden. It grows quickly and can become large and somewhat unruly if not given enough room or occasional pruning right after its spring bloom to keep it in bounds, since it flowers on the prior year's growth and heavy pruning at the wrong time removes the coming season's flowers. It is a good choice for screening a fence or arbor with year-round foliage in the milder parts of its range.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Armenian grape hyacinth is extremely cold-hardy, naturalizes freely, and sends up grass-like foliage in autumn that persists through winter — the foliage is entirely normal and should not be cut back. Plant in large drifts of 25 or more for the best visual effect in spring.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for April-May bloom; Armenian grape hyacinth is the most widely grown and most reliably naturalizing of all the grape hyacinths — a compact, easy, bulb producing dense, upright spikes of tiny, tightly packed, cobalt-blue, urn-shaped flowers with white-rimmed mouths, each spike resembling a miniature bunch of grapes, above narrow, grass-like foliage. In a good form such as 'Valerie Finnis' the color is a brilliant gentian-blue; the straight species is a rich, deep cobalt. Muscari naturalizes prolifically by offsets and self-seeding, forming increasingly large drifts with each passing year — a single bulb may produce dozens of offspring over a decade. The autumn foliage emergence is entirely normal; do not remove it. Works beautifully planted under late-blooming daffodils and tulips, and thrives in the light shade beneath deciduous trees where it receives full sun in spring before the tree canopy leafs out.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Armenian tea olive is tolerant of a range of soils but performs best with protection from harsh afternoon sun in warmer zones.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun; Armenian tea olive is a large, handsome evergreen shrub from the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey with exceptionally large, glossy, lance-shaped leaves that give it a bolder, more tropical texture than most other osmanthus species. In spring it produces clusters of small white flowers with an intensely sweet fragrance that carries far on the breeze, followed by dark blue-black, olive-like fruits. Compared to the popular Osmanthus fragrans (sweet olive), it is considerably more cold-hardy and generally less invasive in North American landscapes. It makes an outstanding large screening hedge or specimen shrub in zones 6–9, and the bold foliage provides strong year-round structure in mixed borders.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; aromatic aster is one of the most drought-tolerant and garden-worthy native asters and performs best in poor to average soils — rich, moist conditions promote floppy growth at the expense of the tightly mounded habit that makes this species so ornamentally distinguished.
directions: Plant in lean, dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun; aromatic aster is widely regarded as one of the finest native asters for garden use, forming a tightly mounded, self-supporting habit — rare among late-season asters, which often flop — covered from September into November with vivid blue-violet to lavender-purple flowers with yellow centers that provide some of the richest, most saturated color of the fall garden. The foliage is intensely aromatic when crushed, with a sharp, resinous scent reminiscent of cedar or pine that is distinctive and deer-deterring. It is outstanding in dry meadows, rock gardens, slopes, and parking-strip plantings where summer drought is routine, and provides critical late-season nectar for migrating monarchs and native bees preparing for winter. Shear plants by half in late May or early June to keep the habit extra compact and encourage denser flowering; no staking is required in poor to average soils.

plant_note: Divide established clumps and plant rhizomes in spring in heavy, fertile aquatic soil in containers placed at the margin of a pond or slow stream in water 0–12 inches deep; arrow arum is one of the most adaptable native emergent wetland plants, tolerating anything from consistently wet soil at the waterline to full submersion of the crown in shallow water. It spreads readily by offsets and can form large, impenetrable colonies in shallow water — divide every 3–4 years to manage spread and maintain vigor.
directions: Plant at pond margins or in shallow water 0–12 inches deep in heavy, fertile aquatic or wetland soil in partial shade to full sun; arrow arum is a bold and architecturally striking native wetland perennial of eastern North America, producing large, glossy, prominently veined, arrowhead-shaped leaves up to 24 inches long that rise from the water on stout stems and create a dramatic vertical accent in naturalistic water gardens, constructed wetlands, and pond edges throughout zones 5–9. The flowers are inconspicuous greenish spathes typical of the arum family (Araceae), emerging in late spring amid the foliage; they are followed by clusters of fleshy green berries that ripen in late summer and are an important food source for wood ducks, mallards, and other waterfowl — making arrow arum an outstanding plant for wildlife ponds and waterfowl habitat restoration projects. Peltandra virginica is not intended for ornamental flower display but earns its place through bold foliage texture, ecological value, and reliable performance in the difficult wet-edge niche where few ornamentals thrive; it is a foundational species for naturalistic freshwater wetland gardens and native pond plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in partial shade to full sun; arrow bamboo spreads by rhizomes but less aggressively than Phyllostachys species. A root barrier is still recommended. More shade-tolerant than most bamboos, tolerating deep shade under trees.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in partial shade to shade; arrow bamboo is a Japanese bamboo widely used in Japanese gardens for its excellent shade tolerance — more tolerant of deep shade than virtually any other bamboo. The large, dark green, lance-shaped leaves on each culm branch tip create a lush, tropical appearance. In Japanese tradition, the straight, strong culms were cut and used for arrows (hence the common name 'arrow bamboo'). A spreading bamboo (running rhizomes) but less aggressive than the Phyllostachys species — still benefits from a root barrier to keep contained. Creates dense, weed-suppressing coverage under trees where few other plants grow. More versatile in shade gardens than other bamboos, making it valuable for shady woodland edge screening, Japanese garden composition, and naturalistic planting under large trees.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix at any time in warm weather; in zone 10–11 plant out after nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F. In zone 9 plant in a sheltered, frost-protected spot or use as a container plant brought inside before frost.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water and plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial to deep shade — arrowhead plant is one of the most adaptable and beautiful shade foliage plants in the world, naturalizing as a groundcover or scrambling vine in zone 10–12 and widely used as a container or houseplant in cooler zones. Young plants produce distinctive arrowhead-shaped leaves that gradually shift to deeply lobed, multi-part leaves as the plant matures and begins to climb or vine. The many cultivars offer an extraordinary range of leaf patterns: solid green, pink, cream-variegated, pale green-silver, and deep burgundy forms are all widely grown. Syngonium thrives in the deep shade of buildings, porches, and mature tree canopies where it provides lush, jungle-like texture. It roots readily wherever stems contact moist soil, spreading to colonize shaded areas in tropical climates; it is considered invasive in Florida and Hawaii when grown outdoors.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; arrowhead violet is one of the more drought-tolerant native violets and grows in open, dry to moist habitats from meadows to woodland margins throughout the eastern US.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; arrowhead violet is distinguished by its distinctively narrow, arrowhead-shaped leaves with pointed, backward-directed basal lobes — a shape quite unlike the typical rounded or heart-shaped leaves of most violets. The deep violet to blue-violet flowers in spring have the typical viola form. Like all native violets, it is an essential larval host plant for multiple fritillary butterfly species and provides nectar for early-season native bees. The arrowhead leaf shape makes it easy to identify and distinguishes it from the common blue violet (V. sororia). More tolerant of dry, open conditions than many woodland violets — suitable for meadow garden and prairie garden plantings as well as woodland edges.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall; arrowwood viburnum is highly adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions from dry to moist and pH from slightly acidic to alkaline. Plant two different clones nearby for reliable fruit set, as cross-pollination improves berry production significantly.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to average soil in part shade to full sun; arrowwood viburnum is one of the most adaptable and wildlife-valuable native shrubs of eastern North America, producing flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring that attract butterflies and native bees in abundance, followed by clusters of metallic blue-black berries in late summer that are among the most preferred fruits of over 35 species of birds including bluebirds, robins, catbirds, cedar waxwings, and wood thrushes. The glossy, coarsely-toothed leaves turn orange-red to purple in fall, making it a multi-season performer. It was named 'arrowwood' because Native Americans used the straight, stiff young stems for arrow shafts. The multi-stem rounded habit is excellent for hedges, shrub borders, and naturalistic plantings. Extremely cold-hardy and adaptable to clay soils.

common_name: Artillery Fern (Tropical Pilea Groundcover Mimicking Fine-Textured Fern Foliage)
plant_note: Plant container transplants after the last frost in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; Artillery Fern's name comes from its ability to explosively discharge pollen in small visible clouds when the tiny flowers are touched or disturbed by insects or wind — a harmless spectacle in the garden.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; Artillery Fern is not a fern at all — it is a succulent-looking tropical groundcover plant (Pilea microphylla, family Urticaceae) that mimics the fine-textured, fernlike appearance of true ferns with its tiny, densely overlapping, bright green succulent leaves on delicate, branching stems. The very small, succulent-textured leaves (2–4mm) are arranged in dense overlapping rows along the stems, creating a texture so fine-grained and bright-green that it closely resembles some delicate maidenhair fern fronds at a distance. The common name 'artillery fern' comes from the plant's unusual reproductive behavior: when the tiny, inconspicuous flowers are ripe, they explosively discharge pollen in small visible clouds when disturbed — a fascinating botanical defense mechanism visible on close inspection on warm, humid days. In zone 9, Artillery Fern is grown as a warm-season annual for shaded beds, container underplanting, and terrace pots — it thrives through Gulf South summer humidity and heat in partial to full shade where it provides lush, fine-textured green coverage from spring through frost. The succulent tissue tolerates brief dry periods better than true ferns. Self-sows in protected positions and may overwinter in zone 9b. Outstanding as a groundcover beneath shade containers and as a fine-textured companion for bold-leaved shade tropicals.

plant_note: Start indoors; cold-moist stratification improves germination.
directions: 'Artisan Red Ombre' is a breakthrough F1 hybrid coneflower, the first individual-color Echinacea from seed, blooming its first year on full, well-branched plants. Start seed indoors and provide cold-moist stratification to encourage even germination. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where it becomes drought tolerant once rooted. The richly saturated red blooms are excellent for cutting and draw pollinators all summer. Leave some seed heads standing to feed birds and add winter interest.

plant_note: Start indoors; cold-moist stratification improves germination.
directions: 'Artisan Yellow Ombre' is an F1 hybrid coneflower that flowers the first year from seed, opening golden yellow and softening to buttery tones for a sun-drenched ombre effect. Start seed indoors and give it cold-moist stratification to improve germination. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where it tolerates drought once established. The cheerful blooms are long-lasting in the vase and beloved by bees and butterflies. Leave spent flower heads for winter interest and to feed finches.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Ashe Magnolia blooms within 3–5 years from seed — much faster than most magnolias — and is appropriate for smaller gardens where Bigleaf Magnolia (Magnolia macrophylla) would be too large.
directions: Ashe Magnolia is one of the rarest magnolias in North America, a critically imperiled native shrub or small tree endemic to the steep, moist, shaded ravines and bluffs of the Florida Panhandle in a handful of counties in far northwest Florida and adjacent Alabama, where fewer than 20 wild populations survive. Despite its rarity in the wild, Ashe Magnolia is relatively easy to grow in cultivation and is widely offered by specialty native plant nurseries; it is often treated as a dwarf or subspecies of the closely related Bigleaf Magnolia (Magnolia macrophylla) but is considered a distinct species by most authorities. The enormous, white, bowl-shaped flowers (12–14 inches across) with purple-spotted centers appear in April and May and are among the most spectacular of any magnolia — attracting native bees and beetles as pollinators. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and protect from drying winds that damage the enormous leaves; it is significantly smaller and faster-blooming than M. macrophylla, making it more suitable for the typical home garden.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or early summer and transplant into well-drained, sandy or sandy-loam soil in full to partial sun after all danger of frost has passed; excellent drainage is essential — this plant is native to xeric sandhill scrub and will rot in wet or clay soils.
directions: Calamintha ashei is a rare aromatic subshrub endemic to the sandhill scrub communities of northwestern Florida and southwestern Georgia, requiring the excellent drainage and low fertility of its native sandy soils. Plant in partial sun with well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil and avoid supplemental fertilization, which encourages rank growth at the expense of its characteristic compact, minty-scented habit. Lavender-white flowers appear from summer through fall and are exceptionally attractive to native bees, including rare scrub specialist bee species that depend on this plant. Because its range is extremely restricted, source only nursery-propagated cuttings from conservation-minded native plant suppliers.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, sandy, or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; ashy sunflower spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes in rich soils and can become invasive — grow in poor, lean, dry soil to limit spread or confine with a root barrier. It is better behaved in difficult, dry conditions that simulate its native habitat of dry, rocky, limestone glades.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; ashy sunflower is a drought-tolerant native perennial sunflower of the central and eastern United States prairies and rocky glades, distinguished from other perennial sunflowers by its covering of soft, dense, gray-white hairs that give the leaves, stems, and even the flower heads a downy, silvery-gray 'ashy' appearance — creating a noticeably silver-gray foliage mass that provides good contrast with the clear, bright golden-yellow daisy flowers (2–3 inches across) produced abundantly in late summer and fall. It is rhizomatous and can spread aggressively in rich, moist soils, but in poor, dry, rocky conditions — its natural habitat — it stays better-contained and is a genuinely useful, drought-tolerant, late-season pollinator plant. Outstanding for dry, lean prairie gardens, naturalistic meadows, and wildflower areas in difficult, dry, sunny conditions where more refined perennials would struggle. The abundant flowers in late August and September are among the most important fall nectar sources for migrating monarchs, native bees, and goldenfinches that consume the seeds.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Asian foamflower is clump-forming rather than stoloniferous and will not spread aggressively, making it suitable for smaller gardens or planting alongside slower-growing companions where T. cordifolia would be too vigorous.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Asian foamflower is the East Asian counterpart to the native North American foamflowers, native to woodland and montane forest habitats across China, Japan, and the Himalayas, producing a similar but distinctly clump-forming habit rather than the stoloniferous spreading growth of Tiarella cordifolia. It forms neat, compact rosettes of lobed, heart-shaped, softly hairy leaves topped in spring and early summer by slender spikes of tiny, starry, white to pale-pink flowers with the same feathery, foamy appearance that characterizes the genus. At 8–12 inches tall and non-spreading, it is well suited to smaller shade gardens, mixed perennial borders in shade, or planting alongside equally well-behaved companions such as small hostas, epimediums, and hellebores. It is slightly less cold-hardy than T. cordifolia, performing best in zones 5–8. An elegant and underused species that rewards close planting and examination of its delicate spring flowers.

common_name: Asian Skunk Cabbage / White Skunk Cabbage
plant_note: Set rhizome divisions into boggy, humus-rich soil at pond or stream margins in early spring; maintain constant moisture and protect from desiccation throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant divisions into perpetually moist, organically rich soil at the edges of a shaded pond, stream, or constructed bog garden, setting the crown level with the soil surface. Pure white spathes appear in early spring before the large, glossy leaves emerge, making this a refined and elegant alternative to its American relative. This species is somewhat smaller and more compact, making it well suited to mid-sized water garden settings where Lysichiton americanus would overwhelm the space. Patience is essential — established clumps improve year over year, eventually forming impressive foliage masses that persist through summer.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline woodland soil in partial to full shade; Asian twinleaf is more persistent through summer than its North American counterpart (J. diphylla).
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; Asian twinleaf prefers the same leaf-mold rich, shaded planting conditions used for trilliums and bloodroot. Jeffersonia dubia is the Asian counterpart to the North American twinleaf, native to woodland and scrub in Manchuria and Korea, producing kidney-shaped leaves with blue-green to purple-flushed coloring alongside lavender-blue cup-shaped flowers in early spring. Unlike the North American species, J. dubia retains its attractive foliage well into fall and is slow-growing but exceptionally long-lived.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich soil; Asian wood poppy self-seeds readily and winter cold provides the stratification needed for reliable spring germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in partial to full shade, or allow established plants to self-seed into adjacent areas; Asian wood poppy performs best in conditions similar to its native Chinese mountain woodland habitat with cool, moist summers. Stylophorum lasiocarpum is the Chinese counterpart to the North American celandine poppy (S. diphyllum), producing deeply lobed, pinnate foliage and large, brilliant golden-yellow four-petaled flowers over a long spring-to-summer season. It self-seeds freely but without becoming weedy, naturalizing into attractive informal colonies beneath deciduous trees where its foliage remains ornamental well past bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Asiatic dayflower self-sows prolifically and spreads easily in garden beds. Often treated as a weed, but its young leaves and stems are edible.
directions: Grows in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Asiatic dayflower is a common garden weed from East Asia, now naturalized throughout North America in disturbed, moist, shaded habitats. While usually regarded as a pest, the plant has significant culinary and ornamental value — the bright blue, three-petaled flowers (two large blue petals and one tiny white petal) are among the most intensely sky-blue flowers of any common plant, and were historically used as a blue dye and pigment for Japanese woodblock printing (aizuri). Young leaves, stems, and flowers are edible raw in salads or cooked as a vegetable in East Asian cuisine. The flowers are also used as an edible garnish. An interesting plant to appreciate as an edible rather than simply eradicate as a weed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall in any well-drained soil in full shade to full sun; asiatic jasmine is extremely adaptable and one of the easiest groundcovers to establish in the South. Space 12–18 inches apart and mulch heavily until the ground is covered — the canopy fills in relatively quickly in warm weather.
directions: Plant in any well-drained soil in full shade to full sun; asiatic jasmine is the premier shade-tolerant groundcover for zone 7–11 landscapes — a dense, weed-suppressing mat of small, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves on wiry twining stems that fills in rapidly and maintains its deep color year-round. Unlike its fragrant relative confederate jasmine (T. jasminoides), asiatic jasmine rarely flowers in the landscape and is grown purely for its exceptional foliage ground cover performance. It is the go-to solution for the problem spots in Southern landscapes: dry shade under large oaks and magnolias, slopes that are difficult to mow, areas around tree roots where nothing else grows. Once established, it requires almost no maintenance — shear or mow to 3–4 inches in early spring every few years to remove the older, woody stems and stimulate fresh, dense regrowth. Remarkably drought tolerant, heat tolerant, and deer resistant. Variegated forms ('Ogon Nishiki') have yellow-green leaves that brighten shaded areas.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring as soon as soil is workable, or in fall for early establishment.
directions: Plant bulbs scales-down at a depth of 3 times the bulb's height, typically 6–8 in deep, in well-drained, humus-rich soil. Lilies prefer cool roots but sunny tops; mulch the soil surface and underplant with low perennials to shade the root zone. Remove only spent flowers, never the stem and leaves, so the plant can photosynthesize and recharge the bulb. Red lily beetle is a serious pest in many regions; inspect plants regularly and remove beetles and larvae by hand.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; asparagus fern is not a true fern but a member of the Asparagaceae family — its feathery, fern-like appearance comes from small, needle-like modified stems (cladodes) rather than true fronds.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade; asparagus fern (plumosa fern, lace fern) is a South African climbing plant grown for its extraordinarily delicate, feathery, bright-green foliage — the flattened, horizontal branchlets bearing tiny, needle-like cladodes create a texture so fine and airy that it appears almost like mist, making it incomparably useful as a filler and softening element in cut flower arrangements and mixed container plantings. The plant climbs by small, hook-like thorns and in tropical gardens can ascend to 10–15 feet, creating a soft curtain of misty foliage over trellises and fences. In cooler climates it functions as a houseplant or annual container filler. Small white flowers followed by dark berries appear on mature plants. It differs from the more robust A. aethiopicus (emerald fern / Sprengeri fern) in producing a finer, more delicate, horizontal branch structure. A staple of the cut flower industry worldwide for its use as foliage filler in arrangements. Note: berries are mildly toxic.

common_name: Asparagus Fern (Emerald Fern, Sprengeri Fern, Foxtail Fern)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in partial shade with well-drained soil; Asparagus Fern establishes quickly and can spread aggressively by bird-dispersed seeds in zone 9b-11 — it is listed as invasive in Florida and Hawaii. Deadhead the red berries to prevent self-seeding. In zone 9a, the plant may be damaged by hard frost but typically resprouts from fleshy, water-storing roots in spring. Excellent in hanging baskets and containers where the arching stems cascade gracefully.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, well-drained soil; Asparagus Fern adapts remarkably well to shaded conditions and grows fastest with morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9 — it tolerates more light than most foliage plants while also performing adequately in fairly deep shade. Asparagus densiflorus is not a true fern but a member of the asparagus family (Asparagaceae), native to southern Africa. Despite the common name, it is closely related to edible garden asparagus (A. officinalis) — the feathery, bright emerald-green foliage that makes it so popular consists of tiny flattened stems (cladodes) that function as leaves. The 'Sprengeri' cultivar produces arching, 2–3-foot stems clothed in fine needlelike cladodes and scarlet berries; the 'Meyeri' (Foxtail Fern) cultivar produces upright, dense, bottle-brush-shaped plumes of bright green. Both forms are outstanding for adding fine-textured, feathery foliage to shaded garden beds, container arrangements, and as groundcovers under trees. The thick, tuberous, fleshy roots store substantial water reserves, giving established plants surprising drought tolerance despite the plant's lush appearance. CAUTION: The berries are mildly toxic if ingested by children or pets. Listed as invasive in some Gulf Coast and Floridian habitats where bird-dispersed seeds colonize disturbed areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, organically rich soil with adequate moisture.
directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1–2 in below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil — astilbe does not tolerate drought and will brown and decline quickly without adequate moisture. The feathery plumes in shades from white through pink to deep red are spectacular in shade and semi-shade gardens from late spring through summer. Leave the russet dried plumes standing through fall and winter for ornamental interest. Divide every 3–4 years in spring when flowering declines or the crown heaves above the soil surface.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in groups in fall in moist, slightly acidic soil; avoid planting in areas that dry out in summer.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; atamasco lily is a native zephyr lily of the Southeast, blooming in earliest spring (often around Easter, hence the common name) with large, pristine white funnel-shaped flowers that emerge from wet, grassy meadows, wet pinelands, and moist woodland openings from Virginia to Florida. Unlike most bulbs, it tolerates and actually prefers seasonally wet soil in spring followed by summer moisture (not drought). Plant in a low spot, under deciduous trees, or at a rain garden margin where it will receive extra moisture. The bulbs are toxic. The plant naturalizes readily in Gulf Coast gardens and may bloom sporadically in fall as well after rain events.

common_name: Atamasco Lily (Native Southeast White Rain Lily for Moist Woodland Gardens)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Atamasco lily naturally grows in moist, seasonally wet areas — along stream banks, low areas, and moist woodland edges — and performs best in garden situations that provide consistent moisture, particularly in spring during its growth and bloom period.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Atamasco Lily is a native southeastern bulb producing exquisitely beautiful, large (2.5–3.5 inch), funnel-shaped flowers of pure glistening white sometimes tinged with pale lavender-pink, emerging on leafless stalks from March through April following spring rains — one of the finest native wildflowers of the coastal plain Southeast and a stunning addition to naturalistic and woodland gardens throughout its native range. The flowers have the clean, pure-white simplicity of a fine amaryllis in miniature, each bloom emerging individually on an upright, hollow stem surrounded by the narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge simultaneously with the flowers in late winter and persist into summer. Unlike many exotic rain lilies, Atamasco lily is indigenous to moist forests, stream banks, and wet meadows from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi — a native plant that evolved in Gulf Coast conditions and thrives without supplemental care in suitable moist sites. In the wild, it frequently grows in such large populations in moist flatwoods and lowland areas that spring bloomings create sweeping drifts of white through the forest understory. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested. Excellent naturalized in moist lawn areas, along stream banks, and in woodland garden understory positions where its preference for consistent spring moisture can be met naturally.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun at woodland edges and stream banks. Atlantic Goldenrod tolerates more shade than most goldenrods, making it useful for shaded or semi-shaded native plant gardens.
directions: Atlantic Goldenrod is a native perennial of moist, open woodlands, forest margins, and stream banks across the eastern United States, valuable as one of the few goldenrods that tolerates significant shade and moist conditions — making it a useful bridge between the sunny meadow and shaded woodland garden. The distinctive, open, arching inflorescence with well-separated clusters of bright yellow flowers differs from the more tightly packed plume of common goldenrod and is produced from August through October, providing late-season nectar for native bees, moths, and migrating monarch butterflies. A versatile native that thrives along shaded stream banks and moist woodland edges, Atlantic Goldenrod fills an ecological niche not covered by most other goldenrod species. Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants spread modestly by rhizomes and are long-lived in appropriate moist, semi-shaded conditions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring or fall in any reasonably well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Atlantic ivy establishes rapidly and provides dense weed-suppressing cover within 1–2 seasons. Do not plant near natural areas in the Pacific Northwest or parts of the Southeast where it is invasive.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average, moist soil in shade to partial shade; Atlantic ivy is closely related to English ivy (H. helix) and often sold mislabeled as such, but it is botanically distinct with larger, broader, 5-lobed leaves on more robust stems. It forms a vigorous, dense evergreen groundcover that suppresses weeds effectively and tolerates heavy shade under mature trees. In humid, mild climates of zones 7–10 it grows especially vigorously; in the Pacific Northwest and parts of the Southeast it can escape cultivation into natural areas and should not be planted near wildlands. The small, nectar-rich flowers in fall are an important late-season food source for ivy bees (Colletes hederae) and other insects. Berries are mildly toxic; all parts of the plant can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by nicking with a file or soaking in warm water for 24 hours before sowing; direct sow in well-drained, lean, sandy, slightly acidic soil after last frost. Atlantic pigeonwings dies back to the ground after frost in zone 7–8 and re-emerges from deep roots in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Atlantic pigeonwings is a native twining vine of open woodlands, sandy roadsides, and pine flatwoods across the Southeast, closely related to the tropical culinary butterfly pea (C. ternatea) but hardier and better adapted to North American conditions. The large, powder-blue to lavender-blue pea flowers are inverted on the plant — the keel points upward rather than downward as in most legumes — with a distinctive white and yellow central mark. The tubular flowers are an important nectar source for bumblebees and sphinx moths that are physically capable of reaching the nectar. At woodland edges and in partial shade gardens, it provides a delicate, trailing structure on fences and shrubs throughout summer. Dies back to persistent roots in winter and re-emerges reliably in spring in zones 7–10. An outstanding native vining legume for the dry, sandy soils typical of the Gulf Coastal Plain.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, highly acidic (pH 3.5–5.5), sandy or peaty soil in full sun. Atlantic White Cedar is a bog and pocosin specialist that requires constantly wet, highly acidic, low-nutrient soil to thrive; it will not prosper in ordinary garden soils or in neutral to alkaline conditions.
directions: Atlantic White Cedar is a graceful, narrow-crowned native conifer, native to the freshwater wetlands, pocosins, and Atlantic white cedar swamps of the eastern coastal plain from Maine south to Florida and along the Gulf Coast to Mississippi, growing in pure stands in permanently wet, highly acidic, peat-based soils where the combination of constant moisture and extreme acidity prevents most other tree species from competing. Its scaly, aromatic, blue-green foliage on a stately, upright, narrow crown makes it one of the most elegant native conifers, and the wood — naturally resistant to decay and reputed to last for centuries — was historically one of the most valuable woods in colonial America, used for ship building, shingles, and water pipes. The dense, humid microclimate within a cedar swamp supports an extraordinary community of rare and specialized plants and animals, and Atlantic white cedar restoration is a major conservation priority along the coastal plain. Grow in full sun in constantly wet, highly acidic, low-nutrient, sandy or peaty soil; it will not adapt to ordinary garden conditions without mimicking the bog environment it requires.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, average to lean soil in full sun; Atlas cedar is tolerant of drought and lean soils once established — native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and Algeria where it grows on dry, rocky limestone slopes. Excellent drainage is critical; wet, heavy clay soil causes rapid decline.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, average to lean soil in full sun; Atlas cedar is prized above all other true cedars for the intense blue-silver to blue-gray needle color of its most striking forms — the blue cultivars, collectively sold as 'Glauca', are among the bluest conifers in cultivation, with a color intensity rivaling or exceeding Colorado blue spruce. The stiff, ascending branches and flat-topped, wide-spreading crown of mature trees develop over decades into magnificent architectural specimens. The weeping cultivar 'Glauca Pendula' is a spectacular accent plant with long, cascading, blue branches that can be trained over walls, pergolas, or staked to create dramatic weeping specimens. More drought-tolerant than deodar cedar once established, native to the semi-arid Atlas Mountain range. The large, barrel-shaped, upright cones take two years to mature. Hardy to zone 6 — more cold-tolerant than deodar cedar.

common_name: Aucuba (Japanese Aucuba, Spotted Laurel, Gold Dust Plant)
