Banana shrub grows as a dense, compact, slow-growing, rounded evergreen shrub with a formal, refined habit and requires minimal care. It tolerates partial shade well and is one of the most versatile and dependable fragrant shrubs for zone 7–11, performing reliably for decades with little attention. 'Port Wine' (deep-burgundy purple flowers with stronger fragrance) is an outstanding cultivar.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub is a classic Deep South garden plant, reliably perennial in zones 7–10 and producing its delightfully banana-scented flowers in spring and summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; banana shrub is a classic evergreen shrub of the South, related to magnolias and producing small, creamy-yellow flowers edged in maroon-purple that emit an intense fragrance reminiscent of ripe bananas — particularly potent in warm, humid air. The fragrance carries considerable distance and can be detected from many feet away when the plant is in full bloom in spring and early summer. The evergreen foliage is attractive year-round. This plant has been grown in Southern gardens for well over a century and is among the most beloved fragrant shrubs for the warm-climate garden. In zone 9a it is a reliable, low-maintenance garden anchor that thrives with minimal care once established. A few individual flowers in a small vase can fill a room with fragrance.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Bangalow Palm is a fast-growing, elegant, slender-trunked rainforest palm native to the subtropical and tropical east coast of Australia (Queensland and New South Wales) — one of the most planted landscape palms in subtropical Australia, California, and similar warm climates for its graceful, tropical appearance, purple-lavender flower clusters, and red ornamental fruits.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Bangalow Palm establishes rapidly and grows relatively fast for a palm — water deeply and regularly in establishment and fertilize with slow-release palm fertilizer containing magnesium; does not tolerate salt spray or cold below 28°F. Archontophoenix cunninghamiana (Bangalow Palm, Piccabeen Palm, or King Palm) is a tall, slender-trunked, elegant feather palm native to the rainforest gullies, creek banks, and rainforest margins of coastal Queensland and New South Wales in eastern Australia, one of the most widely planted and popular landscape palms in subtropical Australia, Hawaii, California, South Florida, and warm Mediterranean climates worldwide. The palm is renowned for its extreme elegance: a straight, smooth, ring-marked trunk supporting a neat, compact crown of arching, pinnate fronds of deep green. In summer, spectacular pendant inflorescences emerge from below the crown shaft — large, branching clusters of small purple-to-lavender flowers that develop into masses of round, bright-red fruits. Bangalow Palms grow at a moderate pace in ideal conditions, reaching mature height of 40–50 feet, and are highly tolerant of partial shade — often planted beneath established tree canopy where many palms struggle — as well as full sun once established. Naturalized and occasionally invasive in parts of Hawaii where it colonizes moist valleys; check local invasive lists.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; banjine is native to the coastal heaths and scrubs of southwestern Western Australia where it receives high rainfall but excellent drainage. It blooms in spring, producing dense, rounded heads of rich rose-pink tubular flowers. It does not tolerate root disturbance well — plant in final position without repotting. Sensitive to overwatering and poor drainage.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; banjine (or rice flower) is a neat, compact, mounding Australian shrub from the coastal heathlands of southwestern Western Australia — producing in spring dense, rounded terminal clusters of many small, tubular, four-petaled flowers in a rich, warm, rosy-pink to deep pink, each small flower head about an inch across and the clusters collectively covering the plant in an abundant pink display. The common name 'rice flower' comes from the appearance of the dense, rounded, tightly packed flower clusters resembling a cluster of tiny rice grains dipped in pink. The compact, neat, naturally mounding growth habit and glossy, small, dark-green leaves provide attractive structure year-round, and the plant maintains a tidy, ornamental character without significant pruning. It is in the Thymelaeaceae family (the same family as daphne), and like daphne, it has a reputation for sensitivity to site conditions — it resents transplanting, requires excellent drainage, and is unforgiving of waterlogged conditions. In the right position in zones 9–11 Mediterranean-climate or warm coastal gardens, however, it is a rewarding, long-lived, compact ornamental shrub.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy prairie soil in full sun; Barbara buttons is a native prairie perennial of the Texas and Oklahoma coastal prairie that is essentially unknown in horticulture despite its charming flowers and adaptability to lean soils — it is an excellent wildflower for prairie-style gardens in the Gulf South.
directions: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Barbara buttons self-seeds modestly in suitable prairie conditions. Marshallia caespitosa (Barbara buttons or white prairie marshallia) is a small, delightful native prairie perennial found in dry, rocky, and sandy prairies from Texas and Oklahoma east to Tennessee — one of the least-known and most charming small wildflowers of the southern prairies. The plant produces low, tufted rosettes of narrow, spatula-shaped leaves and slender, 8-to-20-inch, leafless flower stems each topped with a single, globular, 1-to-1.5-inch flower head composed entirely of white, tubular disc florets (no ray florets) — resembling a small, white, powder-puff button with elongated, protruding style branches giving a fringe-like texture. The effect is unexpectedly refined and delicate for a prairie plant. Barbara buttons blooms in late spring (April–June) in zone 9 and is a quiet, elegant presence in prairie-style wildflower gardens. The flowers attract native bees and small butterflies. A genuinely underused native perennial deserving wider cultivation in southeastern prairies and dry, sunny garden borders.

common_name: Barbara Karst Bougainvillea (Classic Magenta-Red Everblooming Tropical Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average soil in full sun; bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight water and fertilizer stress — avoid overwatering and excessive nitrogen which promote vegetative growth at the expense of flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Barbara Karst is one of the most popular and widely planted bougainvillea cultivars for Gulf South gardens — a vigorous, large-scale vine producing brilliant magenta-red to cerise-red bracts (the showy colored structures surrounding the inconspicuous true flowers) through most of the year in frost-free conditions. In zone 9, Barbara Karst blooms most heavily in spring and fall when temperatures moderate; in winter (November–February) the vine may defoliate partially during cold spells and bloom is reduced. The brilliant magenta-red bract color is one of the most vivid in the warm-climate garden palette and creates an unmistakable tropical visual impact when the vine is in full bloom. Bougainvilleas bloom most prolifically under slight stress — dry-down periods between waterings, lean soil without excessive nitrogen, and root constriction (slightly root-bound in containers) all promote flower production over vegetative growth. This counterintuitive cultural requirement (bloom more when stressed) is the most important management principle for bougainvillea. The thorny stems require careful placement away from pedestrian areas. In zone 9, Barbara Karst may be killed to the ground by severe freezes but returns from the roots; cover with frost cloth during freezes below 28°F. Outstanding trained on walls, fences, and pergolas where the massive bloom display can be appreciated.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Baronii Palm is a graceful, clustering, shade-adapted palm endemic to the rainforests of eastern and northwestern Madagascar — producing multiple slender canes topped by elegant arching fronds — one of the more cold-tolerant Dypsis species from Madagascar's highlands, performing well in zone 9 with protection.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Dypsis baronii is a clustering palm that produces new stems (suckers) from the base — more drought tolerant than many Dypsis species due to its highland Madagascar origin; water moderately and apply palm fertilizer twice yearly. Dypsis baronii (Baronii Palm or Madagascar Bamboo Palm) is a multi-stemmed, clustering palm endemic to Madagascar — one of the most palm-diverse countries on Earth, with over 170 endemic palm species — native to the humid forests of eastern and northwestern Madagascar at moderate elevations. The genus Dypsis (formerly split into Chrysalidocarpus and several other genera) is the largest palm genus in Madagascar. Dypsis baronii produces multiple slender, bamboo-like stems (1–2 inch diameter) in dense clusters, topped by graceful, arching, pinnate fronds with slightly arching, feathery leaflets — creating an elegant, clumping effect. Among the more cold-hardy Dypsis species available, it has performed in zone 9b with some protection in California and Gulf Coast gardens. The clustering habit and moderate size make it suitable for smaller gardens than the more commonly planted Areca Palm (Dypsis lutescens). Excellent as a privacy screen, garden accent, or container specimen in zone 9–11 subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in spring; barren strawberry is among the most tolerant and low-maintenance shade groundcovers for dry, difficult conditions under trees where grass will not grow.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; barren strawberry is a Central European native that superficially resembles a strawberry plant but produces no edible fruit — it is grown as an extremely tough, low-growing, semi-evergreen groundcover that spreads steadily by stolons to form dense, uniform mats of three-part, strawberry-like, glossy leaves that remain attractive through winter. Small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers appear in early spring before most other perennials emerge. It tolerates drier soil conditions than most shade groundcovers, making it exceptionally useful under dense, dry-rooted trees like Norway maples and Norway spruce where few other plants survive. Essentially maintenance-free once established — no deadheading, no division required for years. An underused, genuinely excellent shade groundcover that deserves wider planting. Also useful on dry slopes and as lawn replacement under trees in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; epimediums tolerate dry shade under established trees better than almost any other perennial groundcover. Do not disturb established plantings unnecessarily — they improve dramatically over years.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; epimedium (barrenwort, bishop's hat) is arguably the most underused and underrated of all shade groundcovers — a slowly spreading, low-maintenance perennial that tolerates dry shade under established tree roots better than any other herbaceous perennial. The attractive, heart-shaped leaflets are often mottled with red or bronze when young, and the dainty four-petaled flowers resembling tiny hats or butterflies in yellow, pink, white, red, or bicolor appear in spring. E. x versicolor 'Sulphureum' has pale yellow flowers and reliably semi-evergreen foliage in mild winters. Once established, epimediums are nearly drought proof and essentially pest-free. Cut old foliage to the ground in late winter before new growth begins to showcase the spring flowers. A plant that rewards patience — increasingly impressive each year after establishment.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring onto the surface of moist, sandy or peaty soil; seeds are tiny and light-dependent for germination — do not cover, and keep the seedbed consistently moist until plants are established.
directions: Bartram's Rosegentian is a Florida endemic perennial found in wet flatwoods, moist savannas, and seepage slopes, making it one of the largest-flowered members of its genus with vivid rose-pink blooms up to 1.5 inches across appearing in summer and fall. It requires consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soils in full sun — conditions that mimic its natural flatwoods habitat — and will not tolerate prolonged drought or alkaline garden soils. Sow seeds on the surface of moist, lean growing media in spring without covering, as the fine seeds require light for germination; transplant young seedlings carefully once they reach an inch tall, as the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. This species is an important component of Florida flatwoods wildflower restorations and is a significant nectar source for native bees and butterflies during its long summer-to-fall bloom period.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to clay soil in full sun to partial shade; bastard oak is adapted to the limestone soils and rocky, alkaline, well-drained upland sites of the Edwards Plateau and Gulf Coast prairies, where it grows in conditions that exclude most other oaks.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to clay, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — bastard oak (Quercus sinuata) is a medium to large deciduous white oak of the limestone-dominated Edwards Plateau, Cross Timbers, and Gulf Coast prairies of Texas and adjacent states, notable for its distinctive leaves with deep, rounded, scalloped lobes unlike any other Texas oak. It grows on rocky limestone hillsides and in deep clay draws, tolerating both the thin, alkaline, rocky soils of the Hill Country and the heavy black clay soils of the Blackland Prairie with equal adaptability. The tree is moderately fast-growing for an oak, long-lived, and provides outstanding shade and wildlife value (acorns in the white oak group ripen in one season and are highly palatable to deer and wildlife). An underutilized oak for the challenging alkaline, clay, and limestone soils of central and south Texas garden sites where other oaks perform poorly.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Bat Face Cuphea is grown as a tender perennial in zones 9–11 — it may survive mild zone 9 winters in sheltered locations, behaving as a perennial in warmer areas and a warm-season annual in colder areas of zone 9. Prune lightly in late winter to encourage fresh growth and abundant new flowering. In zone 9 it thrives in the hottest summer months and blooms continuously from spring through frost, becoming more floriferous as heat increases.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — cuphea is drought-tolerant once established and blooms better in lean soil than in rich, consistently moist conditions; Bat Face is a cuphea cultivar with one of the most distinctively shaped and visually memorable flowers in the ornamental plant world — each small, 0.5-inch tubular flower is deep crimson-red with two spreading, rounded purple petals at the tip that create an unmistakable bat face impression when viewed from the front, complete with the suggestion of eyes, nose, and ears in the petal arrangement. The bat face appearance is not accidental or fanciful — the distinctive petal structure is genuinely face-like in a way that is immediately recognized by most observers, making Bat Face cuphea the most conversation-starting small plant in the summer garden. The hummingbird-attractive tubular flower structure, combined with continuous bloom from spring through frost and excellent heat tolerance, makes Bat Face an outstanding zone 9 summer performer. The moderate spreading, bushy habit covers itself in hundreds of the tiny bat-face flowers simultaneously during peak bloom, creating an effect that is both charming and genuinely unusual in the summer garden.

common_name: Bat Flower (Black Bat Flower, Cat's Whiskers)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade to partial shade; bat flower is one of the few tropical ornamentals that genuinely prefers deep shade — direct sun scorches the leaves rapidly. In zone 9 it needs frost protection; grow in a container that can be brought indoors, or mulch heavily and hope for mild winters. High humidity is essential.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in deep to partial shade with high humidity; bat flower produces one of the most extraordinary flowers in the plant kingdom — the inflorescence consists of two large, dark purple-black wing-like bracts (resembling a bat in flight), a cluster of maroon-purple flowers in the center, and up to 28 long, thread-like purple whiskers (bracteoles) hanging down 12–28 inches, giving the flower a ghostly, otherworldly appearance. Native to the forest floor of tropical Southeast Asia from southern China to Malaysia, it requires warm, humid, shaded conditions and is intolerant of direct sun, drought, or temperature below 50°F. In zone 10–12 it is a reliable outdoor perennial shade plant; in zone 9 it is best grown in a container as a specimen that can be overwintered inside. The large, glossy leaves are attractive year-round even when not in flower, and the plants bloom from late spring through autumn.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; bat-faced cuphea is one of the most continuously blooming and hummingbird-attractive annuals available for Gulf South summer gardens.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; bat-faced cuphea (bat's wing cuphea) is a Mexican native grown for its unique and vivid flowers — small, tubular, with brilliant red petals at the base and a pair of purple-red, rounded, ear-like upper petals that give each flower the uncanny appearance of a tiny bat's face, displayed in dense clusters from late spring until frost. The flowers are irresistible to ruby-throated hummingbirds. Plants bloom essentially nonstop in warm weather with no deadheading required. Extremely heat-tolerant and productive in Gulf Coast summer conditions when most cool-season annuals have declined. In zones 9–11 it overwinters as a semi-woody subshrub; in cooler climates grow as a long-season annual. 'Georgia Scarlet' is a popular selection.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep and 6 inches apart in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; bath asparagus tolerates partial shade and does well at the edges of deciduous woodland. In regions where it is edible, the unopened flower spikes may be harvested in May before the flowers open and cooked like asparagus — the remaining stems will still flower normally.
directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for May-June bloom; bath asparagus (Pyrenean star-of-Bethlehem) is a tall, stately, and distinctly unusual ornithogalum producing elegant 12-24 inch upright spikes of numerous small, pale greenish-yellow, star-shaped flowers that open progressively from the base upward through late spring — the overall effect is airy and quietly striking in the border or at a woodland edge. This species is notably edible: the young, tightly furled flower spikes are traditionally harvested before the flowers open, bundled, and boiled or steamed like asparagus, a practice so ingrained in the English city of Bath that the plant acquired its most familiar common name. Native to Mediterranean scrub and grassy slopes and naturalized across parts of southern England and western Europe, it is well adapted to dry summer dormancy and low-maintenance cultivation. It slowly increases by offsets to form modest clumps and rarely becomes invasive. An unusual dual-purpose plant equally at home in the ornamental border and the edible garden.

common_name: Bath's Pink Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Southern Groundcover Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks cultivars are among the most drought- and heat-tolerant perennials available, thriving in lean, rocky, or sandy soils where richer soil causes rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Bath's Pink was discovered and named by a Georgia gardener and has become one of the most reliable cheddar pink selections for hot, humid Southern gardens, forming a dense, low mat of fine, silvery-blue foliage topped in spring with abundant fragrant, soft pink, fringed flowers. It shows notably better heat and humidity tolerance than many other dianthus cultivars, an important quality for gardeners south of the plant's more typical cooler range, and it thrives in the same lean, sharply drained, rocky-to-sandy soil that other cheddar pinks require. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to keep the foliage mat dense and tidy through the rest of the season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bauer's grevillea is notable among grevilleas for being one of the few species that tolerates partial shade — most grevilleas are strictly full-sun plants. It forms a compact, spreading, ground-hugging mound and blooms most heavily in spring but flowers sporadically year-round. No phosphorus fertilizer — fatal to Proteaceae. Named for the Austrian botanical artist Franz Bauer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bauer's grevillea is a compact, spreading, relatively low-growing Australian grevillea — native to the rocky, somewhat shaded forest margins and valley floor habitats of New South Wales — that stands apart from many grevillea species in its greater shade tolerance, making it one of the few Proteaceae useful for planting in the dappled shade or semi-shade of woodland margins and north-facing hillsides. The flowers are in the typical grevillea 'toothbrush' or clustered style — dense clusters of small, curved, tubular red to pink-red flowers with projecting, hooked styles that create the characteristic grevillea flower cluster — produced in greatest abundance in spring but appearing sporadically through the year in favorable mild-winter climates. The foliage is small, dark green, and finely textured, creating a compact, spreading, mat-like mound that works well as a low-maintenance groundcover shrub in the right conditions. Like all Proteaceae, it requires lean soil and absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer. Named for Franz Bauer, the celebrated Austrian botanical artist at Kew whose extraordinary illustrations documented the new Australian flora in the early 19th century.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; beach hibiscus is salt-spray tolerant and grows naturally along tropical coastlines worldwide, making it an excellent coastal garden shrub in zones 9b–12.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, coastal soil in full sun; beach hibiscus is a pantropical coastal shrub or small tree growing naturally at the landward edge of mangroves, sandy beaches, and coastal margins throughout the tropics. The large, round, heart-shaped leaves with their silvery, velvety undersides are distinctive and attractive, and the flowers are a rich yellow with a dark maroon center that changes to pink-red as the flowers age — the color change occurring within hours on the same flower. The wood is very buoyant and was traditionally used throughout the Pacific for outrigger canoe construction. Extremely salt-spray tolerant and useful for coastal hedging and screening. In zone 9, may be killed back by hard freezes but regrows from the base if roots are protected. The fibrous bark has traditional uses in making rope and cordage.

common_name: Beach Morning Glory (Railroad Vine, Bay Hops)
plant_note: Sow scarified seeds directly in sandy, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun; nick the hard seed coat or soak in water 24 hours before planting. Beach morning glory requires pure beach sand or sandy coastal soil — it will not tolerate clay or fertile soil, and actually grows best in the poorest, driest, most exposed coastal conditions.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in sandy, infertile coastal soil in full sun; beach morning glory (railroad vine) is one of the most important native plants of tropical and subtropical beaches and coastal dunes worldwide — a prostrate, creeping vine that can spread 60 feet or more along the sand from a single plant, rooting as it goes, stabilizing shifting dunes against erosion with a mat of large, distinctive bilobed hoofprint-shaped leaves. The large, rose-purple morning glory flowers are produced throughout the growing season and are a beautiful ornamental bonus. Each stem can extend 100 feet, rooting at nodes wherever moisture is available. It is resistant to salt spray, storm surge flooding, and hurricane-force winds in ways that few other plants can match. An outstanding native for coastal restoration, living stabilization of beach dunes, and coastal ornamental planting. It is not invasive in its native coastal range.

common_name: Beach Naupaka (Sea Lettuce Tree, Scaevola, Beach Fan Flower)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun to partial shade in sandy, well-drained coastal soil; Beach Naupaka is exceptionally salt-spray tolerant and perfectly adapted to the hostile conditions of beach dunes, coastal embankments, and barrier island planting where salt wind defeats most ornamentals. In zone 9a, plants may be damaged by hard frost but typically resprout from the crown. Excellent for coastal stabilization and native coastal landscaping in zone 9b-11.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any sandy or well-drained soil — Beach Naupaka is one of the most salt-tolerant and wind-tolerant coastal shrubs available, performing on the front line of beach dunes and oceanfront plantings where few plants survive. Scaevola taccada is a large, spreading, salt-tolerant shrub native to tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean coastlines, found naturally on sandy beaches, dunes, and coastal margins from Hawaii to Australia, through Southeast Asia, and naturalized on Gulf Coast and Florida beaches. The distinctive white to pale lavender, fan-shaped flowers — each one appearing as if cut exactly in half, with all five petals gathered on one side (a characteristic of the Goodeniaceae family that ensures specific pollinator access) — are borne prolifically throughout the warm season. The thick, fleshy, succulent-textured, bright green leaves and extremely deep root system allow the plant to thrive with saltwater spray, drought, compacted sand, and periodic flooding. Beach Naupaka spreads by underground runners to form dense, stabilizing colonies that protect coastal dunes from erosion. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it makes an outstanding low-maintenance native or naturalized coastal shrub for beach properties, waterfront landscapes, and salt-exposed sites where conventional ornamentals fail.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist, sandy or loamy soil in zone 9–12; Beach Spider Lily is a tropical bulbous perennial native to coastal sandy habitats from the Caribbean through Central America and tropical South America — bearing spectacular, large, bright-white, fragrant flowers with long, spidery, reflexed tepals and a prominent central cup, and providing remarkable visual impact in coastal and tropical gardens.
directions: Plant Hymenocallis littoralis bulbs at a depth of about 4 inches, with the neck just at or slightly below soil level, in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, or bright indirect light; water moderately and allow soil to dry slightly between waterings; avoid waterlogged conditions which cause bulb rot. Beach Spider Lily differs from the more commonly grown Hymenocallis latifolia (Coastal Spider Lily) in being a strictly tropical species adapted to seasonally dry coastal habitats throughout the Caribbean and tropical Americas — performing best in zone 10–12 and requiring frost protection in zone 9. The flowers are among the most elegant of all bulbous plants: large, pure white, intensely fragrant (especially at night), with six long, recurving, ribbon-like tepals and a central funnel-shaped corona — strikingly beautiful in the evening garden. Plants produce attractive, broad, strap-like, glossy dark-green leaves year-round in frost-free climates; clumps increase slowly by offsets. In zone 9, plant in a sheltered, south-facing location and mulch heavily in winter; in zone 10–12, grow in the open garden with minimal care beyond occasional irrigation during dry periods.

plant_note: Direct sow seed after last frost in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; beach sunflower is a sprawling, fast-growing annual that self-sows prolifically to naturalize in open, sunny, sandy soils along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry soil in full sun — beach sunflower is a fast-growing, sprawling native annual of Gulf Coast beaches, dunes, sandy roadsides, and open flatwoods, producing cheerful, 2–3 inch yellow sunflowers with dark centers from early summer through frost on prostrate, branching stems that spread to cover large areas with a carpet of flowers. In zone 9–11 it blooms nearly year-round in sunny open spots. Unlike most sunflowers, this species is extremely heat and salt tolerant, thriving in sandy, nutritionally poor soils and handling reflected heat from pavement and buildings without complaint. It is an outstanding, zero-irrigation wildflower for difficult dry, sunny, sandy sites in the coastal South — slopes, parking lot edges, dry medians, and hot foundation exposures. Self-sows prolifically to maintain a persistent colony. The seeds are an excellent food source for goldfinches and sparrows in winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 8–9 plant September–March. Beacon Silver spreads vigorously by surface runners and fills in shade areas quickly — space 12–15 inches apart for a continuous groundcover mat within one season. In zone 9 the plant may go summer-dormant during intense heat; reduce watering in summer and it will rebound in fall. Semi-evergreen in mild winters; provides year-round groundcover in zone 7–9.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Beacon Silver tolerates a wider range of soil conditions than most shade groundcovers; Beacon Silver is among the most effective and reliable shade groundcovers for dry to moist shade conditions, producing a dense, weed-suppressing mat of nearly entirely silver-white leaves with only a thin green margin remaining — the highly reflective silver foliage brightens dark shade areas and makes Lamium an effective lighting element in shaded landscape designs. In spring the mat is covered with delicate pink-lavender flowers that continue for several weeks, adding floral interest during the prime shade gardening season. Spotted dead nettle (Lamium maculatum) is a European woodland native that naturalizes readily in North American garden conditions — it spreads by runners but is not considered invasive in most regions. The combination of easy care, excellent shade performance, dense weed suppression, and ornamental silver foliage that illuminates dark corners makes Beacon Silver one of the most planted shade groundcovers in North America.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial shade for natural winter stratification and spring germination; beaked agrimony thrives in the dappled understory of deciduous forests and is an excellent low-care native for shaded naturalistic plantings.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral forest soil in partial shade; cold stratification over winter improves germination in spring. Agrimonia rostellata (beaked agrimony) is a native perennial of eastern North American deciduous forests, typically found in moist, shaded ravines, hillside woodlands, and forest margins, where it produces erect, slender stems with pinnately compound, coarsely toothed leaves and slender, wand-like racemes of small, bright yellow, 5-petaled flowers from late summer into fall — providing one of the few reliable yellow-flowering options for shaded native gardens in the late season. The hooked seed capsules that follow bloom cling readily to fur and clothing, dispersing by animals in the classic agrimony fashion. This is a quieter, more refined plant than the showier prairie wildflowers, suited to a naturalistic woodland where its delicate flowers and functional seed dispersal biology will be appreciated. Good companion for asters, goldenrods, and wild gingers at woodland edges.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; beaked yucca requires excellent drainage and is killed by waterlogged soils. In humid Gulf Coast conditions, plant on raised berms or in rocky, fast-draining soil to prevent crown rot. It is one of the most cold-hardy of the tree-type yuccas and is reliably cold-hardy to zone 5 with proper drainage.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; beaked yucca is widely considered the most ornamental of the tree yuccas — a slow-growing, single-stemmed Texas native from the Trans-Pecos that develops over many years into a remarkable blue-leaved specimen with a trunk to 10 feet or more, crowned by a perfect, symmetrical pom-pom of hundreds of narrow, powder-blue, rigid leaves that radiate in all directions. The color is among the most intensely glaucous blue-gray of any yucca, creating an outstanding specimen plant with a bold, sculptural presence. In late spring, a tall flower spike emerges from the center bearing a large, dense panicle of white, bell-shaped flowers that are attractive to yucca moths and other pollinators. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert limestone mountains of west Texas and northern Mexico, it is cold-hardy to zone 5 where drainage is excellent. Outstanding as a container specimen, landscape specimen, and architectural focal point — slow-growing and long-lived.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in full sun in sharply drained, rocky, sandy, or caliche soil; bear grass demands excellent drainage and is adapted to alkaline soils. Zero supplemental irrigation is needed after the first growing season.
directions: Plant in full sun in sharply drained, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline soil that mimics its native Hill Country and Trans-Pecos habitat; bear grass forms a ground-hugging rosette of long, thin, strap-like leaves that are tougher than they appear and send up tall, branched flowering spikes covered in small cream-white flowers in late spring to early summer. It is one of the most drought-tolerant, low-maintenance plants available for Texas and the Gulf South, requiring zero irrigation once established and tolerating both extreme heat and occasional hard freezes. The dried leaves are traditionally used by Indigenous peoples for basket weaving. Excellent in rock gardens, dry slopes, and xeriscape plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; bear grass grows naturally in dry open coniferous forests and subalpine meadows of the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies. Individual plants bloom only every 5–7 years; divide for faster establishment.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or gravelly, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; bear grass is an iconic native of the Pacific Northwest coniferous forests and mountain meadows, producing dense, grass-like tufts of long, wiry, evergreen leaves that are surprisingly tough and stiff. The spectacular bloom — a tall spike of thousands of tiny white flowers rising 3–5 feet above the foliage — occurs only once every 5–7 years per individual plant, but in productive stands different plants bloom in different years, creating continuous display. The plume of creamy white flowers is one of the most distinctive sights of the Pacific Northwest high country. The leaves are traditionally woven by Coast Salish and other Pacific Northwest peoples into baskets and decorated ceremonial objects, and the leaves cut from wild stands are widely used in the floral industry. Black bears and elk browse the foliage and flowers. A striking architectural plant for dry, open woodland gardens in the Pacific Northwest.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in dry, sandy or rocky, strongly acidic, extremely well-drained, infertile soil in full sun. Bear Oak is highly specific to acid barrens and pitch pine-scrub oak habitats and will not compete in more productive or shaded soils. It spreads by rhizomes to form dense thickets.
directions: Bear Oak is a low, colony-forming native scrub oak of the acid pine barrens, serpentine outcrops, dry sandy ridges, and coastal heathlands of the northeastern United States, where it is a dominant species of the globally rare pitch pine-scrub oak barrens community from Massachusetts south to North Carolina. The small, irregularly multi-lobed leaves have a distinctive whitish, velvety underside; the abundant small acorns are a critical food source for black bears (the origin of the common name), ruffed grouse, white-tailed deer, and numerous songbirds in the barrens communities where Bear Oak's dense, fire-adapted thickets provide both food and cover. Highly fire-adapted, Bear Oak resprouts vigorously from deep rhizomes after the frequent, low-intensity fires that historically maintained pitch pine barrens and oak-scrub habitats, making it nearly impossible to eliminate once established in appropriate conditions. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Bear Oak requires the same fire-maintained, nutrient-poor conditions as its native barrens habitat.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; in hot summer regions (zones 8–11) afternoon shade is essential as the glossy foliage scorches in direct afternoon sun and the plant often goes semi-dormant in extreme heat.
directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; in hot summer regions (zones 8–11) afternoon shade is essential as the glossy foliage scorches in direct afternoon sun and the plant often goes semi-dormant in extreme heat. Acanthus mollis is the plant whose deeply lobed, glossy leaf shape has been immortalized in the decorative acanthus motif used in Corinthian column capitals, medieval carvings, and ornamental plasterwork for 2,500 years; the plant itself is as bold and magnificent as the art it inspired, with very large (12–18 inch), deeply and precisely lobed, glossy dark-green leaves and dramatic, 3–4 foot spikes of white-and-purple-hooded flowers in late spring and early summer that are architectural and unique. In zone 9–11 gardens it can spread aggressively by root fragments; plant where spread is acceptable or confine with a root barrier. Extremely drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, average to rich soil in full sun to partial shade; bearded beggarticks self-sows prolifically and will naturalize in moist, sunny to partially shaded disturbed areas. In moist conditions, it can become a vigorous self-sowing annual requiring management.
directions: Direct sow in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; bearded beggarticks is a spectacular fall-blooming annual native of moist meadows, streambanks, and disturbed wet areas across the eastern United States. When planted in masses, the plants produce an outstanding, richly colored display of large, golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers with dark disk centers that rivals any cultivated annual in visual impact — and provides dramatic masses of color in the fall landscape when many ornamentals have finished. Named for the narrow, awl-like bristles (aristae) on the seed heads, these barbed seeds disperse by clinging to fur and clothing. The flowers are outstanding nectar sources for migrating monarchs, painted ladies, and sulphur butterflies. Self-sows prolifically in moist conditions, so establish colonies where the annual cycle can continue without intervention. Excellent for moist meadow plantings and naturalized streamside areas.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before frost; divisions planted after midsummer bloom by the following spring.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun — never bury them, as iris borers and rot thrive under covered rhizomes. Plant in late summer after bloom, with the fan of leaves pointing in the direction you want growth to spread. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become overcrowded, discarding the woody center and replanting healthy outer fans. Good drainage is essential; soggy soil causes rhizome rot.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sowing into dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral, calcareous or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Beardtip Prairie Clover is a native perennial of the Texas Hill Country and adjacent south-central states, where it grows on dry, rocky, calcareous hills and limestone-based prairies; its species name pogonathera means 'beard-bearing,' referring to the distinctive bearded tips of its petals that set it apart from other prairie clovers. It produces erect, branching stems with fine-textured pinnate foliage and dense, cylindrical spikes of bright rose-pink to magenta flowers in summer that attract specialist native Dalea bees, bumblebees, and hummingbirds. Grow in dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral, calcareous or sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; scarify seeds before fall direct sowing and avoid supplemental watering once established. It is an outstanding drought-tolerant native for Texas Hill Country xeriscape gardens and limestone glade restorations.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; cold-moist stratification over winter improves spring germination. Container transplants established in fall will bloom the following spring.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall or plant container transplants in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; foxglove beardtongue is one of the most adaptable and deer-resistant native perennials for eastern North American gardens, producing tall, upright stems of tubular white-to-pale-lavender flowers in early summer that are one of the most productive native bee and bumblebee plants available. It thrives in the poor, dry, rocky soils of disturbed areas and prairie edges, and deteriorates in rich, moist, heavily fertilized conditions. The attractive, semi-evergreen, reddish-bronze basal foliage provides winter interest. Self-seeds moderately to maintain a naturalistic colony; popular hummingbird perennial in zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun in very well-drained, dry, rocky to sandy soil; beargrass is long-lived and slow-growing but extremely resilient once established; it rarely needs supplemental irrigation in zones 7-10 and is deer-resistant.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, dry, rocky to sandy soil; beargrass (Nolina microcarpa) is a dramatic desert perennial of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts and adjacent mountains, producing large clumps of long, narrow, grass-like leaves (up to 4 feet long) with finely serrated edges and a tall central flower spike covered in thousands of tiny, cream-white flowers attractive to bees and other pollinators. Despite the grass-like appearance it is related to agaves and yuccas, not grasses. The fibrous, long-lasting leaves were one of the most important weaving materials for Native American peoples across the Southwest for baskets, mats, and ceremonial objects — dried beargrass leaves are still widely sold to florists for arrangements. An outstanding desert specimen plant providing dramatic texture without sharp spines.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in cool soil; soak seed first.
directions: 'Beaujolais' is a Spencer-type sweet pea with deep, wine-red blooms on long, sturdy stems perfect for bouquets. Soak the seed overnight and direct sow in early spring in cool soil, since sweet peas thrive in chilly weather. Provide a trellis or netting for the climbing vines and grow in full sun to part shade in rich, well-drained soil. Keep plants evenly watered and cut flowers often to prolong blooming, which can extend into fall in mild climates. The large ruffled flowers are lightly fragrant.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or layer branches in spring, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; beauty bush is drought-tolerant once established and flowers most freely in full sun — excessive fertility and moisture produce rank growth and reduce flowering.
directions: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; beauty bush is a Chinese monotypic deciduous shrub — the single species in its genus, and one of the last of the great early 20th-century introductions from E.H. Wilson's plant hunting expeditions in western China — that produces a brief but spectacular flowering display in late May to June when the entire large, arching, vase-shaped shrub becomes enveloped from base to tip in masses of small, pale-pink to rose-pink, yellow-throated, tubular flowers in dense clusters, creating a cloud-like, pale-pink effect that gives the plant its perfectly apt common name. After the flowers fall, the bristly, pink seed heads are themselves attractive for weeks. The shrub has a graceful, arching, fountain-like form with peeling, tan-brown bark that provides winter interest. It tolerates a wide range of soils including alkaline and dry conditions. After the spring flowering peak it is relatively plain but does not detract from the garden. 'Pink Cloud' is an improved selection with denser, deeper-pink flower clusters.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Becky is more heat-tolerant than most Shasta daisy cultivars but still performs as a short-lived perennial in zone 9's heat and humidity — expect to divide and replant every 2–3 years for continued vigor. Deadhead spent blooms to extend the flowering season from June–August in zone 9. The tall, upright stems (30–36 inches) produce cut flowers that last 7–10 days in a vase. In zone 9 plants bloom June–August; provide afternoon shade to reduce heat stress during the peak summer bloom period.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Shasta daisies must have excellent drainage and fail in wet, heavy soils; Becky is the most heat-tolerant Shasta daisy cultivar widely available, developed for performance in the hot summers of the American South and named for Becky Stewart, a Georgia gardener who selected the heat-tolerant seedling. The classic single white daisy flowers with golden-yellow central discs on long, sturdy, non-flopping stems represent the archetypal daisy form — clean, cheerful, and versatile in garden designs and cut flower arrangements. Becky's advantage over other Shasta daisies is precisely its ability to produce good quality cut flowers and garden display in zone 8–9 conditions that collapse most other varieties — the upright, non-flopping stems (critical for a quality cut flower), combined with extended blooming and heat persistence, make Becky the definitive Shasta daisy for Southern gardens. The white flowers work with virtually any color palette and any garden style, from formal to cottage to naturalistic, making Becky one of the most broadly useful perennial flowers for zone 9 garden designers.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; bee bee tree is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and establishes readily once planted. It grows quickly and produces flowers in July and August when almost no other trees are blooming — an extremely valuable quality for beekeepers and native bee habitat.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; bee bee tree (Korean evodia) is arguably the most valuable pollinator tree for temperate gardens, producing massive, flat-topped panicles of small white flowers in July and August — a critical period when almost no other trees are blooming — that attract extraordinary concentrations of bumblebees, honeybees, native solitary bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects. A single mature specimen in full bloom is a memorable spectacle of insect activity. Native to China and Korea, it grows as a medium-sized tree 20–30 feet tall with large, pinnate, aromatic leaves that have an interesting citrus-like scent when crushed. In fall, the clusters of small, red to black seed capsules are ornamental and attract birds. The tree was formerly known as Evodia daniellii (or Euodia daniellii) and still appears under the old name in many references. Fast-growing, adaptable to a range of soils, and largely pest- and disease-free in North America where no major insects have adapted to feed on it.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in spring when soil temperature reaches 70°F in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Beehive Ginger prefers the same conditions as culinary ginger — warm, humid, partially shaded, with good drainage. In zone 9, the rhizomes survive mild winters underground but may die in hard freezes; mulch heavily in zone 9a. Divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. The spectacular inflorescences last 4–6 weeks on the plant and 3–4 weeks as cut flowers.
directions: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Beehive Ginger performs best in morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Zingiber spectabile is a large ornamental ginger from Malaysia and Borneo whose primary attraction is its extraordinary inflorescence — a dense, upright, waxy, beehive-shaped structure of tightly overlapping bracts that emerges at soil level on a short stem. The bracts begin cream-white to pale yellow and age through rich golden-yellow to deep orange and finally red as the inflorescence matures, eventually resembling a burning torch. Individual yellow flowers with purple markings emerge from between the bracts. The inflorescence is exceptionally long-lasting — months on the plant — and makes spectacular cut flowers or dried specimens that retain color for years. The plant produces large, dramatic clumps of tall canes with strap-like leaves similar to culinary ginger but much more ornamental. Beehive Ginger is one of the most exotic and conversation-stopping ornamental gingers for zone 9 shade gardens and tropical plantings; its unusual flower form and long season of interest make it a prized specimen in botanical gardens worldwide. The rhizomes are not edible (unlike Zingiber officinale) but have no reported toxicity.

common_name: Bela Lugosi Daylily (Deep Purple-Black Award-Winning Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Bela Lugosi is an award-winning daylily cultivar with large, deep purple-black flowers and a contrasting green throat, among the darkest-colored daylilies widely available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Bela Lugosi is a striking daylily cultivar, named for the classic horror-film actor, bearing large, ruffled flowers in one of the deepest, darkest purples available in the genus, verging on black in certain light, with a vivid chartreuse-green throat that provides sharp contrast. It received the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its exceptional garden performance and distinctive, richly colored blooms produced over a long midsummer season on tall, sturdy scapes. The dramatic dark coloring makes it an outstanding focal point in a mixed perennial border, especially paired with lighter-colored companion plants for contrast. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering and tolerates heat well. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Belinda's Dream Rose (Texas A&M Earth-Kind Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall; Belinda's Dream was bred in Texas and named an Earth-Kind rose by Texas A&M AgriLife for its outstanding heat tolerance and disease resistance without spraying, making it one of the most widely recommended shrub roses for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for good air circulation. Bred by Texas hobbyist Mike Shoup in 1988 and later designated an Earth-Kind rose by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension after years of trial evaluation, Belinda's Dream combines the large, fully double, clear-pink, classically shaped blooms and strong fragrance of a hybrid tea with the toughness and disease resistance of an antique shrub rose. It flowers in repeated flushes from spring through frost and shows outstanding resistance to blackspot even in the humid Gulf South, requiring no fungicide spraying under the Earth-Kind trial protocol. The upright, well-branched shrub works equally well as a specimen, in mixed borders, or massed as an informal hedge, and its blooms hold up well as cut flowers. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage vigorous new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to keep the shrub reblooming steadily.

common_name: Belize Sage (Red-Stem Sage, Central American Tropical Salvia for Zone 9 Gardens)
plant_note: Propagate by stem cuttings (much faster to flowering than seed); Belize Sage is a tropical Salvia from the highlands of Guatemala, Belize, and southern Mexico — hardy to approximately 25–28°F when established, making it reliably perennial in zone 9 in protected microclimates and marginally hardy in zone 8b. In zone 9, Belize Sage behaves as a large, shrubby perennial that blooms nearly year-round in mild winters, with most intense flowering in late spring and fall. It tolerates partial shade, which makes it valuable in the Gulf Coast garden under open tree canopy or on the north side of structures where many salvias perform poorly. Hummingbirds visit the long red tubular flowers intensely during migration periods. Cut back hard after the coldest winter months to encourage vigorous new growth and renewed blooming.
directions: Propagate by cuttings in spring; plant in well-drained soil with afternoon shade in hottest climates. Cut back in late winter. Salvia miniata (Belize Sage, Red-Stem Sage) is a species of the large genus Salvia native to the highlands of Guatemala, Belize, and southern Mexico, where it grows as a shrubby perennial in forest margins and disturbed areas at moderate elevations. The common names 'Belize Sage' and 'Red-Stem Sage' both describe distinctive visual features of the plant: 'Belize Sage' references its Central American provenance, while 'Red-Stem Sage' describes the conspicuous red coloring of the stems, which sets the plant apart visually even when not in flower. The flowers are the primary ornamental draw: long, tubular, bright red blooms produced in upright racemes above medium green, somewhat velvety leaves, with a form and color that makes them exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds — the species has evolved the classic hummingbird-pollination syndrome of long tubular red flowers positioned and structured to deposit pollen on hovering birds. In zone 9, Salvia miniata's tolerance for partial shade — uncommon among the heat- and sun-loving Salvia genus — makes it one of the more versatile of the tropical sages. While full sun produces the most prolific flowering, the plant accepts several hours of afternoon shade without declining, allowing placement in spots where the intense Gulf Coast afternoon sun would stress less tolerant plants. This shade adaptability combined with year-round production in mild winters and hummingbird attraction makes Belize Sage a particularly useful plant for zone 9 gardens with mature tree canopy.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bell agapanthus is deciduous — dying back to ground level in winter — unlike the evergreen A. africanus. This deciduous habit allows it to tolerate harder winters than evergreen agapanthus. Mulch the roots in zones 6–7 in winter. Plants resent disturbance once established and may take 2–3 years after division to flower freely.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bell agapanthus is the most cold-hardy commonly available agapanthus, surviving reliably to zone 6 where its deciduous habit (dying completely to the ground in winter) provides protection against cold that the evergreen species lack. The flowers are typical agapanthus umbels — spherical heads of 20–50 individual, tubular-funnel bells on tall, upright scapes in mid-blue to soft blue-violet — but on a somewhat more compact plant than the large, evergreen A. africanus. The deciduous habit provides a clear spring emerging point that makes the plant easier to manage: when growth emerges in spring, it confirms winter survival and signals when to resume watering. Several white and blue cultivars are available, and it is one of the parent species of many modern cold-hardy agapanthus hybrids that have extended the genus to zone 6. Outstanding for the mixed summer perennial border in zones 6–10 where summer blue flowers and bold scape structure are needed.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in summer or early fall with the neck at or just above the soil surface; the neck should not be buried. True Amaryllis belladonna goes completely summer-dormant before blooming — do not water during the dormant period.
directions: Plant in well-drained, even dry soil in full sun; belladonna lily is a South African native that produces clusters of 6–12 large, fragrant pink to deep rose flowers on bare, leafless stems in late summer and fall. Like red spider lily, the flowers appear before the leaves — hence the name 'naked ladies.' The strap-shaped leaves appear after blooming and persist through winter and spring before dying back completely in summer dormancy. This is a true bulb of the Mediterranean-climate garden: it thrives on summer drought and baking heat while dormant, then blooms with the first fall rains. Requires excellent drainage and does not tolerate wet summer conditions. Very long-lived and increases steadily into impressive clumps.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date; seeds need cool temperatures to germinate and benefit from cold stratification.
directions: Refrigerate seeds for one week before sowing; then direct sow on the soil surface in early spring since seeds need light and cool temperatures to germinate. Thin to 9–12 in apart — crowded plants are prone to powdery mildew. The tall, architectural stems bear small white flowers nestled inside large, shell-shaped green calyces that remain ornamental for months and dry beautifully. Cut stems for fresh or dried arrangements before calyces begin to brown.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: 'Benary's Giant' is a florist favorite with fully double, densely petaled blooms up to 6 inches across in a rainbow of colors on tall, strong stems. Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm, or start indoors a few weeks early. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and space generously for airflow, which helps prevent powdery mildew. The long-lasting flowers hold up to heat and rain and are outstanding for cutting. Cut or deadhead frequently to keep butterflies visiting and blooms coming until frost.

common_name: Bengal Clock Vine (Sky Vine, Blue Trumpet Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; bengal clock vine grows extremely rapidly and requires a very sturdy, large trellis, pergola, or fence — it can cover a large structure in a single season and is considered invasive in Florida and Hawaii. Do not plant near natural areas.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a very large, sturdy support structure; the Bengal clock vine (sky vine) is one of the most spectacular flowering vines available for warm climates, producing pendant clusters of enormous (3–4 inch), lavender-blue to pale blue funnel-shaped flowers with white throats continuously from spring through frost in zone 9–11. The huge, heart-shaped leaves and rampant growth create a dense, cooling shade canopy over pergolas and arbors very quickly. It is an outstanding choice for covering large unsightly structures rapidly. However, this vine is INVASIVE in Florida, Hawaii, and similar warm climates — plant only where you can control its spread and never near waterways or natural vegetation. In zone 9a it often dies back to established roots in hard winters and recovers rapidly; in true zone 10+ it is a permanent, massive vine.

common_name: Bengal Tiger Canna (Yellow-and-Green Striped Foliage Orange-Flowered Canna)
plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Bengal Tiger is grown for its bold yellow-and-green striped foliage, which colors most vividly in full sun.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun, feeding monthly during the growing season for the strongest foliage color and flowering. Bengal Tiger produces bold, paddle-shaped leaves striped lengthwise in vivid yellow and green, similar in effect to the more red-toned Tropicanna but with a brighter, more citrus-toned color scheme, topped with bright orange summer flowers that pick up the warm tones of the foliage. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions into shallow water or saturated marsh soil after soil temperatures reach 65°F; place in full sun for maximum growth and flowering.
directions: Plant divisions in full sun into the shallow margins of a pond, lake, or constructed wetland, setting the crown just at or below the waterline in 2–6 inches of water or in constantly saturated soil. The tall, arching, banana-like leaves create dramatic vertical structure, and long drooping flower stalks bearing small violet blooms attract hummingbirds and native bees throughout the warm season. In zones 8–9 plants may die back to the roots after frost but reliably resprout from the rhizome as temperatures warm; in zones 10–11 they remain evergreen. This southeastern US and tropical native is an excellent large-scale accent for rain gardens, retention ponds, and naturalistic water features.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; bent-awn plumegrass naturally occurs in moist longleaf pine savannas, wet roadside ditches, and boggy depressions — requires consistently moist, acidic soil and full sun.
directions: Bent-awn plumegrass is a spectacular native grass of Gulf Coastal Plain wet longleaf pine savannas and roadside swales, producing large, open, silky plumes of copper-tinted to silvery-white spikelets in fall that shimmer in the breeze and rank among the most beautiful of all native grass seed heads in the Southeast. Each spikelet has a distinctive twisted, bent awn (bristle) that catches the light and gives the plume a textured, almost sparkling appearance — the 'bent-awn' common name accurately describes this key feature. Like its close relative sugarcane (in the same genus), bent-awn plumegrass has reed-like stems with prominent nodes and broad, corn-like leaves that give it a bold, architectural quality during the growing season; the tall, plumed form makes it an excellent vertical accent in wet native meadows and rain garden borders. It grows naturally alongside other savanna species including bladderworts, sundews, orchids, and pitcher plants in the fire-maintained wet pine flatwoods of the Gulf Coast, where it is an indicator of high-quality natural habitat.

plant_note: Sow in spring; seeds benefit from cold stratification, or fall sow.
directions: Surface-sow wild bergamot in spring after a period of cold, moist stratification, or sow outdoors in fall to let winter do the chilling. This native perennial in the mint family spreads into clumps of aromatic foliage topped by lavender, tufted blooms that hum with bees and hummingbirds. Give it good airflow to reduce powdery mildew, and deadhead to encourage repeat flowering. Deer and drought both leave it largely alone once established.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring, just below soil level, with leaves pointing upright; in warm climates fall planting is equally successful.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; the large, leathery, glossy leaves — which turn attractive shades of red and bronze in winter where temperatures drop below freezing — earn this plant a spot as one of the best evergreen shade groundcovers. The clusters of pink or magenta flowers appear in early spring on stout red stems, often before the last frost. Remove tattered older leaves by pulling them sharply downward to snap them free from the rhizome. Divide crowded plants every 4–5 years in spring by cutting through the woody, surface-creeping rhizomes.

plant_note: Seed or sprig in spring when soil temperatures are consistently above 65°F; common Bermuda grass can be established from seed at 1–2 lbs hulled seed per 1,000 square feet. Hybrid Bermuda grass cultivars (like 'Tifway 419', 'Celebration', 'Latitude 36') must be planted vegetatively from sprigs or sod as they produce little viable seed.
directions: Seed or sprig in spring when soil is above 65°F; mow at 1.5–2 inches for common types or 0.5–1.5 inches for hybrid varieties. Bermuda grass (Cynodon dactylon) is one of the most widespread warm-season turf grasses in the world and the dominant sports and athletic turf in zone 7–11, valued for its exceptional heat and drought tolerance, rapid recovery from wear and damage, and aggressive spreading habit via stolons and rhizomes that produces a dense, fine-textured, resilient sward when properly maintained. Common Bermuda grass can be established from seed (relatively inexpensive) but the finest-textured, most attractive Bermuda lawns use sterile hybrid cultivars established vegetatively: 'Tifway 419' (standard athletic and home turf), 'Celebration' (improved color and shade tolerance), 'TifTuf' (exceptional drought tolerance), and 'Latitude 36' (improved cold tolerance). The major limitation of Bermuda grass for residential use is its extremely poor shade tolerance — it requires at least 6–8 hours of direct sun and thins dramatically under trees — making it unsuitable for many residential lots with mature shade trees. In full sun, however, Bermuda grass is unmatched for durability, heat tolerance, and drought resistance. Goes dormant (tan) with first frost, greening up again when soil temperatures rise above 55°F in spring.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Berry Awesome is a Summerific series cultivar with large lavender-pink flowers and dusty blue-green foliage, an unusual soft color palette among typically bold-colored hardy hibiscus cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Berry Awesome bears large, 8-9 inch, soft lavender-pink flowers with a deep rose-red eye, held against distinctive dusty, blue-green foliage that sets it apart from the more common dark-purple or plain-green-leaved hardy hibiscus cultivars. The softer, cooler color palette makes it a versatile choice for pairing with a wider range of companion plants than the bold reds and hot pinks typical of many hardy hibiscus. It blooms in a steady succession of huge flowers from midsummer into fall, each lasting a single day but replaced continuously. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can damage foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Berry Smoothie Heuchera (Pink-Purple Raspberry Coral Bell)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; in zone 9, heucheras benefit from afternoon shade protection — the bright foliage colors fade and the plants decline in intense afternoon sun combined with Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Berry Smoothie is one of the most vividly colored heuchera introductions — producing large, rounded, ruffled leaves in a rich, warm raspberry-pink to deep rose-pink color that is more saturated and vivid than the softer peachy tones of 'Georgia Peach' and the cooler tones of 'Caramel'. The warm raspberry-pink foliage creates a strong color focal point in the partial-shade garden with a boldness that few other heucheras match. The metallic, slightly reflective surface of the leaves catches available light in shade conditions, making Berry Smoothie one of the brightest and most visible heucheras in low-light situations. The color typically deepens to burgundy-raspberry in cooler fall and winter temperatures and lightens slightly in the summer heat. In early summer, small, airy white flower sprays rise above the foliage on slender scapes — delicate accents to the dominant foliage display. Heuchera hybrids like Berry Smoothie are essential partial-shade perennials for zone 9 gardens — they provide multi-season foliage color in areas where most other plants offer only green. Divide heucheras every 3–4 years in early spring when the crown becomes too elevated above the soil surface and performance declines. In zone 9, plant in the shadiest locations available, with consistent moisture and excellent drainage.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; seeds germinate in late winter to early spring.
directions: Bexar Clover is a small native annual of dry, rocky, calcareous, or sandy open ground in Texas and adjacent south-central states, blooming from March through May with compact, globe-shaped cream-white to pale pink flower heads. Sow seeds directly in fall into lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; no soil amendment is needed, and fertility encourages weeds at the expense of this clover. An ecologically valuable species that supports specialist native bee communities in the south-central US, it self-sows freely and naturalizes reliably in open, disturbed ground with minimal competition.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; bidens blooms almost immediately from transplant and continues until frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; bidens (Apache beggartick, golden goddess) is a trailing, fine-textured annual from the arid Mexican highlands that produces a continuous, self-cleaning display of bright golden-yellow, five-petaled daisy-like flowers against the ferny, deeply divided foliage from late spring until frost. The fine texture and trailing habit make it ideal for softening container arrangements and hanging baskets, where it weaves through and around companion plants. Extremely heat-tolerant, drought-resistant once established, and nearly indestructible in containers. Occasionally self-sows in mild climates. 'Goldmarie', 'Peter's Gold Carpet', and 'Golden Goddess' are popular compact selections. Excellent as a combination trailer with salvia, vinca, and zinnias.

common_name: Big Begonia (Large-Scale Landscape Wax Begonia Series)
plant_note: Plant purchased transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; the Big series was bred for unusually large, vigorous plants and flowers compared to traditional smaller wax begonias, making a bold impact in beds and large containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with adequate moisture. The Big begonia series was bred to scale up the classic wax begonia into a much larger, more substantial landscape plant, with glossy leaves and abundant flower clusters in white, pink, or red covering a mounding plant considerably bigger than traditional bedding wax begonias. Its larger size and heat tolerance make it a strong choice for mass plantings, large containers, and borders where a bigger, bolder begonia display is wanted, and it tolerates more direct sun than many begonias provided soil moisture stays consistent. It is largely self-cleaning and needs little maintenance beyond routine watering and fertilizing through the growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, sandy or calcareous, well-drained soil; lightly scarify seeds before sowing to improve germination rates and encourage spring bloom.
directions: The tallest of the Texas bluebonnets, Big Bend Bluebonnet is a native of dry, rocky and sandy desert washes in the Trans-Pecos and Big Bend region of far west Texas, producing dramatic upright spikes of deep blue lupine flowers on stems reaching 4 feet or more in March and April. Direct sow seeds in fall on bare, sandy or rocky, freely draining soil in full sun; lightly scarify or nick seed coats before planting to break dormancy and speed germination. This species thrives in dry, low-humidity climates and is not suited to the humid eastern portions of Texas, performing best in calcareous, well-drained soils of the Hill Country and Trans-Pecos. It does not transplant well and self-sows reliably in suitable desert garden and xeriscape conditions once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Big Blue is the most widely planted clumping liriope cultivar and establishes readily in a very wide range of conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Big Blue is the most commonly grown clumping liriope cultivar — a robust, grass-like perennial ground cover forming dense clumps of arching, dark-green, strap-like leaves about one-half inch wide, topped by erect spikes of dark violet-purple flowers in late summer followed by shiny black berries in fall. It is the workhorse of shade ground covers across much of the South and Gulf Coast, performing reliably under trees, on slopes, and in any location where turf grass fails due to insufficient light. Big Blue is notably more vigorous than the species and maintains its dark color better through the extremes of Gulf Coast summers. The clumping (non-spreading) habit means it stays where planted without becoming invasive, unlike the running lilyturf species. In zone 9, liriope stays green year-round as a fully evergreen ground cover. Mow or cut back to 3–4 inches in late winter (January–February in zone 9) before new growth emerges to remove worn winter foliage and stimulate a fresh flush of clean leaves. Excellent under live oaks, pines, and other established trees where few ground covers survive.

common_name: Big Blue Lilyturf (Border Lilyturf, Muscari Liriope)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; Big Blue lilyturf is the clumping (non-spreading) species of liriope — one of the most widely used shade groundcovers in the American South, with upright to arching, dark-green, grass-like foliage, summer spikes of purple flowers, and persistent black berries — virtually indestructible once established.
