directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade to full sun; shear to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges. Liriope muscari (big blue lilyturf or border lilyturf) is one of the most widely planted and reliably performing shade groundcovers and border plants in the American South and Gulf Coast — a clumping (not spreading) species distinct from creeping lilyturf (L. spicata). The plant produces dense, arching clumps of dark-green, grass-like evergreen leaves 12–18 inches long, topped in summer with upright spikes of small, purple to violet flower clusters resembling grape hyacinth (muscari — hence 'muscari' in the name) rising above the foliage. The flowers are followed by persistent, shiny, black berry-like fruits that provide additional ornamental interest through fall and winter and are eaten by birds. Named cultivars are numerous and widely available: 'Big Blue' (classic standard); 'Monroe White' (white flowers); 'Gold Band' (yellow-striped leaves); 'Silvery Sunproof' (cream-striped, more sun-tolerant). Liriope muscari is extraordinarily adaptable in the Gulf South: it tolerates deep shade, drought, poor soils, salt spray, and competition from tree roots — performing where few other groundcovers survive. Shear clumps to the ground in late winter (use a lawnmower) to remove tattered old foliage before fresh new growth emerges in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring on a firm seedbed once soil temperatures reach 65°F; press seed into the soil surface without deep coverage, as big bluestem needs warmth and light contact to germinate well.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a weed-suppressed, firm seedbed in full sun after the last frost, pressing seed lightly into the surface and keeping the area moist for the first three to four weeks until seedlings emerge. Plants establish slowly in the first season, sending energy into deep roots rather than top growth, so avoid mowing below six inches and withhold fertilizer entirely. By the second and third year, clumps reach their full height of four to eight feet, bearing the distinctive three-branched turkey-foot seed head in August and September. Cut plants back to four to six inches in late winter before new growth begins, and expect spectacular copper-bronze fall color each autumn.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of prepared, weed-free soil in spring; big bluestem seed germinates best with good soil contact. Alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 30 days before spring sowing to improve germination rate.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average, dry soil in full sun; big bluestem is the dominant grass of the tallgrass prairie, once covering hundreds of millions of acres from Manitoba to Texas, and is a cornerstone native grass for prairie restorations, meadow gardens, and large-scale naturalized plantings. The blue-green foliage turns brilliant orange-copper-burgundy in fall and holds through winter as attractive standing tan straw. The distinctive three-parted seed heads — resembling turkey feet in silhouette — are architectural and wildlife-valuable. Deep roots (up to 10 feet) make it exceptional for erosion control and sequestering carbon. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; never needs irrigation or fertilizer in average to dry soil. Cut back to 6 inches in early spring before new growth begins.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly brackish to fresh, sandy or clay soil in full sun; big cordgrass grows naturally along tidal freshwater river margins, freshwater marshes, and the brackish upper zones of estuaries. It spreads by strong rhizomes to form dense colonies.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to brackish, sandy to clay soil in full sun at pond margins, tidal freshwater marshes, and streambanks; big cordgrass is the largest of the native cordgrasses, producing bold, coarse, erect culms to 6–10 feet in height that create an impressive, wetland structural element. Growing naturally along tidal rivers, upper brackish marshes, and freshwater wetland edges from the Atlantic to the Gulf Coast, it tolerates occasional salinity but thrives equally well in fresh water. The large, comb-like seed heads in late summer and fall are distinctive and provide abundant seeds for marsh birds including secretive rails. The dense, vigorous rhizomes are highly effective for shoreline stabilization and marsh restoration along tidal rivers and freshwater margins. A bold, architectural statement plant for large pond edges, wetland gardens, and stream bank stabilization in zones 5–10.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Big Daddy's heavy, deeply puckered leaves are among the most slug-resistant of any large hosta, making it excellent for gardens where slug pressure is high.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Big Daddy is a prized large hosta selected from H. sieboldiana known for exceptionally large, deeply cupped and heavily puckered, powder-blue leaves that hold their blue color well into summer. The thick, waxy leaf texture is among the most slug-resistant available in a large hosta, making it the preferred choice for gardeners who struggle with slug damage. The cupped leaf surface collects dew and light rain, giving the crown water directly. Pale lavender to nearly white flowers appear in midsummer and are attractive though secondary to the bold foliage. Big Daddy is a steady grower that requires 3 years to reach its best appearance but is extremely long-lived. Mulch with 2–3 inches of wood chips to keep roots cool and moist; consistent moisture is essential for maintaining leaf quality and preventing edge browning in warm weather.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (in zone 8–10) or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; big quaking grass is a cool-season annual that germinates in fall, overwinters, and sets ornamental seed heads in spring before dying with summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in fall (in the South) or spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; big quaking grass is a cool-season annual from the Mediterranean region grown for its remarkably ornamental, large, heart-shaped, pendant spikelets that tremble and dance in the slightest breeze — earning it the common name and making it one of the most charming ornamental grasses for cut flower arrangements, dried flower crafts, and naturalistic garden borders. The spikelets begin green and ripen through shades of gold and tan. In zone 9a, it thrives as a fall-sown annual that blooms in spring before dying in summer heat. Self-sows to naturalize in appropriate conditions. The dried seed heads retain their ornamental value indefinitely when cut before fully ripe. A beloved cottage garden and cutting garden grass for spring arrangements.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained conifer forest soil in partial to full shade; big rattlesnake plantain is the western counterpart to the eastern G. pubescens and requires the same mycorrhizal-associated, acidic, needle-mulched forest soil conditions — purchase nursery-propagated stock only.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained conifer forest soil in partial to full shade near established conifers, never in conventional garden beds; big rattlesnake plantain needs mycorrhizal fungal associations to thrive long-term. Goodyera oblongifolia is the Pacific Northwest and western counterpart to the eastern G. pubescens, producing a larger and bolder basal rosette of dark green, oval leaves 2–3 inches long with a single prominent silver-white central stripe (rather than the dense white netting of G. pubescens) that makes the evergreen foliage striking and distinctive year-round on the forest floor. In late summer it produces a leafy stem 8–15 inches tall bearing a spike of small white orchid flowers on one to three sides of the stem. It is the most common and garden-tolerant native orchid of the Pacific coast forest understory, suitable for naturalistic planting in moist, shaded conifer gardens from northern California to British Columbia. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; big red sage grows naturally on rocky limestone outcrops and cliff faces of the Edwards Plateau in central Texas and is adapted to dry, thin, calcareous soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; big red sage is a rare and distinctive Texas endemic of the Edwards Plateau, where it grows on exposed limestone outcrops, ledges, and thin, rocky calcareous soils in areas of central Texas. The flowers are among the largest of any native Salvia — rich scarlet-crimson tubes nearly 1.5 inches long on tall, erect spikes — making it one of the most spectacular fall-blooming salvias in cultivation and an exceptional hummingbird attractor. The common name 'penstemonoides' (penstemon-like) refers to the form of the flower, which somewhat resembles a penstemon in shape. A rare plant in the wild with a limited natural range, it has gained popularity in native plant horticulture as a stunning, drought-tolerant hummingbird and butterfly plant for zone 7–10 dry gardens. Thrives in alkaline limestone soils typical of the Texas Hill Country.

plant_note: Plant seeds immediately upon collection (they lose viability quickly) or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; big-leaf mahogany requires frost-free conditions and grows naturally in tropical and subtropical forests of Central and South America.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; big-leaf mahogany is the commercial mahogany of global trade — the source of almost all mahogany lumber in furniture, cabinets, boats, and fine woodwork worldwide. Native to tropical forests of Central and South America from Mexico to Brazil, it produces spectacular large, compound leaves up to 12 inches long that unfurl pink-bronze before maturing to glossy dark green. The enormous seed pods hang from the canopy and split to release winged seeds. The species is now protected under CITES Appendix II due to severe overharvesting, with few large trees remaining in accessible forests. In zone 10 Florida, it grows as a large ornamental shade tree, widely planted in Miami-Dade parks and neighborhoods. Planting contributes to conservation of this critically important and over-exploited tropical timber species.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; bigleaf aster spreads robustly by rhizomes to form a dense groundcover colony — ideal for shaded slopes where erosion control and low-maintenance ground coverage are desired.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, amended with leaf mold or compost to support the large, coarse foliage that distinguishes this species from all other native asters; bigleaf aster produces the largest basal leaves of any native aster — broad, rough-textured, and heart-shaped, often 4–6 inches across — which emerge as a dense, low rosette in spring and suppress weeds effectively before the 1–2 foot flowering stems rise in late summer, bearing pale lavender to white daisy flowers with yellow centers from August through September. It spreads vigorously by stout rhizomes to form extensive groundcover colonies on shaded slopes and woodland floors and is an excellent, low-maintenance native alternative to invasive groundcovers in areas of dense tree shade and moderate moisture. Divide every 3–4 years to rejuvenate colonies and share divisions; the bold foliage provides strong textural contrast alongside ferns, trilliums, and other fine-leaved woodland plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, amended soil; in zones 8–10, fall planting is preferred. Dig a wide, shallow hole — 2x the width of the root ball — and set the plant at the same depth it grew in the container.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in morning sun with afternoon shade; bigleaf hydrangeas are the classic summer-blooming shrubs with large mophead or lacecap flower clusters in blue, pink, or white. Flower color depends on soil pH — blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5); to maintain blue, add aluminum sulfate and maintain pH below 6.0. In the South (zones 8–9) afternoon shade is essential to prevent wilting and maintain flower quality. Old-wood bloomers (most classic varieties) should be pruned only immediately after flowering — never in fall, as this removes next year's buds. Reblooming types such as 'Endless Summer' bloom on both old and new wood, making them more reliable after hard winters.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; ligularia wilts dramatically in dry conditions or afternoon heat — it requires consistent moisture and shade from afternoon sun.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; ligularia is a bold-textured Asian shade perennial valued for its very large, rounded, kidney-shaped leaves and clusters of bright orange-yellow daisy-like flowers on tall stems in midsummer — providing rare, vibrant color in the shaded garden at a time when most shade plants have finished blooming. The large, purple-backed leaves on named cultivars like 'Desdemona' and 'Othello' are dramatically ornamental even out of bloom. However, ligularia is extremely sensitive to heat and dry air — the large leaves wilt badly in full afternoon sun or dry conditions, recovering at night but looking stressed through the day. It requires consistently moist to boggy soil and cool shade to look its best. Best suited to cool-summer climates (zone 4–7) or consistently moist, shaded stream banks in zone 8. An outstanding plant for boggy shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; bigleaf magnolia requires protection from strong winds, which shred the enormous leaves. Partial afternoon shade is important in zones 7–8.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil sheltered from strong winds in partial shade; bigleaf magnolia holds the distinction of producing the largest simple leaves of any native tree in North America — up to 32 inches long and 12 inches wide — and the combination of these extraordinary leaves with the enormous, intensely fragrant white flowers (up to 16 inches across) makes this one of the most spectacular ornamental trees in the world. The cream-white flowers in late spring to early summer have a distinctive sweet fragrance detectable from considerable distance. It grows naturally as a rare understory tree in moist, protected ravines and hollows of the South Appalachians and Gulf States. Site it in a protected, partly shaded location away from wind — the huge leaves shred easily in exposed sites. The rose-pink fruiting cones in fall are ornamental and provide food for birds.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall after cold stratification (or plant naturally in fall for natural stratification) in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; bigleaf maple grows naturally in moist, coastal forests and stream banks of the Pacific Northwest and is the largest maple in western North America.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; bigleaf maple is the dominant large deciduous tree of moist Pacific Northwest forests, producing the largest leaves of any North American maple — up to 12 inches wide with 5 deep lobes. The massive leaves produce an extraordinary large-textured canopy unlike any other temperate tree. In Pacific Northwest old-growth forests, bigleaf maple trunks and limbs are often draped in thick carpets of mosses, ferns, and licorice fern, creating some of the most magical, fairy-tale forest scenes in North America. Long, pendulous clusters of small, fragrant yellow-green flowers attract early-season pollinators. The paired samaras are large, forming a unique, U-shaped pair. Fall color is golden-yellow to bright orange. The sap can be processed into maple syrup, though production is lower than sugar maple.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade. Bigleaf Snowbell is most spectacular when planted where its pendant white flowers can be viewed from below, such as on a slope above a path or at the edge of a raised bed.
directions: Bigleaf Snowbell is a beautiful native understory shrub or small tree, native to the moist, rich deciduous forests of the southeastern United States from Virginia and Tennessee south to Florida and west to Louisiana, where it grows as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree 6–12 feet tall in the shade of larger hardwoods and pines along stream terraces and ravine slopes. In May and June it produces cascading racemes of fragrant, pure white, bell-shaped flowers with conspicuous yellow stamens that cover the branches in a spectacular display and attract native bees; the flowers are best appreciated from below, where the full pendant clusters are visible against the dark canopy. The large, soft-textured leaves (up to 5 inches long) give the plant its common name and create an attractive bold texture in the shade garden. Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and protect from drought; it is more adaptable to heat and humidity than Japanese snowbell (Styrax japonicus) and is a superior choice for southeastern gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; bigroot geranium tolerates dry shade better than almost any other groundcover and spreads steadily by surface-running rhizomes.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial to full shade; bigroot geranium is arguably the best dry-shade groundcover for temperate gardens, producing a dense, weed-suppressing mat of aromatic, lobed leaves that color beautifully in fall, and producing magenta-pink to white flowers in late spring to early summer. It is one of very few ornamentals that thrives in the challenging dry shade under mature maples and beeches where little else will grow. The sticky, scented foliage is deer-resistant. Semi-evergreen in mild winters. Surface rhizomes spread steadily without becoming invasive. Divide in spring or fall to expand plantings. The aromatic leaves were historically used as a geranium oil source in the perfume industry.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bigtooth aspen is the eastern counterpart to quaking aspen, more common on drier, sandier soils in the Northeast and Great Lakes region. It also spreads by root suckers to form clonal colonies.
directions: Plant root suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bigtooth aspen is distinguished from quaking aspen by its larger, more coarsely toothed leaves with larger, irregular, rounded teeth (reflecting the name 'grandidentata' — large-toothed). More common on sandy, dry soils and mixed hardwood-aspen forests of the Northeast and Great Lakes region. Like quaking aspen, it spreads clonally by root suckers to form groves, and the flat petioles cause the leaves to tremble in the breeze. The bark is greenish-white to cream-colored, somewhat less white than quaking aspen. Fall color is a warm golden-yellow. The bigtooth aspen grove supports important habitat structure — the trees are fast-growing pioneer species that provide early succession habitat for nesting birds and beaver activity. Excellent for naturalistic, large-scale native woodland restoration in appropriate cool climates.

plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light on a moss pole or bark support with chunky, well-draining aroid mix; the striking orange-yellow petioles are the most distinctive identifying feature of this species and develop best color in bright indirect light. Keep consistently moist but not waterlogged — allow the top inch to dry before re-watering. The long, lance-shaped leaves require vertical space. Tolerates humidity levels from 50–80%. Propagate from stem cuttings. A relatively fast grower among collector philodendrons. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-aerated, chunky potting mix with a climbing support — Billie's Philodendron is a hemi-epiphytic climber that grows most vigorously and produces its largest, most dramatic leaves when ascending a moss pole or other support. Philodendron billietiae is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to French Guiana, Suriname, and northern Brazil in the Araceae family, named in honor of Frieda Billiet, a Belgian botanist who collected the type specimen. The plant is distinguished in the Philodendron genus by two immediately striking characteristics: its long, bright orange to orange-yellow petioles, and its narrowly elongated, lance-shaped leaves with distinctly wavy or undulate margins — a leaf shape quite different from the broad, cordate leaves typical of many popular philodendrons. The petioles are a vivid, warm orange-yellow that contrasts brilliantly with the glossy, dark green leaf blade — the orange petioles visible from a distance and making the plant immediately recognizable among a collection of philodendrons. The leaves are large (18–36 inches on mature plants), elongated-lanceolate, with gently rippled margins and a leathery, glossy dark green texture. The mid-rib is pale yellow-green against the dark surface. A popular and relatively fast-growing collector's philodendron valued for its unique petiole color and leaf form. All parts toxic.

common_name: Biloxi Crape Myrtle (Light Pink Vigorous Gulf Coast Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Biloxi grows quickly into a medium-to-large tree and performs especially well in the humid Gulf Coast climate for which it is named.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Biloxi is a vigorous, medium-to-large National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle named for the Mississippi Gulf Coast city, producing clear light pink flower clusters over a long summer bloom season on a fast-growing, upright tree. It shows strong resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars in the humid Gulf South, and develops attractively mottled, exfoliating cinnamon-and-gray bark as it matures. Fall foliage takes on orange to red tones before dropping. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune selectively to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the tree, which spoils its natural vase-shaped form.

subcategory: Pacific island sticky-seeded shade coastal tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in zone 10–12; Bird Catcher Tree (Para Para) is a large-leaved tropical tree native to Pacific islands from New Zealand to Hawaii, Australia, Southeast Asia, and East Africa — famous for its extremely sticky, narrow, club-shaped fruits that trap small birds, insects, and lizards, sometimes fatally — and grown ornamentally for its bold, tropical, large-leaved foliage in shaded or semi-shaded positions.
directions: Plant Pisonia umbellifera in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; young trees prefer some protection from the hottest afternoon sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; the sticky fruits should be considered when siting — place away from areas frequented by small birds and do not plant near bird feeders. Bird Catcher Tree is one of the more ecologically unusual trees of Pacific island forests — its narrow, club-shaped fruits are covered in an extremely sticky, clear resin that adheres to anything that brushes against it, and small birds investigating the fruit clusters can become fatally entangled. This macabre adaptation has made it a subject of scientific and popular fascination: in some Pacific island seabird colonies (particularly on Heron Island, Australia), large numbers of migratory petrels and shearwaters are trapped each breeding season. Despite its sinister seed-dispersal strategy, the Bird Catcher Tree is a handsome ornamental with very large, glossy, paddle-shaped leaves creating a bold tropical texture in the shade garden; it performs well as a specimen or screen in zone 10–12. The variegated form ('Variegata') with green and cream-white blotched leaves is particularly attractive and widely grown as an ornamental across tropical and subtropical regions.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered, frost-free location or in containers moved indoors during cold spells. In zone 9 grow in a protected, deep-shade spot or use as a container plant on a shaded porch. The broad, undivided fronds are unlike typical fern foliage and provide a bold, tropical texture in shade gardens.
directions: Grow in bright to moderate shade in well-draining, humus-rich soil or a loose bark-based potting mix; bird nest fern grows as an epiphyte in nature, perching on tree trunks with its roots in accumulated leaf litter. The glossy, strap-like fronds emerge from a central rosette and can reach 4 feet long in ideal conditions. Avoid pouring water into the central cup where new fronds emerge, as this encourages rot; water the root zone and allow the mix to approach dryness between waterings. Fertilize monthly during the growing season with a dilute balanced fertilizer. This fern is excellent in bathrooms and covered patios where humidity is naturally higher.

subcategory: iconic orange-blue crane-flower South African perennial
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rhizome divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bird of paradise is a slow-growing perennial from the Eastern Cape of South Africa requiring patience — container-grown transplants typically take 2–4 years to reach first flowering, and seed-grown plants 5–7 years. Once established, plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived, blooming continuously for decades. Overcrowded clumps flower best — do not divide unnecessarily. Full sun is essential for flowering; part shade produces foliage but few flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bird of paradise is one of the most internationally recognized flowering plants in horticulture — the floral emblem of Los Angeles, a staple of tropical-theme gardens worldwide, and one of the most distinctive and immediately identifiable flowers produced by any plant. The flowers emerge from a horizontal, boat-shaped, green-purple spathe (the 'beak' of the 'bird') on a tall, stiff scape held above the large, oval, paddle-shaped, blue-green leaves on long petioles. The flower itself consists of three vivid, saturated-orange sepals arranged in a fan and three blue-purple petals — two fused into a pointed, arrow-shaped structure that projects forward — the overall composition creating an unmistakable resemblance to the head and crest of a tropical bird, complete with orange 'crown' and blue 'beak'. The flower's elaborate structure is adapted for pollination by sunbirds in its native South Africa: the weight of the bird on the blue petal structure exposes the pollen-covered anthers that dust the bird's feet. Native to the coastal and riverine scrub of the Eastern Cape of South Africa, it grows in full sun, lean, well-drained soil, and tolerates considerable drought when established. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a reliable, long-lived, repeating-bloom perennial that produces its extraordinary flowers throughout the year when mature.

common_name: Bird's Beak Oncidium (Bird's Mouth Orchid, Dove Orchid, Pink Oncidium)
plant_note: Grow in a small pot with fine to medium bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun; Oncidium ornithorhynchum blooms in fall and winter on long, arching, much-branched racemes that can reach 24 inches and carry 100–200 small flowers in rose-pink to lilac-lavender — the entire inflorescence is extraordinarily floriferous and the fragrance (a sweet, vanilla-baby-powder scent) is among the most pleasant of any orchid. A cool-to-intermediate grower that appreciates nighttime temperatures of 55–62°F in fall to trigger blooming. Protect from frost. One of the best fall-blooming orchids for zone 9-11 outdoor culture. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light in fine to medium bark or on a mount — Bird's Beak Oncidium grows most vigorously in intermediate conditions and produces its most spectacular, multi-branched bloom spikes when given cool, dry fall nights that trigger the inflorescence development. Oncidium ornithorhynchum is a compact, sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Costa Rica, and Colombia — one of the most free-flowering and fragrant of the many smaller Oncidium species, widely grown by orchid enthusiasts for the extraordinary fall flower display and remarkable fragrance. The plant is small and compact — oval, slightly flattened pseudobulbs 2–3 inches tall with 2–3 soft, narrow leaves. In fall and early winter, multiple flower spikes emerge from the base of the pseudobulbs and branch repeatedly to produce long, arching, pendant racemes bearing 50–200 small (0.5-inch) flowers in rose-pink to lilac-lavender, with a small, distinctly shaped lip that gives the species name ornithorhynchum (Greek: 'bird's beak'). The sheer flower quantity on a well-grown, established plant creates a cascade of soft pink-lavender that is exceptional among small orchids. The fragrance is the plant's other outstanding quality: intensely sweet, warm, and pleasant — commonly described as resembling vanilla, baby powder, or sweet clover — produced throughout the day and most concentrated in warm morning conditions. An outstanding fall-blooming orchid for zone 9-12. Non-toxic.

common_name: Bird's Nest Anthurium (Hookeri Anthurium, Lance-Leaf Bird's Nest)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, shaded patio container, or in zone 10-11 outdoor shade gardens; Anthurium hookeri is more tolerant of lower humidity, lower light, and temperature fluctuation than most collector anthuriums, making it a good choice for beginners in the genus. In zone 9b-10 in deep shade, it can be grown as an outdoor tropical groundcover or specimen. Provide moist, well-drained, humus-rich growing medium. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in moderate to deep shade in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or potting medium; Bird's Nest Anthurium is one of the most adaptable and shade-tolerant of the large Anthurium species, tolerating the reduced light and humidity of typical indoor environments better than most of its relatives. Anthurium hookeri is a large epiphytic to terrestrial anthurium from the forests of Trinidad, the Lesser Antilles, Guyana, and northeastern South America, growing in a distinctive bird's nest rosette form — the large, broadly elongated, glossy, dark-green leaves (12–24 inches long) radiate outward in a vase or funnel shape similar to Asplenium nidus, the Bird's Nest Fern, and for the same functional reason: the funnel shape channels rain and falling debris toward the plant's root zone, efficiently gathering nutrients and moisture. The leaves are thick, leathery, glossy, and a rich dark emerald-green with deeply impressed veins. Unlike the demanding velvet anthuriums, A. hookeri tolerates moderate indoor conditions, lower humidity, and even some neglect while remaining attractive. It produces typical anthurium flowers (green-white spathe and spadix) that, when pollinated, develop into small, purple, globose berries along the spadix. An excellent large specimen foliage plant for zone 9 shaded indoor and outdoor spaces. All parts toxic.

common_name: Bird's Nest Fern (Nest Fern, Spleenwort Bird's Nest)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, shaded patio container, or in zone 9b-11 shade garden; Bird's Nest Fern cannot tolerate frost but is one of the more cold-tolerant large tropical ferns, surviving brief temperatures to 32°F if the rhizome is protected. In zone 9-11, plant outdoors in deeply shaded spots with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — outstanding under large trees or in north-facing shaded beds. Avoid getting water into the center rosette cup where it can cause rotting. Do not use neem or oil sprays on the fronds which cause browning.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil or potting mix; Bird's Nest Fern is one of the most shade-tolerant and adaptable of all large ferns, thriving in the deep, dry shade under large trees where most ferns would fail. Asplenium nidus is a large epiphytic fern native to tropical Asia, eastern Australia, and the Pacific Islands that grows naturally anchored to the bark of large trees, its roots drawing moisture and nutrients from accumulated organic matter. The frond pattern is unlike typical ferns: broad, undivided, strap-like, bright-green, glossy fronds up to 4 feet long arch outward from a central rosette in a shape that perfectly mimics a bird's nest — the dense, brown, fibrous mass of old frond bases at the center closely resembles the construction of a large bird's nest, giving the plant its common name. The fronds have an attractive central black midrib. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, Bird's Nest Fern is one of the finest large-scale shade plants for tropical effect, combining bold architectural form, glossy tropical foliage, and shade tolerance that allows it to thrive under oak trees. It also makes a striking large houseplant for bright-to-moderate indoor light.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun for a late winter to spring bloom; self-sows prolifically where happy.
directions: Bird's-eye Gilia is a charming California native annual wildflower bearing masses of small, tubular, violet-purple flowers marked with a ring of deep purple and a yellow-orange throat — the three-toned pattern gives the species both its common name and its epithet tricolor. It is native to the dry, open grasslands and oak woodland clearings of California's Central Valley and Coast Ranges, where it blooms from February through May. Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; seeds require cool, moist conditions to germinate and will sprout through winter rains to bloom in late winter and spring. Bird's-eye Gilia self-sows prolifically in open, sunny, California-native garden beds and makes an excellent companion for California poppies and native clarkia.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or divisions in fall in very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or rocky, dry, poor soil in full sun to partial shade; birdfoot violet will not thrive in clay, wet, or fertile soils — it requires the conditions of the sandy pine barrens and dry rocky glades in which it is native.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, dry, poor soil in full sun to partial shade — birdfoot violet is one of the most beautiful of all native violets, with the largest and most vividly colored flowers of the eastern species — 1 inch lavender to pale violet or bicolored (the classic bicolor form has dark upper petals and pale lower petals with an orange eye). The deeply divided, multi-lobed leaves closely resemble a bird's foot, giving the plant its common name. Unlike most violets that thrive in moist, rich soil, birdfoot violet is strictly a plant of dry, poor, acidic, sandy, or rocky soils — pine barrens, sandstone outcrops, and dry, open glades where soil fertility is minimal. It will languish and die in clay or rich soil. An outstanding and distinctive native for sandy, acidic rock gardens and dry native plant gardens in zones 3–8; a specialist larval host for several native fritillary butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early.
directions: 'Birdhouse' produces hard-shelled gourds that, once cured, can last for decades and be carved, painted, or drilled like wood for countless craft projects. Direct sow after frost in warm soil or start indoors a few weeks early, giving the vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl or a sturdy trellis to climb. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil with steady moisture through the long season. Allow the gourds to fully mature and dry on the vine, then cure them in a dry, airy spot for several months before crafting.

common_name: Bishop of Llandaff Dahlia (Dark Bronze-Foliage Scarlet-Flowered Peony Dahlia Classic)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 inches deep after last frost; Bishop of Llandaff is a peony-flowered dahlia type producing single to semi-double flowers with open centers. In zone 9, plant March–April for summer-fall bloom (July–November). The near-black to very dark bronze-purple foliage is the defining characteristic — this dark coloration is most intense in full sun. Bishop of Llandaff can be overwintered in zone 9 by leaving tubers in the ground with a layer of mulch for frost protection, or by digging tubers after frost kills the tops and storing in a cool, dry location (40–50°F). The contrast between the dark foliage and bright scarlet flowers makes this one of the most visually dramatic garden plants available.
directions: Plant tuber horizontally 4–6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up. Pinch the growing tip when 12 inches tall to encourage branching. Stake plants before they need it. Bishop of Llandaff is a dahlia cultivar of exceptional distinction — one of the small number of dahlia varieties that has achieved genuine iconic status, recognized by name even by gardeners with limited interest in dahlias, for the extraordinary combination of near-black bronze-purple foliage and vivid scarlet-red peony-form flowers. Most dahlias produce green foliage; Bishop of Llandaff's foliage is so deeply pigmented with anthocyanins that it appears nearly black in strong sunlight — a dramatic dark background that makes the bright red flowers appear to glow by contrast. The name honors the Bishop of Llandaff Cathedral in Cardiff, Wales; the variety was hybridized in 1928 by Mr. F. Hyde and has maintained its position as one of the most distinctive and recognizable dahlia varieties across nearly a century of cultivation. The peony-form flowers (semi-double with a visible open center) are 3–4 inches across, a clear, vivid scarlet-red — not the orange-red of some red dahlias but a pure, saturated scarlet — with a yellow-centered disc that provides important pollinator access. Unlike many fully double dahlia types, Bishop of Llandaff's open centers are accessible to bees and other pollinators, making it more ecologically valuable than many showier garden dahlias. It remains one of the most sought-after dahlias in British and European cottage garden traditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; does not transplant well — sow in situ.
directions: Sow seeds directly where they are to grow, pressing them onto moist soil — they need light to germinate; thin to 9–12 in apart. Ammi majus produces flat, lacy white umbels similar to Queen Anne's Lace but with cleaner, more refined flowers that are highly valued by florists. The feathery foliage and long stems make it an ideal filler in bouquets with a vase life of 7–10 days. Successive sowings 3–4 weeks apart extend the harvest period; plants bolt in summer heat so succession-sow in spring only.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost threat; Bismarck palm grows slowly in youth but eventually becomes a dramatic, large-canopy specimen that requires ample space.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Bismarck palm is a massive, solitary-trunked fan palm from Madagascar that is grown for its extraordinarily beautiful, huge, waxy, silvery-blue to silver-gray fan leaves up to 10 feet across — the most structurally dramatic cold-tolerant palm available for zone 9–11 landscapes. Young palms are slow (1–2 feet per year) but eventually reach 30–60 feet with enormous presence. Extremely drought-tolerant once established — deeply water monthly during establishment but then largely ignore. Intolerant of sustained freezes below 22–25°F; mulch the root zone heavily in zone 9 gardens. The silvery blue-leaved cultivar 'Silver' is the most commonly grown form. A fully mature specimen is one of the most spectacular trees achievable in a subtropical landscape.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; IMPORTANT: Install a 30-mil high-density polyethylene rhizome barrier at least 24–36 inches deep around the planting area before establishing any running bamboo to prevent invasive underground spread.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, contained within a rhizome barrier; Bisset bamboo is one of the most cold-hardy of all Phyllostachys species, reliably surviving temperatures to –10°F (–23°C) and making it an excellent choice for cold-climate gardens in zones 5–9. Its dense, upright culms reaching 15–20 feet create superb windbreaks, privacy screens, and living fences that remain evergreen through harsh winters. Like all running bamboos, it spreads aggressively via underground rhizomes and must be contained with a deep barrier or managed by annual rhizome pruning at the grove perimeter. The emerald-green culms hold their color well and are attractive for crafts and garden staking.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; bistort spreads steadily by rhizomes to form ground-covering colonies in moist conditions. The cultivar Superba is more compact and floriferous than the species, with larger, brighter-pink flower spikes. Bistort is also known as snakeweed from its twisted rhizome, and the young leaves and shoots have been used in traditional British cooking.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; bistort is a spreading, rhizomatous European meadow perennial producing soft, poker-shaped, bottlebrush-like spikes of densely packed, pale-pink to deep-rose-pink flowers in May and June — one of the loveliest and most distinctive flower forms of the early summer garden, resembling a soft, elongated pink bottlebrush rather than the typical flat daisy or spike flower. The flower color is a particularly soft, clean rose-pink that harmonizes beautifully with other cool-toned perennials. In moist, partly shaded conditions, bistort spreads steadily to form extensive, weed-suppressing groundcover colonies of attractive, broad, dock-like leaves. The cultivar Superba is the most garden-worthy selection, with larger, more intensely colored pink spikes above compact, dense foliage. Historically, the young leaves were used in the traditional English Lake District dish Dock Pudding. An outstanding plant for naturalizing in moist, partly shaded conditions near water features.

plant_note: Plant small cuttings or divisions at any time in very well-drained, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, sandy, or poor soil in full sun to partial shade; biting stonecrop is extremely easy to establish from cuttings or stem fragments, rooting wherever they contact soil. Perfect for rock walls, dry slopes, and green roofs.
directions: Plant cuttings or division fragments in any well-drained, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, sandy, or lean soil in full sun to partial shade; biting stonecrop is one of the most widely distributed and adaptable low succulent groundcovers in the world — a tiny, mat-forming Eurasian sedum naturalized throughout North America on rocky outcrops, walls, roofs, and disturbed dry ground. The dense mats of tiny, cylindrical, tightly-packed, fleshy leaves turn bright yellow-green with masses of brilliant yellow, star-shaped flowers in early summer. The name 'biting' refers to the sharp, burning taste of the leaves (due to alkaloids) — the plant is slightly toxic and should not be eaten. 'Wall pepper' comes from its habit of growing on old stone and brick walls throughout Europe. Widely used for green roofs (Sedum roofs), rock gardens, rock walls, dry slopes, and paths where few other plants survive. Spreads readily from fragments — a tiny piece rooting anywhere it contacts dry soil.

plant_note: Transplant divisions or plugs in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil directly on dunes or coastal berms; no soil amendment is needed and plants establish quickly in infertile sand.
directions: Set divisions into dry, infertile coastal sand in full sun in spring, spacing plants 24–36 inches apart and watering once to settle roots; after the first few weeks, supplemental irrigation is rarely needed. Bitter panicgrass is one of the most effective native dune stabilizers along the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts, anchoring shifting sand with deep roots while its blue-green foliage tolerates salt spray, wind, and extended drought with ease. Plants spread slowly by rhizome, filling gaps between transplants within two to three seasons without becoming invasive. Avoid fertilizing, as lean sandy soil produces the strongest, most wind-resistant growth.

plant_note: Sow direct around last frost in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; bitterweed is a native annual or short-lived perennial of disturbed roadsides, dry fields, and open sandy ground across the Gulf Coast and South — WARNING: all parts are toxic to livestock.
directions: Sow direct around the last frost date in dry, lean, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in full sun; bitterweed germinates readily in warm soil and grows quickly in poor, dry conditions where richer-soil plants fail — it requires excellent drainage and is intolerant of consistently wet or waterlogged soils. Helenium amarum is a native annual or short-lived perennial of the southeastern United States, ranging from the Gulf Coast states north through the Mid-Atlantic; it produces very fine, thread-like, linear leaves on bushy, much-branched stems and masses of small, bright-yellow, daisy-like flowers with reflexed ray petals around a rounded, yellow-green disk from June through frost. It is an important late-season nectar source for native bees, wasps, and butterflies, particularly on roadsides and disturbed sites where few other natives thrive; it self-sows freely and forms dense colonies in dry, open ground. CAUTION: all plant parts contain bitter sesquiterpene lactones (helenin) that are toxic to cattle, horses, and sheep if consumed in quantity — do not plant in or adjacent to livestock pastures.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; black bamboo is a running bamboo (spreading rhizomes) that requires a root barrier (18-inch deep metal or HDPE sheet) to prevent invasive spread in garden settings.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; ALWAYS install a bamboo root barrier (18-inch deep polypropylene or metal sheet) before planting black bamboo in garden settings — it is a running bamboo with spreading rhizomes that will aggressively colonize surrounding areas without physical containment. The culms (canes) emerge green and gradually turn jet black over 2–3 years as they age — the dramatic contrast between the feathery green leaves and the polished, ebony-black canes is uniquely striking and one of the most beautiful ornamental effects of any bamboo. Widely used in Chinese gardens, Japanese-inspired gardens, and contemporary garden design. The young canes (bamboo shoots) are edible in spring when they first emerge, with a mild flavor. Used decoratively in flower arrangements and for making chopsticks, fans, and bamboo crafts. Container growing in a large barrel eliminates spread concerns.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in deep to moderate shade in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12); Black Bat Flower is a shade-loving tropical rhizomatous perennial native to the humid forests of Thailand, Myanmar, Yunnan, Malaysia, and Borneo, producing extraordinary, bat-shaped, deep maroon-black to purple-black flowers with long, whisker-like purple-black bracts up to 12 inches long — one of the most dramatically bizarre flowers in the plant kingdom.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in deep shade to bright indirect light; Tacca chantrieri demands consistent high humidity, warmth, and shade — it shuts down in direct sun or drought conditions and is best grown under a dense canopy or in a sheltered, humid, north- or east-facing position. Tacca chantrieri (Black Bat Flower, Devil Flower, or Cat's Whiskers) is a dramatic, clump-forming, shade-loving rhizomatous perennial native to the humid tropical forests of mainland Southeast Asia — Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia, Yunnan Province (China), and extending into Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — where it grows in deep forest floor understory in high humidity, filtered light, and rich, moist, leaf-litter soil. The flowers are among the most extraordinary in nature: large, bat-shaped umbels of deepest maroon-black to purple-black, 4–8 inch flowers subtended by similarly dark, wing-like bracts, and accompanied by impossibly long (up to 12–28 inches), threadlike, drooping, black-purple 'whiskers' (bracteoles) that give the plant its common names. The flowers rise singly on long peduncles above the large, broad, glossy, tropical-looking leaves. Tacca chantrieri is challenging to grow outside of tropical climates — it requires high humidity (above 60%), warmth (minimum 60°F), consistent moisture without waterlogging, and deep shade or bright indirect light only. Excellent for tropical shade gardens, humid greenhouse cultivation, and indoor specimen planting in warm, bright interiors. Repot annually and divide clumps when crowded.

common_name: Black Beauty Elderberry (Dark Purple-Leaved Pink-Flowered Elderberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Beauty produces broad, deep purple-black leaves and lemon-scented pink flowers, a bold foliage color combination for a mixed border or large container.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade helpful in preserving foliage color in hot climates. Black Beauty produces broad, dramatic, deep purple-black leaves on a large, vigorous shrub, providing strong foliage contrast in a mixed border throughout the growing season, along with fragrant, lemon-scented pink flower clusters in early summer that mature into small dark berries. Like other ornamental elderberries it is grown primarily for its foliage impact, though the berries can be cooked into syrups and preserves; raw berries and other plant parts are mildly toxic and should not be eaten uncooked. Prune in late winter to control its substantial size and maintain good structure.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or scarify and sow in early spring in humus-rich, well-drained, neutral soil in part shade; black bitter-vetch is an unusual shade-tolerant perennial pea that grows naturally in woodland clearings and scrub. It is slow to establish but long-lived once settled. The common name 'black' refers to the seed color and the way the stem turns black when dried.
directions: Sow in humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in part shade to full sun; black bitter-vetch is a distinctive European woodland perennial pea, related to spring vetchling (Lathyrus vernus) but producing deep burgundy-purple to magenta-purple pea flowers in May and June that fade to blue with age, creating a two-tone flower display. Like spring vetchling, it grows as a non-climbing, bushy perennial with attractive, divided vetch-like foliage and goes dormant after seeding — disappearing by midsummer. It is more tolerant of dry, alkaline soils than many vetchlings and colonizes woodland edges and scrub in calcareous soils across Europe. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves the soil. Unusual and rarely grown in North American gardens despite being an attractive, easy-care shade perennial that fills the early-summer gap in the woodland garden between the spring ephemerals and the midsummer shade perennials. The common name 'black' refers both to the dark seed color and to the black-purple stem color when dried.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; black cohosh is a native woodland plant that establishes slowly but eventually forms large, permanent clumps that should not be moved once established.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; black cohosh is one of the most dramatic native shade perennials of eastern North America — a bold woodland plant with large, deeply divided, compound leaves rising from thick rhizomes to form a substantial mound 3–4 feet wide, topped in summer by extraordinary wand-like flower spikes reaching 4–7 feet. The white flowers on tall bottlebrush-like racemes have a subtle, slightly musky fragrance and are followed by small, round green seed capsules in fall. The rhizomes are widely used in traditional medicine and herbal supplements for menopausal symptoms; over-collection from wild populations makes garden cultivation an important conservation measure. In the garden it is outstanding under tall trees where its white summer flowers illuminate the dark understory. Purple-leafed cultivars such as 'Hillside Black Beauty' and 'Brunette' add dramatic dark foliage interest in addition to the white summer flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions or corms after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Black Coral taro grows rapidly in zone 9's warm, humid summers — reaching full size by midsummer from spring planting. The near-black foliage color is most intense in higher light conditions; deep shade produces slightly lighter green-black leaves. Provide consistent moisture, as colocasia is moisture-demanding during active growth. In zone 9 the corms often survive in the ground through mild winters with heavy mulching; dig and store in frost-free conditions to guarantee survival through colder spells.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Black Coral taro can also be grown in full sun if moisture is consistently high, but the dramatic near-black foliage color is most effective against the lightening backdrop of shaded garden settings; Black Coral is a dark-foliaged cultivar of common taro (Colocasia esculenta) producing heart-shaped, upward-facing leaves in an extraordinary near-black color — the deepest, most saturated dark foliage available among commonly grown elephant ear varieties, with stems and leaf undersides showing deep purple-maroon tones that complement the black-green leaf surface. The near-black foliage creates a dramatic, high-contrast focal point in shade garden settings where it pairs effectively with light-colored companions — chartreuse sweet potato vine, silver-variegated ground covers, and bright-flowered shade annuals all show brilliant contrast against the dark background of Black Coral. This cultivar is particularly valuable in shade gardens precisely because the very dark foliage absorbs and amplifies the subtle light available in shaded conditions, creating a visual depth and shadow play that lighter-foliaged plants cannot achieve. In zone 9 Black Coral grows vigorously in the summer heat and humidity that is its native climate — rapidly producing increasingly large leaves through summer as the corm establishes.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; black cottonwood is the largest native hardwood tree of western North America and grows along mountain rivers and streams from Alaska to California. Plant only where ample moisture is available.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, well-drained riparian soil in full sun along streams and rivers; black cottonwood is the largest native hardwood of western North America, reaching 100+ feet in the riparian forests of the Pacific Coast and Cascades. The deeply furrowed, dark gray bark gives the tree its common name. The buds are large and resinous with a balsamic fragrance similar to balsam poplar. Black cottonwood riparian forests are among the most productive wildlife habitats in the western US — supporting bald eagle nesting, great blue heron colonies, beaver activity, and a rich understory of native shrubs and wildflowers. The brilliant golden-yellow fall color marks every river valley from the Cascades to the Rocky Mountains with spectacular seasonal color visible for miles. The first tree species to have its complete genome sequenced (2006), serving as the model organism for forest tree genomics.

common_name: Black Diamond Crape Myrtle (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Reblooming Series)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Black Diamond is a series distinguished from other crape myrtles by near-black, deep purple-maroon foliage that holds its color through the growing season, providing strong contrast against its bright summer flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Black Diamond is a series of crape myrtles bred for foliage that emerges near-black and holds its deep purple-maroon color through summer heat rather than fading to green, a trait that sets it apart from the many crape myrtle series bred primarily for flower color or mildew resistance. Individual selections within the series bloom in shades from pure white through pink, red, and purple, and the dark foliage makes even pale flower colors read as especially vivid by contrast. Like other modern interspecific crape myrtles (Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei), Black Diamond selections generally show good resistance to powdery mildew, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where older all-indica cultivars mildew heavily. Plants rebloom over several weeks if spent flower clusters are removed, and the naturally attractive, often multi-trunked form with exfoliating bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Avoid the practice of severe annual 'crape murder' pruning, which sacrifices the plant's natural vase shape and delays bloom; instead remove only dead, crossing, or downward-growing branches in late winter.

common_name: Black Dragon Coleus (Deep Maroon-Black Ruffled Coleus)
plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Black Dragon is a coleus cultivar with deeply ruffled, near-black maroon leaves edged in a thin band of bright magenta-red, providing dramatic dark foliage contrast in mixed plantings.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Black Dragon is a dramatic coleus cultivar with deeply cut, ruffled, near-black maroon leaves edged in a narrow band of bright magenta-red, providing some of the darkest foliage color available in coleus and a strong textural accent from the heavily serrated leaf margins. Its near-black coloring makes it an outstanding foil for chartreuse, silver, or brightly colored companion plants in mixed containers and borders, where the contrast draws the eye immediately. Like most coleus, it develops its darkest, richest color with some protection from the most intense midday sun in zone 9, though it tolerates more light than old-fashioned shade-only coleus varieties. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to encourage a full, dense, well-branched habit.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall (September–November in zone 9) for best establishment before spring bloom; spring planting is possible but produces weaker first-year plants. Black Gamecock Louisiana Iris blooms in April–May in zone 9 — the peak of spring when the large, fleur-de-lis-form flowers create one of the most spectacular displays available in moist, native garden settings. Louisiana irises thrive in the moist to wet, acidic soil conditions common in the Gulf South; they naturally grow in swamps, bayous, and stream margins. Divide clumps every 4–5 years when blooming declines. Louisiana iris culture in the Gulf South is supported by the Society for Louisiana Irises, which maintains extensive hybridization and evaluation programs.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, fertile, very acidic to slightly acidic soil — Black Gamecock Louisiana Iris and all Louisiana iris species require the acidic, consistently moist to wet soil conditions that prevail in their native Gulf Coast swamp and stream bank habitats; Black Gamecock is one of the most famous and widely grown Louisiana iris cultivars, producing large, flat, velvety flowers in an intense, nearly pure black-violet — one of the deepest, most saturated dark purple flowers available among all iris types — on 2–3 foot stems above the upright, strap-like foliage. Louisiana irises (Iris x louisiana) are complex hybrids among five native species of the Gulf Coast, bred extensively in Louisiana since the early 20th century into thousands of cultivars spanning almost the complete color spectrum. As a group they are the most heat-tolerant and humidity-tolerant irises available — outperforming bearded iris, Japanese iris, and Siberian iris in the sustained summer heat and high humidity of the Gulf South that limits those species' culture. The fall-to-spring growing period of Louisiana irises aligns perfectly with the Gulf South climate: active growth occurs in the mild fall through spring weather, bloom peaks in April–May, and the plants go semi-dormant in summer heat. Black Gamecock's extraordinary dark flower color makes it one of the most impactful single plants in the spring iris display.

common_name: Black Gold Philodendron (Melanochrysum, Dark Gold Velvet Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio climber in zone 9; Philodendron melanochrysum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or coco coir totem to allow the plant to climb — vining philodendrons produce progressively larger and more dramatic leaves as they climb, while trailing specimens maintain smaller, less impressive leaves. Use a well-aerated mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil. Maintain humidity above 60% for best appearance. Propagate from stem cuttings with a single node and aerial root. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Black Gold Philodendron needs consistent bright indirect light to produce its best, most dramatic foliage, but cannot tolerate direct sun which scorches the delicate velvet leaf surface. Philodendron melanochrysum is a climbing philodendron from the humid tropical forests of Colombia in the family Araceae, prized internationally as one of the finest velvet-leaved collector aroids. The leaves are large (reaching 24 inches or more on climbing specimens), elongated heart-shaped with a long, tapering tip, and velvety dark — a color so deep and saturated that it has been described as 'black-green' or 'midnight green' with a subtle sheen of bronze or gold visible in raking light, the quality that inspired the species name 'melanochrysum' (Greek: 'black gold'). The midrib and primary veins are precisely delineated in pale cream to yellowish-white, creating a striking contrast against the dark velvety surface. New leaves emerge in shades of bright copper-orange before slowly darkening to the mature near-black green. Philodendron melanochrysum has become one of the most desirable collector aroids of the current era, valued for both its exceptional leaf beauty and the dramatic transformation in leaf size as the plant matures on a climbing support. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant container specimens (ball-and-burlap or container-grown) in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; black gum develops a deep taproot and transplants best when young — avoid moving established specimens.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade — black gum consistently ranks among the top native trees for fall foliage color: its leaves turn brilliant shades of scarlet, orange, purple, and wine-red as early as late August in the South, among the first of all trees to change, providing exceptionally early and long-lasting fall color in the landscape. The tree is pyramidal when young and becomes more irregular and picturesque with age; horizontal branching and somewhat layered architecture make it attractive year-round. Small, dark blue to black berries in clusters ripen in September–October and are consumed by over 30 species of songbirds and mammals. Black gum is one of the most important wildlife trees in the eastern US due to its early-ripening, high-fat fruits. Adaptable to a wide range of moisture conditions from dry upland slopes to wet bottomlands — an outstanding landscape tree for native plantings.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; black haw is more drought tolerant than most viburnums and succeeds in drier, shadier conditions that defeat other viburnums.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — black haw is a native multi-stem large shrub or small tree of open woodlands, roadsides, and fence rows throughout the eastern US, valued for four seasons of ornament: flat-topped clusters of white flowers in April, lush summer foliage, brilliant scarlet to burgundy fall color, and clusters of ripening fruit that progress from green to pink to blue-black as fall advances. The dark blue-black berries are edible and have a sweet, raisin-like flavor when fully ripe, used traditionally to make preserves, wine, and fruit leather; they are also heavily consumed by migrating birds in fall. Black haw is one of the most drought-tolerant and shade-tolerant native viburnums — it thrives where other viburnums struggle — and brings exceptional wildlife value to naturalistic plantings and food forest understories.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring as shoots emerge or in fall in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in shade to partial shade; nigrescens hosta is a large, bold species from Japan that is a parent of many popular large blue-gray hosta cultivars including 'Krossa Regal'. It develops into an impressive specimen over several years.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; nigrescens hosta is a large, architectural species from Japan notable for producing unusually tall, upright, vase-shaped clumps — the leaves are held more erect than most hostas, giving the plant a formal, candlestick silhouette quite different from the typical mounding hosta habit. The large, gray-green leaves have a distinctive glaucous bloom and bold corrugation. The flower scapes are exceptionally tall, rising 4–5 feet above the foliage in mid-summer with lavender flowers. This species is an important parent of many prized large blue cultivars including the classic 'Krossa Regal'. In zone 9, hostas appreciate afternoon shade and consistent moisture through summer heat. An impressive, long-lived specimen hosta for large shade gardens and woodland borders.

common_name: Black Knight Butterfly Bush (Dark Purple Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; deadhead regularly to extend bloom season and, critically, to prevent seed formation — Buddleja davidii is considered invasive in parts of the Pacific Northwest and some mid-Atlantic states; remove all spent flower spikes before seeds mature.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Black Knight is the most popular dark-purple butterfly bush — a vigorous Buddleja davidii cultivar producing long (12–18 inch), conical, densely packed flower spikes in a rich, deep violet-purple to nearly black-purple color that is the darkest flower color readily available in any buddleja cultivar. The intense color contrasts dramatically with the silver-gray to gray-green lance-shaped foliage and creates an outstanding late-summer focal point. Like all butterfly bushes, Black Knight is extraordinarily attractive to butterflies, particularly swallowtails, monarchs, fritillaries, and skippers — which visit in such numbers during bloom that a well-established Black Knight shrub becomes a butterfly feeding station rivaling any other garden plant. Bloom runs from July through September (and often through October in zone 9) with regular deadheading. In zone 9, butterfly bush is a woody perennial that dies back significantly in winter and regrows vigorously from the woody base in spring. Cut back hard in February — to 12 inches from the ground — to stimulate vigorous new growth and maximum flower production. Note: Buddleja davidii is listed as invasive or potentially invasive in the Pacific Northwest and some mid-Atlantic regions; in the Gulf South it self-seeds less aggressively, but deadheading before seed set is still best practice. Sterile varieties (Buddleja 'Blue Chip,' 'Miss Ruby') are available for regions where invasive concerns apply.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 6 weeks early.
directions: 'Black Knight' bears almost-black, deep maroon pincushion blooms on long stems, at home in cottage and formal gardens alike. Direct sow after frost or start indoors about six weeks early, barely covering the seed. Grow in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil where it is fairly drought tolerant. It blooms over a very long season and is a magnet for bees and butterflies. Cut flowers freely for arrangements, and let some seed heads dry on the plant for added texture.

common_name: Black Lace Elderberry (Finely Cut Purple-Black Ornamental Elderberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Lace has finely cut, almost fern-like, deep purple-black foliage and pink lace-cap flowers, grown chiefly as an ornamental foliage shrub rather than primarily for its fruit.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helping preserve the deepest foliage color in hot climates. Black Lace is a striking ornamental elderberry cultivar with finely dissected, almost lacy, deep purple-black foliage resembling a Japanese maple more than a typical shrub, topped in early summer by flat clusters of soft pink flowers that mature into small dark berries. It is grown primarily as a dramatic foliage accent for a mixed border rather than for fruit production, though the berries can be used for elderberry syrup and preserves after cooking, since raw elderberries and all other plant parts are mildly toxic. Prune in late winter to control size and maintain a strong branch framework, since it can grow quite large if left unchecked.

subcategory: North Pacific native edible rice-grain bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4–5 inches deep in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained, peaty or woodland soil in zone 3–8; Black Lily (Kamchatka Fritillary) is a stunning, unusual native bulb of the North Pacific Rim — native from Alaska and coastal British Columbia across the Aleutian Islands to Japan, Korea, and Kamchatka — bearing dramatic, nodding, very dark maroon-brown to near-black flowers with a musky, slightly unpleasant scent that attracts flies as pollinators, and historically used as a food source by Alaska Native peoples.
directions: Plant Fritillaria camschatcensis bulbs in fall 4–5 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, peaty, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; keep soil consistently moist through the growing season but not waterlogged; mark planting locations as the summer dormancy period makes the site look bare. Black Lily is one of the most dramatically colored of all bulbs — the nodding, tulip-shaped flowers are an exceptionally deep, near-black maroon, often with a slight greenish sheen to the interior, and are held in whorled clusters of 1–8 blooms at the top of the stem. In its natural habitat — the cool, moist, foggy coastlines, alpine meadows, and forest edges of the North Pacific Rim — it grows in rich, peaty, acidic soil in partial shade, and its cultivation requirements mirror these conditions closely. The bulbs consist of a main bulb surrounded by many small rice-grain bulblets (which multiply readily and produce flowering plants in 3–5 years); a distinct slightly unpleasant musty scent of the flowers attracts fly pollinators rather than bees. The bulbs were an important food for many Alaska Native groups including the Tlingit, Haida, and Aleut — boiled or steamed in baskets or pits, the flavor is said to be bitter-starchy but acceptable after preparation. A wonderful and unusual plant for moist, cool, partially shaded Pacific Northwest gardens.

plant_note: Plant in almost any well-drained soil in full sun — black locust is one of the most adaptable trees available, tolerating drought, poor soil, clay, compacted soil, and urban pollution. It spreads vigorously by root suckers and by seed and is classified as invasive in many eastern states and parts of Europe — verify local regulations before planting and plan to manage suckering. Seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun; black locust is a large, fast-growing native tree of the central Appalachians that has spread across North America and much of the world, valued and controversial in equal measure. In late May to June, mature trees produce spectacular, pendulous clusters of fragrant white pea flowers — some of the most intensely honey-scented flowers of any tree — that are the primary source of the prized 'acacia honey' of Europe (where black locust is widely grown as a honey crop). In the United States, it yields exceptional amounts of nectar for beekeepers. The flowers are edible, with a sweet, floral flavor, and are traditionally dipped in batter and fried as fritters in Appalachian and Eastern European cuisines. Black locust fixes atmospheric nitrogen and rapidly improves poor soil — a valuable quality for reclamation and agroforestry. The wood is extremely rot-resistant and harder than white oak, used for fence posts, outdoor furniture, and boat-building. CAUTION: the tree spreads aggressively by root suckers and seed and is invasive in many states and countries — manage carefully. Seeds, bark, and inner wood are toxic to horses, cattle, and humans if ingested.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; needs darkness to germinate.
directions: 'Black Magic' is a deep, near-black bachelor's button, also called cornflower, prized for cut and dried flowers with edible petals for garnishing. Direct sow in early spring or fall, covering the seed since it needs darkness to germinate. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil where it tolerates drought. It naturalizes readily, self-sowing for a fresh crop the following season. Deadhead to prolong bloom and to keep the plants tidy and productive.

common_name: Black Magic Elephant Ear (Dark Purple-Black Giant Colocasia)
plant_note: Plant tubers or divisions in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 9, tubers can be left in the ground year-round with light mulch protection — they do not need to be lifted for winter storage.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Black Magic is the most celebrated dark-leaved elephant ear cultivar — producing enormous, heart-shaped leaves (up to 30 inches long on established plants) in a uniform, deep burgundy-purple to nearly black color that is unique in the world of large-foliage tropical plants. The consistent, very dark coloration — maintained throughout the growing season without fading to green — creates a dramatic, almost surreal visual impact that makes a single established plant an unmistakable focal point in any garden. The contrast between the near-black leaves and companion plants of lighter color (chartreuse foliage, bright flowers, white flowers) is particularly striking. Black Magic thrives in the heat, humidity, and heavy rainfall of the Gulf South summer — it grows most vigorously in July and August in zone 9, producing new leaves at an impressive rate under optimal conditions. The plant does equally well in standing water (pond margins, boggy areas) as in consistently moist garden soil — its natural habitat includes flooded rice paddies and water garden margins. In zone 9, Black Magic is perennial, dying back in cold winters but reliably re-emerging from the persistent tubers in spring. Mass plantings create a dramatic, dark tropical ground layer beneath light-colored structures or light-foliaged trees.

common_name: Black Magic Taro (Dramatic Near-Black Elephant Ear for Tropical Gardens and Bogs)
