Scarify the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall for the strongest spring display, since the seedlings resent transplanting. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil where it tolerates drought. Plant it in mass for the most captivating effect in naturalized wildflower areas. Allow pods to ripen and it will self-sow to return year after year.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into lean, well-drained soil among established native grasses; close proximity to host grass roots is essential for successful germination and growth.
directions: Bluehearts is a striking native annual hemi-parasite of southeastern coastal plain pine savannas, attaching to the roots of nearby native grasses to obtain additional water and nutrients while still photosynthesizing on its own — for garden success, direct sow seeds into an area already colonized by native warm-season grasses such as little bluestem, wiregrass, or broomsedge, as plants cannot establish without host root contact. Slender, rough-textured stems rise from a basal rosette and bear erect spikes of vivid violet-blue tubular flowers from summer through fall, making Bluehearts one of the most visually stunning of all southeastern savanna wildflowers. It thrives in lean, sandy, or gravelly soils in full sun and does not tolerate shade, competition from dense vegetation, or artificially enriched garden soils. Once sown into a native grass planting, it often self-seeds in subsequent years, gradually becoming a reliable component of a savanna-style wildflower garden.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun. Bluejack Oak demands xeric, nutrient-poor conditions and will not tolerate clay, excessive moisture, or shading from taller vegetation.
directions: Bluejack Oak is a distinctive native tree of sandhills, xeric upland forest, and fire-maintained scrub across the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Texas, immediately recognizable among oaks by its blue-gray, paddle-shaped leaves with pale, hairy undersides that give the small tree a frosted, silvery appearance unlike any other eastern oak. Adapted to the driest, most nutrient-poor sandy soils of the coastal plain, Bluejack Oak is extremely drought-tolerant and fire-resilient, regenerating rapidly from its extensive root system after low-intensity fires that historically maintained the sandhills where it is one of the dominant trees. The small acorns ripen in fall and are a critical food source for white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, small mammals, and Florida Scrub-Jays in dry upland communities where larger mast-producing oaks may be absent. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun — Bluejack Oak will not tolerate clay, excess moisture, or shade.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or direct sow in early spring; bluestem goldenrod is one of the very few native goldenrods that thrives in significant shade, making it invaluable for shaded pollinator gardens.
directions: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, or provide 4–6 weeks of cold stratification before spring sowing; bluestem goldenrod grows in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil and is among the most shade-tolerant of all goldenrods. Solidago caesia is an eastern North American native goldenrod of deciduous forest interiors and edges producing slender, arching, bluish-green stems bearing clusters of small, bright-yellow flowers nestled in the leaf axils along the arching stem length (not in a large terminal plume like most goldenrods) from late summer through fall, creating an elegant, arching spray of yellow that is invaluable for late-season pollinator support in shaded gardens. Unlike most goldenrods that require full sun, bluestem goldenrod is specifically adapted to woodland shade and is an outstanding choice for the transition zone between sunny and shaded garden areas; it is an excellent companion for native wood asters, great Solomon's seal, and native ferns.

plant_note: Surface sow (light required for germination) in moist, slightly acidic soil; the plant self-sows to naturalize in moss gardens, lawn alternatives, and moist, shaded rock gardens.
directions: Scatter seed on moist, acidic soil in partial shade in early spring; this diminutive native wildflower carpets lawns, mossy banks, and lightly shaded meadows with pale blue four-petaled flowers in spring, creating an effect like scattered stars across a green sky. It naturally grows in thin, slightly moist, acidic soil of lawns and forest edges and is a wonderful component of a native lawn alternative. Allow it to go to seed after flowering to maintain the colony. The plant tolerates light foot traffic and can naturalize into an existing lawn if mowing is delayed until it sets seed in late spring. Does not perform well in heavy clay or alkaline soil.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; bluff oak is a white oak group species of bluffs, rocky slopes, and dry uplands of the lower Piedmont and Gulf Coastal Plain. It is closely related to Durand oak and often confused with it in the field.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; bluff oak is a medium to large white-oak group oak of the lower Piedmont and Gulf Coastal Plain, naturally growing on rocky bluffs, dry slopes, and upland sites from North Carolina to Georgia and Alabama. The leaves are variable but typically club-shaped with rounded lobes, resembling a smaller or more graceful white oak leaf. Like all white-oak group oaks, the sweet acorns ripen in a single season and are immediately germinated by squirrels and blue jays. The tree provides important acorn mast for wildlife and supports the full suite of moth and butterfly caterpillars that depend on native oaks. Relatively uncommon in cultivation and underused compared to its relatives, bluff oak is a dependable, drought-tolerant native for dry, upland settings in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; blunt-lobed woodsia is the most drought-tolerant native eastern fern and an excellent choice for dry, rocky shaded slopes and walls.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown plants in spring in dry to moist, rocky, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; blunt-lobed woodsia establishes readily and is among the most drought-tolerant of all native ferns, making it uniquely valuable for challenging dry, rocky, shaded garden situations. Woodsia obtusa is a delicate-looking but tough native fern widely distributed across eastern North America from Canada to the Gulf states, producing compact, 8–18 inch, slightly hairy, light green fronds that are twice-pinnate with distinctive blunt-tipped (obtuse) lobes from which it takes its name; unlike most ferns it thrives in well-drained, even dry, rocky, alkaline soil such as limestone ledges and rocky woods. An excellent candidate for rock gardens, shaded dry walls, and naturalized areas under trees where soil is shallow or competitive. Semi-evergreen in mild winters.

common_name: Blushing Bromeliad (Blushing Neoregelia, Tricolor Bromeliad, Cartwheel Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, shaded container, or in zone 9b-11 outdoor shade gardens; Neoregelia carolinae can survive brief temperatures to 30°F if the central tank is dry, making it one of the more cold-tolerant decorative bromeliads for Gulf Coast zone 9 outdoor use. In zone 9-10, plant in sheltered, shaded spots as a permanent groundcover or accent plant under large trees. Keep the central tank filled with water; empty and refill every 2 weeks. Unlike Vriesea and Guzmania, Neoregelia remains low and flat when in bloom. Propagate by separating and potting pups. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in moderate to bright indirect shade — Blushing Bromeliad adapts to a range of light conditions from deep shade (where it remains green) to bright indirect light (where variegated and colored forms show their best color) but should never receive direct sun, which burns the leaves. Neoregelia carolinae is a flat, spreading, tank bromeliad from the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil, producing a wide, symmetrical, cartwheel-like rosette of broad, strap-shaped leaves in medium to bright green — often with distinctive lengthwise cream-to-yellow stripes in the popular 'Tricolor' cultivar. The most dramatic feature is the plant's response to imminent blooming: weeks before the tiny flowers appear in the central cup, the inner ring of leaves surrounding the center turns brilliant red, crimson, or magenta — the 'blush' that gives the plant its common name. This red central color intensifies over months and persists long after the small, inconspicuous flowers in the central tank have finished — the bromeliad continues to display vivid red center leaves for 6–12 months before eventually declining. Neoregelia carolinae is one of the most widely used bromeliads in zone 9-10 outdoor shade gardens in Florida and the Gulf South, where its flat, spreading growth habit makes it an ideal accent plant, container plant, and groundcover in tropical-style shaded beds. More cold-tolerant than many bromeliads. Non-toxic to pets.

common_name: Blushing Bromeliad (Concentrica Neoregelia, Purple Heart Bromeliad, Bull's Eye Bromeliad)
plant_note: Grow in partial shade in a shallow pot with well-draining bromeliad mix or mounted epiphytically; Neoregelia concentrica is one of the largest and most dramatic of the Neoregelia bromeliads, producing broad, spreading rosettes of wide leaves (3–4 inches wide, 18–24 inches long) with the characteristic Neoregelia quality: the central cup of leaves turns from green to vivid purple, red, and pink around the time of flowering, and small blue flowers appear in the central pool of water held in the cup. Keep water in the central cup, refresh regularly to prevent stagnation. Tolerates brief freezes to 30°F when established. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in partial shade in a shallow pot with well-draining bromeliad mix or mounted on a tree branch — Blushing Bromeliad is one of the most ornamentally striking of the large Neoregelia species, producing extremely broad, spreading rosettes of flat leaves that make a bold statement in shaded garden beds and containers in zone 9-12. Neoregelia concentrica is a large, tank-forming, epiphytic bromeliad in the Bromeliaceae family native to southern Brazil — one of the parent species of many popular Neoregelia hybrids grown for their colorful, blushing inner leaves. The plant produces a broad, spreading, flat rosette of wide (3–4 inch), broadly strap-shaped leaves in dark green with a distinctive pattern of dark purple to black spotting, blotching, or banding. The most distinctive quality of Neoregelia concentrica, shared by Neoregelia species generally, is the dramatic color change that occurs around flowering time: the central leaves (the innermost ring surrounding the water-filled central cup) turn from green to vivid purple-red, pink, or burgundy — the 'blushing' effect that gives the group its common name — creating a brilliant, jewel-like central display that persists for many months. Small, lavender-blue flowers then emerge in the central water cup. Neoregelia concentrica is valued in the bromeliad trade as one of the broadest-leaved, most dramatically spotted and blushing of the species, and as a parent of many large-leaved, heavily-marked hybrids. Excellent in shaded beds, under palms and live oaks, or as epiphytic specimens on tree trunks. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to deep shade in zone 10–12; Blushing Philodendron is a vigorous, climbing, epiphytic aroid native to the Andean foothills and lowland forests of Colombia and Ecuador, the wild parent of many popular cultivated Philodendron varieties, bearing glossy, dark-green, heart-shaped leaves with distinctive red-maroon undersides and red-flushed petioles — producing long aerial-rooting stems that climb tree trunks and walls.
directions: Plant or root cuttings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade with a support — moss pole, tree trunk, or trellis — for climbing; Philodendron erubescens attaches by aerial roots and climbs vigorously in warm, humid conditions; water moderately and maintain high humidity for best growth. Philodendron erubescens (Blushing Philodendron or Red-leaf Philodendron) is a vigorous, hemi-epiphytic, climbing aroid native to the rainforests and cloud-forest edges of Colombia, Ecuador, and adjacent South America — the wild parent species from which many of the most popular commercial Philodendron cultivars were developed, including 'Imperial Red,' 'Painted Lady,' and 'Pink Princess.' In its wild form, P. erubescens produces large, glossy, arrow or heart-shaped leaves (up to 12–16 inches long) with deep-green upper surfaces and distinctive, attractive red-maroon to copper-red undersides — the 'blushing' coloration of the leaf undersides and the reddish-pink to red coloration of new leaves and petioles gives the species its name. The plant climbs vigorously by aerial roots that cling to rough bark, moss poles, or textured surfaces. In tropical outdoor cultivation (zone 10–12), P. erubescens makes an excellent climber on tree trunks, walls, and large trellises, providing attractive, large-leaved coverage in partial to deep shade positions. Contains calcium oxalate crystals — toxic if ingested by humans or pets.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bobo's dwarf stature (2.5–3 feet) makes it proportionate for foundation plantings, containers, and small residential borders where larger panicle hydrangeas would be overwhelming.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bobo is the most compact of the widely available panicle hydrangea cultivars — a dwarf selection staying just 2.5–3 feet tall and wide while producing flower panicles nearly as large as those of full-size cultivars like Limelight. This unusually large flower-to-plant-size ratio gives Bobo a heavily blooming, almost top-heavy appearance at peak bloom that creates a dramatic visual impact from a very compact plant. The large, cone-shaped flower panicles open pure white in mid-summer and transition through blush-pink to dusty rose as fall approaches — a 3–4 month evolving color display. Bobo's compact, mounding habit and relatively sturdy stems that hold the large flower heads erect without flopping make it one of the most practically useful panicle hydrangea introductions for residential landscape use. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Bobo blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter (to 12 inches or shorter) to encourage vigorous new growth and maximum flower production. This new-wood blooming habit means the timing of pruning is not critical — unlike the French hydrangeas that must be pruned at precisely the right time or lose the season's bloom. In zone 9, afternoon shade helps maintain flower color and extend the display season through the intense summer heat.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Bodinier's beautyberry produces more berries per cluster and larger, more metallic berries than the American species. Plant in groups of three or more for best berry production through cross-pollination. Prune hard (to 6 inches) in late winter each year to maintain compact, floriferous growth.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Bodinier's beautyberry is the Chinese species most widely considered superior to the American beautyberry (Callicarpa americana) for ornamental use, producing extraordinarily vivid, metallic violet-purple berries in very large, densely packed clusters along the arching branches in October–November — the intensity of the color approaches an almost unreal, electric quality that is one of the most striking autumn fruit displays in temperate horticulture. The clusters are larger, more densely packed, and the berry color more metallic and saturated than the American native. The cultivar 'Profusion' is the most widely planted and has become a standard of the British and American garden for its exceptional berry production. Unlike the American species, Bodinier's beautyberry is hardy to zone 5 without dieback. The pink to lilac summer flowers are small and inconspicuous. After frost removes the leaves, the vivid purple berry clusters on the bare, arching branches are an extraordinary sight that persists into winter and is eaten by birds.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost in a location with good air circulation. The cultivar 'Profusion' is especially valued for its dense clusters of vivid violet berries.
directions: Set transplants in well-drained soil amended with compost, spacing them 4 to 6 feet apart to allow the arching branches to develop freely. Water regularly through the first growing season to establish deep roots, then reduce irrigation as the shrub becomes more drought tolerant. Cut stems back by about one-third in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and the most prolific berry production the following autumn. The metallic violet-purple berry clusters persist on bare stems well into winter and are a standout in the landscape.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery plants in spring in wet, acidic, peaty or sandy bog soil in full sun to partial shade; bog asphodel requires year-round wet conditions and strongly acidic soil (pH 3.5–5.0).
directions: Narthecium americanum is a rare and beautiful native bog perennial of the Atlantic Coastal Plain, found only in a narrow strip of New Jersey, Delaware, and adjacent states in the open, wet, acidic, sphagnum-moss bog and pine barren habitats of the mid-Atlantic region, where it produces a fan-like tuft of narrow, iris-like leaves and a terminal spike of bright yellow star-shaped flowers with woolly yellow stamens in June and July, followed by ornamental orange-red seed capsules in fall. It requires year-round wet, strongly acidic (pH 3.5–5.0) conditions and is extremely sensitive to soil chemistry — it will not survive in alkaline or enriched soils. Grow in a constructed Sphagnum moss bog or wet sand medium with no added fertilizers; the species is a flagship plant for the globally rare Atlantic Coastal Plain bog community. Available only from specialist native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist to wet, acidic, peaty, poorly drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Bog Goldenrod is specifically adapted to the saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor conditions of sphagnum bogs, fens, and wet meadows — it will not thrive in ordinary garden soil without significant moisture.
directions: Bog Goldenrod is a native perennial of the cool, acidic sphagnum bogs, fens, wet meadows, and peaty swamp edges of the northeastern United States and Canada, occupying a specialized ecological niche shared with carnivorous plants, bog orchids, and other acid-loving bog species that most other goldenrods cannot tolerate. The slender, wand-like spikes of small yellow flowers are produced in August and September in the open, sunny conditions of floating sphagnum mats and sedge fens, attracting late-season native bees and butterflies that visit these specialized wetland habitats. Bog Goldenrod provides an important native plant option for water gardeners, bog garden enthusiasts, and restorers working with cold northern wetland habitats. Direct sow seeds in fall in moist to wet, acidic, peaty, permanently saturated or nearly saturated soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants spread slowly by rhizomes in appropriate bog or fen conditions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in permanently wet, strongly acidic (pH 3.5–5.0), nutrient-poor, sphagnum peat bog or fen conditions in full sun to partial sun. Bog Rosemary requires exceptionally cool, wet, acidic growing conditions and is only suitable for northern bog gardens or cool, high-altitude peat-moss landscapes — it will not survive in warm, dry, or alkaline conditions.
directions: Bog Rosemary is a native circumpolar evergreen shrub of the coldest, wettest, most acidic sphagnum bogs and arctic tundra of the Northern Hemisphere, prized among bog garden enthusiasts for its attractive, narrow, blue-green, rosemary-like evergreen leaves with rolled margins and beautiful clusters of small, pink, globe-shaped flowers in spring. Like other members of the blueberry family adapted to the specialized bog environment, Bog Rosemary requires extreme growing conditions — permanently saturated, strongly acidic (pH 3.5–5.0), nutrient-poor peat — and is entirely unsuitable for conventional garden soil or climates south of Zone 6. All parts of the plant contain grayanotoxins and are toxic to livestock; the specific epithet polifolia ('gray-leaved') refers to the glaucous appearance of the foliage. Plant rooted cuttings in permanently wet sphagnum peat in full sun; Bog Rosemary is an outstanding native specimen for cold-climate bog gardens, peat gardens, and tundra-habitat restorations where its specialized conditions can be maintained.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container transplants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; bog sage spreads aggressively by stolons in ideal moist conditions and requires regular division or containment to prevent it from overwhelming smaller garden neighbors.
directions: Root cuttings and plant in moist to consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade — bog sage from South America produces one of the most pure, clear, vivid sky-blue flower colors available in any garden plant: small, two-lipped, brilliant cerulean-blue flowers in dense terminal spikes from July through hard frost, on tall, gracefully arching stems of narrow, bright green leaves with a pleasant herbal fragrance. It grows naturally in boggy, wet meadows and stream margins and requires consistently moist soil — ideal for rain gardens, wet low areas, and the moist margins of ponds. The plant spreads vigorously by underground stolons in suitable conditions, eventually forming large patches: excellent for covering wet, difficult areas but needs management in smaller beds. In zone 7–8 it may die back in winter but resprouts reliably from established stolons; in zone 9–10 it grows as a large, nearly evergreen perennial. One of the finest late-season blue flowers for the moist garden.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in partial shade after last frost; Bolivian begonia performs best in bright indirect light to partial shade — full sun bleaches and scorches the flowers and foliage.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in partial shade; Bolivian begonia is the wild species parent behind many of the most popular trailing tuberous begonia hybrids (Begonia × tuberhybrida), bearing gracefully pendulous, tubular to saucer-shaped flowers of brilliant vermilion-red to orange in a continuous cascade from late spring until frost — hummingbirds are strongly attracted to the tubular flowers. Unlike wax begonias, Bolivian begonia has a naturally trailing, elegant branching habit that makes it exceptional in hanging baskets, tall containers, and window boxes where stems can arch downward. In zones 9–11 the plant overwinters as a small tuberous perennial. Excellent cultivars derived from this species include the celebrated 'Bonfire' (orange-red, excellent heat tolerance) and the 'Santa Cruz' series. Tubers can be dug before frost in colder zones and stored dry over winter.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring or divide established clumps in spring; boltonia spreads by short rhizomes and self-sows freely in favorable conditions. Tall plants in rich soil may require staking; in lean, dry soil plants are more compact and self-supporting. The cultivar 'Snowbank' is the most widely grown and most compact selection, reaching 3–4 feet rather than the species' 5–6 feet.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun; boltonia is a native North American prairie and wetland-edge perennial that earns its place in the late-season garden through sheer prolificacy — a tall, somewhat spreading plant that in August and September transforms itself into a cloud of thousands of tiny, asterlike daisy flowers in white to pale lavender, each only 3/4 inch across but produced in such extravagant abundance over the entire branch canopy that the plant becomes a mound of white or lavender from mid-summer through frost. The display at peak bloom resembles a multi-branched, five-foot shrub covered in snow — one of the most generous late-season bloomers available in the native plant palette. It thrives in wet or moderately moist soils and is naturally found along stream banks and wet meadows. The widely planted cultivar 'Snowbank' has particularly pure white flowers and a more manageable height. Excellent at the back of the border for late-season impact and valuable to migrating monarch butterflies and other late pollinators. Combines well with ornamental grasses, Joe-Pye weed, and late goldenrods.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost or in fall for winter-spring bloom; in zone 9 sow October–February. Bon Bon is the most compact calendula available — the dwarf 12-inch plants are ideal for containers, window boxes, and small-space gardens where standard 18–24 inch calendula would be too large. Deadhead regularly to extend bloom period. In zone 9 the cool-season fall-through-spring planting produces the most flowers before summer heat ends production.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Bon Bon is the most compact of the named calendula cultivars, forming tidy, mound-shaped plants only 10–14 inches tall and wide — roughly half the size of standard calendula varieties — while producing the same full double flower heads in a cheerful mix of deep orange, golden yellow, cream, and bicolor combinations. The reduced size makes Bon Bon uniquely suited for container growing, window box planting, and tight edging positions in herb and kitchen gardens where the standard species would crowd neighboring plants. Bon Bon calendula retains the same edible and medicinal properties as all Calendula officinalis — the petals are edible garnishes used in salads, soups, and as a natural food coloring, and the flowers are harvested for traditional medicinal preparations including calendula-infused oil and salve. The shorter, more branching habit typically produces more flowers per plant than taller varieties, increasing yield of edible and medicinal petals relative to plant footprint.

common_name: Bonanza Marigold (Compact Uniform French Marigold Series)
plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom; Bonanza is a compact, uniform French marigold series bred for bedding and container use, flowering quickly from seed.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Bonanza is a widely grown, compact French marigold series bred for a uniform, tidy, mounding habit and quick, heavy flowering from seed, making it a reliable choice for bedding displays, edging, and containers where consistent size and abundant bicolor or solid gold, orange, and red-toned blooms are wanted. It flowers quickly after sowing and continues through the heat of summer with good tolerance for poor soil and drought once established. Deadheading spent blooms encourages continued flowering, and the pungent foliage is generally avoided by deer and rabbits.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; boneset is one of the few native perennials that grows happily in both seasonally flooded lowlands and ordinary moist borders.
directions: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; boneset is one of the few native perennials that grows happily in both seasonally flooded lowlands and ordinary moist borders. Eupatorium perfoliatum is easily identified by its most unusual feature: pairs of opposite, lance-shaped leaves whose bases appear to completely fuse around the stem (perfoliate), as if the stem pierces through a single leaf; this trait led to the folk belief that the plant could "set" broken bones, hence the common name, and it was one of the most widely used medicinal plants of Native American and early American herbal medicine. Flat-topped clusters of white flowers bloom from late summer through fall, providing abundant nectar for monarchs, swallowtails, and countless native bees; the plant naturalizes well in moist native meadows, rain gardens, and riparian areas.

plant_note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks early or direct sow after frost.
directions: 'Bonita Top Blue' China aster bears richly saturated purple-blue blooms on sturdy, dark stems all summer long. Start seed indoors four to six weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once frost has passed. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, and rotate its planting spot yearly to reduce disease. The dark stems add contrast in bouquets and hold the blooms upright in the garden. With a long bloom period and excellent vase life, it is a top choice for cutting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil or well-draining potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; Boston fern requires high ambient humidity and consistently moist (never waterlogged) growing conditions — allow the root ball to never dry completely.
directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Boston fern is the most widely grown ornamental fern in the world — a classic porch, patio, and shade garden plant that produces graceful, arching, bright-green fronds of finely divided pinnate leaflets creating the ultimate soft, feathery, tropical foliage effect. In zones 9–12 it thrives as an outdoor perennial in shaded garden beds, under trees, and in shaded container plantings; throughout the United States it is the defining hanging basket plant for covered porches and shaded outdoor spaces in summer, then overwintered as a houseplant. High humidity is essential — in dry indoor air, foliage yellows and drops its leaflets (pinnules) rapidly, a problem solved by misting, pebble-tray humidifiers, or outdoor placement. 'Bostoniensis' is the classic form; 'Dallas' (tolerates lower humidity), 'Tiger' (heavily ruffled), and 'Florida Ruffle' are popular cultivars. The most widely sold fern in the United States by a considerable margin.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Boston fern requires consistently high humidity — the fronds turn yellow and shed leaflets rapidly in dry indoor air or low-humidity outdoor conditions. In zone 9–11 it can be grown outdoors year-round in sheltered, shaded spots.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Boston fern is the world's most widely grown ornamental fern and perhaps the most popular hanging basket plant in temperate and tropical horticulture, with long, graceful, arching fronds of soft, bright green pinnae that cascade elegantly over pot edges, porch railings, and tree branches. In zone 9–12 it thrives outdoors year-round in sheltered, shaded positions on porches, under pergolas, and beneath the canopy of large trees, where the naturally high humidity and warm temperatures suit it perfectly. The key cultural requirement is consistent moisture and humidity — fronds desiccate and shed leaflets rapidly in dry, hot, or low-humidity conditions. In outdoor zone 9 culture, light frost nips the fronds but established plants typically regrow from the crown. Divide congested clumps and remove dead fronds from the crown in spring. The related 'Kimberly Queen' fern (N. obliterata) is generally more heat and drought tolerant and better suited to humid Southern gardens.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in almost any soil in full sun to full shade; Boston ivy climbs by adhesive disc-tipped tendrils that adhere to virtually any rough surface without additional support. It will cover walls rapidly once established and is difficult to remove from masonry — site carefully. The cultivar 'Veitchii' has smaller, more finely textured leaves that turn brilliant crimson.
directions: Plant in almost any soil in full sun to full shade; Boston ivy is the quintessential self-clinging wall vine of ivy-covered colleges and historic buildings, native to China and Japan and widely planted worldwide for its ability to cover brick, stone, and concrete walls with a seamless carpet of foliage. The simple, three-lobed leaves (variable in shape) are overlapping and smooth-textured throughout summer, then transform in autumn to some of the most spectacular fall colors of any vine — brilliant crimson, scarlet, and burgundy, rivaling the finest maples in intensity. Unlike English ivy, Boston ivy is deciduous — letting winter light through the wall and providing summer cooling by shading the masonry while becoming bare in winter. It climbs by tiny, disc-tipped adhesive tendrils that grip masonry firmly without growing into mortar. The small blue-black berries in fall are an important food source for birds. Unlike its cousin Virginia creeper (P. quinquefolia), Boston ivy's three-lobed leaves have a slightly smoother texture and the vine tends to stay flatter against a wall.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained to consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade in spring; seeds require cold stratification (60-90 days at 35°F) to germinate — sow outdoors in fall for natural stratification or refrigerate moist seeds before indoor sowing.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; bottle gentian (closed gentian) is one of the most unusual and intriguing of all native North American wildflowers — the flowers never open. Deep navy-blue to violet, bottle-shaped flowers are clustered at the tops of leafy stems in late August through October, and they remain permanently closed — only large bumblebees are strong enough to force the petals open to access the nectar and pollen within, making them one of the few plants that have evolved an exclusively bumblebee-pollinated flower mechanism. The deep-blue color and late-season bloom make it one of the last truly vivid wildflowers of autumn, blooming alongside native asters and goldenrods. Requires consistently moist, slightly acidic soil and does not tolerate drought. An excellent plant for moist shade gardens, rain gardens, and stream-side plantings where its unique late-season flower adds genuine surprise and interest.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; bottle palm is frost-sensitive (damaged below 32°F, killed below 25°F) and requires a truly frost-free climate. Extremely rare in the wild — only about 10 individuals survive in the wild on Round Island, Mauritius.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–11; bottle palm is one of the world's most distinctive and beloved ornamental palms — the dramatically swollen, bottle-shaped trunk (widest near the base and narrowing dramatically as it rises) topped by a small crown of arching, pinnate fronds is one of the most instantly recognizable palm silhouettes. Native exclusively to Round Island, a small uninhabited island north of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean, where it is critically endangered — fewer than 10 wild individuals survive due to historical invasive species damage. However, it is widely cultivated throughout the tropical and subtropical world as an ornamental, with hundreds of thousands of cultivated specimens in gardens, parks, and streets. The bottle shape is most pronounced in younger trees, typically becoming less pronounced with age as the trunk elongates. Extremely salt-tolerant and well-adapted to sandy, dry, coastal conditions. One of the premier ornamental palms for South Florida, Hawaii, and similar frost-free climates.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Bottle Rocket needs steady soil moisture and wilts dramatically in dry spells, though it recovers with watering — best sited at a pond edge, streamside, or damp low spot.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun and drying wind; mulch to conserve soil moisture and water deeply during dry spells. Bottle Rocket is a compact selection of Ligularia stenocephala, grown for its bold, deeply toothed, dark green leaves and, in mid-to-late summer, dense, upright, narrow spikes of bright yellow flowers that resemble small exploding fireworks or rockets — considerably more compact and garden-friendly than the species and older ligularia cultivars, which can sprawl to 4–5 feet. The strong vertical flower spikes provide valuable late-summer color and form in the shade garden, and the foliage itself is architecturally bold enough to serve as a textural anchor even before bloom. Best used at the moist margins of a shaded water feature, rain garden, or low spot where soil never fully dries out, in zone 4–8.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; bottlebrush buckeye is one of the few large shrubs that genuinely thrives in deep shade. It spreads by root suckers to form colonies — allow adequate space of 8–12 feet diameter per plant.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in deep to part shade; bottlebrush buckeye is one of the most dramatic large shade shrubs in American horticulture, producing spectacular 8–12 inch cylindrical flower spikes (panicles) of densely packed white flowers with long, prominent, reddish-pink stamens in midsummer — hence 'bottlebrush' — at precisely the time when most shade shrubs have finished blooming, filling a critical gap in the summer woodland garden. The bold, tropical-looking, palmately compound leaves (5–7 leaflets each to 8 inches long) create dense shade and turn clear yellow in fall. Native to the understory of moist forests in Alabama and Georgia, it is one of the rare large shrubs that performs as well or better in dense shade as in sun. Spreads by suckers to form broad, dramatic colonies. Hummingbirds and large bumblebees are the primary pollinators. All parts are mildly toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; bottlebrush grass self-sows reliably in appropriate conditions and naturalizes to form a loose colony in moist woodland edge settings.
directions: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade — bottlebrush grass is one of the few native ornamental grasses that genuinely thrives in partial to light shade, making it exceptional for the shaded garden or woodland edge where most grasses cannot grow. The distinctive, upright, cylindrical seed heads — radiating individual spikelets outward from the stem in a perfect bottle-brush pattern — are among the most ornamental of any native grass, remaining attractive from summer through winter as they dry to tan. It grows naturally in moist, rich woodland edges, ravine banks, and moist forest floors throughout the eastern US. Self-sows reliably in appropriate conditions to naturalize. Outstanding for adding native grass texture to shaded areas of the garden or in combination with native wildflowers and ferns along a woodland edge.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; bougainvillea strongly dislikes wet feet and disturbed roots — plant with care, minimizing root disturbance, and do not overwater. Deliberately stressing the plant by slightly withholding water after establishment triggers the most prolific bloom.
directions: Plant in very well-drained soil in full sun; bougainvillea is the quintessential tropical vine of warm-climate gardens, producing massive displays of brilliantly colored papery bracts (the true flowers are small and white at the bract center) in shades of magenta, red, orange, pink, white, and bicolor from spring through fall — especially spectacular in late winter and spring in zone 9. The plant is a vigorous, thorny scrambler that must be trained on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence; it is not self-clinging and must be tied. Light stress (slight drought, slightly root-bound) dramatically increases bloom production. In zone 9, it may suffer frost damage in cold winters but typically regrows from the base; in zone 10–11 it blooms nearly year-round. Prune after each major bloom cycle to encourage re-blooming. Extremely heat, drought, and salt tolerant once established — one of the most spectacular flowering vines available for Gulf Coast landscapes.

common_name: Bougainvillea Spectabilis (Great Bougainvillea, Paper Flower, Bugambilia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in late spring after last frost in full sun on a sturdy trellis, wall, fence, or arbor; Bougainvillea spectabilis is more vigorous and larger than B. glabra and requires stout supports — established plants can carry enormous weight. In zone 9a, freeze damage is common but established plants resprout vigorously; in zone 9b it is semi-evergreen and blooms most heavily in dry, cooler seasons. Withhold water and fertilizer for 4–6 weeks to stress-trigger heavy bloom. The actual flowers are tiny; the spectacular color comes from the papery bracts.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Bougainvillea blooms most prolifically in full sun with moderate stress — overwatering and over-fertilizing produce excessive vegetative growth at the expense of flowering. Bougainvillea spectabilis is a massive, vigorous, thorny, woody climbing vine native to eastern and central Brazil, widely regarded as one of the most spectacular flowering plants in the subtropical and tropical world. Like all Bougainvillea, the apparent flowers are actually highly colored papery bracts (modified leaves) — magenta, purple, crimson, orange, pink, white, yellow, or bicolor depending on cultivar — surrounding the tiny, inconspicuous true flowers within. The bracts persist on the vine for months and are produced so profusely that a specimen in full bloom is literally buried under color. B. spectabilis is one of the two primary species (along with B. glabra) from which nearly all cultivated Bougainvillea hybrids have been developed; it is distinguished by its larger, pubescent (hairy-textured) bracts and more vigorous growth than B. glabra. The iconic vine of Mediterranean and tropical architecture — covering walls, pergolas, gateways, and entire buildings in swaths of brilliant color — Bougainvillea is the definitive plant of zone 9b-11 Gulf Coast, South Texas, California, and Florida landscapes. Sharp, stout thorns require care when pruning.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in cool soil; soak seed first.
directions: Bouquet Blend is a colorful mix of Spencer-type sweet peas with extra-large flowers, long sturdy stems, and many blooms per stem for cutting. Soak the seed overnight and direct sow in early spring in cool soil, since sweet peas relish chilly weather. Provide a trellis or netting for the vines to climb and grow in full sun to part shade in rich, well-drained soil. Keep evenly watered and cut flowers frequently to prolong the lightly scented bloom. Frequent cutting and cool conditions extend the season into early summer.

common_name: Bower Vine (Bower of Beauty, Pink Bower Vine, Jasmine Pandorea)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a trellis, pergola, fence, or arbor in full sun to partial shade; Bower Vine grows rapidly in zone 9 and begins blooming in spring. It is more cold-tolerant than many tropical vines, surviving temperatures to 28°F briefly — established plants in zone 9a often survive winters and resprout from the crown. Prune lightly after the main spring bloom to shape; avoid hard pruning in fall which removes next year's flower buds. The cultivar 'Lady Di' (pure white flowers) and 'Rosea' (deep pink) are widely available. Propagate from stem cuttings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Bower Vine blooms most prolifically in full sun but performs well in partial shade and actually benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Pandorea jasminoides is a vigorous, twining, evergreen vine native to eastern Australia (Queensland and New South Wales) in the Bignoniaceae family, one of the finest Australian native vines for subtropical and warm-temperate gardens worldwide. The plant produces attractive, pinnately-compound leaves with 5–9 leaflets that create a fine-textured, airy, dark-green canopy on whatever structure the vine covers. In spring and intermittently through the warm months, the vine produces clusters of funnel-shaped to trumpet-shaped flowers in shades of white to soft pink, typically with a distinct deep rose-pink to rose-red interior throat — the clean, elegant color combination has made Bower Vine one of the most popular ornamental vines for zone 9-11 gardens, walls, and arbors. The flowers are lightly fragrant in warm conditions. Multiple cultivars are available: 'Rosea' (deeper pink), 'Lady Di' (pure white with no pink throat), and 'Rosea Superba' (larger, deeper flowers). Bower Vine is relatively free of pest and disease problems in zone 9 conditions, making it one of the most reliable and beautiful low-maintenance ornamental vines for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bowie's sorrel is a summer-rainfall species (unlike most Cape oxalis which follow the winter-rainfall cycle) and grows in summer and flowers in late summer and autumn (August–October in the Northern Hemisphere). It has large, attractive, dark-green, three-parted leaves and produces one of the largest and most vivid pink-rose flowers of any oxalis. More vigorous and spreading than most Cape oxalis.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Bowie's sorrel is an unusual South African oxalis that blooms in late summer and autumn rather than the spring of the winter-rainfall Cape species — a summer-rainfall species from the moister, eastern parts of South Africa — and produces what are, for the genus, notably large flowers: loose clusters of 3–5 deep rose-pink to magenta-pink, five-petaled flowers of 1.5–2 inches across (large for an oxalis) above dark-green, medium-sized, three-parted, clover-like leaves. The rich, vivid rose-pink color is deep and saturated, a warm, cheerful autumn pink that provides good late-season color in zones 8–11. More vigorous and spreading than the smaller, more delicate Cape winter-rainfall oxalis species, it builds substantial clumps in well-drained, sunny to partly shaded positions and can be used as an informal groundcover in the right conditions. It was named for James Bowie, the plant collector who introduced it to cultivation in the early nineteenth century during botanical expeditions to South Africa. An excellent autumn-blooming bulb for zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Bowles Vinca Minor is less aggressive than Vinca major (greater periwinkle) — a more restrained spreader that fills in shaded areas without the invasive tendency of its larger relative. In zone 9 the plant remains semi-evergreen through mild winters and spreads gradually via rooting stems. Unlike Vinca major, which can become invasive in mild climates, Vinca minor spreads slowly enough to be manageable in most garden situations. An excellent choice for shaded slopes, under trees, and in areas where conventional lawn grass fails.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Vinca minor tolerates a wide range of conditions and is one of the most reliable shade ground covers for difficult areas; Bowles is a selected cultivar of lesser periwinkle (Vinca minor) with larger flowers than the typical species — the lavender-blue, five-petaled, pinwheel-shaped flowers are noticeably larger (0.75–1 inch across) than standard Vinca minor, making Bowles the showiest of the periwinkle cultivars for ornamental impact in shade gardens. The glossy, small, dark green leaves form a dense, weed-suppressing mat 4–6 inches high that spreads gradually by rooting stems — creating a low-maintenance evergreen carpet under trees and in shaded slopes where lawn grass and most ground covers fail. Unlike the invasive Vinca major, Vinca minor is generally considered manageable in most garden settings, spreading at a modest rate that allows easy control by edging. The spring bloom (April–May) covers the established mat in periwinkle-blue flowers; occasional reblooming occurs in fall. Vinca minor is one of the most reliably effective ground covers for dry shade under mature trees — tolerating the combination of shade and root competition that defeats most other plants.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring and replant divisions immediately into consistently moist to waterlogged soil in partial shade; the golden color intensifies with some direct morning sun but bleaches to pale chartreuse in deep shade or harsh afternoon light.
directions: Divide established clumps in early spring or fall and replant immediately in consistently moist to waterlogged soil at pond edges, bog gardens, or perpetually damp borders in partial shade; Bowles' golden sedge produces arching tufts of brilliant gold-yellow leaves edged with a thin green margin that illuminate shaded spots with a warm, luminous glow all season. Color is most intense in positions with morning sun and adequate moisture, and may bleach in deep shade or prolonged drought. Cut back any tatty foliage in late winter before new growth emerges. An excellent container subject when kept standing in a saucer of water.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Bowman's root is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled — give it 2–3 years to reach full flowering potential.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — Bowman's root is a graceful, airy native perennial of eastern woodland understories, producing a cloud of delicate five-petaled white to pale pink flowers on reddish-tinged branching stems in late spring to early summer — one of the most elegant of all native shade-garden plants. The leaves are trifoliate (three leaflets), giving it the specific epithet, and color attractively to orange-red in fall. It grows naturally in moist, rich, rocky woodland slopes and ravine banks from Ontario south to Georgia. Unlike most shade perennials it has a somewhat shrubby, upright structure rather than a mounding habit, adding height and structure to the shaded border. Bowman's root serves as a host plant for several native moth species and provides nectar for hummingbirds. Once established it is long-lived and low-maintenance. An outstanding native for the woodland garden in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; box honeysuckle is extremely easy to root and establishes rapidly, making it one of the most economical shade hedging options available.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; box honeysuckle is a Chinese evergreen shrub grown as a boxwood alternative for formal hedging in shade and difficult conditions where true boxwood (Buxus) struggles — its small, paired, glossy, oval leaves and dense, twiggy growth habit create the same refined, fine-textured, formal effect that makes boxwood so desirable, but it tolerates more shade, heat, drought, and alkaline soil than boxwood. Small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers appear in spring, followed by small, translucent, purple-red berries. It clips beautifully into formal geometric shapes and responds vigorously to shearing. 'Elegant' and 'Maigrün' (Golden-tipped new growth) are improved selections. An underused, extremely tough alternative to the blight-susceptible boxwoods increasingly being replaced across North American gardens.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in any well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Boxelder self-seeds prolifically and should be planted thoughtfully as a intentional native tree rather than allowed to spread unmanaged in formal landscapes.
directions: Boxelder is a native maple unlike any other — with pinnately compound leaves (3–7 leaflets) that bear no resemblance to the classic maple leaf — native throughout almost the entirety of North America east of the Rockies and naturalized well beyond, growing in river floodplains, bottomlands, stream corridors, and disturbed urban habitats with the same casual colonizing energy as cottonwood. Often dismissed as a weed tree in horticultural circles, Boxelder provides important ecological services that more ornamental trees cannot match: it is the only host plant for the Boxelder bug (Boisea trivittata), a harmless true bug that is a significant food source for many native birds; female trees produce abundant samaras (paired winged seeds) that are an important winter food for evening grosbeaks, finches, and other seed-eating birds; and the fast-growing tree provides rapid canopy cover for riparian restoration. Tolerant of flooding, drought, poor soils, and urban pollution, Boxelder is effectively impossible to kill once established and self-seeds prolifically — use it intentionally in naturalistic, riparian, or wildlife plantings where its resilience is an asset.

plant_note: Surface sow in spring in consistently wet to saturated, acidic soil at pond margins, bogs, or shallow seeps in partial shade; seeds require light for germination and must not dry out — press onto wet substrate and maintain standing shallow water or saturated conditions throughout establishment.
directions: Lobelia boykinii is a federally threatened native lobelia of the southeastern coastal plain, restricted in the wild to shallow ponds, seepage bogs, and wet glades in the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida where it serves as an important indicator of high-quality wetland habitat; it produces pale blue to nearly white flowers on stems that stand upright from shallow standing water or saturated soil from summer into early fall. Because of its federal threatened status, all plants in cultivation must come from legally obtained nursery-propagated stock — never collect from wild populations. Establish in the wettest part of a rain garden, bog garden, or at the margins of a wildlife pond in partial shade; consistent shallow inundation or saturated soil is essential and the plant will not persist through drought.

common_name: Bracken's Brown Beauty Magnolia (Cold-Hardy Southern Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Bracken's Brown Beauty is the hardiest widely available Southern magnolia cultivar and is the best choice where zone 5–6 cold hardiness is needed.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Bracken's Brown Beauty is one of the most exceptional named Southern magnolia cultivars for cold-climate performance — consistently hardy in zone 5 with reliable protection and zone 6 without protection, significantly colder than most Southern magnolia cultivars. It was selected by Ray Bracken of Bracken's Greenhouses in Easley, South Carolina, from seedlings grown at the Secrest Arboretum in Wooster, Ohio — selected specifically for cold hardiness in a climate where Southern magnolias are not traditionally grown. Despite its northern origin, it performs beautifully in zone 9 and throughout the Southeast. The leaves are particularly distinctive: smaller and more densely arranged than many cultivars, with an exceptionally rich, dark cinnamon-brown to rusty-red woolly undersurface (indumentum) that is thicker and more prominent than most selections, creating year-round visual interest as the wind moves the leaves to reveal the contrasting undersides. The medium-sized flowers (5–7 inches) are intensely fragrant and produced prolifically from May through September in zone 9. Bracken's Brown Beauty grows to full tree size (20–30+ feet) and is appropriate for medium-to-large landscape plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in dry, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; does not transplant well and requires infertile conditions to thrive.
directions: Direct sow in spring after all frost danger has passed in dry, sandy, infertile, acidic soil in full sun; avoid enriched garden soils where this species will fail to establish. The plant produces paired leaflets and small bright yellow pea flowers from summer through fall, each blossom tucked behind a distinctive pair of large leafy bracts that give the species its common name. Seeds form in jointed, sticky segments that are consumed eagerly by bobwhite quail and mourning dove, making this species valuable for longleaf pine savanna restorations and wildlife food plots. Avoid irrigation once plants are established, as excess moisture quickly leads to root rot in this dry-adapted native annual legume.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in very dry, well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; cold stratification through winter improves spring germination.
directions: Bractless Blazingstar is a native perennial of the Loasaceae family endemic to the dry, sandy prairies and rocky open ground of the Great Plains, where it produces leafy, branching stems topped with white, star-shaped flowers 2 to 3 inches across — each bloom packed with dozens of long, showy stamens that glow in the fading evening light. The flowers open at dusk and emit a sweet nocturnal fragrance that draws hawk moths and night-flying native bees, making this an exceptional plant for moonlight and pollinator gardens. The barbed, Velcro-like hairs covering the leaves and stems are an adaptation for seed dispersal via animal fur and clothing. Direct sow in fall in extremely lean, sandy or gravelly, fast-draining soil in full sun; established plants develop deep taproots and are among the most drought-tolerant native perennials of the Great Plains, requiring no supplemental water once settled.

plant_note: Plant in crevices of shaded rock walls or outcroppings in moist, humus-rich, very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral substrate in part shade to full shade; Bradley spleenwort is a native American fern naturally adapted to shaded rock crevices and cliffs and requires excellent drainage around the root crown — it will not tolerate waterlogged soil.
directions: Plant in shaded rock crevices or well-drained rock-garden pockets in moist but freely draining, slightly acidic soil; excellent for shaded stone walls and rocky slopes. Asplenium bradleyi (Bradley's spleenwort) is a small, charming native fern found on shaded sandstone and acidic rock outcroppings from Pennsylvania through the Appalachians to Alabama and Arkansas — one of the few ferns naturally adapted to the sharply drained, stressful conditions of vertical rock surfaces. It is a hybrid species (A. montanum × A. platyneuron) producing semi-evergreen, once-pinnate fronds 4–8 inches long with a distinctive dark-brown to nearly black midrib (rachis) contrasting with medium-green leaflets — giving the frond a two-toned, elegant appearance. While rarely available in general nurseries, it is grown by fern specialists and is an outstanding subject for naturalistic rock gardens, shaded stone walls, and terrarium-style displays. The dark midrib trait comes from its ebony spleenwort parent (A. platyneuron). Best planted in fall or early spring; protect from full exposure until established in its rocky pocket.

common_name: Branford Beauty Fern (Vigorous Silver-Painted Hybrid Lady Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Branford Beauty is a sterile hybrid between Japanese painted fern and lady fern, combining painted fern's silvery coloring with lady fern's larger size and greater vigor and heat tolerance.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Branford Beauty is a sterile hybrid between Japanese painted fern (Athyrium niponicum) and the native lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), combining the silvery-gray frond coloring and reddish stems inherited from its painted fern parent with the larger stature, greater vigor, and improved heat tolerance of lady fern. The result is a more substantial, faster-growing plant than a typical Japanese painted fern, better able to hold up through Gulf South summer heat and humidity while retaining much of the ornamental silver coloring that makes painted ferns so popular. Fronds emerge silvery-gray with burgundy-red stems in spring, filling out into an attractive, arching clump that provides season-long texture in the shade garden. As a sterile hybrid, it does not set spores and spread by itself, making it a well-behaved choice for mixed shade plantings alongside hostas, heucheras, and other ferns. Cut back old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors when temperatures approach 50°F. Brasil Philodendron grows as a trailing or climbing vine, extending several feet in a single season when well-grown. Stem cuttings root easily in water or moist potting mix, making propagation simple. Outdoors on a shaded porch or pergola in zone 9, the warm summer humidity promotes rapid growth and large, vivid leaves. In zone 10–11 it can be grown as a permanent outdoor shade plant in protected locations.
directions: Plant in bright indirect light to shade — never in direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil; Brasil is a variegated cultivar of Heartleaf Philodendron (Philodendron hederaceum) producing the familiar heart-shaped leaves of the parent species in a striking bicolor pattern — each leaf displays a central zone of chartreuse to bright yellow-green contrasting with the dark forest green of the leaf margins, with the boundary between the two tones being irregular and painterly rather than a precise stripe. The color pattern creates a vivid, spontaneous, almost abstract effect that gives Brasil philodendron a more artful and dynamic quality than regularly striped or symmetrically patterned foliage plants. The trailing, vining habit makes Brasil excellent for hanging baskets, the edges of containers, and as a trailing accent on shaded shelves and pedestals — the long stems cascading over the container edges to create a flowing, lush effect. Heartleaf Philodendron in general is one of the most genuinely shade- and low-light-tolerant trailing plants available, surviving in conditions where most other ornamental plants decline, making Brasil one of the most practically useful shade container plants for zone 9 covered patios and indoor situations.

Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, cool, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Braun's holly fern needs more consistent moisture and cooler conditions than Japanese holly fern and is best in northern zones and high-elevation gardens. Polystichum braunii is a beautiful, semi-evergreen to evergreen native fern of cool, moist hardwood and mixed forests of eastern North America, Europe, and Asia; its elegant, narrowly lanceolate fronds are densely covered in silvery-white scales when unfurling in spring, creating a striking pewter effect, and the mature fronds are lustrous, deep green with neatly doubly-pinnate, spiny-tipped pinnae giving it the holly-fern look shared by the genus. It is an outstanding choice for shaded rock gardens, cool woodland borders, and naturalizing under conifers in zones 3–7.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile potting mix or garden soil in shade to part shade; Brazilian coleus is a trailing South African plectranthus with distinctive, velvety, rounded, dark-green leaves traced with silver veins on the upper surface and purple on the underside — one of the most beautiful foliage plants for shade containers and hanging baskets.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; water when the top inch of soil dries. Plectranthus oertendahlii (Brazilian coleus or silver spurflower) is a trailing South African succulent-stemmed perennial in the mint family (Lamiaceae), native to the shaded, moist forest floors of KwaZulu-Natal province in South Africa. Despite the common name 'Brazilian coleus,' it is entirely South African in origin — the misnomer likely arises from its use as a tropical shade plant in Brazilian gardens. The plant produces distinctively beautiful, rounded, scalloped-edged leaves (1–2 inches across) with a velvety texture, dark-green with prominently traced, pale-silver veins on the upper surface and a rich purple-burgundy on the underside — one of the most attractive foliage patterns in the plectranthus family. It produces spikes of small, white to pale-lavender flowers but is grown primarily for foliage. As a shade container and hanging basket plant, P. oertendahlii is outstanding — the trailing stems and beautiful leaf patterning make it an eye-catching specimen. It also works beautifully as a shade terrarium subject and as an indoor plant in low-light situations. The cultivar 'Uvongo' has particularly striking leaf markings.

common_name: Brazilian Joseph Coat (Purple Calico Plant, Bloodleaf Joyweed)
plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or purchased transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Brazilian joyweed roots easily from cuttings placed in moist soil or water, making propagation trivially simple for overwintering or expanding plantings.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun (for deepest foliage color) to part shade; tip-prune regularly to maintain bushy, compact growth and prevent legginess. Alternanthera brasiliana (Brazilian Joseph coat) is a fast-growing tropical tender perennial or warm-season annual grown for its spectacular deep-purple to burgundy-purple, bronze, and maroon foliage — among the most richly colored of all foliage annuals. The narrow, lance-shaped to spatula-shaped leaves are a uniform deep burgundy-purple above and lighter purple below; the color is most intense in full sun. Like other alternantheras, it is used extensively as an edging or carpet-bedding plant in formal annual color schemes, and its rich foliage color creates outstanding contrast against chartreuse, gold, or white flowering annuals. Brazilian joyweed grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and provides consistent foliage color from spring through frost without the need for regular deadheading. In zone 9–10, it often survives mild winters and resprouts from roots; take stem cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, lean to average, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 7–10; Brazilian Needle Palm is among the most cold-hardy of all South American palms — native to the campos of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina, tolerating temperatures to 12–18°F when established — with stiff, blue-green fan fronds and a distinctive trunk covered in persistent, matted fiber and needle-like spines.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to average soil; Trithrinax brasiliensis is drought tolerant and adapted to poor, dry grassland soils of the South American campos — requires excellent drainage; water regularly only in establishment, then minimal supplemental water needed in appropriate climates. Trithrinax brasiliensis (Brazilian Needle Palm or Spiny Trunk Palm) is an attractive, slow-growing fan palm native to the subtropical campos (savanna grasslands) of Rio Grande do Sul in southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northeastern Argentina, one of the most cold-tolerant fan palms available from South America. The trunk is distinctive: covered in a dense mat of persistent leaf-base fibers and needle-like spines up to several inches long that give it a rough, armored texture. The stiff, flat fan fronds — divided into narrow segments — have a blue-green to silvery-green color that contrasts beautifully with the dark trunk. Cold hardiness is the plant's outstanding horticultural characteristic: established specimens survive temperatures of 12–18°F (zone 7b–8a) when planted in well-drained soils, making it one of the very few ornamental palms suitable for garden conditions in zone 7. Drought tolerant once established. A valuable, unusual cold-hardy palm for large landscape gardens in the South and Southwest United States where an extremely exotic, palm-like accent plant is desired in zone 7 or warmer climates.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, organically rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade after last frost; Brazilian plume flower blooms most heavily in late summer to fall and again in spring in frost-free climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil in partial to full shade; Brazilian plume flower is a South American native soft-wooded shrub that delivers one of the most spectacular flower displays possible in a shaded landscape — dense, upright, plume-like clusters of tubular rose-pink to deep magenta flowers from late summer through frost, and again in spring. The large, oval, dark-green leaves are handsome throughout the year. Hummingbirds visit the flowers repeatedly. Requires consistent moisture and resents drought; water deeply during hot, dry spells. Cut back by one-half to two-thirds in early spring to promote vigorous, floriferous new growth. In zone 9 it may be killed to the ground by hard frost but re-sprouts from the base; mulch heavily in winter.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in zone 9–11; Brazilian Skyflower is a compact, rounded shrub from the scrubby savannas and forest edges of Brazil — smaller and more cold-hardy than the common Pigeon Berry (Duranta erecta) — producing abundant sprays of small, violet-blue to lavender flowers in dense, narrow racemes throughout the warm season, followed by yellow-orange berry clusters, and making an excellent low hedge or border shrub for warm gardens.
directions: Plant Duranta stenostachya in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; prune after flowering to maintain compact shape; more cold-hardy than Duranta erecta, tolerating light frost to about 28°F. CAUTION: the berries are toxic to humans and pets. Brazilian Skyflower is a close relative of the widely grown Pigeon Berry (Duranta erecta) but with a distinctly different character: where D. erecta is a large, sprawling, vigorous shrub or small tree reaching 15 feet, D. stenostachya stays compact and rounded at 3–6 feet, making it much more manageable in typical garden situations. The flower spikes are narrower and more erect than D. erecta's cascading clusters, giving a slightly different visual effect; the violet-blue to lavender flower color is similar. Originally from the cerrado and forest-savanna transitions of interior Brazil, it is adapted to the seasonal drought and lean soils of tropical savannas — making it more drought-tolerant than D. erecta once established. The compact form makes it an excellent choice for informal hedges, mixed shrub borders, and foundation plantings in zone 9–11 gardens. Butterflies and hummingbirds visit the flowers just as reliably as they visit D. erecta. The yellow-orange berry clusters are ornamental through winter and much appreciated by mockingbirds and thrushes — but should not be eaten by people or pets.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Brazilian tree fern forms a dramatic architectural accent with new fronds emerging in coppery-red before maturing to dark green.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Brazilian tree fern develops a short, scaly trunk over time and produces striking architectural fronds up to 3 feet long with a distinctive ladder-like arrangement of leaflets. New croziers and expanding fronds emerge in vivid copper to red tones before maturing to dark, glossy green. The contrast between the dark mature fronds and the red new growth is especially dramatic in spring. It thrives in sheltered, humid, shaded positions in zones 8b-11, excellent at the base of a building wall or among large tropical perennials in a sheltered courtyard garden.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into a sunny location; thin seedlings to allow ample room for the tall, branching stems to develop.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in a sunny, open site and thin to 18-24 inches apart; plants grow quickly into tall, stiff-stemmed clumps that need no staking in most conditions. From summer through frost, the candelabra-like branching spikes carry masses of tiny purple-violet flowers that are outstanding butterfly magnets, particularly for skippers, painted ladies, and swallowtails. Cut plants back by half after the first flowering flush to encourage a second wave of bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding. This naturalized South American species self-sows prolifically and can spread widely in open, sunny sites across the Southeast, so site it where volunteer seedlings can be tolerated or remove spent flower heads to manage spread.

plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks early; darkness aids germination.
directions: Brazilian vervain, also called tall or purpletop verbena, sends up airy wands of rose-violet to lavender blooms atop tall, slender stems. Start seed indoors six to eight weeks early, covering it since darkness aids germination. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil where it tolerates drought once established. Its see-through height creates a light, floating layer of color in the border and is a magnet for butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds. It reseeds readily as a welcome volunteer and is grown as an annual where winters are cold.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade after frost; Brazilian yellow sage blooms most heavily in fall and winter in frost-free climates and performs best in consistent moisture with partial-shade protection from intense afternoon sun, which causes leaf scorch.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Brazilian yellow sage (yellow jacobinia, golden justicia, golden plume) is a Central American tropical shrub of the family Acanthaceae that produces dense, upright, cone-shaped spikes of bright-yellow, tubular, two-lipped flowers in the fall and winter months — at a time when yellow-flowering shade plants are exceptionally rare. The golden-yellow flower spikes, clustered densely at the tips of the arching stems, provide a vivid autumn-to-winter color display in the warm-climate garden that is nearly unmatched among partial-shade flowering shrubs. The large, soft, oval, velvety-hairy leaves are attractive and provide bold foliage texture in the shade garden. Like other shade-tolerant members of the Acanthaceae, it performs remarkably well in the dappled light of open tree canopies — one of few large-growing shade-tolerant shrubs that produce ornamental spikes of flowers rather than solitary tubular flowers. In zone 9 it freezes to the ground but regrows vigorously in spring. Cut back after flowering to encourage compact regrowth.

plant_note: Direct sow in very early spring or fall; seeds germinate in cool soil and seedlings tolerate frost.
directions: Surface sow by scattering seed on bare ground and pressing lightly without covering, as light aids germination. Breadseed poppies resent root disturbance and must be sown in place. Thin to 6–12 in when seedlings are 2 in tall. The ornamental seedpods are striking after petals drop and are valuable dried; harvest when the cap at the top turns from green to tan.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; breath of heaven requires excellent drainage — it declines quickly in wet, heavy, or poorly-drained soils. Do not over-fertilize; rich soils reduce flowering and shorten plant life. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain compact shape.
