It tolerates more direct sun than many older coleus cultivars while still performing well in bright shade, giving flexibility in siting. Pinch out flower spikes as soon as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage production and to prevent it from becoming leggy, and pinch stem tips periodically to encourage bushy, well-branched growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; camphor daisy grows naturally on Gulf Coast beaches, dunes, and coastal prairies and is highly tolerant of salt spray, sandy soil, and reflected heat.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun — camphor daisy is a native coastal plain annual of the Gulf Coast, naturalized on barrier island beaches, coastal prairies, and sunny, sandy disturbed areas from Texas to Florida, producing masses of small, bright yellow daisy flowers from summer through fall on aromatic, distinctively camphor-scented foliage. The strong, medicinal camphor fragrance is distinctive and immediately recognizable; the plant is named for it. A fast-growing, tough annual that handles the extreme conditions of the Gulf Coast shore: salt spray, drought, nutrient-poor sandy soil, and reflected heat from sand. It self-sows readily to maintain colonies in coastal gardens and is excellent for naturalistic sandy, sunny gardens and coastal erosion-prone areas. Very low maintenance and requires no supplemental irrigation in coastal conditions. The flowers attract small bees and butterflies including skippers and sulfurs.

plant_note: Surface sow without covering seeds — they need light to germinate; keep soil consistently moist.
directions: Pluchea camphorata is a strongly camphor-scented native annual or short-lived perennial in the aster family, producing flat-topped clusters of rosy-purple flowers from July through October that are highly attractive to small native bees, skippers, and monarch butterflies. It is native to moist, open habitats including coastal marshes, streambanks, wet ditches, and pond margins throughout the southeastern US, and grows vigorously in consistently moist to wet, full-sun conditions. Seeds require light to germinate — surface sow and press gently into moist soil without covering. An outstanding choice for native rain gardens, wet meadow plantings, and pond-edge naturalistic gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, disturbed soil in full sun; camphorweed is a native annual or biennial that self-sows prolifically and is commonly found colonizing dry, disturbed, sandy roadsides and open habitats along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Allow to self-sow in dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, open, disturbed soil in full sun; camphorweed is one of the most abundant and ecologically valuable native annual wildflowers of the Gulf Coastal Plain, immediately colonizing bare, disturbed, sandy soil with a profusion of bright yellow daisy-like flowers from late summer through fall. The aromatic, camphor-scented foliage repels deer and rabbits. The plant provides extraordinarily rich late-season nectar for monarch butterflies during their fall migration — a role of critical conservation value along the Gulf Coast migration corridor. Despite its weedy tendency in disturbed areas, camphorweed is a prized monarch nectar plant and should be intentionally maintained in natural garden areas and meadow plantings where its valuable pollinator role can be appreciated. Self-sows reliably to perpetuate populations without replanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Canada anemone spreads aggressively by rhizome and seed and is best used where mass coverage is desired or where natural spreading is welcome — it will crowd out less competitive plants.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — Canada anemone is one of the most vigorous native groundcovers available, producing a long-lasting display of pure white, 1.5-inch five-petaled flowers above attractive, deeply lobed leaves from late spring through early summer, then spreading steadily by rhizome to form a dense, weed-suppressing colony. It grows naturally in moist prairies, stream banks, and moist, open woodland edges from Canada south to the mid-Atlantic states. Its aggressive spreading habit makes it ideal for naturalizing large, moist areas along pond edges, woodland margins, and rain garden overflows — it quickly colonizes disturbed, moist ground and crowd out invasive weeds. Use it with appropriate caution in smaller gardens where it may overwhelm neighbors. An outstanding erosion-control plant for moist, sunny to partly shaded slopes. Important early-season nectar source.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; Canada lily requires consistently moist soil and will not tolerate drought or dry, alkaline conditions — it grows naturally in moist meadows, stream banks, and open woodland edges.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade — Canada lily is one of the most graceful and spectacular of all eastern wildflowers, producing tall, whorled-leafed stems 3–5 feet high topped with pendant clusters of 3–16 large (3-inch), nodding, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to orange to deep red with dark spots inside, held on gracefully recurved pedicels in June–July. The flowers are visited by hummingbirds, swallowtail butterflies, and bumblebees. Canada lily grows naturally in moist meadows, wet prairies, stream banks, and open woodland edges throughout the northeastern and Appalachian US, in conditions that remain consistently moist through the growing season. It is more adaptable to partial shade than most lilies and blooms reliably in dappled light. Naturalize in moist, shaded meadow gardens and along stream banks for a stunning effect.

common_name: Canada Mayflower (Wild Lily of the Valley)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in fall in moist, humus-rich, cool, strongly to moderately acidic soil in partial to full shade; Canada mayflower spreads readily by rhizomes to form dense, low colonies under conifers and is an excellent groundcover in cool-zone shade gardens.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or container plants in fall in moist, humus-rich, cool, strongly to moderately acidic soil in partial to full shade; Canada mayflower spreads readily by rhizomes to form dense, low colonies under conifers and is an excellent groundcover in cool-zone shade gardens. Maianthemum canadense is one of the most abundant and adaptable native woodland groundcovers of the boreal and northern hardwood forests of North America; a diminutive, 3–6-inch-tall perennial with 1–3 heart-shaped, shiny, green leaves and delicate, racemes of tiny, white, 4-petaled flowers in late spring followed by pale red-speckled berries ripening to solid red in late summer, providing abundant food for hermit thrushes and other forest birds. It forms aggressive colonies in cool, acidic, conifer-shaded sites (pH 4.5–5.5) where few other plants thrive, making it an indispensable groundcover in pine and spruce understory gardens in zones 2–6; it is less successful in warm southern climates.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds cold-stratify over winter and germinate in early spring.
directions: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds cold-stratify over winter and germinate in early spring. Canada sanicle is a native biennial to short-lived perennial of eastern North American forests and woodland edges, producing deeply palmate, shiny dark-green leaves and small clusters of tiny white flowers in early summer that are excellent bee forage; it is a specialist forage plant for native mining bees and sweat bees. The plant typically self-seeds in suitable conditions and gradually naturalizes under deciduous trees, particularly in rich mesic forest soils alongside native ferns and woodland wildflowers. Use it as an unobtrusive but ecologically valuable filler in a native shade garden.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or divide clumps in early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Canada violet is one of the tallest and most shade-tolerant native violets, producing flowers over a longer season than most violets.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — Canada violet is one of the most garden-worthy and longest-blooming native violets, producing white, five-petaled flowers with a distinctive purple-veined lower petal and faint purple reverse on the upper petals from spring through early summer on stems 8–16 inches tall — significantly taller than most native violets. It grows naturally in moist, rich, shaded forests and mountain woodland throughout northern North America and is genuinely shade-adapted, performing well in deep woodland conditions where most violets cannot thrive. The heart-shaped leaves are attractive throughout the season. Canada violet spreads moderately by rhizome and self-sows to naturalize, forming groundcover colonies in appropriate conditions. All violet species are larval host plants for native fritillary butterflies, making them essential components of the native butterfly garden. An outstanding shade-garden violet for zones 3–8.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 4 weeks before) in well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; canary creeper prefers cooler conditions than garden nasturtium (T. majus) and blooms most freely in partial shade and cool summers.
directions: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 4 weeks before) in well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; canary creeper prefers cooler conditions than garden nasturtium (T. majus) and blooms most freely in partial shade and cool summers. Tropaeolum peregrinum is a vigorous annual climbing vine from the Andean cloud forests of Peru with deeply five-lobed, gray-green leaves and profuse, small (3/4 inch), bright-golden-yellow flowers with two large, fringed upper petals that create an extraordinary resemblance to small yellow canaries or birds-in-flight, giving the plant its charming common name. It is an outstanding annual climber for a partially shaded trellis, fence, or pergola and is useful where full-sun annuals fail; it provides nectar for hummingbirds and long-tongued bumblebees. Less commonly grown than garden nasturtium but more refined and tolerant of shade and cooler conditions.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Canary Island foxglove is native to laurel forest edges on the Canary Islands and appreciates protection from hot afternoon sun and drying winds. It is damaged below 28°F and thrives in the mild, humid, fog-moderated climates of coastal California and similar maritime conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade; Canary Island foxglove is a tender, shrubby relative of the true foxgloves (Digitalis), native to the laurel cloud forests and scrublands of Tenerife and Gran Canaria in the Canary Islands. Unlike the familiar biennial foxglove, it is an evergreen shrub 3–6 feet tall producing firm, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves and tall upright spikes of densely packed, tubular flowers in a distinctive shade of warm orange-yellow to tawny-amber — one of the few foxglove-family plants producing orange flowers. The flower color is unique among foxglove relatives and is particularly striking in the warm half-tones of the late afternoon light. The flowers are visited by sunbirds in their native habitat and are attractive to hummingbirds in cultivation. Related to Digitalis but classified in the separate genus Isoplexis. A collector's plant of considerable distinction, excellent in mild coastal gardens in zones 9–11 as a specimen in dappled shade.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; candelabra primrose needs steady moisture and is best sited at a pond edge, streamside, or damp low spot rather than an average garden bed.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; never allow the soil to dry out. Primula bulleyana is a Chinese species of candelabra primrose, named for the distinctive way its flowers are arranged in tiered whorls stacked up the flower stalk like the branching arms of a candelabra — in late spring to early summer, the stems carry several tiers of bright orange to apricot-yellow flowers rising well above the coarse, crinkled basal foliage, an especially vivid color break from the pinks and purples of many other primroses. Like other candelabra-type primroses, it thrives at the damp margins of a pond, stream, or bog garden, where reliably moist, humus-rich soil lets it naturalize and self-seed into an increasingly showy colony over the years. A striking, colorful choice for the moist partial shade of a woodland bog garden or streamside planting, zone 5–8.

common_name: Candidum Caladium (Classic Green-Veined White Fancy Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; Candidum has been in cultivation since the 1860s and is the prototype white fancy caladium from which many later white cultivars were derived.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Candidum is the oldest and most historically significant white fancy caladium cultivar — first listed in 1867 and still one of the most widely grown caladiums in the world after more than 150 years of continuous cultivation. The large, heart-shaped leaves are pure white with prominent, contrasting deep-green veins radiating from the central midrib and branching through the white leaf tissue in a clean, bold pattern that is one of the most graphic and visually striking leaf patterns in the plant kingdom. The bright white leaf with crisp green veining creates a unique foliage display that can brighten a deep shade position as effectively as a light fixture — the luminous white reflects available light and makes dark areas appear significantly brighter. Candidum's longevity in cultivation reflects its extraordinary reliability and quality as both a garden plant and a cut-foliage crop (the leaves are used in floral arrangements). The standard white-veined caladium used as a benchmark for all subsequent white varieties, Candidum remains a top choice because no later introduction has consistently surpassed it in the combination of large leaf size, clean white color, bold green veining, and reliable performance in hot, humid Gulf South conditions. A true classic of American horticulture.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for best germination results, as delphinium seed loses viability rapidly and cold stratification through winter triggers more uniform spring germination; alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 2–3 weeks at 40°F and sow indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in cool (55–60°F) conditions.
directions: Plant in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with shelter from strong winds; Delphinium elatum is the species parent of the classic Pacific Giant and Elatum Group hybrid delphiniums — tall, stately cottage garden perennials producing dense, candle-like spikes 3–6 feet tall packed with blue, violet, lavender, or white flowers in late spring to early summer, after which plants can be cut back to the basal foliage to encourage a second flush of bloom in late summer. Delphiniums demand cool summers to perform at their best and decline in zones with prolonged heat and humidity; they are outstanding perennials for the Pacific Northwest, Upper Midwest, and New England, but struggle in the South and southwestern United States. Stake tall stems before they reach full height and protect from slugs in early spring when the new shoots are emerging; divide clumps every 3 years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Candlestick Senna (Empress Candle, Ringworm Bush, Seven Golden Candlesticks)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–May for late summer and fall bloom. Seeds have a hard coat — nick or scarify and soak overnight in warm water for best germination. In zone 9, Candlestick Senna grows as a fast-growing annual or short-lived perennial, dying to the ground in frost but often reseeding prolifically. It self-seeds to the point of becoming weedy in zone 10-11 — deadhead spent spikes before seeds mature if spreading is a concern.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Candlestick Senna grows rapidly — a spring-planted seedling often reaches 6–8 feet and begins blooming by August–September in zone 9. Senna alata (Candlestick Senna or Empress Candle) is a stunning tropical shrub or sub-shrub native to tropical America and now naturalized throughout the world's tropics, producing one of the most dramatic flower displays in the subtropical garden: erect, rigid, conical flower spikes 12–18 inches long closely packed with bright golden-yellow individual flowers that open progressively from the base upward — the unopened buds at the tip are enclosed in overlapping orange-brown bracts that suggest golden candle flames, inspiring the common name. Multiple spikes arise simultaneously from each stem tip in August–November in zone 9, creating an extraordinary golden spectacle when the plant is in full bloom. The large, pinnately compound leaves are architectural and attractive even out of bloom. Senna alata is also famous for its potent antifungal properties — leaf extracts have been shown effective against Microsporum canis, Trichophyton species, and other dermatophytes responsible for ringworm and tinea infections, hence the folk medicine name 'Ringworm Bush.' An outstanding butterfly plant as well — Orange-barred Sulfur and Cloudless Sulphur butterflies use it as a larval host plant throughout the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; candy cane sorrel follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and blooming in winter and spring, going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. The striped appearance of the closed flower buds — crimson on the reverse of petals that are white inside — creates the candy cane effect visible in cold or cloudy weather when the flowers close. One of the most visually distinctive of all Cape oxalis species.
directions: Plant small bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; candy cane sorrel is one of the most visually striking and immediately recognizable of the Cape oxalis species — and the most aptly named. The flowers, when closed (as they are in cold or cloudy weather and at night), display the vivid crimson to red-and-white spiral stripes on the outer (reverse) surface of the petals that wrap around the closed bud in a tight, precise, spiral pattern of alternating crimson and white — exactly resembling a miniature candy cane or barber pole. When the flowers open in warm sunshine, the inside surface of the petals is revealed to be pure white, creating a satiny, pure-white, five-petaled oxalis flower. The transition between the vivid-striped closed bud state and the pure-white open flower state, occurring multiple times daily as sunlight and cloud alternates, is a constant source of small surprise and delight. A short plant producing small flowers, but the visual impact — particularly of a mass planting — is outsized for the plant's dimensions. Native to the sandy coastal fynbos of the Western Cape. Outstanding in pots and rock garden settings in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring bloom; Phlox drummondii is native to the Gulf Coast (Texas) and is well-adapted to zone 9 conditions when fall-sown. The fall sowing strategy allows winter root establishment before the spring bloom flush. Candy Stripe produces a vivid bicolor pattern with a white or pale ground and contrasting deep pink, red, or rose-pink stripes or sectors on each petal — creating a very distinctive and eye-catching pattern not found in other phlox selections. Pinch growing tips when 4–5 inches tall to encourage branching and more flower heads. Plants self-seed reliably in zone 9, naturalizing effectively in sandy soils.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture during the winter growing season — Candy Stripe Annual Phlox requires full sun and cool to mild temperatures for maximum flowering, declining in summer heat; Candy Stripe Annual Phlox is a bicolor selection of Annual Phlox (Phlox drummondii), a Gulf Coast native wildflower that produces clusters of five-petaled, flat-faced flowers in a distinctive pattern of contrasting colors on each petal — the Candy Stripe pattern creating a vivid bicolor effect of deep pink or rose stripes against a lighter ground that makes this selection immediately distinctive among the more uniformly colored phlox selections. Phlox drummondii is native to the Texas Gulf Coast and is naturally adapted to zone 9 conditions — one of the few annual wildflowers that combines native origin with genuine adaptability to fall sowing and winter growing in zone 9. The clustered, domed heads of small flowers on compact, upright plants provide a full, lush bloom display from February through April in zone 9 — the combined effect of many rounded flower heads creating a colorful carpet of bloom that is extremely effective for mass planting and border edging. The strong fragrance of Annual Phlox attracts butterflies and beneficial insects in significant numbers.

common_name: Candy Stripe Creeping Phlox (Bicolor White-Pink Moss Phlox)
plant_note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Candy Stripe requires the same sharp drainage as all creeping phlox — avoid heavy clay or consistently moist soil, which promotes crown rot and decline.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Candy Stripe is the most distinctive bicolor creeping phlox cultivar — producing flowers with a clean white base and a prominent, vivid pink-rose stripe down the center of each petal, creating a candy-stripe pattern that gives each flower an unusual, ornate appearance unlike the solid-colored flowers of most Phlox subulata cultivars. The bicolor striped effect is most vivid when flowers are fully open — the strong contrast between white and pink creates a more complex, visually interesting floral texture across the blooming mat than solid pink or solid white cultivars. In spring (March–April in zone 7–8, February–March in zone 9), the entire plant disappears under a carpet of bicolor flowers — the candy-stripe pattern visible as a mass effect creates a distinctive pink-flushed-white wash rather than either solid pink or solid white. Like all Phlox subulata cultivars, Candy Stripe forms a dense, evergreen, needle-like mat (4–6 inches tall) that is effective as a year-round groundcover on slopes, in rock gardens, and spilling over walls. The sharp drainage requirement is non-negotiable — creeping phlox in heavy clay or consistently moist soil develops crown rot and declines within 1–2 seasons. In zone 9, Candy Stripe performs reliably when sited in well-drained, raised, or slope positions where soil dries between rain events.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; cosmos prefer lean soil and full sun.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in average-to-lean soil, since rich ground reduces flowering. Candystripe bears golden-centered blooms of white edged and streaked in rose, making a sweet cut flower on tall airy stems. Once established these plants are drought tolerant and prefer to be left largely alone. Deadhead for continued bloom or let some flowers set seed, as they reseed readily for the following year.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 3–5 inches deep in moist, rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade after frost danger passes; in zone 8–11 rhizomes can remain in the ground year-round with light mulch.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; canna lilies are among the most spectacular and versatile tropical perennials for southern gardens, producing bold, paddle-like leaves in green, bronze, or striped and large, iris-like flowers in red, orange, yellow, pink, or bicolor from summer through frost. Dozens of named cultivars are available in heights from 18 inches ('Dwarf' types) to 8 feet, suiting them for containers, borders, water's edge, and bold accent planting. In zone 7–11 the rhizomes overwinter in the ground with mulch and re-emerge vigorously each spring. The rhizomes multiply rapidly; divide every 2–3 years. The large tropical leaves make canna an outstanding foliage plant even out of bloom.

common_name: Cannova Canna (Compact Weather-Tolerant Seed Canna Series)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants once soil has warmed; Cannova is a compact, seed-grown canna series bred for improved wind and rain tolerance compared to older tall canna cultivars, staying tidy and upright through summer storms.
directions: Plant rhizomes or seed-grown transplants a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Cannova is a modern canna series bred for a more compact, weather-resistant habit than older, taller canna cultivars, with sturdy stems that hold up better to wind and heavy rain, an important trait during Gulf Coast summer storms that can flatten taller, top-heavy cannas. The series is available in a range of flower colors including scarlet, gold, rose, apricot, and bronze, all on clean green foliage, blooming continuously from early summer through frost. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump over time. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Cantabrian daffodil is the white equivalent of the yellow hoop petticoat (N. bulbocodium), flowering in late winter and early spring. Like N. bulbocodium it naturalizes in thin turf and well-drained rocky grassland. Requires summer dry dormancy — suits Mediterranean-climate gardens or well-drained rockeries that do not receive summer irrigation.
directions: Plant small bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in part shade; Cantabrian daffodil is the white-flowered hoop petticoat species — the smaller, earlier, purer-white counterpart to the familiar yellow N. bulbocodium — producing the same distinctive flower form with an enormous, widely flared funnel-trumpet dominating tiny, vestigial, thread-like outer petals, but in pure snow-white rather than yellow, flowering even earlier (late winter to very early spring, often before N. bulbocodium). Native to the limestone hills, rocky pastures, and open scrubland of the Atlas Mountains of Morocco and the mountains of southwestern Spain and Portugal, it belongs to the drier, more alkaline end of the hoop petticoat daffodil group's habitat range. The little white funnel-flowers, appearing on 4–6 inch stems in February–March, are among the earliest and purest-white of all bulb flowers. Like all hoop petticoat daffodils it naturalizes freely in thin, well-drained grassland and open rocky soils, building colonies over years. A gentle, early-spring treasure for the rock garden, gravel planting, or naturalistic wild area in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Canton fairy bell closely resembles Solomon's seal in form and cultural requirements and makes an elegant, ornamental shade perennial with attractive flowers in spring and colorful berries in fall.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; Canton fairy bell is a Chinese ornamental perennial producing elegant, arching stems 2–4 feet tall with lance-shaped, strongly parallel-veined leaves and clusters of 1–3 small, pendant, cream-white bell-shaped flowers at the stem tips and leaf axils in mid-spring. The flowers give way to attractive, round, red to dark-red berries in fall that are ornamentally valuable and provide wildlife food. Disporum cantoniense spreads slowly by rhizomes to form refined colonies and makes an excellent companion to hostas, ferns, and astilbes in the shaded border; in form and habit it closely resembles Solomon's seal (Polygonatum) and can be used in similar situations. Several ornamental cultivars exist, including dark-foliaged forms; all require consistently moist, humus-rich soil and dislike drought.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; canton fairy bells spreads gently by rhizomes to form expanding colonies in shaded garden conditions. More heat-tolerant than most Asian Disporum species.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in zones 7–10; canton fairy bells is an arching, bamboo-like woodland perennial from southern China and Southeast Asia, producing elegant, leafy stems that arch gracefully under the weight of pendant, tubular white-to-pale-pink flowers in late spring. The stems have an unusual multi-branching habit near the tips, creating a feathery, tiered silhouette in the shade garden. Black berries follow the flowers in fall and are consumed by thrushes and other berry-eating birds. The cultivar 'Night Heron' features striking dark purple-black stems that provide exceptional winter interest after the leaves drop. This species is notably more heat-tolerant than the Japanese species D. sessile, making it a superior choice for zone 7–10 shade gardens. Thrives in the same conditions as hostas, ferns, and hellebores.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, calcareous soil in full sun to partial shade; canyon maple is adapted to the thin, rocky, limestone soils and canyon walls of the Balcones Escarpment in Texas and of canyons throughout the central Rocky Mountains.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, calcareous or sandstone soil in partial shade in the canyon microclimate; canyon maple is the native maple of the Rocky Mountain and Great Basin canyons and the Edwards Plateau of Texas, producing spectacular fall color — brilliant orange, red, and scarlet tones — in otherwise largely dry, autumn-green landscapes. It is the maple that colors the walls of Lost Maples State Natural Area in the Texas Hill Country each October in brilliant red and orange, one of the most spectacular fall color displays in Texas. The tree grows naturally in sheltered canyon walls and north-facing slopes where moisture and shade moderate summer heat, and it is adapted to calcareous, rocky soils unlike the acidic-soil preferences of eastern maples. The small stature (10–30 feet) and excellent fall color make it the ideal native shade tree for small alkaline gardens in central Texas.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; canyon sage is native to rocky canyon walls and slopes in the Chihuahuan Desert at elevations of 4,000–7,000 feet and requires excellent drainage. In humid Gulf Coast conditions, it benefits from raised or rocky beds with lean, fast-draining soil.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; canyon sage is a compact, shrubby perennial salvia from rocky canyon habitats of the Chihuahuan Desert in west Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, producing a long succession of vivid violet-blue flowers throughout the warm season. It forms a dense, dome-shaped subshrub of small, aromatic, gray-green leaves with persistent woody lower stems and soft herbaceous upper growth. The flowers are intensely blue-violet — among the most saturated blues in any salvia — and are produced in whorled spikes throughout spring, summer, and fall with particular abundance after rains. It is a hummingbird magnet throughout its bloom season. Canyon sage combines extreme drought tolerance with outstanding ornamental quality and a refined, compact habit that fits into almost any garden setting. In humid Gulf Coast climates, excellent drainage in lean soil is critical to long-term success; it performs excellently in raised beds, rock gardens, and containers.

common_name: Cape Blue Water Lily (Tropical Blue Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant tubers in aquatic pots filled with heavy garden loam, topped with gravel, and submerged 12–18 inches below the water surface after water temperatures consistently exceed 70°F; Cape blue water lily requires warm water to grow and bloom and will not tolerate water temperatures below 60°F.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy loam aquatic pots submerged 12–18 inches in warm water after temperatures reach 70°F — Cape blue water lily is one of the most spectacularly beautiful aquatic plants for warm-climate water gardens, producing large (6–10 inch), star-shaped flowers in brilliant sky-blue to lavender-blue on tall stems that rise 6–12 inches above the water surface, blooming by day from late spring through fall. Unlike most tropical water lilies, the flowers have an intensely sweet, vanilla-like fragrance and remain open until early afternoon. The large, round, notched floating leaves (12–24 inches across) cover the water surface effectively and provide shade that discourages algae growth and shelters fish and aquatic life. In zone 10–12 the tubers overwinter in the pond; in zone 9 lift and store tubers indoors at 60–65°F over winter. One of the parent species of many popular tropical water lily hybrids and among the finest blue-flowered aquatics available for warm water garden cultivation.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 1–2 inches deep in sharply drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in fall; cape cowslip grows through the cool season (October–April) and must be kept completely dry during summer dormancy (May–September) to avoid rot. In zones 9b–11 it can remain in the ground if drainage is perfect; in other climates grow in pots moved to dry storage in summer.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Cape cowslip is a small, jewel-like South African bulb of the hyacinth family producing compact clusters of pendent, tubular flowers in brilliant combinations of yellow, orange, red, and green that are uniquely striking even compared to other South African bulbs — the color changes along the length of each tube, with the base often yellow-green and the tips flushed orange-red, creating an overall effect of lit-up coral and gold. The two broad, strap-like leaves are typically spotted or mottled with dark purple, adding to the ornamental interest of the plant even before it flowers in winter and early spring. A winter-growing bulb native to the winter-rainfall Cape region of South Africa, it grows through the cool season (November–April) and enters strict summer dormancy. Outstanding as a cool-season container plant and one of the most popular South African bulbs in the British cut-flower and conservatory tradition for over 200 years.

plant_note: Start indoors before the last frost and transplant out after.
directions: Start cape daisy indoors six weeks before the last frost, covering the seed lightly, then transplant to a sunny, well-drained bed once frost danger has passed. It bears elegant white petals around rich purple centers over a long bloom season and is grown as a tender perennial in mild climates. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the display fresh through the warm months. It tolerates some drought but flowers best with steady, moderate moisture.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall with the top half of the bulb above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Cape forest lily grows, flowers, and sets seed in winter and spring, then goes completely summer dormant — do not water during dormancy. Distinguished from V. bracteata by its wavy-edged, glaucous leaves and preference for more alkaline, sandy, well-drained conditions (V. bracteata prefers humus-rich, moist soil).
directions: Plant bulbs (upper half exposed) in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; Cape forest lily is the drier-habitat Veltheimia species — growing naturally in the sandy, well-drained, somewhat alkaline substrates of the coastal scrubland and sandy flats of the Western Cape rather than the more moisture-retaining, humus-rich soils where V. bracteata thrives. Like V. bracteata it is a winter-growing bulb, emerging with the Cape rains in autumn and flowering in late winter (July–September in South Africa, January–March in the Northern Hemisphere), producing the same characteristic dense, bottle-brush-like raceme of pendant, tubular flowers on a sturdy, mottled-purple scape — but in slightly different, usually more pink-flushed or paler-pink shades. The leaves are distinctly glaucous (blue-gray-green) and wavy-edged, contrasting with the glossier, deeper-green flat leaves of V. bracteata. Summer dormancy is complete and mandatory — both species die back entirely and must be kept bone dry. A plant for the specialist collector of South African winter-growing bulbs, particularly valuable for mild-winter Mediterranean-climate gardens in zones 9–11.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates for winter-to-spring bloom; in colder zones, sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Sow seed directly into a sunny, well-drained bed in fall in zones 8-10, pressing seed about one-quarter inch into the soil and firming gently; in colder zones sow in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked. Soil temperatures between 55 and 68 degrees Fahrenheit produce the fastest and most uniform germination, so avoid sowing into cold, wet ground that could cause rot. Thin seedlings to 10-14 inches apart once they are a few inches tall, as crowding reduces air circulation and can encourage mildew. The vivid, sky-blue flowers bloom prolifically through the cool season and will continue until the onset of summer heat, after which plants can be pulled and replaced with warm-season selections.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; cape honeysuckle is extremely drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in lean, dry soil in full sun — rich, moist conditions produce rank foliage with reduced flowering.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; cape honeysuckle is a South African evergreen scrambling shrub-vine that is one of the most reliable and versatile hummingbird plants for Gulf Coast and southwestern zone 9–11 gardens, producing clusters of long, tubular, brilliant scarlet-orange to orange-red, honeysuckle-like flowers in flushes from fall through spring — at the opposite end of the warm season from most summer-blooming hummingbird plants — when migrating and wintering hummingbirds most need reliable nectar sources. It grows as a large, lax, sprawling shrub or a climbing vine if given support, and can be trained against walls, over fences, or left to sprawl as a groundcover on banks. Tolerates partial shade (blooming acceptably in open tree canopy), drought, heat, poor soil, and alkaline conditions once established. In zone 9 it may freeze back in hard winters but recovers quickly from established roots. 'Aurea' (clear-yellow flowers, more refined in habit) is an attractive alternative to the standard orange form. Excellent as a slope cover, espaliered vine, and sprawling hedge.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; cape honeysuckle is extremely adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and is virtually foolproof in warm climates. Train the scrambling stems onto a support structure early — the plant does not twine or cling on its own and must be tied.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — poor, sandy, alkaline, and rocky soils are all acceptable; cape honeysuckle is not a true honeysuckle but a South African scrambling shrub that produces clusters of brilliant orange-red tubular flowers almost continuously from late fall through spring in zone 9 — filling the garden with color exactly when other flowering plants are dormant. It is extraordinary as a hummingbird and butterfly plant. The plant does not twine or cling like a vine but scrambles vigorously through other shrubs or must be tied to a trellis or fence; alternatively it makes an excellent sprawling groundcover on slopes or a large informal mound-shaped specimen shrub. A yellow-orange cultivar ('Aurea') is also available. Cape honeysuckle withstands heat, drought, salt spray, and poor soil with ease once established and grows rapidly in warm weather. In zone 8 it may suffer significant frost damage but recovers vigorously from roots in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool spring soil; blooms open in response to sunshine.
directions: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained soil and full sun, where the flowers can enjoy plenty of light. The daisy-like blooms in orange, yellow, white, and salmon open when hit by the sun to reveal a dark, purple-ringed center that bees and butterflies love. Provide lean soil and let plants dry between waterings, as they tolerate drought well. Deadhead to prolong the display through the cooler part of the season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring (or early fall) in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Nerine bowdenii is the most cold-hardy nerine species — hardy to zone 7 in well-drained soil — producing spectacular clusters of bright-pink, strap-petaled, spidery flowers on bare stems in autumn (September–November), after most other bulbs have finished; flowers appear before or with the strap-shaped leaves; naturalizes readily in mild climates.
directions: Plant bulbs with the tip just at or slightly above soil level in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; do not disturb once established; water sparingly in summer dormancy. Nerine bowdenii (Cape nerine or Bowden lily) is the most cold-hardy species in the Nerine genus — a South African native bulb from the mountains of the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal — and one of the most spectacular bulbs for fall flowering in zone 7–10. The plant produces striking, 2-foot bare stems topped with large umbels (6–8 flowers per head) of bright, vivid pink, reflexed, strap-petaled flowers with distinctively wavy, crinkled petal margins — a uniquely spidery, exotic appearance unlike any other fall bulb. The flowers appear in September through November, after the bulb's strappy, strap-shaped leaves have died back for summer — blooming from apparently bare ground, then producing the strap-like leaves after or alongside the flowers. N. bowdenii naturalizes readily into permanent clumps that increase over years and flower more prolifically as they become established. The bulbs bloom best when slightly crowded and resent disturbance. Unlike its tender relative Nerine sarniensis (Guernsey lily), N. bowdenii is hardy in zone 7 with good drainage and a sheltered position. A classic autumn bulb for the Mediterranean-climate and mild-winter garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger passes in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; plumbago establishes quickly and begins blooming within one growing season. In zone 8 it may die back to the ground in hard freezes but regrows vigorously from the roots in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cape plumbago is one of the most beloved and widely used flowering shrubs of Gulf Coast landscapes, producing continuous clusters of sky-blue to powder-blue flowers from spring through the first frost — a color rarely achieved by other summer-blooming shrubs in the heat. The arching, semi-scandent stems naturally mound and sprawl, making it ideal for slopes, large containers, espalier on fences, or informal hedges. It is remarkably drought tolerant once established and thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9. A white cultivar ('Alba') is also widely available. Prune back by one-third in early spring to encourage fresh, dense regrowth and a compact habit; in zone 9 it remains evergreen year-round. An outstanding long-season butterfly and bee plant, particularly attractive to swallowtail butterflies.

common_name: Cape Primrose (Nodding Violet, Trailing Cape Primrose, Saxicolous Streptocarpus)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-draining, peat-based or coir-based potting mix; Streptocarpus saxorum is particularly susceptible to root rot — use a fast-draining mix and allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings. It thrives in hanging baskets or cascading over the edge of containers. Prefers moderate temperatures (60–80°F) and avoids extreme summer heat. Blooms nearly continuously in good conditions. Propagate from leaf cuttings or stem tip cuttings. Excellent on a bright, cool, shaded porch in zone 9 from spring through fall, with winter indoors.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-draining, porous potting mix — Cape Primrose produces its best bloom in bright indirect light and will fail in dim positions while being scorched by any direct sun exposure. Streptocarpus saxorum is a compact, trailing to semi-prostrate perennial native to Tanzania (and the broader East African highlands) in the Gesneriaceae family, one of approximately 155 Streptocarpus species and one of the most delicate and graceful of the trailing gesneriads for container and hanging basket culture. The plant produces trailing stems of small (0.75–1 inch), round, velvety, mid-green leaves with a softly hairy texture. From among the leaves, delicate, thin flower stalks emerge throughout the growing season carrying one or two pale lavender to soft lilac flowers at the tip — each flower a small (1-inch), tubular, slightly two-lipped bloom with a white throat and five spreading rounded lobes, borne on long, arching pedicels that nod gracefully in the slightest air movement. The overall effect of multiple cascading stems with dozens of nodding lavender flowers is charming, elegant, and refined. S. saxorum's relatively compact form, continuous bloom habit, and tolerance of lower light levels than many flowering plants make it an excellent choice for shaded porches, indoor bright-window positions, and cool, sheltered shade gardens in warm climates. Often grown as a houseplant at the boundary between indoor and outdoor culture. Non-toxic.

common_name: Cape York Lily (Aussie Plume, Native Turmeric)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to dappled shade; Cape York lily is an Australian rainforest curcuma adapted to warm, humid shade conditions and produces a stunning, upright plume of white, pink, or lilac-purple bracts in summer — one of the most ornamental of all gingers.
directions: Plant rhizome sections 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; allow rhizomes to dry and go dormant in winter. Curcuma australasica (Cape York lily or Aussie plume) is an Australian native curcuma — one of very few curcuma species native outside of South and Southeast Asia — found in the rainforests of Cape York Peninsula in far north Queensland. It produces attractive, broadly lance-shaped, medium-green leaves and upright, compact flower 'cones' 10–14 inches tall composed of overlapping, overlapping, boat-shaped bracts in white, pink-tipped white, or lilac-purple, with tiny, cream-yellow true flowers emerging between the bracts. The Australian origin gives it slightly different cultural requirements from Asian curcumas — it prefers the seasonal rhythm of a wet summer and dry winter characteristic of tropical Queensland. As a cut flower, the inflorescences last 2–3 weeks in a vase. In zone 9–12 shade gardens, it thrives in the same conditions as other gingers: moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in dappled shade. A lovely, rarely-grown species for ginger collectors and tropical garden enthusiasts.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early fall or plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; Cappadocian navelwort performs best in dappled or half shade with consistent moisture. The cultivar Cherry Ingram has slightly larger, more intensely blue flowers; Starry Eyes has distinctive blue-and-white bicolor petals. It is more long-lived than the spring-flowering O. verna.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; Cappadocian navelwort is a low-growing shade perennial from Turkey producing small, perfect, pure sky-blue flowers with a white eye — identical in form to forget-me-not flowers but more intensely colored, longer-blooming, and on a more reliably perennial plant. The flowers appear in early to mid spring in loose sprays above neat mounds of dark-green, heart-shaped, somewhat hairy leaves and have a particularly clear, clean blue that is outstanding in the shade garden. Unlike the more common spring navelwort (O. verna), which dies back and goes dormant in summer, O. cappadocica is reliably evergreen or semi-evergreen and maintains its attractive foliage through the growing season as a groundcover. The cultivar Cherry Ingram is the most floriferous selection; Starry Eyes has bicolored flowers with a blue center and white picotee edge to the petals — a genuinely beautiful and unusual flower form. An outstanding companion for hellebores, epimediums, and ferns in the woodland garden.

plant_note: Surface sow, as the seed needs light; Cappuccino blooms the first year from an early start, producing warm mahogany-brown flowers ringed in gold, a distinctive departure from the solid yellow of the classic wild black-eyed Susan.
directions: Surface sow in well-drained, average soil in full sun, since the fine seed needs light to germinate well. Cappuccino produces richly colored flowers with a warm mahogany-brown center zone bordered by a bright golden-yellow edge, a striking bicolor combination that stands out among the many solid-yellow black-eyed Susan cultivars available. Grown as a short-lived perennial or reseeding annual depending on climate, it blooms heavily from summer into fall and makes an excellent cut flower, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its bloom period. Deadheading spent flowers extends the bloom season, and leaving a few seed heads to mature late in the season allows it to self-sow for the following year.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Caradonna is prized for its nearly black flower stems, which contrast dramatically with the violet-blue flowers and remain ornamental even after the petals fade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Caradonna is one of the most widely planted hardy salvias, valued for its slender, nearly black flower stems topped with dense spikes of rich violet-blue flowers that create a striking two-tone vertical accent through the front and middle of a sunny border. Shearing the plant back by about half after the first flush of bloom encourages a strong second and sometimes third round of flowers into late summer. It is drought-tolerant once established, rarely bothered by deer or rabbits, and draws bees and hummingbirds throughout its long bloom season; in hot, humid zone 9 summers it may decline and is best treated as a shorter-lived perennial refreshed every few years.

common_name: Carajuru (Chica Vine, Blood Vine, Bejuco de Indio)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in late spring on a strong trellis or arbor in full sun to partial shade; Fridericia chica (formerly Bignonia chica, Arrabidaea chica) is a vigorous tropical vine suited to zone 10-11 outdoor culture. It grows rapidly and blooms profusely in the warm months with clusters of rosy-pink to magenta trumpet flowers. The leaves have been used for millennia as a source of a red-orange to brick-red natural dye ('chica' dye) by indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin for body painting and ceremonial use. The dye color comes from the carotenoid pigment bixin. Propagate from cuttings.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Carajuru blooms most prolifically in full sun and produces attractive foliage display in partial shade. Fridericia chica (formerly Arrabidaea chica, Bignonia chica) is a vigorous, woody, tendril-climbing vine native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and tropical South America (Peru, Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela) in the Bignoniaceae family — one of the most historically significant ornamental plants of the tropical Americas for a quality beyond its ornamental flower display: its leaves yield 'carajuru' or 'chica,' a brilliant red-orange to brick-red natural dye that has been used by indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin for body decoration, face painting, textile dyeing, and ceremonial preparation for thousands of years, and that remains in use today. The vine produces clusters of attractive, rosy-pink to magenta-pink, 1.5-inch, tubular trumpet flowers with five spreading petal lobes, produced through the warm months and attracting hummingbirds. The compound leaves (2 leaflets + tendril) contain the carotenoid pigment bixin and related compounds responsible for the red dye — the same class of compound that gives annatto its orange color. Beyond its ethnobotanical significance, F. chica is a fast-growing, flowering tropical vine with genuine ornamental value in zone 10-12 warm garden conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Caramel shows better heat tolerance than many dark-leafed heucheras and performs reasonably well in zone 8–9 with afternoon shade and consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Caramel heuchera is one of the most warm-toned and visually distinctive Heuchera x villosa hybrids, producing large, maple-shaped leaves in a glowing amber-to-caramel color that is brightest in spring when leaves first unfurl and in fall when cooler temperatures intensify the coloring. This cultivar has H. villosa parentage that makes it significantly more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many modern heuchera hybrids — an important quality for Southern and Gulf Coast gardens where most coral bells struggle in summer. The loose mound of large, peach-to-caramel leaves acts as a bold ground-level accent that combines exceptionally well with blue-green hostas, blue-leafed ferns, and dark-colored astilbes. Small pinkish flowers appear on wiry scapes in summer. Divide every 3 years when the crown heaves, replanting the youngest outer rosettes at proper soil depth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring when soil is warm; Cardboard Palm grows slowly — a single new set of leaves per year is normal. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. In zone 9a, protect from extended hard freezes; the foliage may brown below 25°F but established plants typically resprout from the crown. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — keep away from children and pets.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy or gritty soil; Cardboard Palm is extremely drought-tolerant once established and will rot in wet, poorly-drained conditions. Zamia furfuracea is a cycad (an ancient gymnosperm, not a true palm) native to the coastal sand dunes and scrub of Veracruz, Mexico. It is one of the most widely planted landscape cycads in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens, prized for its symmetrical rosette of tough, leathery, dark olive-green fronds with broad, felt-covered leaflets that have the exact texture and appearance of corrugated cardboard — the characteristic that gives the plant its common name. The extremely slow growth rate (one complete flush of new leaves per year), prehistoric architectural form, and rugged adaptability to dry, poor, salt-exposed coastal soils make it an ideal low-maintenance specimen for zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes. Cardboard Palm is an excellent partial-shade plant under mature trees where other ornamentals fail — its deep-green leaves brighten shaded spots and it tolerates the root competition and dry shade of live oak canopies. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic to humans, dogs, and cats — the seeds and starchy trunk contain macrozamin and other cycasin compounds that cause liver failure.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; a western North American native perennial with brilliant scarlet flowers that are outstanding for hummingbirds and are held on long sticky stems — the catchfly characteristics give it a distinctive tactile quality in the garden.
directions: Direct sow in spring, or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost risk has passed; cardinal catchfly prefers dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and is drought-tolerant once established. Silene laciniata is a native wildflower of the Pacific Coast ranges and Sierra Nevada foothills, producing long-stemmed, brilliant scarlet flowers with fringed (lacinate) petals on sticky, 12–36 inch stems from spring through fall; the vivid red flowers are a magnet for hummingbirds and are among the most spectacular of all native red wildflowers. It is more heat- and drought-tolerant than many Silene species and is suitable for dry woodland edges, rocky slopes, and naturalized gardens in the western US and in the drier parts of the Southeast. The sticky stems deter crawling insects from reaching the flowers.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed before sowing to speed germination; provide a trellis.
directions: Nick and soak the hard seeds overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis, pole, or fence. This vigorous vine climbs six to twelve feet and carries deep-red, white-throated flowers that hummingbirds and pollinators adore, along with delicate fern-like foliage. Give it full sun and steady moisture through the growing season. Provide sturdy support early, as the twining stems grow quickly once warm weather arrives.

common_name: Cardinal Creeper (Red Morning Glory, Hybrid Cypress Vine)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in full sun after last frost in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil; cardinal creeper is a vigorous annual hybrid vine (cross between Ipomoea quamoclit and I. coccinea) combining the finely divided, feathery foliage of cypress vine with slightly larger, cardinal-red, star-shaped flowers; extremely fast-growing, blooms summer through frost, and attracts hummingbirds prolifically.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms; nick or soak seeds 24 hours before planting; the vine grows quickly to 6–15 feet with minimal care. Ipomoea x multifida (cardinal creeper or cardinal vine) is a naturally occurring hybrid between cypress vine (I. quamoclit) and red morning glory (I. coccinea) — combining the most appealing ornamental features of both parents. From cypress vine, it inherits the deeply pinnately cut, feathery, bright-green foliage that creates an extraordinarily delicate, lacy texture. From red morning glory, it inherits slightly larger, more robust flowers (3/4–1 inch across) of the same intense cardinal-red as its parents. The result is a vigorous, fast-growing, annual ornamental vine that covers trellises, fences, and arbors with a curtain of delicate, feathery foliage and an abundance of small, brilliant-red, star-shaped tubular flowers from summer through fall. The flowers are irresistible to hummingbirds, which visit constantly throughout the day. The vine self-sows readily in warm climates and can be treated as a perennial in zone 9–10. A classic hummingbird garden plant that requires almost no care once established on a trellis.

plant_note: Surface-sow seed (do not cover — seed needs light to germinate) indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; seed requires light and warmth to germinate. Transplant to the garden after frost danger passes, placing in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near water features, rain gardens, or boggy areas; cardinal flower produces brilliant scarlet flower spikes from midsummer into fall that are the premier nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds in eastern North America. The intensity of the red is almost unmatched in the native plant palette. Plants are short-lived perennials that self-seed freely — allow some seedlings to remain to perpetuate the colony, as individual plants typically live only 2–3 years. Division of offsets (basal rosettes) in early fall also maintains the planting. Plants tolerate standing water and thrive along stream banks and pond edges. The great blue lobelia (Lobelia siphilitica) is a closely related blue-flowered species equally valuable for pollinators.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–12; Cardinal's Guard (Firespike) is a large, shade-tolerant tropical shrub from the Caribbean and Central America — naturalized in South Florida and widely grown throughout Gulf Coast gardens — bearing spectacular, tall, brilliant-red, erect flower spikes of small, waxy, tubular flowers in fall and winter that create an extraordinary display in the shade garden and are magnets for hummingbirds during fall migration.
directions: Plant Odontonema tubaeforme in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment and through summer; cut back hard in late winter (before new growth emerges) to encourage compact, bushy growth and prevent woodiness; propagate easily from stem cuttings. Cardinal's Guard is one of the most valuable shade-garden flowering shrubs for the Gulf Coast — its spectacular scarlet-red flower spikes in fall and winter create color in shaded spots at a season when most other plants have stopped blooming, and the flowers are an important fuel stop for hummingbirds during fall migration. The plant performs remarkably well in the partial shade of large trees, where most other fall-blooming shrubs fail to flower well; in deep shade, it will grow vegetatively but reduces flowering. In zone 9, it dies back to the ground after hard frost and re-emerges from the roots in spring, re-establishing quickly to bloom again by October–November. In zone 10–12, it grows as a substantial, multi-stemmed shrub year-round. The tall, elegant flower spikes with their waxy, bright-red individual flowers are also excellent cut flowers. An indispensable plant for Gulf Coast butterfly and hummingbird gardens.

common_name: Carefree Beauty Rose (Cold-Hardy Own-Root Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Carefree Beauty was bred by Iowa State University professor Griffith Buck as part of a program developing own-root, winter-hardy, disease-resistant roses that need no spraying or winter protection, and it performs equally well across a wide climate range from the northern Midwest to the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Bred by Dr. Griffith Buck at Iowa State University and introduced in 1977, Carefree Beauty is one of the best-known results of his decades-long program to develop tough, own-root roses that survive harsh Midwestern winters without protection and resist disease without spraying — goals that happen to also produce excellent performance in the hot, humid Gulf South. It bears large, semi-double, clear pink blooms with a light fragrance in generous flushes from late spring through fall, followed by an abundant crop of showy orange-red hips that provide fall and winter interest and feed birds. The vigorous, upright shrub shows strong resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew and needs minimal care once established. Prune back by about a third in late winter to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new flowering wood, and leave some hips on the plant through fall for ornamental and wildlife value.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings (wear gloves — milky latex is an irritant) or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade after frost; Caribbean copper plant grows fastest and colors most intensely in full sun; partial shade produces somewhat less vivid coloring but is acceptable.
directions: Root stem cuttings (caution — wear gloves, latex is a skin and eye irritant) or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; Caribbean copper plant is a tropical American shrub or small tree grown entirely for its spectacular, deep-mahogany to wine-red, rounded foliage — the constantly produced, oval, alternate leaves emerge in brilliant coppery-red and mature to deep burgundy-maroon, maintaining their rich coloring throughout the season. In the tropical garden it provides a bold, jewel-toned color anchor that contrasts dramatically with lime-green foliage (aralia, euphorbia tirucalli 'Sticks on Fire'), silver-gray plants, and orange-flowered tropical perennials. It is fast-growing to 10–15 feet in tropical climates, functioning as a screening shrub or specimen small tree; in cooler zones 9 gardens it may be damaged by hard frost but resprouts from the roots. Insignificant yellowish flowers. All parts contain toxic, milky latex — handle with gloves and avoid eye contact. Excellent as a bold color contrast in mixed tropical borders.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck just above the soil surface in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Caribbean spider lily is native to the islands of the Caribbean and produces large, white, spider-like flowers with the characteristic Hymenocallis 'cup and strap' form — a central funnel-cup connecting the bases of long, narrow, spreading, strap-like perianth segments. It is strongly fragrant in the evening. In zone 9 it remains in the ground as a perennial; bring indoors in winter in colder zones.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Caribbean spider lily is a bold, tropical Hymenocallis species from the Caribbean islands — producing in summer umbels of large, pure-white, powerfully fragrant, spider-lily flowers in the distinctive Hymenocallis form: a central, flared funnel-cup at the heart of the flower, from the margins of which radiate six long, narrow, reflexed, strap-like perianth segments creating the signature spider-lily silhouette of a central cup surrounded by long, radiating white streamers. Each flower in the 3–8 flower umbel spans 6–8 inches across; a mature clump in bloom is a striking tropical display. The fragrance is very strong and sweet, most intense in the evening, carrying through the summer garden air. The broad, bright-green, strap-shaped, glossy leaves form handsome clumps even when not in flower — providing bold, tropical-looking foliage throughout the summer. It thrives in the warm, humid summer conditions of zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens in partial shade, where it naturalizes into ever-larger, more floriferous clumps over time. Outstanding combined with other bold, tropical-looking shade plants — cannas, elephant ears, gingers — for a lush, tropical summer border.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; caricature plant is excellent in partial shade where other tropical foliage plants such as coleus and impatiens also perform well.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; caricature plant is a tropical shrub from New Guinea and the Pacific Islands that is grown entirely for its extraordinary variegated foliage — large, shiny, oval leaves boldly streaked, blotched, and suffused with yellow, cream, rose-pink, or purple-red markings on a dark-green background, with the irregular patterning suggesting (to imaginative observers) the exaggerated features of cartoon faces or caricatures, giving the plant its common name. The color intensity and pattern of the leaf markings vary with the amount of light — plants in brighter partial shade develop the most vivid contrasts, while plants in deeper shade become more uniformly green. Small, tubular, purplish-red flowers appear occasionally on mature plants in tropical conditions but are secondary to the foliage display. Widely grown as a houseplant and greenhouse specimen in cool climates; in zone 10–12 it functions as a year-round outdoor foliage shrub of considerable ornamental impact.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Carissa is one of the most compact and slow-growing Chinese holly cultivars — maintaining a mounded form of 3–4 feet without frequent pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Carissa is a compact, slow-growing Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta) cultivar with a distinctive characteristic that sets it apart from all other Chinese holly cultivars: its leaves have only a single terminal spine rather than the multiple sharp spines of standard Chinese holly. This makes Carissa the most maintenance-friendly and user-safe holly cultivar for residential settings — plants around walkways, children's play areas, and high-traffic zones where the multiple sharp spines of Rotunda, Burford, and other Chinese holly types would create hazards. The deep, lustrous, dark-green foliage is more elongated and less glossy than some Chinese holly types but still attractive and evergreen year-round. Carissa is a female clone and requires a nearby male Chinese holly for berry production — when pollinated, it produces attractive red berries. The compact, naturally mounded habit (3–4 feet) requires minimal pruning to maintain in typical landscape situations. Extremely tough — tolerating clay soil, drought once established, heat, and partial shade without significant performance loss. Essentially pest-free, deer-resistant, and pollution-tolerant, making it practical for urban and suburban foundation plantings.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–12 weeks before fall planting (August–September in zone 9) in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; carnations are outstanding cool-season flowers in zone 9, blooming prolifically from winter through spring before summer heat stops them — treat as a winter annual in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–12 weeks before transplanting; plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Dianthus caryophyllus (carnation or clove pink) is the florist's carnation — one of the world's most commercially important cut flowers, comprising billions of stems in the global cut flower trade annually alongside roses and chrysanthemums. The classic double-flowered, fringed-petal blooms in red, pink, white, yellow, orange, purple, and bicolor shades have been cultivated for over 2,000 years; the spicy-sweet, clove-like fragrance of old-fashioned varieties is one of the most beloved flower scents. Modern commercial carnations are often scentless but long-lasting; old-fashioned cottage garden varieties retain the characteristic clove fragrance. Carnations are also edible flowers — the petals (with the bitter white base removed) are sweet and mildly spicy, used to flavor wines, liqueurs (Chartreuse), and desserts; they are the traditional garnish for some Spanish and Greek dishes. In zone 9, carnations are outstanding winter-spring bloomers; plant in fall for a February–May flower season. Standard (tall) types need staking; compact border carnations are self-supporting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Carnival's cream-variegated foliage brightens in partial shade — full afternoon sun in zone 9 may bleach the cream margins to white and scorch the leaf tips.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Carnival is a variegated liriope cultivar with cream to creamy-white longitudinal striping on dark-green, strap-like leaves — forming compact, mounding clumps of distinctive two-tone foliage that brightens shade garden areas with the cream-on-green contrast effect common to effective shade variegated plants. Carnival's pink to rose-pink flower spikes (a warmer, pinker color than the purple-violet of most liriope cultivars) rise above the variegated foliage in summer and create an attractive three-color combination of cream-striped green leaves, pink flower spikes, and eventually blue-black berries in fall. The pink flowers rather than typical purple flowers are Carnival's most distinctive attribute among variegated liriope selections — the flower color combines with the cream foliage variegation to create a lighter, airier, more pastel effect than dark-purple-flowered types. Like all liriopes, Carnival is adaptable and low-maintenance in zone 9 — tolerating heat, drought, shade, and root competition from trees while remaining evergreen through mild Gulf South winters. The variegated foliage is most effective when mass-planted in sizeable groupings where the light-reflective cream-and-green texture creates a visual effect visible from a distance. Shear to 3 inches in late winter to remove old foliage before new spring growth emerges.

common_name: Carnivorous Bromeliad (Lantern Bromeliad, Berterone's Catopsis, Tank Trap Bromeliad)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark or cork, or in a small pot with bromeliad bark mix, in partial shade with good air circulation; Catopsis berteroniana is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-12 outdoor culture or protected porch/indoor culture in zone 9. Keep the central tank (cup) filled with rainwater or distilled water — the waxy, pale yellow-white powdery coating on the inner tank walls may trap insects that slide in and drown, contributing to the plant's nutrition. Clean the tank occasionally to remove debris. Propagate from offsets.
directions: Grow in partial shade to bright indirect light in bromeliad bark medium or mounted on bark — Carnivorous Bromeliad performs best in the dappled light of a shaded outdoor position or bright indoor location with good air circulation. Catopsis berteroniana is a small to medium-sized epiphytic bromeliad native to southern Florida (where it is endangered), the Caribbean, Central America, and South America in the Bromeliaceae family, noteworthy as the only bromeliad species with a convincing scientific case for genuine carnivory. The evidence, documented in ecological studies, is based on a distinctive combination of features not found in other bromeliads: the smooth, very steeply angled inner walls of the central tank are coated with an unusual white, powdery, waxy substance (trichomes) that reflects UV light — attracting insects — while simultaneously making the walls so slippery that trapped insects cannot escape. The drowned insects accumulate in the tank and are thought to be digested by the plant's absorptive trichomes. While not as definitively carnivorous as Sarracenia or Nepenthes, the adaptation appears functional. The plant itself is attractive: pale yellow-green to whitish foliage forms an open, lantern-like rosette. It produces a tall, erect inflorescence with small, white to yellow flowers. An unusual and scientifically interesting collector's bromeliad.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina allspice blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates significant shade and is one of the few large flowering shrubs that performs well in light to moderate shade.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina allspice blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates significant shade and is one of the few large flowering shrubs that performs well in light to moderate shade. Calycanthus floridus is a deciduous native shrub of the southeastern United States with a rounded, spreading habit and remarkable, deeply fragrant, strap-petaled flowers with brick-red to burgundy petals that resemble no other flower in the garden; blooming from late spring through summer, the flowers have a complex, spicy-sweet scent compared variously to strawberries, banana, and pineapple, and the aromatic quality extends to the crushed leaves and bark.
