directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or loamy soil in partial to full shade; clasping twisted-stalk is the larger and more widespread of the two North American twisted-stalk species, growing from Alaska and Canada through mountain forests south to California, Arizona, New Mexico, and the Appalachians. The leaves are heart-shaped, with the base clasping the stem (hence 'clasping' and the species name 'amplexifolius'), creating an attractive, layered, overlapping arrangement along the arching, multiple-branched stems. The small, cream-white to greenish-white flowers hang from twisted pedicels in the leaf axils in early summer, followed by oval red berries that smell and taste mildly of cucumber (earning the common name 'cucumber root'). The berries were eaten raw and cooked by Indigenous peoples across the range. Young shoots can be eaten like asparagus. A larger and more imposing woodland plant than rosy twisted-stalk, more tolerant of a wider elevation range and making a bold statement in woodland garden settings.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, replanting immediately in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in deep shade. Handle rhizomes gently as they are slow to re-establish after disturbance.
directions: Clasping Twistedstalk is a graceful native woodland perennial notable for its distinctively zigzagging stems and oval clasping leaves that create an architectural layered effect in the shade garden. Small white to pale pink bell-shaped flowers hang beneath the leaves on twisted pedicels in late spring, giving way to showy red berries in late summer and fall that are relished by thrushes and other forest birds. It thrives in cool, moist, humus-rich soil under a canopy of deciduous trees and performs best where summers are cool. Amend planting areas generously with leaf mold or composted bark and maintain even moisture throughout the growing season.

plant_note: Direct sow at or 2 weeks before last frost; cold stratification of seed for 7 days in the refrigerator improves germination.
directions: Press seed lightly onto the soil surface with barely 1/8 in of cover — light aids germination. Cleome self-sows prolifically and can become weedy; deadhead to limit reseeding if preferred. The tall, airy flower heads open from the base upward over several weeks, providing an extended season of bloom. Handle plants with care as stems bear small spines and the foliage has a musky scent.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Cleopatra is a vigorous, upright grower that can be maintained as a formal hedge or clipped into a topiary form — prune immediately after the bloom season ends to avoid removing next season's flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Cleopatra is a vigorous, upright Camellia sasanqua cultivar producing single to semi-double, rose-pink to deep-pink flowers with prominent golden-yellow stamens from October through December in zone 9. The medium-pink flower color is clear and saturated — a classic, feminine camellia pink that combines well with white-flowering companions, silver-foliage plants, and the dark evergreen foliage of camellias and hollies in the fall garden. Cleopatra is one of the more sun-tolerant sasanqua camellias, performing well in 4–6 hours of direct sun that would stress most japonica camellias, and it is more vigorous and faster-growing than many sasanqua selections. The upright, dense, somewhat narrow-columnar habit (6–12 feet tall, somewhat narrower than its height) makes it useful for screening and hedge applications where height is needed in a limited horizontal space. As with all sasanqua camellias, the fall flowers are mildly fragrant — pleasant but not overwhelming. Cleopatra was one of the foundational sasanqua cultivars widely planted across the Gulf South in the mid-twentieth century and remains a reliable, proven performer for zone 9 camellia gardens. Fertilize with azalea-camellia acidic fertilizer in spring and early fall.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in spring in very well-drained, sunny conditions; Cleveland sage requires excellent drainage and dislikes summer irrigation — it is truly a dry-climate plant that thrives on neglect.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Cleveland sage is a California native aromatic shrub with one of the strongest and most complex sage fragrances in the genus — deeply resinous, herbaceous, and intensely medicinal. The gray-green, deeply textured leaves are used as a culinary sage substitute (particularly appropriate with poultry and game) and were traditionally used by Kumeyaay and other indigenous peoples for ceremonial smudging. It blooms profusely in spring with whorls of lavender-blue flowers on tall spikes that are outstanding for hummingbirds and native bees. In summer-dry Mediterranean climates and warm dry gardens, it is one of the best ornamental shrubs available — extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and low-maintenance once established.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to moderately acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; cleyera is very cold hardy once established but prefers protection from harsh winter winds and reflected heat from walls. It is a slow-growing, long-lived shrub that rarely needs pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly to moderately acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — cleyera is one of the most refined and underused evergreen shrubs for southern shade gardens, producing elegant, glossy, dark green leaves with reddish new growth on a naturally pyramidal to oval form. The small, creamy-white, fragrant flowers in spring are followed by dark red to black berries that attract birds; the plant is sacred in Shinto tradition in Japan, where it is planted at shrines. Cleyera is an outstanding foundation plant, informal hedge, or large specimen for the shaded, acidic, humus-rich conditions under tall pines and oaks throughout zone 7–9. It grows more slowly than many companion plants (camellias, gardenias) but eventually becomes a large, refined, long-lived shrub requiring almost no maintenance beyond an occasional light shaping. Excellent companion plant for camellias and azaleas in woodland garden compositions.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring 3–4 inches deep in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in zone 8–10; Climbing Alstroemeria is a vigorous tuberous climbing vine from the misty Andean cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador — related to Alstroemeria but distinctly different in its twining, climbing habit — producing large, pendant, trumpet-shaped flowers in brilliant orange to red-orange with yellow interiors spotted with brown-purple, held in generous clusters at the ends of long, scrambling stems.
directions: Plant Bomarea multiflora tubers in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; provide support for the twining stems to climb; keep consistently moist through the growing season; in zone 8–9, mulch heavily in winter to protect the tubers from frost. Climbing Alstroemeria is a genus of tuberous, climbing vines closely related to the familiar Alstroemeria (Peruvian Lily) of florists, but with a distinctly different growth habit — the stems twine and scramble through surrounding vegetation to heights of 3–6 feet, decorated with alternate, bright-green, resupinate (twisted) leaves. The large flower clusters at the stem tips bear 10–30 individual pendant, tubular flowers in brilliant orange to deep red-orange (B. multiflora is one of the most vivid-colored species) with a contrasting yellow interior and brown-purple speckling. The genus Bomarea comprises some 120 species throughout the Andes and tropical Americas — an undeservedly neglected group that most temperate gardeners have never encountered despite the extraordinary floral display. Native to the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador at elevations of 6,000–10,000 feet, B. multiflora prefers cool to mild temperatures — making it better suited to the mild climates of the Pacific Coast and zone 8–9 Southeast than strictly tropical conditions. Hummingbirds are the primary pollinators in its native range.

plant_note: Plant near a fence, shrub, or trellis in moist to wet, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; stems scramble and sprawl through surrounding vegetation rather than twining — provide sturdy support or allow it to clamber through a native shrub border.
directions: Climbing aster is the only vining aster native to North America, an extraordinary scrambling perennial from the Gulf Coastal Plain and Florida that clambers 6–15 feet through shrubs and fences to display enormous masses of small, lavender-to-pink flowers with yellow centers in late fall, often blooming well into December in zone 8 and 9 gardens. Because it flowers so late in the season — October through December in the Deep South — climbing aster serves as a critical last nectar source for late-migrating monarchs and queens, sulphur butterflies, and overwintering native bees that remain active through early winter in the Gulf Coast region. Plant it where it can scramble through a wax myrtle, yaupon holly, or native shrub border; its somewhat weedy scrambling stems are hidden by surrounding plants while the spectacular late-autumn bloom is the garden's last big show before frost. Cut back hard in late winter to control spread and encourage vigorous new stems for next season's bloom.

common_name: Climbing Bird's Nest Fern (Common Microsorum, Crocodile Fern, Wart Fern)
plant_note: Grow in shade as a houseplant, on a bark mount, or in zone 9b-11 outdoor shade gardens; Microsorum punctatum is more cold-tolerant than Asplenium nidus and can survive brief temperatures to 32°F if the rhizome is protected with mulch. In zone 9-10, plant outdoors in deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees. The plant naturally creeps and climbs surfaces with its surface-creeping rhizomes — allow it to grow up mossy tree trunks or walls for the most natural appearance. Propagate by dividing rhizome sections with attached fronds.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil or potting medium; Climbing Bird's Nest Fern is highly adaptable and among the most shade-tolerant of the large structural ferns for zone 9 Gulf Coast outdoor shade gardens and indoor use. Microsorum punctatum (also known as Phymatosorus punctatus) is a widespread, variable epiphytic to terrestrial fern distributed across tropical Africa, Asia, the Pacific Islands, and Australia, growing naturally in forest understories, on mossy tree trunks, and on rock faces. The plant produces long, strap-like, undivided fronds of various sizes (depending on cultivar and conditions) — from 12 to 36 inches — in bright to medium green, with the characteristic small, round, orange-brown sori (spore clusters) scattered across the frond undersurface in a dotted pattern that can be visible from above in strong light. Some forms have attractively crested or wavy frond margins. A popular cultivar, 'Grandiceps,' has strongly crested frond tips. The rhizome creeps across surfaces, attaching and climbing — in zone 9-10 outdoor shade gardens it naturally climbs the trunks of large oaks and palms, eventually producing an impressive colony of ferns ascending tree trunks. More cold-tolerant than Bird's Nest Fern (Asplenium nidus), making it preferable for zone 9 outdoor planting. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; climbing bleeding heart is a biennial that germinates in late spring, forms a basal rosette in its first year, then climbs and blooms in its second year. It self-sows freely in moist, shaded conditions and can be treated as a self-perpetuating annual colony once established.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade at the base of a trellis, fence, or scrambling support; climbing bleeding heart is a unique native biennial vine of moist, rocky, shaded slopes and forest margins in the Appalachians and northeastern North America. The lacy, glaucous blue-green foliage is extremely finely divided and feathery, resembling the leaves of bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos/Dicentra) or corydalis, and the plant climbs by means of clinging petioles to reach 6–10 feet. The small, nodding, tubular flowers — white to pale pink — are produced in summer of the second year in clusters from the leaf axils, resembling tiny bleeding hearts. Self-sows freely in appropriate conditions to form a naturalized colony. An unusual and beautiful native vine for shaded woodland trellises and shrub edges, little known in cultivation.

plant_note: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, organically rich soil in partial to full shade near a trellis, fence, or tree; climbing dogbane is a bottomland native that tolerates brief flooding and performs best in the shade of bottomland hardwood forests along Gulf Coast waterways.
directions: Climbing dogbane is a rare native alternative to the widely planted Confederate jasmine (Trachelospermum jasminoides), naturally found in the moist bottomland forests, swamp margins, and stream banks of the Gulf Coast from Virginia to Texas — it is the only species in its genus native to North America. Unlike its Asian relative, climbing dogbane adapts to shaded conditions under bottomland oaks and cypress, making it one of the few woody ornamental vines that will thrive in genuine shade; it produces clusters of small, fragrant, yellowish-white five-petaled flowers in early summer that are visited by native bees and butterflies. The milky latex sap makes it unpalatable to deer, and the plant is host to several specialist milkweed butterflies and moths in the family Apocynaceae. While less commonly available commercially than Confederate jasmine, climbing dogbane is worth seeking out from native plant nurseries for shaded trellises, arbors, and woodland garden structures where a fragrant, native evergreen vine is needed.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, moist to moderately dry soil with support for the tendrils in zone 8–10; Climbing Gazania is a scandent shrub or climbing perennial from the high-altitude shrub zones and forest edges of the Andes in Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru — bearing large (3–4 inch), brilliant orange-red, daisy-like flowers with gold-yellow centers at the stem tips on plants that climb by modified leaf tendrils through surrounding shrubs — a uniquely beautiful, little-known Andean ornamental.
directions: Plant Mutisia clematis in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; provide shrubs, netting, or a trellis for the modified leaf tendrils to grip; keep evenly moist in the growing season; protect from hard frost below 25°F; propagate from stem cuttings in late spring. Climbing Gazania (Mutisia) is one of the most remarkable genera in the Asteraceae (daisy) family — unlike virtually all other members of the daisy family which are herbaceous or non-climbing, Mutisia species are climbing, tendril-bearing, woody-stemmed scandent shrubs that scramble through Andean cloud forest and shrub margins by means of modified leaf extensions acting as tendrils. The large, solitary daisy-like flowers — brilliant orange-red in M. clematis with a golden-yellow center disc — are produced repeatedly at the stem tips and are genuinely spectacular on close inspection, resembling a large, elegant gerbera daisy held by a climbing vine. The approximately 60 Mutisia species are distributed along the length of the Andes from Venezuela to Patagonia; most are challenging to cultivate but M. clematis is considered one of the more tractable in mild climates. A genuinely unusual and conversation-worthy plant for mild, coastal garden climates in zone 8–10 where cool temperatures, consistent moisture, and good drainage can be provided.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; climbing gloxinia grows rapidly and begins blooming in summer. It climbs by twining leaf petioles and needs a trellis, mesh, or shrub for support. In zones 9–10 it may overwinter as a perennial; in colder climates grow as an annual from seed or overwinter cutting-rooted plants indoors.
directions: Start seeds early indoors and train on a trellis or other support in full sun to part shade; climbing gloxinia is a Mexican native vine producing large (2–3 inch), softly tubular, trumpet-shaped flowers in clear, warm rose-pink to soft magenta — a flower form and color closely resembling gloxinia (Sinningia), hence the common name, on a freely climbing vine 6–10 feet long. The hairy, somewhat gloxinia-like leaves contribute to the resemblance. The flowers are abundant from summer through fall and the whole plant has a pleasant, cottage-garden quality — softly colored, generous with bloom, and adaptable to growing up fences, trellises, tripods, and into shrubs. Previously classified as Asarina erubescens, it belongs to the snapdragon family and shares some visual qualities with that family. 'Magic Dragon' is a widely available seed strain in the nursery trade. An excellent companion to softer-colored annual and tender perennial vines on a mixed-planting trellis or fence.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist, rich soil near a trellis or at the margin of a pond, stream, or rain garden; climbing hemp weed is a fast-growing perennial vine in zones 8 and warmer, dies back after hard frost but returns reliably from the roots in Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Climbing hemp weed is a vigorous native twining vine of the aster family (Asteraceae), native to wetland margins, pond edges, freshwater tidal marshes, and moist thickets across the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern United States — despite being little-known in cultivation, it is one of the highest-value native vines for late-season pollinators. Dense clusters of small, fluffy white to pinkish flowers cover the vine from late summer through fall and are magnets for migrating monarchs and a remarkable diversity of native specialist bees; it is among the most important native late-season nectar sources in Gulf Coast wetland habitats. The vine climbs and twines quickly in warm seasons, making it useful for rapidly covering trellises, fences, and chain-link at the edges of rain gardens, constructed wetlands, and moist riparian restoration plantings. In zone 9 and south it remains semi-evergreen; in zone 8 it freezes to the ground but returns vigorously from the roots each spring.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; climbing hydrangea is very slow to establish — it may appear not to grow for the first 2–3 years while developing its root system. After establishment it grows steadily and becomes long-lived and self-sustaining. It climbs by aerial rootlets and requires no additional support on rough surfaces like brick, stone, or wood.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to part shade; climbing hydrangea is among the most valuable vines for shaded positions — one of the few vigorous, ornamental climbers that succeeds and blooms in substantial shade. It clings to walls, tree trunks, and structures by tiny adhesive aerial rootlets without damaging sound mortar and masonry. In June and July, established plants produce large, flat-topped flower heads (lace-caps) up to 10 inches across — creamy white with ornamental sterile flowers surrounding a center of tiny, fertile flowers — in breathtaking abundance that is one of the showiest June spectacles possible on a shaded wall. The bark on mature stems exfoliates in thin, cinnamon-red sheets, creating beautiful winter interest. The broadly oval, glossy leaves turn bright yellow in fall. Native to Japan and Korea, it is slow to begin growing after planting (famously described as 'the first year it sleeps, the second year it creeps, the third year it leaps') but is exceptionally long-lived and essentially maintenance-free once established on a suitable structure.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall against a sturdy wall, fence, or large tree it can cling to.
directions: This vigorous woody vine climbs walls and trees by aerial rootlets, covering surfaces with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant, lacy white blooms in late spring. Plant in part shade to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; it also tolerates morning sun with steady moisture. Be patient, as it is slow to establish but grows rapidly once settled, eventually reaching great heights. Provide strong support and prune after flowering only to control size.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; climbing hydrangea vine is a streamside and swamp-forest plant in nature and requires consistent soil moisture. It climbs by aerial rootlets and establishes well on tree trunks, rough stone, and brick without additional support.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in part to full shade; climbing hydrangea vine is a native eastern North American alternative to the Asian climbing hydrangea (H. anomala subsp. petiolaris), found naturally in moist forests and swamp edges from Virginia to Florida and Louisiana. It climbs trees, walls, and structures by clinging aerial rootlets, and in late spring produces clusters of small, sweet-fragrant, white flowers without the large sterile bracts of the Asian species — more modest but very sweetly scented and genuinely attractive to pollinators. The leaves are glossy, dark-green, and semi-evergreen to evergreen in zones 7–9, making it useful for year-round coverage of shaded surfaces. It tolerates deeper shade than most vines and is one of the few self-clinging climbers native to the southeastern US. Outstanding for climbing shaded tree trunks, stone walls, and other structures in moist, shaded southern gardens where Asian vines perform poorly. Supports the ecology of the forest system it comes from — its berries are eaten by several bird species.

plant_note: Direct sow at last frost in moist, open, well-drained soil in full sun; seeds can also be fall-sown to overwinter in the ground for natural cold stratification and earlier spring germination. Give plants a sturdy fence or trellis to climb — this is a vigorous grower and will quickly cover available support. Best suited to wildlife garden settings where free spreading is acceptable.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun along a fence, trellis, or through a sturdy shrub; Climbing Milkweed (also called Honeyvine) is a vigorous twining native perennial in the milkweed subfamily, producing smooth, heart-shaped leaves and dense clusters of small, sweetly honey-fragrant white flowers from July through September that are outstanding nectar sources for monarch butterflies and many native bees. It is native to moist, open, disturbed ground, fencerows, and thicket edges throughout the eastern and central US, and produces classic milkweed seed pods that split to release plume-tailed seeds. Climbing Milkweed can spread aggressively from both seed and rhizomes in favorable conditions and is best suited to naturalistic or wildlife garden settings where its habit of covering fences and scrambling through shrubs is welcome rather than a problem.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and set out on a trellis, fence, or lattice in partial shade to full sun after frost; climbing snapdragon climbs by twisting its leaf stalks (petioles) around thin supports and is one of the few climbing annuals that flowers well in partial shade.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and set out on a trellis, lattice, or fence in partial shade after frost; climbing snapdragon is a Mexican native annual vine that climbs by twisting its leaf stalks around thin supports, covering itself with snapdragon-like, tubular, two-lipped flowers of rosy purple, lavender, pink, or white from summer until frost. The triangular, softly hairy, ivy-shaped leaves and twining, scandent growth create a soft, romantic effect on trellises, fences, and mailbox posts. It is notably more shade-tolerant than most annual vines and is one of the few that blooms freely in filtered shade — valuable for shaded pergolas, north-facing fences, and areas receiving only 4–5 hours of direct sun. Hummingbirds are attracted to the tubular flowers. 'Bride's White', 'Mystic Pink', and 'Violet Purple' are the most widely available color selections. In zones 9–11, the plant may overwinter as a short-lived perennial.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; climbing snapdragon is a tender perennial from Spain and southwestern Europe typically grown as an annual in North America; it climbs by its petioles and drapes beautifully over walls, containers, and hanging baskets.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 60–70°F; transplant after last frost into partial shade to sun in moist, well-drained soil; climbing snapdragon (Asarina procumbens) is a charming, soft-hairy, trailing vine-like plant native to rocky cliff faces and limestone walls in northeastern Spain, producing snapdragon-like pale yellow flowers with cream-yellow throats throughout the summer. The self-clinging petioles allow it to scramble over rough surfaces and through other plants; it is especially beautiful draping over stone walls, tucked into rock garden crevices, or spilling from containers and hanging baskets. In zone 7–10 it is perennial and can be propagated from cuttings; in colder zones grow as an annual. Distinguished from the related climbing snapdragons (Lophospermum) by its pale yellow flowers rather than pink or red.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; climbing ylang ylang is a tropical Indian and Southeast Asian climbing shrub in the custard apple family with intensely fragrant, yellow-green flowers with the characteristic ylang ylang perfume — the scent is extraordinarily powerful at night and the flowers are used in traditional Indian garland-making.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; provide a strong trellis or allow to scramble through a supporting tree. Artabotrys hexapetalus (climbing ylang ylang or manorangini) is a tropical Indian and Southeast Asian climbing shrub in the custard apple family (Annonaceae) that climbs by means of distinctive hooked, curved peduncles (flower stalks) that become woody and hook-like as the flower develops — anchoring the plant to supporting branches without true tendrils or twining. The plant produces small, pale yellow-green to yellow flowers in clusters, with six tepals (three outer, three inner) — the flowers have an extraordinarily powerful, sweet, heady fragrance almost identical to true ylang ylang (Cananga odorata) — intensely sweet, floral, slightly fruity — and are among the most powerfully fragrant flowers in the tropical garden. The scent intensifies dramatically at night, making this plant outstanding for outdoor seating areas in the tropics. In South India, the flowers are used in temple garlands, hair decorations, and in traditional perfume making — the essential oil extracted from the flowers is used in Ayurvedic preparations and in the perfume industry as a low-cost ylang ylang substitute. A remarkable and underused tropical fragrance plant for zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant in spring once all frost risk has passed and soil has warmed. Choose a sturdy trellis, fence, or tree to support the hooked stems, and site in full sun with fertile, well-drained soil. Mulch generously around the base to retain moisture through the warm growing season.
directions: Take semi-hardwood cuttings 4-6 inches long in late spring or summer, remove lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, and insert into a warm, humid propagation environment with bottom heat near 80°F. Once well rooted, harden off and transplant to a permanent location with robust support, as the vine climbs by means of strong hooked stems that anchor to host structures. Water consistently during establishment, then reduce frequency once the plant is settled; mature plants tolerate brief dry spells but flower most profusely with regular irrigation and monthly balanced fertilization from spring through fall. Prune lightly after each flush of bloom to encourage branching and additional flowering, and position near seating areas or windows to take full advantage of the powerful ylang-ylang fragrance that intensifies in the evening.

plant_note: Plant offsets in well-drained, organically rich soil in full shade to bright indirect light; pot-bound clumps bloom more freely so resist dividing unless necessary.
directions: Plant offsets or container plants in well-drained, organically enriched soil in full shade to bright indirect light, keeping the fleshy roots slightly pot-bound to encourage flowering; clivia produces clusters of brilliant orange or yellow trumpet flowers on tall scapes in late winter to spring when given a 6-week cool, dry rest period (50–55°F) in autumn. Water regularly during active growth but reduce watering sharply in fall to trigger the rest period that promotes next season's bloom. In zone 9 and cooler, grow in containers and bring indoors before frost. Divide large clumps after flowering by severing rooted offsets with a clean knife and allowing cuts to callus before repotting.

common_name: Clog Plant (Guppy Plant, Goldfish Plant, Pouch Flower)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or trailing container in bright indirect light to partial shade; Clog Plant cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It blooms most freely with a brief, dry, slightly cool rest period (6–8 weeks at 55–60°F with reduced watering) in fall before resuming regular care in winter-spring for peak bloom. Propagate from stem-tip cuttings in moist mix. Use a fast-draining, slightly acidic potting mix. Water thoroughly and allow to approach dryness between waterings — the thick stems store water and are susceptible to rot in heavy media.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade as a hanging basket or trailing container plant — Clog Plant flowers most prolifically in bright indirect light (a bright east or north window) and will produce few flowers in dim conditions. Nematanthus gregarius (formerly Hypocyrta radicans and various other synonyms) is a trailing, semi-succulent epiphytic vine from the coastal Atlantic Forest of Brazil in the Gesneriaceae family, closely related to Columnea and Aeschynanthus. The common names — 'Clog Plant,' 'Pouch Flower,' 'Guppy Plant' — all refer to the distinctive shape of the flowers: small (half an inch to an inch), bright orange to orange-red, balloon-shaped or pouch-shaped with a small, pinched opening at one end, the overall silhouette remarkably resembling a tiny Dutch wooden clog, a bloated tropical fish, or a miniature water balloon. The flowers emerge from the leaf axils along the trailing stems in succession throughout the warm months, often blanketing an established hanging basket in dozens of the tiny orange pouches simultaneously. The stems are clothed in small, fleshy, shiny, dark-green, opposite leaves that have a bright, glossy quality. Clog Plant is one of the most rewarding of the trailing gesneriads for indoor hanging baskets — reliably blooming for months once established in appropriate conditions. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, humus-rich soil; cold stratification over winter dramatically improves germination rates the following spring.
directions: Scatter seed onto moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded site in early fall, barely covering with a thin layer of fine soil or leaf mold. Natural winter cold breaks seed dormancy; do not attempt to rush germination with artificial heat. Plants require consistent moisture and will decline in dry or compacted soils, so amend planting beds with compost before sowing. Expect slow establishment over the first two seasons before plants begin reliable late-summer bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta clausa spreads aggressively by stolons compared to most hostas, quickly colonizing large areas in appropriate conditions. Excellent as a shade groundcover for difficult areas.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta clausa is one of the most unusual hostas — a Korean species named for its cleistogamous (closed) flowers that never open fully, staying closed and self-pollinating without releasing pollen or allowing cross-pollination. This botanical curiosity means the flowers, while attractive in bud, never display the characteristic open, funnel-shaped hosta flower. The species compensates with an unusually aggressive spreading habit for a hosta — it sends out stolons to colonize large areas, making it one of the best groundcover hostas for naturalizing in shade gardens. The dark green, medium-sized leaves are attractive and conventional in appearance despite the botanical curiosity of the closed flowers. An excellent choice where spreading shade groundcover is desired without the aggressive nature of English ivy.

common_name: Cloud Nine Dogwood (Heavy-Blooming White Flowering Dogwood)
plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cloud Nine is particularly valued for its prolific blooming even at an early age — often flowering in the first or second year after planting, earlier than many dogwood cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; Cloud Nine is one of the most widely admired white flowering dogwood cultivars — selected for its unusually profuse bloom (the bracts cover the tree so densely at peak bloom that the branches are nearly invisible), its somewhat horizontally spreading branch structure that creates a wider than tall profile, and its ability to bloom as a young tree in its first or second year rather than requiring 5–7 years before flowering as is common with seedling-grown trees. The large, overlapping, pure-white bracts (each slightly overlapping the adjacent bract, creating a solid canopy of white) cover the entire tree at peak bloom in March through April in zone 9 — the flowering display has been described as looking like the tree is covered in white clouds, giving the cultivar its name. The wider-than-tall spreading form gives Cloud Nine a distinctive silhouette even when not in flower — an elegant horizontal branching pattern that is attractive year-round. Excellent red to maroon fall foliage color and red berries for wildlife follow the spring bloom. In zone 9, plant in morning sun and afternoon shade on the north or east side of structures to minimize summer heat stress on this understory native.

common_name: Cloud Nine Switchgrass (Tall Airy Blue-Green Native Switchgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Cloud Nine is one of the tallest switchgrass cultivars, valued for its billowy, airy flower panicles that create a soft, cloud-like effect above the blue-green foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils. Cloud Nine is one of the tallest switchgrass selections commonly grown, producing upright, blue-green foliage topped by unusually large, airy, cloud-like flower panicles in late summer that catch the light beautifully and persist as attractive tan seed heads through winter. Its height and strong vertical presence make it an excellent back-of-border screen or specimen planting, and like other switchgrass cultivars it tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, drought, and periodic flooding with ease. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges to keep the clump tidy and vigorous.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant transplants March–May. Torenia fournieri is one of the few annual flowers that genuinely tolerates and performs well in partial to full shade — making it an invaluable substitute for impatiens in shaded situations. Clown Rose is a compact selection in the Clown series bred for uniform growth, compact habit (8–12 inches), and excellent heat tolerance — an improvement over older, leggier torenia selections that declined in zone 9 summer heat. In zone 9 torenia performs most reliably in spring and fall in full shade; summer heat may reduce flowering but the plant recovers when temperatures moderate. Self-seeds modestly in zone 9, providing some volunteer reseeding.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil — Torenia is one of the few annual flowers that genuinely performs in full shade, making it invaluable for deep-shade situations where most flowering annuals cannot maintain blooming; Clown Rose Torenia is a compact selection of Wishbone Flower (Torenia fournieri), a shade-tolerant tropical annual from Vietnam producing an unusual, bicolor, tubular-to-open flower in rose-pink with a deeper rose-pink lower lip and a bright yellow center spot — a color combination that is vivid and cheerful in the low-light conditions of deep shade where these flowers are most practical. The common name 'Wishbone Flower' comes from the two curved stamens that are fused at the tips inside the flower, forming a wishbone shape visible when the flower is examined closely. Torenia's genuine shade tolerance — it requires shade in hot climates and will bleach and decline in direct sun — makes it one of a very small group of annual flowers that can deliver consistent, colorful bloom in the deep shade under trees, on north-facing walls, and in covered garden structures where no direct sun reaches. In zone 9, where summer shade garden color is particularly difficult to maintain, Torenia provides one of the most reliable warm-season flowering options for genuinely shaded situations from spring through early fall.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost directly into soil already occupied by native warm-season grasses; hemi-parasitic roots require close proximity to host plants for establishment.
directions: Clustered False Foxglove is a native annual hemi-parasite of the southeastern coastal plain, found in pine savannas and flatwoods where it attaches to the roots of nearby warm-season grasses to supplement its own photosynthesis; sow seeds directly among established native grasses such as wiregrass or broomsedge, as plants will fail to thrive in bare soil without host root contact. Its crowded, fascicled (clustered) leaf arrangement gives the stems a distinctively bushy, fine-textured appearance, setting it apart from other Agalinis species. From late summer through fall, it produces abundant rosy-pink trumpet flowers that attract native bees and support specialist pollinators in southeastern savanna restorations. Scatter seeds on the soil surface among host grasses at last frost and avoid transplanting, as disturbed roots disrupt the critical host-parasite connection.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall, or direct sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification; clustered mountain mint spreads moderately by rhizomes and self-seeds in average to moist soils — it is less aggressively spreading than some Pycnanthemum species and is generally well-behaved in garden settings while still forming useful colonies over time.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; clustered mountain mint is widely regarded as the most ornamentally distinguished of all native Pycnanthemum species, set apart from the more common P. tenuifolium and P. virginianum by its large, broad, silvery-white bracts that surround the dense, clustered flower heads and persist long after the small white flowers fade — from midsummer onward the upper portions of the plant take on a striking silver-white frosted appearance that is exceptionally showy and provides weeks of ornamental interest. It is one of the single most valuable native plants for pollinators in eastern North America: studies at the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center have recorded over 60 species of native bees visiting a single planting, along with dozens of butterfly species, making it a keystone resource in any pollinator garden or native meadow planting. The foliage is strongly mint-scented when crushed and deer-resistant; the plant spreads moderately by rhizomes to form a useful, weed-suppressing colony in average to moist garden soils and tolerates partial shade better than most other mountain mints. Clustered mountain mint is a premier native plant choice for rain gardens, stream edges, moist meadow margins, and any garden situation with consistently adequate moisture and partial to full sun.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or scarify and cold stratify seeds for 60 days before spring sowing. Clustered poppy mallow has a deep taproot and transplants poorly — direct seeding in the final location is strongly preferred.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; clustered poppy mallow is a Midwestern prairie native related to the more commonly grown wine-cup (C. involucrata), producing the same vivid magenta-wine to deep purple-red, cup-shaped flowers but with a more upright, clustered growth habit rather than the sprawling form of wine-cup. The flowers are produced in clustered groups near the stem tips from early summer through fall. Like all Callirhoe, it develops a deep taproot that stores carbohydrates and enables the plant to survive drought and fire — making it extremely persistent in lean, dry, well-drained conditions once established. Decline occurs in rich, moist soils. An outstanding drought-tolerant native for dry prairie and meadow gardens where its brilliant color stands out against grasses and other drought-tolerant wildflowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry, lean, sandy or gravelly soil; adapted to California's dry-season blooming cycle.
directions: Clustered Tarweed is a glandular-sticky, resinous native annual of dry, open, disturbed ground, roadsides, and grassland edges in southern California's coastal sage scrub and chaparral zones, bearing tightly clustered heads of small, yellow, 5-rayed composite flowers from summer through early fall on slender, branching, rough-textured stems. It is an ecological specialist of California's summer-dry Mediterranean climate, germinating with spring warmth and blooming through the long rainless months when it serves as a critical late-season pollen and nectar source for native bees. Direct sow in spring after last frost in dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun, pressing seed lightly to the surface; no supplemental irrigation is needed or desired after plants are established. This species is best suited to gardens within its native southern California range where summer drought and heat drive its bloom cycle.

subcategory: shade-tolerant clustering palm with bipinnate fishtail leaves
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; clustering fishtail palm is unique among commonly grown palms in having bipinnate (twice-divided) leaves — the individual leaflets are further divided into irregular, jagged, triangular to wedge-shaped segments with ragged tips that resemble fish tails. The clustering habit (multiple stems per clump) means individual stems can die after flowering without killing the whole plant. In zone 9 it requires a protected, warm microclimate; in zone 10-11 it thrives. Shade tolerant.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; clustering fishtail palm is botanically unique among the commonly grown palms in producing bipinnate leaves — leaves that are divided not once (as in all other feather palms, where a central rachis carries rows of leaflets) but twice, the primary leaflets themselves being further divided into multiple secondary segments. These secondary segments are irregular, asymmetrical, wedge-shaped to triangular, with a jagged, torn, irregular margin at the wide outer tip that closely resembles the tail of a fish — hence the common name 'fishtail palm'. The overall textural effect of the bipinnate, fishtail-segmented leaf is unlike any other palm — a complex, slightly disheveled, fern-like yet bold tropical texture that catches light differently from all directions and creates an immediately distinctive, unusual palm silhouette. The clustering habit (the palm grows as a clump of multiple individual stems) is equally important: because individual caryota stems are monocarpic (they flower from top to bottom over several years and then die), the clustering species maintains the clump indefinitely as new stems continuously replace old ones — unlike monocarpic single-trunk species. More shade-tolerant than most large palms. The sap and fruits of Caryota species contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic to skin and mucous membranes — avoid contact with fruit pulp.

common_name: Clyde Redmond Louisiana Iris (Classic Deep Blue Louisiana Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Clyde Redmond is a widely grown, classic Louisiana iris cultivar producing large, richly colored deep blue-violet flowers in mid-spring, a color long considered one of the standards against which other blue Louisiana iris cultivars are judged. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape where many other perennials would struggle. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in moist to dry, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy, well-drained soil in partial shade; coast azalea is one of the most drought-tolerant of all native azaleas once established and thrives in the sandy, acidic coastal plain soils of the Atlantic Seaboard.
directions: Coast azalea is a compact, stoloniferous native azalea of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain's sandy pine barrens and oak scrublands — producing one of the most intensely fragrant flowers of any native azalea, with white to pale pink blooms that emit a strong, sweet vanilla-clove fragrance in April and May before the leaves fully expand. Unlike most native azaleas that form upright, single-stemmed shrubs, coast azalea spreads slowly by underground stolons (horizontal stems) to form broad, low colonies — a growth habit that makes it one of the finest native azaleas for use as a naturalized groundcover or mass planting under open pinelands and dry oak canopy. Its compact, low stature (rarely over 4 feet) and tolerance of dry, sandy, nutrient-poor acidic soils make it more versatile in the landscape than taller species; it is also more heat-tolerant than northern azaleas and performs reliably in the upper Gulf Coastal Plain. Several hybrid azaleas have been developed from this species for their fragrance and compact habit.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; coast banksia is salt- and wind-tolerant and one of the hardiest banksias, surviving brief temperatures to 23°F (zone 8). Like all Proteaceae, it is severely damaged or killed by standard fertilizers with phosphate. Excellent drainage is essential.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic soil in full sun; coast banksia is one of the most adaptable and cold-hardy Australian banksias, a coastal tree of eastern Australia growing 10–30 feet with distinctive pale-green leaves that are dark green above and silvery-white below — creating a two-toned effect as leaves move in the wind. The characteristic cylindrical banksia flower spikes (4–6 inches long) are produced primarily in autumn and winter in soft, pale-yellow, and are among the richest natural nectar sources of any flowering tree — overwhelming in the volume and concentration of the nectar they produce. This makes them critical wildlife habitat for honeyeaters, lorikeets, bats, and a vast array of insects including native bees. The hardened, woody seed cones that follow the flowers can persist on the branch for years before opening to release seeds in response to fire (a key ecological adaptation). One of the most cold-tolerant banksias and the best starting species for gardens in zones 8b–11 seeking Australian native character.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile to average soil; Coast Coral Tree is a spectacular South African native and one of the most widely planted street trees of Southern California, capable of brief light frosts in zone 8–9, and produces masses of brilliant red-orange flowers on bare thorny branches in late winter and spring before the feathery trifoliate leaves emerge.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Erythrina caffra is drought tolerant once established — water deeply and infrequently during summer in Mediterranean and subtropical climates and rely on winter rainfall in coastal California conditions; avoid heavy clay with poor drainage. Erythrina caffra (Coast Coral Tree or South African Coral Tree) is a large, semi-deciduous tree native to the coastal forests and river margins of Eastern South Africa (KwaZulu-Natal, Eastern Cape) that has become one of the defining ornamental trees of the Southern California street landscape, the official city tree of Los Angeles. Trees lose most of their leaves in late winter and simultaneously burst into spectacular bloom — the dense, columnar racemes of bright coral-red to orange pea-family flowers covering the bare, spiny branches from January through March create an unforgettable winter floral display unmatched by almost any other tree in temperate gardens. The flowers are rich in nectar and attract hummingbirds, lorikeets, and sunbirds across its global planted range. Erythrina caffra is more cold-hardy than the related E. variegata — tolerating brief periods near 25°F when established in well-drained soil — which has made it the standard large coral tree for zone 8b–9 California and Southeastern gardens. A nitrogen-fixer that enriches surrounding soil; useful for large spaces, street medians, and parks.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, moisture-retentive, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; coast redwood grows naturally in the fog belt of the California and Oregon coast where summer fog provides constant atmospheric moisture. It grows best in moist, cool, deep soils.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, moisture-retentive, fertile loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; coast redwood is the world's tallest living tree — the tallest known individual (Hyperion in Redwood National Park) reaches 380 feet. Native to the fog belt of the California and Oregon coast, coast redwood is uniquely adapted to harvest water from fog directly through its needles, supplementing root-absorbed water in the dry California summer. Remarkably fast-growing for such a large tree — growth of 3–5 feet per year is common in ideal conditions in zones 8–10. Distinct from giant sequoia in being taller but much slimmer, with flat needles arranged in two ranks (like yew), and in its ability to sprout vigorously from the base after cutting or fire. Widely planted in California, the Pacific Northwest, and milder parts of the world (Ireland, New Zealand, the UK). Cutting-propagated plants from named selections are more reliable for garden planting than seed-grown trees.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, highly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial to full shade. Coastal Doghobble is one of the most shade-tolerant native broadleaf evergreen shrubs available for southeastern gardens and can thrive under dense tree canopy where few other shrubs persist.
directions: Coastal Doghobble is a graceful, arching, broadleaf evergreen native shrub, native to moist, acidic, shaded streambanks, ravine slopes, and moist, sandy forest understories of the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi, where its arching stems weave through the understory to form dense, impenetrable thickets — hence the 'doghobble' name, as hunting dogs became entangled in the arching stems. In April and May it produces racemes of small, white, urn-shaped flowers along the undersides of the arching branches, followed by attractive dark green, leathery, lance-shaped leaves that turn burgundy-red to bronze in winter, providing excellent cold-season color in the shade garden. One of the most shade-tolerant native broadleaf evergreen shrubs available, Coastal Doghobble thrives under dense tree canopy where azaleas and camellias struggle; provide consistently moist, acidic soil and avoid alkaline conditions or prolonged drought.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Coastal Indigo is a low, spreading native perennial with attractive silvery-hairy, pinnate foliage and clusters of brilliant rose-pink to coral-red pea flowers that continue from spring through fall, making it one of the longest-blooming native legumes of the southeastern coastal plain. It is native to dry, sandy, open ground, pine flatwoods, and roadsides from Georgia to Texas, and is notably more ground-hugging and spreading than most other Indigofera species. Scarify seeds before sowing in spring into dry, sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; amending or over-irrigating the soil will cause decline. An underused, exceptionally long-blooming native perennial for sandy, full-sun Gulf Coast gardens in zones 7 through 10, drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil; inkberry requires acidic conditions (pH 4.5–6.0) and is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, seasonally flooded sites. Plant both male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; inkberry is a versatile native evergreen holly of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain with glossy dark green leaves and small black berries that provide essential winter food for over 35 bird species including bluebirds, robins, cedar waxwings, and hermit thrushes. Unlike many hollies, inkberry tolerates wet, seasonally flooded sites and even some saltwater intrusion, making it ideal for rain gardens, bioswales, and poorly drained sites where most shrubs fail. Numerous compact cultivars have been developed for landscape use, including 'Compacta' (3–4 ft), 'Shamrock' (3–4 ft, very cold hardy), and 'Nigra' (4–6 ft with good fruiting). Both male and female plants are needed for berry production; one male ('Nordic' or 'Strongbox') pollinates several females.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full to partial sun along the coastal plain; coastal Joe-Pye weed is more compact than inland species and thrives in the moist, acidic soils of Atlantic and Gulf coastal lowlands.
directions: Coastal Joe-Pye weed is the compact, coastal-adapted Joe-Pye species of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, typically shorter and more restrained than its inland relatives (hollow Joe-Pye and spotted Joe-Pye) while producing equally beautiful, rounded, domed flower clusters of dusty pink to light purple that smother the plant in late summer and fall. Its compact size (3–5 feet) makes it more appropriate than the 6–8 foot inland species for typical garden borders, perennial beds, and rain gardens where the giant inland Joe-Pye weeds would overwhelm surrounding plants. Like all Joe-Pye weeds, it is a specialist butterfly plant — tiger swallowtails, monarchs, and large skippers congregate on the flower heads in late summer with impressive regularity — and an important late-season nectar source for native bees preparing for winter. It is naturally adapted to the acidic, sandy, moderately moist soils of coastal flatwoods, wet savannas, and streamside thickets of the Gulf Coast Coastal Plain, making it an ideal choice for naturalized woodland-edge gardens in the Deep South.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coastal jugflower requires excellent drainage and lean, low-phosphorus soil — like all Proteaceae, phosphorus fertilizer is lethal. It is native to the coastal sand dunes and heaths of southwestern Western Australia. The primary ornamental value is the extraordinarily fine, soft, silver-gray, silky-textured foliage — the name 'sericeus' means 'silky'. The small, tubular, red flowers in spring are secondary to the foliage in ornamental value.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coastal jugflower is grown almost exclusively for its foliage — one of the finest-textured, most silvery-soft, most ethereally beautiful of all Australian native shrub foliages. The leaves are divided into multiple, extremely fine, thread-like silver-gray segments covered in silky, lustrous, silver hairs that catch light from every angle and create an overall impression of a plant made from fine, soft, silver-gray floss — a shimmering, luminous, soft-silver cloud of extraordinary fine texture. Each leaf has multiple, feathery, thread-like lobes covered in the lustrous, silky hairs of the species name 'sericeus'. The whole shrub creates a medium-to-large mound of incomparably fine, silver-gray, soft-textured foliage that provides year-round textural and color contrast with nearby bold-leaved or dark-leaved plants. In spring it produces small, tubular, red flowers in the leaf axils — pleasant but not the primary ornamental point. Native to the coastal sand dunes and heathlands of southwestern Western Australia where its silver, reflective foliage may reduce water loss and reflect intense sunlight. Outstanding as a silver foliage specimen or contrast plant in zone 9 Mediterranean-climate gardens requiring excellent drainage and lean soil.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial sun to full sun; coastal plain joe-pye weed tolerates periodic standing water and is ideal for rain gardens, bog margins, and low wet areas that challenge most perennials.
directions: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial sun to full sun; coastal plain joe-pye weed tolerates periodic standing water and is ideal for rain gardens, bog margins, and low wet areas that challenge most perennials. Eutrochium dubium is a shorter and more compact species than the common E. purpureum, typically reaching 4–5 feet with distinctive whorled leaves in sets of three rather than four, and large, rounded, mauve-pink flower clusters from July through September that are among the best pollinator resources in the late-summer native garden, drawing monarch butterflies, swallowtails, and dozens of native bee species. It is native to Atlantic coastal plain wet meadows and swamps from Maine to Florida and is particularly well adapted to the heat and humidity of the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in dry to moderately moist, strongly acidic, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun. Coastal Plain Staggerbush is adapted to the xeric, fire-maintained scrub and flatwood habitats of the Florida peninsula and requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate clay, wet soils, or alkaline conditions.
directions: Coastal Plain Staggerbush is a native evergreen shrub endemic to the dry, sandy, fire-maintained scrub and flatwood habitats of the Florida peninsula, where its dense, leathery-leaved growth and small white to pink urn-shaped flowers in spring make it a characteristic component of the open, sunny, infertile sand communities dominated by oaks and palmettos. Adapted to the same xeric conditions as Florida Rosemary, Scrub Hickory, and other Florida scrub specialists, Coastal Plain Staggerbush requires excellent drainage and periodic low-intensity fire to maintain the open, competitive-free conditions it requires. Like other Lyonia species, the foliage contains grayanotoxins and is toxic to livestock if consumed. Plant in dry, strongly acidic, sandy, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun — Coastal Plain Staggerbush thrives in the nutrient-poor, fire-managed conditions of its native habitat and requires no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established.

plant_note: Take hardwood cuttings 8–12 inches long in late winter before bud break and insert directly into moist soil at the water's edge in full sun; rooting is rapid and reliable. Coastal Plain Willow establishes quickly from cuttings and can also be established by planting dormant rooted stems directly in saturated soil.
directions: Coastal Plain Willow is the most abundant native willow of the coastal plain wetlands, stream banks, tidal margins, and disturbed wet soils from Virginia south through Florida and west to Texas and the Caribbean, forming dense multi-stemmed thickets that provide critical cover and nesting habitat for waterfowl, shorebirds, and muskrats. Like all willows, it produces copious pollen and nectar in early spring that are among the first resources available to emerging queen bumblebees, native sweat bees, and early butterflies; the foliage hosts the caterpillars of Viceroy, Mourning Cloak, and numerous native moths. Propagate easily from hardwood cuttings taken in late winter before bud break, inserting 8–12 inch stems into moist, wet soil in full sun; rooting is rapid, establishment reliable, and fallen branches that contact moist soil root naturally. Coastal Plain Willow spreads aggressively by root suckers in wet areas and is best used in large, naturalized riparian settings where its vigorous growth habit is an asset.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with necks at soil surface in moist to well-drained, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 8–11; Coastal Spider Lily is a robust, salt-tolerant native bulb of the coastal scrubs, shell mounds, and beach margins of Florida and the Caribbean — producing large, spectacular, pure-white, intensely fragrant spider lily flowers on tall stems throughout summer — among the most salt-tolerant and coastal-adapted of all native Florida bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs with necks at or just above soil surface in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Hymenocallis latifolia is tolerant of coastal conditions — salt spray, limestone soils, and periodic drought once established — an excellent native bulb for coastal gardens and sandy, alkaline-soil landscapes in zone 8–11. Hymenocallis latifolia (Coastal Spider Lily or Perfumed Spider Lily) is a large, robust, bulbous perennial native to the coastal scrubs, hammocks, rocky pinelands, shell mounds, and beach margin habitats of southern Florida, the Florida Keys, and the Caribbean islands. The large, pure-white, intensely fragrant flowers — the characteristic Hymenocallis 'spider lily' form, with long, narrow, recurving petals surrounding a central, funnel-shaped corona with projecting stamens — are produced in umbels of 3–12 on tall, stout scapes, blooming in summer and fall. The fragrance is extraordinary — sweet, powerful, and vanilla-spice-like — and strongest in the evening, attracting hawk moths and nocturnal pollinators. Hymenocallis latifolia is distinguished from the freshwater-adapted H. littoralis by its preference for well-drained, coastal, limestone, and sandy soils rather than wet or flooded conditions, making it more versatile for typical garden settings. It shows excellent tolerance of salt spray, alkaline limestone soils, and sandy coastal substrates — making it outstanding for coastal Florida, Gulf Coast, and Caribbean garden planting where many bulbs fail.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry to average, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; cobaea penstemon is a calcicole (limestone lover) that absolutely requires sharp drainage and does not tolerate clay or wet soils — excellent for rock gardens and dry limestone slopes.
directions: Cobaea penstemon bears the largest flowers of any native American penstemon — its tubular, inflated blooms in shades of lavender to pale purple (occasionally white) with purple guidelines are two inches or more across, giving a tropical richness that seems almost too spectacular for a native of dry limestone prairies. Native to the rocky, alkaline prairies and cedar glades of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Missouri, it is one of the premier spring-blooming wildflowers of the southern Great Plains, with flower spikes rising from handsome rosettes of glossy, evergreen leaves in April and May. Bumblebees force their way into the large floral tubes to reach nectar, and the plant is an outstanding spring pollinator plant in dry, sunny native gardens. Sharp drainage on limestone or alkaline sandy soil is non-negotiable for this species in cultivation — it thrives in raised beds, rock gardens, and dry stone walls where water runs away quickly; it dies from root rot in typical garden soils with any tendency toward moisture retention.

plant_note: Plant individual rosettes or clusters in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; cobweb houseleek grows naturally on limestone and granite rock faces and cliffs of the Alps and Pyrenees, requiring excellent drainage and lean soils — excess fertility causes lush, open growth that loses the distinctive cobweb effect.
directions: Plant individual rosettes or clusters in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; cobweb houseleek is the most distinctive and charming of all the houseleeks — the small, tight rosettes of succulent leaves are covered in a characteristic network of fine, white, silky threads stretched across the rosette tips, resembling a tiny spider's web or a miniature snowflake. The species name 'arachnoideum' (spider-like) perfectly captures this remarkable feature. In midsummer, bright rose-pink, starry flowers are produced on short stems above the foliage. The cobwebbing is most pronounced and dense in full sun and lean soil conditions — excess moisture or shade causes it to lose its characteristic appearance. Multiplies readily by offsets into growing colonies. A favorite for troughs, rock gardens, dry stone walls, and hypertufa planters where its scale and intricate detail can be appreciated close up.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in warm (75–80°F), well-drained seed-starting mix, do not overwater; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm, spacing 9–12 inches in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in warm (75–80°F), well-drained seed-starting mix, do not overwater; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm, spacing 9–12 inches in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Celosia argentea encompasses the plumed celosia (var. plumosa) with feathery flame-shaped flower heads and the brain-like crested cockscomb (var. cristata), both of which come in brilliant, jewel-toned shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and cream; the flower heads are outstanding dried everlastings and fresh cut flowers. In tropical and subtropical Africa, the leaves and young shoots are an important leafy vegetable (known as "soko" in Nigeria and "quélites" in parts of Mexico), eaten boiled or added to soups and stews; the plant is nutritious and fast-growing. Very heat-tolerant and long-blooming; an excellent zone 9–11 annual.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost in peat pots to minimize transplant shock; celosia dislikes root disturbance. Direct sow outdoors after soil warms to 70°F. In zone 9, start in March for spring planting or in August for fall color.
directions: Start in peat pots indoors or direct sow after soil warms to 70°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Celosia argentea var. cristata (cockscomb) is the most dramatically formed of the celosias, producing a single, large, brain-like, fan-shaped, fasciated (abnormally flattened and broadened) flower head that can reach 4–6 inches wide in deep crimson, scarlet, orange, yellow, pink, or cream — the odd, velvet-textured, convoluted crest is one of the most unusual flower forms in cultivation and has been grown in gardens since ancient times in Asia, where it is used as a temple offering plant. Cockscomb thrives in hot, humid conditions and is outstanding in Gulf South gardens from late spring through frost; it is heat-tolerant and drought-resistant once established. Dwarf types ('Chief' series, 'Jewel Box' series) grow 6–10 inches with proportionally large flower heads; tall types can reach 18–24 inches. All celosias make exceptional dried flowers — harvest the crests before the first frost and hang upside down to dry; they hold color for months.

common_name: Cockspur Coral Tree (Ceibo, Cry Baby Tree, Fireman's Cap)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost; in zone 9, Cockspur Coral Tree dies back to the ground or trunk in cold winters but resprouts vigorously each spring and often blooms in the same year after being cut back. In zone 10-11 it is an evergreen or semi-deciduous tree; in zone 9 it behaves as a large die-back perennial. The thorny stems require care — wear heavy gloves when pruning. Seeds are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Cockspur Coral Tree is quite drought-tolerant once established and tolerates a wide range of soils including sand and alkaline conditions. Erythrina crista-galli (Cockspur Coral Tree or Ceibo) is the national tree and national flower of both Argentina and Uruguay — its spectacular, intense red flowers are also depicted in the coat of arms of Argentina. The flowers are large (2–2.5 inches), waxy, brilliant red, and clustered into drooping racemes at the branch tips in spring and summer; the characteristic 'crista-galli' (rooster's crest) refers to the hooded shape of the large standard petal. In warm climates the tree blooms March–June and again in fall, attracting hummingbirds, orioles, and numerous other nectar-feeding birds. In zone 9, the plant dies back to the root system after hard frost each winter and regrows to 5–8 feet by the following summer, blooming on new wood — acting effectively as a large, spectacular die-back perennial. In zone 10-11 it grows into a 30-foot tree with massive flowering displays. The thorny branches and trunks are a defensive characteristic; all parts of the plant are toxic if consumed. 'Compacta' is a dwarf cultivar reaching 6–8 feet suitable for smaller gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in average, well-drained to moist, adaptable soil in full sun to partial shade; cockspur hawthorn is extremely adaptable to a wide range of soils and moisture conditions and is one of the most drought-tolerant and pollution-tolerant of all native hawthorns.
directions: Cockspur hawthorn is a native small tree or large shrub of the eastern United States named for its long, curved thorns (3–4 inches) that resemble a rooster's spur and made it one of the most effective barrier hedges historically used to create impenetrable property boundaries before barbed wire. Its extremely wide, horizontal branching creates a distinctive, picturesque silhouette that provides year-round interest: white flower clusters in May, glossy red fruits persisting through winter, and spectacular scarlet-to-orange fall foliage color. As a wildlife tree, it is exceptional: the long-persistent red fruits are consumed by cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, robins, and bluebirds through winter when other food is scarce; the dense, thorny structure provides the safest possible nesting habitat for catbirds, thrashers, and wood thrushes. A thornless cultivar ('Inermis') is available for locations where the formidable thorns would be a hazard, providing all the wildlife and ornamental benefits of the species without the thorns.

common_name: Coco Magnolia / Dwarf White Jade Orchid
plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered spot with bright filtered light or morning sun and afternoon shade. Magnolia coco prefers moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil and performs exceptionally well in large containers, which allow the root zone to be protected during unusual cold spells in zone 9.
directions: Take semi-hardwood cuttings in late spring or early summer, wound the base lightly, apply rooting hormone, and root under intermittent mist or inside a humidity tent at 75-80°F with bright indirect light. Transplant rooted cuttings into organically enriched, well-drained soil and avoid heavy clay or sites prone to waterlogging, as Magnolia coco is sensitive to root rot. Unlike most magnolias that bloom in a single dramatic flush, this compact species produces its nodding, creamy-white, intensely sweet-scented flowers from spring through fall, making it especially rewarding near a patio, entryway, or courtyard window. Fertilize with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and midsummer, and deadhead spent flowers to keep the plant tidy and encourage the next wave of bloom.

common_name: Coconut Lime Coneflower (Double Green-and-White Pompom Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Coconut Lime produces fully double, pompom-like flowers combining a creamy white outer ring of petals with a raised, shaggy lime-green center, an unusual double form and color combination quite different from the simple single daisy flowers of the wild species. Its novel double form makes it a strong focal point in a mixed border and a good cut flower, though like other double coneflower cultivars it can be somewhat shorter-lived than the straight species and benefits from sharp drainage, particularly through humid summers. It still draws some pollinators, though double flowers generally offer less accessible pollen and nectar than single-flowered coneflower types.

common_name: Coconut Orchid (Thin-Leaved Maxillaria, Red Coconut Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light; Maxillaria tenuifolia is tolerant of a wider range of conditions than many epiphytic orchids and adapts well to intermediate indoor or shaded porch culture. Water regularly during active growth; reduce watering in winter but do not allow to desiccate completely. The coconut fragrance of the flowers is strongest on warm, sunny days and carries several feet from the plant. Blooms spring–summer. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in coarse bark medium or mounted on cork — Coconut Orchid needs good light to bloom reliably but benefits from protection from the most intense direct summer sun that can scorch the thin leaves. Maxillaria tenuifolia is a small, creeping, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most beloved small orchids in the collector world for a single, unforgettable characteristic: the flowers smell exactly, unmistakably, and powerfully of fresh coconut — a sweet, creamy, tropical fragrance that seems impossible from a small orchid flower but is real and carries several feet from the plant on warm days. The plant itself is modest in stature: a creeping mass of small, oval-to-egg-shaped pseudobulbs each producing a single, narrow (the 'tenuifolia' — thin-leaved), grass-like leaf 8–14 inches long. In spring and early summer, individual flowers emerge one per pseudobulb on very short stems from among the leaves — each flower 1–1.5 inches across, dark red to maroon-red with cream to yellow spotting on the lip, the overall coloration somewhat dark and modest in contrast to the extraordinary fragrance. A container or mounted specimen in full coconut bloom is one of the most pleasant aromatic experiences available from a tropical orchid. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or tubers after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 8–9 plant March–April. Coffee Cups is evergreen and root-hardy in zone 8b–11; in zone 8a and colder, mulch heavily to protect tubers over winter. Prefers partial shade to shade in zone 9 where afternoon sun can scorch the large leaves; full sun is acceptable if consistent moisture is maintained.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade in the heat of zone 9; Coffee Cups is a distinctive Colocasia esculenta cultivar whose large, bright green leaves develop strongly upturned margins as they mature, forming a pronounced cup or bowl shape that collects and holds rainwater — creating a living water feature that attracts wildlife and provides a dramatic focal point in the garden. The cupped leaves can hold several cups of water at a time, glinting and shimmering in dappled light; the effect is most pronounced on leaves of 18 inches or larger diameter. Unlike many dramatic elephant ear varieties, Coffee Cups performs well in partial to deep shade with consistent moisture, making it one of the most useful large-leaf shade plants for zone 8–9 gardens.
