The plant spreads readily by stolons and clumping; divide every 2–3 years to control spread. Provide consistent moisture or even wet-soil conditions, as the plant grows naturally along streamsides and in boggy areas.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring before new growth begins, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Colchis barrenwort is one of the most drought-tolerant and vigorous of all epimediums and is the parent of the widely grown E. × versicolor hybrids — it performs admirably in the dry shade of competitive tree roots where most shade groundcovers fail.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Colchis barrenwort is a Caucasian (Georgian and Iranian) epimedium species recognized as one of the most vigorous, drought-tolerant, and adaptable of the garden epimediums — it forms a steadily spreading, dense, weed-suppressing mat of compound, heart-shaped, spiny-edged, leathery, semi-evergreen leaves that are bronzed on emergence in spring before maturing to glossy, dark green. In spring, airy sprays of small, clear-yellow, four-petaled, spurred flowers — quite different from the long-spurred flowers of E. grandiflorum — rise just above the foliage. The species is one parent of E. × versicolor 'Sulphureum', the most commonly grown yellow epimedium. Colchis barrenwort is exceptional in its ability to spread and provide effective weed suppression in the dry shade under mature deciduous and coniferous trees. The previous season's foliage persists as an attractive bronze groundcover through winter before being replaced by spring growth. Among the very best plants for dry, difficult shade in zone 4–8.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in moist seed-starting mix; do not cover seeds as they require light to germinate. Pinch flower spikes as they form to maintain foliage color and density. In zone 9–11 coleus may be grown as a perennial with winter protection.
directions: Start seeds indoors or root cuttings easily in water; coleus is one of the most versatile and vividly colored foliage plants for shade and part-shade gardens, producing spectacular leaves in virtually every color combination imaginable — red, burgundy, orange, yellow, lime, pink, purple, bronze, and intricate multicolored patterns and textures. Modern sun-tolerant hybrids extend its use to full sun, but traditional coleus is happiest with morning sun and afternoon shade or dappled light under trees, where its colors often intensify beautifully. It is a workhorse of summer container gardening and shade bedding. Pinch the small flower spikes that develop in late summer to maintain bushy growth and color; once allowed to flower and set seed, foliage quality declines. In zone 9–11 old plants often survive mild winters and resprout in spring; take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors in colder zones.

common_name: Color Guard Yucca (Variegated Gold-Striped Adam's Needle)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or pups in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Color Guard is a variegated selection of native Adam's needle yucca, with a bold central gold stripe on each leaf that provides year-round color even without flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Color Guard is a striking variegated form of the native Adam's needle yucca, with each sword-shaped, evergreen leaf marked by a broad creamy-yellow central stripe bordered in blue-green, giving strong architectural color to the garden year-round rather than only during its tall summer flower spike of white bell-shaped blooms. Like the species it is extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and adaptable to poor soils once established, needing almost no supplemental care. It slowly produces offsets (pups) at the base that can be separated to propagate new plants, and spent flower stalks can be cut down after bloom.

plant_note: Start indoors and surface sow, as light aids germination; transplant to well-drained soil.
directions: A hardy, drought-tolerant perennial yarrow blend with feathery foliage and flat flower clusters in red, rose, pink, yellow, and white. Surface sow seed indoors and press it in without covering, since light aids germination. Transplant to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where it needs little water once established. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and cut flowers for fresh or dried arrangements.

plant_note: Start transplants after 4 weeks cold-moist stratification (or direct sow in fall), in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Colorado blue columbine tolerates more sun in cool mountain climates but requires afternoon shade in zone 6–8 heat.
directions: Start transplants after 4 weeks cold-moist stratification (or direct sow in fall), in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Colorado blue columbine tolerates more sun in cool mountain climates but requires afternoon shade in zone 6–8 heat. Aquilegia caerulea is the Colorado state flower and one of the most beautiful native columbines, with large flowers (2–3 inches) of clear, sky-blue sepals and pure-white, flat petals with long, straight blue spurs — a bicolor combination of exceptional purity; it grows naturally in mountain meadows and open forests from Wyoming to New Mexico at elevations of 6,000–11,500 feet and blooms in June–August. It is shorter-lived than some columbines (typically 3–5 years) but self-seeds freely to maintain the colony; remove spent flowers only partially to allow sufficient seed to set. The long spurs are adapted to hawkmoth pollination, and it is an important nectar source for several sphinx moth species.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall with plenty of room for the broad pyramidal form.
directions: This iconic conifer forms a stately pyramid of silvery-blue needles, serving as a striking specimen or windbreak. Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained soil and give it space, as mature trees grow large. Water regularly while young to establish deep roots, then it tolerates cold and moderate drought well. Avoid crowding to reduce needle-cast and canker problems, and prune only to remove dead or damaged branches.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native nodding tiger lily
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4–6 inches deep in full sun to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 4–9; Columbia Tiger Lily is the iconic native lily of the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to California — producing tall, elegant stems bearing numerous nodding, brilliant-orange, Turk's Cap-style flowers with maroon spots — growing naturally in open woodland margins, meadows, and forest clearings, and historically an important food plant for many Pacific Northwest Indigenous peoples.
directions: Plant Lilium columbianum bulbs 4–6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; provide consistent moisture through the growing season and avoid waterlogged conditions; mulch with leaf mold to keep roots cool; allow foliage to die back naturally after flowering. Columbia Tiger Lily is one of the most graceful and naturally beautiful of all North American native lilies — a hallmark wildflower of Pacific Northwest meadows, forest openings, and stream-side clearings that blooms in midsummer with dozens of brilliant orange, reflexed flowers spotted with maroon on each tall stem. The lily grows naturally in the transitional zone between open meadow and forest edge, preferring the soil moisture of forest proximity with the light of open areas — conditions replicated in the dappled shade of garden woodland margins. Many Pacific Northwest Indigenous groups — including the Chinook, Quileute, Klallam, and Quinault — ate the bulbs, roasted or boiled, as a significant starchy food source; the bulbs have a pleasantly mild, slightly bitter flavor similar to other edible lilies. An excellent plant for naturalizing in Pacific Northwest native gardens; it self-sows in suitable conditions and multiplies by bulb offsets to form larger colonies over time. Combines beautifully with Camas, Red Columbine, and native ferns.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify seeds indoors for 3–4 weeks before spring sowing.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly on the soil surface and provide 3–4 weeks of cold stratification (fall sowing outdoors achieves this naturally) to break dormancy. Columbines bloom most freely in their second and third years and are prolific self-seeders that will hybridize freely, creating a constantly shifting mix of colors. Leafminer damage creates white tunnels in the foliage but rarely threatens plant health; remove affected leaves and dispose of them. Plants are short-lived perennials (3–5 years) but the colony self-perpetuates readily through self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or start indoors in late winter with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F followed by germination at 60–70°F; transplant to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or start indoors in late winter with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F followed by germination at 60–70°F; transplant to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost. Thalictrum aquilegiifolium is one of the most beautiful and easily grown European meadow rues; its finely divided, blue-green foliage resembles columbine or maidenhair fern in texture and produces tall, airy stems in early to mid-summer bearing large, fluffy, lavender-purple to white flower clusters composed of prominent stamens rather than petals — a delicate, cloud-like effect outstanding at the back of a shaded border. In full sun it can wilt during heat waves; partial shade improves performance and longevity, especially in the South; it is excellent with hostas, astilbe, and bleeding heart in moist woodland garden borders.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; columbine meadow rue will tolerate full sun if soil remains consistently moist but looks most refined in the dappled shade of an open woodland garden.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; columbine meadow rue will tolerate full sun if soil remains consistently moist but looks most refined in the dappled shade of an open woodland garden. Thalictrum aquilegifolium is arguably the most beautiful of the meadow rues, with large, glaucous, blue-green leaves so similar in shape to columbine (Aquilegia) that the plant appears to be a columbine when not in flower; in late spring and early summer it produces large, fluffy, globe-shaped panicles of tiny flowers in lilac-purple, rose, or white (var. album) formed entirely of prominent stamens without petals, giving the flower heads an unusually light, powder-puff texture. It makes an outstanding companion for hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials and is long-lived and essentially care-free once established.

plant_note: Surface sow, as the seed needs light; stock thrives in cool weather.
directions: Start seed indoors and surface sow, since stock germinates best with light, then transplant while the weather is still cool. This blend forms upright, single-stemmed columns of fully double, clove-scented blooms excellent for bouquets and drying. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and even moisture, and set plants out early because stock dislikes summer heat. It performs especially well in containers and cool spring gardens.

plant_note: Plant in spring once soils have warmed in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun. In zones 7-8 provide a light mulch over the root crown in winter for added protection.
directions: Comfortroot is a native Hibiscus of wet longleaf pine flatwoods, bogs, and seasonal wetlands along the southeastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida, bearing cream-white to pale yellow flowers with a striking dark maroon eye from July through September. Its deeply lobed, palmate leaves give it a distinctive texture among native mallows, and its smaller stature compared to showier rose mallows makes it useful in tighter planting schemes. Grow in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, nutrient-poor soil in full sun, mimicking the conditions of its native longleaf pine savanna habitat. An excellent, low-maintenance native for Gulf Coast landscapes, rain gardens, and longleaf pine ecosystem restorations where most ornamentals would struggle.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into lean, well-drained soil in a sunny spot; cold stratification over winter improves germination, and seedlings emerge reliably in spring.
directions: Sow seed directly into a sunny, lean, and sharply drained site in fall, covering lightly with no more than one-quarter inch of soil and firming the surface. Common Bugloss thrives on neglect in poor, dry ground and will underperform in rich or overly moist soils, so resist the temptation to amend the bed with compost. Space plants generously to allow air circulation around the hairy stems and to accommodate the plant's tendency to self-sow freely; remove spent flower heads if naturalization is not desired. The vivid blue, coiled flower clusters emerge in early summer and are exceptionally attractive to bumblebees, making this plant a high-value addition to dry pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring before new growth emerges. Plant divisions in consistently moist or wet soil in a shaded or partly shaded location. Be aware that this plant spreads aggressively by rhizomes and should be sited with containment in mind.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in boggy or reliably moist ground, spacing them generously to accommodate their eventual spread. Choose a site in partial shade near a pond edge, stream bank, or rain garden where the soil rarely dries out. The dramatic pink flower spikes emerge before the leaves in early spring; the enormous leaves that follow provide bold textural interest through summer. Install a buried root barrier if planting near manicured areas, as rhizomes spread vigorously.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in wet to consistently moist soil; this is one of the few large shrubs that thrives in standing water and wet clay where most plants fail.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, or even periodically flooded soil in full sun to partial shade; buttonbush is a native shrub of swamps, pond margins, and floodplains throughout eastern North America, producing creamy white spherical flower heads resembling pincushions in July and August that are among the most intensively visited flowers by butterflies, native bees, and hummingbirds. The round seed heads provide food for waterfowl and songbirds through winter. It is one of the premier plants for rain gardens, bioswales, and pond edges where periodic flooding occurs. Prune in late winter to shape and stimulate new flowering wood; it can be cut back hard if it becomes too large.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; common camas is historically one of the most important food plants of Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and Great Basin, and a spectacular spring-blooming bulb for naturalized gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in moist, organic soil in a location that stays moist in spring but is not permanently waterlogged; camassia bulbs naturalize readily and spread slowly over time to form dense colonies. Common camas is a western North American native bulb that was historically one of the most important food plants for many Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest and Great Basin, who harvested the starchy bulbs in vast quantities and traded them widely; Meriwether Lewis and William Clark noted large fields of blue camas during their 1805–1806 expedition and remarked on its importance as a food source. The star-shaped, violet-blue to pale blue flowers are held on 12–24 inch stems in late spring and are spectacular when naturalized in masses in moist meadow gardens, under deciduous trees, or along stream edges. Goes dormant by midsummer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; common cinquefoil spreads by long, horizontal stolons (runners) that root at the nodes to form expanding colonies in dry, open conditions. It grows naturally in dry open woods, sandy roadsides, and meadow edges.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; common cinquefoil is a native low-growing groundcover of dry, sandy, open habitats across eastern North America, spreading by long, slender stolons (runners) to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat of small, five-fingered (cinquefoil = 'five leaves') compound leaves. The small, bright yellow, five-petaled flowers bloom in spring and continue sporadically throughout summer. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in lean, sandy, nutrient-poor soils where more demanding groundcovers fail. The spreading stolons root readily to stabilize sandy slopes and disturbed, dry banks. An excellent low-maintenance native groundcover for dry, sunny areas between stepping stones, along driveways, and in hell strips where lawn grass struggles. Unlike many cinquefoils, this species is not aggressive in richer soils.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; common correa is one of the most variable Australian species — occurring naturally in a wide range of habitats from coastal cliffs to mountain forests. Flower color varies from pure red through red-and-green bicolor to pink, white, and yellow-green in different forms. It blooms in winter and spring, providing nectar for honeyeating birds. Several selected cultivars are available.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; common correa is the most widespread Australian Correa species — occurring naturally across the entire southeastern corner of Australia from Queensland to South Australia, in habitats from coastal cliffs and heathlands to mountain forests — and producing in winter and early spring the pendant, tubular, fuchsia-like flowers that give all the correas their common name 'native fuchsia'. The flower form is characteristically correa: a pendant, narrow, tubular or slightly flared tube with four petals that reflex (turn back) at the tip, the whole flower dangling downward from the stem like a small, pendant, delicate bell. The flower color in the wild type is typically red to green-and-red bicolor — a vivid red tube with reflexing green petal tips — but the species is exceptionally variable, with white, pink, salmon, and pure green forms occurring naturally and several selected cultivars now in the trade. The winter bloom timing provides nectar for winter-active honeyeating birds; in cultivation it serves hummingbirds. More shade-tolerant than most Australian natives, growing well in the dappled shade of light-canopy trees. One of the most adaptable and garden-worthy of all correas.

plant_note: Fall sow or early spring; biennial that blooms in its second year.
directions: Surface sow common evening primrose in fall or early spring, pressing the seed in lightly since it needs light to germinate. This hardy native biennial forms a low rosette its first year, then sends up tall stems of fragrant yellow flowers that open at dusk the second season. It thrives in poor, dry soil and tolerates neglect, making it ideal for tough spots and pollinator plantings. Let it self-sow to keep the two-year cycle going in the garden.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in moist, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; afternoon shade in zones 8–10 reduces leaf scorch and prolongs bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil with afternoon shade in zones 8–10 to prevent leaf scorch; gardenia is prized for its intensely fragrant, waxy white flowers that bloom in late spring to midsummer and makes one of the most effective landscape shrubs in the Deep South when sited correctly. Maintain consistent soil moisture but never allow roots to sit in standing water — drought stress triggers bud drop. Fertilize monthly from spring through summer with an acid-type fertilizer; yellowing leaves between the veins (interveinal chlorosis) signal iron or manganese deficiency and respond to applications of chelated iron. Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in late summer for propagation.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; common grape hyacinth is one of the most cold-hardy spring bulbs available, extremely reliable in zones 3-8, and naturalizes freely into large colonies over time. Like M. armeniacum, its foliage emerges in autumn and persists through winter — do not remove it. The white-flowered cultivar 'Album' is particularly elegant.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for March-April bloom; common grape hyacinth (also called blue bottle or bluebells of Spain in older literature) is the hardiest and most northerly-adapted of the grape hyacinths — reliably perennial to zone 3 where M. armeniacum may struggle. It produces the classic dense, cobalt-blue flower spikes on short, compact stems in early spring, often blooming alongside the earliest tulips and late daffodils. The species includes a well-known pure white form, M. botryoides 'Album', which is as vigorous and easily grown as the blue type and useful for combining with blue Scilla or Chionodoxa in mixed spring plantings. Like all Muscari, it thrives under deciduous trees and shrubs where it receives abundant early spring sun before the canopy leafs out, making it an excellent choice for woodland edges and naturalized plantings. Increases steadily by offsets and self-seeding to form sizeable colonies.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in a wide range of soils from dry to moist, full sun to full shade; common greenbrier is extremely adaptable but its thorny stems make placement important — best in naturalized areas or as wildlife cover.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any reasonably fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to full shade; common greenbrier climbs by tendrils and should be given a sturdy support or allowed to clamber through shrubs in naturalized garden areas, as the stout, prickly stems are difficult to remove once established. Smilax rotundifolia is a native vine of eastern North American forests, woodland edges, and disturbed areas; it produces stout, green, thorny stems that climb vigorously by paired tendrils, bearing glossy, round to heart-shaped, evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves, small, greenish, insignificant flowers in spring, and clusters of blue-black berries in fall that are important wildlife food for many species of birds and mammals. The young shoot tips, new leaves, and rhizome tips are edible and have been used as food by Native Americans; the berries are edible but insipid. Best used in naturalized, wildlife-friendly gardens where its aggressive colonizing habit is an asset rather than a problem.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed immediately after collection in late summer to early fall — hepatica seed loses viability within weeks of ripening and must not be allowed to dry out before sowing; sow directly into a prepared woodland bed or into pots kept outdoors through winter. Plants are very slow to establish and may take 3–5 years to bloom from seed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade under a deciduous canopy, enriched with leaf mold; Hepatica nobilis is a diminutive woodland perennial of extraordinary early-season charm, producing small, jewel-like flowers of blue, lavender, pink, or white — sometimes with many petals in the double forms — from February through early April, typically before the new leaves emerge, making it one of the very first perennials to bloom in late winter and a critical early nectar source for queen bumblebees emerging from overwintering. The distinctive three-lobed, leathery leaves (which give the plant its common name, reflecting their resemblance to a human liver) persist through winter, often bronzing handsomely in cold weather, and are replaced by fresh green foliage after bloom. Hepatica is extremely slow to establish from seed — patience of 3–5 years is required before first bloom — but once settled it is very long-lived and essentially permanent in suitable conditions; do not disturb established plants.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost on the surface of moist seed-starting mix (light-dependent germination); or purchase transplants. Avoid downy mildew (Plasmopara obducens) by purchasing disease-resistant varieties such as 'Beacon' or 'Compact Power' series and avoiding overhead irrigation.
directions: Plant transplants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; common impatiens is the world's best-selling bedding plant for shaded areas, producing a continuous flush of flowers from planting until frost without deadheading. Available in red, pink, orange, white, salmon, coral, lavender, and bicolor, it provides reliable, long-season color in the shade garden. A downy mildew outbreak in 2012–2013 devastated impatiens plantings across North America; resistant varieties developed since then should always be chosen over traditional types. Keep soil consistently moist — impatiens wilts dramatically in drought and does not recover well from repeated dry-out. Avoid overhead watering to reduce disease. In zone 9–11 it may overwinter and continue blooming through mild winters; elsewhere treat as an annual.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on bare soil in fall; seeds require cold stratification to germinate well — fall sowing lets winter temperatures do this naturally; thin to 24-inch spacing in spring once seedlings reach 3–4 inches tall.
directions: Common ironweed is a tough, adaptable native perennial found naturally in moist prairies, roadsides, and streambank edges across the central and eastern United States — its compact size (3–5 feet) compared to tall ironweed makes it more useful in typical garden settings while delivering the same brilliant purple pollinator impact. Dense, flat-topped clusters of vivid purple flowers open from midsummer into fall, overlapping with many other prairie perennials and providing critical late-season nectar for migrating monarchs, swallowtails, and native bumblebees. Plants spread slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding, eventually forming clumps that can be divided every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and share plants. Combine with yellow-flowered natives like sneezeweed, black-eyed Susan, and prairie coneflower for maximum visual impact — the complementary warm yellow and cool purple combination is a classic of native meadow plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; one of the earliest-blooming shade perennials, often flowering alongside late snowdrops.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; lungwort is one of the earliest-blooming shade perennials, often flowering alongside late snowdrops, and the spotted foliage provides interest through the entire growing season. Pulmonaria officinalis is a low-growing, semi-evergreen European perennial with hairy, elliptic, white-spotted leaves in the borage family; it produces clusters of small funnel-shaped flowers in early spring that open pink from the bud and change to violet-blue as they age, creating a bicolor effect of pink and blue flowers simultaneously on the same plant — one of the most charming spring displays in the shade garden. The silver-spotted, hairy leaves remain attractive all season and increase the plant's ornamental value beyond bloom time; cut back straggly foliage in mid-summer to promote fresh new growth. Species is the type but many superior-spotted cultivars like 'Sissinghurst White' and 'Trevi Fountain' are widely available.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained soil; flowers open in the morning and close by early afternoon.
directions: Common Madia is a strongly aromatic native annual tarweed with glandular-sticky, resinous stems and bright yellow, daisy-like flowers whose ray petals are marked at the base with a distinctive maroon blotch; flowers open in the morning and close by early afternoon. Native to dry, open grasslands, meadows, and chaparral margins throughout California and the Pacific Northwest, it thrives in lean, sandy or loamy, well-drained soil with no supplemental summer water once established. Direct sow seed in fall in full sun, scattering lightly and pressing into contact with the soil surface; plants germinate with winter rains and bloom from late spring into summer. The sticky resin on the stems reportedly deters deer browsing, making this an excellent, drought-tolerant choice for sunny dry garden borders in Mediterranean-climate gardens.

plant_note: Fall sow or cold-stratify 30 days before spring planting.
directions: Sow common milkweed in fall or cold-stratify the seed for a month before spring planting to break dormancy. This vigorous native perennial grows two to three feet tall with broad leaves and fragrant clusters of pink star-shaped flowers that are vital to Monarch butterflies. It spreads by rhizomes and can colonize, so site it where it has room to naturalize. Give it full sun and average soil, and it will host caterpillars and feed countless pollinators.

common_name: Common Monkey Flower (Yellow Monkey Flower, Seep Monkey Flower)
plant_note: Surface-sow seeds — do not cover, as they require light for germination — in cool, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade or beside water features; monkey flower grows naturally in seeps, wet meadows, and stream banks and requires consistent moisture to perform well.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade beside streams, ponds, or bog gardens; monkey flower is a widely distributed native perennial of the Americas producing cheerful, snapdragon-like yellow flowers spotted with reddish-brown at the throat from spring through fall as long as moisture is adequate. The flowers are genuinely designed for bumblebees, which squeeze the flower open to reach the nectar — an interaction called buzz pollination. Common monkey flower is among the most successful colonizers of disturbed wet habitats in its native western range and has naturalized throughout the eastern US in suitable moist spots. It spreads by stolons in wet conditions to form dense colonies at stream edges and wet seeps. In the garden it is outstanding in rain gardens, bog gardens, and at pond margins where its cheery yellow flowers add color through the season in partial to dappled shade. Plants may behave as perennials or self-seeding annuals depending on climate.

plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade in spring; montbretia spreads rapidly by cormlets along the underground stolons and can become invasive in mild, moist climates — it has naturalized extensively on the coasts of Ireland, Wales, and the Pacific Northwest. In zones 6–7 mulch corms heavily in winter or lift them like gladiolus for frost-free storage.
directions: Plant corms in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; common montbretia is a Victorian-era hybrid (Crocosmia aurea x C. pottsii) that has become one of the most naturalizing of all summer-blooming South African corm plants, spreading by chains of cormlets to form large, grassy colonies and producing, in mid to late summer, arching, branched sprays of funnel-shaped, intense orange-red flowers that bend in graceful, one-sided racemes above fans of broad, sword-shaped leaves — creating one of the most characteristic and cheerful sights of the late-summer garden. The foliage, in pleated fans of bright lime-green, is ornamental from spring through autumn. The flowers, individually tubular and slightly flared, are irresistible to hummingbirds. Modern Crocosmia hybrids and cultivars derived from this cross and other species include the famous 'Lucifer' (flame-red, 4 feet, zones 5–9), 'Emily McKenzie' (large orange flowers with dark mahogany blotch), 'George Davidson' (golden-yellow), and 'Solfatare' (bronze foliage, yellow flowers). The species hybrid naturalized so freely in coastal Ireland and Wales that it has become part of the wild landscape.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; common net bush is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the hot, dry, lean conditions of southwestern Australian coastal heath. It blooms mainly in spring to early summer, producing distinctive, one-sided clusters of crimson flower bundles embedded along the woody stems. More cold-tolerant than many Western Australian natives. The common name 'net bush' refers to the appearance of older specimens.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; common net bush is a large Australian shrub of the southwest with a distinctly unusual flower arrangement — unlike the symmetrical bottlebrush spikes of Callistemon, in which flowers radiate from all sides of a terminal spike, Calothamnus (and its flowers are embedded along the woody, older stems and oriented predominantly to one side of the stem — the 'one-sided bottlebrush' habit that makes the genus immediately distinguishable. The crimson flower bundles appear in spring along the older, needle-leaved, dark-green stems at intervals, the scarlet to crimson stamen bundles projecting to one side of the stem in a bold, contrasting display of rich crimson on dark, needle-like foliage. The effect is unusual and distinctly architectural — red flower bundles appearing at intervals along the dark, spiky-leaved, one-sided bottlebrush stems — and quite different from the familiar symmetrical bottlebrush form. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established, enduring the hot, dry, lean conditions of southwestern Australian coastal scrub without supplemental irrigation in Mediterranean-climate zones. A distinctive choice for water-wise zone 9 gardens seeking Australian flora with unusual flower arrangement.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; common polypody naturally grows on rock outcrops, dry stone walls, and tree bases — it thrives in conditions with excellent drainage and bright indirect light where other ferns fail.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to gritty soil in partial to full shade; common polypody is among the most distinctive of all hardy ferns — its fronds are once-pinnate, with rounded, smooth-edged lobes rather than the further-divided, delicate-looking fronds of most ferns, giving each frond a simple, bold quality like a large green comb. The fronds are evergreen, remaining green through winter and refreshing only in spring. Large, round, golden spore dots (sori) on the underside of the fronds are ornamental features in themselves. The plant grows naturally on dry, shaded rock outcrops, stone walls, and epiphytically on the bark of trees — it is specifically adapted to good drainage and does not tolerate soggy soil. Excellent for shaded rock gardens, dry stone walls, and crevice gardens. The rhizomes have a pleasant, licorice-like scent when cut. A charming, low-maintenance fern for difficult dry-shade situations where most ferns fail.

plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; romulea flowers in late winter to early spring (February–April) in sunny weather — the flowers close at night and in cloudy or cold weather, opening only when the sun reaches them. The whole plant goes summer dormant. Common romulea is widespread across the Mediterranean Basin from Portugal to Turkey, giving it wide climatic tolerance across zones 7–10.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gritty soil in full sun; common romulea is a small but charming Mediterranean iris-family plant — one of about 90 Romulea species distributed between the Mediterranean Basin and southern Africa — that produces in late winter and early spring (February–April in the Mediterranean, opening only in sunny weather and closing at night) cup-shaped to star-shaped flowers in shades of pale to deep lilac-violet to purple, with yellow at the center throat and often with darker veining on the outer surface of the tepals. The flowers are small — 1–1.5 inches across — but produced in such abundance on a naturalized colony that the collective display of small, lilac crocus-like cups opening to the sun is very pretty. The narrow, rush-like leaves, emerging before the flowers, are quill-like and wiry. The whole plant goes completely summer dormant. It is particularly interesting among Mediterranean bulbs for blooming so early — in Feb–March among the earliest of all spring bulbs — and for the behavior of flower opening only in direct sunlight. Naturalizes freely in lean, well-drained, sunny soils of rock gardens and gravel paths.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; common rush is among the most important native emergent wetland plants for rain gardens, bioswales, pond margins, and stormwater management areas, providing erosion control, wildlife shelter, and sediment filtration.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to saturated, slightly acidic to neutral soil; common rush tolerates partial flooding and is excellent for rain garden center zones and pond margins. Juncus effusus (common rush or soft rush) is a widespread native wetland plant found in marshes, wet meadows, stream margins, and pond edges throughout North America; the smooth, cylindrical, deep-green stems (the photosynthetic organs — leaves are reduced to sheaths at the base) emerge in dense, arching clumps 2–4 feet tall and produce branched, brownish flower clusters appearing to emerge from the side of the stem. Common rush is one of the most ecologically valuable native wetland plants for rain garden and constructed wetland design — providing erosion control, bird nesting material, and insect habitat. The cultivar 'Spiralis' (corkscrew rush) with spiral, twisted stems is widely grown as an ornamental water garden plant and is one of the most distinctive ornamental grasses for containers and bog gardens.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; seeds benefit from cold stratification over winter and germinate in spring — common sneezeweed is native to moist prairies, stream banks, and low meadows across most of North America.
directions: Sow seeds direct in fall on the soil surface (light aids germination) in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in early spring — common sneezeweed thrives in consistently moist to wet soils and is poorly suited to dry conditions. Helenium autumnale is a tall, clump-forming native perennial producing winged stems with decurrent leaf bases and large, yellow, daisy-like flowers with distinctively reflexed ray petals fanning backward from a prominent rounded, yellow-brown disk from August through October — one of the most important late-season pollinator plants in North America. It is exceptionally attractive to native bumblebees, sweat bees, and specialist Helenium-foraging bees; the pollen-rich disk flowers support enormous populations of small native bees during the critical late-season period before frost. Divide established clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor and increase bloom; plants in rich, moist soils may need staking if they exceed 4 feet.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring or fall and plant horizontally 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; Solomon's seal establishes slowly from rhizome divisions but becomes very long-lived once settled. Mark the planting location well as it emerges late in spring. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; common Solomon's seal is one of the most graceful and architecturally distinctive of all woodland shade perennials — an arching, unbranched perennial producing elegantly curved stems that emerge in spring and gradually arch to 2–3 feet, lined on both sides with neat, oval, prominently veined leaves that give each stem the quality of a green feather. In May and June, small pairs of white, bell-shaped, pendant flowers dangle beneath the leaf axils along the entire length of the arching stem — tiny, delicate, and sweetly fragrant, entirely hidden beneath the leaves. Blue-black berries follow in autumn. The arching architectural form, with leaves so precisely arranged along each stem, is one of the defining visual qualities of the shaded woodland garden. It spreads slowly by creeping rhizomes, eventually forming expanding colonies. Outstanding as a structural background element for hostas, ferns, and woodland wildflowers in shaded situations. The hybrid Polygonatum x hybridum (P. multiflorum x P. odoratum) and the cultivar 'Striatum' (cream-striped leaves) are also widely grown.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; spiderwort self-sows freely and can become weedy in ideal conditions — deadhead promptly to prevent excessive seeding.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; common spiderwort is a native Eastern North American perennial that produces clusters of striking three-petaled flowers in intense purple-blue, pink, or white from late spring through early summer, with each flower lasting only a single day but continuously replaced from clustered buds. The long, lance-shaped, folded leaves are distinctly grass-like. After the bloom period in early summer, cut the entire plant back by half to two-thirds — it regrows within weeks with fresh, attractive foliage and often a second flush of bloom in fall. Tolerates a wide range of conditions including clay soil, seasonal wet feet, and partial shade. Valuable early-season nectar source for bees. Native ecotype selections include 'Zwanenburg Blue', 'Purple Dome', and 'Osprey' (white).

plant_note: Transplant purchased tubers or divisions in early spring before new growth emerges. Disturb roots as little as possible and plant at the same depth they were growing previously. These orchids depend on specific soil mycorrhizae, so transplanting into undisturbed woodland soil improves success.
directions: Plant in dappled shade at the edge of woodland or under deciduous trees where soil is moist but well-drained. Enrich the planting site with leaf mold rather than fertilizer, as these orchids thrive in low-nutrient conditions similar to their native meadow and open-woodland habitat. The characteristically spotted leaves emerge in early spring; protect plants from slugs during this vulnerable phase. Avoid disturbing established clumps, as the underground tubers are fragile and the mycorrhizal network they depend on is easily disrupted.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep and 6–12 inches apart after last frost in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; sunflowers are extremely fast-growing and drought-tolerant once established but need consistent moisture during germination.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep and 6–12 inches apart after last frost in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; sunflowers are extremely fast-growing and drought-tolerant once established but need consistent moisture during germination. Helianthus annuus is a North American native wildflower domesticated by indigenous peoples in what is now the central United States before 3000 BCE as a seed oil, food, and dye crop long before its introduction to Europe; the wild plant is native to dry, open, disturbed sites from British Columbia to Mexico. In cultivation it produces large, ray-and-disk composite flowers from midsummer through fall that are premier nectar and pollen sources for native bees (particularly long-tongued bumblebees and specialist Melissodes bees) and produce abundant oil-rich seeds harvested by goldfinches, chickadees, and dozens of other birds. Ornamental, edible-seed, and bird-feeding selections range from 2-foot dwarfs to 14-foot giants; all are easy and rewarding.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, slightly acidic soil in full sun; leucadendron is extremely sensitive to phosphorus toxicity — never use standard fertilizers with phosphate. Use low-phosphorus fertilizer labeled for proteas or no fertilizer in appropriately lean soil. Do not amend the soil with compost or manure.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; common sunshine conebush is the most adaptable and widely grown Leucadendron species, a South African fynbos shrub producing lance-shaped leaves that flush brilliant yellow-green to gold in winter and spring — the yellow color intensifying with cooler temperatures and brightening the garden in the season when color is most needed. Male and female plants are distinct (dioecious); female plants produce small, scaled cones surrounded by the colorful bracts; male plants produce more colorful upright flower heads. Many named hybrids including 'Safari Sunset' (dark red), 'Wilson's Wonder,' and 'Cloudbank Ginny' are popular in the cut foliage trade. Like all protea family plants (Proteaceae), leucadendrons require excellent drainage, lean soil with very low phosphorus, and minimal irrigation once established. Outstanding in California Mediterranean climates and dry subtropical gardens; a major component of the international cut-foliage industry.

plant_note: Anchor bunches in pond substrate or allow to float freely; common waterweed is a native, non-invasive oxygenating plant for backyard ponds, water gardens, and natural ponds in zones 4–10. It prefers cooler water temperatures than the invasive Brazilian elodea (Egeria densa).
directions: Anchor bunches in pond substrate or allow to root naturally in the pond bottom in partial shade to full sun; common waterweed is the native North American alternative to the widely used but invasive Brazilian elodea (Egeria densa), providing the same critical oxygenating and water-purifying services in backyard ponds without the risk of invasion in regional waterways. The whorled, small, lance-shaped leaves are arranged in tight spirals along the stems, and tiny, three-petaled white flowers float at the water surface on delicate threads in summer. As a highly efficient oxygenator, it absorbs CO₂ and releases O₂ through photosynthesis, supporting fish and aquatic life. It also absorbs dissolved nutrients, competing with algae for phosphorus and nitrogen. Prefers cool to moderate water temperatures and performs best in ponds with good water movement. The stems are consumed by waterfowl, turtles, and aquatic invertebrates.

plant_note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; common witch hazel is highly shade-tolerant and grows naturally as an understory tree in mature eastern deciduous forests.
directions: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; common witch hazel is highly shade-tolerant and grows naturally as an understory tree in mature eastern deciduous forests. Hamamelis virginiana is the source of the distilled witch hazel extract used in skincare, first-aid, and medicinal products worldwide, and has extraordinary ornamental value as a native shrub/small tree that blooms with wavy, spider-like, bright-yellow fragrant flowers directly on bare branches from October through December — the latest-blooming native woody plant in eastern North America. It also provides outstanding fall foliage color in shades of yellow to orange-red, is a critical late-season nectar source for witch hazel bees (Andrena astragali) and other fall-active insects, and the ballistic seed capsules that eject seeds up to 30 feet give rise to its folk name. Extremely adaptable, cold-hardy, and long-lived.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; this fern is semi-evergreen to evergreen in milder climates, making it a valuable year-round groundcover in shaded gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; common wood fern is among the most widely distributed native ferns in eastern North America and one of the most practical for garden use, being semi-evergreen (holding its green fronds into early winter in most climates), adaptable to both moist and moderately dry soils under forest canopy, and vigorous enough to compete with tree roots. The finely divided, lacy fronds have a fresh, bright green color and a distinctive triangular outline. Unlike the cinnamon or royal ferns, this species grows well in drier shade — under dense deciduous trees where the soil dries in summer — making it invaluable for difficult shaded spots. Provide adequate organic matter at planting and mulch annually with shredded leaves for best results.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; zinnia germinates in 5–7 days and reaches bloom in 60–70 days.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; zinnia germinates in 5–7 days and reaches bloom in 60–70 days. Zinnia elegans is the most important annual butterfly plant in the American garden — in high summer, flowering zinnias attract more butterfly species simultaneously than almost any other plant, hosting swallowtails, monarchs, painted ladies, fritillaries, and dozens of others; they are also the longest-blooming, most heat-resistant summer annual for zones 9–11. Plants bloom continuously from early summer through frost with deadheading, in a full palette of white, yellow, orange, red, pink, and bicolor; they are outstanding as cut flowers. Powdery mildew can be a problem in humid conditions — ensure good air circulation and choose mildew-resistant varieties for zone 8–9.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sowing into very well-drained, dry, calcareous or sandy, lean soil in full sun.
directions: Compact Prairie Clover forms neat, low mounds of fine-textured, pinnate foliage studded in summer with dense, cylindrical spikes of bright purple to rose-violet flowers, making it one of the tidiest and most ornamental of the native prairie clovers for garden use. It is native to dry, rocky limestone glades and open sandy prairies of the south-central US and demands very well-drained, dry, calcareous or sandy, lean soil in full sun to perform well. Scarify seeds before fall direct sowing and avoid any soil that retains moisture, as this plant is prone to root rot in clay or poorly drained sites. Its compact habit makes it well-suited for the front edge of dry native prairie gardens, dry rock gardens, and limestone glade restorations where it also provides important forage for specialist Dalea bees.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall to allow winter cold stratification to break dormancy; do not transplant, as seedlings immediately develop a deep taproot that cannot be disturbed.
directions: Direct sow on the soil surface in fall and allow natural cold stratification over winter to break seed dormancy; germination occurs the following spring. Compass plant is one of the most iconic tallgrass prairie species — its deeply pinnately lobed basal leaves reliably orient their flat faces north and south, giving early settlers a natural compass on the treeless plains. The plant grows slowly for the first several years, investing energy almost entirely in a massive taproot that can reach 10–15 feet deep, which makes it extraordinarily drought tolerant and effectively immortal once established, with individual plants potentially living over a century. Bright yellow daisy-like flowers 2–3 inches across appear on tall branching stems from July through September, providing pollen and nectar for native bees and seeds for birds.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall for spring germination; composite rosinweed is a Coastal Plain species growing in dry, sandy, acidic, open pine flatwoods and sandhills. One of the few rosinweeds adapted to the acidic, sandy soils of the southeastern Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; composite rosinweed is a southeastern Coastal Plain endemic adapted to the dry, sandy, acidic longleaf pine savanna ecosystem — one of the most challenging soil environments for plants. Unlike most Silphiums that prefer richer, more neutral soils, this species is particularly suited to the lean, sandy, infertile soils of pine flatwoods and sandhills. The deeply divided, almost fern-like leaves are ornamentally distinctive and unlike any other rosinweed. Tall branched stems carry numerous small yellow daisy flowers in summer. The seeds attract goldfinches and other seed-eaters. A valuable component of longleaf pine ecosystem restoration plantings and an unusual addition to dry, sandy, native plant gardens in zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Concord Grape tolerates partial shade well and actually benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense heat, which keeps the foliage cleaner through midsummer.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Concord Grape is one of the finest and most striking modern spiderwort cultivars — a compact, well-branched selection producing abundant clusters of rich grape-purple to deep violet-purple three-petaled flowers with bright yellow stamens from late spring through early summer in zone 9. The deep, saturated purple color is more vivid and consistent than older spiderwort cultivars and is outstanding in combination with chartreuse foliage, silver-leafed plants, and yellow companions. The strap-like, blue-green, grass-like foliage makes it attractive even when not in flower — the foliage texture is distinctive and different from most herbaceous perennials. Like most spiderworts, Concord Grape typically declines and becomes messy in midsummer heat — this is normal; cut the plants back hard (to 6 inches) after the main bloom flush, water well, and fresh new growth and often a secondary bloom flush will occur in fall. In zone 9, afternoon shade prolongs the attractive season and reduces the midsummer decline. Spiderworts spread gradually by self-seeding and rhizome expansion — maintain the colony by dividing every 2–3 years. Excellent in naturalistic woodland edges, rain gardens, and moist low spots where many plants fail.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun to partial shade; confederate jasmine is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and thrives in both sun and partial shade. Train onto a trellis or fence early — without support it sprawls as a mounding groundcover.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; confederate jasmine (not a true jasmine but a related genus) is one of the most beloved and widely planted fragrant vines in Gulf Coast landscapes, producing masses of small, pinwheel-shaped, pure-white flowers with an intoxicating, sweet-spicy fragrance that perfumes an entire garden in spring bloom. Glossy, dark-green, evergreen leaves on twining stems provide year-round foliage interest. It is remarkably adaptable — trained on trellises and arbors as a vertical element, allowed to sprawl as a groundcover, used as a sprawling shrub, or pruned as a low hedge. In zone 8–11 it is fully evergreen and essentially indestructible once established, tolerating heat, drought, poor soil, and salt spray. Prune back after flowering to keep it tidy and encourage dense regrowth. One of the most reliable and rewarding plants in the Gulf Coast garden.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring after frost danger passes in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; confederate rose grows rapidly in warm weather and can reach 10–15 feet in a single season from a cutting. It dies back to the ground after hard freezes in zone 7–8 but regrows vigorously from the roots.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; confederate rose is one of the most spectacular autumn-blooming flowering shrubs of the American South, producing enormous (4–6 inch), double, peony-like flowers that open white in the morning and gradually deepen through pink to rose and finally deep red by evening — the color change of a single flower over one day is one of the most remarkable visual effects in horticulture. Single-flowered forms also exist. Blooming from late summer through frost, confederate rose provides critical fall color just when other shrubs are fading. The plant grows very large — a true shrub-tree — and propagates effortlessly from cuttings, which root in a cup of water on the windowsill. It was passed from garden to garden across the antebellum South this way for generations. Prune to 2–3 feet in late winter; the plant regrows vigorously each season and blooms on new wood.

plant_note: Sow in darkness; violas are frost tolerant and thrive in cool weather.
directions: Start seed indoors and cover it, as violas germinate best in darkness, then set out the frost-tolerant plants early. This blend blooms reliably in cool weather and does best with afternoon shade to prolong flowering during warm spells. Keep soil evenly moist and deadhead to encourage continued bloom. Violas often reseed, popping up in unexpected corners the following season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens or offsets in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to average soil in partial to full shade after frost; coontie is extremely drought-tolerant once established and requires virtually no irrigation after its first growing season — one of the most drought-tolerant native shade plants available for zone 8–11.
directions: Plant container specimens or offset divisions in well-drained, sandy to average soil in partial to full shade; coontie is the only cycad native to the continental United States — a living fossil that has been growing unchanged in Florida and the southeastern coastal plain for millions of years. In the landscape it forms a handsome, low-growing rosette of dark-green, stiff, pinnate, fern-like leaves with narrow, pointed leaflets that create an attractive, tropical-textured groundcover in shaded areas. It is critically important as the sole larval host plant for the Atala butterfly (Eumaeus atala), a brilliantly colored Florida native butterfly (black wings with iridescent blue spots and a red abdomen) that was once thought to be extinct due to over-harvesting of coontie for starch production; the recovery of Atala populations has been directly linked to the increase in coontie cultivation in south Florida landscapes. The large, underground root mass stores starch that was harvested and processed by the Seminole, Calusa, and other Florida indigenous peoples for food. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; virtually maintenance-free.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cootamundra wattle is fast-growing and may bloom in 2–3 years from seed. It is short-lived (10–15 years) but spectacular during its prime years. In zone 9 it can be grown as a large shrub or small tree reaching 15–20 feet. Seed coats require nicking or brief boiling water treatment before sowing. In southern and eastern Australia it is listed as invasive outside its native range. All plant parts are potential allergens.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cootamundra wattle is one of the most widely grown and most spectacular of the Australian wattles — a fast-growing, relatively short-lived (10–15 year) small tree or large shrub of exceptional beauty in late winter and early spring when the entire tree is covered in a cloud of hundreds of tiny, intensely fragrant, bright golden-yellow, spherical flower pom-poms against a foil of finely divided, beautiful, silver-blue to blue-gray, twice-pinnate foliage. The silver-blue leaf color and golden-yellow flowers in combination create a vivid contrast of cool silver and warm gold that is one of the most striking color combinations in all of winter horticulture, and a tree in full bloom — the silvery foliage invisible beneath a total coating of brilliant, fragrant, golden-yellow — represents one of the most theatrical winter spectacles in zone 9 gardens. The flowers are intensely fragrant, the sweet, honey-like scent carrying for considerable distances in calm winter air. Fast-growing, drought-tolerant once established, and relatively inexpensive to purchase — making it one of the most rewarding, high-impact winter-flowering investments in the zone 9 garden. Short-lived but worth replanting.

common_name: Copper Canyon Daisy (Mountain Marigold, Lemmon's Marigold)
plant_note: Root tip cuttings easily in spring or plant container-grown transplants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; copper canyon daisy is native to Copper Canyon (Barranca del Cobre) in Mexico and is drought tolerant once established. Prune by one-third after bloom flushes to maintain compact shape.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; copper canyon daisy is one of the finest large perennial flowering shrubs for zone 8–11 gardens — a sprawling, aromatic shrub covered in masses of small, bright golden-yellow daisy flowers in fall and winter (and sometimes spring) when very little else is blooming. The deeply divided, fernlike leaves are pungently aromatic (a strong citrus-mint-marigold scent that is powerfully deer repellent) and retain an attractive gray-green color through much of the year. It is outstanding for fall color, butterfly attraction, and combining with blue salvias or purple ageratum for a stunning gold-and-purple fall combination. Prune back by one-third after each bloom flush to keep the plant compact; an unpruned shrub can spread to 6 feet or more. In zone 8, top growth may be killed by hard freezes but roots resprout reliably.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; fall planting allows roots to establish before winter.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; copper iris is the only native American iris with brick-red to burnt-orange-copper flowers — a unique and striking color that no other wild iris can match. It grows naturally in swamps, bayou margins, and bottomland forests of the lower Mississippi Valley and Gulf Coast, where it tolerates periodic inundation. The plant is one of the parent species of the spectacular Louisiana iris hybrids and contributes their warm red-copper-orange color range to hybrid cultivars. Plant at pond margins, in consistently wet rain garden areas, or in soil that stays moist throughout the growing season. It spreads by rhizome into colonies and can be divided in late summer to expand plantings.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; copper lily is native to the dry, grassy prairies and roadsides of the Gulf Coast and performs best with a summer dry period followed by rainfall to trigger flowering.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — copper lily is a charming, small-bulbed rain lily native to the coastal prairies and grassy roadsides of southeastern Texas and Louisiana, producing star-shaped, copper-pink to rosy-pink flowers on short scapes in late summer and fall following rain events. Like all rain lilies, the flowers appear seemingly overnight after summer storms or irrigation, lasting 2–3 days before fading, with successive flushes following each rain. The narrow, rush-like leaves are nearly evergreen in zone 9–10 and die back in hard freezes. It naturalizes freely in well-drained, open soils, spreading by both offsets and seed to form dense, floriferous colonies in lawn-edge plantings, rock gardens, and sunny to lightly shaded perennial borders. An outstanding low-maintenance bulb for the Gulf Coast that requires no irrigation once established in well-adapted soils.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F and transplant after all frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil in zone 10–12, or use as an annual container specimen in colder climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F and transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; copper plant is a bold tropical foliage shrub whose large, oval, copper-bronze to reddish-burgundy leaves streaked with pink, orange, and green provide unmatched color intensity in summer beds and containers. In full sun the leaf coloration is most vibrant — partial shade produces larger but less intensely colored leaves. Plants grow rapidly to 4–6 feet in a warm season, making them excellent privacy screens and bold border backdrops in zone 10–12. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer for the best leaf color and take cuttings in late summer before frost to overwinter rooted plants indoors; in frost-free zone 10–12 it is a year-round landscape shrub.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; copper rain lily blooms in late summer following rain events, similarly to zephyranthes rain lilies, producing distinctive funnel-shaped flowers held at an angle (not fully upright) in warm coppery-orange to reddish-orange on the outer surfaces, yellow inside. It naturalizes freely by seed in the Gulf Coast region and can become a pleasant garden colonizer in lawns and dry borders.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; copper rain lily is a South American Habranthus species that has naturalized across the Gulf Coast states from Texas to Florida and distinguished itself from the white zephyranthes rain lilies by its warm, coppery-orange to burnt-orange and yellow flower color — a unique warm-toned rain lily that fills a color niche (orange-copper funnel flowers) that no other commonly grown species covers. The flowers are held at a distinctive 45-degree angle (Habranthus, meaning 'graceful flower', characteristically tilts its flowers rather than holding them erect like Zephyranthes), giving each stem a graceful, nodding poise rather than the stiffly upright stance of Zephyranthes. The outer surfaces of the tepals are a warm reddish-copper to coppery-orange; the inner faces are yellow, creating a bicolor effect when viewed from below. Like its zephyranthes relatives, it flowers in flushes following summer rain events, producing masses of small, coppery blooms simultaneously across a naturalized planting. It self-seeds freely in Gulf Coast conditions and can colonize dry lawns and open garden areas without supplemental care. A delightful, self-sustaining small bulb for naturalistic and lawn-edge plantings.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; copperleaf is a bold tropical foliage plant that provides outstanding summer color in zone 9 gardens where it is grown as a summer annual or tender perennial.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; copperleaf holds its most vivid foliage colors in full sun — in shade the color becomes less intense. Acalypha wilkesiana (copperleaf or Jacob's coat) is a tropical Pacific Island shrub grown worldwide as a tropical foliage plant for its spectacularly colorful, large (3–5 inch), copper-red, bronze, maroon, red-orange, yellow, or multicolor variegated leaves in an enormous range of named cultivars — each leaf is often a mosaic of two or three colors in irregular patterns or in distinct margins. The effect in mass plantings is bold and tropical, creating intense color impact that few other foliage plants can match in summer heat. Common cultivar groups include 'Mosaica' (rich coppery-red), 'Marginata' (green leaves with copper-red margins), 'Musaica' (orange to bronze), and 'Tricolor' (red, pink, and green). In zones 9–12, copperleaf grows as a perennial shrub; in colder zones, root cuttings in fall and overwinter indoors. It thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity and is essentially pest-free in those conditions, making it one of the best choices for low-maintenance tropical-themed summer color.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Cora series annual vinca has superior disease resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight — a serious fungal disease of annual vinca (Catharanthus) in hot, humid conditions like zone 9's summer — making it significantly more reliable in the Gulf South than older vinca varieties. In zone 9 annual vinca is one of the most heat-tolerant and long-blooming summer bedding plants available; Cora Cherry thrives in the hottest, most humid summer weeks when most other annuals decline. The plant is self-cleaning — old flowers drop off without deadheading, keeping the plant tidy throughout the season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — annual vinca thrives in heat and performs poorly in cool, wet, or poorly drained conditions; Cora Cherry is an All-America Selections award-winning annual vinca (Catharanthus roseus) from the Cora series, producing vivid, deep cherry-red, five-petaled flowers with a contrasting white eye that bloom continuously from planting until frost without deadheading. Annual vinca (technically not a true vinca but sharing the common name due to similar flower appearance) is among the top performers for hot, humid summer bedding in zone 9 — it genuinely thrives in tropical heat and actually improves in flowering intensity as temperatures rise. The Cora series was specifically bred for resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a fungal disease that devastates vinca plantings in humid summer conditions typical of the Gulf South; this disease resistance makes Cora dramatically more reliable than older annual vinca varieties in zone 9. The intense cherry-red flowers and the plant's exceptional summer performance make Cora Cherry one of the best red bedding annuals available for Gulf Coast summer gardens where heat and humidity challenge most alternatives.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Cora is a vegetatively propagated vinca series from Syngenta Flowers — one of the highest-performing Catharanthus series for heat, humidity, and Phytophthora blight resistance. The Cora series is widely used in commercial landscaping and public plantings throughout the Gulf South precisely because of its superior disease resistance and longer season performance compared to seed-grown vinca series. Cora Strawberry produces vivid strawberry-red to rose-red flowers with a white central eye on plants with notably glossy, dark green foliage — the glossy foliage being a distinguishing trait of the Cora series that provides additional ornamental value between flower cycles.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture during establishment — Cora Strawberry Vinca is extremely heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established, requiring minimal water and no deadheading to maintain continuous bloom; Cora Strawberry Vinca is a premium, vegetatively propagated Catharanthus roseus cultivar producing vivid strawberry-red flowers with a white central eye on compact, well-branched, glossy-leaved plants — one of the highest-rated commercial vinca series for disease resistance, heat performance, and season-long ornamental quality in the Gulf South landscape. The Cora series distinguishes itself from seed-grown vinca series through consistently higher resistance to Phytophthora crown rot — the primary disease that limits annual vinca performance in humid zone 9 conditions — and through the notably glossy, dark green foliage that remains attractive throughout the season regardless of flowering intensity. Catharanthus roseus (annual vinca, Madagascar periwinkle) is the quintessential Gulf South summer annual — heat-thriving, drought-tolerant, self-cleaning, and maintaining its bloom display through the peak summer conditions of July–September that challenge most other annual species. The vivid strawberry-red with white eye of Cora Strawberry provides one of the most visually energetic bicolor combinations available in the vinca color range — the strawberry-red and white creating a lively, high-contrast display effective in both formal mass planting and mixed container compositions.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; coral aloe is the most cold-tolerant flat-leafed aloe and tolerates brief freezes to 25°F. It requires less water than most garden plants but is killed by prolonged wet soil. One of the finest aloes for mild-climate gardens as it is spineless (safe for children), ornamental, and produces outstanding hummingbird-attracting flowers.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; coral aloe is widely considered one of the finest landscape aloes for mild-climate gardens — a flat-growing, rosette-forming South African species completely lacking the teeth and spines that make most aloes difficult to handle. The broad, smooth, glaucous blue-gray to gray-green leaves with thin, pinkish margins are attractive all year, taking on warm peach-apricot tones in cool weather. In winter to spring, dramatic branched flower spikes arise carrying clusters of vivid coral-red to orange tubular flowers that attract hummingbirds in numbers throughout the winter and early spring, providing a critical nectar source when little else is in bloom. Coral aloe spreads slowly by offsets to form impressive colonies and is an outstanding, child-safe alternative to spiny aloes in gardens frequented by children. Its lack of spines, glaucous foliage, spectacular winter flowers, and hummingbird attraction make it arguably the most garden-worthy of the commonly available aloes.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sheltered site with protection from hot afternoon sun.
directions: Prized for its glowing coral-red winter bark, this Japanese maple also offers soft green spring foliage that shifts to golden-yellow in fall. Plant in part shade with rich, moist, well-drained soil, protecting it from drying wind and intense afternoon sun that can scorch leaves. Keep the root zone mulched and evenly moist. Prune minimally in late winter to reveal the colorful stems and maintain the graceful branching form.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 8 the stems freeze to the ground in hard winters but resprout vigorously from the deep, heat-tolerant root system each spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral bean is one of the most striking native shrubs of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, producing brilliant scarlet tubular flowers in long spikes in spring before the leaves emerge — they are among the most important hummingbird nectar plants in the Southeast. In fall the pods split open to reveal vivid coral-red seeds that are highly ornamental but extremely toxic if swallowed. The stems bear recurved spines that deter browsing; the plant dies to the ground in hard freezes in zone 7–8 but regrows rapidly from an established root crown. It tolerates partial shade, sandy soil, drought, and salt spray — making it an outstanding native plant for difficult spots in Gulf Coast gardens. The red seeds were traditionally used as ornamentation and have important Native American cultural uses.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface sow as seeds need light to germinate — do not cover.
directions: Press seeds onto the surface of a moist germination medium — do not cover, as light is required for germination; transplant to a humus-rich, well-drained site after last frost. Grown primarily for their spectacular mound-forming foliage in shades of burgundy, copper, lime, silver, and purple, heucheras also produce airy wands of tiny flowers beloved by hummingbirds. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to rejuvenate the woody crowns; reset divisions with the crown at soil level. Most modern hybrids tolerate more sun with adequate moisture but prefer afternoon shade in hot climates.
