plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; coral bells is the species whose brilliant red flowers gave rise to the name and most early flower-heuchera hybrids.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; coral bells from the Southwest requires excellent drainage and is less tolerant of heavy clay or wet soils than eastern heuchera species. Heuchera sanguinea is a native of the Rocky Mountains and northern Mexico and is the species whose brilliant, bell-shaped, red to coral-red flowers on tall, wiry scapes gave rise to the common name "coral bells"; it produces rounded, scalloped, dark-green leaves with light-silver marbling and bears 12–18-inch flowering stems in late spring and early summer that are exceptional as cut flowers and irresistible to hummingbirds. Unlike the foliage heucheras derived from H. americana and H. villosa, H. sanguinea is grown primarily for its flower show; the named cultivars 'Firefly', 'Splendens', and 'White Cloud' are classic garden selections, and many modern landscape heucheras carry its flower genes.

common_name: Coral Bells Azalea (Classic Coral-Pink Masses-of-Bloom Kurume Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Kurume azaleas perform best in morning sun with afternoon shade protection in Gulf South climates — afternoon shade reduces heat and drought stress during the critical summer period.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Coral Bells is a classic Kurume azalea cultivar — one of the Japanese Kurume (city of origin, Kurume, Japan) hybrids that are among the most widely planted azaleas in the American South, characterized by small, glossy leaves, compact mounding habit, and spring flowering so profuse that the foliage can be completely obscured by flowers. The spring bloom display of 'Coral Bells' — masses of small, hose-in-hose (double) to single, coral-pink to warm rose-pink flowers covering the entire plant simultaneously — is one of the quintessential signs of Gulf South spring alongside dogwood and wisteria. The hose-in-hose flower form (one flower nestled inside another, giving the appearance of a double flower with extra petals) is characteristic of many Kurume cultivars and adds ornamental complexity to each individual flower. In zone 9, Kurume azaleas perform as reliable evergreen foundation and landscape shrubs that require only occasional pruning after bloom to maintain their compact, mounded habit. The small, glossy, dark-green leaves provide attractive year-round structure. Strongly acidic, humus-rich soil and consistent moisture are the most critical requirements — chlorosis from insufficient acidity is the most common cultural problem, corrected by soil acidification with sulfur and acid-forming fertilizers.

common_name: Coral Berry Ardisia (Christmas Berry, Hen's Eyes, Marlberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in partial to deep shade under established trees; Ardisia crenata thrives in the dry, root-competitive shade beneath mature live oaks and other large trees where most ornamentals fail. In zone 9a, plants may freeze to the ground in hard winters but resprout from the crown in spring. INVASIVE NOTE: Ardisia crenata is listed as invasive in Florida, Texas, and other Gulf Coast states where birds disperse seeds into natural areas — do not plant near forests, wetlands, or parks. Legally restricted in some counties.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in any well-drained soil — Coral Berry Ardisia is one of the most shade- and drought-tolerant small shrubs available, performing in conditions of deep dry shade under large oaks that defeat nearly all other ornamentals. Ardisia crenata (also listed as A. crispa) is a small, upright evergreen shrub from India, Southeast Asia, and Japan in the Primulaceae family that produces one of the most striking winter ornamental displays in zone 9 gardens: during November–February, pendulous clusters of bright coral-red to vivid scarlet round berries the size of small pearls hang in dramatic arching sprays below the dark, glossy, wavy-edged, evergreen leaves. The berries persist on the plant for months, and fully loaded plants in December–January are extraordinarily ornamental. The plant blooms in summer with small, inconspicuous white to pinkish flowers that are followed by the developing berries. White-berried ('Alba') and pink-berried forms are available. CAUTION: Classified as invasive in Florida, Texas, Louisiana, Georgia, and other Gulf and Southeast states — birds devour the berries and disperse seeds freely into natural areas where the plant displaces native understory species. Remove berries before they fall if planting in areas with access to natural lands.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after the last frost in a location with partial shade; mulch the root zone to retain moisture and moderate soil temperature.
directions: Carolina Snailseed is a twining woody vine native to woodland edges, thickets, and fencerows across the southeastern United States. It produces small, heart-shaped to kidney-shaped leaves and inconspicuous greenish flowers on female plants in summer, followed by dense clusters of brilliant red berries in fall that persist into winter and provide important food for mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and hermit thrushes. Grow in average to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; it tolerates a range of soil conditions once established. Note that the berries, while highly attractive to wildlife, are toxic to humans — plant where children will not have unsupervised access to the fruit.

plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in fall in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; coral drops grows, flowers, and goes dormant on the Cape winter-rainfall schedule — emerging in autumn, flowering in late winter and spring, then going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. The name 'bulbifera' refers to the bulbils produced in the leaf axils, a common propagation strategy of Cape bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; coral drops is one of the most colorful of the Lachenalia species — producing the characteristic two strap-shaped, often purple-spotted, somewhat succulent leaves and in late winter through spring (February–April in cultivation), dense, upright, bottlebrush-like racemes of pendant, tubular bells in a striking combination of coral-red to orange-red at the top of each tube fading through yellow to greenish-yellow at the tube base — a three-toned color scheme of warm coral, yellow, and green that is visually complex and beautiful. The bright, tricolor flower tubes are surrounded by slightly smaller outer perianth segments. It produces small bulbils in the leaf axils that fall and generate new plants when conditions are suitable — an efficient natural propagation strategy adapted to the Cape fynbos. Outstanding for container culture in zones 8–11, where the pot can be kept dry in summer. One of the most colorful and largest-flowered of the commonly grown lachenalias.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral fountain establishes quickly and roots readily from stem cuttings. It is outstanding cascading over walls, planted at the top of raised beds, or in hanging baskets where the arching stems can drape downward.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; coral fountain (firecracker plant) is a uniquely textural and continuously blooming tropical perennial with masses of thin, arching, rush-like green stems cascading in a weeping habit, studded nearly year-round with small, tubular, coral-red flowers that hummingbirds visit with enthusiasm. The stems have virtually no leaves — the photosynthesis occurs in the green stems themselves, giving the plant an unusual, airy, almost fern-like texture when not in bloom that is strikingly different from any other flowering plant. It is exceptionally drought, heat, and salt tolerant once established and performs at its best cascading over retaining walls, spilling from large containers, or planted in raised beds where the arching, weeping habit shows to best effect. In zone 9 it may suffer frost damage to stems but typically regrows from established roots. A yellow-flowered form is also available. One of the most reliable and continuously blooming hummingbird plants for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Surface sow into warm soil, as the fine seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow into warm soil after frost, since the small seed needs light to germinate. Coral Fountain produces dramatic pendulous tassels in shades of coral that dry beautifully for everlasting arrangements, wreaths, and crafts. Grow in full sun with average soil and moderate water for the fullest tassels. Harvest stems as the flowers reach full color and hang them to dry.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coral gum is from the dry, hot interior goldfields region of Western Australia — requiring hot, dry conditions and excellent drainage. It blooms over a very long period (spring through summer, often year-round in warm climates) producing the distinctive coral-red to pink, ribbed, lantern-shaped buds and flowers. More reliable in hot, dry, inland Mediterranean climates than in humid coastal conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; coral gum is one of the most colorful and most reliably floriferous of all ornamental eucalyptus — a small to medium-sized mallee or tree from the hot, arid goldfields of the Western Australian interior that produces over a very long season (often effectively year-round in warm climates) a succession of distinctive, beautiful coral-red to bright-pink flowers. The flower buds are themselves highly ornamental: angular, ribbed, lantern-shaped, coral-red to pink caps of distinctive sculptural form that remain on the tree in developing clusters for weeks before the cap falls and the dense, pink-red stamen clusters expand. The flowers, when open, are large clusters of vivid coral-red to rosy-pink, crimson-tipped stamens against the gray-green foliage — a rich, warm-pink to coral-red that is among the most vivid flower colors produced by any Australian tree. The combination of long bloom season, ornamental bud form, vivid flower color, and compact size (15–25 feet) makes it one of the best ornamental eucalyptus for the zone 9 garden. Native to the hot, dry goldfields of WA — a landscape of red soils, sparse desert vegetation, and blazing summer heat — it is thoroughly adapted to the hot, dry conditions of zone 9 summers.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring near a trellis, fence, or other support; stems twine and will climb 10–15 feet.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis or fence; unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle this native species is well-behaved and will not escape into natural areas. The long, tubular scarlet-to-coral flowers bloom heavily in spring and continue sporadically through fall, providing the long-tube nectar that ruby-throated hummingbirds require. Prune in late winter or just after the main spring flush to shape the vine and remove dead wood. In the deep South it is semi-evergreen and may retain foliage through mild winters; in colder zones it loses leaves but regrows vigorously from the base in spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Coral Nymph is a distinctive bicolor selection of the native tropical sage with salmon-pink and white two-toned flowers, more delicate in appearance than standard red S. coccinea and outstanding in heat-tolerant garden designs for the Gulf Coast and Deep South.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into well-drained, moderately fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade. Coral Nymph is a bicolor-flowered cultivar of the native American Salvia coccinea (tropical sage), producing distinctive two-toned flowers with salmon-coral upper lips and soft white lower lips on the same spikes — a gentler, more pastel coloration than the vivid red of the species that combines well with soft-colored perennial plantings. Like all S. coccinea cultivars, it is heat- and humidity-tolerant in the extreme, blooming continuously through Gulf Coast and Southern summers without deadheading, and self-seeds prolifically so that a single planting effectively perpetuates itself. Outstanding for hummingbird and butterfly gardens; annual in most zones but naturalized and perennial in zone 9–11.

common_name: Coral Nymph Salvia (Bicolor Coral and White Tropical Sage)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Coral Nymph self-seeds freely in zone 9 — mark seedling locations to preserve self-sown plants that often bloom earlier and more prolifically than transplants.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Coral Nymph is the most distinctive color form of Salvia coccinea (tropical sage or scarlet sage) — producing flowers with a rich salmon-coral upper lip (hood) and a creamy-white lower lip in a distinctive bicolor combination that creates a softer, more complex color effect than the pure red or pure white solid-colored forms. The 18–30 inch upright plants produce slender, whorled flower spikes continuously from late spring through hard frost (and year-round in frost-free zone 9 winters). Salvia coccinea is a Gulf South native — naturally occurring in coastal woods and disturbed areas from the Carolinas to Florida and Texas — making Coral Nymph perfectly adapted to Gulf South heat, humidity, and summer conditions. Unlike many salvias that are sensitive to Gulf South summer heat, S. coccinea thrives through the hottest months and actually intensifies its bloom production in late summer and fall. Coral Nymph self-seeds freely in zone 9 gardens, creating a self-maintaining annual colony that renews itself without replanting. Hummingbirds, sphinx moths, and several butterfly species visit the tubular flowers throughout the long bloom season. The partial-shade tolerance is a practical advantage for gardeners who want color in less-than-full-sun areas — Coral Nymph blooms acceptably in 3–4 hours of direct sun per day.

common_name: Coral Plant (Coral Physic Nut, Multifid Jatropha, Physic Nut)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in full sun with well-drained soil; Coral Plant grows rapidly in warm conditions and can reach 10 feet in zone 9-10. In zone 9a, it freezes to the ground or roots in cold winters but resprouts vigorously in spring; in zone 9b-10 it is a reliable semi-evergreen shrub. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are highly toxic — the seeds in particular contain curcin and ricin-like toxins and are potentially lethal if consumed by children or pets. The milky sap is also irritating.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Coral Plant is drought-tolerant and thrives in the poor, well-drained soils of zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes, tolerating the summer heat and periodic drought that challenges many tropical ornamentals. Jatropha multifida is a large, architectural shrub or small tree from tropical America (Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean) grown throughout the subtropical world for its striking combination of deeply lobed, palm-like leaves and vivid coral-red to scarlet flowers. The foliage is dramatically ornamental: large (up to 15 inches across), deeply cut into 7–11 finger-like lobes reminiscent of a Cannabis or Ricinus leaf, on long, flexible petioles that give the plant a bold, tropical sculptural quality. The flowers are borne in flat-topped clusters of tiny, brilliant coral-red, star-shaped blooms that appear prolifically at the branch tips throughout the warm season, attracting butterflies and occasionally hummingbirds. The interesting three-lobed fruit capsules that follow contain large seeds that, while potentially useful as a biofuel crop in some tropical production systems, are highly toxic and should not be consumed. In zone 9, Coral Plant is a fast-growing tropical accent that provides months of flowering interest and bold architectural foliage through the summer and fall.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; coral plant is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant tropical perennial that produces its best growth and blooms in warm, sunny conditions, yet also tolerates more shade than most flowering shrubs.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; coral plant is drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms more heavily under mild drought stress. Russelia equisetiformis (coral plant or firecracker fern) is a Mexican native producing a dense, weeping, fountain-like mound of slender, rush-like, bright-green to gray-green photosynthetic stems (reduced leaves — hence the species name 'equisetiformis,' meaning 'horsetail-like') hung with hundreds of slender, 1-inch, bright-red tubular flowers from spring through frost. The effect is of an almost waterfall-like cascade of green stems and red flowers — one of the most graceful and romantic ornamental shrubs for tropical and subtropical gardens. Ruby-throated hummingbirds and butterflies visit the tubular flowers extensively. Coral plant is exceptionally heat, drought, and salt-tolerant once established, performing well in coastal gardens, under dry overhangs, and in containers on sunny patios. In zone 9, it dies back in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from roots; in zone 10–12, it is an evergreen perennial. It roots quickly from stem cuttings and can be propagated freely for mass plantings.

plant_note: Plant tubers or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; coral vine is fast-growing and can cover a fence or trellis in a single season. The tuberous roots store carbohydrates and allow rapid regrowth from the base after frost damage in zone 7–8.
directions: Plant tubers in well-drained soil in full sun on a fence, trellis, or arbor; coral vine is one of the most beloved and reliable vining plants of the Gulf South — a fast-growing, drought-tolerant vine from Mexico that covers itself in sprays of small heart-shaped pink to magenta flowers in summer through frost, creating a solid curtain of pink that is irresistible to bees, particularly bumble bees and honeybees. The vine climbs by tendrils and can reach 20–30 feet when established. In zone 7–9 the tops die back in hard frost but established tuberous roots resprout vigorously each spring, often growing 10–15 feet in a single season. The flowers and tubers are edible (tubers roasted like sweet potatoes in Mexico). A white-flowered form ('Album') is less vigorous but charming. A fixture in traditional Gulf South gardens for generations.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors a few weeks earlier for a head start. Coral Zinnia carries four-to-five-inch blooms in sun-kissed coral on sturdy stems that are ideal for cutting and beloved by butterflies. Space plants for good airflow and water at the base to limit powdery mildew. Cut or deadhead often to keep the plants blooming until frost.

plant_note: Divide established suckers or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to alkaline, average to poor soil in partial to full shade in spring; coralberry is the most shade and drought tolerant of the native fruiting shrubs and excels in the deep dry shade under dense tree canopy.
directions: Divide suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained to dry, average to poor soil in partial to full shade; coralberry (Indian currant, buckbrush) is one of the most valuable and underused native shrubs for the most difficult landscape challenge: dry, deep shade under dense tree canopy where most plants refuse to grow. Coralberry not only survives in these conditions but thrives, spreading steadily by suckers to form colonies of arching, wiry stems bearing small, oval, bluish-green leaves and dense clusters of small, coral-pink to rosy-red berries that persist through winter — important food for bobwhite, pheasant, grouse, cedar waxwings, and other wildlife. Unlike most native shrubs, it tolerates alkaline soil, clay, and root competition from established trees. Its stoloniferous spreading habit makes it excellent for erosion control on shaded slopes and embankments. The cultivar 'Foliis Variegatis' has yellow-variegated leaves that are effective in lightening dark shade. Often overlooked by gardeners in favor of showier shrubs, it is irreplaceable for solving the deep-dry-shade problem.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost in warm, well-drained soil and stake tall plants.
directions: Coralie blends the most perfect blush and pink shades, pairing beautifully with other soft-toned flowers in the cutting garden. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil after the ground warms. Because the plant grows tall, provide sturdy staking or support unless you are cutting frequently. Pinch early for branching, cut often to keep blooms coming, and lift tubers to store indoors over winter in cold zones.

plant_note: Plant bulbils or rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade under beech or other deciduous trees; coralroot rarely sets seed (it relies primarily on bulbil propagation) — collect the small, dark, rice-grain-sized bulbils from the leaf axils and plant immediately, or allow them to fall naturally and naturalize. Spring ephemeral: mark locations before the foliage disappears in summer.
directions: Plant bulbils in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full shade under beech or similar large deciduous trees; coralroot is a fascinating and unusual European spring woodland plant, historically classified as Dentaria bulbifera, that reproduces primarily by dropping tiny, dark, oval bulbils from the axils of the pinnate leaves rather than by seed — a vegetative propagation strategy adapted to the deep shade of beech forest floors where seed germination is unreliable. The plant produces handsome, pinnately-divided leaves with narrow leaflets and, in April and May, slender stems bearing loose clusters of pale-pink to lilac-pink, four-petaled flowers. The distinctive bulbils are clearly visible as small, dark, rice-like structures clustered at the base of each leaf through the spring season. Rarely found in cultivation despite its quiet charm; it is a true ancient-woodland indicator species in Britain and Europe, appearing almost exclusively in woodland with unbroken centuries of continuity. Outstanding for the specialist woodland garden under large, established beeches and other canopy trees where its preferred alkaline leaf-mold soil accumulates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; cordyline tolerates wind, coastal salt spray, and brief frosts to about 14°F, making it well suited to zone 8–11 coastal and subtropical landscapes.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; cordyline creates striking architectural focal points with its long sword-like leaves radiating from a central trunk in green, burgundy, bronze, or pink depending on cultivar. Tolerant of wind, coastal salt spray, and brief frosts down to about 14°F, it thrives in zone 8–11 landscapes where it adds unmistakable tropical structure as a specimen, backdrop, or container plant. Growth is moderately fast in warm climates where it can eventually reach 15–20 feet; strip older lower leaves as they dry to maintain the clean, palm-like trunk. Water regularly until established, then reduce to occasional deep watering as it is quite drought-tolerant once roots are set.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date; seeds tolerate light frost and germinate best in cool soil.
directions: Sow seed on the soil surface and tamp lightly; good drainage is essential since coreopsis rots in wet soil over winter. Deadhead regularly to keep the bright yellow flowers coming all summer. Shear plants back by half after the first flush to encourage compact regrowth and a second bloom. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in spring to prevent the center from dying out.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; cork-stemmed passionflower is native to the tropical Americas and naturalized throughout the Gulf South, where it grows in disturbed habitats, forest margins, and coastal thickets.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; cork-stemmed passionflower is a compact, small-flowered passionflower with distinctively corky, ridged stems that distinguish it from other species. The tiny greenish-white to cream flowers are inconspicuous but produce small, dark purple to black berries that are important food for white-eyed vireos, gray catbirds, and other frugivorous birds. Most significantly, it is an essential larval host plant for multiple Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and Julia heliconian butterfly species — its small, tri-lobed leaves are consumed voraciously by caterpillars. In zone 9a, it is a reliable perennial vine that provides critical butterfly habitat with almost no maintenance.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun. Corkwood is a rare species that should only be sourced from specialty native plant nurseries; it is listed as threatened or of conservation concern in most states where it occurs.
directions: Corkwood is one of the rarest and most botanically unusual native shrubs in North America — a monotypic genus (Leitneriaceae family) with no close relatives among living plants, native to the tidal swamps, brackish marshes, and wet bottomlands of scattered, disjunct localities in Georgia, Florida, Texas, Arkansas, and Missouri, where it forms thickets in periodically flooded, organic soils. Its most remarkable characteristic is its wood, which is lighter than cork — making it the least dense wood of any known North American woody plant — and the plant occupies a phylogenetically isolated position in the evolutionary tree of flowering plants. Catkin-like male and female flowers appear on separate plants in spring before the leaves emerge. Despite its rarity, Corkwood is adaptable to a range of wet to moist soil conditions in partial shade to full sun and is occasionally available from specialty native plant nurseries; plant male and female specimens together for seed production. Listed as threatened in several states and on NatureServe's watch list.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in spring in warm, humid conditions. Choose a site with partial shade and moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Polyalthia suberosa naturally grows as an understory shrub and performs best with some protection from intense afternoon sun in zone 10-11 tropical gardens.
directions: Sow fresh seed at a depth of 0.5 inch in moist, well-drained potting mix and maintain temperatures above 72°F to achieve germination within 2-4 weeks; allow seedlings to reach 6-8 inches before transplanting to a permanent understory or semi-shaded garden position. Corky bark polyalthia establishes most successfully in organically enriched, consistently moist soil with good drainage, and benefits from a layer of organic mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds during the first growing season. Once established, this unusual custard-apple family shrub requires minimal maintenance; its small cream to yellow-green flowers attract pollinators and are followed by small black fruits that draw birds, adding wildlife interest to tropical garden compositions. The deeply furrowed, corky gray-brown bark develops distinctive textural character with age, making it a conversation piece as a specimen shrub or informal screen in zone 10-11 tropical and subtropical gardens.

common_name: Corn Cockle (Old-Fashioned Rose-Purple Cool-Season Annual from Grain Fields)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (zone 9: September–November) or early spring where winters are cold; Corn Cockle does not transplant well and is best sown directly where it will grow. In zone 9, fall sowing produces the most robust plants and best flowering (February–April). The plant self-seeds reliably once established and will return each year from dropped seed without further planting. Seeds and all plant parts are toxic if ingested — do not plant where children or animals may eat them. The common name reflects the plant's original habitat as a weed of European cereal (corn) fields, where the purple flowers appeared among wheat and barley.
directions: Scatter seeds on prepared soil in fall or early spring; press in without covering deeply. Corn Cockle does not transplant well — sow in situ. Do not ingest seeds or plant material. Corn Cockle (Agrostemma githago) is a strikingly beautiful old-fashioned annual flower from the pink family (Caryophyllaceae) — a naturalized European wildflower (native to the Mediterranean region) that was once common in grain fields across Europe and Britain as a weed among cereal crops, where the large rose-purple flowers nodding on tall, slender, silvery-hairy stems created a dramatic and romantic visual effect in the spring grain fields. The flowers are 2–3 inches across, with five rounded petals in rose-purple to deep pink with a pale throat and distinctive darker veining and a ring of small dark spots at the base of each petal — a pattern of elegant complexity that makes individual flowers as beautiful when examined closely as the whole plant is from a distance. The long, narrow, silvery-hairy sepals that extend beyond the petals give the unopened buds a distinctive appearance and add texture to flower arrangements. Corn Cockle was once widespread as a grain field weed in Britain and Europe but has declined drastically due to herbicide use and improved grain seed cleaning, making it now more common as a cultivated garden plant than as a wild species — a poignant reversal for a once-ubiquitous wildflower. The seeds are poisonous (containing saponins called agrostemmic acid/githagin) — a significant historical concern when grain contaminated with corn cockle seeds was milled into flour, causing 'githagism' poisoning.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in zones 8–10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in sharply drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; corn lily produces slender, wiry, grass-like stems bearing clusters of star-shaped flowers in luminous shades of white, yellow, pink, orange, red, and blue-green with contrasting dark eyes in late spring. Individual plants are airy and delicate — plant in generous clusters of 25 or more for maximum visual effect. The flowers close in cloudy weather and open fully only in bright sunlight. After bloom, allow foliage to die down completely before removing it; in climates with wet summers, lift corms and store dry until fall. Naturalize readily in well-drained, dry-summer California gardens. Excellent cut flower with long vase life.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade near permanent water; corn lily is a wetland and moist-meadow plant of mountain streams and high-elevation meadows — ALL PARTS ARE EXTREMELY TOXIC.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; corn lily requires consistently moist to wet conditions and is a plant of high-elevation mountain meadows, stream banks, and seepy slopes in western North America. Veratrum californicum is a dramatic, large native perennial closely related to eastern false hellebore (V. viride) producing equally spectacular, tightly pleated, corn-like leaves up to 12 inches wide on stems reaching 3–6 feet tall in early spring, and dense, white-flowered panicles in mid-summer; it differs from V. viride primarily in its white (not greenish-yellow) flowers and western North American range. ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE AMONG THE MOST TOXIC OF ANY NATIVE NORTH AMERICAN PLANT — especially the roots, which have caused fatal poisoning in livestock and have dramatic teratogenic effects on developing lambs if consumed by pregnant ewes early in pregnancy. Grow only in areas inaccessible to livestock, children, and pets.

common_name: Corn Marigold (Field Chrysanthemum, Yellow Oxeye, Segetum Daisy)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 4 weeks before last frost, or in fall in mild climates; corn marigold is a cool-season annual that blooms best in spring and early summer before heat arrives; it is closely related to garland chrysanthemum (Glebionis coronaria) but grown for its ornamental bright yellow daisy flowers rather than for edible greens.
directions: Direct sow on the surface or very shallowly in a weed-free seedbed; thin to 6–10 inches; no fertilization needed — corn marigold blooms best in poor to moderately fertile soil; deadhead spent blooms to extend the season; it self-sows reliably where happy. Corn marigold (Glebionis segetum) is a European and Mediterranean wildflower annual that was once so abundant in grain fields across England, northern Europe, and western Asia that it was considered a serious weed of cultivation — its cheerful bright yellow daisy flowers turning entire wheat and barley fields golden. The common name 'corn marigold' reflects this agricultural history: 'corn' in the old English usage means any small grain (wheat, barley, rye, oats), not maize, and the yellow flowers among the green grain stalks were a familiar sight in pre-herbicide farming landscapes. Despite its weedy past in traditional agriculture, corn marigold has become valued as a garden and wildflower annual for its prolific, long-lasting yellow blooms, its tolerance of poor, dry soils, and its value to pollinators including bees and hoverflies that visit the flowers freely throughout the cool-season bloom period. It is closely related to garland chrysanthemum (Glebionis coronaria) — the Asian edible chrysanthemum greens vegetable — but has narrower, more divided leaves and is grown strictly for ornament. In meadow and wildflower seed mixes for European-style plantings, corn marigold is a standard component for its reliable germination, fast bloom, and cheerful long-season color. The cut flowers are excellent and long-lasting.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors before temperatures approach 45°F. Massangeana corn plant is sensitive to fluoride and boron in tap water, which causes leaf tip and edge burn — use filtered water, rainwater, or allow tap water to sit uncovered overnight to dissipate chlorine. In zone 10–11 it can be grown as a permanent landscape tree reaching 15–20 feet. Outdoors in zone 9's summer humidity, the plant grows more rapidly than indoors. The fragrant white to cream flower spikes that appear on mature plants have an intense, sweet fragrance noticeable across a significant distance.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — never in direct sun, which bleaches and burns the variegated leaves — in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil; allow soil to dry slightly between waterings; Massangeana is the classic variegated corn plant dracaena, producing wide, strap-like leaves with a broad bright yellow to lime-green central stripe on a dark green background — the most distinctive and widely recognized leaf pattern of any tropical foliage plant in the American market. The large leaves (up to 3 feet long and 4 inches wide) are produced in rosettes at the tips of the thick, upright, cane-like stem — a growth form that naturally produces the same architectural, palm-tree-like effect whether grown as a 2-foot houseplant or a 15-foot landscape tree in tropical zones. Corn plant is among the very best shade and low-light tropical foliage plants for zone 9 outdoor display — its tolerance of low light conditions, relative drought tolerance, and ability to go without watering for extended periods makes it practical as an outdoor container specimen on covered patios and porches where access to the plant for watering may be irregular. The plant's ability to shed its lower leaves and expose the attractive, bamboo-like stem as it grows creates an evolving form over years that becomes increasingly interesting as the plant matures.

common_name: Corn Plant Dracaena (Mass Cane, Fortune Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a container specimen in zone 9 and bring indoors when temperatures fall below 40°F; Corn Plant Dracaena is damaged by cold and should not be left outdoors in zone 9a winters. In zone 10-11 it can be planted in the ground in partial shade. The plant is highly toxic to dogs and cats — keep away from pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to low light in well-drained potting mix in containers, or in zone 10-11 landscape shade; Corn Plant Dracaena is one of the most low-light tolerant large foliage plants available and can be maintained in surprisingly dim indoor conditions that would kill virtually any other large houseplant. Dracaena fragrans is native to tropical Africa and has been in cultivation as a houseplant for over 150 years. The most popular cultivar, 'Massangeana' (Mass Cane), features broad, arching, corn-like leaves with a wide yellow stripe down the center — the combination of bold form and golden-yellow variegation makes it one of the most striking large foliage plants for interiors and shaded patios. The thick, woody cane-like stems can be 'cane cut' and new growth will sprout from latent buds — a common propagation technique that also allows the plant to be maintained at a desired height. In zone 10-11 landscapes, the plant grows into a multi-trunked small tree 15–25 feet tall and occasionally produces fragrant white flowers at night. Corn Plant Dracaena removes benzene, formaldehyde, trichloroethylene, xylene, and toluene from indoor air according to the NASA Clean Air Study. CAUTION: Toxic to dogs and cats — causes vomiting, dilated pupils, and weakness; keep away from pets.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall or as early in spring as the soil can be worked by scattering and lightly raking into place; corn poppies do not transplant well and germinate best in cool soil — fall sowing in mild climates produces the most prolific spring display.
directions: Scatter seeds in fall or as early in spring as the soil can be worked by mixing seed with sand and broadcasting over prepared well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; corn poppy is a classic European wildflower meadow plant that germinates only in cool soil and dislikes transplanting. Thin seedlings to 6–9 inches apart — crowding prevents good flowering — and expect blooms within 60–90 days of germination with large, four-petaled, crinkled flowers in scarlet red, salmon, pink, white, and bicolors. Allow seed pods to ripen and shatter in place for natural self-seeding, which will produce larger and larger sweeps in subsequent years. In hot climates the plants die after setting seed in early summer; combine with warm-season annuals to fill the gap.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost in warm, well-drained soil.
directions: Cornel Bronze is a burnt-orange ball dahlia related to Cornel, sharing its prolific bloom, excellent tuber production, and tidy plant habit. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after the last frost. Pinch young plants for bushier growth and harvest the round, tightly petaled blooms frequently for the vase. Lift and store the abundant tubers indoors over winter in regions colder than Zone 8.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost in warm, well-drained soil.
directions: Cornel is the classic burnt-red ball dahlia, a shorter, sturdy plant that often needs no staking and blooms prolifically. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed. Pinch the growing tips to encourage branching and cut the tightly formed blooms often for long-lasting arrangements. In cold-winter regions, dig and store the tubers, which this variety produces reliably, after the first frost.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade after frost; coromandel is one of the best shade-tolerant groundcovers for zone 9–12 and will bloom continuously in quite low light conditions where most flowering groundcovers would fail to produce flowers.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade; coromandel (Chinese violet, Philippine violet, ganges primrose) is a tropical African and South Asian low-growing perennial shrub that has become a widely used low-maintenance flowering groundcover throughout south Florida and Gulf Coast zone 9–12 gardens, prized for its ability to produce its lavender-purple to pale-white, funnel-shaped, foxglove-like flowers on a nearly continuous basis throughout the warm season in partial shade conditions where few other flowering plants bloom reliably. It forms a spreading, mounding mass of lush, dark-green, heart-shaped, quilted leaves with contrasting pale veins that provides attractive foliage coverage even between flowering periods. In frost-free zones it grows as a year-round perennial; in zone 9 it is killed back by frost but typically returns reliably from the root in spring. Spreads vigorously by stem rooting and can naturalize in moist, shaded areas — monitor for invasive tendencies in Florida where it is considered a Category II invasive species in some natural areas. A valuable but potentially invasive shade-garden plant for zone 9–12.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; give the long-season vines a sturdy trellis.
directions: Direct sow after frost in rich soil and full sun, giving the vigorous vines a strong trellis to climb. Corsican produces round, hard-shelled gourds about six to ten inches across that cure to last indefinitely and can be carved, painted, or drilled for crafts. Provide a long, warm growing season and steady moisture while the fruit develops. Harvest before hard frost and cure the gourds in a dry, airy spot for several weeks.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in part shade; Corsican hellebore is the largest and most boldly textured of the evergreen hellebores — a robust, shrubby plant with strongly three-lobed, leathery, spiny-edged leaves and large, open clusters of pale apple-green, cup-shaped flowers in late winter through spring. Native to Corsica and Sardinia. The stems are biennial: they flower in their second year then die back to the crown, which produces new stems continuously. More sun-tolerant than most hellebores.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in part shade; Corsican hellebore is the most robust, most boldly architectural, and largest-foliaged of the hellebores — a native of the rocky hillsides and scrub woodlands of Corsica and Sardinia that grows in cultivation as a dense, shrubby mound of strongly three-parted, leathery, dark blue-green leaves with spiny-toothed margins on stout, erect biennial stems (stems flower in their second year then die to the base; the plant is perennial through the continuous replacement of stems from the rootstock). The bold, spiny, three-lobed leaves give it an architectural foliage texture without parallel among the hellebores — the overall impression, particularly of a mature clump with multiple erect stems of 2–3 feet, is of a substantial, bold, textural shade or part-shade structural plant of considerable presence throughout the full year. In late winter and early spring, the robust stems terminate in large, branched clusters carrying numerous cup-shaped flowers of a characteristic pale, fresh, apple-green to yellow-green color — open-faced, wide, and much more visible than the nodding flowers of H. orientalis hybrids. The pale, fresh-green flower clusters against the dark, spiny, architectural foliage create an elegant late-winter composition. More tolerant of sun and dryness than most hellebores. An outstanding structural shade and part-shade plant for zones 6–9.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil in full sun; cosmos blooms most prolifically in lean, dry soil — rich, moist conditions produce excessive foliage at the expense of flowers.
directions: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil in full sun; cosmos blooms most prolifically in lean, dry soil — rich, moist conditions produce excessive foliage at the expense of flowers. Cosmos bipinnatus is one of the most beloved, easy-to-grow garden annuals, producing feathery, thread-fine leaves on branching stems and a long succession of daisy-like flowers 2–4 inches across in white, pink, rose, burgundy, and bicolors from early summer through frost; individual plants bloom for 3–4 months when kept deadheaded. It is a superb butterfly plant, beloved by monarchs, swallowtails, and skippers, and a major nectar source for bumblebees and honeybees; it self-seeds freely in disturbed soil. Minimal care required — simply thin to 9–18 inches and let it bloom.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; costus is one of the most shade-tolerant of all ornamental gingers and grows naturally as a forest understory plant in tropical Asia. In zone 8–9 the tops die back in frost but roots resprout reliably from established clumps.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; spiral ginger is one of the most structurally unusual and striking plants for the tropical shade garden — the broad, elliptical leaves are arranged in a tight spiral up the stem (giving it the name 'stepladder plant'), and the plant culminates in a dense, pinecone-like terminal inflorescence of overlapping red bracts from which large, white, orchid-like flowers emerge one at a time over several weeks. The architectural form of the spiraling stems creates a dramatic, bold presence in the shaded garden. It is one of the best shade-tolerant tropicals for Gulf Coast gardens and makes an excellent companion for heliconias, anthuriums, and alocasias in the tropical shade garden. Cut old stems to the ground after flowering; new stems arise from the base.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist, loamy to rocky soil in full sun; cottage pinks require excellent drainage and will not survive in wet or heavy clay soils. Avoid overhead watering to prevent crown rot.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — cottage pinks are the classic old-fashioned garden pinks of European cottage gardens, producing intensely fragrant, fringed (hence 'plumarius' — feathery), five-petaled flowers in shades of white, pink, rose, crimson, and bicolors in May–June on a low, spreading mat of glaucous blue-green, grass-like foliage that remains attractive year-round. The rich, spicy-sweet, clove-like fragrance is extraordinary — unmatched by modern hybrid dianthus — and one of the defining scents of the traditional cottage garden. They require excellent drainage and perform best in slightly alkaline soils, making them excellent choices for rock gardens, dry stone walls, gravel gardens, and raised beds with sharply drained soil. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom; shear plants by one-third after flowering to maintain a tidy, compact mound.

plant_note: Start indoors early; tolerant of coastal conditions and needs no cold period.
directions: Start seed indoors several weeks before the last frost and transplant after the soil warms. This blend produces pastel, papery blooms on stems up to eighteen inches long that are prized for fresh and dried arrangements. It grows well in coastal areas and needs no cool period to flower. Harvest stems when the blooms are fully open and hang them upside down to dry for lasting color.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall on the surface of dry, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; seeds are light-dependent germinators and should not be covered — simply press onto the soil surface and allow winter rains to settle them in place.
directions: Cottony Goldenaster is a softly woolly native perennial of dry, open, sandy pinelands, scrub, and coastal plain barrens from North Carolina south through Florida and west to Alabama, where its dense covering of cottony white hairs gives the whole plant a distinctive silvery-white appearance even before it blooms. From September through December — among the latest-blooming native asters in the Southeast — the plant produces masses of small, bright golden-yellow daisy-like flowers that serve as a critical late-season nectar source for lingering monarch butterflies and native bees building their winter reserves. Plant in dry, sandy, acidic, extremely well-drained soil in full sun and avoid clay soils or any site prone to standing water, which will quickly rot the crown. Once established, Cottony Goldenaster is highly drought-tolerant and requires little care beyond removing spent stems in late winter to make way for new basal growth.

common_name: Cowhorn Orchid (Bee Orchid, Antler Orchid, Florida Cowhorn)
plant_note: Mount on rough-barked wood or cork or grow in an open slatted basket with coarse bark; the hollow pseudobulbs of wild plants are naturally inhabited by colonies of biting ants (the ant-orchid relationship is one of the most studied in orchid ecology), but in cultivation the plants grow and bloom without ants. Provide bright indirect to partial direct light. Water regularly in active growth; reduce in winter dry rest. The tall flower spikes (6–10 feet) require space — this is a large orchid. Listed as an endangered species in Florida. In zone 9, protect from hard freezes. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on rough bark or in an open slatted basket in bright indirect to filtered direct morning sun — Cowhorn Orchid grows most vigorously in good indirect light with air circulation and adapts to a range of conditions once established. Myrmecophila tibicinis is a large, epiphytic orchid native to southern Florida (critically endangered), the Florida Keys, the Caribbean, Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most distinctive orchids of the Florida and Gulf Coast region for several remarkable qualities. The pseudobulbs are large (6–18 inches), hollow, and shaped like cowhorns or antlers — clustered in dense masses and, in wild plants, invariably inhabited by colonies of biting ants (genus Crematogaster) that defend the plant aggressively in exchange for shelter in the hollow pseudobulbs. This ant-plant mutualism is one of the best-documented in orchid ecology. The flower display is extraordinary: tall, much-branched inflorescences 6–10 feet tall emerge from between the pseudobulbs and bear hundreds of 1-inch, bright magenta-pink flowers — the sheer height and mass of the branching spike of hot-pink flowers makes a flowering cowhorn orchid one of the most spectacular ornamental displays in Florida and Caribbean tropical gardens. Once an abundant orchid in South Florida hammocks and cypress swamps, it has been decimated by poaching and habitat loss and is now listed as endangered in Florida. A prized specimen orchid for zone 10-12. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; cowpen daisy thrives in disturbed, poor soils and hot, dry conditions that defeat many garden plants — excellent for waste areas, roadsides, and dry hillsides.
directions: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun — cowpen daisy is a bold, fast-growing native annual of prairies, roadsides, and dry disturbed areas throughout the southern US and Central America, producing masses of bright yellow, 2-inch daisies with a yellow central disk from mid-summer through frost on coarse, silvery-white-leaved, branching plants. It grows in some of the most challenging conditions encountered by any garden plant: caliche, dry rocky limestone, alkaline clay, and hot, exposed roadsides, where it seeds into cracks and disturbed patches and blooms prodigiously with zero irrigation. The flowers are reliably visited by monarch butterflies during fall migration and by native bees. An excellent, self-sowing annual for difficult dry, sunny spots in Gulf Coast and Texas gardens where more refined plants would fail. The seeds are an important winter food for mourning doves and other seed-eating birds.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall (they require cold stratification to break dormancy and will germinate in spring), or cold-stratify seeds in the refrigerator for 4–6 weeks before indoor sowing in late winter; cowslip grows best in moist, slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil in part shade or dappled sun. It self-sows freely where happy and forms naturalized colonies in meadows and woodland edges over time.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil in part shade to dappled sun; cowslip is one of the most beloved and historically significant wildflowers of the European countryside — a spring primrose relative producing rosettes of crinkled, oval, downy leaves at ground level and, in April and May, umbels of pendant, deep-golden-yellow, tubular flowers with distinctive orange spots in the throat, all nodding together on a single stem and carrying a sweet, honeyed fragrance uniquely their own. The flowers have been used since medieval times in cowslip wine, mead, and vinegar, and the plant's association with English meadows, hedgerow banks, and woodland clearings is so deep that its decline from agricultural intensification is a touchstone of British conservation. In the garden it naturalizes beautifully in damp meadows, shaded lawns left uncut until after seeding, and lightly shaded borders alongside wood anemones, bluebells, and early forget-me-nots. It hybridizes freely with Primula vulgaris (primrose) to produce the naturally occurring oxlip hybrid Primula x polyantha, from which most garden polyanthus are derived.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; Coyure Palm (Ruffle Palm) is an ornamental, small to medium palm native to the tropical forests and forest edges of the Lesser Antilles and northern South America (Venezuela, Trinidad) — armed with long, black, needle-like spines on trunk and fronds, but producing distinctive, ruffled, bright-green fronds and bright-red ornamental fruits that make it a dramatic specimen plant for tropical gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun — handle with thick gloves as all parts of the trunk and fronds are densely armed with long, sharp, black spines; plant where foot traffic will not encounter the spines. Aiphanes minima (Coyure Palm, Ruffle Palm, or Macaw Palm) is a small to medium, solitary-trunked palm native to the humid tropical forests of the Lesser Antilles (Dominica, Guadeloupe, Martinique) and Trinidad and Venezuela, belonging to the heavily armed Aiphanes genus whose characteristic feature — needle-like, jet-black spines covering the trunk, leaf sheaths, and petioles — makes the palm spectacular but demanding of cautious handling. Despite the forbidding spination, the palm is genuinely ornamental: the fronds are distinctively somewhat irregular and ruffled in their leaflet arrangement (the 'ruffle' appearance) with a fresh, vivid-green color, and the fruits are brilliant red-orange, round, about the size of a cherry — edible with sweet, starchy flesh in its native range and consumed by macaws and other parrots, which explains the common name 'Macaw Palm' in parts of its range. Aiphanes minima is shade-tolerant as a young plant and grows well under the partial shade of taller trees in tropical landscapes. An unusual and dramatic specimen for collectors' gardens in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; crabwood is a characteristic tree of tropical hardwood hammocks in south Florida and the Keys, growing naturally beneath the main hammock canopy as an understory to mid-canopy species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, thin, rocky or sandy, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; crabwood is a native evergreen tree of south Florida tropical hardwood hammocks, typically growing as an understory to mid-canopy species in the diverse, dense hammock forest. The small, dark green, elliptical leaves are glossy and leathery, and the plant produces dense, attractive foliage year-round. The catkin-like flower spikes are inconspicuous. Small, black fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, the indicator bird of the south Florida hammock ecosystem. The wood is dense and hard, used historically for tool handles and small crafts. Crabwood is an important structural species of the Miami-Dade hammock ecosystem — a habitat that has been reduced by over 90% from original extent. Suitable for naturalistic south Florida landscaping under and around larger hammock trees.

plant_note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings 12–24 in long by pushing them 6–8 in into moist streambank or waterside soil in early spring; roots emerge within weeks and growth is rapid. Seeds lose viability within days of ripening and must be sown immediately.
directions: Plant in wet to moist soil in full sun near water features, ponds, streams, or drainage swales; crack willow gets its name from the brittleness of its branches, which snap off at the joints in storms — a trait that is actually part of its natural dispersal strategy, as fallen branches root wherever they land in moist soil. A native of Europe and western Asia now widely naturalized in North America, it grows extremely fast (5–8 ft per year when young) and provides rapid screening and streambank stabilization. The lance-shaped, glossy green leaves appear very early in spring and provide important early-season forage for willow aphids and the beneficial insects that prey on them. Keep well away from septic systems and water pipes, as the roots are highly invasive toward water sources.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom.
directions: Direct sow after frost or start indoors a few weeks early for a jump on the season. Crackerjack is a superior tall blend with a mounding form and sturdy stalks bearing four-inch blooms in tangerine orange, rich gold, and lemony yellow. Grow in full sun with average, well-drained soil and moderate water. Deadhead spent blooms to keep the plants tidy and flowering into fall.

plant_note: Start indoors a few weeks before last frost or sow directly once soil warms.
directions: Crackerjack is a tall African marigold prized for large, showy double pompons in gold, orange, and yellow on sturdy stems. Start seeds indoors for a head start or sow directly after frost danger passes, barely covering them. Plant in full sun where the strong scent helps deter garden pests, making it a classic vegetable-garden companion. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming all summer and pinch young plants to encourage branching.

common_name: Cramoisi Supérieur Rose (Crimson Antique China Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Cramoisi Supérieur is an 1832 French China rose valued for deep crimson-red blooms and the class's characteristic heat and humidity tolerance, making it a long-standing favorite in Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1832, Cramoisi Supérieur ('superior crimson') bears cupped, fully double, rich crimson-red blooms with a light fragrance, borne in small clusters against dark green, glossy foliage typical of the China rose class. It blooms in nearly continuous flushes from spring through the first hard frost and shares the exceptional heat, humidity, and disease tolerance for which China roses are prized in the Gulf South, needing little to no spraying to stay healthy through the growing season. A climbing sport of the variety is also grown, but the shrub form remains the most widely planted, working well in borders, mass plantings, and as a low, informal hedge. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead or crossing wood; heavy pruning is unnecessary since flowering continues on both old and new growth.

common_name: Cranberry Crush Hibiscus (Compact Deep Red Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Cranberry Crush is a compact Summerific series cultivar with deep cranberry-red flowers and green foliage, bred for a shorter, more manageable size than older hardy hibiscus varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Cranberry Crush is one of the most compact cultivars in the Summerific breeding series, staying under 3 feet tall while still producing the enormous, 7-8 inch, deep cranberry-red flowers typical of hardy hibiscus, making it a good fit for smaller gardens and large containers where taller hardy hibiscus varieties would overwhelm the space. It blooms in a steady succession from midsummer into fall, with new flowers opening continuously as each individual bloom lasts only a single day. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can damage foliage and flowers where present.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated corms in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich, undisturbed soil in full to partial shade under mature deciduous hardwoods; crane-fly orchid requires an undisturbed, leaf-littered woodland floor with appropriate mycorrhizal fungi.
directions: Crane-fly orchid is one of the most ecologically fascinating native orchids of eastern North American forests — a shade-dwelling terrestrial orchid that shows a remarkable seasonal reversal: a single, attractively mottled, purple-green leaf emerges in fall, remains through winter as a solitary, easy-to-overlook woodland groundcover, then withers and disappears in late spring as the leafless flowering stalk emerges in midsummer bearing 20–40 tiny, translucent, crane-fly-shaped flowers that give the species its name. This reversed phenology — leafy in winter, leafless when flowering in summer — is unique among North American orchids and perfectly adapted to deciduous forest light patterns: the leaf photosynthesizes during winter when canopy trees are leafless, storing energy in the underground corm for summer flowering. Nocturnal moths are the primary pollinators, attracted by a faint fragrance at night. A subtle, quiet orchid of the undisturbed forest floor that rewards patient observers; best appreciated in its natural woodland setting rather than cultivated, though nursery-propagated corms are occasionally available from specialist orchid growers.

plant_note: Plant dormant corms or container-grown stock in fall (when the winter leaf naturally appears) in moist, acidic, humus-rich, loose leaf-litter soil in deep to partial shade; cranefly orchid depends on an undisturbed mycorrhizal fungal partner in the soil and transplants poorly bare-root — use only nursery-propagated material, never wild-collected plants.
directions: Site in moist, humus-rich, undisturbed leaf-litter soil in deep to partial shade beneath hardwoods; do not rake or disturb the leaf litter over the planting, and never dig plants from the wild. Tipularia discolor is one of the most unusual native orchids of eastern deciduous forests, with a two-phase life cycle that separates its leaf and flower entirely: a single dark green, purple-spotted, pleated leaf emerges in fall and persists through winter, photosynthesizing during the leafless dormant season, then withers away in spring before the summer flower spike — a slender raceme of small, translucent greenish-purple, oddly asymmetric flowers pollinated at night by noctuid moths — rises leafless from the same corm. Because the leaf and bloom never overlap, the plant is easy to overlook except in winter, when its solitary spotted leaf stands out against bare forest floor. A genuinely distinctive conversation piece for a shaded native woodland garden in zone 5–9, best left undisturbed once established.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; crape jasmine tolerates some afternoon shade in the Deep South and actually benefits from partial shading in zone 10–12 summer heat — full sun in zone 10 can stress the plant.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; crape jasmine (pinwheel flower, East Indian rosebay, Adam's apple) is a widely grown South and Southeast Asian tropical shrub that produces pure-white, waxy, pinwheel-shaped flowers with five overlapping, twisted petals throughout the warm season, releasing an intensely sweet, jasmine-like fragrance especially in the evening — making it one of the most fragrant flowering shrubs available for the Gulf Coast and tropical garden. The glossy, deep-green, oblong leaves and neat, dense, rounded growth habit make it attractive even out of flower as a foliage shrub. The double-flowered form, 'Flore Pleno', with ruffled, rose-like double flowers, is the most widely sold cultivar and is particularly ornamental. The plant exudes a milky sap when cut (it is in the Apocynaceae family, related to oleander and plumeria) and all parts are mildly toxic. It is sensitive to frost and is killed back by temperatures much below 32°F, but recovers from the root in zone 9 if given winter protection. Used extensively as a specimen, informal hedge, and container plant throughout tropical and subtropical regions.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in fall or softwood cuttings in summer, or plant container-grown shrubs and trees in spring; crape myrtles are extremely drought-tolerant and heat-loving once established — they bloom best in the hottest, sunniest conditions. Avoid over-watering or over-fertilizing, which produces excessive foliage at the expense of flowers. Never 'crape murder' (severely top the plant) — prune only lightly to shape.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; crape myrtle is arguably the most important ornamental tree of the Gulf Coast, the mid-South, and California, producing dramatic clusters (panicles) of crepe-textured flowers in white, pink, red, lavender, or purple from July through September — among the longest bloom periods of any flowering tree — on plants that range from 3-foot dwarf shrubs to 30-foot trees depending on selection. The modern hybrid varieties (L. indica x L. fauriei) also offer spectacular exfoliating bark in cinnamon, gray, and russet that is ornamental year-round, plus brilliant orange-red fall color. These hybrids are also substantially more mildew-resistant than pure L. indica. Sizes range from true dwarf cultivars ('Petite Embers,' 'Tonto') to large trees ('Natchez,' 'Muskogee'). All are extremely heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and long-lived in zones 7–9. Spring pruning should be limited to removing dead wood and crossing branches — severe topping destroys the natural form permanently.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring or fall (in mild climates) in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; cream cups is a cool-season annual that performs best before summer heat and self-sows to maintain colonies in lean, open soils. It does not transplant well; always direct sow. Best sown in broad drifts for the most attractive meadow effect.
directions: Direct sow seeds in cool weather in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; cream cups is a delicate California native annual, the sole species in its genus, producing grayish-hairy, narrow leaves on spreading stems and in spring (February through May), a succession of small (1 inch), six-petaled, cream-to-pale-yellow poppy flowers of the softest, most delicate, barely-there coloring — the petals creamy-white to very pale butter-yellow, almost translucent in full sun, giving each flower a fresh, light, candlelight quality. In mass plantings or in natural meadow settings with other California native annuals, the cream-colored flowers create a soft, light, airy effect quite different from the stronger colors of California poppy or gilia. It is one of the few California native annuals in this soft, cream-to-pale-yellow range rather than the intense oranges, reds, and blues of other species. Outstanding in native wildflower meadow mixes as a soft foil to bolder-colored companions, and in gravel gardens and the front of lean-soil borders where its modest stature and soft color work well. Native bees forage the flowers readily.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; cream violet is one of the most adaptable native violets for the shaded garden, tolerating a range of moisture conditions and significant shade.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — cream violet is a native woodland violet of eastern deciduous forests, distinguished by its cream to white flowers with distinctive purple veining (striping) on the lower three petals that gives it both the species name striata and the common name striped cream violet. Unlike the stemless violets (V. sororia, V. cucullata), cream violet is leafy-stemmed, growing from branched stems rather than a basal rosette, which gives it a somewhat different growth form in the woodland garden. It blooms in spring and often reblooms again in fall. Grows naturally in moist, rich woodland, stream banks, and moist forest clearings throughout the eastern US. Forms attractive groundcover colonies in shaded settings. Like all native violets, it supports native fritillary butterfly caterpillars as a larval host plant. An excellent white-flowered native violet alternative to the more common blue species.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper or nicking the seed coat before sowing — scarification is essential for reliable germination. Direct sow in fall in a permanent site with well-drained, sandy or loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Cream Wild Indigo is extremely slow from seed (2–3 years to bloom) but is essentially immortal once established; choose the planting site with care as plants resent disturbance and should never be moved.
directions: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or nick the hard coat with a knife before fall sowing — this is critical, as unscarified Baptisia seeds have very low germination rates; direct sow into the permanent site in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun, as Cream Wild Indigo develops a deep taproot and cannot be transplanted successfully once established. This low-growing, sprawling prairie perennial produces creamy-white, downward-nodding pea-flower spikes in early spring (April–May), followed by large, inflated charcoal-black seed pods that rattle when ripe and are prized for dried arrangements. Cream Wild Indigo is one of the slowest native wildflowers to establish from seed — expect 2–3 years before first bloom — but plants are essentially immortal, extremely drought tolerant once established, fix atmospheric nitrogen, and require no care whatsoever once settled; a mature specimen is one of the finest and most trouble-free prairie plants available.

common_name: Creek Sedge (Narrow-Leaf Sedge, Eastern Gray Sedge)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creek sedge is highly adaptable to a wide range of soil moisture conditions, from consistently moist woodland soils to seasonally wet streambanks.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creek sedge is a graceful native sedge of the southeastern and central US, forming upright to arching tufts of narrow, dark-green, somewhat glaucous leaves useful for naturalized streambanks, rain gardens, shaded borders, and moist-shade situations under trees. It is one of the most ecologically important native sedges of the Southeast, providing ground-level structure and habitat in woodland understories and riparian edges throughout the region. The species is widely distributed from New England to Florida and westward to the central plains, demonstrating its adaptability across a broad range of climates. It tolerates both consistently moist garden soils and temporary flooding. In zone 9, it performs as an effective semi-evergreen groundcover in partially shaded areas receiving moderate moisture. An outstanding choice for sustainable landscape plantings, rain garden edges, and woodland restoration.

plant_note: Plant divisions or sow seed in spring in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; creeping baby's breath is a superb rock garden and dry wall plant, forming a dense mat that covers itself in tiny flowers for weeks in summer.
directions: Plant divisions or sow seed in spring in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, gritty soil in full sun; creeping baby's breath requires excellent drainage and performs best in poor, slightly alkaline, gravelly soils similar to its native alpine and subalpine limestone habitats. Gypsophila repens is a low, mat-forming European alpine perennial producing slender, blue-gray leaves on spreading, prostrate stems and masses of tiny, white to pale-pink, 5-petaled flowers in loose panicles from early to mid-summer, creating a frothy, airy effect; it trails attractively over rocks and walls. Unlike the tall, annual or biennial florists' baby's breath (G. paniculata and G. elegans), this is a compact, perennial species ideal for rock gardens, dry walls, and the front of sunny borders. The pink-flowered selection 'Rosea' is particularly popular. Excellent for cutting and drying.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Variegata spreads slowly by rhizome to form a weed-suppressing groundcover mat and is best left undivided for 3–4 years to develop its most effective coverage.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Variegata creeping broadleaf sedge forms a slowly spreading carpet of broad, strap-like leaves cleanly edged with creamy-white margins that appear luminous in shaded positions. The leaves are wider than most sedges — 1/2 to 3/4 inch — giving the plant a decidedly bolder texture than fine-leafed species. The white-margined foliage brightens shaded areas through summer, combining well with dark-leafed hostas, astilbes, and ferns. The plant emerges late in spring and looks freshest from spring through early summer; in hot, humid climates some leaf tips may brown by late summer, which can be trimmed. Semi-evergreen in zone 7–9; may die back in zone 5–6 winters but re-emerges vigorously. Divide when clumps become crowded, about every 4 years, replanting vigorous outer sections and discarding the woody center.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet soil in full to partial sun; creeping eryngo tolerates temporary flooding and is well suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and low, wet areas of the native landscape.
directions: Direct sow in spring in moist to occasionally wet soil in full to partial sun; creeping eryngo is highly adaptable to temporarily flooded sites and performs well in rain gardens and low-lying areas where other perennials fail. Eryngium prostratum is a native eryngo of the southeastern United States, spreading prostrate stems to form low mats studded with small, pale blue to white thistle-like flower heads from summer through fall that attract native bees and beneficial insects. Unlike the showy ornamental eryngos, this species is valued for its ecological function as a native groundcover tolerant of flooding, drought recovery, and partial shade at the woodland edge.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens against a masonry wall, fence, or shaded slope in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full shade in spring; creeping fig adheres by adhesive rootlets and requires no support structure — it anchors directly to masonry, stucco, and wood.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or plant container specimens against masonry, stucco, or wood surfaces in partial to full shade; creeping fig is a vigorous East Asian climbing fig that attaches to vertical surfaces by tiny adhesive rootlets, blanketing walls and fences in a dense, neat carpet of small, heart-shaped, dark-green, juvenile leaves — one of the few true shade vines that thrives in deep shade and provides the distinctive ivy-covered wall effect so prized in formal garden design.
