Juvenile foliage is small and refined; if the vine is not trimmed, the older climbing stems eventually produce larger, leathery, elliptic adult leaves and even figs, but most gardeners trim annually to maintain the juvenile foliage texture. Excellent for covering bare masonry walls, garden structures, and shaded embankments in Gulf Coast landscapes. Can become very large and difficult to remove once established — roots deeply into masonry. Tolerates brief cold snaps to 15–20°F.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Polemonium reptans is a native woodland species distinct from the more commonly grown P. caeruleum, with more deeply shade-tolerant constitution and a looser, more delicate growth habit suited to naturalized woodland gardens.
directions: Plant in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-enriched, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Polemonium reptans tolerates more shade than the European P. caeruleum and is well-suited to naturalized plantings under deciduous trees alongside other spring wildflowers. Polemonium reptans is a native eastern North American woodland wildflower of moist, shaded stream banks, forest floors, and ravines, producing delicate, finely pinnate, ladder-like leaves (the 'Jacob's Ladder' pattern from which the genus takes its name) and clusters of nodding, sky-blue to lavender-blue, five-petaled flowers in April and May that are delicate and beautiful in a woodland setting. It goes dormant by midsummer in heat and drought, making it a spring ephemeral in most of its range; companion it with ferns and hostas that fill the space after it dies back. The cultivar 'Stairway to Heaven' with white-and-green variegated leaves is popular for brightening shade. An underused native for shade gardens in zones 4–8.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem divisions or container plants in moist to wet, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; creeping jenny spreads rapidly by stolons and is ideal for stabilizing stream banks, edging water features, or filling in gaps between stepping stones.
directions: Plant stem divisions in moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun where a rapidly spreading groundcover is desired; creeping jenny forms a dense, mat-forming carpet of round, bright-green (or chartreuse-yellow in the 'Aurea' form) coin-shaped leaves studded with small yellow flowers in late spring. It roots wherever stems touch moist soil and spreads quickly to cover bare ground, suppress weeds, and soften the edges of water features and containers. Excellent for shade gardens, pond banks, and as a trailing container plant that cascades over the edges. Can be invasive in naturalized areas near waterways in some regions — check local guidelines. Trim with shears in midsummer if it outgrows its allotted space.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile to poor soil in full sun; avoid clay soils and any location with standing water, which leads to root rot.
directions: Plant in well-drained, infertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; creeping juniper is a native North American groundcover that naturally carpets rocky outcrops, dry slopes, and sandy barrens from Newfoundland to British Columbia and south to New England. It is extremely cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established, requiring virtually no care on appropriate sites. Many cultivars have been selected for varying habits and needle colors — 'Wiltonii' (Blue Rug) hugs the ground at just 4 inches tall and spreads 6–8 feet; 'Bar Harbor' is denser and turns plum-purple in winter; 'Prince of Wales' has bright green needles. The steel-blue berry-like cones are consumed by juniper hairstreak butterfly caterpillars and numerous birds, especially waxwings and thrushes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, dry, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; cold stratification improves germination rates.
directions: Creeping Lespedeza is a prostrate to spreading native perennial forming low, wiry mats of stems with small, rounded trifoliate leaflets and small pink-purple pea flowers from July through September. It is native to dry, open, sandy or rocky, acidic soil in open woods, barrens, and power-line rights-of-way throughout the eastern US, and its low-growing habit makes it distinctly useful as a drought-tolerant native groundcover on infertile slopes and sandy garden beds. Direct sow in fall in lean, dry, acidic, well-drained soil; cold stratification prior to sowing is beneficial. Plants spread slowly from rhizomes and are highly drought-tolerant once established, requiring little to no supplemental irrigation or fertilization.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creeping lilyturf spreads steadily by stolons and should be planted at 12–15 inch spacing for faster cover — it fills in more quickly than clumping liriope (L. muscari) and will knit into a dense, maintenance-free groundcover within 2–3 seasons.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained to moist, average soil in partial to full shade; creeping lilyturf is the spreading, stoloniferous counterpart of the common clumping liriope (L. muscari) — it produces the same narrow, dark-green, strap-shaped, grass-like leaves but spreads steadily outward from each plant by underground stolons, gradually filling in bare shade areas between plants and creating a dense, low, weed-suppressing groundcover mat without the need for reseeding or replanting. The foliage is evergreen and tidy year-round, and in summer the plants produce small, slender spikes of tiny, pale-lavender to white flowers that are less showy than the larger flower spikes of L. muscari but are still a pleasant ornamental addition. Creeping lilyturf is the preferred liriope for quickly covering large shaded areas under trees and along shaded paths, where its spreading habit is an asset rather than a problem. It is extremely shade-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and adaptable to difficult, dry, root-competitive shade conditions. An outstanding and low-maintenance shade groundcover for zone 7–11.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in partial to full shade; Creeping Lilyturf spreads aggressively by underground stolons and fills in quickly to form a dense groundcover — it is more invasive and faster-spreading than the clumping Liriope muscari and can be difficult to contain. Best used in large areas, under trees, or on slopes where spreading is desired. Mow to 2–3 inches in late winter to remove old foliage before spring flush. Very tolerant of the dry, root-competitive shade under large live oaks.
directions: Plant in full sun to deep shade in any well-drained soil; Creeping Lilyturf is one of the most adaptable and drought-tolerant groundcovers available, thriving in the challenging conditions of dry shade under large trees, compacted soil, slopes, and other difficult sites where few groundcovers survive. Liriope spicata is closely related to and often confused with Big Blue Lilyturf (L. muscari), but the two plants differ in growth habit: L. muscari forms discrete clumps while L. spicata spreads aggressively by underground stolons to form a continuous carpet, making it much better suited as a large-area groundcover but much harder to control in garden beds. In zone 9, the narrow, grass-like, dark-green leaves remain evergreen through most winters; the plant produces spikes of pale lavender to nearly white flowers in late summer, followed by black berries. The spreading habit, extreme shade tolerance, and minimal care requirements make it the standard groundcover under Gulf Coast live oaks and large shade trees across the region. The cultivar 'Silver Dragon' (green-and-white striped leaves) provides bright variegation in shade.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained to somewhat poorly drained soil in full sun to full shade; creeping liriope is far more aggressive and spreading than clumping liriope (Liriope muscari) and is best used where invasive colonization is desired — under trees, on slopes, or in confined beds.
directions: Plant plugs or divisions 12–18 inches apart in spring in virtually any well-drained to moderately moist soil; Liriope spicata spreads vigorously by stolons and quickly forms a solid groundcover mat. Liriope spicata is the strongly spreading (stoloniferous) liriope that forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover mat of narrow, grass-like, dark-green foliage; pale-lavender to near-white flower spikes appear in July–August just above or within the foliage and are followed by black berries. Unlike clumping Liriope muscari (the more commonly planted species), L. spicata spreads aggressively by underground stolons and can become weedy in formal settings — it is most appropriate under large trees, on slopes for erosion control, or in large areas where low-maintenance ground coverage is the goal. In deep shade under mature trees where little else grows well, it performs reliably. The cultivar 'Silver Dragon' has white-striped foliage and somewhat less aggressive spread than the green-leaved species. Shear to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges to refresh appearance and remove winter-damaged foliage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted stolons in early spring in moist, shaded sites; Meehan’s mint roots readily along its running stems and new plantlets can be separated and transplanted during the growing season.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Meehan’s mint is a native North American groundcover in the mint family related to the Asian Meehania species, producing small heart-shaped leaves on creeping stems that root at the nodes as they spread. In spring it produces beautiful tubular purple-blue flowers similar to a scaled-down version of ajuga or lamium. The entire plant is mildly mint-scented. It is genuinely shade-tolerant and performs in the deep, dry shade under large oaks and maples where many groundcovers struggle. It spreads at a moderate pace and is easy to control, making it a refined rather than invasive groundcover choice for woodland gardens. An excellent native companion for jack-in-the-pulpit, ferns, and wild ginger.

common_name: Creeping Oxeye (Bay Biscayne Creeping Oxeye, Wedelia)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; creeping oxeye is an extremely vigorous, salt-tolerant groundcover for hot, sunny locations in zones 9–12 but is INVASIVE in Florida and many tropical regions — verify local regulations before planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; root cuttings root extremely easily in moist soil or water. IMPORTANT NOTE: Wedelia trilobata is listed as invasive in Florida, Hawaii, many Caribbean islands, and other tropical regions where it outcompetes native vegetation — check local regulations before planting. Wedelia trilobata (creeping oxeye) is a low-growing, sprawling, tropical groundcover from the Caribbean and Central America producing cheerful, 1-inch, yellow daisy-like flowers with yellow centers nearly year-round in warm climates, on dense, mat-forming, succulent-stemmed trailing plants with glossy, dark-green, three-lobed leaves. It has been widely planted as a lawn alternative and groundcover throughout the Sunbelt for its heat, drought, and salt tolerance and its continuous yellow flowers; however, it has escaped cultivation and become seriously invasive in Florida and other warm, humid regions, smothering native vegetation and riparian areas. Wherever it is legal to grow, it is an outstanding low-maintenance groundcover for sunny, dry, coastal, or roadside banks; root cuttings root within days in moist soil. Grow with awareness of its invasive potential and do not plant near natural areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; this species (P. stolonifera) is the shade-tolerant creeping phlox, distinct from P. subulata which requires full sun — always confirm species before planting in shade.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; creeping phlox (Phlox stolonifera) is a native Appalachian woodland groundcover distinctly different from the sun-loving moss phlox (P. subulata) — P. stolonifera thrives in partial to full shade, producing spreading mats of rounded, evergreen leaves with runners that root at the nodes and producing saucer-shaped, fragrant flowers in violet-blue, pink, or white in mid-spring. After bloom, the mat provides attractive, year-round groundcover under trees and in shaded woodland beds. Much better for shade than the commonly sold P. subulata. 'Blue Ridge' (blue-violet), 'Pink Ridge' (rose-pink), and 'Sherwood Purple' are excellent named cultivars. Essentially maintenance-free once established in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Sow seed in early fall when soil temperatures are 50–65°F, or in early spring in moist, lean to moderately fertile, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; creeping red fescue spreads by rhizomes to fill in bare spots, unlike sheep's fescue. It establishes readily and requires minimal fertilization — over-fertilizing produces lush, disease-prone growth.
directions: Sow in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; creeping red fescue is the most versatile and widely used fine fescue in lawn and groundcover applications — a cool-season grass of particular value in three difficult situations: shaded lawns under trees (where Kentucky bluegrass and ryegrass fail), dry slopes and banks with minimal irrigation, and low-maintenance meadow and naturalizing applications. Unlike sheep's fescue (F. ovina), which forms non-spreading bunches, creeping red fescue spreads by rhizomes to fill in bare spots and form a continuous cover over time. Its fine, hair-like, dark-green leaves create a soft, elegant texture and remain green in cool weather. It tolerates more shade than any other common cool-season lawn grass, making it indispensable in lawn blends for partially shaded sites. It is the dominant grass in many premium fine fescue lawn blends, often combined with hard fescue (F. brevipila) and chewings fescue (F. rubra subsp. commutata) for all-fescue, no-mow or low-mow lawn applications that require only 1–2 mowings per season.

common_name: Crepe Ginger (Crape Ginger, Spiral Ginger, Cane Reed)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Cheilocostus speciosus grows vigorously in zone 9-10 and can spread aggressively by rhizomes — plant in contained areas or beds where spread is acceptable. In zone 9, the canes are killed by frost but the rhizomes survive and resprout in spring with heavy mulch. Excellent for mass planting in tropical-style shade gardens under large trees. Has naturalized as invasive in parts of Florida, Louisiana, and Hawaii — check local regulations.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Crepe Ginger grows vigorously in both partial shade and full sun, making it one of the most adaptable ornamental gingers for zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes. Cheilocostus speciosus (formerly Costus speciosus, and still widely sold under that name) is a large, rhizomatous, spreading tropical perennial native to South and Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, China, Indonesia, Malaysia) in the family Costaceae, widely naturalized throughout the tropical world. The plant produces the characteristic Costus spiral stem — upright, cane-like stems up to 8 feet tall whose large, broadly elliptical, glossy, dark-green leaves are arranged in a precise clockwise or counterclockwise spiral pattern around the stem. In late summer and fall, the canes terminate in large, cone-shaped to cylindrical inflorescences of overlapping red bracts from which the true flowers emerge: large (3–4 inch), white, crepe-paper-textured petals with a yellow center — the 'crepe' quality of the petals, almost exactly resembling crinkled white crepe paper, is uniquely distinctive and gives the plant its common name. The flowers are produced successively over weeks. The large rhizomes spread aggressively and can form extensive colonies in appropriate growing conditions — the plant has naturalized in parts of Florida, Louisiana, and Hawaii. The rhizomes are used medicinally in traditional Ayurvedic medicine.

plant_note: Cultivation is essentially impossible — this plant has no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesize, surviving entirely by parasitizing soil fungi; transplanting from the wild is both destructive and futile, and no reliable nursery propagation method currently exists.
directions: This record exists for identification and educational purposes only: Crested Coralroot is a mycoheterotrophic orchid with no green tissue whatsoever — it produces no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesize, obtaining all of its carbon and nutrients by parasitizing underground mycorrhizal fungi. Because of this complete dependence on a specific fungal network that is itself tightly bound to the root systems of surrounding trees, the plant cannot survive transplanting and cannot be cultivated in any conventional sense. Do not collect or disturb wild plants under any circumstances; populations are naturally sparse and fragile, and removal kills the plant with certainty. If you find it growing on your property in dry deciduous woodland or cedar glades of the southeastern US, treat the surrounding area as a preserve: avoid soil disturbance, refrain from applying herbicides or fertilizers, and maintain the canopy trees that support the fungal network the plant depends on. The striking purple-brown striped flowers appear on a leafless stalk in June–July and are the only visible sign of a plant that may spend most years entirely underground.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in late summer or early fall in slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; crested dwarf iris spreads by shallow surface rhizomes and should be planted with the rhizome barely covered — not buried deeply — in soils that drain freely.
directions: Plant shallow rhizomes in slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, barely covering the rhizome with soil — planting too deep causes rot; crested dwarf iris is a beloved native woodland perennial that carpets the forest floor with masses of delicate lavender-blue to violet flowers in early to mid-spring, often before surrounding woodland plants have fully emerged. The flowers are typical iris form but dwarf-scaled — 1–2 inches across — with the characteristic crested (raised, ridged) falls that give the species its name. The short, strap-like foliage fans spread to form a dense groundcover 4–6 inches tall that is attractive through summer before dying back. It spreads naturally by branching surface rhizomes to form large colonies along stream banks, rocky slopes, and under deciduous trees throughout the eastern US. A white form ('Alba') is available. Outstanding under azaleas, dogwoods, and spring-blooming trees as a carpet companion that blooms at the same time as its companions. Resents wet soils in summer.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in wet to moist, strongly acidic, peaty or humus-rich, poorly to well-drained soil in partial to full shade; crested wood fern is specifically adapted to wet, boggy, acidic woodland habitats and swamp edges, requiring consistently moist to wet, acidic conditions. An excellent fern for rain garden wet zones and shaded bog garden margins.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in wet to moist, strongly acidic, peaty or humus-rich, poorly to well-drained soil in partial to full shade; crested wood fern is a distinctive native fern of wet, acidic habitats — swamp margins, bog edges, wet forest floors, and poorly drained, shaded depressions from Newfoundland to Florida and west to the Great Plains. The characteristic feature is the pinnae (leaflets) that are held nearly perpendicular (at right angles) to the rachis (frond stalk) and parallel to the ground, creating an unusual, ladder-like appearance quite different from the gracefully arching form of most ferns. The fronds are semi-evergreen, remaining partially green through mild winters. An excellent choice for wet, shaded spots in the garden where standing water or consistently boggy conditions prevent most plants from thriving — crested wood fern actually prefers these conditions and will naturalize in appropriate wet, acidic, shaded settings. Combine with tussock sedge, marsh marigold, and cardinal flower in wet shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers in spring into moist to wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soil in partial shade; never collect plants from the wild — source only from reputable native plant nurseries with documented propagation.
directions: Platanthera cristata is a beautiful and increasingly rare native terrestrial orchid of eastern and southeastern North America, producing a dense spike of brilliant orange-yellow flowers with elaborately fringed lips in July and August that rival any tropical orchid in intricacy and are among the most vivid of all native wildflowers. It grows in moist to wet, acidic, peaty or sandy soils in open bogs, pine savannas, wet meadows, and seepage slopes in partial shade, particularly in Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain communities. Never collect plants from the wild — purchase only nursery-propagated stock from reputable native plant nurseries; the plant requires specific mycorrhizal fungi to thrive and resents root disturbance. An extraordinary addition to a native bog garden or rain garden with consistently high soil moisture.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in shade; Cretan brake fern is one of the easiest and most adaptable ferns for shaded gardens in zones 8-12, tolerating a wide range of soil types and moisture levels.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Cretan brake fern is one of the most widely grown ornamental ferns in warm-climate gardens, with elegant, finger-like fronds divided into narrow, pale green leaflets on dark, wiry stalks. The many cultivars offer striking variation with white-striped or crested leaflet tips. Highly adaptable to both full shade and indirect light, and tolerant of moderate drought once established. Spreads by spores to self-establish in appropriate shaded garden conditions and is one of the best ferns for shaded beds, walkways, and under mature trees in the warm Southeast. Hardy to about 20-25°F; recovers quickly from light frost damage.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in spring; crimson bottlebrush is exceptionally adaptable and establishes quickly. It tolerates brief flooding, salt spray, and a wide range of soil types.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; the crimson bottlebrush is one of the most versatile and widely planted Australian natives in Gulf Coast and California gardens, producing spectacular cylindrical flower spikes 4–6 inches long with hundreds of bright crimson stamens that give the flower its distinctive bottlebrush shape. The nectar-rich flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies and appear primarily in spring and often reflower in fall. Unlike Callistemon viminalis (weeping bottlebrush), C. citrinus grows as a dense, upright to spreading shrub rather than a pendulous tree. It tolerates poor soils, salt spray, drought, and occasional standing water — making it one of the most adaptable ornamental shrubs for challenging coastal and urban conditions. Excellent as a screen, foundation plant, or specimen.

common_name: Crimson Fire Loropetalum (Deep Red Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Crimson Fire maintains its best leaf color intensity with 4–6 hours of direct sun — in deep shade the foliage becomes more green than purple-red.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Crimson Fire is a compact, mounding loropetalum introduced by Monrovia Nursery that combines some of the most intense foliage color in the genus — deep crimson-red to dark burgundy-red new growth that matures to a rich dark purple-red — with a manageable size of 2.5–4 feet tall and wide that fits foundation plantings and shrub borders without requiring constant shearing to control size. The deep pink to magenta fringe flowers appear in spring and intermittently through summer and fall, standing out vibrantly against the dark foliage. Crimson Fire holds its foliage color better through summer heat than some loropetalum selections, maintaining richer red-purple tones rather than fading to green-bronze. The compact size and naturally dense, mounding habit reduce the maintenance requirements that make larger loropetalums problematic in typical home foundation plantings. Loropetalums are some of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant ornamental shrubs for zone 9 and are largely free of serious pest and disease problems in the Gulf South. Provide good drainage — waterlogged soils cause rapid root rot. No pruning is required but plants respond well to light shaping immediately after the main spring bloom.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 1–2 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; crimson flag lily thrives in moist spots alongside ponds and streams and blooms in fall when few other bulbs are in flower.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near pond margins, stream banks, or in rain garden edges; crimson flag lily (formerly Schizostylis coccinea) is a South African plant that produces brilliant scarlet or deep pink star-shaped flowers on slender stems in autumn — September through November — at a time when most flowering perennials are winding down. The grassy, strap-like leaves are evergreen in mild climates. Plants require consistently moist soil throughout the growing season and will not perform well in dry conditions; they thrive where soil is reliably moist in summer. Clumps increase fairly quickly; divide every 3 years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread. 'Major' (large red) and 'Mrs. Hegarty' (pink) are popular cultivars.

common_name: Crimson Queen Japanese Maple (Red Weeping Japanese Maple)
plant_note: Plant container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade; in zone 9, east-facing exposures with morning sun and afternoon shade are essential — Crimson Queen is more sensitive to summer heat than upright red Japanese maples.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, humus-rich soil in dappled to partial shade; Crimson Queen is the most popular and widely planted laceleaf (dissectum) weeping Japanese maple with red foliage — a mounding, cascading, mushroom-shaped small tree reaching 6–10 feet tall with an even wider spread, producing deeply dissected, lace-like, rich crimson-red to burgundy-red leaves that maintain better summer color than most dissectum Japanese maples. The extremely finely cut, feathery foliage drapes from gracefully weeping branches in a soft, cascading curtain of crimson-red — one of the most visually dramatic and elegant small trees available for woodland garden or specimen use. The weeping, mounding habit creates a naturally sculptural form without pruning, and mature specimens become increasingly dramatic focal points over decades. In fall, the foliage transitions to bright scarlet. In zone 9, Crimson Queen requires careful siting to succeed — morning sun and afternoon shade in a location with moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil are the minimum requirements. Plant near water features, in east-facing beds, or under the high canopy of larger trees. Provide consistent moisture during summer. In the right location, Crimson Queen is reliably successful in zone 9 and is widely grown in Houston, New Orleans, and coastal Mississippi.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring, or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; crimson scabious also germinates readily from fall-sown seed. Prefers alkaline to neutral, well-drained soil and is short-lived but self-sows freely.
directions: Sow seed in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; crimson scabious is an outstanding pollinator plant producing dozens of rich crimson to burgundy pincushion flowers on wiry, branching stems from June through frost — one of the longest blooming periods of any perennial. The deep jewel-red color is unusual among summer perennials and combines beautifully with silver foliage plants and pale lavenders. Butterflies, bees, and hoverflies cover the flowers constantly; it is among the top five plants for beneficial insect attraction in European wildflower garden research. It is technically a short-lived perennial but self-sows abundantly enough to maintain a permanent colony. Deadhead spent blooms to extend the flowering season and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rock rose requires excellent drainage and resents summer irrigation once established. It is relatively short-lived (7–15 years) but often self-sows. The sticky aromatic leaves produce labdanum resin that has been collected for perfumery since antiquity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; crimson-spot rock rose is the largest-flowered of the Mediterranean cistus shrubs — producing blooms 3–4 inches across in pure white, each petal bearing a prominent crimson-maroon basal blotch that creates a ring of five vivid spots within the white flower, giving each bloom the quality of a hand-painted botanical illustration. The flowers last only one day each (the petals falling by late afternoon), but are produced in such lavish succession from May through July that the plant appears constantly in flower for weeks. The sticky, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves produce labdanum resin with a distinctive, warm, ambery-woody fragrance that has been harvested for use in perfumery since ancient times — the gum being collected by raking the hillside goats' beards after they browse among the plants. Outstanding as a drought-tolerant flowering shrub for lean, rocky, or sandy soils in hot, dry gardens in zones 8b–10.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to moderately wet, fertile, well-drained to poorly drained soil in partial shade to full sun; crinum thrives in seasonally flooded areas, pond margins, and the wet spots that defeat most other bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to wet, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; crinum lily is one of the most heat-tolerant and moisture-tolerant bulbs available for zone 7–11 gardens, thriving in conditions from boggy pond margins to regularly inundated lawn edges where most ornamentals fail. The intensely fragrant white spider-like flowers appear on tall scapes above the broad, strap-like, semi-evergreen foliage in summer and attract sphinx moths and swallowtail butterflies at dusk. Clumps multiply steadily by offsets and require little care beyond dividing every 5–7 years when they become congested. Hardy to approximately 15°F with heavy mulch in zone 7; essentially evergreen in zone 9–11 coastal Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; the tightly ruffled, crimped leaf margins of Crispatum make it one of the most distinctive-textured leopard plant cultivars for a shady bed or large container.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh sun that can scorch the leaves. Crispatum is a striking cultivar of Farfugium japonicum, the Gulf Coast garden staple known as leopard plant, selected for round leaves with tightly crimped, ruffled margins that give the foliage an almost sculptural, parsley-like texture unlike the flatter leaves of the species. Clusters of small, daisy-like yellow flowers rise above the foliage on tall stems in fall. It spreads slowly into a dense clump, tolerates deep shade better than most broadleaf perennials, and is a favorite container and border plant in Southern shade gardens for its bold, unusual texture.

plant_note: Plant in moist, coarse, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, airy substrate in bright indirect light to deep shade; crocodile fern is an epiphytic Southeast Asian fern best grown in loose, fast-draining, bark-based substrate — treat similarly to an orchid in terms of substrate aeration and avoid dense, waterlogged potting media.
directions: Grow in coarse, airy, humus-rich, well-drained substrate in bright indirect light to shade; allow the top inch to dry slightly between waterings. Microsorum musifolium (crocodile fern or alligator fern) is a distinctive Malaysian and Southeast Asian epiphytic fern producing broad, undivided (simple), banana-leaf-like fronds 12–24 inches long with an extraordinary textural pattern: the entire surface of each pale-to-medium green frond is marked with an intricate network of darker-green veins in a hexagonal, honeycomb-like pattern that uncannily resembles the skin pattern of a crocodile — giving the plant its striking common name and making it one of the most visually interesting tropical foliage plants. Like bird nest ferns, it grows naturally as an epiphyte in the forks of trees in humid tropical forests; in cultivation it prefers a coarse, open, well-aerated substrate rather than dense potting soil. As a houseplant or shade garden plant (in frost-free zones), it is a conversation piece with its uniquely patterned fronds. It requires high humidity and protection from temperatures below 55°F and is best suited to zone 10–12 outdoor gardens or indoor/greenhouse growing.

plant_note: Plant corms in spring around last frost; in zones 6–7 apply a thick mulch in fall to protect overwintering corms.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 in deep in groups of 6 or more for the best visual impact; crocosmia forms clumps through underground stolons. Arching sprays of scarlet, orange, or yellow tubular flowers appear from midsummer into fall and are excellent for cutting. Where hardy, divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to refresh bloom; in zone 5 and colder, lift and store over winter like gladiolus. 'Lucifer' is among the hardiest cultivars, tolerating zone 5 with reliable mulching.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall, 6–10 weeks before the ground freezes, for late-winter to early-spring bloom.
directions: Plant corms pointed side up at a depth of 3–4 in in well-drained soil; they naturalize quickly and look best planted in large, informal drifts. Squirrels frequently dig freshly planted corms, so covering the bed with wire mesh until the ground freezes can protect plantings. Foliage is narrow and grassy; allow it to die back completely before removing. Species crocus tend to be more reliably perennial than large-flowered Dutch types.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun with a sturdy support structure; cross vine is named for the cross-shaped pith visible in a cross-section of the stem and is one of the finest native vines for southern gardens.
directions: Plant in spring in moist, well-drained soil against a sturdy trellis, fence, or tree trunk in partial to full sun; cross vine attaches by tendril-tipped branching structures that grip masonry, wood, and chain link effectively without damaging most structures. This southeastern native semi-evergreen vine produces spectacular clusters of 2-inch, trumpet-shaped flowers in reddish-orange with yellow throats that attract hummingbirds in profusion during its main spring bloom, with scattered rebloom through summer and fall; the glossy, compound leaves remain attractive year-round in zones 7–9 and turn burgundy-red in winter. Cross vine tolerates partial shade remarkably well and is an excellent choice for growing up the trunk of a large tree or covering a shaded fence where other flowering vines would fail. Prune lightly after spring bloom to maintain size and shape.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a sturdy trellis, arbor, fence, or tree; crossvine is a vigorous native climber that attaches by forked tendrils with adhesive discs.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring or fall against a sturdy trellis, arbor, fence, or mature tree in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; crossvine is a vigorous native evergreen vine of the Southeast that produces masses of large, trumpet-shaped, orange-red to yellow flowers in mid-spring that are a critical early hummingbird nectar source just as ruby-throated hummingbirds return to the Southeast from their Caribbean winter. The bicolor flowers (orange-red outside, yellow inside in the species; brick-red in the cultivar 'Tangerine Beauty') cover the mature vine in late April to May in a stunning display. It climbs by adhesive tendrils to 30–50 feet and is semi-evergreen in zone 6–7, fully evergreen in zone 8–9. Once established it is drought-tolerant and self-supporting on any surface it can grip.

plant_note: Plant container stock after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; croton requires warm temperatures (above 60°F) at all times — avoid cold drafts, cold water, and cold soil, all of which cause leaf drop; in zones 9–11, it thrives as a year-round landscape shrub when protected from frost.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to part sun; protect from direct afternoon sun in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, but too little light causes diminished color intensity. Codiaeum variegatum (croton or garden croton) is one of the most spectacularly colored tropical foliage plants in cultivation — a Malaysian native producing thick, leathery leaves in an astonishing variety of shapes (lobed, ribbon-like, twisted, spiral, oak-leaf, or fiddle-shaped depending on variety) in colors ranging from bright yellow and orange to red, maroon, bronze, and multicolor combinations of all these, often changing color dramatically as leaves mature. No two leaves on an established plant may be the same color. Over 100 named cultivars exist including 'Mammy' (twisted red, orange, and yellow leaves), 'Petra' (classic red and yellow lobed leaves), and 'Gold Dust' (green leaves spotted yellow). In South Florida and zone 10+, croton grows as a perennial landscape shrub 3–8 feet tall; in zones 8–9, it is used as a summer patio plant and overwintered indoors. Croton sap is a skin irritant — use gloves when pruning. The sap and seeds are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; crow poison is one of the most abundant native spring bulbs of the Texas Gulf Coast and southern Great Plains, blooming in February–April in lawns, roadsides, and disturbed areas. Despite being called 'crow poison' (Nothoscordum = 'false garlic'), it has no true toxicity; the name reflects the belief that it was toxic to crows. It self-seeds and multiplies freely.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; crow poison is among the most familiar and abundant native spring bulbs of the Texas Gulf Coast, coastal prairies, and southern Great Plains — blooming reliably and prolifically in February through April in lawns, meadows, roadsides, and native areas, often producing large, naturalized sweeps of small, white, star-shaped flowers that are a characteristic sight of the Texas spring. Each individual flower is small, white, six-petaled, held in an open umbel of 6–12 flowers, similar in appearance to wild garlic but distinctly without the garlic-family smell (Nothoscordum = 'false garlic') — the leaves have no onion or garlic odor, which is the practical field characteristic distinguishing it from Allium species. It blooms early in the season, providing nectar for early emerging native bees and small butterflies. Despite the alarming common name 'crow poison', it has no significant documented toxicity to birds or mammals — the name appears to have been based on mistaken observation or transferred from another plant. An excellent, self-sustaining native bulb for lawn naturalizing and prairie garden settings in zones 6–10; one of the plants that makes Gulf Coast spring lawns worth not mowing until April.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered, shaded position; this slow-growing fern benefits from a site with high ambient humidity and minimal disturbance once established.
directions: Plant in deep shade in rich, well-drained but consistently moist, slightly acidic soil, positioning the crown at soil level without burying it — the distinctive rosette form is best appreciated when fully exposed. This is a slow-growing fern requiring patience; avoid disturbing established plants, which resent root disturbance and may take several years to reach full size. Maintain high humidity by mulching with leaf mold around but not over the crown, and site in a naturally sheltered position rather than relying on artificial windbreaks. Protect from frosts below about 23°F (-5°C) with a loose covering of bracken or dry leaves placed over the crown in winter.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; crown flower is one of Hawaii's most beloved lei flowers — its large, waxy, white or purple flowers are the traditional choice for royal leis — and is sacred to Lord Shiva in Hindu tradition; very drought-tolerant once established; ALL plant parts except the outer petals are toxic — wear gloves when pruning and keep away from children.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; crown flower is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives on neglect; CAUTION: All parts except outer petals are toxic — wear gloves when handling. Calotropis gigantea (crown flower, giant milkweed, or mudar) is a large tropical shrub to small tree native to South Asia and Southeast Asia — one of the most important ornamental, cultural, and medicinal plants across the tropics. The plant produces large, thick, ovate, silver-blue-green leaves coated with a waxy, white powder, and spectacular clusters of waxy, star-shaped flowers with a distinctive crown-shaped secondary corona — each individual flower resembling a tiny crown, in white or lavender-purple. In Hawaii, crown flower (particularly the white form) has been the classic choice for making long, fragrant leis for over a century; Queen Lili'uokalani was famous for wearing long white crown flower leis and the plant is deeply associated with Hawaiian royalty. In Hindu tradition across South Asia, the flowers are sacred offerings to Lord Shiva and are used extensively in religious ceremonies and temple garlands. The milky white sap (latex) is toxic and irritating; the bark fiber has traditional uses in rope-making. A magnificent, bold-textured, drought-tolerant ornamental for zone 9–12 that combines ornamental beauty with deep cultural significance.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs 6–8 inches deep on their sides (to prevent water accumulating in the hollow crown and causing rot) in fall in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; crown imperials demand excellent drainage and resent wet, compacted soil.
directions: Plant large bulbs 6–8 inches deep, tilted slightly on their side to prevent crown rot, in fall in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; crown imperial is one of the most magnificent and dramatic spring bulbs, producing bold, upright stems topped with a crown-like ring of large, pendant, orange, red, or yellow bell flowers surmounted by a tuft of glossy green leaves — a regal display unlike any other bulb. Emerging shoots are highly frost-tolerant and may be undamaged even after a hard late freeze. After flowering, the foliage dies back by early summer; mark the location to avoid accidental disturbance. The bulbs have a strong foxy-musky scent that reportedly deters deer, voles, and squirrels. Excellent for imposing structure in spring borders, mixed with tulips and late narcissus. Requires a dry summer dormancy — avoid sites with summer irrigation.

common_name: Crown of Thorns (Christ Plant, Christ Thorn, Euphorbia milii)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun in well-drained soil; in zone 9a, grow as a container plant to protect from frost. In zone 10-11, plant outdoors in a sunny, well-drained location — Crown of Thorns makes an excellent low hedge or specimen plant in frost-free climates. Water carefully: too much water causes root rot, too little causes leaf drop. The thick, milky latex sap is a severe skin and eye irritant — wear gloves when handling. Seeds are also toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in full sun in very well-drained, gritty or sandy soil or potting mix; Crown of Thorns is extremely drought-tolerant and will rot quickly in wet, heavy soils or from overwatering. Euphorbia milii is a semi-succulent shrub native to Madagascar, heavily armed with long, sharp spines on the zigzagging, grayish stems — a characteristic thought to have inspired its Biblical associations with the Crown of Thorns worn by Jesus at the Crucifixion. Despite its formidable armament, Crown of Thorns is one of the most popular and widely cultivated succulent ornamentals in the world, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions where it is grown as an outdoor hedge, container specimen, and cut flower plant. The true flowers are tiny and inconspicuous, but they are surrounded by brilliantly colored, petal-like bracts in vivid scarlet, pink, orange, yellow, salmon, cream, or bicolor combinations — and the plant blooms nearly continuously in warm climates, making it one of the longest-blooming ornamentals available. Modern Thai hybrids (often marketed as 'Giant Euphorbia') produce much larger, showier bracts than the original species and are available in an extraordinary range of colors. CAUTION: The milky white latex sap is highly irritating to skin and eyes and toxic if ingested by humans or pets.

plant_note: Grow in a container in bright indirect light with high humidity (above 60%); Crystal Anthurium is strictly a tropical houseplant or greenhouse specimen in zone 9. It prefers chunky, well-aerated growing media — mix orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil at equal ratios for best results. Water when the top layer of growing medium dries, then water thoroughly. The large leaves are prone to damage from low humidity, tap water fluoride, and direct sun — protect from all three. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Crystal Anthurium needs adequate bright indirect light for vigorous leaf production but cannot tolerate direct sun, which bleaches and burns the dramatic foliage. Anthurium crystallinum is a tropical hemiepiphyte from the cloud forests of Colombia, Panama, and Peru in the Araceae family, prized by tropical plant collectors for its extraordinarily beautiful large leaves — a unique combination of velvety, deep emerald-green to blue-green surface texture and precisely delineated bright silver veins that create an intricate, crystalline pattern resembling etched glass or cut velvet. Young leaves emerge in shades of rose-pink to bronze before expanding and deepening to the mature dark green. As an epiphyte in its native cloud forest habitat, it grows anchored to tree bark in conditions of very high humidity, excellent air circulation, and bright filtered light — conditions that must be approximated in cultivation by using chunky, well-draining growing media and maintaining 60-80% relative humidity. Crystal Anthurium has become one of the most coveted of the 'velvet anthurium' group among tropical plant enthusiasts and collectors worldwide, partly for its exceptional beauty and partly because mature, well-grown specimens are genuinely rare. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

common_name: Crystal Orchid (Crested Coelogyne, Himalayan White Orchid, Snow Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light in well-draining bark medium or mounted on wood in a cool location; Coelogyne cristata is a cool-growing Himalayan orchid that requires cool, dry winters (45–55°F nights in fall and winter) to trigger its spectacular late-winter bloom. Without a cool winter rest with reduced watering, it will not bloom. Grow on a sheltered porch where winter temperatures drop to 45–55°F. Water regularly in summer growth; reduce substantially from October through February. The large clusters of pure white, fragrant flowers emerge in January–March. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in a cool location — Crystal Orchid is a cool-growing orchid that requires genuine winter cool (nights 45–55°F) to initiate its bloom and will not flower in warm indoor conditions year-round, making a cool, sheltered porch in zone 8-10 an ideal environment. Coelogyne cristata is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to the Himalayan foothills of Nepal, India (Sikkim, Darjeeling, Assam), and Bhutan at elevations of 3,000–7,000 feet in oak and rhododendron cloud forests in the Orchidaceae family. The plant produces oval, deeply furrowed pseudobulbs in dense clusters, each bearing 2 long, narrow, grass-like leaves. In late winter and early spring (January–March), the plant produces pendant clusters of 5–10 flowers on gently arching racemes — and these flowers are considered among the most beautiful white flowers of any orchid: large (3–4 inches across), pure crystalline white with a finely textured, glistening surface, and a central three-lobed lip with five prominent, raised, orange-yellow crests that give the species its name 'cristata' (crested). The flowers are lightly sweet-fragrant. On a well-established clump in full bloom with dozens of pendant white flower clusters arching from every side, C. cristata is one of the finest sights in the orchid world. Zone 8-10 gardeners with cool winters have an advantage with this species over those in warmer climates. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; do not cover seeds, as they require light for germination. Transplant outdoors in partial shade as soon as nighttime temperatures remain above freezing; in zone 9 plant September–November for fall and winter bloom, or February–March for spring bloom before summer heat arrives. Crystal Palace is one of the oldest and most widely grown lobelia selections — a compact, mounding (not trailing) form with deep violet-blue flowers and characteristically deep bronze-green foliage that distinguishes it from other blue lobelia selections. In zone 9 lobelia blooms most profusely in the cooler months (October–April); it declines and may die out in July–August heat. Use as a cool-season shade annual rather than attempting summer performance.
directions: Plant in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal in zone 9; deep shade reduces flowering — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil with good drainage; Crystal Palace is one of the most widely grown and historically important compact lobelia cultivars, producing a dense, mounding form covered with the richest, most intensely saturated deep violet-blue flowers of any annual bedding plant commonly available — a color so intense and pure that Crystal Palace lobelia has become the standard reference for deep blue in annual bedding plant design. The characteristic deep bronze-green foliage (rather than the light green of other lobelia cultivars) provides an additional visual distinction that enhances the contrast with the deep blue flowers. Lobelia erinus produces some of the most saturated true-blue color available from any annual flower — a blue so deep and vivid that it provides an invaluable cool-color contrast anchor in mixed planting compositions with yellows, oranges, reds, and whites. In zone 9 Crystal Palace lobelia is primarily a fall, winter, and spring annual — providing exceptional cool-season color October through April in shaded and partial-shade situations where other cool-season annuals (pansies, snapdragons) provide warm-color displays, while lobelia provides the deep blue counterpoint that completes a fully balanced color palette.

plant_note: Surface sow the tiny seed indoors early, as it needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow the fine seed indoors several weeks before the last frost, since it needs light to germinate. Crystal Palace forms compact mounds of rich, dark-blue flowers with bronze-tipped foliage that deepens in full sun, lovely in containers, borders, and baskets. Keep it evenly moist and provide afternoon shade where summers are hot. A light shearing midseason refreshes the plant and renews bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in early spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; cuckooflower naturalizes aggressively in damp meadows and is ideal for wet, shaded naturalistic plantings.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in early spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled light; cuckooflower (lady's smock) produces delicate, lilac-pink four-petaled flowers on slender stems in mid-spring above rosettes of pinnate, watercress-flavored leaves. It is a native of European wet meadows and stream edges and one of the most important larval host plants for orange-tip butterflies. The young leaves have a pleasant peppery, watercress-like flavor and are edible in salads. Naturalizes readily by self-seeding in consistently moist, partly shaded conditions. The double-flowered form 'Flore Pleno' is a long-lived, non-seeding selection that spreads only by offshoots.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; cuckoo flower requires consistent moisture and is ideal for rain gardens, pond margins, and wet, partially shaded spots in the garden.
directions: Direct sow in fall in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; cuckoo flower requires consistent moisture and is ideal for rain gardens, pond margins, and wet, partially shaded spots in the garden. Cardamine pratensis is a delicate, early-spring wildflower of European wet meadows and stream banks, naturalized in northeastern North America; it produces rosettes of pinnate leaves and loose racemes of small, pale lilac-pink to white, four-petaled flowers from March through May, among the earliest spring blooms to appear in moist lowland meadows. It is the primary larval host plant for the Orange-tip butterfly (Anthocharis cardamines) in Europe and is an important early nectar source for queen bumblebees and small native bees; the double-flowered cultivar 'Flore Pleno' is popular in ornamental gardens. The leaves are edible with a mild cress-like flavor, similar to watercress.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, slightly acidic, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; cucumber magnolia is the most cold-hardy of the deciduous magnolias and tolerates more cold than virtually any other Magnolia species.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — cucumber magnolia is the largest and most cold-hardy native magnolia of eastern North America and the only magnolia native to the Great Lakes region and far north, surviving to zone 3. The greenish-yellow flowers (2–4 inches) in spring are not the showiest, but the distinctive cucumber-shaped bright red-pink fruiting cones in summer that split to reveal brilliant orange-red seeds are highly ornamental. The tree develops an impressive pyramidal to broadly rounded form 50–80 feet tall — one of the largest deciduous trees in the native flora. Crucially, it is a parent in the development of numerous hybrid 'yellow magnolias' such as 'Elizabeth' (with Magnolia denudata), which have transformed the magnolia world. The tree produces a yellow pigment in the wood historically used by Native Americans. An excellent choice for large-scale landscape planting and ecological restoration in zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Culver's root is a tall, elegant native prairie perennial that establishes readily from division and rewards patience with one of the most refined flower spikes in the native plant palette.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Culver's root adapts to average garden soils with consistent moisture but performs best in rich, moist conditions and tolerates partial shade better than most tall prairie perennials. Veronicastrum virginicum is one of the most architecturally elegant native perennials of the eastern tallgrass prairie, producing tall, straight, unbranched stems with distinctive whorled leaves arranged in tiers of 3–7 and slender, candelabra-like spikes of tiny, tubular, white to pale lavender flowers from July through August; the multiple flower spikes arising from a single stem create a striking, tiered silhouette that is unlike any other native prairie plant. It is an exceptional native bee plant — the flowers support an extraordinary diversity of specialist and generalist native bees, including long-tongued bumblebees, sweat bees, and mining bees — and is consistently rated among the top native prairie perennials for pollinator value per square foot. Culver's root is slow to establish from seed but long-lived once settled; it naturalizes well in prairie restorations, tall native borders, and rain garden edges, and the dried seed heads provide winter structure and wildlife food — it should not be confused with the related non-native Veronica species.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; cup flower performs well through summer heat and is reliably self-cleaning, requiring no deadheading for continuous bloom.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; cup flower is a South American perennial grown as an annual that produces a continuous carpet of small, upward-facing, violet-blue to lavender-purple or white cup-shaped flowers with a distinctive yellow eye from spring through frost — one of the few reliably violet-blue annuals that performs well in both containers and the garden border through summer heat. Plants are neat, mounding, and self-cleaning (no deadheading required) and are excellent combined with yellow marigolds, orange zinnias, and white petunias for high-contrast container plantings. In zones 7–9 it persists as a short-lived perennial, overwintering and blooming heavily in late winter and spring. 'Purple Robe', 'Mont Blanc' (white), and 'Violet Waterfall' are popular container selections. Excellent for edging, rock gardens, and container edges.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination; cup plant can self-seed aggressively in fertile, moist soils — dead-head promptly after blooming if you wish to limit spreading in smaller gardens.
directions: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification and spring germination, or start indoors with 6–8 weeks of cold stratification; cup plant is a large, aggressive colonizer — plant it where there is space for it to naturalize, not in small, confined garden beds. Silphium perfoliatum is one of the most bold and architecturally striking native prairie plants of eastern North America, growing 5–8 feet tall with stout, square stems and distinctive opposite leaves that are perfoliate (fused at the base to form a cup around the stem) — these cups collect rainwater that provides drinking water for birds and small insects throughout summer. In mid- to late summer it produces an abundance of 2–3-inch, yellow, sunflower-like flowers with prominent yellow rays and dark centers that are magnets for native bees, goldfinches, and many butterfly species. The cup-forming leaves and tall stature make it one of the most distinctive North American prairie plants and a great choice for naturalized areas.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, sowing seeds on their edges 1/2 inch deep to avoid rotting; cup and saucer vine is a vigorous climber that needs a head start and should be set out after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seeds on their edges in moist compost and transplant to a strong trellis or arbor after last frost; cup and saucer vine is a fast-growing Mexican native that can cover 15–20 feet of trellis in a single season, producing an abundance of large, bell-shaped flowers with a prominent ribbed green 'saucer' calyx that makes each flower look like a flower-in-a-cup. The flowers open green-white, then rapidly age to deep purple, so the plant carries both colors simultaneously in an interesting contrast. They are intensely fragrant, with a sweet musky scent. Tendrils at the leaf tips cling to virtually anything with great strength. In zones 9–11 it grows as a perennial woody vine and becomes even more vigorous in its second year.

common_name: Cup of Gold Vine (Golden Chalice Vine, Hawaiin Lily)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; cup of gold vine is one of the most spectacular large-flowered vines for zone 9–12 — the enormous (6–9 inch), golden-yellow, chalice-shaped flowers with five dark-purple stripes in the throat open in late winter and spring, filling the air with a rich, vanilla-coconut fragrance; ALL parts of the plant are toxic; provide very sturdy structural support.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide extremely strong support — this vine becomes enormously heavy; CAUTION: All parts are toxic. Solandra maxima (cup of gold vine or golden chalice vine) is a rampant, large-leafed tropical climbing shrub from Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean — a member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) and one of the most impressively large-flowered ornamental vines available for zone 9–12 gardens. The flowers are exceptional: enormous (6–9 inches across), goblet or chalice-shaped, with five creamy-yellow to golden petals fused into a spectacular cup form, each petal marked with a deep-purple to chocolate-brown stripe running from the center to the tip — an elegant and unusual color combination. The flowers have a powerful, sweet, vanilla-coconut fragrance that perfumes the garden, especially in the evenings. The main bloom period is late winter through spring, when the heavy vine covers itself in the golden chalices. The thick, glossy, leathery leaves are bold and attractive when not in flower. Solandra requires an extremely strong support structure (heavy wooden pergola or steel framework) as established plants can reach 40+ feet and become enormously heavy and woody. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are poisonous; the plants produce tropane alkaloids similar to Datura and Brugmansia.

common_name: Cupani Sweet Pea (Original Fragrant Heirloom Sweet Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for late winter to spring bloom; Cupani is the original wild sweet pea from which all modern fragrant sweet pea cultivars descend, prized for its especially strong, sweet fragrance.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Cupani is the historic parent of all modern sweet pea cultivars, first sent from Sicily to England in the early 1700s by the monk Franciscus Cupani, and it remains treasured today for having by far the strongest, sweetest fragrance of any sweet pea, since much of that intense scent was gradually bred out of later, larger-flowered modern cultivars in favor of bigger blooms. The relatively small, bicolor maroon-and-violet flowers are less showy than modern hybrids but reward growers with an exceptional perfume, especially valuable for cutting and bringing indoors. In mild-winter zones like zone 9, fall sowing allows the vines to establish through the cool season for late winter and early spring bloom before the heat of summer ends the season.

common_name: Cupcake Zinnia (Ruffled Semi-Double Bicolor Cut-Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Cupcake is a semi-double, scabiosa-flowered zinnia mix known for frilly, ruffled center petals in contrasting bicolor combinations, producing unusually textured blooms distinct from flat-petaled zinnia types.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 9-12 inches. Cupcake is a scabiosa-flowered zinnia mix with a distinctive ruffled, cushion-like center of small, tightly packed petals surrounded by a single or semi-double outer ring of larger petals, giving each bloom an unusual layered, textured look often compared to a frosted cupcake. Colors run through mixed pastels and bicolors, with many blooms showing contrasting tones between the outer ring and the ruffled center. Plants are tall and productive, blooming continuously from midsummer through frost with regular deadheading or harvesting, and the unusual flower form makes Cupcake a popular novelty addition to cutting gardens and mixed bouquets alongside more traditional single- and double-flowered zinnia types. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

common_name: Cupid Peperomia (Creeping Peperomia, False Philodendron Peperomia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in well-draining, perlite-enriched potting mix; Peperomia scandens can be grown as a hanging basket plant, a vining plant on a small trellis, or a groundcover on a shaded patio. Allow the top inch to dry between waterings. The variegated form ('Variegata') has cream-margined leaves and is the most commonly available; the solid green form is less common. Prefers temperatures above 60°F. Propagate from stem cuttings. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-draining potting mix — Cupid Peperomia is tolerant of lower light conditions than many other houseplants but produces its most attractive, full growth in bright indirect conditions. Peperomia scandens is a trailing to climbing peperomia native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the Piperaceae family, one of the most widely grown of the larger-leaved peperomias for its attractive trailing habit and appealing heart-shaped foliage. The plant produces long, somewhat fleshy, scandent (vining/climbing) stems with broadly heart-shaped to broadly oval, light to medium-green, slightly glossy, succulent-textured leaves 1.5–2.5 inches long. The most commonly sold form is 'Variegata,' which has the same heart-shaped leaves but with irregular, cream to ivory margins and variegation on the green background — a soft, attractive cream-and-green combination that has made this form popular as a trailing houseplant and basket specimen. The plant's trailing stems can reach 2–4 feet in length, making it effective in hanging baskets and on shelves where the vines can drape. It can also be trained up a small trellis or moss pole, where it produces an attractive, light-textured, climbing display. The common name 'False Philodendron Peperomia' reflects the Philodendron-like appearance of the heart-shaped leaves. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in well-drained, poor to average, dry soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost; cupid's dart is short-lived in heavy or moist soils but self-sows to perpetuate itself in sandy, dry, well-drained conditions.
directions: Direct sow in dry, well-drained, poor soil in full sun; cupid's dart produces lavender-blue, papery, cornflower-like flowers on long wiry stems from early summer through fall, borne above clumps of long, narrow, grayish-green leaves. The semi-papery flowers hold their color beautifully when dried and were historically used in love potions (hence the common name). Plants are short-lived perennials in heavy, wet soils but persist for years in lean, sandy conditions and self-sow reliably. An excellent, low-maintenance border plant for dry, sunny sites that pair beautifully with ornamental grasses, eryngium, and phlomis. Divide in early spring or collect seed annually in humid climates where plants are short-lived.

common_name: Curcuma (Siam Tulip, Hidden Lily, Thai Tulip)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; curcumas emerge from dormancy late (May–June), so patience is required. In zone 8–9 mulch heavily in fall and the rhizomes typically overwinter successfully in the ground.
directions: Plant rhizomes 2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Curcuma alismatifolia (Siam tulip) is one of the most striking ornamental gingers, producing elegant upright flower spikes in late summer with a cone of showy bracts in pink, purple, or white, resembling a large tulip — hence the name. The broad, tropical foliage and exotic inflorescences make curcumas outstanding cut flowers and exceptional accent plants in the shaded summer border. They emerge late in spring from dormancy (don't panic and dig them — wait until June), grow and flower through summer, then die back to the ground in fall. The ornamental Curcumas differ from culinary turmeric (C. longa) but the two are closely related; several curcuma species have both edible and ornamental value.

plant_note: Sow seed shallowly on prepared, firm seedbed once soil temperatures consistently exceed 65°F; stolon-grown transplants establish considerably faster than seed.
directions: Broadcast seed lightly over a firm, weed-suppressed seedbed in late spring, pressing seed into the soil surface rather than covering deeply, as germination requires light and warmth. Keep the seedbed moist for three to four weeks until seedlings are visible, then transition to infrequent deep watering to encourage deep rooting. Once established, this grass spreads by stolons to fill gaps and form a cohesive turf that tolerates heavy foot traffic and prolonged drought. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization, which promotes weedy competition over the grass itself.

plant_note: Sow in fall to allow seeds to naturally stratify; germination is often slow and benefits from the full cold period.
directions: Cusp Blazing Star is a drought-tolerant native of Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico prairies and cedar brakes, producing slender stems densely clad with narrow, pointed leaves topped by vivid lavender-purple flower spikes in late summer. It is an excellent choice for hot, dry south-central gardens where many other Liatris species struggle, offering outstanding ornamental value with almost no supplemental irrigation once established. Direct sow seeds in fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun, as this species does not tolerate wet or heavy clay conditions. Plants bloom most prolifically when grown in poor to moderately fertile soil and left undisturbed to develop their deep corms over several seasons.

common_name: Custard Candy Daylily (Cream-Yellow Ruffled Daylily with Rose Eye)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Custard Candy is a popular reblooming daylily cultivar with creamy pale-yellow flowers marked by a rose-pink eye zone and matching ruffled edge, a soft companion to bolder-colored daylily cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Custard Candy bears soft, creamy pale-yellow flowers accented with a rose-pink eye zone and a matching ruffled picotee edge, a gentle, pastel color combination that pairs well with the bolder reds, purples, and oranges of many other daylily cultivars in a mixed border. It reblooms readily over a long season from early to late summer, producing a steady supply of flowers, and is exceptionally easy to grow, tolerating a wide range of soil types and requiring little care beyond routine watering. The reliable, floriferous performance and soft coloring have made it a popular choice for both dedicated daylily collectors and casual gardeners. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost for fast, easy germination.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors for an earlier display. As the name promises, cutting these old-fashioned two-to-two-and-a-half-inch blooms makes the plants flower more, producing continuously until fall frost. Space for airflow and water at the base to limit powdery mildew. Cut stems often to fill bouquets and keep the plants covered in blooms.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in moist to wet, rich soil in partial shade to full sun; cutleaf coneflower spreads aggressively by rhizomes in moist conditions and should be sited where it has room to naturalize — divide clumps every 2–3 years.
directions: Cutleaf coneflower is the tallest of all North American coneflowers — commonly reaching 6–8 feet or more in moist, rich soil — producing long-stalked, deeply lobed leaves with a coarse, tropical texture and airy sprays of bright yellow, drooping-petaled flowers with a distinctive greenish-yellow dome from July through September. Unlike most other coneflowers that require full sun and dry to average soils, cutleaf coneflower thrives in partial shade in moist bottomland conditions, making it invaluable for the sunny-to-shaded edges of rain gardens, stream banks, and moist woodland borders where a tall, dramatic native perennial is needed. The double-flowered heirloom cultivar 'Hortensia' (Golden Glow) has been grown in American gardens since the 1890s and still persists in old homesteads across the South, where it spreads freely by rhizomes through shaded gardens. It spreads vigorously and can be invasive in small spaces — site it where it can naturalize freely in large native beds or along stream margins.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; the compact cultivar 'Crispa' is lower and more spreading (18 inches tall, 3–4 feet wide) than the straight species and is the preferred selection for groundcover use. Branches root where they touch the ground, increasing spread.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; cutleaf stephanandra is a graceful, arching Japanese shrub in the rose family producing elegantly divided, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves with a refined, lacy texture that gives it its common name. In spring it produces clusters of small, white star-shaped flowers along the arching branches, attractive but secondary to the exceptional foliage. In autumn the leaves turn orange, red, and purple before dropping. The compact cultivar 'Crispa' is particularly valuable as a groundcover — growing only 18 inches tall while spreading 3–4 feet wide, with crimped, finely cut leaves that form a thick, weed-suppressing mat in shade. Branches that touch the ground root themselves (layering), helping the plant colonize large areas under trees where grass and other groundcovers fail. Among the finest shade-tolerant ornamental shrubs for the difficult zone between trees and planting beds, providing excellent weed suppression and year-round ground cover.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in deep shade under deciduous trees. Cutleaf Toothwort goes completely dormant by late spring — mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant rhizomes during summer garden work.
directions: Cutleaf Toothwort is a native spring ephemeral of moist, rich, deciduous woodlands across eastern North America, producing clusters of small white to pale pink flowers on 6–15 inch stems in early to mid-spring, shortly before the forest canopy closes and blocks the light that spring ephemerals depend on. The deeply cut, three-parted leaves with their toothlike lobes give the plant its common name and are an identification feature distinguishing it from the similar Slender Toothwort; the leaves appear in early spring, the plant flowers, sets seed, and retreats entirely underground by early summer, remaining dormant until the following winter. A member of the mustard family, the rhizomes have a mild, peppery, horseradish-like flavor and were eaten raw by various Native American peoples. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in deep shade; Cutleaf Toothwort self-seeds freely in hospitable woodland gardens and gradually colonizes the forest floor.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 3 inches apart in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moisture-retentive soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; narcissus cyclamineus is one of the earliest-blooming daffodil species and performs best in a sheltered position in partial shade with reliably moist, leafy soil — woodland edges, moist grass, and light shade under deciduous trees are ideal. Avoid hot, dry, or exposed sites.
