directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in fall for early spring bloom; Narcissus cyclamineus is one of the most distinctive and botanically fascinating of all daffodil species — a diminutive, early-blooming miniature whose most striking feature is its strongly reflexed perianth segments, swept sharply backward like the petals of a cyclamen flower, exposing a disproportionately long, narrow, tubular golden trumpet and giving the flower a dynamic, wind-blown appearance unlike any other narcissus. It is one of the earliest daffodils to bloom, often flowering in late February or early March before many larger daffodils have emerged. This species is the parent of many of the most beloved small daffodil hybrids, including 'Tête-à-tête', 'February Gold', and 'Jack Snipe', and it naturalizes beautifully in moist grass and light woodland shade, increasing steadily over time to form cheerful early-spring colonies. Native to northwest Spain and Portugal, it is less tolerant of dry summer conditions than most daffodils and performs best where the soil retains some moisture year-round.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or start transplants after cold stratification in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately dry, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cylindric blazing star demands exceptionally sharp drainage and will rot in wet, clay soils.
directions: Direct sow in fall or start transplants after cold stratification in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately dry, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; cylindric blazing star demands exceptionally sharp drainage and will rot in wet, clay soils. Liatris cylindracea is the smallest and most delicate-looking liatris, native to dry, open, rocky prairies and limestone glades of the Great Lakes region and northeastern prairies; it produces small, cylindrical (rather than spherical) flower heads in bright rose-purple from July through August on slender stems, blooming from the top down in the characteristic liatris fashion. An outstanding choice for dry rock gardens, gravel borders, and xeriscape gardens in the northern portion of its range; it is important for specialist native bees and migrating monarch butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in dry, rocky, sandy, or gravelly, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Cylindrical Blazingstar is among the most drought-tolerant of all blazingstars and specifically adapted to calcareous or gravelly prairie and alvar soils.
directions: Cylindrical Blazingstar is a compact, drought-tolerant native perennial of dry prairies, rocky outcrops, calcareous alvars, and gravelly open woodlands of the Great Lakes region and Midwest, producing spikes of few, widely spaced, cylindrical purple flower heads on stiff, slender stems in July and August that are prized for cut flowers and dried arrangements as well as for their wildlife value. Notably more drought-tolerant than most blazingstars and specifically adapted to thin, rocky, calcareous or gravelly soils of limestone outcrops and dry prairie remnants, Cylindrical Blazingstar is an outstanding choice for rock gardens, xeriscapes, and dry native plant gardens across the northern United States. The compact size and long vase life of the cut flowers make it one of the most popular Liatris species among native plant enthusiasts and cut flower gardeners. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in rocky, sandy, or gravelly, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; established corms are extremely long-lived and slowly form clumps.

plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight in warm water before direct sowing after last frost in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; cypress vine self-seeds prolifically in warm climates and can become invasive — deadhead if naturalization is not desired.
directions: Nick or soak seeds overnight in warm water before direct sowing after last frost in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; cypress vine self-seeds prolifically in warm climates and can become invasive — deadhead if naturalization is not desired. Ipomoea quamoclit is a delicate, fast-growing annual vine from tropical America with extraordinarily fine, feathery, deeply pinnate leaves resembling cypress foliage and a long succession of small (1-inch), brilliant scarlet, star-shaped flowers with a white eye from summer through frost that are irresistible to ruby-throated hummingbirds. In zone 9–10 it self-seeds vigorously and can naturalize along fences and into disturbed areas; it has been listed as invasive in some southeastern states, so monitor seedling spread and remove volunteers if they escape the garden area. An outstanding container or trellis plant for attracting hummingbirds.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; allow ample space — D.D. Blanchard grows into a large, pyramidal tree 30–50 feet tall.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; D.D. Blanchard is one of the most magnificent Southern magnolia cultivars — distinguished by exceptionally dark, glossy, almost black-green upper leaf surfaces with a rich, coppery-orange to russet-brown underside that is among the most vivid and attractive of any Southern magnolia selection. The underside color is a significant ornamental feature: when a breeze stirs the branches, the leaves momentarily reveal their orange-bronze undersides, creating a shimmering two-tone effect that no other tree quite replicates. D.D. Blanchard is a large tree with a naturally pyramidal form, growing 30–50 feet tall with a 20–30 foot spread — a specimen tree with an imposing, stately presence appropriate for large residential landscapes and commercial settings. The giant, creamy-white, intensely fragrant flowers (8–12 inches across) bloom from May through July in zone 9, with intermittent bloom through summer. Like all Southern magnolia cultivars, D.D. Blanchard produces large, cone-like fruits with brilliant red seeds that are consumed by birds and wildlife. An outstanding selection for the Gulf South where the tree is most at home — performing magnificently in zone 8–10 heat and humidity.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 4–8 weeks before the ground freezes, for spring bloom.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall at a depth of 3 times the bulb's height (typically 6–8 in) in well-drained soil with the pointed end up. Daffodils naturalize readily and multiply over time; deer and rodents avoid them because the bulbs are mildly toxic. Allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally — at least 6 weeks — so the bulb can store energy for next year's bloom. Divide congested clumps every 5–7 years when flowering diminishes.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring after last frost in lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; in zones 9–11 it self-sows as a short-lived perennial. Dahlberg daisy performs best in hot, dry conditions and declines in heat with excessive moisture. Excellent for filling cracks and edges in hot, dry, sunny spots.
directions: Sow in lean, well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; Dahlberg daisy is a Texas native annual (perennial in zones 9–11) producing exceptionally fine-textured, thread-like, aromatic foliage — almost needle-like and strongly fragrant when crushed — covered throughout the warm season with masses of tiny, bright golden-yellow daisy flowers, each only 1/2 inch across but produced in such uncountable profusion that the plant appears to be a cushion of living gold. The extremely fine foliage texture combined with the continuous small-scale flower display creates an effect unlike any other — a mounding, golden, aromatic, lacy confection that is outstanding for edging, filling containers, and naturalizing in hot, dry, sandy situations. A Texas Hill Country native, it thrives in the exact difficult conditions — poor, dry, alkaline, rocky soil in baking summer sun — that defeat most garden plants. Self-sows freely to maintain colonies in appropriate climates. The foliage releases a pleasant, chamomile-like herbal fragrance when brushed.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 60°F.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4–6 in deep with the eye pointing up after the last frost when soil reaches 60°F; set a stake at planting time to avoid spearing the tuber later. Pinch the growing tip when plants are 12 in tall to encourage branching and more flowers. In zones below 8, dig tubers after the first killing frost, cure them for a week, then store in slightly damp peat at 40–50°F through winter. Disbudding side buds around the main bud produces exhibition-quality blooms.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; dahoon holly grows naturally in swamps, stream banks, and wet flatwoods and tolerates standing water and high water tables better than any other native holly except possumhaw. Plant male and female plants for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — dahoon holly is one of the most beautiful and ecologically important native trees of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, growing naturally in the understory of bottomland swamps, cypress heads, wet pine flatwoods, and stream banks from Virginia to Texas. Female plants (a male nearby is needed for pollination) produce abundant clusters of small, brilliant red to orange-red berries that persist from fall through winter, providing critical food for robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and dozens of other fruit-eating birds during winter when food is scarce. The narrow, elliptic, dark evergreen leaves are attractive year-round. It tolerates flooding and wet soils better than almost any other tree in cultivation and is outstanding for rain gardens, wet low spots, pond margins, and other challenging wet sites in zone 7–11. An excellent winter-interest tree for the shaded, wet areas of Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Daikagura is a classic Japanese camellia cultivar producing very large, peony-form flowers boldly streaked and mottled in rose-red and white, one of the showiest variegated camellia forms.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Daikagura is a centuries-old Japanese camellia cultivar prized for exceptionally large, formal peony-form flowers, densely packed with irregularly waved and twisted petals boldly streaked and mottled in rose-red over a white background, a strikingly variegated pattern unique to each bloom. The dramatic size and coloring make individual flowers a focal point in the winter garden, and the plant's dense, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage provides year-round structure. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it blooms in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9, when little else is in flower. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, which scorches the glossy leaves, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, deep soil in full sun; daimyo oak grows naturally in mountain forests and forest edges of China, Korea, and Japan, producing the largest leaves of any oak — up to 18 inches long — that create a dramatic, bold-textured specimen effect in the landscape.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, deep soil in full sun; daimyo oak (emperor oak) is the boldest-textured oak in the world, producing enormous, deeply lobed, paddle-shaped leaves that can reach 18 inches long and 10 inches wide — the largest leaves of any temperate-zone oak, creating a strikingly coarse, tropical-looking canopy texture completely unlike the small-leaved English oak. Native to mountain forests of China, Korea, and Japan, it is a relatively small to medium oak suitable for residential gardens where its dramatic foliage creates a bold statement. The leaves turn bronze to red-brown in fall and often persist on the tree into early winter before dropping (marcescent). Relatively slow-growing compared to other oaks. The species is the host plant for the silkworm Antheraea yamamai (the Japanese oak silkworm) which produces golden 'tussah' silk. An outstanding specimen tree for gardens where dramatic large-leaved texture is desired.

common_name: Dainty Red and Yellow Lady's Purse
plant_note: Surface sow the fine seed, which needs light; keep cool and evenly moist.
directions: Surface sow the very fine seed indoors, since it needs light and cool conditions to germinate well. This compact, bushy plant produces one-to-two-inch inflated, slipper-shaped blooms in sunny yellow marked with striking red blotches. It performs beautifully cascading from containers, hanging baskets, and garden edges. Keep it consistently moist, give it part shade in warm climates, and protect it from intense heat.

plant_note: Surface sow the fine seed, which needs light; keep cool and evenly moist.
directions: Surface sow the tiny seed indoors, giving it light and cool temperatures for reliable germination. This charming, compact plant bears one-to-two-inch slipper-shaped blooms in sunny yellow dusted with delicate red spots for a hand-painted effect. It shines in containers, hanging baskets, and along garden edges. Keep the soil evenly moist and provide part shade and protection from heat in warm regions.

common_name: Dallas Blues Switchgrass (Extra-Wide-Blade Powder-Blue Native Switchgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun; Dallas Blues has unusually wide, powder-blue leaf blades compared to most switchgrass cultivars, giving it a bolder, more substantial texture in the border.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils. Dallas Blues stands out among switchgrass cultivars for its unusually broad, powder-blue leaf blades, giving it a bolder, coarser texture than the fine-bladed straight species, topped in late summer by large, airy, pinkish flower panicles that age to a warm tan and persist through winter. Like other switchgrass cultivars it is a durable, low-maintenance native grass that tolerates heat, drought, and periodic flooding with equal ease, providing valuable structure, seed for birds, and habitat for beneficial insects. Cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; damianita demands sharp drainage above all else and rots quickly in heavy clay or any soil that stays wet, especially through winter.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; among the most heat- and drought-tolerant native shrublets available, thriving in conditions that kill most perennials outright, but requires perfect drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained gardens. Chrysactinia mexicana (damianita) is a small, rounded, woody-based evergreen shrublet native to the limestone hills and rocky slopes of the Trans-Pecos, west Texas, and northern Mexico, with fine, needle-like, resinous, aromatic foliage that releases a pungent, camphor-like scent when brushed or crushed. From spring through fall, and especially heavily after rain, the plant is smothered in small, bright golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers that draw bees and butterflies and make a vivid mounded splash of color against its dark, textured foliage. Its extreme drought and heat tolerance make it a staple of xeriscape and rock garden design across the drier parts of Texas and the Southwest, and it also tolerates the humidity of the Gulf South reasonably well provided the drainage is sharp. An excellent low-water accent plant for a sunny rock garden or gravel bed, zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant small rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in spring after soil warms to 70°F in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; dancing ladies ginger dies back to the ground each winter in zones 8–9 but reliably re-emerges from the rhizome in spring. Excellent in containers, shade gardens, and as a companion to begonias, caladiums, and ferns.
directions: Plant small rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in spring after soil warms to 70°F in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Globba winitii is a charming, small Thai ginger producing arching, pendant inflorescences with decorative pink to purple bracts and tiny, vivid yellow flowers that dangle in a way that resembles a line of dancing figures, earning its delightful common name; it is one of the finest small gingers for shaded tropical and subtropical gardens. In late summer and fall the bracts are replaced by tiny bulbils that drop to the ground and produce new plants, gradually naturalizing the planting. Dancing ladies ginger dies back to the ground each winter in zones 8–9 but reliably re-emerges from the rhizome in spring. Excellent in containers, shade gardens, and as a companion to begonias, caladiums, and ferns.

common_name: Dancing Ladies Ginger (Nodding Globba, Marantina Globba, Jewel Globba)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Globba marantina cannot tolerate frost but is one of the hardier Globba species, surviving rhizome temperatures to approximately 28°F with heavy mulch in zone 9. The plant goes dormant in winter — leaves die back and rhizomes rest until spring warmth. Propagate by dividing rhizomes in spring or from bulbils (small round propagules) that form in the inflorescence instead of seeds. The arching flower stems need shade to produce their most vivid color.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Dancing Ladies Ginger is among the most shade-tolerant of the ornamental gingers and produces its most delicate and beautiful flower display in the filtered light under large trees. Globba marantina is a small, clump-forming, deciduous ginger native to Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Vietnam, Indonesia) in the family Zingiberaceae, one of approximately 100 Globba species now popular in the ornamental ginger world for their delicate, dancing flower display. The plant produces stems 18–36 inches tall of broad, soft, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive purple blush on the undersides. In summer and fall, arching flower stalks emerge from the leaf tips bearing loosely branched inflorescences of remarkable, pendant, dancing flowers: each individual flower is about an inch long with reflexed, purple-maroon to burgundy bracts and small yellow petals that hang and dangle from thin pedicels in the slightest air movement — the massed, dancing effect of dozens of tiny, pendant purple-and-yellow flowers on arching stems is the quality that earned the genus the name 'Dancing Ladies Ginger.' A distinctive feature of Globba is the replacement of most flowers by small, round, fleshy bulbils — mini-propagules that drop and sprout new plants, forming colonies over time. One of the finest shade-tolerant gingers for zone 9 Gulf Coast woodland gardens.

common_name: Dancing Lady Orchid (Golden Shower Orchid, Tiger Orchid, Sphacelatum)
plant_note: Grow in a slatted pot or basket with coarse bark media in bright indirect to filtered direct light; Oncidium sphacelatum is one of the more tolerant Oncidiums, adapting to a wider range of conditions than many spray orchids. In zone 9, it can grow on a shaded porch in a hanging basket from spring through fall, then moved indoors in winter. The plant blooms from pseudobulbs of the previous season — maintain 3+ mature pseudobulbs for reliable blooming. Water regularly while in growth, reduce in winter rest. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Dancing Lady Orchid produces its best blooms with 4–6 hours of bright filtered light and will not bloom reliably in dim indoor conditions. Oncidium sphacelatum is a large, clump-forming, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Belize, Venezuela, and Colombia, widely distributed in highland tropical forests from sea level to 5,000+ feet. It is one of the largest commonly grown Oncidiums and produces some of the most spectacular spray-type orchid inflorescences available: long, arching, multi-branched panicles 3–5 feet in length carrying hundreds of individual flowers in vivid yellow and chestnut-brown — the small (half-inch to 1-inch) flowers have brown-barred petals and a dominant, bright yellow, flared lip that gives dancing lady orchids their name (the yellow lip resembles the skirt of a dancer twirling in a yellow dress with brown accents). A well-established plant in full bloom with 2–3 long, branching inflorescences simultaneously open is one of the most dramatic of all orchid displays. The plant is a prolific grower that divides readily, forming large clumps. Oncidium sphacelatum has been used extensively in producing the Oncidium intergeneric hybrids now widely sold as potted orchids. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Direct sow, as this ornamental carrot resents transplanting.
directions: Direct sow where plants are to grow, since this ornamental carrot dislikes root disturbance. Also called false Queen Anne's lace, Dara adds soft, airy, lacy umbels to the garden and to fresh or dried arrangements without the aggressiveness of the true species. It is fairly drought tolerant once established, so water moderately. Cut stems when the umbels are freshly open for the longest vase life.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Darcy's sage is hardier than most scarlet salvias and can survive brief dips to about 20 degrees F when established. In zones 8-10 it grows as a long-lived perennial subshrub. Prune back by one-third in early spring to maintain shape and encourage vigorous new growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Darcy's sage is a compact Mexican native from the Sierra Madre Oriental of Nuevo Leon and Coahuila producing an exceptionally long season of brilliant, clear scarlet-red flowers — a deeper, truer red than the salmon-to-pink range of most Salvia greggii cultivars — from spring through frost. The flowers are two-lipped and slightly larger than those of autumn sage, making it particularly effective for hummingbirds. Native to dry, rocky, limestone slopes at 8,000-10,000 feet elevation, it is adapted to hot, dry, alkaline conditions and proves drought-tolerant once established. It was recently discovered by plant explorers and introduced to cultivation in the 1990s, and its combination of true scarlet color, extended bloom season, and drought tolerance has made it a favorite in the heat-tolerant perennial border. Exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds throughout its very long bloom period from April through October in mild climates.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Fuchsia grows as a perennial woody shrub in zones 10–11 and as a season-long annual in zones 3–9. In zone 9 it often survives mild winters — cut back in early spring and the woody base regrows. Hanging baskets require daily watering in summer heat; afternoon shade prevents wilting. Spent flowers drop cleanly, so deadheading is not required for continued bloom.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil or high-quality potting mix in containers; Dark Eyes is one of the most recognizable and widely grown fuchsia cultivars, distinguished by its richly colored double flowers with vivid red-pink sepals spreading backward from a full, rounded, deep violet-purple corolla — a classic fuchsia color combination that is simultaneously jewel-toned and reminiscent of tropical birds in flight. The pendant flowers are borne continuously throughout the growing season on trailing to semi-upright stems that make Dark Eyes ideal for hanging baskets, window boxes, and elevated container positions where the downward-facing flowers are viewed at eye level or from below. Fuchsia flowers are among the most reliably shade-tolerant of all flowering annuals, performing in deep shade conditions where most flowering plants fail to bloom adequately. Hummingbirds are extremely attracted to fuchsia flowers and will visit frequently, making Dark Eyes a reliable hummingbird garden plant in any shaded position.

common_name: Darwin's Orchid (Star of Bethlehem Orchid, Comet Orchid, Christmas Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a slatted basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to filtered morning sun; Angraecum sesquipedale blooms in winter (November–January), triggered by seasonal temperature drops to 55–60°F at night — this natural temperature fluctuation is essential for inducing bloom. Protect from temperatures below 50°F. In zone 9, grow on a shaded porch in a basket from spring through early fall, then move inside to a bright, cool windowsill for the winter bloom period. Water regularly in growth; reduce slightly in winter. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle filtered light in a well-draining bark medium or mounted on cork — Darwin's Orchid grows best in bright, diffuse light similar to dappled forest canopy and will not bloom reliably in dim interior conditions. Angraecum sesquipedale is a large, monopodial epiphytic orchid endemic to Madagascar in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most historically significant plants in all of evolutionary biology — the subject of Charles Darwin's famous 1862 prediction. Examining dried herbarium specimens of A. sesquipedale with their extraordinary flower structure — large (5-inch), waxy, pure white, six-pointed, star-shaped flowers with a single, enormously elongated, thin, whip-like nectar spur hanging below the flower to a length of 11–13 inches — Darwin proposed in his book 'Fertilisation of Orchids' that somewhere in Madagascar, an undiscovered moth must exist with a proboscis long enough to reach the nectar at the base of the spur. Critics ridiculed the prediction. In 1903, 21 years after Darwin's death, a subspecies of the hawk moth Xanthopan morganii was discovered in Madagascar with a proboscis of exactly the predicted length — the confirmation of a prediction from evolutionary logic. The flowers are intensely fragrant at night, attracting their hawk moth pollinators. A large, impressive orchid with stunning winter flowers and extraordinary scientific heritage. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; space at least 18 inches apart — good air circulation is essential to minimize powdery mildew, the primary phlox disease in humid climates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation; David was named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2002 and is widely considered the best white tall garden phlox cultivar ever introduced — selected by David Benner of New Hope, Pennsylvania, specifically for outstanding resistance to powdery mildew, the devastating fungal disease that disfigures most Phlox paniculata cultivars by midsummer in humid climates. Most phlox cultivars develop severe powdery mildew by July or August in the East and Gulf South — their leaves turn white with fungal coating that persists through the rest of the season. David's powdery mildew resistance is dramatically superior to older cultivars, maintaining clean, attractive dark-green foliage well into fall. The large, fragrant, pure white flower heads (panicles) are produced from July through September in zone 8, making it one of the finest long-season white perennials. The intensely fragrant flowers are outstanding for cutting and garden performance. In zone 9, tall garden phlox is not reliably perennial — it performs best as a short-lived perennial in zone 8 and colder. In zone 9's intense summer heat, phlox often declines, but with afternoon shade and consistent moisture it can be maintained for 2–3 years.

common_name: David Verity Cuphea (Prolific Orange-Red Tubular Hummingbird Annual for Summer Heat)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; David Verity is a sterile hybrid that does not set seed — propagated vegetatively by cuttings and sold only as container plants rather than seeds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; David Verity Cuphea is one of the most valuable and consistent hummingbird-attracting annuals for Gulf South summer gardens — a hybrid Cuphea (likely Cuphea ignea x C. llavea parentage) that produces an extraordinary abundance of small, tubular, bright orange-red flowers tipped with purple-black from spring through hard frost, creating a continuous nectar source that ruby-throated hummingbirds and butterflies find irresistible. The small, tubular flower form is precisely calibrated for hummingbird bill access — each flower produces concentrated nectar that makes these plants extremely effective hummingbird magnets in late summer and fall when migrating hummingbirds are actively fueling up for their Gulf of Mexico crossing. The flowers are produced so prolifically and continuously that established plants rarely appear to be between bloom flushes — the orange-red and black color combination creates a vivid display through the longest, hottest Gulf South summer days. 'David Verity' is sterile and propagated by cuttings, making it available only as nursery transplants. The compact, mounding to slightly spreading habit makes it excellent for container culture (where it can be overwintered as a tender perennial) and for summer border edge plantings. In zone 9, it grows as a warm-season annual from spring transplanting through first frost. In zone 10–12, it may survive winter as a subshrub. No deadheading required — spent flowers drop cleanly and new buds open continuously.

plant_note: Plant a young tree in spring after the ground has thawed, in deep moist soil with room to grow large.
directions: Dawn redwood is a fast-growing deciduous conifer often called a living fossil, prized for feathery fern-like foliage that turns coppery orange before dropping in fall. Give it full sun and consistently moist, well-drained soil; it tolerates wet sites and even seasonal flooding better than most conifers. Choose a location with abundant vertical and horizontal space, as mature trees reach 70 to 100 feet with a broad conical form. Water deeply during establishment and through dry spells for the first few seasons. It needs no pruning to develop its naturally elegant shape.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Day Dreamer is a waterlily-form dahlia bearing soft blooms blending apricot, pink, and buttercream on productive plants. Plant tubers horizontally about 4 to 6 inches deep once soil warms, positioning the eye upward, and hold off watering until sprouts emerge to prevent rot. Pinch the growing tip when plants reach about a foot to encourage bushier growth and more blooms. Stake or corral tall stems and cut flowers regularly to keep the plant producing. In zones colder than 8, lift and store the tubers in a cool, dry place over winter.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in spring or fall; set crowns just 1 in below soil level.
directions: Plant fans with the crown about 1 in deep, spreading roots outward over a small mound of soil in the hole. Water thoroughly after planting and keep consistently moist the first season. Divide overcrowded clumps every 4–5 years in early spring or late summer when bloom quality declines. Removing spent scapes after all buds have opened keeps the planting tidy.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seed for a few weeks to improve germination of this perennial.
directions: Cold-stratify the seed for a few weeks and start indoors, since this perennial germinates better after a chill. Dazzler Blend suits any garden and especially rarely watered spots, offering colorful, pollinator-friendly blooms and excellent drought tolerance once established. Grow it in full sun with lean, sharply drained soil, making it a fine choice for rock gardens. Deadhead to tidy plants and encourage additional bloom.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in mild climates (zones 7–10) or in early spring after danger of hard frost has passed in colder zones.
directions: Soak the small, irregular corms in water for 4–6 hours before planting; set them about 2 in deep with the pointed side down (or on their side if unsure). Anemones prefer cool, well-drained soil and perform best where winters are mild and springs are long and cool. Poppy-like blooms in vivid red, blue, purple, white, and bicolors appear over a 6–8 week period in late winter to spring. In cold climates treat as an annual, planting corms in spring for early summer color.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; not suitable for zone 9 and warmer where summer heat causes crown rot.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; dead nettle is one of the most effective and ornamental shade groundcovers for zones 3–8, valued for its silvery-marked, heart-shaped leaves that brighten dark corners throughout the growing season and its whorls of pink or white flowers in late spring and early summer. It is a rapid spreader that forms a dense, weed-suppressing carpet and is easy to propagate by stem cuttings or division. Unlike the weedy annual red dead nettle (L. purpureum), this perennial species is non-invasive and stays where it is planted. Named cultivars like 'White Nancy' (white flowers, heavily silver leaves), 'Beacon Silver', and 'Purple Dragon' are widely available. In the South, plant in a cool, shaded spot and provide afternoon shade from heat; it goes dormant and may die back in high summer in zone 8.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Debutante is best planted in fall in zone 9 so the roots establish during the cool season before facing summer heat — avoid planting in summer.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Debutante is one of the most beloved and widely grown Camellia japonica cultivars — a long-cultivated Southern garden classic producing early to mid-season (December through February in zone 9) flowers in a gorgeous soft light-pink peony form with rows of neatly layered petals that create a formal, rose-like, fully double flower of exceptional elegance. The soft light-pink color — a warm blush to light rose — makes Debutante one of the most feminine and refined camellias for traditional Southern landscape and cut-flower use. The upright, vigorous growth to 6–12 feet tall with dense, glossy dark-green evergreen foliage makes it an outstanding foundation shrub and informal hedge plant for shaded or partially shaded locations. Debutante is known for reliable, abundant bloom production even in zone 9's mild winters — bloom quality does not depend on cold temperatures to trigger flower set. In zone 9, Debutante typically begins blooming in late November and continues through February, often with peak bloom in January. Plant in partial shade — morning sun is acceptable but afternoon shade is essential in zone 9 to prevent sun scorch of the glossy leaves. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil conditions camellias require.

plant_note: Start indoors for earlier bloom; tubers can be lifted and stored over winter.
directions: Start seed indoors about a month before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once weather settles. This very tall blend delivers eye-popping colors on long, sturdy stems, blooming about 90 days from sowing and returning year after year in mild zones. Stake the tall plants and plant them toward the back of the border. Dig and store the tubers over winter in colder climates to replant the following spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade; deer fern requires strongly acidic soil and consistent moisture — it declines in neutral or alkaline conditions. It is best suited to the Pacific Coast, Pacific Northwest, and mild Atlantic coastal gardens with cool summers.
directions: Plant in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade; deer fern is one of the most distinctive of all woodland ferns, producing two very different types of fronds simultaneously from the central crown: outer, spreading, dark-green sterile fronds that lie nearly flat to the ground, and inner, erect, narrowly pinnate fertile fronds that stand upright with narrow, blade-like pinnae bearing the spore-producing sori on their undersides. This dramatic dimorphism makes it immediately recognizable in the forest. It is a characteristic plant of the cool, moist, acidic coniferous and mixed forests of the Pacific Northwest (where it is extremely common) and also occurs in Atlantic coastal forests and in Europe, where it was traditionally fed to deer (hence the common name). It requires cool, humid conditions and consistently moist, strongly acidic soil to thrive — it is less suited to hot, dry interior gardens. An outstanding structural fern for the cool, shaded woodland garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline soil in full sun; deer grass grows naturally in dry washes, chaparral margins, oak woodland edges, and desert grasslands of the southwestern US and Baja California.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; deer grass is a large, dense, mounding native grass of the southwestern US, from California to New Mexico and Texas, growing naturally in dry washes, canyon slopes, and the margins of chaparral and oak woodland. The plant forms an attractive, tight dome of fine-textured, grey-green to blue-green foliage that remains evergreen in mild climates. In summer and fall, long, straight, narrow flower spikes rise well above the foliage like thin wands, creating an architectural effect quite different from the plumed muhly grasses. Extremely drought and heat tolerant — one of the toughest ornamental grasses for hot, dry, western gardens. Deer resistant (as the name implies) and fire-adapted. Widely used in California, Arizona, and Texas in low-water, heat-tolerant landscaping. Division of mature clumps every 3–4 years maintains vigor.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown plants into dry, sandy, acidic soil in spring after the last frost has passed and soil has begun to warm.
directions: Start seeds indoors in fall or winter in a sandy, acidic seed-starting mix and grow on in containers for transplanting the following spring into dry, lean, acidic sandy soil in full sun. This aromatic native perennial of longleaf pine savannas forms a striking basal rosette of broad, strap-like leaves that release a pleasant vanilla-like fragrance when dried, owing to the presence of coumarin, and historically the leaves were used as flavoring and fragrance. From August through October, slender, upright stems rise to 18-36 inches and bear flat-topped or rounded clusters of fluffy, lavender-pink composite flower heads that attract a wide variety of native bees, butterflies, and skippers. Once established in well-drained, acidic, sandy soil, it is reliably drought-tolerant and an excellent choice for longleaf pine savanna restoration or native pollinator gardens in the Southeast.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, partly shaded, humus-rich soil; deertongue grass naturalizes readily once established and spreads slowly by seed without becoming invasive. It can also be divided in spring.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to light shade; deertongue grass is one of the very few native ornamental grasses that thrives in shade, making it a valuable component of naturalized woodland gardens where most grasses fail. The broad, lance-shaped leaves — much wider than typical grass blades — give the plant a lush, tropical appearance that contrasts effectively with finer-textured shade plants. The small flowers and seeds on branching heads ripen in midsummer and provide food for numerous sparrows and other seed-eating birds. Deer browse the succulent foliage (which explains the common name), so it may require protection in deer-heavy areas. Excellent for naturalizing along shaded stream banks, in rain gardens with occasional shade, and in moist woodland edge conditions.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; fresh seed germinates best and benefits from 1–2 weeks of cold stratification.
directions: Use fresh seed — viability drops quickly in storage — and cold-stratify for 1–2 weeks before sowing at 60–70°F for best germination. Transplant after the last frost into rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and stake early, as the tall spikes are highly susceptible to wind damage. Cut flower spikes back to basal foliage after the first bloom to encourage a second, smaller flush in late summer. All parts of the plant are toxic; all plant contact should be followed by hand washing.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow water or wet, slightly acidic to neutral, organic-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; delta arrowhead grows naturally in the sluggish backwaters and river margins of the Mississippi River Delta and Gulf Coastal Plain wetlands.
directions: Plant in shallow water (0–8 inches deep) or consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral, organic-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; delta arrowhead is a robust native aquatic of the lower Mississippi River basin and Gulf Coastal Plain river systems, producing broad, somewhat ovate to broadly arrow-shaped leaves and the characteristic three-petaled white flowers of arrowheads. The plant is valuable in slow-moving water and constructed wetlands, where its dense growth helps stabilize banks, provides fish habitat structure, and produces corms and seeds consumed by waterfowl. An important plant for biological water quality improvement (phytoremediation) in constructed wetlands processing agricultural runoff. In the ornamental pond or rain garden, it creates a bold, native aquatic presence with seasonal white flowers.

common_name: Delta Dawn Heuchera (Delta Dawn Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Delta Dawn is a Heuchera villosa hybrid with excellent heat and humidity tolerance, making it among the best heucheras for the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and zone 8–9 gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Delta Dawn heuchera is a standout among warm-climate coral bells — a Heuchera villosa hybrid that produces large, broad leaves in a striking combination of cherry-red to rose-pink overtones atop a dark purple-black base, giving an almost sunset or tie-dye appearance that changes from season to season. The H. villosa heritage provides the critical adaptation to heat and humidity that allows this cultivar to survive Gulf Coast summers where many northern-bred heucheras fail. The large, thick-textured leaves are characteristic of villosa parentage and hold up better to heavy afternoon sun and humidity than the thinner-leafed cultivars. White to cream flowers appear in summer. In zone 8–9, plant in partial shade with afternoon protection, ensure excellent drainage, and apply 2 inches of organic mulch around (but not on) the crown; the crown must remain at or slightly above soil level to prevent rot.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in deep shade; delta maidenhair requires consistently moist (never waterlogged) soil, high humidity, and shelter from wind and afternoon sun — dry air, cold drafts, and bright direct light will cause fronds to brown and die back rapidly.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade with high humidity — delta maidenhair is the most widely grown maidenhair fern, celebrated for its extraordinary, lacey delicacy: tiny, fan-shaped, bright green leaflets arranged in sprays on impossibly fine, wiry black stems that seem to float the foliage in mid-air. The fronds tremble with the slightest air movement, giving the plant an ethereal, shimmering quality. It demands consistent moisture, high humidity, and shelter from drying winds — the most common failure is under-watering or low humidity, which causes instant browning. Outdoors it is suitable only in zone 10–12 in sheltered, shaded, humid locations; in zone 8–9 it is an outstanding houseplant and covered-patio container plant. The classic indoor maidenhair; cultivars like 'Fragrantissimum', 'Fritz Lüthii', and 'Brilliant Else' are among the most refined forms. Mist frequently, water consistently, and keep away from heating vents and air conditioning.

plant_note: Plant corms or container plants in moist, well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in spring; dense blazing star tolerates clay and periodic wet feet better than most prairie plants and performs reliably in heavy southern soils.
directions: Plant corms or container plants in moist, well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; dense blazing star is the most popular and adaptable liatris species, producing grass-like clumps of foliage topped with striking, bottlebrush-like spikes of fluffy, bright magenta-purple flowers from mid-summer into fall — uniquely, the flowers open from the top of the spike downward (most spikes open bottom-to-top), creating a dynamic visual effect as the bloom progresses. Monarch butterflies use it as a critical nectaring and migration staging plant. Goldfinches eat the seeds through winter. The corms multiply over time to form large clumps that can be divided every 3–4 years in spring. Tolerates clay and seasonal flooding better than most prairie plants. 'Kobold' (compact, 24 inches, rich color) and 'Alba' (white) are fine cultivar selections.

plant_note: Fall sowing provides the cold stratification the seed needs; spring sowing also works after chilling.
directions: This native prairie perennial sends up tall, upright spikes of vivid purple bottlebrush flowers that bloom from the top down. Seeds germinate best after a cold period, so sow outdoors in fall or cold-stratify before spring sowing. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, where the plants are drought tolerant once established and popular with butterflies. The long-lasting spikes make excellent fresh or dried cut flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; dense St. John's wort grows naturally in moist to wet soils at stream banks, pond margins, and in seasonally wet meadows. It tolerates periodic flooding better than most Hypericum species.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; dense St. John's wort is a native shrubby Hypericum of moist streambanks, pond margins, and wet woodland edges across the eastern United States. It produces abundant clusters of small, bright yellow flowers in summer that attract specialized pollen-collecting bees. Unlike the herbaceous St. John's worts used medicinally, this is a woody, multi-stemmed shrub that can reach 6 feet, providing structure in the wet garden. The tiny, linear leaves are produced in dense, crowded clusters along the stems — giving the species its name. It tolerates seasonal flooding and grows naturally in the same wet habitats as cardinal flower, swamp milkweed, and ironweed. An excellent shrub for rain gardens, bioswales, and wet meadow edges where it provides summer blooms and serves as a nectar source for native bees.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; deodar cedar is the most heat-tolerant of the true cedars and the standard large ornamental conifer of the American South and West. Excellent drainage is essential — will not survive in wet, poorly drained soils.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; deodar cedar is the standard large landscape conifer of the American South, widely planted as a specimen and shade tree across the Southeast and Pacific Coast in zones 7–9. The graceful, weeping branch tips and the soft, blue-green needles in clusters of 20–30 create one of the most elegant of all large conifers — the drooping leading shoot and pendulous branch tips are immediately distinctive. Native to the western Himalayas of Pakistan, Afghanistan, and India, where it is a sacred tree — 'deodar' means 'divine tree' in Sanskrit. Grows rapidly (2–4 feet per year) in good conditions. Makes an outstanding specimen for large lawns where it develops its full, sweeping canopy. The golden-yellow cultivar 'Gold Cone' is striking. More heat-tolerant than the other true cedars, making it the best choice for the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun; Desdemona is a classic Ligularia dentata cultivar prized for large, rounded leaves that are deep purple-bronze on top and vivid mahogany-red underneath, though like all ligularias it struggles in zone 9 heat and performs best in cooler climates with consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from afternoon sun and heat. Desdemona is one of the most widely grown Ligularia dentata cultivars, valued for large, rounded, kidney-shaped leaves that emerge deep bronze-purple and hold rich purple-green coloring on top through the season, with a dramatic mahogany-red underside visible when leaves catch the light or wind. In mid-to-late summer, tall stems carry clusters of bright orange-yellow daisy flowers well above the bold foliage. Like all ligularias, Desdemona wilts dramatically during midday heat, looking severely stressed on hot afternoons before recovering fully overnight — normal behavior for the genus rather than a sign of disease, though it signals the plant wants cooler conditions, consistent moisture, and protection from afternoon sun. It performs best in climates with mild summers and struggles considerably in zone 9 heat and humidity, where siting it in the coolest, most sheltered, consistently moist spot available and mulching heavily to keep roots cool gives it the best chance of success. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Desert Four O'Clock / Colorado Four O'Clock
plant_note: Direct sow in spring into dry, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; scarify seeds lightly and sow shallowly, no more than 1/4 inch deep.
directions: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring into dry, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun, pressing seeds just under the surface in a location with good air circulation. This Southwestern native develops a massive woody taproot that anchors it through heat and drought, so choose the permanent planting site carefully as it resents transplanting once established. Deep magenta-pink trumpet flowers open each afternoon and close by morning, providing reliable late-day color and supporting hawk moth populations throughout summer. Once established, avoid irrigation except during extended drought, as excess moisture in heavy soils can cause root rot.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in very well-drained, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert globe mallow is native to Mojave and Sonoran Desert scrub and requires excellent drainage and minimal irrigation once established — it will rot quickly in wet or poorly drained soil.
directions: Sow scarified seeds directly in spring in extremely well-drained, dry, alkaline to neutral, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; germination is improved by lightly nicking the seed coat or soaking in hot water for 24 hours before planting. Desert globe mallow is a native wildflower of the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts producing distinctive cup-shaped, apricot-orange to deep coral-red flowers held in dense spikes above the grey-green, woolly, deeply lobed leaves from spring through fall in desert conditions — the flowers are among the most striking of any arid-region native and are a primary nectar source for the specialist globe mallow bee (Dieunomia). Once established it is extraordinarily drought-tolerant and long-lived; excellent for desert rock gardens, xeriscape plantings, and dry borders in zone 7–11 where summer heat and drought are extreme. The tiny hairs on the foliage can irritate skin and eyes — handle with gloves.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in any very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; desert honeysuckle requires excellent drainage and lean soil — rich, moist soil causes rank growth and reduced flowering. Cut back hard to 12 inches in late winter to encourage compact, dense growth and maximum summer bloom.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert honeysuckle (hummingbird bush) is a native Southwestern shrub with an extraordinarily long season of tubular, orange-red flowers that are among the most powerfully attractive hummingbird plants in the xeric and arid Southwest. Blooming from summer through fall with each successive flowering flush triggered by summer monsoon rains, the plant produces dense masses of 1.5-inch, orange-red tubular flowers that provide rich nectar for migrating and resident hummingbirds. It is extremely drought tolerant and actually declines in fertility and blooming if given rich soil or excess water — thriving in the hard, dry, alkaline conditions of the Southwest and Edwards Plateau. Cut back hard each late winter before new growth begins. The species A. wrightii (flame anisacanthus, Wright's desert honeysuckle) has similar requirements and is equally outstanding as a hummingbird plant; both are outstanding native choices for xeric wildflower and butterfly gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 8–12 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert lily grows at extraordinary depth in nature (bulbs found as deep as 20 inches) to escape summer heat and drought. It requires the hot, dry desert summer dormancy of the Sonoran Desert and is not suitable for areas with wet summers. In its native habitat it flowers only in years with sufficient winter rainfall.
directions: Plant bulbs very deep in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert lily is a remarkable Sonoran Desert native — the only species in its genus — that produces one of the most beautiful and improbable flower displays of the North American desert: slender, upright racemes of 2-inch, pure-white, fragrant, funnel-shaped lily flowers with a pale green stripe down each petal's reverse, appearing in February through April in the sandy washes and desert floors of the Sonoran Desert from southern California to Arizona and Baja California. The plants emerge only when sufficient winter rainfall triggers their growth, disappearing completely in dry years and producing spectacular flowering displays in wet years — creating one of the variable miracles of the desert spring wildflower season. The deep-burrowing bulbs (planted naturally at 12–20 inch depths by small animals and by the force of the plant's contractile roots) are one of the deepest-reaching of all desert bulbs, providing insulation from summer heat. In cultivation it requires the precise conditions of its native habitat — deep, well-drained, sandy, alkaline soil, dry summers, and occasional winter watering to simulate desert winter rain. A collector's plant of special botanical and ecological significance.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun. Thrives in heat, drought, and rocky or caliche-heavy soils common to the desert Southwest. Little supplemental irrigation is needed once established.
directions: Plant in a sunny, open location with fast-draining soil; this desert-adapted shrub excels in rocky, alkaline, or caliche-laden ground where many plants fail. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in midsummer, or cold-stratify seed for 30 to 60 days before sowing in spring. Water to establish during the first growing season, then transition to deep, infrequent irrigation or rely entirely on natural rainfall. Dense branching provides cover and nesting habitat, and the dark blue-black fruits ripen in summer, attracting a wide range of bird species.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; desert phlox grows naturally on rocky, dry slopes, desert scrub edges, and chaparral margins of the Mojave Desert and surrounding mountains — highly drought-tolerant and adapted to low-rainfall desert conditions.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; desert phlox is a low, cushion-forming native phlox of rocky, dry slopes, desert scrub margins, and chaparral edges in the Mojave Desert and surrounding mountains of southern California, Nevada, and Utah. The plant forms compact, spreading mats of needle-like, stiff leaves that are characteristic of desert-adapted phlox. The flowers — white to pale lavender-pink — are profuse in early spring and provide an important early-season nectar source for native bees in desert ecosystems. Extremely drought and heat tolerant, requiring excellent drainage and minimal water; overwatering or clay soil causes rapid decline. An excellent native for dry, rocky, xeric rock gardens, desert-themed gardens, and the margins of gravel paths in arid Southwest gardens. Deer resistant and virtually pest-free in dry conditions.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost danger is past; in zone 9 plant March–May. Desert Rose is grown in containers in zone 9 and brought indoors or to a frost-free location during winter freezes — it cannot tolerate temperatures below 40°F without damage and is killed by frost. It blooms most heavily in full sun and in soil that is allowed to dry between waterings. In zone 9 the active growing season is March–November; reduce water in winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, gritty, low-fertility soil — overwatering and poor drainage are the primary causes of failure; Desert Rose is a succulent shrub native to sub-Saharan Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, producing a stout, swollen stem base (caudex) that stores water and gives the plant its dramatic, bonsai-like silhouette — one of the most architecturally distinctive succulents available to zone 9 gardeners. The brilliant trumpet-shaped flowers in hot pink, red, white, coral, or multicolored forms (depending on variety) bloom profusely from spring through fall, covering the leafy stems in showy clusters. Desert Rose performs best in the hot, bright conditions of the Gulf Coast summer and tolerates the heat that would wilt most ornamentals. In zone 9 it must be container-grown and protected from winter freezes below 40°F; bring containers indoors to a bright, frost-free location from November through March. The sculptural caudex becomes more impressive and valuable as the plant ages — established plants with large caudex formations are prized as living sculpture.

common_name: Desert Sage (Mojave Sage, Gray Ball Sage)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, poor to moderately fertile, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; Salvia dorrii is native to the Great Basin, Mojave Desert, and adjacent dry mountain ranges, requiring excellent drainage and low moisture — it will decline quickly in heavy, moist soils.
directions: Plant in spring in extremely well-drained, dry, alkaline to neutral, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; desert sage is intolerant of heavy clay or summer moisture and is best treated as a xeriscape plant that thrives on neglect in dry, arid conditions. Salvia dorrii (desert sage) is a beautiful, fragrant native sage of the Great Basin, Mojave Desert, and interior mountain ranges of the American West, forming compact, rounded shrubs 18–36 inches tall with densely silver-woolly, aromatic foliage and brilliant purple-violet flowers in spring and early summer that are among the most intensely colored of any western native shrub; the strong, camphor-sage fragrance of the foliage is cleansing and memorable, particularly after rain. Extremely cold-hardy for a desert plant (surviving zone 4 conditions) and exceptionally drought-tolerant once established — it evolved in habitats with 6–12 inches of annual rainfall and grows best in similar lean, dry conditions. An outstanding plant for western xeriscape gardens, rock gardens, and dry borders.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on bare sandy soil in zones 8-11; soak papery seed coats overnight or nick lightly before sowing to improve germination.
directions: Desert Sand Verbena is a stunning desert annual native to sandy flats, bajadas, and washes of the Mojave and Sonoran deserts of California, Arizona, and Baja California — one of the most spectacular early-spring wildflowers of California superbloom events. Its sticky, glandular-hairy, sprawling stems are covered in large dome-shaped clusters of vivid magenta-pink to rose-purple, sweetly fragrant tubular flowers from February through April. Direct sow in fall on bare, sandy, well-drained soil in zones 8-11; soak the papery seed coats overnight or nick them lightly before sowing to improve germination rates. Desert Sand Verbena does not transplant well and should always be direct sown where it is to grow.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in full sun in sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil; desert spoon is highly drought-tolerant once established and demands excellent drainage — clay soils cause fatal root rot.
directions: Plant in full sun in sharply drained, rocky or sandy soil; desert spoon forms a dramatic, spherical rosette of narrow blue-green leaves with toothed, saw-like margins and a spoon-shaped base that gives the plant its common name. After many years (sometimes 10–20), mature plants send up a spectacular flowering spike reaching 10–15 feet tall bearing thousands of small cream-colored flowers. The plant dies after flowering but produces offsets. Desert spoon is native to the Chihuahuan Desert and thrives in hot, dry conditions across the Gulf South and Southwest; it requires absolutely no irrigation once established and is among the most drought-tolerant landscape plants available for zone 7–10 gardens.

common_name: Desert Willow (Flor de Mimbre, Willowleaf Catalpa)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, sandy or rocky, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; desert willow is native to dry arroyos, stream banks, and desert washes of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran Deserts and is extremely drought tolerant — it actually performs better with no supplemental irrigation after the first year.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; desert willow is one of the most beautiful flowering native trees of the Southwest and South Texas, producing masses of showy, orchid-like flowers in pink, lavender, rose, white, or bicolor from late spring through fall in multiple flushes — a spectacular hummingbird and butterfly plant. Despite its name it is not a willow at all but rather a member of the Bignonia family, closely related to catalpa. The long, willow-like leaves emerge late in spring and drop early in fall. It is remarkably drought tolerant once established, thriving on natural rainfall alone in zone 7–11. The decorative seed pods hang on through winter. Many named cultivars are available with different flower colors and forms; 'Dark Storm,' 'Bubba,' and 'Art's Seedless' are popular selections for southern gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or potted plants in spring in rich, moist soil.
directions: Deutschland astilbe is a shade-loving perennial that sends up feathery white plumes above glossy green foliage in early summer. Plant it in partial to full shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, as it dislikes drying out. Work compost into the planting hole and mulch to conserve moisture around its shallow roots. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor. Deadheading is optional; the dried plumes add winter interest, and the flowers attract pollinators.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in any moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; devil's walking stick spreads by suckering roots and can colonize large areas over time — site it where spreading is welcome or in contained plantings.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; devil's walking stick is one of the most architecturally dramatic native plants in eastern North America — a large, coarse shrub or small tree with massive bipinnate-to-tripinnate compound leaves (sometimes 3–4 feet long) arranged in a palm-like whorl at the top of unbranched, viciously prickle-armed stems. The effect in the landscape is aggressively tropical and primitive — unlike anything else in the native plant palette. In late summer, enormous flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers (12–18 inches across) provide a spectacular nectar feast for dozens of native bee and butterfly species. The dark purple berries in fall are consumed by more than 100 bird species during fall migration. It suckers to form dense colonies in moist woodland edges — give it space or contain it.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into lean soil and full sun.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in lean soil and full sun, avoiding rich ground that reduces flowering. Diablo carries vibrant, bold blossoms on tall stems from midsummer until first fall frost, feeding bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies. Once established it is drought tolerant and low maintenance, so water sparingly. Deadhead or cut for bouquets to keep the flowers coming, and let a few set seed to reseed.

common_name: Diabolo Ninebark (Classic Dark Purple-Black Foliage Ninebark)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Diabolo was the breakthrough dark-leaved ninebark cultivar, prized for deep purple-black foliage that holds its color through the growing season better in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Diabolo was the original widely popularized dark-leaved ninebark cultivar, producing deep purple-black, maple-like leaves on a large, vigorous, arching shrub, topped in late spring with clusters of small white-to-pink flowers that draw pollinators, followed by reddish seed capsules and attractive exfoliating bark that provides winter interest. Full sun brings out the darkest foliage color, while shadier sites shift the leaves toward a more muted green-purple. It tolerates a very wide range of soil conditions and needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base each year to keep the shrub full and vigorous.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; one of the most cold-tolerant Clarkia species, seeds overwinter reliably across most of its range and germinate in spring.
directions: Diamond Clarkia is a widespread western US native annual with slender, upright stems and small, 4-petaled flowers in rose-lavender to light purple whose distinctively rhombus- or diamond-shaped petals give the species both its common and scientific names. It is native to dry, open foothill grasslands, oak woodlands, and chaparral margins from British Columbia south to Baja California and east to Utah, making it one of the most broadly distributed and cold-tolerant Clarkia species in the west. Direct sow in fall on dry, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun — it thrives in poor soils and declines in rich, amended ground. It self-sows freely in open, disturbed ground and is an excellent component of native wildflower seed mixes for western US meadow plantings and restoration projects.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in cool weather — the tiny seeds need light to germinate and should not be covered; diamond flower blooms within 4–6 weeks of germination and self-sows freely to maintain naturalized colonies in mild climates. Sow in succession every 3–4 weeks for extended bloom. In mild-winter areas (zones 8–10) sow in fall for winter and early spring flowering.
directions: Surface-sow seeds in cool weather in moderately fertile, moist, well-drained soil in sun to part shade; diamond flower is a Portuguese native miniature annual that is one of the most charming and overlooked small-scale plants in cool-season horticulture — a diminutive, delicate plant only 2–3 inches tall producing tiny, round leaves on thread-fine stems and, from the earliest spring, a constant succession of four-petaled flowers only 1/4 inch across in pale lilac to nearly white with a faint violet vein that gives the flowers a crystalline, diamond-like delicacy when viewed closely. The effect of a large mass is a soft, hazy, low carpet of pale lilac that looks from a distance like a lilac-colored mist at ground level. It self-sows freely between stepping stones, in crevices in paving, at the base of walls, and in any shaded position where the soil stays moist in spring. Outstanding for filling cracks between paving stones and at the base of containers, where its self-sowing habit creates naturalized colonies that need no further effort. The individual plants die in heat but the self-sown seedlings carry the colony through several seasons.

common_name: Diamond Frost Euphorbia (Baby's-Breath-Like Heat-Tolerant Filler Annual)
plant_note: Set out transplants after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Diamond Frost is a sterile Proven Winners hybrid that blooms nonstop from spring through frost without deadheading, tolerating heat, humidity, and drought far better than the baby's breath and gypsophila it visually resembles.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart. Diamond Frost is a sterile hybrid euphorbia introduced by Proven Winners that produces a continuous cloud of tiny white bracts resembling baby's breath, but on a plant that is dramatically more heat-, humidity-, and drought-tolerant than true gypsophila, making it far better suited to Gulf South summers. Because it is sterile, it never sets seed and never needs deadheading, so the airy white cloud of bloom continues uninterrupted from spring through the first hard frost with essentially no maintenance beyond routine watering. Its fine texture and neutral white color make it one of the most useful filler plants in mixed containers and borders, softening bold flower colors and foliage the way baby's breath does in a cut-flower arrangement. It tolerates both full sun and part shade, blooming a bit less densely in shadier spots but remaining attractive, and it shrugs off both drought and the occasional overwatering better than most bedding annuals. Shear back lightly if plants become leggy in late summer to refresh density for fall bloom.

common_name: Diamond Head Elephant Ear (Compact Charcoal-Black Colocasia)
plant_note: Plant tubers or divisions in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Diamond Head is a self-heading cultivar — it does not produce the long runners (stolons) that spread many Colocasia cultivars aggressively through garden beds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Diamond Head is a relatively compact, self-heading dark elephant ear — producing large, heart-shaped, dramatically dark charcoal-to-purple-black leaves similar to 'Black Magic' but on a more compact, controlled plant (3–4 feet rather than 4–6 feet) that doesn't spread aggressively by stolons as many Colocasia cultivars do. The 'self-heading' growth habit is Diamond Head's most practically valuable attribute for garden design: while vigorous Colocasia cultivars like 'Black Magic' spread through underground stolons to create expanding colonies (a quality that is sometimes desirable and sometimes invasive in garden beds), Diamond Head stays as a compact, tidy clump that can be managed like a conventional perennial. The exceptionally dark, glossy leaves — more charcoal than the pure-black of 'Black Magic' and with a distinctive glossy sheen — create a bold tropical accent that is dramatic without the unpredictability of running types. In zone 9, Diamond Head is reliably perennial, dying back in cold winters but returning from persistent tubers in spring. The compact habit makes it outstanding for mixed borders, container plantings, and defined landscape spaces where a controllable but dramatic dark tropical accent is desired.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in sandy, well-drained soil; plants form a rosette in the first year and bolt to flower in the second year, then self-sow to maintain the colony.
directions: Diamond-petal Evening Primrose is a tall, statuesque biennial native to sandy dunes, open disturbed ground, and dry plains of the Great Plains, forming a low, flat gray-green rosette in its first year and shooting up a leafy spike to 6 feet in its second year. The distinctive, large, clear yellow flowers have noticeably diamond- to rhombus-shaped petals 2-3 inches across and open in the evening, attracting hawk moths for pollination before closing by mid-morning. Direct sow in fall in sandy, lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow their architectural second-year form to develop. Plants self-sow reliably in open sandy ground, keeping a self-sustaining colony going year after year without replanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; in zone 8–9 plant September–March. Diana Clare establishes best with consistent moisture during the first growing season. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in fall after foliage declines to maintain vigor. In zone 9 provide reliable shade and moisture to protect from summer heat; mulch heavily around the crown. The plant goes summer-dormant in heat — do not overwater dormant plants.
directions: Plant in full shade to light dappled shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Diana Clare is a highly awarded Pulmonaria cultivar from Terra Nova Nurseries, distinguished by its extraordinarily silver-splashed leaves — the foliage is so heavily overlaid with bright silver that individual leaves appear nearly entirely silver with just a hint of green remaining, creating one of the most dramatic foliage effects of any shade perennial. The plants bloom very early in spring (February–April) with vivid violet-blue to purple-red flowers (the classic lungwort two-tone pink-then-blue color shift as individual flowers age on the same plant) that are among the first nectar sources available to early pollinators including queen bumblebees emerging from winter dormancy. As the flowers fade the striking silver foliage takes over as the primary ornamental feature throughout summer and fall. Lungwort (Pulmonaria) is one of the most reliable low-maintenance shade groundcovers for the mid-Atlantic and Southeast, tolerating dry summer shade once established better than most shade perennials.

common_name: Dinema (Twin Spur Orchid, Polybulbon Epidendrum, Caribbean Creeper)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark or cork, or in a shallow basket with coarse bark; Dinema polybulbon is an excellent beginner orchid for outdoor culture in zone 9-11 — it is cold-tolerant, fast-growing, and produces its modest but pleasant fragrant flowers in late fall and winter. The creeping, spreading rhizomes quickly colonize the surface of a cork mount or flat bark piece. Water regularly in active growth; reduce slightly in winter. Tolerates temperatures briefly to 38–40°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light with moderate humidity — Dinema polybulbon is one of the most cold-tolerant small epiphytic orchids for zone 9-11 outdoor culture and adapts exceptionally well to outdoor mounted culture on a shaded, protected porch. Dinema polybulbon (formerly Epidendrum polybulbon) is a small, creeping, sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Belize, Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, and Puerto Rico in the Orchidaceae family — one of the cold-hardiest of the small, Caribbean-origin epiphytic orchids regularly available in the orchid trade. The plant spreads by creeping rhizomes that slowly colonize the surface of its mount, each section producing a very small, round to oblong pseudobulb topped with 2 narrow, stiff, dark-green leaves about 2–3 inches long. In late fall and winter, short flower spikes (2–3 inches) emerge from between the leaves, bearing 1–2 small (1-inch) flowers in yellow-white with yellow-orange stripes on the sepals and petals and a white to cream lip — modest in size but pleasantly fragrant on warm days. The plant's creeping, mat-forming growth habit, cold tolerance, and unfussy culture make it an excellent starter orchid for zone 9-11 collectors beginning outdoor epiphyte culture. Non-toxic.
