plant_note: Plant tubers after frost; lift and store where not hardy.
directions: Plant dinnerplate dahlia tubers after the last frost, laying them horizontally about six inches deep with the eye facing up. These giant blooms can reach ten to twelve inches across and require staking at planting to support the tall stems. Grow in full sun and rich, well-drained soil, watering deeply once shoots emerge and pinching to promote branching. In cold climates lift and store the tubers in a frost-free place over winter.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade after frost; dipladenia performs best in consistently moist but well-drained soil — waterlogged roots cause yellowing and dieback, while drought stress causes bud drop and leaf loss.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; dipladenia (mandevilla, rocktrumpet) is a Brazilian tropical twining vine widely sold throughout the garden industry as a patio and container flowering plant for its large, trumpet-shaped, glossy-petaled flowers in vivid shades of red, deep-pink, rose-pink, and white, produced continuously throughout the warm season on new growth. It is one of the most extensively-sold container flowering vines in the American nursery trade, marketed under the names dipladenia (for the more compact, less-twining forms) and mandevilla (for the larger, more vigorous climbing forms). The glossy, deep-green, oval leaves and shining, varnished-looking flower petals give the plant a distinctive, tropical-polished appearance. As an outdoor perennial in zone 10–12 it grows vigorously on trellises and arbors; in cooler climates it is used as a summer annual or overwintered as a container plant indoors. The compact cultivars (sold as 'Dipladenia') are bushy and non-vining; the larger forms (sold as 'Mandevilla') climb to 10 feet or more. The plant exudes milky sap; wash hands after pruning.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; disanthus is slow-growing and dislikes root disturbance — plant carefully and do not move. It requires reliably moist, acidic conditions similar to Japanese maples and kalmia, and grows naturally in moist mountain forests of Japan and central China.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil in part shade; disanthus is a monotypic genus in the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) — a single species from mountain forests of Japan and central China that is grown primarily as one of the elite autumn-coloring shrubs. The broadly rounded, heart-shaped leaves closely resemble those of Cercis (redbud) in shape, turning in autumn to some of the most spectacular colors achievable in a garden shrub: brilliant combinations of crimson, orange, purple, and claret, often with all colors simultaneously visible on a single leaf. In October, tiny, deep wine-purple flowers appear directly on the bare and falling-leaf branches — so small and dark that they are easily missed but distinctive and curious up close, with reflexed petals in pairs. A slow-growing, understated but ultimately magnificent shrub for the woodland garden with moist, acidic conditions, outstanding autumn color, and a refined year-round form. Often cited by plantsmen as one of the most desirable garden shrubs, despite remaining little-known outside specialist collections.

plant_note: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full shade to part shade; discolor calanthe is a Japanese native terrestrial orchid and one of the hardiest of all cultivatable orchids, surviving winters to zone 5 when grown in protected, well-drained woodland conditions.
directions: Plant pseudobulb divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), well-drained woodland soil in full shade; allow divisions to establish for a full season before expecting bloom. Calanthe discolor (discolor calanthe) is one of the hardiest and most gardener-friendly of all terrestrial orchids — a Japanese and East Asian species that can be grown as a perennial in the shade garden from zone 5 through zone 9, emerging in spring with attractive, pleated, semi-evergreen basal leaves and producing elegant, upright flower spikes 10–18 inches tall bearing 12–20 graceful, two-toned, purple-and-white orchid flowers in April–May. The contrast between the purplish-brown outer tepals and the pure-white lip (labellum) is striking and distinctive. Unlike epiphytic orchids (which grow in bark mixes), calanthes grow in humus-rich, acidic woodland soil and are treated much like hostas — planted in shaded beds, left to establish, and allowed to slowly clump up over years. In the shade garden, they bloom at an important transition period (April–May) before most summer shade perennials reach peak. C. discolor has been used extensively in breeding cold-hardy terrestrial orchid hybrids.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in zone 9–11; Wallichia disticha (Distichous Fishtail Palm) is a striking, unusual Himalayan palm with a unique flat, fan-like crown — all fronds held in a single plane, giving a two-dimensional silhouette — native to shaded forest margins from Nepal and northeastern India to southern China, and notable for being monocarpic (each stem flowers once, then dies, while the clump persists).
directions: Plant Wallichia disticha in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright partial shade, protecting from harsh afternoon sun and cold below 28°F; water regularly during establishment and provide a balanced slow-release palm fertilizer in spring and summer. The Distichous Fishtail Palm is one of the most architecturally distinctive of all palms — its unique flat crown, with all fronds arranged in a single vertical plane like pages in an open book (the meaning of 'distichous'), creates a dramatic, two-dimensional silhouette unlike any other palm species. Native to the moist, seasonally cool forests of the eastern Himalayas from Nepal through northeast India to southern China and Myanmar, it is adapted to partial shade and cooler conditions than most palms — making it useful in gardens where more tender palms fail. Wallichia disticha is monocarpic like most fishtail palms: each individual stem flowers and fruits once then dies, but the clump produces multiple stems and the overall plant persists. It is not as commonly cultivated as many other palms but is prized by collectors for its unusual form; it makes a spectacular specimen in zone 9–11 gardens in a sheltered, partially shaded position with reliable moisture.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; distylium is exceptional in its tolerance of both full sun and full shade with no significant change in growth quality — a rare characteristic among broadleaved evergreens.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Distylium racemosum is a Japanese evergreen shrub in the witch hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) that is gaining significant recognition as one of the most adaptable and low-maintenance broadleaved evergreens for zone 7–10 landscapes. It produces glossy, leathery, dark-green leaves on spreading, arching branches and bears unusual, petal-less winter flowers with prominent red stamens that emerge in February–March in zone 9, providing early-season color before most shrubs bloom. The strongly adaptable nature of distylium is its defining quality — it thrives in full sun to dense shade, in dry or moist soils, in clay or sandy soils, and in both acid and moderately alkaline pH ranges. This adaptability makes it invaluable for difficult landscape situations where few plants perform reliably. Named compact cultivars have made distylium increasingly available in the trade: 'Cinnamon Girl' (4–5 feet, copper-bronze new growth), 'Vintage Jade' (4 feet, spreading), and 'Coppertone' (2.5–3 feet, compact) are among the most widely sold selections. Distylium is completely free of serious pest and disease problems in zone 9, requires no deadheading or shaping, and is highly deer-resistant — a compelling combination for the low-maintenance Gulf South garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Distylium myricoides (sold as 'Vintage Jade' and related cultivars) has become one of the most popular new evergreen shrubs in the US Southeast for its compact habit, year-round glossy foliage, and exceptional heat and drought tolerance once established.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Distylium is a genus of evergreen shrubs and trees in the witch-hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) from China and Japan, emerging as one of the most important new landscape shrubs for the mid-South and Southeast. The species D. myricoides produces small, glossy, dark green leaves with a neat, compact, spreading habit and unusual winter-to-early-spring flowers — red stamens without petals that create a purplish-red haze across the plant in late winter. Exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and resistant to deer browsing. Widely used in current Southeast US landscaping as a low-maintenance foundation plant; cultivars including 'Vintage Jade', 'Linebacker', and the Coppertone series are widely available. Thrives in part shade and full sun with minimal care. Disease and pest resistant.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost danger passes and soil warms.
directions: Diva is a tall, prolific dahlia producing rich plum blooms with exceptional vase life for a large flower. Set tubers about 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun once soil is warm, and wait to water heavily until growth appears. Because plants grow very tall, install sturdy stakes or a support cage early in the season. Cut or deadhead spent flowers frequently to prolong blooming into fall. Lift and store tubers over winter where the ground freezes.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes and plant in fall or spring in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 6–10; Dixie Iris is the largest-flowered native iris of the Gulf Coast states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Florida Panhandle, and South Carolina — producing spectacular, large, blue-violet to red-purple flowers in spring at pond edges, drainage ditches, bayous, and moist meadows where it is tolerant of prolonged flooding and alkaline as well as acidic soils.
directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade — Iris hexagona is adapted to water-saturated soils and tolerates several weeks of complete flooding; excellent for rain gardens, pond margins, wet ditches, and boggy areas. Iris hexagona (Dixie Iris or Zigzag Iris) is a large-flowered, robust, native beardless iris indigenous to the coastal wetlands, bayous, river margins, brackish marshes, and wet prairie soils of the Gulf Coast states — Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina — and one of the most spectacular native wetland wildflowers of the Deep South. The large, showy flowers (3–4 inches across) are produced in spring in shades of deep blue-violet to rich red-purple, sometimes with yellow signals, held on sturdy, zigzag-branched stalks (hence one common name 'Zigzag Iris') above glossy, strap-like foliage reaching 3–4 feet. Iris hexagona is the dominant native parent species in the development of Louisiana Irises (Iris × louisiana hybrids) — the largest-flowered, most diverse, and most adaptable of all American native iris groups, created by hybridization with I. fulva, I. brevicaulis, and I. nelsonii. Unlike most garden irises, Dixie Iris thrives in wet, boggy, poorly drained, even flooded soils and tolerates wide pH variation. Excellent for Gulf Coast rain gardens, pond edges, and natural wet-area planting.

plant_note: Plant by direct seed or division in spring in any sunny, well-drained soil; dog fennel is a robust, fast-growing perennial throughout the Gulf Coast and effectively self-seeds to return annually even where it is treated as an annual in colder zones — cut back hard in winter.
directions: Dog fennel is a ubiquitous native perennial of roadsides, old fields, and disturbed open areas throughout the Southeast, instantly recognizable by its thread-fine, feathery, intensely aromatic foliage — the camphor-like scent has historically made it a natural insect repellent, and bundles were placed in farm buildings and bedding to repel fleas and lice. Despite its weedy reputation in some circles, dog fennel is an ecologically important native: the clouds of tiny white flowers produced on 3–6 foot wiry stems in late fall are among the final nectar sources of the season for migrating monarchs and late-flying native bees in the Gulf Coast region, often blooming well into November in zone 9. The fine-textured, billowing foliage provides striking textural contrast in the naturalistic garden and is used by some designers as a feathery filler among coarser-leaved perennials. Cut back to a few inches in late winter; it regrows rapidly from the base and will reach full height by midsummer even in the Gulf South's hot climate.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), fertile soil in full shade to part shade; dog hobble is a native Appalachian understory shrub with long, arching branches and glossy, evergreen foliage that turns attractive burgundy-bronze in winter — one of the finest native shade shrubs for woodland gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in deep to part shade; mulch with pine bark or pine needles to maintain soil acidity. Leucothoe fontanesiana (dog hobble or drooping leucothoe) is an elegant native Appalachian understory shrub growing along shaded stream banks and moist forest floors from Virginia south to Georgia and Tennessee. The plant produces long (3–5 foot), gracefully arching stems clothed in glossy, lance-shaped, evergreen leaves — in summer a rich, dark green, transforming to dramatic shades of burgundy, bronze, and red-purple in winter (especially in cultivars like 'Rainbow' and 'Girard's Rainbow'). In late spring, drooping clusters of urn-shaped, white flowers (resembling lily-of-the-valley flowers) line the undersides of the arching branches — fragrant and attractive. Dog hobble earns its common name from the impenetrable tangles it forms along mountain creek banks, through which hunting dogs cannot easily pass. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form colonies. As a shade garden plant, Leucothoe fontanesiana provides outstanding year-round interest: spring flowers, summer foliage, and winter color in sites too acidic and shady for most other shrubs. The cultivar 'Scarletta' has especially vivid scarlet winter color.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or bare-root plants in early spring before leaf break. Cold stratify seeds for 90–180 days at 34–40°F before sowing if starting from seed.
directions: Plant in a sunny, open location with well-drained soil; Dog Rose tolerates poor, rocky, and chalky conditions and does not require amendment or fertilization. Take hardwood cuttings in late autumn or early winter, root them in sandy compost, and overwinter in a cold frame before transplanting the following spring. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and requires little supplemental watering. Prune out oldest canes after flowering to maintain an open framework and encourage vigorous new growth bearing the following season's blooms and hips.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial shade to shade; dogtooth violet goes completely summer-dormant and requires dry conditions during its summer rest. Naturalizes readily under deciduous trees in Europe and in North American woodland gardens.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; dogtooth violet is the European counterpart of the North American fawn lilies — a widespread Eurasian woodland spring ephemeral producing beautifully mottled brown-and-silver basal leaves and nodding, reflexed-petaled flowers in pink, white, lilac, or rose. The common name 'dogtooth violet' comes not from the flower but from the elongated, tooth-shaped corm. The mottled foliage is as attractive as the flowers. Plant in large drifts of 20 or more under deciduous trees for best effect — single corms are easily lost, but a naturalized colony creates a stunning spring display. Goes completely dormant by late spring; suitable for underplanting with summer-dormant perennials or in spots that go dry in summer. More widely available in North American commerce than the native Erythronium species, with many named cultivars in pink, rose, purple, and white.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors, as the seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow the seed indoors several weeks before the last frost, since it needs light to sprout, and transplant after frost. Dondo White forms billowy clusters of fluffy, pure-white blooms on upright plants reaching twenty-four to thirty inches, adding vertical interest and texture to borders and containers. It flowers continuously from summer through frost. Grow in full sun with even moisture and deadhead to prolong the display.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; dotted blazing star is extraordinarily drought-tolerant, developing a deep corm-like root system that enables plants to survive extreme drought conditions. It grows slowly in early years as it develops its deep root system before investing in aerial growth. Established plants can live for 100 or more years in undisturbed prairie conditions.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; dotted blazing star is the most drought-tolerant blazing star species, native to the dry, sandy and gravelly prairies and rocky hillsides of the central Great Plains from Canada to Texas and New Mexico. It is distinguished from other liatris by its very narrow, almost needle-like leaves dotted with small, translucent oil glands (the punctata of the name) and its compact, lower stature compared to the common spike gayfeather. The purple flower spikes open from top to bottom in August and September — the characteristic reverse bloom order of all liatris — providing late-season color and an important nectar source for monarchs and other migrating butterflies. The deep corm-like root system enables plants to survive extreme drought and poor soils, and established plants can live for 100 or more years in undisturbed prairie conditions — one of the longest-lived prairie wildflowers. Slow to establish but extremely long-lived once settled.

plant_note: Surface sow into warm soil, as the fine seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Surface sow into warm soil after frost, since the fine seed needs light to germinate. These low-growing plants form a carpet of brilliantly colored, rose-like double flowers that open on sunny days through the heat of summer. Very drought tolerant, moss rose needs only occasional watering and thrives in dry banks and hot, reflected-heat spots. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil for the best flowering.

plant_note: Often grown as a biennial; sow in spring or summer for bloom the next year.
directions: Sow in spring or summer, since this short-lived perennial is usually grown as a biennial that blooms its second year. Double Blend forms large clusters of edible, double flowers in many colors that rank among the longest-lasting cut flowers. In the garden the sweet, spicy-scented blooms draw butterflies and bees, and the mild clove-flavored petals garnish salads. Grow in full sun to part shade with well-drained soil and even moisture.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or very early spring while dormant, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Double Bloodroot is sterile and spreads only slowly by rhizome, never by seed, so start with nursery-propagated divisions rather than expecting it to naturalize on its own.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees; let the foliage die back naturally in early summer as the plant goes dormant, and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizomes. Sanguinaria canadensis 'Multiplex' is a showy double-flowered form of the native spring ephemeral bloodroot, bearing fully doubled, camellia-like white blooms with dozens of narrow petals in place of the single flower's simple eight to twelve petals. Because the flower is sterile and produces no seed, it never triggers the rapid petal drop that ends the single form's bloom within a day or two of opening — the double flowers instead persist attractively for one to two weeks, a significant advantage for garden display. Like the species, each striking, blue-green, deeply lobed leaf wraps protectively around its flower stem as it emerges in earliest spring; the cut rhizome exudes the characteristic red-orange sap that gives the plant its common name. A prized, long-lived heirloom woodland perennial for a shaded native garden, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in very well-drained, dry, sandy to gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral, poor soil in full sun; double bubble mint is native to rock ledges and dry slopes in the Chihuahuan Desert region and must have excellent drainage — wet soils are lethal.
directions: Start transplants indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in very well-drained, dry, sandy to gravelly, slightly alkaline to neutral, poor soil in full sun; double bubble mint is native to rock ledges and dry slopes in the Chihuahuan Desert region and must have excellent drainage — wet soils are lethal. Agastache cana is a compact, long-blooming agastache native to the Chihuahuan Desert mountains of western Texas and southern New Mexico, producing narrow, intensely bubble-gum-and-licorice-scented leaves (the origin of its common name 'Double Bubble Mint') and dense, fluffy, 6–8 inch spikes of rose-pink to dark-pink tubular flowers from midsummer through hard frost that are exceptional hummingbird and bumblebee forage. It is among the most drought-tolerant and heat-adapted of all Agastache species; deer-resistant, essentially disease-free, and outstanding for rock gardens, dry borders, and xeriscape designs in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into lean soil and full sun.
directions: Direct sow after frost in average-to-lean soil and full sun, since rich ground limits flowering. Double Click produces a profusion of mostly double, some semi-double, chrysanthemum-like blooms in pink, white, and carmine red. Once established it is easy to care for and drought tolerant, so water sparingly. Deadhead or cut for bouquets to prolong bloom, and let a few flowers set seed to reseed.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August for fall bloom. Double Click series cosmos blooms 75–90 days from seed — longer than single-flowered cosmos. The double flowers have significantly longer vase life than single cosmos; harvest as buds begin to open for 7–10 days of cut flower enjoyment. In zone 9 successive sowings 4–6 weeks apart through spring extend the productive season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral soil — cosmos performs best in poor soil and actually blooms less when over-fertilized; Double Click Cranberry is a semi-double to fully double-flowered cosmos variety in a vivid deep cranberry-magenta color — an unusual form for a species (Cosmos bipinnatus) that is normally only available in single-petaled form. The Double Click series from PanAmerican Seed was developed specifically to introduce double-flowered forms to the cosmos genus, creating lush, full, pompom-like flower heads that look more like a small chrysanthemum or dahlia than the familiar daisy form of standard cosmos. The deep cranberry color paired with the full, multi-petaled form makes Double Click Cranberry one of the most distinctive cosmos varieties for cut flower production and ornamental garden use. Like all cosmos, it is extremely heat-tolerant and drought-resistant once established — a remarkable low-maintenance annual that produces continuously from first bloom until frost.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double flowering plum blooms in early spring before the leaves. Prune immediately after flowering to encourage vigorous new growth. The double-flowered cultivar 'Multiplex' is most widely available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; double flowering plum is a Chinese shrub producing double-flowered, rosy-pink blooms so profusely that stems are completely hidden under flowers in very early spring. The popular cultivar 'Multiplex' has fully double, deep rose-pink flowers with a ruffled, peony-like form. This is one of the most spectacularly spring-flowering woody plants for cold climates — reliably cold-hardy to zone 3 with outstanding early season color. Often confused with double flowering almond (Prunus glandulosa) in the garden trade; both are excellent ornamental spring shrubs. The flowers appear before leaves, making the bare-stem flower display especially dramatic. Prune hard immediately after bloom to maintain compact shape and maximize next year's flowering. Short-lived (10–20 years) but easy to propagate from cuttings.

common_name: Double Knock Out Rose (Double Red Knock Out Rose)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Double Knock Out has the same exceptional disease resistance, heat tolerance, and low-maintenance requirements as the original Knock Out.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Double Knock Out rose is the most popular cultivar in the Knock Out series and is now the best-selling landscape rose in America — a double-flowered sport of the original Knock Out selected for its lush, fully double, deep-red to cherry-red flowers that more closely resemble a traditional garden rose than the single-petaled original. While the original Knock Out has 5 petals in the typical wild-rose single form, Double Knock Out produces 18–25 petals in a cupped, decorative double form that most gardeners associate with 'real' roses. This additional petal count gives the flowers a fuller, more luxurious appearance while maintaining essentially all the disease resistance, repeat bloom, and low-maintenance characteristics of the parent. Double Knock Out blooms from spring until hard frost in zone 9, self-cleaning without deadheading, and requires only one annual pruning in late winter (February in zone 9) cutting the plant back to 12–18 inches. Like the original, it shows exceptional black spot resistance — a critical trait in the humid Gulf Coast climate where most roses require weekly fungicide programs. The deep-red flower color is consistent through the season without fading. Numerous Knock Out series siblings exist: Pink Knock Out, Pink Double Knock Out, Sunny Knock Out (yellow), Rainbow Knock Out (coral-pink), and others.

plant_note: Set out the shrub after danger of hard frost; it is a woody deciduous shrub, not typically grown from seed for this cultivar.
directions: Plant this double-flowered althea in full sun with well-drained soil, spacing shrubs 5-8 feet apart to allow their broad upright habit room to mature. It blooms late summer into fall on the current season's growth, so prune in late winter or early spring to shape and encourage flowering wood. Water regularly the first two seasons until the roots establish, after which it tolerates heat and short dry spells. The full, layered pink blooms are sterile, so this cultivar reseeds far less than single-flowered forms.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Double Scoop Cranberry blooms in its first year from well-established container plants and becomes more productive in subsequent years. In zone 9 coneflowers perform best in well-drained to lean soils — the combination of heat and consistently moist soil causes root rot; excellent drainage and lean soil are more important in warm climates than in the North. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering, or leave some seed heads for goldfinches in fall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil — coneflowers are native prairie plants that thrive in poor, dry soil and fail in rich, consistently moist conditions; Double Scoop Cranberry is a double-flowered coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) from the Double Scoop series, producing fully double, pompom-like flower heads in deep cranberry-red — a significant departure from the familiar single daisy form of standard purple coneflower. The double flower heads are completely filled with petals, with no central cone visible, creating a lush, dense flower of a different character than single coneflowers — more like a small dahlia than the familiar Echinacea form. The rich cranberry-red color combined with the compact (18–24 inch) habit and double flower structure makes Double Scoop Cranberry one of the most ornamentally distinctive of the new-generation Echinacea hybrids. As a native North American prairie perennial, coneflowers are strongly adapted to heat, drought, and poor soil — genuine tough plants that perform excellently once established in zone 9 with good drainage. The flowers attract butterflies and bees, and the seed heads feed goldfinches and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost, barely covering seed since light aids germination.
directions: Direct sow or start indoors, pressing the seed onto the surface since light improves germination. This carefree perennial produces semi-double and double golden-yellow blooms from summer until frost and thrives in full sun even in heat, humidity, and poor or dry soil. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong the display and prevent excessive self-seeding. Once established it is quite drought tolerant and needs only occasional watering.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface-sow since light is needed to germinate, and set out hardened plants around last frost.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, pressing seed onto the mix surface as light is required for germination. This variety carries delicate 1.5-inch bicolor blooms in soft pink and white that resemble tiny apple blossoms on heavily branched, wind-resistant stems. Snapdragons prefer cool weather, so transplant early once seedlings are hardened, and pinch young plants to encourage more flowering stems. Regular deadheading and cutting keeps the plants producing long, upright spikes for bouquets.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors early and set out hardened transplants near last frost for cool-season bloom.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost, leaving seed uncovered since light triggers germination. This F1 hybrid bears luminous 1.5-inch open-faced double blooms that shift from peach in cool light to buttery yellow in full sun, on strong branched stems reaching 20-24 inches. Pinch seedlings when a few inches tall to build bushy, floriferous plants and transplant while weather is still cool. Cut and deadhead frequently to keep the wind-resistant stems flowering through the season.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; doublefile viburnum blooms on previous year's wood and should be pruned only immediately after flowering if shaping is needed.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; doublefile viburnum is one of the most architecturally striking flowering shrubs in cultivation — its strongly horizontal, tiered branch structure creates a layered, pagoda-like silhouette that is ornamental year-round even without flowers. In spring, rows of flat-topped lacecap flower clusters are borne in pairs ('doublefile') along the horizontal branches, covering the entire upper surface of each tier in white blossoms — a spectacular display. Red berries follow in summer, turning black and persisting into winter; they are attractive to birds, which rapidly consume them. In fall the leaves often turn wine-red to purplish-red. Popular cultivars include 'Shasta' (large, flat flower clusters and low, wide habit), 'Mariesii' (the most widely grown, strongly horizontal), and 'Summer Snowflake' (an extended blooming selection). Performs best in zone 5–7; in zone 8 it tolerates summer heat with afternoon shade and consistent moisture but may be short-lived.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy soil in partial shade; dove tree grows naturally in cool, moist, mountainous forests of central China and requires adequate moisture, cool conditions, and some shelter from harsh afternoon sun and drying winds. Seeds require double-stratification (2 cold periods) and may take 2 years to germinate.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy soil in partial shade; dove tree is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world, with a legendary history in Western botany — first seen by European plant hunters in Chinese mountain forests and described as a tree covered with fluttering white handkerchiefs or white doves perching in the branches. The 'flowers' (actually a tiny, inconspicuous cluster of flowers) are almost invisible — what creates the stunning display is a pair of very large, unequal, pure white bracts (modified leaves) flanking each flower cluster, ranging from 3 to 7 inches long. When in full bloom in mid-spring, a mature tree covered in hundreds of hanging white bract pairs in a light breeze creates an unforgettable, magical spectacle. The tree requires patience — it typically does not flower until 10+ years from seed. A legendary collector's tree planted in large gardens and arboreta worldwide for this once-yearly flower event. The fruit is a large, olive-like, edible (barely) nutlet. The legendary China plant collector E.H. Wilson nearly died collecting seeds in 1900.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or calcareous soil in partial shade; downy alumroot grows naturally in rocky, limestone outcrops, cliff ledges, and calcareous slope forests of the Appalachians and adjacent regions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or calcareous, humus-rich soil in partial shade; downy alumroot is one of the most rock-garden-friendly native heucheras, naturally growing in the crevices of limestone outcrops and calcareous slope forests of the central Appalachians and surrounding regions. The plant is unusual among heucheras for preferring alkaline to neutral calcareous soils rather than the acidic soils favored by most alumroots. The soft, downy hairs covering the leaves give it an attractive, velvety texture that distinguishes it from harder-textured species. Tall, airy stems of tiny pinkish-white flowers in late spring attract small native bees. In the garden, it performs best in well-drained, calcareous rock garden settings or in partially shaded retaining walls where drainage is excellent.

plant_note: Plant in early spring after frost. Tolerates dry, rocky, and low-fertility soils where other viburnums fail. No supplemental fertilizer needed at establishment.
directions: Plant in a well-draining location with partial shade to full shade; this viburnum thrives in dry, rocky soils and actually struggles in rich, moist conditions. Dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball and backfill with unamended native soil. Water consistently for the first season to establish roots, then reduce irrigation — established plants are notably drought-tolerant. Flat-topped white flower clusters appear in late spring, followed by dark blue-black berries that persist into winter for birds.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall under oaks in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or rocky, lean soil in partial shade; downy false foxglove is hemiparasitic on oak roots — it parasitically taps the roots of nearby oaks for water and nutrients while also producing chlorophyll. Plant near established oaks; it cannot survive without an oak host.
directions: Direct sow in fall near established oaks in slightly acidic, lean, sandy or rocky soil in partial shade; downy false foxglove is a hemiparasitic native perennial of the eastern US woodlands that grows in the company of oaks, tapping their root systems for supplemental water and nutrients while also photosynthesizing. The yellow, tubular, two-lipped flowers in late summer resemble yellow foxglove blossoms, providing nectar for bumblebees, hummingbirds, and clearwing sphinx moths at a time when most summer flowers are finished. The soft, downy, gray-green foliage is attractive. Will not grow without oak root host plants; plant near established black oak, red oak, or white oak for establishment. A fascinating and beautiful shade-garden plant that provides late-season color in oak-dominated woodland gardens. Self-sows under favorable conditions. Increasingly rare in some areas due to oak woodland fragmentation.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, average to sandy soil in full sun; downy gentian grows naturally in dry to average prairies, open oak savannas, and barrens of the upper Midwest where it blooms very late in fall — often the last native wildflower of the season to bloom.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average soil in full sun; downy gentian is a native prairie gentian of the upper Midwest, producing clusters of brilliant, deep blue-violet, vase-shaped flowers at the tips of upright stems in September–October — one of the last native wildflowers to bloom in the prairie season. The closed, finely-pubescent (downy-hairy) flower buds give the species its common name. Like all prairie gentians, the flowers open only in full sunlight and close at night or on cloudy days. A valuable late-season pollinator plant, providing nectar for bumblebees, monarch butterflies, and metallic sweat bees in the final weeks before fall frosts. Best in lean, dry prairie conditions — excess fertility causes lax, floppy growth. Combine with grasses, blazingstar, and other late-blooming prairie species for an authentic fall prairie display. Long-lived in appropriate dry, open prairie conditions.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container specimens after last frost; downy jasmine grows rapidly in zone 9–11 and can be trained as a sprawling groundcover, a low hedge, or a soft mounding shrub depending on how it is pruned.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — downy jasmine is an Indian native jasmine widely grown along the Gulf Coast for its masses of small, starry, pure white flowers with a light, sweet fragrance produced from fall through spring during the cooler months. The soft, downy-hairy leaves and stems give it an appealing, fine-textured, gray-green appearance when out of bloom. It is a sprawling, loose shrub that can be used as a large-scale groundcover, a slope stabilizer, or a mounding informal hedge; with light pruning after bloom it stays tidy and compact. Unlike many jasmines, it tolerates partial shade and performs excellently along the shaded sides of buildings and fences. In zone 9 the foliage may drop or be damaged in hard freezes but the plant resprouts quickly from roots; in zone 10–11 it is fully evergreen. Extremely drought tolerant once established, requiring virtually no supplemental irrigation in adapted soils.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost date; surface-sow on moist medium as seeds need light to germinate. Transplant to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after frost danger has passed. Downy Lobelia re-seeds freely in favorable conditions.
directions: Downy Lobelia is a native perennial wildflower of the southeastern United States, native to moist woodlands, woodland edges, streambanks, and open meadows from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Texas, blooming from late summer to fall with dense spikes of bright blue-violet flowers that are excellent for attracting hummingbirds and bumblebees. Similar in appearance to the more widely cultivated Cardinal Flower (Lobelia cardinalis) and Great Blue Lobelia (Lobelia siphilitica), Downy Lobelia is distinguished by its downy-hairy stems and leaves and its preference for somewhat drier, better-drained soils than its relatives. A robust, short-lived perennial that perpetuates itself by self-seeding in the garden, it is a valuable late-season pollinator plant for naturalistic borders and woodland gardens in zones 5–9. Provide partial shade, moderately moist and slightly acidic soil, and allow seed heads to mature and disperse for natural re-seeding.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; downy maiden fern spreads by spores and short-creeping rhizomes and will naturalize freely in appropriate moist, shaded conditions in zones 8–11.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in zones 8–11; downy maiden fern is one of the most common and adaptable ferns in zone 9–10 Florida gardens, forming lush, bright green colonies in moist, shaded conditions under trees and in streamside settings. The soft, downy texture on the undersides of the fronds gives rise to the common name. Native to tropical Asia, Africa, and the Pacific, it has naturalized across the humid Southeast and behaves as a reliable year-round perennial in frost-free areas, dying back in hard freezes but re-emerging quickly. An excellent filler for wet, shaded spots in tropical and subtropical landscapes where few other groundcovers succeed. Note that this species is considered invasive in Hawaii and in some natural areas — in zone 9 continental Southeast landscapes it is generally well-behaved.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in sandy or well-drained soil in full to partial sun; scarify or nick seed coat lightly before sowing to improve germination, and inoculate with appropriate Bradyrhizobium rhizobial inoculant to activate nitrogen fixation.
directions: Direct sow in sandy or gravelly, low-fertility soil in full to partial sun after last frost; this twining native legume vine thrives in the poor, dry, sandy soils of the southeastern coastal plain where most garden plants fail, and fixes its own nitrogen through root nodule bacteria. Slender twining stems produce small pink-purple pea flowers from midsummer through early fall that are visited by native bees, and the vine is a documented larval host plant for gray hairstreak and other butterfly species, making it valuable in wildlife and pollinator gardens. It is a true perennial in zones 7-10, dying back to the roots after frost and re-emerging reliably from the root crown in spring. Avoid amending soil with compost or fertilizer as rich soils reduce flowering and encourage excessive foliage at the expense of blooms and seed production.

plant_note: Direct sow in autumn to allow seeds to cold-stratify naturally over winter; press seeds onto the soil surface without covering, as light aids germination.
directions: One of the most shade-tolerant goldenrods, Solidago petiolaris thrives in dappled woodland light and humus-rich, well-drained soil — a quality that sets it apart from most goldenrods which demand full sun. Sow seeds directly in autumn onto a lightly raked, moist seedbed and allow winter cold to break dormancy; seedlings emerge in spring and establish slowly before blooming the following year. Arching wands of bright yellow flowers appear August through October, providing a critical late-season nectar resource for bees and butterflies in shaded landscapes where few other plants bloom. Once established it spreads modestly by rhizome and self-seed, forming naturalistic colonies at the woodland edge.

plant_note: Plant only nursery-propagated specimens in fall in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full to partial shade under conifer or hardwood canopy; rattlesnake plantain requires an undisturbed, leaf-littered woodland floor with appropriate mycorrhizal support.
directions: Downy rattlesnake plantain is among the most attractive native orchids for year-round woodland interest — its distinctive rosettes of dark green leaves with a striking network of silver-white veins create a bold, graphic pattern reminiscent of a rattlesnake's scale markings that makes each plant an eye-catching feature of the forest floor throughout the year, regardless of the brief summer bloom. An evergreen, low-growing orchid of the leaf litter under eastern hemlock, pine, and mixed hardwood forests across a broad range from Canada to the Gulf Coastal Plain, it is one of the most shade-tolerant of all native orchids and thrives in the darkest parts of mature forest understory. In summer, a fuzzy, upright flower spike produces small, white, globular flowers pollinated by bumblebees; the spike can reach 16 inches tall and is ornamental in its own right. The striking foliage pattern was historically associated with snakebite medicine by some indigenous peoples — hence the 'rattlesnake plantain' name — though there is no medicinal efficacy. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants; wild plants depend on mycorrhizal fungi and rarely survive transplanting.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, cold-moist stratifying for 30 days first, and transplant into average to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun after frost has passed; downy skullcap tolerates a wide range of light conditions from open woodland edge to full prairie sun.
directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; drought-tolerant once established and tends to flop in overly rich or shady sites, so lean soil and good light produce the sturdiest plants. Scutellaria incana is a tall native mint-family perennial of open woodlands, savannas, and prairie edges across the eastern and central United States, named for the fine, soft, gray-white down covering its stems and the undersides of its leaves. In mid-to-late summer, branching spikes crowded with small, hooded, blue-violet flowers rise well above the foliage, providing a long bloom period that is a magnet for bumblebees and other native pollinators. Its height and airy branching habit make it a good back-of-border native for a sunny to lightly shaded wildflower meadow or woodland-edge planting, where it combines well with other prairie and savanna natives. Zone 4–8.

common_name: Downy Wood Fern (Tropical Woodfern, Shield Fern)
plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in full shade to part shade; downy wood fern is a naturalized tropical fern common across south Florida, the Gulf Coast, and tropical regions — it spreads rapidly and can form dense colonies in moist, shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade to part shade; downy wood fern spreads readily from spores and can naturalize in suitable conditions. Thelypteris dentata (downy wood fern or tropical woodfern) is an Old World tropical fern now naturalized across the Gulf Coastal Plain, Florida, Louisiana, and humid tropical regions of North America. A large, coarse-textured, rapidly spreading fern, it produces lush colonies of once-pinnate fronds 18–30 inches long with broadly lobed, soft-hairy leaflets giving the plant its 'downy' descriptor — the undersurface of the fronds has a distinctly soft, hairy texture when touched. In zone 8–12 shaded gardens, downy wood fern is one of the easiest and most heat-tolerant ferns to grow — it thrives where other ferns fail and spreads vigorously enough to function as a low-maintenance shade groundcover. It tolerates dry shade better than most ferns once established. While sometimes considered a weedy volunteer in tropical gardens (it self-propagates readily from windblown spores), it is genuinely useful for covering large, difficult shaded areas with minimal care. Some authorities include it within the broader Thelypteris palustris complex.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; downy yellow violet is the primary yellow-flowered violet of eastern woodland understories and naturalizes readily by self-seeding in appropriate conditions.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — downy yellow violet is the most common and widespread yellow-flowered native violet of eastern deciduous woodlands, producing bright yellow, purple-veined five-petaled flowers on hairy stems 6–14 inches tall in early to mid-spring, simultaneously with the emergence of the trout lilies and trilliums in the same woodland community. The broad, heart-shaped, softly hairy leaves (giving the common names 'downy' and 'hairy') are attractive throughout the growing season. It grows naturally in rich, moist, deciduous hardwood forest from Canada to the Deep South. Like all violets, downy yellow violet is a critical larval host plant for native fritillary butterfly caterpillars (Speyeria and Boloria species) — the presence of violets in a garden directly supports breeding populations of these spectacular native butterflies. Self-sows modestly to naturalize. Outstanding native for spring woodland wildflower gardens.

plant_note: Plant in spring with the crown a couple inches below the soil surface.
directions: Dr. Ruppel is a vigorous large-flowered clematis with pink, star-shaped blooms accented by a bold magenta bar down each petal. Give it a sunny position for the vines but keep the roots cool and shaded with mulch or low companion plantings. Provide a trellis, arbor, or fence for the climbing stems to grip, and tie in new growth as needed. This variety blooms on both old and new wood, so prune only lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead stems. Water regularly and feed in spring for the best flower show.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; dragon head bamboo is a clumping species that does not spread invasively, making it one of the safest and most garden-friendly hardy bamboos for home landscapes.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from hot afternoon sun; dragon head bamboo is a Chinese clumping (pachymorph) Fargesia that forms a graceful, non-invasive arching clump 10–14 feet tall with abundant small, narrow leaves on slender culms — no rhizome barrier needed. Its cold hardiness to –10°F (–23°C) and preference for partial shade make it an outstanding choice for woodland gardens, shaded borders, and north-facing sites where few large ornamental plants thrive. Unlike many bamboos, Fargesia species prefer cooler summers and may show heat stress in humid southern climates; they are best suited to zones 5–9 with cool to moderate summers. The compact, tidy clumping habit makes it ideal for smaller gardens where running bamboos would be inappropriate.

common_name: Dragon Scale Alocasia (Silver Dragon Alocasia, Baginda Alocasia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; Alocasia baginda is particularly susceptible to root rot — never allow the pot to sit in standing water and ensure the potting medium drains freely. Allow top 1–2 inches to dry before watering. Two cultivars are commonly available: 'Dragon Scale' (dark green with silver-gray scale pattern) and 'Silver Dragon' (pale silver-gray leaves with green venation). Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F. High humidity (60%+) prevents crispy leaf margins. Propagate from corm offsets. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light — Dragon Scale Alocasia needs good light to develop and maintain its distinctive scale patterning but cannot tolerate direct sun, which causes leaf bleaching and scorching on the sensitive leaf surface. Alocasia baginda is a compact, rhizomatous aroid native to Borneo (Sabah, Malaysia) in the Araceae family, one of the most extraordinary of the jewel alocasias for its unique leaf surface texture — a surface so precisely patterned that it bears a startling resemblance to the overlapping scale armor of a mythological dragon. The leaves are thick, leathery, broadly ovate with a slightly cordate base, and covered with a distinctive bumpy to quilted surface texture: each cell group between the veins forms a slightly raised, convex, scale-shaped unit that overlaps adjacent units in a regular, tile-like pattern — the overall impression is unmistakably of reptilian scales. In the 'Dragon Scale' cultivar, the background color is dark gray-green with silvery-gray scale highlights; in the 'Silver Dragon' form, the entire leaf appears pale silver-gray with green veins — a ghostly, luminous coloration unlike any other plant. The undersides are deep burgundy-purple. Two distinct cultivars circulate in the trade, both of extraordinary ornamental value in terrarium, collector shelf, and indoor tropical garden settings. All parts toxic.

common_name: Dragon Tail Plant (Centipede Tongavine, Cebu Blue Pothos, Tibatib)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, hanging basket, or shaded climbing vine in zone 9; Epipremnum pinnatum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or climbing surface to achieve the spectacular adult leaf form — trailing specimens maintain the smaller, silvery-blue juvenile 'Cebu Blue' leaves. In zone 10-11, it grows vigorously outdoors in deep shade, climbing tree trunks to produce enormous adult leaves. Propagate readily from single-node stem cuttings. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Dragon Tail Plant adapts to lower light in its juvenile form but requires adequate light and a vertical climbing support to progress to its spectacular adult leaf form. Epipremnum pinnatum is a large, climbing aroid vine native to Southeast Asia, the Pacific Islands, and northern Australia, distributed across an enormous range from India to Polynesia in the Araceae family. The plant exhibits one of the most dramatic cases of leaf dimorphism in common cultivation: in the juvenile trailing or hanging form, it produces narrow, elongated, slightly iridescent, silvery-blue-green leaves 4–8 inches long with no lobing — the form sold commercially as 'Cebu Blue Pothos' (though not a true Pothos). When the same plant begins climbing a rough surface and receives adequate light, it transitions progressively to the adult form: leaves become dramatically larger (up to 24–36 inches), dark green, and deeply pinnately lobed along the midrib in a pattern resembling a dragon's tail or centipede — giving rise to the common name 'Dragon Tail Plant.' The adult leaves develop fenestrations along the midrib similar to but distinct from Monstera. The transformation from slender blue juvenile to enormous pinnate adult is dramatic and rewarding for collectors who provide climbing support. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

common_name: Dragon Tail Rhaphidophora (Creeping Philodendron, Monster Dragon Tail)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or climbing container vine in zone 9; Rhaphidophora decursiva cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. A moss pole or coco coir totem is strongly recommended — the plant climbs rapidly and produces successively larger, more lobed leaves as it ascends. In zone 10-11 outdoors, it can climb large trees in shaded positions. Propagate from stem cuttings with at least one node and aerial root. Use a well-aerated aroid potting mix. All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Rhaphidophora decursiva transitions from attractive juvenile form to spectacular adult form most quickly in bright indirect light with a climbing support, remaining in the juvenile stage indefinitely if conditions prevent climbing. Rhaphidophora decursiva is a vigorous climbing aroid from South and Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, southern China, and across to the Philippines and Indonesia) in the family Araceae — not a Philodendron or Monstera despite being commonly mislabeled as both in commercial plant sales. The juvenile form produces simple, elliptical, glossy, dark-green leaves that are attractive but unremarkable. As the plant matures and climbs upward, the leaves transform progressively and dramatically: they enlarge significantly and develop deep pinnate lobing — the leaf divides into a row of distinct, finger-like segments radiating from the central midrib — eventually producing 24-inch leaves deeply cut almost to the midrib in a pattern resembling an enormous feather or a prehistoric wing, from which the common name 'Dragon Tail' derives. This adult form is often confused with Epipremnum pinnatum in its adult form (also called 'Dragon Tail') and with large pinnate Monstera species — all three can produce superficially similar adult leaves. Rhaphidophora decursiva is a fast grower that rewards patience with an extraordinary final form. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

common_name: Dragon Taro (Many-Leaved Dracontium, Dragon Arum, Giant Dragon Lily)
plant_note: Plant corm 4–6 inches deep in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, very well-drained, fertile soil; Dracontium polyphyllum is one of the most dramatically exotic-looking of the large tropical aroids, producing a single compound leaf on a single, spectacularly mottled, snake-skin-patterned petiole — the entire leaf can reach 4–6 feet across in mature specimens and is divided into dozens of leaflets arranged like a giant tropical fern frond. The mottled, green-and-brown, snake-skin-patterned petiole 3–5 feet tall is particularly dramatic. The corm blooms underground or near soil level on a short spadix before the leaf emerges, with a strong, fetid odor for 1–2 days. Dormant in winter. CAUTION: toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, fertile soil — Dragon Taro grows most spectacularly in the warm, moist, deeply shaded conditions of a sheltered tropical garden and produces one of the most dramatically exotic single-leaf structures of any ornamental plant when mature. Dracontium polyphyllum is a large, corm-based, deciduous perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to tropical South America (Colombia, Venezuela, Brazil, Peru, Ecuador) — one of approximately 22 species in the genus Dracontium, a group of large, highly ornamental aroids closely related to Amorphophallus. Like the related Amorphophallus, each Dracontium plant consists of a single, compound leaf emerging annually from an underground corm, preceded by an often briefly-fetid inflorescence at or near the soil surface. The leaf is the great spectacle: in Dracontium polyphyllum, it consists of a single, erect petiole (leaf stalk) 3–5 feet tall — dramatically patterned in irregular blotches and spots of brown, green, and gray, like a snake or dragon skin — topped by a massive, spreading, compound blade that divides repeatedly into dozens of individual leaflets arranged in a broad, flat, fern-frond or umbrella-like canopy reaching 4–6 feet across. The overall visual impression of a mature Dragon Taro leaf is extraordinary — an otherworldly, tropical umbrella combining exotic patterning and massive scale. In zone 10-12, the corm overwinters in the ground and produces a new leaf each spring. CAUTION: irritating if ingested raw.

common_name: Dragon Wing Begonia (AAS-Winning Heat-Tolerant Pendulous Annual Begonia)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or purchased transplants after last frost; Dragon Wing Begonia is typically sold as finished plants from nurseries (the standard series is vegetatively propagated). Plant in partial shade to full sun — one of the most heat-tolerant begonias available. In zone 9, Dragon Wing performs throughout the hot summer in areas with morning sun and afternoon shade, where standard impatiens fail from high temperatures. Space 12–18 inches for containers and beds; the cascading habit makes Dragon Wing excellent in hanging baskets.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in fertile, well-drained soil or potting mix after last frost; provide regular moisture and monthly fertilizer. Dragon Wing Begonia received AAS recognition in 2000 (Dragon Wing Red) for exceptional heat tolerance combined with large, pendulous, continuously-blooming performance — two attributes that distinguish it markedly from standard wax begonias (B. semperflorens). Standard wax begonias are compact, mound-forming plants with small flowers (0.5–1 inch) that tolerate heat reasonably well but become stressed in extended high temperatures. Dragon Wing grows as an open, somewhat pendulous plant with large, glossy, dark green, wing-shaped leaves and clusters of large (1.5–2 inch) pendulous flowers in bright red or pink that hang in elegant, semi-cascading clusters. The pendulous, open habit makes Dragon Wing exceptional in containers and hanging baskets where the flowering branches spill attractively over the edge. The extreme heat tolerance — Dragon Wing continues to bloom vigorously in temperatures that shut down impatiens and stress standard begonias — makes it one of the most reliable summer shade container plants for the Gulf South. Dragon Wing performs acceptably in full sun in the Gulf South when moisture is consistent, but performs optimally in partial shade.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Dragon Wing begonias are significantly more heat-tolerant than wax begonias and continue blooming through summer heat that causes other shade begonias to decline — an important advantage in zone 9 summers. In zone 9 the plant often overwinters with frost protection, developing into a large, impressive specimen in its second and subsequent years. Large containers (12–15 gallon) allow the plant to reach its full impressive size.
directions: Plant in partial shade to dappled light in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil or container mix; Dragon Wing Red is a large-growing cane-type (angel wing) begonia with pendant clusters of vivid crimson-red flowers hanging in graceful arching sprays above glossy, wing-shaped, asymmetric dark green leaves — the pendant flower clusters and arching canes create a weeping, tropical appearance unlike the mounded, dense form of tuberous or wax begonias. The large plant size (24–36 inches) and continuous, profuse flowering without deadheading make Dragon Wing Red the most impressive of the summer-blooming shade begonias for large container and landscape use. Unlike tuberous begonias and most wax begonias, Dragon Wing demonstrates significantly better tolerance for summer heat and maintains blooming performance through warm humid conditions — a critical advantage for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens. The showy pendant flower clusters attract hummingbirds and are among the most visually dramatic of any shade-tolerant flowering plant.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Dragon's Blood spreads into a dense, low mat with deep burgundy-red summer foliage tones and clusters of small star-shaped red flowers in mid-to-late summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun. Dragon's Blood is a classic groundcover sedum forming a dense, spreading mat of rounded, fleshy leaves that deepen to rich burgundy-red in full sun and cooler weather, topped in mid-to-late summer with clusters of small, star-shaped, deep red flowers that draw butterflies and bees. It spreads readily by rooting along creeping stems, making it a reliable, low-maintenance groundcover for dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and the edges of paths, and it tolerates poor, lean soil and drought far better than most groundcovers. It needs almost no care beyond an occasional trim to control spread into neighboring plantings.

common_name: Dragon's Breath Celosia (Dark Burgundy Foliage Plume Celosia)
plant_note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or direct sow after soil warms; Dragon's Breath combines nearly black-burgundy foliage with vivid crimson plumes, giving it strong ornamental impact in beds and containers through Gulf South summer heat, which celosia tolerates better than most bedding annuals.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once the soil has warmed, and transplant or thin to 10-14 inches apart in full sun. Dragon's Breath is a wheat-type celosia (Celosia spicata) selected for foliage so dark it reads as near-black in most light, providing dramatic contrast for the slender, upright, bright crimson-red flower plumes held above it from midsummer through frost. Unlike many bedding annuals, celosia thrives in the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer, often blooming most heavily during the weeks when cooler-season annuals have stalled out, and it tolerates considerable drought once established. The dark foliage makes it a striking foil for silver- or chartreuse-leaved companions, and the flower plumes are excellent both fresh and dried for arrangements, holding color and form well after cutting. Deadhead spent plumes to encourage continued branching and bloom, and stake taller plantings in windy, exposed sites since the flower heads can become top-heavy.

common_name: Drake Chinese Elm (Semi-Evergreen Gulf South Shade Tree)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Drake Chinese elm is fast-growing, tolerates heat, drought, and urban conditions well, and is resistant to Dutch elm disease, unlike American elm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Drake is a graceful, fast-growing selection of Chinese elm valued for its attractive mottled, exfoliating bark, fine-textured foliage, and semi-evergreen habit that holds leaves later into fall and winter than most deciduous shade trees across much of the Gulf South. Unlike American elm, it shows strong resistance to Dutch elm disease and also tolerates heat, drought, and compacted urban soils well, making it a popular street and shade tree throughout Texas and the Deep South. Its arching, weeping branch habit gives mature specimens an elegant silhouette, and it needs only routine structural pruning when young to develop strong branch angles for long-term storm resistance.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring in acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: Dream Weaver is a sasanqua camellia bearing abundant double blooms of deep pink to lavender edged in white, flowering from fall into winter. Plant it in partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, and mulch to keep roots cool. Protect from harsh afternoon sun and drying winds, especially in warmer zones. Prune lightly right after flowering to shape the evergreen form. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer in spring for lush foliage and reliable bloom.

common_name: Dressler's Anthurium (Panama Velvet Anthurium, Bullate Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to moderate indirect light in very well-draining, chunky aroid mix; Anthurium dressleri is an epiphytic species that grows naturally in the canopy of Panamanian rainforests and requires excellent drainage and aeration at the root zone — bark-based epiphyte mixes work well. Maintain consistently moist media and high humidity (70%+). Avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 60°F. This is a slower-growing, collector-grade species. Propagate from seed or stem cuttings. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a chunky, bark-based, fast-draining epiphyte mix with high humidity — Dressler's Anthurium is naturally an epiphyte that perches in tree canopies and grows best in conditions that replicate that airy, moist, well-drained environment. Anthurium dressleri is an epiphytic aroid endemic to Panama in the Araceae family, named in honor of botanist Robert Louis Dressler, valued in the collector community for its extraordinarily textured leaf surface and impressive scale. The leaves are large (18–36 inches long), broadly ovate to cordate with a thick, leathery texture, and covered with a dense, velvety, dark emerald-green surface of exceptional quality. The primary feature that distinguishes A. dressleri from related velvet anthuriums is the strongly bullate (quilted or puckered) surface: the spaces between the deeply sunken primary veins are raised, forming a pattern of convex, rounded, pillow-like inter-vein panels that gives the entire leaf a distinctly three-dimensional, corrugated, quilted texture — visually similar to the quilted surface of other prized anthuriums like A. warocqueanum but with its own distinct character. The deeply impressed veins contrast with the raised surface panels to create a strongly patterned, sculptural leaf. An elite collector's anthurium for serious tropical growers with appropriate humidity and temperature conditions. All parts toxic.

plant_note: Divide established clumps every 4–5 years in spring or plant container-grown plants in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Agapanthus inapertus is more cold-hardy than the common Agapanthus praecox, surviving to zone 7 with mulch protection. It blooms later (August–September) than other species, extending the agapanthus season. The pendant, tubular flowers are distinctively different from the more open, funnel-shaped flowers of A. praecox.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; drooping agapanthus is a South African species that extends the agapanthus season into August and September, blooming a full month or more after most agapanthus species have finished. The flowers are distinctively pendant (drooping) and tubular — nodding downward from the umbel rather than opening broadly upward as in Agapanthus praecox — and are an intensely deep, midnight-blue to violet-blue, one of the richest blues achievable in any summer perennial. This combination of late bloom, pendant flower form, and exceptional depth of color makes it unlike any other agapanthus. The narrow, strap-like leaves are somewhat more deciduous than evergreen species. It is one of the more cold-hardy agapanthus species, tolerating zone 7 with adequate mulch. Excellent as a late-season focal point in mixed borders and for extending the agapanthus display well into late summer and fall.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the plant naturalizes by suckering to form attractive colonies along stream banks and shaded slopes.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deeply acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; drooping leucothoe is a graceful native evergreen shrub of mountain stream banks and ravines in the Southern Appalachians, with long arching stems clothed in lustrous lance-shaped leaves that turn bronzy-burgundy-purple in winter — one of the finest winter foliage colors in the shade garden. Tiny white bell-shaped flowers in May are fragrant and nectar-rich for early bees. The plant spreads by stolons to form a layered, naturalistic colony that suppresses weeds effectively. The cultivar 'Rainbow' has cream-pink-green variegated foliage; 'Girard's Rainbow' and 'Zeblid' (Scarletta) are also widely available. All parts are toxic. Excellent massed under rhododendrons, azaleas, or as an understory layer beneath oaks.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, calcareous to slightly acidic, lean, dry soil in full sun; drooping prairie coneflower grows naturally in dry prairies and open roadsides from Texas to Louisiana and the south-central US.
directions: Plant in well-drained, calcareous to slightly acidic, lean, dry soil in full sun; drooping prairie coneflower is a Gulf Coastal Plain relative of the familiar Mexican hat (R. columnifera) and tall coneflower (R. pinnata), producing bright yellow ray petals that characteristically droop or reflex downward around the prominent, elongated central cone — the same growth form that makes all ratibidas distinctive. It is adapted to the calcareous, thin, rocky or sandy soils and harsh summer heat of the Gulf South, making it more heat-tolerant than R. pinnata. The flowers attract numerous native bees and the seed heads provide winter food for goldfinches and sparrows. An excellent, low-water native for dry, sunny, prairie-style gardens and roadsides in zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in well-drained to moderately moist, average to humus-rich soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Drooping Star-of-Bethlehem is excellent for naturalizing under deciduous trees and in dappled shade situations, where it spreads steadily and blooms reliably each spring with little or no maintenance. It is vigorous and can spread extensively by offsets in favorable conditions — site with care if spread needs to be controlled, but it is excellent for filling areas of dry or difficult shade.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained to moderately moisture-retentive, average soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees in fall for April-May bloom; Drooping Star-of-Bethlehem is the most shade-tolerant of the commonly grown ornithogalums and distinguished from the common O. umbellatum by its larger stature, later bloom time, and most distinctively by its elegantly arching, one-sided flower spikes bearing up to 20 large, nodding, white flowers with broad silvery-white inner petals and conspicuous green outer stripes that give the backs of the flowers a bold two-toned appearance — hence the species name nutans, meaning nodding. It blooms in April and May under deciduous trees and naturalizes freely by bulb offsets in suitable shaded conditions, forming expanding colonies year after year in dry or semi-dry shade situations where many other plants fail. The flowers are excellent for cutting and last well in a vase. All parts of this plant are toxic if ingested; handle with normal precautions and site away from areas accessible to children and pets.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall; like all trilliums, drooping trillium takes 5–7 years from seed to first flower and requires 18+ months of stratification for germination. Plant in moist, humus-rich, calcium-rich to neutral, well-drained soil under deciduous trees in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, calcium-rich to slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; drooping trillium is a pedicellate trillium (flower on a stem, held above the leaf whorl) with large, pure white flowers that nod downward or horizontally — the drooping or bending of the flower stalk is the characteristic that gives it both common and scientific names (flexipes = bent foot). It grows naturally in rich, calcium-rich, mesic forests — particularly common in beech-maple forests over limestone — across the central and upper Midwest. One of the taller and more robust pedicellate trilliums, with large, broad leaves and fragrant white flowers that may age to pink or red-purple as they age. The attractive berries in late summer are eaten by birds and small mammals that disperse the seeds. Plant only nursery-propagated stock; wild collection is illegal in most states.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow after frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. This branching mix delivers 4-5 inch florist-quality blooms in deep burgundy, valentine red, and pumpkin-orange-red shades on strong stems ideal for cutting. Sow successively every couple weeks for continuous bouquets through the season. Water evenly while young and stake in windy sites, since heavy branching heads can lean.

plant_note: Divide established plants in spring or fall, or sow seeds in well-drained, lean, neutral to strongly alkaline, chalky or limestone soil in full sun; dropwort is completely distinct from the closely related meadowsweet and queen of the prairie, which require consistently moist soil — dropwort actually prefers dry, calcareous, well-drained conditions and performs poorly in wet soil. The cultivar Multiplex (Flore Pleno) has beautiful double white pompom flowers and is the most widely grown ornamental selection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to strongly alkaline, chalky or gravelly soil in full sun; dropwort is the drought-tolerant, lime-loving member of the Filipendula genus — completely unlike the moisture-demanding meadowsweet (F. ulmaria) and queen of the prairie (F. rubra). It grows naturally in the short-grass calcareous meadows and chalk downs of Europe and Asia where it thrives in the thin, alkaline soils and dry summers that defeat most moisture-loving perennials. The beautiful, finely cut, fern-like foliage forms an attractive mound above which creamy-white to pale-pink flower clusters appear in June and July, fragrant and attractive to bees. The wild species has single flowers, but the cultivar Multiplex (also sold as Flore Pleno) has charming double pompom flowers that give the flower clusters a denser, more ornamental quality. The small, tuberous, carrot-like roots were used as food in early European history. Outstanding for chalk gardens, dry limestone borders, and other alkaline, well-drained positions.

plant_note: Seeds need darkness to germinate; cover completely.
directions: Cover the seed completely because Drummond phlox requires darkness to germinate. Direct sow in early spring in mild climates or start indoors six weeks before the last frost. The clustered flowers come in a wide range of colors and make excellent low bedding and cut arrangements.
