plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; eared lady fern tolerates more warmth and humidity than Japanese painted fern (A. niponicum) and is an excellent choice for warmer temperate shade gardens in zones 5–8.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; eared lady fern is a Japanese native in the same genus as the celebrated Japanese painted fern (Athyrium niponicum 'Pictum') but with distinct and beautiful ornamental qualities — the bipinnate fronds are a rich, lustrous, dark-green color, and the stipes (leaf stalks) and rachises (midribs) are a striking deep wine-red to burgundy color that provides vivid two-tone contrast throughout the growing season. The reddish rachis color persists through the entire frond surface, creating a subtle but attractive color effect visible throughout the growing season. It forms a tidy, non-spreading clump unlike some invasive ferns and is a reliable performer in warmer shade gardens where the Japanese painted fern sometimes struggles. Excellent combined with hostas, Japanese forest grass, and astilbes in classic shade garden compositions.

common_name: Early Amethyst Beautyberry (Compact Early-Fruiting Purple Beautyberry)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Early Amethyst is a compact selection of purple beautyberry that fruits earlier and more heavily than the species, with clusters of vivid violet-purple berries lining arching branches in fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Early Amethyst is a compact selection of Asian beautyberry prized for producing an especially heavy, early display of small, intensely violet-purple berries clustered tightly along graceful, arching branches in fall, after inconspicuous pink summer flowers. Its smaller mature size compared to native American beautyberry makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens, though the vivid fall berry display is just as striking. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so a hard pruning in late winter to a foot or two from the ground each year encourages the most vigorous new growth and heaviest berry set the following fall.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall immediately after collection; early meadow rue seed requires cold-moist stratification and declines in viability quickly — fall sowing is strongly preferred over spring. Plants are dioecious (separate male and female individuals), so sow multiple plants to ensure both sexes for seed set.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade under a deciduous canopy, where early meadow rue takes advantage of the winter-spring light window before the forest canopy leafs out; it is one of the earliest eastern North American native wildflowers to bloom, bearing delicate drooping clusters of greenish-purple, petal-less flowers in April and early May that are wind-pollinated and have a quiet, understated beauty quite unlike showier spring ephemerals. The blue-green, finely divided compound leaves — resembling a miniature maidenhair fern in texture and color — are among the most beautiful in the native shade garden and remain ornamental throughout the entire growing season long after bloom. This species is dioecious: male plants bear conspicuous hanging yellow anthers and are showier in flower; female plants are needed for seed set. Note: all parts are mildly toxic if ingested and the plant should not be consumed. Allow to self-sow undisturbed to naturalize across the woodland floor.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost; soak seed overnight to speed germination.
directions: Soak seed overnight, then direct sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost at the base of a trellis or support. This blend blooms up to two weeks earlier than typical early types, producing mildly fragrant flowers in nearly every color but yellow on long sturdy stems. Keep the roots cool and evenly moist, and cut flowers often to prolong blooming before summer heat. Note that parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or gravelly soil in partial shade to full sun; early saxifrage grows naturally on shaded rock outcrops, rocky slope forests, and gravelly woodland edges across eastern North America.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or gravelly, well-drained soil in partial shade; early saxifrage is one of the earliest native wildflowers to bloom in the eastern woodland, producing sprays of tiny, white, star-shaped flowers on slender stems in late winter to early spring while the woodland floor is still cold. The basal rosette of spatula-shaped leaves remains close to the ground all year, providing evergreen ground cover. The plant grows naturally on rocky outcrops, clifftops, and gravelly, shaded slopes where excellent drainage and relatively sparse competition from other vegetation allow it to persist. An excellent early-blooming native for rock gardens and shaded, well-drained slopes, providing critical early nectar for queen bumblebees and early mining bees. The 'saxifrage' name (rock-breaker) references its habit of growing in rock crevices.

common_name: Earth Star Bromeliad (Starfish Plant, Bi-banded Cryptanthus)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant, terrarium plant, or shaded patio container in zone 9; Earth Star Bromeliad cannot tolerate frost. Unlike most bromeliads, it has no central water cup and grows directly in the soil — use a well-draining, peat or coir-based mix. Unlike the tank bromeliads, water it through the soil like a regular potted plant. High humidity (50–70%) and consistent warmth improve appearance. Excellent for terrariums where humidity is maintained naturally. Propagate by removing pups from the base after the main plant flowers. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Earth Star Bromeliad is one of the most shade-tolerant bromeliads, maintaining its attractive appearance and best color in conditions of moderate indirect light; intense direct sun bleaches the coloration. Cryptanthus bivittatus is a small, flat, terrestrial bromeliad native to Brazil in the family Bromeliaceae, one of approximately 70 species in the genus Cryptanthus (the only bromeliad genus that is entirely terrestrial — all other bromeliads are at least partially epiphytic). The plant produces a flat, star-shaped (hence 'Earth Star') rosette of narrow, stiff, slightly spiny-edged leaves that are wavy and spread horizontally just above the soil surface. In the species and common cultivars, the leaves are marked with two lengthwise stripes (the 'bivittatus' — 'two-banded') of cream-white or pink against a bronze-green to reddish-brown background — but the hundreds of Cryptanthus hybrids and cultivars available today cover an extraordinary range of colors, stripes, waves, and textures in red, pink, purple, bronze, copper, cream, green, and multicolor combinations, making the genus among the most colorful in the bromeliad family. Small, inconspicuous white flowers appear in the center. Unlike the tank bromeliads, Earth Stars absorb water through their roots rather than a central cup, making them uniquely suited to terrarium culture. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil warms.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. Earthwalker is a side-branching sunflower in warm earthy tones of orange, mahogany, coppery brown, and rusty red, excellent for cutting and for feeding bumblebees and seed-eating birds. Because it branches, a single plant supplies many stems over a long period. Water regularly while establishing and stake in exposed sites to keep tall stalks upright.

common_name: East Friesland Salvia (Classic Compact Purple Meadow Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; East Friesland is an older, well-proven German-bred cultivar known for reliable rebloom when sheared after the first flush of flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Introduced from German breeding decades ago, East Friesland was one of the first widely available compact hardy salvias and remains a dependable garden standard, producing dense, upright spikes of rich reddish-purple flowers over a tidy, low mound of aromatic gray-green foliage. Shearing the spent flower spikes back by about half in early summer prompts a strong second flush of bloom later in the season. It is drought-tolerant, deer- and rabbit-resistant, and a strong bee and butterfly attractant, making it a reliable front-of-border choice, though it may act as a shorter-lived perennial in the hot, humid summers of zone 9.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; East Palatka is female and requires a male Ilex opaca or I. cassine within 50 feet for heavy berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; East Palatka holly is a naturally occurring hybrid of Dahoon holly (Ilex cassine) and American holly (Ilex opaca) selected from natural hybrid populations near Palatka, Florida, and has been widely used in southeastern landscape plantings for decades. Like Savannah holly, East Palatka is a large, fast-growing, upright-pyramidal evergreen tree, but it is distinguished by a somewhat more open branching habit and leaves with typically only a single apical spine at the tip rather than the multiple spines of standard American holly, making it less prickly and easier to handle. The single-spined leaves and the plant's natural origin deep in the Gulf Coastal Plain make it exceptionally well-adapted to zone 9 heat and humidity. Female plants loaded with small red berries in fall and winter are spectacular wildlife plants, attracting migrating and wintering songbirds. East Palatka is particularly well-suited to Florida, coastal Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana conditions where the high humidity and heat stress some landscape hollies. Requires a male pollinizer for heavy fruit production. Widely available in Gulf Coast nurseries and highly recommended by the University of Florida IFAS Extension for sustainable Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Heliconia wagneriana is one of the more cold-sensitive heliconias and requires consistently warm conditions — in zone 9a, protect rhizomes with heavy mulch in winter and expect top growth to die back. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a large, reliable perennial with spectacular spring bloom coinciding with Easter. The large inflorescences are among the most prized in the heliconia family for cut flower use — long vase life of 3–4 weeks.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Easter Heliconia grows most vigorously and produces its largest inflorescences with morning sun and afternoon shade protection in zone 9-10's intense climate. Heliconia wagneriana is a large, clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, and Ecuador in the Heliconiaceae family, named for an early botanical collector and commonly called 'Easter Heliconia' because its natural blooming peak in the Northern Hemisphere typically coincides with the Easter season (March–April). The plant produces large, erect inflorescences (flower spikes) 24–36 inches long with 8–12 alternating, boat-shaped bracts in a spectacular color combination: the bracts are bright red to deep orange-red with bright yellow edges and green-tipped margins, giving the inflorescence a multi-colored, rainbow-like appearance that is unique among commonly grown heliconias. The precisely alternating arrangement of the bracts, each perfectly clasping the next, creates an almost geometric, architectural inflorescence. Heliconia wagneriana is highly valued in the cut flower industry for its extraordinary inflorescences, which have vase lives of 3–4 weeks when properly conditioned. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida tropical gardens, established clumps produce multiple inflorescences per season and become impressive landscape features.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall, or divide established clumps in early spring; eastern beebalm is more drought-tolerant and mildew-resistant than the common scarlet beebalm (Monarda didyma) and is better adapted to dry, thin, alkaline soils. It blooms 2–4 weeks earlier than other beebalm species.
directions: Sow seeds or divide in spring in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; eastern beebalm is the most compact and drought-tolerant of the native monardas, producing a tidy mound of aromatic foliage topped in late spring (May–June) with lavender-white to pale pink flowers with distinctive purple-spotted lips that are excellent for bumblebees, native sweat bees, and early-season butterflies. Unlike the taller, powdery-mildew-prone Monarda didyma, eastern beebalm stays under 2 feet and has outstanding mildew resistance even in humid climates. It blooms substantially earlier than other beebalms, bridging the gap between spring flowers and summer bloomers in the pollinator garden. Native to prairies, open woodlands, and rocky roadsides from Illinois to Kansas and south to the Gulf Coast, it is particularly well adapted to the heat and variable moisture of the South and Midwest.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or plant transplants in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; eastern blazing star is adaptable to a range of dry to medium-dry garden conditions and is one of the easiest blazing stars to establish in the Eastern garden.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant transplants in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; eastern blazing star is adaptable to a range of dry to medium-dry garden conditions and is one of the easiest blazing stars to establish in the Eastern garden. Liatris scariosa is one of the showiest of the eastern blazing stars, producing very large (up to 1.5-inch), rounded, button-like purple flower heads on tall stems from August through September; the large flower heads make it easy to identify in the field and give it exceptional ornamental impact compared to the more narrow-flowered species. Native to open woods, rocky slopes, sandy barrens, and open glades from New Hampshire to Georgia, it supports specialist native bees and is an important fall migration nectar source for monarch butterflies; it is the primary blazing star for ornamental use in eastern garden designs.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seeds require chilling to break dormancy and will germinate the following spring.
directions: Eastern Blue-eyed Grass thrives in moist to wet meadows, rain gardens, and pond margins where its slender, grass-like foliage blends naturally into turf or sedge communities. Sow seeds in fall directly onto the soil surface without burial, as light aids germination after cold stratification. Pale to mid-blue, six-petaled flowers with bright yellow centers appear from April through June and are especially attractive to small native bees. Once established, plants self-seed freely in moist, fertile spots and require little maintenance beyond occasional division to prevent overcrowding.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Eastern bluestar is adaptable to a wide range of conditions including clay soil, occasional wet feet, and light shade under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Eastern bluestar is a superb, long-lived native perennial that delivers three distinct seasons of ornamental value — clusters of small, pale powder-blue, star-shaped flowers in mid-spring, dense, shrubby, fine-textured mounds of glossy foliage that never need staking or deadheading all summer, and spectacular golden-yellow fall color that rivals even ornamental shrubs. It is unusually adaptable, performing well in clay, moist soil, partial shade, or full sun. The milky sap is mildly irritating; wear gloves when dividing. Shear plants back by one-third after bloom to maintain compact form. 'Storm Cloud' and 'Blue Ice' (dwarf) are cultivated selections. Deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and virtually problem-free.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants (or hardwood cuttings rooted in moist soil) in spring in moist, well-drained, sandy or loamy alluvial soil in full sun. Eastern Cottonwood grows extraordinarily fast — up to 6–8 feet per year — but is short-lived (60–100 years) and prone to branch breakage in ice storms; plant male cultivars to avoid the cottony seed mess of female trees.
directions: Eastern Cottonwood is the fastest-growing native tree in North America, capable of adding 6–8 feet of height per year in moist, fertile, alluvial soils — a growth rate no other native tree approaches — and is native to the river bars, floodplains, and moist bottomlands of virtually every drainage system in eastern and central North America from Quebec to Florida and west to the Rockies. The triangular (deltoid) leaves tremble and shimmer in the slightest breeze due to their flattened petioles, creating a distinctive rustling sound audible at considerable distances; in late spring, female trees produce enormous quantities of cottony-tufted seeds that fill the air like midsummer snow, settling on every surface and creating what many observers find an enchanting spectacle and others find a nuisance. An important pioneer tree for streambank stabilization and riparian restoration, Eastern Cottonwood provides critical early-successional habitat for many birds and insects. Plant male cultivars to avoid seed dispersal; provide full sun and deep, moist soil near water features or for rapid windbreak and privacy screening.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; eastern gamagrass performs best in deep, rich bottomland soils and tolerates periodic flooding — it establishes from seed slowly but grows vigorously once rooted.
directions: Eastern gamagrass is among the most ancient and important native grasses of North America — as the wild ancestor and closest relative of corn (Zea mays), it was once a dominant grass of the tallgrass prairie and Gulf Coast bottomlands and is now valued both ecologically and for its productive, high-quality forage that can exceed corn in protein content. Dense, arching clumps of broad, corn-like leaves produce jointed seed spikes in summer bearing large, hard, nutritious seeds that are edible and were historically ground into flour by indigenous peoples of the southeastern United States; wildlife from wild turkey to deer consume the seeds and foliage extensively. Eastern gamagrass tolerates partial shade, seasonal flooding, and mowing and can be managed as a productive pasture grass in areas too wet for most warm-season grasses; as a landscape plant its bold, corn-like texture and tolerance of moist bottomland conditions make it ideal for rain garden borders, bioswales, and moist native meadows. Clumps expand slowly over years and can be divided in spring to propagate additional plants.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown shrubs in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline soil in full sun; eastern groundsel tree is extremely adaptable — tolerating salt spray, flooding, drought, clay, sand, and alkaline conditions. It can become weedy by seeding; female plants produce the seed, so male plants are less weedy.
directions: Plant in almost any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; eastern groundsel tree is a large, fast-growing, fall-blooming native shrub of coastal and inland wetland edges from Massachusetts to Texas, valued primarily for its extraordinary fall display when female plants produce dense, silky-white seed heads (pappi) in such abundance that the plant appears to be covered in brilliant white cotton or snow. Male plants produce the inconspicuous but nectar-rich cream-white flowers in September and October that attract monarch butterflies, native bees, and insects before seed set. It is among the most salt-tolerant and flood-tolerant native shrubs of the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts — growing in coastal marshes, salt spray environments, and periodically inundated soils where few ornamentals survive. Equally valuable inland as a fast-growing screen or wildlife shelter shrub. The brilliant white fall seed heads of female plants are stunning in the autumn landscape. A critical ecological shrub for the coastal plain.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or early spring in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, cool, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; eastern hemlock is one of the few conifers that actually grows better in shade than in full sun, especially in zone 6–7 where afternoon shade is essential. Treat proactively for hemlock woolly adelgid in eastern US with imidacloprid soil drench.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, cool soil in partial to full shade — eastern hemlock is the only large native conifer that genuinely thrives in shade and is often the dominant tree in cool, shaded, north-facing ravines and steep, moist slopes where other conifers cannot compete. The delicate, feathery, dark green foliage and graceful, pendulous branch tips create an exceptionally beautiful, textured specimen in the shade garden. It is considered a foundational 'keystone' species supporting 96 species of Lepidoptera caterpillars, and its dense, multilayered canopy provides critical winter shelter for birds. However, the hemlock woolly adelgid, an introduced pest from Asia, has devastated populations throughout the eastern range — all planted trees in the eastern US should receive preventive treatment with systemic insecticide. In zone 3–7, an irreplaceable shade conifer for the woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; eastern larch grows naturally in cold bogs, wet forest edges, and well-drained upland soils across the boreal zone. One of the most cold-hardy trees in North America — tolerating temperatures to -65°F in its northern range.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; eastern larch (tamarack) is the hardiest of North American conifers, native to the boreal forests from Labrador to Alaska and south to northern Minnesota, growing even at the edge of the Arctic tundra. Like all larches it is a deciduous conifer — the soft, blue-green needles emerge in clusters in spring, providing a feathery appearance, then turn a brilliant golden yellow in fall before dropping, producing a spectacular effect unusual among conifers. In bog habitats, tamarack grows in pure stands or with black spruce. The small cones persist on the tree for several years. The flexible, rot-resistant wood was used by many northern indigenous peoples for snowshoe frames, basket ribs, and boat ribs. Excellent for bog gardens, moist areas, and extremely cold climates in zones 1–6 where few other conifers are adapted.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in any well-drained to moist, acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; eastern ninebark is one of the most adaptable and tough native shrubs — tolerating clay, poor soil, drought, flooding, and partial shade once established. Prune out the oldest stems to the base every 2–3 years to maintain vigorous growth; the shrub can also be rejuvenated by cutting to within 6 inches of the ground in late winter.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; eastern ninebark is a native shrub of eastern North America prized for two distinct ornamental features — exfoliating bark that peels and shreds in layers on mature stems (creating year-round textural interest in winter, when the orange-brown inner and grayish outer bark peel apart in curling strips, hence 'ninebark') and, in late spring, dense clusters of small, creamy-white to pale-pink flowers attractive to many native pollinators. The dark-purple to burgundy foliage cultivars such as 'Diabolo' (very deep purple-black leaves) and 'Summer Wine' (somewhat more compact, wine-red foliage) have become mainstays of the mixed shrub border, providing a bold, dark, non-green foliage contrast through the entire growing season. 'Coppertina' has coppery-orange new growth fading to burgundy. The compact cultivar 'Little Devil' stays 3–4 feet. Native across a huge range from Ontario to Georgia in river banks, woodland edges, and bluffs, it is exceptionally tolerant of difficult sites including clay, flooding, and urban conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in fall or early spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; Eastern Red Cedar is extremely adaptable and tolerates poor, thin, rocky, dry, alkaline, and compacted soils where few other trees will grow. Female plants produce berries only when male plants are nearby.
directions: Eastern Red Cedar is the most widely distributed conifer in eastern North America, native from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to the Great Plains, colonizing abandoned fields, roadsides, fence lines, and rocky glades with a tenacity matched by few other native trees — it is the quintessential first colonizer of open, disturbed ground in eastern North America and has expanded its range dramatically following suppression of natural fire and the abandonment of agricultural fields. The aromatic, reddish-brown wood was historically prized for cedar chests, pencils, and fence posts due to its rot-resistance and insect-repelling properties; the fleshy, glaucous-blue, seed-bearing 'cones' (botanically berries) are an essential winter food for cedar waxwings, bluebirds, mockingbirds, and dozens of other birds, and the dense, scale-like foliage provides critical winter nesting cover. Eastern Red Cedar is a host for the alternate life stage of cedar-apple rust (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae), which can infect nearby apple trees — avoid planting within 1,000 feet of apple orchards. An extremely tough, drought-tolerant, adaptable native tree for landscapes from zone 2–9.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or cold-stratify seed 4 weeks before spring sowing. Surface sow only — seed needs light to germinate. Self-seeds freely once established.
directions: Sow on the soil surface in partial shade to full sun in moist to well-drained, average soil; wild columbine is a delicate native perennial of rocky woodlands, ledges, and open forest edges whose unique red-and-yellow nodding spurred flowers in April–June are the primary nectar source for ruby-throated hummingbirds returning from spring migration. The blue-green, lobed foliage is attractive all season. Plants self-seed prolifically and naturalize freely in appropriate conditions — allow seedlings to establish a colony rather than removing all volunteers. Short-lived (3–5 years) but self-perpetuating through seeding. Columbine leaf miners leave unsightly tunnels in foliage; tolerate minor damage or simply remove affected leaves.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; Eastern redbud transplants best when young (4–6 feet) and resents being moved once established. Site in part shade in hot climates — afternoon shade is essential in zones 8–9 to prevent leaf scorch.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Eastern redbud is one of North America's most beloved native understory trees, erupting each spring in clouds of vivid magenta-pink flowers that cover the bare branches for two weeks before the heart-shaped leaves emerge — one of the most spectacular floral displays of any temperate tree. The flat, pea-like flowers are edible and can be added to salads, pickled in vinegar, or used as a colorful garnish. After flowering, the attractive rounded to heart-shaped leaves provide clean summer shade, turning golden-yellow in fall. The species is native from New Jersey to Nebraska and south to northern Florida, making it well-adapted to the Gulf Coast from zone 7 through 9 with afternoon shade; 'Oklahoma' and 'Texas White' are compact heat-tolerant cultivars excellent for the South. The weeping form 'Traveller' and the dark-foliaged 'Forest Pansy' are outstanding landscape selections.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or stratify seeds for 60 days and sow in early spring in dry, lean, sandy or rocky, acidic soil; eastern silvery aster is a specialist of well-drained, infertile, sandy or rocky soils and declines quickly in rich, moist conditions. It spreads slowly by rhizomes in appropriate dry soil.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, sandy or rocky, acidic to slightly acid soil in partial shade to full sun; eastern silvery aster is one of the most distinctive fall-blooming natives of the southeastern Coastal Plain, covered in a dense silver-gray pubescence (fine silky hairs) on the stems, leaves, and involucres that gives the entire plant a soft, felted, gray appearance even before the lavender-pink flowers open in late summer and fall. This distinctive silver foliage makes it attractive from spring through frost as a low-growing, silvery-textured specimen in dry garden conditions. It grows naturally in dry, sandy pine flatwoods and open woodlands along the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain — one of its few real habitats — making it unusually appropriate for zone 9a gardens in lean, sandy soils. The flowers attract migrating monarchs and numerous native bees. Avoid fertilizer and irrigation, which cause floppy, unattractive growth.

plant_note: Start transplants indoors 8 weeks before last frost or direct sow on the soil surface in late fall for spring germination; eastern smooth beardtongue adapts to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light partial shade.
directions: Start transplants indoors 8 weeks before last frost or direct sow on the soil surface in late fall for spring germination; eastern smooth beardtongue adapts to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light partial shade. Penstemon laevigatus is a southeastern native beardtongue that grows naturally along forest margins, roadsides, and moist open woods from Virginia to Florida and west to Louisiana; it produces large, white to pale lavender, tubular flowers with purple guidelines in the throat that are held on tall, upright racemes from late spring through early summer, providing nectar for ruby-throated hummingbirds, long-tongued bumblebees, and native carpenter bees. Unlike many western penstemons, it thrives in the humidity and summer rainfall of the Southeast; it is one of the most reliable and heat-tolerant penstemon species for Gulf Coast and mid-Atlantic gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; eastern turkeybeard is specific to pine barrens and mountain slopes in strongly acidic soils and resents fertile or alkaline conditions.
directions: Plant in dry to moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; eastern turkeybeard grows naturally in pine barrens, sandhills, and rocky mountain slopes from New Jersey to Georgia in strictly acidic, nutrient-poor, fire-adapted communities that are difficult to replicate in gardens but rewarding to attempt. Xerophyllum asphodeloides produces a dense clump of stiff, needle-like, grass-like leaves up to 24 inches long from which arises in late spring a tall, stout flowering stem bearing an impressive, dense, cylindrical spike of tiny, fragrant, creamy white flowers 6–12 inches long that are spectacular in bloom and an important pollen source for native bees. Individual plants may take several years to bloom but are very long-lived; the clump expands slowly. Do not add compost, lime, or fertilizer — this plant thrives on infertility and acidity. An outstanding accent plant for acid-soil gardens and pine barren restoration.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; this is a native alternative to the invasive Asian burning bush (E. alatus).
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; eastern wahoo is a native alternative to the invasive Asian burning bush (Euonymus alatus) and performs the same landscape function — stunning fall color — while supporting native wildlife instead of escaping into woodlands. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant scarlet-red while the seed pods split open to reveal dangling bright coral-pink and orange arillate seeds that attract migratory birds including thrushes, bluebirds, and waxwings. The purple-tinged flowers in late spring are modest but charming. The plant tolerates deep shade and is one of few shrubs that thrives under the dense canopy of mature oaks and maples. All parts are toxic to humans and livestock. This is the true 'burning bush' of the native landscape.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; eastern white pine grows naturally in a wide variety of well-drained, slightly acidic soils but will not tolerate salt spray, heavy clay, or compacted urban conditions. Avoid exposed, windy hilltops.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; eastern white pine is the largest native pine in the eastern US — straight, fast-growing, and graceful, with distinctive soft, blue-green needles in bundles of five and long, curved, resinous cones. At maturity, the old trees develop a characteristic flat, spreading, wind-sculptured crown that is one of the most distinctive silhouettes in the eastern American landscape. Historically one of the most important timber trees in North America — the tall, straight trunks were marked with the broad arrow as masts for the British Royal Navy, a source of colonial conflict. The flexible, soft needles are distinctive among eastern pines. Young trees make fast-growing screens and hedges when sheared. Particularly effective as a windbreak or background planting. Blister rust (Cronartium ribicola) is a serious disease threat in some areas; plant rust-resistant selections when available.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist to well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; eastern woodland sedge spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a low, turf-like groundcover and is much easier to establish from divisions than from seed.
directions: Plant in moist to average, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; eastern woodland sedge is a low, graceful, soft-textured native sedge of eastern US woodlands that forms a loose, arching groundcover in shaded conditions where grass will not grow. Unlike many sedges, it adapts well to moderately dry conditions once established and tolerates the competition of tree roots under mature oaks and maples. The slender, bright green leaves arch gently to about 12–18 inches, providing a fine, grass-like texture in the shade garden. Excellent as a low-maintenance lawn substitute under trees, or as a no-mow groundcover that requires no fertilizer, irrigation, or edging once established. Seeds are eaten by several sparrow species. Naturally colonizes disturbed woodland edges and is one of the most adaptable native sedges for garden use.

common_name: Easy Wave Petunia (Seed-Raised Trailing Spreading Annual Petunia)
plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; petunia seed is tiny and requires light for germination — sow on the surface without covering and keep at 70°F under lights. Easy Wave petunias are more compact than the original Wave series and better suited to containers and hanging baskets. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring bloom; a fall planting in September–October produces excellent winter blooms. Easy Wave tolerates more heat than standard petunias and continues to bloom in conditions that stress standard types.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, sterile starting mix under bright light (no covering — needs light); maintain at 70°F until germination. Transplant carefully after last frost. Easy Wave is a seed-raised version of the famous Wave petunia breeding line from PanAmerican Seed/Ball Horticultural — developed to bring the spreading, trailing habit and continuous bloom of the vegetatively-produced Wave series into a form that home gardeners can grow from seed. The original Wave petunias (Purple Wave, AAS 1995) are vegetatively propagated cuttings sold as finished plants; Easy Wave produces very similar performance from seed. The spreading, trailing habit distinguishes Wave-type petunias from standard petunias: instead of growing as a compact mound, Easy Wave spreads outward (18–24 inch spread) and slightly cascades, creating the 'wave' of color for which the series is named. Easy Wave petunias are low-maintenance — they self-clean (fallen petals drop cleanly), are more heat-tolerant than standard petunias, and bloom continuously without deadheading. The spreading habit makes them exceptional as groundcovers, in hanging baskets where the trailing branches spill over the edge, and in containers where they fill and overflow attractively.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Elaeagnus x ebbingei is extremely adaptable and actually performs best in lean to average soils — avoid planting in rich, heavily amended soil where rank, soft growth is excessive.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ebbinge's Silverberry is a vigorous, large-growing evergreen hybrid elaeagnus — a cross between Elaeagnus macrophylla and E. pungens — producing large, broadly oval, silvery-green to silver-backed leaves on arching, fast-growing stems that create a substantial evergreen screen or windbreak in one to two growing seasons. The large, silvery-underside leaves give the shrub a distinctive, gleaming silver-gray appearance in breezes when the undersides catch the light. In fall, small, creamy-white, intensely sweet-fragrant flowers are produced — remarkably fragrant for small, inconspicuous flowers — followed by small, orange-red berries in spring that are edible (sweet-tart when ripe) and attractive to birds. Like its parent E. pungens, Ebbinge's Elaeagnus is one of the most remarkably tough and adaptable landscape shrubs available: tolerating drought, salt spray, wind, poor soils, alkaline conditions, and coastal exposures that defeat most evergreen shrubs. It grows by nitrogen fixation through root nodules, enriching the surrounding soil. The fast, dense growth and salt tolerance make it outstanding for coastal windbreaks and screening. 'Gilt Edge' and 'Limelight' are named cultivars with bold golden-yellow leaf variegation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist to dry, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; ebony spleenwort is one of the most adaptable and drought-tolerant of all native ferns, succeeding in both moist woodland and dry, rocky conditions in shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist to dry, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade — ebony spleenwort is one of the most widely distributed and adaptable native ferns in North America, distinguished by its narrow, once-pinnate fronds on shiny, dark reddish-brown to black (ebony) stems that give it its common name. It grows in an extraordinary range of conditions: dry, rocky woodland slopes; bases of limestone outcrops; pine forest floors; moist ravine walls; and the dry shade under large trees where most ferns would fail. Unlike many ferns, it tolerates moderately dry, rocky conditions that defeat less adaptable species. The fronds are semi-evergreen in zone 7–9, providing year-round greenery in shaded gardens. It self-sows by spores to naturalize quietly in appropriate shaded, well-drained conditions, never becoming weedy. An outstanding low-maintenance fern for dry shade under trees in southern gardens.

common_name: Echeveria (Hen and Chicks Succulent, Mexican Echeveria)
plant_note: Plant in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, gritty soil in full sun to light shade; Echeveria requires excellent drainage above all else — more plants are lost to overwatering and wet winter soil than to cold. In zone 9, most Echeveria species tolerate brief light frosts to 28–30°F when well-established and dry.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; excellent drainage is the single most important requirement for Echeveria — the plants are extraordinarily tolerant of neglect, heat, and drought but will rot rapidly in waterlogged or continuously moist soil. Echeveria is the quintessential rosette-forming succulent of Mexican origin, encompassing over 150 species and hundreds of named hybrids and cultivars that form the backbone of the global succulent garden hobby — their perfect rosette geometry, frosted or wax-coated silvery-blue to green to purple-red leaves, and jewel-like appearance have made them the most photographed succulents in the world. The rosettes range from marble-sized miniatures to dinner-plate-sized giants; flower spikes rise 6–18 inches above the foliage in spring and summer with bell-shaped, orange, yellow, red, or pink flowers that attract hummingbirds. Echeveria propagates readily from leaf cuttings (leaves gently twisted off and left to callus, then placed on moist gritty soil), stem cuttings, and offsets (chicks) produced by the mother hen rosette. In humid Gulf Coast climates, Echeveria should be planted in raised beds or containers with excellent drainage; humidity-tolerant species like E. peacockii, E. imbricata, and E. runyonii perform better in coastal gardens than the most sensitive species. Outstanding as container specimens, in rock gardens, and in xeric landscape designs.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 16–20 weeks before desired outdoor transplant date; in zone 9 start seeds July–August for fall transplanting (September–October) for winter bloom, or start October–November for February–March transplanting for spring bloom. Lisianthus seed is extremely fine and often comes pelleted for easier handling — do not bury, as light is required for germination. The long lead time from seed to bloom (150–200 days) makes lisianthus one of the longest-season annuals. The Echo series is one of the most reliable lisianthus series for garden performance — bred for heat tolerance and resistance to botrytis. In zone 9 lisianthus blooms November–April; it declines in summer heat and is grown as a cool-season crop.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–7.5) soil with consistent moisture — Lisianthus is unusual among cut flower crops in preferring near-neutral or slightly alkaline soil conditions rather than the acidic soil preferred by most floriculture crops; Echo Blue Lisianthus is a leading commercial lisianthus cultivar producing the double, ruffled, blue-to-blue-violet flowers that represent one of the most elegant and sophisticated floral presentations available from any annual cut flower crop — the multiple layers of tissue-thin, ruffled petals and the rich blue color combining to create a flower that resembles a combination of a rose and a poppy in blue. Lisianthus (Eustoma grandiflorum) is a native wildflower of the US prairies and southern states that has been developed into one of the most valuable commercial cut flower crops in the world — the cut stems lasting 1–3 weeks in a vase, making them among the longest-lasting of all cut flowers. The blue-to-purple color range of Echo Blue is particularly valuable in cut flower work where true blue flowers are rare and high-value. For zone 9 gardeners growing lisianthus as a cool-season annual (November–April), the long growing time required is rewarded with one of the most sophisticated and beautiful cut flower crops available from any home garden.

common_name: Ecuador Velvet Philodendron (Verrucosum Philodendron, Velvet-Leaf Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole or bark support in bright indirect light with chunky, well-drained aroid mix; Philodendron verrucosum is a climbing, hemi-epiphytic species that grows best when its aerial roots have something to attach to. Maintain consistently moist but not saturated media and high humidity (60–80%+) — this species naturally grows in humid cloud forest environments. Cooler nighttime temperatures (60–65°F) can intensify the golden venation on the leaves. Propagate from stem cuttings with a node. All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in chunky, well-aerated potting mix with a climbing support — Ecuador Velvet Philodendron climbs vigorously and produces progressively larger leaves as it ascends a moss pole or bark surface. Philodendron verrucosum is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid from the cloud forests of Ecuador, Colombia, Peru, and Costa Rica in the Araceae family, widely considered one of the most beautiful velvet-leaved philodendrons in the collector trade and globally sought by tropical plant enthusiasts. The leaves are large (up to 18–24 inches on established climbing stems), broadly cordate (heart-shaped), and covered in a dense, velvety, dark forest-green surface with a distinctive iridescent sheen and a bold pattern of yellow-gold to pale gold primary and secondary veins that stand out brilliantly against the dark velvet background. The petioles are clothed in fine, bristly hairs (the 'verrucose' quality — warty or bumpy) in shades of yellow-green to pinkish. The undersides of the leaves are deep maroon-red to burgundy — a rich color contrast visible whenever the leaves catch air movement. The leaf texture, venation pattern, and color combination make P. verrucosum one of the most photographed and desired philodendrons in modern tropical plant collecting. All parts toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost — seeds are extremely fine and should be pressed onto the soil surface without covering; transplant after last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost, pressing the dust-fine seed onto moist surface-sown seed mix without covering — seeds need light to germinate; grow on in a bright window until after last frost, then transplant to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade for best summer longevity. Edging lobelia is a South African native producing masses of small, two-lipped flowers in intense sky-blue, violet, white, or magenta-rose in a continuous cascade from spring through early summer, then again in fall after summer heat abates and it is typically sheared back. The plant blooms most prolifically in cool weather and fades in peak summer heat; afternoon shade significantly extends its performance in hot summer climates. Popular for container edges, hanging baskets, and formal bed borders. 'Crystal Palace' (deep blue, bronze foliage), 'Cobalt Blue', and 'White Lady' are classic selections.

common_name: Edith Bogue Magnolia (Cold-Hardy Upright Southern Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Edith Bogue has a narrower, more upright form than most Southern magnolia cultivars — a significant advantage in smaller spaces.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Edith Bogue is the most cold-hardy Southern magnolia cultivar available for routine landscape use — surviving temperatures as low as -10°F and reliably winter-hardy in zone 5 where no other Southern magnolia cultivar can be grown. The cultivar originated from a tree planted by Edith Bogue in Montclair, New Jersey, that survived severe winters that killed all other Southern magnolia selections in the area. This exceptional cold hardiness expands the range of the magnificent Southern magnolia northward into climate zones previously inaccessible to the species. Beyond cold hardiness, Edith Bogue has a distinctly narrower, more columnar to pyramidal habit than most Southern magnolia cultivars — a significant advantage in residential landscapes where the typical broad, spreading form of standard Southern magnolias would require too much space. The upright form makes Edith Bogue appropriate for tighter spaces along buildings, driveways, and in urban settings. The glossy, dark-green leaves with a lighter underside and the classic creamy-white, deeply fragrant flowers (8–12 inches across) are characteristic of the species. In zone 9, it performs superbly — the superior cold hardiness is not needed in the Gulf South, but the narrow habit is a consistent advantage.

common_name: Edith Wolford Bearded Iris (Blue-and-Gold Bicolor Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Edith Wolford is a multiple-award-winning bearded iris known for its striking two-toned blue-and-gold blooms.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Edith Wolford is one of the most honored bearded iris cultivars of the late 20th century, winning the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal, and is prized for its striking bicolor blooms combining soft butter-yellow standards (upper petals) with deep violet-blue falls (lower petals), a color combination that stands out strongly in the spring border. The tall, sturdy stems hold up well in wind and rain, and the clump multiplies at a good pace, benefiting from division every three to four years after bloom to keep it vigorous. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Edward Goucher blooms continuously from spring through frost, producing successive flushes of the lavender-pink tubular flowers that are distinctly more colorful than white-flowered Abelia x grandiflora. Prune lightly after the first spring flowering flush to maintain shape and stimulate reblooming; avoid heavy pruning that removes flowering wood. In zone 9 this abelia is nearly evergreen, losing only a portion of its leaves in the coldest winters. It tolerates pruning into a formal hedge but looks best when allowed to develop its naturally graceful, arching habit.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Edward Goucher Abelia is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most freely in full to partial sun; Edward Goucher is a hybrid abelia cross between Abelia x grandiflora and Abelia schumannii, producing a medium-sized (4–5 foot), gracefully arching shrub with distinctly more colorful flowers than standard white-flowered abelia — the small, tubular flowers are lavender-pink to lilac-pink, creating a softer, more distinctly colored floral display that continues from late spring through frost. The semi-evergreen to nearly evergreen foliage has a refined, fine texture, and the new growth emerges with a bronze-red tint that transitions to dark green — adding foliage color interest beyond the continuous flower display. Abelia in general is one of the most butterfly-attractive landscape shrubs available in zone 9, and Edward Goucher's colored flowers enhance this quality — the lavender-pink flowers are particularly attractive to swallowtails, skippers, and sulphurs throughout the long bloom season. The combination of zone 9 adaptability, long bloom season, drought tolerance once established, and the graceful natural habit has made Edward Goucher one of the most classic and enduringly popular landscape shrubs for Gulf South gardens since its introduction.

common_name: Egyptian Papyrus (Nile Grass, Paper Reed, Papyrus Sedge)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches deep) or in constantly wet, boggy soil at the pond's edge in full sun to partial shade; Cyperus papyrus grows vigorously in zone 9 humid conditions and spreads by thick rhizomes. In zone 9a, the tops die back in hard frosts but rhizomes survive if the root zone stays above freezing — mulch heavily or maintain in water that doesn't freeze solid. Divide clumps every 2–3 years. Excellent in containers set in decorative water bowls or water features.
directions: Plant in shallow water, boggy pond margins, or constantly wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Egyptian Papyrus requires reliably moist to wet conditions and will decline rapidly if allowed to dry out. Cyperus papyrus is the famous tall sedge of the Nile Delta — the same plant used by ancient Egyptians to produce papyrus paper, one of the earliest writing materials, by splitting and layering the inner pith of the tall stems. In zone 9 Gulf Coast water gardens, it creates an extraordinary tropical effect: triangular, bright green stems rise 5–10 feet tall topped by enormous, spherical, light and airy umbels of thin radiating bracts tipped with tiny flower clusters — the silhouette of a giant, architectural feather duster or sparkler held at the top of a pole. Multiple stems from a single clump sway gracefully in breezes, creating constant motion. The plant also produces smaller stem-tip cuttings that can be inserted upside-down in water to produce offsets (whip propagation). In the humid Gulf Coast climate, Egyptian Papyrus grows with exceptional vigor in water gardens, pond margins, rain gardens, and boggy corners of the landscape. It is naturalized in parts of the Gulf Coast and Florida where escaped plants colonize canal banks and wetland margins.

common_name: Eleanor Taber Indian Hawthorn (Deep Pink-Flowered Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Eleanor Taber is valued for its deep rose-pink flowers, showier than the paler pink or white of many Indian hawthorn selections.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom, though it tolerates partial shade with somewhat reduced flowering. Eleanor Taber is a long-popular Indian hawthorn selection prized for its especially deep, rich rose-pink flower clusters in spring, a stronger color than the softer pinks and whites typical of the species, set against the same leathery, dark green, disease-resistant foliage. Like other Indian hawthorn selections it is outstanding for coastal Gulf landscapes, tolerating salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soil with ease, and needs only a light shaping prune right after spring bloom to keep its naturally tidy, rounded form. Good air circulation helps reduce Entomosporium leaf spot, the main disease concern for Indian hawthorn in humid climates.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil before the last frost; in mild climates sow in fall for winter and spring bloom.
directions: Soak seed overnight and sow in cool soil several weeks before the last frost, or in fall where winters are mild. This blend offers mildly scented, long-stemmed cut-flower cultivars that flower in the short days of winter and cool spring. Provide a trellis, keep roots cool and evenly moist, and harvest often to extend the bloom period. Parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil before the last frost for spring and early summer bloom.
directions: Soak the seed overnight and sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost beside a sturdy trellis. This striking variety bursts with large ruffled blooms in electric magenta-red and a powerful sweet perfume, carrying three to four flowers per long, sturdy stem. Keep roots cool and consistently moist, and cut frequently for vase-worthy bouquets that hold well. Parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, so site it away from children and pets.

common_name: Elegans Camellia (Chandleri Elegans, Pink Anemone-Form Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Elegans has a spreading, somewhat horizontal habit — allow 6–8 feet of space on all sides at planting to accommodate its eventual spread.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Elegans is one of the oldest and most historically celebrated Camellia japonica cultivars in American horticulture — introduced by English nurseryman Alfred Chandler in 1831 and still one of the finest camellias for landscape and specimen use nearly two centuries later. The large, anemone-form flowers display a distinctive structure with five large, broad outer guard petals in deep rose-pink to shell-pink surrounding a central boss of densely packed, smaller, petaloid stamens (petaloids) in the same pink color — creating a unique, shaggy, high-centered flower form quite different from the flat formal doubles or simple singles of other camellias. The large flowers — up to 4 inches across — are exceptionally showy and produced in mid-season (December through March in zone 9). The shrub develops a characteristically spreading, somewhat horizontal habit that is distinctive from the more upright growth of most japonica camellias, eventually reaching 5–10 feet tall and 6–10 feet wide. 'Elegans Champagne' is a sport with white petals and yellow petaloids; 'Elegans Supreme' has ruffled pink petals. Provide morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9, consistent moisture, and acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Elegans develops its best glaucous blue-gray color and largest leaf size in partial to full shade — direct sun bleaches the blue tones to yellow-green and scorches the large leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Elegans is one of the most magnificent large-leaved hostas ever selected — a cultivar of Hosta sieboldiana (the blue siebold hosta) that produces exceptionally large (up to 18 inches long, 14 inches wide), heavily corrugated, intensely glaucous blue-gray leaves arranged in a massive, layered, bowl-shaped mound. The intense blue-gray color, the deeply puckered and corrugated leaf surface that catches shadows and creates dramatic texture, and the sheer scale of a mature plant (2–3 feet tall, 4–6 feet wide after several years) make Elegans one of the most impressive foliage plants available for the shade garden — a bold focal point that commands attention from any distance. In summer, pale lavender-white flowers appear on sturdy scapes above the foliage — modest flowers, but a pleasant accent to the dominant foliage display. Elegans grows slowly but steadily, becoming more magnificent each year; a 10-year-old plant in ideal conditions can reach 5–6 feet in diameter. In zone 9, hostas perform well in deep shade with consistent moisture and mulched soil — the combination of shade, moisture, and mulch moderates soil temperature enough to maintain the hosta through the Gulf South summer. Divide in early spring every 5–8 years when clumps become crowded or vigor declines.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; Elephant Bush tolerates brief temperatures to about 28–30°F when established and dry, making it useful for zone 9b–12 landscapes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun to light shade; Portulacaria afra (Elephant Bush, Dwarf Jade, or Spekboom in Afrikaans) is a South African succulent shrub and small tree that is both one of the most ecologically important plants on earth and one of the most practical ornamental succulents for warm, dry landscapes. In its native South Africa's Eastern Cape, spekboom forms vast thicket ecosystems and is one of the most efficient carbon-sequestering plants known — Kruger National Park estimates that spekboom thicket sequesters 4–10 times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforest. As a garden plant, Elephant Bush is valued for its ease of care, attractive small rounded succulent leaves (resembling jade plant Crassula ovata but faster-growing and more heat-tolerant), and its edible, pleasantly sour leaves used in South African salads and stews. The shrubs grow rapidly in warm conditions (up to 3 feet per year in zones 10–12), are extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established, and root easily from stem cuttings. The leaves are eaten by elephants (hence 'Elephant Bush'), baboons, and other wildlife in the wild. Excellent as a low-water landscape shrub, large container specimen, or informal hedge in zone 9b–12; root cuttings easily to propagate. The similar-looking variegated form (leaves edged in cream) is widely grown as a decorative specimen.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; elephant ear begonia requires good air circulation to prevent fungal issues — in humid climates, overhead watering should be avoided and plants should be spaced to allow air movement around the hairy leaves, which can trap moisture if too crowded.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; elephant ear begonia (Begonia scharffii, syn. B. haageana) is one of the largest and most architecturally impressive of the shrub begonias — it grows with a stout, upright, branching, cane-like habit reaching 3–5 feet, with enormous, asymmetric, heart-shaped leaves that can reach 12 inches or more in length, rich olive-green on the upper surface and vivid deep-red on the undersides, with both surfaces covered with soft, silvery-white hairs that give the foliage a luminous, textured quality in low light. Large, pendant clusters of white to pale-pink flowers with prominent yellow stamens are produced at branch tips throughout the warm season. The hairy, large-leaved, red-backed foliage and the bold shrubby habit combine to make it a commanding specimen in shaded gardens, large containers, and conservatories. It tolerates lower humidity better than most shade-growing tropical plants and is one of the easier large begonias to grow as an overwintering indoor houseplant in cool climates. An outstanding architectural shade specimen for zone 10–12 outdoor gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock or scarified, soaked seeds in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; Guanacaste is the national tree of Costa Rica and one of the most impressive shade trees of Central America — it is fast-growing and drought-tolerant once established but requires protection from frost below 30°F.
directions: Scarify seeds with sandpaper and soak overnight before sowing; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; provide frost protection when young. Enterolobium cyclocarpum (Guanacaste or elephant ear tree) is one of the most massive and magnificent tropical shade trees of Central America — the national tree of Costa Rica — growing to an enormous size with a broadly spreading crown reaching 80–100 feet in diameter that provides extraordinary shade. The common name 'elephant ear tree' comes from the distinctive, flat, dark-brown, ear-shaped seed pods 2–4 inches across that resemble a stylized elephant ear. The tree produces fluffy, white, powder-puff flowers followed by distinctive coiled pods containing 6–15 seeds surrounded by edible, sweet, pulpy flesh used in traditional beverages in Costa Rica. The seeds are high in protein and have been used as animal feed. The wood is valuable for furniture and construction throughout Central America. In zone 10–12 gardens with no frost risk, the tree is a spectacular choice for large-scale tropical landscaping where its enormous size can be accommodated; it grows fast (to 15–20 feet in 3–4 years) and eventually dominates the landscape.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; elephant foot is a native woodland understory perennial of the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern US that thrives in the dappled shade of pine and hardwood forests — an important nectar plant for native butterflies that is rarely available in nurseries but easy to grow from seed in shaded spots.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; thin to 12 inches and allow to self-seed. Elephantopus tomentosus (elephant foot or tobacco weed) is a native perennial wildflower of eastern North American woodlands and the Gulf Coastal Plain — common in the pine and hardwood forest understory from Virginia through Florida and Texas but rarely cultivated, despite being a genuinely useful and attractive shade-garden native. The plant produces a basal rosette of large (6–10 inch), broadly oval, hairy, slightly crinkled leaves (the 'elephant foot' shape that gives it its name) and branching flower stalks 18–30 inches tall in late summer–fall bearing small, lavender-purple, composite flower heads loosely clustered at the branch tips. The flowers, while individually small, are produced in loose, graceful clusters and are strongly attractive to native bees and skippers. A long-lived, easily self-seeding perennial for woodland and shade-garden naturalization, elephant foot is an excellent native companion for ferns, coral bells, and other shade plants in Gulf Coast understory gardens. Essentially maintenance-free in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; Amorphophallus bulbifer is distinguished from A. konjac by producing small aerial bulbils (tiny tubers) in the axils of its leaf divisions — these bulbils fall and self-propagate, making this species the easiest amorphophallus to multiply in the garden.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; elephant foot yam is an Indian tropical aroid that produces a brief, dramatic, pink-green and mottled spathe over a dark, club-shaped spadix in spring (with a mild carrion odor for one day), then emerges with one or two enormous, intricately divided, single compound leaves — each leaf rising from a single upright stem on a dramatically patterned, mottled, snake-skin-like, gray-green and brown-spotted petiole, spreading the leaflets of a single deeply compound leaf into an elegant, tropical umbrella form reaching 2–4 feet across. The most distinctive feature distinguishing A. bulbifer from other amorphophallus is the production of small, brown, edible aerial bulbils (tiny tubers, about the size of large marbles) that form in the leaf axils at the junction of the leaflets — these bulbils drop and self-propagate freely in suitable warm, shaded conditions. More cold-tolerant than the similar A. konjac in zone 7. An outstanding, easily grown, and self-multiplying shade garden aroid for tropical and warm temperate gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in dry to moderately moist, sandy, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; elephant's foot grows naturally in dry to moist, sandy, open pine flatwoods and woodland edges of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; elephant's foot is a distinctive native of the southeastern Coastal Plain, named for its unusually large, rough, basal leaves that spread flat along the ground like the wrinkled feet of an elephant. The plant sends up tall, branched stems in summer topped with small, composite lavender-purple flower heads enclosed in leaf-like bracts — an unusual and ornamentally distinctive inflorescence structure. The flowers attract numerous small bees and butterflies. A shade-tolerant native that provides interest in dry, sandy, partial-shade conditions of pine flatwoods and open woodland gardens in zone 9a. A native plant that is extremely common as a 'weed' but underappreciated as an ornamental.

common_name: Ellamae Agapanthus (Large Blue Lily of the Nile)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ellamae is a large-growing agapanthus that benefits from ample space to form broad clumps — allow 24–30 inches between plants at planting, and resist dividing until the clump is truly overcrowded and bloom quality declines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Ellamae is a robust, large-growing agapanthus cultivar that is one of the most widely grown and best-performing selections for warm-climate gardens — producing large, arching clumps of wide, strap-like, dark-green evergreen leaves from which tall (4–5 foot) flowering scapes rise in summer, each bearing large, dense globular heads of deep blue-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers. The large flower heads are spectacular in mass plantings and outstanding as cut flowers — lasting well in arrangements. Ellamae is more cold-hardy than many agapanthus, tolerating brief freezes to about 10–15°F, and it thrives in zone 7–11 as a reliable perennial where it forms ever-expanding clumps over the years. In zone 9, Ellamae blooms from June through August in full sun, with the season extending into September in partial shade. The large, stately habit — with foliage clumps reaching 2–3 feet and flower scapes rising to 4–5 feet — gives it a sculptural, architectural quality exceptional for creating bold masses along fences, walls, and drives. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. Divide only when clumps become overcrowded — large, mature clumps produce the most spectacular flower displays.

common_name: Ellen Bosanquet Crinum (Classic Wine-Red Fragrant Crinum Lily)
plant_note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Ellen Bosanquet is one of the most celebrated crinum cultivars for its rich, deep wine-red, fragrant flowers.
directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Ellen Bosanquet is widely regarded as one of the finest crinum lily cultivars ever introduced, producing large clusters of intensely fragrant, deep wine-red, trumpet-shaped flowers held on tall, sturdy scapes above strap-like evergreen foliage. Once established, the massive bulb persists and multiplies for decades with essentially no care, making it a classic pass-along plant of old Southern gardens and cemeteries. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil conditions with ease, and division is rarely necessary, since crinum bulbs actually bloom best when left undisturbed and slightly crowded.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall. Elliott's Aster is naturally adapted to wet, seasonally flooded soils in coastal plain habitats from zone 7b–10 and tolerates both extended wet periods and seasonal drought once established. In zone 9 it blooms prolifically in October–November, one of the latest natives to flower, providing nectar at a critical time for migrating monarch butterflies.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained to periodically wet soil; Elliott's Aster is a native fall-blooming aster of the Southeastern Coastal Plain and Gulf Coast, producing spectacular masses of lavender to purple daisy flowers with yellow centers on 3–5 foot stems in October–November — among the latest native wildflowers to bloom in zone 9. The prolific late-season bloom covers the plant in hundreds of small flowers and provides critical nectar for migrating monarchs, native bees, and late-season pollinators when other nectar sources have shut down. Elliott's Aster is naturally adapted to the wet, poorly drained soils of coastal plain habitats, including wet edges of ponds, drainage ditches, and low spots in the landscape where most other ornamentals struggle. It tolerates brief flooding and heavy clay soils far better than most native asters. Cut back to 6 inches in late winter before new growth emerges; divide crowded clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Elliott's bluestem is a warm-season native grass that establishes quickly from seed and is well-adapted to the nutrient-poor, sandy soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Elliott's bluestem is a native warm-season grass of the southeastern Coastal Plain, prairies, and longleaf pine savannas, producing upright clumps of blue-green foliage that turn copper to reddish-bronze in fall — among the finest native grasses for fall and winter color in zone 8–10. The feathery seed heads emerge in late summer, catch the light, and provide winter bird food. It is notably tolerant of the nutrient-poor, well-drained, sandy soils that characterize much of the Gulf Coastal Plain — a quality that makes it excellent for low-maintenance naturalized plantings, coastal restoration, and xeric landscape areas. It performs best in lean soils; rich, amended soil causes excessive growth and floppy stems. An outstanding component of native plant gardens, butterfly gardens, and longleaf pine understory plantings throughout zone 8–10.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, acidic soil; seeds require cold-moist stratification over winter and will germinate the following spring — do not cover seeds, as light aids germination.
directions: Elliott's Gentian is a native perennial of southeastern wet savannas, pitcher plant bogs, and seepage slopes, producing some of the most intensely colored violet-blue tubular flowers of any eastern wildflower during September through November — often the very last wildflower blooming before hard frost. It is genuinely difficult to cultivate and requires close replication of its native habitat: consistently moist to wet, highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), nutrient-poor, sandy or peaty soil in partial sun, as well as the presence of specific mycorrhizal fungal associates in the soil that the plant depends on for long-term survival. Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall without covering them, as they need cold stratification and light for germination; expect very slow seedling growth, with plants typically requiring two or more years to reach blooming size. This species is best established from seed directly into a naturalistic savanna or bog restoration rather than in a conventional garden setting, as transplanting is difficult and container-grown specimens rarely persist without their native fungal partners.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun in spring; Elliott's lovegrass is tolerant of heat, drought, and salt spray, making it ideal for coastal and hot, dry southern landscapes.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, sandy to loamy, poor to average soil in full sun; Elliott's lovegrass (blue lovegrass) is a native southeastern US ornamental grass with unusually attractive blue-gray to silver-blue foliage — the narrow, arching leaves have a distinctly glaucous quality that is rare among warm-season grasses and provides cool, silvery-blue contrast in the summer landscape. Open, delicate panicles of tiny, silvery-purple spikelets appear in summer and fall, creating a misty, translucent effect when backlit. The plant is highly adaptable to the difficult coastal and sandy soils of the Gulf South, tolerating salt spray, drought, and poor soil conditions with negligible care. A natural choice for low-water, native-plant, and coastal landscape designs in zones 7–10. Does not become as weedy as some lovegrass species.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; elm-leaved goldenrod is one of the most shade-tolerant goldenrods in the eastern US, blooming reliably in the conditions of an open woodland understory.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — elm-leaved goldenrod is an eastern North American native recognized by its leaves, which closely resemble elm leaves with strongly toothed, slightly rough-textured blades on short petioles. It grows naturally in moist, open woodland and woodland edges, making it one of a small number of goldenrods genuinely adapted to shaded conditions. The arching, one-sided (secund) racemes of small golden flowers appear in late summer through fall in shaded locations where most goldenrods cannot bloom. Like blue-stemmed goldenrod, it fills an important ecological niche by providing late-season nectar and pollen in shaded settings where pollinators searching for fall resources would otherwise find nothing. Spreads by rhizome to form a colony. An excellent native goldenrod for adding late-season ecological value to the woodland garden.
