plant_note: Direct sow after frost; compact enough for containers.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost about an inch deep in full sun, spacing 8-12 inches apart. This blend of shorter, branching sunflowers includes classic single forms and multi-petaled pom-pom types that draw pollinators and make cheery bouquets. Their compact, drought-tolerant habit suits containers, borders, and small gardens. Water regularly while young and deadhead to keep new blooms coming.

common_name: Emarginate Dimerandra (Pink Rock Orchid, Dimerandra, Caribbean Rock Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork, or in a small slatted basket with coarse bark medium in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun; Dimerandra emarginata is a relatively cold-tolerant epiphytic orchid from lowland tropical areas of the Caribbean and Central America, adapting to zone 9b-12 in warm, protected outdoor positions. It blooms throughout the warm months in zone 9-10 with cheerful small pink flowers. Water regularly in active growth; reduce in winter. The compact, reed-like growth habit makes it easy to mount and display. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light mounted on bark or in a small slatted basket — Emarginate Dimerandra thrives in the open-air conditions of a shaded outdoor porch in zone 9b-12 and benefits from excellent air circulation around its root zone. Dimerandra emarginata is a compact, reed-stemmed, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to the Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico), Mexico, and Central America in the Orchidaceae family, a member of the large and diverse Epidendreae tribe closely related to Epidendrum. The plant produces slender, cane-like pseudostems 10–20 inches tall from clustered, small pseudobulb bases, each cane clothed in overlapping, narrow, distichous (two-ranked) leaves. Through the warm months, terminal flowers emerge from the upper leaf axils — each flower small (0.75–1 inch), in a cheerful, clear rose-pink to cerise pink with a broad lip. While not a dramatic specimen, Dimerandra emarginata is a free-flowering, easy-care, cold-tolerant epiphytic orchid whose continuous summer bloom of fresh pink flowers on reed-like stems makes it an pleasant garden companion for zone 9-11 outdoor orchid collections. Its relative cold-tolerance (withstanding brief dips to 35–38°F on protected porches) makes it one of the epiphytic orchids most likely to succeed in zone 9 outdoor culture. Non-toxic.

common_name: Emerald Blue Creeping Phlox (Sky-Blue Moss Phlox)
plant_note: Plant container plants in late winter or early spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Emerald Blue performs best in sharply drained, lean soil — rich, moist soil promotes lush foliage growth at the expense of flowering and increases susceptibility to crown rot.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Emerald Blue is the standard sky-blue cultivar of Phlox subulata (moss phlox or creeping phlox) — a low, mat-forming native perennial that in early spring (March–April in zone 7–8) produces such a profusion of lavender-blue flowers that the entire plant is obscured under a carpet of blooms. The color of Emerald Blue is a clear, mid-blue lavender — lighter and more purely blue than purple cultivars like 'Red Wings' and 'Scarlet Flame', creating a soft, cool, sky-blue effect that photographs beautifully and reads as a gentle blue sweep across rockeries, slopes, and garden borders. The very dense, needle-like, evergreen foliage forms a tight, weed-suppressing mat year-round; after the brief but spectacular spring bloom, the plant remains attractive as a low, fine-textured, deep-green groundcover through summer, fall, and winter. Creeping phlox is outstanding for slopes, embankments, and rock gardens where its spreading mat anchors soil and outcompetes weeds. Shear lightly after bloom (to 2–3 inches) to encourage dense new growth and a more compact habit. In zone 9, creeping phlox blooms in late February through March — very early in the Gulf South spring — and then serves as an unobtrusive fine-textured groundcover through the warm season. Sharp drainage is the single most critical requirement.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil, spacing for a hedge if desired.
directions: Emerald Green arborvitae is a narrow, upright evergreen with dense sprays of bright green foliage, widely planted in rows for privacy screens and hedges. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants roughly 2 to 4 feet apart for a solid living wall. Water regularly during the first two seasons to establish deep roots and prevent winter browning. It holds its color and slender form well without shearing, though it can be trimmed lightly. Protect young plants from heavy snow load and browsing deer.

common_name: Emerald Ripple Peperomia (Ripple Peperomia, Green Ripple Pepper)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Emerald Ripple Peperomia is not frost-tolerant and must be grown in containers brought indoors when temperatures approach 50°F. It tolerates low light better than most ornamental foliage plants and is an excellent choice for dim indoor spaces. Small pot size is important — root rot from overwatering in oversized pots is the most common failure. Allow soil to dry partially between waterings. Variegated forms ('Variegata', 'Silver Ripple') are equally easy to grow.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to low light in well-drained, peat-based or peat-free potting mix; Emerald Ripple Peperomia is one of the most tolerant of all foliage houseplants for low-light conditions, surviving in dim offices, north windows, and interior rooms that are challenging for most ornamentals. Peperomia caperata is a small, compact, rosette-forming tropical from Brazil in the pepper family (Piperaceae), prized for its deeply puckered, corrugated, heart-shaped leaves whose heavily textured surface creates a striking contrast of dark emerald green in the ridges and pale silver-green in the valleys — a tactile as well as visual interest that makes it one of the most distinctive small foliage plants available. The plant stays small (under 10 inches) indefinitely, making it ideal for terrariums, dish gardens, windowsill collections, and small decorative containers. In late summer and fall, the plant produces interesting, narrow, white rat-tail-like flower spikes — unusual in appearance but not particularly showy. Numerous cultivars exist including 'Rosso' (dark green above, intense red-purple below), 'Variegata' (cream-edged leaves), and 'Silver Ripple' (silver-gray textured leaves). All are easy to grow and safe for pets and children.

common_name: Emerald Vine (Jade Satin Pothos, Amydrium, Green Galaxy)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole or tree support in bright indirect light in well-draining, chunky aroid mix; Amydrium medium climbs vigorously and requires a support to develop its most attractive, large adult foliage — without a support, it trails and the leaves remain smaller. Allow the top inch to dry between waterings. Maintain moderate humidity. Propagate from stem cuttings. As the plant matures on its support, the leaves develop perforations similar to Monstera. Often sold under the incorrect trade name 'Jade Satin Pothos.' All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light on a moss pole or tree support — Emerald Vine is a vigorous climber that produces distinctly larger, more attractive leaves when ascending a support compared to when trailing, and should be provided with a tall support for best ornamental effect. Amydrium medium is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to Southeast Asia (Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Vietnam, Philippines, Borneo) in the Araceae family — a relatively recently recognized genus in the aroid trade, where it is commonly misidentified as a Pothos or Scindapsus species and sold under the trade name 'Jade Satin Pothos.' The plant produces climbing stems with large (8–16 inches), oval to broadly heart-shaped, leathery, deeply glossy leaves in an exceptionally rich, dark emerald-green — the glossy surface of A. medium leaves has a depth and intensity of color that has made it popular in the tropical plant collecting community. In juvenile stage, the leaves are solid, undivided, and simple; as the plant matures and climbs, the leaves develop windows (perforations) scattered across the blade surface, adding visual interest. The intense, varnished-looking green surface combined with the developing perforations on adult leaves makes Amydrium medium one of the most ornamentally appealing of the lesser-known climbing aroids. All parts toxic.

common_name: Emily Bruner Holly (Large Red-Berried Hybrid Holly)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emily Bruner requires a male pollinator (James Swan or other Ilex × koehneana male) nearby for heavy berry production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Emily Bruner is one of the finest large-statured evergreen holly trees for the Gulf South — a hybrid between Ilex latifolia (lusterleaf holly) and Ilex aquifolium (English holly) that combines the large, deep-green, dramatically lustrous leaves of the former with the heavy red berry production and classic holly appearance of the latter. The large, glossy, finely spined leaves (3–4 inches long) create an exceptionally handsome texture — more coarse and more dramatic than American holly (Ilex opaca) and much bolder and glossier than Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta). The tree grows into a broad, pyramidal to oval form reaching 10–25 feet tall with heavy, persistent red berry clusters that develop after cross-pollination from a male plant (James Swan is the recommended male pollinator for Emily Bruner). The massive red berry clusters that develop in October through December are among the most spectacular berry displays of any landscape holly — birds consume the berries through winter. Emily Bruner is excellent as a specimen tree, screening plant, or large accent in mixed shrub borders. The outstanding year-round appearance and heavy berry production make it one of the finest alternatives to American holly for large-scale landscape use in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, very humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; Empress Wu is the largest known hosta and requires enormous spacing — allow 6–7 feet in each direction — taking 5+ years to reach full impressive size.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, very humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep to partial shade; Empress Wu holds the distinction of being the largest named hosta cultivar in existence, with individual leaves measuring up to 18 inches long by 15 inches wide on petioles that themselves can reach 24 inches — the overall plant forms a magnificent mound 3–4 feet tall and 5–7 feet wide after 5+ years of establishment. The large, dark olive-green, heavily textured, deeply veined leaves are outstanding. Pale lavender flowers are produced on tall scapes in midsummer. This hosta is a commitment — it requires years of patience before reaching its full potential — but the result is arguably the most impressive deciduous perennial a shade garden can display. Consistent moisture, deep organic mulch, and protection from afternoon heat in zone 7–8 are essential; in zone 9 it is marginal and benefits from cooling in the hottest months. Empress Wu does not divide easily for several years after planting.

common_name: Empress of India Nasturtium (Dark Red Blue-Green Foliage Nasturtium)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Empress of India is a classic heirloom nasturtium prized for deep crimson-red flowers held above distinctive blue-green foliage, a striking color combination unlike the more common orange-flowered, green-leaved types.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; rich soil produces excess foliage at the expense of flowers. Empress of India is a beloved heirloom nasturtium dating to the Victorian era, valued for its striking combination of deep, velvety crimson-red flowers set against distinctive blue-green, rounded leaves, a more refined and dramatic look than the typical bright orange-and-green nasturtium. Both the peppery flowers and leaves are edible, adding a colorful, spicy accent to salads, and the compact, mounding habit suits containers, edging, and small garden spaces. It blooms continuously through the growing season with essentially no care beyond occasional watering during dry spells, and self-seeds readily if seed pods are left to mature.

common_name: Encore Autumn Bravo Azalea (Reblooming White Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Autumn Bravo is one of the few pure white reblooming azaleas, making it valuable for formal gardens, white-themed borders, and mixed plantings where strong colors are used and a white accent is needed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Bravo is the standard white-flowered Encore azalea cultivar — producing pure white, semi-double flowers with a light touch of pink at the petal edges in spring and again in substantial summer and fall bloom flushes. White-flowered reblooming azaleas are less common than pink, red, and purple reblooming selections, making Autumn Bravo particularly valuable for garden designs that require a white azalea with the extended bloom season of the Encore series. The pure white flowers provide maximum contrast with deep green foliage and make outstanding companions for dark-purple or deep-red flowering companions like Autumn Royalty or Autumn Fire. Autumn Bravo grows as a compact, well-rounded shrub to 2.5–3.5 feet tall and wide, suitable for mixed shrub borders, foundation plantings, and large containers. It shows the Encore series' characteristic requirement for more sun than traditional azaleas — at least 4 hours of direct sun is necessary to achieve reliable summer and fall rebloom. In deep shade, spring bloom may be adequate but fall rebloom will be sparse. The semi-evergreen foliage holds well through zone 9 winters.

common_name: Encore Autumn Chiffon Azalea (Reblooming Light-Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Chiffon is one of the most compact Encore varieties and is excellent for smaller planting spaces and container use.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Chiffon is a refined, compact reblooming azalea producing medium-sized, single, very light pink to blush-pink flowers in spring and again in summer and fall — the palest and most delicate flower color in the common Encore azalea lineup, with petals so light they appear nearly white in bright sun. The softly colored flowers create a particularly elegant effect in combination with deep green foliage and make Autumn Chiffon one of the most useful Encore selections for sophisticated color schemes where pastel blends are desired. The compact habit stays 2–3 feet tall and wide, fitting neatly into smaller foundation plantings, mixed shrub borders, and large containers. Like all Encore azaleas, it requires more direct sun than traditional azaleas for reliable fall rebloom — a minimum of 4 hours and ideally 5–6 hours of daily direct sun produces the best fall bloom quality. The semi-evergreen foliage holds through zone 9 winters with minimal damage. Fertilize with an azalea-specific acidic fertilizer immediately after the spring bloom to support subsequent reblooming.

common_name: Encore Autumn Fire Azalea (Reblooming Red Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Autumn Fire is a compact Encore variety well-suited to smaller spaces, foundation plantings, and containers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun for best rebloom; Encore Autumn Fire is a compact reblooming azalea producing vivid, clear red single flowers in spring and again in summer and fall — one of the few dependably red reblooming azaleas available, as red pigmentation in azaleas can be difficult to achieve with good rebloom habit. The flowers are produced prolifically in spring and recur reliably in summer and fall flushes, making Autumn Fire a standout accent plant for three-season color. The compact habit (24–36 inches tall and wide) fits it well for foundation plantings, borders, and mixed shrub beds where the larger-growing traditional azaleas would overgrow the space. Like all Encore azaleas, it requires more sun than traditional azaleas for reliable fall rebloom — plant where it receives at least half a day of direct sun. The compact size also makes it suitable for large containers. In zone 9 the semi-evergreen foliage typically holds well through winter. Fertilize with an acid-based fertilizer after the spring bloom flush to support subsequent rebloom cycles.

common_name: Encore Autumn Monarch Azalea (Reblooming Lavender-Pink Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade (4–6 hours of sun is ideal for rebloom — more sun than traditional azaleas require); Autumn Monarch is one of the larger-growing Encore varieties and benefits from 4–6 hours of direct morning sun to produce the best fall bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with at least 4 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Monarch is one of the leading cultivars in the revolutionary Encore Azalea series — a breakthrough group of reblooming landscape azaleas that bloom in spring AND again in summer and fall, dramatically extending azalea interest beyond the traditional single spring flush. Autumn Monarch produces large (2.5–3-inch), semi-double, lavender-pink flowers in a spring bloom followed by repeated summer and fall flushes that persist until frost. The Encore series was developed by plant breeder Robert E. Lee (Plant Development Services) over 15 years by crossing traditional azaleas with the naturally reblooming Rhododendron oldhamii from Taiwan. Encore varieties require more sun than traditional azaleas — 4–6 hours of direct sun daily maximizes fall rebloom; in deep shade the spring bloom may be adequate but fall rebloom is sparse. Autumn Monarch is one of the larger Encore cultivars, reaching 3.5–5 feet. Fertilize immediately after spring bloom with an azalea-specific acidic fertilizer to support fall rebloom.

common_name: Encore Autumn Royalty Azalea (Reblooming Purple Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Autumn Royalty is widely considered one of the best-performing Encore azaleas for rebloom quantity and flower color intensity.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Royalty is one of the most popular and widely recommended Encore azalea cultivars — a medium-sized reblooming shrub producing large (2.5–3-inch), bright purple to violet-purple single flowers in spring with reliable and abundant rebloom through summer and fall. The purple-violet flower color is distinctive and unusual among commonly available landscape azaleas, which tend toward pink, red, and white; Autumn Royalty fills an important color range in the landscape palette. It is widely regarded as one of the strongest reblooming Encore varieties, producing substantial fall flushes when given adequate sun. The medium, upright-rounded habit reaches 3–4 feet and fits foundation plantings and mixed borders without overwhelming adjacent plants. Like all Encore azaleas, performance in fall bloom is directly linked to sun exposure — plants receiving less than 4 hours of direct sun may bloom adequately in spring but produce sparse fall color. Amend planting area with pine bark and acidifying fertilizer to maintain the required pH 4.5–6.0 range, especially in alkaline Gulf Coast soils.

common_name: Encore Autumn Sangria Azalea (Reblooming Bicolor Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Autumn Sangria is a vigorous-growing Encore variety that may need occasional pruning immediately after the spring bloom to maintain a tidy size.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with 4–6 hours of direct sun; Encore Autumn Sangria is a distinctive reblooming azalea with flowers in a beautiful, wine-rose to deep rosy-pink color with a lighter center — a rich, saturated color with the warmth of burgundy and the brightness of pink combined in a tone reminiscent of the wine it is named for. This vibrant color is more intense and warm-toned than the cooler lilac-purple of Autumn Royalty or the clear red of Autumn Fire, making it a good companion for rose, salmon, and warm-toned plantings. Autumn Sangria is a medium-large Encore selection, growing 3–4 feet tall and wide with vigorous habit. The spring bloom is particularly heavy, followed by reliable summer and fall rebloom flushes when given adequate sun. In zone 9, Autumn Sangria typically begins its spring bloom in mid-March and continues in flushes through November. The semi-evergreen foliage is attractive and holds well through zone 9 winters. Apply a layer of pine bark mulch 2–3 inches deep to protect the shallow root system from temperature extremes and moisture loss during summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Encore azaleas rebloom in summer and fall in addition to their main spring flush, unlike most traditional azaleas that flower only once.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, protecting plants from harsh afternoon sun in the hottest part of zone 9 summers. The Encore breeding series, developed in Louisiana beginning in the 1990s, was a breakthrough because it combined the classic look of Southern azaleas with genuine repeat blooming, flowering not just in the traditional spring flush but again in summer and often into fall, greatly extending the color season of a plant long associated with a single brief burst of spring bloom. Dozens of named Encore cultivars are now available across a wide range of flower colors and mature sizes, all sharing the reblooming trait and reasonably good heat tolerance for the Gulf South. Water deeply during dry spells, especially heading into the summer and fall bloom flushes, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom to shape without removing the buds that will produce later color.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in rich, moist soil with afternoon shade.
directions: Endless Summer is a reblooming bigleaf hydrangea that flowers on both old and new wood, producing large mophead blooms from spring through fall. Plant it in morning sun with afternoon shade in rich, consistently moist soil, and mulch to keep roots cool. Flower color shifts with soil chemistry: acidic soil yields blue blooms while alkaline soil produces pink, so amend accordingly. Because it blooms on new growth too, light pruning is forgiving, though it rebounds best with minimal cutting. Keep it well watered, as wilting in heat is common.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist to average, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Engelmann spruce grows naturally at high elevations (6,000–12,000 feet) in the Rocky Mountains and requires cool, moist conditions — it does not tolerate heat, drought, or alkaline soils well.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist to average, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Engelmann spruce is the dominant conifer of the subalpine Rocky Mountain forests — the tree that defines the timberline forest from Colorado to British Columbia, often co-occurring with subalpine fir (Abies lasiocarpa) in the classic subalpine parkland just below treeline. The blue-gray to dark blue-green needles are sharp (typical of all spruces) and the crown is narrowly conical with pendulous lower branches. Engelmann spruce wood is valued as a tonewood for acoustic guitar tops, violin tops, and piano soundboards — the finest-grained specimens produce some of the best tonewood available. More cold-tolerant than Colorado blue spruce but generally less drought-tolerant. Best in cool, high-elevation or northern garden sites in zones 2–6 where the cool, moist conditions of its natural habitat can be approximated.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline limestone-based soil in full sun; Engelmann's sage is endemic to the limestone hills of the Edwards Plateau in central Texas and naturally adapted to alkaline, rocky, shallow soils with excellent drainage. It performs poorly in heavy, moist, or acidic soils.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Engelmann's sage is a rare, endemic Texas Hill Country salvia found naturally only on the limestone hills and canyons of the Edwards Plateau in central Texas. It produces dense spikes of vivid violet-blue to blue-purple flowers with white markings from spring through fall, blooming particularly heavily after rains — a characteristic adaptation to seasonal rainfall patterns. The plant forms a compact, drought-hardy subshrub with small, gray-green, aromatic, woolly-textured leaves that are pleasant-scented when brushed. More compact and refined in habit than many salvias and exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established in well-drained soil. It is not widely known outside Texas native plant circles but is an outstanding, drought-tolerant perennial for zone 7–10 gardens with alkaline soil — a category that includes much of the Texas Hill Country, where it can be grown as a true perennial.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; English bluebells naturalize readily over years to form dense, sweeping drifts and should be planted where the foliage can die back undisturbed through spring.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade under deciduous trees; English bluebells are the iconic spring flower of British woodlands, producing drooping, one-sided racemes of deeply fragrant, nodding, narrow-petaled, violet-blue bell-shaped flowers on arching stems in mid-spring that form breathtaking sweeping drifts when naturalized under a deciduous canopy. They reliably self-seed and naturalize to create ever-expanding colonies that need no routine care. The foliage dies back by midsummer. Note: do not confuse with the Spanish bluebell (H. hispanica) which is more robust, upright, and less fragrant — Spanish bluebells hybridize with English bluebells and the hybrid is outcompeting the native in the UK. True H. non-scripta droops distinctly to one side and has a sweet, distinctive fragrance.

common_name: English Edging Boxwood (True Dwarf Boxwood, Dwarf English Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade; Suffruticosa is highly susceptible to boxwood blight — do not plant near existing boxwood plantings where blight has been detected, and avoid planting in humid, poorly drained locations that favor disease.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade with some direct sun; Suffruticosa is the true dwarf English boxwood — the cultivar used for centuries in European formal knot gardens and low hedges, producing extremely dense, slow-growing, fine-textured, bright-green foliage mounds that clip beautifully into precise geometric forms. The very slow growth (6–9 inches per decade) and naturally tidy, globe-shaped habit make Suffruticosa the traditional edging boxwood for formal herb gardens, parterre gardens, and low border edging — a role it has filled in European gardens since at least the seventeenth century. The sweet, resinous fragrance of the foliage is the quintessential boxwood scent, associated with formal gardens throughout the Western garden tradition. However, Suffruticosa is highly susceptible to boxwood blight, the devastating fungal disease (Calonectria pseudonaviculata) that has been spreading across the Eastern United States since 2011 and can kill entire boxwood plantings within a season. For new plantings in areas where boxwood blight is present, disease-resistant Korean boxwood cultivars (Winter Gem, Green Velvet, Green Mountain) are strongly recommended over English boxwood. Where boxwood blight is not a current concern, Suffruticosa remains an outstanding traditional garden plant requiring precise siting in well-drained, aerated soil with good air circulation.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container transplants in fall in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; English ivy is widely adaptable but can be invasive outside cultivated areas — do not plant near forests, natural areas, or unmanaged land. In zone 9a it may struggle in summer heat and drought.
directions: Plant cuttings in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; English ivy is the classic, most widely used shade groundcover in temperate gardens — the glossy, lobed, evergreen leaves in many different sizes and variegations (solid green, silver-variegated, gold-variegated, small-leaved, large-leaved) create a dense, weed-suppressing carpet under trees. It climbs structures by aerial rootlets and has been used for centuries to cover buildings, walls, and slopes. However, English ivy is invasive in many parts of the United States east of the Rockies, smothering native understory plants and climbing trees — where naturalized, it can eventually kill large trees by girdling. Plant only in maintained, contained situations and remove regularly from any areas where it might spread to natural woodland. In zone 9a summer heat and humidity can reduce vigor; the heat-tolerant 'Needlepoint' and small-leaved varieties perform better in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average loamy soil in full sun; English oak is widely adaptable to a range of soil types and is tolerant of clay and somewhat wet conditions, unlike many oaks. Grows more slowly than American red oak but lives for centuries.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile to average loamy soil in full sun; English oak is the archetypal oak of European culture — the 'royal oak,' the great forest tree of England, the sacred tree of the Celts — producing the classic, deeply lobed oak leaf and small, elongated acorns held on distinctive long stalks (peduncles, giving the alternate common name 'pedunculate oak'). English oak has been planted throughout North America in parks, estates, and arboreta for centuries, developing into magnificent specimens in suitable climates. It is more tolerant of clay soils and seasonal wetness than most American oaks. The acorns are consumed by squirrels, jays, deer, and other wildlife. Many cultivated varieties exist, including the fastigiate (columnar) 'Fastigiata' or 'Skyrocket' forms widely used in street tree plantings. A very long-lived tree — English oaks commonly reach 500–800 years of age, and individual trees are counted among the oldest living things in Europe.

plant_note: Start seeds 12–14 weeks before desired transplant date by pressing them onto the surface of moist mix without covering, then cold-stratifying at 35–40°F for 3–4 weeks before moving to 50–60°F bright light; transplant into partial shade in fall or very early spring.
directions: Start seeds at cool temperatures (50–60°F) in moist seed-starting mix with seeds pressed on the surface; germination requires light and cool stratification, so refrigerate freshly sown trays at 35–40°F for three weeks before moving to a bright, cool location. Transplant into partially shaded, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; primroses bloom prolifically in the cool dappled light under deciduous trees where spring sun reaches before the canopy leafs out. In zone 4–6 they are fully hardy perennials that return reliably each spring; in zone 7–8 treat them as cool-season annuals that perform best from fall through late spring and then go semi-dormant in summer heat. Divide overcrowded clumps in early fall every 2–3 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting in late summer and set established transplants into the garden in fall for spring bloom; wallflowers are biennials that overwinter as leafy rosettes and bloom profusely in mid-spring. In zone 8–10 a fall-planted transplant may bloom the same winter-spring season.
directions: Start seeds in late summer in well-drained seed mix and set transplants into the garden in fall in full sun in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil; wallflowers overwinter as leafy rosettes and burst into bloom in mid-spring with intensely fragrant four-petaled flowers in gold, orange, crimson, cream, and burgundy — one of the richest scents in the spring garden. Excellent drainage is non-negotiable; they rot quickly in wet, heavy soils. In zone 8–10 they can behave as short-lived perennials or nearly year-round bloomers in cool seasons. Pull plants after flowering and replace with summer annuals, or allow them to self-seed; volunteer seedlings will often appear but may not come true to the parent cultivar's color.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, or start indoors a few weeks early, spacing plants about a foot apart. This unusual heirloom bears 3-4 inch chartreuse-green edible blooms that are striking in the garden and on the plate. Heat-loving and productive, it flowers endlessly until frost when regularly cut and deadheaded. Water at the base and space for airflow to reduce powdery mildew.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in any well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; once established, epimedium is remarkably drought tolerant and can thrive in the dry root zone under large trees.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; epimedium is among the most valuable groundcovers for difficult dry shade — one of the few plants that genuinely thrives in the dry, root-filled zone under mature maples, beeches, and other large shade trees where almost nothing else survives. The heart-shaped, often evergreen or semi-evergreen leaves are attractive year-round, turn bronze in winter, and the small but intricate crimson and pink bicolored flowers in early spring are delightful at close range before most shade perennials emerge. It spreads slowly but persistently by rhizome to form a dense, tidy, weed-suppressing mat. Shear back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge. The genus contains dozens of outstanding species and cultivars; E. × rubrum is one of the most widely available and adaptable.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March–May. Escargot performs best as a container plant that can be moved indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F — maintaining it as an indoor-outdoor plant allows the spiral foliage to be appreciated year-round. Rex begonias prefer high humidity (above 50%), making zone 9's humid summer climate well-suited to outdoor summer use in deep shade. Avoid wetting the leaves — water at the soil level only to prevent powdery mildew and leaf spotting. Do not overwater — allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings.
directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil — Rex begonias are moisture-sensitive in both directions, suffering from both drought and standing water; Escargot is one of the most famous and distinctive Rex begonia cultivars, producing leaves whose silvery-green surface is marked with a dramatic spiral pattern — the leaf base curls around itself in a tight coil before unfurling, creating a permanent snail-shell spiral pattern on each leaf that gives the variety its name. The silver-green leaf surface with darker green spiral accents and red-purple undersides creates a truly extraordinary visual effect unlike any other commonly grown plant. Rex begonias (Begonia rex-cultorum) are cultivated entirely for their extraordinarily varied and complex leaf patterns rather than their flowers — the small, insignificant flowers are typically removed to redirect energy into foliage production. Escargot is considered one of the most architectural and conversation-starting plants in the shade garden precisely because the spiral leaf pattern is so unexpected and perfect that it appears designed rather than grown. In zone 9 it excels as an outdoor container plant for deep shade areas during the warm months, then transitions easily indoors as a houseplant for cooler periods.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost; surface-sow as light aids germination.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the surface since light aids germination, and transplant once frost danger passes. This blend produces upright architectural spikes of red, purple, white, and Fleuroselect gold-medal coral that bloom nonstop and draw butterflies and other pollinators. Give it full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil. Deadhead faded spikes to keep the color coming through the season.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface-sow and provide light, then set out after frost as a foliage annual.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, leaving it uncovered on the surface where light and cool nights encourage germination. Grown for its fragrant, frosty blue-green rounded foliage, Silver Drop makes long-lasting filler for fresh and dried arrangements. Transplant to full sun after frost and pinch to encourage bushy, well-branched stems. Harvest foliage once stems are firm and cure it upright or hang to dry.

common_name: European Chain Fern / Climbing Chain Fern
plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in a sheltered, shaded position with consistently moist to wet soil; protect from hard frost in the first winter.
directions: Plant in deep shade in rich, permanently moist to wet soil, such as along a stream bank or at the base of a shaded wall where moisture naturally accumulates. Set the crown at soil level and water thoroughly at planting, then maintain consistent moisture throughout the growing season — this fern will not tolerate drying out. The long arching fronds benefit from shelter from wind, which can damage the tips before they harden. Watch for bulbils forming at the frond tips in late summer; peg them gently to the soil surface and they will root and produce new plantlets, a simple way to propagate this impressive fern.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; European columbine is a classic cottage garden perennial that thrives in partial shade and self-seeds freely, creating naturalized drifts in shaded borders and woodland edges over time.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly where plants are to grow, pressing lightly onto the soil surface and allowing winter cold to stratify the seeds for spring germination; European columbine self-seeds readily and does not need to be replanted each year once established. Aquilegia vulgaris is the classic European columbine of cottage gardens and woodland edges, a well-loved perennial with delicate blue-green, clover-like compound leaves and nodding, spurless or short-spurred flowers in shades of blue-violet, purple, white, and pink from late spring through early summer; unlike many North American columbines with long spurs, the European species tends toward shorter spurs and double flowers in garden varieties. The 'Nora Barlow' cultivar with doubled, pompom flowers in red, pink, and white is particularly well-known. Columbines self-seed generously and will hybridize freely among themselves; seedlings may vary in color. Short-lived perennials (2–4 years) that renew themselves by seeding.

plant_note: Plant corms just below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade; unlike other hardy cyclamen that require dry summer dormancy, C. purpurascens remains in leaf year-round and should receive moisture through summer as well as winter. It establishes slowly from corms but is very long-lived once settled.
directions: Plant corms in shade in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; European cyclamen is uniquely distinct from the other two commonly grown hardy cyclamen species (C. hederifolium and C. coum) in two important ways — it is the only hardy cyclamen that blooms in summer (July and August) rather than autumn or winter, and it is the only one that does not require a dry summer dormancy period, remaining in leaf and active year-round. The flowers are sweetly fragrant (unlike most hardy cyclamen), in shades of pale to deep rose-pink, with the typical reflexed, swept-back petals of the genus. The rounded, dark-green leaves are beautifully marbled with silver patterns and are never lost — the plant is essentially evergreen. Native to the shaded limestone woodlands of the Alps and Apennines in central Europe, it requires cool, moist, slightly alkaline conditions under deciduous trees. Slower to establish and rarer in cultivation than C. hederifolium, but uniquely valuable for its summer bloom, fragrance, and year-round leaf retention.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; European hophornbeam is remarkably drought tolerant and limestone-adapted, growing naturally on dry, rocky, calcareous soils in mountain forests of southern Europe where summer drought is common.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; European hophornbeam is a refined, small-to-medium deciduous tree of dry, rocky, calcareous mountain forests from southern Europe through Turkey and the Caucasus — closely related to the American hophornbeam (Ostrya virginiana) but slightly smaller and more drought-adapted. The distinctive fruiting clusters of papery, bladder-like inflated husks enclosing each nutlet hang in loose, pendulous clusters resembling hops (Humulus lupulus) — one of the most distinctive and ornamental fruiting features of any deciduous tree. The finely toothed, birch-like leaves turn gold in autumn. The wood is exceptionally hard and dense. More drought-tolerant than most other deciduous trees, making it an excellent choice for dry, alkaline, rocky garden soils in full sun or light shade. The hop-like fruiting clusters are attractive from summer through winter. An underused but beautiful ornamental tree for dry, chalky, or limestone-based soils where larger trees struggle.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile to average, loamy or clay loam soil in full sun to partial shade; European hornbeam is remarkably adaptable to a wide range of soil types, tolerating heavy clay soils and moderately wet or dry conditions.
directions: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, fertile to average, loamy or clay loam soil in full sun to partial shade; European hornbeam is one of the most important and widely planted trees in the European formal garden tradition — valued both as a large specimen tree and as one of the premier hedging and pleaching trees, because its dense, twiggy branching retains dead tan leaves through the winter (marcescence) just like beech, creating a solid, opaque winter hedge. The wood is extraordinarily hard and tough — 'hornbeam' literally means 'hard tree' — historically used for making cogwheels, tool handles, and cutting boards. The oval leaves turn gold in autumn. The fruiting catkins with their distinctive three-lobed involucres (leafy bracts around each nut) are attractive. Exceptionally pollution-tolerant and adaptable to urban conditions. The cultivar 'Fastigiata' (columnar hornbeam) is one of the premier street trees in European cities. An excellent hedge, screen, and formal pleached allee tree for gardens with the space for its imposing mature size.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; European larch is one of the fastest-growing conifers in European forestry, particularly in the mountains. It requires full sun and good drainage but is tolerant of cold, snow, and wind.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; European larch is the dominant conifer of the Alps, Carpathians, and Sudeten mountains — the classic 'golden mountain' tree whose needles turn brilliant gold in October above the treeline, creating the famous autumn color displays in the Swiss and Austrian Alps. A fast-growing, long-lived, graceful tree producing the characteristic clustered needles on spur shoots of all larches — soft, light green in spring, deepening to rich green in summer, then golden-yellow in fall. The small, oval cones are among the most attractive of any conifer. Widely used in British and European forestry and ornamental planting. The weeping cultivar 'Pendula' is a dramatic, cascading accent tree. More adaptable to garden conditions than western larch, growing in a wider range of well-drained soils in zones 2–7.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to clay soil in shade to full sun; European grey sedge is one of the best groundcover sedges for dry shade — thriving in the dry, dense shade of live oaks and other large trees where few other plants survive — and naturalizing readily into low-maintenance sweeps of arching, fine-textured, deep-green foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile soil in shade to partial shade; drought-tolerant once established in shade; mow or shear in late winter to refresh foliage before spring growth. Carex divulsa (European grey sedge or field sedge) is a clumping evergreen sedge native to the grasslands, roadsides, and dry woodlands of Europe and the Mediterranean region — but now naturalized across much of California, the Pacific Northwest, and parts of the Southeast, where it has been widely adopted in sustainable landscaping for its outstanding performance as a drought-tolerant, shade-tolerant groundcover. In dry shade — the notoriously difficult zone under established live oaks, magnolias, and other large tree canopies where irrigation is restricted and root competition is intense — grey sedge stands out as one of the most reliable and beautiful options: it forms dense, arching, fine-textured mounds of deep-green, grass-like foliage that remain attractive year-round with minimal care. It spreads slowly by seed and division to form a low-maintenance sweep. Unlike turf grass, grey sedge requires no mowing (though shearing in late winter refreshes its appearance), no fertilizer, and little water once established. The thin, arching leaf blades and graceful fountain form give a naturalistic, prairie-edge aesthetic. It is the backbone of California's 'dry shade garden' design movement, used extensively under native oaks in drought-tolerant home landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, rocky, loamy, or sandy soil in full sun; European smoke tree is very drought-tolerant once established and actually produces more vibrant foliage color and a better 'smoke' display in lean, slightly stressed, well-drained to dry soils than in rich, moist, fertile conditions.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, rocky, loamy, or sandy soil in full sun; European smoke tree is one of the most widely grown and loved ornamental shrubs in temperate gardens — famous for the extraordinary summer display of its tiny flowers, which are followed by large, loose panicles of fine, hair-like, pinkish-purple styles (the fuzzy threads remaining after the petals fall), creating the effect of a misty 'smoke cloud' surrounding the entire shrub in summer. The purple-leaved cultivars ('Royal Purple', 'Grace', 'Velvet Cloak') are among the most popular shrubs in the garden center trade — the deep wine-purple foliage contrasting with the ethereal pink-purple smoke creates a striking effect through the entire growing season. Fall color in the purple forms is spectacular: scarlet to orange-crimson. Native to southern Europe and central Asia. Extremely adaptable — tolerating dry, lean, rocky, alkaline soils where other flowering shrubs struggle. The purple-leaved forms are ubiquitous in modern garden design for their dramatic foliage season-long effect.

plant_note: Plant acorns (which take two years to mature) in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; European turkey oak is one of the fastest-growing oaks and adapts to poor, dry soils where other oaks fail. Common name refers to Turkey (the country) where it is widespread, not the bird.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; European turkey oak is a fast-growing, large deciduous oak native to southern Europe and western Asia, named for its abundance in Turkey (not the bird). It produces deeply and variably lobed, bristle-tipped leaves with variable shape, and its most distinctive feature is the acorn cup covered in long, outward-curling, mossy-looking scales — creating some of the most ornamental acorn cups in the genus. The acorns require two full growing seasons to mature, a characteristic of the red oak group. A tough, adaptable tree for poor, dry soils where English oak would fail, commonly used in Europe for woodland planting on difficult sandy or chalk soils. The fall color is variable — yellows and bronzes. Note that in the southeastern US the name 'turkey oak' refers to the native Quercus laevis, an entirely different species.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; European wild ginger is slower to establish than native Asarum canadense but has glossier, more ornamental leaves and is more tolerant of hot, dry shade.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — European wild ginger is a low, slowly spreading shade groundcover with extraordinarily glossy, deep green, kidney-shaped leaves that remain evergreen through winter in zones 5–8, creating a lustrous, polished carpet under trees and shrubs. The leaves are significantly glossier and more ornamental than native wild ginger (A. canadense), which is deciduous. Small, brownish-purple, three-lobed flowers appear hidden at ground level in spring. It spreads slowly and politely by rhizome, creating a refined, weed-suppressing mat in appropriate conditions. It tolerates dry shade better than the native species once established. Unlike native Asarum, the European species does not host certain specialist insects, but its ornamental value is superior. An outstanding foliage plant for shaded woodland gardens in zones 4–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; European wood sedge is a graceful, arching, loosely clumping sedge that naturalizes beautifully in shaded woodland gardens and tolerates deep shade better than most sedges.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; European wood sedge tolerates deep shade remarkably well and makes an elegant, naturalizing ground layer under trees. Carex sylvatica is a fine-textured European sedge that grows in loose, arching clumps 12–24 inches tall with bright green, very narrow leaves that cascade gracefully and slender, nodding, green flower spikes in early summer; it naturalizes slowly by self-seeding under deciduous trees and makes a beautiful, fine-textured woodland ground cover that contrasts well with broad-leaved shade plants like hostas, hellebores, and astilbe. More tolerant of dry shade than many sedges once established, and adaptable to a range of soil types from heavy clay to sandy loam. Largely ignored by deer and rabbit.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost; also sow in fall in zones 8–10 for winter bloom; evening stock closes its flowers during the day — plant near windows, patios, or pathways where fragrance is appreciated at dusk.
directions: Direct sow on the soil surface or barely covered in early spring in cool, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evening stock is grown almost entirely for its intense, sweet, clove-like fragrance that fills the air at dusk and into the night when the small pale purple to white flowers open. Unlike the showy daytime stocks (Matthiola incana), evening stock has modest flowers that close and appear wilted by day — plant it where fragrance matters more than visual impact: beside paths, under windows, or in containers near sitting areas. An outstanding companion to evening gardens, moon gardens, or any planting designed for after-dark enjoyment. Sow in succession every 3–4 weeks for continuous fragrance.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. This branching heirloom bears 4-6 inch sunset-hued blooms with dark centers in many rich tones on one plant, over a long bloom period that keeps vases full and pollinators fed. Because it branches, cut stems regularly to encourage more flowers. Water while establishing and stake tall stalks in windy locations.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in acidic, well-drained soil with afternoon shade.
directions: Ever After Ruby is a reblooming azalea that produces vivid ruby-red flowers in spring and again from summer into fall. Plant it in dappled or partial shade in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to protect the shallow roots. Keep the soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since azaleas resent both drought and soggy feet. Shear lightly right after the spring flush to encourage a fuller shape and stronger repeat bloom. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer in spring.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; evergold sedge provides persistent chartreuse-yellow-and-green foliage that brightens dark shaded corners year-round.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; evergold sedge is one of the most popular shade foliage plants in cultivation, producing dense, arching clumps of narrow leaves with a bright yellow-gold central stripe and dark green edges that glow with captured light even in deep shade. The evergreen foliage provides color through winter and is at its most vibrant in spring, making it an invaluable element in shade gardens for pairing with purple-leaved heucheras, blue hostas, and dark-leaved shrubs. Virtually maintenance-free beyond removing the oldest leaves in early spring. Tolerates clay soil and periodic drought once established. Excellent in containers and as a graceful edging plant along shaded paths.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or fall, or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; candytuft blooms on the previous year's growth — shear back by one-third immediately after flowering to keep plants compact and promote dense new growth for next year's bloom. It dislikes hot, humid summer conditions and performs best in cool climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen candytuft is one of the standard spring-blooming edging and rock garden perennials of temperate gardens — a low, spreading, semi-woody subshrub producing dense, flat-topped clusters of brilliant pure-white flowers from March through May that completely cover the plant and provide one of the most reliable and pristine spring displays available. The flowers are produced in such abundance that the dark-green, narrow, glossy, evergreen foliage is invisible beneath the white bloom. After flowering, light shearing maintains compact, dense growth. It is evergreen through winter (retaining its dark-green leaves), adding ground-level interest even when not in flower. Outstanding for edging paths and borders, cascading over low walls, filling rock garden pockets, and providing a spring carpet in full sun. The cultivar 'Snowflake' is a superior form with larger flower heads and particularly dense, rounded flower clusters.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or plant container-grown plants in fall or winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full shade to part shade; evergreen currant is native to the understory of Coast Live Oak woodland and is adapted to summer-dry conditions under tree canopy. It requires excellent drainage and may struggle in wet clay soils. Established plants need no supplemental water in summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; evergreen currant is one of the finest California native groundcovers for dry shade under oaks and other native trees — a low, spreading shrub from Santa Catalina and Anacapa islands and the adjacent mainland coast that thrives in the same summer-dry, shaded conditions as Coast Live Oak woodland where few other plants succeed. The rounded, dark-green, leathery leaves have an appealing, aromatic, resinous fragrance when crushed. In late winter and early spring it produces small clusters of tiny, deep-wine-red to rose-pink flowers that are disproportionately attractive to hummingbirds for their size. The plant requires essentially no summer water once established and actually resents summer irrigation, making it outstanding for planting beneath oaks where summer watering risks fatal Phytophthora infections of the oaks. An essential plant for California native gardens and water-wise landscapes requiring shade coverage without summer irrigation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Evergreen Giant is more heat- and sun-tolerant than most liriopes and can be used in brighter positions than smaller cultivars while still performing well in shade.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Evergreen Giant is a distinctively large-growing liriope cultivar that reaches 18–24 inches tall — nearly twice the height of standard Big Blue — with correspondingly wide, bold, arching leaves that give it a dramatically different presence in the landscape. Where standard liriope reads as a fine-textured edge plant or ground cover, Evergreen Giant has the bold, architectural quality of a small ornamental grass and can serve as a substitute for clumping ornamental grasses in shade or semi-shade situations where grasses typically fail. The white to pale lavender flower spikes are produced reliably above the foliage in late summer. Evergreen Giant is particularly well-adapted to zone 9 heat and humidity, maintaining better summer appearance than some of the smaller liriope cultivars that can look worn by August in the Deep South. It is also somewhat more drought-tolerant than smaller cultivars once established, performing adequately in drier spots under established tree canopies. Cut back to 4–6 inches in late winter (January in zone 9) before new growth begins to refresh the foliage. Outstanding mass-planted as a bold, low-maintenance ground cover under trees, along driveways, or on slopes.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil in shade; evergreen Solomon's seal is one of the best low-maintenance shade perennials for zones 6–9, combining a beautiful arching habit with year-round foliage in mild winters.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; evergreen Solomon's seal is a Chinese relative of Polygonatum with remarkable ornamental virtues — unlike the deciduous native Solomon's seals, this species retains its lustrous, dark green, arching foliage through winter in zones 7–9, providing year-round structure in the shade garden. The small, white, nodding bell flowers in late spring have a sweet fragrance and the plant spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form an attractive, weed-suppressing groundcover. The combination of shade tolerance, evergreen habit, and adaptability to the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 makes it particularly valuable for Southern shade gardens where deciduous perennials disappear for half the year. Spreads slowly and does not become aggressive.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen wisteria is a Chinese legume vine suited for zones 8–10, where it retains its leaves year-round unlike deciduous wisterias.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; evergreen wisteria is a Chinese legume vine in the same family as wisteria, producing dark, wine-purple to reddish-purple flower clusters from midsummer through fall — a very different bloom time from the spring-flowering true wisterias. The pinnate leaves are glossy and retain their attractive appearance year-round in mild climates. Compared to the aggressive true wisterias, Millettia reticulata is more restrained and less invasive, making it somewhat more manageable in the garden. The deep purple to burgundy flower clusters have a spicy, grapelike fragrance. An excellent vine for providing summer-through-fall fragrant flowering interest on arbors and pergolas in zone 9a gardens, where it is reliably perennial.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Everillo emerges lime-green and matures to a bright, glowing chartreuse-gold, holding its color through the season better than many variegated sedges.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Everillo is a striking sedge cultivar that emerges bright lime-green in spring and matures into a glowing chartreuse-gold that holds its vivid color through summer and into fall, brightening dark corners of the shade garden without needing flowers. Its fine-textured, arching, grass-like form provides an excellent textural contrast to broad-leaved hostas, ferns, and heucheras, and it tolerates both consistently moist soil and brief dry spells once established. It is evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild climates and needs only an occasional combing-out of old foliage in early spring to keep it looking fresh.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; excellent drainage is essential.
directions: Evolution Emerald Ice is a low, drought-tolerant sedum grown as a groundcover, offering fresh green succulent foliage and pink summer blooms that draw pollinators. Plant it in full sun in gritty, sharply drained soil, since wet or heavy ground causes rot. Once established it thrives on neglect and needs little supplemental water. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and tidy. Divide clumps in spring every few years to expand your planting or renew vigor.

common_name: Eyelash Begonia (Tiger Begonia, Miniature Begonia, Bowerae)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded terrarium plant in zone 9; Begonia bowerae is one of the smallest and most manageable rhizomatous begonias, fitting perfectly in a 4–6 inch pot or as a terrarium specimen. It cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Grow in a wide, shallow container to accommodate horizontal rhizome spread. Keep the rhizome at the soil surface. Allow the top half-inch of growing medium to dry between waterings. Excellent for terrariums, dish gardens, and windowsill collections. Propagate from leaf-petiole cuttings.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Eyelash Begonia flowers most freely in bright indirect light (a north or bright east window) and will survive in lower light but produce fewer blooms. Begonia bowerae is a small rhizomatous begonia native to the mountains of Chiapas, Mexico, one of the most charming and widely-grown of the many miniature and compact begonias popular with houseplant collectors. The plant produces a low, spreading rosette of small (2–3 inch), bright emerald-green leaves with a distinctive chocolate-brown to dark maroon edge blotching — a 'tiger' pattern of irregular dark markings around the leaf margins that gives the species its alternative common name 'Tiger Begonia.' The leaf margins are fringed with distinctive white hairs or eyelash-like cilia that stand out against the green leaf surface — the feature that inspired the most widely-used common name 'Eyelash Begonia.' In late winter and spring, the plant produces airy sprays of pale pink to white flowers on long, thin stems well above the foliage — delicate, wispy, and charming in contrast to the bolder leaf display. Begonia bowerae has been used extensively in breeding to produce hybrid miniature begonias (the 'Tiger' hybrids and related compact rhizomatous types). It is one of the easiest begonias for windowsill and terrarium culture, forgiving, compact, and ornamental year-round.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained acidic soil in partial to full shade; this rare species is restricted to the Savannah River drainage in Georgia, South Carolina, and adjacent North Carolina and should only be sourced from licensed nurseries propagating their own stock.
directions: Faded Trillium is a rare and geographically restricted sessile trillium endemic to the Savannah River drainage in the Piedmont and upper Coastal Plain of Georgia, South Carolina, and North Carolina, growing in moist, rich deciduous hardwood forests over well-drained, loamy soils. Its pale yellow to cream-colored sessile flowers are smaller and less showy than many trilliums — giving the species its common name — but the silvery-mottled leaves are attractive throughout the spring season. Classified as a species of conservation concern, this trillium should never be collected from wild populations; it is occasionally propagated by specialty native plant nurseries. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in deep, humus-rich, moist but well-drained acidic soil in the shade of deciduous trees, allowing the plants to emerge and bloom in spring before the canopy leafs out fully.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fairy bells spread steadily by rhizomes and are ideal for naturalizing as a shade groundcover under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade, spacing 12–18 inches apart; fairy bells is an elegant woodland perennial whose arching stems bear alternate, lance-shaped leaves and hang small creamy-white bell-shaped flowers at each tip in mid-spring, followed by glossy black berries that ripen in late summer. The variegated form 'Variegatum' with white-edged leaves is especially striking in deep shade. Plants spread slowly but steadily by rhizomes to form a refined groundcover that tolerates dry shade under established deciduous trees once established. Divide in early spring every 4–5 years to propagate and share; plants need little other maintenance.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil before or around the last frost; it dislikes summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil around the last frost, barely covering the fine seed. Fairy Bouquet is a charming blend of dainty three-quarter-inch snapdragon-like blooms in bright colors above airy foliage, also known as toadflax. It makes a colorful mass planting, container filler, or border edging and attracts pollinators. It prefers cool weather, so sow early and provide even moisture before summer heat arrives.

plant_note: Direct-sow scarified seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to rocky, poor soil in full sun in spring; fairy duster is intolerant of clay, wet, or rich soil — it thrives in the harshest, driest, most alkaline desert and rocky foothill conditions and declines quickly in moist, fertile, or amended garden soil.
directions: Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to rocky, poor soil in full sun; fairy duster is a low-growing native Sonoran and Chihuahuan Desert shrub in the pea family (Fabaceae) — one of the most charming and ecologically valuable small flowering shrubs of the desert Southwest — producing masses of powder-puff-like flower heads composed entirely of long, filamentous, pink-white to deep-pink stamens that give the plant its evocative common name. The silky, feathery flower clusters appear in late winter through spring, just as desert wildflowers peak, and provide an exceptionally early nectar source for emerging queen hummingbirds, sphinx moths, and native bees. The delicate, twice-pinnate, tiny-leafleted, gray-green foliage is drought-deciduous (dropped in extreme drought) and creates a fine, airy texture. Fairy duster grows naturally on dry, rocky, desert foothill slopes and bajadas and demands perfectly drained, lean, rocky soil — it fails in amended or moist garden soil. Its cold-hardiness to approximately 10°F makes it the most cold-adapted of the calliandras, suitable through zone 7. An excellent xeriscape shrub for dry Southwest gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in zone 4–8; Fairy Lanterns (Hooker's Fairy Bells) is a graceful, rhizomatous woodland perennial native to the shaded coniferous and mixed forests of the Pacific Coast from British Columbia to central California — producing arching, leafy stems and pairs of small, nodding, cream-colored bells and bright-red-orange berries that glow like lanterns in the understory shade.
directions: Plant Prosartes hookeri in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade under conifers or deciduous trees; mulch with leaf mold or bark to maintain cool, moist, acidic conditions; the plant spreads slowly from rhizomes to form attractive colonies — divide every 3–4 years if desired. Fairy Lanterns is a beautiful native woodland perennial of the Pacific Coast forests — closely related to and often still listed as Disporum hookeri — forming elegant clumps of arching, leafy stems that emerge in early spring and bear pairs of small, narrow, nodding, creamy-white bell-flowers at the branch tips. The common name comes from the brilliant red-orange berries that follow the flowers in late summer, glowing like tiny lanterns in the deep forest shade. The plant grows naturally in the humus-rich, acidic, perpetually moist soil of Pacific Coast conifer forests alongside Trillium, Oxalis, and ferns; in cultivation it prefers analogous conditions — reliable moisture, acidic soil, and overhead canopy shade. A refined and overlooked native plant that deserves wider use in Pacific Northwest woodland gardens and shady borders; it pairs beautifully with native ferns, bleeding heart (Dicentra formosa), and wild ginger (Asarum caudatum). The berries are not considered edible for humans but are taken by thrushes and other woodland birds.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial shade; fairy wand is dioecious — plant in groups of 3–5 to ensure both male and female plants are present for seed production.
directions: Chamaelirium luteum is an elegant and architecturally distinct native perennial of eastern North American deciduous forests and woodland margins, producing a basal rosette of smooth, spatula-shaped, deep-green leaves from which arise wand-like flowering stems in spring — male plants bearing slender, arching, horizontal spikes of tiny white flowers, female plants bearing stouter, upright white spikes that eventually bear seed capsules — giving the two sexes a strikingly different appearance. It grows in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to light shade from New England to Florida, and the species name luteum (yellow) refers to the yellow-green coloration of the rhizome, called "devil's bit" by herbalists because the tip appears bitten off. Plant in groups of 3–5 to ensure male and female plants are present for pollination and seed set. The plant is slow to establish but extremely long-lived and very deer-resistant.

common_name: Fall Muhly (Purple Muhly, Deer Grass Muhly)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; fall muhly is drought-adapted and performs best in lean soils without supplemental irrigation once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, rocky to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; fall muhly is a western and southwestern native grass closely related to Gulf muhly and pink muhly grass, producing somewhat coarser, denser clumps of deep-green foliage and vivid purple, airy seed plumes in fall — the purple color is more intense and held longer than some other muhly species. It is an outstanding grass for hot, dry, rocky garden conditions in zone 7–10, thriving in the rocky limestone and caliche soils of central Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona where many ornamental grasses struggle. The fall color display — masses of burgundy-purple plumes catching the fall light — is one of the most beautiful seasonal displays available in a drought-tolerant native grass. Excellent for xeriscape, parking lot medians, rocky slopes, and any location that receives reflected heat from pavement. Cut back to 6–8 inches in late winter before new growth begins. Combines beautifully with fall-blooming natives like asters, salvias, and fall-blooming sedums.

plant_note: Plant bulb or container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic soil in zone 5–9; False Aloe is a low-growing native perennial of the eastern and central United States from New York south to Florida and west to Kansas, producing rosettes of narrow, dark-green, purple-spotted succulent-like leaves and tall, slender flower spikes of tubular, greenish-yellow, intensely fragrant flowers in summer — hummingbird and hawk moth magnet.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; Manfreda virginica is highly drought and heat tolerant once established — requires excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water; it is native to rocky outcrops, cedar glades, and dry woodland edges across its range. Manfreda virginica (False Aloe, American Aloe, or Rattlesnake Master) is a low-growing, clumping, bulbous perennial in the Asparagaceae family (closely related to Agave) native to the eastern and central United States from Maryland and Pennsylvania south through the Appalachians and Piedmont to Florida and west through Missouri, Oklahoma, and Kansas. The plant forms loose, ground-level rosettes of narrow, strap-like, semi-succulent, gray-green or dark-green leaves often beautifully marked with purple-red spots and blotches — giving a mottled appearance sometimes compared to a rattlesnake's scales. In summer, a tall, slender, unbranched flower spike emerges from the center of the rosette reaching 2–5 feet, topped with 10–30 tubular, greenish-yellow to brownish flowers that open in the evening and are intensely, sweetly fragrant — powerful enough to perfume a large garden area at dusk. The flowers are excellent hawk moth (Sphingidae) and hummingbird attractors. Unlike agave, Manfreda virginica is not monocarpic — it blooms annually without dying. An outstanding native accent plant for dry, sunny to partly shaded positions in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings under mist or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich, freely draining soil in partial to full shade after frost; false aralia is sensitive to overwatering and root rot — use a freely draining potting mix and allow the top inch to dry between waterings, especially in cooler conditions where the plant's water uptake is reduced.
