directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; false aralia (spider aralia) is a New Caledonian tropical tree in the ginseng family (Araliaceae, now reclassified to Plerandra elegantissima from Schefflera elegantissima) with one of the most dramatic and phase-changing foliage sequences of any tropical plant — juvenile plants (the form most commonly sold as a houseplant) produce long, narrow, deeply serrated, copper-bronze to dark blackish-brown, almost spider-like leaflets radiating from each leaf stalk like the fingers of a dark, elaborately toothed hand, creating an extraordinarily refined and dramatic appearance quite unlike any common houseplant. As the plant matures and reaches tree size, the leaf form transitions dramatically to large, broad, rounded, glossy-green leaflets similar to a large Schefflera, losing the juvenile spider form. In the landscape it becomes a substantial tree to 20 feet. The juvenile, spider-like foliage form is the primary ornamental feature and is best maintained by keeping the plant in a container where root restriction prevents rapid maturation. An exceptional architectural accent for shaded tropical patios and zone 10–12 shade gardens.

plant_note: Scarify seeds and direct-sow in fall in full sun in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; germination is improved by cold-moist stratification. Once established, false blue indigo forms a long-lived, deep-rooted clump that should not be disturbed or moved.
directions: Scarify seeds by nicking or rubbing with sandpaper, then direct-sow in fall in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; false blue indigo is slow to establish but extremely long-lived once rooted — it may take 2–3 years to reach blooming size but plants can survive in the same spot for decades without needing division. The blue-green clover-like foliage is attractive all season; in late spring dramatic spikes of indigo-blue pea-like flowers appear, followed by inflated black seed pods that are decorative through winter and rattle in the breeze. A deep taproot makes it impossible to transplant once established, so siting is permanent. Outstanding as a drought-tolerant native prairie perennial; it is also a host plant for Wild Indigo Duskywing, Hoary Edge, and Orange Sulphur butterfly larvae.

plant_note: Fall direct sowing mimics natural seed dispersal and provides the cold stratification needed for reliable spring germination.
directions: False Boneset is a tough, drought-tolerant prairie and meadow perennial native to central and eastern North America, bearing clusters of creamy white flower heads from late summer into fall when many other wildflowers have finished blooming. It is especially valued as a critical late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and native bees fueling up before migration or overwintering. Sow seeds directly in fall into dry, well-drained soils in full sun; this species tolerates poor, rocky, or clay soils and actually performs best without supplemental fertilization. Once established, False Boneset is long-lived, self-seeds moderately, and integrates well into naturalistic prairie plantings and pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; false goat's beard is the only native North American astilbe species and is more tolerant of summer heat than the Asian-origin hybrid astilbes commonly sold in nurseries.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade — this is the only native US species in the astilbe family and is a magnificent plant for moist, shaded spots in the mid-Atlantic and Appalachian region. The large, pinnately compound leaves are coarser-textured than hybrid astilbes, and the creamy white to yellowish flower plumes in late spring and early summer can reach 4–6 feet tall — among the tallest of any shade perennial. Excellent at the back of a shaded border or naturalized in moist woodland gardens alongside ferns, hostas, and trilliums. More heat tolerant than hybrid garden astilbes and better adapted to the variable rainfall of the Southeast. The dried plumes persist attractively into fall and winter. Unlike the rhizomatous spreading of some astilbes, this species forms upright, gradually expanding clumps.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring as soil becomes workable, in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Astilbe biternata is the only astilbe native to North America and establishes best with consistent moisture during its first season.
directions: Plant crown divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial shade, with the crown set just at or slightly below the soil surface. Astilbe biternata is the only species of astilbe native to North America, occurring naturally in the moist, rich coves and wooded slopes of the southern Appalachians, where it produces bold, bi- to tri-ternate foliage and large, creamy-white plume flowers from June to July — far larger and more architectural than most Asian astilbes. Keep evenly moist throughout the growing season; drought causes premature browning of leaf margins and reduces flowering. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor, as older crowns can die out at the center.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; false hellebore emerges very early in spring and is a bold architectural plant, but all parts are extremely toxic — never allow contact with eyes, mouth, or open wounds.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade near streams, bogs, and moist woodland; false hellebore requires consistently high moisture and is best in permanently wet or seepy sites. Veratrum viride is one of the most dramatic and bold-textured native wildflowers of eastern North American and Pacific Northwest mountain forests; it emerges very early in spring as spectacular, tightly pleated, corn-like leaves that unfurl to produce a towering, 3–6-foot-tall stem bearing large, plume-like panicles of small, yellowish-green, star-shaped flowers in mid-summer. The dramatic tropical appearance belies the plant's extreme cold-hardiness and cold-zone nativity; it is outstanding for bold foliage effect in moist, shaded woodland gardens. ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE EXTREMELY TOXIC — among the most poisonous native plants in North America, causing severe neurological symptoms if ingested. Handle with gloves and keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in deep, cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in full to partial shade; Deinanthe bifida is a rare Japanese woodland perennial that requires protection from afternoon sun and drying winds, and rewards patient cultivation with unusual nodding flowers and bold textured foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in cool, deep, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full shade, enriched with leaf mold or compost; Deinanthe bifida is a rare and prized collector's plant in the hydrangea family (Hydrangeaceae), native to the shaded mountain woodlands of Japan, where it produces bold, deeply textured, wrinkled leaves and nodding, cupped white to pale-blue flowers in summer that are unlike any other shade perennial in appearance. It requires consistent moisture and cool root conditions — mulch heavily to maintain soil temperature and moisture through summer. Protect from deer and slugs, and avoid disturbing established clumps, which resent division and are slow to re-establish.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or scarify and cold-stratify seeds before spring planting.
directions: Scarify seeds and cold-stratify for 4–6 weeks before spring sowing, or direct sow in fall to let natural winter conditions break dormancy. Baptisia is a slow-starting plant — expect minimal bloom for the first 2–3 years, but once established, the clump requires virtually no care and lives for decades. The indigo-blue lupine-like flower spikes appear in late spring and are followed by attractive, inflated seedpods that rattle in the wind. Do not attempt to transplant established plants, as the deep taproot does not tolerate disturbance.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in any moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; false indigo is extremely adaptable to difficult wet, flooded, or droughty conditions once established and can be used for streambank stabilization.
directions: Plant in any moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; false indigo is a large, airy native shrub with pinnately compound leaves and 3–6 inch spikes of unusual dark purple-violet flowers with bright orange anthers in early summer — a striking color combination. It blooms at a time when few other shrubs are flowering, providing important early nectar for native bees and the southern dogface butterfly, whose caterpillars feed exclusively on the plant. It is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, poorly drained soils, riverbanks, and flood-prone areas, tolerating temporary inundation and spreading to stabilize streambanks. After the flowers, clusters of resin-dotted seed pods remain through winter. Prune back by one-third after flowering to maintain a compact form. Despite its common name it has no connection to true indigo (Indigofera).

plant_note: Plant softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, organically rich soil at streambanks, pond edges, or low-lying areas prone to seasonal flooding.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade along streambanks, pond margins, and low-lying areas subject to periodic flooding; false indigo bush is a fast-growing, wide-ranging native shrub found from Ontario to Florida and west to the Great Plains, producing striking 3–6 inch racemes of deep purple flowers with bright orange anthers that create a vivid two-tone contrast in late spring — one of the most visually dramatic native shrubs in flower. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it actively improves soil fertility and is an excellent anchor species for riparian restoration and streambank erosion control projects. The fine-textured, pinnately compound foliage remains attractive through the season, and the plant tolerates brief inundation that would kill most shrubs. Bees — especially bumble bees and native leafcutter bees — heavily visit the flowers. In rich, moist conditions it can sucker to form large colonies, which is desirable for mass plantings and erosion control; remove suckers to keep it shrub-sized in garden settings.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest in late spring directly into the garden; seed requires warm-then-cold double dormancy and will not germinate until the second spring after a double stratification period. Alternatively sow in fall outdoors and allow to stratify naturally over winter for spring germination.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade under deciduous trees or in a shaded rock garden; false rue anemone is a charming and delicate small European woodland perennial in the buttercup family, closely related to the North American native Enemion (with which it was once synonymous), producing a profusion of small five-petaled white flowers on thread-fine stems from March through May before going fully dormant by early summer. The lacy, blue-green, thrice-divided leaves closely resemble those of meadow rue (Thalictrum) and rue anemone (Thalictrum thalictroides), making it a beautiful companion for both in the spring woodland garden. It spreads slowly by self-sowing to form loose, delicate colonies and is especially effective planted in drifts in shaded rock garden crevices, at the base of stone walls, or along woodland paths. A refined and uncommon plant that rewards the collector of shade perennials with its elegant early-spring display.

plant_note: Plant divisions or fresh seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; false rue anemone is a delicate spring ephemeral of moist, rich deciduous forest floors in the eastern and central US, naturalized by spreading tuberous roots into modest patches.
directions: Plant fresh seeds or small tuber divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; false rue anemone is a delicate native spring ephemeral of rich, moist deciduous forest floors across the eastern and central US, producing small, compound leaves very similar to rue anemone (Thalictrum thalictroides) — the two species are similar enough that false rue anemone was long classified with Isopyrum. The small, white, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers are produced in early spring in great profusion on the small, branched plants. Despite the modest size, a naturalized colony provides a lovely, delicate spring display in deep shade where few other plants bloom. The plant is gone by late spring. Spreads slowly by tuberous roots and self-sowing. Easy to overlook if not in flower — pairs well with trilliums, wild ginger, and other spring wildflowers for a rich woodland spring garden composition.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false rue anemone is a spring ephemeral that goes dormant by early summer — it is one of the most delicate and beautiful of all native spring woodland wildflowers.
directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false rue anemone goes dormant by early summer and is a spring ephemeral that should be planted with later-emerging shade plants to cover the gap. Isopyrum biternatum is a delicate, diminutive native spring ephemeral of midwestern and southern floodplain forests, closely resembling rue anemone (Anemonella thalictroides) with its finely divided, ternate, glaucous leaves and white, star-shaped, 5-petaled flowers on hair-fine stems in early spring; unlike rue anemone (eastern), false rue anemone is primarily a midwestern species found in rich bottomland forests from Ontario to Georgia and Kansas. It forms small colonies from fibrous roots in humus-rich, moist soil and is a charming, difficult-to-find native wildflower for collectors of spring woodland plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; false sarsaparilla is a vigorous twining vine or sprawling shrub that blooms in late winter and early spring (July–September in Australia; January–April in zone 9) when little else is flowering. Several selections are available: 'Happy Wanderer' (vigorous vine with deep purple flowers), 'Mini Haha' (compact shrub form), white-flowered and pink-flowered forms. Tolerates moderate drought once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; false sarsaparilla is one of the most widely grown and adaptable Australian native ornamentals outside its homeland — a vigorous twining vine or sprawling groundcover shrub that produces in late winter and early spring a spectacular, prolific display of small but densely clustered, typical sweet pea-family flowers in vivid, rich, deep purple-violet with a distinctive small, contrasting, white-and-yellow mark at the center of each standard petal. The flowers are borne in long, pendant or arching racemes of 20–40 individual blossoms, and a plant in full late-winter bloom — covered in masses of deep-purple flower racemes against the dark, leathery, lance-shaped evergreen leaves — is a very striking sight in the winter-spring garden. The bloom period (late winter to early spring) provides vivid purple color at a time when the garden most needs it, and the flowers are attractive to honeyeating birds and bees. The form 'Happy Wanderer' is among the most commonly available and most vigorous cultivars. Tolerates considerable neglect once established, making it an ideal low-maintenance vine for fences, banks, and ground-covering in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant offsets or direct sow seeds in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, infertile, neutral to alkaline, coastal soil in full sun. False Sisal produces offsets (pups) freely around the base of the rosette — these are the most reliable propagation method. It is monocarpic, blooming once after 10–20 years then dying, but the offsets ensure colony persistence.
directions: False Sisal is a native agave of the coastal scrub, pine rocklands, and coastal dune communities of southern Florida and the Caribbean, producing a dramatic, architectural rosette of long, sword-like, blue-green leaves armed with sharp terminal spines and marginal teeth. Like all agaves, False Sisal is monocarpic — the main rosette blooms once after 10–20 years, sending up a spectacular branched flower stalk reaching 15–25 feet tall bearing thousands of pale yellow flowers that attract a spectacular diversity of moths, bats, and native bees, before the main rosette dies. However, the plant compensates by freely producing offsets (pups) around its base for years before flowering, ensuring colony persistence. Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy to rocky, infertile, neutral to slightly alkaline coastal soil in full sun; False Sisal is highly drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established but cannot tolerate frost, clay, or persistently wet conditions.

common_name: False Solomon Seal (Feathery False Lily of the Valley)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring before new growth in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained woodland soil in part shade to full shade; false Solomon seal spreads slowly by rhizome to form colonies in suitable conditions, providing outstanding woodland texture and wildlife value.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; mulch with leaf litter to maintain the woodland conditions the plant prefers. Maianthemum racemosum (false Solomon seal or Solomon plume, formerly Smilacina racemosa) is one of the most beautiful and important native woodland wildflowers of eastern North America — a rhizomatous perennial producing graceful, arching, unbranched stems 18–36 inches tall with broad, prominently parallel-veined leaves arranged alternately, and ending in a feathery, branching plume of tiny, creamy-white, fragrant flowers in April–May — superficially resembling Solomon seal (Polygonatum biflorum) in stem and leaf but distinguished by the terminal flower cluster rather than axillary flowers. The flowers are followed by attractive clusters of small, green-spotted berries ripening to ruby-red in late summer, which are edible (somewhat bitter-sweet) but more important as bird food for migratory thrushes and other fruit-eating birds. The plant provides bold, tropical-looking foliage texture in shaded woodland gardens, making an excellent companion for ferns, trilliums, and hostas. It is largely maintenance-free in suitable cool woodland conditions but struggles in hot, dry zones without consistent moisture.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false Solomon's seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies and is best left undisturbed once established.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; false Solomon's seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies and is best left undisturbed once established. Maianthemum racemosum (formerly Smilacina racemosa) is one of the most beautiful and versatile native woodland wildflowers of eastern North America; it produces arching stems bearing large, parallel-veined, oval leaves arranged alternately in a pattern nearly identical to true Solomon's seal (Polygonatum), but unlike Solomon's seal it bears showy, frothy plumes of tiny, fragrant, white flowers at the stem tips in late spring — one of the most ornamental flowering effects in the spring shade garden — followed by clusters of ruby-red berries in late summer that are mildly edible when fully ripe but somewhat cathartic. It is an outstanding, all-season shade perennial with interest from spring flowers through red fall berries and golden fall foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost date or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier for bloom the first season.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly in the garden or start indoors; unlike true perennial rudbeckia, heliopsis often blooms robustly in its first season from an early start. Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil; plants tolerate heat and short dry periods better than helenium. Deadhead regularly throughout summer to keep the golden-yellow, semi-double or double flowers coming continuously from July through September. Divide clumps every 3 years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and prevent the center from dying out.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; fan flower tolerates coastal salt spray, heat, and humidity far better than most annuals, making it ideal for Gulf Coast container gardens.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; fan flower is an Australian native that produces an almost continuous cascade of distinctive fan-shaped flowers in lavender-blue, purple, white, or pink — each flower has five petals arranged like an open hand or fan, all on one side (the upper half of the flower is missing, giving it a uniquely asymmetric appearance). It trails attractively from hanging baskets and container edges and tolerates heat, humidity, coastal conditions, and mild drought significantly better than most summer annuals. Self-cleaning (no deadheading required). One of the most heat-tolerant lavender-blue-flowered annuals for Gulf South summer gardens. 'Blue Wonder' and 'Surdiva Blue' are excellent long-blooming selections.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fanal requires consistently moist soil — it will not tolerate prolonged drought, and in zone 9 summer heat the crown should be mulched deeply and irrigation provided during dry periods.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fanal is one of the most widely grown and celebrated astilbe cultivars — a Georg Arends hybrid producing deep blood-red to garnet-red plume-like flower spikes in early summer above a mound of attractive, bronzy-green, finely cut compound foliage. The dark red flower color of Fanal is among the deepest and most saturated in the astilbe genus — a vivid crimson-red that provides maximum color impact in the shaded border when paired with white, pale pink, or silver-foliage companions. The dark, bronzy-tinted foliage is ornamental even when the plant is not in bloom. Astilbes are among the finest shade-garden perennials for moist, humus-rich soils — they thrive in conditions that challenge most plants: deep shade, wet spots near streams and ponds, and the damp cool environments under trees. In zone 9, astilbes require careful siting in deep shade with consistently moist soil and good organic matter to succeed through the summer heat — they are not as reliable in zone 9 as in zone 5–7. Mulch heavily to keep the crown cool and moist. The dried flower plumes remain attractive for weeks after bloom and provide winter garden interest. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant tubers (bulbs) in spring after soil warms to 65°F or above in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; fancy leaf caladiums are among the most spectacular foliage plants for shaded summer gardens in zone 9 and thrive in the hot, humid Gulf Coast summer when planted in shade.
directions: Plant tubers 2 inches deep with the knobby side up in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade after soil warms above 65°F; keep consistently moist. Caladium bicolor (fancy leaf caladium) is among the most dazzling shade plants for Gulf Coast gardens — a Brazilian tropical producing enormous, arrow-shaped, paper-thin leaves 6–18 inches long in spectacular combinations of white, pink, red, rose, and green in hundreds of named cultivars, with intricate patterns including bold veining, freckling, splashing, and marbling that make each leaf look individually hand-painted. The leaves are entirely the spectacle — the small flowers that occasionally appear should be removed to direct energy to foliage. Caladiums thrive in the hot, humid shade that challenges most other plants: full shade under live oaks, dappled light under large canopy trees, and shaded patios are ideal. They go dormant and the tubers can be left in the ground in zones 9–12 through mild winters, or dug and stored at 55–60°F. The 'Strap Leaf' (Caladium picturatum) types have narrower leaves; 'Sun Tolerant' cultivars can handle morning sun. A defining seasonal plant for the humid Gulf South shade garden.

plant_note: Plant tubers 1–2 inches deep, knobby side up, after soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 this is typically March–May. Tubers can be left in ground year-round in zones 9–11 with winter mulch, or lifted after frost kills foliage and stored above 60°F for replanting.
directions: Caladiums are the quintessential tropical shade plant, producing large, paper-thin leaves in spectacular combinations of red, pink, white, and green that brighten dark beds and containers through the summer heat. Plant tubers shallowly in loose, humus-rich, well-drained soil under trees or on the north side of structures where they receive bright indirect light or dappled morning sun; direct afternoon sun bleaches and scorches the leaves. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged — the tubers rot readily in standing water. In zone 9 the long warm season produces lush foliage from May through October; reduce watering as leaves yellow in fall and allow tubers to go dormant in place with a layer of mulch.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation; Fanick's Phlox was discovered thriving in a San Antonio, Texas, nursery where standard garden phlox cultivars had failed, and it is one of the few tall garden phlox selections that reliably survives as a true perennial through Gulf South summer heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Fanick's Phlox was discovered as a chance seedling at Fanick's Garden Center in San Antonio, Texas, where it persisted and thrived for years despite the intense summer heat that typically causes garden phlox (Phlox paniculata) to decline or succumb to powdery mildew within a season or two in the South. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension trials confirmed its outstanding heat tolerance and disease resistance relative to standard garden phlox cultivars, and it was subsequently promoted as one of the few tall phlox reliably perennial in zone 8-9 gardens. It produces large, fragrant clusters of soft lavender-pink flowers from early summer into fall, attracting butterflies and hummingbirds, on sturdy, upright stems that hold up well without staking. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain vigor, and deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding.

common_name: Fannie Munson Caladium (Classic Large Rose-Pink Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fannie Munson produces large, heavy tubers over successive seasons — in zone 9, leave tubers in ground over winter with a layer of mulch protection.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Fannie Munson is one of the most enduring and widely sold large fancy-leaf caladium varieties — a classic pink caladium with large, heart-shaped leaves bearing deep rose-pink to warm-pink centers and veining that radiates from the leaf center, semi-translucent whitish areas between veins that create a luminous, stained-glass effect, and fresh-green margins that frame and contrast the vivid pink interior pattern. The distinctive leaf pattern of Fannie Munson — the combination of deep rose-pink veins, translucent pink-white intervein areas, and the green margin — creates one of the most elegant and recognizable fancy-leaf caladium appearances, more detailed and complex than solid-colored types and more structured than randomly mottled varieties. Fannie Munson has remained in continuous commercial production for many decades because of its reliable performance, vigorous tuber production, excellent leaf quality, and universally appealing soft-pink color scheme. In zone 9, Fannie Munson is outstanding through the entire warm season (May–October), the tubers increasing in size year over year when allowed to overwinter in-ground with protective mulch. The warm-pink coloration pairs beautifully with pure white companions (white impatiens, 'Aaron' or 'Candidum' caladiums, white-flowered begonias) for a soft romantic effect, or with burgundy-to-dark-foliage companions for high contrast.

plant_note: Direct sow in place; tolerates poor dry soil well.
directions: Direct sow this western native in early spring, barely covering the small seed. Farewell to spring produces spikes of ruffled pink to lavender flowers on slender upright stems that make good cut flowers. It prefers lean, dry soil and full sun, blooming as spring transitions into summer. Avoid overwatering and fertilizing, which reduce flowering, and let plants self-sow for future displays.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in part shade to full shade; farfugium establishes readily in moist, shaded locations. In zone 7b–10 it is fully evergreen through winter and thrives year-round. The bold, leathery foliage provides a dramatic tropical effect throughout the growing season; flowers appear in fall to winter.
directions: Plant in part shade to full shade in moist, rich, well-drained soil; farfugium (sometimes called leopard plant) is one of the finest and most underused shade perennials for Southern gardens, producing large, round, leathery, glossy green leaves up to 12 inches across on long petioles — creating a bold, tropical-looking accent in shaded beds where most other perennials look tired. Unlike its cousin Ligularia dentata, farfugium tolerates the heat and humidity of zone 8–9 summers without wilting, making it far better suited to Gulf Coast gardens. Bright yellow daisy flowers appear in November–December, providing rare winter color in shade beds. The standard species has plain green leaves; the cultivar 'Aureomaculata' (leopard plant) features dramatic yellow spots on the foliage. Divide crowded clumps every 3–4 years in early spring; the plant is virtually maintenance-free beyond occasional watering during dry periods.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Fashion is a Glenn Dale Hybrid that tolerates more cold than Southern Indian Hybrids — hardy to zone 6 — while still performing excellently in zone 9 heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Fashion is one of the classic Glenn Dale Hybrid azaleas — a group developed by USDA plant breeder Benjamin Yeo Morrison at the Glenn Dale Plant Introduction Station in Maryland from the 1930s through the 1950s to extend azalea hardiness beyond the frost-tender Southern Indian Hybrids while maintaining large flowers and good landscape habit. Fashion produces distinctive, hose-in-hose (flower-within-a-flower) double flowers in a warm salmon-coral to orange-salmon tone — a color combination unusual among landscape azaleas, where pink, purple, and red predominate. The hose-in-hose flower form gives each bloom a doubled, full appearance that is particularly attractive and distinctive. Plants grow vigorously to 4–6 feet in zone 9, with a broad, mounded to spreading habit and semi-evergreen to evergreen foliage. Fashion blooms in mid-spring and is a single-season bloomer (unlike the Encore rebloomers), but the distinctive flower color and form make it a valued addition to the azalea collection. The Glenn Dale Hybrids as a group are underused in modern landscapes compared to the heavily marketed Encore series; Fashion represents a classic selection worth preserving.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow in warm soil.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in warm soil, spacing plants about a foot apart. Fata Morgana offers soft, ruffled pincushion blooms in shades of peach and apricot on slender stems, lovely in borders, cottage gardens, and bouquets. Deadhead and cut regularly to keep the long-lasting flowers coming and to draw pollinators. Give it full sun and well-drained soil.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Fatshedera is a bigeneric hybrid between Fatsia japonica and English ivy and inherits a sprawling, semi-vining habit that benefits from staking or a support if grown upright.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind. This unusual bigeneric cross between Fatsia japonica and English ivy was first raised in France in 1912 and combines the bold, glossy, lobed foliage of Fatsia with a looser, semi-climbing habit inherited from its ivy parent. Left unstaked it sprawls and roots where it touches soil, making a good shade groundcover or informal hedge, or it can be tied to a support for a more upright accent. It tolerates deep shade better than most broadleaf evergreens, is easy from cuttings, and needs only an occasional light pruning to control its size.

common_name: Fatsia (Japanese Fatsia, Japanese Aralia, Glossy-Leaf Paper Plant)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; fatsia is exceptionally shade tolerant and actually performs better in deep shade than in full sun, where the large leaves can bleach and burn in heat.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fatsia is one of the most dramatic and tropical-looking shade shrubs for zone 7–11 gardens, producing enormous, glossy, deeply lobed leaves 12–18 inches across on bold, multi-stemmed plants that create an instant tropical feel in the darkest garden corners. The leaves hold their rich, dark green color year-round and are remarkably resistant to wind damage. Clusters of small white ball-shaped flowers appear in fall, followed by black berries. It is one of the most shade-tolerant large shrubs available and thrives under the dense canopy of live oaks and other large trees where most plants fail. The variegated form ('Variegata') has attractive white-edged leaves. Equally at home as an outdoor landscape shrub in zone 7–11 and as a bold container plant for covered patios and atriums.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors a few weeks early.
directions: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 4-6 weeks early, spacing compact plants 8-10 inches apart. These single-row-petaled French marigolds make pollen easy for bees to reach, and their tidy, full habit shines at the front of a bed or tucked among vegetables. They grow and flower quickly with continuous blooms from spring to frost. Deadhead for tidiness and prolonged flowering, and water at the base.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; feather celosia is a distinct form of celosia from the cockscomb (cristata) type, producing upright, feathery, silky plume-like flower heads in brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and purple that are among the most striking warm-season bedding and cut flowers for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost (they need some light for germination); thin to 6–12 inches depending on variety size. Celosia argentea var. plumosa (feather or plume celosia) is one of the three main celosia types — the others being the brain/cockscomb cristata form and the wheat-spike spicata form — distinguished by its upright, tapering, silky, feathery plume-like flower heads that resemble ostrich feathers or soft velvet flames in brilliant, saturated colors. The plumosa types are among the most brilliantly colored warm-season annuals available for bedding, cut flower, and container gardens; flowers are extraordinarily heat-tolerant, blooming continuously through Gulf Coast and Southern summers that defeat most other annuals. Colors range from deepest crimson red through orange, gold, peach, pink, and creamy white. Fresh flowers have a unique velvety texture; dried flowers hold their color well for wreaths and dried arrangements. The foliage and flowers of all celosia types are edible (used as vegetables in parts of Africa where Celosia argentea is an important leaf vegetable) and highly nutritious.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring; 'Karl Foerster' is sterile and must be propagated by division.
directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in average, moisture-retentive soil; 'Karl Foerster' feather reed grass is one of the most reliable and widely adapted ornamental grasses, tolerating clay soil, humidity, and cold winters that defeat many others. Strongly upright, narrow clumps emerge early in spring with feathery bronze-pink plumes appearing in early summer that fade to wheat-gold and persist through winter. Cut back to 4–6 in in late winter or early spring before new growth begins. Divide every 4–5 years in spring when the center begins to die out.

plant_note: Plant bulbs or corms in fall 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; situate in a woodland margin or meadow edge with consistent moisture.
directions: Stenanthium gramineum is a striking native bulbous perennial of the eastern United States and Appalachian foothills, producing a basal clump of long, grass-like, channeled leaves and an impressive flowering stem 3–6 feet tall topped with a dramatic, loose, feathery panicle of hundreds of tiny white to greenish-white or purplish-tinged star-shaped flowers from July through September — one of the tallest and most dramatic native wildflowers for moist shade gardens. It occurs naturally in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to acidic soils in open woods, meadow margins, and along stream banks in partial shade to full sun; plant bulbs in fall 2–3 inches deep. The tall flower spikes sway gracefully in summer breezes and provide important late-season nectar for pollinators including native bees and butterflies. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade in spring; rodgersia requires reliably moist to boggy soil and will not perform well if allowed to dry out — a mulched site near a stream, pond, or rain garden is ideal.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial to full shade; featherleaf rodgersia (elder-leafed rodgersia) is a Chinese shade perennial of exceptional character, producing some of the most bold and handsome foliage of any shade garden plant — the large, pinnately divided leaves with five to nine leaflets resemble an oversized elderberry leaf and are arranged in striking rosettes that expand from reddish-bronze emerging buds in spring to large, deep-green, prominently veined, leathery-textured plates that color to rich bronze, copper, and burgundy tones in autumn. In early to mid-summer the plant sends up tall, branching, astilbe-like flower plumes of tiny, pink to creamy-white, starry flowers well above the foliage. The cultivar 'Superba' with deep-pink flowers and bronze-flushed foliage is among the most widely grown, and 'Chocolate Wing' (dark-chocolate-red spring and fall foliage) is exceptional. Rodgersia requires consistently moist to wet soil and dislikes drought — it is ideal beside water features and in wet shade gardens where it can eventually colonize large areas with its slowly spreading rhizomes.

common_name: February Gold Daffodil (Early-Blooming Miniature Cyclamineus Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; February Gold is one of the earliest daffodils to bloom, often flowering in late winter well ahead of most other cultivars, giving an early splash of color in the shade garden's dormant season.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. February Gold is a Cyclamineus-type daffodil, recognizable by its swept-back petals and long trumpet that give the flower a distinctive windblown look, and it is prized above all for being one of the very earliest daffodils to bloom, often opening its golden-yellow flowers in late winter well before most other cultivars have even emerged. Its smaller, more graceful proportions compared to large trumpet types make it a good fit for naturalizing under deciduous trees and shrubs, where it gets adequate sun before the canopy leafs out. It multiplies reliably in climates with sufficient winter chill and, like all daffodils, is completely resistant to deer and rodents.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in very well-drained, lean, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; plants resent wet feet and thrive in rock gardens and dry prairie restorations.
directions: Fendler's Bladderpod (formerly Lesquerella fendleri) is a compact, cushion-forming native perennial in the mustard family, native to dry, calcareous, rocky, or sandy open ground across Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma, and adjacent states. In early spring — often before almost any other wildflower has opened — it covers itself in bright yellow, 4-petaled mustard flowers held just above a silver-gray mat of densely hairy, spatulate basal leaves; the flowers are followed by round, inflated, bladder-like seed pods that persist ornamentally on the plant. These early blooms are a critical first nectar source for native mining bees, mason bees, and other native pollinators emerging in late winter and early spring when forage is scarce. Grow in very well-drained, lean, calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; Fendler's Bladderpod is an excellent and underused native for rock gardens, dry native prairie mixes, and xeriscape plantings across the southern Great Plains.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; Fendler's meadow rue grows naturally in open to lightly shaded canyon slopes, aspen groves, and montane meadow edges of the southern Rockies and Great Basin.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; Fendler's meadow rue is the native meadow rue of the southern Rocky Mountains and Great Basin, growing in aspen groves, canyon-side scrub, and montane meadow margins. Like other meadow rues, it produces elegant, compound, blue-green, maidenhair-fern-like foliage — the primary ornamental feature — and loose panicles of small, wind-pollinated flowers. Fendler's meadow rue is dioecious (separate male and female plants), with the male plants having the showier flowers due to the dangling, yellow-green stamens. Notably more drought-tolerant than its eastern relatives, adapted to the drier conditions of the Rocky Mountain West. The finely textured, glaucous foliage provides excellent texture contrast in dry, shaded or dappled garden sites. A useful native for rock gardens, aspen-garden companion plantings, and dry shade under western native trees.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall or transplant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; fern-leaf corydalis is nearly evergreen in mild climates, providing attractive ferny foliage year-round. It self-sows freely in suitable moist, shaded conditions. Unlike the blue and yellow perennial corydalis species, this one blooms in spring and early summer, producing dense, upright racemes of golden-yellow tubular flowers above the fine, fern-like leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; fern-leaf corydalis is a Chinese woodland corydalis that provides two distinct garden qualities in one compact plant: extraordinary foliage and good spring flowers. The foliage is the main attraction — finely divided, multi-pinnate, lacy leaves of extreme delicacy, closely resembling the fronds of certain ferns or the foliage of fine ferny rock garden plants, in a soft, bronze-tinted green that deepens to bronzy-red in cooler weather and is nearly evergreen in mild climates, providing attractive winter presence in the shade garden. Against this cloud of delicate ferny foliage, dense, upright, cylindrical racemes of small, spurred, golden-yellow tubular flowers appear in spring and early summer — the soft yellow blooms contrasting warmly with the bronze-green fronds. It self-sows freely in cool, moist, shaded conditions, establishing naturalized colonies in suitable woodland garden soil. The combination of fern-like texture, bronze-green color, near-evergreen presence, and yellow spring flowers makes it an unusually versatile and attractive shade groundcover plant for zones 5–8.

plant_note: Direct sow near established oaks in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic, lean, open or rocky woodland soil in partial shade to full sun; fernleaf false foxglove is an annual hemiparasite that self-sows near oak roots in open, dry oak barrens, pine-oak woods, and acidic shale barrens.
directions: Direct sow near established oaks in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic, lean soil in partial shade to full sun; fernleaf false foxglove is an annual or short-lived perennial hemiparasite of dry oak barrens, pine-oak woodlands, and acidic shale barrens of the eastern US, producing deeply pinnately dissected, fern-like foliage (giving the plant its common name) and clusters of bright yellow, tubular two-lipped flowers in summer. The extremely finely cut leaves are among the most distinctive and attractive of any Aureolaria species, making the plant recognizable even without flowers. Like all Aureolaria, it taps the roots of nearby oaks for supplemental water and nutrients; unlike the perennial species, it completes its cycle in a single season and perpetuates by self-sowing. More tolerant of dry, sunny, open conditions than the perennial Aureolaria species. A specialist plant of high ecological value in oak barrens conservation and restoration.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade; scoliopus is a California coastal woodland specialist requiring cool, shaded, consistently moist conditions similar to its native redwood forest habitat.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade; scoliopus must have consistently moist, cool conditions and summer-dry stress will cause premature dormancy or death. Scoliopus bigelovii is one of California's most unusual native woodland perennials, producing mottled strap-like leaves in winter and bearing small brownish-purple veined flowers with a fetid odor from January through March, attracting fungus gnats for pollination. It is native to cool, moist, shaded canyons and redwood forest understories along the California coast and goes dormant by late spring.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade; fetterbush requires very acidic, waterlogged conditions and will not thrive in neutral or alkaline soil.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; fetterbush is a native evergreen shrub of pine flatwoods, pocosins, and bog margins across the coastal South, producing glossy, leathery, sharply ribbed leaves (the midrib runs parallel to the leaf margin — a key identification feature) and small pink to white urn-shaped flowers in early spring that are critically important for native mining bees and early bumblebee queens. The plant naturally grows in waterlogged, very acidic soil and is adapted to conditions that are difficult for most other plants. An outstanding native plant for bog gardens, wet acid borders, and naturally moist sandy soils in the Southeast. All parts are toxic to livestock and humans if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; fever tree grows naturally at the edges of swamps, pocosin bogs, and moist woodlands in the southeastern coastal plain. It requires consistent soil moisture and performs poorly in dry soils or full sun, making it an ideal plant for moist shade or rain garden settings.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in part shade; fever tree is one of the rarest and most unusual native shrubs of the southeastern coastal plain, found naturally only in a narrow band of swampy pocosins and wet pine savannas in coastal Georgia and the Carolinas. In the coffee family (Rubiaceae), it is related to gardenias and quinine trees — and indeed the bark was historically used as a quinine substitute to treat malaria (hence 'fever tree'). In early summer, the plant produces clusters of small, tubular, rose-to-magenta flowers, each surrounded by spectacular, greatly enlarged, rose-pink to rosy-red sepals (calyx lobes) that resemble large pink bracts or petals and create a showy, ornamental display far larger than the flowers themselves — similar in strategy to dogwood bracts. The large, tropical-looking leaves give the shrub a bold texture unusual among native plants. A conservation-significant plant that also makes an outstanding specimen for moist shaded gardens in zones 7–9, appreciating conditions similar to native azaleas.

plant_note: Divide established clumps or plant container-grown plants in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil; fiber optic grass thrives in boggy conditions or at the water's edge and can be grown as an aquatic in shallow water (up to 2 inches deep). Keep consistently moist — it does not tolerate drought.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in part shade to full sun; fiber optic grass is a charming miniature rush-like plant producing dense mounds of very fine, thread-like, bright-green foliage tipped with tiny white to pale brownish flower spikelets that catch the light like the tip of a fiber optic strand — hence the common name. The effect is distinctly whimsical and appealing. It is excellent as a container plant for water features, terrariums, and bog gardens, thriving in consistently wet conditions at pond or stream edges, in water gardens, and as a houseplant in very bright light. In zones 8–11 it grows as a reliable evergreen perennial in wet conditions. Its compact, fine-textured form contrasts beautifully with broad-leafed aquatic plants and it makes an unusual cascading element in container plantings or hanging baskets where moisture is maintained.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist medium, or air-layer branches; fiddle-leaf fig is sensitive to being moved — choose a permanent location with bright, indirect light and consistent conditions. Direct sun causes leaf scorch, deep shade causes poor growth and dropping. Water when the top 2 inches of soil are dry and ensure good drainage to prevent root rot.
directions: Grow in bright, indirect light indoors or in filtered shade outdoors in zones 10–12; fiddle-leaf fig has become one of the most widely grown and immediately recognizable indoor trees of the early 21st century, prized for its enormous, deeply wavy-edged, violin-shaped leaves (12–18 inches long) in rich, dark, glossy green that create an unmistakably tropical and architecturally dramatic statement in interior spaces. Native to the lowland tropical rainforests of West Africa, it grows as a large tree to 50 feet in its native habitat. As a houseplant it requires bright, indirect light (a few feet from a south or west window), consistent watering (allowing the top 2 inches to dry between waterings), and avoidance of both overwatering (the primary cause of root rot and leaf drop) and cold drafts. It dislikes being moved and may drop leaves in response to environmental changes. In zones 10–12 it can be grown outdoors as a specimen tree in partial shade. Cleaning the large leaves with a damp cloth maintains their glossy appearance and maximizes light absorption.

common_name: Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron (Horsehead Philodendron, Panda Plant, Panduraeforme)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Philodendron bipennifolium cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. A moss pole or climbing support is beneficial — the leaves grow progressively larger as the plant climbs. Grow in a well-draining, aroid potting mix. Allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Propagate from single-node stem cuttings in water or moist media. The leaf shape varies greatly between juvenile and mature forms. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron produces its most dramatic and largest leaves with consistent bright indirect light and a climbing support, but adapts to lower light conditions without serious decline. Philodendron bipennifolium (formerly classified as P. panduraeforme, a name still commonly used in horticultural trade) is a climbing philodendron native to Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru in the family Araceae. The common names 'Fiddle-Leaf Philodendron' and 'Horsehead Philodendron' both refer to the distinctive shape of the adult leaves — a broad, slightly elongated outline with two distinctive basal lobes and a characteristic narrowing in the middle that creates a violin or fiddle silhouette, or, from another angle, a horse's head profile. The leaves are glossy, bright to dark-green, leathery, and held on long petioles that give the plant an open, airy structure. In the juvenile form, the leaves are much smaller and simpler; the characteristic fiddle shape develops progressively as the plant matures. As a rapidly growing, adaptable climbing philodendron with an unusual and attractive leaf form, P. bipennifolium has long been popular in cultivation and has been used in breeding the modern 'Philodendron Florida' hybrid series. All parts contain calcium oxalate and are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; nasturtiums resent transplanting.
directions: Direct sow the large seed about half an inch deep after frost, since nasturtiums dislike root disturbance from transplanting. Fiesta Blend brings spicy edible flowers in orange, yellow, and orange-peach bicolors that brighten hanging baskets, containers, and garden walls. Both the peppery blossoms and leaves are edible and prized in salads. Grow in lean soil and go easy on fertilizer, as rich soil favors foliage over flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May. Fiesta del Sol is a compact selection (2–3 feet) of Mexican Sunflower — dramatically smaller than the standard species (5–6 feet), making it practical for mixed borders and small garden spaces where the standard type would overwhelm surrounding plants. The compact size was the primary selection criterion for this All-America Selections winner. Despite the smaller size, Fiesta del Sol produces the same vivid orange flowers as the standard type, beginning to bloom earlier from seed (55–70 days vs 80–90 days for taller selections). Self-seeding occurs in warm conditions; allow a few plants to go to seed in zone 9 for volunteer seedlings in subsequent seasons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Fiesta del Sol Tithonia thrives in the heat and lean conditions that reduce the excessive vegetative growth and delayed flowering of overfertilized plants; Fiesta del Sol is an All-America Selections award-winning compact cultivar of Mexican Sunflower (Tithonia rotundifolia), bred specifically to reduce the scale of this Mexican native from its typical 5–6 foot height to a more garden-friendly 2–3 feet while retaining the vivid, large (3–4 inch), brilliant orange-scarlet flowers and the exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance that make Tithonia outstanding for zone 9 summer gardens. The vivid orange-scarlet flowers are among the most intensely colored of all summer annuals — a warm, saturated orange that is particularly effective in late-summer and fall garden compositions with purple, blue, and cream companions. Tithonia is one of the premier butterfly and pollinator plants available — the large, nectar-rich flowers attract swallowtails, fritillaries, monarchs, and large sulphur butterflies in significant numbers throughout the bloom season. The drought tolerance and heat performance of Tithonia in the peak of Gulf South summer (July–September) when many annuals struggle to maintain quality makes it one of the most reliable high-color, high-pollinator-value summer plants available for zone 9.

plant_note: Sow directly in the garden in spring after the last frost, or start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; fig-leaved hollyhock is biennial, forming a leaf rosette the first year and sending up tall flowering spikes in the second — sow in successive years to ensure bloom every season.
directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after the last frost in spring, pressing seed shallowly into the surface of fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; fig-leaved hollyhock is a biennial that spends its first season as a ground-level rosette of deeply lobed, fig-shaped leaves before sending up tall flowering spikes the following summer. To maintain a continuous display, sow seed each year so that first-year rosettes and second-year blooming plants are always present side by side in the border. The single flowers in warm shades of yellow, apricot, orange, and pink open in succession from the base of the spike upward through midsummer, and the plant's naturally tough constitution makes it notably more resistant to hollyhock rust (Phragmidium malvacearum) than the common A. rosea. After the main spike sets seed in late summer, cut it back to encourage side shoots that may reflower before frost, and allow some seed to fall and self-sow for the following year's plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, dry, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; finger poppy mallow grows naturally in dry, open prairies and rocky, calcareous outcrops of the south-central US from Texas to Kansas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, dry to moderately moist, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; finger poppy mallow is a distinctive perennial winecup with deeply cut, finger-like leaf lobes that give it its common name — the narrow, finger-like divisions distinguish it from other Callirhoe species. The vivid magenta-red, cup-shaped flowers are typical of the genus. It grows naturally in dry, calcareous prairies and rocky outcrops from Texas to Kansas, tolerating alkaline soils and summer drought well once the deep taproot is established. Like all Callirhoe, it develops a large, fleshy, turnip-like taproot that stores water and nutrients, making established plants very long-lived and drought resistant. An excellent native for xeric, prairie-style gardens and calcareous soil landscapes in the south-central US.

common_name: Fingers Anthurium (Cut-Leaf Anthurium, Radiating Finger Anthurium, Mexican Finger Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix; Anthurium pedatoradiatum produces leaves that are deeply and narrowly divided into 9–11 fingerlike segments radiating from a central point — an unusual, dramatically different leaf form from the typical heart-shaped anthurium leaf. The overall leaf can reach 18–24 inches across in mature plants, making it a bold architectural statement in shaded spaces. More tolerant of intermediate conditions than many velvet anthuriums. Keep warm (above 55°F) and moderately moist. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Fingers Anthurium is one of the most structurally unusual of the ornamental anthuriums, producing leaves that are dramatically divided into narrow, spreading, fingerlike segments rather than the entire (undivided) heart-shaped or arrow-shaped form typical of the genus. Anthurium pedatoradiatum is a climbing, hemiepiphytic anthurium in the Araceae family native to southern Mexico (Chiapas, Tabasco, Veracruz) and Central America, one of a handful of Anthurium species that produce leaves divided into multiple narrow lobes or segments (a condition called pedatifid or palmatifid division). The plant produces leaves that are deeply divided into 9–11 narrow, lanceolate to oblong segments (lobes) radiating from a central point in the pattern for which the species name pedatoradiatum ('radiating fingers') was given — the individual segments smooth, dark green, and spreading outward from the center like the fingers of an outspread hand. In juvenile plants, the leaves begin simple and heart-shaped, transitioning to the deeply divided adult form as the plant matures and climbs. Fully adult leaves in well-established plants can reach 18–24 inches across, producing a dramatic, palm-like or philodendron-selloum-like silhouette in a shaded garden. The unusual leaf division makes this one of the most architecturally distinctive anthuriums for interior and shaded tropical garden design. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Light was bred for exceptionally strong, sturdy stems that hold its large flower clusters upright without flopping, even after heavy rain.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Light was bred specifically to solve the floppy-stem problem common in many panicle hydrangea cultivars, holding its large, dense, white flower clusters proudly upright even as they age and turn deep red-pink in late summer and fall. Like other panicle hydrangeas it blooms reliably on new wood, so a hard renewal pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the season's flowers. It tolerates more sun and less consistent moisture than mophead hydrangeas once established, and the sturdy stems make it a good choice for a mixed border where less rigid hydrangea cultivars tend to sprawl after rain.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to rocky, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; fire pink self-sows freely and is best treated as a short-lived perennial that renews by seedlings.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, average to rocky, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fire pink is a native Eastern North American wildflower that produces some of the most vivid scarlet-red flowers in the spring garden, with deeply notched five-petaled blooms on sticky-stemmed plants that hummingbirds visit eagerly from April through June. Plants are short-lived (2–3 years) but self-sow freely in suitable conditions and maintain colonies in rocky woodland edges, dry slopes, and shaded roadsides. Plant in groups for the best visual impact; individual plants are sparse in habit. Combine with native ferns, wild columbine, and foamflower for a diverse native understory planting.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, spacing tall plants about a foot apart for airflow. Fireball Blend delivers intense 4-5 inch blooms that are stunning at the back of a bed or planted in mass. The long-lasting flowers hold well both on the plant and in the vase, so cut and deadhead often to keep them coming until frost. Water at the base and space generously to limit powdery mildew.

common_name: Firebush (Scarlet Bush, Hummingbird Bush, Mexican Firebush)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring after last frost; firebush establishes quickly and begins flowering within the first summer. In zone 9–10, firebush is perennial and grows to 6–12 feet, often dying back to the ground after hard freezes but regenerating vigorously from the root crown. In zone 8, it performs as an annual or a returning perennial depending on winter severity. Established plants require minimal supplemental irrigation except during severe drought.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil of any quality — firebush thrives in poor, sandy, low-fertility conditions and performs well without supplemental fertilization once established. Firebush (Hamelia patens) is one of the highest-value native flowering shrubs for wildlife-friendly Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes — a Florida native and tropical American species that produces tubular, bright orange-to-red flowers in dense, clustered cymes from early summer continuously through the first frost, creating one of the longest-lasting flowering displays of any shrub in the region. The relentless summer bloom makes firebush a magnet for hummingbirds, butterflies (especially Gulf fritillary, zebra longwing, and swallowtails), and native bees throughout the growing season; the small, dark purple-black berries that follow the flowers are eaten by mockingbirds, cardinals, and other berry-eating birds, making firebush valuable at multiple levels of the food web. Unlike many nectar plants, firebush blooms heavily in partial shade as well as full sun, making it one of the few flowering shrubs that reliably attracts hummingbirds in partially shaded sites. The foliage is medium green to bronze-tinged (more colorful cultivars like 'Compacta' exist) with a whorled leaf arrangement that gives the plant a distinctive tropical texture. Firebush is extremely heat and drought tolerant once established, grows rapidly in poor soils, and requires essentially no care beyond occasional pruning to shape — an ideal low-maintenance native for zone 9 wildlife gardens.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist perlite/peat mix or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost; crossandra blooms nearly year-round in warm, humid, frost-free conditions.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; crossandra is an Indian native grown for its salmon-orange to coral-red flowers borne in four-sided spikes nearly year-round in warm, frost-free conditions, making it one of the most continuously blooming ornamentals for shaded areas in tropical and subtropical landscapes. Plants prefer consistent warmth and humidity — they struggle when temperatures drop below 55°F and require protection from direct afternoon sun in hot climates. In the Gulf South grow as a container plant, bringing indoors in winter. Fertilize monthly during active growth. The flowers make excellent leis in Hawaii.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or container plants in well-drained, average-fertility soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; firecracker plant blooms most heavily in full sun and produces flowers nearly year-round in frost-free climates.
directions: Root stem cuttings easily in moist sand or perlite, or plant container specimens in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; firecracker plant produces arching, rush-like, nearly leafless stems covered in tubular scarlet-red flowers that are among the most effective hummingbird and butterfly attractors in Gulf Coast landscapes, blooming almost continuously from spring through fall and year-round in frost-free zones. The plant forms a graceful, weeping mound that drapes beautifully over walls, slopes, and containers. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. Cut back hard in late winter if frost-damaged to encourage fresh growth; plants recover quickly. Coral and yellow-flowered selections are also available.

plant_note: Nick seed and direct sow after frost.
directions: Nick the seed coat and direct sow firecracker vine after the last frost in warm soil. This twining morning glory relative bears small scarlet trumpet flowers with yellow throats that draw hummingbirds. Provide a fence or trellis in full sun and average soil, and it will climb quickly through summer. Deadheading is unnecessary, but remove faded flowers if you wish to limit self-seeding.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil.
directions: Firefly is a compact bush honeysuckle prized for its glowing amber-to-gold foliage and small yellow flowers borne over a long season. Adaptable and tough, it grows in full sun to part shade and tolerates poor, dry, or rocky soils once established. Its dense habit and spreading roots make it useful for erosion control on slopes and banks. Prune in late winter or early spring to renew and control size, since it blooms on new wood. The nectar-rich flowers attract bees and other pollinators.

common_name: Firepower Nandina (Compact Brilliant-Red Winter-Color Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Firepower's most dramatic color display occurs in full sun with cold winter temperatures — the combination of sun exposure and cold triggers the most vivid scarlet-red foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Firepower is a compact, mounded dwarf nandina selection producing some of the most vivid fall and winter foliage color available in any compact evergreen shrub — the fine-textured, compound foliage transitions from lime-green in summer through orange to brilliant scarlet-red in fall and winter, with the most intense red occurring during and after the coldest periods. The bright red winter color of 'Firepower' is significantly more intense than the reddish tones of most other nandina cultivars, making it particularly outstanding in winter landscapes when few other evergreen shrubs provide warm color. In Gulf South winters (mild in zone 9), the red coloration is variable — coldest winters produce the best red; mild winters produce more orange and red-orange. The compact, naturally rounded habit (2–3 feet) requires minimal pruning and maintains its shape without shearing, making Firepower one of the most truly low-maintenance landscape shrubs for Gulf South foundation plantings, parking lot islands, and mass plantings. The fine bamboo-textured foliage creates an appealing contrast with bold-leaved plants. 'Firepower' does not produce berries (it is functionally sterile), eliminating the concern about nandina berry toxicity to birds that has arisen in some regions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after temperatures are reliably above 50°F; firespike establishes rapidly in warm, humid weather in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade. It can also be planted in fall in zone 9–10 and will establish over winter with reduced watering.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; firespike is one of the most valuable shade plants for Gulf Coast gardens, producing tall, dramatic spikes of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers from late summer through frost — at exactly the time when ruby-throated hummingbirds are fueling up for migration, making it one of the premier hummingbird plants of the Southeast. Unlike most flowering plants, firespike performs best in bright shade to partial shade and actually blooms more reliably away from direct afternoon sun in the heat of zone 9. The large, glossy, deep-green leaves provide bold tropical texture throughout the season. Cut back by half in early spring to encourage dense branching and more flower spikes; in zone 8 it may die back to the ground in hard freezes but regrows from the roots reliably. Propagates easily from stem cuttings taken in summer.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; firespike is one of the finest partial-shade hummingbird plants for the Gulf Coast — it blooms most heavily in fall (September–December), providing critical nectar for migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds when few other hummingbird plants are in flower.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; firespike is a Central American tropical shrub of the Acanthaceae family that provides one of the finest fall-season hummingbird plant experiences available to Gulf Coast gardeners — from September through December, when most summer-blooming hummingbird plants have finished, firespike erupts into long, upright, brilliant scarlet-red, tubular flower spikes at the tips of each stem, creating a mass of vivid red color at exactly the time when migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds are moving through the Gulf Coast on their southward migration and actively seeking high-calorie nectar sources. The plants bloom prolifically in fall and the flowering continues until frost kills the stems; in zone 9 the roots survive and regrow reliably in spring, and in zone 10–12 firespike is a permanent, multi-season evergreen perennial. It tolerates partial shade — one of its most valuable attributes — blooming acceptably in the dappled shade of open tree canopies where most hummingbird plants would fail to flower. The glossy, dark-green, oval leaves are attractive year-round. An absolutely essential plant for Gulf Coast wildlife gardens.

common_name: Firestick Plant (Pencil Cactus, Milk Bush, Naked Lady)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown specimens in spring in full sun in any very well-drained soil; Firestick Plant cannot survive frost and should be grown in containers in zone 9 that are brought indoors before frost. In zone 10-11, plant outdoors in a sunny, dry location. CRITICAL CAUTION: The abundant milky white latex sap is one of the most severe plant irritants known — contact with eyes can cause temporary to permanent blindness. Wear heavy gloves, eye protection, and long sleeves whenever working with this plant. Keep away from children and pets.
directions: Plant in full sun in any very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Firestick Plant is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives with minimal water in hot, sunny conditions — overwatering or poor drainage causes rapid decline and root rot. Euphorbia tirucalli is a large, succulent shrub or small tree native to tropical East Africa (Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania) and widely distributed throughout the tropics as a traditional living fence plant, medicinal species, and petroleum-substitute biofuel candidate. The plant consists almost entirely of dense, tangled masses of smooth, pencil-thick, green cylindrical stems with virtually no leaves — the stems perform photosynthesis directly. The 'Sticks on Fire' cultivar (the 'Firestick' form) produces young stem tips in vivid orange, yellow, and red — most intensely colored in full sun and cool weather — creating the appearance of a bush on fire. The effect in winter months when the color intensifies is extraordinary. CRITICAL WARNING: The abundant milky white latex sap that immediately flows from any cut or broken stem is a potent toxin and irritant — it can cause severe skin blistering, is extremely dangerous if it contacts the eyes (potentially causing permanent damage or blindness), and is toxic if ingested. Handle with heavy protective equipment only.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; pyracantha requires full sun for best berry production — plants in shade produce fewer fruits.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; firethorn is an evergreen thorny shrub that earns its place in the landscape through a spectacular fall and winter display of clustered, brilliant orange, red, or yellow berries that cover the shrub in such abundance they literally hide the foliage — providing one of the most eye-catching ornamental fruit displays available in temperate gardens. White flower clusters in spring attract bees. Excellent as an espalier against a wall or fence, as a barrier hedge (the thorns are fierce), or as a freestanding specimen. Cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds flock to the berries. 'Mohave' (orange-red, disease-resistant), 'Lalandei' (orange, vigorous), and 'Teton' (yellow-orange, upright) are widely grown. Berries are mildly toxic to humans; do not eat.

common_name: Firewitch Dianthus (Perennial Plant of the Year Magenta Cheddar Pink)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; cheddar pinks cultivars are among the most drought- and heat-tolerant perennials available, thriving in lean, rocky, or sandy soils where richer soil causes rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Firewitch was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 2006, prized for its dense, low mat of needle-like, silvery-blue evergreen foliage that stays attractive year-round, covered in spring by an abundance of fragrant, clove-scented, vivid magenta-pink flowers.
