plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade; fox sedge tolerates temporary flooding and is highly adaptable to the difficult wet-shade conditions at the edges of wetlands, retention ponds, and shaded ditches.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; fox sedge is a widely distributed native sedge of floodplain forests, wet meadows, marsh margins, and shaded streambanks throughout North America, forming dense, bright-green tussocks of narrow, sharply keeled leaves with distinctive bristly seed clusters in summer. It is an exceptionally important food plant for wildlife — the seeds are consumed by ducks, rails, gallinules, and many wetland songbirds, and the dense stems provide nesting cover for marsh birds. In the restoration and native plant garden, fox sedge is invaluable for stabilizing wet, shaded banks, filling rain garden margins, and naturalizing along water features. It tolerates temporary flooding and clay soils, making it one of the most practically useful native sedges for difficult wet-shade situations in zone 9. The dense tussock growth creates important microhabitat for insects and small animals.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in sharply well-drained, gritty or sandy soil in partial shade in fall, 6–10 weeks before first frost; fox's grape fritillary is native to rocky slopes and meadows in Turkey and Iraq and demands excellent drainage — allow soil to dry out through summer dormancy as wet summer conditions will rot the small bulbs. A sunny or lightly shaded site with lean, well-drained soil gives the best results.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in partial shade in autumn for April–May bloom; fox's grape fritillary is a charming small fritillary from Turkey and Iraq producing slender stems that carry one to three pendant, bell-shaped flowers with a distinctive and striking bicolor pattern — the outer surface of each bell is a rich purple-brown to chocolate color with golden-yellow tips at the petal ends, while the inner surface is washed in the same warm yellow, creating an elegant contrast reminiscent of a dark grape with a glowing interior. At just 6–10 inches tall, it is one of the smaller fritillaries and is best appreciated at close range in a rock garden, raised bed, or front of a mixed border. Like most Middle Eastern fritillaries, it requires dry summer dormancy and will rot in wet or heavy soils; excellent drainage is essential. It naturalizes slowly in suitable conditions. A refined and underused spring bulb for gardeners seeking alternatives to the common snake's head or crown imperial fritillaries.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; seeds need light and should not be covered.
directions: Press seeds onto the surface of moist potting mix under bright light — do not cover, as light aids germination. Foxgloves are biennial or short-lived perennials; most produce a rosette in year 1 and the spectacular tall spikes in year 2 before setting seed and dying. Cutting the main spike after bloom often stimulates smaller side spikes for additional flowers, and self-sowing keeps the planting going indefinitely. All parts of the plant are highly toxic; use caution and wash hands thoroughly after handling.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; foxglove beardtongue adapts to a wide range of conditions including clay and seasonally wet soil.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun; foxglove beardtongue is the most adaptable and widely grown native penstemon in eastern North America, producing tall spikes of white, occasionally pale-pink, foxglove-like flowers in late spring to early summer that are valuable for native bumblebees, which must squeeze inside the flowers to reach the nectar — a striking spectacle of bee behavior. The glossy, semi-evergreen basal rosette and reddish-maroon winter foliage provide year-round interest. Excellent in moist meadows, prairie plantings, and partially shaded woodland edges. 'Husker Red' (intense maroon-purple foliage throughout the season, white flowers) is the most popular cultivar, earning a Perennial Plant of the Year award in 1996 — it delivers bold foliage interest even when not in bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–May or September–October. Foxtail Fern grows from tuberous roots that store moisture, making it more drought tolerant than its lush appearance suggests. In zone 9 it is evergreen to semi-evergreen, surviving mild winters with little damage; hard freezes (below 28°F) will damage or kill the above-ground stems, but the tuberous roots typically survive and resprout. Small white flowers and red berries form on established plants — the berries are mildly toxic if ingested. Despite the common name, this is not a true fern but an asparagus relative with needle-like cladodes.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Foxtail Fern adapts to a wide range of light conditions but produces its densest, most architectural stems in consistent partial shade; Myers Foxtail Fern is distinguished from the better-known Sprengeri Fern (Asparagus densiflorus 'Sprengeri') by its dramatically different growth habit — instead of the loose, trailing, cascading stems of Sprengeri, Myers produces dense, upright, bottlebrush-like stems 12–18 inches long that radiate symmetrically from the center like the tail of a fox, creating an architectural, structural plant form that is highly effective as a container plant, border specimen, and cut greenery. The precise, uniform, densely needled stems are prized by florists and cut flower arrangers for their long vase life, unique texture, and the soft, fine-needle effect that provides exceptional filler material in arrangements. As a landscape plant in zone 9, Foxtail Fern's dense, mounding habit and tolerance for partial shade and occasional drought make it an effective and low-maintenance ground cover or border edging plant. The evergreen to semi-evergreen foliage in Gulf South winters and the container culture versatility (it grows excellently in large pots) add to its practical utility.

plant_note: Plant the spider-like fleshy roots in fall, spreading them horizontally 4 in deep in a well-drained, sunny site.
directions: Spread the octopus-like fleshy roots horizontally over a mound of gritty soil, crown just below the surface, with perfect drainage — wet winter soil rots the crowns quickly. The strap-like foliage emerges in early spring and can be killed by a late frost; a light cover of straw protects emerging growth in zones 5–6. Spectacular bottle-brush spikes up to 8 ft tall erupt in late spring to early summer in shades of white, yellow, orange, and pink. Leaves die back after bloom, so interplant with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap.

common_name: Foxtail Orchid (Gigantea Rhynchostylis, Giant Vanda, Foxtail Vanda)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork or tree fern bark, or in a slatted teak basket with minimal or no media (this species grows best with roots fully exposed to air); Rhynchostylis gigantea is a monopodial orchid that should never be repotted — simply mount or attach to new material as the plant outgrows its mounting. In zone 9, grow on a shaded porch in a hanging basket year-round, protecting from temperatures below 50°F. Natural blooming occurs in fall–winter in the Northern Hemisphere. Water by misting or dunking the roots daily in summer, less frequently in winter. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun with fully exposed aerial roots — Rhynchostylis gigantea, like its Vanda relatives, requires bright light and excellent air circulation to produce its best flower display. Rhynchostylis gigantea is a large, monopodial epiphytic orchid from the tropical forests of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Borneo in the family Orchidaceae, closely related to Vanda and considered by many orchid enthusiasts to produce the most intensely fragrant flowers of any readily available epiphytic orchid. The plant produces a single upright stem clothed in pairs of thick, strap-like, semi-terete dark-green leaves, with long, pendulous, rope-like silver roots hanging below. In fall and winter, the plants produce pendant racemes (the 'foxtails') 8–16 inches long, densely packed with 30–80 small (1–1.5 inch) waxy flowers in white to pale pink with distinctive spots and bars of deep pink-magenta to red-purple — the entire drooping, densely-flowered raceme resembling a fox's bushy tail. The fragrance is extraordinary — sweet, powerful, and pervasive, carrying remarkable distances on warm evenings, often described as combining jasmine, honey, and citrus. Rhynchostylis gigantea is the national flower of Myanmar (Burma). White-flowering albino forms ('Alba') are particularly prized. Non-toxic to pets.

common_name: Foxtail Palm (Wodyetia Palm, Australian Foxtail Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with very well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Foxtail Palm is cold-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting in the US, though it may survive brief temperature dips to 28–30°F as a mature tree. It grows moderately fast in warm, humid conditions. The distinctive arching, full, brush-like fronds (the 'foxtail') give the palm an exceptionally lush appearance. Self-cleaning (old fronds drop cleanly). Provide magnesium and potassium supplements to prevent nutritional deficiencies in Florida and Gulf Coast soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Foxtail Palm grows most vigorously in full sun and becomes thin and elongated in shaded positions. Wodyetia bifurcata is a medium-sized, single-trunked feather palm endemic to a small area of far northeastern Queensland, Australia (Cape York Peninsula) in the Arecaceae family, first described to science in 1978 and named for the Aboriginal elder Wodyeti, the last person to possess traditional knowledge of the species. The palm has become one of the most widely planted ornamental palms in tropical and subtropical gardens worldwide since its introduction, for one primary reason: the extraordinary, immediately distinctive form of its fronds. Each frond arches gracefully outward and is densely clothed with leaflets that radiate in multiple planes around the rachis in a full, brush-like, three-dimensional arrangement that creates the appearance of an enormous, lush foxtail — a completely different silhouette from the flat, two-dimensional frond arrangement typical of most pinnate palms. The combination of the lush foxtail fronds, the clean, smooth, gray-ringed trunk, and the self-cleaning habit (old fronds drop without persistent bases) makes the Foxtail Palm one of the most elegant and low-maintenance ornamental palms available for zone 10-12 landscapes. Moderate growth rate; reaches 20–30 feet at maturity.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky, lean, well-aerated soil in full sun; foxtail pine grows naturally at extreme high elevations on exposed, rocky, nutrient-poor, often serpentine soils in the Klamath Mountains and southern Sierra Nevada — one of the most extreme growing conditions of any tree species in North America.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky, lean, well-aerated soil in full sun; foxtail pine is a rare and distinctive five-needle pine endemic to California — growing in two widely separated populations, one in the Klamath Mountains of northwestern California and one in the high Sierra Nevada above 10,000 feet. Named for the characteristic dense clusters of needles that persist on the branchlets for 10–20 years (rather than the 2–5 years typical of most pines), creating long, bottle-brush-like branch segments resembling a fox's tail. This exceptionally long needle retention is an adaptation to the extreme high-elevation environment where growing season is very short and photosynthetic tissue is valuable. Related to and resembling the bristlecone pine (P. longaeva) in adaptation to extreme subalpine-to-treeline environments, with similar windswept, gnarled growth forms at the highest elevations. Very long-lived — ancient individuals estimated at 2,000–3,000 years exist in the Klamath populations. Rarely grown in gardens but of great interest to conifer collectors.

plant_note: Plant small divisions or pot-grown plants in spring in moist to moderately dry, rocky to humus-rich, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; fragile fern is unusual in tolerating alkaline, rocky, and cliff-face conditions that most ferns cannot — it is often found growing in rock crevices and on mossy outcrops.
directions: Plant in spring in well-drained, moderately moist, rocky or humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fragile fern is well suited to planting in rock garden crevices, along stone walls, on mossy banks, and in shaded rock gardens where its diminutive size suits the scale. Cystopteris fragilis is one of the most widely distributed ferns in the world, found across North America, Europe, Asia, and even South America wherever shaded, rocky slopes and cliff faces provide moisture-retaining crevices; the common name refers to the delicate, brittle stipes (stems) that snap easily when handled, not to the plant's constitution — it is a tough, cold-hardy fern tolerating zones 2–8. The fronds are small (6–15 inches), finely twice-pinnate, lacy, and light green, emerging in early spring and sometimes going dormant in summer drought; in a sheltered, consistently moist spot it may remain lush through the season. An excellent miniature fern for shaded rock gardens, wall crevices, and small-scale woodland plantings.

common_name: Fragrant Aerides (Fox Tail Orchid, Cat's Tail Orchid, Foxtail Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on rough bark or in a slatted basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct light; Aerides odorata is a large, terete-leaved vandaceous orchid from tropical Asia that produces pendant racemes of densely packed, waxy, white-and-rose-purple flowers with a strong, sweet fragrance. One of the most fragrant orchids in cultivation. In zone 9-12, it can be grown outdoors on shaded porches in summer with protection from frost in winter. The pendant flower spikes with their densely packed, jewel-like flowers are extremely ornamental. Water regularly in active growth; reduce in winter. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light mounted on bark or in a slatted basket with very open drainage — Fragrant Aerides grows most vigorously in warm, humid, bright conditions similar to its native lowland tropical forest habitat in Southeast Asia. Aerides odorata is a large, upright, monopodial epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to India, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, and Indonesia — a member of the tribe Vandeae and closely related to Vanda, sharing the same terete (round, cylindrical) leaf form and the same cultural requirements. The plant produces a main stem clothed in distichous (two-ranked), cylindrical, fleshy, dark-green leaves 8–10 inches long that give the plant an unusual, tropical appearance distinct from the broad, flat-leaved vandaceous types. In late spring and summer, long, pendant racemes 8–14 inches long emerge from the leaf axils, densely packed with 20–40 small (1-inch), waxy, long-lasting flowers in white with rose-purple to magenta tips and spotting, and a prominent, spurred, bright rose-purple lip — the densely packed flowers giving the raceme a lush, jewel-studded quality. The fragrance is the outstanding quality: intensely sweet, penetrating, and floral, among the strongest and most pleasant scents of any orchid in cultivation. The species name odorata directly references this fragrance. Aerides odorata has contributed its fragrance and flower density to many hybrid vandaceous orchids. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, dry, lean, slightly acidic to neutral or calcareous soil in full sun; fragrant gaillardia grows naturally in dry, rocky, calcareous, or sandy prairies and open woodlands of the south-central US from Texas to Kansas.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or calcareous soil in full sun; fragrant gaillardia is the only pleasantly fragrant species in the blanket flower genus — most gaillardias are odorless, but G. suavis produces a sweet, clover-like fragrance from its rounded, ball-like flower heads, which lack the ray (petal) flowers typical of the genus and instead produce only disc flowers — giving it a uniquely spherical, pom-pom appearance. It is native to the dry prairies and open rocky soils of the south-central US and is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant. The fragrance makes it unusual and valuable in the sensory or cut-flower garden. An underused native for dry, sunny, prairie-style or xeriscape plantings in zone 9a where it requires minimal care once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; fragrant hosta is more heat tolerant than most hostas and is one of the best hosta species for zone 8–9, where it performs more reliably than the northern-bred cultivars that need cold winters to thrive.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to dappled shade — fragrant hosta stands apart from all other hostas by being the only species with intensely, beautifully fragrant flowers — large, pure white, trumpet-shaped blooms on tall scapes in August that fill the evening garden with a sweet, lily-like perfume. The light-green, glossy, somewhat corrugated leaves are unlike the typical blue-green, waxy hostas — they are brighter and more luminous in the shade garden. Fragrant hosta is also significantly more heat-tolerant than most hosta cultivars, performing reliably in zone 8–9 where most hybrid hostas struggle to thrive without cold winters. The evening fragrance is outstanding when planted near patios, pathways, and windows. Derived cultivars like 'Royal Standard' and 'Aphrodite' (double flowers) extend the bloom period and flower character. Exceptional as a long-lived, low-maintenance shade perennial for warm-climate gardens.

plant_note: Plant dormant tubers or container divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; fragrant ladies tresses is a native North American terrestrial orchid of wet meadows, marsh edges, and moist open woodlands that is remarkably adaptable as a garden plant, naturalizing in moist sites.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; keep consistently moist. Spiranthes odorata (fragrant ladies tresses) is a native North American terrestrial orchid of the southeastern coastal plain — one of the most gardener-accessible native orchids available for cultivation, native to moist meadows, pond margins, and marsh edges from Maryland through Florida and Texas. It produces a slender, erect spike 10–24 inches tall bearing tiny, white, sweetly vanilla-scented flowers arranged in a characteristic spiral pattern (the 'ladies tresses' that gives the genus its name) from September through November — an unusually late bloom time that makes it exceptional for extending the season in native plant gardens. The 'Chadds Ford' selection is particularly vigorous and easy in garden conditions. Unlike many native orchids that are difficult to transplant and resent disturbance, S. odorata is relatively adaptable and can be established in rain gardens, moist meadows, and pond margins where consistent moisture is available. The fragrance of the fall-blooming spikes is notable for its sweet vanilla quality. An underused native orchid for moist southern gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; sweet olive is adaptable but performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade in the hottest climates. It is slow-growing but very long-lived once established.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant olive (sweet olive, tea olive) is one of the most beloved fragrant shrubs of the Gulf South — a classic fixture in old Southern gardens, cherished for its tiny, creamy white flowers that perfume the air with an intense, sweet apricot-like fragrance that can carry 100 yards on a still autumn morning. The plant blooms repeatedly from fall through spring in zone 8–9, often triggered by cool snaps, and the fragrance is one of the most powerful and instantly recognizable in the Southern garden tradition. The large, dense, glossy evergreen shrub makes an outstanding screen, hedge, or specimen. It grows slowly but lives for decades and eventually becomes a small tree. The variety O. fragrans f. aurantiacus has orange flowers; 'Fudingzhu' is a particularly free-flowering white selection.

common_name: Fragrant Pink Camellia (Pioneer Sweet-Scented Small-Flower Hybrid Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Fragrant Pink was one of the first fragrant camellias widely available in the nursery trade and established the concept of fragrant camellia hybrids before the later High Fragrance and other cultivars expanded the group.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; Fragrant Pink is a hybrid Camellia bred to introduce the sweet floral fragrance of Camellia lutchuensis into cultivars with the refined flower form of Camellia japonica — a cross that transformed the possibilities of camellia breeding by combining beauty and scent that had previously been impossible in a single plant. The flowers of Fragrant Pink are small to medium-sized, peony-form to double, in clear soft rose-pink — the individual flower size is smaller than most japonica cultivars, a characteristic inherited from the C. lutchuensis parent, but the sweet, true floral fragrance detectable from several feet away compensates fully for the smaller bloom size. The scent is genuine and pleasant — not a faint hint but a real, detectable, jasmine-like sweetness that makes this camellia suitable for planting near outdoor living areas. Fragrant Pink typically blooms in late winter (January–March in zone 9), filling the period when the garden has few fragrant flowering plants. The plant grows as a compact to medium evergreen shrub — somewhat smaller than most C. japonica cultivars — with a densely branched, naturally rounded habit. In zone 9, it is a reliable landscape perennial performing best with morning sun and afternoon shade. The fragrant flower characteristic and compact habit make Fragrant Pink an ideal camellia for planting near patios, garden seats, and paths where the sweet winter fragrance enhances the garden experience.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into deep, loose, sandy soil; the papery seed bracts can be left intact or removed to improve germination speed.
directions: Fragrant Sand Verbena is a sprawling, glandular-sticky native perennial of dry, sandy prairies, dunes, and roadsides of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain foothills. It produces dense, ball-like clusters of small, intensely fragrant white to pale pinkish tubular flowers in spring and summer that open in the evening and release a powerful sweet vanilla-clove fragrance highly attractive to hawk moths at dusk. Direct sow in fall in deep, loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, or start indoors in deep containers to accommodate the taproot — this plant is not suited to heavy, clay, or waterlogged soils. An outstanding fragrant native for moonlight and pollinator gardens across zones 4-8.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; fragrant snowbell is slow to establish and benefits from mulching to maintain consistent soil moisture during the first 2-3 years.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant snowbell is an underused Japanese deciduous tree distinguished from the common Japanese snowbell (S. japonicus) by its much larger, broadly rounded leaves that can be 8 inches across — giving the tree a bold, almost tropical appearance in summer. In late spring, the long, pendant racemes of white, bell-shaped flowers hang beneath the large leaves in an unusually graceful display with a soft vanilla-like fragrance that is notably stronger than S. japonicus. The combination of bold leaves and hanging flower clusters is architecturally distinctive. The tree tolerates partial shade better than most flowering trees and is excellent as an understory specimen beneath taller oaks and beeches. Yellow fall color.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring before shoots emerge, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fragrant Solomon's seal establishes slowly in the first year but expands steadily thereafter — rhizome divisions should include at least one growth bud and be planted horizontally just below the soil surface.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fragrant Solomon's seal is a Japanese and European woodland perennial celebrated for the extraordinary architectural grace of its arching stems — each unbranched, leafy, gently arching stem carries two alternating rows of oval, deep-green, pointed leaves from whose axils hang paired, small, pendant, white, tubular, bell-shaped flowers with faint green tips in spring, and the flowers are delicately and sweetly fragrant in the cultivar 'Variegatum' (the most widely grown form, with leaves elegantly edged in creamy-white). The naturally arching habit of the stems is one of the most beautiful and refined forms in the woodland garden. After flowering, dark-blue berries develop along the underside of the stems. In fall the foliage turns a warm, clear yellow before dying back to the ground. 'Variegatum' (syn. 'Striatum') is the primary cultivar in commerce, its white-margined leaves providing luminous, long-season color in deep shade. Fragrant Solomon's seal is more strongly scented than the common species (P. multiflorum) and is indispensable in the classic shade garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant sumac is one of the best native shrubs for dry, shaded slopes and is excellent for erosion control.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; fragrant sumac is one of the most versatile, adaptable, and underused native shrubs in North America — tolerating dry shade, rocky slopes, alkaline soil, and drought conditions that defeat most plants. The crushed leaves have a distinctly pleasant lemon-citrus fragrance. Small yellow flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge provide important early nectar for native bees emerging from overwintering. The fuzzy red fruit clusters feed dozens of bird species through fall and winter. The three-parted leaves turn brilliant orange-red and burgundy in fall — among the best native plants for fall color — and the low, spreading form makes it excellent for groundcover use on slopes. The cultivar 'Gro-Low' is a compact, 2-foot-tall groundcover form widely used in landscape planting.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; fragrant tulbaghia is winter-blooming in South Africa (May–September) and produces its beautiful white flowers when little else is blooming. Unlike the violet-flowered T. violacea (Society Garlic), T. simmleri has no garlic odor — the flowers are pleasantly sweet-fragrant instead. More frost-tender than T. violacea.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; fragrant tulbaghia differs from the much more commonly grown Society Garlic (T. violacea) in three important ways: the flowers are pure white rather than violet, the flowers are pleasantly sweet-fragrant rather than garlicky-scented, and it blooms in winter rather than summer. In zone 9 gardens, this combination of white winter flowers and sweet fragrance (rather than the pungent garlic smell that deters some gardeners from T. violacea) makes it a more refined and widely appealing garden plant for positions near paths, entrances, or seating areas where the winter fragrance can be appreciated. The umbels of clean, white, six-petaled, tubular flowers on tall stems above the narrow, strap-shaped, gray-green leaves are elegant and refined; the sweet, light fragrance is detectable throughout the garden from a single established clump. Like T. violacea, it forms steadily expanding clumps that can be divided regularly. Outstanding for zone 9 winter-interest plantings where winter color and fragrance in the garden are otherwise limited.

common_name: Fragrant Water Lily (American White Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant rhizome sections in spring in aquatic planting containers filled with heavy, nutrient-rich clay-based soil submerged 1–2 feet below the water surface in full sun; fragrant water lily is a native North American aquatic plant outstanding for garden ponds, water features, and naturalized wetland gardens from zone 3 through zone 11.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in heavy clay-loam soil in an aquatic basket set 12–24 inches below the water surface in full sun; do not use organic potting mix. Nymphaea odorata (fragrant water lily or American white water lily) is the native water lily of eastern North America — one of the most beautiful and ecologically important aquatic plants of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving waters from Newfoundland to Florida and Texas. It produces the classic, drifting, rounded floating leaves (lily pads) 4–12 inches across and exquisitely beautiful, cupped, multi-petaled white flowers 2–5 inches across with golden-yellow stamens, opening in the morning and closing by midday, with an intensely sweet vanilla-rose fragrance carried over the water surface on warm summer mornings. The flowers are highly attractive to native bees and other pollinators that visit while the flowers are open. The floating leaves provide surface shade that reduces algae growth and provides refuge for fish and aquatic insects. The plant is vigorous and will spread readily by rhizome in natural pond settings — excellent for naturalizing wetland margins and rain gardens. Young buds, seeds, and roots were used as food by many Native American peoples. Grow in full sun for maximum flowering.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, shady soil.
directions: Francee is a classic shade hosta with dark green leaves crisply edged in white, forming a tidy mounded clump and sending up lavender flower spikes in summer. Plant it in partial to full shade in rich, moist, well-drained soil, as too much sun scorches the variegated foliage. Keep the soil evenly moist and mulch to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Divide clumps in spring every few years to propagate or reduce crowding. Watch for slugs, which can chew the leaves, especially in damp conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Frances Williams is a slow-growing giant that takes 3–4 years to reach full size but is extremely long-lived and virtually indestructible once established.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; Frances Williams is one of the most celebrated and widely grown hostas in the world, a giant with distinctive round, deeply puckered, blue-green leaves edged with an irregular golden-to-chartreuse margin 1–3 inches wide. The thick, waxy leaf texture provides moderate slug resistance, a notable advantage over thinner-leafed cultivars. It is a slow grower that requires 3–4 years to develop its full character — a mound 2–2.5 feet tall and 4–5 feet wide that becomes the focal point of any shaded garden. Pale lavender flowers appear in midsummer on tall scapes above the foliage but are considered secondary to the bold leaf display. In zone 8–9, situate it where morning sun reaches the leaves but where it is protected from harsh afternoon heat, and maintain consistent moisture to prevent leaf scorch on the margins. Mulch heavily with wood chips to retain moisture and suppress competing weeds.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Franchet's epimedium is a vigorous Chinese species with unusually spidery, long-spurred flowers in orange-yellow tones that are striking in the spring garden.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Franchet's epimedium is a Chinese species from Hubei and Sichuan with distinctively spidery, long-spurred flowers in warm orange-yellow tones that stand out among the generally purple and white epimediums. The long, curved, orange-tinged spurs give the flowers a dramatic, airy quality when backlit. The foliage is semi-evergreen to evergreen, with attractive bronzy-red mottling on new spring growth. This species is notable for being one of the more vigorous and spreading epimediums, forming good groundcover more quickly than some of the slower-growing species. It is named for the French botanist Adrien René Franchet, who described many plants introduced from China during the late 19th century. Excellent for dry shade under deciduous trees where it competes well with tree roots.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; frangipani is one of the most iconic tropical flowering trees for Gulf Coast and subtropical gardens and performs well in zone 9–12 when given good drainage and full sun.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; allow soil to dry between waterings. Plumeria rubra (frangipani) is one of the most beloved and iconic tropical flowering trees in the world — a deciduous Central American tree or large shrub producing clusters of breathtakingly beautiful, intensely fragrant, 5-petaled flowers in an enormous range of colors (red, pink, orange, yellow, white, salmon, and multicolor) from late spring through fall on bare or nearly bare branches, with the flowers most concentrated when the plant is otherwise leafless. The legendary fragrance of frangipani — sweet, heady, exotic — has made it the quintessential tropical flower scent; the white-and-yellow P. obtusa and related species are used for Hawaiian leis, Buddhist temple offerings, and perfume across Southeast Asia. In zone 9, plumeria grows as a large shrub (6–10 feet) and goes fully dormant and leafless in winter — it should not be watered when leafless to avoid root rot. Rooted cuttings are the fastest way to bloom. Plumeria is surprisingly drought-tolerant and requires perfect drainage to avoid stem rot.

plant_note: Direct sow in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Frank's sedge is particularly well adapted to the heavy clay alluvial soils of floodplains and is a reliable plant for difficult wet clay sites in the Southeast.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, heavy clay to loamy soils in partial shade to full sun in floodplains, swamp edges, and wet gardens; Frank's sedge is a native wetland sedge of the lower Midwest and Southeast, growing naturally in alluvial floodplain forests, swamp margins, and wet meadows from Pennsylvania south to Florida and west to Missouri and Kansas. It is particularly adapted to the heavy, periodically flooded clay soils typical of river bottomlands in the Southeast — a substrate that challenges most other native sedges. The barrel-shaped, spiky seed heads with spreading perigynia resemble those of Carex squarrosa but tend to be more numerous and loosely spaced on the stem. An excellent choice for rain garden plantings in clay soils and for stream bank restoration in the Gulf South. The robust clumps provide winter cover for small birds and the seeds are consumed by waterfowl.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, acid, humus-rich soil with excellent drainage; Franklinia demands perfect drainage and will not tolerate wet or compacted soils — root rot (Phytophthora) is the primary cause of failure in unsuitable sites. Plant in raised beds in heavy clay soils. All cultivated specimens worldwide descend from seeds collected by John Bartram in 1765.
directions: Plant in moist, acid, humus-rich, perfectly drained soil in part shade to full sun; Franklinia alatamaha is the most famous extinct-in-the-wild tree in North America — last seen growing wild along the Altamaha River in Georgia by John Bartram in 1803 and never found wild again, every Franklinia tree alive today descends from seeds or cuttings taken by Bartram before the species vanished from nature. The tree itself is extraordinary: large (3–4 inch) camellia-like white flowers with brilliant golden stamens bloom from August through October at the same time as the leaves turn flaming orange-red, producing a spectacular late-season display unlike any other temperate tree. The flowers are fragrant. It is a rare opportunity to grow a tree that would be extinct today without human cultivation — both a horticultural treasure and a living piece of botanical history.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic, fertile loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Fraser fir is native to the high-elevation spruce-fir forests of the southern Appalachians (above 4,500 feet) and requires cool, moist conditions. Does not tolerate heat or prolonged drought.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic, fertile loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Fraser fir is widely considered the finest Christmas tree in the United States — with a perfect, dense, symmetrical cone shape, outstanding needle retention after cutting, pleasant fragrance, and stiff branches capable of holding heavy ornaments without drooping. The species is native to the high-elevation spruce-fir forests of the southern Appalachians (primarily in western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, and southwest Virginia above 5,000 feet) where it faces severe threat from the introduced balsam woolly adelgid (Adelges piceae), which has killed a large proportion of wild mature trees. Christmas tree farming in the Carolina mountains (particularly around Ashe County, NC) has made Fraser fir a major agricultural crop — North Carolina produces more Christmas trees than any other state. More heat-tolerant than balsam fir, succeeding in zone 7 where balsam fir fails.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Fraser Magnolia is an understory tree that performs best in sheltered positions with protection from late spring frosts that can damage the large, showy flower buds.
directions: Fraser Magnolia is a deciduous native magnolia of the southern Appalachians, native to the rich, moist cove forests and ravine slopes from Virginia and West Virginia south to Georgia and Alabama, immediately recognizable by its enormous leaves (up to 18 inches long) with distinctive ear-like lobes (auricles) at the base — the largest leaves of any magnolia native to the southern mountains. In May and June it produces large, cup-shaped, creamy-white, fragrant flowers 8–10 inches across that emit a sweet, lemony fragrance, followed in fall by striking pink to red cone-like fruit clusters that split to reveal bright red seeds, providing ornamental interest from spring through fall. Fraser Magnolia is a shade-tolerant understory tree that grows naturally in the deepest, richest, most sheltered cove forest conditions alongside cucumber magnolia, yellow buckeye, and basswood, and it translates beautifully to shaded woodland gardens in zones 5–8. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protecting from prevailing wind to prevent the large leaves from tearing.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free areas (zones 9–10) or start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost in cold climates.
directions: Plant corms 2 in deep and 2–3 in apart in gritty, well-drained soil; freesias resent wet conditions especially after bloom. The fragrant, funnel-shaped flowers on arching stems need staking or a grow-through support as stems are slender. In frost-free gardens the corms are perennial and naturalize freely; in colder climates lift after foliage dies, dry thoroughly, and store in a cool dry place. Corms multiply quickly — divide every 2–3 years to maintain bloom quality.

common_name: Freida Hemple Caladium (Classic Bright Cherry-Red Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Freida Hemple is one of the oldest and most famous fancy-leaf caladium cultivars, producing large, heart-shaped leaves in vivid cherry-red centers bordered by a wide, dark green margin, one of the most eye-catching color combinations available among caladiums. Its bold color has made it a mainstay of Southern shade gardens for generations, providing season-long tropical color in beds and containers without the need for flowers. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors over winter in cooler zones ensures better survival.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in late winter to early spring in moist, riparian, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Fremont cottonwood is a riparian specialist requiring consistent access to groundwater. Plant near streams, rivers, and natural waterways, or in sites with high water tables.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings in spring in moist to wet, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along stream banks, river edges, and areas with high water tables; Fremont cottonwood is the dominant riparian tree of the American Southwest, forming gallery forests along desert rivers from California to New Mexico. The massive, fast-growing trees reach 40–80 feet, with deeply furrowed, gray-brown bark and large, triangular, bright green leaves that flutter constantly in desert breezes. In the arid Southwest, riparian cottonwood forests are oases of biodiversity — the trees support more bird species than any other habitat type in the desert, providing nesting sites for endangered southwestern willow flycatchers, yellow-billed cuckoos, and numerous neotropical migrants. The fall foliage is brilliant gold, providing the most spectacular fall color in the otherwise largely evergreen Sonoran and Mojave Desert landscapes. Named for explorer John C. Frémont who documented it in western expeditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; marigolds transplant easily and bloom within 6–8 weeks of transplanting.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; marigolds transplant easily and bloom within 6–8 weeks of transplanting. Tagetes patula is the compact, bushy French marigold with small, double or single flowers in yellow, orange, red, and bicolors that bloom continuously from planting through frost; it has a long history as a companion plant for vegetable gardens, and research has confirmed that high-density plantings suppress root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species) in subsequent seasons. The pungent fragrance of the foliage deters some insect pests; the flowers provide nectar for small native bees, hoverflies, and butterflies; and the plant is heat-tolerant, drought-resistant, and virtually care-free. Deadheading is not required but extends the display.

plant_note: Start indoors for early bloom or direct sow after frost.
directions: This French marigold mix stays compact at about a foot tall with bright, two- to three-inch double blooms in gold, orange, yellow, and red. Sow seeds shallowly after the last frost or start indoors for earlier color, and place in full sun. The tidy mounded plants edge beds neatly and pair well with vegetables to help repel pests. Deadhead often for continuous flowering right up to fall frost.

common_name: Fresh Look Red Celosia (AAS-Winning Compact Vivid-Red Cockscomb Celosia)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting or direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fresh Look Red is a crested (cockscomb) type celosia — the ruffled, velvety, brain-like flower heads are distinctive and maintain their vivid color through the entire warm season without fading.
directions: Transplant after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fresh Look Red is an All-America Selections award-winning celosia in the crested (cockscomb) type — producing the distinctive velvety, ruffled, brain-shaped flower heads in vivid crimson-red. The compact, uniform habit (12–18 inches) with large, well-developed flower heads makes Fresh Look Red more ornamental and practical for garden use than older cockscomb types that were often taller and less uniformly sized. The velvety texture of the crested flower head is unique in summer annuals — the crimped, corrugated surface catches light at different angles to create depth and luminosity in the vivid red color that plain-surfaced flowers cannot match. The color maintains its intensity through the entire warm season without bleaching or browning — one of the few truly summer-proof vivid-red annuals for Gulf South gardens where July–August heat causes many flowers to fade or develop heat-stress brown tones. The compact size and vivid color make Fresh Look Red outstanding for mixed container plantings, border edging, and mass plantings in full-sun summer beds. The flower heads dry well for winter arrangements, maintaining their deep red color for months when dried quickly in a warm, low-humidity location.

common_name: Fresh Look Yellow Celosia (AAS-Winning Bright Yellow Long-Season Cockscomb)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after the last frost, or direct sow after soil is consistently warm (75°F+); Fresh Look Yellow maintains its vibrant golden-yellow color throughout the season without fading, a trait that earned it AAS recognition over earlier yellow celosia selections that tended to fade to cream in heat.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fresh Look Yellow is an All-America Selections winner in the cockscomb (cristata) type of Celosia argentea — producing rounded, brain-like, velvety crested flower heads in clear, vivid golden yellow that maintains its color throughout the long season without fading to cream or pale yellow as earlier yellow celosia varieties tended to do in Gulf South summer heat. The color consistency was the key improvement that earned the AAS award — a true, saturated golden-yellow that holds its intensity from first bloom through fall frost, providing a reliable color anchor in summer and fall mixed borders. The crested, velvety flower heads have a unique texture — velvet-soft, deeply convoluted, with a rich tactile quality that makes them as interesting to touch as to see — and the heads last for months on the plant without deadheading. Fresh Look Yellow is an outstanding cut flower and dried flower plant: the vivid yellow crested heads dry naturally on the stem without significant color loss, making them valuable for dried arrangements that last for months after harvest. Excellent in mixed summer combination plantings with deep blue salvias, orange lantana, and bronze foliage plants. In Gulf South zone 9, celosia can often be direct-seeded in warm soil for a late-summer crop when transplant-grown plants have passed peak.

common_name: Frida Hemple Caladium (Bold Solid-Red Classic Large Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Frida Hemple's solid-red coloration retains its intensity in bright partial shade but may fade to an orange-red in deep shade with insufficient light.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Frida Hemple (also sold as 'Freida Hemple') is one of the most boldly colored and commercially important red caladium varieties — a large fancy-leaf type producing classic heart-shaped leaves in a vivid, nearly solid crimson-red to scarlet-red coloration with only narrow green margins framing the predominantly red leaf surface. The almost entirely red leaf color — covering 80–90% of the leaf surface with no significant white or pink zones — creates a bolder, more saturated red display than varieties with mixed patterns, and makes Frida Hemple one of the most effective caladiums for massing in shade positions where pure, saturated red color is the design goal. The large leaf size (leaves can reach 12–16 inches on established plants) and vivid coloration make Frida Hemple outstanding in formal shade bed plantings, as a front-of-border accent, and in large container designs where the bold red needs to carry over distance. Frida Hemple has been a commercially important caladium cultivar for many decades — its reliable vigor, consistent color, and excellent tuber production have kept it in continuous commercial production. Combine with white companions ('Aaron', 'Candidum', white impatiens) for maximum red-and-white contrast, or with deep green groundcovers (creeping Jenny, carpet bugle) to intensify the red color by contrast. Consistent moisture throughout the warm season ensures largest leaf development.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sheltered spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hotter inland zones. This slow-growing member of the tea family resents root disturbance, so site it carefully from the outset.
directions: Grow in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil similar to what camellias prefer, keeping the pH between 5.0 and 6.5 and the root zone consistently moist but never waterlogged. The large, white, camellia-like flowers with showy yellow stamens open from autumn through winter, providing color when little else is blooming in the garden. Protect young plants from hard freezes with frost cloth, as established specimens tolerate brief dips to the upper teens but young transplants are more vulnerable. Minimal pruning is needed; remove only crossing or damaged branches in late spring after the main flush of bloom.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in rich, moist soil with afternoon shade.
directions: Frill Ride is a bigleaf hydrangea bearing bold mophead blooms with distinctive frilled petal edges in shades that shift with soil pH. Plant it in morning sun and afternoon shade in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil, mulching to keep roots cool. Acidic soil pushes blooms toward blue while alkaline soil yields pink, so amend to steer the color you want. Prune just after flowering, since it blooms mainly on old wood. Water generously in heat to prevent the large leaves and flowers from wilting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Fringe cups is a Pacific Northwest native perennial in the saxifrage family that forms semi-evergreen rosettes of rounded, softly hairy, heart-shaped leaves and sends up elegant, 18–30 inch racemes of small, urn-shaped flowers whose petals are deeply fringed, opening white and aging to pink and red, in spring and early summer. It spreads modestly by seed and rhizomes to naturalize into a graceful woodland groundcover that pairs beautifully with ferns, bleeding heart, and tiarella. Tolerates deep shade under conifers.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fringe cups self-seeds freely in moist shade conditions and may naturalize into a loose colony — deadhead spent flower spikes to reduce self-seeding in formal garden settings or allow to naturalize in woodland garden situations.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; fringe cups is a Pacific Northwest and Western North American woodland perennial in the saxifrage family (Saxifragaceae) that is closely related to heucheras and tiarellas and shares their preference for partial to full woodland shade — it grows as a clump of basal, roundly heart-shaped, hairy, dark-green leaves (remarkably similar to Heuchera leaves) and in late spring produces tall, slender, upright flower stems to 24 inches, each bearing an elegant, elongated spike of small, nodding, greenish-white to cream, urn-shaped flowers with the petals elaborately fringed (cut into narrow, thread-like segments) at their margins — creating a delicate, lacey floral effect along the entire length of the spike. The flowers fade through white to pink to rose-red as they age, so a single spike carries multiple color stages simultaneously. The foliage rosettes are attractive year-round and are semi-evergreen in mild winters. Self-seeds freely in moist shade. A graceful, refined, and underused shade perennial for zone 5–9 woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in early spring in moist, shaded spots; fresh seed can be surface sown in fall for natural cold stratification. Tellima self-sows modestly and can establish small colonies over time.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fringecups is a Pacific Northwest native woodland perennial in the saxifrage family closely related to heucheras and tiarellas. In spring it sends up slender wands of small, urn-shaped flowers with intricately fringed petals that open cream-white and age to rose-pink. The rounded, hairy, semi-evergreen leaves form a dense, attractive clump at the base. It blooms for an unusually long period of 6–8 weeks and performs well in the challenging dry shade of Douglas fir and redwood forests. A reliable, low-maintenance shade perennial that combines beautifully with ferns, native gingers, and bleeding heart.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; fringed bleeding heart remains in bloom from spring through fall in cool climates and does not go summer-dormant like the common bleeding heart.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fringed bleeding heart is a native Appalachian perennial that surpasses the common bleeding heart (Lamprocapnos spectabilis) in most garden settings by blooming continuously from spring through hard frost in cool climates — the deeply ferny, blue-gray, dissected foliage is attractive all season and never goes summer-dormant. The dangling, heart-shaped, rose-pink flowers appear in loose, nodding clusters on arching stems. It tolerates more heat and summer drought than the common bleeding heart. Self-sows gently to maintain a naturalized presence in woodland gardens without becoming invasive. Excellent in combination with hostas, ferns, and astilbes for a year-round shade border. Hybrids such as 'King of Hearts' (compact, deep rose) and 'Luxuriant' (strong bloomer) often replace the straight species in commerce.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; or cold stratify seeds 60 days and sow indoors in late winter. Transplant to very well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to light shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed blue star is a native amsonia of the southeastern Coastal Plain sandhills and pine barrens, adapted to the infertile, droughty, acid soils of longleaf pine habitats where few ornamental perennials survive. The very fine, needle-like foliage is distinctive among amsonias — quite different from the broad leaves of A. tabernaemontana — and turns a glowing golden-yellow in fall, one of the best fall color displays of any low-maintenance perennial. The star-shaped blue flowers in spring are typical of the genus. It performs better in poor, dry, acidic soil than in rich garden conditions — improved soil and irrigation can cause floppy growth. An excellent, low-maintenance native for dry, sandy, acidic sites in the Southeast.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade after frost; aristolochia fimbriata is low-growing and spreading — excellent as a small-scale groundcover or container spiller — and is a key host plant for Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly larvae.
directions: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average soil in partial shade; fringed dutchman's pipe is a compact, spreading, South American perennial grown primarily as a wildlife plant and groundcover for shaded areas — the handsome, heart-shaped leaves are distinctly patterned with silver-white veining against deep green, giving the plant attractive foliage interest independent of its flowers. Small, curved, pipe-shaped, lemon-scented flowers with finely fringed edges appear throughout the warm season, but the plant's greatest value is as a confirmed host plant for the Pipevine Swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor), a stunning iridescent-blue butterfly whose larvae feed exclusively on Aristolochia species. Unlike the larger, climbing Aristolochia macrophylla and A. tomentosa, A. fimbriata stays low and spreading, making it practical for smaller gardens, containers, and shaded garden edges. It is important to note that certain other non-native Aristolochia species (A. elegans, A. littoralis) are actually toxic to Pipevine Swallowtail larvae; A. fimbriata supports them safely. Semi-evergreen in mild winters.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, sandy or silty soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed gentian is a biennial that forms a rosette in its first year and blooms in late summer of its second. It requires moist, lean, calcareous or neutral soil and does not tolerate competition — it thrives in disturbed seep margins, wet meadow edges, and streambanks.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, sandy or silty soil in full sun to partial shade; fringed gentian is one of the most beautiful and coveted native wildflowers of northeastern North America, producing brilliant violet-blue, vase-shaped flowers with dramatically fringed petal margins in late summer and fall — the fringed edges of each petal lobe are deeply cut into hundreds of fine filaments, creating an extraordinarily ornate, lacey appearance unique among North American wildflowers. The plant is notoriously difficult to establish in gardens, requiring very specific conditions — moist, open, lean, near-neutral soils free of competition, such as seep margins, calcareous stream banks, and disturbed wet meadows. Once established in appropriate conditions it self-sows to maintain a colony. John Muir rhapsodized about encountering it in Wisconsin prairies. A specialist plant for wet, calcareous, open sites — immensely rewarding when conditions are right.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; fringed loosestrife spreads by rhizomes and seeds to form colonies in moist woodland edges, stream banks, and wet meadows. The cultivar 'Firecracker' has striking purple-bronze foliage.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun along stream banks, pond margins, rain gardens, and moist woodland edges; fringed loosestrife is a native North American species of the primrose family, producing starry, five-petaled, bright yellow flowers in midsummer that dangle from arching stems above broad, opposite leaves. The common name comes from the distinctive fringe of fine hairs on the leaf petioles. The cultivar 'Firecracker' has become popular in the ornamental trade for its striking, deep purple-bronze foliage that contrasts dramatically with the yellow flowers and adds unusual dark color to the moist shade garden throughout summer. Self-sows and spreads by rhizomes in appropriate moist conditions to form naturalistic colonies. Provides nectar for numerous small native bees and is a host plant for pollen-specialist bees of the genus Macropis.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall; fringed polygala requires moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained forest soil in deep shade and is notoriously difficult to establish from seed or transplant — it grows in association with specific mycorrhizal fungi. Best acquired as established container plants.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained, undisturbed forest soil in deep shade; fringed polygala is a tiny, jewel-like native groundcover of the cool, moist northern hardwood and mixed conifer forests of eastern North America. The small, rose-pink to magenta flowers have a unique, highly ornamental structure — the two wing-like lateral sepals and the fringed lower petal create a shape resembling a miniature orchid or a tiny winged fairy. The flowers are pollinated by large bumblebees that must be heavy enough to depress the flower's structure to reach the nectar. Two types of flowers are produced: the showy open flowers above ground and hidden cleistogamous flowers underground that self-pollinate without opening. A challenging but rewarding woodland plant for undisturbed, acidic, forest-floor conditions; does not tolerate root disturbance or soil compaction.

plant_note: Direct sow in wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fringed sedge grows naturally along shaded stream banks and forested seeps and is one of the few native sedges adapted to deep woodland shade with standing water or continuously saturated soil.
directions: Plant in wet to consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade along stream banks, forested swamp edges, and shaded seeps; fringed sedge is one of the most shade-tolerant of the large native wetland sedges, growing naturally in the deep shade of forested bottomlands and streamside forests across eastern North America. Its most distinctive feature is the long, pendant female spikes — drooping catkins that hang loosely from arching stems, the scales tapering to delicate bristle tips (the 'fringe') — which create a graceful, weeping texture in the woodland garden. The clumps form slowly expanding, elegant tufts of medium-textured, grass-like foliage that remain attractive throughout the growing season. Excellent in rain gardens with overhead tree cover, shaded bioswales, and streamside restoration where full-sun sedges fail due to shade. The seeds are consumed by various marsh and woodland birds.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; in zones 9–11 plants may be started in late winter for earlier establishment. Avoid amended or rich soils — Fringed Twining Milkweed performs best in lean, xeric conditions that mimic its native desert habitat. Provide a low trellis or nearby shrub for the twining stems to climb.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Fringed Twining Milkweed is a drought-adapted native perennial milkweed vine of desert shrubland, washes, and roadsides from California to Texas in the southwestern US. It produces long, narrow to linear leaves and clusters of small, pale to rose-pink, star-shaped flowers with a distinctive fringed corona that bloom across a long summer season. Like true milkweeds it produces latex sap and classic spindle-shaped seed pods with plume-tailed, wind-dispersed seeds. It is a particularly important late-season milkweed resource for monarch butterflies on their fall migration routes through the Southwest, and should be kept dry and given excellent drainage to perform well — it declines quickly in heavy or poorly drained soils.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; fringeleaf coreopsis grows naturally in moist, open woodlands and woodland edges in the southeastern Coastal Plain and blooms in fall — one of the latest-blooming native coreopsis species.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; fringeleaf coreopsis is a fall-blooming native of the southeastern Coastal Plain, extending its bloom season later into the autumn than most coreopsis — a significant advantage in the garden where its bright yellow flowers provide critical fall color and nectar from September through November. The leaves are somewhat different from other coreopsis — broader, almost rounded, with slightly fringed or undulate margins that give the species its common name. It grows naturally in moist, open woodlands, forest edges, and the transition zones between flatwoods and upland habitats, tolerating partial shade better than sun-demanding coreopsis species. The extended fall blooming is exceptionally valuable for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season pollinators. Well-adapted to zone 9a conditions in moist, partially shaded garden situations.

plant_note: Best sown in fall for natural cold stratification over winter, or direct sow in early spring. Seeds may also be cold-stratified for 4–6 weeks in the refrigerator before spring sowing.
directions: Sow seeds in fall to allow natural cold stratification, or cold-stratify refrigerated seeds for 4–6 weeks before a spring direct sowing. Ruellia humilis is a low-growing native perennial that thrives in hot, dry conditions — it is excellent for road cuts, rock gardens, and dry slopes where many other plants struggle. The lavender-blue tubular flowers closely resemble petunias and appear throughout summer, providing nectar for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees. Note that this is the well-behaved native species and should not be confused with Ruellia simplex (Mexican Petunia), which is invasive in the Southeast; established plants spread modestly by self-seeding to form a colony.

plant_note: Plant bulbs just below the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in fall; frizzle sizzle follows the Cape winter-rainfall growth cycle — growing and flowering in winter and spring, then going summer dormant. Keep dry in summer dormancy. Full sun maximizes the dramatic spiral leaf curling — shaded plants may produce less tightly curled foliage.
directions: Plant bulbs near the soil surface in very well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; frizzle sizzle is a South African Cape bulb that has attracted unusual attention from collectors and gardeners primarily for its extraordinary foliage — the leaves are not flat strap-like leaves but tightly spiral, corkscrew-curled, like a pig's tail or a phone cord, creating an immediately bizarre and eye-catching effect quite unlike any other commonly grown plant. The leaves, each spiraling through one to several complete rotations as they grow, create a tightly curled, wispy, almost spring-like cluster of spirals at ground level that is so unusual it reliably draws a second look from every observer. In late winter through spring it produces small, nodding, greenish-yellow to yellow, vanilla-fragrant flowers on short stems — pleasant but secondary to the extraordinary foliage. The spiral curling is a genuine botanical trait of the species rather than a cultivated mutation. It grows naturally in the sandy coastal heathlands of the Western Cape. Outstanding as a container plant where the unique spiral foliage can be examined closely and protected from summer rain during dormancy.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; transplant while cool, or sow in late summer for fall and spring bloom.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before setting out, covering it since pansies germinate best in darkness, and transplant while weather is cool. Frizzle Sizzle Lemonberry features ruffled 2 to 2.5-inch tricolor blooms of lemon, deep burgundy, and berry-purple edges that intensify in cool spring temperatures. These low-growing edible flowers suit beds, borders, and containers. Deadhead to prolong blooming and provide even moisture, as they fade in summer heat.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or plugs in spring in any well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, moist to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; frogfruit is extremely adaptable and roots readily wherever stems contact moist soil, spreading quickly to fill in bare ground.
directions: Plant plugs or rooted cuttings in any well-drained, moist to dry soil in full sun to partial shade — frogfruit is a tough, trailing native groundcover of Gulf Coast roadsides, disturbed prairies, and open woodland margins, hugging the ground so tightly (1–3 inches tall) that it can be used as a low-maintenance lawn substitute or mowed path edge in full sun. Despite its modest appearance, it is one of the most ecologically important low-growing native plants in the South: the tiny white to pink flower heads bloom nearly year-round in warm climates and serve as a critical nectar source for many small native bees and flies, while the leaves are larval host plants for the Phaon crescent and common buckeye butterflies. It roots at stem nodes wherever it contacts moist soil, spreading rapidly to colonize bare areas but never invasively outcompeting other established plants. Heat, drought, and salt tolerant; extremely low-maintenance once established. Blooms are most prolific in spring and fall.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Frohnleiten is a vigorous, evergreen epimedium selection that spreads into a good-sized groundcover patch faster than many slower epimedium species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established. Frohnleiten is a vigorous, evergreen to semi-evergreen epimedium hybrid producing sprays of bright yellow flowers with reddish-bronze centers in spring, held just above heart-shaped leaves that emerge coppery-bronze and mature to leathery green, often taking on burgundy tones again in winter. It spreads at a good pace into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover, faster than many other epimedium species, making it useful for covering larger areas of dry shade under trees or shrubs. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge to keep the planting looking fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, lean to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; frost aster is extremely adaptable and virtually impossible to kill once established — thriving in poor, dry soils of roadsides, old fields, dry woods edges, and disturbed areas. Requires no fertilization and self-sows abundantly.
directions: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, lean to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; frost aster is one of the most widespread, adaptable, and ecologically important native asters in North America — covering vast areas of old fields, roadsides, dry woodland edges, and disturbed areas from eastern Canada to Texas and Florida. The common name 'frost aster' refers to the pure white ray flowers (which remain white even as temperatures drop), the late blooming season (October through November, after the first frosts in northern areas), and the feathery, silvery-white seed plumes that linger through winter, creating a frosted effect in the garden. The 1/2-inch white flowers with yellow centers, produced in massive quantities on highly branched stems, are extraordinarily abundant and valuable as late-season nectar for monarch butterflies, native bees, and many other pollinators. One of the most important late-season nectar sources in eastern North America. Self-sows prolifically in lean soils. An essential native plant for dry old-field restorations and natural-style gardens seeking maximum wildlife value.

plant_note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot.
directions: Frost Proof is a cold-tolerant gardenia bearing intensely fragrant white flowers against glossy evergreen leaves, and it withstands cooler temperatures better than typical gardenias. Plant it in morning sun with afternoon shade in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. Keep watering consistent, as fluctuating moisture causes bud drop. Feed with an acid-loving-plant fertilizer during the growing season and prune lightly after the main bloom. Protect from harsh winter wind at the colder edge of its range.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Frostproof is notably more cold-hardy than standard gardenia cultivars, extending reliable gardenia culture further north than the species typically tolerates.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. As its name suggests, Frostproof was selected specifically for improved cold hardiness compared to standard Gardenia jasminoides, tolerating colder winters with less dieback than most cultivars while still producing the classic, intensely fragrant, creamy white double flowers gardenias are grown for. Its compact, naturally dense habit also makes it a good choice for foundation plantings and smaller borders where a full-sized gardenia would grow too large. Consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential, since gardenias quickly develop yellow, chlorotic foliage in alkaline or poorly drained conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; frostweed grows naturally in moist woodland edges, creek bottoms, and open woods from the eastern US to Texas and tolerates considerable shade while still producing flowers.
directions: Sow seeds in fall or plant transplants in moist, partially shaded woodland-edge soil; frostweed is a tall, commanding native perennial wildflower that earns its evocative name from a remarkable winter phenomenon: when the first hard freeze strikes the green stems, the sap freezes and expands, splitting the bark and extruding curling ribbons and sheets of ice in fantastical flower-like formations called 'ice flowers' or 'frost flowers' that persist for hours after sunrise. This natural ice art is one of the most spectacular surprises in the winter garden. The plant itself produces masses of small white flowers beloved by butterflies — particularly migrating monarchs — from late summer through fall. It is an important nectar source at a critical migration season. Tolerates part shade and moist conditions, making it one of the few native tall perennials suited to moist woodland edges and rain gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate with spring warmth.
directions: Frying Pans is a diminutive California native annual closely related to the California poppy but considerably smaller, with finely dissected, blue-green foliage and tiny, bright yellow, 4-petaled flowers barely half an inch across that spread wide and flat — earning the whimsical common name from their resemblance to a miniature skillet. It is native to dry, rocky foothill grasslands and open chaparral in the Sacramento Valley and Sierra Nevada foothills, where it often grows in thin, gravelly soils with little competition. Direct sow in fall by scattering seed on dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; like its relatives, it resents transplanting and performs best with no soil amendment. It self-sows freely and makes an excellent low-growing native filler for California dry-garden borders, rock gardens, and native meadow mixes.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; fuchsia begonia is more drought-tolerant than most begonias and performs better in lower-humidity environments — allow the top inch of soil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent root rot in the fibrous root system.
