directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–12; the gold tree (golden trumpet tree) produces one of the most spectacular flowering displays of any tree in the world — for 1–2 weeks in late winter or early spring, the entire tree is covered in blazing, golden-yellow trumpet flowers before a single leaf has emerged, creating a vision of solid gold visible from hundreds of feet away. The display lasts only 1–2 weeks and is immediately followed by the production of deeply cut, palmate compound leaves. The species is the national tree of Brazil and widely planted as a street and specimen tree throughout the tropics. Drought-tolerant once established, growing naturally in deciduous tropical dry forest. In south Florida (zone 10), it produces its spectacular bloom in February-March — one of the great floral spectacles of the Miami-Fort Lauderdale area.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or divide established plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; gold and silver chrysanthemum is valued primarily as a foliage plant and groundcover rather than for its flowers. The small, yellow button flowers appear very late — October-November — and may not fully open before frost in northern zones, but the foliage is ornamental from spring through fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; gold and silver chrysanthemum is grown primarily for its exceptionally beautiful foliage rather than its flowers — the deeply lobed, dark forest-green leaves are edged and outlined with a neat, precise border of bright, silvery-white hairs that precisely traces every contour of each leaf lobe and margin, creating the striking two-tone appearance that gives the plant its common name. The contrast between the dark green leaf surface and the precise silver edging is quite extraordinary, particularly in autumn when cooler temperatures intensify both the green and the silver tones. The plant forms a low, mounding, spreading groundcover that is drought-tolerant and adaptable to a range of soils once established. Small, mustard-yellow button flowers appear very late in October and November and may not fully develop before frost in zone 5-6 gardens, but in warmer zones the late bloom adds an additional seasonal interest. Native to coastal cliffs and rocky slopes of Japan, it thrives in well-drained conditions in full sun.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; seed requires 60–90 days of cold, moist conditions before spring germination. Division of established clumps in spring provides faster establishment.
directions: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall or early spring in moist, average to rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this early-blooming native carrot-family plant produces flat-topped clusters of small yellow flowers in April–May, making it one of the earliest sources of pollen for native bees, beetles, and flies at a time when little else is blooming. It is also an important early host plant for black swallowtail butterflies, whose caterpillars feed on the ferny foliage. The plants are short-lived but self-sow reliably in suitable conditions. Excellent at the front of the native plant border or naturalized in a moist meadow.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; alternatively, cold-stratify seeds for 60–90 days in the refrigerator and direct sow in early spring — golden alexanders requires a cold moist period to break dormancy and germinates poorly without stratification.
directions: Direct sow in fall, or cold-stratify for 60–90 days and sow in spring, in moist to average, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; golden alexanders is one of the most shade-tolerant native wildflowers in the carrot family and is an excellent choice for lightly shaded or woodland-edge gardens with moist soil. Zizia aurea is a native North American perennial in the Apiaceae (carrot/parsley) family producing bright, golden-yellow, flat-topped umbels of tiny flowers in April through June — one of the earliest yellow-flowered natives to bloom, bridging the gap between spring bulbs and summer perennials; it is a critical early-season nectar source for native bees and an important larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly (Papilio polyxenes), whose caterpillars feed on the foliage. It tolerates partial shade and moist to periodically wet soils and naturalizes beautifully in rain gardens, woodland margins, and native plant meadows. Dark green, compound leaves remain attractive throughout the season after bloom.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden angel's trumpet produces large, pendant, golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers and is one of the most spectacular large-flowered tropical shrubs. CAUTION: All parts of all Brugmansia species are extremely toxic — do not plant where children or pets have unsupervised access.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden angel's trumpet is an Andean species producing enormous, pendant, trumpet-shaped flowers up to 12 inches long in soft golden-yellow, often with a rich, sweet, tropical fragrance strongest in the evening. A single well-grown plant can carry dozens of pendant blooms simultaneously, creating a spectacular tropical accent. Like all Brugmansia, all plant parts are dangerously toxic — containing tropane alkaloids (scopolamine, atropine) that cause hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, and potentially fatal poisoning. Never use any plant part medicinally without expert guidance. In zone 9, grow as a container plant moved indoors in winter or in a frost-protected location. Fertilize heavily with a balanced fertilizer every 2 weeks during the growing season to achieve maximum bloom production. The large, pendant flowers are adapted for pollination by large hawk moths.

common_name: Golden Angel's Trumpet (Large Pendulous Yellow-Trumpet Brugmansia Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; all parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested — plant away from children's play areas and avoid contact with sap; wash hands after pruning.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Queen is a yellow-flowered Brugmansia (angel's trumpet) producing the spectacular large-scale tropical display characteristic of the genus — very large (10–14 inch), pendulous, trumpet-shaped flowers in warm golden-yellow hanging in clusters from the branch tips, releasing an extraordinary heavy fragrance particularly intense in the evening hours. The golden-yellow flower color of 'Golden Queen' is distinctly different from the white, peach, pink, and apricot tones of other angel's trumpet varieties — a warm, pure yellow that creates a dramatic tropical focal point in partial shade. In zone 9, Brugmansia grows as a large tropical shrub or small tree reaching 6–12 feet, blooming most heavily in spring and fall as temperatures moderate from summer extremes. The plant requires generous water and fertility to produce its finest flower display — large containers require daily watering in summer. All parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested and should be handled with caution; the sap can irritate skin and eyes. In zone 9b and 10, Golden Queen grows as a perennial. In zone 9a, frost may kill the top growth but the plant often returns from the roots with mulch protection; container-grown specimens can be moved indoors before frost. The spectacular flowers and fragrance make angel's trumpets one of the most dramatic ornamentals for Gulf South tropical garden designs.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; golden bamboo REQUIRES a bamboo root barrier (18-inch deep polypropylene sheet) before planting — it is a highly aggressive running bamboo that will invade neighboring properties and is invasive in many southeastern US states without containment.
directions: Plant ONLY within a contained area using an 18-inch deep root barrier in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden bamboo (also called fishpole bamboo for its use in making fishing poles) is the most widely planted and most problematic bamboo in the southeastern US — it has naturalized and become invasive along streams, roadsides, and disturbed areas from the Carolinas to Texas, outcompeting native vegetation. Despite its invasive potential, it remains widely sold and planted because of its fast growth, dense screening ability, and striking golden-yellow canes as they mature. The culms turn yellow-gold with age (green when young), and the distinctive swollen internodes near the base of young shoots are characteristic. If used, ALWAYS contain with a root barrier and remove rhizomes that escape under or through the barrier. Harvest young edible shoots when they emerge in spring. Listed as invasive in multiple southeastern states.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden chain tree grows naturally on alkaline limestone soils and tolerates chalky conditions better than most ornamental trees. The hybrid 'Vossii' produces the longest pendulous chains of flowers and sets fewer viable seeds than the species, reducing the risk of seed toxicity. ALL PARTS ARE HIGHLY TOXIC if ingested — keep away from children and pets.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden chain tree is one of the most spectacular of all spring-flowering trees, producing long, pendant racemes of brilliant, clear-yellow pea flowers up to 24 inches in length in May and June — so dense and vividly colored that the entire tree appears to drip with cascades of golden chains, from which the common name derives. The famous Laburnum Walk at Bodnant Garden in Wales — a 180-foot tunnel of intertwined laburnums, trained overhead to create a tunnel of golden chains — demonstrates the full theatrical potential of this tree. In smaller gardens, a single mature specimen in full bloom against a dark background or blue sky is extraordinary. Native to central Europe and tolerant of shallow, chalky soils and part shade. The hybrid 'Vossii' is the most commonly planted, with the longest flower chains. EXTREME CAUTION: all parts of the plant, especially the seed pods and seeds, contain cytisine (a toxic alkaloid similar to nicotine) and are highly poisonous — the plant should never be planted where children play.

plant_note: Divide and plant rhizomes in spring once water temperatures warm above 60°F, placing crowns in heavy loam or clay aquatic soil in containers submerged 6–12 inches below the water surface; golden club thrives in the still or slow-moving water of ponds, streams, and freshwater wetlands and is among the most shade-tolerant of native aquatic plants. Site in partial shade to full sun — it tolerates considerably more shade than most aquatics. Established clumps can be divided every 3–4 years in spring.
directions: Plant in still to slow-moving water 4–12 inches deep in heavy, nutrient-rich aquatic soil in partial shade to full sun; golden club is one of the most distinctive and visually striking native aquatic plants of eastern North America, producing in early spring — often while other plants are barely stirring — unusual upright flower spathes consisting of a slender, bright golden-yellow spadix on a pure-white stem, held above the water surface like a glowing torch that gives the plant its evocative common name. The large, oblong, blue-green leaves have a remarkably hydrophobic waxy surface coating that causes water to bead and roll off in glistening droplets, a phenomenon known as the lotus effect, making the foliage appear perpetually dry and silvery in wet conditions. Orontium aquaticum is tolerant of considerable shade compared to most aquatics — a valuable trait for water features beneath overhanging tree canopies where many emergent plants fail to perform — and spreads gradually by rhizome to form a handsome colony. A superb choice for naturalistic ponds, rain gardens with permanent water features, and native plant water gardens throughout zones 5–10.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification and spring germination; alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 3–4 weeks at 40°F and sow in early spring. Golden columbine self-sows readily and a well-placed colony will naturalize and self-perpetuate over time.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Aquilegia chrysantha is a native columbine of the American Southwest — native to canyon walls, stream banks, and moist woodland edges in New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico — and is one of the most heat-tolerant and long-blooming of all columbines, producing exceptionally long-spurred, bright yellow flowers on 3–4 foot stems from late spring through summer, with the spurs significantly longer than those of most other columbine species. It is an outstanding hummingbird plant, and the extralong nectar spurs are specifically adapted to hummingbird pollination; both hummingbirds and sphinx moths visit the flowers avidly. More tolerant of heat and dry conditions than European columbines, it performs reliably into zone 9 in the West with afternoon shade. Allow to self-sow freely to build a naturalized colony; plants are short-lived perennials (3–5 years) that persist through abundant self-seeding.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in well-drained, rocky, sandy, or disturbed lean soil in partial shade to full sun; golden corydalis is a winter annual to biennial that germinates in cool weather and blooms in spring through early summer. It self-sows readily in rocky, open, disturbed areas.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, rocky, sandy, or lean disturbed soil in partial shade to full sun; golden corydalis is a charming, finely dissected-leaved native annual of rocky, disturbed soils, stream gravel bars, talus slopes, and sandy open ground across a wide range of North America from Alaska to Texas. The bright, pure golden-yellow flowers are produced in dense terminal clusters on sprawling, succulent stems from spring through early summer. Common names 'scrambled eggs' aptly describes the tumbled, bright yellow flower clusters. Self-sows freely in rocky, open, disturbed garden areas to create naturalized colonies that persist indefinitely. One of the more widespread and adaptable native Corydalis species, tolerating a range of climates from boreal to semi-arid. Visited by bumblebees and long-tongued specialist bees that access the spurred flowers.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or plugs in spring; golden creeping jenny spreads rapidly by surface runners and is particularly effective cascading over container edges or covering shaded slopes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; the golden-leafed cultivar 'Aurea' is one of the most valuable groundcovers for illuminating shaded areas where few plants thrive. The vivid chartreuse-gold rounded leaves create a brilliant carpet that contrasts beautifully with dark green hostas, ferns, and astilbes. Unlike the green species, the gold form needs some shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, but it fades to pale yellow-green in deep shade — dappled light produces the most intense gold color. Small yellow flowers in early summer. Spreads by horizontal stems that root at nodes; divide and replant crowded mats every 2 years.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger passes in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; golden dewdrop grows rapidly in warm weather and can reach 6–8 feet in a single season. Fruit and leaves are toxic to humans and pets — site away from areas frequented by children and animals.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; golden dewdrop is a vigorous tropical shrub that provides two seasons of ornamental interest — lavender to purple tubular flowers from spring through fall, followed by clusters of small golden-yellow berries that drape like strings of dewdrops and persist on the plant for months, creating the common name. The berries are the primary food source for many songbirds, particularly mockingbirds and robins. Be aware that the berries and leaves are toxic to humans, dogs, and cats. The popular weeping cultivar 'Geisha Girl' has larger, richer purple flowers; 'Gold Mound' is a compact, dwarf golden-foliage form. Prune severely in late winter to maintain a compact, manageable shape — unpruned plants can reach tree size. Outstanding as a large informal screen, espalier, or specimen shrub for zone 8–11 gardens where its rapid growth and dual seasonal interest make it highly effective.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Golden Emperor is a large-flowered exhibition chrysanthemum typically grown for cut flowers and fall display — the blooms can reach 4–5 inches across under optimal conditions. Pinch growing tips monthly from spring through early July to promote bushy plants with multiple flowering shoots. In zone 9 plants bloom October–November. Chrysanthemums are short-day plants — they initiate flowers when nights become longer than a critical threshold, making the fall bloom timing predictable and consistent regardless of when plants are pinched. Divide clumps each spring to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Golden Emperor Chrysanthemum performs best with consistent moisture and full sun for maximum flower size and color; Golden Emperor is a large-flowered chrysanthemum cultivar producing the classic double, globe-form flowers in a clean, rich golden-yellow color — the archetypal fall chrysanthemum color that has defined autumn display in American gardens and florist shops for decades. The large, fully double flowers (4–5 inches at their best under greenhouse or exhibition conditions) are composed of hundreds of tightly packed, inward-curving ray florets that create a spherical to slightly flattened globe form. As a short-day plant, chrysanthemum's bloom timing is controlled by day length rather than temperature or calendar date — flowering is triggered when nighttime darkness exceeds the plant's critical threshold, ensuring consistent fall blooming (September–November) regardless of growing conditions. In zone 9 chrysanthemums are less reliably perennial than in cooler zones, often performing as short-lived perennials that benefit from division and replanting every 2–3 years. The rich golden-yellow color of Golden Emperor provides the warm, classic autumnal display that is the most recognizable and widely desired chrysanthemum color for fall landscape and cut flower use.

subcategory: original yellow-orange South African crocosmia species
plant_note: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden falling stars is the parent species of the widely grown hybrid C. x crocosmiiflora (Montbretia) and one of two parents of modern large-flowered crocosmia hybrids. It blooms in late summer (August–September), slightly later than the hybrid Montbretia. The flowers are noticeably larger than those of C. x crocosmiiflora and an attractive golden-yellow to golden-orange. It spreads vigorously by corm chains.
directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden falling stars is one of the two wild South African Crocosmia species — along with C. pottsii — from which the immensely popular hybrid Montbretia (C. x crocosmiiflora) was developed in 1880 by the French nurseryman Victor Lemoine by crossing C. aurea with C. pottsii. In its own right, C. aurea is a very attractive plant: somewhat taller and more imposing than the hybrid montbretia, with larger, more open, golden-yellow to warm golden-orange funnel-shaped flowers on arching, branching stems in late summer and early autumn. The golden-yellow color is more purely yellow and less orange than many crocosmia cultivars, providing a clean, warm-gold effect in the late-summer border. Like all crocosmias it spreads vigorously by producing chains of linked corms underground, forming ever-expanding colonies of the arching sword-like leaves and arching, golden-flowered stems. It tolerates more shade than full-sun crocosmia recommendations suggest, doing well in the dappled shade of deciduous trees or in part-shade border situations. The parent species of the most-planted corm in temperate gardens.

common_name: Golden Fleece Goldenrod (Compact Groundcover Native Goldenrod)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Fleece is one of the most compact, well-behaved goldenrod cultivars, spreading gently rather than aggressively and staying under a foot tall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Golden Fleece is a low, mounding goldenrod selection that stays compact and well-mannered compared to taller, more aggressively spreading goldenrod species, making it a practical choice for a foreground planting or small-space garden without sacrificing the excellent late-season pollinator value goldenrods are known for. In fall it produces abundant sprays of small, bright golden-yellow flowers over glossy, semi-evergreen foliage, drawing large numbers of native bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects at a time when few other plants are still blooming. Contrary to popular belief, goldenrod does not cause hay fever, since its pollen is heavy and insect-carried rather than airborne; it is a valuable, non-allergenic native for the fall pollinator garden.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in any well-drained to moderately moist, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; golden garlic is unusually shade-tolerant for an ornamental allium and will naturalize under deciduous trees where it receives good spring light before the canopy fills in. It multiplies freely to form colonies and the bulbs can be divided and replanted after the foliage dies back in summer.
directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in any well-drained to moderately moist soil in part shade to full sun; golden garlic is the most shade-tolerant of the ornamental alliums — most of which require full sun — naturalizing successfully under deciduous trees where it receives bright spring light before the tree canopy leafs out, then rests dormant through the summer shade. The flowers are bright, clear, golden-yellow — very unusual in the allium genus where most ornamental species are purple, pink, or white — carried in loose, flat-topped umbels in May and June above two broad, gray-green, strap-like leaves with a light garlic scent when bruised. The plant naturalizes freely by offsets, expanding over time into attractive drifts that provide cheerful yellow spring color in the partly shaded garden. Native to rocky slopes and woodland margins of Spain, southern France, and North Africa, it has been cultivated in European gardens since at least the 16th century as 'lily leek.' Excellent for naturalizing at the woodland edge, in drifts under deciduous shrubs, or in massed plantings among hostas and other shade perennials.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; golden groundsel spreads aggressively by stolons to form dense colonies that suppress weeds effectively — choose a site where this colonizing habit is an asset, such as a shaded bank or moist, wooded slope.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade, including deep shade under established trees where spring light penetrates before leaf-out — golden groundsel is one of the finest spring-blooming shade perennials native to eastern North America, producing a semi-evergreen rosette of attractive, heart-shaped basal leaves that remains green through winter and brightens in April and May with brilliant golden-yellow daisy flowers on 12–18 inch stems that stand out vividly against the dark tones of the shaded woodland floor. It spreads steadily and aggressively by surface stolons to form dense, weed-suppressing colonies that are highly effective as a native groundcover on shaded slopes, stream banks, and the moist understory of deciduous woodland; the low, persistent foliage rosettes hold the soil year-round. Note that Packera aurea (golden groundsel, golden ragwort) belongs to a distinct North American genus and should not be confused with the invasive Eurasian Senecio jacobaea (tansy ragwort), which is a different plant and a noxious weed in many states. Divide in spring to expand plantings or control spread.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; golden rain tree is one of the few ornamental trees that blooms in summer (July–August) when most trees are not in bloom, and its papery seed pods provide additional ornamental interest through fall.
directions: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; golden rain tree is very adaptable to poor, dry, alkaline, and clay soils once established and requires minimal irrigation or fertilization. Koelreuteria paniculata is a Chinese ornamental tree 25–40 feet tall that fills a unique niche by blooming in midsummer (July–August) with spectacular 12–15 inch upright panicles of small, bright golden-yellow flowers followed by ornamental papery seed pods (lanterns) that are green, then pink-salmon, then tan, remaining decorative into winter; it is among the most summer-drought-tolerant and adaptable ornamental trees for zones 5–9. The compound leaves turn yellow in fall and the form is broadly rounded with age; plant with adequate space as the canopy spreads widely. Self-seeds freely in some regions — collect seed pods before they shatter to prevent volunteers.

plant_note: Nick or scarify the hard seed coat and soak 24 hours before planting, or plant rooted container specimens in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; golden shower tree is fast-growing and drought tolerant once established. In zone 9a, plant against a south-facing wall for frost protection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; golden shower tree is one of the most spectacular of all tropical flowering trees — the national tree of Thailand — producing cascading chains of brilliant golden-yellow flowers 12–18 inches long that completely cover the tree before the new leaves emerge in spring, creating a breathtaking golden cascade. It grows fast (3–5 feet per year) in frost-free conditions, reaching 25–40 feet, and tolerates drought, alkaline soil, and seaside conditions once established. The flowers are edible in some cultures (flower buds in curries). In zone 9a it may die back in severe freezes but typically regrows from established root systems; site in a protected location sheltered from north winds. A magnificent specimen or street tree for zone 9–11 Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container plants after nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F; golden shrimp plant establishes quickly in warm weather and begins blooming within 6–8 weeks of transplanting.
directions: Root cuttings or plant nursery transplants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun — golden shrimp plant is one of the most continuously showy flowering plants for shaded Gulf Coast gardens, producing upright spikes of overlapping golden-yellow bracts with small white tubular flowers emerging from the tips, blooming nearly year-round in frost-free climates from late spring through fall. The bright golden cones create striking color in shaded beds, under trees, and along north-facing walls where few other flowering plants perform well. Pinch stem tips regularly in the first month after planting to encourage bushy growth; established plants can be cut back by half in late winter to rejuvenate. In zone 9, top growth is killed by frost but plants often resprout from roots if the freeze is brief; in zone 10–11 it grows as a permanent landscape shrub. An outstanding container plant for shaded patios and screened porches.

subcategory: late-summer bulb with brilliant yellow spider-like flowers on bare stems
plant_note: Plant bulbs in late summer to early fall with the neck of the bulb at or just at soil level in excellently well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; golden spider lily requires dry summer dormancy — do not irrigate during the summer when foliage has died. Less cold-hardy than Lycoris squamigera, it is best suited to zones 7–10 and may need mulch protection in zone 7. Foliage emerges in fall after blooming, persists through winter, then dies in spring before summer dormancy. Avoid disturbing established clumps.
directions: Plant bulbs in late summer to early fall with the neck at or just at soil level in excellently well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; golden spider lily operates on the same striking growth cycle as other Lycoris species — strap-like foliage emerges in fall after flowering, persists through the winter months, then dies completely in spring, leaving bare ground through summer before the naked flower stems emerge in late summer bearing brilliant, vivid golden-yellow flower clusters. The flowers themselves are among the most distinctive in the bulb world: the tepals are strongly reflexed and curled back, and the stamens and style extend far beyond the petals in the long, spidery fashion that gives the plant its common name, creating a radiating, starburst effect in an intensely saturated, warm golden yellow. Less cold-hardy than the pink-flowered L. squamigera and L. radiata, it is best suited to zones 7–10 where winters are mild enough to protect the relatively tender bulbs. Like all lycoris, it requires dry summer conditions during dormancy and resents disturbance; established clumps may skip a bloom cycle after transplanting but then flower reliably for many years.

common_name: Golden St. John's Wort (Shrubby St. John's Wort)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in average to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; golden St. John's wort tolerates rocky, shallow, or poor soils and is drought tolerant once established — avoid poorly drained or consistently wet sites.
directions: Golden St. John's wort is a native deciduous shrub of dry, rocky hillsides and cedar glades in the southeastern United States, producing profuse, large, golden-yellow flowers with prominent, brush-like clusters of yellow stamens for several weeks in summer — among the most floriferous and ornamentally attractive of all native shrubs for dry, rocky, or difficult soil situations. Unlike the weedy, herbaceous common St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), this species is a well-behaved woody shrub that stays in bounds without invasive spreading, making it an excellent low-maintenance landscape plant for dry sunny borders, rock gardens, and native shrub masses. The blue-green foliage and exfoliating gray bark are attractive through the growing season, and the persistent, reddish seed capsules provide winter interest; it is deer resistant and tolerates drought, heat, and poor soil with minimal care. An Award of Garden Merit recipient from the Royal Horticultural Society, it is popular in European gardens and deserves much wider use in American native plant landscapes as an alternative to non-native ornamental shrubs.

common_name: Golden Tiara Hosta (Small Gold-Margined Green Hosta)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Golden Tiara is one of the faster-growing hostas and reaches presentable size within 2–3 years of planting — suitable for edging and mass planting where quick establishment is needed.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Golden Tiara is one of the most widely planted small hostas in American horticulture — a compact, fast-growing cultivar producing neat mounds of heart-shaped, medium-green leaves edged with a thin but distinct golden-yellow to chartreuse margin. At 12–18 inches tall and 18–24 inches wide, Golden Tiara is well-scaled for edging shade beds, mass planting as ground cover under trees, and container gardens where larger hostas would overwhelm the space. Golden Tiara is one of the faster-maturing hostas — reaching attractive size in 2–3 years rather than the 5–7 years required by large-growing hostas like Frances Williams. The thin golden margin brightens the leaf edge and catches light in shadowy conditions, creating subtle foliage interest throughout the season. In summer, tall, slender scapes bear purple, funnel-shaped flowers that are mildly fragrant — Golden Tiara is one of the better hostas for flower production relative to its compact size. The compact habit, rapid establishment, and adaptable nature make Golden Tiara an excellent hosta for beginning gardeners who want the lush, tropical effect of hostas without the wait required by large-growing selections. Slug damage is the primary cultural problem; iron phosphate bait or diatomaceous earth applied around the crown helps manage slugs in humid environments.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun in spring; golden trumpet tree is drought-tolerant once established and actually flowers most abundantly after a period of moisture stress followed by rain — a brief dry season before the main wet season triggers the most prolific flowering displays.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; golden trumpet tree (formerly Tabebuia chrysotricha, now Handroanthus chrysotrichus) is one of the most spectacular flowering trees of the Brazilian cerrado and is widely planted throughout tropical and subtropical landscapes for its extraordinary spring flower display — the entire tree becomes covered in large, vivid, deep-golden-yellow to butter-yellow, funnel-shaped, trumpet-form flowers while the branches are leafless or just beginning to leaf out, creating a breathtaking all-yellow display against the blue sky. The flowering season typically lasts only 2–3 weeks but is of extraordinary intensity. The national tree of Brazil is a related species (Handroanthus serratifolius, Tabebuia serratifolia — the Yellow Ipê), and the genus includes pink, purple, magenta, and lavender flowering species as well. Hardy to approximately 28°F in zone 9 with established trees often recovering from frost damage. Excellent as a street tree and garden specimen in zone 9–12. Also known as the golde Ipê.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring after temperatures are consistently above 60°F in moist, very well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; all parts of allamanda are toxic — wear gloves when pruning and wash hands thoroughly. The milky sap causes skin irritation in sensitive individuals.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, very well-drained soil; golden trumpet vine is one of the showiest tropical flowering plants available for Gulf Coast gardens, producing an almost continuous display of large (3–4 inch), brilliant canary-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers from spring through fall on glossy, leathery-leaved vining or shrubby stems. It can be trained as a vine on trellises and fences or pruned as a rounded shrub in formal plantings. The shrubby cultivar 'Cherries Jubilee' has deep rose-purple flowers; 'Hendersonii' bears larger golden flowers. Regular fertilization during the growing season is essential for continuous bloom. All parts of the plant are toxic — wear gloves when handling the milky sap and keep away from children and pets. In zone 9, protect from hard freezes; plants may suffer foliar damage but typically recover from established roots once warm weather returns.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring where plants are to grow; poppies resent transplanting.
directions: This California poppy carries sunny yellow petals with warm orange centers on wispy, blue-green foliage. Sow seeds directly where they are to grow, since the taproot dislikes being moved, and simply press them into the soil surface in early spring. Give it full sun and lean, well-drained ground, where it thrives with little water once established. It self-sows freely and naturalizes beautifully in meadows and dry banks.

plant_note: Sow seed in early spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; the golden cultivar 'Aureum' (Bowles' Golden Grass) seeds true to color and naturalizes readily in appropriate shaded, moist conditions.
directions: Sow seed in early spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; golden wood millet — especially the cultivar 'Aureum' (Bowles' Golden Grass) — is one of the most luminous and valuable shade plants available, producing tufts of graceful, arching bright gold-yellow leaves that seem to glow with internal light in the darkest garden corners. The delicate, open-branched flower panicles appear in spring with golden seeds carried on wispy threads, adding airy texture. A cool-season grass that peaks in spring, goes semi-dormant in summer heat, then revives in fall. It self-sows generously (the golden form seeds true) to naturalize in moist, shaded woodland gardens. Cut back in late summer if it looks tired. Combines beautifully with blue hostas, spring wildflowers, and ferns where its golden light provides striking contrast in deep shade.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring before new growth or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil; golden-scale male fern is more drought-tolerant than many ferns and succeeds in conditions ranging from deep, moist woodland soil to drier positions under tree canopy.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; golden-scale male fern is a robust, semi-evergreen European fern producing large, upright, medium-green fronds that remain attractive from spring through much of the winter in mild climates. The distinguishing feature is the prominent, golden-orange to rust-orange scales that densely cover the crowns, stipes, and midribs, creating a warm, glowing appearance particularly evident in early spring as new fronds emerge. The upright, shuttlecock growth habit is tidy and architectural. Distinguished cultivars include 'Cristata The King,' with elegant, crested frond tips, and 'Pinderi,' which forms a more refined, narrow frond. It is a reliable, long-lived garden fern that gradually forms impressive, multi-crowned specimens over many years. More drought-tolerant than most ferns once established, making it suitable for dry shade under large trees.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; clump-forming cultivars are better-behaved than the straight species.
directions: Plant in full sun in average to poor, well-drained soil; goldenrod thrives in lean conditions and becomes overly lax and floppy in rich, moist soil. The arching plumes of golden-yellow flowers from late summer through fall are essential late-season food for monarch butterflies and dozens of native bee species. Contrary to popular belief, goldenrod does not cause hay fever — its pollen is heavy and insect-carried, not windborne. Choose named compact cultivars like 'Fireworks' or 'Little Lemon' for well-behaved garden varieties; divide every 2–3 years to control spread.

common_name: Goldfish Plant (Flying Goldfish Plant, Columnea gloriosa)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or trailing container in bright indirect light to partial shade; Goldfish Plant performs beautifully on shaded porches, patios, and indoors. It cannot tolerate frost and must be kept above 60°F. A cool, slightly dry rest period for 4–6 weeks in fall (dropping temps to 55–60°F, reduced watering) triggers the winter-spring bloom flush. Propagate from stem-tip cuttings in spring. Use a well-draining, peat-based or coir-based potting mix. Feed monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer during the growing season.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Goldfish Plant flowers most prolifically with good indirect light (bright north or east window or 3–5 feet from a south window) and will produce few flowers in dim conditions. Columnea gloriosa is a trailing, epiphytic vine from Costa Rica and Panama in the Gesneriaceae family, named for its flowers: vivid orange-red, hooded, tubular blooms 2–3 inches long with a small yellow patch in the mouth that, when seen dangling from the trailing stems, precisely resemble a leaping orange goldfish — one of the most charming visual metaphors in the houseplant world. The flowers emerge from small, fleshy, hairy, brown-purple calyx tubes along the trailing stems and at the stem tips, appearing most abundantly after a brief cool, dry rest period in fall. The stems are clothed in pairs of small, thick, fleshy, dark-green, hairy leaves. In excellent conditions with good light and appropriate care, a well-established Goldfish Plant in a large hanging basket produces dozens to hundreds of the characteristic orange flowers simultaneously in winter-spring — an extraordinary display of color at a time of year when few houseplants are blooming. Widely hybridized; many modern hybrids are sold simply as 'Columnea hybrid' with flowers in red, yellow, or bicolor combinations.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Goldflame honeysuckle prefers cool roots and appreciates a mulch layer. Unlike Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), it does not spread aggressively and is well-behaved in the garden — twining habit requires a trellis or support.
directions: Train on a trellis, arbor, or fence in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Goldflame honeysuckle is a hybrid ornamental vine producing exceptionally showy flowers from late spring through summer — the tubular flowers are an intense coral-red to orange-red on the outside with a creamy-yellow interior, presenting a striking bicolor combination as the buds open and the flowers age. The fragrance is moderate to strong, sweet and honeysuckle-like. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), Goldflame is a controlled, twining vine that blooms repeatedly through the season and attracts hummingbirds and butterflies throughout its long bloom period. The foliage is glaucous blue-green, semi-evergreen in mild climates, and attractive in its own right. Particularly valuable for hummingbird gardens as it provides a succession of nectar-rich flowers through most of the warm season. Well-behaved and garden-appropriate for zones 4–9, it thrives even in heat if given consistent moisture and partial shade protection in the afternoon in the hottest climates.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Goldflame develops its best foliage coloration in full sun — the spring bronze-orange new growth becomes more vivid and the summer-to-fall transition colors more intense in direct sun than in shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Goldflame is the premier tricolor Japanese spiraea cultivar — producing a remarkable three-season foliage color progression that provides more sustained ornamental interest than almost any other compact shrub. The new spring growth emerges in a vivid bronze-orange to copper-red color that is one of the most striking spring colors available on any deciduous shrub; through summer the foliage matures to yellow-gold; in late summer and fall the leaves develop orange and red fall tones. The transition from bronze-orange spring → yellow-gold summer → orange-red fall provides effectively continuous color change interest from April through frost. In early summer, small rosy-pink flower clusters add additional color above the evolving foliage. Goldflame's compact size (2–3 feet, slightly wider) makes it proportionate for typical residential borders and it has become one of the most widely planted compact deciduous shrubs in American landscaping. Like other Japanese spiraea cultivars, it is extremely adaptable and tough — tolerating clay, urban conditions, drought, and the heat of zone 9 with minimal care. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush in early summer to stimulate vigorous new growth with fresh bronze-orange coloration.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; goldfussia flowers most heavily in autumn when day length shortens and is an excellent companion to fall-blooming chrysanthemums and asters in the partially shaded border.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; goldfussia is a Thai and Myanmar native shrub that is prized in zone 8–11 gardens for two qualities rare in shade-tolerant woody plants: dramatically iridescent dark-green foliage with a blue-purple metallic sheen in certain light conditions, and a profuse display of soft, powder-blue to violet-blue tubular flowers in autumn and winter — when most garden shrubs have ceased flowering. The combination of semi-glossy, iridescent leaves and late-season blue flowers makes goldfussia an exceptionally valuable plant for providing fall and winter interest in the shaded border. The plant grows as a rounded, mounding shrub with soft, slightly hairy leaves and is somewhat frost-sensitive, typically dying back to the roots in zone 8 winters before resprouting vigorously from the base in spring. In zones 9–11 it grows as a semi-evergreen to evergreen perennial shrub. Excellent combined with autumn-blooming companions in the partially shaded border.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring or fall and plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Goldie's Fern is the largest of the native eastern wood ferns and benefits from deep, rich, consistently moist soil to produce its full-size fronds.
directions: Goldie's Fern is the largest of the native eastern wood ferns, native to rich, moist deciduous forests from Quebec and the Great Lakes south to Georgia and Tennessee, where it grows in deep, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soils — often in ravines, north-facing slopes, and sheltered hollows alongside sugar maple, yellow birch, and basswood. Its massive, arching, golden-green fronds can reach 4 feet in length and create a dramatic bold-textured mass in the shade garden; though deciduous, the fronds remain attractive through much of the season before dying back in late fall. Goldie's Fern is less common in cultivation than many wood ferns but is reliably hardy and long-lived in appropriate conditions — it simply requires the richest, most consistently moist soil and the deepest shade you can provide. Divide clumps in early spring before the fronds unfurl, or plant nursery transplants; mulch heavily with leaf litter to maintain consistent moisture and soil temperature.

Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Goldie's wood fern is among the largest of the North American native wood ferns and prefers reliably moist but not waterlogged conditions in cool, shaded sites. Dryopteris goldiana is a magnificent, stately, semi-evergreen to deciduous native fern of eastern North American hardwood forests; its large, arching fronds reach 3–4 feet long and are broader than most wood ferns, with a distinctively golden-green color when unfurling in spring that matures to deep, glossy green, and the fronds are nearly as wide as they are long, giving the plant an unusually bold, architectural presence. It is an excellent background fern for shaded borders and naturalizes well under large deciduous trees alongside hostas, astilbe, and Solomon's seal.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Goldsturm spreads slowly by self-seeding and rhizome spread to form a colony over years — allow space for gradual spread and divide every 3–4 years when the center of mature clumps begins to die out.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Goldsturm is the most celebrated and widely grown named selection of Rudbeckia — named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 1999 and perhaps the most commonly planted perennial in American horticulture over the past four decades. The golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers with a prominent, dark brown-black central cone are produced in massive, landscape-covering sheets from July through October in zone 9, creating one of the most spectacular and longest-lasting late-summer to fall perennial displays available. The compact, uniform habit (18–24 inches tall) and outstanding flower production make Goldsturm one of the finest mass-planting perennials for full-sun borders, roadsides, and naturalistic gardens — when planted in groups of 5–9 or more, the uniform, floriferous habit creates a golden sea of color through the late-summer garden. Goldsturm is extremely adaptable — it tolerates clay soils, drought, and wet periods better than many perennials and establishes readily from container transplants. The seed heads are left standing through winter as wildlife food for finches and sparrows. Divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. In zone 9, some reduction in bloom quality may occur in the hottest summers — partial shade provides some relief from midday heat stress.

common_name: Goldsturm Black-Eyed Susan (Perennial Plant of the Year Rudbeckia)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Goldsturm is more uniform in habit and flower size than seed-grown Rudbeckia — purchase vegetatively propagated plants or divisions from established clumps for consistent Goldsturm characteristics.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Goldsturm is the Perennial Plant Association's 1999 Plant of the Year — a cultivar of the native orange coneflower (Rudbeckia fulgida) that produces larger, more uniform, and more profuse flowers than the species, on a more compact, tidy plant with better habit control than seed-grown wild types. The 3-inch, golden-yellow, daisy-form flowers with a prominent dark-brown central cone bloom from July through September (zone 7–8) in impressive profusion — a well-established Goldsturm clump at peak bloom can produce dozens of simultaneous flowers that create a brilliant golden-yellow mass effect. The long bloom season (8–10 weeks), drought tolerance, adaptability to clay and average soil, and the persistence of the attractive dark seed cones through fall and winter for wildlife habitat make Goldsturm one of the most versatile and reliably satisfying perennials in American horticulture. The dried seed heads attract goldfinches, chickadees, and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter — leaving the heads standing through winter provides both wildlife value and ornamental winter interest. As a native North American perennial, Goldsturm supports numerous native bee species and monarch butterflies throughout the bloom season. In zone 9, Goldsturm blooms through the summer heat more reliably than many perennials, performing at its peak in July through September when the heat is most intense.

plant_note: Plant small divisions in early fall in consistently moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich, sphagnum-based soil in full shade; goldthread requires cool, consistently moist, strongly acidic conditions (pH 4.0–5.0) and is best suited to naturalized, undisturbed woodland areas under conifers in northern gardens.
directions: Plant small divisions in consistently moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade under conifers; goldthread (canker root) is a tiny native evergreen perennial of cool, northern, moist, acidic forests with three ornamental features: glossy, dark-green, three-part leaves with rounded leaflets like miniature strawberry leaves; brilliant yellow, thread-like roots that give the plant its common name; and small white flowers that appear in spring. The plant is extremely small but forms dense, low, evergreen mats in cool, moist, strongly acidic sphagnum-rich forest conditions. The intensely bitter-tasting, bright-yellow roots have a long history of medicinal use in indigenous traditions and early American herbalism as a treatment for mouth sores and canker sores (hence 'canker root'). The alkaloid berberine gives the roots their characteristic yellow color and bitter taste. Requires strictly cool, northern growing conditions — not suited to gardens south of zone 6.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, peaty, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; goldthread requires cool, moist, acidic conditions and is best in boreal or subalpine woodland gardens with sphagnum moss and native acid-tolerant companions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, peaty, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich or mossy soil in partial to full shade; goldthread requires constantly moist, cool, acidic conditions and grows naturally in sphagnum bogs, mossy boreal forests, and shaded stream margins. Coptis groenlandica (syn. C. trifolia subsp. groenlandica) is a diminutive, evergreen native perennial of boreal North America producing small, glossy, trifoliate leaves resembling miniature strawberry leaves and tiny, white, 5-petaled flowers with prominent, club-shaped golden staminodes in early spring; the bright-yellow thread-like rhizomes (giving rise to the common name) contain berberine and were used medicinally by Native Americans for mouth sores (canker root). It forms a charming, low mat in cool, acidic, bog and woodland gardens alongside pitcher plants, sundews, and native orchids. Best suited to zones 2–6 where cool, consistently moist conditions can be maintained.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. Goldy Honey Bear has thick, multi-branching stalks that stay upright without staking and open to reveal green centers that mature into fully double, solid-gold 5-7 inch blooms. Its nearly pollenless flowers are ideal for clean-cut bouquets. Water while young and cut regularly to encourage more of the branching blooms.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix; soak seed overnight to speed germination. Gomphrena thrives in heat and humidity and is highly drought tolerant once established. The clover-like flowers hold their color and shape exceptionally well when dried — harvest stems just as the heads reach full color. Deadheading encourages continuous fresh bloom throughout the summer.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; contains spreading habit — site where spreading is acceptable or contain with a root barrier.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; gooseneck loosestrife spreads vigorously by runners in moist, fertile soil and should be sited where spreading is acceptable or contained with a root barrier, as it can be invasive in ideal conditions. Lysimachia clethroides is a Japanese and Chinese native perennial grown for its striking, long-lasting flower spikes — narrow, arching, swan-neck-shaped racemes of small, white, star-shaped flowers that curve dramatically at the tip, earning the common name "gooseneck loosestrife" — produced in mid- to late summer when few other shade perennials are in bloom. The foliage turns attractive shades of yellow-bronze-red in fall, providing a second season of interest; it is an excellent cut flower and a valuable late-season pollinator plant. Despite its vigorous spreading habit, it is an outstanding perennial for large-scale naturalistic or semi-wild garden areas.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness and transplant while cool, or sow late summer for fall and spring color.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before setting out, covering it since pansies germinate best in darkness, and transplant while weather is cool. This custom mix brightens the garden with light and dark blue blooms and provides color for spring and fall even in cold climates. The edible flowers are lovely as a garnish on soft cheese or baked goods. Deadhead to prolong bloom and keep the soil evenly moist.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; needs a long season to mature and cure.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm soil, giving the vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to sprawl. This playful blend yields petite festive gourds in warty, smooth, striped, and bumpy shapes in vibrant orange and green, perfect for fall decorating and crafts. Allow the gourds to fully mature on the vine, then cure the hard shells so they last for years. Water evenly during fruit set and keep foliage dry to limit mildew.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; gout plant is a distinctive tropical ornamental shrub with a dramatically swollen, knobby, caudex-like base — resembling a twisted, gout-deformed joint — producing bright coral-red, small, terminal flower clusters above large, deeply lobed, tropical leaves; ALL parts are toxic; minimal water needed once established.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun to bright part shade; the swollen base is the ornamental feature — keep soil dry in winter to prevent rot; CAUTION: All parts are toxic. Jatropha podagrica (gout plant, Buddha belly plant, or tartogo) is a distinctive, slow-growing tropical ornamental shrub native to Central America — a member of the spurge family (Euphorbiaceae) and the Jatropha genus, widely known for its unusual and sculptural physical form. The most dramatic feature of the plant is its pachycaul (thickened-trunk) base: a grotesquely swollen, knobby, gnarled, bottle-shaped or bumpy stem base that looks like a massively enlarged, deformed joint — exactly resembling gout-afflicted knuckles (hence 'gout plant') or the pot-bellied figure of a Buddha (hence 'Buddha belly'). This caudex-like swollen base serves as a water reservoir, making the plant drought-tolerant. Above this remarkable structure, the plant produces large (8–12 inch across), deeply palmately lobed, bright-green leaves with a tropical appearance, and small clusters of vivid coral-red to vermillion-orange flowers on erect peduncles that attract hummingbirds and butterflies. Gout plant is a beloved collector's plant and pot plant in tropical horticulture for its unusual form, easy culture (very low water needs), and colorful flowers. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic, similar to other Jatropha species.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Governor Mouton is an early to mid-season bloomer making it one of the first camellias to flower in November–January in zone 9.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Governor Mouton is a classic, long-cultivated Camellia japonica with distinctive semi-double to peony-form flowers showing a highly variable, bicolor pattern — the base petal color is deep rose-red to carmine-red with irregular splashes, streaks, and flecks of white that create an unpredictable, painterly, somewhat informal flower. No two flowers are exactly alike, which gives Governor Mouton a loose, old-fashioned charm quite different from the geometric precision of formal double camellias like Alba Plena or Pink Perfection. This variability is part of its appeal: the informality suits cottage garden and naturalistic landscape styles. The cultivar is named for Alexandre Mouton, an early Louisiana governor, reflecting its long association with the Gulf South camellia tradition. The upright to spreading shrub reaches 6–12 feet tall and produces dense, dark-green, glossy evergreen foliage. Governor Mouton blooms in early to mid-season (November through February in zone 9), one of the earlier and more reliable bloomers in the japonica camellia lineup. It shows good vigor and adaptability to Gulf Coast conditions. Apply acidic camellia-azalea fertilizer in spring and early fall; maintain 3–4 inches of pine bark mulch at all times to protect the shallow root system.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring bloom; Clarkia amoena does not transplant well and must be direct-sown. Cool soil (50–65°F) is required for good germination. In zone 9 fall sowing is the appropriate approach — spring sowing in warming soil produces poor germination and short-lived, heat-stressed plants. Grace Pink produces large (2–3 inch), semi-double, satiny pink flowers with a slightly darker pink center zone — a classic, clear, pure pink that is effective in mixed cool-season plantings. Plants in zone 9 bloom February–April before summer heat arrives. Self-seeds modestly in zone 9 where soil conditions are appropriate. Godetia (Clarkia amoena) is native to the Pacific Coast of North America.
directions: Direct sow in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent cool-season moisture — Godetia germinates and grows best in cool conditions (50–65°F) and declines rapidly as summer heat arrives; Grace Pink Godetia is a compact selection of Farewell-to-Spring (Clarkia amoena), a Pacific Coast native wildflower producing satiny, semi-double, clear rose-pink flowers (2–3 inches) on upright stems in late winter and spring — one of the most elegantly textured cool-season annuals available, with a silky petal surface that catches and reflects light in a way that gives the flowers an unusual luminous quality. The satiny, slightly translucent texture of godetia petals is entirely different from the matte, paper-like texture of many other cool-season annuals, providing an unusual visual refinement that makes godetia flowers one of the most elegant and graceful cut flowers available from a direct-sow cool-season crop. The clear, pure pink of Grace Pink — without the purple or salmon undertones that characterize many pink annual flowers — works harmoniously with virtually any companion planting in the cool-season garden, from blue violas to white alyssum to yellow snapdragons. In zone 9 fall-sown godetia provides a distinctive and relatively under-used February–April bloom display that is more refined and elegant in character than the more commonly planted cool-season annuals.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to shallow-water conditions in full sun; graceful cattail is a smaller, more refined Eurasian cattail well-suited to smaller water gardens and ponds where the native broadleaf or narrowleaf cattail would be too large and vigorous.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to shallow-water conditions in full sun; graceful cattail is a Eurasian species intermediate in size between dwarf cattail (T. minima) and the common cattails, reaching only 3–5 feet — making it considerably more manageable for smaller water gardens. The brown seed heads are smaller and more graceful than those of common cattails, and the gap between male and female sections is more pronounced and consistent. While spreading by rhizomes as all cattails do, it is less aggressively spreading than broadleaf cattail. Provides excellent wildlife habitat at a human-garden scale: the seed cotton, young shoots, and pollen are all usable as described for other cattail species. A refined and underused alternative to native cattails for ornamental water gardens and small ponds where scale is important.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gracillimus performs best in full sun — in partial shade the arching form becomes loose and floppy, and fall color and flowering are reduced.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gracillimus is the classic maiden grass — the most refined and elegant Miscanthus sinensis cultivar, producing fine-textured, very narrow (1/4-inch wide), arching, medium-green leaves with a thin, white midrib that catches the sun and gives the planting a silver-glinting effect in breeze. The extremely fine leaf texture contrasts beautifully with bold-textured companions like hostas, rudbeckias, and coneflowers. Gracillimus grows into a large, gracefully arching fountain form (5–7 feet tall, 4–5 feet wide) that provides outstanding textural accent in the perennial border and a striking specimen effect when planted singly or in small groups. In late summer and fall, copper-red to bronze flower plumes rise above the foliage and dry to soft tan-gold, providing winter interest that persists until cut back in late winter. The seed heads are attractive to finches and other seed-eating birds. Note: Miscanthus sinensis can be invasive in some eastern states — check local invasive species guidance before planting near natural areas. In zone 9, Gracillimus is reliably perennial and may flower in late summer before cutting back in late winter. Cut to 6 inches in February before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Graffiti pentas is grown as an annual in zones below 10 and as a short-lived perennial in zone 10–11 where light frosts are rare. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages continuous bloom but is not strictly necessary — Graffiti series was selected for its tendency to bloom continuously without requiring deadheading. In zone 9 pentas thrives in the hottest summer weeks when most other flowering annuals decline, blooming most freely from June through October in intense heat.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Graffiti Red is an All-America Selections award-winning compact pentas (Egyptian star flower) from the Graffiti series — a heat-loving tropical annual producing dense, domed clusters of vivid red, five-petaled star-shaped flowers continuously from planting until frost. Pentas is genuinely tropical in its heat preferences, performing most vigorously in zone 9's intense summer months and essentially thriving in the conditions (high temperature, high humidity) that cause most cool-season annuals to fail. The five-petaled star flowers are a key butterfly, hummingbird, and skipper nectar source — the flat, open flower structure accessible to a wide range of pollinators and the brilliant red color attracting hummingbirds make Graffiti Red one of the most effective wildlife garden plants for the Gulf Coast summer. The compact Graffiti habit (12–18 inches vs. the sprawling 3+ feet of older pentas varieties) makes it suitable for container plantings, front-border use, and formal bedding where tidiness is required.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; grand crinum requires ample room to develop — the mature bulb can reach 12 inches across and the leaf spread 5–6 feet. Avoid disturbing established clumps as transplanting sets the plant back significantly.
directions: Plant with the bulb neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained, moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; grand crinum lily is one of the most enduring and spectacular large-scale ornamental bulbs for coastal Gulf Coast landscapes, producing massive strap-like leaves and large, fragrant, spider-like clusters of white flowers with long, recurved petals and prominent red anthers on stout stems 2–3 feet tall — blooming repeatedly from spring through fall. A single well-established bulb produces a clump 4–5 feet wide with multiple bloom stalks simultaneously, creating a dramatic tropical effect. Crinum asiaticum is exceptionally salt tolerant — it is one of the few large ornamental plants that thrives in coastal beachfront conditions right to the edge of salt spray. It also tolerates periodic flooding and waterlogged soils remarkably well, making it valuable for low spots and wet areas where other plants struggle. Essentially indestructible once established; plants decades old are commonly found thriving without any maintenance in old Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Grand Duchess sorrel follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and blooming in winter and spring, going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. Several color forms are in cultivation — 'Grand Duchess White', 'Grand Duchess Lavender', 'Grand Duchess Pink' — all sold as selections of this species. The flowers are notably large for the genus, opening to 1.5–2 inches across.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Grand Duchess sorrel is among the most prolific and showy of all the winter-growing Cape oxalis — producing from winter through spring an extended succession of large (1.5–2 inch), flat-faced, funnel-shaped flowers in clear, vivid purple to rose-purple to lavender or white (depending on the selected form), each flower with a contrasting yellow center, rising above compact, clover-like, dark-green foliage in a continuous, profuse bloom display that can last 3–4 months of winter and early spring. The flowers are substantially larger than most Cape oxalis species, giving the plant a presence disproportionate to its small bulb size. It has been selected into named color forms ('Grand Duchess White', 'Grand Duchess Lavender', 'Grand Duchess Pink') sold in the bulb trade and widely grown in California and Mediterranean-climate gardens. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, it provides a bright, low-maintenance, winter-through-spring color display that requires almost no attention — plant the bulbs in fall, enjoy the flowers from winter through April, water withheld in summer. One of the most rewarding and easy-to-grow winter bulbs for warm-climate gardens.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, fertile, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; grand fir grows naturally in moist river valleys and lower mountain slopes of the Pacific Northwest and inland Rockies. Faster growing than most firs when provided adequate moisture.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, fertile, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; grand fir is the fastest-growing of the true firs (Abies) in the Pacific Northwest — capable of adding 2–3 feet per year in ideal moist, fertile conditions. The largest grand firs reach over 200 feet in the Cascade Range. The needles are distinctively arranged in two flat, horizontal ranks on each branchlet (like a comb), with the dark green upper surface contrasting with the two white stomatal bands on the undersides. When crushed, the needles produce a pleasant citrus-like fragrance. Grand fir is an important component of moist Douglas-fir and western hemlock forest communities at lower elevations. The Christmas tree industry occasionally uses grand fir, but the less-aromatic fragrance and shorter needle retention make it less preferred than noble fir and Fraser fir. An excellent fast-growing ornamental for large, moist landscape sites in zones 5–8.

plant_note: Nick and soak seeds, then direct sow once soil is warm.
directions: This beloved heirloom climbs quickly to produce large, velvety purple trumpets marked with a striking star-shaped center. Nick the hard seed coats and soak overnight, then sow directly against a trellis or fence once the soil is warm. Blooms open in the morning and feed pollinators, with heart-shaped foliage covering the support all season. Provide sturdy vertical structure, as vines can reach ten feet or more.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a support.
directions: Nick the seed coat and soak overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a fence or trellis. This dependable heirloom is a vigorous climber with deep purple blooms and heart-shaped leaves that cover supports, trail on the ground, or spill from baskets. It may self-sow, so remove spent flowers if you want to limit volunteers. Note that parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Install a trellis, arbor, or fence before planting. Plant in early spring in well-drained soil; keep roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into sunlight.
directions: Provide a sturdy support structure such as a trellis, fence, or pergola, and plant in well-drained, dry to average soil in partial shade — this native midwestern vine prefers its roots cool and shaded while its stems climb toward sunlight. Unlike invasive non-native honeysuckles, Grape Honeysuckle is well-behaved and will not spread aggressively or self-seed excessively. Water regularly for the first growing season to establish, then scale back irrigation; established vines are drought-tolerant and thrive with little intervention. The distinctive perfoliate leaves and tubular yellow to orange flowers are magnets for ruby-throated hummingbirds and native bees from late spring through midsummer.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 3–4 in deep; foliage emerges in fall and overwinters, so plant early enough for roots to establish.
directions: Plant small bulbs 3–4 in deep in any well-drained soil; foliage emerges in fall and overwinters as a low ground cover, with tight clusters of cobalt-blue, urn-shaped flowers appearing in early to mid-spring. Muscari naturalizes aggressively by offsets and self-seeding and can spread widely — site where this is desirable or divide clumps every few years in fall to control spread. Excellent planted beneath tulips and daffodils to create complementary color combinations. Deer and rodents generally leave them alone.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; grape ivy is adaptable to a wide range of conditions but requires protection from temperatures below 45°F, which cause leaf drop and defoliation — in zone 9, grow in protected positions against south-facing walls or as a container specimen moved indoors in winter.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; grape ivy is a Venezuelan tropical evergreen vine of the grape family (Vitaceae) that has been among the most widely grown and reliable shade-tolerant tropical foliage vines for over a century — it climbs by tendrils to form dense, leafy masses of three-parted (trifoliate), broadly rhombic (diamond-shaped, hence rhombifolia), glossy, dark-green leaves with prominent, rusty-brown, finely hairy undersides that give the plant an attractive textured quality when the foliage is disturbed. The lustrous, dark-green foliage, reliable shade tolerance, and easy cultivation make it an enduringly popular choice for covering shaded walls, trellises, and structures in tropical and subtropical gardens, and as a trailing vine in large containers and hanging baskets indoors or in sheltered outdoor positions. 'Ellen Danica' (oak-leaf grape ivy) has more deeply lobed, oak-leaf-like leaflets and is slightly more cold-sensitive. Outdoors in zone 10–12 it can reach 15 feet or more on suitable supports in shade conditions where most other vines would fail to thrive.

common_name: Grapeleaf Anemone (Vigorous Pink Fall-Blooming Shade Tolerant Anemone)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Anemone tomentosa is more vigorous and spreading than Japanese anemone hybrids — plant where it has room to expand, or use physical root barriers to contain the spread.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Anemone tomentosa (Grapeleaf Anemone, sometimes listed as 'Robustissima') is a vigorous, spreading species of fall-blooming anemone from China — larger and more aggressive than the refined Japanese anemone hybrids but valued precisely for that vigor and excellent heat tolerance that makes it reliable at the warm edge of the Anemone range (zone 9). The large, lobed, grape-leaf-like foliage (giving the common name 'Grapeleaf Anemone') is bold and attractive in summer, followed by tall (3–4 foot) stalks of simple, cup-shaped, warm-pink flowers with bright yellow centers that bloom in August–October — providing valuable late-season color in shaded garden areas when most shade perennials have finished flowering. The fall bloom season and shade tolerance make Grapeleaf Anemone one of the relatively few plants that provide clear-colored flowers in partial shade through September and October in zone 9. The vigorous stoloniferous spread — more aggressive than Japanese anemone hybrids — is a practical consideration: plant in defined beds with physical edging or barriers, or in naturalistic settings where spreading is welcome. The spreading habit creates an effective groundcover under deciduous trees but can overtake smaller companions.
