More adaptable to clay soil than most anemones; tolerates periodic moisture variability better than the more refined hybrid types.

plant_note: Plant corms from nursery-propagated sources in spring in wet, acidic, peaty or sandy, nutrient-poor soil in full sun to partial shade; grass pink orchid requires an open, wet, acidic bog or seep environment with full sun to partial shade and nutrient-poor conditions.
directions: Grass pink orchid is one of the most common and widely distributed of all eastern North American bog orchids — a single grasslike leaf and an upright flower stem bearing up to 10 vivid magenta-pink flowers with a distinctive bearded lip appear in late spring and early summer in acidic, wet bogs, seepage slopes, pitcher plant savannas, and longleaf pine flatwoods across the Gulf Coastal Plain. Unlike most orchids, grass pink orchid grows from small, underground corms that can be purchased from specialist native plant nurseries and planted in appropriate bog garden conditions, making it more accessible than most native terrestrial orchids. The flowers practice deceptive pollination — the bearded yellow lip (which resembles a pollen-covered stamen to naive bees) flips downward when a bee lands, dropping the bee onto the actual pollen masses on the column below; bees learn quickly and return infrequently, so the plant depends on a steady supply of inexperienced native bees. An important component of Gulf Coast bog gardens when combined with pitcher plants (Sarracenia), sundews, and bog sedges in full-sun, wet, acidic soil.

subcategory: Australian botanical novelty with triggered pollination
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; grass trigger plant is native to the sandy, peaty, often seasonally moist soils of southeastern Australia. The trigger mechanism — the column (fused style and stamens) that snaps to deposit pollen on visiting insects — can be observed and reset by gently touching a flower; it will snap back within a few hours. The plant is partially insectivorous, secreting sticky glands on the stem that trap small insects.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; grass trigger plant is one of the most remarkable and botanically interesting of all commonly grown ornamental plants — a botanical curiosity on par with the Venus flytrap in its unusual adaptation. Each flower of Stylidium contains a 'trigger' — the column, a structure formed by the fusion of style and stamens — that is held under tension and, when touched by a visiting insect seeking nectar, snaps rapidly across the flower in a powerful, spring-like mechanism, depositing pollen onto the insect's body (or collecting pollen from a pollen-carrying visitor). This triggered snap is one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom — occurring in milliseconds — and can be reset: after firing, the column slowly resets to the cocked position over a few hours, ready to fire again. The flowers are small, pink to rose-pink, five-petaled, and produced in many-flowered racemes on stems above the narrow, grass-like (graminifolium = grass-leaved) basal leaf rosette in spring and early summer. Additionally, the glandular-sticky stem hairs trap small insects — contributing to the plant's partially insectivorous nutrition. A plant that combines attractive appearance with a genuinely dramatic and demonstrable botanical mechanism that can be shown to observers in the garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; grass-leaved ladies' tresses thrives in wet, open pine savannas, wet meadows, and roadside ditches of the coastal plain — purchase only nursery-propagated stock.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; grass-leaved ladies' tresses grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, open bogs, moist meadows, and roadside wet ditches throughout the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Texas, often in large populations. Spiranthes praecox is one of the more unusual ladies' tresses species, distinctive for its very narrow, grass-like basal leaves and its relatively early bloom time — the tightly spiraled, pure-white flower spikes appear from March through May, earlier than most other Spiranthes, making it an important early-season nectar source for native bees emerging in spring. It is much easier to cultivate than most native orchids as long as the soil remains consistently moist and acidic; plant at the margin of a rain garden, bog garden, or retention pond. Never collect from the wild; purchase nursery-propagated plants from reputable native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; grass-leaved golden aster grows naturally in dry, sandy pine flatwoods and sandhills of the Coastal Plain from Virginia to Texas, where it is one of the most reliable and abundant wildflowers of the longleaf pine ecosystem.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; grass-leaved golden aster is one of the most characteristic and abundant native wildflowers of the longleaf pine flatwoods ecosystem, producing silvery, silky, grass-like leaves from a rosette and bright golden-yellow daisy flowers in late summer and fall. The silvery-gray leaf surfaces (from dense silky hairs) give the plant a distinctive shimmer in the sun that led to the common name 'silkgrass.' It is adapted to the challenging conditions of deep, white, nutrient-poor sand in full, hot summer sun — conditions that discourage most garden plants. The bright fall flowers are an important late-season nectar source for skippers, hairstreak butterflies, and native bees in the coastal plain. One of the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant native wildflowers for zone 9a sandy gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow on wet, sandy substrate or plant divisions in spring in shallow water or wet soil in partial shade to full sun; grassleaf arrowhead grows naturally in pond margins, slow streams, and other wet habitats with variable water levels.
directions: Plant in shallow water to consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; grassleaf arrowhead is an aquatic native with unusual leaf variation — unlike the typical arrowhead-shaped leaves of most Sagittaria, this species produces narrow, grass-like leaves (particularly when submerged) that give it its common name. The plant adapts its leaf form to water depth: submerged leaves are very narrow and strap-like, emergent leaves may be broader and more typical of the genus. Small, three-petaled white flowers are produced on erect stems above the water. Provides food for waterfowl (the small corms are eaten by ducks) and habitat for small aquatic invertebrates. An adaptable native aquatic for constructed wetlands, bog gardens, and the shallow margins of ornamental ponds in zones 5–10.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil; keep consistently moist throughout establishment.
directions: A delicate native perennial of wet longleaf pine savannas, seepage bogs, and flatwood margins of the southeastern coastal plain, producing narrow, grass-like basal leaves and slender upright flowering stems topped with solitary, fluffy, pink to rose-lavender, powder-puff composite flower heads in late summer to fall. One of several Marshallia species endemic to southeastern US flatwoods and among the most visually charming of the group. Grow in moist to wet, sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor soil in full sun; avoid fertile or amended soils, which suppress flowering and favor rank vegetative growth. An excellent, underused native wildflower for wet garden edges and longleaf pine savanna restorations in zones 7-9.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; gravel bottlebrush is native to the seasonally wet, sandy, gravelly soils of southwestern Western Australia — tolerating periodic waterlogging better than most Australian shrubs, which makes it more adaptable to the wet-summer Gulf Coast conditions of zone 9 than many Australian natives. It blooms in summer (November–February in Australia), providing summer bottlebrush interest. Outstanding for birds.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; gravel bottlebrush is a Western Australian shrub of the Myrtaceae family — related to the true bottlebrushes (Callistemon) and honeymrtles (Melaleuca) — that produces in summer vivid, spherical to rounded, bottlebrush-type flower heads of brilliant orange to orange-red composed of densely massed, projecting stamen bundles in warm, vivid orange, each flower head 2–3 inches across and the plant in full bloom covered in multiple such heads of intense orange. Unlike many Australian shrubs that are summer-dry and drought-tolerant, gravel bottlebrush is native to the seasonally wet, gravelly, sandy flats that experience periodic winter-spring flooding — and therefore tolerates summer moisture and periodic wet conditions significantly better than most Australian ornamentals. This moisture tolerance makes it more suitable for the humid-summer conditions of the zone 9 Gulf Coast than the strictly dry-climate Australian shrubs. The summer bloom timing provides vivid orange bottlebrush flowers in the summer garden season — a different and valuable window from the spring-blooming Australian genera. Outstanding for birds and bees.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; gray beardtongue is one of the most drought-tolerant native penstemons of the Appalachian region.
directions: Sow direct in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; gray beardtongue tolerates dry, rocky, thin soils better than most native penstemons and does not need rich soil to perform. Penstemon canescens is a native penstemon of the Appalachian region from Pennsylvania to Georgia, growing in dry, rocky woods, slopes, and ledges; it has grayish-hairy (canescent) leaves and produces loose, terminal racemes of tubular, lavender to pink-purple flowers with darker veining in late spring and early summer that are visited by native bumble bees, large carpenter bees, and hummingbirds. The soft gray foliage is ornamental even when not in bloom; it naturalizes in rocky, dry-slope native plant gardens and is excellent in combination with native grasses and drought-tolerant forbs.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall; very adaptable — tolerates clay, compaction, and a wide range of moisture levels once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to moderate shade; gray dogwood is one of the most wildlife-friendly native shrubs in the eastern US, producing clusters of white berries on distinctive red pedicels in late summer that attract catbirds, robins, thrushes, and over 90 other bird species. The shrub tolerates dry soil, compacted clay, and partial shade better than most native dogwoods. It spreads by root suckers to form dense thickets valuable for erosion control and wildlife corridors; remove suckers in spring if a more contained form is desired. Small white flower clusters in early summer are visited by numerous native bees and short-tongued pollinators.

plant_note: Scarify or hot-soak seeds before starting indoors; transplant in spring into dry, calcareous or sandy, lean, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Gray Globemallow is a robust, erect native perennial of dry, calcareous grasslands, rocky slopes, and roadsides in Texas and the southwestern United States, distinctive for its densely silver-gray woolly stems and broad, deeply lobed, gray-green leaves that remain ornamental even when the plant is not in flower. From spring through summer it produces upright spikes of salmon-orange to brick-red mallow flowers 1 inch across that are highly attractive to native bees and hummingbirds. Grow in dry, calcareous or well-drained sandy, lean soil in full sun; plants rot quickly in heavy, wet, or organically rich soils. Scarify or soak seeds in hot water before starting indoors, then transplant into the garden in spring — an outstanding xeriscape perennial for Texas Hill Country and southwestern gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, poor to average soil in full sun; gray goldenrod is the most drought-tolerant of the common eastern goldenrods, thriving in dry, sandy, and rocky soils where other goldenrods cannot establish.
directions: Sow seed in fall in well-drained, dry to average, poor to average soil in full sun — gray goldenrod is the most drought-tolerant of the common eastern North American goldenrods, taking its common name from the grayish, downy-hairy stems and leaves that help reduce water loss in its characteristic dry, open habitats: rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, dry roadsides, and dry open woodland edges throughout the eastern US and into the Great Plains. The one-sided arching racemes of golden yellow flowers curve gracefully toward the ground in late summer and fall, providing important late-season nectar for migrating monarch butterflies and a wide range of native bees. While not as showy as some taller goldenrods, gray goldenrod is invaluable for difficult dry, sandy, or rocky sites where creating a pollinator-supporting native planting is otherwise challenging. Historically used by Native American nations as a yellow dye plant.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade at cool higher elevations in the southern Appalachians; Gray's lily is one of the rarest and most beautiful native lilies, limited to a few counties in Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Gray's lily grows naturally in heath balds and moist meadows at 2,500–5,500 feet elevation in the southern Appalachians and prefers cool, moist, acidic conditions. Lilium grayi is one of the rarest and most beautiful native North American lilies, with a restricted natural range limited to a few counties in Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee; it produces small (1.5–2 inch), nodding, reddish-orange to scarlet, bell-shaped flowers with spots (less reflexed than the similar Carolina lily) on slender stems in early to mid-summer. Purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs — never wild-dug plants. It requires cool, acidic, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade and is challenging outside its native climate zone; it is best in cool, humid mountain gardens in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in spring; Gray's sedge grows naturally in wet woodland edges and stream-side meadows and requires consistently moist to wet conditions — it will not thrive in dry soil.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Gray's sedge (morningstar sedge, mace sedge) is a native North American woodland sedge grown primarily for its extraordinarily ornamental seed heads — large, spiky, star-shaped, mace-like fruiting heads that look remarkably like medieval weapons, held on upright stems above the bright-green, arching foliage clumps from summer through early fall. The seed head is the plant's primary ornamental feature and is excellent for both fresh and dried flower arrangements. The plant provides attractive foliage mass in moist, shaded corners throughout the growing season. It grows naturally in wet woodland edges and floodplain forests and is most at home beside streams, ponds, and rain garden margins in partial shade. An excellent specimen plant for rain gardens, bioswales, and wet native plant gardens in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; cold stratification for 30 days improves germination rate. Plants may bloom the first year from an early sowing.
directions: Sow in well-drained, average to poor, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; the gray-headed coneflower is a tall, drought-tolerant prairie native with drooping yellow petals reflexed away from a distinctive elongated gray-brown cone, giving it an unmistakable silhouette in the summer meadow. It blooms from midsummer through fall and spreads gently by self-seeding without becoming aggressive. The crushed foliage smells pleasantly of anise. An important pollen source for prairie bees and the seed is taken by goldfinches in fall. Mixes beautifully with other tall prairie plants like goldenrod and ironweed in naturalistic plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination, or sow in early spring directly on the soil surface as seeds need light to germinate; press seeds gently into the surface but do not cover.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall or early spring, pressing them lightly into contact with soil but not covering, as they require light for germination. Grayhead coneflower is one of the most graceful native prairie composites, with long drooping bright yellow petals reflexed sharply back from a distinctive tall oval gray-brown cone that releases an anise-like fragrance when rubbed — this upright cone distinguishes it clearly from the flatter cones of Rudbeckia. Plants bloom prolifically from July through September on branching 3–5 foot stems clothed in pinnately divided leaves, and they self-seed freely to naturalize into expanding colonies in prairie restorations and meadow gardens. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established, grayhead coneflower thrives in poor, well-drained soils and is an important late-summer nectar source for bees and butterflies.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after cold stratification in very well-drained, rocky, lean, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, dolomitic or limestone-derived soil in full sun; Great Basin bristlecone pine grows naturally on exposed, rocky, dolomitic ridges at 9,000–11,500 feet elevation in the White Mountains and Great Basin ranges. Requires excellent drainage and lean, nutrient-poor soils — very fertile conditions cause early death.
directions: Plant seeds in spring in very well-drained, rocky, lean, slightly alkaline, dolomitic or sandy soil in full sun; Great Basin bristlecone pine is the world's oldest known living organism — individual trees in the White Mountains of California and the mountains of Nevada exceed 5,000 years of age. Methuselah, a named specimen in the White Mountains, is over 4,800 years old. The trees survive extreme conditions of thin dolomitic soil, blistering cold, intense UV radiation, and annual drought that kill competitors, and their resinous, dense wood resists decay for thousands of years after death. In garden culture, bristlecone pines are surprisingly adaptable to lower elevations if given lean, extremely well-drained soil and full sun; they grow very slowly (adding only a few inches per year), making them perfect long-term bonsai subjects or rock garden specimens. The distinctive bottle-brush branch tips (with dense needle clusters on spur shoots) and the distinctive bristly cones are unmistakable. A tree grown from seed will still be young in several human lifetimes.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost on the soil surface without covering (light improves germination); transplant to moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Great blue lobelia thrives at pond margins and rain garden edges.
directions: Start seeds on the surface of moist seed-starting mix under light 8 weeks before last frost; transplant to moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade at pond margins, stream banks, or rain garden edges where soil stays consistently wet. Great blue lobelia produces striking sky-blue flower spikes from late summer through fall that are magnets for hummingbirds and native bumblebees — the only pollinators strong enough to open the flower. It tolerates more shade and more moisture than most flowering perennials. Self-sows readily in moist sites to maintain persistent colonies. The closely related L. cardinalis (cardinal flower) has identical requirements but red flowers; growing them together creates a spectacular two-season hummingbird garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring on moist soil, or divide established clumps in early spring or fall; great burnet transplants easily from container-grown stock and establishes quickly in moist sites.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; great burnet is a stately perennial producing airy, branched stems topped with small oval heads of deep red to maroon flowers from midsummer through fall. The fine-cut blue-green compound leaves have the same cool, cucumber-like flavor as salad burnet (Sanguisorba minor) and can be used fresh in salads and drinks. Great burnet has become fashionable in contemporary naturalistic planting designs, where its tall airy flower stems weave beautifully through grasses and other meadow perennials. Japanese cultivars (S. obtusa, S. tenuifolia) with longer, more elegant flower spikes are widely used in hybrid plantings. Tolerates moist to occasionally wet soil.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4–6 inches deep in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; great camas is the tallest and showiest of the native camas species, with stately spikes of deep blue to cream flowers in late spring that were an important food source for many Native American peoples.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, organic, slightly acidic to neutral soil in a site that is wet in spring but dries out somewhat in summer; camassia naturalizes beautifully in moist meadows, pond edges, and wet woodland margins under deciduous trees. Great camas is the tallest camas species, native to wet meadows and forest openings of the Pacific Coast ranges from British Columbia to California, producing bold spikes 2–4 feet tall of star-shaped flowers in deep violet-blue to creamy white in May and June — one of the most spectacular of all spring bulbs for naturalizing in moist settings. The bulbs were a staple starchy food for many Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest; note that the poisonous Death Camas (Anticlea venenosum) resembles camas in leaf and grows in similar habitats — they are distinguished by flower color (death camas has creamy white flowers, edible camas has blue). Plant in large sweeps for maximum impact.

common_name: Great Expectations Hosta (Large Gold-Centered Blue-Margined Hosta)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Great Expectations was named Hosta of the Year in 1998 for its large, thick, corrugated leaves with a creamy gold center and irregular blue-green margin, one of the most dramatic large hosta cultivars available.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best center color. Great Expectations was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 1998, celebrated for its large, thick, heavily corrugated leaves with a broad, creamy-gold to chartreuse center bordered by an irregular, wavy blue-green margin, creating a bold, three-dimensional textural and color display in the shade garden. Pale lavender-white flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer. As a sport of the popular blue hosta Sum and Substance, it inherits vigorous, substantial growth, forming a large, imposing clump over time that works well as a specimen or focal point. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic contrast. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in fall; cold stratification over winter is essential for reliable germination the following spring. Fresh seed sown immediately after harvest also germinates well. Germination can be slow and uneven.
directions: Direct sow seed in fall into moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded woodland garden or border. The cold of winter naturally stratifies the seed, and germination occurs the following spring; patience is needed as emergence can be slow. Plants reach blooming size in the second or third year, producing their distinctive deep rose-pink pincushion flowers surrounded by decorative pointed bracts from late spring through midsummer. Deadheading prolongs the blooming season, and the plants will self-sow gently once established.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions or container stock in early spring before new growth emerges; seed requires complex double-dormancy stratification and takes 2 or more seasons to germinate — divisions are far more reliable.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; great merrybells is a graceful native woodland perennial that unfurls from tightly rolled shoots in early spring alongside bloodroot and trillium. The arching stems carry large, creamy-yellow pendant bell flowers at the tips — some of the most elegantly proportioned flowers in the native woodland plant palette. After flowering the stems straighten and support handsome, bright green leaves through summer. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a clump; it is not aggressive and pairs beautifully with Solomon's seal, ferns, and wild ginger in a shade garden. Provide consistent moisture and topdress with leaf compost each fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; great Solomon's seal is a bold, architectural species reaching 3–5 feet in height and requires ample space.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; great Solomon's seal requires generous spacing as it reaches 3–5 feet in height and spreads steadily to form large, impressive colonies over time. Polygonatum commutatum is the largest native eastern North American Solomon's seal, an impressive, bold-textured perennial with stout, strongly arching stems bearing large, oval, parallel-veined leaves and 2–8 pendant, greenish-white, tubular flowers per leaf node in late spring followed by dark blue-black berries in summer; the dramatic fall color is a rich, buttery yellow. It is one of the finest and most impressive native shade perennials for large-scale plantings under trees, along fence lines, and in naturalized woodland gardens; it combines well with ostrich ferns, hostas, and ligularia for a bold, tropical-looking shade planting.

common_name: Great Solomon's Seal (Giant Native Woodland Solomon's Seal)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; plant rhizomes horizontally just below the soil surface, 2–3 inches deep; Great Solomon's Seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form expanding colonies.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Great Solomon's Seal is the largest North American native Solomon's seal — a magnificent woodland plant producing arching stems 4–7 feet tall (significantly larger than the common Solomon's seal, P. biflorum, which reaches only 2–3 feet) hung with pairs of pendulous, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers in late spring, followed by ornamental blue-black berries relished by birds in fall. The large, boldly-oval, alternate leaves arranged along the gracefully arching stems create an architectural, tropical effect that is one of the most dramatic structure elements available for the native shade garden. The arching form and large leaves provide outstanding textural contrast with fine-textured groundcovers, ferns, and hostas in the shade border. Great Solomon's Seal spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form expanding colonies that naturalize effectively under the canopy of deciduous trees, creating an increasingly impressive woodland garden planting over years. The native habitat of creek banks and moist woodland edges informs its garden requirements: consistent moisture and humus-rich, acidic soil are essential for the best performance, though established plants show reasonable drought tolerance once roots are deeply established. In zone 9, it thrives under tall pines and deciduous hardwoods where summer shade and organic leaf-litter soil accumulate.

plant_note: Introduce tubers to calcareous or chalk-based soils in open woodland or grassland edges in early spring. Soil pH should ideally be neutral to alkaline; amend acidic soils with horticultural lime before planting. Keep the planting area free of aggressive grass competition, which can crowd out young plants before they establish.
directions: Select a site with calcareous, well-drained soil and partial shade from an open woodland canopy or tall hedgerow. This robust orchid performs best where thin, alkaline soils discourage competitive rank grasses and allow the orchid to access sunlight at ground level. The fragrant greenish-white flower spikes appear in late spring to early summer and attract long-tongued moths after dark. Maintain steady soil moisture through summer, and remove any encroaching vegetation each autumn to prevent smothering the basal leaf rosette that overwinters at ground level.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; greater coreopsis grows naturally in dry, open woodlands, woodland edges, and sandy barrens across the southeastern Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained sandy or rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; greater coreopsis is a tall, robust native perennial of dry, open woodlands and woodland edges across the southeastern United States — a larger, more woodland-adapted alternative to the familiar lanceleaf and threadleaf coreopsis of full-sun meadow gardens. The plant produces bright yellow coreopsis flowers on tall, branching stems in summer, but distinguishes itself by thriving in the partial shade and dry, lean soil conditions of open forest understories where sun-demanding coreopsis decline. The paired (opposite) leaves often consist of three narrow, spreading lobes that can give the appearance of six leaves at each node. Excellent at the woodland edge where it bridges the gap between sun-garden coreopsis and shade-garden plants, blooming prolifically with just a few hours of direct sun. Seeds provide food for native birds in fall and winter.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or stem sections in spring or fall in any moist, well-drained soil in full shade to full sun; greater periwinkle is extraordinarily adaptable and establishes quickly from stem sections placed in moist soil. It spreads aggressively by arching stems that root at the nodes — contain with edging where spread must be controlled.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moderately moist soil in full shade to partial sun; greater periwinkle is a vigorous, trailing, evergreen groundcover with larger, glossier, darker green leaves than the more refined Vinca minor — it covers ground more aggressively and thrives in the heat and humidity of zones 7–11 where V. minor can struggle. Sky-blue, star-shaped, 1.5-inch flowers appear from early spring through summer. Particularly valuable in the hot Southeast and Gulf Coast where its heat tolerance far exceeds V. minor. The variegated form ('Variegata', with leaves edged in creamy white or yellow) provides striking year-round foliage interest in shaded spots. Be aware that V. major can be invasive in riparian zones and warm-climate areas where it spreads into native plant communities — do not plant near natural areas or waterways in warm climates. Excellent for covering slopes, under trees, and in difficult shaded areas in contained residential landscapes.

plant_note: Plant divisions in well-drained to moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; greater wood rush is one of the most tolerant groundcovers for deep shade, dry shade, and acid soil under conifers.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained to moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; greater wood rush forms spreading rosettes of broad, glossy, grass-like leaves with a distinctive fringe of white hairs along the margins, making it one of the most versatile shade groundcovers and one of the very few plants that tolerates the extreme dry shade and acidic conditions under large established conifers. Brown flower spikelets appear in early spring on stems above the foliage. The gold-variegated cultivar 'Aurea' provides year-round bright-gold foliage color even in deep shade and is especially effective along woodland paths. Spreads steadily by stolons; divide every 4–5 years to renew vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring or fall in shaded, moist to moderately dry sites; greater woodrush establishes slowly but once settled it is essentially permanent and requires no maintenance.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; greater woodrush is a broad-leaved, rush-like European woodlander that forms handsome, slowly expanding evergreen clumps of rich green foliage throughout the year. Unlike lawn grasses, it thrives in the deep dry shade under dense tree canopies. In spring it produces airy, branched clusters of tiny rusty-brown flowers on arching stems. The golden-leaved cultivar ‘Aurea’ brightens dark corners with vivid chartreuse-yellow winter foliage that fades to green in summer. It is one of the most effective and lowest-maintenance shade groundcovers for difficult dry shade, and the evergreen foliage provides year-round ground cover where deciduous plants leave a seasonal gap.

plant_note: Soak the small, irregular, dried tubers in water for 24 hours before planting — this step is essential, as dry Anemone blanda tubers absorb water very slowly and will establish poorly if planted without soaking; plant soaked tubers 2-3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart with the concave (hollow) side facing up, in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, 4-8 weeks before first frost. Plant in large quantities for a naturalistic woodland effect and do not disturb established clumps.
directions: Soak tubers overnight, then plant 2-3 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in fall for very early spring bloom; Grecian windflower is one of the most valuable and versatile of all shade-tolerant spring bulbs — a low-growing, spreading, deciduous woodland tuber (technically a rhizome, not a true bulb) from the mountains of southeastern Europe and Turkey that produces daisy-like flowers 1-2 inches across in vivid blue, rich pink, or pure white with a bright yellow center, the petals reflexing in cold weather and closing at night, fully opening only when the sun reaches them. It blooms in March and April, carpeting the ground under deciduous trees and shrubs with jewel-like color at a time when little else is in flower. It is outstanding in deep or partial shade, naturalizing freely by both offset and self-seeding to form expanding colonies beneath trees where many other plants fail. Always soak the dried tubers for at least 12-24 hours before planting as they desiccate during storage and must be fully rehydrated to establish successfully.

plant_note: Plant tubers just below the soil surface with the flat root-side down in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty or rocky soil in full sun to part shade; Greek cyclamen is unusual among hardy cyclamen in tolerating full sun in Mediterranean climates and developing long, thick anchoring roots that contract deeply into the soil — in rocky cliff habitats it may be essentially un-extractable. It flowers in early autumn (September–October) before the leaves. The tuber base produces downward-pointing roots from the center and lower surfaces, unlike C. hederifolium which roots from the sides.
directions: Plant tubers in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Greek cyclamen is the most heat- and drought-tolerant of the autumn-flowering cyclamen species — native to the rocky limestone cliffs, stony garigue, and thin, dry, alkaline soils of Greece, Crete, Turkey, and Cyprus — and therefore an outstanding cyclamen for Mediterranean-climate and warm-winter gardens in zones 7–11 where conditions are too hot and dry for C. hederifolium to thrive consistently. It flowers in early autumn (September–October) producing the reflexed-petaled, pink to rosy-pink or occasionally white shuttlecock cyclamen flowers, often with a magenta marking at the base of each petal, before the leaves unfurl. The leaves, appearing after the flowers, are exquisitely beautiful — dark green, often velvety in texture, with intricate silver-gray zoning and patterning in an infinite variety of marbling patterns, each leaf uniquely marked. It develops thick anchoring roots that pull the tuber deep into rock crevices in nature; in garden conditions the tubers build slowly to impressive size. A specialist plant for collectors and Mediterranean rock gardeners, providing both autumn flowers and outstanding winter foliage.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or balled-and-burlapped stock in early autumn to allow root establishment before winter. Seeds require 60–90 days of cold stratification and are best sown outdoors in autumn for natural stratification and spring germination.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, deep, well-drained to seasonally wet soil; Green Ash is one of the most adaptable native trees in eastern North America and tolerates periodic flooding, clay soils, and urban conditions better than most hardwoods. It is the fastest-growing native ash species and provides dense shade and important wildlife value — the winged seeds are consumed by many bird species including finches and grosbeaks. All plantings of this species should be made with full awareness of the emerald ash borer threat: consult your local extension service for current biocontrol and treatment options and consider whether site conditions justify planting. Established trees need little care beyond occasional formative pruning of crossing branches in late winter; avoid wounding the bark unnecessarily, as entry points can invite opportunistic pests.

common_name: Green Cloud Texas Sage (Dark Green Cenizo with Magenta Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Green Cloud is highly adapted to alkaline, caliche-based soils and will fail in heavy, waterlogged clay — amend with coarse sand and raise planting beds if drainage is questionable.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Green Cloud is a named cultivar of Leucophyllum frutescens (Texas sage, cenizo, Texas ranger) — distinguished by its dark-green foliage rather than the typical silver-gray woolly leaves of the standard species. This green-leaved form creates a different visual effect: while the silver-gray species has a dusty, high-desert texture, Green Cloud has a more lush, conventional-looking green shrub appearance that may integrate more easily into traditional landscape palettes. In both forms, the flowers are identical: vivid, deep magenta-purple, bell-shaped blossoms that emerge in spectacular flushes after rain events (or periods of high humidity) from late spring through fall — a flowering behavior so reliably triggered by moisture that Leucophyllum is sometimes called the barometer bush for its ability to 'predict rain' by blooming just before or after rainfall. The stunning magenta flower display against the dark-green foliage of Green Cloud creates an outstanding ornamental effect. Leucophyllum is one of the most drought-adapted large shrubs for the Southwest and Gulf Coast — native to the Chihuahuan Desert and extremely tolerant of heat, reflected heat, alkaline soil, and periods of drought. In zone 9, it is reliably evergreen and long-lived without supplemental irrigation once established.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; green dragon is closely related to jack-in-the-pulpit but differs in having a single large compound leaf and a dramatically elongated spadix protruding 3–6 inches from the spathe.
directions: Plant corms in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — green dragon is the less-commonly-grown native relative of jack-in-the-pulpit, equally bizarre and fascinating in flower but with a different structure: a single large compound leaf (7–15 leaflets radiating from the tip of the stem) and a distinctive flower featuring a narrow, elongated spadix that projects 3–6 inches beyond the green spathe like the tongue of a dragon — giving both the common name and the specific epithet dracontium. The bright red berries clustered on the spadix in late summer are strikingly ornamental. It grows naturally in moist, rich, shaded bottomland forests and stream banks throughout the eastern US. The corms and all parts of the plant contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if consumed raw; like jack-in-the-pulpit, historically used by Native American nations after careful preparation to neutralize the crystals. Outstanding bold-textured native for shaded, moist woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Green Envy produces distinctive flowers that open a soft lime-green and gradually develop pink-rose tips and undersides as they age, giving each bloom a shifting bicolor effect not seen in typical coneflower cultivars. It blooms over a long summer season, tolerates heat and drought well once established, and draws butterflies and bees like other coneflowers despite its unusual coloring. Leaving spent flower heads standing through winter provides valuable seed for goldfinches and other birds.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; green gentian is monocarpic — it may live 20–80 years as a vegetative rosette before flowering once magnificently, then dying.
directions: Sow direct in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; green gentian is monocarpic (flowers once, then dies) after an extraordinary lifespan as a vegetative rosette of 20–80 years — plant several seedlings to ensure flowering plants at different times. Frasera speciosa is one of the most botanically fascinating native plants of the Rocky Mountain region — it grows as a flat rosette of large, strap-shaped, silvery-veined leaves for many years (sometimes decades), then when conditions are right it sends up an impressive, 3–7-foot-tall flowering spike bearing hundreds of 4-petaled, greenish-white to pale-yellow flowers with purple spots and fringed nectary glands in a spectacular, cathedral-like inflorescence before dying. The ecological synchrony (mass flowering events in some populations) is remarkable; the plant is an important bear food and native bee resource when it blooms. It is an extraordinary garden plant for patient native plant enthusiasts.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Zantedeschia aethiopica is considerably more cold-hardy than hybrid calla lilies, tolerating temperatures to about 10–15°F when the rhizomes are mulched — reliably perennial in zone 7–10 without digging. In zone 9 it grows semi-evergreen to evergreen through mild winters. Thrives in consistently moist to wet soil; it grows naturally in stream banks and wetland margins and tolerates shallow standing water. The large, glossy, arrowhead-shaped leaves are attractive even when not in bloom. Provides exceptional winter and spring interest in zone 9 — blooming January through April when little else is flowering in shaded, wet garden areas.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Green Goddess Calla Lily actually thrives in consistently wet or waterlogged conditions and is one of the few ornamental bulbs that can grow in shallow water; Green Goddess is a distinctive cultivar of Common Calla Lily (Zantedeschia aethiopica) producing unusual, large spathes that are primarily green with white interior patterning — the green coloration of the spathe creates a sophisticated, refined floral effect quite different from the pure white flowers of standard calla lilies. The combination of large, bold, deep green arrowhead leaves and the green-and-white flowers from winter through spring creates one of the most elegant combinations of foliage and flower available for moist, partially shaded zone 9 gardens. Standard calla lily (Z. aethiopica) is one of the most cold-hardy species in the genus — far more winter-hardy than the hybrid colored calla lilies that dominate the commercial market — and reliably perennial in zone 7 without the digging and indoor storage required for hybrid callas. For zone 9 gardeners with wet, shaded areas — pond edges, stream banks, low-lying wet depressions, north-facing beds with poor drainage — Green Goddess Calla provides one of the most ornamentally effective solutions available for these challenging conditions.

common_name: Green Jewel Coneflower (Unusual Solid Green-Flowered Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Green Jewel is a striking coneflower cultivar producing unusual, solid apple-green ray petals surrounding a darker green central cone, an unusual and much sought-after color departure from the typical purple, pink, and orange tones of most coneflower cultivars. It blooms over a long summer season and, like other coneflowers, is drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established, drawing butterflies and bees despite its unconventional color. Leaving spent seed heads standing through winter provides food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; green kangaroo paw is smaller than most other species and more susceptible to ink disease (Alternaria) in humid conditions. It blooms in spring. Division every 2 years maintains vigor. The uniformly bright-green, velvety flower tubes are unusual and striking — one of the few purely green-flowered ornamental perennials.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; green kangaroo paw is the most botanically unusual of the commonly grown Anigozanthos species for a simple reason — all parts of the flower, from the stem to the velvety, six-lobed tube, are the same uniformly vivid, pure emerald-green, creating a flower that is one of the very few purely green-flowered ornamental perennials available to gardeners. True-green flowers — not pale or yellowish-green but clear, vivid, saturated emerald-green — are exceedingly rare in ornamental plants, and the kangaroo paw flower form in vivid green creates an unusual, sophisticated, somewhat shocking effect in the garden: a plant entirely of brilliant green flowers that most observers initially mistake for architectural green foliage until they look closely. Native to the coastal heathlands of southwestern Western Australia in a restricted coastal zone south of Perth, it is smaller and more compact than A. manglesii or A. flavidus, with narrow, strap-shaped leaves and smaller flowering stems. For florists and garden designers seeking the unexpected and rare — a purely green-flowered plant for sophisticated color compositions — green kangaroo paw is one of the very few options.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; green milkweed grows in dry, open prairies, glades, and rocky slopes across the eastern and central US.
directions: Plant in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; green milkweed is the only entirely green-flowered milkweed species in the eastern flora, producing small, compact clusters of unusual lime-green flowers that lack the contrasting hoods of most milkweeds. The subdued coloration makes it a plant that rewards close inspection rather than impressing from a distance. Despite the unshowy flowers, it is a fully functional monarch host plant and provides the same monarch caterpillar habitat value as any other milkweed species. It is adapted to xeric, rocky prairie conditions with very low moisture and nutrient levels. An underappreciated native milkweed for dry, sunny, lean-soil gardens where it completes the spectrum of native milkweed diversity. Specialist bee species that collect milkweed pollen pollinate the flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil around the last frost; it dislikes root disturbance.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil around the last frost since ammi resents transplanting, barely covering the seed. Green Mist produces large rounded umbels that start bold green and turn white as the tiny flowers open, a favorite filler for mixed bouquets. Also called bishop's flower or false Queen Anne's lace, it is nearly carefree and attracts pollinators. Provide full sun and steady moisture, and cut stems for the vase as blooms open.

common_name: Green Mountain Boxwood (Upright Cone-Shaped Hybrid Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Mountain is a hybrid boxwood (B. sempervirens x B. microphylla var. koreana) that naturally grows into an upright, cone-like form, useful for topiary and formal accents without the heavy shearing needed to shape rounder boxwood cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade protection in zone 8-9. Green Mountain is a hybrid boxwood bred for a naturally upright, broadly conical form that holds its shape with minimal pruning, making it a popular choice for formal accents, low pyramidal specimens, or a more structured look in a mixed border without the labor of constant shearing required by rounder cultivars. Like other hybrid boxwoods combining English and Korean parentage, it shows better resistance to boxwood blight than pure English boxwood (Buxus sempervirens) and better summer heat tolerance than English boxwood alone, while retaining rich, deep green, small-leaved foliage year-round. It tolerates the heat and humidity of the Gulf South reasonably well when given afternoon shade and excellent drainage, since boxwood roots are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet, poorly drained soil. Watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary pest in Southern gardens, which causes blistered, discolored leaves; treat with a systemic insecticide if infestation is heavy. Light shearing or hand-pruning in late winter or after the spring flush maintains a crisp, formal outline if desired.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring once the soil is workable; foliage emerges after the last frost.
directions: Green Patriot is a shade-loving perennial grown for its bold foliage of dark-green centers edged in lighter margins, forming a tidy mound. Plant in partial to full shade in rich, moisture-retentive soil and keep it evenly watered. Lavender summer flowers rise above the leaves and attract pollinators. Cut back spent foliage in fall and divide clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor; watch for slugs.

common_name: Green Rose (Viridiflora, Novelty Antique China Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Green Rose is an antique China rose sport first documented in the 1830s-1850s whose blooms are made entirely of sepal-like green bracts instead of colored petals, and it shares the exceptional heat and disease tolerance of other China roses, making it a reliable curiosity for Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Green Rose, also sold as Viridiflora, is one of the odder curiosities in the rose world: a China rose sport whose flowers never develop true petals, instead producing dense clusters of jagged, sepal-like bracts that open bright green and age to a rusty maroon-bronze, giving the plant an unusual, almost floral-arrangement look rather than typical rose color. It has no traditional fragrance but is a favorite of flower arrangers for its novelty and long vase life. Like other China roses it blooms nearly continuously from spring through frost and shares their outstanding tolerance for heat, humidity, and blackspot, needing little spraying or care in the Gulf South. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and expect curious questions from visitors who assume the buds simply haven't opened yet.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after the last frost onto bare, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun; press seed lightly into the surface and water once to settle it, then rely on natural rainfall as seedlings are drought-tolerant from an early age.
directions: Broadcast seed onto bare, well-drained rocky or gravelly soil in full sun at the last frost date, pressing it lightly into the surface and watering once to ensure contact; subsequent irrigation is rarely needed as seedlings establish quickly in warm conditions. Green sprangletop is a native of rocky hillsides, dry plains, and open scrub from the southwestern US through Mexico and into the tropics, where its loose, arching seed heads with multiple side branches add airy, open texture to dry-landscape plantings and wildlife gardens. Established plants are highly drought-tolerant and thrive in the lean, alkaline, or shallow soils that challenge most other grasses, making this species an excellent choice for erosion control on dry slopes and rocky outcroppings. The abundant seed production supports finches, sparrows, and other seed-eating birds through fall and into winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Green Twister produces rosy-pink ray petals edged in lime-green at the tips, creating a distinctive two-toned pinwheel effect around a dark orange-brown central cone, a striking color combination among modern coneflower cultivars. It blooms over a long summer season and shares the classic coneflower traits of drought tolerance, heat tolerance, and low maintenance once established, drawing bees and butterflies throughout its bloom period. Leaving the seed heads standing through winter provides food for goldfinches and adds structural interest to the dormant garden.

common_name: Green Velvet Alocasia (Frydek, Velvet Alocasia, Micholitziana)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; Alocasia micholitziana cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. It requires higher humidity (50–70%) than many common aroids and will develop brown leaf margins in dry air. Use a well-draining aroid potting mix with perlite; this Alocasia is prone to root rot in heavy soils. The plant may go dormant (dropping all leaves) during winter months in low-light conditions — this is normal; maintain minimal watering until new growth appears. Propagate by separating offset corms from the base. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Green Velvet Alocasia produces its best velvety leaf texture and deepest coloration in consistent bright indirect light and will decline in dim, low-light conditions more quickly than many shade tolerant aroids. Alocasia micholitziana is a compact aroid from the Philippines in the family Araceae, most commonly encountered in commerce under the cultivar name 'Frydek' — a name that has become so attached to the plant that 'Alocasia Frydek' is more widely used in retail than the botanical name. The leaves are the primary ornamental feature: narrow, elongated, arrowhead-shaped, dark emerald-green, and covered with a deep, dense velvety texture produced by papillae that give the leaf a rich, soft, matte surface resembling velvet fabric. The veins are precisely delineated in bright white or silvery-white in a strongly contrasting pattern against the dark velvet surface — a combination that makes the plant one of the most striking of the compact Alocasia species. Green Velvet Alocasia is generally regarded as a somewhat challenging but rewarding houseplant — more demanding than common aroids like Pothos or Philodendron, but significantly more manageable than the giant collector Alocasias. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

common_name: Green Velvet Boxwood (Cold-Hardy Rounded Hybrid Boxwood)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Velvet is a hybrid between English and Korean boxwood bred for good winter color retention and a naturally tidy, rounded form that needs little shearing.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade with some afternoon shade in the hottest part of zone 9. Bred in Canada as a cross between English and Korean boxwood, Green Velvet combines the fine, dense texture prized in English boxwood with much better cold hardiness and improved resistance to winter bronzing, holding a rich, consistent dark green color through the year better than many older cultivars. Its naturally tidy, rounded habit needs only light shearing to maintain a formal shape, making it a popular low-hedge and edging plant. Like other boxwoods it requires sharp drainage to avoid root rot and benefits from monitoring for boxwood leafminer, the main pest of concern in Southern gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Green Wizard echinacea blooms in its first year from transplant and more freely in subsequent years as the clump enlarges. Division every 3–4 years in early spring maintains vigor. The green cone and reflexed petals create long-season ornamental interest — even seed heads dry in place and provide winter bird food and structural garden interest through the cold months.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil — established echinacea is drought-tolerant and performs better in lean soils than in rich, moist conditions; Green Wizard is a distinctive echinacea cultivar that produces flowers radically different from the typical purple coneflower form — instead of horizontal ray petals surrounding a dark spiny cone, Green Wizard has strongly reflexed (drooping) greenish-white ray petals that curve sharply backward from a large, greenish-brown, raised cone, giving the flower an architectural, almost alien quality compared to conventional coneflower varieties. The large, prominent cone — which is the echinopsis (spiny sea-urchin-like structure) that gives the genus its name — becomes the dominant feature of each bloom. The unusual green-on-green coloration and the prominent spiny cone make Green Wizard a dramatically effective contrast plant in prairie and pollinator garden designs. Like all echinacea, the plant is highly attractive to butterflies and bees, and the dried seed heads support goldfinches and other small birds through winter.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring (cold stratify for 4–6 weeks before sowing) or plant container-grown plants in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; spider milkweed is taprooted and resents transplanting once established — select a permanent location before planting. It is one of the primary host plants for monarch butterfly larvae in the central and Gulf Coast United States.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; green-flowered milkweed (spider milkweed) is a native of the south-central prairies, glades, and open woodlands from Kansas to Texas and the Gulf Coast, and is one of the most important milkweed species for monarch butterfly conservation in its native range — a primary larval host plant for monarchs during both their northward spring migration and their southward fall migration through the central flyway. The flowers are distinctive: a yellowish-green corona with a contrasting rose-purple center (the hood and horn structures of the milkweed flower), creating a subtle but intricate flower in unusual color combination for a milkweed. They bloom in late spring and early summer and are visited heavily by both monarch adults for nectar and used by females for egg-laying. A deep taproot makes it very drought-tolerant once established. Rarely found at nurseries but easily grown from seed; native plant nurseries in Texas frequently carry it. Outstanding for the monarch garden and any low-maintenance, drought-tolerant native plant planting in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to average soil in partial shade; green-and-gold establishes quickly and spreads by runners and self-seeding to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat, making it an effective low-maintenance groundcover for difficult shaded areas.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic, well-drained to average soil in partial shade; green-and-gold is a cheerful native groundcover from the eastern and southeastern US producing masses of bright-yellow, 5-petaled flowers above a low mat of dark-green, somewhat hairy, scalloped-edged leaves. The common name refers to the yellow flowers above the evergreen-to-semi-evergreen dark foliage. Blooming begins in spring, continues heavily through late spring, then sporadic flowers appear through summer and into fall — making it one of the longest-blooming native groundcovers available. It spreads at a moderate rate by short stolons and self-seeding, eventually forming a solid, weed-suppressing mat 6–12 inches tall. Green-and-gold is notable among native shade plants for its tolerance of dry shade once established — a quality that makes it useful under mature trees where shallow roots and summer drought create challenging conditions. Outstanding for zone 7–9 shade gardens as an evergreen groundcover that blooms from spring well into summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; tolerates light frost and cool weather.
directions: This rare heirloom calendula opens warm gold, peach, and orange blooms each accented by an unusual lime-green center. Sow seeds directly in early spring, covering lightly since they germinate best in darkness, and thin to give plants room. This cool-season annual tolerates light frost and blooms best before summer heat, so successive sowings extend the show. The edible petals brighten salads and the plant has a long history of medicinal use; deadhead often to prolong flowering.

common_name: Greenthread (Hopi Tea, Navajo Tea, Slender-Leaved Thelesperma)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall or after last frost in well-drained, dry soil in full sun; Greenthread is a drought-adapted perennial wildflower of the Great Plains and western Gulf Coast with very fine, thread-like foliage (giving it both its common name and the botanical epithet 'megapotamicum' — of the great river, the Rio Grande) and nodding yellow-orange daisy-like flower heads; the dried stems and foliage make an excellent herbal tea traditionally used by Hopi and Navajo peoples.
directions: Sow seeds directly in fall or early spring in dry, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Greenthread is extremely drought-tolerant once established and does poorly in clay soils or with supplemental irrigation; allow to naturalize and self-sow for the most sustainable establishment. Greenthread (Thelesperma megapotamicum) is a perennial wildflower of the North American short-grass prairie and Chihuahuan Desert region, native from Nebraska and Colorado south through Texas and Arizona and into northern Mexico, where it grows in dry, gravelly, well-drained soils in full sun. The plant is named for its extremely fine, almost thread-like linear leaves — unlike most daisies which have broad, flat foliage, Greenthread has divided, very narrow leaf segments that give it a distinctive wispy, grass-like appearance at a distance. The 1-inch, nodding, daisy-like flower heads have dark orange-yellow ray florets and darker orange-brown central disk florets that together create an attractive burnt orange-to-yellow bicolor effect; the plants bloom in waves from spring through summer. The most significant traditional use of Greenthread is as an herbal tea: the Hopi of Arizona and Navajo of New Mexico and Arizona dry the stems and prepare a reddish-orange tea (called 'Hopi tea' or 'Navajo tea') with a mild, pleasant, slightly sweet flavor that has been used medicinally and as a beverage for generations; the tea contains no caffeine. Thelesperma is related to Coreopsis and Bidens, all in the same tribe (Coreopsideae) of the daisy family.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in spring into dry, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; can also be fall-sown where winters are mild.
directions: Greenthread is a delicate, thread-leaved native of dry prairies and rocky open ground across the Great Plains and Southwest, producing bright yellow, 8-rayed daisy flowers on wiry, much-branched stems from spring through fall. Direct sow seeds in spring after last frost in lean, well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun — do not enrich the soil, as fertility promotes floppy growth and reduces flowering. The dried stems have long been brewed as a mild, pleasant herbal tea by Pueblo and Navajo peoples, earning it the common name Navajo tea or greenthread tea. Plants self-sow prolifically once established and naturalize readily in open, disturbed, or sandy ground.

common_name: Gregg's Mistflower (Gregg's Blue Boneset, Texas Native Monarch Butterfly Perennial)
plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery transplants in spring; Gregg's Mistflower spreads by rhizomes and forms colonies — a useful characteristic for erosion control and naturalizing in dry areas, but worth understanding before planting in confined garden spaces. In zone 9, this Texas native thrives in full sun to partial shade with excellent drainage and low water once established. The fall bloom season (August–November) coincides with monarch butterfly migration through Texas and the Gulf Coast — Gregg's Mistflower is among the most important nectar plants for monarch butterflies, queen butterflies, and many other nectaring species during this critical migration period. Cut plants to the ground in winter or early spring; vigorous new growth emerges from the root system each spring. Once established, Gregg's Mistflower requires virtually no supplemental irrigation in zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun or partial shade; water until established, then minimal irrigation. Cut to the ground in late winter. Gregg's Mistflower (Conoclinium greggii, formerly Eupatorium greggii) is a native perennial wildflower of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Trans-Pecos regions, with a natural range extending into New Mexico and northern Mexico. The plant produces clusters of small lavender-blue to blue-purple powder-puff flower heads in dense flat-topped clusters from August through November — a bloom time precisely coinciding with the southward migration of monarch butterflies through Texas and the Gulf Coast states to their Mexican overwintering grounds. This timing has made Gregg's Mistflower one of the most recommended plants for monarch waystation gardens and wildlife habitat plantings in Texas and the Gulf South, where it provides nectar at a critical period when many other flowering plants have finished their season. The genus name Conoclinium (formerly Eupatorium for most mistflowers) places it in the boneset/Joe-Pye weed group of the aster family — native American plants with a long history of use as medicinal herbs and butterfly garden plants. Gregg's Mistflower distinguishes itself from the more widely distributed Blue Mistflower (Conoclinium coelestinum, eastern US native) by its preference for drier, more alkaline conditions — making it better adapted to the limestone soils and lower rainfall of central Texas and the western Gulf Coast than its eastern relative. The rhizomatous spreading habit gradually colonizes an area and provides increasingly effective erosion control on slopes and rocky terrain.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic soil; grevillea does not tolerate phosphorus-rich fertilizers — use low-phosphorus formulas specifically designed for Australian natives. Most species dislike excessive moisture around the roots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; Grevillea robusta (silky oak) is the most cold-hardy and widely grown grevillea, a fast-growing Australian native that can reach 20–40 feet in frost-free climates and produces spectacular orange-yellow spider-like flowers in spring that are intensely attractive to hummingbirds, honeyeaters, and native bees. Smaller shrubby grevillea species (G. thelemanniana, G. lanigera, G. rosmarinifolia) are excellent for xeriscaping in zones 8–11 and produce red, pink, or orange flowers over much of the year. All grevilleas require excellent drainage and minimal fertilization, as phosphorus-sensitive root systems are easily damaged by standard garden fertilizers. Once established, they are extremely drought-tolerant.

plant_note: Fall sowing into partially shaded, well-drained woodland soil allows natural stratification and reliable germination the following spring.
directions: Gronovius's Hawkweed is a native perennial of dry woodland edges and open forests across eastern North America, producing rosettes of distinctly hairy leaves and airy branching stems bearing small yellow dandelion-like flowers throughout mid- to late summer. It is one of the few native hawkweeds suited to the low-fertility, dry shade conditions under mature deciduous trees where many garden plants fail. Sow seeds directly in fall into a lightly shaded spot with well-drained, lean soil, scattering them onto a raked surface and pressing gently to ensure contact. Once established, plants self-seed modestly to form a low-maintenance ground layer that supports native specialist bees and other beneficial insects.

common_name: Gruss an Aachen Rose (Antique Peachy-Pink Floribunda)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Gruss an Aachen is an 1909 German rose often considered the first floribunda, valued for large, old-fashioned, peachy-pink-to-cream blooms and compact, disease-resistant growth well suited to the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in Germany in 1909, Gruss an Aachen ('greetings from Aachen') is historically significant as one of the roses credited with founding the floribunda class, produced by crossing a hybrid tea with a polyantha to combine large, full-form blooms with the polyantha's compact habit and cluster-flowering vigor. Its large, fully double, old-fashioned-shaped blooms open warm peachy-pink and fade to soft cream, with a moderate, pleasant fragrance, on a low, bushy, well-branched shrub that blooms in generous, repeated flushes from spring through fall. It shows good resistance to blackspot for an early-20th-century rose and needs little care beyond routine watering and an annual light shaping. The compact size makes it well suited to borders, low hedges, and containers. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and maintain a tidy shape.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Guacamole tolerates more sun than most hostas and is notably fragrant, making it an excellent choice for the shadier edges of sunny borders and near seating areas where the evening fragrance can be enjoyed.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Guacamole is a medium-large hosta sporting distinctive avocado-green to chartreuse leaf centers with darker, forest-green margins — the reverse color pattern of most variegated hostas. It was selected as the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year in 2002. Most notably, it inherits outstanding fragrance from its H. 'Fragrant Bouquet' ancestry — near-white, intensely sweet-scented flowers on tall scapes in late summer that are exceptional near sitting areas. Guacamole also tolerates more sun than most hostas, performing well in dappled to partial shade at the sunny edge of a woodland garden as long as soil moisture is consistent. The center of the leaf gradually intensifies to a bright gold-green through summer where it receives light, creating a striking seasonal color change. A fast-growing, vigorous cultivar that establishes quickly compared to larger, slower hostas.

plant_note: Sow in fall directly onto rocky, calcareous, well-drained soil; seeds require winter cold stratification for spring germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall onto extremely rocky, thin, alkaline, calcareous soil in full sun, mimicking the cedar glade and limestone outcrop habitats of the Texas Hill Country and Edwards Plateau where this species is native. Avoid any soil amendment or organic enrichment, as lean, fast-draining conditions are essential to long-term survival and prevent root rot. Plants form compact, mat-like rosettes of narrow, evergreen leaves and send up upright flowering stems bearing dense spikes of violet-blue to lavender, hairy-throated flowers in spring. One of the most drought-tolerant native penstemons available; excellent in rock gardens and dry limestone garden settings in zones 6-9.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–12; Guadua Bamboo is the premier structural and construction bamboo of the Americas — a large, clumping, thorny bamboo native to the Andean foothills and tropical valleys of Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela, producing culms to 100 feet tall and 6 inches diameter with extraordinary tensile strength — used as the primary structural material for earthquake-resistant bamboo construction throughout Colombia and Ecuador.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Guadua angustifolia requires abundant water and high fertility to achieve maximum growth — water deeply and regularly, apply organic mulch, and fertilize generously with nitrogen for maximum culm production. Guadua angustifolia (Guadua Bamboo, Colombian Bamboo, or American Bamboo) is a giant, clumping, thorny bamboo native to the tropical Andean foothills, river valleys, and lowland forests of Colombia, Ecuador, Venezuela, and Bolivia, and one of the most structurally important plants in the Americas. The culms reach exceptional dimensions — 80–100+ feet tall and 4–6 inches in diameter — with extraordinarily thick, dense walls and one of the highest tensile strengths of any plant material, comparable to mild steel on a weight-for-weight basis. Guadua is the traditional structural material for vernacular architecture across the Colombian and Ecuadorian Andean region and has been formally recognized by international structural engineering standards for earthquake-resistant construction — notably, several Colombian cities survived devastating earthquakes in the 1990s with significantly less loss of life in guadua-framed structures than in concrete buildings. The Nobel Prize-winning architect Simón Vélez has pioneered modern guadua structural architecture internationally. Guadua also provides exceptional carbon sequestration, watershed stabilization, and riparian buffer value in tropical environments where it occurs naturally.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in dry, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; guajillo tolerates rocky caliche soils and thrives in the Hill Country and south Texas brush country — avoid clay soils and poor drainage.
directions: Guajillo is a large native shrub or small tree of south and central Texas brush country, producing very fragrant, fluffy white-cream flower heads in late winter and early spring when few other plants are in bloom — its abundant, sweetly scented blossoms make guajillo the most important honey plant in south Texas, where beekeepers prize 'guajillo honey' as a premium single-varietal product with a distinctive, mild floral character. The plant is unarmed (thornless), making it more landscape-friendly than many other native acacias; its feathery, twice-pinnate leaves cast dappled shade and give the plant a graceful, airy appearance throughout the growing season. Dense thickets of guajillo provide critical thermal cover and escape cover for white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and quail in south Texas brush country, and the plant is commonly used in habitat restoration on the Edwards Plateau and south Texas plains. It is highly drought tolerant once established and thrives in the caliche and limestone soils that typify the Texas Hill Country and Winter Garden regions.

subcategory: South American tropical white-flower spiral ginger
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; Guanai Costus is a tall, elegant spiral ginger from the Amazonian lowlands of Bolivia, Brazil, Peru, and Colombia — one of the few white-flowered Costus species — producing long, graceful canes with spirally arranged leaves and terminal white to cream-white flowers with attractive red-flushed bracts in the moist shade of tropical gardens.
