directions: Plant dry tubers barely below the soil surface in late summer in sharply drained, humus-rich soil under deciduous trees where they will receive dappled light; hardy cyclamen naturalize freely under conditions that defeat most shade perennials, producing nodding pink-to-white swept-back flowers in autumn before the ivy-patterned silver-marbled leaves emerge and carpet the ground through winter and spring. The tubers expand slowly into flat pancake-like corms that can live for decades; never bury them deeply or they will rot. Allow the summer dormancy period (foliage yellows and disappears) naturally — do not water when plants are dormant. Self-sown seedlings take 3–4 years to reach flowering size but eventually colonize shady spots without any management.

common_name: Hardy Elephant Ear (New Guinea Shield, Purple-Back Elephant Ear)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown specimens in spring in partial shade with moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Alocasia wentii is one of the more cold-tolerant Alocasias, surviving temperatures to 25–28°F with heavy mulch protection in zone 8b. In zone 9, it grows as a reliable perennial — the rhizomes overwinter underground and resprout in spring. Provide consistently moist soil for best foliage; will go partially dormant in dry conditions. Propagate by dividing rhizome offsets. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in partial shade to dappled light in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Alocasia wentii performs best in the kind of consistently moist, partly shaded conditions found under large trees with moist, humus-rich soil — conditions that approximate its native humid forest habitat. Alocasia wentii is a rhizomatous tropical aroid native to New Guinea in the family Araceae, valued in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens for two qualities that distinguish it from most Alocasias: its relatively greater cold tolerance and its unusually attractive bi-colored leaves. The large, arrowhead-shaped to cordate (heart-shaped) leaves are medium to dark green with a slight bronzy sheen on the upper surface and a distinctive, rich purple-bronze to mahogany-purple on the underside — the purple undersides are revealed whenever the wind moves the leaves, creating a bi-color effect that is particularly striking in a mass planting. The plant produces the modest, spathe-and-spadix flowers typical of the aroid family, but these are secondary to the foliage display. As one of the hardier Alocasia species, A. wentii has become a more reliable choice than the tender A. odora and other commonly grown Alocasias for zone 8-9 gardens where temperatures occasionally drop below freezing. Established clumps divide and spread to form attractive colonies. All parts toxic.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade; hardy fuchsia dies back to the ground in cold winters in zones 6–7 but resprouts vigorously from established roots in spring. In zones 8–9 it remains semi-evergreen to evergreen. Mulch the roots heavily in winter in zones 6–7.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in part shade; hardy fuchsia is the most cold-tolerant fuchsia species — a large shrub from the Andes and Tierra del Fuego that is genuinely perennial to zone 6 where it dies back and resprouts reliably, and in zones 8–9 grows as a substantial, semi-evergreen shrub 5–10 feet tall producing thousands of the characteristic pendant fuchsia flowers — slender, tubular, with four flared scarlet sepals and four shorter purple petals — from early summer through fall. The profuse bloom covers the arching branches in a continuous curtain of red-and-purple miniature pendants that are irresistible to hummingbirds. In the mild, moist climate of the British Isles it has naturalized extensively in hedgerows, particularly in Ireland and western Scotland, creating dramatic late-season floral displays in the wild landscape. Several cultivars include 'Riccartonii' (smaller flowers, more compact), 'Aurea' (golden-yellow foliage), and 'Versicolor' (gray-green and cream variegated leaves).

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall; tolerates a wide range of soil conditions once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in a location with morning sun and afternoon shade; hardy geraniums are adaptable to poor soils and are generally low-maintenance once established. Shear plants back by one-half after the initial bloom to refresh the foliage and encourage a second flush of flowers. The attractive lobed leaves often turn red or orange in fall, extending the ornamental season. Divide every 3–5 years in spring to reinvigorate the planting.

plant_note: Plant pseudobulb divisions 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring after the last frost; space 6–9 inches apart and mulch in zones 5–6 to protect from deep freeze.
directions: Plant pseudobulb (corm) divisions 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade after the last frost; bletilla is the most reliably cold-hardy terrestrial orchid for temperate gardens, producing pleated, grass-like foliage and spikes of 5–8 magenta-pink to white miniature orchid flowers in late spring. The plants naturalize slowly by offsetting and over time form impressive clumps under trees or along shaded path edges. Mulch heavily in zones 5–6 in fall to protect the corms from deep frost; remove mulch in spring as shoots emerge. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring before new growth begins to maintain vigor and increase your planting.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost after nicking the seed coat and soaking 24 hours; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Nick or file seed coats and soak in warm water for 24 hours before sowing to improve germination rates significantly. Plant in full sun in moist, fertile soil — hardy hibiscus is native to wetlands and performs best with consistent moisture but tolerates average garden beds with regular irrigation. This is a late riser in spring; the shoots emerge much later than other perennials, so mark plants to avoid accidental disturbance. The dinner-plate-sized flowers in white, pink, and crimson open each morning and close by evening, with new blooms produced daily from midsummer through frost.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; hardy plumbago emerges late in spring — do not assume plants are dead before late May as they are among the last perennials to re-emerge from dormancy. Mark planting locations to avoid accidental removal.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; hardy plumbago is a low-growing, spreading Chinese perennial groundcover that provides two successive ornamental events: a brilliant display of intensely cobalt-blue, five-petaled, phlox-like flowers from late August through October (at a season when true cobalt-blue flowers are extraordinarily rare in the perennial garden), followed immediately by a striking fall foliage display in deep crimson-red as temperatures drop, often with both blue flowers and red foliage present simultaneously for a breathtaking color contrast. The plant is a semi-woody groundcover that spreads steadily by underground stolons to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat. It emerges late in spring (after most perennials are well established), so patience is required after winter dormancy. Excellent as an edging plant, for slope coverage, and in mixed perennial borders where late-season blue is needed. Drought-tolerant once established, performs acceptably in partial shade but blooms most freely in full sun. Not to be confused with tropical Plumbago auriculata (Cape leadwort), which is tender below zone 9.

common_name: Hardy Water Canna (Powdery Thalia, White Powdered Thalia)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in water 6–18 inches deep or in consistently saturated, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Hardy water canna is a native North American aquatic perennial of the cypress swamps, pond margins, and wet prairies from Missouri south to Texas — it is the hardiest aquatic member of the canna family and provides outstanding ornamental value and excellent wildlife habitat in water gardens and naturalistic pond plantings.
directions: Plant rhizomes in water up to 18 inches deep or in saturated soil in full sun; divide every 2–3 years to manage spread. Thalia dealbata (hardy water canna or powdery thalia) is a native North American aquatic perennial from the cypress swamps, marshes, shallow ponds, and wet prairies of the south-central United States — native from Missouri and Kansas south through Oklahoma and Texas to the Gulf Coast. The plant produces large (12–18 inch), upright, blue-green, canna-like leaves covered with a distinctive waxy, powdery-white coating (the 'dealbata' = whitened) that gives the foliage a handsome, glaucous blue-green appearance. Slender stalks rise 4–6 feet above the water, bearing small but attractive violet-purple flowers in loose panicles; the seeds that follow are eaten by waterfowl. Thalia dealbata is the hardiest aquatic plant in the canna family (Marantaceae) — surviving winters to zone 5 with rhizomes protected under water. In water gardens, it functions as a beautiful, bold-textured marginal plant providing vertical accent, wildlife habitat (hummingbirds and bees visit the flowers), and dramatic blue-green foliage contrast. In zone 9, it grows in full sun in shallow water or wet soil and spreads gradually from rhizomes to form an attractive colony. A wonderful native aquatic for rain garden oases, retention ponds, and naturalistic water features.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions horizontally in a wide, shallow container of heavy clay soil without drainage holes, then submerge 12–24 inches below the water surface in full sun; water lily requires at least 6 hours of direct sun daily for good flowering — too much shade dramatically reduces bloom production.
directions: Plant rhizomes in heavy clay soil in a wide, shallow container submerged 12–24 inches below the water surface in full sun; the fragrant water lily is the quintessential aquatic ornamental — its floating, circular pads 6–12 inches across and beautiful white or pink flowers 3–5 inches wide that open each morning and close by noon are iconic in ponds and water gardens across North America. N. odorata is native to eastern North America and is the most fragrant of the hardy water lilies, perfuming the air around the pond with a sweet, sweet scent. The rhizomes are edible (a traditional Native American food) and the seeds and flower buds were also consumed. Divide rhizomes every 2–3 years when they crowd their container; feed during the growing season with aquatic plant tablets pushed into the soil. In zone 3–7 lower the container to the pond bottom below the freeze line for winter protection.

subcategory: slender South African pendulous wand flower
plant_note: Plant corms or established divisions in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harebell wand flower is smaller and more slender than D. pulcherrimum — more suitable for smaller gardens and for placement in part shade where its more delicate form is appropriate. Like all dieramas, it resents disturbance and may sulk for 1–2 years after transplanting before flowering well. It is a coastal species, more adapted to humid conditions than D. pulcherrimum.
directions: Plant corms in moist to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harebell wand flower is the smaller, more slender, more coastal South African Dierama species — producing the same graceful, pendulous flowering effect as D. pulcherrimum (Angel's Fishing Rods) but on a smaller, more delicate scale: very fine, arching, wiry stems bearing a cascade of small, pendant, bell-shaped flowers in shades of pale pink to rose-pink to mauve-pink that hang on the thinnest of threadlike pedicels, swaying with hypnotic grace in any breeze. The smaller overall scale makes it more appropriate for smaller gardens and for positions in light dappled shade where D. pulcherrimum's greater stature and sun preference would be problematic. The individual bell flowers are slightly smaller and more numerous per stem than those of D. pulcherrimum, and the overall airy, pendulous effect of a colony in full bloom — scores of tiny pink bells hanging from dozens of swaying wiry stems — is arguably even more delicate and beautiful than the larger species. Native to the coastal cliffs, forest margins, and moist grasslands of the southeastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal, it is adapted to higher humidity than D. pulcherrimum, making it suitable for the humid zone 9 Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in zones 8–10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift corms before fall frost. Sparaxis requires a dry summer dormancy.
directions: Plant corms 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in mild-winter zones; harlequin flower is a South African corm-grown plant that produces strikingly colorful, 6-petaled star-shaped flowers in vivid combinations of orange, red, purple, pink, white, and yellow with contrasting dark eyes and yellow centers from mid-spring to early summer. In zones 8–10 with dry summers (Mediterranean climate), corms can stay in the ground year-round; elsewhere dig and store dry over summer. Plant in generous drifts of 25–50 corms for the best effect — individual plants have little visual impact. Excellent in rock gardens, sunny borders, and containers. Naturalize readily in warm, dry California-style climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens or divide root suckers in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; harlequin glorybower spreads by root suckers and should be given adequate space — the suckering habit can be managed by mowing around the perimeter or installing a root barrier.
directions: Plant container specimens or root suckers in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; harlequin glorybower is a large, bold, East Asian deciduous shrub or small tree that provides the most remarkable autumn display of any ornamental tree or shrub in its zone range — the large, dark-purple flower buds open in late summer into clusters of pure-white, intensely fragrant, jasmine-like tubular flowers with long protruding stamens, and as the petals fall, the persistent calyxes remain and flush deep rose-pink to magenta, while the seed inside each calyx ripens to a brilliant, glistening, turquoise-blue to deep cobalt-blue, creating a simultaneous display of vivid blue berries in inflated red calyxes that is completely unlike anything else in the temperate landscape. The large, oval leaves smell unpleasantly if crushed. It tolerates partial shade, spreads by root suckers into colonies (which can be managed by mowing), and blooms most freely in full sun. The blue berries attract and feed birds throughout winter. 'Carnival' (yellow-variegated leaves) is an ornamental selection.

common_name: Harrison's Bifrenaria (Hairy-Lipped Orchid, Harrison's Orchid, Waxy Bifrenaria)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning sun in coarse bark medium or mounted on bark; Bifrenaria harrisoniae is a robust, adaptable epiphyte that tolerates intermediate to warm conditions well. Allow the medium to dry between waterings — this is a relatively drought-tolerant orchid once established. Reduce watering in winter. Blooms in spring on short spikes from the base of the pseudobulbs. Named for Mrs. Arnold Harrison of England, an early collector who first flowered the species in cultivation. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light in coarse, well-draining bark medium — Harrison's Bifrenaria is one of the more tolerant and adaptable orchids for beginners and experienced growers alike, adapting to a range of light and temperature conditions. Bifrenaria harrisoniae is a sympodial, epiphytic to lithophytic orchid native to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most distinctive and immediately recognizable of the Brazilian epiphytic orchids for the combination of its waxy flower texture, color, and hairy lip. The plant produces large, angular, four-ridged pseudobulbs each with a single, large, stiff, leathery, dark-green leaf. In spring, short (4–8 inch) flower spikes emerge from the base of the pseudobulbs bearing 1–4 flowers per spike — each flower is large (2.5–3 inches), waxy, thick, and long-lasting (4–6 weeks), in white to ivory to pale cream with a prominent, three-lobed lip in rich purple-magenta to rose-purple, densely covered in short hairs that give it a softly velvety appearance. The contrast between the clean, waxy, white outer flower and the vivid, hairy, purple lip creates a striking combination unlike most other orchids. The flowers emit a light, pleasant rose-like to violet fragrance. Named in honor of Mrs. Arnold Harrison, an early British orchid enthusiast who first successfully flowered the species from Brazilian collections in the 19th century. Non-toxic.

common_name: Harry Lauder's Walking Stick (Twisted Corkscrew Hazel, Contorted Filbert)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in early spring or fall; Harry Lauder's Walking Stick is a deciduous ornamental shrub with one of the most dramatic branch structures available in temperate horticulture — the stems twist and contort in spiraling, corkscrew patterns that become the primary ornamental feature during the leafless winter months (November–March in zone 9), when the gnarled, spiral branch architecture is fully visible and at its most striking. The contorted growth form originated as a chance mutation in a European hazel hedge in England and was named for Sir Harry Lauder, a Scottish entertainer known for carrying a contorted walking stick cane. In zone 9, Harry Lauder's Walking Stick thrives as a permanent landscape shrub, leafing out in spring with typical hazel foliage and producing ornamental yellow catkins in late winter (January–February) before the leaves emerge — the catkins are particularly charming hanging from the contorted bare branches. The plant is slow-growing and typically reaches 8–10 feet over 10–15 years.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil with morning sun to light shade. Prune out any straight-growing rootstock shoots that emerge below the graft. Harry Lauder's Walking Stick (Corylus avellana 'Contorta') is one of the most prized ornamental shrubs in temperate horticulture, valued primarily for the extraordinary architectural quality of its winter branch structure. The plant is propagated by grafting the contorted cultivar onto straight European hazel (Corylus avellana) rootstock, and all woody growth above the graft union will be contorted; any growth from below the graft union will be normal straight hazel and must be removed as it appears. The contorted growth habit affects every branch and twig, producing a dense winter silhouette of spiraling, twisting branches that catches and holds frost, snow, and ice dramatically and creates complex shadow patterns on winter walls and garden surfaces. When bare of leaves, a mature Harry Lauder's Walking Stick is one of the most winter-interesting plants in temperate gardening — its corkscrew branches have inspired garden designers for generations as structural focal points in winter gardens. In spring, the contorted branches are draped with drooping yellow catkins (male flowers) before the large, slightly crinkled, typical hazel leaves emerge, adding a brief period of early-spring charm before the plant becomes a handsome but unremarkable leafy shrub for the rest of the growing season. The plant produces small nuts in fall, but nut production is typically sparse compared to standard hazel varieties.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, alkaline to neutral, humus-rich, gritty soil in partial to full shade in spring; hart's tongue fern grows naturally on shaded limestone cliffs and in stream gullies and strongly prefers alkaline to neutral soil — acidic conditions are fatal.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; hart's tongue fern is among the most distinctive and beautiful of all hardy ferns, immediately recognizable because its fronds are entirely undivided — they are long, strap-shaped, glossy, bright-green tongues with wavy or crinkled margins, completely unlike the cut or divided fronds of most familiar ferns. The fronds are evergreen and arch gracefully outward from the crown in a vase-shaped rosette. The parallel lines of spore-bearing sori on the underside of the fronds run at precise right angles to the midrib, creating an additional ornamental feature. It grows naturally on shaded limestone cliffs, in stream gullies, and on alkaline soil screes in Europe and eastern North America, and requires near-neutral to alkaline conditions — plants in acid soil decline rapidly. Excellent for limestone rock gardens, shaded walls, and formal shade borders. 'Cristatum' (crested frond tips) and 'Undulatum' (strongly wavy margins) are fine cultivars.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer under mist, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Hartlage Wine is a sterile hybrid and must be propagated vegetatively from cuttings — it does not set seed.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Hartlage Wine sweetshrub is a sterile hybrid (Calycanthus floridus × C. chinensis) developed at JC Raulston Arboretum in Raleigh, North Carolina, that combines the best qualities of both parents into a superior, vigorous, large deciduous shrub with remarkable ornamental value — the outstanding flowers, produced in extraordinary abundance from May through August on a long season matched by few large shrubs, are large (2–3 inches across), multi-petaled, deep wine-red to burgundy, and produced on both old and new wood, maintaining color from late spring through summer. The large, broad, glossy leaves are more refined than those of the native sweetshrub. Unlike the common sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus), Hartlage Wine flowers reliably in partial shade and does not depend on heat or sun for good flower production. It is sterile and non-invasive. One of the finest and most adaptable flowering shrubs introduced in the late 20th century for zone 6–9 gardens, equally at home in sun or partial shade, and exceptionally free-flowering over its long bloom season.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; Hartweg's sundrops is closely related to evening primroses but classified separately. It thrives in the rocky limestone soils of central Texas and is extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established. In zones 8-9 it grows as a subshrubby perennial; in zone 5-7 it is fully herbaceous and more compact.
directions: Sow seeds or plant small container plants in lean, very well-drained, neutral to alkaline, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Hartweg's sundrops is a Texas Hill Country native producing a brilliant, long-lasting display of large, four-petaled, clear lemon-yellow flowers that open each evening and typically remain open through the following morning — giving much better garden visibility than pure evening primroses that close by midday. The flowers are 1-2 inches across, bright as sundrops, and produced nearly continuously from April through October in favorable conditions — an extraordinarily long bloom season. The plant forms a low, spreading, somewhat woody-based perennial mound of narrow, willow-like leaves. Native to the rocky, limestone soils of Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, it is superbly adapted to the dry, alkaline, well-drained soils of the Texas Hill Country and adapts well to similar conditions elsewhere. One of the best-kept secrets of drought-tolerant native horticulture — remarkable persistence and bloom for a compact, low-maintenance native perennial.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, dry to dry-summer clay or sandy loam in zone 7–10; Harvest Brodiaea is a late-spring to early-summer blooming California native corm — native to grasslands, chaparral margins, and oak woodland openings throughout the Sierra Nevada foothills and coastal ranges — bearing rich, deep blue-violet, funnel-shaped flowers in loose, airy umbels held on long, wiry stems above strap-like leaves that die back well before flowering.
directions: Plant Brodiaea elegans corms in fall 3 inches deep in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; leaves appear in winter, wither before flowering; provide no summer water after foliage dies back — summer drought is essential for corm persistence; naturalize in grassland plantings or combine with other California natives. Harvest Brodiaea blooms after its slender, strap-like leaves have already withered and disappeared — the wiry flower stems and brilliant blue-violet flowers appearing in late spring and early summer above bare soil, creating a cheerful, surprising display in naturalistic plantings where their origins might be forgotten. The rich blue-violet flowers (sometimes described as indigo or deep lavender), held in loose, open umbels of 3–12 individual funnel-shaped blooms, are among the most vivid blues in the native California flora. Corms were historically eaten by California Indigenous peoples, boiled or roasted; they have a mild, starchy flavor. An ideal companion for California poppies, blue grama grass, and other dry-summer natives in water-wise California gardens; once established in the right conditions, they naturalize reliably and require no supplemental water or care. In humid summer climates, grown in containers that can be dried out in summer.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring after the last frost into boggy soil or directly into shallow water up to six inches deep; plants establish quickly in warm temperatures and benefit from full sun to light shade.
directions: Set divisions into boggy margins, rain garden bottoms, or pond shelves in spring once nighttime temperatures remain above 50°F, placing crowns at water level or submerging in up to six inches of standing water. Haspan flatsedge produces slender, upright stems topped with delicate, star-burst umbels that resemble miniature papyrus, providing fine-textured vertical interest in water gardens and naturalistic wet-meadow plantings across the Southeast and tropics. In zones 8 and above, roots are typically cold-hardy even when frost kills the foliage; mulch the crown heavily in fall at the cooler edge of its range to improve winter survival. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain the open, airy habit that makes this sedge most ornamentally effective.

plant_note: Plant divisions in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; hay-scented fern spreads aggressively by rhizomes and is best used where large-scale coverage is desired — it is an excellent erosion-control fern for slopes and disturbed woodland edges but can be invasive in smaller gardens.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; hay-scented fern is a highly adaptable native fern of eastern North American forests and disturbed woodland edges that spreads vigorously by rhizomes to form large, dense, arching colonies of bright-green, finely cut, lacy fronds — the fronds exude a sweet, fresh hay-like fragrance when crushed or bruised (the characteristic scent for which it is named). It is one of the most drought-tolerant of all shade ferns, thriving in conditions that would stress or kill more delicate ferns, and it tolerates more sun than most ferns. Turn golden-yellow in fall. Best used where large-scale fern groundcover is needed — on shaded slopes, in natural areas under tree canopies, or as a woodland-edge erosion-control planting. In smaller ornamental gardens its spreading habit can become problematic; use barriers or plant in large naturalized areas. A critical deer-resistant native.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost; this warm-season tarweed blooms through California's dry summer when few other wildflowers remain.
directions: Hayfield Tarweed is a resinous native annual of dry, open grasslands, roadsides, and disturbed hayfields throughout California's Central Valley and Coast Ranges, producing small, yellow, daisy-like composite flowers with toothed ray petals on branching, glandular-hairy stems from summer through early fall. Unlike most California native annuals, this is a warm-season species that should be direct sown in spring after the last frost rather than in fall, as it is adapted to germinate and bloom through California's long dry summers. Sow in dry, lean, well-drained, sandy to clay, slightly acidic soil in full sun with no irrigation needed after establishment. Hayfield Tarweed is a valuable late-season nectar source for native bees at a time when few other wildflowers remain in bloom in summer-dry California landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; heart-leaf flame pea is native to the sandy soils of southwestern Western Australia where it grows in open woodland and heath. It blooms most heavily in late winter and spring. The small leaves with holly-like spiny-toothed margins and the brilliantly bicolored flowers (orange-red with purple/yellow) make it immediately recognizable. Relatively short-lived (5–8 years) but self-seeds in sandy, well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; heart-leaf flame pea is a small Australian shrub of exceptional flower brilliance — producing in late winter and spring such an abundance of vivid, small, sweet pea-family flowers that a plant in full bloom appears entirely engulfed in a smothering cloak of the most vivid bicolor flowers: the standard petal brilliant orange-red to flame-red, the keel and wing petals a contrasting purple to deep violet with a small yellow blotch at the base, the combination of orange, purple, and yellow creating an intense, extravagant, tropical-colored display of remarkable saturation and vibrancy for such a small shrub. The small, heart-shaped to ovate leaves with holly-like, spiny-toothed margins (giving both the common name 'holly flame pea' and the species name cordatum = heart-shaped) provide an attractive, textured foliage background year-round. Native to the sandy soils of the Stirling Ranges and coastal heath of southwestern Western Australia, it requires the lean, well-drained soil conditions of its native habitat to thrive. One of the most brilliantly colored small shrubs available for the zone 9 garden.

plant_note: Plant with surrounding undisturbed Sphagnum or forest soil in spring in moist, strongly acidic, cold, boreal or montane woodland or bog conditions in partial to full shade; heart-leaved twayblade is a tiny circumboreal orchid that requires undisturbed mycorrhizal soil and cool, acidic conditions — strictly a plant for specialized woodland or bog gardens in cold climates.
directions: Plant only with surrounding undisturbed Sphagnum or forest duff soil in spring in moist, strongly acidic (pH 3.5–5.0), cold, boreal or subalpine woodland or bog conditions in full shade; heart-leaved twayblade is extremely sensitive to disturbance and requires specific mycorrhizal fungal associations to survive. Neottia cordata (formerly Listera cordata) is a minute, circumboreal terrestrial orchid of cold, acid, Sphagnum-dominated bogs, conifer forests, and mountain stream banks throughout the Northern Hemisphere; despite its tiny size — the entire plant is 4–8 inches tall — it is a gem of botanical detail, with just two small, opposite, heart-shaped leaves at mid-stem and a slender, loose spike of 6–15 tiny, dark reddish-purple flowers with a deeply forked lip. It is extremely challenging to cultivate outside of Sphagnum bog settings and is recommended only for specialists with bog gardens or cold, moist, acidic woodland conditions. Never collect from the wild. A botanical treasure for naturalistic woodland garden enthusiasts in cold climates.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seed pressed lightly onto prepared soil surface will germinate the following spring.
directions: Sow seed in fall directly into a prepared garden bed or naturalized area, pressing seed gently into the soil surface without covering deeply. Cold winter temperatures provide the stratification needed to break dormancy, and seedlings will emerge in early spring. Plants grow slowly in their first year as they establish a deep taproot, so avoid disturbing the planting site. Once established, Heart-leaved Golden Alexander is long-lived and will self-sow modestly in favorable spots.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; heartleaf aster is one of the few asters that thrives and flowers reliably under deciduous trees, spreading gently by rhizomes and self-sown seedlings.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; pinch or shear by half in early summer to keep the habit compact and floriferous. Symphyotrichum cordifolium (heartleaf or blue wood aster) is a native woodland perennial named for its heart-shaped, toothed lower leaves, sending up airy, branching sprays of small, pale blue-to-lavender, yellow-centered daisies in late summer and fall — exactly when few other shade plants are blooming, making it a critical late-season nectar source for native bees and migrating butterflies. It naturalizes readily under high canopy trees and along woodland edges, spreading by shallow rhizomes and light self-seeding without becoming aggressive in cultivated beds. Combine with ferns, sedges, and other shade perennials for a naturalistic fall display in zone 3–8.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or early fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; heartleaf foamflower spreads by stolons to form a dense groundcover — space plants 12–18 inches apart to allow for spreading, and avoid planting too deeply as the crown must remain at soil level.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; heartleaf foamflower is one of the finest native eastern North American woodland wildflowers and shade groundcovers, producing low rosettes of heart-shaped, lobed, dark-green leaves that develop attractive bronze to maroon central markings in autumn and persist through winter in milder climates. In April and May, slender 6–12-inch spikes rise above the foliage covered in masses of tiny, star-shaped, bright-white to pale-pink flowers with prominent stamens that give a soft, feathery, foamy appearance — the source of its evocative common name. It spreads vigorously by stolons (runners) to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover carpet under deciduous trees and in shaded borders. Unlike the clump-forming Tiarella wherryi, T. cordifolia is a robust, stoloniferous spreader that naturalizes effectively across large shaded areas. It combines beautifully with wild ginger, native ferns, trilliums, and bleeding heart in woodland garden compositions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; cold-stratify for 60–90 days and sow in early spring if fall sowing is not possible — like Z. aurea, heartleaf golden alexanders requires cold moist stratification to germinate reliably.
directions: Direct sow in fall, or cold-stratify for 60–90 days and sow in spring, in moist to average, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; heartleaf golden alexanders is slightly more compact than golden alexanders (Z. aurea) and equally shade-tolerant, making it a versatile native for smaller garden spaces, shaded borders, and rain gardens. Zizia aptera is distinguished from Z. aurea primarily by its simple, heart-shaped (cordate) basal leaves — unlike the pinnately compound lower leaves of Z. aurea — though both species bear bright golden-yellow umbels of tiny flowers in April through June and are nearly identical in garden performance and ecological function; both serve as host plants for the black swallowtail butterfly and provide early-season pollen and nectar for native bees, including specialist carrot-family bees. Heartleaf golden alexanders tolerates a wider range of soil conditions, including drier soils, than Z. aurea, and is somewhat more adaptable in garden settings. It naturalizes readily and combines beautifully with ferns, native sedges, wild ginger, and other shade-tolerant natives.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or direct-sow in fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; telekia self-sows prolifically and can naturalize aggressively — it is better managed at woodland edges where some naturalization is welcome. The large, coarse leaves provide bold structural contrast to finer-textured plants in the semi-shaded border.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; heartleaf oxeye is a large-scale, architecturally dramatic perennial from the Caucasus and southeastern Europe that dominates the semi-shaded woodland edge or large back-of-border position with its enormous, coarsely-toothed, heart-shaped lower leaves (up to 20 inches across) and tall, branched stems reaching 5–7 feet, which in July through September carry loose clusters of bright, golden-yellow, ray daisy flowers (3–4 inches across) with narrow, spreading yellow rays and yellowish-green central discs. The foliage alone is bold and architectural enough to provide strong structural presence through the season, and the tall, branched flower stems create a large, airy cloud of yellow daisies at height in late summer. It self-sows aggressively and is best placed where naturalization is desirable — at the back of large borders, at the woodland edge, or in a wilder part of the garden. The flowers smell strongly, which some find unpleasant at close range. A bold plant for bold situations where its large scale and spreading habit can be accommodated.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in water or moist potting mix at any time of year, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile potting mix in bright indirect light to low light; heartleaf philodendron is the most shade-tolerant and easy-to-root of the landscape philodendrons.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix and grow in partial to full shade; heartleaf philodendron is a classic tropical vining houseplant and shade garden perennial with deep-green, glossy, distinctly heart-shaped leaves (3–4 inches at maturity, much larger when climbing in tropical conditions) on long, trailing stems that root readily at every node. It is considerably more shade-tolerant than pothos and produces a uniformly rich, velvety, dark-green appearance that remains attractive across a very wide range of light conditions — from bright indirect light down to quite dim interior corners. New leaves emerge with a bronze-copper tint before maturing to deep forest-green, a distinctive and attractive feature of the young growth. In zones 10–12 it covers the ground under trees and climbs tree trunks as a large-leaved epiphytic vine. Extremely easy to propagate — a single node cutting placed in water produces roots within days. 'Brasil' (yellow-green variegated center stripe), 'Micans' (velvety bronze-green), and 'Lemon Lime' (chartreuse) are popular cultivars. All parts toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; cold stratify seeds for 30 days before sowing. Transplant to moist to slightly dry, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade after frost has passed.
directions: Heartleaf Skullcap is a shade-tolerant native perennial mint-family herb, native to dry to moist rocky woodlands, forest edges, and limestone bluff bases from Maryland and Ohio south to Florida and west to Texas, blooming from May to July with loose racemes of blue to violet flowers held above large, heart-shaped, opposite leaves. Unlike many skullcaps that prefer full sun, this species thrives in the dappled shade of open woodland and is one of the more shade-tolerant native salvias for the naturalistic shade garden. It provides excellent nectar for bumble bees and is a larval host plant for several native moth species. Grow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; it is notably drought-tolerant once established and performs better in drier shade than most native woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; slow to establish from division but once settled forms a dense weed-suppressing mat. Purchase only from nursery-propagated sources.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; heartleaf wild ginger is the evergreen southeastern counterpart to the deciduous Canadian wild ginger (Asarum canadense), forming a dense, low mat of glossy, evergreen heart-shaped leaves that is one of the finest shade groundcovers available for southern gardens. The curious brown jug-shaped flowers (earning the folk name 'little brown jugs') bloom at ground level in early spring, hidden beneath the leaves, and are pollinated by small ground-crawling insects. The aromatic rhizomes smell and taste of ginger. It colonizes slowly from rhizomes to fill a shaded bed over several years. Plant under oaks, maples, or at the base of large shrubs in woodland gardens. All parts mildly toxic if consumed in quantity.

plant_note: Plant container stock in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; hearts-a-bustin' is an understory shrub of moist hardwood forests and needs consistent soil moisture and protection from hot afternoon sun, especially in the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered, especially through the first two summers, and protect from deer, which browse the foliage and stems readily. Euonymus americanus is an open, airy, native deciduous shrub of eastern woodlands, grown chiefly for its remarkable fruit display: in fall, warty, bright crimson-pink seed capsules split open to reveal glossy orange-red seeds dangling on threads, giving rise to the descriptive common name 'hearts-a-bustin'.' Small, inconspicuous, greenish-white flowers appear in late spring, easy to overlook until the dramatic fruit show follows in September and October. The slender green stems provide winter interest and mild color even when bare. Best used as a specimen at the edge of a shaded woodland garden or native plant border where the fall fruit display can be appreciated up close, in zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; heath banksia is one of the faster-growing and more prolific-flowering banksias — reaching flowering size in 3–5 years and producing from autumn through winter large numbers of the spectacular orange-russet flower spikes that are among the most vivid in the genus. Like all Proteaceae, absolutely no phosphorus fertilizer. Outstanding for nectar-feeding birds including hummingbirds in cultivation.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; heath banksia is one of the most garden-worthy and prolific-flowering of the larger banksia species — producing from autumn through winter striking, cylindrical flower spikes 8–12 inches long in warm, vivid orange to russet-orange to orange-gold, made up of densely packed hundreds of individual small, nectar-rich flowers. The fine, needle-like leaves (resembling heather leaves — hence 'heath banksia' and the species name ericifolia) create a fine-textured, dark-green, somewhat heather-like foliage year-round, providing pleasant contrast to the large, bold flower spikes. The autumn-to-winter bloom time fills a gap in the garden calendar when few other large-flowered shrubs are at peak, and the vivid, warm orange of the flower spikes is particularly welcome in the cooler months. In cultivation the dense, nectar-rich flower spikes are enthusiastically visited by hummingbirds throughout the winter bloom period. One of the more adaptable and garden-practical banksia species for zone 9–11 gardens outside Australia, combining reasonable growth rate, generous flowering, and striking flower color. Requires the same excellent drainage and zero-phosphorus care as all Proteaceae.

plant_note: Set out tubers or divisions in early spring into acidic, moisture-retentive soil. Amend heavy clay with coarse grit and leaf mold to improve drainage while retaining the consistent moisture this species demands. Avoid alkaline or heavily fertilized soils, which suppress the fungal partners these orchids require.
directions: Choose a site with acidic, peaty, or sandy soil that stays consistently moist without becoming waterlogged. This orchid thrives in open woodland, heathland edges, and boggy clearings where it receives bright indirect light through a partial canopy. Mulch lightly with pine needles or acidic leaf mold each autumn to maintain soil acidity and protect the shallow tubers from frost heave. Plants establish slowly and should not be moved once settled, as relocating them typically breaks the essential mycorrhizal associations.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in moist to moderately moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Nandina is one of the most adaptable ornamental shrubs for the Southeast and Gulf Coast, tolerating clay soil, drought, dense shade, and coastal conditions better than almost any comparable plant.
directions: Plant in virtually any well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to full shade; Nandina is one of the toughest and most site-adaptable ornamentals for Southern gardens, though it develops the best red fall and winter foliage color in full sun, and in heavy shade may remain more green year-round. Nandina domestica (heavenly bamboo — not a true bamboo) is an elegant, upright evergreen shrub native to China and Japan with fine-textured, pinnate (bamboo-like) foliage that emerges bronze-red in spring, turns green in summer, and becomes brilliant red to burgundy-red in fall and winter, especially in sun; large, pyramidal clusters of white flowers in May–June are followed by persistent clusters of bright-red berries that last through winter and provide exceptional wildlife value. The berries are relished by Cedar Waxwings and American Robins. Standard Nandina grows 4–6 feet tall; compact cultivars like 'Harbour Dwarf' (2–3 feet), 'Fire Power' (2 feet, intense red fall color), and 'Lemon Lime' (lime-green foliage) are popular. Note: Nandina berries are toxic to dogs and cats; berries may be invasive in some southeastern states — check local regulations.

plant_note: Nick and soak seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a support.
directions: Nick the seed coat and soak overnight, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis or fence. This showy climber opens sky-blue flowers in the cool of morning that close in afternoon heat but stay open all day when cloudy or in fall. Give it full sun and a support to twine up, watering while young until established. Note that parts of the plant are toxic if eaten, so keep away from children and pets.

common_name: Heavy Metal Switchgrass (Steel Blue Upright Switchgrass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Heavy Metal is adaptable to clay, wet, and dry soils — one of the most versatile native ornamental grasses for difficult sites.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Heavy Metal is the most celebrated upright switchgrass cultivar — named for its stiffly vertical, non-flopping growth habit and distinctive steel-blue summer foliage color, in contrast to the arching, floppy form of the switchgrass species and many other cultivars. The rigid, bolt-upright stems (4–5 feet tall) maintain their strict vertical form through all weather without flopping or spreading outward — a critical landscape quality that makes Heavy Metal outstanding for formal accent use, vertical punctuation in borders, and screening where a reliably upright column of foliage is desired. The summer foliage is an attractive steel-blue to blue-green color; in fall it transitions through yellow, orange, and burgundy for one of the finest fall color displays of any native grass. Pink seed heads wave in late summer breezes. Heavy Metal is a prairie native (Panicum virgatum) that is exceptionally adaptable — tolerating clay, periodic flooding, drought, and the full range of Gulf South conditions that challenge many ornamental grasses. The wildlife value is significant: the seeds are eaten by many songbirds, and switchgrass provides nesting habitat and overwintering cover for many native insects and small mammals. Cut to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge bamboo is a CLUMPING bamboo (Bambusa genus) with tight, non-invasive rhizomes — no root barrier needed. This is one of the most reliable non-invasive bamboos for warm climates, ideal for privacy screens and hedges.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; hedge bamboo (and its many cultivars including the striped 'Alphonse Karr' with yellow culms streaked green) is one of the most widely planted bamboos in the southeastern US, Gulf Coast, and California — a clumping bamboo that does not spread invasively but grows into a graceful, dense clump of arching culms perfect for screens, hedges, and specimen plantings. Because it is Bambusa (a clumping bamboo genus), it does not send out long, invasive rhizomes like the Phyllostachys running bamboos — making it suitable for gardens where invasive spread is a concern. The dense, arching clumps provide excellent year-round visual screening. 'Alphonse Karr' with its yellow and green striped culms is one of the most popular ornamental bamboos in warm climates. Grows vigorously in the Gulf Coast and Florida.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil.
directions: Direct sow after frost about an inch deep in full sun, thinning to 12-18 inches apart. This heirloom mix blends the sunny yellows of Lemon Queen, warm tones of Autumn Beauty, and deep reds of Velvet Queen in 4-8 inch multi-branching blooms. Because the plants branch, cut stems regularly to encourage a long succession of flowers for bouquets and pollinators. Water while establishing and stake tall stalks in exposed sites.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant only after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep; germination is slow (14–28 days) and benefits from bottom heat at 70–80°F consistently. Transplant into rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; heat brings out the intensely vanilla-scented, deep purple flower clusters. Pinch tips once or twice before transplanting to produce bushier plants with more flowering heads. In zones 10–11 heliotrope is a shrubby perennial; elsewhere take cuttings in late summer to overwinter prized fragrant selections indoors.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained shade; transplanted divisions establish more reliably than seed.
directions: Plant with the crown at soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade — morning sun is tolerated, but afternoon sun causes leaf scorch. Hellebores bloom in late winter to early spring, often through snow, and the nodding flowers face downward; tipping the pot or planting on a slope allows a better view of the flower interior. Remove old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges to improve air circulation and reduce leaf spot diseases. Hellebores self-sow freely, and seedlings from hybrid plants will vary; divide named selections in early spring to maintain specific colors.

plant_note: Scatter seeds on bare, dry, sandy soil in fall; do not cover, as light aids germination, and avoid compacted or moist ground.
directions: Heller's Cudweed is a southeastern native annual everlasting that produces upright stems densely clothed in white woolly hair, topped in spring with clusters of tiny composite flower heads bearing papery, straw-white bracts that hold their form when dried. The entire plant emits a pleasant, mild balsam-like fragrance when brushed or crushed, making it useful in dried arrangements as well as native habitat plantings. Like other cudweeds, it serves as a critical larval host plant for the American Painted Lady butterfly. Sow seeds on the surface of dry, lean, sandy, well-drained soil in fall and leave them undisturbed through winter; plants self-sow freely in open, sunny ground and need no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–October. Hello Yellow butterfly weed, like all Asclepias tuberosa, is late to emerge in spring — mark plant locations to avoid disturbing dormant roots. Do not transplant established plants as the deep taproot resists disturbance. Plants bloom in their second year from seed; container-grown plants may bloom the first season. In zone 9 butterfly weed is extremely drought-tolerant once established — one of the most drought-adapted native perennials for full-sun locations.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, neutral to slightly acidic soil — butterfly weed must have excellent drainage and thrives in dry, hot conditions; Hello Yellow is a cultivar of native butterfly weed (Asclepias tuberosa) selected for its clear, bright, warm yellow flower clusters — a color variant of the standard vivid orange species that provides a softer, cooler yellow tone for garden designs where the species orange clashes with surrounding plants. Asclepias tuberosa is one of the most ecologically important native plants for monarch butterfly conservation — it is a host plant for monarch caterpillars and an important nectar source for adult monarchs, swallowtails, and other native pollinators. Unlike the common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), butterfly weed does not spread aggressively and does not produce the milky latex sap, making it a much more garden-friendly choice that can be integrated into managed landscape plantings without concern for spreading. Hello Yellow's warm yellow flowers pair naturally with orange, bronze, and gold companion plants, creating summer combinations that reference prairie flower meadows where Asclepias tuberosa is naturally found growing alongside goldenrods, coneflowers, and grasses. Drought tolerance, native provenance, and wildlife value make it a cornerstone plant for responsible zone 9 landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet soil; keep soil evenly moist through the first growing season to establish deep roots.
directions: Henderson's Checker-mallow is a rare native Sidalcea of brackish marsh margins, tidal meadows, and wet coastal lowland habitats in the Pacific Northwest, primarily in Washington and Oregon, where it produces erect spikes of deep rose-pink mallow flowers in summer atop sturdy, upright stems. It is one of the most moisture-tolerant checker-mallows and thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, mucky or heavy soil in full sun — conditions that would be fatal to most ornamental perennials. Plant container-grown transplants in spring and keep soil wet through establishment; once rooted, plants form long-lived clumps that spread slowly by rhizomes and naturalize well in restored wetland settings. It is an important larval host for specialist pollinators in its native range and an excellent choice for rain gardens, wet borders, and Pacific Northwest wetland restoration plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall onto moist, well-drained soil in a lightly shaded site; cold stratification over the Pacific Northwest winter provides the chill needed for spring germination.
directions: Sow fresh seed in early fall directly onto prepared soil in a lightly shaded, well-drained garden bed or open woodland edge, pressing seed into the surface without covering. The corms require a cold, moist winter period to germinate successfully, and seedlings typically emerge among the first wildflowers of the Pacific Northwest spring. Provide consistent moisture through the brief spring growing season, then withhold water as the foliage begins to yellow after flowering, mimicking the plant's natural summer-dry habitat. Once established, Henderson's Shooting Star will form expanding colonies and self-sow reliably under favorable conditions.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Henna is a trailing coleus cultivar with finely cut, lacy, copper-orange leaves edged in chartreuse-green, an unusual warm color combination well suited to hanging baskets and container edges.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Henna is a trailing coleus cultivar with finely dissected, lacy-textured leaves in a warm copper-orange center fading to a chartreuse-green edge, an unusual combination that reads as warm and glowing rather than the cooler purples and reds common among coleus. Its cascading, trailing habit makes it especially well suited to hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of large containers, where it spills gracefully over the rim, and the fine, ferny leaf texture provides contrast against bolder, broad-leaved companion plants. Like most coleus, it performs best with some protection from the most intense midday sun in zone 9, coloring up most vividly with morning sun and afternoon shade. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage denser, bushier trailing growth.

common_name: Henry Duelberg Sage (Perennial Native Blue Texas Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg is a selection of the Texas native Salvia farinacea that is more reliably perennial in zone 9 than the standard Victoria Blue hybrid cultivars used as annuals in northern gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg is a white-flowered selection of Salvia farinacea (mealy cup sage) — the Texas native blue sage that is the parent of the widely grown 'Victoria Blue' annual series, but Henry Duelberg itself is selected as a reliably perennial landscape form for zones 7–11 rather than an annual bedding plant. Wait — Henry Duelberg is actually a white-flowered form. Let me clarify: Henry Duelberg sage produces pure white flowers on silvery-mealy calyces on upright spikes, providing a clean white effect different from the blue-violet standard S. farinacea. The plant grows 2–3 feet tall with an upright, tidy habit and blooms from spring through frost with virtually no deadheading required. Like all S. farinacea selections, Henry Duelberg is highly attractive to butterflies and bees, and the mealy calyx texture persists ornamentally even after individual flowers have dropped, extending the effective display period. In zone 9, Henry Duelberg is reliably perennial — the woody crown overwinters even through moderate freezes and rebounds vigorously in spring. The plant self-seeds mildly, creating a self-maintaining colony without becoming weedy. Outstanding heat, drought, and humidity tolerance make Henry Duelberg one of the most durable and reliable perennial salvias for Gulf South conditions. A Texas native with exceptional local adaptation.

common_name: Henry Duelberg Salvia (Vigorous Native Texas Blue Mealy Sage Selection)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg's exceptional drought tolerance once established makes it ideal for low-irrigation landscapes — water weekly for the first season, then only during extended drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Henry Duelberg is a superior selection of mealy blue sage (Salvia farinacea) — a Texas native wildflower — chosen for its outstanding garden performance: larger, more vigorous plant habit, more robust flower spike production, and excellent persistence compared to typical nursery-grown mealy sage seedlings. Named for Henry Duelberg, a San Antonio area rancher and plant enthusiast who grew this selection for years, the cultivar was popularized by plantsman Scott Ogden and represents one of the most valuable native perennial salvias for Gulf South gardens. The lavender-blue to rich violet-blue flower spikes — each 6–12 inches tall with densely packed whorls of small tubular flowers along white-farinose (mealy-powdery) stems — bloom from early spring through heavy frost, providing an extremely long ornamental season. The extended bloom, exceptional heat and drought tolerance, deer resistance, and powerful attraction to hummingbirds, monarchs, swallowtails, and native bees make Henry Duelberg Salvia one of the top performers for zone 8-10 pollinator gardens and xeriscape designs. In zone 9, established plants are essentially self-sustaining on rainfall alone after the first season. The fine-textured blue flower spikes combine well with coarser-textured native companions — Salvia greggii, Lantana, Gulf muhly — in low-maintenance native plant gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained to evenly moist soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise is native to moist woodland ravines and shaded slopes of central China and demands protection from hot afternoon sun in zones 7–9 or foliage will scorch. Avoid low frost pockets where cold air pools; a sheltered courtyard or north-facing slope provides ideal conditions in the colder end of its range.
directions: Plant in partial shade to deep shade in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with excellent drainage; Henry's anise is one of the finest shade-tolerant broad-leaved evergreen shrubs for gardens in zones 7–9, offering year-round glossy, lance-shaped, deep-green foliage with a distinct anise fragrance when crushed — a characteristic shared with the closely related native Florida anise (Illicium floridanum). Illicium henryi produces charming, star-shaped flowers from spring through early summer in shades of rose-red to deep carmine-pink, with petals arranged in the distinctive multi-layered pattern characteristic of the genus; the flowers are subtly fragrant and appear among the glossy foliage over an extended season. An outstanding plant for shady courtyards, woodland borders, and foundation plantings where a refined, deer-resistant, evergreen structure is needed; it pairs beautifully with Japanese maples, camellias, and Hydrangea quercifolia in the shade garden. CAUTION: all parts are toxic if ingested — do not confuse with culinary star anise (Illicium verum).

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise tree is the hardiest of the Chinese Illicium species and one of the few broad-leaved evergreen shrubs that thrives in deep shade in zones 6–9.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; Henry's anise tree is a Chinese evergreen shrub or small tree prized for its ability to thrive in deep shade — one of the relatively few large-growing broad-leaved evergreens that performs well in the dense shade beneath mature trees where most broadleaf shrubs languish. The large, glossy, dark green, willow-like leaves are aromatic when crushed. The flowers are rosy red to deep pink, star-shaped, and appear in late spring — more showy than those of the native Florida anise (I. floridanum) but less fragrant. Named for Augustine Henry, the Irish plant explorer who collected extensively in China in the late 19th century. Somewhat hardier than Florida anise, tolerating temperatures to 0°F in a sheltered spot. An excellent large screening shrub for shaded gardens in the Southeast.

common_name: Henry's Garnet Virginia Sweetspire (Fall Color Shade Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Henry's Garnet tolerates wet, periodically flooded soils better than most landscape shrubs — it is excellent for rain gardens and moist, low-lying areas.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Henry's Garnet is the most widely grown and most celebrated Itea virginica cultivar — a superior selection chosen by Mary Henry of Gladwyne, Pennsylvania, for its outstanding combination of fragrant summer flowers, exceptional fall color, and adaptability to difficult growing conditions. In late June and July, the shrub produces 4–6 inch, drooping, bottlebrush-like clusters of small, fragrant white flowers that attract bees and butterflies. But Henry's Garnet's most remarkable attribute is its fall color — in September through November, the foliage transitions to vivid burgundy-red to deep garnet, one of the most reliable and intense fall color displays of any native shrub, maintained even in zone 9 where fall temperatures are mild. The fall color persists for 6–8 weeks — far longer than most fall-color shrubs. Henry's Garnet spreads by suckering to form a colony over years, making it effective as a mass planting for naturalizing, rain garden planting, and stream-bank erosion control. Unlike most fall-color shrubs that require full sun for good color development, Henry's Garnet develops excellent color even in partial shade — a notable advantage for shade gardens. The spreading habit and outstanding fall color with shade tolerance make it one of the finest native shrubs for zone 9.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 8-10 inches deep (the stem roots above the bulb, so depth is important) in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Henry's lily is unusual among true lilies in tolerating lime-rich soils and partial shade, making it useful in dappled light under trees where other lilies fail.
directions: Plant bulbs 8-10 inches deep (the stem roots above the bulb, so depth is important) in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; Henry's lily is unusual among true lilies in tolerating lime-rich soils and partial shade, making it useful in dappled light under trees where other lilies fail. Lilium henryi was discovered in central China by Augustine Henry in 1888 and introduced to Western horticulture shortly after; it is a spectacular architectural lily, producing stout stems up to 8 feet tall in full vigor bearing large whorls of leaves and 20-30 pendant, Turk's-cap-type flowers of warm apricot-orange with dark spotting and reflexed petals in late July and August. The plant is vigorous, long-lived, disease-resistant, and increases slowly by bulb offsets; its unusual tolerance of chalk and alkaline soils makes it an outstanding choice for gardens on limestone where most lilies are difficult.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Henryi blooms on old wood in late spring with a possible light rebloom on new growth, so prune only lightly to remove dead or weak stems rather than cutting the vine back hard.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to light shade on a trellis or fence. Henryi is one of the oldest and most classic large-flowered clematis cultivars, producing enormous, creamy white flowers with conspicuous chocolate-brown stamens that create a striking contrast against the pale petals. Because it flowers mainly on old wood from the previous season, heavy pruning removes the coming season's bloom, so gardeners should limit pruning to removing dead or damaged stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole plant back as with Jackmanii-type clematis. It has been a garden favorite for well over a century for its dependable, large-scale white flower display.

plant_note: Plant offsets (chicks) in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun; hens and chicks require virtually no soil depth and thrive in rock crevices, walls, and containers with minimal growing medium.
directions: Plant offsets ('chicks') in spring or fall by pressing them onto the surface of very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, lean soil in full sun — they need almost no soil depth and anchor themselves quickly; hens and chicks are among the hardiest and most drought-tolerant succulents for cold-climate gardens, forming tight rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves in an extraordinary range of colors from green to burgundy, purple, silver, and bicolor depending on cultivar. The 'hen' rosette blooms once (typically in year 2 or 3) with a dramatic starburst flower stalk, then dies, but leaves behind dozens of 'chicks' that fill the gap. Outstanding for rock gardens, green roofs, wall crevices, alpine troughs, dry stone walls, and containers; they thrive on negligence and rot immediately in wet, poorly drained conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in early spring in humus-rich, slightly alkaline soil; purchase only nursery-propagated plants as wild collection is unsustainable and transplants rarely survive.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil (unlike most woodland plants, hepatica prefers near-neutral to mildly basic soil from calcareous bedrock) in full to dappled shade. One of the earliest spring wildflowers in eastern North America, the cup-shaped flowers in shades of white, pink, and lavender open in late February–March before any leaves appear, emerging through snow on fuzzy, insulating stems. The leathery, three-lobed leaves that develop after flowering persist through winter and often have beautiful mottled markings. Extremely slow-growing from seed (3–5 years to bloom); purchase only from ethical native plant nurseries. May live for decades undisturbed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; herald's trumpet is a very large, vigorous vine requiring substantial, permanent support — a mature plant can cover a large pergola or building wall 40–50 feet across. It blooms in spring (April–June), producing large clusters of enormous, white, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers. In zone 9 it may be frost-damaged in hard winters but regrows from the roots. Requires consistent moisture during the growing season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; herald's trumpet is one of the most spectacular of all tropical and subtropical flowering vines — a native of the eastern Himalayan foothills and northern India that produces in spring (April through June) enormous, trumpet-shaped flowers of breathtaking scale: each individual flower is 4–5 inches long and 3–4 inches across at the opening, pure white, five-petaled, with a narrow tube flaring to a wide, rounded, slightly fragrant trumpet that resembles an Easter lily flower of exaggerated dimensions. These enormous white trumpet flowers are borne in large, clustered bunches of 6–20 at the ends of the stems, so that a mature vine in full spring bloom — covering a large pergola or two-story wall — presents hundreds of the enormous, pristine-white trumpets simultaneously in a display of singular tropical grandeur. The large, oval, glossy, dark-green leaves are bold and handsome year-round. The vine is very large-growing, reaching 30–50 feet on suitable permanent support, and is a decades-long commitment. In zone 9a it requires a warm, sheltered position and may suffer frost damage in severe winters but regrows. One of the ultimate ambitions of warm-climate gardeners — a vine you plant and tend for years to achieve an unforgettable eventual spectacle.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, alkaline to neutral woodland soil in full shade; ALL PARTS ARE TOXIC and should not be grown where children or pets have unsupervised access.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full shade, replicating its natural habitat of base-rich European deciduous woodland; herb Paris dislikes acidic conditions and resents disturbance. Paris quadrifolia is a singularly distinctive European woodland perennial producing an unbranched stem topped with a precise whorl of exactly four broad leaves and a single greenish-yellow flower in late spring, followed by a glossy black berry. The entire plant is poisonous (containing steroidal saponins) and should be handled with care; it is slow to multiply but an elegant collector's plant for shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, moderately infertile, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to light shade. Hercules' Club spreads by root sprouts and can form thickets — site accordingly. Handle with care due to the large, sharp spines on trunk and branches.
directions: Hercules' Club is a large, dramatic native shrub or small tree of the coastal plain and piedmont of the southeastern United States, notorious for the massive, knobby, claw-like spines that stud the trunk and branches and make it instantly identifiable from a distance. A member of the citrus family (Rutaceae) and closely related to Sichuan pepper, the aromatic bark and leaves contain numbing, anesthetic compounds that were applied by many Native American peoples directly to sore gums and toothaches — earning it the folk name toothache tree — as well as used as a fish poison and in various medicinal preparations. A primary host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly, one of the largest butterflies in North America, Hercules' Club is an outstanding native choice for wildlife gardens in the Southeast. Plant in well-drained, moderately infertile, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established, it spreads by root sprouts and benefits from open, sunny, naturalized settings.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Heritage is particularly suited to rain gardens, stream banks, and other moist sites where most trees struggle.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Heritage is the premier named cultivar of river birch — introduced by Earl Cully of Heritage Tree Nursery in Jacksonville, Illinois, and selected for outstanding bark exfoliation quality, larger leaf size, and superior heat tolerance compared to unselected species plants. The spectacular bark display is the tree's signature attribute: the outer bark exfoliates in large, curling, papery sheets throughout the year, revealing the inner bark in a complex palette of salmon-pink, cream, cinnamon-brown, and reddish-tan tones — a year-round ornamental effect that is one of the finest bark displays of any tree in cultivation. In winter when the tree is bare of leaves, the multi-trunked form with its layered, peeling, multi-colored bark is truly spectacular against a winter sky. Heritage is also one of the most heat-tolerant birches — unlike white or paper birch that decline in the heat of zone 7 and warmer, Heritage river birch thrives through zone 9 in moist to wet sites, making it the birch of choice for the Gulf South. It is highly resistant to bronze birch borer, which devastates most white birch species in the eastern United States. The naturally multi-trunked form and year-round bark display make Heritage an exceptional specimen and focal-point tree.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Herme is a classic, long-cultivated camellia cultivar with semi-double flowers variably marbled and striped in pink, rose, and white, no two quite alike.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Herme is a long-established, historic Camellia japonica cultivar with roots tracing back to Japan, producing semi-double flowers with an irregular, ever-varying marbled pattern of soft pink, deeper rose, and white, so that individual blooms on the same shrub display a range of patterning rather than an identical, uniform color. This unpredictable variegation has made it a favorite among camellia collectors for generations. It blooms in winter into early spring on an evergreen shrub with the same glossy, dark green foliage typical of the species, and benefits from consistent moisture, acidic soil, and protection from harsh afternoon sun.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens or divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; heucherella is sterile and does not set seed — it propagates only by division and is sold exclusively as named clones.
directions: Plant container specimens or divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; heucherella is an intergeneric hybrid between Heuchera (alumroot) and Tiarella (foamflower) that combines the bold, colorful foliage of heuchera with the running, spreading habit and delicate flowers of tiarella.
