The result is a versatile, shade-tolerant perennial with large, deeply lobed, often intricately patterned or color-contrasted leaves — available in deep burgundy, caramel, chartreuse, and multi-tone combinations — and frothy white to pink flower spikes in spring. The sterile hybrid is generally more heat-tolerant and vigorous than tiarella and holds its ornamental foliage better through summer than many heuchera. Excellent as a shade groundcover, border edger, and container plant. 'Sweet Tea', 'Bridget Bloom', 'Stoplight', and 'Solar Eclipse' are outstanding named selections.

common_name: High Fragrance Camellia (Exceptionally Fragrant Blush-Pink Hybrid Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; High Fragrance is a hybrid between C. japonica and C. lutchuensis — the C. lutchuensis parent contributes the fragrance that is absent in standard C. japonica varieties.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade; High Fragrance is one of the most important fragrant camellia cultivars — a hybrid between Camellia japonica and the fragrant species C. lutchuensis that produces the elegant, refined flowers of japonica combined with a genuine sweet, jasmine-like fragrance that is absent from the vast majority of camellia varieties. Most camellia flowers, despite their beauty, are essentially scentless — the discovery that crossing with the fragrant C. lutchuensis could introduce lasting fragrance into hybrid offspring was a significant horticultural development. High Fragrance produces medium-sized, semi-double to peony-form flowers in soft blush-pink to white-with-pink tones in late winter to early spring — the same season as other camellias — with a sweet, clean fragrance detectable several feet from the plant under favorable conditions. The fragrance intensity is variable with temperature: warm, calm mornings amplify the scent; cold or windy conditions reduce it. The plant grows as a medium-sized, evergreen shrub with the characteristic glossy, dark-green camellia foliage. An outstanding choice for planting near entryways, patios, and garden seating areas where the fragrance can be appreciated. In zone 9, High Fragrance is a reliable perennial shrub that blooms most heavily in late January–March.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; sweet peas thrive in cool weather.
directions: Nick or soak the hard seeds overnight to speed germination, then sow directly 1 inch deep in cool, moist, well-drained soil in early spring. This tall vining variety produces intensely fragrant cream flowers edged in lavender, so provide a trellis or netting 5 to 6 feet tall for support. Keep roots cool and evenly moist, and cut blooms frequently to prolong flowering. Plants fade in summer heat, so start them early where summers are hot.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; highveld protea is distinctly more cold-hardy than the Cape fynbos proteas — native to the summer-rainfall grasslands and rocky highveld of the Drakensberg and Mpumalanga at 4000–6000 feet elevation, where frosts are a regular feature. It tolerates harder frosts than P. repens or P. cynaroides (to zone 7b) and summer rainfall — making it more adaptable to non-Mediterranean climates. Like all Proteaceae, it requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; highveld protea is the most cold-tolerant widely available Protea species — the protea of the summer-rainfall highveld of South Africa, growing naturally at high altitude in the rocky grasslands and cliff faces of the Drakensberg, Mpumalanga, and Limpopo where hard frosts occur regularly in winter. This cold tolerance (to zone 7b) expands the Protea genus into gardens significantly colder than the Mediterranean-climate zones where most proteas are restricted. The flower heads are medium-sized, cup-shaped, white to creamy-white to pale pink, somewhat less flamboyant than the showier Cape species but still distinctively beautiful. It grows into a small tree with a characteristic, gnarled, fire-adapted trunk and gray, fire-resistant bark. Unlike the Cape fynbos proteas adapted to winter rainfall, P. caffra comes from a summer-rainfall climate — making it significantly more tolerant of summer humidity and rain, and suitable for a wider range of garden climates including the Gulf Coast and Southeast where summer dryness cannot be guaranteed. An important species for gardeners who want to grow true Protea in zones 7–9 outside the Mediterranean climate zone.

plant_note: Sow directly in fall onto dry, rocky, calcareous soil; winter cold stratification supports reliable spring emergence.
directions: An endemic Texas penstemon restricted to rocky limestone outcrops and cedar glade openings of the Edwards Plateau; direct sow in fall onto very well-drained, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun and allow winter cold to stratify seed naturally. The flowers are arranged in distinctive whorls of three at each stem node — a reliable identifying trait — and emerge in brilliant magenta-red to carmine in April through June, attracting hummingbirds. Thin established seedlings to 12-18 inches and provide no supplemental water after the first season. An underused, striking native penstemon for Texas limestone gardens and dry, sunny borders in zones 6-9.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; Himalayan bergenia is a smaller, more compact species than the commonly grown B. cordifolia and better suited to small gardens or tight spaces. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become congested and flower production decreases.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; Himalayan bergenia is a compact species from the mountainous regions of Afghanistan, Kashmir, and the Himalayas — smaller in leaf and overall stature than the familiar elephant ears bergenia (B. cordifolia) but sharing its essential character of thick, rounded, leathery, evergreen leaves that develop rich burgundy-red tones in winter cold. The early-spring flowers — appearing in March and April from pink-red flower stems that may even push through snow — are held in neat, rounded clusters of pure white to pale-pink, cup-shaped blooms, each sweetly fragrant (unlike B. cordifolia). The combination of compact size, fragrant white flowers, good winter color, and unusual origin from extreme Himalayan altitudes gives this species a distinctly different quality from the coarser B. cordifolia. A better choice for small shade gardens, containers, and woodland-edge situations where B. cordifolia would be too large. The cultivar 'Bach' is a hybrid derived in part from B. stracheyi with outstanding winter foliage color.

plant_note: Sow seeds indoors in late winter at cool temperatures (50–60°F) without heat; Himalayan blue poppy requires cool germination temperatures and is killed by heat above 75°F during germination. In the first year, remove any flower buds that form (preventing bloom) to allow the plant to build root strength — this greatly increases perennial persistence. It performs as a monocarpic perennial in hot climates, living 2–3 years.
directions: Start seeds at cool temperatures indoors and grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in part shade; Himalayan blue poppy produces flowers of a blue so pure and saturated that they are difficult to believe are real — large, clear sky-blue, silky-petaled flowers 3–4 inches across with golden stamens, carried in loose clusters on hairy stems in early summer. Native to the alpine meadows and open forests of Tibet, Bhutan, and Yunnan at 10,000–16,000 feet elevation, it requires cool summer temperatures to thrive and does not perform well in hot, humid climates. In the Pacific Northwest, Scotland, and the cooler parts of the northeastern US, it is a long-lived perennial; in hot-summer climates it tends toward monocarpic behavior — flowering spectacularly and declining. The key to perennial persistence is removing flower buds in year one to allow full root development. Requires consistently moist, cool, acidic conditions with afternoon shade. For many plantspeople, successfully establishing and flowering this plant is considered an achievement; for others in suitable climates it is surprisingly manageable.

plant_note: Surface-sow fresh seeds in late summer or fall, or cold-stratify for 4–6 weeks and sow indoors in late winter; Himalayan blue poppy requires cool, humid conditions (Pacific Northwest, Scotland, high-altitude gardens) and struggles in hot, dry summers. Plants die after setting seed if allowed to flower in their first year — remove flower buds the first season to build strong clumps. Requires acidic, humus-rich, constantly moist but well-drained soil.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade in cool, humid climates; the Himalayan blue poppy hybrid (M. betonicifolia x M. grandis) is one of the most coveted and difficult plants in temperate horticulture — producing the most impossibly, unreasonably beautiful blue flowers imaginable, enormous (4–5 inch), sky-blue to deep cerulean-blue saucer-shaped poppies with a central boss of golden stamens, held on tall, leafy stems in late spring and early summer. The blue is not merely blue — it is a saturated, luminous, impossible clear blue that appears almost artificially colored to first-time viewers. Achieving this in the garden requires cool, humid summers (the plant's native habitat is the cloud forests of the Himalayas at 10,000–14,000 feet), acidic and constantly moist but excellently drained soil, and the patience to prevent flowering for the first year. In suitable cool, moist climates (Seattle, Scotland, high-altitude gardens) it is achievable; in hot, dry, or alkaline conditions it invariably fails. The cultivars 'Slieve Donard' and 'Lingholm' ('Blue Ice') are vigorous and perennial rather than monocarpic.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Himalayan indigo is drought-tolerant and thrives in lean conditions — avoid rich or wet soils that produce lush but floppy growth. In zone 5–6 it may die back to the ground in hard winters but resprouts vigorously from the base in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Himalayan indigo is a large, graceful, arching shrub or subshrub from the mountain forests and open slopes of the Himalayas, producing an extraordinary profusion of rose-pink to magenta-pink, tiny pea flowers in dense, pendulous racemes from June through September — covering the sweeping, arching branches so densely during the flowering peak that the individual branches are almost obscured by bloom. The elegant, pinnate foliage is soft-gray-green throughout the season, creating an attractive textural complement to the vivid flower clusters. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen and improves poor soils. Himalayan indigo is one of the finest long-blooming shrubs for full sun in temperate gardens — combining drought tolerance, extended bloom, attractive foliage, and a graceful weeping habit in a plant that is still relatively little-known outside specialist gardens. Prune hard to the ground or to 6 inches in late winter to maintain compact, vigorous, floriferous growth.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or early spring, just below the soil surface, in deep shade with consistent moisture; seed germination requires cold stratification and is extremely slow. Himalayan mayapple emerges earlier in spring than the American species and the foliage is more ornamental — deeply lobed with attractive purplish-brown mottling.
directions: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade; Himalayan mayapple is a collector's shade perennial prized for its deeply lobed, marbled leaves with intricate purplish brown and green mottling that emerge in spring with dramatic effect. The single white flower with a pink flush sits at the leaf junction and develops into an ovoid red fruit that is edible when fully ripe — the only edible part of the plant. All other parts contain potent podophyllotoxin, the basis of several cancer chemotherapy drugs, and are toxic. In cultivation P. hexandrum is generally grown as an ornamental curiosity rather than as a fruit plant. It forms spreading colonies in ideal conditions, going fully dormant in midsummer. Closely related to American mayapple (P. peltatum) but considerably more ornamental.

plant_note: Plant out in spring once the soil is workable and hard frosts are unlikely. In colder parts of its range (zones 7–8), choose a sheltered, south-facing wall or overhang to protect the woody base from freezing.
directions: Take softwood cuttings in late spring or early summer and root them in a moist, gritty mix in a shaded, humid environment; pot on once roots are established. Plant in a sheltered, partially shaded position in fertile, moisture-retentive but well-draining soil, and mulch the root zone deeply in autumn to protect the woody crown from winter cold in zones 7–8. Cut back top growth after frost kills it and allow the plant to re-sprout from the base in spring. Divide established clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and to propagate additional plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Hinckley's columbine is a Texas endemic of Brewster County in the Big Bend area and grows naturally in rocky limestone canyons with afternoon shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in partial shade in zones 7–9; Hinckley's columbine is a rare Texas endemic of Brewster County in the Big Bend region of the Chihuahuan Desert, one of the most remote and geologically dramatic counties in Texas. It grows naturally in rocky, limestone canyons and slopes with afternoon shade and intermittent moisture — conditions that would challenge most garden columbines. The distinctive yellow flowers have notably shorter spurs than golden columbine and a different floral geometry. It is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant columbines, making it valuable for zone 8–9 gardens with alkaline, rocky soils where other columbines decline in summer. Often reblooms in fall in zone 9 after summer dormancy. A rare and beautiful Texas native that thrives in the dry, rocky, calcareous conditions of the Edwards Plateau and similar Gulf South situations.

common_name: Hino Crimson Azalea (Brilliant Red Small-Leaf Compact Kurume Azalea)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Hino Crimson's bright red flower color is most vivid with morning sun and afternoon shade — full afternoon sun can cause the red color to fade slightly and increases water stress in Gulf South summers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Hino Crimson is a Kurume azalea cultivar producing one of the most vivid red flower displays of any small-leaf azalea — masses of brilliant, intense red single flowers in spring that cover the plant completely at peak bloom, creating a display significantly more vividly red than the pink-to-pink-red tones of most other azaleas. The very small leaves (typical Kurume fine texture) and compact, mounded habit make Hino Crimson one of the most refined and formal-looking of the spring-blooming azaleas — a tight, dense, naturally rounded shrub that requires minimal pruning to maintain its shape. The cold-hardiness of Hino Crimson (to zone 5) exceeds that of Southern Indica and most other azalea groups, making it adaptable to a broader geographic range, including the cooler portions of zone 9 where indica types can be borderline. In Gulf South zone 9, Hino Crimson is a reliable, long-lived evergreen foundation shrub that blooms dependably each March–April. The intense red color makes it particularly striking in mass plantings along walks and driveways where the simultaneous red bloom creates a powerful seasonal display. Planted where early morning sun can backlight the flowers, the vivid red becomes almost incandescent — one of the most spectacular light effects achievable in the spring garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; hinoki cypress prefers moist, well-drained, slightly acidic conditions and does not tolerate drought, waterlogged soil, or alkaline conditions. Cultivated varieties range from dwarf groundcovers to large trees.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; hinoki cypress is a sacred conifer of Japan, used to build Shinto shrines and the most important temples in Kyoto and Nara — the fragrant, pale-blond wood is the most valued timber species in Japan. An enormous species in the wild (reaching 100+ feet in the mountains of Japan), it is the parent of literally hundreds of cultivated varieties ranging from tiny, 2-inch bun-shaped dwarfs to golden, pendulous, or billowing forms of every size and habit. The distinctive flattened frond-like foliage sprays with bright white markings on the undersides are characteristic. Cultivars such as 'Nana Gracilis', 'Filicoides', 'Crippsii', and 'Gracilis' are among the most popular ornamental conifers in the world. The variable spacing and height reflects the wide range of cultivated forms available.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich woodland or edge soil in partial shade to full sun. Hoary Skullcap tolerates a range of light conditions from partial shade to full sun and is one of the more adaptable native skullcaps for garden use.
directions: Hoary Skullcap is a native perennial of upland woods, forest edges, and open thickets of the eastern United States from New York south to Georgia and west to Missouri, producing spikes of beautiful blue-violet tubular flowers on softly white-hairy (hoary) stems from June through August — an exceptionally long bloom period for a native woodland wildflower. The flowers are specialized for long-tongued native bumblebees that are the primary pollinators, fitting into the bottom lip of each bloom and triggering pollen release; the plant is also an important nectar source for several native skippers and small butterflies. Tolerating partial shade more readily than many native prairie wildflowers, Hoary Skullcap is a versatile native plant that performs well at woodland edges, in dappled shade gardens, and in moderately sunny perennial borders. Direct sow seeds in fall in moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants slowly spread by short rhizomes to form modest colonies.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out in cool spring weather for best bloom.
directions: Hoary stock, also called gillyflower, produces tall stems packed with intensely fragrant blooms in soft shades. Start seeds indoors and set young plants out in cool spring weather, as stock performs best in mild temperatures and dislikes heat. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and even moisture for the fullest flower spikes. Harvest stems for long-lasting, sweetly scented bouquets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; seeds require cold stratification to break dormancy and will germinate the following spring.
directions: Direct sow in fall in dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, pressing seed into the surface without covering deeply. Established plants grow erect to arching stems clothed in soft, hoary white hairs and bear open racemes of small rose-pink to lavender pea flowers from July through September. The jointed, bristly seed segments that follow cling readily to clothing and fur, dispersing naturally without any intervention. This native perennial is highly attractive to specialist native bees in the Desmodium bee guild and requires no fertilization once established in lean, dry soil.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring (cold stratify for 4–6 weeks) in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hoary verbena is taprooted and drought-tolerant once established but may need water during the establishment year. It is a prolific self-sower in disturbed, lean soils — useful for naturalizing in wild areas, but may need management in formal settings.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hoary verbena is a native prairie perennial of the central United States producing distinctively dense, woolly-hairy, grayish foliage that gives both the plant and its common names their character — the leaves, stems, and bracts are covered in such dense, short, white hairs that the plant has a noticeably silvery-hoary appearance. From July through September, upright stems carry elongating, spike-like clusters of small violet-purple to deep-purple verbena flowers, each tiny cluster of tubular florets progressing up the spike from base to tip over several weeks, creating a long-lasting and generous bloom display. It is an important nectar plant for many prairie insects including several specialist native bees that rely on Verbena species, skippers, and other butterflies. The woolly hair covering reduces water loss and helps the plant withstand the extreme summer drought conditions of its native range in the Great Plains. Excellent for prairie restorations, dry meadow gardens, and any lean, disturbed-soil site in full sun where the hoary foliage and long-season purple bloom provide attractive texture and color.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; hollow Joe-Pye weed is the tallest of the common Joe-Pye weeds — regularly reaching 6–12 feet in moist, fertile soil — and requires adequate moisture to achieve its impressive stature.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — hollow Joe-Pye weed is the largest native Joe-Pye weed, regularly reaching 5–12 feet in moist, fertile conditions, making it one of the most imposing native perennials in the eastern flora. It is identifiable by its hollow, purple-spotted stems (the 'fistulosum' meaning tubular, and the purple nodes). Large, domed clusters of mauve-pink flowers in midsummer to late summer are massively attractive to migrating monarchs, eastern tiger swallowtails, fritillaries, and dozens of native bee species — few plants concentrate as many pollinators in a single location as a blooming Joe-Pye weed. It grows naturally along stream banks, moist meadows, and wet open woodland edges throughout the eastern US. Named varieties including 'Gateway' (more compact, 5–6 feet) are widely available. Outstanding back-of-border or screening native for moist, sunny to partly shaded gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; holly fern is one of the most drought-tolerant of all ferns and one of the best for Gulf Coast shade gardens — tolerating clay soil, drought, and considerable heat.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — holly fern is the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of the widely grown shade ferns and one of the finest ferns for Gulf Coast gardens. The bold, lustrous, dark green fronds with glossy, sickle-shaped (falcate) pinnae have an unmistakably bold, coarse texture reminiscent of holly leaves — giving the fern its common name. It is essentially evergreen through zone 6–11, maintaining handsome fronds year-round even through light freezes. Unlike most ferns it tolerates dry spells between watering and grows in relatively dry soil conditions once established. Excellent for shade planting under trees where soil competition and drought would stress more delicate ferns. An outstanding and low-maintenance fern for southern shade gardens in zones 6–11.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun in spring or fall; holly olive establishes readily and requires minimal care once established — it is slower-growing than Chinese holly but ultimately more fragrant and shade-tolerant.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun; holly olive (false holly, holly-leaved osmanthus) is a versatile Japanese evergreen shrub that combines two highly desirable landscape qualities that rarely coexist — the bold, spiny, holly-like foliage that deters deer and unwanted entry, and the extraordinarily fragrant, small, white flowers that perfume the autumn garden with a powerful, sweet, apricot-like scent similar to but distinct from the related tea olive (O. fragrans). The spiny, glossy, dark-green leaves closely resemble English holly leaves, creating a formal, polished effect in the landscape; several cultivars offer gold-, white-, or purple-tinted foliage. It tolerates partial shade, dry soil, and urban conditions far better than most broadleaf evergreens. 'Goshiki' (cream, green, and pink variegated), 'Rotundifolius' (small, rounded, spineless leaves), 'Purpureus' (deep-purple new growth), and 'Gulftide' (compact, cold-hardy) are widely grown selections. More deer-resistant than almost any comparable shrub due to the spiny foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring around the last frost date or in late summer for bloom the following year.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep; hollyhocks are biennial or short-lived perennials that flower the second year from seed and self-sow freely to maintain the planting. Rust fungus is the most common disease — look for orange pustules on leaf undersides and remove affected foliage promptly, avoiding overhead watering. Plant against walls or fences and provide loose staking for the tall, top-heavy flowering spikes. Allow some seed to mature and fall to keep the colony self-renewing.

plant_note: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, dry to average soil in full sun; holm oak is a Mediterranean species adapted to hot, dry summers and mild winters — it thrives in the California and Pacific Northwest coastal climates but is marginal in the humid Southeast. Extremely drought tolerant once established.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, dry to average soil in full sun; holm oak is the iconic evergreen oak of the Mediterranean Basin — a massive, dark, brooding, evergreen tree with small, dark green, holly-like leaves (hence both 'holm' from Old English 'holly' and the species epithet ilex meaning 'holm oak'). It forms the characteristic dark green groves and monte bajo of southern Europe and North Africa. In California, holm oak has been planted for over a century and shows excellent adaptation to the Mediterranean climate — drought-tolerant, long-lived, and providing deep, dense shade year-round. The acorns are small and bitter, but the related Holm oak variety (Quercus ilex subsp. ballota) from Portugal and Spain produces sweet, edible acorns eaten raw or roasted — the famous Spanish 'bellota' acorn eaten by Ibérico pigs. An excellent large evergreen tree for hot, dry climates in zones 7–10.

common_name: Homestead Purple Verbena (Classic Groundcover Southern Verbena)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Homestead Purple is an outstanding, extremely heat-tolerant groundcover verbena that spreads quickly and blooms almost continuously through the long Gulf South growing season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Homestead Purple is one of the most celebrated groundcover verbenas ever introduced, discovered growing at an old Georgia homestead and prized for combining outstanding heat and humidity tolerance with vivid, rich purple flower clusters produced almost nonstop from spring through frost. It spreads quickly into a dense, low mat that suppresses weeds and cascades attractively over walls and the edges of raised beds, and unlike many verbena cultivars it shows good resistance to powdery mildew in humid Southern summers. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs only an occasional trim to keep it dense and encourage continued heavy bloom.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in late summer to early fall in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained soil; seedlings overwinter as rosettes and bolt to bloom in spring of the following year. In mild climates seeds can also be sown in early spring for some first-year bloom.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in late summer or early fall in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; seedlings overwinter as flat rosettes before bolting and blooming in spring of the second year with fragrant clusters of four-petaled purple or white flowers that attract early spring pollinators. After flowering, the large flat oval seedpods develop and ripen to translucent silver-white discs that persist on the stems through autumn and are highly prized in dried arrangements under the common name 'silver dollar plant.' Once established, honesty self-seeds prolifically and reappears each year without deliberate replanting, behaving in effect as a naturalized perennial in most gardens. Thin seedlings to 9–12 inches apart and allow some pods to shatter naturally to perpetuate the colony indefinitely.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or in summer for flowers the following spring; behaves as a biennial in most climates.
directions: Sow seeds in spring or early summer; plants develop as a rosette the first year and flower the following spring — a true biennial. Purple or white cross-shaped flowers appear in mid-spring, followed by the flat, papery-silver seed pods that give the plant its common names 'honesty' and 'money plant.' To harvest pods for dried arrangements, cut when the outer husks have dried and carefully peel away both sides to reveal the lustrous translucent membrane. Plants self-sow freely and once established will perpetuate themselves year after year.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; honey garlic naturalizes reliably by self-seeding and bulb offsets in suitable, freely draining conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade to full sun; honey garlic (Sicilian honey garlic, Mediterranean bells) is an aristocratic ornamental related to alliums, producing slender, tall stems in late spring topped with pendulous umbels of elegant, bell-shaped flowers in a subtle, shaded color palette of creamy-white flushed with rose-purple and green stripes — particularly charming and understated compared to the bolder alliums. After bloom the papery seed heads turn upward and dry to a beautiful silvery-beige, providing weeks of ornamental structure through summer. The plant naturalizes steadily by self-seeding in well-drained soils and once established requires no attention. Useful for filling the late-spring gap between tulips and summer perennials in both sunny and partially shaded borders.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in any well-drained soil — honey locust is exceptionally adaptable to alkaline, compacted, salty, wet or dry soils and urban conditions; thornless cultivars ('Inermis', 'Sunburst', 'Skyline') are preferred over the wild thorny species for landscapes.
directions: Honey locust is one of the most broadly adaptable native trees in North America, tolerating alkaline soils, periodic flooding, urban air pollution, road salt, and heat that defeat other trees — widely planted as a tough street and lawn tree in the form of thornless, podless cultivars developed from its natural variety inermis. The feathery, twice-pinnately compound leaves create dappled shade that allows turf and understory plants to grow beneath the canopy more easily than under most large shade trees; the fine-textured leaves also break down quickly in fall without raking. Wild trees produce massive, twisted, dark brown seed pods up to 18 inches long that contain sweet pulp historically eaten by wildlife and indigenous peoples, and formidable branching thorns several inches long; select thornless, seedless cultivars for most landscape uses. Native pollinators, especially short-tongued bees, visit the inconspicuous but very fragrant creamy-white flower clusters heavily in spring, making honey locust an underappreciated urban pollinator plant.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; honeybush grows rapidly and vigorously in warm conditions and can reach 6–8 feet in a single season. In zone 8–9 it dies back to the roots in hard winters but resprouts vigorously the following spring. The leaves have a strong, pungent smell when brushed — sometimes described as peanut-butter — which is distinctive but not universally pleasant.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; honeybush is one of the most dramatically architectural foliage plants available for warm-climate gardens, native to South Africa and producing enormous, pinnate leaves of a gray-blue to blue-green color with serrated leaflets and a distinctive, almost metallic, blue-gray bloom — like the foliage of a tropical acacia crossed with a glaucous eucalyptus. The blue-gray color is among the most striking leaf colors in any plant and provides a spectacular contrast to darker- or brighter-foliaged plants. In late winter to early spring it produces erect spikes of deep-maroon to brick-red tubular flowers that produce copious, sweet, honey-like nectar — giving rise to both the common name and the species name (melianthus = honey flower in Greek). The flowers are primarily pollinated by sunbirds in South Africa and attract hummingbirds in North America. Honeybush is widely grown in coastal California, the Gulf Coast, and mild British gardens as a bold, exotic foliage specimen for large borders, containers, and tropical-style plantings.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or peaty soil in partial shade. Zenobia is a bog and pocosin specialist that requires consistently acidic, wet conditions — it declines in alkaline or dry soils.
directions: Honeycup (or Powdery Zenobia) is a stunning native shrub, native to wet pine savannas, pocosins, bog edges, and seepage slopes of the coastal plain from North Carolina to northern Florida, where it grows with fetterbush, inkberry, and swamp azalea in highly acidic, peaty, wet soils. In June and July it produces dangling clusters of lily-of-the-valley-scented, white, bell-shaped flowers on gracefully arching stems — the flowers are honey-sweet in fragrance and highly attractive to native bees. The distinctive glaucous (powdery blue-green) leaves are semi-evergreen to deciduous depending on the winter, and the shrub slowly spreads by stolons to form loose colonies. Grow in wet, highly acidic soil in partial shade; it is excellent companion to Atlantic white cedar, blueberries, and swamp azaleas in a native bog or rain garden planting. Avoid alkaline or dry conditions, which are fatal.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in part shade; unlike most fuchsias, F. triphylla tolerates more heat and direct sun than hybrid fuchsias. It is damaged below 28°F. The cultivar 'Gartenmeister Bonstedt' (often simply sold as 'Gartenmeister') is the most widely available selection.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; honeysuckle fuchsia is a Caribbean species from Hispaniola that differs from the hybrid fuchsias in producing long, narrow, trumpet-like flowers in intense orange-red to salmon-red — clustered in pendant bunches at the branch tips — rather than the two-toned, skirted, pendant bells of typical hybrid fuchsias. The flowers are pure nectar-source flowers, highly specialized for hummingbird pollination in their native Caribbean habitat and irresistible to hummingbirds in cultivation. The cultivar 'Gartenmeister Bonstedt' has particularly rich orange-coral flowers with attractive bronze-tinted foliage and is far more heat-tolerant than most fuchsias — thriving in warm summers that would collapse conventional fuchsia hybrids. This heat tolerance, combined with hummingbird-attracting tubular flowers in summer and fall, makes it one of the most valuable warm-climate container plants. Often treated as an annual in zones below 9.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zones 8–11 sow in fall for winter and spring bloom. Cerinthe resents root disturbance and performs best when direct sown.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool weather — cerinthe dislikes transplanting and self-sows freely where happy. The glaucous blue-gray foliage is beautifully paired with deep indigo-purple nodding bracts that surround small tubular flowers adored by bumblebees; the whole plant has a striking silver-blue quality that stands out in a planting. Cerinthe matures quickly and begins flowering in about 10 weeks from seed; in mild-winter areas it blooms from fall through spring as a cool-season annual. The plant self-seeds prolifically in loose soil, returning year after year in the same spot. It pairs well with other cool-season pollinator plants such as phacelia, borage, and annual phlox.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall in zones 7+ for overwintering.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in cool soil; germination is rapid in the 55–65°F range and slows dramatically in warm conditions. The blue-green waxy foliage and pendant, tubular flowers in deep violet-purple with showy blue-purple bracts are a magnet for bumblebees. Cerinthe prefers cool weather and will bolt and die in summer heat; in mild climates it self-sows prolifically and may return year after year. Harvest stems when bracts are fully colored for a distinctive and long-lasting cut flower.

plant_note: Propagate by air-layering or semi-hardwood cuttings (not from seed — this sterile hybrid sets no viable seed) or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; Hong Kong orchid tree is frost-sensitive and should be protected from temperatures below 28°F — established specimens in zone 9 may recover from the roots if frozen back.
directions: Propagate by air-layering or cuttings (this sterile hybrid sets no seed) or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Hong Kong orchid tree is a sterile hybrid flowering tree and the floral emblem of Hong Kong — one of the most spectacular flowering trees for zone 9–12, producing enormous, deep-rose-purple to magenta-crimson, orchid-like flowers up to 6 inches across that appear in great abundance from autumn through late spring on the arching branches, creating a brilliant and prolonged display of large, showy, fragrant tropical flowers at the cooler end of the year. The large, uniquely bilobed, rounded, butterfly-wing leaves (characteristic of all Bauhinia species) are attractive year-round. Because it is a sterile triploid hybrid, it does not set seed and has no invasive potential — unlike many other Bauhinia species that self-seed aggressively — making it the preferred choice for ecological responsible planting. It flowers for the longest season of any Bauhinia and is widely considered the most ornamental. Tolerates partial shade acceptably. Excellent as a specimen or small shade tree in the tropical or subtropical garden.

common_name: Honorine Jobert Japanese Anemone (Classic White Fall Anemone)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Japanese anemones spread by underground stolons to form expanding colonies — plant where they have room to naturalize or where their spreading can be managed.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Honorine Jobert is one of the most beloved fall-blooming perennials in the partial-shade garden — a classic single white Japanese anemone that has been in continuous cultivation since 1858 and is considered the benchmark cultivar for its species. The large, single flowers (2.5–3.5 inches across) are pure white with a slight pink flush on the outside of the petals and a prominent central boss of bright-yellow stamens — a clean, elegant, luminous combination that lights up the partial-shade border in September and October when few other plants are in full bloom. The long bloom season (6–8 weeks) and the timing — bridging the gap between the main summer perennial season and frost — make Honorine Jobert uniquely valuable in the shade garden. Sturdy, 3–4 foot stems rise above the dark-green, deeply lobed foliage and branch repeatedly, producing many flowers per stem over the extended season. Japanese anemones spread by underground stolons to form expanding colonies — a spreading habit that is a practical advantage in naturalizing shade garden beds but requires management to prevent encroachment on neighbors. Divide in spring when clumps become crowded (every 4–6 years) to maintain vigor. In zone 9, Japanese anemones thrive in the partial shade of tall pines or on the north side of structures where summer heat is moderated.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum in full sun to partial shade; hooded pitcher plant adapts to more shaded conditions than other Sarracenia and naturally grows in the light shade of scattered pines in moist flatwoods.
directions: Hooded pitcher plant is a compact to medium-sized native Sarracenia of the southeastern coastal plain with a distinctive domed, helmet-like hood that nearly completely covers the pitcher mouth — this unusual lid design protects the trap from rain diluting the digestive fluid inside, as the plant relies on a different trapping mechanism from most pitcher plants. White transparent windows in the upper pitcher wall allow light in and create 'false exits' that confuse trapped insects; bees and flies follow the light toward the windows and become exhausted trying to escape through the translucent walls, eventually falling into the digestive fluid below. Native from North Carolina to Florida's Ocala National Forest, hooded pitcher plant is among the more heat- and humidity-tolerant of all Sarracenia species, making it an excellent choice for Gulf Coast bog gardens in zones 7–9. Yellow flowers in spring are produced on separate stems before the pitchers emerge; the plant grows as a rhizomatous clump that slowly expands year by year in appropriate conditions without requiring special management beyond pure water and acidic medium.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; a western North American native closely related to Solomon's seal, with attractive spreading rhizomes and cheerful spring flowers followed by ornamental berries in fall.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; Hooker's fairy bell grows slowly but spreads naturally by rhizomes to form loose colonies under trees. Disporum hookeri is a western North American native woodland perennial that resembles a smaller Solomon's seal, with arching, unbranched to slightly branched stems 18–36 inches tall bearing oval, parallel-veined leaves and nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers in early spring followed by red to orange ornamental berries in fall that wildlife eat avidly. It is an elegant and under-used alternative to true Solomon's seal for Pacific Northwest and shaded mountain gardens; in the Southeast, it prefers cool, moist, shaded conditions and is best suited to upper zones of the native range. The berries are not for human consumption.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide established clumps in spring in moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Hooker's inula spreads by underground rhizomes and can colonize large areas in moist, fertile soils. Deadhead regularly to extend the bloom season. Divide every 3 years to prevent clumps from becoming sparse in the center.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Hooker's inula is a Himalayan perennial producing an exceptional late-summer and autumn display — large, soft, somewhat hairy, oval leaves and, from August through October, an abundance of golden-yellow daisy flowers with extraordinarily fine, thread-like ray petals so narrow and numerous (often 100 or more per flower head) that they give each bloom a distinctly shaggy, spidery, or mop-headed appearance quite different from the clean, regular rays of ordinary daisies. The overall effect of each flower is of a golden, shaggy star with a cheerful burst of fine petals radiating outward. It is more floriferous and slightly more compact than the giant Inula magnifica (which can reach 8–10 feet). It spreads by rhizomes in moist soils, eventually forming substantial colonies that provide bold late-season color. Outstanding for the naturalistic border or woodland edge in moist, fertile conditions where other late-season daisies would be routine. One of the finest texturally interesting late-summer perennials for its spidery flower form.

plant_note: Plant in early spring into cool, moist, rich woodland soil with deep shade and excellent drainage. Success depends heavily on intact mycorrhizal associations; source only from reputable nurseries that propagate this species ethically.
directions: Hooker's orchid demands the specific conditions of a cool, shaded northern hardwood or mixed forest understory — rich, moist, well-drained loam with a deep leaf-litter layer and established fungal networks in the soil. Prepare a planting pocket by blending existing woodland soil with well-aged leaf compost, and set the roots at their original depth without burying the crown. Keep the site consistently moist but never waterlogged, and refresh the leaf mulch each autumn to sustain the mycorrhizal partners this orchid relies on entirely for nutrients. Do not fertilize, transplant repeatedly, or remove the surrounding tree canopy, as this rare orchid is extremely sensitive to any disruption of its cool, stable woodland microclimate.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; hoop petticoat daffodil naturalizes freely in thin turf and meadow grass where it can grow undisturbed through the spring and summer to ripen foliage and seed. It is particularly effective mass-planted in grass, where it creates spectacular early spring carpets of the distinctive funnel flowers. Established colonies self-seed freely.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; hoop petticoat daffodil is one of the most charmingly eccentric of all daffodil species — the flower form is virtually the opposite of a typical daffodil: instead of a small cup at the center of large, flat petals, it has an enormous, widely flared, deep funnel-trumpet (the 'petticoat') at the center of tiny, almost vestigial, narrow, thread-like outer petals — the whole flower dominated by the expanded trumpet-funnel that gives it the common name of hoop petticoat. In deep golden-yellow (the typical form) or pale cream-white (var. conspicuus, var. citrinus), the little flared-funnel flowers on short stems create a carpet of unusual, distinctive blooms in early to mid spring that draws immediate attention from anyone who knows daffodils as a class — 'What kind of daffodil is THAT?' is the typical first response. Native to the thin, acidic, peaty, rocky grasslands of Spain, Portugal, and northwest Africa, it naturalizes readily in short, thin turf and meadow grass, returning year after year and self-seeding to extend the colony. Excellent for naturalizing in lawns and wild areas in zones 6–9.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring and plant in wet to seasonally flooded soil with partial shade; hop sedge thrives in the dappled light and saturated soils of bottomland woods and stream edges.
directions: Plant in wet to seasonally flooded soil in partial to full shade at the margins of woodland streams, pond edges beneath tree canopy, or shaded rain gardens; hop sedge is a bold native sedge instantly recognized by its spectacular inflated seed heads — large, cylindrical, bright green perigynia packed tightly on upright spikes that closely resemble the dried cones of the hop vine, making it one of the most ornamentally distinctive native sedges in cultivation. It is particularly valuable for shaded wetland restoration projects where many other native sedges struggle, tolerating heavier shade than Carex stricta while still requiring reliably wet soil. The broad, bright-green strap-like leaves reach 18–30 inches and remain attractive through summer; seed heads mature to straw-tan by fall and persist through winter, providing structure and food for birds. Excellent companion to skunk cabbage, sensitive fern, and lizard's tail in shaded bog gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; hop tree is one of the few native small trees genuinely adapted to understory shade and is an important larval host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly — the trifoliate leaves are the primary food source for giant swallowtail caterpillars east of the Rockies.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; hop tree is a native small tree or large shrub found naturally in woodland edges, river bluffs, and dry rocky hillsides from southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, highly unusual among small trees in its genuine shade-tolerance — it grows in understory conditions beneath taller trees where most ornamentals fail. The common names derive from its two most notable features: the distinctive, round, wafer-like seed capsules (samaras) that ripen in fall and were historically used as a substitute for hops in brewing, and the compound leaves with three leaflets that carry a strong, distinctive aroma when crushed. Clusters of small, greenish-white flowers in early summer attract many pollinators but are unshowy — the ornamental interest lies in the attractive trifoliate foliage, yellow fall color, and the striking, papery, disc-like fruits that hang in clusters and rattle in winter wind. Most importantly, it is the primary and preferred larval host plant of the giant swallowtail butterfly (Papilio cresphontes), North America's largest butterfly, and a significant host for the tiger swallowtail as well.

common_name: Hopi Crape Myrtle (Medium Pink Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hopi is a compact National Arboretum selection reaching 7–10 feet — an excellent size for residential foundations and mixed shrub plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hopi is a compact, semi-dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle that reaches 7–10 feet — smaller than the tree-sized Tonto and Sioux but larger than the truly dwarf compact selections — producing medium-pink to clear rose-pink flowers from July through September in dense, upright clusters. The clear, medium-pink flower color is one of the cleanest and most pleasing pinks in the crape myrtle palette — brighter and more saturated than the light lavender-pink of the large-tree Muskogee but softer and more feminine than the hot-pink Sioux. Hopi has perhaps the best mildew resistance rating of any National Arboretum crape myrtle, making it especially valuable in humid Gulf Coast climates where powdery mildew can be a persistent problem with older crape myrtle cultivars. The compact, upright-spreading habit with attractive exfoliating bark and reliable orange to red fall foliage provides year-round interest. Hopi's manageable size makes it one of the most versatile crape myrtles for typical residential lot sizes, appropriate for foundation plantings, screening masses, and specimen use without requiring restriction pruning that destroys the natural form. Remove only dead and crossing branches; never top.

plant_note: Plant divisions on the surface of wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sand in full sun at the margins of shallow bog pools or on constantly wet sphagnum; horned bladderwort is a terrestrial or semi-aquatic species that grows in the thin, wet soil layer above bog substrate.
directions: Horned bladderwort is a native terrestrial carnivorous plant of open, acidic bogs and wet flatwoods across eastern North America, a plant of deceptively simple appearance — thread-like underground stems bear tiny, hollow trap bladders that vacuum-suck microscopic water organisms (protozoa, tiny worms, and small aquatic invertebrates) through a trap door when prey touches sensitive trigger hairs. The common name refers to the distinctive lower lip of the golden-yellow flower that ends in a downcurved spur or 'horn'; the flowers are beautifully snapdragon-like and appear on leafless stalks 2–10 inches above the substrate in summer, looking almost like a miniature yellow orchid blooming from bare mud. Like all bladderworts, horned bladderwort has no true roots or leaves — the entire plant consists of thread-like, carnivorous stems — and it grows through and over the surface of wet, acidic bog substrates, spreading vegetatively through fragmentation. Combine with sundews, grass pink orchid, and pitcher plants in an authentic Gulf Coast bog garden planting where its delicate golden flowers provide an additional dimension of carnivorous plant diversity.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–12 weeks before fall transplant date in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Viola cornuta is a true perennial violet species (unlike annual hybrid pansies) from the Pyrenees Mountains, blooming prolifically in cool weather and surviving mild winters for multi-year performance in zones 5–9.
directions: Start seeds indoors in late summer or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; transplant in fall in zone 9 for winter-spring bloom. Viola cornuta (horned violet or tufted pansy) is the perennial parent species of the 'viola' group of cool-season flowers — a true perennial native to the Pyrenees Mountains of Spain and France that produces masses of small, 1-to-1.5-inch, five-petaled flowers in purple, blue, white, yellow, and bicolor in spring (and fall in mild climates), on compact, spreading, tufted plants that bloom more prolifically and over a longer season than hybrid pansies (V. × wittrockiana). Unlike annual pansies, V. cornuta comes back reliably from the root each year in zones 5–9 and performs as a cool-season perennial groundcover. The 'Sorbet' series of modern violas is derived largely from V. cornuta and represents the best of the viola type: compact, free-flowering, heat-tolerant, and better adapted to mild climates than large-flowered pansies. In zone 9, violas perform from October through April; shear plants after the main spring bloom flush for compact regrowth and often a second blooming period in fall. All Viola flowers are edible.

plant_note: Anchor bunches loosely in pond substrate or simply allow to float freely; hornwort requires no soil — it absorbs all nutrients directly from the water column. It is one of the most effective submerged oxygenating plants for backyard ponds in zones 4–10.
directions: Place bunches in the pond, anchored loosely in gravel or floating freely; hornwort is one of the most widely distributed native aquatic plants in North America — a rootless, submerged plant with whorled, needle-like leaves arranged in dense clusters that give the underwater stems the appearance of a raccoon's tail (hence 'coontail'). As a highly efficient oxygenator, it absorbs carbon dioxide and releases oxygen into the water column, improving water quality and supporting fish and aquatic invertebrate populations. It also absorbs dissolved nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) directly from the water, competing powerfully with algae for resources and contributing to pond clarity. Unlike most aquatic plants, it requires no soil and can be grown anchored in gravel or floating freely. In winter in the north, it sinks to the pond bottom and re-emerges in spring. Widely used in fish tanks and garden ponds for its efficiency and ease of care.

common_name: Horsehead Philodendron (Oak Leaf Philodendron, Laciniatum Philodendron)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Philodendron pedatum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or rough climbing surface — the leaf lobing becomes progressively deeper and more dramatic on climbing stems compared to trailing ones. Grows rapidly under good conditions. Propagate from single-node stem cuttings in water or moist mix. Use a well-aerated potting mix. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Horsehead Philodendron grows fastest and develops its most dramatic leaf lobing in consistent bright indirect light, though it tolerates lower light levels than many collector aroids without obvious deterioration. Philodendron pedatum is a climbing philodendron native to Venezuela, Trinidad, Guyana, and northern Brazil, readily identifiable by its uniquely shaped adult leaves — deeply and irregularly lobed into three to five distinct sections in a pattern that, viewed from certain angles, resembles the silhouette of a horse's head (hence 'Horsehead Philodendron') or the lobed shape of an oak leaf (hence 'Oak Leaf Philodendron'). The leaf shape is significantly more complex than most climbing philodendrons: a broad primary lobe is flanked by smaller lateral lobes, and the arrangement of these lobes relative to the petiole attachment creates a distinctive, almost sculptural leaf form that changes in complexity as the plant matures on a climbing support. The leaves are glossy, medium-green, leathery, and held on long petioles. Philodendron pedatum is one of the most available and most adaptable of the lobed-leaf climbing philodendrons, growing more vigorously and tolerating imperfect conditions better than the demanding collector types. It has been used extensively in hybridization, notably as a parent of the popular 'Philodendron Florida Green' and related Florida hybrid series. All parts are toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; horsetail spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes in wet conditions — contain with deep buried edging (12 inches or more) or plant in a submerged pot in water gardens to prevent escape into garden beds.
directions: Plant divisions in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil or in shallow water in full sun to partial shade — horsetail is a living fossil, a primitive, spore-reproducing plant that has remained essentially unchanged for 350 million years and was a dominant tree-sized plant during the Carboniferous period. Today it grows as a tall, jointed, leafless, evergreen rushlike plant with hollow, ridged, dark green stems banded with dark nodes that have an extraordinary, architectural, minimalist beauty in garden and water garden design. The silica crystals in the stems were historically used as a natural scouring material for pots and pans (hence 'scouring rush'). In water gardens, containers of horsetail at the margins provide a strongly vertical, Japanese-minimalist aesthetic. It must be contained as it spreads vigorously by rhizome in wet conditions and can become difficult to eradicate once established outside of a designated area. Excellent in containers at pond margins.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring as new growth emerges or in fall at least 6 weeks before frost.
directions: Set crowns at soil level in humus-rich, consistently moist soil; avoid planting too deep or crowns may rot. Hostas tolerate deep shade but produce their best foliage color with 2–4 hours of dappled morning light. Divide large clumps every 4–5 years in early spring by slicing through the crown with a sharp spade. Slugs are the primary pest; use iron phosphate bait around vulnerable new growth.

plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covered, in warm soil after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks early. Upright plumes of caramel-brown seed heads rise on sturdy stems and make excellent fresh or dried cut flowers, especially for autumn arrangements. Heat-tolerant and low-maintenance, this amaranth thrives in full sun and average soil. Cut plumes for drying just as they fully color, and expect self-sowing if seed heads are left in place.

common_name: Hot Lips Salvia (Bicolor Jame Salvia, Red-and-White Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hot Lips requires excellent drainage and lean to average soil — in rich, moist soil it becomes floppy and short-lived.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hot Lips is one of the most popular and widely planted ornamental salvias for Gulf Coast gardens — a Salvia × jamensis hybrid (a cross between S. greggii and S. microphylla) producing a striking and unusual bicolor flower pattern: each small tubular flower displays pure white lower lip with red upper lip, creating a vivid two-toned effect that gives the plant its theatrical name. The bicolor pattern is highly variable and temperature-dependent — in cool weather (fall, spring) the flowers display more white; in heat they shift toward more red; some flowers may be entirely red or entirely white. This variability is part of the cultivar's charm — the same plant displays different flower color proportions through the seasons. Hot Lips blooms continuously from spring through fall in zone 9, with the most intense flower production in the cooler months of spring and fall. Hummingbirds are strongly attracted to the red tubular flowers. The compact, mounding habit stays 18–30 inches and is virtually maintenance-free — light trimming after each bloom flush encourages fresh growth and continued flowering. Unlike larger shrubby salvias, Hot Lips is scaled for small gardens and container culture. Extraordinarily drought-tolerant once established; excellent in rock gardens and full-sun mixed borders.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zones 3–7 plant February–May. Hot Lips Turtlehead is best suited for zones 3–8 where cool summers allow the plant to develop fully; in zone 8 with afternoon shade and consistent moisture it can persist as a short-lived perennial. Requires consistently moist to wet soil — it naturally grows along stream banks, pond margins, and in wet woodland clearings. Provide afternoon shade in the southern end of its range. Divide every 3–4 years when clumps become crowded and flower production declines.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil — Hot Lips Turtlehead requires more moisture than almost any other commonly grown perennial, thriving in the wet soil conditions along stream banks and pond edges where other perennials struggle; Hot Lips is a cultivar of Pink Turtlehead (Chelone lyonii), a native Appalachian perennial producing distinctive, hooded, two-lipped flowers in rich deep pink to rose-pink — the tubular, pinched flower shape resembling a turtle's head or a closed mouth with two pursed lips gives the entire genus its common name. The unique flower structure is not merely descriptive — the narrow, hooded tube admits only bumblebees (one of the few insects strong enough to pry open the partially closed flower and reach the nectar), making turtlehead a specialist bumblebee plant of considerable ecological importance. The late summer to fall bloom time (August–September) fills a critical timing gap in the late-season perennial border, providing fresh, vivid color when many summer perennials have peaked and fall asters have not yet begun. Hot Lips' compact selection (shorter stems, less flopping than the straight species) makes it more suitable for garden use than wild-collected plants, with the rich pink color being more consistent and saturated than typical species variation.

common_name: Hot Papaya Coneflower (Double Orange-Red Pompom Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hot Papaya produces fully double, pompom-like flowers in warm orange-red tones, quite different from the flat, single daisy form of the wild species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Hot Papaya is a striking double-flowered coneflower cultivar, producing dense, shaggy, pompom-like blooms that transition from a fiery orange-red center to a softer orange-gold at the petal tips, an ornamental, almost dahlia-like form quite different from the simple single daisy flowers typical of wild coneflowers. Its unusual double form makes it a strong focal point in a mixed border and an excellent cut flower, though like other novelty double coneflower cultivars it can be somewhat shorter-lived than the species and benefits from sharp drainage, particularly through humid summers. It still attracts pollinators, though double flowers generally offer less accessible pollen and nectar than single-flowered types.

common_name: Hotspot Rose Autumn Sage (Compact Deep-Rose Salvia greggii Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the Hotspot series was selected for more compact, tidy habit than older Salvia greggii selections — making it better suited to formal border placement and smaller landscape spaces.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Hotspot Rose is a compact Salvia greggii cultivar selected for a more refined, tidy habit than older autumn sage varieties — producing the same long-season rose-pink flowers and exceptional drought and heat tolerance as standard S. greggii but on a more compact, self-shaping plant of 18–24 inches that requires less frequent hard cutting back to maintain attractive form. The deep rose-pink to cerise-pink flower color is vivid and saturated — more intensely pink than the pastel pink of some selections — and maintains its color through the Gulf South summer heat without fading. In zone 9, Hotspot Rose blooms continuously from spring through hard frost with particularly heavy flushes in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November). The compact habit makes Hotspot Rose outstanding for defined border edging, container use, and mass plantings in small residential landscape beds where the larger older selections would be out of scale. Like all Salvia greggii cultivars, Hotspot Rose is attractive to hummingbirds and native bees throughout the bloom season and highly resistant to deer browsing. The compact habit means less aggressive annual cutback is required compared to large-growing types — remove the previous year's woody stems to 6 inches in late February to promote vigorous spring growth.

common_name: Hoya pubicalyx (Silver Pink Hoya, Purple Rain Hoya, Wax Vine)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or trellis container in bright indirect to moderate shade; Hoya pubicalyx cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 50°F. It grows faster than many hoyas and blooms more readily — often producing its first flower clusters within 1–2 years of a rooted cutting. Allow to become root-bound before repotting — Hoyas bloom more reliably when slightly pot-bound. Never remove old flower stalks (peduncles) as new flower clusters emerge from the same peduncle each season. Propagate readily from stem cuttings in moist mix.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a fast-draining, well-aerated potting mix; Hoya pubicalyx is one of the most vigorous and free-flowering of the commonly available Hoyas, producing its distinctive clusters of star-shaped flowers more readily than many other species. Hoya pubicalyx is a twining, semi-succulent epiphytic vine from the Philippines in the family Apocynaceae, producing long, trailing stems clothed in narrow, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves that are often lightly flecked or mottled with silver-gray spots — giving the species the common name 'Silver Pink Hoya.' The flowers are the defining ornamental feature: each umbellate cluster contains 20–40 individual star-shaped flowers in shades from deep burgundy-red to pink-purple (varying with cultivar and light intensity), each flower centered with a contrasting pink-white corona — the entire cluster has an almost candied, jewel-like appearance. The flowers exude a sweet, spicy, slightly chocolatey fragrance most intense in the evening. Multiple cultivars exist: 'Silver Pink' (dark burgundy-purple flowers), 'Red Buttons' (deep red flowers), 'Chimera' (variegated form). Like all Hoyas, the plant produces a milky latex sap when cut — avoid skin contact. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as growth resumes, or sow seed in fall after scarification for natural cold stratification; Hubricht's bluestar is slow from seed but long-lived and resents frequent disturbance once established — choose a permanent location in average, well-drained soil in full sun and allow clumps to develop undisturbed for maximum ornamental effect and the spectacular golden-yellow fall foliage color.
directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Hubricht's bluestar is widely acclaimed as one of the finest native perennials in cultivation and is arguably the single best native perennial for fall foliage color — from late September through October the densely mounded, needle-like, thread-fine foliage turns a spectacular luminous golden-yellow that rivals the best of the woody shrubs and trees, providing weeks of brilliant autumn color even in warm climates where other fall color plants underperform. In spring, dense clusters of small, pale blue, star-shaped flowers cover the mounded plant before the full foliage effect develops, providing early-season nectar for native bees; the feathery, almost grass-like texture of the foliage (individual leaves can be 3 inches long and barely a millimeter wide) creates an extraordinary fine-textured mass throughout the growing season. Native to a very restricted natural range in the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas and eastern Oklahoma, it was discovered by amateur botanist Leslie Hubricht in 1942 and has since become one of the most celebrated native perennials in American horticulture, earning the Perennial Plant Association's Plant of the Year award in 2011. It is exceptionally tough, drought-tolerant once established, deer-resistant, and essentially pest- and disease-free — a low-maintenance perennial of outstanding three-season ornamental value that deserves far wider use in the native landscape.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in any well-drained, sunny soil; huisache grows rapidly from seed and tolerates alkaline, clay, caliche, and saline soils — avoid planting in consistently wet or flooded soils.
directions: Huisache is the quintessential flowering shrub/small tree of the Gulf Coast prairies and south Texas brush country — in late winter and early spring, before the leaves fully expand, the tree explodes into thousands of brilliant golden-yellow, intensely fragrant pompom flowers that can be smelled from considerable distance and create one of the most spectacular natural wildflower spectacles of the Gulf Coastal Plain. The flowers are harvested commercially in the South of France for perfume production (the variety 'Cassia' provides notes in many classic French perfumes), and the honey produced from huisache nectar is highly prized among Texas beekeepers for its unusual floral sweetness. Trees grow rapidly in full sun in a wide range of soils including alkaline clay and caliche common to south-central Texas, making them well-suited for low-maintenance landscape uses in zone 8–11 where their winter-to-spring bloom fills the gap when little else is flowering. Armed with paired white spines — use caution when planting near walkways and children's play areas.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or in fall in zones 8–10) in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Huisache Daisy is a small, mounding annual wildflower native to South Texas and northeastern Mexico that blooms from spring through summer with abundant, small, bright yellow daisies with distinctive honey-scented flowers — one of the few wildflowers with a pleasant, notable fragrance.
directions: Scatter seeds in fall or after last frost in poor, dry, sandy, or caliche-based soils in full sun; Huisache Daisy is drought-adapted and performs poorly in rich, moist soils; allow to self-sow for naturalized plantings. Huisache Daisy (Amblyolepis setigera) is a small, mounding annual wildflower native to the hot, dry Tamaulipan thornbrush region of South Texas and northeastern Mexico — the same region famous for the huisache tree (Acacia farnesiana), whose Spanish common name refers to the Nahuatl word for the acacia and from which the daisy borrows its regional name. The plant produces masses of small (3/4 to 1 inch), bright, golden-yellow daisies on branching stems from spring through early summer with a delicate, honey-sweet fragrance unusual in annual wildflowers — the fragrance is distinctive and pleasant, detectable from a short distance on warm days when flowers are fully open. The mounding plants (12–24 inches) with grayish-green hairy foliage are adapted to the challenging conditions of the South Texas brush country: high heat, drought, alkaline soils, and caliche-based substrates that few garden plants tolerate. Huisache Daisy is an excellent choice for xeriscaping in South Texas, the Hill Country, and Gulf Coast zones 8b–10 where water-saving is essential and standard garden annuals fail in summer heat. Excellent nectar plant for native bees and small butterflies.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Hummingbird is a compact, spreading selection of native summersweet that stays smaller than the species and tolerates wet soil well.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade; Hummingbird is a naturally dwarf, spreading selection of the native Southeastern shrub summersweet, staying compact and dense where the wild species can grow considerably taller. In mid-to-late summer it produces upright spikes of small, intensely fragrant white flowers that draw bees and butterflies in large numbers, followed by attractive seed capsules that persist into winter. It spreads slowly by suckers to form a low colony over time, tolerates wet, poorly drained sites better than most shrubs, and is one of the more reliable flowering shrubs for shady, damp corners of the garden.

plant_note: Float a handful of stems in a sunny pond, water garden, or tub without soil; the plant has no roots and anchors itself loosely to substrate or floats freely — use rain or pond water rather than chlorinated tap water.
directions: Place a clump of stems in a sunny, still or slow-moving water body without adding soil — bladderwort floats free or sprawls loosely across shallow mud and requires no planting medium whatsoever. The threadlike submersed branches bear hundreds of microscopic bladder traps that snap shut in milliseconds when a water flea or copepod brushes a trigger hair, sucking the prey inside to be digested. From summer through fall, cheerful bright-yellow snapdragon-like flowers on slender stalks rise an inch or two above the water surface, making the plant unexpectedly ornamental for a carnivore. It spreads vigorously in warm, nutrient-poor, acidic water and can be thinned by simply pulling out excess growth.

plant_note: Divide established clumps carefully in early spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Hungarian acanthus has thick, fleshy roots that break easily and each fragment regenerates into a new plant — making it very persistent once established. It is more cold-hardy than A. mollis (to zone 4) and tolerates drier, more alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Hungarian acanthus is a Balkan native and the most cold-hardy commonly available acanthus — surviving to zone 4 where the more popular A. mollis would perish — with the same fundamental character: enormous, deeply pinnately lobed, shining, dark-green leaves of extraordinary architectural quality (the leaf form that inspired the capital decoration of Corinthian architectural columns in ancient Greece) and tall spikes of hooded purple-and-white flowers in summer. The leaves of A. hungaricus are more deeply and finely cut than those of A. mollis — approaching the quality of deeply incised architectural decorations — and are slightly smaller but not less impressive. Like A. mollis, once planted it is essentially permanent due to its thick, regenerating roots, and can be difficult to remove. Outstanding as an architectural accent plant in the border where bold structural foliage through the entire growing season is more important than flower color. Tolerates more alkaline soil and more drought than A. mollis. The winter-persistent seed heads provide structural interest.
