plant_note: Plant acorns in fall immediately after collection or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; Hungarian oak tolerates a wide range of soils including heavy clays and is more drought-tolerant than most of the large European oaks.
directions: Plant acorns in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile to average, loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; Hungarian oak is one of the most impressive and stately deciduous oaks of southeastern Europe — a massive, broadly spreading tree with exceptionally large, deeply pinnately lobed leaves (up to 10 inches long with large, rounded lobes) that are among the largest of any oak. Native to the open parkland forests, mixed deciduous forests, and scrubland of the Balkan Peninsula, Hungary, Italy, and southeastern Europe. Has become an important ornamental tree in western European and British gardens for its bold, large-leaved texture and massive, spreading form. More tolerant of heavy clay soils and moderate drought than most large-leaved European oaks. Relatively fast-growing for an oak. In the UK, the hybrid with sessile oak (Quercus x hispanica 'Lucombeana', the Lucombe oak) is a very ornamental semi-evergreen cultivar derived from Hungarian oak. An outstanding specimen tree for large landscape sites where maximum leaf impact and bold texture are desired.

common_name: Hurricane Lily (Red Spider Lily, Classic Fall-Blooming Surprise Lily for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall (August–October) with the neck of the bulb at or just below soil surface in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; do not divide bulbs more than necessary — clusters that have not been disturbed for several years produce the most spectacular flowering displays.
directions: Plant bulbs in late summer–fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; the hurricane lily (Lycoris radiata) is one of the most distinctive and eagerly anticipated flowers of the Gulf South fall calendar — a surprise bulb that sends up naked, leafless flower stalks seemingly overnight in late September, producing umbels of intensely red, spidery flowers with dramatically long, curving stamens and petals that reflex backward, creating a starbursting, spider-like form unique among commonly grown bulbs. The common name 'hurricane lily' reflects the Gulf Coast tradition of these blooms appearing around hurricane season in September–October; 'surprise lily' comes from the way they emerge from bare soil with no prior visible foliage to signal their presence. The unusual growth cycle — green strap-like leaves emerge after the flowers die in fall, persist through winter and spring as a ground-level groundcover, then go completely dormant in early summer leaving no trace — means the bulbs are frequently disrupted by gardeners unaware of their presence during summer dormancy. Planting bulbs in a location marked with a stake or near a permanent plant prevents accidental disturbance. Undisturbed colonies naturalize and expand into impressive masses of red over many years; the best displays are typically seen in old Southern gardens where colonies have been undisturbed for decades. The bulbs are toxic if ingested. Excellent under deciduous trees in partial shade where the summer dormancy coincides with leafed-out canopy.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; hurricane palm is extremely wind-resistant (hence the name), salt-tolerant, and fast-growing — ideal for exposed coastal sites in frost-free zones. Frost-sensitive — damaged below 30°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–11; hurricane palm is one of the most graceful and wind-tolerant single-trunk palms available for tropical and subtropical landscapes — a solitary-trunked palm from the Mascarene Islands (Mauritius, Réunion, Rodrigues) with a slender, elegant gray trunk and a relatively small crown of arching, pinnate fronds with distinctive reddish or purplish tinges on new growth, especially the new frond midribs and the underside of pinnae. The name 'hurricane palm' refers to its exceptional resistance to strong winds — the fronds survive wind damage that would destroy less flexible palms. Widely planted in South Florida, the Caribbean, Hawaii, and throughout tropical gardens worldwide as a graceful, medium-sized feature palm. Critically endangered in the wild (it is one of the 'palms of Mascarene' threatened by habitat loss and invasive species on its native islands), but commonly cultivated. Grows at a moderate to fast rate in warm, humid tropical conditions.

common_name: Husker Red Penstemon (Bronze-Red Foliage Native Beardtongue)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Husker Red was named Perennial Plant of the Year for its striking burgundy-red foliage, a dramatic contrast to its white summer flower spikes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade. Husker Red was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 1996 for combining the tough, easygoing nature of native foxglove beardtongue with strikingly dark burgundy-red foliage that provides season-long color, topped in early summer by tall spikes of white, tubular, foxglove-like flowers tinged with pink that draw hummingbirds and bees. It is drought-tolerant once established, tolerates a wide range of soil conditions, and self-seeds modestly, though seedlings often revert toward green foliage rather than staying true burgundy-red. Deadhead spent flower spikes to maintain a tidy appearance and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Husker's Red is among the most heat-tolerant penstemon species but may decline after 2–3 years in zone 9's heat and humidity — treat as a short-lived perennial and divide or replant from seed periodically. Plants bloom in late spring (May–June) and go semi-dormant in summer heat; the dramatic red foliage provides interest throughout the growing year even when not in bloom. In zone 9 light afternoon shade improves persistence and extends the bloom season.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil — penstemon demands excellent drainage and fails in consistently moist or heavy soils; Husker's Red is an All-America Selections award-winning cultivar of Foxglove Penstemon (Penstemon digitalis), a native prairie and woodland edge perennial, selected for its dramatic burgundy-red to maroon foliage that provides striking ornamental value throughout the growing season even when the plant is not in flower. The foliage color is the plant's primary landscape feature — the rich, wine-red rosette of leaves in spring and early summer, the upright dark stems, and the red-tinted bracts on the flower stalks create a dramatic plant that reads as deeply colored even before the pale lavender-white, foxglove-like tubular flowers appear. The spring flower display (May–June) adds a secondary ornamental dimension: tall, airy spikes of white to pale lavender tubular flowers on 2–3 foot stems attracting bumblebees and hummingbirds. As a native North American prairie species, Penstemon digitalis is adapted to the range of conditions typical of the Eastern US, including the heat and humidity of the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall, 4–8 weeks before hard frost, for intensely fragrant spring bloom.
directions: Plant bulbs at a depth of 6–8 in (about 3 times the bulb height) in well-drained soil with the pointed end up; wear gloves as the bulb sap can irritate sensitive skin. Hyacinths produce their most spectacular, dense spikes in year 1; subsequent years yield looser, more relaxed flower clusters that many gardeners find charming. Allow foliage to yellow completely before removing it so the bulb can replenish its energy. In warm climates (zones 8+), lift and chill bulbs for 6 weeks before replanting.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms; loves heat.
directions: Direct sow hyacinth bean after the soil has warmed, or start indoors a few weeks early in cool climates. This ornamental vine bears purple stems, spikes of pea-like lavender flowers, and glossy magenta seed pods. Provide a sturdy trellis in full sun and average soil, and it will climb rapidly in summer heat. The pods are ornamental but require thorough cooking, so it is grown chiefly for its striking display.

plant_note: Set out container-grown plants in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. Softwood cuttings taken in late spring root readily in a humid propagation frame and can be potted on and overwintered for planting the following year.
directions: Plant in full to partial sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Hybrid Deutzia tolerates a wide range of soil types as long as drainage is adequate. In late spring the gracefully arching branches are smothered in clusters of white to pale pink flowers that make this compact 3–5 ft shrub one of the most floriferous in the garden. Prune immediately after flowering by cutting one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each year; this keeps the plant vigorous and prevents the centre from becoming congested. Foliage is notably clean and disease-resistant, making it an easy-care alternative to more demanding flowering shrubs.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid flowering quince tolerates a wide range of soils and is very adaptable. Blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates considerable shade. Do not over-fertilize — excess nitrogen produces excessive leafy growth at the expense of flowering.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; hybrid flowering quince (Chaenomeles x superba) is the cross between the Japanese flowering quince (C. japonica, dwarf) and the Chinese flowering quince (C. speciosa, large) — a group of widely grown, compact, early-spring-flowering shrubs producing an outstanding display of flowers in red, pink, orange, salmon, white, or bicolor combinations before or as the leaves emerge. The parent of many of the most commonly sold cultivars including 'Crimson and Gold' (red with gold stamens), 'Jet Trail' (white), 'Nicoline' (scarlet), and 'Pink Lady' (salmon-rose). Blooms very early in the season — one of the first shrubs to flower in late winter/early spring — and the flowers are frost-tolerant. The small, hard, yellow-green fruits (like tiny hard quinces) that follow are edible when cooked and used for jellies, jams, and flavoring in some Asian and European cuisines. Thorny stems create good wildlife cover. One of the most dependable and widely grown early-spring flowering shrubs in temperate gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; hybrid witch-hazel is best sited where it can be seen and appreciated from inside the house during its January–March bloom period. It grows well in part shade and is excellent near the edge of a woodland garden.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in part shade to full sun; hybrid witch-hazel is a cross between Japanese witch-hazel (Hamamelis japonica) and Chinese witch-hazel (H. mollis) and includes the most spectacular named garden cultivars of any witch-hazel — producing their strap-petaled, spidery flowers in January and February directly on leafless branches, providing color at the darkest time of year when almost nothing else is blooming. The flowers are heavily and sweetly fragrant and can be enjoyed cut indoors. Outstanding named cultivars include 'Arnold Promise' (clear yellow, most cold-hardy), 'Jelena' (luminous copper-orange), 'Diane' (deep red to garnet), and 'Ruby Glow' (copper-red). Fall foliage is outstanding in orange, red, and yellow. Hybrid witch-hazels are larger and more vigorous than either parent, eventually forming large multi-stem shrubs or small trees to 15 feet across.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Hyperion performs best with 6+ hours of full sun and regular fertilization through the growing season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Hyperion is one of the oldest and most beloved daylily cultivars still in wide cultivation — introduced in 1924, it remains a benchmark for fragrance, elegance, and reliability nearly a century later. The tall flower scapes reach 3–4 feet and carry large (4.5-inch), clear canary-yellow, slightly ruffled flowers with an outstanding, intensely sweet, lily-like fragrance that perfumes the garden on warm evenings. It blooms in midsummer for approximately 3–4 weeks and does not rebloom reliably, but the elegance and fragrance of its single season have kept it popular for a century. The tall stems are excellent for cutting and make spectacular vase arrangements. Though long surpassed technically by modern hybrids, its combination of fragrance, classic proportions, and reliable performance makes it a worthwhile choice for the perennial garden. Divide every 4–5 years.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hyssop skullcap tolerates drier, sandier conditions than most native skullcaps and is excellent for naturalized, dry, open woodland plantings.
directions: Sow direct in spring in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; hyssop skullcap tolerates poor, sandy soils and drought better than most native skullcaps and is an excellent choice for dry, open woodland naturalistic plantings in the Southeast. Scutellaria integrifolia is a native eastern US perennial skullcap of dry, open woodlands and sandy slopes producing simple, narrow, lance-shaped to oval, entire (unlobed) leaves and attractive blue-violet, tubular, two-lipped flowers with a large lower lip bearing distinctive markings in late spring and early summer. Like all skullcaps, it has a history of use in Native American and herbal medicine, but modern cultivation is primarily for its ornamental value and its role as a native pollinator plant supporting native bumblebees and long-tongued bees in dry, sunny to lightly shaded landscapes.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hyssopleaf thoroughwort is exceptionally drought-tolerant and adapts to poor, dry, sandy soils.
directions: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hyssopleaf thoroughwort is one of the most drought-tolerant native eupatoriums and thrives in sandy, dry, open woodlands and roadsides in the Southeast. Eupatorium hyssopifolium is an eastern US native perennial with linear, narrow (hyssop-like) leaves arranged in whorls on slender stems and flat-topped clusters of small, white thoroughwort flowers in late summer through fall; it differs from the common boneset (E. perfoliatum) primarily in its narrow leaves and greater drought tolerance. Like all eupatoriums, it is an outstanding late-season nectar plant for monarch butterflies, native bees, and wasps; the small, white flowers attract an enormous diversity of pollinator species in late summer. Excellent for dry, sunny native plant borders and sandy meadow restorations in the Southeast.

common_name: Ice Ballet Milkweed (White-Flowered Swamp Milkweed Selection)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (seeds need 30-day cold stratification) or cold-stratify indoors and start in late winter; Ice Ballet is a pure white-flowered selection of native swamp milkweed, valued equally as a monarch host plant and as a striking, non-pink alternative for white or pastel garden schemes.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Ice Ballet is a selection of native swamp milkweed bred for pure white flower clusters, a striking departure from the rose-pink of the wild species, while retaining all of swamp milkweed's value as an essential monarch butterfly host plant and its unusual tolerance of consistently wet soil, where common milkweed and butterfly weed both struggle. The clean white flowers, fragrant and produced over a long season from early to late summer, work especially well in white or pastel garden schemes and moon gardens, and they draw monarchs, swallowtails, and bumblebees just as effectively as the pink-flowered species. Like other swamp milkweed selections, it stays in well-behaved clumps rather than spreading aggressively by rhizome, making it easy to place in a mixed border, rain garden, or pond margin. Leave seedpods standing through fall and winter for wildlife interest and natural reseeding, or deadhead spent flowers to limit self-sowing. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring or fall; in zone 9 plant September–March. Ice Dance establishes quickly and begins spreading slowly by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing ground cover. It performs best in consistent shade — full sun bleaches the foliage and causes summer decline in zones 8–9. Keep consistently moist during establishment, then water moderate amounts; once established it tolerates periods of dryness under shade trees better than most sedges. Divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor and prevent the center from dying out.
directions: Plant in shade to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Ice Dance Japanese Sedge strongly prefers consistent shade and declines or bleaches in full sun, especially in the South; Ice Dance is a variegated cultivar of Japanese sedge (Carex morrowii) producing arching, strap-like leaves with a bold white margin on dark green centers — one of the most striking foliage combinations available in shade-tolerant ground covers. The clean white-and-green variegation creates a luminous, refined effect under trees and in shaded borders, brightening areas where most plants produce only undifferentiated green foliage. Unlike many variegated plants where the color pattern is subtle, Ice Dance's contrast between bright white margins and deep green centers is bold and distinctive enough to read clearly even in low-light conditions — making it effective as a design element even in deep shade situations. The evergreen to semi-evergreen habit in zone 9 provides year-round foliage interest, making Ice Dance one of the most practically valuable shade ground covers available for Gulf South landscapes. The slowly spreading rhizomes form a dense, low-maintenance colony that suppresses weeds effectively under established trees — one of the most challenging landscape conditions to manage successfully.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall (October–November in zone 9); fall planting is essential for daffodils — they require a period of cool soil temperatures during winter for proper flower development. In zone 9 daffodils do not reliably perennialize due to insufficient winter chilling — treat as annual spring bulbs or purchase pre-chilled bulbs. Ice Follies is widely regarded as one of the most reliable and widely grown daffodil cultivars globally — its adaptability to a wide range of conditions including some heat-tolerance making it more successful in the Gulf South than most large-cupped daffodils. In zone 9 the pale cream to white flowers with the pale yellow cup that fades to cream as the flower ages appear January–February, providing one of the earliest spring flower displays. Allow foliage to die back naturally; do not braid or remove leaves before they yellow.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade — daffodils under deciduous trees receive adequate sun while the trees are leafless during their growing and blooming season — in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil with consistent moisture during the fall and winter growing season; Ice Follies is one of the most widely planted large-cupped daffodils in the world — a Division 2 large-cupped daffodil producing large (4-inch), clean, creamy-white flowers with a broad, flattened, shallow cup in pale primrose-yellow that fades to cream-white as the flower matures, creating a clean, all-white or cream-and-white effect at full maturity. The large flower size, vigorous growth, adaptability to a wide range of climates (zones 3–9), and reliability of bloom have made Ice Follies the standard by which large-cupped white daffodils are evaluated — it remains one of the best-selling and most widely planted named daffodil cultivars in commercial production after more than 60 years in the trade. The naturalizing tendency of Ice Follies — producing multiplying clumps that increase in flower count each year in appropriate climates — combined with the complete deer resistance of Narcissus bulbs and foliage make daffodils one of the most practical long-term spring bulb investments for zone 9 gardeners in cooler microclimates.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed into sharply drained soil.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seeds on moist, gritty mix without covering, as they need light to germinate; avoid overwatering at all stages. Plant in the hottest, driest, sunniest spot in the garden — sandy, rocky, or gravelly soil is ideal, and root rot is the main cause of failure in clay or poorly drained sites. The magenta to purple daisy-like flowers cover the succulent mats nearly all summer and reopen only in bright sunlight. Hardy ice plant spreads steadily to make a weed-suppressing groundcover on slopes and rock gardens.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost once the soil has warmed; lift and store over winter in cold zones.
directions: Ice Tea is a smaller coral-salmon dahlia that shifts through terracotta and vivid coral tones across the season for a chameleon-like display. The sturdy stems often stand without staking, and it is a reliable cut flower and good tuber producer. Plant tubers eye-up in full sun and well-drained soil after frost, and water once shoots appear. Deadhead regularly for continuous bloom, and in cold climates dig and store the tubers dry over winter.

common_name: Iceberg Rose (Schneewittchen Rose, Fée des Neiges)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring in slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), well-drained, fertile, amended soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours); Iceberg is among the most widely planted floribunda roses in the world and performs exceptionally well in warm climates including the Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile, amended soil in full sun; Iceberg is one of the most celebrated and widely grown roses of the 20th century — a floribunda introduced in Germany in 1958 that has been continuously popular for over 60 years for its consistent performance, clean appearance, and prolific production of pure white, lightly fragrant flowers in large clusters throughout the growing season. The flowers are held above glossy, light-green foliage in a clean, attractive arrangement, and the plant shows better disease resistance than many classic floribundas. Iceberg performs excellently in warm climates and is one of the best white roses for zone 8–9. It blooms in flushes through the season, is effectively self-cleaning, and recovers well from pruning. The climbing form ('Climbing Iceberg') is a sport that can reach 12–15 feet on a fence or arbor and is one of the best white climbing roses. Prune bushy plants to 12–18 inches in late winter; cut climbing forms lightly to shape immediately after the main spring bloom.

plant_note: In zones 7–10 sow in fall 4–6 weeks before first frost for winter and spring bloom; in colder zones direct sow in very early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Surface-sow or barely cover seeds on well-prepared, fine-textured soil; seeds need light and cool temperatures (50–60°F) to germinate — warm soil prevents germination. Plants grow as basal rosettes through winter in mild climates before sending up slender stems topped with large, tissue-paper flowers in spring. Iceland poppies are cool-season plants that stop flowering when summer heat arrives; in cold climates treat them as an early-spring annual with fall-sown or indoor-started transplants set out very early. Harvest cut flowers when buds are just beginning to crack open color and sear stem ends in boiling water to maximize vase life.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; Ifafa lily is one of the most shade-tolerant Cyrtanthus species, growing naturally in the forest margins and coastal bush of KwaZulu-Natal near the Ifafa River. It blooms in summer, producing nodding, tubular, white to cream flowers with a light, sweet fragrance. All parts are toxic if ingested. More compact and suitable for containers than the larger Cyrtanthus elatus.
directions: Plant bulbs in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; Ifafa lily is a small, charming, shade-loving South African Cyrtanthus native to the forest margins and coastal bush of the Ifafa River area in KwaZulu-Natal — one of the most shade-tolerant members of a genus that is generally sun-preferring. In summer it produces from each small, narrow-bulbed plant a neat umbel of 6–10 nodding, slender, tubular, pure-white to creamy-white flowers on a thin stem — the individual tubes slightly curved and pendant, slightly fragrant, clustering in a small, graceful, draping umbel. The form is more delicate and smaller than the large, bold C. elatus (Scarborough Lily), and the nodding, white, tubular flowers create a quiet, refined charm suited to woodland and shaded container gardens. The narrow, strap-shaped, bright-green leaves are attractive year-round in mild climates. For zone 9 shade gardens where a small, neat, summer-flowering white lily with genuine shade tolerance is needed, it provides something few bulbs can offer — a compact, shade-happy summer white. Outstanding as a container plant for a shaded terrace or woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant tubers or divisions in spring after the last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Illustris produces its most vivid dark coloration in bright partial shade — deep shade reduces the intensity of the dark patterning while full sun may stress plants in extreme Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Illustris (also called Imperial Taro) is a patterned dark elephant ear producing large, heart-shaped leaves in a distinctive two-tone pattern of dark blackish-purple or dark green-black leaf tissue veined and sectioned with contrasting lighter green veins — creating an intricate, stained-glass effect on each leaf. The veining pattern varies from leaf to leaf but consistently creates an effect of dark panels separated by lighter green margins along each major vein, giving the leaf a sectioned, almost geometric appearance when viewed from above or in backlight. This patterned leaf effect is more complex and visually interesting than the uniform dark color of 'Black Magic' — Illustris provides textural detail and pattern rather than uniform dark mass. Like all Colocasia esculenta cultivars, Illustris thrives in the Gulf South's warm, humid summer conditions — growing most vigorously in July and August and tolerating the heat and humidity that would stress many other large-foliage plants. The plant spreads by offsets to form expanding clumps over time — a self-maintaining quality in zone 9 gardens where the tubers persist year-round. The large dark leaves and intricate veining create an outstanding tropical accent that pairs beautifully with bright flowers and light-colored architectural features.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the top of the neck at or just above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Corsican pancratium is a spring-blooming species (not summer like P. maritimum) with glaucous, gray-green, strap-shaped leaves that are often winter-present. It is more cold-tolerant than P. maritimum and flowers in late spring (May–June). Distinguished from P. maritimum by its earlier bloom time, glaucous leaves, and mountain origins in Corsica, Sardinia, and the Adriatic coast.
directions: Plant bulbs in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Illyrian sea daffodil is a Mediterranean narcissus relative from the rocky limestone mountains, coastal cliffs, and dry hillsides of Corsica, Sardinia, and the eastern Adriatic coast — flowering in late spring (May–June) rather than late summer like the more familiar P. maritimum, and forming attractive clumps of glaucous, gray-blue-green, strap-shaped leaves that persist through winter providing cool-season interest. The flowers are large, white, fragrant, and distinctly narcissus-like in form but with the characteristic pancratium 'daffodil corona' structure — a prominent, fringed or scalloped white cup at the center surrounded by six long, spreading, pure-white perianth segments — carried in umbels of 8–15 flowers per scape in late spring. The fragrance is powerful and sweet, filling the spring garden air. Like all pancratiums, it is a Mediterranean Summer-dry bulb requiring the well-drained, lean, dry conditions of Mediterranean rocky landscapes and withholding of water in summer dormancy. More cold-tolerant than P. maritimum, it suits zones 7–10 garden climates well. An excellent but underused spring-flowering white bulb for dry, sunny Mediterranean-style borders.

common_name: Immortality Bearded Iris (Fragrant Reblooming White Iris)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Immortality is one of the most dependable reblooming bearded iris cultivars, often flowering again in late summer and fall in addition to its main spring bloom.
directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely, since covered rhizomes are prone to rot and iris borer damage. Immortality is widely regarded as one of the most reliable rebloomers among bearded iris, producing crisp white, ruffled, lightly fragrant flowers in the main spring flush and then again in late summer or fall in climates with a long enough growing season, sometimes flowering a third time in mild winters. Divide overcrowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center rhizomes and replanting vigorous outer fans at the soil surface. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; needs a long, warm season.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, transplanting once the weather is warm. This dwarf variety features dramatic bronze-red foliage and scarlet seed heads that give a bold tropical effect. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and attracts hummingbirds. CAUTION: all plant parts, especially the seeds, are highly poisonous if ingested, so keep away from children and pets.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed and nights are warm.
directions: Sow tiny seed on the surface of moist starting mix without covering — light is required for germination. Impatiens are one of the most reliable shade-tolerant annuals and will self-clean most spent flowers. Pinch plants back once after transplanting to encourage compact, bushy growth. Water consistently; wilting in heat is common and plants recover overnight, but chronic drought reduces flowering.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost date; prefers cool conditions for best blooms.
directions: Direct sow shallowly in well-drained soil around the last frost date, as sweet sultan resents transplanting. Airy, softly domed 2 to 3 inch fragrant blooms sway on long, graceful stems and draw bees to the garden. Give plants full sun and average, well-drained soil, and stake in windy sites. Cut flowers just as they open for long-lasting, romantic bouquets, and deadhead to extend the display.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Incrediball requires partial shade in zone 9 — full afternoon sun causes significant wilting and bleaching of the enormous flower heads.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Incrediball is the improved Annabelle — a next-generation smooth hydrangea cultivar bred with significantly stronger, stiffer stems than the classic Annabelle that was notorious for stem flopping under the weight of the enormous flower heads in rain. The problem with Annabelle was that the giant 10–12 inch white flower heads would weigh down and collapse the flexible stems in wet weather, leaving the entire plant prostrate on the ground. Incrediball solves this with substantially stronger stems that hold the enormous flower heads upright even in heavy rain and wet conditions. The flower heads are similarly giant — up to 12 inches in diameter — in the same brilliant white as Annabelle, and the plant has the same new-wood blooming habit (can be cut back hard in late winter and still flowers prolifically the same season). In every practical characteristic, Incrediball is an upgrade over Annabelle: same giant white flowers, same performance in shade, same easy care, but with stems strong enough to support the flowers in all conditions. Like Annabelle, Incrediball is one of the most cold-hardy hydrangeas (to zone 3) and one of the most reliable bloomers across a wide range of conditions in zone 9 with afternoon shade.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost; can also be fall sown in mild climates.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seeds, pressing them into the soil since light aids germination, after the last frost. Tall, bushy plants produce an abundance of swirled bicolor blooms that draw butterflies and bees to a pollinator or cutting garden. Coreopsis is quick, easy, and drought-tolerant, thriving in full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Deadhead regularly to keep blooms coming through the season, and mass plantings for the best show.

plant_note: Plant container stock after last frost danger in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Indian Coral Tree is a fast-growing deciduous tropical tree native to coastal forests and tidal zones of South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Western Pacific, producing spectacular clusters of brilliant red-orange pea-family flowers on bare branches in winter and early spring before the boldly variegated trifoliate leaves emerge.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil; Erythrina variegata is remarkably drought tolerant once established — deep, infrequent watering promotes deep root development, and established trees require little supplemental irrigation in subtropical conditions. Erythrina variegata (Indian Coral Tree, Tiger's Claw, or Variegated Coral Tree) is a large, fast-growing deciduous tree native to tropical coastal forests, mangrove edges, and tidal shorelines from the Indian subcontinent through Southeast Asia to the western Pacific islands, where its brilliant scarlet-to-orange, narrowly cylindrical pea-family flowers appear in dense terminal racemes on bare, thorny branches in the dry season before leaf-out — creating one of the most dramatic floral displays of any large tropical tree. The species epithet 'variegata' references a widely grown ornamental cultivar with bold yellow leaf variegation. The soft, lightweight, easily carved wood has been used across South and Southeast Asia for traditional canoe outriggers, floats, and knife handles, and the tree is deeply woven into Balinese Hindu ritual culture where it appears in temple gardens and ceremonial use. In Southeast Asian countries it is widely planted as a street tree and temple tree, blooming spectacularly in the dry season. A nitrogen-fixer in the legume family, it enriches soils around it. Excellent large specimen tree for tropical and warm subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 1–2 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; Indian crocus flowers in early spring before or as the leaves emerge — the flower display occurs when the rhizomes are planted and warming soil triggers dormancy-break, often producing blooms before any foliage is visible, which is one of the most surprising aspects of this unusual ginger.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian crocus (tropical crocus, resurrection lily) is an Indian and Southeast Asian tropical ginger with one of the most remarkable blooming sequences of any ornamental plant — in early spring (or at the start of the warm season), before or simultaneously with leaf emergence, the plant produces large, showy, pure-white flowers with a prominent, deep-lavender to purple lip that look strikingly like large white crocuses, emerging directly from bare soil above the dormant rhizome before any leaves appear. After the brief, beautiful spring flower display, the broad, attractively patterned leaves emerge — dark-green with silver-green and darker-green feathered markings along the veins — and persist as an attractive foliage groundcover through the summer growing season. It then goes completely dormant again in autumn. The early-spring, leafless flowering sequence makes it appear to bloom from bare earth, creating a startling and beautiful garden effect. The rhizomes and leaves are used medicinally in Ayurvedic medicine. Excellent in shaded borders where the spring flower surprise is particularly appreciated.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions with care in fall in moist, humus-rich, cool, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; Indian cucumber root is notoriously difficult to establish from divisions and is very slow-growing, but it is a uniquely beautiful native wildflower worth the patience and should only be purchased from specialist nurseries.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions with care in fall in moist, humus-rich, cool, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; Indian cucumber root is notoriously difficult to establish from divisions and is very slow-growing, but it is a uniquely beautiful native wildflower worth the patience and should only be purchased from specialist nurseries. Medeola virginiana is a slender, elegant eastern North American native with two whorls of leaves arranged like tiers on a single stem — a lower whorl of 5–9 leaves midway up the stem and an upper whorl of 3 leaves at the summit — producing pendant, small, greenish-yellow, lily-like flowers from the upper whorl in early summer followed by striking clusters of deep purple-black berries on bright red pedicels in fall that are the plant's most ornamental feature. The rhizome tastes like cucumber and was used as food by Native Americans (giving the plant its common name), though digging it kills the plant; it is best appreciated as a living wildflower. It is a colony-forming species that spreads very slowly in undisturbed woodland.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring, lightly covering seed; Indian grass can also be planted from plugs in spring or fall. Weed competition is the primary threat in the establishment year.
directions: Sow seed in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Indian grass is a tall warm-season native grass that anchors native meadows and prairie gardens across North America. It is one of the dominant grasses of the tallgrass prairie, growing alongside big bluestem and switchgrass. The distinctive golden-orange seed heads on arching stems glow in late summer and fall light, and the foliage turns a brilliant copper-orange in autumn before drying to a warm buff that persists through winter. As with all warm-season grasses, growth is slow in spring and accelerates after summer heat arrives. Cut to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth begins. Excellent for birds, which feed heavily on the seeds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall; Indian Hawthorn tolerates transplanting at any time of year in zone 9 but establishes best in spring or fall when root growth is active. Space 3–4 feet apart for a hedge or mass planting; 5–6 feet apart as a specimen. Avoid over-fertilizing — excessive nitrogen reduces flowering and increases disease susceptibility.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Indian Hawthorn (Raphiolepis indica) is arguably the most widely planted evergreen foundation shrub in Gulf Coast landscapes, carpeting suburban front yards from Houston to Jacksonville with its compact mounding form and clusters of fragrant pink or white apple-blossom flowers in February–April. The glossy, dark-evergreen leaves are leathery and handsome year-round; after bloom, small blue-black berries develop that attract mockingbirds and cedar waxwings. Dozens of named varieties exist in commerce ranging from 6-inch ground covers to 6-foot tall hedge plants: 'Olivia' (low-mounding, large white flowers), 'Eleanor Tabor' (pink flowers, dwarf), 'Clara' (white flowers, compact), 'Majestic Beauty' (upright, to 6 feet), and 'Indian Princess' (pink, very dwarf). Indian Hawthorn is exceptionally drought, heat, and salt spray tolerant — making it a top choice for coastal Gulf South gardens, highway medians, and HOA foundation beds that receive minimal irrigation or care. Entomosporium leaf spot is the primary disease in humid conditions; plant in locations with good air circulation and avoid wetting foliage with irrigation. Prune immediately after spring bloom to maintain shape without sacrificing the following year's flower buds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Indian hawthorn is one of the most reliable and widely planted evergreen shrubs in the Gulf South and is extraordinarily tolerant of coastal conditions, salt spray, and poor sandy soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian hawthorn tolerates part shade but blooms more heavily and stays more compact with at least 6 hours of direct sun. Rhaphiolepis indica is a rugged, compact, rounded evergreen shrub native to southern China that has become one of the most widely planted landscape shrubs in the Deep South, Gulf Coast, and California for good reason — it combines attractive dark-green, leathery, serrated leaves with clusters of fragrant, 5-petaled, white to deep-pink flowers in spring (and often again in fall), followed by small, blue-black berries that attract birds, all on a compact, tidy plant that requires minimal maintenance. It is outstanding for coastal landscapes — tolerating salt spray, poor sandy soils, and coastal wind exposure that defeats most shrubs. The cultivar 'Eleanor Taber' has deep-pink flowers; 'Ballerina' is compact with rosy-pink flowers; 'Spring Rapture' has rose-red flowers. Indian hawthorn is susceptible to Entomosporium leaf spot (especially in humid climates) — give plants good air circulation and avoid overhead irrigation to minimize this problem. Prune immediately after spring bloom only to shape.

common_name: Indian Laurel (Chinese Banyan, Laurel Fig, Cuban Laurel)
plant_note: Plant in late spring in a permanent location with adequate space — Indian Laurel develops an enormous spreading canopy and aggressive surface root system; space at least 20–30 feet from sidewalks, driveways, foundations, and utilities. More cold-hardy than Ficus benjamina; established trees can tolerate brief temperatures to 28°F. 'Green Island' is a popular compact cultivar (6–8 feet) with no invasive root problems, suitable for foundation planting.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Indian Laurel is broadly adaptable to soil types but the aggressive surface roots require careful placement away from pavement and structures. Ficus microcarpa (Indian Laurel, Chinese Banyan, or Cuban Laurel) is the Ficus species most commonly used as a street tree in South Florida, Gulf Coast cities, and subtropical regions worldwide — lining downtown boulevards in Miami, Houston, New Orleans, and countless Gulf Coast municipalities with its massive, dense, dark-green canopy. In tropical climates, mature trees develop spectacular aerial roots that cascade from branches and eventually thicken into secondary trunks, creating the multi-trunked banyan tree form. A 150-year-old specimen can cover an acre of ground. The 'Green Island' cultivar (Ficus microcarpa 'Green Island') is a compact, slow-growing selection with small, rounded, thick leaves and a controlled habit (6–8 feet) that makes an outstanding shade-tolerant foundation or container plant without the invasive root system of the straight species. Ficus microcarpa is the primary host plant of the invasive fig gall wasp (Josephiella) and laurel fig thrips in some regions — consult local extension services before large-scale planting in natural areas.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in spring into prepared soil or deep containers, as Polyalthia longifolia does not transplant well once established and is best started in situ or in deep root-trainer pots. Site in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and adequate overhead clearance for the tree's eventual 30-60 foot height.
directions: Sow fresh seed immediately after harvest, as viability declines rapidly; plant one to two seeds per deep root-trainer pot or directly in the ground at a depth of 0.5-1 inch, covering lightly with moist soil. Germination typically occurs within 2-4 weeks in warm, humid conditions above 72°F, and seedlings should be watered consistently but not waterlogged during the first growing season. The Indian mast tree is prized for its dramatically columnar, weeping habit and its tolerance of heat, drought, and urban pollution once established, making it an outstanding choice for avenue planting, windbreaks, or as a vertical accent in tropical landscapes. Feed young trees monthly with a balanced fertilizer through the first two years to encourage rapid development of the characteristic tall, narrow silhouette.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface-sow as seeds need light to germinate.
directions: Surface-sow the fine seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, as light is needed for germination, then transplant after frost. This tall, statuesque plant bears large leaves and drooping clusters of long, tubular white flowers that turn very fragrant in the evening. It shines in a white or moon garden alongside delphiniums or other tall companions. Give it rich, moist soil and part shade in hot climates, and enjoy the perfume from late afternoon into night.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Indian pink is slow to establish but long-lived and low-maintenance once settled. It resents root disturbance — plant at its final location and leave undisturbed.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to light shade — Indian pink is one of the most spectacular hummingbird plants in the eastern native flora, producing clusters of brilliant red tubular flowers with abruptly flared, yellow-green tips in late spring to early summer, providing perfectly shaped perches and nectar reservoirs for ruby-throated hummingbirds. The intensely two-toned coloration — deep red tube, bright yellow mouth — makes it one of the most visually striking wildflowers in the woodland garden. It grows naturally in the moist, humus-rich soils of deciduous forest understories and shaded ravines from Maryland to Kansas and south to Florida. The upright, multi-stemmed clumps produce shiny, dark green, opposite leaves and bloom reliably in dappled shade. Slow to establish but extremely long-lived; pairs beautifully with wild blue phlox, wild columbine, and maidenhair fern in the shade garden.

subcategory: South Asian timber and shade tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile to average soil in zone 8–12; Indian Rosewood (Sheesham) is a large, deciduous to semi-evergreen South Asian legume tree and one of the premier timber trees of the Indian subcontinent — fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing, and drought-tolerant — bearing small, pale-pink, fragrant pea-family flowers and widely planted across South Asia and the Middle East as a street tree and windbreak.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile to average soil; Dalbergia sissoo is drought tolerant once established, fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root symbiosis, and can improve soil fertility on degraded or depleted sites — water regularly only in the first year of establishment. Dalbergia sissoo (Indian Rosewood, Sheesham, or Sissoo) is a large, fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing deciduous legume tree native to the Indo-Gangetic Plain foothills, riverine forests, and lower Himalayan slopes of India, Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan, where it is one of the most important and commercially valuable timber trees of South Asia. The dense, interlocked, dark-brown to reddish-brown heartwood is among the finest furniture, carving, flooring, and musical instrument timbers of the region, with extraordinary durability and beautiful figuring. A nitrogen-fixer in the legume family (Fabaceae), Dalbergia sissoo enriches impoverished soils through atmospheric nitrogen fixation and organic matter return. Small, fragrant, pale-pink to whitish pea-family flowers attract pollinators. Trees are widely planted across India, Pakistan, and the Middle East as street trees, windbreaks, and shade trees for their fast growth, nitrogen-fixing soil improvement, drought tolerance, and ornamental foliage with rounded, tri-foliate, bright-green leaflets. It has naturalized in parts of Florida and the Caribbean and can become invasive — plant with awareness of local invasive status.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; blooms first year from an early start.
directions: Sow seeds barely covered in spring or late summer; this variety is known to bloom in its first season from an early start. Tall spires of single and semi-double pink, rose, and white flowers evoke a classic 1800s English cottage garden. Provide deep, rich soil and ample moisture for best performance, though established plants tolerate some drought. Stake tall stems in windy sites and allow plants to self-sow to maintain the planting year to year.

plant_note: Start indoors, surface-sowing since light aids germination, or fall sow.
directions: Surface-sow the seed since light aids germination, starting indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost or fall sowing outdoors. Large single and semi-double golden flowers with dark centers stand tall in heat and drought without staking. They are excellent, long-lasting cut flowers and lure butterflies while providing seeds for birds in winter. Grow in full sun and average, well-drained soil, and deadhead to prolong the extended bloom season.

common_name: Indian Summer Rudbeckia (AAS 1995 Gigantic-Flowered Black-Eyed Susan Annual)
plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks earlier; Indian Summer's massive flowers need the full growing season to develop. In zone 9, direct sow January–March for spring and summer blooms. Indian Summer produces flowers over an extended season (June through frost in most zones) and the large seed heads left in place provide significant bird food in fall and winter while also self-seeding for subsequent seasons.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (needs light) 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 18–24 inches for full plant development. Indian Summer is a 1995 All-America Selections-winning Rudbeckia hirta variety notable for producing what are arguably the largest flowers of any annual rudbeckia: individual blooms reach 6–9 inches in diameter — roughly the size of a dinner plate — on strong, upright stems 24–36 inches long suitable for cutting. The semi-double to fully double flowers are golden yellow with a large, prominent dark brown central cone that gives the classic black-eyed susan character at an outsized scale. The gigantic flower size is the defining trait and the primary reason for its AAS recognition — at 6–9 inches, Indian Summer flowers are 2–3 times the diameter of standard rudbeckia flowers and have a visual impact that stops gardeners in their tracks. Like all R. hirta selections, Indian Summer is extremely heat-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and adapted to poor, dry soils — the native habitat conditions of the prairie and meadow ecosystems from which the species originates. Plants bloom heavily from early summer through hard frost, and the large seed heads left to dry attract finches and sparrows.

plant_note: Direct sow on prepared, weed-free soil in spring; seed can be surface-sown or barely covered at 1/8 inch depth. Fall dormant seeding (after October) is also effective — natural stratification over winter breaks dormancy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to dry soil in full sun; indiangrass is one of the four dominant tall-grass prairie grasses, companion to big bluestem, switchgrass, and little bluestem. Its narrow blue-green foliage and elegant golden-yellow seed plumes waving in the fall breeze make it one of the most ornamentally beautiful native grasses. Seed heads emerge in August and September with a distinctive twisted 'awns' that catch the light like bronze silk. Fall color is deep orange-gold, and standing winter stems provide bird seed and structure through snow. Like all warm-season prairie grasses, it is slow to start in spring — do not mistake lateness for death. Cut back to 4–6 inches in early spring annually.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 9) for winter establishment and spring bloom; in zone 9 fall sowing is far more successful than spring sowing. Myosotis sylvatica is a cool-season annual that germinates readily in cool soil but struggles in warm-season conditions. Indigo Blue produces the deepest, most saturated blue available in the Myosotis sylvatica color range — a true indigo-blue rather than the lighter sky-blue of standard selections. Partial shade performance is genuine — forget-me-nots grow naturally in shaded woodland settings and perform better in partial shade in zone 9 than in full sun, which causes premature wilting and earlier decline. Self-seeds prolifically in zone 9 cool-season garden beds, creating a naturalizing population that reappears each fall from seed.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun — partial shade is preferred in zone 9 where the cool, moist, shaded conditions of the natural forest understory habitat are approximated under deciduous trees — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Indigo Blue Forget-Me-Not is a deep-colored selection of Woodland Forget-Me-Not (Myosotis sylvatica), producing the characteristic tiny, five-petaled, sky-to-indigo blue flowers with a small yellow eye in dense clusters on low, branching stems — creating a spreading mat of blue bloom that is one of the most universally recognized and beloved cool-season garden flowers. The characteristic tiny blue flowers of forget-me-not have been celebrated in poetry, art, and sentiment for centuries — the simple, vivid blue of the flowers carrying a disproportionate emotional resonance compared to the diminutive scale of individual blooms. As a woodland native, Myosotis sylvatica genuinely tolerates and prefers partial shade conditions — growing naturally beneath deciduous trees where it benefits from winter sun through bare branches and then spring dappled light through emerging leaves. In zone 9 forget-me-nots provide a solid carpet of blue in January–March, naturalizing through self-seeding in appropriate cool, moist, partially shaded sites to create an ever-expanding spring wildflower planting requiring no annual replanting.

common_name: Indigo Spires Sage (Long-Spiked Hybrid Indigo-Blue Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; Indigo Spires is a large, spreading plant that requires ample space — allow 3–4 feet in all directions and position at the back of the border where its 3–5 foot height does not overwhelm smaller plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun after the last frost date; Indigo Spires is one of the finest and most widely grown salvias for the Gulf South — a hybrid between Salvia farinacea and S. longispicata that produces exceptionally long (12–18 inch), spirally twisted flower spikes of deep indigo-violet flowers from late spring through hard frost. The extraordinarily long flower spikes are one of Indigo Spires' most visually distinctive features — the 12–18 inch wands of deep indigo flowers tower above the dark-green foliage in a spiraling, twisted arrangement that creates a unique textural effect unlike any other common garden salvia. Indigo Spires blooms virtually continuously from May through November in zone 9 — one of the longest blooming seasons of any perennial for the Gulf South. Deadheading or shearing back after each main bloom flush stimulates additional growth and prolongs peak appearance. The plant grows vigorously in zone 9 heat and humidity, requiring ample space for its eventual 3–5 foot height and spread. Deep blue-violet to indigo flower color is a scarce and prized quality in summer-blooming perennials — Indigo Spires provides this difficult color reliably through the hottest part of the Gulf South growing season when most blue-flowered plants cease blooming. Outstanding pollinator value — multiple bee and butterfly species visit constantly. Reliably perennial in zone 9.

common_name: Indigo Spires Salvia (Exceptionally Long Blue-Violet Spike Perennial Salvia Hybrid)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Indigo Spires grows to 4–5 feet and should be placed toward the back of mixed borders; the elongating flower spikes continue growing throughout the season, eventually reaching 12–18 inches in length by fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Indigo Spires is a hybrid Salvia (S. farinacea x S. longispicata) producing one of the most spectacular and long-season blue-purple flower displays of any commonly grown perennial — tall, dense, deep blue-violet to indigo flower spikes that elongate continuously throughout the growing season, eventually reaching 12–18 inches in length by fall and creating a dramatic vertical blue accent that persists from late spring through hard frost in zone 9. The elongating spike behavior distinguishes Indigo Spires from most other salvias: rather than producing a flush of flowers and then declining or deadheading the spent portion, the spike continues adding new flowers at the growing tip while maintaining color lower down — a continuously expanding, self-renewing flower spike that becomes more impressive as the season progresses. The deep, rich indigo-blue color is more saturated and richer than standard Salvia farinacea cultivars — closer to a true indigo in the spectrum, creating a deeper, more intense blue effect in the summer border. Hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies visit the flowers extensively. Indigo Spires grows vigorously to 4–5 feet and spreads by underground rhizomes — it naturalizes readily in Gulf South zone 9 gardens, returning from the roots each spring after frost kills the tops and expanding the planting gradually over years. Cut back to 12 inches in late winter to encourage fresh, vigorous regrowth.

common_name: Indonesian Wax Ginger (Pineapple Ginger, Candle Ginger, Small Taper-Lip)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes in spring in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Tapeinochilos ananassae cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It performs best in the warm, humid conditions of zone 10-11 and is best treated as a container plant in zone 9. The spectacular inflorescence emerges at the base of the plant or on separate short stems from the rhizome — place where it can be viewed from ground level. The waxy bracts are exceptionally long-lasting, both on the plant and as cut flowers (2–4 weeks vase life). Divide clumps every 3 years.
directions: Plant in partial shade with consistent moisture — Tapeinochilos ananassae grows best in dappled light with regular watering and performs poorly in full sun or dry conditions. Tapeinochilos ananassae is a rhizomatous tropical perennial from Australia (Queensland) and Papua New Guinea in the Costaceae family (closely related to the spiral gingers, Costus species), producing one of the most extraordinary inflorescences in the entire ginger order. The plant grows as a clump of upright, cane-like stems clothed in spirally-arranged, glossy, dark-green leaves similar to Costus. But the inflorescence is unlike anything else in cultivation: a dense, cylindrical to conical spike of hard, waxy, overlapping, brilliant scarlet-red bracts that build upon each other to create a form strikingly and precisely resembling a miniature red pineapple — complete with the scale-like bract pattern of the pineapple's exterior. From within each bract, small, tubular yellow flowers emerge in succession. The 'pineapple ginger' inflorescence is produced on separate short flowering stems that emerge from the rhizome at ground level, distinct from the leafy canes, making the fiery red pineapple spikes appear at the plant's base surrounded by the taller leafy canes — a dramatic tropical display. The waxy bracts are exceptionally long-lasting as cut flowers (up to a month in water), making Tapeinochilos ananassae important in the tropical cut flower industry.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Unlike Impatiens walleriana (common impatiens), New Guinea impatiens tolerate and actually perform well in partial sun to full sun conditions — they are not exclusively shade plants. The Infinity series was bred specifically for heat tolerance and disease resistance, including resistance to downy mildew (Plasmopara destructor) that devastated common impatiens plantings across North America in 2011–2014. In zone 9 the Infinity series blooms continuously from spring planting through frost with minimal care, making them one of the most reliable continuous-blooming annuals for the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in partial shade to partial sun (2–4 hours of direct sun) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Infinity New Guinea Impatiens performs best with morning sun and afternoon shade in zone 9's climate; Infinity is a New Guinea impatiens series from PanAmerican Seed that represents the modern generation of improved, heat-tolerant, disease-resistant New Guinea impatiens — a step change in reliability and performance over older New Guinea varieties that often struggled in the combination of heat, humidity, and downy mildew pressure that characterizes Gulf South summer conditions. New Guinea impatiens (Impatiens hawkeri), unlike the common bedding impatiens (I. walleriana), has significantly better heat tolerance and sun tolerance — growing and flowering satisfactorily in conditions that would cause common impatiens to collapse. The large, flat, single or semi-double flowers (3–4 inches across in some colors) in a wide range of solids and bicolors bloom continuously and prolifically without deadheading. For zone 9 gardeners frustrated by the decline of common impatiens in summer heat and the susceptibility to downy mildew, Infinity New Guinea impatiens provides a genuine, heat-adapted alternative for partial-shade color through the longest and hottest part of the growing season.

common_name: Inflated Air Plant (Balbis' Tillandsia, Spreading Air Plant, Northern Needleleaf)
plant_note: Wire to rough bark or mount on drift wood in bright indirect light; Tillandsia balbisiana is a medium-sized Florida native Tillandsia with a distinctive inflated, bulb-like pseudo-stem at the base, from which spreading, curved, gray-green leaves emerge. The inflated base gives the plant a characteristic shape unlike most other air plants. Monocarpic — blooms once on a branched spike with violet-blue flowers, then produces pups and dies. Mist or dunk in water 2–3 times weekly. More cold-tolerant than many Tillandsia species. Wild plants are protected in Florida. Zone 9-12. Non-toxic.
directions: Secure to rough bark, cork, or driftwood in bright indirect to partial direct light, misting or dunking regularly — Inflated Air Plant establishes readily on rough-barked surfaces and is one of the more distinctive Florida native tillandsias for its strongly inflated, pseudobulb-like base that sets it apart from the spreading, grass-like or funnel-forming shapes of other species. Tillandsia balbisiana is an epiphytic bromeliad in the Bromeliaceae family native to Florida (Charlotte to Monroe Counties), the Caribbean (Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico), Mexico, Central America, and northern South America — a common and adaptable Tillandsia species across the Gulf Coast and Caribbean regions. The plant is immediately recognizable by its strongly swollen, hollow pseudo-stem base (resembling a small bulb or flask) from which the leaves emerge in a rosette pattern — the base provides water storage and is an adaptation to the seasonally dry conditions of coastal hammock environments. The leaves are narrow, channeled, curved, gray-green to silver-gray from their dense trichome (scale) covering — the typical air plant leaf type that absorbs water and nutrients from rain and atmospheric moisture. When the plant matures, a branched flower spike emerges bearing coral-pink to red bracts and small, violet-blue flowers — a monocarpic bloom after which the rosette produces pups and dies. An excellent, distinctive native tillandsia for zone 9-12 outdoor air-plant collections. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry is one of the most adaptable native shrubs for wet, acidic conditions but also tolerates moderate drought once established.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun — inkberry is a native evergreen holly shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, growing naturally in bogs, pocosins, pine flatwoods, and moist woodland margins. It tolerates shade, wet soil, and flooding conditions that defeat most other shrubs. The small black berries in late summer and fall are consumed by dozens of bird species including wild turkeys, wood ducks, and bluebirds; bees (especially Melittidae oil-collecting bees) work the small white flowers in spring. It spreads steadily by suckering roots and can form dense, wildlife-shelter colonies over time. Named cultivars include 'Shamrock' (compact, mounding) and 'Densa' (dense form). An outstanding native evergreen for wet, acidic soils where Rhododendron and Kalmia cannot be grown. Plants are dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for berry production.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry tolerates wet, poorly drained sites and standing water better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen shrub, making it a strong choice for rain gardens and low, boggy spots. Plant both a male and a female cultivar nearby if berries are wanted, since the species is dioecious.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; inkberry is exceptionally tolerant of wet feet and periodic flooding, unusual among broadleaf evergreens, and also handles drier upland soils once established. Ilex glabra is a native evergreen holly of the wet pinelands, pocosins, and coastal plain wetlands of the eastern and Gulf Coast United States, valued in the landscape as a fine-textured, small-leaved, boxwood-like substitute that thrives in acidic, poorly drained soils where boxwood struggles. Small, inconspicuous white flowers in late spring give way, on female plants, to small black berries that persist into winter and are an important food source for songbirds. The dense, upright to rounded habit takes shearing well, making it a popular choice for a low hedge, foundation planting, or naturalistic screen in a partly shaded woodland-edge landscape. A tough, adaptable, wildlife-valuable native evergreen for difficult wet or acidic sites, zone 4–9.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger has passed. Requires sharp drainage and full sun; does not tolerate wet or poorly drained soils. Avoid transplanting once established, as this shrub develops a deep, fleshy taproot.
directions: Select a dry, rocky, or sandy site in full sun with excellent drainage — this prairie native will not persist in heavy or consistently moist soil. Scarify seeds with sandpaper and cold-stratify for 60 days before sowing, or propagate from softwood cuttings in early summer. Once established, this nitrogen-fixing shrub improves soil and needs little supplemental water. Clusters of small white flowers in late spring attract native bees and butterflies, making it a valuable addition to a wildlife garden.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; also easily started indoors 6 weeks before last frost. Self-sows abundantly once established — remove seedlings where not wanted.
directions: Direct sow in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; inland sea oats is one of the most valuable native ornamental grasses specifically because it thrives in deep shade — a condition that defeats virtually all other ornamental grasses. The flat, bamboo-like leaf blades form a graceful arching clump, but the showstopper is the hanging, oat-like seed clusters that emerge in summer, dangling from slender wiry branches, and persist into winter — turning from green to copper-tan to warm bronze, rattling pleasantly in the wind. It grows naturally along stream banks and in bottomland forests, giving it outstanding tolerance of both shade and periodic wet soils. Self-sows prolifically once established and can become weedy; deadhead if you want to limit spread. The seeds are relished by songbirds in fall.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; intermediate fothergilla is a hybrid between F. gardenii and F. major and is best propagated by softwood cuttings. The cultivar 'Blue Shadow' is most widely available and prized for its intense blue-green summer foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; intermediate fothergilla is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between small fothergilla (F. gardenii) and large fothergilla (F. major), combining the best traits of both parents — the compact habit of the dwarf parent with the larger flower heads and superior fall color of the tall parent. The fragrant, bottlebrush-like white flowers emerge before the leaves in early spring, offering a spectacular display of creamy puffball blooms on bare stems. The summer foliage of the cultivar 'Blue Shadow' is an unusually intense blue-green — among the most striking blue tones of any deciduous shrub — before turning a fiery combination of red, orange, and yellow in fall. A superb specimen shrub for woodland gardens, foundation plantings, and native shrub borders in zones 4–8, combining especially well with azaleas, mountain laurels, and other acid-loving shrubs.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; intermediate periwinkle is less cold-hardy than V. minor (hardy to zone 4) or V. major (hardy to zone 6), surviving reliably in zones 7–9. It blooms in late autumn and winter when temperatures are mild, providing off-season color that the other periwinkles do not offer. It may naturalize in mild climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; intermediate periwinkle is a less well-known Mediterranean species that occupies a horticultural niche distinct from both of the commonly grown periwinkles (V. minor and V. major) in one key way — it blooms in autumn and winter rather than spring. From October through February in zones 8–10, it produces the characteristic five-petaled, pinwheel periwinkle flowers in pale, milky-white to palest lavender-white or soft blue-lavender, adding off-season color to the shade garden when almost nothing else is in bloom. The evergreen to semi-evergreen leaves are narrower and glossier than those of V. major, giving the plant a slightly finer texture. It spreads by trailing, rooting stems to form a weed-suppressing groundcover in dry shade under trees — notably more drought-tolerant than V. minor in warm climates. The cultivar 'Wojo's Gem' has cream-variegated leaves with white margins and is particularly ornamental. A useful addition to the winter-interest shade garden in Gulf Coast and Mediterranean-climate gardens where mild winters allow its distinctive flowering season to be fully appreciated.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; interrupted fern thrives in consistently moist conditions and is particularly effective at pond edges, stream banks, and wet woodland areas. Avoid disturbing established specimens.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; interrupted fern is one of the most distinctive and easily recognized native ferns of eastern North America, named for its unique habit of placing spore-bearing fertile pinnae in the middle section of certain fronds — interrupting the green sterile pinnae above and below with brown fertile segments that drop early in the season, leaving characteristic gaps in the frond's silhouette. This genus (Osmunda) produces the fibrous 'osmunda fiber' root mass prized for centuries as a potting medium for orchids and epiphytes. Interrupted fern grows in moist, shaded conditions similar to cinnamon and royal ferns but tolerates slightly drier slopes within the moist woodland. The large vase-shaped crown makes a bold structural statement in the wet shade garden and the graceful fronds provide excellent textural contrast with broad-leaved hostas and astilbes.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Intrigue is grown primarily for its narrow, dark purple-bronze foliage, an unusual fine-textured leaf form quite different from the broad paddle-shaped leaves of most canna cultivars.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Intrigue is grown chiefly for its distinctive, narrow, deeply colored purple-bronze foliage, a finer-textured leaf shape than the broad, paddle-like leaves typical of most canna cultivars, giving it an almost banana-leaf-meets-grass appearance that stands out in a tropical-themed border. Smaller orange flowers appear above the foliage in summer, though the striking leaf color and texture remain the plant's primary ornamental draw. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant the potted rose in spring after hard frosts; sold as a live plant.
directions: Plant this floribunda rose in spring in a hole amended with compost, keeping the graft at soil level in colder zones. Clusters of richly fragrant purple-plum blooms appear from spring through fall on an elegant upright form, making a bold focal point. Provide full sun, well-drained soil, and consistent moisture, watering at the base to keep foliage dry. Prune in late winter to shape the plant and deadhead spent clusters to encourage repeat flowering.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Invincibelle Spirit was the first pink-flowered selection of native smooth hydrangea, a species traditionally available only in white.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Invincibelle Spirit was a breakthrough introduction as the first pink-blooming cultivar of native smooth hydrangea (the species behind the classic white Annabelle), producing rounded clusters of soft pink flowers on a native plant traditionally available only in white. Like Annabelle, it blooms on new wood, so it can be cut back hard in late winter and still flower reliably the same year, and it rebounds quickly from winter damage in colder zones. Its stems are somewhat sturdier than old Annabelle types but can still benefit from light staking in a very rainy, exposed site. It is a good pollinator plant and, being a native species selection, tends to be adaptable and low-maintenance across a range of soil conditions.

common_name: Ionantha Air Plant (Blushing Bride Tillandsia, Sky Plant)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork bark, driftwood, wire, or shells in bright indirect to direct morning light; Ionantha Air Plant needs no soil whatsoever. Water by dunking in water for 20–30 minutes twice per week in warm months or misting heavily every 2–3 days. After watering, shake off excess water and allow to dry completely within 4 hours — sitting in stagnant water causes rot at the base. A good indirect air source prevents this.
