In zone 9, plants can grow outdoors year-round in protected spots and survive brief temperatures to 32°F dry. Produces offsets (pups) after blooming.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Ionantha Air Plant performs best with 3–4 hours of bright indirect or morning sun and will bleach and dry out in harsh full afternoon sun in zone 9. Tillandsia ionantha is a small, epiphytic bromeliad native to Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and northwestern Venezuela in the family Bromeliaceae, one of the approximately 650 species of Tillandsia and by far the most widely grown and sold air plant in the world. Like all tillandsias, it has no functional roots — the small roots serve only to anchor the plant to its substrate. All water and nutrients are absorbed through specialized scales on the leaf surfaces called trichomes. The plant forms a small, tight rosette of silvery-green, slightly recurved, stiff leaves about 2–3 inches across. Its most dramatic quality is its response to blooming: in spring (or when seasonal cues trigger reproduction), the inner leaves of the entire plant flush brilliant red to rose-magenta over a period of days before the small violet-purple tubular flowers emerge from the center — the entire plant glowing red for weeks. After flowering, the parent plant gradually produces 2–6 pups before declining. The combination of tiny size, no soil requirement, dramatic bloom-time color, and extreme adaptability has made T. ionantha the definitive entry point for air plant collecting.

common_name: Iron Cross Begonia (Iron Cross Plant, Beefsteak Geranium)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Iron Cross Begonia cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It is rhizomatous — grow in a wide, shallow container to allow horizontal rhizome spread. Keep the rhizome at soil level (do not bury it) and allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. High humidity (50–70%) improves appearance and prevents powdery mildew. Propagate from leaf cuttings or rhizome sections. Excellent for terrariums.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Iron Cross Begonia thrives in the bright, indirect light of a north or east window and will scorch in direct sun. Begonia masoniana is a rhizomatous begonia from China (Guangxi province) and South Vietnam with one of the most immediately recognizable leaf patterns in the houseplant world: the large, deeply textured, quilted, bright-green, heart-shaped leaves bear a bold, dark brown to blackish pattern at the center that precisely resembles a German Iron Cross or a four-pointed star within a circle — a marking that appears on every leaf with striking consistency and regularity. The textured, bumpy leaf surface — covered in fine hairs and raised blisters — adds a three-dimensional quality to the ornamental effect. Small, white to pale pink flowers appear in spring but are secondary to the dramatic foliage. Iron Cross Begonia prefers the warm, humid conditions of its subtropical native habitat and will maintain beautiful foliage year-round in appropriate indoor conditions. It is more tolerant of lower humidity than cane-type begonias but still benefits from supplemental humidity in dry indoor environments. The leaf pattern is so distinctive and consistent that it was originally thought to be a deliberate human selection, but it occurs naturally in the wild population.

plant_note: Plant small, scaly bulbs 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in spring after frost danger passes; iron cross oxalis goes dormant in winter and the bulbs can be left in the ground in zones 7–10. In colder zones, lift and store dry indoors. Bulbs multiply freely to form attractive clumps over the seasons.
directions: Plant scaly bulbs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; iron cross oxalis is one of the most cheerful and distinctive small bulbs available, producing four-parted, clover-like leaves in fresh green with a bold, chocolate-purple, cross-shaped zone in the center of each leaflet — the iron-cross pattern that gives it its common name and makes it instantly recognizable. The deep rose-pink to rose-red flowers appear in clusters above the foliage throughout summer, adding color from late spring until fall. A native of the Mexican highlands, it forms compact clumps that multiply steadily from the scaly bulblets and provide a weed-suppressing carpet through the warm season. The foliage folds closed in direct midday heat and at night (a characteristic of all oxalis), reopening in morning and evening light. In mild climates (zones 7–10) the bulbs overwinter in the ground to return dependably each spring. Excellent for container displays, rock gardens, and front-of-border edges where the boldly patterned foliage provides season-long textural interest.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seed, then start indoors; benefits from a chilling period.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds in the refrigerator for several weeks, then sow indoors or direct sow in fall for natural chilling. This swamp milkweed blend produces clusters of pink and rose blooms that are irresistible to monarch butterflies and hummingbirds. It grows best in consistently moist to wet soils such as near a pond or rain garden but adapts to average beds. As a host plant for monarch caterpillars, leave foliage intact and avoid pesticides to support the life cycle.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow in spring.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in spring, barely covering it. Long, wiry stems carry pincushion blooms in white, lilac, and blue shades that are outstanding and long-lasting in bouquets. This tough, fairly drought-tolerant, hardy plant has few pests and blooms over an extended season. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and cut or deadhead frequently to keep flowers coming.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Issai is a dwarf beautyberry that sets fruit reliably even as a young plant, unlike some beautyberries that need a few seasons to bear heavily.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Issai is a compact, dwarf beautyberry selection that reliably sets heavy clusters of bright violet-purple berries even on young plants, without needing the several-year establishment period some beautyberries require before fruiting well. Its small mature size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller gardens where the full-sized native American beautyberry would grow too large. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so cutting the shrub back hard to a foot or so from the ground each late winter encourages vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production the following fall.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Italian arum is winter-active and produces foliage through the cold months, filling the off-season gap when most shade plants are dormant.
directions: Plant tubers in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Italian arum has an unusual reverse-season growth cycle — the large, glossy, dark-green, arrow-shaped leaves emerge in fall, display through winter with striking silver or gray-white marbling, and die back by early summer, then clusters of brilliant orange-red berries on bare stems persist through summer, providing the most visually arresting fruit display of any shade garden perennial. The unusual winter-foliage-summer-berry cycle makes it an invaluable complement to spring- and summer-growing companions. 'Marmoratum' has particularly vivid silver marbling. All plant parts are toxic — the berries are especially dangerous. Naturalizes slowly by self-seeding to form colonies in the deep, undisturbed shade of mature trees where few other plants perform.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun in early spring or fall; Italian bugloss is tap-rooted and resents transplanting once established, so direct seeding or planting very small container plants is preferable. Cut back hard after the first flush of bloom in June to encourage a second flowering in late summer. Short-lived in rich, wet soils; thrives in lean, well-drained conditions.
directions: Sow seeds in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Italian bugloss produces flowers of a true, pure, brilliant blue that is almost unmatched in the late-spring perennial garden — the open, five-petaled, white-eyed flowers are produced in large, branching clusters on tall, leafy stems and are among the most intensely blue of any hardy perennial. As a member of the borage family, it is exceptionally attractive to bees and butterflies throughout its long June-July bloom period, and cutting back the spent flower stalks after the first flush often promotes a secondary flush in late summer. The plant is coarse and hairy in texture — the broad, rough leaves and stems have bristly hairs that can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals — and the tap root makes division impractical, but these characteristics matter little given the breathtaking blue of the flowers. Best planted in the middle or back of a sunny border where the coarser foliage is hidden by neighboring plants. The cultivar Loddon Royalist is the most floriferous and most widely grown selection.

common_name: Italian White Sunflower (Cream-White Branching Beach Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Italian White is a branching, multi-flower type that produces dozens of blooms per plant over a long season, unlike single-stem types that produce one large flower. For cut flower production in zone 9, it can be sown in February–March for spring blooms and again in August–September for fall production. Helianthus debilis naturally tolerates coastal conditions including salt spray and sandy soils.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; Italian White grows well in poor, sandy, well-drained soils and requires minimal fertilization — excess nitrogen produces large plants with fewer flowers. Italian White Sunflower (Helianthus debilis rather than the common H. annuus) is a beloved heirloom cut flower sunflower producing a profusion of small (3–4 inch), cream-white to ivory-colored flowers with dark chocolate-brown to near-black centers — a color combination of remarkable elegance that is unlike any other annual sunflower. The pure cream-white petals surrounding a contrasting near-black center disk create a sophisticated, almost formal aesthetic that pairs beautifully with other cut flowers in arrangements where the standard yellow sunflower would be too assertive. Individual plants are heavily branching and produce 20–50 or more flowers per plant through the summer, providing a continuous supply of cut stems over several months. The species (H. debilis, the cucumberleaf or beach sunflower) is native to coastal dunes of the southeastern United States including Florida's Gulf Coast, giving it genuine native plant credentials for zone 8–10 gardeners and explaining its exceptional drought, heat, and sandy-soil tolerance. Italian White is also an outstanding pollinator plant — the accessible flower centers are visited heavily by bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects throughout the bloom season. A versatile, beautiful, and genuinely useful heirloom annual for both cut flower production and pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, lean, dry to summer-dry soil in zone 6–10; Ithuriel's Spear is a striking California native corm — native to grasslands, chaparral, and woodland edges in the Central Valley foothills and Coast Ranges — bearing large, loose, open umbels of trumpet-shaped, vivid blue-violet to lavender flowers on tall, wiry stems in late spring and early summer, long after the narrow, strap-like leaves have died back completely.
directions: Plant Triteleia laxa corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; leaves emerge in winter and die back by late spring before the flowers appear — mark planting locations carefully; provide no summer water as summer drought is essential; corms naturalize readily and multiply by offsets over several years. Ithuriel's Spear takes its poetic name from John Milton's Paradise Lost, where the angel Ithuriel carries a spear that reveals true forms — a name given to this plant, perhaps, for its dramatic, spear-like, erect flower stems. The loosely arranged umbels of 6–18 trumpet-shaped flowers in vivid blue-violet to pale lavender (occasionally white) are among the most beautiful in the California native flora, appearing in late spring to early summer on tall, wiry, leafless stems at a time when many other spring wildflowers have finished blooming. The cultivar 'Queen Fabiola' is widely available in the trade and has particularly large, rich-violet flowers and reliable performance in cultivation. Unlike many California native bulbs, Triteleia laxa has proven adaptable to some garden irrigation in summer and has naturalized in gardens outside California — though best growth and persistence comes with dry summers. Excellent for cutting; flowers last well in the vase.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost in warm soil; lift and store over winter where it freezes.
directions: Ivanetti is a classic ball dahlia in deep burgundy-to-purple-black tones, a favorite for cutting thanks to its perfect globe form and strong stems. Plant tubers eye-up in full sun and well-drained soil after the last frost, watering only lightly until growth emerges. Pinch the growing tip early to encourage branching and more blooms, and deadhead through the season. In cold regions dig the tubers after the first frost and store them dry until spring.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 10–12; Ivory Cane Palm is a graceful, clustering palm native to the rainforests of Java, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula — one of the most ornamental of the tropical understory palms, producing multiple slender, ivory-white to yellowish-green canes topped by elegant, pinnate fronds with characteristic jaggered, fishtail-tipped leaflets — excellent for shaded tropical garden positions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Pinanga coronata is adapted to rainforest understory conditions and should be protected from direct sun, especially harsh afternoon sun, and from cold below 45°F — mulch deeply and maintain consistent moisture. Pinanga coronata (Ivory Cane Palm or Crowned Pinanga) is a multiple-stemmed, clumping palm in the large Pinanga genus native to the lowland and sub-montane rainforests of Java, Bali, Sumatra, and Peninsular Malaysia, where it is a common and characteristic element of the forest understory. The palm is distinguished by its attractive, ivory-white to pale-yellowish-green cane-like stems — slender (1–1.5 inch diameter), smooth, prominently ringed — arising in clusters to create an elegant, bamboo-like multi-stemmed effect topped by graceful, arching pinnate fronds with attractively jagged (praemorse) leaflet tips. The Pinanga genus contains hundreds of species from South and Southeast Asian rainforests, most of which share the characteristic of being shade-adapted understory palms growing beneath the closed canopy. Pinanga coronata is among the most widely cultivated Pinanga for tropical gardens in zone 10–12, valued for its manageable size, elegant multi-stemmed habit, and tolerance of deep shade. Small red to black fruits appear periodically in colorful clusters. An outstanding shade-tolerant, multi-stemmed palm for tropical garden understory positions.

plant_note: Plant in fall or early spring; this evergreen blooms very early in the season.
directions: Ivory Prince, a Lenten rose, is among the earliest perennials to bloom, opening upright creamy-white flowers flushed with rose and green in late winter to early spring. Its leathery evergreen foliage stays attractive year-round in partial to full shade. Plant in rich, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist while establishing. All parts are toxic if eaten, so site it away from areas where children or pets graze, and remove old leaves in late winter to showcase the blooms.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; ivory sedge is native to rocky, calcareous slopes and performs surprisingly well in dry shade under trees where few other ornamentals survive.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to rocky soil in partial to deep shade; ivory sedge is one of the finest native sedges for extremely challenging shade conditions — it grows naturally on shaded limestone bluffs and rocky slopes where deep shade and dry, rocky soils combine to exclude nearly all other plants. The very fine, delicate, bright-green, almost thread-like leaves form soft, airy tufts 6–12 inches tall that sway gracefully with the slightest air movement, creating a cloud-like texture unlike the bolder carex species. It is one of very few ornamental plants that genuinely tolerates deep dry shade under dense, shallow-rooted trees — a notoriously difficult garden situation. Unlike most sedges, it performs well in neutral to slightly alkaline soils and requires sharp drainage. The delicate texture makes it an outstanding companion to bold-leafed hostas and ferns in the shade border. Semi-evergreen to evergreen in most growing zones.

common_name: Ivy Leaf Morning Glory (Ivy Morning Glory)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost danger in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; nick or soak seeds for 12–24 hours to improve germination; ivy leaf morning glory self-seeds prolifically and can become invasive in warm climates — pull unwanted seedlings when small.
directions: Nick or file seeds and sow directly after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems. Ipomoea hederacea (ivy leaf morning glory) is a native North American morning glory producing ivy-shaped, three-lobed leaves that immediately distinguish it from common morning glories with heart-shaped foliage; the 1.5-to-2-inch flowers are sky-blue to pale blue to violet with a white throat, appearing profusely from summer through frost. The ivy-shaped foliage is the key ornamental distinction — it creates a finer texture and more elegant twining pattern on fences and trellises than the typical morning glory. This species is native to the eastern US and tropics and naturalizes readily in disturbed soils, roadsides, and old fields; it self-seeds abundantly and can spread aggressively in the landscape. It is valuable as a wildlife plant — the flowers provide nectar for bumblebees and the seeds feed native sparrows and mourning doves through winter. Zone 9 and warmer: treat as a warm-season annual that self-seeds reliably.

common_name: Ixora (Flame of the Woods, Jungle Geranium)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; ixora is highly sensitive to alkaline soil and high pH — in alkaline or limestone soils, apply acidifying fertilizer and chelated micronutrients regularly to prevent the severe chlorosis that is the most common problem with this plant in the Southeast.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; ixora is one of the most popular tropical flowering shrubs in the world, producing dense, rounded clusters of small tubular flowers in brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and white nearly year-round in frost-free gardens and spring through fall in zone 9. The flat-topped flower clusters (corymbs) are 3–4 inches across and attract butterflies throughout the bloom season. It is a slow-growing, compact shrub and one of the best choices for formal hedges and foundation plantings in tropical and subtropical landscapes. The main cultural challenge is soil pH: ixora demands strongly acidic conditions (pH 5.0–6.0) and in the alkaline limestone soils of Florida and the Gulf Coast, iron and manganese deficiencies cause chronic yellowing. Use acidifying fertilizer specially formulated for ixora and apply chelated iron if chlorosis appears. Avoid 'lollipop pruning' (shearing into balls) which reduces blooming — prune lightly by selectively removing branches.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to average soil in full sun in spring; jacaranda requires several years of establishment before blooming — trees grown from seed may take 7–10 years; grafted trees bloom much sooner. Frost kills the tops in zone 9 but established trees typically resprout from the base.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; jacaranda is a South American deciduous tree that is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world — in spring, before or as the leaves emerge, the entire tree becomes covered in masses of large, tubular, lavender-blue to violet-purple flowers arranged in billowing panicles that transform the canopy into a breathtaking cloud of blue-purple. The flowering display lasts 6–8 weeks and the fallen flowers carpet the ground beneath the tree in a second violet display. The finely divided, fern-like, bright-green, doubly-pinnate leaves are attractive through the growing season. Jacaranda is the definitive 'purple flowering tree' of warm-climate landscapes worldwide — seen lining streets in Los Angeles, Johannesburg, Sydney, and throughout zone 9–11 in the southern United States. It is frost-sensitive, with established trees tolerating brief dips to approximately 25°F in zone 9 — tops may be killed by hard freezes, but established root systems often resprout. Requires a dry season to flower most reliably. An iconic specimen tree for zone 9–11 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack Frost cannot be grown from seed (it will not come true) and must be propagated from divisions taken in early spring or late summer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack Frost brunnera was the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2012 and remains the most celebrated and widely grown silver-foliage shade perennial available. The large, heart-shaped leaves are almost entirely covered with a brilliant, reflective silver overlay, with only the green primary veins visible — in the shade garden, the silver leaves appear to glow with an inner light and illuminate dark corners as effectively as white flowers. In spring, tiny azure-blue forget-me-not flowers appear on wiry stems above the silver foliage, creating a jewel-like spring display. The silvery foliage remains effective from emergence in spring through summer decline, brightening the shade border for months. Consistent moisture is the most critical requirement — Jack Frost scorches badly in dry conditions and in hot afternoon sun. In zone 8, afternoon shade, consistent watering, and mulching are required to maintain it through summer. It will not produce viable seeds.

common_name: Jack of Diamonds Brunnera (Large Silver-Splashed Heartleaf Brunnera)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jack of Diamonds is a sport of Jack Frost with even larger leaves and bolder silver coloring, and like other named Brunnera cultivars must be propagated from divisions rather than seed to keep the pattern true.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Jack of Diamonds arose as a sport of the celebrated Jack Frost brunnera and is distinguished by noticeably larger leaves and an even bolder, more extensive silver overlay across the heart-shaped foliage, with only fine green veining showing through. In spring, sprays of small, sky-blue, forget-me-not-like flowers rise above the foliage on wiry stems, adding a soft blue counterpoint to the metallic silver leaves. Its large-scale foliage makes a bigger textural and visual statement in the shade border than Jack Frost, useful as a focal point or in bolder plantings alongside hostas and ferns. Consistent moisture is essential — brunnera foliage scorches quickly in dry soil or hot afternoon sun, and in zone 8 gardens it needs reliable afternoon shade and regular watering to look its best through summer. Divide clumps in early spring or late summer when they become crowded, since named cultivars do not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively.

common_name: Jack-in-the-Pulpit (Native Woodland Perennial with Iconic Hooded Spathe)
plant_note: Plant corms (the small, rounded, tuber-like structures) 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; Jack-in-the-Pulpit is a native woodland understory plant that requires deep shade and consistent moisture to thrive. In zone 9, plant fall or early spring in the shadiest, moistest areas of the garden with high organic matter soil. Plants emerge in spring, produce their distinctive hooded flower structure and foliage through summer, then go dormant by midsummer (the foliage dies back to the ground). The corms slowly enlarge over years; established large corms produce female flowers and clusters of red berries in fall. All parts are toxic if eaten raw due to calcium oxalate crystals.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade; keep consistently moist. Do not eat any part of the plant raw. Jack-in-the-Pulpit (Arisaema triphyllum) is among the most recognizable and beloved native wildflowers of the eastern United States — an araceous (Arum family) perennial widely distributed in moist woodland understories from Quebec to Florida and west to the Great Plains. The plant takes its common name from the distinctive reproductive structure: an erect, clublike spadix (Jack) standing inside a hooded, striped spathe (the Pulpit), a form so architecturally precise and recognizable that it has become iconic in American botanical illustration and nature education. The spathe's stripes typically alternate green-white or purple-brown-green, and the entire structure has a jewel-like elegance that makes Jack-in-the-Pulpit one of the most aesthetically sophisticated of native spring wildflowers. One of the most unusual biological characteristics of Arisaema triphyllum is its sexual flexibility: plants can change sex from year to year, typically producing male flowers when small and female flowers when the corm has accumulated sufficient energy reserves, making large, vigorous corms most likely to produce the red-berried fall clusters. The berries (clusters of brilliant red drupes that replace the spathe in fall) provide important fall food for wood thrushes and other migratory birds. Jack-in-the-Pulpit is an excellent choice for deep shade gardens where it naturalizes slowly in moist woodland conditions, providing spring interest in areas too dark for most flowering plants.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the top grows in sun; Jackmanii is one of the oldest and most reliable large-flowered clematis cultivars, blooming on new growth so it can be pruned back hard each late winter.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool (mulch well or shade the base with low companion plants) while the vine climbs into full sun on a trellis, fence, or other support. Introduced in England in 1862, Jackmanii is one of the most enduring and widely grown clematis cultivars ever bred, producing an abundance of large, velvety, deep purple flowers from early summer into fall. Because it flowers entirely on new growth, it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned hard, back to about a foot from the ground, in late winter, which keeps the vine vigorous and full of bloom rather than leggy and bare at the base. It is a tough, adaptable, long-lived vine that has introduced generations of gardeners to clematis.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Jackson brier is the most ornamental of the southeastern Smilax species with glossy, lance-shaped leaves and is commonly used in Southern floral arrangements as greenery — it has been shipped as 'smilax' by florists for over a century.
directions: Plant in spring in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade against a trellis, fence, or tree for support; Smilax smallii climbs by tendrils and can reach 10–20 feet, providing dense evergreen coverage in shaded areas. Jackson brier is the most ornamental of the native southeastern Smilax species, producing long, lance-shaped, glossy dark green leaves on gracefully arching, somewhat thorny stems; it is the 'smilax' of traditional Southern floriculture — the garlands of small-leafed, shiny green vine used to decorate churches, ballrooms, and mantles throughout the South for weddings and holiday celebrations for well over 100 years. Small, greenish-white flowers in early spring are not showy but are fragrant, and small blue-black berries in fall are important food for mockingbirds, catbirds, and other wildlife. Valuable as a native evergreen shade vine in zone 7–10 landscapes.

common_name: Jacob Cline Bee Balm (Red Bee Balm, Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Jacob Cline spreads aggressively by underground stolons — divide every 2–3 years to prevent the colony from expanding beyond its intended area.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Jacob Cline is widely considered the finest red bee balm cultivar for hot, humid climates — selected for its exceptional resistance to powdery mildew, the primary problem that disfigures most Monarda didyma cultivars in Gulf South summer conditions. Most bee balm cultivars develop severe powdery mildew by midsummer in the humidity of the Gulf Coast — white, powdery coating on the foliage that disfigures the plant for the remainder of the season. Jacob Cline was selected from a large planting for the plants that remained cleanest through humid summers, resulting in dramatically superior mildew resistance compared to standard bee balm selections. The large, intense scarlet-red flower heads are exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds, which hover around the tubular flowers seeking nectar — Jacob Cline is one of the finest hummingbird plants available for partial-shade gardens in zone 9. It also attracts bees, swallowtails, and sphinx moths. The aromatic, mint-scented foliage is characteristic of the mint family. Jacob Cline spreads vigorously by underground runners and should be divided every 2–3 years in early spring to contain the colony and maintain plant vigor. In zone 9, it blooms from May through August.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil for spring germination, or start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost after 4–6 weeks of cold stratification at 35–40°F. Transplant in early spring to partially shaded beds.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall or plant container divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; jacob's ladder forms an attractive clump of ladder-like, pinnately compound leaves topped in late spring and early summer with clusters of cup-shaped, lavender-blue flowers with prominent yellow-orange stamens that give the plant an elegant, airy presence in the shade garden. It performs best in cool to moderate climates (zone 3–7) with consistent moisture and afternoon shade; plants often go partially dormant in the heat of summer in warmer climates and may require some shade protection there. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early fall; it self-seeds modestly but not aggressively. The cultivar 'Brise d'Anjou' offers striking cream-variegated foliage that lights up shaded corners.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or stratify and sow in early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Jacob's ladder self-sows reliably in appropriate conditions and forms steadily expanding colonies over time.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — Jacob's ladder is a charming native spring wildflower named for its distinctive pinnately compound leaves whose paired leaflets march ladder-like up either side of the central stem, resembling the Biblical Jacob's ladder to heaven. Clusters of nodding, bell-shaped blue-violet flowers appear in April and May on stems 8–16 inches tall, providing valuable early-season nectar for bumblebees and other native bees. It grows naturally in rich, moist, shaded forest and woodland slopes throughout the eastern US, forming loose colonies in appropriate conditions. The foliage remains attractive through summer in cool, moist locations before dying back in late summer. Self-sows reliably and naturalizes gently without becoming invasive. An excellent companion for native ferns, trilliums, and spring ephemerals in the shaded native plant garden.

plant_note: Divide rhizomatous clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in full to part shade; jade lily tolerates dry shade under trees better than most rhizomatous groundcovers and is semi-evergreen to fully evergreen in zones 7–10. It spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form a uniform colony.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich soil in full to part shade; jade lily is a close relative of liriope and mondo grass but distinctly more shade-tolerant, native to shaded forest floors of China and Japan and producing neat, arching rosettes of narrow, glossy, dark-green, strap-like leaves that remain evergreen to semi-evergreen through winter in zones 7–10. In autumn it produces short spikes of small, fragrant, pale-pink flowers at ground level, followed by red berries that persist ornamentally into winter. It spreads steadily by short underground rhizomes to form a uniform, weed-suppressing carpet in situations where few other plants will grow — including the dry shade under large trees. More refined and denser in habit than liriope, with a lower, more ground-hugging growth, it is outstanding as a close-knit groundcover for shaded walkways, slopes, and woodland floors. Related to but generally better in deep shade than either liriope or mondo grass.

common_name: Jade Plant (Money Tree, Friendship Plant, Lucky Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a container specimen in zone 9 — Jade Plant cannot tolerate freezing temperatures and should be brought indoors or moved to a frost-free area when temperatures drop below 40°F. In zone 10-11, it can be planted outdoors in well-drained, sunny to partially-shaded spots. Jade Plant is one of the easiest succulents to propagate: any detached leaf or stem cutting placed on dry soil will root and form a new plant. Water thoroughly, then allow the soil to dry completely before watering again.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to full sun in very well-drained, gritty succulent potting mix; Jade Plant tolerates lower light conditions than most succulents but develops the most compact, well-colored foliage with bright indirect light or morning sun. Crassula ovata is a succulent shrub native to the Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal provinces of South Africa, where it grows in rocky hillsides and dry scrub in dry, well-drained conditions. Over its decades of cultivation as an ornamental houseplant worldwide, it has become one of the most recognizable and widely-owned plants on earth — practically ubiquitous in offices, homes, and gardens across every continent. The thick, oval, glossy, jade-green leaves with red-edged margins and the stout, woody, trunk-like stems that develop over years give well-grown specimens a miniature tree appearance highly prized in bonsai aesthetics. In zone 10–11, established outdoor plants produce clusters of small, star-shaped, pink to white flowers in winter, creating a charming seasonal display. In Asian cultures, Jade Plant is considered a symbol of good luck, financial prosperity, and friendship — 'money plant' is one of its most common names in Chinese and Japanese contexts. Single leaves placed on gritty soil root readily within weeks, making it one of the most freely propagated of all succulents.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in part shade to full sun; jade vine is a Philippine rainforest species adapted to the dappled shade of forest edges and is most free-flowering with at least 6 hours of sun — it is extremely rare in cultivation outside of specialty botanical gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in bright indirect light to full sun; provide very strong, substantial support structure — jade vine becomes massive. Strongylodon macrobotrys (jade vine or tayabak) is one of the most spectacularly beautiful and rarest flowering vines in cultivation — a Philippine rainforest legume producing extraordinary, cascading, 3-to-5-foot racemes of 75–100 large, claw-shaped, iridescent jade-blue-to-turquoise-green flowers whose unique color is essentially unmatched by any other flower. The jade-green flowers have an almost translucent, gemstone-like quality in sunlight. Jade vine is critically endangered in its native Philippine rainforest habitat due to deforestation and the disruption of its specialized bat and sunbird pollinators. The vine is massive and powerful in ideal conditions — growing to 60–70 feet and requiring very substantial support. It blooms in late winter to spring after a cool dry period. It is extraordinarily difficult to grow outside of tropical conditions (zone 11–12) and is primarily a botanical garden specimen; very rarely available in the nursery trade. For true tropical enthusiasts only. An extraordinary rarity of the plant world.

plant_note: Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring or early fall; avoid heavy clay and alkaline soil — pH 4.5–6.0 is optimal and drainage is essential to prevent root rot.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade, giving each plant 4–6 feet of space; Japanese andromeda is a four-season evergreen shrub notable for chains of white urn-shaped flowers in early spring that hang like lily-of-the-valley, glossy red or bronze new growth that gradually matures to dark green, and persistent buds that decorate the plant through winter. Protect from afternoon sun in hotter zones to prevent leaf scorch; afternoon shade extends its range into zone 7 and 8. Prune lightly after flowering to shape; deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage stronger bud-set for the following year. All parts are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; Japanese anemone is slow to establish in its first year but spreads vigorously by rhizome once settled, producing magnificent late-season blooms in August–October when most shade perennials have finished flowering.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; avoid disturbing the roots once established — plants resent transplanting. Anemone hupehensis (Japanese anemone) is one of the most valuable shade-garden perennials for late-season bloom — a Chinese native that fills the August–October gap when spring-blooming shade perennials have long finished, producing elegant, saucer-shaped, 2-to-3-inch flowers with five or more silky petals in pink, rose, or white surrounding a central cluster of golden stamens, on tall, branching, wiry stems rising 2–4 feet above the bold, dark-green, lobed basal foliage. The flowers have a gossamer, butterfly-like quality and sway gracefully in the breeze; they are excellent for cutting. Plants spread gradually by underground rhizomes to form expanding colonies — welcome in a large shade garden, potentially aggressive in a small one. The species Anemone hupehensis differs from the hybrid A. × hybrida in being slightly smaller and less vigorous; cultivars like 'September Charm' (single pink) and 'Pamina' (semi-double deep pink) are widely grown. Best in zone 9 if given afternoon shade and consistent moisture.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Japanese anemone establishes slowly in year one but becomes progressively more vigorous, eventually spreading by stolons to form large colonies. Do not disturb established plants.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Japanese anemone is one of the most valuable shade perennials for late-season interest, producing graceful 2–4 foot stems of single or semi-double flowers in white or soft pink in late summer and fall when most shade plants have finished blooming. The large, poppy-like flowers — 2–3 inches across — carry prominent yellow stamens that glow against the petal color. The deeply lobed, dark-green, fig-like basal leaves provide attractive texture through summer before the flower stems emerge. Popular cultivars include 'Honorine Jobert' (pure white, single, the most widely grown), 'September Charm' (single pink), 'Max Vogel' (semi-double pink), and 'Whirlwind' (semi-double white). Japanese anemones are slow to establish in their first year but become progressively robust, eventually spreading by underground stolons to form dramatic colonies. They are largely deer-resistant and an outstanding choice for filling the autumn shade garden with graceful color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in full to part shade; Japanese anise is a slow-growing evergreen that thrives in conditions where many broad-leaved evergreens fail — deep shade, dry shade under trees, and difficult urban positions. It is completely heat-tolerant and is more adaptable to humid Gulf Coast conditions than its native range in Japan might suggest.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to part shade; Japanese anise is a slow-growing, densely leafy evergreen shrub native to Japan and Taiwan, closely related to Florida anise (Illicium floridanum) but with wider cold hardiness and glossier foliage with a strong, pleasant anise-clove fragrance when crushed. In spring it produces small, cream-white to pale-yellow star-shaped flowers with many narrow petals — understated but charming close up, with the same star pattern as culinary star anise (I. verum) though unrelated in flavor. The foliage is the primary landscape asset: thick, lustrous, deep-green leaves densely arranged on upright stems creating a solid, refined mound of evergreen texture in shade gardens where few alternatives exist. It is outstanding as a shade-garden shrub under large trees, as an evergreen screen in shade, and in combination with hostas, hellebores, and woodland ferns. CAUTION: all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — the seeds resemble and may be confused with culinary star anise.

common_name: Japanese Aralia (Bold Tropical-Looking Deep-Shade Evergreen Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Fatsia japonica is one of the few large shrubs that performs well in deep shade — it is an outstanding choice for north-facing exposures, under building overhangs, and under large trees where other shrubs fail to thrive.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Japanese Aralia (Fatsia japonica) is one of the most bold-textured, tropical-looking evergreen shrubs available for deep-shade garden positions in the Gulf South — a native of coastal Japan and Korea that produces very large (12–18 inch across), deeply lobed, palmate, glossy dark-green leaves on long petioles, creating an extraordinarily lush and dramatic visual effect in shaded garden spaces. The leaves are genuinely large — among the biggest of any hardy evergreen shrub commonly grown in the Gulf South — and their tropical character is so convincing that Fatsia can appear exotic and out-of-place in naturalistic settings but is perfectly at home in bold subtropical shade designs. In November–December, Fatsia produces large clusters of small, creamy-white flowers in rounded umbels arranged in compound panicles — a winter bloom when virtually no other shade shrubs are flowering — followed by small black berries that provide winter bird food. The winter flowering is unexpected and welcomed in the shade garden during the season's low point. Fatsia grows relatively quickly into a multi-stemmed shrub that spreads by suckers and can form substantial clumps. The plant is remarkably tolerant of deep shade, dry soil (once established), coastal salt spray, urban air pollution, and root competition — a combination of tolerances that makes it one of the most versatile and reliable large evergreen shrubs for difficult Gulf South shade positions. Pruning to reduce height or remove suckers is best done in late winter or early spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, moist, fertile loamy soil in partial shade; Japanese arborvitae grows naturally in humid mountain forests of Japan and requires adequate moisture and humidity — does not tolerate hot, dry, exposed conditions. Thrives in cool, maritime Pacific Northwest climates.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, moist, fertile loamy soil in partial shade; Japanese arborvitae (hiba arborvitae) is the sole species of its genus — a large, impressive conifer from the humid mountain forests of Japan, closely related to Thuja but with distinctly larger, more robust, glossy-green scale leaves and a bold, dramatic texture compared to the finer-textured arborvitaes. The undersides of the branchlets show highly distinctive large, butterfly-shaped white stomatal markings on a dark green background — one of the most ornamentally striking foliage patterns of any conifer. The wood (hiba wood, Japanese: hiba) is exceptionally durable, aromatic, and rot-resistant — valued in Japan for temple construction, shrine buildings, and traditional Japanese architecture. The oils extracted from hiba wood have antifungal and antibacterial properties. In cultivation, it thrives in the cool, moist Pacific Northwest climate of the US and in the UK, where it is more commonly grown than in most of North America. An outstanding specimen conifer for large gardens in cool, humid climates.

plant_note: Divide rhizomatous colonies or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Japanese ardisia spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing, evergreen carpet and is an excellent low-maintenance groundcover for problem shade areas.
directions: Divide rhizomatous colonies or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Japanese ardisia (marlberry, senryo-alternative) is a low-growing, spreading, evergreen Asian shrub that forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover in shaded conditions — the toothed, glossy, oval leaves in whorled clusters give the plant a neat, refined appearance throughout the year. Small, white, nodding flowers in summer are followed by clusters of brilliant red berries that persist through winter and into the following spring, providing attractive color at a season when little else is colorful in the shade garden. Plants spread by underground stolons to gradually colonize shaded areas, creating dense, uniform coverage under trees and in woodland settings. Much more cold-hardy than the invasive coral ardisia (A. crenata) and native to similar garden conditions. 'Hakutsuru' (white berries), 'Chirimen' (crinkled leaves), and 'Nishiki' (variegated) are cultivar selections.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide established clumps in spring; Japanese aster is more mildew-resistant and longer-blooming than most Symphyotrichum asters and does not require staking. Divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. The double-flowered cultivar 'Blue Star' (white with a hint of lavender, pompon-like center) is particularly ornamental and widely available.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Japanese aster is an East Asian native that offers several practical advantages over the North American native asters (Symphyotrichum) commonly grown in temperate gardens — notably its exceptional resistance to powdery mildew (which disfigures many native asters by midsummer), its compact, non-floppy habit that rarely needs staking, and its exceptionally long bloom season from June through October, a span of nearly five months. The flowers are typical small asters — white to pale lavender-blue with a yellow central disc — but produced with remarkable freedom and duration from midsummer well into fall. The cultivar 'Blue Star' has semi-double to double flowers with a distinctive pale lavender-blue, pompon-like, quilted center surrounded by short ray petals — a unique and refined flower form unlike conventional aster flowers. Outstanding for the middle of the summer border where a reliable, long-blooming, mildew-free plant in white-to-pale-blue is needed from midsummer through fall. Often performs better as a garden plant than the more charismatic native asters due to its mildew resistance and more compact habit.

common_name: Japanese Aucuba (Glossy Deep-Shade Evergreen Shrub with Red Winter Berries)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Aucuba is dioecious — plants are either male or female, and both are needed for the female plant to produce its ornamental red berries; plant at least one male within 30–40 feet of female plants.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Japanese Aucuba (Aucuba japonica) is one of the most reliable and widely planted deep-shade evergreen shrubs for Gulf South landscapes, valued for its ability to maintain attractive, glossy, large-leafed evergreen presence in positions of deep, dry shade under large trees where most other shrubs fail completely or perform poorly. The large (4–8 inch), glossy, dark green leaves are the primary ornamental feature in the all-green form — clean, lustrous, and bold-textured throughout the year. Female plants produce clusters of bright scarlet to red berries from December through spring, providing significant winter ornamental interest and bird food; the berry display requires a male pollinator plant nearby. The gold-dust variegated form (A. japonica 'Variegata') with its yellow-spotted leaves is the most frequently grown and most ornamentally dramatic selection — the bold yellow spots on glossy dark-green leaves create a luminous effect in deep shade that no other plant quite matches. Aucuba is exceptionally shade-tolerant, performing in the deep dry shade under large trees where even cast iron plant (Aspidistra) and other ultra-tough shade plants grow poorly. The tolerance for drought, dense shade, and root competition gives Aucuba a practical advantage in Gulf South landscapes that few other evergreen shrubs can match. Avoid direct sun and wet, poorly drained soil — both cause leaf scorch and root rot respectively. An excellent choice for north and east exposures under building eaves.

plant_note: Divide established rhizomatous colonies in spring or plant container stock in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; Japanese bamboo fern spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form a colony in appropriate moist, shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; Japanese bamboo fern is a distinctive fern with unusually large, pinnate fronds where the pinnae (leaflets) are broad and undivided — resembling bamboo leaves more than typical fern fronds. The fronds are held on long, arching stems, creating an elegant, flowing effect quite unlike the lacy texture of most ferns. New growth in spring emerges in shades of yellow-green to lime green before maturing to medium green. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a graceful colony in moist shade. In zone 9, it provides a bold, unique foliage texture in the shade border — different from all other commonly available shade plants. The cultivar 'Flavomaculata' has yellow blotches along the midrib of each pinna, creating a variegated effect.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown shrubs in spring; Japanese beautyberry is more compact than American beautyberry (Callicarpa americana) and better suited to smaller gardens. It blooms and fruits reliably even when cut to the ground each spring — a common practice to maintain compact form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; Japanese beautyberry produces the most vivid violet-purple berries of any ornamental shrub — small, glossy, jewel-like fruits clustered in dense rings along arching stems in late summer and fall, giving a color intensity that photographs cannot fully capture. The effect is stunning both in the landscape and in cut floral arrangements. The foliage turns light yellow in fall before dropping to reveal the berries even more prominently against the bare stems. Unlike American beautyberry (C. americana), which can reach 8–10 feet and become ungainly, Japanese beautyberry stays more compact at 3–6 feet and is better behaved in the border. White-berried ('Leucocarpa') and pink-berried ('Albibaccata') cultivars offer interesting color variations alongside the typical violet-purple.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-aerated soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese bird nest fern thrives in the warm, humid, shaded conditions of Gulf Coast and tropical gardens and is outstanding for shade beds, woodland paths, and shaded patios.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; keep the center crown (the growing point) free of debris and avoid wetting it during watering. Asplenium antiquum (Japanese bird nest fern) is a large, elegant fern from Japan and East Asia producing broad, undivided, strap-shaped, glossy, medium-green fronds 18–30 inches long arranged in a spreading, vase-like rosette around a central cup — the 'bird nest' shape that gives this group of ferns its common name. Unlike the common bird nest fern (A. nidus) with nearly flat, undivided fronds, A. antiquum has gently ruffled, wavy frond margins and a more refined, upright form. In humid, tropical and subtropical gardens (zones 9–11), it thrives outdoors in shade under large trees, along shaded paths, and in understory gardens, creating a bold, architectural statement with its large, glossy fronds. As a houseplant or shade container plant, it is equally outstanding. Grow in acidic, well-drained potting mix that retains moisture; never allow the root ball to dry out completely, but avoid waterlogged conditions. The plant is virtually pest-free in outdoor conditions in warm, humid climates.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Japanese black pine is exceptionally salt- and wind-tolerant, making it the premier coastal landscape pine in the eastern US. It performs well in sandy, well-drained coastal soils but struggles in clay or poorly drained conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Japanese black pine is the premier coastal landscape pine in North America — extraordinarily salt-tolerant and wind-resistant, developing the dramatic, asymmetric, wind-sculpted forms characteristic of shoreline pines in its native Japan. The paired (two-needle) needles are dark green and stiff. Widely used in formal Japanese gardens, bonsai (where it is the premier subject for pine bonsai in Japanese tradition), and coastal landscapes from Cape Cod to the Gulf Coast. The aggressive spring candle growth is the focus of Japanese bonsai 'candle-cutting' technique, which stimulates dense, compact needle growth. Highly susceptible to Pine Wilt disease (Bursaphelenchus xylophilus nematode) in parts of the eastern US — check with local extension services for current disease pressure. The most widely planted Japanese pine in American landscapes.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the blood-red color is most vivid in full sun but tolerates and looks excellent in partial shade. Critically important: remove any all-green shoots immediately and in their entirety — all-green reversion is the invasive form of Imperata and must never be allowed to persist.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese blood grass 'Red Baron' is one of the most visually striking ornamental grasses available, producing upright, narrow blades that emerge green at the base and deepen to an intense, blood-crimson red toward the tips — the color intensifying through summer and fall until the entire blade glows a brilliant red that appears almost translucent when backlit by the sun. It is outstanding as an accent plant among silver or chartreuse foliage, at the edge of water features, or in mixed containers. An important safety note: the cultivar 'Red Baron' (sold as Japanese blood grass) is the non-invasive selection that must be grown from vegetatively propagated red material only. Any all-green reverted shoots that appear must be removed and destroyed immediately, as the green form (cogongrass, Imperata cylindrica) is one of the world's most destructive invasive grasses, classified as a federal noxious weed in the US. Do not allow 'Red Baron' to produce flowers or seeds. Do not plant in warm climates (zone 9+) where conditions favor reversion.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese boxwood tolerates heat and humidity better than English boxwood, making it a common low-hedge choice across the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Japanese boxwood is a heat- and humidity-tolerant relative of Korean boxwood long used across the Southern United States for clipped hedges, foundation plantings, and parterre-style formal gardens, valued for its small, glossy, rounded leaves and dense, easily shaped growth. It handles the long, hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season better than English boxwood, which often struggles in southern zones, though it still requires sharp drainage since all boxwoods are prone to root rot in soggy soil. Shear one to two times a year to maintain a formal shape, or leave it looser and prune selectively for a more natural look, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the main pest to monitor in Southern plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich, moist soil slightly above grade in partial shade; camellia is critical about soil pH and drainage — it will not tolerate alkaline soil, heavy clay, or waterlogged conditions. Fall planting allows root establishment before the winter bloom season begins.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Japanese camellia is the quintessential flowering shrub of the American South, producing large, formal, rose-like flowers in red, pink, white, and bicolor combinations in late fall through early spring — when almost nothing else is in bloom. Over 30,000 named cultivars exist, ranging from single-flowered (most cold-hardy) to fully double (most spectacular). In zone 8–9 it is one of the most spectacular ornamental shrubs available: a mature, large-flowered camellia in full January bloom, covered in hundreds of perfect flowers, is one of the most breath-taking sights in any garden. It requires strongly acidic soil and will show iron and manganese deficiency chlorosis in neutral or alkaline conditions. Prune immediately after bloom in late spring before the following year's buds set. Scale insects and petal blight are the primary concerns — improve air circulation and treat scale with horticultural oil in late winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese cedar prefers moist, well-drained, humid conditions and grows well in the Southeast where summers are warm and humid. Avoid excessively dry or alkaline sites.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Japanese cedar (sugi) is Japan's national tree and most important timber tree, used in shrines, temples, and traditional architecture throughout Japan. The fragrant, reddish-brown wood is prized for its durability and beautiful grain. In gardens, the species has given rise to hundreds of cultivated varieties ranging from dwarf, globose, or prostrate forms for rock gardens to tall, columnar forms for screening. The straight species grows into a large, pyramidal tree with attractive, spirally arranged, bright green to blue-green foliage that turns bronze in cold weather. Particularly well-suited to the humid Southeast (zones 7–9) where it performs better than many other conifers. The cultivars 'Elegans', 'Yoshino', 'Black Dragon', and 'Radicans' are widely used in Southeast American gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Japanese clethra is more tree-like than the native summersweet (C. alnifolia) and suits larger garden spaces. Propagate from softwood cuttings in summer.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese clethra is a multi-stemmed large shrub or small tree from Japan that surpasses the popular native summersweet (C. alnifolia) in ornamental impact at a larger scale. The most distinctive feature is the exfoliating, cinnamon-colored bark that peels in attractive layers on mature stems — providing striking winter interest. The long, arching racemes of fragrant white flowers in midsummer attract countless butterflies and bees. Excellent fall color in shades of yellow and red. More tolerant of dry soil than C. alnifolia once established. An underused, three-season ornamental shrub for shaded woodland gardens, native plant borders, and naturalized settings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to full shade; Japanese euonymus is one of the most shade- and salt-tolerant evergreen shrubs available — tolerating deep shade, coastal salt spray, and air pollution. Highly susceptible to euonymus scale insect — monitor regularly and treat with horticultural oil as needed.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to full shade; Japanese euonymus is one of the most widely used evergreen hedge and foundation shrubs in the southeastern US and mild-climate gardens worldwide — valued for its exceptional tolerance of deep shade, salt spray, air pollution, and a wide range of soil conditions. The thick, glossy, dark green leaves with finely toothed margins are attractive year-round, and the many cultivars offer gold-edged ('Aureomarginatus'), silver-edged ('Argenteomarginatus'), and yellow-centered ('Aureus') variegated leaf forms. A key advantage over many evergreen alternatives is its tolerance of deep shade — growing and maintaining dense, attractive foliage even in the shade of buildings or under tree canopies where most evergreen shrubs become thin and leggy. The main pest is euonymus scale (Unaspis euonymi) — small white and gray scale insects that can defoliate and kill plants if left untreated. An essential versatile evergreen for shaded foundation plantings, formal hedging, and coastal gardens in zones 6–9.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in partial to full shade; Japanese evergreen oak grows as a small understory tree in Japanese forests, tolerating considerable shade in youth. More cold-hardy than other Asian evergreen oaks, surviving brief dips to 10°F when well-established.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in partial to full shade; Japanese evergreen oak (akagashi in Japanese) is one of the most beautiful and important evergreen forest trees of Japan, Korea, and China — a relatively small (by oak standards) evergreen tree with glossy, dark green, simple, lanceolate to elliptic leaves and attractive pale-brown, smooth bark. In Japan it is an important forest tree of the warm-temperate evergreen broadleaf forest (laurel forest) zone along the Pacific coast. More shade-tolerant as a young tree than almost any other oak — it can grow as a woodland understory tree under a partial canopy where most oaks would be severely light-limited. The name 'akagashi' (red oak) in Japanese refers to the reddish new growth rather than any classification similarity to North American red oaks. An excellent evergreen shade tree for southeastern US gardens where a refined, glossy-leaved evergreen tree (unlike the course evergreen oaks) is desired. Rarely available but rewarding when found.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in deep to partial shade in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in zone 4–9; Japanese Fairy Bells is a graceful woodland perennial from Japan, China, and Korea — producing arching, leafy stems and small, nodding, tubular cream-white flowers in spring followed by glossy black berries in fall — a refined addition to shade gardens alongside hostas, ferns, and Solomon's seals.
directions: Plant Disporum sessile in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part to deep shade; mulch with compost or leaf mold to maintain cool, moist soil; divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor; plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form attractive colonies. Japanese Fairy Bells is one of several Asian woodland plants that bring charm to the deeply shaded garden — related to the North American Disporum (Fairy Bells) but native to the rich forest floors of Japan, China, and Korea. The arching stems bear paired, ovate, ribbed leaves and small clusters of nodding, narrow, tubular, cream-white flowers at the tips in spring, followed in late summer and fall by small, round, glossy black berries. Several cultivars have been selected for exceptional foliage: 'Ki-fukurin' has gold-edged leaves, and various variegated forms are prized by collectors of Japanese woodland plants. The spreading rhizome system slowly colonizes woodland settings and pairs beautifully with hostas, hellebores, ferns, and other denizens of the shaded garden. Hardy and reliable in zone 4–9, going dormant in winter and re-emerging from the spreading rhizome system in spring.

plant_note: Divide and plant pups (offsets) in spring after all frost danger has passed, in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. In zones 5–8, mulch the rhizome heavily with 12–18 inches of straw or leaves in fall to protect from deep frost; the pseudostem dies to the ground but the rhizome re-sprouts vigorously each spring.
directions: Japanese Fiber Banana is the hardiest banana in the world, native to the Ryukyu Islands of southern Japan and widely grown worldwide for its ability to provide a lush, tropical effect even in cold climates where true tropical bananas cannot survive — the rhizome is reliably hardy to the ground in zone 5 with heavy mulching, producing new pseudostems up to 12–15 feet tall each growing season in warm, moist conditions. In zones 9–10 the pseudostem survives winter and can eventually produce small flower clusters, though the fruit is not culinary; the plant's value is entirely ornamental, providing dramatic tropical foliage and a bold vertical accent that transforms temperate gardens into apparent tropics for the summer season. Divide pups from the parent clump in spring and plant in the richest, most moisture-retentive soil available in full sun to partial shade; water generously throughout the growing season and fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer for maximum growth. In zones 5–7, cut the pseudostem to within 12 inches of the ground after frost and mulch the root zone with a foot or more of insulating material through winter.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; arguably the most floriferous crabapple species, with deep pink buds opening to white flowers in such abundance that the branches may not be visible at peak bloom.
directions: Plant in spring or fall in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Japanese flowering crabapple is among the most disease-resistant and reliably floriferous of all crabapple species, making it a lower-maintenance choice than many ornamental crabapple hybrids. Malus floribunda is a graceful, wide-spreading Japanese crabapple growing 15–25 feet tall with an equal or greater spread, famous for its spectacular spring display of deep rose-red to carmine buds that open to single white to pale pink flowers so profuse they completely cover the arching branches, followed by tiny (1/4 inch) red-and-yellow fruits that wildlife relish through fall and winter. It has outstanding resistance to apple scab, fire blight, and powdery mildew compared to many hybrid crabapples. Best used as a specimen tree where its graceful, weeping habit and spring floral display can be appreciated; needs full sun to bloom well.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Japanese forest grass grows slowly and is most effective in mass plantings or as an accent against dark stones or deep-shade groundcovers.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Japanese forest grass is one of the finest foliage plants for shaded sites, forming graceful, cascading mounds of arching, golden-yellow or green-and-gold-striped leaves that move elegantly in the slightest breeze and glow with captured light even in deep shade. The golden-variegated 'Aureola' is the most popular cultivar. Avoid hot afternoon sun, which bleaches and burns the foliage; plants perform best in the dappled light of high deciduous canopy or on the north or east side of buildings. Growth is slow but the plant is very long-lived once established. Divide in early spring every 4–5 years to reinvigorate.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade sheltered from wind; glaucidium absolutely must not be exposed to drying winds, drought, or summer heat.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade sheltered from wind; glaucidium requires consistently moist woodland conditions and will fail quickly in dry soil, strong sun, or heat. Glaucidium palmatum is a monotypic Japanese woodland perennial of singular beauty, producing large, deeply palmate, maple-like leaves and exquisite single mauve-to-lavender poppy-like flowers 2-3 inches across with prominent golden stamens in May. It is slow to establish and resents disturbance; established plants are long-lived and virtually pest-free in appropriate cool woodland conditions in the Pacific Northwest, upper Midwest, and New England.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins, ensuring each division retains several healthy roots and at least one growing point. Replant immediately at the same depth in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade. Water in well and keep consistently moist through the first season.
directions: Plant Japanese Hepatica in deep to dappled shade with fertile, humus-rich, reliably moist but well-drained soil; amend with leaf mold or compost before planting. Divide clumps carefully in early spring, replanting each section at the same depth and spacing divisions 6 to 10 inches apart. This variety resents disturbance, so handle the fleshy roots gently and water consistently until re-established. Named cultivars and double-flowered forms are best propagated only by division to preserve their characteristics.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall into rich, consistently moist woodland soil in a deeply shaded site; double dormancy means germination may be delayed across two winters, so patience and an undisturbed site are essential.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall into deeply amended, humus-rich soil in a cool, deeply shaded woodland position, pressing seed just below the surface and covering with a thin layer of leaf mold. Paris japonica exhibits double dormancy, meaning the root may emerge the first winter while the shoot does not appear until the second spring, so do not disturb the planting site for at least two full years. Once seedlings finally emerge, grow them on in consistent moisture and shade, protecting them from slug damage which can devastate the slow-developing shoots. Expect many years of patient cultivation before plants reach flowering size, but the extraordinary rarity and botanical significance of this record-genome species makes it a uniquely rewarding long-term project.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or early fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese holly is one of the most widely used foundation and hedge plants in the eastern US, valued for its fine texture, boxwood-like appearance, and tolerance of shearing.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese holly is a versatile evergreen shrub with small, dark-green, crenate (scalloped-edge) leaves that superficially resembles boxwood but is unrelated — it tolerates the same shearing and formal shaping, making it a popular boxwood substitute in regions where boxwood blight is problematic. The fine-textured, dense foliage is outstanding for formal hedges, mass plantings, and foundation shrubs. Small black berries are produced in fall and persist through winter but are inconspicuous. Key cultivars include 'Helleri' (very dwarf, spreading mound to 3×5 feet), 'Green Island' (open, spreading habit to 3–4 feet), 'Compacta' (dense, globular, 4–6 feet), and 'Sky Pencil' (dramatically narrow, columnar, 6–10 feet tall but only 2 feet wide). Japanese holly tolerates shade better than boxwood and performs reliably in zone 5–9. In zone 9, mulch root zone in summer to prevent heat stress.

Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly to strongly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Japanese holly fern tolerates more heat, drought, and deep shade than most ferns, making it one of the most adaptable and reliable ferns for Gulf Coast and Mid-Atlantic shade gardens. Cyrtomium falcatum is an evergreen Asian fern with a bold, coarse texture quite unlike most ferns; its upright to arching fronds are composed of large, glossy, dark-green, holly-like pinnae with a leathery texture that catches light in shade and remains handsome through winter, making it a standout for year-round interest in shaded borders. It is highly deer-resistant, tolerates clay soil better than most ferns, and is an outstanding choice for zones 7–10 as an evergreen groundcover under live oaks and magnolias; in zone 6 it is marginally hardy and may die back in cold winters.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Japanese honeysuckle is adaptable to almost any site condition but is classified as invasive across much of the eastern United States — consider planting native alternatives such as coral honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) instead.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil; Japanese honeysuckle is an extremely vigorous, twining evergreen vine with intensely fragrant white-to-yellow tubular flowers from late spring through summer that are one of the most recognizable scents of southern summers. However, it is classified as invasive or noxious across much of the eastern US, where it smothers native vegetation in forest understories and disturbed areas. For most planting situations, consider the native alternative coral honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) which is not invasive, hummingbird-pollinated, and equally ornamental. Japanese honeysuckle is useful for erosion control on steep, disturbed slopes where invasiveness is less of a concern.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; Japanese hornbeam grows naturally as an understory tree in Japanese forests and is more shade-tolerant and slower-growing than European hornbeam, making it appropriate for smaller garden spaces and partially shaded positions.
