plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; Kay Parris performs well in partial shade but blooms most prolifically with 6+ hours of direct sun.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Kay Parris is a named Southern magnolia cultivar selected for its superior cold hardiness, narrow columnar form, and early and prolific bloom — a combination of attributes that makes it one of the finest magnolias for zone 6–10 residential landscapes. The naturally narrow, upright habit (20–30 feet tall with a relatively tight 10–15 foot spread) fits medium-sized residential landscapes better than the broadly spreading species without requiring the extremely compact size of Little Gem. Kay Parris begins blooming at young age, producing large (6–8 inch), intensely fragrant white flowers from May through September in zone 9. The cultivar was selected and named by nurseryman David Parris for his wife Kay. A notable characteristic is the exceptionally cold-hardy performance for a Southern magnolia — Kay Parris has been successfully grown into zone 6 with protection, significantly colder than most Southern magnolia selections. The leaves show the characteristic glossy dark-green upper surface and reddish-bronze to cinnamon undersurface. The narrow form suits planting near buildings, driveways, and in limited spaces where the standard Southern magnolia would eventually overwhelm the landscape.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; keeled garlic naturalizes freely from self-sown seed and bulbils produced in the flower heads — it can spread aggressively in favorable well-drained, open garden soils. Subsp. pulchellum (purple-flowered) is more commonly grown ornamentally than the pink-flowered type species. The flowers are attractive to bees and butterflies. Mild garlic scent when foliage is bruised.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; keeled garlic is a European mountain allium — native to the rocky, subalpine meadows and open woodlands of central and southern Europe from the Alps to the Balkans — that is grown ornamentally for its airy, late-summer flower display: loose, open umbels of nodding to spreading, small, pink to reddish-pink to purple (in subsp. pulchellum) bells on slender stems, the individual florets having a pendulous grace that differs from the tight, spherical pompom-type alliums. The flower heads often contain a mix of open flowers and small bulbils — a propagation strategy that makes keeled garlic a prolific self-spreader in open, well-drained garden soils. The bloom period (July–August in most of Europe) provides ornamental value in the midsummer to late-summer garden at a time when many other bulbs have finished. Subsp. pulchellum, with richer purple-pink flowers on taller, more elegant stems, is the form most widely grown ornamentally and is sometimes sold as a separate entity. Outstanding for naturalizing in gravel gardens, dry rock garden slopes, and sunny border fronts where its self-seeding habit creates naturalistic colonies over time.

common_name: Kelvin Floodlight Dahlia (Giant Golden-Yellow Dinnerplate Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Kelvin Floodlight is a classic giant dinnerplate dahlia producing enormous, clear golden-yellow blooms on tall, sturdy plants, one of the most widely grown large-flowered exhibition and garden dahlias. Stake plants early since the very heavy blooms require support.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately, since Kelvin Floodlight produces some of the largest blooms of any commonly grown dahlia. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage a bushier, more floriferous plant. A longtime favorite in exhibition and garden circles, Kelvin Floodlight bears massive, clear golden-yellow, informal decorative blooms that can reach 10-12 inches across on strong, tall stems, giving it a genuinely dramatic presence in the summer and fall border. Its bright, pure yellow color holds up well through the season compared to some of the more subtly toned modern dahlia varieties, providing reliable, bold color from midsummer to frost with regular deadheading. Because the flowers are so large and heavy, disbudding side buds to focus energy into fewer, larger blooms is common practice for exhibition-quality flowers, though leaving buds intact still produces an impressive garden display. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial shade; kentia palm is the most tolerant of all palms of indoor low-light conditions and is the premier interior landscape palm. Outdoors it prefers shade or dappled light and moist, fertile, well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in partial to full shade; kentia palm is the world's most popular indoor palm and one of the most important ornamental plants in the global interior plant industry — exported from its tiny native range (Lord Howe Island, Australia) in the form of seeds and seedlings for over 150 years to supply interior landscape plantings worldwide. The graceful, arching, dark green pinnate fronds and the extremely high tolerance of low light, low humidity, and neglect make it the standard palm for hotel lobbies, office buildings, and living rooms. Outdoors in zones 9–11, kentia palm is an attractive garden palm for shaded or semi-shaded positions under larger trees, unusually shade-tolerant for a palm. The seed germination is notoriously slow and erratic (months to a year). One of the few palms genuinely adapted to deep shade — a valuable characteristic that distinguishes it from almost all other palms.

plant_note: Sow seed in early fall (45–65°F soil temperature) or early spring in well-prepared, fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Kentucky bluegrass establishes slowly from seed (2–4 weeks to germinate, 6–8 weeks to usable turf) but forms a dense, self-repairing sod via underground rhizomes once established. It goes dormant and turns tan during drought or summer heat; resume growth in fall.
directions: Sow in fall or early spring in well-prepared, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; Kentucky bluegrass is the premier cool-season lawn grass of the northern United States — the standard against which other turf grasses are measured for fine texture, dense sod, deep-green color, and ability to repair itself through underground rhizomes (stolons). It produces a rich, blue-green, fine-textured carpet that performs best in cool (55–75°F) temperatures of spring and fall, going summer-dormant in heat and drought only to green up vigorously in autumn. The key advantage over other cool-season grasses is its rhizomatous spread — unlike bunch-forming tall fescue or ryegrass, Kentucky bluegrass fills in bare spots and repairs foot-traffic damage through vegetative spread. Establishing a Kentucky bluegrass lawn is slower from seed than from sod, but the resulting turf is superior in long-term density and durability. It is commonly blended with perennial ryegrass (for fast establishment) and fine fescues (for shade tolerance) in premium lawn seed mixes.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by nicking the hard seed coat or soaking in hot water (not boiling) for 24 hours before planting. Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly alkaline to slightly acidic, deep soil in full sun. Caution: seeds and pods are toxic if ingested raw; roasting destroys the toxic alkaloids.
directions: Kentucky Coffeetree is one of the most architecturally dramatic of the eastern native trees, native to the bottomlands, river terraces, and moist upland woods of the central and mid-south United States from New York and Nebraska south to Tennessee and Oklahoma, immediately recognizable in winter by its massive, stout, few-branched silhouette, deeply ridged gray bark, and enormous, persistent, dark brown seed pods up to 10 inches long that hang through winter — one of the most bold and graphic of all bare winter tree forms. The enormous, doubly-pinnate leaves (up to 3 feet long and 2 feet wide) unfurl very late in spring and drop early in fall, giving it one of the shortest leafy seasons of any native tree; in late spring it produces hanging clusters of fragrant white flowers attractive to long-tongued native bees. The hard seeds were roasted and used as a coffee substitute by early settlers and Native American tribes (raw seeds contain toxic alkaloids destroyed by roasting); the pods were fed to pigs and cattle historically. Extremely drought-tolerant, pollution-tolerant, and adaptable to urban conditions once established; an outstanding underused native street and shade tree.

plant_note: Best planted in early spring in moist, well-drained woodland soil. Prefers sheltered spots near streams or in moist ravines that mimic its native rocky woodland habitat.
directions: Select a site in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil that mimics its native rocky streambank habitat. Plant container-grown specimens in early spring, backfilling with a mix of native soil and compost. Water deeply each week during the first two growing seasons to encourage a deep root system. White flower clusters emerge in late spring and give way to blue-black berries that are a valuable food source for migrating and resident birds throughout autumn.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants (named cultivars are preferred over seedlings for reliable flowering) in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Provide a very sturdy support structure — arbor, pergola, or strong trellis — capable of bearing the substantial weight of a mature plant.
directions: Kentucky Wisteria is the hardiest and most well-behaved of the native wisterias, native to the bottomland forests, streambanks, and moist woodland edges of the south-central United States from Illinois and Missouri south to Louisiana and Texas, producing in late spring (and often again in late summer) dense, fragrant, lavender-to-purple flower racemes 6–12 inches long that are visually spectacular on an arbor or pergola — and doing so while behaving far less aggressively than the invasive Japanese and Chinese wisterias that have escaped cultivation and naturalized throughout the southeastern United States. Named cultivars such as 'Blue Moon', 'Aunt Dee', and 'Thunderstruck' are reliable repeat-bloomers and are the preferred choice over seedlings, which may take years to bloom and produce inferior flowers. Unlike Asian wisterias, Kentucky Wisteria twines in a clockwise direction and is significantly less vigorous and easier to manage, though it still requires a strong support and annual pruning. Grow in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which promotes excessive foliage at the expense of flowers.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; seeds need darkness to germinate.
directions: Sow the fine seed in darkness indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, since light inhibits germination. Also called painted tongue, this variety bears sprays of velvety, deep-blue, trumpet-shaped flowers from summer until frost. It adds rich depth to mixed containers, borders, and cut arrangements while attracting pollinators. Provide full sun, rich well-drained soil, and support for the somewhat lax stems, deadheading to prolong bloom.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil, covering seeds about 1/4 inch, or start indoors a few weeks early. These 4 to 5 inch lime-green and frothy-white blooms dazzle in cottage-garden borders or massed with bachelor's buttons and snapdragons. The edible petals can dress up salads and desserts, and the long stems make superb cut flowers. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce mildew, and cut or deadhead often to keep blooms coming.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy to sandy-loam soil in full sun; Key Thatch Palm is highly salt-tolerant and thrives in coastal Florida conditions of Zone 10–11. Fresh seeds germinate in 2–4 months in warm, moist, well-drained medium.
directions: Key Thatch Palm is a small, slender native palm of the Florida Keys and Caribbean islands, growing in coastal strand, pine rocklands, and scrub habitats where its graceful trunk reaches 15–25 feet topped by a compact crown of fan-shaped leaves with distinctive silvery-white undersides that shimmer in the wind. The small, round white fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, other fruit-eating birds, and small mammals, and the supple, long-lasting leaves were traditionally harvested by Caribbean and Florida Keys communities for thatching roofs, weaving hats, and making baskets. Requiring full sun, excellent drainage, and high salt tolerance, Key Thatch Palm is an excellent choice for coastal landscapes in Zones 10–11 where frost is rare or absent, and its slender, non-invasive root system makes it appropriate for tight spaces near hardscape. Plant fresh seeds in warm, moist, well-drained soil in full sun for germination in 2–4 months; seedlings develop slowly for several years before accelerating in their characteristic warm, sunny, frost-free environment.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, strongly acidic, peaty or gravelly, well-drained to seepage-wet soil in partial shade to full sun; grass-of-parnassus grows in calcareous or acidic seeps, bog edges, and wet limestone glades — moist but never stagnantly flooded.
directions: Plant in moist, peaty or gravelly, slightly acidic to neutral, seepage-wet soil in partial shade to full sun in bog garden or seepage slope settings; grass-of-parnassus is a jewel-like small perennial of cold, wet seeps and bog margins, producing one of the most beautiful and architecturally distinctive flowers of the native flora — a pure white, waxy, five-petaled flower with distinctive green veining and unique, fringe-tipped staminodes (sterile stamens) that are thought to deceive pollinators by mimicking nectaries. The flowers appear in fall, unusually late for such a small, delicate plant. Not a grass at all despite the name, but rather a member of the saxifrage family. A challenging but rewarding native for bog gardens, seepage gardens, and constantly moist, cool, acidic garden settings.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions in moist to wet, fertile aquatic soil at pond margins or in very shallow water (0–3 inches deep); kidneyleaf mudplantain grows naturally in shallow, slow-moving water, pond margins, and muddy shores throughout the eastern US and is excellent for transitional water-to-land margins.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun at pond margins, in emergent zones, and in muddy shores; kidneyleaf mudplantain is a small native aquatic wildflower of still and slow-moving shallow water across the eastern US and tropical America, producing tiny clusters of delicate white and yellow flowers that provide nectar for small native bees and insects at the water margin. The kidney-shaped to oval floating leaves are bright, glossy green. The plant grows in the emergent zone — in muddy shores and water up to 3 inches deep — creating a low, creeping mat that stabilizes muddy pond edges and transitional zones. It is one of the most inconspicuous but ecologically important native aquatics, providing shallow-water cover for small fish, tadpoles, and aquatic invertebrates. Excellent for naturalizing the transitional zone between water and shore in native pond gardens.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring into dry, rocky, well-drained soil; cold stratification of 60–90 days improves seed germination if starting from seed, but transplants are the practical route to a flowering plant.
directions: Kidneyleaf Rosinweed is one of the most architecturally striking native perennials of the piedmont and Blue Ridge of the Carolinas and Virginia, where it grows on rocky, dry outcrops and open, well-drained woodland edges and granite barrens. The plant produces a single enormous, deeply kidney-shaped to cordate basal leaf up to a foot across, from which rises a tall, slender, almost leafless flowering stem topped with bright yellow, daisy-like flowers about 2 inches across that open in July and August. Once the deep taproot is established — a process that takes two to three years from a young transplant — the plant becomes remarkably drought-tolerant and virtually self-sufficient in lean, rocky soil without supplemental irrigation or fertilizer. The resinous seeds are relished by goldfinches, and the unusual growth form — a vast basal leaf paired with a wiry vertical stem — makes this an outstanding structural focal point in rock gardens, dry native meadows, and open woodland settings.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring as shoots emerge or in fall in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; kikutii hosta is a Japanese species prized by hosta specialists for its distinctive narrow, arching leaves and unusually late, prolific flowering in mid-to-late summer.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; kikutii hosta is a species hosta from southern Japan distinguished by notably narrow, channeled, deep green leaves that arch gracefully outward from the center of the clump — quite unlike the broad, flat leaves of most popular hosta cultivars. The plant flowers prolifically and later than most hostas, producing tall scapes bearing pure white, narrowly tubular flowers in August and September. Several interesting varieties exist, including var. caput-avis (with green-striped flower buds resembling a bird's head) and var. polyneuron (with exceptionally prominent veining). A collector's hosta particularly valued for its late-season flowering when most hostas have finished blooming. The narrow foliage type adds textural diversity to shaded borders dominated by broad-leaved hostas.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow when warm.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow when soil is warm, covering about 1/4 inch. This historic variety, the first white marigold introduced in 1975, produces large creamy-white blooms that are rare in the marigold world. Sturdy plants thrive in full sun and average soil and reward regular deadheading with continuous flowers. Grow near vegetables where they may help deter pests, and cut blooms for long-lasting bouquets.

common_name: Kimberly Queen Fern (Upright Heat-Tolerant Australian Sword Fern for Zone 9 Shade Gardens)
plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring through fall; Kimberly Queen Fern is one of the most heat-tolerant and sun-adaptable ferns available for zone 9 landscapes. Unlike Boston fern (Nephrolepis exaltata), which requires significant shade and high humidity and drops leaflets readily in wind or low humidity, Kimberly Queen Fern maintains its upright, compact form, tolerates more direct sun (morning sun to bright shade), and handles the low indoor humidity and outdoor heat of zone 9 much better. In zone 9, Kimberly Queen survives winter outdoors in protected spots near structures and often returns from the roots even after frost damage. The fronds are dark green, upright, and held neatly above the crown without the drooping habit of Boston fern — the more structured, columnar form makes Kimberly Queen particularly attractive in hanging baskets, containers, and landscape beds where a tidy, predictable form is desired.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil or containers with morning sun to bright shade. Water regularly but allow soil to approach dryness before rewatering. Kimberly Queen Fern is native to Australia and was introduced to American horticulture as an alternative to the ever-popular Boston fern (Nephrolepis exaltata) that would be better suited to the warmer, drier conditions of southern homes and landscapes. The Boston fern, despite its widespread popularity as a porch and patio plant, has significant limitations in warm, dry conditions: the fine, arching fronds drop leaflets (pinnae) readily when subjected to wind, low humidity, or temperature stress, creating constant maintenance and mess. Kimberly Queen Fern's fronds are shorter (to 4 feet) and held in a more upright, compact arrangement that resists leaflet drop under stress — a practical advantage for gardeners who want an attractive fern without constant cleanup. In zone 9's landscape applications, Kimberly Queen is one of the most commonly recommended shade ferns for screening, mass planting under trees, and container display on shaded patios and porches. The plant's Australian origin gives it better adaptation to the heat and occasional drought of zone 9 than most other fern species, while its tropical origins provide the moisture and warmth tolerance needed for Gulf Coast conditions. In the warmest zones (9b–11), Kimberly Queen behaves as a fully evergreen perennial; in zone 9a it may be damaged by hard frost but typically regenerates from the crown.

plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Kimi Moragne is a Hawaiian-bred plumeria cultivar with pink-blushed, yellow-centered flowers and a strong, sweet fragrance, popular among collectors and lei makers.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Kimi Moragne is a Hawaiian-bred plumeria cultivar producing flowers that blend soft pink outer petals with a warm yellow throat, a cheerful bicolor combination carrying the strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance prized for lei-making and garden display alike. It is a reliable, well-branched grower that produces flower clusters generously through the warm season. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes.

common_name: King Alfred Daffodil (Classic Large Golden Trumpet Daffodil)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; King Alfred is the archetypal large trumpet daffodil that popularized the type, though in zone 9 daffodils generally do not perennialize reliably due to insufficient winter chilling and are often best treated as an annual spring bulb display or pre-chilled purchase.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting or braiding it, since the leaves recharge the bulb for next year's flowers. King Alfred is the name most people associate with the classic golden daffodil, a large-trumpet type with a long, flaring, deep yellow trumpet surrounded by broad yellow petals, made famous in the early 1900s as one of the first daffodils widely sold and planted at scale. True original King Alfred stock has become rare in commerce and much of what is sold under the name today is actually a similar, very close modern strain, but the bold golden trumpet form it popularized remains the benchmark image of a classic daffodil. It naturalizes well in climates with sufficient winter chill and is completely deer- and rodent-resistant.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light with high humidity (60–80%) and very excellent drainage; Anthurium veitchii is strictly a tropical collector's plant in zone 9, requiring consistently warm temperatures and cloud-forest humidity conditions. Mount on a bark slab like an orchid for the most natural and healthy growth — the pendant leaves hang dramatically from an elevated position. Do not let the plant sit in water. New leaves emerge vertically and slowly unfurl; avoid disturbing them during this process. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on bark or in a hanging basket in bright indirect to moderate shade — King Anthurium's pendant leaves require vertical space to hang freely and display their full ornamental effect. Anthurium veitchii is a spectacular epiphytic anthurium from the cloud forests of Colombia, named for John Gould Veitch, the Victorian-era plant collector and nurseryman who introduced many South American aroids to cultivation. The species is distinguished from all other commonly grown anthuriums by its extraordinary leaves: enormously elongated, strap-shaped or tongue-shaped pendant leaves that in mature specimens can reach 4–6 feet in length, deeply and regularly corrugated (quilted) with a parallel rib pattern, rich bright emerald-green, and hanging gracefully downward from the plant's center — giving the plant the unmistakable presence of a large, dangling exotic that has earned it the title 'King Anthurium.' Young plants produce smaller, more erect leaves that gradually elongate and develop the characteristic corrugated texture and pendant habit as the plant matures. The flowers are the typical Anthurium green-white spathe, inconsequential compared to the dramatic foliage. Anthurium veitchii is among the most valued and sought-after collector aroids worldwide precisely because well-grown mature specimens with fully-developed pendant leaves are extraordinarily beautiful and genuinely rare in cultivation. All parts toxic.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; violas thrive in cool spring and fall.
directions: Sow seed in darkness indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow in cool spring or fall weather. 'King Henry' forms neat little mounds of richly colored royal-purple flowers ideal for garden edges and containers. Violas love cool weather, making them perfect for spring bulb cover or fall color after annuals fade. Grow in part shade with moist soil, deadhead to prolong bloom, and expect self-sowing in favorable spots.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; king palm grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and is one of the faster-growing palms for subtropical landscapes. Frost-sensitive — protect young plants below 28°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile to average, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; king palm is one of the most attractive and widely planted palms in subtropical and warm-temperate regions worldwide — a graceful, fast-growing palm with a distinctive, smooth, gray-green trunk, a bright green crownshaft (the trunk extension formed by the tightly overlapping leaf bases), and a full crown of arching, bright green pinnate fronds. Native to the subtropical rainforest margins of coastal Queensland and New South Wales, Australia, it grows naturally in semi-shade along stream banks. The clusters of bright red fruits produced beneath the crownshaft are ornamental. More cold-sensitive than California fan palm or Canary Island palm. Widely used as a street, avenue, and specimen palm in California, Florida, Hawaii, Australia, and the Mediterranean. Grows in partial shade — unusual tolerance for a large, pinnate-leaf palm.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in sharply drained, lean, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), phosphorus-poor soil in full sun; king protea is fatally sensitive to phosphorus toxicity — never use standard garden fertilizers or composts with phosphate. Use only protea-specific or native plant (Proteaceae) fertilizer. Excellent drainage is non-negotiable; wet feet are the primary cause of death.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, acidic, phosphorus-poor soil in full sun; king protea is South Africa's national flower — the most iconic member of the Proteaceae family and the largest protea species — producing extraordinary globe-shaped flower heads 8–12 inches across with ring upon ring of petal-like bracts in shades of pale silvery-pink to deep rose-crimson surrounding a central dome of silvery-gray florets, the whole resembling a vast artichoke or a jeweled crown. Blooms appear in late winter through summer on plants typically 3–7 feet tall and nearly as wide. It is the dominant species in the South African fynbos (heathland) and requires the same conditions — excellent drainage, lean, low-fertility, low-phosphorus, slightly acidic soil, full sun, and Mediterranean-style dry summers with winter moisture. Phosphorus toxicity from ordinary fertilizers or manure kills it rapidly. Outstanding as a cut flower of extraordinary longevity (lasts 2–3 weeks in a vase). Succeeds in California, coastal Southern California, and similar Mediterranean-climate warm-winter gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost, or direct sow in spring.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in spring, barely covering it. Opulent apricot-toned double blooms stand tall and firm on strong stems, adding elegance to beds and bouquets. China asters make excellent, long-lasting cut flowers and appreciate full sun and rich, well-drained soil. Rotate planting sites each year to avoid soilborne disease, and stagger sowings for a longer season of blooms.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; transplant after frost.
directions: Surface-sow the seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, pressing it in since light aids germination. Papery silvery-rose blooms open into delicate crowns that hold their color beautifully when dried. Well-branched plants reach a good height and supply abundant stems for fresh and everlasting arrangements. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and cut flowers just before they fully open for the best dried results.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; transplant after frost.
directions: Surface-sow the seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, pressing it in since light aids germination. Stately blooms unfurl in layers of soft silvery-white petals for a regal presence in beds and bouquets. Tall, well-branched plants are drought-tolerant once established and provide abundant stems for cutting and drying. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and harvest flowers just as they begin to open for the best dried displays.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; king's mantle is one of the most shade-tolerant of the flowering tropical shrubs and blooms reliably in conditions where full-sun shrubs would fail to flower — it is an excellent choice for shaded courtyards and partially shaded garden borders.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; king's mantle (bush clock vine, royal purple thunbergia) is a West African evergreen shrub of the family Acanthaceae that produces large, trumpet-shaped, deep-purple to violet flowers with pale-yellow to white throats continuously from spring through late fall — the flowers are among the richest and most deeply saturated purple-blue of any flowering shrub available for the Gulf Coast and tropical garden. The dark, metallic, deep-purple flower color against the glossy, dark-green, oval leaves creates a striking combination that remains outstanding throughout the long blooming season. Unlike most purple-flowering tropical plants that demand full sun, king's mantle blooms acceptably in partial shade, making it particularly valuable for lightly shaded garden areas where comparable purple-flowered plants would fail. It grows as a mounding, arching shrub with woody lower stems and softer, freely-branching upper growth that flowers on new wood. In zone 9 it may freeze back but regrows reliably from the roots in spring. Excellent as a specimen, informal hedge, or color accent in the partial-shade border.

common_name: Kirengeshoma (Japanese Wax Bells, Yellow Wax Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in consistently moist, deeply humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial to full shade; kirengeshoma is demanding about soil moisture and acidity — it will not tolerate dry or alkaline conditions and wilts dramatically between watering in summer heat.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deeply humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial to full shade; kirengeshoma is one of the most refined and unusual of all shade garden perennials — a tall, graceful Japanese woodland plant with majestic, deeply lobed, maple-like leaves on arching dark stems, followed by nodding clusters of pendulous, pale yellow, waxy tubular bells in late summer and fall, a season when few other shade plants flower. The flowers last for weeks and have a luminous, translucent quality. It is an outstanding late-season bloomer that fills the gap when hostas and ferns have finished. It requires acidic, consistently moist woodland soil and protection from afternoon sun and summer drought — mulch deeply and water regularly in summer. Combines superbly with late-season hostas, asters, and Japanese anemone in the shade garden.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; transplant after frost.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination. This ornamental oregano drapes in cascading layers of papery green and rosy-purple hop-like bracts that catch the light. Drought-tolerant and pollinator-friendly, it excels in containers, bouquets, and the front of sunny borders. Grow in full sun with sharply drained soil, avoid overwatering, and cut stems for fresh or dried arrangements.

plant_note: Direct sow on surface of well-drained, very lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after soil warms to 70°F+; press seeds lightly into soil surface — do not cover, as seeds need light to germinate; kiss-me-quick is a sprawling tropical ornamental annual related to moss rose (P. grandiflora) but with distinctly hairy stems and small, vivid magenta-pink to rose-purple flowers opening only in morning sun — a classic groundcover for hot, dry, sandy soils in Gulf Coast and tropical gardens.
directions: Surface sow on very lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; needs no fertilizer — excess fertility produces all foliage and few flowers; self-sows freely in tropical climates. Portulaca pilosa (kiss-me-quick, hairy purslane, or pink purslane) is a spreading, mat-forming tropical annual native to the Caribbean, tropical Americas, and warm parts of North America — a close relative of the popular ornamental moss rose (P. grandiflora) and the common edible purslane (P. oleracea). The plant covers itself in tiny, vivid, hot-pink to magenta, 5-petaled flowers from summer through fall, blooming prolifically throughout the growing season with each individual flower lasting only until midday (closing when cloud cover or heat arrives). The stems are covered with hairy, white, silky trichomes (the 'pilosa' = hairy, in the species name), giving the foliage a soft, silvery-white appearance. Like all Portulaca, it is extremely drought-tolerant, thrives in pure sand, and self-sows prolifically in tropical climates where it can naturalize and return annually. Kiss-me-quick is widely grown in Gulf Coast and tropical gardens as a carefree groundcover for hot, dry, difficult sites — sidewalk cracks, sandy berms, and rocky slopes — where more demanding plants fail. A cheerful, low-maintenance plant for challenging hot-dry spots.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; self-sows vigorously and will return year after year without replanting in mild climates — one of the easiest cottage garden annuals to establish.
directions: Direct sow seed on the soil surface after last frost — seed needs light to germinate; kiss-me-over-the-garden-gate is a tall, stately Victorian cottage garden annual that produces long, drooping chains of tiny rose-pink to deep crimson button-like flowers from summer until frost, creating a graceful, old-fashioned effect among dahlias, zinnias, and other cottage favorites. It grows very tall (5–7 feet) and may need staking in exposed sites; allow it to lean into neighboring plants as it does in traditional cottage borders. Self-sows prolifically once established, returning reliably each summer. The large, slightly hairy leaves and dramatic arching flower chains also attract butterflies and bees.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil in partial shade; Kleim's Hardy has notably smaller leaves and flowers than standard gardenia along with improved cold tolerance, and it blooms earlier in spring than most cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to morning sun. Kleim's Hardy is distinguished from most gardenia cultivars by its small, narrow, fine-textured leaves and smaller single-form flowers, giving it a more refined, delicate look than the bold, glossy-leaved standard gardenia. It also blooms earlier in spring than most gardenia cultivars and shows improved cold hardiness, letting it succeed in gardens at the cooler edge of typical gardenia range. Fragrance remains strong despite the smaller flower size, and the compact habit suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and smaller garden spaces. Consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential to avoid the chlorotic yellowing common to gardenias in alkaline conditions.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; likes cool weather.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. This shorter blend delivers a rainbow of lightly scented blooms on knee-high vines that need little or no support. It is ideal for a short trellis, hanging basket, or the front of a border and delights pollinators. Keep roots cool and evenly watered, and cut flowers regularly to prolong the display before summer heat.

common_name: Knock Out Rose (Red Knock Out Rose)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Knock Out roses require at least 6 hours of sun for adequate bloom production — do not plant in partial shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Knock Out rose is the single most significant development in landscape roses in the last century — introduced in 2000 by breeder William Radler after eighteen years of breeding for disease resistance and repeat bloom, it completely transformed the landscape rose market and is estimated to be the best-selling rose in American history with over 80 million plants sold in the first decade after introduction. The cherry-red, single flowers are produced in prolific, continuous flushes from spring until hard frost in zone 9 — a bloom frequency and duration that no traditional hybrid tea, floribunda, or shrub rose approaches. More importantly, Knock Out is essentially disease-immune: it shows extraordinary natural resistance to black spot (the primary rose disease in humid climates), powdery mildew, and rose rosette disease at levels that allow it to be grown without fungicide sprays in virtually all regions of the United States. In zone 9, the cherry-red flowers bloom through the entire warm season with brief pauses between flushes. Prune in late winter (February in zone 9) by cutting the entire plant back to 12–18 inches to stimulate vigorous new growth and maximum bloom. No deadheading is required — the plant is self-cleaning.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist to dry, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Geranium nodosum is exceptional among shade-tolerant hardy geraniums for its ability to bloom under dense tree canopy, in dry shade under shallow-rooted trees, and in difficult spots where other geraniums fail.
directions: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile to poor soil in partial to full shade; Geranium nodosum is remarkably adaptable to dry shade under mature trees — one of the few ornamental geraniums that thrives where other shade perennials struggle with root competition and summer drought. Geranium nodosum (knotted cranesbill) is a compact, rhizomatous hardy geranium native to mountain woodlands of southern Europe, producing deeply lobed, glossy, medium-green leaves and an extended succession of small but attractive funnel-shaped, lilac-pink to magenta flowers with white veining from late spring through midsummer and sometimes continuing into fall; it is evergreen or semi-evergreen in mild climates and one of the most shade-tolerant and drought-tolerant of all hardy geraniums once established. Particularly valued for its ability to thrive in 'problem shade' situations — dry, rooty, competition-laden zones under shallow-rooted trees like maples where most shade plants fail. Spreads slowly by rhizome without becoming invasive.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; knotted rush grows naturally in marshes, shallow pond margins, wet prairies, and stream banks across North America, particularly in the northern and central states where it grows in shallow standing water.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in shallow pond margins, wet prairie gardens, and rain garden wet zones; knotted rush is a small native rush of northern and central North America, growing naturally in the shallow water and saturated soil margins of ponds, marshes, and wet meadows. The stems are distinctively knotted or nodose — with visible swellings or nodes along the stem — a feature that gives the plant its common name. The compact, rounded, dark brown flower and seed heads appear at mid-stem. A fine-textured native for freshwater wet habitats that provides seed food for marsh birds and shorebirds. Self-sows into appropriate wet conditions. Combines naturally with sedges, native wetland wildflowers, and other small rushes at the margins of naturalistic water gardens and pond edges in ecological plantings.

plant_note: Plant corms or divisions in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April or fall September–November. Kobold establishes quickly and blooms in its first year from corms. Unlike most spike flowers that open from bottom to top, Liatris blooms top-to-bottom — an unusual and instantly recognizable feature. In zone 9 Liatris performs as a reliable perennial; mulch crowns lightly in summer to protect from intense heat. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly acidic soil — excellent drainage is essential; Kobold is a compact selection of Liatris spicata (blazing star or gayfeather), a native North American prairie perennial, selected for its shorter, sturdier stems (18–24 inches vs. 36–48 for the species) that resist flopping in garden conditions. The dense, fuzzy, magenta-purple flower spikes bloom from late June through August, opening their small florets from the top of the spike downward — an unusual characteristic that distinguishes Liatris from all other vertical spike flowers and makes it immediately recognizable to garden enthusiasts. Kobold is outstanding for cutting (the spikes last 1–2 weeks in a vase), for attracting butterflies and bumblebees, and for providing late summer color when many perennials have finished blooming. As a native prairie species, Liatris is extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established, thriving in the kind of lean, dry, hot conditions that kill many ornamental perennials — making it particularly well-suited to zone 9 landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; kobus magnolia does not like transplanting once established — plant in a permanent site. Trees grown from seed may take 10–30 years to bloom; grafted plants bloom in 3–5 years.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moisture-retentive, fertile to average soil in full sun to partial shade; kobus magnolia is a Japanese native and the parent of many important magnolia hybrids, producing abundant, slightly fragrant, white flowers with 9–12 petals in early spring before the leaves emerge — similar to star magnolia but on a larger, more tree-like plant. One of the most cold-hardy of the Asian magnolias, reliably hardy to zone 4. The Loebner magnolia hybrids (M. x loebneri), crosses of kobus with star magnolia, are particularly valued for combining cold hardiness with early, profuse blooming and are among the most reliable magnolias for northern gardens. Kobus itself is a stately, large specimen tree when old, eventually becoming a wide-spreading tree of considerable grace. The bark produces fragrant compounds used in Japanese temple incense.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container in zone 9; Kohleria eriantha cannot tolerate frost. It grows from scaly rhizomes — plant the rhizomes in spring in a well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix and allow the soil to approach dryness between waterings, as the rhizomes are prone to rot in wet soil. After flowering, the plant may die back partially in winter — reduce watering and resume in spring when new growth appears. Propagate from rhizome divisions, stem cuttings, or seed. The fuzzy stems and leaves distinguish Kohleria from similar gesneriads. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Kohleria eriantha flowers most abundantly in bright indirect light and will produce sparse blooms in dim conditions, though it tolerates lower light than many flowering houseplants. Kohleria eriantha is a rhizomatous gesneriad from Colombia and adjacent South America in the family Gesneriaceae, closely related to the African Violet (Saintpaulia) and Gloxinia (Sinningia) in the same plant family. The entire plant — stems, leaves, and calyxes — is covered with soft, reddish or white hairs that give it a distinctive furry, velvety texture (the specific epithet 'eriantha' means 'woolly-flowered'). The leaves are large, broadly oval, dark-green with a soft, hairy texture, arranged in opposite pairs on the upright stems. The tubular flowers are 1–2 inches long, orange-red with a yellow throat spotted with red dots, borne in axillary clusters along the upper portions of the stems over an extended bloom period from spring through fall. Modern Kohleria hybrids (often simply labeled 'Kohleria hybrid') are available in colors ranging from pink and red to orange, yellow, and bicolored forms, all retaining the characteristic fuzzy texture and tubular flower form that makes the genus distinctive in the gesneriad family. An underused but rewarding shade houseplant for zones where humidity can be maintained. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Kong Mosaic coleus is a tender perennial that can be kept as a houseplant over winter in cooler climates or maintained as a perennial in zone 9 where light freezes kill back the stems but the roots often resprout. Pinch flower spikes promptly as they appear — coleus flowers are insignificant and pinching redirects energy to larger, more colorful foliage. In zone 9 the long warm season allows Kong Mosaic to develop into a large, impressive specimen.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil or container mix; Kong Mosaic is part of the Ball Horticultural Kong series of coleus — the largest-leaved coleus commercially available — with individual leaves reaching 6–12 inches across in a spectacular mosaic of burgundy, rose-red, chartreuse, and cream in irregular, patchwork-like patterns that vary across each leaf. The scale of the Kong series foliage creates a tropical, dramatic effect unlike any other shade foliage plant — plants placed in shaded beds or large containers make an immediate bold statement that smaller-leaved coleus and impatiens cannot replicate. Coleus has become significantly more versatile since modern selections like the Kong series were developed for improved sun tolerance — Kong Mosaic can be grown in partial shade to nearly full sun in cooler climates, though shade conditions produce the richest, deepest color. In zone 9 partial shade to shade is preferred to prevent leaf scorch. The vivid, multicolored foliage performs throughout the warm season without needing flowers to maintain the ornamental display.

common_name: Kopper King Hardy Hibiscus (Bronze-Leaved Pink-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Kopper King is valued for its coppery-bronze foliage, an unusual contrast to the huge pale pink, red-eyed flowers, and it dies back completely to the ground each winter, emerging late in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season. Kopper King is a striking hardy hibiscus hybrid combining bold, dinner-plate-sized, pale pink flowers with a deep red central eye against dramatic bronze-copper foliage, a foliage color unusual among hardy hibiscus cultivars that makes the plant a strong focal point even before it flowers. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, often causing gardeners to worry it has died, so mark its location and be patient. It flowers from midsummer into fall on a large, robust, well-branched plant, and is generally pest-free and easy to grow given consistently moist soil.

plant_note: Sow seeds in late summer or early fall for spring germination; Korean angelica requires cold stratification and germinates best with exposure to winter cold. Sow direct where plants will grow permanently, as the deep taproot makes transplanting difficult. Allow plants to self-sow to maintain a colony.
directions: Sow seeds in fall in moist, fertile, humus-rich, partly shaded soil; Korean angelica is an exceptionally dramatic biennial or short-lived perennial from Korea and Japan that produces some of the most architecturally impressive flower heads in horticulture — enormous, domed umbels of deep burgundy-maroon flowers, 4–6 inches across, carried in large clusters at the top of stout, dramatically purple-flushed, hollow stems that can reach 6 feet. The entire plant is suffused with rich purple-maroon coloring — stems, leaf veins, flower stalks, and flower heads — making it unlike anything else in the garden. As a biennial, it germinates year one, flowers spectacularly in year two, sets abundant seed, and dies. In moist, partly shaded woodland garden settings it self-sows reliably to maintain a permanent colony. The flowers are magnets for butterflies, bumblebees, and other pollinators. Used medicinally in Korean traditional medicine.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to average, fertile to average loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean arborvitae grows naturally on cool, rocky mountain slopes of Korea and is more cold-hardy and compact than Western red cedar (Thuja plicata), often growing as a low, spreading shrub rather than a tree at high elevation.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to average, fertile to average loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean arborvitae is a distinctive and rarely grown species of arborvitae from the mountains of Korea — quite different in appearance from the familiar American arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis) or western red cedar (T. plicata). The foliage has striking silver-white stomatal marks on the undersides that create a beautiful bicolor effect of dark green above and silvery-white below when the branch tips are lifted or blown by wind. Naturally a variable species from low mounding shrubs at high elevations to narrow upright small trees at lower elevations. Aromatic foliage with a pleasant cedar scent when crushed. Rarely available from nurseries outside of specialist conifer growers, but increasingly of interest to gardeners seeking unusual conifers for their ornamental qualities. More compact and cold-hardy than giant arborvitae, making it appropriate for smaller gardens in colder climates.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Korean fairy bell is a refined, smaller-growing shade perennial best suited to cool-climate gardens where it is an outstanding foliage and flower plant for the woodland garden.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, spacing 12–18 inches apart; Korean fairy bell is a refined, compact shade perennial from Korea and northeast China, producing slender, branching stems 12–18 inches tall with oval, bright-green leaves and solitary, pendant, yellow-green bell-shaped flowers at the stem tips in mid-spring. The flowers give way to single, round, ornamental orange berries in fall that are an attractive fruiting accent in the woodland garden. Disporum uniflorum is an elegant, slow-growing plant that thrives in cool, moist, humus-rich conditions and is best suited to gardens in the northern half of its hardiness range where summer temperatures remain moderate; it is not heat-tolerant and performs poorly in hot, dry summers. Combine with other small-scale shade plants such as wild ginger, bunchberry, and native ferns for a refined woodland effect.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Korean feather reed grass is one of the very few ornamental grasses that performs acceptably in partial shade — a significant advantage in gardens where most grasses would fail to flower or develop properly.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean feather reed grass is a late-flowering Asian ornamental grass that sets it apart from most others by producing its dense, bottlebrush-like, pinkish-silver flower panicles in late summer and early autumn (August–October) rather than in early summer — arriving as many spring-blooming grasses have already set seed and begun to decline. The fluffy, initially pink-tinted, feathery panicles age to a warm, creamy-tan that persists through winter, providing months of multi-season interest on the upright but gracefully arching stems. Importantly, it is one of the very few ornamental grasses that performs in partial shade — maintaining reasonable flowering and attractive foliage in dappled light where most grasses would etiolate and fail to flower. This shade tolerance makes it particularly valuable for partially shaded borders and woodland edges where ornamental grasses are typically unusable. Compact, clump-forming, and non-invasive. Excellent combined with hostas and late asters in partially shaded autumn borders.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean fir prefers moist, cool conditions and does not tolerate hot, dry summers well. Best in zones 5–7 with cool, moist summers. More compact and ornamental than most native firs.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean fir is the premier ornamental fir for garden use, valued above all other firs for a remarkable trait — it begins producing cones at a very young age (sometimes at 5–10 years old), and the upright cones are extraordinarily beautiful, bright purple-violet fading through blue to brown as they mature, prominently displayed on upright branches. The short stature compared to native firs makes it manageable in residential gardens. Cultivated varieties include 'Silberlocke' (with upturned needles that display their white undersides), 'Horstmann's Silberlocke' (more compact), 'Kohout's Ice Breaker' (very compact), and many others. Native to the mountains of South Korea. The compact size, precocious cone production, and beautiful cone color make this the most horticulturally valuable of all the firs for home gardens.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in shade; Korean rock fern is compact enough for small gardens and containers. It tolerates dryness under trees better than many ferns once established and is semi-evergreen to evergreen in mild climates.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; Korean rock fern is one of the most compact, well-behaved, and versatile hardy ferns available, producing neat, glossy, dark-green, finely divided fronds that are more rigid and leathery than most ferns and remain semi-evergreen to evergreen in zones 7–9. The narrow, lance-shaped fronds have small, holly-like pinnae with spiny-toothed margins that give the frond a distinctive texture. It stays under 18 inches and is suitable for small gardens, containers, woodland borders, and shaded corners where larger ferns would overwhelm the space. Native to rocky woodland slopes of Japan, Korea, and China, it is more tolerant of dry shade than most ferns once established. Excellent for the front of a shaded border alongside hostas, hellebores, and woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean spice viburnum blooms on old wood, so avoid pruning until after flowers fade in late spring.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean spice viburnum is arguably the most sweetly fragrant of all flowering shrubs — the dense, rounded heads of small pink buds opening to white flowers in early spring produce an extraordinary spicy-sweet perfume that fills the garden on warm spring days and can be detected from 50 feet away. The fragrance is strongest on still mornings and in the evening warmth. The rounded shrub is neat and symmetrical, reaching 4–5 feet tall and wide over many years, with dull dark-green leaves that turn wine-red to burgundy in fall where summers are not too hot. It performs best in zones 4–7 where winter cold is reliable — in zone 8 and warmer, it often fails to bloom well due to insufficient winter chilling hours and may decline over time. Site it where the fragrance can be fully appreciated: near the entrance, beside a path, or outside a frequently used window. Prune lightly if needed immediately after flowering to maintain shape.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean stewartia resents root disturbance — do not move after planting. Site in a protected location away from hot afternoon sun and drying winds. Mulch to maintain even soil moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Korean stewartia is a four-season specimen tree widely regarded as one of the most beautiful of all small ornamental trees. In summer, it produces large, white, camellia-like flowers with showy orange stamens over several weeks. As summer transitions to fall, the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and purple. In winter and spring, the intricate, flaking bark — peeling in irregular patches to reveal a mosaic of gray, orange, tan, and cinnamon — provides some of the most dramatic winter interest of any tree. The tree is pyramidal in youth and gradually broadens with age. More heat-tolerant than Japanese stewartia and slightly more adaptable to zone 8 conditions. One of the finest specimen trees for the transitional South, performing best in partial afternoon shade in zones 7–8.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings under mist in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Cornus kousa is significantly more resistant to dogwood anthracnose and borers than the native Cornus florida, making it the preferred choice for landscapes where these pests are a serious concern.
directions: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kousa dogwood is a Japanese, Korean, and Chinese small deciduous tree that blooms approximately three to four weeks later than the native flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) — producing its characteristic four-pointed, star-shaped, white or pink bracts in June rather than April — and is considered by many gardeners to be even more ornamental over the full year. The pointed, white (occasionally pink) bracts surround the small true flowers in the center and remain attractive for 4–6 weeks. In late summer and fall, large, bumpy, pink-red, strawberry-like composite fruit clusters ripen and are edible (sweet, slightly grainy, and pleasant-tasting, used to make jam in Japan). The fall foliage is outstanding — purplish-red to scarlet. On mature specimens the bark becomes attractively mottled and exfoliating. It is significantly more resistant to dogwood anthracnose disease and dogwood borer than C. florida — one of the primary reasons for preferring it in areas where these pests are problematic. 'Milky Way' (very heavy flower production), 'Satomi' (deep-rose-pink bracts), and 'Wolf Eyes' (white-variegated leaves) are outstanding cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kramer's Supreme is unusually tolerant of cold — one of the most cold-hardy red camellia cultivars available, surviving temperatures to 10–15°F.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kramer's Supreme is one of the most significant Camellia japonica cultivars because it is reliably fragrant — a quality extremely rare in camellias, which are otherwise almost completely scentless. The large (4–5 inch), peony-form to informal double, vivid turkey-red flowers have a light but distinct, pleasant fragrance that is surprising in a camellia, making this cultivar uniquely valuable for gardens where fragrance is a priority. The flower color is an especially vivid, pure turkey-red without the blue-purple tones of Mathotiana — a clean, electric red that is among the most brilliant flower colors available for the winter garden. Kramer's Supreme blooms in midseason (November–February in zone 9), providing brilliant red winter color when few other shrubs are in bloom. Its exceptional cold hardiness (to zone 6, surviving temperatures to 10–15°F) makes it the most reliably winter-hardy red camellia cultivar, growing further north than most other japonica types. The upright to spreading habit grows 6–10 feet tall with regular pruning. In zone 9, Kramer's Supreme is an outstanding long-lived landscape shrub that requires only light pruning after bloom and supplemental iron (from acidic fertilizer) to prevent chlorosis in alkaline Gulf Coast soils.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Krossa Regal develops a distinctive upright vase-shaped form rather than the mounded habit of most hostas, creating an architectural accent in the shade garden.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Krossa Regal is among the most structurally distinct hostas — rather than forming the typical low mound, it produces large, strongly upright, arching, glaucous blue-gray leaves that create a dramatic vase-shaped form 28–36 inches tall and up to 5 feet wide at maturity. This architectural habit makes it an outstanding focal point in shaded borders, particularly when contrasted with the mounding form of surrounding plants. The tall flower scapes — often reaching 4–5 feet — produce pale lavender flowers that are among the most ornamental of any hosta. The thick, waxy, blue-gray leaf surface is notably resistant to slug damage. It is slow to establish but very long-lived, forming impressive, multi-crowned clumps over many years. Provide consistent moisture and mulch heavily; the upright leaves funnel rainwater to the crown, helping maintain soil moisture during dry spells.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; kuma bamboo spreads by underground rhizomes and can colonize large areas over time — use as a vigorous groundcover or install a rhizome barrier to define boundaries.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to consistently moist soil in shade to partial shade; kuma bamboo is a low-growing Japanese dwarf bamboo celebrated for its dramatic winter foliage effect — the leaf margins die back in cold weather to create a striking natural cream or parchment-colored border around each dark green blade, giving the plant an appearance of variegation through winter and early spring. This leaf withering is a natural adaptation, not a sign of damage, and the distinctive marginal color disappears when fresh green growth emerges in summer. Growing only 2–4 feet tall, it forms a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover ideal for shaded areas under trees, Japanese-style gardens, and naturalistic woodland settings in zones 6–9. Like other Sasa species, it spreads moderately by rhizomes and should be managed to prevent it from overrunning smaller companion plants.

subcategory: Australian native drought-resistant ornamental shade tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained to dry, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline to neutral soil in zone 8–11; Kurrajong is a beautiful, long-lived, drought-hardy Australian native tree from the dry slopes, woodlands, and grasslands of New South Wales and Victoria — bearing attractive, cream-white, bell-shaped flowers with red and purple interior spotting in summer, variable, lobed or unlobed lustrous leaves, and boat-shaped woody seed pods with edible seeds — an outstanding shade tree for hot, dry garden conditions.
directions: Plant Brachychiton populneus in full sun in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, deep soil (it develops a strong taproot); it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and adapts to alkaline, heavy clay soils that challenge most trees; avoid overwatering, especially in youth. Kurrajong is a superlative drought-tolerant ornamental tree for hot, dry climates — native to the slopes, foothills, and grasslands of inland southeastern Australia where it is drought and heat adapted. The leaves are remarkably variable on the same tree: some deeply multi-lobed, others simple and oval, giving the tree a naturally textured, organic appearance. The cream to white, cup-shaped flowers with red and purple interior spotting are produced in summer in clusters and are attractive up close. The woody seed pods (follicles) split to reveal yellow, edible seeds surrounded by irritating hairs — the seeds are roasted to remove the hairs and then eaten or ground into flour; Aboriginal Australians roasted the seeds as a significant food and ground the inner bark fiber for fiber and string. The fat-storing capacity of the young roots was also exploited as a water source in dry conditions. A valuable shade tree for Texas, the Gulf Coast, and dry-summer climates where it withstands drought, alkaline soils, and heat that defeat most ornamental trees. Moderately frost-hardy to about 18–20°F.

plant_note: Plant nursery shrubs in fall or early spring in a sheltered, partly shaded spot.
directions: This evergreen camellia shrub is best planted from a nursery specimen in fall or early spring in a location with morning sun and afternoon shade, sheltered from harsh wind. It thrives in acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, so mulch the shallow roots and avoid planting too deeply. From winter into spring it bears playful blooms of white or soft pink streaked with red, with no two flowers alike. Water regularly during dry spells and prune lightly just after flowering to shape the plant.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Labrador violet is an outstanding self-seeding groundcover for shaded areas, particularly valued for its purple-flushed foliage that adds color contrast to green shade plantings.
directions: Plant in spring or fall in moist, humus-enriched soil in partial to full shade; Labrador violet self-seeds freely once established and naturalizes into a charming, informal ground cover under trees and in shaded woodland gardens. Viola labradorica is a native North American violet of cool woodland, alpine, and subarctic habitats, distinguished from other violets by its distinctively purple-flushed to dark violet foliage — particularly striking in light shade where the leaves often take on a nearly burgundy coloration that contrasts beautifully with the tiny, lavender-purple flowers produced from early spring through summer. It is much smaller than most violet species, forming low mats only 3–6 inches tall that spread by self-seeding and gradually colonize an area; the heart-shaped leaves with their characteristic purple flush make it instantly recognizable among other shade groundcovers. An excellent, low-maintenance companion to hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Labyrinth is a large formal decorative dahlia producing warm blush-to-orange blooms that shift in tone across the flower, a popular cut-flower variety alongside Café au Lait among floral designers. Stake plants early since the heavy blooms on tall stems require support.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake immediately. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching and more blooms per plant. Labyrinth is a large formal decorative dahlia bearing full, densely petaled blooms that open a soft peachy-blush at the center and deepen toward warm orange-apricot tones at the outer petals, a complex, layered coloring that has made it a favorite alongside Café au Lait among wedding and cut-flower growers seeking warm, muted tones. Blooms run 6-8 inches across on strong stems well suited to cutting, and the plant produces continuously from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading and harvesting. In zone 9, peak summer heat can dull flower color and reduce bloom size somewhat, with the best color and largest blooms typically appearing in the cooler weather of early summer and fall. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

common_name: Lady Banks Rose (Thornless Climbing Heirloom Rose)
plant_note: Plant container roses in spring against a strong, large support such as an arbor, pergola, or fence, since Lady Banks eventually becomes an enormous, vigorous climber; it is thornless and blooms only once in spring but very heavily.
directions: Plant against a substantial support in well-drained soil in full sun. A Southern heirloom favorite introduced from China in the early 1800s, Lady Banks Rose is a nearly thornless, extremely vigorous climber that can eventually cover an entire arbor, porch, or old tree with a spectacular single spring flush of small, rosette-shaped flowers, typically pale yellow or white depending on the form grown, often accompanied by a light violet fragrance. Unlike repeat-blooming modern roses, it flowers only once a year but with such abundance that a mature plant can be smothered in thousands of blooms for several weeks. It is remarkably drought-tolerant and pest-free once established, needs only occasional pruning right after bloom to control its size, and is a classic sight on old homes throughout the Gulf South.

common_name: Lady Clare Camellia (Large Semi-Double Rose-Pink Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Lady Clare, also known as Akashigata in Japan, is a classic large semi-double camellia with deep rose-pink flowers and prominent golden stamens, a long-favored Southern garden cultivar.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Lady Clare, known in its native Japan as Akashigata, is a classic large semi-double camellia bearing loosely arranged, deep rose-pink petals surrounding a prominent, showy cluster of golden-yellow stamens, a looser and more informal look than fully double camellia forms. Its vigorous, spreading, somewhat weeping growth habit and large flower size have made it a long-standing favorite for Southern gardens and historic camellia collections, often trained as a specimen or espalier to show off its graceful branching. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9, when little else is in bloom. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

plant_note: Plant crown divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; set the crown at soil level and do not bury; lady fern is the most adaptable and widely grown native fern and succeeds in a very wide range of moist, shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; lady fern is one of the most beautiful, adaptable, and widely grown native ferns in North America, producing finely divided, arching, bright green to chartreuse fronds in graceful spreading clumps that light up dark garden corners throughout summer. Unlike many ferns it is deciduous, going dormant in winter and re-emerging reliably each spring. It tolerates a wider range of conditions than most ferns — moderately dry soil, some drought once established, and varying light levels from dense shade to dappled sun. Dozens of ornamental cultivars exist, including red-stemmed forms ('Lady in Red'), crested forms, and dwarf selections. It naturalizes readily in moist woodland gardens and combines beautifully with hostas, bleeding heart, and native wildflowers. Division every 3–4 years keeps clumps vigorous.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; lady palm is one of the most shade-tolerant palms available — thriving in conditions that would stress most palms, including deep shade, indoor light levels, and enclosed patios. In zone 9 it is an outstanding landscape palm for shaded positions where other palms fail. Slow-growing but very long-lived; old clumps become multi-stemmed specimens of considerable grace. Widely used as an interior plant in subtropical and tropical regions.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; lady palm is one of the most shade-tolerant and most elegantly refined of all the palms — a multi-stemmed, clumping, fan-leafed palm of Chinese origin (native to southern China, probably Guangdong province) that has been cultivated in Japan for centuries as an esteemed garden and indoor specimen, with numerous named cultivars developed over generations of Japanese horticulture. The palm grows as a dense clump of multiple, slender, bamboo-like stems 1–1.5 inches in diameter, each covered in the distinctive dark-brown, woven-fiber leaf-base sheathing, the whole clump increasing in number of stems over the years to form a graceful, multi-stemmed mass of considerable elegance. The fan-shaped leaves are deeply divided into 5–8 broad, blunt-tipped, ridged segments of a rich, deep glossy green, arranged in a spreading, circular pattern at the tips of the slender stems. The overall effect of a mature clump — multiple slender fiber-covered stems of different heights, each topped with a circular fan of broad, deep-green leaf segments — is one of the most graceful and refined of any palm. The exceptional shade tolerance — growing well in conditions equivalent to bright indirect indoor light — makes it uniquely valuable as a landscape palm for shaded positions where most palms fail: under tree canopy, on north-facing walls, in covered outdoor rooms and patios, and in spaces where strong shade prevents the use of most ornamental plants. Slow-growing but very long-lived; established clumps in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens persist for decades.

common_name: Lady Rothschild's Orchid (Rothschild's Bulbophyllum, Red Fan Bulbophyllum)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork or in a slatted basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct morning light; Bulbophyllum rothschildianum is one of the most spectacular of the large Bulbophyllum species, producing pendant, fan-shaped inflorescences 10–14 inches wide bearing 8–12 large flowers arranged in a semicircle — the flowers red-and-white striped with long, thread-like sepal appendages and a small, motile lip. Prefers intermediate to warm temperatures (days 70–85°F, nights 60–70°F). Keep consistently moist. The flowers have an unpleasant odor for a few days but are extraordinarily ornamental. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow mounted on cork or in a slatted basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun — Lady Rothschild's Orchid is one of the most spectacular and sought-after of the large-flowered Bulbophyllum species and rewards careful culture with extraordinary inflorescences that rank among the most unusual flower forms in the orchid family.
