Bulbophyllum rothschildianum is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to India (specifically the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya) and Myanmar, one of the largest-flowered species in the enormous genus Bulbophyllum (which contains approximately 2,000 species, making it one of the largest plant genera in the world). The plant produces oval pseudobulbs spaced along a creeping rhizome, each carrying a single, large, leathery, dark-green leaf. From the rhizome, pendant flower spikes emerge bearing a remarkable inflorescence: a broad, fan-shaped or semicircular arrangement of 8–12 large flowers (2–3 inches each) arranged in a precise, symmetrical arc like a peacock's tail display. Each flower has large, broadly oblong dorsal and lateral sepals in cream-white to pale yellow with vivid red to maroon striping and veining, and extraordinarily long, thread-like extensions (up to 6 inches) from the sepal tips that wave in air movement. The small lip is dark, shiny, and highly motile — moving in the slightest air current to deceive fly pollinators. The flowers produce a smell for a few days that attracts these pollinators but dissipates quickly. One of the crown jewels of Bulbophyllum culture. Named in honor of Lady de Rothschild. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant in fall; perennializes well in warm dry climates.
directions: Plant lady tulip bulbs in fall about five inches deep in sharply drained soil and full sun. Unlike hybrid tulips, this dainty species perennializes reliably and naturalizes in warm, dry climates. The slender flowers are white or yellow with a bold red or pink exterior stripe and open flat in sun. Keep the site dry during summer dormancy to encourage the bulbs to return and multiply for years.

common_name: Lady in Red Fern (Red-Stemmed Lady Fern)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Lady in Red is more tolerant of summer heat and drier conditions than Japanese painted fern, making it somewhat more reliable in zone 9 — though consistent moisture remains important.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Lady in Red is an exceptional and distinctive lady fern selection with bright cherry-red to deep wine-red stems (stipes) that contrast dramatically with the lacy, light-green fronds — one of the most striking color effects in shade-garden ferns. The vivid red-to-burgundy stem color persists from spring emergence through fall, providing a seasonal color effect unmatched by most other ferns. The fronds are finely divided and lacy, with the characteristic lady fern form — lighter and more delicate in texture than southern shield fern or wood fern, creating a soft, airy quality in the shade garden. Lady in Red grows larger and more vigorously than Japanese painted fern (18–30 inches vs. 12–18 inches) and is somewhat more heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant, making it more reliable in zone 9. Like most lady ferns, it is deciduous in zone 9 — dying back in late fall and re-emerging in spring — but the spring growth is vigorous. Outstanding for moist shade situations such as stream banks, bog gardens, and the deep shade of large trees. Pair with hostas, toad lilies, and Solomon's seal for layered shade-garden compositions.

common_name: Lady in Red Salvia (Red Texas Sage, Scarlet Salvia coccinea)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 6 weeks early; in zone 9, Lady in Red often self-seeds so prolifically that it naturalizes as a perennial colony — once established, allow the self-seeded seedlings to fill in around the original planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Lady in Red is a compact, All-America Selections winning selection of Salvia coccinea — the native Texas sage or scarlet salvia — producing vivid, true scarlet-red tubular flowers on compact, well-branched plants from spring through frost in zone 9. Unlike the sprawling, leggy habit of unselected Salvia coccinea, Lady in Red stays compact and bushy at 18–24 inches with neat, square-stemmed, slightly aromatic foliage. The brilliant red tubular flowers are intensely attractive to hummingbirds, which hover around each bloom spike, and the plant is nearly always in active use by feeding hummingbirds during the long Gulf South summer. In zone 9, Lady in Red is treated as a short-lived perennial or vigorous annual that typically self-seeds so freely it naturalizes into a colony that perpetuates indefinitely without replanting. The naturalized seedlings are genetic variations that may range slightly from the named cultivar, but generally maintain the compact habit and red flower color of the parent. The salvia's ability to grow in partial shade as well as full sun makes it more versatile than most red-flowering summer annuals, fitting under light tree canopy and in dappled-light conditions. Outstanding for butterfly and hummingbird gardens.

common_name: Lady of the Night (Night Jasmine, Brunfelsia americana)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil; Lady of the Night thrives in the dappled shade of large trees and performs poorly in full afternoon sun in zone 9. In zone 9a, it requires frost protection or container culture that can be brought indoors; in zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable evergreen shrub. The fragrance is most intense after dark — plant near outdoor seating areas for evening enjoyment. All parts are toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Lady of the Night is one of the finest shade-tolerant fragrant shrubs for zone 9-11 Gulf Coast gardens, where its powerful nocturnal fragrance fills outdoor spaces on warm spring and summer evenings. Brunfelsia americana is an evergreen shrub from the Caribbean (Jamaica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Lesser Antilles) in the Solanaceae family closely related to Yesterday Today Tomorrow (B. pauciflora and B. australis). Its single-day flowers begin as pure white tubes and age through cream to pale yellow — the reverse color change from B. pauciflora's purple-to-white progression. The flower fragrance is released most powerfully after dark and is one of the most intensely sweet and complex fragrances in the plant world — often described as combining jasmine, vanilla, and gardenias — with a reach that can fill a large garden or patio on warm, still evenings. In zone 9, Lady of the Night blooms from spring through fall with peak flowering in late spring and early summer. The combination of shade tolerance and extraordinary nocturnal fragrance makes it one of the most valuable plants for shaded evening garden spaces, planted near patios, decks, and seating areas. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic — contain brunfelsamidine and other alkaloids causing neurological symptoms if ingested.

common_name: Lady of the Night Orchid (Brassavola nodosa, Starwhite Orchid)
plant_note: Mount on cork bark, a tree fern slab, or grow in a slatted orchid basket with bark media; Brassavola nodosa grows in full sun to bright indirect light and cannot tolerate frost. In zone 9b-10, it can be grown outdoors year-round on trees or cork mounts in sheltered spots — it tolerates brief temperatures to 35°F when dry. The plant performs very well in zone 9 on shaded covered porches, blooming multiple times per year. Never let the pseudobulbs dry completely for extended periods. Allow to dry briefly between waterings. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial shade — Brassavola nodosa tolerates brighter light than many orchids but performs well in the bright indirect light of a shaded porch or east-facing window. Brassavola nodosa is a compact, easily grown, free-blooming epiphytic orchid native to coastal and tropical areas from Mexico and the Caribbean through Central America to Colombia and Venezuela, one of the most cold-tolerant and adaptable of the commonly grown tropical orchids. The plant produces clusters of narrow, terete (cylindrical), slightly fleshy leaves and blooms in fall through winter with clusters of 3–7 flowers — the waxy, star-shaped flowers are greenish-white to pure white with a large, heart-shaped white lip fringed with tiny teeth, each flower 3–4 inches across. The flowers are inconspicuously fragrant by day but at night release an intensely sweet, vanilla-lilac perfume to attract pollinating sphinx moths — the nocturnal fragrance, sweet, penetrating, and far-carrying on warm evenings, earned the plant the name 'Lady of the Night' (not to be confused with Brunfelsia americana, another nocturnal fragrant plant with the same common name). Brassavola nodosa is used extensively in hybridization with Cattleya and related genera to produce the 'B. nodosa hybrids' with the characteristic nocturnal fragrance. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in early spring; lady’s mantle can also be direct sown on the soil surface in early spring as the seed needs light and moisture to germinate. It self-sows freely once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; lady’s mantle is treasured for its large, rounded, softly pleated and densely hairy leaves that bead morning dew and rain into perfect silver droplets — one of the most beloved effects in the garden. The frothy sprays of tiny chartreuse-yellow flowers bloom over many weeks in early summer, creating an airy effect that blends beautifully with everything. Shear spent flower stems and old foliage back hard in midsummer to produce a flush of fresh new growth. In warm climates (zone 7 and up) lady’s mantle may go dormant in summer heat — it strongly prefers cool, moist conditions and performs best in the Pacific Northwest and Upper South in partial shade.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lamb's ear requires perfect drainage and actually performs better in dry, poor soil — it rots quickly in wet, humid conditions or heavy clay. In zone 9a, site in a raised bed or slope with excellent air circulation to avoid summer rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun; lamb's ear is prized above all for its extraordinary tactile foliage — thick, felt-like silver leaves 4–6 inches long covered in dense white wool that is impossibly soft to the touch, giving the plant its evocative common name. The silver-gray foliage is among the most effective of all for brightening dark borders, creating contrast with purple or yellow flowers, and providing texture in the dry garden. Tall woolly stems rise in summer carrying whorls of small lavender flowers attractive to bumblebees; the non-flowering cultivar 'Silver Carpet' is a denser, neater groundcover. Lamb's ear requires excellent drainage and good air circulation — in humid zone 9a summers the center of clumps may rot; divide and replant in fall after the heat breaks, selecting drier, elevated sites. Deer resistant.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in poor to average, well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in partial to full sun; lamb's ears struggles in wet, humid conditions — ensure excellent drainage, especially in the humid South, and do not mulch around the crowns.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in poor to average, well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in partial to full sun; lamb's ears struggles in wet, humid conditions — ensure excellent drainage, especially in the humid South, and do not mulch around the crowns. Stachys byzantina is grown almost entirely for its spectacular dense-woolly, silver-white, softly tactile leaves that form a spreading, mat-forming groundcover and make an elegant foil for colorful perennials; in late spring to summer it sends up fuzzy, silver-lavender flower spikes that some gardeners remove to keep the foliage display clean. Divide every 2–3 years in early spring to remove dead centers and maintain a tidy mat. Excellent at the front of borders, edging paths, and as dry-garden groundcover.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors since light aids germination; transplant after frost.
directions: Surface-sow the seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, since light aids germination. This monarda is covered with tiered whorls of lavender-pink flower clusters that attract butterflies, hummingbirds, and bees. The edible petals can replace oregano in savory dishes, be steeped into tea, or float in punch. Grow in full sun to part shade with good air circulation to limit mildew, and deadhead to extend flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; lance leaf coreopsis is one of the most floriferous and reliable native wildflowers for Gulf Coast and southern gardens and naturalized meadow plantings — it thrives on neglect in lean, well-drained soil.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall or early spring by pressing lightly into well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom season. Coreopsis lanceolata (lance-leaf coreopsis or sand coreopsis) is one of the most abundantly flowering native wildflowers of the Gulf Coastal Plain and eastern North America — a long-lived perennial producing masses of bright, 2-to-3-inch, golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers with serrated ray petals on tall, branching stems above narrow, lance-shaped, mostly basal leaves from May through July (and often reblooming in fall). It is one of four coreopsis species designated as the State Wildflower of Florida and one of the most widely used native perennials in southeastern wildflower meadow restorations, roadside plantings, and naturalistic gardens. Unlike many coreopsis species, C. lanceolata is exceptionally drought-tolerant, self-seeds reliably (but not aggressively), and maintains a neat, upright habit in garden settings. The flower heads are extremely attractive to native bees and small native butterflies. It is one of the most recommended low-maintenance native perennials for full-sun, lean-soil garden situations throughout the Gulf South.

common_name: Lance-Leaf Begonia (Amphioxus Begonia, Spotted Sarawak Begonia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, porous potting mix with excellent drainage; Begonia amphioxus is a trailing to semi-erect cane begonia best displayed in a hanging basket or allowed to cascade over a pot edge. Maintain consistent moisture but allow the surface to dry slightly between waterings. This species appreciates moderate humidity (50%+) and good air circulation. Propagate from stem cuttings. A terrarium plant in temperate climates; zone 11-12 outdoor shade garden in tropical conditions. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in moist, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix — Lance-Leaf Begonia performs best in the bright, diffuse light of a shaded indoor position or sheltered tropical shade garden and produces its most vivid leaf spotting in good indirect light. Begonia amphioxus is a small, trailing to semi-erect begonia native to Sarawak, Malaysia (Borneo) in the Begoniaceae family, one of the most visually distinctive of the hundreds of wild Begonia species collected by tropical plant enthusiasts for its remarkable combination of leaf shape and surface pattern. The leaves are the defining feature: narrow, lance-shaped to narrowly ovate (2–4 inches long but only 0.5–1 inch wide — extremely elongated relative to the width), with a strongly tapering, spear-like tip that gives the species its name 'amphioxus' (Greek for 'pointed at both ends'). On this narrow, bright green surface, scattered crimson-red to scarlet spots and blotches of varying sizes are distributed irregularly — the effect is of a thin bright-green ribbon patterned with vivid red paint droplets. The undersides are deep red. The plant also produces small pink flowers in clusters from the leaf axils throughout the growing season. A collector's begonia valued for its completely distinctive and unusual leaf shape — the extreme narrowness distinguishing it from nearly all other cultivated begonia species. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; lance-leaved loosestrife grows naturally in moist woodland openings, stream banks, and meadow edges across eastern North America. It spreads by rhizomes and self-sows to form loose colonies.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in moist woodland borders, stream banks, and rain gardens; lance-leaved loosestrife is a slender, upright native perennial with narrow, lance-shaped leaves and cheerful, star-shaped yellow flowers in midsummer. It is one of the more adaptable native loosestrifes, tolerating somewhat drier conditions than the wetland species while still preferring consistent moisture. The flowers provide nectar for small native bees, including Macropis bees that are specialists on Lysimachia pollen and oil. The plant spreads steadily by rhizomes and seeds to form naturalistic colonies in appropriate moist, shaded areas, combining naturally with native ferns, sedges, and woodland wildflowers. A native alternative to the highly invasive purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria) for moist areas, though unrelated botanically.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in spring after last frost — seeds need light to germinate; in zone 9, sow in early spring (February–March) or in late summer for fall flowers. The plant behaves as an annual in most of the South but sometimes overwinters in zones 8–10.
directions: Scatter seeds on bare, dry, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost — this wildflower requires excellent drainage and poor, even sandy soil; in rich, moist soil it becomes floppy and short-lived. Lanceleaf blanket flower is native to sandy plains and open disturbed ground from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, with narrow lance-shaped leaves (unlike the wider leaves of the hybrid garden gaillardia) and bright yellow to orange-tipped ray flowers with purple-red centers that bloom continuously from summer through frost. A superb plant for hot, dry sandy gardens and roadsides in the Southeast where it attracts skippers, bumblebees, and goldfinches (which eat the seed heads). Minimal care once established — simply leave the seed heads in place for self-sowing.

common_name: Lanceleaf Coreopsis (Native Perennial Yellow Tickseed Wildflower)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in fall or early spring; Lanceleaf Coreopsis is a native perennial that self-seeds prolifically once established — a single planting will naturalize and expand over years without replanting. In zone 9, sow fall (September–November) or late winter (January–February) for bloom in spring (April–June) of the same or following season. Coreopsis planted from fall will frequently bloom the following spring; from spring seed, blooms appear by late summer. The species is extremely drought-tolerant once established — one of the most reliably undemanding native perennials for the well-drained, sunny portions of zone 8–9 gardens.
directions: Scatter seeds on prepared, weed-free soil and press in without covering; coreopsis seeds need some light for germination. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom and prevent self-seeding where not desired. Lanceleaf Coreopsis (Coreopsis lanceolata) is a native perennial wildflower of the eastern and central United States — distributed naturally in open meadows, prairies, roadsides, and disturbed areas from the Atlantic Coast to the Great Plains, south to the Gulf Coast. The bright golden-yellow flowers (1.5–2 inches across) have the characteristic daisy-like form with slightly toothed or lobed ray petals and a central button — instantly recognizable as the defining coreopsis look that has made the genus a staple of native plant and pollinator gardens across North America. As a native plant, Lanceleaf Coreopsis evolved with and provides premium pollinator habitat: the flowers are highly attractive to native bees (bumblebees, mining bees, sweat bees), skippers, and butterflies, providing nectar and pollen from spring through midsummer. The seeds are consumed by native sparrows and small finches, making this a multi-function wildlife plant. Unlike many prairie natives, Lanceleaf Coreopsis blooms heavily in its first year from fall planting, making it more immediately rewarding than species that require two or more seasons to establish before flowering. Its minimal water needs and tolerance of poor, dry soil make it ideal for rain gardens, unirrigated native plantings, and naturalized areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in shallow water or consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil at pond edges; lanceleaf pickerelweed grows in freshwater marshes, shallow ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout the southeastern Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in shallow water (2–6 inches deep) or consistently wet, slightly acidic to neutral, organic-rich soil at pond margins; lanceleaf pickerelweed is a southeastern relative of the common pickerelweed (P. cordata), distinguishable by its narrower, lance-shaped leaves rather than the broad, heart-shaped leaves of P. cordata. The flower spikes bear the same attractive blue-violet flowers as common pickerelweed and bloom from spring through fall, attracting numerous bumblebees and native bees that are essential pollinators of the aquatic flower. The seeds are eaten by wood ducks and other waterfowl. In zone 9a, it performs as a reliable, warm-climate aquatic perennial at pond edges and in constructed wetlands, where it spreads by rhizomes to form naturalistic colonies.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; light aids germination so barely cover seed.
directions: This native perennial coreopsis produces masses of golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers above slender, lance-shaped foliage. Press seeds into the soil surface in spring since light helps them germinate, and keep the bed moist until seedlings establish. It thrives in full sun and lean, well-drained soil, tolerating drought and heat while attracting bees and butterflies. Deadhead to prolong bloom, and let some seed heads mature to feed birds and self-sow.

common_name: Landmark Lantana (Compact Uniform-Flowering Modern Lantana Series)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; the Landmark series was bred for a compact, uniform, well-branched habit and heavy, consistent flowering across a range of colors, making it popular for mass plantings and containers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. The Landmark series was bred as a modern, more compact and uniform alternative to older, taller lantana cultivars, producing dense, well-branched mounds covered in continuous, brightly colored flower clusters across a range of available colors through the entire warm season, with strong appeal to butterflies. Its compact, predictable size makes it especially popular for mass color plantings, hanging baskets, and containers where a uniform habit is valued over the taller, more rambling growth of older cultivars like Miss Huff. It tolerates heat, humidity, and drought with ease once established and needs only light shaping to maintain a tidy mound.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; most gardeners use purchased transplants due to slow, uneven germination.
directions: Sow seeds after lightly scarifying or nicking the seed coat; soak overnight to improve germination, which is slow and can take 4–6 weeks at 70–80°F. Transplant in full sun after all frost risk has passed; lantana thrives in heat, drought, and poor soil and blooms most freely under mild stress. The multicolored flower clusters change color as they age, giving plants a jewel-like effect; deadhead clusters as they fade to keep new flowers coming. Perennial in zones 9–11 where it can become invasive; grow as an annual elsewhere.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in partial shade to full sun. Large Fothergilla tolerates partial shade but produces the best fall color and most flowers in full sun with consistent moisture.
directions: Large Fothergilla is an exceptional four-season native shrub, native to the mountain forests and rocky slopes of the southern Appalachians from Virginia and North Carolina south to Alabama, producing fragrant, white, bottlebrush-like flower spikes of dense stamens in April and May before the leaves emerge — a display that rivals those of its close relative Witch Hazel (Hamamelis). Larger than Dwarf Fothergilla (F. gardenii), it grows 6–10 feet tall and wide and provides multi-season appeal through its dark green, blue-green tinged summer foliage, one of the finest fall color displays of any native shrub (crimson, orange, and yellow often appearing simultaneously on a single leaf), and attractive winter form. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; best fall color develops in full sun, but the plant tolerates partial shade and is easy to establish in typical native plant garden conditions. An outstanding choice for four-season structure in the southeastern native garden.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants (male and female plants together for berry production) in spring in wet to moist, acidic, sandy to peaty soil in partial shade to full sun. Large Gallberry is adapted to the wet pine flatwoods and pocosins of the Gulf Coast and coastal plain.
directions: Large Gallberry is a robust evergreen native holly, native to the wet pine flatwoods, pocosins, bay swamps, and seepage bogs of the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, where it grows alongside inkberry, fetterbush, and pond cypress in permanently moist to wet, highly acidic, sandy or peaty soils. The glossy, dark green, leathery, spine-tipped leaves provide year-round evergreen structure; female plants produce abundant clusters of large black berries in fall and winter that are critical food for bluebirds, hermit thrushes, and other migrating songbirds. Like inkberry (Ilex glabra), Large Gallberry is important for native bees, producing copious nectar that supports early-season bee populations. Plant male and female specimens together for reliable fruiting; provide consistently moist to wet, highly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. An outstanding wildlife shrub for wet native gardens in the lower South.

subcategory: large-flowered South American rain lily bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; large habranthus flowers in summer following rain events or deep irrigation, producing among the largest and most striking flowers in the Habranthus genus — funnel-shaped and held at the characteristic Habranthus 45-degree angle, in deep pink-purple to magenta with a deep maroon-purple central throat marking. One of the boldest and most garden-worthy rain lilies, larger than most zephyranthes species.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; large habranthus — sometimes called simply 'the Paraguayan rain lily' — is the boldest and most showy of the commonly available habranthus species, producing flowers substantially larger than either H. tubispathus or most Zephyranthes species: 3-inch wide, deep pink-magenta to lavender-pink funnel-shaped blooms with a distinctive, contrasting, deep maroon-purple stain at the center of the throat — a bold, eye-catching combination of warm pink-purple outside and dark maroon-purple center that gives each flower a dramatic bicolor appearance. Like all habranthus, the flowers are held at a graceful 45-degree angle rather than strictly upright. The bloom response to summer rainfall is prompt and reliable — a deep irrigation or summer thunderstorm triggers mass flowering 5–7 days later, the classic rain lily response. It is native to open grasslands of Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina, climates with hot, wet summers followed by drier winters, conditions that match the Gulf Coast summer growing season well. Several named cultivars exist, including the popular 'Russell Manning' strain with especially large, rosy-pink flowers. Outstanding naturalized in open, sunny borders where the rain-triggered blooming creates a summer spectacle.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; large poppy mallow grows in dry to moist, open, sandy or clay soils of the southeastern Coastal Plain from Georgia to Texas, often appearing in disturbed roadsides and open fields.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; large poppy mallow is a spreading to erect native perennial of the southeastern Coastal Plain with deeply lobed leaves and large (to 2.5 inches), vivid magenta-pink to wine-red, cup-shaped flowers with white centers — the same brilliantly colored poppy-mallow flowers that make the related Callirhoe involucrata so popular in gardens. This southeastern species is better adapted to the heat and humidity of zone 9a than many of its western relatives. The flowers open in the morning and close by afternoon — best enjoyed in the morning hours. Native bees, particularly long-tongued bumblebees and miner bees, are important pollinators of the nectar-rich flowers. Drought tolerant once established thanks to a deep, fleshy taproot.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide established mats in spring or fall; large self-heal spreads by short stolons and can form a low, weed-suppressing mat. It naturalizes readily in lawns and meadows and will self-sow freely — deadhead to limit spread in formal settings. More ornamental and less aggressive than the common self-heal (P. vulgaris) that is a lawn weed across North America.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; large self-heal is the ornamental European cousin of the common lawn-weed self-heal, producing much larger, more showy flowers in rich violet-purple to rose-pink on a plant that, while still spreading and ground-covering, has showier blooms that merit intentional garden placement. It forms a low, semi-evergreen mat of oval, dark-green leaves with upright, square stems bearing dense, terminal whorls of lipped, tubular flowers from early summer through fall. The flowers are strongly attractive to bumblebees and other long-tongued native bees, making it a valuable pollinator support groundcover for partial-shade situations under deciduous trees or on the shaded side of buildings. Named cultivars and hybrids include 'Loveliness' series (in separate colors: white, pink, lavender, and deep violet) that are more ornamental than the species. Tolerates light foot traffic, making it functional as an occasional-path groundcover between stepping stones in light shade.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun. Large Skullcap adapts to a range of light and moisture conditions and is one of the more forgiving native skullcaps for garden cultivation along the southeastern coastal plain.
directions: Large Skullcap is a native perennial of the southeastern coastal plain, found in dry to mesic, open woodlands, forest margins, and roadsides from Massachusetts south to Florida and west to Texas, producing large, showy blue-violet flowers in May and June that are notably larger than most other native skullcap species — earning the common name. The paired, tubular flowers are specialized for bumblebee pollination and are attractive both in the garden and as a wildflower accent in naturalistic plantings. Adaptable to a range of soil moisture and light conditions along the southeastern coastal plain — from open sandy roadsides to woodland edges with partial shade — Large Skullcap is one of the most garden-worthy of the native Scutellaria species in the Southeast. Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are moderately drought-tolerant and long-lived.

plant_note: Do not attempt to transplant from the wild — collection is illegal in most states and wild-dug plants virtually never survive; sourcing from a specialist native orchid nursery with documented propagation lineage is the only viable path.
directions: This record exists primarily for identification and documentation purposes: Large Whorled Pogonia is one of the rarest native orchids in eastern North America and is essentially impossible to cultivate intentionally — it depends on a precise, poorly understood relationship with specific soil fungi that cannot be reliably recreated, and plants removed from the wild almost invariably die within one to two seasons. Never collect or transplant from wild populations, as this is illegal under state protection laws across most of its range and causes direct population harm. If encountered naturally on a property, the best stewardship is to protect the surrounding soil and woodland canopy, avoid foot traffic near colonies, and note the location for reporting to your state natural heritage program. A single stem bearing a whorl of five to six leaves topped by a solitary maroon-green flower in May–June is the signature form; plants may remain dormant underground for multiple years before re-emerging.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall near established oaks in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, open woodland soil in partial shade; large yellow false foxglove is hemiparasitic on oak roots and cannot survive without an established oak host. Plant near black oak, bur oak, or white oak.
directions: Direct sow in fall near established oaks in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean woodland soil in partial shade; large yellow false foxglove is one of the most striking native hemiparasites of the eastern US oak woodlands, producing large, brilliant yellow, two-lipped tubular flowers — the largest flowers in the genus Aureolaria — on upright stems through late summer. Like all Aureolaria species, it taps the root systems of nearby oaks for supplemental water and nutrients while also producing chlorophyll; it cannot survive without an oak host plant. The deeply cut, almost fern-like foliage is attractive throughout the season. The large, bright yellow flowers are strongly attractive to bumblebees, hummingbirds, and clearwing sphinx moths in late summer when few other native woodland plants are in bloom. A rewarding and ecologically important native for naturalistic oak woodland gardens, particularly in the central US.

plant_note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions in fall or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; bellwort is a slow-growing native woodland perennial that performs best left undisturbed once established.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; large-flowered bellwort is a charming native woodland perennial producing elegant arching stems with perfoliate leaves — the stem appears to pierce through the center of each leaf — and pendant, pale yellow, twisted bell-shaped flowers in mid-spring resembling small, nodding lilies. Plants emerge early and bloom for 2–4 weeks before the woodland canopy leafs out and deep shade closes in. After flowering, stems elongate and the leaves expand to 3–4 inches wide, providing attractive texture through summer. Bellwort slowly spreads by rhizome to form substantial colonies in ideal conditions of consistently moist, acidic, deep, humus-rich soil in dappled shade. It combines naturally with trillium, Virginia bluebells, bleeding heart, and other spring woodland plants. The wide native range (Quebec to South Carolina and westward to Kansas) indicates broad adaptability, and it grows reliably in zone 9 with adequate moisture.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; large-flowered tickseed benefits from natural cold stratification over winter and is one of the few Coreopsis species that performs well in partially shaded woodland edge conditions — avoid heavy, wet, or clay soils.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; large-flowered tickseed is one of the most shade-tolerant Coreopsis species and is the go-to choice for partially shaded native garden situations where the sun-demanding C. lanceolata and C. tinctoria fail to thrive — it is most at home at woodland edges, open pine woods, and the dappled light of thinned forest understory. Coreopsis major is a native perennial of the southeastern United States, ranging from Virginia south to Florida and west to Tennessee and Alabama, where it grows naturally in dry to average, well-drained, sandy or rocky soils in open pine forests, oak-hickory woodlands, and their sunny edges; its leaves are distinctive — the opposite pairs are so deeply divided they appear to be whorls of six narrow, lance-shaped leaflets, giving the plant a delicate, fine-textured appearance — and from June through August it produces a profusion of bright yellow, 1.5–2 inch daisy flowers with a golden-yellow disk, similar in appearance to other tickseeds but borne on a plant comfortable with dappled light. It is an excellent pollinator plant for native bees, including bumblebees and sweat bees that collect its pollen, and supports several specialist Coreopsis-foraging bees in the Southeast; the seed heads are consumed by small finches and sparrows. Large-flowered tickseed spreads slowly by rhizomes to form modest colonies and self-sows lightly in appropriate conditions, making it a well-behaved addition to native garden plantings in partial shade.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before direct sowing in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; large-fruited wild indigo is a southeastern native adapted to bottomland forests and moist, shaded stream margins.
directions: Scarify seeds (nick the hard seed coat with a file or soak in hot water overnight) before direct sowing in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; large-fruited wild indigo is adapted to moist, shaded bottomland forests and differs from most baptisias in its shade tolerance. Baptisia megacarpa is a southeastern US native wild indigo of moist, shaded bottomlands and stream margins in the Florida Panhandle and adjacent Georgia and Alabama; it produces lavender to white, pea-like flowers in spring and very large, inflated, oval seed pods (the largest of any baptisia) that rattle when dry — outstanding as an ornamental dried pod. Unlike the sun-loving prairie baptisias (B. australis, B. bracteata), this species adapts to partial shade and moist soil, making it unusual and valuable in the genus for woodland garden use in zones 7–10.

common_name: Large-Leafed Pothos (Amplissimum Pothos, Silver-Stripe Epipremnum, Giant Pothos)
plant_note: Grow on a rough bark board, moss pole, or tree trunk in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; Epipremnum amplissimum is a large-growing, fast-climbing pothos relative that can reach dramatic adult-leaf sizes in bright indoor to outdoor shaded positions. The adult leaves are long, narrow, and lanceolate (unlike the broader, heart-shaped leaves of juvenile E. aureum), in dark green with a silvery or pale green central stripe. The narrow, lance-shaped leaves distinguish this from all common pothos immediately. Best in warm, humid conditions. CAUTION: all Epipremnum contain calcium oxalate; toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow on a rough support in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained soil — Large-Leafed Pothos climbs rapidly on rough bark or moss poles and develops its most dramatically different adult-leaf form when given a vertical surface to ascend. Epipremnum amplissimum is a climbing, hemiepiphytic aroid in the Araceae family native to the Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, and parts of tropical Asia — a member of the same genus as the ubiquitous common Golden Pothos (E. aureum) but producing a strikingly different leaf form. In juvenile form, E. amplissimum produces standard small, heart-shaped pothos-type leaves. As the plant matures and climbs, the leaves transition to the distinctively adult form: long (12–24 inches), narrowly lanceolate, linear to lance-shaped leaves in dark green with a pale to silver-green central stripe along the midrib — a leaf form that looks almost nothing like the common pothos and is instead reminiscent of a narrow Philodendrum or large Scindapsus. This adult leaf form is quite unusual and ornamentally distinctive, making E. amplissimum one of the more interesting of the Epipremnum relatives for collectors of shade-climbing aroids. The plant grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and covers surfaces quickly. Propagates easily from stem cuttings. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.

plant_note: Scarify seeds with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat and significantly improve germination rates. Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or sow in early spring after last frost. This species develops a deep taproot and dislikes transplanting — sow seeds in their permanent location in well-drained, slightly acidic soil.
directions: Scarify seeds by rubbing with sandpaper before sowing to break the hard seed coat and improve germination; direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or in early spring into permanently selected, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile-to-average soil in full sun. Large-Leaved Lupine is the wild Pacific Northwest perennial that served as the primary parent of the beloved 'Russell Hybrid' lupines, producing tall spikes of blue-violet, white, or bicolor pea flowers in June atop large, palmately compound leaves. This species thrives in the cool, moist summers of the Pacific Northwest and northern gardens but declines in heat and humidity; it is not a good choice for zones 7 and above. Deadhead spent spikes promptly to encourage a second flush of bloom and to prevent aggressive self-seeding, as escapes in the Pacific Northwest have become problematic in some riparian habitats.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in early fall or very early spring; large-leaved pennycress spreads steadily by self-seeding and rhizomes to form a dense weed-suppressing groundcover — a single planting typically produces a self-maintaining colony within 3–4 years.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; large-leaved pennycress is a Caucasian evergreen shade groundcover belonging to the mustard family that is one of the earliest and most reliable shade garden performers of the year — its clusters of small, white, four-petaled, cross-shaped flowers open in very early spring (February-March) before most perennials have emerged, covering the plant with a fresh white display at the same time as snowdrops and early crocuses. The large, thick, kidney-shaped, glossy, dark-green leaves remain attractive throughout the year and create a dense, low-maintenance evergreen groundcover in deeply shaded conditions. It spreads by both self-seeding and creeping rhizomes to form gradually expanding, weed-suppressing colonies under trees, where it requires virtually no maintenance beyond initial establishment. An outstanding and underused shade groundcover for zones 5–9, it tolerates dry shade better than many competing groundcovers once established.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; large-flowered black-eyed Susan is native to dry, open pine woodlands and prairies of the Gulf Coastal Plain from Texas to Alabama.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun; large-flowered black-eyed Susan is a Gulf Coastal Plain native Rudbeckia producing some of the largest individual flower heads in the genus — bright yellow ray flowers surrounding a dark brown central cone on tall, leafy stems. The plant is a hardy, long-lived perennial adapted to the hot, dry summers and mild winters of the Gulf South, making it better suited to zone 9a than the more commonly planted R. hirta (which often behaves as a short-lived biennial in the South's climate). The showy flower heads persist through summer and into fall, providing extended seasonal color and late-season pollen for native bees. The seed heads that follow are consumed by goldfinches. An excellent, low-water native perennial for dry, sunny, Southern gardens.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring after flowering; Epimedium perralderianum is an Algerian species, one of the most vigorous epimediums for dry shade. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Algerian epimedium is native to the Atlas Mountains of northern Algeria and is one of the most drought-tolerant and vigorous ground-covering epimediums available. The bright yellow flowers with distinctive long spurs appear in spring above the bronzy new foliage. The semi-evergreen leaves, which emerge with attractive bronze-red markings and mature to glossy dark green, provide year-round ground cover. It spreads faster than many epimediums, making it effective for quickly covering dry shade areas under deciduous trees. The species has been important in hybridization programs producing vigorous, large-flowered cultivars. A parent of several outstanding garden hybrids. Notable for tolerance of the driest shade conditions — excellent under shallow-rooted trees where little else will grow.

plant_note: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, sandy soil in full sun; large-flowered penstemon requires excellent drainage and fails in heavy clay or consistently moist soils. Stratify seeds in cold (refrigerator) for 30-60 days to improve germination. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and are best left undisturbed as the deep taproot makes division difficult. Short-lived (2-4 years) but self-sows in appropriate conditions.
directions: Sow seeds in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; large-flowered penstemon bears the largest individual flowers of any native North American penstemon — the spectacular, tubular, inflated flowers are lavender-pink to pale violet-pink, up to 1.5 inches long, and carried in dense whorls along tall, upright stems that are very beautiful from May through June. The outstanding foliage is also a distinguishing feature: large, rounded to egg-shaped, intensely glaucous (blue-green, waxy) leaves that are clasped to the stem in pairs and provide exceptional cool blue-green color throughout the growing season even when not in flower. Native to dry, sandy prairies of the central Great Plains from South Dakota and Iowa south to Nebraska and Kansas, it thrives in lean, alkaline, sandy soils and develops a deep taproot that makes it drought-tolerant once established. An important early nectar source for bumblebees, sphinx moths, and ruby-throated hummingbirds. The beautiful blue-green winter foliage rosette is ornamental even in cold months.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to dry shaded soil; this aster spreads by both seed and rhizome to form dense groundcover colonies. It tolerates poor, dry, acidic conditions under oaks and maples better than almost any other flowering perennial.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, acidic, humus-rich to poor soil in partial to full shade; large-leaf wood aster is one of the most shade and drought-tolerant native flowering plants in the northeastern US, forming low-growing groundcover colonies beneath dense oak canopy where few other flowering plants survive. The huge, heart-shaped basal leaves are distinctive and nearly a foot across. Pale lavender to white daisy flowers appear in late summer and fall, providing valuable late-season nectar under closed canopy where most other pollinators run out of food. It spreads vigorously by rhizome in favorable conditions and can be used to suppress weeds and stabilize dry slopes in deep shade.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; largeflower phlox is a tall, shade-adapted native that bridges the gap between sun-loving tall phlox and deep-shade woodland plants.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; largeflower phlox is more shade-tolerant than garden phlox (P. paniculata) and makes an outstanding tall shade garden perennial at the woodland edge. Phlox amplifolia is a native eastern North American phlox of moist woodland borders and river bottomlands with unusually large, broad leaves (giving it the species name "large-leaved") and tall stems bearing large, fragrant, lavender to pale-purple flowers in summer — blooming later than most native phloxes and filling a valuable midsummer gap in the shade garden. It has better resistance to powdery mildew than P. paniculata in humid climates, and the larger, broader leaves create a bolder textural effect; use at the back of shaded borders alongside native grasses, Joe-Pye weed, and elderberry.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, calcareous to slightly acidic, well-drained to seepage-wet soil in partial shade to full sun; largeleaf parnassia grows in calcareous seeps, limestone glade margins, and wet, rocky, open habitats of the central Appalachians and adjacent regions.
directions: Plant in moist, calcareous (calcium-rich) to slightly acidic, constantly moist but well-drained seepage soil in partial shade to full sun; largeleaf grass-of-parnassus is the larger-leaved and larger-flowered of the eastern Parnassia species, producing elegant pure white flowers with green veining and the decorative fringe-tipped staminodes characteristic of the genus. It grows in calcareous seeps and limestone outcrops in the central Appalachians — habitats with constantly moving, mineral-rich groundwater. The white flowers in fall (August–October) provide late-season nectar at a time when few other wildflowers are blooming in its native habitat. A rare find in native plant nurseries but available from specialist native plant sources. Grows best in calcareous, constantly moist conditions that maintain good drainage without waterlogging.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 4–8 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall in mild climates for early spring bloom. Seeds need cold stratification and prefer cool soil to germinate.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep directly in the garden as early as the ground can be worked — larkspur germinates best in cool soil below 65°F and may fail to sprout if the weather turns warm. Do not start indoors, as plants have taproots that do not transplant well. Thin to 9–12 in to promote sturdy stems. Allow some seed to fall for reliable self-sowing in subsequent years.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to average, disturbed or garden soil in full to partial sun; late boneset establishes quickly from seed and spreads via self-seeding and short rhizomes — give it room as it can form large colonies in moist, fertile soil.
directions: Late boneset is the most common and widely distributed of the native Eupatorium species across the South, blooming in late summer and fall — later than most other Eupatoriums, hence its name — with flat-topped clusters of small white flowers that attract an extraordinary diversity of late-season native bees, wasps, flies, and butterflies when few other wildflowers are in peak bloom. It thrives in roadsides, forest edges, disturbed areas, and garden borders with minimal care, tolerating partial shade and a wide range of soil moisture conditions that make it one of the most adaptable of all native wildflowers for the Gulf Coast. Because its white flower clusters resemble those of several other common Eupatorium species, it is often overlooked by gardeners, but it is among the top 10 most valuable native wildflowers in the region for late-season pollinators. Cut back by half in mid-June to reduce height and increase bushiness; divide crowded clumps in spring to rejuvenate and control spread.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Late Goldenrod spreads aggressively by rhizomes in moist, fertile conditions — best used in naturalized settings or managed by dividing every 2–3 years.
directions: Late Goldenrod is one of the most common and widespread native goldenrods of moist, open habitats across North America, blooming later than most goldenrods — from August through October — and providing one of the most important late-season nectar sources for migrating monarch butterflies, native bumblebees, sweat bees, and the last generation of many butterfly species before winter. The smooth stems (a distinguishing feature from the rough-stemmed Solidago rugosa and tall Solidago altissima) support arching plumes of bright yellow flowers that brighten roadsides, stream banks, wet meadows, and moist open disturbed areas from coast to coast. An important host for over 100 species of caterpillars and one of the most ecologically productive native plants in North America by insect diversity supported, Late Goldenrod spreads vigorously by rhizomes in moist soil and is best used in large naturalized plantings or meadow gardens where its spreading habit is an asset. Direct sow seeds in fall or divide established clumps in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; late ox-eye daisy spreads moderately by rhizomes and forms large colonies over time, particularly in moist conditions. It is a very tall plant (4-6 feet) and may need staking or be planted where it can lean against other tall plants for support.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained to moderately wet soil in full sun to part shade; late ox-eye daisy is the autumn counterpart of the familiar ox-eye daisy (Leucanthemum vulgare) — but while the common daisy blooms in May and June, this species from eastern Europe blooms in October and November, making it among the very latest-flowering perennials in the entire garden. The large, pure-white single daisy flowers with yellow centers are produced on tall, clumping, multi-stemmed plants from October until hard frost, providing pure white daisy color at a season when the garden is otherwise dominated by purples, oranges, and golds. The dark-green, narrow, toothed leaves are attractive throughout the growing season and the plants spread steadily to form impressive drifts. Native to moist meadows, stream margins, and forest edges in southeastern Europe from Hungary to Ukraine, it adapts well to garden conditions across zones 4-9 and is outstanding for naturalizing in moist areas where its spreading habit can develop freely.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil; late purple aster self-sows moderately in appropriate conditions and thrives in dry, rocky or sandy soils in full to partial sun. It grows naturally in open woodlands, roadsides, and rocky outcrops across the eastern US.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; late purple aster is one of the most recognizable autumn wildflowers of the eastern United States, distinguished from other fall asters by its clasping leaves — each leaf wraps around the stem at its base in an ear-like fashion — and its intensely clear violet-purple ray flowers that are among the deepest, most saturated shades of any fall aster. It blooms from mid-September into November, providing critical nectar for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season native bumblebees precisely when other late-season resources are diminishing. The plant grows naturally in dry, open woods, rocky roadsides, and pine barrens across the eastern US and is well adapted to zone 9a conditions when planted in well-drained, lean soil. Combine with native grasses, goldenrods, and ironweeds for an outstanding autumn pollinator meadow.

common_name: Laura Bush Petunia (Heat-Tolerant Texas Superstar Petunia)
plant_note: Set out transplants after last frost; Laura Bush is a Texas Superstar-designated petunia selected for outstanding heat and humidity tolerance and a self-cleaning habit, blooming through summer conditions that cause most bedding petunias to collapse.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 10-14 inches apart. Laura Bush is a naturally occurring petunia selection discovered in Texas and named for the former First Lady, then trialed and designated a Texas Superstar by Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for exceptional performance in Texas heat, humidity, and alkaline soil where hybrid bedding petunias typically decline by midsummer. Unlike most petunias, it is self-cleaning — spent flowers drop away on their own without deadheading — and it reseeds readily, often returning the following year in mild-winter zones. Flowers are smaller than hybrid petunias, in shades of light purple to lavender, but are produced in such profusion that the plant is smothered in bloom from spring through fall. It tolerates poor, alkaline soil and considerable drought once established, needing far less water and fertilizer than typical bedding petunias. Shear back by about a third in midsummer if plants become leggy to encourage fresh, compact regrowth for fall bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; provide a sturdy support or allow to scramble into a tree. Laurel Greenbriar is difficult to transplant from the wild due to its deep, tuberous root — use only container-grown nursery stock.
directions: Laurel Greenbriar is an evergreen native vine of moist woods, swamp margins, and thickets of the coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, climbing by tendrils to 30 feet or more with stiff, spiny stems and long, narrow, leathery evergreen leaves that make it the greenest plant in the winter understory forest. The small, dark blue-black berries are produced in clusters and are a critical winter food for wild turkeys, black bears, white-tailed deer, mockingbirds, and cedar waxwings when other food sources are exhausted. The spiny, interlocking stems create impenetrable thickets that provide ideal nesting and escape cover for ground-nesting birds, rabbits, and other small wildlife, and the tubers were historically eaten by Native Americans. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Laurel Greenbriar tolerates periodic flooding and deep shade once established, and requires a sturdy structure or tree to climb.

common_name: Laurel Oak (Diamond Leaf Oak, Swamp Laurel Oak)
plant_note: Plant nursery-grown trees in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; laurel oak tolerates extended flooding and grows naturally in floodplain forests, swamp margins, and wet bottomlands of the coastal plain. It establishes quickly for a large oak when planted small.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; laurel oak is one of the most common and important native trees of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic coastal plain — a large, fast-growing semi-evergreen oak reaching 60–80 feet with a broad crown and distinctive narrowly elliptical, unlobed leaves resembling laurel or willow leaves. Unlike live oak and other southern oaks, laurel oak grows readily in the wet, poorly drained soils of floodplains, swamp margins, and pine flatwoods that define much of the Gulf Coast landscape. It provides outstanding wildlife value — the small acorns are eaten by wood ducks, deer, turkeys, squirrels, and many other species. The semi-evergreen foliage provides moderate winter screening. Laurel oak grows faster than live oak (3–5 feet per year when young) but is shorter-lived (60–80 years). An excellent shade tree for moist, low-lying Gulf Coast sites.

plant_note: Plant in spring in its permanent location — this species has an extensive deep root system and resents transplanting once established; smilax is exceptionally well-adapted to wet, acidic, shaded sites in the Gulf Coast South where it grows naturally in swamp margins and wet woodland.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil; laurel-leaf greenbrier is an evergreen native vine of the Gulf Coastal Plain that uses tendrils to scramble through shrubs and trees, providing year-round cover and valuable black berries for wildlife from fall through winter. The long, lance-shaped, leathery leaves remain glossy dark green through winter, making it valuable for screening and structure in year-round southern gardens. It tolerates flooding, deep shade, and sandy coastal conditions. New shoots in spring are edible and have been used by Native Americans as a vegetable and starch source. The dried rhizomes yield a starchy food and historically formed the basis of a root beer-style drink. Use on fences and naturalized areas where it can spread without becoming a maintenance challenge.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in early spring or late fall; needs light and cold.
directions: Surface-sow the tiny seed in early spring or late fall directly where plants are to grow, since poppies dislike transplanting and need light to germinate. 'Lauren's Grape' produces rich purple single blooms followed by attractive seed pods prized for arrangements and baking. Thin seedlings to give each plant room, and grow in full sun with well-drained soil. Allow some pods to mature and self-sow to bring the poppies back each year.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun in spring or fall; laurustinus is one of the most adaptable and shade-tolerant of all evergreen viburnums.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; laurustinus is a Mediterranean evergreen viburnum that provides exceptional winter interest — the flower buds, held in flat-topped clusters, open from pink buds to white flowers from late winter through spring, providing bloom when nearly nothing else flowers in the garden. After bloom, the fruits pass through a striking metallic turquoise-blue phase before ripening to black, providing a second season of ornamental value. It is one of the most shade-tolerant and adaptable evergreen viburnums, performing well in partial shade, alkaline soil, and coastal conditions. 'Eve Price' (compact, deep-pink buds), 'Spring Bouquet' (compact, freely flowering), and 'Lisarose' (rich pink) are excellent cultivar selections.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; loves heat.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant once the weather is warm. 'Lavender Lady' produces abundant papery, clover-like lavender blooms that shrug off extreme heat and drought once established. The long-lasting flowers are excellent for fresh bouquets and dry beautifully for everlasting arrangements. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and pinch young plants to encourage branching and more blooms.

plant_note: Divide clumps carefully in early spring or sow fresh seed in fall, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; lavender mist meadowrue resents root disturbance and is best left undisturbed once established — it is slower to establish than many perennials but becomes a long-lived and increasingly beautiful garden plant over time.
directions: Divide clumps carefully or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; lavender mist meadowrue is a Japanese tall shade perennial that creates one of the most ethereal and romantic effects in the summer shade garden — rising to 5–7 feet on slender, dark, metallic-purple-blue stems with large, delicate, blue-green, columbine-like, compound leaves, then erupting in mid-summer into enormous, airy clouds of tiny, lavender-lilac to rosy-purple, pendant flowers with long, showy, yellow-tipped stamens that create a hovering, transparent, lavender mist above the foliage. The combination of the dark, metallic stems, the blue-green ferny foliage, and the airy lavender flower cloud creates one of the finest and most distinctive effects available in the shade garden. It is considerably more impressive in stature than the European species (Thalictrum aquilegiifolium) and blooms later, in July–August. It needs staking only in windy or very shaded positions. The dark stem color is a distinctive identification feature. An outstanding background plant for large shade borders.

common_name: Lawn Orchid (Soldier's Orchid, Asian Lawn Orchid, Naturalized Jewel Orchid)
plant_note: Zeuxine strateumatica naturalizes spontaneously in lawns, turf, and disturbed ground throughout zone 8-12 and rarely needs to be intentionally planted — it appears on its own in maintained lawns and garden beds. If introducing deliberately, scatter seed in fall into moist, shaded to partially shaded lawn areas. In zone 9-12, the plant blooms in winter and early spring (November–March), then disappears as summer heat arrives. A delightful, harmless 'lawn weed' orchid that many Florida and Gulf Coast gardeners enjoy discovering for the first time in their St. Augustine or Bermuda grass lawns.
directions: Zeuxine strateumatica naturalizes spontaneously in lawns and turf throughout the southeastern US and requires no cultivation — it simply appears in suitable lawns and is a pleasant discovery rather than a planted species. Zeuxine strateumatica is a tiny, self-seeding, cool-season annual terrestrial orchid native to Southeast Asia and India in the Orchidaceae family — one of the most widely naturalized orchids in North America, now established throughout Florida, Hawaii, Louisiana, Texas, and other Gulf and Atlantic coastal states in maintained lawns, turf areas, and disturbed ground. In cool weather (November through March in zone 9-12), the plant produces small rosettes of narrow, grasslike, dark-green to bronze-green leaves that emerge from the lawn surface — often initially mistaken for a grass seedling or weed — and then an erect flower spike 4–8 inches tall bearing a raceme of tiny (0.25-inch) white to ivory flowers with a golden-yellow center, each flower perfect in miniature orchid form when viewed with a hand lens. The entire plant is small enough to be easily overlooked among lawn grass. Zeuxine strateumatica spreads prolifically by wind-dispersed dust seed and has colonized lawns throughout the southeastern US, the Caribbean, Central America, and Hawaii since its original naturalization in the early 20th century. Mowing is its only control — spring mowing eliminates the season's plants after they flower. A charming lawn companion orchid. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile to average, deep loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Lawson cypress requires adequate moisture and good drainage. Highly susceptible to Phytophthora lateralis root rot — do not plant in poorly drained soils or where water stands. A critical threat to native populations in the Pacific Northwest.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile to average, deep loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Lawson cypress (Port Orford cedar) is one of the most important timber and ornamental conifers of the Pacific Coast — a massive forest tree native to a very restricted range in extreme southwestern Oregon and northwestern California, where it grows in the moist, foggy coast range forests and along mountain stream banks. The wood is extraordinarily lightweight, strong, aromatic, and durable — highly prized for boat-building, archery arrows, and as a Japanese export for shrine construction and coffins. In cultivation (especially in the UK and Europe where hundreds of cultivars have been selected), it is among the most diverse ornamental conifers, with columnar, pyramidal, pendulous, dwarf, and variously colored forms available. Severely threatened in its native range by the introduced water mold Phytophthora lateralis — a catastrophic root disease spread via contaminated water and soil. Widely grown in European gardens and as a hedging plant, where it thrives in cool, moist conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated stock in spring; wild collection is prohibited given the species' rarity.
directions: A rare, conservation-listed native Marshallia endemic to mafic rock outcrops and open rocky woodlands in a small area of the Piedmont of North Carolina and Virginia, producing broad, spoon-shaped basal leaves and slender stems topped with solitary pink to rose-purple, powder-puff composite flower heads in summer. The mafic substrate of its native habitat gives rise to highly specialized, nutrient-limited plant communities with few close parallels in cultivation. Grow in moderately well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in partial to full sun; purchase only nursery-propagated stock from specialty native plant nurseries, as planting cultivated specimens directly supports conservation of this geographically restricted endemic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; leadplant develops an extraordinarily deep root system — mature specimens have roots documented to 15 feet — making it completely impossible to transplant; sow in a permanent location and allow natural cold stratification and scarification over winter; hot-water scarification significantly improves germination rates when spring-sowing.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, dry to average soil in full sun; leadplant is one of the deepest-rooted plants in the world relative to its above-ground size — individual plants develop root systems reaching 15 feet or more into the soil profile, making it one of the most drought-tolerant and fire-adapted shrubs native to North America, and making any attempt at transplanting futile; it must be established from seed sown in place. Amorpha canescens is a low, spreading prairie shrub with distinctive silver-gray, densely canescent (canescens = gray-woolly) pinnately compound leaves that give the whole plant a soft silver-lavender cast; in late June and July it produces spectacular, dense, upright spikes of tiny, deep purple flowers with bright orange anthers, creating a vivid contrast with the silvery foliage that makes it one of the most ornamentally distinguished native prairie shrubs in North America — the plant's association with the deep, lead-gray soils of undisturbed prairie gives it the common name leadplant. It is a nitrogen-fixing legume, an indicator of high-quality, never-plowed prairie remnants, and an exceptional pollinator plant visited by native bumblebees, sweat bees, and mining bees; leadplant is slower to establish from seed than most forbs, taking 2–3 years to begin flowering, but is then extremely long-lived and essentially maintenance-free, resprouting vigorously from its deep root crown after fire or cutting — fire suppression is one reason it has declined in much of its range, and it responds well to periodic cutting or burning that mimics natural disturbance.

common_name: Leather Fern (Giant Leather Fern, Coastal Tropical Fern for Wet Shade in Zone 9-11)
plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery transplants in spring; Leather Fern thrives in consistently moist to wet conditions — it is native to freshwater swamps, brackish wetland margins, and mangrove edges throughout coastal Florida and the Gulf Coast, and requires reliable moisture to perform well. In zone 9, plant in shade to partial shade with consistent water; Leather Fern tolerates brief flooding and is one of the few large ferns that does well in the permanently wet areas of Gulf Coast gardens where most ornamentals struggle. Hardy to approximately 30°F, making it perennial in zone 9 coastal areas but potentially losing fronds in cold winters. The enormous size (fronds to 9 feet) and tropical appearance make Leather Fern a dramatic statement plant for wet, shaded areas. Propagate by division in spring.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; water regularly and never let soil dry out. Acrostichum danaeifolium (Giant Leather Fern, Leather Fern) is one of the largest ferns native to North America — a massive, coarse-textured fern of coastal wetlands and freshwater swamps native to Florida, the Gulf Coast, the Caribbean, and tropical America. The fronds of mature plants can reach 9 feet in length, with a dramatic upright to arching form and coarse, leathery leaflets that give the plant both its common name and its distinctive tropical appearance. Unlike the delicate, feathery texture of woodland ferns (maidenhair, Japanese painted fern), Leather Fern has a bold, architectural presence — the large, firm, deep green fronds are visually striking in the garden and highly resistant to wind damage, making the plant appropriate for exposed positions in wet areas where more delicate ferns would be shredded. The fern produces two types of fronds: sterile (vegetative) fronds with unmodified leaflets, and fertile fronds where the lower leaflets are densely covered with reddish-brown sporangia (spore-producing structures) that give the underside of fertile fronds an entirely different, rusty-brown appearance from the sterile fronds. Leather Fern's ecological niche — coastal freshwater swamps, brackish margins, and disturbed wetlands — means it is one of the few large ornamental plants that thrives in the perpetually wet, sometimes anaerobic conditions of low-lying Gulf Coast gardens where surface water accumulates and most landscape plants decline.

plant_note: Plant with crown at or slightly below soil level in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in partial shade; follow the classic clematis planting advice — head in the sun, feet in the shade — with cool mulch over the root zone.
directions: Leather flower is a graceful native clematis from the moist woodlands and streambanks of the central and eastern United States, distinguished by its nodding, urn-shaped flowers of leathery, thick-textured red-purple to mauve petals — the unusual closed, pitcher-like floral form is adapted for specialist bee pollinators that force their way inside for nectar, preventing nectar robbing by smaller insects. Unlike many showy cultivated clematis, leather flower blooms from late spring through summer with a steady succession of individual flowers rather than one dramatic flush, keeping the vine attractive for months; the feathery, plumed seedheads that follow add ornamental value into fall and winter. Grow on a fence, through a native shrub, or along a trellis in the partial shade of a woodland edge; pair with native ferns, columbines, and spicebush for a layered understory planting. Cut back to 12 inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seeds require 60–90 days of cold-moist stratification to break dormancy and typically germinate the following spring. Plant container-grown specimens in spring near a trellis or shrub for support.
directions: Plant at the base of a trellis, fence, or open shrub in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade; keep the root zone cool and moist with mulch while allowing the vine to climb into brighter light — the classic clematis principle of cool feet and a sunny head. Leatherflower is a native vine of stream banks, forest edges, and thickets across the eastern US, bearing unusually thick-petaled, nodding urn-shaped flowers in shades of pink to reddish-purple that do not open fully, creating a distinctive lantern-like appearance from late spring through summer. The flowers are followed by showy, globe-shaped clusters of feathery-tailed seeds that persist and provide winter interest. Prune back to 12–18 inches in late winter as the plant blooms on new growth.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf fern grows in damp, shaded sites in nature but tolerates surprisingly dry conditions once established. In zone 9 it is often semi-evergreen and benefits from protection from hard freezes.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; leatherleaf fern is the world's most commercially important ornamental fern — the glossy, dark green, triangular bipinnate fronds are the iconic 'greenery' used by florists in cut flower arrangements worldwide, with a global trade worth hundreds of millions of dollars annually. In zone 9–12 landscapes it is a superb, low-maintenance shade groundcover with exceptionally durable, leathery, handsome foliage that maintains its deep-green color year-round. It tolerates drought better than most ferns and grows in a variety of shaded conditions under trees and structures. The fronds hold on the plant for many months and cut fronds last 2–3 weeks in water, making it one of the best cut foliage plants the garden produces. Spreads slowly by creeping underground rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover in shaded beds. One of the most reliable, rewarding, and practical shade plants for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; leatherleaf sedge can be difficult to establish in the hot, humid summers of the Deep South — it performs best in zone 6–8 where temperatures are moderate, and in zone 9 it is often grown as a cool-season perennial or annual in partially shaded, well-ventilated sites.
