Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix and water thoroughly when the top layer dries. The leaves are very large and prone to mechanical damage — handle carefully. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Anthurium magnificum produces its most spectacular foliage in conditions of consistent bright filtered light, ideally from a bright north or east window, and will decline in dim corners. Anthurium magnificum is a large, terrestrial to lithophytic anthurium native to the cloud forests of Colombia, closely related to Anthurium crystallinum and belonging to the same 'velvet anthurium' group. The species name 'magnificum' is apt: the mature plant produces truly magnificent large leaves — broadly heart-shaped, up to 24–30 inches across, with a thickly leathery, velvety texture, very dark emerald-green surface, and a bold network of raised, pale ivory to cream veins that create an intricate pattern across the dark leaf face. The leaves are quadrangular-cordate (squarish heart shape) with distinctly angled basal lobes, a feature that distinguishes it from the more rounded lobes of A. crystallinum. The combination of large size, cardboard-thick leaf texture, dramatic vein pattern, and rich coloration makes A. magnificum one of the most impressive velvet anthuriums available. The species' considerable variation in the wild has led to complex classification and collector debate over 'true magnificum.' All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Magnus performs best in lean soils — overly rich soil produces tall, floppy growth and reduces the intensity of the flower color.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Magnus is the most widely planted and celebrated purple coneflower cultivar — selected in Sweden by Magnus Nilsson and introduced to American horticulture in 1998, when it won the Perennial Plant of the Year award. The large, flat, horizontal petals (ray florets) surround the prominent, spiny, orange-bronze central cone in deep rosy-magenta-purple color that holds through the heat of summer without fading, which was Magnus's breakthrough characteristic over earlier coneflower selections that faded to washed-out pink in midsummer. The petals are notably larger, broader, and more horizontal than the drooping petals of typical wild Echinacea purpurea, creating a bolder, more architectural flower presentation. Magnus grows 30–42 inches tall and is outstanding as a cut flower, garden pollinator plant (monarchs, swallowtails, bees, and goldfinches are all attracted), and naturalizing prairie-style perennial. In zone 9, Magnus blooms from June through October in good conditions. The seed heads left standing through winter provide exceptional goldfinch feeding interest from October through February. Like all coneflowers, Magnus is drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free once established in well-drained soil.

common_name: Mahogany Fern (Maidenhair Tree Fern, Hump Fern, Truncate Didymochlaena)
plant_note: Plant in deep to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil; Didymochlaena truncatula is one of the most elegant and distinctive shade ferns for zone 10-12 outdoor use or a shaded indoor container. The new fronds emerge in rich copper-pink to bronze-mahogany color before maturing to glossy dark green — the color sequence from which the common name 'Mahogany Fern' derives. Sensitive to temperatures below 45°F; bring indoors or protect in zone 9. Water consistently — allow the medium to approach dryness between waterings but never fully dry. Slow to establish but long-lived once settled. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in deep to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil — Mahogany Fern grows most beautifully in the cool, moist, deeply shaded conditions of a sheltered porch, conservatory, or jungle garden in zone 10-12 and is one of the most elegant of all shade ferns when well-established. Didymochlaena truncatula is a large, upright-growing terrestrial fern in the Didymochlaenaceae family (sometimes placed in Dryopteridaceae) with a broadly pan-tropical distribution — native to moist forests in tropical Africa, Madagascar, Asia, Australia, the Pacific Islands, the Caribbean, and tropical Americas. The plant produces a broad, erect rosette of large, bipinnate fronds 24–48 inches long, each frond having a distinctive architectural quality: the individual pinnules (small leaflets) are oblong with truncated (squared-off) bases and tips, giving the frond a clean, precise, almost geometric appearance unlike the delicate filigree of most ferns. The young fronds emerging from the crown are the plant's most spectacular feature — they emerge in rich mahogany-bronze to coppery-pink, a color that glows in shaded light before gradually maturing to glossy, dark forest-green. The contrast between the soft, metallic young fronds and the dark mature fronds creates a year-round multi-tonal display. The trunk gradually develops a short, upright base over many years, giving old specimens a tree-fern-like quality. An elegant, distinctive shade fern of botanical interest. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring when soil has warmed; miscanthus establishes best in warm soil and can be slow in cold springs.
directions: Plant divisions in full sun in any well-drained to moderately moist soil; maiden grass forms large, dramatic clumps with arching, green or variegated foliage and showy, feathery silver plumes in late summer and fall. Cut back hard in late winter or early spring before new growth emerges — use pruners or a chainsaw on large clumps; tie the clump with twine before cutting to simplify cleanup. Divide every 3–5 years in spring when the center of the clump dies out. Some cultivars are sterile; check before planting, as seeding types can naturalize aggressively in some regions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in well-drained soil; maiden pinks germinate readily in cool conditions. Thin to 6 inches and expect first-year flowering. They can also be planted from divisions or plugs in spring or fall.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; maiden pinks is a low, mat-forming European native dianthus that covers itself with small, richly colored flowers in shades of rose, crimson, white, and bicolored combinations. The flowers have toothed or fringed petal margins and many have a darker central ring ('eye'), giving them a jewel-like quality. In flower from late spring through summer, maiden pinks self-sows to naturalize readily in gravel paths, between paving stones, and on dry sunny slopes. It is excellent for rock gardens, cottage garden edging, and low green roofs. The blue-green, needle-like foliage forms an attractive evergreen mat through winter.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or plugs in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches), wet marsh margins, or permanently saturated soil in full sun; maidencane spreads aggressively by rhizomes in aquatic conditions — site where it has room to spread or contain with barriers in smaller water features.
directions: Maidencane is the dominant emergent aquatic grass of the Gulf Coastal Plain's freshwater marshes, lake margins, and slow-moving waterways — forming vast, grass-like stands in shallow water from Texas to Florida that serve as one of the most important waterfowl habitat grasses in the southeastern United States. Dabbling ducks including mallards, teal, mottled ducks, and wood ducks consume the seeds profusely during fall migration; the emergent stands also provide critical nesting cover for king rails, common gallinules, and purple gallinules. In constructed wetlands, stormwater retention ponds, and rain garden overflow areas, maidencane stabilizes wet banks and shallow margins with its extensive rhizome system while providing year-round wildlife value. It spreads rapidly in aquatic conditions by rhizomes and self-seeding and can form dense monocultures in productive conditions — appropriate for naturalized pond and wetland margins but requires management in small water gardens to prevent it from overwhelming other plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; maidenhair fern grows slowly but is long-lived in appropriate conditions with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; northern maidenhair fern is one of the most graceful ferns in cultivation, with distinctive, horseshoe-shaped fronds of fan-shaped, bright-green leaflets carried on delicate, wiry, shining black stems that tremble in the slightest breeze. New growth in spring emerges as coppery-pink croziers (fiddleheads) before expanding to full size. It requires consistently moist soil and fails in dry, compacted, or alkaline conditions. Excellent in combination with trilliums, Solomon's seal, and other woodland perennials. Divide in early spring by lifting and cutting the rhizome mass — do not allow divisions to dry out before replanting. The tropical maidenhairs (A. raddianum and relatives) require completely different culture.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants or small divisions tucked into crevices of a rock garden or dry stone wall in partial to full shade, in neutral to slightly alkaline, freely draining, rocky or gritty soil. Maidenhair Spleenwort is a rock crevice specialist and thrives in the tight drainage and consistent humidity of dry stone walls and rocky outcrops.
directions: Maidenhair Spleenwort is one of the world's most widely distributed and delightful small ferns, native to rock crevices, cliff faces, and mortared stone walls throughout the temperate Northern Hemisphere from North America to Europe, Asia, and beyond, where its neat rosettes of tiny, dark-stemmed, pinnate fronds tuck into the smallest gaps between stones with remarkable grace. The evergreen, arching fronds — typically 4–8 inches long with rounded, alternating pinnae on wiry, dark, lustrous stems — are persistent through winter and provide delicate year-round texture in rock gardens, dry stone walls, and shaded rocky outcrops. Unlike most ferns that prefer moist, humus-rich soil, Maidenhair Spleenwort is adapted to excellent drainage and even slightly alkaline conditions derived from limestone or mortar — making it ideal for growing in rock garden crevices and the joints of dry stone walls, where its fine texture contrasts beautifully with the rugged stone. Plant in tight crevices with minimal amended soil and virtually no supplemental watering once established.

common_name: Majestic Beauty Indian Hawthorn (Tree-Form Large Indian Hawthorn)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring, summer, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Majestic Beauty grows considerably larger than standard Indian hawthorn and can be trained as a small multi-trunked tree or large screening shrub.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Majestic Beauty is a hybrid Indian hawthorn selected for its unusually large mature size, growing into a substantial large shrub or small tree rather than the compact rounded mound typical of most Indian hawthorn cultivars, which makes it useful for screening, specimen planting, or a small flowering tree in coastal landscapes. In spring it produces abundant clusters of fragrant, light pink flowers followed by small blue-black berries that attract birds, all on glossy, leathery, disease-resistant foliage. It shares the species' outstanding tolerance for salt spray, wind, and poor sandy soils, making it a strong performer in exposed coastal Gulf sites, though good air circulation helps minimize the leaf spot disease that can affect Indian hawthorn in humid conditions.

common_name: Major Wheeler Coral Honeysuckle (Best Native Hummingbird Honeysuckle Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Major Wheeler blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates more shade than most flowering vines — half-day sun produces good bloom in Gulf South conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Major Wheeler is widely considered the finest cultivar of native coral honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) — a vigorous, non-invasive, native vine producing intense scarlet-red tubular flowers in large clusters throughout the spring and early summer with rebloom through fall. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), Coral honeysuckle is well-behaved, manageable, and ecologically beneficial — a twining vine that climbs to 6–12 feet without smothering everything in its path, and one of the premier hummingbird plants in eastern North American gardens. 'Major Wheeler' was selected for exceptionally heavy and prolonged bloom compared to the straight species — the flower clusters are larger, more numerous, and the rebloom period more consistent, making it the overwhelming choice among coral honeysuckle cultivars for maximum ornamental and hummingbird value. The vivid red tubular flowers have no fragrance (unlike Japanese honeysuckle) but attract ruby-throated hummingbirds with exceptional consistency from spring through fall. The semi-evergreen, blue-green, oval leaves are attractive even when not in bloom. In zone 9, Major Wheeler performs best with afternoon shade protection during the hottest summers. Red berries persist into fall, providing late-season food for thrushes, mockingbirds, and other frugivorous birds.

plant_note: Plant container vines in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; provide a trellis, fence, or arbor support — Major Wheeler is a twining vine that requires vertical support and will reach 10–15 feet at maturity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with vertical support; Major Wheeler is widely considered the finest cultivar of trumpet honeysuckle (Lonicera sempervirens) — the native American hummingbird vine — selected for its exceptionally prolific and long flower production. While the species is already outstanding for hummingbirds, Major Wheeler produces dramatically more flowers per season and repeats bloom flushes more reliably than unselected species plants. The 1.5–2 inch, tubular scarlet-to-coral-red flowers are produced in dense terminal clusters from spring through fall in zone 9, creating an almost unmatched hummingbird feeding resource — Ruby-throated hummingbirds visit repeatedly, and the vine at peak bloom will attract multiple hummingbirds simultaneously. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica), trumpet honeysuckle is a well-behaved native that does not self-seed aggressively or spread invasively. The semi-evergreen foliage is attractive, with the characteristic perfoliate leaves (the vine stem appears to grow through the center of the leaf pairs) near the flowers. Major Wheeler is drought-tolerant once established and adaptable to a wide range of soils and light conditions from full sun to partial shade. The profusion of red flowers followed by small red berries provides exceptional wildlife value throughout the year.

subcategory: East African and Malagasy ornamental cycad
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–12; Malagasy Cycad is a large, palm-like cycad native to Madagascar, the Comoros Islands, East African coastal forests (Mozambique, Tanzania, Kenya), and the Mascarene Islands — producing an arching crown of long, glossy, bright-green fronds on a stout trunk, and growing to impressive size over many decades in warm, frost-free gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Cycas thouarsii is drought tolerant once established and does not tolerate waterlogged soils — excellent drainage is essential; water deeply but infrequently and apply balanced slow-release fertilizer once or twice per year. Cycas thouarsii (Malagasy Cycad, East African Cycad, or Madagascar Cycad) is a large, striking cycad native to the coastal and lowland forests of Madagascar, the Comoros, and the East African coastline (Mozambique, Tanzania, coastal Kenya), making it the only Cycas species native to Africa or its offshore islands. The plant is a slow-growing, long-lived, architectural specimen cycad developing a stout, palm-like trunk topped by a crown of long (up to 6 feet), graceful, arching, pinnately compound fronds with glossy, bright-green, narrowly lanceolate leaflets. Like all cycads, it is extremely slow-growing but exceptionally long-lived — specimens hundreds of years old are known. Cycas thouarsii is somewhat more cold-tolerant than other large Cycas species and performs well in zones 9–12, making it among the most useful large cycads for Gulf Coast, Florida, and warm subtropical gardens. A distinctive and dramatic specimen plant for large tropical-style landscape settings. All parts of the plant contain cycasin and other neurotoxins — not edible and should be kept away from children and pets.

plant_note: Root stem tip cuttings under high humidity or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, orchid-bark-amended soil in bright indirect light or partial shade after frost; medinilla requires high humidity (above 60%), consistent warmth, and an orchid-like open, free-draining substrate — standard potting soil compacted around its roots causes root rot and decline.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich, acidic, bark-amended soil in bright indirect light or partial shade; Malaysian orchid (rose grape, showy medinilla) is a Philippine tropical epiphyte of the family Melastomataceae — one of the most spectacular flowering plants in the world — that produces enormous, pendant, bougainvillea-like flower panicles composed of clusters of small, deep-rose-pink to magenta flowers hanging from pale-pink to rose-red, waxy bracts, dangling in dramatic, chandelier-like cascades from the tips of the stiff, upright, square stems with large, sessile, dark-green, prominently veined leaves. The entire flower structure is breathtakingly ornamental and can reach 12–18 inches in length on established specimens. As an epiphyte, medinilla naturally grows on tree branches in the Philippine rainforest and is adapted to excellent drainage, high humidity, and warm, bright-shade conditions — it requires an open, orchid-like substrate and consistent humidity rather than consistently moist soil. In zone 10–12 it can be grown outdoors in bright shade; elsewhere it is a challenging but rewarding conservatory or greenhouse specimen.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in spring; male fern is one of the most adaptable of all ferns, tolerating dry shade, poor soils, and challenging urban conditions that defeat most other species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; male fern is one of the most widely grown and adaptable ferns in the world, forming large, vase-shaped, semi-evergreen clumps with lance-shaped, dark-green fronds that are both elegant and extremely tough. It tolerates dry shade, poor soils, periods of neglect, and more urban pollution than virtually any other fern. New fronds emerge as tightly coiled croziers (fiddleheads) in spring. Semi-evergreen in mild winters; cut old fronds to the ground in late winter before new growth emerges to improve appearance. Excellent for difficult, challenging shaded spots. Named varieties include 'Barnesii' (narrow, upright) and 'Linearis Polydactyla' (narrow, crested frond tips). Divide clumps every 5–7 years in spring.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich, poorly drained to seasonally wet soil in partial shade to full sun. Maleberry thrives in the wet, acidic conditions of pocosins, bog margins, and wet flatwoods where most other ornamental shrubs will not succeed.
directions: Maleberry is a native deciduous shrub of wet, acidic soils across the eastern United States, found in pocosins, bog margins, wet flatwoods, and seasonally flooded stream banks from Maine south to Florida and west to Texas. The clusters of small, urn-shaped white flowers in late spring attract native bees and bumblebees, while the attractive fall foliage ranges from yellow to orange-red in appropriate sunlight. A member of the blueberry family (Ericaceae), Maleberry shares the extreme soil requirements of its relatives — strongly acidic, humus-rich, poorly drained to saturated conditions that would stress most landscape shrubs. Well-suited for wet, acidic garden settings including bog gardens, rain garden overflow zones, and moist native plant hedges in acid soil conditions, Maleberry is rarely cultivated but deserves wider use for challenging wet, acidic sites. Plant rooted cuttings in strongly acidic, moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or direct sow in fall for spring germination; Maltese cross self-sows freely and can become a weed in favorable conditions — deadhead before seeds mature to limit spread. It is short-lived (2–4 years) but self-sows to maintain colonies. Plants in poor soil stay compact; rich soil produces tall, floppy plants that may need staking.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Maltese cross is a classic cottage-garden perennial from Russia and Siberia producing one of the most intensely saturated and vivid scarlet reds available in early-summer perennials — upright, bristly-hairy stems topped with flat-topped, dense clusters of small flowers, each petal notched into a distinctive cross shape that gives each floret a Maltese cross outline, and in the aggregate creating round, vivid-scarlet flower heads of high visual impact. The scarlet is hot, clear, and uncompromising — a true scarlet without orange or pink dilution. This saturated color, in combination with the flat-topped, dense cluster form, creates one of the most eye-catching early-summer effects in the mixed border. It is a traditional cottage garden plant with centuries of cultivation. It combines dramatically with blue delphiniums or white Shasta daisies in the classic red-white-blue color schemes of traditional English cottage gardens. Self-sows freely to maintain colonies; the white form 'Alba' is also available. Tends to be short-lived but perpetuates itself by seed.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; likes cool weather.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. Mammoth sweet peas boast extra-large, sweetly scented flowers on long stems that are perfect for cutting. Bred from an Early Multiflora Gigantea Spencer type, this blend offers extra drought and heat resistance for a longer season. Provide a tall trellis, keep roots cool and evenly moist, and cut flowers frequently to prolong the bloom.

plant_note: Plant divisions or corms after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Mammoth grows rapidly in zone 9's warm, humid summer conditions — plants can reach full height and enormous leaf size by midsummer from a spring planting. Provide consistent moisture, especially during peak summer growth; Colocasia thrives in wet to consistently moist conditions and can even grow in shallow water. In zone 9 the corms often survive winter in the ground with heavy mulching; in colder areas of zone 9 dig and store corms above 50°F. The enormous leaves can reach 4 feet across — a single plant in optimal conditions creates a truly dramatic, tropical focal point.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Mammoth Colocasia thrives in consistently moist conditions, bog edges, and even shallow water where drainage is poor; Mammoth is a large-growing selection of common taro (Colocasia esculenta) selected and named for its exceptional leaf size — producing the largest leaves of any widely available Colocasia cultivar, with individual leaves reaching 3–4 feet long and nearly as wide under optimal conditions. The enormous, heart-shaped, velvety, medium-to-dark green leaves on sturdy, upright petioles create an overwhelming tropical presence in the garden that is unmatched by almost any other hardy temperate-climate plant — a single well-grown Mammoth plant is a landscape focal point that demands attention and creates an immediate tropical atmosphere in whatever garden space it occupies. The enormous leaf surface is simultaneously visually dramatic and ecologically functional: Mammoth creates deep shade beneath its canopy (useful for understory shade plants), captures rainfall and funnels it to the soil (an adaptation to tropical forest conditions), and provides cover for garden wildlife. In zone 9 Mammoth thrives in the humid heat that is its native climate — producing increasingly large leaves through summer as the plant approaches its full potential.

plant_note: Soak and sow in cool spring soil beside a trellis.
directions: This mammoth sweet pea mix delivers large, fragrant blooms in soft rose, pink, lavender, and white on vigorous vines. Soak seeds overnight and sow in cool early-spring soil against a trellis, since these cottage-garden climbers love a chilly start. Keep roots cool and moisture steady, and harvest often to encourage a long succession of scented flowers. The five- to six-foot vines need sturdy support to climb.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; likes cool weather.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. This Mammoth selection produces striking, extra-large blooms in deep velvety purple-blue atop long stems ideal for cutting gardens. Bred from Early Multiflora Gigantea, it offers Spencer-type beauty with added drought and heat resistance. Provide a tall trellis, keep roots cool and evenly watered, and cut flowers often to extend flowering.

common_name: Mammoth Russian Sunflower (Classic Giant Single-Stem Sunflower)
plant_note: Sow after the last frost when soil is warm; Mammoth Russian is a classic giant heirloom sunflower producing a single towering stalk topped by an enormous seed head, grown as much for edible, harvestable seed as for ornamental impact.
directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Mammoth Russian is one of the oldest and most iconic giant sunflower heirlooms, reliably reaching ten to twelve feet or more on a single sturdy stalk topped by a massive, heavy flower head that matures into a dense disc of large, striped seeds prized for roasting, snacking, and bird feed. Because of its impressive height and heavy seed head, it benefits from a somewhat sheltered site out of strong wind, and very tall specimens may need staking. Once the back of the flower head turns yellow-brown and petals drop, the seed head can be cut and hung to dry before threshing out the seeds for harvest or leaving it up for birds.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; needs warm soil and full sun.
directions: This giant heirloom sunflower grows on a single stem to ten or twelve feet and crowns it with a massive golden head up to a foot across. Sow seeds an inch deep directly in warm soil after frost, spacing generously so the huge plants have room. Give full sun and steady water, and stake tall stems in exposed sites to keep them from toppling. The abundant seeds are excellent for roasting or feeding birds once heads mature.

common_name: Mammy Croton (Dark Twisted-Leaf Red-and-Gold Croton Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammy's strongly twisted and contorted leaf form is a defining ornamental characteristic — the spiral, corkscrew-shaped leaves distinguish it from all other commonly grown croton cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammy Croton is one of the most distinctive and recognizable croton cultivars — immediately identifiable by its strongly twisted, spiraling, contorted leaves that curl and spiral along their length rather than lying flat, creating an unusual three-dimensional texture unlike any other commonly available ornamental foliage plant. The leaf color is darker and more intensely red-dominated than Petra: deep, burgundy-red to red-and-gold coloring on a dark green base, with the red tones more predominant and the yellow more restricted to the midrib and splashes near the veins. The overall effect is a darker, moodier palette than the brighter, more orange-dominated Petra — making Mammy especially effective in tropical designs with other dark-leaved companions like black elephant ear, purple ti plant, and dark caladiums. In zone 9, Mammy is typically used as a warm-season container plant or annual-style tropical that is moved indoors before frost; in zone 10b-12 it grows as a permanent perennial shrub. The twisted leaf form is most pronounced in high light conditions — leaves in deep shade tend to become more flattened and less dramatically spiral. The unusual form makes Mammy Croton a striking conversation-piece plant in tropical container arrangements.

plant_note: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil or potting mix in full sun to partial shade; mandevilla requires warm temperatures above 50°F at all times — cold damage occurs below 45°F. In zone 9–10 it may be grown in the ground in a protected location; elsewhere treat as a container plant brought indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; mandevilla is one of the most popular tropical vines for patio containers in the United States, producing large, trumpet-shaped flowers 3–4 inches across in brilliant pink, red, or white from spring through frost. The climbing stems have glossy, dark green leaves that are attractive even out of bloom. Modern compact ('Sundaville' and 'Sun Parasol') series stay under 3 feet and are outstanding in large pots and hanging baskets. The larger vining types need a trellis or support and can reach 8–10 feet. Feed every 2 weeks with a bloom-booster fertilizer for maximum flower production. In zone 9–10 mandevilla may be left outdoors year-round in a sheltered location; in zone 8a bring inside at first frost and keep barely moist through winter. Very sap is milky white and mildly toxic — wear gloves when pruning.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, sandy to rocky coastal soil in full sun in Zone 10–11 frost-free landscapes. Mangrove Spider Lily tolerates salt spray and brief flooding once established. Divide overcrowded clumps every 3–4 years in fall to maintain vigor and flowering.
directions: Mangrove Spider Lily is a native bulbous perennial of southern Florida's coastal strand, coastal hammocks, and pine rocklands, as well as much of the Caribbean, producing spectacular, intensely fragrant white flowers with a fringed central cup and reflexed white petals on 18–30 inch stems from late spring through summer. The broad, strap-like evergreen leaves and showstopper flowers make it one of the most spectacular native perennials available for frost-free South Florida landscapes, and its tolerance of salt spray, periodic flooding, and moderate drought makes it practical for a wide range of coastal garden conditions. Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, sandy to rocky coastal soil in full sun; established clumps slowly expand through bulb offsets and become increasingly floriferous as they mature. Mangrove Spider Lily is cold-sensitive and is best suited to Zone 10–11, though it may survive brief cold snaps in protected Zone 9b microclimates.

subcategory: multi-stemmed South African Cape corn lily
plant_note: Plant small corms 3–4 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; many-spiked corn lily follows the Cape winter-rainfall growing cycle — emerging in autumn, blooming in late winter and spring, then going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer. The species name 'polystachya' (many-spiked) reflects its tendency to produce multiple branching flower stems from a single corm, providing more flowers than single-stemmed corn lily species.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; many-spiked corn lily is a South African Cape Ixia that distinguishes itself from other ixias by producing multiple branching flower spikes from each corm — the 'polystachya' habit — creating a more complex, airy, branched flower display rather than the single wand of most corn lily species. The flowers are typical ixia form — small, star-shaped, six-petaled, in white to pale pink to pale violet with a dark center, clustered along the upper portions of very slender, wiry, arching stems. The collective effect of a planting of I. polystachya in full spring bloom is an airy, wiry cloud of small, starry flowers above narrow, grass-like leaves — a delicate, finely textured spring display of considerable charm. Like all Cape Ixia species, it follows the strict Mediterranean-climate cycle of autumn emergence, winter and spring growth and flowering, complete summer dormancy, and requires the corresponding dry summer period in cultivation. An excellent mixing bulb planted through drought-tolerant perennials and grasses in zone 9–11 Mediterranean-climate and Gulf Coast gardens, particularly in the sandy, well-drained soils of coastal areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky, acidic to neutral soil; many-flowered beardtongue is a Florida endemic that grows naturally in dry, open longleaf pine flatwoods and sandy scrub. It blooms in its first year from fall-sown seed.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; many-flowered beardtongue is a Florida and coastal Georgia endemic, notable for producing an exceptionally large number of white tubular flowers densely packed on tall, erect flower stems in late spring — the most floriferous of the native southeastern penstemons. Like all penstemons, it requires excellent drainage and lean soil; rich, amended soils cause rapid decline. The white flowers are pollinated by bumblebees and native solitary bees. This species is well-adapted to the Gulf Coast region and thrives in zone 9 sandy gardens where most penstemons struggle with heat and humidity. An excellent white-flowered native for dry, sunny borders in zone 8–10 where it blooms prolifically in late spring before heat sets in. Short-lived perennial that maintains itself by self-seeding in appropriate sandy soil.

plant_note: Divide established rhizomes in early spring before shoots emerge; Paris polyphylla requires consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full shade. Seeds require double dormancy (warm, then cold stratification) and take 2+ years to germinate; division is far faster. Plants take years to reach flowering size — patience is essential.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in full to deep shade; Paris polyphylla (Chinese Paris, seven leaves one flower) is a remarkable Asian woodland perennial that looks unlike any other garden plant: a single, stout stem rises to produce a precise whorl of 5–10 lance-shaped leaves around its circumference, then produces from the center a single bizarre spidery flower with narrow, thread-like green petals surrounding a prominent ovary, ultimately developing into a dramatic, fleshy red or black seed capsule that splits open to reveal scarlet seeds. The architectural precision of the whorled leaves and the alien appearance of the flower make it one of the most distinctive plants for the shade garden collector. Native to forest understories from the Himalayas through China and Southeast Asia, it is increasingly available from specialty nurseries. It is one of the most important traditional medicinal plants in Chinese herbalism (Yun Nan Bai Yao).

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in dry to moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; this is one of the few viburnums that thrives and fruits in full dry shade under mature trees.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; mapleleaf viburnum is exceptional among viburnums for its tolerance of both dry conditions and full shade — characteristics that together make it one of the most useful native shrubs for planting under established deciduous trees where root competition and low light challenge most plants. The maple-like leaves turn brilliant pink to rose-pink to crimson-magenta in fall, some of the most vivid fall color of any shade-tolerant shrub. Flat-topped white flower clusters in late spring attract native bees, followed by small dark blue-black berries (technically edible but not palatable) that are consumed by songbirds. Spreads slowly by rhizome to form naturalistic colonies; one of the best native shrubs for difficult dry shade situations.

common_name: Marble Queen Pothos (Heavily Variegated White-Green Pothos)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained potting mix in bright indirect light to partial shade; Marble Queen has heavier white variegation than standard golden pothos, which slows its growth rate and makes it need somewhat brighter light to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright, indirect light to partial shade, protected from direct hot sun which can scorch the pale variegated portions of the leaves. Marble Queen is a striking pothos cultivar with heart-shaped leaves marbled in bold patches of creamy white and green, a much more heavily variegated form than standard golden pothos, though the extensive white patches mean it grows more slowly and needs brighter light to stay vigorous and avoid reverting to plain green. It trails or climbs readily and is a popular hanging basket, shelf, or totem-trained houseplant, tolerating average indoor conditions and irregular watering better than most houseplants. In zone 9a it can summer outdoors in a shaded spot but must come indoors well before frost, since it has no cold tolerance.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall immediately after collection, covering 1–2 inches deep; Margaret's oak grows naturally in dry, sandy, infertile soils of scrub and sandhills habitats of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain. An important scrub oak adapted to xeric, nutrient-poor conditions.
directions: Plant in dry to very dry, sandy, infertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Margaret's oak is a scrub white oak complex species of the sandy longleaf pine ecosystem — growing in the xeric sandhills and scrub flatwoods of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain where it forms a key component of the dry longleaf pine savanna understory. The tree is smaller than the closely related post oak (Q. stellata) and more adapted to dry, sandy, low-nutrient conditions. The acorns are an important mast crop for deer, turkey, squirrels, and blue jays in the longleaf pine ecosystem. A valuable restoration species for degraded sandhills and scrub habitats, and an excellent drought-adapted native shade tree for dry, sandy landscapes in zone 9a where it survives with no supplemental water once established.

common_name: Margarita Sweet Potato Vine (Brilliant Chartreuse Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Margarita' maintains its chartreuse-yellow color in more shade than many other chartreuse foliage plants — it tolerates half-day shade while still providing good color, though full sun produces the most brilliant lime-yellow tones.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Margarita Sweet Potato Vine is a cultivar of ornamental sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) producing large, heart-shaped leaves in brilliant chartreuse to lime-green-yellow — one of the most luminous and versatile foliage colors available in an annual, capable of brightening dark garden areas and creating long-distance visual impact with its pure lime-yellow intensity. The heart-shaped leaves are larger and less lobed than 'Blackie', creating a softer, more flowing texture that contrasts well with both fine-textured annuals and bold-leaved tropical companions. 'Margarita' and 'Blackie' are the classic pairing in container and border compositions — the chartreuse and near-black create one of the most dramatic foliage contrasts available from annual plants, each color intensifying the visual impact of the other. The vigorous trailing habit (4–8 foot spread during Gulf South warm season) makes Margarita outstanding as a groundcover annual, as a trailer over pot edges and retaining walls, and as a weed-suppressing annual between permanent plantings. The chartreuse color illuminates shaded border edges and creates visual warmth in combination with cool blue-purple or coral-pink flowers. In Gulf South summer heat, Margarita vines grow rapidly enough to cover significant ground in 6–8 weeks from transplanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; marginal wood fern is one of the most drought- and dry-shade-tolerant native ferns and is an excellent choice for shaded slopes, rocky woodland gardens, and the dry root zones beneath large trees.
directions: Dryopteris marginalis is a handsome, semi-evergreen to evergreen native fern of eastern North American rocky woodlands, prized for its leathery, blue-green fronds that emerge in a graceful vase shape in spring and persist through winter in most of its range, providing exceptional year-round structure in shaded gardens; the sori are arranged in rows along the margins of the pinnules — hence the common name marginal wood fern, also called marginal shield fern. It is one of the easiest and most adaptable native ferns, tolerating drier shade than most Dryopteris species and thriving in well-drained, rocky, or even somewhat gravelly soils under deciduous trees where other ferns decline; it is far more drought-resilient than interrupted fern or cinnamon fern. The evergreen fronds hold their blue-green color through winter, making it an outstanding companion for other winter-interest shade plants such as Christmas fern, hellebores, and native gingers. Divide established clumps in early spring every 4–5 years to maintain vigor and rejuvenate the crown.

common_name: Marguerite Sweet Potato Vine (Chartreuse-Gold Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Marguerite's bright chartreuse-gold foliage color is most vivid in full sun and dims to a softer green in shade.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Marguerite is the classic bright chartreuse-gold companion to the dark-leaved Blackie sweet potato vine, producing large, heart-shaped, glowing yellow-green leaves on fast-growing, trailing vines that quickly spill over the edges of containers, hanging baskets, and garden beds. Its vigorous, weed-smothering growth makes it a popular filler and spiller in mixed plantings, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought well once established, needing only occasional trimming to keep it from overwhelming smaller companion plants. Like other ornamental sweet potato vines, it produces edible tuberous roots, though the plant is grown almost exclusively for its foliage rather than as a food crop.

plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Marie Pavié is an 1888 French polyantha valued in Gulf South gardens for its strong sweet fragrance, compact habit, and outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1888, Marie Pavié is a classic polyantha prized for producing dense clusters of small, fully double, blush-pink-to-white blooms with a strong, sweet fragrance unusual for such a compact rose. The tidy, rounded shrub blooms in flushes nearly year-round in mild climates and shows outstanding resistance to blackspot and powdery mildew, requiring little to no spraying even in the humid Gulf South. Its modest size and dense, twiggy habit make it well suited to borders, low hedges, and containers, and it tolerates part shade better than most roses, though flowering is heaviest in full sun. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing wood and to maintain shape; deadhead spent clusters to encourage continued rebloom.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Marlberry is not to be confused with the invasive Ardisia crenata (Coral Ardisia) — Marlberry is a native species with smaller, less toothed leaves and larger black berries. Always verify you are purchasing the native species.
directions: Marlberry is a handsome native evergreen shrub or small tree, native to the coastal hammocks, tropical hardwood forests, and pinelands of south Florida and the Keys, growing as a common and important component of the hammock understory layer in partial to full shade. It produces clusters of small white flowers from summer through fall, followed by clusters of round, glossy black berries that are one of the most reliable and abundant bird food sources in south Florida's hammock ecosystem — the berries are consumed by dozens of species of warblers, thrushes, vireos, and resident birds throughout fall and winter. An adaptable and attractive native shade shrub for zone 9b–11 landscapes, Marlberry fills the role of native understory shrub in conditions too shaded for most flowering shrubs, providing year-round evergreen structure, summer-fall blooms, and exceptional wildlife value. Important note: always confirm you are purchasing native Marlberry (Ardisia escallonioides) and not the look-alike invasive Coral Ardisia (Ardisia crenata), which has escaped cultivation and invaded Florida's native hammocks.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil; grown mainly for its foliage.
directions: Marmalade is a coral bells cultivar grown for its ruffled amber, caramel, and rose-tinged foliage that holds color through the seasons. It forms a neat mound and sends up airy flower spikes that attract hummingbirds. Plant in partial shade in rich, well-drained soil, keeping the crown at soil level to prevent rot. Water evenly during dry spells and mulch lightly to keep roots cool. Divide clumps every few years in spring to keep the plant vigorous and refresh its color.

common_name: Mars Madness Hibiscus (Giant Deep Red Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Mars Madness is a Summerific series cultivar producing some of the largest flowers in the group, in a rich, saturated red, on a sturdy, well-branched compact plant.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Mars Madness produces some of the largest flowers in the Summerific breeding series, with rich, saturated red blooms that can exceed 9 inches across on a sturdy, well-branched plant that stays more compact than older hardy hibiscus varieties despite the outsized flowers. The strong stems hold up the heavy blooms well without flopping, an improvement over many older hardy hibiscus selections. It flowers in a steady succession from midsummer into fall, with new buds opening continuously as older flowers fade after a single day. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can damage foliage and flowers where present.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in moist to wet, saline or brackish, sandy soil in full sun along the high tide line; marsh elder is a tidal wetland obligate and should not be planted in fresh water or upland sites.
directions: Marsh elder, also called high-tide bush, is a native deciduous shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast salt marshes, growing precisely at the upper limit of regular tidal flooding — its common name 'high-tide bush' describes its ecological niche as the shrubby fringe that marks the upper boundary of the tidal marsh zone on both Atlantic and Gulf shorelines. Despite its unglamorous appearance for most of the year — a stiff, woody shrub with small, succulent leaves and inconspicuous late-summer flowers — marsh elder is ecologically critical: it provides nesting cover for marsh wrens, seaside sparrows, and clapper rails, and its seeds are consumed by dabbling ducks and shorebirds; it stabilizes the marsh-upland ecotone against erosion. In coastal restoration plantings along the Gulf, it is a primary native shrub for establishing the high marsh zone on restored or disturbed shorelines, often planted in combination with black needle rush (Juncus roemerianus) and saltmarsh cordgrass. It also serves as a windbreak and salt spray filter for adjacent upland plantings.

plant_note: Divide rhizome clumps in spring and plant in wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Marsh Fern spreads by long-creeping rhizomes to form colonies and is excellent for naturalizing wet meadows, rain gardens, and pond margins.
directions: Marsh Fern is one of the most adaptable and widely distributed native ferns in North America, native to marshes, wet meadows, sedge bogs, streambanks, and swamp margins from Newfoundland to Florida and west to Alaska and Texas, growing in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil. Its delicate, light green, pinnately divided fronds are deciduous (dying back to the ground in fall) and emerge fresh and bright in spring from long, creeping rhizomes that spread to form open, wispy colonies in wet areas. Unlike many ferns that require deep shade, Marsh Fern tolerates and even thrives in open, sunny wet meadow situations, making it one of the more versatile native ferns for rain gardens, wet roadside ditches, and pond margins. Divide and replant in spring; the plant requires consistently moist to saturated soil and declines if allowed to dry out for extended periods.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring at the margins of ponds, streams, or rain gardens in consistently moist to saturated, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; marsh marigold thrives with its roots in shallow standing water up to 4–6 inches deep.
directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring at the margins of ponds, streams, or rain gardens in consistently moist to saturated, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; marsh marigold thrives with its roots in shallow standing water and can be grown as a true aquatic marginal in up to 4–6 inches of water. Caltha palustris is one of the earliest and most cheerful native spring wildflowers of North American and European wetlands, producing clumps of large, glossy, kidney-shaped, deep-green leaves and brilliant, waxy, golden-yellow, buttercup-like flowers 1–2 inches across in April and May that are among the most vivid yellows in the early spring garden. The plant goes dormant in summer heat; it pairs beautifully with other wetland perennials including blue flag iris, cardinal flower, and lizard's tail for a season-long native water garden display. All parts are mildly toxic if eaten raw.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; marsh muhly grows naturally in moist prairies, wet meadow margins, calcareous seeps, and open wet woodlands across the northern US and Canada. It is one of the more shade-tolerant of the muhly grasses.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; marsh muhly is a more cold-hardy, moisture-loving muhly grass of moist prairies, wet meadow edges, and open calcareous fens across the northern US and Canada, differing from the warm-season ornamental muhlys in its preference for consistently moist soil and its more compact, clumping nature without the dramatic fall plume display of M. capillaris. The dense, upright stems bear tight, clustered (glomerata = ball-clustered) seed heads from midsummer that are attractive in a subtle, native-prairie way. More shade-tolerant than most muhlys and useful in partial shade in moist prairie or savanna edge settings. Provides important food and nesting material for prairie sparrows and other grassland birds. Hardy to zone 3, making it one of the most cold-tolerant muhly grasses.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; marsh violet thrives in the consistently moist to wet conditions of stream banks, pond margins, and rain garden areas where most violets would rot.
directions: Sow seed in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — marsh violet is the native violet of wet, shaded environments, growing naturally along stream banks, pond margins, seepage areas, and wet woodland clearings where it produces blue-violet flowers with distinctive darker veining and a white base on the lower petals, held on stems above the characteristic heart-shaped leaves from spring through early summer. It is distinguished from the common blue violet (V. sororia) by its requirement for consistently moist to wet soil and its preference for shaded sites. An outstanding native for rain garden margins, wet woodland gardens, pond edges, and boggy areas in partial to full shade where few flowering plants thrive. Like all violets, a critical larval host plant for native fritillary butterflies. Forms attractive colonies in appropriate moist, shaded conditions by self-seeding and spreading by runners.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade — martagon lily is one of very few true lilies that genuinely thrives in shade and is the best choice for naturalizing under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade — martagon lily is one of very few true lilies that genuinely thrives in shade and is the best choice for naturalizing under deciduous trees. Lilium martagon is a native of European and Asian mountain woodlands, producing slender, 3-5 foot stems whorled with dark-green leaves and large clusters of 10-50 small, nodding flowers with dramatically reflexed (swept-back) petals in shades of pink-purple to dark rose, with dark spotting, in June-July; the flowers are unpleasantly scented but visually striking, and the variety 'Album' produces elegant pure-white flowers. Once planted, martagon lily strongly resents disturbance and should be left undisturbed in its permanent position where it will slowly increase over decades, self-seeding into a beautiful long-lived colony beneath trees; it is essentially maintenance-free once established.

common_name: Martha Gonzales Rose (Compact Found Texas China Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Martha Gonzales is a compact, red-flowered found rose discovered in a Texas dooryard garden and named for the woman who grew it, prized for its small size and reliable, near-continuous bloom in Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart for a low border or mass planting. Martha Gonzales is a 'found rose' — a once-unnamed variety rediscovered growing in a Texas garden and identified and named for the woman who had grown and passed it down within her family — and it has become a favorite dwarf China-type rose valued for its compact, low-mounding habit rarely exceeding 2 feet, unusual among garden roses. It produces small, semi-double, brick-red blooms with a light fragrance in dense flushes almost continuously from spring through frost, and new foliage emerges with an attractive reddish tint. Like other China-type roses, it is exceptionally tolerant of heat and humidity and shows strong resistance to blackspot, needing no spray program even in the Gulf South. Its diminutive size makes it useful for edging beds, low borders, and containers where larger antique roses would overwhelm the space. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or twiggy growth; otherwise it needs very little maintenance.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost; soak seed to speed germination.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow after the last frost, covering about 1/2 inch. Named for opening in late afternoon, this fast-growing plant flourishes almost anywhere, including hot, windy spots, and tolerates most soils. Fragrant tubular flowers open after 4pm to attract hummingbirds and other pollinators, making it an excellent annual hedge. It reseeds freely and forms tubers that can be dug and stored over winter in cold climates.

plant_note: Set out after frost; treated as an annual in cold zones and a woody perennial in zones 7 and warmer.
directions: Mary Ann is a heat- and drought-tolerant lantana bearing clusters of yellow, orange, and purple-pink flowers from spring through fall. The blooms are a magnet for butterflies and other pollinators while shrugging off humidity and poor soil. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water sparingly once established, as it thrives on neglect. In zones colder than 7 it is grown as an annual or overwintered indoors. Trim back leggy stems midseason to keep the plant compact and flowering freely.

common_name: Mary Helen Plumeria (Fragrant Golden-Yellow Hawaiian Plumeria)
plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Mary Helen is a popular Hawaiian-bred plumeria cultivar with large, bright golden-yellow flowers and a strong, sweet fragrance.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Mary Helen is a popular Hawaiian-bred plumeria cultivar prized for large, rounded, deep golden-yellow flowers with a strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance, considered one of the best solid-yellow cultivars available for both garden display and lei-making. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to avoid stem rot. Established plants bloom heavily through the warm season with waxy, long-lasting flowers held in clusters at the branch tips. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes. Excellent drainage is the single most important requirement for healthy plumeria.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seeds require light to germinate so press onto the soil surface without covering.
directions: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, humus-rich soil in a shaded or dappled-light location in fall, pressing them lightly so they make good contact without being buried. Plants spend their first season establishing a root system and will not produce their tall, branching flower spikes until the second year. Once established, Maryland Figwort self-sows reliably and requires little maintenance beyond removing spent stems in late winter. Site it toward the back of a native planting where its bold height and wildlife value shine without its modest flowers needing close inspection.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; or sow in early spring in a sunny, sandy seedbed and keep lightly moist. Plants bloom the second year from seed.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, sandy or rocky, acidic soil in full sun; Maryland golden aster is a compact, drought-tolerant native with silky-hairy foliage and vivid golden-yellow daisy flowers from late summer through fall, making it among the best native alternatives to common goldenrod for dry, infertile sandy soil. In its natural habitat it occurs on dry pine barrens, sandy woodland margins, and roadsides throughout the coastal plain from New York to Florida and thrives in the heat of zones 8-9. The silver-hairy stems and foliage look attractive all season and provide an important late-season nectar source for specialist bees and monarchs on warm autumn days.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in full sun to partial shade; Maryland meadow beauty requires moist, acidic, nutrient-poor, sandy conditions similar to its natural seepage bog and moist pine savanna habitat. Grows and spreads by rhizomes in appropriate wet, acidic areas.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in full sun to partial shade; Maryland meadow beauty is a widespread native of the eastern Coastal Plain, growing in wet roadside ditches, moist pine flatwoods, and seepage bogs from New England to Texas. The four-petaled pale rose-pink to white flowers with bright yellow, curved anthers are smaller and paler than Virginia meadow beauty, blooming from mid-summer through fall. Like all Rhexia species, it is pollinated primarily by buzz-pollinating bumblebees. The distinctive urn-shaped seed capsule with a distinctive neck ('the jug') is one of the most interesting wildflower fruits in the eastern flora. More adaptable to wet roadside and ditch conditions than many bog plants, making it useful for naturalistic plantings in moist, sandy, acidic areas. Spreads by rhizomes to form loose colonies. Essential for recreating the wet pine flatwood and sandhill bog plant community.

plant_note: Plant divisions or fresh seed in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade in early spring; in cool climates masterwort tolerates full sun if soil stays consistently moist.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart; masterwort produces intricate, old-fashioned flowers that look like pincushions or small Victorian posies — a papery star-shaped collar of white or pink bracts surrounds a dome of tiny individual florets — from late spring through midsummer, with repeat bloom if deadheaded promptly. It performs best where summers are cool and moist; hot, dry conditions cause premature dormancy. Cut flowering stems to the ground after bloom to encourage a fresh flush of foliage and a second round of flowers in early fall in cooler zones. Divide congested clumps every 3 years in early spring.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in almost any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to full shade; mat rush is extraordinarily adaptable and among the most drought-, heat-, and salt-tolerant of all ornamental grass-like plants. Established plants require essentially no supplemental water in zone 8+ after their first summer. The cultivar 'Tanika' is compact and widely used in commercial landscapes.
directions: Plant in virtually any well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; mat rush is an Australian native sedge-like perennial that has become one of the most widely used tough ornamental plants in warm-climate landscaping worldwide — valued for an exceptional tolerance of drought, heat, poor soil, salt spray, waterlogging, shade, and neglect that makes it nearly indestructible once established. The plant produces dense, arching mounds of stiff, strap-like, dark-green leaves 2–3 feet tall and wide, with clusters of small, cream-yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers borne just above or within the foliage in late spring. It is extensively used in commercial streetscaping, highway medians, coastal plantings, and erosion-control work because of its reliability under minimal maintenance. 'Tanika' is a compact cultivar with finer, more graceful foliage that has become the dominant selection in commercial use. Outstanding for mass planting on difficult dry slopes, under trees in dry shade, or as a no-maintenance edging in zone 7–11 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mathotiana is a vigorous grower that benefits from planting in the fall to allow root establishment before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Mathotiana is one of the most enduring and widely grown Camellia japonica cultivars — a large-flowering formal double with rose-form to formal double, deep crimson to purplish-crimson flowers 4–5 inches across that are extraordinarily full and perfectly symmetrical. Mathotiana is sometimes called 'Purple Dawn' due to the purple-red to deep crimson color that distinguishes it from red camellia cultivars — the specific blue-red tone is unique and contributes to the flower's almost imperial visual richness. The flowers bloom in midseason (December through February in zone 9) on a vigorous upright to spreading plant that can ultimately grow 8–15 feet tall if unpruned. Mathotiana has been in cultivation since the early nineteenth century and is one of the foundational camellia cultivars — it has been in continuous cultivation longer than almost any other named japonica cultivar, reflecting its reliability, flower quality, and overall performance. In zone 9, Mathotiana performs as an exceptionally long-lived landscape shrub — camellia specimens of 50–100+ years are common in Southern historic gardens. Prune immediately after flowering (late winter/early spring) to control size and shape; avoid summer pruning that removes the following season's flower buds.

plant_note: Root root cuttings (3–4 inch sections of roots placed horizontally in sand) in late winter, or plant container-grown plants in fall in lean, dry, well-drained soil in full sun; matilija poppy resents disturbance and transplants with difficulty — choose a permanent location and do not move it. It spreads by underground runners and can be invasive in moist, fertile soils. Seed germination requires smoke treatment or fire scarification and is difficult; cuttings are more reliable.
directions: Plant in lean, dry, very well-drained soil in full sun; matilija poppy is one of the most dramatic and spectacular flowering perennials of the western United States — a large, subshrubby California and Baja California native producing glaucous, blue-gray, deeply cut foliage on stems reaching 5–8 feet, and from May through July, flowers of extraordinary size and beauty: pure white, papery-petaled, deeply crinkled blooms up to 9 inches across with a large, rounded, golden-yellow cluster of stamens at the center — the largest flowers of any native plant in North America. The size and purity of the white blooms, combined with the fragrant, crepe-paper quality of the petals and the golden center, make each individual flower an extraordinary sight, and a large, established clump in full bloom is a garden spectacle with few rivals. It evolved in the chaparral and canyon walls of southern California where fire triggers germination of the seeds, and it is perfectly adapted to summer drought, lean soil, and Mediterranean conditions. It spreads assertively by underground runners and can colonize large areas — useful for erosion control on dry slopes, but potentially problematic in small gardens.

plant_note: Sow in darkness indoors; pansies thrive in cool spring and fall weather.
directions: Sow seed in darkness indoors 10 to 12 weeks before the last frost, since light inhibits germination. Matrix Red Blotch bears extra-large 3.5 inch scarlet-red flowers with dramatic dark blotches on compact, well-branched plants. Pansies love cool weather, so plant them out in early spring or fall for lush, tidy color. Grow in sun to part shade with moist, rich soil, and deadhead the edible blooms to keep flowering strong.

plant_note: Sow in darkness indoors; pansies thrive in cool spring and fall weather.
directions: Sow seed in darkness indoors 10 to 12 weeks before the last frost, since light inhibits germination. Matrix Rose Blotch features soft rose petals with dark centers plus occasional creamy-rose blooms for elegant color. Its compact, spreading habit gives lush coverage with little upkeep, and the edible flowers brighten dishes and drinks. Grow in sun to part shade with moist, rich soil, planting in early spring or fall and deadheading to prolong bloom.

plant_note: Sow in darkness indoors; pansies thrive in cool spring and fall weather.
directions: Sow seed in darkness indoors 10 to 12 weeks before the last frost, since light inhibits germination. Matrix Solar Flare dazzles with red, orange, and yellow blooms and burgundy centers outlined in golden yellow. The color shifts with temperature, showing more red in cool weather and brighter yellow tones as it warms. Grow in sun to part shade with moist, rich soil, planting in early spring or fall and deadheading to keep the display vivid.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Matrona's sturdy, dark-tinted stems resist the flopping that affects many taller sedums, especially in richer soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Matrona is a stately upright sedum with thick, dusty-mauve stems and gray-green, purple-tinged succulent foliage that make it an attractive structural presence even before it blooms, topped in late summer by broad, flat clusters of soft pink flowers that age to a rich rusty-bronze and stand through much of the winter. Its sturdier stems hold up better in wind and rain than many older upright sedum cultivars, especially when grown lean rather than overfed. Left standing over winter, the dried flower heads and stems add structure to the dormant garden and offer shelter for beneficial insects, and the clump can be divided every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Maximilian sunflower cold-stratifies naturally over winter and germinates reliably in spring — it can also be spring-sown after the last frost but fall sowing typically produces more vigorous first-year plants; avoid rich, moist soils that encourage excessive vegetative growth at the expense of flowering and increase susceptibility to lodging.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in lean, well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; Maximilian sunflower is the great giant of North American native perennial sunflowers, a towering prairie and Great Plains species that typically reaches 5–10 feet in height and produces hundreds of bright yellow, 2–3 inch daisy flowers in long, arching, leafy-bracted racemes from late September into October — its late bloom season is its defining ecological asset, providing abundant nectar, pollen, and seed when most other wildflowers have finished for the year. Named by German botanist Adelbert von Chamisso in honor of Prince Maximilian of Wied-Neuwied, who documented the species during his famous 1832–34 expedition into the Great Plains, this sunflower is native to the central prairies and plains from Canada through Texas and is one of the most important late-season food plants for migrating monarch butterflies, native bees, and the many sparrows and finches that consume its oil-rich seeds. It spreads by rhizomes to form large, vigorous colonies and can be assertive in rich, moist soils — plant in lean, dry ground to keep it better proportioned and contained; even in good soils it may require staking or the companionship of sturdy native grasses to remain upright. Maximilian sunflower is an indispensable component of tall-grass prairie restorations and naturalistic meadow plantings, providing essential fall resources at a critical time in the migration and overwintering preparation of numerous wildlife species.

common_name: May Night Salvia (Deep Indigo Hardy Meadow Sage)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average soil in full sun; May Night is the Perennial Plant of the Year 1997 — recognized for its outstanding vigor, extended bloom season, and versatility in well-drained perennial borders.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average soil in full sun; May Night (Mainacht) is the Perennial Plant of the Year 1997 and one of the most celebrated hardy perennial salvias — producing exceptionally dense, upright spikes of deep indigo-violet flowers with contrasting purple calyces that intensify the color even after the petals drop. The very deep, saturated blue-violet color (deeper and more blue than most salvias, approaching true indigo) in tight, dense whorls along upright spikes creates a striking vertical accent effect in the mid-border from late May through June, with strong rebloom when sheared to 6 inches after the first flush. The reblooming quality — producing two to three flower flushes per season when deadheaded — extends the ornamental value of May Night through summer and into fall. The aromatic, gray-green foliage is attractive when the plant is not in flower. May Night is an exceptional pollinator plant: bees of all species, hummingbirds, and butterflies feed heavily on the flowers throughout the bloom period. In zone 9a and warmer, May Night may perform as a short-lived perennial rather than a permanent one — the heat and humidity of the Gulf South challenge this plant most severely in its second and third years. Plant in excellent drainage, treat as an annual if it declines in summer, and consider it a reliable cool-season perennial in the milder portions of zone 8.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; set rhizomes horizontally 2–3 inches deep and space generously as mayapple spreads vigorously by rhizomes to form large colonies.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; set rhizomes horizontally 2–3 inches deep and space generously as mayapple spreads vigorously by rhizomes to form large colonies. Podophyllum peltatum is a bold-textured native perennial of eastern North American forests; each plant sends up one or two large, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves up to 12 inches across, and the paired-leaf stems produce a single, nodding, white, waxy flower with 6–9 petals in April–May hidden beneath the leaves, followed in summer by a lemon-sized, yellowish, edible fruit (when fully ripe) with a sweet, tropical flavor that was used by Native Americans. All parts of the plant except the ripe fruit are toxic; wear gloves when handling rhizomes and do not allow children to eat unripe fruits. Mayapple naturalizes rapidly and makes an outstanding large-scale groundcover under deciduous trees.

common_name: Mazari Palm (Dwarf Fan Palm, Ritchie's Nannorrhops, Afghan Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with extremely well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil; Nannorrhops ritchiana is one of the most cold-hardy fan palms, rated to zone 7 and reportedly surviving temperatures to 10–15°F in its native habitat. It requires excellent drainage — root rot in moist, poorly-drained soils is the primary cause of failure. Grows naturally in hot, arid, rocky desert conditions and is extremely drought-tolerant. The clumping habit produces multiple trunks from a shared root mass. Growth is slow. This is a genuinely rare palm in US cultivation despite its exceptional cold hardiness.
directions: Plant in full sun in extremely well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or rocky soil — Mazari Palm is adapted to the arid, rocky mountain deserts of Central Asia and demands the best drainage possible, making raised beds or slope planting essential in humid Gulf Coast conditions. Nannorrhops ritchiana is a clumping, multi-stemmed fan palm native to Afghanistan, Pakistan, Iran, and adjacent regions of Central Asia in the Arecaceae family — one of the most cold-hardy and drought-tolerant of all fan palms and a genuinely remarkable species for gardeners in cold climates who want to grow a palm outdoors. The plant grows naturally at elevations up to 6,000 feet in the arid mountain ranges of Afghanistan and Pakistan, surviving both intense summer heat (110°F+) and winter cold (10–15°F), conditions more extreme than most other palm species can endure. The plant produces a clumping mass of stems that branch from a common base (one of the few monocots that branch), each stem terminating in a rounded crown of stiff, silvery blue-green to gray-green fan leaves 2–3 feet wide with sharply divided segments. The overall appearance is compact, dense, and distinctly silver-gray — quite unlike the tropical-green appearance of most fan palms. Nannorrhops ritchiana blooms terminally — after a trunk blooms (once per stem, after many years), that stem dies but the clump continues via other stems. The fiber of the leaves and stems is used in traditional Central Asian crafts. Exceptional cold hardiness makes it valuable for zone 7-9 palm enthusiasts.

plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seeds directly into warm, well-drained soil once frost danger passes, barely covering them, or start indoors a few weeks before the last frost. This compact variety produces three-inch deep pink blooms with white-tipped petals, so pinch young plants to encourage bushy branching. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to prolong bloom into fall. Zinnias tolerate heat well and make excellent cut flowers and pollinator draws.
