plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained to consistently moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade in spring; mazus is one of the few creeping perennials that tolerates foot traffic and is particularly effective planted between stepping stones in a shaded path.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; mazus is a low, mat-forming Himalayan perennial that spreads rapidly by runners to form a dense, bright-green, weed-suppressing carpet of small, toothed, lance-shaped leaves — one of the few groundcovers that withstands light to moderate foot traffic. In late spring it produces an impressive quantity of small but showy, two-lipped, tubular flowers of purplish-blue with white and yellow spotted throats that, when the plant is in full bloom, cover the mat so densely that nearly no foliage shows beneath. Excellent for use between stepping stones, in rock gardens, in crevices of shaded stone walls, and as a low-maintenance lawn substitute in small shaded areas. The plant spreads quickly in moist conditions. 'Alba' (pure white flowers) is an attractive alternative to the standard blue-purple species. Semi-evergreen in mild climates; goes fully dormant in cold winters.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 9) or start indoors in winter for spring transplanting. Seeds benefit from cold stratification — sowing in fall allows natural stratification. McKana Giant is an All-America Selections winning columbine series producing large (3–4 inch) flowers in an exceptionally wide color range including blue-and-white, red-and-yellow, pink-and-white, and solid yellow, white, and lavender. In zone 9 columbine is a short-lived perennial (1–3 years) rather than a long-lived perennial — it performs best in partial shade with cool, moist conditions and declines in prolonged summer heat. Columbine self-seeds readily to maintain a garden population. The long, nectar-filled spurs are specifically adapted for hummingbird pollination.
directions: Plant in partial shade — morning sun with afternoon shade or filtered light under deciduous trees; full sun in zone 9 causes premature decline and poor performance in summer heat — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist, humus-rich soil; McKana Giant Columbine is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid Columbine series producing the characteristic nodding, long-spurred columbine flowers at an unusually large scale (3–4 inch flowers) in a diverse mix of colors and bicolor combinations — including blue-and-white, red-and-yellow, pink-and-white, and various pastels — that displays the elegant, complex, uniquely structured form of Aquilegia flowers at its most dramatic. The five petals, five petal-like sepals, and five nectar-producing spurs (one per petal) of Aquilegia flowers combine to create one of the most structurally intricate and beautiful flower forms available from any commonly grown garden perennial — the long, curved spurs extending behind the flower in a cluster that gives the whole bloom a distinctly exotic, airborne quality. Columbines are outstanding hummingbird plants — the long, tubular, nectar-filled spurs are perfectly adapted for pollination by Ruby-throated Hummingbirds and other long-billed hummingbirds that feed at the spurs while hovering. In zone 9's partial-shade conditions, McKana Giant Columbines perform as reliable winter-to-spring perennials — the attractive, blue-green, three-lobed foliage providing a lacy texture in the shade garden from fall through the March–May bloom period.

common_name: McKana Giant Columbine (Extra-Large Mixed Hybrid Columbine)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; columbine seeds benefit from cold stratification — fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification for spring germination; McKana Giant columbines are short-lived perennials (2–4 years) that self-seed reliably.
directions: Sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; McKana Giant is the classic large-flowered hybrid columbine series — a mix producing extra-large flowers (3–4 inches across) in an exceptionally wide range of colors including pure white, yellow, pink, red, lavender, purple, and bicolor combinations of these, on plants 24–36 inches tall. The 'Giant' designation refers to the large flower size (two to three times the size of wild Aquilegia canadensis) and long spurs — the elongated petal spurs that project backward from each flower, giving columbines their distinctive, graceful silhouette. The McKana Giant series was introduced by Park Seed in 1955 and won an All-America Selections award — a popular mix ever since for its wide color range and large flowers. Columbines are spring-blooming (April–May in zone 6–7) and fade in summer heat — in zone 9 they bloom February–April and then die back in summer heat. They self-seed reliably, creating a self-maintaining colony that renews itself annually even as individual plants age and decline. McKana Giant is best suited to zones 3–8; in zone 9, treat as a cool-season annual or short-lived perennial that self-seeds to maintain a presence, siting in the shadiest, coolest locations.

plant_note: Cold stratification improves germination; may be fall-sown.
directions: Chilling the seed for a few weeks before sowing, or fall sowing, improves germination for this hardy perennial. Press seeds onto the surface as light aids germination, and keep soil evenly moist. This strain produces large three-inch flowers with long, graceful spurs in a wide color range, blooming in the second year. It thrives in dappled shade in rock gardens and perennial borders and self-sows readily.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or start transplants after cold stratification in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loam soil in full sun; meadow blazing star is adapted to the Great Plains and northern prairies and performs best in cool to moderate summer climates in zones 2-7.
directions: Direct sow in fall or start transplants after cold stratification in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loam soil in full sun; meadow blazing star is adapted to the Great Plains and northern prairies and performs best in cool to moderate summer climates in zones 2-7. Liatris ligustylis is recognized by the Xerces Society and monarch researchers as the single most important plant for migrating monarch butterflies in the northern Great Plains — individual plant blooms in late summer to early fall (August-September) coincide precisely with the peak of the southward monarch migration route, and blooming plants can attract hundreds of monarchs simultaneously. It produces large, rounded, rosy-purple flower heads on sturdy stems and is outstanding for ornamental prairie and meadow gardens in the upper Midwest and northern Plains; it is increasingly difficult to find in commerce but is one of the most ecologically valuable native prairie plants that can be cultivated.

common_name: Meadow Blazing Star (Rocky Mountain Blazing Star)
plant_note: Surface-sow or lightly cover seed in fall for natural cold stratification over winter; plants grow from corms and typically bloom the second year from seed — transplant corms in spring for first-year bloom.
directions: Surface-sow seed in fall to receive natural cold stratification over winter, or cold-stratify for 60 days then transplant corms in spring; meadow blazing star is widely documented as the single most attractive native plant for monarch butterflies during their southward fall migration — densely blooming patches can draw dozens of monarchs during peak flight periods. Stout upright stems bear spikes of rosy-purple flowerheads that open from the top down through August and September, and the nectar-rich blooms are magnets for swallowtails and bumblebees as well. Grows from a fleshy corm that becomes fully drought-tolerant once established; allow seed heads to stand through winter to feed goldfinches.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or fall directly in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; meadow clary self-sows prolifically and naturalizes readily in meadow and prairie-style plantings. It flowers more prolifically in lean, dry, well-drained soils than in rich, moist ones.
directions: Sow in well-drained, neutral to alkaline, lean soil in full sun; meadow clary is a robust European native perennial producing abundant spikes of vivid violet-blue flowers in late spring and early summer — smaller than some of the garden salvias but produced in great quantities on branching plants that naturalize freely in meadows, prairie gardens, and gravel plantings. The crinkled, wrinkled basal leaves form attractive rosettes even out of bloom. Unlike the cultivated Salvia x sylvestris hybrids (S. nemorosa crosses), meadow clary is a true species that flowers from seed the first year and self-sows to form permanent colonies. The 'Haematodes' selection produces unusually large flowers of clear blue. Excellent for dry, chalky, alkaline soils where many other ornamentals struggle. One of the best plants for pollinators in the perennial garden, visited constantly by bumblebees, honeybees, and hoverflies throughout its long bloom season.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; meadow cranesbill is taller and more vigorous than most hardy geraniums and benefits from staking in exposed sites.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; meadow cranesbill is the most robust of the hardy geraniums, forming large clumps that produce clear blue to violet-blue 1-inch flowers with dark veining from early to midsummer in outstanding abundance. After flowering, cut the entire plant back to the ground — it regrows within 3–4 weeks and produces fresh, attractive foliage for the rest of the season, sometimes with a light second flush of bloom. 'Mrs. Kendall Clark' (pale blue), 'Plenum Violaceum' (double purple), and 'Johnson's Blue' (a hybrid) are classic cultivars. Self-sows in suitable conditions; deadhead promptly to prevent seeding if unwanted. Excellent for naturalistic meadow and cottage garden plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; seeds require cold stratification which fall planting provides naturally — meadow parsnip self-seeds reliably in moist woodland gardens and can also be divided in early spring.
directions: Meadow parsnip is a native woodland wildflower of the carrot family (Apiaceae) closely resembling golden alexanders (Zizia aurea) but with distinctly three-parted lower leaves and wider habitat tolerance — it grows in moist to mesic woodland openings, stream banks, and shaded meadow edges where filtered light is available. Flat-topped clusters of tiny golden-yellow flowers appear in late spring and are critically important early-season food for short-tongued native bees, parasitic wasps, soldier beetles, and early butterflies; it is also a documented larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly, making it doubly valuable in the native pollinator garden. The delicate, fernlike foliage remains attractive through the season in shade gardens, providing fine texture among coarser companions like wild ginger and hostas. Combine with Virginia bluebells, native columbine, and other spring ephemerals in a moist woodland garden for layered bloom from late winter through summer.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; meadow phlox is more mildew-resistant than Phlox paniculata and better suited to humid climates.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing 18–24 inches apart with good air circulation; meadow phlox closely resembles garden phlox (Phlox paniculata) but produces cylindrical rather than domed flower clusters, blooms 2–3 weeks earlier in early summer, and is significantly more resistant to powdery mildew — an important advantage in hot, humid climates. Flower color ranges from white to pink-lavender with a darker eye; fragrance is excellent. Shear plants by half after the first bloom flush to encourage a second wave of flowers in late summer. The cultivar 'Natasha' with bicolor pink-and-white flowers is particularly striking and disease-resistant. Divide every 3 years.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root transplants in fall in average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; meadow rose is nearly thornless compared to most native roses and adapts to a wide range of moist to moderately dry soil conditions.
directions: Meadow rose is the most cold-hardy and one of the most nearly thornless of all North American native roses — its species name 'blanda' means smooth, mild, or agreeable, referring to the nearly unarmed (spineless) character of mature stems that make it among the more garden-friendly of all native roses for areas near walkways. Fragrant, five-petaled, medium-pink flowers appear in June on arching stems, followed by small, orange-red hips that persist through winter and are consumed by ruffed grouse, mockingbirds, and a remarkable variety of songbirds. Native to the eastern and north-central United States from Maine to Colorado, it forms slowly spreading colonies by suckers and is among the first plants to colonize disturbed sites and woodland edges, providing excellent wildlife cover and erosion control. Like all native roses, it is host to native mining bees (Halictus and Andrena species) that collect rose pollen as a primary food source, and many moth species use Rosa as a larval host plant. Excellent for naturalizing in prairie and meadow borders, hedgerows, and native garden edges.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with cold stratification; or plant divisions in early spring.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade; tall meadow rue creates an airy, vertical accent with blue-green, columbine-like foliage and billowing clouds of lavender-purple flowers in midsummer. The delicate flowers are held on strong, self-supporting stems and sway gracefully in a breeze. Seldom needs staking if grown in adequate light; divide every 4–5 years in early spring to keep plants vigorous. Excellent in a woodland border or at the back of a shaded perennial bed.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for spring germination or start divisions in early spring; meadow rue self-sows freely in moist, partially shaded situations and requires no cold stratification when sown immediately after harvest.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall or set out container plants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; meadow rue produces delicate, columbine-like glaucous blue-green foliage throughout the season that is handsome even without the fluffy mauve-pink flower clusters that emerge in early summer on stems reaching 3–5 feet. The feathery floral display is excellent for cutting and attracts beneficial insects. Plants are largely self-sufficient in moist shaded borders and woodland edges where they self-sow and naturalize over time. Staking is rarely necessary if plants are grown in sheltered, partially shaded sites; they may flop in exposed positions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; mealy blue sage is a native Texas perennial often grown as an annual in zones north of 7, widely sold as the 'Victoria Blue' bedding plant — one of the most heat-tolerant, long-blooming sages for Gulf Coast and Southern landscapes and an outstanding butterfly and hummingbird plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost into well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Salvia farinacea (mealy blue sage, mealycup sage) is a native Texas perennial sage found naturally on limestone outcrops, cedar glades, and dry prairies from central Texas into New Mexico; it takes its common name from the floury white (farinaceous) coating on the calyces that cradle the spikes of brilliant true-blue to violet-blue flowers, one of the few true, pure-blue flowering plants in the southern landscape. Remarkably heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant, blooming continuously from spring through hard frost in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens without deadheading; 'Victoria Blue' is the most widely sold selection, an AAS winner. Perennial in zones 7–11; self-seeds prolifically; outstanding for butterfly and hummingbird gardens. Can be used as a fresh-cut or dried flower.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; mealy cup sage blooms best with at least 6 hours of direct sun.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; mealy cup sage is a Texas and New Mexico native that produces elegant, white-felted stems topped with intensely blue-violet flower spikes from late spring through hard frost — one of the longest-blooming, most butterfly-attractive perennials for southern and Gulf Coast gardens. The species name 'farinacea' refers to the white, flour-like (farinose) coating on the calyx and stem. Drought-tolerant and deer-resistant once established. Shear spent flower stalks by half in midsummer to refresh growth and extend bloom. In zones 8–10 it overwinters as a woody-based subshrub; in cooler zones grow as an annual. 'Victoria Blue' (deep blue) and 'White Porcelain' are classic cultivar selections.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and overwinter indoors. Medallion Calathea requires consistent temperatures above 60°F and is damaged by temperatures below 50°F — manage as an outdoor summer container plant in zone 9 and bring indoors before fall temperatures drop. Maintain consistently moist soil and high humidity; brown leaf edges indicate low humidity or fluoride/chlorine sensitivity in tap water (use filtered or rainwater when possible). Zone 9's warm, humid summers create ideal outdoor conditions on shaded patios from May through September. The leaves track light through the day and fold partially upward at night.
directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil; Medallion Calathea produces some of the most spectacular patterned foliage of any commonly available houseplant or shade tropical, with large, rounded leaves displaying a complex, symmetrical pattern of dark green and lighter green ovals, chevrons, and feathered markings on the upper surface and deep burgundy-purple undersides. The Medallion pattern — a central lighter zone feathered with dark green radiating from the leaf's midrib, surrounded by progressively darker zones toward the margin — is strikingly ornate and immediately recognizable as one of the most decorative naturally occurring leaf patterns. In zone 9 Medallion Calathea provides an extraordinary level of ornamental interest as an outdoor container plant for covered patios and deep porches during the warm season, where the plant thrives in the humid warmth while providing foliage drama that no temperate shade plant can match. The leaves perform a nyctinastic movement — folding slightly upward and revealing the burgundy underside at night, then relaxing back to horizontal during the day — an unusual biological behavior that adds an additional dimension of interest beyond the static foliage pattern.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Mediterranean fan palm is drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established, making it an excellent landscape palm for coastal gardens in zones 8–11.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Mediterranean fan palm is drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant once established, making it an excellent landscape palm for coastal gardens in zones 8–11. Chamaerops humilis is the only palm native to continental Europe, occurring naturally along the Mediterranean coast from the Iberian Peninsula to Italy and North Africa; it is a slow-growing, multi-stemmed clustering palm with silvery-green to blue-green, stiff fan-shaped fronds on petioles armed with sharp spines, forming a bold, architectural clump 4–10 feet tall over many years. It is highly versatile in the Gulf Coast landscape, functioning as a specimen plant, foundation plant, or tall screening shrub; it tolerates drought, salt spray, and brief cold spells to about 15°F when established.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and set out after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; melampodium requires full sun for best performance and may become leggy or fail to bloom well in partial shade.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and set out after frost in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; melampodium (butter daisy, black-foot daisy annual) is a Central American native that is one of the most heat-tolerant, drought-resistant, and reliably self-cleaning annual daisies available for high-summer performance in the South — the cheerful, bright golden-yellow, one-inch daisy flowers are produced in extraordinary abundance from late spring until frost on dense, mounded, intensely bushy plants. Unlike many summer annuals, melampodium needs no deadheading, tolerates intense heat and humidity, performs well in poor, dry soil, and maintains its compact form without pinching. An exceptional performer where impatiens and petunias fail in midsummer. Excellent in mass plantings, borders, and containers. 'Million Gold' (compact, 10–12 inches), 'Showstar' (heat-tolerant, 18 inches), and 'Derby' (uniform, compact) are widely grown commercial selections.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Merlot is a compact hybrid redbud selected for glossy, heat-tolerant purple foliage that resists the summer fading and leaf scorch common in older purple-leaf redbud cultivars like Forest Pansy.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Merlot is a hybrid redbud, a cross involving Forest Pansy and Texas redbud (Cercis canadensis var. texensis) parentage, bred to combine deep wine-purple foliage with the smaller, glossier, more heat- and drought-tolerant leaves inherited from its Texas redbud heritage. The result holds its rich purple color better through summer heat than older purple-leaf cultivars, which tend to fade to green by midsummer, and shows improved resistance to leaf scorch in hot, humid climates like the Gulf South. Rosy-pink pea-like flowers cover the bare branches in early spring before the foliage emerges, followed by the season-long purple leaf display. Its more compact, rounded habit than standard redbud makes it well suited to smaller landscapes and foundation plantings. Provide afternoon shade in the hottest climates and well-drained soil, since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites; minimal pruning is needed beyond removing crossing or damaged branches in late winter.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; merrybells is slow to establish from division but is virtually permanent once settled and requires no maintenance in woodland garden conditions.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; merrybells (large-flowered bellwort) is one of the loveliest native spring ephemerals of eastern North American woodlands, producing arching stems with twisted, perfoliate leaves (appearing to be threaded onto the stem) hung with one or two drooping, narrow, butter-yellow, bell-shaped flowers in mid-spring. Plants emerge early, bloom briefly and beautifully, then continue producing attractive foliage through summer before going dormant in late summer. They naturalize slowly from division or scattered seed to form small, graceful colonies in woodland gardens. Excellent combined with spring ephemeral companions like trillium, hepatica, and trout lily. Rarely browsed by deer.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; metallic-leaf begonia is particularly sensitive to waterlogging and cold drafts — use a very freely draining potting mix and avoid temperatures below 55°F, which cause the hairy foliage to develop gray patches and increase susceptibility to Botrytis.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; metallic-leaf begonia is a Brazilian shrubby begonia whose primary distinction is the extraordinary, burnished, metallic quality of its foliage — the large, asymmetric, heart-shaped leaves are deep olive-green to rich bronze-green in color but have a pronounced silvery-metallic sheen or gloss over the surface that catches and reflects light in a way that appears genuinely metallic rather than simply shiny, and the leaf surface is marked with prominent, dark-red to deep-purple veining that creates a vivid color contrast against the metallic-green ground. White hairs cover both leaf surfaces. The plant grows with an upright, branching, cane-forming habit and produces loose clusters of pale-pink flowers at the branch tips throughout the warm season. The metallic foliage is the primary ornamental feature and is most vivid in partial-shade conditions where direct light can catch the leaf surface at angles that maximize the metallic reflection. An excellent specimen for shaded tropical patios, conservatories, and zone 10–12 shade gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost has passed.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors for an earlier display. This variety produces vibrant scarlet, semi-double to double blooms four to five inches across on long, sturdy stems ideal for cutting. Give plants full sun and good air circulation to reduce mildew, and deadhead to keep blooms coming through frost. A reliable pollinator and butterfly magnet.

plant_note: Sow scarified seeds directly in warm soil after last frost in full sun in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil; Mexican bird of paradise blooms in its first year from seed when planted in warm conditions and grows very quickly to flowering size.
directions: Sow scarified seeds directly in warm soil after last frost, or nick the hard seed coat and soak overnight before planting in full sun in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil; Mexican bird of paradise grows rapidly to produce large clusters of brilliant orange-and-yellow or all-red flowers with long, showy stamens from summer through fall that are among the finest hummingbird plants in the Southwest and Gulf Coast. Highly drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in the heat, reflected sun, and dry conditions that challenge most other flowering shrubs. In zone 9 it may freeze to the ground in hard winters but regrows vigorously from the deep roots in spring; in zone 10–12 it is a large, semi-evergreen shrub. Prune hard in late winter to maintain shape and renew flowering vigor.

plant_note: Direct-sow scarified seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; Mexican bird of paradise thrives in hot, dry conditions and poor, rocky, calcareous soil — rich, moist, heavily fertilized soil produces rank foliage growth at the expense of flower production.
directions: Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican bird of paradise is a Mexican native evergreen shrub or small tree in the pea family (Fabaceae) that produces upright racemes of bright, clear-yellow, five-petaled, ruffled flowers with showy long, red stamens on a nearly continuous basis from spring through frost — a bloom season that, combined with its tolerance of zone 8 cold and adaptability to dry, alkaline, calcareous soil, makes it one of the most reliably free-flowering large shrubs for Gulf Coast and southern Texas landscapes. It differs from the related red bird of paradise (Caesalpinia pulcherrima) in producing all-yellow flowers (vs. orange-red), being significantly more cold-hardy (to approximately 15°F in zone 8), and having a tidier, less aggressive growth habit. The fine-textured, bipinnate, ferny, dark-green, evergreen leaves remain attractive year-round. It tolerates partial shade significantly better than most drought-tolerant flowering shrubs. Excellent as a specimen, informal hedge, and xeriscape flowering tree in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Mexican blood trumpet produces its most prolific flowering in full sun but blooms acceptably in partial shade — it is one of the better shade-tolerant bignonia-family vines for zone 9–12.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Mexican blood trumpet is a Mexican evergreen vine of the bignonia family that produces large, striking, trumpet-shaped flowers in a dramatic two-toned color combination — the flowers open from orange-red buds into large, flared trumpets in a vivid blood-red to orange-red outer color that fades inside through orange to a yellow throat, creating a warm, vivid, tricolored trumpet effect. The flowers are produced in dense clusters at the branch tips from spring through fall, with the primary flush in spring and a second in fall. The vine climbs by tendrils and can reach 20–30 feet on suitable support. It is more shade-tolerant than Pyrostegia venusta and blooms more reliably in partial-shade conditions, making it a good choice for lightly shaded arbors and structures where the flame vine would fail to produce its best display. Hardy to approximately 25–28°F in zone 9, with established plants typically recovering from frost damage by regrowing from the base. An excellent flowering vine for large arbors, pergolas, and walls in zone 9–12.

subcategory: spectacular silver-blue fan palm for arid landscapes
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Mexican blue palm is native to the Sierra San Pedro Mártir and arid canyons of Baja California — requiring excellent drainage and lean, dry conditions. Hardy to about 12–15°F when established. The nearly pure silver-blue to powder-blue fan leaves are among the most dramatically colored of any palm and provide outstanding year-round structural color in dry-climate landscapes. Produces extraordinary long (15–20 foot) drooping flower stalks in spring. Extremely drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; Mexican blue palm is the most extraordinarily colored of all commonly cultivated palms — a native of the rocky, arid canyons and mountain bajadas of the Baja California peninsula that produces fan-shaped leaves of an almost unreal silver-blue to powder-blue to ice-blue coloration, the pure, cool, metallic blue-silver of the leaf color without parallel in the palm world and arguably among the most striking leaf colors of any large landscape plant. The silver-blue is structural and permanent — not a seasonal phenomenon but the year-round baseline color of every leaf from the moment of emergence, the result of a heavy, reflective, waxy bloom coating that covers the leaf surface and creates the characteristic cool, powder-blue metallic sheen. A mature specimen in full sun — a substantial gray trunk supporting a crown of large, stiffly spreading, circular fan leaves in pure silver-blue against a warm landscape — is one of the most dramatic and architecturally striking plants in all of warm-climate horticulture. In spring, established plants produce extraordinary inflorescences (flower stalks) that can reach 15–20 feet in length, arching dramatically downward from the crown in great, pendulous sweeps and bearing tiny cream-white flowers followed by small, edible, date-like fruits. Hardy to approximately 12–15°F when established in well-drained soil. Extremely drought-tolerant. An outstanding statement palm for dry-climate zone 8–11 gardens where its silver foliage and extraordinary flower stalks create a multi-season spectacle of unmatched drama.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown plants in late winter or early spring; seeds ripen in summer inside distinctive woody pods and germinate the following spring with minimal stratification. Mexican Buckeye grows slowly in the first year but accelerates once established. In zone 9, plant in a partially shaded understory position or along a woodland edge where it receives morning sun and afternoon shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in partial to full shade; Mexican Buckeye (Ungnadia speciosa) is a native multi-stemmed large shrub or small tree indigenous to the limestone hills and cedar brakes of central and west Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico, where it thrives in the dry shade beneath live oak canopies on thin, rocky, alkaline soils. The cloud of bright magenta-pink flowers that appears before the leaves in February–March is startling and beautiful — one of the earliest spring bloomers in the Gulf South native plant palette. The leathery, pinnately compound leaves (resembling the Ohio Buckeye's leaves) turn clear yellow in fall. The distinctive round, woody seed pods split open to reveal 1–3 shiny, mahogany-brown seeds resembling horse chestnuts — they are toxic (containing saponins and cytisine) and should not be eaten. Mexican Buckeye is extremely drought and alkaline-soil tolerant once established; it thrives where soils are too rocky and poor for most other ornamentals. The dense growth provides excellent cover and nesting habitat for mockingbirds and other cavity nesters. A superb native choice for dry shade situations in limestone-soil zone 7–10 gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring after last frost in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Mexican bush sage does not bloom reliably from seed — propagate by stem cuttings taken in spring or early summer.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in zone 8–11 after last frost; Mexican bush sage is one of the showiest late-season salvias, producing arching purple-and-white or all-purple velvety flower spikes from late summer through frost that are among the most effective hummingbird and butterfly plants available in the South. The plant grows quickly to form a large, rounded shrub with soft, grey-green foliage that may look coarse early in the season but becomes spectacular from September onward. Cut to the ground in late winter or early spring before new growth emerges; the root is winter-hardy in zone 8–11 even when top growth is frost-killed. Propagate by stem cuttings rather than seed, as seed-grown plants bloom much later and less reliably.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after cold stratification, or cold-stratify seeds in damp sand for 4–6 weeks in the refrigerator and sow in early spring; Mexican columbine self-seeds readily in suitable conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-enriched soil in partial shade; in hot climates, afternoon shade is essential as this species originates in cool, high-elevation mountain meadows and pine forests in Mexico and Arizona. The bicolored red-and-yellow flowers with shorter-than-average spurs are reliably attractive to hummingbirds and are among the showiest of the native columbines. It tolerates summer heat better than many North American species and makes an excellent companion for native ferns and woodland perennials. Self-sows freely and hybridizes with other columbines if multiple species are grown nearby.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 8–11; Mexican Cycad is a beautiful, medium-sized understory cycad native to the cloud forests and moist mountain forests of eastern Mexico (Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas, Tamaulipas) — one of the most ornamental and relatively shade-tolerant of the Ceratozamia cycads, with glossy, dark-green, arching fronds and good cold tolerance down to zone 8.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; Ceratozamia mexicana is more moisture-demanding than many cycads, reflecting its cloud forest origin — maintain consistent soil moisture with organic mulch and water regularly during dry periods. Ceratozamia mexicana (Mexican Cycad, Chamal) is an attractive, medium-sized cycad genus endemic to Mexico, with C. mexicana occurring primarily in the humid cloud forests, montane forests, and pine-oak forests of eastern Mexico — Veracruz, Tamaulipas, Oaxaca, and Chiapas — at elevations of 1,500–2,500 meters. Unlike many cycads adapted to dry, sunny conditions, Ceratozamia mexicana is a forest understory plant adapted to partial shade, consistent moisture, and cool, humid cloud-forest conditions — making it one of the more shade-tolerant cycads available for garden cultivation. The arching, compound fronds with broad, dark-green leaflets are highly ornamental, and the plants develop a distinctive trunk that remains partially buried or low-growing for many years before elongating. The genus name 'Ceratozamia' (horned zamia) refers to the distinctive paired horn-like projections on the pollen-cone scales. Listed as Threatened on the IUCN Red List due to forest clearance; never collect from the wild. All cycad parts contain neurotoxic cycasin glycosides.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun to partial shade; Dioon edule is one of the most cold-hardy cycads available, surviving brief temperatures to 15–20°F when established. Growth is extremely slow (one set of leaves per year); purchase the largest container size affordable. All parts of the plant contain cycasin and are toxic — seeds require extensive water treatment by indigenous peoples before safe consumption as food.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline-tolerant, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Dioon edule is extremely drought-tolerant once established and adapts to the thin, limestone-based soils of its native habitat. Dioon edule is a cycad (an ancient gymnosperm predating the dinosaurs) native to the dry mountainous regions of Veracruz, Tamaulipas, and Hidalgo states in Mexico, where it grows in thornscrub and deciduous forest on rocky, alkaline slopes. It is the most cold-hardy species in the genus Dioon, surviving brief temperatures to 15–20°F with established trunks, making it one of the most cold-tolerant cycads available for zone 8b Gulf Coast and Texas gardens. The stiff, pinnate, blue-green fronds emerge in annual flushes to form a graceful, palm-like rosette on a slowly developing trunk. Mature specimens produce large, barrel-shaped cones — male cones produce pollen and female cones contain starchy seeds up to 1 inch diameter that indigenous Huastec peoples have historically processed by prolonged water treatment to remove cycasin toxins before using as food flour (hence the common name 'Chestnut Dioon'). As a landscape specimen, Dioon edule is supremely low-maintenance, tolerating drought, alkaline soil, and partial shade that defeats most other ornamentals. An excellent choice for zone 9 xeriscape and rock gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mexican fan palm is extremely fast-growing — potentially reaching 80–100 feet over several decades — and is one of the defining large palms of warm-climate urban landscapes from the Gulf Coast to California. In zone 9 it is a reliable, self-maintaining landscape palm. Unlike W. filifera (California fan palm), it has a notably more slender trunk and faster growth rate. The dead fronds persist as a 'skirt' below the crown unless removed. Hardy to about 20°F when established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mexican fan palm is the tall, slender-trunked, fast-growing signature palm of warm-climate cities from Houston and New Orleans to Los Angeles and Miami — a native of the oases and canyon streams of Baja California and Sonora, Mexico that has been introduced throughout the subtropical and warm-temperate world as one of the most widely planted of all landscape palms. The palm grows with remarkable speed — adding several feet of trunk per year under good conditions — and eventually reaches 80–100 feet or more, developing an extremely slender, slightly tapering, gray-brown trunk (notably more slender than the related California fan palm W. filifera) topped with a compact, dense crown of large, circular, fan-shaped leaves on long, slightly spiny petioles. The dead fronds remain attached below the living crown, forming the characteristic drooping 'skirt' or 'petticoat' of persistent dead fronds that is a recognizable feature of Washingtonia palms and that harbors wildlife habitat (and occasional fire risk — many municipalities require removal). Mexican fan palm is one of the defining skyline elements of warm-climate cities — a tall, slender, vertical accent of pure tropical character growing rapidly to heights that create the subtropical urban landscape visual. Drought-tolerant once established; requires minimal care in suitable climates.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Mexican feather grass self-seeds prolifically in suitable conditions — it is classified as invasive in California and some other western states, so check local regulations before planting.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mexican feather grass forms a billowing clump of hair-fine, bright-green leaves with silky, golden-blond seed tassels from early summer onward that move in the slightest breeze — the most ethereally graceful of all ornamental grasses, giving any planting an airy, meadow-like quality. It performs best in dry, alkaline, or poor soils and in hot, sunny Mediterranean or desert-climate gardens; excessive moisture or fertility produces floppy, disease-prone plants. Self-seeds prolifically in suitable climates and is listed as invasive in California, Australia, and parts of the Southwest — consider this before planting. In zone 6–7 it may die back in severe winters but re-emerges from the roots in spring. Cut back in early spring to remove old, bleached stems.

plant_note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in spring in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, dry to moderately moist soil in zone 7–10; Mexican Flame (Desert Honeysuckle, Hummingbird Bush) is a native Texas and Mexican drought-tolerant shrub — found naturally on rocky limestone slopes, dry creek beds, and desert margins from the Trans-Pecos to the Hill Country — producing an extraordinary abundance of brilliant orange-red, tubular flowers from midsummer through fall that are irresistible to hummingbirds and are among the most important late-season nectar sources in Texas native plantings.
directions: Plant Anisacanthus quadrifidus in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; once established it requires little supplemental water — it is highly drought-tolerant and actually performs better without irrigation in most Texas gardens; cut back hard in late winter to encourage compact, bushy growth and maximize summer flowering. Mexican Flame is one of the premier native hummingbird plants of Texas and the northern Mexico borderlands — a deciduous to semi-evergreen shrub that comes alive in the heat of summer and fall when little else is blooming, producing masses of brilliant orange-red tubular flowers on graceful, arching branches just when hummingbirds are fueling up for their fall migration. In zone 7–9 gardens, it dies back to the root crown after hard frost and re-emerges vigorously in spring; in zone 10 it may remain semi-evergreen. Several flower color variants exist: the most common has bright orange-red flowers, but yellow-flowered forms ('Yellow') are also available and equally valued for hummingbird gardens. A superb plant for xeriscape, wildflower, and native plant gardens throughout the Texas Hill Country, Gulf Coast, and adjacent regions — requiring no fertilizer, no regular irrigation once established, and minimal maintenance beyond annual pruning.

common_name: Mexican Flame Vine (Orange Glow Vine, Fireman's Cap)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Mexican flame vine grows rapidly and blooms from mid-summer through winter in zone 9–11. In zone 8a it may die back in severe frost but resprouts from established roots. Provide a trellis, fence, or large shrub to climb through.
directions: Root cuttings in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a fence or trellis; Mexican flame vine is one of the most spectacular winter-blooming vines for zone 9–11, producing dense clusters of bright orange, daisy-like flowers with contrasting yellow or orange centers from October through March — exactly the cool-season period when most other tropical vines have stopped blooming. The loose, twining stems 6–15 feet long bear small, dark green, slightly succulent leaves and are covered in vibrant orange blooms that attract butterflies. The orange color is exceptionally vivid and warm, excellent for combining with blue salvias or purple queen for autumn and winter color. In zone 8a it is killed to the ground in hard freezes but established root systems resprout reliably each spring to bloom again by mid-summer.

plant_note: Direct-sow or allow to self-sow in almost any well-drained soil including wall crevices, paving gaps, and gravel; Mexican fleabane is a prolific self-seeder that naturalizes readily and is best established by simply allowing seeds to find their own level in the garden. It is short-lived as an individual plant (2–3 years) but self-sows perpetually, filling gaps and softening edges throughout the garden.
directions: Sow in almost any well-drained soil, including crevices in walls and paving, in full sun; Mexican fleabane is one of the most charming and generous self-seeding plants for temperate gardens, producing a near-continuous display of small daisy flowers from late spring through autumn — the flowers open white, then age through blush-pink to deep rose over the course of several days, so a flowering plant simultaneously carries white, pink, and rose flowers creating a multicolor cottage-garden effect. The plants themselves are small and airy, with tiny, narrow leaves, creating fine-textured mounds that tuck into gaps in walls, cascade over stone edges, spill from urns, and fill paving cracks — places where larger plants cannot grow. The combination of extremely long bloom, color change, minimal size, and willingness to grow in dry, lean conditions in full sun makes this one of the most useful 'spontaneous' plants in the garden. Originally from Mexico and Central America, it has naturalized widely in the Mediterranean, parts of Australia, and coastal California and Pacific Northwest in the US.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, lean, rocky to gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in zone 7–11; Mexican Grass Tree is a striking, long-lived architectural accent plant native to the highlands of Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas, Mexico — forming a huge, rounded, porcupine-like mass of extremely long, narrow, unarmed leaves (to 6 feet) radiating from a central stem that eventually develops into a tree trunk, used as a dramatic focal point in hot, dry Southwestern desert and xeriscape gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, rocky to gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Dasylirion longissimum requires excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established — it is highly drought and heat tolerant but will rot in poorly drained, wet, or clay soils. Dasylirion longissimum (Mexican Grass Tree or Toton Palm) is a dramatic, slow-growing architectural succulent in the Asparagaceae family native to the semi-arid highland mountains of Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, and Tamaulipas in northeastern Mexico, where it grows on rocky limestone slopes and ridges in full sun. Unlike the spoon-leaf Dasylirion species (D. wheeleri, D. texanum) whose leaves have serrated or spiny edges, D. longissimum is distinguished by its extremely long (to 6 feet), narrow, strap-like, essentially unarmed and smooth-edged leaves that radiate from the growing center in an enormous, perfect sphere — giving the plant an appearance of a giant teal-green sea urchin or porcupine. Over many years and decades, the plant develops a raised, cylindrical trunk beneath the leaf mass, eventually reaching 10–20 feet in old age. The flower stalk when it finally appears is a spectacular 10–15 foot spike covered with thousands of tiny cream flowers. Excellent for Southwestern desert gardens, xeriscape plantings, and architectural accent positions in hot, dry, alkaline-soil landscapes in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican heather establishes quickly and begins blooming almost immediately after transplanting. In zones 9–10 it often self-sows freely and may behave as a short-lived perennial; it is used as an annual in zones 8 and colder.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican heather is a fine-textured, dense-growing tropical perennial that produces a continuous profusion of tiny lavender, pink, or white flowers on compact mounds of tiny, shiny, narrow leaves — resembling true heather (Calluna) in growth habit and foliage texture but adapted to tropical heat rather than cool climates. It blooms almost without pause from planting through frost and is one of the best butterfly and skipper nectar plants available for Gulf Coast gardens. In zone 9 it is typically a short-lived perennial that often reseeds to maintain a permanent presence. It is outstanding as a low edging plant, in mass plantings, along pathways, or at the front of mixed borders where its fine texture contrasts beautifully with coarser tropical foliage. Requires almost no deadheading or maintenance; simply trim lightly in early spring to refresh the habit.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in partial shade to full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Mexican Honeysuckle grows rapidly in zone 9 and begins blooming in its first season. In zone 9a, plants freeze back in hard winters but resprout reliably from the root crown in spring. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable semi-evergreen perennial shrub blooming nearly year-round. Prune by one-third after each bloom flush to maintain compact form and stimulate reblooming. Roots readily from stem cuttings. An excellent hummingbird plant.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Mexican Honeysuckle blooms most prolifically in full sun but performs well in partial shade in zone 9 and actually benefits from afternoon shade during the peak of summer heat. Justicia spicigera is a large, soft-stemmed, fast-growing shrub from Mexico and Central America in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the more commonly grown Jacobinia (Justicia carnea) and Shrimp Plant (Justicia brandegeana). The species' common name 'Mexican Honeysuckle' refers not to any botanical relationship with true Lonicera honeysuckles but to the nectar-rich tubular flowers, which are intensely attractive to hummingbirds and butterflies — the long, tubular, orange to orange-red flowers emerging from softly fuzzy, velvety calyxes are among the most reliable hummingbird attractants in the zone 9 garden. The flowers are produced in terminal spikes and bloom over an exceptionally long season, essentially year-round in zone 9b-10 with brief pauses between flush cycles. The large, soft, gray-green, velvety leaves give the plant an attractive textural quality even out of bloom. In Mexican folk medicine, Justicia spicigera leaves (Mohintli) have traditional uses as a blue dye plant and herbal remedy. Among the most underused but most hummingbird-effective shrubs for Gulf Coast partial-shade garden beds.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after last frost into well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; in zones 9–10 plants can be direct sown in fall for spring bloom.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant to well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Mexican hyssop is among the best hummingbird and pollinator plants for hot, dry, alkaline conditions across the Southwest and Gulf South, producing dense spikes of tubular rose-pink to cherry-red flowers from midsummer through fall that hummingbirds, hawk moths, and butterflies work heavily. The crushed foliage has a pleasant licorice-mint fragrance. Unlike North American Agastache species, Mexican hyssop is adapted to alkaline, rocky, dry conditions and performs poorly in acidic, heavy soils. Short-lived as a perennial in warm climates but self-sows readily to maintain a colony without replanting. Drought-tolerant once established.

common_name: Mexican Lilac (Quick Stick, Mother of Cocoa)
plant_note: Plant container stock or large hardwood cuttings (which root directly in the soil) in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; gliricidia is one of the world's most important multipurpose tropical trees — outstanding for living fences, shade for cocoa, and nitrogen fixation in tropical agroforestry systems.
directions: Plant container stock or large (2–4 foot) hardwood cuttings directly in the ground in spring; gliricidia establishes from large cuttings planted directly in the soil — a useful trait for creating instant living fence posts. Gliricidia sepium (Mexican lilac, quick stick, or mother of cocoa) is one of the most widely planted multipurpose tropical trees in the world — a Central American legume tree grown throughout the humid tropics for nitrogen fixation, living fences, shade for cacao and coffee plantations ('mother of cocoa' in Costa Rica), green manure, and fodder. The tree has an extraordinary capacity to root from large, dormant hardwood cuttings planted directly in the ground — a common practice for creating instant living fence posts that then leaf out and grow into full trees. In spring (usually January–March when dormant), the bare branches are covered with stunning clusters of bright pink-lavender pea-like flowers resembling redbud (Cercis) — one of the showiest tropical trees in bloom. The leaves and branches are nitrogen-rich and used as green mulch in organic farming; however, the leaves are toxic to mammals (including horses and dogs) if consumed in large quantities. CAUTION: Seeds, bark, and leaves are toxic to mammals — do not plant where livestock have access.

plant_note: Divide offsets in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican lily is damaged below about 15-20 degrees F and is best suited to zones 7-10. The spectacular flower scape, reaching 6 feet or more, appears once after the plant reaches maturity and then the main rosette dies, leaving offsets to continue the colony.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican lily is a dramatic, architecturally imposing relative of the agave from the mountains of central Mexico, forming a bold rosette of broad, soft, blue-green, sword-shaped, yucca-like leaves that are spineless and non-lethal to touch — unlike true agaves. When mature, the plant produces one of the most spectacular flowering events in the succulent world: a massive, arching, coral-red to orange-red flower scape that bends dramatically under its own weight and grows to 5-7 feet, bearing drooping clusters of pendant, tubular, red-and-green flowers along its entire length. The coral-red scape itself is ornamental for weeks before and after the flowers open. The combination of dramatic arching scape, vivid coral-red color, and pendant green-tipped flowers is unlike anything else in hardy horticulture. After flowering, the main rosette dies but produces offsets at its base. An outstanding architectural specimen for warm, sheltered, well-drained gardens in zones 7-10, particularly effective with other bold-textured plants.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; in zone 7 site against a south- or west-facing wall for winter frost protection, as hard freezes can damage the foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; Mexican orange blossom is one of the most popular fragrant evergreen shrubs for warm-climate gardens, producing clusters of pure white, star-shaped flowers with a powerful, sweet orange-blossom fragrance in spring and frequently reblooming again in fall. The glossy, trifoliate leaves are aromatic when crushed, releasing a sharp citrus-like scent. It is borderline hardy in zone 7 and may suffer leaf damage in hard freezes, but typically recovers vigorously from the root system — planting against a warm south-facing wall significantly improves winter survival. The compact cultivar 'Sundance' (golden-yellow foliage) and the more cold-tolerant 'Aztec Pearl' (narrower leaflets, very fragrant pink-tinged flowers) are excellent named selections.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in any moist to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican petunia is extremely adaptable and spreading — contain with deep edging if planting near lawn or naturalistic areas, as it spreads aggressively by underground runners and self-sown seed in warm climates. Use the compact, non-invasive cultivar 'Purple Showers' or 'Katie' in contained plantings.
directions: Plant in any well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican petunia is one of the most widely used and lowest-maintenance flowering perennials in Gulf Coast landscapes, producing a continuous display of funnel-shaped flowers in purple, pink, or white from spring through frost on upright stems with narrow, dark-green leaves. Each individual flower lasts only one day, but the plant produces new flowers in such abundance that the display is uninterrupted throughout the season. It is remarkably drought, heat, and salt tolerant once established and thrives in the conditions that challenge most other perennials. However, it spreads aggressively by underground runners and abundant self-seeding — R. simplex is considered invasive in natural areas in Florida and other Gulf states. Compact, sterile cultivars such as 'Purple Showers' and 'Katie' (dwarf, 8–12 inches) are strongly recommended for residential use as they do not spread by seed. Deadhead or shear to refresh and stimulate new bloom flushes.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in dry, sandy, well-drained soil; seed requires warmth to germinate reliably.
directions: A freely self-seeding annual prickly poppy native to tropical Mexico and the Caribbean, now widely naturalized in disturbed, dry, open ground throughout the southern US and tropical regions worldwide; produces deeply lobed, spine-tipped, silvery-veined, blue-green leaves and golden-yellow, 4-6-petaled flowers 1.5-2 inches across from spring through fall. The yellow sap and seeds are toxic — do not ingest. Direct sow in spring in dry, sandy, well-drained, lean soil; self-sows prolifically and can become weedy in favorable conditions. Grown in folk medicine traditions across tropical America for its analgesic properties.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican redbud requires scarification to break seed dormancy — nick or abrade the hard seed coat and soak 24 hours before planting. It grows naturally on rocky, limestone canyon walls and slopes of west Texas and Mexico.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Mexican redbud is a shrubby to small-tree redbud native to the rocky limestone mountains and canyon walls of west Texas (Big Bend country) and adjacent Mexico, distinguished from eastern redbud (C. canadensis) by its smaller stature, smaller and more rounded leaves with unusually wavy, scalloped margins, and greater tolerance of dry, alkaline, rocky soils. The bright magenta-pink spring flowers appear on bare branches before the leaves, like other redbuds. Heat, drought, and alkaline soil tolerance superior to eastern redbud makes it better suited to the dry limestone terrain of central and west Texas. A fine specimen shrub-tree for the xeric, alkaline, rocky garden in zone 9a where standard redbud struggles on thin, calcareous soils.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 8 it may die back to roots in hard freezes but re-sprouts in spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Mexican sage is a large, bold, shrubby species with broad, deeply veined, highly aromatic leaves and long wands of blue-purple flowers from late summer through fall that attract hummingbirds and bumblebees. It is native to mountain forests and canyon edges in central Mexico at moderate elevation and tolerates partial shade better than most sages, making it useful in the lightly shaded areas of a Gulf Coast or zone 8–9 garden. The foliage has a strong, pleasant herbal fragrance when brushed and is deer resistant. It grows rapidly to a large sub-shrub in one season and may be damaged or killed by hard freezes but typically re-sprouts from the root crown in zone 8. Shear back by half in mid-spring to encourage compact, heavily blooming growth.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican snowball requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of wet soil, especially in the center of the rosette — the most common cause of death is crown rot from standing water.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil or succulent potting mix in bright sun to part shade; allow soil to dry completely between waterings. Echeveria elegans (Mexican snowball) is one of the classic and most widely grown echeverias — a Mexican succulent producing perfect, symmetrical, pale-blue-grey to ice-blue rosettes of dense, fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves 4–6 inches across, with a powdery glaucous coating that gives the rosette a cool, icy-blue appearance and inspired the common name 'Mexican snowball.' In spring and summer, it produces arching, coral-pink flower stems with nodding, yellow-tipped, pink flowers that are attractive to hummingbirds. The plant offsets freely (producing 'chicks' around the central 'hen'), allowing easy propagation by division; leaf and stem cuttings also root readily. Echeveria elegans is the foundation of much of the interest in succulent container gardening and succulent wreaths, and is one of the best echeverias for humid climates (it tolerates more moisture than many succulents if drainage is excellent). In zone 9, it grows outdoors in well-drained rockeries, raised beds, and container gardens; bring indoors during hard freezes.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting (after soil warms to 70°F+) in well-drained, average to poor, neutral soil in full sun; tithonia is extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms better in lean, dry soil.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting (after soil warms to 70°F+) in well-drained, average to poor, neutral soil in full sun; tithonia is extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms better in lean, dry soil. Tithonia rotundifolia is the premier late-summer annual for attracting monarch butterflies, swallowtails, and native bumblebees — in high summer and early fall, a patch of blooming Mexican sunflowers will be covered with butterflies from dawn to dusk. The plant produces vivid, velvety, 3-inch, orange-scarlet flowers with a golden-yellow center on tall, branching, slightly hairy stems from midsummer through frost; hollow stems must be seared before using as cut flowers to prevent wilting. It is an outstanding back-of-border annual for hot, sunny gardens in zones 9–11 and is perennial in frost-free areas.

common_name: Mexican Yellow Water Lily (Yellow Water Lily)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 2–4 inches deep in heavy aquatic planting mix in containers submerged 6–18 inches below the water surface; Mexican yellow water lily spreads vigorously by stolons and can naturalize in shallow ponds and slow-moving water throughout zones 8–11.
directions: Plant tubers in heavy aquatic soil (NOT potting mix — which floats) in containers submerged 6–18 inches below the water surface in full sun; Mexican yellow water lily is a native aquatic perennial of ponds, marshes, and slow-moving waters of the Gulf Coast region from Texas to Florida and into Mexico, producing the classic water lily form — floating, round pads and fragrant, multi-petaled flowers — but in a soft, clear yellow color that distinguishes it from most cultivated water lilies. It is notably more heat-tolerant and better adapted to warm, humid climates than the European water lily (N. alba) or most cultivated tropical water lily hybrids. The cheerful yellow flowers open in the morning and close by afternoon. This species spreads readily by horizontal rhizomes (stolons) to colonize pond edges in warm climates — beneficial in a natural pond setting, manageable in a contained water garden. An excellent choice for water gardens in zone 9a.

common_name: Mexican Zinnia (Little Classic Zinnia, Haage Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mexican zinnia is more drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and disease-resistant than common garden zinnia (Z. elegans) and is outstanding for hot, humid Gulf Coast summers where powdery mildew can devastate Z. elegans plantings.
directions: Direct sow seeds in warm soil in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; thin to 8–12 inches. Zinnia haageana (Mexican zinnia) is a compact, fine-leaved, heat-tolerant Mexican native zinnia species that produces cheerful bicolor and tricolor daisy flowers in orange, red, yellow, and mahogany combinations from summer through frost. Unlike the common large-flowered garden zinnia (Z. elegans), Z. haageana is dramatically more drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and resistant to powdery mildew — the disease that devastates Z. elegans in hot, humid climates. In zone 9, Mexican zinnias perform with vigor through the summer while common garden zinnias may defoliate from mildew. The 'Aztec' series is the most widely grown, with single or semi-double flowers in warm orange-red, yellow-orange, and burnt-orange combinations that are extremely attractive to butterflies, especially Gulf Fritillaries and Sulphurs. The compact habit and narrow, lance-shaped leaves create a finer texture than Z. elegans. Z. haageana is also used as a parent in interspecific zinnia hybrids ('Profusion,' 'Zahara') bred specifically for heat, humidity, and disease resistance.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall into moist, disturbed woodland soil; seeds require cold stratification to break dormancy and will germinate naturally in late winter or early spring for bloom in April and May. Seeds can also be stratified in the refrigerator for 4-6 weeks and sown in earliest spring.
directions: Phacelia purshii is a delicate spring annual native to moist woodland edges and disturbed forest floors across eastern North America, producing loose clusters of finely-fringed lavender-blue and white flowers from April through June. Scatter seeds in fall across bare or lightly raked soil in partial shade; the seeds need a cold, moist period to break dormancy and will germinate on their own schedule in late winter. Plants grow quickly in cool weather, bloom prolifically, then set abundant seed before summer heat arrives, often naturalizing into self-sustaining colonies. It combines beautifully with other spring ephemerals such as Virginia bluebells and wild ginger.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in sharply well-drained, gritty or sandy soil in partial shade or sun in fall, 6–10 weeks before first frost; Michael's fritillary is native to alpine and subalpine meadows in northeastern Turkey and must have excellent drainage year-round, particularly dry conditions during summer dormancy — planting in raised beds or incorporating coarse grit into heavy soils is strongly recommended.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in sharply well-drained, gritty soil in partial shade or full sun in autumn for April–May bloom; Michael's fritillary is one of the most visually striking of all small fritillaries — a compact, 4–8-inch species from the mountains of northeastern Turkey producing clusters of pendant, bell-shaped flowers whose coloring is among the most dramatic of the genus: the upper two-thirds of each bell is a deep, rich purple-maroon to mahogany-purple, shading abruptly to a bright, clear canary-yellow band at the flared petal tips, creating an intensely eye-catching bicolor effect quite unlike anything else in the spring garden. Multiple bells are carried per stem, intensifying the display. Like all Middle Eastern alpine fritillaries, it insists on perfect drainage and a dry summer dormancy; it is intolerant of prolonged wet conditions at any season and will fail in heavy, moisture-retentive soils. Best grown in a gravel garden, raised bed, alpine trough, or bulb frame. When conditions suit, it multiplies freely by bulb offsets. A rare but readily available gem for the enthusiast collector.

plant_note: Sow on bare limestone-derived soil in fall; seeds require cold stratification over winter to germinate in late winter or early spring. Do not add organic matter or compost — this species demands thin, nutrient-poor, calcareous substrate.
directions: Michaux's Gladecress is a tiny, jewel-like native winter annual of limestone cedar glades in Tennessee, Kentucky, and adjacent states, one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom in the entire eastern flora, opening its single white 4-petaled flowers with yellow centers on thread-like stems as early as February through April. It completes its entire life cycle on the exposed, thin-soiled faces of limestone outcrops that experience brief seasonal saturation followed by intense summer drought — conditions nearly impossible to recreate in conventional gardens. Grow in thin, rocky, calcareous, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, deliberately avoiding soil amendments or fertilizer that would favor competing vegetation. It is an ecological specialist of rare, imperiled cedar glade habitat and is best suited for limestone glade restoration projects rather than traditional garden settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, rocky or gravelly soil in partial shade; Michaux's saxifrage is an Appalachian high-elevation endemic growing on moist, rocky, north-facing cliffs and rock outcrops above 2000 feet elevation in the southern Blue Ridge Mountains.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, rocky or gravelly, shaded to partially shaded conditions; Michaux's saxifrage is a rare, high-elevation Appalachian endemic named for the French botanist André Michaux who explored the southern Appalachians in the late 18th century. The plant grows on moist, shaded rock outcrops, north-facing cliffs, and rocky streamsides at higher elevations in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Small white flowers appear in summer. The deeply toothed, spatula-shaped leaves with distinctive reddish-brown dried leaf bases are ornamentally attractive in rock garden and alpine trough settings. Only suitable for cool-summer gardens in zones 4–7; does not tolerate heat. A challenging but rewarding plant for the rock garden specialist — available from native plant specialists and botanical garden plant sales.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall at 3–4 inches depth in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Michigan lily is one of the tallest native lilies and prefers consistently moist, fertile soil along stream banks, moist meadows, and moist prairie edges. Thrives with dappled afternoon shade.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun along stream banks, moist meadows, and moist prairie edges; Michigan lily is a tall native lily of the Midwest and Great Plains, naturally growing in moist prairies, stream banks, and open woodland margins. Like Turk's cap lily (L. superbum), it produces nodding, orange-red, spotted flowers with strongly reflexed petals, but Michigan lily is more common in the central and western part of the range where Turk's cap is absent. The tall stems can reach 7 feet, bearing up to a dozen or more flowers per stem in mid-summer. The drooping flowers are adapted for pollination by large, strong bumblebees and the great spangled fritillary butterfly. A superb native for moist meadow gardens, rain gardens, and naturalistic plantings in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Michigan lily is a superb native Turk's cap-type lily for moist meadows, prairie margins, and stream banks in zones 3–8.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall 4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Michigan lily performs best in consistently moist, fertile soil and is especially beautiful planted at the margins of ponds and along stream banks where consistent moisture is available. Lilium michiganese is a native lily of the upper Midwest and Great Plains tallgrass prairies, moist meadows, and stream margins; it closely resembles the Turk's cap lily (L. superbum) but has smaller, more numerous flowers and a more compact habit. It produces whorled leaves on stout stems reaching 3–6 feet tall and bears 3–10 (occasionally more) nodding, strongly reflexed, orange to orange-red flowers with dark-maroon spots in mid-summer — a spectacular sight when established in large naturalized clumps. Outstanding for moist native plant gardens and prairie restoration plantings.

common_name: Midnight Marvel Hibiscus (Near-Black Foliage Red-Flowered Hardy Hibiscus)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Midnight Marvel pairs near-black purple foliage with huge, vivid true-red flowers, one of the most dramatic color combinations in the Summerific hardy hibiscus series.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Midnight Marvel pairs deep, near-black purple foliage — among the darkest available in hardy hibiscus — with enormous, 8-inch, vivid true-red flowers that create striking contrast against the dark leaves, making it one of the most visually dramatic cultivars in the compact, well-branched Summerific breeding series. It blooms in a steady succession of huge flowers from midsummer into fall, each lasting only a day but replaced continuously by new buds, giving the plant a long, reliable season of color. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring — often not until late May in many climates — so mark its location to avoid accidentally digging into the dormant crown. It is generally trouble-free once established in consistently moist soil, though Japanese beetles can be a significant pest on the foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Midnight Rose Heuchera (Midnight Rose Coral Bells)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Midnight Rose is a sport of Obsidian and shares its parent's need for well-drained soil and partial shade to maintain the characteristic black leaf color with pink spotting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Midnight Rose is a sport of Obsidian heuchera distinguished by its extraordinary foliage — deep black-purple leaves randomly spotted with vivid pink and cream flecks that make the plant appear bejeweled. The spotting is variable and unpredictable from leaf to leaf, ranging from a few small dots to large, splashed pink areas; no two leaves are identical. This speckled pattern creates an arresting, jewel-like effect in the shade garden, especially when the glossy black background reflects light from nearby sources. The pink flecking tends to be more prominent in spring and fall when temperatures are cooler and less distinct in the heat of summer. Small cream to pink flowers appear on wiry scapes in early summer. Like Obsidian, it requires perfect drainage in humid climates and benefits from division every 3–4 years to maintain vigor. An outstanding cultivar for creating focal points in dark, shadowed spots of the garden.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part shade.
