directions: Mighty Chocolate Cherry is a tall astilbe with dramatic cherry-red plumes rising above green-burgundy chocolate-toned foliage. It brings bold vertical color to shaded, moist borders and woodland gardens. Plant in partial shade in rich soil that stays evenly moist, since astilbe suffers if it dries out. Water regularly and mulch to conserve moisture and keep roots cool. Cut back spent foliage in late fall and divide clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Surface sow; needs light and dislikes transplanting.
directions: Direct sow mignonette on the soil surface, as it needs light to germinate and resents root disturbance. The unremarkable greenish flower spikes release an intensely sweet raspberry-like fragrance beloved in Victorian gardens. Grow in full sun to light shade in cool weather and fertile, alkaline soil. Position it near paths and seating where its perfume can be enjoyed, and make successive sowings for a long season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; resents transplanting.
directions: Sow directly where plants are to grow, as California poppies have a taproot and dislike transplanting. Scatter seed on prepared soil in early spring or fall and press in lightly. This selection bears saucer-shaped, bright orange-red flowers that open in sun and close at night or on cloudy days. Heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it needs little care and often self-sows for years of color.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring where plants will grow; do not transplant.
directions: This California poppy strain glows with deep red-orange, saucer-shaped blooms that open in sun and close at night. Sow seeds directly in early spring where they are to grow, pressing them onto the surface since the taproot resents transplanting. Full sun and lean, well-drained soil suit it best, and it needs little water once established. It self-sows reliably to return and naturalize in gardens and meadows.

common_name: Milk and Wine Crinum (Striped White-and-Pink Fragrant Gulf South Crinum Lily)
plant_note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Milk and Wine Crinum prefers planting with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface — planting too deep reduces flowering; divide congested clumps every 5–7 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant large bulbs in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Milk and Wine Crinum is one of the most beloved and long-lived heirloom bulbs of Gulf South gardens — a heritage Crinum hybrid producing large clusters of fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers with white petals boldly striped with wine-red to rosy-pink along the midrib of each petal, creating the distinctive 'milk and wine' appearance that gives the variety its evocative name. The large, heavily fragrant flowers (6–8 per umbel, 4–5 inch diameter) are produced in flushes from late spring through fall, typically blooming most heavily after rainfall events similar to the related Zephyranthes rain lilies. The sweet fragrance — particularly intense in the evening — is one of the most distinctive qualities of Crinum lilies generally, and the large flower clusters create an arresting display at the back of the border or as a specimen planting. Milk and Wine Crinum is extremely long-lived and persistent — established clumps in old Gulf South gardens often persist for many decades, growing into very large clumps with dozens of flowering stalks annually without any attention. The massive bulbs (sometimes reaching the size of a football in old, undivided clumps) have few pests and diseases. The handsome, strap-shaped evergreen foliage (3–4 feet long) provides year-round architectural interest. Tolerates periodic flooding, drought, salt spray, and heavy clay soils — one of the most adaptable ornamental bulbs for challenging Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed or fall sow for best germination.
directions: Cold-moist stratify the seed for several weeks or sow in fall to break dormancy for this heirloom perennial. Direct sow where plants will grow, as the deep taproot resists transplanting. From summer onward it produces clusters of fiery red-orange flowers, a preferred nectar source for monarchs and other pollinators, followed by ornamental seed pods. Drought tolerant once established, it is best left undisturbed to form a long-lived clump.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; million bells is vegetatively propagated (sterile hybrids do not come true from seed) and sold exclusively as rooted cuttings or potted plants.
directions: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile potting mix in full sun to partial shade after last frost; million bells (superbells) are trailing, mounding hybrids derived from South American Calibrachoa species that produce thousands of tiny, one-inch, petunia-like flowers throughout the growing season in virtually every color — from pure white through yellow, pink, coral, red, purple, magenta, and bicolor combinations. They are among the top-selling container annuals in the US for their continuous bloom, compact trailing habit, and resistance to flopping and deadheading requirements (they are self-cleaning). Require consistently moist, well-fertilized growing media — plants in containers quickly exhaust the available nutrients and benefit from weekly liquid fertilizer at half-strength during active growth. Excellent in hanging baskets, window boxes, and as trailers over container edges.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 sow March–May. Million Gold is a compact, very early-flowering melampodium selection that begins blooming in just 50–70 days from seed — among the earliest-blooming selections in this genus. The plant is extremely self-sufficient once established — no deadheading, no pinching, no staking, and minimal water requirements after root establishment. In zone 9 melampodium performs best in the heat of summer (May–October), with declining performance as fall temperatures cool. The bright golden-yellow flowers complement blue, purple, and white companions effectively; excellent with angelonia, vinca, and ornamental sweet potato. Plants can be started from direct sow seed — unusually easy for a warm-season annual.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Million Gold Melampodium thrives in hot, dry conditions and performs most reliably in full sun with minimal water once established; Million Gold Melampodium is a compact selection of Medallion Flower (Melampodium divaricatum), a warm-season annual from Mexico producing a neat, mounding, self-branching plant covered with small (1–1.5 inch), bright golden-yellow, single daisy flowers with deep yellow centers that bloom continuously from late spring through fall frost without any deadheading or flower removal. Melampodium is one of the most genuinely self-sufficient summer annuals available for zone 9 — requiring no deadheading (spent flowers drop cleanly from the plant), minimal water once established, no pinching or shaping, and performing actively through the peak zone 9 summer heat without the bloom reduction or disease issues that affect less heat-adapted annuals. The consistent, clean golden-yellow of the flowers — produced in sufficient quantity to give the plant a solid golden appearance — combined with the dwarf, non-flopping habit and absolute minimal-care requirements makes Million Gold one of the most practical choices for no-maintenance summer color in full-sun beds, borders, and containers throughout zone 9's long summer season.

common_name: Million Hearts Plant (Heart Leaf Dischidia, Rosary Dischidia)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket, mounted epiphyte, or container plant in bright indirect to moderate shade; Million Hearts Plant cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Mount on cork bark or tree fern slabs like an orchid for the most natural display, securing young stems with fishing line until roots establish. In a container, use a chunky mix of orchid bark and perlite with excellent drainage. Water thoroughly then allow to dry almost completely between waterings — overwatering causes rapid stem rot in this epiphyte. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade with exceptional drainage — Million Hearts Plant is a true epiphyte that rots quickly in heavy, moisture-retaining growing media. Dischidia ruscifolia is a small-leafed trailing epiphytic vine from the Philippines and Southeast Asia in the family Apocynaceae (the same family as Hoya and Stephanotis), producing thin, wiry, trailing stems clothed in pairs of tiny, heart-shaped, slightly fleshy, pale to medium-green leaves approximately half an inch across. The massed effect of hundreds of small green hearts cascading from a hanging basket gives the plant its popular common name — 'Million Hearts' — a name that perfectly captures the charming, delicate abundance of the foliage. As a true epiphyte from the humid forests of Southeast Asia, Dischidia grows naturally attached to rough tree bark in conditions of excellent air circulation, bright filtered light, and periodic drought — the small, slightly succulent leaves store water against dry periods between tropical rainstorms. Tiny, white, urn-shaped flowers appear sporadically along the stems. Multiple cultivars exist, including 'String of Nickels' (rounder, slightly larger leaves) and the slightly more compact 'Imbricata.' Non-toxic to pets and children.

common_name: Mine-no-Yuki Camellia (White Dove Camellia, Snow on the Mountain Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Mine-no-Yuki is a low, spreading cultivar well-suited to espalier training against walls and fences where its arching habit can be displayed horizontally.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Mine-no-Yuki (also sold as 'White Dove') is a classic Japanese camellia sasanqua cultivar producing beautiful, fragrant, large, white to cream-white, semi-double to double flowers from October through December in zone 9. The pure white to cream-white flowers with prominent golden-yellow stamens partially visible between the petals create an elegant, refined appearance that is particularly effective against dark evergreen foliage backgrounds, near entryways, or as cut flowers. Mine-no-Yuki has an unusually low-spreading, arching habit that sets it apart from the more upright growth of most sasanqua camellias — it typically spreads wider than it grows tall, which makes it outstanding for espalier training against fences and walls, for draping over retaining walls, and as a low screening or ground-cover plant in sloped situations. The mild, pleasant fragrance of the flowers is another distinctive characteristic — sasanqua camellias are generally more fragrant than japonica types, and Mine-no-Yuki is among the most pleasantly scented selections. The low, spreading habit and arching branches produce attractive natural mounding form without pruning. Provide moist, well-drained, acidic soil and maintain pine bark mulch at the root zone year-round.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite under intermittent mist, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade after frost; ming aralia is sensitive to cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, which cause leaf drop — protect from cold air movement and avoid sites exposed to winter winds in zone 10, where the plant is marginally hardy.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; ming aralia (parsley aralia, wild coffee tree) is an Indo-Pacific tropical evergreen shrub in the ginseng family (Araliaceae) that produces some of the most intricately textured and refined tropical foliage available for shaded garden positions — the leaves are compound and deeply divided, with each leaflet further divided into multiple, small, toothed, crinkled, irregular segments that create a dense, feathery, parsley-like to fern-like appearance at close range and an impression of extraordinary, finely subdivided textural richness from a distance. The thin branches grow in a graceful, architectural, often slightly irregular pattern that resembles a natural bonsai. Ming aralia is frequently grown as an indoor specimen and shaped into bonsai form. Outdoors in zone 10–12 it grows into a substantial shrub or small tree to 15 feet with similarly intricate foliage at a much larger scale. The combination of shade tolerance, fine texture, and elegant form makes it one of the most useful and refined tropical foliage shrubs for shaded positions in the tropical garden.

common_name: Mini Monstera (Piccolo Monstera, Ginny Philodendron, Rhaphidophora)
plant_note: Grow on a moss pole or bark support in bright indirect light in well-draining, chunky aroid mix; Raphidophora tetrasperma climbs vigorously and produces progressively larger, more deeply split leaves as it ascends a support — provide a tall moss pole for best results. Despite widespread common names referencing Monstera and Philodendron, it belongs to neither genus. Allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Maintain moderate humidity (50%+). Propagate from stem cuttings. All parts mildly toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-draining, aerated potting mix on a climbing support — Mini Monstera produces its most attractive, deeply split leaves as it climbs and becomes less impressive when allowed to trail without a support. Raphidophora tetrasperma is a hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to southern Thailand and Malaysia in the Araceae family — not a Monstera, not a Philodendron, despite being widely marketed under both names. The plant produces deeply split, pinnatifid (partially divided rather than fully perforated), glossy, dark-green leaves on slender, fast-growing climbing stems. In young plants, the leaves are small and undivided; as the plant climbs, they become progressively larger (up to 12 inches) and more deeply cut into opposite pairs of oval lobes separated by incisions extending almost to the midrib — a leaf pattern strikingly similar to a miniature Monstera deliciosa. The combination of this attractive, deeply-split leaf pattern, fast growth rate, compact size relative to true Monstera, and ease of cultivation in indoor and tropical garden conditions has made Raphidophora tetrasperma one of the most popular aroids in the contemporary houseplant boom. It grows significantly faster than true Monstera and is substantially more compact, making it better suited to average indoor and small tropical garden spaces. Mildly toxic.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container vine; Rhaphidophora tetrasperma is strictly tropical and cannot tolerate temperatures below 55°F. Provide a moss pole, bamboo stake, or trellis for the aerial roots to attach to — the plant grows much faster and develops larger, more fenestrated leaves when it can climb. Propagate from stem cuttings with one node — root in water or moist sphagnum moss within 2–3 weeks. Despite being commonly sold as 'Mini Monstera,' it is a completely different genus from Monstera.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Mini Monstera grows fastest in bright indirect light (3–6 feet from a sunny window) and develops larger leaves with more pronounced fenestrations when given good light and a climbing support. Rhaphidophora tetrasperma is a fast-growing, climbing tropical vine from southern Thailand and Malaysia that has become one of the most popular houseplants in the recent era of tropical plant collecting, despite being entirely unrelated to the true Monstera genus. It is sold in virtually every garden center and box store under the trade name 'Mini Monstera' because the deeply lobed, fenestrated, bright-green leaves bear a strong resemblance in miniature to Monstera deliciosa — the iconic 'Swiss Cheese Plant' — though R. tetrasperma leaves are smaller (4–8 inches) and thinner. The plant climbs by aerial roots, producing new leaves quickly and making it one of the fastest-growing popular tropical foliage plants. Each new leaf is larger than the last when the plant is given adequate light, warmth, and a climbing structure. Like Monstera, the leaf splits (fenestrations) are thought to be an adaptation for surviving high winds in the rainforest understory by reducing wind resistance on large leaves. Mildly toxic if chewed; the calcium oxalate crystals cause mouth irritation.

common_name: Mini Penny Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Mini Penny is a dwarf sport of the reliable reblooming cultivar Penny Mac, staying compact enough for small gardens and large containers while retaining its parent's dependable rebloom.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun. Mini Penny is a dwarf sport of the widely grown, reliably reblooming Penny Mac hydrangea, retaining its parent's strong performance — flowering on both old wood from the previous season and new wood produced the same year — while staying considerably more compact, typically under 2 feet tall, making it well suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-sized hydrangea would be too large. Because it reblooms on new wood, a late spring frost that damages old buds does not prevent a strong summer bloom. Flower color shifts with soil pH the way most macrophylla hydrangeas do, ranging from blue in acidic soil to pink in more alkaline soil, and can be adjusted with soil amendments. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since heavy pruning removes the old-wood flower buds that provide the earliest bloom flush.

plant_note: Plant small tubers in spring after soil warms in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in deep shade to part shade; miniature caladium is the smallest-leaved caladium species with delicate, naturally small foliage and is an excellent choice for container gardens, terrariums, shaded rock gardens, and fine-textured shade border edging.
directions: Plant small tubers 1 inch deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in deep shade; keep consistently moist and protect from any cold. Caladium humboldtii (miniature caladium) is a distinct Venezuelan caladium species producing naturally compact, small-leaved plants reaching only 6–12 inches tall with small (2–4 inch), elegantly proportioned, arrow-shaped leaves in classic white-with-green-veining coloration that is more restrained and subtle than the bold fancy-leaf cultivars. While less commonly grown than Caladium bicolor cultivars, C. humboldtii is valuable for smaller spaces — terrariums, small container arrangements, fine-textured shade borders, and rock garden pockets — where the scale of fancy-leaf caladiums would be overwhelming. It is also more shade-demanding than C. bicolor and thrives in deeper shade conditions. The species has contributed to miniaturized caladium cultivars bred for compact size. In zones below 10, lift tubers before the first frost and store indoors at 55–60°F; they may be replanted the following spring.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Comins's tulbaghia is a compact, smaller species than T. violacea — ideal for rock gardens, pot edges, and small spaces — that produces fragrant, white flowers. The flowers are sweetly scented rather than garlicky. More tender than T. violacea; in zone 9a it benefits from a sheltered position or container culture for winter protection.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; miniature society garlic is a charming, compact South African Tulbaghia from the rocky grasslands of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape — smaller in all its parts than the familiar T. violacea but similarly clump-forming and similarly prolific in flower production. The small, white, sweetly fragrant (not garlic-scented) flowers are borne in compact, rounded umbels on stems only 8–14 inches tall, above very narrow, grass-like, blue-green leaves that give the plant a delicate, fine-textured appearance well suited to pot edges, rock garden plantings, and small-space gardens where T. violacea's larger clumps would be overwhelming. The sweet flower fragrance (vs the distinctive garlic odor of T. violacea) makes it preferable for positions near paths and sitting areas where one passes close. It flowers over an extended period in late spring through summer. A compact, refined alternative to Society Garlic for the smaller-scale zone 9 garden or for container culture on a shaded terrace.

common_name: Miniature Wax Plant (Wax Bell, Beautiful Hoya, Hoya bella)
plant_note: Grow as a hanging basket or pendant container in bright indirect light; Hoya lanceolata subsp. bella cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Unlike most Hoyas, it prefers slightly more consistent moisture (never fully drying out) because of its naturally epiphytic roots in humid forest understory. Use a fine-textured, well-aerated potting mix. Never remove old peduncles. Propagate from stem cuttings in moist perlite or sphagnum. The naturally pendant growth habit makes it ideal for small hanging baskets. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light to moderate shade — Miniature Wax Plant requires more light to bloom than its size suggests; place within 3 feet of a bright window for reliable flowering, while avoiding direct sun which burns the small leaves. Hoya lanceolata subsp. bella (commonly sold simply as 'Hoya bella') is a small, naturally pendant epiphytic Hoya from Myanmar (Burma) and the eastern Himalayas in the family Apocynaceae — one of the most compact and delicate of the commonly grown Hoyas. The slender, arching stems produce pairs of small, lance-shaped to oval, pale to medium-green, slightly succulent leaves about an inch long in an airy, cascading arrangement naturally suited to small hanging baskets and elevated containers. In bloom, the plant produces pendant umbels of 7–12 tiny, perfectly star-shaped, white flowers with a contrasting center corona of deep rose-purple — each individual flower less than half an inch across, but the massed effect of many clusters simultaneously in bloom creates a charming and delicate display. The flowers are lightly but pleasantly fragrant. Unlike the vigorous, twining large Hoyas, H. lanceolata subsp. bella has a naturally arching, pendant, non-climbing growth habit — it does not reach toward a support or twine but simply cascades downward in long, graceful arches. This makes it one of the finest small Hoyas for hanging baskets and elevated windowsill displays. Non-toxic.

common_name: Mirror Plant (Copper Alocasia, Red Secret Alocasia, Giant Caladium)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in well-drained, chunky, aerated aroid mix — Alocasia cuprea needs excellent drainage and is prone to root rot in dense, moisture-retaining media. Allow the top 1–2 inches to dry before re-watering. Maintain warm temperatures (65–85°F) and moderate humidity (50%+). The metallic sheen of the leaves is a structural color effect and intensifies in bright indirect light. The common name 'Red Secret' refers to the deep red-purple undersides. Propagate by separating corms. All parts toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-draining, aerated potting mix — Copper Alocasia produces its most intense metallic leaf sheen in bright indirect light and becomes dull in dim conditions while being scorched by any direct sun. Alocasia cuprea is a compact, rhizomatous aroid native to Borneo (Sarawak, Malaysia) in the Araceae family, one of the most visually striking of the jewel alocasias and widely coveted among tropical plant collectors for its extraordinary, metallic, iridescent leaf surface. The leaves are broadly oval to cordate, thick and leathery, and covered with a surface that appears to be hammered copper or burnished metal — an intense, reflective, coppery-bronze to deep bronze-green sheen that seems almost industrial in its metallicity, unlike the texture of any other commonly grown aroid. This metallic appearance is a structural color effect produced by specialized leaf cell architecture that acts as a diffraction grating for light. The deeply sunken primary and secondary veins create a strong, dark grid pattern against the bright metallic surface. The undersides are deep purple-red to maroon (the source of the popular cultivar name 'Red Secret'). An established, well-grown Alocasia cuprea with several large metallic leaves simultaneously is one of the most visually arresting of all tropical foliage plants. All parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic.

common_name: Miss Huff Lantana (Cold-Hardy Tall Orange-Pink Lantana)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Miss Huff is notably more cold-hardy than most lantana cultivars, often returning reliably from the roots after winters that kill other lantana to the ground or outright.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Miss Huff is one of the most widely planted lantana cultivars in the Gulf South, valued for a rare combination of vigorous, tall growth, months of nonstop orange-to-pink multicolor flower clusters that draw butterflies in large numbers, and notably better cold tolerance than most lantana, regularly surviving winters as a root-hardy perennial where less hardy cultivars are killed outright. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and poor soil with ease once established, needing only an annual hard cutback in late winter after the coldest weather has passed to remove winter-killed top growth and encourage vigorous new flowering growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; dislikes root disturbance.
directions: Direct sow in early spring since this annual dislikes transplanting; successive sowings extend the bloom. Cover seed lightly and keep evenly moist until germination. Airy, fern-like foliage surrounds jewel-toned blue and pastel flowers that attract pollinators and shine in bouquets. The inflated seed pods that follow are prized for dried arrangements; leave some to self-sow for next year.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–November in zone 9) for winter and spring bloom; in zone 9 fall sowing is strongly preferred over spring sowing — nigella does not transplant well (direct sow only) and performs poorly if sown when soil is warm. Cool soil and winter establishment produces the strongest plants for spring bloom. Miss Jekyll is named for garden designer Gertrude Jekyll and has been in cultivation since the early 20th century. The inflated seed pods that follow the flowers are as ornamental as the flowers themselves — striped green-and-red when fresh and parchment-brown when dry, they make excellent additions to fresh and dried arrangements. In zone 9 nigella blooms February–April and sets seed before summer heat arrives.
directions: Direct sow in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil — Miss Jekyll Nigella germinates best in cool soil (50–65°F) and does not transplant well, requiring direct sowing in place; Miss Jekyll is the standard selection of Love-in-a-Mist (Nigella damascena), producing clear sky-blue flowers — one of the most vivid and pure blues available from any cool-season annual — nestled in an extraordinary collar of finely divided, thread-like, bright green bracts that create a delicate, intricate surround for each bloom. The common name 'Love-in-a-Mist' perfectly describes the appearance: the flowers appearing to float within a misty cloud of finely divided green bracts that blur the boundary between the flower and the stem, creating an unusual, hazy, romantic floral quality distinct from any other annual. After the flowers fade, Nigella produces large, inflated, balloon-like seed pods with prominent purple-red stripes that are fully as ornamental as the flowers and provide some of the most interesting seed pod structures available from any annual garden plant — valuable both in fresh arrangements and dried for winter decorations. In zone 9 Nigella is a fall-sown, winter-growing, spring-blooming cool-season annual that provides unusual sky-blue color in the February–April period when blue-flowering options are limited.

common_name: Miss Muffet Caladium (Dwarf Chartreuse-Speckled Compact Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; Miss Muffet is significantly more compact than standard fancy-leaved caladiums — use it at the front of borders, in containers, and as edging where smaller caladiums are more appropriate.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Miss Muffet is one of the most distinctive dwarf caladium cultivars — producing small (4–6 inch), light chartreuse-green to lime-yellow leaves heavily speckled with small red to pink spots that are scattered across the leaf surface in an irregular, freckled pattern. The unique combination of chartreuse-yellow-green leaf color and contrasting red spotting creates an unusual and eye-catching foliage effect quite different from the large white, red, or pink solid-colored standard fancy caladiums. The chartreuse-yellow tone is particularly effective in creating bright spots in shade — the warm yellow-green color reflects light more than darker greens, providing a light-reflective effect in partial shade similar to but visually distinct from the pure-white of 'White Queen'. Miss Muffet's compact size (8–14 inches tall and wide) makes it appropriate for container gardening, edging uses, and front-of-border plantings where the standard 18–24 inch caladiums would be out of scale. The dwarf strap-leaved habit (some leaves are partially strap-shaped rather than fully heart-shaped) is consistent with other compact caladium forms. Pair with White Queen or Red Flash for a visually interesting mixed caladium planting with complementary color combinations.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall for spring germination or in early spring in cold-stratified conditions; seeds require a period of cold to germinate well. Sow directly where plants will grow permanently, as the deep taproot makes transplanting difficult. Allow plants to self-sow after flowering to maintain a naturalized colony.
directions: Sow seeds in fall in well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Miss Wilmott's Ghost is the most dramatically architectural of all sea hollies, named for the Victorian horticulturalist Ellen Willmott who supposedly secretly scattered seeds in gardens she visited — so the plants appeared mysteriously the following year as her 'ghost.' It produces enormously large, pale silvery-blue-white flower heads and bracts that can reach 4–6 inches across, with a ghostly, pewter-silver appearance unlike the more purely blue Eryngiums. As a monocarpic biennial, it germinates one year, blooms spectacularly the next, sets seed, and dies — but it self-sows so freely in appropriate conditions that it maintains a permanent colony. Combine with blue-gray grasses, dark-leafed salvias, or purple alliums for a dramatic effect. The dried flower heads are unsurpassed for flower arrangements.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; resents transplanting.
directions: Sow seed directly onto prepared soil in early spring or fall, since the taproot resents being moved. This blend produces ruffled, saucer-shaped double and semi-double flowers in rose, red, orange, white, and yellow. Heat- and drought-tolerant, it asks little once established and readily self-sows for years of carpeted color. Grow in full sun for the best flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; cold stratification over winter improves germination rates in spring.
directions: A tall, bold native ironweed of moist prairies, floodplain meadows, and roadsides of the central US, producing flat-topped clusters of intensely vivid, deep purple composite flowers from August through October on upright, stout stems with lance-shaped, somewhat rough-textured leaves. The electric-purple flower color is among the most striking of any native North American wildflower. Direct sow in fall in moist, average to rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; plants spread slowly by rhizomes once established. Excellent as a tall background plant in native prairie gardens, providing late-season nectar for monarchs, native bees, and swallowtail butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall, or transplant divisions in spring, into lean, rocky or gravelly, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Missouri primrose demands sharp drainage and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil.
directions: Plant in lean, rocky or gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established thanks to a deep taproot, and intolerant of wet feet or heavy clay. Oenothera macrocarpa (Missouri primrose, or Ozark sundrop) is a low, sprawling native perennial of limestone glades and rocky prairies in the central United States, grown for producing some of the largest flowers of any native perennial relative to its compact size — brilliant, clear yellow, satiny blooms that can reach 4–5 inches across, opening in late afternoon and evening (a classic evening-primrose trait) to attract night-flying sphinx moths as primary pollinators, then remaining open into the following morning. The trailing stems and narrow, silvery-green leaves form a low mat that works beautifully cascading over a rock wall or spilling along the edge of a raised bed. Its combination of huge flowers, tiny plant footprint, and exceptional drought tolerance make it an outstanding specimen for a rock garden or dry sunny border, zone 4–8.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily by allowing cut ends to callus for a few days, then placing in moist orchid bark or perlite; mistletoe cactus is the only cactus native to the Old World (occurring in tropical Africa and Sri Lanka as well as South America) and requires bright indirect light — NOT direct sun, which bleaches the stems. It grows outdoors in zone 10–11 in shade and as a houseplant in bright indirect light in all zones.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in orchid bark or very well-drained, humus-rich medium; mistletoe cactus is the world's most widely distributed cactus species — uniquely occurring across tropical South America, Central America, the Caribbean, tropical Africa, and even Sri Lanka, making it the only cactus native to the Old World. It is an epiphyte of tropical forest canopies, hanging in long, pendulous, leafless green stems that resemble pencil-thin ropes cascading from tree branches, much like mistletoe (hence the common name). In late winter to spring, tiny, inconspicuous cream-white flowers appear along the stem margins, followed by translucent white berries resembling mistletoe berries. Unlike most cacti, it requires indirect light, moderate humidity, and more frequent watering — much more like an orchid than a desert plant. Excellent as a dramatic hanging basket plant in bright, indirect indoor light or outdoors in frost-free shade. It tolerates neglect and low-light conditions that kill most plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; needs cool soil to germinate.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil in early spring or in fall, as larkspur germinates best at cool temperatures and dislikes transplanting; chilling the seed helps. This variety bears densely packed nine- to twelve-inch spikes of double, ruffled florets in soft greyed lavender and dusty mauve-purple. Provide full sun and support for the tall stems, which make excellent fresh or dried cut flowers. Frost tolerant when young.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Mobile onion is native to the moist, sandy, acidic coastal plain soils of Alabama, Mississippi, and western Florida, where it grows in open longleaf pine savannas, flatwoods, and sandy roadsides. It blooms in spring (March–April) with pink to deep-rose umbels. It prefers the moist, acidic sandy soils of the coastal plain rather than the alkaline limestone soils favored by A. drummond and A. kunthii.
directions: Plant small bulbs in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; Mobile onion is a Gulf Coast endemic allium — found natively in a relatively narrow band of the coastal plain from coastal Alabama through Mississippi and into the western Florida Panhandle — perfectly adapted to the moist, acidic, sandy soils of the longleaf pine flatwood ecosystems of this region. Unlike the limestone-adapted Texas wild onions (A. drummondii, A. kunthii) that favor dry, alkaline substrates, Mobile onion thrives in the opposite soil type: moist, humus-rich, acidic, sandy coastal plain soils of the piney woods and flatwood savannas. It produces in spring (March–April) attractive umbels of rose-pink to deep-pink, star-shaped flowers on stems 10–18 inches tall, providing a native spring pink in the understory of the coastal plain longleaf pine landscape. For gardeners in the Alabama-Mississippi Gulf Coast zone 9a area, this is the most locally native wild allium — a species naturally adapted to the exact soil chemistry, moisture, and light conditions of the local flatwood garden. It represents the native heritage of the specific coastal plain ecosystem of the central Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on moist, acidic soil; seeds benefit from natural cold stratification over winter before spring germination.
directions: A rare and beautiful native coneflower endemic to the wet longleaf pine flatwoods and savannas of Alabama, Georgia, and Florida's panhandle, producing bright yellow ray flowers surrounding a dark-brown, dome-shaped disk on tall, branching stems from July through October. Closely related to Rudbeckia laciniata but restricted to wet, acidic savanna habitats, it is an important component of longleaf pine savanna restoration plantings. Grow in moist to wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun for best flowering; it tolerates periodic inundation but declines in dry or calcareous soils. An excellent and underused pollinator plant for Gulf Coast gardens and rain garden borders in zones 7-9.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1 inch depth in well-drained, dry, rocky, calcareous, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Mohr's oak is adapted to the thin, rocky limestone soils of the Edwards Plateau and trans-Pecos Texas where it forms extensive colonies by sprouting from deep rhizomes after fire or disturbance.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, calcareous, alkaline to neutral, thin soil in full sun; Mohr's oak is a small, shrubby, semi-evergreen oak of the limestone hills and rocky grasslands of the Edwards Plateau and west Texas, forming extensive colonies by clonal spreading from rhizomes after fire — making it an important fire-resistant groundcover in Texas hill country landscapes. The small, leathery, pale green leaves are distinctive and remain on the shrub through most of the winter, contributing to the 'evergreen' characteristic of the Edwards Plateau landscape. Drought and heat tolerant in the extreme, naturally growing on the thinnest, rockiest limestone soils with summer rainfall supplementation only. The very small acorns are eaten by scaled quail, wild turkeys, and deer. Valuable for erosion control on dry, rocky, calcareous slopes in the hill country of central Texas.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall on the surface of moist, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; seeds require exposure to winter moisture and temperature fluctuations to germinate reliably in spring.
directions: Mohr's Thoroughwort is a native perennial boneset of wet longleaf pine flatwoods and seepage slopes along the Gulf Coast, from Alabama through Florida, where it grows in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun. Plant in consistently moist to seasonally wet conditions and avoid letting the soil dry out, especially during the first growing season while plants establish their root systems. From late summer through fall, flat-topped clusters of tiny fluffy white composite flowers attract a remarkable diversity of native bees, wasps, and butterflies. An excellent companion to other wet savanna natives such as Liatris, Helianthus heterophyllus, and Carphephorus species in flatwoods restoration and rain garden plantings.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Mona Lavender is a short-day bloomer — it flowers from late summer through fall when day length shortens, so plants grown through the long days of spring and summer may not flower until September–October in zone 9. In zone 10 it behaves as a year-round perennial; in zone 9 it may die back in cold winters but often resproutes from roots in spring. Take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors. The deep purple undersides of the leaves are a distinctive feature even when the plant is not in bloom.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Mona Lavender performs well in the dappled light under trees and in north-facing shade gardens; Mona Lavender is a hybrid plectranthus (a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae) developed at Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden in South Africa and introduced to the trade as one of the best ornamental shade plants for warm climates. The plant has a striking two-sided leaf appearance: the upper surface is deep, glossy, almost black-green with slightly embossed venation, while the underside is richly saturated deep purple — creating an unexpected color reveal when the leaves catch a breeze or are viewed from below. The flowers, which appear in late summer and fall when day length shortens, are long, elegant spikes of small lavender-purple blooms with a distinct, subtle fragrance. As a heat-tolerant shade plant that performs in zone 9's challenging combination of heat and shade, Mona Lavender fills a niche occupied by few other ornamental plants — providing substantial foliar and floral interest in the difficult conditions of partial to deep shade in humid subtropical climates where most traditional shade perennials struggle.

plant_note: Plant divisions 2–4 inches apart in spring or fall; in warm climates fall planting takes advantage of cooler temperatures for root establishment before summer heat.
directions: Plant divisions in virtually any soil type — from dry sandy to moderately moist — in full shade to partial sun; this tough Asian native is one of the most versatile shade groundcovers for southern gardens. Once established it smothers weeds, requires no mowing, and remains attractive year-round with its dark, grass-like evergreen foliage and small blue-black berries in fall. Mow or shear the entire planting to 2–3 inches in late winter every few years to remove older, ratty foliage and encourage fresh, uniform growth. Divide overgrown clumps every 4–5 years, replanting at the original spacing to maintain density.

plant_note: Sow in spring or fall; as a biennial it flowers the second year.
directions: Money plant, or silver dollar plant, is grown for its charming purple spring flowers and the translucent, coin-shaped seed pods that follow. Sow seeds shallowly in spring or fall, remembering that as a biennial it forms leaves the first year and blooms the second. It grows well in partial shade with average moisture and self-sows to keep returning. Leave the pods to dry on the plant, then peel the papery outer layers for silvery dried arrangements.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm.
directions: Direct sow one inch deep after frost in a sunny, sheltered site protected from strong wind, given the towering height. Each single-stem plant produces one enormous yellow flower up to eighteen inches across filled with large, tasty kernels. Provide rich soil and steady moisture to support the massive growth, and stake in exposed locations. Leave heads to ripen for edible seeds or to feed birds.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Mongolian oak is an extremely cold-hardy Asian oak adapted to the severe winters of Manchuria, Mongolia, and Siberia, tolerating winter temperatures well below -30°F in its native range.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Mongolian oak is one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant of all oak species, native to the boreal and temperate forests of northeastern China (Manchuria), Mongolia, Korea, and the Russian Far East where it is a dominant tree species in continental climates with extreme winter cold and hot, dry summers. In North American gardens, it offers an excellent alternative to overcup oak (Q. lyrata) or white oak for extremely cold climates in zones 3–4 where most oaks would be marginal. The leaves are large, distinctly lobed with very broad, rounded lobes and are clustered at branch tips in a manner reminiscent of daimyo oak. Fall color is yellow to orange-brown. One of the most underused oaks for extremely cold-climate gardens where shade trees are limited.

common_name: Monk Orchid (Spotted Orchid, African Spotted Orchid, Naturalized Shade Orchid)
plant_note: Oeceoclades maculata spreads spontaneously in shaded garden beds throughout zone 9-12 and is commonly encountered as a surprise arrival in mulched shade gardens rather than a deliberately planted species. If introducing deliberately, plant pseudobulbs in well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade under trees. The attractively spotted, succulent foliage is ornamental year-round. The plant produces white, purple-spotted flowers on erect spikes in summer. Has become naturalized and somewhat weedy in Florida and the Caribbean — check local invasive status before planting outside its native range.
directions: Grow in partial to full shade in well-drained, humus-rich, dry to moderately moist soil — Monk Orchid is notably drought-tolerant for a terrestrial orchid and adapts well to the dry-shade conditions under mature trees where many other plants fail. Oeceoclades maculata is a small, drought-tolerant, terrestrial orchid native to tropical Africa, Madagascar, and Réunion in the Orchidaceae family, now widely naturalized throughout the Caribbean, Florida, Central America, and tropical South America. The plant produces clusters of small, oval, gray-green pseudobulbs with one or two succulent, leathery leaves: these leaves are the plant's main ornamental feature, patterned with irregular darker green mottling and spotting on a lighter gray-green background — a pattern similar to a jewel orchid and ornamental enough to make the plant attractive as a groundcover. From the pseudobulbs in summer, erect spikes bear 5–15 small flowers (0.5 inch) in white with purple speckling on the lip. Monk Orchid has naturalized widely in Florida and Caribbean shade gardens, often appearing spontaneously under live oaks, palms, and other shade trees in zone 9-12, spreading by wind-dispersed dust seed. It is considered a minor invasive in some Caribbean islands but is generally a harmless, even ornamental addition to shaded Florida and Gulf Coast gardens where its drought tolerance, attractive spotted foliage, and self-spreading habits make it useful as a low-maintenance shade groundcover. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; monkey grass tolerates a wide range of conditions and is best established by dividing existing clumps or planting rooted container stock.
directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing clumps 12–18 inches apart; monkey grass is one of the most reliable groundcovers for shaded areas under trees where lawn grass thins and fails. Established plants tolerate drought, poor soil, root competition, and deep shade with minimal care, and in zone 5–10 they require no supplemental irrigation once roots are established. The spikes of small violet-to-white flowers appear in late summer above the grassy foliage and are followed by round black berries that persist into winter, providing wildlife value. Shear or mow the entire planting back to 2–3 inches in late winter before new growth begins to refresh the appearance and remove winter-damaged tips.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification; seedlings appear in spring. Established clumps can be divided in early spring or fall. CAUTION: all parts of this plant are extremely toxic — wear gloves when handling.
directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; monkshood is a stately perennial producing dramatic spikes of hooded blue-violet flowers in late summer, providing color at a time when many shade perennials have finished blooming. IMPORTANT: all parts of this plant are acutely poisonous (aconitine) — wear gloves when working with it and keep away from children and pets. It performs best in climates with cool summers and may struggle in zones warmer than 7. Never divide or transplant in late spring or summer. The rich blue flower spikes pair beautifully with golden rudbeckia, white snakeroot, and white turtlehead in naturalistic late-summer plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall to allow natural cold-moist stratification through winter and spring germination; alternatively, cold-stratify seed for 4–6 weeks at 38–40°F and sow indoors in late winter. Do not grow near food gardens and handle plants only with gloves — all parts are intensely poisonous.
directions: Plant in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in cool-summer climates, where the deep purple-blue, helmet-shaped flowers on stately 3–5 foot spikes bloom in mid to late summer and provide strong vertical structure to the cottage or woodland border. WARNING: All parts of Aconitum napellus are extremely poisonous — among the most toxic plants in temperate horticulture — containing the alkaloid aconitine, which is lethal in very small amounts through skin absorption or ingestion; always wear gloves when handling and do not plant near edible gardens or where children or pets may access the plant. Cold stratification is required for germination from seed; fall sowing outdoors is the most reliable method. Divide established clumps every 3–4 years in early fall, replanting the tuberous roots at the same depth, and site where cool nights and moderate shade help prevent summer stress.

plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Monsieur Tillier is an 1891 French tea rose valued in Deep South gardens for its vigorous, drought-tolerant growth and reliable performance in poor soil where many modern roses fail.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart to allow for its large, vigorous size. Introduced in France in 1891, Monsieur Tillier is a robust tea rose bearing large, loosely double blooms in variable shades of pink, salmon, and copper-tan, often several tones within a single flush, with a fruity tea fragrance. It is among the most drought-tolerant and vigorous of the old tea roses, capable of growing into a large shrub 5-6 feet tall and wide, and performs remarkably well in poor, sandy, or infertile soil where many modern roses struggle, a trait that made it a favorite for unattended cemetery and homestead plantings across the Deep South. It shows strong resistance to blackspot and thrives with minimal spraying in the humid Gulf South climate. Prune lightly in late winter to control size and remove dead or crossing wood, since Monsieur Tillier tolerates hard pruning better than many teas if size needs to be reduced.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck of the bulb at or just above soil surface; in zone 9 plant January–March for spring bloom. Mont Blanc naturalizes in the ground in zone 9 as a permanent perennial, multiplying steadily over years to produce increasingly impressive white flower masses in March–April. The pure white flowers show beautifully in evening and shaded garden settings where white flowers reflect and amplify available light. Allow foliage to grow and die back naturally through summer before going dormant; do not remove green leaves prematurely. As a container amaryllis, plant in well-drained potting mix with 1/3 of the bulb above the surface for traditional holiday bloom.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Mont Blanc Amaryllis performs beautifully in partial shade in zone 9 where its pure white flowers are displayed most effectively against shaded backgrounds; Mont Blanc is the definitive pure white amaryllis cultivar, producing the same massive, trumpet-shaped flowers (6–8 inches across, 4 per scape) as Red Lion amaryllis in a clean, brilliant white without markings or color variation — a pristine white that is particularly effective in evening gardens, formal white garden designs, and combination plantings where white provides a neutral, luminous contrast to colored companions. The pure white flower color works with essentially any color palette and any garden design style — mixing harmoniously with both cool-colored companions (blue, purple, silver) and warm-colored ones (red, orange, yellow) while simultaneously elevating the visual quality of each. The large flowers on sturdy scapes combine with the white color to make Mont Blanc one of the most versatile cut flower amaryllis varieties — the flowers last 2–3 weeks in a vase and the striking white color and bold scale make impressive arrangements with minimal other material. In zone 9 outdoor beds, naturalizing white amaryllis provide a reliable spring flower display that intensifies year after year as the clumps expand.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or divide established plants; plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Montauk daisy forms a woody base over time and benefits from hard cutting back in early spring to prevent legginess. Without annual pruning, plants become open and floppy; cut back by one-half to two-thirds in late spring. Salt-tolerant and excellent for coastal gardens.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Montauk daisy earns its place in the garden by being among the very last perennials to bloom, producing large, pure-white, single daisy flowers with bright-yellow centers from September through frost — often into November — when almost no other daisy-family plants remain in bloom. The large, somewhat succulent, dark-green, spoon-shaped leaves are attractive throughout the growing season and the shrubby, woody-based habit gives the plant year-round structure. Native to the coastal areas of Japan, it is famous for its salt tolerance and thrives in sandy, well-drained, seaside conditions that challenge many other perennials. It naturalized along the eastern seaboard of North America and became particularly associated with Montauk Point, Long Island, where large colonies established on coastal bluffs. Annual hard cutting in spring is essential to maintain compact, floriferous form — neglected plants become open and leggy and produce fewer flowers. The cultivar Amelia is a compact selection with larger flowers.

plant_note: Plant corms in spring; naturalizes and can spread widely.
directions: Plant montbretia corms in spring three to four inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. The arching sprays of fiery orange to red tubular flowers in mid to late summer are magnets for hummingbirds. It multiplies rapidly by cormlets and can spread widely, so site it where vigorous growth is welcome. Divide congested clumps every few years and mulch for winter in the colder end of its range.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Monterey pine is native to only three small coastal areas in California and is tender to hard frost, but grows extremely rapidly in mild coastal climates where it is widely used as a windbreak and timber tree.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Monterey pine is paradoxically an extremely rare native tree in the US — naturally occurring in just three small, fog-influenced coastal populations near Monterey, California, Santa Cruz Island, and Cedros Island in Baja California — yet it is the most widely planted timber tree in the Southern Hemisphere, with vast plantations in New Zealand, Australia, Chile, South Africa, and Spain. The species grows extraordinarily fast in moist, mild coastal climates — 6–10 feet per year is common. The cones are serotinous (requiring heat to open) and often remain on the tree for decades, making fire an important part of the species' ecology. In California coastal gardens, it provides fast shade and wind protection. Despite its global importance as a timber tree, the native Monterey pine populations are listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN due to disease, drought stress, and habitat loss.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Montezuma cypress tolerates periodic flooding and performs exceptionally well in the humid, subtropical conditions of Gulf Coast zones 8b–11.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 8b–11; Montezuma cypress is the national tree of Mexico, closely related to but more heat-tolerant and less deciduous than bald cypress (T. distichum). In mild climates, it remains semi-evergreen or evergreen year-round — a significant ornamental advantage over the fully deciduous bald cypress. The ancient Tule Tree (El Árbol del Tule) in Oaxaca, Mexico — a Montezuma cypress — is considered the world's largest tree by trunk circumference at over 40 feet in girth, with an age estimated at 1,400–3,000 years. In zone 9–10 Gulf Coast landscapes, Montezuma cypress makes a superb massive shade tree for moist, low-lying areas and streambanks where its greater heat tolerance makes it more vigorous and longer-lived than the native bald cypress. Knees develop in wet conditions, providing habitat for numerous organisms.

common_name: Moon Bay Nandina (Compact Mounding Heavenly Bamboo)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Moon Bay is a compact, naturally mounding form that requires little to no pruning — it stays under 3 feet without regular shearing.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Moon Bay is a compact, naturally mounding nandina selection staying 18–30 inches tall — smaller and more tightly formed than Gulf Stream or Harbour Dwarf, making it the most compact of the commonly available dwarf nandina cultivars. The graceful, fine-textured, finely divided foliage is a beautiful glossy-green through summer, turning vivid orange-red to scarlet-red in fall and winter when cold temperatures arrive. Moon Bay's compact, mounding form and outstanding fall/winter color combination make it an exceptionally practical and ornamental foundation shrub for zone 9 gardens where its reliability, low maintenance, and multi-season interest make it one of the most useful small evergreen shrubs in the landscape palette. Like all nandinas, Moon Bay is remarkably adaptable — tolerating clay, drought once established, heat, humidity, and partial shade without significant loss of performance or appearance. The foliage compound texture, graceful habit, and outstanding winter red color make it visually effective in all four seasons. Note: Nandina domestica berries are toxic to birds and the plant has invasive potential in some Gulf South natural areas — plant in contained garden settings away from natural areas.

common_name: Moon Vine (Large-Flowered White Night-Blooming Tropical Vine for Evening Gardens)
plant_note: Nick or soak seeds overnight before planting to speed germination; direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Moon Vine is best planted where it can climb a trellis, fence, or arbor and be viewed in the evening when the flowers open — the flowers close by mid-morning each day.
directions: Nick or soak seeds overnight, then direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Moon Vine (Ipomoea alba) is the classic evening and night garden vine — a tropical twining vine that produces extraordinarily large (4–6 inch), pure white, funnel-shaped flowers that open in late afternoon and evening, perfuming the garden with a sweet, rich, jasmine-like fragrance that intensifies as darkness falls. The flowers are among the largest of any commonly grown annual vine and the pure white color reflects low light beautifully, appearing to glow under moonlight, porch lights, or landscape lighting — creating the ethereal moonlit effect that gives the plant its common name. Moon Vine is a rapid, enthusiastic climber, gaining 15–20 feet in a single growing season in warm Gulf South conditions — it covers fences, arbors, pergolas, and mailboxes with dense, large-leaved foliage and a continuous supply of evening flowers from mid-summer until frost. The flowers each last only one evening, but numerous buds open in succession for months of nightly bloom. In Gulf South zone 9, Moon Vine is grown as a warm-season annual from spring through fall. In zone 10–12, it grows as a perennial twining vine. The rapid growth and profuse bloom make it one of the most rewarding evening-garden plants for summer arbors and screens. Often combined with common morning glory (I. purpurea) to create a 24-hour floral display from the same genus.

common_name: Moonbeam Coreopsis (Classic Pale Yellow Long-Blooming Perennial Thread-Leaf Coreopsis)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Moonbeam requires excellent drainage and lean soil — plants in heavy clay or overly fertile soil tend to be short-lived and flop open; raised beds and amended soil provide the drainage needed for long-term success in Gulf South clay soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Moonbeam is one of the most beloved and awarded garden perennials of the late 20th century — a Coreopsis verticillata cultivar that received the Perennial Plant of the Year award in 1992 and remains a gold standard for long-blooming, low-maintenance perennial gardens. The distinctive feature of 'Moonbeam' compared to other coreopsis is its unique pale primrose-yellow to cream-yellow flower color — softer and more subtle than the vivid golden-yellow of most coreopsis cultivars — combined with the fine-textured, thread-like foliage of C. verticillata that creates an airy, delicate visual mass very different from the coarser leaves of C. grandiflora and C. lanceolata. The extremely long bloom season — from early summer through frost with deadheading — and the soft yellow color that harmonizes with virtually every other garden color make Moonbeam one of the most versatile perennials for border combinations. It blooms most prolifically with lean soil and moderate drought stress — overly rich, moist conditions produce lush foliage and reduced bloom. In zone 9, Moonbeam performs best with afternoon shade protection during peak summer and requires well-drained soil to persist as a perennial rather than a short-lived annual-style planting.

plant_note: Start indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost after nicking or soaking seed; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Nick or soak seeds in warm water for 12 hours before sowing 1/2 in deep. Moonflower is a vigorous, fast-growing vine that needs a strong trellis or fence. Unlike morning glories, its large, fragrant white blossoms open in the evening and remain open through the night and into the following morning. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers to encourage blooming.

common_name: Moonflower Vine (Night-Blooming White-Flowered Annual Ipomoea Vine)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. In zone 9, plant March–April; moonflower is a tropical perennial in frost-free areas but grown as a fast annual. Provide sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence — vines reach 10–15 feet in one season. Moonflower's fragrant white flowers open in the evening and close by midmorning, making it the ideal choice for planting near outdoor seating areas or porches used in the evening. Excellent paired with Heavenly Blue morning glory (which opens in the morning when moonflower closes).
directions: Nick seed coat or soak overnight; direct sow 0.5 inch deep after last frost along a sturdy trellis or arbor. Moonflower Vine is the large-flowered night-blooming cousin of morning glory — a tropical Ipomoea species producing enormous (4–6 inch diameter) white, saucer-shaped flowers with a sweet, tropical fragrance that unfurl rapidly at dusk and remain open through the night until midmorning, when they close as morning glories open. The dramatic daily opening — moonflowers can be watched as the buds spirally unfurl in minutes at dusk — is one of the most theatrical performances in the plant world. The very large flowers are pure white, satiny, with a star-shaped pattern visible in the petals, and the heavy, sweet, tropical fragrance carries well on still evening air, perfuming the garden and attracting sphinx moths (hummingbird moths) that are primary pollinators. Moonflower is a fast-growing, robust vine (10–15 feet per season) that covers a standard garden arbor or pergola quickly. The combination of its dramatic evening show and fragrance makes moonflower ideal for planting near outdoor dining or seating areas — evening patio dinners become special when the moonflowers open at dusk around the pergola. In zone 9–10, moonflower is a short-lived perennial that may persist between mild winters.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Moonlight's chartreuse-to-cream coloration makes it one of the brightest caladiums for deep shade illumination.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Moonlight is a large-leaved, predominantly chartreuse to cream-white caladium with an unusual warm, yellow-green to near-white leaf color that creates one of the brightest and most luminous foliage effects of any fancy caladium cultivar. The warm, slightly yellow-tinged white-to-cream color differs from the pure, cool white of 'Candidum' — Moonlight has a warmer, softer quality that creates a glowing, moonlit effect particularly striking in the dim light of deep-shade garden areas at dusk and in low-light conditions. In brighter partial shade, the color is a vivid chartreuse-green that gradually lightens toward cream-white at the center of each leaf as temperatures rise through summer. The large leaf size and predominantly light-colored foliage maximize the light-reflective effect in shade positions — Moonlight is an outstanding choice for illuminating dark corners and brightening shaded foundation areas. The chartreuse-cream color contrasts beautifully with dark-foliaged companions like Black Magic elephant ear, 'Obsidian' heuchera, or dark ajuga groundcovers, creating a vivid light-dark foliage combination. Consistent moisture, humus-rich soil, and protection from direct afternoon sun produce the largest leaves and best color in Gulf South conditions.

common_name: Moonlight Scindapsus (Treub's Scindapsus, Dark Form Scindapsus, Satin Pothos Relative)
plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in well-drained, moist, chunky aroid mix with a moss pole, bark board, or rough surface to climb; Scindapsus treubii has two widely grown forms — 'Moonlight' (silver-green leaves with strong silver-white overlay) and 'Dark Form' (very deep, almost black-green leaves with subtle steel-blue iridescence). Both forms are highly sought collector aroids. The plant is closely related to Scindapsus pictus (Satin Pothos) but produces narrower, more elongated, distinctly different leaves. Keep warm (above 60°F) and provide consistent humidity. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, well-aerated aroid mix with a rough support to climb — Moonlight Scindapsus produces its most ornamental foliage in bright indirect to low light conditions and is an outstanding climbing shade vine for shaded indoor and outdoor tropical positions. Scindapsus treubii is a climbing, hemiepiphytic perennial aroid in the Araceae family native to Borneo, Java, and Southeast Asia — a member of the genus Scindapsus, which is closely related to but distinct from both Epipremnum (pothos) and Monstera, in the tribe Monstereae. The plant produces elongated, narrowly ovate leaves (4–6 inches long, distinctly narrow compared to S. pictus) on climbing stems that ascend with adhesive aerial roots. Two distinct leaf color forms have become highly popular in the collector aroid market: the 'Moonlight' form, which produces silver-green to pale sage-green leaves with a strong silver overlay that gives each leaf a luminous, silver-washed quality — and the 'Dark Form,' which produces leaves of a very deep, saturated dark forest-green to near-black, with a subtle, gunmetal blue-green iridescence in certain light. Both forms are striking and distinctly different from any common houseplant. The plant climbs readily when given a rough moss pole or bark board and develops larger, more lustrous leaves as it ascends. Moderately fast-growing in warm conditions. One of the most sought-after collector aroids of the past decade. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Divide established rhizome clumps in early spring before new growth emerges and replant at the same depth in moist, humus-rich soil; keep consistently moist through the first growing season.
directions: Moonseed is a deciduous, twining native vine of moist woodland edges, stream banks, and thicket margins throughout eastern North America, valued for its bold, broadly shield-shaped leaves and striking blue-black berries in fall. The crescent-shaped seed inside each berry inspired the common name and distinguishes it from the true wild grapes it resembles — the berries are highly toxic and must never be eaten. It spreads readily by underground rhizomes to form dense, colonizing patches, making it ideal for naturalizing moist, shaded slopes and stabilizing stream banks. Grow in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade; it tolerates periodic flooding and deep shade better than most native vines.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; Moonshine requires excellent drainage — it will not survive in heavy clay or wet soil, particularly during summer humidity in zone 9.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; Moonshine is the standard hybrid yellow yarrow cultivar — a cross between Achillea clypeolata and A. taygetea — producing large, flat-topped clusters of rich sulfur-yellow flowers from late spring through midsummer above finely cut, aromatic, silver-gray to gray-green, feathery foliage. The cool, muted sulfur-yellow flower color is softer and more refined than the golden-yellow of species yarrow, making Moonshine a superb mixer in the perennial border — it harmonizes with blue flowers (salvias, catmints), orange and coral tones, and white without the dominating brightness of brighter yellows. The silver-gray foliage is attractive even when the plant is not in flower. Moonshine was named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 1990, recognizing its outstanding landscape performance. Like all yarrows, it is extraordinarily drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant — performing best in lean, dry soils where many perennials struggle. The key limitation in zone 9 is summer humidity: yarrow is susceptible to crown rot and foliar diseases in hot, humid, wet conditions. In zone 9, excellent drainage and lean soil are essential; amended sandy or gravelly soils work better than clay. The dried flower heads are excellent for arrangements. Divide every 2–3 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the top third of the bulb above the soil surface in moist to consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; Moore's crinum is notable among crinums for its strong shade-tolerance — it grows naturally in the moist, shaded, coastal forests of the Eastern Cape. The long, distinctive neck on the bulb (to 12 inches or more in old plants) is a diagnostic feature. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs (upper third exposed) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; Moore's crinum is the most shade-tolerant of the commonly grown crinum species and one of the few large, summer-flowering bulbs that genuinely thrives in the deep, dry shade under large trees — making it exceptional value in the shade garden where bold summer flowers with tropical presence are difficult to achieve. The flowers are large, lily-like, pale to medium pink, funnel-shaped funnels opening to 4–5 inches across, borne in umbels of 5–10 on stout scapes, fragrant in the evening. Unlike many crinums that require full sun and hot conditions, Moore's crinum originates in the moist, shaded, humid coastal forest margins of the Eastern Cape where it grows with clivias and other shade-lovers. In the shade garden it provides a refreshingly bold, tropical-scale bulb plant for positions under tree canopy, combining naturally with hostas, clivias, and other shade perennials. The long, distinctive, elongated bulb neck — a diagnostic feature of the species, sometimes reaching 12 inches long in old specimens — should be left exposed above the soil when planting. One of the parent species of Crinum x powellii (with C. bulbispermum).

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; or nick and soak seed overnight then start indoors 2–4 weeks early.
directions: Nick the hard seed coat with a file or soak in warm water for 8–12 hours before sowing 1/2 in deep to speed germination. Morning glories need a fence, trellis, or other support and are best sown directly at the base of their support. Avoid over-fertilizing, which promotes leaves at the expense of flowers. Blooms open in the morning and close by afternoon on each individual day.

plant_note: Nick seed coat with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing directly in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil after last frost; do not start indoors as tap root is damaged by transplanting.
directions: Nick seed coat with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing directly in well-drained, poor to average, neutral soil after last frost; do not start indoors as tap root is damaged by transplanting. Ipomoea tricolor is the parent of the famous 'Heavenly Blue' morning glory, a fast-growing annual twining vine with heart-shaped leaves and large (3–4 inch), funnel-shaped flowers that open a vivid sky-blue or blue-violet each morning and fade to pink-purple by afternoon — one of the most startling and beautiful morning colors in the annual garden. Provide a trellis, fence, or other support to 8–12 feet; it will naturally scramble up any available structure. The seeds contain lysergic acid amides and are mildly toxic if eaten in quantity. Morning glories bloom most prolifically in lean, dry soil with minimal fertilization; rich soil produces excessive foliage.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Morning Light performs best in full sun — adequate moisture is important during summer in zone 9, where extended drought combined with reflected heat can stress plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Morning Light is widely considered one of the most elegant ornamental grasses available — a refined, fine-textured miscanthus producing very narrow (one-eighth-inch wide) blades edged with a thin white margin that gives the entire plant a silvery-white luminous quality, almost as if the plant is lit from within. The effect is subtle but beautiful: from a distance, the plant appears silver-white; close up, each blade shows a green center stripe and cream-white margins. The narrow, refined foliage and compact, vase-shaped habit reach 4–6 feet, substantially smaller than the larger maiden grass selections. In late summer and fall, feathery, copper-pink plumes emerge above the foliage and last well into winter. Morning Light is notable among miscanthus for being sterile or low-seed-producing in most conditions, which reduces the invasive spread concern that affects some miscanthus selections in the Southeast. In zone 9, flowering typically occurs in September–October; the plant grows as an evergreen or semi-evergreen, requiring cutting back in late winter. An outstanding specimen or mass-planting grass for full-sun locations where its distinctive silver-white effect can be appreciated.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (September–October in zone 9) for winter and spring bloom, or in earliest spring; Moroccan toadflax is a cool-season annual that must bloom before summer heat arrives — it performs best sown in fall in mild-winter climates and in very early spring in colder regions.
