directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface in fall or very early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; press in lightly and keep moist — seeds need light to germinate. Linaria maroccana (Moroccan toadflax) is a slender, delicate, cool-season annual producing miniature snapdragon-like flowers just 1/2 to 3/4 inch long with a small spur on dense, upright spikes in an exceptional range of colors — violet, pink, red, orange, yellow, white, and bicolor — all with a yellow or orange eye that gives the flowers a jewel-like quality at close range. The extremely fine, thread-like foliage is nearly invisible under the mass of flowers. 'Fairy Bouquet' is the classic mixed-color strain; 'Northern Lights' has larger flowers; 'Fantasy' is dwarf (8–9 inches). Moroccan toadflax self-seeds freely in suitable gardens and can naturalize in rock gardens and gravel paths. In zone 9, fall-sown plants bloom from December through March — providing cool-season color when few annuals are in bloom. It is outstanding combined with poppies, larkspur, and bachelor buttons in cool-season cutting gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; golden featherflower is one of the most difficult of all Western Australian natives to cultivate outside its native habitat — it requires perfect drainage, lean soil, and the precise conditions of the sandy coastal plains of the Perth area. Grafted plants on Darwinia or Calytrix rootstocks have improved success. It is the floral emblem of Western Australia's capital region. Not for beginners; a challenge-and-reward plant for dedicated native plant enthusiasts.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; golden featherflower is one of the most spectacular of all the Australian native shrubs in bloom — a Western Australian coastal heath specialist from the sandy coastal plains around Perth (where it is so abundant in spring that it colors whole hillsides brilliant yellow-gold, and is the informal floral symbol of the Perth region) that produces in late winter and spring an astonishing, total-coverage, smothering mass of tiny (0.5 inch), yellow to orange-yellow, feathery-edged flowers covering every stem and twig of the plant in a dense, almost furry, golden-yellow coating. The 'feather' texture of the flowers — each individual flower with finely fringed, feathery-textured petals — gives the genus its common name (Verticordia, meaning 'turning hearts', is sometimes called the featherflower genus), and the density of the yellow flowers on a mature plant in full bloom creates an effect like a shrub dipped in gold or covered in bright-yellow powder. It is considered one of the most spectacular and beautiful spring-flowering shrubs of Australia's west coast. The difficulty of cultivation outside its native sandy coastal habitat is well known — it is considered one of the 'holy grail' plants of Australian horticulture, requiring very specific conditions.

common_name: Mosaica Copper Plant (Multi-Color Tropical Foliage Shrub for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mosaica develops the most vivid multi-color leaf patterning in full sun — partial shade produces larger leaves but significantly reduces the intensity and complexity of the copper, red, orange, and yellow mosaic color pattern.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mosaica is a cultivar of Acalypha wilkesiana (copper leaf, copperleaf, Jacob's coat) — a tropical shrub from the Pacific Islands grown primarily as a foliage plant for the extraordinary multi-color patterning of its large, broad leaves. The 'Mosaica' cultivar produces leaves with a complex, patchwork mosaic of copper, red-orange, bronze, gold-yellow, and reddish-purple tones — different colors appearing as irregular patches, blotches, and streaks across each leaf surface, creating a richly complex pattern that is genuinely different from plant to plant. The result in full sun is one of the most vivid and complex foliage colors available in a commonly grown landscape plant: a tropical tapestry of warm colors that creates intense visual interest in mixed subtropical plantings. Acalypha wilkesiana grows rapidly in Gulf South summer heat, reaching 4–6 feet in a single growing season when planted in warm soil with adequate nutrition. The inconspicuous catkin-type flowers are secondary to the foliage display. In zone 10–12, copper leaf is an evergreen perennial shrub. In zone 9, it grows as a warm-season annual — planted after the last frost and growing rapidly through summer and fall until frost kills it. The rapid growth and striking color make it one of the most effective single-season tropical foliage plants for Gulf South summer borders and container combinations.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings after flowering or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; moss phlox requires excellent drainage and rots in wet soil. Shear or cut back by one-third after flowering to maintain compact mounded form and prevent the center from dying out — this keeps plants attractive and full for many years.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; moss phlox is one of the most spectacular spring-blooming groundcovers in temperate gardens, native to rocky outcrops, sandy barrens, and thin-soiled slopes of eastern North America and covering itself so completely with flowers in April and May that the foliage is entirely hidden — creating a solid carpet of color, typically in shades of pink, white, lavender, or red-purple depending on cultivar. The plant itself is a dense, needle-leaved, semi-evergreen mat barely 4–6 inches tall that cascades beautifully over walls, slopes, and rock garden edges and provides attractive dark-green foliage texture through the rest of the season. After the spectacular spring bloom, trim it back by one-third to maintain dense, compact growth and prevent the center from opening up. Extremely drought-tolerant and cold-hardy once established, and among the few groundcovers that holds its own on steep, dry slopes where nothing else will establish. The cultivar range is enormous — 'Emerald Blue,' 'Candy Stripe,' 'Fort Hill,' 'Scarlet Flame,' and many others offer colors from pure white through pink to deep rose and lavender-blue.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost (seeds need light — do not cover) or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; portulaca demands dry, poor, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and will rot in heavy, moist, fertile conditions — this is the annual for the hot, dry, rocky spots where nothing else will grow.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface after last frost (seeds need light — do not cover) or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; portulaca demands dry, poor, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and will rot in heavy, moist, fertile conditions — this is the annual for the hot, dry, rocky spots where nothing else will grow. Portulaca grandiflora is a prostrate, succulent annual adapted to hot, dry, sandy conditions that makes a spectacular low groundcover with bright green, needle-like leaves and a profusion of large (1–2 inch), tissue-paper-textured, cup-shaped flowers in vivid shades of red, magenta, orange, yellow, and white; flowers are single-day bloomers that open in full sun and close at night or in cloudy weather. It is virtually indestructible in the heat, requires essentially no water once established, is perfect for hot pavement cracks, dry slopes, and rock gardens, and provides important nectar for specialist Portulaca-visiting native bees. Modern double-flowered varieties stay open longer through the day.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Moss Verbena is a sprawling, low-growing perennial (annual in zones 6–7, short-lived perennial in zones 8–10) with finely dissected, moss-like foliage and continuous lavender-purple flowers from spring through frost — it is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and weed-suppressing ground cover plants for sunny dry areas in the Gulf South.
directions: Sow directly or use transplants in full sun; Moss Verbena requires excellent drainage — it thrives in sandy, rocky, or poor soils and dies in heavy clay that stays wet; once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and self-sows freely in warm climates; shear lightly after peak bloom to encourage fresh new growth. Moss Verbena (Verbena tenuisecta) is a sprawling, mat-forming wildflower native to South America but thoroughly naturalized throughout the Gulf South states and Texas, where it has spread along roadsides, rocky disturbed areas, and dry meadows to become one of the most common and beloved wildflowers in the region. The finely dissected, pinnately cut leaves have a delicate, moss-like or fern-like appearance that is distinctly different from the large, lobed leaves of garden verbena; this distinctive leaf texture gives the plant its 'Moss Verbena' name. The small lavender to purple flowers (occasionally white in some populations) are produced in dense clusters at the stem tips from spring through fall, virtually non-stop in warm climates — one of the longest bloom periods of any flowering plant. Moss Verbena is exceptional as a low-maintenance ground cover for dry, sunny areas in zones 8–11 where it spreads by stolons and self-sowing to cover bare ground, suppresses weeds by smothering, and provides continuous bloom with virtually no care. Heavily used by native bees and butterflies as a nectar source. Zone 9a gardens (Chester's area) experience Moss Verbena as a perennial that may die back partially in cold winters but regrows from the base or self-sows prolifically.

common_name: Moth Orchid (Moon Orchid, Amabilis Phalaenopsis, White Moth Orchid)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in zone 9; Phalaenopsis amabilis cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Grow in slatted orchid pots or clear plastic pots in coarse orchid bark media with excellent drainage. Water thoroughly once or twice per week, allowing the media to dry partially between waterings. A brief 2–4 week period of cooler nights (55–65°F) in fall stimulates flower spike initiation. Never remove a green flower spike — reblooming occurs from side branches. Repot every 1–2 years when the bark has decomposed. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Moth Orchid prefers the bright indirect light of an east or shaded south window (direct sun burns the thick leaves) and will rarely rebloom in genuinely dim conditions. Phalaenopsis amabilis is a large, monopodial epiphytic orchid native to the tropical islands of Southeast Asia and northwestern Australia (Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, the Moluccas, and Queensland), discovered in 1750 by Georg Eberhard Rumphius and named 'amabilis' (lovely) for its extraordinary flowers. The species is the primary ancestor of virtually the entire modern commercial Phalaenopsis hybrid industry — the enormous, flat, moth-shaped flowers with rounded sepals and petals, pure white with yellow and red markings at the lip, and the elegant arching stems bearing 10–20 or more flowers simultaneously, established the floral template that modern breeders have reproduced and amplified across thousands of hybrid cultivars. The commercial Phalaenopsis orchids sold at every supermarket, garden center, and box store worldwide are overwhelmingly hybrids in which P. amabilis is a primary parent — the single most economically significant orchid species in global horticulture. The flowers last 2–4 months on the plant and are among the longest-lasting of any floral display. Genuinely non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; dislikes transplanting.
directions: Surface sow the fine seed directly in early spring or fall, as poppies need light to germinate and resent root disturbance. This blend glows in soft shades of pink, white, and purple with crepe-paper petals and contrasting dark centers. Low-maintenance and drought-tolerant, it is stunning massed along borders and self-sows to return each year. Thin seedlings to give plants room.

common_name: Mother-in-law Tongue (Dracaena Snake Plant, Bowstring Hemp)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to full shade; Dracaena trifasciata (the current accepted name for snake plant) grows outdoors year-round only in frost-free zones 10–12 but is widely grown as a houseplant in all zones.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in any light condition; Dracaena trifasciata survives in deep shade but grows more slowly and maintains better leaf color with moderate indirect light. Dracaena trifasciata is the current taxonomically accepted name for the plant long known as Sansevieria trifasciata (which see for the full cultural description); the transfer from Sansevieria to Dracaena was proposed in 2017 based on molecular phylogenetic studies showing that the two genera are not distinct. Garden centers and nurseries continue to sell plants labeled under both names, and both are correct in common usage. The plant is a West African native producing stiffly upright, sword-shaped, succulent-textured leaves with horizontal dark-and-light green banding and often yellow or cream leaf margins. In zones 10–12, it grows outdoors in subtropical and tropical landscapes as a clump-forming ground layer plant; in cooler zones it is one of the most popular and low-maintenance houseplants worldwide. The fiber from the leaves (historical source of the common name 'bowstring hemp') was once used to make rope and bowstrings in West Africa.

plant_note: Plant clump divisions in early spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in deep to partial shade; Mottled Wild Ginger is slow-growing and long-lived. Maintain consistent moisture until established, then reduce watering as the plant is drought-tolerant in deep shade once its root system is developed.
directions: Mottled Wild Ginger is a beautiful native evergreen ground cover of the southern Appalachians and upper coastal plain, producing low mounds of heart-shaped, leathery leaves decorated with silver and pale green mottling against dark green — one of the most ornamentally spectacular native shade plants of the southeastern United States. Unlike the more northern Asarum canadense, which is deciduous, Mottled Wild Ginger retains its attractively patterned foliage through winter and forms a weed-suppressing carpet in dry to moist shade where few other plants grow reliably year-round. The curious, urn-shaped brownish-purple flowers are produced near the soil surface in late spring, hidden beneath the foliage where they are pollinated primarily by ground beetles and ants attracted to their earthy fragrance. Plant divisions in spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in deep to partial shade; plants spread very slowly but are virtually permanent once established, gradually forming dense colonies that suppress weeds under deciduous trees.

common_name: Moulin Rouge Sunflower (Deep Red Pollen-Free Cut Flower Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; for succession harvests, sow every 2–3 weeks through summer. Moulin Rouge is a pollen-free variety, making it exceptional for cut flower arrangements — no pollen drop on tablecloths or clothing. For cut flower production, harvest when the outer ring of petals has fully unfurled but the center disk is still compact and not yet shedding pollen. In zone 9, it can be sown in fall for winter blooms.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches apart for best stem quality and branching. Moulin Rouge is a premium cut flower sunflower developed and popularized by Johnny's Selected Seeds that produces fully double or semi-double flowers in an exceptionally deep, saturated burgundy-red to mahogany-maroon color — the deepest red available among annual sunflowers and a dramatic departure from the yellow, gold, and orange tones that dominate the sunflower palette. The name references the famous Parisian cabaret's signature deep red aesthetic. The deep color is most intense at cool temperatures and when harvested just as the petals fully open; heat and full sun through summer can lighten the red to more orange-red tones, while spring and fall production in cooler conditions maintains the darkest burgundy shades. Moulin Rouge is pollen-free — an important trait for cut flower arrangements, as pollen-producing sunflowers drop yellow pollen onto table linens, furniture, and clothing during vase life. The branching habit produces multiple flowers per plant over an extended summer season when succession-planted. An outstanding specialty cut flower that provides a uniquely dark, dramatic color for flower arrangements and one of the most requested sunflower varieties by florists who want alternatives to the standard yellow.

common_name: Mound Lily Yucca (Spanish Dagger, Glorious Yucca, Soft-Tipped Yucca)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; Yucca gloriosa is native to the southeastern coastal plain from North Carolina to Florida and west through the Gulf Coast, where it grows in dunes, sandy maritime forests, and coastal scrub — one of the most architectural ornamental yuccas for large-scale landscaping in zone 6–10 gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in excellent drainage; Mound Lily Yucca is larger than most garden yuccas and eventually forms a multi-stemmed shrub 5–10 feet tall; remove spent flower spikes after bloom; the species is slower-suckering than many yuccas and generally stays as a single or few-stemmed specimen for many years. Mound Lily Yucca is a large, architecturally bold native yucca of the southeastern United States coastal plain — one of the signature plants of the Atlantic and Gulf Coast dune systems, where it stabilizes sandy soils and provides year-round structural interest with its dramatic rosettes of broad, blue-green leaves. Unlike most garden yuccas, Yucca gloriosa grows to significant size over time, eventually developing a thick woody trunk or multi-stemmed shrub to 5–8 feet (sometimes 10 feet), with large rosettes of stiff, 2–3 foot leaves at the branch tips — creating a palm-like or tree-like silhouette unlike the low ground-hugging form of Yucca filamentosa. The common name 'Spanish Dagger' refers to the stiff, somewhat flexible leaf tip: while sharp, it is softer and less needle-like than the truly dangerous Y. aloifolia (Spanish Bayonet), making Mound Lily Yucca a somewhat safer choice for garden settings near walkways and play areas — though still requiring care. The dramatic 4–6 foot flower spike bearing hundreds of creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers appears in late summer to fall, creating one of the most spectacular flowering events of the late-season garden; the flowers are both edible and attractive to moths that pollinate them at night. Widely used in coastal landscape design for its salt tolerance and sandy-soil adaptation.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain allium is a compact, early-blooming ornamental allium ideal for rock gardens and border fronts. It blooms in late spring (May–June), earlier than the large hybrid alliums, with open, lax umbels of bright, deep-rose-pink star-shaped flowers. It increases by offsets and seeds to form small clumps. Mild garlic scent when foliage is crushed.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain allium is a compact, low-growing allium from the mountain meadows of Central Asia — Turkey, the Caucasus, and Central Asia — that offers one of the most intense, saturated pink-rose flower colors in the ornamental allium range on a plant small enough for the rock garden, border front, or naturalizing in thin, stony turf. The flowers are borne in late spring in rather open, lax, flat-headed umbels of 6–20 individual, six-petaled, starry flowers in a clear, deep magenta-rose to carmine-pink, the petals with a slightly darker central midrib, creating small open umbels of vivid, concentrated pink color on 8–12 inch stems above two narrow, channeled, grass-like leaves. Unlike the large hybrid alliums, the flower head is open and non-spherical, giving it a more informal, naturalistic appearance suited to wild-flower style or rock garden plantings. It blooms before the tall hybrid alliums, filling the late spring bulb gap between the main daffodil-tulip season and the early summer perennial season. Outstanding in combination with Allium hollandicum and later alliums for an extended ornamental allium succession.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring or plant divisions in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain alyssum is drought-tolerant and thrives in hot, dry rock gardens and on sunny, exposed banks.
directions: Sow direct in spring in very well-drained, lean, gritty, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mountain alyssum is intolerant of shade and wet soil — it is a plant of hot, dry, rocky habitats and thrives on neglect and poor soil. Alyssum montanum is a low, mat-forming European perennial alyssum (not to be confused with the annual sweet alyssum, Lobularia maritima) with gray-green, densely hairy leaves and bright-yellow, honey-scented, 4-petaled flowers in dense, rounded clusters in early to mid-spring; the honey fragrance is less pronounced than sweet alyssum but still pleasant. It forms attractive, low mats on dry, rocky banks, in rock gardens, between paving stones, and on dry walls; it is drought-tolerant, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free in appropriate conditions. More compact and lower-growing than gold dust alyssum (A. saxatile/Aurinia saxatilis).

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into gritty, well-drained soil; seeds require cold stratification over winter to germinate in spring. Thin seedlings to final spacing once established.
directions: Direct sow seed in fall into sharply drained, gritty or rocky soil that mimics its alpine home. Cold stratification through winter breaks dormancy naturally, and seedlings emerge in spring once temperatures moderate. This compact perennial prefers cool summers and excellent drainage; it performs best in rock gardens, troughs, or the front of a cool-climate border. Allow the attractive feathery seed heads to develop after the golden flowers fade for continued ornamental interest.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Mountain Camellia is somewhat easier to establish than Silky Camellia (Stewartia malacodendron) and more cold-hardy; avoid waterlogged or alkaline soils.
directions: Mountain Camellia is a striking native understory shrub or small tree, native to rich, moist, wooded slopes, ravine walls, and stream terraces in the southern Appalachians from Virginia and Kentucky south to Georgia and Alabama, blooming in July and August with large, white, five-petaled flowers bearing a prominent cluster of orange-tipped stamens. Larger than Silky Camellia (Stewartia malacodendron) and more cold-hardy (to zone 5), Mountain Camellia blooms later in summer when few other native shrubs are flowering, extending ornamental interest deep into the season. The smooth, exfoliating gray bark provides attractive winter interest, and the foliage turns shades of orange and red in fall. Grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — it is somewhat more tolerant of garden conditions than Silky Camellia and establishes more readily from nursery transplants, though it is still slow-growing and long-lived.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or direct-sow in fall; mountain cornflower spreads by underground rhizomes and self-sows freely — it can be invasive in some regions and should be deadheaded before seeds ripen to limit spread. After the main late-spring flush, shear plants back hard to encourage a fresh crop of foliage and often a second flush of bloom in late summer.
directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; mountain cornflower is the perennial version of the annual bachelor's button — a stout, spreading perennial from European mountain meadows producing large (2–3 inch), spidery, brilliant violet-blue to deep blue-violet cornflower heads with deeper violet centers and contrasting purplish-maroon outer florets, displayed on upright stems above soft, gray-green, woolly foliage from late spring through early summer with a possible second flush in late summer if cut back hard after the first flowering. The cobalt-blue and violet tones are among the truest and most saturated blues available in early-summer perennials, and the large, spidery flower heads have a more romantic, wildflower quality than the more refined blue of delphiniums. White ('Alba'), pink ('Carnea'), and bicolor cultivars exist but the species violet-blue is generally considered the most ornamental. Spreads vigorously and is potentially aggressive in fertile soils; more restrained in lean, dry conditions. Self-sows freely and can naturalize rapidly — an asset in a wildflower garden, a management concern in a formal border.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; mountain death camas requires good winter cold and is best suited to northern regions and mountain elevations.
directions: Anticlea elegans (formerly Zigadenus elegans, white camas) is a graceful bulbous perennial native to moist mountain meadows, subalpine slopes, and streambanks across western and central North America from Alaska to New Mexico, producing a basal cluster of narrow, grass-like leaves and an erect stem in summer bearing a loose raceme of saucer-shaped, creamy white to greenish-white flowers with distinctive greenish glands at the petal bases. Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; the plant requires good winter cold and is best suited to northern regions and mountain elevations. All parts of the plant are highly toxic — it is closely related to and easily confused with edible camas (Camassia), so never harvest from mixed populations without expert identification. An elegant addition to a native wildflower garden in cool climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; mountain devil requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer (like all Proteaceae). It is a slow-growing shrub with unusual, distinctively shaped seed pods — woody follicles with prominent curved, curved horns at the opening — that have given it the common name 'mountain devil' for the devil-like horned silhouette of the pods. The scarlet, tubular flowers bloom intermittently throughout the year in mild climates.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; mountain devil is an Eastern Australian Proteaceae shrub of the Sydney sandstone heathlands that has become well-known for a botanical curiosity: the woody seed pods, when mature and dried, have a distinctive shape with two prominent, curved, tusk-like horns projecting from the opening of each follicle — the overall silhouette of the pod resembling a tiny devil or horned face, giving the plant its memorable and accurate common name. These distinctive horned seed pods have made mountain devil a popular dried-floral material in Australia; the pods are collected, sometimes dyed, and used in wreaths and arrangements. In the garden it is also a rewarding ornamental plant producing throughout the year (most heavily in late winter and spring) terminal clusters of 7 tubular, scarlet-red flowers with prominent, recurving, scarlet petals — vivid, hummingbird-attracting flowers of considerable color impact. Like all Proteaceae it requires excellent drainage and no phosphorus fertilizer. The combination of attractive red flowers and the remarkable, collectible, horned seed pods makes it a plant of multiple ornamental seasons.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into gritty, acidic, rocky or sandy soil in a cool, partially shaded rock garden setting; cold stratification over winter is highly beneficial, and seeds should not be buried — surface sow and firm gently into the growing medium.
directions: Mountain Dwarf Dandelion is a rare endemic native perennial restricted to high mountain rocky summits, cliff faces, and seepage slopes in the southern Appalachians of North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee — far more cold-adapted and persistently perennial than the other species in this small genus. Plants produce slender, leafless scapes topped with solitary, bright golden-yellow dandelion-like flower heads that open in summer above neat basal rosettes of narrow leaves. Grow in cool, well-drained to moist, rocky or sandy, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — conditions that mimic its native mountain seep and rocky outcrop habitats. This species is an exceptional choice for alpine troughs, crevice gardens, and rock garden settings in the upper South but is not suited to hot, humid lowland gardens where summer heat and poor drainage will be fatal.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; mountain fleece is exceptionally adaptable and performs in a wide range of conditions from full sun to quite deep partial shade.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately dry, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mountain fleece (red bistort) is a Himalayan perennial that has become one of the most celebrated and widely grown border perennials in European gardens for its extraordinary five-month flowering period — from late June through November it produces an uninterrupted succession of small, upright, bottle-brush-like flower spikes of rich, deep crimson-red, rosy-red, or white on compact, well-foliaged plants, outperforming most border perennials in duration of bloom by a considerable margin. The plant forms a well-behaved, non-spreading clump of large, heart-shaped leaves that provide an attractive foliage mass independent of the flowers. It tolerates partial shade well, maintaining its blooming performance in dappled light where many full-sun perennials would fail to flower. 'Firetail' (deep crimson-red), 'Golden Arrow' (gold-variegated leaves), 'Album' (white), and 'Inverleith' (compact, dark red) are widely grown cultivars. The flower spikes are attractive to bumblebees throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall after scarifying and cold-stratifying seeds; plant in well-drained soil in full sun and allow natural winter conditions to complete stratification.
directions: Mountain Golden Banner is a showy, robust native perennial in the pea family, producing stout leafy stems with trifoliate lupine-like leaves and dense upright racemes of bright golden-yellow pea flowers in May and June — one of the most striking yellow wildflowers of the Rocky Mountain landscape. It is native to mountain meadows, open slopes, and forest clearings from Montana to New Mexico, spreading by rhizomes to form large, persistent colonies over time. Direct sow in fall after scarifying and cold-stratifying seeds, in well-drained soil in full sun; seeds may take one to two seasons to germinate and plants typically reach first bloom in their second year. This species is intolerant of summer heat and humidity and is not suited to gardens south or east of USDA zone 7, making it ideal for Rocky Mountain and intermountain western gardens.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, deep, humus-rich, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; mountain hemlock grows naturally at subalpine elevations (5,000–11,000 feet) along the Pacific Crest from Alaska to California, requiring cold winters and cool, moist summers. Does not tolerate heat, drought, or alkaline soils.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, deep, humus-rich, rocky or sandy soil in partial shade; mountain hemlock is the most cold-hardy and highest-elevation hemlock of the Pacific Coast — a distinctive subalpine conifer that grows from sea level in Alaska to treeline at 11,000 feet in the Sierra Nevada, forming the picturesque, wind-sculpted, krummholz (twisted) forms near treeline that are among the most iconic images of the high Sierra and Cascades. Unlike eastern hemlock, the needles of mountain hemlock radiate in all directions around the branchlet (like a bottlebrush) rather than lying flat in two rows — an immediately distinctive feature. The cones are proportionally larger than other hemlocks. Mountain hemlock forms pure open groves and mixes with whitebark pine, lodgepole pine, and subalpine fir at the highest tree-elevation zones. In gardens in cool, moist Pacific Northwest lowlands, it makes an outstanding ornamental specimen — more tolerant of cultivation than most subalpine conifers because the lowland maritime climate roughly mimics the cool, moist conditions it prefers.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring as the shoots emerge; mountain hosta is one of the largest-growing Hosta species, eventually forming very large clumps in appropriate conditions. Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; mountain hosta is one of the largest species hostas, producing enormous, glossy, rich green, slightly corrugated leaves that can exceed 14 inches in length on nature plants. The species grows naturally at high elevations in Japan on moist, shaded mountain slopes. In the garden, it forms a bold, weed-suppressing mound with a strongly architectural presence. Large white flowers on tall scapes in late summer. The cultivar 'Aureomarginata' features bold yellow to cream margins on the large leaves, creating a dramatic variegated effect. A species of great horticultural importance as a parent of many large-leaved hosta cultivars. In zone 9, mulch well and ensure consistent moisture through the summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; mountain hydrangea is significantly more shade and heat tolerant than the common bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla) and is the better choice for zone 7–9 shaded garden conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade — mountain hydrangea from the mountains of Korea and Japan is a smaller, more elegant, and significantly more shade and heat tolerant cousin of the common bigleaf hydrangea (H. macrophylla), producing delicate, lace-cap or mophead flower clusters in blue, pink, or white (depending on soil pH and cultivar) in summer on compact, upright shrubs. It is more reliably heat tolerant than bigleaf hydrangea and flowers more consistently in zone 7–9 warm-climate gardens. Like bigleaf hydrangea, flower color shifts between blue and pink based on soil pH (blue in acidic soil, pink in alkaline) and is adjusted with aluminum sulfate applications. Outstanding cultivars include 'Blue Billow' (lacecap, blue), 'Preziosa' (mophead, pink aging to deep rose), and 'Tuff Stuff' (remontant). Its modest size makes it more practical than bigleaf hydrangea in smaller gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in rocky, lean, well-drained, dry to slightly moist soil in full sun; self-sows freely in open ground and adapts to both serpentine and non-serpentine soils.
directions: Mountain Jewel Flower is one of California's most architecturally distinctive native wildflowers, producing erect stems clothed in clasping, ear-lobed leaves that are perfoliate at the base, topped with a raceme of inflated, urn-shaped calyces enclosing purple to cream-white petals that emerge only partially from the swollen sepals — a flower form utterly unlike typical mustard blooms that gives the plant an alien, jewel-like beauty. It is native to dry, rocky mountain slopes, chaparral openings, and serpentine barrens across much of California, and is one of the few wildflowers able to thrive on harsh, heavy-metal-rich serpentine soils. Specialist native bees in the genera Eucera and Anthophora are important pollinators, and some bee species have evolved to specialize exclusively on Streptanthus pollen. Direct sow in fall in rocky, lean, well-drained, dry to slightly moist soil in full sun; plants self-sow reliably in open, gritty ground and are a striking and unusual choice for California native and serpentine garden plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in acid, well-drained, humus-rich soil; mountain laurel requires soil pH of 4.5–5.5 and excellent drainage — soggy soils are fatal. Amend with peat moss or pine bark. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain moisture and acidity. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, avoiding afternoon sun in hot climates; mountain laurel is the state flower of Connecticut and Pennsylvania and arguably the most spectacular native flowering shrub in the eastern United States, producing dense clusters (corymbs) of intricate, bowl-shaped flowers in white, pink, deep pink, red, or bicolored patterns with contrasting star-like markings in late spring — each bud is geometrically folded like an origami flower before opening. The evergreen, lance-shaped leaves provide year-round interest and the gnarled, multi-stem growth habit becomes increasingly sculptural with age. It thrives in the dappled shade of pine and oak forests and is essential to the native woodland garden. Over 80 named cultivars offer great variation in flower color and plant size from dwarf (2 feet) to large (12 feet). All plant parts contain grayanotoxins and are toxic to humans and livestock.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or cold-stratify seeds 3-4 months in the refrigerator and sow in early spring. Mountain maple grows naturally in cool, moist, rocky woodland soils in deep shade.
directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mountain maple is the most shade-tolerant native maple in eastern North America, naturally growing as a small understory tree or large shrub in the deep shade of mixed northern hardwood forests, along rocky mountain streams, and on cool north-facing slopes. The upright flower spikes (distinctive among maples) appear in June after the leaves unfurl. Fall color is outstanding — brilliant scarlet and orange. This is an excellent choice for naturalizing in shaded woodland gardens in cooler climates and is critically important as winter food for moose, who browse the twigs and bark. Not heat-tolerant; best in zones 2-6 where summers stay cool.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring or fall in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mountain phlox is a cool-season annual that performs best before summer heat arrives — time sowing for the cool season in your climate. It does not transplant well; always sow in place. In mild-winter climates (zones 8b–10) fall sowing for winter and spring bloom is ideal.
directions: Direct sow seeds in cool weather in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain phlox is a California native annual of the coastal hills and chaparral that, despite the common name 'mountain phlox,' is unrelated to true phlox — belonging instead to the Polemoniaceae family alongside gilia and cobaea. It produces upright, wiry stems with narrow, divided leaves and large (for its plant size), five-petaled, funnel-shaped flowers in pure white to soft lavender-pink that strongly resemble phlox flowers, opening in the morning and fading by evening, with a faint, sweet fragrance. In mass, it creates a delicate, fresh display of white to pale-pink flowers in spring. The simple, clean, somewhat translucent flower petals have a papery, refined quality that rewards close examination. Outstanding in California native wildflower meadow mixes, cottage garden edges, and as a cool-season filler in dry, sunny gardens before summer annuals take over. Self-sows modestly in appropriate conditions to maintain colonies in mild climates.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 4.5–6.0) soil in part shade; mountain pieris is a native Appalachian shrub for the upper South and is more cold-hardy and less heat-tolerant than its Japanese cousin (P. japonica) — best in zone 9 in morning sun with afternoon shade.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, strongly to moderately acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), well-drained soil in part shade; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity; avoid hot, dry, alkaline conditions. Pieris floribunda (mountain pieris or mountain fetterbush) is a native evergreen shrub of the high Appalachian Mountains of Virginia through Georgia — the North American counterpart to the widely grown Japanese pieris (P. japonica) — producing upright clusters (panicles) of small, white, urn-shaped flowers in March–April at the branch tips, with the characteristic red-to-bronze new growth that distinguishes the genus. Unlike the pendulous flower clusters of Japanese pieris, P. floribunda produces erect, branching flower panicles. The shrub is more compact and slower-growing than Japanese pieris, reaching 2–6 feet in maturity, and is somewhat more tolerant of deer browse. It is an excellent native alternative to P. japonica for acidic-soil woodland and shade gardens in the upper and mid-South. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — it is one of the classic poisonous woodland shrubs of the southern Appalachians. Note: in the lower South and zone 9, Japanese pieris (P. japonica) typically performs better in the heat.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer, or plant container-grown shrubs in spring; mountain sage blooms in fall when photoperiod shortens and is at its peak in October and November when hummingbirds are migrating through Texas and the Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in partial shade to full sun; mountain sage is a large-leafed, shrubby Texas native salvia that lights up in fall with brilliant scarlet-orange tubular flowers precisely when migrating ruby-throated hummingbirds need fuel for their journey to Central America. The flowers are spectacularly hummingbird-attractive and among the showiest of all the fall-blooming salvias. In zones 9–11 it grows as a large, dense evergreen shrub 4–6 feet tall; in zone 8 it is killed to the ground by frost but typically regrows from the roots in spring. It tolerates the dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the Chihuahuan Desert and Hill Country, making it excellent for xeric Gulf Coast gardens with poor, calcareous soil.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer under mist or plant container-grown specimens in moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; mountain silverbell grows naturally as an understory and sub-canopy tree in the southern Appalachian forests and is one of the finest shade-tolerant flowering trees available for eastern North American gardens.
directions: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; mountain silverbell is a large native deciduous tree of the southern Appalachian mountains that produces a spectacularly beautiful spring flower display in April and May, when the entire canopy becomes hung with thousands of small, nodding, pure-white, bell-shaped flowers that dangle in rows from the undersides of the leafing branches, backlit by new green leaves, creating one of the most delicate and ethereal spring effects of any native tree. The flowers are followed by decorative, four-winged, green to tan seed pods that persist through winter. In autumn the foliage turns clear yellow. Mountain silverbell grows naturally as a sub-canopy forest tree and is among the most shade-tolerant of all flowering trees — making it the ideal choice for planting under or alongside taller oaks, maples, and tulip poplars where most flowering trees would fail to bloom. The related Carolina silverbell (Halesia carolina) is similar but smaller; the mountain form (H. monticola, sometimes treated as H. tetraptera var. monticola) is the larger and more tree-like form. An outstanding native tree for the naturalistic woodland garden.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early fall once flowering is fully complete, keeping divisions small — one to three rosettes each — and replanting immediately at the original depth. Use a humus-rich, gritty, well-drained soil mix and firm in gently. Water in well and protect from prolonged winter wet.
directions: Mountain snowbell is slightly more adaptable to lowland conditions than alpine snowbell but still requires cool summers, excellent drainage, and consistent moisture through the growing season. Plant in dappled or partial shade in a rock garden, raised bed, or trough using a mix of loam, leaf mold, and coarse grit. Divide clumps every few years in fall after the foliage dies back, immediately replanting divisions in fresh, enriched mix. The leathery, overwintering leaves are sensitive to crown rot, so avoid mulching directly over the crown and ensure water drains freely away from the plant.

plant_note: Tuck nursery transplants into crevices of acidic rock (sandstone or granite preferred, not limestone) in a shaded to partially shaded rock garden, with excellent drainage and consistent humidity. Mountain Spleenwort is challenging to grow outside of natural rock environments and performs best when the root zone is sheltered within a tight rock crevice.
directions: Mountain Spleenwort is a small, neat, evergreen native fern, native to the shaded, acidic rock outcrops, cliff faces, and boulder crevices of the Appalachian Mountains from New England south to Georgia and Alabama, where it colonizes the smallest cracks in sandstone and granite in the deep shade of north-facing cliffs. Its triangular, twice-pinnate fronds — reaching just 4–10 inches — are dark green, leathery, and persistent through winter, and the plant forms compact tufted rosettes anchored tightly in rock crevices with minimal root access to soil. Unlike the Maidenhair Spleenwort (Asplenium trichomanes), which prefers limestone or neutral-alkaline rock, Mountain Spleenwort is strictly an acidic-rock specialist, growing naturally on sandstone, granite, and quartzite but not on calcium-rich rocks. Most challenging to establish in cultivation outside of natural rock garden conditions — it is best planted directly into a tight crevice in an acidic rock garden or dry stone wall built with sandstone, where the roots can remain sheltered and consistently humid even as the fronds dry rapidly in the open air.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; mountain stewartia is more adaptable than S. malacodendron but still demands excellent drainage, consistently moist soil, and protection from drying winds and hot afternoon sun in zone 7–9.
directions: Stewartia ovata is a large, multi-stemmed, native Appalachian shrub to small tree producing some of the largest flowers of any native deciduous plant — white, camellia-like, five-petaled blooms up to 4 inches across with large, showy orange stamens and dark-purple anthers in June and July — as well as outstanding, multi-season ornamental interest from its handsome, peeling gray-tan-cinnamon mottled bark and brilliant red, orange, and purple fall foliage. Native to moist mountain forest understories from Virginia to Alabama, it is the most widely adaptable stewartia for eastern gardens and is slowly becoming available from quality native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade. Mountain Sweet Pepperbush is more shade-tolerant and grows taller than its coastal relative (Clethra alnifolia) and is better suited to mountain and Piedmont gardens in zones 5–8.
directions: Mountain Sweet Pepperbush is a tall native understory shrub, native to the rich, moist, hardwood forests and mountain cove edges of the southern Appalachians from Virginia and North Carolina south to Georgia and Alabama, growing to 12 feet or more in deep, humus-rich mountain soils and producing fragrant white flower spikes in July and August that attract bumblebees and native butterflies. Distinguished from its coastal relative (Clethra alnifolia) by its greater height, more shade tolerance, and spectacular cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark that peels away in shaggy layers through the winter — an outstanding ornamental feature that rivals the most prized native bark textures. An excellent shrub for the shade garden in zones 5–8, where it tolerates conditions that defeat many other flowering shrubs; grow in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade and mulch deeply with leaf litter to maintain consistent moisture.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or loamy soil in full shade; mountain wood fern grows naturally in cool, moist, shaded mountain forests of northeastern North America, requiring cool temperatures, high humidity, and consistently moist but well-drained, acidic soils.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or loamy soil in full shade to partial shade; mountain wood fern is a graceful, medium-sized deciduous wood fern of cool, moist, northern and mountain forests from Newfoundland and Quebec south through the Appalachians to Virginia, growing on shaded rocky slopes, cool ravine walls, and moist boreal forest floors. The arching, broadly triangular fronds have a characteristic spreading habit and typical Dryopteris appearance — pinnate-pinnatifid to bipinnate, with the light green fronds turning yellow before dying back to the ground in autumn. Like other wood ferns, it is tolerant of moderate drought when established in shaded positions, but requires consistently cool conditions and good drainage with adequate moisture. Best in cool, moist shade gardens of the northeastern US and similar cool-climate gardens. Combines beautifully with hostas, trilliums, and other woodland wildflowers in shaded border plantings.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mountain wood sorrel is a delicate native groundcover of cool northern and high-elevation forests that requires consistently moist, cool conditions and will struggle in hot, dry summers.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in cool, consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil — pH 4.5 to 5.5 — in partial to deep shade; mountain wood sorrel does not tolerate heat or drought and is best suited to USDA zones 2 through 6, where cool summers prevail. Oxalis montana is a charming, low-growing native groundcover of boreal and montane forests from the Appalachians north through Canada, spreading slowly by slender rhizomes to form a soft carpet of clover-like trifoliate leaves that fold downward at night and in response to intense light. In late spring, solitary white flowers with distinctive pink veining appear just above the foliage, creating a delicate, painterly effect on the forest floor. This plant is an excellent groundcover for shaded rock gardens, cool ravines, and the north-facing slopes where few other groundcovers thrive.

plant_note: Plant young transplants in spring into gritty, rocky, freely draining soil in a crevice or rock garden; spores may be surface-sown on moist, sterile medium in late winter indoors.
directions: Mountain Woodsia is a compact, tufted native fern of rocky cliff ledges, talus slopes, and gravelly mountain outcrops throughout North America from Alaska to the southern Appalachians, producing small pinnate fronds 6-18 inches tall with soft glandular hairs that give the plant a slightly sticky, textured appearance. It is highly adapted to thin, rocky, freely draining soil and exposed, dry mountain conditions, making it an outstanding choice for crevice gardens, dry-stone walls, and alpine rock garden collections in cool climates. Plant young divisions or transplants in spring into gritty, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; protect from excessive heat and humidity, as this species is not suited to gardens below USDA zone 7. Water sparingly once established, as consistently moist or heavy soil will cause crown rot.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; mourning widow is one of the most shade-tolerant of all geraniums and self-sows freely to naturalize in shaded situations.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mourning widow produces small, dark, reflexed-petaled flowers in deep purple-maroon (rarely white or lilac) in late spring to early summer — the somber dark color and backward-bending petals account for the mournful common name. It is the most shade-tolerant geranium species, performing well even in the dense dry shade of evergreens. After bloom, cut the entire plant back by half to prompt fresh foliage growth; the leaves re-emerge quickly and remain attractive all season. Self-sows generously to maintain a naturalized presence in shaded woodland gardens. 'Samobor' has strikingly chocolate-marked leaves that are ornamental throughout the growing season.

subcategory: shade woodland novelty arum with mouse-tail spathe
plant_note: Plant small rhizomes or clumps 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; mouse plant spreads by rhizome to form dense groundcover colonies in moist, shaded conditions. It is a cool-season grower — emerging and flowering in early spring, going dormant in summer heat. The common name refers to the tiny, chocolate-and-white spathe-tipped flowers which, viewed from above, resemble small mice diving under the leaves.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; mouse plant is a small, shade-loving, Mediterranean arum relative from the moist, shaded woodlands of Spain and Italy that is one of the most charming and conversation-stopping novelty plants in the woodland garden — producing in early spring, hidden among the glossy, bright-green, arrow-shaped leaves, tiny, peculiar, bicolor flowers: each one a small, tapering spathe that is dark, shining chocolate-brown at the base (the 'body') curving up through a white-and-dark transition into a long, slender, thread-like tail — the 'mouse tail' — up to 4 inches long. The flowers are so cleverly concealed that they appear to be small mice diving nose-first under the leaf canopy, with only the long tail visible above the foliage. The common name 'mouse plant' perfectly captures the instantly recognizable illusion. In a moss-covered, shaded corner of a woodland garden, with a colony of these plants apparently populated by dozens of diving mice tails sticking up among the fresh, glossy leaves, it is an unfailing delight and conversation piece. It spreads steadily by rhizome in favorable moist, shaded conditions to form a groundcover colony. All parts are mildly toxic. An essential plant for the woodland curiosity garden.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring in slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), well-amended, deeply prepared, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mr. Lincoln requires the dedicated care typical of hybrid tea roses — consistent watering, fertilizing, and pest management — but produces some of the finest, most fragrant flowers of any rose.
directions: Plant in slightly acidic, well-amended, deeply prepared, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mr. Lincoln is one of the most fragrant and most widely grown deep-red hybrid tea roses in American horticulture, introduced in 1964 and still listed as one of the best red roses for fragrance by the American Rose Society. The flowers are classic hybrid tea form — high-centered, deeply cupped, velvety dark crimson-red — with an exceptional old-rose fragrance that is among the strongest of any modern rose. The upright canes reach 4–6 feet with dark, glossy foliage. Like all hybrid tea roses, Mr. Lincoln requires more care than modern landscape roses — it is susceptible to black spot and needs regular preventative spraying, consistent fertilization, and precise watering. The reward is extraordinary: no other rose type produces flowers of such classical elegance and overwhelming fragrance. In zone 9, provide deep mulch and consistent irrigation; the plant may go semi-dormant in peak summer heat but returns to bloom in fall.

common_name: Mrs. B.R. Cant Rose (Antique Southern Tea Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Mrs. B.R. Cant is an 1901 tea rose long grown in Deep South cemetery and homestead gardens for its vigor, heat tolerance, and near-total immunity to the blackspot that plagues modern roses in humid climates.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing 3-5 feet between plants since this vigorous tea rose can reach 6-8 feet in warm climates over time. Introduced in 1901 and named for the wife of an English rose nurseryman, Mrs. B.R. Cant became a mainstay of Deep South gardens and old cemeteries because of its extraordinary heat tolerance, vigor, and near-total resistance to blackspot, which lets it thrive in the humid Gulf South with no spraying. Large, cupped, silvery-pink double blooms with a rich tea fragrance appear in flushes from spring through the first frost, most heavily in cooler weather. Like most tea roses, it prefers to be left largely alone — minimal pruning beyond removing dead or damaged wood keeps the plant blooming reliably, since heavy pruning delays flowering and reduces the shrub's naturally graceful, arching form. Established plants tolerate considerable drought and neglect, which is why so many survive today in abandoned Southern homesites decades after they were planted.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; mukdenia is drought-tolerant once established for a shade plant and performs better in drier conditions than many moisture-loving shade perennials.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mukdenia is a Korean and northeastern Chinese shade perennial of the family Saxifragaceae — related to bergenia and heuchera — that produces bold, deeply lobed, glossy-green, maple-like leaves arranged in spreading, basal rosettes that provide an attractive, textural groundcover in the shaded garden. In spring, small clusters of white, star-shaped flowers appear on upright stems before the leaves fully expand. The primary ornamental season extends beyond spring, however, because in autumn the leaves develop brilliant and extensive red, orange, and bronze coloration from the leaf margins inward, creating one of the finest autumn foliage effects of any shade garden perennial — the red-edged, green-centered leaves are striking and long-lasting. More drought-tolerant than most shade perennials. 'Crimson Fans' is the most widely grown selection, with the most vivid and extensive autumn reddening. Excellent as an edging plant in shaded borders.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds or transplant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; mulla mulla is native to the arid interior of Australia and requires excellent drainage and lean, dry conditions. It is often grown as an annual or short-lived perennial. In humid-summer climates it may decline after flowering — treat as an annual. The fluffy, pink, bottlebrush-like flower spikes have made it popular as a cut flower export from Australia.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; mulla mulla is an Australian arid-zone plant of striking visual character — native to the dry inland regions of Western Australia, South Australia, and the Northern Territory, where it blooms after rain in remarkable mass-flowering events that color the usually bare, red-soiled landscape with waves of fluffy pink. The flower spikes are cylindrical to bottle-brush-shaped, 3–6 inches long, composed of hundreds of densely packed, feathery-textured, silvery-pink to rose-pink individual flowers with prominent, silky, feathery bristles that give the whole spike an extraordinarily soft, furry, fluffy texture — exactly like a large pink pussy willow or a fluffy cylindrical brush. Each spike shimmers in the slightest breeze as the silky feathery bracts catch the light. The common name 'mulla mulla' is from the local Aboriginal language of the region. In cut flower trade, the distinctive fluffy pink spikes export well as dried or fresh flowers for the floral industry, where they provide texture and soft pink color unavailable from any other commonly grown cut flower. In the garden it provides a dry-area, full-sun, pink-spike display of entirely unusual texture and form.

plant_note: Plant in fall; wear gloves as bulbs can irritate skin.
directions: Plant multiflora hyacinth bulbs in fall about six inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Unlike single-spike hyacinths, this type sends up several looser, fragrant flower stalks per bulb for a naturalistic effect. Wear gloves when handling, as the bulbs can irritate sensitive skin. Deadhead after bloom and let foliage ripen; flower size may diminish over the years as it perennializes.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Muskogee is one of the largest crape myrtle cultivars — allow 20–25 feet of clear space at planting to accommodate its mature size.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Muskogee is one of the most widely planted large crape myrtle cultivars, renowned for its soft, light lavender flower color — a cool, pale purple-pink that stands apart from the dominant pink and red tones of many crape myrtles and creates a particularly refreshing effect in the intense summer heat of the Gulf South. The flowers are produced in large clusters continuously from June through September in zone 9, covering the canopy with light lavender-purple throughout the peak summer season. Like Natchez (which it was developed alongside at the National Arboretum), Muskogee shows exceptional resistance to powdery mildew and retains attractive multi-trunked form when properly trained. The bark exfoliates to reveal mottled tan, gray, and cinnamon tones in late summer and fall. Fall leaf color transitions to orange-red, providing a third season of ornamental interest. Muskogee is a large-growing tree that can exceed 20–30 feet in height in zone 9 over decades, making it a true tree-scale specimen appropriate only for large planting spaces. Do not top or severely prune — always cut back only to lateral branches of similar diameter when any pruning is needed.

common_name: Mutabilis Rose (Butterfly Rose, Color-Changing China Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring after hard frost, or in fall in mild-winter climates; Mutabilis is an antique China rose first recorded in cultivation in 1894, exceptionally heat- and humidity-tolerant, and one of the most reliable roses for the Gulf South where many modern roses struggle with blackspot.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil enriched with compost, spacing plants at least 4-5 feet apart to allow for its eventual size, since Mutabilis can grow into a large, airy shrub 6-8 feet tall in warm climates over several years. Known as the Butterfly Rose for the way its single, five-petaled blooms seem to flutter above the foliage, Mutabilis opens flame-yellow, ages through pink, and finishes deep crimson, so a single established bush displays all three colors at once. As a China rose it blooms almost continuously from spring through frost with little deadheading required, and it is exceptionally resistant to blackspot and powdery mildew, making it one of the most reliable antique roses for the hot, humid Gulf South. It tolerates poor soil and some drought once established but flowers best and grows most vigorously with regular water and an occasional feeding. Prune lightly in late winter only to shape and remove dead wood, since Mutabilis flowers on both old and new growth and heavy pruning sacrifices bloom.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, sandy, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; myrtle holly is dioecious — plant male and female plants for berry production. Seeds require double dormancy stratification and are most practically grown from cuttings.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 7–10; myrtle holly is a native evergreen shrub of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, named for its unusually small, narrow, glossy leaves that strongly resemble those of true myrtle — quite different from the larger leaves of most native hollies. It grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, pond margins, bogs, and bay swamp edges throughout Florida and the Gulf Coast states, making it one of the most ecologically appropriate native shrubs for zone 9a moist-site plantings. The small, bright red to orange-red berries are highly attractive to bluebirds, yellow-rumped warblers, hermit thrushes, and other fruit-eating birds throughout winter. An underused native alternative to Japanese holly (I. crenata) that offers far greater wildlife value and superior adaptation to Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container plants in fall in dry, white, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; myrtle oak is a scrub obligate that requires the same excessively drained, infertile sands as turkey oak and sand live oak — it will not thrive in typical garden soils.
directions: Myrtle oak is a small-leaved, evergreen scrub oak of the Florida Peninsula and adjacent Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, unique among native oaks for its distinctly myrtle-like, oval, entire (not lobed) leaves that are shiny and dark green above — so different in appearance from typical oak leaves that beginners often fail to recognize it as an oak. It grows in the hottest, driest, most nutrient-deficient white-sand scrub habitats of the Florida interior and coasts, forming dense thickets from ankle height to small tree size depending on fire history and site conditions; Florida scrub habitats maintained by periodic fire have low, clumping myrtle oaks while fire-suppressed scrub develops into tall, dense thickets. Like turkey oak, myrtle oak is a foundational component of the Florida scrub ecosystem, which hosts more endemic species per acre than almost any other habitat in temperate North America, including the federally threatened Florida scrub-jay that depends on scrub oaks as its primary food source. A valuable landscape shrub or small tree for dry, sandy, acidic sites in central and south Florida.

common_name: Mysore Clockvine (Dolls Shoes Vine, Indian Clockvine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a sturdy pergola, arbor, or trellis in full sun to partial shade; Mysore Clockvine is a vigorous, woody perennial vine that can reach 20–30 feet and requires a strong support. In zone 9, it may freeze back in cold winters but resprouts from the crown in spring; in zone 10-11 it is evergreen and blooms nearly year-round with peak bloom in fall through spring. The pendulous flower clusters are best appreciated from below — plant to climb over a pergola or arbor for optimal viewing from underneath.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Mysore Clockvine grows vigorously in zone 9 conditions and produces its most spectacular bloom in fall through spring when temperatures moderate from summer heat. Thunbergia mysorensis is a large, vigorous, woody twining vine from the forests of southern India (Mysore, now Karnataka region), producing one of the most exotic and unusual flower displays of any tropical vine. The flowers are borne in long, pendulous racemes 12–18 inches in length that hang down from the vine canopy like earrings or chandeliers — each individual flower is two-toned, with reflexed outer petals in deep burgundy-red to maroon and a large, flaring, open throat in vivid golden-yellow, creating a striking color combination visible from a distance. The pendant flower clusters are specifically adapted for sunbird pollination in their native Indian forest habitat — the long, tubular corolla and dangling cluster position the flower perfectly for these hovering birds, and in zone 9, hummingbirds fulfill the same function with enthusiasm. In the US, Mysore Clockvine is grown as a spectacular pergola and arbor vine at botanical gardens (it is a signature plant at Balboa Park in San Diego and public tropical gardens nationwide) and is increasingly available at specialty nurseries for zone 9-11 home gardens.

common_name: Mysore Trumpetvine (Lady's Slipper Vine, Dolls Shoes)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Mysore trumpetvine is one of the most spectacular flowering vines for zone 9–12 — the long, pendulous clusters of exotic, red-and-yellow bicolor tubular flowers (looking like a bunch of hanging torches or dancing dolls' shoes) are among the most visually stunning in the tropical plant world, attracting hummingbirds and sunbirds from a distance.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; provide a very strong pergola or trellis — this vine grows vigorously and becomes very heavy; prune after flowering. Thunbergia mysorensis (Mysore trumpetvine, lady's slipper vine, or dolls shoes vine) is a spectacular evergreen climbing vine from the subtropical montane forests of southern India — particularly the Mysore region of Karnataka (where the common name originates) — and one of the most dramatically beautiful flowering vines in tropical horticulture. The vine produces long (12–18 inch), pendulous, racemose clusters of exotic, bicolor tubular flowers: deep red to burgundy-red on the outside with yellow-cream interiors and reflexed lobes, hanging in dense, eye-catching chains that resemble a row of dancing dolls or hanging slippers — hence the evocative common names. The flower clusters drape elegantly over pergolas, fences, and arbors, creating one of the most visually arresting and tropical-looking displays possible in a garden. The flowers are produced abundantly for months in warm climates and attract hummingbirds, bees, and sunbirds. The vine grows vigorously to 20–30 feet on strong support structures. Thunbergia mysorensis is becoming increasingly available through specialty tropical nurseries as awareness of its spectacular ornamental value spreads beyond its native range.

plant_note: Plant container-grown gardenias in spring or fall; in zone 9 spring (February–April) or fall (September–October) planting is appropriate. Mystery is one of the largest-flowered Gardenia jasminoides cultivars — the double, gardenia-scent flowers can reach 4–5 inches across on well-grown plants. Gardenias require acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.0) — test and amend before planting. Apply acid-forming fertilizer in spring and early summer; avoid fertilizing after August. Gardenias are sensitive to iron chlorosis in high-pH soils — yellowing between the veins indicates iron deficiency corrected with chelated iron applications. In zone 9 gardenias bloom May–July with occasional rebloom in fall. Avoid root disturbance once established.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered light — morning sun with afternoon shade is ideal; deep shade reduces flowering while full afternoon sun can cause leaf scorch; Mystery Gardenia (Gardenia jasminoides 'Mystery') is a large-flowered cultivar of one of the most fragrant of all flowering shrubs — producing the classic, intensely sweet, creamy-white gardenia flowers that have defined the concept of floral fragrance in American culture for generations. The 'Mystery' cultivar produces exceptionally large, fully double, pristine white to ivory flowers (4–5 inches across) against a backdrop of glossy, dark, evergreen leaves — creating a floral display of formal elegance and sensory intensity that few other ornamental shrubs can approach. The fragrance of gardenia flowers is one of the most recognizable and universally admired of any flowering plant — the complex, sweet, powdery-floral scent is distinctive and powerful enough to perfume an entire outdoor area when a mature, blooming gardenia shrub is nearby. In zone 9 gardenias thrive in the warm, humid climate that creates their ideal growing conditions — partial shade conditions that are abundant in the Gulf South landscape under pine and hardwood canopy providing exactly the situation they prefer. The combination of spectacular fragrant flowers, elegant glossy evergreen foliage, and cultural fit with zone 9's acid, partial-shade conditions makes Mystery Gardenia one of the most rewarding ornamental shrubs for Gulf South landscapes.

common_name: Mystic Spires Blue Sage (Long-Blooming Compact Indigo Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mystic Spires Blue blooms on new growth — light shearing after each main flush encourages continuous flower production through the entire growing season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; Mystic Spires Blue is one of the most successful and widely planted compact salvias for the Gulf South — a hybrid between Salvia farinacea and S. longispicata that produces long (6–10 inch), dense, indigo-blue flower spikes on a more compact plant (2–3 feet) than the related 'Indigo Spires' (3–5 feet), making it proportionate for typical residential border and container use. The indigo-blue flower color — a deep, saturated blue-violet that maintains its intensity through the Gulf South summer — is among the most valuable flower colors for sun gardens, where true blue is scarce. Mystic Spires Blue blooms continuously from late spring through hard frost in zone 9 — the long bloom season (May through November or longer) and compact habit combine to make it one of the most useful and ornamentally effective salvias for the Gulf South. The deep blue flowers are highly attractive to a wide range of pollinators — bees of many species, gulf fritillary and monarch butterflies, and hummingbirds all visit regularly. Plants are drought-tolerant once established, tolerating clay, heat, and humidity without significant decline. In zone 9, Mystic Spires Blue may be killed by severe cold but the tuberous roots often survive mild zone 9 winters and resprout in spring. A stellar three-season performer for the Gulf South full-sun border.

common_name: Mystic Spires Blue Salvia (Long-Spiked Deep Blue Proven Winners Hybrid Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mystic Spires Blue is a sterile hybrid that does not set seed — reproduction is by division or purchase of new plants. Deadheading spent spikes encourages rapid rebloom and maintains the neat appearance of the plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mystic Spires Blue is a Proven Winners hybrid salvia (Salvia longispicata x S. farinacea) that has become one of the most popular and widely sold salvias in American nurseries — and for good reason. The flower spikes are extraordinary: 12–18 inches long, densely packed with deep cobalt-blue to deep blue-violet flowers, held stiffly upright on branching stems for a display that far exceeds the spike length of standard mealy sage varieties. The extended spikes and prolific branching create a dramatic blue mass effect when established plants are in full bloom — a visual impact that has made Mystic Spires Blue one of the premier blue-flowered annuals and tender perennials for Gulf South summer and fall borders. The sterile hybrid status means no reseeding and no escaping to natural areas — an environmental advantage over some self-seeding sage species. The bloom season runs from spring through hard frost in zone 9, with deadheading of spent spikes promoting rapid, continuous new spike production. Unlike many salvias that slow or pause in peak summer heat, Mystic Spires maintains reasonable bloom production even in July–August in zone 9. In zone 8-9, established plants may survive mild winters and return as perennials; in zone 10-11, they are true perennials.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost into shaded, moist forest soil. Scarify seeds by lightly nicking the seed coat or soaking in warm water for 24 hours before sowing to improve germination rates. Sow at a depth of approximately 1/4 inch.
directions: Naked-flowered Tick Trefoil is a distinctive woodland native that grows in dry to moist deciduous forest shade, where its low-lying leaf stems form a handsome ground-level rosette separate from the tall, arching flowering stalk that rises directly from the root crown. Scarify seeds by rubbing lightly on sandpaper or soaking overnight in warm water, then sow directly in the garden in spring after soil temperatures reach 65 degrees Fahrenheit. Choose a site with dappled to full shade and well-drained, slightly acidic soil with a good leaf litter layer to mimic natural forest conditions. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, this plant benefits surrounding woodland vegetation and requires no supplemental fertilization once established.
