plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the last expected frost date. Surface-sow on moist seed-starting mix and keep under bright indirect light; do not cover seeds as light aids germination.
directions: Sow seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost date, pressing them lightly onto the surface of moist seed-starting mix and providing bright indirect light; germination may be slow and erratic. Transplant seedlings into partial shade once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 50°F, spacing them 8–12 inches apart in rich, humus-heavy soil that drains well. Keep soil consistently moist and avoid allowing plants to dry out, as this species favors the cool, humid conditions of its Himalayan origin. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering and protect plants from drying winds, which can stress foliage rapidly.

common_name: Nana Dwarf Mondo Grass (Miniature Groundcover Mondo Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Nana is a true dwarf mondo grass staying only a couple of inches tall, useful as a fine-textured lawn substitute or filler between stepping stones in shade.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Nana is a true miniature form of mondo grass, staying just two to four inches tall and spreading slowly to form a dense, fine-textured, deep green mat, making it one of the best low groundcovers for shaded areas where regular turf grass will not grow, including narrow gaps between stepping stones and pavers. It is slow to establish but, once mature, forms a durable, low-maintenance carpet that tolerates light foot traffic and needs no mowing. Division of established clumps is the standard way to propagate and expand a planting, and it is otherwise essentially maintenance-free once settled in.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to full shade; nandina is extraordinarily adaptable and one of the easiest landscape shrubs to grow in the South. Note: the berries are toxic to birds and other wildlife — plant non-fruiting cultivars ('Gulf Stream', 'Firepower') to eliminate this concern in naturalistic settings.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; nandina (heavenly bamboo) is one of the most widely planted landscape shrubs in the American South, prized for its four-season ornamental interest: delicate, feathery, compound foliage that emerges pinkish-bronze in spring, matures to bright green in summer, and turns brilliant scarlet-red in fall and winter; clusters of white flowers in late spring; and masses of bright red berries that persist through winter. It is extraordinarily adaptable, tolerating deep shade under trees, drought, poor soil, and heat with minimal care. Important ecological note: Nandina domestica is classified as invasive in many southeastern states as birds spread the seeds into natural areas; furthermore, the berries are toxic to cedar waxwings and other birds that eat them in large quantities. Select non-invasive, non-fruiting cultivars (compact 'Gulf Stream', 'Firepower', 'Fire Power', or dwarf 'Obsession Nandina') for residential use and avoid planting near natural areas. Compact cultivars at 2–3 feet are particularly useful for low-maintenance groundcovers in shade.

common_name: Nanho Blue Butterfly Bush (Compact Blue-Lavender Buddleja)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Nanho Blue is a compact selection reaching 4–5 feet, smaller than standard butterfly bush — suitable for typical residential landscapes. Deadhead regularly to prevent seed formation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Nanho Blue is the most popular compact butterfly bush — a smaller-growing Buddleja davidii cultivar in the Nanho series reaching 4–5 feet tall and wide, compared to the 6–10 feet of standard-sized selections like Black Knight. The reduced size makes Nanho Blue appropriate for typical residential garden spaces where full-size butterfly bush would quickly overwhelm the surrounding plants. The flower color is clear lavender-blue to blue-violet — a cooler, more blue-toned color than many butterfly bush cultivars that trend toward red-violet and purple. The fine-textured, silver-gray foliage is particularly attractive in the Nanho series, with narrower, more delicate leaves than standard cultivars. Like all Buddleja davidii cultivars, Nanho Blue is extraordinarily attractive to butterflies — the honey-scented flowers attract admirals, swallowtails, and fritillaries through the summer. Deadhead regularly to extend bloom and prevent seed set. In zone 9, cut the entire plant back to 12–18 inches in February; vigorous new growth emerges quickly when temperatures warm. Butterfly bush is drought-tolerant once established and actually performs better in lean, somewhat dry soils — in rich, moist soil the growth is rank and floppy.

common_name: Narrow-Leaf Bird of Paradise (Rushleaf Bird of Paradise)
plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; narrow-leaf bird of paradise is slower to establish and flower than S. reginae and more drought-tolerant once established. It takes 3–5 years to flower from division. Requires protection below 28°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; narrow-leaf bird of paradise is a remarkable South African species distinct from the familiar Bird of Paradise (S. reginae) in a unique way — it lacks leaf blades entirely. Instead of the large, paddle-shaped leaves of S. reginae, S. juncea produces erect, cylindrical, rush-like petioles (leaf stalks without a blade) forming a bold clump of upright, gray-green cylindrical stems that gives the plant a dramatic, minimalist, architectural silhouette resembling a cluster of giant rush or bamboo. From within this distinctive foliage emerge the same striking orange-and-cobalt-blue bird of paradise flowers as the common species, appearing on stiff stalks from spring through summer. More drought-tolerant than S. reginae because the reduced leaf surface area minimizes water loss — an elegant adaptation to hot, dry habitats in the South African Eastern Cape. Outstanding as an architectural statement plant in drought-tolerant, Mediterranean-climate, and sub-tropical gardens where its unusual leafless form creates immediate visual interest.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors after 4–6 weeks cold-moist stratification (refrigerator at 40°F) or direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; transplant into well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun after last frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors after 4–6 weeks cold-moist stratification (refrigerator at 40°F) or direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification; transplant into well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun after last frost. Echinacea angustifolia is the coneflower of the native short-grass and mixed-grass prairies of the Great Plains, shorter and more compact than E. purpurea with narrow, lance-shaped, hairy leaves and pale pink to rose-purple flowers with horizontal to reflexed ray petals; it is regarded by herbalists as the most potent of the medicinal echinaceas for immunostimulant use, and the root was one of the most widely used medicinal plants of Great Plains indigenous peoples. Drought-tolerant, long-lived, and difficult to establish from seed — purchase transplants for fastest results.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring on the soil surface, pressing seeds in lightly; narrow-leaf mountain mint also grows readily from stem cuttings taken in late spring or divisions of established clumps.
directions: Sow surface in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; narrow-leaf mountain mint is one of the single most valuable native plants for pollinators, producing tiny white flowers with purple spots from July through September that attract an extraordinary diversity of native bees, beetles, wasps, butterflies, and other beneficial insects. Research has documented more than 100 pollinator species visiting Pycnanthemum in a single season. The slender, needle-like leaves release a strong, pleasant minty fragrance when brushed; the plant can be used as a culinary mint substitute and brewed as a tea. It spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-sows modestly. An essential plant for any pollinator or native plant garden.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in shallow water (0–12 inches deep) or consistently saturated soil in full sun; narrow-leaved cattail is more graceful and less aggressively spreading than the common broadleaf cattail, making it a better choice for ornamental water gardens and small pond margins where containment matters.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions or bare-root plants in spring in 0–12 inches of standing water or in consistently saturated soil at pond margins; in containers, use aquatic planting baskets to control spread. Typha angustifolia (narrow-leaved or lesser cattail) is similar to but more graceful than the common broadleaf cattail (T. latifolia), with narrower strap-like leaves, a slightly shorter stature (4–6 feet), and a distinctive gap between the upper (male) and lower (female) portions of the brown, sausage-shaped flower spike — in T. latifolia the two parts are contiguous. The narrow-leaved cattail is somewhat less aggressively rhizomatous than T. latifolia, making it a better choice for controlled pond margin and water garden plantings. Cattails provide critical wildlife habitat (red-winged blackbird nesting, marsh wren nesting, feeding waterfowl), superior water quality improvement through sediment trapping and nutrient uptake, and the familiar brown seed heads iconic in naturalistic landscape design.

plant_note: Fall sowing or cold stratification improves germination of this native seed.
directions: This prairie native coneflower carries purple-pink blooms with drooping petals around a spiny central cone from early to midsummer. The seed germinates best after cold, so sow outdoors in fall or cold-stratify before spring sowing. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, where its deep taproot makes it very drought tolerant once established. It supports bees and butterflies, and its roots have a long history of medicinal use.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; narrow-leaved hosta is among the most vigorous and adaptable of the species hostas and multiplies quickly into attractive clumps. More sun tolerant than most large-leaved hostas.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; narrow-leaved hosta is distinguished from most hostas by its notably long, lance-shaped (lanceolate) leaves — slender and pointed rather than the rounded, heart-shaped leaves typical of the genus. The glossy, dark green foliage forms attractive, arching, medium-sized mounds that remain fresh and attractive throughout the growing season. Deep purple, funnel-shaped flowers are produced in late summer on tall scapes — one of the latest-blooming species hostas, extending the season of hosta interest in the shade garden. This species has been cultivated in Japan for centuries and was one of the first hostas introduced to Western gardens. It is notably more tolerant of sun and summer heat than the large-leaved blue hostas, making it better suited to southern gardens. A reliable, vigorous species that forms substantial colonies over time in appropriate moist, shaded conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seeds will germinate the following spring when soil warms.
directions: Direct sow in fall onto well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in a full-sun location and allow winter weather to provide the cold stratification needed for reliable spring germination. This slender, upright native perennial produces narrow, toothed leaves and long spikes of small pale lilac-pink flowers from May through August that attract native bees, particularly Augochlora bees that specialize on Verbena species. Once established, plants are highly drought-tolerant and long-lived in lean, dry soils with excellent drainage; they are poor performers in rich, moist, or heavy clay soils. Naturalistic prairie and meadow plantings, rock gardens, and dry roadsides are ideal settings for this understated but valuable native.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow seeds to naturally stratify over winter before spring germination.
directions: Narrowleaf Barbara's Buttons is a low-growing native of longleaf pine savannas and roadsides along the southeastern coastal plain, prized for its soft pink-purple pincushion flower heads that appear from late spring through summer. Sow seeds directly in fall into well-drained, sandy or loamy soil where they will cold-stratify naturally and germinate the following spring. This plant tolerates both full sun and partial shade but performs best with some afternoon protection in the hotter parts of its range. Once established, it spreads slowly into attractive clumps and requires little maintenance beyond removing spent flower heads if self-seeding is not desired.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, moderately dry to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; narrowleaf bluestar is slow to establish from seed but extremely long-lived once settled — the fine-textured foliage and exceptional fall color are among the finest in the native perennial garden.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately dry to moist soil in full sun to partial shade — narrowleaf bluestar from Arkansas is widely considered to have the finest fall color of any perennial plant in North America, its masses of thread-like, willow-narrow leaves turning brilliant, pure golden-yellow in September–October and holding the color for weeks, creating a soft, misty cloud of gold that is breathtaking in mass plantings. The spring bloom of pale blue, star-shaped flowers in May is also very attractive, and the fine, feathery summer texture contrasts beautifully with bold-leaved companions. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established with a deep root system, heat tolerant to zone 9, and completely deer-resistant. The Perennial Plant Association named it Perennial Plant of the Year in 2011. A near-perfect low-maintenance native perennial — plant it in full sun to partial shade and essentially never tend to it again.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; narrowleaf cottonwood grows naturally along mountain streams and rivers of the Rocky Mountain region and is the primary cottonwood of riparian habitats in the high-elevation west. Best propagated by cuttings as seed viability is very short.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; narrowleaf cottonwood is the dominant riparian tree of mountain streams and rivers in the Rocky Mountain west, forming gallery forest along watercourses from Montana to New Mexico. The distinctively narrow, willow-like leaves set it apart from other cottonwoods, giving it a more refined, graceful appearance. In fall, the foliage turns brilliant golden-yellow — a signature of Rocky Mountain fall scenery, particularly in high-elevation valleys where large stands create sweeping landscapes of fall gold against pine forest. The tree provides critical nesting habitat for raptors, heron colonies, and songbirds in mountain riparian corridors. Hybridizes freely with plains cottonwood where ranges overlap, producing intermediate forms. A fast-growing pioneer species of mountain stream banks and flood plains in the intermountain west.

plant_note: Plant divisions or transplants in fall in moist to wet, sandy or loamy, acidic to neutral soil in full to partial sun; narrowleaf false dragonhead is a wetland-edge species that thrives in moist bottomland meadows, streambanks, and the margins of wet prairies.
directions: Narrowleaf false dragonhead is a slender-leaved Physostegia of moist prairies, bottomland meadows, and streambank edges in the central United States — as its name suggests, its leaves are much more narrow and grass-like than those of the common obedient plant (Physostegia virginiana), giving the plant a more delicate, fine-textured appearance in the garden. It blooms in late spring and summer with typical Physostegia spikes of pink-lavender tubular flowers that attract bumblebees and hummingbirds, and like all members of the genus the individual flowers can be physically moved to different positions on the spike — the 'hinged' or 'obedient' characteristic that makes Physostegia one of the more interactive wildflowers for garden visitors. It spreads by rhizomes and self-seeding in moist conditions, forming loose colonies along stream edges and wet meadow borders where it provides good erosion control and continuous summer bloom. In rain garden borders and wet, sunny meadow plantings, it naturalizes pleasantly without becoming overly aggressive.

plant_note: Direct-sow in early spring or fall in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; narrowleaf ironweed is one of the most garden-appropriate Vernonia species because it stays much smaller than the common tall ironweed and does not require staking. The cultivar 'Iron Butterfly' is the most commonly available selection, with an even more refined, mounded habit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; narrowleaf ironweed is a compact, fine-textured species from the Ouachita Mountains of Arkansas and Oklahoma that solves the main problem with common ironweed (V. noveboracensis) — it stays under 24–30 inches in height rather than growing to 6+ feet, making it garden-scale and requiring no staking. The foliage is thread-like and very finely textured, giving the plant a grassy, airy texture through summer that is unusual among ironweeds. In August and September it produces the same brilliant, saturated purple-magenta flowers characteristic of the genus — vivid clusters of tiny brush-like heads — that are magnets for monarchs, swallowtails, fritillaries, and native bees during the critical late-season migration window. The selection 'Iron Butterfly' is particularly uniform and compact. Drought-tolerant, heat-tolerant, and adaptable to clay soils, making it an excellent plant for Gulf Coast and mid-South gardens where its late-season color is most welcome.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in well-drained, moderately moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; narrowleaf mountain mint is more drought-tolerant than P. virginianum and adapts well to average, dry to moist garden soils once established.
directions: Sow direct in fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; narrowleaf mountain mint is more adaptable to dry, average soils than P. virginianum and tolerates poor, sandy, or rocky conditions better — once established it is moderately drought-tolerant. Pycnanthemum tenuifolium is a fine-textured, strongly aromatic native perennial of the eastern United States distinguished by its very narrow, thread-like (tenuifolium = narrow-leaved) leaves that give it an airy, delicate appearance compared to its broader-leafed relatives; it produces an abundance of small, flat-topped clusters of tiny white flowers with faint purple spots from July through September. It is consistently rated among the top three native plants for pollinator diversity in eastern North America — the flowers simultaneously support hundreds of individual native bee species, wasps, flies, and small butterflies over a six-to-eight-week bloom period. Spreads by rhizomes to form dense, weed-suppressing colonies; the minty-fragrant foliage is strongly deer- and rabbit-resistant. Excellent in native meadow plantings, dry to moist borders, and roadsides.

subcategory: California native dry summer ornamental onion
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 2–3 inches deep in full sun in well-drained, dry, lean, rocky to sandy-loam soil in zone 5–9; Narrowleaf Onion (Papery Onion) is a California and Pacific Northwest native — growing in rocky grasslands, hillsides, and serpentine outcrops from British Columbia south through California and east to Nevada — producing small, rounded, papery-white to pale pink flower heads in late spring and early summer above very slender, grass-like leaves.
directions: Plant Allium amplectens bulbs in fall in rocky, well-drained, lean soil in full sun; naturalize in rocky slopes, gravel gardens, or dry native plant meadows; summer drought essential — provide no water from June through September; clumps multiply slowly by offsets. Narrowleaf Onion is a delicate and underused California and Pacific Northwest native ornamental, forming very slender, almost grass-like clumps of leaves surmounted by small, round clusters of papery white to pale blush-pink flowers in late spring. The ultra-narrow foliage and small, neat flower heads create an airy, refined texture that blends gracefully into native grass and wildflower plantings. Like all wild Allium, it has a distinct onion odor when bruised; the bulbs and leaves are edible as a wild onion, used historically by many Pacific Coast Indigenous peoples as a food and seasoning. The dried seed heads are attractive and persist through summer and fall, adding subtle texture to the dry garden. Best grown in thin, rocky soil or gravel — enriched garden soil tends to produce too-lush foliage that flops and reduces flower production. An excellent naturalizing companion for Blue Dicks, Brodiaea, Triteleia, and native bunch grasses.

common_name: Narrowleaf Zinnia (Species Zinnia, Drought and Mildew Resistant Orange Annual)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Zinnia angustifolia is the most mildew-resistant and drought-tolerant of the garden zinnia species, making it significantly more practical in hot, humid zone 9 conditions than the large-flowered Zinnia elegans types that often develop powdery mildew by mid-summer. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer bloom and again August for fall. Narrowleaf Zinnia forms a spreading mound 8–12 inches tall that provides excellent ground coverage in hot, dry conditions — planting closely (8–10 inches) creates a dense carpet of orange flowers. The species is the wild parent of the interspecific Profusion series hybrids (Zinnia marylandica = Z. angustifolia × Z. elegans), which have become among the most popular summer annuals; the species itself is worth growing for its simplicity, easy direct sowing, and exceptional heat and drought resistance.
directions: Scatter seeds on prepared soil after last frost; barely cover with soil. Narrowleaf Zinnia flowers prolifically through the hottest part of summer with minimal deadheading. Zinnia angustifolia (narrowleaf zinnia, spreading zinnia, or Mexican zinnia) is a small-flowered species zinnia native to Mexico and Central America that differs substantially from the large-flowered, upright garden zinnia (Zinnia elegans) in plant habit, flower size, and growing conditions. The leaves are distinctively narrow (hence the common name) compared to the broad, ovate leaves of Z. elegans, and the plant forms a low, spreading mound rather than upright stems. The flowers are small (1–1.5 inches), single, with a simple daisy form in bright orange — a pure, vivid orange that is more intense than many of the blended or muted colors of Z. elegans varieties. The most important practical distinction is disease resistance: Zinnia angustifolia has significant genetic resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that devastates Zinnia elegans plantings in hot, humid climates by mid-summer, leaving plants disfigured and non-productive. In the Gulf South and other hot-humid regions, narrowleaf zinnia is a more reliable long-season annual than Z. elegans because it continues producing flowers through August and September without the mildew damage that typically limits Z. elegans performance. Plant breeders recognized this and created the Profusion zinnia series (Z. marylandica) by crossing Z. angustifolia with Z. elegans to combine the disease resistance of the former with the larger flowers and color range of the latter.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks before last frost; nasturtiums prefer cool soil and bolt in summer heat.
directions: Soak large seeds overnight then direct sow 1/2 in deep in poor, well-drained soil. Avoid fertilizing, as rich soil produces lush leaves at the expense of flowers. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong the season, or allow them to set seed and collect for next year. Both flowers and leaves are edible with a peppery flavor.

subcategory: spectacular winter-flowering South African small tree
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Natal bottlebrush tree flowers spectacularly in late winter and early spring (August–October in South Africa) on bare branches before the leaves appear. In the Northern Hemisphere it flowers January–April. Deciduous in cooler zones; semi-evergreen in frost-free conditions. Outstanding for hummingbirds and sunbirds. Grows slowly to 10–15 feet in favorable conditions. Named for Sir George Grey, Governor of the Cape Colony.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Natal bottlebrush tree is a spectacular South African small tree or large shrub that produces in late winter, on bare leafless branches (flowering before the leaves emerge — a behavior called 'hysteranthous' that creates an unusually dramatic floral display against the bare winter framework of the tree), dense, cylindrical clusters of flowers in vivid scarlet to crimson-red, with prominent, projecting red stamens creating the brushy, bottle-brush-like texture. The individual flowers are composed primarily of conspicuous red stamens projecting from small scarlet sepals, creating the bottlebrush silhouette of the common name, and the color is an intense, clear, fire-engine red. A mature tree in full bloom — red bottlebrush clusters covering every leafless branch against the winter sky — is one of the most dramatically colorful winter spectacles in the zone 9 garden, and an irresistible feeding station for winter hummingbirds. The large, rounded, somewhat fig-like leaves that follow the flowers are also attractive. Related to Melianthus but without the strong odor. A choice specimen tree for warm gardens seeking a spectacular winter-blooming feature tree.

common_name: Natal Bulbine (Orange Bulbine, Red Bulbine, Cat's Tail)
plant_note: Plant transplants or direct sow seeds in spring in well-drained, sandy or gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; Natal Bulbine is drought-tolerant once established and requires excellent drainage — it rots in heavy, poorly-drained clay. It blooms most heavily in cooler weather (fall through spring in zone 9) but continues producing scattered flowers through summer. Can be divided in early fall. In zone 9, it remains semi-evergreen through mild winters; hard frosts kill the foliage but plants resprout from the fleshy roots.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy, or amended soil; Natal Bulbine is a heat-tolerant, drought-resistant South African succulent perennial particularly well suited to zone 9 Gulf Coast conditions. Bulbine natalensis is a clump-forming succulent perennial from Natal province, South Africa, producing loose rosettes of narrow, fleshy, succulent, grass-like leaves and tall, slender spikes of small star-shaped flowers in vivid orange or yellow, each individual flower distinguished by fluffy yellow stamens that give it a bearded appearance. It blooms prolifically in fall through spring in zone 9 (September–May), then rests somewhat in summer heat while maintaining attractive foliage. The orange-flowered form is the most commonly grown and makes a striking groundcover or mass planting with its warm coral-orange flower spikes rising above the textural foliage. The yellow-flowered species B. frutescens (Stalked Bulbine) is also widely grown and produces more of a shrubby habit. The succulent leaves of Bulbine natalensis contain a clear gel similar to aloe vera that has traditional use in South African folk medicine for skin conditions, burns, and wounds. Excellent combined with ornamental grasses, agaves, and other drought-tolerant plants in zone 9 xeriscape plantings.

subcategory: South African monotypic endangered shade cycad
plant_note: Plant in partial shade to bright shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 9–11; Natal Grass Cycad (Stangeria eriopus) is a remarkable, endangered South African cycad — the only member of its family, Stangeriaceae — native to coastal forest margins and grasslands of KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape, with fronds so similar to ferns that 19th-century botanists initially described it as a new fern genus before cycad cones were discovered.
directions: Plant Stangeria eriopus in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; protect from frost (damaged below 28°F), direct sun (which bleaches fronds), and waterlogged conditions; apply a cycad-specific slow-release fertilizer with trace elements in spring. Caution: all parts are toxic if ingested — contain cycasin and other cycad toxins. Natal Grass Cycad is botanically exceptional — the sole species in the family Stangeriaceae, occupying an isolated position in cycad evolution with no close living relatives. It was first described by European botanists in 1853 as a fern (placed in the genus Lomaria) because its soft-textured, pinnate, fern-like fronds are completely unlike the stiff, tough fronds of other cycads — only the discovery of its cone structures confirmed its true identity. Two growth forms exist in the wild: a forest form from shaded coastal forest understory with longer, drooping, dark-green fronds, and a grassland form with shorter, stiffer, sun-adapted fronds. The species is listed as Endangered and is CITES Appendix II listed; over-collection from wild plants for use in traditional Zulu medicine (zulu: isigqiki-somkhovu — 'dwarf's stool') has severely depleted natural populations. Always buy from reputable nurseries propagating from seed.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun (minimum 6 hours direct sun); Natchez is a large-growing crape myrtle — allow 20 feet of space in all directions at planting. Never top or 'crepe murder' — this destroys the tree's natural form permanently.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Natchez is widely considered the finest crape myrtle cultivar ever developed and is certainly the most widely planted — a National Arboretum hybrid of Lagerstroemia indica × L. fauriei introduced in 1987 that combines outstanding white flowers, four-season ornamental value, and exceptional disease resistance. From June through September in zone 9, Natchez produces massive clusters of pure white flowers continuously, creating a spectacular seasonal display that no other white-flowering summer tree rivals in the Deep South. In fall, the foliage transitions to brilliant orange-red — remarkable fall color for a Gulf Coast tree. But Natchez's most distinctive and lasting ornamental attribute may be its bark: the outer gray bark exfoliates in autumn to reveal rich cinnamon-brown, reddish-brown, and cream inner bark in a spectacular mottled pattern that makes the multi-trunked trunk one of the most beautiful in the tree world. The exfoliating bark is excellent as a winter feature when the tree is leafless. Natchez has outstanding resistance to powdery mildew — the primary disease problem of other crape myrtles. NEVER top (cut back major limbs) Natchez or any crape myrtle — this practice creates permanent, ugly knobby heads, destroys the tree's graceful form, and dramatically reduces its ornamental value without providing any benefit.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Natchez is among the largest and fastest-growing National Arboretum crepe myrtle introductions, reaching 20–30 feet at maturity — a true tree-sized specimen, not a large shrub. Do NOT 'crape murder' (top with flush cuts) — this practice produces disfigured trees with weak, gnarled tops that look unnatural and structurally inferior. Instead, remove only crossing branches, suckers, and dead wood in late winter. Natchez's disease resistance (especially powdery mildew and Cercospora leaf spot) is among the best of all crepe myrtle selections, a direct result of the Japanese L. fauriei parentage in the hybrid.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Natchez Crepe Myrtle thrives in summer heat and drought, requiring supplemental water only during establishment and extended dry periods once mature; Natchez is the flagship white-flowered introduction from the National Arboretum's landmark crepe myrtle breeding program, released in 1978 as one of the first L. indica x fauriei hybrids that combined the large, colorful flowers of L. indica with the disease resistance and refined exfoliating bark of the Japanese L. fauriei species. The extraordinary, exfoliating cinnamon-to-chestnut bark that peels to reveal cream, tan, and mahogany underlayers is arguably the most beautiful bark texture of any tree in the Southern landscape — providing striking ornamental interest throughout the fall and winter months long after the white flower clusters have dropped. The pure white flower clusters appear in midsummer (June–August), covering the entire canopy with massive, frothy white blooms before the foliage turns bronze-orange-red in fall. Natchez's combination of spectacular summer bloom, beautiful autumn color, exceptional winter bark, disease resistance, and adaptability to the heat and drought of zones 6–9 has made it one of the most widely planted ornamental trees in the American South for over four decades.

common_name: Native Yellow Canna (Bandana of the Everglades)
plant_note: Divide rhizomes and plant in boggy, shallow water (0–6 inches deep) or in wet, poorly drained soil after last frost; native yellow canna is a true wetland plant adapted to standing water and does not perform as well in ordinary garden beds. It is a parent of many modern canna hybrids and grows as a perennial in zones 8–11.
directions: Divide rhizomes and plant in boggy or shallow-water conditions in full sun; native yellow canna is the sole wild canna species of the southeastern United States, growing naturally in wetlands, pond margins, roadside ditches, and wet meadows from South Carolina to Florida and across the Gulf Coast to Texas. The soft-yellow, iris-like flowers are more delicate and translucent than the bold tropical cannas of cultivation, producing a graceful fluttering display on tall, narrow plants. It is an essential plant for native rain gardens, bioswales, pond edges, and wet meadow gardens in the Gulf Coast region, where it grows as a reliable perennial and provides larval food for Brazilian skipper butterflies. Unlike garden hybrid cannas, native canna self-sows and naturalizes in appropriate wet conditions. It was a primary parent of modern ornamental cannas — most cultivated cannas carry its genes.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost or start indoors 4-6 weeks earlier.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost or start indoors four to six weeks earlier for a head start. This easy garden standard produces single golden-yellow blooms marked with maroon that flower continuously from summer to frost. Fairly drought tolerant, it thrives in full sun and works well as a border, bedding, or companion plant. Deadhead to keep the blooms coming.

plant_note: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the Neches River rose mallow is a federally threatened species endemic to the Neches River bottomlands of East Texas and should only be purchased from reputable native plant nurseries — do not collect from the wild.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the Neches River rose mallow is a federally threatened species endemic to the Neches River bottomlands of East Texas and should only be purchased from reputable native plant nurseries — do not collect from the wild. Hibiscus dasycalyx is one of the rarest members of the North American rose mallow complex; it closely resembles scarlet rose mallow (H. coccineus) and swamp rose mallow (H. moscheutos) in growth habit — producing tall, cane-like stems with deeply palmately lobed leaves — but bears distinctive white flowers with a dark wine-red center eye and a deeply pubescent calyx covered in long, soft hairs that distinguish it from its relatives. Although rare in nature, it is adaptable in cultivation to any wet, sunny site in zones 7–10 and performs well in rain gardens, pond margins, and moist meadows; it is a stunning, large-flowered native rose mallow of significant conservation interest.

plant_note: Sow on bare, thin limestone-derived soil in fall for winter stratification and late-winter germination. This species requires extremely lean, calcareous, open substrate free of competing vegetation; any enrichment of the soil will favor weedy competitors over this diminutive specialist.
directions: Necklace Gladecress is a rare, federally listed native winter annual endemic to limestone cedar glades of central Tennessee and a handful of Kentucky sites, named for the striking bead-like constrictions between the seed compartments of its elongated seed pods that resemble a string of tiny pearls. Like its close relative Michaux's Gladecress, it produces small, white 4-petaled flowers on thread-like stems in late winter and early spring, completing its life cycle on exposed limestone rock faces before summer drought sets in. Grow exclusively in thin, limestone-derived, extremely well-drained, calcareous soil in full sun with no organic amendments; it cannot compete against taller vegetation and must be sited on open, bare rock surfaces or gravel substrate. Essentially unavailable through commercial horticulture, it is planted only in cedar glade conservation restorations — do not collect seed or plants from wild populations.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Necklace Pod is highly salt- and drought-tolerant and is ideal for coastal beach and dune stabilization in zones 8b–11.
directions: Necklace Pod is a striking native coastal shrub, native to the sandy beaches, dunes, and coastal scrub of the Gulf and Atlantic coasts from Florida to Texas, the Caribbean, and tropical Americas, producing long, arching racemes of bright yellow pea-like flowers nearly year-round in frost-free areas that attract hummingbirds, butterflies, and large carpenter bees. The distinctive seed pods are constricted between each seed like a string of beads — giving the plant its common name — and the silvery-gray, velvety, compound leaves provide attractive texture against the beach landscape. One of the finest native plants for coastal stabilization and landscaping in zones 9–11, Necklace Pod tolerates salt spray, poor sandy soil, drought, and heat with equal ease, requiring virtually no care once established in a sunny, well-drained site. Caution: seeds are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade in humid tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12); Needle Flower Tree (Posoqueria latifolia) is a Central and South American understory tree to rainforest edge shrub bearing spectacular clusters of long-tubed, pure-white, intensely fragrant, jasmine-like flowers — each flower tube 4–6 inches long — that open at dusk and are pollinated by hawk moths.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to dappled light; Posoqueria latifolia benefits from consistent moisture and humidity — mulch heavily, water regularly, and protect from strong winds and salt spray. Posoqueria latifolia (Needle Flower Tree or Red Star) is an evergreen shrub to small tree native to humid tropical forests from southern Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean into South America, member of the Rubiaceae (coffee family), and one of the most ornamentally spectacular night-fragrant flowering trees of the tropics. The common name references the long, slender, needle-like flower tubes — each individual flower has a tube 4 to 6 inches long — held in large, globe-shaped terminal clusters that open white at night and release an intense jasmine-like fragrance evolved to attract long-tongued hawk moths (Sphingidae) as pollinators. The round, pale-yellow to orange fruits that follow are edible, mucilaginous, and eaten in some parts of its native range. Posoqueria makes an exceptional accent plant or large container specimen for humid subtropical and tropical gardens where it is a conversation-stopper in bloom; provide shelter, consistent moisture, and protection from frost for best results.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; needle palm is remarkably slow-growing — 5–10 years to a mature specimen — but extremely cold-hardy for a palm, often surviving temperatures down to 5°F when established.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; needle palm is remarkably slow-growing — 5–10 years to a mature specimen — but extremely cold-hardy for a palm, often surviving temperatures down to 5°F when established. Rhapidophyllum hystrix is the hardiest palm in the world, a southeastern US native found naturally in wet flatwoods and hammocks from South Carolina to Florida and Mississippi; it grows as a low, clustering, trunkless to very short-trunked palm with fan-shaped, dark-green fronds on stout stems armed with long, sharp, black needles (giving rise to the common name) that create a nearly impenetrable clump reaching 3–6 feet tall and wide over many years. Despite its slow growth, it is a spectacular specimen palm for zones 7–10 shaded garden borders, and its extreme cold hardiness makes it the top choice for gardeners in zone 7 who want a true, large fan palm; once established it requires virtually no care.

plant_note: Sow on the soil surface in fall and allow winter cold to provide the stratification needed for spring germination.
directions: Needle-tipped Blue-eyed Grass is one of the smallest and most delicate members of its genus, making it well suited to rock gardens, thin turf, and open woodland edges where it naturalizes without becoming aggressive. Its very slender, flattened stems are topped with tiny blue-violet flowers featuring yellow centers that open in spring and early summer. Surface-sow seeds in fall on moist, sandy or thin soil and leave them undisturbed through winter for natural cold stratification. Plants establish slowly from seed but once settled will self-sow modestly, gradually forming loose, charming colonies.

plant_note: Plant divisions or direct sow in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; needlegrass rush grows naturally in shallow water margins, wet meadows, seeps, and ditches across most of North America. It is one of the most widespread native rushes in the US.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in shallow water margins, wet meadows, and rain garden wet zones; needlegrass rush (tapered rush) is one of the most widespread and common native rushes of North America, growing naturally in a broad range of wet habitats from coastal marshes to mountain seeps. The stems bear distinctive, rounded, terminal flower/seed clusters that look like small brown spheres when mature. The seed heads are eaten by various marsh birds and shorebirds. Fine-textured and relatively short compared to soft rush, it naturalizes readily in appropriate wet conditions to create fine, tuft-forming groundcover in wet areas. An excellent native filler for the wet margins of bioswales, rain gardens, and restored wetlands where its widespread adaptability across soil types and moisture levels makes it one of the more reliable wetland natives for mitigation planting.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Needlepoint Holly is parthenocarpic (self-fertile) and sets fruit without a male pollinator — no separate male plant is required for berry production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Needlepoint is a refined, upright Chinese holly cultivar valued for two outstanding characteristics: it is one of the most reliably self-fertile hollies (producing bright red berries without requiring a separate male pollinator), and it has narrower, more elegant leaves with a single prominent terminal spine rather than the multiple spines of typical Chinese holly. The reduced spine count makes it significantly more people-friendly than standard Chinese holly (Ilex cornuta) while maintaining excellent deer resistance and the characteristic waxy, deep-green, evergreen foliage. The heavy annual red berry crop is produced reliably from November through winter, providing outstanding wildlife value — berries are consumed by mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. The upright, pyramidal to oval habit grows 7–12 feet tall with a somewhat narrower spread, making it suitable for foundation plantings, hedges, and screening in spaces where the spreading Burford holly would be too wide. Needlepoint holly tolerates the full range of Gulf Coast conditions — clay soil, drought, heat, and partial shade — that challenge many landscape shrubs. Apply balanced fertilizer in spring; no regular pruning is needed beyond shaping immediately after the berry season ends in late winter.

common_name: Needleroot Airplant Orchid (Florida Needleroot Orchid, Needleroot Epidendrum)
plant_note: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork with the roots exposed to bright indirect light; Harrisella porrecta is a leafless epiphytic orchid that photosynthesizes entirely through its roots — the roots must receive adequate light (bright indirect to partial direct) to support the plant. Extremely slow-growing and highly specialized, this orchid is suited to patient collectors and enthusiasts interested in Florida's rare native flora. Found naturally in Collier and Monroe Counties in Florida on live oak, pop ash, and pond apple trees. Wild plants are protected by Florida law and by CITES — purchase only from nurseries propagating legally. Zone 10-12 outdoors only.
directions: Grow mounted on rough bark with roots exposed to filtered indirect light and high humidity — Needleroot Airplant Orchid is a leafless, photosynthetic-root orchid that subsists entirely on light captured through its chlorophyll-containing roots and nutrients from air moisture and rain, making root light exposure the single most important cultural requirement. Harrisella porrecta is one of the tiniest orchids native to North America — a minute, completely leafless epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family found in southern Florida (Collier and Monroe Counties, including the Big Cypress and Florida Keys) and throughout the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central America. Like the more famous Ghost Orchid (Dendrophylax lindenii) and the related Campylocentrum micranthum, Harrisella porrecta has eliminated its leaves entirely and depends on flat, strap-like, gray-green roots that cling to tree bark surfaces for all photosynthesis. The plant itself is nearly invisible on its host tree — appearing as a few thin, spreading, flatly-appressed roots spreading across bark, indistinguishable from a lichen or bark mark to the untrained eye. In summer and fall, tiny flower spikes (0.5–1 inch) emerge from the root nodes, bearing 3–8 minute (under 0.25 inch) flowers in pale yellow-green with a white lip — flowers that require a hand lens to fully appreciate but are perfectly formed in miniature. Harrisella porrecta is one of the rarest and most specialized of Florida's native orchids, of genuine interest to native plant specialists and orchid collectors fascinated by the biology of leafless, root-photosynthesizing orchids. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped hollies in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Nellie R. Stevens is self-fruitful and does not absolutely require a male pollinizer, though nearby male hollies increase berry production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Nellie R. Stevens is the most widely planted evergreen holly in the American South — a vigorous, broadly pyramidal tree-form shrub reaching 15–25 feet tall with a dense, naturally symmetrical form that requires minimal pruning to maintain its attractive shape. It is a hybrid of Ilex cornuta × Ilex aquifolium, combining the heat tolerance and gloss of Chinese holly with the cold hardiness and berry production of English holly. The dark, glossy, spiny evergreen leaves provide a rich, formal appearance year-round, and the plant produces abundant clusters of bright red berries from fall through winter that are highly attractive to cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and other wildlife. Nellie R. Stevens is considered partially self-fruitful — it sets fruit without a pollinizer, but nearby male hollies (any male Ilex cornuta or I. aquifolium) significantly increase fruit load. It is adaptable to a wide range of soil types and performs well in Gulf Coast clay soils once established. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant. In zone 9, Nellie R. Stevens is one of the most reliable large evergreen hollies, providing both year-round screening and spectacular winter berry displays.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Nellie Stevens is dioecious — plant a male holly nearby for berry production. Edward J. Stevens (the male counterpart) or any other male Ilex x meserveae or Ilex opaca male holly within 50 feet will pollinate. Without a male pollinator, no berries form. Trees begin producing berries 3–4 years from planting and become increasingly ornamental as they mature. Tolerates pruning well and can be sheared into a formal hedge or left to develop its natural pyramidal form.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Nellie Stevens Holly is a hybrid Ilex cultivar (believed to be Ilex aquifolium x Ilex cornuta) that has become one of the most popular evergreen screening trees and specimen hollies for the American South and transition zones — combining the large size and dense pyramidal form needed for privacy screening with exceptional heat tolerance and adaptability to Gulf South conditions. The large, glossy, dark green leaves with spiny margins create an impenetrable, formal-looking screen or hedge that requires minimal maintenance to maintain its naturally tidy pyramidal shape. In winter, heavily pollinated female trees are covered with large clusters of orange-red berries that persist through winter and are an important food source for robins, cedar waxwings, and other berry-eating birds. The combination of year-round ornamental value (evergreen foliage + winter berries), fast growth rate (2–3 feet per year in good conditions), and Gulf South adaptability has made Nellie Stevens one of the most planted ornamental trees across zones 6–9 for the past several decades.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Nelly Moser blooms on both old and new wood, so light pruning after the first flush rather than a hard cutback preserves the most flowers, and the pale flower color fades less in a site with some afternoon shade.
directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into a site with morning sun and afternoon shade, since Nelly Moser's flower color is prone to fading and bleaching in intense, all-day summer sun. Introduced in France in the 1890s, it remains one of the most recognizable clematis cultivars for its large, pale pink flowers boldly striped down the center of each petal with a deep carmine-rose bar. It flowers on old wood in late spring and can rebloom lightly on new growth later in summer, so pruning should be light, removing only dead or weak stems in late winter rather than cutting the whole vine back hard, which would sacrifice the main spring bloom.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–3 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate light frost.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in fine-textured germination mix at 60–65°F; avoid higher temperatures as heat inhibits germination. Plant outdoors in cool weather in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade where summers are hot. Nemesia blooms prolifically in cool conditions with cheerful two-toned flowers in a huge range of colors; it typically falters in summer heat so shear back and move containers to a cooler spot. Plants may revive and rebloom in fall when temperatures drop again.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain consistently above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and bring indoors before temperatures approach 50°F. Neon Robusta produces its most vivid pink coloration in bright indirect light; deep shade causes the foliage to revert toward lighter green with less pink saturation. Stem cuttings root easily in water or moist propagating mix. As the plant matures it transitions from a compact, upright bushy form to a trailing or climbing vine — the juvenile arrowhead-shaped leaves giving way to larger, multi-lobed adult leaves if the plant is allowed to climb. In zone 9 the warm summer humidity promotes vigorous growth.
directions: Plant in bright indirect light to shade — avoid direct sun, which bleaches the distinctive pink coloration — in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist potting mix; Neon Robusta is a pink-leaved cultivar of Arrowhead Plant (Syngonium podophyllum) producing distinctive arrowhead-shaped leaves in a warm rose-pink to dusty mauve-pink that is one of the most unusual and distinctive foliage colors available among commonly grown shade tropical plants. The pink coloration is evenly distributed across the entire leaf surface — not a variegation pattern of green-and-pink like many other pink-leaved plants, but a full-leaf pink that makes Neon Robusta a genuinely unusual and striking specimen in shade garden collections. Arrowhead plants (Syngonium podophyllum) are among the most adaptable and genuinely shade-tolerant tropical foliage plants available — surviving in conditions ranging from bright indirect light to deep shade while maintaining reasonable growth rate and foliage quality. The compact, bushy juvenile form of Neon Robusta (before the plant begins to vine) makes it particularly useful for small containers, terrariums, and tight shade planting situations where a larger trailing plant would be impractical.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings under high humidity or plant container specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade after frost; nerve plant requires the highest consistent humidity of virtually any common tropical foliage plant and fails rapidly in dry air — it is ideally suited to terrariums and glass enclosures that maintain near-100% relative humidity.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full shade; nerve plant (mosaic plant, painted net leaf) is a Peruvian tropical creeping groundcover of the family Acanthaceae, producing small, oval, intensely patterned leaves in which a dense, intricate network of bright-white, pink, or red veins forms a complete lacework overlay on the dark-green leaf surface, creating a mosaic-like pattern that gives the plant its alternative common name. The leaf patterning is extraordinarily precise and complex — the entire leaf surface is filled edge-to-edge with this fine vein network, with no undecorated green area visible. As a creeping, mat-forming groundcover it spreads horizontally across the soil surface to create a dense, living carpet of patterned leaves in terrarium and deep-shade garden conditions. Fittonia is among the most humidity-demanding of all tropical foliage plants — it wilts dramatically at the first sign of dry air, then recovers equally dramatically when humidity is restored. This complete intolerance of dry conditions makes it ideal for terrariums and glass cases but challenging in open interior environments. Pink-veined ('Argyroneura'), red-veined ('Rubra'), and white-veined forms are the primary selections.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container trees in fall in rocky, dry, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; net-leaf hackberry is a tree of canyon walls, rocky arroyos, and desert wash margins in the arid Southwest — it requires excellent drainage and tolerates alkaline soils better than sugar hackberry.
directions: Net-leaf hackberry is the western species of hackberry, found on rocky canyon walls, limestone bluffs, and desert arroyo margins from the Texas Hill Country west to California and south into Mexico, where it often clings to near-vertical cliff faces and survives in conditions of extreme drought and heat. Its distinctive deeply veined, rough, sandpaper-textured leaves (the 'reticulata' means net-veined) and tolerance of alkaline limestone soils make it the hackberry for dry, rocky, alkaline landscapes of the southwest where eastern hackberry (Celtis occidentalis) is poorly adapted. Like all hackberries, it is a primary host plant for hackberry emperor and American snout butterflies, and its small, dark red to black berries are eaten by 30+ bird species including robins, mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and migrating thrushes. In south and central Texas and the southwestern states, it is an important native tree for dry, rocky, alkaline soil landscape situations and for restoring native woodland structure in arroyo and canyon habitats.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; or cold-stratify seeds for 60 days and sow indoors in late winter. This vine dies back to the ground in winter and re-emerges from the root in spring. Plant in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, lean, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; netleaf leather flower is a slender native vine of the southeastern Coastal Plain that scrambles through shrubs and over fences with modest vigor. The unique, urn-shaped flowers have thick, leathery tepals in shades of dull purple with pale-veined markings — resembling tiny pitchers that hang from the vine stems in summer. Unlike the more showy garden clematis, this species is subtle and discovered on close inspection. The feathery seed heads that follow are silvery and attractive. The netted or reticulated (net-like) veins of the leaves give the species its name. This is one of the native leather flower clematis of the Gulf Coastal Plain (related to C. crispa and C. viorna) and a rare but valuable plant for a low-water, naturalistic southern garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in wet to consistently moist, peaty, acidic soil in partial to full shade; netted chain fern is well adapted to boggy woodland margins and shaded swale edges where soils remain saturated for extended periods.
directions: Woodwardia areolata is a small, deciduous native fern of eastern North American bogs, swamps, and shaded wet woodland margins, producing simply pinnate (not bipinnate) sterile fronds with broad, lobed, ladder-like pinnae and a distinctive netted venation pattern that gives the plant its common name; its fertile fronds are narrower with elongated sori arranged in chain-like rows along the midrib of each pinna. It spreads steadily by slender rhizomes to form a low, dense groundcover in wet, acidic, shaded sites and is an excellent native choice for rain garden margins, shaded bog edges, and the wet fringes of pond plantings in zones 3–9. Unlike many ferns, it tolerates standing water and waterlogged soils well, making it one of the few ferns suited to intermittently flooded conditions. Combine with blue flag iris, pitcher plants, and native sedges in naturalized wet woodland or bog plantings.

plant_note: Surface sow seeds in early spring or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade; nettle-leaf bellflower self-sows freely and can naturalize in woodland garden conditions. It has a history as a medicinal herb: the botanical name trachelium refers to the Greek word for throat (trachea) as it was used in folk medicine to treat sore throats.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part to full shade; nettle-leaf bellflower is a shade-tolerant European native of hedgerows, woodland edges, and scrub, producing coarsely toothed, roughly textured leaves reminiscent of stinging nettle (hence the common name, though unrelated and harmless) and in July–August, upright stems bearing clusters of large (1–1.5 inch), broadly cup-shaped, violet-blue to blue-purple flowers — somewhat more openly bell-shaped than C. latifolia and carried in more branching clusters. Like C. latifolia, it is genuinely shade-tolerant and thrives in the moist, lightly shaded conditions where most bellflowers decline. It was used historically in herbal medicine for throat ailments (trachelium derives from the Greek for throat). A traditional English hedgerow plant, it naturalizes readily in the semi-shaded woodland garden. The double-flowered cultivar 'Bernice' (fully double, lilac-blue flowers) is the most decorative available form. Self-sows reliably in moist, shaded situations and can be used to create naturalized colonies under deciduous shrubs and trees.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; nettle-leaf sage is one of the most shade-tolerant native Salvia species in eastern North America and is best suited to woodland edge and dappled-shade settings.
directions: Sow direct in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; seeds benefit from natural cold stratification over winter and germinate in spring — nettle-leaf sage adapts to the kind of moderately moist, shaded woodland floor where most sun-loving sages fail. Salvia urticifolia is a uncommon and underused native perennial sage of the southeastern Appalachians and adjacent piedmont, native to moist, shaded slopes, woodland edges, and stream margins; it is distinguished by its large, nettle-like, coarsely toothed, aromatic leaves (urticifolia = nettle-leaved) that give it a lush, bold texture in shaded garden settings. It produces upright stems bearing whorls of tubular, blue to blue-purple flowers from May through July that are attractive to native bumblebees and hummingbirds — a notable distinction in a genus where most species require full sun. Nettle-leaf sage is an excellent choice for shaded native plant gardens, woodland edges, and naturalistic plantings in the mid-Atlantic and upper South; it self-sows modestly and is not aggressively spreading.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil (do not cover — seeds need light) in early spring or early fall; nettle-leaved mullein is a genuine long-lived perennial, unlike the common biennial mullein, returning reliably year after year. It self-sows moderately to maintain a colony. The cultivar Album has white flowers with the same mauve-purple stamens and is equally ornamental.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; nettle-leaved mullein is the most reliably perennial and garden-worthy of the mulleins, distinct from both the common biennial mullein (Verbascum thapsus) and the silvery Turkish mullein (V. bombyciferum) in being a genuine long-lived perennial that returns each year. The flower spikes reach 3-5 feet and are densely packed with yellow flowers, but the most distinctive and ornamental feature is the prominent, woolly, mauve-purple filaments of the stamens visible in the center of each flower — a striking purple-and-yellow bicolor combination visible across the garden. The cultivar Album produces white flowers with the same contrasting purple-mauve stamens — an unusual and beautiful combination. Native to central and southern Europe, it thrives in the lean, well-drained, alkaline soils of traditional cottage-style dry borders, rock gardens, and gravel plantings. Combines beautifully with Mediterranean herbs, silver-leafed plants, and ornamental grasses.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade after frost; ctenanthe tolerates the deepest shade of the prayer plant family and maintains its leaf coloring in quite low light conditions where stromanthe and calathea would fade.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; never-never plant is a Brazilian tropical perennial of the prayer plant family (Marantaceae) that produces long, lance-shaped leaves with a distinctive, precisely patterned, feathered silvery-gray variegation on a rich dark-green background — the alternating dark and light bands create a herringbone or fish-bone pattern that has a formal, almost graphic quality unlike the more organic markings of calathea. The undersides of the leaves are deep burgundy-red to maroon. It is among the most shade-tolerant of the Marantaceae family, maintaining acceptable growth and variegation in quite dim interior spaces where other prayer plant relatives would decline. Like calathea and maranta, the leaves exhibit nyctinasty (night leaf movement), folding upward in the evening. More tolerant of irregular watering than calathea. 'Tricolor' (cream, white, and green irregular blotching) is the most widely grown cultivar selection.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; never-never plant is an excellent tropical shade perennial for zone 9b–11 gardens or as a container plant brought indoors in winter in cooler zones — grown primarily for its stunning silver and dark green striped foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; never-never plant is intolerant of drought, direct sun, and cold temperatures below 50°F. Ctenanthe setosa is a Brazilian rainforest native in the prayer plant family (Marantaceae) prized for its spectacular foliage: long, oval leaves with dramatic silver-grey stripes on a dark olive-green background and deep burgundy-purple undersides that flash when the leaves move in a breeze. Like other Marantaceae, the leaves fold upward at night in a sleep movement (nyctinasty) that gives the family its common name 'prayer plant.' Grow in deep, consistent shade with high humidity and regular moisture but excellent drainage; use as a bold tropical accent in shaded island beds in zone 10–11 or as a high-impact container plant for patios in cooler zones. Propagate by dividing clumps in spring.

common_name: New Dawn Rose (Ever-Blooming Doctor Van Fleet)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in late winter or early spring against a sturdy support structure; New Dawn requires strong architectural support — a substantial fence, arbor, or pergola capable of supporting a mature plant that can weigh several hundred pounds.
directions: Plant against a sturdy support in slightly acidic, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; New Dawn holds the distinction of being the first plant ever patented in the United States (Plant Patent No. 1, 1931) and remains one of the most beloved climbing roses in cultivation, producing masses of medium-pink, lightly fragrant, semi-double flowers on long, arching canes that can reach 15–20 feet. New Dawn is a sport of 'Dr. Van Fleet' that gained its fame partly by blooming repeatedly rather than once in spring — an unusual quality in vigor climbing roses of its era. The silvery-pink flowers fade gradually to nearly white and are produced in large clusters in spring with reliable repeat bloom in fall. The vigorous, arching canes with glossy, disease-resistant foliage require substantial annual tying and training to maintain the climbing habit; left unsupported it forms a large sprawling shrub. New Dawn tolerates partial shade better than most climbing roses, making it valuable for training on north-facing or partially shaded walls and fences.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; cold stratification for 4–6 weeks improves germination.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4–6 weeks in a damp paper towel in the refrigerator before sowing indoors to improve germination rates. Pinch plants back by one-third in late spring to encourage bushier growth and delay bloom until fall, when their purple flowers are invaluable for pollinators. Tall varieties may need staking or can be grown through a peony cage. Divide clumps every 2–3 years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent the center from dying out.

common_name: New Gold Lantana (Compact Golden-Yellow Gulf Coast Lantana)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Gold is sterile (does not produce fruit) — a significant advantage over fertile lantana cultivars that produce berries consumed by birds and potentially spread invasively in Gulf Coast natural areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; New Gold is the premier golden-yellow lantana cultivar — a Texas A&M University release selected for its uniform, pure golden-yellow flower color (no color changes as in the standard Lantana camara, which shifts from yellow to orange to red as individual flowers age within the cluster), its sterility (no viable seeds — a major ecological advantage in the Gulf South where fertile lantana spreads into natural areas via bird-dispersed berries), and its compact, mounding habit. New Gold blooms continuously from the last frost through hard frost in zone 9 — essentially a 10-month blooming season with no significant dormant period and no deadheading required. The uninterrupted, consistent golden-yellow flower display and the plant's extraordinary heat, drought, and humidity tolerance make New Gold one of the finest low-maintenance flowering perennials for the Gulf South landscape. The golden-yellow flowers are outstanding pollinator magnets — drawing gulf fritillary and monarch butterflies in remarkable numbers, along with many bee species, throughout the long bloom season. New Gold is evergreen and woody perennial in zones 9–11, dying back to the roots in hard freezes but recovering vigorously. Established plants tolerate drought and heat that would kill most flowering perennials. An indispensable plant for zone 9 full-sun borders.

common_name: New Gold Lantana (Sterile Golden-Yellow Pollinator Lantana for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Gold is sterile and will not produce the potentially invasive berries of the straight species — an important environmental advantage for Gulf South Gulf Coast plantings near natural areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; New Gold is a sterile hybrid lantana producing a continuous flush of bright golden-yellow to deep-gold flowers from spring through frost — one of the most floriferous and pollinator-attractive annuals and perennials for Gulf South full-sun gardens. The sterile nature of 'New Gold' is its most important horticultural virtue: unlike Lantana camara (common lantana), which is invasive in coastal areas of Florida and Texas where its berries are consumed and dispersed by birds, 'New Gold' produces no viable seed and no berries, eliminating the invasive spread concern that limits use of the species in sensitive native habitats. The golden-yellow flower color provides a particularly effective nectar resource for monarch and queen butterflies, swallowtails, skippers, and numerous native bee species — the warm-yellow flowers are among the most reliably butterfly-visited of any commonly grown annual in the Gulf South. In zone 8, New Gold is a perennial returning from the root each spring after winter dieback; in zone 10-11, it may persist as an evergreen subshrub. The trailing to mounding habit makes it outstanding for sunny borders, retaining wall edges, and large container plantings where the branches cascade naturally. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; excess water and nitrogen reduce flowering.

common_name: New Guinea Impatiens (Busy Lizzie, Star Impatiens)
plant_note: Plant transplants after last frost in partial to full shade; in zone 9, New Guinea Impatiens performs best March through November when planted in morning sun or dappled shade with afternoon protection from the intense summer sun. Unlike common Impatiens (I. walleriana), it tolerates more direct morning sun and is less susceptible to Impatiens downy mildew. Pinch stem tips at planting to encourage bushy growth and prolific flowering. In zone 9b, it sometimes persists into winter in sheltered spots.
directions: Plant in morning sun to partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained, organically rich soil; New Guinea Impatiens requires more light than common impatiens and will become leggy and bloom poorly in deep shade, but performs best with protection from the harsh afternoon sun of zone 9 summers. Impatiens hawkeri is a species native to Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands that served as the primary genetic source for the large-flowered New Guinea Impatiens hybrids that have become among the most popular shade-tolerant annual flowers in American horticulture since their introduction in the 1970s. The flowers are significantly larger (2–3 inches) and the foliage more diverse than common I. walleriana — leaves may be dark green, bronze, variegated cream-and-green, or deeply colored — and many modern hybrids carry contrasting leaf and flower colors simultaneously. New Guinea Impatiens are critically important for gardeners as a replacement for the traditional common impatiens (I. walleriana) following the widespread outbreak of Impatiens Downy Mildew (Plasmopara obducens) beginning around 2010, which devastated I. walleriana plantings across the US. New Guinea Impatiens are resistant to the mildew and have largely taken the place of common impatiens in commercial and home landscapes. Flowers come in every color except true blue: white, red, orange, pink, salmon, coral, lavender, and bicolors.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; new Jersey tea has an extremely deep taproot and is very difficult to transplant once established — site it carefully the first time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, rocky soil in full sun to partial shade; New Jersey tea is a remarkable native shrub with one of the most interesting histories in American botany — the dried leaves were widely used as a tea substitute during the Revolutionary War when British tea was boycotted. The fluffy clusters of tiny white flowers in early summer are among the most important nectar sources in the native prairie and woodland edge, attracting dozens of bee species, skippers, and hairstreak butterflies. The roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility over time. This shrub is exceptionally drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established, thriving on rocky, infertile, dry soils where few shrubs succeed. The spring bee value alone makes it an outstanding native garden plant. It resents being moved after establishment, so site it correctly from the start.

plant_note: Set out container plants or nursery divisions in spring after the ground is workable. Cold stratification of seeds for 4-6 weeks improves germination rates.
directions: New Mexico Checker-mallow is a native perennial of moist mountain meadows, stream banks, and valley grasslands throughout the southwestern US and Great Basin, thriving across New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, and Arizona. It produces slender, upright spikes of bright rose-pink to lavender-pink mallow flowers from June through August, adding long-lasting color to summer gardens. Plant in well-drained, moderately moist soil in full sun; once established it tolerates periods of dryness better than most other Sidalcea species. Grow from container plants or nursery-propagated divisions for best results, as transplants establish more reliably than direct-seeded plants in garden settings.

common_name: New Mexico Privet (Desert Olive, Elbow Bush)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, caliche, or sandy soil in full sun to part shade; New Mexico privet is native to dry, rocky limestone hillsides and arroyos of the Chihuahuan Desert, Trans-Pecos Texas, and adjacent New Mexico and Oklahoma — it is extremely drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; once established, no supplemental irrigation is needed. Forestiera pubescens (New Mexico privet or desert olive) is a native Texas and New Mexico shrub — a member of the olive family (Oleaceae) producing olive-like, small (1/4-inch), blue-black drupes in fall that are eagerly consumed by migrating and resident birds, including mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings. The shrub is a multi-stemmed, densely branching, semi-evergreen plant with small, light-green, opposite leaves and tiny, inconspicuous, yellowish flowers in early spring before the leaves emerge.
