As a landscape plant, Forestiera pubescens is valued for extreme drought and limestone tolerance, dense wildlife-supporting structure, and use as a native hedge or screen plant that requires no supplemental water once established. It is an outstanding alternative to non-native privets (Ligustrum species) in dry southwestern and southern landscapes, providing equivalent screening value with native habitat benefits. The small, clustered fruits produced in fall are an important berry food source for fall migrants moving through the southwestern plains.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Year lily is a Cape winter-rainfall species that blooms in winter (January in South Africa, its summer; December–February in zone 9 cultivation), producing vivid scarlet-red flowers with white teardrop markings on the lower petals. It is native to wet mountain seeps and waterfall margins (hence 'Waterfall Gladiolus') in the Western Cape. This species is one of the parent plants of the modern garden gladiolus hybrid complex.
directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; New Year lily has a historical distinction that makes it botanically significant beyond its beauty: it is one of the primary wild species from which the entire complex of modern hybrid garden gladioli was developed, contributing especially the brilliant scarlet-red color and the broad, well-formed floret shape that characterize the best hybrid gladioli. In its own right it is a beautiful species — producing in winter (unusually early, hence 'New Year lily') tall spikes of vivid, clear, true-scarlet to cardinal-red, hooded, gladiolus-type flowers with two distinctive, teardrop-shaped, white blotches on the lower three petals, the white markings providing a crisp, contrasting accent to the vivid scarlet. It grows naturally on wet mountain cliffs and waterfall margins in the Cederberg and Hottentots Holland Mountains of the Western Cape — habitats of constant water seepage and mist — and therefore tolerates and prefers the moist conditions of its native waterfall-spray habitat better than most gladioli. The winter bloom timing, in December through February, creates the unusual situation of brilliant-red gladiolus flowers in the zone 9 midwinter garden.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; or divide established clumps in early spring. Division every 2-3 years keeps plants vigorous and prevents the center die-out typical of older clumps.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile to average, well-drained soil in full sun to very light shade; New York aster is among the most profusely blooming of the native fall asters, producing dense masses of violet-blue to purple or white daisy flowers from late August through October and serving as one of the most important late-season nectar sources for migrating monarchs, painted ladies, and bumble bee queens preparing for winter. Divide clumps every two to three years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent the hollow center that develops in older undivided plants. Many cultivars offer compact habits, deeper colors, and extended bloom periods. Susceptible to powdery mildew in hot, humid climates; choose resistant varieties and provide good air circulation.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; New York fern spreads readily by rhizomes and will naturalize to form a weed-suppressing groundcover in moist, shaded woodland settings.
directions: Thelypteris noveboracensis is a light-green, deciduous native fern of eastern North American moist woodlands, instantly recognizable by its distinctive frond shape — the pinnae taper gradually toward both the tip and the base of the frond, creating a narrowed appearance at both ends that has inspired the saying that it "burns at both ends." It spreads steadily by slender, branching rhizomes to form a delicate, airy groundcover that is excellent for naturalizing large shaded areas under deciduous trees, and its light, fresh green color brightens deeply shaded spots in spring and early summer before the fronds fade to yellow and go dormant by fall. New York fern prefers moderately moist, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic woodland soils and does not tolerate waterlogging or drought, though it is more adaptable than many woodland ferns once established. Pair with wild ginger, mayapple, and Solomon's seal for a classic eastern woodland groundcover planting.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; New York ironweed tolerates consistently wet soils and is excellent in rain gardens, moist meadows, and along streams.
directions: Sow direct in spring or start indoors with 4–6 weeks of cold stratification; New York ironweed prefers moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade and is one of the best native perennials for consistently wet, sunny sites. Vernonia noveboracensis is a magnificent, tall (4–7 feet), upright native perennial of eastern North American moist meadows, stream margins, and wet prairies; it produces narrow, lance-shaped, toothed leaves on stout stems and bears large, flat-topped clusters of brilliant, deep royal-purple, fluffy, disc flowers (no ray petals) in late summer through fall — one of the most intensely saturated purples in the native plant palette and a standout in late-season gardens. The flowers are exceptional late-season nectar sources for monarchs, swallowtails, and native bees; the persistent, reddish-brown seed heads provide winter interest. Name does not restrict its range — it occurs throughout much of the eastern and central US.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to part shade; New Zealand flax is extremely adaptable, tolerating coastal salt spray, clay soils, seasonally wet conditions, and moderate drought. Named cultivars with bronze, red, purple, pink-striped, or variegated foliage are widely available and maintain their color best in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; New Zealand flax is one of the most architecturally powerful foliage plants for temperate and warm climates, producing bold, erect, sword-like leaves 3–10 feet long in green or in the many named cultivars, spectacular foliage in bronze, dark purple-red, pink-striped, variegated cream-and-green, or orange-flushed combinations. In summer, mature clumps send up dramatically tall flower spikes (up to 15 feet) bearing tubular red-orange flowers rich in nectar that attract hummingbirds and honeybirds in its native range. The Maori people of New Zealand used the leaf fibers extensively for weaving baskets, mats, and garments — one of their most important fiber plants. In warm-climate landscapes (zones 8–11) it provides bold, year-round architectural structure as a specimen, in mixed borders, or in mass plantings, tolerating coastal exposure, salt spray, wind, and drought once established. Smaller species P. cookianum is more shade-tolerant and suitable for partly shaded positions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; New Zealand iris prefers cool, moist coastal conditions and may struggle in hot, dry summer climates without supplemental irrigation.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; New Zealand iris forms upright, fan-shaped clumps of narrow, rigid, dark-green, iris-like foliage that is evergreen in mild climates and produces clusters of pure white, three-petaled flowers in late spring followed by bright orange seed capsules that persist through fall — providing three distinct seasons of ornamental interest. The neat, architectural foliage clumps are excellent for edging paths, front-of-border placement, and contemporary garden designs. Excellent drought resistance once established but benefits from supplemental water during extended hot, dry spells. In zone 8 the foliage may be damaged by hard freezes; cut back in early spring and new growth re-emerges rapidly.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in moist but well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; New Zealand iris is evergreen and provides structural foliage through the year. It tolerates both dry and seasonally moist conditions once established. The orange-tinted winter foliage (in some forms intensifying to bright orange in cold weather) is a distinctive seasonal feature. Named 'mikoikoi' in Maori.
directions: Plant in moist but well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; New Zealand iris is a structural, evergreen, iris-family perennial from New Zealand that provides year-round interest through two distinct phases: the foliage and the flowers. The sword-shaped, narrow, bright-green to orange-tinted leaves are held in the classic iris-family flat fan arrangement, and in cool weather (particularly winter) the leaves often intensify to bright orange, golden-orange, or bronze-orange in some forms, creating a warm, glowing winter-foliage effect that is particularly striking in a bare-winter border. In spring through early summer the plant produces branching, airy panicles of small, white, three-outer-petaled flowers — each individual flower small, pure white, and open-faced, collectively creating a light, airy, fine-textured spray of white above the structural foliage. The combination of the structural, strap-like fans of orange-tinged leaves with the sprays of white flowers above them is architecturally satisfying throughout the year. The Maori name 'mikoikoi' acknowledges the plant's deep cultural history in New Zealand. Outstanding in zone 9 Gulf Coast borders as a year-round structural foliage plant with spring flowers.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, humus-rich, neutral to slightly acidic soil in part to full shade; New Zealand rock lily is particularly suitable for dry shade under trees where it succeeds where many competitors fail. It tolerates brief frosts to approximately 20°F but performs best in zones 8b–10 in frost-free or near-frost-free conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in part to full shade; New Zealand rock lily is a handsome, clump-forming perennial native to New Zealand's coastal and lowland forests that produces arching rosettes of broad, strap-like, glaucous, gray-green to blue-green leaves in a loosely spreading clump, then in spring sends up branching, airy sprays of small, nodding, pure-white, star-shaped flowers with distinctive reflexed petals that hover above the foliage on slender stems — an effect of elegant, understated refinement. The 'renga' in its Maori name refers to its use as a food source (the fleshy roots were an important carbohydrate in traditional Maori diet). In gardens, it is valued as a shade-tolerant, drought-tolerant groundcover for mild climates — one of the few plants producing genuinely ornamental flowers in dry shade under large trees. The selection 'Te Puna' has especially good, compact foliage. Outstanding as a container specimen and as mass planting in shaded coastal gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors early; surface sow as light aids germination.
directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, pressing the fine seed onto the surface since light aids germination. This spicy-scented snapdragon bears dark red blooms that deepen to near-black in fall, with foliage that darkens too. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and set out after hardening off. A bumblebee favorite that makes long-lasting, striking cut flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Night Before Christmas has wide white centers that intensify in light shade — deep shade may cause the white to become somewhat translucent and less vivid.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Night Before Christmas is a medium hosta producing striking foliage with the color pattern reversed from most variegated hostas — a broad, bright white center surrounded by a dark green margin rather than the more common green center with lighter margin. The wide white center areas create exceptional brightness in dark shaded locations, almost appearing luminous in deep shade, making this one of the most effective hostas for illuminating dark corners of the garden. The white portion may show some sun scorch if exposed to afternoon sun, so full shade or dappled light is best. Near-white flowers appear on tall scapes in midsummer. Night Before Christmas is a steady-growing medium cultivar that reaches mature size in 3–4 years and forms a well-mannered clump without the rapid spreading tendencies of some smaller hostas. The bold, unusual reversed variegation makes it a prized addition to the serious hosta collection.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in cool weather or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; night phlox opens its flowers only at dusk and in overcast conditions, releasing its extraordinary fragrance — the flowers close tightly during daylight hours. Plant near pathways, seating areas, or bedroom windows to experience the nocturnal fragrance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; night phlox is a remarkable South African native that has evolved a unique relationship with night-flying moth pollinators — the flowers close completely during the day and in bright sunlight (appearing as tight, white-edged, crimson-backed buds), then open at dusk to release one of the most extraordinarily powerful and sweet fragrances of any garden plant. The fragrance has been compared to honey, vanilla, almonds, and chocolate, and a single plant in full bloom can perfume an entire garden on a still evening. The opened flowers reveal five petals, white on the inner (upper) face, deep crimson to maroon on the outer (lower) face, creating a white flower with crimson reverse. A South African Cape native, it performs best in cool seasons and mild climates, blooming through spring and into summer before declining in heat. Plant directly beside a path, a garden bench, or beneath a bedroom window to enjoy the extraordinary nocturnal fragrance — during the day the plant with its closed flowers is unremarkable, but after dusk it transforms the garden into something extraordinary.

common_name: Night-Blooming Cereus (Queen of the Night, Dutchman's Pipe Cactus)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in very well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic cactus or orchid bark mix in bright indirect shade; despite being a cactus, this epiphytic species grows naturally in tropical forest canopies and prefers shade and higher humidity than desert cacti. Allow the cut end to callus 1–2 days before planting.
directions: Root cuttings in well-drained cactus or orchid bark mix in bright indirect shade; night-blooming cereus is one of nature's most theatrical performances — the enormous, pure white, intensely fragrant flowers 10–12 inches across bloom only after dark, open for a single night, and wilt before dawn. The flowers, which appear irregularly in summer and fall, often cause garden 'watching parties' when buds are spotted, as the opening in real-time over a few hours is mesmerizing. Unlike most cacti, this epiphytic cactus from tropical forests grows best in partial shade and moist, well-drained organic soil rather than full sun and dry conditions. The flat, leaf-like stems are unremarkable until they flower. In zone 9a it is an outstanding container plant kept on a shaded porch, brought indoors before frost. The fruit is edible and sweet.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix at 70–80°F in spring and plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9–12 plant container-grown specimens directly into the landscape.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in spring after frost danger has passed in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained, moist soil in zone 9–12; night-blooming jasmine is the most powerfully fragrant shrub for warm-climate gardens, releasing an almost overwhelming sweet tropical scent from small, tubular, white-to-yellowish-green flowers that open only after dark and fill the evening air for considerable distances. Flowers appear in clusters multiple times per year in frost-free climates, making it an exceptional plant for near patios, porches, and bedroom windows where the nocturnal fragrance can be enjoyed. Though not a true jasmine (it is in the nightshade family), its fragrance is incomparable; note that the plant is toxic if ingested. Prune lightly after each flowering flush to maintain a tidy, compact shrub form.

plant_note: Plant corms 4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; night-scented gladiolus grows in winter and spring (following the Cape winter-rainfall cycle), producing its pale, cream-ivory flowers in late winter and spring with a powerful evening fragrance. Unlike most garden gladioli, this species grows from autumn through spring and goes summer dormant. Native to wet marshes and seeps of the Cape coastal zone; it tolerates seasonally moist to waterlogged conditions better than other gladioli.
directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; night-scented gladiolus is one of the most fragrant of all gladiolus species — producing in late winter and spring slender, elegant flower spikes bearing 6–10 pale cream-ivory, creamy-yellow, or very pale greenish-white flowers of delicate, almost translucent quality that in the daytime appear quietly beautiful but subdued, and in the evening fill the surrounding air with an extraordinarily sweet, powerfully rich, vanilla-jasmine-like fragrance that far surpasses any hybrid gladiolus in scent intensity. This powerful evening fragrance — evolved to attract night-flying hawk moths — is the species' defining feature and the reason for both the common name (night-scented) and the species epithet 'tristis' (sad, mournful — referring perhaps to the pale, ghostly flowers that show their best quality only after dark when they become intensely fragrant). Native to the moist coastal seeps and wetland margins of the Western Cape, it is unusual among gladioli in tolerating and even preferring seasonally wet conditions, making it valuable for moist borders and rain garden sites in zones 8–11. A plant to site near a window or garden seating area where the evening fragrance can be fully appreciated.

plant_note: Plant the large, flattened, turnip-like tuber with its top just below the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; night-scented pelargonium follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — growing and flowering in winter and spring, going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer dormancy. This species holds the botanical distinction of being the first pelargonium introduced to European horticulture — brought to Leiden Botanic Garden in 1601.
directions: Plant tuber near the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; night-scented pelargonium holds a unique place in botanical history as the first pelargonium species to reach European gardens — introduced to Leiden Botanic Garden in 1601 from the Cape of Good Hope, marking the beginning of the enormously influential European fascination with South African Pelargonium species that eventually produced the entire zonal and regal geranium garden industry. The plant itself is modest but charming: a stout, flattened, turnip-shaped tuber produces in winter and spring a rosette of finely-divided, almost fern-like, deeply-pinnate, dark green leaves of considerable delicacy, and small clusters of typical pelargonium flowers in dull yellow-brown to purplish-brown — not showy in daylight, which gave rise to the species epithet 'triste' (sad, dull) and the common name 'Sad Geranium'. But in the evening, the flowers emit a powerfully sweet, vanilla-like fragrance that explains why this modest-looking plant attracted such attention from seventeenth-century botanists. It is a nocturnal moth-pollinated species, scentless by day, intensely fragrant after dark. A plant of profound historical and botanical significance and unusual sensory quality.

common_name: Nikko Blue Hydrangea (Classic Blue Mophead Hydrangea)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5 for blue flowers), well-drained soil in partial shade; Nikko Blue flowers blue in acidic soil (pH below 5.5) and pink in alkaline soil (pH above 6.5) — add aluminum sulfate to lower pH and intensify the blue color in Gulf South alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Nikko Blue is the most widely grown blue mophead hydrangea cultivar and a classic of the American garden — producing large (8–10 inch), rounded, fully double, sky-blue to cornflower-blue flower heads in early summer from June through August. The iconic blue mophead hydrangea flower is inseparable from the image of the classic American coastal and southern garden, and Nikko Blue has been the most popular blue mophead for decades. The characteristic pH-dependent color change is part of Nikko Blue's management: acidic soil (pH 5.0–5.5) produces the richest true blue; alkaline soil (pH above 6.5) produces pink. In Gulf South alkaline soils, amending with aluminum sulfate (2 lbs per 100 sq ft) and acidifying fertilizers in spring maintains the blue color. Nikko Blue blooms on old wood — meaning the flower buds form in late summer for the following year's bloom. This means the primary rule is: do NOT prune in fall, winter, or spring before bloom; prune only by removing spent flowers immediately after bloom to shape. In zone 9, Nikko Blue is evergreen to semi-evergreen and performs best in morning sun with afternoon protection from the intense Gulf South summer heat.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; nimblewill is naturally adapted to shaded conditions and grows in woodland gardens, dry slopes, and disturbed shaded lawns throughout eastern North America.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; nimblewill is a native creeping muhly grass that is one of the more shade-tolerant warm-season grasses of eastern North America, growing at the edges of woodland gardens, on shaded slopes, and in disturbed areas with some shade. The fine-textured, soft green stems root at the nodes and spread to form a low, soft, mat-like ground cover that turns an attractive warm tan-beige in winter. While sometimes treated as a lawn weed, nimblewill is a native grass providing soft ground cover in the dry shade under trees — one of the few warm-season grasses capable of functioning as a lawn alternative in shade. It is the host plant for the Cobweb Skipper butterfly. In winter, the bleached, straw-colored mat persists and actually has decorative winter interest.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nippon spirea blooms on old wood — prune immediately after flowering (never in fall or late winter) to avoid removing flower buds for the following year. Deadheading extends the flowering display and maintains a tidy appearance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nippon spirea is a Japanese native and one of the finest white-flowering deciduous shrubs for the temperate garden — a rounded, arching shrub producing small, dark blue-green, oval leaves and in late spring through early summer, an exceptional display in which flat clusters of small, pure-white, button-like flowers cover every branch and arching stem so completely that the shrub appears to be draped in white lace, creating the characteristic mounded, snowdrift effect that earns the cultivar 'Snowmound' its name. The small, dark leaves provide an effective foil for the white flowers, and the contrast of the dark foliage and white bloom gives the plant a particularly fresh, clean appearance. Blue-green foliage color is distinctive throughout summer after bloom. Compact enough for foundation plantings and mixed shrub borders, it performs best with consistent moisture and full sun. Other cultivars include 'Halward's Silver' (lower and more compact) and 'June Bride' (particularly dense flower clusters). Widely used in residential landscaping across the northern United States.

common_name: Nirvana Annual Vinca (Disease-Resistant Compact Vinca Series)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; this series shows good resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a serious fungal disease of annual vinca in hot, humid conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; overly wet or poorly drained soil quickly leads to root and stem rot. Nirvana is a compact, uniform annual vinca series bred with strong resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a fungal disease that devastates less resistant vinca plantings during hot, humid, rainy summers typical of the Gulf South. It produces abundant, flat-faced flowers in a range of colors over a dense, well-branched mound that tolerates heat, drought, and reflected heat from pavement better than almost any other bedding annual, blooming continuously from late spring through frost with essentially no deadheading required. It is an excellent low-maintenance choice for hot, sunny beds, medians, and containers where many other annuals struggle.

common_name: Noble Dendrobium (Nobile Orchid, Cane Orchid, Spring Orchid)
plant_note: Grow in a slatted orchid pot or basket with coarse bark media in bright indirect to partial direct light; Dendrobium nobile is one of the more cold-tolerant orchids, surviving temperatures to 40°F if kept dry — its Himalayan origin predisposes it to cool winters. In zone 9, grow on a shaded porch or bright indoor windowsill. CRITICAL for blooming: withhold water almost completely (barely misting monthly) for 6–8 weeks in fall when nights cool to 50–55°F — this cool-dry rest is essential for flower bud development. After rest period, resume normal watering to trigger bud development. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct morning sun — Noble Dendrobium blooms most prolifically in good light with an unobstructed east or shaded south exposure; it will survive but rarely bloom in dim conditions. Dendrobium nobile is a sympodial, cane-forming epiphytic orchid native to the Himalayan foothills of India (Assam, Sikkim, Meghalaya), Nepal, Bhutan, southern China, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam, growing at elevations of 2,000–5,000 feet in a climate with cool, dry winters and warm, wet summers. The plant produces upright, cane-like pseudobulbs (stems) 12–24 inches tall clothed in leaves that are sometimes deciduous in winter. In late winter and spring, after the essential cool-dry rest period, flower buds emerge from the nodes along the previous year's canes and open to clusters of 3–5 flowers per node, covering the entire length of each cane — in a well-bloomed specimen, dozens of clusters may open simultaneously. The flowers are large (2–3 inches), waxy, fragrant, in shades of white to lavender-purple with a dark purple center in the lip — a classically beautiful orchid flower. Dendrobium nobile is the parent species of the large Dendrobium nobile hybrid orchids widely sold as gift plants in spring, which share the clustered-blooming habit. More cold-tolerant than most popular orchids. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; noble fir grows naturally at high elevations (2,000–5,500 feet) in the Cascades and Siskiyous, requiring cool, moist, well-drained conditions. Does not tolerate hot, dry, or poorly drained sites.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; noble fir is the Christmas tree of the Pacific Northwest — the most widely grown Christmas tree in the Pacific Northwest states, valued for its beautiful, stiff branches, perfect conical form, blue-gray needles, and exceptional needle retention after cutting. In the wild it is one of the largest and most impressive native firs, reaching 200+ feet in old-growth Cascade forests. The enormous cylindrical cones — up to 10 inches long — are covered with prominent, downward-pointing bract tips that give them a distinctly bristly appearance and make them the showiest cones of any North American fir. Nobel fir foliage boughs are the primary decorative greenery used throughout the Pacific Northwest holiday season, cut and sold in vast quantities from plantation-grown trees. Widely planted as a specimen ornamental in gardens in zones 4–7.

plant_note: Divide established clumps after flowering or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; nodding clivia has a more pendulous flower than C. miniata and produces longer, narrower leaves. Like all clivias, it requires a dry winter rest period to trigger reliable spring flowering — reduce watering significantly from late autumn through winter. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; nodding clivia is the first described species in the Clivia genus and is the most pendulous-flowered — producing in spring a drooping umbel of 20–40 tubular-funnel flowers that hang downward more decisively than C. miniata, in shades of orange-red to salmon with yellow-green tips on the outer petal margins, creating a pendant, chandelier-like cluster of nodding tubes. The leaf blades are narrower and longer than C. miniata, with a slightly wavy or recurved texture. It grows naturally in the dense, humid, coastal forests of the Eastern Cape near the sea, an environment very different from the drier, higher-altitude KwaZulu-Natal forests of C. miniata. In cultivation it provides the same outstanding shade tolerance — thriving in the deep, dry shade under large trees — with the somewhat less spectacular but more refined pendant flower form. Like C. miniata, it is evergreen, long-lived, and requires the dry winter rest period to flower. A plant for clivia collectors and those who appreciate the more nuanced, quiet elegance of the drooping flower form over the bold upward-facing clusters of C. miniata.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated tubers or transplants in fall in moist to moderately wet, acidic to neutral, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; nodding ladies' tresses is the most adaptable of all native terrestrial orchids and can succeed in a wider range of conditions than most, including moist meadows and roadsides.
directions: Nodding ladies' tresses is the most common and widely distributed of all North American native orchids — a fall-blooming terrestrial orchid found in moist meadows, roadsides, and open woodland edges across virtually the entire eastern United States, producing delicate spiral-whorled spikes of small, pure white, vanilla-scented flowers that are a surprise and delight when discovered blooming in September and October when orchids are the last thing most people expect to find flowering. Its late-season bloom coincides with the final nectar demand of native bumblebee queens preparing for winter, and the white, fragrant flowers are heavily visited by yellow-and-black native bumblebees that are attracted from considerable distance by the fragrance. Unlike most native terrestrial orchids, nodding ladies' tresses is found in a wide variety of habitats including disturbed sites, roadsides, golf courses, and moist lawns, making it potentially the most accessible native orchid for cultivation — it has established itself from naturally windblown seed in appropriate garden conditions without deliberate planting. A beautiful orchid available from specialist native nurseries that can succeed in average moist garden conditions when other native orchids would fail.

plant_note: Divide rhizome clumps in fall or plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Nodding Mandarin is less common in cultivation than Yellow Mandarin but adapts well to the same moist woodland garden conditions.
directions: Nodding Mandarin is a beautiful native woodland perennial distinguished from its close relative Yellow Mandarin (Disporum lanuginosum) by its larger, pure white, purple-spotted, bell-shaped flowers that dangle conspicuously from arching branch tips in April and May — an unusual and eye-catching display in the spring shade garden. Native to moist, rich, deciduous cove forests and north-facing slopes of the Appalachians from Ohio and Pennsylvania south to Georgia and Alabama, it grows in similar conditions to Solomon's seal and False Solomon's seal, with which it often associates. The red-orange berries that follow in summer attract birds and add late-season interest; the plant slowly spreads by rhizome to form loose, graceful colonies over time. Divide clumps in fall, or plant nursery transplants in spring in deeply amended, consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade.

plant_note: Plant fresh rhizomes in late summer or early fall at 2–3 in depth in moist, humus-rich woodland soil; from seed, expect 4–7 years to first bloom as seeds require double dormancy — a warm period followed by cold before germination, then another year before the seedling emerges. Plant divisions are far more practical.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, deep, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in full to partial shade; nodding trillium is distinguished by its white flower that hangs below the leaves on a recurved peduncle, making it easy to overlook in the wild but charming on close inspection. The flower faces downward and is pollinated by bumblebees that must hover or enter from beneath. Plant rhizomes pointed-end up at a depth of 2–3 inches in fall, and mulch with shredded leaves to mimic the natural leaf litter of its woodland floor habitat. Never harvest plants from the wild — all trilliums are extremely slow-growing from seed and wild populations decline quickly when disturbed. Shade and cool, moist conditions are essential throughout the growing season.

plant_note: Plant tubers hollow-side up in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. In zone 9 Nonstop tuberous begonias can be left in the ground in frost-free conditions as tender perennials, returning each spring with increasing vigor. For container growing, use high-quality potting mix with excellent drainage — begonia tubers rot quickly in soggy soil. Remove spent flowers to maintain the display, though the Nonstop series has better self-cleaning ability than older tuberous begonia types.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist, well-drained, rich, slightly acidic soil or container mix; Nonstop Rose is a Benary-bred tuberous begonia series renowned for its continuous, season-long flowering without the summer dormancy period that interrupted flowering in traditional tuberous begonias, and 'Rose' refers to the full, camellia-like double flowers of a rich, warm rose-pink color — among the largest and most impressive of any shade flower available. The tuberous begonia form — with massive, fully double, ruffled flowers reminiscent of garden roses or camellias in size and form — creates a dramatic effect impossible to achieve with fibrous begonias, coleus, or impatiens. The Nonstop series combines this large, showy flower with vigorous, heat-tolerant performance through the entire warm season, creating reliable, low-maintenance shade container displays. In zone 9 the long warm season brings out extended performance from established tubers, and the tropical origin of Begonia means it thrives in the warm, humid conditions of Gulf Coast summers when protected from intense direct afternoon sun.

subcategory: Norfolk Island Pacific coastal ornamental tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in zone 9–11; Norfolk Island Hibiscus (Whitewood, Cow Itch Tree) is a handsome, symmetrical, pyramidal-form tree endemic to Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island in the South Pacific — widely planted as a coastal street tree in Australia and California for its exceptional tolerance of salt winds, poor sandy soils, and coastal exposure — producing large, attractive, pale lavender-pink flowers throughout spring and summer that resemble hibiscus blooms.
directions: Plant Lagunaria patersonia in full sun in well-drained, lean, sandy or loamy soil; exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, coastal winds, poor soils, and drought once established — making it one of the best trees for beachfront and coastal gardens; CAUTION: the brown, dry seed pods contain fine, irritating hairs (similar to fiberglass) that cause significant skin, eye, and respiratory irritation — wear gloves and a mask when collecting or handling seed pods. Norfolk Island Hibiscus is a premier coastal street and garden tree for subtropical coastal areas — its dense, pyramidal crown, salt-spray tolerance, and resistance to sandy, nutrient-poor soils make it an ideal tree for challenging coastal garden sites where most other trees fail. The large, 3-inch, pale mauve-lavender flowers (resembling a subdued hibiscus) appear throughout spring and summer and are genuinely attractive; the tree forms a natural, neat, pyramidal shape requiring little pruning. Endemic to Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island — both tiny, remote South Pacific islands — it has been widely planted as a coastal amenity tree across Australia's eastern coast, California, Hawaii, and Florida. In the Gulf Coast zone 9–10 garden, it performs excellently in exposed coastal positions, along salt air-exposed roadsides, and in hot, sandy inland gardens. The sole species in its genus (Lagunaria), it represents an important isolated branch of the hibiscus family.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; northern bayberry fixes nitrogen through root associations with Frankia bacteria and thrives in infertile, sandy, coastal soils — fertilizing is counterproductive and produces excessive, rank growth.
directions: Plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; northern bayberry is a native, semi-evergreen shrub of eastern North American coastal areas that provides four compelling reasons for wider use: extraordinary tolerance of sandy, nutrient-poor, salty coastal soil where most shrubs fail; dense clusters of small, waxy, blue-gray berries along the stems that provide essential late-autumn and winter food for myrtle warblers (yellow-rumped warblers), tree swallows, and other migratory birds that depend on the high-fat bayberry wax for energy during migration; the rich, resinous, spicy-sweet fragrance of the leaves and berries that perfumes the landscape in warm weather; and the historical use of the waxy berries in traditional bayberry candle-making. Dioecious — plant both male and female plants for berry production. Nitrogen-fixing root associations with Frankia bacteria allow the plant to thrive in infertile soils without fertilization.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, deep loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; northern catalpa is adaptable to a wide range of soils and tolerates both wet and dry conditions once established. Fast-growing — can put on 3–5 feet of height per year when young in moist, fertile conditions.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, deep loamy or clay-loam soil in full sun; northern catalpa is one of the most bold and tropical-looking native trees of the central and eastern US — producing enormous, heart-shaped leaves (up to 12 inches long and wide), spectacular large clusters of white, orchid-like flowers with purple and yellow markings in early summer, and uniquely distinctive long, thin, bean-like seed pods ('Indian cigars' or 'catawba worms') up to 20 inches long that dangle from the tree through winter. The seed pods are entirely unique among North American trees. The catawba sphinx moth (Ceratomia catalpae) larva feeds exclusively on catalpa leaves and is so well-known as live fishing bait ('catalpa worms') that catalpa groves were historically planted near southern fishing ponds specifically to culture the caterpillars. The wood is exceptionally rot-resistant and was widely used for fence posts and railroad ties. A dramatic, fast-growing shade tree for large, open landscape areas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; northern lady fern is adaptable to a range of moisture levels once established and makes a graceful, easy-care addition to shaded borders and woodland gardens throughout northern and mountain regions.
directions: Athyrium angustum (often treated as Athyrium filix-femina var. angustum, the northern lady fern) is a graceful, deciduous native fern of eastern and central North America, producing broadly triangular to lanceolate, bipinnate-pinnatifid fronds with a finely textured, airy appearance on arching, pale-green to reddish-tinged stipes; it is extremely similar to the widely grown common lady fern (A. filix-femina) and shares its elegant, vase-shaped habit. Northern lady fern prefers consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade and tolerates wet conditions well, though it will also persist in moderately dry shade once established, making it more adaptable than many woodland ferns. It is an excellent, trouble-free native substitute for the popular Japanese painted fern (A. niponicum) and its cultivars, and combines beautifully with hostas, astilbe, native bleeding heart, and trilliums. Divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors for earlier bloom. This custom blend produces large four- to five-inch flowers in a dazzling mix of colors that draw butterflies and pollinators. Plant in masses for the best show, give plenty of sun and airflow to limit mildew, and deadhead to extend flowering. Excellent for cutting.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring, barely covering the rhizome with soil; water gently until established.
directions: This elegant native fern requires deep to dappled shade and reliably moist, near-neutral to slightly alkaline soil; it is particularly stunning near water features where humidity stays high. Plant the shallow, creeping rhizome horizontally just below the soil surface and avoid root disturbance once established. The distinctive fan-shaped, horizontally tiered fronds on dark wiry stems die back completely in winter; mark the location to avoid accidentally digging the dormant rhizome. Divide overgrown clumps in early spring by gently separating rhizome sections, each with at least one growing tip.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist to moderately well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Northern Prickly Ash spreads by root suckers and is useful for naturalized thickets and hedgerows; handle with care due to the sharp spines at branch nodes.
directions: Northern Prickly Ash is a native spiny shrub of open woods, thickets, and stream banks across eastern North America from Quebec south to the Gulf states, bearing paired spines at the branch nodes and aromatic compound leaves that release a sharp citrus fragrance when crushed. A member of the citrus family (Rutaceae) and close relative of the southern Hercules' Club, the aromatic bark contains numbing, anesthetic compounds that were applied by many Native American peoples — including the Ojibwe, Chippewa, and Cherokee — directly to sore gums for toothache relief; the bark was also used as a fish poison and to treat digestive ailments, earning the plant the folk name toothache tree. An important host plant for the giant swallowtail butterfly in the northern portion of its range, where it often replaces the closely related Zanthoxylum clava-herculis as the primary larval host plant, Northern Prickly Ash provides dense, spiny nesting cover for birds. Plant in moist to moderately well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; it spreads by root suckers to form thickets and is most useful in naturalized hedgerows and wildlife habitat plantings.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Northwind's strong, upright habit and resistance to flopping make it suitable for windier positions where lower-stature grasses might lodge.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Northwind is the premier tall, strongly upright switchgrass cultivar — reaching 4–5 feet tall with an exceptionally stiff, soldier-straight, non-flopping habit that makes it outstanding for use as a vertical accent, tall screen, or architectural mass planting. The wide, flat, blue-green blades are distinctive and hold their upright posture better through summer heat and fall rains than almost any other switchgrass cultivar. In fall the foliage transitions to yellow-gold, and the airy, open panicle seed heads remain attractive through winter. Northwind was introduced by Roy Diblik of Northwind Perennial Farm in Wisconsin and has become one of the standard switchgrass selections for landscape use due to its exceptional habit consistency. The strong upright form combines beautifully with contrasting horizontal-habit companions like coneflowers and salvias, and the blue-green summer color is cool and sophisticated. Being a native grass, it requires no supplemental fertilization, minimal irrigation once established, and is highly adaptable to the Gulf Coast's clay soils and occasional wet periods. Birds feed on the seeds in winter. Cut back to 6 inches in February in zone 9.

common_name: Nuccio's Gems Camellia (Formal Double White Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Gems is a mid-season japonica blooming January through March in zone 9 — one of the most perfect formal double white camellias in cultivation.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Gems is one of the most celebrated and award-winning Camellia japonica cultivars ever introduced — developed by Nuccio's Nurseries in Altadena, California, and recognized by the American Camellia Society for its exceptionally formal, regular, perfectly arranged double flowers of pure white with a very faint pink blush at times in cool temperatures. The flowers are consistently formal double in form — every petal is precisely arranged in concentric rings with mathematical regularity, with no stamens visible and no disorder of petals regardless of weather conditions. This consistency of form across different temperatures and conditions is the defining quality of Nuccio's Gems and the characteristic most prized by camellia enthusiasts. The blooms are medium-large (3.5–4.5 inches), long-lasting, and borne prolifically over a mid-season period from January through March in zone 9. The upright-growing shrub develops excellent deep-green, lustrous foliage and a clean, compact form reaching 6–10 feet. Like all C. japonica cultivars in zone 9, plant in dappled shade or morning sun with afternoon shade — the flowers burn in full afternoon sun. Mulch heavily, maintain consistent moisture, and feed with acid-forming azalea fertilizer in March and June. The pure white, perfectly formal flowers of Nuccio's Gems are considered among the finest white camellias available to American gardeners.

common_name: Nuccio's Pearl Camellia (Formal Double White-Blushed-Pink Camellia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Nuccio's Pearl produces formal, perfectly symmetrical double flowers in soft white blushed with pale pink at the petal edges.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to filtered light. Nuccio's Pearl, from the renowned Nuccio's Nurseries camellia breeding program in California, produces exquisitely formal, tightly overlapping double flowers in soft white delicately blushed with pale pink along the petal edges, a refined color and form prized by camellia show exhibitors and collectors. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars it blooms in winter into early spring on a slow-growing, long-lived evergreen shrub with glossy, dark green foliage that provides year-round structure even when not in flower. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil, and protect from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can damage both the foliage and the delicate flowers.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring or fall; light aids germination.
directions: Surface sow the tiny seed in early spring or fall, as light is needed for germination and plants dislike transplanting. Often grown as a hardy annual or short-lived perennial, it produces chiffon-like blooms in orange, pale pink, yellow, and white that glow when backlit by the sun. Blooming in spring, it is fairly drought tolerant and prefers cool weather. Deadhead to prolong the display.

common_name: Nun's Orchid (Swamp Orchid, Veiled Nun Orchid, Limestone Orchid)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or container-grown divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil or orchid mix; Phaius tankervilleae is one of the largest and most cold-tolerant terrestrial orchids for zone 9-10 garden use — established clumps have survived brief temperatures to 28°F with heavy mulch in zone 9a. The tall flower spikes (2–4 feet) bearing 10–20 large flowers make this one of the most spectacular orchids for outdoor garden planting. Divide clumps every 3–4 years. Needs consistent moisture during active growth (spring–fall); reduce watering in winter. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Nun's Orchid grows best in the consistently moist, organically rich conditions of a shaded or partially shaded garden bed under large trees, where its tall flower spikes create an outstanding spring display. Phaius tankervilleae is a large, clump-forming terrestrial orchid native from India through Southeast Asia, China, Papua New Guinea to Australia and many Pacific Islands in the Orchidaceae family — one of the most spectacular terrestrial orchids available for outdoor garden planting in zone 9-11 subtropical gardens. The plant produces large, egg-shaped pseudobulbs and tall, broad, pleated leaves (18–30 inches) that create a lush, tropical-looking clump. In late winter to spring, the pseudobulbs send up one to several tall, erect flower spikes 2–4 feet tall, each bearing 10–20 large (3-inch) flowers in sequence from the bottom up. Each flower has an unusual, distinctive color combination: the outer surface of the sepals and petals is white to pale cream, while the inner surface is a rich deep brown-maroon to chocolate-brown with a white-edged, rose-purple to magenta lip — the combination of white outside and dark inside that inspired the common name 'Nun's Orchid' for the resemblance to a nun's habit. The tall spikes with their two-toned flowers are impressive in the shade garden. Naturalized in parts of Florida and considered invasive in Hawaii — check local regulations. Non-toxic.

common_name: Nuttall Oak (Pin Oak, Red River Oak)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile, heavy clay or sandy loam soil in full sun; Nuttall oak is one of the most flood-tolerant of all oaks, native to wet bottomlands that flood seasonally. It is the preferred oak for difficult wet sites in the Mississippi and Red River valleys and Gulf Coast interior.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, clay or heavy soil in full sun; Nuttall oak (Q. texana) is one of the most underused and underrated of all large southern oaks — a fast-growing (3–4 feet per year when young), majestic bottomland tree that reaches 60–90 feet with excellent scarlet fall color and one of the most important acorn crops of any oak, producing large (3/4 inch) acorns in abundance that are critical food for wood ducks, waterfowl, deer, squirrels, and turkeys. It is uniquely adapted to seasonally flooded, waterlogged clay soils where most trees cannot survive, making it the premier oak for wet, poorly drained sites, wet parking lot islands, and retention basin margins. Excellent fall color (brilliant scarlet) distinguishes it from most southern red-group oaks. Not to be confused with Q. nuttallii (same species, now synonymized as Q. texana).

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, humus-rich, shaded woodland soil; winter cold stratifies seed naturally for spring germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall into moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade, allowing winter cold to stratify seed naturally before spring germination; keep soil consistently moist through the first season until plants are well established. This native mint-family perennial is at home on shaded slopes, stream banks, and rock ledges throughout the Appalachians and eastern mountain states, where its square stems with opposite, softly hairy, toothed leaves are diagnostic. Whorled clusters of small, pink to rose-pink, 2-lipped flowers appear along the upper stems in summer and are of particular value to long-tongued bumblebees and bumblebee specialists that cannot access shallower flowers. An understated but ecologically important native shade mint for woodland gardens and naturalized stream bank plantings in zones 4-8.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in lean, very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nuttall's linanthus is native to dry, rocky, chaparral and coastal sage scrub in California and Baja California and requires excellent drainage. It is perennial in zones 8–10 but may be grown as an annual in colder regions. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain compact form.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nuttall's linanthus is a California and Baja California native subshrub of the chaparral, producing exceptionally fine-textured, needle-like leaves that give the entire plant a distinctive, soft, feathery texture strongly reminiscent of heather or fine pine foliage — creating year-round textural interest before the plant flowers. In spring and early summer it produces small, tubular, five-petaled flowers in white to pale lavender carried in tight clusters at the branch tips, and on a mature, well-established plant, these flower clusters can be produced in sufficient abundance to create an attractive display against the distinctive, very fine, needle-textured foliage. Native to dry, rocky, chaparral habitats of the California Coast Ranges where it grows among other drought-adapted shrubs, it is well adapted to the Mediterranean-climate conditions of California and Gulf Coast gardens. The fine, needle-like foliage texture provides year-round structural interest in the dry garden that few other plants can match. Outstanding combined with other California native shrubs — ceanothus, manzanita, and salvias — in low-water native plant gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of wet, sandy, strongly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Nuttall's lobelia grows in wet, sandy, acidic depressions, bog edges, and seepage areas of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain. Seeds are tiny — do not cover.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of wet, sandy, strongly acidic, organic-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Nuttall's lobelia is a delicate, small-flowered annual or biennial lobelia of wet, sandy, acidic habitats — pond margins with sandy, bare substrate, seepage slopes, and wet depressions in pine flatwoods. The tiny, pale blue to nearly white flowers are much smaller than those of cardinal flower and great blue lobelia, but produced in airy, branching sprays on thread-thin stems. The plant is adapted to pioneer conditions on bare, wet, sandy, exposed soil — the same disturbed conditions that characterize the margins of seasonally fluctuating ponds and bog pools. It naturalizes in appropriate wet, sandy, acidic garden conditions by self-sowing. A botanically interesting native for bog gardens and naturalistic wetland features in zone 9a.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat with sandpaper or nicking with a knife; Nuttall's wild indigo requires cold stratification over winter and is slow from seed — expect 2–3 years to first bloom — but once established with its deep taproot it is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially permanent; sow in a permanent, well-drained location in lean to sandy soil in full sun.
directions: Sow direct in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat, in lean, very well-drained, sandy or rocky, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nuttall's wild indigo is a compact, small-statured Baptisia native to the sandy pine woodlands, dry prairies, and open disturbed ground of Texas, Louisiana, and surrounding Gulf Coast states, where it is one of the more drought-tolerant members of the genus — well suited to the thin, acidic, sandy soils of the coastal plain. Named in honor of Thomas Nuttall, the English-American botanist who collected extensively across North America in the early nineteenth century, this species produces small, white to cream-colored, pea-like flowers in slender racemes in spring, followed by the inflated seed pods characteristic of the genus; it is smaller and more delicate in appearance than B. australis or B. sphaerocarpa, making it suitable for scale-appropriate plantings in smaller native gardens. Like all wild indigos it is a nitrogen-fixing legume, develops a deep taproot that makes transplanting impractical, and is very slow to reach first bloom from seed — patience of 2–3 years is required; in return it becomes an essentially permanent, zero-maintenance plant that thrives in the lean, dry conditions that challenge most ornamentals. Nuttall's wild indigo is an important early-season resource for bumblebee queens and specialist native bees in the Southeast and is a valuable addition to native plantings in the Gulf Coast region.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container-grown specimens in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade in spring; oak fern requires cool, consistently moist conditions and is not suited to hot or dry sites — it thrives under conifers and in moist ravines in cool northern and mountain climates.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full shade; oak fern is one of the most exquisitely delicate and beautiful of all small shade ferns — each frond consists of a nearly horizontal, bright apple-green, triangular blade divided into three nearly equal, spreading lobes, held on a slender black stalk so that the fronds appear to float in mid-air at ankle height like a constellation of tiny green triangles. The effect of a colony of oak fern spreading across the dark forest floor is luminous and ethereal. It spreads slowly by underground rhizomes to form a low, delicate, weed-suppressing groundcover under large conifers and northern hardwoods in moist, cool gardens. It requires consistently moist, cool conditions and is best suited to zones 2–7 in cool-summer climates; it struggles in hot, humid summers south of zone 6. An essential fern for naturalistic cool-climate shade garden compositions with mosses, trilliums, and Canada mayflower.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped hollies in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Oakland Holly is a fast-growing hybrid selected for a naturally narrow, dense, oval form that screens effectively in less horizontal space than broader hollies like Nellie R. Stevens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Oakland Holly is a vigorous, fast-growing hybrid holly bred for a naturally narrow, upright, oval form that provides dense, formal screening in a noticeably smaller footprint than broader hollies such as Nellie R. Stevens, making it useful for property-line screens and narrow side yards where space is limited. The glossy, dark green, lightly spined evergreen foliage holds its color and density year-round with minimal pruning required to maintain a neat shape, and the plant produces small red berries in fall and winter that provide food for songbirds. It is heat- and humidity-tolerant, adapts well to Gulf Coast clay soils once established, and shows good resistance to the pests and diseases that can trouble other broadleaf evergreens. Established plants are reasonably drought-tolerant, though regular water during the first one to two years speeds establishment. Prune, if needed, in late winter or after the main flush of new spring growth to maintain the desired screen height and width.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; blooms on old wood — do not prune until after bloom or you will remove next year's flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; oakleaf hydrangea is the premier four-season native flowering shrub for shade, offering showy white cone-shaped flower panicles in early summer that fade gracefully to dusty pink and tan and persist on the plant, then brilliant orange-red-purple fall foliage, and finally striking cinnamon-brown exfoliating bark on thick, architectural stems all winter. It is native to shaded ravines and woodland slopes in the Southeast. The shrub blooms on old wood — do not prune unless absolutely necessary, and only immediately after bloom. Named cultivars like 'Snow Queen' (large upright blooms), 'Pee Wee' (compact), and 'Ruby Slippers' (pink flowers) are widely available and all perform well in zone 8–9 gardens.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring just as growth resumes, or sow seed in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; obedient plant spreads aggressively by rhizomes and self-seeding in moist, fertile soils — divide every 2–3 years to manage spread and maintain vigor, and consider planting in lean, drier soils to limit rhizome spread.
directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained to moderately wet soil in full sun to partial shade; obedient plant is one of the most distinctive late-summer native wildflowers of eastern and central North America, producing stiff, upright square stems topped with dense, tapering spikes of tubular, two-lipped flowers in bright pink to magenta-purple from July through September, at a time when many other wildflowers are past their peak. The common name 'obedient plant' refers to the curious mechanical property of the individual flowers: each floret is hinged on its calyx and will stay precisely where it is manually repositioned on the spike, whether left, right, up, or down — a botanical party trick that has delighted gardeners for centuries and makes it instantly memorable. It is an important late-season nectar plant for ruby-throated hummingbirds, bumblebees, and various long-tongued native bees; the square stems and opposite leaves identify it as a member of the mint family (Lamiaceae), and like many mints it spreads vigorously by creeping rhizomes and can colonize large areas rapidly in moist, fertile conditions. Plant in lean, slightly drier soils to rein in the rhizome spread, or divide and share clumps every 2–3 years; named cultivars like 'Miss Manners' (white, less spreading) are more garden-well-behaved but the straight species has greater wildlife value.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Obsession thrives in partial shade in zone 9 — the bright red winter foliage color develops most vividly with some cold exposure, while full shade reduces the red intensity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Obsession is a distinctive compact nandina cultivar selected for its exceptionally vivid and sustained red winter foliage color — the leaves turn deep fire-engine red in fall and winter, holding this brilliant color for months, creating one of the most eye-catching winter shrubs in the Gulf South landscape. Unlike Firepower nandina (which turns bright orange-red in full sun and greenish in shade), Obsession maintains its rich red color even in partial shade positions, expanding its landscape use to partially shaded areas where Firepower often reverts to less colorful foliage. Obsession additionally produces clusters of red berries — a quality that Firepower lacks — providing bird food and additional ornamental interest through winter. The compact, upright-mounding habit stays 2–3 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning. Like all nandinas, Obsession is remarkably tough — tolerating clay, drought, heat, humidity, and partial shade that challenge many other ornamental shrubs. Note: Nandina domestica and its berries are toxic to birds and the plant is considered invasive in some Gulf South natural areas (particularly the Southeast) — plant in contained landscape settings rather than adjacent to natural areas, and deadhead flowers if self-seeding becomes a concern.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall; in zone 8–9 plant September–March. In zone 9 Obsidian benefits from afternoon shade protection and consistent moisture during summer. Divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor as the crown can lift out of the soil over time — replant divisions slightly deeper than the original position. The nearly black foliage of Obsidian maintains better color in partial shade than in full sun, where high heat can fade the dark pigmentation.
directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Obsidian is a Terra Nova Nurseries Heuchera cultivar producing some of the darkest foliage in the genus — rounded, slightly ruffled leaves of an intense, glossy, near-black purple that approaches true black in shade conditions, creating a dramatic contrast with lighter companion plants in shade garden designs. The deep coloration persists through the entire growing season without fading, which distinguishes Obsidian from many dark-leaved heucheras that lighten to bronze or reddish-purple in summer heat. The dark, satiny leaves create a striking design element when planted alongside silver-leaved plants (Lamium, Pulmonaria), chartreuse-leaved hostas, or bright-flowered shade perennials where the near-black color amplifies the visual contrast. In early summer, Obsidian produces tall, airy wands of small white flowers that hover above the dark foliage — a classic heuchera flowering display that attracts hummingbirds and beneficial insects. The evergreen to semi-evergreen habit provides year-round interest in zone 7–9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Obsidian holds its jet-black leaf color best in partial shade — too much sun fades the leaves toward bronze, while deep shade causes them to green up.
directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Obsidian is widely considered the darkest-leafed heuchera in cultivation — the almost black, very glossy, rounded leaves appear nearly jet-black in partial shade, with the characteristic purple-black lobe color that named the cultivar after the volcanic glass. The high gloss surface reflects light in a way that makes the plant sparkle in shaded settings, creating an extraordinary contrast with chartreuse, gold, or bright-green companion plants. This cultivar was selected for darker color and stronger habit than Palace Purple and other early dark heucheras. Small cream-to-pinkish flowers appear on wiry scapes in early summer. In zone 8–9, afternoon shade, good drainage, and consistent moisture are essential — most heucheras struggle with humid summer heat, and Obsidian is best treated as a perennial that may need replacing after 3–4 years in warm climates rather than as the ultra-long-lived perennial it is in cooler zones.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in fall; Ocean Grape Hyacinth is distinguished from common grape hyacinth (Muscari armeniacum) by its distinctive bicolor flowers — the lower florets are bright, cobalt blue while the upper florets are white or pale blue, creating a sharp two-toned color division. The cultivar Ocean Magic is the most widely available bicolor selection.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; ocean grape hyacinth is the most visually distinctive grape hyacinth, producing compact spikes with a sharply defined two-tone appearance quite unlike the uniform blue of common grape hyacinth — the lower portion of each spike is composed of the typical bright cobalt-blue, closed urn-shaped florets of a grape hyacinth, while the upper quarter to third of the spike bears small, white to pale-blue, open florets that provide an abrupt, clean color transition. The overall effect of a clump in full bloom — dozens of blue-and-white bicolored spikes packed together — is very eye-catching and distinctive. The cultivar Ocean Magic is the standard commercial form of this effect and is widely available as named bulbs. Like all grape hyacinths, it naturalizes freely over time, multiplying by offsets to create expanding drifts. Outstanding when massed under early spring bulbs or planted in drifts with white tulips or yellow narcissus for a spring color combination.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to high, shifting shade under deciduous trees. Oconee Azalea prefers somewhat drier, well-drained upland soils and will not tolerate wet feet or alkaline conditions.
directions: Oconee Azalea is a spectacular native deciduous azalea of dry to mesic upland oak-hickory and pine-oak woods of Georgia and South Carolina, producing some of the most vivid orange, red, and scarlet floral displays of any native North American shrub when it blooms in March and April — before or with the emerging leaves — providing a burst of intense color unlike any other native plant in the early spring landscape. The flowers are not fragrant but are intensely colored in shades of flame orange to deep scarlet, and the plant's natural occurrence is restricted to a relatively small area of the inner coastal plain and piedmont of the Carolinas, making it a regionally rare and culturally significant plant of considerable interest to azalea enthusiasts. A moderate-growing shrub that develops a naturally graceful, open, rounded form, Oconee Azalea provides superior wildlife value to most exotic azalea cultivars and supports native bumblebee queens emerging in early spring. Plant in well-drained, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to high, shifting shade; Oconee Azalea will not tolerate wet feet or alkaline soils.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated transplants in early spring in moist, humus-rich, highly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in deep shade; Oconee Bells is one of the rarest native wildflowers in North America and should only be sourced from specialty nurseries that propagate their own plants.
directions: Oconee Bells is one of the rarest and most celebrated native wildflowers in North America — an Appalachian endemic once thought extinct, restricted to a handful of gorge sites along the headwaters of the Savannah River in western South Carolina, southwestern North Carolina, and extreme northeastern Georgia, where it grows in spray zones of stream gorges in dense, deeply shaded, moist, acidic forests with rhododendron and galax as companions. A compact, slowly spreading evergreen ground cover with rounded, glossy, galax-like leaves and nodding, fringed white to pale pink bell-shaped flowers that emerge from January to March before most woodland plants have awoken, it is one of the first signs of spring in the southern mountain garden. It requires extremely acidic, consistently moist, humus-rich soil with perfect drainage in deep shade, and is notoriously slow to establish — expect 2–5 years before a planting spreads noticeably. Source only from specialty native plant nurseries; wild collection is illegal and has historically devastated native populations.

common_name: October Glory Red Maple (Late-Season Brilliant Red Fall Color Maple)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; October Glory holds its leaves and colors later into fall than most red maples, giving a late burst of brilliant red color after other trees have already dropped their leaves.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. October Glory is one of the most widely planted red maple cultivars for its dependable, long-lasting, brilliant red fall color that develops later in the season than most maples, extending the fall color display after earlier-turning trees have already gone bare. It grows at a moderate-to-fast rate into a dense, rounded shade tree and tolerates a wider range of soil conditions, including occasional wet sites, than many other shade trees, making it a versatile choice for yards, streets, and parks. Like other red maples it has relatively shallow, fibrous roots that can compete with grass and nearby plantings, so avoid heavy underplanting close to the trunk and keep it well watered during establishment and drought.

common_name: October Skies Aster (Compact Lavender-Blue Native Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; October Skies is a compact selection of aromatic aster staying much shorter and more mounded than tall wild asters, and it blooms heavily in fall when few other perennials are still flowering.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. October Skies is a compact cultivar of aromatic aster, native to open prairies and glades of the central and eastern United States, forming a dense, rounded mound of fragrant foliage that becomes smothered in masses of small, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers in fall, providing crucial late-season nectar for migrating monarch butterflies and other pollinators. Its shorter, sturdier habit compared to taller native asters makes it useful at the front of a border without staking, and it tolerates poor, dry soil and drought exceptionally well once established. Cut back by about half in late spring to keep the plant compact and encourage even fuller fall bloom.

plant_note: Plant bulbils (produced prolifically on the flower spike) or offsets in well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; octopus agave is one of the most cold-tender agaves, reliably hardy only to about 25–28°F.
directions: Plant bulbils or offsets in well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — octopus agave is named for its remarkably distinctive rosette of long, twisting, channeled leaves that curl and undulate in organic, sinuous curves resembling the arms of an octopus — a shape unlike any other agave in cultivation. The long, flexible, gray-green leaves have only soft marginal teeth and no dangerous terminal spine, making it one of the safest agaves for garden use. After 10–20 years, the plant produces a tall flower spike densely covered in yellow flowers; unlike most agaves (which produce offsets), octopus agave produces thousands of small bulbils on the flower spike that can be harvested and planted. It is more shade tolerant than most agaves and grows naturally in the rocky slopes and ravines of northwest Mexico, performing well on shaded north or east-facing slopes in Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–6.5), well-drained to poorly drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; odorless bayberry is native to moist pine flatwoods, bay swamps, and wet pocosins of the Gulf Coastal Plain and tolerates brief to extended flooding better than most ornamental shrubs.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained to occasionally flooded soil in full sun to part shade; Myrica inodora tolerates prolonged wet, acidic, poorly drained conditions that challenge most ornamental shrubs, making it excellent for wet spots, pond margins, and rain gardens. Myrica inodora (odorless bayberry) is a seldom-cultivated native shrub of the Gulf Coastal Plain from Alabama to Florida and Louisiana, distinct from the common Southern wax myrtle (Morella cerifera) in its larger, glossier, darker-green, distinctly odorless leaves (as the name implies — wax myrtle leaves are distinctively aromatic when crushed; Myrica inodora leaves are not). It grows as a large evergreen shrub or small tree with an upright, irregular form, producing small, white, clustered flowers in spring and blue-gray, waxy berries in fall and winter that are consumed by Yellow-rumped Warblers and other berry-eating birds.
