directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Pinky Winky is a distinctive panicle hydrangea cultivar distinguished by its unusual two-tone flower display — the large, conical (12–16 inch) flower panicles open pure white in midsummer and then progressively change color from the bottom of the panicle upward, with the lower, older florets turning from white to deep pink to rose-red while the upper, younger florets remain white. This creates a striking bicolor effect of white-on-pink within a single flower head that provides weeks of ornamental interest as the color change progresses. The vigorous, upright-arching habit grows more vigorously than Limelight — Pinky Winky can reach 6–8 feet tall with strong, upright stems. Like all Hydrangea paniculata cultivars, Pinky Winky blooms on new wood and can be pruned hard in late winter to stimulate maximum new growth and flower production. It is among the hardiest of all hydrangeas (to zone 3) and tolerates clay soils, full sun (with adequate moisture), and some drought better than French hydrangeas. In zone 9, the pink color develops most intensely in cooler fall temperatures and may be less vivid in very hot summers.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; pinnate bittercress is a spring ephemeral — it emerges early, flowers, and begins going dormant by early summer. Mark the planting site to avoid disturbance. It spreads by brittle, easily-broken rhizome segments that are scattered around the planting site by digging — each fragment regenerates into a new plant.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; pinnate bittercress is a handsome spring-ephemeral from the beech forests of southern Europe, larger and more boldly architectural than the common weedy bittercresses — producing fresh, bright-green, pinnately-divided leaves with seven (or more) leaflets arranged along the stalk in the neatly ordered pattern characteristic of the genus, and in April through May producing substantial clusters of relatively large, four-petaled flowers in clear white to pale lilac-pink above the attractive foliage. The whole plant is a spring ephemeral — beginning to go dormant by early summer as the tree canopy closes above — but the spring show is attractive and the spreading rhizomes form an effective, gradually expanding colony in moist, shaded conditions. The brittle, white, tooth-like rhizomes break apart easily when disturbed, each fragment capable of regenerating a new plant — making it very easy to propagate by simply working the soil around established plants. Combines naturally with bluebells, wood anemones, and wild garlic in the spring woodland garden.

common_name: Pinstripe Calathea (Pin Stripe Plant, Calathea ornata)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container plant in zone 9; Calathea ornata cannot tolerate temperatures below 60°F or dry air. It requires consistent moisture, high humidity (above 50%), and bright indirect light to maintain its best appearance. Use filtered, distilled, or rainwater — fluoride and chlorine in tap water cause leaf tip browning. Propagate by dividing the rhizome clump at repotting time in spring. Leaves fold upward at night (nyctinasty) and return to horizontal position in daylight.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Calathea ornata performs best 3–6 feet from a bright window and will not tolerate direct sun which scorches the dramatic leaf markings. Calathea ornata is a tropical prayer plant from Colombia and Venezuela in the family Marantaceae, prized for its extraordinary leaf markings: the large, elongated, dark emerald-green leaves are decorated with precise, parallel, feather-like stripes of pale pink to cream in the juvenile phase (turning white as leaves mature) that radiate from the midrib, creating a pattern resembling elaborate hand-painted porcelain. The underside of each leaf is deep burgundy-purple. At night, the leaves fold upward (nyctinasty) — a behavior common to all Calatheas and Marantas that gives them the collective name 'prayer plants.' Calathea ornata's beautiful patterned foliage has made it one of the most sought-after decorative houseplants of the current era, though it has a well-deserved reputation for sensitivity: it is easily stressed by low humidity, fluoride in tap water, cold drafts, and overwatering, developing brown leaf tips and edges. The key to success is consistently warm temperatures, high humidity, and filtered water. Despite the challenges, a healthy, well-grown specimen is extraordinarily beautiful.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; nick and soak seed to aid germination.
directions: Nick and soak the hard seed, then direct sow after frost at the base of a trellis or fence for these quick-growing heirloom vines. Heart-shaped leaves and pinwheel-patterned blossoms open to greet the morning, with a fresh set of flowers each day. Give full sun and support to climb, and avoid overly rich soil, which favors leaves over blooms. Note that morning glory seeds are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, very well-drained soil in partial shade; pinxter azalea requires excellent drainage and strongly acidic conditions — it will not survive in alkaline or clay soils. Mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain acidic soil pH and moisture.
directions: Plant in moist, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, very well-drained soil in partial to dappled shade — pinxter azalea is a graceful, open-branching deciduous native azalea of the eastern piedmont and coastal plain, producing masses of pale to deep pink tubular flowers with long, exserted stamens in April–May before or just as the leaves unfurl, filling shaded woodland gardens with a lovely, sweet-spicy fragrance. Unlike evergreen azaleas, pinxter's open, airy form is beautiful even out of bloom, with yellow-green to orange fall foliage. It grows naturally in acidic, sandy, well-drained soils at the edges of pine and oak woodlands and along stream banks in the Southeast. Slower-growing and longer-lived than most garden azaleas, with exceptional cold and heat tolerance for zone 5–9. An outstanding native alternative to introduced evergreen azaleas that thrives in the challenging, sandy, acidic soils of Gulf Coast pine woodlands without the pest and disease issues of Asian azalea species.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines near a sturdy trellis, pergola, or tree trunk in partial to full shade; the vine grows quickly once established but may be slow to emerge in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; pipevine is a vigorous native climbing vine with enormous heart-shaped leaves that creates a dense, lush shade canopy and unusual curved pipe-shaped brown flowers in late spring that lure and temporarily trap small flies as pollinators. It is the essential host plant for the stunning pipevine swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs exclusively on Aristolochia species — the caterpillars absorb aristolochic acids from the plant, making both larva and adult butterfly toxic to predators. Plant several vines together to provide enough leaf mass for the caterpillars. Train on a sturdy arbor, pergola, or fence; the vine can grow 20–30 feet and covers itself with tropical-looking foliage by midsummer. Cut back hard in late winter to control size.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, infertile soil in full sun; pitch pine is adapted to the poorest, most fire-prone habitats of the eastern US — the Pine Barrens, rocky ridges, and sandy outwash plains where other trees cannot persist.
directions: Plant in dry, strongly acidic, sandy or rocky, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pitch pine is one of the most fire-adapted trees in eastern North America, able to re-sprout from dormant buds in the bark after fire damage — a trait unique among northeastern pines. The New Jersey Pine Barrens, one of the most ecologically important and unusual ecosystems in the eastern US, is dominated by pitch pine, which requires periodic fire to maintain the open, scrubby canopy and prevent succession to other forest types. The tree produces pitch (resin) in extraordinary quantities — historically harvested for naval stores, tar, and turpentine. An extremely tough, gnarled, characterful tree for the driest, most infertile, fire-maintained habitats in the Northeast and Appalachians. Not suitable for zone 9 — limited to zones 4–7.

plant_note: Plant with crown at soil level in well-drained, limestone-based or neutral to slightly alkaline soil in partial shade to full sun; Pitcher's clematis is a prairie-edge species naturally found on limestone bluffs, rocky slopes, and thicket edges in the south-central US.
directions: Pitcher's clematis is a native vine of the south-central United States — Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and adjacent states — producing nodding, pitcher- or urn-shaped flowers of purplish-blue to violet-blue with thick, recurved petal tips from May through August on a twining vine that scrambles through shrubs and fences with a restrained, manageable habit. Its distinctive flowers are adapted to specialist bee pollinators and are particularly visited by native metallic green sweat bees that navigate the closed floral tube; the feathery, silvery seedheads that follow persist into winter as the seed plumes expand and catch the light. As a species adapted to drier, alkaline limestone soils, Pitcher's clematis is among the most heat- and drought-tolerant of all native clematis, performing well in zones 7–9 where summer heat and occasional drought challenge other species in the genus. Cut stems back to 12–18 inches in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth and prolific flowering the following season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring onto a lightly disturbed, open soil surface in full sun; press seed into contact with the soil without deep burial and keep the seedbed evenly moist until germination occurs in two to three weeks.
directions: Scatter seed onto a lightly raked seedbed in full sun in early spring, pressing it firmly into the soil and watering until seedlings emerge and begin to establish their root systems over the first month. Pitchfork paspalum is a native warm-season grass of the southeastern coastal plain and eastern prairies, recognized by its distinctive forked seed heads — two to several spreading racemes that give the species its name — which emerge in mid to late summer and persist attractively into fall. It thrives in open, well-drained prairies, pine savannas, and dry roadsides, tolerating drought and lean soils once the deep root system is established, and providing important seed and cover for grassland birds. Allow plants to self-sow into adjacent open ground to gradually build a naturalized stand; division of established clumps in spring is also effective for expanding plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; nick and soak seed to aid germination.
directions: Nick and soak the seed, then direct sow in spring where plants will grow, as lupines resent transplanting. This compact variety stays just twelve to eighteen inches tall with loose eight-inch spikes in pink, blue, purple, and white, some bicolored. Plant in groups for a splash of color in smaller gardens or containers. Provide full sun and well-drained soil, and deadhead spent spikes to prolong bloom.

plant_note: Surface-sow; needs light to germinate. Self-seeds readily.
directions: Scatter seed on prepared soil and barely press it in, as light triggers germination. This easy native annual, also called calliopsis or golden tickseed, opens bright yellow petals marked with burgundy centers from early summer to fall. It thrives in poor, dry soil and full sun, quickly filling meadows and borders with color. Allow some flowers to set seed and it will reliably return the following season.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; plains cottonwood is the dominant riparian tree of the Great Plains, forming gallery forests along rivers and streams in the otherwise treeless prairie landscape. It grows extremely fast and requires consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to wet, deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral riparian soil in full sun; plains cottonwood is the subspecies of eastern cottonwood (Populus deltoides) adapted to the semi-arid Great Plains, forming the iconic riparian forest galleries along the Platte, Republican, Arkansas, and other prairie rivers of the central US. In the treeless expanses of the Great Plains, cottonwood groves along rivers are biological oases — the only substantial tree cover across thousands of square miles of grassland. They support nesting red-tailed hawks, great horned owls, heron colonies, orioles, and dozens of other bird species that simply cannot exist without tree canopy in the open prairie. The brilliant yellow fall foliage is a spectacular landmark in an otherwise somber fall landscape. The female trees produce cottony seed release in early summer that can be messy — male plants are preferred in urban settings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; plains larkspur is native to dry, open prairies and disturbed ground of the Great Plains and south-central US. Seeds require cold stratification to germinate well.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; plains larkspur is a native perennial of dry prairies and plains grasslands from Manitoba south to Texas and east to Illinois, producing pale white to pale blue flower spikes (more white or cream than the vivid blues of mountain larkspurs) on upright stems in late spring. The foliage and seeds are toxic to cattle and horses — a significant issue for rangeland management in the Great Plains — and all parts should be treated as toxic to humans as well. In the garden, the delicate, lacy foliage and tall flower spikes provide vertical interest in dry, native prairie plantings and meadow gardens. Self-sows in open, disturbed, dry conditions to naturalize over time. Important for pollinators including bumblebees, native bees, and hummingbirds during its spring bloom period.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring into rocky or sandy, well-drained upland soil; can also be fall-seeded to allow cold stratification over winter for stronger spring germination.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in spring on exposed, well-drained soil after the last frost, or fall-sow to let winter cold naturally stratify the seed for improved spring germination. Thin seedlings to 18–24 inches and avoid amending soil with compost, as plains muhly is native to lean, alkaline uplands and tends to flop in overly rich conditions. Plants form tidy, wiry clumps that produce airy seed panicles from late summer into fall, providing both visual interest and forage for native sparrows and finches. Cut clumps back to 4–6 inches in late winter before new growth resumes to keep the planting looking fresh.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of dry, lean, sandy or gravelly soil after last frost; press seed into soil but do not cover deeply, as light aids germination.
directions: A bold, spiny-stemmed native annual or biennial poppy with deeply lobed, blue-gray, spine-tipped leaves and enormous, tissue-paper-white flowers 3-4 inches across with golden-yellow stamens; native to dry, open prairies, roadsides, and disturbed ground of the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain foothills. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested and the milky yellow sap causes skin irritation — handle with thick gloves. Direct sow in spring in dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; self-sows prolifically and naturalizes in open, disturbed, dry ground. An excellent, drought-tolerant native annual for large-scale prairie plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, deep soil in full sun; plains wild indigo has a very deep taproot and resents disturbance once established — sow where it will remain permanently. Scratch seed lightly and cold-stratify before spring sowing.
directions: Sow scarified seed in fall in well-drained, average to poor, deep soil in full sun — plains wild indigo is a low, spreading prairie legume of the Great Plains and midwestern prairies producing dense racemes of cream to pale yellow pea flowers in early spring, among the earliest native prairie plants to bloom. Unlike the tall blue false indigo (B. australis), plants remain compact and spread broadly rather than upright — the procumbent, mounded form covered with 4-inch cream flower spikes is striking in the spring landscape. A nitrogen-fixing prairie legume with an extremely deep taproot that survives drought and fire. Extremely long-lived once established (decades) but slow to establish from seed. Excellent for prairie garden restoration and native plant meadow plantings in zones 4–9. The inflated black seed pods are interesting ornamentally and rattle when dry. A host plant for specialist bees and several moth species.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; plains yellow primrose requires excellent drainage and is native to the dry, calcareous soils of the Great Plains and western prairies. It is very drought-tolerant once established but will rot in heavy, wet soils. A good choice for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and dry prairie restorations in the central states.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; plains yellow primrose is a low-growing, spreading native perennial of the calcareous prairies, rocky glades, and dry bluffs of the central Great Plains — from the Dakotas south to Texas and west to the Rocky Mountains — producing narrow, slightly toothed leaves on spreading stems and a profuse display of clear, bright yellow, four-petaled flowers about 1–1.5 inches across from late spring through summer. The flowers have a soft, crepe-paper texture characteristic of the evening primrose family and open in the morning rather than in the evening, despite the family association. An exceptionally drought-tolerant plant of dry, calcareous soil, it is well-adapted to the same difficult conditions as the central Texas Hill Country where limestone-based, thin, droughty soil is the norm. It spreads moderately by both seed and spreading stems to form a low groundcover in dry, open positions. Excellent for the xeric prairie garden, rock garden, and any lean, calcareous soil situation where a low, spreading, yellow-flowered native perennial is needed. Visited by native bees and other pollinators throughout its extended bloom season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Planer Tree tolerates and prefers seasonally flooded conditions. Seeds should be sown fresh in moist, saturated soil as soon as they ripen in spring, as viability diminishes quickly.
directions: Planer Tree — also called Water Elm — is a small and uncommon native tree of permanently wet swamps, river floodplains, and cypress-tupelo bottomlands of the coastal plain from South Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, where it often grows in the understory beneath bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp cottonwood. The small, rough-textured leaves and warty, inconspicuous drupes superficially resemble those of the closely related elms, but the single nutlet with a distinctly rough, tuberculate surface is the diagnostic feature that separates Planera from Ulmus. Seeds should be collected and planted fresh in moist to wet, acidic soil under light shade, as viability drops quickly; container-grown nursery transplants are the most reliable method for establishing this species in cultivation. Planer Tree is rarely grown in ornamental settings but makes a distinctive small specimen for rain gardens, pond margins, and naturalized floodplain plantings where saturated soils and periodic flooding prevent most woody plants from thriving.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plantain-leaf sedge grows naturally in moist, rocky, north-facing woodland slopes in rich, deep soil and requires similar conditions in the garden.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plantain-leaf sedge is the most architecturally distinctive of all the native shade sedges, immediately recognizable by its unusually broad, pleated, dark green leaves (1–2 inches wide) with prominent parallel veins resembling plantain (Plantago) leaves — a completely different aesthetic from typical narrow-leaved sedges. The leaves remain evergreen or semi-evergreen through winter, providing year-round ground-level interest in the woodland garden. Burgundy-red stems bear small, elegant fruiting spikes in early spring before most other plants emerge. It grows naturally on moist, north-facing, rocky woodland slopes in the Appalachians and eastern US. Slower to spread than some native sedges but forms a beautiful, refined groundcover in appropriate conditions. An outstanding accent plant for the front of a shaded border or as a specimen among ferns and hostas.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in dry to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; plantain-leaf pussytoes tolerates poor, rocky soil and is ideal for naturalizing on dry slopes or beneath high-canopied trees where little else will grow.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in dry, poor to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; plantain-leaf pussytoes is exceptionally tolerant of drought, rocky substrates, and the dense dry shade beneath high-branched deciduous trees. Antennaria plantaginifolia forms dense mats of silvery-gray, woolly foliage that spreads steadily by stolons to create a weed-suppressing groundcover, bearing clusters of tiny white button-like flower heads in early spring that attract native bees before most other plants are in bloom. This dioecious native of eastern North American open woodlands and rocky hillsides thrives where moisture and fertility are too low for conventional groundcovers, making it invaluable for difficult dry-shade situations.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, rocky to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; plateau live oak is significantly more cold and drought tolerant than the coastal live oak (Q. virginiana) and is the live oak of choice for inland Texas gardens away from the mild Gulf Coast climate.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, rocky to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — plateau live oak is the iconic evergreen oak of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Balcones Escarpment, where it forms the defining, spreading, ancient trees of the landscape. Nearly identical to the coastal live oak (Q. virginiana) in appearance, it is distinguished by its superior cold tolerance (surviving zone 6 winter cold without damage) and extreme drought tolerance, adapted to the thin, rocky, alkaline limestone soils of the Hill Country where moisture is scarce. Trees develop the same magnificent, broadly spreading, rounded crown with leathery, dark evergreen leaves and massive, gnarled trunks as coastal live oak but in harsher conditions. Small acorns in the red oak group ripen in two years. This is the live oak for central and west Texas gardens — offering the same magnificent landscape presence as its coastal relative but with dramatically greater cold hardiness and drought performance.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; grass-leaved iris is one of the very few irises that performs well in partial shade and is native to shaded woodland margins in southern Europe.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade; grass-leaved iris is one of the very few irises that performs well in partial shade and is native to shaded woodland margins in southern Europe. Iris graminea is a delightful, small-flowered iris of European woodland edges and shaded grasslands, forming compact clumps of narrow, grass-like leaves among which the small, purple-and-white, typical iris-form flowers are half-hidden in late spring — but the flowers make themselves unmistakably known by their extraordinary fruity fragrance, described universally as exactly like ripe Victoria plums or plum tarts, one of the most surprisingly sweet and specific scents of any iris. The plant is compact, slow-spreading, and absolutely trouble-free in partial shade; use it at the front of a shaded border or beneath deciduous shrubs where its fragrance can be appreciated when passing. It will not tolerate drought or alkaline soil.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring in moist, fertile, well-drained to average soil in full sun to part shade; plume poppy spreads vigorously by rhizomes and can be invasive in ideal conditions — plant only where spreading is welcome or where it can be contained by a barrier. The milky, orange-yellow sap can irritate sensitive skin. In rich, moist soil it may exceed 10 feet in height.
directions: Plant in moist to average, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; plume poppy is a majestic, large-scale perennial from China and Japan that creates an extraordinary tropical effect in the temperate garden. The enormous, deeply scalloped, fig-leaf-shaped leaves — each up to 12 inches across — are carried alternately along tall, glaucous, blue-gray stems and have striking bluish-gray surfaces with contrasting creamy-white undersides that flash pale when the wind moves through them. In mid to late summer, the plant produces enormous, branching plumes of hundreds of tiny, petal-less, buff-cream to pink flowers on stems reaching 6-10 feet, creating an airy, feathery mass that floats above the bold foliage below. It spreads freely by rhizomes and can colonize a large area quickly, but this vigor makes it invaluable for large-scale screening and rapid ground coverage in difficult areas. A single plant creates a dramatic focal point of scale and presence rarely achieved by any other hardy perennial. The orange-yellow sap is irritating to skin; handle with gloves.

common_name: Plumed Celosia (Feathery Plume Cockscomb Summer Annual)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is consistently above 65°F; celosia resents root disturbance and direct sowing usually outperforms transplants. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer and fall bloom. Celosia thrives in heat and humidity — it is one of the summer annuals that blooms more vigorously (not less) in the Gulf South's hot, humid conditions, unlike many other annuals that slow down in summer.
directions: Sow seeds 0.125 inch deep after last frost; thin to 8–14 inches. Plumed celosia is a variety group of Celosia argentea producing feathery, upright, flame-like flower plumes rather than the flat, brain-shaped crests of the cockscomb (var. cristata) type. The plumes are dense, velvety, and upright, ranging from 4–8 inches tall, in brilliant colors: deep scarlet, crimson, orange, salmon, yellow, cream, and hot pink — hot colors that intensify in summer heat. Celosia is one of the most heat-tolerant summer annuals available, thriving in conditions that cause most other plants to retreat — the combination of intense heat, humidity, and high soil temperatures that characterize Gulf South summers promotes vigorous blooming rather than reducing it. The long-lasting cut flowers are prized in both fresh and dried arrangements: the plumes hold their color and shape well when dried, making them valuable for dried flower crafts and fall arrangements. Young leaves and flowers are edible and used as cooked greens in West African and Southeast Asian cooking, where celosia is grown as a vegetable crop. Garden series include Kimono, Fresh Look, and Intenz, each offering improved uniformity and specific color ranges.

plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1–2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; do not water until new growth appears — plumeria cuttings rot easily if kept wet before rooting. Established plants are dormant and leafless in winter and require complete dryness during dormancy.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun — plumeria is a tropical American tree sacred in Buddhist and Hindu cultures, widely planted around temples throughout Asia and used in Hawaiian leis, and one of the most intensely fragrant of all flowering plants. The waxy, 4-inch flowers in white, yellow, pink, red, or multicolor combinations have a powerful sweet tropical scent that is strongest at night. Plumeria is deciduous (leafless in winter), drought tolerant, and thrives in heat — full sun and excellent drainage are its only requirements. In zone 9a it is widely grown in containers: bring indoors dry and leafless when temperatures drop below 40°F, store in a frost-free location, and return outdoors in spring. Hundreds of named cultivars are prized by collectors; the Singapore White (P. obtusa) is an evergreen species suited to zone 10+.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; keep crown at or above soil level. Do not allow to dry out during establishment.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), well-drained soil in partial to full shade; plumleaf azalea holds a unique distinction among native deciduous azaleas — it blooms in July and August, later than every other native azalea species, and is therefore in bloom when every other azalea in the garden has long finished. The large, brilliant orange-red (rarely yellow) flowers appear on the shrub in midsummer, providing color and hummingbird nectar in a season when the woodland garden often lacks bloom. This is one of the rarest native azaleas in the wild, found only in southwestern Georgia and eastern Alabama, but it is a superb and underused garden plant. It tolerates the heat and partial shade of zone 8–9 summers better than most native azaleas. Mulch heavily with pine bark to maintain soil moisture and acidity.

common_name: Pocomoke Crape Myrtle (True Dwarf Groundcover-Type Rose-Pink Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Pocomoke's true dwarf size makes it useful as a low border or mass planting rather than a tree, and it needs little to no annual pruning.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pocomoke is one of the true dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle selections, staying under three feet tall and wide, useful as a low border, mass planting, or large-scale groundcover rather than the shade-tree role most crape myrtles fill. It produces rich rose-pink flower clusters over a long summer season and, like other National Arboretum hybrids, shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Its very small mature size means it needs almost no pruning beyond removing dead wood, in sharp contrast to the standard practice of cutting back larger crape myrtles.

common_name: Poinsettia (Mexican Christmas Star, Easter Flower, Noche Buena Garden Shrub)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil; in zone 9a and the Gulf South, poinsettia is a perennial GARDEN SHRUB growing 6–12 feet tall that blooms every winter in response to the shortening days of November–December — it is NOT just a houseplant; established plants naturalize and self-sow freely in zone 9–10 and bloom reliably each winter without indoor protection.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun or morning sun with afternoon shade; prune heavily after blooming (January–February in zone 9) — cut plants back by one-third to one-half to prevent legginess and encourage compact growth and more prolific flowering the following winter; avoid any artificial light at night in October–November which will delay or prevent flowering since poinsettia requires uninterrupted long nights (14+ hours of darkness) to initiate flower (bract) color. Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) is primarily known as a holiday houseplant in most of the United States, but in zone 9–11 (tropical and subtropical Gulf Coast, California, Hawaii, Florida) it is a perennial garden SHRUB that grows 6–12 feet tall, often becoming a significant landscape element that blooms dependably every winter. In the wild, poinsettia is native to Mexico — particularly the Pacific coastal region of Taxco, Guerrero — where it grows as a semi-deciduous shrub or small tree 10–15 feet tall in the dry tropical forest and blooms in response to the shortening days of November–December, turning entire hillsides red with its bracts (the colorful parts are modified leaves, not petals — the true flowers are the small yellow structures at the center). The plant takes its common English name from Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first U.S. Ambassador to Mexico, who introduced it to the United States in 1825. In zone 9a, poinsettia grown outdoors blooms reliably from November through January with minimal care, and established plants develop woody trunks and can become large impressive shrubs. The characteristic that determines bloom timing is photoperiodism — poinsettia requires uninterrupted dark periods of 14 hours or more to initiate bract coloration, which occurs naturally as nights lengthen in autumn. Streetlights or interior lights shining on the plant at night will disrupt this cycle and delay or prevent coloring.

common_name: Pointleaf Tick Trefoil / Large-flowered Tick Trefoil
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in spring into moist, shaded woodland soil. Scarification by nicking the seed coat or soaking in warm water for 24 hours before sowing is recommended to break seed dormancy. Sow seeds approximately 1/4 inch deep.
directions: Pointleaf Tick Trefoil is a striking native legume for shaded ravines, moist woodland gardens, and naturalized forest understories, where its bold, whorled leaflets and tall racemes of rose-pink flowers make a strong visual statement from midsummer through fall. Sow scarified seeds directly in spring once soil temperatures are consistently above 65 degrees Fahrenheit, pressing them about 1/4 inch deep into moist, humus-rich soil in a partially shaded location. Plants grow slowly in the first year while developing deep roots and will reach flowering size by the second or third season. The sticky seed pods that form after bloom are a valuable food source for wildlife, and the plant serves as a larval host for several skipper and butterfly species, making it an excellent candidate for wildlife-focused woodland plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; poke milkweed is uniquely adapted among milkweeds for shaded conditions, growing naturally in moist, mesic deciduous forests and woodland edges in the eastern US.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; poke milkweed is a critically important species for expanding milkweed diversity in the landscape — it is one of the only milkweeds adapted to partial shade conditions, naturally growing at the forest edge, in woodland openings, and along shaded roadsides in the Appalachians and surrounding regions. Most milkweeds require full sun and would not survive the partial shade gardens where many gardeners could offer milkweed habitat. Poke milkweed fills this niche, producing tall stems with nodding, drooping clusters of white to pale pink flowers with purple hoods that are attractive to monarch butterflies as both larval host and adult nectar source. A tall, imposing plant that fits naturally at the woodland edge or in the back of a shade border.

common_name: Polar Bear Zinnia (Giant Pure White Cut-Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Polar Bear is a giant-flowered white selection from the Benary's Giant zinnia series, producing large, fully double, pure white blooms on tall, strong stems ideal for cutting and white-themed garden or floral designs.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Polar Bear is a giant-flowered white zinnia from the Benary's Giant series, producing large, fully double, dahlia-like blooms 4-5 inches across in a clean, pure white on tall, sturdy stems well suited to cutting. As part of one of the premier cut-flower zinnia series, it shares the group's large flower size, long stem length, and excellent vase life of five to ten days, making it a favorite for white and neutral-toned floral arrangements and weddings. Plants are tall and vigorous, blooming heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production. Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates, and stake in windy sites since the large blooms can be top-heavy on the tall stems.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or water, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade after frost; polka dot begonia requires consistent moisture but is highly susceptible to root rot in compacted, poorly drained, or consistently waterlogged media — allow the top inch to dry slightly between waterings.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in partial to full shade; polka dot begonia is a Brazilian cane-type (angel wing) begonia that has become one of the most vigorously popular houseplants of recent years, with extraordinary social media visibility driven by its remarkable leaf pattern — the large, asymmetric, wing-shaped, olive-green to dark-green leaves are densely covered on the upper surface with a precise, even, all-over pattern of small, perfectly round, silver-white spots, while the undersides are uniformly deep maroon-red, creating a bicolor leaf effect that is striking from both sides. The plant grows with an upright, bamboo-like, cane-forming habit and can reach 4–5 feet indoors or in sheltered outdoor positions. Clusters of small, delicate, pale-pink to white, pendant flowers appear at intervals throughout the year, adding a floral bonus to the outstanding foliage display. It roots easily from stem cuttings in water. 'Wightii' is the most commonly available cultivar, with the densest and most even silver-spot pattern. An excellent outdoor specimen in sheltered shade gardens in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; cover seed as darkness aids germination.
directions: Direct sow in early spring, covering the seed since darkness aids germination and plants tolerate light frost. This dwarf mix averages sixteen to twenty-four inches and blooms in blue, purple, pink, red, and white, making it great for containers. Drought tolerant once established, it flowers from spring into summer and attracts pollinators. Deadhead to extend bloom and let some flowers set seed to self-sow.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or root stem cuttings in moist perlite; plant out after last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Pinch tips regularly to maintain compact, bushy form.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in moist seed-starting mix in a warm, brightly lit location; polka dot plant is a Madagascar native grown for its vivid, spotted foliage — broad, dark-green leaves thickly splashed with pink, white, red, or magenta spots and blotches that give the plant an almost unnaturally colorful appearance, making it one of the most striking foliage plants for shaded containers and garden beds. Pinch growing tips regularly to maintain compact, bushy growth and prevent leggy, flopping stems. Plants flower with small lavender spikes in late season; remove flowers to maintain foliage quality. Overwinters as a tender perennial in zones 10–12; grown as an annual in cooler climates. Excellent in combination with ferns, hostas, and caladiums in shaded container plantings.

common_name: Polly Alocasia (African Mask Plant with Bold White Veining)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Polly Alocasia requires warm temperatures (above 65°F) to thrive — plant outdoors only after night temperatures are consistently above 60°F.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Polly is a compact cultivar of Alocasia × amazonica (the African Mask Plant) — one of the most dramatically graphic foliage plants available, producing arrowhead to shield-shaped leaves 10–16 inches long in deep, glossy, blackish-dark-green with bold, contrasting, creamy-white to ivory-white veins and leaf margins creating a striking graphic pattern reminiscent of tribal masks or stained glass. The contrast between the very dark, glossy leaf surface and the crisp white veins is among the most visually dramatic foliage patterns of any commonly available ornamental plant. Polly's compact size (18–24 inches) makes it more practical for typical garden use than the larger Alocasia × amazonica species (which can reach 4–6 feet). As an outdoor plant in zone 9, Polly performs as a warm-season tropical that requires warm soil and air temperatures — plant outdoors from late April through early October and bring containers indoors before the first frost, or protect in-ground plants with heavy mulch. In frost-free portions of zone 9b and 10, Polly can remain outdoors year-round. The dramatic foliage creates an exotic, jungle-garden aesthetic that is outstanding in large containers, as a shade garden focal point, or in tropical-themed garden designs. Avoid cold drafts, direct sun, and dry soil.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 14–16 weeks before last frost after surface-sowing and cold-stratifying at 35–40°F for 3–4 weeks.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seeds on moist, sterile mix and cold-stratify at 35–40°F for 3–4 weeks to break dormancy, then move to 65°F for germination. Grow on at cool temperatures (55–60°F) since heat causes etiolation; transplant into partial shade in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in early spring. Primroses bloom best in cool, moist conditions — they are outstanding spring plants but typically go dormant in summer heat. Divide crowded clumps after bloom in spring and replant divisions in refreshed, compost-amended soil.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost; excellent long-lasting cut flower.
directions: Plant pompon dahlia tubers after the last frost about four to six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil. The small, perfectly spherical, tightly quilled flowers are outstanding long-lasting cut flowers. Grow in full sun, stake the stems, and pinch young plants to encourage more blooms. Deadhead regularly and, in cold zones, dig and store the tubers over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors in late summer (August–September in zone 9) for fall transplanting, or plant purchased transplants in October–November. Pomponette is a double-flowered English Daisy selection producing button-like, fully double, rounded flower heads in pink, red, and white — one of the most charming and old-fashioned cool-season bedding plant flowers available. In zone 9 Bellis perennis blooms November–April in an essentially continuous display in appropriate shade and moisture conditions. English daisy performs better in partial shade in zone 9 than in full sun, which causes premature wilting and earlier heat decline. As a technically perennial species (Bellis perennis = perennial daisy), it may persist through mild zone 9 summers in cool, moist, shaded situations but is most reliably treated as a cool-season annual.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun — partial shade is preferred in zone 9 where mild winter temperatures and early spring warmth can cause premature heat stress in fully exposed sites — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Pomponette English Daisy is a double-flowered selection of English Daisy (Bellis perennis), the lawn daisy of European meadows and cottage gardens, producing small, fully double, button-like flower heads in pink, rose-red, and white on compact plants — creating an old-fashioned, charming, cottage garden effect that is entirely different from the more modern, large-flowered cool-season annuals that have come to dominate the bedding plant market. The completely double, pompom-form flowers of Pomponette — no visible center disc, entirely composed of tightly packed, inward-curving ray petals — provide an unusual texture compared to other cool-season daisies, producing a more formal, tidier flower form at a compact scale. English daisy's genuine tolerance for partial shade — as a species native to European woodlands and meadows where it grows in both open and lightly shaded conditions — makes it one of the few compact, low-growing cool-season flowering annuals that can deliver consistent bloom in shaded winter and spring gardens in zone 9. The low, compact form (6–8 inches) works particularly well as an edging plant with taller cool-season companions such as snapdragons, pansies, and alyssum.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; pond cypress is more tolerant of still, stagnant water and poor, sandy flatwoods soils than bald cypress and is the better choice for small water gardens, rain gardens with standing water, and sandy coastal plain sites.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — pond cypress is the smaller, more columnar companion to bald cypress (Taxodium distichum), native to the shallow, still, slightly acidic waters of coastal plain ponds, sloughs, bayheads, and flatwoods pools of the eastern Gulf Coast from Virginia to Louisiana. It is more columnar and narrower in crown than bald cypress — an important distinction for smaller water gardens and landscape plantings where bald cypress would eventually become too wide. Like bald cypress, it is deciduous, producing soft, feathery, gray-green needles that turn brilliant orange-brown in fall before dropping, and develops picturesque 'knees' (pneumatophores) in wet soils. It tolerates standing water throughout the growing season and acidic, nutrient-poor, sandy soils that defeat other trees. The ideal tree for small wet garden features, bioswales, and moist low areas requiring a deciduous, fine-textured, low-maintenance large tree.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; the serotinous cones require heat (fire or prolonged heating) to release seeds naturally, so for cultivation purposes collect cones and gently heat them in an oven (250°F for 30 minutes) to open. Pond Pine establishes most reliably in its natural wet, acidic habitat.
directions: Pond Pine is an ecologically fascinating native pine, the dominant tree of the pocosins (shrubby Carolina bogs) and wet pine flatwoods of the southeastern coastal plain from New Jersey to northern Florida, where it grows in the most permanently saturated, acidic, peaty soils of the coastal plain in full sun — a habitat as harsh as any in the temperate world. Its cones are strongly serotinous — sealed shut with resin — and open most reliably after fire, giving Pond Pine a remarkable fire-dependent life history: the dense, wet habitat rarely burns, but when lightning does ignite a pocosin, the heat opens the cones and the charred, open landscape gives the fire-adapted seedlings their best chance for establishment. Pond Pine sprouts vigorously from the root crown after fire, regenerating rapidly even when top-killed. In natural landscape and restoration plantings, Pond Pine is appropriate for the wet, boggy, acidic conditions of pocosins and seepage bogs in zones 6–9, where its tolerance for waterlogged soils matches or exceeds that of any other eastern pine species.

plant_note: Plant outdoors after the last frost once nighttime lows stay reliably above 60°F. Provide a spacious container or garden bed to accommodate the exceptionally large spread of mature foliage.
directions: Propagate from rhizome sections or stem cuttings set in moist, humus-rich mix in a warm location; the thick rhizome should sit at or just above the soil surface. Plant in deep shade or bright filtered light in very rich, moisture-retentive soil and water generously and consistently, as this species is intolerant of drought due to its large leaf surface area. Provide a large container or open garden bed to accommodate the impressive spread, and feed monthly with a balanced fertilizer to sustain vigorous leaf production. Move container plants indoors before the first frost and keep them warm and well-watered through winter.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, deep, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; ponderosa pine is highly drought tolerant once established (after 2–3 growing seasons) but requires regular watering during establishment. Tap-rooted — does not tolerate waterlogging or compacted soils. Grows extremely fast in youth with good water.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, deep, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; ponderosa pine is the most widely distributed pine in North America — covering more land area than any other pine and forming vast, open, parklike forests across the entire western interior from British Columbia to Mexico and from the Pacific Coast ranges to the Great Plains. The mature bark is one of the most distinctive of any tree — developing large, interlocking, jigsaw-puzzle-like plates of orange-cinnamon to yellow-orange bark that, on a warm day, exude a remarkable, unmistakable vanilla and butterscotch fragrance from the bark's resin pockets. The bark fragrance is one of nature's most memorable and beloved scents, often serving as the first signal to hikers that they have entered ponderosa pine forest. The open, parklike ponderosa forests maintained by frequent low-intensity fire have been severely disrupted by a century of fire suppression, creating dangerously overcrowded forests prone to catastrophic crown fire. Among the most important forest restoration and thinning challenges in the western US. Makes an excellent large landscape pine for dry, western gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun after last frost; ponytail palm stores water in its swollen base and demands excellent drainage — clay or consistently moist soil causes fatal rot.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, sandy or rocky, low-fertility soil in full sun; despite its name, ponytail palm is neither a palm nor a tree but a succulent member of the asparagus family from semi-arid Mexico, identifiable by its swollen, barrel-like base (caudex) that stores water and its long, thin, arching, grass-like leaves that cascade from the top like a ponytail. Water deeply but infrequently — monthly in summer, even less in winter — allowing the soil to dry completely between waterings. It is virtually indestructible under hot, dry conditions and tolerates severe neglect, making it one of the best drought-tolerant accent plants for zone 9–11 landscapes. Produces offsets (pups) at the base that can be removed and rooted.

plant_note: Direct-sow outdoors on or just after the last frost date once the soil has warmed. Press seeds onto moist soil surface in a shaded spot; do not bury them, as light supports germination.
directions: Direct-sow seeds on the soil surface in a moist, partially shaded bed after the last frost date, pressing them in gently without covering since light improves germination rates. Thin seedlings to 8–12 inches apart once they reach 2–3 inches tall, choosing the strongest plants and composting the rest. Water consistently throughout the growing season to keep soil evenly moist, especially during dry spells. Allow a few plants to set seed at the end of the season so the colony naturalizes; self-sown seedlings often emerge reliably in subsequent years.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; poor man's rhododendron is a large, shrubby, perennial impatiens from the highlands of East Africa that can reach 4–6 feet in mild climates and blooms nearly continuously with large, lavender-pink to white, spurred flowers throughout the warmer months. In zone 9 it grows as a reliable perennial. Prefers consistent moisture and shade to part shade; wilts in drought or full sun. Outstanding for filling large shady areas with continuous flower color.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; poor man's rhododendron is a large, shrubby, perennial impatiens native to the cool, moist, highland forests and forest margins of East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda), where it grows to 4–6 feet in sheltered, moist situations and blooms almost without pause through the entire growing season. The common name 'poor man's rhododendron' refers to its remarkable capacity to produce continuous, abundant flower color in shade — filling the role that rhododendrons play in cool, acid, Pacific Northwest gardens — but in a warm-climate shade garden context where rhododendrons cannot grow. The flowers are the characteristic impatiens form — five-petaled, flat-faced, with a distinctive curved nectar spur — but much larger than the common bedding impatiens (Impatiens walleriana), reaching 1.5–2 inches across, in clear lavender-pink to soft pink to pale lilac and white. They are produced in continuous succession at the stem tips throughout the warmer months, a single plant carrying dozens of open flowers simultaneously when in full growing mode. In zone 9 it grows as a genuine, long-lived perennial shrub — not an annual — developing woody base stems over multiple seasons and increasing in size to form a large, leafy mound that fills a shady corner with continuous flower color and lush, rich, tropical-looking foliage. Requires consistent moisture and protection from midday sun; wilts quickly in drought or full-sun exposure. Outstanding for large, moist, shaded spaces in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens.

common_name: Popcorn Cassia (Peanut Butter Cassia, Candle Bush, Pois Puant)
plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds or transplant in spring after last frost; Popcorn Cassia germinates quickly in warm soil (70°F+) and grows rapidly to 8–12 feet in zone 9 in a single season. Soak seeds 24 hours before sowing or nick the seed coat to improve germination. In zone 9, treat as an annual or tender perennial; it may resprout from the crown in zone 9b after a mild winter. Self-seeds prolifically — deadhead spent flower spikes to reduce volunteer seedlings. Seeds and foliage are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Popcorn Cassia is adaptable to poor, sandy, or clay soils and tolerates drought once established in zone 9's hot summers. Senna didymobotrya is a large, fast-growing annual to short-lived perennial tropical shrub native to tropical Africa (Kenya, Uganda, Ethiopia), extensively naturalized across the humid tropics as one of the most widely planted ornamental Senna species. The name 'Popcorn Cassia' or 'Peanut Butter Plant' comes from the extraordinary, strong, sweet, peanut-butter-popcorn scent released when the leaves are brushed or crushed — one of the most distinctive and surprising fragrances in the plant world, completely unlike the plant's golden appearance. The flowers themselves are produced in erect, candle-like spikes 6–12 inches long of bright golden-yellow petals emerging from dark brown to black overlapping buds that resemble a stack of poker chips — the visual contrast of black buds and gold flowers is dramatic and unique. The plant blooms from late summer through fall in zone 9 (August–November), providing late-season color when most other ornamentals are past peak. Note that all parts of the plant are toxic, particularly the seeds, which contain anthraquinones causing gastrointestinal distress.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, moist to moderately dry soil with a sturdy trellis or support in zone 9–11; Port St. John's Creeper (Zimbabwe Creeper, Pink Trumpet Vine) is a spectacular, vigorous ornamental climbing vine from South Africa and Zimbabwe — producing large, showy, trumpet-shaped flowers in rosy-pink to soft lilac-pink with darker pink veining in loose terminal clusters throughout summer and fall — one of the most beautiful of all tropical climbing vines.
directions: Plant Podranea ricasoliana in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil with a very sturdy trellis, pergola, or wall to support its vigorous growth; train the initial stems to the support and allow to mature for 2–3 years before expecting heavy bloom; cut back in late winter to encourage compact, manageable growth and maximize flowering. Port St. John's Creeper is named for the coastal town in the Eastern Cape of South Africa near the Pondoland coast, where it scrambles over scrub and along forest margins. The large, broadly funnel-shaped flowers in soft rosy-pink to lilac-pink are produced in loose clusters at the branch tips from late spring through fall; individual flowers are 2–3 inches across, giving the vine a generous, lush appearance when in full bloom. It is similar to the more commonly grown Bignonia capreolata and related trumpet vines but with distinctly softer, more pastel coloring that blends beautifully with other plants. In zone 9, it dies back to the root crown after hard frost and re-emerges in spring; in zone 10–11 it grows as a large, semi-evergreen perennial vine reaching 15–20 feet or more. Butterflies visit the flowers and the vine is generally pest- and disease-resistant in suitable climates. A superb choice for pergolas, fences, walls, and large trellises in Gulf Coast subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy, saline-tolerant, neutral soil in full sun; portia tree is pantropical and highly salt-tolerant, growing naturally along tropical coastlines worldwide. In zone 9, protect from frost as young plants are more sensitive than established trees.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, saline-tolerant soil in full sun in tropical and near-tropical coastal areas; portia tree is a widely distributed pantropical beach and coastal tree in the hibiscus family, producing handsome, broadly heart-shaped leaves and large, yellow, hibiscus-like flowers with a dark maroon center that fade to purple-red as they age. Like beach hibiscus (Hibiscus tiliaceus), the flower color change occurs within hours on the same flower. The portia tree is one of the most salt-tolerant tropical trees available and has been widely planted throughout Pacific island communities for its high-quality, dense, decorative wood used in carving, furniture, and tool handles. The seeds, leaves, bark, and roots have various traditional medicinal applications across tropical Asia and Polynesia. In the US, suitable for south Florida and the warmest Gulf locations.

plant_note: Plant acorns in fall immediately after collection or plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; Portuguese oak is highly drought tolerant and adapted to the hot, dry, Mediterranean-type climate of Iberia. Very adaptable to poor, rocky, shallow soils in full sun.
directions: Plant acorns in fall or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or loamy, lean to average soil in full sun; Portuguese oak is the characteristic semi-evergreen oak of the western Mediterranean — a large, long-lived tree native to the Iberian Peninsula (Spain, Portugal) and northwestern Africa, growing in open forests, dry hillsides, and rocky slopes of the Mediterranean climate zone. Semi-evergreen in character — retaining most of its leaves through mild winters and shedding them in spring as new growth expands. The leaves are deeply lobed to entire, intermediate between deciduous and evergreen European oaks. Highly drought tolerant — one of the most drought-adapted of the European oaks, growing in areas with 12–20 inches of annual rainfall. Historically important in the dehesa (Spanish) and montado (Portuguese) agro-sylvo-pastoral systems — the open, grazed oak park-landscapes of Iberia that support unique biodiversity including Iberian lynx and black vultures. More heat and drought tolerant than English oak, suitable for Mediterranean-climate gardens of the US West Coast and similar warm, dry climates.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs in fall with the nose just at or slightly below the soil surface in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Portuguese squill naturalizes readily in mild climates and spreads slowly by offsets. In zone 8–10 it is reliably perennial and requires no lifting. The misleading name 'Cuban Lily' and 'peruviana' (Peruvian) both result from historical mis-labeling — this plant is actually native to the western Mediterranean.
directions: Plant large bulbs in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Portuguese squill is a large Mediterranean bulb producing one of the most impressive spring floral displays of any small bulb — a massive, domed to conical cluster of 50–100 or more small, star-shaped, vivid blue-purple flowers densely packed into a broad, pyramidal head on a thick, fleshy stem. The overall effect is of a rich, blue-purple dome of stars, 4–6 inches across, carried above a spreading rosette of wide, strap-like leaves. Despite the species name 'peruviana,' it is native to the western Mediterranean (Spain, Portugal, and North Africa) — the name resulted from a 17th-century botanical error. Naturalizes readily in mild climates (zones 8–11) in well-drained soil and slowly multiplies by offsets to form impressive clumps. Unlike the tiny spring squills (Scilla siberica), this is a large, bold bulb that makes a significant visual statement. Goes completely dormant by summer in true Mediterranean bulb fashion.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface after last frost when soil is warm; seed needs warmth and light to germinate.
directions: Scatter seed on the surface of sandy or gritty soil and press lightly — do not cover seed, as light is needed for germination. Portulaca is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant annuals available, thriving in poor, dry soil where other flowers fail. Blooms open in full sun and close at night or in cloudy weather; modern varieties stay open longer. Self-sows readily in warm climates.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix or transplant container specimens in spring; possum grape establishes rapidly in warm weather and is virtually indestructible once established — it tolerates extreme drought, deep shade, and root competition from large trees that kill most other vines.
directions: Root cuttings or plant in virtually any soil type — from dry, rocky, alkaline limestone to moist, sandy loam — in full shade to full sun — possum grape is one of the toughest native vines of the Gulf Coast and South Texas, a member of the grape family with succulent, deeply lobed, somewhat grape-like leaves on twining stems. The succulent stems store water, giving this vine exceptional drought tolerance even under large trees where root competition is intense and soil is bone dry. Small clusters of inconspicuous flowers in summer are followed by small, dark purple to black berries that are eagerly consumed by mockingbirds, cedar waxwings, and other fruit-eating birds. It tolerates the deep shade under live oaks, cedar elms, and other large trees better than almost any other vine and is useful as a tough groundcover or fence cover for difficult, dry, shaded exposures. Deer avoid it. Deciduous in zone 7–8; semi-evergreen in zone 9–10.

plant_note: Plant at least one male and three to five female shrubs for berry production; match male and female cultivar bloom times. The male plant 'Red Escort' is widely used with female cultivars of this species.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; possum haw is a native deciduous holly of the Southeast naturally found in stream margins, swamp edges, and moist bottomland forests, valued for the brilliant orange-red berries that adorn bare branches all winter long after leaves drop in fall. It is an excellent alternative to winterberry (I. verticillata) for zone 8–9 gardens where winterberry can struggle with heat. Like all hollies, it is dioecious — both male and female plants are required for berry set, in a ratio of at least one male per five females. Cedar waxwings, robins, bluebirds, and mockingbirds rely on the persistent berries throughout winter. Named female cultivars like 'Warren's Red' and 'Fineline' are widely available.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw is dioecious — you must plant at least one male within 50 feet of female plants to ensure the heavy berry display. The cultivar 'Red Cascade' and 'Council Fire' are outstanding female selections with brilliant berry color.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic, well-drained to periodically wet soil in full sun to partial shade; possumhaw adapts naturally to floodplains and stream banks and tolerates periodic inundation better than most landscape shrubs. Ilex decidua is a native deciduous holly of the southeastern and south-central US that delivers one of the most spectacular winter berry displays of any North American shrub — after the leaves drop in fall, the bare stems are completely covered in dense clusters of brilliant red to orange berries that persist through February, providing vivid color and abundant wildlife food throughout the dormant season. The berries are heavily utilized by cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and bluebirds during winter irruptions. A male pollinator plant (such as Ilex decidua 'Red Escort' or a male I. opaca) within pollinating distance is essential for berry set on female plants. Outstanding for naturalistic borders, rain gardens, and stream-bank plantings.

plant_note: Plant young, container-grown trees in fall in dry to average, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; post oak has a deep taproot and is extremely difficult to transplant from the wild — only use nursery-grown stock and plant when small for best survival.
directions: Post oak is one of the most drought-resistant and ecologically critical native oaks of the southeastern United States, forming a distinctive cross- or plus-shaped leaf outline (the 'stellata' — starry — refers to the star-shaped hairs on the leaf underside) that makes it immediately identifiable among the dozens of native oaks. Found on dry, sandy, or rocky ridges and uplands across its enormous range from New England to Texas, it is the characteristic oak of the 'post oak savanna' ecoregion of east Texas and the Cross Timbers region — a unique fire-maintained landscape of widely spaced oaks over a diverse grass and wildflower understory. The hard, rot-resistant wood was historically used for fence posts and barn sills (giving the tree its common name), and post oak acorns are among the most important mast crops for white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and dozens of bird species across the Southeast. Post oak supports over 500 species of Lepidoptera (moths and butterflies) as a larval host — making it one of the top native trees for butterfly and moth diversity in the region.

common_name: Postman Joyner Caladium (Classic Red-and-Green Fancy-Leaf Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Postman Joyner is a classic fancy-leaf caladium cultivar known for bold, ruffled leaves splashed with bright red centers and prominent dark green veining against a lighter green background, giving strong color contrast in a shaded bed or container planting. It has been a favorite of Southern gardeners for many decades for its reliable performance and vivid color that holds up through a long summer season in the shade garden. In zone 9, tubers can often overwinter in the ground with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing indoors ensures more reliable survival in cooler climates.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in water or moist potting mix at any time indoors, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained potting mix or garden soil in partial to full shade outdoors after frost in zones 10–12; pothos is the most low-maintenance and forgiving of all tropical foliage plants, tolerating conditions that kill most other plants.
directions: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix and grow in partial to full shade; pothos (devil's ivy, golden pothos) is the most widely grown and universally recognized houseplant in the world — a vigorous tropical vine from the Solomon Islands with glossy, heart-shaped, variably yellow-and-green or solid-green marbled leaves that trails or climbs on virtually any surface, rooting at the nodes to attach to trellises, moss poles, and textured walls. Its legendary low-maintenance character — tolerating low light, irregular watering, low humidity, and neglect that kills competing tropical plants — makes it the most appropriate choice for shaded interior spaces, covered porches, and areas of deep garden shade in zones 10–12, where it covers the ground or climbs trees. Stem cuttings root within days in plain water and can be transplanted to soil or left to grow in vases. Classified as an invasive species in some tropical regions (Hawaii, Florida) because of its ability to smother native vegetation outdoors in frost-free climates. Common cultivars include 'Golden Queen' (yellow-green variegated), 'Marble Queen' (white-splashed), 'Neon' (chartreuse), and 'N'Joy' (white and green). All parts toxic if ingested.

common_name: Pow Wow White Coneflower (Compact White-Rayed Coneflower)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Pow Wow White is more compact than standard Echinacea purpurea cultivars (12–20 inches vs. 24–36 inches), making it proportionate for smaller residential borders and container use.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Pow Wow White is a compact white coneflower selection — bred as part of the Pow Wow series to produce white-rayed flowers with a prominent golden-orange central cone on a plant significantly shorter and more tidy than standard Echinacea purpurea cultivars (12–20 inches compared to the 24–36 inches typical of older selections). The pure white ray petals (held more horizontally than the drooping rays of the species) radiate around the prominent, dome-shaped, golden-orange to bronze cone, creating a classic daisy-form with high visual impact at eye level in a smaller planting space. Pow Wow White provides excellent contrast in mixed perennial plantings when combined with purple or blue companions like Walker's Low catmint, Salvia May Night, or standard purple Echinacea. Like all Echinacea purpurea cultivars, Pow Wow White is a North American native prairie plant that is exceptionally drought-tolerant, heat-resistant, and low-maintenance once established. The flower heads attract goldfinches, chickadees, and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter — leaving the dried seedheads standing through winter provides wildlife habitat value while also providing ornamental winter interest. In zone 9, Echinacea performs reliably as a long-lived perennial; it is one of the most adaptable and drought-tolerant perennials available for the Gulf South border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; PowWow Wildberry is a compact, seed-grown coneflower that flowers reliably in its first year from an early sowing, unlike many coneflowers that need a full season to establish before blooming.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. PowWow Wildberry won an All-America Selections award for its ability to flower heavily from seed in its very first year, along with a notably compact habit that keeps the plant shorter and sturdier than older tall coneflower selections. The flowers are a deep rosy-purple with a slightly upturned, more horizontal petal form than the wild species, held over a long bloom season from early summer well into fall. Like other coneflowers it is drought-tolerant and attractive to butterflies and bees once established, and leaving the spent seed heads standing through winter provides food for goldfinches.

subcategory: Indo-Pacific freshwater mangrove nocturnal flower tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist to wet, acidic to neutral soil or at the margins of ponds and streams in zone 10–12; Powder Puff Mangrove (Freshwater Mangrove, Wild Guava) is a small to medium tree from the freshwater mangroves, river margins, and coastal wetlands of tropical Africa, Madagascar, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific — bearing long, pendant racemes of spectacular, nocturnal, white to pink-tinged, powder-puff flowers with hundreds of long stamens in late night bloom — one of the most beautiful flowering trees of freshwater wetlands.
directions: Plant Barringtonia racemosa in moist to permanently wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun at the margins of ponds, streams, or in any reliably moist lowland position; in dry gardens, regular deep irrigation is needed; highly ornamental when in bloom at night. Powder Puff Mangrove is the freshwater counterpart to Barringtonia asiatica — smaller in overall size, preferring stream banks, pond margins, and freshwater mangrove zones rather than saltwater beaches, but equally spectacular in flower. The long, pendulous flower racemes (each 8–24 inches long) bear dozens of individual flowers that open at night, producing an exquisite display of white, brush-like, many-stamened flowers that fall by morning — the fallen stamens carpeting the ground or water below. The nocturnal blooming strategy reflects pollination by bats and hawk moths; the fragrance is sweet and distinctive. Throughout its vast range across tropical Asia and Africa, the bark, leaves, fruits, and seeds have numerous traditional medicinal applications — used for fever, skin conditions, rheumatism, and as a fish poison (similar to its coastal relative). The fruits are fibrous, oval, and float in fresh water for dispersal along rivers and streams. An outstanding ornamental for tropical water gardens, pond margins, and moist lowland positions in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta hypoleuca produces larger leaves than most species hostas and is a robust grower once established, forming handsome large clumps in appropriate shade conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Hosta hypoleuca is a Japanese species hosta named for its most distinctive feature — the thick, waxy white powder (glaucous bloom) coating the underside of each leaf, creating a dramatic bicolor effect when the large, dark gray-green upper leaf surface is contrasted with the brilliant white underside. Native to rocky cliffs and shaded slopes in central Honshu, Japan. The large, ovate to cordate leaves (up to 12 inches long) and the white-powdered undersides set it apart from all other hosta species. The pale lavender to white flowers are attractive in late summer. A valuable addition to shade gardens where distinctive leaf texture and detail are important design elements. Combines beautifully with ferns and other shade plants where the white leaf undersides catch filtered light and create visual depth in the shaded border.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; powderpuff mimosa spreads by both rhizomes and rooting stems to form a dense, low, weed-suppressing mat, and tolerates light foot traffic and occasional mowing once established.
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; drought-tolerant once established and fixes its own nitrogen, needing little to no supplemental fertility. Mimosa strigillosa (powderpuff mimosa, or sunshine mimosa) is a low, spreading native perennial groundcover of the Gulf South and Southeast, valued as one of the best flowering lawn alternatives for the region — the fine, fern-like, sensitive foliage folds shut when touched, much like its larger relative the sensitive briar, delighting children and adults alike, and the low mat tolerates mowing and light foot traffic once established. From spring through fall, the plant is studded with small, round, bright pink pompom flowers that are a favorite nectar source for native bees and butterflies, including as a larval host for several skipper species. Because it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and spreads to form a dense, weed-suppressing carpet, it also serves as a low-input, ecologically valuable substitute for turf grass in sunny to lightly shaded areas. An excellent pollinator-friendly lawn alternative for the Gulf South, zone 7–10.
