directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for natural cold stratification, or start from transplants; purple coneflower is one of the most ecologically valuable and widely grown native perennials of the eastern and central US prairie, producing large rosy-purple daisy-like flowers with prominent orange-brown spiny central cones from midsummer through early fall that attract an extraordinary diversity of pollinators. The roots and leaves have a centuries-long history as the most widely used plant in North American traditional medicine, and Echinacea extracts remain among the best-selling herbal supplements for immune support. Allow seed heads to mature and stand through winter — they are a primary food source for American goldfinches and many other songbirds. Grows best in lean soil; excessive fertility produces floppy stems and poor flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms, or cold stratify seed for 4 weeks to improve germination.
directions: This native heirloom is a long-lived perennial that blooms for a month or more from midsummer, with pinkish-purple petals surrounding a large dark cone. Sow seed in spring after the last frost, or cold stratify beforehand to break dormancy. Space plants a foot or more apart in well-drained soil and full sun to part shade. Once established it is drought tolerant and self-sows. Leave spent cones standing to feed goldfinches through fall and winter.

plant_note: Scatter seeds on bare, dry, disturbed ground in fall and press lightly into the soil surface; do not cover, as seeds need light to germinate.
directions: Purple Cudweed is a silvery-woolly native annual or biennial that forms a low basal rosette of soft, spatulate leaves coated in white wool before sending up dense leafy spikes of small rose-purple to brownish composite flower heads from spring through early summer. It is an important larval host plant for the American Painted Lady butterfly and attracts small native bees seeking pollen. Grow it in dry, sandy, lean, or disturbed open ground in full sun; rich or moist soils suppress growth and reduce self-seeding. Direct sow on bare soil in fall, pressing seeds lightly against the surface without burying them, and allow plants to complete their cycle and self-sow for a self-sustaining colony.

common_name: Purple Dome Aster (Compact Deep Purple New England Aster)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Dome is a compact New England aster selection that stays low and mounded without the floppy growth and staking that taller New England asters usually require.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Purple Dome is a compact selection of native New England aster, forming a tidy, dense, dome-shaped mound covered in deep violet-purple daisy flowers with golden centers in fall, without the tall, sprawling growth habit that often requires staking in the wild species. This shorter stature makes it far more practical for a mixed perennial border, and like other New England asters it is an exceptional late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and other migrating pollinators. It performs best with consistent moisture through summer and can be divided every few years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Purple Dragon Lamium (Silver-Leaf Deep Violet Dead Nettle)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Purple Dragon has almost entirely silver foliage narrowly edged in green, topped with deep violet-purple flowers, one of the showiest color combinations among lamium cultivars.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Purple Dragon produces nearly solid silvery-white foliage with just a thin green margin, among the most striking silver-leaved lamium cultivars, topped in spring with clusters of deep violet-purple flowers that stand out sharply against the pale foliage. It spreads by surface runners to form a dense groundcover mat fairly quickly, making it useful for brightening a dark, shaded bed under trees or shrubs, and it tolerates fairly dry shade once established better than many groundcovers. Shear back after flowering if the mat becomes tired-looking in summer heat to encourage fresh new growth for fall.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; nasturtiums resent transplanting.
directions: This trailing variety carries deeply veined petals in shades of purple fading to lavender and dusty rose, making it ideal for hanging baskets or as a flowering ground cover. Sow the large seeds directly where they are to grow once the soil has warmed, planting about half an inch deep. Avoid rich soil and heavy feeding, which produces leaves at the expense of blooms. It is fairly drought tolerant once established. Both the peppery blossoms and leaves are edible and add a colorful kick to salads.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in consistently moist to wet soil, preferably at a streambank, pond margin, or rain garden; Physostegia purpurea spreads by rhizomes and will naturalize into a colony in reliably wet conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to saturated soil at a streambank, pond edge, or rain garden where roots can stay consistently wet; this species is distinct from the more common Physostegia virginiana and thrives in wetter, shadier conditions than its relative. The vivid purple-pink tubular flowers appear in fall and are held on upright spikes; each individual flower can be repositioned laterally on the stem and will stay put, a quirk that earns the plant its common name 'obedient plant.' Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent the colony from overcrowding neighboring plants.

plant_note: Root stem-tip cuttings in warm, moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; pseuderanthemum colors most intensely in bright indirect light — deep shade causes the purple coloring to fade toward green.
directions: Root stem-tip cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade; purple false eranthemum (Jacob's coat, eldorado) is a Pacific Islands tropical shrub grown for its spectacular, large, glossy, dark-purple to maroon leaves dramatically overlaid with scattered spots, streaks, and blotches of pink, rose, gold, and white — one of the most richly colored foliage plants available for tropical and subtropical gardens. The unusual combination of dark background coloration with bright-colored irregular markings creates a bold, jewel-like quality unlike any other landscape shrub. Small, pale-lavender to white, tubular flowers appear in terminal spikes throughout the year in frost-free climates but are secondary to the remarkable foliage. Excellent combined with chartreuse-leaved plants (golden pothos, lime coleus) for high-contrast tropical compositions. Grown as a houseplant in cool climates; in zone 10–12 it forms an outdoor foliage shrub of 2–4 feet. 'Tricolor' and 'Rubrum' are cultivar selections emphasizing different color combinations.

plant_note: Direct sow among established native grasses at or just after last frost; seeds require contact with host grass roots for successful establishment.
directions: Purple False Foxglove is a native annual hemi-parasite of eastern North American prairies, pine savannas, and wet meadows, drawing supplemental nutrition through root connections to neighboring grasses while also performing its own photosynthesis. To grow it successfully, direct sow seeds among established native warm-season grasses such as little bluestem or broomsedge in full sun — without host grass roots present, germination and survival rates drop sharply. The plant produces a profusion of showy, rosy-purple, trumpet-shaped flowers with spotted throats from August through October, providing a critical late-season nectar source for native bees and supporting the caterpillars of the buckeye butterfly. Sow seeds on the soil surface at or just after last frost and keep the planting moist until germination; once established, plants are largely self-sufficient.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants after last frost; this cultivar does not come true from seed and is propagated by division.
directions: Plant after last frost in full sun and very well-drained soil; purple fountain grass is grown as an annual north of zone 9 for its arching burgundy-red foliage and showy, rose-tinged plumes from midsummer through frost. It thrives in heat and drought once established but requires consistent moisture the first few weeks after transplanting. In frost-free climates it is a perennial that can become invasive — avoid planting near natural areas and remove flower heads before seeds ripen. Bring container-grown specimens indoors before frost to overwinter as a houseplant in colder zones.

common_name: Purple Globe Amaranth (Heat-Proof Deep Purple Clover-Like Annual for Hot Summers)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Purple Globe Amaranth is among the best summer annuals for sustained performance in brutal Gulf South summer heat and humidity — it actually performs better in August than June in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Purple Globe Amaranth (Gomphrena globosa) produces compact, globe-shaped, clover-like flower heads in rich magenta-purple — papery, button-like structures (1/2–3/4 inch) that maintain their color indefinitely when dried, making globe amaranth one of the premier cut-and-dried flower annuals for summer gardens. The papery bracts retain their vivid purple color when dry because they are composed of pigmented, non-photosynthetic modified leaves rather than the true petals (which would bleach on drying) — the same quality that makes strawflowers, statice, and immortelle persist when dried. In the summer garden, globe amaranth is outstanding for one key quality: it genuinely thrives in the brutal Gulf South summer heat that collapses most other annuals in July and August. The vivid purple clover-like heads continue to produce without pause through extreme heat and humidity, providing consistent garden color when most other summer annuals have declined. Butterflies visit the flowers consistently through the bloom season. The dried flower heads retain their color for months and are outstanding in dry arrangements. Low fertility and good drainage extend bloom; excess nitrogen promotes leafy growth over flowers.

common_name: Purple Glory Tree (Brazilian Spider Flower, Princess Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Purple Glory Tree grows rapidly and should be planted in a location with room to develop a multi-branched canopy 15–25 feet wide. In zone 9a, it freezes back hard in cold winters but resprouts vigorously from the trunk or base in spring; in zone 9b-10, it is semi-evergreen to evergreen. The most spectacular bloom occurs in fall (September–November) and a second flush in spring; do not prune in late summer to preserve flower buds.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, organically rich soil; Purple Glory Tree grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Tibouchina granulosa is a large, fast-growing tree from the Atlantic rainforest of Brazil, producing one of the most spectacular purple floral displays of any tree in the subtropical world. In late summer through fall, the entire canopy becomes covered with large (2–3 inch) royal purple to intense violet flowers borne in broad, flat-topped clusters at every stem tip — the effect is breathtaking, with a well-established specimen appearing as though it has been draped in a cascade of purple velvet. Each flower has prominent purple anthers on curved filaments that give the genus the common name 'Spider Flower.' The large, velvet-textured, dark-green, prominently ribbed leaves are attractive year-round. Tibouchina granulosa (the tree form) is distinguished from the shrubby Princess Flower (T. urvilleana, 6–10 feet) by its potential tree height of 25–40 feet in zone 10-11 and its tendency to develop a single dominant trunk. In zone 9, hard pruning after frost damage stimulates vigorous regrowth and heavy flowering on new wood. An outstanding specimen tree for subtropical Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May or September–October. Purple Heart is a tender perennial in zone 7–9 that may die back to the ground in hard freezes but resprouts reliably from the roots in spring. The trailing, spreading stems root wherever nodes contact moist soil, rapidly covering ground in sunny to partially shaded areas. Stem cuttings root extremely easily — simply cut a stem and place it in moist soil or water, where roots develop within 1–2 weeks. The vivid purple color intensifies in full sun and fades somewhat in shade; in very deep shade the foliage may appear more green-purple than the vivid, saturated purple of full-sun plants.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Purple Heart is drought tolerant once established and blooms most freely with the most vivid purple foliage in full sun, while tolerating partial shade; Purple Heart (Tradescantia pallida, formerly Setcreasea pallida) is one of the most striking purple-foliaged plants available for zone 9 gardens, producing a intense, saturated, clear purple color on both the trailing stems and the large (4–5 inch), lance-shaped leaves that is unique among commonly grown ground covers and border plants. Small, three-petaled, bright pink-magenta flowers appear at the stem tips in summer, providing a complementary floral dimension to the primary foliage display. The trailing, ground-covering habit (stems rooting where they contact soil) makes Purple Heart one of the most effective and low-maintenance purple ground covers available — spreading steadily without becoming invasive in most garden contexts, rooting easily from stem pieces, and recovering quickly from damage or drought when conditions improve. In zone 9 Purple Heart is at its best — thriving in the summer heat that stresses many ornamentals and maintaining its vivid color through the entire growing season from spring through fall. The vivid purple provides exceptional contrast with chartreuse, silver-gray, and gold-foliaged companion plants.

common_name: Purple Heart (Purple Queen, Purple Wandering Jew)
plant_note: Root 3–4 inch stem cuttings in water or moist mix in spring; purple heart roots easily and quickly. Plant in any well-drained soil from full sun to partial shade. Full sun intensifies the deep purple color; shade causes the stems to elongate and the color to fade to green-purple. In zone 7–8 tops die back in frost; roots survive to zone 7.
directions: Root cuttings in water and plant in any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; purple heart is one of the most valuable and widely grown groundcovers for Gulf Coast gardens, producing thick, spreading mats of deep, intensely violet-purple succulent stems and strap-like leaves with a metallic sheen. The color is among the most saturated purple of any plant — a striking design element in the landscape. It produces small pink flowers in summer. Purple heart is nearly indestructible — tolerating drought, heat, salt spray, poor soil, and reflected heat from pavement. In zone 7–11 it is perennial (tops die back in freezes but resprout); it can also be overwintered indoors as a container plant or trailing houseplant. An outstanding container plant for providing dramatic color contrast with silver, chartreuse, or orange-flowering companions. Deer resistant.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost onto dry, lean soil in full sun; seed requires light to germinate — press onto surface without covering.
directions: Direct sow at last frost onto dry, lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun, pressing seed lightly onto the surface without covering since light improves germination. Thin seedlings to 12-18 inches once established and avoid any fertilizer or excess moisture, which promotes rank, floppy growth at the expense of flowering. Whorled clusters of purple to lavender tubular flowers with pale, purple-spotted bracts appear in summer and attract native bees, bumblebees, and hummingbirds; the whole plant releases a strong, spicy-mint fragrance when touched. Allow seed heads to ripen and scatter in place for reliable self-sowing in open, disturbed, sunny ground in subsequent years.

common_name: Purple Hyacinth Bean Vine (Ornamental Heirloom Lablab Bean Vine)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; purple hyacinth bean is a fast-growing tropical vine that can cover an arbor, trellis, or fence rapidly in the Gulf South's warm growing season. In zone 9, plant March–May — the vine grows most vigorously and flowers most prolifically as day length decreases in August and September. The entire plant is ornamental: purple-tinged leaves, magenta-purple pea-like flowers, and spectacular bright purple seed pods that persist for weeks. A perennial in zones 9b–11 but easily grown as an annual from seed.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost near a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor — the vines can reach 10–15 feet and require support. Purple Hyacinth Bean (Lablab purpureus) is one of the most dramatic ornamental vines for the warm-season garden — a fast-growing tropical legume vine with multiple ornamental features occurring simultaneously: dark green leaves with deep purple veining and purple undersides, dense racemes of fragrant, bright magenta-purple pea-type flowers, and after flowering, spectacular flat, bright purple seed pods (2–3 inches long) that persist on the vine for weeks, contrasting strikingly with the continuing flowers and creating a multi-season display. The ornamental pod color is unusual in the plant kingdom — very few plants produce purple pods of this intensity, and the color display is most impressive in late summer and fall when the pods are most abundant. Hyacinth bean is one of the most popular annual vines in American Southern gardens where the long growing season allows it to reach its full potential; it is relatively tender and needs the warmth of a Gulf South spring to establish well. The seeds and pods are edible when cooked thoroughly (raw hyacinth bean contains toxic amounts of cyanogenic glucosides), and the plant is grown as a food crop throughout Africa and Asia.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist soil or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; alternanthera develops its best color in full sun and heat, and is perennial in zones 9–11.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; alternanthera (Joseph's coat) is a tropical foliage plant grown for its intensely colored leaves in burgundy, purple, red, orange, or multicolored patterns that provide vivid, heat-resistant color throughout the summer and fall when many plants struggle. It is widely used in bedding schemes, tapestry plantings, and as an edging plant in formal gardens. Colors intensify with heat and full sun exposure. In zones 9–11 it is a perennial groundcover; elsewhere treat as an annual and either collect stem cuttings to overwinter indoors or replant from cuttings each spring. Shear periodically to maintain dense, compact form.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into very dry, lean, rocky or sandy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; keep away from livestock.
directions: Purple Locoweed is a low-growing, silky-hairy native perennial of dry, open, rocky or sandy prairies and hills throughout the Great Plains, producing basal rosettes of pinnate, silver-hairy leaves and upright stems bearing dense, showy spikes of rose-pink to magenta-purple pea flowers in spring; it is among the most ornamental native prairie legumes in cultivation. CAUTION: all parts are toxic to livestock — cattle, horses, and sheep that graze it in quantity develop a neurological condition known as locoism. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into very dry, lean, rocky or sandy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; germination can be variable, so sow generously. An excellent, deeply drought-tolerant native for xeriscape and prairie gardens in zones 3 through 8 wherever livestock access can be controlled.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring on dry, sandy, well-drained, infertile soil in full sun; purple lovegrass self-seeds freely and forms naturalized colonies in open, dry areas — it establishes quickly and is one of the fastest native grasses to produce ornamental value from seed.
directions: Purple lovegrass is one of the most spectacularly ornamental native grasses of eastern North America — in late summer and fall, the compact, low tufts produce enormous, airy, branching panicles of tiny pink-purple to reddish-purple spikelets that stand well above the foliage and glow with iridescent color in slanted afternoon light, catching the eye from considerable distance in the garden and roadside landscape. The loose, tumbling seed heads eventually break off and roll across fields like tumbleweed, scattering seeds widely — in dry, sandy soils the grass self-seeds prolifically and can form beautiful naturalized meadows without any maintenance. It is one of the lowest-maintenance, highest-reward native grasses available for dry, sunny sites in zones 4–9: remarkably drought and heat tolerant, requiring absolutely no supplemental irrigation or fertilization once established, and producing its spectacular fall display with zero input. Use it in masses on dry slopes, sandy roadsides, and xeric garden borders where its cloud-like purple seed heads create a fall and winter spectacle.

plant_note: Surface sow seed 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; seeds need light to germinate. Can also sow in fall for natural stratification. Plants are dioecious — both male and female plants produce flowers, but only females set seed.
directions: Surface sow seed in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; purple meadow rue is one of the tallest and most architecturally striking native shade perennials, producing airy sprays of lavender-purple to white flowers on dark purple stems in late spring to early summer that rise above bold, blue-green, aquilegia-like foliage. It grows naturally in moist prairies, stream banks, and open woodland edges across the Midwest and Great Plains, tolerating light shade well. The flowers are pollinated by wind and native bees. The plant provides excellent vertical structure in the middle-to-back of a woodland edge border and combines beautifully with native ferns and woodland wildflowers. It spreads slowly by rhizome and self-seeding to naturalize in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold stratification to break seed dormancy; purple milkweed benefits from natural cold-moist treatment over winter and will germinate reliably the following spring.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun, allowing winter cold stratification to trigger spring germination; purple milkweed is slower to establish than common milkweed but grows from a deep taproot and should not be moved once established. Asclepias purpurascens is a native milkweed of central and eastern North America, producing upright stems with large opposite leaves and rounded umbels of intensely deep rose-purple flowers in June and July that are highly attractive to monarch butterflies, which use it as a host plant. It is less commonly grown than A. tuberosa or A. incarnata but is particularly valuable for partial-shade woodland edge gardens where it thrives and provides essential monarch breeding habitat.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring along stream banks, seep margins, or wet meadow edges in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, mineral or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; purple monkeyflower requires consistently moist to wet soil and cool summer temperatures, growing naturally along cold mountain streams and wet subalpine meadows.
directions: Plant or direct sow in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, mineral-rich soil along stream banks, seeps, or wet meadow margins in partial shade to full sun; purple monkeyflower (formerly Mimulus lewisii) is a native perennial of cold mountain streams and subalpine wet meadows from the Rockies through the Cascades, producing large, showy, rose-pink to deep magenta flowers with yellow-bearded lower lips and dark spotting — among the most beautiful of the wild monkeyflowers. Named after Meriwether Lewis of the Lewis and Clark expedition, who collected it during the crossing of the Rockies. The large, tubular flowers are primarily pollinated by bumblebees, but at sites where the species co-occurs with its red-flowered relative E. cardinalis, the two species have been the subject of landmark research demonstrating how pollinator preference drives flower color evolution. An outstanding native for boggy streamside or pond-edge gardens in cool climate zones.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; purple moor grass is a slow-establishing but long-lived grass that improves significantly after the second or third year in the garden — patience is rewarded.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; purple moor grass is a European native of wet heathlands and moors that is grown in the ornamental garden for its exceptional fall color — the foliage and flower stems turn warm golden-orange to amber-yellow in autumn, creating one of the most brilliant grass color displays available. The slender, arching stems bear delicate, purplish flower panicles in summer that arch gracefully and move freely in the breeze. Plants die completely to the ground in winter, making spring clean-up easy (simply pull the old clumps away). Slow to establish but forms handsome, non-invasive clumps that improve over years. 'Variegata' (cream-striped leaves), 'Heidebraut' (upright, tall), and the large cultivar group Molinia caerulea ssp. arundinacea provides taller, more dramatic forms to 5–6 feet. An excellent grass for moist, acidic, partially shaded sites.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, clay-loam to rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple needlegrass is the state grass of California, native to clay grasslands, serpentine outcrops, and coastal prairie. In its native climate it is winter-growing, summer-dormant, and best sown in fall for natural germination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, clay-loam, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun; purple needlegrass is the state grass of California and one of the most important grasses of native California coastal prairie and valley grassland. The fine, dark green foliage forms elegant, upright bunches that are evergreen in mild coastal climates. In spring, the plant produces distinctive, feathery purple-tinted seed heads with long, twisted awns that catch the light and shimmer purple in morning and evening sun — giving the plant its common name. After the summer-dry seed-set period, the awns help the seeds burrow into the soil by hygroscopic twisting, planting themselves. An outstanding low-water, deer-resistant native grass for California-style gardens and drought-tolerant plantings. Winter-active, summer-dry cycle; do not irrigate in summer once established in California climates.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds (nick seed coat with a file or soak 24 hours in warm water before sowing to improve germination) or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun in spring; purple orchid tree germinates readily from seed and self-seeds moderately in warm climates — remove unwanted seedlings before they establish.
directions: Sow scarified seed or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; purple orchid tree is a South Asian deciduous to semi-evergreen flowering tree widely planted throughout zone 9–12 landscapes for its large, showy, fragrant, five-petaled, orchid-like flowers in shades of pink, lavender, purple, and white with crimson veining that appear in autumn through early winter — uniquely, the tree flowers most abundantly after dropping its large, rounded, bilobed leaves in late fall, so the spectacular flower display occurs on nearly bare branches for maximum visual impact. The flowers are followed by flat, woody seed pods that persist through winter. Bauhinia purpurea flowers in fall-winter (August–December in the Gulf South), while the related B. variegata flowers in late winter-spring — together they extend the Bauhinia flowering season. The young leaves and flower buds are edible and eaten in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking. It is one of the most reliable and easily grown flowering trees for zone 9–12 and germinates readily from seed, though seed-grown trees vary in flower color and intensity.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in water or moist perlite, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil or potting mix in bright indirect light to partial shade; the intense purple color develops best in bright indirect light — direct sun scorches the leaves.
directions: Root stem cuttings easily in water or moist perlite; purple passion plant is a Javanese native grown for its extraordinary, intensely purple-violet velvety foliage — the dark-green, toothed leaves are so thickly covered with purple hairs that the entire plant appears to glow with deep, jewel-like purple coloration, a dramatic and unusual effect. The color is most intense in young growth and in bright indirect light; older leaves tend toward green. Pinch regularly to maintain compact, bushy form and prevent the plant from becoming leggy. The orange flowers that occasionally appear are unpleasant-smelling and should be removed — they signal the plant is aging. Excellent in combination plantings with ferns and silver-leaved companions in shaded patios and as an indoor accent plant. Roots in water readily for propagation.

plant_note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss; never use fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain water or distilled water at all times.
directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, acidic medium of pure sphagnum moss or a peat-perlite mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water — tap water, fertilizer, and regular potting soil will kill this plant. The deeply cupped pitchers fill with rain and digestive fluid, drowning insects that slip down the waxy inner walls and providing the plant's sole nitrogen source in its naturally sterile bog habitat. Purple pitcher plant is the hardiest of all Sarracenia, tolerating deep freezes across its native range from Labrador to the Gulf Coast, but it needs a cold winter dormancy with reduced light and moisture. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome and will naturalize in a backyard bog garden or container water feature.

common_name: Purple Pixie Loropetalum (Dwarf Weeping Groundcover Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Pixie's strongly weeping habit makes it exceptional for trailing over retaining walls, spilling out of raised planters, and massing as a groundcover on slopes — uses that exploit rather than fight its natural growth form.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Pixie is a dwarf, strongly weeping Loropetalum cultivar with a radically different growth habit from standard upright loropetalum — growing very low (12–24 inches tall) but spreading wide (3–5 feet) with strongly pendulous, cascading branches that create an elegant, trailing, mounded groundcover form unlike any other commonly available ornamental shrub in the Gulf South. The weeping habit makes Purple Pixie exceptional for uses that standard upright shrubs cannot fill: draping over retaining walls and raised planter edges to create a cascading curtain of burgundy foliage, massing as a groundcover on slopes and banks that are difficult to maintain with upright plants, and providing low-growing, weed-suppressing cover in landscape beds where taller shrubs would block views. The same deep burgundy-purple foliage and bright magenta-pink spring flowers as standard loropetalum cultivars, produced on cascading branches that sweep naturally downward. Extremely drought-tolerant once established, tolerating heat, humidity, and the clay soils of the Gulf South. The very compact, spreading growth means minimal pruning is required to maintain the natural form — periodic tip-pruning to encourage density and remove any particularly vigorous upright shoots maintains the groundcover character.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Pixie is much smaller than standard loropetalums and suits containers, low borders, and groundcover use where the standard-sized plants would be far too large.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Pixie is a breakthrough compact and weeping selection of the purple-leaved loropetalum that stays only 12–24 inches tall while spreading 3.5–5 feet wide, creating a distinctive low, mounding to weeping groundcover effect entirely different from the large-growing standard selections. The deep burgundy-purple foliage is among the darkest and most richly colored of any loropetalum cultivar — maintaining its vivid color through the growing season with more sun intensity increasing the purple intensity. Bright, deep pink fringe flowers appear in spring and intermittently through the season, providing color contrast against the dark foliage. The strongly weeping branch tips cascade down and outward, creating a softening effect at wall edges, raised planting beds, and container rims that the standard upright forms cannot provide. Purple Pixie is an outstanding container plant, groundcover on slopes, and edging plant where its low profile and weeping habit can be showcased. It is Zone Award from the Gulf Coast Plant Introduction Group and performs reliably in zone 9 heat without the pest and disease problems that affect some ornamental cultivars.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native spring iris-family corm
plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple pleat-leaf is native to the moist prairies, roadsides, and open grassy areas of the Texas Gulf Coast and adjacent Louisiana, where it blooms in March–May in dense spring colonies. Each individual flower lasts only one day but the plant produces a long succession of blooms. Goes dormant in summer heat. The pleated, iris-like leaves are distinctive.
directions: Plant corms in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple pleat-leaf is a charming, small native iris-family wildflower of the Texas Gulf Coast — one of those overlooked native plants that is easily passed by in a nursery but produces, in its natural prairie colonies in March and April, an unexpectedly beautiful display of small, brilliant, deep-blue-violet to purple, three-outer-petaled flowers (with white and yellow markings at the throat of each outer petal) that stop observers in their tracks with the intense, jewel-like quality of the color against the pale spring prairie grass. Each individual flower lasts only a single day but the colony produces a sustained succession of blooms over 4–6 weeks. The narrow, pleated, iris-like leaves (giving both the common name 'pleat-leaf' and the family resemblance) emerge in late winter. Native to the Texas coastal prairies from the Houston area to Corpus Christi and adjacent Louisiana, it is precisely adapted to zone 9a Gulf Coast conditions of warm-wet springs, hot-dry summers, and mild winters. An underused Gulf Coast native for spring prairie and naturalistic garden plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for natural stratification and spring germination, or start indoors and transplant in early spring; wine cups develops a deep taproot that makes it extremely drought-tolerant once established but also means it should not be moved after planting — choose the site carefully.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall in sandy, gravelly, or well-drained soil in full sun; do not transplant established plants as the deep taproot is easily damaged. Callirhoe involucrata is one of the most beautiful and drought-tolerant native wildflowers of the central and southern prairies, producing sprawling stems 8–12 inches tall that spread 2–4 feet, covered from late spring through midsummer with brilliant magenta-crimson, cup-shaped flowers 1.5–2 inches across that are outstandingly vivid and seemingly fluorescent in full sunlight — the common name 'wine cups' perfectly captures the color and form. Absolutely drought-tolerant once the deep taproot establishes, and adapted to poor, rocky, and sandy soils; excellent for hot, dry slopes, rock gardens, and prairie plantings in zones 4–9. Native bees and bumblebees visit the flowers constantly.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; purple prairie clover develops a deep taproot and is extremely difficult to transplant — sow in a permanent location and allow natural cold stratification over winter; scarification or a 24-hour cold-water soak improves germination rates in spring-sown seed.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; purple prairie clover develops a deep, woody taproot in its first season and cannot be successfully transplanted — choose a permanent site, sow seeds in place, and allow them to cold-stratify naturally over winter for reliable spring germination. Dalea purpurea is one of the signature wildflowers of the North American tallgrass and mixed-grass prairie, native across a vast range from Canada south through the Great Plains and into the Gulf Coast states; from June through August it produces distinctive, thimble-like cylindrical flower heads densely packed with tiny, brilliant magenta-purple petals that open progressively from the base of the head upward, creating a moving ring of color and pollen that makes it one of the most recognizable and beloved prairie wildflowers. It is a nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil fertility and is a keystone plant in prairie restorations; the flowers are intensely visited by a wide diversity of native bees including mining bees, sweat bees, small carpenter bees, and specialist Dalea-foraging bees, making it one of the highest-value pollinator plants on the prairie. Purple prairie clover is slow-growing in its first year as it establishes its root system but extremely long-lived and drought-proof once established — individual plants may persist for decades in appropriate lean, dry, well-drained conditions, and the attractive fine-textured foliage remains ornamental from spring through fall.

common_name: Purple Queen Bougainvillea (Rich Purple-Violet Bougainvillea Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; promote blooming by allowing slight water stress between waterings and by limiting nitrogen fertilizer — excess fertility and water promote vegetative growth at the expense of flower production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Purple Queen is a bougainvillea cultivar producing bracts in rich, deep purple-violet to blue-purple tones — one of the more purely purple-toned bougainvilleas available, with bracts that lean toward violet-blue rather than the magenta-red of Barbara Karst or the scarlet of San Diego Red. The deeper, cooler purple tone has a different visual quality in the landscape — more sophisticated and less vivid than the hot pinks and reds, creating an elegant effect particularly effective with silver and gray foliage companions. Purple Queen has the same vigorous growth habit as other bougainvillea cultivars, capable of covering large wall areas or pergolas in favorable zone 9-11 conditions. The bloom response to humidity-following-drought, water stress promotion, and lean soil management applies equally to Purple Queen as to other bougainvillea cultivars — slightly stressing the plant consistently produces heavier flowering than well-fed and well-watered specimens. The purple bract color fades to mauve-pink as the flowers age on the plant, providing a naturally occurring color gradient from new vivid-purple bracts at the stem tips to older faded-mauve bracts closer to the main stems — an attractive multi-tone effect during extended bloom periods. Container-grown Purple Queen performs well on patios and in large planters where the root restriction actually promotes flowering.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring or early fall, or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; shear back hard (by half) immediately after flowering to keep plants compact and prevent them from becoming woody and bare in the center. Aubrieta dislikes hot, humid summer conditions and performs poorly south of zone 7 in the American South.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; purple rock cress is among the most brilliant and cheerful spring-blooming groundcovers of rock gardens and dry stone walls — a low, mat-forming perennial from the eastern Mediterranean and southern Europe producing sheets of vivid violet-purple to lavender to lilac to magenta four-petaled flowers that cascade over walls and edges in March through May in an uninterrupted carpet of color. The named cultivars and hybrids span the full range from pure purple-blue to rose-red and bright magenta, and some have variegated foliage. A classic component of the spring rock garden alongside arabis, iberis, and alyssum, forming a traditional tricolor combination of purple, white, and gold. Outstanding cascading over dry stone walls where its natural habitat — limestone cliff faces of the eastern Mediterranean — is well replicated. Shear back hard after blooming to maintain compact form and prevent the center from going bare.

subcategory: hardy Himalayan ginger relative with orchid-like purple flowers
plant_note: Plant fleshy root divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; roscoea emerges late in spring (do not assume dormant divisions are dead) and blooms in early to midsummer with striking purple, orchid-like flowers. It is one of the hardiest ginger relatives available, tolerating winters well into zone 6. Excellent drainage is essential in winter; heavy, wet soils cause root rot. Divide clumps every 3–4 years in spring.
directions: Plant fleshy root divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; roscoea is a remarkable member of the ginger family (Zingiberaceae) native to the high-altitude grasslands and open forests of the Himalayas — Nepal, northern India, and Bhutan — that has evolved to tolerate cold far exceeding what most Zingiberaceae endure, making it genuinely hardy into USDA zone 6 with excellent drainage. The plant emerges very late in spring (mid-May to early June in most zones; do not disturb the site or assume divisions have failed), quickly producing short, compact rosettes of upright, strap-shaped, mid-green leaves from which the strikingly orchid-like flowers emerge on short stems in early to midsummer; the flowers are large for the plant's scale, strongly two-lipped, in shades of rich violet-purple to purple-blue, with a distinctive hooded upper petal and broad, spreading lower lip that creates a strong resemblance to an orchid bloom. Excellent drainage — particularly in winter when the plant is dormant — is essential to prevent rot of the fleshy storage roots. An unusual and rewarding plant for the shade or woodland garden in zones 6–9.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; purple sensation allium naturalizes readily to form expanding clumps and self-sows freely in well-drained, undisturbed soils.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Purple Sensation is the most widely planted of all ornamental alliums, producing perfectly spherical, dense, globe-shaped heads of 100+ tiny, deep rich-violet star-shaped flowers on tall, upright stems in late spring — bridging the blooming gap between late tulips and early summer perennials with striking vertical structure. The globes measure 3–4 inches in diameter and the color is so saturated it appears almost electric. The allium family's typical onion fragrance is only noticeable when the foliage is disturbed. The dried seed heads remain attractive through summer. Excellent combined with catmint, salvia, and tall bearded iris in bold late-spring compositions. Bulbs multiply over years to form expanding clumps requiring no routine care.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in well-drained, fertile to average soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Purple Sensation allium is one of the most reliable and free-flowering of the large ornamental alliums and adapts to a range of well-drained garden soils. Plant toward the middle or back of the border — the large basal leaves die back before or as the flowers open, and surrounding foliage of perennials such as hostas, geraniums, or ornamental grasses will conceal the untidy leaves.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun in fall for May bloom; Purple Sensation allium is among the most popular and widely grown of all ornamental alliums, producing dense, perfectly round, 3-4-inch globes of deep violet-purple flowers on tall, 24-36-inch stems in mid-spring — a vivid and eye-catching display that bridges late tulips and early summer perennials. The cultivar 'Purple Sensation' is particularly prized for its intense, saturated violet-purple color that does not fade as the flowers age, distinguishing it from the more commonly offered seed-grown Allium aflatunense strains which may show paler, more variable coloring. The broad, strap-like basal leaves emerge in early spring and die back as the flowers open, so siting near bushy perennials or ornamental grasses to disguise the foliage is recommended. The dried round seed heads are attractive and long-lasting on the stem, continuing to provide structural interest through summer.

plant_note: Plant small rhizomes (bulblets) 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; purple shamrock grows from small, scaly rhizomes that can be left in the ground year-round in zone 7–10. The plant goes summer-dormant in intense heat and re-emerges in fall.
directions: Plant small rhizomes 1 inch deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; purple shamrock is one of the most charming and versatile small shade plants, producing triangular, folded leaves in deep burgundy-purple with three leaflets that look exactly like large, richly colored shamrocks. The leaves fold downward at night and in strong sun (nyctinasty), 'sleeping' closed before reopening each morning. Small pink flowers are produced on delicate stems above the foliage from spring through fall. It is outstanding in containers, window boxes, and as a low border edging in partial shade. The leaves and flowers are edible with a pleasant sorrel-like tartness (high in oxalic acid — consume only in small amounts). In zone 7–10 the rhizomes overwinter in the ground; the plant may go partly dormant in hot summers and resprout in fall with cooler temperatures.

common_name: Purple Spiderwort (Garden Spiderwort Hybrid with Blue-Purple Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; garden spiderworts tolerate considerable shade — they perform well in positions receiving only 3–4 hours of sun, making them useful in the partial shade category that many bright-colored perennials cannot fill.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Tradescantia x andersoniana (garden spiderwort) is a hybrid group derived from crosses among several native North American Tradescantia species, producing garden perennials with larger, showier, longer-season blooms than any individual parent species. The distinctive three-petaled, blue-violet to purple flowers (individual blooms last only one day but are produced in long succession over many weeks) open primarily in the cooler parts of the day — morning and evening — making garden spiderwort particularly charming at dawn and dusk. Named cultivars include blue-purple ('Zwanenburg Blue', 'Blue Stone'), rose-pink ('Osprey', 'Karminglut'), and white selections, providing a range of color within the hybrid group. In zone 9, garden spiderwort blooms most heavily in spring (March–May) and again in fall (September–October), going semi-dormant in the heat of summer — a pattern characteristic of many cool-season perennials in the Gulf South. The partial-shade tolerance (performing well with only 3–4 hours direct sun) makes garden spiderwort a particularly valuable perennial for the between-full-sun-and-deep-shade positions that are difficult to fill with colorful flowering plants. The strappy, blue-green foliage provides attractive texture even when not in bloom. Divide established clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; soak seed overnight to speed germination.
directions: This unusual heirloom prized since 16th-century England bears nodding, tear-shaped purple bracts on blue-green foliage that pairs beautifully with bronze and deep-purple plants. Soak seed overnight, then sow directly into the garden in early spring for the strongest plants. It thrives in heat and makes a long-lasting cut flower. Give it well-drained soil and full sun. Plants often self-sow to return the following year.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; seeds need light and should not be covered. Linaria self-seeds freely and will naturalize in gravel, dry banks, and cracks in walls.
directions: Scatter seeds on bare, well-drained, lean soil in full sun in early spring or fall, pressing lightly onto the surface without covering; purple toadflax is a slender, airy perennial with delicate narrow leaves and upright spikes of tiny snapdragon-like flowers in lavender-purple (and white in the cultivar 'Canon Went') that bloom from late spring through midsummer and intermittently afterward. Exceptionally drought-tolerant and suited to dry, stony, or poor alkaline soils where it self-seeds and naturalizes freely in gravel gardens, dry banks, old walls, and Mediterranean-style plantings. The main flush of bloom comes in early summer; cutting back spent stems encourages repeat flowering through autumn. Allow some seeds to scatter naturally each year to maintain the colony.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in late summer or early fall in deep, humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in full shade under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizomes in late summer in deep, humus-rich, moist, acidic soil in full shade under deciduous hardwoods; purple trillium is a native woodland wildflower of the Appalachians and Northeast that emerges in mid-spring on erect stems bearing a whorl of three broad leaves and a single dark red to purple flower with a distinctive musky odor that attracts carrion-fly pollinators. Plants enter full summer dormancy by July — mark planting locations to avoid accidental disturbance. Enrich soil with generous amounts of aged leaf mold and fallen oak leaves to mimic the rich forest floor conditions these plants evolved in. Only purchase from reputable nurseries selling nursery-propagated, not wild-collected, stock.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall for winter or early spring germination in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; purple viper's bugloss is a cool-season annual that germinates in autumn or early spring and flowers in late spring. CAUTION: It is classified as a noxious weed and invasive species in California, Oregon, several other western states, and Australia, where it spreads aggressively in rangelands and is toxic to livestock due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid content. Confirm it is legal and non-invasive in your region before planting.
directions: Sow seeds in fall in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; purple viper's bugloss is a Mediterranean annual and biennial wildflower producing masses of brilliantly colored flowers that cycle through a remarkable color change — opening pink in bud, maturing to vivid violet-blue to purple, and sometimes to bright blue or pure pink, creating multicolored mixed clusters on a single plant. The flower color is one of the most intense and vivid purples available in an annual wildflower. It is an extraordinary pollinator plant for bees and butterflies throughout its spring bloom period. As a meadow flower, it has been incorporated into many wildflower seed mixes for its ornamental value. However, purple viper's bugloss has become invasive in many parts of Australia (where it is called Paterson's Curse after the Paterson family on whose property it first appeared in the 1880s), California, and other regions with a Mediterranean climate, escaping cultivation to dominate rangeland and pasture. It contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids toxic to horses and cattle. Always verify local legal status before planting.

common_name: Purple Wave Petunia (Original Groundcover Spreading Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Purple Wave spreads low and wide rather than mounding upright, making it useful as a flowering groundcover as well as a container and hanging basket plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow for their wide spread. Introduced in the 1990s as an All-America Selections winner, Purple Wave was the original cultivar that launched the entire Wave petunia series and transformed the petunia market by introducing a genuinely low, ground-hugging, fast-spreading habit unlike the mounding upright petunias that came before it, making it useful as a colorful flowering groundcover, retaining-wall spiller, or large container filler. It blooms in vivid magenta-purple continuously from spring through frost with good heat tolerance and largely self-cleans without heavy deadheading. Regular fertilizing keeps the vigorous spreading growth flowering strongly through the season.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple wreath prefers bright, hot sun and blooms most prolifically when slightly drought stressed between rain events. In zone 9b–10 it may survive mild winters; established plants freeze-killed in zone 9a often resprout from roots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; purple wreath is one of the most spectacular tropical flowering vines, producing cascading clusters 12–18 inches long of small, star-shaped violet-purple flowers with contrasting deeper purple calyces that remain decorative for weeks after the petals fall — the persistent purple calyces give the vine a second ornamental period. The rough-textured, sandpaper-like leaves give rise to the alternate name 'sandpaper vine.' Established plants bloom in a spectacular spring flush with intermittent repeat bloom through summer and fall. The woody vine can reach 20–40 feet and requires a large, sturdy support. It is drought tolerant once established and blooms most prolifically with minimal irrigation. A stunning specimen for zone 10–12 landscapes; in zone 9b it can survive in sheltered south-facing locations.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade for cold stratification and spring germination; purple-headed sneezeweed is native to moist meadows, stream margins, and wet roadsides across eastern North America.
directions: Sow seeds direct in fall on the soil surface (seeds are light-sensitive and germinate better with some light) in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple-headed sneezeweed thrives in consistently moist to wet soils and is well suited to rain gardens, stream banks, and low wet meadows. Helenium flexuosum is closely related to H. autumnale but is distinguished by its striking, deep purple-brown to chocolate-colored disk (center cone), which creates a vivid color contrast against the bright yellow reflexed ray petals — this dark, globe-shaped disk is its most diagnostic feature and makes it one of the most visually dramatic native sneezweeds. It blooms from June through September across eastern North America from the Midwest to the Atlantic Coast and south to Florida; it is an outstanding pollinator plant supporting native bees, bumble bees, and specialist helenium-foraging native sweat bees. Like H. autumnale, the winged, decurrent stems are a helpful identification feature; divide clumps every 3 years in spring to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in consistently moist, rich soil along a streambank, pond edge, or boggy area in partial shade; seeds lose viability quickly and must be sown fresh to achieve good germination after cold stratification over winter. This is a monocarpic biennial or short-lived perennial that dies after setting seed.
directions: Angelica atropurpurea is a bold, architectural native herb of wet woodland edges and streambanks in the northeastern and north-central United States, reaching 5-8 feet tall with dramatically deep-purple hollow stems and large flat-topped compound umbels of white flowers in June through August. Plant in consistently moist to wet, rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, ideally near a water feature or in a rain garden where roots can stay wet. The large flower heads are major attractions for swallowtail butterflies, native bees, and beneficial parasitoid wasps throughout summer. It is monocarpic — plants flower once, then die after setting seed — so allow seed to fall naturally or scatter it nearby to establish the next generation.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants or root hardwood cuttings in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Pussy Willow catkins can also be cut and displayed indoors in water, where they will root and can be potted or planted out; cut branches in late winter while catkins are still tightly in bud.
directions: Pussy Willow is the beloved harbinger of spring throughout eastern North America, a large native shrub or small tree native to wet meadows, swamp margins, streambanks, and moist thickets from Newfoundland to British Columbia and south to the Appalachians and Pacific Northwest, producing in February and March the large, plump, silvery-gray male catkins that are one of the most universally recognized signals that winter is ending. Male plants produce the showiest catkins (female catkins are smaller and less attractive); catkin branches cut in late winter and placed in water indoors immediately become a beloved floral display that reliably roots — the resulting rooted cuttings can be potted or planted directly in the garden. An important early pollinator plant, providing pollen to native bees, honey bees, and other emerging insects before virtually any other tree flowers; willows in general are one of the most important native pollinator plants in North America. Plant in wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade near pond margins, rain gardens, or wet depressions.

plant_note: Plant corm divisions in early spring before the leafless flowering stalk emerges, or transplant in late summer after the flower has set seed and while the new leaf is just beginning to develop. Place corms at a depth of one to two inches in moist, humus-rich woodland soil in deep shade. Keep surrounding soil consistently moist through the first autumn as the winter leaf establishes.
directions: Grow in deep shade beneath mature deciduous trees in moist, rich woodland soil with a thick layer of decomposing leaf litter. This orchid follows an unusual seasonal rhythm: a single large, pleated, silver-veined leaf appears in late summer and persists through winter, dying back completely before the leafless flowering stalk rises in late spring bearing small, fragrant, yellow-green blooms. Plant where it will receive seasonal moisture from autumn rains and natural snowmelt, as it is adapted to the wet-winter, dry-summer cycle of the eastern deciduous forest understory. Allow fallen leaves to accumulate around plants each autumn rather than raking, as the organic layer is critical to the fungal associations that sustain the corm.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pygmy date palm is the most popular small-scale palm in zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes — a native of lowland river margins in Southeast Asia (Laos and adjacent areas) that tolerates more shade and moisture than most palms. Hardy to about 26–28°F briefly; plants are often damaged by hard zone 9a freezes but rebound from the root. Excellent in containers, courtyards, and as a foundation plant in part shade. Often planted in multiples of 3 for a clumped, multi-trunk effect.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pygmy date palm is the most widely planted small ornamental palm in zone 9 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes — a native of the lowland river margins and forest understory of Laos and adjacent Southeast Asia that has become the standard small-scale, refined, elegant palm for residential landscapes, courtyards, patio containers, and commercial entrances throughout subtropical and warm-temperate America. The palm grows as a single slender trunk (sometimes branched at the base to produce a multi-trunk cluster) to about 6–10 feet, the trunk itself highly ornamental — the surface covered in a decorative, diamond-pattern texture of persistent leaf-base stubs. The arching, pinnate (feather) fronds — each 3–4 feet long and composed of numerous narrow, slightly drooping leaflets — create a graceful, fine-textured, tropical crown of considerable elegance. The overall effect of a mature single-trunk specimen is of a perfectly scaled, fine-textured, refined miniature date palm — all the visual character of a large ornamental feather palm compressed into a manageable, landscape-scale plant. More shade-tolerant than most palms — tolerating significant partial shade and performing well in enclosed courtyard environments with reduced light. Often planted in groups of three or more in close proximity to create the multi-trunk, clumped appearance of a naturally multi-stemmed specimen. The standard small-scale ornamental palm for Gulf Coast zone 9 residential and commercial landscapes.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide clumps in spring or early fall in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun to part shade; pyramid bugle does not produce stolons and forms neat, non-invasive clumps — it is the best choice where the running nature of Ajuga reptans would cause problems in beds or rocky crevices. The cultivar 'Metallica Crispa' has unusual, crinkled, metallic-brown to bronze-purple foliage.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean soil in full sun to part shade; pyramid bugle is a compact, clump-forming European species closely related to the familiar carpet bugleweed (Ajuga reptans) but distinguished by forming non-running clumps rather than the spreading stolons that make A. reptans useful as a groundcover but invasive in gardens. Pyramid bugle is named for its unusually bold, densely pyramidal flower spike — in spring, each clump sends up one to several thick, densely leaved, upright spikes with large, overlapping bracts and rich violet-blue tubular flowers packed tightly in whorls, creating a fuller, more architectural flower spike than the trailing stems of A. reptans. The decorative bracts on the flower spike are larger and more prominent than in the common bugleweed. The cultivar 'Metallica Crispa' is especially ornamental — its leaves are small, strongly crinkled and puckered in texture, and have a remarkable metallic, bronze-purple to chocolate-brown sheen throughout the season. An excellent choice for rock gardens, wall crevices, and edges where a neat, contained bugle that won't run is desired.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Pyramid Magnolia is one of the rarest and least-known native magnolias and should only be sourced from specialty native plant nurseries.
directions: Pyramid Magnolia is a rare native deciduous magnolia of the southeastern coastal plain, found in scattered populations in Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, and Texas, growing in moist, rich, well-drained soil in the understory of mixed hardwood forest — a much more restricted habitat than the closely related Fraser Magnolia (Magnolia fraseri), which it resembles closely but with a more pyramidal form and consistently smaller stature. White, cup-shaped flowers 3–4 inches across appear in April and May before or with the emerging leaves; the large, auriculate (ear-lobed) leaves and attractive pink-red fruit clusters provide multi-season interest similar to its Appalachian relatives. Among the least-known of the native magnolias in horticulture despite being well-suited to zone 7–9 gardens, Pyramid Magnolia is increasingly available from specialty native nurseries as interest in deciduous native magnolias grows. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, deeply amended soil in partial shade; protect from strong winds that damage the large leaves.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: This blend produces bright, papery globe-shaped blooms in warm sunrise tones that add bold color and unique texture to the summer garden. Start seed indoors about six to eight weeks before the last frost, as germination is slow and heat-loving. Transplant into full sun after the soil warms, where the plants tolerate heat and drought with ease. The more you cut, the more it blooms, making it excellent for fresh and dried arrangements. Pollinators are drawn to the long-lasting flowers all season.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; seed germinates best in cool soil and darkness.
directions: Pure white lacy umbels top plants reaching two feet or more, creating an airy, romantic filler for cut-flower bouquets. Sow seed directly in cool early-spring or fall soil and cover lightly, as it germinates best in darkness. Plants produce one strong flush of blooms beloved by pollinators and beneficial insects. Give them full sun to part shade and well-drained soil. Succession sow for a longer supply of the delicate white flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost; safflower has a taproot and dislikes transplanting.
directions: This ornamental safflower opens creamy yellow and matures to deep saffron orange, giving evolving color and thistle-like texture through midsummer. Sow seed directly where plants are to grow, since the taproot resents disturbance. Sturdy upright stems make excellent fresh and dried cut flowers. Full sun and lean, well-drained soil suit it best, and it is quite drought tolerant. The edible petals can be used as a saffron substitute.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers or hardwood cuttings in early spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; quaking aspen is most commonly propagated by root suckers from existing trees, as seed viability is extremely short (germinates within days but loses viability within a week if not planted). Plant in masses for the natural clonal colony effect.
directions: Plant root suckers or cuttings in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; quaking aspen is the most widely distributed native tree in North America, ranging from Alaska to Newfoundland and south through the Rocky Mountains to Mexico. Named for the distinctive trembling of the leaves on their flattened petioles in even the slightest breeze, the constant movement produces a shimmering, glittering effect that is uniquely beautiful. Aspen groves are clonal colonies — all trees in a grove are genetically identical, connected by a single underground root system. The famous 'Pando' clone in Utah is estimated to be 80,000+ years old and weighing over 6 million kilograms, potentially the oldest living organism on Earth. Brilliant golden-yellow fall color; white bark provides winter interest. Best in cool, moist climates of the northern states and mountain West; struggles in hot, humid southern areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; quaking grass thrives in lean, slightly alkaline soils typical of chalk downlands, limestone grasslands, and old meadows. Avoid rich, fertile soils which cause excessive leafy growth at the expense of flowering.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; quaking grass is one of the most charming and distinctive ornamental grasses — producing loose, airy panicles of small, flattened, heart-shaped or teardrop-shaped spikelets that dangle on delicate, hair-thin stalks and tremble and 'quake' in the slightest breeze, producing a soft rustling sound. The Latin 'Briza' comes from Greek for 'food-grain,' though this species is not edible. The spikelets are attractive fresh in arrangements and dry beautifully for dried flower work. Native to limestone grasslands and chalk downlands of Europe and western Asia — natural meadow and grassland habitat — so it thrives in lean, slightly alkaline soils and dislikes fertile, enriched garden conditions. Naturalizes slowly in open, lean meadow conditions. The dried seed heads persist attractively through winter. A lovely addition to cottage-style and naturalistic meadow plantings.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light with very high humidity (70–80%) and exceptional drainage; Anthurium warocqueanum is strictly a tropical collector's plant in zone 9 and requires the closest approximation of Colombian cloud forest conditions — consistently warm temperatures (65–80°F), very high humidity, excellent air circulation, and bright filtered light. Mount on a bark slab or grow in a hanging basket to allow the pendant leaves to hang freely. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in very high humidity — Queen Anthurium requires the consistently warm, humid conditions of its native Colombian cloud forest habitat and will not tolerate the dry air of typical home environments without supplemental humidification. Anthurium warocqueanum is a large epiphytic anthurium from the humid cloud forests of Colombia, named in honor of the Belgian botanist and collector M. Warocqué, and commonly called the 'Queen Anthurium' — reigning alongside Anthurium veitchii (the 'King') as one of the two most desirable large-leaved pendulous anthuriums in collector circles. The leaves are extraordinary: enormously elongated, strap-shaped, pendant, dark emerald-green, velvety, with a precisely delineated network of pale silvery-white veins, reaching 3–5 feet on mature specimens. The velvety texture results from microscopic papillae that scatter light, creating the characteristic soft, deep, matte surface. Unlike Anthurium veitchii, whose leaves are smooth and corrugated, the Queen Anthurium's leaves are velvety and soft to the touch, and the silver venation is more pronounced and ornate. Both species require a mounted or elevated growing position to allow the pendant leaves to hang freely. Anthurium warocqueanum is considered among the most difficult of the collector aroids to grow to its full potential, requiring extremely consistent conditions, but mature specimens with fully-developed pendant velvety leaves are considered among the finest of all tropical foliage plants. All parts are toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Queen Emma lily is a tropical species from Mauritius and adjacent islands that has been long cultivated in warm climates for its striking burgundy-purple-overlaid foliage and deep rose-pink, fragrant flowers. In zones 9b–11 it can remain in the ground year-round; protect or overwinter as a container plant in zone 9a. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Plant bulbs (neck exposed) in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Queen Emma lily is among the most dramatically foliaged of all crinum species — the broad, strap-shaped, glossy leaves are heavily suffused with deep burgundy-purple to mahogany-brown pigmentation that creates a rich, dark-toned foliage effect unlike the all-green leaves of most crinum species. This striking burgundy leaf coloring combined with the flowers — large, fragrant, deep rose-pink to wine-rose, lily-like funnels in umbels of 8–15 blooms per scape in summer — creates a bold, tropical composition of dark foliage and deep-rose flowers of unmistakably exotic character. It is a species of Mauritius and the Mascarene Islands in the tropical Indian Ocean, long grown in historic tropical and subtropical gardens worldwide under the name 'Queen Emma lily' after a Hawaiian queen who grew it extensively. The large bulbs develop into impressive clumps over time, producing multiple flower scapes in summer. Outstanding as a container specimen or tropical-effect border plant in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens where its heat-loving character, tolerance of summer humidity, and dramatic dark foliage make it a premier ornamental bulb.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring when new growth emerges or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; queen lily thrives in the dappled shade under trees and is one of the most shade-tolerant and garden-worthy of all the ornamental curcumas.
directions: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; queen lily (hidden lily) is a Malaysian ginger relative that is one of the most effective shade ornamentals for the warm garden — the broad, tropical-looking, bright-green leaves emerge in spring and rise to 2–3 feet, and in summer the inflorescences emerge directly from the ground on separate stems, displaying stacked, overlapping, salmon-pink to rosy-pink bracts surrounding white to creamy flowers that appear 'hidden' within the bract structure, giving the common name hidden lily. The display is remarkably effective emerging from the ground surrounded by the leafy canopy. Goes fully dormant in winter (rhizomes are cold-hardy to zone 8). An excellent companion for hostas, gingers, and ferns in the summer shade garden. Rhizomes can be lifted and stored indoors in colder zones.

common_name: Queen Lime Zinnia (Trendy Muted Lime-Green Cut Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; Queen Lime is grown chiefly for cut-flower arranging, valued for its unusual muted, dusty lime-green blooms that pair well with almost any other flower color.
directions: Direct sow after frost in warm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Queen Lime has become a favorite of cut-flower growers and florists for its unusual soft, dusty lime-green double blooms, sometimes blushed with pink or rose at the petal tips, a muted color palette that blends easily with nearly any other cut flower rather than competing with it. The tall, sturdy stems make excellent cut flowers with a long vase life, and regular cutting or deadheading keeps the plant producing new blooms over a long summer season. Like other zinnias it thrives in heat and is a strong pollinator and butterfly magnet, though good air circulation helps reduce powdery mildew in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; queen palm needs a slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) to avoid manganese and potassium deficiencies that cause yellowing fronds. Apply palm-specific slow-release fertilizer 3 times per year.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun; queen palm is one of the most popular and widely planted tropical palms in Florida, southern California, and the Gulf Coast, and for good reason — it grows rapidly (3–6 feet per year), has beautiful arching bright-green feather-compound fronds, and produces pendant clusters of small orange-yellow fruit beloved by wildlife. The smooth, light gray trunk has distinctive leaf scar rings that give it a clean, elegant appearance. It is not as cold-hardy as sabal or windmill palms — significant damage occurs below 25°F — making it marginal in zone 9a. Plant in a protected south-facing microclimate for best results. Queen palm is highly susceptible to Ganoderma root rot (avoid wounding roots and overcrowding) and may develop nutrient deficiencies in alkaline soils — regular palm fertilizer applications with micronutrients are essential.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August for fall bloom.
