Queen Red Lime is a large-flowered (3–4 inch) variety that performs best in hot summer conditions — the color is most vivid in heat and loses some intensity in cool autumn weather. The cut flowers last 7–10 days in a vase; harvest when outer petals are open and center is still tight. In zone 9 zinnias thrive in the summer heat that challenges most other cut flowers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Queen Red Lime is one of the most striking and distinctive zinnia varieties available to cut flower growers and garden designers — a large-flowered double zinnia with warm crimson-red petals grading inward to a unique lime-green center, creating a bicolor effect that no other common annual flower replicates. The unusual red-to-lime color combination has made Queen Red Lime a favorite of professional florists seeking distinctive colors for modern, unusual arrangements, and the transition from the outer warm red petals to the inner cool lime-green center becomes more pronounced as the flower ages and the center petals enlarge. Like all zinnias, Queen Red Lime is extremely heat-loving and essentially thrives in zone 9's hottest summer weeks when most cut flowers cannot be grown productively — the brilliant color intensity and large flower size actually improve as temperatures rise. The tall, sturdy stems (30–36 inches) provide excellent cut flower value with long vase life.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; queen sago is a tropical cycad native to India, Sri Lanka, and the Malay Archipelago that is somewhat less cold-hardy than king sago (Cycas revoluta) but produces more elegant, longer, arching fronds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; established cycads are drought-tolerant but prefer consistent moisture while establishing. Cycas circinalis (queen sago) is a large, impressive cycad native to South Asia and the Indo-Pacific — related to but more tropical than the widely grown king sago (C. revoluta). It produces a thick, cylindrical trunk topped with a crown of long (5–8 foot), arching, dark-green, pinnate fronds with narrow, glossy leaflets — more graceful and longer than C. revoluta fronds, with a sweeping, tropical-palm-like form. Cycads are among the most ancient of all living seed plants — living fossils that have changed little in 200 million years and survived the extinction events that eliminated the dinosaurs. Queen sago is dioecious (separate male and female plants) and produces cones on mature plants; the large, orange-red seeds produced by female plants contain starch once used (after processing to remove toxins) by indigenous peoples of the Indo-Pacific as famine food. CAUTION: All parts of the plant (especially seeds) are toxic if ingested — cycad toxins cause neurological damage and cancer in both humans and animals. The plant is stunning as a landscape focal point or container specimen.

common_name: Queen Sago (Rumph's Cycad, Coastal Sago, Queen Cycad)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with fast-draining, well-aerated soil; Cycas rumphii is more cold-sensitive than C. revoluta and best suited to zone 9b-11 outdoors. In zone 9a, container culture is safer — mature specimens can be very large containers to move. The plant produces a single flush of new leaves (a 'crown') each spring — protect the emerging fronds from cold and damage during this period. CAUTION: All parts of cycads (seeds, leaves, stems) are highly toxic to animals and humans.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; Queen Sago is highly drought-tolerant once established and requires excellent drainage — it will not survive waterlogged or poorly draining soils. Cycas rumphii is a large, majestic cycad native to the coastal regions of South and Southeast Asia (India, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Philippines, New Guinea) and the Pacific Islands, where it often grows near coastlines in sandy, well-drained soils close to the sea — a habitat that explains its common salt-tolerance and drought adaptation. Like all cycads, Cycas rumphii is a living fossil, a member of an ancient plant lineage that predates the dinosaurs by more than 100 million years and has changed little since the Jurassic period. The plant produces a stout trunk topped by a crown of long (4–8 feet), arching, pinnately-compound, dark-green, glossy fronds similar to palm fronds. Cycas rumphii is larger and more tropical in appearance than the commonly grown Japanese Sago Palm (Cycas revoluta), with wider, more widely-spaced leaflets and a faster growth rate in warm climates. In zone 9-11 Gulf Coast landscapes, it serves as a dramatic tropical accent and structural focal point. CAUTION: All parts of all cycads, including C. rumphii, contain cycasin and other toxins causing severe liver failure in pets and humans if ingested — plant away from areas accessible to children and pets.

plant_note: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky or gritty, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Queen Victoria agave requires excellent drainage above all else and is killed by wet, poorly drained soil. It is among the hardiest agave species, tolerating temperatures to 10°F or below when dry. In humid climates, plant in raised, well-drained beds with gravel mulch to prevent crown rot.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Queen Victoria agave is generally considered the most beautiful of all agaves — a slow-growing, compact species from the limestone cliffs of the Chihuahuan Desert in Nuevo León and Coahuila, Mexico, producing a dense, geometrically perfect rosette of short, stiff, dark-green leaves with distinctive white edges and markings that create an intricate, almost hand-drawn pattern unique to this species. The narrow, closely packed leaves with their crisp white margins and patterning look sculpted and architectural rather than plant-like. Being monocarpic (flowering once and dying), it produces a magnificent flower spike reaching 10–15 feet after many years (10–30 or more), producing creamy-white flowers before the mother plant dies and offsets develop to continue the colony. Hardy to 10°F when dry, it is suitable for zone 7 in well-drained, rocky situations. A prized collector's plant and exceptional container specimen.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; queen wreath is one of the most spectacular flowering vines for zone 9-11 gardens, producing cascading racemes of violet-purple flowers in spring and sporadically throughout the year, with a main bloom flush of extraordinary beauty.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide strong trellis, fence, or arbor support — queen wreath becomes a large, heavy vine. Petrea volubilis (queen's wreath or purple wreath) is a Mexican and Central American tropical vine producing some of the most spectacular flower displays of any vine in subtropical horticulture — cascading, wisteria-like racemes 10–18 inches long densely packed with tiny, star-shaped flowers in an extraordinary violet-purple color in spring, with a secondary flush after summer rains. Each individual flower consists of a larger, calyx-like structure that outlasts the true petals, persisting as a pale-blue to lavender star shape after the purple petals drop — creating two overlapping color displays as the raceme matures. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves (responsible for the common name 'sandpaper vine') are semi-evergreen. The vine climbs by twining and becomes very large and woody over time; mature plants require substantial support. In zone 9, it may be damaged by hard freezes but typically resprouts from the base. One of the most beautiful flowering vines for Gulf Coast trellises and fences.

plant_note: Divide clumps or plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to deep shade in zone 9–12; Queen of Hearts Homalomena is a compact, shade-tolerant aroid from Southeast Asian forest floors bearing heart-shaped, glossy, deep-green leaves with distinctive red undersides and stems — extraordinarily low-maintenance and excellent for shaded indoor or outdoor positions in warm, humid climates.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Homalomena rubescens tolerates deep shade remarkably well — it actually prefers the low-light conditions of a forest floor and will scorch in direct sunlight; water moderately and avoid overwatering by ensuring the growing medium is well-draining. Homalomena rubescens (Queen of Hearts, Homalomena, or Selva Homalomena) is a compact, clumping, rhizomatous aroid in the Araceae family native to the humid forest floors of Borneo, Sumatra, Peninsular Malaysia, and the Philippines, cultivated as a shade-tolerant ornamental houseplant and outdoor shade-garden plant in warm subtropical and tropical climates. The plant forms dense, tidy clumps of long-stalked, broadly heart-shaped to ovate, glossy, dark-green leaves — often with striking red or burgundy undersides and deep-red petioles that give the plant attractive two-tone coloration. Homalomena rubescens is among the most shade-tolerant of all commonly cultivated aroids — adapted to the near-darkness of deep rainforest floor conditions — and is one of the most effective and low-maintenance shade groundcovers and container plants for zone 9–12 outdoor gardens and indoor positions throughout the world. The genus has an unusual characteristic: many Homalomena species emit a strong, anise-like or spicy aromatic scent from their leaves when handled — a chemotaxonomic trait of the genus. An excellent and underutilized shade garden plant for subtropical Florida, Gulf Coast, and tropical landscapes.

common_name: Queen of Night Tulip (Near-Black Deep Purple Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 8-9 gardens, tulip bulbs generally need to be pre-chilled or treated as annual bulbs, since winters are usually too mild for reliable natural perennializing.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Queen of Night is one of the most famous single late tulip cultivars, prized for its deep, glossy maroon-purple petals so dark they read as nearly black in the garden, especially dramatic when paired with white or pale pastel companions. It blooms late in the tulip season, extending color after earlier cultivars have finished, and is a favorite of flower arrangers for its striking, almost velvety color. In climates with mild winters, tulips generally perform best treated as a fresh fall planting each year rather than a reliable long-term perennial, since they need a sustained period of cold to rebloom well.

common_name: Queen of the Andes (Titanka, Giant Puya, Raimondi's Puya)
plant_note: Grow in full sun in very well-drained, poor to moderately fertile, rocky or gravelly soil; Puya raimondii is a slow-growing Andean bromeliad that tolerates cold (to 15–20°F), heat, drought, and poor soils. It will not tolerate waterlogged or humid subtropical conditions — it is adapted to the cold, dry, sunny, high-altitude grasslands (puna) of the Andes at 10,000–15,000 feet elevation. In zone 7-9 with dry conditions, it can be grown as a specimen plant over many decades, eventually producing the largest bromeliad flower spike in the world after 80–150 years of vegetative growth. A plant of extraordinary ecological and botanical significance — the largest bromeliad on Earth. Monocarpic (dies after flowering).
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, poor, rocky or gravelly soil — Queen of the Andes requires the extremely well-drained, dry, nutrient-poor conditions of its native high-altitude Andean habitat and will rot in any soil that retains moisture for extended periods or in humid subtropical conditions. Puya raimondii is an extraordinary, slow-growing, rosette-forming terrestrial bromeliad native to the high-altitude grasslands (puna) of Peru and Bolivia in the Bromeliaceae family — the largest bromeliad species on Earth, and one of the most remarkable plants in all of biology. The plant spends 80–150 years as a vegetative rosette of stiff, spine-tipped, sword-like leaves 3–6 feet long with upward-curved, sharp, hook-shaped marginal spines, forming a hemispherical mound 5–10 feet across. Then, once in its lifetime, it produces the largest flower spike of any bromeliad on Earth: a towering, erect, densely-branched panicle 25–35 feet tall bearing 8,000–10,000 individual white flowers simultaneously — the floral display visible from miles away in its native Andean habitat. After the flowering — which may take 3–4 months — the entire plant dies (monocarpic behavior), producing thousands of seeds that fall from the massive spike. The spike structure provides critical habitat for Andean birds and insects during bloom. At lower elevations, growth is slower and even less likely to reach blooming size, but the rosette alone — a dramatic, architectural, spine-armed mound — is an extraordinary garden specimen for decades.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in barely moist, well-drained cactus mix or train established plants on a trellis or through a tree in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; queen of the night requires excellent drainage — root rot in wet soil is the primary cause of plant failure.
directions: Root stem cuttings in well-drained cactus mix or plant on a trellis in partial shade to full sun; queen of the night is a Jamaican and Central American epiphytic cactus that is grown for one of the most spectacular and fleeting floral events in horticulture — its enormous flowers, reaching 12 inches or more in diameter, open only once per year, only at night (typically between midnight and 3 a.m.), filling the surrounding air with a powerful, exotic, vanilla-like fragrance, then closing and withering before dawn. The vine itself is a sprawling, multi-stemmed, vinelike cactus that climbs trees, fences, and walls by aerial roots; its flat, jointed stems are unattractive in comparison to the drama of its annual flower event. Dedicated enthusiasts stay up all night to witness the blooming, and the anticipation and communal watching of the opening flower is a celebrated garden ritual in subtropical and tropical neighborhoods. Plants may take several years from cutting to first bloom. In zones 9–12 it grows outdoors on walls and trees; elsewhere it is a large container or greenhouse specimen. A plant whose horticultural impact is entirely disproportionate to its one annual bloom event.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in consistently moist soil; this plant grows best with reliable moisture and will struggle without it.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, rich, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; queen of the prairie is a magnificent native for rain gardens, pond edges, and any low area with reliable summer moisture. The enormous clouds of fluffy, peach-pink flowers on tall stems in midsummer are among the most dramatic native perennial displays available and attract native bees in large numbers. The plant spreads by rhizome to form large colonies and is not suited to small gardens or dry sites. Divide every 4–5 years in spring; each division should include a generous section of rhizome with multiple crowns. Cut back in late fall after frost.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun in spring; queen's crepe myrtle requires consistently warm temperatures to flower — it blooms most reliably in zone 10–12 with a dry period in winter followed by the rainy season, which triggers flower bud initiation; in zone 9 it rarely flowers satisfactorily and is better replaced by the common crepe myrtle (L. indica).
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; queen's crepe myrtle (giant crepe myrtle, banaba) is a large tropical tree native to South and Southeast Asia that is the largest and most spectacular flowering member of the crepe myrtle family — it can grow to 40–60 feet in ideal tropical conditions and in summer and early monsoon season produces enormous, terminal panicles (12–18 inches long) of large, lavender-pink to rose-purple, crinkled, crepe-textured flowers in the characteristic crepe myrtle style, but at a scale dwarfing the common crepe myrtle (Lagerstroemia indica). The bark exfoliates in patches like all crepe myrtles, revealing a smooth, gray-beige inner bark surface that is ornamental year-round. The leaves turn brilliant red-orange in the dry season before falling. Banaba leaf extract has been intensively researched for its anti-diabetic properties and is widely sold as an herbal supplement, particularly in the Philippines, where the tree is called banaba. An outstanding flowering shade tree for zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical landscapes.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade beneath conifers; queen's cup requires cool summer temperatures and the moist conditions of its native montane coniferous forest understory.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in full shade, ideally beneath conifers where needle duff provides natural mulch; queen's cup needs cool, moist conditions year-round and will decline in hot, dry summers regardless of supplemental watering. Clintonia uniflora is a low-growing western North American native of cool, moist coniferous forest understories from Alaska to California and east to Montana, producing 2-3 broad, glossy, basal leaves and a single large, six-petaled white flower in late spring, followed by a single brilliant metallic-blue berry. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form small colonies and is an exquisite native wildflower for cool, shaded Pacific Northwest and Rocky Mountain gardens.

common_name: Queen's Tears Bromeliad (Friendship Plant, Nodding Air Plant)
plant_note: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix or garden soil; Queen's Tears Bromeliad is the most cold-hardy ornamental bromeliad widely available, surviving temperatures to 20–25°F with heavy mulch protection — reliable in zone 8 and very easy in zone 9. In zone 9, grow outdoors as a permanent ground cover, container specimen, or shade garden accent; it naturalizes easily under trees. Keep the central cup filled with water. Divide crowded clumps every 2–3 years by separating rooted offsets. One of the best-sharing plants — divisions and pups establish quickly; hence the common name 'Friendship Plant' reflecting the tradition of sharing it among friends.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-draining, moderately fertile soil; Queen's Tears Bromeliad is highly adaptable to a range of light conditions and is one of the most forgiving and easy-to-grow of all bromeliads, making it an excellent choice for gardeners new to the bromeliad family. Billbergia nutans is a clump-forming, tank bromeliad native to Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina — one of the more southerly-ranging bromeliads, explaining its exceptional cold tolerance relative to other family members. The plant forms erect, tube-like rosettes of dark-green, finely toothed, narrow leaves that grow in dense, spreading colonies. In late winter to spring (and sometimes in fall), the rosettes produce a nodding (the 'nutans' — 'nodding') flower stalk that arches downward, carrying pendant clusters of remarkable, multicolored flowers: drooping green petals edged in blue, emerging from vivid pink bracts, with prominent yellow stamens — a combination of pink, blue, green, and yellow in a single flower cluster that is unique among commonly grown plants. The flowers last 1–2 weeks but are produced abundantly, and established colonies may flower multiple times per year. Among the hardiest, most adaptable, and most readily available bromeliads for zone 8-9 outdoor gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Queensland silver wattle is a phyllode-leaved acacia (unlike A. baileyana which has bipinnate leaves) with large, oval, silver-gray phyllodes (flattened leaf stalks that function as leaves). It blooms in winter–spring, producing masses of fragrant, golden-yellow flower pom-poms. Fast-growing to 15–25 feet. Seed requires hot-water scarification. Notable for its silver-metallic foliage effect year-round.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Queensland silver wattle provides two distinct ornamental qualities in one fast-growing tree: outstanding silver foliage year-round and spectacular, fragrant winter-spring flowers. The large, oval, silvery-gray to blue-silver phyllodes (the leaf-like flattened leaf stalks that the phyllode-bearing acacias use in place of true leaves) create a remarkable, shining, metallic-silver to pewter-gray foliage effect that is one of the most silver of any large tree — the whole tree appearing as if molded from silver-gray metal. Against this striking silver backdrop, winter through spring brings dense, spherical, golden-yellow flower pompoms in long, arching racemes that arch along every stem — the most vivid, warm golden-yellow contrasting brilliantly with the cool silver-gray phyllodes. The flowers are sweetly fragrant. Native to the dry subtropical forests and scrubs of Queensland and New South Wales, it is well-adapted to dry, warm conditions and thrives in zone 9–11 gardens with minimal supplemental irrigation once established. One of the most visually striking large trees for the warm-climate garden, offering both a dramatic, year-round silver landscape presence and a spectacular winter flower display.

common_name: Queensland Trumpet Tree (Deplanchea, Four-Leaf Deplanchea, Yellow Cassod Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil; Deplanchea tetraphylla is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting. The species name 'tetraphylla' (four-leaved) refers to the arrangement of large leaves in whorls of four at each node — a distinctive feature. The massive terminal flower clusters are bright orange-yellow and spectacular — plant where they can be viewed from a distance. Relatively fast-growing for a tropical tree, reaching 30–40 feet at maturity. The tree grows naturally at forest margins and in disturbed forest edges.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Queensland Trumpet Tree grows most vigorously and produces its best flower displays in full sun conditions. Deplanchea tetraphylla is a medium to large, evergreen tropical tree native to northeastern Queensland, Australia (Cape York Peninsula and adjacent Queensland rainforest margins) in the Bignoniaceae family, one of the outstanding ornamental flowering trees of northeastern Australia and one of the least known outside the botanical garden world. The tree has a distinctive, immediately recognizable appearance due to its whorled leaf arrangement: the large, broadly oval to obovate leaves (12–18 inches long) are arranged in precise whorls of four at each node rather than the alternating or opposite arrangement of most trees — giving the tree an architectural, tiered, symmetrical appearance. The flowers are spectacular: large, dense, terminal panicles of bright orange-yellow, tubular flowers crowded into massive heads at the branch tips, each individual flower about 1 inch long with five spreading lobes, produced in profuse display in spring to summer. The orange-yellow flower clusters at the tips of the whorled branches create a striking visual pattern — concentric rings of color and foliage. A rare but genuinely impressive zone 10-12 ornamental flowering tree that deserves wider planting in tropical and subtropical botanical gardens and large residential landscapes.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost; zinnias grow quickly in warm soil.
directions: This tall standout carries an extraordinary lime-and-orange color blend never before seen in a zinnia, with long-lasting blooms on sturdy stems. Sow directly into warm soil after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early in short-season areas. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and cut often to prolong bloom. Full sun and good air circulation help prevent powdery mildew. The flowers attract pollinators and make exceptional cut flowers all summer.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost; zinnias grow quickly in warm soil.
directions: Sturdy plants produce long-stemmed blossoms in a rich lime-and-red blend all summer, drawing in pollinators. Sow seed directly into warm soil after the last frost for fastest growth. Deadhead and cut regularly to keep the plants blooming into fall. Provide full sun and space plants for airflow to reduce mildew. The colorful, edible petals make a pretty garnish for salads and desserts.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Quickfire blooms several weeks earlier than most panicle hydrangeas, with white flowers that begin turning pink to deep rose in midsummer rather than fall.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Quickfire earns its name by flowering several weeks ahead of most other panicle hydrangeas, opening white conical flower clusters in early summer that gradually age to deep pink and finally rich rose-red as the season progresses, giving a longer overall season of color than later-blooming types. Unlike mophead hydrangea, panicle types like Quickfire bloom on new wood, so a hard pruning in late winter does not sacrifice the coming season's flowers and instead encourages a strong flush of new flowering stems. Its sturdy stems hold the flower clusters upright well even in rain, and the plant tolerates more sun and drier soil than mophead hydrangeas once established.

plant_note: Plant in shallow, well-drained hanging baskets or pots allowing the silver-furred rhizomes to drape over the pot edge freely; rabbit's foot fern should be planted at or just above soil level, never burying the decorative rhizomes — the rhizomes creeping over the container edge are a primary ornamental feature of the plant.
directions: Plant in shallow, well-drained baskets allowing the furry rhizomes to drape freely over the edges; rabbit's foot fern is a Fiji native grown as much for its extraordinary rhizomes as for its lacy, dark-green, finely divided fronds — the long, surface-creeping rhizomes are densely covered with silvery-white to light-brown, soft, hair-like scales that have a silky, fur-like texture remarkably similar to a rabbit's foot, draping over the edges of hanging baskets in long, decorative tendrils. The finely dissected, triangular fronds provide a delicate, refined foliage texture above the unusual rhizomes. It is drought-tolerant compared to most ferns, preferring to dry slightly between waterings rather than staying constantly wet. An excellent houseplant and summer shade garden fern that performs well in bright indirect light to partial shade. The fern genus Davallia contains several species with similarly ornamental rhizomes, including D. trichomanoides (squirrel's foot fern) and D. canariensis (hare's foot fern). Easily propagated by cutting and planting rhizome sections.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Radiation Lantana is one of the more cold-hardy lantana selections, surviving mild zone 9 winters as a semi-woody perennial that dies back to the ground in freezes and resprouts vigorously in spring. Prune hard in early spring to remove dead wood and stimulate fresh, heavily flowering new growth. In zone 9 established plants can reach 4–5 feet tall and wide by late summer, producing the most spectacular color display from July through November. Avoid excessive fertilization — lean, well-drained conditions produce more flowers and better drought tolerance than rich, consistently moist plantings.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Radiation Lantana blooms most freely and is most drought tolerant in lean, dry conditions; avoid overwatering and heavy fertilization; Radiation is one of the most consistently spectacular lantana cultivars for the Gulf South — producing large, rounded flower clusters in a brilliant three-color combination of orange, red, and yellow that creates an intense, warm-colored floral display from spring through first frost. The tricolor flower clusters display all three colors simultaneously within each head, with individual florets transitioning from yellow through orange to red as they age — creating the radiating, multi-tonal effect that gives the cultivar its name. Lantana's combination of extreme summer heat and drought tolerance, continuous blooming without deadheading, and exceptional butterfly attraction (lantana is one of the top butterfly nectar plants available, visited by virtually every butterfly species that occurs in zone 9) has made it one of the most widely planted summer ornamentals for Gulf South gardens. Radiation's upright, bushy habit and particularly vivid color combination make it one of the most impactful lantana cultivars for large-scale planting in hot, sunny, drought-prone locations where the heat that defeats most plants allows lantana to reach its full ornamental potential.

plant_note: Plant container-grown palms in spring after temperatures stabilize; in zone 9 plant March–May. Chamaedorea radicalis is among the most cold-hardy of the Chamaedorea palms, tolerating temperatures to about 18–22°F when established — brief dips into the upper teens may cause frond damage without killing established plants. It is extremely slow-growing in cool conditions but accelerates in warm, humid summers. Plant in a sheltered location with northern or eastern shade exposure; deep root establishment takes 1–2 years before visible trunk growth begins. Mature plants produce small clusters of orange to red fruits that attract birds.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Chamaedorea radicalis is a forest understory palm that thrives in the same deep shade conditions that exclude most palms; Radicalis Palm is a small, slow-growing Mexican understory palm that is exceptional among palms for its genuine deep shade tolerance — not merely surviving in shade as most palms will, but genuinely thriving and looking its best in the dappled to dense shade beneath established trees. The plant grows as a low, clumping palm with arching, pinnate fronds of medium-to-dark green leaflets, creating a refined, tropical texture in shaded garden areas at a manageable scale of 3–5 feet. While most landscape palms are unambiguously full-sun plants, Chamaedorea radicalis fills the specific niche of a palm-textured shade plant — providing the tropical character of a palm frond in the shaded woodland garden conditions where conventional palms fail. For zone 9 gardeners working with established oak or magnolia canopy, Chamaedorea radicalis is one of the very few palms that can be successfully incorporated into the understory without the decline and eventual death that shade causes in Queen palms, Windmill palms, and most other landscape palms.

common_name: Radicans Anthurium (Crawling Anthurium, Trailing Anthurium, Rugose-Leaved Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix; Anthurium radicans is a small, creeping, trailing anthurium from Brazil that produces heavily corrugated, bumpy, dark forest-green leaves on trailing to pendant stems — the bumpy, quilted leaf texture is the primary ornamental feature, giving each leaf a three-dimensional, sculptural quality reminiscent of hammered metal or fabric brocade. Excellent in hanging baskets or as a groundcover in shaded tropical gardens. Produces small berry clusters on short spikes. Best in warm, humid, shaded conditions. CAUTION: calcium oxalate in all parts; toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich mix — Radicans Anthurium grows most compactly and textural in warm, humid, deeply shaded conditions and is an excellent choice for hanging baskets, low-light terrariums, or as a shaded ground-cover in zone 10-12. Anthurium radicans is a small, creeping, stoloniferous anthurium in the Araceae family native to southeastern Brazil, belonging to the section Cardiolonchium in Anthurium (the same broad group as A. crystallinum and A. clarinervium) but with a very different, low-growing, creeping habit rather than the large-leaved, upright form of those species. The plant produces stems that trail and creep outward, rooting at nodes where they contact moist substrate, producing a spreading mat of closely-set leaves in shaded locations. Each individual leaf is small to medium (4–8 inches), broadly heart-shaped to ovate, dark forest-green, and densely covered with small, raised bumps and irregular surface corrugations that create a strongly rugose (wrinkled, bumpy) texture — as if each leaf were molded from hammered metal or brocade fabric. This texture is constant throughout the leaf surface and gives the plant a tactile quality unusual in aroids. The creeping, rooting stems make A. radicans naturally well-suited to hanging baskets (where it trails over the edges) or to spreading as a groundcover in shaded tropical planters. It is also commonly grown hybridized with A. dressleri (producing A. ×dressleri hybrids) to enhance the leaf texture. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; ragged robin is an obligate of wet meadows, marshes, and stream banks and will not perform well in dry conditions.
directions: Sow direct in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; ragged robin is a plant of wet meadows, marshes, and stream margins that requires consistently moist to wet soil and will wilt and decline in dry conditions. Lychnis flos-cuculi is a native European perennial wildflower of wet meadows and marshes producing deeply and narrowly cut, feathery, rose-pink to magenta petals (each petal divided into 4 narrow, ragged lobes) on slender, branching stems in early summer — one of the most characteristically "wild" and charming of meadow flowers, excellent in naturalized wet meadow gardens alongside marsh marigold, meadow buttercup, and yellow flag iris. It self-seeds freely in wet conditions and naturalizes readily; an important plant of traditional wildflower meadows that has declined dramatically in Britain and Europe due to agricultural drainage. The white form 'White Robin' is also available.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; rain lilies naturalize freely in lawns and low-maintenance landscapes in zone 7–11 and multiply rapidly by offsets.
directions: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; rain lily earns its name by blooming within days of summer rainstorms, producing clusters of small, white, crocus-like flowers with golden stamens that seem to appear magically from bare, grassy foliage after each significant rainfall in summer and fall. The narrow, dark-green, rush-like leaves are attractive year-round in zone 7–11, forming spreading colonies as the bulbs offset freely. Plant in masses in lawns, borders, and naturalizing areas — it is low-maintenance once established, needing no irrigation beyond natural rainfall. In zone 7–8 mulch heavily in winter to protect the bulbs; in zone 9–11 it is essentially evergreen and fully self-sustaining. The related pink-flowered Zephyranthes rosea and yellow Z. citrina are equally easy and can be combined for a multicolor rain-lily display.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to average soil in full sun after frost; rain of gold is extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established and performs best in hot, bright, dry conditions — rich, moist, or heavily fertilized soil produces rank growth with fewer flowers.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, sandy to average soil in full sun; rain of gold (Galphimia glauca, shower of gold, thryallis) is a Central American and Mexican evergreen shrub widely planted throughout the Gulf Coast and south Florida for its extraordinarily prolonged display of brilliant, clear-yellow, five-petaled, star-shaped flowers borne continuously on the tips of every stem from early spring through frost — the plant is almost never out of bloom during warm weather and functions as a continuous-color shrub requiring virtually no deadheading or care. The flowers are arranged in loose, upright, golden racemes that create an effect of scattered gold stars across the dark-green, glossy, oval-leafed plant. It thrives in the intense heat and drought of zone 9–11 summers, asks for minimal water once established, and rewards benign neglect with the most extended bloom season of any Gulf Coast flowering shrub. It is cold-sensitive and root-hardy to approximately 25–28°F in zone 9 with protection. Excellent massed as a summer-to-fall flowering hedge, in median plantings, and as a low-maintenance xeriscape flowering shrub in hot, sunny areas.

plant_note: Start indoors and surface sow; seed needs light to germinate. Transplant after frost.
directions: Grown for its dazzling foliage in white, bronze, gold, copper, yellow, pink, red, and purple, this blend brightens shady spots where flowers struggle. Start seed indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the soil surface since it needs light to sprout. Transplant after all danger of frost into partial shade and rich, moist soil. Pinch out flower spikes to keep the leaves vibrant and the plants bushy. It also makes an excellent houseplant to add color through winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Rainbow is a variegated selection of native drooping leucothoe with cream, pink, and copper mottled new growth that is showier in some shade than in deep, dark shade.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind, which can scorch the variegated foliage. Rainbow is a colorful sport of the native Appalachian shrub drooping leucothoe, with glossy, arching evergreen leaves splashed in cream, pink, and coppery-red that are showiest on new growth in spring and again in cool fall weather. Small, white, urn-shaped flowers dangle beneath the arching stems in spring, similar to its relatives in the heath family. It spreads slowly by rhizomes to form a graceful, cascading mound, making it a good textural companion for ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials, and benefits from an occasional thinning of old canes at the base to keep growth vigorous.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or start indoors; often blooms the first year from an early start.
directions: In late spring a blue-green mound of foliage is covered with heavily fringed, fragrant, edible blooms in white, pink, lilac, and rose that butterflies adore. Sow seed directly in the garden in spring, or start indoors early for first-year flowers. Give plants full sun to part shade and well-drained soil. Shear after the first flush to encourage a repeat bloom. The lacy flowers make charming, sweetly scented cut arrangements.

plant_note: Surface-sow indoors; seed needs light and warmth to germinate. Transplant after frost.
directions: Start seed indoors on the soil surface under bright light and warmth, as it needs light to sprout. Grown for its painted foliage rather than flowers, this mix shows a wide range of leaf colors and patterns. Move plants outdoors only after all frost danger passes, choosing a spot with partial shade and consistent moisture. Pinch growing tips regularly and remove flower spikes to keep foliage bushy and vivid; it can be overwintered indoors as a houseplant.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in deep shade or bright indirect light in zone 9–12; Rainbow Moss (Peacock Moss) is a creeping, mat-forming, fern ally native to moist forests and rock faces of southern China and Taiwan — one of the most visually stunning groundcovers available for shaded positions, with scale-like, iridescent, blue-green-purple foliage that shifts color like a soap bubble in changing light.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but well-drained soil in deep to moderate shade; Selaginella uncinata requires high humidity (above 60%) and consistent soil moisture — it dries out and browns quickly in dry conditions; excellent for enclosed shade gardens, terrariums, vivaria, and humid greenhouse floors. Selaginella uncinata (Rainbow Moss, Peacock Moss, or Aurora Selaginella) is a delicate, mat-forming, creeping fern ally (Selaginellaceae — the spike mosses) native to the moist, shaded forest floors, rocky outcrops, and stream margins of subtropical southern China (Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian) and Taiwan. The plant is celebrated for its extraordinary iridescent foliage: the minute, overlapping, scale-like leaves are structurally colored like a peacock feather — the surface microstructure diffracts light to produce a shifting blue-green-purple-copper iridescence that changes tone as the viewing angle changes, unlike any color produced by pigment. This optical effect — analogous to the structural coloration of butterfly wings and peacock feathers — is the product of thin-film interference in specialized leaf surface cells. The resulting groundcover appearance is unlike any other plant: a shimmering, metallic, multi-colored carpet perfect for deep shade terrarium displays, forest-floor groundcover in humid tropical gardens, and naturalistic shade vivaria. Maintain high humidity, consistent moisture, and protection from direct sun and cold drafts.

common_name: Rainbow Orchid (Reed Stem Epidendrum, Crucifix Orchid, Fire Star Orchid)
plant_note: Plant rooted divisions or keikis (plantlets) in spring in a sunny to partially shaded spot in well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich garden beds or large containers; Rainbow Orchid is one of the most terrestrial and adaptable of orchids, growing in regular garden soil mixed with bark and perlite. In zone 9, established plants survive mild freezes to 28°F if mulched heavily; in zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable garden perennial blooming year-round. Propagate from keikis (small plantlets that form naturally on the reed stems) — detach when they show several roots and pot or plant in the garden. A truly low-maintenance garden orchid.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Rainbow Orchid blooms most prolifically in full to mostly sunny conditions but adapts to partial shade and typically produces some flowers year-round in zone 9-10. Epidendrum radicans is a reed-stemmed, mostly terrestrial orchid from Mexico, Central America, and northern South America, one of the most adaptable and cold-tolerant of the commonly cultivated orchids. The name 'Rainbow Orchid' comes from the stunning range of cultivated flower colors available — the inch-wide, fringed, miniature flowers are produced in dense, rounded clusters at the tops of 2–3 foot upright canes in shades of orange, red, yellow, pink, lavender, white, and bicolored combinations. The base species produces vivid orange flowers with a bright red-orange lip in a display that resembles tiny crucifix shapes (hence the alternative name 'Crucifix Orchid'). In zone 9-10 Gulf Coast gardens, established clumps of Rainbow Orchid bloom nearly continuously — providing permanent color in landscape beds, container groupings, and butterfly gardens (the flowers are excellent nectaring sources for large swallowtails). Unlike most orchids that require specialized epiphytic media, Rainbow Orchid grows in improved garden soil — one of the most gardener-friendly orchids available for subtropical landscapes.

common_name: Rainbow Spike Moss (Peacock Moss, Iridescent Spike Moss)
plant_note: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Rainbow Spike Moss requires higher humidity and more consistent moisture than most groundcovers and will desiccate quickly in dry conditions. It spreads by creeping stems to form a flat mat; space plants 6–12 inches apart for groundcover use. In zone 9, it performs as an evergreen groundcover in shaded, moist garden spots; it may brown in cold winters but usually resprouts from stem nodes. Excellent under tree fern canopies, in rain gardens, and as a terrarium plant.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil; Rainbow Spike Moss requires more consistent moisture than most groundcovers and will rapidly crisp and die if allowed to dry out. Selaginella uncinata is a primitive vascular plant (a club moss or spike moss, not a true moss) from southern China that produces a remarkably iridescent, structural blue-green sheen on its tiny, overlapping scale-like leaves — an optical interference effect caused by thin-film photonic structures in the leaf cells, similar to the iridescence of a peacock feather or oil film on water. In low light conditions, the iridescence intensifies to an electric blue-teal that creates a jewel-like effect in the shade garden. The plant creeps flat along the ground, building overlapping mats of fern-like, two-dimensional fronds only 1–3 inches high. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens with reliable moisture — under tree canopies, in permanently shaded bed corners, in rain garden margins — Rainbow Spike Moss creates an extraordinary low carpet of living iridescence unlike any other groundcover available. It is equally prized as a vivarium, terrarium, and paludarium plant where its spectacular appearance and humidity requirements make it ideal for closed or semi-closed planted glass environments.

plant_note: Plant rosette divisions in spring into north- or east-facing shaded rock crevices or a sharply drained, humus-rich, gritty medium; Ramonda myconi is a Pyrenean cliff perennial that requires excellent drainage and cool, shaded conditions to perform well, and is considered one of the finest miniature shade perennials for the rock garden.
directions: Plant rosette offsets tilted slightly sideways into shaded rock crevices or in a gritty alpine mix to prevent water from pooling in the crown, which causes rot; Ramonda myconi is a charming miniature rosette perennial endemic to the shaded, north-facing limestone cliffs of the Pyrenees, producing crinkled, dark-green, hairy leaves and bearing remarkably beautiful violet-mauve flowers with a bright yellow anther cone in spring that strongly resemble African violets — to which it is distantly related in the family Gesneriaceae. Like its close relative Haberlea rhodopensis, Ramonda is also a resurrection plant capable of surviving periods of desiccation. It requires cold winter humidity and cool summer conditions, and performs best in climates with cool, moist winters and mild summers; it is not suited to hot, humid summer regions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; Rangoon creeper is one of the most spectacular and fragrant tropical flowering vines — the flowers change color as they age, opening white, turning pink the next day, then deep red by the third day, so the vine always displays all three colors simultaneously, creating a tricolor effect; intensely sweet fragrance strongest in the evening.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; provide strong trellis or fence support; the vine is frost-tender but regenerates from the root in zone 9. Quisqualis indica (Rangoon creeper, Chinese honeysuckle, or drunken sailor) is one of the most flamboyant and unique tropical flowering vines available for zone 9–12 gardens — native to the tropical forests of South and Southeast Asia (India through the Philippines) and now one of the most widely grown tropical ornamental vines worldwide. The vine's most distinctive feature is its color-changing flowers: the 2-inch, long-tubed, star-shaped, fragrant flowers open pure white on the first day, turn soft pink on the second day, and deepen to brilliant scarlet-red by the third day — so the vine simultaneously carries clusters of white, pink, and red flowers at all times, creating a tricolor display unlike any other garden plant. The flowers have a powerful, sweet, jasmine-vanilla-like fragrance that intensifies in the evening, making them extraordinary for garden areas where evening fragrance is desired. The vine is a vigorous grower (reaching 20–30 feet) and blooms prolifically in warm weather. In zone 9, the vine dies back to the root in hard freezes but regenerates vigorously in spring — effectively functioning as a semi-perennial.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Rangoon creeper is a vigorous vine requiring a sturdy trellis or arbor — established plants can cover a fence or shed in a season. In zone 8–9 tops die back in frost but established roots resprout in spring.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis; Rangoon creeper is one of the most spectacular and fragrant of all tropical vines, producing pendant clusters of fragrant tubular flowers that open pure white, then change through pink to brilliant red over 3–4 days — the different-colored flowers at different stages create a stunning three-color display on the vine at all times during the long blooming season from late spring through fall. The sweet fragrance is strongest in the evening and carries widely on still air. In zone 8–9 established plants die to the ground in freezes but resprout vigorously in spring from the established root system. The vine can become very large in warm climates and may need annual pruning to keep manageable. Once established it is drought tolerant. The seeds are edible and have been used medicinally in Asia for centuries.

plant_note: In mild-winter climates (zones 8–10) plant corms in fall for late-winter/spring bloom; in cold climates start indoors and transplant after last frost.
directions: Soak corms in cool water for 4 hours before planting, then set them claw-side down about 2 in deep in well-drained, fertile soil. Ranunculus thrives in cool temperatures (45–65°F) and will decline when heat arrives, so timing is critical. In zones 9–10 plant October through January for blooms from February through May; provide afternoon shade in the warmest areas. After foliage yellows, allow corms to dry in situ or lift, cure, and store in a cool dry location for replanting.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Raspberry Splash flowers very early in spring, often among the first shade perennials to bloom, and its heavily silver-spotted leaves provide season-long foliage interest afterward.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Raspberry Splash produces clusters of small, funnel-shaped raspberry-pink flowers in very early spring, among the first blooms in the shade garden each year, held above heavily silver-spotted, softly bristled leaves that continue to provide strong foliage texture and contrast for the rest of the growing season. Like other lungworts it combines beautifully with hostas, ferns, and hellebores in a woodland border, and it tolerates fairly dry shade once established better than many shade perennials, though consistent moisture during establishment gives the best results. Divide congested clumps in early fall every few years to maintain vigor and refresh the planting.

common_name: Raspberry Wine Bee Balm (Deep Pink-Red Mildew-Resistant Bergamot)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raspberry Wine spreads by underground stolons and benefits from division every two to three years to keep the colony within bounds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew. Raspberry Wine produces large, shaggy clusters of deep magenta-pink flowers in midsummer above aromatic, mint-scented foliage, drawing hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies in large numbers over a long bloom period. It shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older bee balm cultivars, a disease that commonly disfigures monarda foliage by midsummer in humid climates, though good spacing and airflow still help keep plants looking their best. Divide every two to three years in spring to control its spreading habit and maintain vigorous, healthy growth.

common_name: Raspberry Wine Beebalm (Wine-Red Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Raspberry Wine is a tall, vigorous bee balm cultivar with deep wine-red flowers and notably better mildew resistance than many older red and pink Monarda didyma selections.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Raspberry Wine is a vigorous bee balm cultivar bearing large, shaggy flower heads in a deep, rich wine-red color, held on tall, sturdy stems above aromatic, mint-scented foliage. It shows notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older red and pink Monarda didyma cultivars, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where mildew commonly disfigures bee balm foliage by midsummer, though good air circulation and consistent moisture still help keep it looking its best through the season. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit the tubular flowers heavily from early to midsummer. Like other bee balms, it spreads by underground stolons to form an expanding clump; divide every two to three years in early spring to control spread, renew vigor, and reduce crowding that can encourage mildew. Deadhead spent flowers to tidy the plant, or leave some seed heads standing for winter interest and finch forage.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade with tall trees or structures to climb; Rattan (Calamus rotang) is a clustering, spiny, climbing palm native to the tropical forests of India and Sri Lanka — the original source of 'rattan' furniture cane — producing extraordinarily long, flexible, spiny stems that climb forest canopy trees using backward-pointing hook-tipped whips.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with tall trees or very strong support structures for climbing — Calamus rotang is a vigorous, long-stemmed climber that can reach enormous heights in mature forest and requires substantial support to reach fruiting size; handle with thick gloves as the entire plant is armed with sharp, recurved spines and hooks. Calamus rotang (Rattan, Common Rattan, or Indian Rattan Palm) is a clustering, spiny, climbing palm in the Arecaceae family native to the tropical coastal forests, moist forests, and forest edges of southern India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu) and Sri Lanka, and widely naturalized throughout Southeast Asia — the progenitor of the global rattan furniture and basketry industry. Calamus rotang and its relatives (Calamus species are the largest genus in the palm family, with 300+ species) produce extraordinarily long, slender, solid, flexible, spiny stems by climbing to the forest canopy using backward-pointing, hook-covered whips (cirri) that grab onto adjacent vegetation. The harvested and processed stems — stripped of spines, bundled, and steamed — are the 'rattan cane' used worldwide for wicker furniture, baskets, mats, walking sticks, and traditional crafts. Global rattan is a multi-billion-dollar industry, primarily from Indonesian and Malaysian forests. Calamus rotang is one of the few rattan species adapted to cooler, drier conditions outside equatorial rainforest and can be grown as an ornamental curiosity in zone 10–12 gardens with ample space and support.

plant_note: Scarify seeds lightly with sandpaper or soak overnight in warm water before direct-sowing at the surface of well-drained sandy or loamy soil after the last frost; no thinning needed as plants remain compact.
directions: Direct-sow after the last frost in well-drained, infertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; rattlebox thrives in dry sandy fields, roadsides, and open woodland edges where it fixes nitrogen through root nodules and improves soil structure with minimal inputs. Bright yellow pea-like flowers appear from midsummer onward, followed by inflated pods that turn black and papery at maturity, causing the loose seeds inside to rattle audibly in the wind — giving the plant its common name. It is an important larval host plant for the ceraunus blue butterfly and several native moth species. Allow plants to set seed and self-sow freely for a self-renewing colony; the entire plant is toxic if ingested by livestock or humans.

common_name: Rattlesnake Ginger (Yellow Rattle Calathea, Rattlesnake Plant, Yellow Wax Calathea)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in late spring in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Calathea crotalifera prefers partial shade but tolerates full shade — it grows naturally as an understory plant in humid tropical forests. In zone 9, treat as a container plant moved indoors in winter as the plant cannot tolerate frost. The distinctive yellow, waxy, overlapping-bract inflorescences are excellent cut flowers (2–3 week vase life). Propagate by rhizome division. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — Rattlesnake Ginger produces its best foliage and inflorescence display in the bright, filtered light of a shaded tropical garden position or sheltered patio. Calathea crotalifera is a clump-forming, rhizomatous tropical perennial native to Mexico, Central America, and northern South America in the Marantaceae family, grown for its remarkable, novelty inflorescences as much as for its large, paddle-shaped foliage. The inflorescences are 8–14 inches long, erect to arching, and composed of tightly overlapping, waxy, bright yellow to golden-yellow bracts stacked in a precise, shingle-like pattern along the central axis — the bract arrangement, when viewed from the side, closely resembles the segmented rattle of a rattlesnake, explaining the common name 'Rattlesnake Plant.' From between the bracts, small white to pale yellow flowers emerge in succession. The yellow, waxy inflorescences are long-lasting (several weeks on the plant and 2–3 weeks as cut flowers) and have commercial value in the tropical cut flower industry. The large, green, paddle-shaped leaves provide an attractive, lush background to the colorful inflorescences. Multiple inflorescences can be produced simultaneously by established clumps through the warm months. An attractive zone 10-11 shade garden plant and excellent tropical cut flower.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification; transplants poorly due to deep taproot.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in a sunny prairie or meadow garden in lean, well-drained soil; rattlesnake master develops a deep taproot and resents being moved after establishment. The dramatic, yucca-like basal rosette of spiny blue-green leaves is topped by tall branched stems bearing small, spiny, globe-shaped white flower heads in midsummer that are highly attractive to native bees. It is extremely drought-tolerant and actually performs better in poor, sandy or rocky soil than in rich garden beds. The sculptural seedheads provide winter interest and are prized for dried arrangements.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; Rattlesnake Plant requires consistent warmth (65–85°F), moderate indirect light, and high humidity (50%+) for best appearance. Water with filtered or rainwater to avoid fluoride damage to leaf tips. The narrow, upright leaves make it one of the more efficient space users in the Calathea group. Propagate by rhizome division in spring when repotting. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in moist, well-drained, well-aerated potting mix; Rattlesnake Plant is one of the most adaptable Calatheas for indoor conditions, tolerating somewhat lower humidity and slightly less consistent care than many of its relatives while maintaining attractive foliage. Calathea lancifolia (sometimes reclassified as Goeppertia insignis) is a prayer plant from the tropical rainforests of Brazil, producing distinctively narrow, elongated lance-shaped leaves up to 18 inches long decorated with a precise, alternating pattern of dark oval spots along the midrib that graduates to wavy, irregular dark green edges — a marking pattern that strikingly resembles the scale pattern of certain rattlesnakes, particularly the timber rattlesnake, hence the common name. The undersides of the leaves are deep purple-red, creating a dramatic visual effect when the leaves move through their daily opening and closing cycle (nyctinasty). Among the popular Calatheas, Rattlesnake Plant is often recommended as the best choice for beginners due to its relatively higher tolerance for imperfect conditions — it is more forgiving of occasional dry periods, lower humidity, and temperature fluctuation than species like C. ornata or C. makoyana, while still producing the characteristic dramatic patterned foliage that makes the group so appealing.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to poor, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun in spring; ravenna grass thrives in hot, dry, poor conditions and actually performs better in infertile soil — rich, fertile soil produces excessive, floppy growth.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; ravenna grass (Plume grass, Hardy pampas grass, Erianthus) is the cold-hardy alternative to pampas grass for northern zone 6–9 gardens — an enormous, dramatic, clump-forming grass that rises to 8–14 feet with wide, arching, blue-gray-green leaves developing attractive silvery and purplish tones in autumn, and produces enormous, feathery, silvery-white, pampas-like flower plumes in late summer that arch dramatically from the top of the plant and dry to a warm, creamy-tan for winter. The scale is truly impressive — a single established clump rivals the visual impact of a small tree and provides a genuine architectural focal point in the large-scale landscape. Hardy to zone 6 (unlike true pampas grass, Cortaderia selloana, which is limited to zone 7 or 8 in most regions), making it the choice for gardeners in zones 6–8 who want the pampas grass effect. Thrives in hot, dry, poor conditions. Can self-seed in some regions — monitor and remove unwanted seedlings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter for improved spring germination.
directions: A highly unusual native sunflower of the southeastern coastal plain entirely lacking ray flowers, bearing only chocolate-brown disk heads on stiff, upright stems in summer and fall. Native to wet flatwoods, longleaf pine savannas, and bog margins from North Carolina to Florida and Mississippi, it thrives in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun. Despite lacking petals, the dark disk heads attract specialist native bees and provide seed for songbirds through fall and winter. An unusual and conversation-worthy specimen for native savanna gardens and rain gardens in zones 7-9, it pairs well with other wet-flatwoods natives such as Liatris and native sedges.

plant_note: Propagate from tissue culture or sow seeds (slow) or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; red Abyssinian banana does not produce offsets like Musa species and must be propagated by seed, division of the main trunk base, or tissue culture — it is a non-clumping, clonal specimen plant.
directions: Propagate from tissue culture or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; red Abyssinian banana is the most dramatically colored of all ornamental banana plants — a non-clumping, monocarpic (flowers once then dies) Ethiopian banana species in the cultivar 'Maurelii' that produces enormous, paddle-shaped leaves (up to 8 feet long) in a spectacular combination of deep maroon-red midrib, burgundy-red leaf margins and undersides, and dark-green to olive-green central leaf surface, creating a massive, bold, jewel-toned tropical foliage effect that is unlike any other large-leaved tropical plant. The purple-red coloration is most vivid on young leaves emerging from the center and fades somewhat as each leaf matures, but the overall plant maintains its rich, dark, dramatic coloring throughout. Unlike fruiting bananas (Musa), Ensete ventricosum is a non-clumping banana species that grows from a single, non-suckering pseudostem to 10–15 feet in zone 10–12, producing leaves throughout its vegetative phase before the terminal inflorescence and dying after setting seed. In zone 9, it is often grown as a summer annual, started fresh from tissue culture plants each spring for its spectacular single-season tropical display.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Red Alternanthera is used extensively in zone 9 as a colorful, low-growing bedding and border-edging plant — often planted in mass to create geometric patterns (carpet bedding) in formal garden designs. Shear plants lightly every 4–6 weeks to maintain compact, dense form and prevent legginess; unpruned plants become open and produce fewer of the intensely colored leaves. The color is most vivid in full sun; partial shade produces larger, slightly less vivid leaves. In zone 9 it performs as a warm-season annual (tender below about 35°F), though established plants may resprout from stems in mild winters.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Red Alternanthera produces the most vivid leaf color in full sun but tolerates partial shade and is often used in partially shaded border situations; Red Alternanthera (Alternanthera ficoidea 'Red') is a low-growing, densely leafed foliage annual producing small, narrow leaves in vivid shades of red, burgundy, and bronze-red — creating a solid color mass of warm, intensely pigmented foliage that is used in traditional carpet bedding, border edging, and colorful pattern planting. Unlike the more rounded, dark-red-leaved Alternanthera dentata varieties, A. ficoidea has smaller, narrower leaves and a lower, denser growth habit, making it particularly useful for tight geometric patterns and fine-textured edging where a compact, fine-textured plant is needed. The richly colored leaves provide the same seasonal color function as flowering annuals but with purely foliage-based appeal — valuable in designs where consistent, uniform color without the maintenance of deadheading or the variability of flower timing is preferred. Red Alternanthera thrives in zone 9's summer heat and humidity, which would stress many cool-season foliage plants, growing most vigorously and producing its most intensely colored leaves in the hottest months of the year.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or summer; unlike most Brugmansia, B. sanguinea is adapted to cool Andean conditions and actually prefers temperatures of 50–70°F for best bloom. In hot Gulf Coast summers it may decline — site in afternoon shade, keep well-watered, and expect the best display in spring and fall. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Root cuttings and grow in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in part shade; red angel's trumpet is the most distinctive Brugmansia species — unlike the white, pink, and yellow angels' trumpets (B. x candida and relatives) that prefer warm conditions, B. sanguinea is native to the cool, cloud forest elevations of the Andes (5,000–11,000 feet) in Peru, Chile, Colombia, and Ecuador, producing exceptionally large, pendant, bicolored tubular flowers that are red-orange at the flared tip fading to yellow at the base, with a prominent green calyx. The flowers are in continuous production on established plants and are pollinated by hummingbirds in their native habitat — making them strongly attractive to hummingbirds in cultivation. The cool-preference nature makes it better suited to coastal California and mild Pacific Northwest climates than to tropical Gulf Coast summers, where afternoon shade, ample water, and well-drained fertile soil are essential. All plant parts are highly toxic; contain scopolamine, atropine, and related tropane alkaloids.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Red Autumn Sage is a hardy, long-lived perennial shrub in zone 9 — established plants can persist for 10+ years with minimal care. Prune to 6–8 inches in late winter to remove dead wood and stimulate fresh, densely flowering new growth; without annual pruning plants become leggy and produce fewer flowers. In zone 9 blooms most heavily in spring (March–May) and fall (September–November) — flowering is reduced during the heat of July–August but rarely stops entirely. The small, tubular, vivid red flowers are one of the premier hummingbird nectar sources among all landscape plants.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Red Autumn Sage is a Texas limestone native demanding excellent drainage and thriving in the lean, dry conditions that produce the most abundant flowering; Red Autumn Sage (Salvia greggii) is a small evergreen shrub native to the Chihuahuan Desert region of Texas and Mexico that has become one of the most valuable and widely planted ornamental sages for zones 7–9 — providing reliable, continuous flowering from spring through fall in the heat, drought, and alkaline soil conditions where most ornamental plants require intensive support. The vivid scarlet to cherry-red tubular flowers are produced in dense spikes on arching stems in successive flushes through the growing season, with the richest flowering in the cool-weather periods of spring and fall in zone 9. Salvia greggii is one of the most reliably effective hummingbird plants in the Gulf South — the tubular red flowers are specifically adapted to hummingbird pollination and attract Ruby-throated Hummingbirds and other hummingbird species wherever they occur in the plant's range. The combination of drought tolerance, heat tolerance, alkaline soil adaptation, compact evergreen habit, continuous bloom, and hummingbird value makes Red Autumn Sage effectively irreplaceable as a low-maintenance, wildlife-supporting perennial for the warmer, drier parts of zones 7–9.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; red baneberry is easily grown in any cool, moist, shaded site and spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding to form handsome clumps over time.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; red baneberry is easily grown in any cool, moist, shaded site and spreads slowly by rhizomes and self-seeding to form handsome clumps over time. Actaea rubra is a native North American woodland perennial in the buttercup family with large, compound, twice-ternate leaves that give it a delicate, airy texture; in mid-spring it produces fluffy, white bottle-brush-like flower clusters on leafy stems, followed in summer by brilliant, glossy, red (occasionally white in form neglecta) berries in compact clusters on red pedicels that are among the most ornamental of any native woodland fruit but are highly toxic — all parts of the plant are poisonous. It is an excellent companion for black cohosh, white baneberry, ferns, and hostas in shaded woodland gardens; the red berries are eagerly eaten by birds and provide important late-summer wildlife food.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; red barrenwort establishes readily and spreads steadily to form dense colonies, and is one of the most cold-hardy epimedium hybrids available.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this popular hybrid between E. grandiflorum and E. alpinum produces small crimson-red and white bicolored flowers in spring just as striking red-tinted new foliage unfurls. The seasonal foliar interest extends into autumn when leaves again take on red and bronze tints before going fully dormant in colder zones. Cut back old leaves in late winter before new growth emerges to give the delicate spring flowers full prominence. Red barrenwort is one of the most cold-hardy epimedium hybrids, making it a reliable choice for gardens in zones 4–8 where other species may struggle.

plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Philodendron squamiferum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or rough climbing support for best leaf development — the leaf lobes become more deeply divided on climbing specimens. Use a well-draining mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil. Maintain moderate humidity (50%+) for best appearance. Propagate readily from single-node stem cuttings. All parts are toxic if chewed.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Red Bristle Philodendron produces its largest, most dramatically lobed leaves with adequate bright indirect light and a climbing support to grow upward. Philodendron squamiferum is a climbing philodendron from French Guiana, Suriname, and northern Brazil, one of the most immediately distinctive and recognizable collector philodendrons because of its unique combination of leaf shape and petiole texture: the leaves are large (10–18 inches), deeply and irregularly lobed into five distinct lobes (like an oak leaf or a flattened hand), rich dark green, with a thick, leathery texture — but the plant's most distinctive feature is the petioles (leaf stalks), which are covered in dense, soft, bristle-like red hairs or scales. These bright rust-red to coral-red bristled petioles are unique among commonly grown aroids and give the plant the common names 'Red Bristle Philodendron' and 'Hairy Philodendron.' The contrast between the dark green lobed leaves and the vivid red furry stems creates an ornamental effect quite different from the smooth-stemmed philodendrons that dominate the market. The species is generally adaptable and grows well in indoor conditions with moderate care. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; fresh seeds planted immediately after collecting in fall also establish reliably. All parts of the plant are toxic — the seeds especially so.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; red buckeye is one of the finest native shrubs for the shaded garden, producing upright panicles of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers in April and May precisely timed to the return of ruby-throated hummingbirds from migration. The flowers are visited almost exclusively by hummingbirds and are among the most important early-season hummingbird plants available. It grows naturally as a forest understory shrub throughout the Southeast and performs exceptionally well in zone 8–9 Gulf Coast gardens in partial shade. The glossy, palmate compound leaves are attractive all season but the plant goes fully dormant in summer heat — mark its location and interplant with later-season companions. The large, mahogany-colored seeds are toxic to humans and livestock.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; red button ginger blooms most freely in partial shade and is one of the most shade-tolerant of the tropical gingers — it actually produces more flowers in dappled light than in full sun, where the foliage tends to bleach and the plant may experience heat stress.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; red button ginger is a Central American tropical spiral ginger that produces one of the most continuously ornamental flower displays of any shade-tolerant ginger — the inflorescence is a compact, cone-shaped structure of tightly overlapping, bright-red, waxy, button-like bracts from which small, orange-yellow, tubular flowers emerge one or two at a time throughout the warm season. The cone structure persists and remains ornamental even between flowering periods, providing months of red-cone interest. The plant has a distinctive habit characteristic of all Costus gingers — the leaves are arranged in a precise, slightly ascending spiral around each stem rather than the flat-spreading arrangement of other gingers, creating an elegant, corkscrew-like effect that is architecturally attractive. The stems die back after flowering, with new stems emerging from the base the following season. Red button ginger performs at its best in partial shade with consistent moisture, and is an excellent understory plant for the shaded tropical garden. Excellent near water features and in moist, shaded borders in zone 9–12.

common_name: Red Button Ginger / Scarlet Spiral Ginger
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once all danger of cold has passed, setting them 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in a shaded or partially shaded location.
