directions: Plant divisions in rich, well-draining soil in a shaded to partially shaded location, spacing clumps 24-36 inches apart to allow the glossy, spirally arranged leaves to develop their full architectural presence. Water regularly throughout the growing season to keep the soil evenly moist, and feed monthly with a balanced liquid fertilizer from spring through late summer to support the production of the dramatic scarlet cone-like inflorescences. Remove spent flowering canes at the base after blooms fade to encourage fresh new growth and repeated flushes of color. In zone 9 where light frost may occur, cut tops back and mulch the root zone deeply in fall to protect the rhizomes through winter.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring once temperatures are reliably warm, setting them 2-3 inches deep in humus-rich soil in a partially shaded position.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, organically rich soil in partial shade, setting rhizomes 2-3 inches deep and spacing clumps 3-5 feet apart to accommodate their spiraling, upright canes. Water consistently during the growing season, and apply a high-potassium fertilizer monthly from spring through late summer to fuel the production of the vivid red terminal bracts. Cut older canes to the ground after they finish flowering to encourage fresh growth from the base. In zone 9 where light frost may occur, mulch the root zone heavily in fall to protect the rhizomes through winter.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; red campion is dioecious (separate male and female plants) — sow generous quantities so that both sexes are represented. It self-sows prolifically and can naturalize readily in hedgerows, woodland edges, and semi-shaded garden areas. Plants live 2–4 years but self-sow continuously.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to woodland edge; red campion is a widespread European wildflower of woodland edges, hedgerows, and shaded banks — among the most common and cheerful May-flowering wildflowers of the British countryside, producing branched stems of deeply rose-pink, five-petaled, notched flowers from May through September in a cheerful, informal, prolific display that weaves among other wildflowers and garden plants with naturalizing ease. It is dioecious — male and female flowers occur on separate plants, the males slightly smaller and more numerous — and freely hybridizes with the white campion (Silene latifolia) where both occur, producing the intermediate hybrid Silene x hampeana with pale-pink flowers. A classic companion to bluebells and cow parsley in the British spring and early-summer hedgerow. In the garden it naturalizes beautifully in semi-shaded borders, woodland-edge gardens, and cottage-garden plantings, self-sowing to maintain colonies without invasive behavior. Double-flowered forms ('Flore Pleno') with pompom-like blooms are available and particularly ornamental.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for earlier bloom.
directions: Each medium bloom showcases deep, sultry red petals around a vivid yellow center on compact, deer-resistant plants only six to ten inches tall. Sow directly after the last frost or start indoors a few weeks early for a quicker show. These marigolds thrive in full sun and average, well-drained soil. Deadhead regularly to keep them flowering until frost. Their compact size makes them ideal for edging beds, borders, and containers while drawing in pollinators.

plant_note: Surface-sow on prepared soil in early spring or fall; needs light and does not transplant well.
directions: Scatter the fine seed on the soil surface in early spring or fall, as it needs light and resents transplanting. This iconic Flanders poppy opens tissue-paper scarlet petals with dark centers in late spring and early summer. Grow it in full sun and well-drained soil where its deep taproot makes it drought-tolerant. Let flowers form seed pods and it will self-sow generously for years to come.

common_name: Red Drift Rose (Low-Growing Red Groundcover Rose)
plant_note: Plant container roses in late winter through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in full sun; Red Drift requires at least 6 hours of direct sun daily for best flowering; in zone 9 the long warm season allows nearly year-round bloom with only a brief winter rest.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Red Drift is the red-flowered member of the Drift series of groundcover roses — a series developed by Meilland International that combines the disease resistance and landscape adaptability of groundcover roses with the repeat-blooming, dense coverage of modern landscape roses. Red Drift stays very low (12–18 inches tall, 24–36 inches wide), creating a carpet of semi-double, rich red flowers from spring through hard frost. The Drift series was specifically bred to be self-cleaning — spent flowers drop cleanly without deadheading, maintaining a tidy appearance without maintenance pruning. This self-cleaning quality combined with outstanding disease resistance (exceptional black spot and powdery mildew resistance compared to standard tea roses), heat tolerance, and continuous bloom makes Drift roses among the most low-maintenance roses available. Red Drift's low habit makes it outstanding for edging borders, planting on slopes for erosion control, ground covering under taller plants, and mass plantings where its red carpet effect and long bloom season are maximized. In zone 9, Red Drift blooms from February through December with only brief pauses; the disease resistance is maintained even in zone 9's humid summers when black spot devastates unresistant roses. A truly modern, low-maintenance landscape rose.

common_name: Red Emperor Tulip (Fosteriana Type Very Early Giant Red Tulip)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Red Emperor is a Fosteriana-type tulip prized for blooming very early in the tulip season with unusually large flowers on relatively short, sturdy stems.
directions: Plant bulbs six to eight inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in fall. Red Emperor, also known as Madame Lefeber, is a Fosteriana-type tulip celebrated for opening enormous, brilliant scarlet-red flowers very early in spring, well ahead of most other tulip types, giving an early burst of bold color while many other bulbs are just emerging. Its wide, bowl-shaped blooms open fully in sun to reveal a black-based interior that adds drama to the display, and the sturdy, relatively short stems hold up well to wind and rain. As with other tulips, mild-winter Southern gardens generally get the best results treating it as a fresh fall bulb planting rather than relying on it to perennialize reliably.

common_name: Red Flash Caladium (Red-Centered Green-Margined Fancy Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; Red Flash is one of the most sun-tolerant caladium cultivars, performing acceptably in 3–4 hours of morning sun.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade to partial sun; Red Flash is one of the most striking and popular fancy-leaved caladium cultivars — producing large, heart-shaped leaves with vivid red centers, green margins, and distinctive pink to white spots scattered across the red central area, creating a complex, colorful pattern unique among caladium cultivars. The red center, spotted texture, and dark-green margins combine into a leaf with more visual complexity and depth than solid-colored cultivars. Red Flash is notable among caladiums for its higher sun tolerance — it performs acceptably in morning sun positions (3–4 hours direct sun) that would bleach or damage most white-leaved caladiums. This sun tolerance makes Red Flash more versatile for partially shaded locations that receive some direct morning light. The large, boldly patterned leaves create outstanding tropical texture in mixed shade plantings, container gardens, and as mass ground covers under trees. In zone 9, Red Flash produces foliage from late April or May through October before cold temperatures trigger dormancy. The tubers increase in size each year, producing progressively larger and more numerous leaves as the clumps mature. Red Flash is also well-suited to container production, where the combination of good sun tolerance and striking foliage makes it an outstanding patio and deck plant.

common_name: Red Fountain Grass (Burgundy-Purple Tropical Ornamental Grass)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; 'Rubrum' is a sterile cultivar — it does not set viable seed, unlike the invasive straight species Pennisetum setaceum, making it safe to plant without concern for naturalization.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun; Red Fountain Grass ('Rubrum') is one of the most visually dramatic warm-season ornamental grasses for Gulf South gardens — producing mounding, arching clumps of narrow, burgundy-purple to dark wine-red leaves topped by reddish-bronze to copper-colored bottle-brush flower plumes in summer and fall that create an elegant, soft-textured, colorful mass that stands out brilliantly against green or silver companions. The foliage color — maintained throughout the growing season from spring through fall rather than only at bloom time — provides a sustained burgundy accent that few other ornamental grasses offer. The 'Rubrum' cultivar is sterile and does not set viable seed, making it non-invasive despite the parent species (Pennisetum setaceum) being a serious invasive in some warm climates (Hawaii, California) — the sterility of 'Rubrum' is an important ecological distinction. In zone 9, Red Fountain Grass is reliably perennial, dying back in cold winters but returning from the roots in spring; in zone 9b and 10, it may remain semi-evergreen through mild winters. Drought-tolerant once established and excellent in full-sun, reflected-heat positions that challenge many ornamental grasses. Outstanding in containers, as a specimen accent, in mixed borders, and in combination with silver companions (dusty miller, Powis Castle artemisia) where the burgundy-red and silver combination is striking.

plant_note: Divide clumps by separating rhizomes with a sharp spade in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; red ginger blooms best in bright light but tolerates the partial shade under high-canopy trees in zone 10–12 landscapes.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; red ginger (Ostrich plume ginger, pink cone ginger) is one of the most visually dramatic tropical ornamentals available, producing tall, cane-like stems bearing long, glossy, banana-like leaves and topped by spectacular upright or arching flower spikes with densely packed, overlapping bracts in vivid scarlet-red, pink, or white — the bracts (not petals) are the showy feature, lasting for months as both living spikes and cut flower material. The plant is the dominant decorative ginger seen in Hawaiian lei-making and floral arrangements worldwide. Small bulbils often develop in the flower head after bloom and can be removed and replanted. In zone 10–12 it is essentially everblooming. Excellent combined with bird of paradise, heliconias, and tropical foliage plants for a lush, tropical garden effect.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed in spring.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep and maintain even moisture at 65–75°F until germination. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — good drainage is critical, especially in winter, as plants rot in waterlogged conditions. The torch-like flower spikes transition from red or orange in bud to yellow as the florets open, creating a two-toned effect that attracts hummingbirds throughout summer and fall. In zones 5–6 tie the leaves together and mulch deeply around the crown before the first hard freeze to protect the growing point.

subcategory: dark-barked ornamental gum with pink to red flowers
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; red ironbark is one of the more cold-hardy ornamental eucalyptus — surviving to zone 7b in sheltered, well-drained positions. It is a long-lived tree with deeply furrowed, dark-red to almost black, persistent ironbark that provides year-round structural interest. The flower color is variable — white, cream, pink, and deep crimson forms occur, with 'Rosea' being the most ornamental dark-pink selection. Excellent for birds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; red ironbark is the most structurally dramatic ornamental eucalyptus for cold climates (surviving to zone 7b) — a long-lived, stately tree developing over decades a deeply furrowed, persistent, very dark red-brown to almost black-red ironbark (the iron-like, very hard, deeply grooved bark that never sheds as in the smooth gums) that creates a powerful, dark, architectural trunk structure of great character in mature specimens. The contrast of the very dark, almost black ironbark with the blue-gray-green, lance-shaped leaves and, in winter and spring, clusters of white to cream to pink to vivid crimson-rose flowers (depending on form) is a multi-season, multi-textural ornamental composition of considerable sophistication. The dark bark catching winter light against pink flowers in the background blue-gray of the canopy is one of the most striking winter tree compositions available in zones 7–11. The cultivar 'Rosea' produces the most vivid, deep-pink to rose-red flowers. Outstanding as a long-term specimen tree where its slow development into a structurally impressive large tree is a generational investment in a garden.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; Red ivy is a low, spreading tropical Southeast Asian groundcover grown for its distinctive leaves — metallic dark green-gray with a purple reverse and a wrinkled, waffle-textured surface — it is one of the finest shade groundcovers for tropical gardens and performs well in containers and hanging baskets.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to part shade; keep consistently moist for best foliage color. Hemigraphis alternata (red ivy or waffle plant) is a low-growing, creeping tropical perennial from Java and other parts of Southeast Asia in the acanthus family (Acanthaceae), grown primarily as an ornamental for the distinctive foliage: the leaves are oval to heart-shaped, with a deeply wrinkled, puckered, waffle-like texture on the upper surface (hence 'waffle plant') and are metallic dark greenish-gray with silver highlights on top, contrasting with a vivid, wine-red to magenta-purple underside. The undersurface color gives the plant its other common name, 'red ivy,' especially as it spreads along the ground and the underside is visible. Stems root readily at the nodes, allowing the plant to spread as a groundcover in warm, humid conditions. Small, white, tubular flowers are produced but are inconspicuous — the foliage is the feature. As a shade container or hanging basket plant, red ivy is outstanding: the trailing stems with metallic-textured leaves create an elegant, unusual display. In zone 10–12, it functions as a year-round shade groundcover. It is also popular as a tropical aquarium plant and terrarium subject. One of the most distinctive-looking low groundcovers for warm, humid shade.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in its native range (California and Oregon); seeds benefit from cool temperatures and natural cold-moist stratification to break dormancy and germinate in late winter or early spring.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; red larkspur is a California and southern Oregon native of shaded canyon slopes and mixed evergreen forest edges, distinguished from all other delphiniums by its unusual orange-red to scarlet flowers — a color virtually unheard of in the genus. The tubular, upward-facing flowers are exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds. It is a short-lived perennial or annual in cultivation and goes summer-dormant in dry California summers, so allow the foliage to die back naturally without summer irrigation. Like all delphiniums, all parts are toxic.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Red Latan Palm is a striking, slow-growing, large fan palm endemic to the island of Réunion in the Mascarene Islands — critically endangered in the wild — bearing enormous, circular, blue-green fan fronds with distinctive red midribs, petioles, and leaf sheaths in juvenile plants that give it an extraordinary color display unique among fan palms.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy, lean to average, alkaline-tolerant soil; Latania lontaroides is adapted to well-drained coastal soils and tolerates salt spray, drought, and exposed coastal conditions — avoid waterlogged clay soils. Latania lontaroides (Red Latan Palm or Latanier Rouge) is a large, majestic, slow-growing fan palm critically endangered in its native habitat — it is endemic to the island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean Mascarene Islands, where remaining wild populations are severely threatened by habitat loss and invasive species. The palm is celebrated for one of the most spectacular color displays in the palm family: juvenile and young plants (up to 10–15 years old) bear enormous, circular fan fronds with vivid blood-red to crimson midribs, petioles, and sheaths that contrast dramatically against the blue-green frond blades — the color gradually fading to reddish-brown and then gray as plants mature. Even mature plants retain reddish-tinged frond bases and produce an imposing crown of large, slightly glaucous, waxy fan fronds on a stout, prominently ring-marked trunk. Latania lontaroides is dioecious; both male and female plants display the color. Widely cultivated in botanical gardens and by palm collectors worldwide for its extraordinary juvenile coloration. Well adapted to coastal limestone soils, salt spray, and drought conditions in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck of the bulb at or just above soil surface; in zone 9 plant January–March for spring bloom or September for fall bloom. In zone 9 amaryllis bulbs can remain in the ground year-round as permanent perennials, blooming in spring (March–April) and sometimes again in fall. Established outdoor clumps in zone 9 bloom prolifically with minimal care. When grown in containers (as holiday houseplants), plant with 1/3 of the bulb above the potting mix; a single large bulb will typically produce 2 scapes each bearing 4 large flowers. Allow the foliage to grow and die back naturally after flowering to rebuild the bulb for next season.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Red Lion Amaryllis performs best with some shade protection in zone 9's summer heat, which can stress the bulb during summer dormancy; Red Lion is the defining red amaryllis cultivar — a large-flowered, velvety, deep red to scarlet selection that has become the standard commercial red amaryllis in the US market, producing the classic amaryllis flower form: massive, trumpet-shaped blooms 6–8 inches across borne in groups of 4 on thick, hollow scapes that emerge directly from the bulb. The bold, trumpet-form flowers in vivid red with a subtle lighter central stripe represent the most widely recognized and purchased amaryllis color — available in virtually every garden center and holiday gift catalog and producing a dramatic indoor or outdoor floral display that few other bulb flowers can match in sheer size and color impact. In zone 9, outdoors, Red Lion amaryllis is a permanent garden perennial rather than a temporary holiday novelty — the large bulbs naturalize in the ground, multiplying steadily over years and producing spring flower displays of increasing size as clumps develop. The combination of easy culture, spectacular flowers, and permanent naturalization in zone 9 makes amaryllis one of the most rewarding large-flowered bulbs available for Gulf South gardens.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring before flowering or immediately after blooms fade, splitting the crown into sections with both roots and foliage. Replant promptly in prepared, moisture-retentive soil in shade and water thoroughly. Cut back any tattered foliage after dividing to reduce transplant stress.
directions: Grow red lungwort in full to partial shade in soil enriched with compost or leaf mold, where it will spread steadily into an attractive groundcover. Divide clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding, replanting at the same depth and watering well. The unspotted, velvety evergreen leaves are an ornamental feature year-round; cut back any damaged foliage in late winter before new growth emerges. Good air circulation and consistent moisture help prevent the powdery mildew that can affect lungworts in warm, dry conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown propagules or container stock in spring in coastal, estuarine, or tidal wetland substrate in full sun; Red Mangrove is viviparous — the seed germinates on the parent tree, producing a cigar-shaped propagule that drops and anchors in the mud. Planting in protected tidal areas with shallow water and fine sediment gives the best establishment results. Never plant Red Mangrove outside of its natural range.
directions: Red Mangrove is one of the most ecologically important coastal trees in the subtropical and tropical Americas, forming the seaward fringe of mangrove forests along sheltered tidal coasts, estuaries, and coastal lagoons of Florida, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean, where its arching prop roots create a complex three-dimensional habitat supporting hundreds of species of fish, invertebrates, birds, and reptiles. The species is viviparous — the seeds germinate on the parent tree itself, producing cigar-shaped propagules up to 12 inches long that drop into the water and drift with currents before anchoring in tidal mudflats and developing new trees. Red Mangrove forests provide irreplaceable ecological services including coastal erosion control, storm surge buffering, carbon sequestration, and water quality filtration; removing them is illegal in Florida and most coastal states. Plant nursery-grown material only in appropriate tidal coastal zones in full sun in Zones 9–11; Red Mangrove is cold-sensitive and should not be planted north of its natural range.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately wet soil in full sun; red maple establishes readily and grows quickly. Avoid alkaline or compacted soils, which cause chlorosis and stunted growth.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun for best fall color; red maple is one of the most widely distributed and commonly planted native trees in eastern North America, naturally ranging from Newfoundland to Florida and adaptable to an enormous range of soil moisture conditions from wet bottomlands to dry upland ridges. True to its name, red maple puts on a red display in virtually every season: tiny red flowers cluster on bare branches in late winter (often the earliest tree to bloom), red samaras (winged seeds) ripen in spring, the leaf stalks are red through summer, and fall foliage blazes in brilliant shades of orange-red to crimson. The samaras are consumed by squirrels, grosbeaks, and finches; red maple is also a significant larval host plant for the Cecropia moth and numerous other native insects. With a growth rate of 1.5–2.5 feet per year and wide site adaptability, it is one of the most practical large native shade trees for gardens of all sizes.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for earlier bloom.
directions: This color-shifting marigold is deep burgundy in cool weather, then develops splashes of yellow as temperatures warm and reverts to solid burgundy when it cools again. Sow directly after the last frost or start indoors for earlier blooms. Full sun and well-drained soil produce the sturdiest, most colorful plants. Deadhead often to prolong flowering through the season. It makes a striking garden hedge and attracts pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; red milkweed grows naturally in freshwater and brackish marshes, wet pine flatwoods, and tidal ditches of the Coastal Plain. Tolerates seasonal flooding but not prolonged submersion.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun at pond margins, rain gardens, and tidal wetland edges; red milkweed is one of the most brilliantly colored of all native milkweeds, producing vivid, bicolored flowers with red-orange reflexed petals and orange hoods — the most intensely colored flower heads in the Asclepias genus. It grows naturally in freshwater and brackish marshes and wet pine flatwoods of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, making it ideally suited to rain gardens and wet bioswales in zone 9a. The striking flowers attract monarchs, swallowtails, and a wide range of other pollinators, and the plant is an important monarch host plant in Gulf Coast wetlands. The tall, narrow habit with narrow, willow-like leaves gives it a graceful, architectural form in the moist garden.

common_name: Red Porterweed (Cayenne Porterweed, Light Blue Snakeweed)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Cayenne porterweed is a distinct Stachytarpheta species closely related to the more common blue porterweed (S. jamaicensis) — producing lighter blue, smaller flowers on slender, erect spikes, with similar extreme value as a butterfly nectar plant; fast-growing, drought-tolerant, and blooms nearly year-round in zone 9–12 tropical landscapes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; very drought-tolerant once established; self-sows freely in warm climates. Stachytarpheta cayennensis (Cayenne porterweed or light blue snakeweed) is a tropical perennial shrub native to the Caribbean, tropical Americas, and Central America — closely related to the widely-grown blue porterweed (S. jamaicensis) and sharing its exceptional ecological value as a butterfly nectar plant. Like S. jamaicensis, it produces long, slender, erect spikes with small, individual flowers that open one at a time along the spike over an extended period — but the flowers of S. cayennensis are lighter blue to lavender-blue and slightly smaller than those of S. jamaicensis. Both species are among the highest-value plants in the tropical butterfly garden: the elongated flower spike design provides ideal perches for feeding butterflies, and the plant blooms nearly continuously in warm climates. Like S. jamaicensis, S. cayennensis is also used medicinally in tropical traditional medicine across its range — as an anti-inflammatory, antifungal, and general tonic herb in Caribbean and Latin American folk medicine. The two species are nearly identical in garden use and can be distinguished mainly by flower size and shade intensity. Often naturalized as a weed in disturbed tropical habitats worldwide.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; red powderpuff grows rapidly in warm, humid weather and can be blooming within the first season. In zone 8b, protect from hard freezes with frost cloth.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; red powderpuff is one of the most dramatically beautiful flowering shrubs of the tropical and subtropical world, producing spectacular round clusters of deep crimson stamens that form feathery, silky balls 3–4 inches across — the individual flowers have no petals, only hundreds of brilliant red stamens that create the distinctive powderpuff effect. Blooms appear nearly year-round in frost-free areas and intermittently spring through fall in zone 9. The new foliage emerges in shades of copper and bronze before maturing to glossy dark green, providing an additional season of ornamental interest. An outstanding hummingbird and butterfly plant. Prune lightly after bloom cycles to maintain shape but avoid heavy pruning in fall; the plant blooms on old wood. A white-flowered species (Calliandra surinamensis, pink powderpuff) is also widely grown in Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist to average soil in partial shade after frost; red ruellia is one of the better shade-tolerant flowering perennials for zone 8–10, maintaining flower production in quite dim conditions where most red-flowered tropical plants would fail to bloom.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, moist to average soil in partial shade; red ruellia is a Brazilian tropical perennial of the family Acanthaceae that produces bright, clear-red, tubular, flared, funnel-shaped flowers continuously from spring through frost in partial-shade conditions where many red-flowering tropicals would cease blooming — making it particularly valuable as a continuously-flowering red accent plant for shaded gardens. The flowers are individually short-lived (opening for a single day) but produced in continuous succession on the upright stems, creating an ongoing display. The dark-green, lance-shaped leaves provide attractive foliage coverage between flowering periods. Distinguished from the weedy Mexican petunia (Ruellia simplex, previously R. brittoniana) by its non-invasive growth habit, larger flowers, and non-spreading by seed — red ruellia does not naturalize in natural habitats and is safe to plant in ecologically sensitive areas. Excellent as a hummingbird plant, the tubular red flowers attract hummingbirds reliably. In zone 8–9 it freezes back but regrows from roots in spring.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Plant Red Runner tubers 4-6 inches deep once soil warms, laying each tuber horizontally with the eye pointing up. This decorative variety produces dark romantic-red blooms on strong stems well suited for cutting. Pinch the growing tip at 12 inches to encourage bushier plants and more flowers. In zones colder than 8, lift and store the tubers in a cool, dry place over winter. Water deeply once sprouts emerge and avoid overwatering newly planted tubers.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after frost; in zone 9 plant March–May. Red Shrimp Plant is evergreen and root-hardy in zone 8b–11; in colder zone 8a it dies to the ground but recovers from roots if protected with mulch. It blooms year-round in zone 9 with the heaviest flowering in spring and fall. Prune hard in late winter to encourage dense new growth and prevent legginess.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; the Red Shrimp Plant produces distinctive pendulous spikes of overlapping salmon-red to copper-red bracts (modified leaves) that resemble a cooked shrimp in color, shape, and curve — with small white tubular true flowers emerging from between the bracts. The unique flower spikes appear continuously in zone 9 and are extraordinarily attractive to hummingbirds, who hover at each spike to probe for nectar through the entire growing season. The plant performs best in partial shade where it receives bright indirect light or morning sun with afternoon protection — full midday sun in zone 9 causes leaf scorching. It is more compact and floriferous in partial shade than in full sun. Cut back by half in late winter to maintain a bushy, productive habit; plants that are not pruned become tall and leggy with most flowering at the stem tips.

common_name: Red Sister Ti Plant (Brilliant Red-Foliage Cordyline Tropical Accent)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to bright indirect light; protect from direct afternoon sun in summer which can bleach and burn the red leaf pigment in the intense Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to bright indirect light; Red Sister is the most widely planted ti plant (Cordyline fruticosa) cultivar in Gulf South landscaping — producing long, strap-shaped, arching leaves in brilliant burgundy-red to rose-red and magenta-pink tones that provide a year-round tropical foliage focal point in warm-climate gardens. The name 'ti plant' refers to the Pacific Islander cultural significance of Cordyline fruticosa, where the plant carries deep spiritual and traditional meaning and is widely used in ceremonial contexts throughout Polynesia and Hawaii. 'Red Sister' is one of the most intensely and uniformly red ti plant cultivars — the long, lance-shaped leaves (12–24 inches) are a rich, saturated red-magenta through much of the year, sometimes with lighter pink margins that create a luminous, two-tone effect. In zone 9b-12, Red Sister grows as a perennial tropical shrub reaching 3–6 feet with arching rosettes of foliage; in zone 9a, it is often used as a container plant moved indoors before frost or as a warm-season annual-style tropical replaced each spring. The bold red foliage creates outstanding contrast with green-foliaged tropical plants — ginger, elephant ear, bird of paradise — where the red provides the warm color accent that defines a classic tropical border composition.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–5 inches deep in late summer or early fall, before the blooms emerge; do not disturb established clumps as they bloom most prolifically when pot-bound and undisturbed. Plant in a spot where the bare stems will not look odd — flowers emerge without leaves.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; red spider lily is a classic of Southern American gardens, beloved for its startling habit of sending up bright crimson spider-like flowers on bare leafless stems in September and early October — just as the first cool rains return after the summer dry spell, hence the name hurricane lily. The curled, reflexed petals and long projecting stamens give the flowers a wildly exotic appearance unlike any other fall bulb. Strap-like dark green leaves emerge after blooming and persist through winter, providing ground cover. Bulbs naturalize prolifically into large clumps and were traditionally planted on the perimeter of rice fields in Japan as a rodent deterrent — all parts are toxic to mammals.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container stock in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade in zone 9–12; Red Spiral Ginger is a striking, clumping tropical perennial from Costa Rica and Central America bearing spirally arranged leaves on upright canes and producing brilliant scarlet-red, cone-shaped terminal bracts from which small, yellow, tubular flowers emerge — providing months of colorful display in warm, humid gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to bright indirect light; Costus barbatus performs best in high humidity with consistent moisture — mulch heavily, water regularly in summer, and protect from frost; in zone 9 mulch heavily and cut back frost-damaged canes. Costus barbatus (Red Spiral Ginger or Scarlet Spiral Flag) is a clumping, cane-forming, rhizomatous perennial in the Costaceae family — close relatives of the gingers — native to the humid forests and forest edges of Costa Rica, Panama, and adjacent Central America. The hallmark of the plant is its beautiful stem architecture: the broad, lanceolate leaves are arranged in a perfect ascending spiral around each upright cane, giving the plant an elegant, architectural quality even without flowers. The flower heads are spectacular: large, cone-shaped, brilliant scarlet-red bracts tightly overlapping at the top of each cane, from which small, yellow, tubular flowers emerge one or a few at a time over several months — the red bracts persist long after the flowers, extending the display. Hummingbirds work the flowers intensively. Costus barbatus thrives in partial shade, making it an outstanding choice for shadier positions in tropical and subtropical gardens where few other plants produce such vibrant color. Divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor. Excellent for container growing in bright, humid interiors in cooler climates.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or sandy loamy soil in full sun; red spruce grows naturally at high elevations in the Appalachians and at lower elevations in northern New England and Atlantic Canada, requiring cool, moist, acidic, well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, rocky or sandy loamy soil in full sun; red spruce is the characteristic conifer of the southern Appalachian high peaks — the dominant tree of spruce-fir forests above 5,500 feet elevation on the highest summits of the Great Smoky Mountains, Roan Mountain, and the Black Mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee. The 'red' name comes from the reddish-brown young branchlets and the reddish cast of the bark on older trees. The small, reddish-brown cones are distinctive. Widely harvested for pulpwood, resonance wood for violin soundboards (Stradivarius violins were made from European spruce, but red spruce has been used for guitar tops and other musical instruments for its exceptional acoustic properties). Suffered severely from acid rain damage at high elevations in the 20th century; restoration plantings have been underway since the 1990s. One of the most important species for high-elevation Appalachian forest ecology.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline, sandy to rocky, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Red Stopper is best suited to frost-free Zone 10–11 coastal south Florida and the Florida Keys. Berries should be sown fresh as seeds lose viability quickly.
directions: Red Stopper is a native evergreen shrub or small tree of the subtropical coastal hammocks of the Florida Keys and Miami-Dade County, as well as much of the Caribbean, producing small clusters of edible red to black berries that are sweet and aromatic, relished by white-crowned pigeons, mockingbirds, and other subtropical fruit-eating birds. The glossy, elliptical leaves emit a spicy fragrance when crushed, typical of the Eugenia family, and the small, white, brush-like flowers attract native bees and butterflies. A component of the critically imperiled South Florida coastal hardwood hammock community, Red Stopper is an attractive, slow-growing landscape shrub for Zone 10–11 coastal gardens, providing wildlife value, year-round evergreen foliage, seasonal flowers, and colorful edible berries. Plant in well-drained, rocky to sandy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are drought-tolerant and salt-tolerant in coastal settings.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Red Thread is a very low-growing (2–4 inch) alternanthera variety — one of the smallest in the genus — making it ideal for edging, carpet bedding patterns, and fine-scale foreground planting. In zone 9 it thrives in summer heat and performs continuously until frost. Like all alternanthera, it is grown purely as a foliage plant — the tiny, white flowers that may appear are insignificant and the plant should be sheared back if flowering begins to redirect energy into colorful new foliage.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Thread is a low-growing, very fine-textured alternanthera with narrow, thread-like, red-orange to coppery-red leaves — the extremely small leaf size and the thread-like character of the foliage create a fine, delicate texture quite different from the broader-leaved alternanthera varieties. The fiery orange-red to copper-red color of the threadlike leaves provides intense, saturated color in formal edging and carpet bedding where precision and consistent low growth are required. Red Thread is the alternanthera most commonly used in Victorian-inspired carpet bedding designs where differently colored low-growing foliage plants are arranged in precise geometric patterns — the tiny leaf size allows precise edging lines of 2–4 inches high that maintain crisp formal patterns throughout the growing season. In zone 9's summer heat, alternanthera's heat tolerance makes it one of the few ornamental foliage plants that can be used for formal, labor-intensive carpet bedding patterns without the summer decline and replanting that makes formal summer bedding impractical in cool climates.

common_name: Red Tip Photinia (Fraser Photinia, Red Robin Photinia)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; full sun is essential for Red Tip Photinia — shade dramatically increases susceptibility to Entomosporium leaf spot, the primary disease threat, and reduces the brilliance of the red new growth that is the plant's main ornamental attribute.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun with good air circulation; Red Tip Photinia is one of the most widely planted and most recognizable landscape shrubs in the American South — a large, fast-growing evergreen producing stunning flushes of brilliant scarlet-red new growth throughout spring and into summer, creating a spectacular multi-season display as the vivid red leaves mature to glossy dark green. This red new growth is the plant's defining ornamental feature and the reason for its extraordinary popularity. Flat-topped clusters of creamy-white flowers appear in spring. Red Tip Photinia grows vigorously to 10–15 feet tall but responds readily to shearing as a formal hedge at whatever height is needed. However, heavy shearing stimulates rapid new growth — which, while ornamentally attractive for its color, also provides dense, susceptible tissue for the plant's primary disease problem: Entomosporium maculatum leaf spot, which causes spreading purple-red spots with gray centers that disfigure and eventually defoliate plants in humid, warm climates. In zone 9, Entomosporium can be severe in dense plantings with poor air circulation. Planting in full sun with wide spacing and avoiding overhead irrigation reduces, but does not eliminate, the risk. The disease has significantly reduced Red Tip Photinia's use in zone 9 plantings since the 1990s; Ternstroemia gymnanthera is sometimes recommended as a disease-resistant alternative providing similar red new growth.

common_name: Red Tower Ginger (Scarlet Spiral Ginger, Costus barbatus)
plant_note: Plant rhizomes or container-grown clumps in spring when soil temperature reaches 65°F+ in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; Red Tower Ginger grows best in the dappled light of woodland gardens and shaded tropical beds. In zone 9, the rhizomes survive mild winters underground; mulch heavily in zone 9a to insulate roots from hard frost. The striking red cone-shaped terminal inflorescences begin forming in summer. Divide clumps every 3–4 years. The spirally arranged leaves on the canes are the characteristic feature of the entire Costus genus.
directions: Plant in partial shade to dappled light in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Red Tower Ginger thrives in the conditions of its native Costa Rican and Colombian rainforest habitat — warm, humid, partially shaded, with consistently moist soil. Costus barbatus is a dramatic ornamental ginger from Central and South America (Costa Rica, Colombia) in the Costaceae family, distinguished by its tall, cane-like stems whose leaves are arranged in a distinctive spiral pattern rather than the two-ranked arrangement of true gingers (Zingiber) — giving the genus its common name 'Spiral Ginger.' The primary ornamental feature is the inflorescence: a dense, cylindrical to cone-shaped terminal structure of overlapping, hard, bright scarlet to orange-red bracts from which small yellow flowers emerge — like a red torch or pinecone of living fire at the top of each cane. The inflorescences persist for weeks and are occasionally used as cut flowers or in tropical arrangements. Red Tower Ginger is one of the most dramatic ornamental gingers for zone 9 Gulf Coast shade gardens where its bold, architectural form — spirally-leaved canes topped with scarlet torches — creates a powerfully tropical effect in woodland and shaded tropical beds.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, slightly acidic, deeply humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; never dig trilliums from wild populations — purchase only nursery-propagated plants. The rhizome is easily damaged; plant with care at the same depth as grown.
directions: Plant nursery-grown rhizome divisions in fall in deeply humus-rich, moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade — red trillium (T. erectum) is one of the most widespread and variable of all trilliums, producing maroon to dark red (rarely white or pink) three-petaled flowers in mid-spring on erect stalks above a whorl of three broad, mottled leaves. The flower has a distinctive unpleasant odor (resembling carrion) that attracts blow flies and carrion beetles as pollinators. Despite the malodorous flowers, it is a beautiful and ecologically important native wildflower of eastern woodland, associated with rich, mesic forests from Canada to the Appalachians. The seeds are dispersed by ants (a process called myrmecochory) that carry the elaiosome-bearing seeds underground and leave them near established ant colonies. Like all trilliums, red trillium takes 7 years to flower from seed; purchase only nursery-grown, propagated plants — never collect from wild.

common_name: Red Turks Cap (Mexican Sleeping Hibiscus Shade-Tolerant Hummingbird Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; the Mexican Turk's Cap (var. mexicanus) grows larger and more vigorously than the native Texas Turk's Cap (var. drummondii) — allow adequate space, or prune back heavily each late winter to control size.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Red Turk's Cap (Malvaviscus arboreus var. mexicanus) is a Gulf South garden classic and one of the most important hummingbird-attracting plants for the region — a robust, fast-growing shrub producing bright red, tubular, never-fully-opening flowers from summer through frost, the twisted petals and protruding stamens creating the distinctive 'sleeping hibiscus' appearance that gives the plant one of its common names. The flower form — a narrow, twisted tube of red petals rather than the open cup of a blooming hibiscus — is precisely adapted to hummingbird feeding: only a long bill can access the nectar at the base, making Malvaviscus one of the premier hummingbird plants for the Gulf South. The Mexican variety grows larger, more vigorously, and with larger leaves and flowers than the native Texas Turk's Cap (var. drummondii), reaching 6–9 feet in a single growing season in warm zone 9 conditions. One of the exceptional qualities of Red Turk's Cap is its extraordinary shade tolerance — unlike most flowering shrubs, it blooms prolifically in partial to deep shade, filling the critical niche of shade-tolerant flowering shrub that few Gulf South plants can occupy. Under large live oaks and pines, where most flowering plants decline, Turk's Cap thrives and blooms from June through December. In zone 9, the tops may be killed by hard freezes but plants return vigorously from the roots in spring. Excellent for naturalizing in large shade garden areas.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring or fall in moist, consistently irrigated soil; plants establish quickly and begin producing berries in their second or third season.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to full shade; red-osier dogwood produces its most vivid winter stem color in full sun but tolerates significant shade, making it one of the few native shrubs that lights up a shady winter garden with brilliant crimson branches. The white berries ripen in summer and are eaten by over 40 bird species, and the dense thicket provides year-round nesting cover. Rejuvenate the shrub every two to three years by cutting one-third of the oldest canes to the ground in early spring, since the brightest stem color comes from young growth. The stoloniferous habit forms broad colonies excellent for streambank stabilization and erosion control.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown transplants in very well-drained, sandy, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; hesperaloe is extremely drought tolerant once established and grows naturally in the dry limestone hills of south Texas and northeastern Mexico. Never plant in wet or clay soil.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean soil in full sun; despite its common name 'red yucca,' hesperaloe is not a true yucca but a close relative in the Asparagaceae family native to south Texas and northeastern Mexico. It forms striking rosettes of long, narrow, grass-like leaves with thread-like fibers along the margins and produces tall, arching flower stalks 4–6 feet high covered in coral-red tubular flowers from spring through fall — an outstanding hummingbird plant that blooms continuously for months. It is extraordinarily drought tolerant, heat tolerant, deer resistant, and adaptable, thriving in pure gravel or caliche where most plants fail. The yellow form ('Yellow') is an attractive alternative. One of the best xeriscape plants for the Gulf South, equally at home in formal landscapes and naturalistic plantings. Almost no maintenance required after establishment.

plant_note: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix with support for climbing; Philodendron subhastatum is immediately distinguished from other philodendrons by the vivid brick-red to cherry-red undersurface of its leaves — a striking two-tone effect where the upper leaf surface is glossy dark green and the lower surface is bold red. This bicolored leaf quality is especially vivid on young, fresh leaves and fades to duller maroon as leaves mature. Best in warm, humid shade. Protect from temperatures below 55°F. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs — calcium oxalate in all plant parts.
directions: Grow in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Red-Backed Philodendron is one of the most ornamentally distinctive of the climbing philodendrons, valued primarily for the dramatic bicolored nature of its leaves: the upper surface glossy dark forest-green, the lower surface vivid brick-red to cherry-red. Philodendron subhastatum is a hemiepiphytic, climbing philodendron in the Araceae family native to Colombia and Panama — a member of the loosely defined informal group of bicolored-leaf philodendrons within the large and varied genus, sharing the red-undersided quality with species like P. erubescens and some P. gloriosum forms, though subhastatum has a more distinctly elongated, narrow leaf shape. The plant produces elongated, narrowly ovate to hastate (spear-shaped with spreading basal lobes) leaves 10–18 inches long on climbing stems that ascend a support using adventitious roots. The upper leaf surface is dark, semi-glossy green; the lower surface is a vivid, coppery brick-red to cherry-red that is especially striking on young, recently expanded leaves and remains ornamental through the leaf's life. When light comes through the leaf margin or shines on the red underside directly, the bicolor contrast is particularly vivid. In shaded garden settings, hanging leaves and side-light conditions regularly expose the red undersides to good effect. A distinctive collector philodendron with genuine ornamental quality for shaded tropical patios. CAUTION: toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; Mangle's kangaroo paw is the floral emblem of Western Australia. Like all kangaroo paws it is susceptible to ink disease (Alternaria fungal spotting) in humid conditions — improve airflow and avoid overhead watering. It blooms in spring and summer. Division every 2–3 years maintains vigor and flowering. The red-and-green bicolor is the most dramatic and recognizable of the kangaroo paw species.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; red-and-green kangaroo paw is the most iconic and most beautiful of all kangaroo paw species — the floral emblem of Western Australia, recognized internationally as the botanical symbol of Australian flora, and one of the most distinctive and immediately recognizable flowers in the world. The flowers are produced in clusters on upright, branching stems in an extraordinary, vivid bicolor of bright, true-red to crimson-red below (on the stem and lower floral tube) and bright emerald-green on the tubular, six-lobed, velvety upper flower — the combination of saturated red and vivid green in the dense, velvety, fur-textured flower tubes creating a striking, completely unique color contrast that is unlike any other commonly grown ornamental plant. The common name 'kangaroo paw' perfectly describes the shape — the six diverging lobes of the perianth tube spreading and curving like the toes of a kangaroo's paw. It blooms in spring and summer, attracting honeyeating birds (in Australia) and hummingbirds (in cultivation) through the highly productive nectar in the long, tubular flowers. The primary parent species of the many modern Anigozanthos hybrids. A signature plant for zone 9 California and Gulf Coast Mediterranean-style gardens.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; enkianthus requires the same acidic, organic, well-drained conditions as rhododendrons and azaleas and makes an outstanding companion in woodland or shade gardens with ericaceous plants.
directions: Plant in moist, very well-drained, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; redvein enkianthus is an outstanding but underused deciduous shrub with four seasons of ornamental interest. In spring before the leaves emerge, pendulous clusters of small cream-to-pale-yellow bell-shaped flowers delicately striped with red veins are produced at branch tips — the striped pattern gives the species and cultivar names. The neat, whorled foliage arrangement on tiered branches creates an attractive, layered architecture through summer. In fall the foliage turns brilliant shades of orange, red, and yellow — among the best fall color of any flowering shrub. The upright, vase-shaped habit and slow growth make it suitable for smaller gardens. It thrives alongside azaleas, rhododendrons, mountain laurels, and other acid-loving shrubs in woodland settings, requiring the same culture: moist, acidic, organic, well-drained soil and partial shade. Performs best in zones 4–7 where reliable winter cold is available; marginally hardy in zone 8 in cool, shaded, moist sites.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; plants establish readily along streambanks, woodland floors, and shaded rain garden margins where moisture is consistent.
directions: Set divisions into consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial to full shade in spring, pressing crowns to soil level and watering well to eliminate air pockets around the roots. Reflexed sedge is a delicate, fine-textured native of southeastern US woodlands that forms tidy, low clumps ideal for filling shaded understory areas, moist woodland edges, and stream banks where taller plants struggle. The reflexed seed spikes that give this sedge its name arch gracefully outward at maturity, adding subtle texture to the woodland floor from late spring through summer. Divide established clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigorous growth and expand the planting.

common_name: Regal Anthurium (King Anthurium, Giant Velvet Anthurium, Royal Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow in deep shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, chunky aroid mix with excellent aeration; Anthurium regale is one of the most spectacular of the large velvet anthuriums, producing leaves that can reach 36–48 inches or more in mature specimens, in deep forest-green with bold ivory-white primary veins creating a dramatic, architectural display. It requires consistently warm (above 60°F) temperatures, high humidity (60%+), and the well-aerated root medium typical of its epiphytic cloud forest origin. Slow-growing but very long-lived. Highly sought by collectors. CAUTION: calcium oxalate crystals present; toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in deep to partial shade in a well-aerated, humus-rich, chunky mix with consistently warm temperatures and high humidity — Regal Anthurium grows most magnificently in the cool, deeply shaded, perpetually humid conditions of its native Peruvian cloud forest habitat and rewards careful attention to these conditions with some of the most dramatic foliage of any cultivated plant. Anthurium regale is a large, terrestrial to epiphytic anthurium in the Araceae family native to the cloud forests of Peru (primarily the Department of Loreto) in the section Cardiolonchium — the velvet-leaved anthurium group that includes A. crystallinum, A. clarinervium, and A. magnificum. The plant produces enormous, pendant to spreading leaves: in mature specimens, individual leaves can reach 36–48 inches or more in length, are cordate (heart-shaped) at the base, and have a surface texture of deep, velvety forest-green with extraordinarily prominent ivory-white to cream primary veins (midrib and 3–5 main lateral veins) that stand out in brilliant relief against the dark background — creating an effect of dramatic, high-contrast architectural drawing in green and white. The back (abaxial) surface of the leaf is pale, matte green. The velvety upper surface is produced by papillate (bumped) epidermal cells that scatter light diffusely. Anthurium regale is among the largest-leaved and most imposing of the velvet anthuriums and is a prestige specimen for serious collectors of tropical aroids. Slow to reach full size but very long-lived. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect the emerging shoots in spring with a light covering of straw or fleece in zones 3-5 as they emerge early and are susceptible to late frost damage.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect the emerging shoots in spring with a light covering of straw or fleece in zones 3-5 as they emerge early and are susceptible to late frost damage. Lilium regale was introduced from western China to Western horticulture by E.H. Wilson in 1903 and has remained one of the great garden bulbs ever since; it produces large, 6-inch, outward-facing to slightly nodding trumpet flowers with pure white interiors marked with yellow at the center, flushed with wine-purple on the exterior of the petals, and an intoxicatingly powerful fragrance that is unmistakable and carries across the garden on warm evenings. It blooms in midsummer for 2-3 weeks, is easy to grow, and is one of the few lily species that comes reasonably true from seed and flowers in its second or third year; it is excellent cut flower material as well.

common_name: Regal Mist Ruby Muhly Grass (Pink-Red Fall Muhly)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Regal Mist develops its best and most vivid pink-red flower cloud color in full sun — in shade the fall color is significantly less intense.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Regal Mist is a named cultivar of Muhlenbergia capillaris (Gulf muhly grass) — a compact selection bred for improved and more intensely saturated pink-to-red flower cloud color compared to the standard species, and for a slightly more compact, upright habit that is more practical for typical residential garden spaces. In late September through November, Regal Mist produces a spectacular haze of airy, deep rose-pink to magenta-red flower plumes that rise above and envelope the entire plant in a luminous, cloud-like color display — one of the most dramatic fall ornamental effects in American horticulture. The backlit effect when the late afternoon sun shines through the flower cloud from behind is particularly spectacular, creating a glowing, luminous pink-red haze effect that is unforgettable. Muhlenbergia capillaris is a native Gulf Coast grass, naturally occurring from coastal dunes and pine savannas from Virginia to Texas — fully adapted to Gulf South heat, humidity, salt spray, sandy or clay soil, and drought. Regal Mist is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the lean, well-drained conditions where many ornamental grasses struggle. Plant in masses of 5 or more for maximum visual impact — the cloud effect is most dramatic when multiple plants create a sweeping pink-red haze across a broad planting area.

plant_note: Attach small clumps to the rough bark of live oaks, southern magnolias, or other large trees by tying gently with jute twine; keep moist until established. Can also grow on old wooden fences or moss-covered rocks.
directions: Attach small clumps to the rough bark of live oaks, magnolias, cypress knees, or mossy rocks in partial to full shade; resurrection fern is a fascinating native epiphytic fern that grows without soil, anchoring itself to bark and extracting water and nutrients from rain and air. Its extraordinary survival ability allows it to lose up to 97% of its water content and appear completely dead and shriveled in drought, then revive to lush green within hours of rain — earning its dramatic common name. In its natural habitat the bark surface of mature live oaks is often entirely carpeted with this fern, and in rain events the transformation from brown crisp desiccation to vivid green is remarkable and occurs overnight. Establish by tying moist clumps to rough bark in spring; once attached it will spread slowly across the bark surface over time and requires no further care.

subcategory: summer-blooming bulb with bare-stem pink flowers; foliage dies before bloom
plant_note: Plant bulbs in late summer to early fall (after flowering if buying blooming bulbs, or August–September otherwise) with the neck of the bulb at or just below soil level in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; resurrection lily requires excellent drainage and a dry summer dormancy period — summer irrigation will rot the bulbs. The foliage emerges in late winter or early spring, matures and dies completely by early summer, then bare flower stems arise seemingly from nowhere in August without any foliage — giving the plant its common name. Do not disturb established clumps.
directions: Plant bulbs in late summer to early fall with the neck at or just below soil level in excellently well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade under deciduous trees; lycoris squamigera is one of the most dramatic and conversation-provoking bulbs for temperate and subtropical gardens, operating on a uniquely counterintuitive growth cycle that never fails to surprise: broad, strap-like, daffodil-like leaves emerge in late winter or early spring and grow through spring, then die completely and disappear by early summer, leaving bare ground — and then in August, with no warning and no foliage, stout, bare, leafless 18–24-inch stems rise from the ground and open umbels of 6–8 large, fragrant, soft pink to lavender-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers at the top, giving rise to the evocative common names resurrection lily and magic lily. The critical cultural requirement is dry summer conditions: irrigation during the summer dormancy period will rot the bulbs. Plant under deciduous trees (which provide shade and dry conditions under the canopy in summer) or in borders where summer irrigation can be withheld. Bulbs resent disturbance and may skip flowering for 1–2 years after transplanting; once settled, established clumps bloom reliably for decades.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in warm soil in spring in any sunny, well-drained site; retama grows rapidly from seed and tolerates alkaline, poor, dry, or sandy soils — avoid heavy clay and standing water; freezes back in zone 8 but regrows from roots.
directions: Retama is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the Texas coastal region and Gulf South — its weeping, bright green photosynthetic stems and spine-tipped branches give it a distinctive architectural silhouette year-round, and in spring it erupts into cascading sprays of fragrant, bright yellow flowers with an orange-spotted petal that is so showy it has been called 'Jerusalem thorn' in the Anglo tradition and 'retama' in the Spanish South Texas culture. The photosynthetic green bark allows the tree to produce energy even during droughts when leaves (tiny, feathery leaflets on long, drooping rachises) may drop, enabling survival in extreme heat and drought that would kill most trees. Retama grows exceptionally fast — often 6–8 feet per year in good conditions — making it useful for rapid screening and shade creation in south Texas landscapes; it also serves as an important nectar plant for native bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds and provides nesting habitat for orioles and doves. The tree is armed with paired thorns and is not recommended near high-traffic areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained calcareous or sandy soil; established plants are long-lived and persistent with minimal care.
directions: Reverchon's Palafox is a Texas-endemic native perennial, restricted in the wild to dry, sandy, or caliche-rocky soils across central and west Texas prairies and plains. Unlike the annual Small Palafox, this species forms woody-based, mounding clumps with narrow, alternately arranged leaves on branching stems that persist from year to year and expand slowly over time. Clusters of rose-pink composite flowers appear from late summer through fall, reliably drawing monarch butterflies and native bees at a critical time in the migration season. Grow in full sun in dry, lean, calcareous or sandy, sharply drained soil and provide little to no supplemental irrigation once established; it is an outstanding drought-tolerant native perennial for Texas xeriscapes, caliche gardens, and rocky prairie plantings.

plant_note: Plant in shallow, very well-drained, peat-based, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in bright indirect shade; rex begonias have shallow root systems and perform best in wide, shallow containers rather than deep pots. They are sensitive to overwatering — the rhizome rots quickly in wet or poorly drained conditions.
directions: Plant in shallow, very well-drained, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade; rex begonias are grown almost exclusively for their spectacular foliage — the large, asymmetric leaves in patterns of silver, green, burgundy, red, pink, purple, copper, and bronze in bold swirling patterns are arguably the most ornamental of any leaf in the plant kingdom. Each cultivar has a unique, artistic pattern that looks almost hand-painted. They are outstanding container plants for shaded patios and covered porches where their foliage can be admired up close. As an outdoor shade garden plant in zone 10–12, they thrive under trees in similar conditions to calatheas and marantas. They prefer high humidity, bright indirect light, and shallow, moist-but-never-soggy soil. The rhizomes can be divided and propagated; individual leaves can also be rooted in moist peat to produce new plants.

plant_note: Place outdoors only after temperatures remain above 60°F at night. In frost-prone climates, grow in containers that can be brought indoors for the winter.
directions: Propagate by leaf-section cuttings or rhizome divisions placed in a warm, humid propagator on moist perlite or seed-starting mix; avoid burying the cutting deeply. Grow in bright to moderate indirect shade in well-draining, humus-rich potting mix with good air circulation to prevent powdery mildew. Water at the base rather than overhead, allowing the top inch of soil to dry between waterings to discourage root rot. Maintain temperatures above 60°F year-round and bring container plants indoors well before autumn temperatures drop.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in lean, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic soil in full sun; rhizomatous little bluestem differs from common little bluestem (S. scoparium) by having shallow rhizomes that allow it to spread into a loose, spreading mat rather than a tight bunch — making it more effective as a groundcover grass.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rhizomatous little bluestem is a Gulf Coastal Plain endemic closely related to the widely cultivated little bluestem (S. scoparium) but with the important additional trait of short rhizomes that allow the plant to spread into a loose colony — a significant advantage for erosion control on sandy slopes and for naturalizing large dry areas with a weed-suppressing native grass groundcover. The blue-green summer foliage, silvery-white fall seed heads, and brilliant copper-bronze winter color mirror the ornamental qualities of common little bluestem, while the spreading habit provides better coverage of large areas. Native to dry pine flatwoods, sandhills, and sandy openings in the Gulf states from Florida to Texas. An outstanding native grass for large-scale sandy slope plantings and mass groundcover applications in the warm-season Gulf South garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown palms in spring in a wind-sheltered full-sun location with fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 9 choose a warm microclimate near a south-facing wall to protect from brief freezes.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with consistent moisture; the ribbon fan palm is prized for its enormous fan leaves whose outer leaflets droop into graceful, ribbon-like weeping tips that set it apart from other fan palms. Mature specimens can reach 50 feet with individual leaves spanning 10 feet, making this an architectural statement palm for large landscapes and parks. It is among the more cold-tolerant of the Livistona genus and can handle brief dips into the upper 20s°F when established in a sheltered microclimate. Fertilize three times per year with a slow-release palm fertilizer high in magnesium and manganese to maintain the deep green frond color.

common_name: Ribbon Orchid (Long-Petaled Bulbophyllum, Whip Orchid, Long-Sepal Bulbophyllum)
plant_note: Grow mounted on cork or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct morning light with high humidity; Bulbophyllum longissimum is grown for the extraordinary length of its lateral sepals — flowers on well-grown specimens produce thread-like sepal extensions 8–12 inches (sometimes to 20 cm) long that hang from the flower in whip-like filaments. The flowers are pale yellow to cream with pink to purple spotting and the long sepal threads, which wave gently in air movement. The inflorescence itself is only 3–4 inches in main flower size, but the hanging filaments create a dramatically different visual impact. Intermediate to warm temperatures. The flowers have a mild unpleasant odor for the first few days. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on cork bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct light with good humidity and air movement — Ribbon Orchid is one of the most extraordinary of the long-sepal Bulbophyllum species and is grown entirely for the remarkable visual effect of its hanging, whip-like lateral sepal filaments. Bulbophyllum longissimum is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Thailand, Malaysia, and the Malay Peninsula — one of a distinctive group of Bulbophyllum species (section Cirrhopetalum or Cirrhopetalum alliance) in which the lateral sepals of the flowers are extended into long, thread-like filaments that can reach extraordinary lengths. In B. longissimum, the lateral sepal extensions are particularly dramatic: in well-grown specimens, these filaments reach 8–12 inches (to 20+ cm), hanging from the flower in graceful, whip-like threads that wave in the slightest air movement. The flower itself is 3–4 inches in the main sepal-and-petal body — pale yellow to cream with irregular pink to purple spotting — and the thread filaments emerge from the tips of the lateral sepals. The single-flower (or occasionally 2-flower) inflorescences emerge on short stems from the base of the pseudobulbs. The visual effect of several flowers in bloom simultaneously — each with its pair of long, waving white threads hanging from the flower body — is unique and unforgettable among orchids. The flowers produce a mild, unpleasant odor for the first 1–3 days of blooming to attract fly pollinators, then the odor dissipates. An extraordinary orchid for collectors interested in unusual flower forms. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on well-drained to moist, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil; rice button aster self-sows prolifically once established and tolerates a wide range of soil moisture from moist meadows to moderately dry areas. It spreads by rhizomes to form colonies in appropriate conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; rice button aster is one of the most floriferous and adaptable of the native fall asters, producing clouds of tiny white to pale lavender flowers with yellow centers (the disk turns reddish with age) from late August through November on much-branched, bushy stems. The individual flowers are noticeably small — about the size of a grain of rice — but they are produced in such enormous numbers that a single plant in full bloom appears to be covered in a white mist. This is one of the most important late-season nectar plants in the Southeast, attracting dozens of bee species, butterflies, and other pollinators when few other wildflowers remain in bloom. The abundant seeds feed songbirds into winter. Native across the entire eastern US from the Gulf Coast to New England, it is reliably adapted to zone 9a gardens.

plant_note: Divide suckers in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost danger has passed; rice paper plant spreads by underground stolons and requires ample space — allow 6–8 feet on all sides. Cut to ground after frost in zone 8; it rebounds vigorously from the root.
directions: Divide underground stolons or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; rice paper plant (Chinese rice paper plant) is a bold, dramatic Asian shrub that produces some of the largest leaves of any hardy to zone 8 plant — enormous, deeply lobed, palmate leaves that can reach 3 feet or more across on stems that rise to 6–15 feet, creating an instantly tropical, jungle-like effect with no equivalent in temperate gardening. The felted undersides of the leaves provide a contrasting silver-gray texture. The traditional Chinese paper used for making rice paper paintings is made from the pith of the stems. It spreads steadily by underground stolons to form expanding colonies, which can be managed by mowing around the perimeter; this spreading habit also makes it excellent for covering large areas. In zone 8, top growth is killed by frost but the plant rebounds from underground stolons vigorously each spring, often reaching 8–10 feet by summer. 'Steroidal Giant' is a selection with even larger leaves.

common_name: Ring of Fire Sunflower (Bicolor Red-and-Gold Branching Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Ring of Fire is a branching, pollen-free bicolor sunflower with rings of deep burgundy-red at the petal base fading to golden-yellow tips, a striking bicolor pattern popular for cut-flower arrangements.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches for good branching. Ring of Fire produces striking bicolor blooms with a deep burgundy-red ring at the base of each petal fading outward to bright golden-yellow tips, creating a fiery, sunset-like halo effect that stands out clearly from single-toned sunflower varieties. As a branching type, each plant produces multiple flowers over an extended harvest window rather than a single bloom, making it productive for both garden display and cut-flower use, and the flowers are pollen-free, keeping arrangements and clothing free of the yellow pollen standard sunflowers shed. Deadhead or harvest spent blooms to encourage continued branching and flowering through the season. Grow in full sun with support in windy sites, since the branching habit and multiple large flowers can make plants somewhat top-heavy.
