plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; self-sows moderately in open disturbed ground.
directions: Rothrock's Knapweed is a native annual or biennial of mountain meadows, roadsides, and open disturbed ground in Arizona, New Mexico, and adjacent Mexico — one of the few Centaurea species native to the southwestern United States. It produces showy, rose-purple, thistle-like composite flower heads on branching stems from summer through fall, attracting native bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Unlike many knapweeds in the genus, this native species is non-invasive and ecologically appropriate for southwestern US gardens. Direct sow in spring after last frost in dry, well-drained, lean soil in full sun; plants self-sow moderately and establish naturally in open, rocky, or disturbed ground.

common_name: Rotunda Holly (Dwarf Chinese Holly, Mounding Chinese Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter through spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rotunda is a sterile male clone and does not produce berries — it is grown purely for its compact mounding form and dark-green foliage.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rotunda is one of the most widely planted compact foundation shrubs in the Gulf South — a male Chinese holly selection with a dense, rounded, mounding form that stays compact (2–4 feet tall, slightly wider) without the frequent pruning that many other Chinese holly cultivars require to maintain shape. Rotunda does not produce berries (it is a sterile male clone) and is grown purely for its clean, dark-green, heavily spined foliage and reliable, slow-growing mounded form. The extremely sharp, multiple-spined leaves make Rotunda an outstanding security planting under windows and along boundaries — the spines deter entry more effectively than most other barrier plants. Despite the spiny leaves, Rotunda is one of the most versatile, trouble-free foundation shrubs in the Gulf South: it tolerates heavy clay, drought, heat, partial shade, and the year-round humidity without significant pest or disease pressure. In typical residential foundation plantings, Rotunda maintains a clean, tight mound for years with minimal to no pruning — a significant advantage over faster-growing hollies that require aggressive trimming 2–3 times per season. Deer-resistant; essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; sunflowers grow best sown where they will bloom.
directions: This stunning true-red sunflower blooms on multi-branching plants, offering a dramatic accent in beds, borders, and bouquets. Sow seed directly into warm soil after frost, spacing plants closer together for longer stems and smaller flowers ideal for cutting. Full sun and steady moisture produce the best display. Cut stems just before the flowers fully open for the longest vase life. Successive sowings extend the bloom season into fall.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; rough blazing star requires cold stratification for reliable germination and grows from a corm — established corms can also be planted in spring 2–3 inches deep; avoid rich or clay-heavy soils that cause crown rot.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy, loamy, or rocky soil in full sun; rough blazing star is among the most drought-tolerant Liatris species, native to the dry prairies, open woodlands, and rocky glades of the central United States from North Dakota south to Texas and east to Ohio, where it thrives in the kind of lean, dry, well-drained soils where L. spicata fails. Liatris aspera grows from a rounded corm and produces a slender, rough-textured (aspera = rough) stem bearing alternate, linear to lance-shaped leaves and, from August through October, a spike of rounded, button-like, rosy-lavender to pink-purple flower heads with slightly fringed bracts — unlike the more densely spiked L. spicata and L. pycnostachya, the heads are spaced somewhat apart along the spike, giving it a looser, more open appearance; like all Liatris, flowers open from the top of the spike downward. It is an exceptional pollinator plant for migrating monarch butterflies in late summer and fall, and is also heavily visited by native bumblebees, sweat bees, skipper butterflies, and cloudless sulphur; the dried seed heads are eaten by goldfinches and American tree sparrows. Rough blazing star is an excellent choice for dry, lean, native meadow plantings, prairie restorations, and rock gardens where it out-competes weeds once established.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; rough maidenhair fern is more drought tolerant than most adiantums and better adapted to humid subtropical conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rough maidenhair fern is broadly adapted and heat-tolerant, native to tropical Africa, Asia, and Australia, and far better suited to humid subtropical conditions of zone 8-11 than the delicate northern maidenhair fern. New fronds emerge in shades of coppery-pink or bronze before maturing to bright fresh green. The distinctive palmate frond arrangement with leaflets resembling a spread hand is elegant and recognizable. More tolerant of occasional dryness than other maidenhair ferns, making it more forgiving in garden conditions where desiccation is a common maidenhair killer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification over winter; seeds require a cold, moist period to break dormancy reliably in spring.
directions: A native perennial prickly poppy of dry, rocky slopes, canyon walls, and disturbed open ground in the Rocky Mountains and Great Plains; more persistently perennial than annual Argemone species; produces white, tissue-paper-textured flowers 2-3 inches across on densely spiny, branching stems with blue-gray, deeply lobed, spine-tipped leaves. The yellowish sap is toxic. Direct sow in fall in rocky, very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived. Excellent for rocky slopes and xeriscape gardens in zones 4-9.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; rough rosinweed grows in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, open prairie and savanna soils. Develops a deep taproot over years; best sown directly where it is to grow permanently.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rough rosinweed is a drought-tolerant native Silphium of open prairies, dry savannas, and open woodlands across the southeastern US, producing multiple-branched stems with numerous yellow daisy flowers in summer. The stiffly rough, sandpaper-textured leaves give the plant a tactile distinctiveness. Like all rosinweeds, it produces a resinous, aromatic sap and develops a deep taproot that makes established plants very drought tolerant and also nearly impossible to transplant. Direct sow is strongly preferred over transplanting for this species. The seeds are highly attractive to goldfinches and other finches in late summer and fall. A mid-to-tall native prairie plant providing excellent structural interest and wildlife food in naturalistic gardens.

subcategory: South American tropical spiral ginger ornamental
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Rough Spiral Flag is a tall, tropical spiral ginger from the lowland rainforests of Central and South America — bearing rough-textured, spirally arranged leaves on tall canes and distinctive, elongated red-orange bracts with yellow flowers — one of the taller and more architectural of the cultivated Costus species.
directions: Plant Costus scaber divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; provide consistent moisture throughout the warm season and protect from temperatures below 40°F; cut old canes to the ground after they finish blooming and new shoots will emerge from the base; divide clumps every 2–3 years. Rough Spiral Flag is named for the distinctively rough, slightly sandpapery texture of its large, spirally arranged leaves — a texture that sets it apart visually from the smoother-leaved Costus species. The elongated red-orange to brick-red bracts with yellow flowers create a more narrow, torch-like shape than the rounder cones of Costus spicatus. Native to tropical lowland forests and forest margins in Central and South America, it prefers warm, humid conditions in partial shade — making it better adapted to deeply tropical zone 10–12 gardens than the more cold-hardy C. spicatus. Young leaf shoots and tender stem tips of several Costus species, including C. scaber, have been used as edible vegetables by Indigenous peoples throughout their range in tropical America, cooked as pot herbs or eaten raw as salad greens. The plant provides a bold, architectural tropical statement in the garden throughout the warm months and is particularly effective when massed under the canopy of large shade trees.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; rough-leaf hydrangea blooms on old wood — avoid pruning in fall or spring, trimming only immediately after flowering if needed.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; rough-leaf hydrangea is a large, bold-textured shrub from Asia that differs dramatically from the common mophead and lacecap hydrangeas — it produces enormous, velvety, felted leaves up to 10 inches long on stout stems covered with coarse hairs, giving the plant a distinctly tropical, textural quality. The large lacecap flower heads in midsummer bear pale lavender to purple fertile flowers surrounded by white to soft pink sterile ray flowers in a classic lacecap pattern, but on a much larger scale than Hydrangea macrophylla. The combination of the huge, rough-textured foliage and the lacecap flowers makes it an outstanding architectural shrub for woodland shade gardens. It performs better than mophead hydrangeas in zone 7–9 heat and humidity. The subspecies and cultivar 'Macrophylla' (also called villosa hydrangea) is the most widely grown selection. Provide consistent moisture and protection from drying winds.

plant_note: Plant rooted suckers or container plants in fall or early spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; roughleaf dogwood is remarkably adaptable to both dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the southern plains and the moist, acidic soils of eastern woodlands.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — roughleaf dogwood is a tough, suckering native shrub or small multi-stem tree of southern woodlands, thickets, and stream edges, producing flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by pea-sized, creamy-white berries on red pedicels in late summer that are among the most intensely sought fruits by migrating songbirds. The rough-textured, opposite leaves turn attractive shades of maroon and wine-red in fall. It spreads by root suckers to form dense, multi-stem thickets that provide outstanding cover and food for wildlife year-round. Adaptable to dry, rocky, alkaline conditions unusual among dogwoods — an outstanding native for difficult southern sites where flowering dogwood (C. florida) struggles. Prune out oldest stems periodically to maintain vigor and an open, attractive form.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in bright indirect light to part shade; orbifolia calathea requires high humidity and consistent moisture and is intolerant of dry air, direct sun, fluoride, or salt in irrigation water — filtered or distilled water is recommended.
directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in bright indirect light with high humidity; use filtered or distilled water — calatheas are sensitive to fluoride and mineral salts in tap water. Goeppertia orbifolia (round leaf calathea, formerly Calathea orbifolia) is considered by many collectors to be the most beautiful of all prayer plants — a Bolivian tropical producing enormous (12–18 inch across), perfectly round, broadly oval leaves with an exquisitely regular pattern of alternating light silver-green and deeper green stripes of equal width radiating from the midrib, creating a silvered, two-toned effect unlike any other plant. Like all calatheas and prayer plants, the leaves fold upward in the evening ('prayer plant' motion) and open again in the morning — a nyctinastic movement driven by changes in light and temperature. In the home, orbifolia requires high humidity (50%+), bright indirect light (no direct sun), consistently moist but well-drained soil, and fluoride-free water to thrive. In zones 11–12, it can grow outdoors in shade gardens in the tropics. The plant is relatively slow-growing and may need 2–3 years to reach its impressive mature size.

plant_note: Plant fibrous root divisions in fall in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich, stony woodland soil in deep shade. Round-Lobed Hepatica tolerates somewhat drier, sandier, and more acidic soils than Sharp-Lobed Hepatica and is often found in drier oak-hickory woods.
directions: Round-Lobed Hepatica is a beloved native wildflower of eastern North American forests, producing delicate flowers ranging from white through pink to lavender and blue in late winter to very early spring, often blooming while snow still lingers around its base and becoming one of the first wildflowers to greet emerging bees and butterflies each year. The three-lobed, mottled green and reddish leaves remain evergreen through winter as a low basal rosette, distinguished from the closely related Sharp-Lobed Hepatica by the rounded (obtuse) tips of its three leaf lobes and its preference for drier, more acidic, sandy or stony soils in drier oak-hickory forest rather than the rich, base-rich soils of beech-maple forest. A long-lived perennial of extraordinary persistence — individual plants may live for decades — Round-Lobed Hepatica is best established from fall-planted divisions and takes 2–3 years to settle into its permanent location before flowering reliably each spring. Plant in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in deep shade under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination or divide established rhizomatous colonies in spring; round-leaf ragwort grows naturally in moist to well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade in deciduous woodland settings.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; round-leaf ragwort is one of the most useful shade-tolerant native groundcovers of the eastern woodland, with attractive, rounded, evergreen basal leaves that persist year-round and bright yellow daisy-like flowers in early spring — providing crucial early-season nectar when few other flowers are open. The plant spreads by rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing mat in moist, shaded conditions. A superb native lawn substitute or ground layer plant under deciduous trees where it combines evergreen winter foliage interest with important early spring pollinator value. The early flowers are a critical nectar source for queen bumblebees and early mining bees emerging in late winter. One of the best native shade groundcovers for the entire eastern region in zones 4–9.

plant_note: Plant divisions in late summer to early fall in acidic, humus-rich woodland soil with established mycorrhizal networks; pyrola is extremely difficult to establish and transplants should be moved with as much native soil and fungal associations intact as possible.
directions: Plant divisions in late summer in deep shade beneath conifers or mixed woodland, in acidic, humus-rich soil that already supports mycorrhizal fungi; pyrola is obligately mycorrhizal and will fail in any site lacking established fungal networks. Pyrola rotundifolia produces a low rosette of glossy, rounded evergreen leaves that persist through winter, then sends up a slender spike 10-18 inches tall in summer bearing waxy, fragrant white bell-shaped flowers closely resembling lily-of-the-valley. This native wildflower of cool North American and Eurasian forests is one of the most challenging woodland plants to establish and is best acquired from a reputable native plant nursery rather than wild-collected.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; roundhead bush clover fixes nitrogen and thrives in poor, infertile soil — avoid rich, moist conditions which produce excessive, floppy growth. It develops a deep taproot and is difficult to transplant once established; site carefully.
directions: Direct-sow scarified seeds in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; roundhead bush clover is a tall, upright native prairie legume producing dense, rounded, button-like flower heads of small white pea flowers with purple markings in July and August — the spherical, dense heads clustered at intervals along stiff, silver-hairy stems giving the plant its common name. The deeply divided, trifoliate, silver-silky leaves are attractive all season. After flowering, the heads develop into dense, silvery-tan, persistent seed clusters that remain on the upright stems through winter, providing both ornamental structure in the winter landscape and critically important food for wildlife: the seeds are eaten by quail, turkey, pheasants, songbirds, and small mammals and are considered one of the highest-value native wildlife food plants of the eastern prairie. A nitrogen-fixer adapted to dry, lean, infertile soils where the usual prairie companions (big bluestem, coneflowers, black-eyed Susan) also thrive.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sowing into dry, calcareous or rocky, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Roundhead Prairie Clover is a native perennial of dry rocky and calcareous prairies, limestone glades, and open hills from Kansas south to Texas and east to Alabama, distinguished from other prairie clovers by its rounded (rather than cylindrical) flower heads of small white blooms with striking orange anthers. Plant in dry, lean, well-drained calcareous or sandy soil in full sun; scarify seeds before fall direct sowing to improve germination rates. The finely divided, pinnate, gray-green foliage remains attractive even when the plant is not in bloom. It provides important nectar and pollen for specialist native bees of the Great Plains and south-central prairies and is very drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained to moderately dry, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; roundleaf alumroot is one of the most drought-tolerant heucheras and thrives in lean, rocky soils on western slopes and canyon walls where other heucheras fail.
directions: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained to moderately dry, average to poor, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; roundleaf alumroot is one of the most drought-tolerant heucheras and thrives in lean, rocky soils on western slopes and canyon walls where other heucheras fail. Heuchera cylindrica is a native of western mountain cliffs, rocky slopes, and open woodlands from British Columbia to California, with large, rounded, scalloped, maple-shaped leaves and distinctive, tall, slender, cylindrical spikes of greenish-white to cream flowers with no petals but showy creamy-tan calyces in late spring; it is the parent species of several garden hybrids. In the garden it is outstanding in dry shade, rocky walls, and xeric borders in zones 3–8 and is a useful companion to the more ornamental hybrid heucheras where its structural flower spikes provide textural interest.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; roundleaf greenbrier is the most common greenbrier of moist woodlands and thicket edges in eastern North America. It forms dense, thorny, impenetrable tangles that are valuable as wildlife habitat but must be sited carefully in gardens.
directions: Plant in moist to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun for wildlife habitat restoration in naturalistic settings; roundleaf greenbrier is the most widespread and familiar Smilax species of eastern North American woodlands, forming nearly impenetrable thickets of stout, thorny, green-barked stems along forest edges, thicket margins, and disturbed moist areas. The rounded, shiny green leaves with prominent parallel veining are distinctive, remaining deep green through summer before turning a dull yellow in fall. The blue-black berry clusters persist through winter and are among the most important winter food sources for mockingbirds, catbirds, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and wild turkeys. Dense greenbrier thickets serve as critical nesting habitat, providing protection from predators that avoids entering the thorny tangles. Young shoots are eaten in spring. A foundational wildlife plant for large naturalized areas, woodland restorations, and edge habitats.

plant_note: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean, acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; roundleaf tick trefoil is one of the few native nitrogen-fixing legumes adapted to dry shade conditions.
directions: Sow direct in spring in well-drained, lean, acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; roundleaf tick trefoil is adapted to dry, acidic, shaded conditions and is one of the very few nitrogen-fixing native plants that will grow well in dry, poor, shaded soils. Desmodium rotundifolium is a prostrate, mat-forming native perennial of dry oak and pine woods in eastern North America; unlike most desmodiums which are upright, this species lies flat on the ground with very long, trailing stems bearing rounded, velvety, trifoliate leaves (giving rise to the species name) and producing small, pink-purple, pea-like flowers in mid-summer that are visited by specialist bumblebees. The seed pods cling tenaciously to clothing and animal fur (the "stick-tight" quality that gives tick trefoil its name), aiding dispersal; it is the larval food plant of several skippers and grey hairstreak butterflies. Useful as a shade groundcover in native oak woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Route 66 produces striking golden-yellow flowers with a bold burgundy-red central splash that intensifies as the bloom ages, giving each flower a distinctive pinwheel-like pattern.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Route 66 is a bold bicolor coreopsis cultivar producing bright yellow flowers marked with a distinctive burgundy-red central splash that spreads and intensifies as each bloom matures, giving individual flowers on the same plant a range of patterning from mostly yellow to nearly half red. It blooms over a long summer season and, like other coreopsis, tolerates heat, drought, and lean soil with ease once established, making it a low-maintenance choice for a sunny border or mass planting. Deadheading spent flowers encourages continued bloom, and dividing congested clumps every few years in spring helps maintain the plant's vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; soak seed first.
directions: The Royal series offers a majestic mix of colors with larger flowers and better heat tolerance for a longer bloom period than most sweet peas. Soak the seed, then sow directly in very early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, since they love cool weather. Provide a trellis, fence, or netting for the climbing vines. Keep them well watered and cut frequently to prolong flowering. The fragrant blooms lure pollinators and perfume the house when brought indoors.

common_name: Royal Candles Veronica (Compact Long-Blooming Blue Speedwell)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Royal Candles produces dense, upright spikes of true blue flowers over a long summer season and reblooms readily if sheared after the first flush.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Royal Candles is a compact, sterile veronica selection producing exceptionally dense, upright spikes of vivid true-blue flowers over a long bloom season from late spring into summer, one of the truest blue colors available among perennial spike flowers. Being sterile, it never sets seed and instead channels its energy into continuous new flower spikes, and shearing spent spikes after the first flush encourages a strong rebloom later in the season. It forms a tidy, mounding clump that rarely needs division, tolerates average garden soil well, and draws bees readily, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for the front to middle of a sunny border.

plant_note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Press the tiny seed onto the soil surface without covering, since it needs light to sprout. This heirloom sweet alyssum forms a low, spreading carpet of honey-scented violet-purple blooms. Grow it in full sun to light shade as an edging, container filler, or ground cover among vegetables to draw beneficial insects. Shear lightly after the first flush to encourage a fresh round of bloom into cooler weather.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; royal catchfly resents clay and wet soils — excellent drainage is critical. The plant blooms the second year from seed and is very long-lived once established.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; royal catchfly is a spectacular native Midwestern prairie catchfly with intensely vivid, cardinal-red, five-petaled flowers with deeply notched petals that appear on branching stems from June through August — the color is among the most brilliant scarlet-red available in a hardy native perennial. Ruby-throated hummingbirds are powerfully attracted to the flowers and are the primary pollinators. The plant requires excellent drainage and will not tolerate wet or heavy clay soil; it thrives in typical rocky Midwestern prairie conditions. It is considered a rare plant in the wild and is declining across its native range — garden cultivation helps preserve the species. An outstanding plant for hot, dry, rocky prairie gardens and hummingbird borders. Combines beautifully with native prairie dropseed, little bluestem, and wild bergamot in dry, naturalistic plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; royal fern is an ideal choice for pond margins, stream banks, and boggy areas where it may eventually reach 6 feet in height.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun at pond margins, stream banks, and bog garden edges; royal fern is the most massive and architecturally bold of the temperate ferns, eventually forming vase-shaped clumps 4–6 feet tall with large, compound fronds that look more like a tropical plant than a typical fern. The fertile fronds bear distinctive brown, tassel-like spore clusters at their tips from late spring through summer. The unfurling cinnamon-brown croziers (fiddleheads) in spring are edible when young and delicate. The plant is long-lived, building over many decades into a substantial clump with a fibrous rootball of accumulated peaty root material. The closely related cinnamon fern (O. cinnamomea) has very similar requirements.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; royal paulownia is extremely fast-growing — potentially the fastest-growing hardwood tree in temperate cultivation. Self-sows abundantly and is listed as invasive in many eastern US states — remove seed capsules before they open to control spread.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; royal paulownia is the larger-flowered Chinese species of paulownia — a massive, fast-growing tree with enormous heart-shaped leaves (up to 18 inches) and spectacular large, fragrant, pale lilac-white, foxglove-shaped flowers in early spring (before the leaves emerge). The flowers are larger and paler in color than those of the more commonly planted princess tree (Paulownia tomentosa). One of the world's fastest-growing hardwood trees, capable of 10–20 feet of growth in the first year from seed and 8–15 feet per year subsequently in ideal conditions. The exceptionally light, strong, rot-resistant wood dries rapidly without warping and is highly valued in Japan (where it's called kiri) for making chests, musical instruments (koto), and wooden sandals. Produces billions of tiny seeds from its large, oval seed capsules — be vigilant about removing seed pods before they open to prevent invasive spread in moist eastern US forests where it has naturalized. More heat-tolerant than princess tree.

plant_note: Scarify seeds by nicking the seed coat or soaking in hot water (not boiling) for 24 hours before planting; or plant nursery transplants in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun. Royal Poinciana is intolerant of frost, heavy clay soil, and poor drainage.
directions: Royal Poinciana is widely considered the most spectacular flowering tree in the world, native to the dry deciduous forests of Madagascar and now naturalized throughout the tropics and subtropics, producing in late spring and summer an overwhelming canopy of enormous, brilliant scarlet-orange flowers with yellow-tipped petals that can completely conceal the wide-spreading, umbrella-shaped crown — a display so vivid that the tree is visible from miles away. The fine, bipinnate, ferny foliage provides delicate shade during the non-flowering months, and the dark brown seed pods (up to 2 feet long) persist through winter, rattling in the wind. In zones 10–11 it is reliably perennial, and in favorable coastal conditions may be semi-evergreen; it is killed to the ground by even light frost and therefore confined to South Florida, the Florida Keys, and other subtropical areas in the continental US. Grows extremely fast — up to 5 feet per year in good conditions — but needs 5–10 years to reach first flowering. Provide well-drained soil, full sun, and space for its wide-spreading roots and canopy.

common_name: Royal Purple Smokebush (Classic Deep Purple Foliage Smoke Tree)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Royal Purple produces deep wine-purple foliage all season and airy, smoke-like plumes of tiny flowers in summer that give smokebush its common name.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, where drainage is excellent; smokebush dislikes heavy, wet soil. Royal Purple is the classic, most widely planted dark-leaved smokebush cultivar, producing rounded, deep wine-purple leaves throughout the growing season, often shifting to fiery orange-red in fall, combined with airy, wispy, pinkish-purple flower and seed plumes in summer that create the smoky, cloud-like haze giving the plant its common name. It is highly drought-tolerant once established and tolerates poor, lean soil better than rich, moist conditions, which can promote weak, floppy growth. Prune in late winter if a more compact, densely foliaged shrub is wanted, since hard pruning sacrifices the smoky flower plumes that year but produces larger, bolder leaves.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled shade; Royal Standard is one of the most heat-tolerant hostas and performs better in zone 8–9 than most cultivars, particularly when given consistent moisture and morning sun with afternoon shade.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Royal Standard is an exceptional hosta combining fragrance, heat tolerance, and adaptability in a single reliable cultivar — it produces large, glossy, bright-green, heart-shaped leaves and, in late summer, pure white, intensely fragrant funnel-shaped flowers that perfume the evening garden. It is a hybrid of H. plantaginea that inherits the species' notable heat and sun tolerance, making it one of the best hostas for zone 7–9 gardens where many blue-leafed cultivars decline in summer heat. Royal Standard will tolerate more sun than most hostas as long as soil moisture is maintained, even growing in quite open shade near the edge of the woodland garden. The outstanding fragrance of the late-summer flowers makes it an invaluable plant near sitting areas, patios, and paths where the evening scent can be enjoyed. Divide every 4–5 years when the central crown begins to decline.

common_name: Royal Star Magnolia (Large White Star Magnolia)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped plants in late winter or very early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0), fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; the later-blooming nature of Royal Star relative to other star magnolias reduces the risk of frost damage to the open flowers.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Royal Star is the premier star magnolia cultivar — selected for flowers significantly larger and with more petals (25–30 tepals per flower) than the standard Magnolia stellata species (12–18 tepals), creating a fuller, more sumptuous floral display in late winter to early spring. The flowers are pure white, intensely fragrant with a light vanilla-rose scent, and open from fuzzy silver-gray buds in late February through March (in zone 7–8) before any foliage appears — the bare branches covered with star-shaped, multi-petaled white flowers creating one of the most beautiful early spring floral spectacles of any woody plant. Royal Star also blooms approximately one week later than the species — a practical advantage since the open flowers of star magnolia are frequently damaged by late frosts in zone 4–7. The later bloom timing extends the frost-free blooming window significantly. Magnolia stellata and Royal Star are naturally slow-growing, multi-stemmed shrubs to small trees reaching 10–15 feet over many decades. In zone 9, star magnolia blooms very early but may struggle in the hottest, most humid portions — it performs best in zone 5–8 and in the cooler microclimates of zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Rozanne blooms almost continuously from late spring until frost with essentially no deadheading required, unlike most hardy geraniums that flower in a single flush.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Named the Perennial Plant of the Year in 2008, Rozanne is widely considered the best hardy geranium ever introduced, producing large, violet-blue, white-centered flowers almost nonstop from late spring through the first hard frost, far surpassing the brief single bloom flush typical of most cranesbill geraniums. The sprawling, mounding habit weaves attractively through and under other perennials without being aggressive, and the plant is sterile, so it never becomes weedy from self-seeding. In the heat of a zone 9 summer it appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture to keep flowering strong; otherwise it needs almost no care beyond an occasional light trim to keep the mound tidy.

common_name: Rubber Tree (Rubber Plant, Indian Rubber Fig)
plant_note: Grow as a large container or houseplant in zone 9 — Rubber Tree is frost-tender and cannot survive temperatures below 40°F outdoors. In zone 10-11, plant outdoors in partial shade with well-drained soil and room for the massive root system. When moving indoor plants outdoors in spring, acclimatize gradually over 2 weeks to prevent sunburn. The milky latex sap is a severe skin irritant and toxic if ingested — wear gloves when pruning. Repot every 2 years in spring.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light to part shade — Rubber Tree adapts to a wide range of light conditions from low indoor light to outdoor filtered sun, but grows fastest and develops the deepest foliage color in bright, indirect light. Ficus elastica is a tropical tree native to India (Assam, Meghalaya) and Malaysia that grows into a massive 100-foot banyan-form tree in its native habitat, producing aerial roots that descend to form additional trunks — in Indian forests, single trees can span an enormous area. In cultivation worldwide, it is one of the most popular large houseplants and patio container trees, prized for its large (8–12 inch), thick, glossy, dark green leaves that give the plant a bold, tropical presence. The standard green 'Decora' and 'Robusta' cultivars are joined by dark red-burgundy 'Burgundy' (nearly black leaves in high light), cream-edged 'Tineke', and the highly popular tri-color 'Ruby' (pink, green, and cream variegated). In zone 10-11 landscapes, planted outdoors it grows into a large canopy tree eventually. The common name refers to the milky latex sap — exploited commercially before the rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) replaced it as the primary natural rubber source in the 19th century. CAUTION: Sap is a serious skin and eye irritant; all parts toxic if eaten.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in average soil; overly rich soil reduces blooms.
directions: This Fleuroselect award winner bears deeply colored three-inch blooms that open red-wine and age to dusty rose, striking against white flowers and silver foliage. Sow directly after frost into average, well-drained soil, as rich soil produces foliage at the expense of flowers. Full sun and modest water suit it best; it is drought tolerant once established. Deadhead to prolong bloom or leave a few seed heads to self-sow. Butterflies flock to the flowers, which also cut well.

common_name: Ruby Falls Redbud (Weeping Purple-Leaf Dwarf Redbud)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ruby Falls combines a weeping, cascading form with deep purple foliage and a truly dwarf size, making it one of the most useful redbud cultivars for small gardens and container culture.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, siting where its weeping branches can cascade freely. Ruby Falls combines two desirable redbud traits rarely found together — the deep, rich purple foliage of Forest Pansy and the graceful, cascading branch structure of a weeping cultivar — on a genuinely dwarf tree that typically stays under 10 feet tall, considerably smaller than most purple-leaf redbud selections. In early spring, the weeping branches are studded with the species' typical rosy-pink, pea-like flowers before heart-shaped, glossy purple leaves emerge and hold their color well into summer. Its small mature size and weeping form make it an excellent specimen for a small garden, foundation planting, or large container, where its cascading habit and dark foliage stand out against lighter-colored companions. Provide afternoon shade in zone 8-9 to help the purple foliage resist summer fading and scorch, and plant in well-drained soil since redbud roots are prone to rot in wet sites. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.

plant_note: Direct sow seed or plant container-grown plants after the last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; ruby grass grows rapidly in heat and begins blooming within 60–90 days of germination. In zone 9–10 it self-sows to overwinter; in colder zones it is grown as a summer annual.
directions: Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun; ruby grass (Melinis nerviglumis 'Savannah') is one of the most spectacular ornamental grasses available for summer color, producing fluffy, shimmering panicles of tiny spikelets in brilliant shades of ruby-red, rose-pink, and burgundy that catch the light and glow with exceptional luminosity — particularly beautiful in the late afternoon sun when the entire plant appears to be lit from within. The fine-textured, narrow, reddish-tinged leaves complement the flowers perfectly. It begins blooming in early summer and continues through frost, and the dried seed heads add winter interest. Unlike many ornamental grasses, it blooms all season rather than just in fall. As a tender tropical grass, it is grown as a perennial in zone 9–11 and as a summer annual in colder zones, where it self-sows freely in mild winters. Excellent in mixed borders, containers, and as a seasonal accent plant wherever summer color is needed.

common_name: Ruby Loropetalum (Compact Deep-Purple Foliage Gulf South Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Ruby maintains the most intense burgundy-purple foliage color in full sun — partial shade causes the foliage to turn more greenish-purple in color.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Ruby is a compact Loropetalum chinense (Chinese fringe flower) cultivar producing deep, rich burgundy-purple to reddish-purple evergreen foliage throughout the year, punctuated by prolific flushes of bright magenta-pink, fringe-petaled flowers that create a vivid burgundy-and-magenta combination in spring (March–April) and sporadic rebloom through fall. At 4–6 feet with a similar spread, Ruby is one of the most manageable Loropetalum cultivars for typical residential borders and foundation plantings — the compact, rounded habit is more landscape-appropriate than the large-growing species which can reach 10–15 feet. The deep burgundy foliage holds its rich purple color well through the Gulf South summer without the greening that affects some purple-leaf shrubs in high heat. Loropetalum tolerates considerable drought once established and handles the acidic, often clay soils of the Gulf South coast without significant amendment. The spring bloom is one of the showiest shrub floral displays of the Gulf South spring garden — the combination of the bright magenta flowers against the dark burgundy foliage is visually stunning. Minimal maintenance required: prune immediately after spring bloom to maintain size and shape; avoid late-season pruning that removes flower buds developing for the following spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm; can start indoors 3-4 weeks early.
directions: Grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello, this ornamental vine dazzles with pinkish-purple flowers and shiny dark-purple pods against purple-tinged foliage. Sow directly into warm soil after frost, providing a sturdy fence or trellis for the fast, twining stems to climb. Full sun brings out the richest pod color. Keep it evenly watered through the heat of summer. Note that the raw pods and seeds are toxic and should be treated as ornamental only.

common_name: Ruby Slippers Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dwarf Red-Turning Oakleaf)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; Ruby Slippers is a more compact selection than standard oakleaf hydrangea — staying 3–4 feet tall and wide — selected for its distinctive flower color change from white to deep rose-red as the flowers age.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Ruby Slippers is the most distinctive compact oakleaf hydrangea cultivar — selected not only for its reduced size (3–4 feet, compared to 6–8 feet for the species) but for its exceptional flower color change: the large, conical flower panicles open white in early summer and then turn progressively to deep rose-pink and finally rich ruby-red as they age through summer, providing an extended color display that ranges from pure white in June through rich rose-red by August. This color change from white to red is unique among oakleaf hydrangeas and gives Ruby Slippers a dramatically different appearance from the typical white-only oakleaf cultivars. Like all Hydrangea quercifolia cultivars, Ruby Slippers is a southeastern US native fully adapted to the heat, humidity, clay soils, and shade of the Gulf South — requiring no special care and developing excellent reddish-purple fall foliage color and cinnamon peeling bark for winter interest. The multi-season ornamental qualities, compact size, and distinctive red flower color make Ruby Slippers one of the most celebrated oakleaf hydrangea introductions of the early twenty-first century.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade; Ruby Spice tolerates wet, periodically flooded soils and is an excellent choice for a rain garden or pond-edge planting in dappled shade.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade, though it tolerates more sun with consistently wet soil; keep evenly moist, since summersweet does not tolerate prolonged drought. Ruby Spice is a pink-flowered cultivar of the native summersweet, Clethra alnifolia, bred to hold a deeper, more saturated rose-pink flower color through its whole bloom period than older pink selections, which often fade toward white as the flowers age. In mid-to-late summer, dense, upright, bottlebrush-like flower spikes release an intensely sweet, spicy fragrance that carries well through the garden and draws heavy pollinator traffic from bumblebees, honeybees, and butterflies during a period when many other shrubs have finished blooming. The glossy, dark green foliage turns clear yellow in fall before drop. An outstanding fragrant, pollinator-rich choice for a partly shaded, consistently moist border or woodland-edge planting, zone 4–9.

common_name: Ruby Spider Daylily (Giant Red Late-Season Daylily)
plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ruby Spider produces some of the largest flowers of any daylily cultivar, so give plants ample room and stake tall scapes in windy sites if needed.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ruby Spider is celebrated among daylily growers for its enormous, nine-inch, deep ruby-red flowers with a bright yellow-green throat, among the largest blooms of any widely grown daylily cultivar, held on tall, well-branched scapes in mid-to-late summer. The dramatic flower size and rich color make it a strong focal point in a mixed border even though it flowers for a shorter overall season than modern reblooming types. Like other daylilies it is easy to grow in average soil with routine watering, and mature clumps can be divided every three to four years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Plant tuber divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; rue anemone is a delicate spring ephemeral that goes dormant by early summer — plant with ferns to fill the gap.
directions: Plant small tuber clusters in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; rue anemone goes dormant by early summer, so plant near later-emerging hostas or ferns to cover the gap. Anemonella thalictroides (syn. Thalictrum thalictroides) is a diminutive, ethereal native spring ephemeral of eastern North American woodlands; it emerges in early spring with finely divided, three-lobed, glaucous-blue-green leaves resembling miniature meadow rue and bears small (3/4 inch), white to pale pink, 5–10-petaled flowers on delicate, hair-fine stems from March through May, creating a cloud of floating blossoms just inches above the ground. Despite its delicate appearance, it is surprisingly vigorous and long-lived; it spreads slowly by tuberous roots and forms charming colonies under deciduous trees. A very special native wildflower for collectors and connoisseurs of spring woodland plants.

plant_note: Plant small tuber clusters in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; rue anemone is a spring ephemeral that dies back completely by early summer — mark its location to avoid disturbing it during summer dormancy.
directions: Plant small tuber clusters in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — rue anemone is one of the smallest and most delicate of all eastern woodland spring ephemerals, producing clusters of white to pale pink (rarely deep pink) five-petaled flowers on slender stems only 4–9 inches tall in early spring, just as the forest canopy begins to leaf out. The leaves closely resemble those of meadow rue (Thalictrum), explaining both the common name and the former genus placement. Like all true spring ephemerals it dies back completely by early summer, leaving no trace above ground. It is a slow-growing but extremely long-lived native that gradually forms a charming colony when well-sited. Named varieties like 'Shoaf's Double Pink' and 'Betty Blake' (double white flowers) are available from specialty native plant nurseries. An outstanding native for the shaded wildflower garden, best combined with later-emerging foliage plants to fill in after it goes dormant.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to deep shade; Ruffled Fan Palm is a slow-growing, small, understory palm native to Vanuatu in the Pacific Islands, grown as one of the most ornamental shade-tolerant palms available — producing a crown of dramatically large, undivided (or nearly so), circular, pleated, ruffled fan leaves resembling enormous green parasols, set on slender, elegant trunks.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to deep shade; Licuala grandis requires high humidity, consistent moisture, protection from direct sun and wind, and warm temperatures year-round — the large, undivided leaves shred easily in wind and dry out in low humidity; protect from all frost. Licuala grandis (Ruffled Fan Palm or Vanuatu Fan Palm) is a slow-growing, single-trunked, small understory palm native to the rainforests of Vanuatu in the southwestern Pacific, widely cultivated throughout tropical and subtropical gardens worldwide as one of the most architecturally dramatic small palms available. The defining ornamental feature is the extraordinary leaves: among the largest, most perfectly circular, and most undivided of all fan palm species — each leaf a nearly complete, massive, circular 'parasol' up to 2–3 feet in diameter, pleated like an accordion, ruffled at the margin, and held horizontally on a long petiole atop the slender, ringed trunk. The combination of the rounded, parasol-like leaves and slender, elegant trunk is entirely unique in the palm family. Licuala grandis is adapted to deep forest understory in high humidity and will grow in surprisingly deep shade conditions that defeat most palms — making it invaluable as a shade-garden specimen in tropical zone 10–12 gardens. Water consistently, maintain high humidity (>60%), and fertilize lightly with palm fertilizer monthly during the growing season.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade. Rugel's Trillium is a pedicellate species with strongly reflexed white petals that create a nodding appearance distinct from most other trilliums.
directions: Rugel's Trillium is a rare and distinctive pedicellate trillium native to a limited area in the southern Appalachians of Tennessee, North Carolina, and northern Georgia, where it grows in moist, rich hardwood forest coves and sheltered slopes and blooms in April with three white petals that reflex so strongly backward that they resemble a swept-back cap — an appearance unlike any other eastern trillium. The flower hangs on a short pedicel below the leaf whorl, facing downward and sometimes hidden beneath the foliage, and carries a faint fragrance that attracts small fly pollinators. Listed as a species of conservation concern in several states, Rugel's Trillium should never be collected from wild populations; source only from specialty native plant nurseries propagating their own rhizome divisions. Grow in deep, consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade, mulch generously with leaf litter, and allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally by summer.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inch depth in pure, infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun. Runner Oak requires xeric scrub conditions and will not compete in heavier or more productive soils; the rhizomatous root system means it spreads vigorously once established.
directions: Runner Oak is a low, colony-forming native shrub oak of the coastal plain sandhills and fire-maintained xeric scrub habitats of Georgia and Florida, spreading underground by rhizomes to form dense colonies of knee-high stems across expanses of pure white sand where larger trees cannot survive — making it superficially resemble a grass colony more than a tree. Despite its small stature, Runner Oak produces full-sized acorns that are a critical food source for Florida Scrub-Jays, gopher tortoises, and black bears in the imperiled scrub ecosystem where larger mast-producing oaks may be sparse. Highly adapted to fire, Runner Oak resprouts vigorously from its extensive underground rhizome system within weeks of a scrub burn and is a dominant component of the ground-layer plant community in many Florida scrub sites. Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in infertile, pure, sandy, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun — Runner Oak requires the xeric, open, fire-maintained conditions of native scrub and will not thrive in more productive or shaded environments.

plant_note: Transplant nursery-grown plugs in spring into moderately disturbed, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; cold stratification improves germination if starting from seed.
directions: Running Buffalo Clover is a federally endangered native perennial once widespread across open, disturbed, grassy habitats — woodland edges, forest openings, and bison-grazed clearings — throughout the eastern and central US, now restricted to a small number of conservation sites in West Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, and Missouri. It spreads by stolons in a strawberry-like fashion, forming low mats of trifoliate leaves dotted with small cream-white clover flower heads; its decline is directly tied to the loss of frequent, moderate disturbance from bison grazing. Obtain plants from nurseries specializing in federally listed native species and transplant into moderately disturbed, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; periodic light mowing or disturbance mimics the historic grazing regime that this species depends on.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container divisions in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; avoid hot, dry exposures.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; running strawberry bush is a low-growing native groundcover that spreads by layering its trailing stems wherever they contact moist soil, creating dense weed-suppressing mats beneath trees. The plant is most ornamental in fall when the deeply lobed, strawberry-like orange-red fruits split open to reveal bright orange seeds — a striking display that wildlife relish. Unlike the invasive introduced burning bush (Euonymus alatus), this native species is well-behaved and restricted to shady, moist woodland habitats. Excellent for naturalizing dry to moist shaded slopes where little else will grow.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall; in zone 8–9 plant September–March. Running Tapestry is stoloniferous — it spreads by runners along the soil surface, rooting at nodes to create a weed-suppressing groundcover mat. The name 'Running' distinguishes it from clump-forming Tiarella types. In zone 9 provide consistent moisture and afternoon shade to protect from summer heat stress; mulch heavily to keep roots cool. Not suitable for zone 10+ where summer heat and humidity are too intense.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil with generous organic matter content; Running Tapestry Foamflower (Tiarella cordifolia) is a native North American woodland groundcover perennial that spreads via surface runners to create a dense, weed-suppressing carpet beneath trees and in shaded beds where most plants fail. The deeply lobed, maple-like leaves have distinctive dark burgundy-maroon markings along the veins that provide year-round ornamental interest — the pattern of dark veins against bright green leaves creates the tapestry effect that names this cultivar. In spring (April–June) the plant produces airy spikes of delicate white to pale pink foam-like flowers that rise well above the foliage and are highly attractive to early pollinators. Running Tapestry is one of the finest native shade groundcovers for the eastern and central United States — it naturalizes under deciduous trees, slopes, and shaded rock gardens while suppressing weeds far more effectively than mulch alone. The stoloniferous habit allows it to fill in completely within 2–3 seasons to create a low-maintenance, long-lived perennial groundcover.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, well-drained soil to allow cold stratification; seeds require a period of winter cold to break dormancy.
directions: Rush Skeletonweed is a striking native perennial of the central Great Plains, bearing slender, nearly leafless green rush-like stems that give the plant an unusual skeletal texture and provide excellent ornamental interest in dry and xeric garden designs. From June through September the stems are studded with cheerful lavender-pink, dandelion-type flowers that attract native bees and whose seeds are readily eaten by finches and other small birds. Sow seeds directly in fall into poor, dry, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; this species is exceptionally drought-tolerant and will decline rapidly in wet or clay-heavy conditions. It is best used in prairie restorations, gravel gardens, or alongside other low-water natives where its distinctive habit can be appreciated without overwatering from neighboring plants.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; nick or soak the hard seed coat to aid germination.
directions: This 1937 English selection offers an array of colors on tall dramatic spikes that shine when planted in masses or mixed borders. Nick or soak the hard seed coat, then sow directly in spring or fall, as lupines dislike transplanting their long taproot. They prefer full sun, cool summers, and well-drained, slightly acidic soil. In zones 4 to 7 they are short-lived perennials; in warmer areas grow them as annuals. Remove spent spikes to encourage more blooms and support pollinators.

plant_note: Scarify and soak seed before sowing; resents root disturbance so direct sow when possible.
directions: Nick and soak the hard-coated seed overnight, then sow where plants are to grow since lupines dislike transplanting. This perennial hybrid sends up tall spikes densely packed with pea-like flowers in blue, purple, pink, yellow, and white. Plant in full sun and cool, well-drained soil; as a legume it fixes nitrogen and improves the ground. Cut spent spikes to encourage rebloom and let a few set seed for next season's plants.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Russell's sage is drought-tolerant once established. Do not cut the spent flower stems — the dried, brown whorled stem structures are attractive through winter and provide bird food. Divide clumps every 4–5 years in spring to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Russell's sage is a Turkish native and one of the most structurally interesting and drought-tolerant perennials for the sunny border — forming bold, spreading mounds of large, heart-shaped, rough-textured, wrinkled, gray-green leaves and in June through July producing upright stems carrying whorled tiers of soft, butter-yellow, hooded, sage-like flowers arranged in distinct rings at regular intervals up the stem, creating an architectural, tiered candelabra form. After the flowers fade, the calyx whorls remain on the dried stems through autumn and winter as attractive, rigid, tiered seed structures in warm brown, providing months of winter architectural interest and seeds for finches. The dried winter stems are so decorative that Chelsea Flower Show designers have used them as a winterbourne architectural element in naturalistic plantings. Outstanding for the gravel garden, prairie-style border, and drought-tolerant plantings combined with ornamental grasses and other drought-adapted plants. Visited heavily by bumblebees.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into moist, well-drained soil in a partially sunny woodland glade or forest edge. Surface sow or barely cover seeds, as they need light and cold stratification over winter to germinate reliably in spring.
directions: Russell's Wild Bergamot is a rare and regionally distinctive bee balm native to Ozark glades, open woodlands, and rocky forest edges, where it thrives in well-drained soils with dappled to partial sun. Sow seeds in fall by pressing them lightly onto a prepared soil surface in the planting site, as they benefit from natural cold stratification over winter and will germinate the following spring. Space plants 18 to 24 inches apart to ensure good air circulation, which helps maintain the superior mildew resistance this species displays compared to other Monarda. Once established, plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form clumps and can be divided every few years in spring to rejuvenate the planting and propagate new starts.

plant_note: Plant in spring after last frost in lean, well-drained soil; established plants are extremely drought-tolerant.
directions: Plant in poor to average, sharply drained soil in full sun — Russian sage declines quickly in fertile or moist soil and is highly susceptible to root rot in clay. Cut plants back hard in early spring (to about 6 in) just as new basal growth emerges; do not cut back in fall as the woody framework helps protect the crown. The airy silver stems and lavender-blue flowers create a haze of color from midsummer through fall and are beloved by pollinators. Deer avoid this plant due to its strongly aromatic foliage.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; surface sow as seed needs light.
directions: This Asian wildflower has an unusual spiky habit and rosy color that adds welcome contrast to the landscape and long-lasting cut and dried flowers. Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the surface for light. Transplant into full sun and well-drained soil after frost. It tolerates heat and dry conditions once established. Harvest stems when most of the tiny flowers have opened for the best dried bouquets.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist soil in fall for spring germination, or sow in early spring — seeds require light to germinate and must not be covered with soil. Unlike common foxglove which is biennial, Digitalis ferruginea is typically a short-lived perennial persisting 3–5 years in ideal conditions. It self-sows freely to maintain a permanent colony in the garden.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; rusty foxglove is a tall, refined species from southeastern Europe and Turkey producing exceptionally architectural flower spikes — much more densely packed and finely detailed than common foxglove. The flowers are small (3/4 to 1 inch), closely arranged along the spike, and colored in warm, tawny russet-brown to rusty-orange-cream with intricate darker veining and netting visible inside the tube, giving the whole spike a burnished, antiqued quality from which it takes its name. Unlike common foxglove (Digitalis purpurea), which typically dies after flowering, D. ferruginea is a genuine short-lived perennial persisting 3–5 years in favorable conditions while self-sowing freely to maintain a colony. The upright spikes can reach 4–7 feet in excellent conditions and are extraordinarily architectural in the border. Combines beautifully with ornamental grasses, purple-leafed shrubs, and golden-foliaged plants where the warm rusty flower color finds its best complement.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, highly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Rusty Staggerbush is adapted to the dry, scrubby flatwoods and ridge habitats of the Florida peninsula and coastal plain, and requires excellent drainage to thrive.
directions: Rusty Staggerbush is a coarse-textured evergreen shrub or small tree, native to the dry, sandy, scrubby flatwoods, pine ridges, and xeric hammocks of the Florida peninsula and coastal plain from South Carolina to Alabama, distinguished by its large, leathery leaves with rust-colored (ferruginous) scales on the undersides that give the species its common name. In spring it produces clusters of white to pale pink, urn-shaped flowers typical of the heath family (Ericaceae), which are important nectar sources for native bees; the plant may grow 8–20 feet tall in ideal conditions, forming small trees in open scrub habitats. All parts are toxic if ingested by livestock — the 'staggerbush' name refers to the neurological symptoms caused in cattle that graze the foliage. Grow in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it is drought-tolerant once established and an important component of Florida scrub restoration plantings.

plant_note: Plant small divisions in early spring into crevices or well-drained rocky soil; avoid wet or clay-heavy sites.
directions: Grow in a partly shaded rock garden or on a retaining wall with excellent drainage and a gritty, low-nutrient substrate; avoid rich soils which can cause overly lush growth prone to collapse. Tuck small divisions into crevices filled with a mix of grit and coarse humus, mimicking the alpine outcrops where this fern thrives naturally. Water sparingly once established, as this species is notably drought-tolerant once its roots have anchored into the rock substrate. The distinctive rust-colored hairs on the frond undersides intensify in sunnier exposures, making a partly open site preferable to deep shade.

common_name: Rêve d'Or Rose (Golden Noisette Climbing Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall at the base of a trellis, arbor, or fence; Rêve d'Or is an 1869 Noisette climber descended from roses bred in Charleston, South Carolina, and Noisettes as a class are exceptionally well adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil at the base of a sturdy support, allowing 5-8 feet for its mature spread. Introduced in France in 1869, Rêve d'Or ('dream of gold') is a Noisette climbing rose bearing large, fully double, buff-yellow to apricot blooms with a fruity tea fragrance against handsome, glossy, almost evergreen foliage. The Noisette class originated in Charleston, South Carolina, in the early 1800s from roses bred specifically to handle Southern heat and humidity, and Rêve d'Or carries that heritage, blooming repeatedly from spring through fall with strong disease resistance and minimal care once established. Train the long, relatively thornless canes horizontally along a fence or arbor to encourage the most flowers, since roses bloom more heavily from canes trained near-horizontal than from those left to grow straight up. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to remove spent wood and maintain the desired shape, saving hard structural pruning for full dormancy in winter.

plant_note: Plant in spring in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly alkaline soil in full sun. Avoid clay or organically rich soils; this rose is adapted to hot, dry limestone slopes of the American Southwest.
directions: Establish in a hot, sunny spot with extremely well-drained, gritty or rocky soil; Sacramento Rose is native to desert mountain slopes and is uniquely adapted to alkaline, low-nutrient conditions that would stress most cultivated roses. Its unusual gooseberry-like divided leaves and bristly stems make it visually distinctive even when not in bloom. Water sparingly after the first season — established plants are highly drought-tolerant and resent overwatering. Propagate by taking semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer and rooting them in very gritty, low-fertility compost; seeds benefit from a warm stratification period followed by cold stratification before germination.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 70°F; nick or lightly scarify seeds before sowing to improve germination rates.
directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — leaves, flowers, seeds, and roots contain potent tropane alkaloids (scopolamine, hyoscyamine, atropine) that can cause severe anticholinergic poisoning or death; do not plant where children or pets have unsupervised access and wash hands thoroughly after handling. Datura wrightii is a fast-growing native of the American Southwest and Mexico that produces enormous, sweetly fragrant, white to pale-purple funnel-shaped flowers up to 8 inches across that open at dusk and attract sphinx moths in a spectacular display of night-garden drama. Direct sow lightly scarified seeds into well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; this plant thrives on neglect, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. In zones 8–11 it returns reliably from a deep taproot each spring; in zones 7–8 treat it as a warm-season annual, allowing plants to self-seed for natural reestablishment.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; rohdea tolerates the deepest, driest shade of any ornamental perennial for zone 7–10 and is specifically useful in the most difficult dark corners of the landscape.
directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; rohdea (sacred lily, Nippon lily, omoto) is a Japanese native that has been cultivated and revered in Japan for centuries as a symbol of good fortune and longevity, with thousands of cultivars developed by Japanese enthusiasts — some producing extravagantly variegated, ruffled, crested, or otherwise unusual foliage prized as collector's items. For garden use, the plain species produces handsome, glossy, dark-green, strap-shaped leaves in dense, upright clumps and tolerates extreme shade conditions — including the dark, dry shade under mature trees — that defeat most other evergreen perennials. Inconspicuous spike-like flowers in late spring are followed by brilliant red berries in autumn. Extremely long-lived, drought-tolerant once established, and essentially maintenance-free. An excellent deer-resistant shade plant for zone 7–10 gardens. Berries are toxic.

plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Safrano is an 1839 tea rose long grown in Southern gardens for its saffron-apricot buds, strong tea fragrance, and excellent tolerance of Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-3.5 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1839, Safrano is one of the oldest tea roses still in general cultivation and was long prized for its long, elegant, saffron-orange buds that open to loosely double, apricot-to-buff blooms with a rich, classic tea fragrance — the scent for which the entire tea rose class is named. Like other tea roses it flowers almost continuously from spring to frost, with the buds often considered more beautiful than the fully open bloom, and it shows good resistance to blackspot in the humid Gulf South compared with modern hybrid teas. The lightly arching, twiggy shrub works well in mixed borders or as an informal low hedge. Minimal pruning is needed — remove dead or crossing wood in late winter and avoid hard cutting back, which reduces the flush of bloom.

plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Sagae was named Hosta of the Year in 2000 for its large, upright, vase-shaped clump of blue-green leaves broadly margined in creamy white to gold, one of the most architecturally striking hosta cultivars available.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best margin color. Sagae was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 2000, prized for its distinctive upright, vase-shaped growth habit — unusual among hostas, most of which form low, spreading mounds — with large, glossy, blue-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that often deepens to soft gold as the season progresses. Tall scapes of pale lavender flowers rise well above the foliage in summer. Its architectural, upright form and large mature size make it an excellent specimen or focal point at the back of a shade border, distinct in silhouette from the many mound-forming hosta cultivars. The margin coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic contrast. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; perfect drainage is the primary cultural requirement — sago palms decline rapidly in heavy clay or waterlogged soils. All parts of the plant are extremely toxic to humans and pets — manganese deficiency (yellow fronds) is common in alkaline soils and is treated with chelated manganese.
directions: Plant in very well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; despite the common name, the sago palm is not a true palm but a cycad — one of the oldest surviving plant lineages on Earth, essentially unchanged since the Mesozoic Era. The dramatic, crown of stiff, glossy, dark-green fronds radiating from a thick, rough-textured trunk (which grows extremely slowly — gaining only 1–2 inches per year) makes it one of the most architecturally striking landscape plants available for zones 8–12. An established specimen with multiple trunks is an invaluable focal point in any tropical or subtropical garden. The plant produces bright orange-red seeds in large cone-like structures; every part of the plant — seeds, leaves, and trunk — is extremely toxic to humans and pets. In coastal Gulf Coast gardens it is one of the most reliable landscape plants available, tolerating salt, drought, heat, and wind with ease. Apply palm-formulated fertilizer with added manganese in spring to prevent the common yellowing from micronutrient deficiency.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in very well-drained, alkaline, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; saguaro is extremely slow-growing (one inch in the first year from seed) and grows best in the desert Southwest where it is protected by law in Arizona — it is illegal to harvest or damage saguaro on public land or to transplant wild specimens without a permit. Purchase only from reputable nurseries that propagate them legally.
directions: Plant legally sourced transplants in very well-drained, alkaline, desert-type soil in full sun; saguaro is the iconic columnar cactus of the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and northwestern Mexico — recognized worldwide as the symbol of the American Southwest, appearing on the Arizona state seal and in countless Western films. The great columnar stems, which can reach 40–50 feet in extreme old age (100–200 years), develop 'arms' only after 75–100 years of growth. The fluted, ribbed trunks store enormous quantities of water during monsoon rains, allowing the plant to survive extreme drought. In May and June, large, white, night-blooming flowers open at the stem tips — the Arizona state wildflower — attracting white-winged doves, bats, and native bees. The red, fig-like fruits are sweet, edible, and culturally significant to the Tohono O'odham people, who harvest the fruit with long poles to make syrup, wine, and jelly. LEGAL NOTE: saguaro are protected by Arizona law — obtain only from licensed nurseries.

common_name: Salmon Rose Zinnia (Giant Coral-Pink Cut-Flower Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Salmon Rose is a giant-flowered coral-pink selection from the Benary's Giant zinnia series, producing large, fully double blooms in a warm salmon-rose tone popular for soft, romantic floral arrangements.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12-18 inches. Salmon Rose is a giant-flowered zinnia from the Benary's Giant series, producing large, fully double, dahlia-like blooms 4-5 inches across in a warm, soft coral-pink shade that reads as gentle and romantic rather than bold, making it a favorite for wedding and garden-style floral arrangements. As part of one of the premier cut-flower zinnia series, it shares the group's large flower size, long, sturdy stems, and excellent vase life of five to ten days. Plants are tall and vigorous, blooming heavily from midsummer through the first frost with regular deadheading or harvesting to encourage continuous production.
