Grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates, and stake in windy sites since the large blooms can be top-heavy on the tall stems.

plant_note: Plant tubers after frost when the soil has warmed.
directions: Salmon Runner is a well-balanced salmon-colored dahlia that produces abundant cut flowers without needing staking. Plant the tuber 4-6 inches deep in loose, fertile soil after the last frost, eye facing up. This sturdy variety stands on its own but still benefits from pinching to increase stem count. Water deeply and consistently once growth is established, and cut blooms often to prolong flowering. Lift and store tubers over winter in regions colder than zone 8.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring into saline or alkali soils, spacing plugs 12–18 inches apart; plants spread vigorously by rhizome once roots are established and require no soil amendment.
directions: Set divisions into saline, alkali, or seasonally flooded soil in full sun during spring, pressing roots firmly into the planting site and watering in well to eliminate air pockets. Salt grass is one of the few natives that thrives in coastal salt marshes and alkali flats where soil salinity would kill most other plants, making it an excellent choice for erosion control along tidal edges and dune margins. Plants spread steadily by rhizome to form a dense, low mat that suppresses weeds and stabilizes disturbed soils without any supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established. Allow the planting to spread naturally, and mow or cut back only if needed to control boundaries.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to wet, neutral to slightly saline, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; salt meadow cordgrass is one of the most salt-tolerant ornamental grasses and can tolerate periodic inundation with brackish water — essential for coastal restoration and salt marsh edge plantings.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, neutral to slightly saline soil in full sun to partial shade; salt meadow cordgrass (marsh hay cordgrass) is a native grass of coastal salt marshes, barrier island meadows, and estuarine edges from eastern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico that forms graceful, fine-textured, wispy, arching mounds of narrow, wiry, medium-green to golden-green leaves that wave and rustle attractively in coastal breezes, turning golden-tan in autumn. It is one of the most salt-tolerant native grasses and is essential for coastal restoration work, stabilizing salt marsh edges, protecting coastal shorelines from erosion, and naturalizing the transitional zone between dry upland and tidal marsh. The plant is extremely valuable in the ecology of coastal systems — it is a primary nesting habitat for Nelson's sparrows, saltmarsh sparrows, and other coastal specialty birds, and its dense root systems trap sediment and build marsh soil. For ornamental use, it creates a fine-textured, naturalistic groundcover in wet coastal gardens where few grasses perform.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in irregularly flooded high marsh zones, salt flats, or moist brackish soils; salt meadow cordgrass occupies the high marsh zone flooded only by storm tides, above the daily inundation zone of smooth cordgrass.
directions: Salt meadow cordgrass (formerly Spartina patens) is the characteristic grass of the high salt marsh zone — the broad expanses of short, dense, cowlick-patterned grass visible from coastal roads and causeways along both the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Its lower height, finer texture, and characteristic 'cowlick' growth pattern (where wind and tidal currents lay the grass in whirling mats) easily distinguish it from the taller smooth cordgrass of the lower marsh. Historically harvested as 'salt hay' for bedding and fodder from colonial times through the early 20th century, salt meadow cordgrass was the backbone of colonial coastal agriculture; today it is a primary plant for high marsh restoration, living shoreline construction, and tidal wetland mitigation projects throughout the eastern United States. Dense stands provide critical nesting habitat for salt marsh sparrows, seaside sparrows, and willets, and the seeds are consumed by migrating birds; the grass also functions as important muskrat, vole, and meadow mouse habitat in coastal marshes.

plant_note: Plant bare-root plugs or divisions in spring in wet, brackish to saline, sandy or muddy soil at the tidal marsh edge or in wet, salt-tolerant garden settings; saltmarsh cordgrass must have consistent moisture and tolerates flooding and salt spray that would kill most plants.
directions: Plant in consistently wet, brackish to saline, sandy or muddy soil in full sun at tidal marsh edges, coastal restoration sites, or wet, salt-influenced garden areas; saltmarsh cordgrass is the foundational native grass of Atlantic and Gulf Coast salt marshes, forming the vast meadows of gently waving green that define the coastal landscape from Maine to Texas. It tolerates full tidal flooding, saline soils, and constant wave action that no other ornamental grass can withstand, making it irreplaceable for coastal restoration and stabilization. The coarse, upright stems reach 2–6 feet and produce seed heads in late summer that feed coastal sparrows, rails, and other marsh birds. Rhizomatous roots spread to stabilize shorelines, prevent erosion, and trap sediments. Essential for living shoreline projects, coastal restoration, and saline wet-garden situations in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens near the bay or marsh. Not appropriate for ordinary garden use but outstanding in naturalized coastal settings where its ecological function and native character make it irreplaceable.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade; Saltmarsh Fleabane self-seeds prolifically in zone 9-10 moist conditions and will naturalize in wet garden edges, rain gardens, and coastal plantings. It grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions. In zone 9, it may behave as a short-lived perennial in mild winters, returning from the crown for 2-3 years before dying out.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist to wet, average to poor soil; Saltmarsh Fleabane thrives in conditions that challenge most ornamentals — waterlogged clay soils, salt-spray exposure, and the intense summer heat of Gulf Coast wetland margins. Pluchea odorata is a native North American wildflower found in salt marshes, mangrove edges, coastal prairies, disturbed moist areas, and roadsides throughout the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida and up the Atlantic coast to the Carolinas. The plants produce strongly aromatic, camphor-scented foliage (the source of common names 'Camphorweed' and 'Sweetscent') and flat-topped clusters of small rose-pink to violet-pink flowers from July through October that attract skippers, hairstreak butterflies, and small native bees. The plant is valuable in coastal and wetland restoration plantings, rain gardens, and moist meadow plantings where its tolerance of salt, flooding, and poor soils outperforms most cultivated plants. In the wild, it provides critical late-summer and fall nectar for migrating butterflies along the Gulf Coast. The aromatic leaves have traditional use in folk medicine for fever, arthritis, and respiratory complaints in Gulf Coast and Caribbean traditions.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, well-drained, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade.
directions: Sampson's Snakeroot is a native perennial legume of dry, open woods, prairie margins, and rocky or sandy open ground throughout the southeastern and south-central United States. It produces gland-dotted, trifoliate leaves with distinctive purple-black glands visible when held to light, and slender, spike-like racemes of blue-violet pea flowers from May through July that are highly attractive to native bees. Scarify seeds before fall direct sow into dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun to light shade. Drought-tolerant once established, it is an ecologically valuable native legume for dry native gardens, open woodland edges, and dry prairie restoration plantings.

common_name: Samurai Orchid (Fuukiran, Wind Orchid, Japanese Fan Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark, in a small slotted pot with moss, or in the traditional Japanese method of loose sphagnum moss in a ceramic pot; Neofinetia falcata is one of the most cold-hardy of all epiphytic orchids and will survive winter temperatures to 20°F when properly established, making it suited for zone 7-12 outdoor culture in all but the coldest climates. In zone 9, it can be grown outdoors year-round on shaded porches or attached to tree bark. The flowers are small (0.75 inch), pure white, and intensely fragrant with a spicy-sweet vanilla-jasmine scent that is strongest at night. Treasured in Japan for centuries as a formal horticultural art. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial morning sun, mounted on bark, in loose sphagnum moss, or in the traditional Japanese manner in a small ceramic pot with loose moss — Samurai Orchid is remarkably cold-tolerant for a tropical epiphyte and adapts to year-round outdoor culture in zone 8-12 with appropriate moisture and light. Neofinetia falcata is a miniature, monopodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Japan (Ryukyu Islands, Kyushu, Shikoku), Korea, and China — one of the most historically significant and culturally revered orchids in East Asian horticulture. The plant has been cultivated in Japan as a formal horticultural art for over 300 years, with samurai-class collectors developing hundreds of named cultivars (especially variegated-leaved forms called Fuukiran) and specialized cultivation practices that persist to the present day. The plant is small and compact — the fan-shaped rosette of stiff, curved, two-ranked, gray-green leaves rarely exceeds 6 inches in height or spread. In summer, short racemes of 3–7 small (0.75-inch) pure white, long-spurred flowers emerge from the leaf axils. The flowers are the plant's outstanding quality: the long, curving nectary spur (up to 2 inches) and pure white coloration are beautiful, but the fragrance is extraordinary — an intensely sweet, spicy, vanilla-and-jasmine scent produced in the evening hours and capable of perfuming a room or patio. The cold-hardiness (surviving frost to 20°F in established form), small size, fragrance, and cultural history make Neofinetia falcata one of the most appealing miniature orchids for zone 8-12 outdoor culture. Non-toxic.

common_name: San Diego Red Bougainvillea (Vivid Scarlet-Red Large Vigorous Tropical Vine)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to average soil in full sun; San Diego Red is among the most cold-hardy bougainvillea cultivars — it survives brief temperature drops to 25–28°F with some dieback but typically returns from the base.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun; San Diego Red (also sold as 'Scarlett O'Hara' or 'Rosenka') is a large, vigorous bougainvillea cultivar known for its vivid scarlet-red to brilliant red bract color — one of the most intensely red bougainvilleas available, producing masses of brilliant red bracts that create a bold, high-impact tropical display when the vine is in full bloom. The bract color is described as more purely red (rather than the magenta-red of Barbara Karst) — a cleaner, more saturated crimson-to-scarlet tone that creates a different visual temperature in the landscape. San Diego Red is also noted as one of the more cold-hardy bougainvillea cultivars for zone 9 — surviving brief periods below freezing better than many other varieties, with some gardeners in zone 9a successfully maintaining it as a returning perennial with winter protection. Like all bougainvilleas, San Diego Red blooms most prolifically under slightly stressful conditions: periodic dry-down between waterings, lean soil without excessive nitrogen, and full sun exposure produce the heaviest flower display. The large, vigorous vine can reach 20+ feet on a wall or pergola structure in favorable conditions. Outstanding trained against a south or west-facing wall where reflected heat enhances bloom production and the structure protects the vine from cold north winds in zone 9 winters.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix in warmth and humidity, or plant container specimens in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to bright indirect light after last frost; sanchezia colors most intensely in bright indirect light.
directions: Root stem cuttings easily in moist potting mix in a warm, humid environment, or plant container specimens in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect light to partial shade; sanchezia is a Peruvian rainforest shrub grown for its dramatically large, glossy leaves with bold yellow or white veins that glow against the deep green leaf surface — a stunning foliage plant that makes a strong tropical statement in shaded landscapes. Spikes of red-and-yellow tubular flowers appear intermittently. Plants prefer consistently moist, warm conditions and do not tolerate cold, dry winds or temperatures below 50°F. In zone 9 grow in large containers and bring indoors before frost to a warm, bright location. Fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer during active growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into sandy, well-drained soil; seeds benefit from natural winter cold stratification and will germinate in early spring when soil temperatures rise above 60°F.
directions: Sand Blue-eyed Grass is a delicate, grass-like native perennial of the southeastern coastal plain, producing small but jewel-like violet-blue flowers with a bright yellow center from spring through early summer atop flat, iris-family stems that blend naturally into sandy meadows and open pinelands. Despite its common name, it is not a true grass but a member of the iris family (Iridaceae), and its fine, strap-like foliage forms low, slowly spreading clumps that are nearly invisible when not in bloom. It thrives in dry to moist, lean, sandy or gravelly soils in full to partial sun and strongly resents heavy clay, poor drainage, or high-fertility garden beds where competing vegetation quickly overtops it. Sow seeds in fall by scattering them on the surface of sandy soil, allowing winter cold to break dormancy naturally; established clumps can also be gently divided in fall to expand a planting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in any well-drained, alkaline, dry to average soil in full sun; sand hackberry is a thorny, drought-resistant shrub of south Texas and the Rio Grande Valley — it grows rapidly and tolerates poor, alkaline, caliche soils with no irrigation.
directions: Sand hackberry (granjeno in south Texas) is a thorny native evergreen shrub of the lower Rio Grande Valley and south Texas brush country, producing small, yellowish-orange to red fruits abundantly year-round that are among the most important food sources for resident and migratory birds in the region — it is one of the top-ranked native plants for bird feeding in the Rio Grande Valley by wildlife managers and birders. The dense, thorny thickets provide impenetrable nesting and escape cover for green jays, Altamira orioles, and dozens of other brushland birds; the plant is a cornerstone of the native south Texas chaparral community. Hackberry emperor butterflies use this species as a larval host, and white-tipped doves, plain chachalacas, and chestnut-fronted macaws consume the fruits. In south Texas wildlife habitat gardens and Rio Grande Valley native plantings, granjeno is one of the highest-priority native shrubs for creating dense, self-sustaining wildlife habitat that provides food, cover, and nesting resources year-round without supplemental irrigation.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown container trees in fall in dry, sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sand live oak is adapted to deep, excessively drained coastal sands and does not tolerate poorly drained, heavy clay, or alkaline soils.
directions: Sand live oak is a native evergreen tree of coastal sand dunes, scrub habitats, and sandy pinelands of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, closely related to live oak (Quercus virginiana) but distinctly adapted to excessively drained, nutrient-poor, acidic sands of ancient coastal terraces. It is distinguished from live oak by its smaller, more narrow leaves with rolled-under (revolute) margins, lower growth habit, and adaptation to dry sand rather than the moist, fertile soils favored by live oak. In coastal dune restoration and sandy barrier island plantings, sand live oak serves as one of the primary stabilizing species for ancient coastal plain sands, where it eventually develops into sprawling, wind-sculpted specimens of great character; it is more salt spray tolerant than live oak. Like all oaks, it supports an enormous diversity of native moths, butterflies, and beetles as larval hosts; its small acorns feed migrating wood ducks, and the dense evergreen canopy provides nesting habitat for many songbirds. A valuable evergreen tree for coastal sandy sites in zone 7–10 where typical live oak would not thrive.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring on sandy, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; sand lovegrass requires sharp drainage and lean soils — it declines rapidly in heavy clay or moist, fertile garden conditions and is best suited to sandy prairies and xeric landscape situations.
directions: Sand lovegrass is a taller, more robust native lovegrass of deep sandy soils and sandy prairies across the south-central United States, producing large, open, feathery panicles of light pinkish-green to tan spikelets in late summer that wave gracefully in any breeze — its airy, fountain-like form makes it one of the most elegant of all native prairie grasses for dry, sandy garden situations. Found naturally in sand prairies, sandy bottomlands, and open sandy oak woodlands of the Central Plains and Gulf Coast region, it is adapted to deep, well-drained, infertile sandy soils that challenge most ornamental grasses; it is significantly more tolerant of sand and drought than blue grama or buffalo grass while producing a more visually dramatic plant. The seed panicles provide food for native sparrows and finches through fall and winter, and the dried tufts remain attractive through the cold season. Excellent companion for prairie grasses like indiangrass, big bluestem, and prairie dropseed in sandy-soil native meadow plantings from Texas to the Midwest.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in very well-drained, sandy to rocky soil; sand phlox requires excellent drainage and will rot in heavy, wet soils. It also performs well in slightly alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; sand phlox is a low-growing native prairie groundcover that covers itself with fragrant lavender to white flowers with distinctively notched or cleft petals in early spring. It forms a dense mat of needle-like evergreen foliage and blooms so profusely that the foliage is completely hidden by flowers. Unlike the creeping phlox (P. subulata) of garden centers, sand phlox is native to the midwestern prairies and is adapted to slightly drier conditions. Shear or mow lightly immediately after blooming to encourage compact, dense new growth. An outstanding plant for rock gardens, dry slopes, and edging in well-drained sites.

plant_note: Transplant container-grown seedlings in spring in very well-drained, dry, pure white sand in full sun; sand pine is adapted to the most nutrient-poor, droughty, xeric white sand soils in Florida and adjacent states where no other pine survives. Do not amend planting soil.
directions: Plant in dry, infertile, pure white to light-colored, acidic sand in full sun; sand pine is a Florida endemic of the ancient marine sand ridges and white sand scrub habitats of the Florida peninsula and coastal panhandle — one of the most ecologically specialized trees in North America. It is the primary tree of Florida scrub, growing in soil so nutrient-poor and drought-prone that it excludes virtually all other tree species. Two populations exist: a serotinous scrub variety (var. clausa) with cones that remain closed until opened by fire — releasing a mass of seeds after fire removes competing vegetation — and an open-cone variety (var. immuricata) along the Gulf Coast. The scrub habitat it creates is among the most biodiverse ecosystems in Florida, harboring endemic species including the Florida scrub jay, Florida mouse, and dozens of rare plant species. An extremely site-specific tree that should only be planted in authentic white-sand scrub conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring onto bare, sandy, or gravelly soil in full sun; press seed lightly into the surface and keep the site moist until seedlings emerge, then reduce watering as plants develop their deep root system.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a loose, infertile sandy or gravelly seedbed in full sun in early spring, pressing it lightly into the soil surface and watering until seedlings establish over the first few weeks. Sand reed grass is a deep-rooted native of the central Great Plains and interior dune systems, where its extensive rhizome network anchors shifting sand and withstands the full force of plains wind and drought with ease. Plants produce graceful, feathery seed plumes in late summer that persist through winter, providing outstanding visual interest and valuable wildlife cover in prairie restorations, dry meadows, and stabilized dune plantings. Avoid fertilizing or irrigating once established, as lean, dry conditions produce the strongest roots and the most attractive, wind-resilient growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sandankwa viburnum is the workhorse hedge viburnum of the Gulf Coast and central Florida, thriving where northern viburnums struggle in summer heat and humidity. Avoid planting in poorly-drained sites; it tolerates light drought once established but will not stand waterlogged roots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; sandankwa viburnum is the most widely used broadleaf evergreen hedge and screening shrub in Gulf Coast and central Florida landscapes — an easy-growing, tough, relatively drought-tolerant Japanese species that forms a dense, 5–8 foot mound of glossy, dark green, oval leaves and produces clusters of small, fragrant white to pale pink flowers in winter and early spring when few other shrubs bloom. The flowers are followed by red fruits that mature to black, attracting birds. It tolerates partial shade well and performs reliably in the heat and humidity that limits many northern shrubs in zone 8b–10 gardens. Widely used for foundation planting, privacy hedges, and screening in Florida and along the Gulf Coast; easy to shear to a formal shape or allow to grow naturally as an informal screen.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings or stakes directly into moist, sandy, or silty streambank soil in very early spring; stems 12–24 in long can be pushed directly into moist soil where they root almost instantly, making sandbar willow the easiest willow to propagate for streambank restoration.
directions: Plant in wet to moist, sandy or silty soil in full sun along stream banks, pond margins, and flood-prone areas; sandbar willow colonizes bare mineral soils and gravel bars faster than almost any other native woody plant, making it invaluable for erosion control and streambank stabilization following disturbance. The long, narrow silver-green leaves give the plant an elegant, fine-textured appearance that contrasts nicely with coarser riparian vegetation. Mature plants form dense thickets through aggressive root sprouting, providing nesting cover for warblers, wrens, and yellowthroats. The species is ecologically keystone in southwestern riparian corridors where it provides critical streambank structure and willow-dependent pollinator forage.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, sandy, infertile, acidic soil in full sun; sandhill milkweed is native to the dry, sandy pine flatwoods and sandhills of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, where it grows in the challenging, xeric conditions typical of the longleaf pine ecosystem.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, infertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; sandhill milkweed is a prostrate to spreading Gulf Coastal Plain milkweed adapted to the extreme xeric conditions of longleaf pine sandhills — the type of habitat that receives very little soil moisture even during rainy seasons due to the high permeability of deep, white sand. The plant lies almost flat along the ground, with large, round, grayish-green leaves that help reduce water loss, and produces clusters of pale pink to lavender flowers in summer. It is a primary monarch butterfly host plant in the longleaf pine flatwoods ecosystem and an important nectar source for numerous native bees. One of the most drought-tolerant milkweeds available, making it an outstanding pollinator plant for dry, sunny, sandy landscapes in zone 9a.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh acorns in fall in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; sandhill oak is endemic to the ancient scrub habitats of central Florida and is a legally protected Florida state plant. Never collect from the wild — obtain only nursery-grown plants.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, strongly acidic, infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; sandhill oak is a Florida scrub endemic — one of the most specialized and geographically restricted oaks in North America, found only in the ancient inland scrub habitats of central Florida's Lake Wales Ridge and surrounding areas. These scrub habitats on ancient sand dunes are among the most threatened ecosystems in the US, harboring numerous endemic species including the Florida scrub-jay, which depends on low scrub oaks like Q. inopina for acorn food and low, open habitat structure. The plant forms a spreading shrub to small tree with glossy, nearly evergreen leaves and is adapted to the driest, most nutrient-poor sandy soils of the ancient scrub ecosystem. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants from Florida-certified native nurseries; wild collection is illegal.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1 inch depth in well-drained, rocky, calcareous, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sandpaper oak grows on dry, rocky, limestone slopes and desert grasslands of west Texas and New Mexico where it forms dense, scrubby thickets adapted to poor, alkaline, dry conditions.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in well-drained, rocky, calcareous, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sandpaper oak is a small, shrubby to tree-like, semi-evergreen oak of dry, rocky, limestone slopes in west Texas and New Mexico, named for the distinctively rough, sandpaper-textured upper surface of the small, leathery, holly-like leaves with spiny teeth. It forms dense, thorny, impenetrable thickets in its natural habitat that serve as important cover for scaled quail, roadrunners, and various lizards in the Chihuahuan Desert. The small acorns provide food for wildlife in an arid region where food sources are sparse. A tough, dry-land shrub-oak for rocky, alkaline, exposed garden conditions in west Texas and the Southwest where most ornamental plants struggle. Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established. Can form a functional barrier hedge in harsh, exposed xeric conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; sandpaper verbena spreads aggressively by rhizomes in Gulf Coast conditions — it is most appropriate in large open areas or as a slope cover where spreading is desired.
directions: Plant or direct sow in well-drained, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — sandpaper verbena is a tough, spreading perennial from South America that has naturalized widely across the Gulf Coast and Deep South, producing brilliant purple to magenta flat-topped flower clusters almost continuously from spring through hard frost. The rough, sandpapery-textured, deeply veined leaves and stems give it a distinctive texture; the plant spreads rapidly by underground rhizomes to cover large areas in hot, dry conditions where lawn and other groundcovers fail. It is an outstanding butterfly plant with exceptional drought tolerance and makes a bold, colorful slope cover, median planting, or informal groundcover in sunny, dry areas. In zone 7–8 it may die back in winter but resprouts reliably from established roots. The intense purple flower color is unusually vivid in the landscape and combines beautifully with yellow or orange companions. Too aggressive for small formal beds but invaluable for large-scale planting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is native to the sandy, acidic soils of the coastal plain and pineland habitats of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is native to the sandy, acidic soils of the coastal plain and pineland habitats of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma. Echinacea sanguinea is the coneflower of the southeastern coastal plain pineland habitats, producing narrow, strongly reflexed, rose-red to blood-red ray petals and a tall, conical, brownish-orange central disk; its tolerance of sandy, acidic soils and the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast region makes it the best-adapted true-species echinacea for zone 7–9 southern gardens. It is rare in cultivation but increasingly available from native plant nurseries in the South, and is important for ecological gardens in its native range where it supports specialist native bees.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is native to the dry, open pine savannas and sandy, open woodlands of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; sanguine coneflower is a rare Echinacea species endemic to the piney woods of eastern Texas, Louisiana, and neighboring states, producing attractive coneflowers with pale lavender to rose-pink ray petals and the characteristic spiny orange-brown central cone. Named sanguinea (blood-red) for the reddish coloration of the cone at certain stages, it is closely related to and sometimes confused with E. purpurea. The species is adapted to the sandy, slightly acidic soils and mild winters of the East Texas piney woods ecosystem, making it better adapted than many coneflowers to the conditions of zone 9a. An important pollinator plant attracting numerous native bees and monarch butterflies. The seeds are consumed by goldfinches and other finches in fall.

common_name: Santa Barbara Mexican Bush Sage (Compact Mexican Sage)
plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection that grows about half the size of the standard Salvia leucantha and is suitable for smaller garden spaces where the full-size species would overwhelm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection of Mexican bush sage (Salvia leucantha) — a smaller, more garden-friendly alternative to the full-size species that can reach 4–6 feet. Santa Barbara stays 2–3 feet tall and wide, making it practical for smaller beds and borders where the full-size species would quickly become overwhelming. Like the species, Santa Barbara produces spectacular, long (6–12 inch) velvety-purple and white flower spikes from late summer through fall — the velvety-purple calyxes enclose small white flowers in a distinctive bicolor spike that is exceptional for late-season pollinator value and cut-flower use. The long, arching, purple flower spikes of Mexican sage provide the single most dramatic fall display of any commonly grown Gulf Coast perennial — no other plant matches the intensity and quantity of the purple-and-white flower production in September through November. Santa Barbara's compact habit blooms slightly earlier than the full-size species, making it more practical in zone 9 where the species sometimes misses the first frost deadline. Cut back to 12 inches after blooming; the plant regrows vigorously from the woody base. Drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free in well-drained soil.

common_name: Santa Barbara Mexican Sage (Compact Velvety Purple Fall-Blooming Salvia)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Santa Barbara requires the same fall bloom trigger as the species — shorter day length in late summer and fall initiates flowering regardless of other conditions; plants in areas with significant artificial night lighting may not bloom as freely.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Santa Barbara is a compact selection of Mexican bush sage (Salvia leucantha) — more suitable for typical garden spaces than the standard species, which can reach 4–5 feet. At 2–3 feet, Santa Barbara produces the same spectacular display of velvety, deep purple to purple-and-white bicolor flower spikes as the species in a more manageable size. Mexican bush sage flowers in response to shortening day length (photoperiod-triggered), blooming from August through December — one of the most valuable late-season ornamentals for Gulf South gardens that provide important late-summer nectar for migrating monarch butterflies. The flower spikes are composed of velvety, fuzzy purple calyces (even in the bicolor 'white flowers' version, the calyces are purple) with white or purple corolla flowers — the texture is unique among commonly grown sages. In zone 9, Santa Barbara grows as a semi-evergreen perennial, returning from the base after hard freezes; it is at its drought-tolerant best once established in lean soil. Excellent as a late-season companion for fall-blooming Salvia coccinea, Gulf muhly grass, and swamp sunflower. Hummingbirds and gulf fritillary butterflies visit the flowers extensively during the fall bloom period.

plant_note: Plant tubers or seedlings after water temperatures reliably exceed 70°F in full sun in still or slow-moving water 18–36 inches deep in large ponds or water features in zone 9–12; the Santa Cruz Water Lily produces the world's largest floating leaves — circular, up to 5 feet across with upturned edges — and dramatic white to pink-blushed fragrant flowers that open at night over two successive evenings, shifting from white to pink as they age.
directions: Grow Victoria cruziana in full sun in water 18–36 inches deep; pot the rhizome in heavy, unamended clay loam (not potting mix — it floats) in a large aquatic container and submerge; apply slow-release aquatic plant fertilizer monthly and provide water temperatures above 70°F for active growth. The Santa Cruz Water Lily is the hardier of the two Victoria species — native to the rivers and backwaters of Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina — and is more forgiving than its Amazonian relative in temperate and subtropical water gardens. The enormous floating pads, edged with upturned rims 3–4 inches high, can support significant weight; the undersides are covered with sharp spines and a network of air-filled chambers. Flowers are thermogenic, producing heat to attract scarce pollinators: they open white on the first night, trapping beetle pollinators inside; on the second night they reopen as pink and release the pollen-dusted beetles. In zone 9, treat as a tender annual unless overwintered in a heated indoor pool; in zone 10–12, rhizomes may persist for multiple years. Each plant needs at least 100 square feet of open water surface.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Santa Fe phlox grows naturally on dry, rocky limestone and igneous slopes and desert grasslands of the Chihuahuan Desert and southern Rocky Mountain foothills of New Mexico and west Texas.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry to average, rocky or sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Santa Fe phlox is a low-growing native phlox of dry, rocky desert grasslands and limestone slopes of New Mexico, west Texas, and northern Chihuahua, producing clusters of fragrant, rose-pink, lavender, or white flowers in spring. The low, somewhat spreading, semi-evergreen habit makes it well-suited to dry, rocky gardens and the xeriscape. More heat and drought tolerant than most phlox — adapted to the extreme summer conditions of the Chihuahuan Desert where temperatures regularly exceed 100°F — making it valuable for dry gardens in zones 7–9 where other phlox struggle in summer heat. Several named cultivars with improved flower size and color, including selections in deep magenta-pink, are available from xeric native plant nurseries. An excellent pollinator plant for native bees in spring and a good nectar source for tiger swallowtail butterflies.

common_name: Santa Rita Prickly Pear (Purple-Padded Ornamental Cactus)
plant_note: Plant rooted pad cuttings in spring in extremely well-drained, sandy or rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; Santa Rita's signature purple pad color intensifies in cold, dry weather and with stress from drought or poor soil, while it stays greener in richer, wetter conditions.
directions: Plant in extremely well-drained, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun. Santa Rita prickly pear is grown chiefly for its striking blue-gray pads that flush a deep violet-purple in cold or drought stress, providing dramatic color contrast in a xeric or desert-style planting alongside its cheerful yellow spring flowers and edible purple fruit (tunas) later in the season. It is extremely drought-tolerant once established, needing essentially no supplemental water, and propagates easily from rooted pad cuttings allowed to callus for a few days before planting. Handle with heavy gloves, since the pads carry both larger spines and fine, irritating glochids that detach easily on contact.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring after frost danger has passed; Sapphire Showers has a more trailing, cascading habit than upright duranta cultivars, making it well suited to hanging baskets, containers, and spilling over walls.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Sapphire Showers is a trailing form of duranta, producing cascading stems draped in clusters of small, tubular blue-violet flowers over a long warm-season bloom period that draws butterflies and hummingbirds. Its spreading, arching habit sets it apart from the more upright, tree-like duranta cultivars often grown as small specimen trees, making it a good choice for hanging baskets, raised containers, or spilling over a low wall. In zone 9a it typically dies back to the ground after a hard freeze but regrows quickly from the roots the following spring in most winters; in colder zones it is best grown as a container annual or overwintered indoors.

plant_note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall (September–October in zone 8) in well-drained, deeply prepared, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; set the eyes (growth buds) no deeper than 1–2 inches below the soil surface — deeper planting is the most common cause of peonies failing to bloom.
directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, deeply prepared, fertile soil in full sun; Sarah Bernhardt is one of the most famous and most widely grown peony cultivars in the world — introduced by Léon Lemoine of Nancy, France, in 1906 and named for the legendary French actress, it remains the best-selling peony in American commerce after more than a century in cultivation. The enormous, fully double, light apple-blossom pink flowers (6–8 inches across) with a sweet, intensely classic peony fragrance represent the idealized peony — the standard against which other peonies are measured for form, color, and fragrance. The petals are arranged in a lush, layered rosette pattern of exceptional fullness and symmetry. Sarah Bernhardt blooms in late May in zone 8, and the cut flowers last 7–10 days in arrangements. Peonies are long-lived perennials — Sarah Bernhardt specimens planted decades ago continue to bloom reliably without division. The primary zone 9 limitation is insufficient winter chilling — peonies require 500–1000 chill hours to bloom reliably, and in the warmest parts of zone 9 and all of zone 10, the winter chilling requirement is not met. In zone 8 and cooler parts of zone 9 (north Louisiana, central Texas), peonies can succeed. Plant with only 1–2 inches of soil over the crown — deeper planting is the primary cause of peony failure to bloom.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Sardinian glory-of-the-snow is the most uniformly, deeply blue of the chionodoxas — the small white eye of C. luciliae is absent or nearly so, making the entire flower a uniform, intense, gentian-blue. It naturalizes freely by seed and bulb offset, spreading into large colonies in suitable conditions under deciduous trees and in thin turf.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; Sardinian glory-of-the-snow is distinguished from the more commonly grown C. luciliae (forbesii) by its flower color: while C. luciliae has a conspicuous white center eye creating a blue-and-white bicolor pattern, C. sardensis is an intense, uniform, all-blue — a clear, deep, gentian-blue to rich cornflower-blue throughout each small, star-shaped, six-petaled flower with only the slightest trace of white at the very center, if any. The effect of a mass planting or naturalized colony in early spring is therefore a more uniformly intense blue carpet than C. luciliae provides — the even, unwavering, gentian-blue creating an extraordinarily pure, concentrated blue ground-color effect under deciduous trees before the canopy leafs out. It appears early (February–March), pushing through snow if needed (the genus name means 'snow-glory'), and naturalizes freely by self-seeding and offset multiplication into large colonies over years. An excellent and somewhat underused alternative or companion to C. luciliae for mass spring-blue naturalizing in woodland gardens, lawn edges, and rough grass under deciduous trees. Hardy to zone 3.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sargent cherry is one of the largest and most cold-hardy ornamental cherries and one of the few that is genuinely long-lived, persisting as a substantial tree. It also has good early fall color.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sargent cherry is a Japanese species named for Charles Sprague Sargent, director of the Arnold Arboretum, and is one of the largest and most stately of ornamental cherries, developing into a substantial, wide-spreading tree with reddish-brown bark marked by horizontal lenticels. The flowers are deep pink, single, appearing in clusters in early spring — earlier than most Japanese cherries. The fall color is early and vivid — rich orange and crimson tones appearing weeks before most other trees. More cold-hardy and longer-lived than many ornamental cherries and a parent of several widely planted cultivars including 'Accolade'. The small, dark purplish-black fruits are eaten by birds. One of the finest and most substantial ornamental cherry species for long-term landscape use.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Sarvis Holly is dioecious — both male and female plants are required within 50 feet for berry production. It thrives in low, wet, shaded settings where many other holly species struggle.
directions: Sarvis Holly is a rarely cultivated native deciduous holly of moist, low-lying forests, wet woods, and stream margins of the coastal plain from South Carolina to Louisiana, producing clusters of small pink to red berries that ripen in late summer and fall and are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, bluebirds, robins, and other fruit-eating birds during the critical pre-migration feeding period. The name 'sarvis' is a folk rendering of 'serviceberry' or 'service tree,' reflecting the ripening time of its berries relative to other fall food sources. Less commonly cultivated than Possumhaw or Winterberry hollies, Sarvis Holly thrives in the wet, shaded conditions of bottomland forest and stream banks where larger hollies may struggle, and deserves wider use in native plant landscapes. Plant rooted cuttings in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; dioecious, so both sexes are required within pollinator range for berry set.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in well-drained, acidic soil slightly above grade; fall planting allows root establishment before the autumn and winter bloom season begins.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade to full sun; sasanqua camellias bloom in fall and early winter, earlier than Camellia japonica, and are more sun-tolerant and heat-hardy, making them the better choice for Gulf Coast gardens in zones 8–9. Single, semi-double, or double flowers in white, pink, red, and lavender provide vivid color from October through January when little else is in bloom. Unlike japonicas, sasanquas can be trained as espaliers against walls, used as hedges, or even grown as small specimen trees. Apply pine-bark mulch and acid-forming camellia fertilizer in spring. Petal blight and scale are the main concerns; improve air circulation and treat scale with horticultural oil in late winter.

plant_note: Divide or transplant root suckers in early spring, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, average to sandy, dry soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; sassafras transplants poorly due to its deep, fleshy taproot and is best established from small container-grown plants or root cuttings rather than field-dug specimens.
directions: Transplant root suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average soil in full sun to partial shade; sassafras is a native eastern North American deciduous tree distinguished from all other trees by its uniquely variable leaf shape — individual trees simultaneously bear three distinct leaf shapes: simple oval leaves, mitten-shaped leaves with one lobe, and three-lobed leaves — all on the same tree, all with the same distinctive, pleasantly spicy-aromatic, root-beer fragrance when crushed. In spring, small clusters of yellow flowers appear before the leaves. The autumn foliage is among the most brilliantly colored of any native tree — turning orange, red, purple, and scarlet in a spectacular multi-color display. Dark-blue, olive-like fruits on red stalks feed many songbirds in fall. Sassafras was historically important in American commerce — root bark was the original source of sassafras oil and the primary ingredient of traditional root beer and filé powder (an essential Creole seasoning) — though safrole, the active compound, is now restricted as a food additive. Spreads by root suckers to form groves. An excellent native tree for dry, sandy, difficult sites where many trees fail.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in zone 9–11; Satake Palm is a rare, monotypic palm endemic to the Yaeyama Islands of the Ryukyu Archipelago (southernmost Japan), growing in humid subtropical forest — a graceful, solitary-trunked feather palm with a prominently colored, distinctive reddish-brown crown shaft and elegantly arching fronds, one of the rarest palms in cultivation.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Satakentia liukiuensis grows moderately fast for a palm and is reasonably adaptable to subtropical conditions with regular watering and palm fertilizer twice yearly — protect from cold below 26°F. Satakentia liukiuensis (Satake Palm or Ryukyu Palm) is a monotypic genus — a single species known only from the wild in the Yaeyama Island group (Iriomote, Ishigaki) of the Ryukyu Archipelago in southernmost Japan, where it grows in humid subtropical evergreen forest. Named in honor of the Japanese botanist Yoshitami Satake who first described it, the Satake Palm is known to only a small number of palm enthusiasts worldwide. The palm develops a moderately sized, solitary trunk reaching 30–40 feet in maturity, with a distinctive, prominently colored reddish-brown to coppery-red crown shaft — the smooth, enclosed basal section of the fronds just below the crown — that is one of the palm's most ornamental features. The gracefully arching, deep-green feather fronds create an elegant, formal crown. Satakentia is adaptable to subtropical conditions in zones 9–11 and grows reasonably well in South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and California. A genuinely rare and prized collector's palm that is slowly becoming more available through specialized nurseries.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; satin grass grows naturally in coastal scrub, dry sandy pinelands, and coastal strand of south Florida and the Gulf Coast. Division of established clumps in spring is most reliable for propagation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; satin grass (formerly Muhlenbergia filipes, now M. sericea) is a coastal grass of south Florida, the Gulf Coast scrub, and coastal hammocks, producing extraordinary rosy-purple to pinkish plumes in fall that create a shimmering cloud of color above the fine-textured foliage. More cold-tender than the common pink muhly grass (M. capillaris) but similar in appearance, with more delicate, silkier, purple-pink plumes. Native to coastal scrub and dry pinelands of Florida and the Gulf Coast, it thrives in sandy, low-nutrient, well-drained soils where it is drought-tolerant once established. The fall plume display in September–November rivals any ornamental grass for pure visual impact. A superb native for coastal gardens and dry, sandy landscapes in zones 8b–11.

common_name: Satin Pothos (Silver Philodendron, Silk Pothos, Silver Scindapsus)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container vine in zone 9; Satin Pothos cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F and is strictly an indoor or protected container plant in zone 9. It grows equally well as a trailing plant in a hanging basket or as a climbing vine on a moss pole. Propagate from stem cuttings with one or more nodes — root in water or potting mix within 2–3 weeks. Despite the common name, it is not related to true Pothos (Epipremnum aureum) though they share similar care requirements.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade; Satin Pothos tolerates lower light than most variegated plants and can maintain attractive foliage color even several feet from a window, though growth slows considerably in dim conditions. Scindapsus pictus is a climbing tropical vine native to Southeast Asia — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Malaysia, Philippines, Sulawesi, and Sumatra — widely grown as a houseplant for its distinctive, heart-shaped, velvety-textured leaves decorated with irregular silver-gray patches and speckles. The silver variegation has an unusual quality: it appears slightly iridescent or three-dimensional against the dark, matte, blue-green base color, an effect created by air pockets beneath the leaf surface that scatter light — the same optical phenomenon that makes butterfly wings iridescent. The cultivar 'Argyraeus' has smaller, more compact leaves than the species with abundant fine silver spotting; 'Exotica' has larger leaves with more extensive, bold, irregular silver patches. Unlike true pothos (Epipremnum), Scindapsus has single leaves and no overlapping juvenile leaf stages when climbing. Its tolerance for low light, inconsistent watering, and indoor conditions — combined with the beautiful iridescent foliage — makes it a perennial houseplant favorite. Mildly toxic due to calcium oxalate.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; saucer magnolia blooms on bare wood in early spring and is susceptible to late frost damage to the buds — avoid planting in frost pockets or north-facing spots where late freezes are common.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — saucer magnolia is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the world for spring impact, producing enormous, tulip-shaped flowers (4–10 inches across) in shades ranging from deep rose-purple to pale pink to white, borne on bare branches before the leaves emerge in late winter to early spring. A single tree in bloom is visible from hundreds of feet away. The hybrid origin (M. denudata x M. liliiflora) combines cold hardiness and floriferous habit; named cultivars include 'Lennei' (deep rose-purple), 'Alexandrina' (pink and white), 'Brozzonii' (nearly white), and 'Rustica Rubra' (rich rose). The main risk in the South is late frost damage to early-opening buds in zone 5–7; in zone 8–9, this is rarely a problem and plants bloom reliably and abundantly. An outstanding focal point or specimen tree for the front landscape.

common_name: Sausage Tree (African Sausage Tree, Kigelia, Fetish Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Kigelia africana is frost-sensitive and best suited to zone 10-11 for outdoor planting, or zone 9 in containers. The tree grows rapidly in tropical conditions. The enormous, pendulous fruits (1–2 feet long, up to 20 lbs) hang from long, ropy, cable-like stalks from the branches and must not be allowed to fall on people or parked vehicles — site accordingly. The fruits are NOT edible fresh and are considered toxic. Night-blooming red flowers require bat pollination for fruit set.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Sausage Tree grows most vigorously in full sun with adequate water during establishment, becoming drought-tolerant in deep, well-drained soils once established. Kigelia africana is a large, wide-spreading, semi-evergreen tree native to tropical Africa (from Sudan and Ethiopia south to Namibia and South Africa) in the Bignoniaceae family (the trumpet vine family), widely known for producing one of the most extraordinary fruits of any tree. The fruits are enormous, cylindrical, sausage-shaped, hard-shelled, fibrous, gray-brown, and can reach 2 feet in length and 20 pounds in weight — each hanging individually from long, ropy, cable-like stalks attached to the branches, with multiple giant 'sausages' dangling from a single tree creating a surreal, prehistoric appearance. The flowers are deep maroon-red to brownish-red, large, bell-shaped, produced on long pendant racemes and opening at night to release a powerful, somewhat unpleasant odor that attracts bat pollinators — bats visit the flowers at night and transfer pollen between trees. The fruits require bat or other animal dispersal to germinate in the wild. The fresh fruits are toxic if consumed raw; however, the dried or roasted fruits have been used medicinally in traditional African medicine for centuries, and extracts are now investigated for pharmaceutical applications including wound healing and skin conditions. A dramatic, unmistakable specimen tree for large zone 10-11 tropical landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Savannah is a female cultivar requiring a male Ilex opaca pollinator within 50–100 feet for berry production — any male American holly in the vicinity will suffice. Trees bear berries beginning at 3–5 years from planting. In zone 9, Savannah Holly is well-adapted and one of the most prolific berry producers among American holly cultivars. Allow ample space — Savannah grows into a substantial tree (30–45 feet) over decades.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, acidic to slightly acidic soil — American holly adapts to a wide range of conditions but produces the densest berry crops in full sun with consistent moisture; Savannah is one of the most prolific and ornamentally outstanding cultivars of American Holly (Ilex opaca), the native evergreen holly that defines the winter ornamental landscape of the American East and Gulf South. Selected for heavy, consistent berry production, Savannah bears abundant clusters of bright red berries along every branch by November that persist through winter — providing both winter ornamental interest (the classic evergreen holly-and-berry combination) and critical food resources for overwintering birds including robins, cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and yellow-rumped warblers. American holly is the native counterpart to English holly (Ilex aquifolium), with dull rather than glossy leaves and a more open, pyramidal growth habit — less formal than English holly but fully hardy throughout the South and adapted to the heat and humidity that limits English holly below zone 6. Savannah's native provenance means complete adaptation to Gulf South soils, climate, and pest pressure without the cultural requirements or limitations of introduced hollies.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Savannah is female and requires a nearby male holly (Ilex opaca or I. cassine) within 50 feet for reliable berry production.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5) soil in full sun to partial shade; Savannah holly is a naturally occurring hybrid between Dahoon holly (Ilex cassine) and American holly (Ilex opaca) — both southeastern native hollies — producing a fast-growing, upright-pyramidal evergreen tree valued across the Gulf South for its rapid establishment, lighter, finer-textured foliage than other landscape hollies, and exceptional production of small, bright-red berries on female plants throughout winter. The relatively light-weight, less spiny leaves give Savannah a more graceful appearance than the coarser-textured hollies, and the gray bark is attractive. It grows faster than American holly and adapts to a wider range of soil conditions, including periodic wetness, that would stress other hollies. A single female Savannah holly laden with red berries in winter is one of the most attractive of all native evergreen trees for wildlife gardening — the berries are a critical winter food source for cedar waxwings, robins, and mockingbirds. A male pollinator nearby is needed for consistent berry production; any compatible male Ilex opaca or I. cassine in the vicinity will serve. Excellent for screening, naturalizing, and as a specimen tree in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; savin juniper is one of the most widely used evergreen groundcover and bank-stabilization shrubs, with numerous cultivars including the very popular 'Tamariscifolia' (tam juniper). WARNING: All parts of savin juniper are poisonous — do not plant where children may ingest the berries.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; savin juniper is one of the most important ornamental junipers in the landscape industry — a low, spreading, multi-stemmed shrubby juniper of mountain slopes in central Europe and western Asia that has given rise to dozens of widely grown cultivars. The cultivar 'Tamariscifolia' (tam juniper) is one of the most widely planted low-growing evergreen shrubs in North American commercial landscaping. The species and cultivars tolerate heat, cold, drought, and poor soils, making them reliable low-maintenance groundcovers for banks, slopes, and sunny exposed sites. The foliage has a distinctly pungent, somewhat unpleasant odor when crushed — quite different from the pleasant cedar scent of most junipers. All parts are poisonous if ingested; the plant contains savin oil which historically caused miscarriages and was used as an abortifacient in herbal medicine — it should never be used internally. An excellent tough groundcover for full-sun, dry, difficult slopes.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or bird-dispersed seeds in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; saw greenbrier is most useful as a wildlife plant in naturalized settings rather than as a cultivated garden plant — it spreads by extensive underground rhizomes and is very difficult to remove once established.
directions: Allow to naturalize in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in wildlife garden settings; saw greenbrier is a native evergreen vine of the southeastern US, producing stout, angular green stems armed with short, broad spines and thick, leathery, mottled-blotched dark green leaves. The small, shiny black berries in fall and winter are critically important food for mockingbirds, robins, cedar waxwings, bluebirds, and many other birds. The underground rhizomes form large, starchy masses that were roasted and eaten by southeastern Indigenous peoples; young shoots can be eaten as a cooked vegetable. Despite its ornamental berries and ecological importance, it is rarely cultivated — its stiff, sharp thorns and persistent rhizomes make it better suited to wildlife areas than manicured gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; saw palmetto transplants from containers fairly well but is very slow to establish from small plants. The underground root system is ancient and extensive in wild specimens.
directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — saw palmetto is one of the most ecologically important shrubs in the southeastern US, forming the dominant understory layer across millions of acres of Florida and Gulf Coast pine flatwoods and scrub. Individual plants are estimated to live 500–700 years, maintaining an enormous root system that stores carbohydrates and re-sprouts after fire within days. The cream-white flower clusters produce small black berries that are a primary food source for black bears, white-tailed deer, gopher tortoises, and more than 100 bird species. The berries are also harvested commercially as an herbal supplement for prostate health. Saw palmetto tolerates partial shade, salt, drought, and periodic flooding — it is one of the most resilient and valuable native plants for Gulf Coast habitat gardens. The saw-toothed petioles give it its name.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; sawara cypress grows naturally in moist mountain forests of central and southern Japan and requires adequate moisture — do not plant in dry, hot, exposed conditions or in heavy alkaline clay.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile to average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; sawara cypress is the most diverse of the Japanese false cypresses (Chamaecyparis) in terms of cultivated forms — dozens of named cultivars representing completely different appearances have been selected over centuries of Japanese horticulture, including the thread-like drooping forms (Filifera group), the juvenile foliage-forever plants (Squarrosa group) with soft, feathery mossy texture, the dwarf globe cultivars (Nana group), and the golden-foliaged variants of all types. The natural species is a large forest tree in Japan, but the species in gardens is usually encountered as one of its many distinctive cultivars. Requires adequate moisture and good drainage — does not tolerate alkaline soils or drought stress well. The wildly different cultivated forms (some almost unrecognizably different from the species) make this one of the most architecturally diverse of all ornamental conifers. Widely used in Japanese-influenced gardens, conifer collections, and ornamental mixed borders.

plant_note: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy to sandy soil in full sun; sawtooth oak is one of the fastest-growing oaks and is widely planted in wildlife food plots across the southeastern US for its heavy, early acorn production — a full crop typically beginning in 5–8 years from planting.
directions: Plant acorns immediately after collection in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep loamy or sandy soil in full sun; sawtooth oak is an Asian oak (native to China, Korea, and Japan) widely planted throughout the southeastern and mid-Atlantic US as a fast-growing wildlife tree, producing large, chestnut-like acorns in heavy crops beginning at 5–8 years of age — far earlier than most native oaks. The long, narrow, chestnut-like leaves (reminiscent of chestnut rather than typical oak foliage) turn golden yellow in fall. The large acorns are eagerly consumed by deer, turkey, wood ducks, and other wildlife. Its fast growth rate, adaptability, and early, heavy acorn production make it the most widely planted non-native oak for deer and wildlife habitat planting in the Southeast. However, it can naturalize and potentially displace native oaks in some regions — use thoughtfully near natural areas.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or plant transplants in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately dry, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scaly blazing star is more tolerant of clay soil than some liatris species but still requires adequate drainage to prevent crown rot.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant transplants in spring in very well-drained, dry to moderately dry, sandy to rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scaly blazing star is more tolerant of clay soil than some liatris species but still requires adequate drainage to prevent crown rot. Liatris squarrosa is immediately distinguished from other liatris species by the conspicuously reflexed (squarrose), long-pointed bracts of its large, solitary or sparsely clustered flower heads, giving each flower a spiky, star-burst appearance; it produces bold, rosy-purple to rose-pink flowers from July through September on stiff, upright stems. Native to dry, sandy to rocky, open habitats from Delaware to Georgia and west to Kansas, it is an important early fall nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and specialist native bees. More heat-tolerant than many liatris species and a good choice for zone 7-9 dry gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow seeds to undergo natural cold stratification over winter; they will germinate the following spring when soil warms.
directions: Direct sow seeds in fall into well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in a full-sun location, pressing lightly into the surface without covering, and allow winter cold to provide the stratification seeds need to germinate the following spring. This robust southeastern native produces erect stems 2 to 4 feet tall crowned with large, dense magenta-purple flower heads in a distinctive bottom-up bloom sequence from August through October, with distinctly spreading phyllary bracts that give each head a scaly, star-like look unlike other blazing stars. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental watering or fertilizing in lean, well-drained soil. It is an outstanding nectar source for monarchs, swallowtails, and native bees in late-summer and fall pollinator gardens throughout the Southeast.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in dry, rocky or sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; seeds cold-stratify naturally over winter and germinate in spring. Scaly Blazingstar tolerates rocky, calcareous, and sandy soils and is more drought-tolerant than most blazingstar species.
directions: Scaly Blazingstar is a distinctive native perennial of dry, rocky or sandy, open woodlands, prairies, glades, and barrens across the eastern United States from New England south to Florida and west to Nebraska, immediately recognizable among blazingstars by the squarrose (stiffly spreading) tips of its phyllary bracts — the scales surrounding each flower head — that curve sharply outward, giving the flower head a rough, star-like appearance. The large, intensely purple flower heads are produced from July through September on stiff, upright stems, providing outstanding nectar for migrating monarch butterflies, native bumblebees, sphinx moths, and many species of native bees and butterflies. Adapted to lean, infertile soils in full sun, Scaly Blazingstar is longer-lived and more reliably perennial than some blazingstars when grown in appropriate dry, xeric conditions. Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in dry, rocky or sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil; established corms multiply slowly to form impressive, long-lived clumps.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in well-drained, fertile soil in part shade; Scarborough lily blooms best when slightly pot-bound — do not divide unnecessarily. It is semi-evergreen, keeping some leaves through winter, and unlike many South African bulbs does not require a dry rest period. Damaged below 28°F; grow outdoors in zones 9–11 or as a long-lived container plant.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in part shade or as a container specimen; Scarborough lily (formerly Vallota speciosa) is a classic South African bulb in the amaryllis family prized for its outstanding clusters of large, brilliant-red to scarlet, funnel-shaped flowers — 3–4 inches across, borne 3–9 per scape on stout stems rising above arching, strap-like, evergreen leaves in summer (July–September). Unlike most South African bulbs, it does not require a dry rest period and remains semi-evergreen in mild climates, making it simpler to manage than the dormant bulbs. It blooms reliably year after year in the garden in zones 9–11 and is one of the most dependable and longest-lived of all container bulbs in colder climates, where a single large pot can be maintained for decades. The name 'Scarborough Lily' originates from a shipwreck off Scarborough, England in the 1600s — bulbs from the wreck washed ashore and naturalized on the coast, drawing Victorian-era attention to this South African species.

subcategory: East African cat and dog repellent ornamental
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile, moist to moderately dry soil in zone 10–12, or grow as an annual in zone 8–9; Scaredy Cat Plant (Pee-off Plant, Dog's Coleus) is a robust, strongly odorous herbaceous perennial from East Africa and South Asia — with thick, succulent-textured, toothed, bright-green leaves that emit a powerful, pungent odor of skunk and dog urine when touched — reportedly repelling cats, dogs, and other mammals from garden beds when planted around borders and problem areas.
directions: Root Plectranthus caninus cuttings or plant container stock in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; keep moderately moist during active growth; pinch tips to encourage bushy growth; the pungent odor is most effective when leaves are disturbed — plant around garden borders, vegetable beds, or areas where cat or dog activity is a problem. Scaredy Cat Plant (Coleus caninus, now correctly Plectranthus caninus) has an unusual and practical role in the garden — its powerful, highly unpleasant odor (described as a combination of skunk and dog urine, released when leaves are touched or crushed) is claimed to repel cats and dogs from treated garden areas. Scientific evidence for its effectiveness is anecdotal but widespread among gardeners who use it; it is most commonly employed as a border plant around vegetable gardens, bird feeders, and beds where cat digging and fouling are problems. The smell is quite intense when disturbed but less noticeable from a distance — making it an interesting practical solution that doesn't visually disrupt the garden. The plant itself is attractive enough: thick, slightly succulent, bright-green leaves on robust stems with small blue-purple flower spikes reminiscent of other Plectranthus. Native to tropical East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania) and India, it grows as a perennial in zone 10–12 and is easily grown as an annual from cuttings in cooler zones.

plant_note: Start transplants after cold stratification or direct sow in fall in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy to rocky, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; scarlet bugler tolerates heat and some humidity better than many western penstemons and adapts well to garden conditions across a broad range.
directions: Start transplants after cold stratification or direct sow in fall in very well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy to rocky, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; scarlet bugler tolerates heat and some humidity better than many western penstemons and adapts well to garden conditions across a broad range. Penstemon barbatus is the quintessential hummingbird penstemon — long (1–2 inch), narrow, vivid scarlet to coral-red, strongly reflexed tubular flowers on tall, wiry, branching stems in early summer through midsummer are perfectly adapted to ruby-throated hummingbird pollination, and individual flowers are often visited dozens of times per hour by foraging hummingbirds; it is native to dry, rocky slopes from Colorado to southern Mexico and blooms with extraordinary abundance and grace. More heat-tolerant and long-lived than many western penstemons; an outstanding early summer color element in dry pollinator gardens.

plant_note: Plant container plants or root cuttings in spring in dry to moist, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; this native Florida Panhandle plant is exceptionally drought-tolerant and produces spectacular hummingbird-attracting scarlet flowers from late summer through fall.
directions: Plant in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants are highly drought-tolerant and require little supplemental irrigation in zone 8–10. Scarlet calamint is a native Florida and Georgia Panhandle herb in the mint family (Lamiaceae) with an extremely limited natural range in the coastal plain, but it is increasingly available in native plant nurseries and is among the most hummingbird-attractive natives for the Deep South; it produces arching stems with small, slightly fuzzy, aromatic leaves and clusters of brilliant scarlet-red tubular flowers from late July through October that are irresistible to ruby-throated hummingbirds and are rarely touched by deer. The plant has a bushy, somewhat sprawling habit and is excellent in native pollinator gardens, dry herbaceous borders, and naturalistic plantings in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; light cold stratification aids germination.
directions: This southwestern native perennial reaches up to thirty inches and bears deep red flowers that stand out against rich green foliage in pollinator gardens. Sow seed in early spring or fall and give it a cool period to improve germination. It thrives in moderately dry, well-drained soil and full sun to part shade. Once established it is quite drought tolerant. Deadhead to prolong bloom and leave some seed to naturalize.

plant_note: Direct sow in place; short-lived, so succession sow.
directions: Broadcast scarlet flax seed thinly on prepared soil in early spring and rake in lightly. The brilliant red saucer-shaped flowers dance atop wiry stems and are a favorite in wildflower mixes. Because individual plants are short-lived, make successive sowings for continuous color through the season. It thrives in full sun and lean, well-drained soil with minimal supplemental water.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; scarlet gilia is a biennial that forms a rosette in its first year and blooms in its second summer. Self-sows freely to form self-perpetuating colonies in rocky, open, sunny mountain habitats.
directions: Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained, lean, sandy or rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet gilia is one of the most spectacular wildflowers of the Rocky Mountain West, producing tall, slender stems bearing dense clusters of brilliantly scarlet, tubular flowers in midsummer — one of the primary hummingbird wildflowers of mountain meadows and open pine forests from British Columbia to Mexico. The narrow, star-shaped flowers are perfect for ruby-throated, broad-tailed, and calliope hummingbirds. The distinctive finely cut, ferny leaves and the brilliant red color make it immediately recognizable. In areas with both hummingbirds and hawkmoths, the same population shows remarkable flower color variation — red for hummingbirds, white-to-pink for hawkmoths — a famous example of selection pressure from different pollinators. Self-sows readily in open, dry, rocky conditions to form naturalized colonies in mountain or xeric gardens.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring with at least one growing bud per division, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; scarlet ginger is among the hardier hedychiums and establishes more readily than many tender species — rhizomes benefit from mulching in zone 7 gardens to protect against hard freezes, where the tops die back but established rhizomes often persist and resprout.
