directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; scarlet ginger (orange ginger) is a Himalayan species widely recognized as producing some of the most elegantly narrow and intensely fragrant of all hedychium flower spikes — in summer and early fall, dense, 8–12-inch, cylindrical spikes emerge from the tips of the leafy pseudostems and open a succession of narrow-petaled flowers in vivid orange-red to bright scarlet, each with projecting, vivid-red stamens and filaments, creating a spike of spidery, intensely colored, flame-like flowers. The fragrance is deeply sweet, penetrating, and somewhat different from other hedychiums — more spicy and persistent. Scarlet ginger is among the cold-hardiest of the ornamental hedychiums (to approximately 5–10°F in zone 7 when rhizomes are mulched) and one of the most drought-tolerant after establishment. The tall, upright pseudostems clothed in glossy, lance-shaped leaves create an architectural tropical effect in the partial-shade border. An excellent and relatively hardy Himalayan ginger for zone 7–10 gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall after lightly scarifying seeds; cold winter conditions improve germination and establishment the following spring.
directions: Scarlet Globemallow is a low, spreading native perennial groundcover of dry, open grasslands, roadsides, and disturbed ground throughout the Great Plains and western United States, ranging from Canada south to Mexico. From May through August its stems are covered in bright scarlet-orange, 5-petaled mallow flowers 0.75 to 1 inch across, held on upright stems clothed in deeply lobed, gray-green, hairy leaves. Among the toughest of native perennials, it endures extreme drought, heat, and cold across a wide range from zones 3 to 9 and spreads gradually by rhizomes and root sprouts to form open colonies. Lightly scarify seeds before direct sowing in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; established plants require virtually no supplemental water or care.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; scarlet honey myrtle is native to the seasonally moist, sandy soils of southwestern Western Australia and is more tolerant of summer moisture than many other Australian natives. It blooms in spring and early summer, producing vivid, brilliant-red, bottlebrush-like flower spikes outstanding for nectar-feeding birds. Several natural flower-color variants exist: scarlet-red, salmon-orange, pink, and purple-lilac.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet honey myrtle is a medium-sized Australian shrub that produces in spring and early summer one of the most vivid and brilliant-red bottlebrush-type flower displays in the Melaleuca genus: dense, cylindrical, bottlebrush-like spikes of bright, true-scarlet to vivid red flowers composed of numerous stamen bundles projecting from the central axis, each cluster of stamens bright scarlet-red, the whole spike a dense, vivid, bristling cylinder of saturated red from 2–3 inches long. The flower color is among the most intense, pure reds of any commonly cultivated Australian shrub. Natural color variants also occur within the species — including salmon, pink, and purple-lilac forms — providing additional color options from the same species. Like other Melaleuca species it produces nectar that is highly attractive to honeyeating birds in Australia and hummingbirds in cultivation, the bottlebrush structure perfectly adapted for bird pollination by providing a stable perch while the bird probes for nectar. Somewhat more moisture-tolerant than many Australian natives, making it more adaptable to the wet summer conditions of the Gulf Coast in zone 9.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall near the roots of grass species (little bluestem, sideoats grama) for cold stratification; Indian paintbrush is hemiparasitic on grass roots and must be sown in the presence of suitable host grass roots to thrive.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall on the soil surface near the roots of established native grasses such as little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) or sideoats grama (Bouteloua curtipendula); Indian paintbrush is hemiparasitic on the roots of neighboring plants, especially grasses, and MUST have suitable host plant roots to survive — it will not thrive when grown alone. Castilleja coccinea is the eastern native paintbrush, a biennial or short-lived perennial whose brilliant scarlet display comes not from its true flowers but from the brightly colored bracts (modified leaves) surrounding the inconspicuous true flowers; it is one of the most spectacular native wildflowers of prairies and meadows, intensely attractive to ruby-throated hummingbirds. Because of its parasitic requirement, it is challenging to cultivate but rewards the patient gardener who establishes it correctly in a native grass meadow planting. Mix seed with native grass seed and sow together.

common_name: Scarlet Ladies' Tresses (Leafless Beaked Orchid, Red Orchid Weed, Scarlet Sacoila)
plant_note: Grow in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy to loamy, moderately fertile soil; Sacoila lanceolata is a leafless terrestrial orchid — it produces no green leaves, obtaining all nutrients through a mycorrhizal fungal relationship. Despite this, it can be grown successfully from bare-root tubers in sandy garden soil and will naturalize in disturbed, sunny ground in zone 8-12. Avoid heavy, clay-rich soils. Once established in appropriate sandy soil, it multiplies slowly and produces new stems each year. The bright scarlet-red flower spikes are among the showiest of any small native orchid. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy, lean soil — Scarlet Ladies' Tresses is a uniquely leafless terrestrial orchid that grows in open, sunny, disturbed ground and performs best in lean, well-drained, sandy soil typical of Florida roadsides and sandhills. Sacoila lanceolata is a leafless, tuberous, mycoheterotrophic-assisted terrestrial orchid native to the southeastern United States (Florida, Georgia, South Carolina) and throughout the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and South America in the Orchidaceae family. The plant is completely leafless — it produces no photosynthetic foliage whatsoever, obtaining all its carbon from mycorrhizal fungal associates in a partial mycoheterotrophic relationship, supplemented by the chlorophyll that colors the green stem and flower parts. From the underground tubers, an erect, leafless flower spike emerges annually in spring and summer, ranging from 10–24 inches tall, bearing a dense spiral raceme of tubular, scarlet-red to hot coral-red flowers with slightly spreading, recurved petal tips. The intense, vivid red color of the flower spike is extraordinary for a native orchid and makes the plant visible from considerable distance in its native habitat of sunny Florida roadsides, flatwoods margins, and disturbed sandy ground. The species has a remarkable ability to appear and multiply in disturbed, sunny, sandy soil — it can colonize mowed roadsides and open garden beds, making it genuinely useful as a naturalizing native orchid for zone 8-12 landscapes. Non-toxic.

common_name: Scarlet Ladies' Tresses (Mexican Scarlet Orchid, Cinnabar Orchid, Red Spiranthes)
plant_note: Plant tubers in fall or early spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Dichromanthus cinnabarinus grows naturally in open woodlands, rocky slopes, and disturbed areas in the highlands of Mexico and Central America (Guatemala, Honduras). It blooms in late summer to fall on erect spikes. Reduce watering in winter dormancy. The brilliant scarlet-red flower spike is one of the most vivid of any spiranthoid orchid. In zone 9, established tubers may overwinter in well-drained beds with mulch. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately lean soil — Scarlet Ladies' Tresses grows most naturally in the well-drained, rocky to sandy soils of open highland woodlands and performs better in lean, well-drained conditions than in rich, moist garden soil. Dichromanthus cinnabarinus is a small, tuberous, deciduous terrestrial orchid in the tribe Cranichideae (subtribe Spiranthinae) native to Mexico and Central America in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most brightly colored of the ladies' tresses-type orchids. Like the white Spiranthes species of the eastern US, Dichromanthus produces a rosette of basal leaves and a spirally-twisted raceme of flowers along an erect spike — but in place of the white or cream of North American Spiranthes, D. cinnabarinus produces flowers in vivid cinnabar-red to brilliant scarlet, one of the most intense flower colors in the entire ladies' tresses group. The individual flowers are tubular, about 0.5 inch long, in bright scarlet to orange-red, arranged in a one- or two-ranked spiral along the erect, 12–24 inch spike. The flowering season is late summer to fall, triggered by the onset of cooler temperatures. Hummingbirds are attracted to the brilliant scarlet flower spikes. A charming and rarely seen spiranthoid orchid for zone 9-11 collectors interested in hardy, ground-dwelling orchids outside the epiphyte mainstream. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring or fall in dry, sandy, gravelly, or clay, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun. Scarify seed coats with sandpaper or soak in warm water for 24 hours before planting to speed germination. Scarlet Mallow is extremely drought-tolerant once established and will not thrive in wet or overly amended soils.
directions: Scarlet Mallow is a native perennial of the western Great Plains, dry prairies, and desert grasslands from Canada south to New Mexico and Texas, producing clusters of vivid orange-red to coral flowers with a satiny sheen on low, spreading mounds of silvery-gray, lobed foliage from spring through summer. One of the most drought-tolerant of all native wildflowers, Scarlet Mallow thrives in the hottest, driest, most exposed sites — dry roadsides, eroded slopes, rock gardens, and xeric borders — where its cheerful flowers provide an extended season of orange color from May through August in full sun. The gray, star-shaped hairs that cover the entire plant give it a silvery appearance that reflects heat and reduces water loss, making it exceptionally adapted to harsh, sunny, dry conditions. Scarify the hard seed coat before planting by rubbing with sandpaper or soaking overnight; direct sow in spring or fall in dry, well-drained soil in full sun — established plants require no irrigation and resent wet or heavy soils.

plant_note: Surface-sow seeds in cool, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade or start transplants indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; scarlet monkey flower requires consistently wet soil and will not tolerate drought at any stage.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade beside water features, in bog gardens, or at moist streambanks; scarlet monkey flower is a spectacular western native wildflower producing intensely vivid scarlet-red, tubular flowers on upright stems that are outstanding hummingbird magnets — the elongated red tube is precisely designed for hummingbird pollination, with the stamens positioned to dust the bird's head with pollen as it feeds. Plants bloom from late spring through fall in cool, moist conditions. Like yellow monkey flower, it requires consistently wet soil and colonizes stream margins, seeps, and wet rocky canyon walls in its native western habitat from Oregon to Baja California. In the shade garden it is extraordinary for adding hummingbird-attracting red color in moist, shaded spots where most other red flowers fail. Excellent in containers kept standing in water in partial shade. Treat as a tender perennial in zone 9–10, short-lived perennial in zone 5–8.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet morning glory is a vigorous warm-season annual vine native to tropical Americas that self-sows freely in zone 9 and establishes quickly in any sunny, warm location. Scarify seeds for faster germination.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet morning glory (hummingbird vine) produces small, brilliant scarlet, tubular flowers with a yellow throat on vigorous twining stems — like a more compact, finer-textured version of the large garden morning glories, but with a much more intensely colored, tubular flower that is irresistible to hummingbirds and monarch butterflies. The distinctive ivy-shaped leaves (hederifolia = ivy-leaved) distinguish it from other red-flowered morning glories. Native to tropical Americas and naturalized throughout the subtropical US, it self-sows freely in zone 9 gardens where it provides a season-long display on fences, trellises, and shrubs. More drought-tolerant than many morning glories once established. An excellent hummingbird plant for warm-climate gardens that provides continuous summer color with minimal care.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; scarlet oak requires excellent drainage and performs poorly in wet, compacted, or alkaline conditions. It is particularly well-suited to dry, sandy, or rocky upland sites.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, dry to average soil in full sun; scarlet oak is named for the spectacular, deep scarlet fall color — one of the most brilliantly red of all native trees, maintaining its color for 4–6 weeks in fall. The leaves are deeply cut with pointed lobes typical of the red oak group, and the deeply cleft sinuses extend nearly to the midrib, creating a dramatic, finely cut pattern. The tree is naturally adapted to dry, infertile, sandy or rocky upland sites where other oaks struggle, and is a pioneer species on disturbed dry slopes in the East. The acorns are a critical food source for squirrels, blue jays, wood ducks, and wild turkeys. Well-suited as a street tree and park tree in well-drained, slightly acidic urban soils. The spectacular fall color and attractive form make it one of the finest native oaks for landscape use.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry, well-drained ground; cold-moist stratification over winter promotes reliable spring germination.
directions: Scatter seed in fall over dry, calcareous or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, pressing lightly into the soil surface and allowing winter cold to break dormancy naturally. Distinct cupped (perfoliate) leaves clasp the stem, making seedlings easy to identify and protect during thinning to 12-18 inches apart in spring. Plants bloom with vivid scarlet-red, tubular flowers from April through June on tall stems reaching 2-4 feet, drawing hummingbirds throughout the blooming season. Thrives with no supplemental irrigation once established; ideal for Texas Hill Country, post oak savanna, and south-central wildflower gardens in zones 6-9.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade after frost; scarlet plumbago is more shade-tolerant than the common blue plumbago (P. auriculata) and actually performs better in partial to full shade conditions — in full sun in hot climates the leaves tend to yellow and the plant looks stressed, while partial shade produces the healthiest, most attractive growth.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; scarlet plumbago (red plumbago, rose-colored leadwort) is a Southeast Asian tropical shrub entirely different in character from the common, sprawling, blue Cape plumbago (P. auriculata) — it is an upright, non-climbing, softer-wooded tropical shrub that produces long, erect, terminal racemes of tubular, five-petaled flowers in a vivid, rich crimson-red to scarlet-red color, creating a striking and rarely seen red-flowered plumbago display that is particularly effective in the partial shade of a tropical garden. The flowers have the characteristic sticky calyx of all plumbagos and are produced in succession over a long season from spring through fall. The soft, broadly oval, bright-green leaves are larger and less glossy than common Cape plumbago. Scarlet plumbago is a distinctive and underused tropical shrub for zone 10–12 shade and partial-shade gardens, where it provides vivid red color in positions where most red-flowered tropical shrubs would fail to bloom adequately without more direct sunlight.

plant_note: Direct sow seed after the last frost or start divisions in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; scarlet rose mallow thrives in consistently wet to boggy conditions and grows naturally in swamps, marshes, and pond edges. In zone 9 it often reblooms from hard pruning in midsummer.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; scarlet rose mallow is one of the most spectacular native perennials of the eastern and Gulf Coast wetlands, producing enormous (6–8 inch) brilliant crimson-red flowers with a deep red eye on tall, robust, deeply palmate-lobed, dramatically architectural plants that grow vigorously in standing water or perpetually wet soil. The flowers have a uniquely delicate, crepe-paper texture and the color is among the most vivid reds in the plant kingdom. Unlike the hybrid hardy hibiscus (H. moscheutos x) which needs drier soil, H. coccineus must have consistently wet or saturated conditions to thrive — it grows naturally in swamps and tidal marshes. It dies back completely to the ground after frost but regrows vigorously from the roots each spring, emerging late (June in zone 9) and quickly reaching its mature height. An outstanding native for rain gardens, pond margins, water features, and wet spots that are otherwise difficult to plant attractively.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or plant container stock in full sun in moist to wet, fertile soil in zone 6–10; Scarlet Rosemallow is a tall, spectacular native perennial of the coastal marshes, swamps, and wet bottomlands of coastal Georgia, Florida, Alabama, and Louisiana, producing enormous, pure scarlet-red, dinner-plate-sized flowers all summer on tall (5–8 foot) stems — one of the showiest native plants of the southeastern coastal plain.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist to wet, fertile, organically rich soil; Hibiscus coccineus thrives in consistently moist to wet conditions and is ideal for pond edges, rain gardens, and moist low spots — keep consistently moist in summer, water heavily during hot dry periods, and mulch thickly to retain soil moisture. Hibiscus coccineus (Scarlet Rosemallow, Texas Star, or Texas Star Hibiscus) is a tall, robust, herbaceous perennial native to the coastal marshes, tidal swamps, freshwater wetlands, and stream banks of coastal Georgia, Florida (especially the panhandle and northern peninsula), Alabama, and Louisiana — one of the most visually spectacular native plants of the southeastern coastal plain. The enormous, pure scarlet-crimson, 5-petaled flowers — up to 6–8 inches across, with no color variation — are borne prolifically from late June through September on 5–8 foot upright stems above deeply cut, maple-leaf-like, dark-green foliage that is itself ornamentally attractive. The combination of bold tropical-looking foliage and brilliant scarlet flowers over a long summer season makes it one of the most outstanding native perennials for large garden settings, waterside plantings, and bird gardens — hummingbirds and bumblebees work the flowers continuously. Plants die completely to the ground in winter (even in zones 9–10) and re-emerge in late spring; mark locations to avoid disturbing dormant crowns. Excellent for Gulf Coast rain gardens, pond margins, and naturalistic native plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant container stock after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet rosemallow grows naturally along pond margins, wet meadows, and roadside ditches across the eastern and central US.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; scarlet rosemallow is a native wetland hibiscus of the eastern and central US, producing large, pink to pale lavender flowers with the distinctive dark maroon eye typical of the native rosemallows. The three-lobed, halberd-shaped (hastate) leaves distinguish this species from the broader-leaved H. moscheutos and H. grandiflorus. The plant grows naturally in wet to moist, open habitats — pond margins, wet meadows, and roadside ditches — and provides spectacular late-summer flowers that attract numerous native bumblebees. Like all native hibiscus, the seeds are eaten by wildlife and the leaves serve as larval food for several moth species. A bold, showy native for wet, sunny gardens and rain garden features in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; do not plant out until nighttime temperatures remain above 50°F. In zones 9–11, scarlet sage grows as a perennial subshrub and can be planted year-round.
directions: Start seed in warm conditions 6–8 weeks before last frost; scarlet sage is a Brazilian perennial grown as an annual in most climates, producing dense spikes of vivid scarlet flowers that are among the most hummingbird-attractive of all bedding plants. Modern cultivars have expanded the color range to include salmon, coral, white, purple, and bicolors. It performs best in partial shade in hot climates (zone 8 and above), where full sun causes bleaching; in cooler climates it tolerates full sun. The plants bloom continuously from summer until frost without deadheading. In zones 9–11 it grows as a perennial and may persist for several years, becoming more woody at the base. Excellent for mass plantings, containers, and hummingbird gardens.

common_name: Scarlet Star Bromeliad (Guzmania, Tufted Airplant, Carmine Guzmania)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; Guzmania lingulata cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. Grow in well-draining, slightly acidic potting mix or orchid bark. Keep the central leaf cup (tank) filled with water at all times — flush and refill monthly to prevent stagnation. The flower head emerges from the central cup when the plant is ready to bloom; individual bromeliads bloom only once and then die, but produce offsets (pups) at the base that can be separated and grown into new plants. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in moderate to bright indirect shade — Scarlet Star Bromeliad is one of the most shade-tolerant of the commonly grown bromeliads and one of the only popular flowering houseplants that will maintain attractive foliage and bloom in true low-light indoor conditions. Guzmania lingulata is a tanktype bromeliad native to the humid tropical forests of Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America (Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia, Peru), growing as an epiphyte on tree branches in the deep shade of cloud forest understory. The plant forms a rosette of long, smooth, glossy, bright-green, strap-shaped leaves that cup upward to form a central water-collecting tank — a characteristic feature of bromeliad genera adapted to epiphytic life in humid environments. When the plant matures and the environmental conditions trigger blooming, the central rosette produces an erect inflorescence of brilliant scarlet to orange-red bracts (modified leaves) surrounding small, white, tubular flowers — the entire central structure turns a vivid red-orange that provides color for months, far longer than typical flowers. Commercial cultivars include forms in red, orange, yellow, and bicolored bract combinations. After blooming, the parent plant gradually declines while producing 2–4 offsets that grow into new, blooming-sized plants. Among the best choices for low-light indoor flowering color. Non-toxic to pets.

common_name: Scentless Mock Orange / Wild Mock Orange
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown stock in early spring in well-drained to dry soil; this species is native to rocky woodland slopes and bluffs and tolerates lean, shallow soils well. Softwood cuttings taken in early summer root readily and are the most practical propagation method.
directions: Plant in partial sun with good air circulation in well-drained to dry soil; unlike the common Mock Orange, this native species thrives in lean, rocky soils along woodland edges and bluffs without supplemental fertilization. The large, pure white four-petaled flowers appear in late spring and, while scentless, are showy enough to be a garden highlight and attract native pollinators. Allow ample space — established shrubs reach 6–10 ft in both height and spread and develop a bold, multi-stemmed arching form. Prune selectively after flowering, removing the oldest stems at the base every few years to rejuvenate the shrub and encourage strong new flowering wood.

common_name: Schillings Dwarf Yaupon Holly (Compact Rounded Native Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Schillings Dwarf is a naturally compact, dense, mounding male selection of native yaupon holly that needs little to no shearing to stay tidy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Schillings Dwarf (also sold as Stokes Dwarf) is one of the most widely planted compact hollies in the Gulf South, a naturally dense, rounded, slow-growing selection of native yaupon that fits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mass plantings without the constant shearing that fast-growing shrubs demand. Being a male selection it does not set the red berries of the species, but it more than compensates with an extremely low-maintenance, uniformly rounded habit and outstanding tolerance of heat, drought, wind, salt spray, and poor soil, making it a workhorse plant across coastal Gulf landscapes. Established plants need very little supplemental water and only occasional light shearing if a stricter formal shape is desired.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring into dry, rocky clay-loam or well-drained open soil in full sun; source only from nurseries with legally propagated stock, as this is a federally endangered species.
directions: Schweinitz's Sunflower is a federally endangered perennial sunflower endemic to the piedmont of North and South Carolina, where it persists on a small number of dry, rocky clay-loam roadsides and openings in oak-hickory forest that experience periodic disturbance historically provided by fire and bison grazing. Tall, branching stems with large, rough, sessile leaves support bright yellow flowers 2.5 to 3 inches across that open from September through October, providing critical nectar for monarch butterflies during fall migration and seeds relished by goldfinches and other finches. Grow in poor, dry, open, well-drained soil in full sun with excellent drainage — this species is notably intolerant of wet or compacted conditions and actually performs better in lean soil without supplemental fertilizer. Purchase only from specialty native plant nurseries carrying legally propagated stock; cultivating this plant from nursery-grown transplants is an important act of conservation for one of North America's rarest sunflowers.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), lean, sandy or gravelly, peaty soil in full sun; Scotch heather requires extremely acidic, nutrient-poor, well-drained soil and full sun — it fails quickly in fertile, neutral, or alkaline soil or in shade. Do not fertilize.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.0–5.5), lean, sandy or gravelly, peaty soil in full sun; Scotch heather is the defining plant of the British moorlands — the vast open landscapes of Scotland, northern England, Wales, and Ireland carpeted with purple heather in August are among the most iconic and beloved landscapes in Europe. The genus Calluna contains only this single species, distinguished from the related Erica heathers by having the colored sepals (not petals) as the main display. Hundreds of cultivars exist in shades from white through pink, lavender, and deep purple, as well as double-flowered and golden-foliaged forms. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain compact, bushy plants — unsheared plants become leggy and open. Invaluable for dry, acidic, heathland-style gardens in appropriate climates. Late-summer (August) bloom provides nectar for migrating monarch butterflies, honeybees, and native bees during the fall migration period.

plant_note: Plant in early spring in sandy, freely draining soil; Scotch Rose is especially suited to coastal and exposed hillside sites. Division of established clumps or rooted suckers can be transplanted in early spring.
directions: Plant in poor, sandy, or gravelly soil in a fully exposed, sunny location; Scotch Rose is one of the most wind and cold tolerant of all roses and actually performs poorly in rich or waterlogged ground. It spreads steadily by underground suckers to form a low, dense, weed-suppressing thicket, making it excellent for stabilizing dry banks and coastal dunes. The distinctive dark purple-black hips ripen in late summer and persist into autumn, providing food for birds. Propagate by detaching and replanting rooted suckers in early spring, or take semi-hardwood cuttings in mid-summer.

common_name: Scrambling Sky Vine (Purple Thunbergia, Blue Kenya Clockvine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring after last frost on a trellis, fence, or through an established shrub in full sun to partial shade; Scrambling Sky Vine grows rapidly in warm weather and blooms prolifically through the warm months with peak bloom when temperatures moderate in fall. In zone 9a, it freezes back to roots in cold winters but resprouts reliably in spring; in zone 9b-10 it is semi-evergreen and blooms nearly year-round. Excellent for climbing into established shrubs or on wire fencing.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Scrambling Sky Vine thrives in zone 9 humid warmth and produces its best bloom in late summer and fall when daytime temperatures drop below 95°F. Thunbergia battiscombei is a scrambling, semi-woody tropical vine from East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda) in the Acanthaceae family, closely related to the widely-grown Bengal Clockvine (T. grandiflora) but producing smaller flowers in a richer, deeper purple-violet with a contrasting yellow-white throat. The flowers are trumpet-shaped, 2–3 inches in diameter, and borne singly on slender stems along the length of the twining vine — the deep violet-purple with the pale, open throat is one of the most saturated blues available in a tropical vine and blooms continuously from late spring through fall in zone 9. Unlike the enormous, vigorous T. grandiflora which can overwhelm a small space, T. battiscombei is more manageable in scale, typically reaching 10–15 feet and controllable with annual pruning. The common name 'Scrambling Sky Vine' reflects its habit of weaving its way through other shrubs and structures rather than climbing tightly around a support. An excellent choice for informal tropical gardens, butterfly gardens, and screening, where its continuous production of purple flowers provides months of interest.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Screw Pine is a dramatic, architectural ornamental tree from Madagascar and Mauritius — not a true pine or palm — producing a distinctive spirally arranged rosette of long, stiff, spiny-edged, green leaves at the ends of multiple trunks supported by aerial prop roots, and bold, pineapple-sized orange-red fruit clusters that attract wildlife and provide edible starchy pulp in its native range.
directions: Plant Pandanus utilis in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; highly tolerant of salt spray, coastal conditions, and sandy, nutrient-poor soils once established; water moderately during establishment and reduce thereafter; the aerial prop roots that arch from the trunk to the soil are distinctive and should not be damaged. Screw Pine is one of the most architecturally distinctive of all tropical plants — the multiple, branching trunks supported by tall, arching, aerial prop roots and topped by dramatic rosettes of long, spirally arranged, sword-like leaves (the 'screw' pattern of the leaves gives the plant its common name, though it is unrelated to true pines) create a bold, unmistakably tropical silhouette. Native to Madagascar and the Mascarene Islands, it is widely planted as an ornamental throughout tropical and subtropical coastal regions worldwide for its excellent tolerance of salt spray, sandy soils, and coastal exposure. The large, pineapple-like compound fruits (syncarp) are produced by female trees and consist of densely packed wedge-shaped segments; the starchy base of each segment is edible in Madagascar. The long, flexible leaves are woven into baskets, mats, hats, and thatch (the species name 'utilis' means 'useful'). A magnificent specimen or screen plant for zone 10–12 coastal gardens and tropical landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in pure, infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Scrub Palmetto requires the xeric, nutrient-poor conditions of Florida scrub and will decline in clay, irrigated, or heavily amended soils. No supplemental fertilizer or irrigation is needed once established.
directions: Scrub Palmetto is a small, ground-hugging native palm endemic to the ancient, fire-maintained Florida scrub habitats of the central Florida peninsula, growing in pure white sand soils of extreme infertility and drainage alongside the rarest plants and animals in North America. This palmetto typically remains stemless or develops a very short trunk at or below ground level, producing a cluster of bluish-green, fan-shaped leaves 4–6 feet across that emerge directly from the root mass in a way that makes it fire-resistant and able to regenerate rapidly after scrub burns. The small, black, marble-sized fruits are eaten by Florida Scrub-Jays, gopher tortoises, black bears, and other scrub wildlife, making Scrub Palmetto a keystone species in this imperiled ecosystem. Plant seeds in well-drained, infertile, sandy soil in full sun in warm weather; once the root system is established, the slow-growing plants require no supplemental fertilizer, no irrigation, and no soil amendments.

plant_note: Plant small bulbils 1 to 2 inches deep in spring into gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; cool, moist conditions favor establishment.
directions: Plant the small bulbils 1 to 2 inches deep in spring into gritty, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a cool, partially shaded position such as a north- or east-facing rock garden. This Falkland Islands native forms a low, slowly spreading mat of waxy, gray-green multi-leaflet foliage that is distinctive even when out of flower. Large, sweetly fragrant white to pale pink blooms appear in late spring and early summer, sitting just above the foliage on short stems. Avoid hot, dry sites and summer drought; a top-dressing of grit around the bulbils discourages rot while keeping roots cool.

plant_note: Plant divisions or sow seed in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; sea campion is extremely salt- and wind-tolerant and thrives on coastal cliffs and rocky banks.
directions: Plant divisions or sow seed in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; sea campion requires superb drainage and tolerates no shade or waterlogging — a perfect rock garden and dry wall plant. Silene uniflora (syn. S. vulgaris subsp. maritima) is a native coastal European perennial forming compact, cushion-forming mats of blue-gray, glaucous leaves on cliffs, shingle beaches, and rocky coastal outcrops; it produces a profusion of white, deeply notched, 5-petaled flowers with distinctively inflated, bladder-like calyces (resembling small balloons below the petals) from late spring through summer. It is exceptionally salt- and wind-tolerant, making it valuable for coastal gardens, and forms an attractive, low groundcover on dry banks, in rock gardens, and on top of dry stone walls. The double-flowered cultivar 'Flore Pleno' is particularly ornamental.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in late summer with the neck of the bulb just at soil level in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; sea daffodil requires extremely well-drained, sandy or gritty soil and must have dry summer dormancy — wet summer conditions cause bulb rot. It flowers best when crowded and pot-bound, so avoid frequent division.
directions: Plant bulbs in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; sea daffodil is a stunning Mediterranean coastal bulb growing on sandy beaches and dunes from the Atlantic coast of Portugal through the Mediterranean basin, producing pure white, sweetly fragrant flowers resembling a large, elaborate spider lily in late summer — three to twelve large, pure-white, sweetly scented flowers per stem with frilly, fringed petals and a prominent cup. The broad, strap-shaped, glaucous blue-gray leaves are themselves ornamental and persist through the growing season. It thrives in exactly the conditions found in Gulf Coast beach gardens: sandy, well-drained, alkaline, saline soils baked by summer sun. After summer dormancy, the flower stems emerge in August and September before the new season's foliage. It is quite different from the native Hymenocallis (spider lilies) despite the similar flower shape and is an excellent companion to Mediterranean herbs and other drought-tolerant bulbs.

common_name: Sea Foam Rose (Sprawling White Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Plant container roses in late winter through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun; Sea Foam tolerates partial shade better than most roses but flowers most abundantly in full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Sea Foam is an outstanding spreading white shrub rose introduced in 1964 — a low, wide-spreading (6–8 foot spread), semi-evergreen groundcover rose producing clusters of small (1.5-inch), double, creamy-white flowers with a slight blush pink at center from late spring through fall. The sprawling, cascading habit creates an elegant weeping effect when planted on slopes, banks, and over walls where the long, flexible canes cascade downward — one of the finest rose choices for embankment plantings and flowing over retaining walls. Sea Foam has outstanding disease resistance, particularly to black spot — a nearly century-old cultivar that has proven its durability across a wide range of climates without the intensive spraying that hybrid teas require. The semi-evergreen foliage (fully evergreen in zone 9) remains attractive year-round. Sea Foam's low stature (18–36 inches tall) and wide spread make it outstanding as a groundcover, bank stabilizer, and cascading accent. Despite its groundcover habit, established plants are quite drought-tolerant and require minimal irrigation. The creamy-white flower clusters contrast beautifully with the dark-green, glossy foliage. In zone 9, Sea Foam blooms nearly continuously from March through December — one of the longest bloom seasons of any repeat-flowering rose.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall without stratification in very well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; sea holly develops a deep taproot and dislikes transplanting — sow in place or use biodegradable pots for indoor starts.
directions: Direct sow in fall in very well-drained, poor to average soil in full sun, or use biodegradable pots for indoor starts to avoid disturbing the taproot at transplanting; sea holly produces striking metallic blue-violet flowers surrounded by spiky bracts from early to midsummer that are among the most architectural elements available for the sunny border or dry garden. The steel-blue coloring is exceptional for cut flowers both fresh and dried. Sea holly thrives in sandy, gravelly, alkaline soils and is highly drought-tolerant once its deep taproot is established — rich soils cause floppy growth. Plants resent wet winters more than cold; excellent drainage is essential for survival. Self-sows moderately in suitable conditions.

plant_note: Plant in moist to wet, salty or brackish, well-drained sandy or silty soil in full sun; sea lavender is a salt marsh specialist that is difficult to establish from seed but transplants well from container-grown nursery stock — do not attempt in alkaline clay or fresh water sites.
directions: Sea lavender is a native perennial wildflower of Atlantic and Gulf Coast salt marshes, producing dense basal rosettes of leathery, paddle-shaped leaves and tall, branching flower stalks covered in masses of tiny, papery lavender-blue flowers in late summer and fall — the dried flowers retain their color indefinitely and are highly prized in floral arrangements, giving sea lavender enduring commercial value as a cut flower crop. The plant grows naturally in the high salt marsh zone alongside glasswort, saltmarsh cordgrass, and seaside goldenrod, thriving in conditions that kill most garden plants: high salinity, periodic flooding, and exposed coastal wind. In coastal gardens and tidal restoration plantings, it serves as a critical late-season nectar source for monarchs and native bees making their fall southward migration along the Gulf Coast, and the dried seedheads persist through winter as bird habitat. Because it tolerates salt spray and sandy, saline soil, sea lavender is also an excellent choice for stabilizing coastal buffer zones, rain gardens near the coast, and any site with brackish soil conditions.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Sea Mango is a striking tropical coastal tree with fragrant white and pink flowers and large red ornamental fruits — ALL parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are extremely toxic and contain cerberin, a powerful cardiac glycoside — handle with caution and plant away from children and livestock.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Cerbera manghas tolerates brief coastal flooding, salt spray, and periodic waterlogging in its native coastal forest habitat — water regularly in establishment, then moderately once established. Cerbera manghas (Sea Mango or Pong-pong) is an evergreen tropical tree native to the coastal forests, mangrove margins, and beach strands from Madagascar and the East African coast through South Asia, Southeast Asia, and into the Pacific islands, where it is one of the quintessential components of coastal tropical forest. The tree produces clusters of large, intensely fragrant white flowers with a bright pink or red center tube, ornamentally comparable to frangipani, followed by large (3–4 inch), smooth, shiny, green-then-red ornamental fruits resembling a small mango — entirely toxic and not to be eaten. All parts of Cerbera manghas contain cerberin, neriifolin, and related cardiac glycosides among the most toxic plant compounds known; historically the seeds were used in trial-by-ordeal poison rites in Madagascar and across the Pacific. Despite its toxicity, Sea Mango is widely planted as an ornamental street and coastal tree throughout tropical Asia and the Pacific for its compact, attractive form, fragrant flowers, and colorful fruits; it is tolerant of salt, wind, and coastal conditions. Plant in locations inaccessible to children and livestock and always wash hands after handling.

plant_note: Plant plugs or container divisions in spring in very well-drained, sandy, dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sea oats is the primary dune-stabilizing grass of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic shore and plays a critical ecological role in dune formation and erosion control — it is protected from collection in Florida, Georgia, and several other states. Purchase only nursery-grown plants.
directions: Plant nursery-grown plugs in spring in very well-drained, dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun — sea oats is the signature grass of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic barrier islands and beaches, its dramatic, gracefully drooping, flat seed heads swaying in the ocean breeze on tall, upright stems from summer through winter in one of the most iconic images of the southern coast. The long, creeping rhizomes spread underground to stabilize shifting dune sand, building and maintaining the dune systems that protect coastal communities from storm surge and erosion. Sea oats is legally protected in Florida, Georgia, and other states — collect no plants from the wild and purchase only nursery-propagated plants and seed. In coastal garden settings it is outstanding for low-maintenance, drought-tolerant, ornamental dune gardens, beach property landscaping, and sandy, salt-spray-exposed areas where few other plants succeed. The seeds are an important food source for birds in the coastal community.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, sandy, saline to neutral, dry soil in full sun; sea ox-eye daisy is highly salt-tolerant and grows naturally in coastal salt marshes, dune edges, and brackish waterway margins from Virginia to Texas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, saline-tolerant to neutral soil in full sun in coastal gardens; sea ox-eye daisy is a native, low-growing, aromatic subshrub of coastal salt marshes and tidal flats along the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain — one of the most salt-spray and salt-soil tolerant native wildflowers of the coastal zone. The bright yellow daisy flowers with their distinctive button-like centers bloom prolifically from summer through fall, providing extended season color and nectar for coastal butterflies and native bees. The grayish, succulent-like leaves reflect the plant's adaptation to the harsh saline conditions of coastal habitats. In the garden, it spreads by rhizomes to form a dense, salt-resistant ground cover that excels in coastal landscapes where few other flowering perennials survive. An outstanding plant for Zone 9a coastal Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly into sandy, well-drained coastal soil; scarify the hard seed coat with sandpaper or nick with a file before sowing, as sea pea has an exceptionally tough seed coat that delays germination without mechanical assistance.
directions: Scarify seed coats by rubbing on sandpaper or nicking with a file, then sow directly into sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; sea pea is a sprawling perennial native to coastal beaches, dunes, and shore margins throughout the Northern Hemisphere, where it stabilizes sandy substrates with deep, spreading roots and fixes atmospheric nitrogen with rhizobial bacteria. The bicolor purple and pink flowers appear in early summer and are followed by short, curved seed pods. It tolerates salt spray, drought, and nutrient-poor sand once established, but resents transplanting due to its deep root system — sow in situ or use deep biodegradable pots to start seedlings. In gardens it performs best in lean, gritty soils; rich soils promote lush foliage at the expense of flowering.

plant_note: Direct sow at last frost directly onto moist, sandy soil; seeds are tiny and should not be covered — simply press them into the soil surface and keep consistently moist until germination.
directions: Sea Pink is a native annual of Atlantic and Gulf coast salt marshes, tidal flats, and coastal meadows, producing bright pink flowers with a distinctive yellow-green starry center from July through September; it is one of the few Sabatia species truly tolerant of salt spray and brackish soils. Sow seeds directly onto moist, sandy or peaty soil in full sun at last frost, pressing the dust-fine seeds into the soil surface without covering them, and maintain consistent moisture during germination. It thrives in lean, acidic, poorly drained coastal soils that would kill most cultivated annuals and declines rapidly in rich or heavily amended garden beds. Sea Pink is an excellent choice for rain garden edges, coastal restoration plantings, and naturalistic saline meadows where its salt tolerance gives it a distinct competitive advantage.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in average soil; overly rich soil reduces blooms.
directions: These charming cosmos have fluted, seashell-shaped petals in white, pink, rose, and crimson that make an excellent cut flower. Sow seed directly after the last frost into average, well-drained soil, since rich soil reduces flowering. They prefer neglect over pampering and become drought tolerant once established. Deadhead to extend the show or leave seed heads to self-sow. Full sun keeps the tall plants sturdy and blooming into fall.

common_name: Sea Shells Zinnia (Unique Rolled Quilled-Petal Zinnia Mix)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sea Shells is a distinctive zinnia mix whose petals curl and roll lengthwise into tube-like, shell-shaped forms rather than lying flat, giving the blooms a unique, whimsical texture unlike any other common zinnia type.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 9-12 inches. Sea Shells is a novelty heirloom zinnia mix distinguished by petals that curl and roll along their length into narrow, tube-like quills rather than lying flat like typical zinnia petals, giving each bloom a distinctive, whimsical, almost fringed appearance often compared to small seashells or curled ribbons. Flowers come in a mix of pink, rose, orange, yellow, and white on plants otherwise similar in size and vigor to standard zinnias. The unusual petal form makes Sea Shells a popular novelty and conversation-piece addition to cutting gardens and mixed bouquets, standing out clearly next to flat-petaled zinnia varieties. Deadhead or harvest regularly to encourage continuous branching and flowering from midsummer through frost, and grow in full sun with good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew, the primary disease risk for zinnias in humid climates.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sea thrift is extremely salt-tolerant and wind-resistant — ideal for coastal gardens where many other plants struggle. Deadhead spent flower stems promptly to extend the bloom season and prevent the grass-like foliage from becoming bare in the center. Divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sea thrift is a circumboreal coastal wildflower — a salt-spray survivor of sea cliffs and rocky shores across the Northern Hemisphere — forming dense, rounded cushions of narrow, grass-like, deep-green leaves (evergreen to semi-evergreen) and producing from spring through early summer (with possible rebloom in fall) spherical, papery, bright-rose-pink to deep-pink or white flower heads on stiff, upright stems of 6–12 inches, each rounded head tightly packed with tiny florets. The papery bracts persist decoratively as the flowers fade, extending the display. Salt tolerance is exceptional — truly one of the best plants for seaside gardens exposed to ocean spray and saline winds. It thrives in the same difficult conditions as thyme and lavender: lean, dry, well-drained soils in full sun with little competition. A classic edging plant for seaside cottage gardens, rock gardens, and gravel paths. The cultivar 'Dusseldorf Pride' (deep rose-pink) and 'Alba' (pure white) are widely available.

plant_note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in sandy, well-drained to moist, saline or brackish soils in full sun; seashore dropseed is ideal for sandy beach margins, salt flats, coastal erosion buffers, and stabilizing sandy soils in full sun with high salt spray.
directions: Seashore dropseed is a low, mat-forming native perennial grass of coastal sand dunes, beach margins, and salt flats throughout the Gulf and Atlantic coasts — one of the most salt-tolerant of all native grasses, it thrives directly behind the beach berm where salt spray and occasional saltwater flooding eliminate nearly all competition. Dense, creeping rhizomes and stolons knit sandy coastal soils together tightly, making seashore dropseed one of the most effective native plants for stabilizing sandy beaches, eroding shorelines, and coastal buffer strips without the invasiveness problems of non-native beach grasses. The fine-textured, wiry green leaves form attractive low mounds that turn tawny in winter; small, upright seed spikes provide food for ground-feeding birds. In coastal gardens and seaside landscapes, use seashore dropseed as a low-maintenance edging or groundcover grass in areas exposed to salt spray, sandy alkaline soil, and reflected heat from pavement or sea walls — conditions where ornamental grasses and lawn species fail.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring after frost in wet, salt-tolerant, sandy or loamy coastal soil in full sun; scarify the hard seed coat with sandpaper or soak in warm water for 24 hours before planting to speed germination. Seashore Mallow tolerates fresh to brackish coastal marsh conditions and periodic inundation.
directions: Seashore Mallow is a native perennial of coastal marshes, tidal margins, and salt-tolerant wetlands along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Long Island south through Florida and west to Texas, where it produces an extended succession of pink hibiscus-like flowers from midsummer through fall on upright, 3–5 foot stems. The seeds are high in protein and edible fatty acids, the roots are starchy and edible, and the mucilaginous leaves and flowers are used in folk medicine similarly to other Malvaceae family members — making Seashore Mallow one of the few native coastal plants with genuine multi-use potential. An important nectar source for native bumblebees, honeybees, and the Cloudless Sulphur butterfly, it has been studied as a potential grain crop for salt-impaired soils where conventional crops cannot grow. Plant in full sun in wet, coastal, sandy to loamy soil; Seashore Mallow tolerates moderate salinity, fresh to brackish conditions, and periodic flooding, self-seeding readily once established in appropriate settings.

common_name: Seashore Paspalum (Salt-Tolerant Turf Grass, Sea Green Paspalum)
plant_note: Establish from sprigs or sod after last frost; seashore paspalum is primarily used in coastal areas with saline soils, irrigation with brackish water, or sites near salt water where other turf grasses fail. It is the only commonly available turf grass that can be irrigated with recycled wastewater or mild seawater, making it valuable for coastal commercial turf in water-restricted areas.
directions: Establish from sprigs or sod in spring; mow at 0.5–1.5 inches for fine-textured cultivars or 1.5–3 inches for coarser types. Seashore paspalum (Paspalum vaginatum) is the most salt-tolerant warm-season turf grass available for Gulf Coast and tropical applications — used in coastal golf courses, athletic fields, and landscapes where seawater intrusion, brackish irrigation, and high soil salinity exclude other grasses. While common Bermuda grass and St. Augustine grass tolerate moderate salt exposure, seashore paspalum thrives in conditions that would kill those grasses outright, including irrigation with water having electrical conductivity up to 20+ dS/m (seawater is approximately 55 dS/m). This extraordinary salt tolerance has made it the standard coastal golf course turf in Florida, the Gulf Coast, and tropical beach resorts worldwide. Beyond its salt tolerance, seashore paspalum produces a fine-textured, dense, attractive turf with good wear tolerance and moderate shade tolerance, and it can be maintained at golf-green heights (0.5 inches) without scalping. Modern improved cultivars from the University of Georgia breeding program — 'SeaDwarf', 'SeaStar', 'SeaIsle 1', 'SeaIsle 2000', 'Salam' — have dramatically improved the turf quality, cold tolerance, and overall performance compared to common ecotypes. Most valuable in coastal Gulf South locations but also worth considering for any site where recycled or brackish irrigation water is used.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in sandy, well-drained, saline or regular soil in full sun; seaside goldenrod is one of the most salt-tolerant of all native wildflowers and adapts equally well to coastal dunes, inland meadows, and garden borders.
directions: Seaside goldenrod is the salt-tolerant goldenrod of Atlantic and Gulf Coast dunes, salt marshes, and coastal strand habitats — its exceptional salt spray and saline soil tolerance makes it the goldenrod of choice for coastal gardens and living shoreline plantings where other goldenrods would fail. The large, arching sprays of golden-yellow flowers appear from late summer through fall and are among the most important late-season nectar sources on the coastal Atlantic and Gulf Coast, supporting migrating monarchs, native bees, and dozens of butterfly species during their southward migration. Unlike many goldenrod species that spread aggressively by rhizomes to the point of being weedy, seaside goldenrod spreads more moderately and is well-behaved in garden borders; its large, fleshy, salt-tolerant leaves also distinguish it from most other goldenrods. Combine with sea lavender, salt marsh asters, and ornamental grasses in coastal pollinator gardens for a stunning fall display that also provides critical wildlife habitat.

plant_note: Direct sow or plant established divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral, coastal soil in full sun; seaside sandmat is native to coastal dunes, salt flats, and beach margins of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast and is one of the most salt, drought, and heat-tolerant native groundcovers for coastal landscapes.
directions: Sow seeds or plant divisions in very well-drained, lean, sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; seaside sandmat is low-maintenance in coastal sandy soils. Euphorbia mesembryanthemifolia (seaside sandmat or coastal sandmat, formerly Chamaesyce mesembryanthemifolia) is a low-growing, mat-forming native succulent perennial of sandy Atlantic and Gulf Coast beaches, dunes, and coastal salt flats — one of the most salt, drought, and heat-tolerant native groundcovers for challenging coastal landscapes. The plant produces dense, prostrate mats of small, fleshy, succulent-textured, grey-green leaves on trailing stems with tiny, inconspicuous flowers, forming a spreading carpet just 2–4 inches tall. As a coastal revegetation and native beach stabilization plant, it is useful for controlling dune erosion and establishing native cover in infertile, salty, windy coastal conditions where almost nothing else grows. In native plant landscaping, it can be used as a low-maintenance, salt-tolerant groundcover for beach-front or oceanside properties as an alternative to invasive non-native beach groundcovers. The milky latex sap (as in all Euphorbia) is a mild irritant; CAUTION if skin-sensitive.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall; division is easily done by digging and separating rooted stems.
directions: Plant in any well-drained soil — even poor, gravelly soil suits sedum perfectly; overly rich or moist soil causes floppy, open-centered plants. Tall sedums may flop in midseason; pinch once in late spring or grow through a support ring to keep them upright. Leave the russet seedheads standing through winter as they are attractive and provide structure in the dormant garden. Divide every 3–4 years in spring by separating the fleshy crown sections.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, rocky, limestone-derived or calcareous soil in full sun; seep muhly is especially adapted to thin, rocky, alkaline soils over limestone outcrops and caliche in central Texas.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; seep muhly produces an autumn show similar to the more widely planted Gulf muhly (M. capillaris), with long, wispy pink to rose-purple flower plumes in October and November — but on a finer-textured, more drought-tolerant plant better adapted to the alkaline limestone soils of central Texas and the Edwards Plateau. The plumes catch morning light magnificently and the plant is excellent in mass plantings on rocky, dry slopes where Gulf muhly struggles. Unlike Gulf muhly, which prefers more moisture, seep muhly thrives in the xeric, calcareous, rocky soils that define the Hill Country landscape. Named for its natural habitat of seeps and rocky canyon sides, it tolerates both the dry periods between rains and the occasional wet flush. A premium native for zone 7–9 limestone gardens.

subcategory: Utah state flower edible Great Basin native bulb
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in very well-drained, dry, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in zone 4–9; Sego Lily is the state flower of Utah — a beautiful, tulip-like native bulb of the Great Basin and Rocky Mountain West, found in sagebrush steppe, pinyon-juniper woodland, and dry mountain meadows from North Dakota to California — bearing pristine white to pale lavender flowers with distinctive purple, yellow, and brown markings and historically a critical food source that sustained Mormon settlers through the starvation winter of 1848.
directions: Plant Calochortus nuttallii bulbs in fall 3–4 inches deep in extremely well-drained, lean, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; avoid clay soils or areas with summer moisture; provide spring moisture (natural snowmelt or light irrigation) and dry out completely by early summer; mark locations as summer dormancy makes sites look bare. Sego Lily holds a special place in Western American history — the state flower of Utah, it was designated in 1911 to commemorate its role in saving the lives of Mormon settlers during the winter of 1848 when crops failed and settlers dug and ate the small, starchy bulbs to survive. Indigenous peoples of the Great Basin and Rocky Mountain region had long gathered Sego Lily bulbs as a significant food source — boiled, roasted, or dried for storage, the bulbs have a mild, pleasant starchy flavor. The flowers are among the most beautiful of all Western natives: large, three-petaled, cup-shaped flowers in white to pale lavender or pale pink with a bold purple arch and yellow center markings on each petal, creating an almost jewel-like appearance. Like all Mariposa lilies, the primary cultivation challenge is providing adequate summer drought — growing in containers stored dry in summer or in very freely draining raised beds with gravel mulch. The plants self-sow in ideal conditions and can naturalize in Western dry gardens and prairie-style plantings.

common_name: Senita Cactus (Old Man Cactus, Whisker Cactus)
plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; senita cactus is native to the Sonoran Desert of Baja California and the Arizona/Sonora borderlands and requires warm temperatures year-round — it is frost-sensitive below 25°F.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; water rarely — once established, no supplemental irrigation needed in dry climates. Pachycereus schottii (senita cactus or old man cactus) is a distinctive Sonoran Desert columnar cactus forming multi-stemmed clumps of slender, grey-green columns up to 10–15 feet tall. The most distinctive feature is the 'whiskered' appearance of mature stems: the upper portion of older columns becomes densely clothed in long, soft, grey, hair-like bristles (spines), creating a dramatic, shaggy, old-man beard appearance — the source of the common names 'senita' (Spanish: 'old woman') and 'whisker cactus.' In contrast, younger portions of the same stem have few, short spines. Flowers are pink, small, and nocturnal; fruits are red and edible. The senita cactus has a unique, obligate mutualistic relationship with the senita moth (Upiga virescens) — the moth pollinates the flowers while simultaneously laying eggs in them, providing a fascinating example of coevolution. A striking specimen for desert and xeriscape gardens in zone 9–12 where temperatures stay above 25°F.

plant_note: Direct sow after all danger of frost; zinnias grow quickly in warm soil.
directions: This distinguished zinnia produces elegant double three- to five-inch blooms in a dreamy, rare salmon-pink on strong, long stems. Sow directly into warm soil after the last frost for fast growth. Cut and deadhead often to keep the plants flowering all summer. Full sun and airflow between plants help prevent powdery mildew. The edible petals are loved by pollinators and brighten the cutting garden.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Senorita Rosalita is a sterile, non-seeding hybrid cleome — an important improvement over the straight species (Cleome hassleriana) that self-seeds aggressively and can become weedy in zone 9 gardens. Being sterile, Senorita Rosalita blooms continuously throughout the season without the energy diversion to seed set that causes standard cleome to look ragged by midsummer. The plant is also free of the sticky, resinous substance that makes standard cleome unpleasant to handle. As a vegetatively propagated cultivar it is sold as transplants, not seed. Hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies are strongly attracted to the flowers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Senorita Rosalita Cleome thrives in hot, sunny conditions with minimal water and declines in partial shade or consistently moist, fertile soil that promotes excessive vegetative growth; Senorita Rosalita is a sterile, non-self-seeding hybrid Cleome producing the airy, spider-like flower heads of the traditional Spider Flower (Cleome hassleriana) in a compact, non-seeding, non-sticky-stemmed form that eliminates the primary nuisances of the standard species. The flowers — clusters of four-petaled, long-stamened, rose-pink blooms arranged in a rounded, spidery head on tall stems — are produced continuously from late spring through frost because the plant channels all its energy into continuous flowering rather than seed production. Hummingbirds are strongly attracted to cleome flowers, and swallowtail butterflies (Giant, Eastern Tiger, and Spicebush Swallowtail) visit reliably for nectar. The tall, open, airy structure of Senorita Rosalita provides a light, vertical accent in the back of summer borders — the stem-and-flower silhouette visible through the wind and providing a transparency that most tall summer annuals do not offer. In zone 9's long, hot summer, this sterile hybrid maintains its flowering display through the entire season without the decline and seed mess that limits standard Cleome.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in average soil; overly rich soil reduces blooms.
directions: This tall, showy blend produces large three- to four-inch white, pink, rose, and crimson flowers ideal for wildflower plantings and cutting. Sow directly after frost into average, well-drained soil, as lean conditions bring more bloom. Cosmos are drought tolerant and need little attention once up. Full sun keeps the plants upright and flowering; stake in windy sites. An excellent butterfly lure that self-sows for the following year.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May for summer bloom or August–September for fall bloom. Cosmos bipinnatus is one of the most carefree and easy-to-grow annuals from direct seed — germinates rapidly in warm soil, grows quickly to flowering size, and self-seeds abundantly to provide volunteer plants in subsequent seasons. The Sensation series produces the classic tall (3–4 foot) cosmos with large (3–4 inch), single, eight-petaled flowers in a mix of white, pink, rose, and crimson. Avoid overly fertile soil — cosmos in rich soil produces excessive foliage with reduced flowering. Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil without pre-amendment. Self-seeding naturalizes readily in zone 9 sandy soils; allow plants to set seed for the following season's population.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sensation Cosmos demands full sun and poor to moderately fertile, lean soil; in rich, overfertilized soil it produces lush foliage with reduced bloom; Sensation Mixed Cosmos is the classic tall-garden cosmos selection, producing the open, daisy-form, single flowers on tall, feathery-foliaged plants in a harmonious mix of white, light pink, rose-pink, and crimson — creating the airy, naturalistic, cottage-garden floral display that has made Cosmos bipinnatus one of the most beloved and widely grown annual wildflowers in American gardens. The combination of feathery, finely divided foliage and large, simple, flat-faced flowers on tall, open stems creates a transparent, light-catching quality in the garden that many gardeners describe as uniquely beautiful in its combination of substantial flower size and delicate, airy overall appearance. Cosmos is one of the premier butterfly and pollinator annuals available — the large, flat, open flowers with accessible nectar are visited by an exceptional range of beneficial insects including swallowtails, fritillaries, skippers, sulphurs, bees, and beneficial wasps. As a self-seeding species in zone 9, a single planting of Sensation Mixed provides years of successional plants without additional purchase — making it one of the most economical and lowest-effort wildflower annuals for zone 9 sunny borders and wildflower meadow plantings.

plant_note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 60°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April–October and overwinter indoors. Sensation Peace Lily is the largest widely available peace lily cultivar — capable of reaching 4–5 feet tall with leaves 24–36 inches long. Maintain consistently moist soil; peace lily wilts dramatically when dry but recovers quickly when watered. The white spathe-and-spadix flowers appear 1–3 times per year on well-grown plants. Outdoors in zone 9's summer heat and humidity, Sensation performs exceptionally well in deep shade on covered patios. Leaf edges show brown tips if exposed to fluoride in tap water — use filtered or rainwater for best appearance.
directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light — direct sun bleaches and burns the large, dark green leaves irreparably — in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil; Sensation is the large-growing selection of Peace Lily (Spathiphyllum), producing plants two to three times the size of standard peace lily cultivars — creating a dramatic, statement-scale tropical foliage plant for large containers, shaded patios, and indoor spaces with high ceilings. The very large, lance-shaped, deeply ribbed, dark glossy green leaves reach 24–36 inches on mature established plants, creating a bold, lush tropical effect that is impossible to achieve with standard-sized Spathiphyllum varieties. The flowers — pure white, calla lily-like spathes surrounding a cream-white spadix — appear intermittently through the year on well-maintained plants, adding a refined, elegant floral dimension to the dramatic foliage. Peace lily in general is one of the definitive shade and low-light plants — one of very few flowering plants that blooms in genuinely low light conditions — and Sensation simply amplifies all these qualities to a scale appropriate for dramatic indoor or outdoor shaded garden design.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in spring or transplant container plants in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; sensitive briar has recurved prickles along the stems — handle with care.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — sensitive briar is a fascinating native trailing groundcover of the Gulf Coast and southern prairies, with two remarkable properties: the delicate, fern-like, bipinnate leaves fold closed immediately when touched (thigmonastic movement — the same sensitivity as the tropical 'sensitive plant'), providing an entertaining and educational garden element, and the stems are lined with small, recurved prickles similar to rose thorns. The spherical, bright pink pompom flowers in late spring and summer are delightful and attract native bees. It spreads flat along the ground to cover dry, rocky, or sandy open areas. As a legume, it fixes nitrogen from the air, improving soil fertility for neighboring plants. An outstanding native for dry, sunny slopes, caliche hillsides, and disturbed areas where its drought tolerance and sprawling habit control erosion while providing summer bloom and ecological interest.

plant_note: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; sensitive fern naturalizes aggressively in wet areas by underground rhizomes and can become invasive in bog gardens.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun near ponds, streams, and in rain garden edges; sensitive fern produces large, broadly triangular, bright-green fronds that are coarser and less typical-looking than most ferns and die back at the first frost (hence the name 'sensitive'). Separate fertile fronds bear persistent clusters of small, bead-like brown spore cases that remain standing through winter, providing attractive winter silhouette and food structure for birds. The plant spreads aggressively by underground rhizomes in consistently moist conditions and is best used in large-scale naturalistic plantings where its spread can be accommodated. The hardiest fern for wet, disturbed sites across North America.

plant_note: Start indoors; nick or soak the hard seed coat and keep warm. Transplant after frost.
directions: This novelty rapidly folds its fern-like leaves when touched, exposing spines as a defense, delighting children and adults alike. Nick or soak the hard seed and start it indoors in warmth, then grow on as a houseplant or transplant outdoors after frost. Give it bright light, full sun to part shade, and consistently moist, well-drained soil. It is frost tender and typically grown as an annual or potted plant outside the tropics. Handle sparingly to enjoy repeated leaf-folding without stressing the plant.

common_name: September Charm Japanese Anemone (Clear Pink Fall Anemone)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; plant in spring for establishment before the summer heat; newly transplanted Japanese anemones may be slow to establish but become vigorous spreaders once settled.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; September Charm is one of the finest pink-flowered Japanese anemone cultivars — producing clear, medium-pink, single flowers with a slightly deeper pink exterior and prominent yellow stamens on stems somewhat shorter and more compact than Honorine Jobert. The clear, unmuddied pink color (neither the pale blush of some cultivars nor the strong cerise of others) is one of September Charm's most consistently praised qualities: the pink is bright, cheerful, and long-lasting over the 6–8 week fall bloom season. The individual flowers are slightly smaller than Honorine Jobert (2–2.5 inches) but are produced in similar abundance on well-branched stems. September Charm typically begins blooming in late August in zone 7–8 — one to two weeks earlier than many other Japanese anemone cultivars — then continues through October. The earlier bloom start extends the display season significantly. Like all Japanese anemones, September Charm spreads by underground stolons and benefits from spring division every 4–6 years. The dark-green, deeply lobed foliage is attractive from spring through hard frost. Pair September Charm with Honorine Jobert for a contrasting white-and-pink combination in the fall shade garden — the two cultivars bloom simultaneously and create a complementary display.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring or divide established clumps in spring; Serbian bellflower spreads vigorously by surface runners and can become invasive in small rock gardens or between paving stones. It self-sows modestly. Shear back hard after the main June–July flush to encourage a repeat bloom in late summer.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to part shade; Serbian bellflower is one of the most prolific and cheerful bellflowers — a low, trailing, vigorously spreading perennial from the Dalmatian limestone mountains producing a relentless flood of small, star-shaped, lavender-blue to lilac flowers from June through August (with a possible rebloom in fall if cut back), carried on trailing stems 6–8 inches tall that spread outward over rocks, walls, and pavement in a cheerful scrambling cascade. The flowers, though individually simple and small, are produced in such extraordinary abundance that a mature clump is a solid color mass for weeks. Outstanding for trailing over walls, filling cracks between stone, scrambling down banks, and naturalizing in difficult dry positions in part shade. It spreads more vigorously than most bellflowers and can colonize large areas over time. The cultivar 'Stella' has a somewhat more compact habit than the species.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline, average, loamy or clay soil in full sun to partial shade; Serbian spruce is one of the most adaptable and ornamentally outstanding spruces — tolerating both acidic and alkaline soils, air pollution, and a wide range of growing conditions.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline, average, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Serbian spruce is one of the most beautiful and narrowly columnar spruces in cultivation — a naturally slender, spire-shaped tree with gracefully pendulous branchlets, dark green needles with conspicuous silvery-white stomatal bands on the undersides, and very small, dense cones.
