Slow-growing but long-lived, Silver Thatch Palm produces small white flowers in summer followed by round, dark purple berries consumed by birds; historically the leaves were used for thatching (hence the common name). An outstanding specimen palm for the thin, rocky, alkaline marl and limestone soils of South Florida gardens where faster-growing palms would quickly exhaust the substrate — plant in full sun to partial shade, provide excellent drainage, and supply minimal supplemental water once established.

common_name: Silver Trumpet Tree (Caribbean Trumpet Tree, Golden Tabebuia, Aurea Trumpet)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Tabebuia aurea is one of the more cold-tolerant Tabebuia species, surviving temperatures to 25–28°F with damage to young growth. Established trees in zone 9b recover rapidly from cold damage. The tree blooms best after a dry period — withholding irrigation in late winter (February) often triggers the spectacular spring bloom. The silvery-gray, deciduous foliage provides winter interest, and the bare-branch bloom display in spring is extraordinary. Drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to rocky, moderately fertile soil — Silver Trumpet Tree is highly drought-tolerant and performs beautifully in the sandy, alkaline soils common throughout the Gulf Coast and South Florida where many flowering trees struggle. Tabebuia aurea is a medium-sized, deciduous to semi-deciduous tree native to the dry forests and savannas of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina in the Bignoniaceae family, closely related to the widely-planted Pink Trumpet Tree (Handroanthus impetiginosus). In spring, after the dry season has caused leaf drop, the bare, silver-gray branches of Tabebuia aurea produce one of the most spectacular flowering displays of any flowering tree: masses of large, 3-inch, bright golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers covering every branch simultaneously before the new leaves emerge — the tree appears as a golden cloud against the sky when viewed from a distance. The palmate, silver-green, leathery compound leaves that emerge after flowering are themselves attractive in a silvery, semi-succulent way, explaining the common name 'Silver Trumpet Tree.' Tabebuia aurea is considered one of the best-performing and most cold-tolerant of the tropical trumpet trees for zone 9 Gulf South use, and established trees in Houston, New Orleans, and adjacent areas have produced reliably spectacular spring bloom displays for decades. The national tree of Venezuela.

common_name: Silver Vase Bromeliad (Urn Plant, Silver Bromeliad, Aechmea fasciata)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; Aechmea fasciata cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 50°F but is one of the more cold-tolerant bromeliads and can handle brief temperatures to 40°F in dry conditions. Keep the central urn (tank) filled with filtered or rainwater. Grow in a very well-draining mix of bark and perlite. The plant blooms once after several years of growth, then produces pups that will each bloom in 3–5 years. A mature, well-grown plant in bloom is one of the most dramatic flowering houseplants available. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Silver Vase Bromeliad is one of the most shade-tolerant of the larger bromeliads, adapting to the reduced light of typical indoor environments while maintaining its attractive banded foliage even without flowering. Aechmea fasciata is a large, epiphytic bromeliad from the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo states), one of the most widely grown and immediately recognizable bromeliads in cultivation. The plant forms a large, symmetrical rosette of broad, arching, gray-green leaves decorated with irregular transverse bands of silvery-white powder — the bands are silvery because the leaf surface absorbs and scatters light through overlapping silver scales, creating the characteristic silvery sheen that gives the plant its common names 'Silver Vase' and 'Silver Bromeliad.' The broad leaves form a central urn or vase shape that collects rainwater in nature, housing the plant's root zone in a permanent water reservoir. After 3–5 years of growth, the plant produces from its center a spectacular inflorescence: a large, branching, pink to rose-red bract structure studded with small, blue to purple flowers that eventually mature to pink berries — the entire bloom structure persists ornamentally for 3–6 months. Among the most dramatic of all long-lasting indoor flowering displays. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; silver wattle is the primary source of 'mimosa' cut flowers that have been emblematic of late winter in the south of France and the Italian Riviera since the 19th century. It blooms in January–March (late winter), producing masses of fragrant, golden-yellow flower pom-poms. More cold-hardy than some acacias (to zone 8a). Fast-growing; potentially invasive in some Mediterranean climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; silver wattle is the 'mimosa' of European florists and the flower market — the tree that has been synonymous with late winter in southern France and the Italian Riviera since the mid-19th century when Australian plant introductions transformed the Côte d'Azur landscape. Each February the entire region bursts into the golden-yellow bloom of silver wattle, and 'mimosa' trains and festivals celebrate the spectacle; the cut branches of golden pompoms exported to northern Europe each winter have been a staple of the flower market for 150 years. The finely divided, twice-pinnate, silver-gray to blue-green, feathery foliage creates an extraordinarily fine-textured, soft, silver cloud of foliage year-round, and in late winter the entire tree becomes covered in a total coating of hundreds of tiny, spherical, golden-yellow pompoms — each individual head scarcely 0.25 inch across but produced in such astronomical numbers that the tree literally turns from silver to gold. The fragrance, a characteristic warm, sweet, slightly powdery honey-like scent, is the definitive scent of Mediterranean late winter. One of the defining trees of the zone 9 warm-climate Mediterranean-style garden.

plant_note: Start indoors and surface sow; seed needs light. Transplant after frost.
directions: Grown for its striking silvery-white, felted foliage, this plant adds contrast and texture as edging, in moon gardens, and as bouquet filler. Start seed indoors eight to ten weeks before the last frost, pressing it onto the surface for light. Transplant after frost into full sun and well-drained soil. It is drought tolerant and may overwinter in mild climates when mulched. If allowed to flower, the yellow blooms attract butterflies.

plant_note: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed into lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; silverleaf sunflower is native to Texas Gulf Coast sand dunes and prairies and thrives in poor, sandy, drought-prone soil, self-seeding readily where conditions suit it.
directions: Sow directly in lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; highly drought-tolerant once established and best grown without extra fertility, which promotes weak, floppy growth. Helianthus argophyllus (silverleaf sunflower) is a striking native annual sunflower endemic to the Texas Gulf Coast, instantly recognizable for its densely silver-white, velvety, felted foliage and stems — a dramatic textural and color contrast to the green foliage of nearly every other garden sunflower. Large, bright yellow, brown-centered flower heads open over a long summer season atop the tall, branching, silvery stalks, drawing bees, butterflies, and, later, seed-eating songbirds like goldfinches to the ripening seed heads. As a true coastal-plain native, it tolerates poor sandy soil, salt spray, and drought exceptionally well, making it a strong choice for a Gulf Coast xeriscape, dune-style planting, or wildlife garden. It self-seeds readily in favorable conditions, often persisting as a reseeding annual once established, zone 7–11.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in dry to moderately moist, rocky or sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Silverrod is uniquely adapted to the dry, shaded conditions of rocky woodland understories where most goldenrods will not thrive — do not plant in wet, heavy, or overly fertile soil.
directions: Silverrod is the only native goldenrod in eastern North America with white flowers — a distinctive botanical curiosity in a genus that otherwise produces exclusively yellow blooms — and also the most shade-tolerant member of the group, growing in dry to moderately moist, rocky or sandy woodland understories, cliff edges, and open barrens where other goldenrods cannot establish. The wiry stems produce small spikes of creamy-white flowers in late summer and fall that provide nectar for late-season native bees and small butterflies at a time when shade garden options for pollinators are limited. Native to rocky woodlands, sandy barrens, and open forest margins from Quebec south to Georgia, Silverrod is a valuable niche plant for the dry shade garden where its tolerance of drought, poor soil, and low light makes it surprisingly adaptable. Direct sow seeds in fall in dry, rocky or sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; established plants self-seed modestly and form long-lived clumps without aggressive spreading.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; silvery glade fern is named for the silvery-white sori that cover the underside of fertile fronds in early summer, giving the fronds a distinctive shimmering appearance that makes it easy to identify.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-enriched, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; silvery glade fern spreads slowly by rhizomes to form attractive colonies in moist woodland settings. Deparia acrostichoides (silvery glade fern, formerly Athyrium acrostichoides) is a native deciduous fern of eastern North American moist woodlands, producing broad, lance-shaped, softly textured fronds 18–30 inches long on pale, delicate stems; in early summer the undersides of the fronds are covered with elongated silver-white sori arranged in a distinctive herringbone pattern that gives the fern its common name and makes it one of the most beautiful of eastern woodland ferns when backlit. It thrives in the moist, humus-rich soil of stream banks, woodland margins, and shaded ravines, naturalizing readily by rhizome spreading into loose colonies. An underused native fern with elegant foliage and unique ornamental sori; attractive companion to trilliums, Solomon's seal, and hostas.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to deep shade; Silvery Sunproof is one of the few variegated liriopes that maintains its bright cream-and-green color in full sun without bleaching — most variegated liriopes require partial shade for best color.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to deep shade; Silvery Sunproof is the premier variegated sun-tolerant liriope — a striking selection with bold, upright, strap-like leaves striped in green and cream-yellow that maintains its vivid variegation in full sun conditions where most variegated liriopes bleach to pale yellowish white. The ability to perform in full sun without color loss gives Silvery Sunproof greater landscape versatility than variegated competitors, making it effective as edging, ground cover, or accent plant in both shaded and fully exposed positions. In late summer, the plants produce showy spikes of bright lilac-purple flowers above the variegated foliage, providing an attractive contrast to the cream-and-green leaves. Dark blue-black berries follow the flowers and persist into winter, providing additional ornamental interest. Like all liriopes, Silvery Sunproof forms slowly expanding clumps that fill in over 2–3 seasons and tolerate the full range of Gulf South conditions — heat, humidity, drought once established, clay soil, and root competition under trees. In zone 9, it performs reliably as an evergreen to semi-evergreen ground cover and edging plant. Shear to 3–4 inches in February before new growth emerges to remove winter-tattered foliage and encourage fresh, colorful new leaves.

common_name: Singapore Plumeria (White Frangipani, Evergreen Frangipani, Blunt Leaf Plumeria)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with excellently drained soil; Plumeria obtusa is the most cold-sensitive of the common plumerias and is best suited to zone 10-11 outdoors or large containers moved inside in zone 9 winters. Unlike P. rubra, it remains evergreen year-round in frost-free climates, making it excellent for tropical streetscapes. Cuttings 12–18 inches long should be dried for 5–7 days before planting in dry, sandy mix. The milky sap causes skin and eye irritation.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, preferably sandy or rocky soil; Plumeria obtusa is drought-tolerant once established and will rot in heavy, moisture-retaining soils. Plumeria obtusa is a tropical flowering tree native to the Caribbean islands (Cuba, Jamaica, Bahamas, Hispaniola) that has become one of the most widely planted ornamental trees throughout tropical Asia, particularly Singapore and Thailand, where it is now so ubiquitous in Buddhist temple gardens and public landscapes that it has acquired the common name 'Singapore Plumeria,' though it is not native to that region. Unlike the deciduous Plumeria rubra (the most widely planted frangipani in the US), P. obtusa remains evergreen year-round in frost-free climates, retaining its broad, glossy, dark-green, blunt-tipped leaves through all seasons — the specific epithet 'obtusa' refers to the rounded, blunt (obtuse) leaf tips that distinguish it from the narrower-tipped P. rubra. The flowers are pure white with a bright yellow center and produce the classic sweet, tropical frangipani fragrance that is among the most widely recognized flower fragrances in the world. The blooms appear at the stem tips in clusters and are borne for months in warm climates. The milky, latex sap that exudes from cut stems is irritating to skin and eyes. In zone 9, P. obtusa is most practical as a large container specimen brought in during winter.

common_name: Singapore Rhododendron (Indian Rhododendron, Senduduk, Malabar Melastome)
plant_note: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil; Melastoma malabathricum grows vigorously in acidic, moist soils and will tolerate temporarily wet conditions better than many ornamental shrubs. It is half-hardy and can be damaged by frost but often regrows from the root crown in zone 9. In zone 9b-10, it grows as a reliable, free-flowering evergreen shrub blooming nearly continuously through the warm months. The berries turn the mouth and teeth temporarily black-purple when eaten (the name 'Melastoma' means black mouth). Has become invasive in some Pacific Islands and Hawaii — check local regulations.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil — Singapore Rhododendron produces the most flowers in full sun but tolerates and grows attractively in partial shade, which suits its natural habitat as an edge and forest-margin species. Melastoma malabathricum is a fast-growing, evergreen, multi-stemmed tropical shrub native from India and Sri Lanka through all of Southeast Asia to Australia in the Melastomataceae family, widely grown throughout the tropical world as an ornamental flowering shrub for its prolific production of bright, showy, 5-petaled flowers in vivid magenta-pink to rose-purple. The flowers are large for a shrub (2–3 inches across), saucer-shaped, with five distinctly veined petals in intense magenta to hot pink and a central cluster of curved, two-toned stamens in yellow and purple — a flower with genuine ornamental impact. The plant blooms throughout the year in zone 10-11, never without flowers for long. The common name 'Singapore Rhododendron' reflects both its wide use as an ornamental in Singapore and the general resemblance of the flower to a tropical Rhododendron, though the plants are not botanically related. The ripe berries are edible (though they turn the mouth and teeth temporarily black — the genus name means 'black mouth' in Greek), sweet, and consumed in Southeast Asian traditional practice. A robust, reliable, and free-flowering ornamental shrub for zone 9b-11 warm, moist gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; nasturtiums resent transplanting.
directions: This blend blooms in single flowers of scarlet, gold, orange, and yellow on long, trailing stems that can be trained up a trellis or fence. Sow the large seeds directly where they are to grow once the soil warms, planting about half an inch deep. Keep the soil lean, as rich conditions favor leaves over flowers. It is drought tolerant once established and thrives in full sun to part shade. Both the peppery blossoms and leaves are edible and add a watercress-like kick to salads.

plant_note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring after frost danger has passed; plant in well-drained soil amended with organic matter and water in well through the first season.
directions: Abelia uniflora is the wild Chinese species behind the many hybrid abelias common in cultivation, and it deserves far wider use in its own right for its graceful arching habit and long succession of single white-to-pink tubular flowers from summer into fall. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full to partial sun; it tolerates a range of soil types once established and is notably deer resistant. Propagate by softwood cuttings taken in early summer, rooting them in a moist perlite-peat mix under intermittent mist or a plastic tent. Light renewal pruning immediately after flowering encourages fresh branching and extends the bloom season without sacrificing the following year's flower buds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; sinojackia is a rare Chinese woodland tree that establishes best in a sheltered site with protection from desiccating winds and hot afternoon sun, especially in zones 7–9. It is rarely available from mainstream nurseries — seek out specialty native and rare woody plant nurseries or botanical garden plant sales. Soil pH should be kept between 5.5 and 6.5 for best performance.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; sinojackia is one of the rarest and most underused small ornamental trees in cultivation — a member of the Styracaceae family (relatives include Styrax and Halesia), it produces profuse, pure-white, star-shaped flowers with prominent yellow stamens in spring, blooming along the branches as the new leaves emerge and creating an effect reminiscent of a refined, smaller-scale Halesia carolina. Sinojackia xylocarpa is native to a restricted area of eastern China and is considered endangered in its native range, making cultivated plants in gardens an important contribution to ex-situ conservation. The flowers are followed by distinctive woody, beaked fruits that persist into winter and provide additional ornamental interest; the multi-stemmed habit and clean, oval leaves offer good fall color. An exceptional conversation piece for collectors and enthusiasts, best displayed as a specimen or focal point in a woodland garden where its delicate flowers can be appreciated at close range.

common_name: Sinonome Toad Lily (Early-Blooming Purple-Spotted Shade Perennial)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; toad lilies require consistent moisture throughout the growing season — do not allow soil to dry completely between waterings as wilted foliage is slow to recover.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Sinonome is a superior early-blooming toad lily selection — beginning its characteristic purple-spotted, orchid-like flowers in August, several weeks earlier than the standard Tricyrtis hirta species, extending the display season significantly and ensuring a longer bloom period before fall frost in shorter-season climates. The flowers of all toad lily cultivars are botanically fascinating and visually unique: each small (1-inch), upward-facing flower has six white to pale purple tepals heavily spotted with deep purple-violet spots and a prominent, elaborate central column of stamens and style, giving each bloom an orchid-like complexity that is remarkable for a hardy shade perennial. Sinonome's earlier bloom start compared to the species (August rather than September–October) means zone 9 gardeners enjoy the full bloom season without concern about timing. The upright to arching stems (18–30 inches) produce flowers in leaf axils along the upper portion of each stem, creating a long, arching floral display rather than a terminal flower cluster. Consistent moisture is essential — toad lilies will wilt dramatically without water but recover quickly when irrigated. In zone 9, plant in the most shaded locations available (north walls, under deciduous trees) and maintain consistent soil moisture through summer mulching.

common_name: Sioux Blue Indiangrass (Blue-Leaved Native Prairie Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring on well-drained soil in full sun; Sioux Blue is a selection of native indiangrass with notably powdery blue-toned foliage, a cooler color than the yellow-green typical of the wild species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sioux Blue is a blue-foliaged selection of native indiangrass, a tall prairie grass that produces striking, feathery golden-bronze plumes in late summer above upright, powdery blue-green blades, a cooler and more refined color than the more common yellow-green wild-type indiangrass. It combines well with little and big bluestem in a naturalistic meadow or prairie-style planting, and is highly drought-tolerant and adaptable to a range of soils once established, needing only a late-winter cutback to a few inches before new growth begins. The plumes and seed heads provide winter interest and food for birds if left standing through the dormant season.

common_name: Sioux Crape Myrtle (Dark Pink Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sioux is a medium-sized crape myrtle reaching 15–20 feet — appropriate for most residential settings where the large National Arboretum series would be too massive.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Sioux is a medium-sized National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtle producing deep hot-pink to rose-pink flower clusters from June through September — a vibrant, saturated pink that is warmer and more vivid than the typical light pinks common in older crape myrtle cultivars. The flowers are produced abundantly on an upright-spreading, multi-trunked tree reaching 15–20 feet in zone 9, providing both specimen tree and shade-tree functions for medium-sized residential landscapes. Like other National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, Sioux shows good resistance to powdery mildew compared to older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars. The exfoliating bark develops attractively with age, revealing warm tan to cinnamon tones beneath the peeling gray outer bark. Fall leaf color is orange-red. Sioux fills the important mid-sized slot between compact dwarf selections (under 10 feet) and the very large tree-sized Natchez and Muskogee, making it appropriate for typical suburban residential lot sizes where large-tree crape myrtles would eventually overwhelm the space. Remove any suckers that emerge from the base; lightly prune to remove crossing branches and dead wood only — do not top.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun with fast-draining, gritty, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil — tilted at an angle in a rock crevice or raised bed is ideal — in zone 4–8; Siskiyou Lewisia is a jewel of the Pacific Northwest mountains, native to rocky cliff faces and talus slopes in the Siskiyou Mountains of northern California and southern Oregon — producing beautiful rosettes of succulent, paddle-shaped leaves and stunning sprays of multi-petaled flowers in shades of white, pink, salmon, orange, and magenta in spring.
directions: Plant Lewisia cotyledon in a vertical crevice between rocks, in a trough, or in a raised scree bed with extremely well-drained, gritty soil; the crown must stay dry — plant at a slight angle to shed water; water moderately in spring during active growth, reduce sharply in summer, and avoid any water sitting on the crown which causes rot. Siskiyou Lewisia is one of the most beautiful of all rock garden plants — producing from a thick, carrot-like taproot an evergreen rosette of glossy, succulent leaves and abundant branching sprays of spectacular, 1-inch flowers in brilliant shades of white to deep magenta, often with darker veining or striping, throughout spring. The key to success is excellent drainage: in nature it grows in vertical rock crevices where water cannot stand, and replicates this in the garden are best achieved in rock gardens, dry-stone walls, hypertufa troughs, or steeply tilted raised beds with at least 50% grit or coarse sand. In humid summer climates, provide overhead protection during wet summers to prevent crown rot — a classic cause of failure in the Southeast and Pacific Northwest lowlands. Many cultivars have been selected for exceptionally vivid or bicolored flowers; the 'Sunset Strain' and 'Rainbow Series' offer particularly reliable performance and varied color. Divides readily in early spring from offsets.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–November. Siskiyou Pink Gaura is a Texas native (Oenothera lindheimeri, formerly Gaura lindheimeri) that is exceptionally well-adapted to the dry, hot conditions of zone 9 and thrives in the lean, well-drained soils of the Gulf Coast uplands. Provide excellent drainage — gaura is susceptible to root rot in wet or poorly drained soils. In zone 9 it blooms from early spring through frost in an essentially uninterrupted display of the dancing, butterfly-like pink flowers on wiry stems. Cut back by one-third in midsummer if the plant becomes too open and floppy, which stimulates fresh, compact growth.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Siskiyou Pink Gaura demands excellent drainage and thrives in dry, sunny conditions but declines in consistently moist or heavy soil; Siskiyou Pink is a cultivar of Lindheimer's Gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri, formerly classified as Gaura lindheimeri), a native Texas wildflower producing a cloud of small, four-petaled, pink to rose-pink flowers on slender, wiry, arching stems that wave and dance in the slightest breeze — creating a distinctive, airy, naturalistic movement in the garden that earned the plant the descriptive nickname 'whirling butterflies.' Siskiyou Pink is specifically selected for deeper, more saturated pink flower color than the predominantly white or pale-pink straight species, making the floral display more vivid and garden-worthy while retaining the characteristic light, dancing quality of the stem-and-flower form. The combination of essentially continuous bloom from spring through frost, extreme drought tolerance, heat tolerance in zones 6–9, and the light, airy, naturalistic flower form that works in both formal and cottage garden styles has made Gaura one of the most universally successful flowering perennials for the modern Southern garden. Its native Texas origin means full adaptation to the hot, dry conditions of zone 9 summers.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Sitka spruce grows naturally in the moist Pacific coastal fog belt and requires high humidity and consistent moisture — it does not perform well in dry, continental climates. Excellent for coastal planting.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist, deep, fertile to average loamy or sandy soil in full sun; Sitka spruce is the largest spruce in the world and the third largest conifer — reaching up to 300 feet in the old-growth forests of the Pacific Northwest and Southeast Alaska. The Champion Tree in Prairie Creek Redwoods State Park is over 300 feet tall. Native to the Pacific Coast fog belt from northern California to Alaska, it grows in the perpetually moist, fog-drip zone where rainfall can reach 200 inches per year. The characteristic very sharp, stiff needles and the flat, pendant branches create a distinctive large-scale landscape form. Sitka spruce wood has the highest strength-to-weight ratio of any wood and was the primary material for early aircraft construction — nearly all World War I aircraft frames and Howard Hughes's 'Spruce Goose' were built from it. One of the premier coastal windbreak trees where fog and ocean influence moderate summer drought.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; skeleton flower absolutely requires consistent moisture and good drainage — it will not tolerate drought or waterlogging and grows best in cool, north-facing shaded sites.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; skeleton flower absolutely requires consistent moisture and good drainage — it will not tolerate drought or waterlogging and grows best in cool, north-facing shaded sites. Diphylleia grayi is a Japanese mountain woodland perennial that has become increasingly popular for its unique optical phenomenon — its white, waxy petals turn completely transparent when wet from rain, revealing the delicate venation of the petals and earning it the name "skeleton flower"; the large, deeply lobed, peltate leaves superficially resemble umbrella plant or mayapple, and the white flowers are borne in cymes at the leaf axils in late spring. After flowering, it produces striking, deep-blue, grape-like berries on red stems in summer that are the plant's second season of ornamental interest. It demands consistent cool moisture and is challenging but rewarding for shade gardeners in zones 5–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or spring in well-drained soil in full sun; skeleton leaf goldeneye establishes quickly in poor, rocky, or sandy soils with no supplemental irrigation once established. In zone 8–10 it blooms profusely in the fall and often through mild winters; deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom. Cut back hard in late winter to encourage dense new growth.
directions: Plant in full sun in rocky, sandy, or poor, well-drained soil; skeleton leaf goldeneye is a drought-adapted Texas and Mexico native in the sunflower family that produces an extravagant display of bright yellow, 1.5–2 inch daisy-like flowers on feathery, thread-leaved foliage from late summer through frost. The finely dissected leaves give the plant an elegant, airy texture quite unlike the bold foliage of related sunflowers, and the flowering display attracts an exceptional diversity of native bees, butterflies, and skipper moths. It is one of the best plants for establishing Texas-style xeriscape gardens with continuous fall color, performing equally well on rocky limestone slopes and sandy alkaline soils. The plant requires no supplemental irrigation in zone 8–10 once established and actually performs better in poor soil — excess fertility produces lush foliage at the expense of flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in wet, mucky, organic-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; skunk cabbage is very slow from seed (3-5 years to first flower) but establishes a near-permanent presence — the contractile roots pull the rhizome deeper into the soil each year, making mature plants essentially impossible to transplant or remove. Site carefully.
directions: Plant in saturated to wet, mucky, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade along stream margins, seepage slopes, and the perpetually wet fringes of woodland ponds; skunk cabbage is one of the most remarkable native plants of eastern North American woodlands — it generates its own heat through a process of thermogenesis, burning stored starch to raise the temperature inside its hooded spathe by 15–35°F above ambient, allowing it to bloom in late winter while snow still covers the ground. This heat volatilizes the fetid, sulfurous compounds that give the plant its name, attracting early-emerging carrion flies as pollinators. The massive, tropical-looking leaves emerge after flowering and can exceed 2 feet across, creating a bold, lush tropical effect in wet, shaded woodland settings. The plant is essentially permanent once established, with contractile roots that prevent removal. A dramatic native for wet shade gardens where its tropical-looking leaves contrast beautifully with ferns and woodland sedges.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall, pressing lightly into the soil surface without covering; seed requires cold stratification over winter and germinates in early spring. Established plants can also be divided in early spring before significant growth resumes.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, average-fertility soil in partial shade to full sun; skunk meadow rue is distinguished from the closely related purple meadow rue (Thalictrum dasycarpum) by its waxy, glaucous, gland-dotted leaflets with slightly revolute (rolled-under) margins and its musky, skunk-like scent when the foliage is bruised — a distinctive odor that gives the plant its common name. It tolerates drier sites than most meadow rues and performs well in open woodland margins, prairie edges, and sunny borders with average soil. The airy, lavender to white flowers are borne in branched panicles from June through July and are highly attractive to a wide range of native bees, wasps, and beneficial insects. The blue-green, fernlike foliage provides exceptional textural contrast in the mixed border all season. A graceful, underused native that combines beautifully with wild bergamot, rattlesnake master, and prairie dropseed.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sky blue aster is drought-tolerant once established and performs best in poor, dry soils that simulate its native prairie habitat. In rich, moist soil it becomes tall and floppy. Division every 3–4 years maintains vigor.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sky blue aster is a drought-tolerant native aster of the central prairies and dry, rocky, open woods of the central and eastern United States, producing masses of small, clear sky-blue to pale-azure daisy flowers with yellow central discs from August through October — one of the truest and most saturated blues among the native fall-blooming asters. The basal leaves are large and coarse-textured but the stem leaves are smaller and clasping, and the overall plant form is more open and prairie-like than the garden asters bred for showiness. Growing in lean, dry, rocky soils in its native habitat, it is more reliably self-supporting and compact in poor, dry conditions than in the rich soils of typical garden borders. Outstanding for prairie restorations, dry meadow plantings, and late-season native plant gardens where its clear sky-blue color provides distinctive late-season color as well as essential fall nectar for migrating pollinators including monarch butterflies. Combined with late goldenrods, ironweeds, and ornamental grasses in naturalistic fall plantings.

common_name: Sky Pencil Holly (Extremely Narrow Columnar Japanese Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Sky Pencil grows in an extremely narrow, upright column, making it useful for tight spaces where a wide shrub will not fit.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Sky Pencil is a striking Japanese holly selection with an extremely narrow, strictly upright, columnar growth habit unlike almost any other common shrub, reaching several feet tall while staying only a foot or so wide, which makes it a favorite for narrow side yards, tight entryway plantings, and repeated vertical accents flanking a doorway or path. The small, glossy, spineless leaves give it a refined, fine texture, and while it holds its narrow shape naturally, an occasional light shearing keeps individual plants uniform in a formal planting. It prefers consistently moist, well-drained soil, since it can struggle in soggy or very dry sites, and light staking when young helps prevent splaying in heavy snow or wind until the plant matures.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in well-drained, acidic, sandy soil in full sun, pressing seeds into the soil surface; germination occurs in spring. Transplant container-grown nursery trees in fall or early spring for best establishment. Slash Pine grows extremely fast and should be given ample space.
directions: Slash Pine is the dominant pine of the Gulf Coast and Florida peninsula, native to the wet flatwoods, mesic pinelands, and pond edges of the southeastern coastal plain from South Carolina to Florida and west to Louisiana, where it forms the foundational canopy of the longleaf pine savanna ecosystem alongside longleaf and pond pines. One of the fastest-growing native pines — typically adding 3–5 feet per year in good conditions — Slash Pine is widely planted for timber, pulpwood, and naval stores (resin/turpentine), and in Florida it is a primary host tree for the red-cockaded woodpecker and the state champion in terms of longleaf pine savanna ecosystem support. Two varieties occur in Florida: var. elliottii (North Florida and coastal plain, tall and fast-growing) and var. densa (South Florida Slash Pine, shorter, denser, more fire-resistant). Plant in full sun in acidic, well-drained to moderately moist sandy soil; it is intolerant of alkaline conditions, compaction, or prolonged drought once young.

plant_note: Sow direct after last frost in a warm, sunny location with well-drained, lean soil.
directions: Waltheria indica is a velvety-leaved tropical perennial from the mallow family that thrives in full sun and poor, dry, disturbed soils across frost-free climates from Florida and Texas through the tropics. It produces dense clusters of small, bright yellow flowers nearly year-round, making it a reliable nectar source for pollinators in zones 9-12. Plant after all danger of frost has passed and provide excellent drainage; established plants are highly drought-tolerant and require little supplemental water. Leaves are brewed as an herbal tea in Caribbean and Latin American folk traditions, and the plant makes an interesting addition to naturalistic or pollinator-focused plantings.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in sandy, well-drained, infertile, acidic soil in full sun. Slender Blazingstar is adapted to the xeric, sandy coastal plain habitats of the Florida peninsula and adjacent states and will not thrive in clay, irrigated, or overly fertile garden conditions.
directions: Slender Blazingstar is a native perennial of the sandy coastal plain, pine flatwoods, and xeric scrub of the Florida peninsula and adjacent southeastern states, producing feathery, slender spikes of pink-purple flower heads on wiry stems in fall that are a critical nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and native bees traversing the Florida peninsula during their southward fall migration. The narrow, thread-like leaves that cover the slender stems give the plant its common name; the flowers open from top to bottom on the spike, like all Liatris, and are notably fragrant compared to many other blazingstars. Adapted to the poor, sandy, xeric soils of the coastal plain where it often grows in open pine-palmetto flatwoods alongside other fire-adapted wildflowers, Slender Blazingstar requires excellent drainage and periodic burning or mechanical disturbance to maintain its competitive advantage. Direct sow seeds in fall in sandy, infertile, extremely well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; established corms are long-lived and drought-tolerant once settled in appropriate conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow on bare, dry, well-drained, lean soil in fall; seeds cold-stratify over winter and germinate in early spring for late spring bloom.
directions: Slender Clarkia is a graceful California and Oregon native annual with wiry, branching stems and pretty, 4-petaled flowers in shades of lavender-pink to rose, each petal bearing a contrasting darker inner zone that draws specialist native bees. It is native to dry foothill grasslands, chaparral margins, and open woodland clearings throughout the California Coast Ranges, Sierra Nevada foothills, and southern Oregon. Direct sow on bare, dry, lean, well-drained soil in fall — it resents transplanting and performs best with no soil amendment, as it is adapted to the poor, rocky soils of its native habitat. It self-sows freely in suitable conditions and pairs beautifully with California poppies and annual phlox for a naturalistic spring wildflower display in dry California gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; slender deutzia is an adaptable, low-maintenance shrub for borders and foundations.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; deutzia blooms on old wood, so prune immediately after flowering in late spring by removing older canes at the base to renew the plant. Deutzia gracilis is a Japanese native deciduous shrub producing fountains of arching stems smothered in late spring with pure-white, star-shaped, 5-petaled flowers in upright, cylindrical racemes — one of the most reliably and abundantly flowering shrubs for temperate gardens. The slender, arching habit and prolific flowering make it ideal as a specimen, in groups, or as a flowering hedge in zones 4–8; the compact cultivar 'Nikko' (12–18 inches) is particularly useful as a groundcover or edging plant and offers outstanding red-purple fall color.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination or direct sow in spring in well-drained, dry, slightly acidic, sandy to rocky, lean soil in partial shade to full sun; slender goldenrod is a woodland-edge and open woodland species of the southeastern Coastal Plain, more shade-tolerant than most goldenrods.
directions: Plant in well-drained, dry, lean, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun in woodland edges, open woodlands, and dry, sandy gardens; slender goldenrod is a southeastern native with a more upright, slender, unbranched stem than most goldenrods, producing a narrow, terminal, spike-like golden flower cluster in late summer. Unlike many goldenrod species that form large, spreading clumps in sunny meadows, slender goldenrod is more at home in open woodland settings and tolerates more shade than most of its relatives. It is relatively restrained in growth and does not spread aggressively, making it well-suited to the native shade garden where its late-summer yellow flowers provide important nectar for migrating monarchs and late-season native bees. Drought-tolerant once established. An underused goldenrod for naturalistic southeastern gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold stratification; seeds can also be sown in spring after a period of cold-moist stratification.
directions: Slender Greenthread is a compact, clump-forming native perennial distinguished from its relative Thelesperma filifolium by its simple, undivided rather than finely dissected leaves; it bears clear golden-yellow daisy flowers singly on slender, upright stems from late spring through summer. Native to dry, rocky, calcareous or sandy open ground and prairies of Texas and adjacent south-central states, it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established. Direct sow in fall in dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun, or cold-stratify seeds and sow in spring. Like other greenthreads, the stems and leaves can be dried and brewed as an herbal tea, and established plants are long-lived with minimal care in appropriate well-drained soils.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring before new growth emerges, setting roots at their original depth in well-drained, humus-rich soil. Avoid disturbing established plants unnecessarily, as Spiranthes lacera resents frequent division.
directions: Plant slender ladies' tresses in a naturalistic setting with dappled light, such as the edge of a woodland or an open meadow, in well-drained loamy or sandy soil with moderate organic matter. Set divisions shallowly at the depth they were growing, water in gently, and mulch lightly with leaf litter to mimic the forest-floor conditions this orchid prefers. Once established, it requires little supplemental water and benefits from minimal fertilization, which can encourage weedy competition. Allow the basal rosette to die back naturally each autumn and leave surrounding leaf litter in place to support the mycorrhizal fungi essential to its survival.

common_name: Slender Lady Palm (Small Rhapis, Miniature Lady Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in partial to deep shade; Slender Lady Palm is one of the finest palms for shaded garden situations and container culture. It accepts less light than almost any other palm. Protect from temperatures below 25–28°F in zone 9a; established clumps in zone 9b often survive brief cold snaps by resprouting from the base. Excellent as a large container specimen that can be moved indoors during cold snaps.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; unlike most palms, Slender Lady Palm thrives and indeed prefers shaded conditions — it will sunburn in direct afternoon sun in zone 9. Rhapis humilis is a clustering, multi-stem palm from southern China closely related to the Lady Palm (Rhapis excelsa) but more slender-stemmed, more shade-tolerant, and typically shorter (5–10 feet versus R. excelsa's potential 15 feet). The palm forms elegant, slowly expanding clumps of dark-green, glossy, fan-shaped fronds on slim, bamboo-like stems covered with persistent leaf sheaths. In zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes, it is an outstanding shade garden palm — one of the few palms that can be planted in deep shade under large trees and will thrive in the low-light conditions that challenge most ornamentals. Slender Lady Palm is also a classic choice for large container culture: slow growth, elegant form, tolerance of indoor conditions, and tidy habit make it a premier container palm for patios, entryways, and atriums. In zone 9a, established clumps in protected locations often resprout from the base if tops are frozen. Hardy to about 25°F for brief periods with established roots.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall after cold stratification or scarification in dry, lean, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: Slender Lespedeza is a slender, upright native perennial of dry, open woods, barrens, and forest edges throughout the eastern and central US. It produces narrow trifoliate leaves and dense axillary clusters of small rose-purple pea flowers from July through September, followed by single-seeded pods that are eaten heavily by quail and small birds. Sow seeds in fall in lean, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, scarifying or cold-stratifying first to break dormancy. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and serves as a valuable late-season native legume for wildlife food plots and dry native meadow gardens.

plant_note: Surface-sow on moist, sandy-acidic soil at or just after last frost; seeds require light for germination and must not be buried.
directions: Slender Marsh Pink is a graceful annual or biennial of wet pine savannas and coastal plain bogs, producing delicate pink, five-petaled flowers marked with a bright yellow star center on wire-thin branching stems from July through September. Grow in full sun with consistently moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil that mimics its native habitat; it tolerates brief periods of standing water. Surface-sow seeds without covering them, as light is required for germination, and keep the seedbed evenly moist until plants are established. Because plants are short-lived, allow some seed to mature and drop in place each season to maintain a self-sustaining colony.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall or sow fresh seeds in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; slender toothwort is a spring ephemeral of rich, moist, mesic slopes and ravine forests of the eastern US, disappearing completely by early summer.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade to partial shade; slender toothwort is a charming native spring ephemeral of the eastern US, producing narrow, simple or lightly divided leaves (narrower than the more familiar cutleaf toothwort) and clusters of small, white to pale pink four-petaled flowers in early spring — one of the first native wildflowers to bloom in the woodland understory. The plant grows from a toothed, horizontal rhizome (the 'tooth' of the common name) that historically was chewed for a peppery, horseradish-like flavor. Goes completely dormant by late spring. Naturalizes by spreading rhizomes and self-sowing to form loose drifts in appropriate conditions. Best grown in combination with other spring ephemerals — trillium, trout lily, spring beauty — in rich, moist shade gardens. An easy and rewarding native for authentic woodland garden underplantings.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; slender woodland sedge prefers moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in dappled to deep shade. A versatile shade sedge tolerating drier conditions than many of its relatives.
directions: Plant in moderately dry to moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade; slender woodland sedge is one of the most useful native sedges for dry to moderately moist shaded conditions, growing naturally in upland deciduous forests across much of the eastern United States. The narrow, arching leaves are bright green and delicate in texture, creating an airy, graceful effect under deciduous trees. Unlike many shade sedges that require consistent moisture, slender woodland sedge tolerates dry summer shade reasonably well once established — making it valuable for the challenging dry-shade conditions under shallow-rooted trees like maples. The drooping, finger-like spikes (suggested by the species name digitalis) are inconspicuous but produced reliably each spring. An excellent, well-behaved ground layer plant that does not spread aggressively.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing and direct sow in fall into dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; the deep taproot establishes during the first growing season and the plant blooms fully in subsequent years.
directions: Slimflower Scurfpea is a deep-rooted native perennial legume of dry, open prairies, sandy plains, and disturbed ground throughout the Great Plains and south-central US, producing wiry, much-branched stems with delicate pinnate leaves covered in tiny resinous glands and loose clusters of blue-violet, pea-like flowers from May through July. Scarify seeds mechanically or with sandpaper before sowing to improve germination rates, then direct sow in fall into dry, lean, well-drained soil in full sun — avoid fertile or amended soil, which favors weedy competition over this tough prairie native. The extensive taproot makes established plants extremely drought-tolerant and difficult to transplant; plants may go dormant in midsummer drought but return vigorously each spring and serve as an important nitrogen-fixer and nectar source for native prairie bees.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to partial shade. Slippery Elm is moderately susceptible to Dutch Elm Disease but less so than American Elm; it is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions including clay, limestone soils, and occasionally flooded areas.
directions: Slippery Elm is a large, somewhat coarser native elm than American Elm, native to rich, moist forest slopes, bottomlands, and upland woods throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to the Dakotas, named for the distinctive slippery, mucilaginous quality of its inner bark, which has been used medicinally for centuries as a demulcent (soothing agent) for sore throats, coughs, and gastrointestinal inflammation — the FDA has recognized the inner bark as a safe and effective over-the-counter demulcent. The rough, sandpaper-textured leaves are distinctive and diagnostic for the species; the reddish, hairy leaf buds in late winter are among the first signs of life in the spring forest. While moderately susceptible to Dutch Elm Disease, Slippery Elm is adaptable to a wider range of soil conditions than American Elm, tolerating clay, limestone, and occasionally wet soils. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the coarse texture and broad shade make it a valuable native alternative to cultivated elms.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; small anise tree is more shade-tolerant and faster-growing than Florida anise (I. floridanum) and is especially effective as a tall, screening shrub in deep shade situations.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; small anise tree is more shade-tolerant and faster-growing than Florida anise (I. floridanum) and is especially effective as a tall, screening shrub in deep shade situations. Illicium parviflorum is a large, fast-growing, evergreen native shrub or small tree endemic to central Florida and historically occurring only in Volusia and Seminole counties, though now widely cultivated throughout the Gulf South for its outstanding performance as a screening plant in difficult shaded and wet conditions; it produces bright, lime-green to medium-green, aromatic, elliptic leaves and tiny, inconspicuous, pale yellowish flowers in spring. A workhorse screening shrub and hedge plant for zones 7–10 that can reach 8–15 feet tall quickly; it naturalizes along shaded stream banks, pond margins, and moist ravines.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; small crowea is one of the most reliably flowering Australian native shrubs — blooming from late summer through winter with extraordinary prolificacy. The clear, rose-pink, five-petaled star flowers are produced almost continuously for 4–6 months on a healthy plant. Tip pruning after spring promotes dense, bushy growth. More tolerant of shading than many Australian natives.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun to part shade; small crowea is one of the most valuable and reliably long-blooming Australian native shrubs for the garden — producing from late summer through autumn and winter an almost continuous succession of five-petaled, clear rose-pink to deep pink, open-faced, star-shaped flowers on a compact, bushy, densely-leaved mound of narrow, aromatic, dark-green foliage. The bloom period of 4–6 months (August through February in warm climates) makes it one of the longest-blooming of all Australian native shrubs. The flowers are in the clear, clean, warm-pink to deep-rose range — not the orange-red of many Australian natives — providing a color that is unusual in winter-flowering Australian plants. The aromatic, narrow, pointed leaves (the plant is in the Rutaceae family, related to citrus and boronia) release a characteristic pleasant scent when brushed. The compact, neat, naturally rounded habit requires little pruning to maintain. Excellent in part shade — one of the few Australian shrubs that tolerates meaningful shade and continues to flower well. A consistently reliable and rewarding garden shrub for zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; CAUTION — white wandering jew is invasive in Florida, the Gulf South, parts of California, and many tropical and warm-temperate regions where it forms dense mats that exclude native understory plants — verify local regulations before planting.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile soil in shade to part shade; CAUTION — invasive in Florida and warm-temperate regions; never plant near natural areas. Tradescantia fluminensis (small leaf spiderwort or white wandering jew) is a South American succulent trailing perennial closely related to the more commonly grown 'wandering Jew' (T. zebrina) and tradescantia group. This species is smaller-leaved with glossy, oval, bright-green leaves on trailing stems, producing tiny white flowers. It is widely used as a shade groundcover indoors and in warm gardens for its easy growth, shade tolerance, and rapid spreading habit. However, T. fluminensis is classified as an invasive weed in Florida, South Africa, New Zealand, Hawaii, and other warm regions where it escapes cultivation and forms dense, impenetrable mats in woodland understories, smothering native understory vegetation. In New Zealand, it is considered one of the most damaging environmental weeds in coastal forest understories. Where legal and appropriate (i.e., in fully contained indoor or urban settings far from natural areas), it is an effective low-maintenance shade groundcover. Note: causes skin irritation in some individuals. Grow with caution and responsibility.

plant_note: Direct sow on or just after the last frost date; seeds germinate readily in warm sandy soil and plants grow quickly to bloom.
directions: Small Palafox is a slender, branching native annual of the aster family, found naturally in dry, sandy grasslands, prairies, and open roadsides across Texas and adjacent south-central states. It produces clusters of small, rose-pink to pale lavender composite flowers with a deeper rose disc from midsummer through fall, providing reliable late-season color in hot, dry gardens. Sow seeds directly in spring after the last frost into dry, sandy, lean, well-drained soil in full sun; plants thrive on neglect and perform best without supplemental fertilizer or irrigation. Small Palafox self-sows freely in open, disturbed sandy ground, making it a reliable naturalizer and low-maintenance filler for Texas native wildflower plantings and sandy prairie restorations.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky or sandy, calcareous to slightly acidic, very well-drained soil; winter cold provides natural stratification.
directions: Direct sow in fall onto thin, rocky or sandy, calcareous to slightly acidic, very well-drained soil in full sun, pressing seed lightly onto the surface and allowing winter cold to stratify it naturally before spring germination. This diminutive native perennial is one of the smallest-statured Scutellaria species in eastern North America, at home in cedar glades, thin-soiled limestone outcrops, and calcareous prairies from the eastern seaboard through the central states. Tiny, tubular, blue to violet-blue, 2-lipped flowers appear on thread-like stems with small, rounded, often toothed leaves from May through July. Plants spread slowly by shallow rhizomes to form loose, low colonies and are excellent in rock garden crevices, glade restorations, and dry, infertile native plant settings where taller competitors are kept in check.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; small Solomon's seal spreads steadily by rhizomes to form colonies and is best planted in generous drifts of at least 5–7 rhizomes.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; small Solomon's seal spreads steadily by rhizomes to form colonies and provides four seasons of interest — emerging foliage in spring, hanging white flowers in late spring, blue-black berries in summer, and golden-yellow fall color. Polygonatum biflorum is the smaller native eastern North American species of Solomon's seal (compared to the great Solomon's seal, P. commutatum), producing arching stems 18–36 inches long with alternate, oval, parallel-veined leaves and paired, pendant, tubular, white to cream flowers dangling from the leaf axils in late spring, followed by glaucous blue-black berries beloved by wildlife. The common name comes from the circular, seal-like scars left on the rhizome where old stems have attached; the rhizome was used medicinally and the young shoots are edible. Outstanding for naturalizing in shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or early spring in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Small's penstemon tolerates partial shade better than most penstemons and is one of the few species that naturalize reliably in the humid Southeast. It self-sows freely and forms naturalized colonies in appropriate conditions.
directions: Sow seeds or plant divisions in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; Small's penstemon is an Appalachian native producing spikes of large, tubular flowers in a distinctive combination of rosy-purple and white — the wide throat of each flower is striped with purple guidelines on a white background, giving a bicolored effect. It blooms in late spring (May–June), a slightly earlier time than many penstemons. Unlike western penstemons that often fail in humid southeastern gardens, Small's penstemon is native to the humid forest edges and rocky slopes of the southern Appalachians from Virginia to Georgia and is naturally adapted to the summer humidity and rainfall of the Southeast. It is one of the most garden-worthy penstemons for humid zone 7–9 gardens where western species typically struggle or die after one season. An important early nectar source for hummingbirds and native bumblebees.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is a Pacific Northwest native that tolerates deeper shade than most heucheras, making it useful as a shade groundcover under conifers where few perennials survive.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is a Pacific Northwest native that tolerates deeper shade than most heucheras, making it useful as a shade groundcover under conifers where few perennials survive. Heuchera micrantha is the Pacific Northwest native alumroot most closely associated with the famous 'Palace Purple' cultivar and the cascade of bronze- and purple-leafed garden heucheras that followed; the species itself has large, lobed, light-to-medium-green leaves with silver mottling and produces tall, open, airy panicles of tiny white flowers in late spring. It is native to moist, forested cliffs and shaded stream banks from British Columbia to northern California and is an important parent species in Heuchera hybridization programs; in the garden it is a tough, reliable shade perennial for the Pacific Northwest and is more tolerant of dry shade than most species once established.

common_name: Small-Flowered Campylocentrum (Leafless Florida Orchid, Ghost Orchid Relative)
plant_note: Mount on rough-barked wood or cork with exposed aerial roots in bright indirect to partial direct light; Campylocentrum micranthum is a leafless epiphytic orchid — like the related Ghost Orchid (Dendrophylax lindenii), it produces no leaves and obtains all photosynthesis through flat, green, chlorophyll-containing roots. The roots must receive light (bright indirect to partial direct) to support the plant. A very slow-growing, specialist orchid for patient collectors with appropriate high-humidity conditions. Wild plants are protected. Zone 10-12 outdoors. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow mounted on rough bark or cork in partial indirect to dappled direct light with high humidity — Small-Flowered Campylocentrum is a leafless, photosynthetic-root orchid that requires light on the roots and consistently warm, humid conditions to thrive. Campylocentrum micranthum is a minute, leafless, epiphytic orchid native to southern Florida (Collier and Miami-Dade counties), Puerto Rico, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, and South America in the Orchidaceae family, representing one of the fascinating group of 'ghost orchids' — orchids that have eliminated their leaves entirely and adopted a photosynthetic root system. The plant is visible only as a mass of flat, strap-like, green to gray-green roots spreading across the bark surface of its host tree. From these roots in summer and fall, tiny (2–3 mm) cream-white to yellowish flowers emerge on short racemes — the flowers microscopic by orchid standards, requiring a hand lens for appreciation, but formally complete with sepals, petals, lip, and column. Campylocentrum is a genus of approximately 60 species distributed from the Caribbean through tropical America, related to the more famous Dendrophylax genus that includes Florida's Ghost Orchid (D. lindenii). In south Florida, C. micranthum grows naturally on live oaks, pond apples, and other hardwood trees in hammock forests. A specialist's orchid of genuine ecological interest, particularly for collectors drawn to Florida's remarkable native orchid flora. Non-toxic.

common_name: Small-Flowered Cuphea (Candy Corn Cuphea, Micropetal Cuphea)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil after last frost; Cuphea micropetala is one of the more cold-tolerant Cuphea species, surviving temperatures to 25–28°F in established plants and often regrowning from the root crown after light freezes in zone 9. The orange-and-yellow tubular flowers are exceptionally attractive to hummingbirds and are produced almost continuously from spring through frost. The common name 'Candy Corn Cuphea' reflects the bicolored orange-yellow flower resembling candy corn. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Small-Flowered Cuphea blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates partial shade and is more drought-tolerant than many tropical-looking ornamental shrubs once established. Cuphea micropetala is a compact, semi-woody, perennial shrub native to Mexico and Guatemala in the Lythraceae family, one of the most cold-hardy and ornamentally valuable of the approximately 260 Cuphea species for zone 8-11 gardens. The plant produces a dense, upright to somewhat mounding form with narrow, lance-shaped, dark-green leaves and an exceptionally free-flowering habit — producing dozens to hundreds of tubular flowers at the leaf axils simultaneously through the warm months from spring through fall. Each flower is a small (0.5-inch), tubular, slightly curved structure in orange to orange-red with a yellow-green tip — a bicolored orange-and-yellow pattern that strongly resembles a piece of candy corn, explaining the marketing name 'Candy Corn Plant' sometimes applied to this species. The nectar-rich, tubular, hummingbird-adapted flowers attract Ruby-throated, Rufous, and other hummingbird species reliably, with hummingbirds visiting and revisiting a flowering Cuphea micropetala plant dozens of times daily during migration. Greater cold hardiness (to zone 8) than most ornamental Cuphea species makes this a particularly valuable selection for zone 9 gardens. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, rocky or sandy soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is a limestone cliff and cave-entrance specialist native to the Appalachians, preferring the cool, consistently moist, very well-drained conditions of shaded rock overhangs and cliff faces.
directions: Plant in moist, very well-drained, humus-rich, rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; small-flowered alumroot is an Appalachian native of limestone cliffs, cave entrances, and shaded rocky outcrops, naturally growing in the perpetually cool, moist, well-drained environment of rock overhangs where moisture seeps through rather than pooling. The rounded, maple-like, dark green leaves form low, neat rosettes and are attractive year-round as a semi-evergreen groundcover in appropriate rocky, shaded garden settings. The tiny, white flowers on airy, branching panicles in late summer are less showy than garden heuchera cultivars but provide nectar for small native bees. An excellent choice for shaded rock gardens, crevices in stone walls, and the base of large boulders in woodland gardens in zones 4–8.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; small-headed blazing star grows naturally in dry, rocky, calcareous soils of the Cumberland Plateau and surrounding Appalachian region, in open glades and rock outcrops in full sun.
directions: Plant in dry, rocky, calcareous or slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; small-headed blazing star is a distinctly more slender, more narrowly adapted liatris than the widely cultivated Liatris spicata, native to the open rocky glades and dry, calcareous slopes of the Cumberland Plateau of Tennessee and surrounding areas. The small flower heads give it a more airy, delicate appearance than the more robust blazing stars, and it blooms in late summer with the typical rose-purple liatris color. Like all Liatris species, the flowers open from the top of the spike downward, and it serves as an important late-season nectar source for monarch butterflies and native bees during their fall migration period. An excellent, drought-tolerant species for dry, rocky, calcareous garden soils.

plant_note: Surface-sow on moist soil at or just after last frost; do not cover seeds, as light aids germination.
directions: Slender, freely branching native annual or short-lived perennial smothered in masses of small white to pale lavender daisy-like flowers with yellow centers from late summer through October. Native to moist, open, disturbed habitats, ditches, and pond margins throughout the southeastern US, it is much more delicate in appearance than the larger Boltonia asteroides. Surface-sow on moist soil in full sun after last frost; plants naturalize readily by self-seeding in consistently moist sites. An excellent fine-textured filler for the back of rain garden borders and native wetland restorations where consistent moisture is available.

plant_note: Lightly scarify seeds with sandpaper or soak overnight in warm water before sowing to improve germination, though seeds will often sprout without treatment.
directions: Sow seeds in spring directly into their permanent location or into deep containers to accommodate early taproot development. Plant in full sun in dry to moderately moist, well-drained soil — this shrub thrives in poor, alkaline, or sandy conditions where most plants struggle. Once established it requires virtually no supplemental irrigation and tolerates wind, drought, and severe cold with ease. Use in mass plantings for erosion control, shelterbelts, or wildlife hedgerows across challenging exposed sites.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into sandy, rocky, or gravelly well-drained soil in full sun; Nuttall's milkvetch is adapted to naturally disturbed, nutrient-poor ground and requires excellent drainage — it will rot in heavy, wet, or clay soils.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall into sandy, rocky, or gravelly well-drained soil in full sun; nick the hard seed coat lightly before sowing to improve germination and inoculate with a legume rhizobium inoculant to encourage nitrogen fixation from the outset. Astragalus nuttallianus is a native annual of the south-central United States — primarily Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico — producing small purple pea-like flowers in spring on low, spreading stems that thrive in the same disturbed, calcareous, sandy soils where it naturally occurs along roadsides, cedar glades, and open rangeland. This inconspicuous but ecologically significant species is a documented larval host for the Reakirt's Blue butterfly, a specialist of leguminous plants found across the arid Southwest, making it a valuable addition to native wildflower mixes in its natural range.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; smooth aster tolerates a wide range of soils, from lean prairie ground to average garden soil, and is one of the more adaptable native asters for general garden use.
directions: Plant in average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and generally sturdy and self-supporting without staking. Symphyotrichum laeve (smooth aster, or smooth blue aster) is a native tallgrass prairie perennial distinguished by its smooth, waxy, blue-green foliage — a notable contrast to the coarser, hairier leaves of many other native asters — and its clouds of lavender-blue, yellow-centered flowers that open from late summer into fall. It is considered one of the most valuable late-season native asters for pollinators, providing critical nectar for native bees, honeybees, and migrating monarch butterflies as they refuel for their journey south, and it also serves as a larval host plant for pearl crescent butterflies. Its sturdy, upright habit and long fall bloom period make it an excellent choice for the middle of a sunny native perennial border or prairie-style planting, zone 3–8.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days; often blooms the second year.
directions: Give seed a month of cold-moist stratification, then sow in spring. This dependable native perennial bears clouds of small lavender-blue, daisy-like flowers in late summer and fall. Plant in full sun and average, well-drained soil where its smooth blue-green foliage resists disease. It provides critical late-season nectar for bees and migrating butterflies as other flowers fade.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Bougainvillea glabra blooms most heavily under mild drought stress (slightly dry) and full sun — avoid rich, wet soil or excessive fertilization, which promotes vegetative growth at the expense of the showy bracts.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide a sturdy trellis, wall, or fence for climbing support. Bougainvillea glabra (smooth bougainvillea) is the species most commonly sold as 'bougainvillea' in the nursery trade — a vigorous, thorny, sprawling vine or shrub from Brazil producing masses of small, white, tubular true flowers surrounded by the magnificently colored bracts (modified leaves) in magenta, purple, red, orange, yellow, white, or bicolor combinations that are the ornamental feature of the plant. B. glabra differs from the common hybrid Bougainvillea spectabilis in having smooth (glabrous, as the name implies) stems and leaves vs. hairy stems and is generally considered more free-blooming and compact. Bougainvillea blooms most heavily after mild water stress in full sun; withhold water before anticipated bloom periods to trigger flowering. In zone 9, it may die back in hard freezes but resprouts vigorously from roots when established; in zones 10–12, it is a dramatic year-round bloomer. Stems are armed with sharp thorns; handle with heavy gloves.

plant_note: Direct sow cold-stratified seed in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to gravelly, thin soil in full sun to partial shade; smooth coneflower is a Federally Threatened species adapted to disturbed, thin-soil openings in cedar-hardwood woodland — it requires good drainage and open mineral soil.
directions: Sow cold-stratified seed in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky to gravelly soil in full sun to partial shade — smooth coneflower is a Federally Threatened native coneflower of the Appalachian piedmont and Blue Ridge foothills, declining primarily due to habitat loss and canopy closure over its characteristic thin-soil, semi-open woodland and roadside habitats. It is distinguished from the more common purple coneflower (E. purpurea) by its smooth (not rough) stems and leaves and its adaptation to disturbed, thin, rocky soils — often in partially shaded situations unlike most other Echinacea. The pale to deep rose-purple ray flowers and prominent central cone are characteristic of the genus and equally attractive to pollinators and beneficial for gardens. Growing this species supports its conservation by maintaining cultivated populations and seed banks. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants from reputable native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Plant plugs or bare-root divisions in spring in regularly flooded tidal flats, muddy marsh edges, or constructed tidal wetlands; smooth cordgrass must be planted in the intertidal zone where it is flooded by saltwater twice daily — it will not persist in fresh water or fully upland sites.
directions: Smooth cordgrass (formerly Spartina alterniflora) is the dominant grass of tidal salt marshes along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of North America — arguably the single most ecologically important native grass on the eastern seaboard, as it forms the structural foundation of the salt marsh ecosystem.
