directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; southern live oak is the quintessential evergreen tree of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, forming massive, wide-spreading crowns with horizontal limbs draped in Spanish moss that define the character of the region. This long-lived giant is remarkably tough — salt spray, poor sandy soils, periodic flooding, and coastal winds are all tolerated once the tree is established, and mature trees are exceptionally drought-tolerant. The small, dark acorns are produced in generous quantities and are critically important food for wood ducks, mallards, squirrels, and deer. Acorn production begins at 25 years and peaks in trees 75 years and older, underscoring that this is a multigenerational planting that rewards patience with an irreplaceable landscape anchor.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter or spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; southern magnolia tolerates a range of soils but performs best in fertile, moist, slightly acidic conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; southern magnolia is the defining icon of the Deep South, a massive evergreen tree with leathery, glossy dark green leaves (with rusty-brown undersides) and enormous, intensely fragrant white flowers up to 12 inches across that open from May through September — among the largest flowers of any native North American tree. The tree is native to the coastal plain from North Carolina to Texas and is the state flower and tree of Mississippi and Louisiana. Compact cultivars like 'Little Gem' (20–25 feet, repeat-blooming) and 'Brackens Brown Beauty' make it accessible for smaller gardens. The cone-like fruit with brilliant red seeds is highly ornamental and provides important food for gray squirrels, turkeys, and songbirds. Plant away from foundations, driveways, and structures to allow for its eventual large size.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring and plant in moist, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Southern Maidenhair Fern is unusual among native ferns in preferring neutral to alkaline soil and often grows naturally on moist limestone outcrops, seep ledges, and waterfall spray zones.
directions: Southern Maidenhair Fern is the subtropical maidenhair native to the Gulf Coast and southern United States, native to moist limestone ledges, cave mouths, waterfall spray zones, and moist shaded cliffs from Virginia to Florida and west to California and south through the tropics, where it grows in the constant moisture of seeping or spray-wetted rock faces in deep shade. Its delicate, fan-shaped, bright green leaflets on arching, wiry black stems make it one of the most graceful and ornamental of all ferns; in zones 8–11 it is semi-evergreen to evergreen in the garden, providing year-round texture in the deep shade. Unlike most native ferns, Southern Maidenhair Fern prefers neutral to slightly alkaline soil and is naturally found on limestone substrates — amend planting areas with crushed limestone or dolomite and keep the soil constantly moist. An exceptional fern for shaded water features, seep gardens, or moist rockeries.

plant_note: Establish divisions in early spring into permanently moist or wet, nutrient-poor to moderately fertile soil in partial shade or open sun. Avoid rich garden soils, which encourage lush foliage at the expense of flowering.
directions: Plant southern marsh orchid in a rain garden, bog margin, or consistently moist border where the soil stays wet through the growing season; the tuberous roots tolerate standing water in winter but prefer slowly draining, moisture-retentive soil in summer. Amend heavy clay with coarse grit to prevent anaerobic conditions while maintaining the high moisture this species requires, and incorporate a modest amount of leaf mold to improve structure. Set divisions at their original depth in early spring, water generously to eliminate air pockets, and top-dress lightly with a grit-and-leaf-mold mix each autumn. Once established, clumps can be divided every three to four years in early autumn after flowering and the divisions used to create naturalistic drifts in wet meadow or pondside plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; southern meadow rue requires consistently moist, humus-rich soil and partial to deep shade — it does not tolerate drought or full sun in hot climates.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — southern meadow rue is a rare Appalachian native of moist, rich, shaded mountain woodlands and stream-bank forests in Virginia, North Carolina, and Tennessee, producing the classic meadow-rue effect at an impressive scale: tall (3–6 foot) stems clothed in beautiful, blue-green, columbine-like compound leaves, topped in summer with loose, airy panicles of small white flowers with prominent stamens that create a soft, misty cloud-like effect above the foliage. The delicate, divided foliage is exceptionally ornamental throughout the season. It is one of the taller native shade perennials available, providing dramatic vertical interest in shaded borders, woodland gardens, and moist stream-bank plantings. At the northern edge of zone 8 in moist, deeply shaded, well-drained positions it can succeed, but it is most reliable in zone 4–7 woodland conditions.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in fall or early spring in well-drained, sandy or loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Southern Red Cedar is highly salt-tolerant and is an excellent windbreak and wildlife tree for coastal landscapes in the Gulf states.
directions: Southern Red Cedar is the coastal plain and Gulf Coast counterpart to Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana), native to the sandy soils, coastal hammocks, maritime forests, and barrier islands from North Carolina through Florida and around the Gulf Coast to Texas, where it is distinguished from J. virginiana by its more pendulous (weeping) branch tips and overall softer appearance. Salt spray-tolerant, drought-tolerant, and adapted to the sandy, low-nutrient soils of the coastal plain, Southern Red Cedar is an excellent native windbreak, privacy screen, and wildlife tree for Gulf Coast landscapes in zones 7–11. Like Eastern Red Cedar, it produces fleshy blue-green berries (technically seed cones) that are consumed by dozens of bird species including cedar waxwings and bluebirds, and provides dense, year-round nesting cover; plant male and female trees together for consistent berry production. Grow in full sun in any well-drained soil; it is notably more heat-tolerant than Eastern Red Cedar and performs better in the lower South and in coastal situations.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist to slightly dry, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; southern shield fern is exceptionally heat and drought tolerant for a fern once established and is one of the most reliable shade ferns for Gulf Coast and Deep South gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade — southern shield fern (Thelypteris kunthii) is the workhorse fern of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, naturalized along stream banks, drainage ditches, woodland edges, and the shaded understory of pine and live oak forests from Virginia to Texas. It spreads by creeping rhizomes to form large colonies, deciduous in the upper zones but semi-evergreen in zone 9–10, and tolerates more heat, drought, and root competition from large trees than virtually any other native fern in the South. The fronds are medium green, 2–3 feet tall, with pinnate-pinnatifid division and a soft texture; they emerge in spring and provide lush, layered textural coverage all season. Establish with regular water, then let it fend for itself — a uniquely low-maintenance shade groundcover for difficult dry-shade situations under mature trees. Remove old fronds in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants from cuttings in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade; southern spicebush is a federally threatened species and should only be planted from nursery-propagated stock, never from wild collection.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to deep shade at wetland edges, spring-fed areas, and depression swamps; southern spicebush is a federally threatened native shrub of the southeastern United States, growing naturally in small, disjunct populations in depression swamps, bay swamps, and spring-fed wet areas from Missouri to Florida. A close relative of the common spicebush (L. benzoin) but adapted to wetter conditions and deeper shade, it produces the same intensely aromatic, spicy-fragrant foliage and stems when crushed. Like common spicebush, it is the larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail butterfly. The beautiful yellow flowers in early spring emerge before the leaves, and the bright red drupes in fall provide excellent wildlife food. Growing this plant in the garden directly supports conservation of a federally threatened species while providing exceptional wildlife value in shaded, wet-site conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or transplants in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; southern spiderwort naturalizes freely in shaded gardens by self-seeding and division of the fibrous root clumps.
directions: Southern spiderwort is a shade-tolerant native Tradescantia of the moist, rich, rocky slopes and ravines of the Appalachian foothills and Ozarks to the Gulf Coastal Plain — the species name 'subaspera' means 'somewhat rough,' referring to the slightly hairy stems and leaves that distinguish it from the smooth Ohio spiderwort. Like other spiderworts, it produces vivid three-petaled flowers of brilliant blue-violet with bright yellow stamens that open in the morning and close by midday, continuing to produce new flowers throughout a long season from late spring through summer; each flower lasts only a few hours but the plant produces dozens in succession. It grows well in the partial to moderate shade of mature deciduous trees and is one of the few genuinely shade-tolerant native wildflowers with a long bloom season — most shade perennials bloom only briefly in spring. The clumping habit and bold, strap-like leaves provide attractive foliage interest even when not in flower; divide clumps every 2–3 years in fall to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall immediately upon ripening (they lose viability quickly) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; southern sugar maple is the heat-adapted southern relative of sugar maple, native to mixed hardwood forests of the coastal plain and piedmont from Virginia to Texas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; southern sugar maple is the heat-tolerant, summer-drought-adapted southern counterpart to the familiar sugar maple (Acer saccharum), differing in smaller leaf size, lighter texture, and significantly greater heat tolerance, performing well in zones 7–9 where northern sugar maple languishes or dies in the summer heat. The fall color is outstanding — rich orange, red, and yellow tones that rival northern sugar maple in many years — providing some of the best native fall color in the South. The bark is more furrowed and less smooth than northern maple. Although not tapped commercially for syrup, the sap does contain sugar. A superb native shade tree for southern gardens providing habitat, fall color, and a graceful canopy that suburban northern sugar maples cannot achieve in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in any well-drained to moist soil in any light condition from full sun to deep shade; this is one of the most adaptable native plants for the South.
directions: Plant in any soil — wet or dry, acidic or alkaline, rich or poor, sun or deep shade — wax myrtle tolerates virtually every condition in zone 7–11 once established and is arguably the Gulf Coast's most versatile and valuable native shrub. The aromatic, evergreen foliage provides year-round screening and privacy; both male and female plants produce tiny waxy blue-gray berries that encrust the branches in fall and winter, providing essential food for yellow-rumped warblers, tree swallows, and many other bird species that can digest the high-fat wax. The root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil over time. Prune heavily at any time to maintain a desired size, or allow it to develop naturally into a multi-trunked small tree 15–20 feet tall. The aromatic leaves have traditional use as an insect repellent.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in spring into consistently moist or wet soil in partial to full shade; plants adapt well to swamp margins, rain gardens, and shaded stream banks where standing water is intermittent.
directions: Plant divisions in spring into moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, setting crowns at soil level and watering thoroughly to establish firm root contact. Southern waxy sedge is native to swamp margins and moist woodland understories throughout the southeastern United States, where its glaucous blue-green leaves provide year-round color in spots too wet and shaded for most ornamental grasses. Keep the root zone consistently moist, especially during the first growing season, and apply a light layer of leaf mulch to replicate the forest-floor conditions this sedge prefers. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to refresh vigor and propagate new plants for expanding a shaded rain garden or streamside planting.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring in moist to moderately dry, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; southern wild ginger is slow to spread but forms attractive evergreen colonies and is more heat and drought tolerant than the northern wild ginger (A. canadense), making it the better choice for zones 7–9.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade — southern wild ginger is an elegant native groundcover of the southeastern US Piedmont and coastal plain, producing attractive, arrowhead-shaped evergreen leaves that are beautifully mottled with silver-gray markings along the veins. Unlike its deciduous northern relative (Asarum canadense), this species holds its foliage through winter in zones 7–9, maintaining year-round groundcover. The curious jug-shaped, brown-purple flowers emerge at soil level in early spring and are pollinated by ground beetles — they are almost entirely hidden by the foliage and go unnoticed, but the effect in leaf is outstanding. The foliage has a mild gingery fragrance when crushed. It spreads slowly by rhizome to form dense mats that suppress weeds under trees and in shaded beds, making it an excellent choice for dry to moderately moist shade in southern gardens.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant nursery transplants in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Southern Wood Fern tolerates seasonal flooding and thrives at the margins of ponds, streams, and swamps throughout the Gulf Coast region.
directions: Southern Wood Fern is the premier native wood fern for Gulf Coast gardens, native to the wet bottomland forests, swamp edges, and rich floodplains of the southeastern coastal plain from South Carolina and Georgia west to Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, where it grows alongside cypress, tupelo, and swamp chestnut oak in semi-permanently wet soils. Its large, dark green, leathery fronds are semi-evergreen to evergreen in zones 8–10, providing year-round structure in the shade garden, and the plant tolerates seasonal flooding better than almost any other wood fern. An outstanding choice for wet, shaded rain garden depressions, pond margins, and the moist shade under magnolias and live oaks in Gulf Coast landscapes. Divide clumps in spring; plant in heavily amended, consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade, and mulch deeply to retain moisture during dry spells.

common_name: Southern Wood Fern (River Fern, Kunth Maiden Fern)
plant_note: Plant container stock or rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full shade; southern wood fern is native to moist, wooded stream banks and shaded bottomlands from South Carolina to Texas and is exceptionally well-adapted to Gulf Coast shade gardens — thriving in the heat and humidity of zone 9.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part to full shade; keep consistently moist. Thelypteris kunthii (southern wood fern or river fern) is the most commonly encountered native fern of the Gulf Coastal Plain understory — a vigorous, deciduous-to-semi-evergreen, colony-forming fern found naturally along shaded stream banks, bottomland forests, and moist woodland margins from the Carolinas through Florida and west to Texas. The fronds are once-pinnate (single-divided) with narrow, soft, light-to-medium-green leaflets and a somewhat delicate texture, produced in graceful, arching, spreading colonies that can cover large areas of shaded ground. Unlike many ferns that struggle in the heat and humidity of southern summers, T. kunthii actively thrives in Gulf Coast conditions, making it an outstanding — and underused — native groundcover for shaded areas. It spreads moderately by underground rhizomes to form weed-suppressing colonies. In zone 9, fronds may go partially or fully dormant in a hard freeze but the plant resproutes vigorously in spring. As a low-maintenance native shade groundcover, southern wood fern has few equals for moist, shaded sites in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil; this southeastern native is distinct from the more northern E. americanum and is the appropriate trout lily species for Gulf Coast-adjacent woodland gardens in zones 6–9.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep immediately after division in late summer or early fall in moist, leafy, slightly acidic woodland soil under deciduous trees; do not let corms dry out before planting. Southern yellow trout lily (Erythronium rostratum) is the southeastern counterpart to the familiar E. americanum, native to the coastal plain and adjacent Piedmont from Kentucky south to Louisiana and east to Georgia, blooming in February through April with nodding yellow flowers with distinctly reflexed petals and a characteristic beaked (rostrate) capsule that distinguishes it from other yellow Erythronium species; the green leaves with mottled brown spots are the same beautiful trout-spotted appearance as other species. This is a spring ephemeral that goes fully dormant by late spring — pair with late-emerging hostas or ferns to cover the gap. A valuable species for regional provenance in Gulf South woodland gardens.

common_name: Souvenir de la Malmaison Rose (Classic 1843 Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in a site with excellent air circulation; Souvenir de la Malmaison is an 1843 Bourbon rose named for Empress Josephine's garden and prized for huge, quartered, intensely fragrant blooms, though its densely petaled flowers can ball and fail to open in prolonged Gulf Coast humidity, so afternoon shade and open air movement help performance.
directions: Plant in full sun with excellent air circulation in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart. Introduced in France in 1843 and named for the rose garden of Empress Josephine at Château de Malmaison, this Bourbon rose is famous for enormous, flat, quartered blooms in soft blush-pink packed with dozens of petals and a rich, classic old-rose fragrance considered among the finest of any rose. It blooms in flushes from spring through fall on a compact, sturdy shrub, but in the humid Gulf South its densely petaled blooms can 'ball' — swelling with trapped moisture and failing to open — so siting it where morning sun dries the foliage quickly and air moves freely improves bloom quality. It is more disease-resistant than most Bourbons but still benefits from being kept away from overhead irrigation. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to remove spent flowers and shape the plant, and avoid heavy pruning, which reduces flowering.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container specimens in spring in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; handle with extreme caution — the leaf tips are rigid, needle-sharp, and can cause serious eye and skin injury. Spanish bayonet is one of the most salt-tolerant yuccas, thriving in coastal conditions.
directions: Plant offsets or container specimens in very well-drained, dry, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — Spanish bayonet is the most commonly encountered native yucca of the Gulf Coast and Southeast Atlantic coast, forming dramatic, architectural rosettes of rigid, dark green leaves tipped with needle-sharp points (hence 'bayonet') on stems that can grow 6–10 feet tall and develop a trunk-like stem over years. Mature plants are truly striking landscape specimens. Enormous panicles of white, pendulous, edible flowers appear in spring-summer; the large, fleshy fruit capsules and flowers are both edible and were important food sources for Native Americans. Plant well away from foot traffic areas — the razor-sharp leaf tips are a serious safety hazard. Extraordinary drought, salt spray, and wind tolerance makes it one of the best structural plants for coastal, dune, and xeriscape landscapes. Deer-proof, essentially pest-free, and immortal in adapted sandy soils.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall; naturalizes readily in shade.
directions: Plant Spanish bluebell bulbs in fall about four inches deep in moist, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade. The upright stems carry many bell-shaped blue, pink, or white flowers in mid to late spring. It naturalizes vigorously beneath trees and shrubs and can spread aggressively, so site it thoughtfully. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back naturally to feed the bulbs for next season.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in well-drained to moderately moisture-retentive, humus-enriched soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Spanish bluebells are vigorous and adaptable, thriving particularly well in partial shade beneath deciduous trees where they receive bright spring light before the canopy leafs out. Plant in large informal drifts for best effect and avoid mixing with sites near native English bluebells (H. non-scripta), as the two species hybridize freely and the resulting hybrids can threaten native bluebell populations.
directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade in fall for April-May bloom; Spanish bluebells are among the most vigorous and freely naturalizing of all spring bulbs, producing upright, arching stems bearing loose, one-sided racemes of pendant, lightly fragrant, bell-shaped flowers in shades of blue-violet, pink, or white above strap-like, bright green foliage. They are outstanding shade garden bulbs, naturalizing with exceptional ease under the canopies of deciduous trees and shrubs — conditions that suit them perfectly, as they receive full sun in early spring before the trees leaf out, then retreat into dormancy under dappled summer shade. Over time they spread by offsets and prolific self-seeding to form large, informal colonies that provide a reliable mid-spring floral display year after year without any maintenance. Note that Spanish bluebells hybridize readily with the rarer, native English bluebell (Hyacinthoides non-scripta) where the two grow in proximity; they should not be planted near naturalized stands of the native species.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost, nicking or soaking seeds first; Spanish flag grows quickly and appreciates a head start. In zones 9–11 it can be direct sown in warm soil after last frost and grows as a perennial.
directions: Start indoors and transplant to a sunny trellis or fence after last frost; Spanish flag is an unusual and showy Ipomoea vine producing one-sided clusters of tubular flowers that dramatically change color as they age — opening bright scarlet red at the tip of the cluster, fading through orange to yellow to white at the base, so that a single flower cluster simultaneously displays four different colors like a living color gradient. The palm-shaped, deeply lobed leaves are attractive even without flowers. The plant climbs quickly to 10 feet or more and blooms from midsummer through frost. It is an outstanding plant for adding tropical flair to a trellis, arbor, or fence and the constant succession of multicolored flower clusters is endlessly interesting.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in moist but well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Spanish hyacinth is exceptional among small spring bulbs for its genuine shade tolerance and thrives under the canopy of deciduous trees and shrubs where it receives bright indirect light but little direct sun. It naturalizes freely under trees where most spring bulbs struggle and is most effective planted in generous informal drifts of 20 or more.
directions: Plant small bulbs 2-3 inches deep in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in fall for May bloom; Spanish hyacinth is a charming and genuinely shade-tolerant small bulb from the Pyrenean mountains, closely related to Hyacinthus but far more tolerant of woodland conditions, producing slender 6-8-inch stems bearing loose, one-sided racemes of 6-12 pendant, bright blue, tubular bells with slightly flared mouths that closely resemble a miniature grape hyacinth in form but are a more vivid, pure blue. It is one of the most valuable of all shade-tolerant spring bulbs precisely because so few small bulbs bloom well in the deep, root-filled shade under established deciduous trees — a position where it thrives and naturalizes freely by offsets and occasional self-seeding into charming informal colonies. A white-flowered form ('Alba') is also available. Excellent for underplanting shrubs, naturalized in woodland gardens, or interplanted with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials for a layered spring display.

plant_note: Hang clumps of fresh material on tree branches or structures in any location with bright indirect light and high humidity; Spanish moss requires no soil — it absorbs all moisture and nutrients from the air through tiny scales on its leaves. It grows naturally throughout the Gulf Coast from the Carolinas to Texas.
directions: Hang fresh clumps on tree branches or wire supports in partial shade with good air circulation and humidity; Spanish moss is one of the most distinctive and iconic plants of the American Deep South, the gray-green curtains draping from live oaks and cypresses that define the visual landscape of the Gulf Coast. Despite its name, it is neither a moss nor Spanish — it is an epiphytic bromeliad native from Virginia to Argentina that attaches to tree branches without parasitizing them, absorbing rain, dew, and nutrients from airborne dust through thousands of tiny absorptive scales covering each silvery-gray thread. It provides critical nesting habitat for bats, birds, and jumping spiders, and was historically used as mattress and upholstery stuffing, building insulation, packing material, and for making mud-and-moss wattle walls. It produces tiny, fragrant yellow-green flowers in spring. A piece of living southern heritage for zone 8–11 landscapes.

common_name: Spanish Needles (Beggar's Ticks, White Bidens, Shepherd's Needle)
plant_note: Spanish Needles establishes spontaneously throughout zone 8-12 in disturbed sunny areas and is more often managed than planted — most gardeners encounter it as a beneficial 'weed' rather than deliberately sowing it. Allow patches to self-establish in sunny, informal areas of the garden, wild garden edges, or meadow plantings. It is classified as native to the Caribbean and tropical Americas, naturalized broadly in the southeastern US. The barbed seeds (the 'needles') attach to clothing and animal fur — plant away from high-traffic areas to minimize this nuisance, but retain at garden margins for exceptional pollinator value. Non-toxic.
directions: Grows in full sun in any disturbed, well-drained soil — Spanish Needles is an opportunistic colonizer of open, sunny ground and once established in a garden, perpetuates itself by prodigious self-seeding, requiring only that it be tolerated in appropriate areas. Bidens alba is a fast-growing annual to short-lived perennial forb native to the Caribbean, Florida, and tropical America in the Asteraceae family, now naturalized and extremely common throughout the southeastern US, the Gulf Coast, the Pacific Islands, Asia, and tropical regions worldwide. The plant produces upright stems of opposite, dark-green, pinnately compound leaves and, from late spring through fall (essentially year-round in frost-free conditions), quantities of small white daisy flowers with 5–8 white ray petals surrounding a yellow disk center — modest in size (0.75–1 inch) but produced in remarkable abundance. The ecological value of Bidens alba as a pollinator plant in the southeastern US and Gulf Coast is genuinely extraordinary: it is documented as one of the single most important nectar and pollen sources for honey bees (Apis mellifera), native bees, hoverflies, and butterflies throughout Florida, where it is considered the most important honey bee nectar plant of the fall season. The small, barbed, twin-pointed seeds ('needles') attach easily to clothing and animal fur, explaining the spread of this plant. A keystone pollinator plant for Florida and Gulf Coast wild gardens. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Spanish rockrose requires excellent drainage and tolerates no waterlogging. It is closely related to Cistus and requires similar cultivation: lean soil, full sun, no summer water once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Spanish rockrose is a close relative of the cistus family shrubs, native to dry, sandy, and rocky scrublands of the Iberian Peninsula, producing spreading mounds of gray-green to silver-gray aromatic foliage and in late spring through early summer, vivid bright-yellow flowers 1–2 inches across, each with a distinctive dark reddish-brown to purple-black basal blotch on each petal — a spot pattern producing a strong eye at the center of each flower in dramatic contrast to the yellow. The dark basal markings against clear yellow create a flower of considerable visual impact. Like the cistuses, each flower lasts only a day, but is replaced in rapid succession over several weeks. Often crossed with Cistus species to produce the hybrid genus x Halimiocistus, which shows the qualities of both parents. Outstanding for lean, dry, hot sunny gardens in zones 8b–10, particularly in combination with other Mediterranean scrub plants.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun. Spanish Stopper tolerates salt spray, drought, and partial shade and is an excellent evergreen screening shrub for coastal landscapes in zones 9–11.
directions: Spanish Stopper is an attractive evergreen native shrub or small tree, native to the coastal hammocks, scrub, and pinelands of south Florida and the Florida Keys, with a natural range extending through the Caribbean and tropical Americas. Small, oval, aromatic, dark green leaves densely clothe the branches and produce a thick, fine-textured screen when planted as a hedge; clusters of small white flowers in summer are followed by round black berries that are avidly consumed by mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings. Highly adaptable to a range of coastal conditions including salt spray, drought, and partial shade, Spanish Stopper is an excellent foundation plant, hedge, or specimen for south Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes in zones 9b–11. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants require little care and tolerate periodic drought with minimal stress.

plant_note: Sow after frost danger passes in warm, well-drained soil.
directions: This South African annual thrives in hot, dry sites and forms a low, spreading carpet of succulent foliage topped with neon 1.5-inch daisy-like blooms. Direct sow into fast-draining soil after the last frost, barely covering the fine seed and keeping it lightly moist until germination. Give plants full sun; flowers open in bright light and close at night or under clouds. Space plants so they can knit together along borders, between pavers, or in rock gardens. Avoid overwatering, as soggy roots quickly rot in this drought-loving species.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to average soil in partial to full shade; Sparkler sedge establishes quickly and maintains its striking variegated appearance throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to average soil in partial to full shade; Sparkler sedge is one of the most visually distinctive ornamental sedges available, forming a compact, upright mound of narrow, strap-like dark-green leaves boldly edged and striped with creamy-white margins that appear almost neon in shaded positions. The variegated foliage is at its most brilliant in partial shade; deep shade causes some fading but the plant remains ornamental. Sparkler is more heat-tolerant than most variegated sedges, performing well in zones 7–10 where many Carex cultivars struggle. The upright form and strongly contrasting variegation make it an outstanding accent or groundcover in Southern shade gardens, particularly under live oaks and in the dappled shade of urban tree canopies. In zone 9–10 it may be semi-evergreen or evergreen in mild winters; cut back any winter-damaged foliage in early spring before new growth emerges. Excellent container plant for shaded patios.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring; seed benefits from cool soil and light to germinate.
directions: Sparky produces charming double and semi-double blooms in warm apricot tones with burgundy undersides on compact 8-to-10-inch plants. Scatter the tiny seed on the soil surface in early spring, pressing it in without covering since it needs light to sprout. Poppies resent transplanting, so direct sow where they are to grow and thin seedlings to prevent crowding. Drought-tolerant and deer-resistant once established, this variety draws bees and butterflies to the garden. Let a few blooms go to seed and it will often self-sow for the following year.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections in 6–18 inches of water in pots of aquatic soil set on the pond bottom, or directly into pond mud in spring; spatterdock thrives in more shade than true water lilies and tolerates slow-moving or slightly turbid water that would defeat Nymphaea species.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in 6–18 inches of still to slow-moving water in full sun to partial shade — spatterdock is the toughest and most shade-adaptable of all North American native water plants, growing in slow streams, ponds, lakes, ditches, and bayous throughout the continent where it produces large, heart-shaped, floating and emergent leaves up to 16 inches across that provide outstanding surface coverage and shade for fish and frogs. The distinctive globe-shaped, 2-inch yellow flowers with conspicuous red stamens appear above the water surface from spring through fall and are pollinated by beetles attracted to the sweet scent. Unlike true water lilies (Nymphaea), spatterdock tolerates shade, slow-moving water, turbidity, and some salt influence, making it the water plant of choice for shaded natural ponds, sluggish streams, and bayou margins. The rhizomes were an important food source for Native Americans. Spreads vigorously in ideal conditions; contain in pots for small water gardens.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, coniferous duff or peaty soil in full shade; speckled wood lily grows naturally under the deep shade of conifer forests in the Pacific Northwest and Sierra Nevada, requiring cool temperatures, consistently moist (but not wet) acidic, humus-rich soil, and low light. Difficult to establish outside these conditions.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, strongly acidic, cool, humus-rich, coniferous duff or peaty soil in full shade; speckled wood lily is a tiny, enchanting woodland native of Pacific Coast and Rocky Mountain conifer forests — the western counterpart of the eastern yellow clintonia (Clintonia borealis), but producing a single, upward-facing, white flower (rather than multiple yellow flowers) above a small rosette of large, shiny, oval basal leaves. The single white flower with its delicate speckles is borne on a short stem and is followed by a striking, metallic blue-purple berry in late summer. The blue berries are distinctive and beautiful but inedible. Found in cool, moist, deeply shaded Douglas-fir, hemlock, and red fir forests from southern Alaska through British Columbia and cascading through the Sierra Nevada. Requires essentially the same conditions as its habitat: deep conifer shade, consistently cool temperatures, and acidic, humus-rich soil with good moisture retention. A gem for conifer shade gardens in the Pacific Northwest and mountain climates.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; tolerates cool weather.
directions: This vigorous, late-flowering Spencer type bears fragrant ivory ruffled blooms 1 to 2 inches wide that resemble delicate confections. Sow seed directly in early spring in rich, well-drained soil, providing a trellis or netting for the climbing vines to grab. Nicking or soaking the hard seed coat overnight speeds germination. Keep roots cool and evenly moist, and harvest flowers often to keep the plants producing through the season. Its slightly shorter stems and late bloom time extend the sweet pea season for intimate bouquets.

plant_note: Sow in early spring as soon as soil is workable; likes cool roots.
directions: Princess Elizabeth blends peachy salmon and soft cream tones in romantic, lightly fragrant blooms ideal for cottage-style beds and vertical gardens. Direct sow in early spring in cool, fertile soil, soaking or scarifying the seed first to improve sprouting. Set up a sturdy trellis for the vigorous vines and keep the soil consistently moist. Frequent cutting encourages the plant to produce armfuls of blooms over a longer window. Plant in full sun with cool roots, mulching to buffer summer heat.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in deep shade to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 10–12; Spicate Calyptrocalyx is a striking, clustering, understory palm native to the lowland and hill rainforests of New Guinea, grown for its highly attractive, bright orange to red new leaf growth (new fronds emerge copper, orange, and red before maturing to green) and its excellent tolerance of deep shade — outstanding for shaded tropical garden positions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in deep to moderate shade; Calyptrocalyx spicatus requires consistently high humidity and moisture — mulch heavily, water regularly, and maintain shade protection; excellent for tropical understory and shade garden settings. Calyptrocalyx spicatus (Spicate Calyptrocalyx or New Guinea Understory Palm) is a clustering, suckering, small to medium understory palm native to the humid lowland and hill rainforests of New Guinea (Papua New Guinea and Irian Jaya), grown primarily for an ornamental characteristic shared by many Calyptrocalyx species: the spectacular orange-to-red coloration of emerging new fronds. Each new leaf unfurls in bright copper, orange, or red tones before gradually maturing to standard deep green — creating a continuously colorful display as new leaves emerge throughout the growing season. This 'colored new growth' trait makes Calyptrocalyx spicatus an exceptionally attractive shade-garden palm. The multiple clustering stems are slender, graceful, and reach moderate heights (4–10 feet). The species is also notable for its tolerance of deep shade — genuinely adapted to the rainforest floor — making it useful for shaded positions where most palms would struggle. Calyptrocalyx spicatus is rarely seen in North American collections due to limited distribution, but is cultivated by tropical palm enthusiasts in South Florida and Hawaii for its remarkable new-growth coloration.

plant_note: Plant bulb or container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 7–10; Spice Lily is a small native bulbous perennial of south Texas and northeastern Mexico — forming compact rosettes of narrow, purple-spotted, semi-succulent leaves and producing tall flower spikes of tubular, brownish-purple to greenish flowers with a remarkably strong, sweet spice fragrance strongest at dusk — an outstanding hummingbird and hawk moth nectar plant.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline-tolerant soil in full sun; Manfreda maculosa is adapted to shallow, calcareous, rocky soils of the Texas Edwards Plateau and Rio Grande Plains — excellent drainage is critical; avoid clay and overwatering; requires no supplemental water once established in appropriate xeric conditions. Manfreda maculosa (Spice Lily or Mottled Tuberose) is a compact, bulbous perennial in the Asparagaceae family native to the rocky, calcareous soils and cedar-oak scrub of the Edwards Plateau and Rio Grande Plains of south Texas and extending into Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas, Mexico. The plant forms ground-level rosettes of narrow, strap-like, gray-green leaves beautifully decorated with irregular dark-purple spots and blotches — giving an ornamental mottled appearance similar to its relative M. virginica. In summer, slender, branching flower spikes emerge to 3–5 feet, bearing small, brownish-green to brownish-purple, tubular flowers that are powerfully and sweetly fragrant — a spicy-sweet scent strongest at dusk and into the night, designed to attract hawk moths (Sphingidae) as pollinators alongside hummingbirds. Like M. virginica, it is not monocarpic and blooms reliably each year. An outstanding native accent plant for rock gardens, dry borders, and xeriscape plantings in zones 7–10 across Texas and the Southwest.

plant_note: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spicebush is one of the most shade-tolerant of all native shrubs and grows naturally as a dense understory shrub in moist, rich, deciduous forests — it is exceptional in deeply shaded garden spots where few shrubs thrive.
directions: Plant container or field-grown stock in spring or fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spicebush is one of the most shade-tolerant of all native shrubs and grows naturally as a dense understory shrub in moist, rich, deciduous forests — it is exceptional in deeply shaded garden spots where few shrubs thrive. Lindera benzoin is one of the most valuable native shrubs for wildlife gardens: the aromatic, spicy-scented foliage is the exclusive larval host plant for the spicebush swallowtail (Papilio troilus) and the promethea silk moth; small, bright-yellow flowers appear in late winter to early spring before the leaves, providing critical early nectar; glossy, red, waxy berries in fall are greedily consumed by migrating songbirds, especially wood thrushes and veeries; and brilliant yellow fall foliage lights up shaded woodland garden interiors. Dioecious — plant male and female for berries.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Jatropha integerrima is one of the best year-round blooming shrubs for South Florida and zone 10 gardens and performs well as a warm-season annual or container plant in zone 9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Jatropha is drought-tolerant once established and blooms most heavily in full sun. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — keep away from children and pets. Jatropha integerrima (spicy jatropha or peregrina) is a Cuban native tropical shrub producing dense, rounded clusters of brilliant scarlet-red, star-shaped flowers 1 inch across almost continuously throughout the warm months in zones 10–12, and reliably spring through fall in zone 9. The flowers are irresistible to butterflies (especially Sulphurs, Zebra Longwings, and Gulf Fritillaries) and hummingbirds, making it an outstanding wildlife plant for tropical gardens. The attractive, slightly lobed, dark-green to bronze-tinged leaves add ornamental interest between bloom flushes. Despite the toxicity of its seeds and sap (all Jatropha species contain toxic diterpenes), the plant is widely grown as a landscape shrub in South Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical regions; wear gloves when pruning. It grows rapidly from cuttings and can be trained as a small tree for greater impact.

plant_note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, limestone-derived soil in partial to deep shade; spider brake is a limestone-loving fern that self-sows into cracks in walls, sidewalks, and stone paving in the humid South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, limestone-derived or mortar-rich soil in partial to deep shade; spider brake is a delicate, lacy fern from eastern Asia that has naturalized extensively in the humid American South, particularly in shaded walls, the cracks of old brick buildings, mortar joints, and limestone outcrops — wherever moisture collects in alkaline, calcium-rich substrates. The narrow, ribbon-like pinnae arranged around the rachis give the frond an elegant, spider-like appearance that makes it ornamentally distinctive. It is one of the few ferns that prefers alkaline conditions, making it valuable for shade gardens with limestone-derived soils or on the north-facing walls of masonry structures. An excellent fern for naturalizing in the mortar joints of shaded stone walls and pathways in zone 9a.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds on prepared soil surface in full sun after last frost — seeds need light to germinate — or refrigerate seeds for 2 weeks before sowing to improve germination rate. Spider flower self-seeds freely and will naturalize in a sunny bed.
directions: Direct-sow seeds on prepared soil surface in full sun after last frost — seeds need light and should not be covered — and thin to 18–24 inches; spider flower grows quickly into a bold, tall annual with distinctive globe-shaped heads of pink, white, or purple flowers with extraordinarily long, spider-like stamens that protrude dramatically beyond the petals, giving each bloom its spider-like appearance. Blooms continuously from midsummer through frost and self-seeds so prolifically that it naturalizes readily in a sunny border, reappearing every year without replanting. Highly drought-tolerant and unfazed by summer heat; the flowers are excellent for cutting and attract swallowtail butterflies, sphinx moths, and hummingbirds. The sticky stems and leaves have a strong scent that most people find disagreeable up close; plant away from areas where the foliage will be touched or brushed against.

common_name: Spider Flower (Garden Cleome, Spider Legs, Hassler's Spider Flower)
plant_note: Direct sow at the soil surface (seeds require light to germinate — do not cover) after last frost in full sun; Spider Flower grows rapidly in warm conditions and tolerates summer heat and drought better than most tall annuals. Self-seeds prolifically, often naturalizing in gardens. Thin to 18–24 inches apart for best development. The sticky, slightly fragrant foliage and stems deter many pests. Excellent for hummingbirds and butterflies; a host plant for some Sphinx moth larvae. Deadheading is not needed — the elongating seed pods below the active flower cluster are ornamental.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Spider Flower grows vigorously in hot, dry, sunny conditions and is one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant of the tall summer annuals, making it well-suited to Gulf Coast zone 9-11 conditions where many other tall annuals struggle. Tarenaya hassleriana (formerly Cleome hassleriana) is a tall, fast-growing annual native to South America (Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay) in the Cleomaceae family, widely grown throughout the world's warm-climate gardens as one of the finest tall background annuals for hot summer gardens. The plants produce large, rounded, domed clusters of flowers at the tips of their erect, branching stems — each individual flower has four narrow petals in pink, rose, white, or lavender-purple, but the defining feature is the extremely long, thin, prominent stamens (6) and style that project far beyond the petals like the legs of a spider — earning the plant its common name. Below the active flower cluster, the developing seed pods (5–8 inches long, narrow, cylindrical) hang on thread-like stalks, extending the ornamental interest below the flower head. The whole elongating display — active flowers above, pendant seed pods below — creates an unusual, multi-dimensional ornamental effect. The cultivar series 'Queen' (in pink, white, violet, rose, and mixed) is the standard commercial form. Self-seeds abundantly.

plant_note: Plant corms 2 inches deep in sharply drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; spider iris is a winter-growing South African fynbos plant requiring dry summers and moist cool winters. In zones 9–10 with excellent drainage it can be grown in the open garden with a reliable summer dry period. Naturalizes freely in California coastal climates similar to its native habitat.
directions: Plant corms in fall in sharply drained, lean, sandy soil in full sun; spider iris is among the most bizarre and visually fascinating members of the iris family — a South African fynbos endemic producing flowers of extraordinary complexity, with six wavy, crinkled, spider-leg-like tepals in cream, brown, purple-black, and maroon arranged in intricate combinations and textures, the wavy margins and darkly mottled patterns creating a flower that resembles a small, ornate mosaic. The flowers are short-lived (each lasting a single day or two) but appear successively over several weeks in winter and spring and carry a distinctive, musky-vanilla fragrance that is strong and reminiscent of chocolate to some observers. It grows through the cool season of its native winter-rainfall Western Cape habitat and must be kept completely dry in summer. Related to the moraeas, it belongs to the same iridaceae tribe and requires identical cultivation. A collector's plant of unique character, grown for its botanical bizarreness as much as its fragrance.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist to wet, well-drained to moderately drained fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; hymenocallis thrives near water features, pond margins, and in moist low-lying areas of zone 7–11 gardens.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above the soil surface in moist, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun near water features, pond edges, or in moist low spots; the spider lily produces one of the most structurally distinctive flowers in the summer garden — a white central cup is surrounded by six long, narrow, arching white petals that give each flower an elegant spider-like form, and the intensely sweet perfume is released especially in the evening hours. The broad, strap-like, semi-evergreen foliage remains attractive throughout the year in zone 9–11. Established clumps multiply by offsets and require minimal care; divide every 4–5 years in late fall after the foliage dies back when clumps become crowded. In zone 7–8, lift bulbs after the first frost and store in a cool, dry location through winter.

common_name: Spider Orchid (Arching Brassia, Colombian Spider Orchid, Arcuigera Brassia)
plant_note: Grow in a medium-to-large pot with medium bark or in a slatted basket in bright indirect to partial direct light; Brassia arcuigera is one of the largest-flowered Brassia species, with individual spidery flowers reaching 6–10 inches tip to tip of the longest extended sepals. The flowers are vivid yellow-green to yellow with brown to cinnamon spotting and blotching on the sepals and petals, with a light, pleasant fragrance. Blooms primarily in spring. The spidery flowers mimic female spider wasps, and male wasps attempt to mate with the lip, effecting pollination. Intermediate temperatures preferred. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light in medium bark — Spider Orchid grows most vigorously in intermediate temperatures with bright, filtered light and produces its extraordinary long-sepaled flowers most freely when given generous pot size and adequate root room. Brassia arcuigera is a robust, sympodial, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru — one of the larger-flowered Brassia species (a genus sometimes called 'spider orchids' for the elongated, spreading, insect-leg-like sepals of their flowers). The plant produces flattened, compressed pseudobulbs 4–5 inches tall with 2–3 broad, somewhat fleshy, strap-like leaves. In spring, long (to 24 inches), arching flower spikes emerge bearing 6–10 large flowers, each one remarkable for the extraordinary length of the sepals: the lower lateral sepals extend downward and outward in a strongly arching pattern (giving the species name arcuigera, 'bearing an arch') to total flower widths of 6–10 inches tip-to-tip. The flower color is vivid yellow-green to bright yellow with irregular brown to cinnamon spotting concentrated toward the sepal bases, and the broad lip is white with brown spots. The spidery appearance of the flower is an adaptation to its pollination system — male spider wasps (Pepsis species) mistake the lip for a large female wasp and attempt to mate with it, picking up pollinaria in the process. A spectacular orchid of extraordinary flower form. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root plantlets (spiderettes) by pinning them to moist soil or placing in water; in zone 9b–11, spider plant can be grown as an outdoor groundcover in deep shade where its stolons will root and spread to cover ground. In zone 8–9a, treat as a container plant or protect from frost.
directions: Root spiderette plantlets in water or moist soil and plant in any moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade — spider plant is one of the world's most popular houseplants and a valuable outdoor shade groundcover in tropical and subtropical gardens, producing fountains of long, arching, strap-like leaves (solid green or with bold cream-white centers or margins) and long, arching stolons tipped with miniature plantlets that root wherever they contact moist soil. In zone 9b–11 it grows as a naturalized groundcover in deep shade under trees, producing a lush carpet that requires almost no care. It tolerates deep shade, inconsistent watering, and low soil fertility better than almost any other shade groundcover. The variegated form (cream-and-green striped) is especially bright in dark shade. NASA studies identified spider plant as one of the most effective air-purifying houseplants, removing formaldehyde and other volatile organic compounds from indoor air.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring around last frost date; cold stratification for 4 weeks improves germination of seed.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds for 4 weeks before sowing; established divisions establish more reliably than seed-grown plants and can be done in spring or fall. Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, average to rich soil; plants tolerate wet conditions and make excellent rain garden plants. The three-petaled flowers in purple, blue, pink, or white open only for a single morning but are produced in rapid succession over many weeks. Shear the entire plant to 8 in after the main bloom flush to stimulate fresh foliage and a second round of flowers in fall.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; spike winter hazel is among the most widely available Corylopsis species in US nurseries and is known for unusually long, many-flowered racemes. Site in a sheltered location to protect from late winter frosts.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade, sheltered from late winter frosts; spike winter hazel is a Japanese species distinguished from other Corylopsis by the unusually long, cylindrical racemes containing up to 20 lemon-yellow flowers each — the longest pendulous flower clusters of commonly grown winter hazels. The flowers are slightly larger than those of C. pauciflora and carry a soft, sweet, cowslip-like fragrance that is particularly pleasant in the mild days of late winter and early spring. The purple-tipped stamens create a colorful contrast with the pale yellow petals. Leaves emerge with an attractive reddish-purple flush that matures to blue-green, turning golden yellow in fall. Hardy to zone 5, this is one of the more reliable winter hazels for cold-climate gardens. Combines beautifully with early-blooming witch hazels (Hamamelis) for an extended winter flowering display.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 9–12; Spiked Costus is a Caribbean and tropical American native spiral ginger — naturalized in Florida and widely found in Gulf Coast gardens — producing tall, spiraling, leafy canes topped by brilliant scarlet-red, pine-cone-like flower spikes from which small, bright-yellow flowers emerge successively from spring through fall, and thriving in the partial shade of large trees.
directions: Plant Costus spicatus rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; mulch well to retain moisture and protect the rhizome in zone 9 where frost kills the tops but the roots re-emerge in spring; divide clumps every 2–3 years to maintain vigor and increase; harvest the mature scarlet bracts for use as attractive cut foliage. Spiked Costus is native to the West Indies and adjacent mainland tropical Americas and has become naturalized in moist, disturbed areas of South and Central Florida, where it thrives in partial shade under oaks and palms in the Gulf Coast climate. The spirally arranged leaves on the tall, cane-like stems and the handsome scarlet-red, waxy, bract-covered cone at the tip — from which small, yellow, tubular flowers emerge one at a time — create a bold, tropical effect in the shade garden from late spring through fall. The bracts and stems are decorative in arrangements, lasting well. A highly reliable and tough plant for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens — dying back to the ground after frost in zone 9 and re-emerging vigorously each spring from the spreading rhizome. Hummingbirds visit the flowers regularly. The stems have been used in traditional medicine in the Caribbean. Naturalizes readily in suitable moist, shaded conditions and can spread to form large colonies.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or divide clumps in spring; spiked wood oats is more shade and drought tolerant than the related inland sea oats (Chasmanthium latifolium) and performs well in dry to moderately moist conditions in full to partial shade.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in spring in dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — spiked wood oats is a fine-textured native grass of the southeastern and south-central US, closely related to inland sea oats (C. latifolium) but notably more drought and shade tolerant and somewhat smaller and narrower in leaf. It grows naturally in dry, rocky, or sandy woodland soils under hardwood forest canopies and along dry bluffs and ridges, where its minimal water requirements make it a standout among shade grasses. The attractive seed heads emerge in summer, erect rather than pendulous, and turn a warm tan by fall, providing winter interest and wildlife food. An excellent grass for filling dry shade under oaks and other trees where irrigation is unavailable, or for naturalizing in shaded woodland garden settings. Self-sows moderately; cut back to the ground in late winter to encourage fresh growth.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; spindle palm is frost-sensitive and requires frost-free conditions. Native to Rodrigues Island (Mauritius), where it is critically endangered in the wild with fewer than a few dozen specimens remaining.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun in frost-free zone 10–11; spindle palm is closely related to bottle palm (both in the genus Hyophorbe), and while both have distinctively shaped trunks, spindle palm's trunk swells in the MIDDLE rather than at the base, creating a spindle or fusiform shape — widest in the center of the trunk and tapering toward both the base and the crownshaft. The taller, more slender crown of arching pinnate fronds and the graceful spindle-shaped trunk distinguish it clearly from the squat bottle palm. Like bottle palm, it is critically endangered in the wild (native to Rodrigues Island, Mauritius), but very widely cultivated as an ornamental throughout the tropical world. Slightly taller and more slender than bottle palm, with a more graceful overall form. Both Hyophorbe species are outstanding ornamentals for small garden spaces in frost-free climates where their compact size and architectural trunks are advantages.

common_name: Spineless Yucca (Soft Leaf Yucca, Giant Yucca)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in any well-drained soil; Spineless Yucca grows quickly in warm conditions and requires excellent drainage — it will rot in clay that stays wet after rain. Plant 6–10 feet from buildings and walkways to allow for mature spread. In zone 9a, plants may defoliate in hard freezes but resprout from the trunk if the growing tips are not frozen.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Spineless Yucca is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives on neglect in appropriate conditions. Yucca elephantipes (also sold as Yucca gigantea) is a native of Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico that has become one of the most widely planted tropical accent plants in Gulf Coast zone 9–11 landscapes and a standard large houseplant and container specimen throughout the world. Unlike most yuccas whose stiff leaf tips can pierce skin (earning the family name 'needles and thread'), the Spineless Yucca's long, dark-green, strap-like leaves have soft, flexible tips that cause no injury — making it safe around children and pets and usable in high-traffic landscape situations where spiny yuccas would be hazardous. The plant develops multiple trunks over time, each eventually producing dramatic 3–4 foot spikes of creamy-white, pendant, bell-shaped flowers. It makes an excellent large container specimen for patios, entryways, and atriums where the bold form contrasts with fine-textured plants. When planted directly in the ground in zone 9b–11, it can grow to 30 feet with multiple branching trunks and a truly impressive specimen presence. Very popular in formal tropical and Mediterranean-style Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Divide crowns in early spring or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; spinulose wood fern tolerates a range of moisture conditions from consistently moist to moderately dry under tree canopy once established. It is one of the most widely distributed ferns in the temperate Northern Hemisphere and adaptable to a wide range of shaded garden conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; spinulose wood fern is one of the most common and widely distributed woodland ferns in the temperate Northern Hemisphere, found across North America, Europe, and Asia in moist, deciduous and coniferous forests. The medium-sized, triangular, lacy fronds are elegantly divided two or three times, with small, sharply toothed (spinulose) segments that give the fronds a fine, delicate texture distinguishing them from the coarser Dryopteris filix-mas. The plant forms vase-shaped clumps of light-green to medium-green fronds that are semi-evergreen in mild winters. It is one of the most adaptable, tolerant, and widely planted ferns for woodland gardens, succeeding in a wide range of shade and moisture conditions. It hybridizes freely with other Dryopteris species, including producing the common hybrid D. x complexa with D. affinis. An excellent, dependable fern for naturalizing in woodland settings and for combining with hostas, hellebores, and woodland wildflowers.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; spiny acanthus is more drought-tolerant and more deeply cut in its foliage than soft acanthus (A. mollis) — it is also more heat-tolerant and better adapted to dry summer conditions. Wear gloves when handling as the leaf tips bear sharp spines.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun to part shade; spiny acanthus is the superior species for hot-summer and dry-summer gardens — the deeply lobed, spiny-tipped, dark-green leaves are more dramatic in outline than soft acanthus (A. mollis), and the plant is more cold-hardy, more drought-tolerant, and more adaptable to a wide range of conditions. The leaves inspired the capital designs of Corinthian columns in classical Greek and Roman architecture, one of the most ancient uses of any plant in decorative art. In summer, spectacular vertical spikes 3–5 feet tall arise carrying hooded, two-toned flowers: purple-maroon bracts surrounding white flowers with prominent spiny bracts between each flower. These spikes are among the most architecturally impressive flower structures of any perennial and the flowers are visited by bumblebees that are strong enough to push into the hooded blooms. Once established, acanthus spreads by thick underground roots and can be difficult to eradicate — site it where it can expand freely.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; spiny black olive grows naturally in tropical coastal hammocks and the edges of mangrove in south Florida and the Caribbean, tolerating salt spray, thin alkaline soils, and drought.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy, coastal soil in full sun; spiny black olive is a native tree of tropical coastal hammocks and scrub of south Florida and the Caribbean, not related to the olive (Olea) but named for the dark, fleshy, olive-like fruits. The tree has an attractive, fine-textured, weeping canopy with long, drooping branchlets bearing small, leathery, elongated leaves and (on young growth) short, stiff spines that have given it one common name. The small fruits are eaten by tropical birds. Well adapted to coastal conditions including salt spray, rocky limestone soil, and drought — all characteristic of the Keys habitat. Widely used as an ornamental and windbreak tree in South Florida coastal landscapes. A smaller relative of the commonly planted (and non-native) black olive (Bucida buceras), which is the dominant street tree of Miami.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun. Suited to California and mild coastal climates; protect from hard freezes. Once established, this shrub thrives on neglect and minimal water.
directions: Choose a sunny site with fast-draining, lean soil — rich or moist soils encourage weak growth and root rot in this chaparral native. Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in late summer, or transplant nursery-grown starts in spring. Water only to establish during the first season, then reduce to occasional deep irrigation in summer. The spiny branches form an effective barrier hedge while the bright red berries draw birds throughout fall and winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rhizomes in spring after soil warms in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Spiral Ginger is one of the most cold-tolerant Costus species — surviving to zone 9 (and marginally zone 8) with root protection during freezes.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Spiral Ginger is a tropical shade perennial in the Costus genus — producing erect, cane-like stems with the characteristic spiral arrangement of broad, tropical-looking leaves that give the entire Costus group their common name. The leaves are arranged in a beautiful, precise spiral up each cane that is architecturally distinctive and visually arresting. In late summer and fall, large (3–4 inch), white, tissue-paper-thin flowers emerge from reddish-brown cone-like terminal bracts, providing a dramatic contrast against the deep-green foliage. Spiral Ginger creates outstanding tropical shade garden effects in zone 9–11, where its combination of bold, spiraling foliage and dramatic late-season flowers provides multi-season ornamental interest. In zone 9, the tops are killed by hard freezes but the underground rhizomes typically survive to zone 9a when mulched, re-sprouting vigorously in spring. The bold tropical foliage texture combines beautifully with other shade tropical plants — caladiums, gingers, and philodendrons — to create a lush, jungle-like understory effect under high-canopy trees. Division of established clumps every 3–4 years maintains vigor and provides divisions for expanding the planting.

subcategory: deep blue spectacular South African Cape corm
plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; splendid wine cups follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle — autumn emergence, winter-spring bloom, complete summer dormancy. Keep bone dry in summer. The species name 'splendidissima' (most splendid) is justified: the flowers are among the most intense, saturated, pure deep blue of any plant in the world. Best in containers in areas with wet summers to control summer moisture.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; splendid wine cups — the botanical superlative in the species epithet 'splendidissima' (most splendid) is fully earned — is one of the most intense, saturated, deep-blue flowering plants in existence, producing in late winter and spring wide-open, cup-shaped flowers of extraordinary, gemlike, deep ultramarine-blue to dark royal-blue that is so saturated and vivid it appears almost luminescent in sunlight, with a small, contrasting white or very pale center zone at the base of each petal that intensifies the optical power of the surrounding dark blue. Unlike the bicolor G. radians (blue with red center blotches), G. splendidissima achieves its beauty through the purity and depth of a single, extraordinary, supremely saturated blue — arguably the deepest, most intense, most unmistakably magnificent pure blue of any spring-flowering plant regularly available to gardeners. Native to a restricted area of the coastal Western Cape fynbos where it grows in sandy, peaty, seasonally moist soils on the coastal flats. A collector's prize — not widely available but obtainable from specialist Cape bulb suppliers — of singular botanical distinction for the quality of its flower color alone.

common_name: Split-Leaf Monstera (Pinnatipartita, Peru Monstera, Broad-Leaf Monstera)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio vine in zone 9; Monstera pinnatipartita cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Provide a moss pole or climbing support to achieve the dramatically pinnate adult leaf form — the transformation from juvenile simple leaves to deeply split adult leaves is one of the most striking in the genus. In zone 10-11 outdoors, it can climb tree trunks in deep shade. Propagate from stem cuttings with at least one node. Use a well-draining aroid potting mix. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Monstera pinnatipartita transitions from its juvenile to its extraordinary adult leaf form most rapidly with adequate bright indirect light and a climbing support. Monstera pinnatipartita is a climbing aroid from Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia in the Araceae family, producing one of the most dramatically transformative leaf progressions in the genus Monstera — the group named for their 'monstrous' leaves. In the juvenile trailing or hanging phase, the plant produces relatively small (4–6 inch), simple, elongated, glossy dark-green leaves that give no indication of what is to come. As the plant climbs a vertical surface and matures, the leaves transform dramatically: they enlarge significantly and become deeply pinnately lobed — divided almost to the midrib into numerous (8–12 pairs or more) distinct lobes — creating a leaf structure that is deeply slashed rather than fenestrated (holed), with the individual lobes remaining attached to the central rib like a feather. The adult leaves, reaching 24 inches or more, are among the most striking in the genus. Monstera pinnatipartita is frequently confused in commerce with Monstera siltepecana (which is similar in juvenile form), Rhaphidophora decursiva (similar in adult form), and even Epipremnum pinnatum — accurate identification is helpful for appropriate care and expectation setting. All parts are toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on sandy, well-drained, acidic to neutral, dry soil in full sun; splitbeard bluestem is a low-nutrient-requiring grass that performs best in poor, sandy, acidic pine flatwoods soils — excessive fertilization leads to rank growth and reduced ornamental quality.
directions: Splitbeard bluestem is one of the most ornamentally appealing native grasses of the Gulf Coastal Plain and Atlantic Coastal Plain pine country — in fall, the paired flower spikes develop silky, glistening white or silvery seed heads with a distinctive forked, Y-shaped arrangement that gives the species both its common names (splitbeard for the paired stalks, chalky for the whitened seed heads). The plants have a somewhat tufted, wiry character and typically stay shorter than big bluestem or bushy bluestem, making them appropriate for small to medium native garden settings; their chalky-white winter seedheads contrast beautifully with the coppery-bronze stems and leaves. Naturally found in open, dry, longleaf pine savannas, sandhills, and coastal plain flatwoods, splitbeard bluestem is adapted to the fire-maintained, nutrient-poor sandy soils of the Gulf South — combine with native wildflowers like blazing stars, black-eyed Susans, and goldenrods for an authentic pine flatwoods meadow garden.

plant_note: Sow in fall into sandy, well-drained soil to allow natural cold stratification before spring germination.
directions: Spoonleaf Barbara's Buttons is a compact southeastern native wildflower adapted to the sandy, nutrient-poor soils of longleaf pine uplands, where it produces distinctive spoon-shaped basal leaves and delicate white to pale pink pincushion blooms in spring. Direct sow seeds in fall into well-drained, acidic sandy soil with good sun exposure, spacing plants at least 9 inches apart to accommodate their slow-spreading habit. This drought-tolerant perennial is well-suited to rock gardens, native plant borders, and open pine understory plantings where many other flowers struggle. It thrives with minimal fertilization, as overly rich soils can reduce flowering and encourage lush but bloom-sparse foliage.

plant_note: Surface-sow; light aids germination. Short-lived but self-sows.
directions: Surface-sow the seed and press it in, as light helps it germinate. Also called dotted horsemint, this native produces tiered whorls of yellow flowers spotted with purple, set off by showy pink bracts. It thrives in full sun and sandy, dry soil, and its aromatic foliage deters deer. A biennial to short-lived perennial, it self-sows freely and is a magnet for bees, wasps, and other beneficial pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; spotted beebalm requires excellent drainage and is intolerant of heavy or consistently moist soils — it thrives in the kind of dry, sandy, or rocky ground where most other wildflowers struggle, cold-stratifying naturally over winter for spring germination.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or rocky soil in full sun; spotted beebalm is strictly a plant of dry, open ground and will not tolerate heavy clay or consistently moist soils — it is one of the finest native wildflowers for hot, dry, infertile conditions where richly blooming plants are difficult to establish. Monarda punctata, also called horsemint, is one of the most botanically unusual native wildflowers in eastern and central North America: its flowers are small, spotted yellow-white with purple-brown dots and held in multiple tiered whorls along the stem, each whorl subtended by showy, leaf-like bracts in soft pink, lavender, or white that persist long after the flowers fade, giving the plant a dramatic, sculptural appearance from July through September that is wholly unlike any other native wildflower. It is one of the very best native plants for small native bees, including many specialist solitary bees that visit Monarda; it is also heavily worked by bumblebees, sweat bees, long-tongued bees, and various wasps, and the aromatic foliage contains high concentrations of thymol, the same antiseptic compound found in garden thyme.
