Spotted beebalm is a short-lived perennial or biennial that self-sows prolifically in appropriate dry, sandy soils — allow seed heads to ripen and fall in place to maintain a self-sustaining colony, and avoid amending or irrigating the soil, which dramatically shortens the lifespan of individual plants.

plant_note: Sow seeds in spring or divide established clumps in spring or fall; spotted bellflower spreads by underground rhizomes and can be aggressive — choose a site where some spread is welcome or confine with a root barrier. It is notably heat-tolerant among bellflowers and performs well in the warmer parts of its zone range.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; spotted bellflower is a Japanese and Korean native that produces some of the largest, most unusual flowers in the bellflower genus — long (2 inches), drooping, tubular bells in cream to soft pink, each distinctly spotted and freckled inside with red-purple dots, hung in nodding clusters on plants only 12–18 inches tall. The interior spotting, only visible by looking up into the pendant flower, is exquisite and gives the flowers a quality more reminiscent of foxglove or digitalis than of typical bellflowers. It blooms in early summer and spreads vigorously by underground rhizomes to form colonies in semi-shaded woodland conditions. Several cultivars and hybrids are available including 'Cherry Bells' (deep rose-pink) and 'Bowl of Cherries.' The rhizomatous spread, while vigorous, makes it an effective groundcover under shrubs and trees. Somewhat more heat-tolerant than most temperate bellflowers, succeeding in the warmer zones of its range.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes 3–4 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile soil in spring; spotted calla lily requires dry summer dormancy (unlike Z. aethiopica which is summer-active) — stop watering when leaves yellow after flowering and keep dry through summer. It is the parent species of many hybrid calla lilies with spotted, translucent-spotted leaves. Suitable for zones 8–11 outdoors; lift and store dry in colder zones.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in part shade; spotted calla lily is the primary parent species of the hybrid calla lily group with the characteristic white-spotted, translucent-spotted foliage — the dark-green, arrow-shaped leaves are decorated with numerous white, translucent dots and spots of varying size, creating an attractively patterned foliage effect even before the flowers appear. The flowers are typical calla-form — a creamy-white to pale-yellow or greenish-white spathe surrounding a yellow spadix — smaller and more elegant than the large Z. aethiopica. Unlike Z. aethiopica, it follows a summer-dormant, winter-active pattern (reflecting its summer-dry South African native habitat) and must have dry conditions during summer dormancy to prevent rhizome rot. In zones 8–11 it can remain in the ground with withheld summer water. It is the parent of most hybrid calla lily cultivars with spotted foliage, now available in a wide range of spathe colors from white through yellow, orange, pink, and dark burgundy-purple. Outstanding in containers where the summer dormancy can be easily managed by simply withholding water.

plant_note: Transfer small divisions of the coral-like rhizome in early spring, taking care to keep a portion of the surrounding native soil attached to preserve active fungal partners. Plant in undisturbed forest duff beneath mature deciduous or coniferous trees where leaf litter accumulates naturally. Do not attempt to grow in sterile or amended potting mix; success depends entirely on intact mycorrhizal networks already present in the native soil.
directions: Establish divisions beneath a closed woodland canopy in rich, humus-laden soil where minimal light reaches the forest floor, as this plant produces no chlorophyll and gains all nutrition through its fungal symbiont. Because it never photosynthesizes, it is entirely invisible above ground for most of the year, emerging only as a leafless reddish-brown stem bearing small spotted flowers in late spring or summer. Mark planting locations carefully to avoid accidental disturbance during the dormant season. Supplemental watering is rarely needed where natural leaf litter maintains consistent soil moisture, but avoid flooding or allowing the soil to dry out completely.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the upper half exposed above the soil surface in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; spotted crossyne flowers in late summer and autumn (February–April in South Africa) before the leaves emerge (hysteranthous). Keep dry in summer. The species name 'guttata' means spotted — the individual flowers are white to pale pink and often marked with darker spots or streaks. A rare collector's bulb native to the fynbos of the Northern Cape.
directions: Plant bulbs (upper half exposed) in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; spotted crossyne is a rare, collectible South African bulb in the Amaryllidaceae family — related to Brunsvigia and Boophone — from the arid, rocky, fynbos and Namaqualand landscapes of the Northern Cape. Like Brunsvigia and Boophone it flowers in late summer and autumn on a leafless scape that emerges before the leaves (hysteranthous), producing a rounded, somewhat hemispherical umbel of 20–40 individual, tubular-funnel, white to pale pink flowers that are frequently spotted or streaked with darker markings — the 'guttata' (spotted) character. The whole flower head has a somewhat informal, airy quality compared to the more spectacular Brunsvigia josephinae or the bizarre Boophone disticha, but it provides the authentic autumn bloom timing and the spotted flower pattern that make it of botanical interest for the collector of South African autumn-blooming amaryllids. After the autumn flowers, the strap-shaped, grey-green leaves emerge and persist through winter and spring. A specialist plant for the dedicated Cape bulb collector; not widely available in commerce.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant divisions in spring; spotted dead nettle establishes quickly and begins spreading within the first season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; spotted dead nettle is one of the most reliable shade groundcovers available, prized for its silver-marked leaves that light up dim spaces under trees. The small hooded flowers in pink, white, or purple appear in spring and continue sporadically through summer. Shear plants back by one-third in midsummer if they become straggly to promote fresh new growth. Named cultivars with highly silvered or patterned foliage — 'White Nancy', 'Beacon Silver', 'Hermann's Pride' — are superior to the straight species. Tolerates dry shade once established but performs best in consistently moist conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; space 12–18 inches apart for quick coverage.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, avoiding heavy clay that stays waterlogged in winter; spotted deadnettle forms a quick-spreading mat of silver-marked foliage that suppresses weeds effectively under trees and shrubs. The small pink, white, or purple flowers appear in late spring and continue sporadically through summer. Cut plants back hard in midsummer if they become leggy or stressed by heat to encourage a flush of fresh foliage. The silver-splashed leaves of popular cultivars like 'White Nancy' and 'Beacon Silver' brighten dark corners more effectively than most groundcovers. Divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

plant_note: Cold-moist stratify seed for 30 days; surface-sow as light aids germination.
directions: Cold-stratify the seed for a month and surface-sow, since light improves germination. This tall native perennial produces large, domed clusters of fragrant rose-pink flowers from August into September. Grow it in full sun to part shade and consistently moist to wet soil, ideal for rain gardens and pond edges. Its towering stems are a butterfly favorite and add bold structure to the back of the border.

common_name: Spotted Leopard Plant (Yellow-Spotted Bold-Leaf Shade Perennial for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; the yellow spotting of Aureomaculatum is caused by viral variegation and is therefore heritable but not transmissible to other plants — propagate only by division to maintain the spotted pattern.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Aureomaculatum is the spotted form of Farfugium japonicum — the same bold-textured, large-leaved shade perennial as the green species but with distinctive irregular yellow spots and blotches distributed randomly across the dark green leaf surface, resembling paint splattered across the leaves and creating a strikingly unusual variegation pattern not found in other commonly grown shade perennials. The yellow spots of Aureomaculatum are the result of a viral variegation — genetically stable but caused by a specific viral interaction in the plant tissue — which means the spotting pattern is propagated faithfully by division but cannot be transmitted to adjacent plants. Each leaf produces a uniquely arranged set of yellow spots, and the number and size of spots varies from leaf to leaf, creating an irregular, artistically random variegation that is more visually interesting than uniformly-patterned variegation. The spotted pattern brightens deep shade positions significantly — the yellow spots appear luminous in low-light conditions, functioning like scattered points of light in the dark garden. Otherwise, the cultural requirements and fall yellow flowers of Aureomaculatum are identical to the green-leaved species. In Gulf South shade gardens, the spotted form provides a higher ornamental value than the straight species and is worth seeking out from specialty nurseries and plant societies. Both forms are equally cold-hardy and reliable in zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic to slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade. A coastal plain specialist, Spotted Trillium thrives in the warm, moist forests of Georgia, Alabama, and the Florida panhandle.
directions: Spotted Trillium is a sessile trillium of the southeastern coastal plain, native to moist, rich hardwood forests from South Carolina south to Florida and west to Alabama, where it often grows with sweetbay magnolia, titi, and evergreen shrubs in lowland forest understories. Its heavily marbled, silver-spotted leaves and nearly black maroon sessile flowers make it one of the more dramatic members of the genus, and the flowers carry a faint spicy scent that attracts fly pollinators. Rhizome divisions establish best when planted in fall in deeply amended, consistently moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.0) in full shade; the plants go completely dormant by early summer and should never be disturbed while dormant. Source only from reputable nurseries growing their own stock — this species is never legitimately available from wild collection.

plant_note: Carefully transplant small rooted sections with attached soil and intact root structure in early spring; spotted wintergreen requires very specific conditions — dry, infertile, sandy or rocky, strongly acidic soil in deep shade with established ectomycorrhizal fungi. Only plant nursery-propagated stock; never collect from the wild.
directions: Plant in dry, lean, sandy or rocky, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in deep shade; spotted wintergreen is one of the most beautiful native evergreen groundcovers of the eastern forest understory — a low, spreading plant with glossy, dark green leaves dramatically patterned with white or pale silver along the veins, creating a vivid variegated effect. Small, waxy, fragrant white flowers are produced in summer on upright stalks. The plant requires the presence of specific ectomycorrhizal fungi and strongly dislikes root disturbance, fertilization, or soil amendments — making it notoriously difficult to establish in cultivated settings. The best approach is to acquire nursery-propagated plugs (never wild-collected), plant in dry, acidic, sandy soil near the base of oaks or pines that support appropriate mycorrhizal networks, and then largely leave it undisturbed. Once established, it spreads slowly to form colonies that are permanent features of the native shade garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Spotty Dotty is a hybrid mayapple selection prized for enormous, deeply lobed leaves boldly splashed with chocolate-maroon spots, providing dramatic textural impact in the shade garden well beyond its brief spring bloom.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, sited where its bold foliage has room to spread. Spotty Dotty is a hybrid Podophyllum selection, likely involving the Chinese species P. delavayi, bred for enormous, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves heavily marbled and spotted with chocolate-maroon blotches over rich green, a striking effect that makes it one of the boldest textural statements available for a shaded border. In spring, dark maroon-red, nodding, cup-shaped flowers appear beneath the emerging foliage, followed later by red fruit, though the flowers are often hidden by the leaves and the foliage display is the plant's main draw. Unlike the common native mayapple (Podophyllum peltatum), which spreads by rhizome and goes dormant by midsummer, Spotty Dotty forms a slowly expanding clump and holds its dramatic foliage well into fall in consistently moist soil. Mulch with leaf litter or compost each fall to mimic its native woodland habitat, and avoid letting the soil dry out during the growing season, since drought causes the large leaves to scorch.

plant_note: Divide established mats or plant small rooted sections in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade; spreading club moss requires constantly moist soil and high humidity — it desiccates rapidly in dry conditions. Excellent for terrariums, woodland floors with consistent moisture, and the margins of streams and ponds in zones 7–10.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full shade; spreading club moss is a South African moss-relative (actually a vascular plant, unrelated to true mosses) that creates a dense, emerald-green to bright-golden-green flat mat of exceptionally fine-textured, scale-like leaves that spreads steadily over moist shaded surfaces — creating a seamless carpet of living green over forest floors, terrarium floors, and other consistently moist, shaded situations. The golden-green cultivar 'Aurea' (gold club moss) is especially popular in terrariums and miniature gardens for its warm, luminous color in deep shade. It spreads by prostrate stems that root at intervals, eventually covering large areas where the consistently moist conditions it requires are maintained. Not drought-tolerant at all — the foliage wilts and browns rapidly if allowed to dry out. An ideal companion to ferns, mosses, and woodland wildflowers in moist, shaded sites with reliable moisture. Also widely used in vivaria and terrariums as a naturalistic ground layer.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spreading sedge colonizes slowly by long stolons to form a low groundcover that is easy to control if needed.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spreading sedge is a low-growing native sedge of eastern woodland floors, distinguished by its unusually wide leaves (up to 3/4 inch wide, broad for a sedge) that are a beautiful glaucous blue-green color with a matte, almost frosted surface. The prostrate to arching leaves spread loosely to form a lax groundcover very different in character from the more upright native sedges — relaxed, natural-looking, and graceful. It spreads slowly by long stolons to form a loose, open mat. The cultivar 'Hobb' (sold as 'Blue Bunny') offers especially pronounced blue-green foliage and is widely available in the native plant trade. An outstanding groundcover for the shaded woodland garden in zone 4–8, especially effective paired with native spring wildflowers, ferns, and bleeding heart.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in shade to dappled light; tolerates heavier moisture than many wood ferns and spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form a weed-suppressing colony.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full shade to dappled woodland light; the spreading wood fern produces broad, arching, triangular-ovate fronds on dark stalks, forming graceful mounds that soften woodland garden paths and shaded borders with fresh spring-green color that deepens to rich forest green through summer. Semi-deciduous to deciduous, it spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a natural-looking weed-suppressing colony. Tolerates heavier moisture than many wood ferns and establishes readily in the humus-rich leaf-mold soils typical of mature deciduous woodland.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Sprenger's tulip is the latest of all tulip species to bloom (June in northern gardens) and is among the very best naturalizers — spreading freely by seed in garden conditions when allowed to set seed without cutting. A single planting builds into large colonies over 5–10 years. Bulbs are small and difficult to source; seed or specialist tulip nurseries are the main supply route.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in part shade; Sprenger's tulip has two unique distinctions that set it apart from all other tulip species: it is the latest to bloom (flowering in late May through June after all other tulips have finished, bridging the gap between spring bulbs and summer perennials), and it is arguably the best naturalizer in the tulip genus — self-seeding freely in garden conditions to build large, spreading colonies of plants that increase reliably year after year without lifting, dividing, or replanting. The flowers are a vivid, warm, scarlet-red to deep orange-red (with occasional yellow-flushed outer petal surfaces), starry, six-petaled, pointed-oval in bud and opening to a broad, open, star-like display of satiny red in bright sun. For a species that blooms so late and self-seeds so freely, it is perplexingly rare in general cultivation — partly because the small bulbs are difficult to produce commercially and mostly available through specialist sources and from seed. A colony established from seed or a first planting of small bulbs gradually becomes a self-sustaining treasure in the garden, the late-season red tulip display filling a slot in the spring bulb calendar that nothing else occupies. Naturalized colonies have been established in old gardens and appear completely at home in the borderline-shade of deciduous tree canopy.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–May or September–October. Sprengeri Fern grows from tuberous roots that allow it to survive periods of drought and some winter cold. In zone 9 it behaves as a semi-evergreen perennial, surviving mild winters with minimal damage and resprouting vigorously after hard freezes kill the above-ground stems. The trailing, cascading stems make it excellent in hanging baskets, window boxes, and container plantings where the growth can hang freely. Small, fragrant white flowers appear on established plants followed by red berries — attractive but mildly toxic if ingested. Can become invasive where birds drop seeds in warm, frost-free areas.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sprengeri Fern adapts to a wide light range but produces the most lush, dense growth in consistent partial shade with regular moisture; Sprengeri Fern is the most widely grown ornamental asparagus cultivar — a trailing, cascading, arching plant with airy, needle-like cladodes (the green, needle-like modified stems that function as leaves) clothing long, flexible stems that naturally arch and cascade 2–4 feet from their point of origin. Despite the common name, Sprengeri is not a true fern but an asparagus relative (Asparagus densiflorus) native to South Africa, sharing only the fine, feathery texture that gives it a fern-like appearance. The light, airy, bright green texture of cascading Sprengeri stems is one of the most versatile elements in both container design and cut flower arranging — the stems add a loose, naturalistic, fine-textured complement to virtually any floral combination, and the sprays remain fresh for an extended period after cutting. As a container plant for shaded patios and porches in zone 9, Sprengeri's cascading habit and fine texture provide an essential design element that trails gracefully from the edges of containers while tolerating the heat and partial shade conditions of covered outdoor spaces.

plant_note: Plant small corms in early fall in deep, moist, well-drained, rich woodland soil in full shade under deciduous trees; spring beauty naturalizes by self-sowing and corm offsets into large, sweeping colonies over many years.
directions: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in early fall in moist, rich, well-drained woodland soil in full shade under deciduous hardwoods; spring beauty is one of the quintessential Eastern North American spring ephemerals, forming extensive carpets that produce thousands of small pink-striped white flowers in earliest spring before the tree canopy leafs out, then disappearing completely by late spring. The dime-sized corms are edible, with a starchy-sweet flavor resembling water chestnuts, and were an important food source for Eastern Native peoples. Plants naturalize slowly by both self-seeding and corm offsets to create breathtaking sweeps of spring color in undisturbed woodland gardens. Purchase nursery-propagated corms only.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Spring Bouquet is a compact selection of laurustinus (Viburnum tinus) valued for dense evergreen foliage, winter-into-spring flower clusters, and a naturally tidy rounded form that requires little pruning.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge. Spring Bouquet is a compact cultivar of laurustinus, prized for its dense, dark green, glossy evergreen foliage and abundant clusters of small, fragrant, pinkish-white flowers that open from reddish-pink buds in late winter and early spring, one of the earliest flower displays in the evergreen shrub border. Flowers are followed by small blue-black berries that add fall and winter interest and attract birds. Its naturally rounded, well-proportioned habit holds a tidy shape with far less pruning than many broadleaf evergreens, making it useful for foundation plantings, informal hedges, and mixed borders. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soil types once established, though good drainage improves long-term performance, and it shows good resistance to the pests and diseases that trouble some other Southern landscape evergreens. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering to avoid removing the next year's flower buds.

plant_note: Plant small corms just below the soil surface (1 inch deep) in humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil under deciduous trees; spring cyclamen grows and flowers in winter and spring while deciduous trees are leafless, then goes dormant in summer when tree shade intensifies. Dry summer dormancy is essential — do not water during this period.
directions: Plant corms just below the surface in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade under deciduous trees; spring cyclamen is the third species of hardy garden cyclamen (after the autumn-blooming C. hederifolium and the winter-blooming C. coum) — a Mediterranean native of olive groves and deciduous woodlands in southern Europe that flowers in spring (March–April) with elegantly reflexed, rose-pink to carmine, fragrant flowers above beautifully silver-marbled, ivy-shaped leaves. Like its relatives, it grows actively in winter and spring when deciduous tree canopies are open, then retreats into summer dormancy under the dense shade of summer foliage. The flowers have a subtle, sweet fragrance uncommon in this genus. Hardier than the florist cyclamen (C. persicum) but somewhat less cold-tolerant than C. hederifolium, thriving in sheltered woodland gardens in zones 7–9. Together, C. hederifolium, C. coum, and C. repandum extend hardy cyclamen interest from August through April — nearly year-round in mild gardens.

plant_note: Plant tubers 2–3 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall before ground freezes; spring fumewort is a spring ephemeral — it emerges and blooms early, sets seed, and then dies down completely by early summer, leaving bare soil, so mark its position and interplant with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in fall; spring fumewort (fumitory, bird-in-a-bush) is a European woodland spring ephemeral bulb in the fumitory family — one of the earliest woodland bulbs to flower, emerging and blooming in early spring (March–April) simultaneously with snowdrops, early crocuses, and Scilla sibirica, before the deciduous tree canopy leafs out and shades the ground. The compact plants produce racemes of small, tube-spurred, two-lipped flowers in shades of deep rose-pink, magenta, red, lilac, or white with darker purple tips, above finely divided, gray-green, fernlike leaves. Like other spring ephemerals, it completes its entire growth cycle — emergence, flowering, seed-set, and dormancy — before deciduous trees fully shade the ground. It naturalizes readily under deciduous trees, spreads by self-seeding and by the division of the solid round tubers. The named cultivar 'George Baker' (deep, vivid salmon-red) is considered the finest individual form. Plant in large drifts of 25 or more bulbs for best effect under deciduous shade.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Spring Green is an eye-catching celosia standing about 40 inches tall with fresh lime-green plumes that thrive through late summer heat. Start seed indoors 6 to 4 weeks before the last frost, barely covering it and keeping soil warm around 75 degrees F for best germination. Transplant into full sun after frost danger passes, spacing plants for good airflow. The long, sturdy stems make excellent fresh or dried cut flowers and attract pollinators. Deadhead or harvest regularly to keep the display coming through the growing season.

plant_note: Transplant divisions in early spring into consistently moist, open ground with full sun to light shade. Incorporating organic matter improves establishment in heavier soils, but avoid excessive fertility.
directions: Site spring ladies' tresses in a moist meadow, rain garden, or roadside planting with full sun to partial shade and consistently moist, humus-enriched soil that does not dry out in summer. Prepare the planting area by removing competing sod and loosening the soil to allow the fleshy roots to establish without obstruction. Plant divisions at their original depth, firm the soil around the roots, and water thoroughly; continue to keep the soil evenly moist through the first growing season. This orchid blooms in spring rather than fall, making it an excellent companion to other early-season natives, and it will slowly colonize suitable areas once the mycorrhizal community is established.

plant_note: Start indoors in cool conditions; transplant in early spring or fall.
directions: Midnight Glow features rich velvet-purple petals with glowing yellow centers that fade into deep purple edges, producing large 3-inch blooms on uniform, well-branched plants. Start seed indoors in cool conditions and dark until germination, then grow on in bright, cool light before transplanting. Pansies thrive in cool, short-day weather, making them ideal for early spring and fall displays. Set plants in full sun to part shade in rich, moist soil and deadhead to prolong bloom. The edible flowers make a colorful garnish for salads and desserts.

plant_note: Divide and replant established clumps in early spring before new growth emerges, setting pseudobulbs just at the soil surface in a fast-draining orchid mix in a shaded location.
directions: Grow in a fast-draining mix of bark, perlite, and leaf mold in a deeply shaded location that receives bright indirect light, spacing clumps 9-15 inches apart to allow the narrow grassy foliage to form tidy mounds. Water moderately during the growing season, allowing the mix to approach dryness between waterings, and reduce water significantly in late autumn to encourage the formation of spring flower spikes. Apply a dilute balanced orchid fertilizer every two to three weeks from spring through summer, switching to a low-nitrogen formula in fall to harden growth. Divide clumps every three to five years in early spring, ensuring each division retains at least three to five pseudobulbs to guarantee flowering within one to two seasons.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spring snowflake is one of the earliest bulbs to bloom, often flowering before the last frosts, and naturalizes steadily to form increasingly beautiful drifts over time.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in fall in moist, well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; spring snowflake blooms in very early spring — often alongside snowdrops and well before most bulbs — producing one to three white, drooping, bell-shaped flowers per stem with distinctive green (sometimes yellow) spots at the tip of each petal, creating a dainty, charming display. Unlike the taller summer snowflake (L. aestivum), L. vernum is dwarf and delicate, blooming for 2–3 weeks in late winter to early spring. It naturalizes steadily by bulb offsets in suitable moist, shaded conditions and is one of the finest companion bulbs for snowdrops, winter aconites, and early crocus under deciduous trees. All parts are mildly toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Texas spider lily is native to wet meadows, creek margins, and roadside ditches in south Texas, Louisiana, and the Gulf Coastal Plain and thrives in seasonally moist to wet conditions where many other bulbs fail.
directions: Plant bulbs 4–6 inches deep in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Texas spider lily tolerates and even prefers seasonally flooded or consistently wet conditions. Hymenocallis liriosme (Texas spider lily or spring spider lily) is a native Gulf Coastal bulb producing one of the most elegantly beautiful flowers of any native American plant — strikingly large, pure-white flowers with narrow, reflexed, spider-like tepals (petals) 3–4 inches long radiating from a central, cup-shaped corona (like a small daffodil cup), produced on 18-to-30-inch naked stems in March–May before the leaves fully emerge. The fragrance is intensely sweet and vanilla-like, especially in the evening. The plant is native to wet prairies, roadside ditches, creek margins, and moist meadows from south Texas through Louisiana, blooming prolifically in the moist springs of the Gulf Coastal Plain. In garden conditions, it thrives in rain gardens, pond margins, boggy areas, and any consistently moist to seasonally wet location. The broad, strap-shaped, bright-green leaves remain attractive after flowering. Unlike many spider lilies that need dry summers, H. liriosme tolerates summer moisture. An outstanding native bulb for zone 9 gardeners seeking spectacular spring flowers in wet spots.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; spring starflower is tolerant of a wide range of soil conditions and partial shade, making it useful for naturalizing in difficult garden areas such as dry shade under trees, grassy banks, or the edges of paved surfaces. It spreads steadily by offsets to form dense, weed-suppressing clumps without becoming invasive.
directions: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for early to mid-spring bloom; spring starflower is a delightful, low-growing, easy-care bulb from South America that produces solitary, upward-facing, pale lavender-blue to silvery-blue, six-petaled, star-shaped flowers on slender stems above narrow, grass-like, bright green foliage that smells faintly of onions when crushed — betraying its relationship to the allium family. It blooms freely over several weeks from early spring, performing equally well in open sunny borders and in partial shade under deciduous trees and shrubs, where it tolerates surprisingly dry summer conditions once established. The bulbs multiply readily by offsets, slowly building into dense, attractive clumps that are excellent for edging, rock gardens, or naturalizing in rough grass and lightly shaded areas. The cultivar 'Wisley Blue' is a particularly fine selection with larger, deeper blue flowers.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Spring Symphony forms a slow, well-behaved clump and spreads gently by short stolons, making it suitable for smaller shaded beds and edging.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; mulch with leaf litter or shredded bark to keep roots cool and moist through summer. Spring Symphony is a foamflower cultivar prized for its finely cut, deeply lobed, almost fern-like leaves with a distinct central dark red-brown blotch that intensifies in cooler weather, providing months of foliage interest before and after the bloom period. In mid-spring, slender spikes densely packed with small, star-shaped flowers in soft pink emerge just above the foliage, creating a frothy, foamy display that gives the genus its common name. Its compact, restrained spreading habit makes it easier to keep within bounds than many stoloniferous native Tiarella cordifolia selections, while still knitting together into an attractive, weed-suppressing shade groundcover over a few seasons. Zone 4–9.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall for spring germination or scarify and sow in early spring; spring vetchling is slow to establish but forms long-lived clumps once settled. It grows naturally in deciduous woodland understory and performs best in similar conditions in the garden — dappled shade with humus-rich, well-drained soil. Plants emerge very early in spring and complete most of their growth before the tree canopy leafs out.
directions: Sow in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; spring vetchling is a small, woodland perennial pea from European forests — one of the earliest-blooming perennials in the spring garden, producing clusters of pea-shaped flowers in a distinctive color change: buds opening deep crimson-purple, flowers fading to violet-blue as they age, creating a plant with two or three colors simultaneously visible. The whole plant is delicate and compact — just 10–14 inches tall — with attractive, divided, vetch-like foliage and a non-climbing, bushy habit unlike most peas. It grows from a woody crown that becomes long-lived, slowly forming tidy, self-contained clumps in the shade garden without spreading aggressively. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves woodland soil fertility. It goes completely dormant by midsummer and disappears underground — an important consideration when siting it, as the empty space can be filled by later-blooming companions. Perfect for the woodland garden alongside trilliums, hepaticas, and bleeding hearts that bloom at the same season.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, loamy soil in partial shade to full sun. Spruce Pine is ecologically unique among eastern pines in its ability to establish and grow in the partial shade of mixed hardwood forests — the only pine native to the Southeast that tolerates significant shade.
directions: Spruce Pine is the most ecologically unusual of the southeastern native pines — the only pine in eastern North America that regularly grows as an understory component of bottomland hardwood forests and shaded mixed woods, native to the coastal plain and lower Piedmont from South Carolina to northern Florida and west to Louisiana, where it occurs in moist, fertile, loamy soils in the shade of sweetgum, water oak, and magnolia rather than in the open pinelands where other southeastern pines grow. Its smooth, gray bark (glabra means smooth or glabrous) is distinctive among pines and gives the tree an appearance reminiscent of a smooth-barked hardwood; the short, clustered needles and small cones distinguish it from other southeastern species. A valuable native pine for moist, shaded woodland gardens and naturalistic landscapes in zones 7–9 where its unusual shade tolerance sets it apart from all other native conifers. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; it is not drought-tolerant and requires consistently moist conditions.

plant_note: Plant divisions in fall or spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 7–10; Square Bamboo is a unique ornamental running bamboo native to southern China and Japan, the only widely cultivated bamboo species in which the mature culms develop distinctively square (4-sided) cross-sections — making it a horticultural curiosity and conversation piece, prized in Japanese tea garden design for its unusual geometry.
directions: Plant with rhizome barrier in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Chimonobambusa quadrangularis is a running bamboo — install deep HDPE rhizome barrier before planting to prevent spreading into neighboring areas; an interesting choice for Japanese garden or tea garden settings where the unusual square culms create visual interest. Chimonobambusa quadrangularis (Square Bamboo or Japanese Square Bamboo) is a distinctive, medium-sized running bamboo native to southern China (Fujian, Hunan, Guangdong) and long cultivated in Japanese gardens and tea garden design. The unusual and botanically remarkable feature is the development of distinctly 4-angled (square in cross-section) culms on mature plants — a property unique among commonly cultivated bamboos and caused by differential cell growth at the node internodes. Young shoots are round or only slightly angular; older culms develop the pronounced square shape that makes this bamboo instantly recognizable. The culms grow 4–15 feet tall, 0.5–1 inch in diameter, slender, and often sport decorative spine-like branch remnants at the nodes on mature culms. Chimonobambusa is a fall-shooting bamboo (unusual — most bamboos shoot in spring), producing its new culms September through November. It is moderately spreading (runner) and should be contained with rhizome barrier; the rhizomes are fairly superficial and relatively easy to manage by annual cutting. An outstanding and unusual addition to Japanese-style, contemplative, or tea garden designs.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; squarrose sedge grows naturally in forested floodplains and shaded swamp margins. Plants grow slowly from seed but divide readily in spring or early fall.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in forested wetland gardens and shaded rain gardens; squarrose sedge is a native sedge of swamp forests, forested floodplains, and shaded stream banks across the eastern United States, distinguished from related species by its unique fruiting heads in which the perigynia (seed cases) spread outward at nearly right angles to the stem axis — giving the spike a distinctly square-shouldered, cylindrical appearance. The reflexed perigynia tip creates a rough, bristly texture on the seed heads that provides excellent habitat texture in woodland plantings. Tolerates partial shade better than many wetland sedges and is excellent in rain garden plantings with overhead shade from existing trees. The seeds are consumed by various wetland birds. Forms tidy, non-aggressive clumps that stay in scale for residential rain garden plantings.

plant_note: Plant pea-sized yellow tubers (which resemble corn kernels, giving the plant its name) 1–2 inches deep in fall in groups for a natural display; interplant with hostas or ferns.
directions: Plant the small, yellow, corn-kernel-like tubers 1–2 inches deep in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; squirrel corn is a spring ephemeral closely related to Dutchman's breeches (D. cucullaria) but with rounded, heart-shaped flowers instead of pantaloon-shaped ones, and it has a hyacinth-like fragrance that D. cucullaria lacks. The finely dissected gray-green foliage and delicate white flowers appear in March–April then disappear completely by early June. The plant produces its namesake yellow tubers rather than the white grain-like tubers of its close relative. Entirely toxic — do not confuse with any edible plant. Forms small colonies over time as tubers multiply.

common_name: Squirrel's Foot Fern (Ball Fern, Rabbit's Paw Fern)
plant_note: Grow in a hanging basket or on a moss ball/kokedama in bright indirect to moderate shade; the creeping rhizomes of Squirrel's Foot Fern naturally cover the outside of containers and hanging baskets, creating a striking shaggy-rhizome display. Do not bury the rhizomes under growing medium — they need to be exposed on the surface. Water thoroughly and allow to approach dryness between waterings (more drought-tolerant than most ferns due to its epiphytic roots). Propagate by cutting rhizome sections with fronds attached and pressing them to moist growing medium.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Squirrel's Foot Fern is one of the most shade-tolerant and drought-forgiving of the epiphytic ferns, making it an ideal choice for indoor hanging baskets in low to moderate light. Davallia trichomanoides is a small, epiphytic fern native to Malaysia, Java, and Borneo in Asia, growing naturally on tree bark and rocky outcrops in humid tropical forests. The plant's defining and immediately captivating feature is its rhizomes: thick, creeping, furry brown surface rhizomes that radiate outward from the center of the plant and cascade down and over the edges of containers, covered in dense, soft, pale brown to rust-colored scales that give them the precise texture and appearance of a small squirrel's or rabbit's foot — the quality that inspired the plant's common names. From these distinctive rhizomes emerge small, finely divided, triangular, lacy fronds of deep medium-green that create an attractive, textured canopy above the showier rhizomes. The combination of the ornamental creeping rhizomes and the finely cut fern fronds makes Davallia trichomanoides particularly striking in hanging baskets, where both elements can be fully appreciated from below. Unlike most ferns, it tolerates periodic drying of the fronds and can be revived from apparent dessication by a thorough soaking. Non-toxic to pets.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to dry, well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; St. Andrews Cross is a small, adaptable native shrub of the southeastern United States bearing distinctive cross-shaped, 4-petaled yellow flowers in summer — the only North American St. John's Wort with only 4 petals — and is exceptionally shade and drought tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, acidic, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Hypericum hypericoides establishes readily in poor, infertile, acidic soils and is excellent for shaded edges, pine understory plantings, and woodland gardens — requires no supplemental fertilizer or irrigation once established in appropriate soil. Hypericum hypericoides (St. Andrews Cross) is a small, multi-stemmed, deciduous native shrub of the eastern and southeastern United States, ranging from New England south through Florida, west through Oklahoma and Texas, and into the Caribbean, where it grows in dry to moist pine flatwoods, sandhills, woodland edges, and stream banks. The common name and species epithet both reference the unusual cross-like arrangement of the 4 petals — unique among North American Hypericum species, all others of which have 5 petals — resembling the X-shaped cross of St. Andrew (the Saltire). Small, bright-yellow flowers appear prolifically in summer, followed by small, 2-valved capsules. A remarkably adaptable native shrub that performs well in both dry and moist conditions, acid soils, sandy substrates, full sun and deep partial shade — one of the most useful native shrubs for low-maintenance naturalistic planting in the Southeast. Valuable for pollinators, particularly native bees that collect pollen from the numerous stamens.

common_name: St. Cecilia Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)
plant_note: Set out container plants in spring or fall; St. Cecilia was one of David Austin's earlier English roses, introduced in 1987, combining old-rose cupped form and myrrh fragrance with repeat bloom, and performs through Gulf South heat with better disease resistance than many roses of its class.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil, spacing plants 2.5-3.5 feet apart. Introduced by David Austin in 1987, St. Cecilia was among his earlier English roses and remains a favorite for its soft, blush-apricot, cupped, old-fashioned-looking blooms and strong myrrh fragrance, an unusual scent profile distinct from the classic damask or tea fragrances of most roses. The relatively lax, arching shrub blooms in flushes from late spring through fall and shows better disease resistance than many early English roses, though like most of the class it benefits from good air circulation and occasional attention to blackspot in humid climates. It works well in mixed borders and cottage-style plantings, where its graceful, informal habit and soft coloring blend easily with perennials. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage a compact shape and vigorous new flowering growth.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring or fall; St. Joseph's Lily is one of the oldest garden hybrids in cultivation, dating to about 1810, and has naturalized so widely around old homesites across the Gulf South that it is often found blooming decades after a house and garden have vanished.
directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; in zone 9 gardens bulbs can stay in the ground year-round without lifting. St. Joseph's Lily, botanically Hippeastrum x johnsonii, is among the oldest amaryllis hybrids still grown, raised around 1810 by an English watchmaker crossing two South American species, and it proved so tough and long-lived that it spread through Southern gardens for two centuries, often persisting and naturalizing at abandoned homesites long after the rest of the garden is gone. Each stout stem carries several large, trumpet-shaped, red blooms with a distinctive white central stripe down each petal in mid-to-late spring, appearing before or with the strap-shaped foliage. Clumps increase steadily by offsets and are best left undisturbed for years, since flowering improves as the clump matures; divide only when clumps become congested, replanting divisions immediately since the bulbs dislike prolonged storage out of soil. It tolerates part shade better than most amaryllis, making it useful under high tree canopy, and needs no winter protection in zone 7 and warmer.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained to moderately wet, strongly acidic, sandy to loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. All parts of Staggerbush contain grayanotoxins (andromedotoxins) and are poisonous to livestock — do not plant where grazing animals have access.
directions: Staggerbush is a graceful native deciduous shrub of the coastal plain's moist to moderately dry, acidic soils from New England south to Florida and west to Texas, producing elegant, pendulous clusters of white to pink, urn-shaped flowers in May that hang gracefully from the branches before the leaves fully expand. The common name 'staggerbush' refers to the plant's toxicity to sheep and other livestock that consumed the foliage; like all Lyonia species, the leaves contain grayanotoxins (andromedotoxins) that cause staggering, drooling, and potentially fatal poisoning in grazing animals. Despite this toxicity, Staggerbush is an attractive ornamental native shrub with graceful spring flowers, attractive summer foliage, and modest red to orange fall color that supports native bees when in bloom. Plant in moist, well-drained to moderately wet, strongly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; keep away from livestock.

plant_note: Mount on boards covered with sphagnum moss or plant in hanging baskets in bright indirect light in partial shade; staghorn ferns are epiphytes that root into organic material rather than soil — soak the entire root mass in water for 15–20 minutes weekly, allow to drain fully, and never allow to stand in water. Offsets (pups) can be removed and mounted separately.
directions: Mount on sphagnum-covered boards or plant in hanging baskets in bright indirect light; staghorn fern (elkhorn fern) is one of the most dramatic and sculptural of all ferns — an epiphytic Australian native that produces two distinct frond types: flat, sterile 'shield fronds' that clasp the mounting surface and accumulate organic matter for nutrition, and large, upward-spreading, branched, antler-like 'fertile fronds' that give the plant its extraordinary architectural quality, resembling the antlers of a stag or elk. Plants are mounted on wooden boards, cork slabs, or tree trunks covered with moist sphagnum moss and hung on shaded walls, fences, or tree trunks to create a remarkable living-sculpture effect. Watering consists of soaking the entire root mass weekly (or more frequently in hot weather), then allowing to drain. In zones 9–12 they grow outdoors on trees and fences; elsewhere they are striking houseplants. Offsets (pups) that form around the base can be removed and separately mounted for propagation. Long-lived and can grow to enormous size over decades.

plant_note: Divide root suckers or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; staghorn sumac suckers aggressively — plant where spreading can be tolerated or mow around the perimeter annually to contain the colony.
directions: Divide root suckers or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; staghorn sumac is a fast-growing, large native shrub or small tree that provides one of the most spectacular multi-season landscape performances of any woody plant: bold, tropical-looking, compound leaves with 11–31 leaflets create a dramatic summer canopy; brilliant, fire-engine-red to orange-scarlet fall foliage among the most vivid of any temperate tree or shrub; fuzzy, cone-shaped clusters of deep-red, acidic berries (drupes) that persist through winter and provide critical food for ruffed grouse, robins, thrushes, bluebirds, pheasants, wild turkeys, and numerous other birds; and the distinctive, densely furry, brown-velvet branch tips that resemble the antlers of a stag in velvet — the most distinctive structural feature of any dormant shrub. Berries are used to make a pleasantly tart, pink lemonade-like beverage (sumac-ade) in indigenous and folk traditions. 'Laciniata' (cut-leaf/dissected foliage) is a particularly elegant ornamental cultivar. The suckering habit makes it excellent for erosion control on slopes.

common_name: Stained Glass Hosta (Fragrant Gold-Centered Hosta of the Year)
plant_note: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Stained Glass was named Hosta of the Year in 2006 for its large, glossy, gold-centered leaves with a wavy blue-green margin and its unusually fragrant white flowers, a rare trait among hostas.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, with morning sun or dappled light for the best gold color. Stained Glass was named the American Hosta Growers Association's Hosta of the Year for 2006, recognized for large, glossy, rounded leaves with a bright golden-yellow center bordered by a wavy, blue-green margin, along with fragrant, near-white flowers on tall scapes in summer — a genuinely useful trait, since most hostas have little to no fragrance. Its large, well-proportioned clump size and reliable, vigorous growth make it an excellent specimen or anchor plant in a shade border. The gold coloring develops most fully with some morning sun, though the plant tolerates deeper shade with somewhat less dramatic coloring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring as new growth emerges. Watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage, and apply iron phosphate bait around vulnerable new growth if damage appears.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; standing cypress is biennial — it forms a flat rosette of feathery foliage in the first year and produces its dramatic flower spike in the second year before setting seed and dying. Sow every year to maintain a continuous supply of blooming plants.
directions: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun — standing cypress is a native biennial of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf Coast, producing one of the most dramatic and unique effects in the spring-summer garden: an erect, rigid, 3–5 foot spike densely clothed in feathery, bright green, cypress-like foliage, then crowned the second year with hundreds of tubular, brilliant scarlet-orange flowers from May through July. The flowers are among the most intensely attractive to ruby-throated hummingbirds of any plant in the eastern flora — a single plant in bloom will hold hummingbirds all day. Because it is biennial, sow seed each fall to maintain continuous bloom from a mixture of first- and second-year plants. It self-sows reliably in sandy, open, sunny soil to maintain naturalized colonies. An outstanding plant for formal and naturalistic gardens alike wherever a vivid vertical accent and hummingbird attraction are desired.

common_name: Standing Ovation Little Bluestem (Extra-Sturdy Non-Flopping Native Grass)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Standing Ovation was bred specifically to solve the late-summer flopping that affects many little bluestem selections in humid, rainy climates, staying upright and tidy all season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Standing Ovation was specifically selected and trialed for its exceptional stem strength, staying upright through humid, rainy Southern and Midwestern summers where many little bluestem cultivars and the wild species itself tend to splay open or flop by late summer. It carries the same attractive blue-green summer foliage that turns warm orange-copper in fall, along with fluffy silvery seed heads that provide winter interest and bird food. Its reliably upright, dependable form makes it a strong choice for a formal or repeated planting where consistent structure matters, and like other little bluestem selections it is highly drought-tolerant and thrives in poor, lean soil. Cut back to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

common_name: Standing Winecup (Finger Poppy Mallow, Tall Winecup)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (October–November in zone 9) for spring blooming; established plants develop a deep, fleshy taproot that resents transplanting — direct seeding in permanent position is strongly preferred. In zone 9, fall-sown seed germinates in cool winter weather and plants bloom April–June. Excellent drainage is essential; plants rot in heavy clay or poorly drained soils. Do not mulch deeply over the crown.
directions: Direct sow in very well-drained, lean, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; rich soils produce weak, floppy stems with reduced flowering. Callirhoe digitata is an upright native prairie perennial from the tallgrass and mixed prairies of Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas, distinguished from the sprawling Winecup (C. involucrata) by its erect, branching habit on wiry stems reaching 2–3 feet, and by its deeply digitately-lobed leaves that resemble a spread hand (digitata = finger-like). The vivid magenta-crimson flowers are identical in brilliance to those of its sprawling relative and bloom April–July. The plant develops a deep, fleshy carrot-shaped taproot that stores water and nutrients — allowing well-established plants to survive extreme summer drought without irrigation and to regrow vigorously from the root crown when the above-ground portion dies back in heat. Once the taproot is established (2nd year), the plants are essentially indestructible in appropriate well-drained soils. Native American peoples reportedly used the taproots as a cooked vegetable. Standing Winecup self-seeds modestly in suitable conditions, slowly naturalizing in dry, gravelly garden spots. An outstanding choice for dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and xeriscape plantings in zone 9 where summer drought eliminates most other flowering plants.

plant_note: Plant crown divisions in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this small Japanese astilbe is ideally suited to the front of shaded borders and woodland edges, where its compact habit and glossy, simple leaves provide year-round textural interest.
directions: Plant crown divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil with the crown set just at soil level; this small Japanese species is distinguished from other astilbes by its undivided (simple or shallowly lobed), glossy dark-green leaves — an unusual trait in the genus. Astilbe simplicifolia produces graceful, arching sprays of star-shaped pink or white flowers in midsummer, and has been widely used as a parent of many popular dwarf hybrid astilbes valued for their compact size and refined foliage. Keep consistently moist and apply a mulch to protect shallow roots from summer heat and winter freeze-thaw cycles. Divide every 3 years in spring to prevent crown congestion and sustain flowering.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings under mist in early summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; star magnolia is one of the few magnolias that tolerates partial shade and maintains good flower production — but flowers may be damaged by late spring frosts, which is one reason for siting it in a position with some north or east exposure to delay bloom until frost risk has passed.
directions: Root softwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; star magnolia is a Japanese deciduous shrub-tree that flowers earlier than virtually any other ornamental tree in the temperate garden — in late March to April (zone 5–7), or even late February to early March in milder zones, the still-bare, furry-budded branches burst open into masses of large, multi-petaled, pure-white (or pale-pink in 'Rosea'), star-shaped flowers with 12–18 narrow, strap-like petals that radiate in all directions from the center. The pure-white, star-like flowers cover every branch and create an extraordinary white cloud effect before a single leaf has emerged. It blooms 2–3 weeks before Magnolia x soulangeana and considerably earlier than most garden shrubs, making it the first dramatic flowering statement of the temperate garden year. The narrow petals give it a distinctive, finely structured appearance quite different from the cupped, tulip-flowered magnolias. It is smaller and more shrubby in habit than many magnolias. 'Royal Star' (late-flowering, avoiding late frosts, particularly large flowers), 'Waterlily' (pink-budded, white-opening, very fragrant), and 'Centennial' are excellent cultivars.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep and 8-10 inches apart in sharply well-drained, dry to average soil in fall, 4-8 weeks before first frost; Star of Persia demands excellent drainage and tolerates poor, dry, stony soils well — bulbs will rot in heavy clay or persistently moist conditions. Plant in large groups of 5 or more for the most spectacular display, and allow the giant dried seed heads to remain on the plant through summer for continued ornamental impact.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in sharply well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun in fall for May-June bloom; Star of Persia produces the most spectacular flower head of any ornamental allium — enormous, globose umbels 8-12 inches in diameter composed of up to 100 individual metallic, star-shaped flowers in shimmering lilac-purple, each petal with a deeper central stripe, held on stiff, 12-18-inch stems above broad, strap-like, somewhat untidy basal leaves. The giant spherical heads are extraordinarily long-lasting, both on the plant and when cut and dried, and the papery star-shaped seed heads persist through summer and into autumn, turning a warm silvery-brown that is as beautiful as the flowers themselves. It performs best in hot, dry, well-drained sites that approximate its native Central Asian steppe habitat, and is outstanding in gravel gardens, rock gardens, and dry Mediterranean-style borders. It may be left to self-seed, and the resulting seedlings, while slow to reach flowering size, gradually build into naturalistic colonies.

plant_note: Direct sow; drought tolerant and heat loving.
directions: Direct sow star of the veldt in warm, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. This South African annual bears glowing orange and apricot daisies that open in bright sun and close on cloudy days. It thrives in heat and lean soil with minimal water, making it excellent for dry sunny beds and containers. Deadhead spent blooms and avoid overwatering, which can cause rot.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3-4 inches apart in well-drained, average soil in fall, 6-10 weeks before first frost; star-of-Bethlehem is extremely adaptable and will naturalize readily under deciduous trees and in grassy areas, thriving in the partial shade that filters through open tree canopies. Be aware that it spreads aggressively by offsets and self-seeding and is listed as invasive in several eastern US states — site it thoughtfully.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade in fall for April-May bloom; star-of-Bethlehem is a low-growing, cheerful spring bulb producing loose, flat-topped clusters of starry white flowers, each petal boldly striped green on the outside, that open fully only in bright light and close at night and on overcast days — a habit reflected in the old country name 'nap-at-noon.' The narrow, grass-like leaves are dark green with a distinctive pale central stripe, and the plant thrives especially well in the dappled shade beneath deciduous trees, where it receives full spring sun before the canopy closes. It naturalizes freely by offsets and self-seeding, eventually forming large, long-lived colonies that require no attention — a quality that is both a virtue and a caution, as it is considered invasive in parts of the eastern United States and should not be planted where it can escape into natural areas. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

plant_note: Direct sow around the last frost in full sun.
directions: Starflower opens delicate pale blue and white blooms, but its real magic is the spherical seedhead covered in papery, striped cups each cradling a five-pointed dark star. Direct sow in spring around the last frost, lightly covering the seed and keeping it evenly moist until seedlings emerge. Grow in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained soil. Cut blooms for fresh arrangements or leave them to mature into the ornamental seedheads prized for dried bouquets and crafts. The flowers draw bees and butterflies through summer.

common_name: Stargazer Oriental Lily (Iconic Pink-White Spotted Cut-Flower Bulb Lily)
plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall (November–December) in zone 9 for late spring to early summer bloom; orient bulbs pointed end up, 5–6 inches deep. In zone 9, Stargazer performs best when given afternoon shade — the hot summer sun can scorch the blooms and reduce vase quality. In zone 9's warm winters (insufficient chilling), Stargazer may bloom reliably for 1–2 seasons and then decline; for ongoing performance, lift and refrigerate bulbs for 8 weeks at 34–40°F before replanting each fall.
directions: Plant bulbs 5–6 inches deep in fall with pointed end up; mulch over the planting area to moderate soil temperature. Stargazer is the world's most recognized and widely grown Oriental hybrid lily — an F1 hybrid lily developed in 1974 by California lily breeder Leslie Woodriff, who reportedly said of the upward-facing flowers 'it's looking at the stars,' giving the variety its name. Before Stargazer, Oriental lilies typically produced downward-facing blooms (like the tiger lily form), but Stargazer's upright, upward-facing flowers were a breakthrough — placing the spectacular blooms where they could be seen clearly and making them dramatically more impactful in the garden. The individual flowers are among the most beautiful in the plant kingdom: 6–8 inches across, with 6 recurved tepals in deep carmine-pink with white edges and margins, heavily spotted with dark maroon spots, and a deep red central stripe — the combination of colors, spots, and form creating an appearance of almost artificial perfection. The intense fragrance is as remarkable as the appearance: sweet, heavy, exotic, and pervasive — a single vase of Stargazer can fill an entire room with fragrance. Stargazer has remained the dominant Oriental lily after 50 years of continuous commercial production.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall into dry to moist rocky woodland soil; cold stratification over winter triggers spring germination — do not cover seed as light improves germination rates.
directions: Silene stellata is an elegant native woodland campion of eastern North America, producing whorled, lance-shaped foliage on tall, slender stems and loose panicles of small but intricate, pure-white flowers with five deeply fringed petals in late summer — July through September — that look lacy and star-like even at close range. It grows naturally in dry to moist, rocky, slightly acidic to neutral woodland slopes and open forest understories and is one of the few native wildflowers that blooms reliably in late summer in partial shade. Hummingbirds visit the flowers, and the seeds ripen in ornamental, inflated capsules. Direct sow in fall for spring germination, or transplant divisions in early spring.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; starry false Solomon's seal forms spreading colonies by rhizomes and is more adaptable to dry shade and sandy soils than its larger relative M. racemosum.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; starry false Solomon's seal forms spreading colonies by rhizomes and is more adaptable to dry shade and sandy soils than its larger relative M. racemosum. Maianthemum stellatum (formerly Smilacina stellata) is a delicate, smaller relative of false Solomon's seal found across a wide range of North American habitats from moist woodlands to sand dunes and dry prairies; it has slender, arching stems with narrower, clasping leaves and bears loose racemes of 5–15 star-shaped, white flowers with 6 distinct petals in mid-spring, followed by greenish berries that turn dark red-striped then black as they ripen in late summer. It is among the most adaptable of native woodland perennials, tolerating a wider range of soil conditions than most shade plants, and makes an excellent naturalizing groundcover under deciduous or mixed-conifer trees in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in early spring or fall in full sun in well-drained to average soil; starry rosinweed is tap-rooted and difficult to transplant once established. It tolerates poor, dry soils and is considerably smaller than cup plant or compass plant, making it more suitable for residential gardens.
directions: Sow seeds in well-drained, average to lean, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; starry rosinweed is the most compact and garden-appropriate of the silphiums — a southeastern native prairie wildflower producing cheerful, bright-yellow daisy flowers 2–3 inches across with many narrow petals in a starry arrangement from July through September on plants that stay 2–5 feet tall rather than the 8–10 feet of compass plant. The rough, hairy, paired leaves are distinctive, as is the clear yellow of the ray flowers. It thrives in dry, poor soils where it needs no fertilization and minimal supplemental water once established. Native to dry, open woods, roadsides, and pine flatwoods from Virginia south to Florida and west to Texas, it is reliably perennial in the Southeast and Gulf Coast and grows considerably better in hot, humid conditions than many other prairie composites. Goldfinches consume the seeds in fall.

common_name: Starry Solomon's Seal (Star-Flowered False Solomon's Seal)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade; starry Solomon's seal spreads slowly by rhizomes to form colonies — plant 6-inch-deep rhizome divisions horizontally and allow several years to establish before dividing.
directions: Starry Solomon's seal is a native woodland perennial closely related to the more common false Solomon's seal (Maianthemum racemosum) but producing star-shaped white flowers spaced individually along the arching stems rather than in a terminal plume — the small, starry flowers have a delicate, precise symmetry that rewards close inspection. Like its relatives, it grows in moist to dry, rich woodland soil across a broad range of habitats from Pacific coast to Atlantic, forming slowly expanding colonies of arching, parallel-veined stems that emerge fresh green in spring and age to attractive copper-bronze in fall. Small striped berries (green to red-striped when young, darkening to deep red or black at maturity) are consumed by thrushes, towhees, and small mammals in fall; the berries and foliage are mildly toxic to humans and should not be consumed. Its compact stature and tolerance of dry shade make it one of the most versatile native groundcovers for both moist and moderately dry woodland gardens — use as an edging or naturalizing groundcover under deciduous trees.

common_name: Stars and Stripes Cast Iron Plant (Yellow-Spotted Deep-Shade Aspidistra)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Stars and Stripes maintains best leaf coloration in good indirect light — too-deep shade reduces the yellow spotting intensity while direct sun causes leaf bleaching and burning.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; Stars and Stripes is a variegated Aspidistra elatior cultivar with a distinctive speckled-and-streaked variegation pattern — small to medium yellow-gold spots and short streaks distributed across the dark green leaf surface create a starry, speckled appearance rather than the longitudinal stripe pattern of 'Variegata'. The spotting pattern is dense enough on good specimens to create a significant lightening of the overall leaf tone in mass plantings, brightening deep shade areas with the small yellow spots that gave the cultivar its name. Cast iron plant (Aspidistra elatior) is the standard-bearer for deep-shade ornamental groundcovers in Gulf South landscapes — routinely thriving under live oaks, Southern magnolias, and other dense-canopy trees where root competition, deep shade, and summer drought create hostile conditions for most other plants. The 'Stars and Stripes' variegation provides additional ornamental interest over the solid-green species while maintaining the same extraordinary shade and drought tolerance. The broad, strap-shaped, leathery leaves are deeply green with the scattered yellow speckle pattern that is attractive in both formal and informal shade garden settings. The small, inconspicuous, maroon flowers produced at soil level in late winter are characteristic but rarely noticed. Division of established clumps is slow — patience is required for new plantings to develop into full groundcover masses.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3-4 times their diameter deep in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in fall for spring flowering; Stars of Persia requires excellent drainage and dislikes wet soils, especially in summer when the bulbs are dormant. The enormous dried seed heads persist ornamentally for months and are excellent for drying. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after flowering.
directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Stars of Persia produces some of the most spectacular flower heads of any ornamental allium — enormous, perfectly spherical umbels reaching 8-12 inches across that are composed of scores of individual starry, metallic silvery-purple to amethyst-pink florets, each on its own slender stem radiating outward from the center like a perfect starburst or fireworks explosion. The overall effect of a fully open flower head is unlike anything else in the spring garden — a huge, airy, three-dimensional sphere of metallic purple stars that seems to float above the ground. After the flowers fade, the seed heads dry in place and remain ornamental for months — often through the entire summer and into fall — their silver-gray skeletal structure providing exceptional structural interest. The florets of the dried head are used in dried flower arrangements. Plant in drifts for maximum impact; best combined with late-season perennials that will cover the fading foliage.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger passes in warm soil.
directions: State Fair Mix is a pollinator magnet producing immense flowers dominated by reds and purples with orange, pink, white, and yellow scattered throughout. Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil and full sun, thinning seedlings to give these tall plants room to branch. Zinnias grow quickly and bloom heavily until fall frost when kept deadheaded or cut. The long, sturdy stems make outstanding cut flowers for arrangements. Provide good airflow and water at the base to reduce foliar disease.

common_name: State Fair Zinnia (Tall Classic Large-Flowered Mixed Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; State Fair is among the tallest zinnia varieties (30–36 inches) and produces sturdy stems for cutting. In zone 9, direct sow March–May for summer bloom or August for fall. Stake if necessary in exposed windy sites. State Fair zinnia petals are thick and durable — the flowers hold up in the garden through rain and heat better than thinner-petaled varieties.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. State Fair is a classic large-flowered zinnia mix producing very tall plants (30–42 inches) with large double flowers (4–5 inches) on stems long enough for impressive cut flower arrangements. State Fair represents the traditional American zinnia ideal — the tall, robust, large-flowered zinnia that was grown in American gardens for decades as the primary summer cutting flower before hybrid varieties introduced more compact, uniform types. The flowers come in the full zinnia color range: scarlet, rose, salmon, orange, gold, cream, lavender, white, and bicolors — the mixed seedling planting creating a naturalistic, abundant, old-fashioned garden scene. The thick petals and sturdy stems make State Fair excellent for cutting at the bud-opening stage for 7–10 day vase life. Plants bloom prolifically from midsummer through frost with regular harvesting or deadheading. The tall habit (30–42 inches) distinguishes State Fair from compact modern types and suits it for the back of borders, cutting garden rows, and locations where height is desired.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–3 weeks before last frost as plants tolerate mild frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/8 in deep in moist starting mix; seeds come in a papery casing and germination is slow. Statice prefers cool conditions early in the season. Harvest flower stems for drying when 75% of the florets on each branch have opened. The papery calyces — which hold their color dried — are the ornamental part; the true petals are tiny and brief.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Steeds is a slow-growing, upright, densely branched Japanese holly cultivar long used as a boxwood substitute in Southern landscapes for its fine texture and tolerance of shearing.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 3-4 feet apart for a hedge or screen.
