The plant twines naturally and needs a trellis, fence, pergola, or other structure to climb. In zone 9 it grows vigorously from spring through fall, blooming continuously without deadheading from first planting through first frost. In the warmest zone 9 locations the plant may survive mild winters as a semi-woody perennial; in most of zone 9 treat as an annual or move container-grown plants indoors before frost. The milky sap is irritating to some people — wear gloves when pruning.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Sun Parasol Crimson Mandevilla blooms most abundantly in full sun with consistent moisture; Mandevilla (Mandevilla x amabilis) is a tropical twining vine producing large, funnel-shaped flowers with five broadly overlapping petals in a classic five-lobed arrangement — the Sun Parasol Crimson selection bearing vivid crimson to deep rose-red flowers 3–4 inches across that create a striking, uninterrupted bloom display from late spring through frost. Mandevilla's combination of tropical flower size (far larger than most annual vines), glossy deep green foliage, continuous bloom without deadheading, and ability to quickly cover a trellis, pergola, or fence with an impressive tropical display makes it one of the most impactful ornamental vines for zone 9 summer gardens. The large, funnel-shaped flowers are hummingbird-attractive — the trumpet form, bright crimson color, and sweet nectar production make mandevilla a reliable hummingbird plant wherever hummingbirds occur. In zone 9's warm, humid climate, mandevilla performs as one of the finest summer flowering vines available — thriving in the heat that defeats many vine species and providing the tropical character that suits the Gulf South climate.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. SunPatiens are a Sakata Seed trademark and are sold as vegetatively propagated transplants only — not as seed. The Compact series plants are smaller (18–24 inches) than the Vigorous series (24–36 inches), making Compact Pink better suited to containers and formal beds. SunPatiens bloom continuously without deadheading and are self-cleaning. In zone 9 they perform well from spring through fall in both sun and partial shade, withstanding summer heat and humidity significantly better than traditional bedding impatiens.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil — SunPatiens tolerate more sun than traditional impatiens and are suitable for both shaded and full-sun locations; SunPatiens Compact Pink is part of the SunPatiens line from Sakata Seed — an interspecific impatiens hybrid (Impatiens x hybrida) developed to solve the critical problem of impatiens downy mildew (Plasmopara obducens) that devastated traditional bedding impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) populations beginning around 2011–2012. The interspecific hybrid parentage gives SunPatiens resistance to this downy mildew disease that rendered conventional impatiens unreliable for shade garden use in warm, humid climates. SunPatiens Compact Pink produces large (1.5–2 inch), bright candy-pink flowers continuously from planting until frost, with glossy, slightly succulent foliage that is more heat-tolerant than standard impatiens. The unique sun-and-shade tolerance allows SunPatiens to be used across a wider range of light conditions than any traditional impatiens variety — from deep shade to full sun — making it one of the most versatile summer annuals for varied garden situations.

common_name: SunRich Sunflower (Pollen-Free Single-Stem Cut Flower Series)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; for succession harvests, sow every 1-2 weeks through summer. SunRich is a major commercial single-stem, pollen-free cut-flower sunflower series bred for uniform bloom timing and strong stems, widely used alongside ProCut in professional cut-flower production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in full sun after last frost; grow on a tight spacing of 6-9 inches to encourage the single, unbranched flowering stem this series is bred to produce. SunRich is one of the leading commercial cut-flower sunflower series, offering pollen-free flowers in gold, lemon-yellow, orange, and other colors on strong, straight, single stems bred specifically for uniformity, making it a favorite of market growers who need predictable, evenly timed harvests. Because plants do not branch, close spacing maximizes stem count per bed, and the whole planting typically matures and is harvested together roughly 55-65 days after sowing. The pollen-free trait keeps arrangements and clothing clean of the yellow pollen that standard sunflowers shed heavily once open. Harvest when petals have just begun to unfurl but the center disk remains tight for the best vase life, and succession sow every one to two weeks through the growing season for a continuous cut-flower supply.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm. In zone 9 plant March–May. Sunday Orange celosia is heat-loving and actually blooms better and more vividly as temperatures increase — it is one of the few annuals that performs better in summer heat rather than declining. The large, feathery plumes are excellent for fresh cutting and dry extremely well on the plant, making them outstanding for dried flower arrangements.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Sunday Orange is a plume-type (feather) celosia producing dramatic, soft, feathery plumes in vivid pure orange — one of the most saturated and vividly colored of any annual flower, with an almost unreal intensity of color that makes it instantly eye-catching in summer garden displays and mixed cut flower arrangements. The plume-type celosia (as opposed to the crested cockscomb type) has soft, delicate, branching flower heads that resemble bright-colored feathers or flames, which explains the common name 'plumed cockscomb' or 'feather celosia'. Sunday Orange was developed for uniformity, large plume size, and early bloom — beginning to flower 60–75 days from transplant and continuing continuously until frost without requiring deadheading. Celosia is genuinely heat-loving: plants grow slowly in cool weather and then rapidly accelerate in hot summer conditions, blooming most freely in zone 9's intense summer heat. The flowers dry in place on the plant and can be cut for dried arrangements at any stage of development.

plant_note: Fall sow or cold-stratify seed; taproot resents transplanting.
directions: Sundial lupine, also called wild lupine, is a heirloom perennial native to the eastern U.S. and a vital host plant for the Karner blue butterfly. Scarify or cold-stratify the hard seed and direct sow in fall or early spring, since the deep taproot dislikes transplanting. Grow in full sun in lean, sandy, well-drained soil where it naturalizes in wildflower gardens and meadows. Its blue flower spikes appear in late spring to early summer and draw many pollinators. Avoid rich soil and excess water, which this drought-tolerant native does not need.

common_name: Sundial Mango Portulaca (AAS-Winning Warm Mango-Orange Moss Rose for Summer Heat)
plant_note: Surface-sow seeds after the last frost in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; do not cover seeds — portulaca seeds require light for germination; Sundial Mango blooms reliably even in cloudy conditions unlike older portulaca varieties that closed their flowers on overcast days.
directions: Surface-sow seeds on well-drained, lean to sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sundial Mango is an All-America Selections award-winning portulaca (moss rose) — part of the Sundial series selected for an important improvement over older portulaca varieties: the ability to remain open and in bloom on overcast days. Traditional portulaca varieties close their flowers in shade, cloudy weather, and in the afternoon, significantly limiting their ornamental value to only the sunniest morning hours. The Sundial series maintains flower opening throughout the day in typical light conditions, including partial overcast. The Mango color — warm, sunny, deep apricot-orange to mango-orange — is one of the richest and most distinctive in the Sundial color range, producing a warm, vibrant display in the rock garden, gravel mulch, and dry border positions where portulaca excels. Portulaca is one of the most truly drought-tolerant and heat-resistant summer annuals for full-sun Gulf South positions — thriving in lean, sandy, or gravelly soil where other annuals would fail, and continuing to bloom through the driest and hottest periods of Gulf South summer. The succulent stems and leaves store water to bridge dry periods without wilting. The low, spreading mounding habit (6–8 inches tall, 12–18 inches wide) makes portulaca ideal for rock walls, gravel gardens, and the fronts of full-sun borders.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May. The Sundial series is one of the most widely grown portulaca series in North America, selected for flowers that remain open longer than older portulaca — traditional portulaca closes in shade and on cloudy days, while Sundial remains open in lower light conditions. Do not cover seed — portulaca requires light for germination. Direct sow on the soil surface and press in lightly. Thin seedlings to 8–10 inches. In zone 9 portulaca is one of the most dependably heat and drought-tolerant annuals available — thriving in the harshest summer conditions while continuing to flower prolifically. Excellent for rock gardens, sandy banks, and other hot, dry situations where few other annuals can perform.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Portulaca demands full sun and excellent drainage; it thrives in the dry, hot conditions that defeat most other annuals and declines rapidly in shade or wet soil; Sundial Orange Portulaca is a compact, semi-double to double portulaca producing vivid orange flowers in the Sundial series, one of the most improved portulaca strains available — with flowers that remain open in lower light conditions than older portulaca varieties that close completely on cloudy days and in shade. The succulent stems and leaves of Portulaca grandiflora (from its South American native range) store water and enable the plant to withstand drought conditions at which most annual flowers wilt and decline — making portulaca uniquely valuable for hot, dry, full-sun situations including sandy banks, rock gardens, paving cracks, and dry border edges where conventional annuals would require frequent irrigation to survive. The brilliant orange of Sundial Orange provides one of the most saturated and vivid warm-color tones available from a low-growing annual — particularly effective as an edging or mass planting against stone or gravel surfaces where the orange flowers glow against neutral backgrounds. In zone 9's peak summer heat portulaca improves in performance while most other annuals decline, making it the go-to choice for reliably colorful, extremely low-maintenance summer color in the most challenging hot, dry sunny situations.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–June. Sundial series portulaca flowers stay open later into the afternoon than older varieties (which close in overcast or afternoon conditions), making them more useful as a continuous-color bedding plant throughout the day. In zone 9 portulaca thrives in the hottest, driest summer conditions — a perfect full-sun annual for hot, dry slopes, rock gardens, and containers where irrigation is minimal. Sow seeds thinly on the surface of the soil (do not cover — seeds require light to germinate) and mist gently until seedlings establish.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, neutral to slightly acidic soil — portulaca demands excellent drainage and actually blooms best in poor, dry soil, languishing in rich or wet conditions; Sundial Pink is a large-flowered (1.5-inch) semi-double portulaca (moss rose) with bright cerise-pink blooms from the Sundial series, which was specifically developed to solve portulaca's traditional failing: the original moss roses closed their flowers in afternoon heat, overcast conditions, and late in the day, leaving the plant bloomless for much of the day. The Sundial series flowers stay open significantly longer than older varieties — an important improvement for a plant intended to provide continuous color in hot, sunny garden locations throughout the day. The succulent, needle-like leaves store water in their tissues, giving portulaca remarkable drought tolerance that allows it to survive periods of complete neglect and to thrive in the kind of hot, dry, reflected-heat locations (paved beds, rocky slopes, container walls) that would kill almost any other flowering annual. In zone 9's brutal summer heat, portulaca is among the very few flowering plants that genuinely improves in performance as temperatures rise.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring around or just before the last frost date in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; sundrops self-seeds readily once established and spreads by rhizomes to form attractive colonies — site it where it has room to naturalize.
directions: Direct sow in early spring in lean, well-drained, average to poor, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; sundrops is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, dry soils — rich, moist conditions produce weak, floppy growth and reduce flowering. Oenothera fruticosa is a native eastern North American perennial evening primrose relative that, unlike most of its nocturnal relatives, opens its bright, butter-yellow, 4-petaled, 1–2-inch flowers in full daylight throughout the day — making it a true daytime ornamental rather than a night-bloomer; the clear yellow flowers appear abundantly from May through July atop reddish, upright stems with lance-shaped, glossy, dark-green leaves that often develop attractive red and bronze tints in fall and spring. It is an excellent native wildflower for sunny, dry, low-maintenance borders and meadow plantings, spreads gradually by rhizomes and self-seeding to form colonies, and is highly attractive to bees and other native pollinators. The red-budded subspecies glauca (sometimes sold as ssp. glauca or 'Fyrverkeri'/'Fireworks') has particularly ornamental red flower buds that contrast vividly with the yellow open flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall to allow cold stratification through winter; seeds will germinate in spring as soils warm.
directions: Sunflower-leaved Coreopsis is a robust southeastern native perennial distinguished by its broad, undivided leaves that closely resemble small sunflower leaves — quite unlike the finely cut foliage of most other Coreopsis. Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; it tolerates a wider range of conditions than many of its relatives and is more forgiving of heavier soils. Classic bright yellow daisy flowers with maroon-tinged central discs appear on upright stems from June through August, reliably attracting bees and butterflies. The plant spreads slowly by rhizomes to form attractive, long-lived clumps that require little maintenance in prairie gardens or open sunny borders.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; good for containers due to compact habit.
directions: Sow seed one inch deep after the last frost once soil warms. This dwarf heirloom grows just two to three feet tall, producing dozens of fluffy, double golden-yellow pom-pom blooms. Its compact, branching habit suits containers, borders, and small gardens, and the sturdy stems make fine cut flowers. Give it full sun and moderate water, and deadhead to keep new blooms coming through the season.

common_name: Sunkiss Coreopsis (AAS-Winning Bicolor Red-Ringed Yellow Coreopsis)
plant_note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sunkiss is an AAS-winning bicolor coreopsis blooming heavily the first year from an early start.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Sunkiss is an All-America Selections-winning coreopsis producing bright golden-yellow flowers marked with a bold burgundy-red ring around the center, a striking bicolor pattern that stands out against the plain gold of most coreopsis cultivars. It blooms heavily from its first year onward and continues over a long summer season with regular deadheading, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil with ease once established. Like other coreopsis, it performs best in lean soil with sharp drainage, since overly rich or wet conditions promote excess foliage and shorten the plant's life; dividing congested clumps every few years helps maintain vigor.

common_name: Sunny Border Blue Veronica (Perennial Plant of the Year Deep Blue Speedwell)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Sunny Border Blue was named Perennial Plant of the Year for its long bloom season, glossy dark green foliage, and dependable performance across a wide range of conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Sunny Border Blue was named the Perennial Plant Association's Perennial Plant of the Year in 1993 and remains one of the most reliable, widely grown veronica cultivars, producing dense spikes of rich violet-blue flowers over glossy, deep green, crinkled foliage from early summer well into fall with deadheading. Its exceptional garden performance and long bloom season across a wide range of soil and climate conditions have made it a benchmark perennial for sunny borders, and it draws bees and butterflies reliably throughout its bloom period. Divide the clump every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor as the center becomes congested.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; soak or nick seed to speed germination.
directions: Sunrise Blend offers a colorful assortment of trumpet blooms that flutter against vigorous heart-shaped foliage from midsummer to the first fall frost. Soak or nick the hard seed coat, then direct sow after the last frost near a trellis, fence, or arbor for the climbing vines to scale. The flowers open in early morning and may stay open on cloudy or cool days. Grow in full sun in average soil, avoiding overly rich ground that favors leaves over flowers. Note that the seeds are poisonous if eaten, so keep them away from children and pets.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to a very well-drained site in full sun; sunset hyssop requires excellent drainage and thrives in lean, rocky, alkaline soils — rich, moist soils promote disease and weak growth. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and heat-loving.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; sunset hyssop is a native agastache of the dry mountains of New Mexico and Arizona, producing aromatic, narrow, gray-green leaves with an intensely pleasant combined licorice-mint-root-beer fragrance and long, narrow spikes of small tubular flowers in a spectacular orange-pink to salmon-coral color that shades toward orange at the base of the tube and pink at the tip — precisely the color of a sunset sky. The blooms appear from midsummer through fall and are intensely attractive to hummingbirds throughout the season. Unlike the more common anise hyssop, sunset hyssop is more heat-tolerant, much more drought-tolerant, and thrives in the hot, arid, alkaline soils of the Southwest and Gulf Coast. It is short-lived (2–4 years) but self-sows readily. Deer resistant.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; loves heat and dry soil.
directions: Sunshine Blend gazania is a heat- and drought-loving groundcover in warm colors from yellow to mauve, with lush low foliage and blooms held high on their stems. Start seed indoors 6 to 4 weeks before the last frost, covering lightly since darkness aids germination, then transplant after frost danger passes. Grow in full sun in sandy, well-drained soil where the daisy-like petals unfurl in sunshine and close under clouds. Water sparingly once established, as this tough plant tolerates drought and poor soil. Deadhead to keep the color coming through summer.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for best golden color; Sunshine Ligustrum is a sterile, non-fruiting sport selected specifically to avoid the invasive seeding of common Chinese privet.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, where the foliage colors most brightly; in shadier sites the leaves stay more chartreuse-green than gold. Sunshine Ligustrum was selected as a sterile, non-flowering, non-fruiting sport of common Chinese privet specifically to provide the same tough, brightly colored foliage without the invasive seeding that has made the wild species a serious problem in Southern woodlands. Because it never flowers or sets berries, it channels its energy into dense, compact growth and vivid golden-yellow foliage color that holds through the heat of summer, making it a popular low hedge, mass planting, or color accent shrub. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil with ease and needs only occasional shearing to maintain a tidy shape.

plant_note: Plant plugs or divisions in spring in any well-drained, sunny soil; sunshine mimosa spreads vigorously by stolons to form a dense mat — excellent for replacing lawn areas in full sun, but control spread in small gardens by periodic edging.
directions: Sunshine mimosa is the premier native groundcover lawn substitute for the Gulf Coast region — a low-growing, stoloniferous perennial that forms dense, fine-textured mats covered with pink, feathery pompom flowers from spring through fall, handling foot traffic better than most native groundcovers. As a member of the legume family, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, improving soil fertility as it spreads, and it tolerates the heat, drought, and poor sandy soils of Gulf Coast gardens that defeat other groundcovers. The sensitive leaves fold slightly when brushed or walked on — a charming touch-me-not response that delights children — and the spectacular pink pompom flowers are a prolific nectar source for native bees and butterflies throughout the growing season. In lawn renovation projects in zone 8–11, plant plugs on 12-inch centers in spring and within one growing season they will knit together into a solid, mowable (3-inch mow height) lawn alternative that needs no irrigation, no fertilizer, and no pesticides once established.

plant_note: Set out container-grown or bare-root plants in early spring in a sunny, open location with well-drained to dry soil. Native prairie gravel or loam is ideal; avoid clay-heavy or amended soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in dry to average, well-drained soil typical of central US prairies; this species is native to open grasslands and woodland edges and does not tolerate wet feet or heavy shade. Once established, it is highly drought-tolerant and spreads by root sprouts to form a low thicket useful for erosion control and wildlife cover. Deep pink blooms appear in late spring to early summer and are followed by small, globe-shaped red hips that persist into winter, providing important food for birds. Propagate from hardwood cuttings in late autumn or by carefully digging and transplanting rooted root sprouts in early spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Sunspot delivers large sunflower heads on surprisingly dwarf 18-to-24-inch stalks, making it a favorite for kids and small gardens. Direct sow the seed about an inch deep after the last frost in warm soil and full sun. Thin seedlings so each plant has room to develop its outsized bloom. The short stature makes dramatic cut flowers and container plantings, and the heads later provide seeds for birds. Provide steady moisture while young and full sun throughout the season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost or plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant transplants March–May. Sunstander is a sun-tolerant impatiens selection developed in response to the nearly complete collapse of Impatiens walleriana production caused by impatiens downy mildew (Plasmopara obducens), which devastated annual impatiens plantings across the Eastern US starting around 2012. The Sunstander series was selected for greater sun tolerance than standard walleriana — making it useful in partial shade and high-light situations where standard impatiens produce leggy, sparse growth. In zone 9 impatiens perform best as a spring and fall annual, declining in peak summer heat; plan for replacement or expect reduced flowering in July–August.
directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered light in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich, consistently moist soil — Sunstander impatiens tolerates more sun than standard Impatiens walleriana and performs well in morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9; Sunstander is a sun-tolerant selection of Common Impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) developed to address the practical limitations of standard impatiens in higher-light situations — the standard selections requiring deep shade conditions that limit planting flexibility in many garden situations. Impatiens walleriana remains one of the most valuable shade-garden annuals available — producing a continuous, weed-suppressing carpet of single or double flowers in essentially every color except true blue, requiring almost no deadheading, and delivering consistent performance from planting through frost in shaded beds, window boxes, and containers. The Sunstander selection expands the practical planting range of walleriana impatiens by tolerating the dappled light and part-sun conditions that cause standard impatiens to become leggy and produce sparse flowers rather than the dense, mounding bloom mass they produce in appropriate shade. In zone 9 impatiens are most valued as spring and fall annuals — planted in March for spring display and replaced or supplemented in fall (September–October) when they recover from summer heat stress.

common_name: Sunstorm Coral Vinca (Heat-Proof Coral-Orange Madagascar Periwinkle Annual)
plant_note: Plant container transplants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Vinca requires good soil drainage — plants in poorly drained soils develop Phytophthora root rot rapidly; raised beds and well-amended garden beds provide the drainage needed for reliable performance.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sunstorm Coral is a coral-orange to warm-peach-orange Catharanthus roseus (Madagascar periwinkle, vinca) — one of the most important and reliable summer annuals for Gulf South full-sun gardens, blooming prolifically and continuously through the brutal July–August heat that collapses most other summer annuals. Catharanthus roseus is native to Madagascar and specifically adapted to hot, humid conditions — its heat performance in Gulf South summers is among the best of any commonly grown annual. The Sunstorm series was bred for improved heat and humidity tolerance, early and continuous flowering, and mounding, well-branched plant habit. The warm coral-orange color of 'Sunstorm Coral' creates a vivid summer display that works with both warm tropical companions (lantana, blue salvia) and cooler purple and chartreuse foliage plants. The waxy, glossy leaves and five-petaled, flat-faced flowers are characteristic of the species. Deadheading is not required — vinca naturally drops spent flowers and produces new blooms continuously. Good drainage is the critical cultural requirement — Phytophthora root rot in poorly drained soil is the primary cause of vinca failure in Gulf South gardens. Vinca is toxic if ingested and contains alkaloids with significant pharmacological properties that have been the basis for cancer chemotherapy drugs (vincristine, vinblastine).

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Sunstorm Pink is a selection in the Sunstorm series of vinca bred for enhanced heat tolerance and mildew resistance. Annual vinca (Catharanthus roseus) is susceptible to aerial Phytophthora blight in conditions of poor drainage and water on the foliage — plant in raised, well-drained sites and avoid overhead irrigation or overhead watering. In zone 9 annual vinca is one of the most reliable and self-cleaning summer annuals available — requiring no deadheading, maintaining compact form without pinching, and blooming continuously from late spring through frost. Seeds require light for germination — do not cover; bottom heat improves germination speed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil — Annual Vinca performs best in heat and full sun, declining in shade and in wet, poorly drained conditions; Sunstorm Pink Vinca is a compact selection of Annual Vinca (Catharanthus roseus), a heat-tolerant tropical annual from Madagascar producing a continuous cascade of five-petaled, flat-faced, bright pink flowers (each with a lighter central eye) that are self-cleaning, requiring no deadheading, and bloom from first warm weather through frost. The Sunstorm series was developed specifically for improved Phytophthora blight resistance and superior heat performance — addressing the primary weakness of older vinca series in the humid Gulf South climate where standing water or overhead irrigation created disease pressure on less resistant selections. Annual vinca is among the most genuinely heat-tolerant and low-water-demand flowering annuals available for zone 9 — thriving in the peak summer conditions of July–September when temperatures exceed 95°F and rainfall may be irregular. The combination of continuous self-cleaning bloom without deadheading, excellent drought tolerance once established, compact mounding habit, and genuine heat performance that improves through the hottest months of zone 9 summer makes Sunstorm Pink one of the most practically reliable summer flowering annuals for full-sun beds, borders, and containers.

common_name: Super Blue Liriope (Bold Deep-Blue Flowering Lilyturf for Shade Borders)
plant_note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Super Blue's heavy flowering is maintained in partial shade — one of the few ornamental groundcovers that produces significant flower display without requiring full sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Super Blue is a Liriope muscari cultivar selected for exceptionally heavy and prolific flowering — producing dense spikes of rich lavender-blue to deep violet-blue flowers in August–September well above the dark-green foliage, creating one of the best flower displays of any commonly grown liriope. The flower spike quality distinguishes Super Blue from standard liriope varieties: the spikes are longer, more densely flowered, and more vivid in color than typical Liriope muscari cultivars, creating a stronger ornamental statement in the late-summer border when few other shade perennials are actively flowering. Liriope is one of the most important and versatile groundcover plants for Gulf South landscapes — tolerating the full range of conditions from full sun to deep shade, from clay soils to sandy soils, from moist to periodically drought-stressed, and from salt spray to inland heat. Super Blue is an outstanding choice for border edges, the fronts of foundation plantings, and mass groundcover plantings in partial-shade positions under trees and along shaded building foundations. The dark-green, strap-shaped leaves provide clean, year-round evergreen structure even when the plant is not in bloom. Black berries persist through fall and winter, providing interest and food for small birds. Divide established clumps every 3–5 years when they become overcrowded and productivity declines.

common_name: Superb Anthurium (Puzzle Anthurium, Bird's Nest Bird's Nest)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light; Anthurium superbum is more adaptable than many collector anthuriums, tolerating lower humidity (though preferring 50–70%) and moderate temperature fluctuation. Use a well-draining, humus-rich potting mix. The rosette growth habit means the plant grows outward rather than upward — allow adequate horizontal space. Propagate from offsets or fresh seed. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in moderate to bright indirect shade — Anthurium superbum is among the most shade-tolerant of the commonly available anthuriums, thriving in lower light conditions where other large Anthuriums would struggle. Anthurium superbum is a large rosette-forming anthurium native to Ecuador, producing a bold, bird's-nest or fountain-like rosette of large, broadly strap-shaped, leathery leaves that arch outward from the center in a vase-like arrangement superficially resembling large Bird's Nest Ferns (Asplenium nidus) or the rosette form of Anthurium hookeri. The leaves are distinguished by their unusual surface texture: the upper surface is covered with irregular, slightly raised areas and depressed zones — a rough, bumpy, puzzle-like texture that gives the species the alternative common name 'Puzzle Anthurium.' The undersides of the leaves are dark violet-purple, creating a striking color contrast visible when the large leaves arch outward. Anthurium superbum produces long flower spadices that develop into dense, elongated clusters of deep purple-to-black berries when fertilized — the berry-laden spadix is itself ornamental. This species is one of the larger-growing of the commonly available bird's nest-type anthuriums, eventually forming an impressive specimen suitable as a floor plant in appropriate indoor spaces. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring; Salvia x superba is a sterile hybrid and must be propagated vegetatively by division or cuttings. After the first main flush (typically June–July), shear the entire plant back hard by one-half to two-thirds — this will produce a second, often more prolific flush of bloom by August–September and prevent the plant from going to seed before it can rebloom.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; superb sage is one of the foundational hybrid garden salvias — a sterile perennial hybrid related to Salvia nemorosa and S. sylvestris that produces dense, erect spikes of small, rich violet-purple to blue-violet, hooded flowers with contrasting dark, wine-purple calyces, giving the spike a two-toned color effect. The dense spikes appear on bushy, upright plants in June–July and, if the whole plant is cut back hard after the first flowering, again in August–September — one of the most reliable and rewarding reblooming perennials if the shearing step is reliably performed. The cultivar 'Superba' has been in cultivation since the 1930s and spawned a large group of related hybrids now grouped under Salvia nemorosa and S. x sylvestris. Outstanding for the sunny, drought-tolerant border combined with yellow achillea, silver artemisia, and ornamental grasses. The flower spikes retain their decorative character as they age, the dried calyces remaining attractive for weeks after the petals fall. Reliably attractive to bees — particularly bumblebees — throughout the bloom period.

plant_note: Plant transplants in spring as soon as last hard freeze danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring bloom. Superbells Yellow is part of the Superbells series from Proven Winners — one of the major Calibrachoa breeding programs. Calibrachoa requires excellent drainage and acidic conditions (pH 5.5–6.0); alkaline soils cause iron deficiency (interveinal chlorosis) corrected with chelated iron. Feed regularly with an acid-forming fertilizer as heavy feeder. In zone 9 calibrachoa performs best February–May and September–November; summer heat causes decline. It is not grown from seed — all Superbells calibrachoa are vegetatively propagated to maintain the specific cultivar. The trailing habit makes it ideal for hanging baskets and container edges.
directions: Plant in full sun — calibrachoa requires full sun for maximum flowering; partial shade reduces bloom significantly — in well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.0), fertile potting mix or garden soil; feed regularly with acid-forming fertilizer; Superbells Yellow Calibrachoa is a trailing, small-flowered annual producing hundreds of small (1-inch), bright yellow, petunia-like flowers on trailing stems that cascade elegantly over container edges — earning the common name 'Million Bells' for the sheer quantity of flowers produced per plant throughout the cool-season bloom period. Calibrachoa (Calibrachoa x hybrida) is a relatively recent container annual that emerged commercially in the 1990s and rapidly became one of the most important container and hanging basket plants in the North American market — providing the prolific, self-cleaning, non-deadheading flower production of wave petunias at a smaller, finer scale. The self-cleaning habit — spent flowers fall from the plant without leaving behind brown, dried remains that require removal — makes Superbells Yellow a maintenance-free container plant that requires only regular watering and fertilization to maintain its bloom display from spring through early summer in zone 9. The bright, clean yellow color provides a warm, sunny complement in mixed container compositions with blue, orange, and white companion plants.

plant_note: Plant transplants in spring as soon as last hard frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant February–April. Superbena is a trailing verbena series bred for superior heat tolerance, powdery mildew resistance, and continuous flowering without deadheading — improvements over older verbena selections that were problematic in Gulf South summers due to mildew and heat decline. As a vegetatively propagated cultivar it is sold as transplants, not seed. In zone 9 trailing verbena performs best February–May and September–November; midsummer heat may reduce flowering but the plants recover in fall. The burgundy-red color provides an intense, jewel-toned warm color for mixed container compositions. Excellent butterfly and pollinator plant.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with consistent moisture — Superbena Burgundy Verbena requires full sun for maximum flowering and good air circulation to prevent powdery mildew; Superbena Burgundy is a trailing verbena hybrid producing clusters of small, five-petaled, rich burgundy-red to deep wine-red flowers in dense, rounded heads on trailing stems — creating a cascading display of intense, saturated warm color that is particularly effective in elevated containers, hanging baskets, and raised beds where the trailing stems can cascade freely. The Superbena series was developed specifically for improved performance over older trailing verbena in hot, humid conditions — addressing the primary failure mode of older verbena (powdery mildew and summer heat decline) through breeding rather than fungicide management. Verbena flowers are among the most effective pollinator plants available for warm-season annuals — the flat-topped, nectar-rich flower clusters attract a wide range of beneficial insects including bees, skippers, painted ladies, and fiery skippers throughout the bloom season. The rich, jewel-toned burgundy color of Superbena Burgundy provides a deep, saturated warm tone that pairs elegantly with yellow, white, and silver companions while providing strong color presence in mixed container compositions from late winter through the first flush of summer heat.

plant_note: Start indoors in darkness; transplant after frost.
directions: Salpiglossis, or painted tongue, produces velvety, trumpet-shaped flowers with striking metallic coloration and intricate veining in a range of jewel tones. Start seed indoors 8 to 6 weeks before the last frost, covering it fully since the seed needs darkness to germinate, and keep soil warm. Transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with shelter from strong wind. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and stake the somewhat lax stems. Deadhead regularly and enjoy the blooms as long-lasting cut flowers.

plant_note: Plant transplants in spring after last hard frost danger passes; in zone 9 plant February–April. Supertunia Royal Velvet is a vegetatively propagated cultivar — not available as seed — producing the characteristic large, single, trailing petunias of the Supertunia brand (Proven Winners). The series was bred specifically for improved heat tolerance, self-cleaning (no deadheading required), and continuous flowering that surpasses seed-grown petunias in hot, humid conditions. In zone 9 trailing petunias perform best February–May and September–November; midsummer heat reduces bloom but the plants recover well in fall. The deep, rich purple of Royal Velvet is one of the most saturated and vivid flower colors available in the petunia category — a jewel-tone purple-violet that provides exceptional intensity in container compositions.
directions: Plant in full sun — petunias require full sun for maximum flowering; partial shade causes leggy growth and sparse bloom — in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist potting mix or garden soil; feed with a balanced fertilizer every 1–2 weeks; Supertunia Royal Velvet is a trailing, vegetatively propagated petunia cultivar producing large (2–3 inch), single, deep purple-violet flowers on cascading stems that can extend 2–3 feet from the container center in hanging baskets and elevated containers — creating one of the most dramatic and voluminous container annual displays available in the spring and fall season. The Proven Winners Supertunia series was one of the breeding programs that established the modern standard for trailing, self-cleaning, high-performance petunias — combining the trailing habit, large flower size, and extended bloom without deadheading that define the contemporary container petunia market. The deep, saturated purple-violet of Royal Velvet is one of the richest and most intense colors in the petunia palette — providing a strong, vivid color anchor in mixed container compositions with white, yellow, and pink companions that would disappear if paired with a less saturated purple. In zone 9's spring and fall container garden, trailing purple petunias remain one of the most visually striking and high-impact annual container options available.

common_name: Supertunia Vista Bubblegum Petunia (Extremely Vigorous Spreading Pink Petunia)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Supertunia Vista Bubblegum spreads much more vigorously than a typical petunia, easily covering three to four feet, making it better suited to large containers, hanging baskets, and landscape beds than small pots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, giving it ample room to spread since it is far more vigorous than a standard petunia. Supertunia Vista Bubblegum produces an enormous mounding, trailing plant covered in clear bubblegum-pink flowers from spring through frost, largely self-cleaning so it needs little deadheading to keep flowering heavily. Its exceptional vigor makes it a favorite for large mixed containers, hanging baskets, and mass landscape plantings where a smaller petunia would be overwhelmed by neighboring plants. Regular fertilizing supports its vigorous growth and continuous bloom, and a mid-season trim can rejuvenate the planting if it becomes overly leggy in the heat of summer.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately wet soil in partial to full shade; supplejack is a woody vine that forms thickets and climbs high into the forest canopy — site it where it has room to naturalize or provide a large, sturdy arbor.
directions: Supplejack is a vigorous native woody vine of bottomland forests, swamp margins, and moist woodland edges across the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, climbing high into the forest canopy by twining and branching through the upper shrub and tree layers. Its flexible, wiry stems gave rise to the common name — the wood was historically used to make walking sticks, basket frames, and tool handles because of its exceptional suppleness and strength. Small, inconspicuous greenish-white flowers in late spring produce blue-black drupes that ripen in fall and are consumed by wood ducks, wild turkeys, and at least a dozen species of songbirds and small mammals, making supplejack one of the highest-value wildlife vines in the region. In naturalized woodland gardens or large-scale habitat restorations, allow it to climb through native trees and form dense thickets that provide both food and nesting cover; it is too vigorous for small spaces but invaluable for restoring native forest understory structure.

plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Surdiva Blue is a selection from the Surdiva series bred specifically for heat and humidity tolerance — making it more reliable than older scaevola selections in Gulf South summer conditions. The trailing, spreading habit makes scaevola ideal for hanging baskets, container edges, and window boxes where the long, cascading stems create a flowing effect. Scaevola is propagated vegetatively from cuttings — not available as seed. It performs well in both full sun and partial shade in zone 9. The unique, fan-shaped flower form — five petals all arranged on one side of the flower, leaving the other side open — is botanically unusual and immediately recognizable.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately moist soil — Surdiva Blue Scaevola performs well in both sun and partial shade, making it one of the more flexible summer annuals for zone 9 mixed container planting; Surdiva Blue Scaevola is a trailing annual from Australia producing unusual, fan-shaped, lavender-blue to blue-violet flowers in which all five petals are arranged to one side of the bloom — a unique floral structure called a zygomorphic or bilateral flower that gives scaevola an immediately recognizable, unusual appearance among commonly grown annuals. The common name 'Fan Flower' describes this distinctive one-sided petal arrangement that distinguishes scaevola from every other commonly grown annual. The trailing stems (extending 18–30 inches from the container center) covered with the lavender-blue fan flowers create an airy, flowing cascade that is particularly effective in hanging baskets and elevated containers where the trailing stems are visible from below. In zone 9's warm, humid summer climate, scaevola maintains active growth and bloom through the peak heat that reduces flowering in many spring annuals — the native Australian origin giving it natural adaptability to warm, dry to moderately moist conditions similar to zone 9's summer.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, freely draining, acidic to neutral soil or container mix in zone 8–11; Sutherland Begonia is a compact, trailing, tuberous begonia native to the moist forests, cliff faces, and stream banks of the Drakensberg mountains of KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape of South Africa — bearing abundant, small, bright-orange to salmon-orange flowers on reddish stems throughout summer and fall in partial shade.
directions: Plant Begonia sutherlandii tubers in partial shade in humus-rich, freely draining, slightly acidic potting mix or garden soil; keep evenly moist during active growth; allow to dry down after fall frost or when foliage yellows, then store tubers dry and cool for winter in zone 8–9; repot in spring. Sutherland Begonia is one of the more cold-tolerant of all tuberous begonias — its native Drakensberg habitat experiences occasional light frost — and performs well in zone 8 with good drainage and a protective mulch over the dormant tubers. The bright, clear-orange single flowers are produced in cheerful clusters throughout summer and into fall, even in quite deep shade where few other flowering plants perform; this makes it exceptionally valuable for the shaded garden. The trailing, red-stemmed habit makes it ideal for hanging baskets, container edges, rock walls, and woodland garden borders. Unlike the large-flowered hybrid tuberous begonias which require careful culture, Sutherland Begonia is relatively easy to grow and increases by offset tubers over time. In fall, distinctive bulbils (tiny aerial tubers) form in the leaf axils and can be collected and potted to produce new plants. The species has been used extensively in hybridization programs to introduce trailing habit and orange-flame coloring into modern begonia hybrids.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp aster is native to wet meadows, streambanks, and open swampy areas and requires consistently moist to wet soil — excellent in rain gardens and bog borders.
directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp aster is native to wet meadows, streambanks, and open swampy areas and requires consistently moist to wet soil — excellent in rain gardens and bog borders. Symphyotrichum puniceum is one of the tallest and showiest native fall asters, producing large (1–1.5 inch), vivid violet to purple ray flowers with orange-yellow centers on reddish-purple, somewhat hairy stems in September and October; the stems and leaves have a distinctive reddish to wine-purple color that extends the ornamental season beyond bloom. It is native to wet, open habitats from Newfoundland to Georgia and is one of the most vigorous and cold-hardy fall asters for moist conditions, supporting monarch butterflies, bumblebees, and specialist aster bees during the critical fall migration and foraging period.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil; do not allow to dry out during establishment. Do not plant too deeply — keep the crown at or above soil level.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, deeply acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to light sun; swamp azalea is the most fragrant of all native North American deciduous azaleas, producing intensely clove-spice-scented white flowers (often pink-flushed) in late June through July, extending the native azalea bloom season well into summer after all other species have finished. It grows naturally in swamps, bogs, stream banks, and wet woodland margins from Maine to Florida, and tolerates standing water better than any other Rhododendron. The plant spreads slowly by rhizome and root sprouts to form a colony; purchase container-grown propagated plants only. Mulch with pine bark or pine needle litter to maintain soil acidity and moisture. Never allow to dry out in summer.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp bay grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, pond margins, swamps, and bottomlands of the Gulf Coast and Southeast — it requires consistently moist to wet soil and does not tolerate drought.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun — swamp bay is a native evergreen tree of Gulf Coast wetlands, closely related to the edible bay laurel and redbay, with aromatic leaves historically used as a bay leaf substitute in Creole and Southern cooking. The glossy, elliptic evergreen leaves have a whitish-downy underside and are fragrant when crushed with the characteristic bay laurel scent. Small, yellowish-green flowers in spring attract native bees; dark blue-black berries feed songbirds and the palamedes swallowtail butterfly uses the foliage as a larval host. It grows naturally in cypress swamps, wet flatwoods, and bay swamps throughout the Gulf Coast and is one of the best choices for naturalizing in wet, low areas where other trees refuse to grow. The wood is durable and aromatic; the tree is long-lived and forms the canopy of classic southern bay swamp ecosystems.

plant_note: Plant divisions or bare-root stock in spring in consistently wet to moist, acidic soil at the edge of a pond, stream, or bog garden; this species requires wet feet and will not thrive in well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant in wet to constantly moist, acidic, organic-rich soil in full sun to partial shade at pond edges, stream banks, and bog gardens; swamp candles produces slender candle-like racemes of small bright yellow star-shaped flowers in early to midsummer, lighting up wet shaded areas where little else will bloom. Unlike the invasive purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria), this species is a well-behaved native of eastern North America that stays in manageable patches without aggressive invasion. The plant often produces small plantlets at the leaf axils that drop and establish near the parent, gradually spreading into attractive colonies. An excellent choice for rain gardens, bioswales, and persistently wet spots that are too soggy for most perennials.

common_name: Swamp Chestnut Oak (Basket Oak, Cow Oak)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, rich bottomland or floodplain soil in full sun to partial shade; swamp chestnut oak is native to the rich bottomland hardwood forests of the Southeast and produces the largest acorns of any American oak — critical for wildlife at a time when few other mast crops are available.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, slightly acidic bottomland soil in full sun to partial shade; swamp chestnut oak is a magnificent large native oak of the rich bottomland forests of the Southeast, reaching 60–100 feet with a straight trunk and broad, open crown with large, chestnut-like leaves 5–9 inches long. The large, sweet acorns (up to 1.5 inches) ripen in a single season and are the largest, most palatable acorns produced by any American oak — they were eaten by Native Americans and early settlers and are readily eaten by deer, turkeys, squirrels, and wood ducks. The handsome, ridged, grayish bark and excellent fall yellow-orange color make this a valuable landscape tree where space permits. Tolerates seasonal flooding but also grows well in moist, well-drained upland soils. Somewhat more tolerant of partial shade when young than most oaks. A premier wildlife and landscape tree for zone 5–9.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp coreopsis grows naturally in moist to seasonally flooded pine flatwoods, wet prairies, and pond margins of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp coreopsis is the wetland-adapted coreopsis of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, growing naturally in moist pine flatwoods, wet prairies, and seasonal pond margins where most other coreopsis would drown. It produces the classic bright yellow, daisy-like coreopsis flowers from summer into fall on stiffly erect, branching stems. Unlike the drought-tolerant species commonly sold in garden centers, this species requires consistent moisture and even tolerates seasonal flooding. An excellent choice for rain gardens, moist meadow plantings, and boggy areas where it blooms prolifically through the summer months. Provides nectar for swallowtail butterflies, native bees, and goldenrod soldier beetles. Seeds are consumed by goldfinches and other small birds in fall and winter. Highly appropriate for zone 9a wet-site plantings.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants or root hardwood cuttings in spring in wet, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, rich alluvial or clay-loam soil in full sun. Swamp Cottonwood thrives in the deepest, most permanently wet bottomland soils where Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides) begins to struggle.
directions: Swamp Cottonwood is the wetland specialist of the cottonwood family, native to the permanently flooded swamps, blackwater river bottoms, and cypress-tupelo swamp margins of the southeastern coastal plain from Connecticut to Florida and west to Indiana and Oklahoma, where it tolerates deeper and more prolonged flooding than any other native cottonwood. Its leaves are distinctly broader and more rounded than those of Eastern Cottonwood (Populus deltoides) — hence the species epithet heterophylla (variable-leaved) — and the tree often develops a tall, straight trunk in the competitive light environment of bottomland forest. Like other cottonwoods, Swamp Cottonwood is a fast-growing pioneer tree important for rapid canopy establishment in wetland restoration projects; it roots readily from hardwood cuttings pushed into wet soil in early spring. The cottony seeds of female trees are dispersed by wind and water in late spring and early summer. An excellent riparian tree for the restoration and naturalization of permanently wet bottomland habitats in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.0–5.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; this plant grows naturally in very acidic, boggy, waterlogged conditions and will not thrive in alkaline or neutral soils.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp cyrilla (also called titi or leatherwood) is a distinctive multi-season native shrub of coastal plain bogs, swamp margins, and pocosins in the Southeast, producing long racemes of small white flowers in June and July that are intensely fragrant and among the most important summer nectar sources for native bees and the basis of the highly prized 'titi honey' produced by southeastern beekeepers. The semi-evergreen leaves turn brilliant orange-red in fall before dropping, and in warm winters may persist through spring. The plant is adapted to very acidic, poorly drained soils where it has little competition. An outstanding specimen for bog gardens, rain gardens, and acid pond margins in zone 7–9.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade along stream banks or in seasonally wet, shaded woodland settings. Swamp Doghobble requires consistently moist, shaded conditions and performs best at the shaded edge of streams and wet woodland understories.
directions: Swamp Doghobble is a graceful native deciduous shrub of moist to wet, shaded, acidic habitats along shaded stream banks, boggy swamp margins, and wet woodland understories of the eastern United States, producing fragrant, white, cylindrical flowers in drooping clusters along the stems in spring before the leaves fully emerge. Unlike the evergreen leucothoes, Swamp Doghobble is deciduous and displays outstanding orange, red, and purple fall foliage color that rivals the showiest cultivated shrubs. The arching, fountain-like growth habit and multi-season ornamental interest — spring flowers, attractive summer foliage, and brilliant fall color — make Swamp Doghobble a highly desirable native shrub for shaded, moist, acid garden settings. Plant in strongly acidic, moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Swamp Doghobble will not tolerate alkaline soil, drought, or prolonged direct sun.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Swamp Dogwood thrives along stream banks, pond margins, wet meadow edges, and seasonally flooded areas; it is excellent for rain gardens and bio-retention swales where the soil remains consistently moist.
directions: Swamp Dogwood is a large, multi-stemmed native shrub native to wet thickets, streambanks, pond margins, and swamp edges throughout eastern North America from New Brunswick to Florida and west to Oklahoma, tolerating prolonged seasonal flooding and thriving in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. It produces flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in June and July that attract a wide variety of native bees and other pollinators, followed by striking porcelain-blue fruits on red-stemmed clusters that ripen in August and September and are eagerly consumed by over 40 species of songbirds, including wood thrush, catbirds, and warblers. The purplish-red winter stems provide attractive four-season interest, and the shrub suckers readily to form dense thickets that stabilize streambanks and provide excellent nesting cover for wildlife. An outstanding plant for wet native gardens, rain gardens, or bio-swales where its moisture tolerance is an asset rather than a compromise.

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring and plant in wet to moist, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun. Swamp Fern spreads aggressively by stolons in moist soil and should be given ample room or used where it can naturalize freely.
directions: Swamp Fern is an aggressive, colony-forming native fern of the Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida, native to wet flatwoods, swamp margins, cypress sloughs, seepage slopes, and roadside ditches from Florida west to Texas, and throughout the Caribbean and tropical Americas, where it thrives in warm, wet, acidic conditions that few other ferns tolerate. The upright, glossy fronds — both sterile (wider, with toothed pinnae) and fertile (narrower, with elongated sori) — are produced from creeping stolons that spread widely in saturated or permanently moist soil, forming dense colonies that effectively suppress weeds and stabilize wet soil. An excellent low-maintenance groundcover for the permanently wet spots in Gulf Coast landscapes where most ornamental plants drown; it is fully evergreen in zones 9–11 and semi-evergreen in zone 8. Divide and replant in spring in any moist, acidic, low-lying area.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer to early fall in moist to wet, acidic soil at the water's edge or in shallow water; fall planting allows roots to establish before winter dormancy and spring bloom.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this native species is the parent of the beloved Louisiana iris hybrid group, growing naturally in swamps, bayou margins, ditches, and wet flatwoods of the Gulf Coast from Florida to Texas. The large, elegant blue-violet flowers (occasionally varying to pink or white) in spring are extraordinary among native wildflowers for their sophisticated form and vivid color. Louisiana iris hybrids have expanded the color range to include burgundy, yellow, white, pink, and bicolors — if you want color variety, seek out named Louisiana iris hybrids from specialty nurseries; for native restoration, stick with the true species. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested. Plant at pond margins, in rain gardens, or in any consistently wet spot.

common_name: Swamp Jessamine (Rankin's Jessamine, Scentless Yellow Jessamine)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist to wet, partially shaded sites; Swamp Jessamine naturally grows in floodplain forests, swampy margins, and moist woodland edges. Unlike Carolina Jessamine (G. sempervirens) which thrives in dry, sunny sites, Swamp Jessamine needs consistently moist soil and partial shade. All parts of the plant are toxic — like all Gelsemium species, do not confuse with edible plants.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, acidic soil along a fence, trellis, or arbor; Swamp Jessamine twines to 10–20 feet and can cover a large support structure. Gelsemium rankinii is a native evergreen vine closely related to Carolina Jessamine (G. sempervirens) but adapted to entirely different habitat — wet, shady floodplains and swamp margins rather than dry, sunny slopes. The yellow, tubular, slightly fragrant flowers (though less intensely fragrant than G. sempervirens) appear in two distinct blooming periods: late winter–spring (like Carolina Jessamine) AND again in fall (October–December), making it a unique vine that provides yellow blooms in both early spring and late fall when few other plants are in color. The glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage is attractive year-round. Swamp Jessamine fills a specific ecological niche as a shade-tolerant, moisture-loving native vine for moist woodland settings in zone 6–9 where Carolina Jessamine would fail in the shade and wet conditions. CAUTION: Like all Gelsemium species, all parts of the plant are highly toxic — containing gelsemine and other alkaloids that can be fatal. Do not confuse with edible plants. Plant away from children and pets.

plant_note: Plant near a trellis or fence in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp leather flower is one of the most flood-tolerant native clematis, naturally occurring along streambanks, swamp margins, and bottomland forest edges.
directions: Swamp leather flower is a native clematis of the Gulf Coastal Plain, blooming from late spring through summer with distinctive nodding, urn-shaped flowers in soft lavender to blue-purple with flared, recurved petal tips that give the flowers a crisp, sculptural quality unlike any other vine — it is one of the finest ornamental native vines of the American South yet remains underutilized in cultivation. The vine is naturally found in swampy thickets, bottomland forests, and moist shrub borders from Virginia to Texas, making it ideally suited to rain garden edges, pond margins, and low-lying moist areas of Gulf Coast gardens that challenge other vines. Unlike many Clematis species, it handles the heat and humidity of the Gulf South reliably without the mildew and root rot problems that affect hybrid large-flowered types in zones 8 and 9. Plant through a native shrub or on a fence in partial shade; cut back hard to the ground each winter to maintain a neat, vigorous plant.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil and allow to cold-stratify over winter; alternatively plant container-grown vines in spring near a light trellis, shrub, or fence in partial sun with consistently moist to wet soil.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial sun along woodland edges, swamp margins, stream banks, or moist fence lines; swamp leatherflower is one of the most beautiful native vines of the Gulf Coast and southeastern US, producing delicate, nodding, urn-shaped flowers with flared, crisped petal tips in shades of lavender-blue to pale violet throughout summer. Unlike many clematis it thrives in poorly drained and seasonally flooded soils, making it invaluable for wet spots where other vines fail. It climbs by twining leaf petioles to 3–6 feet through shrubs, other vines, or light structures and pairs naturally with buttonbush, swamp rose, and Virginia willow in wet garden borders. The feathery seed heads are ornamental in fall. This species is best grown from nursery-propagated plants; purchase from reputable native plant nurseries as wild collection is discouraged.

plant_note: Plant large bulbs with the neck just at or above soil level in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade; does not tolerate dry conditions. Excellent for pond margins and rain gardens.
directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in consistently wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; swamp lily is a stunning native bulb of the Gulf Coast, Florida, and Caribbean, growing naturally in freshwater swamps, bog margins, stream banks, and wet ditches. It produces large, fragrant, spider-like white flowers with narrow strap petals in summer and into fall — often repeatedly after summer rain events — on upright stalks among bold, strap-like evergreen leaves. Plant at pond margins, in consistently moist rain garden hollows, or in large containers kept in saucers of water on the patio. The bold foliage and exotic flowers provide a tropical look in Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens. Divide crowded clumps every 4–5 years by removing and replanting offsets.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (seeds need 30-day cold stratification) or cold-stratify indoors and start in late winter; transplant to the garden in spring. Unlike butterfly weed, swamp milkweed germinates more reliably after stratification.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, average soil in full sun to partial shade; swamp milkweed is an essential monarch butterfly host plant that tolerates wet conditions where common milkweed struggles, making it ideal for rain gardens, pond margins, and low-lying areas. The bright rose-pink to mauve flower clusters bloom from June through August and are heavily visited by monarchs, swallowtails, and bumble bees. Unlike other milkweeds, it does not spread aggressively by rhizomes and stays in well-behaved clumps, making it one of the best milkweed species for garden planting. Leave seedpods on through winter for wildlife interest and natural reseeding. The white-flowered cultivar 'Ice Ballet' is also excellent.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall in wet, peaty, acidic soil in partial shade; swamp pink is federally threatened — purchase only nursery-propagated stock and never collect from the wild.
directions: Helonias bullata (swamp pink) is a federally threatened native perennial found in a handful of isolated, high-quality, seepage-fed bogs and wet woods in the mid-Atlantic and upper Southeast, where it produces an overwintering rosette of lustrous, strap-like, evergreen leaves and a dramatic, hollow stem bearing a dense, cylindrical spike of fragrant, bright rosy-pink flowers with blue anthers in March and April — one of the earliest and most vivid wildflowers of the eastern bog flora. It requires permanently wet, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), peaty, oxygen-poor soil in partial shade with steady seepage from upslope, making it a challenging but rewarding plant for constructed bog gardens or reliably wet rain garden margins. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants from specialists — the species is protected and increasingly rare due to wetland drainage and deer browsing. An extraordinary native gem for conservation-minded gardeners.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants (male and female plants together) in spring in wet to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Swamp Privet is excellent for naturalizing wet bottomlands, streambanks, and seasonally flooded areas throughout zones 5–9.
directions: Swamp Privet is a large, multi-stemmed native deciduous shrub, native to the riverine swamps, oxbow lakes, backwater floodplains, and cypress-tupelo swamps of the southeastern and mid-South United States from South Carolina to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas, tolerating prolonged inundation that few other native shrubs can survive. Inconspicuous yellow flowers appear in February and March before the leaves emerge, providing critical early-season nectar and pollen for native bees emerging from winter dormancy; small, dark blue-purple olive-like drupes ripen in summer and are avidly consumed by wood ducks, mallards, and other water-dependent birds. A valuable plant for the restoration and naturalization of wet bottomland and floodplain habitats, Swamp Privet tolerates prolonged flooding up to 4–6 months and is one of the few native shrubs that can establish in true swamp conditions. Plant male and female individuals together for fruit production; it requires no maintenance once established.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil; ideal for rain garden edges, stream banks, and pond margins.
directions: Swamp Rose is a robust, upright-arching native rose naturally found along stream banks, swamp margins, and moist open meadows from Nova Scotia to Florida, and is the most flood-tolerant of all native eastern rose species. Plant rooted cuttings in spring into moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing plants 4 to 6 feet apart to accommodate their vigorous suckering habit. Deep rose-pink, 5-petaled, fragrant flowers 1.5 to 2 inches across appear on recurved-prickled arching canes from June through July, followed by round red hips that persist through winter and are eaten by dozens of bird species. Allow plants to spread naturally by suckers to colonize wet areas, stream banks, and rain garden berms where few other flowering shrubs will thrive.

plant_note: Nick or soak seed in warm water 24 hours before sowing indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes when soil has warmed. Alternatively, direct sow in very late spring. Plants emerge late — do not assume they are dead until June.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, rich soil in full sun; swamp rose mallow produces the largest flowers of any perennial hardy to zone 4 — dinner-plate sized blooms up to 10–12 inches across in white, pink, red, or bicolor from July through September. It is native to wetlands, marshes, and stream margins throughout eastern North America and thrives in rain gardens and pond edges where few other plants bloom so dramatically. Plants emerge very late in spring — sometimes not until late May or early June — so mark their location to avoid digging them. Numerous cultivars with red, pink, white, and bicolor flowers are available (Luna series, Disco Belle, Summerific series). Cut stems to the ground in winter after they die back.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant to moist to wet, fertile soil after last frost; Hibiscus grandiflorus is a wetland species that thrives in consistently moist soil and tolerates periodic flooding. Nick or soak seeds before planting to improve germination. In zones 8–11 it grows as a persistent perennial; in cooler zones it is killed by frost but may reseed.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; swamp rose mallow is the most dramatic of the native hibiscus species, producing enormous flowers — among the largest of any hardy perennial — reaching 8–12 inches across in blush pink with a deep crimson center eye, on plants that can reach 10 feet in ideal moist conditions. The large leaves are softly velvety-pubescent on the undersides, giving the plant its common name velvet mallow. Native to freshwater marshes, tidal flats, and pond margins in the Florida Peninsula and Gulf Coast, it is one of the showiest native wildflowers of the Southeast and a hummingbird magnet. The flowers bloom from June through September and the large seed capsules that follow are decorative into fall. It is more heat-tolerant and moisture-demanding than the closely related rose mallow (H. moscheutos) and is the best choice for wet sites in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3–4 inches deep in wet to moist, slightly acidic, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; swamp spider lily thrives in pond margins, wet ditches, and boggy, shaded spots where few other bulbs will grow. It is winter-hardy to zone 7 and resprouts reliably from established bulbs.
directions: Plant bulbs in wet to moist, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun — the swamp spider lily is a spectacular Gulf Coast native wildflower found naturally in wet prairies, swampy ditches, stream banks, and the margins of cypress swamps from Texas to Georgia. In spring it produces clusters of 3–6 intensely fragrant, spider-like white flowers on leafless scapes 18–24 inches tall — the long, narrow, reflexed petals surrounding a prominent cup-like corona are architecturally striking and fill the garden with a rich, sweet perfume. The broad, strap-like leaves emerge in spring and die back by late summer. It naturalizes freely in wet conditions, forming spectacular colonies in roadside ditches and pond margins throughout the Gulf Coast region. Unlike many spider lilies, it thrives in partial shade and wet soils where most other bulbs fail. Excellent at the edge of rain gardens, retention ponds, and boggy low spots.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full to partial sun; plants can also be started from divisions in spring for faster bloom.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; swamp sunflower is arguably the most spectacular of the native sunflowers for fall bloom, producing hundreds of bright yellow flowers on tall multibranching stems from October through frost — often when almost nothing else is blooming. It grows naturally in wet pine flatwoods, swamp margins, and roadside ditches across the coastal South and is perfectly suited to Gulf Coast zone 8–9 gardens where the late season heat and moisture support its growth. The plant spreads aggressively by rhizome and self-seeding; give it space or divide annually in spring. Monarch butterflies and native bees mob the flowers. Pinch tips twice in early summer for a shorter, more compact plant.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; swamp titi tolerates periodic flooding and grows naturally in bog margins, cypress swamps, and pitcher plant bogs of the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain. Propagate from softwood cuttings in summer.
directions: Plant in wet to moist, acidic, peaty or humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade; swamp titi is a native Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain shrub of remarkable ornamental and ecological value that is still underused in landscape horticulture. The long, drooping racemes of small white honey-scented flowers in late spring and summer are among the most important nectar sources for honey production in the Florida Panhandle, where 'titi honey' is a regional specialty. The semi-evergreen to evergreen, leathery leaves turn vivid red and orange in fall before dropping. It tolerates flooding, poor acid soil, and full sun in swampy conditions — exactly the site conditions where most ornamental shrubs fail. In zone 9a, it makes an excellent native screen in wet or poorly drained areas.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in wet to moist, acidic, slightly sandy or loamy soil in full sun to partial shade. Swamp Tupelo is adapted to seasonally or permanently flooded conditions and develops distinctive swollen (buttressed) trunk bases in very wet soils; it is most appropriate for rain gardens, wet bottomlands, and natural pond margins.
