directions: Thread-leaf sundew is one of the most spectacular of all North American carnivorous plants — producing upright, thread-like leaves up to a foot tall that are covered along their entire length with long, glistening, red-tipped tentacles dripping with sticky mucilage, making the plant look like something from a science fiction film. Native to coastal plain bogs of New Jersey and the Carolinas, it is one of the largest and most dramatic of all North American sundews, capable of trapping insects as large as damselflies and small bees on its long, adhesive leaves. Pink flowers appear on tall stalks in summer; the plant goes dormant in winter in zones 5–7, forming a tight, dry bud (hibernaculum) at the soil surface that is cold-hardy to well below freezing, making it one of the more cold-tolerant carnivorous plants for outdoor bog gardens. It produces gemmae (vegetative propagules) in fall that can be planted to create new individuals — an easy propagation method that makes it more accessible than many other carnivorous plants. Grow in the standard wet, acidic, nutrient-poor bog conditions with pure water only.

plant_note: Surface sow seed in early spring or start transplants; threadleaf coreopsis is more reliably propagated by division than seed — divisions establish quickly in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Grow in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade — threadleaf coreopsis is the most finely textured and perhaps the most garden-adaptable of all native coreopsis species, producing a season-long display of bright golden-yellow daisy flowers above delicate, needle-like whorled foliage from early summer through fall frost. Unlike most coreopsis, the thread-like leaves create an exceptionally fine-textured mound that contrasts beautifully with bold-leafed perennials. It spreads steadily by rhizome to form wide, weed-suppressing clumps and thrives in poor, dry soils where richer garden perennials struggle. Named cultivars 'Moonbeam' (pale yellow), 'Zagreb' (bright gold, compact), and 'Golden Gain' are widely available and extremely garden-worthy. Deadheading is optional — the plant reblooms regardless, but removing spent flowers extends peak flowering. One of the longest-blooming native perennials available.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or divide established mats in early spring; three-leaf bittercress spreads by creeping rhizomes and over time forms an effective, low groundcover in moist, shaded situations. It is semi-evergreen to fully evergreen in mild winters, maintaining its attractive dark-green, trifoliate leaves year-round. Best planted in drifts for maximum groundcover effect under deciduous trees.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; three-leaf bittercress is a quietly attractive European woodland groundcover producing neat, dark-green, three-parted (trifoliate) leaves that have the quality of large, dark, clover-like foliage and are semi-evergreen through mild winters — forming a low carpet of attractive rounded leaflets that suppresses weeds and covers ground effectively under trees. In spring it produces a cloud of small, four-petaled, pure-white cruciform flowers on 4–6 inch stems that hover just above the foliage in a brief but cheerful display before the tree canopy closes above. The simple white flowers and clean, dark, rounded foliage make it quietly pleasing throughout the season. Spreads steadily by creeping rhizomes to form expanding patches — useful in competition with tree roots, where it can make progress without heavy soil disturbance. An underused woodland floor plant for temperate shade gardens, valuable for its evergreen quality and ability to spread slowly in competition with the root systems of large trees.

common_name: Thryallis (Galphimia, Rain of Gold, Golden Thryallis)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Galphimia glauca is one of the most heat-tolerant flowering shrubs for zone 9 Gulf Coast landscapes, blooming continuously from spring through fall and tolerating brief frosts to about 25–28°F when established.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in full sun; Galphimia glauca (commonly called Thryallis, Rain of Gold, or Golden Thryallis) is a Mexican and Central American shrub that is one of the most reliably blooming and low-maintenance flowering shrubs for Gulf Coast and South Texas zone 8–10 landscapes — producing a nearly continuous shower of small, five-petaled, bright golden-yellow flowers on terminal spikes from spring through fall (and sometimes year-round in zone 10+). The effect of hundreds of small golden flowers covering the fine-textured, blue-green foliage is spectacular and sustained, unlike many flowering shrubs that bloom only briefly. Thryallis tolerates heat, humidity, and drought exceptionally well once established, requires minimal fertilization, and is rarely bothered by pests or diseases — the combination of beauty, durability, and low maintenance makes it one of the finest choices for reliable color in challenging Southern landscapes. The shrub grows into a well-behaved, rounded mound (4–8 feet tall and wide over time) without aggressive spreading. Excellent as a specimen, mass planting, or informal hedge. Freezes to the ground in hard winters in zone 8 but resprouts from roots with vigor; essentially evergreen in zone 9b–12.

common_name: Thryallis (Shower of Gold, Rain of Gold)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; thryallis is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant Mexican native shrub producing masses of small, brilliant-yellow flowers on gracefully arching branches nearly year-round in warm climates — one of the most reliable and cheerful flowering shrubs for zone 9–12 Gulf Coast and tropical gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after flowering to maintain compact shape. Galphimia gracilis (thryallis, shower of gold, or rain of gold) is a graceful, fast-growing, shrubby Mexican native in the Malpighiaceae family — one of the most reliably cheerful and floriferous flowering shrubs for zone 8–11 Gulf Coast and tropical gardens. The plant produces long, arching branches tipped with clusters of small (1/2-inch), five-petaled, brilliant golden-yellow flowers produced abundantly almost year-round in warm, frost-free climates — hence the evocative common names 'shower of gold' and 'rain of gold.' In zone 9–11, thryallis blooms nearly continuously from spring through fall, pausing only during the coldest months. The fine-textured foliage, graceful, fountain-like habit, and prolific golden flower production make it outstanding for mixed borders, foundation plantings, and as a flowering accent in drought-tolerant landscapes. It is also highly attractive to butterflies. Thryallis is more cold-hardy than many Mexican tropical shrubs, surviving brief dips to about 25°F once established in zone 8b; it dies back in cold winters but regrows from the root. A tremendously reliable and low-maintenance choice for hot, sunny, dry gardens throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall; space 5-6 ft apart for a solid privacy screen.
directions: Thuja Green Giant is a fast-growing evergreen conifer widely used as a living privacy hedge, adding several feet of dense, rich green foliage each year. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants 5 to 6 feet apart for a continuous screen. Water regularly the first season to establish deep roots; once mature it tolerates heat, humidity, and brief drought. Its naturally pyramidal habit rarely needs pruning, though it takes shearing well if a formal shape is desired. It resists deer browsing and most pests.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in a sunny, well-drained spot.
directions: Thuja Virginian is a compact arborvitae hybrid that offers the dense evergreen screening of Green Giant in a more manageable size for smaller yards. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently through the first growing season to establish. Its tight, upright pyramidal form makes an excellent privacy hedge or specimen without heavy pruning. Mature plants tolerate heat and humidity and stand up to deer better than many evergreens. Mulch the root zone to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Thumbelina is a charming dwarf zinnia and 1963 All-America Selections winner, producing abundant cheerful blooms in a wide range of colors on compact plants. Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil and full sun, thinning seedlings for good airflow. Its small stature suits containers, edging, and the front of borders. Deadhead spent blooms to keep flowers coming through summer and into fall. Water at the base to reduce foliar disease, and enjoy the pollinators the flowers attract.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in summer or divide established crowns in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Thunberg's bush clover dies back to woody crowns each winter and may appear dead long into spring before new growth emerges — do not prune until new growth confirms the crown is alive. It grows very rapidly each spring. The cultivar Gibraltar is the most widely grown, with particularly deep rose-purple flowers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Thunberg's bush clover is one of the most spectacular late-season perennials available, producing dense, cascading wands of small, rosy-pink to rose-purple pea flowers in August and September — when almost nothing else in the garden is blooming with this abundance — on long, gracefully arching branches that create a weeping, fountain-like form of exceptional elegance. Each individual stem carries hundreds of small flowers in a dense, continuous spike, and a single established plant produces dozens of such stems that cascade toward the ground under their own weight, creating a foamy, waterfall effect of pink bloom that can span 5-7 feet. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves soil over time. Native to China and Japan, it dies back to the woody crown each winter and emerges late in spring, growing rapidly to blooming size by midsummer. Extraordinary for filling the late summer gap in the perennial border with a dramatic, long-lasting display highly attractive to bees and butterflies.

common_name: Thunder Cloud Texas Sage (Deep-Purple Compact Cenizo Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–8.0), lean soil in full sun; Thunder Cloud absolutely requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate standing water or heavy wet clay, and root rot in poorly drained soil is the primary cause of failure in humid Gulf South gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; Thunder Cloud is one of the most compact and richly colored Texas sage (cenizo) cultivars — producing the species' characteristic silvery-gray, small, soft-textured foliage on a more restrained 3–4 foot plant, with deep purple-violet flowers that are more saturated and darker than the typical medium-purple of the species and many other cultivars. The compact habit makes Thunder Cloud proportionate for typical residential borders and containers where the sprawling, larger selections would overgrow the planting space. Like all cenizo, Thunder Cloud blooms in remarkable, synchronized flushes triggered by periods of high humidity or moisture after dry weather — the sudden appearance of masses of purple flowers across an entire planting following a rain or fog event is one of the most dramatic of Gulf South garden phenomena. The silvery foliage is attractive year-round — the pale gray-silver leaf color provides an effective contrast to green or dark foliage companions. Leucophyllum requires excellent drainage — in the humid Gulf South east of San Antonio/Houston, site in raised beds, berms, or rocky slopes where water moves away from roots quickly. Once established in appropriate drainage conditions, Thunder Cloud requires virtually no supplemental watering or fertilization. An outstanding choice for xeriscaping, reflected-heat positions, and caliche/alkaline soils where other ornamental shrubs struggle.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in spring in a hot, sunny location.
directions: Thunderstruck Coral Boom is a fast-growing crape myrtle that produces large panicles of vivid coral-pink blooms from early summer into fall. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; more sun means more flowers and better mildew resistance. Its multi-season interest includes attractive exfoliating bark in winter and colorful fall foliage. Prune in late winter to remove crossing branches and shape the canopy, avoiding heavy topping. Water regularly while establishing, after which it becomes notably heat- and drought-tolerant.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in a warm, sunny spot.
directions: Thunderstruck Rumblin' Red is a crape myrtle celebrated for its fiery red summer blooms and strong year-round interest. Site it in full sun in well-drained soil, where abundant light maximizes flowering and helps prevent powdery mildew. The dark-tinged foliage and smooth exfoliating bark add appeal beyond the long bloom season. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain a tree-like structure rather than topping it hard. Once established it is quite tolerant of heat and dry conditions, needing supplemental water only in extended droughts.

plant_note: Root tip cuttings or 'log' sections in moist potting mix or water at 70–80°F; in zone 10–12 plant outdoors in partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained fertile soil. Grow as a container plant in colder climates, bringing indoors before frost.
directions: Root tip cuttings or stem sections ('logs') in moist potting mix or water at 70–80°F, then plant outdoors in partial shade in moist, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile, well-drained soil in zone 10–12; the ti plant has been a sacred and culturally significant plant in Pacific Island and Hawaiian cultures for millennia, prized for its deep burgundy, pink, green, or tricolor strap leaves and grown outdoors year-round in tropical gardens. Bright filtered shade deepens the leaf coloration — full sun bleaches the colors and deep shade reduces vibrancy and causes leggy growth. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged and fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer during the growing season. Outside zone 10–12, grow as a houseplant or deck container in the highest indirect light available and bring indoors before the first frost.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a warm, sheltered location with high humidity. Prefers rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. In zone 9, site against a south-facing wall or in a container that can be moved indoors during cold snaps.
directions: Propagate from softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings in summer, keeping them warm and humid until well rooted before potting on. Transplant to the garden only in frost-free zones 10-11, or grow in a large container in zone 9 and overwinter indoors above 55°F. Maintain consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and fertilize monthly with a balanced tropical-plant fertilizer throughout the growing season. The pinwheel-shaped white flowers bloom repeatedly in warm weather and are at their most fragrant in the evening, making this tree a standout near patios and entryways.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tibetan cherry is grown primarily for its extraordinary bark — not its flowers. Site it where the trunk is visible in winter and where you will brush against it to feel the satiny surface.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tibetan cherry from western China is grown almost exclusively for its extraordinary, burnished, mahogany-red to copper-brown bark that peels in horizontal strips to reveal gleaming, polished, metallic-looking new bark beneath — arguably the most ornamental bark of any tree in temperate gardening. The effect is amplified in winter sun when the bark catches raking light and glows like burnished copper. The flowers are white and relatively small, appearing with or just before the narrow, willow-like leaves in spring. The dark red fruits are small but attractive to birds. Position where winter sun will illuminate the trunk, and keep it clear of competing vegetation at the base. The bark develops its best coloring as the tree matures — young trees are less impressive. A specimen tree for its stem and bark character.

plant_note: Sow in fall or early spring; a reliable wildflower for meadows.
directions: Scatter tidy tips seed on cool, moist soil in fall or early spring and rake in lightly. This California native produces cheerful yellow daisies tipped in white that attract native bees and butterflies. It thrives on lean soil with minimal water once established, making it ideal for wildflower meadows and drought-tolerant plantings. Allow some flowers to set seed for reliable self-sowing in future seasons.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tiffany is a mid-to-late season camellia blooming January through March in zone 9, providing winter interest when many other landscape plants are dormant.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Tiffany is a magnificent large-flowered Camellia japonica cultivar producing extremely large (4.5–5 inch), semi-double to loose peony-form flowers in a distinctive warm orchid-pink to light lavender-pink color with slightly wavy, cupped petals surrounding a prominent cluster of bright-yellow stamens. The large, open, somewhat informal flower form and the distinctive orchid-pink color (neither the deep red of Mathotiana nor the pure pink of Debutante, but a warm intermediate with lavender tones) make Tiffany instantly recognizable and uniquely beautiful among red and pink camellia cultivars. Tiffany was selected from a seedling in California and has become one of the most popular and widely grown large-flowered japonica cultivars in American gardens. The blooms are produced mid to late season (January through March in zone 9) on an upright, vigorous shrub that can reach 6–12 feet with excellent annual growth rate. As with all Camellia japonica cultivars in zone 9, plant in dappled shade or morning sun with afternoon shade; consistent moisture and acidic soil are essential for healthy growth and maximum bloom production. Supplement iron with chelated iron fertilizer if leaves show yellowing between veins (chlorosis) — a common sign of iron deficiency in alkaline Gulf South soils.

plant_note: Plant offsets or container plants in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; tiger aloe naturally grows in rock crevices and the partial shade of cliff faces in its native South Africa and is one of the few aloes that actively prefers some shade in hot climates.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade — unlike most aloes that demand full sun, tiger aloe is unique in preferring partial shade or bright indirect light, making it one of the most valuable and unusual succulents for shaded dry garden conditions. The compact, triangular, dark green leaves arranged in three ranks are beautifully marked with irregular white horizontal bands and spots — a striking, ornamental pattern that gives rise to the common names tiger and partridge breast. The salmon-pink to coral-red tubular flowers on tall stalks appear in winter and spring, providing color when the garden needs it most. Compact enough for windowsills, containers, and small garden pockets; it produces offsets slowly to form small clusters. Native to the scrubby karoo shrubland and rocky hillside outcrops of South Africa. Outstanding as a houseplant in bright indirect light or as an outdoor container plant in shade in Gulf Coast zone 9–11.

plant_note: Plant bulbs after all frost danger passes in spring, once soil has warmed above 60°F.
directions: Plant bulbs 3–4 in deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; each exotic three-petaled flower lasts only one day but new buds open in succession over weeks. The vivid blooms come in yellow, orange, red, pink, and white, typically with a heavily spotted or blotched center cup. Plant in groups of a dozen or more for a showy display from midsummer into fall. In zones colder than 8, dig bulbs after first frost, dry thoroughly, and store in paper bags in a cool, frost-free location.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep and 12 inches apart in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light partial shade in early spring; tiger lily multiplies rapidly from the characteristic black bulbils that form along the leaf axils in summer and can be planted immediately for new plants.
directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep and 12 inches apart in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light partial shade in early spring; tiger lily multiplies rapidly from the characteristic black bulbils that form along the leaf axils in summer and can be planted immediately for new plants. Lilium lancifolium is the showiest, most vigorous, and most carefree of all garden lilies, producing 4-6 foot stems in midsummer with up to 20 pendant, strongly reflexed flowers of vivid orange with black spots and recurved petals that are among the most dramatic mid-summer ornamentals in any garden; individual plants bloom for 2-3 weeks and clumps increase rapidly. This lily can carry Lily Symptomless Virus without showing symptoms and can transmit it to other lily species via aphids — plant it away from other Lilium species, especially the more susceptible Asiatic and Oriental hybrids.

common_name: Tiger Stanhopea (Downy Stanhopea, Inverted Orchid, Upside-Down Orchid)
plant_note: MUST grow in an open slat basket or mesh basket — NEVER in a solid pot; Stanhopea's flower spikes grow downward and penetrate through the basket bottom to bloom below the plant. A solid pot prevents flowering entirely. Use coarse bark medium. Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning sun. Water regularly in active growth; reduce slightly in winter. The flowers last only 3–5 days but the fragrance is extraordinary. Bloom season is summer. Protect from temperatures below 50°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in a slatted or open-mesh hanging basket in bright indirect to filtered direct light — Tiger Stanhopea MUST be grown in an open-bottom container because its flower spikes emerge from the base of the pseudobulbs and grow downward through the basket medium to bloom below the plant — a pot with a solid bottom prevents flowering. Stanhopea tigrina is a sympodial, epiphytic orchid native to Mexico (Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas, Puebla) in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most fascinating orchids in cultivation for several reasons: its extraordinary downward-blooming habit, its large and complex flowers, and its remarkable fragrance. The plant produces oval pseudobulbs with broad, heavily-veined leaves, and in summer, one to four flower spikes per pseudobulb emerge from the base, push through the bark medium, and emerge hanging downward below the basket — where they open simultaneously into 3–8 of the most bizarre and dramatic flowers in the orchid family. Each flower is large (4–5 inches), waxy, and complex in shape: the sepals and petals are pale yellow heavily spotted and blotched with maroon-purple spots (the 'tigrina' — tiger-spotted), with a sculptural, two-part, boat and hook-shaped lip. The fragrance is powerful, complex, and sweet-spicy (vanilla, cinnamon, and eucalyptus are described), used by male Eulaema bees to attract females. Flowers last 3–5 days. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant in spring or early fall in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade.
directions: Tilt-A-Swirl is a bigleaf hydrangea whose mophead blooms shift through pink, red, and green as the season progresses, with flower color influenced by soil pH. Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil where it gets morning sun and shade during the hottest part of the day. Keep the soil consistently moist, especially in summer, as this species wilts quickly when dry. It blooms on old and new wood, so avoid heavy pruning; simply remove spent flowers and dead stems in late winter. Amend soil with aluminum sulfate for bluer tones or lime for pinker ones.

plant_note: Surface sow in early spring; seed needs light to germinate.
directions: Tiny Tim is a compact, honey-scented sweet alyssum that stays covered in tiny flowers all season with no need to shear back. Surface sow the seed in early spring since light aids germination, pressing it into the soil without covering. Grow in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained soil where it forms a fragrant, spreading groundcover. It withstands heat and drought while drawing beneficial insects and pollinators. Use it to edge beds, tuck between pavers, or spill from containers and hanging baskets.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in well-drained soil; ideal for containers or small beds.
directions: Tiny Tower is a very slow-growing dwarf Alberta spruce that keeps a naturally dense, narrow pyramidal shape without shearing, making it perfect for small gardens, entryways, and containers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and provide good air circulation to discourage spider mites, its main pest. Water regularly the first two seasons and mulch to keep roots cool and moist. In hot climates give it some afternoon shade to prevent needle scorch. Its compact evergreen form also serves as a living holiday tree.

plant_note: Soak seed overnight and sow deep; resents transplanting so direct sow.
directions: Soak the large seed overnight and sow about half an inch deep directly in the garden after frost. This dwarf, non-trailing variety produces a cheerful mix of yellow, red, and orange blooms held above the foliage. Both the peppery leaves and flowers are edible, making it a favorite for salads and companion planting. Grow in full sun and lean soil, since rich ground yields lots of leaves but fewer flowers.

common_name: Tipu Tree (Pride of Bolivia, Rosewood of Bolivia, Tipu)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Tipu Tree grows rapidly in zone 9-10 and can add 3–5 feet of height per year in good conditions. It is semi-evergreen to briefly deciduous in zone 9, dropping leaves in late winter before the spring leaf flush and peak bloom. The flower display occurs just after (or just before) the new leaf flush — the entire tree covered in yellow-orange flowers is a spectacular annual display. The distinctive single-winged seed pods (samaras) are ornamental. Root system is invasive — plant away from paving and structures.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Tipu Tree grows most vigorously in full sun and well-drained soil, becoming drought-tolerant once established. Tipuana tipu is a fast-growing, large, semi-evergreen to deciduous ornamental tree native to Bolivia, Argentina, and Brazil in the legume family (Fabaceae), monotypic in its genus. The tree has become one of the most widely planted street and shade trees in Mediterranean-climate cities worldwide (particularly in California, Spain, Argentina, South Africa, and Australia) and in zone 9-11 Gulf Coast and Florida landscapes. In late spring to early summer, the tree produces its annual bloom: an explosion of small, pea-like flowers in rich apricot-yellow to golden-orange covering the entire canopy — the display can be so dense that the foliage is temporarily obscured by the flowers, and the falling petals create a golden carpet beneath the tree. The flowers are followed by distinctive single-winged samara seed pods that spin as they fall. The broad, spreading canopy (often exceeding the tree's height in spread) provides exceptional shade on large lawns and public spaces. The compound leaves — each composed of 13–21 paired leaflets — are a fine-textured, light green that dances in the breeze. A magnificent specimen tree for large residential and public zone 9-11 landscapes.

common_name: Titan Annual Vinca (Large-Flowered Vigorous Vinca Series)
plant_note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; this series shows good resistance to Phytophthora aerial blight, a serious fungal disease of annual vinca in hot, humid conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; overly wet or poorly drained soil quickly leads to root and stem rot. Titan is a vigorous annual vinca series bred for unusually large, bold flowers relative to plant size, along with the same excellent heat and drought tolerance and good disease resistance typical of modern vinca breeding. It produces a dense, mounding plant covered in wide, flat-faced blooms across a range of colors from late spring through frost, thriving in the hottest, sunniest, most exposed parts of a Gulf South garden where many other bedding annuals fail. It requires minimal maintenance beyond routine watering during establishment and is an excellent low-water, low-input choice for mass plantings, medians, and containers.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring as growth begins; they establish quickly and bloom in their first season from divisions.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained shade; toad lily is an elegant late-season bloomer that produces exotic-looking, orchid-like flowers in white, purple, or lilac with dark spots from late summer through fall. The arching stems with clasping leaves create a graceful, architectural presence throughout the season. Consistent moisture is essential — plants decline in dry soil; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and temperature. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to manage the slowly spreading clumps.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist to wet, compacted or disturbed, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; toad rush is a cosmopolitan annual of seasonally moist, disturbed, and compacted ground — path edges, tire ruts, pond margins, and mudflats. It establishes and sets seed rapidly before conditions dry out.
directions: Scatter seed on moist, compacted, disturbed soil at the margins of ponds, seasonal wetlands, and wet disturbed areas; toad rush is a tiny, nearly grass-like annual rush that grows naturally in the muddy margins of ponds, seasonal pools, tire tracks, path edges, and any temporarily moist, disturbed ground across virtually all of North America and most of the world. The very small stature and wiry stems bear tiny flowers along most of their length. While not ornamental, toad rush is an important ecological pioneer plant that quickly colonizes bare, moist, disturbed soil before other species establish, providing early ground cover and preventing erosion. The tiny seeds are eaten by various shorebirds and wading birds that forage in its typical shallow-water and mudflat habitat. It self-sows automatically in any appropriate seasonal mud habitat without management.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; never collect toadshade from wild populations — purchase only nursery-propagated plants. The stalkless (sessile) flower sits directly atop the three mottled leaves.
directions: Plant nursery-grown divisions in fall in humus-rich, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade — toadshade trillium is one of the most distinctive of the eastern native trilliums, recognizable immediately by its sessile (stalkless) dark maroon flower that sits directly upon the three large, dramatically mottled leaves without an intermediate stalk. The heavily mottled, silver-and-green leaves are among the most beautiful of any native spring wildflower, providing ornamental interest even before the flowers open. A wide natural range stretches from New York west to Kansas and south to Georgia, growing in rich, moist hardwood forests and along stream banks. Like all trilliums, toadshade takes 7 years to bloom from seed — always purchase nursery-propagated plants and never collect from wild populations. The flowers attract small flies and beetles as pollinators; the seeds are dispersed by ants. An outstanding native wildflower for the shaded woodland garden.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Toffee Twist produces fine, curling, warm bronze-copper foliage that forms a graceful cascading mound, an unusual foliage color for a shade-tolerant sedge.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Toffee Twist is a distinctive New Zealand sedge grown for its fine, thread-like, warm bronze-copper foliage that curls and cascades into a loose, tousled, fountain-like mound, an unusual warm color that contrasts beautifully with green- and blue-leaved shade perennials like hostas and ferns. It tolerates a range of light from fairly sunny to shaded sites and adapts to both moist and moderately dry soil once established, needing only an occasional combing-out of old, dead foliage to keep the mound looking fresh. Its arching, tactile texture makes it a favorite for containers and border edges where its curling leaves can be appreciated up close.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring as shoots emerge; tokudama hosta is slow-growing but extremely long-lived once established. Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Takes 3–5 years to reach mature size — plan to leave it undisturbed long-term.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tokudama hosta is one of the most prized species hostas in cultivation, valued for its exceptionally deeply cupped, puckered, glaucous-blue to blue-gray leaves that are among the most intensely textured of all hostas. The deep cupping and puckering of the heavy, corrugated leaf surface gives an almost sculptural quality that makes each plant a focal point in the shade garden. It is a slow-growing hosta species that takes several years to reach full size, but its garden longevity and unique foliage quality make it worth the wait. Several important hosta cultivars derive from this species, including the famous 'Halcyon' (via hybridization). Pale lavender flowers in mid-summer. Slug damage is less severe on the heavily puckered, waxy leaves than on smooth-leaved hostas.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost into part shade.
directions: Tom Thumb Blend is a compact, shade-loving balsam standing 12 to 16 inches tall with bushy plants that come alive with violet, white, and rose double flowers. Start seed indoors and barely cover it, keeping soil warm, then transplant after frost into part shade and rich, moist soil. Bumblebees and hummingbirds are drawn to the array of blooms tucked along the stems. Keep the soil consistently moist, as balsam wilts quickly when dry. Its tidy size makes a charming centerpiece for shady beds and containers.

common_name: Tomato Soup Coneflower (Vivid Red Double-Layered Echinacea)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tomato Soup produces vivid, saturated red flowers, a bold departure from the purple-pink of the wild species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Tomato Soup is a modern coneflower cultivar bred for intensely saturated, brick-red flowers with broad, slightly overlapping petals surrounding a coppery-orange central cone, a bold, warm color unlike the softer purple-pinks of the wild species. It blooms over a long summer season, draws butterflies and bees, and holds its color well in the heat rather than fading, though like many of the newer colorful coneflower hybrids it can be somewhat shorter-lived than straight Echinacea purpurea in humid climates, benefiting from excellent drainage. Leaving spent seed heads standing through winter provides food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

common_name: Tonto Crape Myrtle (Red Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tonto is a semi-dwarf selection reaching 8–12 feet, making it suitable for smaller landscapes and foundation plantings where full-size crape myrtles would be overwhelming.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tonto is a compact, semi-dwarf National Arboretum crape myrtle cultivar reaching 8–12 feet — smaller than the large tree-form selections but larger than the truly dwarf compact types — producing rich fuchsia-red to magenta-red flower clusters from midsummer through fall. It occupies the important size category that bridges the gap between full-size landscape trees and dwarf shrub-form crape myrtles, making it appropriate for foundation plantings of large structures, medium-sized residential landscapes, and situations requiring a crape myrtle that provides substantial presence without becoming a full-scale tree. Tonto shows exceptional resistance to powdery mildew — one of the best in the National Arboretum series for disease resistance — and produces glossy, deep mahogany-red fall foliage color that is among the finest in any crape myrtle selection. The developing exfoliating bark provides winter interest. Tonto benefits from annual removal of small crossing and rubbing branches and removal of sucker growth from the base to maintain an attractive multi-stemmed form. The fuchsia-red flower color is particularly vivid against light-colored walls and combines boldly with contrasting white or silver companion plantings.

plant_note: Plant rhizome segments 1–2 inches deep in fall in moist, deeply humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained woodland soil in full shade; toothwort is a spring ephemeral that goes completely dormant by early summer — mark its location carefully to avoid disturbing the rhizomes when dormant.
directions: Plant rhizome segments in fall in deeply humus-rich, moist, slightly acidic woodland soil in full shade; toothwort is among the most charming native edibles of the eastern woodland, producing pairs of deeply cut, coarsely toothed leaves on erect stems topped with clusters of small white to pale pink four-petaled flowers in early spring alongside trout lilies and trilliums. The toothlike, segmented underground rhizomes have a sharp, peppery wasabi-horseradish flavor and were gathered by Native Americans and early colonists as a condiment; they can be grated fresh or fermented like horseradish sauce. A true spring ephemeral, the entire plant disappears by late spring after setting seed, forming expanding colonies in rich, shaded conditions. Plant with other spring ephemerals — trout lily, bloodroot, Virginia bluebells — in a rich, shaded woodland garden for a sequence of color from late winter through May before the canopy closes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in very well-drained, rocky or sandy, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; cold stratification over winter in the ground produces reliable germination.
directions: Direct sow in fall in very well-drained, rocky or sandy, dry to moderately dry soil in full sun; cold stratification over winter in the ground produces reliable germination. Echinacea atrorubens is one of the most vividly colored of the true species coneflowers, native to dry limestone and rocky prairies of Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, with dark red-crimson to deep magenta ray petals that are much more intensely saturated than typical pink species; it is adapted to alkaline, rocky, dry soils in the south-central prairie region and blooms in June–July. A species for true prairie garden enthusiasts in zones 5–9, it is excellent in dry prairie plantings, gravel gardens, and xeriscape designs in its native range; plants develop a deep taproot and are extremely drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Take offsets or stem cuttings and allow to callus for a week before planting in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; torch aloe is one of the most cold-tolerant of the large, branching aloes, surviving brief dips to 25°F once established. It is widely planted along the California coast and Gulf Coast and is an outstanding hummingbird plant throughout the winter when few other flowers are available.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; torch aloe is a large, branching, multi-stemmed aloe from South Africa that makes one of the most dramatic winter-blooming landscape plants for zone 8–11, producing tall, erect torches of brilliant red-orange tubular flowers from November through February — the peak of the hummingbird-lean winter season — in such abundance that mature clumps appear ablaze with color. Each established clump can have dozens of flower spikes simultaneously, creating a spectacular display that attracts Anna's hummingbirds, Allen's hummingbirds, and other hummingbird species in the Pacific Coast states in large numbers. The plant itself is strongly architectural: many-stemmed and branching, with rosettes of thick, gray-green, toothed leaves at each branch tip, reaching 6–10 feet tall on mature specimens. It is faster-growing and more vigorous than Aloe vera, eventually forming large, impressive clumps. Like aloe vera, the gel is soothing and medicinal. More cold-tolerant than most large aloes, surviving brief freezes to 25°F once established.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade after frost; torch ginger demands rich, moist, organic soil and regular fertilization — in poor or dry soil it produces few flowers and its growth is stunted; top-dress with compost annually and fertilize monthly with a balanced fertilizer during the growing season.
directions: Divide rhizomes or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; torch ginger (red ginger lily, Philippine wax flower, bunga kantan) is a Southeast Asian tropical perennial that produces one of the most dramatic and architecturally striking flower structures of any plant in the tropical garden — the individual flowers emerge directly from the ground on separate, erect stems distinct from the leafy shoots, opening into large, ornate, waxy, pink-to-red, cone-shaped, artichoke-like flower heads composed of tightly overlapping, waxy, pink or red petals arranged in a perfect geometric spiral, rising above the garden floor at the end of stout, 3–5-foot stalks as solitary flame-like torches. The entire structure has an almost architectural, sculptural precision. The large, lance-shaped, deep-green leaves on the vegetative stems rise to 8–15 feet. In addition to its ornamental value, the flower buds and young shoots are used in Southeast Asian cuisine (Thai, Malaysian, and Indonesian cooking) as an aromatic flavoring ingredient. Requires genuinely tropical conditions (zone 10–12) and rich, moist organic soil. An essential large-scale tropical specimen.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Torch is a tall variety (4–6 feet) that blooms from midsummer through fall frost — the long season of vivid orange flowers makes it outstanding for back-of-border use in zone 9's summer gardens. Cut flowers require careful handling — the hollow stems can be sealed by searing the cut end in boiling water immediately after cutting to extend vase life to 5–7 days. Pinch seedlings at 12 inches to encourage branching. Plants may require staking in windy locations due to the tall stems.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral soil — Mexican sunflower thrives in poor soil and blooms better with less fertilizer; Torch is an All-America Selections award-winning Mexican sunflower cultivar selected for its intense, saturated, vivid orange-vermilion flowers — a color so vivid and warm that it reads as almost electric in summer garden displays. Tithonia rotundifolia (Mexican sunflower) is native to Mexico and Central America and is perfectly adapted to the kind of relentless summer heat that defeats many ornamentals — it genuinely thrives in zone 9's brutally hot summer months, growing rapidly and blooming prolifically precisely when most cool-season flowers have long since burned out. The large, 3-inch daisy flowers on long, sturdy, slightly fuzzy stems attract monarch butterflies, swallowtails, and bumblebees in remarkable numbers, making Torch one of the most effective butterfly plants for summer garden use. The sheer height (4–6 feet) and continuous production of vivid orange blooms from July through frost makes Torch visually commanding in any summer garden, and the cut flowers bring a tropical warmth to arrangements.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; thrives in heat.
directions: Torch is a genuine heat lover, setting the dog days of summer ablaze with sizzling 3-inch orange flowers on a large, multi-branching plant for the back of the border. Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil and full sun, barely covering the seed. It tolerates infertile soil, drought, and neglect, so avoid overwatering and rich ground. The tall stems benefit from spacing for airflow and may need staking in exposed sites. Its nectar-rich blooms are irresistible to butterflies and other pollinators.

common_name: Totally Tangerine Dahlia (Single Collarette-Type Orange Dahlia)
plant_note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Totally Tangerine is an award-winning single/collarette-type dahlia with airy, semi-double burnt-orange blooms on tall, branching stems, prized by pollinator gardeners and cut-flower growers alike for its open, bee-accessible flower form.
directions: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep with the growth eye facing up; stake plants as they grow. Pinch the growing tip when about 12 inches tall to encourage branching. Totally Tangerine bears distinctive, semi-double, burnt-orange blooms with a prominent open center and slightly twisted, waterlily-like petals, a looser, airier flower form than the fully double blooms of most decorative and ball dahlias. That open center makes the flower's pollen and nectar accessible to bees and butterflies, which most fully double dahlia forms block entirely, making Totally Tangerine one of the more pollinator-friendly dahlia choices without sacrificing garden impact. It won the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its outstanding, prolific, long-season bloom on strong, well-branched plants that need less disbudding and staking effort than giant dinnerplate types. Deadhead regularly to keep the plant flowering continuously from midsummer through the first frost. Lift and store tubers after frost blackens the foliage in zones colder than 8, or mulch heavily and leave in the ground in zone 8-10.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; tough bumelia grows naturally in dry, sandy, open scrub and upland pine flatwoods of north-central Florida. Seeds benefit from scarification and warm stratification. A relatively rare Florida endemic.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average soil in full sun; tough bumelia (Alachua buckthorn) is a native evergreen shrub or small tree of north-central Florida's dry, sandy scrub and upland pine habitats — one of several Sideroxylon species native to Florida, related to the widespread tough buckthorn (S. tenax) of the Coastal Plain but with a more restricted distribution centered on Alachua County, Florida. Like other bumpelia/sideroxylon species, it produces leathery, elliptic, dark green leaves, small white flowers in clusters that attract pollinators, and small, oval, dark purple-black drupes that are eaten by mockingbirds, catbirds, and other fruit-eating birds. The spiny branches (typical of the genus) provide excellent nesting cover. An important but rarely cultivated native for the dry, sandy, acidic scrub gardens of north-central Florida.

plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil in full sun to part shade; trailing acalypha produces a nearly continuous display of tiny, fluffy, bright-red to magenta caterpillar-like flower spikes on trailing, cascading stems — outstanding in hanging baskets, over walls, and as a colorful tropical groundcover in zone 10–12.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; pinch stems to encourage branching and more prolific flowering. Acalypha reptans (trailing acalypha or dwarf acalypha) is a small, trailing tropical ornamental perennial in the euphorbia family (Euphorbiaceae), closely related to the larger chenille plant (A. hispida) but compact and trailing rather than erect. The plant produces a nearly continuous display of distinctive, fluffy, caterpillar-like flower spikes (chenille flowers) in bright red to deep magenta-red, 1–2 inches long, dangling from the trailing, cascading stems. The flowers are exclusively ornamental — purely decorative with no food or fragrance value — but are intensely colorful and long-blooming over the warm season. In hanging baskets, trailing acalypha is spectacular — the masses of red caterpillar spikes and the cascading growth habit create an eye-catching display. As a groundcover in zone 10–12 tropical gardens, it spreads rapidly at ground level, providing low color and weed suppression. The plant thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast and tropical conditions and blooms most prolifically in bright indirect light or morning sun with afternoon shade. Easily rooted from stem cuttings in water or moist medium.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in strongly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained, undisturbed forest soil in deep shade; trailing arbutus depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi and is highly sensitive to root disturbance. Only plant nursery-propagated stock — collection from the wild is illegal in many states.
directions: Plant in strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, perfectly drained, undisturbed woodland soil in deep to partial shade; trailing arbutus is the beloved state flower of Massachusetts ('Mayflower') and one of the most fragrant of all native wildflowers — the clusters of small, waxy, white to pink flowers in late winter to early spring have an intense, sweet fragrance disproportionate to their modest size. The plant is notoriously difficult to grow — it requires specific mycorrhizal fungal associates, strongly acidic soil, excellent drainage, and undisturbed native woodland conditions. It will not survive in average garden soil or compost-amended beds. A protected species in several states; never collect from the wild. Suitable only for established, undisturbed acidic woodland gardens in cool climates where its specific soil requirements already exist naturally.

common_name: Trailing Jade Peperomia (Round-Leaved Peperomia, Creeping Peperomia)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in very well-draining potting mix (adding 50% perlite to standard potting mix works well); Peperomia rotundifolia is particularly prone to root rot if overwatered — allow the top half of the soil to dry before re-watering. The trailing stems look beautiful cascading over the edge of a hanging basket. Maintain temperatures above 50°F. Mist the leaves occasionally to maintain humidity. Propagate from stem or leaf cuttings. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in well-draining, perlite-enriched potting mix — Trailing Jade Peperomia tolerates lower light than many other peperomias but produces the most compact, attractive growth in bright, indirect conditions. Peperomia rotundifolia is a small, trailing, epiphytic peperomia native to tropical South America (Peru, Ecuador, Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia) in the Piperaceae family, one of the most delicate and graceful of the trailing peperomias for hanging basket culture. The plant produces very slender, wiry, trailing or creeping stems with small (0.25–0.5 inch), round to nearly circular, thick, succulent, bright medium-green leaves spaced along the stems — the round leaf shape (the 'rotundifolia' — round-leaved) and the fine, delicate stem combined create a trailing pattern of fine-textured, emerald-green circles that looks unlike most other peperomias. The semi-succulent nature of the leaves makes it more drought-tolerant than many tropical houseplants while keeping the foliage fresh and full. In a hanging basket, the trailing stems can reach 24 inches or more, creating a fine-textured, green curtain effect. Excellent in terrariums where its delicate scale is appreciated. One of the easiest peperomias to maintain in appropriate conditions. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in any well-drained soil in full sun; trailing lantana is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant and establishes rapidly. Unlike L. camara, it rarely self-seeds invasively in zone 9 and is generally less aggressive in landscapes.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — poor, sandy, and rocky soils are ideal; trailing lantana is a low-growing, wide-spreading groundcover form of lantana that smothers slopes, spills over walls, and covers large areas with a continuous carpet of small lavender-rose to purple flower clusters from spring through frost. Unlike the more common Lantana camara (upright lantana), trailing lantana (L. montevidensis) has a naturally prostrate, cascading growth habit making it superb for slopes, raised beds, and retaining walls where it can drape downward. It is more frost-hardy than upright lantana, less invasive in seed production, and almost indestructible once established. In zone 9 it often persists as a semi-evergreen perennial year-round. An outstanding butterfly and pollinator plant — particularly attractive to skippers and small native bees. Prune back by one-third in late winter to prevent woody buildup and encourage fresh, dense regrowth.

plant_note: Propagate from softwood or semi-hardwood cuttings taken in spring or summer; root cuttings in warm, moist medium and transplant to full sun, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed. In zones 8-9 plants may die back to the roots in frost but regrow vigorously from the base; in zones 10-11 trailing lantana is evergreen and blooms nearly year-round.
directions: Lantana montevidensis is a sprawling, trailing, woody-based perennial groundcover shrub native to South America, producing a near-continuous succession of dense, rounded clusters of small, lilac-purple flowers from late spring through hard frost — one of the longest and most reliable bloom periods of any ornamental shrub in warm climates, while also serving as an important nectar source for butterflies and hummingbirds. Propagate from cuttings in a warm, bright location; once transplanted to full sun and well-drained soil, trailing lantana is highly drought-tolerant and heat-loving, making it ideal for dry slopes, rock gardens, raised beds, and hanging baskets where it will cascade attractively over edges. Note that Lantana montevidensis is considered invasive in parts of the Gulf Coast (Florida, Texas, and Hawaii) where it escapes cultivation into natural areas — always check local regulations before planting outdoors, and prefer growing it in containers in regions where it may naturalize aggressively. Shear plants back by one-third in early spring to encourage fresh, vigorous growth and prevent woody, leggy stems; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, particularly the unripe green berries, so plant with caution in gardens accessible to children or pets.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; trailing wild bean is adapted to dry, sandy, open habitats including beach dunes, prairie margins, and sandy roadsides. Scarifying the hard seed coat before planting improves germination speed.
directions: Direct sow in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost, lightly scarifying the hard seed coat to improve germination; trailing wild bean is a native annual legume vine of prairies, sandy open woodlands, beach dunes, and disturbed sandy soils across eastern North America. The small, pink to rose-purple pea flowers, produced throughout summer and into fall, are visited by native bees including specialist legume bees, and the slender bean pods that follow are consumed by Northern Bobwhite, Wild Turkey, and other ground-feeding birds. As a nitrogen-fixing native annual it builds soil fertility on sandy, nutrient-poor sites where few other plants will grow and self-sows reliably to maintain itself in open, sunny, sandy areas year after year. The trailing and twining stems weave through low grasses and shrubs, creating naturalistic low cover that is excellent for dry prairie restoration, sandy slope stabilization, and wildlife-focused native garden plantings.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, near-neutral soil; Transvaal Gardenia is a deciduous southern and East African savanna tree adapted to seasonal drought and poor, sandy soils — it is more cold-tolerant than most gardenias, surviving light frosts in zone 9, and bears large, creamy-white, intensely fragrant flowers on bare branches before the new leaves flush in spring.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil; Gardenia volkensii is deciduous in seasonal dry conditions — water regularly during the growing season but allow a pronounced dry rest in winter, mimicking its native seasonal-rainfall savanna habitat. Gardenia volkensii (Transvaal Gardenia) is a deciduous shrub or small tree native to the bushveld, miombo woodland, and seasonal savanna of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Kenya, and East Africa to the Mozambique coast, where it produces spectacular, large, creamy-white, 6–8-petaled flowers with a powerful sweet fragrance on bare branches in late winter and early spring before leaf flush — making it one of the most dramatic late-winter flowering trees of the African dry savanna. The trees produce oval to oblong, distinctively ribbed, green to yellow fruits, nutritious to wildlife including elephants, baboons, and hornbills, and used medicinally across its range for skin conditions, fever, and eye ailments. It is hardier to cold than Gardenia thunbergia, tolerating brief periods at or just below freezing in dry winter conditions, making it suitable for protected spots in zone 9. Excellent drought-tolerant specimen or fragrant accent plant for hot, dry, sunny gardens.

plant_note: Propagate from suckers (offsets from the base) or plant container-grown specimens in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile soil in full sun after frost; traveler's palm grows from the center of a single, expanding fan and should be given ample space for the spread to develop symmetrically — planting in windy areas without protection will tear the large paddle-shaped leaves and destroy the ornamental symmetry of the fan.
directions: Propagate from suckers or plant container specimens in moist to well-drained, humus-rich, fertile soil in full sun; traveler's palm is a Malagasy giant of the bird-of-paradise family (Strelitziaceae) — not a true palm — that creates one of the most architecturally dramatic plant forms in the tropical landscape: an enormous, perfectly flat, two-dimensional fan of enormous, paddle-shaped, banana-like leaves aligned precisely in one plane, held on long, smooth, gray-green leaf sheaths that arch outward from the base and, as the plant matures, from an increasingly tall trunk. The fan alignment was traditionally said to run roughly east-west, allowing travelers to orient themselves — giving the plant its common name. The leaf sheaths hold reservoirs of fresh water at their bases. In established plants, small, white, bird-of-paradise-like flowers emerge from boat-shaped bracts along the upper stem. The plant produces basal offshoots (suckers) that can be separated to propagate new specimens. Traveler's palm is one of the most iconic and unmistakable specimens of the tropical landscape, widely planted throughout zone 10–12 botanical gardens, resorts, and private estates.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost, or transplant purchased bedding plants after frost danger; in zones 9–11, Gazania rigens grows as a perennial groundcover that blooms most heavily in spring and fall, blooming lightly through summer heat but persisting year-round.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow after frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; gazanias perform best and bloom most profusely in hot, dry conditions. Gazania rigens (treasure flower) is a South African native that produces brilliantly colored, 2-to-3-inch daisy flowers with a distinctive, contrasting dark eye ring and ornately patterned petals — in colors ranging from brilliant orange, yellow, and red to pink, white, and multicolor bicolor combinations — on compact, rosette-forming plants with silvery-gray, hairy, lobed leaves. The flowers close in shade, on cloudy days, and at night (a characteristic of the genus); they open fully only in bright sunshine, making them most spectacular on warm, sunny days. Gazanias are outstanding in hot, dry, infertile conditions (poor sandy soil, coastal exposure, reflected heat from pavement) where most annuals fail. In zones 9–11, they may persist as tender perennials; elsewhere treat as summer annuals. The 'Daybreak' series has early, reliable blooms that stay open somewhat longer than older types.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings or container stock in fall or spring in well-drained, moderately lean, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy-loam soil in full sun to part shade; aeoniums are winter-growing, summer-dormant succulents from the Canary Islands that prefer the opposite season from most succulents — they grow actively in cool, moist winters and go dormant in hot, dry summers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; water moderately in fall through spring; withhold water in summer when the plant is dormant. Aeonium arboreum (tree aeonium or Irish rose) is a Canary Islands succulent remarkable for its unusual growth rhythm: unlike most succulents, aeoniums grow actively in cool, moist winters and go dormant in summer heat — the rosettes may drop most of their leaves and appear stressed in hot weather but revive with fall rains. The plant produces branching, succulent stems topped with large, flat rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves in bright green ('normal' form), or deep burgundy-purple to nearly black in the popular 'Zwartkop' (Black Rose) cultivar. Mature plants eventually produce a central rosette that elongates into a tall (2–3 foot) cone of small yellow flowers — after which that rosette dies (monocarpic), but side branches continue. The 'Zwartkop' cultivar with nearly black foliage is one of the most dramatically dark-leafed plants in horticulture. In zone 9, aeoniums perform well in the mild climate; avoid summer irrigation. An outstanding architectural container or rock garden plant.

plant_note: Allow stem segments to dry for 2–3 weeks before planting in very well-drained, dry, alkaline to neutral, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; tree cholla is among the hardiest of the cholla cacti, surviving to zone 5 in dry, well-drained conditions.
directions: Plant in dry, well-drained, rocky or sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tree cholla is the most architecturally striking of the upright cholla cacti, producing a distinctive, branched, tree-like form with heavily ribbed, cylindrical joints covered in sheathed, retrorsely barbed spines. The magenta-pink flowers in late spring are surprisingly large and showy for a cholla, and the yellow, spine-covered, persistent fruits remain on the plant through winter — attractive and wildlife-valuable. This is among the cold-hardiest cholla cacti, native to the Great Plains and Chihuahuan Desert from Colorado and Kansas south to Mexico, and survives temperatures as low as zone 5 in dry soils. The densely spiny structure provides excellent nesting habitat for curve-billed thrashers and cactus wrens. The dried skeleton of old plants — the woody, latticed, hollow tubes — is used in crafts and decoration. An outstanding drought-tolerant specimen for dry, sunny gardens from zone 5 to 11.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (3–4 node sections of the hollow stems) horizontally 2–3 inches deep in moist, fertile soil after last frost; tree dahlia's hollow, bamboo-like stems can be harvested in fall before frost, dried briefly, then cut into sections and planted like bamboo cuttings in spring. In zones 9–10 it is perennial above ground; in zone 8 it dies back to tuberous roots and resprouts.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; tree dahlia is the species dahlia from which all hybrid garden dahlias are partly derived — an enormous perennial of the Mexican highlands that grows 10–20 feet tall on stout, hollow, bamboo-like stems in a single season, then bursts into bloom in October through December with masses of large, 4–5 inch, lavender-pink single flowers with golden-yellow centers arranged along towering stems. The timing is critical and remarkable: tree dahlia is strictly day-length sensitive and will not initiate flowering until autumn days shorten in October, meaning it produces all of its spectacular display in the final weeks of the season, providing late color when everything else has finished. In zone 9 and frost-free areas it becomes a permanent perennial shrub, eventually developing thick, persistent stems from year to year. The hollow stems can be harvested, dried, and replanted as cuttings the following spring for easy propagation. An extraordinary statement plant for large gardens seeking drama at tropical scale in the fall.

common_name: Tree Marigold (Mexican Sunflower Tree, Wild Sunflower, Nitobe Chrysanthemum)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in full sun after last frost; Tithonia diversifolia grows extremely rapidly (up to 10 feet in one season) and requires space — do not plant near small shrubs or perennials it will overwhelm. In zone 9, it grows as a large, multi-stemmed perennial shrub; in zone 9b-10, it becomes a large, woody, tree-like shrub. The plant makes an outstanding green manure — cut and incorporate the nitrogen-rich foliage into garden beds to improve soil. Excellent for pollinators, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Self-seeds moderately. Prune hard after fall bloom to prevent becoming too massive.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — Tree Marigold is one of the most fast-growing, adaptable, and drought-tolerant ornamental shrubs for zone 9-12 conditions and will establish vigorously in poor soil where many plants fail. Tithonia diversifolia is a large, fast-growing, woody-based perennial shrub native to Mexico and Central America in the Asteraceae family — not the annual marigold of the flower garden but a large, semi-woody to woody, perennial plant that can reach 10–15 feet in height in zone 9-12 and produces masses of bright orange-yellow, daisy-like flowers 3–4 inches across on the branch tips through fall and early winter. In zone 9, the plant cuts back to the ground in hard freezes and regrows vigorously from the root in spring; in zone 10-11, it forms a large, multi-stemmed shrub of impressive presence. The flowers are powerfully attractive to Monarch butterflies, Gulf Fritillaries, native bees, and hummingbirds — one of the most valuable late-season butterfly nectaring plants for zone 9-12 gardens. Beyond its ornamental value, T. diversifolia has attracted significant interest in organic agriculture as a 'biomass' green manure plant: the thick, succulent, nitrogen-rich foliage contains nutrients that, when cut and incorporated into the soil, release nitrogen and organic matter at rates comparable to commercial fertilizers. Used as a living mulch and soil-building green manure throughout tropical Africa. An outstanding, multipurpose native-range plant for zone 9-12 landscapes. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Divide basal offshoots or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade to full shade after frost; tree philodendron becomes very large over time — a mature specimen can spread 6–10 feet — and its massive leaf stalks and trunk-like base require adequate space, so site with its eventual size in mind.
directions: Divide basal offshoots or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; tree philodendron (lacy tree philodendron, selloum, horsehead philodendron) is a South American tropical perennial that is among the most architecturally dramatic shade plants available for zone 9–12 gardens — a non-climbing, self-heading philodendron that develops a trunk-like stem and spreads outward from its center with enormous, deeply divided, glossy, dark-green, pinnately lobed leaves that can reach 3 feet across on mature specimens, creating a bold, sculptural, rainforest-understory effect. Now correctly classified as Thaumatophyllum bipinnatifidum, it was long known as Philodendron bipinnatifidum or Philodendron selloum in horticulture. In zone 9 it is often frozen back but regrows vigorously from the roots; in zone 10–12 it is a permanent, year-round architectural specimen. It develops aerial roots that anchor it and absorb moisture. The large, tropical form and remarkable leaf shape make it a definitive specimen plant for shaded tropical-style gardens and large container plantings.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in shade; tree selaginella is one of the best selaginellas for outdoor shaded garden use in zones 7-10, forming attractive miniature fern-like clumps that spread slowly.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full shade; tree selaginella is an arching, bush-like fern ally from China that resembles a miniature tree fern with delicate, lacy branches of bright green scale-like foliage arranged in flattened, frond-like planes. Unlike prostrate mosses, tree selaginella forms an upright, branching structure 12-18 inches tall that creates ornamental textural accent in deeply shaded areas. Excellent as a groundcover under large ferns or hostas, or as a container specimen for shaded patios. The iridescent blue-green sheen on the leaves in certain light conditions makes it particularly attractive. More cold-tolerant than most selaginellas and one of the most reliable for outdoor shade garden use in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant in spring in moist soil; tolerates wet sites well.
directions: The Tri-Color Dappled Willow is a fast-growing deciduous shrub whose new spring growth emerges in variegated green, white, and soft pink, with coral-red stems adding winter interest. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, fertile soil; it thrives in damp spots where many shrubs struggle. Prune hard in late winter to encourage a fresh flush of the brightest variegated foliage. Water generously, as willows are thirsty plants that dislike drying out. Grow it as a rounded shrub in a mixed border or shear it into a formal shape.

plant_note: Plant in spring in moist, fertile soil; tolerates wet ground.
directions: This is the standard, tree-form version of the tri-color dappled willow, grafted atop a single trunk to create a lollipop-shaped canopy of green, white, and pink variegated leaves. Plant in full sun to light shade in consistently moist, fertile soil where it can show off its cascading foliage. Prune the head in late winter to keep it dense and to renew the most colorful new growth. Keep the soil evenly moist, as willows demand regular water and tolerate wet feet. Remove any suckers that sprout below the graft to preserve the tree form.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; triangle palm is highly drought tolerant once established and thrives in dry, fast-draining soils. Frost-sensitive — protect young plants below 28°F, established palms may tolerate brief 25°F dips.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; triangle palm is one of the most architecturally distinctive palms in the world — the fronds arise from the trunk arranged in three distinct ranks (rows), creating a perfectly triangular cross-section visible from above and giving the entire crown a dramatic, sharply geometric triangular silhouette unlike any other palm. Native to the dry, rocky spiny forest of southern Madagascar, it is exceptionally drought-tolerant and well-adapted to hot, dry, sandy soils. The stiff, strongly arched fronds are blue-gray-green and held erect, creating a bold, sculptural presence. One of the most popular ornamental palms for dry, warm tropical and subtropical gardens in California, Florida, Arizona, and similar climates. Not tolerant of wet, poorly drained soils. The triangular arrangement of leaves (tristichous phyllotaxy) is one of the most unusual and recognizable features of any landscape palm — a genuine conversation piece in the garden.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Tricolor is a classic variegated camellia cultivar with formal double flowers striped and streaked in red, white, and pink, no two blooms exactly alike.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade. Tricolor is a classic Japanese camellia cultivar bearing formal double flowers with neatly layered petals variably streaked and marbled in red, white, and pink, a variegation pattern that varies noticeably from bloom to bloom and even from year to year on the same plant depending on growing conditions. This unpredictable, ever-changing coloring has made Tricolor a favorite among camellia collectors for generations, since every flush of bloom offers a slightly different show. The dense, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage provides reliable year-round structure between bloom seasons. Like other Camellia japonica cultivars, it flowers in the cool season, typically midwinter in zone 9. Plant in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun, and mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to protect the shallow, fibrous root system and maintain the acidic soil camellias require.

common_name: Tricolor Chinese Evergreen (Camouflage Plant, Aglaonema pictum)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant in bright indirect to low light; Aglaonema pictum cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Unlike the common Chinese Evergreen cultivars, A. pictum is more demanding — it prefers higher humidity (above 50%) and more consistent warmth than typical indoor conditions. Use a well-draining potting mix with added perlite. Water when the top inch dries. The camouflage leaf pattern is most vivid in consistent moderate indirect light. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to low light — Aglaonema pictum is one of the most shade-tolerant of the ornamental foliage plants and one of the very few popular houseplants that can maintain its decorative appearance in genuinely low light conditions, though growth slows considerably. Aglaonema pictum is a species of Chinese Evergreen from the tropical forests of Sumatra and nearby islands in Indonesia, producing one of the most immediately arresting leaf patterns in the houseplant world. The large, elongated, matte, dark-green leaves are decorated with irregular patches and blotches of medium sage-green and silvery pale green-white in a distribution pattern so precisely resembling military camouflage fabric that the plant has become universally known as the 'Camouflage Plant.' The three-toned pattern — dark base, mid-green mottling, bright silver-white patches — is produced by irregular distribution of chloroplasts and other pigments, and the pattern is never repeated identically across any two leaves, creating a naturally varied ornamental effect. Aglaonema pictum is considerably more demanding than the common hybrid Chinese Evergreens (Aglaonema commutatum varieties) typically seen in commercial settings — it requires higher humidity and more consistent warmth — but its unique camouflage pattern has made it a coveted collector plant among houseplant enthusiasts. Multiple 'tricolor' forms exist with varying intensities of the three-color pattern. All parts toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in bright indirect light to part shade; stromanthe requires high humidity and consistent moisture and thrives in outdoor shade gardens in zones 9b–12 or as a striking indoor/patio plant in cooler zones.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in bright indirect light to deep shade; consistent moisture and humidity produce best foliage color. Stromanthe thalia (formerly S. sanguinea, tricolor prayer plant) is a spectacular Brazilian tropical in the Marantaceae family — closely related to calatheas — producing large, lance-shaped, 12-to-18-inch leaves with a stunning three-color pattern: the upper surface is dark green with irregular, creamy white variegation along the midrib and lateral veins, while the leaf underside is vivid, deep magenta-crimson — creating a dramatic contrast when leaves move or catch light from below. Like calatheas, stromanthe displays daily leaf movement (prayer plant behavior). The 'Triostar' cultivar is the most widely grown, with particularly bold cream-and-green upper surfaces and magenta undersides. In zone 9b and warmer, stromanthe can be grown outdoors as a perennial in shaded tropical borders; in cooler zones it is an outstanding indoor plant.
