plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; Fargesia bamboos are clump-forming (not running/invasive) and can be planted without containment barriers, unlike Phyllostachys and other runner bamboos.
directions: Divide established clumps or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; umbrella bamboo (Chinese fountain bamboo) is one of the most ornamental and garden-appropriate of all bamboos for temperate gardens — a graceful, arching, clump-forming (non-invasive) bamboo that produces dense clusters of slender, elegant culms (canes) that arch gracefully outward and downward like a fountain of cascading foliage, bearing short, narrow, lance-shaped leaves that create a rustling, whispering sound in the breeze. Unlike the running bamboos (Phyllostachys, Pseudosasa) that spread invasively by underground rhizomes, Fargesia bamboos form compact, tightly restrained clumps that expand slowly and require no containment barriers. Tolerates shade better than most bamboos. Excellent as a screen, specimen, or large container plant. Unlike some Fargesias, this species flowers infrequently. 'Simba' and 'Jumbo' are popular cultivar selections.

plant_note: Transplant divisions with a section of the stout rhizome in early fall, or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic, cool, shaded soil near a stream or seepage area in early fall; umbrella leaf requires constantly moist, cool conditions and is best planted beside permanent water features or in north-facing slopes.
directions: Transplant divisions in early fall in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in full shade near streams or seepage areas; umbrella leaf is a rare and spectacular native perennial of high Appalachian mountain stream edges, grown for a sequence of three distinct ornamental features across the season — in spring, each stem bears two enormous, deeply lobed leaves that spread horizontally like open umbrellas up to 20 inches across (one of the most dramatic basal leaf effects in hardy perennials), followed by flat-topped clusters of white flowers in early summer, followed in turn by the most prized feature: clusters of vivid, intensely blue berries on bright red stalks in late summer — a color combination of scarlet stems and brilliant blue-purple fruits that is uniquely eye-catching in the shade garden and is the plant's greatest ornamental asset. Requires constantly moist, cool, shaded conditions similar to its streamside mountain habitat. Fairly difficult to establish but long-lived and spectacular when content.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; umbrella magnolia grows naturally as an understory tree in moist ravines and shaded slopes and tolerates deep shade better than most flowering trees.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; umbrella magnolia is a distinctive native understory tree of the Appalachians and Southeast named for the pattern of its enormous leaves — 12–24 inches long — arranged in a dramatic whorl around the branch tips like the spokes of an umbrella, creating a striking bold-textured tropical effect in the shaded garden. The large creamy-white flowers (6–10 inches) in late spring have an unusual, slightly unpleasant fragrance but are still attractive from a distance. Red cone-like fruit clusters in late summer and fall are ornamental and eaten by songbirds. It grows naturally as a subcanopy tree in moist, acidic ravines and tolerates shade better than most Magnolia species, making it one of the few flowering trees that performs well in partial to light shade. The extraordinarily large leaves and exotic texture make it an excellent specimen in shaded woodland gardens.

plant_note: Root stem tip cuttings in moist potting mix or plant container specimens in well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun after last frost; schefflera grows rapidly in warm climates — up to 2–3 feet per year — and becomes a large specimen tree in frost-free zones.
directions: Root stem tip cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun; umbrella plant grows rapidly to become a large, multi-stemmed tree in zones 10–12 with bold, palmate, compound leaves of 7–16 leaflets arranged like the ribs of an umbrella, creating a striking tropical silhouette. Mature trees produce dramatic, upright clusters of small red flowers that attract birds. Outdoors it can reach 40 feet tall; as a container plant or indoor specimen in filtered light it stays manageable at 4–8 feet. Plant has become invasive in Florida and Hawaii — consider the smaller, non-invasive Schefflera arboricola (dwarf schefflera) as an alternative in those states. Container plants tolerate low light exceptionally well.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beside ponds, streams, and in rain gardens in spring; umbrella plant thrives in shallow water (up to 6 inches deep) and wet boggy soil and requires consistently moist conditions throughout the growing season.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beside water; umbrella plant (Indian rhubarb) is a native Californian and Oregon perennial of streambanks and wet canyon floors with two distinct ornamental seasons: in early spring, before any leaves emerge, clusters of small, flat-topped, pale-pink flowers appear on 3-foot, bare, hairy reddish stems — a surprising and charming early display; then throughout summer and fall, enormous, round, peltate (stalked from the center) leaves up to 2 feet across rise on tall, thick, hairy petioles to 3–4 feet, creating a bold, parasol-like effect that is one of the most architecturally dramatic of any streamside or bog perennial. The leaves turn to rich coppery-orange in autumn before dying back. An excellent specimen plant for large-scale naturalistic plantings beside ponds and streams where its scale and requirement for constantly wet soil can be accommodated. Similar in scale to Petasites (butterbur) but native to western North America and much better-behaved (non-spreading).

plant_note: Divide clumps in spring or plant container-grown specimens in consistently wet to standing-water conditions in full sun to part shade; umbrella plant grows in boggy soil, shallow water up to 6 inches deep, or ordinary moist container mixes. It can be overwintered indoors as a houseplant in cold climates and is one of the most popular container and pond plants.
directions: Grow in consistently wet soil, boggy margins, or shallow standing water in full sun to part shade; umbrella plant is a Madagascar native sedge in the papyrus family producing tall, straight, triangular stems topped with graceful, radiating whorls of narrow, grass-like bracts that spread like the ribs of an umbrella — an architectural silhouette immediately distinctive in any water garden or container planting. It grows best in shallow water (2–6 inches) or in saturated boggy soil at pond margins, and is equally successful as a houseplant in a water-filled saucer. The upright, bamboo-like stalks create bold vertical interest in water features, and the plant is prolific enough to supply cut foliage for arrangements. In zones 9–11 it is perennial outdoors; in colder climates it is widely grown as a pool ornamental moved indoors for winter or maintained as a houseplant year-round. Propagation is uniquely simple — cut off a head of bracts and float it upside-down in water, where it will root from the bracts.

common_name: Umbrella Tree (Octopus Tree, Queensland Umbrella Tree)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; umbrella tree is adaptable to a wide range of conditions but prefers bright indirect light for best indoor performance — outdoors in zone 9b-12 it is a fast-growing shade tree. CAUTION: Listed as invasive in Florida — check local regulations.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade to full sun; CAUTION — invasive in Florida and Hawaii; do not plant near natural areas. Schefflera actinophylla (umbrella tree or octopus tree) is an Australian tropical tree that has become one of the most popular houseplants in the world while simultaneously becoming a serious invasive species in Florida and Hawaii. As a landscape tree in zone 10–12, it grows to an impressive 25–40 feet with a distinctive canopy of large, palmate (hand-shaped) compound leaves with 5–16 leaflets radiating like the ribs of an umbrella — each leaflet 4–10 inches long and glossy. The common name 'octopus tree' comes from the bizarre flowering structure: dark-red, finger-like flower spikes emerging from the branch tips like tentacles — striking in flower and producing small, dark-red berries consumed by birds (which has spread the plant into natural areas). As an indoor plant, the large-leafed forms create a bold tropical statement; 'Amate' is a popular, more compact cultivar. CAUTION: Listed as an invasive Category I exotic pest plant in Florida — do not plant near wild areas or waterways.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Underwood's Trillium is a warm-climate sessile species suited to the moist hardwood and mixed pine-hardwood forests of the Florida panhandle, Georgia, and Alabama.
directions: Underwood's Trillium is a southeastern sessile trillium native to the moist, mixed hardwood forests of the Florida panhandle, Georgia, and Alabama, where it blooms in February through April with dark maroon to nearly black sessile flowers nestled among three strongly mottled, glossy leaves. It occupies an ecological niche similar to other coastal plain sessile trilliums but tolerates somewhat warmer and more humid conditions than its montane relatives, making it an appropriate choice for gardeners in zones 7–9 seeking native spring woodland plants. Obtain only nursery-propagated plants, as wild collection is destructive and in many areas illegal; plant rhizome divisions in fall in well-amended, moist, acidic soil in the shade of evergreen or deciduous trees. Like all trilliums, it blooms for only a few weeks before going dormant, so interplant with later-emerging shade perennials to fill the gap.

common_name: Unicorn Monstera (True Swiss Cheese Plant, Obliqua Monstera, Ghost Monstera)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-draining, chunky, highly aerated aroid mix; true Monstera obliqua is one of the rarest Monsteras and most plants sold under this name in the trade are actually Monstera adansonii. Genuine M. obliqua has leaves where the fenestrations (holes) exceed the remaining leaf tissue in area — the leaf appears to be more hole than leaf. Requires high humidity (70%+), warm temperatures (65–85°F), and a climbing support. Very slow-growing. Propagate from stem cuttings. All parts toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to medium indirect light in chunky, well-aerated aroid potting mix with a climbing support — true Monstera obliqua is an extremely slow-growing, delicate climbing aroid that requires consistent warmth, high humidity, and careful watering to thrive. Monstera obliqua is a rare, hemi-epiphytic climbing aroid native to Panama, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, and Brazil in the Araceae family, one of the most coveted and least commonly available plants in the tropical collector world. The reason for its rarity and fascination is its extraordinary leaf fenestration pattern: true M. obliqua produces thin, delicate leaves in which the holes (fenestrations) are so large and numerous that they actually occupy more area than the remaining green leaf tissue — the leaf is literally more hole than leaf, a lace-like structure of the most extreme fenestration of any Monstera species. This quality makes the true plant fragile, photosensitive, and extremely challenging to cultivate compared to the robust Monstera adansonii that is frequently sold as 'M. obliqua' in the plant trade. Collectors who obtain true M. obliqua consider it one of the pinnacles of the aroid hobby. Important note: the vast majority of plants labeled 'Monstera obliqua' in commercial horticulture are actually Monstera adansonii, which is more robust and has much less fenestration. All parts of true M. obliqua are toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; unlike its relative wild ginger, Saruma has upright stems rather than a low creeping habit and self-seeds modestly in a favorable woodland setting.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade. Saruma henryi is a monotypic Chinese woodland genus closely related to wild ginger, but unlike its low, creeping cousin it grows upright stems clothed in heart-shaped, softly hairy leaves, forming a small clump rather than a mat. In late spring it produces small, nodding, pale yellow flowers shaped much like those of wild ginger, followed by modest self-seeding in a hospitable shade garden. It combines well with hostas, ferns, and hellebores in a woodland border, tolerates a range of shade conditions once established, and needs little care beyond a yearly topdressing of leaf compost.

plant_note: Direct sow in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–May for summer bloom or August–September for fall bloom. Uproar Rose is a tall variety (24–30 inches) that may benefit from staking in exposed locations. For the longest bloom season, deadhead spent flowers regularly — though Uproar Rose blooms profusely with or without deadheading. Thin to 12 inches apart for best air circulation; zinnias are susceptible to powdery mildew when crowded, especially in humid conditions. The large, rose-pink flowers are outstanding cut flowers lasting 7–10 days in a vase.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — zinnias thrive in hot, sunny, moderately fertile conditions; Uproar Rose is an All-America Selections award-winning zinnia producing particularly large (4–5 inch), fully double, deep rose-pink flowers on tall, sturdy stems that are among the most impressive cut flowers available from direct-sown seed in the summer garden. The rich, saturated rose-pink color — more vibrant and deeper than pale pink varieties — maintains its intensity through summer heat, making Uproar Rose one of the most reliable large-flowered pink zinnias for the hot conditions of zone 9 summers. Zinnias in general are the quintessential summer annual for the Gulf South — they thrive in the heat that defeats many summer flowers, blooming continuously and heavily from planting through frost with minimal care. The large flowers are exceptional butterfly magnets, attracting swallowtails, fritillaries, monarchs, and sulphurs throughout the summer season, making zinnia plantings important pollinator habitat during the hottest months when many other nectar plants are stressed. Uproar Rose's combination of cut flower quality, striking color, heat tolerance, and pollinator value makes it one of the most multi-purpose zinnias available.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to poor soil in partial shade in spring; dicliptera is drought-tolerant once established and actually blooms better in poor, dry soil than in rich, fertile conditions — avoid heavy fertilization which produces rank foliage at the expense of flowers.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in partial shade; Uruguayan firecracker plant (hummingbird plant) is a South American perennial of the family Acanthaceae that stands out from other hummingbird plants by its distinctive silvery-gray, softly hairy foliage — the felt-like, silver-green leaves create a refined, cool-toned foliage effect that combines beautifully with the bright, tubular, orange-red flowers borne in clusters at the stem tips from late spring through fall. The silver foliage and orange-red flowers together create a sophisticated color combination that is warm, vivid, and unusual. It is notably drought- and heat-tolerant, shade-tolerant, and hardy to approximately 15°F in zone 8 (freezing back and regrowing reliably from the root). The clusters of bright-orange tubular flowers are irresistible to hummingbirds and produce nectar continuously through the warm season. It spreads moderately by underground stolons to form manageable colonies that make it effective as a groundcover on slopes and dry, shaded areas. An outstanding plant for hot, dry, partially shaded conditions in zone 8–11 where many flowering perennials fail.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural cold stratification or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to arid, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Utah juniper is supremely adapted to the cold desert climate and thin soils of the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau at 3,000–8,000 feet elevation.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to arid, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; Utah juniper is the defining tree of the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau desert — the dominant woody plant of the vast juniper-sagebrush and piñon-juniper woodlands that characterize the landscape of Nevada, Utah, western Colorado, and adjacent states at mid-elevations. More adapted to the cold desert continental climate (extreme heat, extreme cold, minimal rainfall) than almost any other tree species. Often grows in nearly pure stands on rocky mesas, canyon slopes, and valley floors. The species name 'osteosperma' means 'bony-seeded' — the hard seed within the fleshy berry-like cone. Important forage and browse plant for deer, pronghorn, and other wildlife. The berries are a critical food source for many birds. An excellent xeriscape tree for high desert gardens (zone 4–8) where water conservation is paramount — virtually no irrigation needed after establishment.

plant_note: Plant fresh acorns in fall at 1–2 inches depth in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, valley or foothill soil in full sun; valley oak requires deep soil to accommodate its extensive taproot. It grows naturally in deep valley soils and does not tolerate shallow, rocky, or waterlogged conditions. Never summer-irrigate established trees.
directions: Plant fresh acorns in fall in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; valley oak is the largest of California's native oaks, reaching 40–100 feet tall with massive, sprawling crowns up to 80 feet wide — widely regarded as one of the most majestic and iconic trees of California. It grows naturally in deep valley soils and oak savanna throughout California's Central Valley and coast ranges. Valley oaks can live over 600 years and develop massive, deeply furrowed, gray trunks and wide-spreading canopies of graceful, deeply-lobed leaves. The large acorns were the primary food staple of numerous California indigenous cultures. CRITICAL: never irrigate established valley oaks in summer — summer water near the root zone encourages Phytophthora root rot (sudden oak death) and kills otherwise healthy trees. Plant away from irrigated lawns and landscapes. A landmark tree requiring ample space but magnificent at maturity.

plant_note: Plant tubers after all danger of frost when soil has warmed.
directions: Valley Porcupine is a spiky, pink-and-white cactus-type dahlia that is both an excellent cut flower and a reliable tuber producer, making it a great choice for beginners. Plant tubers horizontally about 4 to 6 inches deep after the soil warms in spring, with the eye facing up. Site in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and stake tall plants to support the heavy blooms. Pinch the growing tip when plants are about a foot tall to encourage bushier growth and more flowers. In cold zones, lift and store the tubers indoors over winter after the first frost blackens the foliage.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost when soil is warm.
directions: Valley Rust Bucket is a smaller red-orange dahlia whose warm autumn tones blend beautifully with bronze and copper companions in the cutting garden. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Stake the plants and pinch the central shoot early to promote branching and a fuller flush of blooms. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep the plant producing through the season. Lift the tubers before hard freezes in colder regions and store them in a cool, dry place for replanting.

common_name: Van Houtte Sage (Van Houtte's Scarlet Sage, Red Velvet Sage)
plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings in spring after last frost in partial shade to full sun; Van Houtte Sage grows vigorously in zone 9 and can reach 4–6 feet in a single season. It roots readily from tip cuttings in water or moist soil. In zone 9a, plants may be damaged by hard frost but resprout from the root crown in spring; in zone 9b-10, it overwinters reliably as a semi-evergreen perennial. Prune by half after each bloom flush to stimulate repeat blooming and maintain compact habit.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Van Houtte Sage grows fastest in full sun but tolerates and even appreciates afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat, where it continues blooming through July–August when other sages shut down. Salvia van-houttei is a large, vigorous, soft-stemmed tropical sage from Brazil that produces some of the most theatrical and unusual flowers in the genus. The whorled flower spikes are covered with large, deeply-veined, velvety, dark burgundy-red to wine-colored calyxes that persist long after the scarlet corolla flowers inside them have fallen — the persistent, showy calyxes give the entire spike a dramatic deep-red to black-purple appearance and extend the ornamental interest of each bloom spike for weeks. The flowers themselves are tubular, bright scarlet, and intensely attractive to hummingbirds and large butterflies including swallowtails. The large, soft, dark-green, pebbly-textured leaves are aromatic and give the plant a bold, tropical presence even out of bloom. Van Houtte Sage is one of the most underused and undervalued of the tropical sages available for zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens — combining long bloom season, hummingbird attraction, heat tolerance, and an exotic tropical appearance that rivals showier but less adaptable ornamentals.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanhoutte spiraea blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering to avoid removing the following year's flower buds.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanhoutte Spiraea, commonly called Bridal Wreath, is one of the most beloved flowering shrubs in American horticulture — a large, wide-arching shrub that in April and May (zone 7–8) produces such a profusion of small, pure-white flower clusters along the entire length of each cascading branch that the branches appear covered with a white veil, creating the bridal wreath effect that gives the plant its common name. The arching, fountain-like form with flowers distributed along every branch tip is one of the most graceful and spectacular spring flowering shrub effects available in the northern and mid-South garden. Vanhoutte spiraea is a hybrid of Spiraea cantoniensis and S. trilobata that has been cultivated since the 1860s — more than 150 years of continuous popularity testify to its landscape merit. Unlike summer-blooming Japanese spiraea (S. japonica) cultivars that bloom on new wood, Vanhoutte blooms on old wood and must be pruned immediately after flowering — never in fall or winter, which would remove the following year's flower buds. In zone 9's heat, Vanhoutte performs best in zone 8 and colder; in the hottest parts of zone 9a, the summer heat can stress the plant.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil and full sun.
directions: Vanilla Ice brings a creamy, light-yellow color to the garden on multi-branched plants about 5 feet tall bearing sweet 3-to-5-inch flowers. Direct sow the seed about an inch deep after the last frost in warm soil and full sun. Thin seedlings so the branching plants have room to develop their many blooms. Practically care-free, these sunflowers provide months of color and lovely cut flowers, and are striking in a moonlit garden. Water steadily while young and enjoy the pollinators and birds they attract.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanilla Strawberry blooms on new wood — prune hard in late winter to stimulate vigorous new growth for maximum flower production.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Vanilla Strawberry is one of the most spectacular and distinctive panicle hydrangea cultivars — producing enormous, upright, conical flower panicles (up to 12–16 inches long) that undergo a dramatic color transformation through the growing season: opening pure creamy-white in early summer, then progressively blushing from the base of each panicle upward from pink to vivid strawberry-red as summer advances, creating a bicolor white-and-strawberry effect that is unlike any other hydrangea. At peak color in late summer and early fall, the large panicles display a gradient from strawberry-red at the base through pink to creamy-white at the tip — an extraordinary color combination that has made Vanilla Strawberry one of the fastest-selling new shrubs since its introduction. The shrub grows 6–8 feet tall and 4–6 feet wide with a strong, upright habit and sturdy stems that support the heavy flower panicles without flopping — an advantage over some other large-flowered H. paniculata types. Like all H. paniculata, it blooms on new wood and is pruned hard in late winter. In zone 9, morning sun with afternoon shade produces optimal results — the intense strawberry-red color develops best with some direct sun but the flowers hold color better if protected from the intense afternoon Gulf South sun.

common_name: Variable Maxillaria (Yellow and Red Maxillaria, Tufted Maxillaria, Variabilis Orchid)
plant_note: Grow mounted on bark or in a small basket with coarse bark in bright indirect to partial direct light; Maxillaria variabilis is one of the most tolerant and adaptable of the Maxillaria species, growing in a wide range of temperature and light conditions — cool, intermediate, and warm — and producing single, small (0.75-inch) flowers in variable colors (yellow, orange-red, red, or brown) singly from between the pseudobulbs and leaf bases on short stems. The plant forms increasingly large clumps over time, eventually producing dozens of flowers simultaneously over many months. A good beginner orchid for zone 9-11 outdoor culture. Tolerates brief temperatures to 35°F. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to partial direct morning light mounted on bark or in a small basket — Variable Maxillaria is one of the most adaptable and undemanding of the smaller Maxillaria species, tolerating cool to warm temperatures, a range of light conditions, and irregular watering better than many more exacting orchids. Maxillaria variabilis is a sympodial, clustering, epiphytic orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, and Colombia — widely distributed in the cloud forests and humid montane forests of Central America and northern South America. The plant produces compact, somewhat flattened pseudobulbs 1–2 inches tall arranged tightly on a clustering rhizome, each topped with a single, narrow, grass-like leaf 4–8 inches long. The species name variabilis refers to the remarkable variation in flower color across the natural range: from clear, bright yellow in some populations to orange-red, brick-red, deep red, or brown-red in others, with all intermediate shades represented. The flowers are small (0.75 inch), produced singly on short stems from the bases of the pseudobulbs, and are faintly fragrant. The real value of the plant lies in its clumping habit: over several years, a plant develops into a large, multi-headed clump producing dozens of flowers simultaneously over the extended blooming season (spring and early summer primarily, with scattered bloom at other times). Very adaptable and rewarding in zone 9-11. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist to dry, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; variable panicgrass is a woodland species native to the understory of open deciduous and mixed forests, one of the few native grasses truly adapted to shaded conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; variable panicgrass is one of the most important native Dichanthelium species of woodland and forest-edge habitats across eastern North America. The Dichanthelium grasses are a unique genus of native panicgrasses that form rosettes of broad basal leaves in fall and winter, bloom in spring, then produce a second wave of smaller flowers through summer — an unusual bimodal blooming pattern shared across the genus. This species occupies the woodland understory with particular success, tolerating a degree of shade that excludes most native grasses. The fine, loosely branched seed panicles are a critical, high-quality food source for woodland-edge sparrows, juncos, and other granivorous birds. Excellent in the shaded section of a rain garden, at woodland edges, and as a low-growing grass layer beneath canopy trees in native plant gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall on moist, acidic, sandy soil; cold stratification over winter improves germination rates.
directions: Native perennial sunflower of wet pine flatwoods and longleaf pine savannas of the southeastern coastal plain, producing bright yellow daisy-like flowers 2-3 inches across in late summer and fall on tall, upright stems. The narrow, rough basal leaves differ markedly in shape from the smaller stem leaves, giving the plant its common name. Grows best in moist to wet, sandy, acidic soil in full sun but tolerates seasonal standing water; plant in mass for the most striking late-season display. Seeds attract finches and sparrows, making it an underused native sunflower for wet, full-sun pollinator and bird gardens in the Gulf Coast region.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; varicolored angel's trumpet is notable for flowers that change color as they age — typically opening white and gradually turning peach, apricot, or orange. CAUTION: All parts extremely toxic.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; varicolored angel's trumpet is an Ecuadorian species named for its distinctive flower color change — the enormous pendant trumpets open white and gradually transition through cream, peach, and apricot to a final orange tone as they age, so a single plant displays multiple flower colors simultaneously, creating an exceptional multicolor effect rare in tropical ornamentals. The flowers, up to 14 inches long among the largest in the genus, have a pleasant, sweet fragrance. Like all Brugmansia, all parts are dangerously toxic and the plant must be sited away from children and animals. The enormous, tropical-looking foliage and dramatic pendant flowers create the most architectural and dramatic tropical statement in the warm-climate garden. Heavy fertilization and consistent moisture are essential for maximum performance; drought or nutrient stress cause immediate flower drop.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Variegata holds its cream-edged foliage as a bright accent through the growing season, well after the spring flowers fade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. A long-established classic among variegated shrubs, Variegata weigela produces soft green leaves broadly edged in creamy white that brighten a mixed border all season, paired with clusters of soft pink, trumpet-shaped flowers in late spring that draw hummingbirds. The variegated foliage provides ongoing visual interest well beyond the relatively brief flowering period typical of weigela cultivars. It performs best with a light shaping prune right after flowering, since blooms form on the previous year's wood, and is otherwise a tough, easy shrub tolerant of average soil and normal garden care.

common_name: Variegated Cast Iron Plant (Cream-Striped Deep-Shade Aspidistra Groundcover)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; the variegated form is somewhat slower-growing than the all-green species and slightly less tolerant of extreme neglect — provide consistent moisture and avoid direct sun which burns the cream variegation.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade; Variegated Cast Iron Plant is a stunning selection of the legendary Aspidistra elatior — the most shade-tolerant of all commonly grown ornamental plants — producing the same broad, strap-shaped, leathery evergreen leaves as the green species but with distinctive cream-white to ivory longitudinal stripes that create a luminous, light-reflecting effect in the deepest, darkest shade positions where few other plants survive. The cream stripes typically run the length of the leaf blade in widths varying from thin lines to broad bands, producing a gently variegated pattern that brightens dark garden areas while maintaining the bold, tropical foliage character that makes cast iron plant a cornerstone of Gulf South shade gardening. Aspidistra elatior earned its common name through extraordinary tolerance of neglect, drought, poor light, dry soil, and root competition from trees — but the variegated form is slightly more demanding than the green species and produces its best appearance with consistent moisture and protection from sun. In zone 9, Variegated Cast Iron Plant grows as a reliable perennial groundcover under live oaks, magnolias, and other dense-canopy trees where the combination of root competition, deep shade, and summer drought would eliminate most alternatives. The cream stripes are most vivid in the variegated form grown in good but indirect light — deep shade in poor soil dulls the variegation over time.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Variegata performs best in partial shade — the cream-yellow leaf margins may bleach or scorch in full hot afternoon sun, especially in zone 9 summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Variegated Lilyturf is a widely grown selection of clumping liriope distinguished by its creamy-yellow to cream-white leaf margins that contrast brightly with the dark-green central stripe — providing far more visual interest in shaded situations than the all-green types. In the shade garden, the yellow-variegated foliage acts as a natural light reflector, brightening dark areas and creating the appearance of filtered light even in deep shade. The lavender flower spikes in late summer are produced reliably through the variegated foliage and add seasonal interest. In zone 9, the foliage remains evergreen year-round but benefits from being cut back to 3–4 inches in late January or early February before new growth begins to maintain a fresh, clean appearance. The variegated form is somewhat slower-growing than Big Blue but reaches the same density with patience. Use as edging along shaded beds, in sweeping masses under trees, or as a foliage accent in shade container plantings. Deer typically avoid established liriope once it is recognized as unpalatable.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegata pittosporum is highly salt-tolerant and is an excellent choice for coastal landscapes within a mile of the Gulf or Atlantic coast.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Variegated pittosporum is one of the most reliable and widely planted foundation and landscape shrubs for zone 8–11 coastal and Gulf Coast gardens — a compact, rounded, evergreen shrub producing distinctive, leathery, spatula-shaped leaves in dark green irregularly edged and streaked with creamy white to gray-green variegation. The variegated foliage provides year-round visual interest and brightness in both full sun and partial shade conditions. In spring, the shrub produces small, creamy-white, intensely orange-blossom fragrant flowers — the fragrance is remarkably strong for such small flowers and perfumes the surrounding garden. Variegated pittosporum is among the most salt-tolerant and wind-tolerant of common landscape shrubs, making it exceptional for coastal exposures where most shrubs struggle with salt spray and marine wind. The compact, naturally mounding habit stays 3–5 feet tall and wide with minimal pruning, though it can be pruned to control size immediately after spring bloom. Extremely drought-tolerant once established; tolerates clay soil, alkaline conditions, and reflected heat from paving. Avoid wet, poorly drained sites where Phytophthora root rot can be a problem. Essentially pest-free in zone 9. The standard green species Pittosporum tobira grows larger and is also widely planted in Gulf Coast landscapes.

common_name: Variegated Shell Ginger (Cream-and-Green Striped Tropical Ginger Specimen)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Variegated Shell Ginger prefers afternoon shade protection — full-day direct sun can cause the cream variegation to bleach to white and the leaf margins to burn in Gulf South summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to partial sun; Variegated Shell Ginger is one of the most spectacular foliage plants for Gulf South tropical garden designs — a large, bold ornamental with broad, strap-shaped leaves (12–18 inches long) brilliantly streaked with alternating bands of deep green and creamy-white to ivory-yellow variegation that creates one of the most visually striking striped foliage effects of any commonly available ornamental plant. The creamy-white striping covers 30–50% of each leaf surface in irregular, painterly bands that vary in width and distribution, creating a luminous effect in partial shade where the cream bands glow against the dark-green background. In spring or early summer, mature established clumps produce pendant clusters of shell-shaped white flowers with yellow and red markings — beautiful but secondary to the spectacular foliage display. The variegated form is significantly more ornamental than the solid-green Alpinia zerumbet (shell ginger) but slightly slower-growing and more heat-sensitive — the cream portions of the variegated leaves are more vulnerable to sun scorch than the all-green type. In zone 9, Variegated Shell Ginger is a perennial that may be top-killed by hard freezes but returns from the rhizome in spring — heavy mulching protects the roots through zone 9a winters. The bold, tropical scale and spectacular variegation make this an outstanding specimen plant for partially shaded entryways, courtyard gardens, and tropical-theme garden designs.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, moderately fertile soil in part shade to full sun; variegated shell ginger is more shade-tolerant than common shell ginger and the variegated foliage is brightest in morning sun with afternoon shade — full shade produces less crisp variegation but plants still thrive.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; provide morning sun for best foliage color. Alpinia vittata (variegated shell ginger) is a Pacific Island native ginger producing one of the most striking foliage displays of any tropical plant — upright, 3-to-5-foot stems with long (18-inch), lance-shaped leaves dramatically striped with alternating bands of green and creamy yellow, creating a bold, bright, bamboo-like architectural effect. Unlike common shell ginger (A. zerumbet) which is grown for both foliage and flowers, variegated shell ginger is primarily a foliage plant — the striped leaves are the main ornamental feature, providing year-round tropical color in shade and part-shade situations. The shell ginger flowers (nodding racemes of white and pink flowers resembling porcelain shells) are less freely produced than in the straight species. In zone 8–12, the plant persists as a perennial; the above-ground parts may die back in a hard freeze but the rhizomes survive in the ground with mulch protection. An outstanding tropical foliage specimen for part-shade situations in Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Place outdoors in shade to partial shade after temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9 use outdoors April–October and bring indoors when temperatures approach 45°F. Laurentii is a variegated cultivar with the distinctive bright yellow margin stripe — this variegation is propagated by division only (leaf cuttings revert to plain green). Dracaena trifasciata 'Laurentii' (formerly Sansevieria trifasciata 'Laurentii') is one of the most studied plants for indoor air quality — NASA's Clean Air Study identified it as effective at removing formaldehyde, benzene, and other VOCs from interior air. The upright, strap-leaved form takes up minimal floor space relative to its visual impact, making it effective in confined container situations.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — tolerates extremely low light conditions where most plants cannot survive, while also adapting to bright indirect light — in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil or potting mix; Variegated Snake Plant (Dracaena trifasciata 'Laurentii') is the classic variegated form of Mother-in-Law's Tongue, producing the familiar upright, stiff, strap-shaped leaves with the distinctive pattern of dark green cross-banding on a lighter green ground — and in the 'Laurentii' form, an additional bright golden-yellow stripe running the full length of both leaf margins. The combination of the detailed cross-banded central pattern and the bold, clean yellow margin stripe creates a more visually striking and decorative effect than the plain green species, making 'Laurentii' the most commonly sold and planted snake plant variant worldwide. Dracaena trifasciata tolerates neglect — infrequent watering, low light, temperature fluctuations, and irregular fertilization — at levels that would kill most other decorative foliage plants, making it genuinely practical for situations (covered porches, low-light indoor corners, weekend homes) where consistent care cannot be guaranteed. The extremely low water requirement (tolerating complete drought for weeks) combined with the low-light tolerance and the clean, architectural upright form makes the Variegated Snake Plant one of the most practically useful shade and low-light ornamentals available.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring just as new growth emerges, or plant in early fall, placing rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; variegated Solomon's seal establishes slowly but becomes a long-lived, low-maintenance shade perennial. Mark the planting area as it emerges late in spring.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally 1–2 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; variegated Solomon's seal is the most widely grown and most ornamentally striking form of Polygonatum odoratum (angular Solomon's seal), bearing the same elegantly arching unbranched stems as the species but with each oval leaf edged in a broad, creamy-white to pale-cream margin that provides striking variegated foliage from emergence in spring through autumn dormancy. In late spring, small pairs of white, sweetly fragrant, tubular pendant bells dangle beneath the leaf axils along the full length of the arching stem, followed by blue-black berries. The arching stems with their precisely alternating variegated leaves create one of the most refined and architecturally graceful effects available for the shaded garden, combining beautifully with hostas, ferns, hellebores, and dark-leaved plants where the creamy leaf margins glow in low light. It spreads slowly by rhizomes into gradually expanding colonies. All parts are toxic if ingested. An indispensable classic of the shade garden.

plant_note: Place outdoors in shade to partial shade after temperatures remain above 50°F; in zone 9 use outdoors April–October and bring indoors before freezing temperatures. Vittatum produces the classic center-white, green-margined stripe pattern — the reverse pattern from 'Variegatum' (which has green centers and white margins). Spider plants produce long, arching runners bearing miniature plantlets (spiderettes) that can be snipped and rooted in water or moist soil. In zone 9 outdoors in summer, spider plants grow vigorously in the humid heat, producing abundant runners and plantlets. The thick, fleshy roots store water, making spider plants more drought tolerant than their lush appearance suggests.
directions: Plant in shade to bright indirect light — spider plants tolerate extremely low light conditions and are among the most adaptable shade container plants available — in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral potting mix with consistent moisture; Variegated Spider Plant (Chlorophytum comosum 'Vittatum') is one of the most widely grown and genuinely shade-tolerant foliage plants in cultivation — producing gracefully arching rosettes of long, narrow leaves with a central white stripe and green margins, and sending out long, arching stolons that produce miniature plantlets (spiderettes) at their tips that dangle in the air like a cascade of tiny spiders. The vittatum pattern — white center stripe, green margins — creates a bright, luminous effect in shaded settings where the white stripe catches and reflects available light, making spider plants one of the most effective brightening plants for deeply shaded corners and covered patios where other plants would fade to monotone green. The cascading runners and plantlets extend 2–3 feet below the container in a hanging basket, creating a dramatic, lush, cascading display with almost no care beyond periodic watering. The combination of extreme adaptability to low light and neglect, air-purifying capability, prolific production of easily shared plantlets, and the bright variegated foliage makes spider plant one of the most practical and rewarding shade foliage plants for zone 9 porches, patios, and interiors.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Variegatus requires full sun to keep its crisp white-and-green striped blades from reverting toward plain green in shade.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Variegatus is one of the oldest and most classic maiden grass cultivars, producing arching, gracefully drooping blades boldly striped lengthwise in crisp white and green, creating a luminous, almost silvery effect in the garden that brightens even from a distance. In late summer it sends up tall, feathery, coppery-pink flower plumes that age to fluffy tan seed heads persisting through winter for structural interest. The large, fountain-like clump makes an excellent specimen or screen, though it needs a good amount of room to display its full arching habit; cut the entire clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth emerges.

plant_note: Direct sow in early autumn or divide established clumps in spring; autumn sowing allows roots to establish before winter.
directions: Direct sow in early autumn onto a lightly prepared seedbed under deciduous trees or in dappled shade, pressing seed into the soil surface without covering deeply, as light aids germination. Unlike most ornamental fescues that demand full sun, this species genuinely performs well in moderate to full shade, maintaining attractive dark-green, thread-fine foliage throughout the season. Plant or thin to 12 to 18 inches apart to allow each clump to develop its full, loose arching character. Divide clumps every three years in early spring to prevent center die-out and to maintain the fresh, dense texture that makes this fescue a standout groundcover in shaded situations.

plant_note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in deep, moist, rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade in a woodland garden setting. Vasey's Trillium is a large pedicellate species that blooms somewhat later than sessile trilliums — April to May in the Southern Appalachians.
directions: Vasey's Trillium is one of the largest and most striking of the native eastern trilliums, native to rich, moist cove forests and sheltered ravines of the southern Appalachians from Virginia and North Carolina south to Georgia and Alabama, where it blooms from April through May with dramatic, deep wine-red petals that recurve strongly back toward the stem, hanging below the leaves and emitting a strong, sweet fragrance to attract fly pollinators. It grows markedly larger than most sessile trilliums, with broad three-parted leaves and stems reaching 24 inches, and its flowers hang on a distinct pedicel below the leaf whorl — a characteristic setting it apart from sessile species. Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in the deepest, most richly amended soil you can provide — cove forest conditions with high organic matter, consistent moisture, and full shade — and mulch heavily with leaf litter. Vasey's Trillium takes 5–7 years to reach blooming age from seed, making nursery divisions the only practical route for most gardeners.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring just as new growth begins. Replant divisions immediately at the same depth in consistently moist, humus-rich soil. Shelter from afternoon sun to prevent leaf wilting.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in moist to wet, organically rich soil with dappled or partial shade, particularly protection from harsh afternoon sun. Ligularia veitchiana is one of the most dramatically scaled perennials for the moist shade garden, with leaves that can exceed 18 inches across and flower spikes rising 4 to 6 feet in midsummer. Keep soil consistently moist throughout the growing season, as plants will wilt dramatically during dry spells even in shade. This bold specimen works well planted in large groups near water features or as a backdrop plant in sheltered woodland borders.

common_name: Veitchii Gardenia (Classic Florist Gardenia with Everblooming Double White Flowers)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Veitchii was historically the standard florist gardenia for cut flowers and corsages and produces more compact, more regularly shaped flowers than the larger, showier 'Fortuniana' — both fragrant but with different use profiles.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) soil in partial shade; Veitchii is the classic florist and corsage gardenia cultivar — the variety that shaped the public image of gardenia for most of the 20th century as the preferred white flower for corsages, wedding bouquets, and cut flower arrangements, valued for its perfectly formed, fully double, pure-white flowers and the intense, sweet, iconic gardenia fragrance that makes it one of the most recognizable flower scents in the world. The flowers of Veitchii are somewhat smaller than those of the larger-flowered 'Fortuniana' and 'Mystery' cultivars but are more precisely and symmetrically formed — tight spirals of white petals forming a perfect double flower that is simultaneously elegant and lush. The key practical advantage of Veitchii over earlier cultivars is repeat or continuous bloom (sometimes described as 'everblooming') — unlike once-blooming gardenias that flower only in spring, Veitchii produces flowers from late spring through summer and into fall, a trait that made it invaluable commercially. The intense gardenia fragrance is full and true across all blooming periods. The plant grows as a compact to medium evergreen shrub (3–5 feet) with the characteristically glossy, deep-green foliage of gardenia. In zone 9, Veitchii is somewhat cold-sensitive — mulching the roots and planting against a south-facing wall provides winter protection in zone 8–9a. Strongly acidic soil and iron availability are the most common cultural challenges.

common_name: Velvet Arrowhead (Wendland's Syngonium, Silver Goosefoot Plant, Dark Velvet Syngonium)
plant_note: Grow in full shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil or on a moss pole for climbing; Syngonium wendlandii is the darkest and most velvety of the commonly cultivated Syngonium species, producing deeply colored, dark forest-green leaves with a striking white central stripe and a velvety texture from tiny, light-scattering surface hairs. It is an outstanding indoor or sheltered outdoor shade plant for zone 10-12 or a protected outdoor position in zone 9b. Keep from temperatures below 50°F. The leaves are beautiful when backlit. CAUTION: all Syngonium parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested by pets or children — toxic to cats and dogs.
directions: Grow in full to partial shade in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil — Velvet Arrowhead is one of the most shade-adapted and visually distinctive of the Syngonium species and thrives in the low-light conditions of a shaded porch, bright interior room, or understory garden in zone 10-12. Syngonium wendlandii is a climbing, rhizomatous tropical vine in the Araceae family native to Costa Rica and Central America, one of the most sought-after species in the genus for the extraordinary visual quality of its leaves. The leaves are a deep, saturated dark forest-green on their upper surfaces, with a broad, brilliant white to silver-white midrib and primary veins creating a dramatic two-tone pattern of dark and light. The surface of the leaf has a distinctly velvety texture from tiny surface papillae that scatter light in a way reminiscent of velvet fabric — making the leaves appear almost three-dimensional, like cut velvet or dark plush. Juvenile plants produce smaller, arrowhead-shaped leaves on compact, low-growing stems. As the plant matures and begins to climb a support, the leaves take on a larger, more broadly lobed form up to 10–12 inches across, with the white markings becoming even more pronounced. Syngonium wendlandii is one of the classic collector aroids now widely appreciated both as a houseplant and as a shaded outdoor container or landscape plant in frost-free climates. The deep shade tolerance, compact juvenile form, and extraordinary leaf pattern make it ideal for shade gardens and sheltered patios. CAUTION: toxic to pets if ingested — keep away from cats and dogs.

common_name: Velvet Cardboard Anthurium (Clarinervium, White Veined Anthurium)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light; Anthurium clarinervium requires consistent warmth (65–85°F), high humidity (60–80%), and excellent drainage. Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil — never dense potting compost. Water thoroughly when the top layer of the mix dries; the plant is more drought-tolerant than humidity-tolerant, and chronic overwatering causes rapid root rot. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Anthurium clarinervium needs adequate light for healthy leaf production but will bleach and burn in direct sun. Anthurium clarinervium is a terrestrial to epiphytic anthurium endemic to the limestone cliff faces (karst) of Chiapas, Mexico, where it grows in the crevices and rock faces of cloud forest — an unusual natural habitat that explains its particular cultivation requirements: excellent drainage, high humidity, and bright filtered light in a calcareous substrate. The leaves are the defining ornamental feature: large, broad, heart-shaped, and thickly textured with a distinctive velvety or cardboard-like feel (giving the species the common name 'Cardboard Anthurium'), rich dark emerald-green to blue-green, covered with a network of precisely delineated, bright white to silvery-white raised veins in a complex branching pattern. Young leaves emerge in shades of rose to bronze before deepening to the mature dark green. The combination of bold leaf shape, velvety texture, and dramatic white venation has made Anthurium clarinervium one of the most sought-after velvet anthuriums among tropical plant collectors worldwide. The spathe flowers are small and inconsequential. All parts are toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; branching habit produces many blooms.
directions: Sow seed one inch deep directly in the garden after the last frost once soil warms. This heirloom bears velvety, multi-toned blooms in mahogany, bronze, and burnt orange on branching five- to seven-foot stems. Its many pollen-rich flowers make excellent cut material and feed bees throughout summer and fall. Give it full sun and moderate water, staking tall plants in exposed sites to prevent lodging.

plant_note: Plant container trees in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0) soil in partial shade; Venus is more heat-tolerant and disease-resistant than Cornus florida and performs better in zone 9 than the native species.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Venus is the US National Arboretum's most celebrated hybrid dogwood introduction — a first-generation hybrid between the native American flowering dogwood (Cornus florida) and the Chinese kousa dogwood (C. kousa) that produces flower bracts of extraordinary size: individual bracts (modified leaves surrounding the true flowers) reach 3–4 inches long, making the overall flower display twice the visual impact of either parent species. The enormous, pure-white, overlapping bracts create a spectacular late-April to May floral display (blooming slightly later than C. florida, extending the dogwood season) on a vigorous, upright tree. Venus inherits the best qualities of both parents: the early spring bloom timing and dense flowering of C. florida, combined with the superior heat tolerance, drought resistance, and disease resistance of C. kousa — specifically resistance to dogwood anthracnose that has devastated native C. florida populations. In zone 9, Venus performs reliably where native dogwood often struggles — the C. kousa genetics provide significantly better adaptation to Gulf South heat, humidity, and the summer conditions that stress C. florida. The large fruits that follow bloom are more showy than those of either parent. A landmark introduction for southern gardeners who love dogwoods.

plant_note: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, nutrient-poor, acidic medium (50/50 peat moss and perlite or long-fiber sphagnum moss) in full sun; water only with rain water or distilled water — tap water minerals and all fertilizers will kill plants. Venus flytrap requires a winter dormancy period (50°F for 3–4 months).
directions: Venus flytrap is the world's most famous carnivorous plant — a native of the Green Swamp region of North and South Carolina, where it grows in wet, nutrient-poor, acidic pine savannas maintained by periodic fire, trapping and digesting insects and spiders with its hinged, toothed, snap-trap leaves to supplement the minimal nutrients available in its impoverished native habitat. Each trap closes in milliseconds when two trigger hairs inside the trap are touched in quick succession — a failsafe mechanism that prevents wasted closure on raindrops or wind-blown debris; the trap then seals tightly and secretes digestive enzymes over 7–10 days to dissolve the prey. Despite its exotic appearance, Venus flytrap is hardy to zone 7 and requires a cold winter dormancy of 3–4 months (50°F) to remain healthy long-term; in zones 7–9 it can be grown outdoors year-round in appropriate bog conditions. Grow in a mix of 50% peat moss and 50% perlite or sand (no potting soil, no fertilizer), keep the medium wet using rain water or distilled water only, and provide maximum sun — the most common causes of failure are tap water, fertilizer, and insufficient sun.

common_name: Vera Cruz Rose Plumeria (Fragrant Deep Pink Plumeria)
plant_note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Vera Cruz Rose is a widely grown plumeria cultivar with rich, deep pink flowers and a strong, sweet, classic tropical fragrance.
directions: Plant cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Vera Cruz Rose is a widely grown, long-established plumeria cultivar producing rich, saturated deep pink flowers with a lighter blush toward the yellow-white center, carrying a strong, sweet, classic plumeria fragrance that intensifies in the evening. It is one of the more reliably vigorous and free-flowering pink plumeria cultivars, making it a popular choice for both garden specimens and lei-flower production in Hawaii. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids, it is deciduous in cooler weather, dropping its leaves and going fully dormant in winter, and requires complete dryness during that dormant period to prevent stem rot. In zone 9a it is best grown in a container: bring indoors dry and leafless once temperatures drop below 40F, store in a frost-free location without watering, and return outdoors in spring as new growth resumes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist to moderately moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel tolerates moist soil and periodic flooding along streams better than most other witch hazels.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade — vernal witch hazel is the earliest-blooming native Hamamelis species, opening its strap-petaled flowers in January through March while the plant is still dormant, even in the coldest conditions of zone 4–5. The flowers come in shades from pale yellow to orange to deep brick-red (dark orange-red in the commonly grown form) and have a sweet, spicy fragrance. Unlike the common witch hazel (H. virginiana), which blooms in fall, H. vernalis blooms in late winter and is the best native species for early-season pollinator value — providing nectar for early queen bumblebees and native mining bees on warm winter days. It is native to the gravel bars and rocky streambanks of the Ozarks and tolerates moist to wet conditions. The fall foliage is brilliant orange-yellow.

common_name: Vernal Witch Hazel, Ozark Witch Hazel
plant_note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel is native to the Ozark plateau and grows naturally along stream gravels — it is more tolerant of dry, calcareous soils than H. virginiana and slightly more drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant container or balled stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; vernal witch hazel is native to the Ozark plateau and grows naturally along stream gravels — it is more tolerant of dry, calcareous soils than H. virginiana and slightly more drought-tolerant once established. Hamamelis vernalis is among the first woody plants to bloom in late winter, producing intensely fragrant, small, yellow to reddish-orange, ribbon-petaled flowers on bare stems from January through March, filling the dormant winter garden with a spicy-sweet scent on any mild winter day; the flowers close when temperatures drop below freezing and reopen when temperatures rise, allowing them to survive late-winter freezes. The fall foliage is outstanding in shades of gold and orange; it is a major improvement over Asian witch hazels for naturalizing in eastern North American native gardens because it supports specialist witch hazel bees and other native insects.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil; excellent drought tolerance once established.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; speedwell is notably drought-tolerant and performs poorly in soggy or heavy clay conditions. The upright spikes of blue, pink, or white flowers bloom from late spring into summer and are excellent for cutting. Deadhead by removing spent spikes back to a lateral bud or leaf to extend the flowering period and prevent excessive self-seeding. Divide every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and an attractive mounding habit.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring before new growth begins or in fall, or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade; versicolor barrenwort tolerates dry shade under large conifers and shallow-rooted trees better than almost any other ornamental groundcover — it is one of the first plants to try in those notoriously difficult positions.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in well-drained, humus-rich to average soil in partial to full shade; versicolor barrenwort (Epimedium × versicolor) is a hybrid between E. grandiflorum and E. pinnatum subsp. colchicum that is widely regarded as the most vigorous, adaptable, and drought-tolerant of the garden epimediums — the cultivar 'Sulphureum' is particularly popular, with semi-evergreen, heart-shaped, compound leaves that emerge with a rich copper-red mottling in spring before maturing to medium green, and bright-yellow, four-spurred flowers produced in loose, airy sprays in mid-spring. The plant spreads more vigorously than the straight species epimediums by rhizomes, forming an increasingly dense, weed-suppressing groundcover mat that is exceptional in dry shade under conifers, maples, beeches, and other notoriously difficult root-competitive trees. In mild winters the foliage is semi-evergreen, providing year-round cover. Once established it is extraordinarily drought-tolerant and requires essentially no supplemental irrigation. 'Sulphureum' remains the standard against which other yellow-flowered epimediums are measured.

common_name: Vestitum Calanthe (Swan Calanthe, Christmas Calanthe, White-Cloaked Calanthe)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-draining terrestrial mix (bark, perlite, coco coir); Calanthe vestita is a deciduous orchid that loses its large, pleated leaves in fall as the pseudobulbs ripen — this is normal and expected. Reduce watering as leaves yellow in fall, then keep dry through the winter blooming period. The arching flower spikes bearing 10–25 large, white to pale rose flowers emerge from the leafless pseudobulbs in late fall and winter, making this an outstanding Christmas-season bloomer. Resume watering as new growth starts in spring. Tolerates brief temperatures to 35–40°F when dry. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-draining terrestrial orchid mix — Vestitum Calanthe grows most successfully when its seasonal deciduous cycle is respected: active growth and heavy watering in spring and summer, a gradual dry-down in fall, a dry winter rest during bloom, then resumption of watering with new spring growth. Calanthe vestita is a deciduous, terrestrial to semi-terrestrial, sympodial orchid in the Orchidaceae family native to Myanmar (Burma), Thailand, Laos, and Malaysia — a member of the large, diverse genus Calanthe which includes both evergreen and deciduous species. Among the deciduous Calanthe species, C. vestita stands out for its large, elegant flowers and its bloom timing: the arching flower spikes, 18–24 inches long and bearing 10–25 flowers, emerge from the leafless pseudobulbs in November through January — making it one of the finest winter-blooming orchids. Each flower is large (1.5–2 inches), long-lasting, and elegant: the broad, spreading sepals and petals are pure white to very pale pink, framing a large, four-lobed or three-lobed lip that is white with a distinctive orange, yellow, or rose-red callus or marking at the center — the 'cloak' (vestita, meaning cloaked) of the species name. The flowers are unscented but of a clean, formal beauty appropriate to their winter blooming season. Calanthe vestita contributed important parentage to many classic Calanthe hybrids developed in Victorian times, when deciduous Calanthe orchids were among the most popular orchids in cultivation. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late autumn or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; vetchleaf sophora is adapted to dry, rocky, alkaline hillsides in China and tolerates drought, poor soils, and extreme heat better than most flowering shrubs. Avoid rich, moist soils which produce lush but uncharacteristically vigorous growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; vetchleaf sophora is a spreading, elegant Chinese shrub in the pea family producing silvery-gray, pinnately divided foliage that has a delicate, fern-like texture throughout the season — and producing in May and June loose clusters of small, pale-blue to lilac-white pea flowers flushed with purple that are attractive to bees and butterflies. The combination of silvery, soft-textured foliage and subtle blue-white flowers gives the shrub a refined, mediterranean quality, somewhat resembling a drought-tolerant version of false indigo (Baptisia). It develops a somewhat stiff, twiggy branching structure that can be shaped to enhance the garden form, and the dried seed pods are ornamental in winter. Very drought-tolerant once established, it thrives in lean, rocky, alkaline soils similar to those of the Chinese highland slopes where it grows naturally — an excellent plant for dry, alkaline sites where most flowering shrubs perform poorly.

plant_note: Plant divisions or slips 18–24 inches apart in rows along the contour of a slope in full sun; vetiver is sterile and does not self-sow, making it non-invasive in spite of its vigorous growth. Established plants tolerate drought, flooding, and extreme heat.
directions: Plant slips or divisions along contour lines on slopes in full sun in any well-drained soil; vetiver is the world standard for low-cost erosion control on steep slopes — a tropical grass from South Asia with an extraordinary root system that penetrates 6–10 feet straight down (not laterally) and holds soil with remarkable efficiency against both water and wind erosion. The World Bank promotes vetiver hedgerow systems in developing countries as the most effective and affordable slope stabilization technology available. The aromatic roots are distilled to produce vetiver essential oil, a base note used in hundreds of fine perfumes. Unlike most grasses used for erosion control, vetiver is sterile and non-invasive — it produces no viable seed and spreads only by division. In zone 8–11 it is an outstanding low-maintenance erosion control plant for steep slopes, stream banks, and road cuts.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before first fall frost for spring bloom; in zone 9 sow October–November for February–April flowering. Victoria Blue forget-me-not is typically grown as a winter annual in zone 9 — seeds sown in fall germinate through cool weather, overwinter as small rosettes, and produce flowers in late winter through spring before setting seed and dying as temperatures rise. The self-seeding characteristic means a planting once established will typically reseed itself year after year in favorable locations. In zone 9 partial shade extends the blooming season by keeping the soil cooler and delaying bolting.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — forget-me-nots prefer cool, moist conditions and partial shade in warm climates; Victoria Blue is a compact, early-flowering forget-me-not cultivar producing an exceptional azure-blue that is one of the most intensely saturated blues available among spring-blooming cool-season plants. The tiny (0.25-inch), five-petaled flowers in the classic azure-blue with a white or yellow eye completely cover the low, mounding plant in a carpet of pure blue in late winter and spring — creating a luminous blue ground-level effect that is unmatched by any other cool-season annual. The 'Victoria' in the name refers to the compact, mounding habit selected by breeders for more formal garden use — unlike the sprawling, loose habit of wild forget-me-not, Victoria Blue forms tidy compact mounds ideal for edging, underplanting spring bulbs, and filling in between larger plants in spring garden combinations. The traditional spring combination of azure forget-me-nots with orange or yellow tulips creates one of the most visually striking color contrasts in the spring garden. In zone 9 forget-me-nots bloom in late winter (February–March), providing garden interest in the color-limited cool season.

plant_note: Sow in spring or summer; biennial that blooms the following spring.
directions: Victoria Blue is a darling, compact forget-me-not with petite, star-shaped blue flowers perfect for the front of a shade garden or alongside spring bulbs. Direct sow the seed in spring or summer, covering it lightly since darkness aids germination. As a biennial or short-lived perennial it often blooms the spring after sowing and then self-sows to return. Grow in part shade in moist, rich soil where it heralds spring with its cheerful color. Keep the soil evenly moist and let plants naturalize for a lasting display.

common_name: Victoria Blue Salvia (Classic Dark-Blue Compact Mealy Sage for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Victoria Blue is one of the most reliable cut flowers for Gulf South summer arrangements — the flower spikes hold their color well for 7–10 days in water.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Victoria Blue is the classic, standard-setting Salvia farinacea (mealy blue sage) cultivar — one of the most widely planted blue-flowering perennials for Gulf South gardens, producing dense spikes of deep violet-blue flowers with the white-powdery (mealy) stems that give the species its common name. The flower color of Victoria Blue is one of the most purely blue and deeply saturated available in a commonly grown summer perennial — the cobalt-blue to violet-blue spikes are more intensely colored than most Salvia farinacea varieties, providing a vivid blue accent in summer borders where true blue is difficult to achieve. Victoria Blue is seed-grown and therefore more variable than named vegetatively-propagated cultivars — but the best plants from a seed-grown flat are outstanding. In Gulf South zone 9, Victoria Blue grows as a short-lived perennial that often persists 2–4 years with occasional winter dieback and spring regrowth; it also performs as a long-lived annual from winter-grown transplants set out in spring. The long bloom season (spring through frost), excellent heat and drought tolerance, and outstanding cut-flower quality make Victoria Blue one of the most versatile blue annuals/perennials for Gulf South summer gardens. An excellent companion for Rudbeckia, Lantana, and Gulf muhly grass in summer and fall borders.

plant_note: Sow in spring or summer; biennial that blooms the following spring.
directions: Victoria Pink is a compact forget-me-not with petite, star-shaped pink flowers that attract pollinators and pair beautifully with spring bulbs. Direct sow the seed in spring or summer, covering it lightly since darkness helps germination. As a biennial or short-lived perennial it typically blooms the spring after sowing and self-sows to return year after year. Grow in part shade in moist, rich soil, keeping it evenly watered. Let plants naturalize at the front of shady beds for a soft, spreading carpet of color.

common_name: Victoria Water Lily (Royal Water Platter, Queen Victoria Water Lily)
plant_note: Start from seed indoors in warm water (80–90°F) in late winter and transplant to an outdoor pond or large water feature after last frost when water temperature reaches 75°F+; Victoria amazonica grows extremely rapidly once established in warm water. It requires a large water feature (minimum 20×20 feet, 3–4 feet deep) to reach its full glory. In zone 9, grow as a warm-season annual — plants cannot survive cold water below 60°F. Botanical gardens and public water gardens throughout the Gulf South grow Victoria species annually as statement plants.
directions: Plant in full sun in large, warm, fertile ponds or water features — Victoria amazonica requires the warmest, sunniest conditions and a large volume of nutrient-rich water for its enormous, rapid growth. Victoria amazonica is the world's largest water lily, producing the most spectacular leaves of any aquatic plant: circular, flat, floating pads up to 10 feet across (in exceptional specimens) with upturned margins 4–8 inches high that give them the appearance of enormous green trays or pizza-pan platters on the water surface.
