The berry clusters are produced abundantly in August through November, persisting on the bare stems into winter after the leaves fall, providing food for at least 40 species of songbirds and game birds. The leaves of American beautyberry contain callicarpenal, a compound with documented mosquito-repellent activity that has long been used in folk tradition. Beautyberry grows as a loose, arching shrub that benefits from hard pruning in late winter — cutting back by one-third to one-half stimulates vigorous new growth that produces the most prolific berry clusters in the same year. Self-sows in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Divide basal suckers in spring or plant large container-grown specimens in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; white bird of paradise grows slowly to tree proportions and requires ample space — allow at least 10 feet on all sides for a mature specimen.
directions: Divide basal suckers or plant large container specimens in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; white bird of paradise is the giant tree-form relative of the familiar orange bird of paradise (S. reginae), developing massive, paddle-shaped, blue-green leaves up to 6 feet long on tall, bamboo-like trunks — producing a dramatic, tropical architectural effect in the landscape. The flowers are spectacular when they appear: large, boat-shaped spathe bracts of deep purple-blue cradle blue-and-white flower petals. The plant is extensively used as a dramatic indoor specimen (the most popular tropical foliage plant in US interior landscaping) and as an outdoor landscape focal point in zones 10–12. Tolerates partial shade and indoor low light better than most tropical trees, though outdoor plants in full sun are most vigorous. Outstanding as a large-scale specimen in courtyards, entrances, and pool gardens in zone 10–12 landscapes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; white boneset grows naturally in dry to moist, sandy, acidic, open pine woods, flatwoods, and sandhills of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain. It is better adapted to dry, sandy conditions than common boneset.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, sandy, lean, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; white boneset is a Coastal Plain native eupatorium of dry sandy pinewoods and sandhills, particularly common across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain from Virginia to Texas. Unlike the moisture-loving common boneset (E. perfoliatum), white boneset thrives in dry, sandy, acid soils of longleaf pine flatwoods — making it an outstanding native pollinator plant for dry, infertile, sandy soils where few other flowering perennials excel. The flat-topped clusters of pure white flowers in late summer attract an extraordinary diversity of small native bees, wasps, flies, beetles, and butterflies including both skippers and swallowtails. Plant in dry, sandy naturalistic garden settings in zone 9a where it requires almost no supplemental water once established.

common_name: White Burma Orchid (Snow-White Thunia, Phaius Thunia)
plant_note: Plant divisions or detached leafy stem sections in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained orchid bark and soil mix; Thunia alba is a deciduous orchid — its tall, reed-like canes grow actively in spring and summer, flower at the tips in early summer, then shed their leaves in fall as the canes die back, leaving dormant cane bases. Keep nearly dry through winter. Requires cool to moderate winter temperatures (45–60°F) for best performance. The terminal clusters of large white flowers in June–July are spectacular. Propagate from stem cuttings or by removing offsets. Zone 9 in containers; outdoors zone 10+. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil or orchid bark mix during the active growing season — White Burma Orchid grows vigorously in warm, humid conditions from spring through early fall and requires consistent moisture to develop its tall, leafy canes. Thunia alba is a deciduous terrestrial to semi-epiphytic orchid native to Myanmar (Burma), Yunnan Province of China, northeastern India, and Nepal in the Orchidaceae family, producing one of the most spectacular terminal flower displays of any terrestrial orchid relative to its size. The plant grows tall, upright, reed-like canes (2–4 feet) clothed in alternate, elliptical, gray-green leaves throughout the growing season. In early summer (June–July), the growing tip of the cane produces a large, pendant, multi-flowered inflorescence of 5–12 large (2–3 inch) flowers: pure white petals and sepals with a yellow-orange to orange, fringed lip decorated with purple veins — the combination of the pure white outer parts and the brightly colored, frilled, intricate lip creating a flower of considerable beauty. After blooming, the canes continue to grow slightly, then begin shedding leaves from the base upward as the plant enters dormancy. The leafless canes can be detached and rooted as cuttings — a convenient propagation method. A showy and relatively easy deciduous orchid for zone 9-11 with cool winters. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; white butterfly ginger is one of the most powerfully fragrant flowering plants cultivated in warm climates — the pure white, butterfly-shaped flowers releasing an intense, sweet, exotic fragrance that carries a considerable distance in evening air. It is the national flower of Cuba (known as Mariposa) and has naturalized throughout the tropical world. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a reliable perennial, dying back in winter and resprouting vigorously in spring. Thrives in moist, boggy conditions; can grow at pond margins.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, moderately to richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; white butterfly ginger is regarded by garden enthusiasts in warm climates as one of the most intensely fragrant of all flowering plants — a native of the Himalayan foothills of India and Nepal (naturalized throughout tropical Asia, the Caribbean, and subtropical America) that produces in summer and autumn large, terminal spikes of pure-white, butterfly-shaped flowers with an extraordinarily powerful, sweet, exotic, slightly jasmine-like fragrance of unusual complexity and intensity that fills the garden air, particularly in the warm evenings when the fragrance intensifies and carries for considerable distances. The individual flowers are the distinctive hedychium form: a long, narrow, trumpet tube opening to three spreading, pure-white upper petals (the 'butterfly' shape) with a central, broad, pure-white labellum and two narrow, lateral staminodes creating the characteristic butterfly appearance. They are produced in succession on terminal spikes held above the long, lance-shaped, bright-green, ginger-family foliage for weeks in summer and fall. In zone 9 the rhizomes survive winter underground and resprout with considerable vigor each spring, producing clumps of erect, 5–7-foot stems by midsummer. Cuba named it the national flower under the name 'Mariposa' (butterfly). The national flower of Cuba and one of the quintessential plants of tropical and subtropical garden traditions worldwide.

common_name: White Calanthe (White Nun Orchid, Triple-Winged Calanthe, Evergreen Calanthe)
plant_note: Plant pseudobulbs or container-grown divisions in spring in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Calanthe triplicata is one of the most cold-tolerant Calanthe species, surviving brief temperatures to 28–30°F with mulch protection in zone 9a. It is evergreen (unlike the deciduous Japanese ebine calanthes), requiring moisture year-round. The tall spikes of white flowers with orange-red centers are produced in spring. Excellent for naturalistic shade gardens under large trees. Divide every 3–4 years. Non-toxic.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil — White Calanthe thrives in the deep, moist, organic-rich conditions of a shaded garden bed under large trees and will decline in dry or sunny positions. Calanthe triplicata is a clump-forming terrestrial orchid with an exceptionally wide natural range — one of the most geographically widespread of all orchid species, native from Japan, China, and India through all of Southeast Asia to Australia, New Zealand, and many Pacific Islands in the Orchidaceae family. The plant produces robust, oval pseudobulbs and 3–4 broad, pleated, rich-green leaves (12–20 inches) per pseudobulb. In spring, one or more erect flower spikes 18–36 inches tall emerge from the base, each bearing 10–25 flowers in a showy raceme. The flowers are white to pure white, approximately 1.5 inches across, with the central lip distinctly yellow-orange to orange at the center and three-lobed — the 'triplicata' (triple) refers to this three-lobed lip structure. The two-toned white and orange center creates a clean, elegant flower display. As one of the most cold-tolerant of the Calanthe species (rated to zone 9), and as an evergreen species requiring no winter rest period, C. triplicata is among the most adaptable and reliable of the terrestrial orchids for zone 9-12 shade garden planting. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall for spring germination, or sow in early spring; white campion self-seeds freely to naturalize and often behaves as a short-lived perennial or biennial in garden conditions.
directions: Sow direct in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; white campion self-seeds freely and often naturalizes in gardens, roadsides, and meadows without intervention once established. Silene latifolia (syn. Melandrium album) is a common European short-lived perennial or biennial weedy wildflower naturalized throughout North America; it produces softly hairy, sticky stems bearing oval leaves and sweetly fragrant, pure-white, 5-petaled flowers with deeply notched petals that open in the evening and at night, making it particularly attractive to moth pollinators. The nocturnal fragrance is delightful in the summer garden; white campion is an important pollinator plant and naturalizes beautifully in wildflower meadows and cottage-garden borders. Male and female flowers are on separate plants (dioecious); both are needed for seed production.

common_name: White Cedar (Pink Trumpet Tree, Variable-Leaf Tabebuia, Caribbean Lapacho)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun with well-drained soil; Handroanthus heterophyllus is one of the more cold-tolerant Handroanthus species, surviving temperatures to 24–28°F with some damage. In zone 9, established trees produce reliable spring bloom and may recover well from cold damage. Like other trumpet trees, it blooms best on bare branches after a dry period. Semi-deciduous — the leaves drop before spring bloom in cool or dry conditions. The common name 'White Cedar' reflects historical Caribbean timber use; the wood is extremely hard and durable.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to moderately fertile soil — White Cedar is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in the sandy, alkaline soils of coastal Gulf and Florida landscapes. Handroanthus heterophyllus (formerly Tabebuia heterophylla) is a medium-sized, semi-deciduous flowering tree native to the Caribbean islands (Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, Cuba, Jamaica, and the Lesser Antilles) in the family Bignoniaceae, the national tree of Puerto Rico. The species name 'heterophyllus' (variable leaf) refers to the variation in leaf form on individual trees — sometimes simple, sometimes 3-leaflet, sometimes 5-leaflet compound. In spring, the tree produces clusters of large (3–4 inch), trumpet-shaped flowers in soft lavender-pink to light rose-pink, blooming on bare or nearly bare branches before the new leaf flush — the delicate pink coloration is softer and more pastel than the vibrant magenta-pink of H. impetiginosus, creating a distinctly elegant bloom display. The tree is widely used in Caribbean and tropical American landscapes as a medium-sized flowering shade tree, and has proven successful in zone 9 Gulf South conditions where its relative cold tolerance, drought adaptability, and spring flower display make it one of the better choices among the many beautiful but sometimes tender Handroanthus trumpet trees.

plant_note: Plant tubers in spring when soil temperature reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant April–June. In zone 9 caladiums are perennial — leave tubers in the ground year-round in frost-free areas, but lift and store in mild zones where frost occurs. White Christmas is particularly striking in dappled shade under trees, where the bright white leaves illuminate dark areas. Reduce water and allow tubers to go dormant when foliage declines in fall; store at 60°F minimum if digging.
directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, acidic soil — caladiums require warmth above all else and tolerate deep shade better than most foliage plants; White Christmas is one of the most classic and enduring caladium cultivars, producing large, arrow-shaped leaves with dramatic nearly all-white blades set off by bright green veins and a narrow green margin — the effect of a mass planting under tree shade is startlingly bright and luminous, as the white leaves reflect available light and appear to glow in shade conditions where most plants would appear dull. Caladium is among the most effective plants for brightening dark, shaded areas of the landscape, and White Christmas is specifically sought for high-contrast shade planting because its white leaves provide the maximum illuminating contrast. The tropical foliage effect — large, bold, dramatic leaf patterns — also works extremely well in containers on shaded patios and porches. In zone 9 White Christmas performs as a reliable perennial, returning each summer from established tubers with increasing size and vigor each year.

common_name: White Cloud Muhly Grass (White-Flowered Gulf Coast Muhly Grass Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Cloud produces its best display in late September through November in the Gulf South — plant in spring for full development by fall bloom time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Cloud is the pure-white-flowered cultivar of Gulf Coast muhly grass (Muhlenbergia capillaris) — producing the same spectacular fall display of airy, cloud-like flower and seed head masses as the standard pink-to-reddish-pink species, but in a pure, soft white rather than the warm pink-magenta of the species. The white flower clouds have a cool, ethereal quality — a mist of white above the fine-textured green foliage — that creates an entirely different aesthetic from the warm, romantic pink of standard muhly: White Cloud works beautifully in white-and-silver garden themes, with blue-violet companions (blue salvias, ageratum, fall asters), or in naturalistic plantings where a softer, more naturalistic tone is desired. The fall bloom season (September–November) is identical to the species — a time when few other native grasses or perennials are at peak display, making White Cloud outstanding for fall garden interest. Like the species, White Cloud is exceptionally drought-tolerant, adapted to full sun, and thrives in poor, lean soils where fertility is minimal and drainage is good. Shear close to the ground in late winter before new growth begins. White Cloud is native in origin, supports a wide range of native seed-eating birds through winter, and requires absolutely minimal maintenance once established.

common_name: White Cloud Texas Sage (White-Flowered Cenizo Shrub)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–8.0), lean soil in full sun; White Cloud absolutely requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate standing water or heavy wet clay soil; plant in raised beds or berms in the humid eastern Gulf South.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, alkaline to neutral, lean soil in full sun; White Cloud is the white-flowered cultivar of Texas sage (cenizo, Leucophyllum frutescens) — producing the same outstanding silver-gray, small, soft, woolly foliage and the remarkable humidity-triggered synchronized blooming behavior as the purple-flowered species, but with pure white flowers that create an entirely different aesthetic. The white-flowered display is particularly striking against the silver-gray foliage — an all-silver-and-white combination that has a cool, refined quality in contrast to the warm purple-on-gray of standard cenizo cultivars. White Cloud's bloom response to humidity or rainfall (a sudden mass flowering of white across the entire shrub following a rise in relative humidity or rain event) is one of the most dramatic natural phenomena in southwestern ornamental horticulture. The white flowers pair beautifully with blue-purple companion plants (blue salvias, Russian sage) for a traditional blue-and-white planting combination, and with ornamental grasses whose warm golden tones provide contrast. Like all Leucophyllum, White Cloud requires excellent drainage and lean soil — excessive water and fertility produce soft growth and reduce the tight, silver-gray character of the natural plant. In zone 9 west of the high-humidity coastal zone (San Antonio area, central Texas), White Cloud is exceptionally hardy and reliable; in the humid Gulf Coast proper, good drainage is essential.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in moist to wet, strongly acidic, sandy or peaty soil in partial shade to full sun; white colicroot grows naturally in acidic, seasonally wet savannas, flatwoods, and bogs and requires specific acidic, low-nutrient soil conditions — do not add lime or fertilizer.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), sandy or peaty, low-nutrient soil in partial shade to full sun; white colicroot is a native perennial of the eastern and southeastern US coastal plain and Piedmont, growing naturally in open, wet, acidic savannas, pine flatwoods, bogs, and roadside ditches, where it produces a flat basal rosette of smooth, pale-green, lance-shaped leaves and a tall, wand-like spike of small, mealy-white, tubular flowers with a distinctive bumpy, granular texture — the species name farinosa means 'floury' and refers to the rough, mealy surface of the flower tube. In bloom from May to August, the white wand-like spikes are one of the more distinctive and unusual native wildflower forms and are excellent for naturalistic planting with pitcher plants, sundews, and other bog-community species. The plant has a long history of use in traditional Appalachian and Native American medicine for digestive ailments. Never add lime, compost, or fertilizer to the planting site.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; white correa is the most salt-tolerant and coastal-hardy of the commonly grown correas — native to the exposed coastal cliffs and headlands of southeastern Australia where it experiences constant salt spray and wind. It blooms in autumn through winter, providing white star-shaped flowers when few other correas are in bloom. The dense, rounded habit with attractive silver-green foliage provides year-round interest.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; white correa differs from the pendant-tubular C. reflexa in producing starry, white, open, four-petaled flowers — the petals reflexing fully to create an open, flat, white star rather than a hanging tube. The flowers are produced in autumn through winter from terminal clusters on the tips of arching branches covered in attractive, oval, gray-green leaves with a slightly woolly or tomentose texture underneath. The overall effect of a plant in flower — masses of small, clean, white, four-petaled stars scattered across the dense mound of gray-green foliage — is simple and elegant. Native to the exposed, salt-sprayed coastal cliffs and headlands of southeastern Australia from New South Wales to South Australia and Tasmania, it is the most salt-tolerant and wind-resistant of all the commonly grown correas — thriving in positions that defeat most ornamental shrubs. An excellent, reliable plant for coastal gardens in zone 9 where salt spray, wind, and lean, sandy soil combine to limit the range of ornamental shrub choices. Provides winter flowers, attractive foliage, and year-round bird habitat.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring after frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–May. Plant with the neck of the bulb at or just below soil surface — do not bury too deep. Crinum x powellii 'Album' is among the most cold-hardy of all crinum lilies, tolerating temperatures to about 5°F when the bulbs are well-mulched — hardy in zones 7–10 as a permanent landscape bulb. In zone 9 it is essentially evergreen, with the large, strap-like foliage persisting through mild winters. Established clumps multiply freely; dig and divide offsets every 4–5 years when blooming declines. The large bulbs resent disturbance once established — site carefully and allow permanent placement.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained to moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Crinum x powellii 'Album' adapts to a wide range of soil and light conditions and is one of the most versatile large bulbs for zone 9; White Crinum is one of the most reliably large and spectacular summer-blooming bulbs for Southern gardens, producing huge, fragrant, pure white funnel-shaped flowers (4–5 inches across) on tall, sturdy scapes that emerge above the broad, strap-like foliage in July and August — the peak of summer when most spring bulbs are long finished and fall-blooming plants have not yet begun. Crinum x powellii 'Album' is a hybrid between two South African species that has proven exceptionally cold-hardy for a crinum, extending the growing range well north of most other crinum lilies. The pure white, lily-like flowers (each scape bears 6–12 blooms in succession) are powerfully fragrant in the evening — a feature that makes White Crinum particularly effective near patios, walkways, and outdoor living areas where the fragrance can be appreciated. As a permanent, low-maintenance, long-lived landscape bulb for zone 9 that returns reliably year after year and gradually multiplies into impressive clumps, White Crinum fills the large-scale, summer-blooming bulb niche with a kind of reliable permanence that annual summer bulbs cannot match.

common_name: White Duranta (White-Flowered Golden Dewdrop Shrub with Golden Berries)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the golden-yellow berries of Duranta are toxic if eaten by humans and pets — plant away from areas where berry consumption is likely.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; White Duranta ('Alba') is the white-flowered form of golden dewdrop (Duranta erecta) — a widely grown tropical shrub native to the Americas that produces arching, cascading branches of small, white flowers (rather than the blue-purple of the species) followed by the showy strings of golden-yellow berries that give the plant its common name 'golden dewdrop'. The white flower and golden berry combination creates an elegant, clean color scheme distinct from the blue-and-gold of standard Duranta. Duranta is one of the most important butterfly and hummingbird plants for Gulf South gardens — the flowers attract monarch butterflies, queen butterflies, sulphur butterflies, and a wide range of native bees throughout the long bloom season (summer through fall), making it an outstanding pollinator plant in full-sun borders and along fence lines. The golden-yellow berry clusters persist through fall and are consumed by mockingbirds, catbirds, and other frugivorous birds. In zone 9, Duranta grows as a perennial shrub in protected locations, often killed to the ground by hard freezes but returning vigorously from the roots in spring. The fast-growing, arching habit means established plants can reach 6–8 feet in a single warm season. The berries are toxic if eaten — a caution for households with small children or pets that might be attracted to the colorful fruits.

subcategory: Egyptian sacred night-blooming aquatic water lily
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring in full sun in aquatic pots with heavy clay loam under 6–18 inches of warm water in zone 9–12; the White Egyptian Lotus is a tropical night-blooming water lily native to the Nile Delta, East Africa, and Southeast Asia — one of the most ancient sacred aquatic plants in human history — bearing large, fragrant, white flowers with prominent yellow stamens that open at dusk and close by midmorning.
directions: Plant Nymphaea lotus tubers in heavy, unamended clay loam in large aquatic pots submerged under 6–18 inches of warm water in full sun; top-dress monthly with aquatic fertilizer tablets and maintain water temperatures above 65°F for active growth; lift tubers and overwinter indoors in a bucket of water in zone 9 and colder. The White Egyptian Lotus is a night-blooming tropical water lily sacred in ancient Egyptian religion and art — depicted extensively on temple walls, papyrus scrolls, and tomb paintings, where it symbolized creation, rebirth, and the sun. Unlike the Blue Lotus (Nymphaea caerulea) which opens at sunrise, Nymphaea lotus opens at dusk and closes the following morning; flowers are strongly fragrant, white to pale pink at the tips, 6–10 inches across, and held well above the water on strong stalks. The toothed, slightly wavy leaf margins distinguish Nymphaea lotus from other white water lilies. Native to the Nile Delta and East Africa, the species has also become naturalized throughout Southeast Asia where it grows wild in rice paddies and irrigation canals. In zone 9, overwinter as for other tropical water lilies; in zone 10–12, it may persist year-round in garden ponds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 10–12; White Elephant Palm is an extremely rare, slow-growing, understory fan palm endemic to just two forest areas in peninsular Thailand (Khao Nor Chuchi in Krabi Province) — critically endangered in the wild — producing a crown of large, circular fan fronds with brilliant white undersides that flash silvery-white when the fronds move in the wind.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly to strongly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; Kerriodoxa elegans requires consistently moist, humid, shaded conditions — protect from direct sun, cold below 45°F, and dry winds; the white frond undersides are the primary ornamental feature and must be positioned where they can be viewed from beneath. Kerriodoxa elegans (White Elephant Palm or Elegant Kerriodoxa) is an exceptionally rare, slow-growing, monotypic fan palm endemic to an extremely restricted habitat: the lowland rainforests of Khao Nor Chuchi and one or two adjacent forest areas in Krabi Province, peninsular Thailand, making it one of the rarest palms in the world by natural distribution — classified as Critically Endangered by IUCN. The name 'White Elephant Palm' references both the rarity (white elephants being considered sacred and extremely rare in Thai culture) and the striking ornamental feature: large, circular fan fronds (2–3 feet across) with deep-green upper surfaces and brilliant, chalky-white to silver-white lower surfaces — when the fronds move in a breeze, the alternating flash of green and white is spectacular. The palm is short to medium-trunked, reaching 10–15 feet in cultivation over many years, with a compact, elegant habit. Primarily of interest to specialized tropical palm collectors and botanical gardens. Always purchase nursery-propagated specimens — never wild-collected.

subcategory: Pacific Northwest native shade spring bulb
plant_note: Plant corms in fall 3–4 inches deep in partial to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in zone 4–8; White Fawn Lily (Oregon Fawn Lily) is a graceful, spring-blooming native bulb of Pacific Northwest open woodland and forest edges from Vancouver Island and western Oregon to northern California — producing beautiful, reflexed, pure-white flowers with creamy-yellow centers above pairs of handsomely mottled, bronzy-green and silver-grey leaves.
directions: Plant Erythronium oregonum corms in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; keep consistently moist in spring and allow to dry out somewhat in summer during dormancy; plant in colonies of 10–25 for the best naturalistic effect; mark planting areas as the plants disappear completely by midsummer. White Fawn Lily is one of the most elegant of all Pacific Northwest native wildflowers — blooming early in spring before the tree canopy leafs out in the dappled shade of western red cedar, Douglas-fir, and bigleaf maple forests. The reflexed, nodding flowers with their upswept petals (resembling the style of a Turk's Cap lily) are pure white with bright yellow anthers and a cream-yellow center; below the flower, a pair of broad, succulent leaves with beautiful maroon-and-silver mottling emerges from the ground. Naturally forms spreading colonies from corm offsets and self-sowing; in suitable woodland garden conditions it will slowly naturalize and spread to carpet large areas. The mottled leaves are among the most attractive foliage patterns in spring bulbs. An outstanding companion for Trillium, native ferns, Dicentra, and spring wildflowers in Pacific Northwest woodland gardens; tolerates more summer moisture than many Erythronium species.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; white fir is the most drought-tolerant of the native North American firs, adapting to drier, more continental conditions than other firs. More tolerant of heat and drought stress than Engelmann spruce or balsam fir.
directions: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; white fir is among the most elegant and garden-worthy of the native North American firs — notable for its long, curved, distinctively blue-gray to blue-green needles that are arranged in a beautifully symmetrical pattern on each branch. The blue-gray form (sometimes called 'concolor fir' in the nursery trade) has striking, ice-blue foliage that rivals Colorado blue spruce in color intensity but with a much more graceful habit. White fir is significantly more drought tolerant than most firs, native to the drier mountain forests of the Sierra Nevada, Rocky Mountains, and Great Basin from Colorado to southern California. The Christmas tree industry uses white fir as an alternative to Fraser and balsam firs in western states, and it is one of the premier ornamental firs for large landscape settings in the West. Relatively more tolerant of dry summers than other firs.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring after temperatures are reliably above 50°F in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white firespike is even more shade tolerant than red firespike and performs beautifully as an understory plant under large shade trees in humid Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; white firespike is a lesser-known but equally attractive relative of the scarlet-flowered firespike (Odontonema tubaeforme), producing tall, graceful spikes of pure white tubular flowers on dark, glossy-leaved plants in late summer and fall. It is an outstanding shade-garden perennial for zone 9–12, providing important late-season white flower color in deep shade conditions where most other white-flowering plants require more light. The white flowers are particularly effective at brightening dark corners of the garden and glow beautifully in evening light. Like red firespike, it grows most vigorously and productively in the bright shade of large trees or pergolas; it is somewhat more cold-sensitive than the red species and benefits from mulching in zone 9. Propagate from stem cuttings taken in summer. White firespike is less commonly available than red firespike but increasingly offered by specialty nurseries in the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped specimens in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; white fringetree establishes slowly but is long-lived and exceptionally adaptable once rooted in. It is dioecious — female plants produce ornamental blue-black fruits attractive to wildlife if a male is nearby, though both sexes flower showily. Seed requires warm stratification followed by cold stratification and may take 18 months to germinate; nursery-grown transplants are strongly preferred.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; white fringetree is one of the most spectacular native flowering trees of the eastern United States, erupting in late April and May in airy, drooping panicles of pure-white, strap-like petals that give the effect of shimmering white fringe covering the entire canopy — often before or just as the leaves emerge, which amplifies the floral display dramatically. Chionanthus virginicus is dioecious: female plants produce loose clusters of olive-sized, blue-black, grape-like fruits in late summer that are highly attractive to birds, particularly thrushes, mockingbirds, and waxwings; male plants typically produce slightly showier and more fragrant flower clusters. Exceptionally adaptable to a wide range of soil types including clay, loam, and sandy soils, and tolerant of urban conditions, air pollution, and occasional flooding once established — making it an outstanding choice for residential landscapes, streetscapes, and naturalistic borders throughout zones 3–9. Grows slowly at 6–10 inches per year; patience yields a magnificent specimen that can live for decades with virtually no maintenance.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall where plants are to grow, or allow existing plants to self-sow freely; white fumewort self-sows into cracks and crevices in walls, steps, and paving where it often thrives better than in cultivated soil. It tolerates dry shade under trees. Unlike blue-flowered C. flexuosa, this species blooms continuously from spring through fall without a summer rest.
directions: Sow seeds in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; white fumewort is one of the finest and most long-blooming shade perennials available — a European native producing delicate, finely divided, blue-green foliage resembling bleeding heart or maidenhair fern, topped continuously from April through November with clusters of small, tubular flowers in creamy-white with a yellow tip. Unlike many shade perennials with limited bloom seasons, this species is genuinely in flower for most of the growing season in mild climates, filling the shade garden with a constant veil of soft white. It is a natural wall and pavement plant, spontaneously colonizing cracks in stone, brick, and mortar where it often self-sustains indefinitely, and is particularly charming growing from walls and between paving stones where organic soil would be unsuitable. Related to the blue C. flexuosa and yellow C. lutea, it occupies the same garden role as the yellow species but in white — longer-blooming and more shade-tolerant than many competitors.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant in spring into well-drained soil.
directions: White gaura brings airy elegance with long, delicate stems and butterfly-like white blooms that dance in the breeze above the foliage. Start seed indoors 8 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Its deep taproot makes it drought-tolerant once established, so avoid soggy ground and heavy feeding. Cut back spent flowering stems to encourage a fresh flush of bloom through summer and fall. Hardy in zones 5 to 9, it adds graceful height and motion to beds and borders.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–4 inches deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun after soil warms above 60°F; white ginger lily thrives in dappled light under tall trees and along stream banks in zone 7–11.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 2–4 inches deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered light in spring after soil warms above 60°F; white ginger lily is outstanding for Gulf Coast and zone 7–11 gardens where its intensely fragrant butterfly-white flowers perfume the garden in late summer and fall with one of the sweetest scents in the plant world. The tall, reed-like stems with broad tropical-looking leaves create bold textural interest from late spring through frost, making it an excellent specimen and a striking backdrop in mixed borders. In zone 7–8 the rhizomes may freeze to the ground in hard winters but re-emerge reliably from the roots in spring if protected with a thick mulch layer; in zone 9–11 it is evergreen. Divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in spring to maintain vigorous summer-to-fall flowering.

common_name: White Ground Orchid (Pure-White Hardy Chinese Terrestrial Orchid)
plant_note: Plant corms in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; 'Alba' is the white-flowered form of the Chinese ground orchid — the pure white flowers have a more refined, elegant quality than the typical magenta-pink of the species.
directions: Plant corms in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; 'Alba' is the pure-white flowered form of Bletilla striata (Chinese ground orchid) — one of the easiest and most rewarding terrestrial orchids for shade garden planting, producing clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), delicate, pure-white orchid-form flowers in April–May on upright stems above pleated, strap-shaped foliage. The flowers are genuinely orchid-shaped — the characteristic labellum (lip) and lateral petals are clearly visible in each small flower — providing the exotic quality of an orchid in a remarkably hardy, easy-to-grow terrestrial bulb that naturalizes reliably in zone 9 shade gardens. 'Alba' differs from the standard pink-magenta Bletilla striata in its pure-white flower color — a crisp, clean white with no pink tones that creates a refined, elegant effect in woodland shade plantings. The pleated, strap-shaped foliage (12–18 inches) is attractive through the growing season and the winter dormancy is unobtrusive. Ground orchids naturalize slowly over years, forming expanding clumps that can be divided in early spring before new growth begins. In zone 9, ground orchids grow best in the partial to full shade of deciduous trees where they receive some winter sun and full summer shade — the classic woodland edge condition of their natural habitat. Combine with hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials for spring bloom in the shadow garden.

plant_note: Scatter seeds in fall onto dry, open ground in partial sun to light shade along woodland edges or roadsides — this adaptable southeastern native tolerates a range of well-drained soils from sandy loam to clay as long as drainage is adequate. Press seeds into the soil surface and allow natural winter precipitation to provide cold stratification. Plants form arching, billowy mounds that are especially effective massed on dry slopes or as an informal hedge along woodland margins.
directions: Direct-sow seeds in fall by broadcasting them onto bare, dry, well-drained soil and pressing them lightly against the surface without covering. Cold winter temperatures stratify the seeds naturally, and germination occurs in spring when soil temperatures climb above 55°F. This vigorous and drought-tolerant aster will form full, arching clumps of small-leaved stems by the second season, then erupt in masses of tiny white flowers with yellow centers in late fall — a critical late-season nectar source for migrating monarchs and native bees. Divide clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigor and control spread.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; white indigoberry is extremely tolerant of salt spray, sandy soil, and coastal conditions — one of the most salt-tolerant native shrubs available for south Florida and Gulf Coast landscapes.
directions: Direct-sow or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun to partial shade; white indigoberry (milkberry, prick-wood) is a spiny, evergreen native shrub of south Florida, the Caribbean, and coastal tropical Americas that is one of the most reliable and wildlife-valuable small shrubs for zone 9b–12 coastal and dry upland landscapes. Its small, white, fragrant, tubular flowers produce an indigo-blue to white, waxy berry that is a critical food source for mockingbirds, thrashers, bluebirds, and over thirty additional bird species — making it one of the most bird-attractive native shrubs of south Florida. The sharp, paired spines make it an excellent barrier hedge for security plantings, and the plant's extreme tolerance of salt spray, drought, and poor sandy soil makes it ideally suited to the harsh conditions of coastal landscapes where few other shrubs thrive. Slow-growing to 3–10 feet, it can be used as a hedge, a natural barrier, or allowed to grow as a specimen with an attractive, irregular branch structure. Largely absent from commercial nurseries but available from native plant nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white ironbark is more moisture-tolerant than most ornamental eucalyptus — native to the woodland and mallee scrub of southeastern South Australia and western Victoria where annual rainfall is higher. It blooms in winter through spring, with flower color varying from white to cream to pink to vivid red (subsp. rosea, the most ornamental pink form). One of the most cold-tolerant ornamental flowering eucalyptus, surviving moderate frosts.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white ironbark is one of the most adaptable and widely planted ornamental flowering eucalyptus — valued for its very long winter-to-spring blooming period, its moderate cold hardiness compared to tropical Australian species, and the variable, attractive flower color that ranges from white through cream, pink, and crimson depending on form. The subspecies rosea produces particularly vivid rose-pink to crimson-red flowers and is the most commonly grown ornamental form. The flowers are typical eucalyptus form — dense, brush-like clusters of stamens expanding from the falling operculum cap — in white, cream, or pink/red, providing nectar for birds throughout the winter and spring. The bark is smooth and white to pale gray-cream with shed patches of darker bark creating a mottled or streaked appearance. It is native to the drier woodlands of southeastern South Australia and western Victoria — a Mediterranean-climate woodland eucalyptus that tolerates more winter rainfall and moderate frost than the arid interior species, making it among the most adaptable ornamental gums for zone 9 coastal gardens. Outstanding as a street tree and garden specimen where both form and winter flowers are valued.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky, thin, oolitic limestone soil in partial shade to full sun; white ironwood grows naturally in the tropical hardwood hammocks of the Florida Keys where it is an uncommon component of the mature hammock canopy. It is rare and declining.
directions: Plant in well-drained, thin, rocky, slightly alkaline to neutral oolitic limestone soil in partial shade; white ironwood is a rare native tree of the tropical hardwood hammocks of the Florida Keys, a member of the soapberry family (Sapindaceae) producing trifoliate compound leaves with small, leathery leaflets and small white flower clusters followed by black, fleshy fruits. The black fruit gives the tree its alternate common name 'inkwood.' The extremely hard, dense wood was historically used for construction and tool handles, and the tree is sometimes confused with paradise tree (Simarouba). Critically threatened in the wild due to habitat loss in the Keys, white ironwood is an important species for native plant restoration in the Florida Keys and extreme south Florida. The fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons and other subtropical birds. A conservation plant worth growing in appropriate south Florida native gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, fertile, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 9–12); White Ixora (Ixora finlaysoniana) is a Southeast Asian native shrub bearing large, domed clusters of pure-white, 4-petaled, tubular fragrant flowers — far more fragrant than the common red Ixora coccinea — and is valued in Thai and Indian temple gardens for its pure white flower color and sweet honey-jasmine scent.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, acidic (pH 5.0–6.0), well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; White Ixora requires consistent moisture, good drainage, and acidic soil — iron chlorosis (yellowing leaves) occurs in alkaline soils and should be treated with acidified water and chelated iron supplements. Ixora finlaysoniana (White Ixora, Petch Lan Fah in Thai) is an evergreen shrub native to Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam, grown throughout tropical Southeast Asia, South Asia, and the Pacific for its large, rounded corymbs of pure-white, tubular, 4-petaled flowers held above glossy, dark-green foliage — and for its notably stronger, sweeter honey-jasmine fragrance compared to the familiar red-flowered Ixora coccinea of commerce. White Ixora carries deep cultural significance in Thai Buddhism, where the white flowers are offered at temples, shrines, and merit-making ceremonies, and in Hindu ritual use across South and Southeast Asia. Plants bloom continuously in warm, humid conditions and respond well to light pruning after each flush to encourage dense, compact growth and continuous flower production. Excellent for hedges, foundation plantings, and container specimens in subtropical and tropical gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; cool temperatures aid germination.
directions: White Lace produces pure-white, lacy flowers in stunning 3-to-5-inch clusters on strong stems and a compact, bushy habit that suits gardens large and small. Direct sow in early spring or fall, as the seed benefits from cool temperatures and darkness to germinate. Grow in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained soil. This long-lasting cut flower is striking massed or intermingled with colorful blooms. Deadhead to prolong flowering, and let some seed drop to encourage self-sowing.

common_name: White Lightning Trailing Lantana (White Spreading Weeping Lantana)
plant_note: Plant container plants after the last frost date in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; trailing lantana (Lantana montevidensis) is the lower-growing, spreading species compared to the upright Lantana camara — it stays under 18 inches but spreads 4–6 feet, making it outstanding for banks and slopes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; White Lightnin' is a white-flowered selection of Lantana montevidensis — the trailing or weeping lantana species that produces a prostrate to mounding, wide-spreading (4–6 feet wide) form that is fundamentally different in habit from the upright Lantana camara. While L. camara grows upright to 3–4 feet, White Lightnin' spreads along the ground and over embankments in a wide, horizontal carpet that is outstanding for slope stabilization, bank coverage, and flowing over retaining walls. The pure white flowers (unusual among lantanas, which are predominantly yellow, orange, and purple) create a clean, bright effect that combines well with any color of companion planting — providing the extraordinary heat tolerance and butterfly attraction of lantana without the color constraints of the more common yellow-orange-red types. Like all trailing lantanas, White Lightnin' is continuously blooming from last frost through hard frost in zone 9 with no deadheading required. The sterile or nearly sterile nature of L. montevidensis reduces the invasive concerns associated with L. camara berries. Outstanding for slopes, embankments, and as a spreading groundcover in hot, dry, difficult-to-water areas where most plants fail. Gulf fritillary and monarch butterflies visit the flowers constantly throughout the long bloom season.

plant_note: Plant container-grown vines after last frost in full sun to partial shade on a trellis, obelisk, or fence; White Mandevilla grows rapidly in warm conditions and can be kept in a container for portability. In zone 9, treat as a warm-season annual or bring containers indoors before frost. The species is slightly more cold-sensitive than red-flowered Mandevilla hybrids. Train the twining stems onto supports early — stems can become tangled if left to sprawl.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; White Mandevilla blooms most prolifically in full sun but tolerates morning sun with afternoon shade in zone 9, where this combination can extend the flowering season through the hottest months. Mandevilla boliviensis is a twining tropical vine from Bolivia and Ecuador that produces pure white, 3-inch, funnel-shaped flowers with a contrasting yellow center — a clean, elegant color combination that pairs beautifully with other tropical colors or with purely white garden designs. The flowers are produced profusely and continuously throughout the warm months on vigorous, evergreen stems clothed in glossy, dark-green, lance-shaped leaves. White Mandevilla is the primary white species used in breeding the modern 'White' selections of Mandevilla sold in mass-market retail — though most commercial 'white' Mandevillas are actually complex hybrids combining M. boliviensis with other species for improved plant size and flower production. Like all Mandevilla relatives (family Apocynaceae), the plant produces a milky latex sap when cut that is irritating to skin and eyes. In zone 9, it is one of the finest annual or temporary perennial vines for rapid seasonal color on trellises and fences, growing 6–10 feet in a single season.

plant_note: Plant nursery-grown stock in spring in sheltered coastal, estuarine, or tidal sites in full sun in Zone 10–11. White Mangrove typically occupies slightly higher, less frequently flooded ground than Red Mangrove. The seeds germinate rapidly after dropping; propagules should be planted immediately in appropriate coastal substrate. Never plant outside of natural range.
directions: White Mangrove is the most frost-sensitive of the three Florida mangrove species, typically occupying the landward fringe of the mangrove forest on slightly higher ground that is less frequently inundated than the zones occupied by Red and Black Mangrove. Distinguished by its pale, yellowish-gray bark and distinctive pairs of salt-excreting glands (nectaries) at the base of each leaf, White Mangrove lacks the dramatic prop roots of Red Mangrove and the pneumatophore air-root mats of Black Mangrove, though small peg-like root structures occasionally develop in waterlogged conditions. The flowers attract native bees and produce nectar, and the dense canopy provides critical nesting habitat for ibis, egrets, herons, and spoonbills in Florida's coastal rookeries. Restricted to frost-free Zone 10–11 coastal settings in the United States, White Mangrove is protected under Florida law and should only be planted from nursery stock within the appropriate coastal habitat.

plant_note: Plant divisions in early spring in consistently moist to saturated, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun at the margins of streams, ponds, or bog gardens; caltha leptosepala grows along snowmelt streams and is one of the earliest bloomers in mountain gardens, often flowering while snow still remains nearby.
directions: Plant divisions in early spring in consistently moist to saturated, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun at the margins of streams, ponds, or bog gardens; caltha leptosepala grows along snowmelt streams and is one of the earliest bloomers in mountain gardens, often flowering while snow still remains nearby. Caltha leptosepala is the white-flowered western counterpart to the familiar yellow marsh marigold (C. palustris), native to cold, high-elevation bogs, stream margins, and subalpine meadows from Alaska to New Mexico; it produces large, kidney-shaped, glossy, dark-green leaves and glistening, white, buttercup-like flowers 1–1.5 inches across with a central cluster of yellow stamens in early spring, often among the very first wildflowers to bloom after snowmelt. It is less commonly grown than C. palustris but adapts well to water garden edges and bog gardens in zones 3–7 where it blooms several weeks earlier than most spring perennials.

common_name: White Mexican Petunia (Compact White-Flowered Ruellia for Gulf South Borders)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; note that Ruellia simplex (including white-flowered cultivars) is listed as invasive in Florida due to prolific seeding — plant responsibly in Florida and consider sterile or non-seeding dwarf cultivars in sensitive areas.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; White Mexican Petunia is the white-flowered form of Ruellia simplex — a perennial Gulf South garden standard valued for extreme drought tolerance, long bloom season, and adaptability from full sun to deep shade, producing funnel-shaped, petunia-like flowers in pure white from spring through hard frost. The white flower color is cleaner and more visually versatile than the dominant purple of the straight species — more useful in moonlight gardens, white-themed borders, and combinations with deep blue or rich red companions where purple flowers would reduce contrast. Like all Ruellia simplex cultivars, the white-flowered form performs through brutal Gulf South summer heat without wilting, stopping, or requiring deadheading — the flowers drop cleanly in the morning and new blooms open daily throughout the growing season. The extreme heat, drought, and shade tolerance make Ruellia simplex uniquely versatile among perennial flowers: few plants perform acceptably in the full range from full sun to deep shade AND from drought to seasonal flooding. In zone 9, Mexican petunia grows as a reliable perennial, returning from the roots each spring and expanding by spreading rhizomes and self-seeding. The seeding behavior should be noted: the species is considered invasive in Florida wetlands and naturalized areas; plant responsibly and deadhead before seed set in ecologically sensitive areas. Outside of Florida, white Ruellia is widely used and appreciated as a versatile, near-indestructible perennial for difficult Gulf South garden positions.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost in a location with full sun and rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. In zone 9, choose a warm microclimate sheltered from cold north winds, and mulch deeply to protect roots from any winter cold snaps.
directions: Propagate from semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer, treating the basal cut with indole-butyric acid rooting hormone and maintaining high humidity and bottom heat of 75-85°F until rooting occurs in 6-10 weeks. Transplant rooted cuttings into fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in a warm, protected site and water thoroughly to settle the roots. Fertilize with a balanced slow-release fertilizer in spring and again in early summer, supplementing with a micronutrient drench if foliage yellows on alkaline soils. The intensely fragrant pure-white flowers are produced year-round in the warmest climates and peak in spring and summer; harvest individual blooms in the early morning for use in garlands or hair ornaments, as the fragrance is most potent just after opening.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for cold stratification and spring germination; or cold stratify seeds for 30 days and sow indoors 8 weeks before last frost. White milkweed grows naturally in dry to well-drained upland woods and woodland edges, tolerating more shade than most milkweeds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; white milkweed is one of the few native milkweeds adapted to grow in the dappled shade of open woodlands and forest edges rather than in open sun — a significant advantage for gardeners who want to support monarchs and other milkweed-dependent species in partially shaded situations. The rounded clusters of pure white flowers with a distinctive dark purple crown in the center are among the most attractive of any milkweed, combining visual elegance with remarkable fragrance. Growing naturally in dry to well-drained upland forest understories across the southeastern US, it is more drought-tolerant than its woodland habitat would suggest. An excellent companion for native ferns, wild ginger, and other woodland plants where it provides the critical role of milkweed host in shaded garden zones.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, lean, dry to moderately dry soil in partial shade; white mistflower is native to limestone hills and canyon slopes in south-central Texas and northeastern Mexico and thrives in rocky alkaline conditions where few other plants survive.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; white mistflower is one of the most spectacular fall-blooming native shrubs of the Texas Hill Country and Gulf South, covering itself in dense clusters of pure white, fluffy, ageratum-like flowers in October–November just when most other plants are going dormant. The fragrant flowers are outstanding for butterflies and late-season pollinators, including migrating monarch butterflies that use them as a critical nectar source during the fall migration. The plant is semi-evergreen in mild winters. It grows naturally in the shade of limestone canyon walls and cedars, making it one of the more shade-tolerant native fall-blooming shrubs available. The common name 'mistflower' refers to the soft, misty appearance of the white flower clusters. Cut back by one-third in early spring to encourage compact, dense growth.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most artemisias, white mugwort requires consistent moisture and shade tolerance makes it the best Artemisia for partially shaded positions.
directions: Artemisia lactiflora is exceptional among artemisias for its large, deeply divided, rich-green (not silver) foliage and for its tall panicles of creamy-white, softly fragrant flower plumes in late summer and fall that closely resemble astilbe or meadow rue; the flowers are excellent for cutting. It is the go-to artemisia for partially shaded mixed borders and is not invasive like many other species; it requires staking in windy positions and produces its best display in reliably moist, fertile soil enriched with compost. The cultivar 'Guizhou' has dark-purple-flushed foliage that is especially ornamental.

common_name: White Mussaenda (Philippine Mussaenda, White Flag Bush, Donna Luz)
plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late spring in full sun to partial shade with well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; White Mussaenda grows rapidly in zone 9-11 and blooms most heavily from late spring through fall when temperatures are warm. In zone 9a, it is frost-tender and must be protected — use as a large container specimen brought indoors in winter. In zone 9b-10, it can be grown outdoors as a large shrub. The Donna Luz and related hybrid forms produce vastly enlarged, more numerous white bracts than the original species.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; White Mussaenda grows most vigorously and blooms most heavily in full sun but tolerates and benefits from afternoon shade in zone 9's intense summer heat. Mussaenda philippica is a large tropical shrub from the Philippines in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that has produced some of the most spectacular ornamental hybrids in tropical horticulture — particularly through the Philippine breeding program that developed the 'Dona' series (Dona Aurora, Dona Carmen, Dona Luz, Dona Esperanza) named in honor of Philippine First Ladies, in which the small, typically 5-petaled flowers are surrounded by greatly enlarged, pure white, snowflake-shaped sepals (not petals) that cover the entire branch tips in a cloud of brilliant white. The ornamental display comes entirely from these enlarged sepals, which function to attract pollinators to the small true flowers within — a strategy shared with bougainvillea and poinsettia. The Dona Luz cultivar has become one of the most widely planted tropical ornamentals in zone 10-11 landscapes worldwide for its exceptionally long bloom season (essentially year-round in zone 10-11), clean white appearance, and dramatic presence as a large specimen shrub.

common_name: White Nancy Lamium (Classic Silver-Leaf White-Flowered Dead Nettle)
plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; White Nancy is one of the most widely planted lamium cultivars, forming a dense, silvery groundcover mat topped with pure white flowers in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. White Nancy is a longtime favorite lamium cultivar, producing heart-shaped leaves that are almost entirely silver with a narrow green edge, brightening dark shade year-round, and topped in spring with clusters of pure white, hooded flowers that add a further layer of light to a shaded bed. It spreads readily by surface runners to form a dense, quick-filling groundcover mat, making it useful under trees and shrubs where grass and many other groundcovers struggle, and it tolerates fairly dry shade once established. Shearing the mat back partway through summer, if it looks tired from heat, refreshes the foliage for a strong fall appearance.

common_name: White Nun Orchid (Monja Blanca, Skinner's Lycaste, Guatemala's National Flower)
plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in bark-based medium in a clay pot; Lycaste skinneri is a cool-growing orchid from Guatemala's highlands (4,000–8,000 feet) and requires cool nights (50–60°F) in fall and winter to trigger bloom. Without a cool-dry winter rest, the plant will not flower. Allow the potting medium to dry significantly between waterings during the winter rest (October–February); resume regular watering as new growth starts in spring. The flowers appear on separate stems from the base before or alongside new growth in late winter. Protect from temperatures below 40°F. Non-toxic to pets.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct morning light in bark medium in a clay pot — White Nun Orchid grows best in the cool, moist, well-ventilated conditions of highland cloud forest and appreciates the lower temperatures and clay pots that help the roots cool at night. Lycaste skinneri is a deciduous, sympodial epiphytic orchid native to Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Mexico in the Orchidaceae family, bearing the singular distinction of being Guatemala's national flower — honored as the 'Monja Blanca' (White Nun) for the pure white to pale pink of its large, waxy, fragrant flowers and the robe-like arrangement of the broad petals around the smaller, white lip. The plant produces large oval pseudobulbs with broad, pleated leaves that drop in fall before the winter bloom. From the leafless or newly leafing pseudobulbs in late winter to spring, 2–6 individual flowers emerge on separate, erect stems from the base of each pseudobulb — each flower is large (4–6 inches across), waxy, long-lasting (4–6 weeks), with three large, spreading, broadly oval white to pale pink sepals framing two smaller white petals and a small, three-lobed, white, slightly hairy lip. The flowers are lightly fragrant. Wild populations are critically endangered in Guatemala due to habitat loss and collection — all cultivated plants must be from legally propagated nursery stock. Lycaste skinneri has contributed to numerous hybrid orchids. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or early spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; white oak develops a deep taproot early and transplants best when small. Plant as a long-term investment — this is a multigenerational tree that rewards patience with an irreplaceable landscape presence.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white oak is one of the most majestic and ecologically important trees in eastern North America, growing slowly into a massive, wide-spreading giant with deeply furrowed gray bark and a broad, rounded crown that can span 80 feet or more. White oak acorns are widely recognized as the single most nutritious acorn for wildlife — lower in tannins than red oak acorns, they are eagerly consumed by white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, wood ducks, blue jays, and at least 180 other vertebrate species, making white oak the keystone wildlife tree of the eastern deciduous forest. The deeply lobed leaves turn attractive wine-red to russet-brown in fall. Growth is slow but steady — expect 12–15 inches per year — and the tree is exceptionally long-lived (centuries to over 500 years in natural settings). Despite the slow start, there is no native tree that surpasses white oak in landscape longevity, wildlife value, and grandeur.

plant_note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or slightly above the soil surface (unlike most bulbs) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to sandy soil in partial to full shade; white paintbrush lily is evergreen and should not be allowed to dry out completely — unlike most amaryllid bulbs, it does not require a dry dormant period and performs best with consistent, moderate moisture year-round.
directions: Plant bulbs with neck at or above soil level in well-drained, average soil in partial to full shade; white paintbrush lily is a South African evergreen bulb of the amaryllis family that is one of the easiest and most adaptable shade bulbs available for zone 9–12 gardens — a low-growing, tough, long-lived, evergreen plant producing a pair of broad, strap-shaped, dark-green, leathery, persistently glossy leaves that lie nearly flat on the ground and persist year-round, providing attractive foliage groundcover even out of flower. In autumn and winter, short stems bear compact, white, paintbrush-like flower heads — dense spherical clusters of small, white, tubular flowers with prominent white stamens creating a soft, fluffy, white-brush effect — followed by orange-red berries that are ornamental through winter. The primary virtue of white paintbrush lily is its exceptional shade and drought tolerance among evergreen bulbs; it grows remarkably well in the dry, deep shade under mature trees where most other bulbs and plants fail. It clumps and multiplies slowly by offsets. An underused but reliable and handsome shade groundcover bulb for zones 9–12.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after all frost danger has passed in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full to partial sun; white passionflower is frost-killed to the ground in zone 9 but reliably resprouts from the root, and is fully evergreen in frost-free zones 10-11.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after all frost danger has passed in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full to partial sun; white passionflower is frost-killed to the ground in zone 9 but reliably resprouts from the root, and is fully evergreen in frost-free zones 10-11. Passiflora multiflora is a vigorous native vine of Florida, the Caribbean, and Central America, producing an abundance of small, intricate white flowers with the characteristic passionflower structure that attracts pollinators throughout the warm season; it is a critical larval host plant for the Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterflies, making it an essential addition to Florida and Gulf Coast butterfly gardens. The vine climbs readily by tendrils and can be trained over a trellis or fence, or allowed to ramble as a groundcover in frost-free settings.

plant_note: Root cuttings 12–18 inches long in dry, gritty mix — allow cut ends to callus for 1–2 weeks before planting; grows readily as a container plant brought indoors in frost-prone areas.
directions: Root branch cuttings (allow cut ends to callus for 1–2 weeks) in gritty, very well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; white plumeria (Plumeria alba) is the species native to the Caribbean and Puerto Rico, prized for its narrow leaves and pure white flowers with a yellow eye that are intensely fragrant with a sweet, tropical, honeysuckle-like scent. The flowers are the classic blooms used to make Hawaiian leis and Indian garlands (gajra). Grows as a deciduous to semi-deciduous shrubby tree in the tropics and subtropics; in zone 10 it loses its leaves during the cool dry season but is cold-sensitive and damaged below 32°F. Extremely drought-tolerant and resistant to most pests once established. An iconic tropical ornamental suited to containers for gardeners in cooler zones.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; white prairie clover develops a deep taproot that makes transplanting very difficult — sow in a permanent location and rely on natural cold stratification over winter; light scarification or a 24-hour cold-water soak improves germination in spring plantings.
directions: Sow direct in fall in lean, very well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; white prairie clover is essentially the white-flowered counterpart to Dalea purpurea, sharing the same deep-taproot habit, prairie origin, and cultural requirements — it cannot be transplanted once its root system is established, so sow seeds in a permanent location and cold-stratify naturally over winter. Dalea candida is a nitrogen-fixing legume native to the same vast range of tallgrass, mixed-grass, and shortgrass prairies as purple prairie clover, from Manitoba and Saskatchewan south through the Great Plains to Texas and New Mexico; from June through August it produces the same elegant cylindrical flower heads as D. purpurea but in pure white with golden-yellow anthers, giving a cleaner, crisper floral effect that is especially striking when the two species are planted together in a prairie planting or pollinator meadow. The flowers are rich in nectar and pollen and attract a broad range of native bees, including specialist Dalea-foraging bees, mining bees, and many small sweat bees; like purple prairie clover it is a keystone species in prairie ecosystem restorations and is considered a high-value component of any native seed mix for the central United States. White prairie clover is slow to establish but essentially immortal once its deep root system is in place — it is drought-tolerant, fire-adapted, long-lived, and one of the finest native wildflowers available for lean, dry, sunny sites.

plant_note: Scarify seeds before sowing in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white prairie wild indigo develops a deep taproot and is very slow the first 2–3 years as it builds root mass. Do not move established plants — the deep taproot makes transplanting almost impossible after the first year. Plants become very long-lived and increasingly spectacular over decades.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; white prairie wild indigo is a tall, bushy native legume of the central prairie and open woodland edges, distinct from the Atlantic white wild indigo (Baptisia alba) in its more upright, taller habit and its preference for drier, leaner prairie soils. It produces tall spikes of pure-white pea flowers in May and June that are striking against the three-parted, blue-green leaves — one of the most architecturally impressive native wildflowers in bloom. The inflated seed pods that follow are dark purple to black and ornamentally striking, rattling in the wind and providing excellent dried flower material. As a deep-rooted nitrogen-fixing legume, it improves poor, lean soils over time and is drought-tolerant once established. An important pollen source for native bumblebees, particularly specialist bees that extract pollen by sonication (buzz-pollination) from the flowers. Once established, plants are extremely long-lived — potentially persisting 50 or more years without disturbance.

plant_note: Direct sow on the surface of bare, dry, lean, sandy or gravelly soil around last frost; does not transplant well due to a sensitive taproot.
directions: A southeastern US native prickly poppy of dry, sandy or rocky, disturbed open ground from Virginia to Florida and Texas; produces spiny, deeply lobed, silvery-veined, blue-green leaves and pure white, 6-petaled, crinkled-tissue-paper flowers 2-3 inches across with prominent yellow stamens from spring through summer. The yellow sap is toxic if ingested. Direct sow in spring on bare, dry, lean, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; does not transplant well and self-sows readily in open ground. An excellent low-care annual for dry, naturalistic Gulf Coast gardens and native roadsides.

common_name: White Queen Caladium (Classic Large White-Veined Fancy Caladium)
plant_note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 65°F; plant 1–2 inches deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade; White Queen is one of the finest white caladiums for brightening deep shade areas.
directions: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade; White Queen is one of the most classic and widely grown fancy-leaved caladium cultivars — producing large, heart-shaped leaves with pure-white centers, green margins, and distinctive red veins radiating from the central midrib through the white tissue, creating a dramatic three-color leaf pattern. The large white leaf areas reflect light effectively in shaded positions, making White Queen one of the brightest and most illuminating shade plants available — a single established clump can dramatically lighten a dark corner. Caladiums are among the premier foliage plants for Gulf South shade gardens, thriving in the hot, humid conditions that challenge many other shade plants. They emerge from tubers in late spring, develop through summer, and go dormant with the first cool fall temperatures (typically October in zone 9). In zone 9, the tubers can be left in the ground over winter if protected with 4 inches of mulch, or lifted and stored in a dry, warm location. For best performance, provide consistent moisture and avoid direct afternoon sun, which bleaches the white foliage and scorches the leaf margins. Feed monthly with a balanced fertilizer during the active growing season. The combination of heat tolerance, low light requirement, and spectacular foliage makes caladiums essential for Gulf South shade garden design.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 2–3 inches deep and 3–4 inches apart in spring or fall in any well-drained, moist to moderately dry soil in full sun to partial shade; white rain lily is extremely adaptable and easy to grow, naturalizing freely under lawn conditions and in garden borders. Plant in masses for maximum impact — a single bulb produces a modest display, but hundreds of bulbs blooming simultaneously after rain is spectacular.
directions: Plant bulbs in any well-drained, moist to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; white rain lily is one of the most reliable and effortless naturalizing bulbs for zones 7–11, producing masses of pristine white, crocus-like flowers — about 1.5 inches wide with yellow stamens — in late summer and fall, typically triggered to bloom within days of a summer rain after a dry period. The narrow, rush-like, grass-green leaves are present most of the year and are attractive in their own right; the plant multiplies freely by offsets to form an expanding clump over time. In zone 9 it is fully evergreen or semi-evergreen and blooms repeatedly through the warm season with each significant rainfall. It naturalizes beautifully in lawns, under trees, in borders, and in rock gardens, requiring essentially no care once established. Combine with pink Zephyranthes grandiflora, yellow Z. citrina, and salmon-peach Z. 'Grandjax' for a succession of bloom from spring through fall.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Costus arabicus tolerates brief drought better than some gingers once established but prefers consistently moist conditions and partial shade to prevent leaf scorch. One of the most shade-tolerant of the spiral gingers, making an attractive medium-sized specimen for partially shaded tropical-style gardens in zones 9–11.
directions: Plant rhizomes in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Costus arabicus (syn. Costus spicatus in some references) is a tropical Americas spiral ginger with the characteristic spiraling leaf arrangement of the Costus genus and attractive cone-like terminal flower heads producing white, orchid-like flowers with orange centers from summer through fall; it is one of the most shade-tolerant of the spiral gingers and makes an attractive, medium-sized specimen for partially shaded tropical-style gardens in zones 9–11. The rhizomes are used in traditional Caribbean and South American folk medicine as a diuretic and anti-inflammatory remedy.
