directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; wild tulip is a species tulip that dramatically differs from the large hybrid garden tulips in its ability to reliably naturalize and return year after year — spreading vegetatively by underground stolons to form expanding colonies that flower more profusely over time rather than declining as do most hybrid tulips. The flowers are smaller and more delicate than hybrid tulips, elegantly star-shaped when fully open, in clear, warm, soft yellow with a faint greenish flush on the outer petals — and they have a pleasant, sweet fragrance absent from most tulips. Native across a vast range from the Mediterranean to central Asia, it has naturalized in historical European orchards and vineyards where it was planted during the Renaissance. Outstanding for naturalizing in grass under deciduous trees, in orchard lawns, and in rock gardens where its modest size and naturalizing habit suit semi-wild plantings. One of the few tulips that succeeds in zone 9 because it does not require deep cold to perform.

common_name: Will Fleming Yaupon Holly (Narrow Columnar Native Holly)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, upright male selection of native yaupon holly that never needs shearing to maintain its columnar shape.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Will Fleming is a naturally narrow, strictly upright, columnar selection of the Gulf Coast native yaupon holly, discovered and named for a Texas landscape architect, and valued for providing the vertical accent of a formal columnar evergreen without any shearing or shaping required to maintain the shape. As a male selection it does not produce the red berries typical of yaupon holly, but its extreme drought tolerance, adaptability to both wet and dry soils, and complete indifference to heat and poor soil make it one of the toughest, most maintenance-free narrow accent shrubs available for Gulf Coast gardens. It works well as a narrow screen, foundation accent, or repeated vertical element along a walk or drive.

plant_note: Plant small container trees in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; willow oak transplants more easily than most oaks and is one of the best native trees for urban street and lawn use in the Southeast.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun; willow oak is one of the most graceful and distinctive of the native oaks, bearing narrow, willow-like leaves that give the tree an unusually fine-textured, airy appearance very different from other oaks. It grows naturally in moist bottomland forests and upland slopes throughout the Southeast and is one of the most widely planted native oaks as a street and lawn tree, valued for its tolerance of urban soils, relatively fast growth (1–2 feet per year), and adaptability. The small acorns produced abundantly from age 15 onward are a critical food source for wood ducks, mallards, wild turkeys, and many songbirds. The fine foliage turns attractive golden-yellow in fall before dropping cleanly, and the tree's upright-oval form matures into a large, handsome landscape specimen.

plant_note: Sow seeds in early spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; willow-leaf ox-eye thrives in poor, dry, alkaline, limestone-derived soils that are typical of its native Alpine meadow habitat. In rich soils it becomes floppy and short-lived. Deadhead regularly for a long bloom season; divide every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; willow-leaf ox-eye is a useful and underused European native perennial from Alpine and subalpine meadows of central and southern Europe, producing slender, willow-like leaves on upright stems and a prolonged succession of yellow, asterlike daisy flowers (1.5–2 inches across) with slightly twisted ray petals and darker yellow disc centers from June through September — one of the longest natural bloom seasons of any daisy-type perennial in undemanding conditions. The slightly twisted ray petals give the flowers an informal, loosely spidery quality distinguishing them from the more precisely regular rays of Leucanthemum or Helenium. It thrives in the poor, dry, alkaline soils of limestone gardens where more demanding perennials decline, making it a good choice for difficult, free-draining situations. Excellent for prairie-style plantings, gravel gardens, and naturalistic wildflower areas on calcareous soils. Long-lived in lean conditions, shorter-lived in rich soils. Attractive to bees and butterflies throughout its long season.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in lean, well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; willowleaf sunflower cold-stratifies naturally over winter and germinates reliably in spring; like Maximilian sunflower it benefits from lean, drier soils that keep stems upright and plants better proportioned — rich, moist soils encourage excessive vegetative growth and floppy stems.
directions: Direct sow in fall in lean, very well-drained, dry to average soil in full sun; willowleaf sunflower is one of the most architecturally distinctive native perennial sunflowers in North America, immediately recognizable by its exceptionally long, narrow, willow-like leaves (4–8 inches long, less than half an inch wide) that clothe the stem in dense, drooping, grass-like foliage from base to tip, creating a feathery, almost bamboo-like texture that is unlike any other sunflower species. From September through October the stems are topped with clusters of bright yellow, 2–3 inch daisy flowers with yellow-brown disk centers, providing the same important late-season food resources as Maximilian sunflower for pollinators and seed-eating birds at a critical time when most wildflowers have finished. Native to the rocky, dry prairies, limestone glades, and rocky hillsides of the south-central United States from Nebraska to Texas and Louisiana, it is naturally adapted to thin, alkaline, rocky soils and extreme drought — it performs best in lean, dry conditions that emphasize its graceful texture rather than producing excessive, floppy vegetative growth. Willowleaf sunflower spreads by rhizomes into handsome colonies and is an excellent structural plant for the back of a sunny native border, tall prairie planting, or naturalistic meadow where its fine-textured foliage provides visual interest from spring through frost.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a sunny, well-drained spot or a container that can move indoors in cold zones.
directions: Wilma Goldcrest is a lemon cypress with glowing golden-green foliage that releases a fresh citrus scent when brushed, and a narrow, upright form perfect for tight spaces. Grow it in full sun to keep the foliage brightest, in fast-draining soil that never stays waterlogged. In containers it stays around 3 to 5 feet, while in the ground in mild climates it can reach 10 feet. In zones colder than 7, grow it in a pot and bring it indoors near a bright window over winter. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and avoid soggy roots.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in midsummer under mist or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Wilson's magnolia is best appreciated when planted at the top of a slope, retaining wall, or above a path so that the pendulous, nodding flowers can be admired at face level or viewed from below.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Wilson's magnolia is a Chinese deciduous magnolia introduced from Sichuan province by plant hunter E.H. Wilson in 1908 that produces, in May and June, the most exquisitely formed pendant flowers of any magnolia species — pure-white, circular, saucer-shaped, deeply cupped flowers about 3–4 inches across, with nine large, rounded, pure-white petals surrounding a magnificent, bold, central boss of deep crimson-red to rose-red stamens, hanging nodding on slender stalks from the tips of the branches so that they look directly downward, like ornamental lanterns. The brilliant contrast of the white petals against the vivid crimson stamen cone makes each flower a miniature work of art. Like M. sieboldii, it performs well in partial shade — making it particularly valuable for the woodland garden — and the late flowering season (May–June) means frost damage to the flowers is rare. A connoisseur's magnolia for zone 6–9 gardens seeking unusual shade-tolerant flowering trees. Closely related to and similar to M. sieboldii, distinguished by its slightly larger flowers and different leaf shape.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in California; seed requires cool, moist conditions to germinate and blooms in spring before summer heat arrives.
directions: A delicate California native annual related to the California poppy, producing slender, upright stems with finely cut leaves and vivid brick-red to salmon-orange, 4-petaled flowers with a deep maroon basal blotch in spring; native to grassy chaparral burns, open hillsides, and disturbed ground of California's Coast Ranges and foothills. Often appears in abundance after wildfire, earning it the name 'fire follower.' Direct sow in fall in dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; does not transplant well. An outstanding, rarely cultivated annual for California native gardens and fire-follower wildflower mixes.

subcategory: most cold-hardy fan palm for temperate gardens
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; windmill palm is the most cold-hardy fan palm widely available, surviving to about 5–10°F (-15 to -12°C) when established. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a reliable, permanently hardy landscape palm reaching 20–30 feet over decades. In part shade it grows more slowly but maintains its characteristic single, slender, fiber-covered trunk with spreading fan leaves. Produces fragrant yellow flower clusters in spring, followed by blue-black fruits on female plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; windmill palm is the most cold-hardy fan palm in general cultivation — a native of the mountain forests of central China and Japan at elevations up to 7,500 feet, where it endures significant cold, frost, and even snow on its characteristic fan-shaped leaves. The hardiness extends to approximately 5–10°F (-15 to -12°C) when the palm is established and planted in a sheltered, well-drained position, making it a genuine, permanent landscape palm for gardens as cold as zone 7b — including much of the mid-Atlantic coast, the Pacific Northwest, the British Isles, and large areas of the American Southeast where other palms cannot survive. The distinctive characteristic of the species is the single, slender trunk covered in dense, dark-brown, burlap-like fibrous matting — the remains of old leaf bases — giving it an instantly recognizable, rough-textured, shaggy appearance quite unlike the smooth, gray trunks of many tropical palms. The circular, fan-shaped, blue-green leaf blades, divided into numerous stiff, radiating segments, are held on long petioles at the top of the trunk. In spring, the palm produces arching clusters of small, fragrant, yellow flowers from among the leaf bases; female plants (the species is dioecious) subsequently produce small, blue-black, waxy fruits. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it is a completely reliable, permanently established landscape palm that grows steadily over decades. One of the defining plants of warm-climate gardening in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Set pseudobulbs half-buried in a gritty, well-drained orchid mix in early spring just as new growth begins, positioning them in a shaded to partially shaded location that stays cool and frost-free through winter.
directions: Half-bury pseudobulbs in a gritty mix of fine bark, perlite, and leaf mold in a shaded position, placing them 4-6 inches apart in a shallow pan or raised bed where their shallow roots can spread freely. Water sparingly when new growth first emerges in spring, gradually increasing moisture as the single pleated leaf and showy pink to lilac flowers develop, then reducing water steadily as foliage yellows in autumn. Keep pseudobulbs cool and nearly dry but frost-free during their winter dormancy, as prolonged freezing will kill them even in zone 7 without protective mulch or cold-frame shelter. Each autumn, lift and separate the daughter pseudobulbs that form alongside the original, discarding the spent parent bulb and replanting the offsets to steadily increase your colony.

subcategory: spectacularly bicolored South African Cape corm
plant_note: Plant small corms 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, lean to slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; wine cups follows the Cape winter-rainfall growth cycle — emerging in autumn with rains, blooming in late winter and spring (August–October in South Africa, February–April in the Northern Hemisphere), then going completely summer dormant. Keep bone dry in summer dormancy. One of the most spectacularly colored small Cape corms. Best in containers in areas with wet summers.
directions: Plant corms in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic, sandy soil in full sun; wine cups is one of the most dramatically, improbably beautiful small Cape corms — a botanical rarity that produces flowers of such striking, sharply contrasting bicolor perfection that the first sight of a blooming plant reliably produces disbelief. Each flower is a shallow, open, wide-faced cup (the 'wine cup') of pure, deep, vivid blue-violet to royal blue — and at the center of each petal, precisely positioned, a bold, dark wine-red to maroon-red blotch that creates a starburst pattern of wine-red at the center of the blue cup, the two colors absolutely saturated and sharply demarcated in a bicolor combination of electric blue and blood-red that appears painted by an artist rather than produced by a plant. The common name 'Sentry-in-a-Box' refers to the traditional observation that the red markings look like a small figure standing in a blue sentry box. Native to a small area of the Western Cape around Darling in the sandy coastal fynbos, it is one of the Cape's many microendemic botanical wonders — a plant of restricted range but astonishing floral beauty. Outstanding in pots and alpine house conditions where summer dryness is easily controlled; a collector's gem of the highest order.

common_name: Wine and Roses Weigela (Dark Purple-Leaf Pink-Flowered Weigela)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Wine and Roses holds its dark purple foliage color best with at least six hours of direct sun.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Wine and Roses was a breakthrough weigela introduction for combining rich, dark burgundy-purple foliage that holds its color through the growing season with abundant clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped spring flowers that stand out sharply against the dark leaves. Hummingbirds are drawn strongly to the tubular flowers, and the plant provides months of foliage-color interest even after the main spring bloom flush ends. It is generally trouble-free, tolerating heat and average garden soil well, and needs only a light shaping prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood and heavy pruning at the wrong time removes the next season's flower buds.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in early spring in well-drained to moderately moist, loamy or clay soil in full sun to light shade. Winged Elm seeds ripen in early spring before leafout and must be sown fresh immediately upon collection, as viability is lost within days; transplanting from nursery stock is the practical choice for most gardeners.
directions: Winged Elm is a medium-sized native tree of dry to mesic upland woods, rocky slopes, fence rows, and disturbed roadsides across the southeastern and south-central United States from Virginia to Florida and west to Kansas, readily identified by the distinctive corky, wing-like ridges that develop along younger branches — a feature unique among eastern elms. The seeds ripen in early spring before the leaves emerge and must be sown fresh in moist, well-drained soil immediately upon collection, as germination viability drops to near zero within days of ripening; nursery transplants are the practical method for establishing this species. Winged Elm is among the toughest and most adaptable of the native elms, tolerating drought, compacted clay, alkaline soils, and periodic flooding, and shows some tolerance to Dutch elm disease, making it a useful native tree for difficult urban sites and naturalized roadsides. The vase-shaped canopy, small rough-textured leaves, and light-yellow fall color provide multi-season ornamental interest with minimal maintenance.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in mild climates (zones 8–10) sow in fall for winter-spring bloom; winged everlasting is an Australian native grown worldwide as an everlasting cut flower — the papery white flower heads with yellow centers dry beautifully on the plant and retain their papery texture for 1–2 years in dried arrangements.
directions: Surface sow or barely cover seed; winged everlasting tolerates poor, dry, sandy soils and needs excellent drainage; harvest stems for drying when the yellow central disc is still tight and the papery white bracts are just opening; hang upside-down in small bundles in a dry, airy location to dry; the papery quality is retained for years in dry conditions. Winged everlasting (Ammobium alatum) is an Australian native wildflower grown around the world as a premier dried-flower crop and garden annual, valued for its distinctive papery flower heads that retain their appearance almost indefinitely after drying. The plant grows from a basal rosette of leaves with woolly-white undersides, sending up erect, distinctively winged stems (the 'alatum' = 'winged' in Latin refers to the prominent flanges running down the length of each stem) topped by clusters of small, round, papery-bracted flower heads about 3/4 inch across — white papery outer bracts surrounding a compact yellow central disc. The white papery bracts have the characteristic texture of everlasting flowers: they are neither petals nor sepals in the conventional sense but specialized, scale-like bracts that are naturally dry and paper-textured even on the living plant. When cut and dried, the flowers maintain their white color and papery texture with minimal shrinkage and no loss of the characteristic form, making Ammobium one of the longest-lasting and most reliably drying of all the everlasting flower genera. The flowers are freely produced over a long season (6–8 weeks or more), and plants often self-sow reliably in well-drained garden situations. Used extensively in dried flower arrangements, wreaths, and craft projects.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow after soil warms to 70°F in full sun; wingpod purslane requires no watering once established in sandy or gravelly soil. Unlike moss rose (P. grandiflora), the flowers of P. umbraticola (used to breed most modern Portulaca hybrids) do not close in cloudy weather — an important horticultural advantage. Most nursery 'Portulaca' sold as 'Sundial', 'Yubi', or 'Pazzazz' series are derived from or are this species.
directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, sandy to gravelly soil in full sun; wingpod purslane is a heat-loving succulent annual native to the southern United States and tropical America that is the primary parent species behind most modern portulaca hybrids sold under names like 'Sundial', 'Yubi', and 'Pazzazz.' It produces succulent, cylindrical to flat, glossy, bright-green leaves on sprawling, succulent stems and from early summer through frost, vivid, tissue-paper-textured flowers (1–2 inches across) in the full range of hot portulaca colors — crimson, scarlet, magenta, orange, yellow, white, and bicolors — that, importantly, stay open longer in cloudy conditions than the related moss rose (P. grandiflora), making them a better choice for regions with overcast summer weather. Absolutely the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of all colorful summer annuals, thriving in pure sand or gravel with no supplemental irrigation in the hottest summer conditions. Outstanding for the tops of dry stone walls, sandy road edges, the front edge of gravel driveways, and any impossible, hot, dry location where virtually nothing else will flower. An essential plant for Gulf Coast and zone 9 summer gardens where heat and drought defeat most annuals.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in moist, fertile soil in partial shade; plants establish readily and spread by rhizome and self-seeding, naturalizing aggressively once happy. Do not plant in small gardens without containment.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; wingstem is a bold, tall native wildflower of moist woodland edges and stream banks with distinctive narrow wings running down the length of the stem (giving it the common name), topped with loose clusters of raggedy yellow flowers in August through October that are outstanding late-season nectar sources for bees, wasps, and butterflies. The plant is one of the most shade-tolerant of the tall native yellow-flowered composites, blooming reliably in significant shade where few similar plants perform. It spreads aggressively by rhizome and should be given a naturalized area of its own or managed by division. The persistent seed heads are eaten by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds through fall and winter.

plant_note: Plant the potted or bare-root climber in spring after hard frosts.
directions: Winner's Circle is a vigorous climbing rose with bright, cherry-red double blooms and a strong, upright habit that flowers spring through fall. Plant the potted or bare-root rose in spring in full sun and rich, well-drained soil near a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence to support the canes. Tie in the long canes as they grow and train them horizontally to encourage more blooms. Water at the base to keep foliage dry, mulch to conserve moisture, and prune in late winter to shape and remove old wood. Hardy in zones 4 to 10, it rewards care with repeat flushes of color.

plant_note: Plant tubers (actually small, knobbly rhizomes) 2-3 inches deep as soon as they are available in late summer or very early fall — ideally in August or September while the tubers are still plump and fresh, as they dry out and fail quickly if stored; soak dry tubers in water for 24 hours before planting to rehydrate them. Winter aconite establishes most reliably when planted immediately after purchase into moist, humus-rich, alkaline-leaning soil beneath deciduous trees.
directions: Plant tubers 2-3 inches deep as early as possible in fall in moist, humus-rich, preferably alkaline soil in partial shade beneath deciduous trees for late January to March bloom; winter aconite is the earliest of all spring bulbs — it blooms while snow is still on the ground, often beginning in January or February, producing solitary bright golden-yellow, buttercup-like flowers cupped in a distinctive ruff of bright green, finely cut leaves that makes the flower look as though it is wearing a small green collar. It is the perfect companion for snowdrops (Galanthus) — the golden flowers of winter aconite and white flowers of snowdrops bloom simultaneously, creating one of the most celebrated sights of the late-winter garden. Unlike most bulbs, winter aconite is actually a small tuber (rhizome) that performs best in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil that stays cool and slightly moist even in summer, and it thrives under the light shade and root competition of deciduous trees — conditions it encounters in its native woodland habitat across southern Europe. It self-seeds freely once established to form large colonies, but initial establishment can be slow, particularly from dried tubers; fresh tubers or green transplants succeed best.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in partial to full shade or full sun in spring; winter creeper is extremely adaptable and tolerates a wide range of soil types, sun levels, and difficult conditions including drought and air pollution.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in shade to full sun; winter creeper is one of the most versatile and widely planted evergreen groundcovers in North American landscaping — a trailing to climbing shrub with glossy, dark-green, oval leaves that naturally roots where stems contact soil, making it an effective weed-suppressing groundcover on slopes and under trees, or a wall-covering vine when given support. Numerous cultivars offer varying leaf size, growth habit, and variegation: 'Coloratus' (leaves turn purple-red in winter, excellent groundcover), 'Emerald Gaiety' (white-margined, compact), 'Emerald 'n Gold' (yellow-margined, colorful), and 'Vegetus' (large-leaved, vigorous). Very tolerant of shade, drought, poor soil, air pollution, and pruning. Important caution: in parts of the eastern US and Midwest it can escape cultivation to become invasive in woodland settings; check local invasive species listings before planting in naturalized areas.

plant_note: Plant corms 1–2 inches deep in fall (with the flat side down) in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; winter cyclamen goes dormant in summer and should be planted where it will not receive summer irrigation.
directions: Plant corms flat-side down, 1–2 inches deep, in fall in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; winter cyclamen (Eastern Mediterranean cyclamen) is a delightful small hardy cyclamen that blooms in late winter to early spring — often from December through February — producing tiny, swept-back, bright carmine, pink, or white flowers and beautifully marbled, kidney-shaped silver-patterned leaves that emerge in fall and persist through winter, disappearing entirely in summer dormancy. The plant naturalizes slowly by self-seeding to form expanding colonies under deciduous trees and in sheltered rock gardens. Less demanding than the tender florist's cyclamen; this species is reliably hardy and garden-worthy. Best planted in masses of 25 or more for a significant winter flowering effect.

plant_note: Plant in early fall or spring in sharply drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; daphne is notoriously difficult to transplant — choose the permanent location carefully as plants do not move well.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade and choose the site carefully — winter daphne resents transplanting and should be considered permanent once established. The intensely sweet fragrance of its pink-purple flower clusters from late winter to early spring is one of the most powerful and pleasant in the garden and can perfume the air for 20 feet or more. Excellent drainage is the single most critical cultural requirement; root rot in wet soil kills plants quickly and without warning, a phenomenon so common that gardeners joke that daphne 'dies for no reason.' Keep well-watered during dry spells in summer. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested — handle with care and wash hands after pruning.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Winter Gem requires protection from hot afternoon sun in zone 9 — partial shade is preferred and helps prevent the bronzing and bleaching that can affect boxwood foliage in intense summer heat.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with afternoon shade protection; Winter Gem is the most widely planted Korean boxwood cultivar — a tight, globe-forming selection that maintains exceptional dense, rounded form with small, dark-green, lustrous leaves that hold their color better than many boxwood cultivars through winter and summer. The deep, rich green color with a slightly glossy sheen is particularly attractive as a formal edging or clipped topiary subject. Unlike many Buxus sempervirens cultivars, Winter Gem shows markedly superior resistance to boxwood blight (Calonectria pseudonaviculata), which has devastated English boxwood plantings across much of the Eastern United States — this disease resistance is a major reason Korean boxwood cultivars have increased in popularity. Winter Gem tolerates zone 9 summer heat better than English boxwood selections, provided afternoon shade protects from the most intense sun. Boxwoods require well-drained soil — they are extremely susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet, poorly drained sites. No serious pests affect boxwood in Gulf Coast gardens except the boxwood leafminer, which causes blistering of the leaves; treat with systemic insecticide if infestation is severe. Shear or hand-prune to maintain desired formal shape in late winter or after spring flush.

plant_note: Plant at least one male and three female shrubs for berry production; one male can pollinate up to five females. Match the male cultivar's bloom time to the female's — choose male cultivar recommendations from the nursery that match your female selection.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; winterberry is a spectacular native deciduous holly that produces brilliant red (or yellow or orange in some cultivars) berries that encrust every branch after leaf drop in fall, providing dazzling winter interest from October through February when birds finally strip them. It grows naturally in swamps, stream banks, and wet woodland margins and performs best with consistent moisture. This species is dioecious — you must plant both male and female plants, matching cultivars that bloom at the same time, to get berries. Named female cultivars like 'Winter Red', 'Sparkleberry', and 'Red Sprite' (compact) are widely available; match them with the appropriate male. Mulch to maintain soil moisture and acidity.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wintergreen is a fast-growing, cold-hardy Korean boxwood valued for holding good green winter color better than many boxwoods, which often bronze or yellow in cold weather.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun with afternoon shade protection in the hottest climates. Wintergreen is a Korean boxwood selected for faster growth than many boxwood cultivars along with good, consistent green foliage color through winter, when many boxwoods bronze, yellow, or bleach in cold weather. Its rounded, dense, small-leaved habit makes it useful for hedging, edging, and foundation plantings, and its Korean boxwood parentage gives it noticeably better resistance to boxwood blight, a fungal disease that has devastated English boxwood plantings across much of the eastern United States, than straight Buxus sempervirens cultivars. It tolerates Gulf South heat reasonably well given afternoon shade, but like all boxwoods requires sharp drainage, since the roots are highly susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet or poorly drained sites. Watch for boxwood leafminer, which causes blistered foliage, and treat with a systemic insecticide if infestation is significant. Shear or hand-prune in late winter or after the spring growth flush to maintain a formal shape.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed.
directions: Surface-sow tiny seeds on moist mix without covering; they need light to germinate at 70–75°F. Torenia is one of the best flowering annuals for shaded and part-shaded spots in hot, humid climates where impatiens are lost to downy mildew. The bicolored, snapdragon-like flowers in purple, pink, white, or yellow bloom profusely without deadheading throughout summer. Keep soil consistently moist, as plants wilt quickly when dry but recover readily; fertilize monthly with a balanced liquid feed.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in early spring or late fall in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the plant transplants well from container stock but is slow to establish from seed. The species blooms October–December; vernal witch hazel (H. vernalis) blooms in late winter.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; American witch hazel is the latest-blooming native shrub, producing clusters of fragrant, spidery yellow flowers on bare branches from October through December — often while the leaves are still falling around the flowers. It is a stunning sight in the November woodland garden when nothing else is in bloom. Growing naturally as a multi-stemmed understory tree in moist woodland slopes and ravines across eastern North America, it tolerates full shade but blooms more heavily with some dappled light. The bark and leaves are the botanical source of witch hazel astringent. Allow it to grow naturally as a large multi-stemmed specimen; it resents heavy pruning. The seed pods pop open explosively to disperse seeds.

plant_note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Wizard Sunset coleus grows quickly and fills in beds and containers with brilliant warm-toned foliage. Pinch flower spikes as soon as they appear to maintain the foliage color and compact shape — flowering signals the end of the plant's productive foliage season. In zone 9 the long warm season allows extended growth; the plants can be maintained as large specimens through the year in frost-free areas.
directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Wizard Sunset is part of the Wizard coleus series — a compact, seed-grown coleus series known for uniform habit and a wide range of color selections. The Sunset color in the Wizard series features leaves in a warm blend of sunset orange, gold, red-orange, and bronze arranged in irregular patterns, capturing the warm glow of an evening sky. The compact, 12–18 inch height and dense branching habit of the Wizard series makes it one of the most practical seed-grown coleus for formal bedding patterns, edging, and container planting where a consistent, predictable size is required. Unlike the large-leaved vegetatively propagated coleus varieties, seed-grown Wizard types are uniform in size, color, and habit — each plant from the same packet is nearly identical, making them reliable for mass planting effects. In partial shade the warm sunset colors are often most vivid; deep shade tends to deepen the red tones while reducing the gold and orange.

plant_note: Direct-sow in fall for biennial flowering in spring of the second year, or sow in very early spring; woad is a biennial or short-lived perennial in the mustard family. INVASIVE WARNING: Woad is a listed noxious weed in multiple western US states (Idaho, Colorado, Utah, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, and others) and should not be planted in those states. Check local regulations before planting.
directions: Sow in well-drained, average soil in full sun — INVASIVE in western US states: check local regulations; woad is the ancient European source of blue dye that predates the introduction of tropical indigo (Indigofera tinctoria) — the same compound, indigotin, is present in both plants, but in smaller concentrations in woad. The blue woad dye produced from fermented, composted leaves was the primary blue textile dye of Europe for thousands of years, from prehistoric times through the Middle Ages, and was used to produce the blue in medieval stained glass pigments, illuminated manuscripts, and textiles. The Picts of Scotland famously used woad to paint their bodies blue. The plant itself is an upright biennial producing rosettes of blue-green basal leaves in the first year and tall branching flower stalks bearing masses of small, bright-yellow flowers in the second year, followed by distinctive, hanging, black, paddle-shaped seed pods that are ornamental. It was supplanted by imported indigo in the 16th–17th centuries. Now grown primarily as a historical, educational, and natural dye plant.

common_name: Woman's Tongue (Siris Tree, East Indian Walnut)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Woman's Tongue is a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing, tropical legume shade tree famous for its persistent, flat, papery seed pods that rattle noisily in the wind (hence the evocative common name) — CAUTION: classified as a Category I invasive exotic in Florida where it naturalizes aggressively in disturbed areas and natural habitats.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established. CAUTION: invasive in Florida — do not plant near natural areas. Albizia lebbeck (woman's tongue or siris tree) is a large, fast-growing, deciduous-to-semi-evergreen tropical legume tree native to South Asia and tropical Africa, now widely naturalized throughout the tropics as both a valued shade tree and an invasive species. The plant is named 'woman's tongue' for its persistent, flat, tan, papery, 6–10 inch long seed pods that hold their seeds loosely and rattle loudly in the slightest breeze — the metaphorical association being obvious. As a landscape tree, Woman's Tongue is excellent: it grows rapidly (3–5 feet per year), provides dense, spreading shade, fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root bacteria, produces attractive cream-white, fragrant, powder-puff flower clusters in late spring, and is extraordinarily drought-tolerant on poor soils. The bark has traditionally yielded saponins used as a soap substitute in India. The wood is highly valued as a timber for furniture and construction in South Asia. IMPORTANT CAUTION: In Florida, coastal Gulf South states, and Hawaii, Albizia lebbeck is classified as an invasive exotic pest plant — it naturalizes in disturbed areas, roadsides, and natural areas aggressively. Do not plant in proximity to natural lands in Florida or coastal Gulf states.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; plant in generous drifts of at least 25–50 rhizomes for best effect.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; wood anemone spreads steadily by rhizomes to form extensive, low carpets under deciduous trees and looks best when planted in generous drifts of at least 25–50 rhizomes. Anemone nemorosa is a diminutive, spring-ephemeral European woodland perennial producing a low carpet of deeply cut, dark-green, three-lobed leaves above which rise slender, 6–12-inch stems each bearing a single, star-shaped, white (sometimes pink or pale blue in cultivars) flower with 6–8 petal-like sepals and a ring of golden stamens in early to mid-spring; the plant goes completely dormant by early summer. It naturalizes beautifully under deciduous trees and in combination with spring bulbs such as snowdrops, glory of the snow, and miniature daffodils; cultivars include the lavender-blue 'Robinsoniana' and the pure white, semi-double 'Vestal'. All parts are mildly toxic.

plant_note: Plant divisions near suitable host plant roots in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; wood betony is hemiparasitic primarily on grasses and some forbs — it performs best in native plant communities with a diversity of host species.
directions: Plant divisions or carefully transplant container-grown plants in spring near the roots of grasses and native forbs in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade or light dappled sun; wood betony is hemiparasitic and performs best embedded in a diverse native plant community with ample grass and forb roots to tap. Pedicularis canadensis is a native eastern North American hemiparasitic perennial of woodland edges, prairies, and open rocky slopes; it produces attractive, deeply pinnately lobed, fernlike leaves in a basal rosette and stout spikes of clustered, tubular flowers with distinctive, hooded upper lips in colors ranging from yellow through red in mid-spring, one of the most beautiful and architecturally interesting of the spring wildflowers. It is among the most important early-season nectar plants for queen bumblebees emerging from hibernation. Like paintbrush, it benefits from diverse host-plant associations and is most successful in native meadow and woodland garden settings.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall at 3–4 inches depth in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; wood lily is one of the few native lilies that holds its flowers upright (facing the sky) rather than drooping. It requires good drainage and benefits from light shade in warmer zones.
directions: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy or loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; wood lily is one of the most striking native wildflowers of eastern and central North America, producing upward-facing, brilliantly orange to orange-red, spotted flowers on relatively short stems — unlike the drooping, turk's-cap form of most other native lilies. The upright orientation makes wood lily a natural hummingbird flower, and ruby-throated hummingbirds are among its most important pollinators. The plant is increasingly rare in the wild due to deer browsing, loss of fire-maintained habitat, and illegal collection. In the garden, wood lily requires excellent drainage and is short-lived in rich, moist conditions. Plant in sandy soil on a slope or raised bed with consistent but moderate moisture and light afternoon shade in warmer zones.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; wood melic grass grows naturally in shaded woodland on alkaline or neutral soils and is specifically suited to shade conditions — it does not perform well in full sun.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, average to humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; wood melic grass is a European woodland grass that is one of the few true ornamental grasses suited to deep shade — it forms loose, delicate tufts of soft, flat, rich-green leaves and produces loose, arching panicles of nodding, dark-purple to bronze, single-spikeleted flowers from late spring through early summer that glisten with a silky, metallic quality when backlit. The overall effect of wood melic in flower is ethereal and refined — far more subtle and naturalistic than most ornamental grasses. Excellent for naturalizing as a groundcover in shaded woodland gardens under deciduous trees and in formal shade borders where a soft, grassy textural element is needed without the full-sun requirements of most grasses. The cultivar 'Variegata' (cream-striped leaves) is slightly more ornamental. Self-sows moderately in suitable shaded, humus-rich conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in moist woodland soil for natural cold stratification and spring germination; this native shade perennial naturalizes readily from self-seeding and is among the brightest and longest-blooming yellow wildflowers for shaded sites.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; cold stratification occurs naturally over winter and seeds germinate in early spring. Wood poppy is a native eastern North American woodland perennial in the poppy family with deeply lobed, blue-green, poppy-like leaves and large (1.5–2 inch), brilliant golden-yellow flowers with four petals that bloom from early spring through summer in shaded conditions, making it one of the brightest and most prolific yellow-flowering shade plants for the eastern US — a standout with spring bloomers like wild ginger, bleeding heart, and ferns. It self-seeds freely without becoming invasive, gradually naturalizing into a cheerful drift under deciduous trees. All parts of the plant exude orange sap when broken; do not ingest.

common_name: Wood Rose (Yellow Morning Glory, Hawaiian Wood Rose)
plant_note: Direct sow or plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; wood rose is a vigorous tropical vine grown for its extraordinary, large, pale-yellow morning glory flowers and, uniquely, for the spectacular dried seed pods — the opened, star-shaped, woody calyces resemble carved wooden roses and are prized in dried floral arrangements.
directions: Direct sow scarified seeds in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; wood rose is drought-tolerant and vigorous once established — provide a very strong support. Merremia tuberosa (wood rose or Hawaiian wood rose) is a large, fast-growing tropical vine in the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae) native to Mexico and Central America, now naturalized and widely grown throughout the tropics. It produces large (3-inch), beautiful, pale golden-yellow, funnel-shaped morning glory flowers throughout the warm season. But the real treasure of wood rose is its extraordinary seed pod: as the flower fades and the fruit ripens, the calyx (the five-lobed green backing of the flower) expands and stiffens into a large, starfish-shaped, papery-woody structure 2–3 inches across, remaining on the vine to dry naturally. When fully dry, these calyces are deep chestnut-brown, rigid, and resemble intricately carved wooden roses — hence the name. The dried pods are highly prized in the craft and dried flower market, used in wreaths, arrangements, and floral crafts. Seed the pods during summer, collect in fall, and air-dry for use. In Hawaii, where the vine has naturalized widely, it is considered invasive in some native plant habitats. NOTE: Seeds may contain mildly psychoactive ergot alkaloids (similar to morning glory seeds) — do not ingest.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring or root basal cuttings in early summer; Salvia x sylvestris is a sterile hybrid and must be propagated vegetatively. After the first main bloom flush, cut the entire plant back by half to two-thirds to promote a reliable second flush of bloom in late summer. It is drought-tolerant once established and performs best in lean, well-drained soils.
directions: Plant in lean, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; woodland sage hybrid is the parent species of many of the finest cultivated garden salvias — a complex hybrid (S. nemorosa x S. pratensis) producing dense, bushy, upright plants clothed in aromatic gray-green leaves and, from late spring through summer (with reblooming after cutting back), dense upright spikes of rich violet-blue, blue-violet, or pink tubular flowers with contrasting bracts that maintain their color and decorative quality even after the flower petals drop. The named cultivars derived from this hybrid group are among the most widely planted perennials in temperate horticulture: 'May Night' ('Mainacht', deep violet-blue with dark bracts, Gold Medal Award winner), 'Blue Hill' ('Blauhugel', clear sky-blue), 'Rose Queen' (rose-pink), and 'Caradonna' (violet flowers on distinctive dark, near-black stems). Drought-tolerant, long-blooming with proper deadheading, and reliable across a wide zone range from 4 to 9 — qualities that make this hybrid group among the most useful and versatile of all garden perennials for the sunny, low-maintenance border.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil with the roots shaded and the stems in sun; woodbine tolerates partial shade better than Japanese honeysuckle and is preferred for informal hedgerows and native garden settings across Europe.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone cool and shaded while allowing stems to climb toward light; woodbine is the native European honeysuckle celebrated in Shakespeare's writings and the source of the intensely sweet evening fragrance associated with English cottage gardens. Unlike the invasive Japanese honeysuckle (L. japonica), this species is non-invasive and suitable for planting in naturalistic gardens. The tubular flowers, creamy-white flushed with pink and purple, are exceptionally fragrant in the evening and attract hawk moths; the red berries feed warblers, thrushes, and other birds in late summer. Popular cultivars include 'Serotina' (late Dutch, deep purple outside), 'Graham Thomas' (creamy white aging to yellow), and 'Belgica' (early Dutch honeysuckle). Prune lightly after flowering to shape.

plant_note: Plant divisions or nursery transplants in fall or early spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; woodland phlox naturalizes by self-sown seed and stolons. If starting from seed, cold-stratify 60–90 days before sowing; germination is slow and erratic.
directions: Plant divisions in partial shade in moist, humus-rich soil in fall or early spring; woodland phlox is one of the most beautiful native spring wildflowers of eastern North America, producing masses of fragrant flat-faced flowers in shades of pale blue, lavender, violet, and white in mid-spring — blooming at the same time as Virginia bluebells and trilliums to create spectacular native wildflower combinations. The semi-evergreen foliage forms spreading mats that suppress weeds throughout the growing season, and unlike tall garden phlox (P. paniculata), woodland phlox is rarely troubled by powdery mildew when given good air circulation in a shaded site. Selected cultivars include 'Clouds of Perfume' (fragrant blue-violet), 'London Grove Blue' (deep blue), and 'Fuller's White' (pure white). An excellent pollinator plant attracting hummingbirds, swallowtail butterflies, and long-tongued native bees. Spreads slowly by rooting stolons to fill woodland edges and shaded borders naturally.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall in dry to average, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; woodland sunflower spreads by rhizome to form large colonies and is best used where aggressive naturalization is welcome — it is exceptionally effective at naturalizing along dry woodland edges and under oak canopies.
directions: Sow seed in fall or divide in spring in dry to average, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade — woodland sunflower is one of the very few perennial sunflowers genuinely adapted to partial shade, producing 2–3 inch yellow daisy flowers in mid-to-late summer on upright stems 3–6 feet tall in conditions where most sunflowers refuse to bloom. It grows naturally in dry, open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout the eastern US and is especially common along the edges of oak woodland, thriving in the dry shade beneath the oak canopy that challenges most sun-loving perennials. It spreads vigorously by rhizome — use this to advantage in naturalizing dry, shaded areas with low-maintenance native cover and late-season pollinator value. The seeds are eaten by goldfinches and other seed-eating birds. An outstanding native for filling the challenging dry, part-shade niche.

plant_note: Surface sow (seeds need light) indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost on moist seed-starting mix; do not cover seeds. Transplant to partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil after last frost.
directions: Surface sow (seeds need light) indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost on moist seed-starting mix; do not cover seeds. Transplant to partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil after last frost. Nicotiana sylvestris is a spectacular ornamental tobacco from northwestern Argentina, producing enormous (up to 24 inches wide), rough-hairy, basal rosettes of bold, dark-green leaves and tall, candelabra-like clusters of long, pendant, tubular white flowers in early summer that are intensely, sweetly fragrant — particularly at dusk and night, when the fragrance carries 50 feet or more. The flowers are adapted to sphinx moth pollination and their nocturnal fragrance attracts hawkmoths in the evening; they also attract hummingbirds. All parts are toxic; do not ingest. A spectacular annual for the back of shaded or partially shaded borders, where its bold texture and evening fragrance create a dramatic effect.

common_name: Woolly Congea (Shower Orchid Vine, Lilac Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; woolly congea is a spectacularly beautiful tropical vine from Thailand and Southeast Asia — the ornamental display consists of large clusters of pale-lavender to white, woolly, three-lobed bracts (petal-like modified leaves) that cover the vine in winter and early spring in a display sometimes compared to seeing falling lavender snow; actual flowers are tiny, hidden within the dramatic bracts.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; woolly congea is a vigorous vine requiring strong support and can become very large — provide a sturdy pergola or large fence. Congea tomentosa (woolly congea, shower orchid vine, or lilac vine) is one of the most spectacular and unusual tropical flowering vines available for zone 10–12 gardens — a native of Thailand, Myanmar, and Southeast Asian dry tropical forests where it scrambles over trees in the deciduous forest canopy. The ornamental display of congea is completely different from most flowering vines: the actual flowers are tiny and inconspicuous, but each small cluster is surrounded by three large, petal-like, woolly bracts (modified leaves) that are the true ornamental display. These bracts, 1–2 inches long, are produced in enormous quantities in dense, cascading clusters that cover the vine during the cool, dry season (winter to early spring in zone 10–12) — pale lavender-lilac when fresh, fading to silvery-white as they age. The overall effect of a flowering congea is one of cascading pale-lavender to white woolly clusters hanging in billowing masses from the vine — sometimes compared to a waterfall of lavender or a shower of lilac snow. The vine can reach enormous size (30–50 feet) on a large pergola or tree. After flowering, the silvery dried bracts persist attractively for weeks. A breathtaking and rare ornamental vine for large tropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant container vines or rooted cuttings in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; woolly Dutchman's pipe is the southeastern-native species of Aristolochia, hardier and better adapted to Gulf Coast conditions than A. macrophylla.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun with a sturdy support structure; woolly Dutchman's pipe is the southeastern US native species of Aristolochia, distinguished from A. macrophylla by its dense woolly coating of soft hairs on the leaves and stems — a beautiful textural detail. Like all native Aristolochia species, it is the exclusive larval host plant for the pipevine swallowtail butterfly (Battus philenor), one of the most spectacular black-and-iridescent-blue native butterflies in eastern North America. A single established vine supports dozens of caterpillars each season. The unusual curved, yellowish-green to brown pipe-shaped flowers are insect-trapping devices that temporarily trap small flies for pollination. Twining stems reach 10–20 feet and provide rapid screening in partial shade. Highly recommended for butterfly gardens in zones 5–9, particularly in the Southeast where this species is native.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall into dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, matching the open pine flatwood conditions this southeastern native prefers. Rake seeds shallowly into the soil surface and allow winter rains to settle them in place. Avoid clay-heavy or moisture-retentive soils, which cause root rot; established plants are highly drought-tolerant and require little to no supplemental irrigation.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly onto a prepared, lean, sandy or gravelly seedbed in full sun — this species from the dry southeastern coastal plain requires excellent drainage and will not persist in heavy soils. Lightly rake seeds into the top quarter-inch of soil and water once to settle; subsequent rains will carry the seeds through winter stratification. The distinctive silvery-woolly basal rosettes appear in early spring and the bright yellow flowers open in mid-spring, often before most summer wildflowers have emerged. Once established after the first season, plants are reliably drought-tolerant and will self-sow modestly into bare soil nearby.

plant_note: Plant transplants in fall in moist, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; woolly sunbonnets is adapted to the longleaf pine savanna and flatwood conditions of the southeastern coastal plain and performs best with periodic disturbance or open canopy that mimics its native fire-maintained habitat.
directions: Plant transplants in fall in moist, well-drained sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun, choosing a site that approximates the open longleaf pine flatwood conditions of its native range in the southeastern coastal plain. Chaptalia tomentosa produces a flat basal rosette of leaves that are deep green on top and strikingly white-woolly on the undersides, giving the plant year-round textural interest even out of bloom. The unusual daisy-like flowers appear from winter through spring, nodding in bud like a sunbonnet before opening to reveal white to pale lavender rays, making this native wildflower a valuable cool-season bloomer in mild southeastern gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial shade; woolly sweetspire is a Coastal Plain relative of the common summersweet (C. alnifolia) with notably woolly-hairy leaves and stems.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; woolly sweetspire is a native ericaceous shrub of wet, acidic Coastal Plain habitats — pocosins, bay edges, moist pine flatwoods, and the margins of Carolina bays — from Virginia to Georgia. The dense, white, fragrant flower racemes in midsummer are intensely perfumed and highly attractive to native bees, particularly bumblebees, which find the tubular flowers accessible. The woolly-textured leaves and stems (more densely hairy than C. alnifolia) give the plant a distinctive soft appearance. Fall foliage turns orange to red. As with all sweetspires, it thrives in moist, acidic woodland gardens and wetland edges — excellent for rain gardens and moist shade borders in zones 5–9. Spreads slowly by stolons to form colonies.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; woolly-stemmed sage is frost-tender and is damaged below 30 degrees F. In zones 9-11 it grows as a large, shrubby perennial; in colder zones it can be grown in large containers and overwintered frost-free. It is a large plant — allow 3-4 feet of space. Fertilize monthly to support its vigorous growth and abundant flowering.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; woolly-stemmed sage is a dramatically bold Brazilian salvia producing some of the most visually striking flower spikes in the genus. The entire plant is covered in a dense layer of russet-orange to tawny-brown woolly hairs — on the stems, leaf undersides, and calyx — that create a warm, velvety texture throughout. The flower spikes, which appear from late summer through frost, carry deep orange-red to crimson-scarlet tubular flowers from rusty-orange woolly calyces in dense, compact whorls, creating a warm, glowing effect unlike the typically blue or purple tones of most salvias. The large leaves are roughly textured and prominently veined, with hairy surfaces on both sides. At 4-6 feet tall and as wide, it is a commanding plant in the late-season border or tropical-style garden. It is powerfully attractive to hummingbirds throughout the bloom period. In zones 9-11 it grows into a large perennial shrub; elsewhere it is a dramatic container specimen.

common_name: Wormvine Vanilla (Leafless Vanilla, Barefoot Vanilla, Florida Vanilla)
plant_note: Grow on rough-barked trees or cork with exposed aerial roots in partial shade; Vanilla barbellata is a leafless, photosynthetic-root Vanilla species — unlike V. planifolia, it produces no leaves, obtaining all photosynthesis through its flat, green, chlorophyll-containing aerial roots. These roots must be exposed to light (partial shade to filtered light) for the plant to thrive. Wild plants are protected in Florida (endangered) — only cultivate from legally propagated nursery stock. Hand pollinate the short-lived flowers for occasional pod set. Zone 10-12 outdoors. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow on rough-barked trees or cork mounts in filtered, indirect light — Wormvine Vanilla is a leafless climbing orchid that obtains all its photosynthesis through chlorophyll-containing aerial roots that must receive adequate light, making it unlike most orchids in its light requirements for the roots rather than the leaves. Vanilla barbellata is a leafless, climbing, epiphytic orchid native to the Florida Keys, the Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola, and Jamaica in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most distinctive of the Vanilla species and a genuinely fascinating botanical curiosity. The plant produces no leaves at any life stage — instead, the flat, strap-like, dark-green aerial roots serve dual function as both anchoring/water-absorbing organs and as photosynthetic structures, containing chloroplasts and performing all the plant's carbon fixation. The stems are thin, wiry, and flexible, climbing by these flatly-adhering roots up tree trunks and branches. The flowers (produced on short racemes from leaf axils) are pale green to white with a white lip, short-lived (single day), and produce occasional small vanilla pods with some fragrance but of much less commercial value than V. planifolia. As a native Florida Keys and Caribbean species, V. barbellata is protected under Florida law and by CITES. In cultivation, it provides a fascinating example of leafless photosynthesis. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep and 3 inches apart in early to mid-fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; Woronow's snowdrop establishes best when planted 'in the green' immediately after flowering in late winter, but dry bulbs planted promptly in fall will succeed in suitable shade conditions.
directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in early to mid-fall in moist, humus-rich, woodland soil in partial to full shade; Woronow's snowdrop is one of the most shade-tolerant snowdrops available and excels under deciduous trees and shrubs where it naturalizes freely. Galanthus woronowii is a Caucasian species snowdrop immediately distinguished from the common snowdrop (G. nivalis) by its exceptionally bright, glossy, apple-green, strap-shaped leaves that remain vivid and fresh-looking even in the coldest weather — giving rise to the common name 'Green Snowdrop'; the white, nodding, single flowers with green-marked inner petals appear from January through March, pushing through snow and frozen ground. It naturalizes readily by offsets and self-seeding under deciduous trees and performs particularly well in shaded gardens where it receives winter and spring sunlight through bare branches and summer shade; this dappled-shade tolerance makes it one of the most reliable snowdrops for woodland gardens. Like all snowdrops, it goes dormant by early summer and benefits from undisturbed, leaf-mold-enriched soil.

plant_note: Plant tubers in fall 3–4 inches deep in full sun in very well-drained, lean, sandy or gritty, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 7–9; provide complete summer drought; Wreath Nasturtium is a spectacular, large-scale trailing Chilean nasturtium from the Atacama-Andes transition zone — producing masses of brilliant golden-yellow flowers on long, far-spreading stems with distinctive, pale blue-green, glaucous, many-lobed leaves — one of the most striking of all tuberous nasturtiums in cool-winter gardens.
directions: Plant Tropaeolum polyphyllum tubers in fall in extremely well-drained, lean, sandy to gritty soil in full sun; provide absolutely no summer water — summer drought is essential; the plant grows over winter and spring in the cool, moist season, dies back completely in early summer, and re-emerges the following fall. Wreath Nasturtium is one of the largest and most spectacular of the Chilean tuberous nasturtiums — producing wide-spreading, mat-forming or trailing stems that can travel 3–6 feet in a single season, bearing distinctive blue-grey-green, multi-lobed, glaucous leaves that emerge with a smoky bloom and masses of bright golden-yellow flowers along the entire length of the stems. The effect in full bloom is extraordinary: a wide sweep of yellow flowers over a blue-grey foliage carpet, created from a single tuber that develops into a substantial, carrot-like storage root. Native to the Atacama Desert transition zone in Chile and Argentina, where winter rains trigger growth and summer drought forces dormancy, its cultivation requires strict adherence to this rainfall pattern — no summer water whatsoever. Grow in raised beds, scree, or containers moved under cover in summer. The tuber grows very large over successive years (sometimes reaching over a foot long); the large, gnarled tubers are occasionally used as an edible root vegetable in its native Chile, with a pleasant, slightly peppery flavor.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall or early spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; wrinkleleaf goldenrod tolerates consistently wet soil and is one of the best goldenrods for rain gardens, pond margins, and moist meadows.
directions: Direct sow in fall or provide 4–6 weeks of cold stratification before spring sowing; wrinkleleaf goldenrod thrives in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade and is one of the best native goldenrods for persistently wet, difficult sites. Solidago rugosa is a robust, upright to arching eastern North American goldenrod with wrinkled, rugose (rough and deeply veined) leaves and arching, one-sided racemes of bright yellow flowers in late summer through fall; it tolerates consistently wet soil better than most goldenrods, making it valuable for rain gardens, pond margins, and moist meadow restorations. The cultivar 'Fireworks' is a spectacular garden selection with strongly arching, fountain-like flowering branches creating a dramatic display; it spreads vigorously by rhizomes in moist, fertile soils. Outstanding late-season pollinator plant for monarchs, bees, and wasps.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Wushan epimedium is an evergreen species from Chongqing and Sichuan provinces of China, named for the Wushan Gorge area of the Three Gorges. It is one of the most dramatic large-leaved epimediums and exceptionally ornamental.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in shade to partial shade; Wushan epimedium is one of the most dramatic and large-growing epimediums in cultivation, producing very large, evergreen, narrowly ovate leaflets with a fine, spiny-toothed margin and a bold, dark green appearance that persists through winter. The flower display in spring is spectacular — large racemes of pale yellow to soft yellow flowers with slightly reflexed outer petals and long, curved, slightly orange-tipped spurs, born on tall, airy stems well above the foliage. One of the largest-growing and most vigorous epimediums, it can form substantial clumps in good woodland soil. The evergreen foliage makes it an excellent year-round groundcover that suppresses weeds effectively even in dry shade under trees. The cultivar 'Caramel' is particularly sought after for its rich caramel-bronze new growth.

plant_note: Plant tubers after the last frost once soil has warmed.
directions: Wyns New Pastel is a tall, vigorous dahlia bearing big pink-and-yellow blended blooms all season on a well-branched, hedge-like plant. Plant tubers 4 to 6 inches deep in full sun and rich, well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed. Because of its height, provide sturdy staking early and pinch the central shoot to encourage branching. Cut flowers freely and deadhead to keep new buds forming through summer and fall. In cold climates, dig and store the tubers over winter, replanting them the following spring.

plant_note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Wyoming is a classic large canna cultivar with dark bronze-purple foliage and bright orange flowers, a long-standing favorite for tropical-style borders.
directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Wyoming is a classic, long-cultivated canna bearing large, deep bronze-purple leaves that provide dramatic dark color and bold tropical texture through the growing season, topped with bright, true-orange flowers that stand out sharply against the dark foliage. Its substantial size and strong color contrast make it a favorite anchor plant for tropical-themed borders and mixed plantings alongside cannas of contrasting leaf color. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

plant_note: Plant outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain above 45°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. In zone 9a Xanadu Philodendron is borderline hardy — the rhizome may survive light frost when mulched, but temperatures below 28°F will kill the above-ground foliage. Manage as a container plant on a shaded porch or patio and bring indoors when frost threatens, or plant in the ground in the most frost-protected garden microclimate. In zones 10–11 it grows as a fully hardy landscape shrub reaching 4 feet by 5 feet. The deeply lobed leaves create a refined tropical effect in shaded outdoor living spaces, and the plant handles zone 9's summer heat and humidity well if maintained with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant in partial to deep shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil — Xanadu Philodendron thrives in the shade conditions of tropical forest understories, performing best where direct sun is excluded; Xanadu (Thaumatophyllum xanadu, formerly Philodendron xanadu) is a compact, self-heading philodendron producing a dramatically architectural mound of deeply pinnately lobed, dark glossy green leaves that create a refined, sophisticated tropical texture at a manageable scale — growing to a tidy 2–4 foot mound rather than the sprawling, climbing habit of many philodendron species. Each large leaf (up to 18 inches long on established plants) is divided into deeply cut lobes along the length that create a feathery, textured appearance fundamentally different from the entire or shallowly lobed leaves of most shade tropicals. Xanadu's architectural foliage — the precise, repeating cut-leaf pattern, the glossy dark surface, the mounding form — creates a modern, clean aesthetic that works well in contemporary landscape design as well as in tropical garden styles. As an outdoor shade plant for zone 9 patios and covered garden areas, Xanadu provides a tropical character with more refined foliage texture than elephant ears or cannas, creating a sophisticated shade garden texture suitable for formal as well as casual landscape settings.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in full sun; blooms quickly from seed.
directions: Xanthos is a breakthrough soft-yellow cosmos, an award winner that is early to flower on well-branched, shorter plants ideal for containers and the front of the border. Direct sow after the last frost in full sun and average, well-drained soil, barely covering the seed. It thrives in lean soil, so avoid overfeeding, which produces foliage at the expense of blooms. Deadhead or cut flowers often to keep the plant producing through summer. Drought-tolerant once established, it draws bees, butterflies, and other pollinators.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; prefers to be direct sown as transplants disturb its taproot.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun with lean, well-drained soil; xeranthemum is one of the easiest everlastings to grow and tolerates poor, dry conditions well. The papery, daisy-like flowers in shades of lavender, pink, purple, and white are naturally self-preserving and air-dry on the stem. Harvest stems for drying when flowers are about two-thirds open; hang upside down in a warm, airy location for 2–3 weeks. Successive sowings 2–3 weeks apart can extend the harvest season into early fall.

common_name: Xerographica Air Plant (King of Air Plants, Silver Ball Tillandsia)
plant_note: Display on open cork board, in a bowl, or mounted in bright direct to indirect light; Tillandsia xerographica is native to dry tropical forests (the specific epithet means 'dry writing') and is significantly more drought-tolerant than most tillandsias. Water by misting heavily once per week in summer or dunking briefly for 5–10 minutes monthly — overwatering is the primary killer. Allow to dry within 4 hours. In zone 9, it can be grown outdoors year-round in exposed, bright spots and tolerates temperatures to 32°F when dry. One of the slowest-growing tillandsias — a large silver ball represents many years of growth.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to direct morning sun — Tillandsia xerographica is more sun-tolerant than most tillandsias and actually requires brighter light than T. ionantha and other small species to look its best; it will become loose and etiolated in inadequate light. Tillandsia xerographica is a large, slow-growing, epiphytic bromeliad native to the semi-arid tropical dry forests of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and southern Mexico, listed as a protected species in CITES Appendix II due to over-collection from the wild. It has been called the 'King of Air Plants' — a title that reflects both its commanding size (a mature specimen forms a rounded silver ball 12–30 inches across) and its dramatic appearance. The long (12–24 inch), silvery-white to pale gray, curling, strap-like leaves spiral outward and curl back at their tips in a loose, sculptural, spherical arrangement that is among the most architecturally elegant of all bromeliads. The silver color comes from the dense coating of trichomes that cover every leaf surface, maximizing atmospheric moisture absorption from the dry habitats where the plant grows. In spring or summer, a tall flower spike rises from the center producing an inflorescence of pink, green, and purple bracts surrounding small violet tubular flowers. Tillandsia xerographica is extraordinarily long-lived and slow-growing — a prized, prestigious specimen plant for distinctive decorating.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in early spring (seeds need light to germinate) or plant divisions in spring or fall in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yarrow thrives in poor, dry soil and actually performs better without fertilizer — rich soil causes floppy, weak growth.
directions: Direct sow or divide in spring in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; yarrow is one of the most drought-tolerant and adaptable native perennials of North America, producing flat-topped clusters of tiny flowers in white (wild type) or warm shades of yellow, gold, salmon, pink, and red in named cultivars from summer through fall. The ferny, deeply divided aromatic foliage is attractive throughout the season. Yarrow is exceptional for dry, sunny, difficult sites — it tolerates poor soil, heat, drought, and deer grazing and is one of the best perennials for planting on slopes and in gravel gardens. The flat flower heads are important landing platforms for beneficial insects including parasitic wasps, lacewings, and hover flies. Cut stems back by half after the first flush to encourage reblooming; divide every 3 years as plants spread outward. Outstanding long-lasting cut and dried flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost into open, sandy soil near the root zones of oaks or native shrubs that will serve as hosts for this hemi-parasitic annual.
directions: Yaupon Blacksenna is a native annual hemi-parasite of the southeastern United States, growing in open, sandy longleaf pine habitats and roadsides where it parasitizes the roots of oaks and native shrubs to supplement its photosynthesis — direct sow seeds near the root zones of established native oaks or shrubs, as plants depend on host root contact and will not persist in open, host-free soil. Its finely dissected, ferny, Senna-like foliage gives plants an airy, lacy texture quite unlike most other native annuals, and small bright yellow flowers appear throughout summer and fall. It performs best in poor, well-drained, sandy soils in full sun and declines quickly in heavy clay or high-fertility garden beds. Yaupon Blacksenna is an excellent botanical specimen for longleaf pine garden restorations and is an important nectar plant for specialist native bees.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown stock in spring or fall in virtually any soil type in full sun to full shade; yaupon holly is one of the most adaptable native shrubs in North America, tolerating drought, flooding, poor soils, salt spray, and heavy shade. It is dioecious — plant at least one male for every 3–6 females to ensure berry production on female plants.
