plant_note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yellow Rain Lily naturalizes freely in zone 8–10 gardens, self-seeding and producing offsets to form expanding colonies that require minimal maintenance — plant and allow to spread.
directions: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Zephyranthes citrina (Yellow Rain Lily) is one of the finest low-growing, naturalizing bulbs for Gulf South gardens — producing small (2–3 inch), bright golden-yellow, funnel-shaped flowers on 6–8 inch stems in flushes that follow rainfall events from summer through fall. The characteristic blooming response to rainfall gives rain lilies their common name: a period of dry weather followed by rain triggers an almost simultaneous flowering display across an established colony — hundreds of flowers opening within days of a rain event, creating a carpet-effect display that is one of the most charming garden phenomena. Yellow Rain Lily is distinguished from the more common pink and white species by its pure, vivid golden-yellow color — a bright, clean yellow with no orange or orange tones. The small flowers are jewel-like individually and spectacular en masse. Zephyranthes citrina is among the most heat-adapted and drought-tolerant of the rain lilies — naturally adapted to Mexican and Central American seasonally dry habitats and outstanding in the heat and periodic drought of the Gulf South. Established bulbs multiply rapidly by offsets and self-seeding to form large, low-maintenance colonies that naturalize freely in turf edges, rock gardens, and border edges. Plant in masses of 25–50 or more for best display effect — individual bulbs disappear among other plantings.

plant_note: Plant corms in fall in dry to moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; yellow star grass blooms prolifically in spring and early summer and is one of the native wildflowers that tolerates the light shade and root competition under pine trees — a very useful quality for southern landscapes.
directions: Plant small corms 1–2 inches deep in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; yellow star grass tolerates both dry and moderately moist conditions and is easily established in open woodland, pine barrens, and prairie settings. Hypoxis hirsuta is a tiny, charming native wildflower found throughout eastern North America from the Great Plains to the Atlantic coast, producing grass-like, hairy leaves 4–8 inches long and star-shaped, six-petaled, brilliant yellow flowers 1/2–3/4 inch across held on slender stems above the foliage from April through June; despite its small stature, a colony in full bloom is eye-catching. It grows from a corm and tolerates a wide range of conditions from dry pine woods to moist meadows, making it an adaptable choice for naturalizing in rough grass, woodland edges, and pollinator gardens. Native bees visit the flowers readily for pollen.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring as new growth begins, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yellow toad lily requires consistently moist, humus-rich soil and mulching to maintain the cool, moist root zone it prefers — avoid dry, exposed, or hot positions where the shallow rhizomes will suffer drought stress.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; yellow toad lily is a Japanese woodland perennial toad lily of exceptional and rare distinction — while the vast majority of toad lily species (Tricyrtis) produce white or pale-lavender flowers spotted with purple or maroon (the pattern that gives them their toad-spotted common name), T. macranthopsis produces large, clear, unspotted, bright-golden-yellow to warm-yellow, nodding, six-petaled, bell-shaped flowers hanging from the leaf axils along the arching stems in late summer and fall, with just light maroon spotting in the throat. The clear yellow, large, pendant-bell flower form is unique in the genus and exceptionally beautiful in the partial-shade garden where yellow is a relatively scarce flower color. The arching, leafy stems carry broadly oval, clasping, bright-green leaves similar to other toad lilies. It blooms in late summer and fall, extending toad lily color later in the season. A treasured, somewhat difficult-to-source but readily grown toad lily for shade gardens in zone 4–9.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring before emergence or in fall after dormancy in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil; trilliums are slow to establish and resent disturbance — never purchase wild-collected plants. Yellow trillium goes summer-dormant in June–July in the wild but may remain green longer in cultivation with consistent moisture.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in humus-rich, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; yellow trillium is a native woodland wildflower of the southern Appalachians — common in rich cove forests of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia — producing the characteristic trio of leaves and a single erect, sessile (stalkless) flower in clear, warm yellow. The lemon-yellow petals and prominent maroon-yellow stamens give the flower a tropical richness distinct from the white and red trilliums. The mottled silver-green leaves are attractively marked year-round. Yellow trillium is notable as a lemon-scented trillium — the flowers have a pleasant citrusy fragrance that distinguishes it from other sessile-flowered trilliums. It is among the showiest of the sessile trilliums and particularly well suited to shade gardens in the Upper South. Purchase only nursery-propagated plants, as collection from the wild is illegal and ecologically harmful.

plant_note: Plant corms immediately after division in late summer or early fall in moist, humus-rich woodland soil; do not let corms dry out before planting; yellow trout lily is a spring ephemeral that emerges and blooms in early spring then goes fully dormant by early summer.
directions: Plant corms 3–4 inches deep in moist, leafy, woodland soil under the canopy of deciduous trees in early fall; yellow trout lily is a true spring ephemeral native to eastern North American forests, emerging from snow-covered ground in early spring with pairs of beautifully mottled green-and-brown leaves that resemble the markings of a brook trout — hence the name — followed by solitary nodding yellow flowers with reflexed petals and prominent orange anthers in March and April. The entire plant goes dormant by June as the tree canopy fills in, leaving no trace above ground until the following spring; plant in large colonies with later-emerging companions such as hostas or ferns to fill the gap. Slugs and snails are the main pests; avoid planting near areas of heavy slug pressure.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun in spring; yellow trumpet tree grows quickly — 2–3 feet per year in warm climates — and can be used as a street tree, patio specimen, or large accent plant.
directions: Plant container specimens in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; yellow trumpet tree is one of the most spectacular flowering trees in the tropical and subtropical world, producing an explosion of brilliant golden-yellow trumpet-shaped flowers completely covering the bare branches in late winter to early spring before the new leaf flush — the brief but unforgettable show stops traffic when the tree is in peak bloom. Trees grow 15–30 feet tall and wide and tolerate drought, poor soils, and salt once established. Established plants are somewhat cold-hardy to 28°F for brief periods; young trees require frost protection in zone 9 until established. The wood is extraordinarily dense and durable, historically used for bow-making and tool handles.

common_name: Yellow Trumpet Tree (Yellow Tabebuia, Golden Tree, Ipe Amarelo)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun; formerly classified as Tabebuia chrysantha; the yellow trumpet tree is the national tree of Brazil and one of the most admired ornamental trees for zone 10+ gardens in the United States.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, any-type soil including alkaline limestone soils in frost-free locations; yellow trumpet tree (Handroanthus chrysanthus, formerly Tabebuia chrysantha) is a semi-deciduous tree producing spectacular clusters of brilliant golden-yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers in late winter before the new leaves emerge, creating a breathtaking solid-yellow canopy for one to three weeks — among the most stunning floral displays of any tree in the world. It is the national tree of Brazil (ipê amarelo) and commonly planted as a street and park tree in south Florida and along the Gulf Coast. Exceptionally drought-tolerant, hurricane-resistant, and adaptable to poor soils once established. Plant as a specimen in a lawn or as an avenue tree where its brief but extraordinary bloom can be fully appreciated.

common_name: Yellow Trumpet Vine (Chamberlain's Anemopaegma, Golden Bignonia)
plant_note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence in full sun to partial shade; Anemopaegma chamberlaynii grows vigorously in zone 9-10 and may freeze back to the ground in zone 9a winters but regrows from the root system. The vine climbs by tendrils and can reach 20–30 feet on adequate support. Flowers appear primarily in spring and fall, resembling yellow Allamanda or Trumpet vine flowers. Prune after each bloom cycle to maintain shape. Propagate from cuttings or seed.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Yellow Trumpet Vine blooms most prolifically in full sun and produces fewer flowers and more vegetative growth in shaded positions. Anemopaegma chamberlaynii is a vigorous, tendril-climbing, woody vine native to Brazil in the Bignoniaceae family, grown for its display of large, bright yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers that closely resemble those of Allamanda or the yellow form of Bignonia capreolata. The flowers are large (2–3 inches long), funnel-shaped to trumpet-shaped, bright golden-yellow, with five spreading, slightly frilled petal lobes — produced in terminal and axillary clusters throughout the spring and fall. The vine has attractive, pinnately compound leaves with 2 leaflets and a terminal tendril that grips supports for climbing. In zone 9-10 Gulf Coast conditions, Anemopaegma chamberlaynii is valued as a less common but ornamentally rewarding alternative to more frequently planted Bignoniaceae vines like Bignonia capreolata and Campsis radicans, producing the same general 'trumpet vine' aesthetic but in a pure, clear yellow. The genus name 'Anemopaegma' comes from the Greek for 'playing in the wind' — referring to the delicate, light movement of the flowers in a breeze. A handsome and underused flowering vine for zone 9-11 fences and arbors.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; kirengeshoma is intolerant of alkaline or dry soil and resents drought — consistent moisture and acidic conditions are non-negotiable for successful cultivation.
directions: Plant divisions in moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; yellow waxbells is a Korean and Japanese shade perennial of exceptional refinement — an elegant plant with large, soft, palmate, maple-like leaves on dark-purple stems and, uniquely among shade perennials, producing nodding clusters of distinctive, thick-petaled, waxy, pale-yellow bell-shaped flowers in late summer and early autumn (August–September), at the tail end of the shade garden season when most shade perennials have completed their flowering. The flowers have a subtly understated quality — pale, pure yellow, waxy, and perfect — that perfectly complements the architectural plant habit. It requires the cool, moist, acidic conditions of a Japanese woodland garden to perform at its best; it resents alkaline soil and dryness and will not perform satisfactorily in the South. The related Korean species Kirengeshoma koreana (synonym K. palmata 'Koreana') is slightly more upright and open in habit. An exceptional plant for the connoisseur shade garden in zones 5–8 with naturally acidic, cool, moist conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat with sandpaper; yellow wild indigo requires natural cold stratification over winter and is slow from seed — expect 2–3 years to first bloom — but forms a long-lived, deep-rooted plant that resents disturbance once established; sow in a permanent location in lean to average, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun.
directions: Sow direct in fall after scarifying the hard seed coat, in lean to average, well-drained, sandy to loamy, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yellow wild indigo is a nitrogen-fixing legume native to the Gulf Coast states and south-central United States that develops a deep, woody root system making transplanting inadvisable — establish from seed in a permanent location and cold-stratify naturally over winter. Baptisia sphaerocarpa is the yellow-flowered counterpart to the more widely grown blue wild indigo (B. australis), distinguished by its bright golden-yellow, pea-like flowers held in upright racemes from April through May — it typically blooms earlier in spring than blue indigo and is one of the finest yellow-flowered native perennials for hot, dry, sunny conditions in the South. Like all Baptisia species it is extraordinarily long-lived and slow to establish from seed, requiring 2–3 years before first bloom and reaching full maturity and maximum ornamental effect after 5 or more years; once established it is essentially indestructible, surviving extreme drought, poor soils, and neglect. The inflated, rounded seed pods (sphaerocarpa = round-fruited) are ornamentally attractive in fall, and the blue-green, trifoliate leaves provide handsome fine-textured foliage from spring through frost; it is an important early-season nectar and pollen plant for queen bumblebees and specialist native bees before most other prairie wildflowers have opened.

plant_note: Scarify or nick seeds before sowing in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yellow wild indigo is extremely slow the first 2–3 years as it develops a deep taproot, then becomes very long-lived and drought-tolerant. Do not move established plants — the deep taproot makes transplanting nearly impossible after the first year. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it gradually improves soil over time.
directions: Sow scarified seeds in lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; yellow wild indigo is a bushy, rounded native legume of eastern North America, native to dry, sandy woodlands, pine barrens, and open ridges from Maine to Florida, producing bright, clear-yellow pea flowers in loose clusters along upright stems from June through August — a different bloom time than the blue (B. australis) and white (B. alba) species. The attractive three-parted blue-green leaves turn black after frost, and the inflated, rattling seed pods are ornamental in fall and winter. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it gradually improves surrounding soil fertility and thrives in dry, lean soils that challenge most garden plants. It is extremely long-lived once established — plants can persist 50 or more years in appropriate conditions without disturbance. A critical late-summer nectar source for bumblebees and specialist native bees that depend specifically on baptisia flowers for pollen collection.

plant_note: Plant rhizomes horizontally 2–3 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in fall in shade; yellow wood anemone goes dormant by early summer — mark the planting site to avoid disturbing the rhizomes. It spreads slowly into expanding colonies. All parts are toxic if ingested and the sap may cause skin irritation.
directions: Plant rhizomes in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to part shade; yellow wood anemone is a European counterpart to the familiar white wood anemone (Anemone nemorosa), producing the same low, spreading, rhizomatous mats of deeply divided, three-parted leaves in early spring and similarly ephemeral flowers — but in clear, warm golden-yellow rather than white, each bloom a simple, cup-shaped, buttercup-like star of 5–8 petals that appears singly on 4–8 inch stems in March through April before the forest canopy closes. A true spring ephemeral — the entire plant emerges, flowers, sets seed, and dies back to the underground rhizome within 8–10 weeks, completely disappearing by early summer. The warm yellow color, contrasting with the cool whites and blues of woodland wildflower companions (wood anemone, bluebells, grape hyacinth), adds a welcome warmth to the spring woodland tapestry. Both species hybridize naturally where they meet, producing the hybrid Anemone x lipsiensis with pale primrose-yellow flowers. Outstanding for massing under deciduous trees in naturalistic woodland gardens.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this plant establishes quickly and spreads by rhizome to form a dense colony. Tolerates periodic flooding.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained to moist soil in partial to full shade; yellowroot is a low, colony-forming native shrub of Appalachian stream banks and moist woodland slopes, grown for its ferny, compound foliage that provides attractive, fine-textured groundcover in shade, its drooping panicles of small maroon-purple flowers in early spring, and its outstanding orange-gold fall color. The roots and inner bark are vividly yellow from the alkaloid berberine (also found in goldenseal), historically used as a natural yellow dye and for medicinal purposes. As a groundcover, it spreads vigorously by rhizome to form weed-suppressing mats under trees, on moist slopes, and along shaded stream banks. One of the best native low-maintenance groundcovers for moist shade.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; brunfelsia requires consistently moist soil and a regular fertilization program for best flowering — iron deficiency chlorosis on alkaline soils is the most common cultural problem.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; yesterday today tomorrow (Paraguayan brunfelsia, Paraguay raintree) is a South American evergreen or semi-evergreen shrub whose flowers perform the unique trick of opening deep violet-purple on the first day, fading to lavender on the second, and turning pure white on the third — so that at any one time the shrub simultaneously displays all three color stages in a captivating three-tone effect that gives the plant its evocative common name. The intensely sweet, jasmine-like fragrance of the flowers is strongest in the evening. Brunfelsia australis is the hardier of the commercial species, surviving brief cold snaps to around 25°F in protected locations, making it more suitable for zone 8 than the less cold-tolerant Brunfelsia pauciflora. All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested, particularly the berries, and represent a significant risk to dogs who may be attracted to the fallen fruit. Thrives in the dappled light of an open tree canopy. Excellent as a fragrant specimen or informal hedge in warm coastal gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile soil in part shade to full sun; yesterday today and tomorrow is a popular subtropical landscape shrub for zones 9–11, flowering most heavily in spring and sporadically year-round in frost-free conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) produces best performance. Brunfelsia pauciflora (yesterday today and tomorrow or morning noon night) is a Brazilian tropical shrub famous for one of the most charming color-change performances of any flowering plant — new flowers open deep violet-purple ('yesterday'), fade to lavender the next day ('today'), and become nearly white by the third day ('tomorrow') — creating a three-toned tapestry of violet, lavender, and white flowers simultaneously visible on the plant at all times, against a backdrop of glossy, dark-green, somewhat wavy leaves. The flowers are sweetly fragrant, especially in the evening. The shrub is compact (3–6 feet), with a naturally tidy form that requires little pruning; it blooms most heavily in spring and may rebloom after summer rains. In zone 9, it typically survives mild winters with light frost damage, rejuvenating vigorously in spring; protect from hard freezes below 28°F. CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic if ingested; the berries are especially dangerous to children and pets.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; brunfelsia prefers bright, indirect light or morning sun with afternoon shade in the heat of zone 9. All parts of the plant are toxic to pets, particularly dogs — the alkaloid brunfelsamidine causes severe neurological symptoms.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; yesterday-today-and-tomorrow takes its name from one of the most enchanting flower color-change sequences in horticulture: the fragrant, flat-faced flowers open deep violet-purple ('yesterday'), fade to lavender ('today'), and turn white ('tomorrow') before dropping — so at any given moment a single plant displays all three colors simultaneously, creating a remarkable polychrome effect. The sweetly fragrant flowers appear in spring and intermittently through summer and fall. This attractive, moderate-growing evergreen shrub performs best in the bright shade of a pergola or lath house where it is protected from scorching afternoon sun. A critical caution: all parts of the plant are highly toxic to dogs, causing severe neurological symptoms including tremors and seizures — it should not be planted where dogs can access the fruit or flowers. Prune lightly after the main spring bloom flush.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; podocarpus tolerates drought and coastal salt spray well once established and is one of the most versatile and low-maintenance evergreen shrubs for Gulf Coast landscapes.
directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; yew podocarpus (Buddhist pine, shrubby podocarpus) is one of the most widely planted evergreen trees and hedge shrubs throughout the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, prized for its long, flat, dark-green, yew-like leaves on densely branching upright stems that create an elegant, refined, and formally refined appearance whether grown as a specimen tree, a clipped hedge, a privacy screen, or a foundation shrub. Unlike most conifers, podocarpus tolerates significant shade, clay soil, urban heat, salt spray, and drought, making it one of the most adaptable broadleaf conifers available for challenging southeastern growing conditions. It is slower-growing than many hedging plants but ultimately more durable. Left unclipped, it grows eventually to 40 feet as a narrow columnar tree; clipped regularly it maintains any desired height. The small, fleshy, red-purple receptacles bearing the seeds are attractive to birds. Virtually pest-free in the Gulf Coast South.

plant_note: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; ylang-ylang grows very rapidly (6–15 feet per year when young) and produces the characteristic drooping, chandelier-like crown. It is frost sensitive and suited to outdoor culture in zone 10–12 only.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; ylang-ylang is the source of one of the most important perfume ingredients in the world — the intensely fragrant yellow-green flowers with long, drooping petals are steam-distilled to produce the essential oil used in Chanel No. 5, Joy, and countless other perfumes. The scent is rich, heavy, and intensely sweet with notes of jasmine, narcissus, and banana. The tree grows remarkably fast — producing a graceful, weeping tropical specimen in just a few years — with pendulous branches and large, oval leaves. Flowers are produced year-round in tropical climates and are used fresh in garlands and as bedroom perfumers throughout Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Ylang-ylang is the national flower of the Philippines, where it is called 'poor man's perfume.' Only suited to outdoor culture in frost-free zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant in spring or fall in full sun and well-drained soil.
directions: The Yoshino cherry is the classic flowering cherry famed for its spring canopy of fragrant, blush-white blossoms that open before the leaves emerge. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, giving it plenty of room for its broad, spreading crown. Water regularly while young and mulch the root zone, keeping the mulch off the trunk. Prune sparingly and only just after bloom, since cherries are susceptible to disease through large wounds. It provides light shade in summer and golden-bronze foliage in fall, making it a beloved landscape specimen.

plant_note: Divide clumps in early spring before flowering or plant container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part to full shade; Young's barrenwort is semi-evergreen to deciduous — cut back old foliage to the ground in late winter before new growth and flowers emerge. It tolerates dry shade under trees better than most shade perennials once established.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; Young's barrenwort is a hybrid epimedium (between E. diphyllum and E. grandiflorum) producing some of the most delicate and refined foliage and flowers in the genus. The heart-shaped, finely textured leaves emerge in spring with attractive bronze-red coloring before maturing to fresh, light green, then turning bronzy-crimson in autumn. In spring the flowers rise just above the new leaves on wiry stems — small, spurred, in 'bishop's hat' form in pure white ('Niveum') or soft pink ('Roseum') — giving the plant a quality of refined, airy delicacy unlike the bolder epimedium species. It spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a carpet in shaded areas and tolerates the difficult dry-shade conditions under large trees where few groundcovers thrive. Part of the invaluable epimedium genus — collectively the finest group of shade groundcovers for dry, difficult woodland conditions with year-round seasonal interest.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yuletide blooms in December–January in zone 9 — one of the latest-blooming sasanqua camellias — making fall planting ideal for root establishment before the bloom season.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Yuletide is perhaps the most distinctive and widely grown Camellia sasanqua cultivar for its brilliant red flowers with a contrasting boss of bright golden-yellow stamens — a vivid red-and-gold color combination that perfectly matches the traditional holiday color palette, earning the cultivar its name. While most sasanqua camellias bloom in October–November, Yuletide blooms in December–January in zone 9, providing genuine holiday-season color at the precise time when few other plants are in flower. The single, bright red flowers with the prominent golden stamens are smaller than japonica flowers but produced prolifically, covering the upright shrub with vivid color during the typically brown and gray winter garden season. The compact to medium-sized, upright habit grows 5–10 feet tall with dense, small, glossy, dark-green evergreen foliage. Yuletide tolerates more sun than most camellias — sasanqua types generally prefer more sun than japonica camellias — and performs well in 4–6 hours of direct sun with some afternoon protection. The late bloom season makes Yuletide less susceptible to freeze damage on open flowers than earlier-blooming camellias, though the flowers will be damaged by hard freezes below 28°F. Maintain consistent moisture and acidic soil pH for best performance.

plant_note: Divide clumps carefully in early spring or sow fresh seed in fall in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade in spring; Yunnan meadowrue resents disturbance and establishes slowly — plant in its permanent position, mulch well, and leave undivided for the best long-term performance.
directions: Divide clumps or plant container specimens in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Yunnan meadowrue (Delavay's meadow-rue) is a Chinese shade perennial that produces one of the most refined and beautiful flower clouds of any tall shade perennial — the slender, wiry stems rise 4–6 feet above large, delicate, glaucous, blue-green, columbine-like compound leaves, then branch into enormous, open, airy panicles of hundreds of small, pendant, lilac-purple to lavender flowers with large, showy, creamy-yellow stamens in mid-summer. The effect is supremely light and airy — a transparent wash of purple above the foliage — and the long, wiry flower stalks move gracefully in the slightest breeze. 'Hewitt's Double' (sterile, fully double, deep-mauve pompon flowers with no stamens) is the most widely grown cultivar and has the most ornamental and longest-lasting flowers. Slightly more tolerant of warmer climates (to zone 9) than T. rochebrunianum. An exceptional specimen for the back of large shaded borders and cottage-style shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a spot that receives morning sun and some afternoon shade in zone 9 summers. This Chinese species tolerates drier conditions than its American cousin Itea virginica, making it a versatile choice for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist soil and water regularly until established, after which the shrub shows good drought tolerance compared to other sweetspires. Long, arching racemes of fragrant white flowers appear in early summer, followed by excellent red to orange-red fall foliage color that holds late into the season. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain a tidy shape and encourage branching, removing any dead or crowded stems at the base. Mulch annually to protect the root zone and retain soil moisture through the hottest months.

common_name: ZZ Plant (Zanzibar Gem, Aroid Palm, Eternity Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in zone 9; ZZ Plant cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 55°F. It is one of the most drought-tolerant foliage plants available — the thick rhizomes store water and the plant can survive neglect that would kill any other indoor plant. Allow the soil to dry completely between waterings (every 2–4 weeks in winter, monthly in summer for bright-lit specimens). Repot every 2–3 years when roots fill the container. Propagate by leaf cuttings inserted in moist mix — roots and a small rhizome develop within 4–6 months. All parts are toxic if ingested.
directions: Grow in low to bright indirect light; ZZ Plant is the definitive choice for extremely low-light situations — it can survive in conditions (dim office corners, fluorescent-lit rooms, north windows) where virtually no other decorative foliage plant remains healthy. Zamioculcas zamiifolia is a tropical perennial from the dry forests of East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Zimbabwe, Zambia) that stores water in its underground rhizomes and the thick, succulent stems of its compound leaves — an adaptation to the extended dry seasons of its native habitat that translates to extraordinary drought and neglect tolerance in cultivation. The plant produces arching, glossy, pinnately-compound leaves of glossy, dark, almost waxy, deep green oval leaflets that give it a clean, architectural, perpetually healthy appearance. ZZ Plant has become one of the most universally planted commercial interior foliage plants — used in office lobbies, shopping malls, airports, and dim indoor spaces worldwide precisely because it maintains its attractive appearance under conditions that defeat any other ornamental. The 'Raven' cultivar produces dramatic near-black to dark purple foliage. CAUTION: All parts of the plant contain calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested; the sap can irritate skin and eyes.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Zagreb is the most compact commonly available threadleaf coreopsis, making it excellent for foreground positions, edging, and container planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Zagreb is the most compact and upright of the commonly grown threadleaf coreopsis cultivars — a tidy, mounding plant reaching only 12–18 inches tall and wide, with the same fine, thread-like foliage and long succession of bright golden-yellow daisy flowers as the larger threadleaf selections but in a more restrained package that fits small borders, edging positions, and containers that would be overwhelmed by standard coreopsis. The bright, clear golden-yellow flowers are more saturated in color than the soft Moonbeam, making Zagreb a higher-impact plant for positions where its color can be used as an accent rather than a blender. It blooms reliably from late spring through fall in zone 9, with light shearing after heavy bloom periods encouraging additional flush. Zagreb is exceptional for mass planting along walks, in rock gardens, and as a long-season foreground plant in full-sun mixed borders. Like all threadleaf coreopsis, Zagreb is self-seeding and will naturalize in appropriate conditions — seeds germinate readily and maintain the compact habit characteristic. Extremely low-maintenance, drought-tolerant, and resistant to deer browsing.

common_name: Zahara Zinnia (AAS-Winning Heat-Tolerant Mildew-Resistant Landscape Zinnia)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4–6 weeks earlier; Zahara is slightly larger than Profusion zinnia (15–20 inch plants vs. 10–16 inch) with bigger individual flowers. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer bloom. Zahara's exceptional powdery mildew resistance and heat tolerance make it among the most reliable summer annual flowers for the Gulf South, where it blooms continuously without disease intervention.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep after last frost; no deadheading required. Zahara is another interspecific hybrid zinnia (Zinnia marylandica) from Ball Horticultural, closely related to the Profusion series — a compact to medium landscape zinnia with improved flower size over Profusion (2.5–3 inch flowers vs. 2–2.5 inch) while maintaining the same extraordinary disease resistance and self-cleaning, continuously-blooming habit. Zahara received AAS Awards in multiple colors including Zahara Coral Rose (2010), Zahara Sunburst (2010), Zahara White (2006), and others — a testament to the quality of the series across color ranges. The larger individual flowers compared to Profusion give Zahara a more showy appearance suitable for both landscape mass plantings and mixed containers. Like Profusion, Zahara virtually eliminates the maintenance burden of deadheading and disease management that standard zinnia types require in the Gulf South. The plants are bushy, well-branched, and mound-shaped, producing dense coverage that discourages weeds in landscape beds. Colors include fire, scarlet, coral, rose, white, yellow, orange, and bicolors.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in early spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Zawadski's chrysanthemum is notably more heat- and humidity-tolerant than many chrysanthemums and succeeds in the Southeast better than most garden mums. Divide every 2-3 years to maintain vigor and prevent center die-out.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; Zawadski's chrysanthemum is the earliest-blooming species in the genus, flowering from August into September — considerably earlier than most garden chrysanthemums that bloom in October — and filling a valuable mid-to-late-summer gap. The flowers are single or semi-double daisies in shades of pale pink to rose-pink to nearly white, with a more informal, naturalistic quality than the large, pompom garden mums, more closely resembling small, elegant wild daisies. Native to Korea, northeastern China, Siberia, and Japan, it is fully cold-hardy to zone 3 — far hardier than tender garden mums sold as container plants in autumn — and reliably perennial as a clumping, non-invasive perennial. It is also notably more tolerant of summer heat and humidity than many Chrysanthemum species, making it better adapted to southeastern US gardens where common garden mums often fail as perennials. The cultivar Clara Curtis (pink) is the most widely grown selection.

common_name: Zebra Alocasia (Zebra Elephant Ear, Tiger Leg Alocasia)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container in zone 9; Alocasia zebrina cannot tolerate frost or temperatures below 60°F. Use a well-draining mix with added perlite; Alocasias are prone to root rot in heavy soils. Allow the top inch to dry between waterings. The plant may go dormant (losing leaves) during cool or low-light winter months; resume watering when new growth appears. Propagate by separating offsets (pups) from the base of the main plant. All parts are toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Zebra Alocasia maintains its most vibrant appearance with consistent bright indirect light and will become etiolated and lose leaf intensity in very dim conditions. Alocasia zebrina is a striking tropical aroid native to the Philippines in the family Araceae, but its most distinctive ornamental feature is not the leaves alone but the combination of leaf and stem: the plant's petioles (leaf stalks) are dramatically marked with alternating bands and stripes of pale cream-yellow and dark olive-green in a bold pattern that precisely resembles the markings of a zebra — giving the plant its common name 'Zebra Alocasia,' 'Tiger Leg,' or 'Zebra Stem Elephant Ear.' The large, arrowhead-shaped leaves (typically 12–18 inches on established plants) are glossy, medium-green with a smooth surface, elevated on the uniquely patterned long petioles that form the primary ornamental display. The combination of large glossy arrowhead leaves and eye-catching banded stems creates a tropical accent plant with strong architectural presence. Alocasia zebrina is more tolerant of indoor conditions than many Alocasia species and is a good choice for collectors new to the genus. Like all Alocasias, it produces corms (small underground bulblets) that can be separated and grown into new plants. All parts toxic due to calcium oxalate crystals.

common_name: Zebra Calathea (Zebra Plant, Zebra Prayer Plant)
plant_note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded container plant in zone 9; Zebra Calathea cannot tolerate temperatures below 60°F or drafts from air conditioning and heating vents. It requires high humidity (50–70%) for best appearance — leaves will curl and develop brown edges in dry air. Use a pebble tray with water or a humidifier nearby. Water with filtered, distilled, or rainwater (tap water fluoride causes leaf tip burn). Propagate by rhizome division in spring.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade — Zebra Calathea performs best with consistent bright indirect light (avoid direct sun which bleaches the markings) and will tolerate lower light better than most ornamental tropicals, though growth slows considerably. Calathea zebrina is a large, bold tropical from the humid forests of southeastern Brazil, prized for the extraordinary pattern on its large, elongated, velvety leaves: vivid alternating stripes of dark emerald-green and pale lime-green radiate from the central midrib in precise, regular bands like the markings of a zebra, while the undersides of the leaves are deep burgundy-purple. The velvety, matte leaf surface (from microscopic papillae) absorbs light rather than reflecting it, creating an unusually rich, deep color. As a prayer plant in the Marantaceae family, the leaves fold upward at night and open horizontally during the day — when a large clump of Zebra Calathea opens in morning light, the movement is visible. This is one of the largest and most dramatically marked of the popular Calatheas, making it an excellent statement foliage plant for shaded indoor spaces and sheltered outdoor patios in warm climates. Non-toxic to pets and children.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Zebrinus requires full sun to develop and maintain its distinctive horizontal yellow banding — in shade or partial shade, the bands fade and the plant loses its defining characteristic.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Zebra grass is a dramatically variegated miscanthus selection producing broad, arching leaves marked with horizontal bands of creamy yellow that alternate with the green blade tissue — a unique pattern unlike any other common ornamental grass and instantly recognizable at a distance. The horizontal banding is striking and bold, creating a tropical effect that combines exceptionally well with late-summer tropical perennials, dahlias, and other high-impact plants. The plant grows large — 5–7 feet tall and nearly as wide — creating a bold specimen or backdrop presence in the landscape. In late summer and fall, copper-red plumes emerge above the striped foliage. The horizontal banding (as opposed to the longitudinal white stripes of 'Variegatus') is caused by a genetic trait that develops only after temperatures warm — bands may not be visible in spring and early summer but become vivid through the heat of summer. 'Strictus' (Porcupine Grass) is a very similar selection with a more upright habit and slightly narrower habit than 'Zebrinus'. Zebrinus leans with age — staking or dividing every 3–4 years helps maintain an upright stance. Cut back hard in late winter. Miscanthus can self-seed in some areas of the Southeast; remove seed heads before they disperse if invasive spread is a concern.

plant_note: Separate offsets from established rosettes and pot in well-drained cactus mix or gritty succulent soil; zebra haworthia requires bright indirect light indoors — a north or east window or a position several feet from a bright south or west window. It is one of the best succulents for low-light conditions and succeeds where most cacti and succulents would fail. Outdoors, grow in shade or dappled light in zone 9–11.
directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-drained cactus mix; zebra haworthia is one of the most widely grown succulent houseplants in the world — a small, compact South African succulent forming a neat rosette of dark-green, firm, triangular leaves marked with distinctive horizontal bands of white, pebbly tubercles that exactly resemble zebra stripes, making it immediately recognizable. Unlike most succulents which require bright direct sun, zebra haworthia is naturally adapted to growing in shade under shrubs and rocks in South Africa's Eastern Cape, making it an outstanding indoor succulent for bright but indirect light conditions — windowsill plants, offices, and rooms with east or north light. It produces offsets freely, forming multi-rosette clumps, and can be divided regularly to propagate new plants. Small, tubular, whitish flowers appear on long, thin stems in summer. Easy to grow, forgiving of occasional neglect in watering (but not of overwatering), and remarkably long-lived — a well-maintained plant can grow for decades. Formerly classified as Haworthia fasciata or H. attenuata.

plant_note: Root stem tip cuttings under high humidity or plant container-grown specimens in consistently moist, strongly acidic to slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright indirect light or full shade after frost; zebra plant is extremely demanding of high humidity (above 60%), warm temperatures, and consistent moisture — drought causes rapid leaf drop, and direct sun scorches the leaves severely.
directions: Root stem tip cuttings or plant container specimens in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in bright indirect light or full shade; zebra plant is a Brazilian tropical evergreen perennial of the family Acanthaceae prized for both its dramatic foliage and its unique flower display — the large, bold, dark-green, glossy, oval leaves are boldly striped with ivory-white midrib and lateral veins in a precise, high-contrast pattern that exactly resembles a zebra's stripes, creating an intensely graphic, formal appearance that makes it immediately recognizable. In addition to this year-round foliage display, zebra plant produces an upright, bright-yellow to golden, pagoda-like flower spike — a dense, overlapping stack of yellow-green bracts from which small, tubular, yellow flowers emerge one or two at a time — that lasts for 4–6 weeks and is quite decorative. As a tropical shade plant, it requires genuinely high humidity, warmth, and consistent moisture; it is challenging to maintain in excellent condition and is best treated as a temporary specimen brought to peak condition for seasonal display rather than a long-term evergreen. One of the more demanding but rewarding tropical foliage plants for the shaded garden.

plant_note: Sow outdoors around the last spring frost; tolerates light frost and can also be sown in late summer for fall bloom.
directions: Direct sow seeds about a quarter inch deep once the soil is workable in spring, or start indoors a few weeks before the last frost. This cultivar produces bronzy-orange petals that fade to soft pink over a maroon-backed, yellow-centered flower. Deadhead regularly to keep the edible blooms coming and prevent early fade in summer heat. Petals are edible and make a colorful addition to salads or as a garnish. Calendula self-sows readily and thrives in cool weather.

common_name: Zephirine Drouhin Rose (Thornless Fragrant Climbing Bourbon Rose)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring against a fence, arbor, or wall; Zephirine Drouhin is one of the few climbing roses with no thorns, making it a good choice for planting near walkways, and it tolerates partial shade better than most roses.
directions: Plant against a sturdy support in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Introduced in France in 1868, Zephirine Drouhin is a Bourbon climbing rose beloved for two rare qualities in one plant: it is almost completely thornless, making it pleasant to train and prune, and it is intensely, classically rose-scented, with large, cerise-pink, semi-double flowers produced in repeated flushes through the growing season rather than once. It tolerates more shade than most roses, which makes it useful on a partly shaded fence or arbor where sun-hungry modern roses would struggle. It is more susceptible to black spot in humid climates than newer disease-resistant roses, so good air circulation and occasional fungicide treatment in wet years help keep the foliage healthy.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container transplants in spring in well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline to slightly acidic, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; zexmenia is native to the rocky limestone hills and caliche prairies of central Texas and is extremely well adapted to alkaline, dry Gulf Coast soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky to loamy, alkaline to neutral, dry soil in full sun to light shade — zexmenia is a tough, sprawling Texas native perennial that produces cheerful, bright orange-yellow daisy-like flowers nearly continuously from spring through frost in zone 8–9, and virtually year-round in zone 10–11. The rough, hairy leaves and stems give it a slightly weedy texture that suits naturalistic plantings, wildlife gardens, and dry slopes; in borders it benefits from cutting back by one-half in late spring to keep it compact and floriferous. It spreads slowly by both rhizome and self-sowing to form a modest groundcover in dry conditions. Outstanding for wildlife: the flowers are rich in nectar for monarch butterflies, skippers, and native bees. Essentially zero-maintenance once established in well-drained soil — requires no supplemental irrigation in adapted alkaline or caliche soils. A mainstay of the low-water Texas Hill Country garden.

common_name: Zhuzhou Loropetalum (Tall Vigorous Purple-Leaf Fringe Flower)
plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Zhuzhou grows considerably larger and faster than the many compact loropetalum cultivars now common in the trade, making it useful as a large screening shrub or small multi-trunked tree.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade for the deepest foliage color. Zhuzhou is one of the larger, more vigorous loropetalum selections, growing into a substantial evergreen shrub or small tree rather than the low, compact mounds bred more recently for foundation plantings, making it valuable where a tall screen or specimen with the same rich burgundy-purple foliage and fringy hot-pink spring flowers is wanted. It flowers heavily in spring with a lighter rebloom possible later in the season, and the deep foliage color holds well through summer heat given adequate sun. It tolerates a range of soil conditions once established and needs only occasional structural pruning to maintain a strong framework as it reaches its larger mature size.

plant_note: Sow direct in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; zigzag goldenrod is the most shade-adapted of all native goldenrods and grows naturally in the understory of mature deciduous forests.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; zigzag goldenrod is specifically adapted to woodland interior shade and is one of the finest native goldenrods for true shade gardens alongside ferns, Solomon's seal, and shade-tolerant asters. Solidago flexicaulis is named for its distinctively zigzagging stem that changes direction at each leaf node — a unique and charming characteristic; it produces broad, toothed, oval leaves (broader than most goldenrods) and clusters of small, bright-yellow flowers at the leaf axils along the zigzag stem in late summer and fall. Like bluestem goldenrod (S. caesia), it provides critical late-season nectar for pollinators in shaded woodland gardens where few other plants are in bloom at that time; it spreads slowly by rhizomes to form loose, naturalistic colonies under deciduous trees.

plant_note: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; zinnias resent cold, wet ground.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost about a quarter inch deep, or start indoors a few weeks early for an earlier show. This scabiosa-flowered blend yields 2 to 2.5 inch double, semi-double, and occasional single blooms in soft pastel shades where no two flowers are alike. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and more stems for cutting. Cut or deadhead frequently to keep the plants productive all season. Provide good air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature is above 65°F; also easy to start indoors 4–6 weeks early.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep directly in the garden once frost risk is past and soil is warm. Pinch seedlings at 6 in tall to promote branching and a fuller plant with more stems for cutting. Cut flowers frequently to the next set of leaves to stimulate continuous bloom through summer. Avoid overhead watering to reduce powdery mildew; water at the base.

plant_note: Sow directly after the last frost; successive sowings every couple of weeks extend the bloom season.
directions: Direct sow about one inch deep after the last frost once soil has warmed. This branching, pollenless-style florist sunflower blooms roughly two months from sowing, bearing golden-yellow 4 to 6 inch flowers on tall, sturdy stems ideal for bouquets. Space plants closer for single-stem cut flowers or wider to encourage branching and more blooms. Its long vase life makes it a favorite for the backyard florist. Stake in windy sites to keep the tall stems upright.

plant_note: In zone 8–10, plant in fall for a winter-spring bloom season; zonal geraniums perform best in cool weather (50–70°F) and decline or stop flowering in summer heat above 85°F. In zone 9a, fall-through-spring is the preferred season. Start cuttings in late summer to have blooming plants ready for fall planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; despite being called 'geraniums,' these plants are Pelargonium — South African natives in the family Geraniaceae. They are among the most popular and widely grown bedding plants in the world, producing heads of bright red, pink, salmon, white, or bicolor flowers on compact mounds of velvety, horseshoe-zoned foliage. In zone 9a, where summers are too hot for them to thrive, they are grown as cool-season annuals from fall through spring — planted in October and blooming through March or April before summer heat causes decline. Take cuttings in late summer before heat ends the season, root them indoors or in shade, and use them as next fall's transplants. Excellent for containers, window boxes, and cool-season borders.

common_name: Zoysia Grass (Japanese Lawn Grass, Emerald Zoysia)
plant_note: Establish from plugs or sod in spring and early summer; zoysia is slow to establish (plugs typically take a full season to fill in) but extremely persistent once established. Plugs planted 6 inches apart in late spring fill in within 8–12 months in zone 9 conditions. Seeded zoysia (Zoysia japonica cultivars only) is available but slow; plugs and sod are preferred.
directions: Establish from sod or plugs in spring; mow at 1.5–2.5 inches and maintain consistent moisture during establishment — once established, irrigation needs decrease significantly. Zoysia grass encompasses several species (Zoysia japonica, Z. matrella, Z. tenuifolia) and numerous cultivars, ranging from coarse-textured 'Meyer' (Z. japonica) to ultra-fine-bladed 'Zeon' and 'Emerald' (Z. matrella x japonica hybrids), and the thread-fine 'No-Mow' Z. tenuifolia — the variation in texture between cultivars is greater than any other warm-season turf grass. Zoysia's outstanding characteristics are its excellent drought tolerance (deep root system), relatively good shade tolerance (better than Bermuda, approaching St. Augustine), superior cold tolerance (among the hardiest warm-season grasses), dense sod that suppresses weeds, and attractive, dense, fine-textured appearance at maturity. The major limitation is its slow establishment rate — a full season or more to fill in from plugs — and its tendency to go dormant earlier in fall and green up later in spring than other warm-season grasses, giving it a longer dormant brown period in transitional zones. In zone 9, zoysia typically remains green from March through November. Popular cultivars include 'Meyer' (coarse, very cold-hardy), 'Emerald' (fine-textured, shade-tolerant, Gulf South standard), 'Palisades' (excellent drought and shade tolerance), and 'Zeon' (ultra-fine, premium home lawns).

plant_note: Start indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant out once frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant after the weather warms, or direct sow in warm regions. Also called Monarch of the Veldt, this heat- and drought-tolerant South African annual produces 3 to 4 inch daisy-like flowers above silver-tinged foliage from midsummer to fall. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid overwatering as it prefers drier conditions. The blooms attract bees, birds, and butterflies. Flowers close at night and on cloudy days.

common_name: Zuni Crape Myrtle (Compact Lavender-Pink Semi-Dwarf Crape Myrtle)
plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Zuni's smaller mature size makes it a good fit for tight residential spaces where larger crape myrtles would eventually crowd the site.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Zuni is one of the smaller National Arboretum hybrid crape myrtles, producing lavender-pink flower clusters from summer into early fall on a compact, semi-dwarf tree well suited to smaller residential landscapes and foundation plantings. Like other National Arboretum hybrids it shows good resistance to powdery mildew, a common disease problem on older Lagerstroemia indica cultivars, and develops attractive exfoliating bark with age. Fall foliage turns shades of orange-red. Remove root suckers as they appear and prune only to remove crossing or dead branches rather than heavily topping the plant.

plant_note: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in well-draining bark-based medium (not mounted); Zygopetalum mackayi grows naturally at moderate elevations (2,000–5,000 feet) in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil and appreciates cooler nights (50–60°F) that are essential for triggering bloom — without cool nights in fall and winter, the plant may not flower. Water regularly during active growth; reduce in winter. Blooms fall–winter, emitting a powerful, sweet, hyacinth-like fragrance. One of the more cold-tolerant sympodial epiphytic orchids. Non-toxic.
directions: Grow in bright indirect to filtered direct light in well-draining bark medium — Zygopetalum mackayi needs good light to bloom and will not flower in dim conditions, but is damaged by direct summer sun on the foliage. Zygopetalum mackayi is a sympodial, epiphytic to semi-terrestrial orchid native to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil (Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo) at elevations of 2,000–5,000 feet in the Orchidaceae family, one of the most distinctive and ornamentally striking orchids in terms of flower coloration. The flowers of Zygopetalum are immediately recognizable: large (3–4 inches), with three sepals and two petals in the same rich coloration — a combination of green with broad bands and blotches of chocolate-brown to deep maroon — and a dramatically contrasting broad, spreading lip in pure white to pale lilac heavily marked with bold veins of deep purple to dark violet, creating a complex pattern of purple lines and dots on a white or pale background. The color combination of maroon-spotted green petals against a purple-veined white lip is unique among commonly grown orchids and immediately eye-catching. The flowers are strongly, sweetly fragrant — a powerful, hyacinth-like scent that fills a room. Multiple flowers per spike (5–12), with tall erect spikes in fall and winter. A prized and underused orchid for zone 9-11 collectors who can provide cool nights in fall to trigger bloom. Non-toxic.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; abiu is a South American tropical tree suited to zones 10–12 that performs best in consistently warm, humid conditions with ample rainfall or irrigation. Grafted trees from superior selections begin fruiting in 3–4 years and produce smooth, bright yellow fruits with translucent, very sweet, jelly-like flesh.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 10–12; abiu (Pouteria caimito) is a tropical Sapotaceae tree native to the Amazon basin that produces smooth, glossy, bright lemon-yellow fruits with a custardy, translucent white flesh of exceptional sweetness — often described as tasting of caramel, vanilla, or crème brûlée — that clings to a small number of large seeds. The fruit is eaten fresh by scooping out the flesh, taking care to avoid the slightly sticky latex in the skin, which can irritate the lips if left in contact. Abiu is widely grown in Brazil and Queensland, Australia, where its productivity and flavor have made it one of the most popular exotic Sapotaceae fruits among tropical fruit enthusiasts. Trees respond well to regular fertilization with a balanced tropical fruit fertilizer and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development; mulch heavily to conserve soil moisture and maintain root health.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or grafted stock in spring after all frost danger; in zone 9 site against a south-facing wall for extra warmth.
directions: Acerola produces cherry-like fruits with one of the highest natural concentrations of vitamin C of any food plant — up to 65 times that of an orange. The shrubby tree is self-fertile and can bear multiple times per year in truly frost-free climates; it is very sensitive to cold below 30°F and root systems are damaged below 28°F. Plant in well-drained, slightly acid to neutral soil and fertilize lightly with a balanced fertilizer three times per year. Fruit ripens very quickly from green to red and is extremely perishable — harvest when fully red and process (freeze, juice) within 24–48 hours for maximum vitamin C retention.

common_name: Acerola Cherry (Barbados Cherry, Highest Vitamin C Natural Tropical Fruit)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery plants in spring after last frost in full sun; acerola is a frost-sensitive tropical shrub that is damaged below 28°F and killed by temperatures below 25°F. In zone 9, plant against a south-facing wall for frost protection, in containers that can be moved indoors, or in frost-protected microclimates. Acerola produces 3 or more fruit crops per year in frost-free conditions — the plant blooms and fruits almost continuously in warm, humid conditions. The fruits should be harvested at full red ripeness and consumed or processed immediately — acerola loses Vitamin C rapidly after harvest (50% within 24 hours at room temperature). Stem cuttings root readily.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; protect from frost. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain shape and encourage new fruiting wood. Acerola Cherry (Malpighia emarginata, Barbados Cherry, West Indian Cherry) is a tropical American shrub producing small, bright red, cherry-shaped fruits with the highest Vitamin C content of any commonly cultivated fruit — measured at 1,600–4,700 mg per 100 grams of fresh fruit, compared to 50–90 mg per 100 grams in oranges. This extraordinary Vitamin C concentration — 30–100 times that of citrus — makes acerola one of the most nutritionally significant fruits available to home gardeners in zone 9–11, where the plant is well-adapted to the heat and humidity of the Gulf South. The fruits are small (0.5–1 inch), three-lobed, brilliantly red at ripeness, with soft, juicy, somewhat tart flesh — the tartness masks the sweetness but reflects the very high ascorbic acid content. Acerola fruit has extremely limited commercial availability in North America because the ripe fruits are too soft and perishable for commercial shipping; the best quality fruit is available only to gardeners who can harvest and consume them immediately. Acerola is used for fresh eating, juicing, smoothies, and is commercially important in South America (especially Brazil) for vitamin supplement production from the concentrated juice.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; achachairu is more cold-tolerant than mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) and reportedly survives brief dips to 28–30°F when established. Young trees are more sensitive to cold than mature ones — protect for the first several years. It is commercially grown in Bolivia at elevations up to 3,000 feet.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade; achachairu is a Bolivian fruit tree in the same genus as mangosteen (Garcinia) and widely considered the superior subtropical Garcinia for warm temperate gardens — significantly more cold-tolerant than true mangosteen (which requires tropical conditions) while producing excellent fruit. The oval, orange-yellow fruits are 2–3 inches long with a thick, hard rind and sections of white, juicy, translucent flesh with a flavor profile that directly recalls mangosteen: sweet, tropical, slightly acidic, and complex, with an aromatic quality unique in temperate fruits. The tree is dense, dark-green, and attractive as an ornamental, with glossy leaves and a naturally compact, rounded form. Commercially grown in Bolivia, the fruit is popular fresh and in juices, ice creams, and desserts. It grows much faster than mangosteen and begins fruiting in 7–10 years from seed. Australia has embraced it as a commercial orchard crop, and it is increasingly available in subtropical zones 9–11 in the United States.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; ackee requires warm tropical conditions in zones 10–12 to fruit reliably; in zone 9, it may survive in protected locations but rarely fruits without summer heat accumulation.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; avoid planting in frost-prone sites. Blighia sapida (ackee) is a West African tree that became the national fruit of Jamaica, where the arils (fleshy seed coverings) of the opened, ripe fruit are the key ingredient in Jamaica's national dish, ackee and saltfish. The three large, black seeds of each red ackee pod are surrounded by creamy-yellow, buttery, scrambled-egg-textured arils that taste mildly savory and are typically sautéed with salt cod, onions, and peppers. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unripe ackee (pods not fully opened naturally) contains hypoglycin A, a toxin that can cause Jamaican Vomiting Sickness — consume only the fully ripe arils after the pod has opened completely on the tree and seeds have developed fully. The ripe arils are nutritious, high in protein, fat, and niacin. The tree is an attractive, medium-sized evergreen with pinnate leaves and small white flowers. Fresh ackee is available in Jamaican and Caribbean communities in South Florida; canned ackee (already safely processed) is widely available.

common_name: Adams Elderberry (Classic High-Yield Large-Cluster American Elderberry Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Adams is one of the best pollinators for Bob Gordon and Nova elderberry cultivars — planting two or more different cultivars consistently produces 30–50% heavier fruit crops than single-variety plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Adams is one of the oldest and most widely established named elderberry cultivars — selected from wild American elderberry (Sambucus canadensis) populations and long used as the benchmark for comparison in elderberry cultivar trials. It produces large, flat-topped flower clusters (cymes) in June–July — among the largest of named elderberry cultivars — followed by heavy, pendant clusters of small, dark purple-black berries in late August–September. Adams is valued not only for its direct productivity but as an exceptionally effective cross-pollinator for other cultivars: planting Adams near Bob Gordon, Nova, or other cultivars consistently boosts overall production across the planting. The heavy, well-formed berry clusters of Adams are well-suited to all standard elderberry processing: elderberry syrup (a popular immune support product), elderberry wine, elderberry jelly, and elderflower preparations from the spring flowers. The large flower clusters are among the most attractive of any elderberry cultivar for elderflower cordials, fritters, and other culinary uses. As with all American elderberry, Adams spreads vigorously by root suckers and can naturalize in favorable moist conditions — manage the suckering to maintain a defined shrub rather than a spreading thicket. In zone 9, elderberry performs best in the slightly cooler, moister areas — near water features or in low spots where soil moisture is consistent.

common_name: Advance Loquat (Early-Ripening Gulf Coast Orange-Fleshed Loquat)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Advance is one of the earliest-ripening loquat varieties available, with fruit typically mature 2–3 weeks ahead of standard varieties like Premier or Champagne — a significant advantage in the Gulf South where early spring frosts sometimes damage late-blooming varieties or where extended harvest overlapping with other fruit crops creates scheduling conflicts.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil; Advance loquat ripens earlier than most other varieties, often beginning in January–February in zone 9a, making it the first fresh tree fruit of the year in Gulf Coast gardens; fruits are medium, orange-fleshed, and sweet with moderate acidity; harvest sequentially as individual fruits ripen since this variety does not ripen all at once. Advance is an early-ripening loquat cultivar prized in Gulf Coast and Florida gardens for its ability to bring the first fresh homegrown tree fruit of the year to the table — typically ripening in January or February in zone 9a, 2–3 weeks ahead of the standard loquat season. This early ripening characteristic is agriculturally significant in two ways: it extends the effective loquat season (allowing home growers to plant multiple varieties for a longer fresh-fruit window from January through April), and it potentially reduces frost-damage risk to the developing fruit since early-ripening varieties complete their fruit development before the most severe January-February cold events. The fruits of Advance are medium-sized, rounded, with orange to golden-orange skin and firm, sweet orange flesh that is well-flavored without being as intensely aromatic as some other varieties. The tree is moderately vigorous and productive, and its earlier bloom time (September–October) compared to later-season varieties means some cross-pollination timing considerations when planting alongside other loquat varieties. Advance is a standard recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension for Gulf Coast home gardeners who want reliable loquat production.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; African breadfruit is a large, majestic West African tree — the largest member of the breadfruit/jackfruit family (Moraceae) — producing enormous globose fruits (12–36 inches across, up to 65 lbs) unlike common breadfruit: the edible part is the large starchy seeds rather than the flesh, and they are a major dietary staple in Nigeria, Cameroon, and Central Africa.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; a very large tree requiring considerable space — suitable primarily for large tropical properties in zone 11–12. Treculia africana (African breadfruit or ize) is one of the most ecologically and nutritionally important food trees of West and Central Africa — a massive, buttressed tropical tree native to the humid forests of Nigeria, Cameroon, Gabon, DRC, and Central Africa, producing the largest fruits of any species in the breadfruit/jackfruit family (Moraceae). The enormous globose fruits (12–36 inches across, weighing 10–65 lbs) erupt directly from the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) and are technically similar to jackfruit or breadfruit in structure, but used very differently: unlike common breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis, where the flesh is eaten) and jackfruit (where the flesh is the food), in African breadfruit, the edible product is the starchy, protein-rich seeds embedded in the fibrous flesh. The seeds are extracted, boiled or roasted, ground into flour, fermented (to make ugba or ukpaka — a traditional condiment in southeastern Nigeria), made into porridge, or pressed for oil. The fermented seed product (ukpaka) is a major flavor ingredient in Igbo cuisine, used similarly to cheese or miso as an aged, complex-flavored condiment. African breadfruit seeds are exceptionally protein-rich (21%) compared to other starchy staples. The tree is too large and slow-growing for most home gardens but represents one of the most important indigenous food forest trees of sub-Saharan Africa.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical climates (zone 11–12) in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil; African Bush Mango (Ozigo) is a large rainforest tree of Central and West Africa in the same genus as Safou (D. edulis) — bearing elongated, oblong, oil-rich, dark-blue to black fruits boiled and eaten as a sauce or condiment in Central African Gabonese and Cameroonian forest communities.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Dacryodes buettneri requires consistently high rainfall and humidity typical of tropical rainforest conditions — water abundantly during dry spells, mulch heavily, and maintain high organic matter content. Dacryodes buettneri (African Bush Mango, Ozigo, or Arbre à Beurre in French) is a large, emergent to canopy rainforest tree native to Gabon, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, and the Congo Basin forests, a member of the same Burseraceae genus as the widely grown African olive (Dacryodes edulis / Safou). Like safou, D. buettneri produces oblong, oil-rich fruits with thin, waxy skin ripening from green to dark-blue or black-purple, cooked (boiled or roasted) rather than eaten raw — the soft, creamy, rich, butter-like pulp develops a flavor somewhat reminiscent of avocado or a rich olive when heated. The fruits are an important food and oil source for forest-dwelling communities in Gabon and Cameroon, and the extracted fat is used for cooking and traditional personal care. Dacryodes buettneri is a tall-growing, high-humidity, tropical rainforest species best suited to humid equatorial climates in zones 11–12; it does not tolerate drought, salt, or cold and needs rich, moist, forest-type soils to perform well.

subcategory: African dryland cucurbit ornamental fruiting vine
plant_note: Direct sow or plant tuber divisions in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in zone 9–12; African Cucumber is a drought-adapted cucurbit vine from sub-Saharan Africa — producing charming, small, green-and-white striped, oval fruits that ripen to bright orange and red, and growing from a large, water-storing tuberous rootstock that allows it to survive months-long dry seasons — ornamental and wildlife-valuable in dry gardens and xeriscape plantings.
directions: Plant Kedrostis africana seeds or tuber sections in very well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; water sparingly during establishment and infrequently once growing — the large tuberous roots store water for extended dry periods; allow to dry down significantly in winter (the plant may appear dead); new growth emerges from the tuber in spring. African Cucumber is one of the most drought-adapted vines in the Cucurbit family — a member of the extraordinary African flora adapted to seasonal drought — growing from a large, knobby, water-storing tuber (caudex) that can persist underground through months-long dry seasons without any rainfall. Slender, twining vines emerge from the tuber in the wet season and bear small, deeply lobed leaves and clusters of tiny, exquisite, green-and-cream-striped oval fruits that look like perfect miniature watermelons as they develop, then ripen through yellow-orange to bright scarlet-red, splitting to reveal black seeds. In African folklore and traditional medicine, the tuberous roots and fruits of related Kedrostis species have various documented uses; the fruits are eaten by birds and mammals in the wild. The ornamental miniature fruits make it a conversation piece in the dry garden; it is well suited to succulent gardens, xeriscapes, and dry South Africa-inspired plantings in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, deep, sandy to loamy, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in zone 9–12; African Fan Palm is the African counterpart of the Asian Toddy Palm (Borassus flabellifer) — a massive, stately, long-lived fan palm native to the savanna, woodland, and floodplain regions of sub-Saharan Africa from Senegal to Kenya and south to Zimbabwe, producing very large, heavy, orange-brown fruits whose jelly-like germination tissue, fleshy mesocarp, and young shoots are all consumed as food.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, sandy to loamy, alkaline-tolerant soil; Borassus aethiopum is drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry periods of African savanna — water regularly only in the first few years of establishment; growth is very slow initially as the palm develops its extensive root system before vertical growth. Borassus aethiopum (African Fan Palm or African Palmyra) is one of the largest and most ecologically important palms of sub-Saharan Africa — a massive, solitary-trunked fan palm native to the savanna, woodland, and seasonal floodplain ecosystems of tropical and subtropical Africa from Senegal east through Nigeria, Sudan, Kenya, Tanzania, and south to Zimbabwe and Mozambique. The closely related Asian Toddy Palm (Borassus flabellifer) is a separate species adapted to South and Southeast Asian monsoon climates. The African Fan Palm reaches impressive dimensions — trunks to 80+ feet topped by a large, rounded crown of enormous, pleated, circular fan fronds up to 10 feet across. The large (4–6 inch), smooth, orange-brown fruits are economically important: the jelly-like germinating seed tissue is eaten by children and livestock; the fleshy mesocarp is eaten raw or cooked; palm sap tapped from the crown is fermented into 'African palm wine.'
