directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — root rot in heavy wet soils is the primary avocado killer and is not recoverable; Brogdon is a Florida-developed avocado cultivar prized as one of the most cold-hardy named avocado varieties, making it the top choice for gardeners in zone 9a and the warmer parts of zone 8b who want to grow avocados at the northern edge of their hardiness range. The medium-to-large fruits develop deep purple-black skin when ripe — the color change from green to dark purple indicates increasing maturity, but fruits may be harvested slightly early and ripened indoors. The flesh is creamy, rich, and flavorful with excellent avocado oil content. Brogdon has Guatemalan race genetics that contribute its cold hardiness — Guatemalan race avocados are considerably more cold-tolerant than West Indian race types and can survive light frosts. In zone 9 Brogdon is one of the few avocado varieties that can survive the occasional subfreezing nights that occur during cold winters, making it the recommended variety for the most frost-challenged avocado planting sites.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a frost-free or nearly frost-free location.
directions: The bronze loquat is grown both for its striking coppery new foliage and small, tart edible fruit. Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered position, as the flowers and young growth are frost-sensitive. Water regularly while establishing, then only during dry spells once mature. Prune after fruiting to shape the canopy and remove any frost-damaged tips.

common_name: Brown Select Satsuma (Premier Gulf Coast Satsuma Mandarin, Louisiana Commercial Standard)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in spring after frost risk passes; Brown Select Satsuma is one of the most important and widely grown satsuma mandarin selections for the Gulf Coast region, particularly in Louisiana, Mississippi, and southern Alabama where it was selected and evaluated for superior performance under Gulf Coast conditions. It ripens earlier than Owari (the other leading Gulf Coast satsuma) and produces exceptionally sweet, rich juice with the characteristic easy-peel, seedless Satsuma profile. The trees are moderately cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures to around 28°F briefly without major damage) and perform best in zone 8b–9b. Brown Select is named for L.H. Brown, the Louisiana citrus enthusiast who selected it. In zone 9, the fruit typically ripens October–November, making it one of the earliest fresh-tree-ripened citrus available in the season. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil with full sun. Protect from frost below 28°F by covering young trees. Harvest October–November when fully orange. Brown Select Satsuma is a mandarin orange selection developed and popularized in Louisiana, where Satsuma mandarins have been grown commercially and in home gardens along the Gulf Coast since Japanese immigrants introduced the variety to Louisiana in the late 19th century. Satsuma mandarins (Citrus reticulata, specifically the 'Unshiu' or 'Satsuma' group) became an integral part of Gulf Coast culture — Louisiana's St. Bernard Parish and adjacent areas were once a significant commercial Satsuma production center, and Satsuma season (October–December) remains a beloved Gulf South annual event with home trees producing for family and community distribution. The name Satsuma comes from the Satsuma Province of Japan, where the variety was cultivated for centuries before reaching the United States. Brown Select's primary distinction from the more widely distributed Owari Satsuma is earlier ripening (Brown Select ripens 2–3 weeks earlier, in October rather than November) and what many Gulf Coast growers consider superior juice quality — slightly richer, sweeter, and with more complex flavor than Owari in typical Gulf Coast growing conditions. The tree is vigorous and productive under good culture, reliably producing heavy crops of 2-inch flattened-round fruits with loose, easy-peel skin, seedless flesh (typically zero to few seeds per fruit), and intensely sweet, juicy mandarin character. For zone 9 gardeners seeking a productive citrus tree, Brown Select Satsuma is often the first recommendation — earlier than most other mandarins, reliably productive, cold-tolerant enough for zone 9, and producing fruit of exceptional quality.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Brown Select is among the earliest-ripening of all satsuma mandarins — ripening in late September to October, 3–4 weeks earlier than Owari Satsuma. This earliness is its key distinguishing advantage, providing fresh homegrown citrus before any other commonly grown mandarin ripens. Cold hardiness is comparable to Owari (to approximately 15°F when fully dormant). Trees begin producing their first significant crop in the third or fourth year and reach full production in 6–8 years. Protect young trees with frost cloth during the first 2–3 winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Brown Select is a distinctly early-ripening Satsuma mandarin developed and selected in Louisiana as an improvement on Owari Satsuma in terms of harvest timing — the trees produce ripe, full-flavored, easy-peeling mandarins in late September to October, making Brown Select the first commonly grown citrus to ripen in the Gulf South citrus season. The flavor at peak ripeness is comparable to Owari — sweet, aromatic, with the characteristic Satsuma complexity — but the earlier timing extends the homegrown citrus season by 3–4 weeks before Owari becomes ready. Brown Select carries the same exceptional cold hardiness as Owari (among the hardiest of all citrus to freezing temperatures) and the same practical advantage of loose, easily peeled skin and nearly seedless, juicy flesh. The combination of extreme cold hardiness, high productivity, and early ripening makes Brown Select specifically important to Gulf South citrus culture in the zones where winter cold is a genuine risk factor for citrus growing, and where starting the fresh fruit season as early as possible is valuable.

plant_note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in spring; in zone 10 plant March–June. Sapodilla is best suited to zones 10–11 but can be grown in protected zone 9b microclimates. Established trees tolerate brief temperatures to 27–28°F; young trees are damaged below 32°F. Brown Sugar is the preferred cultivar in South Florida for home orchards due to its superior flavor and consistent production. Trees fruit throughout the year with peaks in spring and fall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, alkaline-tolerant soil — sapodilla is one of the few tropical fruits that tolerates the alkaline, rocky soils of South Florida; Brown Sugar is a Florida-selected sapodilla cultivar named for its extraordinary sweetness and distinctive brown-sugar-molasses flavor that sets it apart from standard sapodilla varieties. The medium-sized, round to slightly oval, brown-skinned fruits have grainy, sandy-textured, translucent tan flesh that is so sweet it rivals candy — one of the sweetest fruits grown in North America, with a caramel-brown-sugar-molasses flavor that is universally appreciated even by people unfamiliar with the species. Sapodilla latex in the flesh (chicle, historically the base of chewing gum) gives the texture a slightly sticky, granular quality that is distinctive. Brown Sugar is considered the finest-flavored sapodilla cultivar for fresh eating and is the recommended variety for home orchards in zone 10 South Florida. The evergreen, windproof tree is also extremely drought-tolerant once established.

plant_note: Plant after the last hard frost; in colder zones grow in a container that can be moved to shelter.
directions: This cold-hardy fig tolerates temperatures near 10 degrees F, making it a good choice for cooler regions where most figs struggle. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and provide consistent moisture while fruit is developing for deep burgundy fruit with a pink center. In borderline zones, mulch heavily around the base or grow in a pot to overwinter in a protected spot. Prune in late winter to keep the tree at a manageable height and encourage a strong branching structure.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; Bruce is partially self-fertile but bears more heavily when cross-pollinated by Methley or another low-chill Japanese plum variety; requires 250–400 chill hours.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Bruce is a classic Gulf Coast Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) developed by B.W. Stone at the Texas A&M Experiment Station in the early twentieth century and released in 1952 — one of the first specifically developed low-chill plum varieties adapted to the warm winters of the Gulf South. Bruce requires only 250–400 chill hours and ripens in late May to early June in zone 9, producing heavy crops of medium to large, red-skinned, yellow-fleshed plums with sweet, juicy, pleasant flavor that makes it excellent for fresh eating, jams, and preserves. The tree is vigorous, productive, and fairly disease-resistant under Gulf South conditions — it handles the humid climate better than many other plum varieties. Bruce is partially self-fertile but benefits significantly from cross-pollination: planting with Methley or another low-chill Japanese plum reliably doubles production. Prune annually in late winter to maintain open-center structure at 10–12 feet; thinning fruit to 3–4 inches after June drop produces full-sized, high-quality plums. Brown rot is the primary disease challenge for plums in humid climates; preventive fungicide applications during bloom and as fruit develops reduce losses significantly.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, average to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Brunswick has been grown in the southeastern United States for generations under the name 'Magnolia fig' and is one of the most widely distributed Southern heirloom figs, well-adapted to humid Gulf Coast conditions and reliable in zones 7–10.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Brunswick is a common fig type requiring no pollinator and one of the most widely grown figs in the American South under various regional names. Brunswick (known throughout the southeastern United States as 'Magnolia fig' and occasionally as 'Madonna fig') is an old European fig variety that has been grown in Southern gardens for at least 150 years, widely distributed through cuttings exchanged between generations of gardeners in the Gulf Coast states; the very large (3–5 oz), pear-shaped to oblong fruits have thin, pale yellowish-green to bronze-green skin, prominent ribs, and dark amber to brownish-strawberry interior flesh with moderately sweet flavor and good quality. A vigorous, large-growing tree that tolerates the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers better than many European fig varieties. Excellent for preserves, fresh eating, and drying. Because of widespread cutting-sharing over generations, plants sold or shared under the name 'Magnolia fig' may vary somewhat; most are similar to or identical with Brunswick.

common_name: Brush Cherry (Magenta Brush Cherry, Australian Cherry)
subcategory: tropical evergreen hedge and fruit shrub
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Brush cherry is an Australian native Syzygium grown in zone 9–12 primarily as an ornamental hedge and specimen tree, but producing abundant small, bright magenta-pink, edible fruits with a mild, slightly astringent, rose-water-like flavor.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; shape with hedge shears for formal use or allow to grow naturally as a specimen. Syzygium paniculatum (brush cherry or magenta brush cherry) is an Australian native tree or large shrub in the rose apple family (Myrtaceae) — closely related to rose apple (S. jambos) and other Syzygium fruit trees — that has become one of the most widely planted evergreen hedge, screen, and topiary plants in zone 9–12 landscapes in Florida, California, and the Gulf Coast. The plant produces glossy, lance-shaped, dark-green new growth that flushes copper-red to bronze-red as it emerges — making it attractive year-round — and responds well to shearing into formal hedge shapes. It produces abundant, 1/2-inch, bright magenta-pink fruits in summer that are edible but primarily astringent and mild, with a rose-water and mild apple flavor; they are eaten fresh in small quantities, made into jams, or used in drinks. The flowers are fluffy, cream-white, and produced in clusters; they attract bees and butterflies. As a hedge plant, brush cherry is outstanding: it maintains dense, dark-green foliage, responds well to clipping, and is salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant once established. More widely available in the nursery trade in Florida and California than most other Syzygium species.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring; pair with another Japanese or American plum for cross-pollination.
directions: This cold-hardy hybrid plum produces juicy reddish-purple fruit with a distinctive sweet, spicy flavor often compared to bubblegum. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and include a compatible pollinizer nearby since Toka also serves as an excellent pollinator for other plums. Water consistently during fruit set and thin heavy fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune in late winter to an open-center form for good light penetration and air flow.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; buckthorn bumelia grows naturally in moist to mesic forests, forest edges, and bottomland woodlands across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in woodland garden settings; buckthorn bumelia is a native thorny shrub of the eastern Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, growing naturally in moist, mixed woodlands and forest edges from Virginia to Texas. Unlike the more drought-adapted gum bumelia, this species prefers moist woodland soils and grows in shade-adapted situations at woodland margins and in the forest understory. The small, black fruits in fall are eaten by numerous species of birds and the thorny branches provide valuable nesting habitat. A useful shrub for creating dense, bird-friendly hedgerows at the edge of native woodland garden designs in zones 6–9. The small white flowers in summer attract pollinators.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; Buddha's hand is very cold-sensitive and ideal for container culture.
directions: Buddha's hand is a citron variety bearing distinctive finger-like lobes that contain only aromatic peel with no juice or pulp; it is valued entirely for its intensely fragrant zest used in baking, cocktails, and as a natural air freshener. Trees are self-fertile and small enough to grow in 15–20 gallon containers, making them suitable for patios and sunrooms in colder climates; bring indoors before temperatures fall below 32°F. Fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year and maintain consistent moisture to prevent fruit drop. Harvest when the fingers have turned fully yellow and the fragrance is intense; fruit can be stored at room temperature for 1–2 weeks.

common_name: Burbank Plum (Luther Burbank's Japanese Plum, Red Plum Classic)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Burbank requires cross-pollination from another Japanese plum such as Santa Rosa, Beauty, or Methley for reliable fruit set — it is not reliably self-fruitful; requires approximately 600–700 chill hours, making it adaptable to zones 5–9 with adequate winter cold; in zone 9a, a nearby companion is essential.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit in spring to 4–6 inches apart; plant with a companion Japanese plum for reliable fruiting; Burbank produces medium to large round, dark red to mahogany-red fruits in mid-July to early August with amber-yellow flesh; the flavor is very sweet with tropical-fruity notes and low acidity — one of the best fresh-eating Japanese plums. Burbank plum is Luther Burbank's most famous and historically significant Japanese plum variety, released by the legendary plant breeder in the 1880s from his Santa Rosa, California plant breeding operations where he created an extraordinary number of new fruit varieties through deliberate hybridization and selection from germplasm imported from Japan. Burbank introduced Japanese plums (Prunus salicina) to American horticulture, obtaining seeds directly from Japan through the USDA and developing multiple varieties — but 'Burbank' became the most widely planted and commercially important of these, establishing the Japanese plum as a standard American backyard fruit and farm market crop throughout zones 5–9. The fruits are medium to large, round, with a distinctive deep red to mahogany skin and amber-yellow flesh that is firm, juicy, and very sweet with characteristic Japanese plum flavor — a somewhat tropical, stone-fruit sweetness with lower acidity than European plums. The combination of low chill requirement (approximately 600–700 hours), broad adaptability from zone 5 to zone 9, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Burbank one of the most successful home garden stone fruits of the 20th century. Santa Rosa plum (also by Luther Burbank) is considered the superior variety by many modern tasters, but Burbank predates it and remains widely planted and recommended.

common_name: Burgundy Plum (Small Dark-Red Japanese Plum for Zone 9, Very Low Chill Requirement)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Burgundy requires approximately 200–250 chilling hours — among the lowest chill requirements of any plum variety — making it one of the most reliable Japanese plum choices for zone 9 conditions where many standard plums (requiring 500–800 chill hours) fail to bloom and produce reliably. Plant with a cross-pollinator (Santa Rosa, Methley, or Beauty plum) within 50 feet for best fruit set, as Burgundy benefits significantly from cross-pollination. Burgundy ripens June–July in zone 9, producing small to medium fruits with deep red-burgundy skin. The compact tree size (smaller than most Japanese plum types) makes Burgundy practical for smaller home gardens where a standard-sized plum would be impractically large. Excellent for Gulf Coast gardens where low-chill performance is essential.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters to 3–4 inches when marble-sized. Harvest when deep burgundy-red and slightly soft. Burgundy Plum is a Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) variety originating in California that has become one of the most valued low-chill plum varieties for gardeners in zones 8–10 where the winter chilling hours required by standard plum varieties are inconsistently accumulated. The variety takes its name from the fruit's distinctive deep red to burgundy-purple skin color — one of the darkest red Japanese plum varieties — which covers a sweet, amber-yellow flesh with good sweetness and mild plum flavor. The fruit is smaller than most Japanese plum types (typically 1.5–2 inches) but produced prolifically in good crop years, and the deep color makes Burgundy one of the most visually attractive plums when displayed at market or in fresh fruit arrangements. California agriculture recognized the low-chill potential of Burgundy and similar varieties in the warm Central Valley and southern coastal regions, leading to its adoption as a commercial variety in some California districts and its recommendation by cooperative extension services in low-chill regions nationwide. For Gulf Coast and Gulf South gardeners in zone 9, Burgundy represents one of the few plum varieties that can be grown reliably without the risk of insufficient chilling — a real advantage in an area where most stone fruit production is challenging.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Burmese Grape (Latka, Mafai) is a medium-sized tropical tree native to Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, and Southeast Asia that produces its clustered grape-like fruits directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory) — round, yellow to pinkish-red, thin-skinned fruits with juicy, sweet-sour white pulp surrounding large seeds.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Baccaurea ramiflora benefits from consistent moisture, high humidity, and protection from strong drying winds — mulch heavily and water regularly throughout the growing season. Baccaurea ramiflora (Burmese Grape, Latka, or Mafai) is an evergreen to semi-deciduous tree of the Phyllanthaceae family native to Bangladesh, Myanmar, Bhutan, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, and south into the Malay Peninsula, where it is cultivated and semi-wild in forest edges, village gardens, and homestead agroforestry systems. The tree exhibits cauliflory — fruiting directly on the trunk and large branches in dense, pendulous racemes — producing small (1–2 inch), round to slightly oval, yellow-to-pinkish-red, thin-skinned fruits with translucent, white, sweet-sour, mucilaginous pulp around large seeds. The fruits are eaten fresh when ripe, made into jams, pickles, and fermented drinks, and are an important local market fruit in Bangladesh (where it is called Lotkon), Thailand (Mafai thet), and Myanmar. The tree is dioecious — male and female trees are separate — so plant at least one male with every 4–6 female trees. Baccaurea ramiflora is related to rambai (B. motleyana) and shares the genus's characteristic trunk-borne fruiting and acid-sweet flavor profile popular across Southeast Asian tropical fruit markets.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Burro is suited to zones 9b–12 and does not tolerate hard freezes well, though the rhizome may survive brief dips to 28–30°F with heavy mulching and a warm microclimate.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Burro banana (also called 'Chunky Banana', 'Horse Banana', or 'Bluggoe') is a distinctive ABB genome banana producing uniquely short, thick, blocky fruits (4–6 inches long but very broad and nearly square in cross-section with squared-off ridges) that stand out visually from the typical elongated banana shape. The fruits ripen from green to yellow and develop a characteristic tangy, lemon-tinged sweetness with a slightly chewy texture when fully ripe (skin may be greenish-yellow outside but flesh is cream-colored and sweet); when eaten green-ripe or cooked, the starchy texture is similar to plantain, making Burro a dual-purpose banana suited to both fresh eating when ripe and cooking applications when green. The trees are medium-large (10–14 feet) and vigorous in tropical to subtropical conditions, producing large bunches with up to 8 hands. Burro is well adapted to Gulf Coast humidity and heat in zones 9b–11 and is particularly popular in Mexican and Central American households for its unique dual-use character.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky calcareous or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; bustic grows naturally in tropical hammocks and rockland habitats of south Florida and the Keys, tolerating thin, rocky, alkaline oolitic limestone soils well.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; bustic (false mastic) is a medium to large evergreen tree native to the tropical hammocks and rockland forests of south Florida and the Caribbean, producing a dense, spreading canopy of large, glossy, leathery leaves. The small, white, fragrant flowers are produced throughout the year in clusters, followed by small, yellow to orange edible fruits with a sweet, apricot-mango-like flavor. The fruits are eaten by white-crowned pigeons, gray catbirds, and numerous other birds as a critical food source in the south Florida hammock ecosystem. The wood is extremely hard and durable — historically used for railroad ties and boat building. A superb shade tree for south Florida native landscapes, providing an evergreen canopy, wildlife food, and attractive flowers. One of the characteristic dominant trees of the endangered Miami rock ridge hammock ecosystem.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; choose disease-resistant hybrid selections due to butternut canker pressure on the native species.
directions: Butternut, or white walnut, produces rich, oily nuts with a milder, sweeter flavor than black walnut and is native to eastern North America. The species is severely threatened by Sirococcus clavigignenti-juglandacearum (butternut canker), so seek out canker-resistant cultivars or hybrids (butternut x heartnut crosses, or selections from university breeding programs) rather than straight-species seedlings. Like other walnuts, butternut is monoecious and partially self-fertile but benefits from a second tree nearby; it also produces juglone that can inhibit nearby sensitive plants. Harvest when the sticky, hairy green hulls begin to soften and turn yellow-brown in early to mid-fall; hull promptly and dry nuts for 2–3 weeks before cracking or storing.

subcategory: Brazilian Atlantic Forest myrtaceous berry tree
plant_note: Plant in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 9–11; Cabeludinha (Hairy Jaboticaba, Peluda) is a small to medium fruiting tree in the Myrtaceae family from the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, São Paulo) — closely related to the jaboticaba complex — producing clusters of small, round, yellowish-orange to golden fruits covered in short, fine hairs, with sweet-tart, grape-like translucent pulp used for fresh eating, juices, and liqueurs in the region.
directions: Plant Cabeludinha in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water consistently; maintain high organic matter; protect from hard frost below 28°F; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Myrciaria glazioviana is one of the lesser-known but highly regarded wild fruits of Brazil's endangered Atlantic Forest — a small to medium-sized tree whose golden, hairy fruits are prized locally though almost unknown internationally. The fruits (roughly 0.5–1 inch diameter) are covered in short, fine hairs that give them a distinctly fuzzy appearance, unlike the smooth skin of the closely related jaboticaba (Myrciaria cauliflora). The pulp is translucent, juicy, sweet-tart, and grape-like in texture — excellent eaten fresh directly from the tree and used for juices, fruit wines, and liqueurs in the same tradition as jaboticaba. Unlike jaboticaba, Cabeludinha produces its fruits on the branch tips rather than cauliflorous directly on the trunk, giving a different fruiting habit. Growing naturally in the understory to mid-canopy of Atlantic Forest remnants, it tolerates partial shade better than full-sun species. Part of the rich Myrtaceae fruit tree diversity from Brazil that includes Cambuci (Campomanesia phaea), Grumixama (Eugenia brasiliensis), and Araçá (Psidium cattleianum), representing an extraordinary regional flora of underexploited edible berries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; cacao is a true understory tree requiring shade, warmth above 60°F year-round, and consistent humidity. In zone 10–12 only outdoors; grow in a warm greenhouse or as a houseplant in zone 9.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade — cacao is the source of chocolate, one of the world's most important food crops, and is an understory tree of the tropical rainforest that grows naturally in partial to deep shade. The unusual cauliflorous flowering habit (flowers and fruits growing directly from the main trunk and large branches rather than at branch tips) produces football-shaped pods in vivid yellow, orange, red, or purple at maturity, each containing 30–50 seeds (cocoa beans) embedded in sweet white pulp. The pulp is eaten fresh in cacao-growing regions; the seeds are fermented, dried, and processed to produce cocoa powder and chocolate. In South Florida and tropical zones, small cacao trees fruit in as little as 3–4 years and produce two crops per year. An exceptional specimen plant for the tropical garden that actually prefers shade over full sun.

common_name: Caddo Pecan (Scab-Resistant Productive Mid-Season Pecan, Type II Gulf South Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil; Caddo is a Type II pollinator — plant with Type I varieties including Desirable, Cape Fear, or Pawnee for maximum nut set; Caddo is particularly recommended for the humid, scab-prone Gulf Coast regions of Louisiana, Mississippi, and coastal Texas where its above-average scab resistance reduces the need for intensive fungicide spray programs.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile soil in full sun; Caddo is consistently high-yielding and somewhat more scab-resistant than varieties like Desirable and Wichita in humid conditions; nuts are medium-sized (50–55 per pound) with excellent filling and flavor; a good choice for home orchards in the humid Gulf South where scab management is a primary concern. Caddo pecan is a USDA-released variety that has become an important recommended variety for the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States, particularly valued for its combination of reliable productivity, above-average scab resistance, and good nut quality in the hot, humid growing conditions of the Gulf South. In the humid pecan-growing regions of Louisiana, Mississippi, and coastal Texas, pecan scab disease (caused by the fungal pathogen Fusicladium effusum) is the primary limiting factor in pecan production — attacking leaves, shoots, and developing nuts in wet spring and summer conditions, reducing kernel quality and yield. Varieties with good scab resistance are substantially more forgiving for home orchardists who cannot maintain the intensive fungicide spray programs used by commercial producers. Caddo's above-average scab tolerance compared to Desirable (which is quite scab-susceptible in humid conditions) makes it a more practical choice for many Gulf South home orchards. The nuts are medium-sized with an attractive appearance, good kernel percentage (57–60%), and solid, sweet pecan flavor. Caddo is also considered a relatively good cross-pollinator as a Type II variety paired with Type I varieties in mixed plantings. Louisiana State University's AgCenter has included Caddo as a recommended variety for Louisiana pecan production for many years.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Calabash Tree is frost-sensitive and best suited to zone 10-11 for outdoor planting. In zone 9, container culture is practical for young trees. The tree blooms on old wood (trunk and major branches), so pruning removes future fruiting wood — prune minimally. The large, round fruits (4–14 inches in diameter) hang directly from the trunk and branches by short stems in a phenomenon called 'cauliflory.' Fruits are ornamentally striking but the pulp is mildly toxic and used medicinally, not eaten fresh.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil — Calabash Tree grows most vigorously with full sun and regular water during establishment, then tolerates periods of drought in sandy and rocky soils once established. Crescentia cujete is a medium-sized tropical tree native to Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America, widely distributed by pre-Columbian peoples throughout tropical America as a utilitarian and sacred plant — the large, round, hard-shelled fruits of the calabash have been among the most widely used natural containers, bowls, cups, ladles, and musical instrument bodies across all cultures of the tropical Americas for thousands of years. The tree is immediately recognizable by its phenomenon of 'cauliflory' — flowers and fruits borne directly on the trunk and major branches rather than on the growing tips, a strategy that attracts bat pollinators that can access the flowers and fruits by hovering next to the trunk. The greenish-white, bell-shaped flowers open at night for bat pollination, and the mature fruits are perfectly round to slightly ovoid, 4–14 inches in diameter, hanging directly from the bark on short stalks. The fruit shell is extraordinarily hard when dried — traditionally cut in half for bowls, carved and decorated as art objects, or used as maracas. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida landscapes, the Calabash Tree is a distinctive tropical ornamental valued for its unusual fruiting display.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Calamansi is the most widely used citrus in Philippine and Southeast Asian cooking, with tiny, round, intensely aromatic fruits used as a souring agent in virtually every aspect of Filipino cuisine — a must-have for Filipino cooks.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; calamansi is self-fruitful and produces small, round fruits year-round in warm climates. Citrofortunella microcarpa (calamansi, calamondin, Philippine lime) is a kumquat-tangerine hybrid that is the most important souring citrus in Filipino cuisine and widely used in Southeast Asian cooking generally; the tiny (1–1.5 inch), round, orange-rinded fruits with intensely tart, aromatic green to orange juice are used in Philippine cooking the way lemons and limes are used in Western cuisine — squeezed over virtually every savory dish, mixed with soy sauce as the ubiquitous sawsawan dipping sauce, squeezed over grilled meats, noodles, soups, and rice. The distinctive, intensely floral-tart flavor is quite different from standard lime or lemon. Bears fruit almost continuously in warm climates; highly ornamental with glossy foliage. Outstanding as a large container citrus that can be moved indoors in colder zones.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; calamondin is excellent for container culture in zones 7–8, where it can be brought indoors in winter.
directions: Calamondin is a hybrid between a kumquat and a mandarin orange, producing prolific small, sour-sweet fruits that are eaten whole like kumquats or used as a lime substitute in Southeast Asian cooking. The tree is self-fertile, nearly thornless, highly ornamental with fragrant white flowers, and among the easiest citrus to grow in containers — it tolerates indoor conditions better than most citrus. It tolerates brief dips to about 20°F when established. Fruit ripens from late autumn through spring; harvest when fully orange for best flavor, though the rind remains sweet while the flesh is tart even at the green-orange stage.

plant_note: Grow outdoors only in frost-free zones; elsewhere keep in a container that overwinters indoors.
directions: This ornamental citrus, a kumquat-mandarin cross, bears a heavy crop of small, round, tart fruit prized for marmalades and drinks. Grow in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and feed regularly with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In non-tropical climates keep it potted so it can move to a bright indoor spot before frost. Fragrant white blossoms and glossy evergreen leaves make it as decorative as it is productive.

plant_note: Plant outdoors in warm zones; grow in a movable container in colder regions.
directions: This compact mandarin produces sweet, juicy, easy-peeling fruit and stays small enough for patios or sunny indoor rooms. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and water deeply but allow the top inch to dry between waterings. Feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season and protect from frost, moving containers indoors when temperatures drop. Light pruning after harvest keeps the canopy open and the tree productive.

common_name: Calville Blanc d'Hiver Apple (French Culinary Heirloom Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Calville Blanc ripens very late and needs a long growing season, developing its full flavor and characteristic vitamin C content only after several weeks of storage.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Documented in France since the 1500s, Calville Blanc d'Hiver is one of the oldest named apple cultivars still grown and became the classic dessert and pastry apple of French cuisine, famously used in tarte Tatin and other traditional preparations. The irregularly ribbed, pale greenish-yellow fruit has a distinctive, complex, almost pineapple-like flavor and unusually high vitamin C content for an apple. It ripens quite late in the season and improves with several weeks of storage, but the tree can be a light or biennial bearer and benefits from a warm site and careful thinning.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full sun; cambucá is a rainforest understory tree from Brazil's Atlantic Forest that tolerates and even prefers some afternoon shade, making it a candidate for food forest mid-canopy positions. Use fresh seed, as viability drops sharply within a few weeks of extraction.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full sun in zones 10–11; cambucá is a rare Atlantic Forest gem in the Myrtaceae family (closely related to jaboticaba) that produces large, round, yellow-green fruits directly on its trunk and major branches — a phenomenon known as cauliflory that makes the tree a striking spectacle when loaded with fruit. The thick-skinned fruits hold exceptionally sweet, white, juicy flesh with a fragrant, complex flavor described as a blend of mango and passion fruit, and are eaten fresh or made into artisanal jams and wines in the Brazilian coastal states where it is native. Cambucá prefers the high humidity and warm temperatures of its coastal rainforest home and performs best with regular deep watering and organic mulch kept away from the trunk. Seed must be planted fresh — sow immediately after extraction from ripe fruit, as viability falls dramatically within two to three weeks.

plant_note: Plant in full to partial sun in moist to wet, acidic soil; camu camu is native to seasonally flooded Amazonian riverbanks and tolerates waterlogging far better than most fruit plants — it can actually grow with its roots in standing water for months. Zone 10-12 only in the US.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; camu camu (Myrciaria dubia) is a shrubby Amazonian Myrtaceae producing small, cherry-like, reddish-purple fruits with a powerfully acidic, cranberry-passion-fruit flavor that are virtually inedible raw due to their extreme sourness but are valued as one of the highest natural sources of vitamin C on earth — 20–60 times more vitamin C per 100g than oranges. The fruit is processed into powders, juices, and health supplements widely sold in health food stores; home production is possible in south Florida and Hawaii with specimens growing in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil or at pond edges. An outstanding addition to a food-forest understory in zone 10+, where it also provides white, fragrant flowers and attractive foliage.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Canada plum is the most cold-hardy native North American plum and is invaluable for fruit production in zones 2–6 where other plums cannot survive.
directions: Plant grafted trees or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Canada plum is the most cold-hardy of the native North American plums, surviving temperatures to -40°F and producing fruit reliably in zones 2–6 where most stone fruit trees would be killed by winter cold. Prunus nigra is a native small tree or large shrub of eastern and central Canada and the northern US producing prolific white flowers in early spring (before leaves) and medium-sized, oval plums ripening yellow to red to deep purple in late summer with a tart, wild-plum flavor excellent for jams, jellies, and sauce. Cross-pollinate with American plum (P. americana) or another Canada plum seedling for best fruit set; it also attracts wildlife heavily — the fruit is avidly eaten by bears, raccoons, foxes, and many bird species.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Canary Island date palm is tolerant of salt spray and coastal conditions. It tolerates light frost to about 15-18°F when established but young plants need protection below 25°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Canary Island date palm is the most majestic and widely planted ornamental palm in the world — a massive, slow-growing palm with an immense crown of arching, dark green, pinnate fronds each up to 18 feet long, creating a fountain-like canopy of extraordinary scale and beauty. The pineapple-like patterned trunk develops from years of old frond bases and becomes a powerful architectural statement in landscapes. Native to the Canary Islands, it has been planted throughout the Mediterranean, California, Florida, and worldwide tropical and subtropical climates. The orange-yellow fruits produced in massive pendant clusters are date-like and technically edible but too astringent for pleasant eating. Mature trees create the grandest scale of any landscape palm — worth every inch of space. Widely used as street trees in California, Spain, Portugal, and Florida. Fusarium wilt disease (Fusarium oxysporum) is a serious and fatal threat; purchase only certified disease-free specimens.

plant_note: Plant seedlings or cuttings in full sun in well-drained soil; candlenut is the state tree of Hawaii (kukui) and can be grown throughout zone 10–12; it tolerates a wide range of soils and is relatively fast-growing. Note: raw nuts are toxic — they must be roasted or cooked before eating.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil in frost-free conditions; candlenut (Aleurites moluccanus, kukui in Hawaiian) is an extremely versatile tree native to tropical Asia and the Pacific Islands, widely cultivated for its large, oily nuts that are a critical ingredient in Indonesian (kemiri), Malaysian, and Hawaiian cuisine — the roasted kernels are ground into pastes, sauces, and curries. Caution: raw candlenuts are toxic and mildly purgative due to saponins; always roast or cook before eating. The nuts have the highest oil content of any edible nut and burn like candles, giving the tree its common name; the oil was traditionally used for lighting, wood finishing, and skin care. The Hawaii state tree (kukui), with distinctive silvery-green foliage visible from a distance.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Candy bears at a young age and requires a compatible Type I pollinator such as Pawnee or Kanza for best nut set.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA pecan breeding program, Candy is valued for bearing precociously, often producing a crop within a few years of planting, well ahead of many older commercial cultivars. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality and a well-filled, attractive shell, and the tree tends to crop reliably from a young age rather than needing a long establishment period before its first real harvest. As with other pecans, supplement with zinc on alkaline soils and monitor for scab disease pressure in humid climates.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; canistel is limited to truly frost-free zones in the continental U.S.
directions: Canistel is an evergreen tropical tree that produces smooth, orange-yellow fruit with dense, dry, egg-yolk-colored flesh — hence the common name egg fruit. Grafted trees are strongly preferred over seedlings; seedlings may take 5–7 years to fruit and show variable quality, while grafted plants can begin bearing in 2–3 years. The tree is drought-tolerant once established and tolerates a range of well-drained soils but is damaged by temperatures below 32°F even briefly. Harvest when the skin turns fully golden-yellow and yields firmly to pressure; ripen indoors at room temperature for 3–5 days until completely soft and sweet.

common_name: Cannonball Tree (Nagalingam, Sala Tree, Shivalinga Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun with well-drained, fertile, moist soil; Cannonball Tree is frost-sensitive and suitable only for zone 10-11 outdoor planting. In zone 9, it can be grown as a large container specimen. Cauliflorous (trunk-flowering) trees like this one should never be heavily pruned — the permanent framework of the trunk and branches is the bearing surface for all flowers and fruits. Site where the striking trunk flowers and falling fruits can be appreciated — do not plant where falling cannonball fruits (6–12 inch diameter, 5–10 lbs) could fall on people or vehicles.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil — Cannonball Tree grows most rapidly and blooms most prolifically in full sun with regular watering, becoming a dramatic, multi-season ornamental after 5–10 years. Couroupita guianensis is a large tropical tree native to tropical South America (Guiana, Venezuela, Peru, Brazil) in the Brazil-nut family (Lecythidaceae), famous for two simultaneous ornamental spectacles occurring directly on its trunk and branches. The flowers are produced year-round on long, pendant cauliflorous racemes (flower stalks) that hang directly from the trunk and major branches — each fragrant, complex, waxy flower 3–4 inches across with large, creamy-white to pale pink petals surrounding a modified stamen structure in pink, orange, and yellow that creates an exotic, orchid-like appearance. Simultaneously, the tree bears the previous season's fruits: enormous, perfectly spherical, hard-shelled, rust-brown fruits 6–12 inches in diameter (the 'cannonballs') that are attached in clusters to the same trunk racemes as the flowers — so the tree often displays flowers and fruits simultaneously. The fruits fall explosively when ripe, with a loud impact that explains the 'Cannonball Tree' name. In Hindu and Buddhist temple gardens throughout South and Southeast Asia (where the tree is sacred as the 'Shivalinga Tree' and 'Sala Tree'), the trunk-borne flowers and spherical fruits have profound religious symbolism.

common_name: Cape Elderberry (Bourtree, Southern Elder, Yellow Elderberry)
plant_note: Root cuttings in spring or autumn; cape elderberry is an Australian elder native to humid subtropical forests and rainforest margins, suited to zones 9-11 in the US where it can be grown as an alternative to the northern elderberries.
directions: Root stem cuttings in spring or autumn in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; plant in partial shade to full sun; cape elderberry (Sambucus australasica) is an Australian species native to Queensland and New South Wales rainforest edges and creek margins, producing large clusters of small, bright yellow berries (distinct from the dark purple-black of northern elderberries) that ripen in summer. The berries are edible when fully ripe and can be used in the same applications as European elderberries — jams, jellies, syrups, and wines — though they are reportedly less intensely flavored. The flowers are also edible as elderflower tea and fritters. An attractive subtropical alternative to common elderberry for zone 9–11 gardens, with similar wildlife value and similar requirements for moist, moderately fertile soil.

common_name: Cape Fear Pecan (Mid-Atlantic Southeastern Pecan, Type I Reliable Cross-Pollinator)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cape Fear is a Type I pollinator (protandrous — sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) and is frequently recommended as a cross-pollinator for Type II varieties including Desirable, Wichita, Pawnee, and Elliott; the Pawnee pecan entry in this database explicitly mentions Cape Fear as one of the recommended Type I companion varieties.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained loam in full sun; Cape Fear is a reliable medium-to-large nut producer with moderate scab resistance; it is widely adapted throughout the southeastern states from coastal North Carolina through the Gulf South; trees are vigorous and come into production in 5–7 years; supplement with zinc spray in spring. Cape Fear pecan is a variety developed by the USDA Pecan Breeding Program and named for the Cape Fear River valley of North Carolina, where the variety demonstrated particularly reliable production under the moderately humid coastal plain conditions of the mid-Atlantic South. The variety has proven broadly adapted throughout the southeastern states from eastern North Carolina through the Gulf Coast, performing reliably under a range of humidity levels and soil types typical of the coastal plain and river bottom land of the region. Cape Fear produces medium-to-large nuts (45–52 per pound) with good kernel percentage (57–61%) and solid pecan flavor — not the exceptional nut quality of Desirable or Wichita but consistent, reliable, and commercially acceptable. The variety's primary contribution to many home orchard designs is as the Type I cross-pollinator for the more challenging-to-fruit Type II varieties: since pecan varieties are strongly cross-pollinated (most nut set requires pollen from a different variety), placing Cape Fear alongside Type II varieties like Desirable, Wichita, Elliott, or Stuart ensures reliable pollination and heavier crops on both trees. Cape Fear is also the companion pollinator recommended in many pecan extension publications for home gardeners planting the newer precocious varieties like Pawnee.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil after frost danger has passed. In zone 9–11 it acts as a short-lived perennial; cut back by half in late winter to encourage fresh growth.
directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant to well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost; cape gooseberry is a South American relative of tomatillo with intensely flavorful, tangy-sweet golden berries enclosed in papery brown husks — the same fruit sold as 'golden berries' or 'physalis' in supermarkets and restaurants worldwide. The distinctive papery husks enclose 3/4-inch golden-orange berries at maturity; berries are eaten fresh, dried, in salsa, preserves, and baked goods. Each plant produces hundreds of berries over a long season from midsummer to frost. In zone 9–11 it overwinters as a perennial and becomes a shrubby plant 3–5 feet tall producing fruit year-round. It self-sows generously in warm climates and can naturalize. An outstanding fruit crop for the Gulf Coast garden.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted tree; move outdoors after frost.
directions: The Cara Cara is a sweet, low-acid navel orange distinguished by its rosy-pink flesh and berry-like flavor. This adaptable citrus performs well in the ground in mild regions or in a large container that can be moved indoors where winters are cold. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed it a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season. Water deeply but allow the top of the soil to dry between waterings, and protect it from frost.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; young trees need protection from cold and wind for the first two seasons.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; carambola is sensitive to flooding and cold below 27°F even briefly, limiting outdoor cultivation to frost-free zones. The tree blooms multiple times per year and produces fruits along the trunk and main branches — a trait called cauliflory — so hang fruit-protection bags in commercial settings to prevent blemishes. Harvest when the ribs have turned fully yellow and the fruit has slight give; overripe fruit browns quickly at the tips. Fertilize with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer 3–4 times per year to sustain heavy bearing.

common_name: Carlos Muscadine Grape (Classic Bronze Self-Fertile Wine-Quality Gulf South Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Carlos has perfect (self-fertile) flowers and is one of the best pollinators for female-flowered muscadine cultivars — planting Carlos near female cultivars consistently improves production in mixed plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Carlos is the benchmark bronze muscadine cultivar — one of the most widely planted and historically important Gulf South muscadines, valued equally for fresh eating quality and as the primary variety for muscadine wine production in the Southeast. The medium to large, round grapes ripen to bronze-tan to bronze-gold color with thick skin and sweet, aromatic, musky flesh typical of the muscadine type; the flavor profile is somewhat more refined and balanced in acidity than many other muscadine cultivars, which is why Carlos is the preferred variety for wine production and has long been the standard against which other muscadines are evaluated. Muscadine wine from Carlos has a characteristic sweet, floral, musky quality — distinctively Southern and quite unlike any European wine style — with enough natural acidity to provide balance. Carlos is self-fertile with perfect flowers and is an outstanding cross-pollinator for female-flowered cultivars including Fry, Higgins, and others. The vines are vigorous and productive, disease-resistant to the fungal diseases (black rot, downy mildew, powdery mildew) that make growing European grapes nearly impossible in Gulf South conditions, and adapted to the heat, humidity, and long growing season of zones 6–10. Grapes ripen in August through September, with individual grapes in each cluster ripening sequentially. Excellent for fresh eating, juice, muscadine wine, jelly, and preserves.

common_name: Carmel Almond (Reliable California Pollenizer Almond, High-Production Soft-Shell Almond)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, fertile soil in full sun; Carmel is self-incompatible but is one of the best cross-pollinators available for Nonpareil — its bloom time overlaps extensively with Nonpareil, and its very abundant pollen production and early bearing habit make it the most commonly planted companion variety for Nonpareil in California commercial orchards; requires approximately 300 chill hours.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained fertile soil in full sun; Carmel is primarily planted as a companion and cross-pollinator for Nonpareil in commercial orchards but also produces its own crop of soft-shell almonds with good flavor; it ripens slightly after Nonpareil (mid-August); kernels are slightly smaller than Nonpareil but of good quality for snacking and roasting. Carmel almond is a UC Davis release developed specifically to serve as the ideal companion and cross-pollinator for Nonpareil — the two are now the most common planting pair in California commercial almond orchards, with the standard three-variety system often being Nonpareil + Carmel + Mission or Butte. Carmel's most important attribute in commercial production is pollination efficiency: its bloom time coincides precisely with Nonpareil, it produces abundant viable pollen, and it bears its own crop reliably and heavily — making it productive as both a pollinator and a production variety rather than just a sterile companion tree. The variety was developed at UC Davis by Floyd Zaiger and William Sims and has been important in the rapid expansion of California almond acreage since the 1970s because its reliable early bearing and high productivity complemented Nonpareil's commercial requirements. Carmel produces soft-shell almonds of moderate size with a sweet, mild almond flavor somewhat similar to Nonpareil — entirely acceptable for all uses including direct consumption, roasting, and confectionery — while its primary role remains as the preferred pollinator in the world's most important almond-producing region.

common_name: Carmine Jewel Cherry (Cold-Hardy Dwarf Bush Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Carmine Jewel is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator, and its compact, shrubby form fruits at a young age, often within 2-3 years of planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Carmine Jewel tolerates a wide range of soils and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Carmine Jewel is a University of Saskatchewan-bred dwarf sour cherry hybrid, part of a breeding program aimed at producing extremely cold-hardy, compact cherry shrubs for the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies, where standard sweet and tart cherry trees cannot survive. The dense, shrubby plant stays under 8 feet tall, bears dark red, sweet-tart fruit good for fresh eating, baking, and preserves, and is self-fertile, bearing reliably without a second pollinator. Because of its extreme cold hardiness (surviving winter lows well below -40°F), it is grown mainly in northern climates outside the Gulf South's typical range, but is included here as a distinctive, easy-care option for gardeners in colder zones who want cherries without the size and chill-hour demands of standard cherry trees. Prune only lightly, removing dead or crossing wood, since the shrub form needs little training.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring after frost; carob is well-suited to dry Mediterranean-climate zones 9–11 and tolerates alkaline, rocky soils.
directions: Carob is a slow-growing evergreen legume tree that fixes atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils where few other fruits survive; it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established. Trees are dioecious — plant one male for every 8–10 female trees, or choose hermaphroditic cultivars such as Santa Fe and Clifford that produce fruit without a separate male. The long, dark-brown seed pods ripen in late summer and fall and are left on the tree to dry and sweeten; they are harvested when fully brown, dry, and the seeds rattle inside. Carob pods are sweet and chocolatey and used ground as a cocoa substitute or in stock feed.

common_name: Carolina Red June Apple (Early-Ripening Southern Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Carolina Red June is one of the earliest-ripening Southern heirloom apples, producing small, deep red fruit as early as June, well ahead of most apple varieties, with low chill requirements suited to the warmer parts of the South.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Carolina Red June is a Southern heirloom apple documented since at least the early 1800s and grown widely across the antebellum South, valued above all for its extremely early ripening, often ready to pick in June, weeks ahead of nearly every other apple variety and giving Southern growers fresh apples at a time of year when no other apple is available. Fruit is small to medium, deep red over a yellow background, with crisp, juicy, mildly tart flesh good for fresh eating, sauce, and early-season pies. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the variety's relatively low chill requirement makes it one of the more Gulf-South-adapted heirloom apples compared with higher-chill Northern varieties. Because it ripens so early and doesn't store particularly long, plan to use or process the crop promptly rather than relying on it for winter storage. Plant with another apple variety nearby for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Carpathian strains tolerate far colder winters than typical English walnut and can be grown well outside the mild-winter regions most walnuts require.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, away from vegetable gardens and other sensitive plants since walnut roots exude juglone, a compound toxic to many other species. Carpathian refers to a cold-hardy strain of the common English (Persian) walnut originating in the mountainous Carpathian region of Poland, introduced to North America in the mid-20th century specifically because it tolerates far colder winters than typical English walnut selections from milder climates. The thin-shelled, easily cracked nuts have the classic mild, rich English walnut flavor, and the trees are large, long-lived, and productive once mature, typically beginning to bear within five to seven years of planting.

plant_note: Plant fresh cashew seeds (the actual nuts before roasting) 1 inch deep in well-drained, sandy, lean soil after last frost in zone 10–11; in zone 9, cashew is best grown as a container plant moved indoors in winter or in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic to neutral, infertile to average soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; cashew is native to northeastern Brazil and now cultivated throughout the tropics as one of the world's most important nut crops. The 'nut' is actually a large seed attached to the outside of a swollen, fleshy, pear-shaped 'cashew apple' (pseudofruit) which is edible fresh, juiced, or fermented into cashew wine. The seed shell contains urushiol — the same irritating compound in poison ivy — and must never be handled or roasted without protection. Commercial cashews are processed to remove this compound before the familiar pale nut is edible. The cashew apple, rarely seen in North America, is highly perishable and consumed fresh throughout tropical regions as a vitamin-C-rich refreshing fruit. In zone 9, treat as a container specimen moved indoors in winter.

common_name: Cedar Bay Cherry (Beach Cherry, Reinwardtiana Berry)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy coastal soil in full sun to part shade; cedar bay cherry is an Australian native Eugenia (related to Surinam cherry) from tropical Queensland and the Northern Territory coastal regions — producing abundant small, round, bright orange-red to red berries with sweet-tart, pleasant flavor, and tolerant of salt spray, wind, and sandy coastal soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; excellent salt and wind tolerance makes it outstanding for coastal gardens. Eugenia reinwardtiana (cedar bay cherry or beach cherry) is an Australian native Eugenia shrub or small tree from the tropical beaches, coastal scrub, and dry vine thickets of far north Queensland and the Northern Territory — one of the few Eugenia species native to Australia (most Eugenia, including the commercial Brazilian cherry group, are from the Americas). The plant bears small (1/2-inch), round, bright orange-red to scarlet fruits in clusters along the branches — similar in size and color to Surinam cherry (Eugenia uniflora) but with a different, distinctly sweet-acid, pleasant flavor without the resinous undertone characteristic of Surinam cherry. The fruits are eaten fresh as a snack and used in jams and beverages. Cedar bay cherry is especially valued in coastal tropical gardens for its outstanding tolerance of salt spray, wind, sandy soils, and coastal drought — growing naturally on exposed beaches and coastal headlands. The plant can be grown as a low shrub or allowed to develop into a small tree; it responds well to pruning for hedge use. The attractive, glossy, oval leaves and prolific berry production make it ornamentally pleasing. Very rare in cultivation outside tropical Queensland and the Pacific Islands.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil; in zone 7–8, plant against a south-facing wall for warmth and protection. Container culture is excellent for bringing indoors during harsh winters.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; Celeste is the most popular and cold-hardy fig in the Deep South, producing small to medium, violet-brown figs with a honey-sweet, rose-pink interior that ripen mid-July through August. It is the standard home garden fig from Virginia to Texas and is considered by many to have the best flavor of any common fig variety. Figs fruit on second-year wood and on new growth late in the season — do not prune heavily in winter. Mulch roots in zone 7 to prevent root freeze-kill. Trees rarely need fertilizer and will produce heavy crops with minimal care once established. Other excellent Gulf Coast cultivars include 'Brown Turkey', 'LSU Purple', and 'LSU Gold'.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; cempedak is a Southeast Asian Artocarpus fruit tree closely related to jackfruit but considered by many connoisseurs to produce richer, sweeter, more aromatic fruits — with the flesh also frequently battered and fried in Malaysia; the tree tolerates more shade than jackfruit, making it useful in multi-story food forests.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; cempedak tolerates partial shade better than jackfruit — useful in the middle canopy of tropical food forests. Artocarpus integer (cempedak or champedak) is a Southeast Asian fruit tree in the breadfruit family (Moraceae) — a close relative of jackfruit (A. heterophyllus) native to the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, and Sumatra. Like jackfruit, cempedak produces large composite fruits on the trunk and branches through cauliflory, but the fruits are smaller than jackfruit (typically 6–15 inches long, 4–6 inches diameter), cylindrical, and covered in small, soft, hexagonal-patterned protrusions with a yellow to orange-green exterior. The interior fruit segments are rich, sweet, aromatic, and exceptionally good — widely considered by Malaysian and Indonesian fruit lovers to be superior in flavor to jackfruit, with a denser, creamier, more strongly tropical-fruit character combining mango, banana, and custard apple notes. Cempedak is particularly popular in Malaysia fried: the individual fruit segments are battered and deep-fried as a street food (exactly like a tropical doughnut), which is a major culinary tradition. The seeds are edible when roasted or boiled. Cempedak is more shade-tolerant than jackfruit, making it useful as a middle-canopy tree in multi-story agroforestry systems. Requires genuinely tropical conditions (zone 11–12) without frost.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings with at least one node in moist medium; monstera grows outdoors year-round only in frost-free climates and is damaged below 30°F. In zones 9 it can be grown in a sheltered location with frost protection but typically dies to the ground in cold winters and regrows from the roots.
directions: Root cuttings in moist mix and transplant to rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Monstera deliciosa (ceriman, Mexican breadfruit) is the beloved houseplant grown everywhere, but in frost-free zones 10–11 it grows outdoors as a vigorous climbing vine with its characteristic enormous, deeply split and hole-perforated leaves reaching 3 feet across, producing exotic 6–8 inch cone-shaped edible fruits that taste like a combination of banana, pineapple, and vanilla. The fruit takes over a year to ripen from flower to harvest — it ripens from the base upward as the hexagonal scale-like sections of the outer husk lift and fall away, revealing the white, creamy, flesh underneath. Unripe fruit contains oxalate crystals that cause severe mouth irritation; only fully ripe sections should be eaten. The flavor of ripe ceriman is exceptional and unlike any common fruit. It climbs vigorously by aerial roots and makes a dramatic specimen in tropical landscapes.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; Ceylon gooseberry grows rapidly and begins fruiting in 3–4 years from seed; it is dioecious (separate male and female plants needed for fruit), so plant at least one male for every 3–5 females.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; plant both male and female trees for fruit production. Dovyalis hebecarpa (Ceylon gooseberry or kitambilla) is a Sri Lankan thorny shrub or small tree producing small, 1-to-1.5-inch, velvety, dark-purple to maroon fruits with an intensely tart, acidic flavor somewhat resembling a sour cranberry or gooseberry crossed with tamarind — extremely sour fresh but outstanding for jams, jellies, preserves, and syrups when sweetened. The plant is densely armed with sharp thorns and can be grown as an impenetrable security hedge while also producing edible fruit — a combination making it practically useful as a barrier plant in tropical gardens. In Sri Lanka, the fruits are made into a traditional preserve and the juice is used as a refreshing tart drink. The tree tolerates moderate drought and poor soils once established and can be used as a rootstock for grafting related Dovyalis species. It is dioecious — plant both male and female plants for fruiting. The compact form and spiny character make it useful as a living fence.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 8–10; Chamburo is a drought-adapted, dryland papaya relative native to the dry intermontane valleys of the Andean highlands of Ecuador and northern Peru (200–2,800m elevation) — producing oblong, yellow-green, aromatic fruits the size of an egg with white papaya-like flesh and a mild, sweet, papaya-lemon aroma, cooked in Ecuadorian traditional cuisine.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, dry to moderately moist soil; Vasconcellea candicans is adapted to dry inter-Andean valley conditions and is considerably more drought tolerant than common papaya — water moderately and avoid overwatering or waterlogged soils. Vasconcellea candicans (Chamburo or White-flowering Papaya) is a small tree in the Caricaceae family native to the dry inter-Andean valleys and hillside scrub of Ecuador and northern Peru at elevations of 200 to 2,800 meters — adapted to significantly drier conditions than most Vasconcellea species, which are predominantly cloud-forest plants. The white-flowered trees (the species name 'candicans' means 'becoming white' in reference to the flowers) produce clusters of elongated, oval, pale-yellow to white-green, fragrant fruits about the size of a large egg, with soft, white, papaya-textured flesh and a mild, sweet-sour, papaya-lemon-vanilla aromatic flavor. Chamburo fruits are traditionally cooked in Ecuadorian highland cuisine — used in the classic dish cuy al horno (roasted guinea pig with vegetable accompaniments) and in fruit preserves and juices. The plant tolerates dry conditions, shallow soils, and light frost considerably better than common papaya, making it potentially useful for drier zone 8b–10 gardens in the southwestern United States and similar Mediterranean climates. Dioecious; plant male and female trees.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Champagne is well adapted to hot, humid summers and performs reliably in Texas and Gulf South dooryard plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Champagne is a light greenish-yellow fig long grown in Texas dooryards, prized for its thin skin, amber-pink pulp, and very sweet, honeyed flavor that many gardeners rank above darker-skinned figs for fresh eating. It fruits on both old and new wood, giving a small early-summer breba crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer. Trees tolerate heat and humidity well and need little fertilizer once established, though a summer mulch layer helps even out soil moisture during fruit ripening. Protect young trees during hard freezes in the cooler end of its range; established plants regrow readily from the base after cold damage.

common_name: Champagne Loquat (White-Fleshed California Loquat, Golden Yellow Loquat)
plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring in full to partial sun in well-drained soil; Champagne is the most widely grown and commercially important loquat variety in California and the standard variety in California commercial loquat production — it produces medium to large, pale yellow to golden-orange fruits with white to cream-colored flesh and an unusually mild, sweet, almost champagne-like delicate flavor that makes it the most refined-tasting commonly available loquat.
directions: Plant grafted tree in well-drained soil in full sun; loquats tolerate poor soils and occasional drought once established but produce much better fruit with regular moisture; thin fruit clusters to 3–5 per cluster for larger individual fruits; harvest when fruit is fully colored and slightly soft to pressure — loquats do not ripen further after picking. Champagne is the premier commercial loquat variety of the American Pacific Coast — the standard variety grown in California's loquat orchards and the type most commonly available in specialty markets and Asian grocery stores on the West Coast. The fruits are medium to large (1.5–2.5 inches), pear-shaped to rounded with a pale yellow to warm golden-yellow skin, and the flesh inside is distinctively cream-white to very pale yellow — unlike the deeper orange flesh of most loquat varieties. The white-fleshed characteristic is associated with a milder, more delicate, slightly acidic-sweet flavor profile that many tasters consider the finest among loquats, with a subtle fragrance sometimes compared to mild apricot or very ripe melon. The 'Champagne' name captures this refinement of flavor. Trees are vigorous and productive, blooming in fall-winter and fruiting in late winter to spring — one of the earliest fruit trees to ripen in the year, providing fresh fruit in February to April when little else is available. In zone 9a and the Gulf Coast, Champagne loquat reliably crops when winter temperatures stay above 26°F; the developing fruits are the most frost-sensitive part of the plant.

common_name: Chandler Walnut (California Commercial Standard Walnut, UC Davis Walnut)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep (4+ feet), well-drained, fertile loam or sandy loam; Chandler is protandrous (sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) and benefits from cross-pollination with a companion variety; requires approximately 700–800 chill hours and is best adapted to the California Central Valley and similar zones 6–9 climates; avoid sites with heavy clay or poor drainage — walnuts are sensitive to Phytophthora root rot in waterlogged soils.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Chandler benefits from cross-pollination though it will produce some crop alone; the large, thin-shelled nuts ripen in September–October and are harvested by mechanical knock-down or hand-collection when hulls begin to split; allow nuts to dry at 100°F for several days after harvest to reduce moisture content for storage. Chandler walnut is the most widely planted commercial English (Persian) walnut variety in California and among the most important walnut varieties in the world — released by UC Davis in 1979 from the UC Walnut Improvement Program as a selection with exceptional combination of large nut size, very thin shell, high kernel percentage (above 50%), and excellent kernel color and quality. California produces approximately 75% of the world's English walnut supply, and Chandler accounts for more than half of that production — making Chandler the single most economically important walnut variety on earth. The variety produces very large (28–30 mm), well-shaped nuts with a thin shell that cracks easily and yields plump, light-colored halves with mild, sweet walnut flavor and high oil content typical of premium English walnuts. The light kernel color (essential for premium market pricing, where darker kernels command lower prices) and consistent quality in the drying and processing process made Chandler the preferred commercial variety over the older standards (Franquette, Hartley, Serr). For home orchards in zones 6–9, Chandler delivers premium walnut quality with good productivity.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, in a site sheltered from north wind; Changsha is among the most cold-hardy true mandarins available, tolerating brief drops into the low teens (°F) once mature, though young trees still need winter protection for the first several years.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, sheltered from cold north winds; mulch well and protect young trees through their first few winters until established.
