Changsha is a small-fruited mandarin native to Hunan Province, China, valued above nearly all other citrus for its exceptional cold hardiness — mature trees have survived and fruited after temperatures well below 10°F, making it one of the few true mandarins that can be grown outdoors, unprotected, in the Gulf South and even into the coastal Southeast beyond typical citrus range. The small, flattened, deep orange fruits are intensely sweet with a rich, aromatic mandarin flavor, though they are notably seedy, which has historically limited commercial interest despite the outstanding flavor and hardiness. Changsha is widely used by cold-hardy citrus breeders and hobbyists both as a garden fruit tree in its own right and as breeding stock for hardier hybrid mandarins. A rewarding choice for Gulf South gardeners who want the flavor of a true mandarin from a tree that can survive outdoors through a hard winter, zone 8–10.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring for reliable fruiting.
directions: Che, sometimes called the Chinese mulberry, produces round, red, fig-like fruit with a mild, melon-melon flavor. It is drought-tolerant and adaptable once established, growing well in full sun on well-drained soil. Seedling trees can be thorny and slow to bear, so plant a grafted, female cultivar for earlier crops; a male tree nearby can improve set. Prune to keep it manageable and net the sweet fruit against birds as it ripens in autumn.

plant_note: Plant grafted or air-layered container plants in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; chempedak is very frost-sensitive and is primarily for South Florida and tropical areas. Grafted plants begin fruiting at 3–5 years vs. 10+ years from seed.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; chempedak is a close relative of jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus), native to Southeast Asia from Indonesia to Thailand, producing large, barrel-shaped compound fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches like jackfruit but typically smaller and sweeter. The fruits have a strongly aromatic, intensely sweet, almost fermented flavor that is more pronounced than jackfruit — considered by many Southeast Asian aficionados to be superior to jackfruit for fresh eating. The soft, yellow-orange arils surrounding the seeds are eaten fresh, fried in batter (a popular street food in Malaysia), or incorporated into desserts. The seeds are roasted or boiled and eaten. More tolerant of wet, poorly drained soils than jackfruit, making it suitable for sites that jackfruit would struggle in. An outstanding choice for tropical South Florida gardens seeking an alternative to the more common jackfruit.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade; Cherapu is a small to medium Garcinia fruit tree endemic to Peninsular Malaysia bearing small, thin-skinned, orange to mandarin-orange-colored fruits with sweet-sour, soft, orange-yellow aroid pulp — among the most popular small Garcinia fruits of Malaysian tropical gardens and markets.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Garcinia prainiana requires consistent moisture, high humidity, and protection from wind and cold — mulch well and water regularly throughout the growing season. Garcinia prainiana (Cherapu or Button Mangosteen) is an evergreen fruit tree endemic to the lowland and hill forests of Peninsular Malaysia and southern Thailand, member of the Garcinia family (Clusiaceae) and closely related to the famous Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana). The fruits are distinctive: small (1.5–2 inch), round, with thin, orange to mandarin-colored skin (not the thick, purple rind of mangosteen) that peels easily to reveal 4–5 segments of soft, sweet-sour, orange-to-white, juicy, aromatic pulp with a complex tropical flavor — often described as a blend of sweet orange, lychee, and tangy passion fruit. The tree is compact and ornamental with glossy, dark-green, opposite leaves, and suits smaller tropical gardens better than the slower-growing mangosteen. Like all Garcinia species, G. prainiana is slow-growing and requires patience — typically 5–8 years from grafted stock to first fruit. A prized and rarely exported tropical fruit tree for serious tropical fruit collectors in zone 10–12.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; cherimoya is suited to zones 10–12 and sheltered zone 9b microclimates where brief cold to 25–28°F may be tolerated by established trees. Hand-pollination is strongly recommended in cultivation, as the flowers' protogynous timing and lack of natural pollinators in many regions results in poor fruit set without human intervention.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; cherimoya (Annona cherimola) was famously described by Mark Twain as "the most delicious fruit known to men," and it remains one of the most sought-after fruits in the world among tropical fruit enthusiasts, producing heart-shaped, scaly green fruits with a snow-white, custardy flesh of extraordinary sweetness and complexity — with flavors of pineapple, banana, vanilla, and cream all at once. Native to the Andean highlands of Ecuador and Peru, cherimoya prefers a mild, subtropical rather than hot tropical climate and performs best where summers are warm but not brutally hot, and winters are cool but frost-free. Hand-pollination is essential in cultivation: transfer pollen from freshly opened male-phase flowers to receptive female-phase flowers using a small brush or cotton swab in the morning for reliable fruit set. Grafted trees of selections such as 'Lisa,' 'Booth,' and 'McPherson' begin bearing in 2–4 years and produce superior fruit size and flavor compared to seedling trees.

plant_note: Plant container stock or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to clay-loam soil in full sun; cherry plum is one of the earliest-flowering and most adaptable small fruit trees, native to Western Asia but naturalized throughout Europe — it serves as one of the primary rootstocks for grafted plums worldwide, and the edible cherry-sized fruits (red, yellow, or purple) can be used like small plums for eating fresh, making jam, and flavoring wine.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; self-fertile but produces better with a second tree for cross-pollination; cherry plum is extremely adaptable and flowers early. Prunus cerasifera (cherry plum or myrobalan) is a small deciduous tree native to Western Asia and southeastern Europe — one of the earliest flowering Prunus species in spring, often opening white or pale-pink blossoms in late winter or very early spring even before peaches or almonds, creating a spectacular early-season display. The cherry-sized (3/4–1 inch) fruits ripen in summer in a range of colors from bright yellow to red to dark purple-black depending on variety, with sweet to sweet-tart, plum-like flesh that can be eaten fresh, cooked into jam, preserved as conserves, or fermented into wine or vinegar. Cherry plum is enormously important horticulturally as one of the primary rootstocks onto which commercial plum, apricot, and nectarine varieties are grafted. Several ornamental purple-leaved forms (particularly 'Atropurpurea' and the popular 'Thundercloud' and 'Purple Pony') are among the most commonly planted street and specimen trees in zone 5–9 landscapes for their deep maroon-purple spring foliage and masses of pink flowers. The species naturalizes readily and has escaped into the wild in parts of North America and Europe.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; cherry of the Rio Grande is relatively slow growing and blooms most heavily in spring with fruit ripening in early summer. Self-fertile, but cross-pollination with a second plant increases fruit set.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; cherry of the Rio Grande is a Brazilian Eugenia species prized by subtropical fruit enthusiasts for its exceptional flavor — the dark red to purple, oblong, cherry-sized fruits have a rich, complex flavor that blends cherry, wine, and grape notes with a slight aromatic complexity that is unique in the subtropical fruit world. It is one of the most sought-after specialty fruits for zone 9 food gardens. The dense, glossy, evergreen foliage is attractive year-round and the showy white flowers appear in spring. It grows as a medium shrub or small tree and tolerates partial shade well, making it suitable as an understory specimen in the food forest. The fruit ripens from May through June on the Gulf Coast and must be harvested promptly as it ferments rapidly after picking. In zone 9a it may need frost protection in hard winters; established plants recover readily. One of the top five subtropical fruits for Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring; chestnuts strongly prefer acidic, well-drained soil.
directions: Chestnuts require cross-pollination between at least two different cultivars or seedlings — plant them within 50 feet of each other for reliable nut set. American chestnut was devastated by blight, so choose blight-resistant Chinese, European, or hybrid selections (such as Dunstan Chestnuts). Trees strongly prefer acidic soils (pH 4.5–6.5) and perform poorly in alkaline or wet conditions. Harvest in fall when burs open and nuts fall; collect daily as nuts on the ground deteriorate quickly. Fresh chestnuts are perishable — refrigerate promptly and use or freeze within a month.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Cheyenne bears young and needs a Type II pollinator such as Elliott or Desirable, and its compact size suits closer spacing than many standard pecan cultivars.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Released by the USDA breeding program, Cheyenne is notable for its smaller, more compact tree size compared to many pecan cultivars, along with excellent kernel quality and a high percentage of kernel to shell. It tends to bear at a younger age than older heirloom cultivars, giving growers an earlier return on a new planting, though it is more susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and benefits from good spacing and airflow. Its compact habit makes it a reasonable option where space is more limited than a full commercial pecan grove requires.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost; in cold zones the tops may die back and regrow from the roots.
directions: One of the hardiest figs available, Chicago Hardy can be grown down to Zone 5, where the tops may freeze back but resprout from the roots to fruit on new wood. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and mulch heavily over winter in colder regions to protect the crown. Water steadily while fruit develops for the best sweetness. In the coldest zones, grow it in a container that can overwinter in a garage or basement.

plant_note: Plant bare-root stock or container plants in early spring before bud break in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Chickasaw plum is one of the toughest native fruits for the Southeast and Gulf South, tolerating sandy soils and drought that defeat most fruit plants.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chickasaw plum thrives on neglect and is essentially care-free once established. Prunus angustifolia (Chickasaw plum or sand plum) is one of the most important native fruit plants of the Gulf Coastal Plain, East Texas, and Piedmont Southeast — a tough, fast-growing, suckering shrub or small tree producing abundant 1/2-to-3/4-inch, bright-red to orange-red or yellow plums in May–June that are tart-sweet and excellent for jellies, preserves, wines, and eating out of hand. The tree is one of the earliest flowering native plants of the Southeast, producing dense clusters of small white flowers in February–March (before the leaves emerge) that provide extremely valuable early nectar for native bees emerging from winter dormancy. Chickasaw plum forms thickets by root suckers, creating dense, thorny hedgerows that provide outstanding nesting cover and food for a wide range of wildlife. It is self-fertile (though cross-pollination improves yields) and one of the most heat, drought, and disease-resistant of all stone fruits for southeastern gardens.

common_name: Chilean Wine Palm (Coquito Palm, Honey Palm)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Chilean wine palm is the world's most cold-hardy large palm, tolerating temperatures down to approximately 20°F (-7°C, zone 8 briefly) — its exceptionally massive trunk stores huge quantities of water and nutrients that protect it from cold; it is extremely slow-growing and may take 40–80 years to reach full height.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; exceedingly drought-tolerant once established. Jubaea chilensis (Chilean wine palm or coquito palm) is the world's most cold-hardy large-growing palm species — native to the central Chilean Andes coastal valleys where it experiences occasional frost and cold winters — and the most massive palm in terms of trunk girth, with a single trunk reaching 3–5 feet in diameter at maturity. It tolerates temperatures briefly to approximately 18–20°F (zone 8) — making it growable outdoors in zone 8 or warmer, far colder than any other large pinnate palm. The 'wine' in the common name refers to the traditional Chilean practice of felling mature trees to tap the sap as it flows from the cut stump — producing large quantities of sweet sap boiled to 'miel de palma' (palm honey, a thick, dark, amber, molasses-like sweetener), or fermented to palm wine ('chicha de palma'). CAUTION: The traditional sap harvest requires killing the tree. The small fruits ('coquitos,' little coconuts) contain a sweet, coconut-flavored seed that is sold commercially as a snack in Chilean markets. Jubaea is critically endangered in the wild due to centuries of sap-tapping and habitat loss; it is protected in Chilean national reserves. An extraordinary garden palm for warm-temperate climates where most large palms fail.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; in zone 9 plant December–February. Chinese Apricot is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator, though fruit size and yield improve with a nearby pollinizer. Chill hour requirement is approximately 400–500 hours, making it viable in the colder parts of zone 9. Late spring frost after bloom is the primary risk — site in a well-drained location with good cold air drainage and avoid frost pockets. Fruits ripen in May–June in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil on a gently sloping site to encourage cold air drainage away from spring blossoms; Chinese Apricot (also known as 'Chinese Sweet' or 'Mormon Apricot') is an heirloom apricot variety valued for its early and reliable fruiting in warm-climate zones, exceptional ornamental spring bloom of pure white blossoms (among the most beautiful of any stone fruit), and large, orange-blushed fruits with rich, sweet, classic apricot flavor. The self-fertile habit — rare among apricots, which are often incompatible — makes Chinese Apricot practical for small gardens with space for only a single tree. The primary challenge in zone 9 for any apricot is that the early bloom (January–February) may be damaged by late frost; selecting a well-drained site with good cold air movement significantly reduces frost-damaged crop losses. Chinese Apricot has demonstrated better heat tolerance in warm-summer climates than most European apricot selections, contributing to its success in the South and Southwest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; Chinese bayberry prefers slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil and tolerates partial shade. In zone 7b–9 the tree is root-hardy and fully perennial; the top may suffer cold damage in severe zone 7 winters. Females require a male pollinator tree nearby. Trees fruit beginning at 5–7 years from transplant; produce large crops in June–July.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Chinese bayberry (yang mei, yumberry) is one of China's most celebrated fruits — a small, deep red to purplish, lychee-like berry on a large, shade-tolerant evergreen tree that is almost unknown in American gardens despite growing well in zone 7–9. The fruits, borne in June–July, are intensely flavored with a sweet-tart taste similar to a cross between pomegranate and raspberry, with a slightly grainy texture around a central pit. Chinese bayberry is rich in anthocyanins and vitamin C. The tree is dioecious — female trees bear fruit when pollinated by a male; most nurseries sell sexed trees. It grows slowly to 25–35 feet but can be kept smaller with pruning. The dark, glossy, evergreen foliage is attractive year-round.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall or container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), sandy to loamy, deep soil in full sun; Chinese chestnut requires two or more genetically distinct trees for cross-pollination and nut production. Plant in well-drained soil — chestnuts are extremely susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in wet, poorly drained soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun — Chinese chestnut is the blight-resistant alternative to the devastated American chestnut, producing sweet, edible nuts very similar to the native species. It grows naturally in China where it evolved resistance to the fungal blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) that destroyed American chestnuts, and is now the primary species used in chestnut restoration hybrids and in commercial chestnut orchards throughout the eastern US. The tree is medium-sized (30–50 feet), requires two or more trees for cross-pollination, and begins producing nuts within 3–5 years from a grafted tree. The burr-enclosed nuts ripen in fall and are harvested fresh for roasting, boiling, grinding into flour, and use in stuffings and desserts. Chinese chestnut wood is also blight-resistant and durable. An important and practical nut tree for the food forest and home orchard in zone 4–9.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees or container-grown saplings in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese hawthorn produces the largest-fruited hawthorn berries available in cultivation and is widely grown as an orchard tree in northern China.
directions: Plant grafted trees or container saplings in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese hawthorn is extremely cold-hardy, surviving temperatures to -30°F, and is one of the most productive and large-fruited hawthorns available for northern gardeners. Crataegus pinnatifida is the most commercially important hawthorn in China where it is grown in extensive orchards for its unusually large (up to 1 inch across), bright-red, shiny fruits with white-speckled skin; the tart, apple-like fruits are eaten fresh, candied (as Chinese candied hawthorn skewers — tanghulu), made into jams, dried, and used extensively in traditional Chinese medicine for digestive health. The tree is heavily thorned, produces profuse white spring flowers, and has attractive, deeply lobed leaves with good fall color. It adapts readily to a wide range of soils and climates in zones 3–8.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Chinese quince is a spectacular small ornamental tree with beautiful exfoliating bark, large quince-like fruits, and vivid fall color — it is more cold-tolerant and more tree-like than flowering quince (Chaenomeles), reaching 15–20 feet.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Chinese quince (Pseudocydonia sinensis) is a small ornamental tree related to quince and pear but in its own monotypic genus, producing magnificent exfoliating bark (flaking in irregular puzzle-piece patches of green, cream, and tan like a camouflage pattern), beautiful pale pink spring flowers, and large, 6-inch, yellow, pear-shaped fruits in autumn with a powerful quince-like fragrance that fills a room. The fruits are too astringent to eat raw but make outstanding jelly, paste (membrillo), and syrup; the trees are also spectacular in fall when the leaves turn brilliant orange, red, and yellow. One of the most ornamentally distinguished small trees available for zones 5–9, combining beautiful bark, flowers, fruit, and fall color in a single specimen.

common_name: Chinese White Mulberry (Silkworm Mulberry, King White Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant grafted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chinese white mulberry is the silkworm's preferred host plant and produces sweet, large white-to-lavender mulberry fruits — grown for both sericulture (silk production) and as an edible fruit tree in warm climates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mulberry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions once established. Morus multicaulis (Chinese white mulberry or silkworm mulberry) is the mulberry species most important to global sericulture (silk production) — the leaves are the sole or preferred food source for the silkworm (Bombyx mori), whose cocoons are processed into silk thread. The species is a distinct subspecies or variety within the Morus alba complex, selected over millennia in China, Japan, and Korea for large, tender, nutritious leaves with high silkworm productivity. It produces sweet, large, white-to-pale-lavender to white-pink fruits that ripen in early summer — slightly milder and sweeter than red mulberry, excellent fresh, in pies, jams, syrups, and wine. The tree is fast-growing and quite large, eventually reaching 20–30 feet with a spreading canopy that provides excellent summer shade. In zone 9, the large, sweet fruits ripen in May–June; the tree is deciduous and provides summer shade then winters interest with a distinctive, broadly spreading branch structure. An underused fruit tree for Gulf Coast food gardens where its heat and drought tolerance are genuine assets.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil; prefers Pacific Northwest conditions.
directions: Chinkapin (Castanopsis chrysophylla, also called golden chinquapin) is a large Pacific Coast evergreen related to chestnuts and oaks, bearing small, intensely sweet nuts in spiny burs — often considered the finest-flavored nut native to the Pacific Northwest. Unlike American chestnut it is not susceptible to chestnut blight, making it a valuable blight-free nut tree for western gardeners. Trees are monoecious but require cross-pollination between at least two seedlings or distinct cultivars for reliable nut production; wind and insects both carry pollen. Burs take two years to mature and split open in autumn — collect nuts promptly before squirrels and jays claim the entire crop, and consume or freeze within a month as the small nuts dry out quickly.

plant_note: Collect and sow acorns in fall immediately after they drop, pressing 1 inch deep into moist, well-drained soil; acorns germinate readily in spring without stratification. Transplant seedlings to final location before taproots become too long — typically in the first year.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, calcareous or acidic soil in full sun; chinkapin oak is among the most drought-tolerant native oaks and the only species that thrives naturally on dry limestone outcrops and bluffs — a trait that makes it excellent for rocky, alkaline soils where most oaks fail. The toothed, chestnut-like leaves are distinctive and turn attractive gold and brown in fall. The sweet, small acorns are among the least bitter of any oak, maturing in a single season and consumed immediately by deer, turkeys, squirrels, and wood ducks. The tree adapts to a wide range of soils including limestone-derived clays, shallow rocky hillsides, and deep loams, making it one of the most landscapeable native oaks for challenging sites.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chocolate is a PVNA persimmon — it becomes non-astringent and develops brown flesh when pollinated and seeded, but remains astringent without seeds if grown without a pollinator nearby.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chocolate is a PVNA (Pollination Variant Non-Astringent) Japanese persimmon — a type that produces sweet, non-astringent, crunchy-when-firm fruit with distinctive brown ('chocolate') flesh when pollinated and seeds are present, but remains astringent if no seeds develop from lack of pollination. The presence of a pollinator tree (Gailey, Maru, or another male or seeded cultivar) within 50 feet allows Chocolate to develop its characteristic dark brown, sweet, crunchy flesh that can be eaten firm at the orange-yellow stage — unlike astringent types that must be soft. This firm-eating non-astringent quality (shared by Fuyu) makes Chocolate outstanding for fresh use, salads, and eating out of hand. The unusual brown flesh color — resulting from tannin-anthocyanin reactions stimulated by seeds — is distinctive and has no direct equivalent among common temperate fruits. With a pollinator nearby, Chocolate produces medium-large, flat to slightly rounded, orange fruits with brown flesh that are ready from late September through November in zone 9. Without a pollinator, fruits are astringent and must ripen soft (similar to Hachiya) before eating. For maximum enjoyment, plant Chocolate near another persimmon variety for cross-pollination.

common_name: Choctaw Pecan (Large-Nut Premium Gulf South Pecan, Type II Late-Season Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Choctaw is a Type II pollinator — plant alongside Type I cultivars such as Desirable, Cape Fear, or Pawnee for reliable nut set; Choctaw produces some of the largest individual pecan nuts of any variety, rivaled only by Mahan, making it particularly prized for fresh-eating and gift pecans where presentation size matters.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Choctaw is a late-season variety ripening in October–November, later than most other pecans; supplement with zinc spray in spring; Choctaw is somewhat susceptible to pecan scab in very humid coastal conditions and benefits from fungicide applications in wet years; best in zones 7–9 with adequate growing season length. Choctaw pecan is a USDA-ARS variety (released 1959) known primarily for producing some of the largest individual nuts of any commercial pecan variety, with nut counts typically running 35–40 per pound compared to the 50–60 nuts per pound typical of smaller varieties — in pecan marketing, where size commands premium prices, Choctaw's exceptionally large nuts give it distinct commercial value. The nuts are well-filled, with 60–64% kernel percentage, and the kernel quality is excellent — bright golden color, plump halves, and a rich, sweet buttery flavor. Choctaw has broader adaptation through the Gulf South than some varieties, performing reasonably well in the humid coastal plain from eastern Texas through the Florida Panhandle, though like most pecans it requires fungicide management for scab control in high-humidity years. The trees are vigorous and upright-growing, ultimately becoming very large specimens, and are somewhat slow to come into production compared to precocious varieties like Pawnee. The late ripening season (October–November) is an advantage in areas prone to early fall wet weather — the nuts are harvested and on the ground before the worst scab-spreading conditions of mid-fall. A prestige variety for home orchards and direct-market operations where extra-large nut size commands attention.

common_name: Chojuro Asian Pear (Brown Russet Japanese Pear, Butterscotch Asian Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Chojuro requires cross-pollination from another Asian pear variety — Hosui, Shinseiki, or Nijisseiki are compatible; Chojuro is one of the oldest named Japanese pear varieties still in commercial production, noted for distinctive butterscotch and caramel notes in the flavor that no other variety replicates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Chojuro requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in late August to mid-September when the skin color transitions from greenish-brown to warm brown-russet; Chojuro stores well under refrigeration (2–3 months) longer than many other Asian pears; flavor improves slightly with 2–4 weeks of cold storage after harvest. Chojuro is one of the oldest named Asian pear varieties in continuous cultivation, developed in Japan from a cross of two traditional Japanese pear varieties in the late 1800s and widely grown there for well over a century before introduction to North American home orchards. The variety's distinguishing characteristic is a unique flavor profile — described as butterscotch, caramel, or anise-like by different tasters — that is completely unlike any other Asian pear variety and arguably more complex than the straightforward crisp sweetness of varieties like Shinseiki and Hosui. The nuts are medium to large, round to oblate, with a rich brown-russet skin that is slightly rough in texture, and crisp, dense, white flesh with the characteristic refreshing juiciness of Asian pears combined with the distinctive butterscotch flavor undertone. Chojuro has become popular among specialty Asian pear growers and farmers' market vendors precisely because its unusual flavor creates a point of differentiation from the more neutral-flavored standard varieties — customers who taste it for the first time often find the flavor complex and memorable. Good fire blight resistance compared to some other varieties.

plant_note: Plant bare-root stock in late winter or early spring; seed requires 90–120 days cold stratification and is best sown outdoors in fall for spring germination.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry soil in full sun to partial shade; chokecherry is one of North America’s most cold-hardy and adaptable native fruiting shrubs, ranging from Alaska to Tennessee and coast to coast. Fragrant white flower racemes appear in spring followed by clusters of small dark red to purple-black fruits in mid-summer. The astringent, very tart fruits are too acidic to eat raw in quantity but cook into outstanding jams, syrups, and wines with a flavor reminiscent of Concord grape; the juice has been used by indigenous peoples for centuries as a food, dye, and medicine. It suckers freely to form thickets, providing excellent wildlife habitat. Cultivars 'Schubert' and 'Canada Red' have striking purple summer foliage.

plant_note: Crack the hard stone carefully with a nutcracker to extract the inner seed before sowing, as the endocarp significantly delays germination if left intact.
directions: Remove the seed from its hard stone before sowing, then plant 1 inch deep in sandy, well-drained soil in a warm, sunny location once all frost risk has passed. This tree demands heat and full sun and will not tolerate waterlogged or heavy clay soils; raised beds or slopes with excellent drainage are ideal in marginal climates. Protect young trees from frost in zones 8 and 9 during their first few winters until the trunk thickens and cold hardiness improves. Fruit production begins within three to five years of transplanting and increases substantially as the tree matures.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free areas; very cold-sensitive.
directions: Citron is an ancient citrus grown mainly for its thick, fragrant rind, which is candied or used in preserves. It is among the most frost-tender citrus, so grow it in full sun in the warmest possible spot or in a container to move under cover. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, feeding regularly during growth. Prune to remove the plant's stout thorns and dead wood, and harvest the large fruit when fully colored.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; clammy ground cherry spreads by underground rhizomes and can become weedy in garden beds. Best in open areas where some naturalization is acceptable. The plant and all parts except the ripe berry inside the husk are toxic.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; clammy ground cherry is one of the most common and widespread native ground cherries of the eastern and central US — a perennial, rhizomatous plant producing the typical Physalis papery husk (the inflated calyx) surrounding a small, round, yellow berry when ripe. Named 'clammy' for the sticky, viscid glandular hairs covering the stems and leaves. The ripe yellow berries inside the papery husks have a pleasant, sweet-tart, slightly tropical flavor and are eaten fresh, used in jams, preserves, and pies, or dried like raisins. The fruits are ripe when the papery husk has turned tan and papery and the berry inside has turned from green to yellow. Like all Physalis, only the ripe berries are edible — unripe berries and all other plant parts contain toxic alkaloids. A weedy but edible native for natural gardens and food forests. Spreads aggressively by rhizomes. Tolerates partial shade — more shade-tolerant than tomatillo.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free citrus zones or grow in a container.
directions: Clementines are sweet, seedless, easy-peeling mandarins that ripen in early winter. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, sheltered from frost, or in a large pot to overwinter under glass in cool climates. Some cultivars fruit more reliably without a cross-pollinator, which keeps them seedless. Feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season and harvest as soon as the fruit colors, since it holds only briefly on the tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted stock in spring in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, fertile soil in full sun; clementines perform best in zones 9–11 with a warm, dry fall ripening season — zone 9a is the northern limit of reliable outdoor production for this mandarin hybrid.
directions: Plant grafted stock in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; water deeply and infrequently once established; fertilize with citrus-formulated fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and early fall. Citrus × clementina (clementine mandarin) is the small, seedless, thin-skinned, intensely sweet mandarin orange known worldwide as the holiday tangerine — a hybrid of mandarin and sweet orange discovered in Algeria around 1900 by Brother Clément Rodier (for whom it is named). The clementine is distinguished from ordinary mandarins by its typically seedless fruits (in isolated plantings without cross-pollination), deep-orange, extremely glossy, smooth peel that peels effortlessly, and exceptional sweet flavor with minimal tartness. In zone 9, clementines ripen from November through January — the ideal cool-season ripening period that concentrates sugars. Trees are moderately compact and more cold-tolerant than many citrus types, surviving brief drops to 28°F when established. Plant only grafted trees (not seedlings) for true-to-type fruit and quicker bearing; trees typically bear first fruit 2–3 years after planting. A reliable, productive choice for Gulf Coast home orchards.

plant_note: Plant container trees in spring after danger of frost has passed in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Clementines are slightly more cold-hardy than navel oranges but should still be protected from temperatures below 28°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Clementine is the most widely grown and beloved easy-peel mandarin orange in the world — the source of the small, bright-orange, seedless (when grown without cross-pollination) tangerines marketed as 'Cuties' and 'Halos' in American grocery stores. The fruit is small (2–2.5 inches diameter), very easy to peel with virtually no pith, with 8–14 segments of rich, sweet, complex mandarin flavor and distinctive floral aroma. The thin, glossy, bright-orange rind peels effortlessly, making Clementines the most practical fresh-eating citrus for children and adults who want convenient, mess-free citrus. Fruit ripens in November through January in zone 9 — the holiday season — making it one of the most seasonal and eagerly anticipated citrus fruits. The tree is compact, well-shaped, and attractive, with glossy dark-green foliage and fragrant white spring flowers. Clementines can produce seeds if cross-pollinated by other mandarin or sweet orange varieties growing nearby — for seedless fruit, avoid planting near other mandarins, or select a seedless clementine variety. In zone 9, Clementines should be sited in warm, protected locations and protected from temperatures below 28°F. Apply citrus fertilizer three times annually: February, May, and September.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 8–11; Cliff Date Palm is a graceful, medium-sized date palm native to rocky cliff faces and hill forests of the eastern Himalayas (Sikkim, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Assam) — producing remarkably elegant, arching, dark-green, soft-textured fronds and edible, small, orange date-like fruits, with considerably more cold-hardiness and shade tolerance than the common date palm.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Phoenix rupicola is among the more shade-tolerant date palms — adapting to filtered light beneath taller trees — and tolerates moderate drought when established; water deeply but infrequently in subtropical and Mediterranean conditions. Phoenix rupicola (Cliff Date Palm or Rupicola Date Palm) is one of the most elegantly formed and ornamentally refined of all Phoenix date palm species, native to the rocky escarpments, cliff faces, and hill forests of the eastern Himalayan foothills — Sikkim, Bhutan, Assam, and Meghalaya in northeast India, and Bangladesh. The common name 'Cliff Date Palm' accurately describes its native habitat: the palm naturally grows in rock crevices and on steep, exposed cliff faces at elevations of 1,500–5,000 feet. The fronds are the defining ornamental feature: extraordinarily graceful, arching, and soft-textured — lacking the stiff, rigid quality of many Phoenix palms — with a deep, rich green color and a naturally weeping, 'fountain' form that makes the plant immediately distinctive in a landscape setting. Phoenix rupicola shows more shade tolerance than most date palms due to its cliff-forest habitat and is one of the better date palms for partially shaded landscape positions. The small, orange, date-like fruits are eaten locally. Among the best date palms for compact landscapes, courtyard gardens, and partial-shade positions in zones 8–11.

plant_note: Plant outdoors in warm zones; grow in a container that can move indoors in cooler regions.
directions: This semi-dwarf grapefruit-pomelo hybrid produces juicy, sweet-tart, low-acid fruit on a compact tree ideal for patios or small yards. Grow in full sun in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil and water deeply while letting the surface dry between waterings. Feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season for good fruit development. Move container trees to a bright indoor location before frost, as grapefruit is cold-sensitive.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a frost-free site in moist to wet, sandy or alkaline coastal soil; coco plum is extremely tolerant of salt spray, waterlogged soils, and alkaline conditions that challenge most fruiting plants, making it one of the few edible fruiting shrubs well-suited to South Florida and Gulf Coast coastal conditions.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained to seasonally wet, sandy, alkaline, or coastal soil; coco plum is a versatile South Florida and Caribbean native that ranges from a 3-foot groundcover to a 15-foot shrub depending on the cultivar and site conditions. The round to oval fruits ripen to white, red, or dark purple depending on variety and are eaten fresh when ripe — they have starchy, mildly sweet, coconut-flavored flesh around a large seed — or made into jam and jelly. The seed kernel contains a fat that is extracted for cosmetics in South America. Coco plum is both a valuable wildlife plant, supporting many birds and butterflies, and one of the few edible natives for South Florida's challenging alkaline, salty, and wet conditions. Tolerates periodic flooding and salt spray better than almost any other fruiting plant.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant in warm season in frost-free or container conditions; cocona is a short-lived perennial grown as an annual in temperate gardens and as a productive perennial in zone 10–12.
directions: Start seeds in warm, moist mix at 75–85°F indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moist soil after soil warms; cocona (Solanum sessiliflorum) is a tomato relative from the Amazon basin of Colombia, Peru, and Brazil, producing 2–4 inch yellow to orange fruits that resemble a slightly fuzzy tomato with a pleasant, acidic, tomato-citrus flavor widely used in Amazonian cuisine for juices, jams, and salsas. The plants are large-leafed and fast-growing, producing fruit 6–9 months after transplanting in suitable tropical conditions. Rich in iron and an important component of the diet of indigenous Amazonian peoples; increasingly available as a specialty crop in Florida and Hawaii. Thrives in humid tropical conditions with good rainfall or irrigation.

plant_note: Plant container-grown seedlings or place a partly husked seed nut on its side with one-third buried in moist, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; coconut palm is strictly limited to frost-free zones and cannot survive freezing temperatures even briefly.
directions: Plant container-grown seedlings in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; coconut palm is the most widely cultivated and economically important palm tree in the world — a single tree provides coconut fruit (with meat, milk, water, and oil), fibrous husk (coir), palm fronds (for thatching and weaving), and palm heart, making it one of the most useful food trees in human history. In zone 10–12 Florida, Hawaii, and tropical coastal areas it grows to 30–60 feet with a gracefully curving trunk and a spreading canopy of long, feathery fronds. Trees begin producing coconuts 6–10 years after planting and can remain productive for 70–80 years. Excellent salt tolerance makes it one of the best trees for coastal landscapes. 'Malayan Dwarf' cultivars are shorter, earlier fruiting, and moderately hurricane-resistant. Growth is faster in deep, moist, sandy soil with access to groundwater. Extremely frost-sensitive — any freezing temperature causes permanent damage; restricted to southernmost Florida and Hawaii in the US.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a frost-free site; tolerates salt, flooding, alkaline soils, and sandy coastal conditions.
directions: Cocoplum is an extremely adaptable native Florida and Caribbean shrub-tree that tolerates salt spray, periodic flooding, alkaline soils, and full sun — one of the toughest edible landscape plants for coastal south Florida. Plants are self-fertile and fruit reliably as hedges or specimens; the white, pink, or purple oval drupes ripen sporadically through the warm months. The sweet, mildly flavored flesh is eaten fresh or made into jams and jellies; the large oily seed is edible and has a coconut-like flavor when roasted. Harvest when fruit has reached its full color (cream, pink, or deep purple depending on ecotype) and is soft to the touch.

plant_note: Plant container specimens in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade; coffee grows naturally in the forest understory at elevation in Ethiopia and requires shade from direct afternoon sun, consistent moisture, high humidity, and frost-free conditions — zone 10–11 in the ground, or a large container in cooler zones.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial shade — coffee is an attractive, glossy-leaved tropical shrub or small tree native to the forest understory of Ethiopia, grown worldwide in tropical highlands for the seeds (coffee beans) contained inside the red or yellow 'cherry' fruits, which ripen 9–12 months after the heavily fragrant white flowers bloom. As an ornamental plant it is outstandingly handsome: the dark green, glossy, waxy leaves are beautiful year-round; the clusters of jasmine-scented white flowers in spring are intensely fragrant; and the red coffee cherries are decorative and visually striking in fall and winter. Coffee is a genuine shade plant, preferring filtered light under taller trees rather than full sun, which scorches the leaves and stresses the plant in warm climates. In zone 10–11 it can be grown outdoors permanently; in cooler zones it is a remarkable large container plant for bright indoor spaces or protected outdoor areas in summer.

common_name: Coffee Plum (Indian Plum, Rhoea Plum, Puneala Plum)
plant_note: Plant in well-drained tropical conditions; this species has some hermaphroditic flowers and can set fruit without a separate male plant, making it more garden-friendly than Flacourtia indica.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in frost-free tropical conditions; coffee plum (also known as Indian plum or Puneala plum in India and Sri Lanka) is a Southeast Asian Flacourtia related to governor's plum but distinctly different — producing attractive clusters of small red to deep red-purple fruits with a sweet-acidic, slightly astringent flavor reminiscent of sour plum combined with cherry. The name 'coffee plum' is used in southern India where it is made into jams and pickles and eaten fresh when fully ripe. Often hermaphroditic and self-fertile, making it easier to grow than most Flacourtia species. An attractive thorny shrub with glossy leaves, useful as a security hedge in subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Coffeecake is a PVA (pollination-variant astringent) persimmon — cross-pollination from a male persimmon or another D. kaki cultivar within 50 feet causes the flesh to develop rich, dark cinnamon-brown coloration and complex, non-astringent sweetness even before the fruit softens. Without pollination the fruit remains astringent until fully soft-ripe.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Coffeecake is a PVA (pollination-variant astringent) Japanese persimmon selected for its distinctive deep cinnamon-brown flesh coloration and extraordinary flavor when cross-pollinated — the richly colored flesh has a complex, spiced sweetness reminiscent of warm cinnamon and brown sugar that gives the variety its distinctive name. The medium to large, flat-round, orange-skinned fruits develop their characteristic dark interior progressively as pollination stimulates dark flesh development, and fully pollinated fruits may have almost entirely dark, non-astringent, sweet, dense flesh while still firm enough to slice. The flavor of cross-pollinated Coffeecake is considered among the finest of any persimmon type — complex, sweet, and aromatic with none of the astringency that makes unripe persimmons inedible. In zone 9 Coffeecake ripens in late October–November and the tree is vigorous and productive with attractive form and good fall leaf color.

common_name: Col de Dame Blanc Fig (Neck of the Lady Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun against a warm south-facing wall for best fruit development; Col de Dame Blanc is a rare and highly sought-after Spanish heirloom from the Catalonia region particularly associated with Sitges, prized by serious fig collectors and chefs for an extraordinary, concentrated honey sweetness that many consider unmatched among all fig varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile to average soil in full sun; Col de Dame Blanc performs best with reflected heat from south or west-facing walls and requires genuine summer heat to ripen its fruit fully — not recommended for cool-summer Pacific Northwest climates. Col de Dame (literally 'neck of the lady' in Catalan, for the fruit's distinctive elongated, graceful neck) is a group of heirloom Spanish figs from the Catalonia region particularly associated with the town of Sitges; the Blanc (white) form produces elongated, pear-necked, greenish-white to pale yellow fruits with exceptionally thin skin and almost liqueur-like white interior flesh with a concentrated honey sweetness and complex figgy aroma that experienced fig growers frequently describe as among the finest flavors of any variety. A common fig type requiring no pollinator. Less cold-hardy and less vigorous than many commercial varieties but the extraordinary flavor rewards the extra attention; increasingly popular among American fig collectors and now more readily available from specialty nurseries than a decade ago.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost in a hot, sunny site with sharp drainage.
directions: This cold-tolerant pomegranate bears vibrant red-fruited crops and handsome orange-red flowers on a large, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it thrives in heat and tolerates drought once established. Water deeply but infrequently, easing off as fruit ripens to prevent splitting. In the colder end of its range, site it against a warm south wall and mulch the base for winter protection.

common_name: Colossal Chestnut (European-Japanese Hybrid Chestnut, California Large Chestnut, Giant Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, fertile loam in full sun; Colossal requires cross-pollination from another chestnut variety for good nut set — plant with another Colossal or with a compatible European-Japanese hybrid; the variety is adapted to the mild-winter climates of California, Oregon, and Washington (zones 6–9) but is less cold-hardy than Dunstan or Chinese chestnut, performing best where winter temperatures rarely drop below 0°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Colossal requires cross-pollination; harvest nuts in October when burrs open and nuts fall naturally; collect promptly from ground; Colossal chestnuts are among the largest available — single nuts can reach 30+ grams, comparable to the best Italian and French chestnuts — with sweet, creamy flesh excellent for roasting, marrons glacés, and fresh cooking. Colossal chestnut is a hybrid of European sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa) and Japanese chestnut (Castanea crenata) developed in California in the late 1800s by Felix Gillet, a French-born nurseryman who operated the Nevada City Nursery in northern California and imported and trialed numerous European and Asian chestnut varieties and crosses. The variety became the standard commercial chestnut in California and the Pacific Northwest, where it grows vigorously in the mild, well-drained soils of the region and produces exceptionally large individual nuts — among the largest of any named chestnut variety, comparable to the finest Italian and French chestnuts in size and flavor. The large nut size (a single nut can weigh an ounce or more) and good flavor — sweet, starchy, and rich — make Colossal the variety of choice for specialty fresh-market chestnut sales, marron glacé (candied whole chestnuts), and roasting. It has been widely planted in California's chestnut-growing regions (Nevada County, the Sierra Nevada foothills) and in Oregon and Washington for commercial and home production.

common_name: Comice Pear (Doyenné du Comice, Christmas Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break; Comice requires 600–900 chill hours and a cross-pollinator (Bosc or Bartlett recommended) within 100 feet; it is more demanding than other pears, requiring premium soil, careful thinning to 1–2 fruits per spur, and the ideal climate of Oregon's Rogue Valley or similar conditions for the finest quality fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun in rich, deep, well-drained soil with pH 6.0–6.5; Comice is the most demanding major pear variety for soil quality, climate precision, and careful management — thin fruits to 1–2 per cluster for maximum quality; pick before full ripeness and ripen indoors at room temperature. Comice (full name Doyenné du Comice, 'Doyenne of the Show') was raised by the Comice Horticole d'Angers agricultural society of Angers, France in 1849 and rapidly gained recognition as the finest dessert pear in the world — a reputation it has maintained for 175 years among pear enthusiasts and chefs. The large (8–16 oz), roundish-oval to slightly pear-shaped fruits have greenish-yellow skin with slight red blush and are the pears most associated with luxury gift boxes, cheese pairings, and the finest fresh-eating experience: the flesh is extraordinarily buttery, creamy-smooth, and dripping with juice, with an intense pear fragrance and honey-sweet flavor with vanilla and floral overtones that is unmatched by any other pear variety. Oregon's Rogue Valley is the primary American commercial production area for Comice, where the specific valley climate — hot days, cool nights, volcanic soil — allows the fruit to reach a quality level rarely achieved elsewhere. Ripens late (October–November); requires careful storage and monitoring for peak ripeness.

subcategory: fruiting banana, tropical perennial for zone 9-11
plant_note: Plant rooted suckers (pups) in moist, well-drained, richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; fruiting banana requires deep, fertile, consistently moist soil and full sun for fruit production. In zone 9a it may suffer pseudostem dieback in hard winters but regrows from the rhizome — however, fruit production requires 10–14 months of uninterrupted warm-season growth. In zone 9b and 10 it fruits reliably. Feed heavily with a high-potassium fertilizer monthly. Each pseudostem fruits once then dies; new suckers take over. Provide wind protection for the large leaves.
directions: Plant rooted suckers (pups) in moist, well-drained, richly fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; common banana is the species underlying the world's most important fruit crop — the seedless, triploid Cavendish and related commercial cultivars that supply the global banana market, all derived from the diploid wild species Musa acuminata native to tropical Southeast Asia. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, selected cultivars including 'Dwarf Cavendish' (6–8 feet), 'Grand Nain' (the commercial Cavendish, 8–12 feet), and 'Goldfinger' produce genuine, edible, sweet bananas from plants grown in-ground as perennials. Each pseudostem (the apparent trunk, composed of tightly overlapping leaf-base sheaths) grows for 10–14 months, then produces a pendant inflorescence from which the banana bunch develops — the large, pendulous, purple-red flower bract opening to reveal successive 'hands' of bananas along the central axis. After fruiting, the fruited pseudostem dies and is cut to the ground; the continuously produced suckers (pups) at the base replace it, maintaining the clump and producing the next generation of fruiting pseudostems. The plant requires consistently rich, moist soil and heavy feeding with high-potassium fertilizer during the growing season for optimum fruit production. In zone 9a the pseudostems may be killed back to the ground by hard freezes but the rhizome resprouts in spring; however, this resets the 10–14 month fruiting clock, often preventing fruit set before the next winter. In zone 9b and 10 the pseudostems persist year-round and fruit reliably.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring after all frost risk has passed; in frost-free zones fall planting avoids summer heat stress.
directions: Guava is self-fertile and productive as a single tree; grafted selections of known cultivars (Ruby Supreme, Thai White) are superior to seedlings for flavor and bearing consistency. Trees tolerate a wide range of soils but are sensitive to standing water and prolonged frost — temperatures below 28°F damage foliage and below 24°F kill established trunks. Prune annually to 10–12 ft to simplify harvest and improve light penetration; guava bears on new growth so heading-back encourages productivity. Harvest when the skin softens, the color shifts from green to yellow or pink, and the fruit is intensely fragrant.

plant_note: Plant bare-root transplants in late winter or early spring while dormant; seed requires warm stratification (3 months) followed by cold stratification (3 months) and takes 2 seasons to germinate naturally when fall-sown.
directions: Plant in any well-drained soil in full sun; common hawthorn is an exceptionally tough small tree or large shrub valued for its dense thorny habit providing excellent wildlife cover, profuse white spring flowers, and abundant red berries (haws) that feed birds through winter. The haws are edible — mildly flavored, slightly mealy, and high in antioxidant flavonoids — and are used to make jellies, wines, and medicinal syrups with a long history in European herbal medicine. Tolerates urban pollution, heavy clay, coastal exposure, and severe pruning. For hedging, plant 18 inches apart and shear twice yearly; the dense spiny habit makes a stock-proof barrier within a few years.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall for natural double stratification (seeds require two winters to germinate), or plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; common juniper is extremely adaptable, growing on rocky ledges, exposed hillsides, and tundra margins across the Northern Hemisphere.
directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; common juniper has the largest natural distribution of any woody plant in the world — native to and present across the entire Northern Hemisphere from the Arctic Circle to the mountains of Mexico, Morocco, and the Himalayas. The small, blue-black, resinous berry-like seed cones (juniper berries) are the essential flavoring of gin — virtually all gin production worldwide uses common juniper berries to achieve the characteristic piney, resinous flavor. The berries also flavor sauerkraut, game dishes, and aquavit across Scandinavia and central Europe. The needled, prickly foliage creates excellent wildlife habitat — the berries feed waxwings, thrushes, and other birds through winter. Garden forms range from prostrate, low-growing groundcover types to loose, upright shrubs. The species is dioecious — both male and female plants are needed for berry production.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Conadria was selected by USDA breeder Ira Condit in 1955 for outstanding fresh-eating and drying quality, large attractive fruit, and high productivity — a premium commercial and home-garden fig variety particularly suited to hot, dry California and Western conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; Conadria is a common fig type (no pollinator needed) and one of the most productive figs per tree, bearing heavily in its second and third years. Conadria was released in 1955 by USDA fig breeder Ira J. Condit from the Riverside California station after decades of fig selection work; it was selected for exceptional fruit quality combined with high yields, producing large (3–5 oz), turbinate, greenish-white to pale yellow fruits with strawberry-pink interior flesh and very sweet, rich flavor comparable to the finest White Adriatic and Calimyrna types. Outstanding for fresh eating and particularly excellent for drying, producing firm, sweet dried figs with good shelf life. A vigorous, upright, productive tree that performs exceptionally in hot, dry Western climates (Central Valley California, Arizona, Texas, Gulf Coast) and ripens reliably in the main crop (August–October). Somewhat more heat-tolerant than many high-quality white figs.

common_name: Concord Grape (American Blue Grape, Slip-Skin Grape, New England Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Concord is the most widely grown home garden grape in North America — a slip-skin American Labrusca grape that produces large clusters of deep blue-purple grapes with the iconic 'Concord grape' flavor universally associated with American grape juice, grape jelly, and Welch's products; best in zones 4–7 where its high chilling requirement is reliably met.
directions: Plant on a trellis or arbor in full sun in well-drained soil; prune heavily each winter — Concord is cane-pruned, leaving 2 strong canes per vine; fruit ripens in September in most zones; Concord is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator; the berries slip easily from their skins ('slip-skin'), which facilitates juice making but means they are not firm enough for shipping. Concord grape is the foundational American table and juice grape, developed in 1849 by Ephraim Wales Bull in Concord, Massachusetts, from a chance seedling of Vitis labrusca — the native American 'fox grape' species of the northeastern forests. Bull spent six years selecting seedlings for fruit quality from a wild Labrusca vine growing on his property before exhibiting the named variety at the Massachusetts Horticultural Society in 1853, where it immediately attracted attention and within decades became the most widely planted grape in the United States. The Concord grape flavor — simultaneously musky, sweet-tart, and intensely 'grapey' in a way that European vinifera grapes are not — became the defining American grape taste through Welch's grape juice (first produced in 1869 to provide an unfermented communion grape drink by Dr. Thomas Welch) and the ubiquitous grape jelly that made the PB&J sandwich a cultural icon. The flavor compound primarily responsible for the characteristic Concord aroma is methyl anthranilate, a naturally occurring ester found at high concentrations in Labrusca-type grapes and essentially absent from European vinifera varieties. Concord is a seeded grape (seeds are a minor inconvenience for fresh eating but irrelevant for juicing and jelly making) producing large, round, blue-black berries in substantial clusters in mid-to-late September. The vines are cold-hardy to -20°F and require 100–150 chill hours, which are met in zones 4–8 but rarely in zones 9+.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in a sunny, well-drained site.
directions: Contender is a disease-resistant, cold-hardy, self-pollinating peach that produces abundant medium-to-large juicy freestone fruit across many climates. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water consistently during fruit development. Thin young fruit to about 6 inches apart to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape for light penetration, and apply dormant sprays as needed to manage common peach diseases.

plant_note: Plant in spring in mild-winter regions.
directions: Coolidge is a self-fertile pineapple guava selection, useful where only one plant can be grown. Set it in full sun on well-drained soil and water consistently through the fruiting season for the best crop. It tolerates coastal conditions and light frost once established, and can be grown as a shrub or clipped hedge. Fruit is ripe when it drops naturally, so gather it daily from the ground beneath the plant.

plant_note: Plant acorns in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean soil in full sun; cork oak is native to the western Mediterranean and requires excellent drainage, moderate to low fertility, and dry summer conditions. It tolerates moderate drought and salt spray but not wet, heavy clay soil.
directions: Plant acorns in fall in very well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; cork oak is the source of virtually all wine and champagne cork in the world — the extraordinarily thick, spongy, deeply furrowed outer bark is harvested every 9–12 years from mature trees (a process called 'cork stripping') that does not harm the tree, as the bark regenerates completely. Portugal and Spain produce about 80% of the world's cork. The tree is an evergreen with a broad, spreading canopy and small, evergreen, slightly holly-like leaves. First cork harvest is typically at age 25 years; subsequent harvests every 9–12 years for the remaining 150–200 years of the tree's life. In California, cork oaks have been grown for over a century as ornamentals and heritage trees, thriving in the Mediterranean climate. An interesting tree with historical and economic significance for home gardeners in zones 7–10.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter to early spring before bud break; fall planting also works in zones 5–7.
directions: Cornelian cherry is one of the earliest-blooming woody plants — small yellow flowers appear in late winter before the leaves — and the small, olive-shaped drupes ripen in late summer to a rich ruby red. Plant at least two seedlings or cultivars for best fruit set, as it is partially self-fertile but cross-pollination greatly improves yields. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and urban pollution once established. Harvest when fruit is fully dark red and slightly soft; it is too tart to eat out of hand but makes outstanding preserves, syrups, and fruit leather.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; cornelian cherry is exceptionally cold-hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of soil conditions and even modest drought once established.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; cornelian cherry tolerates a wide range of soil conditions. Cornus mas (cornelian cherry dogwood) is a large, multi-stemmed European and Asian shrub or small tree producing one of the very earliest spring flower displays of any hardy plant — tiny, bright-yellow flowers clustered in small, button-like heads that cover the bare branches in February–March (often while snow still falls) before any other spring-blooming shrub. The flowers are followed by oval, cherry-like fruits that ripen to deep scarlet-red in August, tasting like a tart-sweet cranberry crossed with a sour cherry — used in jams, jellies, liqueurs (the Georgian chacha), and sauces throughout Eastern Europe and the Caucasus, where the sour flavor is prized in cooking much like tamarind. The tree is also fall-ornamental with excellent red-pink fall foliage and attractive peeling bark. 'Golden Glory' and 'Redstone' are widely grown cultivars. At the warm edge of its range (zone 8), it grows best with afternoon shade and consistent moisture; it is marginal in zone 9 and does best in the cooler northern parts of zone 8.

common_name: Cortland Apple (McIntosh × Ben Davis Cross, Non-Browning Salad Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Cortland requires approximately 1000 chill hours and is well-adapted to zones 4–7; it is an excellent cross-pollinator for McIntosh and other varieties — Cortland pollen is compatible with a very wide range of apple varieties.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cortland is an excellent cross-pollinator for many other apple varieties including McIntosh; ripens mid-season (September–October); the non-browning flesh makes it uniquely valuable for salads, charcuterie boards, and fresh-cut preparations where apples must remain attractive for hours without discoloring. Cortland apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1915 from a cross of McIntosh and Ben Davis — two of the most important apple varieties of the early 20th century. Cortland inherits McIntosh's aromatic, sweet-tart flavor character in a larger, firmer fruit with significantly better keeping quality than McIntosh. However, Cortland's most famous and unique characteristic is the slow-browning tendency of its flesh when cut: while most apple varieties brown rapidly after cutting due to enzymatic oxidation, Cortland flesh is notably slower to brown, making cut pieces remain white and attractive for much longer than most varieties. This property makes Cortland uniquely valuable for fresh preparations where apple slices need to remain appealing: fresh fruit platters, salads, charcuterie boards, and school lunch boxes where the apples won't be eaten immediately after cutting. The fruit is large, round, red over greenish-yellow skin with very white, juicy, tender flesh and the characteristic McIntosh aromatic quality. It is an excellent cross-pollinator for most other apple varieties due to its abundant, viable pollen. A classic in northeastern U.S. home orchards.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Costa Rican Guava (Cas Guava, Cas, Guayaba Agria) is a small to medium fruit tree native to Costa Rica, Panama, and adjacent Central America — highly important in Costa Rican national cuisine and culture — bearing abundant small, tart, white-fleshed fruits with a refreshing, lemon-bright guava flavor that is more acidic than common guava, prized for fresh juice, agua de cas, and in cooking.
directions: Plant Psidium friedrichsthalianum in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment and fruit development; tolerates some frost once established but best in zone 10–12; harvest fruits when they turn fully yellow and give slightly under gentle pressure. Costa Rican Guava ('cas' in local parlance — a word so fundamental it has no direct English translation outside of the botanical name) occupies a unique place in Costa Rican culture — the guava-sized, white-fleshed, intensely tart fruits are the basis of agua fresca de cas (the most popular fresh juice in the country), used in refresco mixtures, ice creams, jams, and as a souring agent in cooking. The flavor is bracingly tart and intensely guava-fragrant, with significantly more acidity than the common tropical guava (Psidium guajava) — more similar to a tart lemon guava in flavor profile. The tree is somewhat smaller and more cold-tolerant than the common guava, performing well in humid subtropical conditions. In zone 10–12 Gulf Coast gardens and Florida, it fruits reliably and heavily with minimal care. The fruit's high pectin content makes it excellent for jams and jellies without needing commercial pectin. For Costa Rican immigrants and lovers of Central American cuisine, this tree represents home in a way that the common guava cannot replicate.

common_name: Cox's Orange Pippin Apple (World's Finest Eating Apple, English Dessert Apple Standard)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun in a sheltered location with good air circulation; Cox's Orange Pippin requires approximately 800–900 chill hours and cross-pollination from a compatible variety (Bramley's Seedling, Worcester Pearmain, or Egremont Russet); it is challenging to grow in the humid eastern United States (susceptible to apple scab, mildew, and fire blight) but flourishes in the Pacific Northwest and UK maritime climate.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun with good air movement; Cox's Orange Pippin is highly susceptible to apple scab and powdery mildew in humid climates — a preventive spray program or planting in the dry Pacific Northwest is strongly recommended; it requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in October when fully colored and giving slightly to pressure, then store 4–6 weeks to allow flavor to fully develop. Cox's Orange Pippin is the variety most consistently named by apple connoisseurs worldwide as the finest-flavored dessert apple in existence — a small to medium English heirloom discovered as a seedling by retired brewer Richard Cox in his garden at Colnbrook Lawn in Slough, Berkshire, England around 1825, and distributed commercially from 1850 onward. The flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinarily complex and rich by apple standards: intense, spicy-sweet, aromatic, with distinct notes of pear, mango, honey, and fresh nuts that no other apple variety precisely replicates — and which Cox's defenders argue no modern commercial variety (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) can equal in flavor depth and complexity. Cox's became the dominant apple of British gardens and orchards for 150 years and remains the benchmark of the English fresh-eating apple tradition. In the United States, Cox's is most successfully grown in the maritime Pacific Northwest (Oregon and Washington's western valleys, similar in climate to England) where the cool, moist summers allow the apple to develop its characteristic complex flavor without disease pressure overwhelming the susceptible trees. In the humid eastern states, disease resistance is a significant challenge that requires diligent management.

plant_note: Plant dormant trees in early spring or fall in mild areas.
directions: Crabapples bear small, tart fruit excellent for jelly and serve as reliable pollinizers for dessert apples. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, choosing disease-resistant selections to limit scab and rust. They are extremely cold-hardy and adaptable, tolerating a wide range of soils. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy, and harvest the high-pectin fruit after the first firm color develops.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Creek Plum tolerates a range of soil types from sandy loam to clay. It spreads by root sprouts to form thickets — a valuable quality for erosion control but plan for the eventual colony footprint. Seeds require 90–120 days of cold stratification.
directions: Creek Plum is a native shrubby plum of stream banks, creek margins, woodland edges, and disturbed open lands across Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and adjacent states, producing clusters of small, bright red to yellow plums in mid-summer that are sweet, tart, and excellent fresh or for jams, jellies, and preserves. The profuse clusters of white flowers that cover the branches in early spring before leaf emergence are as ornamentally striking as any cultivated ornamental plum, making Creek Plum a multi-season landscape value as well as an edible landscape plant for zone 6–9 gardens. Spreads readily by root sprouts to form dense, multi-stemmed thickets that provide valuable wildlife habitat — nesting cover for mockingbirds and other birds, and the plums are consumed by mockingbirds, thrashers, raccoons, and white-tailed deer. Plant in full sun in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic soil; Creek Plum tolerates heat, periodic drought, and moderate clay once established.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very moist, highly acidic, peaty or sphagnum soil in full shade; creeping snowberry requires extremely specific conditions — cool, wet, acidic, shaded bogs or mossy, acid conifer forest floors in the boreal zone. It does not tolerate heat, dryness, or neutral to alkaline soils.
directions: Plant in very moist, highly acidic, peaty or sphagnum-based, humus-rich soil in full shade in cool, humid climates zones 2–6; creeping snowberry is a delicate, thread-like native evergreen groundcover of boreal bogs, mossy conifer forests, and cool, acid swamps across Canada and the northern United States. The tiny, rounded, glossy evergreen leaves form a fine mat just 1–3 inches tall, and the tiny white berries that form in late summer are pure white, edible, and have the characteristic wintergreen flavor of the Gaultheria genus. They were collected and eaten by indigenous peoples and early settlers as a minor food source. Like all Gaultheria, the leaves contain methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) and have been used as a flavoring. This species requires very specific, cool and perpetually moist conditions and is not appropriate for most garden settings, but excellent for recreating boreal bog gardens in the northern states and Canada.

common_name: Cripps Pink Apple (Pink Lady, Late-Season Low-Chill Sweet-Tart Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Cripps Pink has a comparatively low chill requirement (around 400–500 hours) and needs a very long, warm growing season to ripen fully, so it is best suited to areas with mild winters and hot, extended autumns.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator, since this cultivar is not self-fertile. Bred by John Cripps in Western Australia from a cross of Golden Delicious and Lady Williams, it is marketed commercially as Pink Lady and is among the latest-ripening apples grown, often left on the tree into late autumn to fully develop its rosy-pink blush and dense, crisp, sweet-tart flesh. Its lower chill requirement compared to classic northern apples makes it one of the more workable dessert apples for warmer growing regions. Fruit stores exceptionally well and resists browning better than many varieties once cut.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April.
