Croisic is primarily valued for its breba crop (early summer figs on previous season's wood); in zone 9 the first breba figs ripen in late May–June, providing some of the earliest figs of the season. The main crop matures August–September.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Croisic is a French fig variety named for the coastal commune of Le Croisic in Brittany, notable primarily for its prolific breba crop — the early-season figs produced on previous year's wood that ripen in late May to early June in zone 9, weeks ahead of the main crop figs on most other varieties. The early-ripening breba figs are medium to large, with a yellow-green to yellow skin and amber to orange-tinged flesh with a mild, honey-sweet flavor. In zone 9 the Croisic fig provides the earliest fresh fig harvest of the season and is particularly valued by gardeners who want to extend the fig-eating season by starting early. The main crop figs on new wood ripen in August–September and are similar in quality to the breba crop. In zone 9 the mild winters and long growing season allow Croisic to produce heavy breba crops — the consistently warm temperatures maintain the tree's vigor for prolific breba production.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part shade to full shade; cupuassu is an understory tree native to the Amazon rainforest that produces its remarkable cauliflorous fruits (borne directly on trunk and main branches) in dappled shade — do not plant in full sun, which causes leaf scorch.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in part to full shade; cupuassu requires consistent moisture and high humidity and will not tolerate any frost or prolonged dry periods. Theobroma grandiflorum (cupuassu) is a Brazilian Amazon rainforest relative of cacao (T. cacao) producing large, 8-to-12-inch, oblong, woody fruits borne directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflorous), each containing 20–50 seeds surrounded by a thick, creamy-white, intensely fragrant pulp with a flavor combining chocolate, pineapple, banana, and guava — considered by many food scientists to be one of the most complex and delicious tropical flavors in the world. The pulp is used to make juices, ice creams, yogurts, and confectioneries throughout Brazil, where it is the second most important Amazonian fruit after açaí. The seeds can be fermented and processed into a chocolate-like product ('cupuaçu butter') and are the basis of a proprietary chocolate-substitute trademarked as 'cupulate.' Growing cupuassu outside zones 11–12 requires a greenhouse; at the frontier of zone 10b, protected microclimates may support growth. A rare and extraordinary specialty fruit for true tropical enthusiasts.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Curtis is a Type II pollinator and needs a Type I cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination and full nut set.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Curtis is an old, Florida Panhandle-origin pecan cultivar valued for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab and other humid-climate fungal diseases, making it one of the most reliable low-spray options for Deep South home orchards. The nuts are smaller than many modern commercial cultivars but well filled, with good flavor, and the tree bears consistently and precociously once established. Because of its disease tolerance and long track record along the Gulf Coast, Curtis is frequently recommended as a dependable, low-maintenance pollinator and production tree for home growers who do not want to run a fungicide spray program. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in full sun after soil has warmed; custard apple prefers well-drained soil and does not tolerate waterlogging. Grafted trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years, while seed-grown trees take 5–7 years.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; custard apple is a deciduous to semi-evergreen Annona tree producing round to heart-shaped yellow-green to brownish fruits 3–4 inches in diameter with a reticulated (net-patterned) skin. The creamy white flesh inside is sweeter and softer than sugar apple, with a custard-like texture and a mild, slightly musky flavor. It is the Annona most widely grown across tropical Latin America, the Caribbean, and South Asia, where it is known variously as bull's heart, corazon, nona, and anon. Hand-pollinate flowers using a small brush in the morning to transfer pollen between flowers on the same tree; like other Annona species, the stigma and anther are not receptive at the same time.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring with a compatible pear nearby for pollination.
directions: D'Anjou is a vigorous, productive European pear yielding sweet, juicy fruit excellent for fresh eating, baking, and canning. Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and include a different pear variety nearby for cross-pollination. Water consistently during fruit development and prune in late winter to a central-leader form. Harvest the fruit while still firm and ripen it off the tree in cool storage for the best texture.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring; tolerates cooler, wetter sites than dessert plums.
directions: The damson is a hardy, self-fertile culinary plum whose tart, astringent fruit shines in jams, gins, and preserves. It thrives even on heavier soils and in exposed positions where dessert plums struggle. Plant in full sun to partial shade and keep young trees weed-free and mulched. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood in summer; expect reliable heavy crops after three to four years.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring before bud break in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Damson plum is an ancient European plum type with smaller, more astringent, intensely flavored oval fruits that are outstanding for preserves, jams, gin, and damson cheese — it requires less winter chill than Japanese plums and is one of the hardiest and most disease-resistant plum types.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; prune to open center form after harvest. Prunus domestica 'Damson' (Damson plum or Blue Damson) is an ancient, small-fruited European plum type — distinct from both Japanese plums (P. salicina) and common European plums in being smaller, more astringent, and more intensely flavored when raw, but superb when cooked or preserved. The small (1-inch), oval, blue-purple to nearly black fruits ripen in late summer through fall with a rich, complex, winelike, slightly tannic flavor that becomes sweet and luscious when cooked with sugar. Damson plum is the traditional fruit of English damson jam, damson cheese (a firm fruit paste), damson gin (sloe-gin equivalent made with damsons rather than sloes), and damson wine. The Shropshire Damson is the most celebrated English variety; Merryweather is the largest-fruited commercial type. Damson trees are notably hardy, long-lived, disease-resistant, and productive — often naturalizing at hedgerow edges across England — and require less winter chill than Japanese plums. Generally self-fertile or partially self-fertile; a pollination partner improves yields.

plant_note: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; damson plum is more tolerant of thin, alkaline, and dry soils than most plums and produces astringent, aromatic, dark-purple fruit exceptional for preserves.
directions: Plant grafted or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; damson is more self-fertile than most plums and often sets good crops without a pollinator, though cropping improves with cross-pollination from another plum. Prunus instititia is the wild source of the cultivated damson, a small tree or large shrub producing small, oval, blue-black to purple plums in late summer with dense, richly flavored, astringent flesh quite distinct in character from the sweet, fresh-eating Japanese plums; damsons are the traditional plum for cooking, being too astringent to eat in quantity raw but transforming into superb jam (damson jam is one of Britain's most prized traditional preserves), jelly, cheese, wine, and gin. The tree is extremely long-lived, hardy, and productive even in cold, exposed, and acid soils where other plums fail.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost risk; Dancy tangerine requires well-drained soil — standing water even briefly can cause root rot. In zone 9, Dancy ripens December through January, making it a classic Christmas citrus fruit. Protect from frost below 27°F with frost cloth or row cover when young; established trees tolerate brief exposure to 25–26°F. Space trees 12–15 feet apart, or prune to maintain compact 6–8 foot size for easy harvest.
directions: Plant grafted nursery trees in full sun, well-drained soil; fertilize with a citrus fertilizer 3 times per year (February, May, September). Dancy is the original American tangerine — named for Col. George L. Dancy of Orange Mills, Florida, who cultivated this variety beginning around 1867, making it one of the oldest named tangerine cultivars in the United States. For over a century, 'Dancy tangerine' was synonymous with 'tangerine' for most Americans — it was the predominant commercial tangerine grown in Florida and the citrus most commonly associated with Christmas stocking traditions, the holiday season timing of its December–January ripening. The fruits are medium-small, oblate, and deep orange-red at maturity with a distinctively loose, easily peeled 'zipper-skin' — the loose skin peels away from the flesh with minimal effort, releasing the fruit in clean, separate segments. The flavor is the classic tangerine profile: tart, sweet, aromatic, and intensely citrus with the characteristic spicy-sweet note that distinguishes tangerines from oranges. Dancy has substantial seeds (8–15 per fruit), which reduces its appeal compared to modern seedless mandarin hybrids; however, the intense traditional tangerine flavor is considered by many to be unmatched by the sweeter but blander modern seedless types. Trees are productive and long-lived in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Collect and plant acorns immediately after they fall in autumn; press 1 inch deep in moist, well-drained to moist soil. Darlington oak is native to upland dry sandy soils of the Coastal Plain, distinct from the closely related Q. laurifolia which grows in moist lowlands.
directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; Darlington oak is a medium-sized semi-evergreen oak of the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain, often confused with the closely related laurel oak (Q. laurifolia) that grows in moister soils. The elliptical leaves are semi-evergreen to evergreen in the deep South, making this an excellent year-round shade and wildlife tree for zone 8–10 landscapes. Like most oaks, it produces abundant small acorns that provide essential food for wild turkeys, wood ducks, blue jays, and white-tailed deer. It is one of the most commonly encountered oaks in dry upland portions of the Florida peninsula and the Gulf Coastal Plain, thriving in the kind of deep, dry, infertile white sand that challenges most trees. An excellent canopy tree for naturalistic landscapes in the coastal Southeast where heat, drought, and sandy soils limit tree choices.

plant_note: Plant offshoots or container stock in spring when the soil is warm; dates require the specific combination of desert heat and dry air to ripen properly.
directions: Dates are dioecious — you need a male tree to pollinate female trees, with one male sufficient for up to 50 females; commercial growers hand-pollinate by shaking male flower strands over female inflorescences in spring. Ripe dates require extremely hot, dry summers (110°F daytime heat preferred) with very low humidity during the ripening period — this limits quality fruit production in the continental U.S. almost entirely to the Coachella Valley and low desert Arizona. Offshoots from the base of female palms are the preferred planting material as they preserve the sex and fruit type of the parent; seed-grown palms yield 50% males and highly variable fruit. Harvest in fall when fruit reaches the desired stage: khalal (crisp, astringent), rutab (partly soft, sweet), or tamr (fully dried).

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in moist, well-drained soil in spring or fall; date plum is adaptable to a wide range of soil conditions and is notably more cold-hardy than Asian persimmon. Female trees require a male pollinator for reliable fruit set. It is commonly used as a rootstock for grafting Diospyros kaki.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; date plum is a medium to large tree native from the Caucasus and Mediterranean to eastern Asia, producing small (1/2–1 inch) yellow to blue-black persimmon fruits in October–November that resemble tiny plums and have a sweet, date-like flavor — hence 'date plum.' The fruit contains high tannin levels when unripe (astringent like American persimmon) but becomes sweet after frost or extended hanging on the tree. Historical records suggest the fruit may be the legendary 'lotus fruit' of Homer's Odyssey that made Odysseus's sailors forget their homes. The tree is highly ornamental with glossy, dark-green leaves that turn yellow and red in fall, interesting orange bark on mature specimens, and small, attractive cream-colored flowers. More cold-hardy than Asian persimmon and easier to establish in temperate gardens, it is used as a rootstock for kaki persimmons.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; dattock or sweet detar is a large West African forest tree producing small, round, date-like fruits with sweet-acid, edible brown flesh that is exceptionally rich in vitamin C — one of the sweetest and most pleasant wild fruits of the West African coastal forests, eaten fresh throughout Senegal, Guinea, and Sierra Leone.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun to part shade; dattock is a forest tree that benefits from some shade protection when young. Detarium senegalense (dattock or sweet detar) is a tall leguminous tree from the coastal forests, gallery forests, and moist woodland savannas of West Africa — native across Senegal, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea, Sierra Leone, Ivory Coast, Ghana, and Nigeria. The tree produces round to slightly flattened, 1–1.5 inch, thin-shelled fruits containing large, flat, hard seeds embedded in sweet, brown, fibrous, edible mesocarp with a distinctive sweet-acid, almost tamarind-like flavor. The fruits are exceptionally rich in vitamin C (up to 100 mg per 100g — roughly twice that of orange juice), and are eaten fresh as a pleasant sweet-sour snack across rural West Africa. The hard seeds contain a starchy meal used in traditional foods. The tree yields a useful timber and a resin used in traditional medicine. In Senegal, the sweet detar fruits are particularly popular and are sold in local markets. Sweet detar (D. senegalense) is the sweet-fruited species, distinguished from bitter detar (D. microcarpum), which has similar fruits but with an unpleasantly bitter taste — an important distinction for edibility. A largely unknown and underexplored fruit tree outside West Africa.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Dauphine is a main-crop variety producing its heaviest harvest in August–September in zone 9. The vigorous, large tree requires generous spacing. It is known for exceptional productivity and large fruit size.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Dauphine is a French fig variety named for the Dauphiné region of southeastern France, producing large, round to flattened fruits with violet to brown-purple skin and pink to reddish-amber flesh with a rich, sweet, mild flavor. The large fruit size (2–3 inches) is among the biggest in the fig world and makes Dauphine figs particularly impressive for fresh eating and market presentation. The vigorous, productive tree performs well in zone 9 heat and provides abundant harvests of the large, handsome fruits from August through September. Dauphine figs are best eaten fresh at peak ripeness; the large size can lead to cracking if late-season rains arrive during ripening. The French Dauphiné region has a tradition of fig cultivation in its milder southern valleys, and Dauphine represents the large-fruited table fig tradition of this region. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast conditions closely approximate the warm, humid conditions of the Dauphiné valleys.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Davidson's plum is a rainforest understory tree from tropical and subtropical Queensland, producing large, dark-purple to almost-black, very tart, sour plums on the trunk and branches (cauliflorous) — the primary fruit of the Australian native food industry for jams, sauces, cheeses, desserts, and gin liqueurs — and remarkably rich in antioxidants and vitamin C.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Davidson's plum grows naturally as a rainforest understory tree and requires protection from direct hot afternoon sun. Davidsonia pruriens (Davidson's plum or ooray) is a rainforest understory tree native to the tropical and subtropical rainforests of Queensland, Australia — one of the most commercially important fruits in the Australian native food industry. The tree is notable for its highly unusual growth habit: the large (1.5–2.5 inch), dark-purple to burgundy-black, plum-like fruits grow directly from the trunk and main branches in dense clusters (cauliflory), similar to cacao and jaboticaba. The fruits are intensely, mouth-puckeringly tart — far too sour to eat fresh in quantity without processing — but with extraordinary depth of flavor that has made them the darling of Australian native food chefs and product makers. Davidson's plum jam, Davidson's plum sauce (excellent with game, lamb, and dark meats), Davidson's plum sorbet, Davidson's plum wine and gin, and Davidson's plum dried food products are among the most celebrated products of the native food movement. The fruits are extremely rich in antioxidants — anthocyanins, ellagic acid, vitamin C — with a deep, complex, sour-fruity character that processing and sweetening reveals as intensely flavorful. Hardy to light frost in zone 9, Davidson's plum is increasingly available from Australian specialty nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Davis needs a second, genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Davis is one of the oldest widely propagated named pawpaw cultivars, selected by Michigan pawpaw breeder Corwin Davis in the mid-20th century from wild seedling trees and long valued for its consistent, reliable production and good flavor. Fruits are medium-sized with smooth, pale yellow, fiber-free flesh and a rich, sweet, banana-custard flavor, though the seeds are somewhat larger in proportion to flesh than in some newer cultivars. Davis ripens in the early-to-mid part of the pawpaw season and, alongside cultivars like Sunflower and Taytwo, played a foundational role in the mid-20th-century revival of interest in pawpaw as a cultivated fruit. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, since pawpaw's natural pollinators (flies and beetles, drawn to the maroon flowers' faint carrion scent) are often scarce in home gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy, dryland soil in full sun; desert date is an extremely drought-tolerant, thorny, small tree of the African and Middle Eastern drylands — producing oval, olive-sized, yellow-brown fruits with sweet-bitter, date-like flesh around a hard seed — one of the most drought-resistant multi-use trees in the Sahel, used across the semi-arid belt of Africa from Senegal to Ethiopia and into the Middle East.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to loamy dryland soil in full sun; one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available — tolerates 3–6 months of complete drought once established. Balanites aegyptiaca (desert date, heglig, or soap berry tree) is a thorny, slow-growing tree native to the arid and semi-arid regions of sub-Saharan Africa, the Sahel, and the Middle East — one of the most widely distributed and ecologically important trees of the African drylands, found from Senegal and Mauritania east through Sudan and Ethiopia and into the Arabian Peninsula. The tree produces oval, olive-sized, yellow-brown to dark-brown fruits (drupes) with fleshy, oily mesocarp that is sweet-bitter with a date-like character; the fruits are eaten fresh, used to flavor traditional porridges, fermented into beer, and pressed for oil. The seed kernel yields an edible oil used in cooking and as a skin preparation. The bark, leaves, and fruit rind contain saponins traditionally used as soap — hence 'soap berry tree' — and in traditional fish stunning for fishing (the saponins narcotize fish). The tree has extensive traditional medicinal applications across Africa (treatment of malaria, diabetes, skin conditions) and is increasingly studied for bioactive compounds. One of the premier trees for the dryland agroforestry systems of the Sahel, where it withstands extreme drought, poor soils, and degraded conditions that defeat most other trees.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Desert King is the most widely grown and most reliably productive fig for the Pacific Northwest and similar cool-summer climates, where it produces an abundant breba crop that ripens reliably even in cool, short summers that defeat most other fig varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun against a south-facing wall in cooler climates to maximize heat accumulation; Desert King is a San Pedro type that requires no pollinator for its reliable breba crop but benefits from caprification for main crop development in warm climates. Desert King is the dominant fig cultivar in Pacific Northwest gardens (Oregon, Washington, British Columbia) where it excels for its large, spectacular breba crop (early summer, June–July) that ripens reliably without the extended heat required by most other figs; the very large (3–6 oz), flattened-turbinate fruits have thick, green to greenish-yellow ribbed skin and dark strawberry to amber-red interior flesh with rich, sweet flavor. In warm climates (California, Gulf Coast) it also produces a substantial main crop in August–October. Among the most cold-hardy of all quality fig varieties, surviving to about 10–12°F when established and dormant. A vigorous, large tree that requires space; well-suited to training as an espalier against south-facing masonry walls.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January–February in zone 9); Desirable requires a cross-pollinator such as Stuart, Elliott, or Caddo for reliable nut production since it is a Type II pollinator (pistillate flowers receptive before pollen shed). Space 50–60 feet apart for full-sized trees, or 30–35 feet for orchard plantings.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun; Desirable is the most widely planted named pecan cultivar in the United States and the benchmark against which other commercial varieties are measured. Developed by the USDA and released in 1940, it produces large, well-filled nuts (50–55 per pound) with an excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and superb flavor — considered by many pecan growers to be the highest-quality commercial pecan available. It is a consistent, reliable producer in zone 7–9 and well-adapted to the Gulf Coast South from Texas to Georgia. The principal challenge is susceptibility to pecan scab disease (Fusicladium effusum) in humid climates — in very humid areas like coastal Louisiana and Mississippi, it may require fungicide protection in wet years. Space trees widely: pecans ultimately become very large trees (60–80 feet tall, 40–60 feet wide) that shade out everything below. Supplement with zinc spray in spring; pecan is notorious for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils.

common_name: Dorset Golden Apple (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf Coast Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; Dorset Golden requires only 100–200 chill hours — it is one of very few apple cultivars that reliably produces fruit in zone 9a where chill hours frequently fall below 500 hours in warm winters.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Dorset Golden is one of the two or three apple cultivars with the lowest chill requirements that can be reliably grown in Gulf South zone 9 gardens — requiring only 100–200 chilling hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break and fruit set. This ultra-low chill requirement makes Dorset Golden one of the very few apples that can be grown productively in the Gulf South where total winter chill hours range from 200–600 hours in zone 9, often falling short of the 700–1,000+ hours required by standard northern apple varieties. Dorset Golden originated as a chance seedling in the Bahamas — an unexpected confirmation that apples with very low chill requirements can produce high-quality fruit in tropical and subtropical climates. The fruit is medium to large, golden-yellow with a light blush, and has a firm, crisp texture with a good balance of sweetness and mild acidity — far superior in flavor to most other low-chill apple varieties. In zone 9, Dorset Golden ripens in June — exceptionally early for a full-sized apple. It is partially self-fertile but produces larger crops when cross-pollinated with Anna (another ultra-low-chill variety). For Gulf South apple growing, pair Dorset Golden with Anna for reliable cross-pollination.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in winter dormancy (December–February in zone 9); Dorsett Golden requires only 100–200 chill hours — the lowest requirement of any widely grown apple cultivar — making it viable in zone 10 and parts of south Florida where Anna struggles. Partially self-fertile but produces better crops with Anna or Ein Shemer nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dorsett Golden originated as a chance seedling discovered in the Bahamas by Irene Dorsett in the 1950s, thriving in a climate with almost no winter chill. It requires only 100–200 chill hours — the lowest of any significant apple cultivar — and produces reliable crops in zone 9b–10a where even Anna struggles. The medium-large, golden-yellow fruits resemble Golden Delicious in appearance but ripen 2–3 weeks before Anna (April–May in zone 9), making it the first ripe apple of the season in the deep South. Flavor is sweet, mild, and pleasant with moderately crisp flesh. Dorsett Golden is partially self-fertile but sets significantly heavier crops when cross-pollinated with Anna or Ein Shemer. In zone 10, this trio of low-chill apple varieties (Anna, Dorsett Golden, Ein Shemer) makes apple growing possible where it would have been considered impossible a generation ago. Fire blight can be a problem — avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes lush growth susceptible to infection.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; seeds require warm followed by cold stratification (double dormancy) and typically germinate in their second spring — patience is essential with this species.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun along forest edges, stream banks, or open lowlands; dotted hawthorn is among the showiest of the eastern native hawthorns, producing broad, flat-topped clusters of white flowers in spring that are excellent pollinator forage, followed by heavy crops of round, dull-red to yellow haws distinctively spotted with pale lenticels — the 'dots' that give the species its name. The persistent haws are eagerly consumed by cedar waxwings, robins, grouse, and foxes through fall and early winter, making this one of the most productive wildlife trees in its native range. It forms a dense, thorny canopy well suited to wildlife hedgerows or naturalized areas where its formidable spines can serve as a living fence. Seeds require double dormancy and may take two full seasons to germinate; container-grown transplants establish most reliably.

subcategory: Egyptian and East African branching palm
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to rocky, alkaline to neutral, arid soil in zone 8–11; Doum Palm is one of the only true branching palms in the world — native to Egypt, the Nile Valley, and sub-Saharan Africa — with naturally dichotomously branching trunks producing multiple growing tips, and bearing large, orange-brown, gingerbread-flavored fruits sacred to ancient Egypt and still an important food across northeastern Africa.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to gravelly, alkaline, lean, arid soil; Hyphaene thebaica is adapted to extreme desert and semi-arid conditions — drought tolerant, heat tolerant, alkaline-soil adapted, and saline-tolerant; avoid clay or wet soils. Hyphaene thebaica (Doum Palm, Gingerbread Palm, or Egyptian Doum) is a large, majestic, fan palm native to the Nile Valley, northeastern Africa, and the dry savannas and deserts of sub-Saharan Africa from Egypt and Sudan through East Africa to South Africa — one of the most distinctive and botanically remarkable palms in the world because of its naturally dichotomously branching trunk. Unlike virtually all other true palms (which are monocots and cannot branch), Hyphaene thebaica produces true dichotomous bifurcation at each growing point, creating a naturally multi-headed, tree-like branching architecture that makes it instantly recognizable and utterly unlike any other palm. The large (2–4 inch), smooth, orange-brown fruits have a hard, starchy, dry, reddish inner mesocarp with a flavor and texture remarkably similar to gingerbread — giving the common name 'Gingerbread Palm.' The fruits were a significant food source in ancient Egypt — doum fruit has been found in Egyptian tombs dating to 3200 BCE and is depicted in reliefs at Luxor and Karnak. The hard endosperm ('vegetable ivory') is carved into buttons and small ornaments. Excellent accent palm for hot, dry, alkaline-soil landscapes in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown specimens in spring in full sun in any well-drained to moist soil; downy hawthorn is one of the largest-fruited native hawthorns, producing deep red to orange-red fruits nearly 1 inch in diameter — much larger than most other hawthorn species.
directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in any fertile, well-drained to moist soil; downy hawthorn (Crataegus mollis) is among the largest-fruited native hawthorns in the eastern United States, producing abundant clusters of large, red-orange fruits (haws) nearly 3/4 to 1 inch across in late summer — far more substantial than most hawthorn species — that are suitable for making jelly, jam, and fruit leather with a pleasant, apple-like flavor. The tree itself is large and spreading with downy (hairy) leaves and branchlets and spectacular white flowers in spring. An outstanding wildlife tree providing critical food for over 100 species of birds and mammals, and exceptional browse habitat for deer and rabbits. The thorny branches also provide nesting protection for songbirds.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring; this species tolerates a wider range of soil moisture than Amelanchier canadensis and can be grown as a single-trunk tree.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike the colonial serviceberry (A. canadensis), this species develops a single trunk to form a graceful multi-season small tree with spectacular clouds of white flowers in early spring, blueberry-like fruit in June, and brilliant orange-red fall foliage. The sweet berries ripen all at once in early summer and are excellent fresh, dried like raisins, or used in pies and jams; birds compete fiercely for the crop. Prune to remove crossing branches in late winter; do not top the tree. Cedar-apple rust and fire blight are potential problems in humid climates — ensure good air circulation around the canopy.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings after frost danger passes; overwinter indoors in cold climates.
directions: Dragon fruit is a climbing, white-fleshed cactus that produces dramatic sculptural stems and sweet fruit following its large night-blooming flowers. Grow it in fast-draining cactus soil and provide a sturdy trellis or post for the heavy vining stems to climb. Water only when the soil dries out, since the plant stores moisture and is prone to rot if kept wet. It needs warmth above 40 degrees, so grow it in a container to move indoors where frost occurs. Hand-pollinate the evening flowers for reliable fruit set.

plant_note: Root 12–18 inch stem cuttings in well-drained, sandy or cactus-mix soil with at least 4 hours direct sun; allow cut end to callus 3–5 days before planting. A sturdy 5-foot post or trellis is needed as a climbing support from the start.
directions: Root cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy or amended cactus soil in full sun; dragon fruit is a climbing cactus native to Central America that produces spectacular night-blooming white flowers 12 inches across, followed by the familiar large, brightly colored fruit with its distinctive pink-magenta or yellow skin and speckled white or red flesh. Plants take 1–2 years from cuttings to first fruit, then produce prolifically. The vine-like stems climb via aerial roots and require a sturdy post or trellis. In zone 9a, protect from hard freezes with frost cloth — stems will die back at 28°F but established plants often resprout from the base. Fruit ripens 30–50 days after flowering; harvest when the pink color fully develops and the wings begin to wilt. Multiple varieties exist including red-fleshed 'American Beauty' and yellow-skinned Selenicereus megalanthus.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Duncan is seedy but widely regarded as having the richest, most complex flavor of any grapefruit, and the tree is notably cold-hardy for the species.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Traced to a tree found growing on Florida's Gulf Coast in the 1830s and later propagated commercially in 1892 by A. L. Duncan, this is the oldest named grapefruit cultivar still grown today and the ancestor of most modern seedless grapefruit varieties. The pale yellow, white-fleshed fruit is notably seedy by modern standards, but its tart, deeply flavored juice is prized by grapefruit enthusiasts and is still used in breeding programs for flavor quality. The tree is vigorous, productive, and among the more cold-tolerant grapefruit selections, making it a reasonable choice at the cooler edge of the grapefruit-growing range.

common_name: Dunstan Chestnut (Blight-Resistant American-Chinese Chestnut Hybrid, Food Forest Nut Tree)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees or seedlings in spring; Dunstan Chestnut trees require cross-pollination — plant at least two seedlings or grafted trees for nut production, as chestnuts are not self-fertile. Dunstan Chestnuts bear their first modest crop in 3–5 years and reach full production in 7–10 years. In zone 9, the combination of heat and humidity can stress chestnut trees; plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) in a location with good air circulation to reduce fungal disease pressure. Unlike other chestnut species, the Dunstan hybrid has demonstrated substantially greater resistance to chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) — the fungal disease that eliminated virtually the entire American chestnut population from eastern North American forests in the early 20th century. The Dunstan provides a practical avenue for home orchardists who want to grow chestnuts without the catastrophic cankers that terminate American chestnut trees before they reach nut-bearing size.
directions: Plant two or more trees for cross-pollination; harvest nuts in September–October when burrs split and nuts fall naturally. Dunstan Chestnut is a hybrid between American chestnut (Castanea dentata) and Chinese chestnut (Castanea mollissima) that was developed by plant breeder Robert Dunstan beginning in the 1950s after he obtained blight-resistant American chestnut seedlings identified by plant pathologist Arthur Graves. Dunstan crossed these blight-resistant American chestnut trees (which retained their blight resistance while displaying more American-type tree form) with Chinese chestnut to create offspring that combined the superior nut quality, upright tree form, and improved blight resistance of the selected parent material. The Dunstan Chestnut is commercially distributed by Chestnut Hill Nursery in Alachua, Florida — itself a significant note, as Alachua/Gainesville, Florida is in zone 9, confirming that Dunstan Chestnut grows in zone 9 conditions. The nuts are large to very large (often 1 inch diameter), sweet, richly flavored — closer to American chestnut quality than Chinese chestnut — and produced in large quantities in well-established trees. Chestnuts have significant nutritional value: high in complex carbohydrates (unusual among tree nuts, which are typically high in fats), relatively low in fat, and with a flavor and texture that makes them excellent roasted, boiled, pureed into soups and stuffings, or ground into flour for baked goods. Chestnut trees are also long-lived, productive wildlife food trees: the nuts are consumed by deer, turkey, squirrel, and many other wildlife species, making Dunstan Chestnut valuable for food forest and wildlife habitat plantings in the Gulf South.

common_name: Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut (American-Chinese Hybrid Chestnut, Blight-Resistant Eastern Chestnut)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), deep, sandy loam or loamy soil in full sun; Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut is self-fertile and can produce a crop as a single tree, though yields improve with cross-pollination from another chestnut variety; avoid heavy clay or waterlogged sites — chestnut does not tolerate wet feet and is susceptible to Phytophthora root rot in poorly drained conditions; does NOT require the blight fungus management needed for American chestnut.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, sandy loam or loamy soil in full sun; Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut is self-fertile; mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and acidity; harvest nuts in September–October when burrs split open and chestnuts fall; gather from ground promptly as ground moisture causes rapid spoilage; refrigerate fresh nuts within days of harvest since they are perishable. Dunstan Hybrid Chestnut represents one of the most important advances in American chestnut restoration, developed by Dr. Robert Dunstan of Greensboro, North Carolina in the 1950s and 1960s after discovering a surviving American chestnut tree in Ohio (the Graves tree) that appeared to have some natural resistance to the chestnut blight (Cryphonectria parasitica) that wiped out approximately 4 billion American chestnut trees from the eastern forest between 1904 and 1950. Dunstan crossed this apparently blight-resistant American chestnut with Chinese chestnut (Castanea mollissima), which has co-evolved with the blight fungus in Asia and carries true genetic resistance, to produce a hybrid combining the large size and straight timber form approaching American chestnut with the blight resistance of the Chinese parent. The Dunstan Hybrid produced nuts with excellent size and sweet flavor — closer to American chestnut sweetness than to the less-flavorful Chinese chestnut — while demonstrating substantially better blight resistance than standard American chestnut. Dunstan Hybrids have been widely planted in the southeastern and Mid-Atlantic states for orchard nut production, wildlife habitat (deer, turkey, and squirrels relish chestnuts), and as a productive native-type chestnut for home orchards where the formerly dominant American chestnut once grew.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a humid, frost-free tropical climate; durian requires consistent warmth above 50°F.
directions: Durian demands deep, fertile, well-drained soil, high humidity, and temperatures between 75°F and 95°F year-round; it is the most climate-specific of the major tropical fruits and can only be grown outdoors in the most tropical parts of the continental United States (extreme south Florida). Flowers open at night and are primarily bat-pollinated, so maintain nearby native habitat and avoid pesticide applications at dusk; hand-pollination improves set in enclosed settings. Fruit develops over 3–5 months and the spiny husk is potentially dangerous — trees should be netted and fruit harvested from the ground after it falls naturally. The ripe flesh has a rich custard flavor with a pungent sulfurous aroma that intensifies rapidly after harvest; consume or freeze within 24–48 hours.

plant_note: Plant after frost danger; grow in a container to overwinter indoors in cold climates.
directions: Dwarf Cavendish is a compact banana cultivar that fruits at a manageable height, making it well suited to containers and small spaces. Grow it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, feeding heavily through the warm season since bananas are gross feeders. Keep the soil consistently moist and shelter the large leaves from strong wind that can shred them. Where temperatures drop below the mid-50s, move the plant indoors to a bright, warm spot for winter. Each stem fruits once, after which it is cut down and replaced by new pups from the base.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown plants in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Dwarf Everbearing stays small enough for a large container or tiny yard while still producing a long, extended crop of sweet berries.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container where its compact size is a real advantage. Dwarf Everbearing is a naturally small mulberry, reaching only a fraction of the size of standard mulberry trees while still producing a long, extended harvest of sweet, dark berries over many weeks rather than the shorter few-week fruiting window of many fruit trees. Its small size makes it one of the few mulberries practical for a small urban yard, patio, or large container, and it can even be grown as a modest specimen shrub rather than needing the space of a full-sized shade tree. It fruits at a young age and requires only routine pruning to control size and shape.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in sandy, dry, acidic soil in full sun; seeds undergo double dormancy and typically germinate in the second spring — direct sowing at the permanent site is preferred because dwarf hawthorn resents root disturbance.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), infertile soil in full sun; dwarf hawthorn is one of the few native woody plants genuinely adapted to the challenging conditions of pine barrens and sandhills, where richer soils and supplemental moisture will actually harm it by promoting overly lush growth susceptible to disease. Unlike all other native hawthorns, which bear flowers in corymbs, this species bears a single white flower at each thorn tip in spring — an unusual and botanically distinctive habit. The small, round red haws that follow are an important food source for songbirds in the dry-woods habitats where little else fruits abundantly. Its thicket-forming habit makes it useful as a wildlife brush pile and nesting cover in naturalized dry-soil gardens and restorations.

plant_note: Plant pups (suckers) or tissue-culture plants in spring after danger of frost; in zone 9 plant March–May. Dwarf Orinoco is one of the most cold-hardy edible banana cultivars, surviving temperatures down to 20–22°F at the roots even when the above-ground pseudostem is killed to the ground — the rhizome survives and sends up new suckers in spring. In zone 9 the pseudostem typically survives mild winters intact, allowing it to reach the fruiting stage in the first or second season.
directions: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil with high organic matter; Dwarf Orinoco is a compact, cold-hardy edible banana producing medium-sized, angular, somewhat starchy fruits that can be eaten fresh when fully ripe (developing a rich, sweet-tart flavor) or cooked as a plantain when green. The Orinoco type bananas (also called 'Horse Banana') are among the most cold-hardy fruiting bananas in cultivation, with Dwarf Orinoco selected for a shorter stature (6–10 feet) that is more manageable in home gardens and more wind-resistant than tall-growing types. In zone 9 Dwarf Orinoco regularly produces edible fruit clusters on pseudostems that survive mild winters without die-back, making it one of the most reliably productive edible banana choices for the Gulf South. Feed generously with high-potassium fertilizer during the growing season to support fruit development.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade; small-flower pawpaw tolerates significantly drier conditions and more shade than the common pawpaw (A. triloba) and naturally grows in the understory of longleaf pine flatwoods and dry woodlands.
directions: Plant in moist to dry, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in partial shade — small-flower pawpaw is the native pawpaw of the southeastern coastal plain, growing in the dry understory of longleaf pine flatwoods and open, sandy woodlands from Virginia to Florida and west to Louisiana. It is more shade-tolerant and drought-tolerant than the common pawpaw (A. triloba) and produces smaller but similarly flavored fruits — small oblong yellow-green pawpaws 1–2 inches long with the characteristic sweet, custard-like tropical flavor of the familiar large pawpaw. Like all Asimina species, it is the exclusive larval host plant for the zebra swallowtail butterfly, which depends entirely on Asimina for its caterpillars. The small maroon flowers in early spring resemble the larger common pawpaw flowers. A valuable native plant for the shaded, dry woodland garden in the Southeast, supporting both edible fruit production and butterfly habitat.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall in a well-drained seedbed; this vigorous suckering shrub establishes readily from seed and will spread by root sprouts once established.
directions: Sow seeds in fall directly into a prepared bed with lean, well-drained soil, pressing them just below the surface and allowing winter cold to provide the stratification needed for spring germination. Dwarf Serviceberry spreads aggressively by root sprouts and will form dense thickets over time, so site it where naturalized spread is welcome rather than in manicured borders. The profuse white spring flowers provide early nectar for pollinators, and the sweet blue-black berries that follow are among the first wild fruits to ripen each summer. Established colonies are highly drought-tolerant and require virtually no maintenance, making this shrub an outstanding choice for habitat restoration, erosion control, or low-maintenance edible landscaping.

common_name: Early Golden American Persimmon (Pre-Frost Ripening Persimmon, Historic Illinois Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Early Golden is notable for ripening in September — before hard frosts — unlike most American persimmon cultivars that require frost softening to become non-astringent; this early ripening is especially valuable in zones 7–9 where autumn frosts arrive late or for gardens where early harvest is desired; plant with a male tree or self-fertile variety for best fruit set.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Early Golden is adapted to a wide range of soil types including poor, clay, and acidic soils; grafted trees first fruit in 3–5 years; harvest when fruits soften and color fully to light orange-yellow and test a fruit for astringency before consuming — fully ripe Early Golden fruits are sweet, non-astringent, and rich with apricot flavor. Early Golden is one of the oldest named American persimmon cultivars, with documentation extending back to the 19th century from Illinois nursery records, making it among the earliest formal selections of Diospyros virginiana evaluated for garden culture rather than simple wild harvest. The variety's primary distinction is its unusually early ripening season: fruit matures and becomes non-astringent in September — sometimes as early as late August in warm years — typically 4–6 weeks ahead of most American persimmon selections, and often before hard frosts occur. This early ripening is particularly valuable in warm-climate gardens (zones 7–9) where autumn frosts arrive in November or later, and for zones 4–5 gardeners who want ripe persimmons before early fall frost events. The fruits are small to medium (1–1.25 inch diameter), light orange to yellow-orange at maturity, with sweet, mild, complex flavor when fully ripe.

plant_note: Grown from a rooted cutting; a climbing cactus needing sturdy support.
directions: Edgar's Baby is a compact dragon fruit, a climbing epiphytic cactus that rewards growers with sweet, vividly colored fruit on a manageable plant. It produces large, fragrant night-blooming flowers followed by fruit and thrives with warmth and strong support to climb. Grow from a rooted cutting in full sun and fast-draining, sandy soil, watering only when the mix dries since the cactus rots in soggy conditions. Provide a trellis or post, feed lightly, and shelter it from any frost.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 9b–12) in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Egg Fruit (Canistel, Tiesa) is a medium-sized evergreen sapotaceous tree native to Central America and Mexico bearing oval to pear-shaped fruits with smooth, vivid orange-yellow skin and dense, dry, sweet, orange-yellow flesh of a texture and richness so similar to a hard-boiled egg yolk that it is called Egg Fruit in English and compared to sweet potato in flavor.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pouteria campechiana benefits from regular water during fruiting but tolerates brief drought once established — maintain good drainage and avoid standing water around the root zone. Pouteria campechiana (Egg Fruit, Canistel, or Tiesa) is an evergreen or briefly deciduous tree native to the tropical forests of Central America — Guatemala, Belize, Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula — and introduced throughout the Caribbean, South Florida, the Philippines, Southeast Asia, and tropical West Africa. The fruit is one of the most distinctive of the sapote family: ovoid to pear-shaped, 2–4 inches long, with smooth, waxy, vivid orange to golden-yellow skin, and dense, dry, smooth, richly sweet orange-yellow flesh with a starchy texture remarkably similar to a hard-boiled egg yolk — sometimes described as sweet potato crossed with pumpkin pie. The flesh is eaten fresh, made into egg fruit nog, smoothies, ice cream, jam, and pies; it is particularly popular in Cuba, the Philippines, and South Florida ethnic markets. Trees require grafted or air-layered specimens to fruit true-to-type and within 3–5 years; seedling trees may take 6–8 years to fruit. A productive and adaptable tropical fruit tree for South Florida, the Gulf Coast, and similar warm subtropical climates.

common_name: Ein Shemer Apple (Very Low-Chill Gulf South Apple for Zone 8-9)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Ein Shemer needs only about 300 chill hours, making it one of the few apples that reliably fruits in the Gulf South, and it doubles as an effective pollinator for Anna and Dorsett Golden, which bloom at a similar time.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; unlike most apples, Ein Shemer was selected in Israel specifically for regions with mild, short winters and thrives where classic high-chill apples like Red Delicious or Fuji fail to break dormancy properly. The medium, yellow-green fruit is mild and sweet with a soft, quick-to-ripen texture, best eaten soon after picking rather than stored long term. It ripens early in the season, generally ahead of most other low-chill apples, and its abundant, well-timed bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator in a mixed low-chill apple planting. This is one of the more dependable apple choices for zone 9a gardens along the Gulf Coast.

common_name: El Dorado Nectarine (Genetic Dwarf Low-Chill Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; El Dorado is a genetic dwarf that tops out at a fraction of standard tree size, making it well suited to containers and small gardens, with a low chill requirement good for zone 8-9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; bred by Floyd Zaiger, El Dorado is a genetic dwarf nectarine that naturally grows to only six to eight feet, a fraction of a standard tree's size, while still producing full-sized, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit. Its low chill requirement of around 300 hours lets it fruit reliably in mild-winter regions like the Gulf South where standard nectarines often fail to break dormancy evenly. The compact size makes it an excellent choice for large containers or small yards, though the dense, naturally rounded canopy still benefits from light annual thinning to let light into the interior. Fruit ripens in early summer and is self-fruitful, requiring no separate pollinator.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) before the trees break dormancy in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Elberta requires approximately 800 hours of chilling (temperatures below 45°F) — verify local chill hour accumulation before planting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile, deep soil in full sun; Elberta is the single most historically significant peach cultivar in American horticulture — developed in 1875 by Samuel Henry Rumph of Marshallville, Georgia, from a cross of Chinese Cling × Early Crawford, and for a century it was the standard commercial and home-garden freestone peach across the South. The large, yellow-fleshed, freestone fruit has a rich, full peach flavor with the balanced sweetness and acidity that defines the classic Southern peach flavor profile. Despite the development of countless newer peach cultivars with improved disease resistance and self-fertility, Elberta remains widely grown for its outstanding flavor quality, large fruit size, and proven production in zone 9 with sufficient chill hours. Elberta requires approximately 800 chill hours (hours below 45°F), which accumulates reliably in zone 9a and most of zone 9 during normal winters, though borderline years may occur. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart after petal fall to achieve maximum fruit size. Prune annually to an open-vase form to maintain production. Peach leaf curl, brown rot, and oriental fruit moth are common pests; a preventive fungicide and dormant oil spray program beginning at bud swell is essential for disease management.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Elephant Heart is a Luther Burbank introduction from around 1929 and one of the most distinctive and impressive Japanese plums for fresh eating — very large, dark, blood-fleshed fruits with an exceptionally rich, sweet-tart, wine-like flavor that sets it apart from more mildly flavored modern varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires cross-pollination with Santa Rosa, Shiro, Satsuma, or another Japanese plum. Elephant Heart is a Luther Burbank plum introduced around 1929 and named for the large, heart-shaped fruits that can weigh 4–6 oz each — unusually large even among Japanese plums. The dark red to near-black skin encloses blood-red to deep crimson flesh with intensely rich, sweet-tart, wine-complex flavor that many consider the most interesting and complex of the Japanese plum flavors; it is notably more flavorful and less mild than Shiro or Santa Rosa when eaten at peak ripeness (late August to September, relatively late for Japanese plums). The depth of pigmentation (both in skin and flesh) makes Elephant Heart particularly striking and flavorful for fresh eating, jam, and preserves. Chill requirement is approximately 400–500 hours. The distinctive, intense flavor comes through even when cooked; a justly famous heirloom plum maintained by Slow Food and heirloom orchardists.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (dormant) or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 plant January–February. Elliot pecan requires 1,500–2,000 hours below 45°F for optimum production — easily met in zones 6–9. Plant two varieties for cross-pollination (pecans are wind-pollinated and most cultivars benefit from another variety nearby). Elliot is a Type II variety — releases pollen after female flowers are receptive; pair with a Type I variety (Stuart, Cape Fear) for best production. Trees become significantly productive in 7–10 years and can remain productive for 100+ years.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep (6+ feet), well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — pecans are deep-rooted trees that require deep, fertile bottomland or well-amended upland soil for maximum production; Elliot is one of the most important pecan cultivars for the Gulf South, selected specifically for its outstanding resistance to pecan scab (Venturia effusa) — the most damaging fungal disease of pecans in the humid Gulf Coast climate where without resistance, pecan production requires intensive fungicide programs that make orchard production impractical. Elliot's scab resistance means it can produce quality nuts in the humid Gulf South with minimal or no fungicide applications — a fundamental practical advantage for home orchard growers. The small-to-medium, ovate nuts have thin shells and a high kernel percentage (approximately 52%), with the sweet, rich, buttery, distinctively pecan flavor that makes Gulf South-grown pecans the gold standard among nut crops. Elliot's consistent production, excellent kernel quality, and scab resistance make it the recommended home orchard pecan for Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and the Texas Gulf Coast — the regions where pecan is culturally important and where Elliot's disease resistance matters most.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees January–February in zone 9; Elliott is a Type II pollinator and pairs best with Desirable (Type I) or Curtis (Type I) for cross-pollination. Its exceptional scab resistance makes it the recommended variety for humid coastal zone 8–9 areas where scab disease is a persistent problem.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Elliott is a Florida-origin pecan variety selected for commercial production in the humid Gulf Coast Southeast because of its outstanding resistance to pecan scab disease — the most economically damaging disease of pecans in the humid South. While Stuart and Desirable require protection in rainy years, Elliott produces consistent yields without fungicide programs in most Gulf Coast locations, making it the variety of choice for low-spray and organic home orchards in zone 8–9. Nuts are smaller than Desirable or Stuart (60–70 per pound) but kernel quality is excellent — thin shells, high kernel fill (55–60%), and very good flavor. Elliott is a late-season variety, maturing in October–November after most other varieties. Its smaller stature (60–70 feet mature) compared to some pecan giants also makes it slightly more manageable. An excellent choice for humid coastal and transitional zone 9 gardens where disease pressure is high.

common_name: Emerald Blueberry (UF Southern Highbush Excellent-Flavor Low-Chill Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root plants in late fall to early spring in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Emerald requires cross-pollination from another southern highbush variety (Jewel, Southmoon, O'Neal) for maximum fruit production — plant two or more compatible varieties within 50 feet.
directions: Plant in well-drained, very acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun; Emerald is a University of Florida IFAS southern highbush blueberry introduction recognized as one of the finest-flavored and most productive low-chill blueberry varieties for Gulf South gardens — producing large, round, sky-blue to medium-blue berries with a desirable balance of sweetness and mild acidity, firm texture, small dry scar, and excellent fresh-eating quality that compares favorably with the best northern highbush varieties. Emerald requires only approximately 200 chill hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break and reliable annual fruit production — far fewer than the 700–1,000+ hours required by northern highbush varieties, making it fully adapted to zone 9 winters where chill accumulation frequently falls in the 200–400 hour range. The early to mid-season ripening (March–May in zone 9) provides fresh local blueberries before summer heat arrives. Soil pH management is the most critical cultural requirement: blueberries in general, and southern highbush especially, require very acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5) — outside this range, nutrients become unavailable regardless of fertilization, causing slow growth, yellowing foliage, and poor production. Amend soil with sulfur well before planting to lower pH; maintain with acidifying fertilizer (azalea/camellia formulas) and pine bark mulch. For maximum production, plant Emerald with at least one other southern highbush variety for cross-pollination.

common_name: Empire Apple (McIntosh × Red Delicious, Cornell Commercial Release Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Empire requires cross-pollination from a compatible apple variety — Cortland, Honeycrisp, Gala, or McIntosh are all compatible pollinators; requires approximately 800–900 chill hours; best adapted to zones 4–7; Empire is an early-to-mid-bearing variety that begins producing good crops by its 4th–6th year on standard rootstock.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Empire requires a cross-pollinator; fruits ripen in September–October with medium to large, deep red to nearly all-red skin and crisp, firm, creamy-white flesh; Empire stores significantly better than McIntosh — refrigerated fruits hold quality for 3–5 months — making it preferable for wholesale and storage. Empire apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva in 1945 from a deliberate cross of McIntosh and Red Delicious, and released for commercial planting in 1966 — named for 'The Empire State' of New York to honor the variety's state of origin. The cross combined the aromatic, sweet-tart character and eating quality of McIntosh with the firmer flesh and better keeping quality of Red Delicious, achieving an apple that outperformed both parents in commercial viability: Empire is significantly firmer than McIntosh (which quickly becomes soft and mealy after harvest), stores considerably longer under refrigeration, and maintains its crispness and good flavor for months. Today Empire is one of the most important commercial apple varieties in New York State — which produces the second-largest apple crop in the United States — and is widely planted throughout the northeastern states and eastern Canada. For home gardeners, Empire's earlier bearing age (compared to Northern Spy), reliable productivity, and superior storage compared to McIntosh make it an excellent choice for the home orchard where both fresh-eating and winter storage apples are desired.

plant_note: Plant pad cuttings in spring or early fall; allow cut surfaces to callus for 1 week before planting in dry, sandy or rocky, well-drained soil. Engelmann prickly pear tolerates rocky limestone soils and extended drought. Fruits (tunas) ripen deep red-purple in late summer through early fall — harvest with heavy gloves and tongs.
directions: Plant paddles vertically with the cut end 2–3 inches deep in very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; Engelmann prickly pear is the most widespread cactus of the American Southwest, ranging from Texas to California and into Mexico, and the principal source of edible tunas (fruits) and nopales (young pads) used in Mexican and Southwestern cooking. The large, red-purple tunas that ripen in late summer are exceptionally sweet with a flavor reminiscent of watermelon and bubblegum, high in antioxidants and vitamin C — they are eaten fresh, juiced into agua fresca and syrups, or made into jelly and candy. Harvest fruits with tongs and singe off glochids over a flame or scrub under running water before eating. This native cactus requires essentially zero maintenance once established in appropriate soil and will not tolerate standing water or clay soil.

plant_note: Root pad cuttings in spring in full sun in fast-draining, sandy or rocky, lean soil in zone 5–11; Engelmann's Prickly Pear is a large, native prickly pear cactus of the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts of the southwestern US and northern Mexico — one of the most widespread and ecologically important cacti in Texas — producing abundant waxy yellow flowers in spring followed by deep purple-red edible tunas (fruits) in summer, with edible green pads (nopales) harvested year-round.
directions: Root Engelmann's Prickly Pear pad cuttings by allowing the cut surface to callus for 1–2 weeks before placing upright in dry, sandy soil; water sparingly; once established, this cactus thrives on neglect and natural rainfall in zone 5–11. Opuntia engelmannii is the quintessential Texas prickly pear — a large, sprawling native cactus forming dense clumps to 3–6 feet tall with round to oval, blue-green pads armed with clusters of stiff white to yellow spines. In spring the cheerful, waxy yellow flowers (2–3 inches across) open in profusion, attracting native bees and providing critical early-season pollen; by midsummer the flowers give way to deep reddish-purple tunas (prickly pear fruits) 1.5–2.5 inches long and sweet-tart with a distinctive watermelon-like flavor. Both the fruits and the young, spine-free green pads (nopales) are important traditional foods throughout Texas, Mexico, and the Southwest: fruits are eaten fresh, made into juices, jellies, syrups, and candy; nopales are sliced and grilled, sautéed with eggs (nopalitos), or pickled. Handle pads and fruits with tongs — both the large spines and tiny hair-like glochids cause intense skin irritation. Exceptional drought tolerance, native wildlife value, and dual culinary uses make this a natural choice for xeriscape gardens in zone 7–11.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring or fall in well-drained soil; seeds require a complex double dormancy (18+ months of stratification) and are best started from nursery stock. Named cultivars like 'Paul's Scarlet' and 'Crimson Cloud' are propagated by grafting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; English hawthorn is the traditional hedgerow hawthorn of Britain and Europe, historically used to create stockproof field boundaries and now cultivated primarily for its spectacular late-spring flower display. The popular double-flowered cultivar 'Paul's Scarlet' (Crimson Cloud in North America) produces vivid deep pink to red double flowers that smother the thorny branches before the leaves fully emerge. The small red fruits (haws) ripen in fall and are consumed by thrushes, waxwings, and numerous other birds. The thorny dense habit makes it one of the most effective wildlife-friendly hedging plants for gardens. More susceptible to leaf blight diseases than native American hawthorns in humid summer climates.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring; in mild-winter zones fall planting works well.
directions: English walnuts are monoecious — male (catkins) and female flowers occur on the same tree — and most cultivars are partially self-fertile, though a second tree improves yields. The tree produces juglone, a chemical that inhibits growth of many plants beneath its canopy; avoid planting near vegetables, berries, or sensitive ornamentals. Grafted Carpathian-strain trees are more cold-hardy and begin fruiting in 4–7 years; seedling trees may take 10+ years. Harvest in fall when hulls begin to crack and turn dark; remove husks promptly and cure nuts for 2–3 weeks before storing.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Enterprise ripens in October, later than most main-season apples, and its disease-resistant genetics mean it needs little or no fungicide spraying in most home gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding program and released in the early 1990s, Enterprise is immune to apple scab and resists fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it a strong choice for low-spray or organic orchards. The medium-large, dark red fruit is crisp, firm, and sweet-tart with flavor that holds up well and even improves somewhat in storage. It ripens late in the season and keeps for several months under cool conditions.

common_name: Esopus Spitzenburg Apple (Thomas Jefferson's Favorite Rich-Flavored Heirloom Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Esopus Spitzenburg is a light, somewhat biennial bearer and benefits from thinning and a vigorous rootstock to encourage more consistent annual crops.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating in Esopus, New York in the 1700s, this heirloom became famous as the reported favorite eating apple of Thomas Jefferson, who planted it at Monticello. The bright red-orange fruit, dotted with pale russet, has firm, yellow, intensely rich and spicy-sweet flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all apples, though the tree can be a shy, uneven bearer compared to modern commercial varieties. It ripens in mid-to-late fall and keeps reasonably well in cold storage, developing more complexity over several weeks.

plant_note: Plant grafted or rooted-cutting trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; etrog citron is among the most cold-sensitive of all citrus and requires a frost-free microclimate in zone 9b or container culture that can be moved indoors in zone 9a and below.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in the warmest available microclimate; Etrog citron (Citrus medica 'Etrog', also spelled 'Esrog') is the specific cultivar of citron used for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles), where it serves as one of the Four Species (arba minim) central to the religious observance — a use with over 2,000 years of continuous documented history, making it one of the oldest cultivated citrus varieties still grown for a specific purpose. The fruits are very large (4–8 inches long), yellow, highly aromatic, with a very thick, white-fleshed rind and very little juice; the entire fruit, including the extraordinarily thick, sweet, resinous peel, is the primary edible product, commonly candied, used in liqueurs and confections, or made into jam. The strongly ribbed, warty, irregular shape and intense, complex citrus-resin fragrance make etrog citron immediately distinctive. Ritual-quality etrogs (used for Sukkot) must meet specific halachic requirements — fully yellow, unblemished, with the pitam (style/stigma) intact at the blossom end — and command very high prices. Etrog trees are quite ornamental, with large leaves and dramatic fruit, but are tender and need winter protection in most of zone 9.

common_name: Eureka Lemon (Standard Lemon Tree, Four-Season Lemon)
plant_note: Plant container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Eureka lemon is among the most cold-sensitive of commonly grown citrus — protect from temperatures below 28°F, which can cause significant damage to the tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Eureka is the standard lemon cultivar in American commercial production and one of the most widely grown home-orchard lemons in zone 9–11 — a vigorous, nearly thornless tree that is truly everbearing, producing lemons year-round with peak crops in winter and spring. The classic medium-to-large, yellow lemons have thin, smooth skin, high juice content, classic lemon acidity, and excellent fragrance — the gold standard of lemon flavor for culinary use. The everbearing production habit means there is nearly always some fruit on the tree in zone 9, even if the heaviest crops come in winter and early spring. The tree reaches 8–15 feet with glossy, aromatic leaves and fragrant white flowers that bloom repeatedly throughout the year. Eureka is slightly more cold-sensitive than Lisbon lemon and significantly more cold-sensitive than mandarins or kumquats; temperatures below 28°F for more than 4 hours can cause fruit and leaf damage. In cooler parts of zone 9, Lisbon lemon (more cold-tolerant) or Meyer lemon (much more cold-tolerant) may be better choices. Fertilize with a citrus-specific balanced fertilizer three times annually; iron and zinc deficiencies are common in alkaline soils and should be corrected with chelated micronutrient sprays.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eureka is astringent until fully soft-ripe, so let fruit color deep orange-red and soften completely on the tree or after picking before eating.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Eureka is a long-established Southern astringent persimmon valued for its reliable heavy production and good cold tolerance compared to many Asian cultivars. The medium, flattened, deep orange-red fruit must fully soften after ripening before eating, since the tannins in unripe flesh are strongly puckering, but once jelly-soft it turns richly sweet and custardy, excellent fresh or baked into puddings and breads. Trees are self-fruitful, precocious, and tend to bear reliably once established, with fruit typically ripening from October into November after color develops fully.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; European hazel is wind-pollinated and requires at least two genetically different plants (or two named cultivars) for reliable nut production — one plant alone may produce few or no nuts.
directions: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; European hazel is wind-pollinated and requires at least two genetically different plants (or two named cultivars) for reliable nut production — one plant alone may produce few or no nuts. Corylus avellana is the hazel of European woodlands and hedgerows, grown for millennia for its nutritious hazelnuts (cobnuts and filberts in commerce); flexible, coppiced stems have been used for furniture, wattling, and charcoal production since prehistoric times; and the soft, round catkins that dangle from every bare stem in February and March are one of the earliest and most important pollen sources of spring for emerging native bees, including queen bumblebees and early Andrena mining bees. The large, rounded leaves turn golden-yellow in fall; the twisted cultivar 'Contorta' (Harry Lauder's Walking Stick) is a popular ornamental selection. Plant two different cultivars for best nut yield.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Eustis is the original and most widely grown limequat, a cross of Key lime and kumquat developed in Florida in 1909, combining true lime flavor with cold hardiness well beyond that of any true lime.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a lime-flavored citrus, tolerating temperatures that would kill true Key lime and Persian lime trees outright. Eustis limequat was developed in Eustis, Florida, in 1909 by USDA citrus breeder Walter Swingle as a cross between Key lime and kumquat, aiming to combine the tart, aromatic lime flavor with the cold hardiness of kumquat, one of the toughest edible citrus species. The resulting small, oval, yellow-gold fruit has a genuinely lime-like tart flavor along with an edible, sweet-tart rind in the kumquat tradition, making the whole fruit usable — sliced fresh, juiced, or preserved in marmalade — without peeling. The compact tree bears prolifically and tolerates cold that would damage or kill a true lime, making it one of the few practical ways to grow lime-flavored citrus in the cooler parts of zone 8-9 outside the true lime-growing range. Protect young trees through their first few winters; mature wood handles cold considerably better. Harvest fruit once it colors up gold, and use promptly, as limequats do not store as long as some other citrus.
