plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Eversweet is a unique pomegranate variety with clear, non-staining juice — unlike all other common pomegranates whose deep red juice stains hands and clothing permanently, Eversweet has very soft pink arils that produce a light pink juice that does not permanently stain — a practical advantage for families with children or for fresh eating over white fabric or clothing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Eversweet is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant once established, requiring little irrigation in most Gulf Coast settings after the first year; harvest when fruits are fully colored (rosy-orange to red skin) and sound hollow when tapped; fruits are sweet enough to be eaten with minimal mess. Eversweet is a distinctive pomegranate variety unlike any other in its combination of extreme sweetness, very soft (almost absent) seeds, and clear non-staining juice. Most pomegranates have deep red to crimson arils producing intensely colored red juice — the juice stains are notorious and pomegranate processing indoors is typically done over the kitchen sink with care to avoid contact with clothing. Eversweet breaks this rule: the arils are a soft rose-pink rather than deep red, and the juice they produce is clear to very light pink rather than the deep crimson of standard pomegranates, and crucially, it does not stain permanently. This characteristic makes Eversweet a more family-friendly choice for fresh eating, especially with children, and allows pomegranate eating and juicing without the usual mess concerns. The flavor is very sweet with low acidity — milder and less complex than Parfianka or Wonderful, but consistently rated among the sweetest pomegranates available. The seeds are extremely soft and virtually undetectable when eating the arils fresh. The exterior of the fruit is more orange-pink than red, making it visually distinct from other varieties at harvest.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cutting transplants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Excel figs begin producing in their second year and become increasingly productive as trees establish. In zone 9 figs typically produce two crops: a small breba (early) crop on the previous season's wood in June–July, and the main crop on new wood in August–October. Excel is well-adapted to the Gulf South climate and produces good crops even in partial shade. Prune lightly in late winter to shape the tree and remove dead wood; heavy pruning reduces fruit production.
directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage; Excel is an LSU (Louisiana State University) AgCenter-developed fig cultivar released specifically for Gulf South production, selected for its large, distinctively yellow-skinned fruit with rich amber flesh and the high resistance to fruit souring that is a serious problem for figs in the humid Gulf Coast climate. While traditional Southern figs like Celeste and Brown Turkey are prone to splitting and souring in rainy, humid conditions at harvest time, Excel was specifically bred for improved resistance to these problems — producing firmer skin that resists splitting and reduces the entry of yeasts that cause souring. The large, sweet fruits have an extremely rich, complex, honey-fig flavor that is the archetypal fresh fig experience — one of the most sophisticated and complex flavors of any temperate fruit. Figs are the quintessential Gulf South home fruit tree: tolerant of heat, humidity, and occasional drought once established, self-fruitful (no cross-pollination required), highly productive, and producing fruit of exceptional quality that cannot be found in stores (fresh figs ship and store very poorly, making the homegrown experience irreplaceable).

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Excel is a Type I pollinator (sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) and needs a Type II cultivar such as Elliott or Desirable nearby for cross-pollination and full nut set.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Excel is a modern Louisiana-bred pecan cultivar selected for strong resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum), the humid-climate fungal disease that plagues many older commercial cultivars along the Gulf Coast, reducing or eliminating the need for fungicide sprays in home plantings. It produces large, well-filled nuts with good kernel quality and ripens relatively early, helping it escape late-season disease and weather pressure. Because of its disease tolerance, Excel is increasingly recommended for Gulf South home orchards where spray programs are impractical. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and watch for zinc deficiency on alkaline soils, correcting with a foliar zinc spray in spring.

plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Fairchild tangerine requires cross-pollination from a compatible citrus variety (such as Dancy tangerine, Orlando tangelo, or other mandarins) for adequate fruit set — plant a pollinizer within 50 feet.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fairchild tangerine is a Clementine x Orlando tangelo hybrid developed by USDA breeders in 1964, producing deep reddish-orange, medium-sized (2.5–3 inch) fruits with rich, sweet-tart, spicy-aromatic tangerine flavor — one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available. The skin is thin, slightly rough, and adheres somewhat to the flesh (tighter than most loose-skinned mandarins but peels relatively easily by hand); fruits typically contain 6–12 seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor. Fairchild is one of the earlier-ripening mandarins in the California/Gulf South season, ripening November through December, and is an excellent choice for gardeners who want full-size mandarin flavor earlier in the season than the late-ripening Honey or Murcott types. The tree is medium-sized (8–14 feet), well-branched, and productive under good conditions with a cross-pollinator present. Trees in zone 9 should be sited in the warmest available microclimate as Fairchild is somewhat cold-sensitive; it tolerates brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established but young trees need frost protection in the first 2–3 years.

common_name: Fantasia Nectarine (Large-Fruited California Standard Nectarine, Freestone Commercial Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile soil in full sun; Fantasia requires approximately 400–500 chill hours and is self-fertile; best adapted to the warm interior valleys of California, the Pacific Northwest, and zones 6–9 where summer heat ripens fruit fully; in the humid Southeast, standard fungicide spray programs for brown rot are required as nectarines' smooth skin (unlike peach fuzz) allows brown rot spores to penetrate more readily.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Fantasia is self-fertile; thin to 5–6 inches in spring for maximum fruit size; Fantasia ripens mid-to-late season (late July to mid-August in California) producing very large, red to yellow-red blushed freestone nectarines with firm, yellow flesh and excellent sweet-tart flavor; outstanding for fresh eating and fruit stands. Fantasia nectarine is one of the most widely planted mid-season nectarine varieties for commercial and home production in California and the warmer western states, developed by Zaiger Genetics and released in the 1970s as part of the wave of nectarine variety improvement that transformed nectarine from a specialty fruit to a mainstream commercial crop in California's San Joaquin Valley. The variety's primary attributes — very large fruit size (among the largest freestone nectarines available), excellent red skin color with bright yellow background, firm flesh for shipping and handling, and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor — made it ideal for the fresh market where visual appeal and size command premium prices. Fantasia consistently produces one of the largest individual fruits of any nectarine variety, with well-colored red-over-yellow skin that is visually very attractive, and the freestone flesh separates cleanly from the pit at full maturity — a practical advantage for home eating and cooking. The variety's moderate chill requirement (400–500 hours) makes it reliable in zone 7–9 climates beyond California, including the Pacific Northwest and some parts of the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; feijoa is one of the hardiest subtropical fruit plants, tolerating temperatures to about 12–15°F when established, making it viable in zones 8–11 and an outstanding dual-purpose ornamental and fruiting shrub for Gulf Coast and Southeast gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; established feijoas tolerate drought but produce better fruit with regular moisture during flowering and fruit development. Acca sellowiana (feijoa or pineapple guava) is a South American evergreen shrub native to southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and northern Argentina, producing exceptionally ornamental flowers in May — petals of white and crimson with red stamens that are edible and sweet, often harvested from the ground — and unique oval fruits in fall that have an intensely aromatic, tropical, pineapple-guava flavor unlike any other temperate-climate fruit. The silvery-green leaves with white undersides are attractive year-round; the plant is exceptionally cold-hardy for a subtropical fruiting plant, tolerating 12–15°F and making it viable throughout the Gulf Coast, the Southeast, and mild West Coast gardens. Most selections require two plants for cross-pollination, though self-fertile cultivars like 'Coolidge' and 'Pineapple Gem' are available.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root figs after the last frost date when soil has warmed; in mild climates, fall planting works well.
directions: Common figs (the type grown in most gardens) are parthenocarpic and self-fertile — no pollinator or fig wasp is needed. In zones 6–7 protect the trunk and lower branches over winter by wrapping with burlap or mounding mulch; established roots often resprout even after top-kill. Figs bear two crops on some cultivars: a small breba crop on old wood in early summer and a main crop on new growth in late summer. Harvest when the neck droops, the skin splits slightly, and the fruit is soft and fragrant; a drop of syrup at the eye signals perfect ripeness.

plant_note: Plant after frost danger; grow in a pot to overwinter indoors in cold zones.
directions: Fignomenal is a true dwarf fig reaching only 2 to 3 feet, making it ideal for containers and small patios while still producing full-sized sweet fruit. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently, easing off as fruit ripens to concentrate flavor. Its compact size makes it easy to move indoors to a cool bright space for winter in colder regions. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove weak wood. Feed during the growing season for steady production of its self-fertile crop.

plant_note: Plant bare-root stock in early spring while dormant, or container-grown plants any time in the growing season; plant at least two different varieties or seedlings for cross-pollination, as filberts are largely self-infertile.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, spacing at least 10–15 feet from other plants to allow for the naturally wide-spreading form; filbert (Corylus maxima) is the large-fruited European hazelnut, distinguished from Corylus avellana by its longer tubular husk that completely encloses the nut, and is the parent of many named cultivars including 'Butler', 'Ennis', and 'Tonda di Giffoni'. A multi-stemmed deciduous shrub that bears pollen-heavy catkins in late winter while fully dormant — one of the earliest signs of spring — with small red pistillate flowers that require wind cross-pollination from a second genetically distinct plant to set nuts. Harvest when husks begin to brown and nuts release easily; dry in a single layer before storage to prevent mold.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; finger lime tolerates brief frosts to about 22–25°F once established.
directions: Finger lime is an Australian rainforest citrus producing cylindrical finger-length fruits filled with spherical pulp vesicles that burst on the palate like caviar — highly prized in fine dining as a garnish. Grafted trees are strongly preferred over seedlings, which are slow to fruit and thorny; grafted plants begin fruiting in 2–3 years and are more manageable in size. The tree is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator; it performs well in containers and espalier forms. Fruit ripens in late autumn through winter; harvest when the skin (green, yellow, red, or black depending on variety) is fully colored and the fruit releases easily with gentle pressure — avoid overripening, as the vesicles lose their pop.

plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Fire Cherry is a fast-growing pioneer species that thrives in disturbed, open, forest-gap conditions; it grows too fast to compete well in established forest understory. Seeds require 90–150 days of cold stratification before spring germination.
directions: Fire Cherry — also called Pin Cherry — is a fast-growing native pioneer tree of disturbed forest openings, clear-cuts, burned areas, and roadsides across the northern United States and Canada, where it is usually the first woody species to colonize forest gaps and recently disturbed sites, earning the name 'fire cherry' for its rapid colonization of burned forest. The clusters of bright red, pea-sized cherries ripen in summer and are among the most important late-season wildlife fruits in northern forest ecosystems, heavily consumed by American robins, cedar waxwings, grosbeaks, ruffed grouse, bears, and deer during the late summer fattening period before winter. Short-lived by nature — typically 15–30 years in the wild — Fire Cherry grows extremely fast for a native cherry, reaching 20 feet in just a few years and serving as a pioneer nurse species that modifies the site for longer-lived forest trees to follow. Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Fire Cherry thrives in open, disturbed conditions and makes an excellent fast-growing wildlife planting for northern gardens, fields, and woodland restoration projects.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Flame is a seedless red grapefruit selected in the Texas Rio Grande Valley and ripens over a long winter window, developing its deepest red flesh color with cool nights.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected and released by Texas A&M's citrus breeding program in 1987 from the Rio Red lineage, Flame produces medium-large, seedless fruit with intensely red-pigmented flesh and a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. It is one of the reddest-fleshed grapefruit cultivars commercially grown and holds its color reliably even in warmer winters that can wash out the blush in older red grapefruit types. Fruit matures from late fall through winter and holds well on the tree, allowing a long, flexible harvest window.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun.
directions: Flame Red Seedless is a vigorous grape producing sweet, juicy, ruby-red seedless berries in large clusters. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis or arbor to support the heavy vining growth. Train a permanent trunk and cordons the first years, then prune hard every dormant season to a few productive spurs or canes, as grapes fruit on the current year's growth. Water steadily while fruit swells but reduce moisture as harvest approaches for sweeter grapes. Good air circulation helps prevent mildew.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; Flanders is notably more cold-hardy than most fig cultivars, tolerating winter dieback and regrowing reliably from the crown even after a hard freeze, making it a good choice at the cooler edge of fig-growing range.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the more cold-hardy fig cultivars available, reliably resprouting from the roots after winters that kill back the top growth of less hardy varieties. Flanders is an old Belgian fig cultivar long grown in home gardens and small orchards for its dependable production of medium, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber flesh and good flavor, and for its resilience in marginal fig-growing climates where winter cold is a limiting factor. It typically produces a modest breba (early summer) crop followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and the fruit holds reasonably well against splitting in humid weather. Its cold tolerance makes it a valuable choice for gardeners at the northern edge of the fig range, or in a Gulf South garden where an occasional hard freeze is a risk, zone 6–10.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container specimens in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; flatwoods plum grows naturally in the sandy, acidic, dry soils of pine flatwoods and woodland edges throughout the Gulf Coast and adapts well to similar garden conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to loamy, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — flatwoods plum is a spectacular native small tree of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf Coast pine flatwoods, producing masses of pure white five-petaled flowers on bare branches in February–March, among the earliest and most profuse of all native spring-blooming trees and a critical early nectar source for native bees before other flowers open. The small round fruits (3/4 inch) ripen in July to purple-black with a blue bloom; they are tart to sweet depending on the tree, used for preserves, jellies, wine, and as wildlife food for deer, foxes, and dozens of bird species. An excellent candidate for wildlife food plots and naturalistic plantings in the pine flatwoods region. Many individual trees have superior fruit; select superior-fruiting trees to propagate for orchard use. Drought tolerant once established in adapted sandy soils.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring in full sun.
directions: Flavortop is a fast-growing nectarine producing large, juicy, well-balanced freestone fruit that ripens in mid to late summer. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, avoiding low frost pockets that harm early bloom. It is self-fruitful, so one tree will bear without a partner. Prune yearly in late winter to an open-center form for light and airflow, and thin developing fruit to boost size and prevent limb breakage. Provide steady water while fruit develops, and manage peach leaf curl with dormant sprays if needed.

common_name: Flordaglo Nectarine (University of Florida Very Low-Chill Yellow Nectarine for Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Flordaglo requires only 150–200 chilling hours — among the absolute lowest chill requirements of any nectarine variety, making it one of the only nectarines reliably producible in zone 9b-10 where mild winters rarely accumulate the 500–700 hours needed by standard nectarines. In zone 9 on the Gulf Coast, Flordaglo ripens in late May to early June — very early for a nectarine. The tree is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator, though yield may improve with nearby compatible stone fruit. As with all nectarines in humid climates, bacterial spot and brown rot can be significant; preventive copper and fungicide sprays during bloom and leaf-out help maintain plant health and fruit quality in the Gulf South's humid conditions.
directions: Plant bare-root tree in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart. Harvest when fully yellow-orange and gives slightly to pressure. Flordaglo Nectarine was released by the University of Florida IFAS as part of the same low-chill stone fruit breeding program that produced Flordaking, Flordaprince, and other Gulf South-adapted peach and nectarine varieties. Nectarines (smooth-skinned peaches, genetically a single-gene variant of the standard fuzzy peach) are typically even more demanding in their chill hour requirements than their peach counterparts, making the development of a reliable very low-chill nectarine a significant achievement. With approximately 150–200 chilling hours required, Flordaglo can be grown in most of Florida and the Gulf Coast — conditions under which virtually all standard nectarine varieties fail to bloom and set properly. The fruit is medium-sized, with a yellow-red skin and yellow freestone flesh — the smooth nectarine skin distinguishing it visually from the closely related fuzzy peaches. The flavor is typically sweeter and slightly more aromatic than many standard low-chill peaches, with the characteristic nectarine quality that growers in cool climates take for granted but that gardeners in zone 9 rarely get to experience from home-grown fruit. For zone 9 home orchardists who want to grow nectarines — generally considered nearly impossible in the Gulf South — Flordaglo is one of the very few varieties with a realistic chance of success.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; Flordahome requires only 150–200 chill hours and is the best pear choice for zone 9b–10 and the warmest portions of zone 9a where other pear varieties fail to produce consistently.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Flordahome is a University of Florida-developed pear cultivar requiring only 150–200 chill hours — the lowest chill requirement of any commonly available pear cultivar, making it the primary choice for zone 9b, zone 10, and any warm-winter location where standard pear varieties (which require 600–1000+ chill hours) consistently fail to bloom and fruit adequately. Flordahome produces medium-sized, yellow-green, round fruits with mild, sweet flesh that ripens in early summer — often in June in zone 9 — earlier than most other pear varieties. The fruit quality is pleasant but not as buttery or complex as high-chill European pears; it is best enjoyed fresh at peak ripeness or processed into preserves and sauces. Plant with Hood or Orient pear for cross-pollination — Flordahome is not self-fertile and requires a pollinizer. Fire blight resistance is moderate; preventive copper sprays at bloom reduce fire blight incidence in humid Gulf South climates. Flordahome trees grow vigorously in zone 9 and may need pruning to maintain manageable size — prune annually during dormancy to develop and maintain an open-center structure.

common_name: Flordaking Peach (University of Florida Low-Chill Early Freestone Peach for Zone 9)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Flordaking requires only 250–350 chilling hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the lowest-chill peach varieties adaptable to zone 9 conditions where winters are mild. In zone 9 (Gulf Coast region), the standard 400–500 chill hours required by most standard peach varieties are often not accumulated, leading to poor bloom and production; Flordaking's low chill requirement allows reliable production in zone 9. The fruit ripens in May–June — relatively early in the peach season — before summer heat becomes intense. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; peach trees are susceptible to root rot in poorly drained soils. Flordaking is self-fertile and does not require a cross-pollinator, though cross-pollination with another early-blooming peach may increase fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; prune to an open-vase shape in year 1. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches between fruits when marble-sized. Flordaking Peach was released by the University of Florida Tropical Research and Education Center (then Florida Agricultural Experiment Station) in 1957 as one of the pioneering low-chill peach varieties specifically bred for Florida and Gulf Coast conditions. The development of low-chill peach varieties began in earnest at the University of Florida under the leadership of George Lyrene and others who recognized that the warm-winter climate of Florida and the Gulf Coast made it impossible to grow standard peach varieties requiring 600–800+ chilling hours. Flordaking became one of the landmark early low-chill releases: a freestone variety (the pit separates easily from the flesh at full ripeness) with medium-large fruit, yellow skin blushed with red, and yellow flesh of good eating quality for a low-chill variety. The variety's reputation for reliability in low-chill conditions — producing consistent crops when other peach varieties bloom prematurely or fail to set properly in zone 9's mild winters — established Flordaking as a foundation variety in Gulf Coast peach production, and it remains planted and recommended decades after its introduction. For zone 9 gardeners, Flordaking represents one of the most accessible routes to growing tree-ripe peaches at home in a climate where most stone fruits are impractical.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in January–February in zone 9, containerized trees through early spring; Flordaprince requires only 150–200 chill hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the very few peach varieties that fruits reliably in zone 9a–9b and coastal zone 8. Requires a cross-pollinator or self-fruitfulness depends on climate — plant with Tropic Beauty for best yields.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–6.5) in full sun; Flordaprince is a very-low-chill peach released by the University of Florida's fruit breeding program in 1982, bred specifically for the Gulf Coast and central Florida where most standard peach varieties fail to fruit because winters are too mild to accumulate sufficient chill hours. With only 150–200 chill hours required, Flordaprince blooms and sets fruit consistently across zone 9. The fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, semi-freestone, with a pleasant mild peach flavor ripening in mid-April to early May — remarkably early compared to northern varieties. Trees grow vigorously and require annual pruning to an open-center form to maintain size and fruit quality. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart in April for large fruit size. Protect blooms from late cold snaps in zone 8b; blooms appear in January–February and can be damaged by freezes below 28°F. Fire blight can be a problem — remove affected wood promptly.

common_name: Florida Beauty Strawberry (Day-Neutral Gulf Coast Strawberry)
plant_note: Transplant plugs or bare-root plants in fall (October–November in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile, sandy loam in full sun; Florida Beauty is a day-neutral variety developed for Gulf South production — it does not require the long cold periods needed by June-bearing northern varieties.
directions: Transplant plugs or bare-root plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, sandy loam in full sun; Florida Beauty is a University of Florida IFAS strawberry introduction developed specifically for Gulf Coast production — a day-neutral cultivar adapted to the warm winters and mild springs of zone 8–10 where standard June-bearing northern varieties (Chandler, Camarosa) perform unreliably in recent warmer winters. Day-neutral strawberries are not dependent on day length for flower initiation — they flower and fruit based on temperature rather than photoperiod, making them more reliably productive across a range of winter weather patterns in the Gulf South. Florida Beauty produces attractive, large (medium-to-large), bright red, excellent-flavored fruits with firm texture and good fresh-eating quality. In zone 9, transplant in October–November for a production window from January through April — the peak of Gulf South strawberry season when temperatures are ideal for fruit development and quality. The plants are treated as annuals in commercial production (removed after the spring harvest) but can be maintained as short-lived perennials in home garden beds. Florida Beauty represents the most recent generation of Gulf South strawberry breeding that addresses the challenges of warm-winter climate change on traditional day-length-sensitive cultivar performance.

common_name: Florida King Peach (Large Low-Chill Yellow Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun; Florida King requires approximately 450–500 chill hours (hours below 45°F) for adequate dormancy break — it is suited for zone 8–9a where chill hours are sufficient but temperatures are mild enough for low-chill fruit production.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Florida King is one of the premier low-chill peach cultivars for the Gulf South — a large-fruited, yellow-fleshed, freestone peach that produces high-quality fruit with approximately 450–500 chill hours of cold requirement, making it adapted to the winter climate of zone 8–9a where higher-chill northern peach varieties fail to break dormancy properly. The large fruits (2.5–3 inches diameter) have golden-yellow skin with an attractive red blush, yellow-orange flesh, small pit (freestone type), and excellent sweet peach flavor. Florida King ripens in May in zone 9 — one of the earliest major peach harvests, ahead of the intense summer heat that can reduce quality in later-ripening cultivars. Like all peaches, Florida King must be thinned aggressively after set: thin to one fruit every 6–8 inches on each branch to allow the remaining fruits to develop to full size — unthinned trees produce large numbers of small, inferior fruits. Prune annually in late winter (February in zone 9) to maintain tree size at 10–12 feet, promote new wood development on which next season's crop will form, and open the canopy to air circulation that reduces disease pressure. Peach leaf curl and brown rot are the primary disease challenges in the humid Gulf South — preventive dormant sprays with copper fungicide are standard practice.

common_name: Florida Prince Peach (Low-Chill Gulf South Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in January–February in zone 9 in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), deep, fertile soil in full sun; Florida Prince is a true low-chill peach requiring only 150 chill hours, making it appropriate for the warmest parts of zone 9 and zone 10 where standard peaches fail.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), deep, fertile soil in full sun; Florida Prince is the standard low-chill peach cultivar for Gulf Coast zone 9–10 production — requiring only approximately 150 chill hours (hours below 45°F), compared to 800–1000 hours required by standard northern peach cultivars. This dramatically low chill requirement allows reliable peach production in coastal Louisiana, southern Texas, central Florida, and other warm winter areas where standard peach cultivars receive inadequate chilling to bloom and set fruit properly. Florida Prince produces medium-sized, round, yellow-fleshed, semi-freestone to clingstone fruit with a red blush on the sunny side — quality is good for fresh eating and suitable for canning and preserves, though not equal to the finest high-chill peach cultivars in flavor complexity. Fruit ripens in late April through May in zone 9 — very early in the season — which helps avoid much of the summer disease pressure that affects later cultivars. The tree is vigorous, productive, and well-adapted to the clay and sandy loam soils of the Gulf Coastal Plain. Thin fruit heavily (6–8 inches between remaining fruits) after natural June drop to develop full-sized fruits. Annual pruning to maintain an open-vase form is essential for air circulation and disease management in humid Gulf Coast conditions.

plant_note: Plant seeds in spring after removing the fleshy seed coat in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or well-drained soil in full sun; Florida soapberry grows naturally in upland sandy forests and sandhills of the Florida Peninsula and is adapted to poor, sandy, well-drained soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Florida soapberry is a native tree of the Florida Peninsula, growing naturally in upland sandy forests, sandhills, and dry flatwoods. Like its relative western soapberry (S. drummondii), it produces fleshy, translucent, amber fruits high in saponins that lather in water and have been used as natural soap. The pinnately compound leaves turn yellow in fall. Florida soapberry tends to be smaller and more restricted in distribution than western soapberry, naturally adapted to the sandy, acid, well-drained soils of Florida's uplands rather than the calcareous plains soils of the central US. The fruits are eaten by mockingbirds and robins. An underused drought-tolerant native for sandy, dry garden conditions in Florida and adjacent Gulf States where its multiple seasons of interest — spring flowers, fall color, and persistent amber fruits — make it a useful ornamental native.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida strangler fig is native to subtropical hammocks and rockland habitats of south Florida and the Florida Keys. It typically starts as an epiphyte but can also be planted as a free-standing tree from container stock.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Florida strangler fig is the only native fig species of the continental United States (excluding Hawaii), naturally occurring in the subtropical hammocks and rockland of south Florida and the Keys. In nature it begins as an epiphyte — a seed dropped by a bird into a tree crotch germinates and sends aerial roots down to the soil that eventually engulf and 'strangle' the host tree. As a free-standing garden tree it simply grows as a magnificent, large-canopy evergreen. The small yellow-orange figs are eaten by an extraordinary variety of wildlife — dozens of bird species, Florida panthers, and raccoons — making the strangler fig one of the most ecologically productive trees in south Florida. The dense canopy provides important nesting habitat for raptors. A keystone species of the south Florida hammock ecosystem.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late autumn or plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; flowering quince is extremely adaptable, tolerating clay, sandy, poor, and alkaline soils once established. It blooms on old wood — prune only immediately after flowering, never in late summer or fall, or next year's flowers will be removed.
directions: Plant in any well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; flowering quince is one of the earliest-blooming ornamental shrubs of the temperate garden — producing brilliant flowers in red, scarlet, orange, salmon, pink, or white directly on the bare, thorny stems in late winter and very early spring (February–March in the mid-South), often through snow. The dense, interlocking thorny growth makes it an impenetrable barrier hedge as well as an ornamental specimen. After the flowers, the shrub produces hard, green to yellow-green quincelike fruits 2–3 inches across that are not particularly palatable raw but make excellent jelly, preserves, and liqueurs — a quality long exploited in Japanese and Chinese cuisine. The fruits are high in pectin, which makes them particularly valuable for preserving, and have an intense quince fragrance when ripe. Extremely cold-hardy, drought-tolerant once established, and adaptable to a wide range of soils. The many named cultivars span the full color range from pure white ('Jet Trail') to deepest blood-red ('Crimson and Gold').

plant_note: Plant in spring; a dwarf, contorted form of the hardy orange.
directions: Flying Dragon is a dwarf, contorted selection of trifoliate orange with curved thorns and twisting stems, valued both ornamentally and as a size-controlling rootstock. It bears the same small, aromatic fruit and shares the species' extreme cold hardiness. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, where its sculptural winter silhouette is a feature. Prune minimally to preserve the natural twisting form, and use the tart autumn fruit for preserves.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant (January-February in zone 9); Forkert is a Type II pollinator and needs a Type I cultivar such as Excel or Cape Fear nearby for reliable cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil (pH 6.0-7.0) in full sun; Forkert is a classic Mississippi pecan cultivar valued for its thin, papery shell that cracks out easily in large, whole kernel halves, along with rich flavor and good kernel percentage. It bears precociously and produces consistent crops in the Gulf South, though like many older cultivars it benefits from a fungicide program in wet years to manage pecan scab. Forkert is commonly recommended alongside scab-resistant cultivars in home orchard plantings to diversify harvest timing and pollination. Space trees widely, since mature pecans become very large shade trees, and correct zinc deficiency with a foliar zinc spray each spring on alkaline soils.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full to partial sun; provide a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence from the start, as fox grape is a vigorous vine that can reach 30 feet and requires strong support to realize its full fruit production potential.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full to partial sun; provide a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence from the start, as fox grape is a vigorous vine that can reach 30 feet and requires strong support to realize its full fruit production potential. Vitis labrusca is the native northeastern grape species that gave rise to the Concord, Catawba, and Niagara cultivated varieties; it produces large, round, purple to amber grape clusters with the characteristic musky, distinctly "foxy" flavor in September and October, beloved by wildlife and humans alike. The dense summer canopy provides excellent nesting habitat and cover for songbirds, and the ripe fruit draws foxes, raccoons, deer, turkeys, and a wide array of frugivorous birds including mockingbirds, catbirds, and thrushes.

common_name: Franquette Walnut (Late-Leafing French Walnut, Frost-Safe Walnut, Isère Valley Walnut)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained loam; Franquette is late-leafing (3–4 weeks later than Chandler), which substantially reduces the risk of late spring frost damage to developing catkins and leaves — a significant practical advantage in climates with variable spring frosts; it requires cross-pollination from Chandler, Hartley, or another compatible variety for best nut set; requires approximately 700 chill hours.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile loam in full sun; Franquette requires cross-pollination; the late leafing habit means the catkins emerge significantly later than standard varieties — reducing spring frost damage that can eliminate the entire nut crop in frost-prone sites; Franquette ripens late (October–November), producing medium to large nuts with moderately thin shells and good flavor. Franquette walnut is a French variety with origins in the Isère department of southeastern France, where it was grown as a commercial production variety long before California walnut production began, and was one of the first named walnut varieties introduced to the Pacific Coast of North America in the 1870s and 1880s when California's walnut industry was developing. The variety's most important attribute is its late-leafing phenology — Franquette emerges from dormancy 3–4 weeks later in spring than most other walnut varieties, including Chandler, Hartley, and Serr. This late emergence is critically important in frost-prone regions: walnut catkins (male flowers) and developing leaves are extremely frost-sensitive, and an unexpected late spring frost at the critical bloom period can eliminate the entire nut crop for the season — a problem that Franquette largely avoids due to its delayed bud break. This characteristic made Franquette the variety of choice for sites at higher elevations, more northerly latitudes, or valleys prone to late spring frosts where earlier varieties fail too frequently. Franquette also serves as an important cross-pollinator for Chandler and other protogynous varieties in commercial orchards.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or potted tree; plant after frost.
directions: Frantoio is a renowned Italian olive prized for producing high-quality oil and rich, dark fruit that ripens mid-season. This evergreen brings old-world Mediterranean character to the garden and tolerates heat and drought once established. Grow a young tree in full sun with lean, well-drained soil, watering sparingly since olives dislike wet roots. Prune to an open framework for light and air, and in marginal climates grow it in a container to shelter from hard freezes.

common_name: Friar Plum (Dark-Skinned California Japanese Plum with Mild Sweet Amber Flesh)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Friar requires a cross-pollinator for good fruit set — plant with Santa Rosa, Burgundy, Methley, or another compatible Japanese plum within 50 feet. Requires approximately 400–500 chilling hours, placing it on the upper end of what zone 9 reliably provides in most years; it performs most consistently in zone 8 and cooler zone 9 locations with 500+ chill hours most winters. In the Gulf South, Friar ripens July — one of the latest Japanese plum varieties to mature, following the earlier summer plums by several weeks and extending the fresh plum season. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage. Friar Plum is widely available in California-adapted nursery stock and from mail-order nurseries serving the southeastern US.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit to 4–5 inches. Harvest when skin is fully dark purple-black and fruit gives slightly under firm pressure. Friar Plum is a California-developed Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) released by the University of California Cooperative Extension in the 1960s as part of a systematic program of plum variety evaluation and selection for California commercial production — a program that produced several varieties (Santa Rosa, Friar, Laroda, Casselman) that became mainstays of California plum production and eventually found their way into home garden cultivation throughout the United States. Friar is distinguished by its very dark, near-black skin — the dark purple-black coloring that covers the entire fruit surface at maturity — contrasting with the amber-yellow flesh beneath, which creates a dramatic visual contrast when the fruit is cut. The skin color of Friar is among the darkest of any common Japanese plum variety. The flesh is firm, sweet, and mildly flavored with moderate acidity — less acid than Santa Rosa — creating a mild, sweet eating character that appeals to consumers who prefer less tangy plum flavor. The fruit is large (often 2–2.5 inches), globe-shaped, and produced in good quantity on a moderately vigorous tree. Friar's late ripening (July in California, slightly earlier in the humid South due to the longer season) helps extend the Japanese plum harvest season beyond the earlier-ripening varieties, providing fresh market plums during a period when earlier types have finished. In zone 9, Friar benefits from the long growing season but requires adequate chill to set reliably.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring in full sun.
directions: Frost is a hardy peach bred for cooler climates, offering sweet, juicy fruit and notable resistance to peach leaf curl. Plant it in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, and it tolerates spring frosts better than many varieties. It is self-fruitful, producing a crop from a single tree. Prune annually in late winter to an open-center shape and thin the young fruit to improve size. Water deeply during fruit development for the best harvest.

common_name: Fuerte Avocado (Former Commercial Standard Avocado, Type B Large Green Avocado)
plant_note: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring after all frost danger; Fuerte is a Type B avocado (flowers open female in the afternoon, male the following morning) and produces best when planted with a Type A companion — Hass or Mexicola are ideal Type A companions for Fuerte; requires excellent drainage and does not tolerate wet feet; zones 9–11 (damaged below 26–28°F); in zone 9a, plant in a frost-protected microclimate near a south-facing wall or structure.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Fuerte performs best with a Type A companion (Hass, Mexicola) for maximum fruit set; mulch heavily over roots; apply balanced citrus/avocado fertilizer in spring; Fuerte ripens from November through March in California, producing large, pear-shaped, dark green fruits that remain green (do not darken) when ripe — test ripeness by cutting, as the skin color is not a reliable indicator. Fuerte avocado was the dominant commercial avocado variety in California and globally from the 1920s through the 1950s, named for the Spanish word 'strong' after the tree demonstrated remarkable cold-hardiness during a destructive California frost in 1913, surviving when other avocado varieties died — leading to its commercial selection and widespread planting. For three decades, Fuerte was the avocado that most Americans encountered in markets, setting the standard for avocado flavor and quality. It was gradually displaced by Hass after Hass's commercial introduction, primarily because Hass's pebbled skin turns black when ripe (providing a reliable harvest indicator that Fuerte's green skin lacks) and Hass handles shipping better. The Fuerte fruit itself is large, pear-shaped with smooth, thin, bright green skin and rich, creamy, pale green flesh with a moderately nutty, rich flavor — many avocado connoisseurs consider its flavor superior to Hass, with a richer oil content and more complex character, though the harvest timing challenge (no color change at ripeness) makes it less practical for commercial sales. A winter-ripening variety (November–March in California), it extends fresh avocado season when Hass is between crops.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; in zone 9 plant December–February. Fuji requires 300–500 chill hours (hours below 45°F) to break dormancy and fruit reliably — borderline for zone 9a (Houston receives approximately 300–400 chill hours annually). Plant in the most elevated, coldest microclimate available. Fuji requires a cross-pollinator (Gala, Granny Smith, or any other non-Fuji apple) planted within 50 feet for adequate fruit set.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic soil in the best-drained location available; Fuji was developed in Japan in the 1930s and released in 1962 as a cross between Red Delicious and Ralls Janet — it has become one of the most popular apple varieties in the world and is now the leading apple in Japan, China, and a major variety in American specialty markets. The large, firm, round fruits with distinctive pink-red and yellow-green streaked skin contain exceptionally crisp, dense, very sweet flesh with a high sugar content (typically 15–18 brix) and mild, pleasant apple flavor that has made Fuji the preferred apple for fresh eating in Asian markets and increasingly in mainstream American grocery stores. The flavor is distinctly sweeter than Gala or Honeycrisp with low acidity. In zone 9 Fuji is a marginal but feasible apple choice in areas that receive adequate winter chilling — inland areas and northern parts of zone 9 typically accumulate more chill hours than coastal areas. Low-chill Fuji selections ('Fuji Babe', 'Low-Chill Fuji') have been developed for warmer climates.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring in full sun.
directions: Fuji is a Japanese-bred apple beloved for its exceptionally sweet flavor and crisp, dense texture that stores well. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil, and provide a compatible pollinating apple nearby since Fuji is not self-fertile. Prune each dormant season to a central-leader or open form for light and air, and thin fruit clusters to improve size. Water consistently during establishment and dry spells. Fuji ripens late in the season, so allow ample time on the tree for full sweetness.

plant_note: Plant after frost danger; grow in a container to move indoors in cold climates.
directions: Fukushu is a compact kumquat producing small oval citrus with an edible sweet rind and tart flesh, well suited to container growing. Grow it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil and water when the top inch dries, avoiding both drought stress and soggy roots. In climates with frost, keep it potted so it can move to a bright indoor spot for winter. Feed regularly with a citrus fertilizer during active growth. It is self-fertile, so a single tree will set fruit.

common_name: Fuyu Persimmon (Non-Astringent Flat Asian Persimmon for Gulf Coast)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun; Fuyu is non-astringent — unlike Hachiya and most native persimmons, Fuyu can be eaten firm like an apple without puckering astringency, making it the most practical fresh-eating persimmon for home gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Fuyu is the most popular non-astringent Asian persimmon for home garden production — producing flat, tomato-shaped, medium-large (4–6 oz), deep-orange fruits that can be eaten while still firm, like an apple, without the intense mouth-puckering astringency that makes other persimmons (including Hachiya) inedible until fully soft. The flat shape, firm texture when ripe, sweet flavor, and brilliant orange color make Fuyu the most practical and versatile fresh-eating persimmon. Fuyu ripens in October–November in zone 9, producing fruit after the summer growing season has ended and providing sweet, colorful fresh fruit at a time when few other locally grown fruits are available. The attractive deciduous tree puts on a spectacular fall display of orange to red fall foliage as the persimmons ripen — a visual combination that is outstanding in the autumn landscape. Fuyu is self-fruitful (does not require a pollinator tree) and produces reliable annual crops on mature trees with minimal pest and disease pressure. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and require minimal fertilizer input — excessive nitrogen encourages vegetative growth at the expense of fruit production. Japanese persimmons (D. kaki) require approximately 100–200 chill hours — readily accumulated in Gulf South winters — making Fuyu well-adapted to zone 9 production.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun with well-drained soil.
directions: Fuyu is a non-astringent persimmon whose sweet, firm fruit can be eaten crisp like an apple while still firm. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fruitful and needs no pollinator. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit develops, then it tolerates some drought. Prune in dormancy to build a strong framework, since heavy fruit can break branches. The fruit ripens in fall and holds on the tree well after the leaves drop, creating an ornamental display.

plant_note: Plant tuber divisions or started plants after last frost; provide a strong trellis — vines reach 30 feet.
directions: Gac is a vigorous, tuberous-rooted perennial vine in the cucumber family that regrows each year from a starchy tuber in zones 9–11 and can be grown as an annual elsewhere; it requires a sturdy trellis or fence. Plants are dioecious, so grow at least one male and several female plants together; bees transfer pollen between the separate male and female flowers. The football-sized, brilliant orange-red fruit is among the richest known sources of lycopene and beta-carotene; the red aril surrounding the seeds is the edible portion, traditionally mixed into Vietnamese sticky rice (xôi gấc). Harvest when the skin is fully orange-red and the surface texture softens from spiny to smooth; fruit is mature approximately 4–5 months after planting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; in zone 8–9 plant December–February. Gala requires 500–600 chill hours (hours below 45°F) to break dormancy — viable in zone 8 and in colder parts of zone 9 that accumulate adequate chilling. Plant with a compatible cross-pollinator (Fuji, Honeycrisp, Granny Smith) within 50 feet for good fruit set. Gala is among the earlier-ripening apple varieties (August in zone 8–9), well ahead of the fall apple season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — apples require excellent drainage and are not adapted to clay-heavy sites; Gala is a New Zealand-developed apple variety (Golden Delicious x Kidds Orange Red) released in 1934 that has become one of the top-selling apple varieties in the world and the most planted apple in the United States as of the 2010s. The medium-sized, striped red-and-gold fruits have a distinctive mild, sweet, honey-like flavor with very low acidity that makes them exceptionally popular for fresh eating across all age groups — the approachable, sweet flavor profile has made Gala the preferred apple in school lunch programs, grocery stores, and fresh snacking applications. The crisp, fine-grained texture holds up well for several weeks in refrigerator storage. Numerous Gala strains and sports ('Royal Gala', 'Regal Prince', 'Galaxy') offer improved color or earlier ripening but share the same flavor profile. The early-to-mid season ripening (August in warm climates) makes Gala one of the first fresh apples available each year.

plant_note: Plant while dormant in early spring in full sun.
directions: Gala is a widely grown apple with a sweet, mild flavor and firm, crisp flesh that suits fresh eating and cooking alike. Plant it in full sun in well-drained soil and include a compatible pollinating apple nearby, as Gala benefits from cross-pollination. Prune every dormant season for structure and light, and thin fruit clusters to improve size and prevent limb breakage. Water steadily during establishment and dry periods. Gala ripens in late summer to early fall, earlier than many other apples.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; Galip Nut (Canarium Nut, Pili relative, Nuss) is a large evergreen timber and nut tree of the Burseraceae family native to the humid lowland forests of Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, and adjacent Melanesia — the most economically important indigenous nut tree of Papua New Guinea — producing clusters of dark purple, olive-like drupes enclosing hard-shelled nuts with rich, sweet, high-fat kernels eaten fresh, roasted, and processed for cooking oil.
directions: Plant Galip Nut in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in zone 10–12; water regularly during establishment; large trees are fairly drought-tolerant when established; harvest nut clusters when the outer drupes turn dark purple-black. Canarium indicum produces clusters of dark purple, almond-sized drupes resembling large olives, each enclosing a very hard, triangular-ridged shell containing a single cream-colored kernel of exceptional quality. The kernels are rich (approximately 70% fat) with a sweet, mild, buttery flavor reminiscent of a combination of almonds and macadamia nuts — widely considered among the finest edible nuts of the Pacific region. They are eaten fresh directly from the shell, roasted over fire, and processed into oil for cooking and for use in traditional body oil preparations. Galip nuts are the single most important indigenous tree nut of Papua New Guinea, traded widely in coastal markets, and of growing international interest as a specialty nut crop. The large trees (reaching 60–80 feet in their native forest habitat) are also highly valued for their straight-grained, durable timber. Closely related to the Pili Nut (Canarium ovatum) of the Philippines, which is also commercially grown; both species deserve wider cultivation in tropical Pacific and Caribbean gardens.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; gambooge (Malabar tamarind) is a South Indian and Sri Lankan tropical tree producing pumpkin-ribbed, sour, yellow-orange fruits whose dried rind is an essential souring agent in Kerala and Konkani coastal cooking — and the source of hydroxycitric acid (HCA), the controversial supplement compound marketed for weight loss.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; plant multiple trees for cross-pollination as the species is polygamous. Garcinia cambogia (gambooge or Malabar tamarind) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Malabar Coast of India and Sri Lanka, producing small (2–3 inch), distinctively pumpkin-ribbed, yellow-orange, extremely sour fruits. The fresh fruit pulp is too acidic to eat raw, but the dried rind (kokum or kodampuli, depending on region) is an essential souring agent in Kerala, Konkani, and Sri Lankan coastal cooking — adding a fruity-tart, slightly sweet tartness to fish curries, sambars, and the famous Goan sol kadhi coconut drink. The dried rind is also used in Sri Lankan fish preparations and as a food preservative in traditional coastal cuisine. The fruit rind gained enormous international attention in the 1990s–2010s as a weight-loss supplement ingredient: it is the primary natural source of hydroxycitric acid (HCA), which was heavily marketed as a fat-burning compound — though clinical evidence for significant weight loss has been mixed. The tree is also the source of gamboge resin (from incisions in the bark), a yellow pigment historically used as a watercolor pigment. The tree needs multiple trees for fruiting as it is polygamous (different trees have different flower types).

plant_note: Plant container stock or fresh seed in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; gandaria is a Thai and Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree in the mango family (Anacardiaceae) that produces oval, mango-scented fruits ranging from tart-green to sweet-golden at full ripeness — eaten fresh, in Thai somtam salads, and as a souring agent in curries.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; gandaria prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Bouea macrophylla (gandaria or Marian plum) is a Thai, Malay, and Indonesian tropical fruit tree in the mango family (Anacardiaceae) — closely related to mango (Mangifera) and producing small (1–1.5 inch), oval, egg-shaped fruits with a thin, smooth skin progressing from bright green through yellow-orange to golden when fully ripe, surrounding a large seed. The fruit's flavor profile is remarkably mango-like — fragrant, sweet-tart, resinous — but in miniature form; the flesh is juicy, fibrous, and intensely aromatic. Unripe fruits are highly acidic (like green mango) and are used as a souring agent in Thai and Malay curries, fish dishes, and the Thai-Malay salad-style dish 'rujak.' Ripe fruits are sweet enough to eat fresh. The tree is dense, compact compared to true mango, with large, glossy, dark-green leaves and clusters of small cream flowers. Gandaria is extremely popular in rural and home gardens of Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand but is almost completely unknown in Western horticulture. For tropical zone 11–12 gardeners seeking unusual, genuine Southeast Asian fruits.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter; Garber requires 150–200 chill hours and is partially self-fertile but crops better with LeConte, Orient, or Kieffer nearby for cross-pollination. Ripens August–September in zone 9 — a mid-season Southern pear.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Garber is an old American hybrid pear selected around 1880 in Florida and one of the most fire-blight resistant pear varieties known — it is sometimes used as a rootstock for other pears specifically for its superior adaptability to Southern soils and resistance to the fire blight (Erwinia amylovora) that devastates European pear varieties in humid climates. The large, roundish-pear-shaped fruits are yellow to golden at maturity with crisp, gritty, mildly sweet flesh good for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. Garber ripens mid-season (August–September) and is widely planted in the Gulf South as a dual-purpose tree: ornamental landscape specimen with beautiful spring bloom and reliable production under low-spray conditions that would be impossible for Bartlett or d'Anjou. Long-lived, vigorous trees are productive for decades in zone 7–9. Harvest when fruit begins to soften at the blossom end; Garber pears ripen better when picked slightly underripe and allowed to ripen at room temperature.

plant_note: Plant the dormant tree in early spring after the ground is workable; a self-fertile genetic dwarf, it fruits in a container or small bed.
directions: This genetic dwarf peach tops out around 4-6 feet, making it ideal for large containers or tight yards while still yielding full-size, sweet yellow freestone fruit. Site it in full sun with well-drained soil and give it consistent moisture through the growing season. Thin the young fruit to about 6 inches apart so remaining peaches size up well. Prune lightly in late winter to keep an open, vase-shaped canopy, and expect a harvest beginning two to three years after planting.

common_name: Gefner Atemoya (Nearly Self-Fruitful Popular Home Garden Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant grafted container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; atemoya generally needs hand pollination for reliable fruit set in US gardens, since its natural beetle pollinators are absent.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Gefner is the most widely planted atemoya cultivar for home gardens, valued for setting a reasonable crop with less hand pollination effort than most other cultivars, since it is considered nearly self-fruitful under good conditions, though hand pollination still improves fruit set and size. The rich, creamy white flesh has the classic atemoya flavor of custard, vanilla, and tropical fruit notes, and the tree bears at a relatively young age once grafted. Fruit ripens in fall and should be picked when it just begins to soften and change from green to a slightly yellow-green color, then allowed to finish ripening at room temperature indoors.

plant_note: Set out after all danger of frost; grow in a pot to overwinter indoors in cold climates.
directions: Introduced from Genoa, Italy, this productive lemon bears juicy, tangy fruit much like Eureka. Give it at least 8 hours of sun, fast-draining slightly acidic soil, and a dedicated citrus fertilizer during the growing season. In zones colder than 9 grow it in a container and move it indoors near a bright window before frost. Water deeply but let the top inch of soil dry between waterings to avoid root rot.

plant_note: Plant grafted bare-root or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Giant Fuyu is the largest-fruiting of the non-astringent Fuyu-type Japanese persimmons, producing fruits that can reach 1 pound each and are eaten crisp like apples when fully colored — no need to wait for softening.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; persimmons are drought-tolerant once established but benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development. Giant Fuyu is a large-fruited, non-astringent Japanese persimmon cultivar, an improved selection from the standard 'Fuyu' producing much larger fruits (often 8–16 oz per fruit, compared to 4–6 oz for standard Fuyu) while retaining the outstanding non-astringent quality of the Fuyu type — meaning the fruits can be eaten firm and crisp right off the tree when fully orange without any astringency, like eating a sweet, spiced apple. An excellent choice for Gulf Coast, California, and mild-climate gardens where it ripens in October–November; trees are self-fruitful, moderate in vigor, and begin producing in 3–5 years from grafted trees. The fruit has beautiful fall color and the bare orange fruits persisting on leafless branches in late fall are ornamentally striking.

plant_note: Plant only in frost-free gardens or large containers moved under cover in winter; requires a very robust support structure — mature vines and their heavy fruits demand strong anchoring.
directions: Plant in deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun with an extremely sturdy support capable of handling 8-pound fruits; giant granadilla produces the world's largest passion fruits — 6 to 12 inches long and weighing up to 8 pounds — with whitish-yellow skin, a thick edible rind used as a vegetable, and seedy interior pulp that makes refreshing juice and drinks popular across tropical Latin America. The vine is extraordinarily vigorous, growing 30–50 feet annually, and requires rigorous pruning after harvest. Flowers measure 4–5 inches across with a remarkable corona of purple, white, and pink filaments. In Central America, the unripe fruit rind is cooked as a vegetable in soups and stews; the ripe pulp is eaten fresh or juiced.

common_name: Ginger Gold Apple (First-of-the-Season Crisp Yellow-Green Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Ginger Gold ripens in mid-to-late summer, well ahead of most other apples, so pick promptly since fruit can go soft quickly on the tree in warm weather.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator such as Gala or Fuji. Found as a chance seedling near a Golden Delicious orchard in Nelson County, Virginia after Hurricane Camille in 1969, the tree was named for the discoverer's wife, Ginger Harvey. It is prized as one of the very first apples ready to harvest each year, well before Gala, with crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh that resists browning after slicing. The pale yellow-green skin sometimes develops a light pink blush in full sun. Because the fruit softens quickly once ripe, it is best picked promptly and used within a few weeks rather than stored long term.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring; site male trees downwind of living areas to avoid the malodorous female fruit.
directions: Ginkgo is dioecious — only female trees produce the edible nut, but a male is needed nearby for pollination; purchase named female cultivars (Tit, Megi, Oishi) or graft known female wood to avoid planting only males, which cannot be sexed until first flower at 20+ years. The outer fleshy seed coat (sarcotesta) smells powerfully of rancid butter when ripe and contains urushiol-related compounds — wear gloves when handling and process outdoors; the inner cream-colored nut inside the hard shell is the edible portion. Harvest when the fleshy coating has turned yellow-orange and fallen from the tree in autumn; clean immediately, dry the shells, and roast or steam before eating. Do not eat ginkgo nuts raw or in excessive quantities — they contain 4-O-methylpyridoxine, which is toxic in large amounts.

common_name: Gold Kist Apricot (Low-Chill Southern Apricot, Gulf South Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Gold Kist has one of the lowest chill requirements of any named apricot (approximately 300 hours below 45°F), making it the standard recommended apricot for the mild-winter Gulf South, central Texas, the San Joaquin Valley, and similar climates where higher-chill varieties like Moorpark and Harcot receive insufficient winter cold to bloom and fruit reliably; self-fertile.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Gold Kist is self-fertile and drought-tolerant once established; thin fruits to 3–4 inches after natural fruit drop; Gold Kist ripens early (May in the Gulf South and central Texas), one of the earliest-ripening apricots; harvest when fully orange and beginning to soften for best flavor. Gold Kist apricot was developed by Zaiger Genetics in California and released in the mid-1980s specifically to address the near-absence of suitable apricot varieties for mild-winter regions — the Gulf South, South Texas, the lower San Joaquin Valley, and other areas where winter temperatures rarely accumulate the 700+ chill hours required by standard apricot varieties. With a chill requirement of approximately 300 hours, Gold Kist dramatically expanded the geographic range of apricot production in the United States, particularly through the deep South and the Gulf Coast where no practical apricot had previously been available. The fruits are medium-sized, golden-orange to light orange at full ripeness, with good sweet-tart apricot flavor — somewhat milder than the finest California varieties like Blenheim but very acceptable for fresh eating and preserves. The early ripening season (May in zone 8–9) is an important characteristic: Gold Kist delivers fresh apricots weeks before any other stone fruit of comparable quality, giving it a clear market window at farmers' markets and roadside stands. It remains the primary recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Louisiana State University's AgCenter for home garden apricot production in the Gulf South.

common_name: Gold Nugget Loquat (Yellow-Fleshed Small-Seeded California Loquat)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; Gold Nugget is valued for its small to medium fruits with unusually small seeds and deep yellow flesh — a combination that maximizes the ratio of edible flesh to seed and produces a distinctive golden-yellow color and rich, sweet flavor at full maturity; excellent as a backyard tree in zones 8–10.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Gold Nugget produces abundant crops of small to medium golden fruits from February through April in California and similarly timed in the Gulf Coast; the small seed size is a significant advantage for fresh eating and processing; no thinning is generally necessary due to the naturally smaller fruit size. Gold Nugget is a California loquat selection noted primarily for two characteristics: the unusually small seeds relative to fruit size, and the deep golden-yellow to amber flesh color that gives the variety its name. While most loquat varieties have relatively large seeds that reduce the proportion of edible flesh in each fruit, Gold Nugget produces a seed that is noticeably smaller than average, leaving more of the interior as eating flesh — a practical advantage for fresh eating and for any processing application (jams, preserves, sauces). The flesh color is a rich golden-yellow rather than the white of Champagne or the orange of Premier and Big Jim, and the flavor is sweet, richly aromatic, and quite juicy at peak ripeness. The tree is moderately vigorous and productive, and the smaller fruit size (typically 1–1.5 inches) means higher fruit counts per cluster compared to large-fruited varieties. In the Gulf Coast zone 9a, Gold Nugget blooms in fall and ripens in late winter to spring alongside other loquat varieties. An excellent choice for gardeners who want to maximize edible yield and minimize the frustration of handling large seeds.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; GoldRush ripens very late and benefits from as much hang time as the season allows, developing its full rich, spicy-sweet flavor and honeyed texture only after several weeks in storage.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Released in 1994 from the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois breeding program, GoldRush carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with strong resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust, making it one of the most reliable choices for growers who want to avoid a heavy fungicide program. The yellow-green, russeted fruit is quite tart and firm at harvest in October but mellows over weeks of cold storage into a dense, complex, honey-sweet apple that keeps for months, rivaling many classic long-keeping heirlooms. Pick late and store cool for the best eating quality.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Goldcot blooms slightly later than many apricots, which helps its crop escape some late frosts that damage earlier-blooming cultivars in cold-winter regions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. Developed at Michigan State University for reliable cropping in colder apricot-growing regions where most cultivars bloom too early and lose their crop to frost, Goldcot combines good winter hardiness with a comparatively later bloom time that improves the odds of a successful harvest. The medium, deep orange, firm-fleshed fruit is sweet and well flavored, suitable for fresh eating, canning, and drying, and ripens in mid-summer. The tree is self-fruitful and productive, making it a dependable choice for northern home orchards that struggle with more tender apricot varieties.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown shrubs in moist to dry, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; golden currant is adaptable to a wide range of soils including clay and dry rocky soils, and tolerates partial shade well. It spreads by suckers to form colonies — remove unwanted suckers to contain its spread.
directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; golden currant is a broadly adaptable native shrub of western and central North America producing intensely fragrant yellow flowers in spring — fragrant with a spicy clove-like scent that carries in the air, giving rise to the alternate common name 'clove currant' — that are followed in summer by round currants ripening from red to black-purple, sweet-tart and edible fresh or made into jelly, jam, and wine. The spring floral fragrance is among the most remarkable of any native shrub, detectable at a distance on warm spring days. The attractive foliage turns red and orange in fall. Unlike European black currant (Ribes nigrum), golden currant has no unpleasant 'catty' flavor and produces a pleasant, gently flavored fruit. It is one of the most important nectar sources for early hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees in the western states. Drought-tolerant once established, adaptable to part shade, and much more garden-friendly than many currant species.

plant_note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; golden kiwi (A. chinensis) is a separate species from the fuzzy kiwifruit (A. deliciosa) — distinguished by its smooth golden-yellow skin, golden-yellow to bright-yellow flesh, and sweeter, less acidic flavor — the source of Zespri Gold and similar gold kiwifruit commercial varieties; requires 1 male plant per 6–8 female plants for pollination; plant 2 or more for fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; provide a very sturdy trellis or pergola — mature vines are extremely vigorous and heavy; one male plant pollinates up to 8 female plants. Actinidia chinensis (golden kiwi or yellow kiwifruit) is a separate species from the common fuzzy kiwifruit (A. deliciosa), native to the forests of central and eastern China — though the two species are closely related and sometimes hybridized commercially. The golden kiwi is distinguished from fuzzy kiwifruit by its smooth, thin, golden-yellow to bronze skin (no fuzzy brown hairs), golden-yellow to bright-orange-yellow flesh, and distinctly sweeter, tropical, less acidic flavor profile with notes of mango, papaya, and vanilla in addition to the classic kiwifruit taste. Golden kiwis are now among the most commercially valuable kiwifruit worldwide; the New Zealand-bred 'Zespri SunGold' variety (patented) dominates the premium market, but non-patented gold kiwi cultivars are available to home growers. Like fuzzy kiwifruit, A. chinensis is a vigorous deciduous vine requiring a substantial support structure, annual dormant pruning, and separate male and female plants (dioecious). It is somewhat less cold-hardy than A. deliciosa and requires mild winters without late spring frosts to protect the early-emerging shoots.

plant_note: Plant container stock or hardwood cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun; golden mombin is a fast-growing tropical tree well-suited to zone 10 and warm zone 9 coastal areas, producing abundant oblong golden-yellow fruits with a sweet-tart, mango-like flavor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; golden mombin is fast-growing and may produce fruit within 3–4 years from cuttings. Spondias dulcis (golden mombin, ambarella, or June plum) is a Polynesian and Melanesian tropical fruit tree — widely cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and tropical Americas — producing oblong, golden-yellow, 2-to-4-inch fruits that ripen to orange-yellow with a fibrous central pit and flesh with a flavor combining mango, pineapple, and tart apple. The fruits are eaten fresh when ripe, or green (unripe) as a crisp, tart, mango-like condiment in curries, chutneys, and salads across Southeast Asian cuisines — particularly popular in Vietnam and Cambodia where unripe ambarella is eaten with salt, chili, and sugar. The tree is fast-growing and highly productive once mature, often requiring thinning of the heavy crop to prevent limb breakage; it is semi-deciduous in seasonal climates.
