The leaves are also edible as a vegetable in some Pacific Island cuisines. In zone 9, grow as a container plant or in the most frost-protected locations, bringing indoors or covering when frost threatens.

common_name: Golden Nugget Loquat (Large-Fruited Sweet Named Loquat Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container trees in fall through spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Nugget is self-fruitful and does not require a second tree for fruit production — a significant practical advantage for small home gardens where space for two large trees may not be available.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Golden Nugget is one of the best-fruiting named loquat cultivars for Gulf South gardens — producing larger, sweeter, better-quality fruits than seedling loquats with the same outstanding adaptability to Gulf Coast conditions that makes loquat one of the most reliable subtropical fruit trees for zone 8b–9. The round to oval, deep golden-orange fruits are substantially larger than typical seedling loquat (1.5–2 inches diameter compared to 1–1.5 inches for seedlings) and have excellent sweet flavor with a mild, tropical quality. Loquats bloom in fall and winter (November–January in zone 9) and ripen fruit in early spring (February–March) — providing fresh tree fruit at a time when virtually no other locally grown fruit is available. The winter flowering is the primary limitation of loquat production in zone 9: the flowers and young fruit are frost-sensitive, and a hard freeze during the fruit development period can eliminate the entire crop. In years without hard freezes, Golden Nugget produces heavy crops of high-quality fruit. The evergreen tree is attractive year-round with large, bold, dark-green leaves and is suitable for use as a landscape tree as well as a fruit producer. Loquat tolerates a wide range of soils, partial shade when necessary, and is highly adapted to Gulf Coast humidity and heat.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; this compact columnar tree needs a second apple variety nearby for good pollination.
directions: This columnar Fruit Snacks apple grows tall and narrow, producing sweet snack-size fruit in as little as 2 feet of width, perfect for patios and small gardens. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and provide a compatible apple pollinator blooming at the same time. Water regularly the first two seasons while roots establish. Its naturally slim habit needs minimal pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood in late winter.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Goldfinger is a FHIA-bred hybrid known for disease resistance and acceptable cold hardiness, with rhizomes surviving light freezes in zone 9 and reliably resprouting in spring.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Goldfinger banana (FHIA-01) is a tetraploid hybrid developed by the Honduran Foundation for Agricultural Research (FHIA) in the 1980s, bred specifically for resistance to Black Sigatoka leaf disease, Fusarium wilt (Panama disease), and moko bacterial wilt — the three most destructive banana pathogens — making it a significant improvement over susceptible Cavendish varieties for home gardeners in humid subtropical climates. The fruit clusters are large, with medium-sized, slightly angular fruits ripening yellow that have sweet, full banana flavor with a hint of apple when fully ripe; texture is firmer than Cavendish and the fruits resist bruising and handle well. Goldfinger is productive (producing 40–70 pounds of fruit per pseudostem) and regrows quickly from the rhizome after freeze dieback in zone 8b–9, typically reaching fruiting size within 12–18 months of resprouting. An excellent choice for Gulf South food gardens where disease pressure is high and cold resilience is valued.

common_name: Goldmine Nectarine (White-Fleshed Sweet Nectarine, New Zealand White Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep fertile soil in full sun; Goldmine requires approximately 500 chill hours and is self-fertile; it is the most widely planted white-fleshed nectarine in home gardens in the western United States, prized for a sweeter, less acidic flavor profile than yellow-fleshed nectarines — white-fleshed stone fruits have lower acidity and higher sugar, giving them a distinctly floral, very sweet flavor character.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic fertile soil in full sun; Goldmine is self-fertile; thin to 5–6 inches; Goldmine ripens mid-season (late June to mid-July in California) producing medium-sized, reddish-white to pale red blushed nectarines with cream-white flesh and a very sweet, low-acid flavor with floral aromatic notes — quite different from yellow-fleshed varieties and appealing to those who find standard nectarines too tart. Goldmine nectarine is a New Zealand variety that became widely grown in California and Australia as the premier white-fleshed nectarine for home orchards — belonging to the white-fleshed stone fruit category that is vastly more popular in Asia (Japan, China, Korea) and is now gaining appreciation among Western fruit connoisseurs for its distinctly different flavor profile: lower acidity, higher sugar concentration, and floral aromatic notes that distinguish white nectarines from the familiar sweet-tart profile of yellow-fleshed varieties. White nectarines like Goldmine are at their best consumed very ripe — the flesh is tender and can bruise easily, making them poorly suited to commercial shipping but excellent for home-grown fresh consumption. At peak ripeness, Goldmine is exceptionally sweet and fragrant with honeyed floral notes, and the white flesh is tender, melting, and extraordinarily juicy — a texture and flavor profile that many white-flesh enthusiasts consider superior for fresh eating to even the best yellow nectarines. Best in zone 7–9 climates with warm, dry summers for ripening.

plant_note: Plant both male and female plants for reliable fruiting (plants are dioecious); some nurseries offer self-fertile selections that fruit without a pollinator.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average soil — tolerates drought, poor soils, and coastal conditions once established; governor's plum is a thorny tropical small tree or large shrub from Africa and Asia producing prolific clusters of small (1/2–1 inch) dark red to purple-black fruits with a flavor blending cherry and plum with pleasant tartness. One of the most reliable and productive tropical fruit plants for the subtropical home garden, fruiting heavily from a young age with minimal care beyond adequate drainage. The spiny branching habit makes it a formidable security hedge. Fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe, made into jams, jellies, and juices, or fermented into alcoholic beverages in East Africa.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average soil in zone 8–11; Governor's Plum is a thorny, fast-growing shrub or small tree native to tropical Africa and Asia producing small, round, deep-red to dark-purple berries with a sweet-astringent-plum flavor widely eaten across its range — a tough, drought-tolerant fruiting shrub adaptable to poor soils and also valued as an impenetrable, thorny security hedge.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to poor soil; Flacourtia indica is drought tolerant once established, adaptable to a wide range of soil types including lateritic and calcareous soils, and grows vigorously with minimal care — prune to shape after fruiting and to maintain desired height. Flacourtia indica (Governor's Plum, Ramontchi, or Madagascar Plum) is a thorny, fast-growing, many-branched shrub or small tree native to tropical and subtropical Africa and South Asia from Madagascar, the East African coast, and sub-Saharan Africa east through India, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia to the Philippines. The small (0.5–1 inch), round to slightly flattened fruits ripen from green through red to deep red-purple or nearly black, with tart-sweet, juicy, dark-red flesh eaten fresh, made into jams, jellies, syrups, and fermented into wine across its broad native range. The flesh is astringent when underripe but richly sweet-tart and plum-like when fully ripe. Governor's Plum is a tough, adaptable, undemanding fruiting plant tolerant of poor soils, drought, alkalinity, and partial neglect — an excellent productive hedgerow plant or edible security hedge plant for zone 8–11. The plants are dioecious (separate male and female trees required for fruit set). Naturalized and sometimes invasive in tropical regions outside its range.

plant_note: Plant tissue-culture plants or rhizome pups in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Gran Nain performs best in zone 9b and 10 where winters rarely damage the pseudostem. In zone 9a mulch heavily around the base in fall and provide frost protection for the pseudostem during hard freezes to preserve the harvest timeline.
directions: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained, moisture-retentive soil with abundant organic matter; Gran Nain is the world's most commercially important banana — the standard Cavendish-type export banana sold under the Chiquita and Dole brands. The medium to large, curved, smooth-skinned, sweet, mild-flavored fruits are the archetype of the supermarket banana and are grown on multi-stem mats that require minimal specialized knowledge. Gran Nain grows 8–12 feet tall — moderately tall for a Cavendish type — and produces large, heavy bunches of 7–9 hands when given full sun, abundant water, and high nitrogen and potassium fertilization throughout the growing season. In zone 9 the long, hot growing season produces excellent banana development; the main challenge is protecting pseudostems from the occasional hard freeze. Zone 9 gardeners who can grow Gran Nain successfully typically achieve production equivalent to small commercial planting density.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; provide a compatible apple variety nearby for cross-pollination.
directions: The iconic tart green Granny Smith is prized for baking and long storage as well as fresh eating. It needs a long, warm season to fully ripen and a second apple variety nearby for pollination. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and water consistently while the tree establishes. Prune in late winter to maintain an open canopy that ripens fruit evenly and improves air circulation.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk has passed; requires the longest, hottest growing season of any common citrus.
directions: Grapefruit is self-fertile and produces best in the warmest citrus climates — the prolonged heat of south Texas and southern California delivers better sugar development than coastal or inland zones 9. Trees are large and vigorous; allow 20–25 feet between them and avoid overcrowding with other trees. Ruby Red and Flame are popular pink-fleshed varieties with good cold tolerance for zone 9. Fruit takes 12–18 months from bloom to full ripeness; taste-test from late autumn onward — the peel may remain slightly greenish even when the juice is sweet.

plant_note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; the cultivar 'Winter King' is vastly superior to seed-grown trees for ornamental effect and berry production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; green hawthorn — especially the cultivar 'Winter King' — is one of the finest native small trees for four-season ornamental value and wildlife habitat. In spring the tree is covered with small white flowers that are excellent bee forage; in fall the foliage turns burgundy-orange; and in winter the persistent glossy orange-red berries shine against bare branches well into February, providing critical food for cedar waxwings, robins, and thrushes. The tree has a vase-shaped form with slightly pendulous branches and is relatively free of the fireblight and cedar-apple rust that plague many hawthorns. The thorns are formidable — plant away from walkways. Excellent as a wildlife garden specimen or fall/winter focal point.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Green Ischia is one of the oldest continuously grown fig varieties, documented in cultivation since at least the 16th century, producing small to medium, greenish-yellow fruits with sweet amber flesh that are exceptional for both fresh eating and drying.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average soil in full sun; Green Ischia is a common fig type (no pollinator required) and typically produces both a reliable breba crop and a main crop. Green Ischia (also called Ischia Verde or simply 'Ischia') is one of the oldest continuously documented fig cultivars in European cultivation, with recorded references going back to at least the 16th century — one of the ancient Italian figs associated with the island of Ischia in the Bay of Naples. The small to medium, round to pear-shaped fruits have greenish-yellow skin that turns to golden-yellow when fully ripe; the interior flesh is pale amber to strawberry-amber with excellent sweetness and mild, delicate fig flavor with a gentle honey note. A two-crop variety that typically produces a moderate breba crop in early summer and a more abundant main crop in August–September. The small tree size (usually 8–15 feet with mature girth) makes Green Ischia more manageable than large fig varieties and an excellent choice for container culture in zones north of 7 where frost protection is needed. Outstanding fresh and dried.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; green sapote takes 5–10 years from seed but grafted trees fruit faster. More cold-tolerant than mamey sapote (to about 28°F) and can survive in the warmest microclimates of zone 9.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 9–11; green sapote is a Central American relative of the mamey sapote, producing large, round fruits with an olive-green skin and a rich, caramel-flavored orange flesh that is eaten fresh, in milkshakes, and in ice cream. It is less commonly cultivated than mamey sapote but produces equally delicious fruit and is somewhat more cold-hardy — able to tolerate brief dips to 28°F with some defoliation but surviving in protected locations in zone 9b. The fruits ripen in winter, providing fresh tropical fruit at a time when most trees are bare. In zone 9a, plant against a south-facing wall or in the warmest microclimate available and protect from frost when young. Grafted trees from named selections begin fruiting in 3–5 years.

plant_note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break.
directions: Greengage is an old European dessert plum prized for its honeyed, amber-green fruit. Give it a warm, sheltered site with fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil to ripen its sugars fully. Many greengage selections benefit from a compatible European plum pollinator planted within about 50 feet. Prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit for best size and sweetness.

common_name: Grimes Golden Apple (West Virginia Heirloom Parent of Golden Delicious)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Grimes Golden is a reliable annual bearer and a useful pollinator for many other apple varieties.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Discovered as a chance seedling on Thomas Grimes' farm in Brooke County, West Virginia in the early 1800s, this heirloom is historically significant as the presumed parent of Golden Delicious, one of the most commercially important apples of the 20th century. The medium, deep yellow fruit has dense, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh with a wine-like richness that many old-apple enthusiasts consider superior to its more famous offspring. It ripens in early-to-mid fall and was historically valued both fresh and for cider, keeping reasonably well in a cool cellar.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade; grumichama tolerates brief temperatures to 28–30°F once established, making it suitable for zone 9b–12. The plant grows slowly but is long-lived and very ornamental.
directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to partial shade — grumichama is a beautiful small-to-medium Brazilian Eugenia producing glossy, deep burgundy-to-black cherries (3/4 inch) with sweet, soft, slightly acidic flesh and 1–3 seeds, eaten fresh, made into preserves, or used in beverages. The trees are ornamental year-round with attractive smooth, pinkish-brown peeling bark, handsome dark glossy leaves, and masses of white flowers before fruiting. Unlike many tropical fruits it tolerates partial shade and moist conditions and has some cold hardiness to about 28°F. The fruits are produced in late spring and are consumed enthusiastically by birds. Closely related to jaboticaba and surinam cherry, the grumichama is one of the finest but least known of the Brazilian Eugenia fruits, producing a fruit that resembles a cherry in size and sweetness.

common_name: Guabiyú (Uruguayan Guabiju, Black Cherry of the Forest)
plant_note: Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; guabiyú is a subtropical Myrtaceae from southern Brazil, Uruguay, and Argentina, tolerating light frosts and making it suitable for zone 9 in sheltered locations — one of the hardier South American Myrtaceae for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; guabiyú (Myrcianthes pungens) is a subtropical rainforest tree of southern South America producing small, round, deep purple to black berries in clusters, with a sweet, aromatic, cherry-like flavor and a pleasant Myrtaceae fragrance — consumed fresh, in jams, juices, and liqueurs throughout its native range. The tree is more cold-hardy than most Myrtaceae relatives, tolerating temperatures down to 25°F (-4°C) when established, making it potentially the most cold-tolerant South American Myrtaceae and an excellent candidate for zone 9 Gulf Coast fruit gardens. The attractive, reddish-barked tree also provides ornamental value year-round with glossy leaves. A growing interest among Gulf Coast gardeners and subtropical fruit collectors.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring; Guadalupe Palm is slow-growing and may take 5–10 years to develop a visible trunk from a container plant. It is more cold-hardy than most feather palms and more drought-tolerant than other Brahea species. Plant in a hot, sunny, extremely well-drained spot — it fails in wet clay soils.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained soil; Guadalupe Palm requires excellent drainage and is highly drought-tolerant once established — it will not tolerate poorly-drained or consistently moist soils. Brahea edulis is a single-trunk fan palm endemic to Guadalupe Island, a remote volcanic island 150 miles off the Baja California coast of Mexico, where it survived in harsh, wind-scoured, fog-desert conditions for millennia. In cultivation it has proven to be among the most drought-tolerant and cold-hardy fan palms available for zone 9 Gulf Coast and California gardens — surviving brief dips to 20°F and thriving in the extreme summer heat and drought of zone 9. The crown of large, fan-shaped, bright mid-green fronds has a full, lush appearance that contrasts beautifully with the more compact, gray-green look of Mexican Blue Palm (Brahea armata). Guadalupe Palm produces edible dates — round, black, cherry-sized fruits with sweet, date-like flesh that was an important food for the indigenous people of Guadalupe Island and is still eaten fresh or dried. The species is rare in its native habitat due to feral goat browsing and is considered vulnerable in the wild. In zone 9 landscapes, it is a prized specimen palm for dry gardens and xeriscape plantings.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost risk passes; in zone 9 protect young trees from frost their first two winters. Guava bears fruit year-round once established in frost-free conditions, typically 2–4 years from transplant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; guava tolerates a wide range of soil types including sand and clay but performs poorly with standing water. Young trees are frost-sensitive — provide frost cloth when temperatures threaten to drop below 28°F; mature trees can survive brief dips to 24°F but may lose production for a season. Prune after each fruiting flush to control size and encourage new wood, which bears the heaviest crop; a light annual fertilization with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer maintains vigor. Harvest fruit when the skin transitions from bright green to pale yellow-green and the aroma becomes noticeable — guavas ripen rapidly off the tree in 2–5 days.

common_name: Gulf Crimson Peach (UF IFAS Low-Chill Freestone Peach for the Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) while dormant; Gulf Crimson requires approximately 300–350 chilling hours (hours below 45°F), which is reliably met in zone 8–9 most winters. Bloom occurs January–February in zone 9 and late frost can damage blossoms — plant in areas with good cold-air drainage to minimize frost pocket risk. Gulf Crimson is a freestone peach with yellow flesh and red skin that ripens in late April through May in the Gulf South, making it one of the earliest-ripening peach options and providing fresh peaches 4–6 weeks before later-season varieties. Thin fruit to 4–6 inch spacing when walnut-sized for maximum fruit size.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; stake young trees and train to an open-center form. Thin fruit aggressively in the first weeks of fruit set for maximum size. Gulf Crimson is one of the University of Florida IFAS releases from the peach breeding program that has made commercial and home peach production possible throughout the Gulf South — a region where most standard peach varieties fail because they require 700–1,200 chilling hours that the mild Gulf South winters cannot provide. Gulf Crimson's low chill requirement (300–350 hours) means that even in the warmest parts of zone 8–9, the tree accumulates adequate winter dormancy to bloom and set fruit reliably each year. The fruit is medium to large-sized, with attractively red-blushed skin over a yellow-green ground color, and yellow flesh that is sweet, aromatic, and freestone — the pit separates cleanly from the flesh at ripeness. Gulf Crimson's early ripening (late April to May in zone 9) means the harvest precedes the peak summer heat that stresses trees and reduces fruit quality in later-season varieties. The University of Florida peach breeding program (which also produced Gulf Gold, Gulf King, and Gulfrose) developed Gulf Crimson specifically for the low-chill peach market across zone 7–9 of the Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coastal Plain.

common_name: Gulf Gold Peach (Low-Chill Early Yellow Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile loam in full sun; Gulf Gold requires only 150 chill hours and is one of the earliest-ripening, most reliably productive peaches for zone 8–9.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Gulf Gold is a low-chill peach cultivar developed by the University of Florida — requiring only 150 chill hours (hours below 45°F) to break dormancy reliably, making it one of the most dependable peach varieties for the Gulf Coast where chill hours are consistently limited. The fruit is medium-sized with yellow flesh, excellent eating quality, and very good flavor for a low-chill peach variety — ripening in late May to early June in zone 9, well ahead of standard-chill peaches that struggle to fruit in the Gulf South. Gulf Gold is a white-flowering, self-fertile peach that does not require a pollinizer, though planting two low-chill varieties together improves yield. Prune annually after harvest to maintain an open-center tree structure at 10–12 feet — reducing disease pressure and making fruit easier to harvest. Peach leaf curl, brown rot, and bacterial spot are the primary disease challenges in humid Gulf South climates; copper fungicide applied at dormant bud swell and follow-up fungicide applications through bloom are essential for reliable production. Thin fruit to 6 inches apart after natural fruit drop (June drop) for full-sized, high-quality peaches.

common_name: Gulfcrest Peach (University of Florida Release, 450-Chill Gulf South Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Gulfcrest requires approximately 450 chilling hours — more than the lowest-chill varieties but within reach of most zone 9 locations in north and central Louisiana, Mississippi, and East Texas that accumulate 400–600 hours most winters. In years with warm winters, production may be reduced or delayed; in years with adequate chill accumulation, Gulfcrest produces reliably. Ripens late June in zone 9. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage. Gulfcrest is self-fertile but may benefit from cross-pollination with other mid-season peach varieties. The variety has been grown in the Gulf South region for decades and remains recommended by Louisiana and Mississippi extension services as a reliable mid-chill variety for the region.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches. Harvest when skin is yellow with red blush and fruit gives slightly to firm pressure. Gulfcrest Peach was released by the University of Florida IFAS (then Florida Agricultural Experiment Station) in 1978 as part of a series of Gulf South-adapted peach releases that included Flordaking, Flordaprince, and other low-to-moderate chill varieties developed specifically for Florida and Gulf Coast conditions. The UF peach breeding program, which began producing named releases in the 1950s and accelerated in subsequent decades, addressed the fundamental challenge of growing peaches in warm-winter climates: standard commercial peach varieties requiring 700–900+ chilling hours bloom prematurely, fail to set adequate fruit, or produce poor-quality fruit in zone 8–9 where winter temperatures inconsistently meet chill requirements. Gulfcrest occupies a specific niche in the low-to-moderate chill continuum — with approximately 450 hours required, it demands more winter cold than very low-chill varieties like Flordaking (250–350 hours) but considerably less than standard northern varieties. This positions Gulfcrest as a practical option for the transition zone between the lowest-chill Gulf Coast locations and the higher-chill interior areas, providing good fruit quality in locations where the very lowest-chill varieties may over-bloom or produce poor quality in warmer-than-average years. The fruit has yellow skin with good red blush, yellow freestone flesh, and adequate flavor quality for fresh eating and preservation.

common_name: Gulfking Peach (Texas A&M Low-Chill Gulf Coast Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in January-February while dormant; Gulfking requires only about 400 chill hours, part of the Texas A&M 'Gulf' series bred for zone 8b-9 coastal Texas and Louisiana where winters are too mild for standard peach varieties. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; Gulfking is a freestone peach developed by Texas A&M AgriLife as part of its low-chill 'Gulf' series (alongside Gulfprince and Gulfcrest) bred specifically for the mild-winter Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast. With a chill requirement of roughly 400 hours, it sets a reliable crop in zone 8b-9 areas where standard peach varieties bloom erratically or fail from insufficient winter chilling. Fruit is medium-large, yellow-fleshed, and fully freestone with good classic peach flavor, ripening in late May to early June. Trees are vigorous and self-fertile. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart in April to size the crop properly, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop to maintain good light penetration and airflow in humid Gulf Coast conditions.

common_name: Gulfprince Peach (Texas A&M Low-Chill Gulf Coast Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in January-February while dormant; Gulfprince requires roughly 400 chill hours and ripens earlier than Gulfking, part of the Texas A&M 'Gulf' series bred for zone 8b-9 coastal Texas and Louisiana. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; Gulfprince is a freestone peach from the Texas A&M AgriLife low-chill 'Gulf' series, bred alongside Gulfking and Gulfcrest for the mild-winter Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast where standard peach varieties fail to accumulate enough winter chilling. It requires about 400 chill hours and ripens slightly earlier than Gulfking, giving Gulf Coast growers a way to extend the harvest window when the two are planted together. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good flavor for a low-chill selection, ripening in mid-to-late May. Trees are vigorous and self-fertile. Thin fruit to 6-8 inches apart in April, and prune to an open-center vase shape after leaf drop to maintain airflow and reduce brown rot pressure in humid conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh seeds in fall or cold-stratify 60–90 days; gum bumelia prefers well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline soil in full sun to light shade. A slow-growing, long-lived, tough native of dry, rocky, or sandy upland sites.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, slightly acidic to neutral or alkaline soil in full sun; gum bumelia is a thorny native small tree or large shrub of dry uplands, rocky hillsides, and dry woodlands across the south-central US from Kansas to Florida. The small, black, olive-like fruits are edible and mildly sweet — consumed by numerous birds including mockingbirds, thrushes, and cedar waxwings — making it an outstanding wildlife plant for dry, sunny, naturalistic landscapes. The thick, spiny branches provide secure nesting habitat for mockingbirds and other cavity-nesters and the dense crown offers excellent cover. The milky sap was historically chewed as gum by Indigenous peoples (hence 'gum elastic' and 'gum bumelia'). Extremely drought tolerant and long-lived. The thorny habit makes it effective as an impenetrable wildlife hedge or barrier plant.

plant_note: Plant in early spring or fall as bare-root or container stock; gumi establishes best in cool soil and is very adaptable to poor soils — its nitrogen-fixing root nodules allow it to thrive where most fruiting shrubs struggle. A single plant can self-fruit but cross-pollination with a second plant increases yields substantially.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil of any fertility — gumi fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root symbiosis with Frankia bacteria, improving the surrounding soil and feeding itself even in infertile, sandy, or rocky ground. The shrub produces silvery-speckled dark red to cherry-red fruits in early summer that are sweet-tart with a slight astringency that some compare to a tangy cherry; they are excellent eaten fresh, dried, or made into preserves and juice. The fragrant creamy-yellow flowers in spring attract pollinators. Unlike its invasive relative autumn olive (E. umbellata), gumi is a well-behaved garden shrub that doesn't spread aggressively. It makes an excellent companion plant in food forests and permaculture systems, enriching the soil for neighboring fruit trees and shrubs.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Hachiya must be completely soft and jelly-like before eating — firm Hachiya fruits contain high soluble tannins and are intensely astringent.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Hachiya is the classic large acorn-shaped astringent Japanese persimmon, with deeply orange 6–12 oz fruits harvested in late October and November that must fully soften (bleten) to jelly-like consistency before eating — frozen overnight or left on the counter for 1–3 weeks achieves this, producing a rich honeyed, spiced flavor. Excellent for making Japanese dried persimmon (hoshigaki), baked goods, puddings, and purées. Trees are remarkably drought-tolerant once established, require minimal spraying, and bear reliably in warm temperate to subtropical gardens — one of the most rewarding and lowest-maintenance fruit trees for zones 7–10.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring; one of the most adaptable native trees, tolerating compacted soil, air pollution, and urban conditions where other trees fail.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; hackberry is among the most adaptable native trees, thriving in urban heat, clay soils, drought, flooding, and alkaline conditions that defeat many other species. The small dark-purple berries that ripen in September–October have a sweet, date-like flavor and are edible directly from the tree; the thin skin is nutritious and the sweet pulp surrounds a hard seed. The berries are a critical fall food source for over 50 bird species, including cedar waxwings, robins, bluebirds, and many migrating warblers. The distinctive corky bark warty growths are a natural feature, not a disease. Excellent choice for difficult urban sites or as a wildlife anchor tree.

common_name: Hall's Hardy Almond (Cold-Hardy Almond, Northern Almond, Zones 5-8 Almond)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Hall's Hardy is believed to be a peach-almond hybrid with cold-hardiness to approximately -15°F or below — significantly more cold-hardy than standard California almonds; it is partially self-fruitful but benefits from cross-pollination with a companion tree; the late-blooming habit of Hall's Hardy (several weeks after pure almond varieties) significantly reduces the risk of spring frost blossom kill that devastates standard almonds in the Midwest and mid-Atlantic.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, deep soil in full sun on a protected slope or elevated site to reduce late spring frost damage to blossoms; Hall's Hardy blooms later than standard almonds, reducing but not eliminating frost risk to flowers; harvest nuts in September when hulls split; the small to medium kernels have a mild almond flavor but thicker shells than California varieties — crack-in-shell type. Hall's Hardy almond occupies a unique market niche as essentially the only widely available almond variety for cold-climate gardeners in zones 5–8 of the northeastern and Midwestern United States, where the low temperatures that standard California almonds cannot survive and the late spring frosts that kill the early-blooming California almond flowers make standard almond production impractical or impossible. Hall's Hardy is believed by many pomologists to be a hybrid between Prunus dulcis (almond) and Prunus persica (peach) rather than a pure almond — it demonstrates characteristics of both parents, including cold-hardiness exceeding pure almond by a substantial margin, later bloom time, and nuts with a thick shell and moderate almond flavor. These characteristics — while reducing the quality compared to premium California almonds — allow Hall's Hardy to produce viable almond-type nuts in zone 5–8 climates where no standard almond variety will survive reliably. The nuts are smaller and have a thicker shell than Nonpareil or Mission, with a mild but acceptable almond flavor that is usable for cooking, baking, and direct consumption. For cold-climate home orchardists interested in growing their own almonds, Hall's Hardy is essentially the only viable option.

common_name: Hamlin Orange (Early Cold-Hardy Sweet Orange, Standard Florida Juice Orange)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in early spring after cold risk has passed; Hamlin is one of the hardier sweet orange varieties, tolerating brief temperatures to 26–27°F when the tree is established and cold-hardened — making it one of the most cold-tolerant choices for the northern margins of zone 9. In zone 9 (Louisiana, Mississippi Gulf Coast, eastern Texas), plant in a sheltered, south-facing location for maximum cold protection. Hamlin oranges ripen October through December — earlier than most other sweet oranges — making them valuable as the first tree-ripe citrus of the season. Fruit should be left on the tree until color has fully developed; unlike many citrus, Hamlin does not improve significantly in storage and is best used for juice immediately after harvest.
directions: Plant grafted tree in full sun, well-drained soil; protect from frost in zone 9 when young. Fruit in October–December. Hamlin Orange is the most commercially important sweet orange in Florida — the variety that produces the majority of Florida's fresh-squeezed and not-from-concentrate orange juice, and the dominant early-season orange in Florida commercial groves. The variety was discovered as a chance seedling in Glenwood, Florida in 1879 by A.G. Hamlin, who recognized its value and began propagating it; the combination of very early ripening (October–December harvest, months ahead of navel oranges), excellent cold hardiness for a sweet orange, prolific bearing, and high-quality juice made Hamlin rapidly popular among Florida citrus growers. The fruit is medium-sized, round, smooth-skinned, thin-skinned, with pale orange-yellow to bright orange exterior. The flesh is tender, very juicy, with excellent sweet-acid balance and nearly seedless character (typically 1–3 seeds per fruit) — qualities that make Hamlin ideal for juicing, where seed count affects yield and flavor extraction. Hamlin's cold hardiness is one of its most significant practical attributes for zone 9 gardeners: it is more reliably cold-hardy than navel orange, Valencia, or most other sweet orange varieties, making it the recommended choice for zone 9a plantings where severe freezes are possible. Established trees in good health can survive temperatures to 26°F briefly without significant damage, though young trees and flowers are more sensitive.

common_name: Harcot Apricot (Canadian Disease-Resistant Apricot, Northeast-Adapted Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep fertile soil in full sun on a protected slope or elevated site to minimize spring frost risk; Harcot is self-fertile and requires no cross-pollinator; it requires approximately 800–900 chill hours and is one of the most cold-hardy named apricot varieties available, making it the premier recommendation for northeastern United States and Canadian gardens where standard California varieties lack sufficient winter hardiness or cold resistance in the buds.
directions: Plant on a north-facing slope, elevated ground, or north side of a windbreak to delay bloom and reduce late spring frost damage to blossoms; Harcot is self-fertile; thin fruits to 4–5 inches after natural drop; fruit ripens in July producing medium to large, firm, orange fruits with very good sweet-tart flavor and above-average resistance to brown rot — a critical advantage in humid northeastern climates. Harcot apricot was released by Agriculture Canada's Harrow Research Station in Ontario in 1977 as part of a breeding program aimed at developing apricot varieties with improved cold-hardiness and disease resistance for production in eastern Canada and the northeastern United States, where the combination of cold winters, late spring frosts, and humid summer conditions had historically made reliable apricot production difficult or impossible. Harcot achieved a combination of characteristics that made it the premier recommended apricot for the northeastern states and eastern Canada: significantly better cold-hardiness than California-bred varieties (surviving winters in zone 4), self-fertility requiring no companion tree, above-average resistance to the brown rot disease that devastates apricots in humid climates, and good fruit quality — medium to large fruits with firm, orange flesh, a pleasant sweet-tart balanced flavor, and good fresh-eating quality. University cooperative extension services throughout the northeastern states from New England through the Mid-Atlantic list Harcot as their primary or sole recommended apricot variety for home orchards in the region, reflecting its exceptional combination of hardiness, disease tolerance, and quality under northeastern conditions.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; this self-fertile variety needs no second tree to set fruit.
directions: Hardired is a cold-tolerant, self-fertile nectarine known for smooth-skinned, freestone fruit and good resistance to bacterial spot and brown rot. Plant in full sun with well-drained soil and thin the fruit to about 6 inches apart for larger nectarines. Prune each late winter to an open-center vase shape to maximize light and airflow. Consistent watering during fruit development keeps the flesh juicy and sweet.

common_name: Hardy Orange (Trifoliate Orange, Japanese Bitter Orange)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; trifoliate orange is the most cold-hardy citrus relative, surviving temperatures to -10°F when dormant — it is the primary rootstock for grafting other citrus species and an important cold-climate curiosity.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, moderately fertile soil in full sun; hardy orange is deciduous (unusual for citrus) and leafless in winter. Poncirus trifoliata (trifoliate orange or hardy orange) is the most cold-hardy member of the citrus family — a deciduous, thorny Chinese shrub or small tree that survives temperatures to -10°F when dormant, making it the only citrus relative that can be grown permanently outdoors through USDA zone 5. The small, 1.5-to-2-inch, round, yellow fruits resemble a tiny orange but are intensely bitter and unpleasant raw (high limonin content) — technically edible as marmalade or preserves if the bitterness is accounted for, but not for fresh eating. The plant's primary horticultural importance is as a dwarfing, cold-hardy rootstock for grafting edible citrus — trifoliate orange rootstock limits tree size, improves cold hardiness, and increases fruit quality in grafted sweet oranges, grapefruits, and mandarins. As an ornamental, it is a thorny barrier or specimen plant with fragrant white flowers in spring (before the leaves emerge), attractive yellow fall fruits, and interesting green-barked, zig-zag winter branch structure. A novel cold-climate citrus curiosity.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Harrow Sweet is a Canadian-bred European pear released by Agriculture Canada's Harrow Research Station with outstanding fire blight resistance and excellent sweet, buttery fruit — one of the most disease-resistant European pears available for humid climates.
directions: Plant two different pear varieties for cross-pollination; in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Harrow Sweet pear was released in 1964 by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Harrow Research Station in Ontario specifically for its outstanding fire blight resistance (a major disease problem for European pears in humid eastern climates) combined with excellent fruit quality; the medium-large, short-necked, golden-yellow fruits with some russeting ripen in September and have sweet, juicy, buttery flesh with exceptional flavor and keeping quality — storing for 2–3 months in refrigerated storage. Harrow Sweet was selected to fill the gap between early-ripening Bartlett (poor storage) and late-ripening D'Anjou/Bosc types; it is particularly valuable in humid southeastern climates where fire blight pressure makes most European pears unreliable. Partially self-fruitful but yields better with a pollinator.

common_name: Harvester Peach (Mid-South Early Freestone Peach, Gulf South Yellow Freestone)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) deep soil; Harvester requires approximately 750 chill hours, making it suitable for zones 6–9 and well-adapted to the mid-South and upper Gulf South from east Texas through the Carolinas; trees are self-fruitful; early-ripening season makes Harvester a valuable first-of-season peach for markets.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit in April to 6–8 inches; Harvester matures early (late May to mid-June in most of the Gulf South), making it one of the earliest large-fruited peaches; prune annually to open-vase form; good for direct-market sales and home fresh eating — early ripening gives it a market window before the main-season varieties arrive. Harvester is an early-season yellow freestone peach variety developed by North Carolina State University and the USDA (released 1971) that became an important variety for mid-South commercial peach production throughout the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee, and the Gulf South for its ability to deliver large, well-flavored, fully freestone yellow peaches earlier in the season than the standard mid-season benchmarks like Elberta and Loring. Early-season peach varieties command premium prices in direct farm markets because consumers are eager for the first fresh peaches of the year, and Harvester's ripening time — typically late May to mid-June in zone 7–9 — puts it among the first significant-sized freestone peaches available in most markets. The fruits are medium to large, round, with an attractive red blush over yellow skin, firm yellow flesh, and a clean freestone pit at full maturity. The chill hour requirement of approximately 750 hours fits the mid-South and Gulf South climate well in most winters, making Harvester a reliable producer under typical zone 7–8 conditions. Trees are vigorous and productive with moderate disease susceptibility requiring a standard spray program for brown rot and other peach diseases. An excellent choice for home orchardists who want the earliest possible fresh peach harvest.

plant_note: Plant after frost danger passes; grow in a container to move indoors in zones colder than 9b.
directions: The world's most popular avocado, Hass produces rich, buttery fruit with pebbly skin that darkens as it ripens. Grow in full sun with fast-draining soil, as avocados are extremely sensitive to soggy roots. Water deeply but infrequently and protect from frost, growing in a large pot indoors where winters are cold. It is partly self-fertile, though a second avocado nearby improves fruit set.

plant_note: Plant bare-root shrubs/trees in late winter to early spring; hazelnuts establish readily and tolerate a range of soils.
directions: Hazelnuts require cross-pollination and are wind-pollinated, so plant at least two different cultivars within 20 feet of each other; pollen is shed in late winter before leaves emerge. American hazelnut (C. americana) is hardier and more disease-resistant than European types; many gardeners grow hybrid selections for both traits. Eastern filbert blight (Anisogramma anomala) is a serious fungal disease in the eastern United States — choose blight-resistant cultivars such as Jefferson or York for eastern plantings. Harvest in late summer when nuts begin to fall from the husks on their own.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in early spring; heartnut adapts to a wide range of soils and is one of the most productive walnuts for northern growers.
directions: Heartnut is a variety of Japanese walnut bearing distinctively heart-shaped nuts that crack open cleanly along a suture to release a whole kernel — unlike black walnut, which requires significant effort to extract meat. Trees are monoecious and partially self-fertile but yield better with a second tree; they begin bearing in 4–7 years from grafted stock. Heartnut is notably less allelopathic than black walnut, making it more garden-friendly as a specimen tree. Nuts fall in clusters in late summer to early fall; hull and dry for 2–3 weeks before cracking and storing.

plant_note: Plant grafted named varieties in spring in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained soil; hicans require a cross-pollinator from either pecan or shagbark hickory for reliable crop; named hican varieties include 'McCallister', 'Pleas', and 'Burton'.
directions: Plant grafted named-variety trees in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained bottomland soil in full sun; hicans are natural and intentionally bred hybrids between pecan (Carya illinoinensis) and various hickory species (most commonly shagbark or bitternut), combining traits of both parents — the nuts are usually larger and easier to crack than hickory but with a richer, more complex flavor than straight pecan, with less oil and a firmer, drier kernel. Trees are typically very vigorous and disease-resistant, combining pecan's productivity tendency with hickory's cold hardiness and adaptability. Suitable for zones 5–9 where pecan may be too tender or unreliable; an excellent choice for nut tree diversification in humid eastern forests. Requires cross-pollination from pecan or a compatible hickory nearby.

common_name: Hog Plum (Wild Olive, Seaside Plum, Tallow Wood)
plant_note: Plant in well-drained coastal or dry tropical soils; hog plum is extremely drought-tolerant once established and thrives in thin sandy or rocky soils where little else grows.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil — tolerates poor, rocky, and alkaline soils exceptionally well once established; hog plum is a pantropical shrub or small tree with strongly fragrant white flowers and small oval fruits that ripen from green to yellow-orange then red, with thin skin, juicy sour-sweet flesh, and a large oily seed. The fruit is eaten fresh when fully ripe but is very sour; it makes excellent jellies, juices, and fermented drinks popular across sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean, and coastal Brazil. The seeds contain a high-quality oil used for cooking and cosmetics in West Africa. A superb drought- and salt-spray-tolerant fruiting hedge plant for coastal gardens.

common_name: Honey Jar Jujube (Small Sweet Early Chinese Jujube)
plant_note: Plant grafted tree in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Honey Jar is an early-maturing jujube variety producing small, very round fruits that ripen weeks ahead of Li and Lang — it is considered by many tasters to be the sweetest-flavored jujube available, with a flavor that lives up to its name of a fruit as sweet as concentrated honey.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Honey Jar is among the earliest jujubes to ripen (mid-August in many areas, 3–4 weeks before Li and Lang); the small fruits are best consumed fresh at peak ripeness rather than dried; trees are moderately compact compared to other jujube varieties. Honey Jar is widely regarded as the sweetest-tasting jujube variety available in American nurseries — the fruits are small (about 3/4 to 1 inch), round, and at perfect ripeness have a flavor described as pure concentrated honey with very little acidity and no bitterness, earning the variety its descriptive name. The small size, while meaning less fruit per piece, is actually an advantage in fresh eating situations where you want to pop a whole fruit in your mouth without cutting — Honey Jar is the jujube equivalent of a cherry tomato or Champagne grape, perfectly sized for snacking directly from the tree. The early ripening season (mid-August in zones 6–8, somewhat earlier in zone 9a) makes Honey Jar valuable for extending the fresh jujube harvest over the longest possible season when planted alongside the mid-season Li and the late-season Lang — a three-variety planting can provide fresh jujubes from late July through October. The trees are somewhat more compact than Li and Lang, making Honey Jar a good choice when space is limited. Cross-pollination with Lang or Li improves fruit set on Honey Jar trees significantly.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seeds in spring in dry, alkaline, well-drained soil in full sun; honey mesquite has an extraordinarily deep taproot that allows it to reach permanent water tables — do not transplant seedlings once established, and plant only in permanent locations.
directions: Honey mesquite is the defining native tree of Texas plains and prairies, a thorny, nitrogen-fixing legume of unmatched drought resilience that has sustained both wildlife and indigenous cultures of the semi-arid Southwest for thousands of years — its sweet, nutritious seed pods were ground into mesquite meal (pinole) by many Southwestern and Gulf Coast tribes and are the source of distinctively flavored mesquite honey produced by Texas beekeepers from the abundant, fragrant yellow catkin flowers in spring and summer. The hard, dense wood is the premier smoking wood for Texas barbecue and is also used in flooring, furniture, and decorative woodworking; charcoal from honey mesquite burns hotter and longer than most other hardwoods. Honey mesquite is an important wildlife tree: the pods are consumed by deer, javelinas, coyotes, and dozens of bird species; the canopy provides nesting habitat for doves, mockingbirds, and scissor-tailed flycatchers across Texas ranchlands. Long-paired spines on the branches can be hazardous — site away from foot traffic, but within wildlife habitat and native plantings it is invaluable.

plant_note: Plant grafted container trees in spring after cold risk; in zone 9 plant February–April in full sun with southern exposure protection. Honey tangerines are tender and more cold-sensitive than navel oranges — require protection below 28°F. Late-season (January–March) ripening makes them the last mandarin of the season.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in the warmest available location in full sun; Honey tangerine (also called Murcott or Murcott honey mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored and sweetest commercial citrus varieties — the name 'Honey' reflects its extraordinary sugar content (Brix up to 14–16) and rich, honeyed, complex flavor that combines mandarin aromatics with tangerine sweetness and a characteristic mild tartness. The fruit is medium-sized, deep orange, with thin, peelable skin and tender, very juicy flesh. Ripening in January–March, Honey tangerines extend the citrus season into late winter and early spring when other citrus is winding down. They have seeded flesh (unlike some modern mandarins) but flavor more than compensates. Trees are productive and attractive landscape specimens; they can have alternate-bearing tendencies (heavy crop one year, lighter the next) that are managed by thinning in the on-year. Feed with citrus fertilizer; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Florida produces commercial quantities in Polk and Highlands counties.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; requires a second apple variety nearby for pollination.
directions: Honeycrisp is beloved for its explosively crisp texture and balanced sweet-tart flavor, and it is notably cold-hardy. It needs a compatible pollinating apple variety and thrives in cooler northern climates. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and water steadily through the season. Thin fruit clusters and prune in late winter to promote large, well-colored apples and reduce disease pressure.

subcategory: East Asian small-fruiting Garcinia ornamental tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Hong Kong Garcinia is a small to medium ornamental and fruiting tree native to southern China, Hong Kong, and Vietnam — bearing small clusters of bright-orange to red fruits with sweet-sour, translucent flesh above attractive, glossy, oblong leaves — relatively cold-tolerant compared to tropical Garcinias and adaptable to humid subtropical conditions.
directions: Plant Garcinia oblongifolia in humus-rich, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to dappled sun; maintain consistent soil moisture and avoid prolonged drought; protect young plants from temperatures below 32°F; established trees tolerate light frost. Hong Kong Garcinia is one of the more cold-hardy Garcinia species — adapted to the subtropical climate of South China and Hong Kong where winters can be cool with occasional brief frost — making it more tractable in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens than strictly tropical Garcinias. The ornamental value is high: the tree has a neat, dense, compact form with attractive, glossy, oblong, dark-green leaves and produces small clusters of bright orange-red fruits that are decorative on the tree. The fruits have a sweet-sour, juicy, translucent-white pulp somewhat resembling a small mangosteen in flavor — less rich than Purple Mangosteen but pleasant and refreshing. The tree is appreciated in Hong Kong and southern Chinese traditional culture both as an ornamental and for the edible fruits; it also has traditional medicinal uses in Chinese herbal medicine, particularly the dried rind of the fruit (similar to Garcinia cambogia). Relatively uncommon in Western cultivation but deserves wider planting in humid subtropical gardens as a hardy, attractive alternative to more tropical Garcinias.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in winter dormancy (December–February in zone 9); Hood requires only 100–150 chill hours, making it one of the lowest-chill pear cultivars available and successful in zone 9b–10a where most pears cannot fruit. Plant with Pineapple or Floridahome for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Hood is a low-chill European pear cultivar developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program, requiring only 100–150 hours of chilling — one of the lowest chill requirements of any successful pear. This makes Hood exceptional for zone 9 and even zone 9b–10a, where most European pear varieties fail to produce consistent crops. The fruit is large, greenish-yellow to yellow at maturity, with sweet, white, juicy flesh ripening in June–July in zone 9 — much earlier than conventional pear season. Flavor is mild and pleasant, suitable for fresh eating and canning. Fire blight can be a problem in humid conditions; prune out infected wood promptly and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization. Cross-pollination with Pineapple pear or Floridahome significantly improves yields. Hood is one of the three low-chill pears (with Orient and LeConte) most reliably recommended for Gulf Coast zone 9 home orchards where conventional Bartlett and Bosc fail to fruit.

common_name: Hosui Asian Pear (Japanese Golden-Russet Round Asian Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Hosui requires approximately 400–450 chilling hours (hours below 45°F) — achievable in most of zone 7–9 in most years. Asian pears are not self-fertile — plant at least two different Asian pear varieties (Shinsei, Twentieth Century, Olympic, or another Pyrus pyrifolia) within 50 feet for pollination; European pears (Pyrus communis) are generally not compatible pollinators. Hosui fruit ripens in August in zone 9 — earlier than most Asian pears — and should be harvested when still firm on the tree (unlike European pears, Asian pears do not improve in storage and should be harvested at full ripeness). Fruits do not ripen after harvest the way European pears do.
directions: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; thin fruit clusters to one fruit per cluster when fruits are marble-sized for maximum size. Asian pears need no post-harvest ripening period. Hosui is a Japanese-bred Asian pear (nashi pear, Pyrus pyrifolia) — one of the finest Asian pear varieties available in North America for both flavor quality and adaptability to warmer zones (zone 5–9 with adequate chill). The fruit is large (8–12 oz), round to slightly oblate, with distinctive golden-brown russeted skin — the russet texture of Hosui's skin is one of its defining aesthetic characteristics, giving it a warm, autumn-toned appearance that differs from the smooth green or yellow skin of other Asian pear varieties. The flesh is the extraordinary feature: extremely crisp, almost crunchy — quite unlike the soft, butter-like texture of ripe European pears — with very high juice content and a sweet, aromatic, complex flavor with notes of honey and vanilla. Asian pears are eaten fresh at harvest, when crisp and juicy at peak quality; they do not improve with storage and are not used for cooking or canning the way European pears are. Hosui is among the most popular and widely planted Asian pear varieties in Japan and California, where its early ripening, excellent flavor, and moderate chill requirement make it adaptable to a wider range of climates than many Asian pear types.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups/suckers) after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Ice Cream banana is one of the more cold-tolerant banana varieties — the rhizomes survive frost to about 22°F if heavily mulched, and the plant resprouts vigorously from the rhizome in spring even when the above-ground pseudostem is killed. In zone 9 a plant that survives multiple seasons as a ratoon crop (resprouting from the surviving rhizome) will bloom and produce fruit within 9–12 months of the spring resprouting. Allow suckers to develop as replacement ratoon plants when the main pseudostem flowers, since banana plants fruit only once per pseudostem.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil with consistent moisture — banana requires abundant water, nutrients, and heat to produce fruit; Ice Cream banana (also called Blue Java) is a cold-tolerant banana cultivar notable for its distinctive blue-green to silvery-blue coloring on unripe fruits and the unusually rich, creamy flavor of ripe fruit described as reminiscent of vanilla ice cream — a flavor and texture quality that sets this cultivar apart from the standard Cavendish banana flavor most North Americans are accustomed to. The ripe fruits develop a pale yellow to creamy-white flesh with a particularly soft, smooth, melting texture and vanilla-banana flavor that is among the finest of all banana varieties for fresh eating. Ice Cream's relative cold tolerance compared to Cavendish and other commercial varieties (the rhizome surviving to approximately 22°F with mulching) makes it one of the most practical banana varieties for zone 9 Gulf South gardens where winter freezes regularly kill the above-ground pseudostem. In zone 9 the combination of the summer heat, humidity, and rain that banana requires, combined with the cold-hardiness that allows ratoon production from surviving rhizomes, makes Ice Cream banana one of the most rewarding tropical fruit plants available.

common_name: Ice Cream Banana (Blue Java Cold-Hardy Vanilla-Flavored Banana)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Java tolerates frost to approximately 20°F (-7°C) — the pseudostem may be killed but the rhizome survives most zone 9 winters and regenerates new shoots in spring.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Blue Java (Ice Cream banana) is one of the most cold-hardy banana cultivars available for Gulf South gardens — tolerating frost temperatures to approximately 20°F, allowing the rhizome to survive most zone 9 winters even when the pseudostem is frozen to the ground and regenerate productive new shoots in spring. The variety name 'Blue Java' refers to the distinctive blue-green color of the unripe fruit bunches; the 'Ice Cream' name describes the rich, creamy, vanilla-like flavor of the ripe fruit — a flavor profile distinctly different from the standard Cavendish banana of commerce and more complex, with smooth, creamy, slightly vanilla-custard characteristics that justify the evocative name. The medium-length (6–8 inch), pale-yellow ripe fruits have a soft, creamy texture that reinforces the ice cream comparison. In zone 9, Blue Java typically requires the full warm season (May–October) for pseudostem development, and established plants with multiple offsets may fruit in warm years with protection through mild winters. Even when pseudostems are killed by frost, the vigorous rhizome system regenerates multiple new shoots in spring, making Blue Java a reliable ornamental tropical even in years when fruit production is not achieved. Heavy mulching around the base protects the rhizome during cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant the pup after frost; grow in a large pot to shelter indoors in cold climates.
directions: Also called Blue Java, this banana yields creamy, vanilla-flavored fruit and tolerates more cold and wind than most bananas. Give it full sun, rich soil, and abundant water plus regular feeding to fuel its fast growth. The bluish fruit ripens to pale yellow and is best eaten fresh. In marginal climates grow it in a large container and overwinter the plant in a bright, frost-free spot.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; ice cream bean grows rapidly and begins fruiting in 2–3 years from seed. Hardy to about 29°F; zone 9b–12 in the ground, containers in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade — ice cream bean is a fast-growing Central and South American legume tree producing enormous pods (12–30 inches long) filled with white, cottony, sweet pulp that wraps the seeds and tastes unmistakably of vanilla ice cream. The white pulp is eaten fresh directly from the pod; it melts on the tongue with a sweet, mild, creamy vanilla flavor that surprises everyone who encounters it for the first time. Beyond the extraordinary fruit, ice cream bean is a nitrogen-fixing legume that improves soil fertility, an excellent shade and windbreak tree (growing 30–40 feet), and a valuable component of agroforestry systems throughout the tropics. The fragrant white flower pompoms attract hummingbirds and native bees. It grows rapidly in the frost-free tropics and sub-tropics, beginning to fruit in 2–3 years from seed.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Ichang lemon is one of the most cold-hardy citrus species, with mature wood tolerating temperatures down to around 0°F, and is often grown as much for its hardiness and rootstock value as for its tart fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; among the hardiest citrus species available, surviving winter conditions that kill standard lemons and limes outright. Citrus ichangensis (Ichang lemon, or Ichang papeda) is a wild citrus species native to the mountainous borderlands of China, prized by cold-hardy citrus breeders and enthusiasts as one of the parents behind many of today's cold-tolerant citrus hybrids, thanks to its unusual combination of true citrus flavor and genuine winter hardiness. The rough-skinned, lemon-like fruit is highly acidic and aromatic with a distinct floral note, used much like a true lemon for juice, zest, and flavoring rather than fresh eating out of hand. Its glossy, deep green, notably large-winged leaves and modest thorns give it strong ornamental value even apart from fruiting. A rewarding choice for gardeners in the Gulf South and Southeast who want to grow citrus outside the usual protected range, and a useful parent plant for anyone interested in breeding hardier citrus hybrids, zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Ichang Papeda is among the most cold-hardy citrus species, tolerating temperatures to about 0–5°F when established — making it suitable for zone 7 and a nearly indestructible rootstock or ornamental in zone 9. It is primarily grown as an ornamental, rootstock, or specimen tree for its exceptional cold hardiness; the fruits are used for juice and flavoring but are not eating citrus. Ichang Papeda has contributed cold hardiness to many citrus breeding programs.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Ichang Papeda (Citrus ichangensis, Ichang lemon) is a wild citrus species from the mountains of central China near Yichang on the Yangtze River — the hardiest true citrus species, capable of surviving brief temperatures near 0°F and making it valuable for cold-climate citrus experimentation far beyond the normal range. The large, fragrant, lemon-yellow fruits are highly aromatic but extremely acidic and seedy, used for juice, fragrance, and culinary flavoring rather than fresh eating. The distinctive winged petioles on the leaves identify the plant and give it an interesting ornamental appearance with an almost tropical look. In zone 9 Ichang Papeda grows vigorously and produces abundant, highly aromatic fruit with a distinctive floral-citrus fragrance used in Chinese cooking and perfumery. Ichang Papeda is a parent of the Yuzu lemon hybrid and has contributed cold hardiness to many important citrus breeding programs; it thrives in zone 9 as an ornamental citrus tree with exceptional cold insurance.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a frost-free setting with a distinct dry season to stimulate bloom.
directions: Ilama is a semi-deciduous Annona from Mexico and Central America that tolerates drier conditions than most of its relatives, preferring a pronounced dry season to trigger leaf drop and subsequent flowering. Like other Annonaceae, flowers are protogynous and benefit strongly from hand-pollination — collect pollen in the afternoon from half-closed male-stage flowers and dab onto receptive stigmas of newly opened female-stage flowers in the morning. Fruit comes in pink-fleshed and white-fleshed strains; the pink-fleshed type has a slightly acidic flavor while the white is sweeter and more custard-like. Harvest when the skin has slightly separated at the segment lines and the fruit gives to gentle pressure; shelf life at room temperature is only 1–2 days.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Illinois Everbearing is one of the most cold-hardy mulberry cultivars and produces fruit over an exceptionally long season (6–8 weeks vs 2–3 weeks for single-crop varieties). Trees are fast-growing, reaching significant size (30–35 feet) quickly — allow ample permanent space. The fruit stains everything it contacts — plant away from walkways, patios, and vehicles. In zone 9 mulberries produce prolifically in April–May and may fruit again in fall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — mulberry is adaptable to a wide range of soil types and conditions; Illinois Everbearing is a hybrid mulberry (Morus alba x Morus rubra) that produces the longest fruit season of any widely available mulberry cultivar — harvesting over 6–8 weeks from late spring into early summer compared to the brief 2–3 week window of standard mulberry varieties. The large, cylindrical, 1–1.5 inch fruits ripen from red through dark purple-black over the extended season, with the sweet, mild, slightly bland flavor characteristic of mulberries — less complex than blackberries, softer-textured, and milder-tasting, primarily valued for fresh eating, smoothies, and baked goods where the abundant, easily harvested fruit compensates for the relatively mild flavor. The practical appeal of Illinois Everbearing is unambiguous: a single established tree produces quantities of fruit (hundreds of pounds in a mature tree) over an extended period with essentially zero cultivation requirements beyond harvesting. As a wildlife plant, mulberry is unparalleled — the fruit is consumed by more than 60 species of birds and dozens of mammal species — making it the single most productive wildlife-supporting tree available for home landscapes.

common_name: Illinois Everbearing Mulberry (Long-Season Red Mulberry Hybrid, Eastern Standard Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring; Illinois Everbearing is self-fertile and produces without a pollinator; it is a hybrid between white mulberry (Morus alba) and red mulberry (Morus rubra) with the cold-hardiness of the white parent (zones 4–8) and the superior fruit flavor of the red parent; it is the most widely recommended mulberry variety for home orchards in the eastern United States by most university cooperative extension services.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Illinois Everbearing is self-fertile; the trees are fast-growing and begin bearing in year 2–3; fruit ripens over an extended 4–6 week season (June–July in zones 5–7) rather than dropping all at once; the long harvesting period makes it practical to collect ripe fruit repeatedly from the ground or by shaking branches. Illinois Everbearing mulberry is a naturally occurring or deliberately selected hybrid of Morus alba (white mulberry) and Morus rubra (red mulberry) that was selected and propagated in Illinois in the mid-20th century and subsequently became the standard recommended mulberry variety for home orchards in the eastern and midwestern United States. The variety combines the key qualities of both parent species: from Morus rubra, it inherits superior fruit flavor — significantly more complex and berry-like than the often bland white mulberry — along with better fresh-eating quality; from Morus alba, it inherits cold-hardiness to zone 4 and adaptability to a wide range of soils and climates. The most practically important feature reflected in its name is the extended ripening season — berries mature gradually and drop over a period of 4–6 weeks rather than all ripening within 1–2 weeks as many mulberry seedlings do. This extended season makes it much more manageable for home fruit harvesting and wildlife feeding, and reduces the dramatic mess that concentrated mulberry drop can create on driveways, paths, and patios. The fruit quality is good: long (1–1.5 inch), dark red to black-purple berries with sweet, mild, pleasant mulberry flavor — not as intensely sweet as Pakistan Mulberry but far superior to most seedling trees.

subcategory: Brazilian Caatinga native dryland fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to stony, poor to average soil in zone 9–11; Imbu (Umbuzeiro) is a remarkable drought-adapted fruit tree endemic to the Brazilian Caatinga semi-arid scrubland — one of the most important wild food trees of the Brazilian Northeast — that stores water in massive, starchy, underground tubers and produces small, round, yellow-green, sweet-sour fruits vital to subsistence food security in one of the world's driest inhabited regions.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, sandy to stony, poor to average soil; Spondias tuberosa is exceptionally drought tolerant — the underground water-storage tubers allow the tree to survive months of total drought; overwatering or waterlogged soil is fatal. Spondias tuberosa (Imbu, Umbú, or Umbuzeiro) is a drought-deciduous, small to medium tree endemic to the Brazilian Caatinga (semi-arid thorny scrubland) of the northeastern states of Pernambuco, Bahia, Sergipe, Piauí, and Ceará — one of the most important and beloved wild fruit trees of the Brazilian Northeast. The tree's defining ecological adaptation is remarkable: a system of massive, water-filled, carrot-to-sweet-potato-sized underground storage tubers (technically water-storing roots) that can accumulate hundreds of kilograms of water, allowing the tree to survive the brutal, multi-month droughts of the Caatinga and burst into fruit production with the first rains — typically January through March. The small (1–1.5 inch), round, pale-yellow to yellow-green fruits have juicy, sweet-sour, tropical, mango-lychee-like pulp eaten fresh, made into the beloved Brazilian drink umbuzada (fruit pulp boiled with milk and sugar), jams, and fermented into Caatinga wine. The tree has become a symbol of northeastern Brazilian cultural identity and food resilience. Spondias tuberosa is well adapted to dryland gardens in zone 9–11 where excellent drainage and full sun are provided; it is one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available.

common_name: Improved Brown Turkey Fig (Larger-Fruited Brown Turkey Selection)
plant_note: Plant after the last hard frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Improved Brown Turkey is a selection valued for producing somewhat larger fruit than standard Brown Turkey while retaining the same reliable cold hardiness and heavy production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Improved Brown Turkey is a selection of the classic Brown Turkey fig valued for producing somewhat larger, bronze-brown fruit with sweet, amber-pink flesh compared to standard Brown Turkey, while keeping the same dependable cold hardiness and heavy, reliable production that has made Brown Turkey one of the most widely planted figs in home gardens. Like other figs it bears on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by the main crop in late summer, and it needs minimal care beyond routine mulching and occasional pruning to control size. In colder zones, grow in a container that can be moved to shelter for winter.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. The 'Improved' designation refers to the virus-indexed, certified clean version released by UC Davis following the discovery that the original Meyer lemon carried citrus tristeza virus — all nursery-sold Meyer lemons are now this certified clean selection. Meyer lemon is the most cold-hardy of all true lemons, tolerating temperatures to about 22–24°F — borderline zone 8b/9a. In zone 9 it produces fruit through winter (harvest November–March), providing fresh lemons when the tree is at peak ornamental interest with simultaneous flowers and fruit. Grow in containers in colder zones to move indoors when freezes threaten.
