Kishu mandarin is cold-hardy to about 24°F, making it more vulnerable to hard freezes than navel oranges — protect young trees in zone 9a winters with frost cloth or heat lamps when temperatures drop below 28°F. Trees are self-fertile and begin bearing within 2–4 years.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–7.0) soil; Kishu mandarin (Kishu mikan) is a tiny Japanese mandarin producing small, round, intensely sweet, completely seedless fruits — typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, roughly the size of a large grape. The combination of total seedlessness and extraordinary sweetness makes Kishu the darling of high-end specialty markets, where the small size makes it a perfect one-bite citrus snack. The paper-thin skin peels effortlessly in a single piece, and the flavor is intensely sweet with rich tropical complexity that surpasses most commercial mandarins. Trees are compact and manageable at 6–10 feet, well-suited to zone 9 and container growing. Kishu ripens in December–January, slightly earlier than most clementine-type mandarins. Although small trees, they bear prolifically and a single established tree can produce hundreds of fruits. Avoid planting in frost pockets where cold air settles.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; kiwano thrives in hot, dry conditions and is more drought-tolerant than common cucumber — plant in zone 9 for summer harvest of the dramatic, spiny, orange-gold fruits.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in warm soil in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; provide trellis support; kiwano tolerates more drought than most cucurbits once vines are established. Cucumis metuliferus (kiwano or African horned melon) is an extraordinary African cucurbit producing one of the most visually dramatic fruits in horticulture — an oblong, 3-to-5-inch fruit covered in prominent, rigid, pointed spines (horns), ripening from green to brilliant deep orange-gold that looks almost artificial in its intensity. The jelly-like interior flesh is lime-green and gelatinous, with a mild, refreshing flavor combining hints of banana, cucumber, and lime. Kiwano is grown commercially in New Zealand, Kenya, and California for specialty markets and upscale grocery stores where the exotic appearance commands premium prices. The fruit is eaten by scooping out the jelly-like flesh with a spoon, used in tropical fruit salads, blended into smoothies, or used as a dramatic edible vessel for other foods. As an annual vine, it is easy to grow in zone 9 summers — direct sow after the last frost, provide trellis support, and harvest when the skin turns deep orange. The vines are vigorous and productive under heat.

plant_note: Plant air-layered or container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Kohala longan requires a brief cool-dry period (cool temperatures below 59°F for several weeks) to trigger flower induction — this chilling occurs naturally in zone 9 winters, making zone 9 a better longan climate than zone 10. Do not overwater in winter; allow the tree to experience mild stress during the cool season to promote flowering. Young trees are frost-sensitive; protect below 30°F.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Kohala is the most widely planted named longan cultivar in Hawaii and South Florida, selected at the University of Hawaii for consistently large, sweet, reliable fruit production in tropical and subtropical conditions. The large clusters of walnut-sized fruits with tan-brown papery shells and translucent white sweet flesh ripen in August–September — the classic longan flavor is a delicate sweetness with floral notes and a refreshing juicy texture, less intense and more floral than lychee. In zone 9 the mild winter temperatures provide the natural chilling that longan requires to initiate flower buds, making zone 9a an ideal longan climate. Kohala trees are vigorous growers that can eventually reach 30–40 feet in favorable conditions but are maintained smaller by selective pruning. The species produces abundantly once established, with mature trees bearing hundreds of pounds of fruit in a good year.

common_name: Korean Giant Asian Pear (Olympic Pear, Jumbo Asian Pear, Large Korean Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Korean Giant requires cross-pollination from another Asian pear variety — Hosui, Chojuro, or Shinseiki; Korean Giant ripens very late (September–October in most locations), later than most other Asian pears, requiring a long growing season; it is one of the largest Asian pears available — individual fruits commonly weigh 1–2 lbs.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Korean Giant requires a cross-pollinator; thin fruit clusters in May to 1 fruit per spur for maximum fruit development — this variety has the capacity to produce extremely large fruit when properly thinned; harvest in late September to October when skin color shifts from green to yellow-green and fruit gives very slightly to pressure. Korean Giant (also marketed as 'Olympic Pear' in American nursery trade, named for the 1988 Seoul Olympics) is a Korean variety that produces some of the largest Asian pear fruits available to home growers and specialty markets — single fruits commonly weigh 1–1.5 lbs and exceptional fruits can reach 2 lbs, making them dramatically larger than the typical 6–10 oz fruits of Hosui, Shinseiki, and Nijisseiki. The size is the variety's primary market distinction: Korean Giant pears make a striking visual impression at farmers' markets and gift fruit presentations, where the giant, pale gold-green to golden-brown skin and exceptional juicy-sweet flavor create a memorable product. The flavor at peak ripeness is excellent — sweet, refreshingly crisp, and juicy with a clean, mild pear flavor — and the very late ripening season (September–October) extends the fresh Asian pear harvest window well after early and mid-season varieties have finished. Korean Giant requires careful fruit thinning to develop full-sized individual fruits; without thinning, trees set too many fruits and individual nuts remain smaller.

plant_note: Plant in early spring before bud break; Korean pine is a cold-hardy alternative to Stone pine for producing large, commercially sized pine nuts in the northern U.S.
directions: Korean pine is a large, ornamental five-needle pine that produces the large, wingless pine nuts commonly sold in Asian markets — seeds are bigger than those of Italian stone pine and have a rich, buttery flavor. Trees are monoecious and bear cones that ripen over two growing seasons; significant cone production typically begins at 15–25 years from seed. Cones are harvested in early autumn when the scales begin to separate; spread cones on tarps to dry and then beat or tumble to dislodge seeds. The outer seed coat must be cracked to access the edible kernel, which is high in oil and should be refrigerated or frozen to prevent rancidity.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or potted tree; plant after frost.
directions: Koroneiki is a productive Greek olive celebrated for generous harvests and a compact, easygoing habit that suits both orchards and patios. Its small fruit yields a robust, high-quality oil, and the silvery evergreen foliage lends year-round Mediterranean charm. Grow a young tree in full sun with sharp drainage and minimal water once established. Prune to keep light reaching the interior, and where winters are cold, grow it in a pot to move to shelter during freezes.

common_name: Kosui Asian Pear (Early Sweet Japanese Pear, Small Golden Russet Asian Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Kosui requires cross-pollination from a compatible variety — Hosui or Chojuro are recommended companions with overlapping bloom times; Kosui is an early-season Asian pear (ripening in late July to August), providing ripe Asian pears several weeks before mid- and late-season varieties, giving it value as a season-extender from the beginning of the harvest window.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Kosui requires a cross-pollinator; harvest in late July to August when the golden-brown russet skin reaches full color and fruit gives very slightly under thumb pressure; Kosui has somewhat shorter shelf life than later-season varieties — best consumed within 2–4 weeks of harvest; the small to medium size makes it ideal for single-serving eating straight off the tree. Kosui is a widely grown Japanese pear variety developed through deliberate cross-breeding at the National Institute of Fruit Tree Science in Japan and released in 1959, becoming one of the most popular fresh-eating Asian pear varieties in Japan and increasingly common in American specialty orchards and Asian-American community gardens. The variety's most important attribute for home orchardists is its early ripening season — Kosui typically ripens in late July to August in the Pacific Northwest and mid-Atlantic, 3–6 weeks before mid-season varieties like Hosui and 6–8 weeks before Korean Giant, allowing fresh Asian pear harvest to begin at the height of summer rather than early fall. The fruits are small to medium-sized with golden-brown russet skin and crisp, juicy, very sweet white flesh with a clean, refreshing flavor and aromatic quality. The sweetness and early ripening of Kosui — combined with its thin, tender skin that doesn't need peeling — make it an appealing variety for fresh eating directly from the tree. Productive and reliable in zones 5–9.

plant_note: Plant in spring; kumquats are the hardiest citrus relative and tolerate brief dips to 18°F.
directions: Kumquats are the hardiest of the citrus family and the only ones whose entire fruit — sweet peel and tangy flesh — is eaten whole. They are self-fertile and well-suited to container growing in zones 7–8, where they can be overwintered indoors. Unlike other citrus, kumquats go dormant more readily in winter, which improves their cold hardiness. Fruit ripens from late autumn through winter; harvest when fully orange and sweet-peel is prominent.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Kuwini mango is a Southeast Asian relative of common mango producing smaller, intensely fragrant, oval fruits with an aroma so powerful and distinctive that it can be detected from meters away — the fruits are primarily used for juice and drinks rather than eaten out of hand due to the fibrous flesh.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Kuwini mango is similar in requirements to common mango but more frost-sensitive. Mangifera odorata (Kuwini mango or fragrant mango) is a species in the Anacardiaceae family related to common mango (M. indica), native to the Malay Peninsula and the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, producing small to medium-sized, oval, green to yellowish fruits with extraordinarily intense mango-floral fragrance — the most powerfully aromatic of all Mangifera species. The fresh fruit has a strong turpentine-floral aroma detectable at a considerable distance, with yellow-orange flesh that is significantly more fibrous than commercial mangoes and with more resinous flavor notes. While less pleasant to eat out of hand than polished commercial mango varieties, Kuwini is prized in Malaysia and Indonesia for juice, juice blends, mango lassi-type drinks, ice cream, and traditional sambal sauces where the intense fragrance shines through processing. The skin of the fruit also yields a yellow dye. The tree is also notable as one of the parents in the natural hybrid origin of common mango's wild ancestors. In zone 11–12 tropical fruit collections, Kuwini is a valuable diversity addition for those wanting the full spectrum of Mangifera species. Very rare in cultivation outside Southeast Asia.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.5), fertile soil in full sun; figs tolerate poorer soils than most fruit trees but perform best with good drainage and protection from late spring freezes that can damage the crop.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; LSU Gold is a golden-yellow fig cultivar developed by the Louisiana State University Agricultural Center's renowned fig breeding program — one of several outstanding cultivars released by LSU specifically for Gulf Coast garden conditions. The medium-sized fruits have golden-yellow to amber skin and rich, sweet, amber-colored flesh with excellent flavor and lower acidity than common brown-skinned fig varieties. The golden skin and rich, honey-sweet taste make LSU Gold particularly attractive for fresh eating and fresh presentations where the unusual color adds visual appeal. LSU Gold ripens with a main crop in July through September in zone 9 and often produces a lighter breba (early crop) in June. LSU-developed figs are specifically selected for performance in the hot, humid Gulf South — resistance to fig mosaic virus, quality fruit production in high heat and humidity, and productivity in the long Gulf South growing season. Figs are among the easiest and most productive fruit trees for Gulf Coast gardens — drought-tolerant, naturally pest-resistant, fast to bearing (often fruiting in the second year from cuttings), and requiring minimal care beyond keeping the soil moist during fruit development. Propagate easily from dormant hardwood cuttings taken in late winter.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; LSU Purple was specifically developed for the humid, disease-prone Gulf Coast climate and significantly outperforms other fig varieties under these conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; LSU Purple fig was developed by Louisiana State University specifically for the Gulf Coast and Deep South, where high humidity, summer rains, and soil fungal diseases typically prevent figs from performing as reliably as in Mediterranean or California climates. It produces an abundant main crop in summer of medium-sized, deep purple-skinned figs with a rich, sweet, dark-red interior. The variety has superior resistance to fruit splitting and souring — common problems in humid regions where rain during ripening ruins the crop on other varieties. It ripens earlier than most, avoiding the worst of hurricane season. An outstanding choice for zone 8‑9 gardeners in the humid Southeast.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; LSU Tiger was developed by the LSU AgCenter fig breeding program specifically for Gulf Coast disease pressure and humidity, and shares the program's characteristic split- and souring-resistance.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; like its LSU AgCenter sibling releases, LSU Tiger fig was bred specifically to perform reliably in the humid, disease-prone conditions of the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Its most distinctive feature is its striking immature fruit — young, unripe figs are boldly striped in yellow-green and dark green, giving the variety its 'Tiger' name — before ripening to a bronze-brown skin with sweet, richly flavored, amber-to-strawberry-colored flesh. The variety carries useful resistance to fruit splitting and souring, common problems for figs grown where summer rains fall during ripening, and its ornamental striped immature fruit makes it a conversation piece in the garden even before harvest. A good choice for Gulf South growers who want the LSU program's disease resistance along with a visually distinctive fruit, zone 7–11.

plant_note: Plant bare-root in January–February in zone 8–9; La Feliciana requires 450 chill hours, making it best suited for zone 7b–8b inland areas of the Gulf South where winter temperatures regularly dip below 45°F. Not recommended for coastal zone 9b where chill accumulation may be insufficient.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic loam in full sun; La Feliciana is a freestone peach developed by Louisiana State University AgCenter and released in 1978, specifically bred for the Gulf Coast South and named for the historic peach-growing region around St. Francisville, Louisiana. With a chill requirement of approximately 450 hours, it is well-matched to the inland Gulf South (zones 7b–8b) where more heat-sensitive northern varieties struggle through summer but standard low-chill Florida varieties lack enough winter cold. Fruit quality is excellent — large, yellow-fleshed, fully freestone with rich, classic peach flavor ripening in late May to June in Louisiana and Mississippi. Trees are vigorous and productive, with good disease tolerance under Gulf Coast conditions. La Feliciana is considered a benchmark variety for Louisiana peach production and is widely sold at regional nurseries. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches in April for full-sized fruit; prune to an open center after leaf drop.

common_name: Lady Finger Banana (Sugar Banana, Fig Banana)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Lady Finger banana performs best in zones 9b–11 and needs frost protection in zone 9a, though the rhizome may survive light freezes with heavy mulching.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Lady Finger banana (also called Sugar Banana, Sucrier, or 'Fig Banana') is an AAB genome group banana producing long, thin, elegant fruits (4–5 inches long but unusually slender) with delicate, thin, easily peeled skin and exceptionally sweet, rich, aromatic flavor — widely regarded as one of the finest-flavored fresh-eating bananas available, with a honey-like sweetness and floral aroma that surpasses standard Cavendish bananas. The fruits are produced in large bunches of 12–20 fingers per hand, and the delicate thin skin means they do not ship well commercially (hence their relative scarcity in supermarkets despite their superior flavor), making Lady Finger an excellent choice for the home gardener who wants superior banana flavor and can eat the fruits promptly at ripeness. The tall (12–18 foot) plants produce large ornamental pseudostems with broad tropical leaves; they are truly tropical and suffer pseudostem dieback in any freeze but the rhizomes can survive to about 28–30°F with heavy mulching in zone 9b. Grow in the warmest, most protected microclimate available in zone 9.

plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant, in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lakota is a Type II pecan and needs a Type I pollinator such as Kanza, Pawnee, or Elliott within about 150 feet for reliable fertilization and a full crop.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually and prune to maintain an open canopy for airflow and scab management. Lakota Pecan was released through the USDA Agricultural Research Service pecan breeding program as a scab-resistant alternative to older, disease-prone standards, combining good resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum) with a large, attractive, thin-shelled nut and high kernel percentage that appeals to growers who want commercial-quality size without the heavy fungicide program that susceptible varieties demand in humid regions. The tree bears at a moderate age and produces consistent, mid-season crops of good-quality nuts well suited to both fresh eating and baking. Its disease resistance and nut size make it a strong choice for Gulf South and Midsouth home orchards and small commercial plantings seeking reduced-spray management, in zone 6–9.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from gardens and other juglone-sensitive plants; Lamb is a named black walnut cultivar selected for a strong combination of nut size, cracking quality, and consistent annual production.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to the juglone this species releases into the surrounding soil. Lamb is a named black walnut selection valued by nut growers for combining good kernel percentage and cracking quality with strong, consistent annual bearing, an important trait in a species that can otherwise produce heavily only every second year. Like other grafted black walnut cultivars, it grows into a large, long-lived shade tree over time, so it is best suited to a large property, orchard row, or field edge rather than a small home garden. Nuts drop in a thick, dark, staining husk in early fall that should be removed promptly to prevent kernel discoloration, and grafted trees typically begin bearing within six to ten years, considerably sooner than seedling trees. Rake and dispose of fallen husks away from lawns and walkways, since they stain concrete and skin on contact.

common_name: Lang Jujube (Pear-Shaped Chinese Jujube, Large Late Jujube)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained soil; Lang is one of the two most widely planted jujube varieties in the United States alongside Li — they are often planted together because cross-pollination between Lang and Li dramatically increases fruit set on both trees; Lang produces elongated, pear-shaped fruits that are larger than most jujubes and mature later in the season than Li.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — jujubes thrive in poor, alkaline, rocky soils where other fruit trees fail; Lang and Li are the classic companion pair for maximum fruit set; harvest fruits when they turn from green to mahogany-red and reach full size; air-dry excess harvest at room temperature for preserved 'dried dates.' Lang jujube is one of the two most important cultivated jujube varieties in American horticulture, planted alongside Li jujube (the other dominant variety) throughout the jujube-growing regions of the United States. Lang differs from Li in fruit shape and season: where Li produces round to oval fruits that ripen relatively early, Lang produces elongated, pear-shaped to teardrop-shaped fruits that are noticeably larger than Li (typically 1.5–2.5 inches long) and ripen later in the season. The larger, more elongated fruit shape of Lang also makes it particularly excellent for drying into Chinese-style red dates (hong zao / hóng zǎo), where the pear shape produces attractive elongated dried fruits with a pleasant chewy texture and concentrated honey-sweet flavor. Cross-pollination between Lang and Li is well-documented to significantly increase fruit set on both trees, making them the classic companion pair for backyard jujube plantings — planting one of each type provides mutual pollination benefits that result in substantially heavier crops than either variety planted alone. Like all jujubes, Lang is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant, thriving with no supplemental irrigation once established in most of the country. An exceptional choice for zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardeners who want a reliable, low-input fruit tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in late spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, humid, fertile soil; Langsat is strictly tropical and frost-tender, suitable only for zone 10b–11 outdoor planting or for large containers in zone 10a. It is one of the most shade-tolerant of tropical fruit trees and actually benefits from some overhead protection when young. Very slow to reach bearing age from seed — grafted trees produce fruit in 4–6 years. The tree prefers high humidity and consistent moisture similar to its humid lowland forest native habitat.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Langsat is more shade-tolerant than most tropical fruit trees and performs well with overhead canopy protection when young, mimicking its native understory forest environment. Lansium parasiticum (formerly L. domesticum) is a medium tropical tree native to the Malay Peninsula, the Philippines, and Indonesia, where it is one of the most beloved native fruits — at once common enough to be sold from roadside carts throughout Southeast Asia and exotic enough to be a premium market item in Japan and specialty stores. The fruits are produced in long, grape-like clusters directly on the main trunk and branches (cauliflory), each fruit a small (1–2 inch) oval, pale yellowish-tan berry with thin, papery skin. Inside are 3–5 segments of translucent, juicy, sweet-tart flesh with a flavor variously described as combining grape, grapefruit, longan, and rose water — extraordinarily refreshing in tropical heat. The 'Duku' form (sometimes listed separately) produces larger, thicker-skinned, sweeter fruits than the standard Langsat; 'Longkong' is a selected clone from Thailand with very sweet, thin-skinned fruits highly valued in Southeast Asian markets. Virtually unavailable commercially outside Southeast Asia and rare specialty markets, Langsat is a coveted addition to zone 11 South Florida tropical fruit gardens.

plant_note: Plant dormant in early spring; self-fertile, so no second cherry is needed.
directions: Lapins is a self-fertile sweet cherry producing large, firm, dark-red fruit without needing a pollinator, ideal for smaller gardens. Plant in full sun with deep, well-drained soil and water steadily as fruit develops. Prune in late winter or after harvest to keep an open canopy and reduce disease. Netting the tree near ripening helps protect the crop from birds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; large sourplum is a thorny shrub or small tree from the savanna and bushveld regions of eastern and southern Africa — bearing single-seeded, oval, orange-red to scarlet, cherry-sized fruits with very sour, vitamin C-rich flesh and an almond-flavored kernel — one of the most widely used wild food fruits across sub-Saharan Africa.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — adapted to seasonally dry African bushveld. Ximenia caffra (large sourplum or wild sourplum) is a thorny deciduous shrub or small tree from the dry savannas, bushveld, and woodland margins of eastern and southern Africa — native across South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Tanzania, and Kenya. The plant produces small (1-inch), oval, single-seeded drupes that ripen from green to bright orange-red to scarlet, with very tart, astringent, vitamin C-rich flesh surrounding a large seed — eaten fresh across rural sub-Saharan Africa (often with salt to balance the sourness), and made into jam, chutney, beer, and preserved sour fruit drinks. The seed kernel has an almond-like flavor and is pressed for Ximenia oil (sour plum oil), one of the most sought-after African cosmetic oils, with excellent skin-conditioning properties rich in long-chain polyunsaturated acids — increasingly used in high-end African cosmetics, hair oils, and skin care. Distinguished from the smaller X. americana (tallow wood) by its larger fruits, larger leaves, and preference for drier, more seasonal climates. As a water-wise shrub for zone 9–11 gardens, large sourplum is extremely tough and attractive, with white, almond-scented flowers in spring.

common_name: Laroda Plum (Large Late-Season Red California Japanese Plum with Rich Flavor)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Laroda requires a cross-pollinator — plant with Santa Rosa, Burgundy, or another compatible Japanese plum within 50 feet for reliable fruit set. Requires approximately 400–500 chilling hours, placing it on the upper margin of what zone 9 reliably provides; it performs most consistently in zone 8 and cooler zone 9 locations. In the Gulf South, Laroda ripens late July to August — among the latest Japanese plum varieties to mature — extending the fresh plum season significantly beyond the earlier summer varieties. The combination of late ripening and large fruit size has made Laroda commercially important in California and a sought-after variety for home orchardists wanting fresh plums into late summer. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; requires cross-pollinator. Thin fruit clusters to 4–5 inches. Harvest when red skin is deep and fruit gives to gentle pressure. Laroda is a California-developed late-season Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) that has been grown in California commercial orchards and home gardens since the mid-20th century, selected from the same broad program of California stone fruit development that produced Santa Rosa, Friar, and other standard Japanese plum varieties. The name Laroda is of uncertain derivation — unlike Luther Burbank's poetically named plum introductions, Laroda was likely a station selection name from one of the California experiment station programs that systematically evaluated Japanese plum seedlings for commercial quality. The fruit is one of the largest Japanese plum types: large to very large globose fruits, 2–2.5 inches in diameter, with deep red to dark red skin that becomes almost black at full maturity. The skin has a slightly mottled appearance with a light bloom (waxy surface coating). The flesh is amber to yellow, firm and juicy with rich, full plum flavor and moderate sweetness — more complex and less bland than some of the large-fruited Japanese plums selected primarily for size. The late season (July-August in California, somewhat earlier in the humid South) means Laroda provides fresh plums after most other Japanese varieties have finished — a practical attribute for home orchard planning where sequential harvests are desirable. Cross-pollination from Santa Rosa plum or another compatible Japanese plum is needed for full crop set.

subcategory: Caribbean Lauraceae wild avocado relative tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Laurel Avocado (West Indian Laurel, Palo de Laurel) is a medium to large forest tree of the Lauraceae family — related to true avocado (Persea americana) — native to tropical forests of the Caribbean, Central America, and northern South America, bearing oval to pear-shaped fruits resembling small avocados with greenish to purple-black skin and oily, avocado-like green flesh with a distinct laurel-leaf flavor.
directions: Plant Beilschmiedia pendula in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees are fairly drought-tolerant; harvest fruits when fully colored and give slightly to gentle pressure. Laurel Avocado is one of numerous wild Lauraceae fruit trees related to the cultivated avocado — in the Beilschmiedia genus, distributed across tropical Asia, Africa, and the Americas. The Caribbean species B. pendula produces fruits that closely resemble small avocados in appearance and texture: oval to pear-shaped, 2–3 inches long, with dark greenish to purple-black skin and green, oily, smooth-textured flesh surrounding a single large seed. The flavor is avocado-like but distinctly different — the laurel-family heritage shows in a subtle aromatic note reminiscent of bay leaves, giving the fruit a more complex character than standard avocado. Eaten fresh with salt and lime, used in local Caribbean cooking as an avocado substitute, and occasionally used to press for oil. The tree grows naturally in humid Caribbean forest and coastal woodland environments and tolerates periodic flooding better than cultivated avocado. Of interest as a potential rootstock for avocado cultivation research and as a wild relative for avocado breeding programs.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9); LeConte is partially self-fertile but produces heavier crops when cross-pollinated with Orient, Garber, or Kieffer. It requires 150–200 chill hours — excellent for zone 8–9. Site in full sun with good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; LeConte is a historic American hybrid pear (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) developed in the 19th century in the United States and named for John LeConte, Georgia naturalist. It was one of the dominant commercial pear varieties in the Deep South from the 1850s through early 20th century because of its combination of fire blight resistance (far superior to European Bartlett types), low chill requirement (150–200 hours), and productivity under Gulf Coast conditions. The large, yellowish-green pear-shaped fruits are crisp and mildly sweet — good for fresh eating, canning, and preserves, though not as richly flavored as Bartlett. Trees are vigorous, productive, and extremely long-lived; old LeConte pear trees planted before 1900 still stand and fruit in some Southern gardens. Modern pear growers in the humid South should choose LeConte over Bartlett specifically for its far superior fire blight resistance. Prune in winter to an open-center or modified central-leader form; remove water sprouts that attract fire blight. Harvest when fruit lifts easily from the branch but before fully soft.

common_name: Legacy Southern Highbush Blueberry (Late-Season Highbush Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in late winter in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Legacy is a late-season, lower-chill highbush cultivar making it more suitable for zone 8 than standard northern highbush varieties; plant with O'Neal or Bluecrop for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Legacy is a vigorous, productive, late-season highbush blueberry with relatively low chill requirements (approximately 400–600 hours) that extends the highbush blueberry season well into late summer and performs reliably in zone 8 and warmer parts of zone 9. Developed by USDA in New Jersey and released in 1993, Legacy produces medium to large, firm, sweet, aromatic berries with exceptional flavor that is considered by many blueberry connoisseurs to be among the finest-tasting highbush cultivars. The berries ripen late in the season (3–4 weeks after Bluecrop) and hold on the bush without dropping, extending the harvest window for the home garden. The vigorous, upright shrub produces attractive white spring flowers and outstanding red-orange fall foliage — one of the better blueberries for fall landscape interest. Legacy is semi-evergreen to evergreen in zone 9, which reduces winter chilling compared to deciduous cultivars — this is actually advantageous in zone 9 where chilling is the primary production limitation. For zone 9 production, pair with other low-chill southern highbush cultivars like Sunshine Blue or O'Neal. Soil pH management is critical: maintain pH between 4.5 and 5.5 using elemental sulfur treatments and acidic mulch such as pine bark or pine straw.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk has passed; in frost-free zones plant any time but avoid midsummer planting.
directions: Lemons are self-fertile and can bloom and fruit year-round in frost-free climates; Eureka and Lisbon are the commercial standards, while Meyer lemon is hardier (damaged below 22°F) and better suited to containers in cooler climates. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and fertilize with citrus-specific fertilizer three times per year. In zones 8–9, grow in large containers and bring indoors when temperatures drop below 28°F. Fruit is ready when fully yellow, slightly soft, and the rind is thin — do not wait for it to fall off the tree.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; lemon aspen is a Queensland rainforest tree producing small, round, pale-yellow fruits with intensely concentrated, complex lemon-eucalyptus-pine flavor — unrelated to true lemons (Citrus) but with a remarkably bright, complex citrus character prized in Australian native food cuisine for sauces, drinks, dressings, and as a lemon substitute.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; lemon aspen grows as a rainforest understory tree and performs best with some afternoon shade protection. Acronychia acidula (lemon aspen) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the tropical and subtropical rainforests of northeastern Queensland — one of the most distinctive flavor ingredients in Australian native cuisine and a rising star of the Australian native food industry. The tree produces small (1/2–3/4 inch), round, pale-yellow to white fruits with highly aromatic, intensely concentrated lemon-pine-eucalyptus flavor — a unique, complex, bright citrus character that is entirely different from true lemons (Citrus limon) but provides a distinctively clean, intense, herbal-citrus punch that chefs value highly. The flavor profile is often described as lemon with eucalyptus, thyme, and pine notes — a complexity that normal citrus lacks. Lemon aspen is entirely unrelated to true citrus but has evolved a remarkably similar citrus flavor independently through different chemistry. The fruits are too intense and sharp to eat fresh in quantity but are used in small amounts as flavor accents in dressings, seafood sauces, marinades, desserts, and beverages — both fresh and as preserves, oils, and freeze-dried powder. Commercially produced lemon aspen products are increasingly available in Australian specialty food stores and international gourmet markets.

subcategory: Central American small citrus-flavored Garcinia fruit
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in zone 10–12; Lemon Drop Mangosteen (Imbe, Chaparrón) is a small- to medium-fruiting Garcinia from the humid lowland forests of Costa Rica, Panama, Guatemala, and Belize — producing clusters of small, round, bright-golden-yellow to orange fruits with sweet, intensely citrus-flavored, translucent-white pulp surrounding a single seed — a unique and highly esteemed rare fruit in Central American tropical gardens.
directions: Plant Garcinia intermedia in fertile, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; provide consistent moisture throughout the year — Garcinia species do not tolerate prolonged drought; protect from cold below 40°F, especially in youth; dioecious species (both male and female plants needed for fruiting, or select self-fertile named varieties if available). Lemon Drop Mangosteen is one of the most exquisitely flavored of all Garcinia fruits — smaller than the Purple Mangosteen (Garcinia mangostana) but with a uniquely intense, sweet-tart, citrus-dominant flavor profile quite different from other Garcinias. The bright golden-yellow to orange, golf-ball-sized fruits contain translucent-white, juicy pulp segments of remarkable flavor — combining intense lemon, lime, and sweet tropical fruit notes in an almost sherbet-like profile. In Central America, the fruits are eaten fresh, used in drinks, and made into preserves; the yellow skin contains bitter compounds similar to other Garcinias and is not eaten. In zone 10–12 gardens and collections, Lemon Drop Mangosteen grows as a slow-growing, handsome ornamental tree with attractive, glossy, dark-green leaves; fruiting begins after 5–7 years from seed. An excellent greenhouse tree in cooler climates.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; lemon guava is more cold-tolerant than tropical guava, surviving brief temperatures to 22-25°F when established. The yellow-fruited variety (var. lucidum) has a milder, sweeter flavor than the red-fruited strawberry guava. INVASIVE in Hawaii and parts of Florida.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; lemon guava (yellow-fruited variety of strawberry guava) produces small, round to oval, yellow-skinned fruits with white flesh and a sweet, aromatic, guava-strawberry-lemon flavor that is milder and less acidic than the red-skinned strawberry guava (var. cattleyanum). The glossy, dark green, evergreen leaves and attractive smooth bark are ornamental year-round. Fruits eaten fresh, used in jams, jellies, and juices. Like the red strawberry guava, it is extremely adaptable and has become seriously invasive in Hawaii's native forests and in parts of Florida and the Caribbean, where it forms dense thickets that displace native vegetation. In cultivation outside of tropical areas (zone 8), it is well-behaved; in zone 9–11 it should be monitored for self-seeding. Birds are the primary seed dispersers. More cold-tolerant than tropical guava, growing in zone 8 with some frost protection. The lemon-yellow skin makes ripe fruits easy to identify for harvest.

common_name: Lemonade Berry (Lemonade Sumac, California Lemonade Berry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in fall for best establishment; lemonade berry is a California coastal native requiring excellent drainage, minimal summer water, and full sun; once established it is extremely drought tolerant and fire resistant. Best in zones 9–11 in the western US.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean soil in fall or early spring; lemonade berry is a coastal chaparral shrub of southern California prized for edible red-orange berries (technically drupes) covered in a sticky, tart coating — the berries can be soaked in cold water for 15–30 minutes to make a refreshing, pink, lemonade-like drink that indigenous Chumash and Cahuilla peoples have used for centuries. The berry flavor is strongly acidic and lemony with a resinous undertone. Absolutely drought-tolerant once established, thriving on coastal rainfall with no supplemental water after the first year — an ideal California-friendly landscape plant combining edibility with low maintenance and excellent wildlife value. Makes an attractive hedge or screen and tolerates salt spray.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the soil has warmed; tolerates heat and drought.
directions: Li is a large-fruited jujube cultivar producing sweet, apple-crisp fruit that can be eaten fresh or dried like dates. It thrives in hot summers and tolerates drought, alkaline soils, and neglect once established. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage; a second cultivar such as Lang nearby improves fruit set. Prune in late winter to remove suckers and thin the canopy, and harvest when the fruit turns fully brown.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Liberica coffee is the rare third major commercial coffee species — larger in all respects than arabica or robusta (larger tree, larger leaves, larger fruits, larger beans) — with an unusual, divisive flavor: strongly fruity, somewhat smoky, with distinctive jackfruit, dark chocolate, and floral notes that make it controversial but passionately loved by some specialty coffee drinkers; the national coffee of the Philippines (barako).
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in part shade; Liberica coffee grows as a larger tree than arabica and needs more space; tolerates slightly drier conditions than arabica. Coffea liberica (Liberica coffee or barako) is the rare third major commercial coffee species — a larger, bolder, more assertive plant than arabica (C. arabica) or robusta (C. canephora). Native to the lowland forests of Liberia and West Africa, C. liberica is a substantial tree reaching 20–35 feet (much taller than the 10–15 foot arabica shrub), with large, glossy leaves, large white flowers, and large, asymmetric, elongated coffee fruits (cherries) containing unusually shaped, irregular beans. The flavor of Liberica coffee is perhaps the most controversial in the coffee world: strongly fruity with jackfruit-like, slightly funky, floral-aromatic, sometimes smoky notes — entirely different from the clean, nuanced arabica profile or the bold-bitter robusta profile. Some specialty coffee drinkers consider Liberica's complex, funky, tropical fruit character uniquely wonderful; others find it off-putting. Liberica coffee is of particular importance in the Philippines, where it is known as barako (from a Tagalog word for a virile bull) and has strong cultural identity as the traditional Filipino coffee — once produced in significant quantities on Luzon until coffee rust devastated plantations in the 1880s. Today barako is a prized specialty product in the Philippines.

common_name: Liberty Apple (Disease-Resistant Organic Apple, Cornell Scab-Free Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Liberty requires approximately 800 chill hours, is best in zones 4–7, and is particularly recommended for home gardeners wanting to minimize or eliminate fungicide spray programs — it has strong resistance to apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew, the four most important apple diseases in the humid East.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Liberty is self-unfruitful and requires a nearby apple of a compatible variety for pollination; in disease-resistant plantings, pair with Freedom or Enterprise for cross-pollination; Liberty ripens in October producing medium to large, red-blushed fruit with good sweet-tart flavor — quality significantly above what one might expect from a disease-resistant variety. Liberty apple is a Cornell University-developed disease-resistant variety (released 1978) that has become one of the most important apple varieties for home organic production in the eastern United States, where the humid climate creates severe pressure from the four major apple diseases — apple scab, cedar-apple rust, fire blight, and powdery mildew — that require intensive fungicide spray programs to manage on standard susceptible varieties like Fuji, Gala, and McIntosh. Liberty's multiple-disease resistance package was assembled through deliberate crosses at Cornell that combined resistance genes from multiple sources: the apple scab resistance comes from Malus floribunda 821 (the same source as the PRI disease-resistant breeding program), while fire blight and rust resistance come from other wild Malus species in the parentage. The result is an apple variety that can be grown essentially spray-free in home gardens — a significant advantage for organic-minded gardeners — while still producing attractive, well-flavored fruit that compares favorably with commercial varieties. The fruit is medium to large, red-striped over yellow-green skin, with crisp, juicy, moderately sweet flesh and a pleasant balance of sweet and tart flavor. Liberty has been the recommended variety for organic home orchards from Cornell Extension for over 40 years.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed; limes are the most cold-sensitive citrus.
directions: Key lime (C. aurantiifolia) is the most cold-sensitive common citrus and is reliable only in zones 10–11; Persian lime (C. latifolia) is somewhat hardier and suits zone 9 in sheltered spots. Both are self-fertile and produce almost continuously in warm climates with adequate water. Container culture in a large pot (25+ gallons) allows limes to be grown farther north and moved indoors during frost. Fruit is best harvested while still green and fully sized — if left to yellow on the tree it becomes dry and flavorless.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring; limequat's kumquat parentage gives it excellent cold tolerance for a lime-flavored citrus.
directions: Limequat is a Key lime × kumquat hybrid combining the intense lime flavor of Citrus aurantiifolia with the cold hardiness of Fortunella, tolerating temperatures down to about 20°F — the hardiest of the lime-flavored citrus. Like kumquat, the entire fruit — sweet edible peel and sour juice pulp together — can be eaten whole or sliced into drinks and salads. Trees are self-fertile, compact, and well-suited to container culture in zones 7–8, where they can be moved indoors during hard freezes. The small oval to round fruits ripen from green to yellow in autumn through winter; harvest when fully yellow for the sweetest peel, or use while still green for the most intense lime flavor.

plant_note: Set out grafted trees after all danger of frost; grow in a large container where winters drop below 25 F.
directions: Lisbon is a vigorous, cold-tolerant lemon that fruits heavily and produces classic tart, juicy fruit almost year-round in warm regions. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and keep the graft union above the soil line. In zones colder than 9, grow in a pot that can be moved indoors or to a bright greenhouse for winter. Feed with a citrus-specific fertilizer during active growth and water deeply but allow the top inch of soil to dry between waterings. Thin fruit lightly on young trees so the branches are not overloaded.

common_name: Litchi Tomato (Morelle de Balbis, Sticky Nightshade)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil after all frost danger; litchi tomato is an extremely robust, thorny, and productive plant that self-seeds prolifically in warm climates — handle with care as the numerous spines can be painful.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; wear gloves when handling — plants are densely spiny. Solanum sisymbriifolium (litchi tomato or morelle de Balbis) is a South American tomato relative producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red berries resembling tiny tomatoes, enclosed in a spiny, papery calyx that peels back to reveal the glossy red fruit at maturity — the resemblance to lychee fruit when partially enclosed in its papery husk gives the plant its common name 'litchi tomato.' The flavor is sweet-tart, similar to a cherry tomato but with a distinct floral undertone; fruits are eaten fresh, used in jams, pies, and salsas, or dried. The plants are extremely productive in warm climates, bearing prolifically from midsummer through frost. The entire plant is covered with numerous, sharp, reddish-orange spines on stems, leaves, and calyces that make handling without gloves painful; despite this deterrent, the plants are interesting and productive specialty edibles. CAUTION: Like all nightshades, the leaves, stems, and unripe berries are toxic; consume ripe fruits only. The spiny character makes litchi tomato a useful barrier or living fence plant.

plant_note: Plant after frost; this dwarf fig stays small enough for containers that can be sheltered over winter in colder zones.
directions: Little Miss Figgy is a naturally dwarf fig reaching only about 4 to 5 feet, making it ideal for patios and small gardens. It produces sweet, deep-purple figs on new growth, often with a light second crop later in the season. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water consistently while fruit is sizing up. In zones below 7, grow it in a container and move it to an unheated garage or shed during hard freezes. Prune lightly in late winter to shape the plant and encourage fruiting wood.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun near a river bottom or moist woodland edge; double dormancy means germination occurs in the second spring — container transplants from native nurseries are the most practical establishment method.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained to occasionally wet soil in full sun along river banks, flood plains, or moist forest margins; littlehip hawthorn is one of the most graceful of the southeastern native hawthorns, with an elegant form, attractive spatula-shaped to shallowly 3-lobed leaves, and masses of tiny (1/4-inch) brilliant red haws that ripen in fall and persist on the branches well into winter. The persistent fruit crop is exceptionally valuable to winter-resident thrushes, cedar waxwings, and other berry-eating birds when larger food sources have been exhausted. White flower clusters in spring provide pollen and nectar for native bees and early butterflies. The tree's smaller stature relative to other hawthorns makes it well suited to suburban wildlife gardens and riparian restoration plantings where a medium-scale fruiting tree is needed.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; littleleaf sumac is native to dry, rocky, calcareous soils of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau and is among the most drought-tolerant native shrubs of the Southwest. Once established, it requires no supplemental irrigation.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; littleleaf sumac is a small-leaved, drought-adapted native shrub of the Chihuahuan Desert and Edwards Plateau of west and central Texas, recognized by its unusually tiny compound leaves with small, dark green, heat-tolerant leaflets. White flowers in early spring before leaf emergence are followed by small, sticky, tart red berries that are edible as a lemonade-like beverage (native peoples soaked them in water to make a refreshing drink, similar to other Rhus species). The persistent small red fruits are important food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and other desert birds through summer. Outstanding fall color — brilliant orange-red — followed by attractive winter structure. An extremely drought and heat tolerant native shrub for xeric, rocky, alkaline gardens in central and west Texas and adjacent areas.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees after all cold weather has passed; young trees are cold-sensitive and need protection until the trunk is well established.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5–6.5) in full sun; longan will not tolerate standing water or saturated roots. A brief winter cool-dry period — temperatures in the mid-40s°F for several weeks — is essential to trigger reliable flowering, making coastal south Florida and extreme south Texas the two viable zones in the continental United States. Fruit clusters ripen in summer and should be harvested by cutting whole panicles with scissors when the skin turns tan to light brown and the flesh is translucent and sweet. Prune annually after harvest to keep the canopy to a manageable height and promote new fruiting wood.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Longue d'Aout (Long of August) is named for its August ripening peak in France. In zone 9 it ripens July–September. The elongated, pear-shaped fruits distinguish it visually from round-fruited varieties. It produces moderate breba crops and abundant main crops.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Longue d'Aout is an old French heirloom fig variety named for its August ripening season, producing distinctive elongated, pear-to-tear-drop-shaped fruits with violet to purple-brown skin and amber to pink-tinged flesh with a sweet, mild, honey-fig flavor and very few seeds. The unusual elongated shape (2–3 inches long, narrowing to a pronounced neck) makes this variety immediately identifiable among more common round-fruited fig varieties and creates an elegant presentation at table. Longue d'Aout is a main-crop variety producing its primary harvest in August–September in zone 9. It grows as a moderately vigorous tree with good productivity once established. This variety is well-regarded in French fig traditions and has been grown for centuries in the south of France; its elongated form makes it particularly distinctive for display and specialty market use.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk has passed; in zones 9–11 fall planting is preferred.
directions: Loquat is an evergreen tree that flowers in fall and winter and ripens its fruit in late winter to early spring — one of the earliest fruiting trees of the season. Most varieties are self-fertile, though two trees increase crop size. Fruit clusters can be thinned at golf-ball size to produce fewer but larger fruit. Harvest when fruit is fully golden-yellow to orange, slightly soft, and sweet-tart; the thin skin is edible but seeds are large and should be discarded. Trees are cold-hardy to about 12°F but flowers and developing fruit are damaged below 28°F.

common_name: Loring Peach (Mid-South Commercial Standard Yellow Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep fertile soil; Loring requires approximately 750 chill hours, making it adaptable to zones 6–9 and well-suited to the mid-South and upper Gulf South where its chill requirement is reliably met; trees are self-fruitful but produce heavier crops with a nearby companion peach.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; thin fruit to 6–8 inches after petal fall for maximum fruit size; Loring ripens mid-season (late June to mid-July in zone 7–9) with large, well-colored yellow-fleshed freestone fruit; apply preventive fungicide starting at bud swell for brown rot and peach leaf curl control. Loring peach is one of the most widely planted commercial peach varieties in the mid-South and a benchmark mid-season variety throughout the southeastern United States, developed at the Missouri Agricultural Experiment Station (USDA collaboration) and released in 1944. The variety takes its name from Mount Loring, a traditional Missouri peach-growing area. For decades, Loring was the dominant commercial peach in Tennessee, Missouri, Arkansas, and adjacent southeastern states, praised for its reliable high yields, large fruit size, excellent flavor, and shelf life compared to other varieties of its era. The fruits are large to very large, round to slightly oblate, with a predominantly red skin over a yellow-orange background — very attractive at roadside markets and farm stands. The flesh is yellow, firm, and fully freestone at full maturity, with a well-balanced rich peach flavor that compares favorably with Elberta while generally producing larger, better-colored fruit under mid-South conditions. Loring's moderate chill requirement (approximately 750 hours) fits the climate of the mid-South better than Elberta (which needs 800–1000 hours) in years with insufficient winter cold. It has been partially replaced by newer varieties with improved disease resistance in commercial production, but remains a standard recommendation for home orchardists throughout the Southeast.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall into well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; the shrub's natural habitat preference makes it well suited to difficult sites where improved soils are unavailable.
directions: Sow fresh seeds in fall directly into sandy, well-drained soil, as Low Serviceberry is adapted to dry, rocky ground and performs poorly in rich or consistently moist conditions. Winter cold provides the stratification seeds need, and seedlings emerge in spring when soil temperatures warm to 40–55 degrees Fahrenheit. This spreading, colony-forming shrub is excellent for naturalizing slopes, stabilizing sandy soils, and providing wildlife habitat; allow adequate space for root-sprouting colonies to develop. Expect the first berry crop 2–5 years after transplanting; the sweet, dark blue fruits ripen in midsummer and are relished by birds and mammals.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free to near-frost-free conditions; lucuma is damaged below 28–30°F but tolerates brief cool temperatures better than most tropical fruit trees. Grafted trees begin fruiting in 3–5 years versus 7–10 years for seedlings. Good drainage is essential — it does not tolerate waterlogged soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun in a frost-free location; lucuma is a Peruvian fruit tree native to the Andean valleys, where it has been cultivated since ancient times and was called the 'Gold of the Incas.' The large, oval fruits (3–4 inches) have a dry, starchy, bright orange-yellow flesh with an extraordinary flavor — intensely sweet with a rich, complex caramel-maple-sweet potato quality that is completely unlike any familiar fruit. The taste is so distinctive and rich that lucuma powder (dried, ground lucuma flesh) is used as a natural sweetener and flavoring for ice cream, smoothies, pastries, and confections in Peru, where lucuma ice cream outsells chocolate and vanilla in many surveys. The flavor is particularly popular as a low-glycemic sweetener alternative. Fresh lucuma is eaten locally in Peru and Chile but ships poorly, so it is rarely found fresh outside its home region. An exceptional specialty fruit tree for collectors in frost-free zones.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost risk; in zone 9 plant March–May. Lula is a hybrid avocado with West Indian and Guatemalan ancestry that provides moderate cold tolerance — surviving temperatures down to approximately 24–26°F when established. Plant in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate available: south-facing walls, raised beds, and sheltered positions increase cold tolerance significantly. Young trees under 3 years are more frost-sensitive than established trees.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — avocados are extremely sensitive to root rot in poorly drained or clay soils; Lula is a historic Florida avocado cultivar developed by George Lula in Homestead, Florida in the 1920s and valued for its combination of good cold hardiness, large fruit size, and excellent fresh-eating quality. The large fruits (often 12–18 ounces) have smooth green skin that remains green when ripe — ripeness is determined by giving the fruit a gentle squeeze, not by color change. The flesh is pale yellow-green, creamy, and mild-flavored with good avocado oil content. Lula is classified as a hybrid between West Indian and Guatemalan race avocados, inheriting moderate cold tolerance from its Guatemalan genetics and fruiting reliability from its West Indian parentage. In zone 9 Lula is one of the more reliable cultivars for home production; the long, warm growing season develops the oil content that gives mature fruits their buttery richness. Cross-pollinate with a Type A avocado such as Bacon for best fruit set.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost risk has passed; in zones 10–11, fall planting after summer heat breaks is preferred.
directions: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) in a site sheltered from salt spray and drying winter wind; lychee cannot tolerate waterlogged roots at any age. Trees require a cool-dry stress period of 4–6 weeks in late autumn — nights reliably below 59°F — to trigger flower bud development, so hold irrigation during that window rather than watering on a regular schedule. Fruit clusters develop rapidly after bloom and benefit from thinning to 3–5 fruits per panicle when marble-sized to improve final fruit size and reduce limb stress. Harvest clusters when the rough, bumpy skin has turned fully red to pinkish-red and the aroma is distinctly floral and sweet, typically 90–112 days after bloom.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost; macadamias grow best in frost-free zones with well-distributed rainfall.
directions: Macadamias are self-fertile but cross-pollination between two or more varieties meaningfully increases yields; grafted trees start bearing at 3–5 years, while seedlings can take 10–15 years. The tree prefers well-drained, slightly acid soil (pH 5.5–6.5) and is sensitive to root disturbance — plant without disturbing the root ball. Trees produce racemes of cream-white flowers that fall and create a slippery surface; harvesting is done by collecting nuts that have dropped naturally as the green husk splits and the nut falls. Shell and dry nuts for 3–4 weeks before cracking; the shells require a commercial or heavy-duty nut cracker as they are among the hardest of any food nut.

plant_note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; grafted trees produce in 4–6 years vs. 8–12 from seed; macadamia is native to the subtropical rainforests of southeast Queensland and northeast New South Wales — the only major commercial nut crop to originate from Australia — producing the world's most expensive commercial nut, with creamy, buttery, sweet, incomparably rich flavor.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; protect from frost below 26°F until established; plant 2+ varieties for cross-pollination and better yields. Macadamia integrifolia (smooth-shell macadamia) is one of the world's most celebrated nut trees and the only major food crop originating in Australia — native to the subtropical rainforests of southeast Queensland. The macadamia nut is universally recognized as one of the finest-flavored nuts in the world: round, ivory-white, buttery-smooth, with an extraordinarily rich, creamy, sweet flavor unlike any other nut. The fat content (75%) is predominantly monounsaturated, making macadamia oil one of the most desirable culinary and cosmetic plant oils. The smooth-shell species (M. integrifolia) is the primary commercial macadamia — most Hawaiian, Australian, South African, and Kenyan commercial orchards are primarily or entirely M. integrifolia or its hybrids. Trees are evergreen, grow slowly to 25–35 feet, produce dark-green, glossy, leathery leaves, and begin bearing in 5–7 years from grafted stock. The extremely hard shell (requiring 300+ psi to crack) requires a specialized macadamia cracker. Zone 9b–11, damaged below 26°F. Hawaii, California, and South Florida can grow macadamia commercially; zone 9a gardens can succeed with protected sites.

common_name: Macoun Apple (Beloved Northeast Eating Apple, McIntosh-Type Geneva Station Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Macoun requires approximately 1000 chill hours and cross-pollination — plant with Cortland, Empire, or McIntosh; Macoun is a mid-to-late-season variety (ripening October in most of New York and New England) with a high chill requirement that limits it to zones 4–7; the trees are moderately biennial-bearing, often producing a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter crop the next.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic fertile soil in full sun; requires cross-pollinator; thin biennial crops by hand-removing half the fruit clusters in early summer to encourage annual bearing; Macoun ripens October and must be harvested at peak ripeness — slightly soft at the stem end, fully red, and with characteristic spicy aroma — as it deteriorates quickly after peak. Macoun apple was developed at the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva from a cross involving McIntosh, and named for W.T. Macoun, Dominion Horticulturalist of Canada who made significant contributions to fruit breeding and evaluation — released in 1923, making it roughly contemporary with McIntosh's commercial rise. Among apple connoisseurs of the northeastern United States, Macoun occupies a unique status: it is considered by many the finest-eating apple of any variety available in New York and New England, with a complex, spicy-sweet, intensely aromatic flavor at peak ripeness that exceeds even McIntosh in intensity and depth. The fruit is medium-sized, dark red (often nearly all-red with a purple-red hue at full maturity), with pure white, tender, very juicy flesh and the characteristic McIntosh floral fragrance amplified. Macoun's intense flavor comes with a significant limitation: the variety has a very short window of peak eating quality — typically 1–2 weeks at the height of ripeness in October — after which the flesh softens rapidly and flavor diminishes. This poor keeping quality has limited Macoun's commercial viability but made it a cult variety among farmers' market customers who know to seek it out during its brief peak season.

common_name: Madison Peach (Cold-Hardy Virginia Heirloom Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep, fertile soil; Madison requires approximately 850 chill hours and is one of the most cold-hardy named peach varieties, with flower buds tolerating temperatures down to 0°F or below — significantly more cold-resistant than Elberta and other standard varieties, making it the premier choice for orchards in zones 4–6 where late spring frosts or severe winter cold reduce peach production reliability.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Madison is self-fruitful; thin fruit in spring to 6–8 inches; this variety is particularly valuable where late spring frosts endanger developing blossoms — its cold-hardy flower buds and frost resistance make it among the most reliable peach varieties in colder zones. Madison peach was developed at the Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (released 1963) as part of a program to develop peach varieties combining high fruit quality with improved cold-hardiness of the flower buds — addressing the primary limitation on peach production in the colder parts of the South and the lower Midwest where late spring frosts can destroy the blossoms of standard varieties like Elberta even in years when winter temperatures are adequate for the trees to survive. The key innovation of Madison is its extraordinary flower bud cold-hardiness: Madison buds have been documented surviving temperatures of -5°F to 0°F with minimal damage in some trials, making it significantly more frost-resilient than Elberta (whose buds are damaged at 28–30°F during bloom). This characteristic translates to reliable cropping in zones 4–6 where other varieties fail every few years due to late frost blossom kill. The fruits are medium to large, red-blushed over golden-yellow skin, with firm, yellow, fully freestone flesh and a well-flavored, balanced sweet-tart peach quality. Madison ripens in mid-season (late July to mid-August in its Virginia homeland, somewhat earlier in warmer zones). It remains one of the most important variety recommendations for cold-region home orchardists in the Mid-Atlantic, Appalachian, and upper Midwest states.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Mahan produces some of the largest pecan nuts of any cultivar but has a lower kernel percentage and is more prone to alternate bearing than modern selections.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. One of the earliest widely planted named pecan cultivars, dating to the early 1900s, Mahan is known for producing exceptionally large nuts, among the biggest of any pecan cultivar, though the kernel fill and disease resistance lag behind modern breeding selections. It remains of historical interest and is still grown in some older orchards and by collectors of heirloom pecan varieties for its striking nut size, even though it has largely been superseded commercially by higher-yielding, more scab-resistant cultivars.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained to moderately well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Mahua is a large tropical tree of paramount economic and cultural importance in India — the fleshy, sweet, edible flowers are used to distill a traditional fermented spirit (mahua liquor), the seeds yield a high-quality edible and industrial fat (mahua butter), and the tree is sacred to numerous Indian tribal communities.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, deep soil in full sun; mahua is drought-tolerant once established and thrives on poor soils. Madhuca longifolia (mahua or Indian butter tree) is a large, slow-growing tropical tree native to the forests of central and southern India, deeply woven into the culture and economy of indigenous tribal communities across Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, and Madhya Pradesh. The tree provides multiple distinct food, economic, and cultural products: the fleshy, sweet, cream-colored flowers (corollas) that drop prolifically in spring are edible and extremely sweet — they are eaten fresh (tasting like a mild honey-flower combination), sun-dried and used as a sweetener, fermented into mahua wine, and distilled into mahua liquor, one of India's most important traditional tribal spirits and an important livelihood product. The seeds contain 30–40% mahua butter (a semi-solid vegetable fat) with a composition similar to cocoa butter, used in traditional cuisine, soap-making, and cosmetics. The leaves provide fodder; the bark and flowers have Ayurvedic uses. Mahua is considered a 'tree of life' by many Indian adivasi (tribal) communities — the flowers are economically critical, often constituting a significant fraction of tribal household income in forest villages. A remarkable tree with enormous cultural depth and genuine multiple-use value.

common_name: Malabar Chestnut (Money Tree, Guiana Chestnut, Saba Nut)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; in zone 9a protect from frost — young trees are killed by hard freezes, though established trees may resprout from the base after a light freeze. Full sun to partial shade; tolerates wet or seasonally flooded soils well, which makes it valuable near ponds or in low spots where other trees struggle.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained to seasonally wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Malabar chestnut is best known to most people as the ornamental 'money tree' with braided trunks sold as a houseplant across the world, but it is also a genuine food plant producing 12-inch oval pods filled with 20–25 large, edible seeds that taste remarkably like chestnuts or roasted peanuts when cooked — the seeds can be roasted, boiled, or ground into flour, and the young leaves and flowers are edible as vegetables. As a landscape tree in zone 9b–12 it can reach 30–40 feet in the ground with a spreading tropical canopy, but is easy to keep pruned to 10–15 feet. The large, palmate leaves and buttressed trunk give it outstanding ornamental character. Native to the seasonally flooded forests of Central and South America, it tolerates both dry periods and extended flooding — a rare combination that makes it valuable for challenging low-lying sites.

common_name: Malay Apple (Mountain Apple, Jambu Bol, Rose Apple Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Malay Apple is frost-sensitive and suitable for zone 10-11 outdoor planting or zone 9 container culture. The tree exhibits cauliflory — flowers and fruits emerge directly from the trunk and major branches, not the growing tips. Fruiting begins within 3–5 years of planting. The fruits mature in spring to early summer and must be harvested promptly as they do not store well.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Malay Apple grows most rapidly with regular watering and fertilization in the warm humid conditions of zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and South Florida. Syzygium malaccense is a large, fast-growing, evergreen fruit tree native to Malaysia and the Indonesian islands, now cultivated throughout the tropics from the Pacific Islands to Central America, Africa, and the Caribbean. The tree is doubly ornamental: in spring, it produces spectacular displays of crimson-red to deep rose-purple flowers that emerge directly from the bark of the trunk and major branches (cauliflory), creating an extraordinary effect of flowers growing from the wood — dozens to hundreds of 1-inch flowers with brush-like clusters of bright crimson stamens covering the trunk in a fiery display. These flowers are followed by the fruits: dark red to magenta, pear-shaped, 2–3 inch fruits with white, spongy, mildly sweet flesh and a faint floral flavor — eaten fresh throughout Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands and used in jams and beverages. The tree is an important crop and dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical Oceania and Southeast Asia. The Hawaiian name 'Ohia Ai' (mountain apple) reflects its long cultivation history in the Hawaiian Islands. In zone 10-11 South Florida landscapes, it serves as both an ornamental shade tree and a productive home fruit tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; mamey apple is killed by any frost and requires a truly tropical or subtropical climate. It is slow-growing but extremely long-lived — trees in the Caribbean are known to exceed 100 years in age. Grafted trees bear fruit earlier than seedlings.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; mamey apple is a large, stately fruit tree native to the Caribbean, Mexico, and northern South America, producing round to oval fruits 3–8 inches across with a thick, rough, bitter brown-russet skin enclosing firm, apricot-orange to yellow flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavor suggesting apricot, vanilla, and almond — quite unlike most other tropical fruits. The flavor is complex and distinctive: the outer flesh directly under the skin can be slightly bitter, while the inner flesh is sweet and aromatic. The tree is magnificent as a landscape specimen — densely leafy, with thick, glossy, oval leaves and a formal, dome-shaped crown. Small, white, fragrant flowers appear on the branches directly. The timber is dense and valuable. Not to be confused with Mamey Sapote (Pouteria sapota), an entirely different fruit despite the similar name. Mamey apple was a staple food of the Taino people of the Caribbean before European contact and was described by Columbus's men. It is now primarily grown in Cuba, the Dominican Republic, and Mexico.
