plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mamey sapote is a Central American tropical tree suited to zones 10–12, with mature established trees tolerating brief drops to 28–30°F in protected zone 9b microclimates. Named grafted varieties such as 'Magaña' and 'Pantin' begin producing the distinctive brown-skinned, salmon-fleshed fruits within 3–5 years of planting.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; mamey sapote (Pouteria sapota) is a majestic Central American tree in the Sapotaceae family that produces one of the most beloved tropical fruits in Caribbean and Latin American cuisine — a large, russet-brown, football-shaped fruit with vivid salmon-to-brick-red flesh of exceptional richness, sweetness, and smooth texture, often compared to a pumpkin-sweet potato-almond fusion. The fruit is eaten fresh, blended into milkshakes and batidos (a staple across Miami's Cuban community and throughout the Caribbean), made into ice cream, and used in desserts. Only grafted trees of named selections should be planted, as seedling trees can take 10–15 years to fruit and produce variable quality; grafted trees begin bearing in 3–5 years. Mamey sapote is moderately drought-tolerant once established but produces larger, higher-quality fruit with consistent irrigation and regular fertilization with a balanced citrus-type fertilizer.

plant_note: Plant grafted or air-layered trees in warm, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed; mamoncillo is strictly tropical and is damaged below 28°F. Grafted trees may begin fruiting in 5–8 years versus 10–15 years for seedlings. A single tree may produce fruit but two trees of different seedling origin improves fruiting.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun in frost-free climates; mamoncillo (Spanish lime, quenepa, genip) is a large tropical tree native to Central America and the Caribbean that produces clusters of golf-ball-sized green fruits with a brittle outer skin concealing a translucent, salmon-colored pulp clinging tightly to a large seed. The flavor is a unique combination — simultaneously sweet-tart, tropical, and faintly lime-like with a passionfruit quality — that is utterly distinctive among tropical fruits. Fruits are eaten by biting through the skin and sucking the pulp off the seed, which is the traditional way to consume them across the Caribbean. They are also made into juice, fermented into wine, and processed into candy. Mamoncillo is an important street-food fruit in Puerto Rico, Colombia, Cuba, and throughout the Caribbean, where it is eaten fresh out of hand in large quantities. The tree is drought-tolerant once established and very long-lived.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost; mandarins are among the hardiest citrus, tolerating brief dips to 24°F.
directions: Mandarins (including tangerines, clementines, and satsumas) are the most cold-hardy of the common sweet citrus, with satsumas surviving to about 15°F and thriving in zone 8. Most are self-fertile, though some varieties set more fruit with a compatible pollinator nearby. Fruit tends to ripen earlier in the season than oranges — from October through January depending on variety — and the loose peel and sweet-tart flavor make them popular for fresh eating. Avoid overwatering, as mandarins are somewhat drought-tolerant and susceptible to root rot in wet soils.

plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; mandarins are generally more cold-hardy than sweet oranges and many are self-fruitful, though cross-pollination from other citrus usually improves fruit set and fruit size.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Citrus reticulata is the species encompassing all mandarins, tangerines, satsumas, clementines, and most mandarin-type hybrids — a diverse group of loose-skinned, easily peeled, aromatic citrus originating in Southeast Asia and southern China that includes hundreds of named varieties ranging from tiny, seedless clementines to large, deeply flavored Ponkans. As a group, mandarins are the most cold-hardy common citrus (Satsuma types tolerating temperatures to 18–22°F when established) and one of the most adaptable to Gulf South conditions, performing well in zones 8b–11 where sweet oranges or grapefruit might struggle with cold or humidity-related issues. Key mandarin varieties for Gulf South gardens include Satsuma (most cold-hardy), Owari Satsuma, Owens Navel, Clementine, Ponkan, Murcott (Honey mandarin), and Dancy tangerine. Most mandarins ripen November through February, and the loose skin that peels easily by hand makes them the most user-friendly fresh citrus. The species is very adaptable to container culture, making it practical for zone 8 gardeners who want moveable citrus.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after all frost risk has passed; in zones 10b–11 the rainy-season break in early spring is the optimal planting window.
directions: Plant grafted trees of named cultivars (Kent, Tommy Atkins, Haden, Keitt) rather than seedlings; grafted trees fruit in 3–5 years and produce fruit true to type. Mangoes require a cool-dry period of 4–6 weeks during winter — nights below 60°F without frost — to trigger uniform flowering; excess rainfall during bloom causes anthracnose and poor fruit set. Prune after harvest each year by removing one-quarter to one-third of the outer canopy to keep the tree at a manageable height and promote fresh fruiting wood. Fruit is ripe when the shoulders near the stem fill out, color develops according to the cultivar, and the flesh yields slightly to pressure; the stem end is often the last to color.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; in zone 9 plant February–March. Mango is a named cultivar from the USDA breeding program at Beltsville that produces distinctly mango-like fruit flavor. Requires a second pawpaw variety for cross-pollination; use another named cultivar within 50 feet. Avoid disturbing the fragile taproot at transplanting.
directions: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Mango Pawpaw is a named USDA-selected cultivar known for producing fruits with a distinctly tropical, mango-like flavor quality that is more pronounced than in typical seedling pawpaws — a richer, more aromatic, tropical sweetness beyond the standard banana-vanilla pawpaw flavor. The medium to large fruits weigh 6–12 ounces with bright yellow flesh and a creamy, custard-like texture. Mango is considered one of the finest-flavored named pawpaw cultivars in the Corwin Davis breeding tradition and is widely used in taste trials as a benchmark for outstanding pawpaw flavor. Like all pawpaw cultivars, Mango requires cross-pollination from a different named cultivar — plant alongside Overleese, Wells, or NC-1 for reliable fruit set. Ripe fruits fall from the tree in September–October and must be refrigerated or eaten within a few days; the short shelf life is inherent to the species.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a site with reliably warm temperatures year-round; mangosteen is extremely sensitive to cold and drought stress.
directions: Mangosteen is one of the slowest-growing and most demanding tropical fruit trees, requiring deep, rich, well-drained, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5), humidity above 80%, and temperatures that never fall below 40°F or rise above 100°F. It is apomictic — seed-grown trees are genetically identical to the mother, eliminating the need for pollinators, though fruit set is parthenocarpic in cultivation. Young trees require shade for the first several years; gradually transition to full sun as the canopy develops. Harvest when the thick purple rind has deepened to a dark maroon-purple and yields slightly to thumb pressure, typically 5–6 months after fruit set.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Manila Tamarind is more cold-hardy than most tropical fruits — established trees survive light frosts to approximately 24–26°F and quickly resprout from the roots if frozen back. In zone 9 the tree is semi-deciduous in cold winters. The twisted, ornamental seed pods ripen from December through May. Trees may naturalize in zone 9 conditions and should be sited where fruit drop is not a nuisance.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, poor-to-fertile soil — Manila Tamarind is extremely drought-tolerant and thrives in lean, sandy, even compacted soils where most fruit trees fail; Manila Tamarind (also known as guamúchil, Madras thorn, or camachile) is a thorny, tropical legume tree from Mexico and Central America that produces coiled, bright red-and-white seed pods containing sweet, fibrous white pulp surrounding shiny black seeds. The sweet-tart, cotton-candy-like flavor of the fresh white aril (the edible fleshy layer around the seeds) is popular in Mexican street food markets and throughout tropical Asia where the tree has naturalized. Despite the common name, Manila Tamarind is not related to true tamarind (Tamarindus indica) but belongs to the legume family with nitrogen-fixing roots. The tree is highly productive and drought-tolerant, making it valuable for edible landscape use in hot, dry zone 9 conditions. Pods are harvested when the husks split open to reveal the red-pink exterior and white interior with sweet pulp.

common_name: Manzanilla Olive (Spanish Table Olive Standard, Green Martini Olive, Seville Table Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Manzanilla is self-fertile and produces well as a single tree though cross-pollination with Sevillano, Frantoio, or another olive variety increases yields; it requires approximately 300–400 chill hours, well-suited to California, the Gulf South, and similar zones 8–10 climates; Manzanilla blooms somewhat earlier than some other varieties, extending the effective pollen window.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Manzanilla is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for green table olives in October when fully sized but still green; harvest for black table olives in November–December when fully ripe; home-cured Manzanilla olives require brine treatment for 6–12 months to remove bitter oleuropein before eating. Manzanilla (meaning 'little apple' in Spanish, for the round fruit shape) is the dominant commercial table olive variety in the world — the variety behind the iconic green olives stuffed with pimentos found in cocktail jars and martini glasses throughout the Western world, and a major component of Spanish, American, and Mexican table olive production. Its origin is in the Seville region of Spain (particularly the province of Huelva), where it has been the foundation of the Spanish table olive trade since the 1800s, and it was introduced to California (where it is called 'Manzanillo') in the 19th century with California's Spanish-mission heritage, becoming established in the central California olive-growing regions (Fresno, Madera counties) and eventually as the dominant commercial table olive variety in the United States. The olives are medium-sized, round to slightly oblate, with firm, meaty flesh and a relatively small pit that makes them ideal for stuffing — the characteristic American 'green olive' of commercial production is almost always a Manzanilla cured at the green stage. The trees are medium-sized (15–25 feet), productive, and adapted to a wide range of California and Gulf South conditions with adequate drainage and minimal rainfall during the ripening period.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Manzanillo is largely self-fertile though a compatible pollinizer such as Mission improves fruit set, and it grows into a larger, traditional-sized tree than compact modern cultivars like Arbequina.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Manzanillo is a classic Spanish olive cultivar and the most widely grown table olive variety in the world, valued for its large, plump, meaty fruit with a favorable flesh-to-pit ratio that makes it the standard choice for brine-cured green and black table olives found in grocery stores worldwide. The tree bears heavily and reliably, and while it can also be pressed for oil, its primary use and reputation is as a table olive. Harvest green in fall for green-cured olives, or let fruit ripen to black for black-cured olives, then cure in brine or lye solution for several weeks to months to remove natural bitterness before eating; olives are inedible straight off the tree. The tree grows to a more traditional, larger size than modern compact cultivars, so allow ample space.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Manzano is less cold-hardy than Cavendish or Orinoco types and is best suited to zone 9b–11 or container culture in cooler climates where it can be overwintered indoors.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Manzano banana (also called Apple Banana, Finger Banana, or 'Bocadillo' in Colombia) is a widely grown short-fruited banana popular throughout Latin America and the Caribbean, producing plump, stubby fruits (3–5 inches long, broader in proportion than Cavendish) with a distinctive, complex flavor reminiscent of strawberry and apple when fully ripe — a significantly more aromatic and interesting eating experience than a standard Cavendish. The fruits turn bright yellow and then develop black skin patches as they ripen, and the flesh remains firm even when sweet and fully ripe, giving them better shelf life than many banana types. Manzano banana plants are more compact than Cavendish (8–12 feet versus 12–20 feet) making them practical for smaller yards. Manzano is moderately susceptible to Black Sigatoka and should be grown in well-drained, well-fertilized conditions with regular irrigation; it thrives in Gulf Coast conditions (zones 9b–11) but pseudostems are killed by even brief freezes.

plant_note: Sow 3 seeds per planting spot 1/2 inch deep after frost danger passes, thin to strongest plant; or start transplants 6 weeks early and transplant after frost; 'Maradol' plants include males and females — plant 2–3 plants to ensure a bisexual or female plant is included, and remove male plants (identified by long-stalked tubular flowers) after sex is determined, keeping one male per 8–10 females if needed.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Maradol is the dominant commercial papaya of Mexico and the variety most commonly sold in American supermarkets, producing very large, oblong fruits (3–8 pounds, sometimes to 10 pounds) with distinctive salmon-red to deep orange flesh, moderate to high sweetness, and a mild, pleasant, non-musky flavor that appeals to consumers who find tropical Solo papayas too strongly flavored. The skin turns from green to yellow-orange at ripeness, with clear indicator spots appearing near the stem. 'Maradol' plants are dioecious (separate male and female plants) which means planting multiple trees is necessary to ensure fruiting; approximately one-third of seedlings are male. The tall plants (10–18 feet under optimal conditions) bear heavily from the main trunk, with fruits maturing in dense clusters below the umbrella of large leaves. Originally developed in Cuba, 'Maradol' is now the main papaya in Mexico's Veracruz and Tabasco production regions and thrives in Gulf Coast conditions — hot humid summers, mild winters, and fertile lowland soils of zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant seedlings or air-layered cuttings in deep, moist, fertile, well-drained tropical soil; marang requires genuine tropical conditions (zone 11-12) and high humidity; it is cultivated in southern Mindanao (Philippines), Borneo, and throughout Southeast Asia as a valued fruit tree.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, rich, consistently moist, well-drained tropical soil; marang (Artocarpus odoratissimus) is a close relative of breadfruit and jackfruit, native to Borneo and Mindanao, producing rounded, yellow-green fruits about the size of a small jackfruit with an extremely sweet, creamy white flesh surrounding large, edible seeds — many who have tasted it rank it among the finest tropical fruits, with a rich, sweet, almost vanilla-custard flavor with a fragrant aroma. The seeds are also edible when cooked (roasted, boiled, or ground) and have a pleasant chestnut-like flavor. Strictly tropical and not tolerant of any frost; best suited for south Florida and Hawaii collections and food-forest enthusiasts in zone 11+. Less well-known outside Southeast Asia but increasingly available from specialty nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil; Marbrite is an Italian fig variety valued for its pale green skin and sweet, amber-white flesh, offering a distinct fresh-eating alternative to the pink- and red-fleshed figs most common in Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun. Marbrite is an Italian fig cultivar bearing medium-sized figs with pale green to yellow-green skin and sweet, translucent amber to white flesh, a lighter-colored departure from the deep pink and red interiors of Gulf Coast standards like Celeste and Brown Turkey. It typically produces two crops in warm climates: a smaller breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer, followed by a larger main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Figs fruit on both second-year wood and current-season growth, so avoid heavy winter pruning, which removes the breba crop; light shaping after the main harvest is sufficient. Trees are vigorous and productive once established and rarely need fertilizer, though a layer of mulch over the root zone helps in zone 7-8 where occasional hard freezes can damage unprotected roots. Harvest when fruit softens and the neck bends over, since figs do not ripen further once picked.

common_name: Marcona Almond (Spanish Queen of Almonds, Round Blanched Premium Almond)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun in a Mediterranean or dry-summer climate; Marcona is self-incompatible and requires a companion almond variety for pollination; requires approximately 200–300 chill hours, making it suitable for warmer zones 8–10 with mild winters; it is specifically adapted to the dry, calcareous soils and Mediterranean climate of coastal Spain.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile soil (calcareous or sandy loam preferred) in full sun; Marcona requires a companion pollenizer variety; harvest in late summer when hulls begin to split; the round, flat kernels are best roasted in olive oil and sea salt in the traditional Spanish preparation — the rich, buttery texture of roasted Marcona is distinctly different from any California variety. Marcona is a Spanish almond variety traditionally grown along the eastern Mediterranean coast of Spain (the Valencian Community and Murcia region) that has become known internationally as the 'queen of almonds' for its extraordinarily rich, buttery flavor and distinctive round, flat shape that makes it immediately recognizable on a charcuterie board or tapas spread. The flavor difference between Marcona and California varieties (Nonpareil, Mission, Carmel) is significant and immediately apparent to tasters: Marcona has a much higher fat content and a softer, more buttery texture with a sweeter, more intensely almond-flavored profile — often described as having hints of marzipan and fresh sweetness that California varieties cannot replicate. The traditional preparation — blanched (skin removed), roasted in olive oil, and salted — is the standard presentation in Spanish tapas and increasingly common in American specialty food and charcuterie culture. Marcona's very low chill requirement (200–300 hours) makes it the almond most adapted to warm-winter zones 8–10 where standard California varieties may also grow, but Marcona's flavor sets it apart for culinary use. Not as productive as California commercial varieties in California growing conditions.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun; Marigoule bears young and reliably and benefits from a second chestnut cultivar nearby for best pollination.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety nearby. Bred in France from a cross of European and Japanese chestnut, Marigoule combines good resistance to chestnut blight and ink disease with large, easy-to-peel nuts and a precocious habit, often bearing within a few years of planting. It has become a popular choice in North American chestnut orchards specifically because its hybrid vigor and disease tolerance let it thrive where the straight American chestnut has been devastated by blight. The tree is moderately vigorous and more compact than a full-sized American chestnut, making it a practical choice for a home orchard or food forest planting.

common_name: Marsh Grapefruit (Seedless White Grapefruit, Marsh Seedless)
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; grapefruit trees are large and require adequate space (20–25 feet diameter at maturity), so site carefully; Marsh is self-fruitful and productive without a pollinator.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; Marsh grapefruit (introduced commercially around 1860 from a seedling found in Florida) is the foundational white grapefruit of the citrus industry — virtually all seedless white grapefruits sold commercially today are Marsh or descended from it. The large, round, pale-yellow fruits (4–5 inches diameter) are nearly or completely seedless (a major practical advantage over older seedy varieties like Duncan), with pale-cream to light-yellow flesh, balanced sweet-tart grapefruit flavor, and abundant juice. The flavor is the benchmark classic grapefruit flavor — moderately tart with characteristic bitterness from naringin — excellent eaten fresh (halved and sectioned with a serrated spoon), juiced, or used in salads and cocktails. The large tree (15–20 feet when mature, larger on vigorous rootstocks) is cold-hardier than many citrus and can tolerate brief temperatures to about 26–28°F when established. Marsh grapefruit is the parent of most modern grapefruit varieties, including Ruby Red (a bud sport of Marsh) and Thompson Pink. Ripens November through May in Florida; the fruits hold on the tree exceptionally well, improving in flavor through winter.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in early spring; in zone 9 plant January–March. Maru is a pollination-variant astringent (PVA) persimmon — when unpollinated, the fruit remains astringent until fully soft; when cross-pollinated, the seeds stimulate the flesh to develop dark-colored, non-astringent regions (jelly-like, very sweet spots) even before the fruit softens. Plant with a male persimmon or another D. kaki cultivar within 50 feet for full PVA expression.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Maru is a Japanese persimmon cultivar that exemplifies the PVA (pollination-variant astringent) type — uniquely, the flavor and texture of its fruit changes dramatically based on whether the flower was pollinated. Unpollinated Maru fruits are uniformly orange-colored and astringent until fully ripe-soft; pollinated fruits develop dark brown or black spots and streaks in the flesh (called 'chocolate flesh') around the seeds, and these dark regions are sweet, jelly-like, and completely non-astringent while still firm — a prized texture and flavor combination. Fully pollinated Maru fruits may have most of the flesh dark-colored and sweet, making them among the most interesting persimmon-eating experiences available. In zone 9 Maru produces reliable crops of medium-sized, round to slightly oblate fruits ripening in October–November. The dark flesh and sweet, pudding-like texture of cross-pollinated fruits makes Maru an outstanding garden and fresh-market variety.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in late spring in full sun with very well-drained, deep soil; Marula is highly drought-tolerant once established but intolerant of waterlogged soils. Marula is dioecious — separate male and female trees are required for fruit production; purchase sexed (grafted) stock from specialty nurseries or plant 2–3 seedlings and hope for mixed sexes. Established trees in zone 9b have survived brief dips to 26–28°F. Young trees require frost protection for the first 2–3 winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil of any type — Marula is remarkably adaptable to poor, sandy, or rocky soils and intensely drought-tolerant, thriving in conditions that challenge most fruit trees. Sclerocarya birrea subsp. caffra (Marula) is a large, spreading, deciduous African fruit tree native to the woodlands and savannas from Ethiopia and Nigeria south to South Africa, famous throughout sub-Saharan Africa as one of the most important traditional food and beverage trees of the continent. The plum-sized fruits (1–1.5 inches diameter) ripen in December–March in South Africa; in zone 9 they ripen in late summer–fall. When ripe, the thin, pale yellow skin covers soft, extremely juicy, intensely aromatic flesh with a rich, complex flavor combining tropical fruit notes reminiscent of mango, pineapple, and lychee — prized fresh, fermented into a traditional beer, and distilled into the popular Amarula Cream liqueur (produced commercially in South Africa). The large, brown, extremely hard seeds inside each fruit contain edible kernels with a rich, nutty flavor and high oil content used in traditional African cosmetics. Elephants travel great distances to feed on fallen marula fruits, giving rise to the folklore that they become inebriated — a myth, though the fruits do ferment rapidly when fallen. Marula is increasingly grown as an edible landscape tree in zone 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Marumi is among the most cold-hardy kumquats and, like other kumquats, is eaten whole, skin and all, since the sweet rind contrasts with tart flesh.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Marumi is one of the oldest kumquat cultivars grown, producing small, round fruit with thin, sweet, edible skin surrounding a tarter, seedier pulp, eaten whole rather than peeled. It is among the more cold-hardy kumquats and, being a naturally small, dense shrub, adapts well to container culture and can be moved under cover during hard freezes in the cooler parts of its range. Fruit ripens in winter and holds on the tree for weeks without dropping, giving a long, flexible harvest window; established plants are otherwise low-maintenance and require only routine citrus fertilizing.

plant_note: Plant only where winters stay above freezing; young trees are very frost-sensitive and benefit from wind protection.
directions: Mauritius is a productive lychee bearing rough-skinned red fruit with sweet, fragrant, translucent flesh. It needs a frost-free subtropical or tropical climate with a brief cool, dry period to trigger flowering. Plant in full sun in deep, acidic, well-drained soil and protect young trees from wind and cold. Water generously during flowering and fruit development but ease off during the winter rest period. Mulch heavily to keep the shallow roots moist and feed with a balanced fertilizer through the growing season.

common_name: Maxine Pear (Starking Delicious Fire Blight-Resistant Southern Pear)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Maxine, also sold as Starking Delicious, is a large-fruited fire blight-resistant pear developed for Southern growing conditions, similar in use and reliability to Moonglow and Orient.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maxine cross-pollinates well with Moonglow, Orient, Kieffer, and most other fire blight-resistant Southern pear varieties. Maxine, also marketed as Starking Delicious, was developed for good disease resistance and reliable production in the humid Southeast, where fire blight quickly kills susceptible European pear varieties like Bartlett. It produces large, smooth, yellow-green fruit with sweet, juicy, only lightly gritty flesh, notably larger than many of its fire-blight-resistant peers, ripening in late summer. Like most Southern-adapted pears, it should be picked while still firm and green and ripened off the tree in a cool spot for the best texture and flavor, since fruit left to ripen on the tree tends to soften unevenly from the core outward. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the strong disease resistance means Maxine needs little to no fungicide spraying to produce a reliable crop in Gulf South conditions. Plant with another European pear variety for best cross-pollination and yield.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained, limestone-tolerant soil in full sun; Maya nut is a large canopy tree of Mesoamerican tropical forests that grows in zones 10–12 and can tolerate brief cold to about 32°F in protected zone 9b microclimates. The seeds must be planted fresh, as viability drops rapidly; sow immediately after extraction from ripe fruit.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil — including rocky, limestone-based soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; Maya nut (Brosimum alicastrum) is a towering canopy tree in the Moraceae family that the ancient Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples relied upon as a critical famine food for thousands of years, with seeds that are extraordinarily nutritious — high in protein, calcium, potassium, iron, zinc, and B vitamins — and can be boiled, roasted, dried, and ground into flour. The ripe purple-skinned fruits are also edible fresh, with a sweet, fig-like flavor, and the abundant leaves serve as high-quality livestock fodder. Trees are long-lived, moderately drought-tolerant once established, and grow naturally in limestone-rich soils where other fruit trees may struggle. Though primarily a large timber and food tree rather than an orchard crop, Maya nut is gaining recognition as an exceptionally valuable multipurpose agroforestry species, with first seed harvests typically beginning 5–10 years after planting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter to early spring in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich, occasionally flooded soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw is native to bottomlands, pond margins, and stream banks in the Gulf South and requires moist to seasonally wet acidic soils for best production.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to occasionally flooded soil in full sun; mayhaw thrives in the heavy, wet, acidic soils of the Gulf Coast plain that frustrate most fruit trees. Crataegus aestivalis (mayhaw) is the iconic native fruit tree of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, producing small (1/2-to-3/4-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-like fruits in April–May (hence 'may haw' — haw is an old name for hawthorn fruit) that are traditionally harvested by spreading sheets under the tree or raking from the water's surface when the tree grows over ponds and bayous. Mayhaw jelly is a Southern culinary tradition — the vivid, translucent, coral-red jelly with a unique tart-sweet, apple-berry flavor is considered a regional treasure and a gift-worthy specialty product throughout Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi. The tree is also highly ornamental — producing masses of white flowers in February–March (often among the first spring blossoms), followed by the distinctive April berry crop, then good fall foliage color. Named cultivars for improved fruit production include 'Big Red,' 'Crimson,' 'Super Berry,' and 'Texas Star.' Mayhaw grows naturally in wet bottomland forests, bayou margins, and pond edges throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in late winter or spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw is native to the river bottomlands and swampy depressions of the Gulf Coastal Plain from east Texas to the Carolinas — it thrives in seasonally wet soils and is the source of the most beloved traditional preserve of the Deep South, mayhaw jelly.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to part shade; mayhaw naturally grows in wet bottomlands and tolerates seasonal flooding. Crataegus opaca (Western mayhaw or May haw) is a native hawthorn of the Gulf Coastal Plain — a small to medium deciduous tree growing in the wet, seasonally flooded bottomlands, bayous, and boggy depressions of eastern Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia. It is the source of one of the most prized and distinctively Southern traditional preserves: mayhaw jelly, made from the small (1/2-inch), bright-red to orange-red, apple-flavored fruits that ripen in April and May (hence 'mayhaw' — haw ripening in May). Mayhaw jelly has a uniquely mild, apple-quince-like flavor with subtle floral notes that makes it a beloved regional specialty — spread on hot biscuits, it represents the taste of the Gulf South spring. The fruits must be harvested from the ground or water (they drop when ripe, sometimes into shallow water) and are processed immediately — too sour and dry to eat fresh, but exceptional for jellies, preserves, and syrup. Many improved fruiting cultivars have been selected in Louisiana, Texas, and Georgia; 'Super Berry,' 'Texas Star,' and 'Crimson' are productive modern selections. Mayhaw is notably tolerant of wet soils and occasional flooding, making it valuable for rain gardens and wet spots in Gulf Coast landscapes.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds after last frost or plant bare-root transplants in full to partial sun in well-drained soil on a fence or trellis; maypop spreads by underground runners and a sturdy support is needed for the vigorous vines.
directions: Direct-sow seeds or plant transplants in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil against a trellis, fence, or arbor; maypop is one of the most ornate native vines of the Southeast, producing intricately structured lavender-and-white flowers all summer followed by fragrant, egg-sized, yellow-green edible fruits that ripen in fall and make excellent juice and jam with a tropical guava-like flavor. The vine spreads vigorously by underground runners and can colonize an area quickly — provide a sturdy trellis and monitor spread, or allow it to naturalize along a fence row. Maypop is the sole or primary host plant for Gulf Fritillary and Zebra Longwing butterfly larvae in the Southeast, making it one of the most ecologically valuable native plants for zone 5–9 pollinator gardens. Despite top growth dying back in zone 5–7, the deep roots re-emerge dependably each spring.

common_name: McIntosh Apple (Mac Apple, Original Red Apple, Northeastern Apple Classic)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile, deep soil in full sun; McIntosh requires approximately 900 chill hours and is best adapted to zones 4–7 where reliable winter cold accumulates; it requires cross-pollination from a compatible variety such as Cortland, Honeycrisp, or Golden Delicious.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; McIntosh requires cross-pollination; ripens early season (early September in New York), making it the first major commercial apple of the fall; fruit should be harvested when fully red and slightly soft to pressure — McIntosh doesn't firm up like later-season apples and is at its best when slightly tender and very aromatic. McIntosh apple is the foundational variety of the northeastern American apple industry and for decades was the dominant commercial apple in New England, New York, and eastern Canada. The variety was discovered as a chance seedling on John McIntosh's farm in Dundas, Ontario (near present-day Morrisburg) around 1811 — one of the most consequential accidental apple discoveries in North American horticultural history. The young seedling was found growing on his property, probably a wild seedling from a previous homestead planting, and John McIntosh and his son Allan grafted and propagated the tree beginning around 1835, eventually distributing trees throughout eastern Canada and New England. McIntosh produces distinctively aromatic fruit with a characteristic sweet-tart flavor and very soft, juicy, bright white flesh that is immediately recognizable to anyone who grew up in the Northeast. The red-green skin deepens to full red with harvest, and the flesh is softer than modern popular apples (Honeycrisp, Gala, Fuji) — McIntosh is what older generations mean when they say 'the way apples used to taste' — a tender, juicy, very fragrant apple with complex flavor. McIntosh is also the primary parent of many important modern apple varieties including Cortland, Empire, Jonamac, Macoun, and others.

common_name: McMillan Pecan (Highly Scab-Resistant Native-Type Gulf South Pecan)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant, in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; McMillan is a Type II (protogynous) native-type pecan and needs a Type I pollinator such as Kanza, Elliott, or Oconee within about 150 feet for a full crop. Its exceptional scab resistance makes it especially valuable for low-spray or organic Gulf South orchards, where humidity makes pecan scab the primary disease pressure.
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually to prevent rosette symptoms common in Gulf South pecan production. McMillan is a native-type pecan selection out of Mississippi long favored by Gulf South growers for its outstanding, near-immune resistance to pecan scab (Fusicladium effusum) — the single most damaging disease of pecans in the humid Southeast — which allows it to produce consistent, high-quality crops with little or no fungicide input, unlike scab-susceptible standards such as Desirable and Stuart. The nuts are smaller than many commercial cultivars, in keeping with its native-type parentage, but the kernel quality and flavor are excellent, and the tree bears reliably and precociously. Because of its disease resistance, McMillan is frequently recommended for backyard, homestead, and low-input orchard plantings across the Gulf South where fungicide spraying is impractical, and it pairs well with a Type I pollinator for full production. Zone 7–9.

common_name: Meader American Persimmon (Self-Fertile Northern Persimmon, UNH Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; Meader is the most widely grown named American persimmon cultivar specifically because it is reliably self-fertile — a critical advantage since the species is typically dioecious and requires separate male and female trees — making Meader the practical choice for small properties or gardeners who can only plant one tree; cold-hardy to -25°F or below, adapted to zones 4–9.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Meader persimmon is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in poor, clay, or sandy soil where most fruit trees would struggle; grafted trees first fruit in 3–5 years, producing 1–1.5 inch orange fruits that ripen in October–November and become honeyed and non-astringent after the first hard frosts. Meader American persimmon was selected by Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire and released in the 1950s as one of the first named American persimmon cultivars evaluated through a university research program, becoming the defining benchmark for improved American persimmon culture in the northeastern and upper Midwestern United States. The cultivar's most important characteristic is its self-fertility: standard American persimmon is dioecious and typically requires separate male pollinators, but Meader reliably produces fruit without a pollenizer — either through true self-fertility or parthenocarpy — making it the practical choice for gardeners with room for only one tree. Fruit quality is very good: medium-sized (1–1.5 inch diameter), bright orange, intensely sweet and honey-rich when fully ripe after frost softening, with a complex apricot-plum flavor that surpasses most wild American persimmon in consistency and richness.

subcategory: Premium Moroccan fresh-eating date palm cultivar
plant_note: Plant tissue-culture offshoots in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in zone 9–11; Medjool Date Palm is the most prized of all date palm cultivars — originally from the royal palm gardens of Morocco and the Middle East — bearing exceptionally large (1.5–3 inch), soft, caramel-sweet, fresh-eating dates with rich, complex flavor considered superior to all other date varieties, and producing a strikingly ornamental, stately palm with gracefully arching, blue-green pinnate fronds.
directions: Plant Medjool Date Palm offshoots (tissue-culture plants or basal offshoots from certified, disease-free sources) in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; requires hot, dry summers (ideally above 95°F) for fruit development and very low humidity during the fruit ripening period — high humidity causes fungal problems with the developing fruit clusters; irrigate deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry between waterings. Medjool dates are among the most commercially valuable date palm products in the world — large, soft, caramel-brown dates with rich, complex sweetness described as a combination of honey, caramel, and dried fruit; they are the 'fresh date' sold in upscale markets and gourmet stores. Originally from the royal date gardens of Morocco and the Middle East, Medjool was brought to the United States in 1927 by Walter Swingle of the USDA, who rescued eleven offshoots from a diseased date garden in Morocco; this small genetic founder population gave rise to the entire US commercial Medjool industry centered in the Coachella Valley of California and the Yuma area of Arizona. For fruiting in Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens, Medjool requires the dry, intensely hot summers of desert climates; in humid coastal areas like Houston, fruiting is unreliable but the palm grows magnificently as an ornamental. Must be hand-pollinated by transferring pollen from male palm flowers to female date clusters to ensure fruit set in home gardens.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while dormant; fall planting suits zones 6–8.
directions: Medlar is a small, gnarled tree that tolerates a wide range of soils and needs minimal pruning beyond removing crossing branches; it is largely self-fertile and rarely needs a pollinator. Fruit is harvested in late autumn after the first light frost when the skin has turned brown and slightly wrinkled, then 'bleted' (stored at room temperature for 2–4 weeks) until the flesh softens to a custard-like consistency and loses its harsh astringency. The bletted fruit tastes of apple butter with wine overtones and is traditionally made into jelly or cheese. Few pests bother medlar, making it one of the easiest heritage fruits for a low-spray garden.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Meiwa is generally considered the finest-flavored kumquat for fresh eating, with thick, unusually sweet skin and sweeter interior flesh than Nagami, making it the most pleasant to eat whole without the intense pucker of standard kumquats.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Meiwa is self-fruitful and does not require a pollinator. Meiwa kumquat (also spelled Miehua or called 'Sweet Kumquat') is a round-fruited species hybrid distinct from the elongated Nagami, with notably thicker, sweeter edible peel and somewhat less acidic interior flesh than Nagami — making it the most approachable and pleasant kumquat for direct, whole-fruit eating without the sharp pucker of standard types. The round to slightly oval, golden-orange fruits (approximately 1 inch in diameter) ripen November through February and hold well on the tree. Meiwa trees are somewhat more compact than Nagami and are among the most cold-hardy citrus available, tolerating brief temperatures to 16–18°F. An outstanding ornamental container citrus for temperate climates and an excellent Gulf Coast landscape tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile soil in full sun; kumquats are among the most cold-hardy citrus, tolerating temperatures to about 18–22°F, making them suitable for zone 8b–9 with minor frost protection.
directions: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Meiwa is the sweetest and most widely recommended kumquat cultivar for fresh eating — a round-fruited kumquat (distinct from the oval Nagami kumquat) with notably sweeter, thicker, nearly non-acidic edible skin and sweet-tart flesh. The sweet skin makes Meiwa kumquats the superior choice for eating whole — both skin and flesh are consumed together, and the sweetness of the Meiwa skin dramatically reduces the puckering tart bite that makes Nagami less pleasant for casual snacking. The small, round, golden-orange fruits appear in clusters on a compact, attractive, evergreen tree that makes an outstanding ornamental specimen even when not in fruit. Kumquats are among the most cold-hardy true citrus — surviving to 18–22°F — which makes them excellent choices for the entire Gulf South and even zone 8b gardens with minor winter protection. The trees are naturally compact and can be maintained at 6–10 feet for easy harvesting. Meiwa kumquat fruit is excellent fresh, sliced in salads, made into marmalade, and candied. The attractive, shiny, dark-green foliage and white, fragrant flowers make it an excellent landscape specimen year-round. Excellent container plant for patios and small gardens.

common_name: Melogold Grapefruit (UC Melogold, Sweet White Grapefruit)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Melogold is self-fruitful and productive without a pollinator; the large tree needs adequate space — allow 20–25 feet diameter at maturity.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Melogold is a pomelo x white grapefruit hybrid developed by the University of California alongside Oro Blanco from the same breeding program (both released 1980), but with a subtly different flavor — where Oro Blanco has a pomelo-forward character with slightly dry, mealy flesh, Melogold has juicier flesh and a flavor closer to a very sweet, very mildly bitter grapefruit, with somewhat more grapefruit character and slightly more juice than Oro Blanco. Like Oro Blanco, Melogold lacks the bitter naringin flavanone that makes standard grapefruit bitter, but retains more of the characteristic grapefruit aroma and slight tartness, making it a good bridge between grapefruit lovers and those who normally avoid grapefruit bitterness. The large, greenish-yellow to pale-yellow fruits (4–6 inches) ripen October through February and must be tasted to judge ripeness since the skin stays green or pale yellow even when fully ripe. The very large tree is suitable for large home landscapes and the Southern California and Gulf Coast climate in zones 9–11.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Methley is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer — an important advantage for small home orchards with space for only one plum tree. It requires only 250–350 chill hours, making it one of the best plum selections for zone 8–9.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Methley is one of the best Japanese plum cultivars for warm climates — a highly productive, self-fertile tree requiring only 250–350 chill hours (hours below 45°F), making it one of the most reliable plum choices for zone 8–9 Gulf Coast gardens where most other plum cultivars fail due to insufficient winter cold. The medium-sized fruit has red-purple skin and distinctive red flesh with a sweet-tart, juicy flavor. Methley is an early-season plum that ripens in May or June in zone 8–9, which allows the harvest to be completed before summer heat and disease pressure peak. It is also an effective pollinizer for many other Japanese plum cultivars. Trees are vigorous and productive, beginning to bear 2–3 years after planting. Prune annually after harvest to maintain tree structure and control size. A consistent performer in the Gulf Coast South where it is one of the standard recommendations from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension.

plant_note: Plant seeds in fall or plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; Mexican pinyon is the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant of the pinyons, native to the dry mountain ranges of northern Mexico and trans-Pecos Texas at 4,000–8,000 feet elevation.
directions: Plant seeds in fall or container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to average, rocky or sandy, lean to average soil in full sun; Mexican pinyon is the most widely distributed of the Mexican pinyon pines — a three-needle pinyon (three needles per bundle, distinguishing it from the two-needle Colorado pinyon) of the dry mountain ranges of Mexico and into trans-Pecos Texas, southeastern Arizona, and southern New Mexico. The most important commercial pine nut tree in Mexico and an important food plant for Indigenous peoples of northern Mexico. More heat-tolerant than Colorado pinyon, extending into warmer, drier climates of zones 6–9 in the Southwest — an excellent xeriscape tree for hot, dry Texas Hill Country, west Texas, and similar climates where Colorado pinyon is marginally hardy. The nuts are smaller than Colorado pinyon nuts but comparable in flavor and nutritional quality. Slow-growing but long-lived — old trees develop picturesque, gnarled forms on rocky, exposed slopes. An underused edible landscape tree for dry southwestern gardens.

plant_note: Root large stem cuttings (allow cut ends to callus 1–2 weeks) in very well-drained cactus mix in full sun; Mexican pitaya is damaged below 28°F and requires frost-free conditions for long-term success. It is cultivated in dry regions of Mexico and the Caribbean for its edible fruit, which ripens in early summer and is a prized seasonal treat in the markets of Oaxaca, Yucatan, and Colombia.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, dry, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Mexican pitaya is a large, multi-stemmed columnar cactus native to the dry coastal and lowland regions of Venezuela, Colombia, the Caribbean islands, and Mexico, grown for centuries in tropical America for its edible fruits — the pitayas are oval to round, 2–3 inches long, with a thin, red or yellowish skin studded with clusters of spines and translucent white to reddish, sweet, refreshing flesh surrounding the seeds, with a flavor combining gentle sweetness with a slightly acidic, wine-like finish. In Oaxacan markets, fresh pitayas are a beloved seasonal delicacy sold from June through August. The plant grows as an upright, branching, candelabra-shaped cactus that makes an impressive landscape specimen reaching 10–20 feet. The white, night-blooming flowers are adapted for bat pollination. Different from the pitahaya/dragon fruit (Selenicereus undatus) in being a columnar cactus rather than a climbing vine cactus. An outstanding ornamental and edible cactus for zone 9–12 landscapes.

common_name: Mexican Plum (Big Tree Plum, Creek Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root stock in early spring in well-drained, limestone, caliche, or loamy, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Mexican plum is native to limestone cedar glades, stream banks, and forest margins in central Texas and Oklahoma and is exceptionally adapted to alkaline, calcareous soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral or slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Mexican plum tolerates rocky, shallow, limestone soils that defeat most fruit trees. Prunus mexicana (Mexican plum or big tree plum) is the largest native plum of Texas and a landscape-worthy ornamental tree as well as a valuable food plant — more tree-like in form than the suckering Chickasaw plum, growing to 15–25 feet as a single-trunked specimen with attractive, exfoliating, reddish-brown bark. The 1-to-1.5-inch, dark-red to purple-red plums ripen in August–September with a rich, sweet-tart flavor excellent for jams, jellies, preserves, and fresh eating. Clouds of fragrant white flowers smother the bare branches in February–March, making it one of the most spectacular early-flowering native trees in the Texas landscape. Mexican plum is self-fertile, requiring no cross-pollination; it is also one of the most limestone and drought-tolerant of the native plums, thriving in the alkaline, rocky soils of the Texas Hill Country, Edwards Plateau, and Post Oak Savanna. Wildlife value is high — the large fruits are consumed by deer, foxes, raccoons, and many bird species.

common_name: Mexicola Avocado (Most Cold-Hardy Avocado, Mexican Race Black Avocado, Edible-Skin Avocado)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger; Mexicola is one of the most cold-hardy avocado varieties available (surviving to approximately 18–22°F when mature and established), opening avocado growing in zones 8b–9 where standard Hass and Fuerte would be killed; Mexicola is a Type A avocado and is pollinated by Type B companion varieties (Fuerte, Bacon, Zutano); the edible, anise-flavored skin is a distinctive culinary characteristic of this variety.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Mexicola is more compact than most avocados; plant with a Type B companion (Fuerte, Bacon) for best fruit set; harvest August–October (earlier than most avocados) when the small fruits turn glossy purple-black; the thin, papery skin is edible and contributes an anise-herb flavor to the fruit; slice and eat with skin on for the full flavor experience. Mexicola avocado is a pure Mexican race avocado (Persea americana var. drymifolia) with remarkable cold-hardiness traceable to its highland Mexican origin, where ancestors of this variety grew at elevations above 6,000 feet where frost is common — making Mexicola and its relatives the most frost-tolerant avocados that produce edible fruit, with documented survival at 18–22°F that no Guatemalan-race variety (Hass, Reed) can approach. This cold-hardiness has made Mexicola the recommended avocado for zone 8b gardens in the Gulf South, California's inland valleys, and anywhere else where an extra 6–8°F of frost protection would make the difference between avocado success and failure. Mexicola's distinctive features beyond cold-hardiness include small fruit size (3–6 oz compared to Hass's 6–12 oz), very thin, edible skin with an anise or licorice flavor that is typically eaten along with the flesh, and a very high oil content with a rich, complex flavor. The trees are relatively compact (15–25 feet) compared to standard avocados. Mexican race avocados like Mexicola also produce aromatic leaves used as a culinary herb in Oaxacan and other Mexican cuisines.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; Meyer lemon is the hardiest true-fruiting lemon and can be grown in containers in zones 7–8 with winter protection.
directions: Meyer lemon is a natural hybrid between a lemon and either a mandarin or sweet orange, resulting in a thinner-skinned, less acidic, and more cold-tolerant fruit than standard lemon varieties; it tolerates brief dips to about 22°F once established. It is self-fertile, blooms nearly year-round in frost-free climates, and is exceptionally well-suited to container culture — a 20-gallon pot allows the plant to be moved indoors in zones 7–8. Plant in fast-draining citrus mix or well-amended garden soil and fertilize with citrus-specific fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer. Fruit is ripe when the skin turns deep golden-yellow and yields to gentle pressure; the rind is thin and zests well for culinary use.

common_name: Mid-Pride Peach (California Low-Chill Yellow Freestone Peach with Excellent Flavor)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; Mid-Pride requires approximately 250–300 chilling hours — one of the lowest chill requirements of any high-quality yellow freestone peach, making it an excellent choice for zone 9 conditions along the Gulf Coast where full-chill varieties (requiring 700–900 hours) consistently underperform. In zone 9, Mid-Pride ripens in late June–early July, slightly later than very early varieties like Flordaking, providing sequential harvests when planted alongside earlier types. The variety is self-fertile — no cross-pollinator is required, though nearby peach trees may improve fruit set. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage. In the Gulf South's humid climate, annual copper and fungicide applications are advisable to manage bacterial spot and brown rot.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit clusters to 6–8 inches when marble-sized for maximum fruit size. Harvest when skin background has transitioned from green to yellow-orange and fruit gives slightly to firm pressure. Mid-Pride is a California-developed low-chill peach variety considered by many low-chill peach enthusiasts to be among the finest-flavored low-chill varieties available in North America. The variety was selected from University of California breeding programs that worked systematically to reduce chill hour requirements while maintaining the fruit quality characteristics (flavor complexity, sugar-acid balance, flesh texture) that distinguish premium peaches from the bland, fibrous fruit that many early low-chill releases produced. The fruit is medium to large, with yellow skin blushed red and yellow freestone flesh — the freestone character (flesh separates cleanly from the pit at full ripeness) makes Mid-Pride practical for fresh eating, canning, preserving, and freezing without the effort of separating clingstone flesh. The flavor is genuinely excellent for a low-chill variety: sweet with good acid balance, peach aroma, and the melting, juicy flesh texture that characterizes premium peaches. For Gulf Coast zone 9 gardeners, Mid-Pride represents one of the most reliable paths to growing truly excellent-quality peaches in a climate that limits most other stone fruit production.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; midland hawthorn is the woodland-edge species of hawthorn native to the deciduous forests of Europe — slightly more shade-tolerant and adapted to heavier soils than common hawthorn (C. monogyna) — producing abundant dark-red to deep-scarlet haws (berries) used for jelly, wine, and hawthorn cordial.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; midland hawthorn tolerates heavier clay soils and partial shade better than common hawthorn. Crataegus laevigata (midland hawthorn or English May) is a native European hawthorn species closely related to — and often confused with — common hawthorn (C. monogyna), but botanically distinguished by having 2–3 styles per flower (instead of one in C. monogyna), deeply lobed but less deeply cut leaves, and preferring the partial-shade, moist-soil woodland-edge habitat rather than open scrub and hedgerows. Both species are called 'May' or 'May blossom' in England, referring to the masses of white (or in cultivated forms, pink or red) flowers in May that were traditionally brought into homes for May Day celebrations. The deep-red to scarlet fruits (haws) are similar to those of C. monogyna: small, oval, containing 2–3 seeds, with a mild, floury, slightly sweet-tart flavor. In European herbal tradition, hawthorn berries and flowers are among the most important cardiovascular herbs — widely used in European phytomedicine for mild heart conditions, improving coronary blood flow, and supporting healthy blood pressure. The double-flowered pink ornamental forms ('Paul's Scarlet' and 'Rosea Flore Pleno') are among the most popular ornamental flowering trees in British gardens.

common_name: Miho Satsuma (Early Compact Gulf South Satsuma)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Miho is an early-ripening satsuma widely planted in Gulf South home orchards for its compact size and reliably sweet, seedless fruit.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Another early-ripening Japanese satsuma selection similar in season to Okitsu, Miho has become one of the most commonly sold satsuma cultivars in Gulf Coast nurseries because of its naturally compact, rounded growth habit and dependable early crop of small, sweet, essentially seedless fruit. Fruit typically colors and ripens in October, ahead of standard-season satsumas, with loose rind that peels away easily in segments. The tree's smaller stature also makes it a good option for large containers that can be moved under cover during hard freezes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Minneola tangelo requires cross-pollination from a compatible citrus (Temple orange, Dancy tangerine, or Orlando tangelo) for reliable, heavy fruit set — plant at least one pollinizer tree within 50 feet.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Minneola tangelo is a hybrid of Duncan grapefruit and Dancy tangerine developed by USDA breeders at the University of Florida in 1931, producing the largest and most dramatically flavored tangelo available — large (3–4 inch diameter), deep reddish-orange fruits with a characteristic knobby protrusion at the stem end (giving them the nickname 'Honeybell' from their bell-like silhouette) and intensely aromatic, sweet-tart juice that is considered by many citrus enthusiasts to be among the finest citrus flavors of any variety. Minneola typically ripens January–March in Florida and California (one of the latest-ripening citrus), and the fruits hold on the tree for 2–4 weeks allowing flexible harvest. The skins peel easily (a peel-and-eat citrus), and the flesh separates into 10–12 clean segments with very few seeds. The tree is medium-sized (8–15 feet), moderately vigorous, and somewhat cold-hardy for a tangelo. Minneola requires cross-pollination — plant a Temple orange, Dancy tangerine, or Orlando tangelo within 50 feet for adequate fruit set; trees planted alone may produce poorly. Outstanding for Gulf Coast gardens in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed and soil is warm, or start indoors in short-season areas.
directions: Direct sow this compact heirloom melon in warm soil, or start indoors a few weeks early in short-season climates. Introduced in 1948, it produces loads of small 4 inch fruits that are sweet and juicy right to the rind, on short vines well suited to small gardens and containers. Give plants full sun and steady moisture while fruits develop, then ease off watering as they ripen to concentrate the sugars. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and smells fragrant.

plant_note: Best planted dormant in early spring in a warm, sunny position.
directions: Mirabelles are small, round, golden plums famed in Lorraine for tarts and eau-de-vie. Plant in full sun on fertile, free-draining soil and provide shelter from late frosts that can damage the early blossom. Most are self-fertile, so a single tree will crop, though a European plum companion boosts yields. Thin the abundant fruit set and prune lightly in summer to keep the canopy open.

plant_note: Plant in spring; grows well in large containers that can be overwintered indoors in zones 9 and below.
directions: Plant in highly acidic soil (pH 4.5–5.5), which is critical — miracle fruit performs poorly above pH 6.0 and the leaves turn chlorotic in alkaline conditions. It requires consistently warm temperatures and suffers at any temperature below 40°F; container culture in large pots using acidic potting mix is the most practical approach outside zones 10–11. The small red berries contain miraculin, a glycoprotein that binds to taste receptors and makes sour foods taste sweet for 30–60 minutes after eating one fruit; harvest when berries are fully red and soft. Although individual plants are self-fertile, cross-pollination by insects improves berry set, so grow multiple plants together.

common_name: Mission Almond (Texas Mission Almond, California Mission, Hard-Shell Commercial Almond)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Mission is partially self-fruitful and will produce some crop alone, though yields improve substantially with a companion pollinizer variety; requires approximately 250–300 chill hours; it blooms 1–2 weeks later than Nonpareil, making it more frost-resistant in frost-prone almond-growing areas; Mission is the standard recommendation for Texas almond production.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mission is partially self-fruitful but benefits from a companion variety; harvest in late August to September — later than Nonpareil — when hulls split naturally; the thick, hard shell requires a nutcracker rather than the light hand pressure sufficient for Nonpareil; kernels are round, plump, and darker than Nonpareil with a richer, slightly more intense almond flavor. Mission almond (also called Texas Mission) is one of the oldest continuously grown named almond varieties in California, historically associated with the California Spanish mission system and possibly introduced to California with Spanish colonization in the late 1700s — though the exact origins are contested. It was one of the first California almond varieties to reach commercial significance and for many years was the second most planted California variety after Nonpareil. Mission's hard, thick shell — a significant disadvantage for fresh-cracking and processing — became an asset in the shell-on almond market, where the hard shell protects the kernel during shipping and storage, and in the roasted-in-shell specialty market. Mission almonds also have a distinctly different flavor from the mild Nonpareil — slightly richer, with a more intense almond character — making them preferred by some specialty roasters and confectioners. The variety's later bloom time (1–2 weeks after Nonpareil) reduces spring frost risk at the critical blossom stage, a practical advantage in frost-prone almond sites. In Texas, Mission is the primary recommended almond variety where it often goes by the name 'Texas Mission.'

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or potted tree; plant after frost.
directions: The Mission olive, first cultivated in California, is a versatile favorite valued for both flavorful oil and classic table olives. It is a hardy, resilient evergreen that adapts to a range of conditions and delivers reliable harvests for home growers. Plant a young tree in full sun with well-drained soil and water sparingly once it establishes. Prune for an open canopy and good airflow, and in cold-winter regions grow it as a container specimen that can be sheltered from hard freezes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, sandy loam in full sun; plant with another low-chill southern highbush (O'Neal, Sharpblue, Emerald) for cross-pollination; Misty requires only 150–300 chill hours and excels in zone 8b–10.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, sandy loam in full sun with another southern highbush cultivar for cross-pollination; Misty is an outstanding low-chill southern highbush blueberry cultivar developed by the University of Florida — requiring only 150–300 chill hours, making it one of the best blueberry choices for the Gulf Coast, Central Florida, and other warm-winter regions where northern highbush varieties consistently fail to produce. Misty is additionally distinctive for having attractive ornamental value beyond its fruit production — it has an elegant, upright habit with attractive dark-green foliage that turns red in fall, and in spring produces showy clusters of white to pink, urn-shaped flowers before leaf-out. The medium to large, light-blue fruits ripen in April through May in zone 9, with a somewhat mild but pleasant blueberry flavor. As a very early ripening variety (among the earliest of all southern highbush types in zone 9), Misty gives Gulf Coast gardeners fresh blueberries in April when markets charge premium prices. Plant Misty in raised beds or in containers with acidified peat-based potting mix — most Gulf Coast clay and native soils are too alkaline and must be heavily amended or blueberries will fail regardless of cultivar. Pair with O'Neal or Sharpblue for best cross-pollination and maximum yields.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or bare-root trees in spring; mockernut hickory has a deep taproot and should be planted young — larger transplants rarely establish successfully; requires deep, well-drained soil.
directions: Plant young container or bare-root trees in full sun in deep, well-drained, moderately fertile to fertile soil in spring; mockernut hickory is the most common hickory in the eastern United States and among the most beautiful, with dramatic large compound leaves that turn brilliant golden-yellow in fall. The nuts are enclosed in a very thick husk (giving the 'mockernut' name — the husk 'mocks' the nut inside), and the kernel is small but has a rich, full, classic hickory flavor. A critical wildlife tree, providing extremely high-value mast for deer, turkey, squirrels, and many other species; the very dense, strong, flexible wood is commercially valuable for tool handles and sporting goods. An outstanding native shade tree for large properties that also provides excellent wildlife food.

plant_note: Plant container stock or seeds in spring in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; money tree is a Central American wetland tree that tolerates significant flooding and poor drainage (naturally growing along streams and floodplains), making it excellent for consistently moist to wet sites in tropical gardens.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; money tree tolerates periodic flooding and poor drainage. Pachira aquatica (money tree or Malabar chestnut) is a Central American tropical tree famous in two quite different contexts: as a beloved ornamental houseplant (braided trunk forms sold under the 'money tree' name, associated in Feng Shui with prosperity) and as a significant wild and semi-cultivated food tree in its native tropical Central and South American habitat. The tree produces large, distinctive, 5-to-7-fingered, palmate leaves and spectacular, large (8–12 inch), creamy-white flowers with hundreds of long, red-tipped, brush-like stamens — one of the showiest flowers of any tropical tree. The large, woody fruits contain edible seeds (Malabar chestnuts) with a nutty flavor when roasted or boiled — eaten throughout Central America as a nutritious food. Braided trunk forms (produced by braiding multiple young seedlings while soft) have become extremely popular houseplants worldwide. In zone 10–12, money tree grows as a large landscape tree; in zone 9, it requires frost protection.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in zone 10–12; Monkey Jack (Lakuch, Barhal, Monkey Fruit) is a medium to large evergreen tree of the Moraceae family — related to Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) and Breadfruit (A. altilis) — native to humid tropical forests from India and Sri Lanka through Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia, producing round to irregularly lobed, golden-yellow to reddish composite fruits with sweet-sour, aromatic, slightly astringent yellow flesh, widely consumed fresh and in regional cooking throughout South and Southeast Asia.
directions: Plant Monkey Jack in deep, fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zone 10–12; water well during establishment and dry seasons; harvest fruits when they turn golden-yellow and yield to gentle pressure — use gloves as the latex sap stains skin and clothing. Artocarpus lacucha produces round to irregularly shaped compound fruits 3–6 inches across — structurally similar to small jackfruits, formed from fused fruitlets on a central core — with golden-yellow to orange-red skin studded with small bumps and sweet-sour, aromatic, slightly astringent yellow flesh. The flavor is described as a complex blend of mango, pineapple, and slightly acidic tropical notes; the fruits are eaten fresh, pickled, cooked in curries, and used in chutneys and preserves throughout its native range. The starchy seeds are also edible when boiled or roasted, similar to jackfruit seeds. Various parts of the tree are used in traditional Ayurvedic and Thai medicine — the bark yields a yellow dye used for dyeing Buddhist monk robes in Thailand and Myanmar. A productive and ornamentally handsome tree for large tropical gardens, with attractive compound leaves and interesting fruits hanging from the main trunk and larger branches.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; monkey jack is a medium-sized Artocarpus species from lowland Southeast Asian forests producing round cauliflorous composite fruits with orange-yellow sweet flesh — smaller and more manageable than jackfruit, and more shade-tolerant.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; monkey jack is more shade-tolerant than jackfruit and suited to multi-story food forest understory planting. Artocarpus rigidus (monkey jack, pingan, or terap hutan) is a tropical Artocarpus species from the lowland dipterocarp forests of Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines — one of several dozen Artocarpus species in the breadfruit and jackfruit genus, most of which produce edible composite fruits through cauliflory (fruiting on the trunk and main branches). Monkey jack produces round to oval, 2–4 inch composite fruits with a spiny-bumpy, green exterior and orange-yellow, sweet, somewhat sticky flesh surrounding multiple seeds. The flavor is sweet, fruity, and pleasant when fully ripe, though less refined in flavor than the closely related cempedak (A. integer) or jackfruit (A. heterophyllus). It is primarily a forest fruit eaten opportunistically in Malaysia and Indonesia rather than a major cultivated crop, and is notable mainly to tropical fruit collectors and ethnobotanists documenting the edible Artocarpus species of Borneo. As a garden tree, monkey jack is smaller and more manageable than jackfruit, with good shade tolerance making it useful in food forest designs. Restricted to zone 11–12 humid tropics.

common_name: Monstera (Swiss Cheese Plant, Fruit Salad Plant)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings with at least one node in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in deep shade to partial shade; monstera grows naturally as a forest understory vine and performs best with dappled light or bright indirect light — direct sun in warm climates bleaches and burns the foliage.
directions: Plant in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in deep to bright indirect shade; monstera is one of the world's most recognizable houseplants in temperate climates but grows as a large, vigorous outdoor vine in zone 10–12, where it can climb 20 feet or more up trees, walls, and structures by aerial roots. In the wild it migrates from deep shade toward brighter light as it matures, producing the characteristic deeply lobed and perforated leaves only in brighter conditions — deeply shaded plants have smaller, unlobed juvenile leaves. The edible 'fruit' is actually a cone-like cluster of hexagonal segments that ripens from the base upward over 10–12 months; fully ripe segments slip off cleanly and taste like a blend of pineapple, banana, and coconut. Unripe fruit contains calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense mouth irritation — harvest only segments that have separated naturally from the base.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in early spring.
directions: Montmorency is the classic self-fertile tart pie cherry, so a single tree will crop heavily on its own. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil, avoiding frost pockets that damage the early bloom. It is more compact and cold-hardy than sweet cherries, making it well suited to northern gardens. Prune to an open center in late winter and net the ripening fruit against birds.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Moonglow is a USDA-released pear variety with good fire blight resistance, soft, sweet, mild, very early-ripening fruit, and adaptability to Southern climates that makes it one of the most recommended pear varieties for zone 6–8 southern gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Moonglow cross-pollinates well with Seckel, Bartlett, Harrow Sweet, and most other European pear varieties. Moonglow pear was released by the USDA in 1960 from a breeding program targeting soft-fleshed, early-ripening pear varieties for Southern gardens; it produces medium-large, pyriform (classic pear-shaped), pale yellow to greenish-yellow fruits that ripen in late July to August — the earliest of the commonly grown European pears.
