The flesh is white, very soft, mild, and sweet without the grittiness of some older pear varieties; it is a dessert pear best for eating fresh as it does not hold well after picking (must be ripened off the tree like Bartlett). Good fire blight resistance makes it more reliable than Bartlett in humid southeastern gardens. Partially self-fruitful; cross-pollinate with another European pear for best yields.

common_name: Moorpark Apricot (Classic English Heirloom Apricot, Large-Fruited Heritage Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral (pH 6.5–7.5), deep, fertile soil in full sun; Moorpark requires approximately 700–900 chill hours and a cross-pollinator — it is not reliably self-fruitful — pair with Harcot, Blenheim, or another compatible apricot; best adapted to zones 5–8 where adequate winter cold accumulates and late spring frosts do not regularly destroy the early-blooming blossoms.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Moorpark requires a cross-pollinator; thin heavy crops to 4–6 inches after natural fruit drop for maximum size; harvest when fruit is deep orange, fully colored, and gives slightly to pressure — Moorpark is at its best consumed fresh within days of picking, as the extraordinarily rich, honeyed flavor at peak ripeness is what makes this variety historically important. Moorpark apricot is one of the great classical apricot varieties of the English-speaking world, an heirloom dating to at least the early 1600s in England and named for Moorpark House in Hertfordshire where it was grown extensively — though its origins may be even earlier and possibly Italian or Continental European. For centuries, Moorpark was the standard of apricot excellence in England, appearing in historic orchards of country houses and kitchen gardens throughout the British Isles, and was the variety which set the benchmark against which all other apricots were evaluated. The fruits are large (for the era), round to oval, deep orange to orange-red with a distinctive dark blush, with firm, richly sweet-tart, intensely flavored orange flesh that is considered among the finest flavors of any apricot variety even by modern standards — a rich, honeyed, complex flavor that distinguishes it from the milder, blander commercial varieties selected for shelf life. Moorpark is not self-fertile and requires cross-pollination; the spring blossoms appear very early and are vulnerable to late frosts, making site selection on a frost-protected slope or south-facing wall important for reliable fruiting.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Moreland shows good resistance to pecan scab, an important trait in the humid Gulf South, and needs a Type I pollinator.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Selected for reliable production and notably good resistance to pecan scab, a fungal disease that is a major limiting factor for pecan growing in humid Gulf Coast climates, Moreland has long been a dependable choice for growers in Louisiana, Mississippi, and neighboring states where less resistant cultivars require heavy fungicide programs. Nuts are medium-sized with good kernel quality, and the tree is a consistent annual bearer under good management, making it a solid choice for growers prioritizing lower-input disease tolerance over maximum nut size.

common_name: Morello Cherry (English Morello, Dark Sour Cherry, Culinary Sour Cherry)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Morello is self-fertile and more tolerant of partial shade than any sweet cherry variety, making it one of the few cherry trees that can produce a useful crop on a partly shaded north-facing wall or in a garden with reduced sun exposure; requires approximately 700–800 chill hours.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun or partial shade; Morello is self-fertile; the dark red to nearly black fruits ripen in late July to August — later than most sweet cherries — and are very tart, intended for cooking, preserves, and culinary preparations rather than fresh-eating; harvest when fully black for maximum color in jams and liqueurs. Morello cherry is the classic European culinary sour cherry — a dark-skinned, dark-fleshed variety with deep red to nearly black skin and dark red juice that distinguishes it from the clear-juiced Montmorency type — grown for centuries in English, Dutch, and German cottage gardens as the primary cherry for preserves, pies, tarts, cherry brandy, and the fermented cherry preparations traditional in continental Europe. The dark flesh and juice of Morello give it distinct advantages over Montmorency in certain culinary applications: cherry jam, jelly, and liqueurs (including the famous Schwarzwälder Kirschwasser of the Black Forest and the maraschino cherry liqueur of Central Europe) derive their deep red-purple color from Morello's dark pigments, producing a dramatically richer-colored product than would result from clear-juiced cherries. Morello is also notable for being one of the few cherry varieties that will bear adequate crops in partial shade — a practical advantage in British and northwestern European cottage gardens where full sun is not always available. The fruit is very tart at all stages of ripeness, with a complex sourness and rich cherry flavor that intensifies with cooking and makes it the definitive variety for traditional European cherry cookery.

plant_note: Plant container trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Moro blood orange requires cool nights (45–55°F) to develop its characteristic red pigment (anthocyanins) — in areas with warm winters the flesh color may be reduced or absent.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Moro is the deepest-colored blood orange cultivar — a Sicilian selection producing dramatic, dark crimson to near-black flesh with a striking red-streaked rind exterior. The flavor is distinctly more complex than standard sweet oranges, with a pronounced berry-like, raspberry-blackberry tone layered over the sweet orange base — a flavor unlike any other citrus. The deep red color comes from water-soluble anthocyanin pigments that develop only when cool nights (below 55°F) occur during fruit development; in very warm winters the flesh may show less red coloration but still produces the characteristic flavor. In zone 9, Moro blood oranges ripen in December through February — the coolest months — when the anthocyanin development is most favorable. The small to medium, round to slightly oval fruits have a thin, smooth rind. Blood oranges are highly valued in cooking for their dramatic color in fresh-squeezed juice (which turns deep ruby-red to purple), salad dressings, sauces, and cocktails. The juice color provides a culinary application that no other citrus can replicate. Protect from temperatures below 28°F; site in thermally protected areas of zone 9 gardens.

common_name: Morris Burton American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Seedless Indiana Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun in any well-drained to average soil; Morris Burton is an Indiana-origin American persimmon selection noted for good cold hardiness and reliable production of seedless fruit without a male pollinator. Adapted to zones 5–9.
directions: Plant in well-drained to average soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and undemanding of fertile soil. Morris Burton is a named American persimmon cultivar out of Indiana grown for its combination of dependable cold hardiness, early bearing age, and consistent production of medium, seedless orange fruit without requiring a nearby male tree. The fruit ripens in mid-fall and, like other American persimmons, must fully soften on the tree or after a hard frost to lose its raw astringency, at which point the flesh turns sweet, thick, and richly flavored — excellent fresh, or processed into persimmon pudding, bread, and butter. Its good cold tolerance and self-fruiting habit make it a popular choice for northern-edge persimmon growers and for gardeners who want a single reliable tree without pollination logistics, in zone 5–9.

common_name: Morris Plum (Texas A&M Low-Chill Self-Fertile Japanese Plum for the Gulf South)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February) while dormant; Morris requires approximately 400–450 chilling hours, suitable for most of zone 7–9. Morris is one of the few Japanese plums reliably self-fertile — it can set a good crop without a pollinator, though planting a second Japanese plum (Methley, Bruce, Santa Rosa) will improve fruit set and crop size. Fruit ripens late May through June in zone 9 — earlier than most Japanese plums. Thin fruit to 3–4 inch spacing at marble size for maximum fruit development.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil; prune to open-center form. Thin fruit heavily at marble size for maximum size and quality. Morris Plum is a Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) developed at the Texas A&M University Agricultural Experiment Station in Montague County, Texas — one of the primary low-chill Japanese plum varieties released specifically for the hot, humid climate of the South and Gulf Coast region where most standard Japanese plum varieties from California require too many chilling hours or fail to set fruit reliably. Morris carries a low chilling requirement (400–450 hours) that is reliably met throughout most of zone 7–9, and the variety's self-fertile nature (it can pollinate itself and set a full crop without a second plum nearby) makes it particularly practical for home gardeners with space for only one tree. The fruit is medium-sized, round, with mahogany-red skin and amber to yellow flesh — freestone at full ripeness — with good sweet-tart plum flavor. Morris is notably productive for a low-chill plum, bearing heavily in most years when the chilling requirement is met. Texas A&M's stone fruit breeding program (which also produced Bruce plum and other Gulf South stone fruit varieties) made commercial and home plum production viable across zone 7–9 of Texas and the surrounding Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Morton is a cold-hardy citrange, a hybrid of trifoliate orange and sweet orange, valued for tart, orange-flavored fruit on a tree that tolerates significantly colder winters than any true orange.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for citrus, with mature wood able to withstand temperatures well below what standard sweet orange trees survive, thanks to trifoliate orange parentage. Morton citrange is a hybrid between trifoliate orange (Poncirus trifoliata) and sweet orange, bred primarily to extend cold-hardy citrus growing further north than standard oranges allow. The fruit is tart, seedy, and more acidic than a true sweet orange, generally used for juice, marmalade, or as an ade rather than fresh eating out of hand, though well-ripened fruit mellows considerably. Trees show the trifoliate parent's deciduous or semi-deciduous habit in colder winters and small, three-part leaves, along with light thorns typical of trifoliate hybrids. Because of its unusual hardiness, Morton citrange has been of particular interest to cold-climate citrus hobbyists pushing the edible citrus range into zone 6-7, well beyond where standard citrus survives. Protect young trees for the first few winters; established trees are considerably tougher. Harvest fruit once fully colored for the best balance of sweetness and acidity.

common_name: Mount Royal Plum (Canadian Cold-Hardy European Freestone Prune Plum)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mount Royal is self-fruitful (one of the most reliably self-fruitful European plums available) and is especially valued in zones 4–5 where it can be grown reliably without a cross-pollinator in climates too cold for many other European plums; it originated in Montreal, Quebec, where it was selected for hardiness in the severe Canadian climate.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mount Royal is self-fruitful and very cold-hardy; the round to oval blue-purple fruits ripen in late August to mid-September; flavor is rich, sweet, and high-quality — one of the best-tasting cold-hardy European plums; suitable for fresh eating, preserves, cooking, and drying. Mount Royal plum is a Canadian-origin European prune plum (Prunus domestica) that has been widely grown in Quebec and the northeastern states since its selection in the Montreal area (likely in the late 19th century), where it consistently demonstrated the cold-hardiness and reliable self-fruitfulness that make it particularly valuable in zones 4–5 where standard European plums like Stanley and Italian Prune may suffer winter damage or require cross-pollination to set adequate crops. The name reflects its Canadian origin — Mount Royal (Mont-Royal) is the mountain in the heart of Montreal, and the variety's proven performance in that zone 5 climate is its primary recommendation. Mount Royal produces medium-sized, round to slightly oval, blue-purple to dark blue fruits with firm, yellow-green, freestone flesh and a sweet, rich European plum flavor with balanced acid and sugar that makes it excellent for all purposes: fresh eating at peak ripeness, preserves and jam, plum butter, cooking in tarts and cakes, and drying into prunes. It is considered one of the best-tasting cold-hardy European plums available, with quality comparable to Stanley but with significantly better cold-hardiness and self-fruitfulness. An essential variety for home orchards in zones 4–5 where plum options are limited.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 8–10; Mountain Papaya (Chamorro, Babaco relative) is a small, fast-growing tree native to the Andean highlands of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Colombia at 5,000–10,000 feet elevation — producing clusters of small, oblong, yellow-orange fruits with white papaya-like flesh and a sharp, acidic, fragrant flavor used in Latin American cooking and juices, while tolerating cool, even light-frost temperatures that kill common papaya.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Vasconcellea pubescens is remarkably cold-tolerant compared to common papaya (Carica papaya) — tolerating brief temperatures to 26–28°F when established, making it the best papaya-like fruit tree for zone 8 climates — water regularly, fertilize monthly with balanced fertilizer, and prune to maintain tidy form. Vasconcellea pubescens (Mountain Papaya, Chamorro, or Chihualcan Papaya) is a small to medium-sized, fast-growing, short-lived tree in the Caricaceae (papaya) family native to the Andean highlands of Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Colombia at elevations of 1,500–3,200 meters, where the cool, moist, frost-prone mountain climate would immediately kill common papaya (Carica papaya). As one of the papaya family's most cold-hardy species, V. pubescens withstands light frosts that damage the common papaya — making it the most appropriate papaya relative for cultivation in mild-winter zone 8–10 climates across southern North America and the Mediterranean. The clusters of small (2–4 inch), oblong, yellow-orange, smooth-skinned fruits contain firm, white, strongly aromatic, papaya-like flesh with a distinctive, sharp, tropical-citrus-sour flavor — eaten raw, cooked in stews and soups (popular in Chilean cocina criolla), juiced, and made into jam and preserves across its Andean native range. Plants are typically dioecious and very fast to first fruit (1–2 years from seed), making them productive even as short-lived trees.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mountain papaya requires male and female plants for fruit set — unless a hermaphrodite form is obtained. This species tolerates light frost better than common papaya.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mountain papaya is a cool-climate relative of common papaya from the Andes of Colombia and Ecuador, adapted to elevations of 5000–10,000 feet where it tolerates light frost to 28°F — considerably more cold-hardy than the common papaya (Carica papaya). The small, yellow-green fruits are high in papain enzymes — even higher than common papaya — and must be cooked before eating, as the raw fruit is too enzyme-active to eat comfortably. Cooked, the flesh is used in jams, jellies, and stews throughout the Andes. In zone 9, mountain papaya can be grown outdoors year-round and provides a more climate-appropriate alternative to common papaya. The plant is dioecious; obtain plants of both sexes for fruiting.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; mountain soursop grows and fruits faster than common soursop (A. muricata) and shows slightly more cold tolerance, performing in zone 9b–12.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun — mountain soursop is the larger-fruited relative of common soursop (Annona muricata), native to the rainforests of the Amazon basin, and is considered more vigorous and faster-fruiting than its more common relative. The spiny, ovoid fruits (3–6 inches) have white, fibrous, juicy flesh with a strong tropical flavor used to make juice, ice cream, and desserts similar to soursop. The tree is faster-growing than common soursop and shows slightly greater cold tolerance. Like all Annona species, the flowers produce heat and attract beetle pollinators overnight — cross-pollination with another tree improves fruit set significantly. The handsome, large, dark-green glossy leaves make it an attractive ornamental even when not in fruit. A productive, fast-bearing tropical fruit tree for zone 9b–12 gardens.

subcategory: Mediterranean and Middle Eastern wild pistachio tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, lean, rocky to sandy soil in zone 7–10; Mt. Atlas Pistachio is a large, extremely drought-tolerant, long-lived pistachio species native to the Atlas Mountains of North Africa, Turkey, and the Middle East — the primary rootstock for commercial Pistacia vera pistachio grafts — bearing small, resinous, edible pistachio-like nuts and exceptional autumn color in cold-tolerant zone 7 climates.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, lean, rocky or sandy soil; Pistacia atlantica is remarkably drought tolerant and thrives in conditions too harsh for most fruit trees — avoid clay, overwatering, and excess fertility, which promote lush growth at the expense of drought adaptation and cold hardiness. Pistacia atlantica (Mt. Atlas Pistachio, Mastic Pistachio, or Bene) is a large, long-lived, drought-adapted deciduous to semi-evergreen tree native to the Atlas Mountains of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia, and extending across the Middle East to Central Asia — the wild pistachio tree most widely used as the cold-hardy rootstock upon which commercial Pistacia vera (edible pistachio) varieties are grafted, conferring exceptional drought tolerance, deep-rooting habit, and disease resistance to the scions. The tree itself produces small clusters of small, pea-sized, resinous, edible nuts resembling tiny pistachios — edible and pistachio-flavored when roasted, historically used as a seasoning and oil source across the Middle East and North Africa. Pistacia atlantica is also the source of a gum-resin historically used as a primitive chewing gum and incense in the Middle East. As an ornamental landscape tree, it is exceptional: extremely long-lived, deeply drought-tolerant, with elegant pinnate foliage and spectacular orange-red-purple autumn color in cooler climates. Planted in California's pistachio-growing regions as a street and shade tree for its drought tolerance.

plant_note: Plant in early spring; mulberries establish readily from container stock.
directions: Red mulberry (native to eastern North America) and white mulberry (Morus alba, from Asia) are both grown for fruit; white mulberry is more tolerant of heat and alkaline soils. Most mulberries are self-fertile or near-enough so that a single tree crops well. Trees require very little care once established — no regular spraying or thinning is needed. Fruit ripens over several weeks and drops when ripe; lay a tarp beneath the canopy for easy collection, as the juice stains pavement and clothing permanently.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Mundu is a Philippine and Southeast Asian Garcinia species producing golf-ball-sized, round, golden-yellow fruits with sweet-tart, apricot-mango-flavored flesh — less complex than its famous relative mangosteen but easier to grow and more productive in tropical home gardens.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Garcinia dulcis is slow-growing and prefers consistent moisture. Garcinia dulcis (mundu or sweet mangosteen) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Philippines, Indonesia, and Malaysia — a member of the mangosteen family (Clusiaceae) and related to the famous mangosteen (G. mangostana) but distinctly different in fruit character. Mundu produces round, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits with smooth, thin, golden-yellow to orange-yellow skin and bright-yellow, juicy, mildly sweet-tart flesh with a flavor profile combining apricot, mango, and a slight citrus note — pleasant, refreshing, and more accessible in flavor than mangosteen's complex floral-tropical character. The yellow latex (gamboge) in the skin and pith is mildly bitter and slightly resinous (as in all Garcinia species) — peel carefully and avoid including the skin in the edible flesh. Mundu is significantly easier to grow than true mangosteen, which is notoriously difficult and slow; mundu is faster-maturing, more forgiving of less-than-perfect conditions, and more productive. The tree is also useful as a rootstock for grafting true mangosteen in regions where mangosteen is difficult to grow on its own roots. In the Philippines, the fruit is eaten fresh and made into jam; the large seeds contain a fat used in traditional cosmetics.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; Murcott is self-fruitful but benefits from cross-pollination for maximum fruit set; it is strongly alternate-bearing and benefits from fruit thinning in heavy years to promote consistent annual production.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Murcott honey tangerine (also called Murcott mandarin, Honey mandarin, or Spring mandarin) is one of the most intensely flavored mandarins available — a complex tangor (mandarin x sweet orange hybrid) with deep reddish-orange skin, extremely sweet, rich, honey-like juice with excellent aromatic complexity, and medium-thick skin that peels relatively easily. The fruits are medium-sized (2.5–3.5 inches), slightly flattened, and typically contain 15–25 small seeds, which is a trade-off for the exceptional flavor profile that many citrus enthusiasts consider the finest of all mandarin types. Murcott ripens late in the season (January–March in Florida; February–April in California), and the fruits hang on the tree well, gradually increasing in sweetness through the winter; the tree can be used as a reliable late-season fresh citrus source when earlier varieties have finished. The California Citrus Research Board markets Murcott as 'Honey mandarin' and sells significant quantities at premium prices. Trees are moderately cold-sensitive (damaged at 28°F) and are best in the warmest sites in zone 9.

common_name: Mutsu Apple (Crispin, Large Honeyed Japanese-Bred Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Mutsu is a triploid and produces very little viable pollen, so it needs two different diploid pollinator varieties planted nearby rather than a single partner.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible diploid pollinator varieties nearby, since triploid cultivars cannot pollinate themselves or each other. Bred in Aomori Prefecture, Japan from a cross involving Golden Delicious and released in the late 1940s, Mutsu produces very large, greenish-yellow fruit with dense, juicy flesh and a rich, honeyed sweetness that intensifies in storage. It is sold in Britain and parts of Europe under the name Crispin. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the fruit holds its shape well when baked, making it a favorite for pies alongside fresh eating.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; in zone 9 plant February–March. NC-1 is a very cold-hardy cultivar selected in Canada and also one of the most productive named pawpaw varieties — a combination that makes it the top choice when heavy production and flavor quality are both priorities. Requires cross-pollination from a second variety for maximum fruit set.
directions: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; NC-1 is a named pawpaw cultivar selected in Ontario, Canada by Richard Campbell and subsequently widely adopted in North American pawpaw cultivation for combining two usually separate virtues: exceptional cold hardiness (rated to USDA zone 4) and superior fruiting productivity in the upper part of its range. The medium-large fruits (8–14 ounces) have cream-to-yellow flesh with a rich, complex, sweet flavor rated highly in Kentucky State University pawpaw taste evaluations. NC-1 is noted for its consistent, reliable fruiting on young trees — often beginning to bear meaningfully in 3–4 years from transplant, ahead of the 5–7 year wait common for seedling pawpaws. Its northern Canadian selection history means it leafs out slightly later in spring, reducing the risk of late frost damage to flowers — a significant advantage for zone 9 gardeners where erratic late-winter weather can damage early flowers. Cross-pollinate with Mango, Overleese, or Shenandoah for best results.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Nagami kumquat is the most widely grown and most readily available kumquat, the classic oval-fruited type with sweet edible skin and intensely tart flesh that are eaten whole.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; kumquats are more cold-hardy than most citrus and can tolerate temperatures briefly to about 18–22°F when mature. Nagami kumquat is the most widely grown kumquat worldwide, producing oval (1–1.5 inch long), bright orange fruits with a sweet, aromatic edible peel and intensely sour-tart flesh and juice — the unique flavor is experienced by eating the entire fruit in one or two bites, allowing the sweet peel flavor to intermingle with the tart interior. The contrast of sweet and sour in a tiny package is delightfully surprising and different from any other citrus. Nagami fruits from November through January and holds on the tree for 3–4 months; the laden branches are extraordinarily ornamental and the trees make outstanding large container specimens that can be moved indoors in zones north of 8 for winter protection. Self-fruitful; no pollinator needed.

plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Namwa is an ABB genome banana with greater cold and drought tolerance than pure Cavendish types, and the rhizome reliably resurfaces after freeze damage in zone 8b–9.
directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; Namwa (also spelled 'Nam Wa', 'Kluai Nam Wa' in Thai, meaning 'water banana') is an ABB genome banana that is among the most widely grown commercial and home garden bananas in Southeast Asia, particularly Thailand, where it is the dominant fresh market variety. Its great popularity stems from its compact size (8–12 feet tall), reliable productivity, good flavor (sweet, slightly tangy, slightly firmer than Cavendish), and significantly greater drought and cold tolerance than Cavendish types — the ABB genome contributes Musa balbisiana cold and stress resistance that allows the rhizome to survive temperatures to about 22–25°F, making Namwa useful in zone 8b–9 Gulf South gardens. The medium-sized, plump, round-tipped fruits (5–6 inches) ripen to creamy yellow with a thin skin and dense, sweet, slightly chalky-creamy flesh; they are excellent fresh, and the slightly starchy texture when green-ripe makes them suitable for cooking or frying as well. A productive, compact, and cold-resilient choice for Gulf South banana cultivation.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a frost-free site; nance tolerates poor, well-drained soils exceptionally well.
directions: Nance is a tough, drought-tolerant shrub-tree native to tropical America that thrives on poor, acidic, sandy or rocky soils where other fruit trees struggle, and is among the most fire-tolerant tropical fruit plants. It is partially self-fertile, but fruit set improves significantly when multiple plants are grown together; bees are the primary pollinators. The small yellow drupes ripen over an extended season and have a distinctive pungent, waxy, cheese-like aroma that intensifies when processed; they are consumed fresh, frozen in syrup, fermented into a popular Central American drink called chicha, or cooked into preserves. Harvest when the fruit has fully yellowed and drops freely from the clusters, then refrigerate or process immediately.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in sandy, dry, acidic soil in full sun; cold stratification over winter triggers spring germination — established clumps can also be divided in early spring by carefully separating rooted suckers from the parent plant.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy, acidic (pH 4.5–6.0), infertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nantucket serviceberry is one of the most compact and low-growing serviceberries in cultivation, native to coastal pine barrens, heathlands, and sandy outwash plains from Cape Cod and Nantucket south through the mid-Atlantic — conditions that most other fruiting shrubs find inhospitable. Its small scale makes it one of the few fruiting native shrubs suited to tight urban lots or coastal cottage gardens where larger serviceberries would overwhelm the space. White flowers appear in early spring and sweet blue-black berries ripen in early summer, attracting catbirds, robins, and warblers. Because it is endemic to a restricted range and specialized habitat, sourcing plants or seed from reputable native plant nurseries rather than wild-collecting is strongly encouraged to protect remaining natural populations.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in warm, humid conditions; transplant outdoors in a sheltered, partially shaded location after soil warms to 65°F.
directions: Start seeds in warm, moist seed mix at 75–80°F; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in a location sheltered from strong afternoon sun, as the large tropical leaves burn easily. This Andean highland fruit naturally grows at elevations where temperatures rarely exceed 85°F — it prefers the cool tropics and will struggle in humid Gulf Coast summers; maritime California and high-altitude zones 9–10 are ideal. The orange, tomato-like fruits are covered with soft hair when immature and ripen over several months; the intensely tart, aromatic pulp is used for juices, smoothies, and ice cream in Colombia and Ecuador. Prune to remove dead or crossing branches after harvest.

common_name: Natal Orange (Kaffir Orange, Spiny Monkey Orange)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Natal orange is a thorny deciduous tree from sub-Saharan Africa producing hard-shelled, yellow-green fruits resembling small oranges — the sweet-acid, jelly-like pulp is edible (unlike the toxically famous S. nux-vomica); the hard shell is used traditionally for containers and decorative gourds.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; very drought-tolerant once established; the thorny nature deters browsing animals. Strychnos spinosa (Natal orange, spiny monkey orange, or kaffir orange) is a thorny deciduous tree from sub-Saharan Africa — native to the savanna, bushveld, and dry woodland regions of South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and eastward to Kenya and Tanzania. The tree bears the most remarkable fruits in the genus: large (3–4 inch diameter), perfectly round, hard-shelled, bright yellow-green when ripe, strongly resembling oranges externally despite being completely unrelated (in the Strychnaceae family). IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: Unlike Strychnos nux-vomica (the strychnine tree, which has highly toxic seeds), S. spinosa fruit pulp is edible — the sweet-acid, jelly-like, cream to yellow flesh surrounding the large seeds inside has a pleasant, fruity, somewhat date-like flavor and is widely eaten in rural southern Africa. The seeds are bitter and should be avoided. The extremely hard shell of the dried fruit has been used for millennia as a container, bowl, and decorated gourd throughout sub-Saharan Africa. The roots, bark, and leaves have extensive traditional medicinal applications in southern African herbalism. A remarkably tough, drought-resistant tree for dry subtropical collectors' gardens in zone 9–11.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil; navel oranges require hot summers and mild winters to produce the sweetest fruit and are best grown in zone 9–11 or in large containers moved indoors during frost.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the Washington Navel is the world's most widely grown eating orange, identifiable by the small secondary fruit (the 'navel') embedded in the blossom end of each fruit. Navel oranges are seedless, easy to peel, and have exceptionally rich, sweet, non-bitter flavor when fully ripe. They ripen in winter (November through March), making them a precious fresh fruit at a time of year when few other fruit trees are bearing. Trees are self-fruitful and require no pollinators. Feed monthly with a citrus fertilizer, maintain good drainage, and protect from frost — even brief exposure to 28°F will damage fruit. In zone 9 the trees are hardy but fruit may be damaged in hard freezes.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Nazemetz is partially self-fertile but produces significantly heavier crops when cross-pollinated with another feijoa cultivar such as Coolidge, Apollo, or Mammoth. In zone 9 feijoa flowers and fruits reliably; harvest fruits by collecting those that fall naturally from the shrub October–December. Fruits must be harvested promptly when dropped as they do not store well at room temperature.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Nazemetz is a California-selected feijoa (pineapple guava) cultivar prized for producing the largest fruits of any commonly available named variety — round to slightly pear-shaped fruits typically reaching 4–8 ounces, significantly larger than the 2–4 ounce fruits of unnamed seedling plants. The rich, complex, aromatic flavor combines pineapple, mint, guava, and strawberry notes into a unique tropical flavor that is highly distinctive and unlike any other common fruit. Feijoa (Acca sellowiana) is a South American fruit increasingly popular in California, New Zealand, and the Gulf South for its exceptional zone 8–10 adaptability, drought tolerance, and ornamental value — the spring flowers with white petals and red stamens are edible and delicious eaten directly from the plant as a sweet-spicy spring treat. In zone 9 Nazemetz produces fruit reliably with minimal care; the fruit drops naturally when ripe and is harvested by collecting fallen fruits.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring before bud break.
directions: Nectarines are essentially smooth-skinned peaches and share the same culture — self-fertile, open-center pruning, and annual heading-back of one-year-old wood. Because nectarines lack the peach's fuzzy skin barrier they are somewhat more susceptible to brown rot and bacterial spot in humid climates, so good air circulation is critical. Chill requirements range from 250 to 900 hours depending on cultivar; select accordingly. Fruit is ready when it gives slightly to thumb pressure and the background color has shifted from green to creamy yellow.

common_name: Newtown Pippin Apple (Albemarle Pippin, Thomas Jefferson's Apple, First American Exported Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Newtown Pippin requires approximately 800 chill hours and cross-pollination from a compatible variety (Cortland, Winesap, or Golden Delicious); best adapted to zones 5–8; the variety produces its finest quality in climates with cool summer nights and good light — the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia and the Pacific Northwest valleys produce exceptional Newtown Pippin fruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Newtown Pippin requires a cross-pollinator; the greenish-yellow to yellow fruit with some russet ripens very late (October–November) and benefits from 4–6 weeks of cold storage before eating, during which the flavor mellows, sweetens, and develops complex aromatic notes; an outstanding cider apple as well as a fresh eating variety. Newtown Pippin is one of the oldest American apple varieties in continuous cultivation, discovered as a chance seedling in the early 1700s in what was then the town of Newtown on Long Island, New York (now the neighborhood of Elmhurst in Queens), and is distinguished by a historical record rivaling any apple variety in the world. Benjamin Franklin shipped Newtown Pippin to England as early as the 1750s, where it was received with acclaim; it was later selected as the apple to be presented to Queen Victoria in the early 19th century — and became so popular in England that the British Parliament waived the apple import duty on American Newtown Pippins, the only American apple to receive such distinction. Thomas Jefferson planted Newtown Pippin at Monticello, where the variety is now called 'Albemarle Pippin' for its long association with Albemarle County, Virginia, and still grown in the restored Monticello orchard today. The fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to yellowish with russet patches, with crisp, dense, moderately tart, richly flavored flesh that becomes complex and aromatic after storage — nutty, slightly spicy, and quite unlike most commercial varieties. An important cider variety as well.

common_name: Niagara Grape (White Concord, Golden Grape, American White Table Grape)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines in early spring; Niagara is the most widely grown white (green-gold) American home garden grape — the white counterpart to Concord with the same Labrusca slip-skin character and musky-sweet flavor but in a golden-green berry; developed in Lockport, New York in 1872 and the standard pairing for Concord in northeastern home vineyards and U-pick operations.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun in well-drained soil; train to a 4-arm Kniffin system or similar; cane-prune in late winter; Niagara ripens 1–2 weeks before Concord in most regions (late August to early September); the berries are pale green to amber-gold at full ripeness, very juicy, with the classic musky Labrusca fragrance and flavor. Niagara is the second most important American Labrusca grape after Concord, developed in Lockport, New York in 1872 by C.L. Hoag and B.W. Clark as a cross of Concord and Cassady — two Labrusca-type grapes. Where Concord produces blue-black fruit with the iconic musky-sweet Concord flavor, Niagara produces pale green to golden-amber fruit with an equivalent but distinct flavor: the same Labrusca 'foxiness' but in a lighter, more delicate package that is closer to traditional white grape flavors when eaten fresh, yet unmistakably American in its musky, aromatic character. Niagara has been widely grown in the northeastern and midwestern states since its introduction and is the standard white-fruited companion to Concord in home vineyards across the grape belt of New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan, and similar regions. The grapes are seeded (like Concord) with the same slip-skin characteristic — the skin separates easily from the pulp — and produce excellent fresh-eating fruit, white grape juice (with a distinctive musky-sweet flavor that distinguishes American white juice from European-style products), and white jellies and preserves with a characteristic Labrusca fragrance. The vines are vigorous and highly cold-hardy, equivalent to Concord in frost resistance, and similarly require adequate chilling hours that limit their usefulness in zones 9+.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Nichols is a Louisiana-developed fig selection valued for good cold hardiness and reliable production in Gulf South dooryard plantings.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Nichols is a fig selection developed in Louisiana and long grown across the Gulf South for its reliable production of medium-large, brown-skinned figs with sweet, amber-pink flesh, along with good cold hardiness that lets it recover well after occasional hard freezes common at the northern edge of fig-growing country. Like other figs it fruits on both old and new wood, giving an early breba crop in late spring followed by a heavier main crop in late summer, and needs minimal care once established beyond an annual mulch layer and light pruning to manage size. Established plants regrow readily from the base if winter cold kills back the top growth in an unusually harsh year.

plant_note: Plant in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nijisseiki (20th Century) is the historic benchmark Asian pear variety, discovered in Japan in 1888 and still the standard against which all others are measured — producing large, juicy, round, yellow-skinned fruits that exemplify the classic Asian pear form and flavor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; requires cross-pollination with another compatible Asian pear. Nijisseiki (20th Century, in Japanese literally 'twentieth century') is perhaps the most historically significant Asian pear cultivar, discovered as a chance seedling in Matsudo, Chiba Prefecture, Japan in 1888 by Chuhei Matsudo and eventually named for the approaching new century; for most of the 20th century it was Japan's most widely grown pear and still accounts for significant commercial production. The fruits are large (8–12 oz), perfectly round, smooth-skinned, pale yellow-green, and juicy with a mild, refreshing, lightly sweet flavor and crisp, white flesh. Reasonably low chill requirement (approximately 400–500 hours) makes it viable in California, Gulf Coast, and mild Southern gardens. Ripens in August; stores well for 2–4 months refrigerated.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring; Nikita's Gift is a hybrid between the American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) and the Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki) developed at the Nikita Botanical Garden in Yalta, Ukraine — combining the extraordinary cold hardiness of the American parent (to about -25°F when dormant) with the large fruit size and non-astringency of the Oriental parent, resulting in one of the most cold-hardy large-fruited persimmons available.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Nikita's Gift is notably drought-tolerant when established and thrives without supplemental fertilization in most soils — avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that encourage excessive vegetative growth. Nikita's Gift was hybridized at the Nikita Botanical Garden (Nikitsky Botanic Garden) in Yalta, Crimea, Ukraine by crossing the cold-hardy American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) with the large-fruited Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki); the goal was to produce a persimmon with fruit size, quality, and non-astringency approaching the Japanese cultivars while withstanding the much harsher winters of continental and cold-temperate climates where standard Asian persimmons die back or fail to fruit. The result is a very cold-hardy tree (to approximately -25°F when fully dormant) producing large (6–12 oz) fruits with reddish-orange to brick-red skin resembling the appearance of Asian varieties; the fruits are astringent when unripe but become non-astringent and sweet after frost or artificial treatment (the PVNA type characteristic of some Asian varieties). The flavor of fully ripe Nikita's Gift is rich, sweet, and honeyed — superior to American persimmon and comparable to the finest Japanese types. Self-fruitful; produces best without a pollinator. One of the most important persimmon introductions for cold-climate gardeners.

subcategory: tidal mangrove edible palm Southeast Asia
plant_note: Plant propagules or container stock in spring in full sun in tidal or permanently wet, brackish to fresh, low-salinity soil or at the edge of still, warm water in zone 10–12; Nipa Palm is a remarkable, stemless, tidal palm native to mangrove estuaries from the Indian subcontinent through Southeast Asia and the Pacific — one of the oldest flowering plants on Earth with a fossil record of 70 million years — grown for its edible young endosperm (kaong), palm wine tapped from the flowering stalk, and leaves used for traditional thatching (nipa huts) throughout Southeast Asia.
directions: Plant Nypa fruticans propagules (the large, floating seeds germinate readily and can be pressed into waterlogged soil) in tidal freshwater to slightly brackish mudflats or pond margins with permanently saturated soil in full sun; the rhizome spreads horizontally underground and produces new upright frond clusters periodically; plants tolerate some saltwater intrusion but grow best in low-salinity or freshwater tidal conditions. Nipa Palm is one of the most ancient and ecologically important palms in the world — with a fossil record extending back 70 million years to the Cretaceous period — and is the only member of the subfamily Nypoideae, making it botanically unique among all living palms. Unlike all other palms, Nypa is essentially stemless: its massive, horizontal trunk lies underground or just at the water surface, sending up large, pinnate fronds 10–15 feet tall directly from the horizontal stem. The spherical, rugose fruit clusters yield young, jelly-like endosperm (kaong or palm toddy in the Philippines) eaten fresh or preserved in syrup; the developing floral stalks are tapped for sap (up to 8 liters/day) fermented into palm wine (tuba) or boiled to make palm sugar (gula atap). Millions of acres of Nipa stands form critical tidal mangrove habitat across Southeast Asia, storing substantial carbon and protecting coastlines from erosion. Cultivation outside its natural range requires a very wet, frost-free environment.

common_name: Noble Muscadine Grape (Large Dark-Purple Self-Fertile Gulf South Muscadine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Noble has perfect (self-fertile) flowers — it will set fruit without a pollinator but produces better crops when planted with another muscadine cultivar nearby. Provide a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence; muscadines are vigorous climbers.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Noble is one of the most widely planted and highly regarded purple muscadine grape cultivars for Gulf South home gardens and small vineyards — a vigorous, productive vine producing large (1–1.5 inch), round, deep purple-black to dark purple grapes with thick, slightly tough skin and sweet, musky, richly flavored flesh that is the definition of classic muscadine flavor. Muscadine grapes (Muscadinia rotundifolia) are the grape of the American Southeast — a separate species from European and California wine grapes, native to the coastal plain from Florida to Virginia, and extraordinarily well-adapted to the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of Gulf South summers that devastate Vitis vinifera varieties. Noble bears perfect (hermaphroditic) flowers and is self-fertile, a major advantage over the older cultivars that required a male or bisexual pollinator; it is also an excellent pollinator for female-flowered cultivars like Fry and Higgins. The large grape clusters ripen in August–September and are harvested individually as grapes ripen separately within each cluster — a distinctive feature of muscadine harvesting. Noble is used for fresh eating, juice, jelly, wine, and vinegar. The thick skin and seeds are the main characteristics distinguishing muscadine from table grapes — some people find them unpleasant, while others consider them inseparable from the authentic flavor experience. Noble wine produces a characteristically sweet, richly flavored muscadine wine very different from European wine styles.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Noire de Caromb is a main-crop fig ripening August–September in zone 9. It is a moderately vigorous tree well-suited to zone 9 heat. The dark fruit absorbs heat well and ripens thoroughly even in partial shade conditions.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Noire de Caromb is a French dark-skinned fig from the Caromb commune in Vaucluse, Provence — part of the rich fig heritage of Provence where the warm, dry Mediterranean climate has sustained diverse fig cultivation for millennia. The medium-sized, round to slightly flattened fruits have very dark purple to nearly black skin and deep red-to-garnet flesh with an intensely rich, complex, sweet flavor with pronounced winey depth that characterizes the best Provençal dark figs. Noire de Caromb is considered one of the finest-flavored dark-skinned fig varieties by European fig enthusiasts, though it remains less well-known in North American markets than brown Turkey or Celeste. In zone 9 the Gulf Coast heat produces fig flavor of excellent quality, and Noire de Caromb performs well in the long, warm growing season. Its primary advantage over more common dark-skinned figs is the depth and complexity of flavor.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, sandy, or rocky, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; noni is a remarkably adaptable small tree suited to zones 10–12 that tolerates poor, infertile, saline, and even volcanic soils where other trees would struggle. It is one of the fastest-bearing tropical fruit trees, often producing its first fruits within 12–18 months of transplanting.
directions: Plant in well-drained sandy, rocky, or infertile soil — including saline and coastal soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; noni (Morinda citrifolia) is a small, fast-growing evergreen tree in the Rubiaceae family native to Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands that has been one of the most important plants in Pacific Islander traditional medicine for over 2,000 years, with virtually every part of the plant — fruit, leaves, bark, seeds, and roots — used in traditional preparations throughout Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia. The distinctive, lumpy, pale greenish-white to translucent fruits have an extremely pungent, cheese-like odor when ripe that makes them challenging to consume fresh, yet the juice has become a globally marketed health supplement product worth billions of dollars annually, prized for antioxidant compounds including iridoids, scopoletin, and various polysaccharides. Trees produce fruit year-round in frost-free tropical conditions, bear their first crop remarkably quickly — within 1–2 years of transplanting — and are exceptionally drought-tolerant once established, requiring irrigation only during establishment. Noni is one of the most salt- and wind-tolerant of all tropical fruit trees, making it well suited to coastal planting in South Florida and the Gulf Coast.

common_name: Nonpareil Almond (California Commercial Standard Almond, The World's Almond)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Nonpareil is self-incompatible and requires two cross-pollinating varieties — plant with Carmel plus one of (Mission, Butte, Padre, or Fritz) for reliable three-variety pollination system used in California commercial orchards; requires approximately 250–350 chill hours; strictly zones 7–9 in hot, dry summer climates — almonds require a Mediterranean climate with dry summers to ripen properly and avoid hull rot diseases.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Nonpareil requires two cross-pollinating companion varieties for fruit set; irrigate deeply but infrequently once established; harvest in late July to August when hulls split open naturally; shake trees to dislodge nuts and allow to dry on tarps for 1–2 days before hulling and drying. Nonpareil is the most widely planted almond variety in the world and the variety that defines the global almond market — approximately 40–50% of California's almond production, which itself supplies roughly 80% of the world's almonds, comes from Nonpareil trees, making it the single most economically important tree nut variety on earth. The variety was selected in California in the 1870s by A.T. Hatch and propagated by Sexton & Lewelling Nurseries of San Leandro, California, quickly becoming the commercial standard because of its combination of easily-shelled, very thin shell, high kernel percentage (around 62–65%), excellent kernel quality (smooth, flat shape ideal for processing and sliced almonds), and early ripening that opens the harvest season before other varieties. Nonpareil kernels set the price benchmark in global almond markets — the Nonpareil grade commands the highest premiums for direct consumption, whole roasted almonds, and retail packaging because of the variety's consistent appearance, mild sweet flavor, and thin, papery shell. The variety is not self-fertile and requires two companion varieties with overlapping bloom times for reliable nut set.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; North Star is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, making it ideal for smaller gardens with space for only one cherry tree.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; North Star is a naturally dwarf tart cherry developed at the University of Minnesota that reaches only 8–12 feet tall — significantly smaller than standard sour cherry trees — making it manageable for home gardens and usable on semi-dwarfing rootstocks for even smaller trees. The fruit is tart, dark-red, with a short stem that makes hand harvesting easier than Montmorency. It is self-fertile, needing no pollinizer, and is exceptional for its hardiness — surviving zone 3 winters reliably. Like all tart cherries, North Star fruit is used primarily for pies, jams, juices, and preserves rather than fresh eating, but the intense cherry flavor is prized in those applications. Trees bear heavily and begin producing within 2–3 years of planting. North Star is more disease-resistant than sweet cherries, requiring less intensive management. An excellent choice for the northern home orchard where sweet cherries may be unreliable.

common_name: Northern Spy Apple (Classic New York Pie Apple, Late-Season Northeastern Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Northern Spy requires approximately 1000 chill hours and is best adapted to zones 4–7; it requires a cross-pollinator (Cortland, McIntosh, or Empire) and is notably slow to come into bearing — grafted trees on standard rootstock may take 6–10 years to produce significant fruit — but the trees are extremely long-lived, productive, and cold-hardy once established.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pair with McIntosh, Cortland, or Empire for cross-pollination; thin fruits in June for maximum size; Northern Spy ripens October–November — later than almost all other apple varieties — producing very large, greenish-yellow to red-striped fruits with exceptional crispness, complex sweet-tart flavor, and outstanding keeping quality. Northern Spy apple was discovered as a chance seedling in East Bloomfield (Ontario County), New York around 1800, taking its unusual name from political associations of the era; it was introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s and rapidly became one of the most important commercial and home orchard apples of the northeastern United States and Canada. The variety has characteristics that make it consistently beloved by serious apple enthusiasts: very large size (sometimes exceeding one pound per fruit), exceptional crispness and juiciness, a complex, rich sweet-tart flavor with floral notes that compares favorably with any modern variety, and excellent keeping quality (fruits store 3–5 months under proper conditions). Northern Spy is the definitive pie apple of the northeast American tradition — the variety that old-time New England and New York pie recipes specify by name — because its firm flesh holds structure through baking and its tart, complex flavor creates an extraordinary pie filling. The trees are notably long-lived and become very large, with documented trees 150+ years old still producing; the long juvenile period (5–10 years to significant bearing) is a trade-off for extreme longevity.

common_name: Nottingham Medlar (Classic Bletted European Medlar Tree for Unusual Jelly and Wine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nottingham is the most widely grown and most readily available medlar cultivar in commerce — selected for more open, easier-to-pick fruit structure than the species and reliable flavor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Nottingham Medlar is the best and most widely grown cultivar of one of the most unusual and historically significant fruits in the European garden tradition — the medlar (Mespilus germanica) is a small deciduous tree that produces brown, apple-like fruits with an open calyx end that must undergo 'bletting' (controlled softening through frost damage and fermentation) before becoming edible. Freshly picked medlar fruits are hard, astringent, and unpleasant; after bletting — either on the tree after frosts or stored in a cool location for several weeks — they transform into soft, brown, date-like paste with a rich, wine-like flavor combining apple, date, and brown sugar notes that is quite unlike any other fruit. Bletted medlar flesh is used for medlar jelly (a beautiful, rose-colored preserve with complex flavor), medlar wine, and eaten fresh as a confection. The tree itself is ornamentally beautiful: a small, naturally gnarled and picturesque deciduous tree (10–15 feet) with large white flowers in spring, handsome broad leaves that color well in autumn, and the unusual open-calyx brown fruits hanging from the branches through fall and into winter. The late-season beauty and ancient cultural history — medlar appears frequently in medieval and Renaissance English literature and was a common kitchen-garden tree for centuries — give this fruit exceptional interest for historically minded gardeners. Zone 9 is at the warm edge of its range.

common_name: Nova Elderberry (Early-Ripening High-Yield Canadian Elderberry Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Nova is a good pollinator for Bob Gordon and Adams cultivars — planting two or more different cultivars consistently increases fruit production.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Nova is a Canadian elderberry cultivar developed by Agriculture Canada that produces large, dense, heavy berry clusters ripening one of the earliest in the American elderberry season — typically 7–10 days earlier than Adams and other mid-season cultivars. The large, heavy clusters of very dark purple-black berries — dense and pendant when fully ripe — combine good fresh eating quality with excellent processing characteristics for elderberry syrup, juice, wine, and jelly production. Nova produces abundant flat-topped flower clusters in June–July, providing one of the most productive native pollinator resources in the early summer garden — elder flowers are visited by extraordinary numbers of native bees, small native bees, and beneficial insects that use the pollen and nectar. The compact cyme structure of Nova clusters makes harvesting somewhat easier than looser-clustered varieties. Nova's combination of early ripening, high production, and compact plant habit (slightly smaller than some other cultivars at 5–10 feet) makes it a practical choice for home gardens. As with all American elderberry, Nova spreads by root suckers to form colonies — plan for the suckering habit and remove suckers regularly to maintain the desired planting footprint.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 2–3 inch depth in moist, deep, slightly acidic, loamy bottomland soil in full sun; cold stratification of 90–120 days over winter is required before spring germination. Nutmeg Hickory develops a deep taproot early and transplants poorly once established — direct seeding or very young container stock is strongly preferred.
directions: Nutmeg Hickory is the rarest of the true hickories native to North America, found scattered in moist to wet bottomlands, alluvial flats, and river swamps of the southeastern coastal plain from South Carolina west to southeastern Texas, where it reaches its greatest abundance in Louisiana and Mississippi. The round, dark nuts — resembling nutmegs in shape and borne in thick, 4-parted husks — are smaller than those of most hickories but are relished by squirrels, white-tailed deer, and wild turkeys, and were historically gathered and eaten by Native Americans. Plant fresh nuts directly in fall in deep, moist, slightly acidic loamy soil in full sun, allowing 90–120 days of cold stratification over winter before spring germination; the deep taproot that forms in the first growing season makes older trees virtually impossible to transplant. Trees grow steadily in bottomland soils and develop spectacular golden-yellow fall color and deeply furrowed gray bark that make them outstanding additions to naturalized floodplain or riparian plantings.

common_name: O'Neal Southern Highbush Blueberry (Low-Chill Highbush Blueberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in late winter in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; O'Neal requires only 200–400 chill hours, making it one of the best highbush blueberries for zone 9; plant with another low-chill southern highbush cultivar like Legacy or Sunshine Blue for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; O'Neal is widely considered the finest-tasting southern highbush blueberry cultivar — a North Carolina State University release with remarkably low chill requirements (200–400 hours) that makes it appropriate for zone 9 and even warmer parts of zone 8, where northern highbush cultivars receive insufficient chilling. The large, medium-blue berries have exceptionally complex, aromatic, rich blueberry flavor — consistently rated among the best-tasting of all blueberry cultivars in taste trials by the North Carolina breeding program. The flavor profile is described as rich, aromatic, and complex with a good balance of sweetness and acidity. O'Neal is an early-season cultivar, ripening in April–May in zone 9, which helps avoid peak summer heat and provides early-season fruit at a premium time. The bush grows vigorously to 5–7 feet with attractive white urn-shaped flowers in late winter and outstanding fall color (orange to red) that makes it an ornamental landscape plant as well as a fruiting shrub. Plant with at least one other southern highbush cultivar (Legacy or Sunshine Blue) for cross-pollination, which dramatically increases berry size and total yield. Maintain strict soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5 — blueberries fail in soils above pH 6.0.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings after last frost; in zone 9 plant February–April. O'Rourke is a biennial bearer, producing a Breba crop in June and a main crop in August–October. Well-suited to humid Gulf Coast conditions where many fig varieties suffer from souring (internal fermentation) caused by rainfall splitting ripe fruit — O'Rourke's closed eye greatly reduces this problem.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; O'Rourke is a fig developed by the LSU AgCenter and named for Dr. Ed O'Rourke, the Louisiana fruit breeder who led decades of fig research at LSU. Released in the late 20th century, it was bred specifically for Louisiana and Gulf Coast conditions, where the challenges of summer rain, humidity, and insect pressure at the eye (ostiole) cause fruit souring and internal pest damage in many standard varieties. O'Rourke has a distinctively tight, nearly closed eye that greatly reduces fruit souring caused by rain entering the ostiole and internal splitting — making it one of the best varieties for humid Gulf Coast gardens. Fruit is medium-sized, greenish-yellow to tan at maturity with amber-pink flesh, very sweet with complex fig flavor. The breba crop on old wood in June is modest; the main crop in August–October is abundant. Trees are vigorous and well-adapted to heavy clay soils when drainage is adequate.

common_name: Oconee Pecan (UGA Scab-Resistant Southeastern Pecan, Type I Mid-Season Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; Oconee is a Type I pollinator (sheds pollen before its own pistillate flowers are receptive) — plant with Type II varieties including Stuart, Elliott, Caddo, or Wichita for reliable cross-pollination; Oconee is one of the premier recommendations from University of Georgia Extension for home and commercial pecan production in the southeastern states, specifically selected for performance under southeastern humidity and scab pressure.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained to moderately moist fertile soil; Oconee is a mid-season variety (ripening October in the Gulf South) with large nuts and good kernel fill; its scab resistance makes it particularly valuable in the humid southeastern states from Virginia through the Gulf Coast; trees are moderately vigorous and productive. Oconee pecan is a University of Georgia-developed variety (released in the 1990s) that has become one of the most highly recommended pecan cultivars for the southeastern United States, specifically bred and selected for performance under the humid conditions, disease pressure, and climate of the southeastern coastal plain and Gulf South. The breeding program at the University of Georgia's Tifton Campus has focused on developing pecan varieties with significantly improved scab resistance compared to the older standard commercial varieties (Desirable, Stuart, Schley) while maintaining nut quality comparable to those benchmarks — and Oconee represents one of the successful outcomes of this program. The nuts are large (40–48 per pound), well-filled, with good kernel percentage (58–62%), and produce a clean, sweet, buttery pecan flavor that compares favorably with the best commercial varieties. Oconee's most important attribute is its considerably better scab resistance than Desirable or Schley in the humid conditions of Georgia, Alabama, and the Gulf South — in UGA variety trials under disease pressure, Oconee consistently shows significantly lower scab infection rates on leaves and shucks, resulting in cleaner nuts and more consistent yields without the intensive fungicide programs that scab-susceptible varieties require. A premier choice for home orchard planting throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Okitsu ripens earlier than standard satsuma and its seedless, easy-peel fruit develops full sweetness ahead of most other citrus in the garden.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Selected at Japan's Okitsu horticultural research station as an early-ripening sport of common satsuma, this cultivar produces small, flattened, deep-orange fruit that colors and sweetens several weeks before standard satsuma, often ready by October. The seedless, loose-skinned segments are tender and richly sweet with low acidity, and the compact tree bears reliably from a young age. Its early ripening window makes it especially useful in areas where an early hard freeze can threaten later-maturing citrus.

plant_note: Plant in spring after the last frost; in Mediterranean-climate zones fall planting is also suitable.
directions: Olives thrive in the classic Mediterranean climate — hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters — and are extremely drought-tolerant once established, but they require 200–400 chill hours to set fruit reliably. Most cultivars are self-fertile, but cross-pollination with a second variety improves yields significantly. Trees are long-lived and slow-growing; minimal pruning is needed beyond thinning for light penetration. For table olives, harvest when fruit is still green-to-straw colored; for oil, pick when about half the fruit has turned black.

plant_note: Plant after frost; grow in a container in zones colder than 8 so it can shelter indoors over winter.
directions: The olive is a slow-growing Mediterranean evergreen with silvery foliage, gnarled character, and small fruit ripening from green to black. It thrives in hot, dry conditions and needs a stretch of winter chill to set fruit well. Plant in full sun in fast-draining, even rocky soil and water deeply but infrequently once established. In zones below 8, grow it in a large pot and move it to a cool, bright indoor space during hard freezes. Prune in late winter to open the canopy and cure the fruit before eating, as fresh olives are bitter.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Olosapo (Zapotillo, Cacaito, Olosapo de Playa) is a medium-sized tropical fruit tree from the Pacific coast lowland forests of Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica — bearing oval to pear-shaped, russet-brown, thin-skinned fruits with rich, creamy, yellow flesh of exceptional flavor combining avocado, sweet potato, and almond — a prized traditional food of coastal Mesoamerica.
directions: Plant Couepia polyandra in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; water regularly during establishment; trees begin fruiting at 5–8 years and can produce heavy crops of excellent-quality fruit once mature. Olosapo is a member of the Chrysobalanaceae family (relatives of coco plum) native to the Pacific coastal lowlands of Mesoamerica, where it is a traditional food tree in local communities in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Costa Rica. The russet-brown to olive-green, oval fruits (resembling a small russet potato externally) contain very rich, creamy, yellow-orange flesh surrounding a single large seed; the texture is smooth and buttery, not unlike a ripe avocado, and the flavor is sweet and complex — combining notes of sweet potato, almond, and a mild tropical richness. The fruit is eaten fresh out of hand (removing the thin skin) or processed into beverages. The tree produces attractive, large, oval, glossy leaves and clusters of small white flowers followed by the distinctive fruits. Rarely seen outside its native range but considered by those who know it to be one of the finest-flavored Pacific coast Mesoamerican fruits; deserving wider cultivation in zone 10–12 tropical gardens in Florida, Hawaii, and southern California.

common_name: Olympian Fig (Exceptionally Cold-Hardy Brown-Skinned Productive Fig)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Olympian is one of the most cold-hardy fig cultivars — suitable for zone 6-7 gardens where most other figs are marginal, and exceptionally reliable in the Gulf South where cold hardiness is rarely a limiting factor.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Olympian is a fig cultivar noted for exceptional cold-hardiness and reliable productivity — it is one of the hardiest named figs commercially available, surviving temperatures well below those that damage other cultivars, making it the preferred choice for gardeners at the northern edge of fig culture (zone 6-7) and an extremely reliable fruiting tree throughout zone 8-10. The medium to large fruits have brown to brown-violet skin, amber flesh with reddish tones, and a pleasant sweetness — not as dramatically flavored as Violette de Bordeaux but consistently good and productive. Olympian typically produces a breba (early summer) crop on previous year's wood in addition to the main crop on current year's wood, extending the harvest season. The cold-hardiness advantage of Olympian is most significant in zone 9a and northward, where occasional cold snaps below 20°F would damage less-hardy cultivars; in zone 9b-10, it provides a comfortable margin of cold tolerance safety. Self-fertile, like all common figs, and a vigorous, productive tree that begins bearing in its second or third year from planting. The large, distinctive lobed leaves of all figs provide attractive tropical-looking foliage through the growing season. Figs produce two crops in warm climates: the early breba crop in June and the main crop in late summer through fall.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; in frost-free zones, spring or early fall planting is ideal.
directions: Sweet oranges (Citrus sinensis) are self-fertile; navel oranges and many blood oranges are seedless because they are parthenocarpic. Most oranges need warm nights to develop sweetness and cannot be grown outdoors north of zone 9; the Hamlin and Navel types are slightly more cold-tolerant. Fruit can stay on the tree for weeks to months after ripening, extending harvest, but may re-green in warm weather without losing quality. Apply a balanced citrus fertilizer in late winter, late spring, and midsummer for best production.

common_name: Orange Quince (Classic Round Golden American Heirloom Quince)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Orange Quince is a long-established American heirloom cultivar producing large, round, golden-orange fruit with a strong, sweet fragrance, among the most widely planted quince cultivars in home orchards for its reliable production and good flavor when cooked into preserves, jelly, and paste. Like other quince it is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, blooming with attractive pale pink flowers in spring before the hard, aromatic fruit develops and ripens in fall. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and needs only routine pruning to maintain an open form that allows good air circulation, which helps reduce fire blight, the main disease concern for quince in humid regions.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors in spring in very well-drained, sandy, neutral to alkaline cactus mix; transplant into the garden when several inches tall. In zone 8-9, site in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate available. Organ pipe cactus is slowest to mature from seed; cuttings root more readily.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly, neutral to slightly alkaline, lean soil in full sun in zones 9–12; organ pipe cactus is a multi-stemmed columnar cactus native to the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, Mexico — the signature species of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. The dark green, 20+ ribbed columns eventually reach 15–20 feet in height in a candelabra form. The night-blooming, pale lavender to pink-white flowers are pollinated by long-nosed bats, which migrate northward from Mexico specifically to feed on cactus blooms. The reddish-purple, spiny fruits — the pitaya dulce (sweet pitaya) — are among the most important traditional foods of the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert, eaten fresh or dried into fruit leather. A freeze-sensitive cactus (damaged below 26°F) best suited to the warmest, driest areas of zone 9 and the true desert Southwest.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees January–February in zone 9; Orient is partially self-fertile but benefits from cross-pollination with LeConte, Kieffer, or Garber. Low chill requirement (100–150 hours) makes it one of the best pears for zone 9. Ripens July–August in zone 8–9 — earlier than most European pears.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Orient is a hybrid between European and Asian pear species released by the USDA in 1945 and one of the most recommended pears for zone 7–9 because of its exceptionally low chill requirement (100–150 hours), outstanding fire blight resistance, and reliable productivity in the humid South. The large, yellow-brown, russeted fruits are sweet and juicy with a slightly gritty, Asian pear texture — firm enough to eat fresh immediately after harvest (unlike European varieties that must ripen off the tree) and excellent for canning, preserves, and cooking. Orient trees are vigorous, productive, and relatively easy to grow in zone 9.
