The early ripening (July–August in most of the Gulf South) makes fresh pears available in midsummer — a time when pear production from the northern states is still weeks away. Orient is considered slightly more fire blight resistant than Kieffer and a better fresh-eating pear. One of the most reliably productive pear choices for Gulf Coast zone 8–9 home orchards.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant; in zone 9 plant December–February. Orient pear is partially self-fertile and will produce some fruit without a cross-pollinator, but production increases substantially when planted with Kieffer, Moonglow, or another pear variety within 50 feet. Chill hour requirement is approximately 350–450 hours below 45°F, making it one of the more widely adapted pears for zone 9 inland gardens. Fruits ripen in August–September in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, deep, slightly acidic to neutral soil — like the Kieffer, Orient pear tolerates the heavier clay soils common in the Gulf South better than most fruit trees; Orient is a Southern-bred pear hybrid (Pyrus communis x Pyrus pyrifolia) released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1945, developed specifically for the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the American Southeast. The large, golden-yellow, round to bell-shaped fruits are among the largest of any pear variety commonly grown in the South, with smooth, butter-textured, mildly sweet flesh that ripens earlier than Kieffer (August rather than September-October). Orient's exceptional resistance to fire blight — the bacterial disease that devastates pears in humid southern climates — was the primary breeding objective that made it a success in the Southeast. The combination of large fruit size, fire blight resistance, adequate flavor, and low chill hour requirement makes Orient one of the most reliably productive pears for zone 9 conditions in the inland South.

common_name: Orinoco Banana (Very Cold-Hardy Cooking and Eating Gulf South Banana)
plant_note: Plant divisions (pups) after the last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Orinoco is one of the most cold-tolerant banana cultivars — the rhizome survives temperatures into the high teens (°F) and regenerates reliably from the roots in spring in zone 8b–9.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Orinoco is among the most cold-hardy banana cultivars for Gulf South gardens — a large, vigorous variety with remarkable rhizome hardiness that allows reliable regrowth from the roots even after severe freezes that kill the pseudostem entirely. The cold hardiness is Orinoco's primary practical advantage over most other banana cultivars in zone 8b–9: while the aboveground pseudostem is typically killed in hard freezes below 25–28°F, the underground rhizome system survives temperatures into the upper teens (°F), regenerating aggressively in spring and frequently reaching full pseudostem height again within a single growing season. Orinoco produces medium-large, thick-skinned, angular-ribbed fruits that are excellent for cooking when green (plantain-like, with a slightly starchy, mild flavor that takes on seasonings well in frying, baking, and sautéing) and sweet for fresh eating when fully ripe and yellow to black. The thick skin provides good shelf life and handling resistance. The very large, bold tropical foliage (8–12 foot pseudostems with 4–6 foot leaves in Gulf South conditions) creates dramatic tropical landscape impact even in years when fruit production is not the priority. Orinoco has been grown in Gulf South gardens for generations and is particularly favored in coastal Louisiana where its heat and humidity tolerance are well-matched to the climate.

scientific_name: Citrus grandis x C. paradisi 'Oro Blanco'
plant_note: Plant container-grown, grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Oro Blanco is self-fruitful and sets good crops without a cross-pollinator, though bee activity always improves fruit set.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Oro Blanco ('White Gold' in Spanish) is a remarkable hybrid of pomelo (Citrus grandis) and white grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) developed by University of California breeders in the 1950s and released in 1980, producing pale greenish-yellow to yellow fruits that appear externally unripe but are actually fully ripe and extraordinarily sweet — completely lacking the bitter notes of standard grapefruit due to the absence of the flavanone naringin, the compound responsible for grapefruit's characteristic bitterness. The result is a large citrus (slightly larger than grapefruit) with thick, spongy peel, white, juicy flesh, and a flavor that is pure sweet citrus without any bitterness — outstanding for people who love grapefruit flavor but dislike the bitterness, and for those who take medications contraindicated with grapefruit. Fruits ripen October through February (one of the earliest-ripening grapefruits) and hold on the tree for months; the thick peel insulates the flesh and extends storage life. The large tree (12–18 feet) is handsome in the landscape and produces heavily. A superb and under-known citrus for Gulf South zone 9 gardens.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Oroblanco is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid developed by UC Riverside, released in 1981 — less cold-hardy than grapefruit or satsuma, tolerating temperatures only to about 27–28°F. In zone 9a plant in the most protected microclimate (south or west wall exposure) and protect young trees with frost cloth during the first 3–4 winters. Harvest in winter (December–February) when the thick, pale yellow-green rind begins to yellow — the fruit does not need to fully color for the flesh to develop full sweetness. The flesh is notably sweeter than standard grapefruit, with lower acidity and bitterness.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil with consistent deep watering during the growing season — Oroblanco citrus requires full sun, good drainage, and regular irrigation for fruit production; Oroblanco is a grapefruit-pomelo hybrid (Citrus x paradisi) developed at UC Riverside specifically to combine the large, sweet, low-acid flesh of pomelo with the familiar grapefruit flavor profile — producing a fruit that is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than standard white or pink grapefruit while retaining the clean, refreshing citrus character that makes grapefruit family fruits distinctive. The large, pale yellow-green to yellow fruit (5–6 inches in diameter) has a thick rind and abundant, juicy, very pale yellow-white flesh with the reduced bitterness that makes Oroblanco accessible to consumers who find standard grapefruit too bitter without sugar. Oroblanco is one of the most productive and consistent hybrid citrus varieties for zone 9 — the combination of large fruit size, high juice content, and notably superior eating quality compared to bitter grapefruit types makes it a practical and rewarding home citrus tree in the warm, protected microclimates of zone 9 where adequate winter temperatures allow year-round outdoor culture.

plant_note: Cold-stratify seeds for 30–60 days, or wash seeds from the large fruits and plant in spring; seeds germinate readily in warm soil. For hedgerow use, plant small potted plants 3–4 feet apart in a row and trim annually to form a dense, impenetrable barrier.
directions: Plant in virtually any well-drained soil in full sun — osage orange is extraordinarily tough and tolerates drought, flooding, extreme heat, alkaline soils, heavy clay, and compaction better than almost any other large deciduous tree; it was originally native to a small area of Texas and Oklahoma but was spread across much of North America in the 19th century for use as a living fence (a hedge of osage orange is literally 'horse-high, bull-strong, and hog-tight'). The dense, thorny branches form impenetrable barriers; the orange-colored heartwood is one of the most rot-resistant and hardest of any American wood, traditionally used for fence posts, bows (the tree's French name 'bois d'arc' means 'bow wood'), and railroad ties. The large, lumpy yellow-green fruits (osage oranges or hedge apples) are not edible for humans but are consumed by squirrels and, historically, by mammoths and ground sloths — the tree is a relic of the Pleistocene megafauna era.

common_name: Osborne Prolific Fig (San Francisco Bay Fig, Cool-Climate California Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring after frost danger; Osborne Prolific is particularly well-adapted to the cool maritime climates of the San Francisco Bay Area, coastal Oregon, and Washington State, where it ripens well even in cool foggy summers that prevent many other fig varieties from fully maturing — it is the most recommended fig for Pacific Coast cool-summer gardens and bears two crops: a breba crop in early summer on old wood and a main crop in late summer.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Osborne Prolific is drought-tolerant once established and requires minimal fertilization; prune in late winter to maintain desired size; fruits ripen brownish-purple to dark reddish-purple and should be harvested when completely soft and sweet — they do not store or ship well and are best eaten immediately. Osborne Prolific is an heirloom California fig variety of unknown but apparently pre-1900 California origin, named for and associated with the nursery trade of the San Francisco Bay Area region where it became the standard recommended fig for maritime and cool-summer Pacific Coast gardens. Its primary distinguishing attribute is its ability to ripen fruit adequately in the cool, foggy summers of the Pacific Coast, where the heat units accumulated from May through October are significantly lower than in the Sacramento Valley or Central Valley fig-growing regions — conditions under which varieties like Calimyrna, Kadota, and Brown Turkey may fail to fully sweeten or ripen the main crop before autumn. Osborne Prolific's adaptation to cool conditions appears to involve both earlier ripening of the main crop and a reliable breba (first) crop in early summer that provides fruit even if the main crop is delayed by a cool summer. The fruits are medium-sized, brownish-red to dark reddish-purple, with amber to strawberry-pink flesh and an excellent rich, sweet, honey-fig flavor that is considered one of the finest of any California fig variety. Very productive and reliable — living up to the 'Prolific' in its name — it is also a good choice for mild-winter coastal gardens in the Southeast.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun to part shade; Otaheite gooseberry is a Southeast Asian tropical tree producing dense clusters of small, ribbed, waxy, pale-yellow fruits with intensely sour, vitamin-C-rich flesh — they grow directly on the branches and main trunk (cauliflory) and are used throughout Southeast Asia as a sour flavoring in curries, pickles, and relishes.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; tolerates short dry periods once established. Phyllanthus acidus (Otaheite gooseberry or star gooseberry) is a pantropical small tree native to Madagascar and widely grown throughout Southeast Asia, India, and the Caribbean, producing dense clusters of tiny (1/2-inch), deeply ribbed, 6–8 angled, pale cream to yellow fruits that grow directly from the branches and main trunk in a striking display of cauliflory. The fruits are extremely sour and high in vitamin C — almost inedibly tart fresh — but excellent when cooked with sugar to make preserves, pickles, chutney, and a distinctive sour relish used in Filipino and Southeast Asian cooking as a souring agent (similar to tamarind) in soups, stews, and curries. In India, the fruits are pickled in salt and used in rice dishes. The tree is ornamental in its own right — the delicate, deciduous, compound-leafed branches resembling fine fern fronds contrast with the heavy clusters of waxy fruits on the bare branches. In zone 9, the tree may be damaged by hard freezes but usually recovers from the roots. A neglected tropical food tree that produces abundantly with minimal care in warm climates.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring before bud break; in zone 9 plant February–March. Pawpaws have a fleshy, easily-damaged taproot that makes transplanting difficult — purchase container-grown trees and disturb the root ball as little as possible at planting. A second variety is required for pollination; use hand-pollination with a small brush between different pawpaw varieties for best fruit set. Trees need 2–3 years of establishment before significant fruiting begins.
directions: Plant in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun as the tree matures; Overleese is a named pawpaw cultivar selected by Charles Zimmerman from southern Indiana, producing very large, high-quality fruits — among the largest of any named pawpaw variety at 6–16 ounces per fruit, with a distinctive elongated shape. The creamy, custard-like yellow flesh has a rich tropical flavor combining notes of banana, vanilla, and mango with a dense, smooth texture and relatively few, large seeds. Overleese is regarded as one of the premier flavor varieties in the Corwin Davis and Neal Peterson selection programs and produces heavy crops on mature trees. Pawpaws are the largest edible fruit native to North America and require cross-pollination from a different named variety — plant two or more cultivars within 50 feet, or hand-pollinate using a brush to transfer pollen between flowers on different trees. Ripe fruits fall from the tree in September–October and must be eaten or refrigerated within a week; they do not ship well, which is why pawpaws remain a local specialty.

plant_note: One of the more cold-tolerant citrus; grown from a grafted tree.
directions: The Owari satsuma is the early bird of citrus, ripening juicy, seedless, easy-peel mandarins in early winter. It is among the most cold-tolerant citrus, making it a good choice for growers in warm-temperate regions or in containers that overwinter indoors. Grow a grafted tree in full sun with well-drained soil and feed with a citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Water deeply but allow the surface to dry between waterings, and give some frost protection during hard cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April or September–October. Owari Satsuma is the most cold-hardy mandarin and one of the most cold-hardy of all citrus — tolerating temperatures down to about 15°F for brief periods when fully dormant and acclimated, significantly hardier than navel oranges or other citrus. Trees produce their first significant harvest 3–4 years after planting and reach full production in 5–7 years. Fruit ripens October–December, earlier than most citrus, providing fresh citrus before other varieties are ready. Protect young trees with frost cloth for the first 2–3 winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, sandy loam soil — satsuma mandarins require excellent drainage and regular deep watering during the growing season; Owari Satsuma is the most widely grown mandarin in the Gulf Coast region and one of the best-adapted citrus for zones 8–9 where its exceptional cold hardiness (among the hardiest of all edible citrus) allows reliable production in climates that would damage other mandarin varieties. The medium-sized, flattened-globe fruits with loose, easily peeled orange skin and nearly seedless, exceptionally sweet, aromatic flesh begin ripening in October — well before navel oranges and most other citrus — providing fresh homegrown citrus through December from a single, low-maintenance tree. The loose peel (puffy skin that separates easily from the fruit segments) makes Satsumas the easiest-to-eat citrus variety for fresh consumption, requiring no knife and no mess — a significant practical advantage over oranges and grapefruits. Owari Satsuma's cold hardiness has made it the standard citrus for the Gulf South, where it is grown commercially in Louisiana and Texas as well as throughout zone 9 home gardens.

common_name: Ozark Beauty Strawberry (Reliable Everbearing Strawberry for Home Garden Production)
plant_note: Plant bare-root crowns in late winter to early spring (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; in zone 9, fall planting (October–November) is often preferred as it allows plants to establish during the cool season and produce a heavy spring crop before summer heat declines production.
directions: Plant bare-root crowns in late winter–early spring (or fall in zone 9) in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Ozark Beauty is one of the most widely grown and long-proven everbearing strawberry varieties for home gardens — producing two to three crops annually (spring, summer, and fall in cooler regions; spring and fall in the Gulf South) versus the single annual spring crop of June-bearing types. The everbearing fruiting habit provides strawberries across a much longer season than June-bearers, making Ozark Beauty the preferred choice for home gardeners who want a sustained harvest rather than the concentrated single-season production of June-bearing varieties. The medium-to-large fruits are bright red, firm, and sweet — not quite the exceptional fresh flavor of the best June-bearing varieties (like Chandler) but reliably good across all crop flushes. The everbearing habit is maintained by growing the plant without harvesting runners during the first year, allowing energy to concentrate in fruit production rather than vegetative spread. In zone 9, Ozark Beauty performs best when planted in fall (October–November) to allow establishment during the cool season — spring transplants in zone 9 have limited time to establish before summer heat reduces productivity. Mulching with straw or pine straw conserves soil moisture, maintains even soil temperature, and keeps fruit clean. Remove runners from plants dedicated to fruit production to maintain fruiting energy.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall at 2 inches depth in well-drained, acidic, rocky to loamy soil; Ozark chinkapin grows in dry, rocky, ridge-top conditions and requires good drainage. Plant two trees for cross-pollination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, acidic, rocky or loamy soil in full sun; Ozark chinkapin is a native chestnut relative endemic to the Ozark Highlands of Arkansas and Missouri, historically less severely impacted by chestnut blight than the eastern American chestnut and still producing viable nuts in remnant populations. The tree occupies a niche on dry, rocky, acidic Ozark ridges where it was a valuable food resource for both wildlife and people — the sweet, thin-shelled nuts were gathered and eaten raw, roasted, and dried for winter storage. Like other American Castanea species, it is threatened by chestnut blight, though some individual trees show variable resistance. Conservation organizations actively collect seeds from resistant individuals for propagation and restoration. The nuts are smaller than Japanese chestnut but excellent in flavor, with a rich, sweet taste.

common_name: PA Golden Pawpaw (Pennsylvania Selection with Rich Golden Flesh)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; PA Golden needs a second, genetically distinct pawpaw cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; PA Golden is a Pennsylvania-origin pawpaw selection prized for its rich, deep golden-yellow flesh, smooth fiber-free texture, and intensely sweet, tropical flavor that many growers rank among the best-tasting named cultivars available. The medium-to-large fruits ripen over a relatively long window in the mid-to-late season, and the tree is a consistent, productive bearer once established. Because of its outstanding flavor and reliability, PA Golden is one of the more widely recommended cultivars for new home pawpaw plantings. Hand-pollinate with a small brush during the brief flowering window to improve fruit set, and plant with a second distinct cultivar such as Sunflower, Shenandoah, or Susquehanna for cross-pollination.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Page is a compact hybrid mandarin that ripens in winter and performs well in containers, making it a good choice for gardeners with limited in-ground space.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Developed by USDA researchers in Orlando, Florida in 1963 from a cross of Minneola tangelo and Clementine mandarin, Page produces small, deep reddish-orange fruit with very sweet, richly flavored, easy-peeling segments. The compact, dense growth habit makes it well suited to smaller yards and large containers that can be moved to shelter during hard freezes. Fruit ripens from December into February, and the tree benefits from thinning in years of especially heavy fruit set to maintain size.

common_name: Pakistan Mulberry (Giant Mulberry, Long Mulberry, Sweet Giant Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger; Pakistan Mulberry is self-fertile and produces without a pollinator; it thrives in zones 7–10 with warm summers and mild winters, performing particularly well in the Gulf South, California, and similar climates; the extraordinarily long fruit (up to 3 inches) is the defining characteristic that distinguishes Pakistan Mulberry from all other mulberry varieties — no other named mulberry produces fruit even close to this size.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pakistan Mulberry is drought-tolerant once established; trees bear in year 2–3 from transplant; fruit ripens May–June, producing very long (2–3 inch), deep red to black-purple mulberries with extraordinary sweetness — far more intensely sweet than red or white mulberry; spread a sheet under the canopy and shake branches to harvest ripe fruit. Pakistan Mulberry is a named selection of Morus macroura (the long mulberry of South Asia and Central Asia) introduced and popularized in American home orchards in the late 20th century, valued almost entirely for its exceptional fruit size — the berries of Pakistan Mulberry are dramatically longer than any other mulberry variety, with ripe fruits reaching 2–3 inches in length, nearly twice the length of the longest standard mulberries. This extreme length gives Pakistan Mulberry a visual impact unlike any other berry and a practical advantage in harvesting and fresh eating — the long, cylindrical berries are easy to pick individually and contain more juice and sweetness per fruit than shorter mulberries. The flavor of ripe Pakistan Mulberry is exceptional: intensely sweet, deeply fruity, and far richer than the wild red or white mulberry, with a complex sweetness that improves significantly on the flavor of seedling-grown mulberry trees. The trees are large and vigorous (30–40 feet on standard, smaller with pruning), adapting well to the hot summers of the Gulf South, central California, and the lower Midwest. In zone 9a, Pakistan Mulberry performs very well and has become one of the most-sought specialty fruit trees at Gulf Coast nurseries.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, sandy, slightly acidic soil in full sun; pale pawpaw is a Florida/Georgia endemic of dry, sandy soils and sandhills — unlike common pawpaw (Asimina triloba), which prefers moist, rich bottomland, this species is adapted to xeric, nutrient-poor, sandy habitats in the lower South.
directions: Plant in well-drained to dry, sandy, slightly acidic, infertile soil in full sun; pale pawpaw is a shrubby member of the custard apple family endemic to dry sandhills, sandhill scrub, and dry oak-pine woodland of northern and central Florida and southern Georgia — a very different habitat than the moist bottomlands of common pawpaw (A. triloba). The white flowers with pale cream to white petals are produced before leaf emergence, showy against the bare stems in late winter to early spring. The small, oval fruits are edible and custard-flavored like common pawpaw but smaller. The larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus) feed exclusively on Asimina species, making all pawpaws critically important for this distinctive butterfly. A rare and threatened species in its native Florida sandhill habitat, valuable for ecological restoration of dry, sandy, native ecosystems.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; palillo is a South American tropical fruit tree in the guava family producing small (1-inch), round to oval, yellow-orange fruits with creamy, sweet-aromatic flesh resembling a cross between guava and mango custard — an important native fruit tree of the Andean and Amazon foothills of Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun; palillo prefers consistent moisture and excellent drainage. Campomanesia lineatifolia (palillo or yellow guabiroba) is a Colombian, Peruvian, and Ecuadoran tropical fruit tree in the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) — the same plant family as guava, feijoa, and jaboticaba — producing small, round to oval, bright-yellow-orange fruits with smooth, thin, aromatic skin and a small quantity of cream to golden, very fragrant, sweet-rich flesh surrounding a few small seeds. The flavor is described as combining guava, mango, and custard in one fruit — aromatic, sweet, with pronounced tropical fragrance. The fruit is eaten fresh or made into juice, ice cream, and preserves; it is an important traditional food of indigenous Andean communities in Colombia and Peru. The genus Campomanesia encompasses many species of native Brazilian and South American myrtle-family trees — some famous (like guabiroba, C. xanthocarpa), most virtually unknown outside their native regions. Palillo is the Colombian and Peruvian name for C. lineatifolia; the tree is an important ornamental in Bogotá urban parks. Extremely rare in cultivation outside South America.

plant_note: Plant seedlings in spring in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; Palmyra palm is one of the most economically important and versatile palms in all of Asia and Africa — documented to yield more than 800 distinct products from its sap, fruit, leaves, and timber — it is the national tree of Cambodia (Kingdom of Cambodge) and the state tree of Tamil Nadu, India.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy soil in full sun; Palmyra palm is remarkably drought-tolerant once established. Borassus flabellifer (Palmyra palm or toddy palm) is one of the oldest cultivated plants in Asia — documented in Tamil literature for over 2,000 years — and one of the most economically important multi-use palms in the tropics. The tree is the national tree of Cambodia and the state tree of Tamil Nadu (India), reflecting its profound cultural and economic significance. The sap (toddy) tapped from the immature flower stalks is an extremely important product: fresh, it is a sweet, mildly alcoholic fermented drink; boiled down, it produces palm jaggery (tan-neera sugar), one of the most traditional sweeteners of South and Southeast Asia; left to ferment fully, it produces palm wine. The young, firm, jelly-textured fruit segments inside the unripe fruit are 'ice apples' (nungu) — refreshing, mildly sweet, hydrating; eaten as a summer cooling food throughout South India. The ripe orange-yellow outer flesh is edible; seeds are cooked and eaten when young. The leaves are used for traditional palm-leaf manuscripts (the medium of Southeast Asian scripture and literature for millennia), baskets, mats, and roof thatching. A truly remarkable plant of civilization.

common_name: Panache Tiger Fig (Ornamental Yellow-Green Striped Fig with Strawberry-Like Flavor)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Panache requires maximum sun to develop the best striped skin coloring and fruit sweetness — shaded fruits tend to be less sweet and less distinctively striped.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Panache (Tiger Fig, Strawberry Fig) is one of the most visually distinctive and ornamentally beautiful fig cultivars — producing medium-sized fruits with unmistakable yellow-to-green and darker-green vertical striping on the skin that resembles the pattern of a tiger or the appearance of a watermelon rind, creating an arresting visual display unlike any other commonly grown fig. The striped skin pattern is formed by differential ripening of the fruit skin, with the yellow portions ripening ahead of the green stripes and both shifting gradually toward gold-and-green as the fruit matures. The interior flesh is light strawberry-red to pale rose — the flesh color and an unusually sweet, almost strawberry-like flavor that gives 'Strawberry Fig' its other common name. The ornamental quality of Panache at all stages of fruit development makes it an outstanding specimen tree for edible landscape use — the striped fruits hanging in clusters from late summer through fall are genuinely decorative. Production is somewhat lower than some other cultivars — Panache prioritizes flavor quality over quantity. In zone 9, Panache is grown successfully as a standard landscape fig tree; it is somewhat less cold-hardy than varieties like Celeste and may need frost protection below 20°F.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Panamint has a low chill requirement well suited to zone 8-9 and produces reliably where standard nectarines struggle to break dormancy.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Panamint is a low-chill freestone nectarine developed for mild-winter growing regions, producing medium-to-large, richly flavored yellow-fleshed fruit with a sweet-tart balance typical of good dessert nectarines. Its comparatively low chilling requirement lets it flower and fruit reliably in areas like the Gulf South and lower South where standard high-chill nectarines fail to leaf out and bloom evenly. The tree is self-fruitful and ripens in early-to-mid summer; thin fruit to four to six inches apart along the branch in years of heavy set to improve size and reduce limb strain.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted tree; more frost-tolerant than most avocados.
directions: Pancho is a cold-hardy Mexican-type avocado that shrugs off chills that would damage tender varieties, extending avocado growing into cooler regions. It is low-maintenance and rewards patient growers with creamy, homegrown fruit. Plant a grafted tree in full sun with deep, fast-draining soil, since avocados are extremely sensitive to soggy roots and root rot. Water regularly but never let the tree stand in water, mulch well, and protect young trees during their first few winters.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all cold risk has passed; even a light frost kills papaya plants.
directions: Papaya is one of the fastest-bearing fruit plants — grafted or transplanted seedlings can fruit within 6–12 months of planting. It is highly sensitive to frost, waterlogged soil, and root disturbance; plant in well-raised, excellently drained beds and never let roots sit in water even briefly. Most commercial papaya is hermaphroditic (self-fertile), allowing a single tree to produce fruit; dioecious types require a male plant within 20 feet. Cut the growing tip back at 3–4 ft to encourage a compact, easily harvested form. Harvest when at least one-quarter of the skin has turned yellow; ripen fully at room temperature and refrigerate only after fully ripe.

common_name: Paradise Nut (Zabucajo, Monkey Pot, Sapucaia Nut)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in partial shade to full sun with consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Lecythis zabucajo is frost-sensitive and suitable only for zone 10-11 outdoor planting. The tree is related to the Brazil Nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and requires similar conditions — warm, humid, and fertile. The famous 'monkey pot' fruits open with a lid (operculum) to release the seeds — the narrow pot opening allows monkeys to reach in for the nuts but traps their closed fist. The seeds (Paradise Nuts) are considered superior in flavor to Brazil Nuts.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, fertile, slightly acidic, deep soil; Paradise Nut Tree grows best in conditions that approximate the humid, fertile soils of its native Amazonian rainforest habitat — deep, moist, well-drained, organic-rich soil with regular rainfall. Lecythis zabucajo is a large, majestic tropical tree from the Amazon Basin (Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, Brazil) in the Brazil-nut family (Lecythidaceae), grown for its edible seeds and as a remarkable ornamental specimen. The tree is closely related to the Brazil Nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and produces similar large, round, woody pods — but with a crucial difference: the pod of L. zabucajo has a natural operculum (lid) that opens at maturity to release the seeds, while the Brazil Nut pod does not open and must be cracked. The open-lidded pods ('monkey pots') have a narrow neck opening that is a natural primate trap: a monkey can reach in and grab a nut, but cannot withdraw its closed fist, and must release the nut or remain trapped — a phenomenon documented and described by naturalists since the 16th century. The Paradise Nuts themselves — large, brown, oily, rich — are considered by those who have tasted both to be superior to Brazil Nuts in flavor and richness. In zone 10-11 collections and botanical gardens, L. zabucajo is grown as both an edible nut tree and an ornamental specimen for its year-round beauty, including attractive pink flowers.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds in spring in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; paradise tree is native to tropical lowland forests of Central and South America and requires frost-free conditions. It is being promoted as a multipurpose agroforestry and bioenergy tree in tropical regions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zone 10–12; paradise tree is a multipurpose tropical tree from Central and South America producing large, pinnately compound leaves that create a lush, tropical canopy effect. Small, fragrant, yellowish flowers produce clusters of small, dark purple olives containing seeds with 60–75% oil content — one of the highest vegetable oil contents of any plant, approaching the palmitic/oleic profile suitable for both food use and biodiesel production. The tree is extremely fast-growing (20+ feet per year in tropical conditions), drought-tolerant once established, and being actively developed as a low-input bioenergy crop in tropical developing countries. The red-and-yellow immature fruits and the dark purple ripe fruits are ornamentally attractive. Of very limited landscape use in the US outside zone 10–11 Florida, but grown as an agroforestry specimen.

common_name: Parfianka Pomegranate (Central Asian Premium Pomegranate, Soft-Seeded Supreme)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or grafted trees in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Parfianka is widely considered by fruit connoisseurs to be the best-tasting pomegranate variety available in the United States, combining exceptional sweetness with complex flavor, very tender seeds (soft-seeded), and brilliant deep red arils — it consistently outranks all other varieties in blind tasting trials at California Rare Fruit Growers events.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate drought, alkaline soils, and heat — ideal for zone 9a; harvest when the skin deepens to full deep red and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped (late September–November in the Gulf South); Parfianka arils are strikingly deep red and the juice intensely colored. Parfianka is a Central Asian pomegranate variety (originally from Uzbekistan or the broader Turkestan region, where pomegranates have been cultivated for millennia) that has become the acknowledged gold standard of pomegranate flavor among American pomegranate enthusiasts, consistently winning blind tasting competitions at California Rare Fruit Growers Society events and receiving the highest ratings in UC Cooperative Extension pomegranate variety trials. The arils are brilliant deep crimson-red — darker and more richly colored than Wonderful (the commercial standard) — and have a flavor combination that separates Parfianka from other varieties: intensely sweet with balanced acidity, complex fruity aromatics, and remarkably soft, almost undetectable seeds. The seed softness (characteristic of the 'soft-seeded' varieties from Central Asia) means the arils can be eaten whole without the crunching sensation that bothers some pomegranate consumers. The juice is vivid deep red, exceptionally flavorful, and produces the finest pomegranate juice of any commercially available variety. For zone 9a and Gulf Coast gardeners willing to invest in the best possible fresh-eating pomegranate, Parfianka is the clear first choice — a tree that rewards with the finest-quality pomegranates available in home production.

common_name: Parson Brown Orange (Oldest Commercial Florida Sweet Orange)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Parson Brown is a self-fruitful, early-ripening sweet orange first found growing near Webster, Florida around 1856 and named for the Reverend N.L. Brown who propagated it. It became the first Florida orange of the season to reach market each fall, historically important for growers wanting fruit before Hamlin or Valencia came in. The medium-large fruit has a moderate number of seeds and a mild, sweet flavor that is less intensely sweet than modern seedless oranges but appreciated for its historical role and reliable early cropping. Its relative cold-hardiness among sweet oranges made it a mainstay of the northern Florida citrus belt before hardier hybrids became available.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Parson Brown is the earliest-ripening common sweet orange, ready from October, and is notably more cold-tolerant than later-season Florida oranges, which historically made it valuable for the northern edge of the citrus belt.

plant_note: Plant in deep shade to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in zone 10–12; Pataste (Wild Cacao, Cacao Silvestre) is a small, shade-tolerant understorey tree in the cacao family (Malvaceae/Theobromaceae) from the Amazonian lowlands of Brazil, Colombia, and Peru — producing cacao-like pods directly on the trunk and major branches (cauliflory) with sweet, white pulp around bitter seeds used locally to make traditional chocolate drinks and as a wild cacao substitute.
directions: Plant Herrania mariae in deep to partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil with consistently high humidity; maintain soil moisture year-round; protect from all frost and dry winds. Pataste is a close relative of cultivated cacao (Theobroma cacao) in the same subfamily Byttnerioideae, sharing cacao's characteristic cauliflorous pod production — the colorful, oval to elongated pods emerge directly from the trunk and major branches rather than at the branch tips. The pulp surrounding the seeds is white, translucent, and sweet (similar to cacao pulp, eaten fresh or fermented for beverages); the seeds themselves are bitter and high in theobromine like cacao, and have historically been used by Amazonian peoples as a cacao substitute or mixed with true cacao for chocolate preparation. Herrania is a genetically diverse cacao relative of significant interest to cacao breeders for disease-resistance genes, and several species produce viable chocolate-flavored pods. Growing in the deep, humid, understory shade of Amazonian forests, Pataste is adapted to conditions of very high humidity, no frost, and dappled to deep shade — making it a perfect choice for shaded positions in zone 10–12 tropical gardens where true cacao may grow poorly in full exposure.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–7.0), fertile, deep soil in part shade; pataste (Theobroma bicolor) is the 'other cacao' — a close relative of chocolate cacao (T. cacao) native to Central America and the Amazon, cultivated since pre-Columbian times as a chocolate substitute and flavoring; the seeds can be fermented like cacao, the white pulp around the seeds is sweet and edible, and the species was widely used by the Maya and Aztec as a flavoring for chocolate drinks.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in part shade; pataste grows naturally as an understory tree and requires shade protection, especially when young. Theobroma bicolor (pataste, mocambo cacao, or two-colored cacao) is a close relative of chocolate cacao (T. cacao) — one of the approximately 20 edible Theobroma species native to the tropical Americas — and one of the most historically significant secondary cacao species. Like T. cacao, it is native to the humid forests of Mesoamerica and the Amazon basin and produces large, ribbed, gourd-like fruits containing seeds embedded in white, sweet, edible pulp. The seeds of T. bicolor were used by the pre-Columbian Maya and Aztec as a cacao substitute and flavoring in chocolate beverages — often blended with T. cacao to modify flavor, reduce cost, or add specific aromatic notes. The seeds can be fermented and processed similarly to cacao beans to produce a chocolate-like paste and beverage. The white, sweet, mucilaginous fruit pulp surrounding the seeds (similar to the cacao pulp used in Colombia and Ecuador) is pleasantly sweet-acid and is eaten fresh or processed into juice, ice cream, and fermented beverages. T. bicolor was once more widely cultivated than it is today; it is currently grown in home gardens and small farms across Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico, but has been largely displaced by T. cacao in commercial production. A fascinating collector's tree connecting to chocolate's deep pre-Columbian history.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in late winter to early spring in very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich, sandy loam in full sun; plant at least two cultivars for cross-pollination; Patriot requires 800–1000 chill hours and is best suited to zone 8 and colder rather than the warmer portions of zone 9.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5–5.5), humus-rich soil in full sun with at least one other blueberry cultivar for cross-pollination; Patriot is a cold-hardy northern highbush blueberry cultivar developed by the University of Maine — selected for extreme cold hardiness (to -20°F), compact upright habit, and good resistance to root rot (Phytophthora cinnamomi), which makes it more adaptable to heavier or less-than-perfectly-drained soils than most highbush cultivars. The large, firm, aromatic, medium-blue berries ripen in early-to-midseason (July in zone 5–6) with a sweet, excellent blueberry flavor and very good shelf life. Patriot is widely grown in the Northeast and upper Midwest where its cold hardiness is the decisive advantage. In zone 8 it performs well with sufficient soil acidification — a reliable producer where winter temperatures regularly drop below 10°F. In zone 9, Patriot's 800–1000 chill hour requirement is not reliably met in the warmest locations; southern highbush cultivars (Misty, O'Neal, Sharpblue) are better adapted to zone 9. Patriot is a good pollination partner for Bluecrop, Blueray, and other midseason northern highbush varieties. Amend soil with peat moss, sulfur, or acidifying fertilizers to maintain the essential low pH.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.5), fertile loam in full sun; Pawnee is Type II for pollination scheduling (sheds pollen after the female flowers are receptive) — plant with a Type I cultivar (Desirable, Cape Fear) for best cross-pollination.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, deep, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Pawnee is one of the finest pecan cultivars for the Gulf South — a USDA Agricultural Research Service introduction that has become one of the most widely planted pecans in the region for its combination of outstanding nut quality, large nut size, excellent kernel percentage (55–57%), early maturity, and partial scab resistance. Pawnee's most significant attribute is its very early maturity: it ripens 2–3 weeks earlier than Desirable, Stuart, and other standard cultivars, meaning Pawnee nuts are falling in late September to early October in zone 9 — well ahead of the alternating wet/dry weather cycles of mid-fall that cause many pecan cultivars to develop scab and quality losses. The large, thin-shelled nuts have excellent quality with bright, sweet-tasting kernels and very good percentage fill. Pawnee is a Type II pecan (protandrous pollen shedding) — it produces pollen when its own female flowers are not yet receptive, requiring cross-pollination from a Type I cultivar (like Desirable) for maximum yields. This cross-pollination requirement is easy to meet in the Gulf South where multiple pecan cultivars are commonly grown in close proximity. Pawnee is moderately susceptible to pecan scab — preventive fungicide applications during leaf-out and through spring are important in humid Gulf South conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown pawpaws in late spring after frost; avoid bare-root stock as the taproot is easily damaged.
directions: Pawpaws require two genetically distinct seedlings or named cultivars for cross-pollination; hand-pollinating flowers with a small brush greatly improves fruit set. Young trees need shade for the first one to two seasons — plant under a light canopy or use a shade cloth — but mature trees prefer full sun to fruit well. The taproot makes transplanting difficult, so use container-grown stock and disturb roots as little as possible. Fruit ripens in late summer to fall and goes from firm to custardy-soft within days; refrigerate immediately after picking as shelf life is very short.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter before bud swell; in zones 8–9 fall planting is also successful.
directions: Most peaches are self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, but they need 600–1000 chill hours — choose low-chill varieties (below 400 hours) for zones 8–9. Train to an open-center (vase) shape to allow sunlight deep into the canopy, and prune out about one-third of last year's growth each dormant season because peaches only fruit on one-year-old wood. Thin fruit to 6–8 inches apart after June drop to size up remaining fruit and reduce limb breakage. Harvest when the green ground color fades to cream and the fruit yields to gentle pressure.

plant_note: Plant in frost-free conditions in spring; peach palm requires consistently warm, humid conditions.
directions: Peach palm is clump-forming, producing multiple spiny stems from the base; plant suckers or container-grown plants in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent irrigation. It is dioecious in the wild but many cultivated selections are monoecious and self-productive; planting in clusters of 3–5 stems improves pollination and yield. The starchy, oily orange-red drupes are rich in beta-carotene and must be boiled or roasted before eating as raw fruit contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals. Harvest bunches when fruit has turned fully orange to red and softens slightly; boil or cook within a few days as the starchy fruit does not store well raw.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; peanut butter fruit is more shade-tolerant than most tropical fruit shrubs and can produce fruit in filtered light, making it useful for partially shaded garden positions in zone 9–11.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zones 9–12; peanut butter fruit earns its name from the distinctive flavor of the ripe orange-red fruits — the flesh surrounding the seeds has a rich, somewhat sticky texture and flavor uncannily reminiscent of peanut butter, combined with subtle sweet notes. Native to Peru and the Andes, this ornamental shrub is surprisingly adaptable to Gulf Coast conditions in zones 9–11, where it fruits prolifically on an almost continuous basis in warm seasons. The small, bright yellow flowers are attractive and produced repeatedly throughout the year in warm climates. The fruit are eaten fresh from the shrub or used in smoothies, ice cream, and desserts throughout South America. Unusually shade-tolerant for a fruiting tropical — it can produce reasonably well in the bright filtered light beneath a high canopy, making it valuable for partially shaded garden positions.

common_name: Peanut Butter Fruit (Amazon Peanut Butter Tree, Peanut Butter Plant)
plant_note: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Bunchosia glandulifera is a compact, evergreen tropical shrub-tree that produces small oval fruits turning from green to orange to deep red when ripe — the ripe flesh has a thick, sweet, pasty, distinctly peanut-butter-like flavor that makes this one of the most unique subtropical fruits. Excellent in smoothies, eaten fresh, or used as a sweet spread. Very productive in zone 9b-12; in zone 9, established plants cut back in freezes but regrow from the base. Propagate from seed (germinates in 2-4 weeks) or cuttings. Best harvested when the fruit turns fully orange-red and yields to gentle pressure.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Peanut Butter Fruit is adaptable to a range of soil types and is moderately drought tolerant once established, performing reliably in zone 9b-12 as an evergreen fruiting shrub-tree. Bunchosia glandulifera is an evergreen to semi-deciduous, large shrub to small tree native to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, and the Amazon basin in the Malpighiaceae family — the same family as Acerola (Malpighia emarginata), from which the distinctive wing-petaled yellow flowers of Bunchosia are recognizable. The plant produces ovate, dark-green, glossy leaves and clusters of small (0.5-inch) yellow flowers with the characteristic wing-petaled (fringed petal margin) form typical of the Malpighiaceae. The flowers are followed by oval fruits, 1–1.5 inches long, that ripen progressively from pale green through yellow-orange to deep red-orange. The ripe flesh of Bunchosia glandulifera fruit is thick, sweet, slightly dry in texture, and has a flavor that is remarkably and unmistakably reminiscent of smooth peanut butter — sweet, rich, and nutty, without any actual peanut content. The fruit can be eaten fresh at the ripe orange-red stage (before it becomes overripe), blended into smoothies, used as a natural sweet spread on crackers, or incorporated into desserts. Plants are highly productive in warm climates and begin fruiting within 1–2 years from a large transplant or seedling. An unusual and genuinely delicious tropical fruit for zone 9b-12 gardens. Non-toxic.

common_name: Peanut Butter Fruit (Silver-Leaved Bunchosia, Gold Cherry)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in partial shade to full sun with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Bunchosia argentea is frost-sensitive and best suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting or zone 9 containers. It is fast-growing and begins bearing fruit within 1–2 years from transplant. The small, yellow-orange fruits ripen throughout the warm months and are eaten fresh — they do not store or ship well. Two plants improve fruit set but a single plant often fruits acceptably. The fruit is best eaten before it becomes very soft.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Peanut Butter Fruit grows and fruits well in partial shade, making it useful for under-story tropical food garden positions under larger fruit trees. Bunchosia argentea is a fast-growing, evergreen shrub or small tree from Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia in the family Malpighiaceae, widely grown as a dooryard fruit tree throughout tropical America and increasingly available in South Florida and zone 10-11 Gulf Coast fruit collections for one of the most remarkable flavor descriptions in the tropical fruit world: the flesh of the ripe fruit has the precise taste and texture of smooth commercial peanut butter — sweet, nutty, slightly dry, and unmistakably peanut-like, despite having no botanical relationship to Arachis hypogaea (the peanut). The fruits are small (half to 1 inch), oval to oblong, and ripen from yellow-orange to orange-red, produced in clusters along the branches from the warm months. A single ripe Bunchosia argentea fruit consumed fresh is a memorable culinary experience — the resemblance to peanut butter is genuine and immediate. The plant is a rapid grower that begins bearing fruit within one to two years of planting and produces through the warm months. The silver leaf undersides (the 'argentea' — 'silvery') give the plant an attractive bi-colored appearance. An excellent, unusual addition to any tropical or subtropical home food garden.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while dormant; fall planting works in zones 7–9.
directions: European pears require 700–1200 chill hours and almost always need a second compatible cultivar for adequate pollination; Bosc and Anjou cross well with each other. Pears are prone to fire blight, so choose resistant varieties and prune out any infected wood well below the canker margin. Train to a central leader and avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes lush growth susceptible to blight. Pick pears while still firm and ripen indoors at room temperature — they go mealy if left on the tree too long.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring; pecans have a deep taproot — handle carefully and plant immediately.
directions: Pecans are protandrous or protogynous depending on variety — pollen shed and receptive female flowers rarely overlap on the same tree — so always plant at least two cultivars of opposite types (Type I with Type II) to ensure cross-pollination. Northern varieties (Hark, Kanza, Lakota) are bred for shorter growing seasons and suit zones 5–7; southern varieties need 250+ frost-free days. Pecans are heavy zinc feeders; apply zinc foliar spray in spring if leaves show rosette symptoms. Harvest when shucks split open in autumn and nuts fall freely.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown transplants in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep-soiled sites in full sun; pecan develops a taproot up to 5 feet deep within its first few years and requires deep, loose, non-compacted soil for best growth and production — avoid shallow, rocky, or compacted sites.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; pecans require at least 30–40 feet of space in all directions and are best suited to large properties with deep, loamy soil. Carya illinoinensis (pecan) is the iconic native nut tree of the American South and Southwest — the only major North American nut to have achieved worldwide commercial importance — producing sweet, buttery, thin-shelled nuts from September through November that are consumed fresh, candied, in pies (pecan pie is the most iconic Southern dessert), and in a vast range of confectioneries and baked goods. The pecan is native to the Mississippi-Ohio River basin and Gulf Coastal Plain, reaching 60–100 feet tall and living for centuries; established trees are drought-resistant and incredibly long-lived. Two trees with different bloom times (Type I — shedding pollen before receptive to it; Type II — the opposite) are needed for reliable cross-pollination and maximum nut production. Named varieties for the Gulf South include 'Desirable,' 'Candy,' 'Caddo,' 'Cheyenne,' 'Kiowa,' and 'Oconee' — all selected for disease resistance to pecan scab, the primary disease problem in humid southeastern climates. The trees also have significant wildlife value as a mast crop for deer, turkeys, and squirrels.

plant_note: Start from cuttings (roots readily) or transplant after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; pepino performs as a short-lived perennial in zone 9 and south, surviving mild winters and producing fruit repeatedly — protect from frost below 28°F.
directions: Pepino melon is a perennial fruiting shrub from the Andes of South America, belonging to the same genus as tomatoes and eggplants — its smooth-skinned, oval fruits are pale golden-yellow with distinctive purple streaks when ripe, with sweet, mild, melon-like flesh that has been compared to a blend of cantaloupe and cucumber. The plant blooms and sets fruit best in cool to mild temperatures (50–75°F) rather than peak summer heat, making the fall through early spring season the most productive in the subtropical Gulf Coast; in zone 9 it often survives mild winters to fruit again the following cool season. Propagate easily from stem cuttings like tomatoes — a rooted cutting can fruit within 75–100 days of transplanting. Stake plants like a tomato or pepper to keep fruits off the ground; harvest when fruits develop a fully golden background color and give slightly to thumb pressure, typically 3–4 months after transplanting; let fully ripen at room temperature after picking for peak sweetness.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or transplants after last frost in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil in zone 9–11; Pepino Dulce (Sweet Cucumber, Pepino Melon) is a sprawling Andean subshrub of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) from the highlands of Peru, Colombia, and Ecuador, producing distinctive oval to pear-shaped fruits with smooth, creamy-yellow to pale green skin streaked with purple, and sweet, juicy, melon-flavored flesh — eaten fresh as a dessert fruit or in fruit salads.
directions: Plant Pepino Dulce in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; water consistently and feed monthly with balanced fertilizer; stake or cage as plants sprawl; harvest fruits when fully colored and aromatic, giving slightly to gentle pressure. Solanum muricatum is a domesticated Andean crop related to tomato, potato, and eggplant — one of the less commonly grown members of the Solanaceae family that produces a genuinely delicious and distinctive dessert fruit. The oval fruits, ranging from 2–4 inches long, develop beautiful purple streaking on a pale yellow base as they ripen, and the flesh has a mild, sweet flavor combining melon, pear, and cucumber notes with very low acidity — a refreshing warm-season treat eaten fresh, chilled, or in fruit salads. Propagation from stem cuttings is faster and more reliable than from seed, yielding fruiting plants within the same season; plants grown in zone 9–11 behave as short-lived perennials and may be cut back after fruiting for regrowth. In frost-prone zones it is grown as a warm-season annual from transplants started indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings, which root easily in moist potting mix; pepino does not breed true from seed. Plant after frost risk passes in full sun. In zone 9 it can be grown as a perennial subshrub, often persisting for several seasons if protected from the rare hard freeze. A single plant can produce dozens of fruits.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; pepino melon is a relative of tomato and eggplant that produces cream to pale-purple-striped fruits shaped like a pear or egg, with flesh tasting of a mild blend of melon and cucumber. Grow on a stake or trellis to keep fruit off the ground and improve air circulation. The plant benefits from regular fertilization with a tomato-type fertilizer and consistent watering; fruit quality declines with drought stress. Harvest when fruits turn golden yellow with purple stripes and yield slightly to pressure — they are eaten fresh, in fruit salads, or as a savory side dish in Andean cuisine where they originate.

subcategory: Brazilian Cerrado iconic oilseed and fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained to dry, deep, sandy to sandy-loam, acidic, lean cerrado-type soil in zone 10–12; Pequi is the defining fruit tree of the Brazilian Cerrado (tropical savanna) — a symbol of Minas Gerais and Goiás states — bearing unusual, golf-ball-to-softball-sized fruits with a hard outer husk enclosing a spiny, golden-yellow inner seed coat covered with intensely aromatic, oily, yellow-orange flesh with a distinctive, powerful, cheese-and-mango-and-toasted-nut flavor revered in central Brazilian cuisine.
directions: Plant Caryocar brasiliense in deep, well-drained, sandy, acidic, very lean cerrado soil in full sun; the tree is adapted to nutrient-poor savanna soils and performs poorly in rich, fertilized conditions; water moderately during establishment, then sparingly — it is drought-adapted. CAUTION: the inner seed coat (endocarp) is covered with sharp spines; eat the oily flesh from the outside of the seed coat with extreme care, using a scraping motion, or you will be impaled. Pequi is an ingredient of such cultural importance in Minas Gerais and the Cerrado of central Brazil that it has been called 'the soul of sertanejo cooking.' The intensely aromatic, golden-yellow oily flesh surrounding the spiny inner stone is eaten by scraping with the front teeth — a culturally specific technique that everyone from the region knows — in dishes like Galinhada com Pequi (chicken and rice with pequi), pamonha, and various cerrado preparations. The flavor is extraordinary and polarizing: powerful, complex, unmistakably distinctive, combining notes of ripe mango, roasted nuts, pungent tropical cheese, and a rich, almost buttery oiliness. The fruit oil is pressed for cosmetics, cooking, and traditional medicine. A crucial food for wildlife in the Cerrado: jaguars, tapirs, and many birds consume the fallen fruits. The tree is the symbol of Minas Gerais state and a cultural keystone of the cerrado region.

plant_note: Plant dormant, grafted trees in early spring; expect long establishment before cropping.
directions: Perry pears are tannic, high-acid cultivars grown to ferment into perry, the pear equivalent of cider. These are famously long-lived, slow-to-fruit trees that eventually reach great size, so give them ample space and patience. Plant at least two varieties for pollination in deep soil and full sun. Little pruning is required once a strong framework is established; harvest the astringent fruit slightly underripe and let it sweat before pressing.

plant_note: Plant after frost danger; grow in a container where winters drop below 30 F.
directions: Persian Bearss is a prolific, thornless lime producing juicy, seedless fruit perfect for cooking and drinks. It is one of the more cold-tolerant limes but still needs protection below freezing. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil and keep the graft union above the soil line. Water deeply and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, feeding with a citrus fertilizer during active growth. In zones colder than 9, grow in a large pot that can move to a bright indoor location for winter.

plant_note: Plant grafted container trees after last cold risk in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April in a protected southern exposure. Persian lime is seedless and not reproduced true-to-type from seed — always purchase grafted nursery trees. More cold-hardy than Key lime (tolerates 26–28°F briefly) but requires protection in zone 9a during hard freezes.
directions: Plant in excellent drainage in full sun; Persian lime is the lime sold in virtually every grocery store worldwide — the standard 'lime' of commerce in the United States and Europe. The large, seedless, thick-skinned fruits (much larger than Key lime) are harvested green and provide the characteristic lime flavor of margaritas, guacamole, and countless beverages. Unlike Key lime, Persian lime is technically a triploid (3 sets of chromosomes), which makes it seedless and somewhat more vigorous and cold-tolerant than Key lime. It produces fruit year-round in tropical climates and has peak seasons in spring and fall in zone 9. Trees are also more cold-tolerant than Key lime (surviving to 26°F vs. 28–30°F for Key lime) and are larger and more productive under zone 9 conditions. Feed 3–4 times yearly with a complete citrus fertilizer; supplement with chelated micronutrients if leaves show yellowing. Freeze protection below 28°F is recommended; wrap trunks with frost cloth or move container trees indoors.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in late spring or summer by allowing cut ends to callus for 1–2 weeks before planting in very well-drained cactus mix; Peruvian apple cactus establishes rapidly from large cuttings. It is damaged at 28°F and killed below 25°F, making it suitable for zones 9–11 outdoors or as a dramatic container specimen moved indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean cactus or sandy soil in full sun; Peruvian apple cactus is a large, multi-branched columnar cactus native to South America and widely planted as an ornamental, living fence, and fruit tree throughout the Caribbean, tropical America, and the Mediterranean. The stout, blue-green to gray-green columns branch freely to form impressive upright clumps reaching 10–25 feet, with prominent ribs and clusters of short spines. In summer, it produces large, showy, white funnel-shaped flowers up to 6 inches across that open at night and are pollinated by bats and hawk moths — a remarkable natural spectacle. The flowers are followed by the edible 'Peruvian apples' — oval red to dark-magenta fruits 2–3 inches long with sweet, translucent white flesh and small black seeds, having a mild, pleasant flavor. Related to and confused with the queen of the night and night-blooming cereus, but distinct. Excellent as a living fence, architectural garden specimen, or screening plant in zone 9–11 landscapes.

common_name: Peter's Honey Fig (Small Yellow-Green Sweet Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; figs are self-fertile and need no pollinator. Peter's Honey fruits on both old wood (breba crop) and new growth (main crop), giving two harvest windows in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate poor soil but grow and fruit best with consistent moisture during fruit development. Peter's Honey is a fig cultivar collected and popularized among southern fig enthusiasts for its small-to-medium, pale yellow-green fruit with a honeyed, richly sweet flavor that belies its modest size and unassuming skin color. The tree is productive and vigorous, producing a light breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer followed by a heavier main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Because the fruit does not need to color up to signal ripeness, harvest by feel — ripe figs soften and the neck droops — rather than by color change. Prune in late winter to control size and remove any winter-killed tips, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summers.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Petite Aubique is a compact-to-medium fig suited to container growing or small gardens. In zone 9 it produces a breba crop in June–July and a main crop in August–September. The compact size makes it excellent for patio containers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Petite Aubique is a French compact fig variety producing small to medium, teardrop-shaped fruits with violet to brown skin and amber flesh — a mild, delicate, honey-sweet flavor suitable for fresh eating and preserves. The compact tree habit (smaller than most standard fig varieties) makes Petite Aubique one of the better options for container growing in large pots or half-barrels on patios and decks. The smaller plant size does not compromise productivity significantly; established container-grown Petite Aubique can produce 50–100 fruits annually. The small fruit size (1–1.5 inches) makes them a good all-in-one fresh-eating fig — no slicing required. In zone 9 the compact habit and full-sun requirement make it an excellent choice for warm south-facing walls or enclosed courtyards where reflected heat can accelerate ripening. The name 'Petite Aubique' is also found in the literature as 'Petite Grise,' indicating possible synonym use in some regions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cutting transplants in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Petite Negra is naturally dwarf, remaining under 5 feet without pruning — ideal for container growing, patio culture, and small garden spaces where standard fig trees (8–15 feet) would be too large. In zone 9 it produces two crops: a small breba (early) crop in June–July on previous season's wood, and the main crop in August–October. The dark purple to near-black skin and sweet, amber-to-red flesh distinguish the fruit visually from brown or green-skinned fig varieties. In containers, repot every 2–3 years and feed regularly with balanced fertilizer during the growing season for maximum fruiting.
directions: Plant in full sun to light partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — figs are adaptable to a wide range of soils but require good drainage and at least 8 hours of sun for maximum fruit production; Petite Negra is a naturally compact, dwarf fig cultivar producing small, round to pear-shaped fruits with dark purple to nearly black skin and amber to red, rich, sweet flesh — delivering the characteristic fresh fig flavor at a manageable plant scale that makes fresh fig production accessible to gardeners with limited space. The dwarf habit (3–5 feet in the ground, 2–3 feet in containers) is the primary distinguishing feature: Petite Negra produces full-sized, high-quality fruit on plants small enough to grow as container specimens on patios, to fit in small garden beds, or to overwinter indoors in containers in marginally cold climates. Container-grown fig culture allows gardeners outside the traditional fig belt (zones 7–10) to grow figs by moving plants indoors or into garages during winter; zone 9 gardeners can grow Petite Negra in the ground as a permanent, productive perennial shrub or in large containers for patio display. The self-fruitful nature (no cross-pollination required) and rapid return to bearing (often in the first or second year) make Petite Negra one of the most immediately rewarding fruit plants available.

plant_note: Plant in spring; phalsa is coppiced annually in India but can be trained as a small tree in warmer zones.
directions: Phalsa is a fast-growing shrubby tree from South Asia that tolerates drought, heat, and a range of soils, fruiting reliably within 1–2 years of planting — one of the quickest-bearing subtropical fruits. In traditional cultivation it is heavily pruned (nearly to the ground) each year after fruiting, which promotes vigorous new fruiting wood; in zone 9 this also serves as winter frost management. The small, dark purple-red drupes ripen over several weeks in summer and have a refreshing sweet-sour flavor prized in Indian cooling drinks (phalsa sherbet) and jams. The fruit is extremely perishable — harvest when fully dark purple and soft and use within 24 hours; it does not store or ship well.

common_name: Picholine Olive (French Dual-Purpose Table and Oil Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, low-fertility soil in full sun; Picholine benefits from a compatible pollinizer nearby for the best fruit set, and it is somewhat more cold-tolerant than many olive cultivars.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; established trees are drought-tolerant and should not be over-fertilized or over-watered. Picholine is a classic French olive cultivar from the Languedoc region, valued as a dual-purpose variety producing both high-quality table olives — elongated, firm, green-cured olives with a distinctive nutty flavor — and good oil with a peppery, herbaceous character typical of southern French olive oils. The tree is notably vigorous and relatively cold-hardy for an olive, tolerating brief winter dips better than some more tender cultivars, which has made it a popular choice for marginal olive-growing climates. Harvest green in fall for classic Picholine table olives, curing in a lye or brine solution over several weeks to remove bitterness, or allow fruit to ripen further for oil pressing in early winter.

common_name: Picual Olive (World's Most Planted Oil Olive, Jaén Spain Olive, Stable High-Polyphenol Olive)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained, low-fertility, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Picual is largely self-fertile and produces good crops as a single tree, though yields improve with cross-pollination from Koroneiki, Frantoio, or another companion; requires approximately 300–400 chill hours; Picual is one of the most cold-tolerant major olive varieties (surviving to approximately 18–20°F when established), making it suitable for zones 8–10.
directions: Plant in well-drained, low-fertility, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Picual is extremely drought-tolerant once established; harvest for oil production in November–December when olives shift from green to purple-black; Picual oil is known for its stability and resistance to oxidation — it keeps significantly longer than most olive oils and maintains its flavor profile without going rancid. Picual olive is the most widely planted olive variety in the world, accounting for approximately 20% of total global olive production — concentrated primarily in the province of Jaén in Andalusia, Spain, which alone produces more olive oil than the entire country of Greece. The variety's global dominance is built on a combination of practical attributes: very high oil content (22–27% by weight, among the highest of any variety), exceptional oil stability and shelf life (Picual oil has very high oleic acid and polyphenol content that makes it resistant to oxidation — a critical commercial advantage since most olive oil goes rancid within 1–2 years), strong cold-hardiness relative to other major varieties, and vigorous, productive trees adaptable to the challenging calcareous, poorly-drained soils of the Spanish meseta. Picual oil has a distinctive flavor profile: robust, fruity, slightly bitter and peppery in the fresh-pressed (unfiltered) state — characteristics that reflect its high polyphenol content (polyphenols provide both the peppery sensation and the health benefits of olive oil). For home oil production, Picual's high oil content and excellent stability make it the most efficient variety for pressing, and its robust flavor is well-suited to the strong tastes associated with premium extra-virgin olive oil.

common_name: Pieper American Persimmon (Named Female Midwestern Persimmon Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant grafted container or bare-root trees in spring in full sun; Pieper is a named female cultivar requiring a nearby male American persimmon or the self-fertile Meader cultivar for reliable fruit production; adapted to a very wide range of soil types and tolerates the clay-heavy and poorly-structured soils of the Midwest and mid-Atlantic states where most tree fruits fail; cold-hardy to zone 4.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained to average soil; Pieper is adaptable to clay, sandy, or poor soils and very drought-tolerant once established; harvest by collecting fallen fruits from the ground after frost softening — fruits that separate easily from the calyx are ready; ripe fruit is completely soft and uniformly orange. Pieper is a named American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) selection that has been propagated through Midwestern and eastern nurseries as a reliable female cultivar with above-average fruit size and consistent productivity — characteristics that distinguish it from seedling trees of variable quality. American persimmon is a dioecious species, meaning most trees produce only pollen (male) or only fruit (female), so named female cultivars like Pieper must be planted alongside a male tree or a self-fertile cultivar (Meader) for reliable cropping. Pieper produces medium to large American persimmon fruits (1.25–1.75 inch) that ripen in October–November following hard frosts, developing the characteristic sweet, honey-apricot flavor of excellent American persimmon at peak ripeness. The trees are vigorous, drought-resistant once established, and productive across the range of Midwestern soils — making them a practical native fruit for home orchards where Asian persimmon would be marginally hardy.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost risk passes; pigeon plum is frost-sensitive and suitable outdoors only in zone 9b–11. In zone 9a grow in large containers that can be moved to shelter during freezes. This is a slow-growing, shade-tolerant understory tree that thrives in partial shade and salt-spray tolerance makes it excellent for coastal gardens.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in sandy, well-drained soil; pigeon plum is a native Florida and Caribbean understory tree related to sea grape (Coccoloba uvifera) that produces dark purple, grape-like fruits in hanging clusters that ripen in fall and winter — an important food source for birds and wildlife. The small fruits have a thin, sweet skin covering minimal flesh around a large seed, similar to wild grape, and are used in the same ways as sea grape fruits: fresh eating, jelly, wine, and juice. The tree is highly salt-tolerant, drought-tolerant once established, and pollution-resistant, making it valuable for coastal landscapes where other fruit trees struggle.
