plant_note: Plant bare-root in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil; Reliance requires approximately 850 chill hours and is one of the most cold-hardy peach varieties available, with dormant wood hardy to -25°F and flower buds among the most cold-tolerant of any named variety — the premier peach for zones 4–6 where winter hardiness and late-frost resilience are paramount; self-fruitful.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; thin to 6–8 inches in spring; Reliance is self-fruitful and requires no cross-pollinator; the trees are vigorous and productive, delivering reliable crops in zones where other peach varieties fail due to winter cold; fruit ripens early-mid season (late July to mid-August in zones 4–6). Reliance peach is the most cold-hardy named peach variety in widespread cultivation in North America, developed by F.H. Emerson at the University of New Hampshire (released 1964) specifically for the challenging peach-growing conditions of New England and the northern United States where standard peach varieties like Elberta, Loring, and Madison lose their flower buds to winter cold or late spring frosts too frequently to be reliable crops. The extraordinary cold-hardiness of Reliance is its defining characteristic: dormant wood has survived -25°F in New Hampshire orchard trials, and the flower buds show significantly better cold-tolerance than most other varieties. In comparative cold-hardiness tests, Reliance consistently outperforms all other widely-available named peach varieties, giving it a unique market niche as 'the peach you can actually grow in the North.' Fruit quality is good but not exceptional compared to premium mid-South varieties — the fruits are medium-sized, round to oval, with a red blush over yellow background, and a pleasant yellow-fleshed, sweet, fully freestone flavor. The flavor is somewhat mild compared to full-sun, high-quality southern peaches, reflecting the shorter, cooler northern growing season. However, for gardeners in zones 4–6 where reliable peach production from standard varieties is difficult or impossible, Reliance delivers consistent, acceptable-quality fresh peaches from a tree that simply survives winters that would kill other varieties.

common_name: Reliance Seedless Grape (Red Seedless Home Garden Grape, Hardy Seedless)
plant_note: Plant bare-root vines or container plants in early spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Reliance is the most widely planted seedless red table grape for home gardens in the northern and central United States, bred by James Moore at the University of Arkansas for its combination of seedlessness, cold-hardiness (to -15°F), excellent fresh-eating quality, and reliable production in zones 4–8 — filling the niche for an easy-to-eat, sweet, seedless home grape in climates where the Thompson Seedless (a warm-climate variety) is not reliably productive.
directions: Plant on a sturdy trellis in full sun; spur-prune in late winter to 2 buds per spur; Reliance is self-fruitful; fruit ripens mid-August in most zones; the medium-sized, rose-red to red berries are seedless, tender-skinned, and sweet with a mild, pleasant flavor more subtle than Concord; excellent for fresh eating, fruit salads, and home winemaking. Reliance seedless grape is a University of Arkansas-bred red seedless table grape (released 1982, bred by James Moore) that became the most widely planted cold-hardy seedless home garden grape in the United States, filling a genuine need for a sweet, seedless fresh-eating grape that could be grown reliably in zones 4–8 where the California-bred Thompson Seedless and Flame Red Seedless (developed for California's mild winters and low humidity) perform poorly or inconsistently. The breeding background of Reliance includes multiple American Labrusca and hybrid species crosses selected for cold-hardiness, which gives the variety a very cold-tolerant profile — mature canes are hardy to -15°F and the variety tolerates late spring frosts reasonably well. The berries are medium-sized, red-rose to medium red (lighter than dark blue varieties like Mars), round to slightly oval, and truly seedless with a tender, non-slip skin (unlike the slip-skin character of Concord and Niagara). The flavor is sweet, mild, and pleasantly fruity without the strong Labrusca 'foxiness' of slip-skin varieties — closer to the flavor profile of commercial seedless grapes but with its own mild aromatic quality. Reliance is a productive, reliable variety that earns its place as the standard seedless home garden grape for most of the northern and central United States.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; riberry is an Australian native rainforest tree producing abundant, small (1/2-inch), vivid crimson, pear-shaped fruits with a sour-sweet, spicy flavor combining apple and clove-cinnamon notes — widely used in Australian native food products and highly regarded as a bushfood ingredient.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; riberry can be pruned as a formal hedge or left to grow as a specimen small tree. Syzygium luehmannii (riberry or small-leaf lillypilly) is an Australian native rainforest tree from the subtropical and warm-temperate rainforests of New South Wales and Queensland — one of the most commercially important of the Australian lilly pilly (Syzygium) species in the native food industry. The tree produces abundant clusters of small (1/2-inch), teardrop-shaped, vivid magenta-crimson fruits, and is one of the most prolific and reliable fruiting lilly pillies in the genus. The riberry flavor is unique and highly prized: sour, fruity, and sweet with distinctive warm cinnamon-clove spice notes from the high eugenol content — a flavor combination with no equivalent in European or American fruits. In Australian native food (bushfood) cuisine, riberries are used in jams, sauces, wines, ice creams, vinegars, and as a garnish for savory dishes — particularly with game, lamb, and cheese. As a landscape plant, riberry is compact, attractive, and responds very well to formal clipping into hedge shapes; the coppery-red new growth flushes make it ornamentally outstanding. Its combination of ornamental and food value makes it one of the best lilly pillies for zone 9–12 edible landscapes.

plant_note: Plant grafted container trees in spring after last cold risk; in zone 9 plant February–April in the warmest location with excellent drainage. Grapefruit requires more accumulated heat units than oranges to develop full sweetness — site in the hottest spot available. Rio Red ripens October through March in Texas and Florida.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, the warmest available location; Rio Red is a grapefruit cultivar developed at Texas A&M University through irradiation mutagenesis of Ruby Red stock and released in 1984 — and has since become the dominant commercial grapefruit variety in Texas, replacing both Ruby Red and Star Ruby on most commercial acreage. The fruit is the gold standard for Texas red grapefruit: large, with yellow skin blushed deep red-pink, and flesh that is deep crimson-red, very sweet (low acidity), with complex flavor and very few seeds. Rio Red's flesh has the deepest, most consistent red color of any commercially significant grapefruit variety, a characteristic valued by both fresh market buyers and for appearance when halved. The trees are vigorous and productive. Feed with citrus fertilizer 3–4 times annually and supplement with zinc and manganese chelate if leaves show deficiency symptoms on alkaline soils. Protect below 28°F. In zone 9 the long hot summers develop excellent sweetness and color in the fall crop.

plant_note: Plant hardwood cuttings in spring in moist to average, well-drained soil; riverbank grape is one of the most cold-hardy native grapes and has been used extensively in cold-climate wine grape breeding programs. It prefers moist, fertile bottomland soils but adapts to upland conditions.
directions: Plant in moist to well-drained, fertile, loamy soil in full sun along riverbanks, fences, and arbors; riverbank grape is native to streambanks and forest edges across most of North America, from Quebec to Texas, and is one of the most cold-hardy wild grapes — surviving to zone 2. The small, highly fragrant flowers in spring are intensely honey-scented and attract numerous pollinators. The small, blue-black, tart grapes ripen after the first fall frost (hence 'frost grape'), becoming slightly sweeter and less astringent with cold exposure. This species has been critically important in wine breeding — it is a parent of numerous cold-hardy wine grape cultivars including 'Marquette', 'Frontenac', and 'Frontenac Gris' developed for cold northern climates. Also an important source of phylloxera-resistant rootstock for European wine grapes.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; robusta coffee (C. canephora) is the second most important commercial coffee species after arabica (C. arabica) — more disease-resistant, more drought-tolerant, and higher in caffeine than arabica, but with a harsher, more bitter, earthier flavor; widely grown for espresso blends and instant coffee production; the natural understory habitat of the species makes it well-suited to part-shade garden positions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.0–6.5), fertile, loamy soil in part shade; robusta coffee grows naturally as an understory shrub and performs best with afternoon shade in hot climates. Coffea canephora (robusta coffee or Congo coffee) is the second major commercial coffee species, accounting for approximately 40% of world coffee production — ranking second only to arabica (C. arabica) but distinctly different in origin, physiology, flavor, and agricultural use. C. canephora is native to the humid tropical forests of central and West Africa (particularly the Congo Basin region — hence 'Congo coffee'), where it grows as a spreading, multi-stemmed understory shrub. Robusta coffee has several significant differences from arabica: it is more disease-resistant (particularly to coffee leaf rust — Hemileia vastatrix — the devastating fungal disease that has devastated arabica crops worldwide); it is more drought-tolerant; it contains approximately twice the caffeine content of arabica (2–4% vs. 1.2–1.5%); and it can be grown at lower elevations and in hotter, more humid climates than arabica. These traits make robusta the preferred crop for hot, humid, lower-elevation tropical regions including Vietnam (the world's largest robusta producer), India, Ivory Coast, Uganda, and Indonesia. The flavor profile of robusta — stronger, more bitter, earthier, with woody and chocolate-cocoa notes — suits espresso blends (where it adds body and crema), instant coffee, and cold brew. In zone 10–12 gardens, both coffee species can be grown for home production and as ornamental shade-tolerant specimens.

plant_note: Plant in spring in extremely well-drained or rocky soil in full sun; avoid any soil that holds moisture as this palm of dry limestone mountains is prone to root rot in poorly drained sites.
directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining, lean soil — this native of dry Mexican limestone mountains thrives on neglect and is one of the most drought-tolerant palms available for zone 8-9 gardens. The silvery-blue fan leaves are similar to other Brahea species and provide striking year-round color; the palm is slow-growing but extremely long-lived. Small, dark, date-like fruits are produced in pendant clusters and are sweet and edible, though they are used mainly by local communities in Mexico for food, wine, and traditional crafts. Once established, reduce irrigation to near zero; overwatering is the most common cause of failure with this species.

plant_note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in a frost-free tropical site; biriba is among the faster-fruiting Annona relatives.
directions: Rollinia / biriba is an Annona relative from Amazonia that prefers deep, fertile, consistently moist soil and produces fruit faster than cherimoya or soursop under hot, humid conditions. Like other Annonaceae, the flowers exhibit protogynous dichogamy — the female stage opens first, closes, then reopens in the male stage — so hand-pollination at the correct time greatly increases fruit set: collect pollen from half-open flowers in the afternoon and apply to fully open receptive stigmas the following morning. The soft, custard-flavored fruit is covered in soft yellow spines and must be handled very gently — it bruises and ferments within hours of reaching peak ripeness. Harvest when the spines have softened and yellowed and the fruit gives noticeably to pressure; consume immediately or refrigerate for no more than 24 hours.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rollinia is damaged below 30°F and should be protected from frost. It grows faster and bears fruit at a younger age than cherimoya — typically fruiting within 3–4 years from seed. It tolerates wet soils better than most Annonaceae and thrives in high humidity.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free conditions; rollinia (biribá) is a South American tropical tree in the custard apple family, native to the Amazon basin and considered by fruit connoisseurs one of the finest fruits in the Annonaceae family — potentially superior to cherimoya and sugar apple in flavor. The fruits are large (often 4–6 inches across) and round to heart-shaped with distinctive, pointed tubercles (bumps) on the yellow-green exterior that turn golden-yellow at maturity. The interior is snow-white, sweet, translucent, and juicy — much moister and more refreshing than cherimoya — with a flavor combining banana, pineapple, and caramel with a sweet lemon-custard quality. The texture is extremely delicate, almost like thick cream, and it must be eaten immediately after harvest as it deteriorates within 1–2 days of ripening. Rollinia is faster-growing and more prolific than most Annonaceae and is better adapted to humid tropical conditions. It tolerates wet soils and high humidity better than cherimoya or atemoya. An important and growing orchard crop in tropical South America.

common_name: Rome Beauty Apple (The Baking Apple, Ohio Heirloom Baker, Rome)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep fertile soil in full sun; Rome Beauty is partially self-fruitful and will produce some crop without a pollenizer, though yields improve significantly with a companion variety; requires approximately 800 chill hours; well-adapted to zones 5–8, where late ripening (October–November) in the open orchard is feasible before killing frost; blooms late, reducing frost risk.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Rome Beauty is the classic baking apple and benefits from being cooked rather than eaten fresh — its firm, low-acid flesh holds structure beautifully under heat; harvest in October when fully colored deep red, typically after McIntosh and Empire are finished; baked whole apples with butter and brown sugar are the signature preparation. Rome Beauty (often sold simply as 'Rome') is an Ohio heirloom apple discovered as a branch sport on a seedling tree near Rome, Ohio (Lawrence County) by Joel Gillett around 1816, propagated by his neighbor Alanson Gillett, and introduced to the nursery trade in the 1840s where it rapidly became one of the most important American commercial apples of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The variety has an unusual characteristic that defines its culinary use: the flesh is relatively low in acid and somewhat dry in texture compared to most eating apples, which means it is not the most interesting variety for fresh consumption but becomes exceptional when baked — the firm flesh holds its shape without collapsing, the mild, sweet flavor concentrates under heat, and the large round shape makes it the ideal vessel for a whole baked apple filled with butter, sugar, and spices. For a century, 'Rome' and 'baking apple' were nearly synonymous in American cookery. The round, symmetrical, deep red to all-red appearance also made Rome Beauty particularly popular with retailers when unblemished fruit mattered; a barrel of large, perfectly round, uniformly deep-red Romes was among the most visually impressive of any apple variety.

plant_note: Plant dormant trees in early spring once the soil is workable.
directions: Romeo and Juliet are a pair of compact, extremely cold-hardy bush cherries that produce sweet, robust fruit good for snacking and baking. Plant both varieties near each other in full sun with well-drained soil to improve cross-pollination and yields. Space plants 5-8 feet apart and water consistently while young to establish strong roots. Prune lightly in late winter to maintain an open, productive shape. These dwarf trees stay small enough for backyard gardens and fruit reliably even in harsh winter regions.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Ronde de Bordeaux is a compact-to-medium fig tree well-suited to container growing and small gardens. In zone 9 it produces a breba crop in June–July and a main crop in August–October. The compact habit makes it one of the better figs for container growing in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Ronde de Bordeaux (Round Bordeaux) is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region producing small, round, dark-purple to nearly black-skinned fruits with brilliant deep red to garnet-colored flesh — one of the most richly colored of all fig varieties. The dark skin and brilliant interior make Ronde de Bordeaux a spectacular fresh eating fig and an equally attractive fig for jam and preserves where the deep color produces richly-hued products. The flavor is very sweet, rich, and slightly winey with the complexity associated with dark-skinned fig varieties. The compact tree habit makes Ronde de Bordeaux one of the most practical figs for home gardens and container growing — it produces prolifically despite its modest size. It is an early-maturing variety with the main crop ripening in late July–August in zone 9, among the earliest of the dark-skinned European fig types. This fig has become very popular among fig enthusiasts in zone 9 and zone 10 for its combination of early ripening, outstanding flavor, and manageable tree size.

plant_note: Plant in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rose apple is a medium-sized Myrtaceae tree suited to zones 10–12 that is prized for its ornamental showy white to pale yellow pompom flowers as much as for its fruit. Trees naturalize readily in humid tropical climates and are considered invasive in parts of Hawaii and other Pacific Islands — check local invasive species regulations before planting.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in zones 10–12; rose apple (Syzygium jambos) is a medium-sized evergreen tree in the Myrtaceae family native to Southeast Asia that produces waxy, pale yellow to cream or blush-pink, oval fruits with a uniquely crisp, crunchy texture and a delicate, unmistakable flavor of rose water — floral, lightly sweet, and aromatic in a way unlike any other fruit. The fruits are primarily eaten fresh out of hand, and their distinctive rose fragrance also makes them popular for flavoring drinks, syrups, and desserts across Southeast Asia and the Caribbean. The tree produces spectacular ornamental flower clusters of long, creamy-white stamens resembling shaving brushes before fruit development, making it a dual-purpose landscape tree. Rose apple is adaptable, moderately fast-growing, and performs well with consistent moisture and regular balanced fertilization.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root grafted trees in spring; Rossiyanka is a cross between the American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) and the Oriental persimmon (Diospyros kaki) bred in Russia for extreme cold hardiness, tolerating winter lows to roughly -25 to -30°F once dormant while retaining the larger, less astringent fruit of its Asian parent.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established trees are drought-tolerant and need little supplemental fertilization beyond a light annual feeding. Rossiyanka is a Russian-bred hybrid between the native American persimmon and the Asian kaki persimmon, developed to combine the extreme winter hardiness of the American parent with fruit size and eating quality closer to Asian types. The medium-large orange fruits are strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point they turn sweet and jammy with a rich, honeyed flavor; frost or a period of cold storage speeds the softening. Self-fruitful and reliably productive once established, it is a good choice for growers who want Asian-persimmon-quality fruit in a climate too cold, or on a rootstock too marginal, for standard kaki cultivars, and it also performs well in the milder Gulf South.

plant_note: Plant grafted container stock in spring in well-drained, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; rough-shell macadamia (M. tetraphylla) is marginally more cold-hardy than smooth-shell M. integrifolia, tolerating brief dips to about 24–26°F in established trees — slightly extending the zone range into protected zone 8b–9a sites; the prickly-edged leaves (unlike the smooth-edged M. integrifolia) distinguish the species.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5), deep, loamy soil in full sun; M. tetraphylla is slightly more cold-tolerant than M. integrifolia and may succeed in protected zone 8b sites. Macadamia tetraphylla (rough-shell macadamia or prickly-leaf macadamia) is the second of the two commercially important macadamia species — closely related to the smooth-shell macadamia (M. integrifolia) but distinguishable by its prickly-edged leaves arranged in whorls of four (the species name 'tetraphylla' means 'four-leaved'), and by the rough, ridged texture of its nut shell. Both species produce equally delicious, buttery, rich macadamia nuts with the same world-class flavor, and in commercial macadamia production, the two species and their hybrids are grown side by side with little practical flavor difference noted by consumers. The practical distinction for home growers is cold tolerance: M. tetraphylla is marginally more cold-hardy than M. integrifolia, typically tolerating temperatures of 24–26°F in established trees — potentially extending the range to protected zone 8b–9a microclimates in warm-wall or frost-pocket-free sites. M. tetraphylla is also slightly smaller in tree size. Both species benefit from cross-pollination, and planting one of each species is commonly recommended to ensure good nut set.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall on rocky or sandy, well-drained soil; this species naturally colonizes exposed outcrops and barrens where soil is thin and lean.
directions: Harvest berries when fully dark blue-black and extract seeds by mashing and rinsing before sowing in fall into lean, well-drained soil in a sunny outdoor bed. The round, coarsely toothed leaves that give this species its name are a useful identification feature as seedlings mature through their first growing seasons. Roundleaf Serviceberry tolerates shallow, rocky soils and gravelly barrens far better than most shrubs, making it a strong candidate for challenging landscape sites. Plants begin bearing their sweet, dark berries within 2–5 years of transplanting and attract a wide variety of frugivorous birds during the midsummer ripening period.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Roxburgh fig is a large-leafed fig native to the foothills of the Himalayas and Southeast Asia, producing enormous, rounded, elephant-ear leaves 12–24 inches across and clusters of large, brownish-red, edible figs that form directly on the trunk and main branches (cauliflory), similar to jackfruit.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; Roxburgh fig grows rapidly and produces large clusters of edible figs. Ficus auriculata (Roxburgh fig or timla fig) is one of the most ornamentally dramatic and useful fruiting figs in tropical horticulture — a large, fast-growing tree from the Himalayan foothills and Southeast Asia producing the largest leaves of any commonly cultivated Ficus: enormous (12–24 inch), rounded, dark-green, slightly hairy leaves with a bold, tropical texture that gives the plant a genuinely dramatic visual presence, resembling a cross between a giant philodendron and an elephant ear. The figs are equally remarkable: large (1.5–2.5 inch), distinctly ribbed, brownish-red when ripe, produced in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory) — the same unusual fruiting pattern as jackfruit. The figs are sweet, moist, seedy, and pleasant to eat fresh when ripe, with a mild, sweet flavor; they are also eaten as a cooked vegetable when unripe in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking (stewed, pickled, or curried). In Himalayan and hill-station gardens in India, Roxburgh fig is grown as a major multi-use tree; in zone 9–12 Gulf Coast gardens, it is an outstanding bold-textured ornamental that also produces an edible crop.

common_name: Roxbury Russet Apple (Oldest Documented American Apple Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Roxbury Russet is vigorous and productive, and its thick russeted skin gives the fruit outstanding storage life compared to smooth-skinned apples.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. First recorded in Roxbury, Massachusetts in the 1630s, this is the oldest apple cultivar documented as having originated in North America, predating the country itself by well over a century. The medium, dull yellow-green fruit is almost entirely covered in rough golden-brown russet, with firm, crisp, sweet-tart flesh well suited to fresh eating, cider, and long winter storage, since the thick skin sheds moisture slowly and resists shriveling. It ripens in mid-fall and was historically prized precisely because it kept so well through the winter months before refrigeration existed.

common_name: Ruby Red Grapefruit (Original Texas Pink Grapefruit, First US Plant Patent Recipient)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in spring; Ruby Red grapefruit is most successfully grown in the Rio Grande Valley of south Texas (zone 9b-10) and the Gulf Coast where the combination of warm summers and cooler winters produces the best red pigmentation development — the pink-red color intensifies with cooler temperatures and the fruit may remain pale in very mild winters. In zone 9 (Louisiana, Mississippi), grapefruit trees are near the northern cold limit and require frost protection when young and during severe cold events; mature trees can tolerate brief temperatures to 26–28°F. The fruit matures late (November–June), with peak quality typically in January–April. Ruby Red grapefruit should hang on the tree until fully mature — the bright pink flesh and sweet-tart flavor develop fully only at ripening and do not improve if picked early.
directions: Plant grafted tree in full sun, deep well-drained soil; mulch for moisture retention. Protect from frost in zone 9. Ruby Red is the original pink/red-fleshed grapefruit variety and one of the most historically significant citrus varieties in American horticulture: it holds the distinction of being the first variety to receive a US plant patent, issued February 4, 1930 (US Plant Patent 1), when Bonnie Nance's discovery of a pink bud sport on a Thompson grapefruit tree in Weslaco, Texas in 1929 was submitted by Stark Brothers Nursery. The story of Ruby Red begins in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas — one of the finest grapefruit-producing regions in the world — where the combination of warm days, cool nights, and alkaline soil produces grapefruit of exceptional sweetness and flavor. Ruby Red's pink flesh coloration comes from lycopene (the same pigment in tomatoes and watermelons) — a pigment that accumulates in the fruit's flesh during the cool nights of the growing season. The variety has less red pigmentation than its descendants (Rio Red and Star Ruby, which were developed specifically for deeper coloration), but it was the original breakthrough that made pink grapefruit a distinct commercial category. The fruit is large (3–5 inches), mildly fragrant, with blushed pink skin and sweet, mildly acidic, aromatic flesh that made pink grapefruit the preferred fresh-eating grapefruit variety in American markets through the mid-20th century.

plant_note: Grown from a grafted or potted tree; move outdoors after frost.
directions: Ruby Supreme is a tropical guava that bears fragrant fruit with sweet, pink-red flesh rich in flavor and nutrition. This fast-growing evergreen fruits young and adapts well to containers, making it accessible even where winters are cold. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and feed regularly during the warm season for the heaviest crops. Keep the soil evenly moist, prune to maintain a manageable size, and bring potted trees indoors before frost.

plant_note: Plant bare-root shrubs in late winter or early spring; rugosa rose establishes quickly and begins producing hips in its second or third year.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil including poor sandy or salty soils where few shrubs survive; rugosa rose is extraordinarily tough and requires almost no maintenance once established. The intensely fragrant single or semi-double flowers in magenta, pink, or white bloom repeatedly from late spring to fall, followed by the largest and most nutritious rose hips of any commonly grown species — orange-red to scarlet tomato-shaped hips up to 1 inch in diameter that are exceptionally rich in vitamin C. Hips are harvested after the first frost when fully soft and red for rosehip tea, syrup, jam, and wine. The dense, thorny habit makes an excellent barrier hedge. Remove only dead wood; avoid hard pruning, which disrupts repeat flowering.

plant_note: Plant in humid tropical lowlands with well-drained soil; requires separate male and female trees for fruiting unless self-fertile selected varieties are obtained.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained, fertile soil in humid tropical lowland conditions; rukam is a large Southeast Asian fruiting tree in the same genus as governor's plum but bearing larger, rounder fruits (3/4–1 inch) with dark red to purple-black skin and acidic flesh that sweetens with full ripeness and can be eaten fresh or preserved. A handsome ornamental tree with large glossy leaves, it is grown in home gardens across Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines as both ornamental and fruit tree. Much less commonly grown than governor's plum but produces superior fruit quality and larger individual fruits. Slow to bear from seed — grafted plants fruit several years earlier.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted hardwood cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Russian 26 is one of a group of cold-hardy pomegranate selections imported from the former Soviet Union, tolerating temperatures into the low teens °F once established. Self-fertile; no separate pollinator required.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate poor, alkaline, and clay soils far better than most fruit trees. Russian 26 is one of several numbered cold-hardy pomegranate cultivars brought into North American cultivation from Russia and Central Asia, prized for combining good winter hardiness with heavy, precocious production of medium-sized fruit. The rind is typically pink to red and the arils are juicy, sweet-tart, and well flavored, ripening in early-to-mid fall. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and long-lived, and the compact, multi-stemmed shrub form makes it easy to manage as a large shrub or small espaliered tree. In the Gulf South, Russian 26 fruits reliably and its cold tolerance provides insurance against occasional hard freezes that can damage less hardy pomegranate selections.

common_name: Ruston Red Peach (Louisiana Heirloom Clingstone Peach for Gulf South Gardens)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter; Ruston Red requires approximately 400–450 chilling hours — more than low-chill varieties like Flordaking, but still within reach of most zone 9 locations in Louisiana, Mississippi, and East Texas where winters accumulate sufficient chill. In years with warm winters, Ruston Red may bloom poorly; in years with adequate chill, it produces reliably. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun. The variety produces fruit in June–July in zone 9, slightly later than very early low-chill peaches, and the fruit keeps better on the tree and post-harvest than very early types. Ruston Red is particularly well-adapted to the humidity of the Gulf South and is considered one of the better locally-adapted peach varieties for the Midsouth region.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun, well-drained soil. Thin fruit when marble-sized to 6–8 inches apart. Ruston Red is an heirloom peach variety associated with Ruston, Louisiana — a city in Lincoln Parish in north Louisiana that became famous for its peaches and has celebrated an annual Peach Festival since 1951. Ruston is located in a sweet spot for peach production in Louisiana: elevated enough above the Gulf Coast to accumulate adequate winter chill hours for most peach varieties, yet with a long enough warm season for fruit development, making the area one of the most productive peach regions in the Deep South. Ruston Red is a clingstone variety (the flesh adheres to the pit, making fresh eating more effortful but canning and preserving easier), with deep red skin and yellow to orange flesh, good sweetness, and the rich peach flavor associated with tree-ripened southern peaches. The variety has been grown in Louisiana for multiple generations and represents the type of locally-adapted, regionally-specific heirloom fruit variety that is increasingly important to preserve as commercial agriculture standardizes toward nationally-marketed varieties. Ruston Red's reputation in Louisiana is one of strong local association and pride: the name carries the flavor of place, as fruit varieties often do in American agricultural tradition, linking the eating experience to a specific region's history and soil.

plant_note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, alkaline to slightly acidic, rocky to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; rusty blackhaw is particularly well-adapted to limestone soils of the Southeast and Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; rusty blackhaw is one of the most beautiful and underused native fruiting shrubs of the Southeast, producing spectacular flat clusters of creamy white flowers in early spring, followed by clusters of dark blue-black berries with a raisin-like, sweet-tart flavor that can be eaten fresh or used for jelly and wine. The leaves have rusty-red fuzzy undersides (giving the species name) and turn deep burgundy-red in fall. It grows naturally on dry, rocky, limestone slopes and woodland edges and is extremely drought tolerant once established. The berries provide fall food for mockingbirds, bluebirds, and thrushes. It can be trained as a specimen shrub or allowed to develop into a small multi-trunk tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Sabara jaboticaba is slow-growing but long-lived and extremely productive once mature. In zone 9 the tree requires frost protection when young (below 28°F); established trees of 5+ years tolerate brief temperature drops to 24–26°F. Plant in a sheltered microclimate if hard freezes occur in your area. The tree is self-fertile and bears without a cross-pollinator.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil — jaboticaba tolerates a wider pH range than most tropical fruits and performs well in amended Gulf Coast soils; Sabara is the most widely grown jaboticaba cultivar, a selection of the Brazilian grape tree (Plinia cauliflora) renowned for its unique and visually remarkable fruiting habit — the small, grape-like fruits emerge directly from the trunk and main branches of the tree rather than on terminal shoots, covering the bark in dense clusters of dark purple fruits that look like the tree has been decorated with purple grapes. The fruits are eaten fresh (popped open to reveal the sweet, translucent white pulp inside a thick purple skin), or processed into jams, wines, and liqueurs. Jaboticaba trees fruit multiple times per year in zone 9 after triggering by rain or irrigation following a dry period, providing periodic fresh fruit throughout the growing season. Sabara is the highest-quality eating variety, with sweet, rich, complex fruit flavor and good fresh-eating skin-to-pulp ratio.

common_name: Sacred Fig (Bodhi Tree, Peepal Tree, Bo Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with well-drained soil; Ficus religiosa is frost-sensitive and best suited to zone 10-11 for outdoor planting. In zone 9, it can be grown as a large container specimen or bonsai. Keep away from structures — the roots and canopy are powerfully invasive. Unlike most figs, it is semi-deciduous, briefly dropping its distinctive heart-shaped leaves before quickly producing new ones. The milky sap irritates skin.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Sacred Fig grows vigorously in tropical and subtropical conditions and should be sited away from all structures, pipes, and paving. Ficus religiosa is a large, semi-deciduous fig tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia, one of the most sacred plants in human history. It is the tree under which Siddhartha Gautama achieved enlightenment, becoming the Buddha, at Bodh Gaya in present-day India — an event considered so significant that the tree, and its descendants propagated from that original specimen, are venerated throughout the Buddhist world. The plant is equally sacred in Hinduism and Jainism. Its distinctive heart-shaped to ovate leaves have an extraordinarily elongated drip tip — sometimes 2–3 times the length of the leaf blade — that evolved to channel water rapidly off the leaf surface in the heavy monsoon rains of its native habitat. These trembling, long-tipped leaves create a distinctive rustling sound in the slightest breeze, a quality noted in both botanical and spiritual literature. In zone 10-11 Gulf Coast and Florida, Sacred Fig is grown as a significant landscape specimen and street tree. In zone 9, it is best maintained as a large container tree or bonsai subject, moved to protected locations in winter. Small, inedible figs are produced and consumed by birds.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; safou or African pear is one of the most nutritionally important indigenous fruit trees of Central and West Africa, producing clusters of deep purple-blue, olive-shaped fruits rich in essential fatty acids and protein — grilled or boiled, the flesh softens to a buttery, avocado-like consistency and is a dietary staple in Cameroon, Nigeria, DRC, and across the humid tropical forest zone.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; young trees benefit from partial shade and consistent moisture. Dacryodes edulis (safou, African pear, or bush butter tree) is one of sub-Saharan Africa's most culturally and nutritionally important indigenous food trees, native to the humid tropical forests of West and Central Africa — particularly Cameroon, Nigeria, Gabon, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. The fruits are produced in large pendant clusters directly on the branches: deep purple-blue to violet, oval-oblong, 2–4 inches long, resembling a fat olive. The fruit is not eaten raw — the hard, firm flesh must be boiled or flame-roasted to soften, at which point it transforms into a rich, buttery, smooth, avocado-like consistency with a unique, savory-nutty flavor profile. The fruit pulp contains 35–55% oil with a composition similar to olive oil and palm oil combined, making safou one of the most calorie-dense and nutritionally complete forest fruits in Africa. It is also a significant protein source compared to most fruits. In its native range, safou is widely eaten alongside corn, cassava, and plantain as a major dietary fat source, and is sold extensively in West African urban markets. Outside Africa, safou is almost entirely unknown but is gaining interest as a potential food security crop and agroforestry tree in tropical regions worldwide.

plant_note: Plant container stock or suckers in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Sago Palm is a large, clustering, monocarpic palm native to the peat swamps and lowland swamp forests of Southeast Asia — the primary source of sago, the starch extracted from the pith of the trunk immediately before flowering — a fundamental starch staple for millions of people in Indonesia, Malaysia, and Papua New Guinea.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun in tropical conditions; Metroxylon sagu thrives in peat swamp conditions with consistently high water table — it tolerates seasonal flooding and requires consistently moist to wet soil; do not allow the root zone to dry out. Metroxylon sagu (Sago Palm) is a large, clustering, monocarpic palm native to the peat swamps, freshwater swamps, and lowland swamp forests of the Malay Archipelago — Borneo, Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, the Moluccas, and Papua New Guinea — where it is the primary source of 'sago,' a powdery starch extracted from the pithy interior of the trunk immediately before the palm flowers and dies. Each trunk accumulates up to 150–300 kilograms of starch over 7–15 years before flowering, fruiting, and dying (monocarpic); the clusters produce multiple offshoots (suckers) that replace the mother stem, so the clump persists indefinitely. Sago is a fundamental caloric staple for millions of people across Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, and the Pacific Islands — prepared as papeda (sago porridge), sago pancakes, sago noodles, and diverse traditional foods. It has been called 'the staff of life of swamp peoples' and feeds communities in areas too wet, flooded, or acidic for rice or other crops. Globally important as a swamp-agroforestry tree for waterlogged, acidic, peat-swamp soils where no other major food crop survives.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile soil in full sun; Saijo is astringent when firm and must be fully soft before eating; it is self-fertile and requires minimal chill hours (100–200).
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Saijo is an astringent Japanese persimmon of Japanese origin — widely considered one of the finest-flavored of all persimmon cultivars, with elongated, narrow, yellow-orange to orange fruits and exceptional rich, honey-sweet flavor that persimmon enthusiasts describe as superior to any non-astringent variety. Saijo is astringent when firm — meaning the fruit must fully ripen and soften to a jelly-like texture before the astringency disappears and the full sweetness and flavor develop. This is not a defect but a different style of persimmon use: fully ripe Saijo is spooned from the skin like a pudding. Saijo ripens in September to October in zone 9, requiring only 100–200 chill hours, making it one of the lowest-chill persimmon cultivars and extremely well adapted to Gulf Coast climates. The tree is handsome, drought-tolerant once established, and remarkably free of serious pests and diseases — one of the easiest fruit trees for Gulf South gardens. The striking orange fruit and vivid orange fall foliage create exceptional ornamental value in the landscape. Saijo can be dried (hoshigaki) to make the traditional Japanese dried persimmon candy — a process that concentrates the intense natural sweetness into a complex, mellow confection.

plant_note: Plant in frost-free, humid tropical conditions with deep, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; salak is a clumping spiny palm — plant male and female plants together for fruiting, or obtain a hermaphroditic variety.
directions: Plant in deep, moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade in frost-free tropical conditions; salak (snake fruit) is a dramatic spiny clustering palm from Indonesia and Malaysia producing clusters of pear-shaped fruits with distinctive reddish-brown scaly skin that closely resembles a snake's skin — hence the common name. The fruit has three lobes of crisp, dry, sweet-acidic flesh (texture somewhat like a dry apple) with a complex flavor variously described as sweet, astringent, honey-like, and reminiscent of cinnamon, varying considerably by variety. The most prized variety is 'Salak Bali' from Bali. High humidity and consistent moisture are essential; this is one of the most challenging tropical fruits to grow outside its native range.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Salavatski is one of the most cold-hardy pomegranate varieties, tolerating temperatures to about 10–15°F when established — substantially hardier than most other fruiting pomegranates and suitable for zone 7b–11. Trees are self-fertile; no cross-pollination is needed. Pomegranates fruit on new wood; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils; Salavatski (also spelled Salavatsky, Salavatskij) is a Central Asian pomegranate from the Caucasus region of Russia and Azerbaijan, valued primarily for its exceptional cold hardiness among fruiting pomegranate varieties — it survives temperatures to 10–15°F that would kill most other cultivars, making it the go-to choice for zone 7b–8 growers and providing extra insurance in zone 9a. The large, deep-red to garnet fruits ripen in September–November with tart-sweet, ruby-red arils surrounding tender seeds — the flavor is typically more tart than softer varieties like Wonderful, which suits pomegranate juice, grenadine, and Persian cooking better than fresh eating. Trees are extremely drought-tolerant once established and long-lived; established specimens may produce fruit for decades or even centuries. In zone 9 pomegranates produce heavily and reliably; Salavatski offers cold-hardiness insurance for zone 9a gardens where rare hard freezes occasionally occur.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 2–3 inch depth in dry, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; cold stratification of 90 days over winter is required before spring germination. Sand Hickory develops a long taproot and is best established by direct seeding or very young container-grown transplants.
directions: Sand Hickory is a native nut tree specially adapted to the dry, sandy, acidic soils of pine-oak barrens, sandhills, and upland forest margins across the southeastern coastal plain from New Jersey south to Florida and west to Kansas, where it thrives in conditions too infertile and dry for most other nut trees. The compound leaves are distinctively pale and silvery-hairy on the undersides — a useful field character separating it from the similar Pignut and Mockernut hickories — and produce brilliant gold fall color. Nuts are moderately thin-shelled with mildly bitter to slightly sweet kernels eaten by squirrels, white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, and black bears; direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 2–3 inch depth in sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun, allowing 90 days of cold stratification before spring germination. Once established, Sand Hickory is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental irrigation, making it the ideal native nut tree for dry, infertile, xeric sites.

plant_note: Plant dormant trees in early spring; tolerates humid, warm climates well.
directions: The sand pear is a vigorous, disease-resistant Asian pear species valued for its gritty, juicy fruit and tolerance of hot, humid summers. Plant two compatible cultivars for cross-pollination in full sun and deep, well-drained soil. Train young trees to a central leader and thin fruit clusters to one per spur to improve size. Its strong fire-blight resistance makes it a dependable choice where European pears fail.

plant_note: Plant bare-root while dormant in early spring or in fall in mild climates.
directions: Plant this popular Japanese plum in deep, well-drained loam and full sun, setting the graft union a few inches above the soil line. Though partially self-fruitful, yields improve dramatically with a second Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination. Prune to an open-center vase shape during the dormant season to admit light and air. Thin heavy fruit sets to 4-6 inches apart to size up the crop and prevent limb breakage.

plant_note: Plant in the humid tropics; intolerant of any frost.
directions: Santol is a fast-growing Southeast Asian tree bearing round, downy fruit with sweet-sour, cottony pulp surrounding large seeds. It requires a hot, humid, frost-free climate and deep, fertile, well-drained soil with steady moisture. Plant in full sun, allowing ample space for the large canopy to develop. Grafted trees fruit within a few years; harvest when the skin turns yellow and use the pulp fresh or in preserves and candies.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; sapodilla is one of the most drought- and salt-tolerant tropical fruit trees available, making it well-suited to South Florida's sandy, alkaline soils and coastal conditions. Mature established trees tolerate brief cold to 26–28°F, which allows planting in protected zone 9b microclimates.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — including sandy, rocky, and calcareous soils — in full sun in zones 10–12; sapodilla (Manilkara zapota) is a long-lived, slow-growing Mesoamerican tree that ranks among the most drought- and wind-tolerant of all tropical fruit trees, making it exceptionally well adapted to South Florida's coastal sandy soils, salt air, and seasonal dry periods. The small to medium-sized, rough brown-skinned fruits reveal a translucent, grainy, caramel-brown flesh of extraordinary sweetness — often described as tasting of brown sugar, pear, and malt — that must be fully ripe and soft before eating, as unripe fruits are astringent from tannins. Grafted trees of selections such as 'Prolific' and 'Tikal' begin bearing in 4–6 years; seedling trees may take 8 years or more. The tree also has historical industrial significance as the source of chicle, the natural latex once used as the base of chewing gum, harvested by the Mesoamerican chiclero tradition for centuries.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sapucaia or paradise nut is a large canopy tree of the Brazilian rainforest — closely related to Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) — producing large, woody, barrel-shaped capsules (the 'monkey pots') containing edible nuts considered by many tasters to be superior to Brazil nuts in creaminess and flavor, with oil composition similar to macadamia oil.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile, deep soil in full sun to part shade; sapucaia requires genuinely tropical conditions and a long time to first fruiting — a tree for patient collectors in zone 11–12. Lecythis pisonis (sapucaia or paradise nut) is a massive canopy tree of the tropical rainforests of Brazil, Venezuela, and the Guianas — in the lecythis family (Lecythidaceae), closely related to Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) and sharing its remarkable botanical story. The tree produces large, barrel-shaped, very heavy woody capsules (4–6 inches wide) that remain on the branches and open via a detachable 'lid' at the top — these are the famous 'monkey pots' or 'monkey cups': animals (monkeys, squirrels, agoutis) reach into the narrow opening to grab the nuts, but if they grab too many, their fist is too large to withdraw, trapping them. The nuts inside (5–40 per capsule) are considered by nut connoisseurs to be superior to Brazil nuts: milder, creamier, less waxy, with an exceptionally smooth texture and rich flavor, very high in healthy fats similar to macadamia oil composition. Sapucaia nuts are almost entirely unknown in commerce despite their exceptional quality, because they do not store as well as Brazil nuts (the high oil content means they go rancid quickly) — making them a fresh-nut delight available primarily near their source. A magnificent collector's tree for zone 11–12 tropical gardens.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root specimens in spring; saskatoon is the prairie serviceberry of western Canada and the northern Great Plains, adapted to cold, dry, alkaline to neutral soils — it tolerates pH up to 7.5 and drought far better than eastern serviceberry species.
directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, moderately fertile soil; saskatoon (Amelanchier alnifolia) is the primary serviceberry of the Great Plains and Canadian prairies, producing abundant clusters of sweet, blueberry-flavored, dark purple berries in June that have been one of the most important food plants of the North American plains — used fresh, dried, and in pemmican by indigenous peoples including the Cree, Assiniboine, and Blackfoot, and now commercially cultivated across western Canada as 'saskatoon berries' for pies, jams, and wine. One of the most cold-hardy edible berry shrubs available, surviving to -40°F. Named cultivars including 'Thiessen', 'Smoky', and 'Martin' produce particularly large, sweet fruits. An outstanding prairie food-forest plant and edible landscape shrub.

plant_note: Plant in spring in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 9b–11; Satin Leaf is a small to medium native evergreen tree of the Sapotaceae family — native to South Florida hammocks, the Caribbean, and Central America — famous for leaves with a lustrous coppery-gold silky underside that flash dramatically when breezes turn them over, producing small, purple-black, edible Sapotaceae fruits similar in family to Star Apple and Mamey Sapote.
directions: Plant Satin Leaf in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; water regularly during establishment; mature trees tolerate brief cold to 28°F; protect young plants from hard frost; no significant pruning required. Chrysophyllum oliviforme is among South Florida's most striking native trees, instantly recognized by the extraordinary bicolor leaves — dark glossy green above and covered with dense, copper-golden, silky hairs below — that shimmer and catch light dramatically when wind moves through the canopy. The tree grows in South Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks alongside Gumbo Limbo, Strangler Fig, and Pigeon Plum, and is a highly recommended native alternative to non-native ornamental trees for South Florida landscapes. Small clusters of tiny white flowers give rise to small, dark purple, oval fruits (less than 1 inch) — technically edible and sweet when fully ripe, similar in structure to small star apples (in the same family), though the thin flesh makes them a minor snack rather than a major crop. The fruits are enthusiastically consumed by mockingbirds, robins, and migrating warblers in winter. An excellent shade tree for South Florida native gardens, providing year-round color interest through the glinting copper undersides of its foliage.

plant_note: Plant nursery transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun. Satinleaf tolerates a range of soil types including marl and sandy soils and is moderately drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Satinleaf is one of the most visually striking native trees of south Florida's tropical hardwood hammocks, native to coastal hammocks, marl prairies, and pinelands from Brevard and Hillsborough counties south through the Keys and into the Caribbean, recognized immediately by its distinctive two-toned leaves — rich, dark, glossy green on top and brilliant coppery-golden on the undersides — that shimmer and flash in the breeze with each passing gust. Small white flowers produce small, dark purple to black berries (1–1.5 cm) that are sweet and edible and an important food for mockingbirds, robins, and migrating warblers; the fruit is also edible for people, with a flavor reminiscent of a mild grape. In south Florida native landscapes it works beautifully as a specimen tree, understory tree under larger canopy, or informal screen in partial shade; it tolerates the thin, rocky, alkaline marl and limestone soils of Miami-Dade County where many plants struggle. Grow in well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full sun in zones 9b–11.

plant_note: Plant in spring; among the most cold-tolerant of the sweet citrus.
directions: The satsuma is a nearly seedless, cold-hardy mandarin that ripens early and peels with ease. It survives brief dips near the low twenties Fahrenheit once established, making it the best citrus for marginal areas. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and protect young trees during hard freezes. Harvest promptly when the rind colors, as the fruit puffs and loses quality if left too long on the tree.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Satsuma is an early 20th century Japanese plum introduction with one of the lowest chill requirements of any high-quality Japanese plum (approximately 200–300 hours), making it one of the best plum varieties for Gulf Coast zone 8 and mild California coastal gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Satsuma cross-pollinates best with Santa Rosa, Beauty, Methley, or other Japanese plums. Satsuma is a distinctive Japanese plum selection of early 20th century origin whose most striking characteristic is its blood-red to deep crimson-purple interior flesh — unlike most plums with yellow or amber flesh, Satsuma's flesh is the same deep red as the skin, producing richly pigmented juice and a distinctive wine-like, full-flavored sweetness with more depth and richness than most yellow-fleshed Japanese plums. The medium-large, round fruits have deep red to maroon-black skin; they ripen in late July to August. With only approximately 200–300 chill hours required, Satsuma is one of the most reliably productive Japanese plums for Gulf Coast zone 8 and similar low-chill climates. The deep red flesh makes spectacular jam, preserves, and fresh eating; the color intensifies when cooked. Outstanding for Gulf Coast, Texas, and Central and Southern California gardens where insufficient chill makes most European plums unproductive.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, acidic to neutral, lean to moderately fertile soil in zone 9–12; Savanna Guava (Guisaro, Brazilian Guava, Cas Silvestre) is a sprawling, drought-resistant shrub or small tree from the tropical savannas (cerrado) of Brazil and adjacent South America — producing abundant small, round, yellow-green fruits with sweet-tart, white to cream flesh and a pronounced guava aroma — highly drought and cold tolerant compared to common guava.
directions: Plant Psidium guineense in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly acidic, lean soil in full sun; once established it is highly drought-tolerant — one of the most drought-resistant of all Psidium species — and performs well in sandy, poor soils where common guava struggles; prune lightly after fruiting to maintain a manageable size. Savanna Guava is the wild guava of the Brazilian cerrado (tropical savanna) — a shrubby, fire-resistant, drought-adapted species that has co-evolved with the deep-rooted, seasonally dry ecosystems of central Brazil. The small (golf-ball-sized to slightly larger), yellow-green fruits are produced in abundance from a relatively young age; the flavor is sweet-tart with an assertive, complex guava aroma — often described as more intensely flavored than common guava — and the fruits are eaten fresh, used for juice, made into jellies, and fermented into guava wine. The plant's tolerance of poor, sandy, acidic soils and periods of summer drought make it an excellent choice for Gulf Coast zone 9 gardens where common guava might be marginal; it is hardy to about 25–27°F with protection. The white, four-petaled flowers are attractive and produced throughout the warm season; birds relish the ripe fruits. A productive, low-maintenance, wildlife-supporting fruit shrub for hot, dry garden conditions.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; scarlet kadsura is dioecious — plant male and female plants for fruit production. It grows naturally in shaded woodland understory conditions and tolerates full shade.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to deep shade in zones 7–10; scarlet kadsura is a semi-evergreen to evergreen twining vine native to Japan, Korea, and southern China, valued for exceptional seasonal interest across multiple seasons: glossy, dark green, leathery leaves that may turn burgundy in cool weather; small, pale yellow, fragrant flowers in summer; and spectacular, showy clusters of scarlet-red, coral-like fruiting bodies in fall — each cluster up to 2 inches in diameter and resembling a bunch of tiny rubies. The fruits are edible and used in traditional Chinese medicine. It grows naturally in shaded forest understories and tolerates deep shade better than most fruiting vines — one of its most valuable garden traits. An outstanding shade vine for zone 7–10 gardens where its combination of handsome evergreen foliage, fragrant flowers, and dramatic red fruit clusters provides year-round ornamental interest in difficult, shaded positions.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Schley requires a Type II pollinator such as Desirable or Elliott and is more susceptible to scab than newer disease-resistant cultivars, so it benefits from good air circulation.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile bottomland-type soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety. Introduced in the early 1900s, Schley became one of the foundational commercial pecan cultivars of the 20th-century South and is still valued for its thin, easily cracked papershell and rich, high-quality kernel. It has been widely used as a parent in breeding programs that produced many of today's more disease-resistant cultivars, since it passes along excellent nut quality even though the tree itself is fairly susceptible to pecan scab in humid climates and may need fungicide protection in wet years. It remains a good choice in drier pecan-growing regions or where scab pressure is manageable.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to moderately moist, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; screwbean mesquite grows naturally in desert washes, riverbanks, and seasonally moist floodplains of the southwestern US and Mexico. The uniquely spiraling seed pods are highly distinctive.
directions: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; screwbean mesquite is immediately recognizable by its uniquely coiled, spiral seed pods — tightly twisted into a tight helix resembling a screw or corkscrew — unlike the straight or gently curved pods of other mesquites. The common name 'tornillo' (Spanish for screw) reflects this distinctive pod shape. The pods are edible, sweet, and nutritious, and were processed into food by Sonoran Desert indigenous peoples. The tree grows naturally along desert washes and dry riverbanks of the Southwest, tolerating the highly alkaline, sometimes saline soils of desert floodplains. The cream-colored flower spikes are fragrant and heavily visited by native bees. Increasingly rare in some areas due to agricultural development of desert floodplains. A distinctive, drought-tolerant native for desert Southwest gardens with excellent wildlife value.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall at 1–2 inch depth in dry, pure sandy, acidic, infertile, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; Scrub Hickory will not tolerate clay, wet feet, or excessive organic amendments. Mimicking the open Florida scrub habitat is essential for successful establishment.
directions: Scrub Hickory is a rare and imperiled native nut tree endemic to the ancient, fire-maintained Florida scrub habitats of the central Florida ridge, where it grows in pure white sand soils of extremely low fertility that are inhospitable to most other plants. A small tree rarely exceeding 25 feet, it produces small, round, thick-shelled nuts with bitter kernels that are eaten by Florida Scrub-Jays, fox squirrels, gopher tortoises, and other scrub wildlife, making it a keystone component of the Florida scrub food web. Plant fresh nuts in fall in pure, infertile, sandy, extremely well-drained soil in full sun — excessive water, clay, or organic matter quickly kills this species. In cultivation, Scrub Hickory performs best in open xeric settings that mimic native scrub conditions, and benefits from the periodic, low-intensity fire that characterizes and maintains the Florida scrub ecosystem.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in late winter to early spring; Scuppernong is self-fertile but benefits from a second muscadine variety nearby for maximum berry set. Build a strong arbor or trellis before planting — mature Scuppernong vines are massive and heavy with fruit. In zone 9, plant February–March for maximum first-season growth.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Scuppernong is a bronze-skinned muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) that is arguably the oldest cultivated grape in North America — the original 'Mother Vine' on Roanoke Island, North Carolina, is estimated to be over 400 years old and still produces fruit. It is the ancestral cultivar of the entire muscadine grape industry in the southeastern United States. Scuppernong grapes are large (1–1.5 inches), round, bronze-green to golden when ripe, with a distinctively musky, sweet, complex flavor very different from European grapes — they are used for fresh eating, wine, juice, and preserves. Muscadines are extremely well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf South, where they naturally resist Pierce's disease, black rot, and other diseases that devastate Vitis vinifera grapes. Vines are vigorous and long-lived, requiring a strong overhead arbor or high-wire trellis. Harvest in late August–September when berries drop from the cluster at a touch. Prune heavily each winter, leaving only short spurs on the permanent arms.

subcategory: Southeast Asian coastal ornamental fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Sea Apple is a large, handsome, coastal rainforest tree native to the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, and surrounding region, widely planted in Singapore and Malaysia as a shade and ornamental street tree for its attractive form, large glossy leaves, and spectacular masses of white powder-puff flowers followed by round, red, edible apple-like fruits.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained, acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Syzygium grande is fast-growing and tolerates brief waterlogging and coastal conditions — water regularly in establishment, then water deeply and infrequently once the tree is established. Syzygium grande (Sea Apple or Jambu Bol) is a large, handsome, fast-growing evergreen tree native to the coastal and freshwater-edge rainforests of the Malay Peninsula, Borneo, Sumatra, and the Philippines — one of the most important and beautiful tropical street and shade trees of Singapore and Peninsular Malaysia, where it is widely planted in parks, streets, and public spaces as one of the city's signature urban trees. The tree is spectacular in flower: enormous, cloud-like masses of small, white, 'powder-puff' flowers (characteristic of the Syzygium genus) cover the tree canopy in brilliant white floral displays multiple times per year. The round, green-to-pink-red fruits — 1–2 inches across, resembling small apples — are crisp, watery, mildly sweet, and edible fresh in the same way as the related rose apple (Syzygium jambos), though less flavorful. The fruit is also attractive to birds and wildlife. Syzygium grande is among the fastest-growing and most heat- and humidity-tolerant of the large Syzygium species and is well-suited to the humid tropical climate of coastal south Florida and Hawaii.

plant_note: Plant in spring in a coastal or frost-free site; sea grape is among the most salt-tolerant fruiting trees available.
directions: Sea grape is dioecious — male and female plants must both be present for fruit production — so purchase nursery plants that have been confirmed female, or graft from a known fruiting specimen and include a male pollinator nearby. It is one of the most wind- and salt-spray-tolerant fruiting trees available and naturally colonizes beach dunes and coastal scrub; it thrives on sandy, alkaline soils where most fruit trees fail. The grape-like clusters of purple-red fruits ripen in late summer to fall and are used to make a tart, mild jelly; individual fruits must be fully purple before picking as unripe fruit is astringent. Sea grape is legally protected in some coastal states — confirm local regulations before heavy pruning.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in sandy, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; seagrape is extraordinarily salt- and drought-tolerant once established and grows in pure sand just above the tide line on Florida's coasts.
directions: Plant in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; seagrape is one of the most iconic plants of Florida and Caribbean coastal areas — a native evergreen shrub or small tree with enormous, nearly round leaves 6–12 inches across with distinctive red veining that deepen to a rich burgundy in winter. It grows naturally in coastal dune scrub and maritime hammocks, one of the very few trees adapted to grow in pure beach sand with salt spray exposure. The clusters of grape-like fruits ripen to deep purple in late summer and fall, eaten fresh (moderately tart) or made into jelly and wine. Seagrape is critical habitat for coastal wildlife and an important sea-turtle nesting beach plant; it is legally protected in Florida — never collect from wild populations. It is used extensively as a hedge, screen, and windbreak in zone 10–11 coastal gardens.

plant_note: Plant dormant bare-root trees in early spring.
directions: Seckel is a small, intensely sweet American dessert pear often called the sugar pear. It shows useful resistance to fire blight and crops reliably in home orchards. Plant a second European pear such as Bartlett nearby for cross-pollination, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil. Train to a central leader, thin the abundant fruit, and pick while still firm to ripen in cool storage.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown palms in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Senegal date palm is adaptable to moist and occasionally flooded soils near streams, unlike most palms. More cold-hardy than other Phoenix species other than Canary Island palm — tolerating brief freezes to about 22°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Senegal date palm is the most important palm of tropical Africa — a naturally multi-trunked, suckering palm (producing clusters of arching trunks that grow to 25 feet and lean outward from a common base) native to riverbanks, lake margins, and moist savannas across tropical Africa from Senegal to Tanzania. The multi-stemmed, arching, clustering growth habit creates an instantly recognizable, lush tropical silhouette quite different from the single-trunked date palms. The small date-like fruits are edible, used locally for food and wine. More cold-hardy than most Phoenix species other than the Canary Island date palm, tolerating brief temperatures to about 22°F when mature and established — making it one of the hardiest of all fruiting palms. An outstanding ornamental for large spaces where its spreading, multi-stemmed habit can develop. Widely naturalized and invasive in Florida.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seeds require extended chilling near freezing to break dormancy and will germinate the following spring.
directions: Collect ripe fruits in autumn and extract seeds, then sow directly in a prepared outdoor seedbed or in deep pots left outside to receive natural winter chilling. Seeds require 90–180 days near freezing to break dormancy and will not germinate reliably without this cold period. Transplant seedlings to their permanent location in well-drained soil once they reach 6–12 inches tall, ideally in their second or third year. Patience is essential: trees take 7–15 years to bear their first crop of small, astringent sorbets, which soften and sweeten after a frost or brief bletting period.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container seedlings in early spring; shagbark hickory has a deep taproot and strongly resists transplanting once established — site carefully.
directions: Shagbark hickory is a stately native North American tree recognized by its exfoliating, shaggy gray bark; it produces small, round nuts with thin shells and exceptionally sweet, richly flavored kernels prized over pecans by many nut connoisseurs. Trees are monoecious and wind-pollinated; two or more trees improve nut set but a single tree can produce modest crops. Seedlings bear unpredictably and may take 10–20 years to fruit; grafted improved selections (Grainger, Wilcox) begin bearing in 5–7 years. Nuts drop in autumn when the four-sectioned husk splits open; collect promptly before squirrels take them and cure for 2–3 weeks before cracking.

common_name: Shangri-La Mulberry (Everbearing Compact Gulf South Mulberry)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shangri-La mulberry is everbearing — fruiting over multiple extended periods rather than in one concentrated flush, providing an extended picking season compared to standard spring-bearing types.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Shangri-La is a compact, everbearing mulberry selection valued for Gulf South gardens where the combination of heat tolerance, low chill requirement, extended fruit production, and moderate size makes it one of the most practical fresh fruit trees for zone 9 home landscapes. The long, cylindrical, dark-purple to black fruits (1.5–2 inches) are sweet, juicy, and excellent for fresh eating, jam, jelly, and freezing — the rich, complex mulberry flavor is one of the finest of any easily grown fruit tree. 'Shangri-La' fruits over an extended season (typically March through June in zone 9, with some additional fall fruiting) rather than in a single compressed flush — providing weeks of fresh mulberry harvest rather than an overwhelming glut. The tree's smaller mature size (8–12 feet compared to 20–30 feet for seedling mulberries) makes it manageable in typical home landscapes and allows netting to protect fruit from birds, which are very competitive with human harvesters for mulberry fruit. Mulberries in the Gulf South require very few chill hours (100–200 hours) and fruit reliably in warm winters that defeat other tree fruits. Established trees are highly drought-tolerant and require minimal care — the most significant maintenance is the control of surface root spread and the cleanup of fallen fruit on paved surfaces.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or early fall; in zone 9 plant October–March. Shasta Gold is self-fertile and does not require cross-pollination. Protect young trees from hard freezes below 27°F with frost cloth; established trees tolerate brief dips to 25°F. Ripens January–March in zone 9, which is later than many mandarins and extends the fresh citrus season into late winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Shasta Gold is a University of California-developed mandarin hybrid combining the superior flavor of Murcott mandarin with improved disease resistance and the late-season ripening of Encore — producing large, orange, flattened fruits with a very low seed count (typically 2–5 seeds), deep-orange flesh, and a rich, complex sweetness that many citrus experts rate among the finest mandarins available. The fruit holds on the tree without internal quality loss for 6–8 weeks after ripening (January–March), allowing extended harvest over a long window. The moderate-sized tree is easy to manage and produces heavy crops once established. In zone 9 Shasta Gold benefits from afternoon heat reflected from walls or pavement to ensure full fruit ripening; place against a south-facing wall in marginal locations. Trees are typically grafted onto trifoliate or flying dragon rootstock for cold hardiness.
