directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor; Summit is a bronze (amber-green) muscadine grape cultivar released by the University of Georgia — selected for its combination of large berry size, excellent fresh-eating quality, self-fertility, and late-season ripening. Bronze muscadines are generally milder and sweeter in flavor than black muscadines, making Summit particularly outstanding for fresh table use, wine production (bronze muscadines produce white/rosé wines), and juice. The large, uniform berries ripen in mid-to-late season (September in zone 9) in loose clusters that fall into collection bags or tarps for easy harvesting — a distinct muscadine characteristic compared to bunch grapes. Summit's self-fertility makes it an excellent standalone vine for gardeners with limited space, though yields are typically improved with a male or other self-fertile pollinizer within 50 feet. Muscadines are the native grapes of the southeastern United States — naturally adapted to Gulf South heat, humidity, and disease pressure that make European (Vitis vinifera) grapes impractical without intensive spray programs. Summit is disease-resistant, long-lived, and productive — established vines 20–30 years old commonly produce 30–50 pounds of fruit per year. The vine becomes a significant landscape feature as it ages, with thick, gnarled main canes and attractive fall foliage.

common_name: Sumner Pecan (UGA Release Large-Nut Type II Southeastern Commercial Pecan)
plant_note: Plant grafted nursery trees in late winter while dormant; Sumner is a Type II (protogynous) pecan — the pistillate flowers become receptive before the pollen is shed from the same tree's catkins, requiring a Type I pecan pollinator within 150 feet for reliable fertilization. Pair Sumner with Stuart, Desirable, Pawnee, or another Type I pollinator for full crops. In zone 9, pecan trees require deep, fertile soil with good internal drainage; shallow or waterlogged soils dramatically reduce production and tree longevity. Apply zinc sulfate foliar applications each spring before leaf-out to prevent zinc deficiency, which is extremely common in Gulf South pecans and causes rosette (distorted small leaves clustered at branch tips). Trees produce significant crops beginning 6–8 years after planting and are long-lived (50–100+ years in suitable conditions).
directions: Plant grafted trees in deep well-drained soil; pair with Type I pollinator. Apply zinc sulfate foliar sprays annually. Harvest when husks split and nuts fall. Sumner Pecan was released by the Georgia Agricultural Experiment Station (now part of the University of Georgia) as a named cultivar selected for the southeastern United States — a region that represents one of the traditional heartlands of US pecan production, with Georgia consistently among the top pecan-producing states nationally. Sumner is classified as Type II (protogynous) in the pecan flowering system that categorizes varieties by the relative timing of pistillate and staminate flower emergence: Type II varieties have pistillate (female) flowers ready to receive pollen before the same tree's catkins shed pollen, creating a natural cross-pollination requirement and making mixed-type plantings more productive than single-variety blocks. The nuts are large to very large for a southeastern pecan variety, with a good shell thickness-to-kernel ratio and above-average kernel quality — the kernel is plump, well-filled, and has good flavor. Sumner's relatively good resistance to pecan scab (compared to varieties like Desirable and Curtis, which have significant susceptibility) has made it a practical choice for home orchards and small commercial operations in humid areas where fungicide application is difficult to maintain consistently. The variety is widely available from Gulf South and southeastern nurseries and has remained in commercial production for decades despite the introduction of newer scab-resistant varieties.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sumo mandarin requires more careful management than standard mandarins and trees benefit from removal of excess fruit (thinning) to prevent biennial bearing and maintain large fruit size, which is a hallmark of the variety.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sumo mandarin — sold under the trademarked name 'Sumo Citrus' in North America and known as 'Dekopon' in Japan and 'Shiranui' by its cultivar name — is a premium mandarin hybrid (Kiyomi tangor x Ponkan mandarin) developed in Japan and widely considered one of the finest fresh mandarin fruits in the world: extraordinarily sweet (very high Brix), completely seedless, easily peeled with thick, bumpy, loose skin, and so large (typically 3–4 inches in diameter) that a single fruit is a generous one-person serving. The characteristic topknot bump at the stem end and enormous size make Sumo instantly recognizable in markets, where it commands premium prices ($3–5 per fruit or more). The flavor is intensely sweet with very low acid and a honey-like aromatic quality unlike any other mandarin, and the peel comes off in large easy-to-remove sections. Sumo/Dekopon trees are slow to come into full production (4–5 years from grafted trees to reliable crops), somewhat demanding in their cultural requirements, and require fruit thinning to produce the signature large fruits — but the result is exceptional. A wonderful specialty tree for zone 9–11 home orchards and edible landscapes.

common_name: Sunburst Tangerine (Deep Orange-Red Florida Hybrid Mandarin)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Sunburst ripens from November into January and is a heavy, reliable bearer, though fruit should be thinned in on years to avoid excessive limb breakage from heavy crop loads.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Released by the USDA in 1979 from a cross of Robinson and Osceola mandarins, Sunburst produces medium-sized fruit with a strikingly deep orange-red rind and sweet, juicy, richly flavored flesh with relatively few seeds. It is one of the more widely planted modern mandarin cultivars in Florida and the Gulf South because of its dependable, heavy annual production and attractive fruit color. The tree bears young and can overbear, so removing some fruit in spring helps maintain fruit size and reduce alternate-year bearing.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young; Sunflower is self-fertile to a degree but performs much better when cross-pollinated by another cultivar such as Shenandoah, Wells, or Susquehanna.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, full sun at maturity; Sunflower is a named pawpaw cultivar selected in Ohio from wild seedlings notable for its large, somewhat self-fertile nature (better fruit set when grown alone than most pawpaw cultivars), medium-large fruit size, and rich, sweet, yellow-gold flesh with excellent banana-custard flavor. The 'sunflower' name refers to both the yellow-gold flesh color and the cultivar's tendency to produce better solo fruit set than most pawpaws, though production is still significantly improved with a cross-pollinator. Sunflower's partial self-fertility is its most important practical attribute for gardeners who have space for only one tree — it will produce some fruit without a pollinator while most other pawpaw cultivars produce little or none. The medium-to-large fruits (4–6 oz average) have green to yellowish-green skin that softens slightly and turns more yellow-toned when fully ripe; the rich, sweet, banana-custard flesh is among the most popular of named pawpaw selections. Harvest by feel rather than appearance — ripe pawpaws yield to gentle pressure like a ripe peach. As with all pawpaws, the very short post-harvest shelf life (2–5 days at room temperature) makes them a specialty fruit for home gardeners and local direct-sale; they cannot be commercially distributed through standard grocery supply chains.

common_name: Sunred Nectarine (Ultra-Low-Chill Gulf South Nectarine, Florida-Texas Nectarine)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, deep fertile soil in full sun; Sunred has an extraordinarily low chill requirement of approximately 150–200 hours below 45°F — the lowest of any widely available named nectarine — making it the standard recommended nectarine for the Gulf South, central and south Texas, and the southern half of Florida where winter temperatures are too mild for standard nectarines; self-fertile, no cross-pollinator needed.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sunred is self-fertile; thin fruits to 6 inches after natural drop; Sunred ripens early (May in zone 8–9, one of the earliest nectarines available), producing medium-sized, bright red, freestone fruits with yellow flesh and good sweet-tart flavor — the first fresh nectarines of the season in Gulf Coast markets. Sunred nectarine is the primary low-chill nectarine for Gulf South and Florida gardening, selected for its exceptionally low chill hour requirement (approximately 150–200 hours) that allows it to bloom and fruit reliably in the mild winters of Houston, New Orleans, Tampa, and similar Gulf Coast cities where the 400–600 chill hours required by standard California nectarines are rarely accumulated in a typical year. The variety was developed through University of Florida and related southern breeding programs specifically to fill the gap in the Gulf South stone fruit palette, where peaches had low-chill options (Flordaking, Florida Crest) but the nectarine category was essentially absent for warm-climate gardeners. Sunred ripens in May in zone 8–9 — among the very earliest of any nectarine — providing a fresh stone fruit harvest at a time when nothing else is ripe, giving it a clear market window at Gulf Coast farmers' markets and specialty farm stands. The fruits are medium-sized, bright red, with yellow freestone flesh and a pleasant sweet-tart nectarine flavor that, while not matching the complex richness of premium California nectarines in cool growing conditions, is excellent for the region.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Superior is a University of Minnesota 1957 release combining Japanese and American plum genetics for outstanding cold hardiness and excellent fruit quality — one of the best plum varieties for zones 4–6 where most Japanese plums winter-kill or fail to fruit reliably.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Superior is partially self-fruitful but produces heavier crops cross-pollinated with Toka, Pipestone, or another Minnesota plum hybrid. Superior plum was released in 1957 by the University of Minnesota fruit breeding program, which developed a series of plum hybrids combining Japanese plum (Prunus salicina) quality and fruit size with the extreme cold hardiness of native American plum species (Prunus americana); these hybrids fill an important niche for gardeners in zones 4–6 where winters regularly kill Japanese plums or prevent adequate chill hours for European varieties. Superior produces large (2–3 inch), dark red-maroon, round fruits with yellow flesh and excellent sweet-tart flavor — one of the largest and best-flavored of the Minnesota hybrids and clearly superior in fruit quality to earlier hybrid selections. Very cold-hardy (surviving to –40°F) and blooms late enough to avoid most late spring frosts. A large, vigorous, productive tree suited to the Upper Midwest and Northern Plains where most stone fruits struggle.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Surinam cherry is a frost-sensitive tropical fruiting shrub native to Brazil and Paraguay that has naturalized extensively in South Florida, Gulf Coast, and tropical regions worldwide as both an ornamental hedge and food plant.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants are drought-tolerant but produce best fruit with consistent moisture during the fruiting period. Eugenia uniflora is a glossy-leaved evergreen shrub or small tree native to tropical South America, widely naturalized in Florida, the Gulf Coast, Hawaii, and subtropical regions worldwide; the deeply ribbed, round, eight-segmented fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally to deep red or nearly black, with a distinctive sharp-sweet, resinous flavor that is immediately distinctive — excellent fresh when fully ripe (dark red to black stage), in juices, jellies, ice cream, and fermented beverages. The foliage is beautifully aromatic when crushed. It is commonly planted as a fast-growing hedge or screening shrub in zone 9–12 and has become naturalized (and invasive in some areas of Florida). Hardy to about 28°F; protect from frost in zone 9a.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Suruga is a Japanese astringent persimmon that must be fully soft (bletted) before eating, unlike non-astringent types like Fuyu. Trees are partially self-fertile but produce more heavily with cross-pollination from another Japanese persimmon variety. In zone 9 Suruga ripens October–November; the orange fruits color up dramatically and can be harvested for drying while still firm.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile soil; Suruga is a large-fruited astringent persimmon from Japan, producing brilliant deep-orange fruits of 8–14 ounces with smooth, thin skin and exceptionally rich, complex, honey-sweet flavor when fully bletted (softened to near-liquid jelly consistency). Astringent persimmons like Suruga contain high tannin levels when unripe that create an intensely mouth-puckering sensation; the astringency disappears completely when fruits are allowed to ripen and soften fully on or off the tree. Suruga is specifically valued in Japan for hoshigaki — traditional Japanese dried persimmon — where peeled fruits are hung on strings and massaged daily over 4–6 weeks to produce a sweet, concentrated dried fruit with a crystalline sugar bloom on the surface. In zone 9 Suruga trees are productive and long-lived, with spectacular fall foliage adding ornamental value. The large fruits are less susceptible to fruit fly damage than non-astringent types because they are harvested firm and ripened off the tree.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0) soil in partial shade when young; Susquehanna pairs effectively with Shenandoah or Wells for cross-pollination, as the Peterson pawpaws were selected to maximize cross-productivity with one another.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Susquehanna is one of the flagship 'Peterson Pawpaws' — the group of named cultivars selected and introduced by Neal Peterson from decades of pawpaw breeding aimed at developing the largest, sweetest, and most productive cultivars available. Susquehanna produces some of the largest individual pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with exceptional fruits reaching 12–16 ounces — two to three times the average size of a good seedling-grown pawpaw — on a productive, healthy tree. The extraordinarily large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with rich banana-custard-vanilla character, and low seed-to-flesh ratio (maximum edible flesh per fruit) make Susquehanna the top choice among pawpaw enthusiasts seeking maximum yield from a home orchard planting. Cross-pollination from Shenandoah, Wells, or another unrelated cultivar is required for reliable production — plant two or more different named cultivars within 50 feet. Because pawpaw flowers have an unusual pollination mechanism (receptive to pollen only briefly, with fly/beetle pollinators), hand-pollination using a small brush to transfer pollen between flowers at different stages significantly improves fruit set. In zone 9, pawpaws perform in the northern portions of the zone; deep South heat and insufficient winter chilling can limit production in zones 9b and warmer.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall directly in a sheltered seedbed; the cold of winter provides the stratification needed for spring germination.
directions: Harvest berries in early autumn and mash to separate seeds from pulp, then rinse seeds thoroughly before sowing to remove germination inhibitors in the flesh. Sow in a prepared seedbed or deep containers left outdoors to experience natural winter cold, which substitutes for manual stratification. Swedish Whitebeam is exceptionally adaptable and tolerates coastal winds, compacted urban soils, and exposed hillsides better than most ornamental trees. Move seedlings to their permanent site by the second year, choosing a location with full sun and good drainage where the tree can develop its distinctive white-backed foliage.

common_name: Sweet Calabash (Sweet Granadilla, Hard-Shell Passion Fruit)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or seedlings in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; sweet calabash is a Caribbean and northern South American passionflower that produces round, hard-shelled, brownish-yellow fruits with intensely sweet, aromatic, orange-yellow juice — considered by many Caribbean islanders to be the best-flavored of all wild passionfruits, far sweeter than common purple passionfruit.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide very strong trellis or arbor support. Passiflora maliformis (sweet calabash or sweet granadilla) is a passionflower native to the Caribbean islands and northern South America that produces one of the sweetest and most intensely aromatic of all passionfruits. The fruits are rounded to slightly apple-shaped, roughly 2–3 inches across, with a hard, woody, yellow-brown to dark-brown shell when ripe (much harder than purple or yellow passionfruit shells), protecting an extremely sweet, aromatic, orange-yellow pulp with a flavor that combines passion fruit, apricot, and guava with a honeyed sweetness rarely found in cultivated passionfruits. The hard shell makes it less susceptible to insect damage than thin-shelled species, and the fruits can be stored for weeks at room temperature. To eat, crack the hard shell and scoop out the aromatic pulp with seeds; the juice is excellent mixed with water as a tropical drink. Sweet calabash is prized in Caribbean home gardens and is occasionally grown in tropical botanical gardens worldwide; it remains very little known in commercial cultivation despite its outstanding fruit quality. The attractive, divided leaves and intricate blue-and-white flowers are typical of the genus. In zone 10–12, the vine is vigorous and productive in full sun.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring before buds swell.
directions: Sweet cherries require 700–1100 chill hours and are among the least self-fertile of the stone fruits — always plant at least two compatible varieties, choosing cultivars from the same incompatibility group (or self-fertile types such as Stella and Lapins). They prefer well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and dislike wet feet, which promotes root rot and crown rot. Protect ripening fruit with bird netting. Harvest when fruit is deeply colored, fully sweet, and the stem parts cleanly from the spur.

plant_note: Thrives in cool tropical highland conditions at 60–75°F; not suited to hot, humid lowland tropics where flavor and sugar content diminish — plant at elevation where temperatures are mild.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun with wire or trellis support; sweet granadilla is widely considered the sweetest and most delicately flavored of all passion fruits, with a brittle hard shell that rattles when ripe and a translucent sweet-gelatinous interior pulp eaten with a spoon — the dominant commercial species in Colombia, Peru, and Venezuela. It differs from P. flavicarpa in preferring cool highland conditions (3,000–8,000 feet elevation in the tropics, or mild Mediterranean climates); excessive heat reduces sugar content significantly. Harvest when the shell becomes brittle and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped. A single established vine on a strong trellis can yield 100 or more fruits per season.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free areas or grow in a container to overwinter indoors.
directions: Sweet lime yields mild, low-acid fruit prized in South Asia and the Mediterranean for fresh juice. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, protecting it from any frost, or keep it in a large pot to shelter indoors in cold climates. Feed with a citrus fertilizer through the growing season and water deeply but infrequently. Harvest when the rind turns pale yellow-green and the fruit yields slightly to pressure.

subcategory: tropical Southeast Asian cauliflorous fruit tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; sweet rambai (Baccaurea dulcis) is a small tropical fruit tree from the lowland forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula, producing clusters of small, round, yellowish to orange-red, sweet, jelly-fleshed berries — cauliflorous, forming on the trunk and branches — the sweetest of the Baccaurea fruit species, with mild, sweet, pleasant flavor; dioecious (male and female plants needed for fruiting).
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; plant at least one male and one female tree for fruiting — Baccaurea dulcis is dioecious. Baccaurea dulcis (sweet rambai or jentik-jentik) is a small tropical fruit tree from the humid lowland forests of Borneo and the Malay Peninsula — one of the sweetest and most pleasant of the Baccaurea fruit species (the species name 'dulcis' means sweet in Latin). The tree is a compact size compared to other Baccaurea relatives, making it somewhat more suitable for home tropical gardens. Like other Baccaurea species, the fruits are cauliflorous — forming in pendant clusters directly on the trunk and main branches in the distinctive pattern shared with cacao, jackfruit, and related tropical trees. The small (1/2-inch), round to oval fruits ripen to yellowish to orange-red with thin skin and translucent, white, jelly-like flesh; the flavor is genuinely sweet and mild, with less of the tartness characteristic of other rambai relatives (B. motleyana). The tree is dioecious, requiring both male and female plants for fruit production. Sweet rambai is largely unknown in cultivation outside its native Borneo and Malaysian range; a rare collectors' fruit tree for dedicated tropical fruit enthusiasts in zone 11–12.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Sweetheart is self-fertile and does not require a pollinizer, though yields improve with a compatible sweet cherry nearby.
directions: Plant in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; protect ripening fruit from birds with netting and avoid low, frost-prone planting sites. Sweetheart is a Canadian-bred sweet cherry from the Summerland research station in British Columbia, valued for being self-fertile — unlike Bing and many other sweet cherries, it sets a reliable crop without a separate pollinizer tree, making it a practical choice where space allows for only one cherry tree. It ripens notably late in the sweet cherry season, extending fresh harvest well after earlier cultivars like Bing and Rainier have finished, with medium-large, bright red, firm, sweet fruit of good flavor. The tree is vigorous and productive, and its self-fertility combined with late ripening has made it a popular choice for home orchards and small commercial plantings alike. Provide consistent moisture during fruit development to avoid cracking, especially if rain falls as fruit nears full ripeness.

common_name: Sylvester Date Palm (Silver Date Palm, Wild Date Palm)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring when soil is warm (70°F+); Sylvester Date Palm establishes best in warm soil. Purchase the largest container size affordable — palms cannot branch to compensate for a frozen or damaged growing tip, so a wider, established trunk is more cold-resilient in zone 8b. Space 15–20 feet from structures. Plant with the root ball slightly above grade in clay soils to prevent crown rot.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil — clay, sand, alkaline, or loam — Sylvester Date Palm is broadly adaptable and extremely drought-tolerant once established; avoid waterlogged soils. Phoenix sylvestris (Wild Date Palm or Silver Date Palm) is native to Pakistan, India, and Sri Lanka, where it is heavily tapped for the sweet sap used to produce date palm jaggery, a prized molasses-like sweetener throughout South Asia. In Gulf Coast zone 9 landscapes it is one of the most dramatic and widely-planted feather palms, prized for its striking silvery blue-green fronds — significantly more silver-blue than the commercial Date Palm (P. dactylifera) — and its distinctive diamond-patterned trunk that becomes increasingly textured and photogenic with age. Unlike P. dactylifera, Sylvester Date Palm tolerates more cold (zone 8b, to about 20–22°F with brief exposure), adapts to the high humidity and rainfall of the Gulf South, and resists the root and crown rots that plague commercial date palms in wet climates. The palm produces clusters of small, yellow to orange-red date-like fruits that ripen in fall and are edible fresh or used for making jaggery syrup. An outstanding statement palm for large residential properties and commercial streetscapes in zone 9, frequently planted in staggered triple groups for maximum visual impact.

common_name: Szukis American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Selected Native Persimmon Cultivar)
plant_note: Plant nursery-grown grafted trees in late winter or early spring; Szukis is self-fertile and produces without a cross-pollinator, though crop size may improve with a second American persimmon nearby. Plant in a permanent location — persimmons develop a deep taproot that makes transplanting difficult after establishment. In zone 9, Szukis ripens in September–October. American persimmons are astringent until fully ripe — do not harvest until the fruit is extremely soft (almost jelly-like) or until after a hard frost — premature consumption produces an intensely astringent, mouth-puckering effect from the tannins in underripe fruit.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained soil in full sun or partial shade; American persimmons tolerate poor, dry, acidic soils that challenge most fruit trees. Allow fruit to ripen fully and become very soft before harvesting. Szukis is a selected cultivar of the American Persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) — a native North American tree with a natural range from Connecticut to Florida and west to Nebraska and Kansas, making it one of the most widely distributed native fruit trees in eastern North America. The American persimmon was an important food for Indigenous peoples and early European settlers, who ate the ripe fruit fresh, dried, and fermented into persimmon beer; persimmon pudding remains a traditional Appalachian and Midwestern dessert made from the pulp of ripe fruit. Szukis was selected from the wild by Larry Szukis for its exceptional fruit size for an American persimmon — the fruits can reach 1.5–2.5 oz, substantially larger than typical wild American persimmon fruits. The flavor of fully-ripe American persimmon is dramatically different from the popular Asian persimmons (Diospyros kaki) — more complex, intensely sweet, winey, and honey-like, with a jammy quality that many consider superior to the blander sweetness of the kaki types. As a native plant, Szukis/American persimmon provides exceptional wildlife value: the fruits are eaten by deer, raccoons, foxes, and over 40 bird species.

plant_note: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting and move to the garden after frost danger passes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Tainung No. 1' is a bisexual (hermaphrodite) variety that sets fruit alone without a pollinator, and fruits very early — often within 7 months of germination under warm conditions.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting or sow directly in warm soil in full sun after frost; Tainung No. 1 ('TN1') is a bisexual F1 hybrid papaya developed by the Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute that has become the leading papaya variety in Taiwan and is widely grown throughout East and Southeast Asia for its combination of early bearing, excellent fruit quality, and bisexual flower type that allows single-plant fruiting. The compact trees (8–14 feet) begin fruiting at a very low trunk height (1–2 feet from the ground), allowing easy harvest and a shorter time from planting to first fruit than many papaya varieties. Fruits are medium-large (2–4 pounds), oblong-cylindrical, with moderately thick yellow-orange skin and deeply orange to salmon flesh with high sugar content (Brix 12–14°), excellent fragrance, and small seed cavity. Tainung No. 1 has reasonable tolerance of cooler subtropical conditions and is less sensitive to temperature fluctuations than some papaya varieties, making it a useful choice for zone 9 where temperatures occasionally drop in winter; the tree is killed by frost but seeds easily and can be replanted each year as a productive warm-season fruiting crop in frost-marginal climates.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in warm, moist conditions; transplant outdoors after soil warms to 65°F in a sheltered spot with afternoon shade.
directions: Start seeds in warm, moist potting mix at 75–80°F and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from cold wind and afternoon heat; tamarillos are frost-sensitive but also dislike sustained temperatures above 90°F, thriving best in cool subtropical climates such as coastal California, highland tropics, or mild maritime zone 10. The smooth-skinned red or yellow egg-shaped fruits ripen 18 months from seed and have a rich, complex flavor — tangy and tomato-like — excellent in salsa, chutneys, smoothies, and cooked dishes. Shallow roots make the tree drought-sensitive; water deeply but infrequently. Prune after harvest to maintain a manageable 6–8 foot height.

plant_note: Plant in spring after all frost danger has passed; tamarind tolerates coastal conditions and is surprisingly drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Tamarind is a massive, long-lived tropical tree that can take 6–8 years from seed or 3–5 years from grafted stock to begin bearing the distinctive hard-shelled brown pods. It is self-fertile and thrives in hot, dry conditions; it is one of the most drought-tolerant tropical fruit trees. The interior pulp surrounding the seeds is intensely sour when young and sweet-sour when fully ripe; pods are harvested when the shell is brittle and the pulp is sticky, fibrous, and deep brown. Trees require no significant pruning and are largely pest-free in the continental U.S.; remove only dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Tamopan Persimmon (Large Ringed Chinese Astringent Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Tamopan is astringent and must fully soften after harvest before eating, and its very large fruit benefits from thinning to reduce limb strain.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Tamopan is a distinctive Chinese persimmon cultivar known for its unusually large size and a visible constriction ring around the middle of the fruit that gives it a pumpkin- or acorn-like shape unlike most other persimmons. The deep orange fruit is strongly astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point the flesh becomes sweet, thick, and custard-like, well suited to fresh eating and baking. The tree is vigorous and productive, and because individual fruits can grow quite large and heavy, thinning excess fruit helps prevent broken branches in a heavy year.

common_name: Tanenashi Persimmon (Large Seedless Astringent Japanese Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile to average soil in full sun; Tanenashi is self-fertile and does not require a pollinator — its consistent seedlessness (which requires no pollination) is one of its primary commercial and home garden advantages.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tanenashi is the most widely planted Japanese persimmon cultivar in the American South — an astringent persimmon variety that produces large (3–4 inch diameter), round to slightly conical, bright orange-red fruits without seeds when grown without pollination. The seedless quality is one of Tanenashi's most important practical attributes — all commercial packing persimmons are seedless, and home-garden fresh eating quality improves without seeds in the soft, jellylike flesh. As an astringent persimmon, Tanenashi must be fully ripe (soft, completely yielding to pressure, like a water balloon) before eating or the tannins create an unpleasant mouth-puckering sensation; picking at the orange-red but still-firm stage and allowing to ripen at room temperature completes the conversion. The rich, sweet, pumpkin-like flavor of a fully ripe Tanenashi has no equivalent in temperate fruits. In zone 9, Tanenashi ripens in October through November and is one of the finest fall orchard fruits for the Gulf South — virtually pest-free, drought-tolerant once established, and producing heavily within 3–5 years of planting. The tree itself is ornamental: attractive dark-green summer foliage, spectacular orange-red fruit display in fall, and good fall foliage color before leaf drop.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free citrus regions.
directions: The tangelo is a juicy, loose-skinned cross between a mandarin and a grapefruit or pomelo, often bearing a distinctive neck at the stem. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil in a frost-protected location, and note that some cultivars set better crops with a pollinizer nearby. Water deeply and feed with citrus fertilizer during the growing season. Harvest when the fruit is fully colored and heavy with juice, typically from midwinter onward.

plant_note: Plant in spring in frost-free areas.
directions: A tangor is a mandarin-sweet orange hybrid, combining easy peeling with rich, full orange flavor. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil and protect it from frost, which readily damages leaves and fruit. Apply a balanced citrus feed in spring and summer and mulch to conserve soil moisture. Harvest when fully colored and sweet, and prune lightly after cropping to remove crossing or weak wood.

plant_note: Plant in spring in full sun in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 10–12; Taraw Palm is a tall, stately, single-trunk fan palm native to lowland forests, riverbanks, and coastal zones of the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea — one of the tallest and most impressive Livistona species — producing large drooping skirts of deeply divided fan leaves on a robust gray-brown trunk, with clusters of small, blue-black, edible fruits used locally in traditional food preparations.
directions: Plant Taraw Palm in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; water regularly during establishment and in dry seasons; young plants tolerate partial shade for the first few years; mature palms are self-cleaning (old fronds drop cleanly) and require no pruning. Livistona saribus is among the larger and more majestic members of the Livistona genus — the widespread Asian fan palm group represented in cultivation by the Chinese Fan Palm (L. chinensis) and Australian Fan Palm (L. australis). The Taraw Palm develops a single straight gray-brown trunk up to 40–80 feet tall, topped by a graceful crown of large, deeply divided fan leaves whose drooping tips give the crown a characteristic pendulous, elegant character. A fast grower by palm standards in good conditions, it is widely used as a landscape palm in Southeast Asian cities and is gaining favor in zone 10–12 tropical and subtropical gardens globally. In its native range, the leaves are traditionally harvested for weaving baskets, mats, and hats; the blue-black clustered fruits are eaten by local wildlife and occasionally by people as a minor food. An excellent large specimen palm for tropical gardens where a dramatic, fountain-crowned palm silhouette is desired.

plant_note: Plant dormant trees in early spring once the soil can be worked.
directions: Tasty Red is a narrow, columnar apple that produces sweet, bite-sized red fruit with a refreshing crunch while taking up very little space. Its upright growth habit makes it ideal for containers, patios, and small yards, and several can be planted close together. Set the tree in full sun with well-drained soil and water regularly during establishment. Plant a second apple variety nearby for cross-pollination and better yields. Minimal pruning is needed thanks to the naturally compact columnar form.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained soil; Temple is a tangor (mandarin-orange cross) that ripens mid-to-late winter and is somewhat more cold-sensitive than true sweet oranges, so it is best sited with wind protection in the cooler parts of its range.
directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with some wind protection, since Temple is more cold-sensitive than sweet oranges. First found growing in Jamaica and brought into Florida commerce in the early 1900s, it is classed as a tangor, a natural mandarin-orange hybrid, and produces a deep reddish-orange, easy-peeling fruit with an exceptionally rich, aromatic, sweet flavor that many consider superior to either parent type. It ripens January through March, later than most satsumas, giving a late splash of fresh citrus in the garden. Trees are moderately vigorous and benefit from regular citrus fertilizer and consistent moisture during fruit development.

plant_note: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; terebinth is extremely drought-tolerant once established and grows slowly but lives for centuries in the wild.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, calcareous to neutral, poor to moderately fertile soil; terebinth is an ancient Mediterranean tree whose small red fruits (similar to tiny pistachios) have been consumed since prehistoric times and are still eaten in Greece and Turkey, where they are roasted, ground into a coffee-like drink, used to flavor spirits, and pickled in brine. The tree also historically yielded the original terebinth resin (turpentine) used in ancient medicine and as a paint vehicle. Closely related to the pistachio (Pistacia vera) and sometimes used as a pistachio rootstock. Extremely drought-adapted, thriving on poor limestone hillsides where little else will grow. The autumn foliage turns brilliant red before leaf drop.

subcategory: Mediterranean wild fruit and spice tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or gravelly, limestone-derived soil in full sun; terebinth is an ancient Mediterranean deciduous shrub or small tree — the wild ancestor of the cultivated pistachio (P. vera) — producing small, olive-shaped berries that dry to a deep red-brown; widely used in Turkish cuisine as 'menengiç' for a traditional coffee-substitute beverage, and as a spice throughout the Middle East.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky or limestone-derived soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established — a true Mediterranean xerophyte. Pistacia terebinthus (terebinth or turpentine tree) is an ancient wild Mediterranean tree in the cashew family — the wild relative of the commercial pistachio (P. vera) — native to the dry hillsides, maquis, and garrigue scrublands of the Mediterranean basin from Portugal and Morocco east through Turkey and the Levant. The terebinth is one of the most historically significant trees of the ancient world: it appears in the Hebrew Bible (the 'elah' of the story of David and Goliath), in Greek mythology, and throughout classical Mediterranean literature. It produces small (1/4-inch), olive-shaped drupes that dry from red to dark brown-purple — the 'terebinth berries' or 'menengiç' used in Turkish cuisine as a traditional spice and, most distinctively, as a caffeine-free coffee substitute: roasted and ground terebinth berries are brewed exactly like coffee (menengiç kahvesi — terebinth coffee), producing a thick, rich, slightly bitter, nutty, resinous beverage beloved in southeastern Turkey and the Levant. The tree also produces a historical resin (Chian turpentine) used in medicine and varnishes in antiquity. As a garden plant, terebinth is an attractive, hardy, drought-tolerant Mediterranean small tree or large shrub with graceful pinnate leaves turning brilliant red-orange in autumn.

plant_note: Plant container stock or bare-root in spring in well-drained, rocky, caliche, or sandy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Texas persimmon is native to rocky limestone soils of central and south Texas and northern Mexico and is extremely drought-tolerant and heat-adapted.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky to sandy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; once established, Texas black persimmon requires little to no supplemental water. Diospyros texana (Texas black persimmon or Mexican persimmon) is a native small tree or large shrub of rocky Texas Hill Country limestone and the brushlands of south Texas and northern Mexico, producing small, 1-inch, round, jet-black fruits in July–September that taste intensely sweet — like dark plums or figs with a honey-like richness — and stain everything they touch with deep-purple-black juice (historically used as a fabric dye by Native Americans and early settlers). The tree is highly ornamental in addition to its fruit value: an attractive, multi-stemmed form with flaky, pale-gray bark that exfoliates to reveal silvery, cream, and pale-orange patches; small, glossy, semi-evergreen leaves; and outstanding fall-winter structural interest. It is adapted to full sun and extreme drought and alkaline soils where most fruit trees struggle. Wildlife (deer, wild turkey, quail, and many bird species) consume the fruits eagerly. Texas persimmon is dioecious (separate male and female trees needed for fruit); plant at least one male per 3–5 female trees.

plant_note: Plant fresh nuts in fall at 2-3 inches depth in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil; Texas black walnut grows in challenging, dry, rocky, alkaline limestone soils where eastern black walnut fails. Squirrels often cache and forget nuts, naturally regenerating the species.
directions: Plant in well-drained, rocky, chalky, or limestone-derived soil in full sun in central and south Texas; Texas black walnut is the small, drought-tolerant walnut native to the rocky limestone hills and creek drainages of central Texas, Oklahoma, and New Mexico. Unlike the towering eastern black walnut (J. nigra), this species stays at 20-30 feet with a spreading, multi-stemmed habit. The small nuts are round and dark-shelled with a proportionally small but edible, walnut-flavored kernel — historically gathered and cracked by Indigenous peoples and early settlers. The tree produces juglone in its roots and leaves like all walnuts, inhibiting the growth of some nearby plants, especially tomatoes, peppers, and certain other species. An excellent native tree for dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the Texas Hill Country and adjacent areas where eastern black walnut cannot thrive.

common_name: Texas Blue Giant Fig (Large Purple-Black Texas Fig)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; figs are self-fertile and need no pollinator. Texas Blue Giant produces very large fruit on vigorous growth, so give it plenty of room and rich soil for the best fruit size.
directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; figs benefit from consistent moisture during the fruiting season to size fruit well and avoid splitting. Texas Blue Giant is a large-fruited fig popular among Texas and Gulf South fig growers, producing sizeable, deep purple-black fruit with sweet, richly flavored strawberry-red flesh on a vigorous, spreading tree. Its large fruit size and dark, attractive skin color make it a favorite for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree is well adapted to regional heat and humidity, cropping over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to manage its vigorous size and remove any winter dieback, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system through summer heat and occasional winter cold snaps.

common_name: Texas Everbearing Fig (Texas Everbearing Brown Turkey)
plant_note: Plant container or rooted cuttings in spring after frost danger; Texas Everbearing is the most widely recommended fig for Texas and Gulf Coast gardens in zones 7b–10, bearing two crops — a breba (early summer) crop on old wood and a main crop (late summer through fall) on new wood — with adaptations for hot, humid Gulf Coast conditions that make it superior in performance to many imported fig varieties not selected for this climate.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; established Texas Everbearing figs are drought-tolerant and require minimal care; protect roots with 4–6 inches of mulch in zones 7–8 where temperatures occasionally drop below 15°F. Texas Everbearing is a fig variety specifically selected and propagated in Texas for its exceptional performance in the hot, humid climate of the Gulf Coast and Central Texas, where it is the most commonly grown and recommended home garden fig; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension has long listed it as a top variety for the region. The medium to large, pear-shaped fruits have brownish-purple to brown skin (similar to but distinct from standard Brown Turkey) with strawberry-pink to amber flesh; the flavor is rich, honeyed, and sweet with the characteristic caramel-fig quality characteristic of the best common-type figs. As an everbearing type, Texas Everbearing produces two crops: breba fruits on previous year's wood in early summer (June) followed by the main crop on current season's wood from late summer through frost (August–November); this extended fruiting season is a practical advantage over single-crop types for home garden production. Excellent fresh, dried, or preserved; very productive in Gulf Coast zone 8–10 conditions.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in dry to moist, rocky to sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas mulberry is the native mulberry of the dry Trans-Pecos region and Hill Country, extremely drought-tolerant and valuable for wildlife food in xeric landscapes.
directions: Plant container-grown trees or hardwood cuttings in spring in dry to moderately moist, rocky, sandy, or caliche soils in full sun to light shade; Texas mulberry once established is highly drought-tolerant and requires no supplemental irrigation in zone 7–10. Texas mulberry is a small native tree or large shrub (8–20 feet) of the dry Hill Country, Trans-Pecos, and Chihuahuan Desert of Texas and New Mexico, with smaller leaves and a more drought-tolerant constitution than any other native American mulberry; the sweet, dark purple to black mulberries ripen in late spring and are an extremely important food source for numerous bird species including cedar waxwings, mockingbirds, and orioles, as well as mammals from foxes to deer. Excellent as a water-conserving landscape tree for dry zone 7–10 gardens where conventional mulberries may struggle; the fruit is edible and excellent fresh or in pies and preserves.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in late winter or spring in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or caliche soil; this is a separate-sex species — both male and female trees are needed for fruit, though female trees can produce some fruit without pollination.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; Texas persimmon is a small native multi-trunked tree of the Texas Hill Country and Rio Grande Plains with distinctive smooth, peeling gray bark revealing white-green underbark (one of the most beautiful native bark patterns in the Southwest). The small round fruits ripen jet black in August–September and are intensely sweet when fully ripe, though the black pulp stains everything permanently — including lips, fingers, and clothing. They are eaten fresh, dried, or cooked into syrup and are an important food for coyotes, bears, gray foxes, and birds. The tree is extremely drought tolerant once established and requires alkaline, well-drained soil. Both male and female trees are needed for fruit production.

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost danger passes, or grow in a patio container in colder zones.
directions: Texas Pink is a pomegranate valued for its large rosy-pink blushed fruit and its ornamental, gnarled bonsai-like bark and bright orange-red flowers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, allowing plenty of room for the shrubby tree to develop. Once established, it is quite drought-tolerant and needs only occasional deep watering. In zones colder than 7, grow it in a patio container and move it to shelter over winter. Prune to a single trunk or multi-stemmed form and thin fruit to improve size.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, alkaline, limestone-derived or rocky soil in full sun; Texas pistache is native to canyon limestone and requires excellent drainage — it will not tolerate wet feet or heavy clay soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline, limestone-based or rocky soil in full sun; Texas pistache is a handsome small multi-trunked native tree of the limestone canyons of southwest Texas and northeast Mexico, prized for one of the most spectacular fall color displays of any native Texan woody plant — the compound leaves turning brilliant shades of orange, red, and scarlet before dropping. Small red fruits are eaten by birds and wildlife, and the tree is often suggested as a superior native alternative to the widely planted Chinese pistache (Pistacia chinensis). It is extremely drought tolerant once established and well suited to xeric landscapes, parking lot edges, and small residential lots in zones 7–10. Growth is slow to moderate, so purchase the largest container specimen available for faster landscape impact.

common_name: Thomas Black Walnut (Classic Thin-Shelled Named Black Walnut)
plant_note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from gardens and other juglone-sensitive plants; Thomas is grafted onto black walnut rootstock and grows into a very large shade tree over time.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from tomatoes, apples, and other plants sensitive to the juglone this species releases into the surrounding soil. One of the oldest named black walnut cultivars, Thomas was selected in Pennsylvania in the 1880s for producing an unusually high percentage of kernel relative to shell for a species notorious for its thick, hard shell, along with the bold, distinctively rich, earthy flavor prized in baking. The tree is vigorous, cold-hardy, and eventually becomes a massive shade tree, so it is best suited to a large property or orchard edge rather than a small home garden. Nuts drop in a thick, dark, staining husk in early fall that should be removed promptly, and the tree may take eight to ten years to begin bearing from a graft.

plant_note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Thomasville citrangequat is among the most cold-hardy edible citrus hybrids available, with mature wood tolerating temperatures down to near 0°F, making it plantable well outside the range of standard citrus in the Gulf South and Southeast.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; exceptionally cold-hardy for a fruiting citrus, tolerating hard freezes that would kill standard citrus outright, though a sheltered microclimate still improves fruit set and tree vigor. Thomasville citrangequat is a three-way citrus hybrid — a cross of citrange (trifoliate orange × sweet orange) with kumquat — developed by USDA citrus breeder Dr. Walter Swingle in Thomasville, Georgia in the early 20th century specifically to push the boundary of cold-hardy edible citrus northward out of Florida. The small, oval, orange-yellow fruits have an aromatic, tart-sweet, marmalade-quality flavor with edible skin in the kumquat tradition, best used for marmalade, candying, or juice rather than fresh peeling and eating. The tree also carries attractive small trifoliate-influenced leaves and light thorns, and its extreme hardiness has made it a mainstay of cold-hardy citrus hobbyist plantings from the Gulf Coast through the Southeast. A rewarding novelty citrus for growers pushing the cold edge of the citrus range, zone 7–10.

plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring; three-leaf sumac adapts to a very wide range of soils and climates across the western US and is one of the most versatile native shrubs for dry gardens, slopes, and erosion control. Extremely cold hardy to -20°F once established.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in any well-drained soil from rocky to clay; three-leaf sumac (Rhus trilobata) is a wide-ranging, cold-hardy western sumac producing small, sticky, red-orange berries used identically to lemonade berry — soaked in water to make a tart, refreshing beverage — and was one of the most important wild food and medicinal plants of western Native American tribes from the Great Plains to California. The flexible young branches were traditionally used for basket weaving by many indigenous peoples. Exceptional for erosion control on dry slopes, with beautiful orange-red fall color, excellent wildlife value, and extraordinary drought tolerance. Does not sucker aggressively. The common name 'skunkbush' refers to the strong, somewhat pungent smell of the crushed foliage.

plant_note: Plant two specimens (cross-pollination improves fruit set) in spring in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in zone 5–9; Three-leaf Akebia is a vigorous, twining climbing vine from China, Korea, and Japan — semi-evergreen in mild winters — producing fragrant vanilla-scented flowers in spring and remarkable sausage-shaped, purple to pale lavender fruits in autumn, with sweet edible white pulp surrounding black seeds, and occasionally used young shoots as a vegetable in East Asian cuisine.
directions: Plant Akebia trifoliata at the base of a sturdy trellis, pergola, or fence in partial to full sun; plant two or more seedlings of different genetic origin for cross-pollination and reliable fruiting; water regularly; harvest pods in autumn when they split open along the seam. Three-leaf Akebia is a fascinating edible ornamental vine producing unusual fruits that are rarely seen outside Japan and China but are gaining interest among adventurous Western growers. The pale purple to lavender sausage-shaped pods (3–5 inches long) split open in autumn to reveal sweet, translucent white pulp — the pulp is eaten fresh by scooping around the embedded seeds, which are not eaten. The flavor is mildly sweet, subtle, and aromatic — not intensely flavored but pleasantly unique. Beyond the fruit, young spring shoots are blanched and eaten as a vegetable (akebi no tsuru) in Japanese mountain cuisine. The intricate, three-leaflet foliage on twining stems is ornamentally attractive, and the small, dark purple flowers in spring are fragrant with a vanilla scent. A related species, Akebia quinata (Five-leaf Akebia), is very similar but with five leaflets and is widely grown ornamentally — both are vigorous and need substantial support.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; threeleaf akebia is slightly more vigorous than fiveleaf akebia (A. quinata) and produces larger fruits. Cross-pollinate with plants from different sources for best fruit set.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun in zones 5–9; threeleaf akebia is closely related to the more commonly grown fiveleaf akebia (A. quinata) but is distinguished by having only three leaflets per leaf (vs. five in A. quinata) and generally larger fruits — the sausage-shaped, blue-purple pods can reach 4–5 inches long in good specimens. The pale purple, vanilla-fragrant flowers in spring are striking and ornamental. The ripe fruits split open along one side to reveal white, jelly-like pulp surrounding black seeds — the pulp is eaten fresh, tasting sweet and somewhat like lychee, while the empty pods are used as a vegetable in Japan. A vigorous, somewhat twining vine that can be invasive in some regions; grow on a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence where its vigor can be managed by pruning. A productive edible vine for the partial shade garden in zones 5–9.

common_name: Tilton Apricot (California Canning Apricot, Late-Season Commercial Apricot)
plant_note: Plant bare-root in late winter in deep, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Tilton is self-fertile and a reliable heavy producer; it requires approximately 600–700 chill hours and is well-adapted to the San Joaquin Valley, the Pacific Northwest, and similar zones 6–9 climates; it blooms later than other apricots, making it somewhat more frost-resistant in regions with unreliable late-spring temperatures.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Tilton is self-fertile; thin to 3–5 inches after June drop; Tilton ripens mid-to-late season (July in California), about 2 weeks later than Blenheim, providing a fresh apricot harvest window after the main-season varieties finish; firm flesh holds quality after picking and is excellent for drying, canning, and jam. Tilton apricot is a California variety with origins in the San Joaquin Valley community of Tilton (now part of Hanford), from which it takes its name, and it was one of the primary commercial canning apricot varieties in California's Central Valley from the late 19th century through much of the 20th century alongside Blenheim. Where Blenheim is the benchmark for fresh-eating quality, Tilton became the commercial preference for processing — its firmer flesh holds structure better through the heat of canning and cooking than the softer, more aromatic Blenheim, producing intact apricot halves that maintain attractive color and firmness in the can. Tilton fruits are medium-sized, round to oval, pale orange to golden-orange with a slight reddish blush, with firm, moderately sweet, mildly tart flesh and a pleasant though not exceptional apricot flavor. The variety blooms somewhat later than Blenheim and Moorpark — an advantage in regions with late spring frost risk — and the firm flesh makes it better for shipping and home drying into dried apricots. A solid production variety for home orchards where a large canning crop is desired.

common_name: Toddy Fishtail Palm (Wine Palm, Jaggery Palm)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; toddy fishtail palm is an Indian and Sri Lankan multi-use palm grown for palm wine (toddy), jaggery sugar production, and as an ornamental with distinctive bipinnate (doubly compound) leaves with unique fish-tail-shaped leaflets — it is monocarpic, dying after it completes a single multi-year flowering cycle.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; note that Caryota urens is monocarpic and dies after completing its single flowering sequence. Caryota urens (toddy fishtail palm or wine palm) is a large, single-stemmed Indian and Sri Lankan palm remarkable for several unique characteristics: it is one of very few palms with bipinnate leaves (doubly compound — each leaf divided into segments, each segment then further divided into individual fishtail-shaped leaflets), giving it a dramatically different appearance from most other palms; and it is monocarpic — it flowers only once in its life, then dies. The flowering sequence begins at the top of the trunk and proceeds downward over several years (from the highest leaf axil to the lowest), with the entire tree dying when the last inflorescence at the base completes seed set — a spectacular but terminal process. The palm is the primary source of kithul jaggery in Sri Lanka (considered the finest quality palm sugar in Asia) and a major source of toddy (palm wine) in South India. The sap from tapped flower stalks is collected daily; fresh it is sweet and mildly fermenting; processed it produces kithul honey, jaggery, and vinegar. The seeds and unripe fruits contain oxalate crystals — do not eat raw. The palm is ornamentally outstanding — unique bipinnate fronds create an unmistakable tropical texture.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Trazels are hybrids between American hazelnut and the Turkish tree hazel, bred to grow as a single-trunked tree rather than a suckering shrub while carrying strong resistance to Eastern filbert blight, the fungal disease that devastates orchard plantings of European hazelnut through much of North America.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil, allowing 15-25 feet between trees for their eventual size. Trazels are named for their parentage — a cross between the native American hazelnut (Corylus americana) and the Turkish tree hazel (Corylus colurna) — combining the American parent's cold hardiness and blight resistance with the Turkish parent's strong single-trunk, tree-like growth habit, unlike the suckering thicket form typical of most hazelnuts. This tree form makes Trazels far easier to manage in an orchard row or as a landscape specimen than shrubby hazelnut types, and their resistance to Eastern filbert blight — a fungal canker disease that has devastated commercial plantings of European hazelnut (C. avellana) across much of the eastern and midwestern United States — makes them one of the more dependable hazelnut options outside the Pacific Northwest. Nuts are borne in husked clusters and ripen in late summer to early fall; because most Trazel seedlings show variable nut size and quality, growers select and propagate individual trees for improved nut characteristics. Plant two or more seedlings for best pollination, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and largely self-incompatible.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in zone 8–10; Tree Tomato (Tamarillo) is a fast-growing, small ornamental tree native to the Andean highlands of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, and Chile — bearing prolific clusters of egg-shaped, deep-red to orange-yellow, glossy, thin-skinned fruits with tangy-sweet, tomato-passionfruit-flavored flesh popular across Latin America, New Zealand, and increasingly in international markets.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Solanum betaceum grows fast but has brittle branches — provide wind protection and stake when young; water deeply and regularly and fertilize monthly for maximum fruiting; prune after fruiting to maintain shape and encourage new productive growth. Solanum betaceum (Tree Tomato or Tamarillo, syn. Cyphomandra betacea) is a fast-growing, soft-wooded, small tree in the Solanaceae (nightshade) family native to the semi-arid and sub-humid Andean highlands of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Colombia, and northern Chile at elevations of 5,000–10,000 feet. The tree produces prolific clusters of glossy, egg-shaped, thin-skinned fruits — deep red, orange, or yellow depending on cultivar — with tangy-sweet, intensely flavored flesh combining tomato, passion fruit, and tropical notes, surrounding a central core of dark-purple seeds. Tamarillos are extensively eaten fresh (the skin is typically removed), made into juice, jams, chutneys, salsas, and cooked sauces across Ecuador, Peru, Colombia, and especially New Zealand, where the industry was developed from Andean introductions in the mid-20th century. Trees fruit prolifically in 1–2 years from transplants, providing remarkable returns for a tree-fruit crop. The plants are susceptible to tobacco mosaic virus, cold below 28°F, and water stress — they perform best in cool, frost-light subtropical conditions (zone 8b–10) with consistent moisture. Named a 'new world food' candidate for its high vitamin C, antioxidant, and nutritional content.

plant_note: Plant in spring; exceptionally cold-hardy for a citrus relative.
directions: The hardy trifoliate orange is a deciduous citrus relative bearing small, aromatic, seedy fruit used for marmalade and flavoring. Remarkably cold-tolerant, it survives well below freezing and is widely used as a dwarfing rootstock for other citrus. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; its dense, fiercely thorny growth makes an effective barrier hedge. Harvest the downy yellow fruit in autumn, using the tart juice and rind rather than eating it fresh.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5), fertile loam in full sun; Tropic Beauty requires only 150 chill hours and ripens earlier than Florida Prince, making it a valuable option for hot Gulf Coast climates where the growing season is long but chill hours are limited.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile loam in full sun; Tropic Beauty is a University of Florida-developed low-chill peach cultivar requiring only 150 chill hours — making it adapted to the warmest portions of zone 8b, all of zone 9, and zone 10 in protected locations. Tropic Beauty produces medium to large fruits with yellow flesh and good sweet peach flavor, ripening in late April to May in zone 9 — one of the earliest-ripening yellow-flesh peaches available and a particularly valuable trait in Gulf South climates where spring arrives early and summer heat quickly limits the harvest window. The tree has an upright, vigorous growth habit and adapts well to the pruning required to maintain an open center structure for air circulation in humid climates. Like all peaches in the Gulf South, Tropic Beauty requires preventive fungicide management (copper at dormancy, follow-up fungicides through bloom) for disease control in the humid climate. Self-fertile — produces without a pollinizer, though cross-pollination with another low-chill variety improves yield. Thin fruit aggressively to 6 inches after June drop for maximum fruit size and quality; unthinned trees produce many small fruits that are commercially worthless and exhaust the tree.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter dormancy (January–February in zone 9); Tropic Snow requires only 200 chill hours — well-suited to zone 9a and reliable in zone 9b. Self-fertile. An early-season variety ripening in April in zone 9 — among the earliest white-flesh peaches for the Gulf Coast.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tropic Snow is a low-chill white-flesh peach developed by the University of Florida's fruit research program, requiring approximately 200 chill hours. It is one of the earliest-ripening white peaches in zone 9, typically producing fruit in mid-April — sometimes the first peach of the season in Gulf Coast gardens. The medium-sized fruits have creamy white flesh with a red-blushed, white skin, a freestone pit, and a distinctive sweet, low-acid flavor with floral, honeyed notes characteristic of the finest white peaches. Flavor quality is superior to most yellow-flesh peaches when eaten at perfect ripeness. The trees are productive and self-fertile. White peaches were historically preferred by many southern peach connoisseurs over the higher-acid yellow types, and Tropic Snow is one of the best white varieties for low-chill climates. Prune to an open-center form in late winter; thin fruitlets to 6 inches apart in early spring for full-sized fruit. Protect blooms from late cold snaps.

common_name: Tropic Sweet Apple (Large Sweet Low-Chill Gulf South Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tropic Sweet requires approximately 150–200 chill hours and is best cross-pollinated with Dorsett Golden or Anna for maximum fruit set.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Tropic Sweet is a University of Florida low-chill apple introduction specifically developed for production in zone 8–10 gardens where chill hours are insufficient for standard northern apple cultivars. With only 150–200 chill hours required, Tropic Sweet is adapted to the winter climate of zone 9a where standard apple varieties cannot break dormancy properly. The fruits are large, round, yellow with a light blush, and distinguished by outstanding sweetness with very low acid content — a flavor profile that differs from the balanced sweet-tart quality of northern apples and appeals strongly to those who prefer sweet, mild apples. Tropic Sweet ripens in June in zone 9 — the June ripening window is well ahead of most summer fruit production and provides fresh orchard fruit at a time when few other tree fruits are ready. Like all low-chill apples, Tropic Sweet performs best when cross-pollinated with another low-chill cultivar such as Dorsett Golden or Anna. Proper dormant pruning (in late January–February) and fire blight management (preventive copper sprays during bloom) are the primary cultural practices for Gulf South apple production. The outstanding sweetness and large size make Tropic Sweet one of the finest fresh-eating apple choices for Gulf South gardeners willing to manage fire blight, which is the primary disease challenge in the humid Gulf South climate.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant February–April. Guava is frost-sensitive — temperatures below 27°F can kill established trees, though mature trees may resprout from the roots after moderate freezes. In zone 9a plant in the warmest, most frost-protected microclimate (south or west wall exposure with thermal mass). Trees typically begin bearing fruit within 2–3 years of planting and produce two crops per year in zone 9 — spring and fall. Psidium guajava is highly invasive in Hawaii and other Pacific island ecosystems; confirm planting is appropriate for your location.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — guava is adaptable to a wide range of soils and is drought tolerant once established; Tropical White is a white-fleshed guava cultivar producing medium-sized, round to oval fruits with pale green to yellow skin at full ripeness and cream-white to pale yellow flesh with a mild, sweet, aromatic flavor and a texture ranging from smooth to granular depending on harvest timing. The flavor of white-fleshed guava is milder and less intensely tropical than pink-fleshed varieties — appealing to consumers who find the strong, musky, distinctive guava flavor of red-fleshed types overpowering. Common guava (Psidium guajava) is one of the most productive and easily grown tropical fruit trees in zone 9 — adapting to a wide range of soils, producing fruit year-round, and growing rapidly from a young tree to full bearing size. The highly aromatic fruit — which contains more vitamin C per gram than citrus — is consumed fresh, in juice, paste (guava paste is a classic Latin American confection), jam, and desserts across the tropical world. In zone 9 the combination of easy culture, fast production, and highly aromatic fruit that cannot be found in commercial distribution makes guava one of the most rewarding tropical fruit trees available.

plant_note: Grown from a pup or potted plant, not seed; move outdoors after frost.
directions: Truly Tiny is a miniature Dwarf Cavendish banana that stays compact enough for a container or a bright corner indoors while still producing edible fruit. Its bold tropical leaves make it an ornamental standout, and its small size suits patios and sunrooms. Grow from a potted plant or pup in full sun with rich, moisture-retentive soil, feeding heavily during active growth. Keep the soil consistently moist since bananas are thirsty, shelter it from wind, and move it indoors before frost.

plant_note: Propagate by detaching and allowing pads to callus for 2 weeks before planting in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tulip prickly pear requires excellent drainage and establishes in almost any well-drained, dry condition. Handle with extreme care using thick gloves and tongs — the tiny glochids (hairlike spines) embed in skin and are difficult to remove.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; tulip prickly pear is one of the most widely distributed native cacti of the American Southwest and southern Plains, producing large, satiny, lemon-yellow flowers with orange centers in May and June that are among the most beautiful cactus flowers — 2–3 inches across, silky-textured, and glowing in full sun. The pads are flat, blue-green, and covered with clusters of spines. The fruits (tunas) ripen from green to deep red-purple in late summer and fall and are edible fresh or cooked into juice, jelly, candy, and syrup, having a sweet, watermelon-like flavor. The young pads (nopales) are also edible as a vegetable when the spines are removed. This species is one of the most cold-hardy prickly pears, surviving to zone 4 in well-drained conditions. It naturalizes across the Southwest and Texas and is an important wildlife plant — the fruit feeds desert tortoises, coyotes, javelinas, and birds. CAUTION: the tiny glochid spines embed invisibly in skin and cause intense, persistent irritation.

common_name: Tung Oil Tree (China Wood Oil Tree)
plant_note: Plant seeds in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist soil in full sun; tung oil tree was extensively planted in the Gulf South from the 1930s–1950s as a commercial oil crop. It tolerates mild frosts but is killed back to the ground by hard freezes in zone 8, often resprouting from roots.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; tung oil tree is a Chinese tree cultivated throughout zone 8–11 for its seeds, which yield tung oil — a fast-drying, water-resistant drying oil used extensively in paints, varnishes, wood preservatives, and wood finishing products. The spring flower display is spectacular — large clusters of white flowers with red or pink veining cover the bare branches before leaf emergence, followed by bold, large, heart-shaped leaves. The golf-ball-sized fruits contain 3–7 seeds with 50–60% oil content. The entire plant is poisonous if consumed — the seeds, leaves, and oil are toxic. The Gulf South has abandoned remnant tung orchards from a failed commercial industry of the mid-20th century. Now a naturalized, occasionally invasive ornamental/landscape tree notable for its spring flower show. Caution: all plant parts are toxic.

plant_note: Direct sow nuts in fall for spring germination after cold stratification; or cold-stratify nuts for 90-120 days in the refrigerator and sow in early spring. Turkish hazel is one of the best hazelnut trees for challenging urban conditions.
directions: Plant in well-drained, alkaline to neutral, even dry or compacted soil in full sun; Turkish hazel is the most drought-tolerant and urban-adaptable of all hazelnuts, renowned in the horticultural trade as one of the few large nut trees that tolerates dry, alkaline soils, compacted city conditions, and air pollution — a remarkable feat for any tree. It is used as a rootstock for grafting cultivated filbert and hazelnut varieties, and the straight species produces small edible nuts enclosed in deeply fringed husks. The distinctive corky, deeply ridged bark and broadly pyramidal form make it an ornamental specimen tree even when not in nut. Long-lived and very low-maintenance; used extensively in European forestry and urban planting programs.

common_name: UFBest Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in December-January while dormant; UFBest is a University of Florida IFAS release bred alongside UFSun and UFGold for an extremely low chill requirement, letting it fruit reliably through the warm winters of central and south Florida. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, siting trees away from low frost pockets since bloom can begin in December during mild winters. UFBest is one of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill peach releases, developed to give growers south of the traditional Gulf Coast peach belt a dependable home-orchard option despite winters too warm for standard varieties. Fruit is medium to large, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with good sugar and a bright red blush, ripening in mid-to-late April. Because such a low chill requirement makes bloom erratic and extended in unusually warm years, watch closely through late winter and be ready to cover young trees if a hard freeze threatens; otherwise care follows standard peach practice — thin fruit to about 6 inches apart and prune annually to an open, low vase shape to keep the tree productive and easy to harvest.

common_name: UFSun Peach (University of Florida Ultra-Low-Chill Freestone Peach)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in December-January while dormant; UFSun was released by the University of Florida IFAS stone fruit breeding program with a chill requirement of only about 100 hours, letting it fruit reliably in central and even south Florida where standard 'Gulf' series peaches (about 400 hours) can bloom erratically. Self-fertile, no pollinizer required.
