directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, choosing a site without a low-lying frost pocket since bloom can begin as early as December in warm winters. UFSun is one of the University of Florida's ultra-low-chill releases, bred to extend backyard and commercial peach production into areas of central and south Florida too warm for even the Texas 'Gulf' series. Fruit is medium-sized, yellow-fleshed, and freestone with a mild, sweet flavor and an attractive red blush, ripening in April, well ahead of most other peach varieties. Because bloom happens so early, protect trees from a late hard freeze with row cover if a cold snap threatens, and thin fruit to about 6 inches apart once set to improve size. Prune annually to an open-center vase shape after harvest to keep the canopy low and to renew the one-year-old wood that peaches fruit on.

plant_note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Unryu is grown primarily as an ornamental specimen for its dramatically twisted, contorted branch structure, which is especially striking in winter when leafless.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Unryu, meaning 'dragon's claw' in Japanese, is an ornamental white mulberry selection grown chiefly for its strikingly twisted, corkscrew-contorted branches, a dramatic sculptural feature that is most visible and prized in winter after leaf drop, and which also makes the cut branches valued by florists and flower arrangers. It produces small, sweet, mild-flavored white-to-pinkish mulberries in season, a secondary bonus to its main ornamental appeal. Because the twisted branch character can be lost in overly vigorous growth, avoid heavy nitrogen fertilization, and prune minimally, removing only dead or crossing wood, to preserve the natural contorted form. Like other mulberries, ripe fruit drops and stains, so site it away from paved areas.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ussurian pear is the most cold-hardy of all pear species and is widely used as a rootstock and breeding parent for ultra-cold-hardy hybrid pears in Canada and northern US.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Ussurian pear tolerates temperatures to -40°F and is the hardiest pear species available, making it the only viable pear for zones 2–3 where European pears cannot survive. Pyrus ussuriensis is a large, ornamental, extremely cold-hardy pear species from northeastern China and Siberia; it bears masses of white flowers in early spring before the leaves, followed in fall by small (1–2 inch), round, green to yellow-green, gritty-fleshed fruits with a rough texture that are best cooked or used for preserves rather than fresh eating. Its primary agricultural value is as a rootstock for grafted pear varieties and as a breeding parent for cold-hardy pear cultivars (e.g., 'Ure', 'Rescue', 'David', 'Nova') developed by Canadian and university breeders for the northern Great Plains. The glossy, dark-green leaves turn brilliant red in fall, making it an outstanding ornamental even where fruit quality is secondary.

plant_note: Plant container-grown shrubs or bare-root plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Utah serviceberry is the most drought-tolerant of the native serviceberries and is excellent for arid western landscapes and wildlife gardens.
directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, lean, rocky, or sandy soil in full sun to light shade; Utah serviceberry thrives in dry, rocky, alkaline soils of the West and Great Basin where other serviceberries would fail. Amelanchier utahensis is a native shrub of dry foothills, rocky slopes, and canyon walls from the Great Basin west, producing white spring flowers, small (1/3 inch) dark-blue berries with a sweet, mild, blueberry-like flavor in early summer (ripe very early, often by late May-June), and outstanding fall color in shades of orange and red. The berries are an extremely important wildlife food — essentially every frugivorous bird and mammal in the arid West relies on serviceberries during the brief ripening window. Extremely drought- and cold-hardy, this is the recommended serviceberry for xeric and high-altitude western gardens. Use for wildlife plantings, erosion control, and native landscaping.

plant_note: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; uvaia prefers subtropical to tropical conditions and can tolerate brief light frosts once established — suited to zone 9b-12 in the US.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soil; uvaia (Eugenia pyriformis) is a beautiful Brazilian Myrtaceae tree closely related to Surinam cherry and pitanga, producing pear-shaped to round yellow fruits about 1 inch in diameter with a juicy, aromatic, sweet-acidic flesh — the flavor is often described as a complex blend of passion fruit, citrus, and Eugenia aromatics with a pleasant acidity that makes the fruit excellent fresh, as juice, in ice cream, and as jams. The tree has attractive bronze-red new growth and small white flowers. Increasingly popular among Brazilian native fruit enthusiasts and tropical fruit collectors in south Florida and Hawaii; one of the finest of the genus Eugenia for flavor. Fruits appear in clusters along the branches and trunk.

plant_note: Plant container citrus in spring after cold risk passes; in zone 9 plant February–April. Valencia oranges require 3–5 years from grafted transplant to first significant crop. Site in the warmest, most frost-protected location available — south or southeast exposure near a masonry wall is ideal in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil (pH 6.0–7.0) in full sun in the warmest available location; Valencia is the world's most important juice orange and the benchmark orange of Florida's commercial citrus industry. The medium-large, thin-skinned, deep-orange fruits mature in March–June — uniquely late for citrus, which is why Valencia becomes the dominant fresh-market and juice orange in late spring when all other oranges have finished. The juice is abundant, sweet-tart, and intensely flavored. Valencia is known for re-greening: mature ripe fruit turns orange during cool weather, then re-greens as temperatures warm in spring — this does not affect juice quality but can confuse growers expecting a uniformly orange skin. In zone 9, Valencia is one of the most cold-tolerant sweet oranges and often survives temperatures to 25°F with minimal damage; below 20°F the tree may be severely damaged. Feed with citrus fertilizer (including zinc, iron, and manganese) three times per year and maintain a 3–4 inch citrus mulch ring. Excellent fresh or for juice.

common_name: Variegated Pink Lemon (Pink Eureka Lemon, Eureka Variegated Pink)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Variegated Pink Lemon performs best in full sun but is slightly more shade-tolerant than standard lemon trees; the variegated foliage is attractive enough for use as a decorative container specimen or landscape accent.
directions: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Variegated Pink Lemon (sold as 'Pink Eureka Lemon' or 'Eureka Variegated Pink') is a striking sports mutation of the standard Eureka lemon, valued both as a productive lemon and as a highly ornamental landscape or container specimen. The foliage is distinctively variegated in green and cream-white patterns that remain attractive year-round; the unripe fruits are dramatically striped in green and yellow (somewhat like a watermelon in miniature), and the flesh is pale pink when cut — a surprise and visual delight that makes this lemon memorable and photogenic. As the fruit ripens to full yellow, the pink-flesh color fades but remains just slightly pink in fully ripe fruit; the flavor is standard Eureka lemon — tart, aromatic, excellent for culinary use in anything requiring fresh lemon juice, zest, or slices. Production is good but somewhat lighter than standard Eureka. An outstanding choice for container culture, ornamental edible gardens, and any setting where visual interest in the plant matters as much as production.

common_name: Velvet Apple (Mabolo, Butter Fruit, Kamagong Fruit Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in full sun to partial shade with well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Velvet Apple is frost-sensitive and suited to zone 10-11 outdoor planting. In zone 9, container culture is practical for young trees. Trees are dioecious — plant male and female trees for fruit production. Fruits have a peculiar strong cheese-like or onion-like odor when just picked that dissipates as the flesh ripens fully; the mature flesh itself has a sweet, mild, mango-banana flavor. Considered a luxury fruit in Filipino markets.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — Velvet Apple grows most vigorously in full sun but tolerates and often benefits from afternoon shade protection in the intense heat of zone 9-10 summers. Diospyros blancoi is an evergreen fruit tree from the Philippines in the family Ebenaceae (the ebony and persimmon family), producing one of the most striking and unusual fruits in the tropical fruit world. The ripe fruits are perfectly round (3–4 inches in diameter), covered in a dense coat of fine reddish-brown to coppery velvet-soft hairs — like an incredibly large, round, red-brown cherry with velvet skin — from which the common name 'Velvet Apple' derives. Beneath the velvety skin is a firm, creamy-white to pink flesh with a sweet, mild flavor combining banana, cream, and mango notes and a dry, slightly astringent texture similar to some persimmons. The fruits have a striking, pungent odor when freshly harvested that many people find unpleasant (sometimes compared to ripe cheese or onion), but this odor dissipates with ventilation and does not affect the pleasant flavor of the flesh. In the Philippines, the tree is doubly valued: for its edible fruit and for its heartwood (called 'kamagong' — Philippine ebony), one of the hardest and heaviest woods in Southeast Asia, used for fine furniture and tool handles. The tree is also an ornamental specimen with glossy, dark-green foliage.

plant_note: Plant scarified seeds in spring (soak in boiling water and cool overnight before planting) in well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep soil in full sun; velvet mesquite grows naturally in desert grasslands, dry washes, and desert scrub of southern Arizona and Sonora, Mexico.
directions: Plant scarified seeds in spring in well-drained, dry to average, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep, well-aerated soil in full sun; velvet mesquite is the dominant mesquite of Arizona desert grasslands and saguaro cactus country, nearly identical to honey mesquite (P. glandulosa) but more densely hairy (velutinous) on the leaves and pods, tolerating the extreme heat and seasonal drought of the Sonoran Desert. The long, flat, tan seed pods mature in late summer and are very high in sugar and protein — edible by humans (ground into mesquite flour), consumed by coyotes, javelinas, deer, and dozens of bird species. The fragrant, cream-colored flower spikes in spring attract swarms of native bees. Deep taproots (up to 60 feet) access groundwater far below the surface. An important nitrogen-fixing tree that improves soil fertility. The aromatic wood produces some of the finest barbecue smoke in the world — prized for smoked meats throughout the Southwest.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Verte de Bordeaux is a productive, compact-to-medium fig tree well-suited to zone 9 conditions. It produces two crops in zone 9: a breba crop on old wood in June–July and a main crop on new wood in August–September. Prune lightly after harvest to maintain size and encourage productive new wood.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil — figs produce best in lean conditions and can become overly vegetative in rich, heavily fertilized soil; Verte de Bordeaux is a French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of southwestern France, producing small to medium, pear-shaped fruits with green to greenish-yellow skin that remains green even when fully ripe — a distinctive appearance that surprises consumers expecting a ripe fig to be darker. The deep burgundy-red interior flesh has an intensely rich, wine-like, complex sweetness that fig connoisseurs often rate among the finest flavors in the Ficus carica species. The petite size (1–2 inches) and striking green skin with deeply colored interior make it a specialty market favorite. In zone 9 Verte de Bordeaux produces consistently and handles the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers well. The green skin can be confusing to novice growers who may pick the fruit too early — harvest when the neck of the fig bends and the fruit softens.

common_name: Violette de Bordeaux Fig (Negronne Fig, Petite Negri Fig)
plant_note: Plant in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Violette de Bordeaux is a small-statured fig tree (6–8 feet) highly suited to container growing and small urban gardens. It produces predominantly on the main crop (August–October in zone 9) with a modest Breba crop in June.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Violette de Bordeaux (called Negronne in California and known as Petite Negri in some American nurseries) is a small-statured French heirloom fig from the Bordeaux region of France — one of the most beloved fig varieties among connoisseurs because of its extraordinary flavor. The small (1.5–2 inch), deep purple-violet to nearly black berries have blood-red interior flesh with a rich, complex, intense sweetness with strawberry-raspberry undertones — a flavor profile significantly deeper and more complex than larger, milder figs. The tree's compact size (6–8 feet tall and wide) makes it an ideal container specimen for patios, balconies, and small urban gardens where a standard fig would overwhelm the space. Violette de Bordeaux is the go-to container fig recommended by specialty nurseries. The skin is quite thin and fruits bruise easily, limiting its commercial shipping potential but making it perfect for eating fresh off the tree. In zone 9, it fruits reliably August–October and can be moved into protected areas during cold snaps in zone 9a.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Violette de Sollies is primarily a fall-ripening fig; in zone 9 the main crop ripens September–October, later than most other varieties. The late ripening extends the fresh fig season into fall. It produces minimal breba fruit and is primarily valued for its exceptional main crop quality.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Violette de Sollies has Protected Designation of Origin (AOP) status as the primary fig of Sollies-Pont commune in Var, Provence — the most commercially important fig production area in France. It accounts for approximately 80% of French commercial fig production and is the fig you encounter in French supermarkets and on French cheese boards. The large, round to pear-shaped fruits have dark violet to nearly black skin and deep red to garnet flesh with an exceptionally creamy, melt-in-the-mouth texture and rich, complex sweetness. The PDO designation reflects the specific microclimate of the Var region and the care taken to produce the variety at optimal quality. Violette de Sollies is a fall-ripening variety, producing its main crop in September–October in zone 9 — later than most other figs and extending the fresh fig season into autumn. The exceptional flavor quality and French culinary prestige make it a premium choice for zone 9 gardens where the warm fall provides ideal ripening conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; wampee is sensitive to cold and is best protected from any frost. It is smaller and more compact than most tropical fruit trees, reaching 10–20 feet, and can be grown in large containers in cooler climates and moved indoors in winter.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-protected conditions; wampee (wampi) is a Chinese subtropical fruit tree in the citrus family (Rutaceae) producing large drooping clusters of small, round, yellowish-white to golden fruits about the size of a large grape, with a thin, slightly oily skin and aromatic, translucent flesh that ranges from sweet to pleasantly acid-sweet, with a distinctive, complex, resinous-floral fragrance from essential oils in the skin. The flavor profile has notes of citrus, lychee, and a slight bitterness that makes it uniquely refreshing. Native to South China and widely grown in southern China, Vietnam, and Thailand, it has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and is a significant regional fruit crop in Guangdong. The fruits are eaten fresh, made into preserves and wine, and the essential oil from the rind is used in Chinese medicine and as a fragrance. It grows well in the humid subtropics of zones 9–11 and is more compact and manageable than many tropical fruit trees.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; Wani or Binjai mango is a Borneo and Sumatra native Mangifera species producing large, pale-green to whitish-green, very heavy fruits with sweet-tart, somewhat turpentine-flavored white to pale-yellow flesh — one of the most important traditional fruit trees of Malaysian Borneo.
directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, deep soil in full sun; requires consistent rainfall or irrigation during fruit development. Mangifera caesia (wani mango or binjai) is a large Mangifera species native to the humid lowland rainforests of Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula — one of the most important traditional fruit trees of Sarawak and Sabah (Malaysian Borneo), where it is planted around villages and sometimes bears enormous quantities of fruits. The fruits are remarkable: large (4–6 inches long), elongated-oblong to kidney-shaped, pale green to yellowish-white when ripe — larger on average than common mangoes — with white to pale-yellow flesh. The flavor is more distinctly turpentine-acidic than common mango, with a sweetness that varies considerably by seedling; selected clones can be mild and pleasant. The flesh is rather fibrous and the skin is not eaten. In Sarawak, wani fruits are sold fresh in markets and eaten as a fresh fruit, in rujak (spicy fruit salads), and processed into pickles. The bark and young leaves have traditional medicinal uses in Malaysian herbal medicine. Wani requires a genuinely tropical, hot, humid, low-frost-risk climate and is suitable only for zone 11–12 in the continental United States (extreme South Florida, Hawaii). A collectors' fruit tree for the most dedicated tropical fruit enthusiast.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile loam in full sun; plant two different pear cultivars for cross-pollination (Hood, Kieffer, Ayers); Warren pear requires only moderate chill hours (600–800) and excels in zone 7–9.
directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile loam in full sun; Warren is an outstanding southern heirloom pear discovered in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, by T.O. Warren around 1960 — a chance seedling that produces buttery, very sweet, nearly grit-free fruit with the silky texture of a fine European dessert pear. This exceptional fruit quality, combined with good fire blight resistance (the most devastating pear disease in humid southern climates), has made Warren one of the most highly regarded pear varieties for the Gulf South in recent decades. Most European pears are highly susceptible to fire blight (Erwinia amylovora), the bacterial disease that kills branches and causes heavy losses in hot, humid climates — Warren's relative resistance makes it a practical choice where standard European pears like Bartlett routinely fail. The medium-to-large, greenish-yellow fruits ripen in August in zone 9 and require off-tree ripening (store at room temperature after harvest) to reach their full, buttery sweetness. Plant with Hood or Kieffer for cross-pollination. Warren is not always easy to find at nurseries but is available from regional southern specialty nurseries and bare-root mail-order sources.

common_name: Water Apple (Watery Rose Apple, Bell Fruit)
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to periodically waterlogged, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; water apple is a Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree that tolerates wet soils and periodic flooding and produces crisp, bell-shaped, mildly sweet, extremely watery fruits — very distinct from the rose apple (Syzygium jambos) in fruit size, texture, and tree form.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; water apple tolerates periodic waterlogging and is well-suited to wet, low-lying areas. Syzygium aqueum (water apple or watery rose apple) is a Southeast Asian tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Indonesia that produces the most 'watery' of all the rose apple relatives — distinctive, bell-shaped to pear-shaped fruits (1.5–2 inches long) in white, pale pink, or red, with an extremely high water content (as the name suggests), a thin, glossy skin, crisp texture, and a very mild, barely-sweet, cucumber-like flavor. The fruit is refreshing rather than richly flavored — in tropical heat, the high water content makes water apple a thirst-quenching fruit eaten fresh as a hydrating snack, cut into slices and served with salt and chili, or made into a light agua fresca. The tree is notably tolerant of wet soils and periodic flooding compared to other Syzygium species — it grows naturally along stream banks and in seasonal swamps in its native habitat. It is distinctly different from the rose apple (S. jambos) in its smaller, lighter, more watery fruit, smaller tree size, and tolerance of wet conditions. Widely grown in home gardens throughout Southeast Asia and the Philippines.

plant_note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall in moist to wet, slightly acidic, deep alluvial soil in full sun. Water Hickory is adapted to the seasonally flooded bottomlands and swamp edges of the Gulf Coast and should be sited in low-lying areas that experience periodic flooding.
directions: Water Hickory is the hickory of the riverine swamps, bottomland hardwood forests, and floodplain edges of the southeastern coastal plain, native from Virginia to Florida and west to Illinois and Texas, where it grows alongside bald cypress, water tupelo, and swamp chestnut oak in the seasonally flooded alluvial soils of river terraces and floodplain edges. Its small, thin-shelled nuts are very bitter and not generally eaten by people, but they are an important food for wood ducks, squirrels, and wild turkeys in bottomland habitat — waterfowl consume large quantities of the nuts that fall into flooded bottomland pools in fall. Like all hickories, Water Hickory is slow-growing but extremely long-lived, with the deep taproot making transplanting nearly impossible after the first year of growth; direct-seed into the permanent planting site in fall for best results. Grow in moist to periodically flooded, rich, slightly acidic alluvial soil in full sun — the only hickory species reliably tolerant of extended seasonal flooding.

plant_note: Plant fresh seeds indoors in warm, moist, fertile soil; water rose apple is frost-tender and suited only for zones 10–12 outdoors or container culture in zone 9 brought indoors before frost. Plant in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; water rose apple is a tropical Asian Syzygium closely related to the wax jambu (S. samarangense) and produces similar bell-shaped, hollow fruits that are crunchy, mildly sweet, and extremely refreshing with a high water content — as the name suggests. The fruits range from white to pale pink and are eaten fresh as a cooling fruit, particularly popular in Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines where they are sold by street vendors. The tree is medium-sized and can be kept more compact than many tropical fruit trees. It bears fruit prolifically in the tropics and is beginning to appear in specialty tropical fruit nurseries in Florida. In zone 9a, grow in a large container and move indoors in winter; the fruits are produced year-round in frost-free conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, well-drained, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wax apple requires tropical to warm subtropical conditions (zones 10–12) to fruit reliably, though established trees may survive light frosts in zone 9 with damage — protect with frost cloth below 28°F.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wax apple thrives in tropical lowland conditions with high humidity and warm temperatures year-round. Syzygium samarangense (wax apple or Java apple) is a tropical fruit tree native to the Malay Peninsula and Andaman Islands, widely cultivated throughout Southeast Asia for its distinctive, pear-shaped to bell-shaped fruit with thin, waxy, translucent red to deep-red (or white, green, or pink depending on variety) skin, crispy, spongy, mildly sweet flesh, and a hollow, air-filled core with a rose-water scent — the fresh eating experience is unlike any other fruit, refreshingly crisp and very mildly sweet. The tree is evergreen with large, oval, glossy leaves and produces clusters of showy white to pale-pink, brush-like flowers (typical of the Myrtaceae family) followed by fruits in clusters. In the United States, wax apple cultivation is primarily limited to southern Florida and Hawaii; in zone 9, container culture or greenhouse growing is required. Named varieties include 'Jambu Air' (very dark red, sweet) and 'Pearl' (white-green, milder flavor).

plant_note: Plant in spring after frost risk passes; trees are damaged below 28°F but recover from brief cold if the trunk is protected.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; wax jambu tolerates brief flooding better than most tropical fruits and grows well near water features. Trees are self-fertile and fruit heavily along the branches — a single mature tree produces hundreds of bell-shaped, crisp, mildly sweet fruits per season. Fertilize three times per year with a balanced fertilizer; maintain a regular irrigation schedule during flowering and fruiting to prevent premature fruit drop. Harvest when fruits reach their full color (pink, red, or white depending on variety) and the waxy skin is firm and glossy; the spongy flesh has a very short shelf life and is best eaten within a day or two of picking.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 5.5–7.0) soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at maturity; Wells pairs well with Shenandoah or Susquehanna for cross-pollination — two cultivars are needed for reliable fruit production.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade when young, transitioning to full sun at fruiting age; Wells is a named pawpaw cultivar selected from a wild tree in Maryland — valued for its exceptionally large fruit size, excellent sweet flavor with classic banana-custard character, and good productivity. Wells produces some of the largest pawpaw fruits of any named cultivar, with individual fruits commonly weighing 6–12 ounces and occasionally larger — a significant attribute for a species where fruit size varies enormously between seedling selections. The large, heavy fruits have creamy-yellow flesh with minimal fiber, full banana-vanilla custard flavor, and a smooth texture that makes them outstanding for fresh eating and pawpaw-based recipes (ice cream, smoothies, bread, beer). Wells ripens mid-to-late season (late September to early October in zone 7–8, slightly earlier in zone 9) and requires cross-pollination from a different named cultivar such as Shenandoah or Susquehanna for maximum fruit set. The very short shelf life inherent to all pawpaw fruit (2–4 days at room temperature, up to 2 weeks refrigerated) limits commercial distribution but is not a problem for home gardeners harvesting on demand. Hand-pollination with a small brush during the brief flowering window significantly improves fruit set in home orchard settings where natural fly and beetle pollinators may be scarce.

subcategory: Tropical American food and timber tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in tropical or subtropical climates (zone 10–12) in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil; West Indian Locust is a large, long-lived tropical timber and food tree of the Caribbean and tropical Americas bearing hard, woody pods enclosing a dry, starchy, edible flour-like pulp with a distinctive sweet-sour flavor — highly nutritious and an important traditional food source — and producing the hard, amber-colored Jutahy copal resin used for varnishes and incense.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Hymenaea courbaril is drought tolerant and adapted to seasonal dry periods once established — water regularly in establishment years, then rely primarily on rainfall in tropical conditions. Hymenaea courbaril (West Indian Locust, Jatobá, or South American Locust) is a massive, long-lived, evergreen to semi-deciduous tree native to the Caribbean islands, Central America, and tropical South America from Mexico through the Amazon Basin, where it is one of the dominant canopy trees of seasonally dry and humid tropical forests. The tree produces large, hard, oblong, woody, dark-brown pods enclosing a dry, starchy, sweet-sour, floury pulp around the seeds — an important traditional food of indigenous peoples throughout its range, eaten directly, ground into flour for bread and porridge, or fermented into beverages. The pulp is nutritionally dense, rich in carbohydrates, protein, and calcium. Hymenaea courbaril is also one of the primary historical sources of Jutahy (or jatobá) copal resin, exuded from the trunk and roots as a hard amber-colored substance used in traditional varnishes, incense, and folk medicine for respiratory conditions and skin ailments. The extremely dense, hard, durable heartwood — among the hardest commercial timbers of the Americas — has been used for heavy construction, flooring, furniture, and tool handles for centuries. A very slow-growing, exceptionally long-lived tree requiring 10+ years to first fruit.

common_name: Western Schley Pecan (Widely Planted Southwestern Irrigated Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Western Schley is one of the most widely planted pecan cultivars in irrigated Southwestern orchards and needs a Type II pollinator such as Desirable or Elliott.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator variety, and provide consistent irrigation during nut fill, since this cultivar was developed for and performs best under the irrigated growing conditions of the arid Southwest. Often simply called Western in the trade, it produces a thin-shelled, well-filled nut with good flavor and has become one of the most heavily planted commercial pecan cultivars in New Mexico, Arizona, and West Texas orchards. It shows somewhat better tolerance of drier climates than many Southeastern-bred cultivars but still performs acceptably in the more humid Gulf South when given good air circulation and disease management.

common_name: White Adriatic Fig (Classic Italian Green-Skinned Honey-Flavored Jam Fig)
plant_note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Adriatic is a traditional Italian fig variety commercially cultivated in California and historically along the Gulf Coast — the thin skin and high sugar content that make it exceptional for fresh eating and jam also make it less suitable for humid climates where skin cracking and splitting can be a problem in rainy weather at ripening time.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Adriatic is a classic Italian fig cultivar grown commercially in California (it is the primary variety used for dried figs and fig paste in California production) and traditionally cultivated in Gulf South kitchen gardens for its exceptional fresh-eating quality. The medium-to-large fruits have green-to-yellow-green skin at full ripeness with amber to light strawberry-rose interior flesh of unusually high sweetness and a clean, honey-like flavor that ranks among the most highly regarded of all common fig varieties for fresh use. The flavor of fully ripe White Adriatic fresh from the tree — warm, sweet, delicate — is the benchmark against which many other figs are judged. The thin skin is part of what makes the fresh flavor exceptional; it also means ripe fruits are delicate and should be harvested promptly before rain or excess humidity causes splitting. White Adriatic is a vigorous, productive fig tree that typically begins bearing in its second year from planting and reaches full production by year 3–5. In Gulf South zone 9, the main crop ripens in late July through September; a breba (early) crop may develop on previous year's wood in June in years when the wood survives winter undamaged. Self-fertile, requiring no pollinators. Best eaten fresh within a day or two of harvest; or made into fig preserves and jam where the delicate honey flavor is retained.

plant_note: Root hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant container-grown trees in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. White Genoa is productive in zone 9 and grows well in the Gulf Coast climate. In zone 9 it produces a main crop in August–September and may have a light breba crop in June. The light-colored fruit skin does not camouflage ripeness well — monitor for softening as the harvest cue.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; White Genoa is an Italian light-skinned fig producing medium to large, greenish-yellow to pale gold fruits with amber to pink-tinged flesh and a mild, sweet, delicate flavor — one of the milder-flavored fig varieties, with a honey-sweet taste that lacks the robust winey complexity of dark-skinned varieties but is exceptionally appealing for fresh eating by people who find strong fig flavor too intense. The pale skin and light flesh of White Genoa produce an elegant presentation as fresh fruit or in light-colored preserves; it makes an outstanding pale-gold fig jam. It is widely grown in Australia and California where it performs well in Mediterranean-type climates and is considered one of the best light-skinned figs for fresh eating. In zone 9 and the Gulf Coast, White Genoa performs comparably to its reputation in warm Mediterranean climates. The light-colored fruits are prone to souring and cracking if they crack near the eye in wet weather; plant in locations with good air circulation.

plant_note: Set out after frost has passed; grow in a container to overwinter indoors outside frost-free zones.
directions: This evergreen tropical bears fragrant white-fleshed guavas with a flavor blending passion fruit and sweet melon, rich in vitamin C. Give it full sun and warm, humid conditions in rich, well-drained soil. Water regularly and feed with a balanced fertilizer during active growth for the heaviest fruiting. In climates that dip below freezing, grow it in a large pot and shelter it indoors during cold snaps.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. White Indian Guava is slightly more cold-hardy than pink-fleshed types, tolerating brief temperatures to about 26°F. In zone 9b–10 it fruits reliably year-round with peaks in summer and winter. Protect young trees from freezes below 28°F with frost cloth in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil — guavas tolerate a wide range of soil types including sandy and slightly alkaline soils; White Indian Guava is a white-to-cream-fleshed cultivar of common guava producing round to oval fruits with yellow skin when ripe, white to pale-cream flesh, and a sweeter, milder, less musky flavor than pink-fleshed guava varieties — the gentler flavor makes White Indian more approachable for people who find the distinctive strong fragrance of pink guava overpowering. The fruits have very few, soft seeds and a texture similar to a ripe pear. White-fleshed guavas are preferred in some Asian cuisines where they are eaten fresh with salt and chili or blended into drinks; they also make exceptional guava paste, jelly, and guava cheese when cooked. The trees are prolific once established and produce two or more crops annually in zone 9 and 10. Thin fruits to 4–6 inches apart to encourage larger fruit development.

plant_note: Plant seeds or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; white jaboticaba is frost-sensitive (damaged below 30°F) and requires a frost-free climate. Like all jaboticabas, it is slow-growing but long-lived, producing fruit on the trunk and main branches in a spectacular cauliflorous display.
directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic, fertile, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; white jaboticaba (also called yellow jaboticaba) is a Brazilian species of jaboticaba producing smaller fruits than the common jaboticaba (Plinia cauliflora), with the distinctive yellow-green to white skin of the ripe grape-like fruits distinguishing it from the deep purple-black common jaboticaba. Like all jaboticabas, the fruits grow caulifloresly — directly on the trunk and main branches of the tree rather than on the branch tips — creating the remarkable, otherworldly spectacle of hundreds of fruits clustering directly on the bark. The flavor of white jaboticaba is sweeter and less astringent than the more common purple types, with a delicate, pleasant muscat-like sweetness. Used for fresh eating, jams, and fruit wines. Rare and highly prized even in Brazil, much rarer outside its native range than the common jaboticaba. A prized collector's fruit for zone 9–11 gardens where unusual tropical fruits are cultivated.

common_name: White Marseille Fig (White Fig of Marseille)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Marseille is one of the oldest known fig cultivars in continuous cultivation, grown in European gardens for centuries and valued for its exceptionally sweet, honey-vanilla flavor and pale greenish-yellow skin ripening to creamy white.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; figs tolerate poor, dry soils better than most fruit trees and perform well in raised beds and large containers where root pruning encourages fruiting. White Marseille (also spelled 'Marseilles') is one of the oldest fig varieties in documented cultivation, known in European gardens since at least the 16th century and praised in early horticultural literature for its sweet, honey-like flavor; the medium to large, turbinate fruits have pale greenish-yellow to creamy-white skin and translucent white to pale amber interior flesh with a mild, delicate sweetness and gentle fig fragrance unlike the darker, richer intensity of dark figs. A common fig type that requires no pollinator; produces a reliable main crop (August–September) and often a smaller breba crop in early summer. Excellent container and espalier candidate; protect from frost below 15°F as a large container specimen that can be moved indoors.

common_name: White Marseilles Fig (Lattarula Italian Honey Fig, Sweet Golden-Fleshed Mediterranean Fig)
plant_note: Plant cuttings or nursery plants in spring in full sun; White Marseilles (also sold as 'Lattarula,' 'Italian Honey Fig,' and 'Blanche') produces fruits with very thin, tender, pale green to yellow-green skin that turns translucent at full ripeness. In zone 9, White Marseilles produces a breba (early) crop on old wood in June and a main crop on new wood in August–September. The thin, tender skin is a premium eating quality attribute but also a minor limitation for handling — harvest gently and consume quickly. Protect from frost below 18–20°F when young; established plants tolerate brief periods to 15°F.
directions: Plant nursery trees or rooted cuttings in full sun, well-drained soil; prune in late winter to shape. White Marseilles is one of the oldest documented fig varieties in European cultivation — referenced in 17th-century English garden literature and grown continuously in Mediterranean European gardens for centuries under various local names including Lattarula (Italian, meaning little bottle), Blanche (French), and White Marseilles (English, after the port city of Marseilles from which it was widely distributed). The fruit is medium to large, turbinate (pear-shaped) to round, with pale green to yellowish-green skin that becomes translucent amber-green at full ripeness — visually distinctive from the dark-skinned black and brown figs that are the most common fig types sold in American nurseries. The flesh is pale amber, extremely sweet and rich with a honey-like quality — the Lattarula name acknowledges the syrupy honey character of the ripe fruit — and the flavor is described as one of the finest among common fig varieties, with a complex sweetness that surpasses the simpler flavor of standard commercial brown turkey types. White Marseilles performs well in the warm, long growing seasons of zone 8–10, where the extended summer gives the main crop time to fully develop the honey concentration that distinguishes it.

plant_note: Plant in spring; extremely adaptable to poor soils.
directions: White mulberry is a fast-growing, exceptionally hardy tree bearing sweet, mild fruit and historically grown to feed silkworms. It tolerates drought, heat, and poor soils, thriving in full sun in a very wide range of conditions. Plant a fruiting cultivar rather than a fruitless ornamental, and site away from walks since the ripe fruit drops freely. Prune in winter to control size, and expect abundant crops within a few years.

plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring after frost danger; established trees tolerate brief dips to 22°F and suit zone 9 in sheltered microclimates.
directions: White sapote is a fast-growing, drought-tolerant evergreen tree that bears creamy, custard-flavored fruit often compared to a blend of peach and vanilla. Grafted cultivars (Vernon, Suebelle, Cuccio) fruit in 3–5 years and produce more reliably than seedlings, which can take a decade or more and show highly variable fruit quality. Trees are self-fertile, though two cultivars nearby increase set. Harvest when fruit is light green to yellowish, yields slightly to palm pressure, and separates easily from the stem; it ripens to soft within 3–5 days at room temperature and has very short shelf life.

plant_note: Sow freshly cleaned seeds in fall to undergo natural cold stratification; germination will occur the following spring after the chilling requirement is satisfied.
directions: Sow cleaned seeds directly into a nursery bed in autumn, covering lightly with 1/4 inch of soil; the distinctive white-felted leaves of seedlings make them easy to identify and separate from weeds in spring. Whitebeam is notably tolerant of shallow, alkaline, and chalky soils, making it one of the few ornamental fruiting trees suited to difficult chalk downland conditions. Grow in full sun for the most compact habit and the best berry production; established trees are drought-tolerant and require little supplemental watering except during prolonged dry spells. Allow five or more years from seed for the tree to reach flowering size and begin producing its scarlet autumn berries.

common_name: Wichita Pecan (Western High-Quality Pecan, Type II Commercial Pecan)
plant_note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter (January–February in zone 9) in deep, well-drained fertile soil; Wichita is a Type II pollinator (pistillate flowers receptive before pollen shed) — plant with a Type I cultivar such as Desirable, Cape Fear, or Western Schley for reliable cross-pollination and maximum yield; Wichita is best adapted to the drier conditions of western Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona where it is one of the two most important commercial varieties.
directions: Plant in deep (4+ feet), well-drained loam or sandy loam in full sun; Wichita is very productive and precocious, bearing significant crops at 5–6 years after planting, earlier than most other varieties; supplement with zinc foliar spray in spring to prevent zinc deficiency; in humid southeastern conditions, Wichita is susceptible to pecan scab and may require fungicide protection. Wichita pecan is one of the most widely planted commercial pecan varieties in the southwestern United States — the dominant variety in the major commercial pecan production areas of western Texas and New Mexico where supplemental irrigation is available and the dry summer climate limits scab disease pressure. The variety was released by the USDA in 1959 and quickly achieved widespread planting in the irrigated orchards of the West Texas Pecan Belt (around San Saba, San Angelo, and the Pecos River region) and New Mexico's Mesilla Valley, where the combination of hot days, cool nights, low humidity, and fertile alluvial soils creates ideal pecan-growing conditions. Wichita produces large to very large nuts (40–45 per pound) with excellent kernel percentage (58–62%) and an exceptional, rich buttery flavor — consistently rated among the highest-quality pecans for flavor by tasting panels. The kernels are plump and well-filled, bright golden-yellow in color, and have the mild, sweet, buttery flavor characteristic of high-quality western-grown pecans. Wichita is a Type II protogynous variety — meaning the pistillate (female) flowers become receptive before the pollen is shed — so it requires pairing with a Type I variety for reliable pollination. Early-bearing, high-quality, and widely available — Wichita is an excellent choice for zone 8–9 home orchard plantings where summer humidity is not extreme.

common_name: Wild Banana (Balbis Banana, Saging na Saba)
plant_note: Plant corm divisions (pups/suckers) in spring after last frost in full sun in rich, well-drained, moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Musa balbisiana is more cold-tolerant and drought-resistant than the common dessert banana and is one of the parents of most cultivated banana varieties.
directions: Plant suckers in deeply cultivated, rich, well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Musa balbisiana is more drought-tolerant than Musa acuminata and can tolerate brief dry spells once established, but performs best with regular moisture. Musa balbisiana (wild banana) is one of the two ancestral wild banana species from which virtually all cultivated banana and plantain varieties worldwide derive — along with Musa acuminata, it contributed the 'B' genome to many banana cultivars (Cavendish bananas are triploid AAA; plantains are typically AAB or ABB — the B refers to M. balbisiana's genetic contribution). The species produces seedy, starchy fruits that require cooking and are eaten in Asia, but its primary horticultural significance in Western gardens is as an ornamental banana and as an ancestor of cultivated types. It produces striking, large, paddle-shaped leaves on a 10-to-15-foot pseudostem — similar in appearance to the plantain but slightly smaller — and is among the most cold-hardy Musa species, surviving temperatures to 22–25°F when well-mulched, making it more reliable as a zone 8 ornamental landscape plant than most banana species. In zone 9, it grows as a near-permanent perennial specimen.

plant_note: Sow pits in fall at a depth of 1-2 inches to allow natural cold stratification over winter; seeds typically germinate reliably the following spring after the chilling requirement is met.
directions: Plant pits in fall in a sunny, well-drained spot with slightly acidic to neutral soil; this heat-tolerant native plum performs exceptionally well in the southeastern and south-central United States where many other plums fail. Thin seedlings to the strongest individual and allow it to develop naturally; wild goose plum will begin producing fruit within three to six years from a strong seedling and often spreads via root suckers to form a productive thicket. Cross-pollination with another wild plum or a compatible named variety will significantly improve fruit set and yields of the flavorful red-yellow fruits. This species is an important parent of many named southern plum varieties and provides early spring blooms that are a critical food source for native pollinators emerging from winter.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; wild medlar is a tough, drought-resistant shrub or small tree from the dry bushveld of southern and eastern Africa — producing round, yellow-brown, sweet-acid fruits eaten fresh, dried, or fermented into traditional beer across the region from South Africa to Kenya.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; exceptionally drought-tolerant once established — a true bushveld species. Vangueria infausta (wild medlar or African medlar) is a deciduous shrub or small tree from the dry savanna and bushveld regions of eastern and southern Africa — common across South Africa, Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique, and Kenya in seasonally dry habitats. The plant produces round to slightly flattened, 1–2 inch fruits that ripen from green to yellowish-brown, with soft, sweet-acid, mealy flesh and 4–5 large seeds. The flavor when fully ripe is pleasant — sweet with fruity-acid notes somewhat reminiscent of a tart apple-medlar — and the fruits are eaten fresh throughout rural sub-Saharan Africa, as well as dried into a concentrated fruit leather, fermented into traditional beer, or made into jams and sauces. The tree is highly drought-resistant, adapted to seasonally dry and poor soils of the African bushveld, making it a candidate for water-wise agroforestry in dry subtropical climates. The leaves, bark, and roots have extensive use in southern African traditional medicine. As an ornamental and food plant in zone 9–11 dry climates, wild medlar is a low-maintenance, wildlife-friendly tree that produces an edible crop under difficult conditions.

plant_note: Sow seeds immediately after harvest in fall; seeds require extended cold stratification and germination may be uneven, sometimes occurring over two seasons.
directions: Harvest fruits in late autumn and clean the seeds free of pulp before sowing 1/4 inch deep in a nursery bed; expect germination to be slow and potentially staggered over one to two springs, as wild service tree seeds are notoriously variable in their dormancy. Grow in well-drained loamy or clay soil in full sun to light shade, as this species thrives on the woodland edge in its native European habitat. The russet-brown berries are astringent when first ripe but become sweet and date-like after frost or bletting; harvest after the first hard frost for the best flavor. This rare woodland indicator species is long-lived and slow-growing, rewarding patience with outstanding maple-like autumn foliage and excellent value for pollinators and wildlife.

common_name: William's Pride Apple (Very Early Disease-Resistant Dark Red Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; William's Pride ripens in midsummer, among the very earliest apples of any kind, and fruit should be picked promptly since it softens quickly once ripe.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Also a product of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois disease-resistance breeding effort, William's Pride carries genetic immunity to apple scab along with resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and powdery mildew. The dark red, medium fruit ripens unusually early, often before the Fourth of July in warmer growing areas, with crisp, aromatic, mildly tart flesh. Because it softens fast after ripening, plan to harvest over a short window and use the fruit fresh rather than storing it.

common_name: Winesap Apple (Virginia Heirloom Keeper Apple, Self-Fertile Cider Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), deep fertile soil in full sun; Winesap is one of the few apple varieties that is reliably self-fruitful — it will produce a good crop without a cross-pollinator — though planting with a companion variety improves yields; requires approximately 800–1000 chill hours; best adapted to zones 5–8 where consistent winter cold accumulates.
directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Winesap is self-fruitful but yields improve with a cross-pollinator; harvest in October–November when deep red and firm; Winesap is an outstanding storage apple — sound fruits keep 3–6 months in a cool root cellar (32–40°F) while maintaining flavor and crispness far longer than most modern varieties. Winesap is one of the great classic American apple varieties, documented in Virginia since at least 1817 and possibly earlier, with origins that suggest development in New Jersey in the late 1700s before spread throughout the Shenandoah Valley and Appalachian apple-growing regions that became its primary production territory. The variety has a characteristic that made it enormously valuable before refrigeration: extraordinary keeping quality — Winesap apples stored in a cool root cellar or spring house could remain crisp, tart, and flavorful from harvest in October through March or April of the following year, making Winesap the standard winter apple of Appalachian farmsteads for generations. The fruits are medium-sized, deep red to almost black-red with yellow-green patches, with firm, dense, creamy-yellow flesh and a distinctive spicy-winy flavor with pronounced tartness and aromatic quality — unlike the mild sweetness of most modern commercial apples. Winesap is excellent for fresh eating (for those who appreciate tart, complex flavor), cider making, cooking, and drying. Its self-fruitfulness and cold-hardiness make it a practical single-tree orchard choice for zones 5–7.

common_name: Winged Passion Fruit (Fragrant Granadilla, Sweet Calabash, Red Passion Fruit)
plant_note: Plant container-grown transplants or rooted cuttings after last frost in spring, providing a strong trellis, fence, or arbor for the vigorous vines; Passiflora alata climbs by tendrils and can cover 15–20 feet of support within a single growing season. In zone 9–10, plants are perennial and develop a permanent woody framework; in zone 8b they may die to the ground in hard winters but often regenerate from roots. First fruit set typically occurs in the second season after planting.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and provide a sturdy trellis or fence; established plants fruit more reliably than recently transplanted ones, so patience through the first season is required. Passiflora alata (winged passion fruit) is a Brazilian passion fruit species that stands out from the more commonly grown P. edulis for two extraordinary qualities: its flowers and its fruit fragrance. The flowers are among the most beautiful of any Passiflora — large (3–4 inches across), deeply colored in crimson-red sepals with purple-and-white banded corona filaments, strongly fragrant, and produced in profusion from summer through fall. The aroma alone makes this an exceptional garden plant. The large, oval to oblong fruits (3–5 inches long) are distinctly fragrant when ripe, with a sweet, aromatic, tropical scent often described as more complex and perfumed than standard purple passion fruit (P. edulis); the golden-orange interior pulp is sweet and aromatic with a flavor that is mellower and less acidic than standard passion fruit, more approachable for fresh eating. The vine grows vigorously in zone 9–10, covering trellises and fences rapidly with glossy dark green leaves that have distinctly winged (four-angled) petioles — the characteristic that gives the species its common name. Pollination by large bees (especially carpenter bees) or hand-pollination improves fruit set. One of the most rewarding edible passion fruits for Gulf Coast gardens where it performs as a true perennial.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or bare-root specimens in spring; winged sumac spreads by root suckers and forms colonies — excellent for naturalizing large areas, slopes, and wildlife corridors but may spread more than desired in small gardens; control by mowing the perimeter.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil in spring; winged sumac (Rhus copallinum) is the most widely distributed sumac in the eastern United States, recognizable by the distinctive 'wing' of tissue along the central leaf stem, and producing brilliant, glossy clusters of small red berries that can be used to make sumac-ade (sumac lemonade) or dried and ground as a tart, tangy spice similar to Middle Eastern sumac (Rhus coriaria). The fall foliage color of winged sumac is among the most spectacular of any native shrub — blazing scarlet, orange, and crimson in October — making it a superb ornamental as well as a food plant and wildlife species. High-value wildlife shrub providing critical late-season fruit for birds (songbirds, turkeys, quail) and dense thicket cover.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; witherod is naturally a swamp and bog-edge shrub that tolerates consistently moist and occasionally wet soils better than most viburnums. It forms multi-stemmed clumps that can be selectively pruned to maintain size.
directions: Plant in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; witherod is a multi-season native shrub of wet woodland edges, swamp margins, and boggy thickets from Newfoundland to Florida, producing flat-topped clusters of small, white flowers in spring, followed by berries that go through an extraordinary color sequence as they ripen from early summer through fall: green, then pink-salmon, then red, then blue, and finally blue-black, with the multiple colors sometimes present simultaneously on a single cluster. The fully ripe blue-black berries are edible and have been eaten by Indigenous peoples and settlers — they have a sweet, raisin-like flavor, giving rise to the name 'wild raisin.' The fall foliage turns brilliant red to burgundy-red, often among the best fall color of any viburnum. Outstanding for moist sites, rain gardens, and naturalistic plantings where its tolerance of consistently wet soil is invaluable. The fruit is an important wildlife food for migrating birds in fall.

plant_note: Plant container or bare-root plants in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; witherod viburnum spreads by suckers to form dense thickets in moist conditions. Fruit production is better with multiple plants. Cuttings root readily in summer.
directions: Plant in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial shade to full sun; witherod viburnum is a native shrub of moist, acidic habitats across eastern North America — bog edges, streambanks, moist meadows, and pond margins from Newfoundland to Alabama. The berries pass through an extraordinary sequential progression of colors as they ripen — starting green, then turning through pink, blue-pink, and finally blue-black — so that clusters simultaneously display three or four colors. The fully ripe blue-black berries, called 'wild raisin,' are edible and sweet enough to eat raw or dried. Spectacular scarlet to burgundy fall foliage adds further season-long interest. Plant 2 or more plants of different clones for improved berry set. An exceptional wildlife shrub offering berries for over 30 bird species and the flowers feed numerous native bees and pollinators.

common_name: Wolf River Apple (Giant Wisconsin Heirloom Baking Apple)
plant_note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Wolf River produces unusually large fruit, so thin clusters to a single apple to prevent limb breakage and improve size further.
directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Originating near the Wolf River in Fremont, Wisconsin in the mid-1800s, this heirloom is famous chiefly for the sheer size of its fruit, with individual apples sometimes weighing over a pound and reportedly large enough that a single apple can fill a whole pie. The pale yellow-green skin blushed with red covers soft, mild, mellow flesh that is better suited to baking and sauce than fresh eating, since the flavor is pleasant but unremarkable on its own. The tree is extremely cold-hardy and vigorous, and its dramatic fruit size has kept it a curiosity and conversation piece in heirloom orchards for generations.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; wonderberry grows quickly in warm weather and produces abundantly. Only fully ripe, black berries should be eaten — cooked or raw (some people cook them for better flavor). Do not confuse with true huckleberries (Vaccinium) — these are Solanums.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; wonderberry (also sold as 'garden huckleberry') is a Solanum species grown for its small, jet-black berries — promoted by plant breeder Luther Burbank in the early 1900s as 'the most delicious berry in the world' but received with disappointment because fresh berries have a bland, somewhat bitter, black-nightshade flavor. Cooked into pies, jams, and sauces (with generous sugar) the flavor improves considerably and is quite pleasant. An annual bush producing enormous quantities of marble-sized black berries through the growing season, making it productive even if the flavor is underwhelming fresh. Distinguished from black nightshade (S. nigrum) by its larger plant size, larger berries, and slightly different botanical characteristics. Like all black-berried Solanum, only fully ripe (jet-black) berries should be eaten; all green parts and unripe berries are potentially toxic. An easy-to-grow novelty edible for those interested in unusual fruits.

plant_note: Plant after the last frost in a hot, sunny location; grow in a pot in cold zones.
directions: Pomegranate 'Wonderful' is the most popular home-garden variety, forming a large shrub or small tree that produces glossy red fruit filled with tangy-sweet, ruby-colored seeds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; it is self-fertile, so a single plant will fruit. Water regularly during establishment and while fruit is developing, then reduce as fruit ripens to prevent splitting. In climates colder than zone 8, grow it in a large container and move it to a protected spot over winter. Prune in late winter to shape and remove suckers, and harvest fruit in fall when it colors up and sounds metallic when tapped.

common_name: Wonderful Pomegranate (Classic Large Deep-Red Gulf South Pomegranate)
plant_note: Plant container or bare-root trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral to slightly alkaline (pH 5.5–7.5) soil in full sun; Wonderful is highly drought-tolerant once established — it is one of the most xeric fruit trees available and performs well on minimal irrigation in well-drained Gulf South soils.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to alkaline soil in full sun; Wonderful is the dominant commercial pomegranate variety of California and the standard against which all other pomegranate varieties are evaluated — producing very large (10–16 oz), round, deep-red to scarlet-red fruits with a thin, hard rind enclosing hundreds of ruby-red arils (the juicy, seed-containing sacs) with a complex tart-sweet, deeply flavored, astringent juice that defines the classic pomegranate flavor profile. The ornamental quality of pomegranate is exceptional — showy orange-red flowers (May–July in zone 9), then large, jewel-colored fruits that ripen to deep red-purple by October–November. Pomegranate is an ancient cultivated fruit (documented cultivation for 4,000+ years) that is one of the most drought-tolerant, heat-adapted, long-lived fruit trees available for Gulf South gardens. In zone 9, pomegranate thrives in the hot summers and mild winters — requiring only 150–200 chill hours — and established trees are remarkably long-lived, with historic specimens surviving 50–100+ years with minimal care. The ornamental summer flowers and autumn fruit make pomegranate as valuable as a landscape specimen tree as it is as a fruit producer. Self-fruitful (does not require a pollinator) and resistant to most pests and diseases common in Gulf South gardens. Harvest fruit when the exterior skin has fully colored and the fruit sounds hollow when tapped.

plant_note: Plant in spring in well-drained, even poor soils; wood apple is extremely drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Wood apple is a deciduous tree from South and Southeast Asia related to bael; it tolerates poor, rocky, alkaline soils and drought conditions that defeat most fruit trees, making it valuable for arid-zone agroforestry. The spherical, gray-shelled fruits have a hard woody shell that must be cracked open with a hammer; the dark, pungent, sticky flesh inside is strongly acidic and astringent and is usually mixed with sugar, coconut, and spices or blended into drinks rather than eaten plain. It is self-fertile and pollinated by insects; a single tree crops reliably after the first 5–7 years. Harvest when fallen fruit has fully ripened on the ground, or remove from the tree when the gray shell turns slightly yellowish and sounds hollow when struck.

plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile to average soil in zone 9–11; Wooly-leaf White Sapote is a close relative of the common White Sapote (Casimiroa edulis) native to highland Mexico and Guatemala, somewhat hardier to cold, with distinctively soft-woolly leaf undersides and the same smooth, green-skinned fruits with creamy, sweet, custardy white flesh — considered by some sapote growers to have superior flavor to the more common C. edulis.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile to average, neutral to slightly acidic soil; Casimiroa tetrameria tolerates brief light frost once established — provide winter irrigation in dry climates and mulch the root zone against cold. Casimiroa tetrameria (Wooly-leaf White Sapote or Matasano) is an evergreen to briefly deciduous tree native to the highlands of central Mexico and Guatemala, closely related to the more widely cultivated White Sapote (Casimiroa edulis) and distinguished by its distinctively velvety-woolly leaf undersides (the species name 'tetrameria' references the 4-merous flowers, while the woolly leaves differentiate it visually from C. edulis). The smooth, round to oval, 2–3 inch, green-skinned fruits contain creamy-white to cream-yellow, smooth, dense, rich, sweet flesh with a buttery-custard flavor and soft, satiny texture — eaten fresh, chilled, or pureed into smoothies and ice cream. Casimiroa tetrameria is considered by some tropical fruit enthusiasts to produce sweeter, richer fruit than the common white sapote, and the tree shows somewhat improved cold tolerance, performing well in zone 9 with good drainage. Graft onto Casimiroa edulis rootstock for earlier fruiting and better uniformity. The seeds contain mildly sedative alkaloids (casimiroin) and should not be eaten; wash hands after seed handling.

common_name: Yamhill Hazelnut (OSU EFB-Resistant Compact Hazelnut, Eastern-Adapted Filbert)
plant_note: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yamhill requires a cross-pollinating companion variety — plant with Jefferson, Wepster, or other EFB-resistant OSU releases; Yamhill is a 2009 OSU release specifically bred with Eastern Filbert Blight resistance, making it suitable for planting in eastern North America (from the Mid-Atlantic through the Midwest) where the standard Barcelona variety is killed by endemic EFB; it is also suitable for Pacific Northwest gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Yamhill requires a cross-pollinator (Jefferson, Wepster, or another EFB-resistant OSU variety); it is semi-compact and tends to produce a shorter, multi-stemmed bush form; nuts ripen September and fall naturally — harvest promptly from the ground; Yamhill typically begins bearing in year 3–4, earlier than some older varieties. Yamhill hazelnut is an Oregon State University variety released in 2009 from the OSU hazelnut breeding program — one of the first wave of EFB-resistant named hazelnut varieties developed specifically to allow hazelnut production throughout the eastern United States, where Eastern Filbert Blight (Anisogramma anomala) has prevented the success of standard European varieties including Barcelona. The OSU breeding program incorporated EFB resistance from the wild Turkish hazelnut (Corylus colurna) and other resistant species into productive, quality-fruited cultivars adapted to commercial and home hazelnut production. Yamhill's EFB resistance is now documented in variety trials throughout the mid-Atlantic and Midwestern states where EFB pressure is severe, showing dramatically better survival and production than Barcelona and other susceptible varieties. Yamhill tends to have a compact, bushy habit (shorter than Barcelona) and produces medium-sized, round nuts with good flavor and moderate kernel percentage — suitable for home fresh use, roasting, and processing. The combination of EFB resistance, compact habit, and earlier bearing age than older varieties makes Yamhill one of the most important hazelnut releases for home orchardists east of the Cascades.

common_name: Yates American Persimmon (Heavy-Bearing Virginia Persimmon, Wildlife Persimmon)
plant_note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in well-drained to average soil; Yates is a named female cultivar of Diospyros virginiana requiring a male pollinator or self-fertile Meader for reliable fruit production; particularly noted for heavy and consistent annual cropping once established, making it productive for wildlife food plots — deer, turkey, raccoons, opossums, and many songbirds are strongly attracted to the fallen fruits — as well as human harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; Yates American persimmon is drought-tolerant and productive in a wide range of conditions including poor and clay soils; harvest fruits from the ground after frost softening in October–November; the heavy fruit production of Yates makes it particularly attractive for wildlife plantings, permaculture food forests, and home orchards where a sustained fall crop of native fruit is valued. Yates is a named American persimmon cultivar known primarily for its exceptional productivity — consistently producing heavy crops of medium-sized fruits that ripen and drop over an extended period in October and November, making it valuable for both human harvest and as a wildlife-attracting planting throughout the mid-Atlantic and southeastern states. The extended fruit-drop period provides a sustained food source for deer, raccoons, foxes, opossums, and many songbirds rather than a brief burst of fruit, making Yates a popular choice in wildlife habitat plantings and food forest designs where the ecological role of the persimmon is as important as human harvest. For human use, the fruits are medium-sized (1–1.5 inch), deep orange to reddish-orange at maturity, with the intensely sweet, slightly grainy, honey-apricot flesh characteristic of excellent American persimmon after frost softening — a quality that exceeds most commercial fruit in richness when fully ripe. The trees are extremely adaptable across the range of Virginia and mid-Atlantic climates from zone 4 through 9.

plant_note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees spring through fall; Yates is a small-fruited 19th-century Southern heirloom apple valued for exceptional disease resistance, reliable annual bearing, and outstanding storage life, making it one of the most trouble-free apples for Deep South orchards.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun. Yates is a Georgia heirloom apple dating to the early-to-mid 1800s, prized by Southern orchardists for its outstanding resistance to fire blight, cedar-apple rust, and other diseases that plague apple growing in the humid South, along with dependable annual production even in years when other varieties bear poorly. The fruit is small, red-striped over yellow, with firm, crisp, tart-sweet flesh better suited to cider, preserves, and cooking than fresh eating, though many old-time growers enjoy it fresh once it mellows in storage. Its most celebrated trait is exceptional keeping quality — properly stored fruit holds firm and flavorful for months longer than most apples, historically making it a reliable source of fresh fruit through winter before refrigeration was common. Because it requires a moderate chill accumulation, it performs best in zone 6-8 and is marginal in the mildest parts of zone 9. Plant with another apple variety for cross-pollination, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good air circulation and disease prevention.

common_name: Yellow Dragon Fruit (Yellow Pitahaya, Cactus Pear Pitaya)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings in well-drained cactus mix in warm conditions; yellow pitahaya is self-fertile — a single plant will set fruit without hand pollination, unlike most other dragon fruit species.
directions: Root stem cuttings in gritty, well-drained cactus mix and grow on a strong post or trellis in full sun; yellow pitahaya is considered by many tasters to be the sweetest and most flavorful dragon fruit — its white interior flesh with tiny edible black seeds is measurably higher in sugar than red or white-flesh types, with a rich, tropical, almost honey-like sweetness and no bitterness. The fruits have yellow, spiny (not scaly) skin without the prominent pink 'scales' of other types. A significant advantage over other dragon fruits: yellow pitahaya is self-fertile and does not require hand pollination or a second plant to set abundant crops. Grows slower than Selenicereus undatus but the superior flavor makes it the most prized of the dragon fruit species.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; install a 30-mil rhizome barrier 24–36 inches deep before planting. Yellow groove bamboo is among the easiest and most rewarding hardy bamboos for edible shoot production in zones 5–9.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, contained within a deep rhizome barrier; yellow groove bamboo is distinguished by its attractive yellow sulcus — a distinctive yellow groove running along one side of each otherwise green culm — making it one of the more ornamental of the hardy Phyllostachys species. The spring shoots are edible, milder than many bamboo species, and are considered among the better-tasting shoots of temperate bamboos; harvest them while still below knee height before sheaths open. Culms reach 15–25 feet at maturity and tolerate temperatures to –10°F (–23°C), rivaling Phyllostachys bissetii for cold hardiness. Containment with a rhizome barrier is mandatory, as this running bamboo spreads vigorously by underground rhizomes.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed directly in fall in sandy, dry, acidic soil in full sun; as with most hawthorns, seeds require double dormancy and will germinate in their second spring — sow on-site whenever possible, as transplanting established plants is difficult.
directions: Plant in dry, sandy or rocky, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun along the Coastal Plain; yellow haw is a rare and botanically distinctive native hawthorn prized for its fall display of attractive yellow to greenish-yellow, pear-shaped to rounded haws that are notably sweeter and more palatable than those of most other hawthorns. Its spring flowers provide nectar for early native bees, and the fruit is consumed by mockingbirds, brown thrashers, and other birds that frequent the dry, sandy-woods habitats where this species thrives. It performs best in lean, well-drained soils and is intolerant of heavy clay, standing water, or overly enriched garden beds. Yellow haw's rarity in the wild makes cultivating it from locally sourced seed a valuable contribution to the conservation of Coastal Plain plant diversity.

common_name: Yellow Mangosteen (Mysore Gamboge, Yellow Gamboge, Egg Tree)
plant_note: Plant container-grown specimens in late spring in partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Garcinia xanthochymus is frost-sensitive but somewhat more cold-tolerant than the Purple Mangosteen (G. mangostana), surviving brief temperatures to 32°F if the soil drains well. In zone 9b-10, it can be tried as a large container or borderline landscape tree in sheltered spots. The yellow fruits ripen summer–fall; the sweet-sour flesh is eaten fresh or used in preserves and beverages. Trees are self-fertile — a single tree produces fruit.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in consistently moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Yellow Mangosteen grows best in the filtered light and moist, rich conditions of its native South Asian forest habitat and benefits from shade protection during establishment. Garcinia xanthochymus is an attractive, medium-sized, evergreen tree native to the Western Ghats and Mysore region of India and adjacent Burma (Myanmar) in the family Clusiaceae — the same family as the famous Purple Mangosteen (G. mangostana). The tree has a naturally elegant form: a pyramidal to columnar crown of large, glossy, deep-green, lance-shaped leaves that hang in graceful, slightly pendant arrays from the branches.
