This is a slow-growing, at-risk native species; growing your own reduces pressure on wild populations, but expect 4–6 years before roots are substantial enough to harvest. Harvest small portions of the golden rhizome in autumn of the fourth or fifth year, leaving the majority of the root system intact for continued growth.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; seeds may need cold stratification for best germination.
directions: Cold-stratify seeds in the refrigerator for 2–4 weeks before sowing to improve germination rates; sow 1/4 in deep in moisture-retentive, fertile soil. This old European cottage garden vegetable-herb was once widely grown for its young shoots (used like asparagus), leaves (used like spinach), and flower buds (used like broccoli). Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; plants are long-lived perennials once established and require little care. Harvest young shoots in spring, leaves throughout the season, and flower buds before they open; do not harvest heavily in the first year to allow the plant to establish.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Gorizia is an Italian heirloom rosemary cultivar prized for unusually large leaves and a milder, less resinous flavor than standard rosemary, along with strong, upright, vigorous growth.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil. Gorizia is an heirloom Italian rosemary cultivar, named for the city in northeastern Italy, valued for producing notably larger leaves than standard rosemary along with a milder, sweeter, less resinous flavor that many cooks find more versatile in the kitchen since it is less likely to overpower a dish. It grows into a large, vigorous, upright shrub, often taller and more substantial than typical rosemary cultivars, making it a good choice as a specimen shrub, informal hedge, or the backbone of a culinary herb bed where its size and productivity provide a generous, continuous harvest. Like other rosemary, it thrives in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil and struggles in heavy clay or soil that stays wet, so raised beds or berms are useful in areas with poor drainage. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than selections like Arp and performs best in zone 8-10, where it can remain evergreen and productive year-round. Prune after flowering to maintain shape and encourage bushy new growth for continued harvest.

plant_note: Transplant rooted runners after all frost danger has passed into a warm, moist location; propagation from stolons is far more reliable than seed.
directions: Propagate from stolons (creeping stems with nodes), which root readily in moist potting mix or at the edges of ponds; plant in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade, as gotu kola thrives in the margins of water bodies in its native tropical Asian habitat. In zones below 9, grow in containers that can be overwintered on a warm, bright windowsill with consistently moist soil. Harvest the small, fan-shaped leaves regularly once the plant is established; the fresh leaves are eaten in salads in Sri Lankan cuisine and used in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine as a cognitive tonic and wound-healing herb. Harvest leaf material by snipping stems without uprooting the plant to allow continued production.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade after last frost; in zones 9–11 plants can be grown outdoors as perennials. In colder climates grow as a container plant and bring indoors for winter.
directions: Plant rhizomes in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; grains of paradise is a West African ginger relative producing striking orchid-like pink to purple flowers at the base of the plant, followed by red oval fruits each containing 60–100 small brown seeds. The seeds have a complex, layered flavor combining warm pepper heat, floral cardamom, and citrus — used historically in European medieval cooking as a pepper substitute and today experiencing a culinary revival in craft brewing, gin production, and spice-forward cooking. In Ghana it is known as efom wisa and is used in traditional stews and spice blends. The ornamental foliage and unusual basal flowers make this a beautiful specimen plant for warm-climate shade gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; scarlet passionflower is frost-tender and must be grown in containers in zones 9 and below, or in frost-free zones 10–12.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in a frost-free location; in zone 9 and cooler, grow in large containers that can be moved indoors or to a greenhouse in winter. Passiflora vitifolia is a spectacular tropical passionflower vine native to Central and South America producing three-lobed, grape-like leaves (giving the species its name) and the showiest flowers in the genus — brilliant scarlet-red, 4-inch flowers with a striking corona of white-tipped, red filaments in the center; it blooms nearly continuously in tropical climates. The edible fruits are small, oblong, and yellow-green when ripe with a sweet-tart, grape-like flavor. It is one of the finest tropical passionflowers for greenhouse culture and large patio containers, with some of the most intensely colored and beautiful flowers in the genus; it requires warm temperatures year-round.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, in deeply dug, loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; burdock produces a very long taproot and requires deeply prepared, stone-free soil for straight, smooth roots suitable for culinary use — raised beds or deeply tilled rows at least 18 inches deep are recommended.
directions: Arctium lappa (great burdock, gobo) is a large, vigorous biennial native to temperate Asia and Europe, prized in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese cuisine for its long, slender, sweet, earthy taproot (gobo) which can reach 3 feet or more in depth; roots are best harvested in the first year of growth (before the plant flowers and sets seed in the second year) when they are most tender and flavorful. Direct-sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in early spring in deeply dug, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; the soil must be worked to at least 18 inches depth to allow the taproot to develop without forking — closely spaced rows of 6–8 inches produce slender, straight roots ideal for the table. In traditional Western herbalism, the root is used as a blood-purifying and liver-supportive tonic, and both the root and seed have a long history of use in treating skin conditions; the immature flower stalks can also be peeled and eaten like celery in spring of the second year. Do not allow plants to set seed and self-sow freely as burdock can become weedy in disturbed soils; harvest all roots before the plant flowers in the second year.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade to part shade; greater celandine self-sows prolifically and can naturalize aggressively — in some regions it is considered a weed or invasive species (check local regulations before planting). All parts are toxic if ingested; the orange-yellow latex sap causes skin irritation in some individuals.
directions: Plant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in shade to part shade; greater celandine is a European and western Asian member of the poppy family that has naturalized extensively in North America in disturbed, shaded situations — old walls, woodland edges, shaded garden corners, and waste ground — where it grows as a short-lived, freely self-sowing perennial producing pale-blue-gray, deeply lobed, softly hairy foliage and small, four-petaled, cheerful-yellow flowers from spring through summer in a nearly continuous display. When the stems or leaves are broken, they exude a bright, intense orange-yellow latex sap that has been used since antiquity to treat skin conditions, particularly warts (the name tetterwort refers to its historical use for skin eruptions). The sap is caustic and can irritate skin and is toxic if ingested. In the garden it is best used as a shade-tolerant naturalizing plant under trees and shrubs where its self-sowing habit creates a tapestry of bluish foliage and yellow flowers without requiring care. The double-flowered cultivar 'Flore Pleno' has attractive pompom-like flowers and is somewhat less freely self-sowing than the species.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; greater galangal is a large, robust ginger relative from coastal Southeast Asia that thrives in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens as a clumping perennial, reaching 4–8 feet with large, handsome, lance-shaped leaves. The white-striped-red rhizome is harvested year-round once established and used fresh in Thai curries, soups (tom kha), and marinades. It has a distinctive flavor quite different from culinary ginger — more piney, citrusy, medicinal, and peppery. Tender; damaged below 28°F.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; greater galangal is the essential culinary rhizome of Southeast Asian cooking — a large, handsome ginger-family plant native to coastal Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand) that provides the distinctive aromatic flavoring in Thai tom kha soup, Thai curry pastes, Indonesian rendang, Cambodian dishes, and numerous other Southeast Asian preparations where it is as fundamental an ingredient as garlic or lemongrass. The flavor of galangal rhizome is completely distinct from culinary ginger (Zingiber officinale): sharper, more medicinal and piney, with strong citrus-pepper notes and a resinous, camphor-like quality that is immediately recognizable in the cuisines that use it — the characteristic flavor that makes tom kha soup taste like tom kha and nothing else. The rhizome is distinguished visually from ginger by its dense, concentric-ringed, smooth skin with distinctive rose-pink to red-tinged growing points (unlike the warty tan skin of ginger). In the garden it is a very handsome, bold, tropical plant — a large, upright clump of robust stems with broad, dark-green, somewhat glossy, lance-shaped leaves reaching 4–8 feet, with attractive white-and-maroon-striped flowers occasionally in summer. In zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens it grows as a reliable perennial in sheltered positions with consistent moisture. Once established, rhizomes can be harvested year-round as needed by carefully digging at the clump margin.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights are reliably above 50°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm, moist seed-starting mix and thin seedlings to avoid crowding once they have two true leaves. Greek basil forms a naturally compact, globe-shaped mound with tiny, intensely aromatic leaves — no pinching required to maintain shape, though removing flower buds prolongs leaf harvest. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the petite habit makes it an excellent edging plant or container herb. Harvest by snipping small stem tips; the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of the small leaves delivers concentrated flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes into very well-drained, rocky or sandy soil.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep in well-drained, alkaline starting mix and keep warm at 68–72°F until germination; use gritty, mineral-rich mix to mimic its rocky Mediterranean mountain habitat. Plant out in the poorest, most well-drained spot in the garden — excess moisture and rich soil are the primary causes of failure. The silver-felted stems and leaves are harvested in full bloom in summer when the yellow flowers are visible; cut entire stems and hang in bundles to dry in a warm, airy space. Brew the whole dried stems as an herbal tea by simmering 5–10 minutes; the resulting infusion has a mild, honey-and-herb flavor and is traditionally consumed throughout Greece for immune support and as an everyday tonic.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Surface-sow seeds by pressing them into barely moist, well-drained seed-starting mix without covering, as they need light to germinate. Greek oregano (also called Italian or true oregano) is the pungent, white-flowered subspecies prized in Mediterranean cooking; it has far stronger flavor than common Origanum vulgare. Plant in lean, gritty, alkaline-leaning soil in full sun — excessive fertility dilutes the essential oils that give it its distinctive bite. Cut plants back by one-third after flowering each year to keep them compact; harvest just as buds begin to open for peak aroma.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow in early spring; in zone 9 plant September–November or January–March. Kaliteri grows best in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil — avoid rich, moist conditions that dilute essential oil content and reduce flavor intensity. The name 'Kaliteri' means 'the best' in Greek. Harvest before flowering for peak essential oil concentration; cut back by half after each flush to maintain compact habit.
directions: Plant in full sun in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil — avoid overwatering and rich fertilization; Greek Oregano Kaliteri is a select strain of true Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) chosen for exceptionally high essential oil content and intense, pungent flavor — the variety name means 'the best' in Greek. The aromatic, white-woolly leaves are strongly pungent with the hot, spicy, complex oregano fragrance that defines Mediterranean cooking from Greek salads to Neapolitan pizza to Spanish sofrito. Most oregano sold at grocery stores is mild and nearly flavorless compared to properly grown Greek oregano subsp. hirtum; Kaliteri represents a selected high-oil strain of an already superior subspecies. The small, compact mound of woolly gray-green leaves is attractive in the herb garden and the white summer flowers are valuable to bees. In zone 9 the plant grows vigorously in fall, winter, and spring but may become semi-dormant in peak summer heat. Soil drainage is more critical than fertility — soggy soil kills Greek oregano quickly.

plant_note: Root cuttings in spring or start from seed; Greek sage is more heat and drought tolerant than common sage (Salvia officinalis) and thrives in the alkaline, rocky, dry conditions of Mediterranean-type climates and zone 8–10 gardens; excellent in raised beds with sharp drainage.
directions: Root stem cuttings or sow seeds in well-drained, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Greek sage (Salvia fruticosa) is the wild sage of the eastern Mediterranean islands — the primary sage of Greek, Cypriot, and Turkish cuisine and the sage used in dried herb mixes sold as 'mountain tea' throughout Greece and the Middle East. The flavor is fuller, more complex, and somewhat milder than common garden sage, with distinctive 3-lobed leaves (giving it the name 'three-lobed sage') and lavender-pink flowers. More heat tolerant and longer-lived than common sage in hot-summer climates, making it an excellent culinary sage for zones 8–11 where Salvia officinalis tends to decline. Used fresh or dried in Greek lamb dishes, lemon-sage teas, and Mediterranean marinades.

plant_note: Plant tuberlets or bulbils 2-3 inches deep in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; pinellia multiplies rapidly by producing abundant bulbils along the leaf petioles and at the stem base and can spread aggressively in ideal conditions.
directions: Pinellia ternata is a small Asian aroid grown in traditional Chinese medicine gardens for its tubers (ban xia), which are used dried and processed as an anti-nausea and antiemetic herb — the raw tubers are toxic and cause intense oral irritation and burning; always handle with care. The plant produces trifoliate leaves on long petioles and a slender, hooded spathe in late spring, followed by a spike of tiny orange-red berries; it grows happily in the deep shade of trees where few other plants thrive and makes a useful, if spreading, shade groundcover in Asian herb gardens. In zone 9, it may behave as a cool-season annual.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface (seeds need light to germinate); in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Green shiso self-seeds prolifically — allow a few plants to go to seed at end of season and a permanent self-seeding colony will establish. In zone 9 the long warm season allows continuous leaf harvest from spring through early fall before the shorter days trigger flowering. Harvest young, large leaves frequently to stimulate continued growth; flowers and seeds are also edible and flavorful.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Green Perilla Shiso (the green-leaved form of Perilla frutescens var. crispa) is the standard Japanese culinary shiso used extensively in Japanese cuisine — the large, ruffled, bright green leaves with their distinctive complex fragrance combining mint, anise, cinnamon, and citrus are served with sashimi, used to wrap sushi, sliced into cold noodle dishes, tempura-battered and fried, and used as a garnish for countless Japanese preparations. Green shiso is the preferred type for fresh-leaf use, having a brighter, more delicate flavor than red shiso (which is primarily used for coloring and flavoring pickled umeboshi plums). The large, attractive, deeply ruffled leaves have an impressive appearance for a kitchen herb, growing to 4–5 inches across on robust plants that do not require much care. Green shiso thrives in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf South and tolerates some shade, making it practical for partially shaded kitchen herb gardens.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; green santolina has bright-green, more feathery foliage than gray santolina and is slightly more tolerant of moisture and humidity.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; green santolina requires the same excellent drainage and sunny, dry conditions as gray santolina but has slightly more tolerance of humidity and moisture. Santolina rosmarinifolia (syn. S. viridis) is a green-leaved counterpart to the familiar gray cotton lavender; it produces feathery, bright-green, rosemary-like foliage with a similar strong, herbal, camphor-like scent and equally bright-yellow button flowers in summer. The contrasting use of gray (S. chamaecyparissus) and green (S. rosmarinifolia) santolinas is a classic technique in traditional knot garden design; the green species' brighter, more vivid foliage makes it excellent as a companion to silver or purple-leaved plants in formal herb plantings. Shear after flowering to maintain shape.

common_name: Green Shiso (Japanese Culinary Herb for Sushi and Tempura)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; green shiso self-sows prolifically once established — allow some plants to go to seed at the end of the season to ensure a volunteer crop the following year; or collect seeds for replanting.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Shiso (Perilla frutescens var. viridis) is the standard culinary form of Japanese perilla — the bright green, deeply toothed, wrinkled leaves with their distinctive aroma (a complex combination of mint, cinnamon, anise, and citrus that is unique and difficult to compare to other herbs) are an essential ingredient in Japanese cuisine. The large leaves (2–4 inches) are used as wrappers for grilled meats and fish, shredded as a garnish for sashimi and sushi, fried as tempura, pickled (shiso pickles), and used in a range of salads and rice dishes throughout Japanese cooking. The aroma and flavor are entirely distinct from red shiso (var. crispa) used primarily for coloring umeboshi and other preserved items — green shiso has a brighter, more herbal, slightly minty quality versus the more intensely aromatic and slightly sharper red shiso. Green shiso grows vigorously in Gulf South summer heat, reaching 2–3 feet and self-sowing prolifically at the end of the season. The ornamental quality is significant — the large, bright-green, textured leaves with purple tinges on the undersides and pink flower spikes in late summer are decorative in both herb and ornamental gardens. Regular harvest of the growing tips delays bolting and maintains leafy production through summer.

plant_note: Seed needs light and benefits from chilling; press onto surface and do not bury.
directions: Also called Japanese basil or beefsteak plant, shiso carries a complex flavor blending cinnamon, mint, and clove with hints of cumin, and this mix offers both green and red-leaved plants. Surface-sow seed indoors as it needs light to sprout, and set out only after the soil has warmed. Heat- and drought-tolerant, it makes a handsome bedding plant that attracts pollinators. Pinch growing tips to encourage branching and harvest young leaves for wraps, pickles, and garnishes.

common_name: Grosso Lavandin (Commercial Fragrance Lavender, Provence Lavender)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage; Grosso is a lavandin hybrid (L. angustifolia × L. latifolia) that is sterile and must be propagated by cuttings; it grows larger and faster than English lavender with much longer flower spikes that are the dominant type grown for the commercial lavender oil industry in Provence, France.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained to dry soil; Grosso grows larger than English lavenders and needs 24–36 inches of space; shear spent flower stalks after bloom to prevent woody sprawling; in zones 8–10 where summer humidity is high, Grosso performs better than English lavender due to the L. latifolia parentage contributing some heat tolerance. Grosso is the world's dominant commercial lavender variety — it covers the rolling purple fields of the Provence and Drôme regions of France that define the iconic 'lavender landscape' image of southern France, and it is the primary source of lavender oil in the global fragrance and cosmetics industry. As a lavandin hybrid (a sterile cross between English lavender, L. angustifolia, and spike lavender, L. latifolia), Grosso inherits characteristics of both parents: the floral-sweet fragrance of English lavender combined with the higher camphor content, larger plant size, and greater heat tolerance of spike lavender. This combination makes the Grosso essential oil slightly different from pure English lavender oil — with a more complex, slightly camphor-accented fragrance that is valuable in perfumery but considered less pure for culinary use. For garden use, Grosso produces the longest, most striking flower spikes of any commonly grown lavender — up to 12–16 inches — in a dense, voluminous display that is far more dramatic than any English lavender. Harvested just before fully open for maximum essential oil content; used in sachets, potpourri, culinary (in small amounts), and craft arrangements.

plant_note: Plant rooted divisions in spring or fall in any moist, well-drained to moderately moist soil in partial to full shade; ground ivy establishes rapidly and spreads by rooting stolons — site it where spreading is desirable and use edging to contain it in formal plantings. It naturalizes readily in shaded lawns and under trees where grass struggles.
directions: Plant in partial to full shade in any reasonably moist soil; ground ivy is a creeping, mat-forming member of the mint family with distinctively kidney-shaped, scallop-edged leaves that release a pleasantly pungent, minty-medicinal aroma when crushed — small purple to blue flowers appear in whorls along the stems from spring through early summer. The young leaves and shoots are edible: they were used in medieval Europe to clarify and bitter ale before hops (earning the name 'alehoof'), and are used today in small amounts as a bitter herb in salads, soups, and herbal teas. Medicinally, ground ivy has a long tradition in European herbal medicine as an anti-inflammatory and respiratory herb. It is one of very few plants that will produce a dense, attractive groundcover in deep, dry shade under trees — a condition that defeats almost everything else. Can be invasive in favorable, moist conditions; contain with edging where needed.

plant_note: Plant stem cuttings (which root readily) in spring in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; guduchi is a vigorous climbing vine native to tropical and subtropical India that thrives in Gulf Coast heat and humidity and grows as a perennial in zone 9b-12, spreading vigorously over trees and structures.
directions: Plant stem cuttings 6–8 inches long directly in moist, moderately fertile soil in spring; provide trellis or tree support — guduchi is a vigorous climber. Tinospora cordifolia (guduchi or giloy) is one of the three most revered medicinal plants in Ayurvedic medicine (the others being ashwagandha and shatavari) — a tropical Indian climbing vine that has been used continuously in Ayurvedic medical practice for over 3,000 years. Modern research has identified numerous bioactive compounds including tinosporin, berberine, and various alkaloids and glycosides with anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, antipyretic, and hepatoprotective properties. The stem is the primary medicinal part — consumed as a decoction, powder, or extract. The plant is a vigorous, twining vine with broad, heart-shaped, bright-green leaves resembling a large morning glory vine in appearance. In India, a respected folk tradition holds that guduchi plants growing on neem trees (Azadirachta indica) — absorbing constituents from the host — have enhanced medicinal potency. The plant naturalizes readily in tropical and humid subtropical climates; it spreads vigorously and may require management to prevent overgrowth in frost-free zones.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; gymnema is a woody climbing vine from the tropical dry forests of India and Sri Lanka — famous for its ability to temporarily suppress the sweet taste: chewing fresh leaves makes sweet foods taste like they have no sweetness at all for 1–2 hours; used in Ayurvedic medicine for over 2,000 years to treat diabetes and sugar cravings, and now clinically studied for blood sugar management.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in part shade; provide a trellis or support structure; propagate by stem cuttings. Gymnema sylvestre (gymnema, sugar destroyer, or gurmar — Hindi for 'destroyer of sugar') is a woody climbing vine native to the tropical dry forests of central and southern India and Sri Lanka, famous in both traditional medicine and modern nutritional science for one of the most remarkable food interactions known in botany. The fresh leaves of gymnema contain gymnemic acids — triterpene saponins that temporarily bind to and block the sweet taste receptors on the tongue — causing a complete, reversible suppression of the ability to taste sweetness for 1–2 hours after the leaves are chewed. After chewing gymnema leaf, eating sugar tastes like sand, honey tastes like nothing, chocolate loses all sweetness, and sweet fruits taste only of their sour or astringent components — a dramatic, repeatable, pharmacological food interaction. This property has given gymnema both its ancient role in Ayurvedic medicine (used for 2,000+ years for 'sweet urine' — now understood as diabetes) and modern research interest: clinical studies suggest gymnemic acids may reduce sugar absorption in the intestine and support healthy blood glucose management. Gymnema is now one of the most widely sold botanical supplements for blood sugar support worldwide. In zone 9–12, it grows as an ornamental vine with elliptical leaves and small, yellow, tubular flowers.

plant_note: Direct sow or allow to self-seed in any well-drained, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; hairy beggartick is a Pantropical annual that volunteers in disturbed soil and garden margins throughout the Gulf Coastal Plain — it is a widely used edible and medicinal herb in African, Asian, and tropical American cuisines and folk medicine.
directions: Sow seeds or allow to self-seed in any well-drained, moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; harvest young leaves and shoots for culinary use before flowering. Bidens pilosa (hairy beggartick or black jack) is one of the world's most widespread tropical annual herbs — a common 'weed' of disturbed soils throughout the tropical and subtropical world that is simultaneously one of the most widely used edible and medicinal plants in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. In many African countries (particularly Kenya, Zimbabwe, and Central Africa), the young shoots and leaves are a major leafy vegetable cooked in stews and soups; in Asia, it is cooked like spinach; in Brazil and the Caribbean, it is used as a medicinal tea. The plant is a prolific producer of small, black seed-needles with two barbed prongs (the 'beggar ticks' or 'Spanish needles' that attach to clothing and animal fur). Despite its weedy character in gardens, the small, white, daisy-like flowers with yellow centers are important nectar sources for native bees and butterflies. Young leaves are mildly flavored and nutritious, used in many cultures as a green vegetable. A genuinely dual-use plant — volunteer edible and medicinal herb.

plant_note: Divide in spring or fall; hairy mountain mint self-seeds moderately and can naturalize in meadows and garden beds — a valuable addition to pollinator gardens that spreads slowly to form attractive colonies. Performs well in average to dry garden soils.
directions: Plant divisions or transplants in full sun to light shade in average, dry to moist, well-drained soil; hairy mountain mint (Pycnanthemum pilosum) is a native prairie and woodland-edge mint of the central and eastern United States with strongly aromatic foliage — the intense spearmint-oregano fragrance is released when leaves are brushed — and masses of small white flowers with purple spots that are exceptionally attractive to native bees, butterflies, and wasps from July through September, making it one of the highest-rated native plants for pollinator gardens. The dried leaves can be used as a mild mint tea or herb. Unlike invasive common mint (Mentha), mountain mints spread slowly and politely. An outstanding native herb for the meadow garden, pollinator strip, and naturalizing in dry to average soils.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in a woodland bed; seeds require cold, moist stratification over winter and germinate in early spring. Hairy sweet cicely is a native carrot-family herb of eastern North American forests with mild anise-scented foliage and lacy white umbel flowers that attract small native bees and flies in early spring.
directions: Sow fresh seed in fall directly in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; seed must not be allowed to dry out before sowing, as viability drops sharply with desiccation. Osmorhiza claytonii is one of the earliest-blooming native herbs in eastern deciduous forests, producing soft, fernlike, anise-scented foliage in early spring and flat-topped white umbels that serve as critical early nectar sources for small native bees and beneficial insects before most woodland flowers open. The plant naturalizes readily by self-seeding in moist shaded areas and is a useful addition to native woodland gardens, forest edges, and streamside plantings. Roots and young leaves carry a mild, pleasant anise flavor and have a long history of food and medicinal use by Indigenous peoples of eastern North America.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; hairy wood mint grows naturally in moist to mesic deciduous forest understory, shaded stream banks, and moist woodland margins throughout the eastern US.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in woodland gardens, shaded borders, and moist shaded areas; hairy wood mint is a little-known native perennial of the mint family (Lamiaceae) with distinctively hairy stems and leaves and whorled clusters of small, two-lipped, white to pale lavender flowers with purple spotting in midsummer. The minty-aromatic foliage is pleasantly fragrant. An outstanding native for the challenging combination of shade and adequate moisture — one of the few mint-family plants truly adapted to woodland understory conditions. The flowers are visited extensively by small native bees, bumblebees, and butterflies. The leaves can be brewed as a mild mint tea with a pleasant oregano-mint blend flavor. Self-sows modestly in appropriate conditions to naturalize in the shade garden.

plant_note: Root cuttings in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in zone 6–10; Hart's Pennyroyal is an unusual Mediterranean aquatic mint — native to stream banks, wet meadows, and seasonal wetlands from Iberia and southern France through North Africa — bearing very narrow, rush-like leaves and small spikes of pale lavender flowers, with a strong, clean spearmint fragrance and excellent culinary and ornamental value in moist to wet garden situations.
directions: Plant Mentha cervina in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; it tolerates standing water and grows well at the margins of ponds, in bog gardens, or in any reliably moist position; contain in pots as with other mints to prevent spreading; harvest stems for fresh use throughout the growing season. Hart's Pennyroyal is a distinctive and underused culinary mint — rare in cultivation but increasingly recognized for its ornamental value and culinary merit. Unlike most mints, it is adapted to aquatic or near-aquatic conditions and grows naturally in the beds of seasonal streams that dry in summer and flood in winter across the Iberian Peninsula, southern France, and North Africa. The very narrow, almost rush-like leaves are unlike any other mint and give the plant a unique, fine texture in the water garden. Culinary use closely mirrors that of spearmint: the leaves have a clean, fresh, strong spearmint fragrance with overtones of peppermint, and can be used fresh in teas, cocktails (particularly in Iberian cuisine), desserts, and savory dishes. In Portugal and Spain, it is used to make 'hortelã-da-ribeira' tea (riverside mint tea). Unlike some Mentha species, it does not spread as aggressively as peppermint or spearmint; still, container culture is advisable in mixed herb gardens. A charming, refined, and genuinely useful mint for the aquatic herb garden.

plant_note: Divide established clumps in spring once soil is workable and replant divisions at the same depth in consistently moist soil.
directions: Plant Hart's Pennyroyal in moist to seasonally wet soil along pond edges, rain gardens, or stream margins where its narrow, peppermint-scented foliage can spread freely. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding. Harvest stems for culinary or herbal use by cutting back to just above a leaf node, which encourages bushy regrowth. Although more drought-tolerant than common pennyroyal, it performs best when soil moisture remains consistent through summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination; or sow in earliest spring in a shaded, cool, moist seedbed. Herb Robert self-sows prolifically once established and typically perpetuates itself without intervention once a colony is started.
directions: Direct sow or allow to self-sow in moist, shaded, rocky or well-drained soil under trees, along walls, or in shaded garden beds; herb Robert is a dainty annual or biennial with deeply cut, ferny foliage that smells of turpentine when bruised — a scent that may repel insects, which accounts for part of its old folk-medicine reputation as a pest deterrent. The small, bright magenta-pink flowers appear from spring through fall and attract small native bees. In traditional European herbal medicine, the plant was used as an astringent and anti-inflammatory poultice; modern research has found antibacterial compounds in the leaf. In partly shaded rock gardens, walls, and woodland edges, herb Robert forms charming self-sustaining colonies without becoming aggressive. The foliage turns bright red in fall, giving rise to the common name 'red robin.'

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow February–March or September–October. Dill does not transplant well — always direct sow in place. Hercules is a compact, slow-to-bolt variety particularly suited for maritime and warm climates where standard dill bolts too quickly for a full herb harvest. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide continuous leaf harvest. In zone 9 the fall sowing typically provides the longest harvest before bolting.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — do not transplant; Hercules is a compact, bolt-resistant dill variety developed for gardeners and market growers who need an extended leaf harvest before the plant flowers. Unlike standard dill that rushes to bolt in warm weather, Hercules delays flowering by 2–3 weeks under similar conditions, producing a longer window of dense, feathery, aromatic foliage harvest — the primary advantage over standard open-pollinated dill types. The plant grows to a more compact 24–36 inches rather than the 4–5 foot height of standard dill, making it easier to grow in containers or small spaces without the flopping and staking required for large dill plants. The leaf flavor is identical to standard dill — fresh, bright, anise-like — and is equally useful in all dill applications from cold fish preparations to tzatziki, potato salads, and dill pickles. In zone 9 the compact habit makes Hercules the better choice for the brief spring dill season before heat ends production.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring; in zone 9 plant September–April. Hi Ho Silver creeping thyme makes excellent groundcover for dry, sunny slopes, rock gardens, and stepping stone pathways where foot traffic does not crush the low-growing stems. The silver-edged variegated foliage and pink-lavender bloom in spring create a tapestry effect when mass-planted. Provide very good drainage — standing water kills creeping thyme quickly.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to rocky, lean soil — creeping thyme fails in wet or heavy soils; Hi Ho Silver is a variegated creeping thyme (Thymus praecox) with silver-margined leaves that create a two-tone silver-and-green appearance across the mat-forming plant, making it one of the most ornamentally attractive thymes available for groundcover use. The tiny, silver-edged leaves are fragrant when brushed or crushed and are mildly culinary — suitable as a garnish and for light flavoring, though not as potently flavored as upright culinary thyme varieties. In spring (March–April in zone 9) the entire mat is covered with small pink-lavender flowers that are highly attractive to bees and beneficial insects. Hi Ho Silver is widely used in rock gardens, between stepping stones where foot traffic releases the fragrance, as an edging plant, and as a fragrant groundcover in herb gardens. The prostrate, spreading habit fills in gaps efficiently without becoming invasive in well-drained soils.

common_name: Hidcote English Lavender (Compact Deep-Purple English Lavender)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; 'Hidcote' does not come true from seed and must be propagated by cuttings or purchased as a named cultivar; it is compact and well-suited to formal plantings, edging, container growing, and small gardens where standard English lavender varieties grow too large.
directions: Plant in full sun with excellent drainage (amended sandy or gravelly soil if needed) and avoid heavy clay or consistently moist soils; trim after flowering to maintain compact shape; in zones 8–9 plant in fall for establishment before summer heat; Hidcote lavender requires excellent air circulation to prevent fungal issues in humid climates. Hidcote is one of the most beloved and widely planted English lavender cultivars in the world, named for the famous English Arts and Crafts garden Hidcote Manor in Gloucestershire — a National Trust property renowned for its rare plants and structured garden design, where this compact, very dark-purple lavender was popularized. The cultivar has been a standard in English lavender since the early 20th century and is recognized by its distinctive characteristics: very compact, tightly mounding habit (12–18 inches rather than the 24–36 of open-pollinated English lavenders), intensely deep purple-violet flowers (darker than almost all other English lavender varieties), and silver-gray foliage. The deep color makes Hidcote one of the most visually striking lavenders for formal planting designs, knot gardens, edging borders, and formal herb gardens. The fragrance is intensely sweet in the characteristic English lavender style — considered by many perfumers to be the most refined and complex of all lavender types, with a floral-camphorous-sweet balance that is the reference fragrance for culinary lavender and lavender products. Hidcote is the lavender for people who want compact, tidy, deeply colored plants for formal or small-space settings.

common_name: Hill Hardy Rosemary (Madalene Hill Cold-Hardy Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring or fall in full sun, well-drained soil; Hill Hardy is one of the most cold-hardy rosemary selections available, tolerating temperatures well below the range that damages standard rosemary when grown in a sheltered, well-drained site.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; like other rosemary cultivars it dislikes rich, moisture-retentive soil, which encourages soft, frost-tender growth at the expense of cold hardiness. Hill Hardy is a cold-hardy rosemary selection associated with Madalene Hill, the pioneering Texas herb grower who also introduced Arp rosemary, and is prized alongside Arp as one of the more winter-tolerant named rosemary cultivars available to home gardeners in marginal climates. Its habit is semi-upright to spreading, somewhat looser than a compact culinary type, with the same piney, resinous fragrance and flavor as any standard rosemary, making it fully usable in the kitchen for roasting, grilling, and seasoning. Prune after flowering to maintain a dense, shapely plant, and avoid overwatering or heavy mulch against the crown, which invites root rot in humid Gulf South summers.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, average to slightly lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; hoary mountain mint is tolerant of a wider range of soil conditions than many mountain mints and grows naturally in open woodlands, woodland edges, rocky slopes, and dry meadows.
directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; hoary mountain mint is one of the most distinctive mountain mints, immediately recognizable by the striking silvery-white, downy (hoary) coating on the upper leaves and bracts surrounding the flower clusters — creating a bold, almost mealy-white appearance in midsummer that makes the plant ornamentally attractive even before and after bloom. The white bracts below the small lavender flowers are so conspicuous that they resemble petals, creating an unusual effect in the garden. Like all mountain mints, the flowers attract an extraordinary diversity of native bees — documented as supporting over 50 native bee species at a single planting. The aromatic foliage is repellent to deer. More tolerant of dry, rocky soils and partial woodland shade than Virginia mountain mint, hoary mountain mint is excellent in the transitional zone between sunny meadow and shaded woodland.

plant_note: Plant divisions or rooted suckers after last frost; in zones below 8 grow in large containers and overwinter indoors.
directions: Divide established clumps in spring by separating rooted suckers from the base of the mother plant and replanting in rich, moist soil. Hoja santa grows rapidly in warm, humid conditions and prefers partial shade with consistent moisture; the enormous heart-shaped leaves can reach 12 in wide and emit a distinctive anise–root beer aroma from their essential oils. In Mexican cuisine the leaves are used to wrap tamales, season mole verde, and envelop fish for grilling. In zones 8–9, plants die to the ground after frost but reliably regrow from the roots; mulch heavily to protect the root zone through winter.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; or direct sow on the soil surface after last frost when soil is warm. Seed needs light to germinate — do not cover.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; holy basil (tulsi) is the sacred herb of Hindu worship and traditional Ayurvedic medicine, with an intensely spicy, clove-and-pepper scented flavor distinctly different from sweet Italian basil. The purple-stemmed Kapoor and Krishna varieties are most fragrant; the green-stemmed Vana type has a stronger, more medicinal flavor. Holy basil makes excellent Thai cooking, fresh teas, and pesto, and is reputed to have adaptogenic properties. Grow exactly as sweet basil — pinch flowers early and often to extend the harvest. In zones 10–12 it grows as a short-lived perennial; everywhere else it is grown as an annual. Seed is produced prolifically if a few flower stalks are allowed to mature.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; do not transplant until nights are reliably above 55°F as cold soil stunts growth.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix at 75–85°F; germination is swift when soil is adequately warm. Transplant after night temperatures stay above 55°F and pinch growing tips immediately to promote bushy growth. Regular pinching and removal of flower spikes prolongs the leaf harvest and delays bitterness; harvest leaves in the morning after dew has dried for the most aromatic result. Fresh or dried leaves are used in adaptogenic teas, Ayurvedic preparations, and as a sacred plant in Hindu tradition.

plant_note: Plant container stock or root divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun in zone 7–11; Honduran Sarsaparilla is a thorny, woody, climbing vine native to the humid forests of Central America — Honduras, Mexico, Jamaica, and Guatemala — whose aromatic, starchy rhizomes are the authentic source of the flavoring used in traditional root beer and the original sarsaparilla beverages, and a valued traditional medicine for joint pain and skin conditions.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with trellis or other support for climbing; Smilax ornata is adaptable to a range of conditions including full sun with consistent moisture and deep shade — mulch heavily to maintain soil moisture and supply organic matter to the root zone. Smilax ornata (Honduran Sarsaparilla, Zarzaparilla) is a thorny, woody, perennial climbing vine in the Smilacaceae family native to humid tropical forests, forest edges, and riparian corridors of Central America — particularly Honduras, Guatemala, Mexico (Veracruz and Chiapas), Cuba, and Jamaica — where it climbs through the understorey using tendrils. The long, aromatic, reddish-brown rhizomes are the authentic source of 'true' sarsaparilla flavoring — the complex, vanilla-anise-wintergreen root flavor historically used in 19th-century American sarsaparilla beverages and root beer before artificial flavors displaced it. Medicinally, sarsaparilla root was a major export from Central America and the Caribbean to European pharmaceutical markets in the 16th–19th centuries for treatment of syphilis, psoriasis, rheumatism, and as a blood-purifying tonic. Modern phytochemical research confirms anti-inflammatory steroidal saponins (sarsasaponin, smilasaponin) in the rhizomes. The rhizomes are harvested by carefully digging, removing a portion, and replanting the crown; the vine regenerates. Excellent shade-tolerant medicinal vine for forest-garden and woodland-garden settings in zones 7–11.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; honewort self-sows freely and can naturalize in the shade garden. A perennial herb that dies back in winter and re-emerges in early spring from a taproot.
directions: Honewort is a shade-loving native edible herb, native to moist, rich woodlands and forest edges throughout eastern North America from Quebec to Florida and west to Kansas, producing tender, edible leaves and stems in spring and early summer that taste mildly of parsley and celery — used raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb. It is closely related to Japanese mitsuba (Cryptotaenia japonica) and can substitute for it in East Asian cooking; the young leaves are particularly flavorful in early spring. A self-seeding perennial that naturalizes freely in the shade garden, it fills in the difficult deep-shade spaces where most vegetables fail, providing a continuous harvest of tender greens from early spring to summer heat. Harvest outer leaves regularly to maintain plant vigor; allow some plants to set seed for natural self-renewal.

plant_note: Start from cuttings or transplants; in zone 9 plant March–May. Honey Stevia flowers profusely in September–October when days shorten — harvest leaves for drying before flowering begins, as the sweetness is highest in pre-flower leaves. In zone 9 the plant is a short-lived perennial, often surviving 2–3 years before requiring replacement. Provide light shade during the hottest summer weeks to prevent leaf scorch and premature bolting.
directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil; Honey Stevia is a named cultivar of stevia (Stevia rebaudiana) selected for a smoother, more honey-like sweetness compared to the standard species, which can have a distinct licorice-menthol aftertaste that some people find unpleasant in large quantities. The sweetening compounds in stevia (steviosides and rebaudiosides) are 200–350 times sweeter than sugar by weight, so only small amounts of fresh or dried leaf are needed to sweeten foods and beverages. The Honey cultivar has been selected to emphasize the rebaudioside-A fraction (which provides the cleaner, honey-like sweetness) relative to the stevioside fraction (associated with the bitter aftertaste) — making it the preferred variety for fresh leaf use in teas, lemonades, and fresh preparations where subtle sweetener differences are most noticeable. Leaves are used fresh in drinks and food, or dried and powdered for longer storage.

plant_note: Plant rhizome cuttings ('rhizomes') horizontally 2–3 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; hops climbs vigorously (up to 20 feet in a single season) — provide a very strong trellis or support. Only female plants produce usable cones.
directions: Plant rhizomes horizontally in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; hops is the perennial vine whose dried female flower cones ('hops') are the essential bittering and preserving agent in virtually all beer styles. Native to temperate North America and Europe, it is a vigorous, tendriled vine that dies to the ground each fall and re-emerges rapidly each spring to climb 15–20 feet on strings, trellises, or arbors. The soft green hop cones (strobiles) ripen in late summer; harvest when papery and fragrant, then dry immediately for use in home brewing. The young spring shoots emerging from the ground are edible as a vegetable, cooked like asparagus. The dried seed cones have traditional medicinal use as a mild sedative. Ornamental cultivars like 'Aureus' (golden-yellow foliage) are widely grown for their dramatic summer screening effect. Performs best in cool-summer climates (zones 3–7); struggles in the persistent heat of zone 8+.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow as seeds are small and benefit from light for germination.
directions: Surface-sow onto moist mix 6–8 weeks before transplanting; horehound germinates readily in warm soil but can be slow and erratic. Plant in dry, well-drained, even rocky or sandy soil where most plants would struggle — fertile, moist conditions cause leggy, weak growth. Harvest stems and leaves before flowering for the most potent bitterness, bundling for drying or infusing fresh into candy and cough syrups. Shear plants back in late summer to keep growth compact and prevent excessive self-seeding.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings or root division in spring; horse mint spreads vigorously by underground runners like all mints and is best contained in a pot or a bed with root barriers. Plant in moist soil in partial shade.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, contained in pots or with root barriers to limit spreading; horse mint is a European native mint with long, lance-shaped, silver-green leaves that are more strongly and sharply aromatic than spearmint, with a mentholated, camphor-like fragrance. The dense, elongated spikes of small lavender flowers in late summer are exceptionally attractive to bumblebees, honey bees, and numerous other pollinators. The leaves can be used as a tea, culinary seasoning, or insect repellent — the intense menthol content makes it more suited to teas and infusions than to fresh eating. In South Africa it is widely used as a traditional medicine and culinary herb (called 'ballerja'); it naturalizes in moist streamside habitats across North Africa, Europe, and western Asia. Contrast with 'horse mint' used in the US (Monarda punctata), which is an entirely unrelated native wildflower.

common_name: Hot and Spicy Oregano (Compact High-Oil Pungent Culinary Oregano)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Hot and Spicy oregano is a compact (12–15 inch) shrubby perennial in zones 5–9 that grows well year-round in zone 9 with some protection from extended hard freezes. Can also be direct sown outdoors in spring. In zone 9, plant in well-drained, somewhat poor soil in full sun — rich, moist soils reduce the concentration of aromatic oils that give the variety its name. Harvest stems before or during early bloom for maximum essential oil content and flavor intensity.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct sow in spring; transplant to full sun, well-drained soil. Harvest stems for drying just as flower buds begin to open. Hot and Spicy Oregano is a compact cultivar of common oregano (Origanum vulgare) selected for higher essential oil content and more pronounced, pungent flavor compared to the bland, low-oil common oregano that grows widely in American gardens. Standard common oregano (Origanum vulgare) grown in the United States often has relatively low essential oil content and mild flavor — the reason that most dried commercial 'oregano' products in American grocery stores are a blend of Origanum vulgare with Greek oregano (O. heracleoticum) or marjoram. Hot and Spicy represents a more flavorful selection of the common oregano type, with significantly more essential oil and a more robust, peppery, slightly camphoraceous character approaching that of true Greek or Italian cooking oregano. The compact habit (10–15 inches), fine texture, and purple-tinged flowers make Hot and Spicy also ornamentally attractive in herb gardens and Mediterranean-style plantings. The variety is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in containers where watering can be controlled.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; can also be started indoors 4 weeks early for a longer season.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in well-drained soil after last frost; thin to 18–24 in apart as huacatay grows into a tall, upright plant. This Andean herb — essential in Peruvian cuisine for dishes like ocopa sauce and anticuchos marinades — has a complex flavor combining mint, tarragon, and citrus. Plants are day-length sensitive and flower in late summer to fall; harvest leaves and stem tips throughout the vegetative season before flowering commences. Grow in full sun with moderate fertility; the plant is drought-tolerant once established and spreads by self-seeding in warm climates.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential — this plant rots in heavy, moist clay. Excellent in gravel gardens and rock gardens.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; hummingbird mint is a native sage relative of the Texas-New Mexico border region with the most extraordinary foliage fragrance in the genus — a pure, sweet bubblegum-spearmint scent that fills the air when brushed. The deep rose-pink tubular flowers from summer through frost are consumed almost exclusively by hummingbirds, which are so attracted to the flowers that the plant earns its common name. It is genuinely drought tolerant and thrives in hot, dry conditions where it has excellent drainage. The plant self-sows modestly and is short-lived as a perennial (3–5 years); take cuttings in summer to maintain the garden. Deer resistant. An excellent choice for zone 8–9 pollinator gardens in full sun with excellent drainage.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean, rocky or loamy soil in partial shade; hummingbird sage spreads by underground rhizomes to form dense, weed-suppressing groundcover colonies under oaks and in dappled shade, making it an excellent low-maintenance native California groundcover.
directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to lean soil in partial shade; hummingbird sage is one of the most useful native California salvias for gardens, tolerating more shade than most salvias while producing large, striking, rose-magenta flower spikes on tall stems — among the largest flowers of any native California sage, strongly attractive to Anna's hummingbirds and rufous hummingbirds throughout the blooming season from late winter through spring. The large, crinkled, gray-green aromatic leaves smell strongly of fresh pineapple and sage when crushed. Spreads by rhizomes to form gradually expanding colonies that provide excellent, drought-tolerant groundcover under California oaks and in dappled shade. One of the best California natives for replacing invasive English ivy under trees while maintaining shade coverage and providing outstanding wildlife value for hummingbirds and native bees.

common_name: Huntington Carpet Rosemary (Extremely Prostrate Groundcover Rosemary)
plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Huntington Carpet is one of the most prostrate rosemary selections available, hugging the ground closely and spreading widely, making it a strong choice as a large-scale groundcover on a sunny slope.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Huntington Carpet is among the most flat-growing, ground-hugging rosemary cultivars available, spreading widely while staying only a few inches tall, making it an excellent choice for covering a sunny bank or slope, cascading over a wall, or filling a large container where a true groundcover habit is wanted rather than an upright shrub form. It shares the same fragrant, culinary-quality foliage as other rosemary cultivars and produces small blue flowers in season. Excellent drainage is essential, since rosemary is highly prone to root rot in heavy or poorly drained soil, and it needs very little pruning to maintain its naturally flat, spreading form.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface-sow or cover lightly with 1/8 in of fine mix.
directions: Sow seeds 1/8 in deep indoors in warm starting mix; germination is fast and reliable at 65–70°F. Plant in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil — hyssop is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in conditions similar to lavender. Prune plants back by about one-third after flowering to keep them from becoming woody and to promote a compact, bushy habit. Harvest leafy stems and flowers in the morning just as the blossoms begin to open, drying them for use in expectorant teas, culinary herb blends, and potpourri.

plant_note: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring, since Icterina does not come true from seed. Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun after last frost.
directions: Root tip cuttings in moist potting mix in spring or summer and plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Icterina is a variegated culinary sage with soft gray-green leaves broadly edged in gold, giving a brighter, more luminous look to an herb garden or mixed border than plain green sage while carrying the same savory, slightly peppery flavor used in stuffings, poultry dishes, and herb butters. It stays a bit more compact than green garden sage, making it useful for edging or container plantings. Cut back hard in early spring to remove winter-worn growth and encourage fresh, well-colored new leaves.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Indian coleus is related to ornamental coleus (Plectranthus scutellarioides) and is an easy-to-grow perennial herb in warm climates, roots are harvested for the compound forskolin.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; root cuttings readily in moist soil or water. Plectranthus barbatus (Indian coleus or forskohlii) is a fragrant-leaved tropical herb closely related to ornamental coleus, native to East Africa and tropical Asia and used extensively in Ayurvedic medicine under the name 'makandi' or 'coleus.' The roots of P. barbatus contain the diterpene compound forskolin, which has been extensively studied for its ability to activate the enzyme adenylate cyclase, increasing cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels in cells — a mechanism that has been researched for effects on weight management, glaucoma, and thyroid conditions. Forskohlii supplements (standardized root extracts) are widely sold in the herbal supplement market. As a garden plant, Indian coleus is an attractive, square-stemmed, aromatic, soft-leaved herb with pale-blue flower spikes in late summer — resembling a coarser-leaved version of its ornamental coleus relatives. It roots readily from stem cuttings and grows vigorously in humid, subtropical conditions. CAUTION: May interact with anticoagulants and medications metabolized by the CYP system; consult healthcare provider before medicinal use.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds where plants are to grow permanently in spring (or fall in mild climates) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian dill does not transplant well due to its taproot. It can be sown more thickly than European dill and the young plants thinned for fresh leaf use while remaining plants mature for seed harvest. The seeds are larger than common dill and more pungently aromatic.
directions: Direct sow seeds in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Indian dill is a distinct species from the common European dill (Anethum graveolens), native to South Asia and widely used throughout Indian, Sri Lankan, and Iranian cuisines where it occupies a culinary role analogous to but distinct from European dill — the seeds are larger, more flattened, with a stronger, earthier, more camphoraceous aroma than common dill, and the fresh leaves have a more pungent, slightly different flavor profile that is essential to certain South Asian fish curries, lentil dishes, and the Persian herb-rice dishes that are among the oldest continuously prepared foods in culinary history. The whole plant is taller and somewhat coarser than common dill. The seeds are used both whole in tempering (bloom in hot oil to release aromatics) and ground in spice blends. The essential oil chemistry differs meaningfully from A. graveolens, containing higher carvone concentrations that give the seeds their more assertive character. It is used medicinally throughout South Asia as a carminative and digestive herb. Excellent for South Asian herb gardens and cross-cultural culinary herb collections.

common_name: Indian Mulberry Root (Bai Ji Tian, Morinda Root)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in part shade; Morinda officinalis (Bai Ji Tian) is one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine, used for over 2,000 years to tonify Kidney Yang, treat impotence, lower back pain, and bone weakness — the starchy, medicinal roots are harvested after 3–5 years of growth.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in part shade; harvest roots after 3–5 years. Morinda officinalis (bai ji tian or Indian mulberry root) is a trailing and climbing vine from southern China and Southeast Asia in the coffee family (Rubiaceae) — one of the 50 fundamental herbs in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and a plant used continuously in Chinese medical practice for over 2,000 years. The medicinal part is the dried root (bai ji tian in Chinese, meaning 'a hundred joints stretching to the sky') — starchy, slightly sweet, mildly warming — used in TCM specifically to tonify (strengthen) Kidney Yang energy, treating impotence, infertility, lower back and knee pain and weakness, fatigue, and osteoporosis from a TCM perspective. It is one of the principal herbs in many male reproductive tonifying formulas (like the classic Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan). The root contains anthraquinones, polysaccharides, and flavonoids with studied effects on testosterone levels, bone density, and adaptogenic activity. As a garden plant in zone 8–12, it is an attractive, semi-woody vine with glossy, ovate leaves and small white flowers in rounded clusters, followed by compound, white, aggregate fruits similar to noni (M. citrifolia) but smaller. Quite different from commercial noni in use and chemistry despite being in the same genus.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds on the surface of moist soil in partial shade after last frost; do not cover seeds with soil as they require light to germinate. Indian tobacco self-sows freely once established in a woodland garden.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the soil surface (do not cover) in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade after last frost; Indian tobacco is a native annual wildflower of eastern North American woodland clearings and disturbed areas, recognized by its inflated, balloon-like seed capsules after the small, pale lavender-blue flowers fade. It is an important plant in the history of American botanical medicine — the leaves and seeds contain lobeline and related piperidine alkaloids that act as respiratory stimulants and were traditionally used by Indigenous peoples and 19th-century physicians for asthma, croup, and as an emetic. IMPORTANT CAUTION: All parts of the plant are toxic in quantity; it should be used medicinally only under professional guidance. Do not confuse with garden lobelia cultivars (L. erinus) which are ornamentals. Indian tobacco is primarily of botanical and ethnobotanical interest rather than general garden use.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Irene is a vigorous, low, trailing rosemary well suited to cascading over a wall, raised bed edge, or large container.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Irene is a vigorous, low-growing, trailing rosemary selection that spreads and cascades rather than growing upright, making it an excellent choice for spilling over a retaining wall, raised bed, or large container edge. It carries the same fragrant, needle-like foliage and culinary use as upright rosemary types, along with small blue flowers in spring, and it tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established. Good drainage is essential, since rosemary quickly develops root rot in heavy, wet soil, and only minimal pruning is needed to keep the trailing habit tidy.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; tolerates light frost.
directions: This heirloom flat-leaf parsley produces broad, dark green leaves with a clean, robust flavor prized in Mediterranean cooking. Soak seed overnight to speed the naturally slow germination, then sow shallowly and keep the soil consistently moist for the two to four weeks it takes to sprout. Thin seedlings to about eight inches apart in rich, well-drained soil and full sun. Harvest outer stems first so the plant keeps producing tender new growth through the season.

plant_note: Set out only after nights stay reliably above 50 F.
directions: Genovese is the classic Italian basil, offering the traditional fragrance and flavor that make it the top choice for pesto and countless summer dishes. Start seed indoors in warmth and transplant after the soil is warm and settled weather has arrived, as cold stunts young plants. Give it full sun, rich soil, and even moisture for lush growth. Pinch out flower buds and harvest from the top to keep plants leafy, tender, and productive all season.

common_name: Italian Large Leaf Basil (Oversized Smooth-Leaf Classic Pesto Basil)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Italian Large Leaf basil bolts quickly in Gulf South summer heat — pinch flower stalks immediately and repeatedly to extend leaf production; succession sowings every 3 weeks from April through August ensure continuous fresh basil.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Italian Large Leaf basil produces very large (3–4 inch), smooth, flat, slightly cupped, glossy leaves with the classic sweet, aromatic, clove-and-anise basil flavor of traditional Italian cooking — the preferred basil for pesto, where the large leaf size dramatically reduces the time and effort required to harvest sufficient leaf mass for a batch. The large, smooth leaves with their flat, relatively unwrinkled surface represent a distinctly different basil character from small-leaf and ruffled types — they are easier to clean, process, and stack, and produce a cleaner pesto with less stem fiber. The vigorous plants reach 2–2.5 feet with regular harvesting that removes flower buds and promotes continued vegetative growth. In zone 9, Italian Large Leaf basil grows throughout the warm season (April–October) and succession planting every 3 weeks maintains continuous fresh supply despite the tendency of summer heat to promote bolting in individual plants. For maximum leaf harvest, remove flower stalks immediately when they appear — flowering redirects plant energy from leaf production and quickly reduces the quality and flavor of remaining leaves. A single-season basil capable of producing many pounds of leaves from a short row under good management.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Italian oregano is a natural hybrid and does not come true from seed — propagate from cuttings or purchase plants. It is cold hardier than sweet marjoram and more flavorful than common oregano, making it the most versatile culinary oregano for most American gardens.
directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Italian oregano (Origanum x majoricum) is a naturally occurring hybrid between sweet marjoram (O. majorana) and Greek oregano (O. vulgare subsp. hirtum) that combines the complex, warm sweetness of marjoram with the earthy intensity of oregano to produce the characteristically mild, aromatic flavor used in Italian cuisine — the flavor profile preferred for pizza, pasta sauces, and Italian-American cooking. It is more cold-hardy than sweet marjoram, more flavorful and complex than ordinary wild oregano, and easier to grow with consistent harvest quality. The small, oval, gray-green leaves are harvested before flowering for maximum essential oil content; dried Italian oregano is far more intensely flavored than the thin, often stale commercial product and vastly superior for cooking. Excellent for container growing and performs well in zone 9 heat if given good drainage and lean soil.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in spring after the last frost; established clumps expand steadily and are divided every 3–4 years. In zone 7–9 myoga grows as a fully perennial ground cover in part shade to full shade, dying back to the ground each winter and re-emerging reliably in spring. The harvest season for the edible flower buds is August–September in zone 9.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 2–3 inches deep in rich, moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese ginger (myoga) is a shade-thriving edible perennial rarely seen in American gardens despite being widely grown in Japan for its prized flower buds. The plant's ginger-scented strap leaves reach 24–36 inches in shade conditions, forming a handsome ground cover through the growing season. The harvest is the unopened flower buds, which emerge at soil level in August–September — these small, pink-tipped buds are sliced thin and used as a pungent, mildly spicy garnish in miso soup, sashimi, noodle dishes, and pickled in vinegar. Young spring shoots are also edible with a more delicate flavor. The flavor is distinctly gingery but milder and more aromatic than culinary ginger root. Plants naturalize slowly and are nearly care-free once established in a shaded spot with consistent moisture.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 start February–March and transplant March–April. Japanese Indigo is a warm-season annual harvested before flowering for the highest leaf indican content; harvest the first flush of leaves when plants are 12–18 inches tall, then allow regrowth for a second harvest. In zone 9 the long warm season allows 2–3 harvests before fall. The plants self-sow readily in zone 9 conditions and may naturalize in moist garden areas.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Japanese Indigo (Ai, Tade Ai) is the traditional indigo dye plant of Japan, used for over 1,500 years to produce the brilliant blue textile dye that colors traditional Japanese fabrics including indigo-dyed cotton, shibori tie-dye, and katazome stencil-printed cloth. The blue dye precursor indican is stored in the fresh leaves and requires a fermentation vat (sukumo) or direct fresh-leaf dyeing process to produce the indigo pigment that bonds to fiber. Unlike the tropical indigo plant (Indigofera), Japanese Indigo thrives in temperate garden conditions and is accessible to North American home growers. Fresh leaves yield blue dye directly when crushed and applied to cotton in the sun — a simple process known as 'leaf printing' that produces soft blue marks without a dye vat. The ornamental plants with reddish stems and oval, deep green leaves and pink flower spikes in fall are attractive in the garden and valuable to craft dyers, fiber artists, and natural dye enthusiasts.

common_name: Japanese Pepper Vine (Fuji Kadsura, Asian Pepper Vine)
plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full shade; Japanese pepper vine is a tropical Asian climbing vine related to black pepper that grows as an understory climber in humid, shaded forest conditions — it can be used as a shade-tolerant ornamental and culinary herb in warm gardens.
directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in part to full shade; provide trellis or tree trunk support. Piper kadsura (Japanese pepper vine) is a Japanese and East Asian climbing vine in the pepper family (Piperaceae) — related to true black pepper (P. nigrum) but native to the humid, shaded forests of Japan, China, and Korea. The plant produces attractive, heart-shaped, deeply veined, dark-green leaves with conspicuous venation and a mildly spicy pepper aroma when crushed. Small, string-like flower spikes produce tiny, red to dark-purple peppercorns-like berries in fall that are mildly peppery-spicy and have been used as a seasoning and traditional medicine ingredient in East Asian cuisine and herbal practice. The vine climbs by adhesive stem roots similar to Virginia creeper and can attach to rough stone, brick, and wood surfaces. As a shade-tolerant ornamental vine for zone 9–12, it provides year-round interest with its attractive foliage and subtle fruiting display. Used in Japanese herbal medicine (kampo) for joint pain and circulation. Extremely rare in Western horticulture.

common_name: Japanese Sweet Flag (Dwarf Sweet Flag, Grassy-Leaved Sweet Flag)
plant_note: Plant clump divisions in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or in containers submerged up to 2–3 inches of water in shade to part shade; Japanese sweet flag is a small, grass-like aquatic-marginal perennial from East Asia — the mildly anise-scented leaves are used in traditional Japanese ikebana arrangements, as a marginal water feature plant, and in various ornamental cultivars with variegated gold-and-green foliage.
directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil or in containers in shallow water (up to 3 inches deep) in shade to part shade.
