Acorus gramineus (Japanese sweet flag or dwarf sweet flag) is a small, compact, grass-like aquatic-marginal perennial from Japan and China — a diminutive relative of the larger sweet flag (A. calamus) — producing dense tufts of narrow, grass-like, slightly arching, aromatic leaves in solid green or with variegated golden-yellow striping. The leaves, when crushed, release a mild, pleasant anise-cinnamon fragrance similar to (but softer than) the larger A. calamus. Several ornamental cultivars are widely grown: 'Ogon' (yellow-green striped leaves), 'Variegatus' (white-striped leaves), and the miniature 'Pusillus' (just 3–4 inches tall). Japanese sweet flag naturally grows along stream margins and in wet meadows in Japan and Korea, tolerating conditions from moist soil to shallow water up to 3 inches deep; it is an ideal marginal plant for water garden pots, pond edges, and shade rain gardens. In Japanese flower arranging (ikebana), the upright leaves provide linear structure. In Chinese and Japanese traditional medicine, the root and leaves are used as a mildly stimulating tonic and insect repellent herb. A wonderfully versatile plant for moist shade situations.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; Java citronella is the primary commercial source of citronella essential oil worldwide — a large, clumping aromatic grass closely related to lemongrass, grown in Java, Sri Lanka, Taiwan, and Central America for its leaves, which distill to produce the citronella oil used in insect repellents, candles, and soaps.
directions: Plant clump divisions in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; harvest leaves after 4–6 months and steam-distill or use fresh as repellent. Cymbopogon winterianus (Java citronella) is a large, clumping tropical aromatic grass that is the world's primary commercial source of citronella essential oil — one of the most commercially important aromatic crop plants globally, with the highest geraniol and citronellal content of any Cymbopogon species. Java citronella oil (named for its origin in Indonesian cultivation on Java) is the primary active ingredient in citronella candles, insect repellent products, and many natural insect-deterrent sprays worldwide. The plant is named for Cornelius de Winter, a Dutch botanist. Java citronella (C. winterianus) is distinct from Ceylon citronella (C. nardus) — Java citronella has significantly higher citronellal and geraniol content and produces a superior, more commercially valuable oil. The plant resembles lemongrass but has a more pronounced citrus-floral-rose fragrance (from geraniol content) rather than purely lemon. As a garden plant in zone 10–12, Java citronella forms an attractive, 4–6 foot clump of narrow, arching, blue-green leaves with a strong pleasant scent when crushed. Fresh stems placed around outdoor seating areas provide some mosquito deterrence, though less than the concentrated essential oil.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed as young plants are cold-sensitive.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm, moist starting mix and provide a trellis or support on which the vigorous twining vine can climb; jiaogulan grows 10–20 ft if given the right conditions. Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in hot climates; consistent moisture promotes the most lush and harvestable leaf growth. In zones 7–8 the plant dies to the ground in winter but regrows from the root; in zone 9 and above it may be evergreen. Harvest the five-lobed leaflets throughout the growing season for fresh or dried tea; known as southern ginseng, the leaves contain saponins similar to those in Panax ginseng and are used in adaptogenic preparations.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, slightly acidic soil; in zones 9–10 it can remain outdoors year-round. In zones 7–8 grow in containers and overwinter indoors above 50°F.
directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; makrut lime is grown primarily for its distinctive double-lobed leaves, which are the indispensable aromatic herb of Thai and Cambodian cooking, used in curries, soups, and stir-fries to impart an intensely floral, citrusy perfume that no other herb can substitute. The bumpy, knobbly green fruit has very little juice but extremely aromatic zest used in marinades and Thai curry pastes. Leaves can be harvested whenever new growth appears; young leaves have the strongest flavor. In containers (the most practical approach north of zone 9), use a quality potting mix, fertilize monthly with citrus fertilizer spring through fall, and overwinter indoors in a bright window above 50°F.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or transplant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; kalmegh thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast summer and is one of the most important medicinal herbs in Indian Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, used for immune support and respiratory infections.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; harvest aerial parts when plants begin to flower for maximum andrographolide content. Andrographis paniculata (kalmegh, green chiretta, or king of bitters) is one of the most important and widely researched medicinal plants in Asian traditional medicine systems — a tropical Asian annual herb producing intensely bitter leaves (among the bitterest of any plant) containing the bioactive diterpene compound andrographolide. Clinical research has documented significant efficacy for andrographolide in reducing the severity and duration of upper respiratory infections (common cold and flu) — it is one of the better-supported herbal remedies for viral respiratory illness. The plant is used extensively in Ayurvedic medicine (as kalmegh), traditional Chinese medicine, and Southeast Asian folk medicine for fever, liver conditions, and infections. Despite its extreme bitterness, the plant is consumed as an herbal tea, tincture, and tablet supplement throughout South and Southeast Asia. The plant grows as an upright, branching annual with lance-shaped leaves and small, white, pink-speckled flowers; it is well-adapted to hot, humid conditions and grows vigorously through Gulf Coast summers.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; kalonji prefers cool spring conditions and dislikes heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep directly where they are to grow; kalonji has fine, thread-like foliage similar to its ornamental cousin love-in-a-mist and dislikes transplanting. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; the plant bolts quickly in summer heat, so time sowing for a cool-season harvest. Harvest the swollen seed pods when they begin to turn tan and paper-like, cutting whole stems into bags before the pods split and release the seeds. The intensely aromatic black seeds are used in South Asian cooking on naan breads and in spice blends, and have a long history of medicinal use; they are not to be confused with black cumin (Bunium persicum).

plant_note: Start indoors 4 weeks early or direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring and August for fall. Kapoor is heat-tolerant and well-adapted to Indian-subtropical growing conditions that resemble the Gulf Coast climate, making it one of the better basil varieties for sustained summer production in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Kapoor is a compact Indian sweet basil cultivar selected for high essential oil content and strong clove-camphor aroma with a distinctive spicy note absent from European Genovese varieties. The small-to-medium dark green leaves have a more robust, pungent flavor than Genovese basil and are used extensively in Indian cooking — in chutneys, raitas, and as a fresh herb added to dals and curries. Kapoor's compact habit and heat tolerance make it particularly suitable for year-round indoor container growing and for outdoor herb gardens in subtropical zone 9 where it often survives mild winters as a short-lived perennial. The slightly camphoraceous aroma also has medicinal uses in Ayurvedic tradition, closely related to but distinct from true holy basil (tulsi).

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May. Kapoor tulsi is a compact (12–18 inch) holy basil that thrives in zone 9's warm, humid summers and often self-seeds to create a self-perpetuating colony. In Ayurvedic tradition the plant should not be harvested after dark or on certain days; for culinary and medicinal use, harvest fresh leaves continuously to prevent bolting. In zone 9 the plant can overwinter in frost-free spots as a short-lived perennial, but is best treated as an annual that self-seeds.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kapoor Tulsi is a named variety of holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) selected for compact habit and exceptionally high eugenol content — the volatile oil component that gives tulsi its characteristic warm, clove-like fragrance is highest in the Kapoor selection, making it the preferred variety for medicinal use in Ayurvedic preparations where eugenol concentration matters. In Hindu tradition, Tulsi (also called Vrinda or the Holy Basil) is the most sacred plant in the home, representing Lakshmi and kept in a tulsi pot on the veranda of traditional Indian homes where it is tended daily. Beyond its religious significance, Kapoor Tulsi is used medicinally for digestive support, as an adaptogen for stress, in tea blends for respiratory health, and as an aromatic in Indian and Southeast Asian cooking where the clove-camphor notes are distinctly different from sweet basil. The compact Kapoor selection fits easily in container or herb garden cultivation and grows robustly in the warm conditions of the Gulf South.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September for a fall harvest. Kaprao holy basil thrives in zone 9's heat and humidity — unlike sweet basil which may decline in extreme summer heat, holy basil actively thrives in tropical-humid conditions. In zone 9 Kaprao can be grown as a perennial in frost-free microclimates, returning from roots or self-seeding abundantly. The plants flower quickly in long summer days — pinch frequently to maintain vegetative growth if leaf production is the goal.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Kaprao (กะเพรา in Thai, pronounced 'kra-pao') is the specific holy basil type used in Thai cooking — its clove-and-pepper-forward flavor with a faint anise note and spicy heat is the defining herb of pad kra pao (stir-fried basil), Thailand's most popular everyday dish. While all holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum) has the characteristic clove-spice aroma from eugenol, the Kaprao type selected for Thai cooking has a particularly pungent, peppery quality and narrow, slightly serrated leaves that are used exclusively in their cooked form — unlike Italian sweet basil or Vietnamese basil, Kaprao is wilted into hot wok dishes where the heat activates and transforms the volatile oils. The fresh leaves cannot be substituted by Italian sweet basil in pad kra pao, as the clove-pepper flavor profile is essential to the dish. In zone 9 Kaprao thrives in the hot, humid summers that are close to its native tropical Thai climate, performing far better than sweet basil in the season's peak heat.

plant_note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall; in zone 9 plant year-round except in peak summer heat. Kentucky Colonel spreads aggressively by underground runners — plant in a buried container or with root barriers to prevent takeover of surrounding beds. In zone 9 partial shade reduces aggressive spread while maintaining large, high-quality leaves; harvest frequently to prevent flowering, which diminishes leaf flavor. Cut to the ground after flowering and the plant will regenerate with fresh, flavorful new growth.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil — mint thrives with consistent moisture and morning sun with afternoon shade protection; Kentucky Colonel is widely considered the finest spearmint cultivar for culinary use, producing very large, broad, slightly crinkled, bright green leaves with a smooth, intensely sweet, clean spearmint fragrance and flavor that is more refined and less harsh than standard commercial spearmint. The large leaf size makes Kentucky Colonel practical for fresh cocktail garnishes (mint juleps, mojitos), cold drinks, and herb preparations where leaf presentation matters — the substantial leaves are picked individually for floating in glasses or bruising for infusions, rather than stripped from stems. The Kentucky Colonel name connects this variety to the classic bourbon-and-mint culture of Kentucky where spearmint was historically associated with the mint julep tradition — the sweet spearmint character complements bourbon's caramel and vanilla notes without the sharp mentholated edge of peppermint. Kentucky Colonel is also excellent in iced tea, fruit salads, desserts, and fresh herb sauces where a classic spearmint flavor is desired.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4–6 weeks early in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean mint self-sows freely and often maintains a persistent colony by self-seeding in suitable conditions.
directions: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Korean mint (Korean hyssop) is an East Asian culinary and medicinal herb with large, anise-mint-scented leaves used fresh in Korean, Vietnamese, and Chinese cooking — particularly in ssam (lettuce wrap), salads, and teas — and dense spikes of lavender-purple to pink flowers from midsummer through fall that attract extraordinary numbers of bees and swallowtail butterflies. Distinctly different from the North American native A. foeniculum (anise hyssop) in flavor and growing conditions, though botanically similar. More heat-tolerant and easier in southern gardens. Self-sows freely once established; leave some spent flower stalks for seed to maintain the colony.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil or transplant seedlings; Korean perilla (kkaennip) is distinct from Japanese shiso in having larger, thicker, rounder, more strongly aromatic leaves with a more complex anise-mint-basil fragrance used extensively in Korean cuisine as a ssam wrap leaf, banchan pickle, and seasoning — one of the most important herbs in Korean cooking.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface (they need light to germinate) or barely cover; Korean perilla self-seeds prolifically and will return each year once established — deadhead if you want to control spread. Perilla frutescens var. japonica (Korean perilla, kkaennip, also called Korean sesame leaf or Korean mint) is distinct from the Japanese shiso (var. crispa) in its larger size, rounder leaf shape, flat rather than crinkled leaf margin, thicker leaf texture, and stronger, more complex fragrance — a blend of anise, mint, basil, and sesame that is deeply characteristic of Korean cuisine. The large (3–5 inch), round-oval, bright green leaves (occasionally flushed with purple on the underside) are used in Korean cooking in numerous ways: as ssam wraps for grilled meats (samgyeopsal, bulgogi), as perilla kimchi (kkaennip kimchi), marinated in soy and sesame as a banchan side dish, fried in batter as pajeon ingredients, and as a culinary herb in soups and stews. Distinguished from Japanese shiso by larger leaf size and the more potent, less floral fragrance. Excellent for hot, humid Gulf Coast gardens where it thrives in summer heat; tolerates partial shade.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Korintje cinnamon is slightly more cold-tolerant than Ceylon cinnamon and may survive light frosts to 28°F in protected locations in zone 8b.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist to well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun in zones 9–12; Korintje cinnamon is an Indonesian species from Sumatra that is actually the most commonly sold type of cinnamon in the United States under the generic label 'cinnamon' — accounting for the majority of commercial cinnamon imports. Named for Kota Kerinci in Sumatra, it produces thick, dark-brown bark quills with a strong, mildly sweet flavor intermediate between Ceylon and Chinese cassia cinnamons. The bark is harvested from trees 3–4 years after planting by stripping young branches; coppicing the trees stimulates new shoot production for repeated harvests. Like all commercial cinnamon, the attractive, broad, three-veined leaves are also aromatic when crushed. In zone 9–11, it grows well outdoors as a multi-stemmed shrub or small tree; regular harvesting of branches maintains a bushy, productive form suitable for the home garden.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; seed needs light to germinate and should not be covered.
directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; pinch flower spikes regularly to keep the plant bushy and productive. Krishna is the deep purple-leaved, purple-stemmed form of holy basil (tulsi), named for the Hindu deity traditionally depicted with dark blue-purple skin, and valued both for its striking ornamental coloring and its more intensely spicy, peppery, clove-forward flavor compared to the milder green Rama type. The rich purple foliage and purple-tinged flower spikes make it as much an ornamental accent for a sunny herb bed as a culinary and tea herb, and its stronger flavor makes it a favorite for those who prefer a more assertive tulsi tea. Like other holy basil types, it is considered sacred in Hindu tradition and is easy to grow in a warm, sunny herb garden through the summer. Zone 10–12 or as a warm-season annual elsewhere.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in fall for cold stratification over winter, or sow in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline, calcareous soil in full sun to light partial shade; lady's bedstraw is a plant of dry grasslands, hedgerows, and coastal dunes — it spreads by slender rhizomes to form loose, scrambling mats and naturalizes readily in dry, sunny, wild garden settings.
directions: Galium verum is a slender, scrambling, rhizomatous perennial herb of dry grasslands and hedgerows throughout Europe and temperate Asia, producing whorls of very fine, needle-like, dark-green leaves along square stems and masses of tiny, four-petaled, honey-scented, bright-yellow flowers in dense, frothy panicles from early to mid summer; the whole plant when dried emits a pleasant, sweet, coumarin-like (new-mown hay) fragrance. Direct-sow seeds in fall in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline, calcareous soil in a sunny or lightly shaded position; seeds benefit from cold stratification and germinate most reliably after a natural winter cold period — established plants spread by shallow rhizomes to form loose, weed-suppressing mats. Lady's bedstraw has a rich history of traditional use: the flowering tops were used to curdle milk in cheese-making (especially for Cheshire and Gloucester cheeses, as a vegetable rennet substitute), and the roots yield a warm red to orange dye with an alum mordant, while the stems and flowers produce yellow; the dried plant was historically stuffed into mattresses and strewn underfoot for its pleasant scent and supposed flea-repelling properties. Tolerant of drought and coastal conditions once established; excellent for naturalizing in wild or meadow gardens with other dry-grassland species.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant only after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: This sweet Italian basil is grown for its unusually large, aromatic leaves and slow-bolting habit that stretches the harvest for pesto and fresh cooking. Start seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost and keep it warm, since basil resents cold soil. Transplant into rich, well-drained ground in full sun once nights stay reliably above fifty degrees. Pinch flowering tips regularly to keep the plant bushy and encourage a steady supply of tender leaves.

plant_note: Plant container plants or start from seed (seeds are tiny; surface-sow in spring on moist medium and do not cover) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; calamint prefers a position sheltered from drying winds and produces the most flowers with a few hours of afternoon shade in hot climates.
directions: Calamintha grandiflora is the showiest of the calamlints, producing soft, aromatic, mint-scented foliage and large (for the genus), vivid pink, tubular, two-lipped flowers in whorled clusters from late spring through early fall that are extraordinarily attractive to bumblebees and are among the most bumblebee-visited ornamental herbs in British and European garden trials. The leaves and young shoots have a strong, pleasant, minty-oregano flavor and can be used fresh or dried as a seasoning and herbal tea; the flavor is similar to but more delicate than wild mountain oregano.

plant_note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer or plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; lavandin does not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively. It is more vigorous and faster-growing than English lavender. Grosso is the most widely planted cultivar for oil production and dried bundles; Provence and Fred Boutin are also excellent landscape cultivars.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; lavandin is a naturally occurring and cultivated hybrid between English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) and spike lavender (L. latifolia) that has become the dominant commercial lavender worldwide — over 90 percent of the lavender essential oil sold globally comes from lavandin rather than true English lavender. It is larger, more vigorous, and more heat- and drought-tolerant than English lavender, with longer, more branched flower spikes and a stronger scent that is higher in camphor and has a slightly sharper, more penetrating quality than the pure English lavender fragrance. As a sterile hybrid, it produces no viable seed but blooms heavily and reliably. The cultivar Grosso produces the most oil and the largest, most dramatic dried bundles; Provence is the classic lavender-field cultivar of the Provence region of France. Excellent for mass planting, dried flower production, cut flowers, and herb gardens. Slightly less cold-hardy than English lavender but more heat-tolerant in zones 7-8.

common_name: Leisure Cilantro (Classic Open-Pollinated Slow-Bolt Cilantro for Leaf Production)
plant_note: Direct sow only in cool soil; does not transplant well. In zone 9, plant October–November for fall-winter production or February–March for a brief spring crop. Leisure is one of the classic open-pollinated slow-bolt cilantro varieties — selected specifically for delayed bolting (the rush to flower and seed that ends leaf production) compared to standard varieties. The 'slow-bolt' trait means Leisure stays in leaf-producing mode for a longer period under warming conditions than standard cilantro varieties, extending the productive harvest window in spring gardens. This is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the spring temperature rise is rapid and cilantro planted in late February may have only a short window before bolting; Leisure's extended slow-bolt characteristic can add 2–3 weeks of productive leaf harvest in spring conditions. The leaves are typical broad, flat cilantro foliage with the standard cilantro flavor.
directions: Direct sow thinly in cool soil; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest outer leaves successively before bolting. Leisure Cilantro is one of the most widely recommended open-pollinated cilantro varieties for home gardeners specifically wanting maximum leaf production before the plant bolts to seed. All cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) is genetically programmed to flower — it is an annual that must complete its seed cycle — but the timing and speed of this transition from vegetative (leaf-producing) growth to reproductive (flower/seed) growth varies considerably among cultivated varieties, and selecting for delayed bolting has been a primary breeding objective in cilantro improvement since leaf herb production became the primary commercial use of the crop in North America. Leisure was selected from open-pollinated cilantro populations for its consistent tendency to remain in vegetative leaf production mode longer than standard unselected populations, particularly as temperatures increase in spring. This character is not the same as the more dramatically extended bolt resistance of F1 hybrid varieties like Calypso, but it is meaningfully better than generic cilantro seed and substantially better than truly fast-bolting varieties. For zone 9 gardeners, the distinction matters: in the rapid spring temperature rise of the Gulf Coast (February through April), even 2–3 extra weeks of leaf production before bolting is a meaningful difference in total harvest. Leisure's open-pollinated status means seed can be saved from selected late-bolting individual plants to potentially improve the variety further for local conditions over successive generations.

plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost or start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; lemon balm germinates readily in cool soil and grows vigorously in full sun to partial shade, tolerating more shade than most herbs.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or direct sow outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon balm tolerates more shade than most herbs and is one of the few culinary herbs that produces acceptable quality even in partially shaded sites. Melissa officinalis is a vigorous, lemon-scented European perennial in the mint family producing wrinkled, oval, toothed leaves with a delightful fresh lemon fragrance used in teas, lemonade, salads, fish dishes, poultry, desserts, and liqueurs; it is much milder and more pleasant than lemon verbena for fresh use. Cut plants back hard after flowering to prevent aggressive self-seeding and to stimulate a flush of fresh, fragrant new leaves; in the Gulf South it often dies back in summer heat but re-emerges in fall. Harvest before flowering for best fragrance and flavor.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall; Aurea lemon balm establishes readily in cool, moist conditions. In zone 9 plant September–November for fall establishment or January–March for spring. The golden variegation is most intense in spring and fall; summer heat may cause the foliage to revert to mostly green. Divide crowded clumps every 2–3 years in early spring.
directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, well-drained soil; Lemon Balm Aurea (also known as Golden Lemon Balm or Variegated Lemon Balm) is a cultivar of common lemon balm distinguished by brilliant gold-splashed, yellow-green variegated foliage in spring and early fall — the leaves are irregularly mottled with golden-yellow against the base green, giving the plant an ornamental quality entirely absent from plain lemon balm. The lemon fragrance is identical to the species, and the leaves have the same culinary and herbal uses — teas, desserts, liqueurs, and salads — with the added benefit of attractive foliage that makes this herb garden-worthy as an ornamental. In hot zone 9 summers the gold variegation tends to fade to mostly green as the plant responds to heat stress; for the best color effect, grow in partial shade and harvest the brightest spring leaves for culinary use. The plant spreads by self-sowing in fertile soils; deadhead before seed set to prevent naturalizing.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 9 sow March–June. Lemon basil matures and begins bolting earlier than sweet basil — pinch flower buds regularly to extend the leaf harvest. In zone 9 it thrives in the summer heat and high humidity that sometimes stresses sweet basil with fungal issues; lemon basil's somewhat different metabolism makes it a useful alternative for summer herb gardens. The fresh lemon fragrance is particularly strong when leaves are pinched or bruised. Plants self-seed freely in warm conditions — allow a few plants to set seed for volunteer seedlings in subsequent seasons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Lemon Basil is a hybrid basil (Ocimum basilicum x O. americanum) producing smaller, narrower leaves with a distinctive, intense lemon-citrus fragrance and flavor that is completely different from the clove-anise profile of sweet basil — substituting citrus brightness for the classic basil complexity. The lemon flavor is genuine and strong, derived from citral and other lemon-fragrance compounds in the leaf oils, making lemon basil specifically useful in preparations where lemon and herb flavors are desired simultaneously: Thai cuisine (where it is a traditional herb in certain dishes), lemon herb sauces, seafood seasoning, herbed rice, and tea. The compact, fine-textured leaves and upright, branching habit create a smaller, more refined plant than sweet basil — typically 18–24 inches tall with many small branches each tipped with the small, narrow, lemon-scented leaves. Lemon basil is one of the most immediately identifiable herb plants in the garden for visitors unfamiliar with it — the combination of basil's visual character and the unexpected lemon fragrance when leaves are touched creates a memorable sensory experience that makes it a particularly effective plant for teaching about herb gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant only after nights are reliably above 50°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 in deep in warm seed-starting mix at 70°F or above; germination is rapid once soil temperature is adequate. Transplant into rich, well-drained garden soil in full sun and pinch the growing tip early to encourage a bushy, multi-stemmed plant. Lemon basil is compact compared to sweet basil and has a distinct citrus fragrance from the presence of citral; it pairs well with fish, poultry, and Southeast Asian cuisines. Harvest by snipping stems just above a leaf pair once plants are well established, and pinch flower buds promptly to extend the harvest season.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4 weeks before last frost; lemon catnip self-seeds freely once established.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of well-drained starting mix and press in lightly; fresh seeds germinate readily in 1–2 weeks. Lemon catnip has all the nepetalactone chemistry of common catnip (making it equally irresistible to cats) but its foliage carries a pleasant lemon-mint scent suitable for tea and aromatherapy. Grow in full sun in any well-drained soil; cut plants back by half after the first flush of flowers to encourage a second bloom and fresh aromatic foliage. Harvest stems before flowers fully open for the best flavor in herbal teas; dry quickly in a warm, airy spot and store in airtight containers.

common_name: Lemon Frost Thyme (Variegated Lemon-Scented Groundcover Thyme)
plant_note: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun; Lemon Frost combines finely variegated, cream-edged foliage with a strong lemon fragrance, providing both ornamental interest and culinary use as a low, spreading thyme.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in sharply drained, alkaline to neutral, poor to average soil in full sun. Lemon Frost is a variegated selection of lemon thyme, its small, gray-green leaves edged in creamy white for a frosted, two-tone effect that stands out clearly against plain green groundcovers and adds brightness to a rock garden or herb bed even before it flowers. Crushed foliage releases a strong, clean lemon fragrance along with the characteristic thyme aroma, and the leaves are fully usable in the kitchen anywhere a citrusy thyme flavor is wanted, from roasted chicken to herbal tea. Small pale lavender-pink flowers appear in early summer and attract bees, though the foliage color and fragrance remain the plant's main appeal through the rest of the season. Like other creeping thymes, it thrives in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and struggles in rich, moist, or poorly drained conditions, which promote rot and reduce the intensity of both flavor and fragrance. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, tidy mat and encourage fresh, brightly variegated new growth.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist perlite or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile potting mix or garden soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; lemon geranium prefers slightly drier conditions than many herbs — allow the soil to dry moderately between waterings to avoid root rot.
directions: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; lemon geranium is a South African scented-leaf pelargonium with intensely lemon-scented, small, crinkled, fan-shaped leaves that release a remarkably true, clean lemon fragrance — not the synthetic-citrus scent of lemon verbena but a pure, fresh, clear lemon aroma that is one of the finest natural citrus scents available in an herb garden plant. The leaves are used to flavor sugar, baked goods, tea, jellies, and custards; placed in the bottom of a greased cake pan before adding batter, they impart a delicate lemon perfume to pound cake and sponge cakes. Small, pale-pink to lavender flowers appear at intervals. Unlike most pelargoniums, lemon geranium tolerates partial shade acceptably, though it flowers most heavily in full sun. In zones 9–11 it grows as a perennial sub-shrub; elsewhere it is grown as a container plant brought indoors in autumn. 'Prince Rupert' (upright, strong-growing), 'French Lace' (compact, cream-variegated leaves), and 'Cy's Sunburst' are notable cultivars.

plant_note: Surface sow; benefits from a period of cool moisture to break dormancy.
directions: Also called lemon bee balm or horsemint, this aromatic Monarda produces tiered whorls of lavender-pink blooms that draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. Surface sow the seed where plants are to grow, pressing it in for good contact, and expect uneven germination over two to three weeks. It thrives in full sun and average, well-drained soil and self-sows to return year after year. Harvest fragrant foliage for tea and leave some flowers standing to feed pollinators.

plant_note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, moist soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon myrtle grows slowly, reaching 6–8 feet over many years in most garden situations. It is frost-sensitive and performs best in zone 9b–11 where freezes are rare or light.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; lemon myrtle is an Australian native rainforest tree with the most intensely concentrated lemon fragrance of any plant on Earth — the essential oil content of the leaves (95% citral) vastly exceeds that of lemon balm, lemon verbena, or lemon thyme. Fresh or dried leaves are used in cooking exactly as lemon is used, in teas, baked goods, sauces, marinades, ice cream, and fish dishes, with a clean, pure lemon flavor that holds up better to heat than actual lemon juice. It is increasingly popular as a culinary specialty herb in Zone 9–11 gardens in the US, particularly in coastal California and the Gulf Coast. The shiny, oval, evergreen leaves are attractive year-round, and small clusters of white flowers appear in summer. It makes an excellent large container specimen in colder zones that can be moved to protection before frost. Harvest leaves fresh as needed or dry for long-term use.

plant_note: Root softwood cuttings in spring or summer in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; lemon thyme does not come true from seed and must be propagated vegetatively to maintain the lemon fragrance. Cultivars include Aureus (gold-variegated leaves) and Silver Queen (cream-variegated leaves), both ornamental and culinary. Trim after flowering to prevent woodiness.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; lemon thyme provides the same low-growing, woody-stemmed, small-leafed thyme habit as common thyme but with distinctly and strongly lemon-scented foliage from the volatile oil constituents geraniol and linalool. The lemon fragrance is immediately apparent on touching the leaves and makes lemon thyme particularly valuable for fish dishes, roasted poultry, herb butters, cream sauces, and lemon-scented baked goods where a citrus-thyme combination is desired. Pale-pink to lavender-pink flowers in early summer attract bees and other pollinators. The variegated cultivars Aureus (golden-edged leaves) and Silver Queen (cream-variegated) add bright foliage color to the herb garden edge, rock garden, or container planting while retaining the full lemon-thyme culinary flavor. Grows identically to common thyme in its requirements for very well-drained, lean soil and full sun exposure.

plant_note: Plant container divisions in spring in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; lemon thyme requires excellent drainage and lean soil — in zone 9's summer heat and humidity, poorly drained soil causes crown rot. Raised beds and containers with gritty mix are ideal in zone 9.
directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral, gritty soil in full sun; Lemon thyme is a hybrid thyme with an intensely pleasant lemon-citrus fragrance and flavor overlaid on the traditional thyme aromatic — the combination of thyme's herbal character with a bright, clean citrus note makes lemon thyme one of the most useful and distinctive culinary herbs for fish, poultry, tea, desserts, and anywhere a citrus-thyme combination is desired. The low, spreading, mat-forming habit (4–8 inches tall, spreading 12–18 inches) is elegant in rock gardens, between stepping stones, and as a fragrant ground cover in well-drained, sunny areas. In summer, small pale-pink to lavender flowers attract bees. The most commonly grown lemon thyme cultivar is 'Silver Queen' — a variegated selection with silver-margined green leaves that adds ornamental value to the culinary utility. 'Aureus' (Gold Lemon Thyme) has yellow-variegated leaves. The plain green form provides the most intense flavor. In zone 9's summer humidity, lemon thyme is the most heat-sensitive common thyme — it benefits from afternoon shade during peak summer heat and absolutely requires sharp drainage to survive zone 9 summers. Container culture in a porous mix with excellent drainage is often the most reliable approach in Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Transplant rooted cuttings outdoors after all frost danger has passed; bring containers indoors before the first autumn frost.
directions: Propagate from softwood cuttings taken in summer rather than from seed, which has poor viability; root cuttings in moist perlite under plastic until rooted. Plant in full sun and well-drained soil; in zones below 8 grow in containers that can be overwintered indoors in a cool, bright spot. Prune hard in spring when new growth emerges from what may look like dead wood — lemon verbena is often a slow riser after dormancy. Harvest leaves any time for intensely lemon-scented tea, dessert flavoring, and potpourri; fragrance peaks just before the plant begins to flower.

plant_note: Transplant divisions or rooted stalks after last frost when soil is reliably warm.
directions: Propagate by placing fresh grocery-store stalks (with roots intact) in water until roots develop, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Lemongrass needs heat and consistent moisture; water deeply and regularly during the growing season. In zones below 10, grow in large containers and bring indoors before first frost, cutting back to 6 in tall. Harvest outer stalks by cutting or twisting at the base when they reach pencil thickness; use the pale, tender base for cooking.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds in spring in well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; lesser calamint thrives in dry, sunny conditions and poor, stony or chalky soils — rich, moist soil reduces the intensity of its minty-peppery fragrance and flowering abundance.
directions: Calamintha nepeta is a compact, bushy, aromatic perennial of the mint family (Lamiaceae) native to dry, sunny grasslands, rocky hillsides, and chalky banks throughout southern and central Europe, producing small, softly hairy, gray-green, rounded leaves with an exceptionally pleasant minty-peppery-oregano fragrance and an unusually long succession of tiny, two-lipped, white to pale-lilac flowers from July through September that make it one of the single best perennial plants for attracting native bees, bumblebees, and other pollinators. Direct-sow seeds in spring in very well-drained, lean, neutral to alkaline, preferably chalky or stony soil in full sun; it is summer drought-tolerant once established, requiring minimal irrigation in well-drained soils, and will decline in rich, moist, or waterlogged conditions. Lesser calamint has an ancient culinary history in Mediterranean Europe: the leaves and flowering tops are used fresh or dried as a flavoring for roasted meats (particularly in Italian cuisine, where it is sometimes called nipitella and used with porcini mushrooms), as a tisane, and as an aromatic addition to salads. Shear plants by about one-third after the first main flush of bloom to maintain tidiness and encourage a second flowering period; plants self-sow moderately and naturalize well on dry banks, gravel paths, and in dry-stone wall crevices.

common_name: Lesser Galangal (Small Thai Cooking Galangal Root Herb)
plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; lesser galangal is smaller and more compact than greater galangal (A. galanga) and appropriate for container growing — a useful option for zone 9 gardeners who want to move the plant indoors during hard freezes.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Lesser Galangal (Alpinia officinarum) is a rhizomatous herb from southern China and Southeast Asia grown for its aromatic rhizomes, which provide the distinctive peppery-gingery-citrusy flavor that is essential to Thai tom kha soup, Thai curries, Indonesian laksa, and numerous other Southeast Asian dishes. The flavor differs significantly from ginger — sharper, more peppery, with pine and citrus overtones — and from greater galangal (A. galanga) which is milder and more floral. The smaller stature of lesser galangal (2–3 feet) compared to the 5–6 foot greater galangal makes it more manageable in typical garden settings and suitable for large containers. The rhizomes can be harvested from the edge of established clumps after the first year without disturbing the entire plant — a sustained harvest approach that allows the clump to continue producing indefinitely. In Gulf South gardens, lesser galangal thrives in the warm, humid conditions similar to those of its native growing range. The ornamental narrow leaves and occasional small white-and-red flower spikes provide year-round interest as a foliage plant in partial-shade tropical herb gardens. The rhizomes freeze and can be grated directly from frozen state for cooking, making storage simple.

plant_note: Warmth-loving; transplant after soil warms.
directions: This exceptionally productive sweet basil produces huge, light green leaves nearly the size of your hand that are more sweet than spicy. The broad leaves make an excellent lettuce substitute in wraps and sandwiches or a bold layer in a caprese salad. Start seed indoors in warmth and move to a sunny bed only after frost danger has passed. Keep soil evenly moist, pinch off flower spikes, and harvest whole leaves to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost after scarifying or soaking seed overnight; transplant carefully after frost danger passes to avoid disturbing roots.
directions: Scarify seed coat lightly with sandpaper or soak overnight before sowing 1/4 in deep in warm starting mix; germination improves significantly with this treatment. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — licorice develops an extensive, deep root system and resents being moved. Roots are ready to harvest in the third or fourth autumn when they are at least pencil-thick, digging carefully to extract as much of the lateral root run as possible. The dried root is used medicinally as a demulcent and anti-inflammatory for digestive and respiratory conditions; note that excessive consumption raises blood pressure.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 weeks early or direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring and August for fall. Licorice basil's anise oils are most concentrated when the plant is slightly stressed from heat — zone 9 summer conditions bring out the best aroma. Pinch flower heads regularly to maintain leaf production and oil concentration.
directions: Transplant or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; licorice basil is a large-leaf sweet basil cultivar with an extraordinarily intense anise-licorice aroma — significantly more pronounced than standard Genovese basil — arising from exceptionally high methyl chavicol (estragole) concentration in the essential oil. The wide, dark green, slightly cupped leaves are 2–3 inches long with purple-tinged flower bracts that make the plant quite ornamental when in bloom. Licorice basil is prized for Thai-inspired cooking, Vietnamese-style salads, and beverages where a prominent anise note is desired — it is also used in cocktails, syrups, and infused vinegars. The flavor is distinctly different from Cinnamon or Thai basil types despite also containing high methyl chavicol. In zone 9 the plant performs best in spring and fall, but continues producing through summer with regular pinching and irrigation.

plant_note: Chartreuse foliage; light-dependent seed.
directions: Surface-sow indoors 8 weeks before last frost, leaving seed uncovered since light aids germination. This golden-leaved anise hyssop offers licorice-scented foliage for teas and blue flower spikes for pollinators. Transplant to full sun in well-drained soil, spacing to allow good airflow. Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering into fall and prevent excessive self-seeding. Harvest leaves and flowers fresh or dried and cut plants back after frost.

plant_note: Plant root divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained, deeply tilled, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep, sandy-loam soil in full sun; licorice root requires a deep, well-drained, fertile growing site and 2–3 years of growth before the roots are ready to harvest — the sweet, anise-flavored roots contain glycyrrhizin, a compound 50 times sweeter than sucrose, used in confectionery, pharmaceuticals, and herbal medicine.
directions: Plant root divisions in deeply tilled, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, deep soil in full sun; harvest roots in fall of years 2–3. Glycyrrhiza glabra (licorice root or Spanish licorice) is the plant behind all licorice flavoring in candy, herbal teas, and medicine — a perennial Mediterranean and Central Asian leguminous herb producing sweet, tan-skinned taproot stubs extending 3–4 feet into the soil. The roots contain glycyrrhizin, a saponin compound approximately 30–50 times sweeter than sucrose, responsible for the characteristic sweet, anise-like, distinctive licorice flavor. Licorice root has been used medicinally for over 4,000 years — in ancient Egypt, China, India, and Greece — as a treatment for coughs, digestive disorders, and ulcers; it remains one of the most widely used herbal medicines worldwide, used in pharmaceuticals as a sweetening and flavoring agent for bitter medicines (the name 'licorice' comes from the Greek for 'sweet root'). CAUTION: Overconsumption of licorice root or glycyrrhizin can cause hypertension, potassium loss, and hormonal effects — not for excessive use, and problematic for those with high blood pressure or heart conditions. As a garden plant, licorice grows as a multi-stemmed, pinnately-leafed, attractive perennial shrub with pale lavender flowers — harvest roots in the fall of year 2 or 3 for best glycyrrhizin content.

plant_note: Direct-sow into warm soil after frost.
directions: Direct-sow after the soil warms past 65F, scattering seed thinly and thinning to a hand's width apart. The bright citrus scent makes this basil superb in Southeast Asian dishes and cold drinks. Give it full sun and steady moisture in rich, free-draining soil for the best oil content. Pinch growing tips early to build a bushy plant and delay bolting. Harvest leaves in the morning when the fragrant oils are most concentrated.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March–May and again in August–September for a fall crop. Lime Basil prefers slightly cooler conditions than standard sweet basil and may bolt more quickly in extreme heat — providing afternoon shade in zone 9 summer extends the productive season. Pinch flower buds regularly to keep plants productive. The small leaves and compact habit make it well-suited to container growing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Lime Basil is an Ocimum x citriodorum hybrid selected for an intense natural lime-citrus fragrance and flavor derived from high concentrations of limonene, citral, and related volatile compounds in the leaves — the aroma is strikingly and unmistakably lime, not just vaguely citrus as with some other basil varieties. The small, pointed bright green leaves have a fresh, bright citrus-lime character distinctly different from standard sweet basil (which contains primarily linalool and estragole). The lime flavor makes it a natural pairing for Thai and Vietnamese cuisines where lime leaves are traditional (dried Lime Basil can partially substitute for kaffir lime leaf), in fresh salsas, tropical fruit salads, seafood dishes, limeade, and cocktails. The compact, neat habit with small leaves is attractive in herb gardens. Like all basil, Lime Basil is frost-tender and performs best in warm weather, though it is somewhat more heat-tolerant than lemon basil.

plant_note: Set out after frost danger; grow in a pot where winters fall below 20 F so it can overwinter indoors.
directions: Little Ragu is a compact, upright form of culinary sweet bay with aromatic evergreen leaves used fresh or dried in soups and stews. It stays tidy at 6 to 8 feet and takes well to pruning or shaping in containers. Plant in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil and let the surface dry slightly between waterings, as it dislikes soggy roots. In cold-winter areas grow it in a pot and bring it into a cool, bright spot before hard frost. Harvest mature leaves any time and dry them for the strongest flavor.

plant_note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container-grown young trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil; linden is one of the great street and park trees of Europe and North America, tolerating pollution, pruning, and urban conditions better than most large trees.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, fertile soil; littleleaf linden (Tilia cordata) is one of the most important medicinal trees of Europe, grown primarily for its fragrant, pale yellow flower clusters (collected with the distinctive wing-like bract) that are dried to make tilleul tea — one of the classic European herbal teas with a pleasant mild flavor and traditional use for relaxation, sleep, cold and flu, and anxiety. The flowers, which appear in June-July, are intensely attractive to bees and are considered one of the finest sources of honey in Europe; linden honey is a premium product. The tree itself is magnificent, developing deeply furrowed bark and a broad, rounded crown that provides excellent shade. Leaves are edible as salad greens in spring when young and tender.

common_name: Long Island Improved Dill (Classic Standard Dill Variety for Leaf and Seed Harvest)
plant_note: Direct sow only — dill does not transplant well; plant in early spring several weeks before last frost or in fall in zone 9. Long Island Improved is one of the classic American dill varieties, selected as a standard cultivar for both dill weed (leaf) production and dill seed harvest. In zone 9, plant October–November for fall-winter production (the best season) and February–March for a short spring crop that bolts with summer heat. Unlike Dukat dill (selected for leaf oil content), Long Island Improved is a dual-purpose variety with good leaf production and large, well-formed seed heads appropriate for dill seed harvest and pickling. The plants grow tall (3–4 feet) with the characteristic blue-green ferny foliage, and produce flat-topped flower umbels that dry to attractive seed heads.
directions: Direct sow in cool soil; thin to 6–12 inches. For seed harvest, allow plants to flower and seed heads to mature and begin to brown. Long Island Improved Dill is a classic American named dill variety that has been one of the standard cultivars in the United States seed trade for many decades — one of the most widely available and commonly grown dill varieties in home and market garden production. The 'Long Island' designation reflects its association with New York's Long Island, which was a major center of market garden and specialty crop production in the 19th and early 20th centuries, with many vegetable varieties named for the region (Long Island Cheese Pumpkin, Long Island Improved Brussels Sprouts). Unlike the more recent specialty dill cultivars selected for specific properties (Dukat for high leaf oil, Fernleaf for dwarf compact habit), Long Island Improved is a classic standard selection valued for its combination of good leaf production and excellent seed head development — the characteristic that makes it a true dual-purpose variety useful for both dill weed (fresh and dried leaf) and dill seed harvest. The seed heads of Long Island Improved are large, flat-topped umbels that dry well for use in pickling (dill seed is the primary flavoring agent in dill pickles), in dill vinegar, and as a dried floral/culinary ingredient. The seeds are held firmly in the umbel until fully ripe and begin to shatter as the seed head fully dries — harvest by cutting the entire seed head when seeds have changed from green to tan-brown but before significant shattering begins. For zone 9 gardeners wanting dill seeds for pickling their summer cucumbers, Long Island Improved's good seed head development makes it the classic choice.

plant_note: Propagate from stem cuttings — seed is rarely available; grow in tropical conditions or in containers brought indoors in winter; requires high humidity and consistent warmth.
directions: Root stem cuttings in warm, humid conditions and grow in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade to dappled light; long pepper is the historical precursor to black pepper in European and Mediterranean cuisines, used extensively from ancient Rome through the medieval period before the black pepper trade displaced it. The elongated catkin-like fruits (1–2 inches long) have a rich, complex heat distinct from black pepper — sweeter, more aromatic, with a slight numbing quality and notes of cinnamon and ginger. A tropical climbing vine that needs support and high humidity; it performs year-round outdoors in zone 10–12 and makes an unusual and rewarding container plant moved inside during cool months. Harvest green or ripe red and dry completely for long storage.

plant_note: Direct sow in succession; cilantro dislikes transplanting and bolts in heat.
directions: Also known as Chinese parsley, this variety is selected for excellent flavor, extra leafiness, and slow bolting, giving you a longer cilantro harvest. Direct sow into cool soil since the taproot resents transplanting, and make successive sowings every few weeks for a steady supply. Provide full sun in cool weather or light afternoon shade as temperatures climb to delay flowering. Let some plants bolt and set seed to harvest coriander for the spice rack.

plant_note: Direct-sow fresh seed in fall as soon as it ripens, or in early spring in moist, fertile, deeply dug soil in full sun to partial shade; lovage seed loses viability quickly — always sow fresh seed and expect germination in the first spring after fall sowing, or within 2–3 weeks of spring sowing at cool soil temperatures.
directions: Levisticum officinale is a bold, statuesque perennial herb of the carrot family (Apiaceae) native to the mountains of southern Europe, producing deeply divided, dark, glossy-green leaves with a powerful, unmistakable flavor of intensified celery — a single large plant can supply a household with celery-like flavoring throughout the growing season from every part: leaves, stems, seeds, and roots. Direct-sow fresh seed in fall in moist, deeply dug, fertile, well-drained to moisture-retentive soil in full sun or light partial shade; seed viability drops sharply after the first year, so always sow the freshest seed available. Once established, lovage grows to 4–6 feet tall with hollow, celery-scented stems and large umbels of small, greenish-yellow flowers in early summer — plants should be cut back hard after flowering to encourage a second flush of tender, flavorful young foliage. Harvest young leaves and stems freely throughout the season for use in soups, stocks, stews, and salads where celery flavor is desired; seeds can be used as a spice and dried roots are used in traditional herbal preparations.

plant_note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost (cold-moist stratify 3–4 weeks for best germination) and transplant out after frost, or divide established clumps in spring or fall, into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.
directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near pond edges, rain gardens, or low woodland spots; does not tolerate prolonged drought. Scutellaria lateriflora (mad-dog skullcap) is a native wetland and streamside perennial in the mint family, grown for its small blue-to-violet, two-lipped flowers that line the leaf axils in a distinctive one-sided (lateriflora) arrangement, and for the aerial parts, which are harvested at flowering and dried for traditional calming herbal preparations. Despite the common name, the plant is not associated with rabies — the name stems from historical folk use as a treatment for rabid-animal bites. It spreads by rhizomes into loose colonies in reliably damp ground and is a good choice for the moist partial-shade margins of a rain garden or bog bed, where it also attracts small native bees. Zone 3–9.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, deeply cultivated soil in full sun in zone 5–9; Madder is a sprawling, climbing perennial native to the eastern Mediterranean and Western Asia that has been cultivated since ancient times as the primary source of red natural dye — the rose-to-scarlet-to-orange-red pigment alizarin and purpurin extracted from the roots colored textiles, rugs, and art from ancient Egypt through the 19th century until synthetic dyes replaced it.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral, deeply loosened soil in full sun; Rubia tinctorum tolerates drought once established and benefits from calcium-rich soils — add lime to acidic soils and avoid waterlogging. Rubia tinctorum (Madder or Dyer's Madder) is a rambling, rhizomatous, rough-stemmed perennial climbing herb in the Rubiaceae (coffee) family native to the eastern Mediterranean, Turkey, and Central Asia, now widely naturalized across Europe and cultivated by natural dyers worldwide. For more than 5,000 years — documented in Egyptian tomb textiles dating to 1500 BCE, Indian trade records, and Islamic textile traditions — Madder root was the primary source of red, orange, and coral dyes for textiles, wool, silk, and cotton worldwide. The roots contain alizarin (1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone) and purpurin, which when mordanted with alum produce clear reds, with iron produce purples and browns, and with other mordants produce a full spectrum from coral to brick-red to burgundy. Madder root cultivation was an enormous agricultural industry in the Netherlands, France, Turkey, and India from the medieval period until the synthesis of alizarin from coal tar by Perkin in 1869 collapsed the natural dye industry almost overnight. Today Madder is grown by natural dyers, craft textile artists, and historical recreationists who value plant-based dyes. The plants need 2–3 years to produce roots of harvestable size.

plant_note: Plant container-grown or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant year-round, with spring and fall preferred. Majorca Pink rosemary thrives in zone 9 and can be grown as an evergreen perennial shrub. It requires excellent drainage — water pooling around roots is the main cause of failure. Once established it is very drought-tolerant and requires minimal supplemental irrigation. The pink flowers are particularly showy from February through April in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — excellent drainage is more important than soil fertility for rosemary; Majorca Pink is a named cultivar of culinary rosemary distinguished by its delicate pink flowers in contrast to the blue-purple blooms of most rosemary varieties, making it equally valuable as an ornamental flowering shrub and a culinary herb. The upright to slightly spreading habit and profuse pink spring bloom (February–April in zone 9) create a spectacular display in herb gardens, Mediterranean-style landscapes, and edible ornamental borders. The foliage flavor and aroma of Majorca Pink is equivalent to standard rosemary — potent, resinous, piney, with notes of camphor — and it can be used in all the same culinary applications: roasting meats and vegetables, infused oils, herb breads, and as a fresh garnish. In zone 9 Majorca Pink is particularly drought-tolerant and heat-adapted, thriving in the intense summer sun that would stress less robust varieties.

plant_note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; makrut lime is more cold-sensitive than common lime or lemon and requires frost protection below 30°F — best in zone 9b and warmer, or grown in containers brought indoors in winter in zone 9a.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moist, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; protect from temperatures below 28°F. Citrus hystrix (makrut lime, formerly and controversially called kaffir lime) is a Southeast Asian citrus grown primarily for its extraordinary, hourglass-shaped double leaves — two leaves joined end to end — which have an intensely aromatic, complex lime-floral fragrance unlike any other citrus and are indispensable to the flavor profiles of Thai, Indonesian, Cambodian, and Lao cuisines. The fresh or dried leaves flavor curries, soups (Tom Yum), coconut-milk dishes, and rice; they are among the most important flavoring ingredients in Southeast Asian cooking. The small, warty, dark-green, rough-skinned fruits are highly acidic and used primarily for their zest (makrut lime zest is a key ingredient in Thai curry pastes) rather than their juice. The plant is an extremely popular container herb in Thai and Southeast Asian communities across the Gulf South — grown in pots for easy access to fresh leaves year-round and brought indoors when cold threatens. Makrut lime is also used in some natural beauty products for its essential oil.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 transplant February–March and again August for fall production. Mammoth's large leaf size makes it particularly prone to slug and snail damage at transplant; protect young plants until established. Pinch flower stalks promptly to maintain leaf production.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Mammoth basil is prized for its extraordinarily large leaves, regularly reaching 4–6 inches long and 3–4 inches wide — far larger than standard Genovese varieties. The oversized leaves are ideal for making whole-leaf Caprese salad arrangements, individual-leaf wraps, and for presentations where a single perfect leaf is the feature rather than chiffonade. Flavor is standard Genovese-type — sweet, clove-like, aromatic — with no sacrifice in quality for the size increase. The relatively compact plant habit for a large-leaf variety makes Mammoth more manageable than some other large basil types. Pinch flower buds as soon as they appear to maintain leaf production; in zone 9 the plant will bolt in May–June but often rebounds for fall production.

plant_note: Direct sow where it is to grow; the long taproot resents transplanting.
directions: Mammoth dill lives up to its name, reaching at least three feet and sometimes towering to five, with feathery foliage prized for cooking and pickling. Its large flower umbels are magnets for beneficial pollinators, and the plants readily self-sow once seed matures. Direct sow into full sun since the taproot dislikes being moved, and sow in succession for a continuous supply of leaves. Provide staking or a sheltered spot for the tallest plants, and harvest foliage before flowering for the best flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring production or September for fall. Mammoth Long Island dill grows best in cool weather and bolts in summer heat — in zone 9 the spring planting window is brief, making the fall-sown crop the primary harvest. Time sowing so the plant is producing mature seed heads when cucumbers are ready for pickling. The plants can reach 4–5 feet and may need staking in exposed locations.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun — do not transplant; Mammoth Long Island Dill is the classic tall, open-pollinated dill variety grown for over a century in the truck-farming regions of Long Island, New York, and is still the standard for dill pickle production. The large plants reach 4–5 feet with broad, flat seed heads (umbels) 6–8 inches across carrying hundreds of seeds — the seed-head size is the key advantage over compact varieties when the goal is fresh dill seed for pickling, dill vinegar, or dill oil. The seed flavor is stronger, more pungent and aromatic, and more concentrated than leaf dill flavor, and Mammoth Long Island is timed and sized to produce mature seed heads concurrent with cucumber harvest. Both the fresh foliage (dill weed) and the mature seeds are usable. The very tall habit makes the plants dramatic in the back of the herb or vegetable garden and provides early habitat for swallowtail butterfly caterpillars, which feed exclusively on Apiaceae family plants.

common_name: Mammoth Long Island Dill (Tall Classic Dill for Pickling and Abundant Seed Heads)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds thinly in fall (September–November in zone 9) or very early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammoth Long Island can be direct-sown in fall in zone 9 for winter and spring herb harvest and seed production — fall-sown plants often overwinter as rosettes and produce the largest seed heads of any sowing time.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mammoth Long Island is the tall, large-seed-head dill cultivar traditionally grown for pickling and dill seed production — producing the largest seed heads and highest seed yields of common dill varieties, along with an abundance of feathery foliage for fresh and dried dill weed use throughout the season. The name reflects the cultivar's origins in Long Island, New York pickling operations where large seed heads were needed to efficiently pack dill into pickle jars — those large, flat compound umbels of yellow flowers and, later, of aromatic dill seed are the defining feature of the variety, producing proportionally more seed per plant than dwarf and compact varieties. The tall habit (3–5 feet) provides visual presence in the herb garden and creates the feathery, vertical texture that makes dill an attractive ornamental companion for low-growing vegetable crops. In Gulf South zone 9, dill is best grown as a cool-season herb: fall-sown plants establish through the cool months, producing foliage for harvest through winter and spring, then flower and set seed in March–April before summer heat. Fall-grown plants self-sow freely, naturalizing the dill into the garden as a self-renewing herb. Dill foliage is the host plant for black swallowtail butterfly larvae — accepting this graciously means dill does double duty as both herb and butterfly garden plant.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in spring in moist, fertile, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade in zone 8–11; Mango Ginger is a distinctive Indian Curcuma species prized for rhizomes with an unmistakable raw mango (green mango / Mangifera indica) aroma and flavor — without any turmeric or ginger heat — used fresh in South Indian pickles, chutneys, and salads as a seasonal delicacy.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, fertile, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Curcuma amada is dormant in winter — cut back dead foliage after frost, mulch the root zone heavily in zone 8–9 to protect against freezing, and replant or divide in spring. Curcuma amada (Mango Ginger or Amba Haldi) is a clumping, rhizomatous ginger-family perennial native to subtropical India (West Bengal, Odisha, northeast India) and cultivated throughout South Asia for its plump, whitish to pale-yellow rhizomes — valued for the extraordinary raw green mango scent and flavor profile unique to this species within the Curcuma genus, with no heat or turmeric bitterness. The fresh rhizomes are sliced, pickled, or grated in South Indian and Sri Lankan seasonal preparations — particularly the South Indian festival pickle ambahaladi or amada pachadi — and are sold fresh at South Asian markets during the brief harvest season (October–January). The flavor is genuinely mango-like, mild, slightly sour, and entirely distinct from all other gingers. Mango Ginger is an excellent culinary novelty for partial-shade herb gardens in zone 8–11, dying back completely in winter and re-emerging reliably from its persistent rhizome in spring. The inflorescences are also ornamentally attractive: pale-pink, cone-shaped spikes that emerge before the foliage in spring.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring when soil temperature reaches 68°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Mango turmeric thrives in partial shade and performs well under the dappled light of tall trees or on the east side of structures. Harvest rhizomes in late fall when the foliage yellows and dies back, typically October–November in zone 9. In zone 9 the rhizomes can overwinter in the ground with heavy mulching.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in rich, well-drained, moist, humus-rich soil; Mango Turmeric (Curcuma amada) is an Indian ginger-family plant producing rhizomes with a pronounced raw mango aroma and flavor when cut — distinctly different from the warm, earthy, peppery flavor of regular turmeric (Curcuma longa). When the fresh rhizomes are sliced, they release a strongly fruity, tropical aroma with pronounced mango-citrus notes, making them a completely different culinary ingredient from turmeric despite their similar appearance. In Indian cuisine, Mango Turmeric rhizomes are used primarily as a pickle vegetable — sliced and preserved in salt, lemon juice, or vinegar where the bright mango flavor develops into a tart-fruity preserve used as a condiment. The plant is also used in Ayurvedic medicine (called Ambi Haladi in Sanskrit) for its anti-inflammatory and digestive properties. The attractive flowering tropical foliage with large, paddle-shaped leaves adds ornamental value to partially shaded garden areas in zone 9.

plant_note: Surface sow indoors; press seed in and keep warm.
directions: Sweet marjoram is a Mediterranean culinary herb with a warm, gently spicy flavor softer than its relative oregano. Surface sow the fine seed indoors about six weeks before the last frost, pressing it into the mix and keeping it warm and lightly moist. Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, spacing plants around ten inches apart. Grown as a tender perennial, it is best treated as an annual in cold climates or potted up to overwinter indoors.

plant_note: Fall sowing supplies cold stratification; spring sowing works after chilling the seed.
directions: Marsh mallow is a tall perennial herb with soft gray-green foliage and pale pink flowers, long valued for its soothing roots and leaves. The seed germinates best after a cold period, so sow outdoors in fall or cold-stratify before a spring sowing. Give it full sun and consistently moist soil, reflecting its natural home in damp meadows and marshy ground. Plants may be slow the first year but form deep roots that can be harvested from established clumps.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; scarifying the seed coat lightly with sandpaper or soaking overnight in warm water speeds germination.
directions: Scarify or soak seed overnight before sowing 1/4 in deep; marshmallow appreciates consistent moisture, particularly during its establishment period. Plant in deep, moderately moist soil as the tap root grows substantial in mature plants. Harvest leaves and flowers in summer for use in soothing teas and poultices; the fleshy root is the most mucilaginous part and is best dug in the plant's second or third autumn. The dried root can be sliced, powdered, or made into a cold-water infusion to extract its slippery mucilage for throat-coat and digestive preparations.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in dry, rocky, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Maryland dittany grows naturally in dry, rocky, open woodlands and woodland edges across the eastern United States, preferring thin, well-drained, slightly acidic soils.
directions: Plant in dry to moderately moist, rocky or sandy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; Maryland dittany — also called stone mint or wild oregano — is a low-growing native perennial herb of dry, rocky woodland edges and open, thin-soiled habitats across the eastern United States. It produces small lavender-pink flowers in late summer when most other native herbs have finished blooming, making it valuable for late-season nectar. The entire plant is strongly aromatic with a fresh, oregano-like fragrance when bruised, reflecting its culinary history as a wild herb — the dried leaves can be used as a substitute for oregano or dittany in cooking and teas. One of the few native mints that blooms in late summer and fall, providing critical resources for migrating monarch butterflies and late-season native bees. Extremely drought tolerant once established in appropriate dry, rocky conditions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown plants in very well-drained, lean, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; mastic tree requires excellent drainage and is killed by waterlogged soils. It tolerates drought, salt spray, rocky soils, and alkaline conditions that defeat most ornamental shrubs. It establishes slowly but becomes extremely drought-tolerant once established.
directions: Plant in sharply drained, lean, alkaline to neutral, rocky or sandy soil in full sun; mastic tree is the source of the original mastic gum — the resinous, pine-scented exudate collected by scoring the bark of trees on the Greek island of Chios, used for at least 2,500 years as a chewing gum, food flavoring, incense, varnish, and medicine. Greek mastic ('Chios masticha') is a protected designation of origin product used in the liqueur Mastika, Greek chewing gum, breads, pastries, and Turkish delight. As a landscape plant, mastic tree is an outstanding drought-tolerant, evergreen shrub for Mediterranean-climate and Gulf Coast gardens, producing aromatic, glossy, pinnate leaves and small clusters of red to black berries that attract birds. It is excellent for coastal gardens due to its salt tolerance and thrives in the hot, alkaline, well-drained conditions of the Texas Hill Country and Gulf Coast. A relative of the pistachio tree (Pistacia vera).

plant_note: Plant small bulbs in fall 2–3 inches deep in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; meadow garlic naturalizes readily and can form dense colonies in moist meadows and open woodland.
directions: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained to moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; meadow garlic naturalizes readily by bulbils (produced instead of seeds in many populations) and will colonize moist meadows and woodland edges over time. Allium canadense is a native North American wild onion found across the eastern and central US in moist meadows, open woodlands, and disturbed areas; it produces slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and 12–24-inch stems bearing rounded umbels that typically produce bulbils (small bulbs) rather than flowers or a mixture of both in spring. All parts are edible and have a mild onion-garlic flavor; the leaves, young bulbs, and bulbils were widely used by Native Americans and are excellent as a wild substitute for chives or green onions in cooking. It is extremely adaptable and tolerates light shade, wet soils, and neglect, making it one of the easiest native edibles to establish.
