plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun; balsam apple is closely related to but distinct from bitter melon (Momordica charantia). It requires a trellis and warm, humid conditions. Native to tropical Africa and naturalized across many tropical regions.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average soil in full sun; balsam apple is the African species of the bitter gourd group — a climbing vine with deeply lobed, attractive leaves and small, oval, prominently warty orange-yellow fruits (smaller and rounder than bitter melon) that split dramatically when ripe to reveal bright scarlet-coated seeds in a striking display. Native to tropical and subtropical Africa and widely naturalized across Africa, South Asia, and northern Australia. The leaves, young shoots, and unripe fruits are eaten as cooked vegetables across Africa, where it is an important pot herb and relish ingredient in many regional cuisines. The ripe fruit is ornamental and was traditionally used medicinally as a topical treatment for skin conditions (the name 'balsam' refers to the resinous, aromatic properties historically attributed to the fruit). More compact and less bitter than bitter melon (M. charantia). The red-seeded, splitting fruit display is striking and ornamental in the garden.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature exceeds 65°F; like peanuts, the flowers bend downward and developing pods push underground to mature — grow in loose, easily penetrated, well-drained soil.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after last frost in loose, sandy to loamy, well-drained soil in full sun; bambara groundnut is a West African staple legume that forms its nutritious pods underground after pollination — a fascinating growth habit that requires loose, easily penetrated soil for the gynophore (pod peg) to bury itself. The seeds contain 19–21% protein and 40–65% carbohydrate with a nutty, slightly sweet flavor; they are boiled fresh or dried for storage, ground into flour, or fermented into condiments. Among the most drought-tolerant and heat-tolerant legumes in cultivation, outperforming cowpeas and soybeans on poor dry soils where other legumes fail while fixing nitrogen and improving soil structure.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. Banana Legs is indeterminate and benefits from staking or caging. The golden-yellow paste tomatoes are sweet enough for fresh eating — useful as a dual-purpose paste/fresh tomato. In zone 9 fall planting in August extends the productive season well into December.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with stake or cage support; Banana Legs is a yellow paste tomato producing clusters of elongated, banana-shaped fruits (4–5 inches long, 1–1.5 inches across) with pale golden-yellow skin that deepens to a richer yellow at full ripeness. The low-acid, sweet, mild flavor of yellow paste tomatoes like Banana Legs fills a different culinary niche than standard red paste tomatoes — the mildness and sweetness make Banana Legs outstanding for golden tomato sauces, sun-dried yellow tomatoes, and fresh eating as a snack tomato, where the sweet, non-acidic character appeals to people who find standard red tomatoes too sharp. The thick walls and small seed cavities are characteristic of paste tomatoes, making Banana Legs efficient to process for sauce and giving it a meaty, dense texture when eaten fresh. Unlike many paste tomatoes that are primarily functional, Banana Legs produces well-flavored fruits suitable for both cooking and fresh eating.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and keep at 75–80°F until sprouts appear. Transplant to the garden after last frost and water evenly to maintain steady growth and prevent fruit splitting. Banana peppers are mild and productive; pick fruits at 4–6 inches long when pale yellow for the mildest flavor. Leaving fruits to mature to orange or red increases both sweetness and slight heat.

plant_note: Plant sets pointed tip up with the neck just above soil.
directions: A large elongated shallot combining the size of an onion with a shallot's refined flavor. Plant individual sets in early spring with the tip barely showing, spacing them 6 inches apart. Unlike clustering shallots, banana shallots often size up as a single large bulb, so give each room. Keep weeded and evenly watered until tops begin to yellow in midsummer. Lift, cure thoroughly, and store the papery bulbs in a cool dry place for months.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Banana squash is one of the largest commonly grown winter squash varieties, producing enormously long (18–36+ inches), cylindrical, banana-shaped fruits in pale pink-orange-salmon skin with dense, sweet, golden-orange flesh — a Western US market and home-garden staple sold in cut wedges because the fruits are too large for whole-fruit sale.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows; Banana squash requires a long season (105–120 days) and is best suited to zones 5–11 with warm summers; in short-season areas, start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting. Banana squash is a Cucurbita maxima type producing some of the longest and heaviest fruits of any winter squash, with cylindrical, slightly curved, banana-shaped fruits typically 18–36 inches long and weighing 10–35 lbs; the distinctive pale pink-salmon to peachy-orange skin makes it instantly recognizable and it is commonly sold in cut wedges at Western US grocery stores and farmers' markets where the whole fruit would be too large for most households. The flesh is dense, smooth-textured, golden-orange with excellent sweetness and a rich, slightly nutty flavor excellent for roasting, soups, and pies. A vigorous, sprawling vine requiring considerable space (at least 8 feet in each direction); store harvested fruits in a cool, dry location where they keep for 3–6 months.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights remain above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a productive spring through fall season. Barker's Hot is one of the hottest New Mexico type varieties, producing 10,000–15,000 SHU, and thrives in the heat and low humidity of zone 8–9.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Barker's Hot is a New Mexico State University-developed hot New Mexico-type chile with significantly higher heat (10,000–15,000 SHU) than standard Hatch and New Mexico No. 9 varieties, making it the choice for gardeners who want traditional New Mexico flavor with serious heat. The long, 7–8 inch fruits are produced in abundance on large, productive plants and are harvested green for roasting or left to ripen and dry red for red chile powder and ristras. Roasting mellows the heat while concentrating the flavor; roasted Barker's Hot chiles freeze well for year-round use. This variety is particularly well-suited to hot, dry climates but also performs in the humidity of zone 9 Gulf Coast with good air circulation.

common_name: Beauregard Sweet Potato (Louisiana-Developed Leading Commercial Orange Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, sandy loam to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Beauregard produces best in loose, deep soil — heavy clay limits tuber expansion and produces misshapen roots; raised beds with amended soil are ideal in clay-heavy Gulf South soils.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips (rooted cuttings) after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Beauregard is the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States — developed by Louisiana State University AgCenter and released in 1987 to address both production efficiency and consumer preference for the deep-orange-fleshed sweet potato that now defines the American market standard. The deep orange-copper skin over vivid orange flesh, consistently uniform tuber shape, and high sugar content that develops fully after curing represent the qualities LSU breeders targeted: a variety that performs reliably in the humid Gulf South climate while producing the attractive, sweet, deeply colored roots that American consumers prefer. Beauregard matures in 90–110 days from slip transplanting, making it one of the faster-maturing sweet potato varieties and allowing good production within the Gulf South warm season. Sweet potatoes require curing to develop their characteristic sweetness — newly harvested tubers are starchy and less sweet than properly cured ones. Cure at 85–90°F with high humidity (85–90%) for 5–7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars. Plant certified virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery store sweet potatoes to avoid introducing sweet potato virus diseases that reduce yield. As a Gulf South native crop commercially centered in Louisiana, Beauregard performs with particular reliability in zone 8-10 humid conditions.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Beefmaster requires a very sturdy support system — heavy cages or strong staking — due to the extreme weight of mature fruit clusters.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beefmaster is one of the most popular extra-large slicing tomato hybrids in American home gardens — an indeterminate hybrid producing truly giant fruits averaging 16–32 ounces (1–2 pounds) or more per fruit, with the classic beefsteak form: large, meaty, low-seed, deep-red flesh with rich, balanced tomato flavor that makes it the premier choice for thick-sliced tomatoes for sandwiches and BLTs. The extremely heavy fruit size requires robust support — the vines need strong cages or stakes and should have the heaviest fruit clusters supported or tied as they develop to prevent stem breakage. Beefmaster was developed to combine maximum fruit size with disease resistance (V, F, N, T, A resistance package) that most older beefsteak heirlooms lack, making it significantly more reliable in warm, humid Gulf South climates. In zone 9, Beefmaster performs best in the spring window (February–May transplanting) when temperatures allow the large fruits to develop without excessive heat during fruit set — temperatures above 95°F can cause blossom drop and inhibit fruit development on large-fruited varieties. Consistent, deep watering reduces blossom-end rot, which can affect the large-fruited types more than small-fruited varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and keep the mix warm for even sprouting. This century-old indeterminate heirloom produces thick, meaty slices prized for sandwiches and any dish wanting rich tomato flavor. Vines are extremely vigorous, reaching 6 feet or more, so provide a sturdy cage or wire support and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and harvest fruit fully colored.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F; transplant in full sun in very fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil and provide heavy-duty caging or staking as beefsteak plants grow large and carry heavy fruit that requires strong support.
directions: Start seeds 1/4 inch deep indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–85°F and transplant in full sun in deeply cultivated, very fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; beefsteak tomatoes produce the largest fruits of any tomato type, with individual fruits commonly weighing 1–2 pounds and sometimes exceeding 3 pounds in favored varieties. They are indeterminate and long-season (78–95 days to first harvest), requiring heavy-duty caging or staking and consistent, deep watering throughout the season. Prune to one or two main stems for the largest individual fruits; allowing multiple stems produces more but smaller fruits. The unrivaled flavor and meaty, low-seed flesh make beefsteaks the top choice for fresh slicing, caprese salads, and sandwiches. Popular heirloom varieties include 'Brandywine' (pink), 'Cherokee Purple', and 'German Johnson'.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This determinate type delivers a rich, umami-packed flavor that finishes with smoky, fire-roasted notes, ripening most of its crop over a concentrated window. Stake or cage the compact bushes to keep fruit clean and support the yield. Water consistently at the base to avoid cracking, and harvest tomatoes when fully colored and slightly soft.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost; make a second sowing in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow beet clusters (each is a multi-seeded fruit) 1/2 in deep in rows 12 in apart. Because each corky seed can produce 2–3 seedlings, thin early to 3–4 in to avoid crowding, and use the thinnings as salad greens. Maintain even soil moisture to prevent woody, cracked roots. Harvest globe roots at 1.5–3 in diameter; larger roots become pithy and lose sweetness.

plant_note: Grown indoors on trays; soak the corky seed clusters before sowing to improve germination.
directions: Presoak the multigerm seed balls for several hours so they sprout more evenly, then sow them densely across a moist tray. Beet microgreens germinate a little slower than brassicas, so keep them covered and warm until shoots emerge, then move to bright light to develop their deep red stems. Water carefully from below or with a fine mist to avoid crushing the delicate seedlings. Harvest the striking crimson-stemmed greens at the cotyledon or first-true-leaf stage for their mild, earthy sweetness.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms; can start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: Beit Alpha is a burpless, thin-skinned heirloom cucumber that is parthenocarpic, setting smooth, mild fruit without pollination and free of bitterness. Direct-sow after the soil warms to 70F, or start indoors three weeks early, and grow up a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Harvest at 4-6 inches while the skin is deep green and tender, picking often to keep the vines producing. Because no peeling is needed, these cucumbers are ideal for fresh salads and snacking.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Beit Alpha is heat-tolerant and parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination), making it excellent for hot, enclosed or pest-challenged gardens.
directions: Trellis for best results; sow 3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thinning to the strongest when 3 inches tall. Beit Alpha is the classic Middle Eastern cucumber type — short (4–6 inches), thin-skinned, virtually seedless, and extremely crisp and sweet, with no bitterness even at room temperature. It is parthenocarpic, meaning it sets fruit without pollinator visits, and gynoecious (predominantly female flowers), resulting in extremely heavy production from compact vines. The thin skin requires no peeling and wilts less in high summer heat than standard American slicing cucumbers. Harvest frequently — the fruits reach ideal eating size within 24–48 hours in zone 9's summer heat and become puffy if left too long.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings easily in moist soil or water; bele grows as a perennial shrub in zones 9–11 and cuttings establish quickly. It thrives in hot, humid conditions and tolerates partial shade — often growing more productively in light shade in the hottest months, which reduces leaf toughening and extends the harvest season.
directions: Root cuttings and plant in fertile, well-drained to moderately moist soil in full sun to part shade; bele (aibika) is a large-leafed tropical relative of okra grown widely across Papua New Guinea, the Pacific Islands, and Southeast Asia as one of the most important leafy vegetables — the large, soft, mucilaginous leaves are harvested young and eaten as a cooked green vegetable, used to thicken soups and stews, or wrapped around other foods before cooking, exactly as collard or banana leaves are used. The mucilage thickens soups in the same way okra does. The large, showy yellow hibiscus flowers with dark centers are ornamental and also edible. Bele is heat-tolerant, productive, and thrive in Gulf Coast zone 9 summers when other leafy greens bolt and fail. It grows as a perennial shrub in frost-free conditions and can be harvested continuously. Rich in protein relative to most leafy vegetables.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring for summer root production, then force roots in fall or winter indoors; in mild climates, sow in late summer for fall root harvest followed by winter forcing. Do not direct sow too early — chicory bolts in the long days of late spring if sown too early.
directions: Sow seeds thinly in rows 12–18 in apart in late spring; thin to 8–10 in spacing when seedlings reach 2–3 in tall. Grow the plants through summer, then in fall dig the roots (which resemble fat parsnips), trim tops to 1 in, and store in a cool, dark, humid place. To force the distinctive tight pale chicons (the white-leaved heads sold in stores), pack roots vertically in a box of moist sand, cover to exclude all light, and keep at 50–60°F for 3–4 weeks — the blanched white chicons emerge from the root tops. The bitter, tender chicons are excellent braised, roasted, or eaten raw. Never allow light to reach the forcing roots or the chicons will turn green and bitter.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2 weeks after frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix; peppers germinate best when soil stays above 75°F. Harden off transplants over 7–10 days before planting, and wait until soil temperature reaches at least 65°F. Keep moisture consistent to prevent fruit drop, and apply a balanced fertilizer once flowering begins. Pick green for mild flavor or leave on the plant to ripen to red, yellow, or orange for maximum sweetness.

common_name: Bella Rosa Tomato (Disease-Resistant Gulf South Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting to harvest in May–June. Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid recommended specifically for Southern gardens where diseases and heat are primary challenges.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid tomato developed for disease resistance and heat adaptation in humid Southern gardens, an AAS (All-America Selections) winner that earned recognition for reliable production in difficult growing conditions. The medium-large (8–12 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have excellent flavor — more complex and acidic than purely mild hybrids but not harsh — with thick walls and small seed cavity that make them suitable for slicing, sandwiches, and fresh preparations. The broad disease resistance package (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and gray leaf spot) addresses the main failure modes of standard tomatoes in humid Gulf South gardens where disease pressure is severe. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for gardeners who want a concentrated harvest for preserving, sauce-making, or sharing with neighbors. An excellent choice for zone 9 spring and fall tomato seasons where disease resistance is more important than variety novelty.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for spring, or midsummer for fall.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. Selected for heat tolerance, this variety suits both spring and late-summer sowings and forms large, 6 to 8 inch, tightly packed blue-green heads. After the main head is cut, many smaller side shoots follow for continued harvests, and it grows well through winter in mild climates. Cut the central head while buds are tight, then keep harvesting side shoots.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring crop, or start in late July for transplant mid-August for fall. Better Boy is an indeterminate that benefits from sturdy staking or caging to support 4–5 foot plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–75°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Better Boy is a Petoseed Company introduction from the 1960s that became one of the best-selling tomato varieties in US history, consistently appearing in Guinness World Records lists for the heaviest yields from a single plant — a Better Boy at the Chattanooga Times Free Press Demo Garden reportedly produced 342 pounds of fruit from a single plant. The large (8–16 oz), smooth, deep-red fruits are meaty with thick walls, excellent rich-sweet tomato flavor, and few seeds — the archetype of what many American gardeners consider an ideal home garden tomato. Indeterminate vines continue growing and producing until frost, requiring substantial staking or a heavy-duty cage. Disease resistance covers Fusarium wilt (race 1) and Verticillium wilt. Better Boy's long production season, large fruit size, and excellent flavor have kept it among the top five best-selling tomato varieties in the US for over 50 years. In zone 9, it thrives as a spring crop and can resume production in fall after summer heat subsides.

common_name: Better Bush Tomato (Compact Semi-Determinate Container Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Better Bush is outstanding in containers (at least 15-gallon) — its compact habit and sturdy self-supporting stems are ideally suited to patio, deck, and balcony growing.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Better Bush is one of the finest compact tomatoes for container gardening and small-space production — a semi-determinate hybrid that naturally stays 3–4 feet tall with sturdy, stocky stems that are largely self-supporting (minimal or no staking required), compact enough for large containers, and productive enough to provide a meaningful harvest without the sprawling, aggressive growth of indeterminate types. The medium-sized (8–10 oz), round, globe-shaped, bright-red fruits have good flavor and firm texture appropriate for fresh eating and all standard culinary uses. Better Bush carries disease resistance to V, F, and N — a standard Gulf South disease package. The compact size, self-supporting habit, and container suitability make Better Bush the first recommendation for zone 9 gardeners growing tomatoes on patios, balconies, or in raised beds where space is limited. For best container production, use containers of at least 15 gallons with premium potting mix and consistent watering and fertilization — container-grown tomatoes require more frequent irrigation and feeding than in-ground plants. Two plants per patio can provide significant summer tomato production with only 30–40 square feet of container space.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Bianca Riccia is the standard Italian fine-cut white endive for winter production, producing a naturally pale center without tying. In zone 9 the cooler temperatures from October through December provide ideal growing conditions.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bianca Riccia (White Curly) is an Italian fine-cut curly endive producing a loose, open rosette of very finely divided, heavily frizzy white-to-cream leaves — naturally self-blanching at the center without the tying required by some other frisee types. The fine cutting and natural pale color of the interior make Bianca Riccia one of the most elegant frisee types for Italian insalata recipes and for the French frisee au lardons preparation where the delicate pale center is the centerpiece. The outer leaves, being more exposed, are darker green and more bitter; the pale interior heart is the culinary prize with its mild, slightly bitter, elegant flavor. Unlike darker-centered frisee varieties, Bianca Riccia requires little or no artificial blanching because the dense, overlapping outer leaves naturally shade the center as the head matures. In zone 9 fall planting produces heads of excellent quality through November and December.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; Bibb lettuce is a Kentucky heirloom developed by Jack Bibb of Frankfort around 1865, a butterhead type producing small, loose, cupped heads of buttery, sweet, tender leaves — the definitive American butterhead lettuce and considered by many the most flavorful lettuce for salads.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil; thin to 9–12 inches and harvest the whole head when the center begins to feel firm. Bibb lettuce was developed by amateur horticulturist Jack Bibb of Frankfort, Kentucky around 1865 and was distributed to neighbors and friends for decades before entering commercial seed trade; it is a butterhead-type lettuce producing small, loose, semi-cupped heads of exceptionally tender, silky, buttery leaves with a mild, sweet, distinctive flavor that many consider the finest of any lettuce for raw salads. The original Limestone Bibb (named for the limestone water of Kentucky) is more delicate and refined than commercial butterhead varieties but slightly slower and less uniform; it is the 'real' Bibb for flavor purists. Modern hybrid butterhead varieties ('Boston,' 'Summer Bibb,' etc.) are improvements in yield and bolt-resistance but lack some of the exceptional flavor of the true heritage Bibb.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Big Beef is an All-America Selections winner hybrid that combines the large, meaty fruit of a beefsteak with broad disease resistance and consistent productivity — one of the most widely grown large-fruited tomatoes in American home gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide sturdy caging or staking for the vigorous indeterminate vines, which can reach 6 feet or more. Big Beef was introduced by Seminis Vegetable Seeds and won the All-America Selections award in 1994 — it has since become one of the best-selling tomato varieties in the United States, valued for combining the large size and exceptional flavor of old-fashioned beefsteak types with outstanding disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt, nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus) that makes it more reliable across a wide range of climates and conditions. Fruits are large (8–12 oz or more), round to slightly oblate, meaty with few seeds and small blossom scars, and richly flavored — among the best-tasting large hybrid tomatoes available. Widely adaptable from cool northern gardens to Gulf Coast conditions.

common_name: Big Bertha Bell Pepper (Giant Extra-Large Sweet Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Big Bertha's exceptional fruit size benefits from consistent fertility — apply balanced fertilizer at transplanting and again when fruits begin to size up for maximum development.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Bertha is one of the largest bell pepper varieties in general cultivation — producing extra-large, four-lobed fruits 7 inches long and 3.5–4 inches wide with very thick, crunchy walls and excellent sweet flavor. The enormous fruit size makes Big Bertha outstanding for stuffed pepper preparations where the cavity size determines how much filling can be used, and for slicing use where individual slices are large, substantial, and visually impressive. Big Bertha is a hybrid variety with disease resistance that includes tolerance to tobacco mosaic virus — an important practical quality in zone 9 gardens where virus pressure is a consistent challenge for sweet peppers. Fruits ripen from green to red, with the sweet flavor deepening and vitamin C content increasing significantly as the pepper fully ripens red. However, the thick-walled green stage is also excellent for fresh use. Big Bertha plants are vigorous and produce prolifically through the long Gulf South pepper growing season. The combination of extra-large fruit, good disease tolerance, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Big Bertha one of the most popular large-fruited bell pepper varieties in American home gardening. Support plants with a stake or cage as the heavy fruits can cause branches to break.

common_name: Big Boy Tomato (Classic Large Beefsteak Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9 (Houston/New Orleans area), transplant in mid-February for spring production before summer heat ends fruit set.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after last frost; Big Boy is one of the most historically important and widely grown large-fruited tomato cultivars in American home gardens — introduced by Burpee in 1949 and still one of the most recognizable tomato names in American horticulture. The large beefsteak-type fruits typically weigh 1–1.5 pounds with deep red, meaty, flavorful flesh and the classic balanced tomato flavor — rich, full, and aromatic without the extreme acidity of some heirloom beefsteaks. Big Boy is an indeterminate, vining cultivar that continues to grow, flower, and fruit until killed by frost — it requires a strong cage or staking support to manage its vigorous 4–7 foot growth. The large fruit production and classic flavor made Big Boy the standard large-fruited tomato in American garden catalogs for decades. In zone 9, tomatoes should be transplanted in mid-February for the spring window, with the goal of harvesting as much as possible before temperatures consistently exceed 95°F (at which point pollen viability fails and fruit set stops). A second planting in late August captures the fall window. Prevent blossom end rot with consistent irrigation and calcium-balanced fertilization. Better Boy is the improved hybrid successor with added disease resistance — both are widely grown.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and keep the mix warm for even germination. This hybrid crosses Big Dwarf with Brandywine to yield dark pink, ribbed fruits of 12 to 15 ounces with rich flavor and productive, nearly blemish-free yields. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly at the base to prevent cracking, and harvest tomatoes when fully colored.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–April for fall harvest in August–September. Big Max requires 120–130 days and substantial space — vines spread 8–15 feet. For maximum size, remove all but one or two developing fruits per plant, allowing the plant to concentrate energy into a single massive fruit. Provide a piece of cardboard or wood under developing fruits to prevent rot where they rest on soil. In zone 9 the extreme summer heat can cause pollination failure during the hottest weeks — hand-pollination in early morning may be needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with ample room for the extensive vines; Big Max is the standard large pumpkin variety for home gardeners seeking impressively large fruits — a Cucurbita maxima (not the common Cucurbita pepo pie/carving pumpkin) that can reach 100 pounds or more under ideal growing conditions, though typical well-grown specimens are 50–80 pounds. The large, round, ribbed, salmon-pink to orange fruits with thick orange flesh are primarily grown for fall display and competition rather than culinary use — the flesh is edible and has a sweeter, less stringy character than standard carving pumpkins, but the enormous size and thick shell make kitchen preparation challenging. The fascination with growing large pumpkins — a pursuit that becomes genuinely competitive at county fairs and pumpkin festivals across North America — has made Big Max and its descendants the gateway variety for the hobby of giant pumpkin growing, which extends through increasingly specialized varieties into fruits exceeding 2,000 pounds. For zone 9 gardeners, Big Max must be started in time to mature before the most intense summer heat — a March planting targets a July–August harvest that avoids both late spring cold and late summer heat extremes.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes; needs a long, warm growing season.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, richly amended soil and give each vine ample space to run. This heirloom is a favorite of giant-pumpkin growers, producing round fruits with smooth, light-orange skin well suited to Halloween carving and decorating. For maximum size, grow one pumpkin per vine and water and feed generously through the season. Leave fruit on the vine until the rind hardens, then cut with a length of stem attached.

common_name: Big Rainbow Tomato (Very Large Bicolor Gold-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Big Rainbow is a very large-fruited heirloom requiring a long growing season — start seeds 8 weeks before last frost in zone 9 to ensure adequate development time before summer heat arrives.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Rainbow is one of the most spectacular large bicolor heirloom tomatoes — a giant beefsteak type producing very large (1–2 lb), irregularly shaped, heavily ribbed fruits with a stunning golden-yellow to orange base skin suffused, streaked, and marbled with bold crimson-red blushing, creating a vivid yellow-and-red bicolor display on the exterior that is dramatically beautiful when the massive fruits are displayed sliced. The cut interior reveals the full character of the variety: a yellow-gold to orange flesh with red sectors and mottling arranged in irregular patterns — each fruit slightly different in its specific bicolor expression but consistently vivid and visually remarkable. The flavor is excellent: very sweet, fruity, and low-acid with a tropical, complex quality comparable to the Pineapple tomato in style but with a distinctly different appearance — Big Rainbow's background color tends toward deeper gold-orange while Pineapple's is more lemon-yellow. Big Rainbow is a Minnesota heirloom variety believed to have been maintained by northern seed savers. The very large fruit size requires the full spring growing season in zone 9 (February–June) to develop properly before summer heat diminishes fruit quality. As with all large bicolor heirlooms, Big Rainbow plants require sturdy cage or stake support and benefit from consistent moisture and fertility for maximum fruit development.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth; transplant well after frost.
directions: Big Red is a sweet heirloom bell pepper with thick walls and large, blocky three-to-four-lobed fruits that ripen from green to deep red and grow sweeter as they color. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, and transplant only after nights stay above 55F. Space plants 18-24 inches apart in full sun and stake taller plants to keep the heavy fruit off the ground. Pick green for a crisp, mild flavor or leave on the plant to ripen fully red for maximum sweetness.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall; extremely cold-hardy for winter harvest.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in cool soil in late summer or fall, since mache germinates best in cool conditions. This big-seeded variety tolerates heat better than others without turning bitter and is also very cold-hardy, often surviving to about 10 degrees. Enjoy the tender rosettes alone as a salad, mixed with other greens, or lightly cooked like spinach. Harvest whole rosettes at the base as needed through cool and cold weather.

common_name: Biker Billy Jalapeño Pepper (AAS-Winning Long Mild Jalapeño)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Biker Billy is an All-America Selections winning jalapeño bred for unusually long, slender fruit and earlier, more prolific production than standard jalapeños, with milder, more consistent heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Biker Billy, named for a television chili-pepper personality, was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for producing notably long, slender jalapeño fruits, up to 5-6 inches, considerably longer than standard jalapeño varieties, along with earlier maturity and heavier overall yield. Heat is milder and more consistent than many jalapeño varieties, which can vary widely in spiciness depending on growing conditions, making Biker Billy a more predictable choice for recipes needing reliable, moderate jalapeño heat. Fruits ripen from dark green to red and can be harvested at either stage, with red fruit slightly sweeter. Its high productivity and vigorous, disease-resistant plants make it a dependable choice for home gardens and market growers alike. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season.

plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in cool soil; Bintje is a late-season, high-yielding Dutch heirloom potato dating to the early 20th century. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10-12 inches apart, 3-4 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling twice as plants grow. Bintje is a classic Dutch potato bred in 1904 and, for much of the 20th century, one of the most widely grown potato varieties in Europe, prized for its pale yellow, moderately starchy flesh, excellent all-purpose cooking qualities, and reliable, heavy yields. It is especially well regarded for frying — Bintje is a traditional choice for Belgian and French fries — while also performing well boiled, mashed, or roasted, making it one of the more versatile heirloom varieties available. Tubers have smooth, light tan skin and store reasonably well after curing. Harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or let vines die back fully for mature tubers with the best storage life and frying quality.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms and frost risk has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant March–April. Bishop Crown behaves as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — cut back to 6–12 inches in late winter and the woody base will regrow vigorously, producing earlier and more heavily than first-year plants. Mature perennial plants can reach 4–5 feet tall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Bishop Crown is a South American aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) with an extraordinary, immediately recognizable shape — a round, slightly flattened main body like a small bell pepper, with 3 or 4 small, prominent, finger-like lobes hanging from the bottom equator like a bishop's miter or crown. This unusual shape (also sold as 'Chapeau de Frade' or 'Balloon Pepper') is unique among peppers and makes it instantly identifiable at markets and in the garden. The flavor is fruity, slightly sweet, and aromatic — mild to medium-hot (5,000–10,000 Scoville) with the distinctive citrusy, tropical fruitiness characteristic of Capsicum baccatum. The thick, crisp walls make it excellent for fresh eating and stuffing — the hollow interior and large body are well-suited to filling with cheese, meat, or grains. The bright red color at full ripeness is vivid and attractive. In zone 9 the perennial habit allows Bishop Crown plants to develop into productive multi-year specimens.

common_name: Bishop Crown Pepper (Balloon Pepper, Three-Lobed Ornamental South American Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Bishop Crown is a Capsicum baccatum species requiring the same germination conditions as other hot peppers, but Capsicum baccatum species can be slower to germinate than Capsicum annuum — use a heat mat and be patient. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. The distinctive three-winged crown shape is fully visible from early in the fruit's development and becomes more pronounced as the pepper ripens through yellow to orange to deep red. Harvest at green for mild heat; red ripe for full flavor and slightly higher heat. The thin walls and hollow interior make Bishop Crown unsuitable for thick-walled fresh preparations but excellent for pickling, roasting, and as a garnish where the unusual shape is displayed.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost. Harvest green for mild use or red for maximum flavor. Bishop Crown (also called Balloon Pepper, Christmas Bell, or Joker's Hat) is a Capsicum baccatum variety named for the distinctive three-pointed crown shape of the fruit — which resembles a bishop's mitre hat from above, or a three-winged balloon when viewed from the side. The fruit has three prominent shoulder lobes that extend outward with a small pendant point below, creating a completely unique silhouette among commonly grown peppers. This shape is genetically characteristic of the Capsicum baccatum species (the Andean peppers, including the ají varieties of South America), where several related varieties share the winged crown form under different names. Bishop Crown fruits measure 2–3 inches in diameter and 1–2 inches in length — small but with a visually complex three-dimensional shape. The walls are thin and crisp, the interior is hollow with minimal placental tissue, and the heat level is mild to moderate (5,000–15,000 Scoville units) — substantially less hot than habanero types but with a fruity, slightly acidic flavor characteristic of the baccatum species. The visual novelty of Bishop Crown makes it one of the most attention-getting peppers in garden displays and at farmers markets, and its mild heat makes it accessible to gardeners who want interesting pepper shapes and flavors without extreme heat levels.

common_name: Bishop's Crown Pepper (Christmas Bell Pepper, Joker's Hat, Capsicum UFO)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Capsicum baccatum varieties are slower to establish than C. annuum types and benefit from an extra 2 weeks of indoor growing time. In zone 9, Bishop's Crown often functions as a short-lived perennial, developing into a woody shrub that overwinters in protected sites and produces more heavily in its second year. Harvest at any color stage — green, yellow, orange, or red — each offers slightly different flavor intensity.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun, well-drained soil, spacing plants 18–24 inches apart. Bishop's Crown is one of the most visually distinctive peppers available to home gardeners — a South American Capsicum baccatum variety that produces fruits with an unmistakable three-lobed shape resembling a bishop's crown or mitre when viewed from above, or an upside-down hat when viewed from the side. The fruits are typically 2–3 inches wide and 1.5–2 inches tall — flat, wide, and three-winged with a central pointed lobe — and they ripen from green through yellow and orange to deep red. The three-winged shape is unique among commercially available peppers and makes each fruit instantly recognizable. Beyond the striking visual character, Bishop's Crown delivers the distinctive fruity, citrusy flavor characteristic of Capsicum baccatum varieties — sweeter and more tropical-fruity than C. annuum types with a pleasant heat in the mild-to-medium range (approximately 5,000–20,000 SHU, varying with growing conditions) that builds gradually rather than hitting all at once. The thin walls make the fruits excellent for fresh eating, stuffing with soft cheeses, or quick-pickled as a garnish. The unusual shape makes every bite a conversation starter and the fruits are genuinely beautiful sliced or whole in salads. Very productive and beautiful in the garden as an ornamental-edible plant.

plant_note: Root 6–8 inch stem cuttings in moist soil; bitter leaf roots readily in warm weather and can be planted outdoors after the last frost. In zones 9–11 it persists as a woody perennial shrub.
directions: Root stem cuttings in moist soil at 75°F; bitter leaf establishes quickly from cuttings in warm weather and begins producing harvestable leaves within a few months. The large, dark green leaves have an intensely bitter flavor that is fundamental to West African cooking — particularly egusi soup, ofe akwu (palm nut soup), and a wide range of Nigerian, Cameroonian, and Ghanaian stews. Fresh leaves are squeezed and rinsed repeatedly in water to reduce bitterness before cooking; or bitter leaf powder (dried, ground leaves) is used in smaller quantities. The bitterness decreases with cooking. The plant is used medicinally throughout sub-Saharan Africa for treating fever, malaria, and hypertension. In Gulf Coast gardens it grows as a large semi-woody perennial.

plant_note: Direct sow (nick or soak seeds 24 hours) or start transplants indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9, sow in March–April for summer harvest, or again in August for fall harvest; bitter melon requires a trellis or fence to climb and produces prolifically in Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
directions: Nick seeds and sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained, fertile, moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on a trellis or fence; keep soil consistently moist. Momordica charantia (bitter melon, bitter gourd, or karela) is one of the most widely consumed vegetables across South and Southeast Asia, East Africa, and the Caribbean — a fast-growing tropical vine producing distinctive, warty, oblong to tapered green fruits 3–10 inches long that contain a bold, intensely bitter flavor considered an acquired taste but essential in dozens of traditional Asian dishes: Indian karela sabzi (stir-fried bitter melon with onions and spices), Chinese stir-fries with black bean sauce, Filipino ginisang ampalaya, Japanese goya champuru (the classic Okinawan dish). The bitterness decreases substantially when seeds are scooped out and the flesh is salted and rinsed; parboiling further reduces bitterness. Bitter melon has significant traditional medicinal use for blood sugar regulation and is the subject of ongoing pharmaceutical research for antidiabetic compounds. In zone 9, it thrives in summer heat and produces abundantly from June through October; harvest fruits when fully green and before yellowing begins.

plant_note: Plant tuber sections in warm soil in full sun with sturdy trellis support; WARNING — bitter yam contains toxic alkaloids (dihydrodioscorine) that cause paralysis if consumed raw or insufficiently processed — tubers must be peeled, boiled in multiple changes of water, and soaked before eating; do not consume raw under any circumstances.
directions: Plant tuber pieces in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun; bitter yam is a tropical African species of yam that produces clusters of small to medium tubers with intensely bitter flavor from toxic alkaloids — these require thorough processing (peeling, boiling in multiple changes of water, and prolonged soaking) to make safe for consumption. Despite this challenge, it is an important food crop in West Africa during food shortages and is also grown for its edible aerial tubers (bulbils) that have lower toxin levels and require less processing. Primarily of interest to gardeners interested in West African food plants, ethnobotany, or food security crops; properly prepared, the tubers have an earthy, slightly sweet flavor similar to other yams.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth; transplant well after frost.
directions: Black Beauty is the classic heirloom eggplant, producing large, glossy deep-purple fruits with tender, mild flesh perfect for grilling and roasting. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with warm soil, and transplant only after nights reliably stay above 55F. Space plants 18-24 inches apart in full sun and stake them to support the weight of the fruit. Harvest while the skin is firm and glossy, cutting rather than pulling; picking regularly keeps the plants productive.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest plants per hill. This highly productive bush-type zucchini from the 1920s takes little space and yields dark green, glossy fruits with tender skin. Harvest fruit young, around 6 to 8 inches, for the best texture and to keep plants producing. Pick every day or two at peak season, as fruit sizes up fast and overgrown squash slows further set.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm.
directions: Black Beauty is a dependable, prolific heirloom zucchini bearing glossy dark-green fruit on compact, bushy plants. Direct-sow two or three seeds per hill after the soil warms to 70F, then thin to the strongest seedling, spacing hills two to three feet apart. Harvest zucchini young at 6-8 inches for the best texture, and pick every day or two at peak season to keep the plant producing. Water evenly at the base and mulch to reduce disease and keep fruit clean.

common_name: Black Beauty Zucchini (Classic Dark Zucchini, Italian Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2 plants per hill) after soil warms to 70°F; in zone 9, zucchini can be planted in February–March for spring harvest and again in late August for fall harvest — summer heat reduces pollination and triggers powdery mildew.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Black Beauty is the classic standard-setting zucchini cultivar — the benchmark dark-green zucchini against which other varieties are measured, widely grown since the mid-twentieth century and still the most recognizable and most-planted zucchini in American home gardens. The compact, bush-habit plant (non-vining, unlike winter squash) produces very dark green, slightly speckled, tender-skinned fruits with mild, slightly sweet flavor and excellent firm texture. Harvest at 6–8 inches for the best eating quality — zucchini left on the plant more than a day or two at peak size rapidly grows into oversized clubs with tough skin and poor flavor. Check plants daily during peak production. Black Beauty is remarkably productive for its compact habit, typically producing more fruit per plant than the garden can reasonably consume during the peak summer weeks. In zone 9, plant in late February to March for the spring window before summer heat triggers powdery mildew and reduces production; a fall planting in late August extends the season. Squash vine borers can devastate plants — check the base of stems for entry holes and use row covers to exclude the moth. Powdery mildew appears in summer heat; newer disease-resistant cultivars extend the productive season where mildew is persistent.

plant_note: Start indoors, transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Black Cherry is an indeterminate heirloom producing clusters of round, dark mahogany cherry tomatoes with a sweet, rich, and complex flavor. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant sturdy seedlings once nights stay above 50F, setting them deep. Give the vigorous vines a tall cage or trellis and prune suckers for airflow, since they can top six feet. Harvest when fruit turns deep purple-brown and gives slightly to the touch; frequent picking keeps the clusters coming all season.

common_name: Black Cherry Tomato (Dark Purple-Red Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Black Cherry is a true open-pollinated heirloom with seed that can be saved true-to-type.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Black Cherry is one of the most unusual and striking cherry tomato varieties — an heirloom producing small (1-inch), round fruits in a deep mahogany-purple to almost black color with brick-red flesh, offering a distinctly rich, complex, wine-like flavor with chocolate-tomato undertones that is remarkably different from standard red or yellow cherry tomatoes. The dark color comes from high anthocyanin content in the skin — the same antioxidant pigments responsible for the dark color of blueberries and black raspberries — giving Black Cherry a distinctive nutritional profile alongside its unusual flavor. The complex, slightly smoky, wine-tomato flavor makes Black Cherry outstanding in raw preparations where the flavor stands alone: fresh from the vine, in caprese-style salads with mozzarella and basil, or in mixed cherry tomato platters where its dark color contrasts dramatically with red Sun Gold and yellow pear tomatoes. The indeterminate vine produces prolific clusters from transplanting through the end of the warm season. As an open-pollinated heirloom, true seed can be saved from season to season. Resistance to cracking (a weakness of many dark-colored tomatoes) is better than many purple/black tomato varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Black Diamond was the dominant commercial and roadside-stand watermelon of the American South in the 1950s and 1960s, producing very large, nearly spherical fruits with dramatically dark blue-green skin and exceptionally sweet red flesh — a classic variety now prized by home gardeners and heirloom melon enthusiasts.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, warm soil after last frost; Black Diamond needs full sun and warm nights — it performs best in zones 7–11 and Gulf Coast gardens where the long, hot summers allow the large fruits to fully develop. Black Diamond was one of the most important commercial watermelon varieties of mid-20th century America, grown throughout the South for roadside stands, truck farming, and local markets; the very large (30–50+ lbs), round to oblong fruits have an unusually dark, blue-green skin that approaches black in color and firm, bright red flesh with excellent, classic sweet watermelon flavor. The tough skin and firm flesh gave Black Diamond reasonable shipping quality in an era before refrigerated transport was universal. Now prized as an heirloom variety for gardeners wanting the authentic large-fruited Southern watermelon experience. Days to maturity of 85–90 make it best for long-season Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a Russian black tomato from the city of Tula, south of Moscow; this and similar Russian black heirlooms have become staples of the dark tomato connoisseur community for their striking color and complex flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, planting deeply and staking firmly. Black From Tula is a Russian heirloom beefsteak tomato from the Tula region south of Moscow, producing large 8–16 ounce fruits with very dark brownish-purple skin and deep reddish-brown flesh similar to Black Krim but with slightly more robust structure and a complex, smoky, earthy-sweet flavor; it is among the finest of the Russian black-type heirlooms and is particularly well adapted to conditions where hot days are followed by cool nights, which intensifies the dark pigmentation. Harvest when the blossom end yields to gentle pressure and the dark color has fully developed around the equator of the fruit.

common_name: Black Futsu Squash (Japanese Heirloom Kabocha-Type Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash known for deeply ribbed, warty, near-black skin that fades to a warm tan-orange as it cures in storage, with dense, sweet, chestnut-flavored flesh prized by chefs.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing plenty of room for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash valued for its striking appearance — small, flattened, deeply ribbed fruit covered in a warty, near-black rind when first harvested, which fades over several weeks of storage to a warm tan-orange with a slight bloom, a color transformation that also signals improving flavor and sweetness. The dense, dry, deep orange flesh has a rich, sweet, chestnut-like flavor considered among the best of any winter squash by many chefs, excellent roasted, pureed into soup, or used anywhere a rich kabocha-type squash is called for. Vines are vigorous and productive, typically setting several fruit per plant, each running 2-3 pounds, a manageable size for a single meal without excess storage bulk. Harvest when the rind resists a fingernail and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before eating — Black Futsu's flavor and sweetness improve markedly with curing and continue to develop in storage over the following months.

common_name: Black Gram (Urad Dal, Urid Bean, Black Lentil)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; black gram is extremely heat-tolerant and drought-resistant once established, making it an excellent summer legume for zone 8–11 gardens.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile to poor soil in full sun; black gram (urad dal) is one of the most important legumes in South Asian cuisine — the small, shiny black pods and seeds are the basis of dal makhani, idli, dosa, pappadams, and dozens of other dishes in Indian, Sri Lankan, and Southeast Asian cooking. The mature dried seeds are split (urad dal) for cooking or used whole; young green pods can also be eaten fresh like snap beans. Unlike many legumes, black gram fixes substantial atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in hot, dry conditions where other beans struggle. An outstanding heat-tolerant food-garden legume for the South and Southwest.

common_name: Black Grape Tomato (Dark Purple-Black Grape Cluster Tomato with Complex Rich Flavor)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Black Grape is a compact to medium-sized indeterminate cherry tomato that produces clusters of elongated grape-shaped fruits. In zone 9, transplant March–April. Black Grape is one of the most distinctive cherry tomatoes visually — the fruits are uniformly dark purple-black when ripe, with no streaking or green shoulders, and in good growing conditions may have a slight sheen to the skin. The dark color comes from high anthocyanin content in the skin (the same pigments that make black tomatoes distinctive), which combines with lycopene in the flesh to produce the characteristic complex, sweet-rich flavor. The anthocyanin content of Black Grape and similar dark tomatoes is higher in plants grown in high-light conditions, so zone 9's full sun intensifies both the color and the antioxidant content compared to lower-light growing environments.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and stake. Harvest when fruits are uniformly deep purple-black throughout the cluster. Black Grape Tomato is a compact indeterminate variety producing clusters of small, oval to elongated-grape-shaped fruits that ripen to a very dark purple-black color — one of the darkest small-fruited tomato varieties commercially available. The dark coloration results from high anthocyanin content in the skin (the same class of pigments responsible for the color of blueberries, eggplant, and purple cabbage) combined with the lycopene that gives tomatoes their characteristic red color. When anthocyanins are expressed strongly in tomato skin and lycopene is present in the flesh, the result is a dark fruit that appears almost black in good light. This anthocyanin content has nutritional significance — anthocyanins are potent antioxidants, and dark-fruited tomatoes contain higher concentrations than red or yellow types. The flavor of Black Grape combines the sweetness of a cherry tomato with additional complexity and depth — a rich, almost wine-like quality that distinguishes dark tomatoes from standard red types. The texture is firm and the grape shape (elongated, 1–1.5 inch) makes Black Grape practical for packing and transporting without the splitting that affects rounder cherry types. This firmness combined with the dramatically dark color makes Black Grape particularly popular at farmers markets and in restaurant settings where visual distinction is valued. The variety's compact growth habit relative to Sweet 100 and similar indeterminate cherry types makes it easier to manage in average-sized garden spaces.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil once frost danger has passed, giving vines room to sprawl. These dramatic, deeply ribbed pumpkins darken as they mature until nearly black and weigh only 1 to 2 pounds, making tidy personal-sized decorations. Group several together for striking fall displays. Leave fruit on the vine until the rind hardens and color fully develops, then cut with a bit of stem attached for the best keeping quality.

plant_note: Sow spring and late summer; very cold-hardy.
directions: Black Knight tatsoi is a heirloom Asian green forming tidy rosettes of dark, spoon-shaped leaves with a sweet, mild mustard flavor. Direct-sow shallowly in early spring and again in late summer, thinning plants to 6-10 inches for full rosettes or leaving them close for baby greens. Harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut the whole rosette; the plant tolerates hard frost and sweetens in cold weather. It grows quickly and does well in containers and cold frames for winter harvests.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This Russian heirloom produces baseball-sized, 10 to 12 ounce fruits with reddish-brown flesh and a rich, slightly salty flavor, and it sets fruit well in heat. Provide a sturdy stake or cage for the indeterminate vines and prune suckers for airflow. Water evenly to reduce cracking, and harvest when shoulders take on their characteristic dusky color.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; darker-colored tomatoes absorb more heat and can sometimes ripen faster in cool seasons; stake firmly — indeterminate and vigorous.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost risk passes into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Krim is a heirloom beefsteak tomato originating from Crimea (the Black Sea region of Ukraine), producing medium-to-large fruits with a distinctive deep brownish-red to almost black skin with green shoulders, and dark red marbled flesh with a rich, complex flavor that is earthy, smoky, and slightly sweet. One of the most striking and flavorful of the dark or 'black' tomato types. Fruits show their best color in warm weather with cool nights; in hot climates the colors may be less dramatic but flavor remains outstanding. Harvest when the skin darkens significantly and gives slightly to pressure.

plant_note: Start indoors, transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Black Krim is a Crimean heirloom beefsteak bearing large, dark purple-brown fruits with a rich, full-bodied, faintly smoky and salty flavor. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights are reliably warm. Support the indeterminate vines with a strong cage or stake and prune suckers for air movement to reduce cracking in the shoulders. Harvest when the fruit develops its dark color and gives slightly; the color deepens in hot weather and sun.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; WARNING: unripe green berries and all green parts contain solanine — a toxic alkaloid. Eat ONLY fully ripe, cooked berries and well-cooked young leaves. In Africa and Asia it is an important food plant when properly prepared; in Western gardens it is considered a weed.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; black nightshade is a widespread, weedy annual cosmopolitan plant whose cultural significance varies dramatically by geography — considered an undesirable toxic weed in Europe and North America, but an important traditional vegetable food plant across Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, where the young leaves and fully ripe berries are eaten after cooking (boiling, sautéing, or stewing). The leaves are cooked as a pot herb (like spinach) across many African countries where it is called 'mnavu' (Swahili) or 'imboga' (various East African languages). The fully ripe, jet-black berries (glossy, round, about 1/4 inch) are cooked into sauces and stews or made into jam. IMPORTANT: unripe green berries contain toxic solanine and must never be eaten raw or unripe — only fully ripe (jet-black), well-cooked berries are safe. Young leaves are also cooked, not eaten raw. Self-sows readily in disturbed, rich soil. Tolerates partial shade.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant March–April. Black Pearl is compact (18–24 inches) and extremely ornamental — it is widely grown as a container plant where the black foliage and shiny black fruits transitioning to red create continuous seasonal interest. In zone 9 the plant can overwinter as a perennial woody shrub, regrowth from the base producing even heavier crops in subsequent seasons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Black Pearl is an All-America Selections award-winning ornamental pepper notable for its intensely dark, shiny, almost black foliage throughout the growing season — one of the darkest-leaved edible plants available for ornamental garden use. The small, round, pea-sized fruits emerge shiny black, gradually transitioning through red-black to a final vivid red as they mature, so that at any moment the plant displays all three colors simultaneously against the near-black foliage — creating a dramatically ornamental display that performs equally well as a container specimen and in ornamental borders. The fruits are genuinely hot (approximately 10,000–30,000 Scoville) and fully edible — suitable for hot sauces, dried chiles, and as a garnish for dishes where both heat and visual drama are desired. The compact size and outstanding ornamental value make Black Pearl one of the most popular choices for edible ornamental garden design.

common_name: Black Plum Tomato (Russian Heirloom Dark-Red Paste Cherry)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Black Plum is an indeterminate heirloom that requires staking or caging and produces prolifically throughout the season. In zone 9, transplant February–March for May–July harvest. The distinctive dark, mahogany-red to near-black skin color intensifies with warm temperatures and full sun exposure; the rich flavor is best appreciated at room temperature rather than refrigerated.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with strong cage or stake support and consistent, even moisture. Black Plum is a Russian or Eastern European heirloom paste-type cherry tomato that has become one of the most appreciated 'dark' tomato varieties in American heirloom tomato culture — producing small (1.5–2 inch), plum-shaped fruits with an extraordinarily dark skin color ranging from deep mahogany-red to near-black-purple on the sun-exposed surface and shoulders. The dark color comes from high levels of chlorophyll that breaks down to brownish-red tones in the skin, combined with the fruit's deep red flesh, creating an intensely rich, almost chocolatey appearance that makes Black Plum one of the most visually distinctive cherry/paste types. The flavor is equally distinctive: rich, complex, and deeply sweet with more winey, umami-forward notes than typical sweet red cherry types — a sophisticated flavor more commonly associated with large beefsteak types than small tomatoes. Black Plum produces in abundant clusters throughout the season and is excellent fresh in salads, halved on cheese plates, dried whole, or roasted — the meaty, paste-type interior with relatively few seeds makes it particularly good for drying and roasting. One of the most beautiful and flavorful of all dark tomato varieties.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Black Prince is a Siberian heirloom dark tomato producing medium-sized, round to slightly oblate fruits with dark red-purple to almost-black coloring at the shoulders that transitions to deep burgundy-red — an early, flavorful representative of the 'black tomato' category with a rich, earthy, complex taste profile associated with the high anthocyanin content of dark-skinned varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Black Prince performs exceptionally well in cool climates due to its Siberian origin and can be transplanted earlier than most heat-requiring varieties. Black Prince is a Russian heirloom tomato from Siberia, where it was developed to produce ripe fruits under cool growing conditions with a shorter summer season than most tomato-growing regions — a characteristic that makes it one of the earliest-maturing of the 'dark tomato' class, which typically run late. The medium (3–6 oz), round to slightly flattened fruits develop dark red-purple to near-black pigmentation in sun-exposed areas of the skin (from anthocyanin development under UV exposure), while shaded areas remain deep burgundy-red; the interior flesh is dark red to mahogany with dense, meaty texture and a distinctively complex flavor profile — sweet and rich with earthy, slightly smoky undertones and good acid balance. Black Prince is an excellent introduction to the 'dark tomato' flavor category for gardeners unfamiliar with the type; it is earlier, more compact, and more productive than larger dark varieties like Cherokee Purple or Paul Robeson, making it particularly suitable for containers, short seasons, and cooler gardens.

plant_note: Sow 8–10 weeks before first fall frost; black radish stores well into winter and is best harvested after light frosts improve flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in loose, deeply prepared, fertile soil in late summer for fall harvest; thin seedlings to 6–8 inches to allow the large roots to develop fully. Black radish is an ancient European winter storage root with rough, jet-black skin and crisp, pungent white flesh — significantly hotter than spring radishes and reminiscent of strong horseradish. Harvest after light frost, which mellows the intense pungency; roots can reach 3–4 inches in diameter and 4–6 inches long. The robust flavor is best appreciated when the flesh is grated raw into salads with sour cream, pickled in brine, or cooked in soups where the heat moderates pleasantly.

common_name: Black Radish (Spanish Black Radish, Winter Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow 6–10 weeks before first fall frost in well-drained, deeply cultivated, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; black radish is a large, winter-storage radish with a dramatically pungent, horseradish-like flavor that mellows considerably when cooked — plant in fall for harvest before hard freezes.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in deeply cultivated, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 4–6 inches for large root development. Raphanus sativus 'Black Spanish' (black radish or Spanish black radish) is a large, ancient European winter radish producing round to turnip-shaped roots with jet-black, rough, firm skin and strikingly white, dense, extremely pungent flesh — the flavor is intensely sharp, mustard-hot, and horseradish-like when raw, making it far more assertive than common spring radishes. Black radish is one of the oldest cultivated radish types — documented in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome — and remains popular in Eastern Europe, Germany, and France as a traditional winter vegetable. Raw, it is grated and dressed with salt, sour cream, or vinegar as a condiment (German Schwarzer Rettich); cooked, the pungency mellows considerably and the radish becomes milder and sweet. The roots store exceptionally well in cool conditions for weeks to months — a genuine winter storage vegetable unlike spring radishes, which must be used immediately. Black radish is also highly valued in naturopathic medicine for liver-supportive and digestive-stimulating properties attributed to high glucosinolate content.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate in cool soil. A garden favorite since 1850, this loose-leaf variety yields full-sized, frilly leaves in just over a month and baby greens in about three weeks. It withstands hot, dry conditions and light frosts better than many other lettuces. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again supply, or cut the whole plant before it bolts in heat.

plant_note: Succession sow spring and fall; light aids germination.
directions: Black Seeded Simpson is a fast, reliable heirloom loose-leaf lettuce with tender, light-green ruffled leaves and a mild, crisp flavor. Direct-sow shallowly, barely covering the seed since light aids germination, and thin plants to 6-10 inches apart. Harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again for a prolonged supply, and succession-sow every two weeks from early spring through fall. Provide afternoon shade in hot weather to delay bolting; it also grows well in containers and hydroponics.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–June for a summer harvest. Black sesame requires the full warmth of the Gulf Coast summer to set and ripen seed pods. The plants are drought-tolerant once established and require no fertilization beyond initial soil preparation. Harvest when the lower pods begin to turn yellow-brown and before they split open and shatter — losing the seed. Cut the entire plant and hang upside down over a tarp to capture falling seeds.
directions: Direct sow thinly in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; black sesame is a color variant of common sesame producing jet-black seeds with a distinctly richer, nuttier, and more complex flavor than the pale white sesame seeds familiar from Western cooking — the higher pigment content is associated with higher concentrations of antioxidant sesamin, sesamolin, and lignans. Black sesame is the standard seed for traditional East and Southeast Asian preparations including black sesame paste (used in tang yuan rice balls and Asian pastries), black sesame ice cream, Japanese gomashio (sesame salt), Korean jook (sesame rice porridge), and black sesame halva. Toasted black sesame seeds have an almost smoky, deep nutty profile that white sesame cannot replicate. The slender, upright, ornamental plants with white-to-pink tubular flowers are attractive in the garden. Harvest by cutting and hanging entire plants over a cloth when pods begin to ripen — mature pods open at the top and shed seeds readily.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for a December–February harvest. Black Spanish radish is a large winter storage type that requires the full 55–70 days of cool weather to develop properly — it is not a quick spring radish. In zone 9 fall planting is the primary season; spring planting usually bolts before the roots size up. Harvest roots before heavy spring rains cause them to split or become pithy.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches in loose, deep, well-prepared soil in full sun; Black Spanish Radish is an ancient winter storage radish documented in cultivation since at least the 1500s and widely grown in France, Germany, and Eastern Europe as a cold-season storage crop. The round to slightly elongated roots are 3–4 inches across with striking jet-black skin and brilliant white, very firm, pungent flesh inside — the flavor is substantially stronger and more peppery than spring radishes, with a dry, dense texture and a sharp spicy bite that is characteristic of all large winter radish types. The traditional preparation is sliced paper-thin and eaten with butter and salt as a crudité, or grated raw into salads where the pungency is diluted by other ingredients. Black Spanish radish stores for 2–3 months in cold storage with the greens removed, making it a genuine cold-pantry root crop unlike the quick-to-deteriorate spring radish types. The distinctive black skin and white interior create dramatic visual contrast in raw preparations.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, warm, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after last frost and when soil reaches 60°F; black turtle beans perform as either bush or climbing types depending on variety. For dry bean production, harvest when 90% of pods have turned brown and dry.
directions: Sow 1–2 inches deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; black turtle beans are the standard black bean of Latin American, Caribbean, and American cuisine — the dense, shiny black seeds are rich in protein (15g per cup) and antioxidant anthocyanins, used in black bean soup, rice and beans, burritos, tacos, and countless other dishes. Both bush and pole varieties are available; the most common home-garden varieties include 'Black Valentine' (bush) and 'Black Coco' (bush).
