Allow pods to dry completely on the plant for dry bean harvest — seeds should rattle in the pod. Thresh by spreading dried plants on a tarp and walking on them, then winnow. In zone 9a, plant in spring for a late-summer dry bean harvest; the plants fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil for subsequent crops.

common_name: Black Valentine Bush Bean (Heirloom 1897 Bush Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Black Valentine shows better tolerance for cool soil germination than many snap beans, germinating as low as 55°F, allowing earlier planting. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall harvest. Black Valentine is also grown as a dry shell bean — allow pods to dry completely on the vine for black-seeded dry beans excellent in soups.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest pods when 5–6 inches long and still tender before seeds swell. Black Valentine is one of the oldest continuously maintained snap bean varieties in American cultivation, introduced around 1897 — a bush snap bean with more than 125 years of documented garden history, making it one of the few surviving American snap bean varieties from the pre-hybrid, pre-modern-breeding era. The black seed (from which the name derives) is the seed coat color at the dry stage: the seeds are jet black when fully dried, producing a useful dry black bean with excellent flavor for soups and stews. As a snap bean, Black Valentine produces dark green, round to slightly flat pods of good length (5.5–6.5 inches) on compact, bushy 18–22 inch plants. The flavor is richer and more complex than most modern bush snap bean hybrids — characteristic of traditional open-pollinated varieties that were selected for eating quality over the decades of their use. Black Valentine shows good tolerance for cool soil germination (as low as 55°F, versus the 60–65°F requirement of most snap beans), which allowed earlier planting in the pre-modern gardening era when it was a primary garden staple.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil is warm; thrives in heat.
directions: Black-eyed peas are a heat-tolerant cowpea grown for their nutritious seeds and their ability to fix nitrogen and improve soil. Direct-sow after the soil warms to 70F, planting an inch deep and thinning to 3-6 inches apart, since the plants dislike transplanting. They tolerate heat and drought well, so water moderately and avoid overly rich soil, which favors foliage over pods. Harvest young pods for fresh snap peas or leave them to dry on the plant for shelling and storage.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; sow succession plantings every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest; widely available and one of the most heat-tolerant loose-leaf lettuces for warm-climate spring gardens.
directions: Broadcast or direct sow seed on the soil surface (light aids germination — do not cover) in early spring, thinning to 8–12 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall; Black-Seeded Simpson is the most widely grown American heirloom loose-leaf lettuce, documented since at least 1850 and still one of the best choices for the home garden due to its excellent heat tolerance (bolts much more slowly than most head lettuces), fast maturity (45–50 days), light green crinkled leaves with a pleasant, mild flavor, and the heavy yields of a cut-and-come-again plant. Harvest outer leaves when plants are 6–8 inches tall, leaving the center growing point to continue producing. Self-shades the soil and benefits from afternoon shade in warm climates.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-prepared soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for early summer harvest and June–July for a fall crop. Despite being bred for short northern seasons, Blacktail Mountain performs well in zone 9's heat — the early maturity allows harvest before the most intense late-summer heat, and the dark rind absorbs heat efficiently in cooler spring soil. Check for ripeness by thumping (hollow sound) and examining the tendril nearest the fruit, which should be dried and brown.
directions: Direct sow in hills or rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Blacktail Mountain is an early-maturing open-pollinated watermelon developed by Glenn Drowns of Seed Savers Exchange to produce reliably sweet, ripe melons in the short summers of northern Idaho and the northern Plains. The small to medium round fruits (8–12 pounds) have a strikingly dark — almost black-green — rind that distinguishes them instantly from most other watermelon varieties. The bright red, sweet, juicy flesh is comparable to the best commercial watermelons in flavor, with a thin rind and few seeds. In zone 9 the early maturity (70–80 days from direct sow) means it finishes before the most brutal August heat and is particularly useful for succession-planted summer crops that bridge the gap between spring and fall production. The dark rind warms faster in cool spring soil, giving Blacktail Mountain an advantage early in the season when soil temperatures are marginal.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; bladder campion self-sows freely once established and naturalizes readily in meadow conditions.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or fall in poor to moderately fertile, well-drained, preferably neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; bladder campion is a European native naturalized throughout North America that has long been eaten in Mediterranean countries — particularly Italy and Spain — where the young spring shoots and leaves are gathered and cooked like asparagus or used raw in salads, with a flavor often described as fresh, pea-like, and slightly peppery. The inflated silvery-white balloon-like calyx is highly ornamental, and white five-petaled deeply notched flowers appear from late spring through fall with an evening fragrance. Naturalizes readily in dry meadows and borders and is fully drought-tolerant once established.

common_name: Bleu de Solaise Leek (Blue of Solaise)
plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors in spring; harvest runs from autumn through winter, with flavor and hardiness improving after frost. Bleu de Solaise is a renowned French winter leek from the commune of Solaise in the Rhône valley near Lyon — prized for its extraordinary cold hardiness and the dramatic blue-green to steel-blue coloration the foliage develops in response to frost, one of the most visually striking of all leek varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost date; sow 1/4 inch deep in flats or cell trays at 60–70°F. Bleu de Solaise is a traditional French winter leek from the Rhône valley region near Lyon, classified as a winter-type leek because it is sown in late winter or early spring, transplanted in late spring, and harvested from autumn through the following spring — the main harvesting season runs from November through February in most climates. The most distinctive characteristic of Bleu de Solaise is its dramatic foliage color: the leaves develop an intense steel-blue to blue-violet pigmentation in response to cold temperatures through the anthocyanin response, making each plant increasingly vibrant and beautiful as winter progresses; in hard frosts the blue becomes almost purple-blue. Transplant seedlings in late spring when 6–8 inches tall, planting deeply in a trench or dibbling holes 6 inches deep to blanch the shanks and develop long, tender white stems; the thick shanks (6–8 inches long) have a sweet, mild, sophisticated flavor that intensifies rather than diminishes in cold weather. One of the most cold-tolerant of all leeks, surviving temperatures well below 0°F when established.

plant_note: Sow very early in spring in persistently moist or wet ground; blinks thrives in cold conditions and will often germinate through the remnants of snow cover. It is best suited to naturally wet areas rather than standard garden beds.
directions: Broadcast seeds across the surface of very moist, even waterlogged soil beside a spring, seep, stream edge, or perpetually wet bed, and do not cover them as they need light for germination; blinks is an inconspicuous but historically valued wild potherb of cool, wet habitats across Europe, Asia, and North America, producing mats of tiny, fleshy, bright-green leaves with a clean, mild, slightly succulent flavor reminiscent of purslane. Gather the young shoots and leaves by the handful for use raw in salads or cooked briefly as a light pot herb alongside other spring greens. Blinks is seldom deliberately cultivated and is far more commonly encountered as a volunteer in damp garden corners, irrigation runnels, and beside water features; the gardener's role is more to encourage and harvest it than to manage it as a conventional crop. It self-sows abundantly in suitable wet conditions and will naturalize into a permanent spring presence in any reliably wet microhabitat in the garden.

common_name: Blondkopfchen Tomato (Little Blonde Girl German Heirloom Cherry)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Blondkopfchen is an indeterminate heirloom that requires strong staking or caging (6 feet minimum) and produces prolifically throughout the warm season. In zone 9, transplant late February–March for a May–July harvest. The extremely long clusters (30–50 small tomatoes per cluster) are one of the most visually remarkable features of this variety — a single plant in full production is spectacular.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with a sturdy cage or tall stake. Blondkopfchen (German for 'little blonde girl' or 'little blondie') is a German heirloom cherry tomato that produces one of the most spectacular fruiting displays of any tomato variety — extremely long, drooping clusters of 30–50 or more tiny (0.5–0.75 inch), round, clear golden-yellow to light lemon-yellow fruits that cascade like bunches of golden grapes from indeterminate vines growing 6+ feet. The fruits are uniformly pale golden-yellow, translucent-skinned, and have an exceptionally sweet, mild, almost honey-sweet flavor with very low acidity — a delicate sweetness that is quite different from the richer red cherry types and makes Blondkopfchen appealing to those who find red cherry tomatoes too tart. The combination of the fruit's pale golden color, the translucent skin through which the interior is visible, and the long hanging clusters makes Blondkopfchen one of the most beautiful tomato plants in the garden — genuinely ornamental as well as productive and delicious. Very popular in European heirloom gardens and increasingly appreciated in the US by tomato collectors who value both visual character and eating quality. Seed Savers Exchange and specialty seed companies carry this variety as an example of German heirloom tomato excellence.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination. Blondy's compact size (3–4 feet vs. the 5–6 feet of standard okra) makes it appropriate for smaller gardens. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer and fall harvest. Harvest pods every 2–3 days when 2–4 inches long — Blondy pods stay tender longer than dark green types, remaining usable up to 5–6 inches without becoming tough and fibrous.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest cream-colored pods every 2–3 days at 2–5 inches. Blondy is a 1986 All-America Selections-winning okra that earned recognition for two distinguishing traits: compact plant size and distinctive cream-white to pale chartreuse pod color. Standard okra varieties like Clemson Spineless and Emerald are tall plants (5–7 feet) that require staking and become difficult to harvest at the top as the season progresses; Blondy stays compact at 3–4 feet, keeping all pods within easy reach throughout the harvest season. The pale cream-colored pods are the most visually distinctive feature — where standard okra is dark forest green, Blondy's pods are almost white-green to cream-yellow, giving a noticeably different appearance both in the garden and on the table. Beyond the visual novelty, the pale pods have a slight cooking advantage: they do not contribute the dark green color that sometimes bleeds into dishes, making them preferable for light-colored preparations like cream soups, gumbo with light roux, or pickled okra where visual clarity is desired. The pods remain tender at larger sizes than dark-green types, providing a more forgiving harvest window. Blondy produces heavily on its compact plants, making it particularly well-suited to small gardens and raised beds.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 55°F; Bloody Butcher is a 150+-year-old Appalachian and Virginia heirloom dent corn with dramatic deep blood-red and red-flecked kernels, used for meal, hominy, roasting ears, and heritage bourbon production — and one of the most visually striking of all heirloom corns.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows to ensure cross-pollination; plant in fertile, well-amended soil with consistent moisture during pollination and kernel fill. Bloody Butcher is a tall, vigorous Appalachian heirloom dent corn documented in Virginia and the Appalachian region since at least the 1840s; the plants are impressive, reaching 10–12 feet, and produce 2–4 ears per stalk of medium-length (10–14 inch) ears with kernels that are dramatic deep blood-red to red-brick with darker red cob — the most vividly colored of the traditional red dent corns. Dried, the kernels are ground into deeply flavored, reddish-tinged cornmeal with a rich, earthy, sweet corn taste that is distinct from modern yellow dent meal. Also used for hominy, grits, masa, and heritage whiskey distilling. At the milk stage (80–90 days) the ears can be eaten as roasting ears; for grain and meal, allow to dry on the stalk or cure indoors.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full shade; bloody dock thrives in shaded woodland gardens and is one of the most ornamental leafy greens for shaded spots, producing glossy, dark-green leaves with vivid crimson-red veins and midribs.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or fall in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; thin to 12 inches. Rumex sanguineus (bloody dock or red-veined sorrel) is a European perennial dock producing some of the most visually striking leaves of any vegetable — glossy, lance-shaped, medium-green leaves dramatically marked with vivid crimson-red veins and midribs, creating a graphic color contrast that makes this plant as ornamental as it is edible. Young leaves are harvested like sorrel and used raw in salads, where the mild, slightly acidic flavor adds interest; older leaves become more strongly acidic (from oxalic acid) and are best cooked briefly like spinach or used sparingly as a flavoring. Unlike common garden sorrel, the leaf flavor is milder and the visual interest much greater. Plants are long-lived perennials that die back in hard winters and regrow in spring; in zone 9, they may persist semi-evergreen through mild winters. The tall, reddish flower stalks should be removed as they develop to keep plants producing leaves rather than going to seed. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Sow early spring and fall; germinates in cool soil, bolts in heat.
directions: Bloomsdale is a cold-hardy heirloom spinach with heavily crinkled, deep-green leaves and a sweet, mild flavor that stands up well in cool weather. Direct-sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked and again in late summer, since seed germinates poorly in warm soil. Thin plants to 4-6 inches apart and harvest outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut whole plants before hot weather triggers bolting. In mild zones a fall planting under cover can overwinter for an early spring harvest.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes.
directions: Separate bulbs into cloves at planting and set each clove pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes. This Turban-type hardneck forms large, plump bulbs with violet-streaked wrappers and 8 to 10 easy-peel cloves. Mulch after planting to protect roots over winter, and cut off the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy place before storing.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; a compact, single-serving size blue-grey squash in the Hubbard family — ideal for gardeners who want the exceptional Hubbard flavor in a size manageable for a single meal.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, composted soil; Blue Ballet is a compact vine type needing 4–6 feet of space, much more manageable than giant Hubbard types while retaining the same outstanding eating quality. Blue Ballet is a small, 2–4 pound, blue-grey teardrop-shaped winter squash in the Cucurbita maxima (Hubbard) family, with dense, smooth, bright orange flesh that is extraordinarily dry, sweet, and nutty — essentially the same outstanding Hubbard flavor in a size perfect for a single serving or small family portion that eliminates the wrestling match of cutting a 15-pound Blue Hubbard. Excellent for roasting halved in the oven with butter and maple syrup; the small size also makes it practical for stuffing. Cure for 10 days and store for 3–4 months.

common_name: Blue Curled Scotch Kale (Classic Tightly-Curled Dwarf Blue Kale)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. sabellica 'Blue Curled Scotch'
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Blue Curled Scotch is a dwarf type (12–16 inch plants) appropriate for small gardens and container growing. In zone 9, transplant August–September for fall and winter harvest. The tightly curled leaves trap water in their crinkles, so watering and harvest timing after heavy rains requires slightly more care than with flat-leaf kale types. Multiple light frosts improve the sweetness significantly — the flavor peak is November–January in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun or partial shade. Blue Curled Scotch (also called Dwarf Blue Curled Scotch or Blue Curled Dwarf) is one of the oldest and most recognized curly kale varieties in American cultivation — a compact, very tightly-curled kale with deeply blue-green, intensely frilled and crinkled leaves on a low, spreading, dwarf plant. The very dense curling of Blue Curled Scotch is the most extreme in the curly kale category — each leaf is curled and recurled into a compact, almost cabbage-like head of texture that is visually striking and creates distinctive culinary behavior when cooked (the very curly leaves trap oils and seasonings in their folds). The tightly frilled leaves also create the most decorative appearance among common kale varieties, making Blue Curled Scotch useful in ornamental kitchen gardens and edible landscape plantings where visual appeal is important. The dwarf habit (12–18 inches) is practical in raised beds and containers. Like all curly kales, flavor improves dramatically after frost — the sweetness increases and the bitterness decreases as cold temperatures convert starches to sugars, making fall and winter the optimal harvest window.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; a drought-tolerant heirloom flour corn.
directions: Sow seeds about 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure good wind pollination. This Hopi heirloom tolerates dry, hot conditions better than most corn, so avoid overwatering once established. Allow the ears to dry fully on the stalk before harvesting the deep-blue kernels for grinding into flour or cornmeal.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2 plants per hill) after soil warms to 70°F and all frost danger passes; Blue Hubbard requires a long, warm growing season and is best planted in late July in zone 9 for fall harvest, allowing 100–110 days before the first expected fall frost.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Blue Hubbard is a classic, large-fruited heirloom winter squash producing enormous, blue-gray, warty, thick-skinned fruits typically weighing 15–35 pounds — the quintessential large storage squash that has fed families through winter for generations in American kitchen gardens. The flesh is deep orange, very dry and dense, richly flavored, and exceptional for pies, soups, and roasting — the flavor is often described as richer and more complex than the more commonly grown butternut squash. The thick, warty, blue-gray skin provides outstanding storage capacity — well-cured Blue Hubbard fruits store at room temperature for 6 months or longer. The vine is vigorous and space-demanding, spreading 8–15 feet — provide ample space and consider training the vine to maximize space efficiency. In zone 9, plant in late July for fall harvest (counting back 100–110 days from the average first frost date). Harvest after the skin hardens and turns fully blue-gray; cure in a warm location for 10–14 days before storage to harden the skin and improve sweetness. The large fruits are sometimes sold cut into sections at farm stands — cut pieces must be refrigerated and used within a week.

common_name: Blue Jade Sweet Corn (Dwarf Blue Sweet Corn, Container Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; Blue Jade is unique among sweet corns for its genuinely dwarf plant size (3–4 feet tall) that makes it the most practical sweet corn for container growing, small raised beds, and gardens where standard 6–8 foot corn stalks are not practical; the vivid blue to near-black kernels turn steel-blue when cooked and have a sweet, tender flavor despite their striking color.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for pollination — even dwarf corn requires block planting; thin to 6–9 inches; Blue Jade can be grown in large containers (15+ gallons) for patio gardens; harvest when kernels exude milky liquid when punctured; Blue Jade silk is blue and the husk has blue streaks; eat immediately for best sweetness as the sugars convert rapidly. Blue Jade is the most practical sweet corn for small gardens and containers — a genuinely dwarf sweet corn variety (plants only 3–4 feet tall) that was selected specifically for its compact habit, making it the rare sweet corn that can be grown in large containers, small raised beds, or urban gardens where standard corn's height and space requirements are prohibitive. The kernels are a vivid blue-purple when raw, turning a distinctive slate-blue when cooked — a color unlike any other common sweet corn, derived from the same anthocyanin pigments found in blue tortilla corn, blueberries, and purple cabbage. Despite the striking color, the flavor at the perfect milky stage is sweet and tender, comparable to standard sweet corn, though with a slightly more complex, starchy background flavor reflecting the corn's partial flint heritage. Blue Jade is classified as a sugary-enhanced (se) type sweet corn — not as sugary as supersweet (sh2) types but sweeter than old su types, with a longer window between milk and dough stages than original open-pollinated sweet corns. The entire plant is attractive: blue silk, blue-streaked husks, and blue-purple stalk coloring make Blue Jade an ornamental as well as productive corn. Excellent for children's gardens for its manageable size and dramatic appearance.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; an heirloom storage pumpkin with slate blue-gray skin.
directions: Plant seeds an inch deep in hills once the soil is thoroughly warm, thinning to the two strongest vines per hill. Give these sprawling plants plenty of room and a steady supply of water and compost to size up the deeply ribbed fruits. Cure the blue-gray pumpkins in a warm, dry spot after harvest for long winter storage and sweet, dense flesh.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans dislike transplanting and rot in cold ground. This variety produces a very large concentrated crop of round, 6 inch pods on 16 to 18 inch bushy, disease-resistant plants. Because it crops all at once, sow in successions two weeks apart for a steady supply. Harvest pods while young and tender before the seeds swell, and pick frequently to encourage more pods.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy trellis or pole in warm soil once frost danger has passed. Vigorous 5 to 8 foot vines are high-yielding and produce a bounty of 5 to 7 inch, white-seeded pods excellent fresh, canned, or frozen. Provide strong support before the vines begin to climb. Harvest pods while young and tender, picking every few days to keep the vines producing over a long season.

common_name: Blue Lake Pole Bean (Classic Climbing Standard Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Blue Lake Pole requires a 6–8 foot trellis, fence, teepee poles, or other support structure — the vines will climb any vertical support readily using their tendrils. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and August–September for fall; pole beans are more heat-tolerant than bush types in high summer because the vine continues producing new flowers above the canopy where slightly cooler air circulates. Harvest when pods are 5–6 inches long and still tender and snappy; over-matured pods become fibrous and tough. Pick regularly to extend production — unpicked pods signal the plant to stop flowering.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost near trellis support; harvest pods at 5–6 inches length for best eating quality. Pick every 2–3 days to encourage continued production. Blue Lake Pole is the climbing, vining form of the Blue Lake bean family — the standard against which all green snap beans are measured in American vegetable gardening. The Blue Lake name comes from Blue Lake, California, where commercial snap bean growers in the Humboldt County area developed and refined the variety for the canning industry in the early 20th century. The Blue Lake type (both bush and pole forms) became the dominant American snap bean because it set the standard for straight, dark green, round pods with excellent tenderness, stringlessness, and flavor — characteristics that made it both the go-to home garden bean and the standard for the commercial canning and frozen bean industry. Blue Lake Pole's climbing habit (6–8 feet) gives it significant advantages over the bush form: the vine continues producing over a longer season (12–16 weeks vs. 6–8 weeks for bush), the elevated flowers and pods are slightly cooler and better-ventilated in humid conditions, and the vertical growth makes efficient use of small garden space with a supporting trellis. The beans are indistinguishable in flavor from the bush form — round, meaty, stringless, medium-dark green, with excellent eating quality fresh, frozen, or canned.

common_name: Blue Max Collards (Large Upright High-Yield Smooth-Leaf Collard Hybrid)
plant_note: Direct sow 10–12 weeks before the first frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Max is a hybrid collard — it will not come true from saved seed but produces more uniform plants and potentially higher yields than open-pollinated varieties when purchased as fresh hybrid seed each season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Max is a hybrid collard variety valued for its large, smooth, blue-green, broadly rounded leaves and high-yield production — producing some of the largest, most productive collard plants available for home garden and small-farm production. The large leaf size (leaves reaching 18–24 inches across on well-fed plants) and tall, upright habit produce an impressive harvest volume from each plant. As a hybrid variety, Blue Max produces uniform, vigorous plants with excellent disease tolerance and the high-yield characteristics that result from hybrid vigor. The smooth, thick, waxy leaf surface holds up well in cooking and has good culinary quality in traditional preparations — braised with smoked meats, in Southern-style stewed greens, and in other long-cooked preparations where the thick leaves benefit from extended cooking time. Blue Max is cold-hardy and continues producing through Gulf South winters, sweetening after frost exposure as starches convert to sugars — the post-frost harvest typically produces the finest-flavored greens. In zone 9, plant in August–September for fall/winter production and harvest outer leaves progressively through November–February. The very large leaves and tall plants provide ample harvest from relatively few plants in a garden bed.

common_name: Blue Taro (Purple Taro, Violet-Stemmed Taro, Black Taro)
plant_note: Plant corms or divisions in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to consistently moist soil; Xanthosoma violaceum tolerates more shade than most edible aroids and performs well under high canopy in zone 9-12, making it particularly useful for shaded food gardens where few edible plants thrive. The striking dark purple leaf stems (petioles) and blue-green, slightly glaucous leaf blades make this a highly ornamental edible. The corms are edible when cooked (similar to taro) and are consumed throughout the Caribbean and Pacific. In zone 9, plants cut back in frost but regrow vigorously from corms in spring. CAUTION: all Xanthosoma parts contain calcium oxalate crystals and must be thoroughly cooked before eating — raw consumption causes severe mouth irritation.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to moderately moist soil — Blue Taro grows vigorously in a range of light conditions and is notably more shade-tolerant than many edible root crops, making it a valuable choice for partially shaded food gardens in zone 8b-12. Xanthosoma violaceum is a large, corm-forming, rhizomatous perennial aroid native to the Caribbean and tropical Americas in the Araceae family — closely related to the Dasheen/Taro group (Colocasia) but in the distinct genus Xanthosoma, which tends to have larger, lighter-colored leaf undersides and edible corms with a different starch profile. The plant is most immediately distinguished by its spectacular petioles (leaf stems) in very deep purple-violet to almost black — a color so intense it verges on the appearance of metal or wood rather than a plant part. The large, sagittate (arrowhead-shaped) leaf blades are blue-green with a slightly waxy, glaucous surface. The overall effect is of a large, bold-textured tropical plant of great ornamental impact. The corms (and young leaves, when properly prepared) are used throughout the Caribbean, West Africa, and Pacific Islands as a starchy vegetable similar to taro. Both the corms and young leaves must be thoroughly cooked to neutralize calcium oxalate crystals. The plant provides excellent large-scale ground cover in shaded areas and combines dramatically with lighter-textured shade plants. CAUTION: toxic if eaten raw; cook thoroughly.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for spring germination after natural cold stratification; or cold stratify seeds for 60 days and sow in late winter. Waterleaf grows naturally in rich, moist woodland soils in deep shade and self-sows readily in appropriate conditions.
directions: Direct sow in fall or plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in deep shade to partial shade; blunt-leaved waterleaf is a native woodland ephemeral-like perennial of rich forest floors across eastern North America, valued as an early spring edible — the young, furled leaves before flowering are among the most easily harvested native spring greens, with a mild flavor suitable for salads, soups, and sautéing as a pot herb. Unlike Virginia waterleaf (H. virginianum) which has sharply pointed leaflets, this species has distinctly rounded, blunt leaflet tips. The white to pale lavender flowers in spring attract specialist native bees. The plant dies back in summer heat, so it pairs naturally with summer-active ferns and hostas that fill in as it goes dormant. An excellent deep-shade groundcover for moist, woodland gardens that doubles as a spring salad green.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches at least 65 degrees.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination. This sugar-enhanced hybrid produces 8-inch ears packed with 16 rows of juicy golden kernels that hold their sweetness well after harvest. Sturdy stalks carry a strong disease package for consistent yields. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, and harvest when silks brown and kernels are plump and milky.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for the main crop; bok choy grows best in cool weather (50–70°F) and bolts to seed quickly in heat or when days lengthen in spring. Fall plantings are more successful than spring plantings in most climates.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing 6–12 inches apart; bok choy (pak choi) is the most widely grown Chinese vegetable outside of Asia, producing compact plants with crisp, white-ribbed stalks and dark-green, spoon-shaped leaves used in stir-fries, soups, braises, and salads. It grows rapidly in cool weather and is one of the best fall vegetables for zone 5–11, tolerating light frosts and continuing to produce into early winter in mild climates. Harvest either the entire plant when mature or individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest. Baby bok choy varieties (Shanghai, Toy Choy) mature in 30–40 days and are ideal for tender whole-plant harvest. Keep evenly moist to prevent premature bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or summer; this variety tolerates heat for extended sowing.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to about 4 inches apart, or grow in containers. This baby bok choy tolerates heat, so you can sow it through summer, harvesting at about 4 inches tall for delicate, crisp, mild-flavored leaves. The uniform green plants are an indispensable stir-fry ingredient and also good fresh or marinated. Keep soil evenly moist to keep growth tender, and harvest whole heads while young for the best texture.

common_name: Boldor Golden Beet (Deep-Gold Bejo F1 Hybrid Non-Bleeding Yellow Beet)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (zone 9: August–October) for winter harvest; each beet 'seed' is actually a corky seed cluster that may produce 2–3 seedlings — thin to the strongest plant at 3–4 inches. Boldor is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid selected specifically for the most vivid, deep golden-yellow root color of any golden beet variety, with the additional quality of very low bleeding — golden beets in general bleed far less than red types, and Boldor bleeds less than most golden varieties. The yellow color holds surprisingly well in cooking compared to red beets (which turn everything they touch crimson) — roasted Boldor can be served alongside lighter-colored ingredients without color contamination.
directions: Direct sow seed clusters 0.5 inch deep; thin to 3–4 inches. Harvest roots at 2–3 inches diameter for best texture; harvest greens at any size. Boldor is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid golden beet developed specifically to maximize the golden-yellow pigmentation of the root while maintaining the culinary qualities — tender, sweet, earthy — of the best red beet types. Golden beets (yellow beet varieties) differ from standard red beets in their pigmentation: instead of betacyanin (the red-purple betacyanin of standard beets), golden beets produce betaxanthin — a yellow-orange pigment in the same betacyanin family but in the yellow portion of the spectrum. This difference creates the visually striking golden color and the important culinary advantage of significantly reduced bleeding: while red beets stain everything they contact an intense crimson, golden beets' yellow betaxanthin pigment migrates far less during cutting and cooking, making golden beets practical for preparations where color bleeding would be problematic (roasted vegetable mixes, salads with white cheese, light-colored sauces). Boldor consistently achieves the most saturated, vivid golden color of any commonly available golden beet variety — the deep gold interior is visually striking when roasted and served as golden rounds, and the Bejo breeding produces more uniform root sizing than many open-pollinated golden beet types.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; a widely adaptable Nantes-type hybrid carrot with outstanding disease resistance to leaf blight, powdery mildew, and cavity spot — one of the most reliable carrots for home gardens in hot and humid zones 8–11.
directions: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall to allow roots to develop fully. Bolero is an outstanding Nantes-type hybrid carrot developed for exceptional disease resistance, particularly to alternaria leaf blight and carrot fly, with excellent tolerance to heat and humidity that makes it one of the most reliable carrots for gardens in zone 7–11 where summer heat normally makes carrot culture difficult. The 6–8 inch, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange, smooth-skinned, and have a sweet, mild flavor with good core-to-cortex ratio and excellent storage quality — they can be left in the ground for weeks without going woody. In zone 8–9, sow in late winter for spring harvest and again in late summer for fall harvest.

common_name: Bolita Bean (New Mexico Traditional Round Pueblo Indian Dry Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Bolita is a dry bean requiring the full growing season to dry. In zone 9, plant April–May for fall dry bean harvest. Bolita plants are semi-vining and may benefit from light support (a fence or string trellis) though they often sprawl adequately without staking. The beans are round (bolita = little ball in Spanish), cream to tan-pink at full dry maturity, and are harvested when pods are completely dry and papery. Bolita is adapted to the hot, dry, high-altitude conditions of the Southwest but grows well across a wide range of zones when given adequate heat during the growing season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when pods are completely dry and papery; beans are round, cream to pinkish-tan. Shell and store in airtight containers. Bolita Bean is the traditional dry bean of New Mexico and the Pueblo cultures of the American Southwest — a variety with documented cultivation in New Mexico and Pueblo Indian communities for centuries, predating European contact and representing one of the most important food plants of southwestern Indigenous agriculture. The name 'bolita' (little ball in Spanish) describes the characteristic round, rotund shape of the dried seed, distinctly rounder than most common beans and immediately recognizable in any collection of dried bean varieties. The dried seeds are cream to pinkish-tan with a slightly glossy surface — a modest appearance that belies the exceptional culinary quality Bolita is known for among Southwest cooks and food historians. The flavor is earthy, slightly sweet, and deeply savory when slow-cooked — Bolita makes extraordinary refried beans (frijoles refritos): the beans cook to a very creamy, smooth texture when mashed and fried, with a richness that commercial pinto beans rarely achieve. Bolita is the traditional bean of New Mexican red and green chile preparations, cooked simply with onion, garlic, and salt or with rendered lard in the traditional method. Seed Savers Exchange and Native Seeds/SEARCH maintain diverse traditional Bolita strains.

common_name: Bolivian Rainbow Pepper (Ornamental-Edible Multicolor Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Bolivian Rainbow is particularly effective as a container plant, where the compact habit and upward-pointing multicolor fruits create an outstanding ornamental display. In zone 9, it often survives as a perennial in sheltered positions, developing into a woody shrub with increasing productivity in subsequent years.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; Bolivian Rainbow is one of the most visually spectacular ornamental-edible peppers available — a compact plant that simultaneously displays fruits at multiple stages of ripening, cycling through purple, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, creating a stunning multicolored display that earns it a place in ornamental borders and container arrangements as much as in vegetable gardens. The plants are dense, attractive, and heavily loaded with small (1–1.5 inch), upward-pointing conical fruits; the visual effect of dozens of multicolored fruits pointing upward from the dark green foliage is genuinely striking and unlike any other common garden plant. The fruits are very hot (50,000–100,000 Scoville units), with a clean, direct heat appropriate for hot sauce, spicy condiments, or any preparation where decorative whole dried peppers provide both heat and visual interest. The purple stage is particularly ornamental (purple pigmentation rarely seen in fruiting stage of other varieties) and fades to yellow, then orange, then the final red as the fruit matures. In zone 9+, established plants often behave as perennials, developing increasingly thick, woody stems and producing heavier crops each successive season.

common_name: Boniato (White Sweet Potato, Cuban Sweet Potato, Batata)
plant_note: Plant slips (rooted cuttings) after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm above 65°F; boniato slips root readily; plant in well-mounded ridges for best tuber development and drainage.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam, enriched ridges in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; boniato is the traditional sweet potato of Cuban, Caribbean, and Latin American cuisine, prized for its dry, fluffy, white to pale cream flesh that is less sweet, less moist, and more starchy than orange sweet potatoes — more similar in texture to a russet potato and much preferred in savory preparations. The skin is irregularly shaped, pinkish to light brown, and the plants are slightly more drought-tolerant than standard sweet potatoes. Excellent roasted, mashed, or fried; does not have the cloying sweetness that makes American orange sweet potatoes unsuitable for some savory applications. Stores well in a cool, dry location.

plant_note: Plant slips (rooted stem cuttings) after soil has warmed to 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant April–June. Bonita is adapted to the Gulf Coast's hot, humid summer conditions and produces reliably even in the high-heat periods of July–August when some varieties reduce tuber set. Harvest when vines begin to yellow and die back, or after 100 days. In zone 9 a second planting in late July can produce a fall harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to sandy-loam soil — sweet potatoes do not tolerate waterlogged or compacted soil; Bonita is a white-fleshed sweet potato released by the Louisiana State University AgCenter specifically for Gulf Coast production conditions, selected for its firm, dry, mildly sweet flesh that is used as a staple starchy vegetable rather than as a dessert-sweet orange-fleshed type. The large, oblong, tan-skinned tubers have creamy white flesh with a dry, starchy texture more similar to a dry-type white potato than to the moist, orange Beauregard type — making Bonita suitable for soups, stews, fried preparations, and the Latin American-style cooking (boniato) where a dry, non-sweet white sweet potato is traditional. The vine shows good heat and humidity tolerance and is specifically tested for performance in the Gulf South's challenging summer conditions. Bonita is popular in Louisiana and Gulf Coast markets catering to Caribbean and Latin American culinary traditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Bonny Best is a classic 1908 American heirloom slicing tomato — one of the most widely grown varieties in early 20th century American home gardens and commercial fields — valued for its reliable production, attractive round-globe shape, good acid-sweet balance, and relatively early maturity for a full-sized slicer.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Bonny Best performs well with or without staking — it is an indeterminate but moderately compact type compared to most indeterminate heirlooms. Bonny Best was introduced in 1908 (previously distributed as 'John Baer') and rapidly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in early 20th century America, prized for reliable, heavy production of attractive, round to slightly oblate, medium to large (6–10 oz), uniformly red fruits with a classic balanced sweet-acid flavor that home gardeners and canners found superior to the watery commercial varieties of the era. Bonny Best's particular virtues are its productivity, disease resilience, and flavor — a reliable old-fashioned tomato that consistently produces good crops without fuss. By midcentury it was eclipsed in commerce by hybrid varieties but remained in home garden cultivation; it is now maintained by seed savers and available from heritage seed companies as one of the historically important American tomato varieties. Good canning and fresh-eating tomato.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Boothby Blonde is best harvested young at 3–4 inches for fresh eating; at full maturity the fruits are 5–6 inches and still mild but beginning to yellow. Remove overripe fruits promptly to keep the vine producing. Bush habit is compact; no trellis required but vines benefit from light support.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Boothby Blonde is a Maine heirloom cucumber preserved by the Boothby family of Livermore Falls and introduced to the broader seed-saving community through Seed Savers Exchange. The small, oval fruits are ivory-to-pale-yellow with black or white spines — the pale color is the key distinguishing feature that makes identification by color a reliable harvest guide. Harvest when the fruits are still ivory-white at 3–5 inches; yellowing indicates over-maturity. The flesh is exceptionally crisp, mild, and sweet with thin skin that does not require peeling — the flavor is more delicate than standard green cucumbers, with less bitterness and a refreshing, clean taste ideal for fresh eating, simple salads, and sliced into yogurt or dressings. The unusual pale exterior makes it a novelty in the garden and at farmers' markets. Heat tolerance is adequate for zone 9 spring crops, but fall production is best.

common_name: Boothby's Blonde Cucumber (Maine Heirloom Cream-Yellow Oval Cucumber, Seed Savers Classic)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Boothby's Blonde is a semi-vining variety (grows 3–4 feet before trailing) that can be trained up a trellis for cleaner fruit or allowed to sprawl. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall production. Harvest fruits when cream-yellow in color (3–4 inches long) — do not allow to become large and yellow-orange, which indicates overripeness, bitterness, and seed hardening. The pale skin of Boothby's Blonde makes it easy to spot overripe fruits before they develop bitterness, unlike dark-green varieties where overripeness is harder to detect. The black spines (as opposed to the white spines of burpless/European types) indicate this is a traditional pickling-style heirloom, though it is most often eaten fresh.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when cream-yellow and firm. Boothby's Blonde is a Maine family heirloom cucumber preserved by the Boothby family from Livermore Falls, Maine, and shared through the Seed Savers Exchange — the network through which most American home-saved heirloom vegetable varieties have been maintained and distributed since the organization's founding in 1975. The cucumber is immediately distinguishable from every other commonly grown variety by its fruit color: the skin is creamy white to pale yellow at harvest maturity, oval to oblong in shape (3–4 inches long), with black spines on the surface ribs rather than the white spines of European or Asian cucumber types. This combination of cream-yellow skin and black spines produces a visual character unlike any other cucumber commonly available — the pale fruit with dark spines stands out dramatically in the garden and on the plate. The eating quality is excellent: thin skin (no peeling needed), crisp and juicy flesh, mild sweet flavor with no bitterness, and a good seed cavity for a traditional cucumber type. Boothby's Blonde exemplifies the category of heirloom vegetables that persist not because of exceptional yield or disease resistance but because of unique visual and flavor qualities unavailable in commercial varieties — preserved specifically because gardeners valued those qualities enough to maintain the seed across generations.

common_name: Borettana Cipollini Onion (Flat Golden Italian Onion)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in early spring; Borettana is an Italian heirloom cipollini type prized for its flat, disc-like shape that makes it ideal for whole-onion roasting and pickling.
directions: Direct sow or set transplants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. This Italian heirloom produces distinctively flat, disc-shaped bulbs with coppery-gold skin and sweet, mild flesh, and is the classic cipollini used in Italian agrodolce (sweet-and-sour) roasted onion dishes as well as pickling, since the flat shape cooks evenly and looks attractive whole on the plate. It matures relatively quickly for an onion and the small-to-medium bulbs cure and store reasonably well for a sweet type. Space plants a bit closer than standard globe onions, since the flattened bulbs take up less lateral room, and reduce watering as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over near harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-amended soil; one of the oldest American heirloom squashes, documented in New England gardens since the 1830s, with vibrant orange-red skin and superb flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, enriched soil, spacing hills 4–6 feet apart and thinning to 2 plants per hill; Boston Marrow requires 90–100 days of warm weather, so plant promptly after last frost. Boston Marrow is one of the oldest American heirloom winter squashes, offered by commercial seedsmen in New England since the 1830s; it produces round to pear-shaped fruits 6–10 pounds in weight with spectacular, deep orange-red skin and extremely sweet, fine-grained, nearly stringless flesh of exceptional quality — it was reportedly the standard squash for pies before Hubbard types became popular. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin is fully colored; cure for 10 days and store in a cool, dry place for 2–3 months.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; one of the oldest American pickling cucumbers, documented since the 1870s, producing short, blocky, thin-skinned fruits ideal for dill pickles and fermented pickles.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Boston Pickling is a fast-maturing (55–65 days) pickling type that produces very early and keeps producing well if harvested at 2–3 inch length for small dill pickles or 3–4 inch length for whole dill pickles. Boston Pickling is an American heirloom documented since the 1870s, producing short, blocky, light-to-medium green fruits with slightly ridged skin, crisp white flesh, and a small seed cavity that gives pickles an excellent bite; the skin absorbs brine beautifully, producing crunchy pickles that store for months. Harvest at least every two days when production peaks to keep the vine producing; fruits left to yellow dramatically slow new production. Both vine-type and bush selections exist.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; direct sowing is also possible once soil is warm.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in warm mix or directly in warm soil; nick the seed coat or soak overnight to speed germination. Bottle gourd is a vigorous, tropical vine that requires a sturdy trellis or fence and very warm conditions to thrive. Harvest immature fruits when they are 6–8 inches long (or the desired shape depending on variety) for vegetable use — they are delicate and best cooked; allow fruits to mature fully and dry on the vine if growing for use as a gourd vessel. Pollination requires both male and female flowers to be open simultaneously; hand-pollinate in the morning if fruit set is poor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a reliably productive red beefsteak heirloom with excellent disease resistance that performs consistently in both humid and dry climates — a good choice for beginners seeking a dependable large heirloom tomato.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil. Box Car Willie is an American heirloom red beefsteak tomato named with Old West flair and popular for its reliable productivity, large 8–14 ounce fruits with smooth, meaty red flesh and excellent balanced sweet-acid flavor, and its relative disease resistance compared to many other heirlooms — it typically outproduces more famous heirlooms like Brandywine under variable conditions. The vigorous, indeterminate vines need staking or caging; fruits are round to slightly flattened with smooth, crack-resistant skin. A solid everyday heirloom choice for gardeners who want large, flavorful tomatoes without the fussiness of some heritage types.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 6–10 feet of room to sprawl and handle ripe fruit gently, since the thin, tender rind that gives Bradford its sweetness also makes it far more bruise-prone than commercial shipping melons.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Bradford Watermelon is a South Carolina heirloom dating to the 1840s, developed by the Bradford family of Sumter County and grown continuously within the family for over 170 years before nurseryman Nat Bradford reintroduced it commercially in the 2010s. Large oblong fruits (often 25–40 pounds) have a distinctive soft, thin rind and exceptionally sweet, deep red flesh — historically prized enough that the whole melon, rind included, was cooked down into watermelon rind preserves and syrup. That same soft rind made it too fragile for the rail-shipping trade of the early 20th century, which nearly drove the variety extinct as tougher-rinded shipping melons took over the commercial market; it survived only because the Bradford family kept saving and replanting seed on their own land. A true living-history heirloom for the home garden, where a thin, easily bruised rind is no obstacle, in zone 4–11.

plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This classic heirloom, thought to date to the late 1800s, has distinctive potato-leaf foliage and produces massive 16 to 24 ounce pink fruits with rich, old-fashioned flavor. The indeterminate vines need a tall, sturdy stake or trellis and benefit from suckering for airflow. Water evenly at the base to reduce cracking, and harvest fruit when fully colored and slightly soft.

common_name: Brandywine Red & Yellow Blend Pole Tomato
plant_note: Start indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply once nights stay warm. This blend pairs Red Brandywine, with its rich, well-balanced flavor, and golden Yellow Brandywine, which is sweet-tart, both producing large fruits often near a pound and sometimes close to two. The indeterminate vines need a tall, sturdy support and benefit from pruning for airflow. Water evenly to prevent cracking, and harvest each color when fully ripe and slightly soft.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost risk passes; a potato-leaved variety that benefits from deep planting and very sturdy staking as the large fruits make vines top-heavy.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant after frost risk passes, burying the stem deeply to encourage rooting; Brandywine is arguably the most celebrated American heirloom tomato, a large pink-red beefsteak type with potato-leaved foliage and 1–2 pound fruits that ripen slowly but reward the patient gardener with extraordinarily rich, complex, sweet-acidic flavor widely considered the gold standard of tomato taste. Stake or cage firmly — the vigorous indeterminate vines grow to 6 feet and heavy fruits weigh branches down without support. Days to maturity are long, making it best suited to long-season gardens; in the south, plant early for spring harvest before summer heat sets in.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix after nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F; plants establish rapidly in warm weather.
directions: Plant cuttings in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; this low-growing groundcover from Brazil spreads to fill in bare areas beneath shrubs and fruit trees, providing a living mulch while yielding edible leaves. The slightly succulent, wavy-edged leaves are harvested young and used raw in salads or briefly cooked like spinach, with a mild, pleasant flavor free of bitterness. It is extremely productive in the subtropics, rooting wherever stems contact moist soil. Take cuttings in early fall to overwinter indoors in a sunny window, or treat as an annual in zone 8 with fresh transplants each spring.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate in cool soil. This variety holds its pretty leaves high above the core for easy cutting and forms compact heads that yield well in a small space. Strong bolt resistance extends the harvest, and it resists downy mildew, lettuce leaf aphid, and Fusarium wilt. Keep soil evenly moist, provide afternoon shade in warm weather, and harvest outer leaves or the whole head as needed.

common_name: Bright Lights Swiss Chard (AAS-Winning Rainbow Multi-Color Stem Swiss Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Bright Lights is a cool-season biennial treated as an annual. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter production, or February–March for spring. Swiss chard tolerates light frost but is damaged by hard freezes — in zone 9, plants grown through the mild winter provide harvest from fall through spring. Bright Lights produces a mix of stem colors (yellow, orange, red, pink, white, purple, and intermediate shades) within each packet, creating a visually striking garden planting and a colorful harvest of mixed-stem bunches.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; each chard 'seed' is actually a seed cluster that may produce 2–3 seedlings — thin to the strongest. Harvest outer leaves at any size; plants continue producing from the center. Bright Lights is a 1998 All-America Selections-winning Swiss chard — a variety selection that produces the same flavor and productivity as standard chard while dramatically expanding the visual appeal of the garden. Each individual plant in a Bright Lights planting develops stems of a single color, but a planting from any seed packet includes plants with yellow, orange, red, pink, white, lavender, and purple stems, with the blade of each leaf complementarily colored against the bright stem. Photographed in morning light, a mature Bright Lights planting is among the most colorful edible garden plantings available in any vegetable category. The flavor is identical to standard Swiss chard — the young leaves are mild and spinach-like for raw salads; the mature leaves are substantial and slightly earthy-sweet when cooked. The colored stems and midribs hold their color reasonably well through cooking (yellow and white stems hold best; red and pink stems bleed somewhat). Bright Lights is valued in both edible gardens and ornamental-edible plantings where it provides extended color through the cooler months.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 the ideal sowing windows are September–November for fall/winter crop and February–March for spring. Bright Lights tolerates light frost and light heat but bolts in sustained high temperatures. In zone 9, fall-sown chard is often the finest and can continue through winter.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6–9 inches; chard seed is a cluster (multigerm) so thinning is essential. Bright Lights is an All-America Selections winner rainbow chard that transformed chard's reputation from a workmanlike spinach substitute to a showstopping ornamental-edible. The plants produce stems in a vivid spectrum of yellow, orange, red, pink, purple, and white — a single bed creates extraordinary visual impact in the garden. Leaves are tender, mild, and slightly earthy, superior to red chard for flavor; stems are crisp and colorful even when cooked, with a mildly sweet, earthy flavor that stands up to sautéing, braising, and pasta dishes. For zone 9 fall gardens, Bright Lights is one of the most reliable cool-season crops: it germinates quickly in September warmth, grows through October–November, survives light freezes, and can continue producing into January–February. Harvest outer leaves regularly for continuous production; plants can produce for months. Tolerates partial shade in hot weather, which extends the harvest season significantly.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in cool soil.
directions: Quinoa is an ancient, nutritious South American grain, and this rainbow blend adds striking seed-head colors of hot pink, burgundy, red, orange, yellow, white, and green. Direct sow in early spring in cool soil, in full sun and well-drained ground. The tender young leaves can be cooked like spinach, while the protein-rich seeds are harvested when the plants dry down. Rinse the harvested seeds well to remove the naturally bitter saponin coating before cooking. Give the tall plants room, as they can reach 4 to 6 feet.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant August–September for harvest November–January. Batavian endive takes longer to mature than frisee; allow the full 80–95 days from transplant. Blanch the center by tying outer leaves together for 10–14 days before harvest to reduce bitterness and lighten the interior. The large, robust heads store well for 2–3 weeks under refrigeration.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Broad-Leaf Batavian Endive is the flat-leafed, large-headed escarole-type endive — distinct from frizzy curly endive in having broad, wavy, slightly ruffled leaves rather than finely cut, frilly ones. The large, open heads weigh 1–2 pounds with pale green to cream-white interior leaves (if blanched) and a mild, slightly bitter flavor that is more approachable than radicchio or frisee. Broad-Leaf Batavian endive is extensively used in Italian cooking — sautéed with garlic and olive oil, incorporated into soups and braised bean dishes, and used as a pizza or pasta topping where its mild bitterness counterbalances richer ingredients. It is also used raw in salads when blanched to a creamy interior. The large, substantial leaves hold up better to cooking than frisee or standard lettuces. In zone 9 it is a reliable fall crop that matures through November and December for harvest into January.

plant_note: Plant corms or rhizome divisions in spring into saturated mud or shallow water up to 12 inches deep; push corms just below the surface of heavy aquatic soil and keep continuously submerged or wet throughout the growing season. Broadleaf arrowhead spreads by stolons to produce new corms at their tips — harvest corms in fall after the foliage dies back.
directions: Plant corms in heavy aquatic soil in saturated mud or standing water 2–12 inches deep in full sun; broadleaf arrowhead thrives in freshwater marshes, pond edges, slow streams, and ditches across most of North America and is both a highly ornamental aquatic perennial and a traditional Indigenous food plant. Sagittaria latifolia produces bold, arrowhead-shaped leaves on long petioles rising 1–4 feet above the water surface, and attractive whorled racemes of bright-white, three-petaled flowers with yellow stamens from midsummer through early fall — providing valuable nectar for native bees. The starchy, potato-like corms produced at the tips of underground stolons were a critical food source for many Native American and First Nations peoples and were gathered in enormous quantities, especially by Plains tribes — Meriwether Lewis and William Clark documented their use extensively; the corms can be baked, boiled, roasted, or dried and ground into flour. Outstanding for naturalizing pond margins and rain gardens while providing important food and cover for ducks (hence 'duck potato'), muskrats, and other wetland wildlife.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost once seedlings are stocky.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in starter mix and keep at 70–75°F until germination, then grow on in bright light to prevent leggy transplants. Set out 2–4 weeks before last frost and fertilize with a nitrogen-rich feed at planting and again when heads begin to form. Harvest the central head while florets are still tight and dark green, before any yellow shows. Cut with a few inches of stem to encourage side-shoot production after the main head is removed.

plant_note: One of the easiest microgreens; sow densely on a moist tray and blackout for two to three days.
directions: Broadcast broccoli seed thickly across an evenly moist tray and cover for the first couple of days to encourage strong, uniform germination. Once shoots stand up, uncover and give them bright light so the stems stay short and sturdy. Keep the medium consistently moist and provide gentle airflow to prevent damping-off. Harvest the crisp, mild greens at the cotyledon stage in about a week for the sweetest flavor and best texture.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring crop; sow again in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/4 in deep and thin to 4–6 in; rapini grows quickly and is best as a cool-season crop because heat intensifies bitterness and accelerates bolting. Side-dress with nitrogen once plants are established to encourage the leafy shoot growth that is the primary harvest. Harvest when flower buds are visible but before they open fully, cutting the top 6–8 in of the shoot with leaves included. Repeated cuts extend the harvest, as side shoots continue to develop after the main stem is removed.

plant_note: Grown indoors year-round in a jar or sprouting tray; not sown in garden soil.
directions: Rinse seeds and soak overnight, then drain and spread in a sprouting jar or tray kept out of direct sun. Rinse and drain two to three times daily to keep sprouts moist but never standing in water. Harvest tangy, nutrient-dense sprouts in four to six days once the first true leaves show and greening begins. Refrigerate harvested sprouts and use within a week for the best crunch and peppery bite.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–February for fall through spring harvest. Bronze Mignonette is a miniature butterhead that forms small, tight heads 3–5 inches across — perfect spacing is 6–8 inches in a grid pattern for maximum production in a small space. The tight, compact heading habit makes it one of the best lettuces for containers and small patio gardens. In zone 9 it performs excellently from fall through early spring; thin sowing in partial afternoon shade extends the season. Harvest the entire small head at once or harvest as baby leaves from the outside.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil — lettuce requires steady moisture and cool temperatures; Bronze Mignonette is a miniature French heirloom butterhead lettuce forming small, compact, dense heads with deeply bronze-tinged outer leaves grading to butter-yellow in the blanched interior — the same color pattern as a large butterhead but scaled down to a single-serving head of 3–5 inches across. The Mignonette name (French for 'small and delicate') describes both the size and the tender, buttery character of these compact heads, which provide the soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth texture of butterhead lettuce in a size perfectly proportioned for a single-person salad. Unlike large butterhead varieties where a single head may be too much for one meal, Bronze Mignonette heads can be harvested and eaten in one serving — a practical advantage for small households and container growers who want variety without waste. The bronze outer leaves and buttery-sweet interior flavor make Bronze Mignonette one of the most attractive and best-tasting small lettuces for kitchen garden edging, window boxes, and mixed salad plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out; a cold-hardy drumhead cabbage for fall and winter harvest.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in summer for a fall crop. This heirloom forms dense, flattened drumhead heads that tolerate hard frosts and store well. Keep the soil evenly moist and feed with nitrogen to build large heads, and harvest after cool weather sweetens the leaves.

plant_note: Start indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost so plants mature in cool autumn weather.
directions: Sow 1/4 in deep indoors under bright lights; transplant into deeply prepared soil and stake tall plants against wind. When sprouts at the base reach marble size, remove the growing tip (topping) to concentrate energy and speed maturation of the remaining sprouts. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward once they are 1–2 in across and tight. Flavor peaks after exposure to a hard frost.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; buckler sorrel (Rumex scutatus) is a distinct species from common garden sorrel (Rumex acetosa) with smaller, shield-shaped leaves, a lemony-tart but notably milder flavor than common sorrel, and better tolerance for light shade and dry conditions — the preferred sorrel of French cuisine for cream of sorrel soup, chiffonade in salads, and fish sauces.
directions: Sow directly in spring or fall in any well-drained soil; buckler sorrel is drought-tolerant when established and tolerates light shade, making it useful under taller plants; harvest young leaves by cutting 2–3 inches above the crown; remove flowering stalks to encourage continued leaf production; plants are perennial and will regrow from the crown each spring. Buckler sorrel (Rumex scutatus) is a European perennial herb closely related to but distinct from common garden sorrel (Rumex acetosa) — the differences are important for culinary use: where common sorrel has large, elongated arrow-shaped leaves with a strong, pungent, distinctly acidic flavor, buckler sorrel has small, rounded, shield-shaped (scutate — hence 'scutatus') leaves with a more delicate, lemony-tart flavor that is fresh and citrusy without the harsh tang of the larger-leaved species. The name 'buckler' refers to the small round medieval shield (a buckler) that the leaf shape resembles. Buckler sorrel is considered the superior culinary sorrel in French cooking: it is used in the classic potage à l'oseille (cream of sorrel soup), as a chiffonade in salads where the milder flavor is more versatile, in sauce oseille served with fish and eggs, and as an herbal flavoring in vinaigrettes where lemon-acid flavors are desired without citrus. The leaves are high in oxalic acid (as is common sorrel), so large quantities should not be eaten regularly, but culinary use in normal amounts is entirely safe. Once established, buckler sorrel is a tough, long-lived perennial that self-sows readily and can spread if not managed.

plant_note: Use unhulled seed and soak overnight; grown indoors on trays year-round.
directions: Soak the unhulled buckwheat seed overnight and rinse it before spreading it densely on a moist tray. Cover for a few days while the heart-shaped cotyledons push up, then expose to bright light and mist as needed. Keep an eye out for seed hulls clinging to the leaves and mist them off before harvest. Cut the tender, lightly nutty greens once the cotyledons have fully opened, generally around a week to ten days.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; an African-American heirloom pepper from Philadelphia with striking color changes through the ripening cycle — highly ornamental as well as edible.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Buena Mulata is a treasured African-American heirloom pepper with roots in Philadelphia's Black community, saved for generations and brought to wider attention through Seed Savers Exchange; it produces thin, cayenne-shaped pods 4–5 inches long that pass through a remarkable spectrum of colors as they ripen — pale cream to lavender-purple to orange to red — making the plant highly ornamental at every stage. The flavor is moderately hot (about 30,000 SHU) with a distinctive spicy, slightly fruity complexity; use fresh at any stage or dry to a rich red powder. This is a historically significant cultivar that deserves preservation and wider growing.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring after last frost in any well-drained to dry, slightly alkaline to neutral, sandy to rocky soil in full sun; buffalo gourd has a massive perennial taproot that can reach 100+ pounds and regrows aggressively after frost or cutting — it is best suited to large-scale naturalistic plantings where the extensive spread (15–30 feet) is acceptable.
directions: Direct sow in spring after last frost in any well-drained, dry to moderately moist, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — buffalo gourd is one of the most extraordinarily drought-tolerant plants native to North America, a perennial-rooted annual vine of dry prairies, roadsides, and desert washes from Nebraska to California, extending its large, rough-textured, gray-green leaves on trailing stems up to 30 feet in a single season. The plant has a distinctly unpleasant, musky-fetid odor when handled (hence the species name 'foetidissima' — most stinking). Round, striped, baseball-sized gourds develop in summer that are toxic and extremely bitter when raw (cucurbitacins); these were used by indigenous peoples after processing to remove bitterness, and the seeds are oil-rich and nutritious. The massive taproot (potentially hundreds of pounds on mature plants) stores enormous water reserves. Most appropriate for large-scale wildlife habitat plantings, erosion control on dry slopes, and arid restoration projects rather than conventional garden settings.

plant_note: Plant sets or transplants 2–4 weeks before last frost; onions from sets mature faster and are simpler for home gardeners.
directions: Press sets or transplants 1 in deep with the pointed tip facing up in rich, well-drained, loose soil. Onion bulb size is determined by the number of leaves at the time of bulbing: each leaf corresponds to a ring, so healthy top growth is essential throughout spring. Reduce watering once the necks begin to soften and tops start to fall over naturally. Cure harvested bulbs in a warm, airy spot for 2–3 weeks before moving to dry, cool storage.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk passes and soil has warmed; this Bulgarian heirloom produces carrot-shaped, brilliant orange fruits that are thin-walled but very prolific.
directions: Start seed at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost in a moist starting mix and pot up once the first true leaves appear; transplant after frost danger passes and begin fertilizing with a low-nitrogen, high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage fruit set. Bulgarian Carrot is an eastern European heirloom producing vivid orange, carrot-shaped fruits 3–4 inches long with thin, crispy walls and a surprising fruity, almost apricot-like sweetness that precedes a sharp, clean, medium heat (5,000 SHU). It is exceptionally productive, with dozens of fruits per plant, and is highly ornamental as fruits turn from yellow to brilliant orange at maturity. Use fresh in salsas and relishes where the fruity flavor is showcased, or pickle whole for a pantry staple.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for fall harvest; Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet grown as much for its strikingly deep burgundy-red, ornamental foliage as for the edible roots, making it one of the most beautiful of all vegetable garden plants and an outstanding edging or salad green.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden 2–4 weeks before last frost in fertile, deeply worked, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil; soak seeds overnight to improve germination and thin to 3–4 inches when plants are 3 inches tall. Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet first listed in Burpee's catalog in the 1840s, grown for 175+ years for its spectacular deep burgundy-red to near-purple foliage that is among the most vivid of any vegetable; the young leaves and stems are intensely colored and are prized as a microgreen, baby salad leaf, and ornamental edging plant. The roots are also deep red, sweet, and excellent at any size from marble (35–40 days) to mature golf ball (55–60 days). The dramatic foliage remains strongly colored through the season and is highly heat-tolerant for a beet. An outstanding dual-purpose ornamental-vegetable for edible landscaping, container growing, and intensive salad gardens.
