French Fingerling is valued primarily for its visual distinction and culinary versatility: the combination of rose-pink skin and cream-yellow flesh with distinctive pink marbling through the interior makes French Fingerling one of the most visually striking fingerling varieties when halved or sliced — the pink marbling pattern within the creamy flesh is unique and makes the roasted or halved potato distinctly attractive in presentations. The texture is waxy and firm — a characteristic of fingerling potato varieties that have lower starch content than baking types (Russet Burbank) and retain their shape well through cooking. This waxy texture makes fingerlings the preferred choice for roasting whole (they develop a crispy exterior while staying firm inside), for potato salads (they don't become mushy when dressed), and for sautéed preparations where pieces need to hold their shape. French Fingerling's flavor is described as nutty, sweet, and complex — more interesting than the relatively neutral flavor of standard Russet types, with a richness that farmers market customers and restaurant chefs find particularly valuable. The variety performs well for small-scale and home garden production, producing enough tubers per plant for household use without requiring the large-scale inputs (cool storage, extensive land) of commercial Russet production.

plant_note: Plant sets (small bulbs) in early spring 4 weeks before last frost or in fall in zone 7 and warmer for overwintering; set each bulb pointy-end up, 1 inch deep, spaced 6–9 inches apart in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil.
directions: Plant small bulbs (sets) pointy-end up, 1 inch deep and 6–9 inches apart in well-drained, fertile soil in early spring or fall; the true French gray shallot (échalote grise) is considered the premier shallot of French haute cuisine, with a distinctive grayish-purple skin, elongated teardrop shape, and more complex, less harsh flavor than common shallots. Each planted bulb divides into a cluster of 8–12 daughter bulbs by harvest time in midsummer when the tops fall over. Lift, clean, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 2–3 weeks before storing. Save the smallest bulbs as next year's planting sets. Do not overwater — shallots are prone to rot in wet soils.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil warms; succession sow for extended harvest.
directions: This compact haricot vert produces slender, stringless pods with fine flavor on tidy dwarf bush plants ideal for small spaces and containers. Sow seed about an inch deep directly in warm soil, as beans dislike transplanting. Keep moisture even through flowering and pod set, and avoid handling wet foliage to reduce disease. Harvest the pencil-thin pods often while young and tender to keep the plants producing over several weeks.

plant_note: Sow direct or plant divisions in early spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; French sorrel is lower and more sprawling than garden sorrel with smaller, more arrowhead-shaped leaves and a more refined, less harsh acid flavor.
directions: Sow direct or plant divisions in early spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; French sorrel is more drought-tolerant than garden sorrel and thrives in poor, well-drained soils — rich, moist soil produces rank growth with coarser flavor. Rumex scutatus is a low-growing, somewhat sprawling European perennial herb with small, distinctive, shield-shaped or hastate (arrowhead-shaped) leaves that have a milder, more refined, less harsh acid flavor than the common garden sorrel (R. acetosa) and are preferred by many chefs for their superior taste — it is the traditional sorrel used in fine French cuisine and is sometimes called "true French sorrel." It is an excellent perennial groundcover in the kitchen garden, spilling attractively over path edges and walls; unlike R. acetosa it tolerates dry, rocky conditions. Harvest the small leaves continuously and remove flower stalks to prevent self-seeding.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is above 60°F.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep in warm mix at 80°F and pot up once seedlings have two true leaves; transplant to the garden after last frost. Fresno peppers resemble jalapeños but are slightly thinner-walled, fruitier in flavor, and ripen from green to bright red, with heat increasing as they mature (2,500–10,000 Scoville units). Harvest green fruits at 70 days for a jalapeño substitute, or ripen fully to red for a sweeter, hotter pepper that is excellent in hot sauces and salsas. Consistent deep watering (rather than frequent shallow watering) produces the best quality fruit and reduces stress-induced heat spikes.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Direct sowing is also possible. Frisee blanches naturally at the center as the outer leaves close over the interior; for the maximum pale center and milder flavor, tie the outer leaves loosely with twine 2 weeks before harvest. In zone 9 fall planting gives the most reliable head development; spring planting bolts too quickly in warming conditions.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Frisee is the fine-leaved, deeply curled, frizzy form of curly endive — a classic French bistro salad ingredient produced by its pale, blanched interior heart surrounded by a halo of fine, frizzy dark-green outer leaves. The pale interior (the blanched portion) has a mild, gently bitter, nutty flavor that is the defining taste of the classic frisee salad with lardons and a warm poached egg — one of the most recognizable French bistro dishes. The dark green outer leaves are more bitter and are usually removed or used for cooking. Frisee blanches naturally when the outer leaves overlap and shade the center, but deliberate blanching (tying the outer leaves for 1–2 weeks before harvest) produces a larger, more uniform pale center. In zone 9 frisee is a fall-through-winter crop that produces its characteristic delicate, pale center in the cool, short-day conditions from November through February.

plant_note: Sow in late summer or early fall for a fall and winter harvest; frisée produces best in cool weather and can be blanched by gathering and tying outer leaves around the head for 7–10 days to whiten and sweeten the center. In zone 9, direct sow September–October for harvest November through February, when the cool weather produces the most tender, flavorful heads.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; frisée (curly endive or fine curled endive) is the distinctive French salad green with deeply cut, finely fringed, pale green to yellowish leaves that create a loose, finely textured head with a pleasantly bitter flavor — one of the defining ingredients of classic French and Belgian cuisine. Unlike its flat-leaved cousin escarole, frisée has intensely ruffled, narrow, spiky-looking leaves that form a sprawling head; the outer leaves are dark green and quite bitter, while the interior (naturally or artificially blanched by excluding light from the heart for 7–10 days) turns pale yellow and becomes substantially more tender and mild. Frisée is the traditional green in salade lyonnaise (the classic Lyon salad with poached egg, lardons, and mustard vinaigrette) and in the Belgian warm salad tradition. The moderately bitter flavor pairs beautifully with rich dressings, warm bacon vinaigrettes, and strong cheeses. In zone 9, frisée is grown as a fall-through-winter crop when cool temperatures bring out its best flavor; summer production results in extremely bitter, loose plants that quickly bolt. Extremely cold-hardy once established, tolerating frosts to about 22°F.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant August–September for harvest November–January. Full Heart Batavian self-blanches at the center more reliably than other escarole types as the outer leaves naturally close over the heart. In zone 9 the mild fall allows slow, steady head development from September transplants through November harvest.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Full Heart Batavian is the classic escarole for Italian home cooking — a broad-leaved chicory endive forming a large, dense head with a characteristic self-blanching, creamy-yellow interior heart surrounded by darker outer leaves. The center heart has the mildest, most tender flavor of any escarole or endive type; the outer leaves are more bitter and are often removed or reserved for long-cooked soups and braises. Full Heart Batavian is the standard escarole used in Italian-American cooking — the primary green in Italian wedding soup (minestra maritata), in braised escarole with white beans and garlic, and as a pizza topping. The dense, substantial head stores well for 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator after harvest, making escarole one of the most practical winter greens for home cooks. In zone 9 the fall growing season from August transplants produces excellent heads by November; the plants are cold-hardy and withstand light frosts that improve flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer for fall/winter harvest in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; swollen-stem mustard (zhacai type) requires a full cool season to develop the characteristic swollen basal stem that is the primary edible portion — it grows slowly in cool weather and will bolt without making a proper stem if planted too late.
directions: Direct sow in late summer for fall/winter harvest in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; gai choy (swollen-stem mustard, zhacai type) is the Chinese mustard grown for its enlarged, knobby, swollen basal stem that forms a distinctive corm-like structure — salted, dried, and fermented with chili and Sichuan pepper to produce 'zhacai' (榨菜), the pickled Sichuan preserved vegetable that flavors noodle soups, fried rice, and countless Chinese dishes. The peppery, pungent young leaves are also edible as cooking greens. Growing your own allows fresh stem harvest for home pickling or fresh use. Requires a long, cool growing season for the stem to swell to usable size — an autumn crop planted 10–12 weeks before frost in zones 7–9 works best. A fascinating vegetable for those interested in Asian fermentation and pickling traditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: This pungent Chinese mustard, also called Indian mustard or Swatow mustard, forms curled leaves and wide, crunchy stems favored in Chinese, Korean, and Japanese cooking and pickling. The flavor is milder when young and grows sharper with maturity and heat. Grow in cool weather in full sun to partial shade, sowing in spring and fall. Keep soil evenly moist to slow bolting and keep flavor mild. Harvest whole heads or outer leaves as needed.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall harvest; gai lan is one of the most heat-tolerant and productive of the Asian brassica vegetables, more bolt-resistant than most and a particularly good choice for Gulf Coast fall and spring production in zones 8–11.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 9–12 inches for best results. Gai lan (also written kai-lan or gai laan) is the Chinese broccoli or Chinese kale of Cantonese cuisine, a leafy brassica producing thick, succulent stems, broad blue-green leaves, and small clusters of white flower buds that are harvested together as the edible vegetable; unlike Italian broccoli where the heads are the prize, gai lan is prized for its juicy, thick stems with a clean, mild, slightly bitter flavor that takes well to the intense heat of a wok and oyster sauce. Harvest when the first buds are just beginning to open for peak flavor and tenderness; the plants regrow from the base for additional cuts. More heat-tolerant than most brassicas and an excellent vegetable for Gulf Coast fall and spring seasons when traditional broccoli bolts quickly. Essential in Chinese restaurant cooking — the vegetable in classic 'Chinese broccoli with oyster sauce.'

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil is warm; needs a long season.
directions: This French heirloom, nicknamed peanut pumpkin for the sugar-crystal warts on its peach-colored skin, is prized for its supremely sweet, velvety orange flesh in soups and sauces. Fruit weighs 10 to 15 pounds and needs a long warm season to mature fully. Sow into rich, well-drained soil in full sun and give vines ample room to sprawl. Water deeply and feed for best size. Harvest when the rind hardens and cure in a warm, dry place before storage.

common_name: Galia Melon (Israeli Hybrid Netted Green-Flesh Muskmelon)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Galia requires warm conditions throughout its development and performs well in the Gulf South's warm summer climate. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–August harvest. Reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to golden-yellow and a sweet, tropical fragrance is detectable at the stem end — the skin color change from green to yellow-gold is the primary harvest indicator for Galia.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns yellow-gold and a sweet tropical aroma is detectable at the stem end. Galia is an Israeli hybrid muskmelon type developed in the 1970s at the Newe Ya'ar Research Center by Dr. Zvi Karchi, named for his daughter — an F1 hybrid that combines the netted, aromatic skin characteristics of cantaloupe/muskmelon with the pale green, spicy-sweet flesh of honeydew, creating a novel flavor profile found in no other commonly available melon type. The round to slightly oval fruits (3–5 lb) have heavily netted, yellow-green to yellow-gold skin at maturity (the skin begins green and transitions to yellow-gold as the melon ripens — a useful visual harvest cue not present in cantaloupe types that stay tan). The flesh is pale green to cream-green, aromatic, and extremely sweet with a distinctive tropical character — floral, spicy, and complex, distinctly different from both orange-fleshed cantaloupe and the blander honeydew. Galia melons are widely grown and marketed throughout Europe, Israel, and Central America and have become increasingly available in American specialty markets, where they are often sold under the name 'Israeli melon.' The flavor is among the most complex and interesting of any melon type, making Galia a top choice for gardeners who want to explore beyond standard cantaloupe.

plant_note: Sprout indoors year-round in a jar or tray; no garden bed required.
directions: Garbanzo bean sprouts are easy to grow indoors and rich in vitamins and protein for snacking or adding to many dishes. Rinse and soak the seeds overnight, then drain and rinse two to three times a day in a sprouting jar or tray. Keep them at room temperature out of direct sun and harvest in just a few days when short sprouts appear. Cook lightly or eat the crisp sprouts fresh. Refrigerate promptly after harvest to keep them fresh.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes in a partially shaded to full-sun spot. Garden huckleberry grows quickly in warm conditions and tolerates more shade than most fruiting vegetables — a good choice for lightly shaded food gardens in zones 3–10 (grown as annual).
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, moist but well-drained soil; garden huckleberry is an African cultivated nightshade that produces abundant clusters of small, round, glossy black fruits about the size of a large pea. Unlike its wild nightshade relatives, the ripe fruits are edible but ONLY when fully cooked — raw berries contain solasodine alkaloids that cause digestive upset. When properly cooked, they lose their bitterness and make good pies, jams, and preserves with an earthy, slightly tart flavor. Harvest only fully black, ripe berries. The plant is extremely productive in warm climates and tolerates partial shade, making it useful for lightly shaded food gardens. It is distinct from the true huckleberry (Gaylussacia species) and true blueberry, and should not be eaten raw under any circumstances.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep as soon as soil can be worked in spring — peas tolerate light frosts and germinate in cool soil; in zone 6–9 a fall crop planted 6–8 weeks before first frost is often the most productive.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep and 4–6 inches apart as early in spring as the ground can be worked, well before the last frost; garden peas are cool-season vegetables that thrive in cool, moist conditions (45–75°F) and deteriorate rapidly when temperatures exceed 80°F, so early planting is essential for a good harvest before summer heat arrives. Bush types (60–80 cm) need no support; climbing types need a trellis or netting. Keep the soil consistently moist from flowering through pod fill — inconsistent watering causes poor pod fill. Harvest shelling peas when pods are plump but still bright green; snap peas when pods are full and sweet; snow peas when pods are flat and before seeds swell. Peas fix their own nitrogen and improve soil for subsequent crops.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is a unique and charming heirloom tomato that genuinely resembles a peach — producing small, round, blush-yellow to pale cream fruits covered in a delicate fuzz of dense trichomes that gives them the texture and appearance of a ripe peach skin — one of the most visually distinctive and surprising novelty tomatoes available.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is an indeterminate, moderately sized variety requiring staking or caging; it is quite productive and continues bearing through the season. Garden Peach tomato is a remarkable heirloom curiosity that mimics a real peach in appearance with unusual fidelity — the small (2–3 oz), round fruits have pale cream to blush-yellow skin covered in tiny dense hairs (trichomes) that create a distinctly fuzzy, velvet-textured surface virtually identical to peach fuzz; when held in the hand, a ripe Garden Peach tomato is nearly indistinguishable from a small peach by touch alone. The flavor is sweet and mild with a hint of fruity peach character, very low acidity, and soft, juicy texture — appealing to those who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The novelty factor is considerable: Garden Peach tomatoes generate immediate curiosity and conversation, and children in particular are captivated by the peach resemblance; they are excellent for farm stands and markets as well as home garden curiosity. The fuzzy skin, unlike most tomatoes, does not split in rain or overhead irrigation. A productive and reliable variety for any garden where the growing season exceeds 70 days.

plant_note: Sow direct in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; garden sorrel is extremely easy to grow and will produce harvests within 2 months of sowing.
directions: Sow direct in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost in moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; garden sorrel is one of the easiest and most productive perennial vegetables — once established, remove flowering stalks to maintain leaf production and divide clumps every 3–4 years to rejuvenate. Rumex acetosa is a European native perennial herb grown for its large, arrow-shaped leaves with a distinctive, bright, lemony-sour flavor from oxalic acid that is the defining ingredient in classic French sorrel soup, sorrel sauce (excellent with fish), and sorrel-cream pasta; the leaves can be used fresh in salads when young and small, or cooked and pureed when larger, though they turn an unappetizing khaki color on cooking. The plant is extremely cold-hardy, re-emerging reliably in early spring, and is one of the first fresh greens available in the spring garden; harvest leaves continuously from the outside of the clump. Consume in moderation due to oxalic acid content.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out after frost danger passes.
directions: This 1950s German heirloom is often praised as one of the best cherry tomatoes, with extra-sweet, flavor-packed fruit borne in clusters of 6 to 12 all summer until frost. The vigorous indeterminate vines easily reach 6 feet or more. Provide tall, sturdy support and prune suckers for airflow and larger clusters. Start seed indoors early and transplant into full sun after frost. Water consistently to prevent cracking and pick often to keep vines producing.

plant_note: Plant cloves 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes in autumn so roots establish before winter; spring planting produces smaller bulbs.
directions: Break bulbs into individual cloves and plant each 2 in deep, pointed tip up, in well-amended soil enriched with compost; hardneck varieties are better for cold climates while softneck types store longer. Mulch the bed with 4–6 in of straw after the ground freezes to insulate and prevent heaving. Snap off hardneck scapes in early summer to redirect energy to the bulb. Harvest when the lower 4–5 leaves have dried to brown but 5–6 green leaves remain, then cure in a shaded, breezy spot for 3–4 weeks.

common_name: Garnet Sweet Potato (Red Garnet Moist-Flesh Orange Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant sweet potato slips (rooted cuttings) after the last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F or above; Garnet sweet potato produces slips from mature tubers grown in a warm, moist environment (place in a jar of water or bury in moist sand at 80°F for 2–4 weeks until sprouts are 4–6 inches long). In zone 9, plant April–June for fall harvest; sweet potato vines grow vigorously in Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Dig roots before the first frost (or in zone 9 before sustained temperatures below 55°F, which can cause chilling injury to stored roots). Cure at 85°F and 90% humidity for 4–7 days after harvest to sweeten and harden the skin before storage.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, loose soil; do not overwater or over-fertilize with nitrogen (promotes vine over root). Cure harvested roots before storage. Garnet Sweet Potato (also sold as 'Red Garnet') is one of the most widely grown and commercially important sweet potato varieties in the United States, recognizable to millions of shoppers as the 'yam' with reddish-purple to copper-red skin and brilliant orange flesh sold in most American supermarkets. The confusion between true yams (Dioscorea species, tropical tubers with starchy white flesh) and sweet potatoes is a historical American marketing accident: in the mid-20th century, Louisiana farmers and marketers began calling their orange-fleshed sweet potatoes 'yams' to distinguish them from the paler-fleshed Northern sweet potato types, and the term 'yam' became permanently associated with moist, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes in American grocery retail. Garnet's moist orange flesh has the classic American sweet potato eating character: very sweet, soft when baked, and vibrantly orange — characteristics that come from a high beta-carotene content (beta-carotene is the pigment in carrots, orange squash, and other orange vegetables that converts to Vitamin A in the body). The roasted Garnet sweet potato is one of the most nutritionally dense foods in regular American cooking: high in complex carbohydrates, very high in beta-carotene (Vitamin A precursor), and a good source of potassium, fiber, and Vitamin C.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms to well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist loamy soil in full sun. Gboma eggplant is a vigorous grower in warm, humid conditions and produces large plants requiring staking. More heat and humidity tolerant than standard eggplant cultivars.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting after last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, moist loamy soil in full sun; gboma eggplant is one of the most important vegetable plants of tropical West and Central Africa — a large, robust eggplant species (distinct from the common eggplant Solanum melongena) with large, lobed, hairy leaves and rounded to oblong, whitish-green to purple-streaked fruits. The leaves, young shoots, and immature fruits are all cooked and eaten as vegetables in West African cuisine — the leaves are particularly important as a cooked vegetable eaten with fufu (pounded starchy staples) and soups across Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, and neighboring countries. An important traditional African food plant adapted to hot, humid tropical conditions where standard eggplant varieties may struggle. The fruits can also be used like conventional eggplant in curries and stews. More robust and heat-tolerant than standard eggplant cultivars. A valuable addition to home gardens in zone 9–12 where traditional West African vegetables are of interest.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost once soil is warm.
directions: This German heirloom pattypan bears vibrant yellow, scalloped fruit with creamy yellow and light-green striping. For the best flavor and texture, harvest squash starting at about 2 inches wide up to 4 inches. Pick young and often to keep the plants producing all season. Sow directly into warm, fertile soil in full sun. Water consistently and allow good airflow to limit powdery mildew.

common_name: Gem Squash (South African Baby Round Squash, Bush Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Gem squash is a South African heirloom summer squash producing compact, round, dark green fruits the size of a tennis ball to softball (3–4 inches diameter) that are harvested at a small, tender stage unlike other summer squashes — the immature Gem squash is cooked whole or halved rather than sliced, and is the most widely grown squash in home gardens throughout South Africa.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; Gem squash grows as a compact bush (unlike most squash vines) and is excellent for small gardens and containers; harvest when fruits reach 3–4 inches (tennis-ball to softball size) with dark green skin — do not allow to mature to yellow or tan as flavor and texture degrade; cook whole (boiled, steamed, or baked) until just tender. Gem squash is a South African heirloom variety with deep roots in the home gardens of South Africa, where it is so culturally central that it appears in traditional Afrikaner recipes, South African school cookbooks, and family food traditions going back to the early colonial period. The small, round, dark green fruits are harvested at a much smaller stage than American summer squash — when they are about the size of a tennis ball to softball, with soft seeds and tender flesh — and are traditionally cooked whole rather than sliced. The most common preparation in South Africa involves boiling or steaming the whole small squash in salted water until tender, then halving and scooping out the seeded core, filling the cavity with butter, cream cheese, or condensed milk (a classic dessert preparation), and serving the squash halves on the plate. The flavor of properly young Gem squash is milder and sweeter than zucchini, with a delicate texture that makes it very versatile. The bush-type plant (not a vine) is exceptionally productive, producing many small fruits from a compact plant, making it practical for small raised-bed gardens. Increasingly available in American specialty and heirloom seed catalogs as gardeners discover this productive, compact, and culturally interesting vegetable.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+); traditionally interplanted at the base of standing corn stalks, which the vigorous climbing vines use as a living pole in the old 'three sisters' style of companion planting.
directions: Sow at the base of standing corn or a sturdy pole in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a true climbing type, it needs tall support to perform well. Genuine Cornfield Bean is an old-time American heirloom pole bean, so named because it was traditionally grown climbing up living corn stalks in the cornfield rather than on a dedicated trellis — a direct descendant of the indigenous 'three sisters' companion-planting tradition of interplanting corn, beans, and squash, in which the bean's nitrogen-fixing roots benefit the heavy-feeding corn while the cornstalk provides the bean a ready-made climbing pole. The vigorous vines produce a heavy crop of medium green pods good for snap use when young, or left to mature and dry for a flavorful winter soup bean. A practical, space-efficient heirloom for gardeners who want to grow beans and corn together in the traditional way, zone 4–10.

plant_note: Direct sow shelled peanuts (seed) after last frost when soil temperature is reliably above 65°F; in zone 9 sow March–May. Plant shell-on or shelled peanuts (not roasted) 1.5–2 inches deep; do not remove the seed coat. Georgia Green is the leading commercial Virginia-type peanut variety in the US, widely grown across the South for its disease resistance, high yield, and excellent flavor. Peanuts form their pods underground — after the yellow flower petals fall, the fertilized ovary elongates into a 'peg' that grows downward and pushes into the soil where the pod develops. In zone 9 dig peanuts when the inner pod shell shows the characteristic veining pattern and the pods have formed mature kernels (110–130 days from planting). Sandy, well-drained, calcium-rich soil is ideal — peanuts require calcium around the developing pods.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, calcium-rich soil — peanuts require loose, deep, well-drained soil for the pegs to penetrate easily and the pods to develop properly; Georgia Green is the leading commercial and home garden Virginia-type peanut variety in the United States, released by the North Carolina State University breeding program and immediately adopted across the peanut belt for its superior resistance to late leaf spot (Cercosporidium personatum) and Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) — the two most economically important peanut diseases in the Southeast. The Virginia type produces larger kernels than Spanish or Valencia peanuts, with the characteristic elongated, two-kernel pods and excellent roasted flavor that make Virginia peanuts the preferred type for in-shell roasting, boiling, and gourmet peanut products. Georgia Green has maintained commercial adoption for over 25 years — an unusual longevity for a field crop variety — because the disease resistance package continues to provide practical advantages over older and newer alternatives under Gulf South conditions. In zone 9 the long, hot growing season (110–130 days) and sandy coastal plain soils are ideal for peanut production, making Georgia Green one of the most naturally adapted and rewarding warm-season food crops available for Gulf South gardens.

plant_note: Plant slips after last frost when soil is warm above 65°F; Georgia Jet is one of the most early-maturing and productive sweet potato varieties for northern and transition-zone growers, reaching harvest in 90 days — useful in zone 9 as a reliable second crop that fits in a shortened growing window. Excellent for home slips from purchased roots.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; Georgia Jet is a productive open-pollinated sweet potato variety that reaches harvest in 90 days — one of the earliest-maturing sweet potatoes available, making it a reliable choice for shorter growing seasons and for gardeners in zones 5–7 who need a variety that matures before fall frost. In zone 9 it is equally useful as an early-maturing variety that can be planted as a second crop after spring vegetables finish. The deep reddish-purple skin and vivid orange flesh are very attractive; the flavor is sweet, moist, and rich — considered excellent for baking, steaming, and as a dessert sweet potato. An outstanding heirloom variety that produces well without synthetic fertilizers and stores reliably.

plant_note: Sow after frost in warm soil; long vines need plenty of room.
directions: This Southern heirloom from the 1830s produces oblong, green-striped fruits of 25 to 35 pounds with sweet, rosy-red flesh. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and give the sprawling vines abundant space. Water consistently while fruits swell, then ease off as they near ripeness to concentrate sweetness. Look for a curled, dry tendril near the stem and a creamy ground spot as ripeness cues before cutting the melon.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. In zone 9 collards are best grown as a fall-through-spring crop when temperatures are cooler — frost actually improves the flavor by converting starches to sugars in the leaves. Summer heat causes bitterness and reduced quality. Georgia Southern is especially heat-tolerant compared to most collards and can be harvested in zone 9 from October through April. Harvest outer leaves as needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Georgia Southern is the original Southern heirloom collard variety — one of the oldest and most historically significant vegetables in American Southern cooking, with documented continuous cultivation in the southeastern United States for well over a century. The large, smooth, blue-green leaves with a prominent pale midrib are the defining collard green appearance in traditional Southern cuisine — different from the crinkled leaves of kale and the heading structure of cabbage, collards are a non-heading form of Brassica oleracea that produces large individual leaves harvest continuously from the outer portions of the plant. The slow-cooked Southern preparation — simmering collards with smoked pork (ham hock, fatback, or smoked turkey) for hours with salt and vinegar until tender — transforms the tough, slightly bitter raw leaves into silky, rich, deeply flavorful cooked greens that are a cornerstone of Southern food culture. Georgia Southern is particularly valued for its mild flavor, large leaf size, and exceptional heat tolerance that allows spring and fall production in zone 9.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; flavor improves after fall frost.
directions: This time-tested Southern heirloom yields large, tender, blue-green leaves with a rich, traditional flavor and strong vigor. Sow seed a quarter to half an inch deep and thin plants so the broad leaves have room to develop. Harvest lower leaves as needed for cut-and-come-again picking, leaving the growing tip intact. Highly cold hardy, the greens sweeten noticeably after fall frost and produce reliably in both spring and fall gardens.

common_name: Georgia Southern Collards (Classic Old-Fashioned Southern Heirloom Collard)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12–14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August–September for fall and winter production or February–March for spring. Georgia Southern is the traditional large, open, heat-tolerant collard of the Deep South — it grows larger and more productively in zone 8–9 than most other collard varieties and is particularly adapted to the Gulf Coast's mild winters. Light frost improves the flavor; hard freezes below 20°F can damage large plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil. Georgia Southern (also simply 'Georgia Collards' or 'Old Georgia') is the foundational heirloom collard variety of the American South — an open-pollinated type with a continuous documented growing history in Southern gardens spanning well over a century, representing the traditional collard before the development of modern compact hybrids. Plants grow 3–4 feet tall and 2–3 feet wide, producing large, broad, blue-green, relatively smooth leaves with a somewhat open, non-heading habit. The flavor is the classic Southern collard character: substantial, slightly bitter when raw, sweet and savory when cooked slowly with salt pork, ham hocks, or smoked turkey — the traditional pot-likker preparation where the cooking liquid becomes as important as the greens themselves. Georgia Southern is notably heat-tolerant for a brassica, surviving Gulf South summers better than most collard varieties, and produces some of the most vigorous growth in the warm, humid conditions of zone 8–10 fall and winter gardens. Its open-pollinated nature allows seed saving from the most productive plants year after year.

common_name: Georgian Crystal Garlic (Large-Clove Mild Porcelain Hardneck)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Georgian Crystal is a porcelain hardneck that needs a real winter chill for good bulb formation and performs best in zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Crystal is a porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating in the country of Georgia, valued for its large, glossy white bulbs with just 4-6 very large cloves that are quick and easy to peel, along with a mild-to-medium, clean garlic flavor that works well both raw and cooked. It is a vigorous, reliable producer that adapts well across a range of cold-winter climates. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct energy into bulb growth; scapes are excellent sautéed or made into pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; storage life is moderate, typically 5-7 months in a cool, dry location.

plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; German Butterball is a German heirloom potato renowned as one of the most richly flavored and richly colored yellow-flesh potatoes available — the name accurately describes the extraordinary buttery, creamy flavor and golden-yellow flesh that makes it the benchmark yellow potato for flavor among heirloom enthusiasts.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; German Butterball is a late-mid-season variety (70–90 days) that produces medium-large, round to slightly oval, netted-skin, golden-fleshed tubers. German Butterball is a traditional German heirloom potato that entered American heirloom potato circles through the Rodale Institute and seed saver networks in the 1980s; it is consistently rated among the finest-flavored potato varieties by tasting panels — the rich, buttery, dense golden-yellow flesh has a flavor intensity that significantly exceeds Yukon Gold (the most popular yellow potato commercially) and makes German Butterball a benchmark for those seeking the very best potato flavor. The tubers have thin, netted tan-gold skin and deep golden-yellow flesh with a texture that is semi-waxy when young and becomes more floury when mature, making it excellent for all cooking purposes: baked, roasted, mashed, boiled, or fried. The exceptional flavor when simply roasted or baked with olive oil is what defines German Butterball's reputation — no other potato consistently delivers this depth of rich, buttery potato flavor without any embellishment. One of the most sought-after varieties in the specialty potato market.

common_name: German Extra Hardy Garlic (Robust Cold-Climate Porcelain Hardneck)
scientific_name: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'German Extra Hardy'
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so roots establish before dormancy; German Extra Hardy is a porcelain hardneck bred for exceptional winter survival and needs a real cold period to form well-divided bulbs, making it best suited to zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. German Extra Hardy is one of the most popular and reliable porcelain hardneck garlics for cold-climate gardeners, prized for its outstanding winter hardiness and consistent production of large bulbs with 4-5 big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, sometimes with faint purple streaking. Flavor is strong and full-bodied raw, mellowing to a rich, savory sweetness when roasted. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location, then trim and store; German Extra Hardy has only moderate storage life, typically 4-6 months, so use it earlier in the year relative to longer-storing softneck types.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall.
directions: This aptly named radish can be pulled small at quarter size or left to grow as large as a tennis ball while staying crisp and flavorful. It is crack-resistant and holds its texture without turning woody or spongy as it matures. Sow directly in cool weather and thin seedlings to give the large roots room. Keep soil evenly moist for the best flavor. Grows well in spring and fall in full sun to partial shade.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; German Johnson is a large, pink-fleshed Southern heirloom widely grown across the Mid-Atlantic and Gulf Coast states for its outstanding flavor and generous yields of meaty, 1–2 pound fruits with a classic old-fashioned tomato taste.
directions: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. German Johnson is a large-fruited, indeterminate, pink-fleshed heirloom long popular throughout the American South and Mid-Atlantic states — it is considered a parent variety of the famous Mortgage Lifter, crossed by M.C. Byles of Logan, West Virginia to produce that legendary tomato; the fruits themselves are large, slightly irregular, meaty, and deeply flavored with a rich, slightly acidic, classic old-fashioned tomato taste and minimal gel content. The plants are vigorous and highly productive, with good resistance to common foliar diseases in hot, humid Southern conditions. Excellent for slicing, sandwiches, and home canning.

common_name: German Red Hardneck Garlic (Rocambole Type Hardneck)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost in fall; German Red is a Rocambole-type hardneck garlic originally from Germany and popularized in the Pacific Northwest — it produces 8–12 cloves per bulb with a rich, complex, full-bodied flavor considered among the finest of all Rocambole garlics; harvest in early to midsummer when scapes have curled and straightened and 5–6 lower leaves remain green.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart, in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch with 4–6 inches of straw after ground cools; keep consistently moist in spring and remove scapes when they curl to redirect energy to bulbs; stop watering as lower leaves yellow and harvest in early to midsummer. German Red is a Rocambole-type hardneck garlic with origins in Germany, gaining wide recognition in North America through garlic enthusiast and seed-saver networks in the Pacific Northwest and through specialist growers like Filaree Garlic Farm — Rocambole types are considered by many garlic connoisseurs to produce the finest flavor of all garlic types, and German Red is consistently ranked among the best Rocamboles for its deep, rich, complex, slightly spicy flavor and the full-bodied pungency that distinguishes well-grown Rocambole from milder softneck types. The bulbs produce 8–12 large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer, with brownish-purple outer skin typical of Rocamboles; the cloves are rounded-edged and notably easy to peel (another Rocambole characteristic). The flavor is excellent when raw but truly reveals its complexity when roasted, sautéed, or used in slow-cooked dishes. The main limitation of Rocambole types including German Red is storage life — typically only 3–5 months under good conditions, compared to 10–12 months for softneck types; grow what you will use by midwinter and source next season's seed before that.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; German Stripe is a large Mennonite heirloom beefsteak tomato with stunning bicolor red and gold-yellow striped and marbled flesh — the visual effect when the fruit is sliced is extraordinary, with crimson and golden streaks radiating through the flesh in an irregular pattern, accompanied by an outstandingly rich, honey-sweet flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil; provide substantial staking or caging as plants reach 5–8 feet. German Stripe (also sometimes called 'Old German' or 'Old German Stripe') is a large Mennonite heirloom beefsteak tomato of the bicolor class — producing very large (12–28 oz), flattened to slightly lobed fruits that are visually unremarkable from the outside (reddish-gold exterior) but stunning when sliced: the interior flesh is dramatically streaked and marbled with alternating crimson red and golden yellow in bold, irregular patterns radiating from the blossom scar, making each cross-section unique and visually captivating. The flavor matches the dramatic appearance — exceptionally sweet and rich with a honey-complexity that is one of the hallmarks of the best bicolor heirlooms; the sweetness from the golden areas contrasts with the more acid-forward richness of the red portions to create a layered, complex taste. One of the finest beefsteak heirlooms for fresh eating, tomato salads, and caprese where the bicolor slices can be displayed to advantage.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes.
directions: This porcelain hardneck garlic, also sold as German Extra-Hardy, forms impressive 2 inch or larger bulbs with 4 to 7 fat, easy-peeling cloves and a strong, robust flavor. Plant individual cloves in fall, pointed end up, in fertile, well-drained soil, then mulch for winter protection. Cut the scapes in early summer to channel energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown and cure in a dry, airy place. It stores well and is very cold-hardy.

common_name: Gete Okosomin Squash (Ancient Native American 'Get Big' Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost, giving vines ample room to sprawl; Gete Okosomin, meaning roughly 'big old squash' in Anishinaabemowin, is an ancient variety grown by the Miami and other Great Lakes Native nations, propagated from seed found in a centuries-old archaeological cache and reintroduced to cultivation by tribal seed-saving efforts.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, giving the vigorous, sprawling vines generous room. Gete Okosomin — an Anishinaabemowin name often translated as 'big old squash' or 'cool old squash' — is an heirloom traced to seed recovered from a centuries-old clay pot in an archaeological context associated with Native peoples of the Great Lakes region, and subsequently grown out, verified, and shared by Miami Nation seed keepers and Native seed-saving networks, making it one of the oldest documented squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. Fruits are large, often 10-15 pounds, striped in shades of green, orange, and cream on a somewhat elongated, ribbed form, with dense, deep orange, sweet flesh well suited to baking, soups, and pies. As a Cucurbita maxima type, it needs a long, warm growing season and ample space for its long vines, along with consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Beyond its culinary value, growing Gete Okosomin is a way for gardeners to participate directly in the ongoing revival of an Indigenous foodway; seed saved from open-pollinated fruit can be replanted, continuing a lineage that stretches back many generations. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and the stem has dried, then cure for two to three weeks before storing in a cool, dry location.

plant_note: Start indoors early; the long season and warmth-dependent germination make transplanting after all frost danger essential.
directions: One of the hottest peppers on earth at over one million Scoville units, so wear gloves when handling ripe fruit. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and provide bottom heat around 85F for reliable germination. Transplant into the warmest spot in the garden after nights stay above 55F. Fruits ripen slowly from green to fiery red; dehydrate and grind them into flakes for a fruity, intense heat.

plant_note: Start indoors 12–14 weeks before last frost to allow enough growing time; transplant only after nights are reliably above 60°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and maintain a constant soil temperature of 85–90°F; germination is slow and irregular, so start more seeds than needed and be patient. Transplant to a sheltered, heat-retaining bed after all frost danger has passed, and protect young plants from cool nights with row cover. Fruits turn from green to red (or yellow in some strains) at full maturity; wear gloves and avoid touching the face when harvesting, as the heat exceeds one million Scoville units. The extremely long growing season makes this pepper best suited to zones 9–12 or greenhouse culture in cooler regions.

plant_note: Plant container-grown rhizome divisions or culm cuttings in spring in deep, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil in full sun; giant bamboo is one of the largest bamboos in the world and is clump-forming (not running) — a critical distinction that makes it manageable and non-invasive, unlike running bamboo species.
directions: Plant in deep, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide deep, consistent irrigation — giant bamboo is a water-demanding tropical plant. Dendrocalamus asper (giant bamboo or dragon bamboo) is one of the largest bamboo species in the world — a clumping (not running, not invasive) tropical giant native to Southeast Asia producing massive culms (stems) that can reach 20–40 meters tall and up to 20 cm in diameter in tropical climates, although in zone 9 conditions it is somewhat smaller (20–30 feet) and more manageable. The young shoots are among the most commercially important bamboo shoots in Southeast Asia — extraordinarily large, thick, and mild-flavored, sold fresh and canned throughout the region. Unlike running bamboo (Phyllostachys and others), Dendrocalamus asper forms a tightly clumped, slowly expanding clump and does not send runners underground to colonize surrounding areas — making it vastly more manageable in a garden setting. The mature culms are used for structural bamboo construction, furniture, crafts, and musical instruments. In zone 9, the clump will be killed to the ground by hard freezes but may resprout from the base if the root zone is well-mulched.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Giant Belgium Pink is a large-fruited heirloom beefsteak tomato producing flattened, deeply lobed pink-red fruits frequently exceeding 1–2 lbs, with sweet, rich, low-acid flesh similar in character to Brandywine but from a distinct European heirloom lineage — one of the great large pink beefsteak tomatoes for home garden growing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil. Giant Belgium Pink (also called Belgian Giant) is an indeterminate heirloom tomato with large, flattened, sometimes deeply lobed, pink to pinkish-red beefsteak fruits that frequently weigh 1–2+ lbs, rivaling Brandywine in size and beauty; the flesh is dense, meaty, sweet, and low-acid with a rich complexity suited for fresh slicing and sandwich use. The fruits share the large-pink-beefsteak class with Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter, providing an additional option with slightly different flavor character for gardeners who prize this class of tomato. Indeterminate; stake or cage as plants reach 5–8 feet; productivity is good for a giant beefsteak but individual fruits require time to develop fully. Outstanding for Gulf Coast spring tomato production planted February through March for May–June harvest.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; giant cane spreads by rhizome to form extensive canebrakes — use underground barriers if confined space is required.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; giant cane is the only bamboo native to North America, once forming vast canebrakes across the South and Mississippi Valley that were critical habitat for the now-extinct Carolina parakeet and Bachman's warbler, as well as important forage for Swainson's warbler. The young shoots in spring are edible, similar to commercial bamboo shoots, and were an important food source for Native American peoples. The mature canes were used for tools, weapons, and construction. As a landscape plant it provides fast-growing subtropical screening and naturalistic structure. It spreads aggressively by rhizome and should be managed; use underground root barriers to contain it in smaller spaces. The plant supports several rare specialist moth species.

plant_note: Start indoors early and transplant into deep holes to blanch the stalks.
directions: This AAS-winning heirloom leek produces thick, mild, onion-flavored stalks that store well through cold weather. Start seed indoors about ten weeks before the last frost, then transplant the pencil-thick seedlings into deep dibbled holes to blanch the lower stems. Water steadily and hill soil around the shafts as they grow to lengthen the tender white portion. Harvest as needed through fall and winter, since the hardy plants tolerate hard freezes.

common_name: Giant Marconi Sweet Pepper (AAS-Winning Italian Roasting Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Giant Marconi is an Italian frying/roasting pepper type that produces best with consistent moisture and good fertility. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall harvest. Harvest green for frying and grilling, or allow to ripen red for sweeter roasting and antipasto use. The very large, thick-walled fruits hold up exceptionally well to heat for frying, stuffing, and grilling.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Giant Marconi is a 1997 All-America Selections-winning Italian sweet frying/roasting pepper that produces some of the largest and most productive sweet non-bell peppers available to home gardeners — long (7–10 inch), slightly tapered, blocky-shouldered fruits with very thick flesh and virtually no heat. The distinctive form is characteristic of Italian frying peppers: longer and more tapered than bell peppers, with a ridged, slightly irregular exterior and a meaty, thick-walled interior with surprisingly few seeds relative to total volume. The large, thick-walled fruits are extraordinary for roasting and grilling — the thick flesh holds its structure as the skin blisters and chars, and after peeling, the roasted flesh is silky, sweet, and rich with concentrated pepper flavor. Giant Marconi is the ideal choice for Italian peperonata (braised peppers with olive oil and garlic), stuffed peppers, antipasto, and any application calling for large quantities of roasted sweet pepper. The plants are tall and productive, often requiring staking when heavily loaded; they produce heavily from midsummer through fall in zone 9. The very sweet, mild flavor at the red-ripe stage is excellent raw in salads and on cheese boards where the visual impact of the large, vivid red fruits is attractive.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: This classic heirloom spinach forms large, deep-green leaves with a mild, tender flavor, spreading widely as it grows. Direct sow seed half an inch deep in cool, fertile soil as early as it can be worked, since spinach bolts quickly in heat. Keep moisture even and thin plants so leaves size up fully. Harvest outer leaves or cut whole plants young, and sow again in late summer for a productive, cold-tolerant fall crop.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost transplant date; in zones 5–7 start in January–February and transplant in March–April. Celeriac requires a very long cool growing season of 110–120 days from transplant and cannot tolerate summer heat — zones 3–7 are ideal growing regions. Consistent moisture throughout development is critical; uneven watering produces cracked, malformed roots. Remove side shoots and small roots from the base of the developing globe to concentrate growth. In zone 9 celeriac is very challenging due to limited cool season length.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, consistently moist, very fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — celeriac demands high fertility and absolutely consistent moisture throughout its long development; Giant Prague is the standard open-pollinated celeriac variety — celery root — one of the most important and widely grown vegetables in European cuisine that remains dramatically underutilized in American cooking despite its extraordinary culinary versatility. The edible part of celeriac is not a root but a swollen hypocotyl (the base of the stem) that develops into a large, round, rough-surfaced globe of dense, white flesh with an intense, concentrated celery flavor — pure celery essence without the stringy fiber or water content of celery stalks. Celeriac's culinary applications are among the most diverse of any European vegetable: raw in the classic French preparation celeriac rémoulade (grated raw celeriac in mustardy mayonnaise), pureed into silky soups and mashes as a potato alternative, roasted, braised, or added to stocks for their distinctive aromatic depth. The dense, concentrated flavor means a small amount of celeriac adds substantial impact — a quarter of a root can flavor an entire pot of soup that whole bunches of celery stalks would struggle to match.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or late summer; heat prompts bolting.
directions: This heirloom mustard combines ornamental burgundy-red leaves brushed with green and a bold, spicy flavor that mellows with cooking. Direct sow seed a quarter to half an inch deep and thin for baby leaves or fuller plants. Harvest young leaves for a milder bite in salads or let them mature for cooking greens. Grow in cool spring and fall weather with steady moisture, since heat pushes plants to bolt and turns the flavor sharp.

plant_note: Plant rhizome offsets or divisions in spring after soil warms to 65°F. In zone 9 Alocasia macrorrhiza typically suffers freeze damage to the tops in hard freezes but resprouts from the rhizome in spring; mulch heavily in winter. Established clumps can produce enormous, upward-facing leaves reaching 4–6 feet long.
directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in bright indirect light or dappled shade; unlike Colocasia (which faces its leaves downward and outward), Alocasia macrorrhiza holds its enormous leaves facing up and skyward on stout, upright petioles, creating a dramatic architectural effect in tropical gardens. The stems and corms are edible after extensive cooking in many Pacific Island and Asian cuisines, but all parts contain high levels of calcium oxalate and must be boiled for at least 45 minutes to neutralize the crystals. Water generously during the growing season and reduce irrigation in cooler months; the large leaves transpire heavily and wilting is the first sign of drought stress. Clumps spread slowly by offsets that can be separated and replanted.

subcategory: Clumping timber and edible shoot bamboo
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 7–11; Giant Timber Bamboo (Oldham Bamboo) is the most widely planted clumping bamboo in the Southern United States and California — a large, non-invasive clumper native to Taiwan and south China producing straight, thick-walled culms to 65 feet tall and 4–5 inches diameter, used for timber, stakes, furniture, and edible young shoots.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Bambusa oldhamii is a clumping bamboo that does not run — the rhizomes are pachymorph (tightly clumping), so it stays where you plant it and never invades neighbors; water deeply and regularly in establishment and during summer heat. Bambusa oldhamii (Giant Timber Bamboo, Oldham Bamboo, or Eating Bamboo) is a large, fast-growing, non-invasive clumping bamboo native to Taiwan and adjacent southeastern China, and the most widely planted timber bamboo in California, Florida, and the Gulf Coast states due to its massive size, non-running growth habit, and cold hardiness to zone 7b. The culms (canes) grow rapidly to 50–65 feet tall and 3–5 inches in diameter, straight-walled and deep green when young, maturing to yellow-green or golden. The shoots produced in spring are among the largest, most palatable, and best-tasting of any bamboo available in the United States — harvested when 6–12 inches tall, boiled to remove bitterness, and used in Asian cooking exactly like commercial canned bamboo shoots. Giant Timber Bamboo also produces outstanding landscape screening, windbreak, and carbon-sequestration value — fully grown culms can be harvested every 3–5 years as timber for furniture, flooring, fencing, and structural poles. Excellent Gulf Coast and zone 8–11 privacy screen, grove specimen, and food-producing landscape plant.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Tomatillos require two plants for cross-pollination and fruit set; always plant at least two plants regardless of variety. Gigante produces the largest fruits of commonly available tomatillo varieties, making it the choice for recipes requiring large quantities of salsa verde with minimal prep work.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gigante (also called Grande) tomatillo is a large-fruited Mexican selection producing fruits 2–3 inches in diameter, substantially larger than the standard tomatillo — each fruit can weigh 3–4 ounces, compared to 1–2 ounces for standard types. The large fruit size dramatically reduces the number of fruits needed per batch of salsa verde and makes individual-fruit processing (husking, cleaning) more efficient. The flavor is bright, mildly tart, and herbal — characteristic of the tomatillo — without the papery, husked fruit becoming bitter at full size. Harvest when husks begin to split and feel papery but before they yellow significantly. Plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination, which is essential for good fruit set. Plants sprawl widely and may benefit from staking or support.

common_name: Gilfeather Turnip (Vermont State Vegetable, Heirloom Turnip-Rutabaga Cross)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer for fall and winter harvest; Gilfeather turnip develops best in cool weather and improves significantly in flavor after light frosts. In zone 9, direct sow late August through September for harvest November through January. The very large roots (up to 5 pounds) require adequate space and a full growing season of cool weather for best development.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly in well-tilled, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, thinning to 8–12 inches when plants are 3 inches tall; harvest in late fall after light frosts have sweetened the roots. Gilfeather turnip is one of the most historically significant and culinarily distinctive heirloom vegetables in New England — the Vermont state vegetable, named for John Gilfeather of Wardsboro, Vermont, who reportedly kept this variety secret by cutting off the tops and bottoms of roots before selling or trading them to prevent others from saving seed, maintaining a monopoly on his exceptional variety for decades in the early 20th century. The Gilfeather is not a standard turnip but appears to be a cross between turnip (Brassica rapa) and rutabaga (Brassica napobrassica), inheriting characteristics of both — the roots are large (up to 5 lbs), elongated to round with a distinctive greenish-white skin, and the white flesh is significantly sweeter, milder, and less peppery than standard turnips, with a creamy texture when cooked that many tasters prefer to either parent species. The flavor is sweet, rich, and substantial — excellent mashed, roasted, or in soups and stews — without the sharpness that can make standard turnips polarizing. A unique and genuinely outstanding heirloom vegetable with an authentic piece of New England agricultural heritage behind it; a excellent fall/winter root vegetable for zone 9 production.

plant_note: Start rhizome pieces indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; move outside only after all danger of frost has passed and temperatures are consistently warm.
directions: Break fresh ginger rhizomes into 1–2 in pieces each with a visible growth bud and pre-sprout them in a warm, moist environment for 2–3 weeks before planting 2 in deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil. Ginger thrives in dappled shade and resents direct afternoon sun in hot climates. Keep soil consistently moist and avoid letting it dry out. Harvest young ginger in as little as 4–5 months for milder flavor, or leave in the ground until foliage yellows for full-size, more pungent roots.

plant_note: An early determinate type; start indoors and set out after frost for very early fruit.
directions: A cold-tolerant bush tomato that sets fruit in cooler temperatures than most, giving you some of the earliest ripe tomatoes of summer and a long fall harvest. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and harden off before transplanting. The compact 30-inch plants stay tidy and do well in containers, though a small cage helps. Pick the 2-inch flavorful slicers as they color up to keep production going.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Glacier is a notably early-maturing, cold-tolerant slicing tomato capable of setting fruit when nighttime temperatures fall to 45–50°F — ideal for short-season northern gardeners, high-altitude gardens, or Pacific Northwest coastal conditions where most tomatoes fail to set fruit in cool summers.
directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; Glacier is a determinate to semi-determinate variety that does not require extensive staking; it produces most of its fruit in a compressed season (excellent for northern and coastal climates) and can be grown without pruning. Glacier is an open-pollinated early-season slicing tomato specifically suited to cool-summer and short-season climates: it sets fruit at nighttime temperatures as low as 45–50°F, a capability that distinguishes it from most standard tomato varieties (which require consistent nighttime temperatures above 55°F for pollen viability and fruit set). This cold-setting ability makes Glacier valuable for Pacific Northwest coastal gardens where summer temperatures rarely exceed 75°F, high-altitude Rocky Mountain gardens with cool nights, and short-season northern gardens (zones 3–5) where the growing season is compressed. The medium-small (3–4 oz), round to slightly oblate, red fruits ripen early (55–65 days from transplant) and have good flavor for an early variety — pleasantly sweet-acidic balance with classic fresh tomato character; the flavor intensifies if warm conditions prevail at harvest time. The determinate to semi-determinate plants (36–48 inches) do not require the extensive staking that indeterminate varieties need, making them convenient for short-season production in smaller garden spaces.

plant_note: Intermediate-day onion; start indoors early and transplant as soon as soil is workable.
directions: An intermediate-day onion that forms clean, crisp white bulbs 4 to 5 inches across with a mild, sweet flavor good for fresh use. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings once the soil can be worked. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist, tapering off water as the tops fall over near harvest. Cure bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing.

common_name: Glass Gem Corn (Rainbow Jewel-Toned Ornamental Flour Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of 4+ rows for adequate wind pollination; isolate from other corn by 300 feet to preserve jewel-color purity, though crossing with other corn simply diversifies the colors in interesting ways. In zone 9, plant March–May. Glass Gem requires a long season (100–120 days) and must be harvested as a dried corn — leave ears on the plant until husks are completely dry and papery. The translucent jewel colors are most vibrant after drying.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4 rows after last frost; harvest ears 3–4 weeks after the husks become fully dry and papery. Peel back husks and hang in a dry, well-ventilated place for additional drying before storage or decorative use. Glass Gem is a visually extraordinary ornamental flour corn that became an internet sensation in 2012 when photographs of its polychrome, jewel-toned ears went viral — sparking massive interest in heirloom and decorative corn that had not previously existed in the gardening public. The corn was developed by Carl Barnes, a half-Cherokee seed saver from Oklahoma, who spent decades crossing and back-crossing different traditional Cherokee corn varieties to create a flour corn capable of producing kernels in any color of the rainbow — deep red, crimson, burgundy, purple, violet, blue, aqua, green, gold, orange, pink, cream, and white, often on the same ear in translucent, jewel-like forms. Barnes shared seed with fellow seed saver Greg Schoen, who further developed and distributed the variety through Native Seeds/SEARCH. Each ear is unique — no two are identical — and the translucency of the kernels in bright light has no equivalent in any other corn or vegetable. While Glass Gem can be ground into flour (it is a genuine flour corn with functional starch composition), its primary use is ornamental — for corn arrangements, wreaths, and displays where the extraordinary color variation is the attraction.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil has warmed; plant in blocks for pollination.
directions: A stunning ornamental flint corn with kaleidoscopic, translucent rainbow kernels that can also be dried for cornmeal, flour, or popcorn. Direct sow after the last frost in blocks of at least four short rows so wind pollination fills out the ears. Give steady water during tasseling and silking for well-filled cobs. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure indoors before shelling or displaying.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; expose seedlings to cool temperatures (50°F) for 2 weeks before transplanting to vernalize and trigger bud set.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors and expose young plants to 2 weeks of 50°F nights to vernalize them for first-year bud production. Transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil in a permanent location, as plants are long-lived when winters are mild enough. Harvest the central bud first, while bracts are tight and the stem snaps cleanly, then side buds as they develop. In zones 7–9, cut plants back to 12 in after harvest and mulch heavily for overwintering; divide clumps every 3–4 years to maintain vigor.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Glory of Enkhuizen'
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop in mild-winter climates; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once seedlings have 4–5 true leaves.
directions: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the round, dense heads benefit from consistent moisture to avoid splitting as they finish sizing up. Glory of Enkhuizen is a classic Dutch heirloom cabbage introduced in the late 19th century from the seed-growing town of Enkhuizen in the Netherlands, long one of Europe's most important vegetable-seed production centers. It forms medium-large, round to slightly flattened, blue-green heads with a tender, sweet, finely grained interior that holds its quality well both fresh and cooked, and it has a good reputation for splitting resistance and reasonable storage life for a mid-season type. Widely grown across Europe and North America through the 20th century as a dependable, high-yielding main-crop cabbage, it remains a favorite heirloom for gardeners wanting classic round-head cabbage with proven, old-world reliability, in zone 3–9.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. Provide sturdy cage or stake support for the large, indeterminate vines. The bicolor flesh — yellow-gold base with red internal streaking — makes Gold Medal one of the most beautiful tomatoes when sliced. In zone 9 fall planting in August produces exceptional flavor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy stake or cage support; Gold Medal (also known as B&L's Gold Medal) is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing spectacular bicolor fruits with bright golden-yellow skin blushed with red and dramatically marbled interior flesh — when sliced, the cross-section reveals a swirled pattern of deep red-orange and golden-yellow that makes Gold Medal arguably the most beautiful heirloom tomato variety for fresh-cut presentations and tomato salads. The flavor combines the mild, low-acid sweetness characteristic of yellow tomatoes with the rich, complex notes of a large beefsteak type, producing a fruit that is simultaneously sweet and substantial in flavor without the sharp acidity of most large red heirlooms. The low-acid, sweet character makes Gold Medal appealing for people who enjoy the fresh sweetness of yellow tomatoes but want a larger, meatier fruit. Large fruits commonly reach 1–2 pounds and have meaty walls with small seed cavities, making them outstanding for fresh slicing.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; beans resent transplanting and cold soil.
directions: A golden-yellow wax bean whose bright pods stand out against green foliage, making picking quick and easy. Direct sow after the soil warms past 65F, spacing seeds a few inches apart in rows. This compact, disease-resistant bush type does well in containers and holds quality both on the plant and after harvest. Pick pods young and often to encourage continued production.

common_name: Gold Rush Potato (Golden-Flesh Russet-Type Baking Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.8–6.5) soil in full sun; Gold Rush is a longer-season potato (90–100 days) — in zone 9, plant as early as January to ensure tubers mature before summer heat arrives; protect young shoots from late frost with row cover.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Gold Rush is a North Dakota State University russet-type potato introduction combining the classic russet potato appearance (oblong, netted-brown skin) with the bright golden-yellow flesh of yellow-flesh varieties — providing a visually distinctive combination of the familiar russet form with surprisingly vivid yellow-gold interior color. The golden-yellow flesh — darker than standard Russet Burbank white flesh and more intense than the pale yellow of Yukon Gold — creates an attractive visual quality in baked, mashed, and roasted preparations where the golden color adds visual appeal to the finished dish. Gold Rush has the high-starch, dry, fluffy interior texture of classic russet-type potatoes — ideal for baking (fluffy, dry-textured baked potato), French fries (crispy exterior, dry interior), and mashed potatoes where a light, dry texture is desired. The russet skin type and long oblong shape produce the classic large baked potato form. In zone 9, Gold Rush's longer season (90–100 days) requires early planting (January) to ensure harvest before summer heat ends the cool potato growing season. Plant deeper than most varieties (6–8 inches) and hill aggressively to promote maximum tuber development in the long cool season before heat forces harvest.

common_name: Gold Rush Wax Bean (Bright Yellow Stringless Bush Wax Bean with Straight Pods)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; Gold Rush is a compact stringless yellow wax bush bean producing uniform straight pods (5–6 inches) in a concentrated set over 2–3 weeks. The bright golden-yellow color of the pods makes harvesting easy — the pods stand out clearly against green foliage, reducing the chance of overlooking mature pods that would become tough and seedy if missed. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through midsummer extend the harvest; in zone 9, sow February–April for spring and again September–October for fall production. Gold Rush is one of the highest-yielding yellow wax bush beans, with pods borne in dense clusters just above the soil surface on a compact upright plant.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest when pods reach 5–6 inches before seeds swell noticeably inside. Gold Rush Wax Bean is a high-yielding yellow wax bush bean developed by Burpee for home garden production, distinguished by the uniformity and straightness of its bright golden pods and its concentrated harvest set that makes it one of the most productive yellow wax types per planting. The wax bean category — yellow-podded varieties that lack the green chlorophyll of standard snap beans — developed historically as a distinct preference in European-American cooking traditions where the pale color was associated with tenderness and delicacy; wax beans are botanically identical to green snap beans, with the yellow coloration resulting from the absence of chlorophyll development in the pod walls, allowing carotenoid pigments (which would normally be masked by green) to express visibly.
