Cushaw's mild flesh is used in pies (a Southern tradition), as a cooked vegetable, and in Mexican and Central American cuisines where the species originated.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Green Thai Eggplant is exceptionally heat-tolerant and continues producing through zone 9 summer heat when other eggplant varieties slow. Multiple plantings (February and July) provide nearly year-round production in zone 9. Plants may survive mild winters in zone 9b as short-lived perennials and re-grow from the base.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with warm soil temperatures; Green Thai Eggplant produces small, round to oval, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits in bright green to greenish-white with striping or mottling, harvested young at marble to golf ball size for the best flavor and texture. The flesh is firmer, drier, and significantly more bitter than standard globe eggplant — the characteristic bitterness and firm texture are intentional qualities in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking, where the small green eggplants are sliced and added raw to green curry pastes or braised whole in red curry. They absorb coconut milk and spice sauces without becoming mushy, maintaining their distinctive firm bite even in extended cooking. Unlike the standard Italian or Japanese eggplants where bitterness is considered a defect, the natural bitterness of green Thai eggplant is a flavor feature that rounds and deepens the overall taste of Thai curries. In zone 9 the plants are extremely heat-tolerant and productive through the hottest months.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; the standard green heirloom tomatillo produces medium to large (1.5–2 inch) green to yellow-green fruits in papery husks and is the backbone of Mexican salsa verde, enchiladas verdes, and countless other dishes — plant at least two plants for cross-pollination.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil; stake or cage plants as they sprawl. Green tomatillo is the standard culinary tomatillo of Mexican cuisine — not a green tomato but a distinct species (Physalis ixocarpa) with a characteristic papery husk that expands around the developing fruit; fruits are harvested when the husk splits and the fruit fills it completely, at a bright green to yellow-green stage with a tangy, tart, citrus-herbal flavor that is distinctly different from any tomato flavor. The tart flavor of the fresh tomatillo is the foundation of salsa verde, a primary sauce in Mexican cooking alongside salsa roja; tomatillos are also used in mole verde, enchiladas verdes, chile verde, and canned as salsa. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; does extremely well in Gulf Coast and Southwestern gardens. Two or more plants are needed for pollination — a single plant produces little to no fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall crop. Green Wave is cold-tolerant to about 15°F when established, making it one of the most cold-hardy mustards for Gulf Coast winters.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–18 inches; Green Wave is an AAS winner mustard green producing large, beautifully ruffled, deep green leaves with a distinctive curled and frilled edge that gives it strong ornamental value as well as excellent eating quality. Flavor is pungent and spicy like Southern Giant Curled but with finer leaf texture and more cold-hardiness. Green Wave is the recommended mustard green for raw use in salads (young leaves) and sautés where texture is prized; the intricate ruffling and curling increases leaf surface area, creating both a decorative appearance in the garden and a textural interest on the plate. In zone 9, fall-planted Green Wave produces beautifully through winter, the cold sweetening and mellowing its characteristic spicy bite — the finest mustard green eating comes after temperatures drop below 40°F. Harvest outer leaves regularly; the plant regrows vigorously. An excellent substitute for kale or collards in anyone who wants a faster-maturing, more flavorful cooking green.

plant_note: Start indoors; transplant after frost and provide sturdy support for tall vines.
directions: A gourmet indeterminate tomato bearing smooth, crack-free 2 to 3 inch fruits striped golden green and forest green, with a slight amber blush when ripe. Start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply after the weather warms. Stake or cage the vigorous 6-foot-plus vines and prune suckers for airflow. Judge ripeness by softness and blush rather than color, since the fruit stays green when ready.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; ripeness is tricky to judge by appearance — harvest when the skin softens slightly, shows yellow-green stripes against deeper green, and gives to gentle pressure.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to deeply prepared, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Green Zebra is a modern heirloom tomato developed by Tom Wagner in 1983, producing attractive 2–3 inch fruits with distinctive lime-green skin and dark green stripes that warm to yellow-green stripes against chartreuse skin when ripe, with a bright, tangy, acidic flesh that is a refreshing counterpoint to sweeter tomatoes. Excellent sliced fresh in salads, as a garnish, or for green salsa — one of the most visually striking tomatoes available. An indeterminate vine, it tends toward compact growth relative to larger beefsteak heirlooms. Yields prolifically over a long season.

common_name: Gretel Eggplant (AAS-Winning White Mini Eggplant, Tender Bitter-Free Companion to Hansel)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Gretel is the white-fruited companion variety to Hansel (purple), both from PanAmerican Seed and both AAS winners in consecutive years. Gretel produces clusters of 3–4 inch white eggplants on the same compact (20–24 inch) upright bush plant. In zone 9, start seeds January–February for March–April transplanting. Gretel's most important characteristic beyond its striking pure-white color is the complete absence of bitterness — white eggplants generally lack the anthocyanins and related phenolic compounds responsible for bitterness in purple eggplants, and Gretel has been bred for minimal astringency and very sweet, mild flavor. The flesh is tender and creamy-white with minimal seeds at proper harvest size (3–4 inches); left to overripen, the skin yellows and seeds increase. Unlike purple eggplants that can turn bitter when cut and exposed to air, Gretel's white flesh remains stable. Harvest before any yellowing appears on the skin.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches while skin is pure white; yellowing indicates overripeness. Gretel Eggplant won the All-America Selections award in 2009, one year after its companion Hansel (purple mini eggplant), both from the same PanAmerican Seed breeding program and sharing the same compact plant habit, prolific cluster fruiting, early maturity, and exceptional eating quality. Gretel's white fruit color distinguishes it visually and culinarily from standard purple eggplants: the white coloration (caused by the absence of the anthocyanin and chlorogenic acid pigments present in purple eggplant skin) correlates with a fundamentally different flavor profile — white eggplants, including Gretel, are consistently sweeter, milder, and less bitter than purple varieties because they lack the phenolic compounds that contribute bitterness. This means white eggplant varieties like Gretel can be used raw in preparations where purple eggplant's bitterness would require salting to draw out (a traditional technique for reducing eggplant bitterness before cooking): Gretel's naturally sweet, mild flesh is pleasant raw in thin slices or cubed in salads. The AAS recognition of Gretel in consecutive years with Hansel highlighted the appeal of offering home gardeners a white-fruited alternative to the standard purple that combined the same outstanding productivity and compact habit with meaningfully different flavor characteristics. For zone 9 gardeners growing multiple eggplant varieties for culinary diversity, Gretel and Hansel planted together provide a visually striking paired harvest of white and purple mini eggplants from compact, easily managed plants.

plant_note: Sow after frost when soil is warm; tolerates heat well.
directions: This heat-tolerant heirloom produces smooth, straight fruits with mottled silver-grey skin on compact, heavy-yielding bush plants. Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil and space plants for good airflow. Water at the base to keep foliage dry and harvest fruits young, around six to eight inches, for tender flesh. Pick frequently during the peak of summer, as fruits size up quickly and steady harvest sustains production.

plant_note: Start indoors well before the last frost; transplant only after soil has warmed.
directions: This heirloom Physalis produces small golden fruits inside papery, lantern-like husks with a sweet pineapple-vanilla flavor. Start seeds indoors six to eight weeks before your last frost and set out sprawling plants once nights stay warm. Fruits are ripe when the husks turn tan and drop naturally to the ground, so harvest from the soil below the plant. Let them cure a few days in their husks to develop full sweetness for fresh eating or preserves.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost in warm (70–80°F) conditions; transplant after all frost danger passes. In zone 9, plant in fall for a winter crop — ground cherry performs as a cool-season vegetable in the Gulf Coast South where it fruits prolifically through winter and spring before summer heat causes decline.
directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; ground cherry is an often-overlooked member of the Physalis family closely related to the tomatillo, producing small, marble-sized golden-yellow fruit enclosed in papery tan husks like a miniature tomatillo. The flavor is remarkable — simultaneously sweet, tropical, and slightly vanilla-like, unlike any other common garden vegetable. The plants are bushy and sprawling, reaching 2–3 feet high, and produce prodigiously once established. Fruit drops to the ground when ripe (hence the name), where it can be left in its husk for several weeks without deteriorating. Eat fresh, bake in desserts, make preserves, or dry for extended storage. In zone 9, treat as a cool-season annual planted in fall for winter through spring production. The husk protects the fruit from pests and makes storage easy. Self-seeds prolifically in warm soils and will naturalize in suitable areas. Not to be confused with the cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana), though they are closely related.

common_name: Ground Elder (Goutweed, Bishop's Weed, Herb Gerard)
plant_note: CAUTION — ground elder is one of the most aggressive garden weeds in North America and Europe; once established it is nearly impossible to eradicate; only plant in buried containers or completely isolated beds, and choose the variegated form 'Variegatum' which is less invasive.
directions: Plant only in buried containers with solid bottoms, or in walled raised beds with no soil contact — ground elder spreads by deeply rooted, tenacious rhizomes that regenerate from small fragments and are nearly impossible to eradicate once established in open soil. Despite this invasive tendency, it is a genuinely useful shade edible: young spring leaves have a pleasant, lightly celery-like, slightly peppery flavor and have been eaten across Europe and Asia since medieval times, used in salads, soups, and as a potherb. The variegated form 'Variegatum' with cream-edged leaves is less vigorous and a better garden choice. For foragers, it is easily identified in spring before any other look-alikes emerge.

plant_note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, loamy to rocky, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun; ground plum has a deep taproot that makes it drought tolerant but very difficult to transplant — sow directly in its permanent location.
directions: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, dry to moderately moist soil in full sun — ground plum is a native sprawling legume of the southern Great Plains and central prairies, historically one of the most important native edible plants of the southern prairie, producing clusters of purple to reddish-purple pea flowers in April–May followed by the remarkable, plum-like fruit pods — green when young, reddish when ripe — that gave the plant its common name. The young, unripe pods have a mild, slightly sweet, pea-like flavor and were eaten raw by Plains peoples as a seasonal vegetable and green snack food on the prairie. The pods are edible raw when fully green and firm, but become papery when ripe. An important nitrogen-fixing prairie legume that improves soil for neighboring plants. Outstanding for prairie restoration plantings in well-drained, alkaline, or rocky soils in zone 3–9.

plant_note: Plant small tubers 2–3 inches deep in spring after last frost; provide a trellis or fence for the twining stems. Tubers from the previous year planted in spring produce the largest harvest in fall.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun near a support for the twining stems; this native leguminous vine was a staple food for many Indigenous nations and early European settlers and was considered for commercial cultivation before potatoes became dominant. Harvest the small, walnut-shaped tubers strung along underground rhizomes in fall after frost kills the vines; they taste like a richer, nuttier potato and can be boiled, baked, or roasted. The fragrant reddish-purple flowers in midsummer fix atmospheric nitrogen. Tubers are small in the first year but grow larger each subsequent year — the plant becomes more productive the longer it is left undisturbed.

plant_note: Sow in midsummer (July in most climates) for a spring harvest; the plants survive winter and produce their distinctive rosette heads in early spring from the overwintered root. In zone 9, sow September–October for harvest in January–March.
directions: Sow seeds in late summer and allow plants to grow through autumn; after hard frosts, the tops die back and the plant enters semi-dormancy before the root drives up a tight, flat rosette of dark green leaves in late winter or early spring — a delicacy treasured in northern Italy as a salad green when little else is available. The name 'grumolo' means 'little cluster' in Italian, describing the compressed button-rosette form. Grumolo verde is exceptionally cold-hardy and virtually maintenance-free through winter. The bitter, nutty flavor is characteristic of chicory; young spring leaves are the most tender and least bitter. In warm-winter climates like zones 8–9, the plants may not go fully dormant but still produce acceptable rosettes in winter.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; a widely used dried Mexican chile that requires a long warm season — ideal for zone 8–11 where it can produce two harvests in warm years.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost, harden transplants thoroughly, and plant into warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil after all frost risk has passed. Guajillo is one of the most commonly used dried chiles in traditional Mexican cooking, the dried form of the Mirasol pepper, producing long (3–5 inch), tapered, shiny red fruits with smooth, thin skin that dries to a deep red-brown; heat is mild to medium (2,500–5,000 SHU). The distinctive sweet, tangy, slightly fruity flavor with mild heat makes guajillo an indispensable base for authentic red enchilada sauce, pozole rojo, and adobo marinades. Harvest fully red and dry slowly on the plant or by hanging in a warm, ventilated space; dried guajillos store for 6–12 months.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Gypsy's earlier maturity (60–70 days) compared to bell peppers (70–80 days) gives zone 9 gardeners an earlier start on sweet pepper harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Gypsy is an All-America Selections winner (1981) — a sweet, elongated, tapering pepper that produces medium-sized (4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), semi-thick-walled fruits that ripen through a distinctive color progression from pale creamy-yellow, through orange, to bright red, with excellent flavor at every stage. The early maturity (60–70 days) gives Gypsy a head start on the sweet pepper season compared to larger bell types, and the disease resistance package includes tobacco mosaic virus tolerance — a significant advantage. Gypsy is a semi-sweet, elongated type rather than a classic blocky bell — closer to an Italian frying pepper shape but with thicker walls and a sweeter, less pungent flavor than traditional frying types. The elongated fruits are outstanding for fresh eating, stuffing (the tapering shape holds stuffings differently than blocks), grilling, and roasting. The color progression from pale yellow through orange to red creates an attractive multi-colored harvest display when fruits at different maturity stages are present on the plant simultaneously. Plants are productive, compact, and well-suited to both spring and fall production in zone 9. An outstanding early-maturing sweet pepper for home garden use.

plant_note: Start indoors early with strong bottom heat; transplant only after nights are warm.
directions: An intensely hot pepper prized for its fruity aroma as much as its fire, said to be many times hotter than a jalapeno. Start seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost with warmth around 85F for even germination. Transplant into a warm, sunny spot after nights stay above 55F, and mulch to keep roots evenly moist. Wear gloves when picking and processing the ripe orange fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost due to the long growing season; transplant 2 weeks after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and maintain soil temperature at 85–90°F to achieve reliable germination, as Capsicum chinense species are notably slow to sprout. Transplant into the warmest, most sheltered spot in the garden once conditions are fully settled. Consistent feeding with a potassium-rich fertilizer during fruiting will maximize yields. Harvest when fruits reach their characteristic orange or red color and feel firm; handle with gloves due to extreme capsaicin levels.

plant_note: Hairy bittercress is primarily harvested as a foraged weed that appears in garden beds in early spring and fall; if growing intentionally, direct sow in late summer or early fall in moist, shaded, or partly shaded soil. Harvesting small plants before they flower keeps the bed clean while providing fresh greens.
directions: Harvest young plants from shaded garden beds and pathways in late winter through early spring when they appear as small rosettes; hairy bittercress is a widespread annual or overwintering weed of gardens, nurseries, and cultivated ground throughout North America that is almost universally underappreciated as food. The small, watercress-like leaves have a pleasant, sharp, peppery flavor exactly like watercress and can be eaten raw in salads, added to sandwiches, or used as a garnish — ideally harvested before the white flowers open when flavor is best. The spring-loaded seed capsules shatter explosively when ripe, scattering seeds widely; harvesting before flowering prevents this and gives you both the greens and a cleaner garden. An excellent early-spring foraged green requiring no cultivation whatsoever.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring crop; in zone 9 the ideal window is January–February for spring and September–November for fall, when mild temperatures produce the sweetest roots. Fall crops are typically superior in taste and texture.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-prepared, loosened soil and thin to 3–4 inches apart; crowding produces forked or stunted roots. Hakurei is a Japanese F1 hybrid turnip bred to be eaten raw: the pure-white, smooth globe roots (2–3 inches in diameter at harvest) are remarkably sweet, mild, and almost fruity — nothing like the sharp, peppery flavor of conventional turnip varieties. Unlike storage turnips, Hakurei is best harvested small and young; roots toughen and lose their fresh crispness if left past 2 inches. The greens are also tender and mild and excellent raw or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, fall-sown Hakurei seeded in October is often the finest salad turnip in the cool-season garden, maturing just before the holidays. A favorite for farmers' market growers because of its eye-catching appearance and reliably sweet flavor.

common_name: Hale's Best Cantaloupe (Classic California Heirloom, Sweet Orange-Flesh Standard Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F); in zone 9, plant April–May. Melons need full sun, warm soil, and consistent moisture from transplant through fruit development. Hale's Best develops fruits 5–7 inches in diameter on trailing vines 4–6 feet long. Detect harvest maturity by smell (strong sweet melon aroma from the blossom end), the fruit slipping slightly from the vine, and the underlying skin color shifting from white-green to creamy yellow. In the Gulf South, mildew can affect melon foliage by late summer; early planting for a June harvest before peak humidity helps maintain plant health. In zone 9's hot, dry springs (before the summer humidity builds), melons are ideally suited — the combination of heat and adequate moisture produces the sugar development that distinguishes a good cantaloupe from a bland one.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when slip from vine and fragrant. Hale's Best is the quintessential American heirloom cantaloupe — a variety that defined the flavor standard of what a good cantaloupe should taste like for generations of American home gardeners and market growers. The variety was developed in the early 20th century by Paul Halladay of Turlock, California, from melon seed brought from Japan, and selected specifically for shipping quality, flavor, and thick, deeply netted skin. The resulting variety — medium to large, round to slightly oval, covered in a thick network of raised tan netting over a gray-green background, with a heavily perfumed blossom end and deeply orange, very sweet flesh — became so widely grown in California's San Joaquin Valley melon production region that 'Hale's Best' essentially defined the commercial cantaloupe market in mid-20th-century America. The flesh is thick, dense, and intensely orange — higher in beta-carotene than pale-fleshed cantaloupe varieties — with genuine sweetness and the rich, complex melon aroma that distinguishes a truly good cantaloupe from a bland one. The Brix (sugar content) of properly grown, vine-ripened Hale's Best in warm conditions can reach 14–16, producing sweetness comparable to the best modern hybrid melons. Several numbered strains of Hale's Best were selected for regional performance: Hale's Best #36 and Hale's Best Jumbo are among the subvarieties that have remained in commerce through heirloom seed preservation.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost, or start indoors briefly to get a jump.
directions: A classic heirloom muskmelon with exceptionally sweet, thick-walled flesh and a small seed cavity, in 3 to 5 pound fruits. Direct sow two or three seeds per hill once soil warms past 70F and thin to the strongest plant. Water deeply while vines grow and fruit sizes up, then ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine and smells fragrant.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Hale's Best is a classic heirloom cantaloupe prized for exceptional sweetness, tender juicy flesh, and a small seed cavity that yields more edible fruit. Sow seeds in warm soil once frost has passed, giving vines several feet to sprawl. Water consistently while fruit develops, then ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the melon separates cleanly from the vine with a light pull.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; plant 4–5 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thin to 2 strongest plants when 3 inches tall. In zone 9 plant March–April for summer harvest; Halona's short season (73–80 days) makes it one of the better choices for zone 9's limited spring melon window before extreme summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Halona is a 2015 All-America Selections Gold Medal winner cantaloupe — one of the most highly awarded AAS winners in recent years — developed for exceptional eating quality combined with early maturation and disease resistance. Halona produces medium-sized (4–5 pound), deeply netted, tan-skinned fruits with dense, deep orange flesh and exceptional sweetness (Brix 14–17°, very high for an open-pollinated type) with complex, honey-like flavor that compares to the finest specialty melons. The fruit set is consistent and the plants show resistance to powdery mildew — a significant disease in humid climates. Halona's early maturation (73–80 days) and compact vine habit make it suitable for small gardens and shorter growing seasons; two plants produce more than enough for a family. The small seed cavity and thick, firm flesh give excellent eating quality with no watery texture. Halona is the recommended first melon for new growers due to its reliable production, disease resistance, and superior flavor — and one of the best choices for zone 9 spring production where a short fruiting window requires a reliable early variety.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; the long growing season requires an early start and the slow germination period means pre-soaking seeds is beneficial.
directions: Soak seeds in warm water for 24 hours before sowing to improve germination; sow 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, stone-free soil in rows, as seeds germinate slowly and unevenly over 2–4 weeks. Thin seedlings to 6–8 inches apart once established; the flat-leaf parsley-like foliage is edible throughout the season as an herb. The ivory-white, parsnip-like root develops slowly all season and tastes like a concentrated, slightly sweet parsley-parsnip hybrid — exceptional in Central European soups and stews. Harvest in fall after light frost improves sweetness; roots left in the ground over winter in milder climates will re-sprout in spring but roots lose quality as the plant prepares to bolt.

common_name: Hannah Sweet Potato (White-Fleshed Dry-Type NCSU Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; Hannah is a white-fleshed sweet potato that produces in approximately 90–100 days and is harvested before the first fall frost. In zone 9, set slips in late March through April for a July–September harvest; mulch beds to conserve moisture and suppress weeds through the hot summer growing period.
directions: Plant rooted slips after last frost when soil is above 65°F, setting each slip 3–4 inches deep with the crown at or just above soil level; Hannah is a white-fleshed, cream-to-tan skinned sweet potato developed by North Carolina State University that has become one of the most popular white-fleshed varieties in US production — offering a substantially different culinary experience than the familiar orange-fleshed types. The flesh is cream to pale ivory, firm, and notably dry (less moist than orange varieties), with a mild, subtly sweet flavor that reads more like a russet potato than a typical sweet potato — making Hannah uniquely versatile for preparations like roasted potato dishes, gratins, soups, and anywhere a firm, dry-textured potato is preferred. The dry, non-gummy texture means it mashes cleanly, holds together in casseroles, and is excellent when baked whole with a crisp skin. Hannah produces smooth-skinned, uniform tubers in a standard 90–100 day window and yields reliably in Southern and Gulf Coast production areas. For gardeners familiar only with orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, Hannah represents a practical bridge variety that can replace russet potatoes in the garden while still being a true sweet potato culturally and agronomically.

common_name: Hansel Eggplant (AAS-Winning Slender Mini Purple Eggplant, Prolific and Early Cluster Producer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Hansel is a compact eggplant variety producing prolific clusters of slender, 3–4 inch long deep purple eggplants on an upright, bushy plant reaching 20–24 inches. In zone 9, start seeds January–February for March–April transplanting. Hansel was an All-America Selections winner in 2008, recognized for its extraordinary productivity, early maturity (55–60 days from transplant — faster than most large eggplant varieties), compact habit suitable for container growing, and excellent eating quality: the slender fruits are tender-skinned with virtually no bitterness, very few seeds, and flesh that stays white and creamy without the sponginess or discoloration that can affect larger eggplant varieties. The cluster fruiting habit — multiple fruits set in groups at each branch node rather than singly — contributes to the spectacular production that made Hansel notable in AAS trials. Harvest at 3–4 inches for best texture; fruits become slightly seedy and tough-skinned if left much longer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches when skin is glossy deep purple. Hansel Eggplant was developed by PanAmerican Seed and won the All-America Selections award in 2008, one of a pair of complementary mini eggplant varieties (Hansel purple, Gretel white) from the same breeding program that were recognized in consecutive years for their outstanding performance in AAS trials. The Hansel and Gretel naming reflects the paired nature of the complementary varieties and their petite, fairy-tale proportions compared to standard full-sized eggplants. Hansel's outstanding AAS trial performance was attributed to several factors that distinguish it from both standard large eggplant varieties and other small-fruited eggplants: the combination of extremely early production (55–60 days from transplant, compared to 70–80+ days for large varieties), prolific cluster fruiting (multiple fruits per node vs. one to two for standard types), compact plant size (20–24 inches, easily managed in containers), and excellent eating quality (tender skin with no bitterness, minimal seed content, clean white flesh) created a variety with compelling advantages in every direction. For zone 9 gardeners, Hansel's short days-to-maturity is particularly valuable: zone 9 eggplant production spans March–October, but the most productive and high-quality harvest period is before the peak summer heat (June–July); Hansel's early maturity allows significant harvest before conditions become stressful.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Haogen is a celebrated Israeli melon developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz, prized for its extraordinarily sweet, aromatic flesh of exceptional quality — considered by melon enthusiasts and chefs to be among the finest-flavored melons in the world, the Israeli equivalent of the French Charentais for concentrated sweetness and intense melon aroma.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun; Haogen is ready to harvest when the skin transitions from green to orange-yellow in patches and the fruits slip from the vine with minimal pressure — like all aromatic melons, it deteriorates rapidly after peak ripeness. Haogen (also spelled Ogen) was developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz in Israel and remains the most celebrated Israeli melon variety, known throughout the melon-growing world for its extraordinary flavor; the small to medium (1–3 lb), round fruits start with pale green skin that develops orange and gold patches and creeping yellow-green net as they ripen. The flesh is salmon-orange to greenish, with an intensely sweet, highly aromatic, complex melon fragrance and flavor with notes of honey and tropical fruit that many consider the finest melon eating experience available. Short shelf life after harvest (1–2 days at room temperature, 3–5 days refrigerated) means Haogen is fundamentally a garden and local market melon rather than a commercial shipping variety — its reputation rests on the incomparable quality of fruit eaten within hours of harvest. Widely grown in Israel, Netherlands, and by American melon enthusiasts.

common_name: Hardy Tapioca (Cold Hardy Cassava, Argentine Cassava)
plant_note: Plant rooted stem cuttings in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Hardy tapioca is an Argentine relative of cassava (M. esculenta) that is far more cold-tolerant than true cassava — surviving freezes to zone 8 and dying back to the ground but regrowing in spring — primarily grown in warm-temperate and subtropical gardens as an ornamental foliage plant for its deeply-cut, tropical-looking leaves.
directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings in well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established; dies back to roots in freezes but regrows. Manihot grahamii (hardy tapioca or Argentine cassava) is a cold-hardy Argentinian relative of true cassava (M. esculenta) — closely resembling its famous edible cousin in leaf shape (deeply palmately lobed, tropical-looking) and stem structure but significantly more cold-tolerant, surviving hard freezes to zone 8 (approximately 15°F) by dying to the ground and regenerating from tuberous roots the following spring. In zone 8–11, it is grown primarily as an ornamental for its dramatically tropical-looking, deeply cut, dark-green leaves (8–12 inches across) — creating a convincing tropical garden effect at far lower temperatures than true cassava (zone 10+). The plant can reach 4–8 feet in a single growing season, creating rapid impact as a tropical accent. The roots are reportedly edible (similar to cassava) but much less developed than commercial cassava and require the same caution about proper preparation to remove cyanogenic glycosides. Hardy tapioca is drought-tolerant, grows rapidly on poor soil, and is extremely low-maintenance — simply cut to the ground after frost and let it regrow. A remarkably useful plant for zone 8–9 gardeners seeking a tropical aesthetic without the winter protection demands of true tropical plants.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring — parsnip requires a long, cool growing season of 100–130 days and cannot tolerate summer heat. Germination is notoriously slow (14–28 days) and erratic; sow thickly and thin to 3–4 inches after germination. Parsnip performs best in zones 3–7 where hard fall frosts convert the roots' starches to sugars — the classic technique of leaving roots in the ground through fall frosts and harvesting in late fall/winter produces the sweetest, most intensely flavored roots. Zone 9 gardeners will find parsnip very challenging due to insufficient cold for sweetness development.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil — parsnip requires the same deep, uncompacted growing conditions as carrots but needs even more space due to the larger root; Harris Model is the standard American parsnip variety, selected in the 1880s by the Joseph Harris Seed Company as a smooth, uniform improvement over the traditional English Hollow Crown parsnip — fewer hollow crowns, smoother skin, and better root uniformity make Harris Model the most widely grown American parsnip. The long, tapering, ivory-white roots develop a rich, complex flavor that is unmistakably its own: sweet and aromatic with earthy, celery-like, and nuttily caramelized notes when roasted — a flavor that lacks any close comparison among other vegetables. The signature technique for maximizing parsnip flavor is 'frosting' — leaving harvested or in-ground roots exposed to repeated hard frosts that convert starches to sugars, creating a dramatically sweeter root than summer-harvested parsnips. Roasted parsnips (with butter, herbs, and honey) are one of the great classic British-American root vegetable preparations, where high heat caramelizes the natural sugars and transforms the texture from firm-and-dense to tender and lightly crisp at the edges.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; multiple varieties exist under the 'Hatch' name (Big Jim, Joe Parker, 6-4, Sandia) — all are New Mexico-bred long green chiles best harvested green and roasted.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil rich in phosphorus after all frost risk has passed. Hatch green chile refers to New Mexico-style long green chiles — varieties such as NuMex Big Jim, Joe Parker, and the heritage 6-4 — bred at New Mexico State University and grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico; they produce 6–10 inch, elongated, thick-walled green pods with heat levels ranging from mild to hot depending on cultivar and growing conditions. The distinctive flavor comes from the dry, high-altitude climate, but home gardeners in zones 7–11 with hot, dry summers can produce excellent results in-ground. Harvest green when pods are fully sized and char-blister them on a grill or under a broiler; the roasted flavor is unmatched for green chile sauces, stews, and salsas.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights remain above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a productive spring through fall season; New Mexico type chiles produce heavily through summer heat and can be roasted and frozen in quantity for year-round use.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the New Mexico type chile, particularly Hatch and its relatives, is the defining pepper of Southwestern cuisine, eaten green (roasted), red (dried), or ground into chile powder. This long, mildly hot pepper (1,500–3,000 SHU) averages 6–8 inches and is the standard for roasting — the thick walls blister perfectly under a broiler or over an open flame, and the roasted, peeled chiles freeze beautifully for months. Harvest green through September, or leave some to ripen red for a fully different flavor profile. The Hatch designation technically refers to chiles grown in the Hatch Valley of New Mexico, but the variety performs excellently throughout zone 9.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; alternately start cabbage for the fall crop in midsummer (10–12 weeks before first fall frost) for transplanting in early fall.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant out 2–4 weeks before last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; cabbage is a cool-season crop that tolerates hard frosts once established, and fall crops initiated in midsummer often produce the best heads as the crop matures into cool autumn weather. Space plants widely — 18–24 inches — as crowding produces smaller heads. Water consistently throughout head development, as irregular watering causes the heads to crack open; harvest immediately if heads show any cracking. Cabbage is susceptible to clubroot, cabbage worms, and aphids; row covers over young transplants provide excellent pest protection. Head types range from small early varieties (70 days) to large late storage types (120 days) suitable for long-term kraut fermentation.

plant_note: Sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring crop; sow again in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: Sow seed at 1/8 in depth and thin to 8–12 in once seedlings are 2 in tall; butterhead types form loose, tender heads with buttery inner leaves. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch to maintain cool root temperatures, as heat quickly triggers bolting. Harvest heads by cutting at the base when they feel moderately firm but before the center begins to elongate, which signals imminent bolting. Outer leaves can be removed as the head develops to stretch the harvest period over several weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm soil; suited to shorter seasons.
directions: A productive heirloom muskmelon well suited to short-season climates, bearing round 3-pound fruits with dark orange, firm, aromatic flesh. Direct sow into warmed soil after frost, or start indoors a couple of weeks early in cooler regions. Give vines room to sprawl and keep them evenly watered until the fruit begins to net and ripen. Harvest at full slip when the fruit releases from the vine with gentle pressure.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil warms and frost risk is gone.
directions: Hearts of Gold is a beloved heirloom cantaloupe with fragrant, honey-sweet orange flesh, usually maturing at two to three pounds. Sow directly into warm, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Keep moisture even during fruit set and growth, then reduce watering as the melons ripen to boost flavor. Harvest when fruit slips easily from the vine and gives off a strong sweet aroma.

common_name: Heat Wave II Tomato (Gulf South High-Heat Fruit-Setting Hybrid Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Heat Wave II's primary advantage is fruit set at temperatures above 95°F — when most standard tomato varieties drop flowers without setting fruit, Heat Wave II continues to produce.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Heat Wave II is one of the most important tomato introductions for Gulf South gardeners — a hybrid specifically developed for heat tolerance to maintain fruit set during the high-temperature periods (daytime highs above 90–95°F) that cause standard tomato varieties to drop flowers without setting fruit. In zone 9, most standard tomato varieties produce well in spring (March–May) then cease fruiting when summer heat arrives in June; Heat Wave II's genetic ability to set fruit at high temperatures extends the productive season into summer conditions that defeat other varieties. The medium-large (6–8 oz), round, globe-shaped fruits have bright-red color, firm flesh, and good fresh-eating flavor — not the finest gourmet tomato, but extremely reliable production in conditions that eliminate the competition. Heat Wave II is a determinate (bush-type) tomato growing 4–5 feet that can be grown with minimal staking. Disease resistance includes V, F, FF, N, T — a comprehensive disease package for Gulf South conditions where soilborne disease pressure is high. For zone 9 gardeners who want tomatoes through the summer rather than only spring and fall, Heat Wave II is the primary recommendation.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring crop. Heatmaster is specifically bred to set fruit when nighttime temperatures remain above 75°F — the primary reason most tomatoes fail in Gulf Coast summer. It is the recommended choice for gardeners who want a spring crop that extends into early summer in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Heatmaster is a hybrid tomato developed specifically for gardeners in hot-summer climates (USDA zones 8–10) where standard tomato varieties drop their blossoms and fail to set fruit when nighttime temperatures exceed 70–75°F and daytime temperatures exceed 95°F. The proprietary Seminis breeding program tested hundreds of crosses before selecting a plant that maintains viable pollen and fruit set under extreme heat — making it one of the most important varieties for Gulf Coast, Southwest, and Deep South gardeners who struggle with the narrow spring window before heat arrives. Fruits are medium-large (8–10 oz), red, globe-shaped with good flavor and firm flesh. The indeterminate plant continues producing through periods of heat that stop Celebrity and Better Boy cold. Disease resistance includes Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium, Tobacco mosaic virus, and nematodes. For zone 9 gardeners frustrated by tomatoes that stop producing in May, Heatmaster extends the harvest window by 3–5 weeks.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Heinz 1350 is a determinate canning tomato that ripens a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for processing in large batches — time transplanting to allow harvest before peak summer heat in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Heinz 1350 is the classic determinate processing tomato developed by the H.J. Heinz Company, once widely grown commercially for ketchup production, that became a home garden favorite for anyone serious about canning, sauce-making, or tomato processing — it produces a concentrated set of uniform, medium-sized (5–6 oz), globe to slightly blocky, bright-red fruits with thick, meaty walls, small seed cavities, and very firm texture that holds up exceptionally well to cooking and reduces beautifully to rich tomato sauce without excessive water. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce the entire crop within a 3–4 week window, which is exactly what canners need — a predictable large harvest all at once rather than a continuous trickle. VF resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt) keeps plants healthy through the season. For zone 9, plant in late January to early February so the harvest window falls in late April through May before summer heat stresses the plants. An outstanding choice for serious home canning enthusiasts who want a reliable, high-yield processing crop.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; succession sow for a steady supply of mixed leaves.
directions: A blend of four red and green lettuces including bibb, romaine, crisphead, and leaf types for varied color and texture in one bed. Direct sow in cool soil and thin as plants grow, eating the thinnings as baby greens. Keep the soil consistently moist and give afternoon shade in warm spells to slow bolting. Harvest outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again supply or cut whole heads at maturity.

plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Helios is a golden-yellow-skinned spring radish with crisp white flesh and mild flavor, an unusual color choice that stands out in mixed radish plantings and relish trays.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Helios is a round spring radish with smooth, bright golden-yellow skin and crisp, mild white flesh, an eye-catching alternative to standard red radishes that adds warm color contrast to salads, relish trays, and mixed radish plantings. Flavor is clean and only mildly peppery, similar to other fast-maturing spring radish types. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, since radishes left too long in the ground become pithy and hollow; succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.

plant_note: Sow at or just after last frost; hemp grows very quickly and tolerates light frost at seedling stage but is damaged by hard freezes.
directions: Drill seed 3/4–1 in deep at 20–30 lb/acre for grain production (denser stands reduce branching and improve yield); hemp requires a federal or state license to grow legally in the United States. Plants are dioecious — female plants produce the seed-bearing flowers; for grain production allow plants to go naturally to seed and harvest when seeds are firm and no longer milky. Thresh and dry seed to below 10% moisture for storage; hulled hemp seed (hearts) is nutritionally rich in protein and balanced omega-3/6 fatty acids. Do not confuse grain hemp with high-THC varieties; certified grain cultivars contain less than 0.3% THC.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Henderson is very sensitive to cold soil and seed will rot rather than germinate in cold wet ground — be patient and wait for warm conditions.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost in full sun, in fertile, well-drained soil; Henderson Bush Lima is the standard small-seeded bush lima bean, an heirloom selection dating to the 1880s that remains the most widely grown small white lima because of its outstanding heat tolerance, compact growth requiring no staking, and prolific production of small, tender, buttery beans in a compressed time frame. The small seed size means faster cooking than large limas and a creamier texture; it is excellent fresh, frozen, or dried as a dry bean. Space rows 18–24 inches apart for good air circulation and reduce disease pressure. Mulch to keep soil moist as pods develop.

plant_note: Sow directly after the soil is reliably warm; lima beans rot in cold ground.
directions: This compact heirloom butterbean, introduced in the late 1800s, is loved for its reliability, mild flavor, and easy sprouting. Sow seeds directly into warm soil, as lima beans germinate poorly in cold or wet ground. The bushy plants need no staking and produce flat pods of small, creamy beans. Pick pods when plump for shelling fresh, or leave them to dry on the plant for storage beans.

common_name: Henderson Lima Bean (Baby Bush Lima, Heat-Tolerant Gulf South Butter Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil (65°F minimum); Henderson is a baby lima (smaller seed than Fordhook types) that excels in hot weather — it sets pods reliably in the Gulf South heat that causes many bean varieties to drop flowers. In zone 9, plant April through July for summer production; late plantings mature in September when temperatures moderate for the fall harvest. The bush habit (no staking needed) and compact plant size (18–24 inches) make Henderson practical for raised beds and small gardens. Plant at 4-inch spacing in rows 24 inches apart for the highest yield per square foot. Henderson is widely available as a named 'baby butter bean' in Gulf South seed racks and is one of the most heat-adapted dry and fresh lima bean types for the region.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest green for fresh use when pods are plump; leave to dry on the plant for dry beans. Henderson is a small-seeded bush lima bean — one of the most widely grown lima bean varieties in the American South and Gulf Coast region, where it is often marketed and sold as 'baby butter bean' or 'speckled butter bean' (referring to the speckled seed coloring of some strains). Henderson was introduced in the 1880s and has remained a staple in Southern gardening for over a century, valued for its small, tender seeds, heat tolerance, and reliable production in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf South that challenge larger-seeded lima types (such as Fordhook). The primary distinction between Henderson and Fordhook-type limas is seed size: Henderson produces small seeds roughly half the size of Fordhook, with a more tender skin and a creamier texture when cooked fresh or dried. In the Gulf South culinary tradition, 'butter beans' (the Southern name for fresh lima beans) are a staple of summer cooking — simmered low and slow with fatback or ham hock until very tender, the small Henderson seeds achieve a creamy, buttery texture that the variety's Southern common name accurately describes. Henderson also performs well as a dry bean: the small seeds dry quickly on the vine and cook to a smooth, creamy texture in soups and stews without requiring the long soaking and cooking time of larger bean types. The heat tolerance of Henderson is a practical advantage in zone 9: while cool-season beans (snap beans, peas) cannot be grown in summer, Henderson sets pods reliably in July-August temperatures that stop production in more sensitive varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after frost for good wind pollination.
directions: Hickory King is a historic heirloom white dent corn with unusually large kernels, ideal for grits, hominy, masa, and cornmeal. Sow directly into warm soil in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good pollination. Give plenty of nitrogen and steady moisture as the tall stalks develop. Let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvesting for grinding or long-term storage.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; a Native American heirloom dry pole bean from the Hidatsa people of the northern Great Plains, traditionally grown in the Three Sisters system with corn and squash; plant at the base of corn stalks for traditional companion planting.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6 inches apart along a trellis or the stalks of sweet corn in the traditional Three Sisters companion planting arrangement. Hidatsa Red is a Native American heirloom dry pole bean from the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River region (present-day North Dakota), with deep maroon-red seeds that cook to a creamy, full-bodied texture with an earthy, robust flavor well-suited to soups and stews; the variety was collected and preserved through the work of Alfred Mandan and introduced more widely by Seed Savers Exchange. Allow pods to ripen and dry completely on the vine; pods are tan with dark mottling when ready. An important cultural heritage bean that rewards the grower with both excellent eating and connection to a long agricultural tradition.

common_name: Hidatsa Red Indian Bean (Plains Native American Dry Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Hidatsa Red is a traditional bean of the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River valley in North Dakota, traditionally grown as one of the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) in the fertile bottomlands of the Missouri and its tributaries, producing striking dark red, kidney-shaped seeds with excellent rich flavor that made it a staple of Hidatsa cuisine.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; Hidatsa Red is a bush dry bean that does not require staking; harvest when pods are fully dry and papery, typically 85–100 days from planting. Hidatsa Red is a traditional bean variety of the Hidatsa people (also called Minitari or Gros Ventre), a Native American nation of the upper Missouri River valley in what is now North Dakota, where they cultivated beans, corn, and squash in the fertile bottomlands for centuries before European contact; the bean entered American heirloom preservation networks through ethnobotanical work documenting traditional Plains agriculture and was distributed by the Seed Savers Exchange. The medium-sized, kidney-shaped seeds are an unusual deep brick-red to maroon-red color — distinctive enough to recognize immediately among other dry beans — and cook to a tender, creamy texture with rich, earthy, complex flavor somewhat similar to kidney beans but with more character. In traditional Hidatsa cooking, the beans were dried and stored for winter use, then slow-cooked in stews with dried meat and corn; they are equally excellent in modern preparations — chili, soups, slow-cooked bean dishes, and baked beans where the robust flavor is showcased. Well-adapted to short seasons and the variable conditions of the Northern Plains; good drought tolerance.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–July. Hill Country Heirloom Red is a Texas heirloom variety adapted to deep summer heat and limestone-influenced soils, producing earlier and more prolifically than most standard green okra varieties under Central Texas and Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in full sun in any well-drained soil; Hill Country Heirloom Red is a striking Texas heirloom okra with deep burgundy-red pods, stems, and leaf veins that make it as ornamental as it is productive. The pods are smooth with 5 ridges and should be harvested at 3–4 inches for peak tenderness; like all okra, the pods become fibrous if left to exceed 5–6 inches. The red pigmentation fades to green when cooked, similar to red-pod okra generally. Plants grow vigorously in the limestone soils and intense heat of Central Texas, where this variety has been grown by generations of families in the Hill Country region. Soaking seeds overnight in warm water before planting speeds germination. Harvest every 2–3 days in summer.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after the last frost when nights stay above 50F.
directions: This West Virginia heirloom produces huge one-to-two-pound beefsteak fruits with striking yellow-and-red marbled coloring and sweet, low-acid flavor. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. The indeterminate vines can reach five feet or more and need sturdy staking or caging. Support heavy fruit clusters and harvest when the marbled fruits give slightly to gentle pressure.

common_name: Hillbilly Tomato (Appalachian Bicolor Yellow-Orange Striped Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Hillbilly is an Appalachian heirloom from West Virginia that has been preserved and distributed through regional seed-saving networks for decades before entering the commercial heirloom seed trade.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Hillbilly (also called Hillbilly Potato Leaf) is a West Virginia heirloom beefsteak tomato of Appalachian origin — a large (12–24 oz), irregularly shaped, golden-yellow-orange fruit streaked and mottled with red to produce the characteristic bicolor pattern of this historic mountain heirloom. The Hillbilly's distinctive coloration differs from closely related varieties (Pineapple, Big Rainbow) in its specific yellow-orange background tone and the characteristic way the red streaking distributes across the fruit surface in bold, irregular patches. The flavor is outstanding: very sweet, fruity, and low-acid with a mild, rich character that has made Hillbilly one of the most enthusiastically recommended heirlooms by those who have grown it. 'Hillbilly Potato Leaf' plants display the characteristic potato-leaf (undivided, smooth-margined) foliage common among certain old Appalachian heirloom lineages. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds save true to type season after season. In zone 9, Hillbilly produces best in the spring window (February–June) before summer heat arrives — the very large fruits require the full spring season to reach their finest size and flavor quality. Sturdy support is required for the vigorous indeterminate vines.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring after danger of frost passes in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Scarify hard seed coats lightly with sandpaper or soak overnight before planting to speed germination. Hog Peanut grows best in light shade and will not thrive in exposed, dry, or heavily fertilized soil.
directions: Hog Peanut is a delicate, twining native legume vine of moist forest floors and shaded stream banks across eastern North America, producing two types of flowers: small lavender blossoms on climbing aerial stems that rarely set fruit, and inconspicuous cleistogamous flowers near the soil surface that produce fleshy, one-seeded pods underground — a remarkable adaptation for seed burial and dispersal. The underground fleshy seeds are rich, sweet, and bean-like in flavor, and were a significant food source for many Native American peoples including the Meskwaki, Cherokee, and Iroquois, who harvested them in fall; settlers called them hog peanuts because pigs eagerly rooted them from the soil. A nitrogen-fixing perennial that returns from taproots each spring in zones 5–9, Hog Peanut adds valuable biodiversity and soil health to shaded native plant gardens and woodland edges while providing food and cover for small wildlife. Direct sow after frost in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; established plants self-seed freely and colonize gradually.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; trellising saves space for the long vines.
directions: A gherkin cucumber producing seedless, bitter-free, uniform fruits perfect for cornichons and sweet pickles, best used from 1.5 to 4 inches long. Direct sow after the soil warms, spacing plants along a trellis for the vines that can reach 6 feet. Keep the soil evenly moist and mulched, since drought stress causes bitterness and misshapen fruit. Harvest small and often to keep the plant setting new cucumbers.

common_name: Hollow Crown Parsnip (Classic American Heirloom Parsnip Variety)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall in zone 9 (September–October) for winter and spring harvest; parsnip takes 14–28 days to germinate and must be sown in loose, deep (12+ inch), stone-free soil for straight root development. In zone 9, parsnip is a fall-sown root vegetable harvested January–March; the roots require exposure to cold (below 40°F for several weeks) to convert starches to sugar — this 'sweetening by frost' is essential to the parsnip experience and in zone 9's mild winters the temperature drops are sufficient, especially at night. Use fresh seed each year — parsnip seed has notoriously short viability (1–2 years under good storage conditions, far less under poor conditions). Mark the row well as emergence is slow and the seedlings are easy to miss or accidentally weed out.
directions: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in loose, deep, well-prepared soil; thin to 3–4 inches when 2 inches tall. Keep soil consistently moist during germination. Hollow Crown Parsnip is the standard American garden parsnip — an open-pollinated variety that has been the dominant parsnip type in American kitchen gardens and seed catalogs since at least the 1820s. The name 'Hollow Crown' describes a shallow depression or crown at the top of the root where the leaves emerge — a characteristic of this variety's root shape rather than an internal hollowness. The roots are long (10–16 inches), creamy-white, tapered, and aromatic — a distinctive sweet, earthy, and spicy character that is unlike any other common vegetable. Parsnip's flavor transformation with cold exposure is the most dramatic of any commonly grown root vegetable: fresh-dug roots in warm weather have a starchy, slightly bitter character, but roots exposed to several weeks of near-freezing temperatures convert their starch to sugar and develop a rich, complex sweetness with spicy, aromatic notes that make parsnips one of the great vegetables of the cold-season kitchen. Roasting parsnips at high heat caramelizes the surface sugars and creates the classic preparation: crisp, brown-edged exterior with creamy, sweet interior. Hollow Crown has remained the standard parsnip in American catalogs because no modern breeding has significantly exceeded its combination of good flavor, long roots, and reliable production.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm soil; compact vines suit containers.
directions: A heavy-yielding pickling cucumber ready early, with the ideal interior texture for pickles though also good fresh, harvested anywhere from 1.5 to 6 inches long. Direct sow after frost into warm soil and mulch to hold moisture. The compact 4 to 5 foot vines do well in containers or on a small trellis. Pick frequently and evenly water to keep fruits crisp and the plant productive for canning batches.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; a spring and fall tomato for zone 9–11. Homestead 24 is one of the most heat-tolerant open-pollinated tomatoes available, developed for the intense summer heat of South Florida where standard tomatoes fail.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in full sun, fertile soil with good drainage; Homestead 24 is a University of Florida IFAS heirloom bred at the Homestead Experiment Station in Homestead, Florida, selected for heat tolerance and disease resistance under South Florida's extreme subtropical growing conditions. The '24' designation indicates a selection within the Homestead series, the result of many generations of selection for performance in tropical heat and humidity. Determinate plants produce medium (6–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits with good flavor, firm flesh, and resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. An important open-pollinated variety for zone 9b–12 gardeners who want to produce tomatoes reliably in hot, humid summer conditions where most varieties fail to set fruit — one of the trio of UF heirlooms (with Tropic and Walter) that carried South Florida vegetable gardening through decades before modern disease-resistant hybrids became available.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Homestead was bred at the University of Florida to set fruit in high heat and humidity, making it one of the classic Southern tomato varieties. Also plant in late July for fall production.
directions: Transplant into fertile, deeply amended, well-drained soil and stake or cage; Homestead 24 is a determinate variety developed by the University of Florida that bears a concentrated crop of medium-large, smooth, red fruits ideal for canning and fresh use in hot, humid climates. Its primary attribute is heat tolerance — the variety was specifically selected to set fruit when night temperatures remain above 75°F, a condition that causes blossom drop in most standard varieties. Fruit size averages 6–8 ounces with good wall thickness for slicing or canning. This heirloom-type determinate variety has been a Southern garden standard since the 1950s and remains popular throughout the Gulf Coast.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; in zones 8–11 make a second sowing in early fall for a mild-winter crop.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; plants establish quickly in cool weather and are ready to harvest in about a month. Cut the entire plant at 3–4 inches above the soil or snap off individual stems with leaves and emerging flower buds, the most prized part. The vivid purple stems, dark green leaves, and yellow flower buds are equally edible — stir-fry briefly over high heat or blanch and toss with sesame oil. Flavor is mild and sweet before the plant bolts; harvest frequently to delay bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for a June harvest and August for fall. Honey Bear's compact vine habit makes it suitable for smaller garden spaces than standard sprawling acorn squash vines. The small, single-serving fruit size means home gardeners can harvest as needed without worrying about using a large squash before it spoils.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Honey Bear is a 2009 All-America Selections-winning acorn squash that produces a compact, semi-bush vine with small, single-serving fruits — typically 1 pound, the perfect size for splitting and roasting as one serving for two. The deep green, ribbed, acorn-shaped fruits have exceptionally sweet, dry, nutty flesh — rated significantly sweeter in taste trials than standard acorn squash types including Table King and Table Queen. The compact plant habit (3–4 feet spread versus 8–12 feet for standard acorn squash) makes Honey Bear one of the few winter squashes genuinely suitable for raised beds and smaller gardens. Each plant produces multiple fruits over the harvest season. Cure harvested fruits at room temperature for 10 days to convert starches to sugar and extend storage life to 3–4 months.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; needs a full warm season to mature.
directions: A delicata-type winter squash with rich, golden-orange flesh and a sweet, nutty flavor that is excellent baked and buttered. Direct sow into warm soil after frost, giving the trailing vines plenty of room to run. Water steadily while fruit forms, then let the rinds harden as the plants wind down. Harvest before hard frost when the skin is tough, and cure in a warm spot to deepen the sweetness for storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Honeydew requires the longest growing season of any common melon (90–110 days) and the most heat to develop full sugar. Unlike cantaloupe, honeydew does not 'slip' from the vine when ripe — check for ripeness by skin color (cream to white-green), slight giving when pressed at the blossom end, and a characteristic sweet aroma. In zone 9 the heat of June through August is ideal for honeydew sugar development; consistent moisture during fruit development then reduced irrigation as fruits approach maturity produces the sweetest flesh.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil — honeydew requires warm soil, abundant heat, and consistent moisture during fruit development; Honey Dew is the standard honeydew melon variety — a winter melon type (Cucumis melo, Inodorus group) producing large (5–8 pound), oval to round fruits with a distinctive smooth, creamy-white to pale green skin that develops a subtle gold or cream color at full ripeness. The flesh is pale green, firm but juicy, with a mild, clean, very sweet flavor that is quite different from the musty, complex, aromatic sweetness of cantaloupe — honeydew's sweetness is cleaner and more neutral, making it the preferred melon for many people who find cantaloupe flavor too strong. Honeydew's longer shelf life and later harvest timing compared to cantaloupe made it historically important as a late-summer melon that could be stored and shipped where cantaloupe could not. Zone 9 is ideal for honeydew production — the extended summer heat and long growing season align perfectly with honeydew's need for consistently warm conditions over a long development period.

common_name: Honey Nut Squash (Cornell Mini Butternut Sweet Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 2–3 weeks earlier for zone 5–6 shorter seasons; in zone 9, plant March–April for fall harvest. Honey Nut requires the same long season as standard butternut (100–110 days) but stores well through winter (3–4 months in a cool, dry location) and cures similarly — allow 2 weeks at warm temperatures (80–85°F) to harden the skin after harvest. The mini size (5–6 oz) means individual fruits serve 1–2 people perfectly.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Cure harvested fruits at 80–85°F for 2 weeks to harden skin, then store in cool, dry conditions. Honey Nut is a miniature butternut-type winter squash developed at Cornell University by plant breeder Michael Mazourek, introduced commercially around 2011–2015 — a squash that has rapidly gained status as one of the most innovative new vegetable introductions of the decade. The standard butternut squash (Waltham Butternut and similar) is widely considered one of the best-flavored winter squashes but weighs 3–5 lbs — more than most households can comfortably consume in one meal. Honey Nut produces single-serving-sized fruits of only 4–6 oz, with the same classic butternut shape (pear-shaped with a long cylindrical neck and round base) compressed to a palm-sized scale. Beyond the practical size advantage, Honey Nut has exceptional flavor that often outperforms standard butternut in blind tastings — the small size means the fruits must mature fully before harvest, when starches have converted to sugar, resulting in a consistently sweeter, more intense squash flavor. The deep orange flesh is very sweet, smooth-textured, and rich — ideal for roasting (a single halved fruit roasts in 30–35 minutes, faster than the 45–60 minutes for full-size butternut), soups, and purees.

plant_note: Sow directly once frost is past and soil is warm.
directions: Honey Rock, an All-America Selections winner from 1933 also known as Sugar Rock, offers honey-sweet salmon-colored flesh and dependable performance. Direct sow seeds in warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Keep vines evenly watered during growth, then reduce moisture as fruit ripens to intensify sweetness. Harvest at full slip when the melon parts easily from the vine and smells fragrant.

common_name: Honey Select Sweet Corn (AAS-Winning Bicolor Synergistic Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; Honey Select is a synergistic (sy) type combining sh2 and su kernels on the same ear — it does not need isolation from su/se types but should be isolated from other sh2 varieties by 250 feet or staggered planting dates. Soil should be 65°F minimum for reliable germination. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest or in August–September for a fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress at knee height with nitrogen. Honey Select is a 1999 All-America Selections-winning bicolor sweet corn from Rogers Brothers/Syngenta that represents one of the most successful expressions of synergistic (sy or triplesweet) sweet corn genetics — a breeding system that places approximately 75% supersweet (sh2) kernels and 25% standard su kernels randomly across each ear, creating a flavor profile that integrates the long-lasting sweetness and slow starch conversion of sh2 types with the richer, more complex corn flavor that su kernels contribute. The resulting flavor is considered by many tasters to be more balanced, complete, and authentically corn-flavored than pure sh2 types (which can be very sweet but thin in traditional corn character) while retaining the extended harvest window advantage of sh2 genetics. The bicolor (yellow and white) ears are large (8–8.5 inches, 16 rows), well-filled, and visually attractive; the synergistic type's mixed kernel genetics produce slightly irregular but appealing ear fill. Honey Select has been a top-selling sweet corn variety since its release and remains one of the most consistent performers in home garden and market garden trials, with good disease resistance including tolerance to Stewart's wilt, NCLB, and SCLB. An outstanding all-around bicolor corn for any climate where premium flavor and extended postharvest quality are priorities.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Plant in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for good wind pollination — single rows pollinate poorly. Isolate from field corn, popcorn, and other sweet corn varieties by at least 250 feet or stagger planting dates by 2 weeks to prevent off-type pollination. Honey and Cream is a standard su (normal sugary) type — harvest promptly at peak ripeness and use quickly, as sugar conversion to starch begins immediately after harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Honey and Cream is a classic bicolor sweet corn producing attractive ears with alternating yellow and white kernels in the traditional American bicolor pattern — it was among the earliest widely available bicolor sweet corn varieties and remains popular for its straightforward, reliable, pleasant sweet corn flavor without the extreme sweetness of modern super-sweet types. Honey and Cream represents the standard sugary (su) bicolor corn flavor profile that defined American sweet corn for most of the 20th century — rich, substantial corn flavor with moderate sweetness and a tender, slightly milky kernel texture when eaten at peak ripeness. The reliable production, good ear appearance, and familiar flavor make it a trusted heirloom-style bicolor variety for home gardeners seeking a classic sweet corn experience. The ears are well-filled and typically 7–8 inches long — a proper size for fresh eating and corn-on-the-cob presentations.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; plant in blocks for good pollination.
directions: A bicolor sweet corn with a luscious blend of white and yellow kernels bursting with flavor and tenderness far above store-bought. Direct sow after the last frost once soil warms, planting in blocks of at least four rows so wind pollination fills the ears. Feed with nitrogen and keep well watered through tasseling and silking. Harvest at the milk stage when silks brown and kernels squirt milky juice when pressed.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; compact semi-bush habit saves space.
directions: An All-America Selections winning butternut-type hybrid that is very productive, setting numerous 1 to 2 pound fruits on compact 2 to 3 foot vines with some powdery mildew resistance. Direct sow into warm soil after frost, thinning to the strongest seedlings per hill. The semi-bush habit suits smaller gardens; keep evenly watered through fruit set. Harvest when rinds turn tan and hard, then cure before storing.

plant_note: Best in hot-climate gardens; direct sow after frost into warm soil.
directions: Honeydew produces sweet, refreshing melons with crisp pale-green flesh that thrive in hot summer gardens. Sow seeds directly in warm soil and full sun after all frost has passed, giving the long-season vines ample room. Provide steady water during fruit development and a long, warm growing season for the fruit to sweeten fully. Unlike cantaloupe, honeydew does not slip, so harvest when the rind turns creamy and the blossom end softens slightly.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil is warm; in short-season climates, start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in hills of 4–5 seeds thinned to 2. Honeydew requires a longer, hotter season than cantaloupe; black plastic mulch is helpful in northern climates to boost soil warmth. Unlike cantaloupes, honeydews do not slip from the vine when ripe, so judge by skin color changing to creamy white, a waxy feel, and a sweet aroma from the blossom end. Cut fruits from the vine with a knife rather than pulling.

common_name: Honeynut Squash (Mini Intensely Sweet Butternut-Type Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer (July–August in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; Honeynut is a moschata type with better heat tolerance than pepo squash types, making it more reliable for late-season zone 9 production.
