Kossak is a late-maturing giant kohlrabi variety (80–100 days) developed specifically for the ability to grow very large bulbs without becoming woody or pithy — a problem that plagues standard small-bulb kohlrabi varieties when they overstay their welcome in the garden. While standard varieties turn fibrous and tough above 3–4 inches, Kossak can be harvested at 6–10 inches diameter (tennis ball to softball size) and remain tender and sweet. In zone 9, fall planting allows a December–March harvest window before spring heat terminates cool-season growth. Kossak tolerates light frost well, making it a good choice for zone 9 winter gardens.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in cool soil; keep consistently moist for best growth. Harvest from 3 inches up to 10 inches diameter. Kossak is an F1 hybrid kohlrabi variety developed and introduced by Bejo Seeds (Dutch seed company) specifically for the giant kohlrabi market — a category of extra-large kohlrabi varieties that can reach 6–10 inches in diameter while remaining tender and palatable, unlike standard kohlrabi varieties that become woodily fibrous above 3–4 inches. The distinction between Kossak and standard kohlrabi varieties is fundamental: standard types (Purple Vienna, White Vienna, Early White Vienna) must be harvested promptly at small size or become inedible, while Kossak was specifically selected for an extended harvest window at large sizes. This makes Kossak practical for gardeners who cannot monitor their garden daily, for home gardeners who want a few large plants rather than many small ones, and for fall gardeners who want kohlrabi that overwinters in the ground without quality loss. The bulbs are pale green (white type), extremely smooth-skinned, and can reach weights of 1–2 pounds or more while retaining the characteristic kohlrabi flavor — mild, sweet, slightly peppery, somewhere between broccoli stem and turnip — without the harsh bitterness and woodiness of overmature standard types. The flesh is very juicy and crisp, excellent raw in slaws and salads (where the sweetness is most apparent), roasted (where it caramelizes beautifully), or braised. Kossak is also more cold-hardy than many kohlrabi varieties, holding quality in the garden through light freezes, which extends its usability in zone 9 winter gardens.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Kunth's wild onion is native to the rocky, limestone-based hills, prairies, and open woodlands of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, where it blooms in spring and early summer. The bulbs are edible — both leaves and bulbs — and have been used as a food plant by indigenous peoples of the Southwest and Mexico for centuries. The strong, garlicky-onion scent distinguishes it readily from non-edible similar plants.
directions: Plant small bulbs in well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Kunth's wild onion is one of the most widespread and important edible native alliums of Texas and the American Southwest — a spring-blooming, small wild onion native to the limestone hills, Rocky Mountain foothills, and Chihuahuan Desert mountains of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and northern Mexico, where it has been harvested and eaten by indigenous peoples for thousands of years as a wild food plant. The bulbs and leaves both have a strong onion-garlic flavor and aroma, usable in the same ways as domestic onions and garlic — raw, cooked, pickled. The spring flowers are produced in small, rounded umbels of white to pale pink to deep pink star-shaped florets on stems 8–16 inches tall, serving as pollinators for native bees and beetles. In the garden it provides both a wildflower display in spring and an edible wild-food plant for harvesting — a dual-purpose native species for the Texas-Southwest edible landscape and native plant garden. The strong garlic-onion scent immediately identifies it as edible and distinguishes it safely from the non-scented, potentially toxic Nothoscordum bivalve (crow poison) with which it sometimes grows.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Direct sow this compact Japanese kabocha after the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep in hills spaced 3 to 4 feet apart in full sun. Each vine produces small 3 to 4 pound fruits with sweet, fine-grained flesh reminiscent of sweet potato. Allow the squash to mature fully on the vine until the rind hardens and the stem corks, then cure in a warm spot to improve storage and flavor. Give the vines room to sprawl and provide steady moisture, especially while fruit is sizing up.

common_name: La Ratte Fingerling Potato (Classic French Gourmet Fingerling)
plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. La Ratte is a classic French fingerling potato long prized by chefs for its exceptionally rich, nutty, almost chestnut-like flavor and dense, waxy, pale yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled or roasted whole. The small, knobby, finger-shaped tubers mature over a somewhat longer season than standard round potatoes and yield less per plant, but the superior flavor has made it a long-standing favorite for specialty and high-end cooking. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and die back, and handle the thin-skinned tubers gently, since they bruise more easily than thicker-skinned storage potatoes.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Sow this 18th-century Tuscan heirloom in early spring for a summer harvest or in mid to late summer for fall and winter greens, as its flavor sweetens after frost. Direct sow a half inch deep and thin seedlings to 12 to 18 inches apart. Harvest tender young leaves as salad greens in about 21 days, or let plants mature for full-size, strap-shaped dark blue-green leaves prized by cooks. Pick outer leaves first to keep plants producing over a long season, and provide steady moisture for tender growth.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Also known as dinosaur or Tuscan kale, this heirloom features deep blue-green, bumpy-textured leaves with rich, mild flavor. Sow directly in spring or late summer, as it is a cold-hardy crop whose flavor sweetens after a frost. Thin plants to give the tall, upright rosettes room to develop. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up, letting the center keep producing for a long, continuous cutting season.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for the main crop; alternatively start indoors 4–6 weeks before last spring frost. Lacinato kale matures more slowly than curly kale but holds better through winter and regrows vigorously in spring.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep 8–10 weeks before first fall frost or start indoors in early spring; lacinato kale (also called dinosaur kale, Tuscan kale, or cavolo nero) forms tall, upright plants with long, strap-like, deeply puckered, blue-black to dark-green leaves with a more tender texture and milder, slightly sweeter flavor than curly kale. It is one of the foundational vegetables of Tuscan cuisine, essential in ribollita and minestrone. Harvest by removing outer leaves as needed, working from the bottom of the stem upward — plants will continue producing from fall through winter and into spring in mild climates. Flavor intensifies significantly after frost exposure. A more elegant, slower-maturing, and culinary-preferred alternative to curly kale for the kitchen garden.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil after last frost; Lady pea is one of the smallest of the Southern peas with very small seeds, so somewhat more of them are required per planting. It is heat tolerant and produces reliably in zone 8–10 Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in any well-drained, lean soil in full sun after last frost; Lady cream pea is a traditional Southern heirloom cowpea producing small, white, round peas with a notably sweet, mild, delicate flavor — milder and less earthy than crowder peas or black-eyed peas, and considered by many Southern pea aficionados to have the finest flavor of all the cream peas for fresh eating and freezing. The small size and mild sweetness make it the variety most often served to guests unfamiliar with Southern peas, as the flavor is more approachable and universally liked. A true bush-type plant that is drought-tolerant once established; performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast. Excellent boiled simply with butter and salt and served as a side dish, or incorporated into succotash, hoppin' John, and traditional Southern vegetable plates.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost into warm, rich soil.
directions: This heirloom is grown for its unique hulless seeds, which are soft-shelled pepitas that need no peeling for roasting or snacking. Sow directly into warm, rich soil after frost, giving the vines plenty of room to spread. Keep moisture and nutrients steady as fruit develops. Harvest the mature pumpkins, then scoop and dry the green hulless seeds for a homegrown supply of pepitas.

common_name: Lakota Squash (Native American Heirloom Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Lakota is a striking Native American heirloom winter squash with vivid deep orange skin dramatically marked with irregular dark green and black mottling — one of the most visually beautiful and historically significant native food squashes, producing teardrop-shaped fruits of 5–8 pounds with exceptionally sweet, rich, deeply colored orange flesh.
directions: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after soil warms; provide 4–8 feet of vine space; harvest when the skin hardens completely and can no longer be dented with a fingernail, and the stem begins to dry and cork; cure at room temperature for 10–14 days after harvest to develop optimal flavor and maximize storage life. Lakota squash is an heirloom winter squash associated with the Lakota (Sioux) people of the Great Plains, one of the native peoples of North America who cultivated squash as a primary food staple long before European contact. The variety produces one of the most visually distinctive squashes in cultivation: teardrop or pear-shaped fruits with deep orange-red skin boldly marked with irregular splotches and streaks of dark green and near-black — a coloration so striking that Lakota is as ornamental as it is edible. The flesh is the intensely orange, dry, sweet, and finely textured type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties: rich enough to need nothing added beyond butter and salt, sweet enough to serve as dessert, and dry enough to bake or purée without becoming watery. The flavor is often compared favorably to kabocha and red kuri squash — comparable sweetness and dryness but with a distinctive terroir-like richness that differentiates it from commercial varieties. Lakota stores exceptionally well — 4–6 months under cool, dry conditions — making it a true long-keeping winter provision. Average fruits weigh 5–8 lbs with moderate vine length suitable for home gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow this vigorous heirloom squash in warm soil, planting in hills spaced well apart to accommodate 10 to 20 foot vines. Beyond its striking orange and green coloring, Lakota is a superior baking variety with fine-grained, sweet, nutty flesh. Let the pear-shaped fruits ripen fully and the rind harden before harvesting, then cure in a warm, dry spot to improve storage life. Give the sprawling vines full sun and consistent moisture while the fruit develops.

plant_note: Direct sow around the time of last frost; seeds are very small and germinate best when pressed into moist soil without covering. Plants self-sow prolifically once established.
directions: Scatter seeds on bare soil and press firmly; lamb’s quarters germinates readily and requires virtually no care once established. Harvest young leaves and stem tips continuously — they taste similar to spinach, raw or cooked, and are exceptionally high in vitamins A, C, and calcium. The mealy white coating on new leaves is a natural wax secretion. Allow a few plants to set seed each year to maintain a self-sowing colony; mature seeds can be dried and cooked like quinoa. Plants grow rapidly in rich soil and may reach 6 feet if left unchecked.

plant_note: Lambsquarters is more typically managed as a welcome weed than deliberately sown; if intentionally growing, scatter seeds on the soil surface as they need light to germinate, from early spring through early summer. Self-sows prolifically and will naturalize in any disturbed garden soil.
directions: Allow to grow voluntarily in garden beds or scatter seeds on soil surface in early spring; lambsquarters is arguably the most nutritious common garden weed available as a potherb, with leaves containing more calcium, iron, and vitamins A and C than most cultivated greens. The young growing tips and leaves have a mild, spinach-like flavor that is excellent raw in salads when small or steamed, sautéed, or added to soups and egg dishes when older. The mealy white coating on young leaves is normal and edible — it is not pesticide or mildew. The seed heads, when mature in late summer, can be eaten cooked as a grain similar to quinoa (they are closely related). Control by harvesting regularly before seed set; one plant can produce 70,000 seeds that remain viable for decades.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Lancelot is an early-season leek variety (70–85 days from transplant) with more slender, tender stalks than overwintering types — it is harvested in summer and early fall while still tender, rather than being held through winter; ideal for gardeners who want leeks available early in the season before winter storage types are ready.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 65–75°F; transplant outdoors after last frost, setting transplants 4–6 inches apart in a trench 4–6 inches deep to blanch the shafts; gradually backfill the trench as plants grow; harvest beginning at 1 inch shaft diameter for best tenderness. Lancelot is a European-bred early-season leek variety that fills an important niche in the leek production calendar: unlike the classic overwintering leek varieties (such as Bleu de Solaise or Giant Musselburgh) that require 130–150+ days from transplant and are intended to overwinter in the garden for winter and spring harvest, Lancelot matures in just 70–85 days from transplant and is harvested in late summer and early fall while stalks are still slender, tender, and at their best eating quality. The stalks are typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter at harvest — more refined in texture and milder in flavor than fully mature overwintering leeks — making Lancelot the superior choice for preparations where tenderness and delicate leek flavor are paramount: vichyssoise, leek gratin, braised leeks, and fresh leek salads where the young stalks are excellent raw. The blue-green foliage and cylindrical white shaft create an attractive plant in the garden from late spring through summer. Lancelot does not have the cold hardiness or overwintering capability of late types but excels as a summer-season leek in climates too hot for fall-planted overwintering types.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade as early in spring as soil can be worked, or sow in late summer for a fall and overwintering crop; land cress is a cold-hardy watercress substitute that thrives in ordinary garden soil without the running water watercress requires.
directions: Direct sow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun as soon as soil can be worked in spring or in late summer for fall harvest; land cress (upland cress, American cress, creasy greens) is a biennial European native grown as an annual salad herb that provides a peppery, watercress-like flavor in ordinary, moist garden soil — without the stream or pond edge that true watercress (Nasturtium officinale) requires. The deeply lobed, rounded basal leaves have intense, hot, peppery bite that mellows considerably with cooking. Plants remain edible through light frosts and can often be overwintered under cold frames in zones 5–7, providing very early spring greens. Harvest outer leaves beginning at 4–6 inches in height; plants withstand multiple pickings before bolting in warm weather. Sow every 4 weeks for succession harvests through the cool season. Excellent raw in small quantities to add zip to salads, or blanched and wilted as a cooked green.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost once soil warms.
directions: This classic indeterminate variety yields abundant clusters of bright red cherry tomatoes with fresh, zesty flavor all summer. Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil warms. Stake or cage the vigorous vines and remove suckers if you want to manage the sprawl. Pick tomatoes as they ripen to keep the plants setting new fruit continuously through the season.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Late Flat Dutch'
plant_note: Start seed 12–16 weeks before the first fall frost for a fall/winter-maturing crop, or start in very early spring for a summer harvest in cooler climates; in zone 8–9, Late Flat Dutch is best grown as a fall-planted crop that matures through winter, since it tolerates hard freezes and stores in the garden far better than it handles summer heat.
directions: Set transplants 24–30 inches apart in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the large, heavy heads need ample room and rich soil to size up properly over their long season. Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom prized for producing enormous, flattened, blue-green heads that commonly reach 10–15 pounds and can grow considerably larger under good conditions, with dense, crisp interior leaves that make it an outstanding keeper — heads store for months in a root cellar or cool garage, and the variety was historically favored for large-batch sauerkraut and winter storage before refrigeration was common. Its long season and excellent cold hardiness make it best suited to fall planting in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South, where the heads mature slowly through the cool months and can stand in the garden through hard freezes without splitting. A workhorse heirloom for gardeners who want maximum storage cabbage from a single planting, in zone 3–9.

plant_note: Direct sow 12–16 weeks before first fall frost so roots mature in cool fall weather; in zones 3–7 sow June–July. Rutabaga requires a long, cool growing season — unlike turnips, which can be harvested young in 50–60 days, rutabagas need the full 85–95 days to develop their full size and flavor. Frost dramatically improves rutabaga flavor by converting starches to sugars — leave roots in the ground through hard frosts and harvest in late fall or winter. Thin to 6–8 inches apart. In zone 9 the late-fall/winter growing season is too short for full rutabaga development — zones 3–7 are the primary growing regions.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil; Laurentian is the standard North American rutabaga variety — a natural hybrid between turnip and cabbage producing large, round to slightly elongated roots with the characteristic purple shoulder above ground and yellow-tan below, with golden-yellow, dense, starchy flesh distinctly different from the white flesh of turnips. Rutabaga (called 'swede' in British English, reflecting its Swedish origin) has a richer, more complex flavor than turnip — the yellow flesh is denser, starchier, and more nutrionally robust with a sweeter, more earthy, complex flavor that becomes significantly more intense and sweet after hard frost exposure. The classic rutabaga preparations — mashed ('neeps' in Scotland, traditionally served with haggis), chunked in beef stew, roasted with butter and herbs, or pureed into soups — take full advantage of the dense, deeply flavored flesh that holds its shape better than potato while contributing its own distinctive sweetness and earthiness. Laurentian's large size (roots can reach softball size in good conditions), excellent storage quality (roots keep for months in cool storage), and consistent purple-top appearance make it the most reliable and widely grown rutabaga for home and market garden production.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Sow Lavewa spinach directly in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since spinach bolts in heat and long days. This open-pollinated variety offers good heat tolerance and mildew resistance, rivaling hybrids for flavor. Thin seedlings to about 4 to 6 inches apart and keep the soil consistently moist and cool. Harvest outer leaves individually or cut whole plants, and provide light afternoon shade to extend the harvest in warm weather.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Lazy Housewife is an 1810 German heirloom pole bean that is one of the oldest and most historically significant American heirloom beans, documented in German seed catalogs since the early 1800s and named for the ease of shelling — the pods are stringless and the beans pop out with minimal effort.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis, teepee poles, or corn stalks; provide 6 feet of vertical support for the vigorous vines. Lazy Housewife is one of America's most documented heirloom pole beans, appearing in American seed catalogs since at least 1810 and recorded by seed historian William Woys Weaver as a bean brought to America by German immigrants; the name refers to the ease of preparation — the pods are stringless when harvested young as snap beans, and the mature white seeds shell out of the dried pods with minimal effort, hence 'lazy housewife.' The pods are 5–7 inches long, round, and stringless, with plump white seeds marked with a distinctive black eye at maturity. Equally excellent as a snap bean (harvest young), shell bean (harvest green pods when seeds have filled), or dry bean; the cooked flavor of the mature seeds is rich, creamy, and outstanding.

common_name: Lazy Wife Pole Bean (Stringless German Heirloom Pole Bean, 1810 American Classic)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Lazy Wife requires a pole or trellis 6–8 feet tall and produces abundantly over a long season. In zone 9, plant April–May; the variety performs adequately but prefers somewhat cooler conditions than the peak Gulf South summer. A late-July or August planting for fall production is often more productive in zone 9 than a late spring planting that encounters July-August heat. The 'lazy' in the variety's name refers not to any person but to the ease of preparation: Lazy Wife is stringless and requires no tedious stringing of the pods before cooking — a significant advantage in the era when most snap beans had tough, fibrous strings running the length of each pod. This stringless quality was unusual and highly valued when the variety was widely grown in the 19th century.
directions: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost; provide tall support (6–8 feet). Harvest at 5–7 inches as snap bean or leave to dry for shell/dry use. Lazy Wife is a German immigrant heirloom pole bean that was introduced to American seed catalogs around 1810 and became one of the most popular snap beans in the 19th century — a status maintained until modern stringless hybrid varieties provided equivalent ease of preparation with higher yield. The name 'Lazy Wife' refers to the bean's stringless character: in the 19th-century farm kitchen where snap bean preparation required long sessions of stringing pods by hand before cooking, a truly stringless bean required no stringing at all — hence the tongue-in-cheek name suggesting the homemaker could be 'lazy' about bean preparation. The implied humor of the name was accepted in its era; the bean's quality was the real selling point. Lazy Wife produces broad, flat, pale green pods (5–7 inches long, 0.75 inches wide) with a somewhat different form than round-pod types — the flat pod shape and relatively thick walls give Lazy Wife a characteristic visual distinction from most modern snap beans. The pods are truly stringless through their snap-bean stage and have rich, full flavor that heirloom enthusiasts prize. The seeds are creamy-white and excellent as a shell bean (picked young) or dry bean (left to fully mature), giving Lazy Wife three-stage versatility as a snap, shell, or dry bean from a single planting.

common_name: Leaf Amaranth (Chinese Spinach, Callaloo, Joseph's Coat)
plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface or barely covered — seeds need light to germinate; in zone 9 plant from March through September for continuous warm-season production. Leaf amaranth is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens available, thriving when spinach and lettuce have long since bolted.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface or barely 1/8 inch deep in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; leaf amaranth germinates quickly in warm conditions and grows rapidly to a productive harvest-ready size in as little as 30 days. The young leaves taste mild and spinach-like when harvested small; older leaves are cooked like spinach, steamed, sautéed, or stewed into the Caribbean callaloo and West African soups that this plant anchors. It is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens for southern gardens, producing abundantly through summer temperatures that wilt most other greens. The tricolor varieties display striking red, gold, and green foliage useful as an ornamental. Pinch the growing tip frequently to encourage bushy lateral branching and delay seed formation; once the plant flowers heavily, leaf quality declines.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; succession sow every 2 weeks through spring, then again in fall.
directions: Scatter or row-sow seed on the surface or barely cover with 1/8 in of soil, as light aids germination. Thin to 6–10 in and use thinnings as baby greens in salads to avoid waste. Harvest outer leaves continuously once plants are 4–6 in tall, or cut the entire plant an inch above the soil line for a cut-and-come-again harvest. Bolting in warm weather makes leaves bitter; provide shade cloth in late spring to extend the season.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; transplant seedlings into deep trenches after the last frost date.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors in flats and thin to 2 in; transplant pencil-thick seedlings into 6-in-deep trenches, dropping each plant into a dibber hole and filling with water rather than soil to encourage a long white shank. Gradually fill trenches and hill up soil around stems as they grow to blanch the shanks. Leeks tolerate hard frost and can be left in the ground well into winter for a late harvest. Dig as needed once shanks reach 1 in or more in diameter.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is an Oregon State University tomato released in 1996 with the highest level of late blight (Phytophthora infestans) resistance available in an open-pollinated tomato variety — developed specifically for the damp, foggy conditions of the Pacific Coast where late blight is a persistent annual challenge that can devastate unprotected tomato crops.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage prevents fruit from resting on the soil; provides excellent production without fungicide sprays in conditions where late blight is present. Legend was released in 1996 by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University, culminating many years of breeding for late blight resistance in open-pollinated tomatoes; at the time of release it had the highest documented level of late blight resistance in any open-pollinated variety, making it a breakthrough for organic and low-spray gardeners in humid, blight-prone climates. The large (10–16 oz), round to slightly flattened, smooth, uniform deep red fruits have thick walls, good meaty texture, and classic sweet-balanced tomato flavor superior to most disease-resistant commercial varieties; the determinate plant ripens a heavy concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks rather than producing continuously. Legend performs exceptionally well in the Pacific Northwest and humid Eastern climates; it is also valuable in Gulf Coast gardens planted in fall (August–September) when late blight risk from summer thunderstorm humidity is highest. One of the most important contributions to open-pollinated tomato breeding in the late 20th century.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; one of the most reliable large yellow tomatoes available, with good disease resistance and consistent fruit set even in warm, humid conditions — well-suited to zone 8–10 spring planting.
directions: Start seed indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and providing a sturdy cage or stake from the outset. Lemon Boy is one of the most widely grown large yellow tomatoes, an F1 hybrid introduced in 1984 that remains a top performer for home gardeners seeking a reliable, large, lemon-yellow salad tomato; it produces 6–8 ounce round fruits with smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and mild, sweet, very low-acid flesh that is ideal for slicing fresh, for guests who find red tomatoes too acidic, and for adding visual contrast in salads and on plates. Disease resistance to verticillium, fusarium, and nematodes makes it particularly valuable in humid southern gardens. Water consistently and stake firmly as the indeterminate vines are tall and productive.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for a spring crop and again July–August for fall. Lemon Cucumber is best harvested when pale yellow to ivory colored — fully yellow fruits are overripe and develop a slightly bitter skin. The round shape and distinctive color make it easy to spot on the vine when it's time to harvest. Plants are productive and compact enough for small trellises and can be grown in containers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with trellis support; Lemon Cucumber is an 1894 American heirloom producing distinctive round to oval, lemon-sized fruits with pale yellow-white skin when ripe — the resemblance to a lemon is strictly visual, as the flavor is mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the tartness of actual lemon. The thin skin, small seeds, and crisp, sweet, very low-bitterness flesh make Lemon Cucumber one of the most palatable cucumbers for fresh eating without peeling — the skin remains tender and palatable throughout the eating-ripe stage (pale yellow to ivory) unlike the tough skins of slicing cucumbers. The round shape also makes Lemon Cucumber excellent for serving as a natural bowl — hollow out the round fruit and fill with dips, salads, or other fillings. The mild, sweet flavor and easy digestibility (lower cucurbitacin bitterness than many cucumbers) makes it popular for people who find regular cucumbers hard to digest.

plant_note: Sow in warm soil; seedlings resent cold, wet conditions.
directions: This heirloom bears round, yellow, lemon-sized fruit with sweet, mild, non-bitter flesh. Sow seeds an inch deep in warm soil and grow on a trellis to keep the round fruit clean and easy to spot. Keep evenly watered to avoid bitterness and misshapen fruit during dry spells. Harvest while the skin is still pale yellow and before it turns deep gold and seedy. Frequent picking keeps the prolific vines producing until frost.

common_name: Lemon Cucumber (Crystal Apple Cucumber, Round Yellow Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Lemon cucumber (Crystal Apple) produces round to oval, tennis-ball-sized, pale-creamy-yellow fruits with exceptionally mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor — harvest when the skin is pale yellow to white; allowing it to turn deeper yellow indicates overripeness and seed development.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil reaches 65°F; thin or transplant to 18–24 inches; harvest when pale yellow. Cucumis sativus 'Crystal Apple' (Lemon cucumber) is a heritage cucumber variety — one of the best-loved heirloom types — producing distinctive round to oval, tennis-ball-sized fruits with pale cream to pale yellow skin and white flesh that is exceptionally mild, sweet, and non-bitter compared to most standard cucumbers. Despite the name, the flavor is not lemony — it tastes like a very mild, sweet, refreshing cucumber. The thin skin makes peeling unnecessary, and the mild flavor means the seeds and seed cavity are also mild and not bitter, unlike some full-sized cucumbers. Lemon cucumbers are extremely popular with home gardeners for several reasons: the unusual round shape is attractive and different from grocery store varieties; the mild, non-bitter flavor appeals to people who find standard cucumbers too strong; and the fruits are easy to spot when harvesting (by size and color rather than hunting in dense vines). The variety produces prolifically over a long season. Best harvested young — large, deep-yellow specimens tend toward bitterness and seedness. An excellent choice for fresh eating, quick pickles, and cucumber water.

plant_note: Start indoors early; this species is slow to germinate and needs a long, warm season.
directions: Start this Peruvian aji pepper indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, as baccatum peppers germinate slowly and need a long, warm growing season. Provide bottom heat and warm soil around 80 degrees for best germination, then transplant out well after frost when nights stay warm. The bright yellow, wrinkled pods rate 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville units with a distinct citrus flavor and lemony aroma. Give plants full sun, stake them if they grow tall, and harvest fruits fully colored for the best flavor.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum baccatum species takes longer to germinate and matures more slowly than C. annuum. In zone 9 start in January and transplant March–April. Lemon Drop thrives as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — cut back hard in late winter and the plant will regrow from the roots, producing earlier and more heavily in its second year.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Lemon Drop is a Peruvian aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) producing small, wrinkled, bright lemon-yellow fruits that ripen from pale green through various shades of yellow with a distinctive fruity, citrusy, bright heat very different from the harsher burn of jalapeños or the floral heat of habaneros. The heat level is medium-hot (15,000–30,000 Scoville units) with a pronounced fruity, lemony flavor note that makes Lemon Drop one of the most culinarily versatile hot peppers — used in salsas, ceviches, hot sauces, and Peruvian-style pepper pastes where the citrus-forward flavor complements seafood and poultry. Capsicum baccatum species peppers are widely grown in South America and increasingly popular in North American specialty gardening. In zone 9 the perennial habit is a major advantage — the plant can grow to a small shrub 4–5 feet tall over multiple seasons, producing far more fruit than annual plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; aji limon is a Peruvian species (Capsicum baccatum) that germinates more slowly than C. annuum peppers and benefits from a longer indoor growing period. Needs consistently warm conditions to thrive.
directions: Start indoors in warm conditions and transplant after frost danger has passed; lemon drop pepper (aji limon) is a Peruvian Capsicum baccatum cultivar producing small, tapered, bright yellow fruits 2–3 inches long with a distinctive intensely fruity, citrusy, lemon-like flavor combined with a clean, building heat (30,000–50,000 SHU). The lemon aroma and flavor make it quite different from other yellow hot peppers and it is used extensively in Peruvian cuisine — in ceviche, aji de gallina, and fresh salsas where its fruitiness and brightness are essential. The plants are productive and quite ornamental with their pendant yellow fruits. Fresh or dried and ground, it is one of the most versatile and distinctive of the South American aji peppers.

common_name: Lemon Drop Pepper (Fruity Lemon-Yellow Peruvian Hot Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting (C. chinense is slower to germinate and develop than C. annuum); transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Lemon Drop requires a long warm season — in zone 9, the long growing season supports full production.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Lemon Drop is a traditional Peruvian pepper (Ají Lemon in Peru) — a small (1–1.5 inch), thin-walled, conical fruit with a distinctive bright-lemon-yellow color at maturity and a unique combination of intense heat (15,000–30,000 Scoville units — comparable to a serrano but with more heat variability) and fruity, distinctly citrus-lemon flavor. The characteristic lemon flavor — a fruity, citrus-forward quality quite unlike the neutral heat of jalapeños or the fruity sweetness of habaneros — makes Lemon Drop one of the most flavorful hot peppers for cooking applications where heat AND flavor complexity are desired simultaneously. The dried and powdered fruit has an exceptional flavor that is widely used in traditional Peruvian cuisine for adding heat and bright citrus notes. As a Capsicum chinense species, Lemon Drop requires somewhat higher temperatures for germination (80–90°F) and a longer season than C. annuum peppers — start seeds 10–12 weeks before transplanting for adequate development time. The plant is productive in zone 9's long warm season, producing prolifically from late spring through frost. Fresh fruits, dried fruits, and powder form are all excellent culinary applications. The vivid yellow color and intense fruity aroma make Lemon Drop a distinctive addition to the pepper garden.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in early spring, 2–4 weeks before the last expected frost, as young plants tolerate light frost and benefit from a long, cool growing period. Inoculating seeds with a legume-specific rhizobium inoculant before planting improves nitrogen fixation and yields.
directions: Direct-sow lentils in early spring as soon as the soil is workable, planting seeds 1 inch deep in rows 12–18 inches apart; they germinate readily in cool soil and tolerate light frost. Choose a well-drained bed in full sun and avoid high-nitrogen soil, which promotes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Plants need little water once established and are highly drought-tolerant. Harvest when the lower pods turn tan and begin to rattle but before the stems dry completely; pull the entire plant and hang it upside down in a dry, airy space to finish curing before threshing.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; lentils prefer cool growing conditions and deteriorate in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1 in deep in rows 18 in apart in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that delay podding. The slender, branching plants benefit from brushy twigs as supports to keep pods off the ground and improve air circulation. Harvest the entire plant when the majority of lower pods have turned tan but before they shatter. Thresh by beating dried plants on a tarp and winnow lightly to clean seed before storage.

plant_note: Scatter seeds thinly on prepared soil and press lightly onto the surface without covering — lettuce seeds need light to germinate; start as early as soil can be worked in spring, 2–4 weeks before last frost. Seeds germinate poorly above 80°F; refrigerate them for 1–2 days before sowing in summer.
directions: Scatter seeds on the surface of moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil and press lightly without covering — lettuce seeds need light for germination; succession-sow every 2–3 weeks from early spring through fall for a continuous harvest. Thin seedlings to 6–12 inches apart (wider spacing produces larger heads). Lettuce prefers cool temperatures (60–70°F) and bolts quickly in summer heat, becoming bitter and inedible; choose heat-tolerant varieties for summer planting and provide afternoon shade in hot climates. The four main types — crisphead, butterhead, loose-leaf, and romaine — have different maturity times and uses but similar growing requirements. Harvest leaf types by cutting outer leaves; harvest head types when the head feels firm.

plant_note: Light-sensitive seed germinates best cool; sow shallow on moist medium.
directions: Sow lettuce seed thinly pressed onto the surface of a moist tray, since it germinates best in cooler conditions and with some light. Keep only a light cover for a day or two, then bring the seedlings into bright light to prevent leggy growth. Mist gently and avoid overwatering, as tender lettuce seedlings rot easily. Harvest the mild, sweet, crunchy greens after about ten days to two weeks once the cotyledons are fully expanded.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Leutschauer Paprika is a slow-to-ripen variety — allow the full season for fruits to turn deep red; in zone 9 the long warm season suits this variety particularly well and allows full color development without rushing.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Leutschauer Paprika is a Slovak heirloom paprika pepper that produces elongated, pendant, 5–6 inch fruits with exceptionally thin walls and high sugar content — characteristics that make it one of the premier varieties for drying and grinding into fresh paprika. The bright red, fully ripe fruits are dried whole in strings (paprika ristras) or sliced and dehydrated before grinding. The flavor is sweet, slightly fruity, and aromatic — quite different from commercially ground paprika that has lost volatile compounds in processing. Plants are productive on fertile soil with consistent moisture; fruit set can stall during the hottest weeks in zone 9 but resumes in September. This is primarily a drying variety, though the fresh ripe fruits are also edible.

plant_note: Sow 2–3 weeks after last frost; lima beans demand warm soil and will rot in cold, wet ground.
directions: Sow seeds 1 to 1.5 in deep in loose, warm soil with the eye of the bean facing downward. Lima beans are sensitive to drought during flowering; irregular moisture can cause blossom drop and reduced pod set. For fresh shell use, harvest pods when they are bright green and plump but before they begin to fade or yellow. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine for dry bean storage.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Lincoln (also sold as Homesteader, the same variety under a different name) is one of the most highly regarded American shelling peas for flavor — a mid-season bush pea with wrinkled seeds and large, well-filled pods that many home gardeners consider the finest-flavored of all commonly available shelling peas.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep, 2–4 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; direct seed as soon as soil can be worked in early spring. Lincoln (sold as Homesteader in Britain and by some American companies — both names refer to the same variety) is a mid-season American shelling pea considered by many gardeners and seed savers to produce the finest overall flavor and texture among commonly available bush peas; the compact plants produce blunt-tipped pods with 7–9 large, wrinkled (sweeter) peas each, ripening in 65–70 days from sowing. The wrinkled seed type indicates higher sugar content compared to smooth-seeded varieties; like all garden peas, Lincoln must be harvested at precise peak ripeness and eaten promptly before sugars convert to starch. An excellent variety for freezing as well as fresh eating; it remains the benchmark for shelling pea flavor among serious home gardeners.

common_name: Lipstick Pepper (AAS-Winning Sweet Pimento-Type Pepper, Compact and Prolific)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Lipstick is a compact sweet pepper producing small to medium pimento-shaped fruits (about 4 inches long, heart-shaped with a pointed tip). In zone 9, transplant March–April. Lipstick produces prolifically on compact plants (18–24 inches) suitable for containers and small gardens. Harvest green or allow to fully ripen to deep red for sweetest flavor — red-ripe Lipstick has exceptional sweetness and thick walls ideal for roasting, fresh eating, and stuffing. The compact plant habit means Lipstick can be grown in 5-gallon containers on patios, making it useful for zone 9 gardeners without significant ground space. Unlike the large, blocky bell pepper types that often struggle to set fruit in zone 9's summer heat, the pimento type peppers like Lipstick are generally more heat-tolerant and continue producing through the Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or red; red is sweeter. Lipstick Pepper is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the sweet pepper category, recognized for its combination of compact plant size, prolific productivity, and exceptional fruit quality in the pimento pepper class. The variety belongs to the pimento type — a group of sweet peppers distinct from bell peppers in fruit shape (heart-shaped, conical, or tapered rather than blocky), flesh thickness (very thick walls with small seed cavity), and flavor (sweeter, with less of the grassy quality of green bell peppers). Pimento peppers have a long history in American cooking: the red pimento paste used to stuff olives and fill pimento cheese sandwiches is made from this type, and the pimento's thick, sweet walls make it the preferred pepper for roasting, where the flesh caramelizes to an exceptional sweetness. Lipstick's AAS recognition was awarded specifically for its performance across diverse North American climates — including hot-summer regions where standard bell peppers underperform — making it a practical choice for gardeners in zone 9 who find that large bell peppers drop their blossoms or produce poorly during the Gulf South's summer heat peak. The fruit is medium-sized (3–4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), heart-shaped to conical with a small pointed tip, and ripens from green to a deep, brilliant red. The skin is thinner than a bell pepper and the flesh is proportionally thicker, with a small, easily removed seed cavity. The flavor at red-ripe stage is very sweet, almost candy-like, with none of the bitterness that some tasters detect in green bell peppers.

common_name: Lipstick Sweet Pepper (Pimiento-Type Mini Sweet Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Lipstick is a compact plant (24 inches) bearing 3–4 inch pimiento-type fruits that ripen from green to deep, vivid red. Unlike most bell peppers, Lipstick ripens to red relatively quickly (70–80 days) without the extended 3-week+ green-to-red window of larger types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; plants often continue producing into fall. Lipstick does not require as much fertilizer as standard bell types — moderate fertility produces best flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost with spacing of 15–20 inches. Lipstick is a Burpee-developed pimiento-type sweet pepper that produces small to medium (3 x 3.5 inch), heart-shaped, very thick-walled fruits of the pimiento class — a pepper type characterized by a rounder, more compact form than standard bell peppers, extraordinarily thick walls relative to total size, very few seeds, and exceptional sweetness. The pimiento type has been prized by Spanish and Mediterranean cooks for centuries for its superior eating quality (pimientos are what give pimento-stuffed olives their distinctive flavor and the Spanish name 'pimiento' itself means pepper in Spanish). Lipstick delivers the classic pimiento character in a compact, prolific plant suitable for small gardens and containers: the fruits have very thick walls that hold up to heat, an extremely sweet, mild flavor with no heat, and the characteristic heart-shaped cross-section when sliced that makes them visually distinctive from bell peppers. The vivid, saturated red color at full ripeness is striking and the thick walls make Lipstick excellent for roasting, stuffing with cheese, and eating raw where the thickness provides a satisfying crunch. Ripens more completely and uniformly than many larger bell types, making it practical for gardeners who want to harvest primarily red-ripe peppers.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; an early-maturing pimento-type pepper that performs well in shorter seasons; transplant after all frost has passed and soil warms to 60°F.
directions: Start seeds at 75–85°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Lipstick is an early-maturing sweet pimento-type pepper that produces heart-shaped, 4-inch fruits with thick, candy-sweet walls, minimal seed cavity, and zero heat; they ripen from green to a brilliant lipstick red earlier than most pimentos, making it one of the better sweet pepper choices for northern gardens and short-season growers. The fruits are remarkably thick-walled and sweet when roasted, and they peel cleanly after charring, making them ideal for preserving as roasted red peppers. Compact plants are well-suited to containers.

plant_note: Heat-loving Spanish heirloom; mulch to retain warmth and moisture.
directions: A Spanish heirloom with teardrop fruit striped purple and white and a notably sweet, mild flavor. Give it a long warm season, starting seed indoors early and transplanting into the warmest bed available. Fruit skin is thin and bruises easily, so handle carefully and harvest with shears. Pick when fruit is 5 to 7 inches and still shiny, before seeds harden. Steady watering prevents blossom-end problems and keeps flesh creamy.

common_name: Listada de Gandia Eggplant (Striped Italian Heirloom Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9 also transplant in August for a fall crop — eggplants often produce their most abundant crop in the cooler fall weather.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Listada de Gandia is one of the most beautiful and visually distinctive eggplant varieties — a traditional Italian heirloom from the Valencia region of Spain producing oval to oblong, medium-large fruits with a stunning two-tone pattern of cream-white base with vivid purple-lavender stripes or splashes covering much of the surface. No two fruits have exactly the same pattern, making each harvest visually unique. Beyond its striking appearance, Listada de Gandia is prized for its exceptionally mild, tender, low-bitterness flesh — the thin skin and low seed content make it one of the finest eggplants for fresh preparations, grilling, and Italian dishes where eggplant bitterness would be unwelcome. The mild, creamy flesh has a slightly sweet, delicate flavor that is quite different from the stronger flavor of large black globe eggplants. Harvest at medium size (4–6 inches long) when the skin is shiny — the stripes fade and seeds become noticeable if left too long. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved true-to-type. The ornamental quality of the fruits and foliage makes Listada de Gandia attractive even as an edible ornamental in mixed garden beds and containers. In zone 9, eggplants are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables, thriving in the Gulf South summer.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; carrots resent transplanting so always sow in place.
directions: Direct sow this French baby carrot in loose, stone-free soil, since carrots dislike transplanting and forked roots result from compacted ground. Sow seed shallowly and keep the surface consistently moist until germination, which can take two to three weeks. Thin seedlings to about an inch apart so the slender 3 inch roots can size up sweet and crisp. Little Finger is ideal for shallow beds and containers and is best harvested young; succession sow every few weeks for a continuous supply.

common_name: Little Finger Eggplant (Slender Baby Asian Finger Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Little Finger is a productive, compact eggplant that performs extremely well in zone 9 hot summers. In zone 9, transplant March–April for June–November production. Harvest fruits when 3–5 inches long and deep purple-black — do not allow to over-ripen, as the thin skin becomes tough and the few seeds develop rapidly. The plants produce prolifically in clusters, and frequent harvesting encourages continued production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Harvest slender purple-black fruits at 3–5 inches. Little Finger is a slender, finger-shaped Asian eggplant — a compact variety producing clusters of elongated, narrow fruits (2–5 inches long, 0.5–1 inch in diameter) of the finger eggplant type. The finger eggplant category is distinct from the large, globe-shaped Italian types and the longer Asian slicers: finger eggplants are the smallest category, producing bite-sized to small fruits in prolific clusters on bushy plants. Little Finger's small fruits are characterized by very thin, tender skin; virtually no seeds; and mildly sweet, creamy flesh without the bitterness sometimes found in large-fruited types. The thin skin means no peeling is required — fruits can be cooked whole (roasted, grilled, or sautéed) without preparation. The compact cluster-fruiting habit makes Little Finger one of the most productive eggplants per plant for its size, making it excellent for small gardens and containers. The fruits are harvested frequently (every 2–3 days at peak production), and the small size makes them ideal for stir-fries, kebabs, and preparations where bite-sized pieces are desired.

plant_note: Direct sow; ideal for containers and shallow beds.
directions: This heirloom baby carrot produces small, vibrant orange roots packed with sweet flavor, bred originally for canning but excellent fresh or in containers. Sow seeds directly into loose soil and keep the bed evenly moist during the slow germination. Thin seedlings so the short roots can size up cleanly. Harvest while the roots are still small and tender for the sweetest, most delicate flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Little Gem is a miniature romaine-butterhead cross that produces small, compact, dense heads of exceptional quality — the 'sucrine' of French cuisine, considered by many the most flavorful lettuce for whole-head salads and prized by restaurant chefs for its combination of crunch and buttery flavor.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50–70°F. Little Gem is a miniature romaine/butterhead cross producing small (4–5 inch), compact, upright heads with firm, crunchy outer leaves and a sweet, butter-cream interior heart — essentially a mini Caesar salad head in one plant. Also known as 'Sucrine' in France (from the French for 'sugar'), it has become extremely popular in restaurant and farmers market contexts as a whole-head salad lettuce grilled or served halved with dressings. The outer leaves have romaine's crunch while the hearts are as sweet and buttery as buttercrunch — the best of both types in a small, space-efficient package. 4-6 inch spacing allows intensive planting; harvest the whole head when firm and compact. More heat-tolerant than standard butterhead and holds well in the garden without bolting quickly.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and succession sow; sow in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow this English heirloom mini-romaine directly in cool weather, barely covering the seed since lettuce needs light to germinate. The petite heads reach just 6 inches tall and 4 inches wide, forming the perfect size for a single-serving salad with tender, sweet, succulent leaves. Thin plants to 6 to 8 inches apart and keep them evenly moist to prevent bitterness and bolting. Succession sow every couple of weeks and give afternoon shade in warm weather to extend the harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Little Marvel is a 1934 All-America Selections winner — a remarkably compact dwarf bush pea (15 inches tall) that produces an outsized crop relative to its tiny size, making it ideal for small-space gardens, raised beds, containers, and intensive succession planting.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep; Little Marvel can be planted in raised beds at 15-inch row spacing due to its dwarf habit and needs only minimal support. Little Marvel pea won an All-America Selections award in 1934 and remains one of the most productive and most compact garden shelling peas available — the dwarf 15-inch plants are among the shortest of all shelling peas while producing an outsized crop of well-filled pods with 6–8 wrinkled, sweet peas each. The compact habit makes Little Marvel excellent for small raised beds, succession planting in containers, and tight-spaced intensive gardens where full-sized pea varieties would be impractical. Does not require staking even in wind, though a small 12–18 inch support fence improves harvestability. The 60–65 day maturity is relatively early for a sweet wrinkled-seeded pea.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, and again for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow this compact heirloom shelling pea as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since peas thrive in cool weather. The short vines grow only 18 to 24 inches tall and do not require support, making them ideal for small gardens and containers. Plants produce an abundance of 3 to 4 inch pods filled with sweet, tender peas perfect for fresh eating. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod fill, and harvest promptly to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Lolla Rossa can be harvested as baby leaves (cut 2–3 inches tall) or allowed to develop to full rosettes. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide a continuous supply. The red color is most intense in cool weather; warm temperatures reduce pigmentation.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Lolla Rossa is an Italian looseleaf lettuce producing rosettes of tightly frilled, deeply ruffled, deep burgundy-red to crimson leaves — the most intensely frilled and ruffled of all red lettuces, with a texture often compared to coral or ruffled fabric. The heavy frilling maximizes surface area and catches dressings exceptionally well, making Lolla Rossa a favorite in mixed salad bowls and mesclun mixes where its dramatic appearance creates visual impact. The flavor is mild and tender with a slight bitterness from the red pigments that is barely perceptible in young leaves and becomes slightly more pronounced in older, larger leaves. The deep red color makes Lolla Rossa one of the highest-anthocyanin lettuces, providing significant antioxidant content. It is the standard red frilly lettuce in European market and supermarket displays, where it has been in continuous commercial production since the 1970s, and is equally valuable in North American specialty salad production and home gardens.

plant_note: Sow in spring or late summer; heat causes bolting and bitterness.
directions: This Italian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce forms frilly rosettes of magenta-red and green leaves with mild flavor and striking color. Sow directly in cool weather, spring or late summer, since heat prompts bolting and bitterness. Sow in succession for a continuous supply of tender leaves. Harvest outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut whole rosettes when full, keeping soil evenly moist throughout.

common_name: Lollo Bionda Lettuce (Italian Ruffled Green Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly with minimal soil coverage; grow as cut-and-come-again from 40 days or harvest whole heads at 55–65 days. Often grown alongside Lollo Rosso for visual contrast in mixed salad plantings. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter production and February–March for spring. Performs best in cool weather and does not tolerate summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or barely cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; maintain consistent moisture through germination. Lollo Bionda (Italian for 'blonde curly') is the green counterpart to Lollo Rosso — sharing the identical intensely frilled, ruffled leaf margin and open loose-leaf habit but expressing uniformly bright chartreuse-green to golden-green coloring throughout rather than the Rosso type's red pigmentation. The two varieties are frequently grown together in alternating rows or blocks, where the intense green-and-crimson contrast creates a visually striking planting that is both ornamental and practical. Mixed bags of Lollo Bionda and Lollo Rosso leaves form the foundation of the Italian insalata mista tradition. Like Lollo Rosso, Lollo Bionda has a mildly bitter, distinctly Italian loose-leaf character — more complex and interesting than flat-leafed American loose-leaf types — and the same extremely frilled, ruffled texture that gives the leaves visual and textural interest in salads. Lollo Bionda is somewhat more heat-tolerant than Lollo Rosso in some trials, extending the spring salad season by 1–2 weeks before bolting. Both Lollo types are excellent for cut-and-come-again harvesting, where the plant continues producing from the center after outer leaves are removed, providing multiple harvests from a single planting.

common_name: Lollo Rosso Lettuce (Italian Ruffled Red Loose-Leaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly and barely cover with fine soil (lettuce needs light for germination); Lollo Rosso is best grown as a cut-and-come-again crop, harvesting outer leaves from 40 days onward or cutting the whole plant at 55–65 days when full size. In zone 9, sow September through November for fall and winter harvest, and again February through March for spring. Lollo Rosso performs best in cool weather (50–70°F) and tends to bolt quickly in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; keep moist until germination. Lollo Rosso is the defining Italian loose-leaf lettuce — a variety whose intensely frilled, ruffled, deeply cut leaf margins and vibrant crimson-red to dark wine-red coloring at the leaf tips (fading through red-purple to green at the base) have made it the visual centerpiece of European mixed salad culture and one of the most recognizable lettuce varieties in the world. The name means 'red curly' in Italian, describing both the color and the extraordinarily frilled leaf margin that distinguishes Lollo Rosso from all other common loose-leaf types. The frilling is dramatic and consistent — the leaf margins curl so tightly that they create a lace-like appearance when the lettuce is displayed whole, making Lollo Rosso not only a component of salads but a visual garnish in its own right. The flavor is mildly bitter in the Italian leaf lettuce tradition — more complex and interesting than bland American loose-leaf types but not unpleasantly so — and pairs well with vinaigrette-dressed salads where the slight bitterness provides welcome contrast. Lollo Rosso is the standard accompaniment to Italian prosciutto and melon, appears in mixed salad bags throughout Europe as the red accent component, and is excellent alone dressed simply with olive oil and sea salt.

common_name: Long Black Spanish Radish (Winter Storage Radish with Black Skin)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer/early fall for fall and winter harvest; Long Black Spanish is a winter radish that requires a longer growing time than spring radishes (60–70 vs. 25–35 days). In zone 9, sow August–September for November–January harvest. Winter radishes should not be planted in spring — they bolt quickly in warming temperatures. Harvest when roots reach 6–8 inches; they keep in the ground for weeks and can be stored in damp sand in a cool location for months.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fall in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when roots are 6–8 inches long; peel before eating as the black skin is tough and astringent. Long Black Spanish Radish is a winter storage radish with a very distinctive appearance: the long (6–10 inch), cylindrical root has deeply black skin — nearly jet black — contrasting with crisp, white flesh within. It is one of the oldest documented European radish varieties, with references dating to the 16th century; it was the standard large winter radish of European cuisine before the introduction of Asian types and remains common in Polish, German, and Ashkenazi Jewish food traditions where it appears in salads (grated with onion and oil) and as a medicinal digestive herb. The flavor is significantly sharper and more pungent than spring radishes — a biting, horseradish-adjacent pungency that mellows somewhat when the grated flesh is salted and rested. The winter storage capability distinguishes Long Black Spanish from spring radishes: properly harvested and stored in damp conditions near freezing, the roots keep for 3–4 months, providing a root vegetable throughout the winter.

plant_note: Direct sow in rich, well-drained soil 1–2 weeks after last frost; Long Island Cheese is a Cucurbita moschata type (related to butternut squash) with exceptional disease resistance and heat tolerance compared to jack-o-lantern types — excellent for zone 8–10 gardens. Vines are vigorous, reaching 10–15 feet.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2; Long Island Cheese Pumpkin is a large, flat, deeply ribbed, tan-buff heirloom that looks remarkably like a wheel of French cheese — hence its popular name. Developed by Long Island market gardeners in the 19th century, it was once the dominant commercial pumpkin variety in the northeastern United States because of its excellent eating quality, dense orange-yellow flesh with a smooth, rich, sweet flavor particularly prized for pumpkin pies (significantly better than jack-o-lantern types). Being a Cucurbita moschata variety, it is substantially more resistant to squash vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat than C. pepo types, making it one of the most practical large pumpkins for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast gardens where summer disease and pest pressure is high. Fruits weigh 8–15 pounds and store well for months.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera 'Long Island Improved'
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date, transplanting 12–16 weeks before first expected frost; in zones 3–7 start in late spring for fall harvest. Brussels sprouts require a very long cool growing season (90+ days) and develop best flavor only after exposure to hard frost — zones 3–7 are ideal, with zones 8–9 being very challenging due to insufficient sustained cool weather for quality sprout development. In zone 9 Brussels sprouts may produce a partial crop in the coolest winters but results are often disappointing compared to more appropriate cool-climate growing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Brussels sprouts are heavy feeders requiring substantial nitrogen throughout their long growing season; Long Island Improved is the standard open-pollinated Brussels sprouts variety — the classic 'compact' type (as opposed to taller, older varieties) that has dominated American horticulture since the early 20th century. The small, round, tightly packed miniature cabbage heads (sprouts) that form along the stem are harvested from bottom to top as they mature, with each stem producing dozens of 1–2 inch sprouts over several weeks of harvest. Brussels sprouts' reputation for strong, unpleasant flavor is entirely a product of poor growing conditions — specifically, heat stress — rather than the plant's inherent flavor. Brussels sprouts grown to maturity in cool weather with frost exposure are mild, nutty, sweet, and completely different from heat-stressed sprouts with the intense sulfurous off-flavors that give the vegetable its negative reputation. The conversion of starches to sugars after frost exposure transforms Brussels sprouts from a challenging, strong-flavored vegetable into a genuinely delicious one — a transformation that zone 9 gardeners rarely witness but that northern gardeners who harvest after repeated freezes experience routinely.

plant_note: Time so the long crop matures into cool fall weather; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: This time-tested heirloom from the late 1800s is valued for compact plants, dependable yields, and excellent cold tolerance. Start seeds indoors and transplant so the long-season crop matures into cool fall weather, when the sprouts taste sweetest after light frosts. Keep plants well watered and side-dress with nitrogen for steady growth. Harvest the firm sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach about an inch across.

plant_note: Start indoors in early to mid summer and transplant for a fall harvest; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: Start this heirloom Brussels sprout indoors and transplant for a fall harvest, as the sprouts sweeten and firm up after light frosts. Give plants plenty of water, rich soil, and a long season, spacing them 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. Row covers help protect young plants from cabbage worms and other pests. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach about an inch in diameter, and top the plants a few weeks before harvest to encourage uniform sizing.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth and transplant well after frost when soil and nights are warm.
directions: Start this heirloom eggplant indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, providing bottom heat and warm soil for good germination. Transplant only after nights are reliably warm, as eggplant is very cold sensitive, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. The long, slender purple fruits are flavorful in countless dishes and are best harvested young when the skin is glossy. Stake taller plants, keep them evenly watered, and pick fruits regularly to encourage continued production.

common_name: Long Red Cayenne Pepper (Classic American Cayenne)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Long Red Cayenne is the standard, classic cayenne pepper variety — a long-season heirloom producing pencil-thin, wrinkled, 6–8 inch red pods with 30,000–50,000 SHU heat, the benchmark from which all other cayenne peppers are measured and the source of commercial cayenne powder, hot sauce, and the classic Louisiana-style hot sauce heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil; Long Red Cayenne is a vigorous grower that benefits from staking when loaded with fruit; pick all red and drying fruits promptly to encourage continued production through the season. Long Red Cayenne is the classic cayenne pepper — an old heirloom open-pollinated variety that represents the original 'cayenne' type from which the broad category of cayenne peppers takes its name (likely from Cayenne, French Guiana, where related chiles were grown). The fruits are distinctive: pencil-thin (1/2 to 3/4 inch in diameter), 6–8 inches long, wrinkled and irregular in cross-section, tapering to a point, and ripening to a bright red — characteristics that make Long Red Cayenne immediately identifiable and distinct from the smooth-skinned, shorter 'Ring of Fire' type. The heat level of 30,000–50,000 SHU is moderate-hot — significantly hotter than jalapeños but substantially milder than habaneros — in the range that defines 'cayenne heat' in American cuisine. Long Red Cayenne is the source (via cultivated strains) of commercial cayenne powder, an essential spice in Cajun and Creole cooking, Indian cuisine, and most dry spice blends; of Louisiana-style hot sauce; of the dried cayenne pods used in Chinese and Sichuan cooking; and of the classic sriracha-style sauces. Prolific production on vigorous plants (24–36 inches) in warm climates; excellent for drying on the plant or on strings.

common_name: Long Red Slim Cayenne Pepper (Classic Slender Drying Cayenne)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Long Red Slim produces the classic thin, wrinkled, fiery red cayenne pods traditionally strung and dried for homemade cayenne pepper powder and pepper flakes.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Long Red Slim is a classic, widely grown cayenne cultivar producing narrow, tapering, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to bright red, packing substantial heat in a lightweight, easily dried pod. The thin walls make it ideal for stringing into traditional pepper ropes (ristras) or oven-drying and grinding into homemade cayenne powder or crushed red pepper flakes. Plants are productive over a long season and tolerate heat well, making cayenne one of the more reliable hot peppers for Gulf South summers; pick pods at full red color for maximum heat and flavor when drying.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March. Long Slim Cayenne is highly productive in zone 9's long warm season and often overwinters as a perennial — cut back in late winter and the woody plant regrows to produce even more heavily the next year. For dried cayenne, harvest fully red fruits and dry on strings or in a dehydrator. The thin-walled fruits dry quickly and completely.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Long Slim Cayenne is the standard form of cayenne pepper — the elongated, thin-walled, moderately wrinkled red pepper that is one of the most important culinary chile peppers in the world and the source of commercial cayenne pepper powder and red pepper flakes. The fruits are 4–6 inches long, pencil-thin, and bright red when fully ripe, with heat levels typically measuring 30,000–50,000 Scoville Heat Units — a penetrating, clean, sharp heat that has made cayenne the dominant hot pepper in Louisiana Cajun and Creole cuisine, Indian cooking, and dozens of other culinary traditions. Long Slim Cayenne dries easily and completely due to the thin walls, and the dried pepper grinds to the characteristic bright red powder of commercial cayenne spice. Fresh red cayenne peppers are also used in hot sauce production — Tabasco-style sauces use fermented cayenne-type peppers as their primary ingredient. In zone 9 the plants bear enormous crops of drying-quality peppers over the full warm season.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring and August for fall. Long of Naples produces very long vines (12–15 feet) requiring generous space or a large trellis. The moschata type is more heat-tolerant and powdery mildew-resistant than pepo squashes, making it a better choice for zone 9 summer production. Harvest immature fruits at 12–18 inches for summer squash use, or leave to mature fully for winter storage.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Long of Naples (Lunga di Napoli, Serpentina di Napoli) is a renowned Italian heirloom squash from the Campania region surrounding Naples, producing extraordinarily long cylindrical fruits of 24–36 inches or more — occasionally reaching 4–5 feet under optimal conditions. At maturity the tan-to-buff skin covers dense, deep-orange flesh with a sweet, rich flavor similar to butternut but with a creamier texture and less watery flesh. Immature fruits at 12–18 inches can be harvested and used as a superior summer squash — far more flavorful than standard zucchini, with firmer flesh and more concentrated sweetness. Fully mature fruits cure well and store for 6–12 months in a cool, dry location. As a Cucurbita moschata type, Long of Naples shows excellent heat and humidity tolerance, resistance to vine borers, and superior performance in zone 9 compared to pepo-type squashes. The vines are vigorous and spreading — allow 8–12 feet per plant.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil has warmed; plants spread by rhizomes and will naturalize readily.
directions: Long-leaf Ground Cherry is a hardy native husk tomato found across central and eastern North America in prairies, disturbed areas, and open woodlands, producing small yellow fruits enclosed in papery husks similar to a miniature tomatillo that are edible fresh or cooked. Direct sow seeds after the last frost into well-drained soil in full sun, as this perennial spreads vigorously from spreading rhizomes and will naturalize in favorable conditions. Plants are extremely drought-tolerant once established and require little care beyond occasional thinning to prevent them from crowding out neighboring plants. Harvest fruits when the husk has turned tan and dried, and the berry inside has dropped naturally, as this indicates peak ripeness and sweetness.

plant_note: Root 4–6 inch stem cuttings in water or moist mix after last frost; they root in 1–2 weeks and are ready to transplant when roots reach 1 inch.
directions: Root cuttings easily in water and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; the plant sprawls attractively as a groundcover or can be trained onto a low trellis. Harvest leaves and shoot tips regularly; the raw leaves have a crunchy, mild, slightly succulent texture and are popular in Southeast Asian salads and as an anti-diabetic traditional food. Unlike the closely related Okinawa spinach, this species has smooth (not wavy-edged) leaves without the purple underside. Bring cuttings indoors before first frost for overwintering; in frost-free areas it grows year-round and can be lightly sheared to encourage fresh growth.
