plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March after nights stay above 55°F. Lorz Italian is productive through the Gulf Coast summer and performs best when harvested green; if left to ripen red, pick before fruits become overripe and mushy in summer humidity.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lorz Italian is a Washington State heirloom sweet frying pepper, a classic Italian-style variety with thin-walled, pendent fruits that are 8–10 inches long — among the longest sweet peppers available. The mild, sweet flesh is nearly seedless and ideal for the classic Italian-American preparation of frying in olive oil with garlic and salt (peperonata), as well as roasting, stuffing, and fresh eating. The thin walls roast and collapse beautifully without the wateriness of thicker-walled sweet peppers. Plants produce prolifically once established, with multiple fruits per branch; the long, elegant fruits are also ornamental hanging from the plant. Harvest green for crispest texture or allow to ripen red for sweetest flavor.

common_name: Lorz Italian Softneck Garlic (Pacific Northwest Italian Immigrant Heirloom)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall around the time of first frost; Lorz Italian is a softneck Artichoke-type garlic brought to the Walla Walla area of Washington State by Italian immigrant Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 1800s, where it was grown and preserved through generations of Italian-American farming families in the Columbia River valley before entering heirloom seed networks.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall; softneck types like Lorz Italian can be planted over a wider window than hardnecks — from 4 weeks before first frost to a week or two after; mulch after planting; keep weed-free in spring; harvest when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly. Lorz Italian is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic with a remarkable Italian-American immigrant story: it was brought to the Walla Walla Valley of eastern Washington State by an Italian immigrant named Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 19th century, where it became a staple of the Italian immigrant farming community in the Columbia River valley region, passed down through family seed-saving for generations before being preserved by heirloom garlic collectors and specialist growers. The large, roundish bulbs typically contain 12–20 cloves arranged in multiple overlapping layers (characteristic of Artichoke types), with white to pale ivory outer skin; the cloves are plump, meaty, and moderately spicy — a full-flavored softneck with more character than commercial supermarket garlic but without the intensity of the finest Rocambole hardnecks. The great practical advantage of Lorz Italian and other Artichoke softnecks is excellent storage — bulbs typically keep 9–12 months in good conditions, far outlasting any hardneck type; the flexible stems also make it excellent for braiding. Adapted to a wide range of climates from cool Pacific Northwest conditions to warm Southern winters.

plant_note: Plant rhizome sections in still or slow-moving water 1–2 feet deep after last frost when water temperature stays above 65°F.
directions: Plant intact rhizome sections (with at least one growing tip) horizontally in the mud bottom of a pond, tub, or container submerged under 12–18 inches of still water; never allow the growing tip to dry out. Full sun is essential — lotus will produce only foliage and few flowers in shade. Harvest rhizomes in fall once foliage dies back by reaching into the mud and carefully pulling out the chain of large, starchy sections; the distinctive lacy, hole-patterned cross-section is a signature feature. Rhizomes must be cooked before eating; they are eaten stir-fried, pickled, or braised throughout East and Southeast Asia and have a crunchy texture even after cooking.

common_name: Louisiana Green Velvet Okra (Long Smooth Dark Green Southern Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; Louisiana Green Velvet is a smooth-podded, heavy-yielding heirloom okra variety that produces long (5–7 inch), straight, smooth dark green pods with minimal ribbing and particularly tender texture — one of the top-recommended varieties by LSU AgCenter for Gulf Coast okra production, prized for consistent tenderness and yield through humid Louisiana summers.
directions: Soak seeds overnight before planting; direct sow 1 inch deep 12–18 inches apart after soil warms; harvest pods at 4–5 inches for the finest texture; once production begins, harvest every 2 days during peak summer heat as pods elongate rapidly. Louisiana Green Velvet is an heirloom open-pollinated okra variety with a strong association with Louisiana and Gulf Coast traditional food culture — it is one of the most historically prominent varieties in the region and has been grown by Louisiana gardeners for generations as the standard for gumbo okra and fresh summer side dishes. The pods are smooth, deep green, and slightly ridged rather than heavily ribbed like Clemson Spineless, with a velvety (not bristly) surface texture that makes handling comfortable and gives the variety its name. 'Green Velvet' pods remain tender at 4–5 inches under high summer temperatures — a practical advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat causes many okra varieties to become tough and fibrous quickly if not harvested every day. The variety is adapted to the humid, hot climate of coastal Louisiana and the Gulf South and performs especially well in the clay soils and high humidity of the Louisiana bayou region where it originated as a preferred variety. Louisiana Green Velvet is the traditional okra of Cajun and Creole cooking — most commonly used in gumbo, where the natural mucilage (thickening quality) of properly cooked okra is considered essential to authentic texture and flavor.

common_name: Louisiana Long Green Eggplant (Old South Elongated Green Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Louisiana Long Green is particularly productive in the Gulf South's long, hot growing season — transplant in spring and again in August for maximum productivity.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Louisiana Long Green is a traditional old-South eggplant variety producing elongated, cylindrical fruits 8–12 inches long in an unusual pale green to light green-white color that stands in stark contrast to the standard purple-black American eggplant. The pale green color indicates ripe fruit — unlike purple-black types where color darkens as they ripen, Louisiana Long Green turns a light, creamy green to yellow-green when mature. The flesh is white, mild, and very low in bitterness — outstanding for frying, grilling, and the classic Louisiana preparation of eggplant dressing (a traditional Gulf South casserole combining eggplant with shrimp, crabmeat, bread crumbs, and Cajun seasonings). Louisiana Long Green is a regional heirloom that has been grown continuously in Louisiana and lower Mississippi kitchen gardens for generations — selected by Southern gardeners for its outstanding heat tolerance, prolific production in the Gulf South summer, and excellent culinary qualities in traditional regional recipes. Harvest when fruits are 8–10 inches long with pale, slightly shiny skin — over-mature fruits become yellowish and develop more seeds and bitterness. Plants are vigorous and can reach 4 feet tall in the long Gulf South growing season, requiring staking when heavily loaded with fruit.

common_name: Louisiana Purple Pod Bean (Heat-Tolerant Southern Heirloom Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Louisiana Purple Pod is a vigorous heirloom pole bean bred for Gulf South heat and humidity, and its deep purple pods stand out sharply against the green foliage for fast harvest. In zone 9, plant March-May for a summer crop and again in August for a fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis or pole support after the danger of frost has passed. Louisiana Purple Pod is a Deep South heirloom pole bean selected over generations for reliable production through the heat and humidity that stall many snap bean varieties, and it shows good resistance to common bean mosaic virus and rust compared to older commercial types. Pods emerge deep purple, which makes them easy to spot among the leaves at harvest time, and the color cooks away to ordinary green so the beans can be prepared exactly like any other snap bean. Pick pods at 5-6 inches long while still tender for the best snap texture, and pick regularly to keep vines producing; left longer, pods can also be shelled fresh or dried for winter storage. Vines climb vigorously and benefit from consistent moisture during flowering and pod set to prevent blossom drop during extreme heat.

common_name: Louisiana Ribbon Cane (Heirloom Striped Syrup Cane)
plant_note: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Ribbon Cane is a traditional Gulf South heirloom variety grown chiefly for syrup rather than table sugar, prized for its distinctive green-and-purple striped stalks.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Ribbon Cane is a historic heirloom sugarcane variety, distinguished from modern commercial hybrids by its slender, green-and-purple striped stalks, that has been maintained by Deep South farm families and seed savers for generations specifically for making cane syrup rather than refined sugar. It is traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, then stripped, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked down into dark, richly flavored cane syrup, a staple of Louisiana and Georgia country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass also makes a striking, fast-growing screen or accent planting; in zone 9 it typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze and regrows vigorously each spring.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a large bicolor beefsteak with stunning golden-orange skin blushed red and equally beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh — one of the most visually dramatic heirloom tomatoes available.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the large, heavy fruits. Lucky Cross is an exquisite heirloom bicolor tomato producing large, 1–2 pound beefsteak fruits with golden-yellow to orange skin blushed with a red blush at the blossom end and extraordinarily beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh that is as ornamental sliced on a plate as it is delicious — the flavor is sweet, low-acid, and tropically fruity with exceptional richness. Its rarity and stunning appearance make it a prize at farmers' markets and seed saving circles. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive; harvest when fruit softens at the blossom end and the skin transitions fully from green.

common_name: Lucullus Chard (Heirloom White-Stemmed Large-Leaf Swiss Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; Lucullus produces very large plants and benefits from wider spacing (9–12 inches) than many chard varieties for full-sized leaves. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, February–March for spring. Lucullus is one of the most productive and heat-tolerant chard varieties for warm climates, making it particularly well-suited to the Gulf South winter garden where it can be grown nearly year-round with mild management.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fertile, well-amended soil; thin to 9–12 inches for full-sized production. Harvest outer leaves regularly from 40 days onward; the plant continues producing new leaves from the center for months with consistent harvesting. Lucullus is one of the oldest and most established Swiss chard varieties in American cultivation — named after Lucullus, the Roman general and gourmet famous for his extravagant feasts, a name that captures both the impressive size of the plant and the generous quality of its harvest. Lucullus produces very large (18–28 inch tall), broadly spreading plants with thick, heavily crinkled, dark green leaves and thick, ivory-white to pale green stems and ribs — a classic white-stemmed chard in the traditional style before the development of colored-stem varieties. The large, deeply savoyed leaves have substantial texture and rich, minerally chard flavor that is excellent cooked — wilted with olive oil and garlic, added to soups and pasta, or incorporated into quiches and casseroles. The very large leaf size makes Lucullus impractical for baby salad mixes (too coarse when young) but exceptionally productive for cooked greens — a single plant at peak production can provide a large bundle of cooking greens per week. Lucullus is often noted for better heat tolerance than some other chard varieties, making it one of the more productive summer leaf vegetables in hot climates.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. Luffa requires a long, hot season.
directions: Nick or soak seeds for 24 hours before sowing 1/2 inch deep indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost to give this long-season crop a head start. Provide a very sturdy trellis, as vines can reach 15 feet and carry heavy fruit. For eating, harvest young fruits at 4–6 inches before the fibrous skeleton hardens. For sponges, allow fruits to fully mature and dry on the vine until the skin browns, then soak in water, peel, and rinse out the seeds.

plant_note: Needs a long, hot season; start indoors and transplant onto a strong trellis.
directions: This vigorous climbing gourd serves two purposes: harvest young fruits as a tender, okra-like vegetable, or let them mature and dry into natural loofah sponges. It needs a long, hot season, so start seeds indoors and transplant onto a sturdy trellis once soil is warm. The heavy vines produce long, hanging fruits that require strong support. For sponges, leave the gourds on the vine until the skin browns and the interior fibers dry, then peel, shake out the seeds, and rinse.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; luffa needs a long season (150+ days frost-free) and benefits from the head start in all but the Deep South. In zone 9 the long summer provides ample time for full maturation when started in March. Direct sow is possible in late March–April.
directions: Grow on a strong trellis, arbor, or fence — luffa vines are extremely vigorous and can cover a large structure in a single season. The large yellow flowers are showy and attract bees and pollinators. Young fruits at 4–6 inches long are eaten as a tender vegetable in Asian cuisines (similar to zucchini but with a silkier texture); for sponge production, allow fruits to mature fully on the vine until the skin turns brown and papery, then soak in water to loosen and remove the outer skin, revealing the fibrous interior skeleton. Dry the sponge in the sun and rinse several times until the fiber is clean and pale yellow. Each vine can produce dozens of sponges.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a white-skinned pumpkin that makes a striking alternative to orange jack-o'-lanterns for fall decoration and has sweet, edible flesh that works well in baking.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-amended soil, spacing hills 5–6 feet apart; Lumina is a vigorous vine type that needs plenty of room and full sun. Lumina is the most widely grown white pumpkin, producing round, 10–20 pound fruits with a smooth, creamy-white to ghostly-white exterior rind that makes it one of the most sought-after decorative pumpkins for Halloween and fall displays; the interior flesh is orange, sweet, and of good quality for cooking and pies — better than many orange carving pumpkins. The white skin provides an excellent canvas for painting, engraving, or decorative carving. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin resists puncture with a thumbnail; cure for 1 week and store in a cool, dry location for 2–3 months.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Lunchbox is an AAS-winning series of compact plants producing abundant small, sweet, snack-sized peppers in red, orange, and yellow, perfect for eating whole straight from the garden.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Lunchbox is a popular sweet pepper series bred to produce large numbers of small, thin-walled, crunchy, sweet fruit about the size of a large grape or small egg, perfect for snacking whole, tossing into lunchboxes, or adding to salads without any need to slice. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and work well in both garden beds and containers. Harvest continuously as pods ripen to their full color (red, orange, or yellow depending on the specific variety) to keep the plant producing more fruit.

common_name: Lutz Green Leaf Beet (Winter Keeper Storage Beet)
plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; Lutz is a late-maturing beet bred specifically for long storage rather than early eating, so allow it a full season to size up.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody roots. Lutz Green Leaf, also called Winter Keeper, is a classic American heirloom beet bred to grow to a large size (often 3-5 inches or more) without becoming woody, fibrous, or losing its sweet flavor the way most beets do when oversized — a trait that makes it uniquely suited for fall harvest and long winter root-cellar storage. The tender, mild, sweet flesh holds its quality even at full size, and the abundant deep green tops are excellent cooked as beet greens. Because it needs a longer season to develop its full storage-quality size, plant it in time to mature before hard frost, then harvest and store roots in damp sand or a root cellar for use well into winter.

common_name: Lychee Tomato (Litchi Tomato, Morelle de Balbis)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; germination can be slow and erratic — nick the seed coat or soak seeds for 24 hours before sowing. Transplant after frost danger passes in full sun. In zone 9, start in January–February for the best spring crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil — lychee tomato is remarkably drought-tolerant and thrives in poor soils where other nightshades would struggle; provide gloves when handling since the entire plant is covered in sharp spines up to 1.5 inches long. The cherry-sized, bright red fruits are enclosed in spiny green husks that split open at full ripeness, revealing smooth, glossy berries with sweet-tart, lychee-flavored flesh containing small seeds. Fruits are delicious eaten fresh when fully red or cooked into sauces, jams, and pies. In zone 8–9 this perennial-in-origin plant often naturalizes and re-seeds, becoming a productive self-sustaining patch. It is also studied as a biocontrol host against nematodes and as a trap crop for Colorado potato beetle. Wear thick gloves during any maintenance or harvest.

plant_note: Sow seeds directly in the garden around the time of last frost; maca thrives in cool, high-altitude conditions and actually benefits from frost exposure during growth. In lowland climates it performs best in cool coastal or mountainous regions.
directions: Sow seeds directly into deep, well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in a cool climate or cool season, barely covering them and keeping the seedbed consistently moist until germination; maca is a compact, low-growing brassica relative native to the high Andes above 13,000 feet, where it produces a flat, radish-like hypocotyl in colors ranging from cream and yellow to red, purple, and near-black. The edible hypocotyl has a butterscotch-malt flavor when fresh and intensifies to a deeper, richer taste when sun-dried — the traditional Andean preparation — and is used in porridges, stews, baked goods, and fermented drinks. In temperate lowland gardens, maca is challenging but achievable in cool-summer climates; gardeners in maritime regions of the Pacific Northwest, the UK, and New Zealand have had the most consistent success. Harvest when the central rosette begins to decline, usually in autumn of the planting year.

plant_note: Sow 4–6 weeks before first frost for fall and winter harvest; also sow in very early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed at 1/4 in depth in cool soil and keep moist; mache is extraordinarily cold-tolerant and grows slowly through winter in mild climates. Thin to 4–6 in for well-formed rosettes, though closer spacing produces acceptable baby greens. Harvest entire rosettes by cutting at the soil line, or pinch individual rosettes for salad use. Mache does not tolerate heat and will quickly bolt and disappear as spring temperatures rise; enjoy it as a winter green.

common_name: Mad Hatter Pepper (Unique Flying-Saucer-Shaped Mild Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Mad Hatter produces distinctive flattened, lobed, flying-saucer-shaped pods with mild heat and a fruity, citrusy flavor, an AAS award-winning novelty pepper as much for its shape as its flavor.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mad Hatter is an All-America Selections winner grown for its unusual, whimsical, flattened flying-saucer-shaped pods with distinctive lobed edges, a shape unlike almost any other common pepper, combined with a mild, sweet, subtly citrusy flavor reminiscent of its Capsicum baccatum relatives like aji peppers. It works well fresh in salads, pickled whole for a striking presentation, or lightly cooked, and the productive plants continue setting fruit over a long summer season. Harvest at any color stage from green to ripe yellow-orange, since the mild heat and flavor are enjoyable throughout ripening.

plant_note: Plant divisions in spring with STRONG root barrier (minimum 30-inch deep HDPE rhizome barrier buried 28–30 inches deep) in full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in zone 5–10; Madake is the premier Japanese giant timber bamboo and one of the largest of all Phyllostachys species — a running bamboo that WILL spread aggressively without containment — producing straight, thick-walled culms to 75 feet tall used for traditional Japanese flutes, tool handles, and as the finest furniture bamboo.
directions: Plant with strong, deep rhizome barrier (30-inch HDPE sheet) to prevent running — Phyllostachys bambusoides sends rhizomes 20–30+ feet in a season and will colonize large areas without containment; install barrier before planting and inspect annually for rhizome escape. Phyllostachys bambusoides (Madake, Japanese Giant Timber Bamboo, or Matake) is one of the largest and most culturally important bamboos in the world — native to China but cultivated in Japan for at least 1,500 years, where it is the premier timber bamboo of Japanese traditional crafts. The culms grow to extraordinary dimensions in optimal conditions: 50–75 feet tall and 4–6 inches in diameter, with thick, straight, dense walls, outstanding tensile strength, and beautiful, lustrous, deep-green color that ages to golden-yellow. Madake is the traditional material for shakuhachi (Japanese end-blown flutes), kendo practice swords (shinai), fishing rods, scaffolding, architectural elements, and fine bamboo furniture — the culm quality is unsurpassed among temperate bamboos. The young spring shoots are edible. As a Phyllostachys (running bamboo), however, it produces aggressive, far-traveling monopodial rhizomes that can penetrate asphalt, damage foundations, and invade neighbor properties if not properly contained by deep rhizome barriers. Never plant without barriers in place. Extremely cold hardy to zone 5 when established.

common_name: Madame Jeanette Pepper (Surinamese Lantern Pepper, Intensely Hot Caribbean Capsicum chinense)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Madame Jeanette, like all Capsicum chinense, requires very warm germination temperatures (80–95°F) on a heat mat and is slow to germinate compared to C. annuum — allow 14–21 days. In zone 9, transplant March–April into full sun. Capsicum chinense thrives in Gulf Coast heat and may overwinter as a perennial in zone 9b if protected from frost, sometimes producing for 2–3 seasons and yielding heavier crops in subsequent years. Harvest when fruits have fully transitioned from green to their ripe yellow color — do not harvest green. The heat level (150,000–300,000 SHU) makes Madame Jeanette one of the hotter commonly grown Capsicum chinense varieties; handle with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face.
directions: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest when fully yellow. Madame Jeanette is a Surinamese Capsicum chinense variety that is one of the most important chiles in Dutch-Caribbean cuisine — particularly in the culinary traditions of the Surinamese and Antillean communities that immigrated to the Netherlands beginning in the mid-20th century. The pepper is named after a legendary entertainer from Paramaribo, Suriname's capital, and carries strong cultural significance in Surinamese cooking, where it is used to season traditional dishes such as pom (tayer root casserole) and various rice preparations. Morphologically, Madame Jeanette produces elongated, lantern-shaped to irregular pendant fruits — 2–3 inches long, tapering to a point — that ripen from green to yellow (occasionally to orange or red in some strains). The shape is somewhat different from the round, wrinkled habanero and the bell-shaped Scotch bonnet, falling between those types and the elongated fatalii in form. The heat level is substantial (estimated 150,000–300,000 Scoville units) with the characteristic fruity, floral habanero-type aroma of C. chinense — sweet, tropical, and intensely fragrant. The flavor that accompanies the heat is distinctly fruity and aromatic with apricot-like qualities that distinguish C. chinense from the more neutral heat of cayenne. In zone 9, Madame Jeanette performs exceptionally well — the heat and humidity that challenge cool-season crops are ideal conditions for this tropical species, which can produce abundant fruit through summer and fall.

subcategory: South American tropical climbing leafy vegetable
plant_note: Plant aerial tubers or root divisions in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, moderately moist soil in zone 9–12, or as an annual in zone 6–8 after last frost; Madeira Vine (Mignonette Vine) is a fast-growing tropical perennial climber from South America — cultivated for its edible, fleshy, heart-shaped leaves (rich in vitamins and minerals, cooked like spinach) and small, warty aerial tubers — with fragrant white flower spikes and remarkable speed of growth in warm conditions.
directions: Plant Anredera cordifolia tubers or divisions in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide a trellis, fence, or other support as it is a vigorous climber; water regularly during active growth; harvest young, tender leaves as needed throughout the warm season; contain carefully as the aerial tubers can spread and the plant is invasive in warm climates. Madeira Vine is native to tropical South America and has spread as a culinary crop throughout Asia, where the leaves are eaten as a nutritious cooked green vegetable in the same manner as spinach or Malabar spinach — particularly popular in the Philippines (alugbati companion), Taiwan, and Indonesia. The succulent, heart-shaped leaves are harvested continuously from the vigorous vines and cooked briefly in stir-fries, soups, and wilted salads; they have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to New Zealand spinach. The plant produces numerous small, warty aerial tubers along the stems as well as underground tubers, all of which are edible cooked. WARNING: Madeira Vine is classified as a serious environmental weed in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, and some US states; never plant near natural areas, and dispose of all plant material including tiny aerial tubers carefully, as even small fragments can establish new plants. Grow in containers or in contained raised beds in frost-free areas.

common_name: Magda Squash (Lebanese Cousa-Type Summer Squash, Superior Nutty-Sweet Flavor)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Magda is a bush-type squash (no trailing vines) that produces compact, upright plants suitable for small gardens and raised beds. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and August for fall. Harvest Magda squash at 3–4 inches for best flavor — the nutty, sweet quality that distinguishes cousa-type squash from standard zucchini is most pronounced at this young harvest stage. Slightly larger fruits (4–6 inches) are good for stuffing; overripe fruits become bland and seedy. The pale, almost celery-green skin of Magda is a useful visual cue for harvest maturity — harvest when skin is pale and slightly waxy. In hot Gulf Coast summers, squash plants typically decline after 6–8 weeks; replanting in August extends the season through fall.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches for best flavor; up to 6 inches for stuffing. Magda is a cousa-type Lebanese summer squash — a form of summer squash with a fundamentally different eating character from the Italian zucchini types (such as Black Beauty, Costata Romanesco) that dominate American garden squash production. The cousa squash group, originating in the Middle East and Mediterranean, produces fruits that are pale sage-green to celery-green, cylindrical to club-shaped with a distinctively bulging blossom end, and with a pale, waxy skin surface that is noticeably different in appearance and texture from the darker, shinier skin of Italian zucchini types. The defining characteristic of cousa squash flavor — and the reason Magda has a devoted following among cooks — is a nutty, creamy sweetness distinctly different from the mild, slightly vegetal flavor of standard zucchini. Cousa squash flesh has a firmer, drier texture and more pronounced sweetness than Italian types, making it the preferred squash for Middle Eastern preparations: the primary culinary use of cousa squash in Lebanese, Syrian, and Egyptian cooking is kousa mahshi (literally 'stuffed squash') — the small fruits cored and filled with a spiced meat and rice mixture before being simmered in tomato sauce, a preparation where the firmer flesh and nutty flavor of the cousa type are essential to the dish's character. Magda is an F1 hybrid cousa-type that produces prolifically with good uniformity, adapts well to North American growing conditions, and provides the cousa flavor character more reliably than open-pollinated Middle Eastern varieties.

common_name: Magic Molly Potato (Deep Purple High-Anthocyanin Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in cool soil; Magic Molly is a late-season, high-anthocyanin purple potato. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10-12 inches apart, 3-4 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling twice as plants grow to boost yield and prevent tuber greening. Magic Molly is a striking purple potato with deep violet-black skin and vivid, uniform purple flesh throughout, prized for its exceptionally high anthocyanin content, dense, moist texture, and rich, earthy flavor that some describe as slightly nutty. Unlike some older blue and purple varieties, Magic Molly holds its intense color well through cooking, making mashed potatoes a striking lavender-purple and roasted wedges deep violet inside. The medium-sized, round-to-oval tubers form in good numbers per plant, and the variety performs reliably across a range of climates. Harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or wait until vines die back for full-sized, better-storing tubers.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes for harvest the following summer.
directions: Plant this Porcelain-type hardneck garlic in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, so cloves establish roots before winter. Separate the bulbs into individual cloves just before planting and set them pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 to 8 inches apart, then mulch heavily. Each bulb yields 4 to 7 jumbo cloves with an assertive flavor. In early summer, snap off the curling scapes to direct energy into the bulbs, and harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy spot.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow this AAS-winning purple pole bean once the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep at the base of a tall trellis or pole. The vigorous climbing vines produce striking 5 to 6 inch pods with rich purple skins and tender green interiors that offer sweet, crisp flavor. The purple color also makes the pods easy to spot at harvest. Pick regularly to keep the vines productive, and provide full sun with consistent moisture during flowering and pod set.

plant_note: Sow direct or transplant 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; in tropical zones 10–11, sow year-round — Malabar spinach thrives in the heat and humidity that makes true spinach bolt immediately.
directions: Sow direct or start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting, placing seeds in warm soil after last frost and providing a trellis, fence, or other support — Malabar spinach is a vigorous twining vine that can climb 10 feet or more in a single season. Basella alba is an excellent warm-season substitute for true spinach in hot, humid climates where conventional spinach bolts; the thick, fleshy, glossy leaves have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture when cooked and hold up better than spinach in stir-fries, soups, and curries, and the young leaves are pleasant eaten raw. It grows rapidly in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, fertile soil and high humidity, making it ideal for gulf-coast and tropical gardens. Harvest by snipping young stem tips every 1–2 weeks to encourage bushy regrowth; the plant is killed by the first frost but self-seeds freely in frost-free zones.

common_name: Malaga Violet Radish (French Purple-Skinned Spring Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Malaga Violet is a French heirloom radish with striking violet-purple skin, white flesh, and a slightly milder flavor than many spring radishes.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Malaga Violet is a classic French heirloom radish valued for its striking, uniform violet-purple skin over crisp white flesh, a distinctive color that stands out clearly from the more common all-red or bicolor spring radishes. The round to slightly oval roots have a clean, mild, only lightly peppery flavor, and the purple skin holds its color well even as the radish sizes up, unlike some varieties that fade. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, since radishes left too long in the ground become pithy and hollow; succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.

plant_note: Plant cormels (side shoots from the main corm) or divide corms in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich, fertile, deep soil in partial shade after frost; malanga requires a long, warm growing season (8–10 months) and will not mature tubers properly if planted too late or harvested too early.
directions: Plant cormels or divide corms in moist, humus-rich, fertile, deep soil in partial shade; malanga (yautia, cocoyam, tannia, new cocoyam) is a tropical American root crop closely related to taro (Colocasia esculenta) and widely cultivated throughout the Caribbean, Central and South America, and tropical Africa as a major starchy staple food. The underground corms and cormels are large, starchy, and nutritious — boiled, baked, fried, or mashed in a broad range of Caribbean and Latin American dishes including Cuban malanga fritters (frituras de malanga), pasteles, soups (sancoche), and as a potato substitute. Unlike true taro, malanga corms are generally considered easier to digest and are less irritating to people with taro sensitivities. The above-ground plant is ornamental in itself — the large, arrowhead-shaped, deep-green leaves on tall, mottled petioles create an impressive tropical foliage display while the roots develop. It grows well in partial shade and moist, fertile, organically rich soil. Harvest corms 8–10 months after planting when the lower leaves begin to turn yellow. An important crop in Caribbean communities and a worthwhile tropical edible for zone 9–12 food gardens.

plant_note: Plant corms or corm pieces with at least one eye, 4–6 inches deep, after soil warms to 65°F and all frost danger is past. Keeps producing side corms for subsequent harvests.
directions: Plant corms in fertile, loose, consistently moist but well-drained soil in partial shade; malanga grows naturally in Caribbean and South American forest edges and is more tolerant of shade than taro. The arrow-shaped leaves are ornamental as well as edible (properly cooked), and the large starchy corms have a nuttier, creamier flavor than taro. All parts must be thoroughly cooked before eating as raw malanga contains calcium oxalate crystals. Harvest corms when leaves begin to yellow and die back, typically 7–9 months after planting; the central corm and surrounding cormels can all be harvested. In zone 9 store unharvested corms with heavy mulch over winter or dig and store indoors above 50°F.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Direct sow this heirloom snow pea in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, since peas prefer cool conditions. The vigorous vines reach 5 to 6 feet tall and benefit from a trellis or netting to keep pods clean and easy to pick. Harvest the large, sweet, tender flat pods before the peas swell for the best flavor in stir-fries and fresh eating. Keep the soil evenly moist during flowering and pod development, and pick frequently to prolong the harvest.

plant_note: Sow in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost; a tall climber to 4–5 feet requiring netting or trellis support; harvest young pods before seeds begin to swell for best eating quality.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, fertile soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost, providing 4–5 feet of netting or trellis support; Mammoth Melting Sugar is the most widely grown heirloom snow pea, an heirloom variety documented since at least the early 1900s producing large (4–6 inch), flat, tender pods with a delicate, melt-in-the-mouth texture when harvested young and cooked lightly in stir-fries or eaten raw. The pods are stringless when young and the standard against which other snow peas are judged for tenderness and flavor. Harvest when pods are 3–4 inches long and absolutely flat with no seed bulge visible for the premium eating experience.

scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Mammoth Red Rock'
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start August and transplant September–October for a December–March harvest. Mammoth Red Rock is a late-season storage type that needs the full fall-to-winter growing period to develop its characteristic large, dense heads — rushing it with too-late planting produces undersized heads. In zone 9 the purple-red color deepens and intensifies after frost, which converts some starches to sugars and improves flavor.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Mammoth Red Rock is a large, late-season red cabbage heirloom that forms very dense, dark red-purple heads of 8–10 pounds — among the largest and densest of red cabbage types. The firm, tightly-packed heads have a robust, slightly peppery flavor that mellows to rich sweetness after frost exposure and is perfect for braised red cabbage with apples and vinegar (the classic Scandinavian and German preparation), coleslaw, sauerkraut, and long-storage use. Red cabbage keeps far longer than green cabbage — 3–4 months in cold storage at near-freezing temperatures — making Mammoth Red Rock particularly valuable for homesteaders and home food preservation. The deeply saturated red-purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that are natural pH indicators, turning more blue-purple in alkaline cooking water and more red in acidic conditions (add vinegar to fix the red color when braising). In zone 9 Mammoth Red Rock is a fall-planted crop that matures through the winter months.

common_name: Mammoth Sandwich Island Salsify (Vegetable Oyster Edible Root, Biennial Cool-Season Novelty)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (zone 9: August–September) in deep, loose soil; salsify has a long taproot that requires 12+ inches of loosened, stone-free soil. In zone 9, sow August–September for harvest December through March — the roots improve in flavor after cold temperatures sweeten them. Salsify is a long-season crop (120–150 days) requiring a full cool season to develop; the roots can be left in the ground through winter and dug as needed since they keep best in the ground. Fresh seed germination is much higher than old seed — use seed from the current year when possible.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in deeply loosened soil; thin to 3–4 inches. Do not transplant — the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. Harvest roots at 1 inch diameter or larger by carefully loosening the soil with a fork. Mammoth Sandwich Island Salsify is the standard American garden salsify — a biennial root vegetable in the daisy family grown as an annual for its long, tapering, white-skinned edible root. Salsify occupies an unusual position in the vegetable world: it is one of a handful of vegetables whose flavor genuinely resembles a different food — in this case, oysters. The cooked root has a subtle, oceanic, slightly mineral quality reminiscent of mild oysters, earning salsify its traditional common name 'Vegetable Oyster' and giving it appeal in preparations that highlight this unusual flavor character. Salsify was widely grown in American kitchen gardens in the 18th and 19th centuries when root vegetables formed a much larger portion of the winter diet than today, and Mammoth Sandwich Island was the primary named variety in this period. The roots are peeled (the skin oxidizes brown immediately, like artichokes — drop into acidulated water) and boiled, roasted, or prepared like other root vegetables. In zone 9, salsify provides a distinctive cool-season root that few gardeners grow, offering variety from the more standard parsnip, turnip, and carrot roots.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 both a spring and a fall planting are productive — Manalucie's resistance to gray leaf spot makes it particularly reliable in the high-humidity conditions of Gulf Coast summers where this disease devastates susceptible varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Manalucie was developed by the University of Florida in the 1950s and named for the Manalucie experimental farm in Homestead, Florida — one of several important tomato varieties developed by UF plant breeders for subtropical Florida conditions. An indeterminate variety producing large, red, globe-shaped fruits (8–12 oz) with solid flesh, good flavor, and outstanding resistance to gray leaf spot (Stemphylium solani), a fungal disease that is especially destructive in Florida and humid Gulf Coast conditions but for which most tomato varieties have no resistance. Manalucie was for decades the standard large beefsteak-type tomato for Florida home gardens because of this specific disease resistance. It remains valuable today for any gardener in zone 8b–11 who has struggled with leaf spot diseases in tomatoes.

scientific_name: Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris var. crassa
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in a deep, loose seedbed; mangel-wurzel produces very large roots (5–20 lbs) requiring deep, stone-free soil to develop properly; widely adapted to poor soils and drought conditions.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in deeply worked, loose, fertile to moderately fertile soil after last frost; mangel-wurzel is a large-rooted beet developed in Europe for winter livestock feed and human food in times of scarcity, producing enormous roots (up to 20 lbs) with reddish-yellow or white flesh that stores through winter in a root cellar. Young leaves are edible as greens, and the roots (when young, under 3 lbs) can be cooked and eaten like regular beets with a slightly coarser, starchier flavor. Of growing interest to market gardeners, homesteaders, and traditional food preservers for its extraordinary storage qualities and very high yields per square foot.

plant_note: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall crop; this winter radish needs cool, shortening days to size up.
directions: Sow this Chinese beauty-heart radish in summer or early fall, as it needs cool weather and shortening days to develop its large, mild roots. Direct sow a half inch deep and thin seedlings to 3 to 4 inches apart to give the 3 inch round roots room to swell, some reaching up to a pound. The greenish-white exterior hides a vivid fuchsia interior that is crisp and mildly sweet. Keep the soil evenly moist for tender roots and harvest before hard freezes.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost due to the long germination and growing period; manzano peppers prefer cooler temperatures than other peppers (60–70°F ideal) and may not set fruit well in very hot summer climates. They perform best in the mild coastal climates of California and the Pacific Northwest.
directions: Start indoors early and transplant after all frost danger has passed; Capsicum pubescens is a unique pepper species easily identified by its distinctive purple flowers, hairy leaves and stems, and black seeds — features shared by no other cultivated Capsicum. The apple-shaped (manzano = apple in Spanish) fruits ripen from green to red, orange, or yellow and contain extremely hot flesh (100,000–200,000 SHU) with a thick, fruity wall — quite different from the thin, papery walls of most hot peppers. In Peru and Bolivia, rocoto is used whole to make rocoto relleno (stuffed pepper), as the thick walls hold up to cooking. Unlike other Capsicum species, it tolerates light frost and can survive as a perennial in mild climates. The black seeds are distinctive in culinary use.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant into warm soil after frost with warm nights.
directions: This classic Italian heirloom produces long, slender six-to-eight-inch peppers with thin skin, tender flesh, and sweet mild flavor, excellent roasted or grilled. Start seeds indoors about eight weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm. Support the plants as the heavy fruits develop. Harvest green for a milder taste, or let the peppers ripen to deep red for their fullest sweetness.

common_name: Marconi Red Sweet Pepper (Italian Frying Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Marconi Red is a traditional Italian sweet frying pepper producing long (6–8 inch), slender, deeply ribbed, bright red fruits with thin walls and exceptional sweet, rich flavor — outstanding for frying in olive oil, roasting, and sautéing, used throughout Italian cuisine where its sweetness intensifies dramatically with heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Marconi is productive and begins bearing early for a long sweet pepper; the fruits can be harvested green or left to ripen fully red for the sweetest, richest flavor. Marconi Red is an Italian heirloom sweet frying pepper producing long, tapering, deeply lobed, 6–8 inch fruits that ripen from green to brilliant red; unlike blocky bell peppers, Marconi has thin, tender walls with very sweet, rich, slightly smoky pepper flavor that intensifies dramatically when fried in olive oil or roasted over a flame. Used throughout Italian and Mediterranean cooking as the classic 'frying pepper' for peperonata, antipasto, and pan-fried pepper dishes. The thin walls mean the fruits cook quickly and evenly without becoming tough; they also need minimal or no skin removal after roasting. Marconi is one of several related Italian frying pepper varieties (along with Corno di Toro and Jimmy Nardello) that together represent the tradition of Italian long sweet peppers, each with slightly different fruit shape, texture, and flavor profile. Very productive plants set fruit continuously through summer.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil has warmed; a compact bush type requiring no trellis; one of the earlier-maturing heirloom dry beans, well-suited to shorter seasons and successive plantings.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, spacing 4–6 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart; Marfax germinates quickly in warm soil and the compact bush plants require no staking or support. Marfax is a New England heirloom bush dry bean with attractive tan-and-brown mottled seeds that are smaller and rounder than kidney-type beans and have a creamy, buttery texture when cooked with a mild, nutty flavor excellent in baked beans, soups, and salads. Allow pods to fully mature and begin to yellow and rattle before harvesting; if a wet spell threatens, pull plants and hang them under cover to finish drying. Marfax stores well for a year or more when dried thoroughly and kept in an airtight container at room temperature.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Marglobe was a landmark All-America Selections winner in 1925 when it became the first widely adopted disease-resistant tomato, and for decades it was the standard commercial and home garden tomato across the United States.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes and stake plants early. Marglobe, introduced by the USDA in 1925 and awarded the first All-America Selections Gold Medal, was the standard American home and market tomato for much of the twentieth century; bred at the Arlington, Virginia USDA experiment station to resist Fusarium wilt and nailhead rust, it was the first widely successful disease-resistant tomato and allowed commercial tomato production to expand dramatically into areas where disease pressure had previously made growing difficult. The fruits are medium-sized (6–8 oz), round to slightly globe-shaped, smooth, bright red, and of solid, crack-resistant construction with a firm skin and classic tomato flavor; Marglobe Supreme is a later improved selection. Grows as an indeterminate vine; productive over a long season and well-suited to home gardens, canning, and fresh market.

common_name: Mariachi Pepper (AAS-Winning Mild Fruity Pepper with Multicolored Cluster Fruits)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mariachi is a prolific, compact pepper plant that produces clusters of 3-inch elongated fruits in colors that transition through ivory, yellow, and orange to red as they mature — multiple colors appear simultaneously on the plant, creating a colorful and ornamental appearance. In zone 9, start seeds in January–February and transplant March–April. Mariachi won the All-America Selections award in 2006 for its outstanding productivity, compact plant habit, and unique combination of mild fruity flavor with very low heat (500–600 SHU, far below the heat level of jalapeño) that makes it versatile for both fresh eating and cooking without the heat restriction of spicier varieties. The individual fruits are tapered and elongated (3–4 inches) with a slightly irregular shape; the mild heat level means even heat-averse eaters can enjoy Mariachi fresh.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at ivory-yellow for mild flavor or let ripen to red for maximum sweetness. Mariachi Pepper is a 2006 All-America Selections winner in the vegetable category, developed for its extraordinary visual display of multicolored fruits at different ripeness stages and its mildly spiced fruity flavor that makes it accessible to a wide range of palates. The name 'Mariachi' evokes the colorful, festive nature of the plant at peak production, when ivory, yellow, orange, and red fruits appear simultaneously in clusters on the same compact plant — the visual effect is immediately striking. Unlike standard bell pepper development where fruit transitions from green to fully ripe (green→red, green→yellow, etc.), Mariachi's fruit transition from ivory cream through progressive warm tones to red creates a more complex visual palette on the plant. The heat level of Mariachi is technically mild rather than sweet — at 500–600 SHU (Scoville Heat Units), it is substantially less hot than a jalapeño (2,500–8,000 SHU) but not as completely heat-free as a standard bell pepper. This small amount of heat adds a fruity warmth that enhances the flavor without causing heat discomfort for most people, making Mariachi useful in both sweet pepper contexts (fresh eating, salads) and mild chili contexts (salsas, roasting, stuffed preparations). The compact plant habit (24–30 inches) and prolific production of Mariachi's clusters make it an excellent candidate for container growing on patios and decks where the ornamental and culinary value combine effectively.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting; sow after last frost in warm soil; a traditional Italian heirloom from the Chioggia coastal region near Venice that stores exceptionally well into winter.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost, or start 3–4 weeks early indoors; plant in hills of 2–3 seeds per mound spaced 5–6 feet apart and thin to the strongest plant. Marina di Chioggia is a prized Italian heirloom winter squash from the Chioggia lagoon region, producing large 8–15 pound fruits with deeply ridged, blue-green skin covered in grey-green bumps and warts, and brilliant orange flesh that is dense, sweet, nutty, and nearly stringless — among the finest-flavored winter squashes. Cure fruits for 2 weeks in a warm, dry location after harvest to harden the skin and concentrate the sugars; properly cured fruits store for 4–6 months. The large vines need ample space; train them onto a trellis or let them sprawl in open ground.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and again August–September for fall. Cucumbers grow fastest with soil temperatures above 70°F and decline in extreme summer heat above 95°F; fall plantings often outperform spring in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow 3–4 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, then thin to the 2 strongest seedlings; trellis to maximize air circulation and fruit quality. Marketmore 76 is the Cornell University-developed standard slicing cucumber, bred for disease resistance to multiple fungal and viral pathogens including cucumber mosaic virus, scab, and powdery mildew — resistance that makes it especially valuable in humid Southern gardens. The smooth, dark-green fruits are 8–9 inches long with crisp, bitter-free flesh and very small seed cavity. Consistent, even watering is the most critical cultural practice — irregular moisture leads to bitter-tasting fruits. Harvest daily when fruits reach full size before they yellow.

plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; in zone 9, sow spring cucumbers in February–March and fall cucumbers in late July–August for the best production in the shoulder seasons before summer heat or fall cold limits the crop.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Marketmore 80 is a Cornell University slicing cucumber introduction that has become one of the most widely grown home garden cucumbers in America — producing straight, cylindrical, 8–9 inch, deep-green cucumbers with excellent fresh-eating flavor, thin skin, and small seed cavities. The significant disease resistance package — scab, cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), and angular leaf spot resistance — makes Marketmore 80 substantially more reliable in Gulf South gardens where summer humidity drives disease pressure. The 'Marketmore' series from Cornell represents a succession of improvements beginning with the original Marketmore in the 1960s; Marketmore 80 was selected for improved scab resistance and CMV tolerance critical for humid-climate production. The non-bitter fruits have classic cucumber flavor and good crispness. Plants are indeterminate vines that perform best on a trellis or fence where air circulation reduces disease and fruits hang straight. In zone 9, cucumbers are most productive in the spring season (March–May) and fall season (August–October) — summer heat causes reduced fruiting and increased disease. Succession sowing every 2–3 weeks through spring extends the harvest window. Harvest fruits at 6–9 inches for best flavor; over-mature cucumbers become bitter and seeds harden.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; arguably the most widely grown slicing cucumber in American home gardens, selected at Cornell University for disease resistance and consistent productivity.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost risk has passed, in hills of 3–4 seeds thinned to 2, or in rows 12 inches apart against a trellis; cucumbers germinate quickly in warm soil and grow fast — do not plant in cold ground. Marketmore 76 was developed at Cornell University and released in 1976 as an improvement on the original Marketmore line, and for decades it has been the benchmark slicing cucumber for home gardeners: a vigorous, disease-resistant vine producing straight, dark green, 8–9 inch fruits with thin, non-bitter skin and crisp, mild white flesh that stays productive over a long harvest window. The variety carries resistance to cucumber mosaic virus, angular leaf spot, powdery mildew, and scab. Pick fruits when uniformly dark green and firm, before any yellowing begins, to encourage continued production; cucumbers left on the vine too long signal the plant to stop setting new fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil in blocks of several short rows for good pollination.
directions: Direct sow this open-pollinated corn in warm soil, planting in blocks of at least four short rows rather than a single long row to ensure good wind pollination. The purple stalks and husks yield ears with white kernels and a traditional, slightly-less-sweet corn flavor, rich in anthocyanins. Give plants full sun, fertile soil, and steady moisture, especially during tasseling and ear fill. Harvest when the silks brown and the kernels are plump and milky for the best eating.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest October–February. Maruba Santoh can also be sown January–March for a spring crop before summer heat causes bolting. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide continuous harvest. The round, smooth leaves are harvested young at 3–4 inches for baby greens or at full size at 35–50 days. More heat-tolerant than most mustard types.
directions: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Maruba Santoh is a Japanese mustard green distinct from other Asian brassicas in having smooth, round, paddle-shaped leaves rather than the lobed or frilly leaves of most mustard types — the name 'maruba' means 'round leaf' in Japanese. The flavor is much milder than standard mustard greens, with a mild, slightly mustardy-sweet taste closer to bok choy or spinach, making it one of the most versatile and approachable cool-season greens for raw use in salads, stir-fries, soups, and braising. The smooth, non-frilly texture of the leaves holds dressings well without wilting and is preferred over crinkled-leaf types in delicate preparations. Maruba Santoh is faster-maturing than most brassicas and can produce a baby green harvest in 25–30 days from sowing. In zone 9 it is an excellent gap-filler for the fall and winter garden, tolerating light frosts and growing through the cool months without the bitterness that develops in other mustard greens exposed to heavy cold.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Marvel Stripe is a large bicolor heirloom from Oaxaca, Mexico with stunning golden-yellow fruits streaked with red and orange, mild tropical flavor, low acidity, and a reputation as one of the most striking visually dramatic heirloom tomatoes for the kitchen and market table.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and stake early as plants produce large, heavy fruit on indeterminate vines. Marvel Stripe is a large bicolor heirloom tomato of reported Mexican (Oaxacan) origin, producing very large (1–2 pound), oblate fruits with a striking golden-yellow exterior streaked and flamed with red and orange that is visually one of the most dramatic tomatoes in the garden or at a farmers market; when sliced, the interior shows a beautiful bicolor pattern of orange-gold and red. The flavor is mild, sweet, and tropical with notably low acidity — more fruity and candy-like than most large red tomatoes — making it particularly appealing to those who find red tomatoes too sharp. An outstanding choice for fresh slicing, caprese salads, and market display where visual drama matters.

common_name: Marvel of Four Seasons Butterhead Lettuce
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer; this adaptable variety grows across seasons.
directions: Sow this 1800s French butterhead directly in cool weather, barely covering the seed since it needs light to germinate. The tender, sweet leaves are green at the base and turn a beautiful cranberry-red, forming a crinkly rosette that resembles a flower. Keep plants consistently moist to preserve the coloring and prevent bitterness, and thin to about 8 to 10 inches apart. This adaptable variety performs across the seasons; give it afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting.

plant_note: Start seed indoors, transplant crowns after danger of frost; establish in a permanent bed.
directions: Mary Washington is a classic heirloom asparagus producing thick, straight green spears with a faint purple blush at the tips. Start seed indoors early and transplant seedlings or crowns into a deeply worked, well-drained permanent bed. Resist harvesting for the first two seasons so plants build strong root reserves, then cut spears for several weeks each spring. A single planting can yield reliably for fifteen years or more with annual mulching and feeding.

common_name: Masai Bush Bean (French Filet Bush Bean, AAS Winner)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F; Masai is a compact bush-type filet bean that stays productive over a longer window than most bush filet types before needing succession sowing.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 3-4 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest every 1-2 days once pods reach 4-5 inches and are still pencil-thin. Masai is an American Award of Merit-winning French filet bush bean, prized for combining the slender, tender, seedless-tasting pods typical of haricots verts with a compact, upright, easy-to-harvest bush habit that needs no trellising. The plants hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, making picking fast and keeping pods cleaner and less prone to soil-splash disease than sprawling bush types. Because filet beans mature quickly from flower to overgrown pod, harvest frequently to maintain the fine, tender texture; pods left even a day or two too long become coarser and more fibrous. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the season for a continuous harvest, since bush types produce a concentrated flush rather than the extended season of pole filet beans.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November or January–February. Mascara holds dark red color remarkably well in warm fall conditions that cause most red lettuces to revert toward green. Harvest outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest or pull entire plants at maturity.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Mascara is a deeply red-colored romaine-type lettuce producing upright, compact heads of dark wine-red to nearly black-red leaves with the crisp, crunchy texture and pronounced midrib of romaine — combining the structural quality of cos-type lettuces with an extreme depth of red pigmentation that rivals the darkest red looseleaf varieties. The dramatic, almost black-red color maintains well through the warm fall temperatures that cause most red lettuces to lighten; Mascara's consistent dark color regardless of temperature makes it valuable for market growers who need reliable color in variable fall conditions. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — very similar to standard romaine in taste despite the striking color difference. In mesclun and mixed salad plantings, the very dark Mascara leaves provide the strongest color contrast against green lettuces. The intense red-black coloring indicates very high anthocyanin content and corresponding antioxidant value.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow this compact white acorn squash after the soil warms, planting in hills spaced a couple of feet apart. Its restricted vines reach only about 45 inches, making it a good choice for smaller gardens, and each plant usually sets three to four fruits. Let the squash mature fully until the rind hardens, then harvest with a bit of stem attached and cure in a warm spot for storage. Provide full sun and steady moisture while the fruits are developing.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mashua is a short-day plant that initiates tubers only as days shorten in fall, making it best suited to zones with mild fall weather. Spring through fall is the growing season.
directions: Plant tubers in spring in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mashua is one of the 'lost crops of the Andes' — a climbing nasturtium relative that produces edible tubers at the base of its twining stems. It is the most productive of the Andean tuber crops (producing more calories per unit area than potato under appropriate conditions) and is naturally resistant to insects and some nematodes through bitter compounds in its tissues. The tubers have a distinctive sharp, peppery, mustard-like raw flavor that mellows dramatically when cooked (especially by frost exposure) to a sweet, starchy taste similar to parsnip. The attractive red and orange tuberous nasturtium flowers are edible and ornamental. Mashua is a short-day plant that forms tubers only when days shorten in fall — it performs best in zone 7–9 where frost is not severe but fall days are distinctly short.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Sow Matador spinach directly in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop, as spinach bolts quickly in heat. This variety offers good heat tolerance and holds a while before bolting, with smooth, dark green oval leaves suited to salads and cooking. Thin seedlings to 4 to 6 inches apart and keep the soil cool and evenly moist. Harvest baby leaves for salad mixes or let plants mature for cooked dishes like risotto.

common_name: Matina Tomato (German Heirloom Ultra-Early Small-Medium Red Salad Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Matina is one of the earliest-maturing indeterminate tomato varieties, producing ripe fruit as soon as 58–65 days from transplant — which in zone 9 (transplant February–March) can mean first ripe tomatoes as early as late April. This ultra-early production window before June heat arrives is Matina's primary advantage for zone 9 gardeners, where the spring tomato season is compressed. The variety is indeterminate and continues producing over a long season, but the earliest flush of fruit in late spring before heat stress is when Matina shows its greatest advantage over later-maturing types. Stake or cage plants at planting — though not as large as full-season indeterminate types, Matina reaches 3–4 feet and produces enough to require support.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage plants. Harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Matina is a German open-pollinated heirloom tomato from the Quedlinburg region of Saxony-Anhalt — a historically important German seed-saving and plant breeding center that preserved many traditional German vegetable varieties through the 20th century. Matina is among the most respected early tomatoes in European heirloom tomato tradition: a variety that consistently delivers ripe, flavorful tomatoes earlier in the season than almost any other indeterminate heirloom, making it a first-pick benchmark for season extension and early production. The fruits are small to medium (2–3 oz), round, smooth, and deep red at full ripeness — the classic small salad tomato form used throughout Germany and much of northern Europe for sliced tomatoes, salads, and fresh eating where the relatively small size provides good proportionality for whole slices. The flavor is exceptional for an ultra-early variety: sweet with a good acid balance and genuine tomato complexity that many early-maturing hybrid tomatoes lack. Early-ripening tomato varieties often sacrifice flavor to achieve early maturity; Matina demonstrates that early harvest and excellent flavor are compatible. In zone 9 gardens, Matina's ultra-early ripening makes it particularly practical: the variety delivers its best production before the June-July heat that suppresses fruit set in most tomato varieties, allowing harvest of the critical first tomatoes of the season before summer limits production.

common_name: Matt's Wild Cherry Tomato (Wild-Type Tiny Red Cherry)
scientific_name: Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme 'Matt's Wild Cherry'
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Matt's Wild Cherry is a variety collected from a wild or semi-wild population in the Hidalgo region of Mexico by Matt Liebman and introduced to the seed-saving community — it produces extremely small (pea-sized, 3/8–1/2 inch), intensely flavored red fruits with a bold, complex, acidic-sweet tomato flavor that recalls the taste of truly wild tomatoes and is unlike any commercial cherry tomato.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Matt's Wild Cherry is an extremely vigorous grower requiring sturdy staking; the pea-sized fruits are prone to cracking when ripe and should be harvested frequently; self-sows readily in mild climates — may reappear without replanting. Matt's Wild Cherry is a tomato variety with an interesting origin: it was collected by Matt Liebman from a wild or semi-wild population (possibly a naturalized escape) in the Hidalgo state of Mexico — an area near the center of origin of the domestic tomato — and introduced to North American seed-saving networks through the Seed Savers Exchange and similar organizations. The variety is classified as Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme, the wild cherry tomato type considered ancestral to all cultivated tomatoes, and it displays many wild-type characteristics: extremely small fruits (pea-sized, only 3/8 to 1/2 inch in diameter), prolific production (literally hundreds of fruits per plant), high seed-to-flesh ratio, thin skin prone to cracking, and exceptional flavor intensity that is quite different from cultivated cherry tomatoes. The flavor is extraordinarily complex for such small fruits — intensely tomato-ish, with high acidity balanced against good sweetness, and a deep, earthy, wild tomato character that reflects the original tomato flavor before centuries of breeding selected for larger, milder, less acidic fruits. For flavor enthusiasts and tomato purists, Matt's Wild Cherry offers a connection to the ancestral tomato that no commercial variety can provide.

plant_note: Plant root cuttings or divisions at or just after last frost; mauka is an Andean high-altitude perennial grown as an annual in temperate climates. It performs best in cool summers and will not thrive where summer heat is prolonged.
directions: Plant root sections or divisions in deep, well-drained, fertile soil after danger of hard frost has passed, setting them 3-4 inches deep in a site that receives full sun but stays cool through summer; mauka is a striking Andean perennial in the four-o'clock family (Nyctaginaceae), producing large, somewhat fleshy leaves on multi-branched stems above a cluster of thick, parsnip-like storage roots that can reach 12-18 inches in length under ideal conditions. The roots are not edible raw — they contain calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense oral irritation — but a traditional sun-curing process of several days substantially reduces the oxalate content and transforms the flavor to a mildly sweet, starchy quality reminiscent of parsnip. In the high Andes, mauka was once a staple crop of the pre-Columbian era but is now rare even in its native range; outside of botanical gardens and specialty growers in cool-climate gardens, it is extremely uncommon in cultivation and represents a living piece of agricultural heritage worth preserving. Harvest roots in autumn after the first frost kills the tops, and save a few root sections in cool, dry storage to replant the following spring.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow this golden zucchini after the soil warms, planting a couple of seeds per hill and thinning to the strongest plant. The long, straight fruits have a small seed cavity and firm, flavorful flesh, and their bright color makes them easy to spot for harvest. Pick fruits young at 6 to 8 inches, checking daily during peak season since summer squash grows fast. Give plants full sun, rich soil, and consistent moisture, and harvest frequently to keep the plant producing.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Direct sow this French filet bush bean after the soil warms, planting seeds an inch deep in full sun. The compact plants need no support, making them well suited to containers and small beds. Harvest the slender, stringless haricots verts at their peak between 6 and 8 inches long and about a quarter inch wide for the best texture and flavor. Pick every couple of days to keep the plants productive, and sow in succession for a steady supply through the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Medallion is compact and fast-maturing, making it excellent for succession planting every 2–3 weeks to maintain a continuous supply of small heads. In zone 9 the relatively quick maturity (45–55 days) allows multiple crops in the cool season window. Pull entire plants at harvest.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Medallion is a mini-romaine type lettuce producing compact, upright, 5–6 inch heads with tightly wrapped inner leaves and crisp, crunchy texture — the small-head format that has become standard in grocery produce departments and upscale food service. Mini-romaine heads like Medallion are harvested at one-quarter to one-third the size of full-sized romaine but with the same crunchy, mild, slightly sweet romaine flavor in a single-serving portion size. The compact heads also allow significantly closer spacing (6–8 inches) than full-sized romaine, making them more efficient in raised beds and small gardens. The crisp, upright inner leaves hold dressings exceptionally well for Caesar-style preparations, and the compact whole head can be split lengthwise and grilled or broiled as a dramatic presentation. Medallion has been widely adopted in restaurant supply chains precisely because the single-serving size reduces food waste compared to large head lettuces.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil is warm.
directions: Start this large jalapeno indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm for reliable germination. Transplant seedlings out only after nights stay above 55 degrees, spacing plants 18 to 24 inches apart in full sun. Megatron produces extra-large, thick-walled peppers up to 4.5 inches long and matures earlier than many jalapenos, giving an abundant crop ideal for stuffing. Provide consistent moisture and a light feeding once fruit sets, and harvest green or let peppers ripen red for a sweeter, hotter flavor.

subcategory: tropical seed and leaf edible tree
plant_note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; melinjo is a remarkable tropical tree distantly related to conifers rather than flowering plants — one of very few gymnosperms with edible seeds and leaves — the seeds are the basis of emping crackers (kerupuk melinjo), one of Indonesia's most distinctive traditional snack foods.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun to part shade; melinjo grows slowly and tolerates light shade when young. Gnetum gnemon (melinjo or paddy oat) is one of the most botanically unusual food plants in cultivation: it belongs to the Gnetaceae, a group of gymnosperms (cone-bearing plants related to conifers) rather than flowering plants — making it one of very few non-angiosperm food trees (alongside ginko, cycads, and pines). Despite looking superficially like a tropical flowering tree with broad, opposite, shiny green leaves and red seed pods, it is more closely related to conifers than to any fruit tree. In Indonesia and Malaysia, both the leaves and seeds of melinjo are important food ingredients.
