The young leaves are used in Javanese vegetable stews (sayur asem) and soups; the seeds, after roasting and pounding flat, are fried to make emping melinjo (also called emping crackers or gnemon chips) — thin, translucent, slightly bitter crackers that are a standard accompaniment to Indonesian nasi goreng, rijsttafel, and as a snack. The ripe red fruits (technically the sarcotesta, a fleshy seed coat rather than true fruit) are boiled and the starchy, mildly bitter seeds inside are peeled, pressed flat, and sun-dried before frying. CAUTION: High in purines — not recommended for gout sufferers.

plant_note: Start indoors early since celery is slow to germinate and needs a long season; transplant around last frost.
directions: Start Merengo celery indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, as the seed germinates slowly and needs a long season; barely cover the tiny seeds since they need light. Transplant hardened seedlings out around the last frost, spacing them 8 to 12 inches apart. Celery is a heavy feeder that demands consistently moist, rich soil to produce tender, flavorful stalks free of stringiness. Water generously and mulch to retain moisture, and harvest whole plants or individual outer stalks as needed.

common_name: Merveille des Quatre Saisons Lettuce (Marvel of Four Seasons, French Red Butterhead)
plant_note: Direct sow in early spring through early summer (succession sow every 3 weeks), or in late summer for fall harvest; Merveille des Quatre Saisons (French for 'Marvel of Four Seasons') is one of the most beautiful French butterhead heirlooms, producing bicolor heads of deep red-bronze outer leaves surrounding creamy pale-yellow inner leaves — a centerpiece of the classic French kitchen garden for more than a century.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 10–12 inches apart; Merveille des Quatre Saisons produces its most stunning red coloration when nights are cool (45–55°F); succession sow every 3 weeks for continuous harvest; harvest full heads by cutting at the base or harvest outer leaves as cut-and-come-again. Merveille des Quatre Saisons is a classic French butterhead heirloom lettuce with roots in the traditional potager (kitchen garden) of France, where it has been grown and selected for generations as both an ornamental and culinary variety of exceptional beauty. The heads are distinctly bicolor: the outer leaves are deep crimson to mahogany-bronze with the red intensifying dramatically in cold weather, while the inner leaves are creamy pale yellow-green — the contrast between brilliant red outer leaves and golden interior makes this one of the most photographed and admired lettuces in the garden. The 'quatre saisons' (four seasons) name reflects its traditional use throughout the growing year in French kitchen gardens. The flavor is excellent: sweet, buttery, and mild with the silky tenderness characteristic of well-grown butterhead types. The name and variety appear in French seed catalogs dating to at least the 1880s, making it among the oldest continuously cultivated lettuce varieties still widely available.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist, fertile soil 4 weeks before last spring frost or 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for the main autumn crop; mibuna is closely related to mizuna but bears smooth, narrow, strap-like leaves rather than mizuna's feathery, deeply lobed fronds — both are excellent cut-and-come-again greens.
directions: Direct sow in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun 4 weeks before last frost in spring or 8–10 weeks before first frost in fall; mibuna is a Japanese mustard green that produces smooth, narrow, rounded-tip, dark-green leaves distinctly different from the deeply lobed, feathery leaves of its close relative mizuna — the mild, slightly peppery, clean flavor of mibuna is excellent raw in salads and wilted in stir-fries, soups, and noodle dishes. It is harvested by cut-and-come-again method — cut outer leaves at 4–6 inches tall, leaving the center growing point intact, and plants regrow multiple times. Extremely cold-tolerant (withstands light frost) and among the fastest-maturing of all brassica greens. Bolt-resistant in cool conditions but seeds quickly in heat. Outstanding value as a winter salad green in zones 7–10 where it can be grown year-round with cold frame protection.

common_name: Midnight Snack Tomato (AAS-Winning Indigo Anthocyanin Cherry Tomato that Changes Color at Ripeness)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Midnight Snack is an indeterminate cherry tomato developed through the Oregon State University anthocyanin tomato breeding program and received All-America Selections recognition for its unique color-change ripeness indicator: the fruit develops deep blue-black (anthocyanin) coloring on the sun-exposed upper portions of the cherry while the shaded underside remains red, and when fully ripe the red area spreads to cover the underside — providing a clear ripeness signal without needing to squeeze or taste individual cherries. In zone 9, transplant March–April and provide cage or stake. The dark anthocyanin coloration in the sun-exposed skin has nutritional significance — anthocyanins (the same pigments in blueberries and blackcurrants) are potent antioxidants, and Midnight Snack's production is maximized in high-light conditions like zone 9's full sun. The cherry-red underside plus dark-blue top creates a striking bicolor appearance unlike any other cherry tomato.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake. Harvest when underside turns fully red to match upper blue-red skin. Midnight Snack Tomato is one of the most visually distinctive cherry tomato varieties available — a product of the Oregon State University tomato breeding program's work on anthocyanin accumulation in tomato fruit skin. Anthocyanins are a class of pigments responsible for blue, purple, and red colors in many plants (blueberries, purple cabbage, red grapes, black currants), and OSU researchers identified and bred for a trait that causes anthocyanins to accumulate in tomato fruit skin in response to light exposure. In Midnight Snack, the sun-exposed upper portion of each cherry develops a dramatic deep blue-black to dark indigo color while the shaded underside remains the conventional cherry-red of a ripe tomato — creating a two-toned fruit unlike any traditional tomato variety. When fully ripe, the red color from the underside gradually encompasses the fruit, providing a visual cue: as the red progresses upward to meet the darkening blue-black, the fruit is at peak ripeness. The flavor combines genuine sweetness with a fruity, complex quality that reflects the improved eating quality bred into OSU's anthocyanin lines beyond their visual novelty. Beyond appearance, the high anthocyanin content of Midnight Snack skin provides measurable antioxidant value — anthocyanins contribute to the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant capacity associated with blueberry and dark fruit consumption — with zone 9's intense sun exposure maximizing anthocyanin production in the fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow after soil warms and all frost has passed.
directions: Midori Giant is a compact heirloom edamame that sets large, plump pods packed with tender, protein-rich beans. Sow seed directly into warm soil in full sun once frost danger has passed, spacing plants a few inches apart in rows. The bushy plants stay tidy and are well suited to smaller gardens and raised beds. Harvest pods when they are bright green and full but before they yellow, then steam or freeze promptly.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; eggplant requires sustained warmth and benefits from bottom heat during germination. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a long growing season through October–November. Millionaire thrives in summer heat and continues setting fruit when cooler-season crops fail.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Millionaire is a Japanese-type hybrid eggplant producing long (8–10 inch), slender, deep purple-black fruits of exceptional quality and high yields — the name reflects its extraordinary productivity under good growing conditions. The thin, tender skin and nearly seedless, non-bitter flesh make it ideal for slicing, stir-frying, and grilling without peeling or salting. It is a high-yield variety developed in Japan and widely grown in zone 9 commercial and home gardens for the Southern Asian food market. The plants are vigorous and productive from summer through fall, with fruit set continuing reliably even in the peak heat of Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when skin is deep purple and glossy at 6–8 inches — fruits become seedy and bitter if allowed to grow to full size.

plant_note: Direct-sow in fall (or spring in cool climates) in almost any soil in shade to part shade; miner's lettuce germinates best in cool, even cold soil and will germinate through winter in mild climates. It self-sows prolifically once established, creating a permanent volunteer colony that reappears each autumn without replanting. In zone 9, fall through spring is the prime growing window.
directions: Direct-sow in fall in moist, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; miner's lettuce is a western North American native cool-season annual producing the most distinctive leaf form of any salad green — later-produced stem leaves are perfectly round, like a disc, with the stem growing through the center of the leaf, giving the appearance of a small lily-pad with the flower stalk emerging from the middle. Earlier leaves are long-stalked and spade-shaped. The plant was a critical winter and spring food source for California Native Americans and was later eaten by gold rush miners (hence the name) to prevent scurvy. The flavor is mild and succulent, similar to spinach or purslane, and the entire plant is edible raw or cooked — leaves, stems, and small white flowers. It thrives in shade where most vegetables fail, making it invaluable for shaded vegetable gardens. In zone 8–10, it grows abundantly through fall, winter, and spring and dies back in summer heat. Self-sows reliably to maintain a self-perpetuating colony that requires no maintenance.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Start this compact mini bell pepper indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm for reliable germination. The plant stays a tidy 24 inches tall, making it well suited to containers and small spaces. Transplant out after nights warm and space plants 12 to 18 inches apart in full sun. Each little pepper is about 1.5 inches with smooth, thick, juicy flesh; harvest them fully red for peak sweetness, and pick regularly to encourage more fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant only after nights stay warm.
directions: This rare Peruvian heirloom produces petite creamy-white pods roughly three-quarters to two inches long with intense, fruity habanero heat. Start seed indoors under warm conditions well before your last frost, as germination is slow and needs consistent warmth. Transplant into full sun once nights are reliably warm, and the ornamental, productive plants thrive in containers. Wear gloves when handling the ripe pods, which are excellent in salsas and hot sauces.

plant_note: Direct sow thickly in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; minutina germinates rapidly in cool conditions and is one of the most cold-tolerant salad greens available. Make successive sowings every 3 weeks from late winter through early spring, then again from late summer through fall.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; minutina (erba stella, or 'star grass') is one of the most unusual and sought-after Italian salad greens, producing rosettes of narrow, deeply toothed, antler-like leaves that have a pleasantly mild, slightly nutty to salty flavor and a satisfying crunch — a standout texture in any mixed salad. Unlike most salad greens, minutina is very tolerant of light frost and can be harvested almost year-round in mild climates; in the Southeast it is a fall-through-spring crop that withstands temperatures down to the mid-20s°F. The leaves are cut at the base and the plant regrows from the crown for multiple harvests. It tolerates partial shade better than most salad crops, making it productive in spots that receive only 3–4 hours of direct sun. Slow to bolt even in cool, bright conditions. Outstanding in the cut-and-come-again salad garden.

plant_note: Plant the entire fruit (not just the seed inside) sideways in a hole with the narrow tip pointed slightly upward and the stem end just below the soil surface; the whole fruit germinates and sprouts a single vine.
directions: Plant the entire fruit whole — chayote has a single large seed that cannot be separated from the flesh and the whole fruit is the planting unit. Dig a hole 4 inches deep and set the fruit at an angle with the narrow stem end barely covered. Once sprouted, provide a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor; the vine grows 20–40 feet and is extremely productive in zones 9–11 where it overwinters and bears fruit in fall and again in early spring. In New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, a single vine can produce hundreds of mirlitons per season. Fruits are eaten at all stages: stuffed and baked when large, stir-fried or pickled when small. The tender young leaves and shoot tips are edible greens, and the large starchy tubers that develop on established plants are edible as well.

common_name: Misato Rose Radish (Beauty Heart Radish, Rose Heart Radish)
plant_note: Best as a fall crop — direct sow in late summer 10–6 weeks before first frost; Misato Rose is a Japanese winter radish with green or greenish-white exterior skin and a spectacular vivid rose to magenta-pink interior flesh — one of the most visually stunning root vegetables available, making it a centerpiece of any vegetable display and exceptionally attractive in slaws, salads, and pickles where the color impact is full.
directions: Direct sow in late summer or fall; thin to 4–6 inches for full root development; Misato Rose grows to 3–4 inches in diameter over 60–70 days — much longer than spring radishes; harvest before hard freeze; the vivid interior color intensifies in cool fall weather; slice thin to showcase the color in salads. Misato Rose is a traditional Japanese winter radish (daikon type) from the Misato region of Japan, where it has been grown for centuries as a specialty vegetable known for its extraordinary interior color. The exterior of the root is pale green to greenish-white — completely unremarkable from the outside — but when the root is cut crosswise, the interior reveals a brilliant ring of vivid rose to magenta-pink extending from the interior outward, with a paler white core and a narrow white zone just inside the green skin. The effect is striking: the pink-fleshed cross-section looks like a small decorative disc with a rose-colored center zone. The vivid pink color comes from betalain pigments similar to those in beets and watermelon radishes, and it intensifies dramatically in the cooler temperatures of fall growing. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — much milder than the small red spring radishes most American gardeners know, and excellent for slicing thin in Japanese-style pickles (where the pink color turns the pickling liquid a beautiful deep rose), for raw salads where the color provides visual drama, and for Korean-style seasoned vegetable preparations. Also called 'Beauty Heart Radish' in some markets.

common_name: Mississippi Cream Pea (Traditional Gulf South Small-Seeded Cream Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mississippi Cream peas can be planted in succession every 3–4 weeks from April through August for continuous summer production — they thrive in the summer heat that limits most other garden vegetables.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mississippi Cream is a traditional Gulf South cream pea variety — producing small to medium-sized, cream-white seeds with the mild, sweet, nutty flavor characteristic of cream peas that distinguishes them from the earthier, bolder flavor of blackeye peas and cowpeas. Mississippi Cream is a semi-bush type with good productivity in Gulf South conditions and excellent heat tolerance — continuing to produce through the summer heat of zone 9 when most cool-season vegetables have ended. As a cream pea type, Mississippi Cream has slightly smaller seeds and a sweeter, more delicate flavor than standard crowder or blackeye types — the creamier texture and milder flavor of cream peas generally makes them preferred for certain traditional preparations including fresh summer pea succotash, cream peas and okra, and fresh peas braised with ham or fatback. Southern peas as a group are the most important summer legume vegetable of Gulf Coast traditional gardens — providing fresh protein through the hottest months when other vegetables fail. The nitrogen-fixing root system enriches garden soil for subsequent crops. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage (well-filled hulls but still green) for fresh eating or continue to dry maturity for storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Mississippi Crowder is a vigorous bush variety with higher tolerance for clay soils than many southern pea types — particularly valued in heavy Gulf Coast soils.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any reasonably well-drained soil; Mississippi Crowder is a bush-type crowder pea with tightly packed seeds that turn light brown at maturity. It is a traditional Mississippi variety well-adapted to the heavy clay soils common along the Gulf Coast and Mississippi Delta, where it tolerates temporary waterlogging better than many other cowpea types. The crowder seeds develop a creamy texture when cooked with excellent flavor for fresh-shell eating, and they also dry well for storage as dried beans. The vigorous vines shade out weeds effectively once established, and the roots fix substantial nitrogen, improving soil for the following season.

common_name: Mississippi Purple Hull Pea (Deep South Garden Crowder Cowpea)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature is reliably above 65°F; Southern peas are extremely heat and drought-tolerant once established and require no special soil preparation. In zone 9, plant April–August — Southern peas can be succession-sown throughout the Gulf South summer for continuous harvest. Mississippi Purple Hull is a crowder-type pea with distinctive purple pods that turn green when shelled and cooked. Harvest at the green shell stage (pods are fat and round but before they begin to dry) for fresh eating, or allow to dry fully for storage. The purple pod color makes the harvest stage visually easy to determine.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in rows 24–30 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. No fertilizer needed on most soils — cowpeas fix nitrogen. Harvest at the green shell stage for the best fresh flavor. Mississippi Purple Hull Pea is a Southern pea (cowpea, Vigna unguiculata) — a warm-season legume that is one of the most historically important and widely grown vegetables of the American Gulf South and Deep South, where the hot summers that challenge many other vegetables are actually the conditions Southern peas thrive in. The name 'purple hull' describes the distinctive coloration of the pods at harvest: the pods are vivid purple-red, making the harvest stage visually unmistakable in the garden and distinguishing purple hull types from the silver/green pods of cream peas and the tan pods of blackeye peas. Mississippi Purple Hull is a crowder-type pea (the seeds are crowded tightly in the pod, creating the characteristic dimpled, round shape of the shelled peas) — crowder types are considered by many Gulf South cooks to have the richest, meatiest flavor of the Southern pea types, ideal for the slow-cooked preparations that are central to Gulf South foodways. Southern peas are nitrogen-fixing legumes that improve soil fertility while producing — one of the most productive and soil-improving summer crops for zone 8–10 gardens.

common_name: Mississippi Silver Southern Pea (Silver-Hull Crowder Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; Mississippi Silver is a semi-erect bush type Southern pea producing distinctive silver-tan, slightly inflated pods with a speckled cream-and-purple seed — one of the most productive and flavorful crowder-type Southern peas grown in Mississippi and the Gulf South, and a staple of traditional Southern summer gardens for many decades.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun, well-drained soil; Mississippi Silver can be succession-planted every 3–4 weeks from spring through late summer for continuous production; plants fix atmospheric nitrogen and require no supplemental fertilizer in average garden soil; harvest at the green-shell stage when pods are well-filled and slightly silvery-tan in color. Mississippi Silver is a traditional open-pollinated Southern pea variety that derives its name from the distinctive silvery-tan to pale buff color of its mature pods — a different visual marker from the purple-hull and black-eyed types more familiar to outside the South. The variety is classified as a crowder type because the seeds are tightly packed ('crowded') inside the pod, causing them to develop flat sides from pressing against each other — the classic crowder characteristic that gives the type its name. The seeds are cream-colored with purple or red-purple speckled markings that fade to a uniform tan when cooked, as with most field peas, and the flavor is the rich, earthy, savory character of Southern field peas that is quite different from garden peas or snap beans. Mississippi Silver is one of the most widely recommended varieties by Mississippi State University Extension and LSU AgCenter for home garden Southern pea production — consistently rated highly for both yield and eating quality in regional trials. Like all Southern peas (Vigna unguiculata), it thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South through summer months when most other vegetables have ended, making it one of the primary summer food crops of the region.

plant_note: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall crop, as daikon needs cool, shortening days.
directions: Sow this Japanese daikon in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since it is a winter radish that needs cool weather and shortening days to size up. Direct sow in loose, deeply worked soil so the long white roots can grow straight, and thin seedlings to 4 to 6 inches apart. Keep the soil evenly moist for tender, mild roots with a lightly spicy flavor. Harvest before hard freezes; use young roots shredded fresh, or pickle and cook mature roots in stir-fries and soups.

plant_note: Direct sow thickly in early spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; mizuna germinates rapidly and is ready for baby-leaf cutting in as few as 21 days. Make successive sowings every 2–3 weeks through cool weather for continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow in cool weather in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; mizuna is one of the most popular Japanese salad greens and one of the fastest, easiest cool-season crops available, producing deeply cut, feathery, pale green leaves with a mild, slightly peppery, refreshing flavor that is pleasantly tender when harvested young. It is one of the most cold tolerant of all the Asian brassicas and continues growing through light freezes, making it an outstanding fall and winter crop in zones 7–9. Begin harvesting as baby leaf at 21 days by cutting the outer leaves; the plant regrows for multiple harvests before bolting in warm weather. Bolt resistance is better than arugula, and the plant handles light shade well, making it productive in partly shaded plots. Red-leaved mizuna cultivars ('Red Kingdom', 'Mikado Red') add color to salad mixes. An outstanding addition to spring and fall salad mixes, stir-fries, and as a garnish in Japanese cuisine.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring; carrots resent transplanting so always sow in place.
directions: Direct sow this Nantes-type hybrid carrot in loose, stone-free soil, since carrots dislike transplanting and rocky ground causes forked roots. Sow shallowly and keep the surface evenly moist until the slow-germinating seeds sprout, then thin seedlings to about an inch apart. Mokum stays sweet even in warmer weather and its slim, nearly coreless roots are crisp whether pulled as baby carrots or grown to a full 6 to 8 inches. Provide steady moisture and full sun for smooth, snappy roots.

plant_note: Heat-loving green; thrives in the hottest part of summer.
directions: Also called Egyptian spinach or jute mallow, molokhia is a heat-loving green that thrives when other leafy crops bolt. Direct sow after the soil is thoroughly warm, since seedlings need heat and stall in cool weather. Pinch the growing tips to encourage bushy branching and a continuous supply of young leaves. Harvest the tender upper leaves and stems, which turn silky and thicken soups and stews when cooked. Keep it well watered through summer, and pick regularly to delay flowering.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production and again late July–August for fall. Momotaro requires staking or caging as an indeterminate vine and benefits from consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking in summer heat.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake; Momotaro is Japan's most celebrated fresh tomato — an indeterminate, pink-fruited hybrid with exceptionally low acidity and high sugar content that has dominated the Japanese fresh tomato market since Sakata Seed Company introduced it in 1985. The smooth, round, 6–8 ounce fruits have thin, tender skin, almost no gel around the seeds, and a dense, sweet, mild flesh that requires no sugar addition in cooked preparations and is prized for fresh eating. The plant produces steadily over a long season and shows better resistance to blossom-end rot than many large-fruited varieties. In zone 9 the flavor is best in spring and fall crops; the fruits produced through peak summer heat tend toward milder, less complex flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out several weeks before the last frost.
directions: Start Monastrell onions indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant the seedlings out several weeks before the last frost since onions are cold tolerant when young. This late-season variety forms uniform, slightly flattened red globes 3.5 to 4 inches across with strong sunscald resistance. Match the variety to your latitude, as onion bulbing is triggered by day length. Keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist, then stop watering once tops fall over and cure the bulbs for storage of up to six months.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Start this indeterminate heirloom indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply once nights warm, burying part of the stem to encourage strong roots. Moneymaker earned its name through uniform, reliably heavy yields of medium-sized, meaty, sweet fruits. Provide a tall stake or cage since the vines keep growing all season, and prune suckers to improve airflow. Water consistently at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot, and harvest fruits as they ripen to keep the plant producing.

plant_note: Sow in cool soil; germination fails above 75 F.
directions: This large French heirloom spinach produces enormous smooth leaves and is known for fast, heavy yields. Sow seed half an inch deep in cool soil as early as it can be worked, since heat prevents germination and triggers bolting. Thin to 6 inches and keep beds evenly moist and rich in nitrogen for lush leaves. Harvest whole plants or pick outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again supply. Sow again in late summer for a fall crop that sweetens with frost.

plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes for harvest the following summer.
directions: Plant this vigorous Porcelain-type hardneck garlic in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, so the cloves root before winter. Break the bulbs into individual cloves just before planting and set them pointed end up 2 inches deep and 6 to 8 inches apart, then mulch heavily for winter protection. Each bulb yields 4 to 7 large, pink-wrapped cloves with a buttery, nutty, low-heat flavor. Remove the scapes in early summer to boost bulb size, and harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy place.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, deeply enriched soil; Montreal Muskmelon is a large, historic Canadian heirloom that dominated North American melon production from the 1860s through the 1920s and was once the most celebrated melon on the continent, shipped to New York and Boston in elegant straw-packed wooden crates as a luxury product.
directions: Sow in deeply enriched, well-drained hills after last frost; Montreal Muskmelon is a large, demanding variety that needs rich soil and ample space — traditional Montreal growers would excavate three-foot-deep planting holes and fill them with aged manure before planting. Montreal Muskmelon was the most celebrated North American melon from roughly 1850 to 1920, grown on the Island of Montreal (particularly in the Rivière-des-Prairies area) in intensively managed, manure-enriched beds and shipped to Montreal, New York, and Boston as a luxury fruit commanding premium prices; the Ferme Onésime Pépin operation shipped 11,000 melons daily at peak production. The large (10–15 lb), deeply ribbed, heavily netted fruits have orange flesh with a rich, intensely sweet, musky perfume that made it the yardstick by which all other melons were judged. It went extinct in commercial production by the 1940s but was revived from Seed Savers Exchange members; now being recultivated by slow food advocates in Montreal.

common_name: Moon and Stars Watermelon (Star-Speckled Heirloom Watermelon)
plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 8-10 feet of room to sprawl.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness. Moon and Stars is a striking American heirloom watermelon, first documented in the late 1800s and rescued from near-extinction in the 1980s after seed saver Merle Van Doren shared surviving seed with Kent Whealy of Seed Savers Exchange, reviving a variety that had all but vanished from commerce. Its dark green rind is scattered with one large yellow 'moon' spot and many smaller yellow 'star' speckles, a genetically distinctive and instantly recognizable pattern; the leaves also show smaller yellow speckling, making the plant ornamental even before fruiting. Flesh is sweet, deep red, and classic in flavor, and large fruits commonly reach 20-40 pounds. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners who want to preserve genetic and horticultural history alongside a tasty harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow or start indoors 3 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 direct sow February–April for summer harvest or August for fall. Moranga does best with a long, warm growing season and heavy, fertile soil; in zone 9 it benefits from fall planting to avoid peak summer heat during fruit development.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in deeply amended, fertile soil and thin to the strongest plant when 3 inches tall; Moranga is a large, flat-ribbed, orange-red Brazilian pumpkin (Cucurbita maxima) with deep orange, dense, sweet flesh used throughout Brazil as the traditional vessel for stuffed shrimp dishes (camarão na moranga) and as a soup tureen. The large fruits, averaging 15–25 pounds, are oval to flat with a warty, orange skin and extraordinarily thick, starchy-sweet flesh with minimal seed cavity. The Moranga type is closely related to Hubbard squash and has been cultivated in Brazil for centuries. The flesh makes exceptional purées, soups, and savory stuffings. Store cured fruits for 3–4 months in cool conditions.

common_name: Moringa (Drumstick Tree, Miracle Tree, Horseradish Tree)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds (pointed end down, 1 inch deep) or set stem cuttings directly in the ground after last frost in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; moringa grows extremely rapidly in warm conditions and should begin producing harvestable leaves within 2–3 months of planting.
directions: Direct sow or plant stem cuttings in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; moringa is extremely drought-tolerant once established and actually performs better in poor, dry soil than in rich, wet conditions. Moringa oleifera (moringa, drumstick tree, or miracle tree) is a North Indian native now cultivated throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide as one of the most nutritionally dense multipurpose food trees known — virtually all parts are edible and extraordinarily nutritious: the young leaves are exceptionally high in vitamins A, C, B6, calcium, iron, potassium, and protein and are eaten steamed, added to soups and curries, or dried and powdered as a nutritional supplement; the immature green seed pods (drumsticks) are used in curries; the mature seeds are pressed for edible, high-quality oil (moringa or ben oil); and the roots have a flavor similar to horseradish and are used as a condiment. In zone 9, moringa grows as a fast-growing perennial that may die back to the roots in hard freezes but resprouts vigorously in spring; in zone 10–12, it is a permanent tree. Cut back to 4–5 feet annually to maintain productive, harvestable leaf growth rather than letting it become a large tree.

plant_note: Direct sow or set transplants 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, Morris Heading can also be sown in late winter for a spring crop, but the fall-sown crop is sweetest since frost converts starches to sugars.
directions: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24–30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wider spacing than most collards is needed because Morris Heading forms a loose, cabbage-like head rather than a simple open rosette of leaves. This old Southern heirloom collard is distinctive among collard varieties for its semi-heading habit — the inner leaves cup and fold inward to form a loose head reminiscent of a savoy cabbage, while the outer leaves remain harvestable individually as with any collard. The smooth, tender, blue-green leaves have a sweeter, milder flavor than many open-leaf collard varieties, and the heading habit helps blanch and protect the inner leaves from cold and insect damage. Long grown in home gardens across the Carolinas and Georgia, it is well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, where fall-planted crops can be harvested over many months. Zone 6–10.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again July–August for fall. Mortgage Lifter is a pole type requiring a sturdy trellis 6 feet or taller. In zone 9 the vines produce prolifically through the long warm season and may survive mild winters as short-lived perennials, returning from the roots.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mortgage Lifter lima bean is an Appalachian heirloom from Virginia and West Virginia — an exceptionally productive, large-seeded pole lima with big, flat seeds that can reach half an inch across and fill the pod tightly with 3–5 massive seeds per pod. The sheer yield of these large limas made the variety valuable for subsistence gardeners who could shell, cook, and preserve enormous quantities of butter beans from a small planting, historically giving the variety its name. Fresh-shelled Mortgage Lifter limas have an exceptionally creamy, buttery, starchy flavor — richer than most commercial lima beans and similar in quality to the best Virginia butter beans. Like all limas, they thrive in Gulf Coast heat and continue producing through summer when most other legumes have failed. Harvest pods when plump and the seeds inside are full but still green for fresh eating; allow to fully dry on the vine for dry beans.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Start this classic indeterminate beefsteak indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply after frost danger passes, burying part of the stem for strong roots. The Halladay strain produces hefty 1 to 2 pound pink beefsteak fruits with crack-resistant skin on vigorous vines. Provide a sturdy tall cage or stake, prune suckers for airflow, and water consistently at the base to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot. Harvest the big fruits as they ripen to keep the plant setting more.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; this is an indeterminate variety that benefits from robust caging or staking to support the 1–2 pound fruits; excellent disease resistance for an heirloom.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, amended soil after frost risk passes; Mortgage Lifter is a legendary American heirloom developed by M.C. Byles of Logan, West Virginia in the 1930s by crossing four large tomato varieties over six years — the resulting tomatoes sold so well at 50 cents each that he paid off his mortgage in six years, giving the variety its unforgettable name. Fruits are very large (1–2 pounds), pink-red, with meaty flesh, few seeds, and a mild sweet flavor excellent for fresh eating and slicing. One of the most reliable and high-yielding large heirloom beefsteak types, with better disease tolerance than many heirlooms.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Mortgage Lifter is a famous indeterminate heirloom beefsteak known for enormous, meaty pink-red fruits that often top two pounds. The rich, mild, low-acid flavor makes it a favorite for slicing and sandwiches. Start seed indoors several weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the soil is warm, burying the stem deeply. Provide sturdy staking or caging, since the tall vines carry very heavy fruit and keep producing until frost.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed; this variety tolerates cool nights.
directions: Start this early Russian indeterminate indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply after frost danger passes. Bred in the early 1970s near Moscow, Moskvich withstands cool weather and is often the first tomato to ripen, offering round, deep-red fruits with rich flavor. Provide a tall stake or cage since the vines keep growing all season, and prune suckers for better airflow. Water consistently at the base and harvest as fruits color up to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; moso bamboo is a running bamboo requiring a bamboo root barrier (24-inch deep minimum for this large species) to prevent aggressive spreading. A single established grove can produce hundreds of edible shoots annually.
directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained loamy soil in full sun; moso bamboo is the most economically important bamboo in the world — the source of most commercial bamboo timber, flooring, furniture, textiles, and paper produced globally. It also produces the most prized bamboo shoots in Chinese cuisine, harvested in spring when they emerge from the ground. The new shoots can be harvested before they emerge from the soil (the pale, tender, underground form) or just as they break the surface. ALWAYS install a deep root barrier (24 inches minimum) before planting — moso is an aggressive running bamboo that can devastate surrounding plantings and structures without physical containment. The towering, green culms with their distinctive white waxy powder on new growth reach 40–90 feet tall, creating a dramatic grove effect reminiscent of Chinese mountain paintings. Once established, a well-managed grove produces an annual harvest of both timber culms and edible shoots.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; moth bean thrives in hot, dry conditions and should not be overwatered or grown in heavy, poorly drained soil.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hot, dry conditions; moth bean is one of the most drought-tolerant grain legumes in the world, capable of producing a crop on as little as 8 inches of annual rainfall. The small, cylindrical pods contain tiny tan or speckled seeds prized in South Asian cooking — sprouted or cooked whole in dal preparations, ground into flour for papadums, and used in the Rajasthani specialty moth ki dal. The spreading, leafy vines make an excellent cover crop for hot, arid, or sandy soils with the added benefit of nitrogen fixation. An outstanding plant for warm, dry climates where most legumes struggle; ideal for zone 9–11 summer gardens.

common_name: Moulin Rouge Beet (Uniform Cylindrical Hybrid Beet)
plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; succession sow through the cool season for a continuous harvest.
directions: Sow half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly shaped roots. Moulin Rouge is a modern hybrid cylindrical beet, similar in form to heirloom cylindrical types like Forono but bred for more uniform root shape, smoother skin, and reliable germination and sizing, making slicing and pickling more efficient with less trimming waste. The deep red, sweet, tender flesh holds its color well when cooked, and the long, straight roots make it a favorite for home canning and pickling where consistent slice size matters. Because the roots grow mostly upright rather than wide, plants can be spaced somewhat closer than round beet varieties for the same yield. The greens are also edible and good cooked as beet greens.

common_name: Mountain Fresh Plus Tomato (Southern Disease-Resistant Slicer)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Fresh Plus is a determinate hybrid well-suited to Southern spring and fall growing windows. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring harvest and August for fall harvest.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Mountain Fresh Plus is a North Carolina State University-bred determinate hybrid tomato from the Mountain series (which also includes Mountain Merit, Mountain Spring, and Mountain Pride), developed to combine excellent fruit quality with broad disease resistance for Southern and transitional-climate production. The large (8–12 oz), globe, bright red fruits have firm, crack-resistant skin, good internal color, and balanced sweet-acid flavor — a reliable all-purpose slicing tomato without the flavor complexity of heirlooms but with vastly superior disease resistance and shelf life. Disease resistance includes Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, gray leaf spot, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes (races 0, 1, 2, 3) — one of the broadest resistance packages available in a Southern-bred tomato. An excellent choice for zone 8–10 home gardens and market growers who need reliable, marketable tomatoes with broad disease protection in humid, challenging Southern conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Start this determinate slicer indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant deeply after frost danger passes, burying part of the stem. As a 2014 All-America Selections winner, Mountain Merit offers strong disease resistance including to Fusarium wilt and produces a beautiful red beefsteak on compact plants suited to containers. Its condensed harvest period is handy for preserving a large batch at once. Support the plants with a cage, water consistently at the base, and harvest fruits as they ripen.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic, loose soil; in zone 9 plant January–February for April–May harvest before summer heat sets in. Mountain Rose is a mid-season variety well-suited to zone 9's cool winter potato-growing window.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 2–3 inches deep 4–6 weeks before last frost, after curing cut surfaces for 1–2 days; Mountain Rose is a striking and delicious red-fleshed potato — the skin is red, but when cut, the flesh is also vivid rose-red to pink throughout, distinguishing it from standard red-skinned potatoes (like Red Pontiac) that have white flesh inside. The rosy-red flesh is high in anthocyanin antioxidants (the same pigments that color red cabbage, blueberries, and beets) and retains some color through cooking, making baked, mashed, and roasted Mountain Rose potatoes visually dramatic. The flavor is rich and earthy with good potato character; the texture is medium-moist and moderately waxy, excellent for baking, roasting, and boiling. Mountain Rose is a versatile all-purpose potato that performs well in both Southern cool-season production and in more northerly climates, and its beautiful color makes it outstanding for farmers' markets and gourmet home cooking. The red flesh fades somewhat during boiling or steaming but is better maintained when roasted or baked.

plant_note: Sow in warm soil after all danger of frost; needs a long, hot season.
directions: This heirloom yields large oblong melons of 20 to 35 pounds with sweet, juicy yellow flesh inside a dark green striped rind. Give each hill rich, well-drained soil and full sun, and allow long vines plenty of room to sprawl. Water steadily while fruit sets, then ease off as melons ripen to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit dries and the ground spot turns creamy.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; slow to germinate so give it warmth.
directions: These grape-sized fruits look like miniature watermelons but taste like tart cucumber, perfect for pickling or garnishing drinks. Vines can reach 10 feet, so provide a trellis for tidy growth and easy picking. Harvest fruits when firm and about the size of a grape, before they soften and turn sour. Plants tolerate heat well and produce steadily until frost.

common_name: Mr. Stripey Tomato (Large Bicolor Yellow-Red Striped Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Mr. Stripey is not the same as the British 'Tigerella' tomato — Tigerella is a smaller red-and-yellow striped variety; Mr. Stripey is a larger American heirloom bicolor with different size and flavor characteristics.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Mr. Stripey is a large bicolor heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (10–20 oz), somewhat flattened, irregularly shaped fruits with a yellow-to-golden exterior prominently striped and mottled with red or pink-red in an irregular, abstract pattern across the fruit surface. The bicolor exterior reveals a matching interior when sliced — yellow and red-tinted flesh arranged in an irregular pattern that makes each fruit slightly different in cross-section. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity — characteristic of yellow-dominant bicolor tomatoes — and with a melon-like, fruity quality that is outstanding in fresh eating. Mr. Stripey is an indeterminate heirloom with vigorous vines requiring sturdy support throughout the season. The very large size of the fruits makes them slow to mature — zone 9 gardeners should start seeds early (8 weeks before last frost) and plant out as early as safely possible to maximize the spring growing window before summer heat arrives. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, the thin skin requires careful handling. Not to be confused with the British variety 'Tigerella' which shares a similar name but is a much smaller (4–6 oz), earlier-maturing, red-with-yellow-striped variety of completely different character.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mt. Washington was selected and released for its ability to set fruit in cold conditions similar to those at the summit area of Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — one of the coldest and windiest spots in the eastern United States — making it among the earliest-producing cherry tomato varieties available and suitable for the most challenging cold-summer and short-season climates.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Mt. Washington is a compact, determinate-type cherry tomato that does not require staking; the plants concentrate production in a relatively tight window (good for canning or preserving in quantity); harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Mt. Washington is an ultra-early cherry tomato selected specifically for cold-tolerance and short-season performance, named for Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — famous for its extreme weather (the site held the world record for the highest surface wind speed ever recorded at 231 mph in April 1934) and the notoriously harsh conditions of its summit area. The variety produces small, round, red cherry tomatoes (about 1 inch) with good, sweet-tart flavor in 52–60 days from transplant — one of the fastest-maturing cherry tomatoes available. The compact, determinate plants (24–36 inches) are appropriate for container growing and produce a compressed flush of fruit ideal for gardeners who want to can or preserve cherry tomatoes in quantity rather than harvest over an extended season. Cold tolerance allows fruit set at nighttime temperatures approaching 45°F, making this variety one of a handful suitable for truly short growing seasons with cold nights throughout the summer.

common_name: Mucho Nacho Jalapeño Pepper (Extra-Large AAS Jalapeño)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections award-winning jalapeño variety producing exceptionally large fruits (4–5 inches long versus standard jalapeño's 2–3 inches) with thick, meaty walls and heat in the 10,000–12,000 SHU range — hotter than TAM Jalapeño but similar in shape, designed for nachos and poppers where large size matters.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Mucho Nacho is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast and Southern growing seasons. Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning jalapeño developed specifically to produce extra-large (4–5 inch long), thick-walled jalapeño fruits that are large enough for easy stuffing for jalapeño poppers and have enough surface area for maximum nacho topping use — the name directly references its intended use. The heat level (10,000–12,000 SHU) is somewhat hotter than many standard jalapeño varieties and significantly hotter than TAM Jalapeño, making it authentic jalapeño heat in a much larger package. The very thick walls (up to 1/4 inch) make Mucho Nacho excellent for grilling whole (the thick walls hold up without burning through) and for stuffing with cream cheese or other fillings. Ripens from dark green to red; can be harvested and used at the green stage (most common) or allowed to ripen red for a slightly different, sweeter flavor. High productivity and disease resistance make it one of the most reliable jalapeño varieties for home garden use.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring through late spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop; Muir is notably heat- and bolt-tolerant for a loose-leaf lettuce, extending the harvest window later into warm weather than most leaf types.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; thin to 6–10 inches and harvest as cut-and-come-again or as full heads. Muir is a French heirloom oakleaf-type loose-leaf lettuce developed as a heat-tolerant selection, producing a loose, upright rosette of thick, savoyed, chartreuse-green leaves with a distinctively crisp, succulent texture and mild, sweet flavor that holds up better than most leaf lettuces once temperatures start climbing. Its unusually thick, crinkled leaf texture also makes it more forgiving of the wilting summer sun than thinner-leafed varieties, and it is slower to turn bitter as it approaches bolting. A useful bridge variety for gardeners who want fresh salad greens into the early part of a Gulf South summer before switching to heat-adapted greens, in zone 3–10.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist soil or water, or plant container-grown specimens in moist, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade after frost; mukunuwenna roots readily from stem cuttings placed in moist soil or water and can be harvested repeatedly by tip-pruning, which also promotes bushy new growth for subsequent harvests.
directions: Root stem cuttings or direct-sow in moist, average to fertile soil in partial shade; mukunuwenna (sessile joyweed, dwarf copperleaf, alternanthera) is a pantropical low-growing perennial herb widely consumed as a leafy vegetable throughout South and Southeast Asia — the young shoots and leaves are a staple green vegetable in Sri Lanka (where it is a major ingredient in mallung, a coconut-based herb salad), and in Indian, Thai, and Vietnamese cooking. The mild, slightly crunchy leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked briefly in stir-fries, curries, and soups. The plant is exceptionally shade-tolerant for a warm-season leafy green, maintaining vigorous production in partial shade where spinach and lettuce would bolt in summer heat, making it a highly practical leafy green for Gulf Coast and tropical summer shade gardens. It grows along the margins of streams, ponds, and wet ditches in its natural habitat and tolerates wet, waterlogged soil conditions. Multiple harvests per season are obtained by tip-pruning. In zone 9–12 it persists as a perennial; elsewhere it is grown as a summer annual.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Mulato Isleno is a dried chile variety that requires the full summer season to develop and ripen; allow fruits to turn chocolate-brown on the plant before harvesting for drying. In zone 9 the long, warm growing season is ideal for this variety's development.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato Isleno is a poblano-type dried chile grown specifically for its distinctive chocolate-brown dried form rather than for fresh use — unlike the more common ancho (dried red poblano), the mulato is harvested at a later stage when fruits turn from green directly to dark brown, producing a darker, smokier, more complex dried chile with chocolate, coffee, and dried fruit undertones. It is one of the three chiles traditionally used in mole negro (with ancho and pasilla), contributing a smoky depth that neither ancho nor pasilla provides alone. Dry fully ripe, dark-brown fruits in a dehydrator or low oven for 2–4 hours until leathery and pliable. Plants are productive on fertile soil in zone 9 and tend to be tall with upright growth habit.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start January–February and transplant February–March. Mulato is a full-season pepper requiring 80–100 days to first mature fruit — start early for best zone 9 production before summer heat peaks.
directions: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato is a Mexican dried chile closely related to poblano but from a distinct gene pool (the seed color is tan, versus black for poblano/ancho) that produces heart-shaped, medium-large fruits, dark green turning dark brownish-black (rather than red) when fully ripe and dried. In dried form, mulato is one of the trio of chiles (together with ancho and pasilla) used in traditional Mexican mole negro sauce — its distinctive contribution is a dark, chocolate-tobacco, raisin-like complexity that makes mole negro deep and bittersweet. Heat level is mild to moderate (500–2,500 Scoville). Fresh mulato fruits are used in chiles rellenos and sauces; dried mulatos are rehydrated for mole and enchilada sauces. The plants are productive in zone 9's warm season and the fruits dry naturally on the plant in hot, dry conditions or can be dried in a dehydrator. An essential ingredient for serious Mexican cooking and home food preservers.

plant_note: Plant sets (small bulbs) in fall — September through November in zone 9 — for harvest the following spring. Multiplier onions form clusters of 4–12 small bulbs underground; the cluster is divided at harvest, with the largest bulbs eaten and the smallest saved for replanting. They can also be planted in late winter for a summer harvest.
directions: Plant small sets 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; multiplier onions are a perennial system that perpetuates itself through vegetative division rather than seed. One planted bulb will produce a cluster of 4–12 bulbs at harvest; sort the cluster at harvest, eating the largest and replanting the smallest to maintain the planting year after year. The flavor is milder and sweeter than common onions, and the green tops can be harvested as scallions throughout the growing season. In zone 9 they perform best planted in fall; in hot, dry summers the tops die down and the bulbs go dormant, much like garlic. This heirloom vegetable was once widely grown in kitchen gardens before commercial onions became cheap.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: Muncher is a burpless heirloom cucumber prized for mild, low-acid flavor and thin, tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest fruits young at four to six inches for crisp snacking, or let them size up to eight or nine inches for slicing. Direct sow in warm soil in full sun after frost, or start early indoors, and grow on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Pick regularly and keep the plants evenly watered to prevent bitterness.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil once frost has passed.
directions: This mini slicing cucumber produces tender, burpless, thin-skinned fruits with a crisp bite, best picked around 5 inches long. High yields come from steady moisture and full sun, so water consistently to avoid bitterness. Train vines on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive throughout the season.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills or rows after last frost; Munchkin pumpkin vines are shorter and more compact than full-sized pumpkin vines, making them suitable for smaller garden spaces. For fall decorative harvest, count back 100 days from desired harvest date. In zone 9, plant May–June for a September harvest. Each vine typically produces 8–15 miniature pumpkins; harvest when rind is hard and fully orange.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun; harvest when rind has hardened completely and is uniformly deep orange. Munchkin is a 1996 All-America Selections-winning miniature pumpkin that produces perfectly proportioned, small (4–5 inches in diameter, 3–5 oz) pumpkins with the classic Halloween pumpkin shape — deeply ridged, round, bright orange, with a proportionally large corky stem — in quantities of 8–15 per vine. The scale and perfect form of Munchkin pumpkins have made them the dominant decorative miniature pumpkin in the American market: they look like standard pumpkins shrunk to one-tenth their normal size, with all the visual appeal intact. Their most popular use is as tabletop decorations, door step arrangements, and centerpieces for autumn events; the small size and hard rind give them good postharvest longevity (4–8 weeks in cool conditions) for extended decorative use. Munchkin also has the distinction of being edible — the sweet, dense flesh makes excellent pumpkin puree, though the small size means significant work for a small yield — but most growers treat it purely as a decorative crop. Very productive and highly marketable at farm stands, farmers markets, and pumpkin patches where customers specifically seek miniature varieties. A top-selling item for autumn specialty crop producers.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil reaches 65°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; mung bean grows rapidly in warm conditions and is ready for harvest in 55–80 days — multiple successions can be planted from spring through early fall in zone 9 for continuous production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; inoculate with Rhizobium legume inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Vigna radiata (mung bean or green gram) is among the most widely consumed legumes in the world — a staple of Indian, Chinese, Southeast Asian, and Korean cuisines in its many forms: whole cooked beans in dal and soups, split (moong dal) for creamy lentil dishes, sprouted (bean sprouts) as a fresh vegetable, ground into flour for cheela pancakes, and processed into bean thread (glass) noodles. The bean is particularly nutritious — high in protein, folate, magnesium, and iron — and easier to digest than many other legumes, producing less flatulence. Mung beans are also the most common source of fresh bean sprouts: seeds germinate and develop edible sprouts in just 3–5 days at room temperature, making them one of the few vegetables that can be produced entirely indoors year-round. In the garden, mung bean grows as a fast-maturing, upright, bushy annual producing small, cylindrical black or brown pods with 8–15 seeds each, harvested when pods turn black-brown and dry.

plant_note: Soak seed overnight; often grown as sprouts or in trays with frequent rinsing.
directions: Soak mung beans overnight so they swell and sprout rapidly, then spread them in an even layer on a tray or in a sprouting jar. They germinate within a day or two and thrive in warmth, so keep them covered and rinse or mist frequently to prevent souring. If growing as tray microgreens, give them light once shoots appear to green them up slightly. Harvest the crunchy, protein-rich shoots after roughly a week, or eat earlier as classic bean sprouts.

plant_note: Sprout indoors year-round in a jar; no field planting needed.
directions: Mung beans are prized for quick, protein-rich sprouts used in stir-fries, egg rolls, and salads. Soak seeds overnight, then rinse and drain two to three times daily in a sprouting jar kept out of direct sun. Sprouts are ready to eat in four to seven days once the shoots are an inch or two long. Keep them moist but well-drained to prevent souring.

common_name: Murasaki Sweet Potato (Japanese Purple Sweet Potato)
plant_note: Plant slips 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Murasaki requires a full 95–110 days, so plant as early as possible in the South. It performs well in the Gulf Coast heat and produces excellent tubers with a slightly longer season than standard varieties.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; murasaki (purple in Japanese) sweet potato is a Japanese-origin variety producing long, slender tubers with striking dark purple skin and off-white to cream-colored flesh — a distinct and useful contrast to the Okinawan purple-flesh type, with a dry, chestnut-like sweetness and firm texture that holds up beautifully in roasting, frying, and sautéing where orange-flesh sweet potatoes would become too soft. The flavor is rich, mildly sweet, and nutty with a savory quality that makes it more versatile in non-sweet preparations than moist orange types. Widely grown in Japan and increasingly popular in the United States as interest in Asian sweet potato varieties grows; excellent for Japanese-style roasted sweet potatoes, tempura, and savory preparations that benefit from a firmer texture.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes; harvest the following summer.
directions: This porcelain hardneck cultivar produces very large bulbs with 4 to 6 big, easy-to-peel cloves and excellent cold tolerance. Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, mulch heavily, and let them overwinter. Snip the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into the bulbs. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure in a dry, airy spot for storage.

common_name: Musica Romano Pole Bean (Wide Flat Italian-Style Pole Bean with Exceptional Tenderness)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; Musica is a Dutch-bred flat Romano-type pole bean with unusually wide, flat pods (up to 1 inch wide) reaching 8–10 inches long. It requires a trellis or pole support to 6–7 feet. Unlike round-podded pole beans that become stringy and coarse as they size up, Musica maintains remarkable tenderness and sweet flavor well past the size at which most beans become tough — pods can be harvested at full size (9–10 inches) without significant loss of texture. This characteristic makes Musica one of the most forgiving pole beans for busy gardeners who cannot harvest daily. In zone 9, direct sow March–April after last frost for spring production and again August–September for fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide a sturdy trellis or poles to 7 feet and harvest pods when flat and full-length (8–10 inches) but before seeds develop prominently inside. Musica Romano Pole Bean is a Dutch commercial variety developed specifically to combine the flat Romano-style pod shape beloved in Italian cuisine with the productivity and extended harvest window of a modern pole bean. The flat pod shape — wide (nearly 1 inch across) with a slightly rectangular cross-section rather than round — is the defining characteristic of the Romano bean type, which originated in Italy and represents a fundamentally different pod morphology from the round, pencil-thin beans of French filet types or the oval cross-section of standard American snap beans. Romano types are prized for a distinctive beany, almost meaty flavor that is more pronounced than round-podded types; this flavor intensity comes partly from the thicker pod walls and slightly higher dry matter content of the flat pod structure. Musica improves on older Romano varieties in two key ways: pods remain tender and stringless at large sizes (a significant practical advantage, since older Romano types become stringy once pods exceed 6–7 inches), and the plant produces heavily over an extended harvest window rather than the concentrated burst typical of bush bean types. The vigorous climbing plant (to 7 feet) is highly productive in warm conditions and particularly well-suited to zone 9's long warm season, where it can continue producing through fall when given a midsummer break from heat. Steam or blanch briefly for the best texture; Musica also holds up well in longer-cooked dishes like minestrone where flat Romano beans contribute body without dissolving.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–June. Musquee de Provence requires a long, warm growing season — at least 110 days of warm weather. In zone 9 planting in April gives the fruit time to cure fully on the vine. As a Cucurbita moschata, it has better heat and humidity tolerance than Cucurbita maxima types. The large fruits (12–20+ lbs) benefit from being elevated on boards or straw to prevent rot where soil stays moist.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, rich, slightly acidic soil; Musquee de Provence (Musk of Provence) is a magnificent French heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region, producing large, deeply ridged, flat-round fruits with a muted tan to bronze-brown skin that develops rich russet-copper tones when fully mature. The deep orange-yellow flesh is exceptionally sweet, dense, and aromatic — the 'musquee' (musky) name refers to the intensely sweet, rich, slightly musky fragrance and flavor of the ripe flesh, considered among the finest-flavored of any large pumpkin. Fully matured fruits from this Cucurbita moschata variety develop complex flavor notes beyond ordinary pumpkin sweetness. The large, photogenic fruits (often 12–20 pounds) are classic French market pumpkins seen in Provençal farmers' markets in fall. In zone 9 the summer heat and humidity are well tolerated by this C. moschata type, which is more disease-resistant in warm climates than C. maxima varieties.

common_name: Musquée de Provence Pumpkin (Fairytale Pumpkin, Cheese Pumpkin)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Musquée de Provence is a large, sprawling Cucurbita moschata pumpkin requiring substantial space (15–20 feet vine length) and a long, warm growing season of 95–115 days, making it well-suited to the Gulf South's extended warm season.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thinned to 2) after last frost in warm, rich soil; Musquée de Provence is a spectacular heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region of southern France that produces deeply ribbed, flat-lobed, heavily textured fruits that turn from dark green to a rich tan-bronze at maturity, resembling giant rounds of aged cheese (it is often sold under the marketing name 'Fairytale Pumpkin' in the US). The large fruits (10–20 pounds, sometimes to 30 pounds) are as stunning ornamentally as they are culinarily valuable — the deep orange, dense, sweet flesh is comparable to butternut squash in flavor (Musquée de Provence is Cucurbita moschata, the same species as butternut) with excellent sweetness, minimal stringiness, and superb flavor when roasted, pureed into soups, or made into pie. The thick skin and hard rind give outstanding storage life (6–12 months in a cool, dry location), and the impressive size and dramatic appearance make the fruits valuable for both Thanksgiving decorations and serious cooking. Well-adapted to the heat and humidity of Gulf South summer production and a rewarding long-season crop in zone 8–11.

plant_note: Very winter-hardy; can stand in the ground for winter harvest.
directions: This hardy Scottish heirloom leek withstands hard freezes and can be harvested through winter in many climates. Start seed indoors early, then transplant seedlings into deep dibble holes so the shanks blanch white. Hill soil around the stems or drop plants into holes to lengthen the tender white portion. Keep well watered and side-dress with nitrogen midseason for thick shanks. Dig leeks as needed all winter, lifting the last before spring regrowth begins.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost; mustard greens are extremely fast-growing and can be harvested within 40 days of sowing. Fall crops are preferred in zone 7–10 where they continue producing through mild winters.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring, or 4–6 weeks before first fall frost for the preferred fall crop; mustard greens are a staple leafy vegetable of Asian and Southern US cuisines, prized for their pungent, peppery, mustardy flavor that ranges from mildly spicy to intensely sharp depending on variety. Young leaves are used raw in salads; mature leaves are braised, stir-fried, or cooked with salt pork and vinegar in Southern tradition. They bolt quickly in summer heat but tolerate light frosts, improving in flavor after cold exposure. In zone 7–10 fall-planted mustard greens can produce through winter; Southern flat-pod varieties like 'Florida Broadleaf' and Asian varieties like 'Mizuna' and 'Red Giant' are popular choices.

plant_note: Fast, spicy brassica microgreen; mucilaginous seed sown dry on moist trays.
directions: Sow mustard seed dry and dense on a moist tray, since it develops a gel coat when wet that makes presoaking messy. It sprouts fast, so keep the blackout period short and move it into bright light within a couple of days. Mist to keep the surface moist and provide airflow to keep the fast growth healthy. Harvest the zesty, peppery greens at the cotyledon stage in about a week for maximum heat and aroma.

plant_note: Sow direct from late summer through fall in any reasonably fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; mâche germinates best in cool soil and is one of the most cold-hardy salad greens, surviving hard freezes to 10°F.
directions: Sow direct from late summer through fall (or in early spring in cold climates) in any reasonably fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; thin to 4–6 inches apart and harvest the outer rosettes, or pull entire plants at 45–70 days. Valerianella locusta is the premier winter salad green for cold-hardy production; a small-rosette-forming annual with smooth, oval, soft, blue-green leaves and a distinctively mild, nutty, slightly sweet flavor quite unlike any other green — the taste that makes genuine French salade de mâche so sought-after in winter bistros. It is among the most cold-hardy of all salad crops, surviving temperatures to 10°F under light row cover or as low as 20°F with cold frames; in the Gulf South (zones 8–10) it can be harvested from October through April as a continuous cool-season salad. It self-seeds readily and often naturalizes in garden beds.

common_name: München Bier Radish (German Beer Garden White Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow in spring 2–6 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall harvest; München Bier (Munich Beer) is a large, round, white-skinned German radish cultivated specifically for the traditional Bavarian custom of serving thick radish slices with beer — large (tennis ball to baseball-sized) round roots with pure white skin and flesh, mild-to-moderate radish bite, and a dense, juicy texture ideal for the accordion-sliced 'Radi' presentation traditional in Bavarian beer gardens.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart (important for large root development); keep consistently moist to prevent cracking; harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for best flavor — overripe roots become pithy and hot. München Bier is a traditional Bavarian radish variety with an intimate connection to German beer garden culture: in Munich's famous outdoor beer gardens and throughout Bavaria, a 'Radi' (the Bavarian German word for radish) served alongside a Masskrug (liter) of beer is as traditional and culturally fixed as pretzels and sausages. The Bavarian Radi is always München Bier or a similar large, white, round variety — never the small red radishes of American experience — and it is served in a specific traditional way: the entire large root is scored with a spiral cut from top to bottom using a special tool (a Radihobel), accordioned apart to fan out into a long, beautiful spiral, rubbed with salt to draw out the juices, and eaten slice by slice as an accompaniment to beer. The flavor is mildly peppery and refreshing, with good crunch and juiciness, and the large size allows the elaborate spiral cutting presentation impossible with small radishes. München Bier is one of the few radish varieties specifically sized and textured for this presentation; it is also excellent sliced thick for salads, grated for German-style radish salads with vinegar and oil dressing, or pickled.

common_name: Nadia Eggplant (Heat-Tolerant Glossy Italian Hybrid Eggplant)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Nadia is a vigorous, heat-tolerant hybrid that sets fruit reliably even in the hottest part of a Gulf South summer, when many eggplant varieties slow production.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Nadia is a widely grown hybrid eggplant producing glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with tender, non-bitter flesh and few seeds, on a vigorous, high-yielding plant especially valued for continuing to set fruit through peak summer heat when many other eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, soft skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and tougher flesh. Regular harvesting every few days keeps the plant productive over a long season, and staking helps support the heavy fruit load on the branches.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in loose, deep, stone-free soil; Nantes-type carrots are virtually coreless and have a nearly cylindrical shape that requires deep loose soil — break up any compaction to 12 inches before sowing.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches when 2 inches tall; Nantes is the most widely grown home garden carrot type, originating in Nantes, France — producing 6–7 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical carrots with remarkably sweet, crisp, virtually coreless flesh and thin skin that doesn't require peeling. The standard against which other home garden carrots are judged for flavor and tenderness. Requires loose, deep, stone-free soil for best shape; rocky or compacted soils produce forked, stunted roots. Excellent raw, steamed, or roasted; also one of the best for juicing.

plant_note: For fall crop, direct sow 8–10 weeks before first frost; for spring, sow as soon as soil can be worked and harvest before summer heat triggers bolting.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to 12–18 in once seedlings are 3–4 in tall. Water regularly, as dry spells encourage premature bolting in warm weather. Fall planting generally produces better-quality heads with fewer pest problems. Harvest when heads feel firm and compact, cutting at the base before temperatures drop below 20°F.

plant_note: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest.
