common_name: Orient Express Eggplant (AAS Early Japanese-Type Hybrid)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Orient Express is an All-America Selections award-winning Japanese-type eggplant producing long (8–10 inch), slender, dark purple fruits in 58–68 days from transplant — one of the earliest-maturing eggplants available — making it the top choice for northern gardeners with short seasons and for Gulf Coast gardeners who want eggplant harvest to begin before peak summer heat reduces fruit set.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Orient Express benefits from staking in windy locations; harvest fruits when 6–10 inches long and the skin is glossy dark purple — do not allow to over-ripen; continuous picking encourages continued fruit production. Orient Express is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Japanese-type eggplant that combines the long, slender fruit shape, thin skin, and tender flesh of Asian eggplant varieties with very early maturity (58–68 days from transplant) — a combination that makes it highly productive across a wide range of climates. The long (8–10 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter) fruits have glossy, near-black purple skin and white, very tender flesh with minimal seeds and virtually no bitterness — the thin skin makes Orient Express excellent for eating with skin on in stir-fries, Japanese-style preparations (nasu dengaku — miso-glazed grilled eggplant), grilling, and dishes where the skin texture would be noticeable in a thick-skinned globe eggplant. The early maturity is particularly valuable for Gulf Coast and Southern gardeners who want to get the eggplant harvest in before peak summer heat reduces fruit set, and for northern gardeners who need production in 60–70 days rather than 80–90 days. Highly productive — a well-grown plant can produce 6–10 fruits at once — and the early season timing allows for multiple successive harvests.

common_name: Orient Wonder Pole Yard Long Bean
plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; loves heat and humidity.
directions: Also called Chinese long beans, this dark green pole variety produces smooth, slender pods that stay tender because the seeds develop slowly. It tolerates weather swings from cool and dry to hot and humid better than common beans. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous vines. Harvest pods young at 12 to 18 inches, picking often to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Start mid to late summer for fall and winter color; frost intensifies the hues.
directions: Ornamental kale, a flowering cabbage, forms compact rosettes of frilly leaves in pink, purple, cream, and white that light up cool-season beds and containers. Start seed in mid to late summer so plants color up as temperatures drop, since the vivid hues develop with cold. Give full sun and steady moisture for full, dense rosettes. Frost only deepens the color, making this a standout for fall and winter displays; the leaves are edible but grown mainly for looks.

plant_note: Purchase rooted slips or root cuttings from an overwintered tuber; transplant only after last frost when soil is warm, in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil — morning sun with afternoon shade extends the display in hot climates.
directions: Purchase rooted slips or start cuttings from overwintered tubers and transplant after last frost in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil; ornamental sweet potato vine is one of the most dramatic foliage plants for containers, hanging baskets, and ground cover use in warm-season gardens, producing an exuberant cascade of heart-shaped to deeply lobed leaves in purple-black, chartreuse, bronze, or tricolor combinations depending on cultivar. Growth is vigorous in summer heat, easily spreading 4–6 feet per season to fill containers and cascade elegantly over walls. The small tubers that form underground are edible but bland compared to culinary sweet potato varieties; the ornamental appeal is entirely the foliage. In zone 9–11 leave tubers in the ground year-round as a perennial; elsewhere dig tubers after the first light frost and store overwinter in a cool, dry location.

common_name: Osaka Purple Mustard (Japanese Purple Leaf Mustard)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall (zones 7–11) or early spring (zones 3–7); Osaka Purple is a distinctive Japanese mustard green with round, semi-blistered, bright purple-red leaves — the color intensifies in cool weather, making it one of the most visually striking cool-season greens; the flavor is milder than large-leaved Southern mustard types when young, making it excellent for fresh salads and Asian-style applications.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 6–12 inches for mature plants or sow thickly for baby leaf harvest at 3–4 inches; the rich purple color intensifies dramatically as temperatures cool (40–55°F); harvest outer leaves for cut-and-come-again production or harvest whole plants at the baby leaf stage. Osaka Purple is a Japanese mustard green variety with notably different characteristics from the large-leaved American mustard green types — rather than elongated, flat leaves, Osaka Purple produces compact, round, slightly blistered leaves (mildly puckered like a miniature Savoy cabbage) with an intense purple-red color on the upper surface that deepens in cold weather, making it among the most visually attractive winter vegetables for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 'Osaka' name references Japan's second-largest city and its long vegetable-growing tradition. The flavor is milder and more delicate than large-leaved mustard greens — a gentle mustard note and pleasant sweetness that make it excellent raw in salads and fresh spring rolls, as a substitute for radicchio in salad mixes, or lightly stir-fried in Japanese and Korean cooking. Osaka Purple is one of the most visually useful plants for fall and winter salad mixes, providing intense purple-red color that contrasts beautifully with pale green lettuces and white mizuna; it pairs particularly well with arugula, watercress, and baby spinach for color and flavor contrast in mesclun-style mixes.

common_name: Otto File Corn (Tuscan Eight-Row Corn, Otto Fila Giallo)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in blocks of at least 4 rows; Otto File is a Tuscan yellow flint corn named for its defining characteristic — exactly eight rows of kernels on each ear (otto = eight, file = rows in Italian) — and the traditional grain for authentic Tuscan polenta, where its deep yellow color and nutty flavor produce a superior porridge distinct from the pale commercial product.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-prepared, fertile soil; Otto File is an eight-row flint corn that produces compact ears with exactly 8 rows of golden-yellow kernels; allow ears to dry fully on the stalk; stone-grind for the authentic coarse-textured, deeply flavored polenta that is standard in Tuscany and distinguishes Italian-style polenta from American cornmeal mush. Otto File (Italian: otto fila = eight rows) is the traditional polenta corn of Tuscany, the Italian region where polenta — while less dominant than in the Venice region of northeastern Italy — has been made from this specific eight-row flint corn for generations. The variety name precisely describes the defining characteristic of the ear: each cob bears exactly eight rows of kernels, a consistent genetic trait that is visible at harvest and that Italian farmers used for centuries as a way to identify and maintain the variety. The yellow flint kernels are deeply golden to amber-yellow at maturity, and when stone-ground they produce a meal with a rich, nutty, complex flavor and a pleasantly coarse, somewhat granular texture that gives polenta its characteristic hearty body. Otto File is shorter-season than the Floriani Red Flint (90–110 days versus 100–120) and adapts well to a wide range of climates including the humid Southeast and Gulf South. The compact plant height (5–7 feet) makes it somewhat easier to manage in wind-prone garden situations than taller heritage corns. Otto File is prized by Italian-American home cooks and professional chefs who seek the authentic grain for traditional polenta preparations.

common_name: Outredgeous Lettuce (Deep Red Romaine, First Lettuce Grown in Space)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Outredgeous is a deep burgundy-red romaine lettuce famous as the first crop grown and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station, and a reliable, richly colored performer in the home garden.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Outredgeous is an open-pollinated romaine lettuce selected for intensely dark red-burgundy outer leaves that shade to green toward the crisp, upright heart, giving each head striking two-tone color as well as classic romaine crunch and mild, sweet flavor. It gained widespread recognition in 2015 as the first food crop grown, harvested, and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station as part of NASA's Veggie experiment, chosen partly for its rich anthocyanin pigmentation and reliable performance. In the home garden it is simply a vigorous, dependable, good-flavored red romaine, harvested either as whole heads once firm or as individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again approach. It bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best quality in zone 9, providing afternoon shade for plantings that overlap with warm weather.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Oxheart Pink is a vigorous indeterminate heirloom producing large, heart-shaped fruits with smooth skin, deep pink flesh, and a firm, meaty texture with few seeds. The dense flesh makes it excellent for sauces as well as fresh slicing. Start seed indoors before the last frost and transplant into full sun in warm soil, planting deeply. Provide strong support for the heavy fruit and keep watering even to reduce cracking and blossom-end rot.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: This Italian heirloom, also known as Cuore di Bue, bears heart-shaped, meaty fruits that are dense with few seeds and cook down into a robust sauce. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and need staking or caging. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water evenly to prevent cracking and blossom-end rot. Prune suckers lightly to improve airflow and fruit size.

subcategory: East African tropical oilseed and edible seed vine
plant_note: Direct sow seeds in spring after frosts in full sun in fertile, moist, well-drained, deep loamy soil in zone 10–12; Oyster Nut is an enormous tropical vine from East Africa — native to Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, and Mozambique — grown for its exceptionally large seeds (resembling giant sesame seeds) that are eaten roasted, boiled, or ground into a protein-rich paste; a close relative of the West African Fluted Gourd (Telfairia occidentalis) but larger-fruited, with fruits weighing up to 70 kg.
directions: Plant Telfairia pedata seeds in fertile, deep, well-drained, moist soil in full sun; provide the sturdiest support structure possible as this vine can climb 30–50 feet and bears massive, heavy fruits; water deeply twice weekly during active growth; harvest mature fruits when the skin yellows and splits; dry and shell seeds before eating. Oyster Nut is among the most impressively large of all tropical vines — a forest-margin climber capable of ascending trees to 100 feet and producing enormous, football-shaped to cylindrical gourds that can weigh 40–70 kilograms (100–150 lbs), making them among the largest fruits of any plant. The fruits contain 30–100 large, flat, ovoid seeds (resembling giant sesame or pumpkin seeds) with a thin, papery shell and rich, oily, protein-dense kernel. The seeds are roasted and eaten as a snack, ground into a protein-rich paste for cooking (similar to egusi), or pressed for a cooking oil with a mild, distinctive flavor. In East Africa, particularly in Tanzania and Kenya, Oyster Nut is an important food security crop and commercial oil crop; efforts are underway to expand cultivation. The vines require massive, strong trellises or tree support and will break lightweight structures; plant near a sturdy tree or build a purpose-made strong support before planting.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring harvest or August–September for fall. Packman is an early variety well-adapted to the shorter cool seasons available in zone 9's spring and fall broccoli windows.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 60–75°F; Packman broccoli is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning hybrid that remains one of the most widely grown garden broccoli varieties — an early-maturing variety (65–75 days from transplant) producing large, blue-green central heads with a domed, attractive appearance and good flavor. After the central head is harvested, Packman produces generous side shoots that continue through the season, extending harvest considerably beyond what determinate, single-head broccoli types provide. The early maturation is particularly valuable for zone 9 gardeners who need a broccoli that produces before summer heat terminates the season, and for northern gardeners who want to beat early fall frosts. Packman is dependable, widely available, and well-adapted to a range of growing conditions — making it an excellent beginner's broccoli and a reliable backbone variety for any broccoli production.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after frost when soil warms.
directions: This early, thin-skinned Spanish pepper is a classic tapas appetizer, mostly mild but with the occasional fiery pod for a game of Spanish roulette. Pick fruits small at 1 to 1.5 inches for the best texture and flavor. Start seeds indoors early and transplant into warm, sunny beds. Harvest frequently while green, blistering the pods in hot oil for the traditional dish.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; plant in blocks for good pollination.
directions: This colorful open-pollinated sweet corn was bred from a cross of Luther Hill sweet corn and Painted Mountain flour corn, giving it kernels in many hues and adaptation to short, cool seasons. Sow in warm soil in blocks of at least four rows so wind pollinates the ears well. Keep evenly watered, especially as tassels and silks form. Harvest in the milk stage when kernels are plump and juicy.

plant_note: Direct sow at last frost — Painted Mountain tolerates light frost and can be planted earlier than most corns; it was developed in Montana by Dave Christensen specifically for cold, short-season mountain growing conditions, maturing in 65–85 days from seed at altitudes over 5,000 feet.
directions: Sow in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Painted Mountain is shorter than most corns and somewhat drought-tolerant once established. Painted Mountain corn was developed over 30 years by Dave Christensen of Montana through selection from hundreds of traditional Native American and pioneer corn varieties, specifically to produce an open-pollinated flour corn that matures in 65–85 days in the short growing seasons of Montana mountain communities; the resulting variety is extremely early-maturing, cold-tolerant, and drought-resistant compared to most corns. The ears are 6–8 inches long with strikingly beautiful, multi-colored kernels in a palette of crimson, blue, gold, yellow, orange, and white that can produce rainbow-like color gradients even on a single ear. The flour ground from Painted Mountain has sweet, complex flavor; the variety is also grown as a ornamental corn and for whole-grain cooking.

common_name: Painted Pony Bean (Speckled Heirloom Dry Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Painted Pony is a determinate bush dry bean that sets pods over a 2–3 week window. Allow pods to dry on the vine until the pods are tan, papery, and the beans rattle inside, then harvest and finish drying indoors before shelling. In zone 9, a short spring sowing (March–April) before summer heat sets in is ideal.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; allow pods to fully mature and dry on the vine before harvesting. Painted Pony is a visually spectacular heirloom dry bean producing medium-sized beans with a beautiful swirled pattern of deep maroon-red, tan, and cream — each bean unique in its markings, resembling the coat of an Appaloosa or pinto horse, which gives the variety its evocative name. The ornamental markings unfortunately fade significantly when cooked (as with most colorfully marked dry beans), but the flavor is excellent — rich, slightly earthy, and starchy with the substantial body that makes it outstanding in soups, chilis, stews, and baked bean preparations. Painted Pony beans hold their shape reasonably well when cooked, making them suitable for preparations where bean integrity matters. A productive bush-type bean (no staking required) that fits well into small gardens and is an outstanding choice for seed saving due to its distinctive and reliably reproduced markings. An excellent heirloom variety for bean enthusiasts who value genetic and visual diversity in their garden and pantry.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest, or in late summer 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; pak choi (bok choy) is the quintessential cool-season Asian green, harvested as a whole plant or as individual outer leaves, with crisp, succulent stems and tender, mild leaves that are fundamental in Chinese stir-fry and soup cooking.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep in spring or late summer in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; thin to 6–12 inches depending on desired head size. Pak choi (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) is the quintessential Chinese white-stemmed leafy vegetable grown throughout East Asia for thousands of years and now foundational in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Southeast Asian cooking; the distinctive appearance — a rosette of smooth, deep-green leaves on broad, crisp, white to pale green, fleshy stems — is immediately recognizable. Both the leaves and stems are edible and have different textures: the stems are crisp, juicy, and mild; the leaves are tender and slightly more bitter. Used in stir-fries, soups (pho, hot pot, won ton), dumplings, and braised dishes throughout Asian cuisines. Bolts quickly in heat but is excellent as a fall-through-spring crop in zones 8–11. Baby pak choi (harvested at 3–4 inches) is increasingly popular for microgreens and market sales.

plant_note: Sow in mid to late summer so heads form in cool fall weather.
directions: Palla Rossa is an Italian radicchio-type chicory that forms tight, round heads of deep burgundy leaves with crisp white ribs and a pleasantly bitter flavor. It grows best as a fall crop; the cool weather colors up the heads and mellows their bitterness. Direct sow in mid to late summer in full sun and thin to give each plant room to head up. Harvest when heads feel firm, and a light frost only improves flavor and color.

plant_note: Sow in summer for a fall crop; color and heads develop best in cool weather.
directions: This radicchio forms firm red heads whose color and flavor develop best in cool fall weather, and it overwinters well in zone 4 and warmer. The mildly bitter leaves sweeten after frost. Sow in mid to late summer for heading in autumn, keeping soil evenly moist. Cut heads at the base, and if cut correctly the plants may regrow a second flush.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for winter harvest or January–February for spring. Parade is a non-bulbing type that produces a single upright stem rather than multiple small bulbs, giving cleaner, more uniform appearance. Successive sowings every 4 weeks provide continuous harvest of young green onions. Plants can also be harvested at baby green stage (25–30 days) or at full size at 60–70 days.
directions: Direct sow thinly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Parade is a bunching onion (Japanese-type scallion or green onion) producing straight, uniform, single-stemmed plants with bright white bases, upright green tops, and a clean, mild, sweet flavor — the ideal scallion for fresh eating, garnishing, and all uses where an attractive, uniform appearance matters. Unlike multiplying types that form clusters of small bulbs, Parade produces a single straight stem that is easier to harvest, wash, and present. The non-bulbing, perennial-type Allium fistulosum species tolerates more cold, heat, and wet soil than common bulbing onions, making it well-suited to zone 9 year-round production. Parade is widely used in commercial food service and restaurant settings precisely because the straight, single-stem habit provides uniform portions without the cleaning and sorting of cluster types. In zone 9 plant Parade in fall for the cleanest, sweetest harvest through winter and spring.

plant_note: Round roots tolerate heavy or shallow soils where long types fail.
directions: This round French heirloom carrot forms golf-ball-sized roots that thrive in clay or rocky ground where long carrots struggle. Sow seed thinly and shallowly, keeping the surface damp until the slow seedlings emerge. Thin to 2 inches to allow the little globes to plump up evenly. Because roots are short, they mature quickly and are excellent for containers. Harvest young at about 1 to 1.5 inches across for the sweetest, most tender roots.

common_name: Parris Island Cos Romaine (Classic Upright Tall Romaine Lettuce)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Parris Island Cos is the standard tall romaine lettuce of American commercial production and home gardens — a variety so widely planted that it defines the romaine category for most American growers. In zone 9, transplant September–November for fall and winter production, or February–March for spring. Romaine lettuces tolerate light frost (28–30°F) but are damaged by hard freezes. In zone 9, romaine's best quality window is November–April when temperatures keep heads tight and prevent bolting. Direct sowing works well for romaine: scatter seeds 0.25 inch deep and thin to 8–10 inches for full-sized heads, or 4–6 inches for harvesting as cut-and-come-again.
directions: Transplant or direct sow; thin to 8–10 inches for full heads. Harvest whole head or pull outer leaves. Parris Island Cos is a tall romaine (cos) lettuce — named for Parris Island, South Carolina, from the coastal region where the variety was developed and popularized — that became the dominant commercial romaine type in the United States during the mid-20th century and has remained the standard against which other romaine varieties are measured. Romaine (cos) lettuce differs from butterhead and loose-leaf types in its characteristic tall, upright, tightly folded form — the outer leaves are held upright and pressed together, creating a tall, narrow head with a pale, creamy, slightly blanched interior of great crispness and sweetness that is unavailable in the more loosely arranged butterhead types. The inner heart leaves of Parris Island Cos are the hallmark of a proper Caesar salad — the firm-textured, slightly bitter, crisp interior ribs and pale yellow-green heart that define the authentic Caesar experience. Parris Island Cos has good bolt resistance for a romaine (better than some other varieties) and thrives in the cool fall-through-spring window of Gulf South gardens in zone 8–9, where it produces high-quality heads with the sweetness and crispness that makes this variety so widely planted.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; sow again in late summer for fall.
directions: This classic romaine, developed by the USDA and Clemson around 1950, forms upright 10 to 12 inch heads with crunchy sweet leaves and a buttery green heart. It shows good heat tolerance and vigor. Sow shallowly in cool soil and keep evenly moist for tender leaves. Harvest whole heads or pick outer leaves, and offer light shade in summer heat to delay bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Parris Island is a classic romaine (cos) heirloom forming large, upright heads up to a foot tall with firm green outer leaves and tender, blanched hearts. It shows good heat resistance for a lettuce, making it dependable into early summer. Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer, keeping soil consistently moist. Give full sun in cool weather, and harvest whole heads when firm or take outer leaves as needed.

plant_note: Sow fresh seed 2–4 weeks before the last frost; parsnip seed has a very short viability window so always use seed from the current season.
directions: Sow 3 seeds per station 1/2 in deep in very deeply dug, stone-free soil and thin to the strongest seedling; long taproots will fork in compacted ground. Parsnip germination is notoriously slow and erratic — sowing radish seed in the same row acts as a quick-germinating row marker. Leave roots in the ground through autumn frosts, which convert starches to sugars for a sweeter harvest. Wear gloves when handling foliage in bright sun to avoid phototoxic sap burns.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after frost when soil warms.
directions: The fresh chilaca pepper dries into the dark, wrinkled pasilla that is essential to traditional mole and adds depth to enchilada sauces and salsas. Heat runs a mild 1,000 to 2,000 Scoville units. Start seeds indoors early and set transplants into warm soil in full sun. Let pods ripen to dark brown for drying, or use them fresh, harvesting regularly to keep plants productive.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; the chilaca/pasilla is used fresh when dark green and dried (as pasilla) for authentic Mexican sauces and moles — most gardeners grow it specifically for drying.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed. Pasilla Bajio — meaning 'little raisin from the lowlands' — is the dried form of the fresh chilaca chile, producing narrow, 6–9 inch, wrinkled dark green to near-black fruits that dry to a very dark reddish-black with a distinctive fruity, dried-fruit, earthy flavor and medium heat (1,000–2,500 SHU). Pasilla is one of the three essential dried chiles used together in authentic Mexican mole negro (along with mulato and ancho) and is used extensively in Oaxacan and central Mexican cooking. The tall, upright plants produce cascading clusters of long, drooping fruits; harvest green for fresh use or allow to ripen fully dark and dry on the plant.

common_name: Pasilla Negro Pepper (Mexican Mole Chile, Long Dark-Fruited Dried Chile)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Pasilla Negro is typically harvested at the dark chocolate-brown to very dark green stage (not fully red — though the fruits do ripen through dark brown to red). In zone 9, transplant March–April. Allow some fruits to dry completely on the plant or harvested and air-dry for storage as the dried pasilla chile used in mole negro, enchilada sauces, and other traditional Mexican preparations. Fresh pasilla is used as a stuffed pepper (chile relleno) and in sauces.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Pasilla Negro (also called Chile Pasilla, Chile Negro, or Pasilla Bajío) is a long, narrow, dark-fruited Mexican chile pepper that, when dried, becomes one of the essential dried chiles of Mexican cuisine alongside ancho and mulato. The fresh pepper is 6–9 inches long, narrow (1–1.5 inches diameter), and deep dark green to near-black at the harvest stage — the name 'Pasilla' (little raisin) refers to the wrinkled, dark, raisin-like appearance of the dried pepper. The heat level is mild to medium (1,000–2,500 Scoville units) — substantially milder than serrano or jalapeño — making the peppers appropriate for use in larger quantities in sauces and moles. The flavor is rich, earthy, and slightly fruity with a complex character that makes pasilla one of the most important 'flavor' peppers in Mexican cooking rather than primarily a heat source. Mole negro, the complex black mole of Oaxaca and southern Mexico, typically uses pasilla negro (along with mulato and ancho) as its primary chile base, and the dried, toasted pasilla contributes the dark color and deep, earthy flavor that defines the sauce.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring in moist, fertile soil; or transplant container plants in spring or fall. Once established, patience dock is virtually maintenance-free and returns reliably from the root each spring even in zone 3.
directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; patience dock is a large, handsome perennial with broad, spinach-like leaves that are harvested as a pot herb from earliest spring through late fall. Unlike the sharply acid sorrel (Rumex acetosa), patience dock has a mild, slightly earthy flavor with very little oxalic acid bitterness, making it more broadly useful as a cooked green. The huge leaves (up to 12 inches long) are excellent sautéed with garlic and olive oil, stirred into pasta, or used in savory pies in the way southern Europeans have used them for centuries. The plant has been cultivated in European cottage gardens for hundreds of years and was historically considered one of the most valuable early-spring pot herbs. Divide large clumps every 3-4 years to keep them productive.

common_name: Patio Choice Yellow Bush Cherry Tomato
plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: This compact determinate bush tomato is ideal for containers and small spaces, yielding abundant sweet half-ounce yellow cherry tomatoes. Its tidy habit needs little staking, making it good for patios and mixed pots. Start seeds indoors, transplant after frost, and water evenly to keep fruit from splitting. Pick ripe tomatoes often to encourage a steady flush.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Patio Pride is an early, compact heirloom shelling pea that grows just eight to twelve inches tall, making it ideal for containers, window boxes, and small raised beds. Despite its small stature it produces a generous early crop of sweet peas. Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, sowing thickly since the dwarf plants support each other. Harvest promptly once pods fill for the best flavor, and enjoy a quick turnaround for succession planting.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as soon as it can be worked; great for containers.
directions: This early snap pea is a 2017 All-America Selections winner, ready in about 40 days on compact plants perfect for containers. It yields sweet, uniform 2 to 3 inch pods that are tender when picked young. Sow directly in cool soil for a quick spring or fall crop and keep evenly moist. Harvest pods when plump but still crisp to keep the vines producing.

common_name: Patio Snacker Cucumber (Compact Container-Friendly Snacking Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Patio Snacker is specifically bred for container and small-space growing — the compact vines require minimal support and grow well in large containers (5-gallon minimum) where standard vining cucumbers would be impractical.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Patio Snacker is a compact, semi-vining cucumber variety selected for container and patio growing — producing shorter, more manageable vines (18–30 inches) than standard cucumber varieties while maintaining prolific fruit production of small (3–4 inch) snacking-size cucumbers. The small fruit size and compact plant habit are ideally matched for patio container growing: the cucumbers are sized for fresh snacking without slicing, and the plant fits in a large container (5-gallon minimum, 10-gallon ideal) with a simple stake or small trellis. Patio Snacker produces crisp, thin-skinned, nearly seedless cucumbers with mild, sweet flavor and no bitterness — characteristic of the modern small-cucumber/snacking types bred for fresh eating without the preparation steps (peeling, seed removal) required for large slicing varieties. In zone 9, cucumbers are most productive in the spring shoulder season (February–April) and the fall shoulder season (August–September) — summer heat reduces fruiting and increases disease pressure. The compact size and container suitability make Patio Snacker particularly useful for zone 9 gardeners who can move containers to optimize microclimate conditions during the challenging summer transition period.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Patterson is a long-day (14–16 hour) hybrid yellow storage onion widely recognized as one of the most reliable and highest-yielding yellow onions for northern gardens — it produces large, globe-shaped, golden-yellow-skinned bulbs that store exceptionally well for 8–12 months in ideal conditions, making it the premier variety for northern gardeners who want a full year's supply from a single planting.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; space 4–6 inches apart in rows 12–18 inches apart; Patterson is a long-day variety requiring 14+ hours of daylight to form bulbs — performs in zones 3–8 north of the 35th parallel; harvest when 80% of tops fall naturally and cure 3–4 weeks in a warm, dry location with good airflow. Patterson is a long-day hybrid yellow storage onion widely considered one of the gold standards for reliable, high-yielding yellow onion production in northern gardens (zones 3–8); it has been a staple recommendation of Johnny's Selected Seeds — the primary commercial source — and university extension services throughout the Northeast and Midwest for its combination of high yield, consistent bulb quality, and exceptional storage performance. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have smooth, dark golden-amber skins that cure tightly and resist breakdown in storage; the flesh is white, firm, moderately pungent, and full-flavored in the traditional yellow onion style — excellent for all cooking purposes: caramelizing, soups, stews, roasting, and pickling. The standout characteristic that makes Patterson the choice of serious northern vegetable gardeners is storage life: under ideal conditions (33–40°F, low humidity, good airflow), Patterson onions store 8–12 months — essentially the full year from one harvest to the next — with far less deterioration, sprouting, or softening than most other onion varieties. This durability in storage is the result of tight, multiple layers of dry outer scales that seal the bulb against moisture and pathogens.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; pattypan grows on a compact bush plant about half the size of trailing squash. In Gulf Coast gardens, sow in spring and make a second planting in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost; pattypan (also called scallop or flying-saucer squash) is a bush summer squash producing flat, round, scallop-edged fruits in white, yellow, green, or bicolored versions that look entirely different from the cylindrical zucchini or yellow straightneck. Harvest at 2–3 inches in diameter for the most tender flesh; larger fruits become tough and seedy. The hollow center makes them ideal for stuffing: scoop out the interior, fill with cheese, herbs, or seasoned meat, and bake. The compact bush habit makes pattypan suitable for smaller gardens. 'Sunburst' (yellow) and 'Patio Star' (white) are popular named cultivars.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil temperature is at least 65°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil in hills of 2–3 seeds, thinning to the strongest plant. Consistent moisture at the root zone keeps the bush compact and productive throughout the season. Pattypan's distinctive flying-saucer shape makes sizing easy. Harvest when fruits are 2–3 inches across for the most tender flesh; over-mature fruits become tough and seedy.

common_name: Paul Robeson Tomato (Complex Deep Brick-Red Russian Dark Heirloom)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Paul Robeson is named in honor of the American singer, actor, and civil rights activist Paul Robeson — a Russian heirloom commemorating a figure celebrated in the Soviet Union for his commitment to racial justice.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Paul Robeson is a celebrated Russian heirloom tomato that is consistently rated by connoisseurs as one of the finest-flavored dark tomatoes available — producing medium-large (7–10 oz), round to oblate fruits in a distinctive deep brick-red to mahogany-brownish-purple color with dark-green shoulders that is the hallmark of the 'black' Russian tomato aesthetic. The flavor is remarkable: deeply complex, rich, smoky, and earthy with a balanced sweetness and moderate acidity that creates a dimensional, wine-like flavor profile that many experienced tomato tasters consider superior to any other tomato type. The flavor intensity — often described as the most complex and layered of all dark heirloom tomatoes — makes Paul Robeson outstanding for fresh eating (particularly with nothing more than salt and olive oil), in Caprese-style presentations, and in cooking where the rich, smoky character concentrates further. Paul Robeson was introduced to American seed savers from a Russian collection by Marina Danilenko in the 1990s and has become one of the most respected and sought-after heirlooms in the American seed-saving community. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds save true to type. In zone 9, Paul Robeson produces best in the spring growing window (February–June) and requires the long spring season to develop its finest fruit quality.

plant_note: Soak peas overnight before sowing thickly; shoots can be cut and regrow once.
directions: Soak the pea seed overnight so it germinates quickly and evenly, then spread it thickly across a moist tray. Keep the seeds covered under weight for a couple of days to encourage strong, upright shoots, then bring them into bright light. Water from below to keep the dense mat hydrated without inviting rot. Harvest the sweet, tender pea shoots at three to six inches tall; many growers get a second cutting from the same tray.

plant_note: Sow thickly in cool soil or trays; harvest young as tender shoots.
directions: Harvested young, pea shoots are a tender, versatile green for salads, sandwiches, soups, and stir-fries. Sow the seeds thickly in a container or garden bed and keep them evenly moist. Snip the shoots with scissors when a few inches tall, cutting above the lowest leaves so plants can regrow for a second cutting. They grow quickly in cool conditions and tolerate part shade.

common_name: Peach Habanero Pepper (Pale Peach-Fruity Habanero Variety with Full Heat)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Peach Habanero, like all Capsicum chinense, requires very warm germination temperatures (80–95°F) and is slow to germinate compared to Capsicum annuum — allow 14–21 days and use a heat mat. In zone 9, transplant March–April; Capsicum chinense thrives in Gulf Coast heat and can produce abundantly through summer and fall. Peach Habanero plants may behave as short-lived perennials in zone 9b if protected from frost, potentially living 2–3 years and producing heavier crops in subsequent seasons. The pale peach color of ripe fruits is the defining characteristic — do not harvest until the green fruits have fully transitioned to the cream-peach color.
directions: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest when fully peach-colored. Peach Habanero is a color variant of the habanero pepper group (Capsicum chinense) producing fruits that ripen to a distinctive peach to pale apricot-cream color rather than the familiar orange of standard habanero. The heat level is comparable to orange habanero (100,000–350,000 Scoville units) — full habanero-class heat that demands careful handling and measured use — but the flavor character is perceived by many tasters as slightly different: more floral, sweeter, and with a pronounced fruity quality that some describe as reminiscent of apricot or tropical fruit. The habanero group includes color variants ranging from white through yellow, orange, peach, red, chocolate, and nearly black, with all variants sharing the distinctive fruity-floral habanero aroma that distinguishes Capsicum chinense from the more neutral Capsicum annuum species. Peach Habanero is valued by hot sauce makers, hot pepper enthusiasts, and gardeners interested in the visual diversity of the habanero color spectrum — the pale peach fruits are visually striking against the deep green foliage and make an attractive presentation in fresh pepper mixes and hot sauce. In zone 9, Peach Habanero is one of the most productive hot peppers available: the combination of the species' heat and humidity tolerance with the long Gulf Coast growing season produces prolific crops of fruits through summer and into fall.

common_name: Peaches and Cream Sweet Corn (Bicolor Sweet Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 8–12 inches apart in blocks of at least 4 rows (not single long rows) for adequate pollination; in zone 9, plant in February–March for spring harvest or late July for fall harvest; sweet corn requires a large block planting for wind pollination — isolated rows produce poorly filled ears.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate cross-pollination; Peaches and Cream is the most popular bicolor sweet corn cultivar in American home gardens — producing medium-large ears with yellow and white kernels in a random bicolor mosaic pattern that gives the variety its name and provides both sweet varieties in a single ear. The flavor is typically described as rich, sweet, and complex — the combination of white (typically sweeter) and yellow (typically more 'corny' in flavor) kernels in each bite creates a distinctive eating experience that many gardeners prefer to all-yellow or all-white varieties. Peaches and Cream is an 'SE' (sugar-enhanced) sweet corn type — sweeter than standard su sweet corn but not as sweet or tender-skinned as sh2 (supersweet) types. The SE type is more forgiving of growing conditions and holds its sweetness longer after harvest than standard sweet corn. In zone 9, sweet corn is a spring and fall crop — plant in late February for June harvest and in late July for October harvest. The hot summer is too demanding for quality corn. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder — side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer when plants are 12 inches tall and again when tasseling. Corn earworms are the primary pest and must be managed with Bt applications at silk emergence.

plant_note: Sow 2–4 weeks after last frost; peanuts need a long, frost-free growing season of at least 120 days.
directions: Shell peanuts and plant seeds 2 in deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil; heavy clay prevents proper peg penetration and pod development. After flowering, keep the area around plants free of weeds and loosen surface soil lightly so fertilization pegs can easily enter the ground. Harvest when foliage begins to yellow and the inner shell veins turn dark, by lifting the entire plant with a fork. Cure plants upside-down in a warm, airy location for 2–3 weeks before removing pods.

plant_note: Sow thickly and do not thin; crowding keeps bulbs small.
directions: Tiny pearl onions are grown deliberately crowded so each bulb stays small and round for pickling and boiling. Direct sow densely in a wide band and skip thinning, since competition limits bulb size. Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free during the short growing period. Harvest when tops yellow and fall, then cure the little bulbs before storing or pickling. Blanching the cured bulbs in hot water makes peeling far easier.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in blocks of 4+ rows; Pencil Cob is a distinctive North American heritage corn with narrow, pencil-thin cobs densely packed with small, cream-to-yellow kernels — used primarily as a flour corn for fine-grained, delicate-flavored cornmeal and grits prized in the Appalachian and mid-Atlantic tradition.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of 4+ rows for good pollination; thin to 9–12 inches within the row. Pencil Cob corn (sometimes called Cob Corn or Ashworth type) is a distinctive Appalachian and Midwestern heritage flour corn named for the distinctive narrow, slender cob (roughly pencil-diameter, compared to the fist-thick cobs of modern hybrids) that is densely covered in small, tightly packed kernels; the cobs are long for their diameter (8–12 inches) and produce flour corn with a fine-grained texture and delicate, sweet corn flavor that is different from the coarser, more assertive flavor of modern hybrid cornmeal. Ground into a fine, cream-colored meal that makes exceptionally tender and flavorful cornbread; many Southern cornbread enthusiasts claim it produces the finest cornbread of any heritage variety. Also used for hominy, grits, and polenta.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Pencil Pod Black Wax is an 1880s heirloom yellow wax (golden) bush snap bean, producing round, cylindrical (pencil-shaped), golden-yellow pods with black seeds — one of the classic American wax beans prized for its crisp texture, mild flavor, and beautiful color that holds when canned or cooked.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest through spring. Pencil Pod Black Wax is an American heirloom wax bean introduced around 1880, named for its distinctive round, cylindrical pods (resembling a pencil in shape — round rather than flat) and black seeds; the 'wax' designation refers to the golden-yellow color of the pods, which are more ornamentally attractive than standard green beans and have a somewhat different, milder flavor. The pods are harvested at 4–6 inches when crisp and tender; like all wax beans, the yellow color holds through cooking and canning better than green beans, making the finished product more visually appealing in jars. Black Wax beans were a standard American commercial canning variety in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; now maintained by heirloom seed companies. One of the most productive and reliable early wax beans for succession planting.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; needs a long season to mature.
directions: This Pennsylvania heirloom is a long-necked butternut type with rich, smooth flesh and excellent keeping quality. The elongated necks are nearly solid flesh, ideal for roasting and soups. Give the vigorous 6 to 8 foot vines full sun and plenty of room to sprawl. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot to deepen flavor and improve storage life.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 75–85°F soil temperature — peppers germinate poorly below 70°F; transplant only after nights consistently stay above 55°F as cold soil dramatically stunts growth.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 75–85°F soil temperature — peppers need warm soil to germinate and grow; transplant after nights consistently stay above 55°F in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Water consistently but do not overwater — even moisture is essential for preventing blossom drop and fruit set; inconsistent watering causes blossom drop during pollination. Peppers are one of the most productive vegetables for hot-summer climates, producing continuous harvests from midsummer through frost. Green peppers can be harvested at any time; allowing them to mature to red, yellow, or orange increases sweetness and vitamin C content significantly. In zone 8–11 peppers can be overwintered as perennials if protected from frost.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January and transplant February–March. Pepperoncini is harvested green (2–3 inches long) for pickling, or allowed to turn red for a sweeter, riper flavor. In zone 9, the long warm season enables outstanding production through spring and fall.
directions: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pepperoncini is the classic Italian pickling and frying pepper, widely grown throughout Tuscany and the Greek Peloponnese for centuries and the pepper that fills the olive bar jars in every American grocery store. The thin-walled, mildly hot (100–500 Scoville), wrinkled fruits are harvested at 2–3 inches when bright green for pickling in white wine vinegar — the standard preparation produces the distinctive brine-pickled pepperoncini familiar from Italian sub sandwiches and antipasto. When allowed to ripen fully red, the fruits sweeten considerably and are excellent fresh or roasted. The plants are productive and undemanding, bearing heavily over a long season in full sun with consistent moisture. In Italian cooking, fresh pepperoncini are used whole in pasta sauces (arrabbiata), braised with olives and capers, and roasted under poultry. The Greek variety (often called 'Golden Greek' or 'Greek Golden') is essentially the same pepper and is the primary type pickled for commercial sale in the US.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; in zones 8–11 pequin pepper can be grown as a perennial woody shrub and wild populations persist through mild winters in south Texas. Native populations tolerate brief light freezes and resprout from roots.
directions: Start indoors and transplant to well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; pequin pepper (also spelled piquin) is a wild-type species pepper native to South Texas and northeastern Mexico, where it grows as a woody perennial shrub in dry, rocky, calcareous soils — often under the shade of mesquite, oak, and other native trees. The tiny, egg-shaped fruits (1/4 to 1/2 inch) pack an intense concentrated heat (40,000–100,000 SHU) with a distinctive citrusy, nutty flavor beloved in Tex-Mex cooking, particularly in traditional Mexican salsas and vinegar-based hot sauces. Wild-harvested pequin peppers are prized over cultivated ones in parts of northern Mexico. Birds that eat the fruits are immune to capsaicin and disperse the seeds. An excellent native plant for hot, dry, alkaline Texas and Gulf Coast gardens.

common_name: Peredovik Black Oil Sunflower (Russian High-Oil Bird-Feeding and Oil-Production Sunflower)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Peredovik is a multi-stemmed, multi-head oilseed sunflower producing many 3–5 inch flower heads per plant (unlike the single giant-headed ornamental sunflowers grown for show). In zone 9, plant March–May; for fall dove season, plant July–August to time seed maturity with the September–October dove hunting season. The oil sunflower habit (shorter, multi-branching, many small heads) maximizes seed yield per plant and provides more uniform ripening than single-headed types. Harvest when seed heads are thoroughly dry and birds begin eating the seeds.
directions: Direct sow 0.5–1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest when seed heads are completely dry and brown. Peredovik (also spelled 'Peredovik') is a Russian open-pollinated oilseed sunflower developed in the Soviet Union specifically for oil production — one of the most widely planted sunflower varieties in the world and the standard variety used in commercial sunflower oil production globally before the development of modern high-oleic hybrids. The Peredovik breeding emphasized oil percentage over seed size: the thin, black seeds contain 42–45% oil by weight (compared to 24–28% for striped ornamental/snack sunflower types), and this high oil content is what gives 'black oil sunflower' its distinct value. In the bird-feeding context, black oil sunflower seeds (Peredovik or similar black-seeded varieties) are universally recommended as the premier wild bird food: the thin, easy-to-crack shell is accessible to a wider range of small songbirds than the thick-shelled striped types, and the high oil content provides superior energy density for birds — particularly important for overwintering and migratory species. For wildlife food plots in the Gulf South, Peredovik-type black oil sunflower is one of the primary dove and songbird attractants planted specifically for the September-October dove season. The seeds are also excellent for human consumption (roasting, pressing for oil) though small in size.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an 1890s heirloom okra that produces very long (up to 8–10 inch), slightly ridged, green pods with outstanding flavor and a notably long harvest window before pods become tough — a longtime favorite in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is warm; soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an heirloom okra variety introduced in the 1890s that produces exceptionally long (6–10 inch) ribbed green pods with a more tender quality at larger sizes than most okra varieties — meaning the pods remain acceptable for eating somewhat longer than standard varieties, which quickly become fibrous and tough once they exceed 3–4 inches. The plants are vigorous (5–8 feet), highly productive, and heat-tolerant, performing well throughout the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Harvest pods at 4–6 inches for optimal tenderness; though the pods can be eaten somewhat larger, regular harvesting every 1–2 days in hot weather is essential to keep production high — missed pods left on the plant stop production quickly.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; the biennial keeps producing into fall.
directions: Perpetual spinach is actually a leaf chard grown for tender, mild leaves that eat like true spinach but far more heat- and bolt-resistant. As a cut-and-come-again crop it produces for months, and being biennial it can carry over for a second season in mild areas. Direct sow in spring in full sun to partial shade and keep evenly watered. Harvest outer leaves regularly and the plant will keep pushing out new growth well into fall.

plant_note: Direct sow around last frost; keeps producing through the season.
directions: Despite its name this thin-ribbed Italian heirloom is a Swiss chard grown for its tender, spinach-like leaves, and it is slow to bolt in hot weather. Sow directly and thin seedlings, then harvest outer leaves regularly so the plant keeps producing new growth for months. Keep the soil evenly moist and feed occasionally for lush leaves. It tolerates both spring and fall conditions and mild frost.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon type popular in California and the American West, producing large (8–15 lb), round, deeply netted, fragrant fruits with deep salmon-orange flesh of excellent sweetness — one of the standard commercial and home-garden melons for hot, dry Western climates.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Persian melon requires hot, dry conditions for best sweetness and is most successful in California, Arizona, Texas, and Gulf Coast gardens. Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon of Middle Eastern origin that became a California commercial standard in the early 20th century; the large (8–15 lb), round to slightly oval fruits have a thick layer of fine, closely woven gray-green netting over dark green skin that transitions to golden-green at maturity, with deeply aromatic, thick, deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, spicy sweetness. Persian melon is rounder and larger than cantaloupes and has thicker, denser flesh with a more pronounced, spicy aromatic complexity than American cantaloupe types. It requires a longer season (90–100 days) and performs best in hot, dry conditions; California's Central and Imperial Valleys have historically produced most commercial Persian melons sold in Western markets. The thick rind and firm flesh give Persian melon better shipping quality than more delicate muskmelon types, and it stores 1–2 weeks refrigerated after harvest.

common_name: Persian Star Hardneck Garlic (Marbled Purple Stripe, Samarkand Heritage)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost in fall; Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan (the historic Silk Road city) by John Swenson for the Seed Savers Exchange in 1989 — it produces strikingly beautiful bulbs with vivid violet-purple inner clove skins and a rich, earthy, complex flavor characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe type.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch after planting; keep weed-free and consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl; harvest in early to midsummer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure in a warm, dry, airy location. Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe-type hardneck garlic with a remarkable provenance: it was collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan — the ancient Silk Road city at the crossroads of Central Asia — by John Swenson, a garlic enthusiast and Seed Savers Exchange member who traveled to the former Soviet Union in 1989 collecting traditional garlic varieties grown in the region for centuries. The provenance from Samarkand, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and a center of Central Asian agricultural tradition, gives Persian Star historical and botanical significance as a window into the genetic diversity of garlic in its center of diversity (Central Asia is believed to be the region where cultivated garlic first developed). The bulbs are 2–3 inches across with 8–12 cloves; the outer skin is white with subtle purple striping typical of the Marbled Purple Stripe group, while the inner clove skins are often vivid violet-purple — beautiful when peeled. The flavor is rich, earthy, moderately pungent, and complex — slightly different from Rocambole types with a distinctive minerality. Storage life is better than Rocambole (5–7 months) but less than softneck types.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; a large, golden-orange beefsteak heirloom with very low acid and sweet, fruity flavor — an excellent choice for gardeners who want an orange type that ripens reliably in hot summer conditions.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and staking or caging firmly. Persimmon is a Ukrainian heirloom beefsteak tomato with fruit that resembles the color of a ripe persimmon — vivid golden-orange — with very meaty flesh, a small seed cavity, extraordinarily sweet, low-acid, fruity flavor, and fruits weighing 10–16 ounces; it is among the finest-tasting orange or golden beefsteak heirlooms and has been prized by serious tomato growers since its introduction through Seed Savers Exchange. The vigorous indeterminate vines produce steadily through the season; stake firmly and maintain consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot. Harvest when fruits are fully colored and yield slightly to pressure at the blossom end.

common_name: Peruvian Purple Pepper (Ornamental Edible Hot Pepper with Purple Foliage and Upright Fruits)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Peruvian Purple is a compact ornamental edible pepper (18–24 inches) with distinctive deep purple-black foliage, purple stems, and small upright fruits (1.5–2 inches) that mature from purple-black through a transitional stage to vivid red. The purple pigmentation in both foliage and immature fruits results from anthocyanin accumulation triggered by light exposure, making it one of the most visually striking ornamental peppers available. Heat level is high (estimated 50,000–80,000 SHU), reflecting the small fruit size typical of high-heat Capsicum annuum types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the compact habit makes it excellent for containers and ornamental mixed plantings where edible and decorative plants are combined.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun and harvest fruits at any stage from purple-black (immature, high heat) to fully red (ripe). Peruvian Purple Pepper is a compact ornamental-edible hot pepper variety distinguished by its unusual anthocyanin-rich foliage — a deep purple-black that makes the plant visually dramatic from seedling stage through maturity. The purple coloration in the leaves and immature fruits results from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to high light intensity; the same plant grown in reduced light will show less purple coloration and more green foliage, making sun exposure a direct visible factor in the plant's ornamental effect. Fruits emerge deep purple-black and upright — pointing skyward rather than pendant — which is a characteristic of many small ornamental hot pepper types and adds visual interest as the small fruits are held prominently above the purple foliage. As fruits ripen to full maturity they transition through a mottled purple-and-red stage before reaching solid vivid red; many gardeners harvest throughout this color progression since the flavor and heat level remain high at all stages. The heat level is substantial for a Capsicum annuum variety — comparable to Thai or bird's eye types — and is proportional to the small fruit size, as capsaicin concentration tends to increase as fruit diameter decreases within the species. Culinary uses mirror those of other small hot peppers: used fresh in salads, salsas, and stir-fries; pickled; or dried whole for later use. As a compact container plant with dramatic foliage, Peruvian Purple also functions effectively as a purely ornamental annual in mixed containers where its purple leaves provide contrast against chartreuse, silver, or deep green companions.

common_name: Petai (Stink Bean, Bitter Bean, Twisted Cluster Bean)
plant_note: Plant container-grown seedlings in well-drained, deep, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free zones 10–12; petai is a tall tropical legume tree that requires many years to fruit — it is rarely grown outside of its native Southeast Asian range except in southern Florida, the Caribbean, and similar frost-free climates.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in frost-free tropical conditions; petai requires a long growing season with warm temperatures year-round. Parkia speciosa (petai or stink bean) is a large, tropical legume tree of Southeast Asia producing distinctive, long (12–18 inch), flat, twisted seed pods containing 10–18 large, flat, bright-green seeds with an intensely pungent, sulfurous odor (similar to but stronger than garlic and fenugreek combined) that is a celebrated ingredient in Malaysian, Indonesian, and Thai cooking. The seeds are eaten raw, stir-fried with shrimp, added to curries and sambals, or mixed with garlic, chili, and shrimp paste — those accustomed to the flavor consider it a prized delicacy despite (or because of) its extreme pungency. Like asparagus with certain compounds, petai causes urine to smell strongly of its sulfurous compounds for several hours after eating — considered a normal, if somewhat inconvenient, effect. The tree is a nitrogen-fixer (fixing atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules) and has been used in agroforestry systems throughout Malaysia and Indonesia. Rarely available in the continental US except in specialty tropical fruit nurseries.

common_name: Peter Pan Pattypan Squash (AAS-Winning Green Scallop Summer Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Peter Pan is a bush-type pattypan suitable for smaller gardens than vining summer squash. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August for fall harvest. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter for best flavor and texture — pattypan squash becomes seedy and watery if allowed to grow much beyond 4–5 inches. The scalloped edges that give pattypan its distinctive star or UFO shape become more pronounced and decorative as fruits approach full harvest size.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest fruits at 3–4 inches diameter for best eating quality. Peter Pan is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning pattypan (scallop) summer squash — an early-maturing, bush-habit variety producing pale green, disc-shaped fruits with the characteristic scalloped, fluted edges of the pattypan type. The distinctive flat, disc-like shape with scalloped margins distinguishes pattypan squash from all other summer squash types (zucchini, yellow crookneck, yellow straightneck) and has no equivalent in other vegetable categories — the shape makes individual fruits look like tiny flying saucers or UFOs and creates an unusually attractive presentation on the plate when halved or stuffed whole. Peter Pan's light green color is gentler and less common than the white pattypans that dominated before its introduction. The flavor is mild and slightly sweet — similar to other summer squash but with a distinctive nuttiness that develops in the scallop varieties at the ideal 3–4 inch harvest size. The bush habit (24–36 inch spread vs. the 6–8 foot spread of vining squash) makes Peter Pan practical for smaller raised beds and gardens.

common_name: Peter Pan Squash (AAS-Winning Pale Green Scallop Squash, Early and Compact)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Peter Pan is a scallop (pattypan) squash that produces pale sage-green to silvery-green flat, scallop-edged fruits on a compact bush plant. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September for fall production. Harvest Peter Pan at 3–4 inches when the skin is still tender and the green color is uniform and pale — the skin toughens significantly if the squash is left to grow beyond 4–5 inches. The distinctive pale green-grey color (lighter than most green summer squash) and scalloped edge make Peter Pan one of the most immediately recognizable summer squash varieties at harvest. The flavor is mild and nutty, somewhat different from zucchini in a pleasant way — scallop types have a slightly different flesh texture and a subtly nuttier quality that distinguishes them from elongated zucchini types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when pale sage-green and tender. Peter Pan Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the summer squash category, honored for its early production, compact plant habit, and the distinctive pale sage-green to silvery-blue-green color of the scallop-shaped fruits. The AAS recognition confirmed Peter Pan's performance advantage over other scallop squash varieties of its time in trials across multiple growing regions and climates. The scallop squash form — a flat, disc-shaped fruit with distinctively scalloped or fluted edges — is one of the oldest American summer squash forms, with historical precedent in both Native American cultivation and early colonial American gardens. Peter Pan's F1 hybrid vigor contributes to both its compactness (more manageable plant than many bush zucchini) and productivity (abundant fruit set throughout the season). The color is a notable characteristic: the pale, muted sage-green to silvery green of Peter Pan is unlike the darker green of standard zucchini or the yellow of Sunburst, occupying its own distinctive color space that many gardeners find attractive for mixed variety plantings and market displays where color diversity is valued. The flat scallop form also makes Peter Pan an exceptionally attractive stuffed squash: the naturally hollow interior of the scallop form (relative to the solid flesh core of zucchini) allows more filling capacity per fruit when halved for stuffing, and the shallow depth of the squash makes even cooking possible at the small sizes most suitable for stuffing preparations.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat; transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has fully passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; stake taller plants if heavily loaded with fruit. Peter Pepper is a well-known Southern heirloom hot pepper, famous for its unmistakably novelty shape, which has made it a popular curiosity and conversation piece for generations of home gardeners across Texas and Louisiana. The medium-heat fruits (roughly 10,000–25,000 Scoville units, comparable to a strong jalapeño or mild cayenne) ripen from green to red and carry a fruity, tangy flavor good in salsas, pickling, and hot sauce once the novelty value has been enjoyed. Plants are productive and reasonably compact, performing well in containers as well as garden beds, and the fruit's thick walls hold up nicely to stuffing or pickling whole. A fun, genuinely productive heirloom for gardeners who want something distinctive alongside their standard pepper lineup, in zone 4–11.

common_name: Petit Gris de Rennes Melon (French Heirloom Gray-Green Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Petit Gris de Rennes is a French muskmelon type that requires warmer growing conditions than some European varieties — it performs well in the Gulf South's warm summer climate but needs protection from excessive humidity that can cause Alternaria blight. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The 'Petit Gris' (little gray) refers to the grayish-green skin when fully ripe.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to gray-green (the characteristic 'petit gris' color) and the stem cracks slightly at the base — this muskmelon type does not 'slip' from the vine like American cantaloupes but has a less decisive harvest cue. Petit Gris de Rennes (small gray of Rennes) is a traditional French muskmelon heirloom from Brittany, the coastal region of northwestern France, where it has been grown for centuries as the area's distinctive local melon. In France, Petit Gris de Rennes has Slow Food Ark of Taste recognition as a threatened traditional variety of significant cultural importance. The small to medium (1–2 lb) round fruits are distinguished by their unusual grayish-green to slate-green skin coloration with shallow ribs and fine, irregular netting — a very different appearance from the tan-netted American cantaloupe standard. The deeply orange, firm-textured, extremely sweet and aromatic flesh has a rich, complex character that many tasters consider superior to standard Western cantaloupe types — more complex in flavor, with floral and spicy notes beyond simple sweetness. Petit Gris de Rennes represents the French horticultural tradition of flavor breeding, where appearance is secondary to eating quality, and is a fascinating variety for gardeners interested in growing traditional European melon types beyond the standard muskmelon.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, moist soil; in zone 9–11 sow year-round as a perennial, cutting plants back periodically to encourage fresh tender growth.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in warm, moist soil; talinum is an exceptionally heat-tolerant tropical leafy vegetable used across West Africa, the Caribbean, and Southeast Asia as a spinach substitute that thrives in hot weather that destroys most other greens. The thick, succulent leaves and stems cook quickly and have a mild, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to purslane. Harvest by cutting stem tips with young leaves regularly; plants regenerate vigorously from the base. In zones 9–11 it becomes a woody perennial subshrub 2–3 feet tall; cut back to 6 inches periodically to keep growth tender. Very drought-tolerant once established and requires little fertilizer. Also known as Lagos spinach and waterleaf.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Phoenix continues setting fruit through the high daytime and nighttime temperatures of a Gulf South summer that cause blossom drop in most other tomato varieties.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent watering reduces blossom end rot in humid conditions. Phoenix is a tomato variety developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife vegetable breeding program specifically to keep setting fruit through the extreme heat of a Texas and Gulf South summer, when night temperatures above 75°F cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in most standard varieties. The medium-sized, firm, deep red globe fruits also carry useful resistance to common soilborne diseases and cracking, and the vines continue producing through the hottest stretch of summer that typically causes a production gap in southern tomato gardens. It also carries a degree of protection against sunscald thanks to good foliage cover. A dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want tomatoes to keep coming through July and August rather than stalling out, in zone 4–11.

common_name: Pickle Bush Cucumber (Compact Bush-Habit Pickling Cucumber for Small Spaces)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush's compact, bush-habit vines (18–24 inch spread) make it excellent for raised beds and container growing — no trellis required and the plants are self-supporting.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush is a bush-type pickling cucumber producing compact, self-supporting vines 18–24 inches across rather than the sprawling 4–6 foot vines of standard pickling cucumbers — making it the preferred choice for raised beds, containers, and small gardens where trellises are impractical and space is limited. The short (3–4 inch), blocky, warted, pickling-type cucumbers mature very early (48–55 days) in prolific clusters that concentrate harvest in a short window ideal for batch processing and canning. Pickling cucumbers are specifically bred for thin, tender skin that absorbs brine quickly, mild-to-bland flavor that allows pickle seasonings to dominate, and firm flesh that maintains crunchiness through the pickling process — qualities that distinguish them from slicing cucumbers in important culinary ways. In zone 9, the very early maturity (48–55 days) of Pickle Bush is a practical advantage — it completes its production cycle before summer heat drives cucumbers into bitter, poor-quality fruit stage. The bush habit allows high-density planting in raised beds (18 inches apart) compared to the 3–4 foot spacing required for trellised vining types. AAS Honorable Mention recognized Pickle Bush's outstanding performance in the small-space home garden category.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills or rows 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; pickling cucumbers are typically bush or short-vine types that produce prolifically over a short concentrated harvest period suited to batch pickling.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun 1–2 weeks after last frost, thinning to 12–18 inches apart; pickling varieties such as National Pickling, Calypso, and Boston Pickling bear shorter, blockier, thinner-skinned fruits than slicing types and set fruit more uniformly over a compressed harvest window — ideal for making dill pickles and bread-and-butter chips in a single session. Harvest at 2–4 inches for gherkins, 4–5 inches for standard dills; leaving even one overripe fruit on the vine significantly slows further production. Keep soil evenly moist — irregular watering causes bitter fruits. Succession-plant every 3 weeks for a season-long supply.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; in zone 9–12 pigeon pea grows as a short-lived perennial woody shrub and may produce pods for 2–5 years before needing replacement. In cooler zones grow as an annual and start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; pigeon pea is a deep-rooted, drought-tolerant shrubby legume that is one of the world's most important tropical food crops — the yellow, green, or red seeds (arhar dal, toor dal) are a dietary staple across the Caribbean, South Asia, and sub-Saharan Africa, used in dals, stews, rice dishes, and soups. The plants fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules and thrive in poor soils without supplemental fertilizer; overly rich or wet soils reduce pod production. Harvest green pods when plump for fresh use or allow to fully dry on the plant for dried dal; in zone 9–12 plants become woody perennial shrubs and will continue producing pods for several years if pruned back hard after the main harvest to stimulate new growth. In zone 8 and below, grow as a warm-season annual and expect a single late-season harvest.

plant_note: Sow seeds in fall in partial shade in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist woodland or hedgerow soil in zone 5–9; Pignut (Earth Chestnut, Earthnut) is a slender, delicate, native British and European woodland herb — once eaten by children and common folk throughout Britain for its small, brown-skinned, sweet, nutty-flavored underground tubers — bearing finely divided, carrot-family foliage in hedgerows, meadows, and oak and beech woodland understories, and an important food plant for dormice, wild boar, and other woodland wildlife.
directions: Sow Conopodium majus seeds in fall in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; plants are slow to establish and the small underground tubers take 2–3 years to reach harvestable size; avoid disturbing the soil around plants once growing; harvest small tubers with a trowel in summer as foliage dies back. Pignut is one of the most charming native edibles of British and European woodlands — a slender, graceful plant of meadows, hedgerows, and open woodland that has been gathered for its sweet, nut-flavored tubers by country people for centuries.
