The small, round to irregularly shaped tubers (technically a corm-like swelling of the underground stem) are covered in brown skin and have cream-colored, very sweet, crunchy flesh with a flavor reminiscent of sweet chestnut or hazelnut — edible raw or cooked. Foragers prize them but they are difficult to dig without following the thin, brittle stem underground without breaking it (hence their reputation for elusiveness). Wild populations are protected in Britain, but cultivation from seed is permitted and encouraged for those wishing to grow them. The plant is an important food source for dormice, wild boar, and other wildlife in European woodland ecosystems. A genuinely rare and unusual woodland garden plant with culinary value and strong ecological connections.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and transplant to fertile, well-drained garden soil once the risk of frost has fully passed. The heart-shaped, thick-walled fruits ripen from green to deep red and are sweeter and more aromatic than most bell peppers, with a rich, almost spicy fragrance that is distinct to the type. Harvest at full red for fresh use, or roast and peel for preserving in oil — pimento is the classic stuffing for green olives. High yields from compact plants make this a productive choice for containers or small beds.

common_name: Pimiento Pepper (Classic Sweet Thick-Walled Pimento Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Pimiento is the traditional variety for making pimiento cheese — the classic Southern spread requiring the specific thick-walled, sweet, very mild flesh of the true pimiento variety.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pimiento (also spelled pimento) is the traditional thick-walled sweet pepper of Spanish and Southern American tradition — producing heart-shaped to rounded, medium-sized (3–4 inches) fruits with exceptionally thick, sweet, juicy walls and very mild, sweet flavor with no heat. The thick walls and very sweet, low-acid flesh are the defining qualities that distinguish pimiento from other sweet peppers: the wall thickness (often twice that of standard bell peppers) makes pimiento ideal for roasting, stuffing, and jar-packing, while the sweetness and mildness make it the original pepper for stuffed olives and the authentic ingredient in Southern pimiento cheese. The fruits ripen from green to a deep, vivid red and are at their best flavor when fully red. Pimiento is less commonly found in grocery stores than bell peppers (most commercial pimiento production goes to food processing), making it a particularly worthwhile home garden variety for cooks who want the authentic ingredient. The plants are productive, compact, and well-adapted to Gulf South growing conditions. In zone 9, pimiento peppers have two productive seasons: spring planting (February–March transplant, harvest May–July) and fall planting (August transplant, harvest October–November). The rich red color and exceptional thick-walled quality make pimiento one of the finest peppers for roasting whole.

common_name: Pimiento de Padrón Pepper (Spanish Tapas Pepper, One-in-Ten Hot Novelty Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Padrón peppers are harvested very young (1.5–2 inches long) at the green stage before any heat develops — the occasional hot fruit is random and appears even in young peppers. Harvest when fruits are small, bright green, and smooth; larger, older fruits are more likely to be hot. In zone 9, transplant March–April for spring and summer production. Padrón plants are prolific and compact (18–24 inch), making them well-suited to container growing and small gardens. The tradition of gambling on which pepper will be hot is a cherished element of eating Padrón peppers in Spanish culinary culture.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 78–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest peppers when small (1.5–2 inches), bright green, and tender. Cook whole in a screaming-hot cast iron skillet with olive oil and coarse salt — the classic preparation. Pimiento de Padrón (Padrón Pepper) is a small Spanish sweet frying pepper from the municipality of Padrón in Galicia, northwestern Spain — famous throughout Spain and now internationally for its unusual roulette-like characteristic: most fruits (roughly 9 in 10) are mild and sweet, but a small percentage of fruits within any given harvest are randomly and intensely hot (estimated 5,000–20,000 Scoville units). The heat distribution is random — you cannot visually distinguish hot from mild fruits, and the proportion of hot fruits increases as the season progresses and when plants are under stress. This unpredictability makes eating Padrón peppers a social ritual: they are placed in a bowl and eaten communally, with everyone alerting the group when they encounter the occasional hot pepper, providing a light gambling element to the meal. The Galician expression 'os pementos de Padrón, uns pican e outros non' ('Padrón peppers: some are hot, some are not') has become one of the most recognized food sayings in Spanish culture. The traditional preparation — whole peppers blistered in very hot olive oil and salted — is now a standard tapas preparation across Spain and in Spanish restaurants worldwide.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pineapple ground cherry is a named selection of the cape gooseberry type with especially sweet, intensely tropical pineapple-vanilla flavor in small, papery-husked fruits that drop from the plant when ripe — an extraordinary, underused fruit for snacking, baking, and preserves.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Pineapple Ground Cherry is a named selection of the ground cherry (Physalis pruinosa) grown for its small (1/2–3/4 inch), golden-yellow fruits enclosed in dry, papery, tan husks (lantern-like husks much smaller than tomatillo husks) with an intensely sweet, tropical flavor reminiscent of pineapple, vanilla, and caramel — completely unlike tomatillos in flavor despite being related. The fruits drop from the plant when fully ripe and are gathered from the ground (hence the name); this drop-when-ripe characteristic is the easiest ripeness indicator. Extraordinarily productive in warm weather, with hundreds of fruits per plant. Delicious eaten fresh, in pies (often compared to cape gooseberry pies), in jams, and dried like raisins. A charming and unusual fruit for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that is barely known to most gardeners.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: This high-yielding beefsteak ripens to yellow-orange marbled with red streaks running through the meaty, low-acid flesh. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and need strong staking or caging. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water consistently to reduce cracking on the large fruit. Prune suckers lightly to boost airflow and support ripening of these big tomatoes.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring and July for fall. Tomatillos require at least two plants from different seed sources for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set; plant Pineapple Tomatillo alongside a green-fruiting type for maximum production. The papery husk turns tan and splits as fruits mature to gold-yellow.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pineapple Tomatillo is a named selection of Physalis ixocarpa that ripens to a distinctive golden-yellow rather than the standard tomatillo green, with a noticeably sweeter, more tropical flavor that includes a pineapple-like brightness absent from green-fruiting types. The medium-sized fruits, typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, fill and split the papery husk as they ripen to gold, at which point they are at peak sweetness. The sweeter profile makes Pineapple Tomatillo less acidic than standard green tomatillos and more suitable for fresh eating out of hand, in fruit salsas, or in preparations where a less tart tomatillo flavor is desired. Standard green tomatillos provide better classic salsa verde acidity; Pineapple works best where a milder, sweeter, more unusual tomatillo experience is the goal. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination.

common_name: Pineapple Tomato (Giant Bicolor Yellow-Red Heirloom Beefsteak)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Pineapple produces very large fruits that take significant time to develop — start seeds early to maximize the harvest window before summer heat causes fruit quality to decline.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pineapple is one of the most visually spectacular heirloom beefsteak tomatoes — producing enormous (1–2 lb), irregular, slightly ribbed fruits with a stunning bicolor pattern of golden-yellow base skin marked with bold red and orange streaking and marbling that creates a stained-glass appearance when sliced. The cut surface reveals a similarly bicolor red-and-yellow flesh pattern — an ornamental quality that makes Pineapple outstanding for fresh salads and sliced presentations where the visual effect can be appreciated. The flavor matches the visual quality: intensely sweet, fruity, and complex with a low-acid, tropical quality that justifies the variety's evocative name — the combination of golden-yellow color and sweet, fruity flavor genuinely suggests tropical fruit. Large, vigorous indeterminate plants require sturdy support (minimum 6-foot cage or stake). As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from the most characteristic fruits for replanting. In zone 9, Pineapple produces best in the spring season (March–June) before summer heat arrives; the very large fruits require a relatively long, cool growing period for maximum development.

common_name: Ping Tung Long Eggplant (Taiwanese Heirloom Slender Purple Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Ping Tung Long is a Taiwan heirloom adapted to hot, humid conditions, making it an excellent choice for Gulf South gardens. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall harvest. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches long and still deep lavender-purple before any brown coloration develops at the calyx. Plants benefit from staking when fruit load is heavy — the long fruits can cause branches to lean.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches and still vivid lavender-purple. Ping Tung Long (named for Pingtung County in southern Taiwan where it originates) is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant representing the classic Asian long eggplant type at its finest — producing exceptionally long (12–16 inch), slender, slightly curved, vivid lavender-purple to violet fruits with thin, tender skin. The variety is among the most widely grown and highly regarded long Asian eggplants in Taiwan and throughout the Chinese-American gardening community in the United States, where it has been maintained as an open-pollinated heirloom for multiple generations. The fruits are characterized by extremely thin, tender skin (no peeling needed), virtually no seeds, and very sweet, mild flesh with no bitterness — a flavor profile considered superior for raw preparations and quick stir-fries where the tender skin softens immediately without extended cooking. The vivid lavender-purple color is particularly attractive in the garden and at the table. Ping Tung Long's heat tolerance and prolific production in hot conditions make it especially well-suited to southern gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; eggplant needs sustained warmth and benefits from bottom heat during germination. Transplant in zone 9 February–March for a long growing season; eggplant thrives in the heat and often continues producing through October–November.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pingtung Long is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant that produces slender, 12–18 inch fruits in a vibrant lavender-purple, among the longest eggplant fruits available. The skin is exceptionally thin and tender with minimal bitterness, making it prized for quick stir-fries and grilling without peeling. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, continuing to set fruit through the hot zone 9 summers when other eggplant varieties may pause. Harvest fruits young when skin is glossy and before seeds develop; overripe fruits become seedy and bitter. A heavy producer that may need light staking to support the long, heavy fruits.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after all frost danger.
directions: Pink Banana is a large heirloom winter squash producing elongated, pink-skinned fruits with sweet, tender orange flesh on vigorous vines that can run fifteen feet. The big fruits store well for months in a cool, dry place. Direct sow into warm, rich soil in full sun after frost, giving the sprawling vines plenty of space. Harvest when the rind hardens and skin turns pink, then cure the squash before storing.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pink Brandywine is the original pink-fleshed Brandywine heirloom and the one that gave the variety its legendary reputation for flavor — the Sudduth strain and Platfoot strain are the two main true-breeding lineages, both producing large, pink, irregular fruits of extraordinary depth of flavor.
directions: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost, burying 2/3 of the stem, and stake or cage immediately — Pink Brandywine produces tall, sprawling, potato-leaved vines that are challenging to support and slow to set fruit. Pink Brandywine (distinct from the yellow Brandywine and red Brandywine strains) is widely considered by heirloom tomato enthusiasts to be the definitive Brandywine — a large (12–24 oz), oblate to irregular, deep pink-skinned, pink-fleshed tomato with extraordinary, complex, sweet-rich flavor that lacks the sharp acidity of red tomatoes; many growers consider it the best-tasting tomato they have ever grown. The Sudduth and Platfoot strains (the two main documented lineages preserved by Seed Savers Exchange) are both potato-leaved (a genetic marker associated with the true Brandywine) and behave similarly in the garden. A notoriously slow, difficult, but rewarding grow — plants are late to mature and require long, warm seasons, but the fruit quality when conditions are right is unmatched.

common_name: Pink Eye Purple Hull Pea (Classic Gulf South Dual-Color Summer Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull peas are highly heat-tolerant — they thrive and produce abundantly in Gulf South summer heat that limits production of most other vegetables.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull is one of the most widely grown and deeply traditional southern pea varieties of the Gulf South — a semi-bush to vining type producing distinctive purple-hulled pods that make harvest timing and identification visually clear (green hulls shade to purple as the peas approach maturity), with cream-white peas marked by a distinctive pink to rose-colored 'eye' or hilum that gives the variety its evocative name. The pink eye is the identifying mark: when a pot of fresh-shelled Pink Eye Purple Hull peas is spread on the counter, the cream peas with their small pink-rose eye marks are immediately recognizable as this specific variety. The flavor is excellent — classic southern pea quality with a rich, earthy, beany sweetness that is characteristic of the Gulf South summer pea tradition. Pink Eye Purple Hull is extremely productive in Gulf South conditions, continuing to produce through summer heat that limits most other garden vegetables. It is among the most important vegetable crops of the traditional Gulf South summer garden, providing fresh food through July, August, and September when garden production from other crops has ended. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. The purple hulls are ornamentally attractive in the garden and make identifying ripe pods easy and unambiguous.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in February–March for a spring crop. Stake or cage heavily — Pink Ponderosa vines are tall (5–7 feet) and produce very large, heavy fruits that require solid support. In zone 9 a fall planting in August for October–November harvest often produces better-quality fruit with fewer cracks.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy staking; Pink Ponderosa (also called 'Henderson's Pink Ponderosa') is a late 19th-century American heirloom tomato introduced by the Henderson seed company around 1891, noted for producing enormous, beefsteak-type fruits of a distinctive deep rose-pink color — the 'pink' refers to the red flesh showing through the colorless (no yellow pigment in skin) skin, creating the characteristic pink-red appearance of traditional beefsteak-type heirlooms. The very large fruits (often 1–2 pounds each) are meaty, low-acid, and juicy with a mild, sweet, rich tomato flavor that made Ponderosa-type tomatoes the standard fresh-eating tomato for most of the 20th century before uniform-color commercial hybrids replaced them. The indeterminate vine produces continuously until frost and can be especially productive in zone 9's long growing season. The mild, low-acid flavor makes Pink Ponderosa particularly appealing for sliced tomatoes where the full fruit flavor is experienced without cooking.

plant_note: Direct sow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade as soon as soil can be worked in spring; pink purslane self-sows prolifically in suitable shaded, moist conditions and will naturalize to provide a self-replenishing supply of edible greens in the woodland garden.
directions: Direct sow in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade as soon as soil can be worked; pink purslane (Siberian miner's lettuce) is a small, delicate annual or biennial native to Siberia and the Pacific Coast of North America that produces a rosette of fleshy, pale-green, succulent leaves and distinctive stems that pierce directly through their paired leaves (perfoliate, like its American relative Claytonia perfoliata), topped with clusters of small, pink, five-petaled flowers in spring. All parts are edible — the tender leaves, stems, and flowers are mild, slightly succulent, and pleasant in salads. Unlike most salad greens, pink purslane grows enthusiastically in full shade and can be naturalized as a self-sowing edible groundcover in shaded woodland gardens and under deciduous trees, where it self-sows to provide a recurring supply of early spring greens. Goes to seed quickly in heat but will resow for fall crops.

common_name: Pinkeye Purple Hull Cowpea (Southern Pea, Purple Hull Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep, 3–4 inches apart in rows 24–36 inches apart after soil thoroughly warms to 65°F and all frost danger passes; in zone 9, plant from late March through late July for successive harvests — Pinkeye Purple Hull is one of the most heat-tolerant crops and thrives in the peak Gulf South summer.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; Pinkeye Purple Hull is the most widely grown and most beloved Southern pea (cowpea) cultivar in Gulf South gardens — a semi-vining bush variety producing pods with a distinctive purple hull (pod exterior) that turns from green to vivid purple-magenta at the ideal harvest stage for fresh-shelling, making it easy to identify perfect harvest timing. The peas inside have the distinctive pink 'eye' (hilum marking) characteristic of this type, with a rich, full, starchy-creamy flavor that is the authentic taste of Southern cooking — distinctive, earthy, and satisfying in ways that fresh garden peas cannot replicate. Cowpeas are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables in cultivation and actually perform best during the hottest summer months when most other crops fail — the Gulf South summer that defeats beans, cucumbers, and squash is ideal cowpea growing weather. They fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule bacteria, enriching the soil for follow-on crops. For fresh eating, harvest when the majority of the pod has turned purple and feels firm and fully rounded but before the pod dries. For dried peas, allow the pods to turn tan and dry completely on the vine. The dried peas store indefinitely and are the foundation of traditional Southern New Year's black-eyed pea dishes.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; grow to full maturity for dry beans.
directions: Pinto is a heat- and drought-tolerant bush bean grown as a dry bean, producing pods of speckled beans on upright plants with short runners. Direct sow after frost into warm soil in full sun, and let the pods dry fully on the plant. Water moderately during flowering and pod set, then ease off as pods mature. Harvest when pods are brown and brittle, then shell and dry the beans further for storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring and July–August for fall. Pinto beans are primarily a dry bean — the plant must be allowed to fully mature and dry before harvest, which takes the full season. In zone 9 the spring crop typically produces dry beans by June–July; a fall planting dried in November–December. Bush habit requires no staking.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; pinto beans are the most widely grown dry bean in the United States, accounting for nearly half of all dry bean production, and the foundation of Southwestern and Mexican cooking — the primary bean in refried beans (frijoles refritos), bean soup, and chili. The tan seeds with reddish-brown speckles (the Spanish name 'pinto' means 'painted') turn uniformly tan-brown when cooked, at which point the flavor is rich, earthy, and starchy with a creamy texture that falls apart when mashed. Bush-habit pinto plants are compact and self-supporting, producing a single concentrated harvest suitable for home-scale production and storage. The dry beans store for 2–3 years in a cool, dry location. In zone 9 the plants are susceptible to bean rust in humid conditions; provide adequate spacing for air circulation.

common_name: Piquillo Pepper (Spanish Roasting Pepper, Lodosa Piquillo)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes; piquillo is a compact, highly productive sweet Spanish pepper turning vivid red at maturity with a characteristic pointed tip (piquillo = 'little beak') — the most important preserved pepper in Spanish cuisine, roasted and packed in jars, and a staple ingredient in tapas, pintxos, and modern Spanish cooking.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after frost danger passes; piquillo plants are compact and productive, setting numerous small, triangular fruits; harvest at full vivid red maturity; roast over open flame or under a broiler until charred, steam to loosen skin, peel and seed for the classic preparation. Piquillo is the defining preserved pepper of northern Spain, particularly the Navarra region around the town of Lodosa (in the Ebro River valley) where the Denomination of Origin 'Piquillo de Lodosa' protects the traditional pepper and its preparation. The pepper is small (2–3 inch), triangular to slightly flattened-conical with a characteristic pointed 'beak' tip (piquillo = 'little beak'), vivid scarlet-red at maturity, and sweet to very mildly pungent with no significant heat. The flesh is thin but intensely sweet and slightly fruity, with a subtle bitterness that is balanced by the roasting process — fire-roasting is inseparable from the piquillo's culinary identity. The traditional preparation involves hand-roasting individual peppers over wood fires, peeling and seeding each one by hand without any water washing (to preserve flavor and sugars), and packing them in their own juices in jars or tins without any additional preservation except salt. The result is one of the most refined and flavorful preserved vegetables in world cuisine. Jarred piquillo peppers are a staple of Spanish kitchens and are used stuffed with salt cod or cheese, arranged on pintxos, layered in pasta dishes, and pureed into smooth sauces. Growing piquillo at home and roasting them yourself produces a quality that commercially jarred peppers rarely match.

common_name: Piracicaba Broccoli (Heat-Tolerant Brazilian Sprouting Broccoli for Warm Climates)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting to garden; in zone 9, start seeds in August–September for fall transplanting in September–October, targeting harvest December–March. Piracicaba was developed in Brazil for production in subtropical warm-winter conditions where standard heading broccoli (such as Packman or Marathon) struggles with heat-induced bolting and premature heading. Rather than forming a single large central head, Piracicaba produces an abundance of small, tender loose florets on branching side shoots over an extended harvest period — a sprouting habit similar to De Cicco broccoli but with dramatically better heat tolerance. In zone 9, Piracicaba can be harvested continuously through the mild winter rather than requiring a single-harvest timing, and it continues producing side shoots well into spring when standard broccoli bolts.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant to garden in fall for zone 9 winter harvest. Harvest loose florets continuously. Piracicaba Broccoli originated at the Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) and agronomic research stations near Piracicaba, a city in São Paulo state, Brazil — a major center of Brazilian tropical agricultural research. The variety was developed specifically to address the fundamental incompatibility between standard broccoli breeding (which targets cool-climate heading formation) and the subtropical conditions of southern Brazil and other warm-climate growing regions. Standard broccoli varieties were bred primarily in Europe and California's cool coastal fog belt, where temperature ranges precisely suited to head development allow reliable production; in warm climates, standard broccoli heats prematurely, forms loose, open heads of poor quality, or bolts before any marketable crop develops. Piracicaba's breeding solution was to select for a sprouting growth habit that produces continuously rather than forming a single marketable head — an approach that converts the temperature sensitivity of head formation from a problem into an advantage. Since the plant never forms a central head to be ruined by heat, there is no precise temperature window to miss, and the plant produces usable florets across a much broader temperature range. The florets of Piracicaba are small and tender, with a delicate texture superior to the sometimes-coarse texture of oversized main-head broccoli, and the continuous harvest over weeks or months provides far greater total yield per plant than single-harvest heading types in favorable conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Capsicum frutescens peppers benefit from a longer indoor growing period than C. annuum. In zones 9–11 the plants grow as woody perennials and become increasingly productive in their second and third years.
directions: Start indoors early and transplant to warm, well-drained soil; piri piri is an African cultivar of Capsicum frutescens (the same species as tabasco pepper) producing small, erect, vivid red to orange fruits 1–2 inches long with an intense, bright heat (50,000–175,000 SHU). It is the essential ingredient in the famous Portuguese piri piri sauce, brought to Portugal from its colonies in Angola and Mozambique in the 1500s, and is now central to Portuguese, South African, and Mozambican cuisines. Nando's Peri-Peri sauce is based on this pepper. The fruits are blended with garlic, lemon, and oil to make a marinade-sauce for grilled chicken. Plants become perennial subshrubs in zones 9–11 and produce prolifically year-round.

common_name: Plum Regal Tomato (Disease-Resistant Plum Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Plum Regal is a determinate paste-type tomato that sets a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks. In zone 9, aim for spring harvest in May–June by transplanting in early March.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Plum Regal is a determinate plum-type paste tomato developed by Cornell University's tomato breeding program specifically to improve on the disease susceptibility of heirloom Roma and similar paste types while maintaining the thick walls, dense flesh, and low moisture content that make plum tomatoes superior for sauce-making and processing. Plum Regal carries resistance to late blight (Phytophthora infestans) — the disease that wiped out heirloom paste tomatoes across much of the Northeast during the late blight epidemic of 2009 — as well as Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt. The medium-large (3–5 oz), deep red, oval fruits have very thick walls, small seed cavities, and excellent sauce-making characteristics with rich, concentrated tomato flavor. An outstanding choice for humid-climate paste tomato production, for home canners who want reliable crops without the disease susceptibility of traditional paste heirlooms, and for any gardener growing tomatoes where late blight or Fusarium are recurring problems.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant 2 weeks after frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in warm starting mix and provide bottom heat around 80°F to speed germination. Transplant to fertile, well-drained soil once nights are consistently above 55°F. Water deeply but infrequently to encourage deep rooting and reduce disease pressure. Harvest dark green fruits at 4–5 inches long for fresh use, or allow to turn red and dry them for ancho chiles.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost date; transplant into warm, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February for spring production and again in late July for fall production.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Poblano is the classic Mexican culinary pepper — a mildly hot (1,000–2,000 Scoville units), wide, heart-shaped to triangular pepper that is the foundational ingredient in chiles rellenos, mole negro, and dozens of traditional Mexican dishes. Harvested green (poblano) or dried red (ancho or mulato depending on variety), these peppers have a rich, complex, slightly smoky flavor with moderate heat that defines the deep, layered character of traditional Mexican cuisine. The large, thick-walled fruits reach 4–5 inches long and 2.5–3 inches wide, with deep green color maturing to red-brown. Poblano is one of the most heat-tolerant culinary peppers and performs exceptionally well in zone 9's summer temperatures — unlike many sweet bell peppers, poblano tolerates the high summer heat of the Gulf South and continues producing through the hottest months with consistent irrigation. In zone 9, the plant can become a perennial woody shrub if protected from hard freezes, producing for 2–3 years from a single planting. Dry ripe red-brown poblanos to make ancho chiles — a key ingredient in red mole — by hanging in bundles in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 3–4 weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Poinsett 76 is a Clemson University breeding program selection from the original Poinsett variety, released in 1976 and still widely grown in the Southeast for its outstanding combination of disease resistance, heat tolerance, and production in hot, humid conditions that challenges most cucumber varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; provide support or allow vines to sprawl with 3–4 feet between hills. Poinsett 76 was developed by the Clemson University vegetable breeding program in South Carolina and released in 1976 as an improved selection of the original Poinsett cucumber (released 1966) — both named for Joel R. Poinsett, the South Carolinian who brought the poinsettia plant from Mexico. Poinsett 76 is distinguished by its outstanding disease resistance package (angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy mildew, mosaic, and powdery mildew resistance) and heat tolerance that makes it the cucumber of choice for hot, humid Southeastern gardens where most varieties decline quickly in summer; fruits are 7–8 inches long, dark green, cylindrical, and of good eating quality. An open-pollinated, seed-saveable classic that remains one of the best choices for Gulf Coast and Deep South summer cucumber production.

plant_note: Propagate from stem or root cuttings — both male and female plants are required for fruit production, so plant at least one of each; pointed gourd is dioecious and does not fruit from seeds alone without confirmed plant sex. Grows perennially in zones 10–12 and as an annual in zones 8–9.
directions: Propagate from rooted stem cuttings or root sections, planting male and female plants together (ratio of 1 male per 4–6 females); train on a strong trellis in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; pointed gourd is one of the most popular vegetables in Bengali, Odia, and North Indian cuisine, prized for its tender 2–6 inch elongated fruits with green-and-white striped skin that are stuffed, curried, fried, or used in sweets when fully mature. Distinct from snake gourd (Trichosanthes cucumerina) in being much smaller, more compact, and preferred for cooking fresh and stuffed. Plants in zone 9 may freeze to the ground in winter but resprout from the roots in spring; mulch heavily in the first winter. Harvest fruits when they reach 3–4 inches for best culinary quality.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is warm; erect a trellis or pole structure before sowing to avoid disturbing roots later.
directions: Plant seeds 1 in deep at the base of a sturdy trellis or teepee of poles set 6–8 ft tall, spacing 3 seeds per pole. Vines twine naturally but may need early guidance toward supports. Harvest pods before seeds bulge prominently for the tenderest texture. Pole beans produce over a longer season than bush types, so keep picking to prevent pod maturation from stopping new flower set.

common_name: Polish White Softneck Garlic (Eastern European Heirloom Artichoke Garlic)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves in fall at or around first frost; Polish White is a traditional Eastern European softneck garlic (Artichoke type) with origins in Poland and surrounding countries, where garlic has been grown as a staple crop for centuries — it produces medium-large bulbs with 10–16 tightly packed cloves, clean white skins, and a reliable, full-flavored character suited to all cooking uses and excellent storage of 10–12 months.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall from 4 weeks before first frost to shortly after; Polish White performs well in both cold northern climates and mild southern winters; harvest in summer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly before storage; braid the flexible stems for attractive long-term storage. Polish White is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic originating in Poland and the broader Eastern European garlic-growing tradition, where garlic has been a staple culinary and medicinal crop since ancient times; it entered the North American heirloom garlic collection through the immigrant communities and seed-saver networks that preserved traditional European agricultural varieties throughout the 20th century. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) with tightly packed multiple layers of cloves (10–16 per bulb) in the characteristic Artichoke arrangement, with clean white to ivory outer skins and a compact, rounded shape. The flavor is full, moderately pungent, and satisfying — not as complex as the finest Rocambole or Marbled Purple Stripe hardnecks, but very reliable and versatile for all cooking uses from fresh salsas and aioli to long-cooked soups, stews, and roasted garlic. The primary virtues of Polish White are reliability (excellent performance in a wide range of climates), productivity (high-yielding compared to hardneck types), and outstanding storage life of 10–12 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark) — making it the garlic of choice for those who want a year-round supply from a single fall planting.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions 3–4 inches deep in moist, well-drained, organically rich soil after temperatures remain above 65°F; this understory plant prefers partial shade and consistent moisture year-round in its tropical range.
directions: Plant rhizome pieces in humid, tropical or subtropical gardens in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil; this Pacific island staple grows naturally in coastal and forest-edge habitats from East Africa to Polynesia. The deeply lobed leaves are attractive, and by 6–9 months the underground rhizomes are large enough to harvest; raw rhizomes are bitter and mildly toxic due to tannins and must be grated, washed repeatedly in water, and dried to yield a pure white starch. The fine arrowroot-like starch, called pia in Hawaii and Polynesia, was a critical famine food and is used to thicken sauces and puddings; it is entirely gluten-free and easily digestible. Outside zones 10–12 grow as a container plant brought indoors for winter, maintaining warmth and humidity.

plant_note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-draining soil once temperatures are consistently above 70 degrees F, in a partially shaded to bright-indirect light location.
directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, organically rich, well-draining soil in a partially shaded location, spacing them 3-5 feet apart to accommodate the large, deeply lobed umbrella-like leaves. Water moderately and consistently through the growing season, allowing the top inch of soil to dry slightly between waterings to prevent tuber rot. The plants go dormant during dry seasons, so reduce water and allow the tops to die back naturally before lifting or leaving tubers in place in frost-free areas. To process tubers for starch, grate and thoroughly wash the flesh through multiple changes of water, then allow the settled starch to dry completely before use as a fine, high-quality thickener.

common_name: Poona Kheera Cucumber (Indian Heirloom Color-Changing Cucumber)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Poona Kheera is an Indian heirloom cucumber that dramatically changes color as it matures — from white to pale yellow to apple-yellow and finally to russet-tan — and is prized for its exceptional flavor at the yellow stage and above, good heat tolerance, and thin, easily digestible skin; one of the most beloved traditional cucumber varieties in the Pune (Poona) region of Maharashtra, India.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep and provide a trellis for best production; harvest at any stage from white (mild, crisp) to apple-yellow (sweetest, most complex) to russet (mellow, slightly sweet and aromatic); the yellow-to-russet stage is the traditional eating stage in India but many American gardeners prefer the pale yellow stage for fresh salads. Poona Kheera is an heirloom cucumber from the Pune (formerly Poona) region of Maharashtra state in western India, where it has been grown for centuries as the primary cucumber of the region and is still widely available in Indian markets. The most distinctive characteristic of this variety is its remarkable color change through the maturation cycle: young fruits are white or pale ivory, then transition to pale yellow, apple-yellow, golden-yellow, and finally to a warm russet-tan at full maturity — no other commonly grown cucumber goes through such a dramatic color progression. The flavor also changes with color: white fruits are mild, crisp, and relatively bland; yellow fruits have developed characteristic cucumber fragrance, sweetness, and complexity; russet fruits have an almost apple-like sweetness and aroma distinct from young cucumber flavor. In the Indian culinary tradition, the yellow-to-russet stage is preferred for eating raw out of hand, in raitas, and for cooking; American gardeners often prefer the yellow stage for salads where the flavor is sweet and the flesh remains crisp. Poona Kheera has good heat tolerance compared to standard slicing cucumbers and adapts well to Gulf Coast and Southern growing conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow at or up to 2 weeks after last frost once soil reaches at least 60°F. Isolate from sweet corn by at least 250 feet or time plantings to avoid simultaneous silking.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for proper wind pollination, isolating from sweet corn to prevent cross-pollination that ruins eating quality. Side-dress with nitrogen at knee-height and again when tassels appear. Leave ears on the stalk past eating stage until husks are completely brown and papery; pull husks back and hang ears in a dry, ventilated spot for 4–6 weeks until kernels release from the cob easily. Kernels are ready to pop when moisture content drops to around 14%.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost when soil is warm.
directions: Bred by Wild Boar Farms, this true-yellow beefsteak has a sweet flavor with citrus notes and slightly flattened 8 to 12 ounce fruits. Being indeterminate, the vines grow tall and benefit from sturdy staking. Start seeds indoors, transplant into warm soil, and water evenly to prevent cracking. Let fruit ripen fully to yellow for the sweetest flavor, picking regularly to sustain production.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Porter is an outstanding heat and drought-tolerant tomato for Texas and the Gulf Coast — historically the most widely grown home garden tomato in Texas, it performs reliably in hot, dry conditions where other varieties wilt and fail to fruit.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Porter tomato is a Texas heirloom introduced around 1897–1900 by the Porter & Sons seed company of San Antonio, developed or selected specifically for the demanding conditions of Texas summers — heat, drought, and alkaline soils that would destroy most Eastern varieties. The small to medium (4–6 oz), pinkish-red, slightly oval fruits grow in clusters and have rich, concentrated flavor enhanced by mild water stress. Porter is genuinely drought tolerant and produces in Texas summer heat when standard varieties quit blooming. Historically the most important garden tomato in Central and South Texas, where generations of families grew it through conditions that would kill Brandywine or Cherokee Purple. For any gardener in the hot, dry interior South or Southwest struggling with summer tomato production, Porter is the essential starting point.

plant_note: Plant slips (rooted cuttings from sprouted storage roots) after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant April–June for a September–November harvest. Porto Rico is a full-vine variety that spreads more widely than bush types and is best grown with ample space or on a mound system to control spreading.
directions: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained, slightly sandy soil amended with organic matter in full sun; Porto Rico is one of the oldest named American sweet potato varieties, recorded since the early 1900s and widely grown in Louisiana, Mississippi, and the Gulf Coast region for generations before the introduction of Beauregard and Covington. The medium-sized, copper-skinned tubers have bright orange, moist flesh with a rich, sweet, creamy flavor — considered by many Southern gardeners to have superior taste to modern commercial varieties. The vining plants spread widely, up to 10 feet, and should be positioned in open areas or at garden edges. Cure harvested roots at 85°F with high humidity for 7–10 days before storage to maximize sweetness and shelf life.

common_name: Portuguese Kale (Tronchuda Kale, Couve Tronchuda, Caldo Verde Cabbage)
plant_note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost for spring planting; for fall production in zones 7–10, direct sow or transplant 10–12 weeks before first fall frost.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to well-enriched, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Portuguese kale (couve tronchuda) forms large, loose heads with broad leaves featuring wide white midribs that are milder and more tender than common kale — both the leaf blades and the thick midribs are cooked, the midribs simmered until very tender in the traditional Portuguese soup caldo verde where the leaves are sliced into thin chiffonade with potatoes and chouriço. More heat-tolerant than most kales and excellent in zone 8–10 gardens where it can be grown nearly year-round; harvest leaves from the outside in, leaving the center growing point intact.

common_name: Pot-a-peno Pepper (Compact Container Jalapeño, AAS Winner)
plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Pot-a-peno is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for container growing, producing a full crop of true jalapeño-flavored peppers on a compact plant well under a foot tall.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into a large container or garden bed after danger of frost has passed. Pot-a-peno was bred specifically to solve a common problem with growing jalapeños on a patio or balcony — most jalapeño varieties grow too large and sprawling for small containers — by combining a genuinely dwarf, compact plant habit with full-sized, full-flavored jalapeño fruit and strong productivity. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining container-friendly size with reliable yield and classic jalapeño heat and flavor, unlike many ornamental dwarf peppers bred for looks rather than culinary use. Fruits mature from green to red if left on the plant, with red fruits noticeably sweeter and slightly hotter than green. Because the plant is so compact, it benefits from a slightly richer potting mix and more frequent watering and feeding than an in-ground pepper, since a small root zone dries out and depletes nutrients faster. Harvest fruits at the green stage for classic jalapeño flavor or let them ripen to red for a sweeter, smokier heat, useful for chipotle-style drying.

plant_note: Plant seed pieces 2–4 weeks before last frost when soil reaches 45°F; in warm climates a second planting is made in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Plant certified seed potatoes cut to egg-sized pieces (each with 1–2 eyes) 4 in deep in trenches spaced 30 in apart. Hill soil up around the stems as they grow, keeping tubers covered to prevent greening from light exposure. Water consistently and watch for late blight in humid weather — infected foliage should be removed promptly to protect tubers. Harvest new potatoes when plants flower, or cure full-season types for a week at room temperature before long-term storage.

plant_note: Plant bulbs in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze in zones 5–9; in zones 3–4, plant as early as possible in spring.
directions: Plant individual bulbs 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile soil — large bulbs planted in fall will multiply into a cluster of 8–12 medium onions, while small bulbs tend to produce fewer but larger bulbs. Potato onions are a multiplier onion type that propagates entirely by bulb division, forming a cluster of bulbs in the same way shallots do; no seed is needed or typically produced. Allow tops to fall over and begin to yellow before harvesting the entire cluster; cure in a warm, airy spot for 2–3 weeks. Save the smallest bulbs from the cluster for replanting, perpetuating the variety indefinitely without seed purchases.

plant_note: Transplant into a warm, sunny spot in well-drained or sandy soil after last frost has passed and nighttime temperatures are reliably above freezing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant to a dry, sunny location with sandy or well-drained soil after frost danger has passed. This compact native perennial produces small, sweet-to-tart yellow berries enclosed in papery husks that ripen from midsummer through fall. It is notably more drought-tolerant than tomatillo or cape gooseberry and thrives on neglect once established. Plants spread slowly by rhizomes to form loose colonies, making them a productive and low-maintenance addition to dryland food gardens or prairie restoration plantings.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs 2–3 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil; prairie onion naturalizes readily and will self-seed to expand its colony over time. Seeds can also be sown in fall for spring germination.
directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained to dry soil in full sun; prairie onion is a native North American allium of the central prairies and upper South, producing attractive spherical clusters of rose-pink to lavender flowers in late summer when few other bulbs bloom. All parts are edible — bulbs, leaves, and flowers — with a mild onion flavor used by Plains indigenous peoples as a wild food and flavoring. The upright, flat leaves emerge in spring, provide texture through summer, and the flowers appear in August and September when hummingbirds and late-season butterflies are active. It is both a functional edible garden plant and a beautiful native wildflower for dry, sunny prairie or meadow gardens. Increases steadily by bulb division and self-seeding.

plant_note: Sow scarified seeds in very well-drained, lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; prairie turnip develops a deep, starchy taproot and requires 2–3 years to reach harvestable size. It absolutely requires excellent drainage and resents transplanting once the root has formed. Native to the dry, lean shortgrass and mixed-grass prairies of the Great Plains.
directions: Sow in very well-drained, lean, prairie-type soil in full sun; prairie turnip (tipsin, breadroot) is one of the most important food plants of the North American Plains tribes — a critical starch staple for the Lakota, Blackfoot, Comanche, and many other Plains peoples, who harvested, dried, and braided the turnip-like starchy roots for winter storage. The roots, which resemble parsnips with a brown outer skin and white starchy interior, were eaten raw, boiled, roasted, or ground into flour. Lewis and Clark documented trading for them with the Mandan people. The plant itself is small and unobtrusive — a low-growing perennial with gray-green, divided leaves and small clusters of lavender-blue pea flowers in late spring. The root can reach 2–4 inches in diameter and 4–8 inches in length on mature plants. As a nitrogen-fixing legume of the dry prairie, it improves lean, poor soils. An important plant for food forest, edible prairie, and cultural heritage gardens and for ecologically-minded gardens on the Great Plains.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; also sow in late summer for fall and winter harvest.
directions: This blend mixes Dwarf Blue Curled, Dwarf Siberian Improved, Lacinato, and Red Russian kale for a range of colors, textures, and flavors. Harvest baby greens in about 25 days or let plants size up for full leaves. Sow directly in cool soil and thin as they grow, picking outer leaves so plants keep producing. Frost sweetens the flavor, making it a great fall and winter crop.

subcategory: aquatic edible seed Asian water lily
plant_note: Sow seeds in shallow water or press seeds into aquatic container soil in late spring when water temperatures exceed 70°F in full sun in zone 8–12; Euryale ferox (Prickly Water Lily, Gorgon Plant, Fox Nut) is a monotypic Asian aquatic grown primarily for its starchy, popped seeds — makhana — a major crop in Bihar, India — and ornamentally for its enormous spiny floating leaves that can reach 5 feet across.
directions: Direct sow Euryale ferox seeds in warm, still, shallow water in full sun; press seeds into heavy clay loam at the pond bottom or in sunken aquatic pots, spacing plants 5–10 feet apart to accommodate the enormous leaves; fertilize with aquatic tablets monthly for maximum leaf and seed production. The Prickly Water Lily is an annual or short-lived perennial aquatic in the Victoria family, native to southeastern Asia from India to Japan — the only species in its genus. Its enormous spiny floating leaves (up to 5 feet across, dark green above and deep purple-red below), covered in sharp prickles on both surfaces, are among the most dramatic of all aquatic plants. The seeds — dried and popped to make makhana (fox nuts) — are a prized crop in the Mithila region of Bihar and widely consumed across India, Nepal, and China for their high starch content and nutty flavor. In warm climates, the plant grows extremely fast and can form a dense, nearly impenetrable floating mat; harvest seeds in late summer as seed pods ripen and begin to sink. In zone 8, it may self-sow from seeds that overwinter in pond mud; in zone 10–12, it may behave as a short-lived perennial.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; amaranth is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant grain crops available and requires little supplemental water once established.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun; amaranth is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant grain crops available and requires little supplemental water once established. Amaranthus hypochondriacus was one of the three staple crops of Aztec civilization (along with maize and beans), consumed as grain in porridge and flatbreads (tamales de alegría) and in ritual religious offerings to Huitzilopochtli; the Spanish conquistadors banned its cultivation as part of their campaign against Aztec religion, contributing to the decline of amaranth as a staple food. The grain is nutritionally exceptional — 14–18% protein with a balanced amino acid profile including lysine — and is now being rediscovered as an important gluten-free alternative grain. The dramatic tall stems with enormous, feathery, dark-red to magenta to gold plumes are visually spectacular in the garden and support abundant seed for birds in autumn.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; this determinate variety requires only modest staking; prolific bearer best harvested in quantity for drying or canning.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to full sun after frost risk passes; Principe Borghese is the traditional Italian tomato for sun-dried tomatoes, a compact determinate vine bearing enormous clusters of small (2–3 oz) plum to egg-shaped fruits with thick dry flesh, thin skin, few seeds, and very low moisture content — the characteristics that make it ideal for halving and drying in the sun or dehydrator. The variety's name refers to the Borghese family of Rome who historically grew them on terraced hillsides; the dried product is intensely flavored and chewy. It bears all at once in a concentrated flush, making it excellent for large-batch canning and preserving as well.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil; sow again in late summer for fall.
directions: This heirloom leaf lettuce dating to at least 1881 forms large, loose green leaves with bronze-red margins and an upright habit. Slow to bolt with good heat tolerance, it offers a tender texture and mild sweet flavor. Sow shallowly in cool soil and keep evenly moist. Harvest outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop, and shade lightly in summer heat to prolong the harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring or September–October for fall. Prizehead is one of the fastest-maturing looseleaf lettuces and can be harvested as baby leaves in 25–30 days or at full size in 45–55 days. The quick maturity makes it excellent for succession planting every 2 weeks through the cool season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Prizehead is a classic American heirloom looseleaf lettuce developed by W. Atlee Burpee Company in the 1880s and still widely grown for its exceptional flavor and striking red-bronze tipped leaves. The large, frilly, bright green leaves are broadly and dramatically tipped in red-bronze to burgundy at the leaf edges, creating a distinctly two-toned effect that makes Prizehead one of the most ornamental of all heirloom lettuces and an enduring favorite in kitchen gardens. The flavor is superb — mild, tender, and buttery with a crisp texture that surpasses many newer commercial varieties in taste trials — and the quick maturity (45–55 days to full size) allows it to be harvested before summer heat arrives. The frilly, slightly ruffled leaf texture holds dressings well. In zone 9 Prizehead is equally at home in spring and fall gardens; the red tips intensify in cooler weather and provide the most dramatic color in fall plantings.

plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow; kale is also an excellent fall crop, since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves' flavor.
directions: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Prizm is an All-America Selections-winning kale bred for a compact, dense, more uniform habit than older kale varieties, with tender, tightly curled, blue-green leaves that hold good quality and mild flavor even as the plant matures. Its smaller stature makes it well suited to containers and smaller garden beds, and the tender texture requires less cooking time than some older, tougher kale cultivars, making it popular for salads as well as cooked greens. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production, and like other kale, flavor sweetens after light frost in a fall crop.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool soil as soon as it can be worked.
directions: This heavy-producing heirloom shelling pea, also called Laxton's Progress #9, fills each 5 inch pod with 7 to 9 plump, sweet peas. Sow directly in cool spring soil and keep evenly moist for good pod fill. The compact vines need little support. Harvest when pods are rounded and full but still bright green, shelling promptly for the freshest flavor.

common_name: Progress No. 9 Garden Pea (Laxton's Progress Classic English Wrinkled Shell Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked; Progress No. 9 is a semi-dwarf shelling pea (18–24 inch plants) that may need light support (twiggy branches pushed in near plants works well) but is manageable without formal trellising. In zone 9, direct sow November–February for spring harvest (February–April); peas are a cool-season crop that thrives in zone 9's mild winter and will bolt and die in summer heat. Harvest pods when plump and round — shell immediately or refrigerate for up to one week. Progress No. 9 is one of the earliest shelling peas, producing usable pods at 60–68 days.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in rows 18 inches apart; thin to 2–3 inches. Support with short twiggy branches or a low string trellis. Shell pods when plump and round; do not allow to over-mature. Progress No. 9 (also called Laxton's Progress or simply Progress) is a classic English garden pea with a history in British kitchen gardens extending back to the work of Thomas Laxton, the 19th-century English plant breeder who made significant improvements to pea varieties through systematic cross-breeding. The variety produces heavy yields of large, dark green, round pods containing 6–9 large, sweet, wrinkled peas — the wrinkled seed (rugose type) is a characteristic of sweeter, higher-sugar garden peas versus the smoother seeds of field peas, and Progress No. 9 exemplifies the sweet, tender, wrinkled-pea style. The semi-dwarf habit (18–24 inches) makes Progress No. 9 more manageable in home gardens than the tall pole peas like Alderman (Telephone) that require 4–5 foot trellises, while still producing full-sized, well-filled pods of excellent quality. Progress No. 9's early maturity (60–68 days) is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the window between suitable pea-growing temperatures and summer heat is brief — earlier-maturing varieties like Progress complete their harvest before heat stress arrives.

plant_note: Sow after last frost; proso millet is the shortest-season grain available to home gardeners, maturing in as little as 60 days.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed 1/2 in deep at roughly 20–25 lb per acre in home-scale rows and thin to 4–6 in; proso millet germinates quickly in warm soil and produces an open panicle of seed in just 60 days, making it practical even in short-season gardens above zone 4. Harvest entire stalks when the lower seeds are hard and the panicle begins to droop; hang bundles upside-down over a tarp for 2 weeks to finish drying. Thresh by beating bundles against the inside of a barrel and winnow outdoors; the hull is loose and comes free with light rubbing in warm water. Proso millet is gluten-free and has the lowest water requirement of any grain crop.

common_name: Provider Bean (Cold-Tolerant Dependable Bush Snap Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow starting 2 weeks before last frost; Provider germinates in cooler soils (as low as 50°F) than most beans, allowing earlier planting. In zone 9, sow February–April for spring production and August–September for fall production. The cold-soil tolerance allows earlier planting and fall planting into cooling soils, extending the productive season at both ends.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep; Provider is one of the most widely grown and recommended bush snap bean varieties in the United States — a 1965 release that has remained a cornerstone home garden and commercial variety for 60 years due to its combination of reliable production, consistent quality, and unusually cold-tolerant germination. Provider's ability to germinate reliably in cooler soils (down to about 50°F, compared to the 60°F minimum for most beans) allows it to be planted 1–2 weeks earlier than standard beans in spring and later into fall, giving it a significant practical advantage for extending the bean season in both directions. The round, medium-length (4–5 inch), dark green pods are harvested when young and tender and have clean snap-bean flavor — honest, straightforward, and pleasant rather than refined. A vigorous, upright bush habit requires no staking and produces heavily over a 2–3 week period per planting; successive sowings every 2–3 weeks provide continuous harvest. Provider has been the standard reliable bush bean against which others are compared — not glamorous, but dependable, productive, and universally adaptable from the earliest spring planting to late fall production in virtually any vegetable garden climate.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost; tolerant of cool soil for early sowings.
directions: Provider is an early, dependable bush snap bean valued for germinating well in cooler soil and adapting to a wide range of climates. It sets straight, stringless, tender pods with good flavor in a heavy early flush. Direct sow after frost, or slightly earlier than most beans since it tolerates cool soil, in full sun. Pick pods young and often to keep the plants producing over several weeks.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pruden's Purple is a large, potato-leaved, purple-pink beefsteak tomato saved by William Pruden of Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina, closely related to Brandywine in flavor and character but often producing more reliably and slightly earlier — considered by many tomato enthusiasts an excellent alternative or companion to Brandywine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost into fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil. Pruden's Purple was saved by William Pruden of Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina and entered the Seed Savers Exchange network in the 1980s; it is a large, indeterminate, potato-leaved (smooth, undivided leaf form, as in Brandywine) beefsteak tomato producing very large (12–24 oz), flattened, lobed, dusky rose to purple-pink fruits with dense, meaty, sweet, complex flesh with the rich, full tomato flavor characteristic of the best pink beefsteak heirlooms. Many tomato growers consider Pruden's Purple slightly more productive and reliably earlier than Brandywine Sudduth while producing nearly identical flavor; the two make excellent companions in the garden. Days to maturity of 65–80 from transplant make it one of the earlier large beefsteak heirlooms. A consistently excellent performer in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Plant slips (rooted vine cuttings) 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Puerto Rico sweet potato thrives in zone 9's long, warm season and requires no supplemental care once established. Harvest when the skin resists scratching and vine leaves begin to yellow. Cure harvested roots at 85–90°F with high humidity for 2 weeks to convert starches to sugars and develop sweetness; uncured sweet potatoes taste bland and starchy.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, loose, slightly acidic, moderately fertile sandy soil — sweet potatoes require loose soil for the roots to expand and develop properly; Puerto Rico was the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States for much of the 20th century, and under various synonyms ('Southern Queen', 'Vineless Puerto Rico') it formed the backbone of American sweet potato production in the Southeast, where it became the foundation of Southern sweet potato cuisine. The moist-flesh, orange sweet potato familiar as a Thanksgiving side dish, sweet potato pie filling, and candied yam is essentially the Puerto Rico type — the moist, sweet, orange-fleshed character that most Americans think of as the defining sweet potato quality. The large, uniform, blocky-to-slightly-tapered roots have deep orange skin and vivid orange flesh with an intensely sweet, moist, smooth texture after curing and baking. Puerto Rico is well-adapted to Gulf Coast conditions and produces very large yields in zone 9's long, warm growing season with minimal care.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost; time planting to mature before the first fall frost.
directions: Sow 3–4 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in deeply worked, compost-rich soil once soil temperature is at least 65°F, then thin to the 2 strongest seedlings. Large-vined types need 6–10 feet of space per plant; choose bush types for smaller gardens. Place a piece of cardboard or straw under developing fruits to prevent rot. Harvest when the shell is fully orange, the rind is hard throughout, and the stem has begun to dry and cork.

common_name: Pumpkin on a Stick Ornamental Eggplant
plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after frost when soil warms.
directions: This 1800s ornamental eggplant produces clusters of small, ribbed fruits that look like tiny pumpkins, prized for fresh and dried fall arrangements. Grow it like eggplant, starting seeds indoors early and transplanting into warm, sunny soil. The fruits ripen from green to orange-red on sturdy branching plants. Cut stems when the little fruits color up, and hang to dry for lasting decorations.

plant_note: For the traditional Italian winter harvest, direct sow in late summer (late July to August in zone 9) so heads form during cool weather; puntarelle is a cool-season biennial that bolts quickly in warm weather — its distinctive hollow asparagus-like shoots only form after the plant experiences cool autumn temperatures.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and thin to 18–24 inches; puntarelle is a treasured Italian winter vegetable from the Lazio region, prized for its hollow, asparagus-like inner shoots that emerge from the center of the large chicory head. After harvest, the shoots are shaved or sliced thin, soaked in cold water to curl and reduce bitterness, and served raw in the classic Roman preparation with anchovy-garlic-lemon dressing. The outer leaves are also edible and mildly bitter in the chicory style. Sow in late summer for fall and winter harvest — in zone 8–10 this is an excellent late-season crop that matures when few other vegetables are producing. The plant is a biennial that sends up a tall flower stalk in its second spring; grow as an annual for the best eating shoots.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for a fall-winter-spring harvest; in zone 8–10, sow in September for a winter harvest of the tender inner shoots that are the prized Roman 'puntarelle' salad vegetable; the plant survives light freezes and is best treated as a cool-season crop.
directions: Direct sow in late summer in rich, well-drained soil; thin to 12–18 inches once established. Puntarelle is the Italian Catalogna-type chicory grown for its distinctive hollow, asparagus-like inner shoots that emerge from the crown in fall and winter and are the centerpiece of the classic Roman winter salad — thin strips of the shoots are soaked in cold water to curl them, then tossed with a pungent anchovy, garlic, and olive oil dressing in one of Rome's most iconic dishes. The outer leaves are cooked like bitter greens or braised, while the inner shoots and their hollow stems (the puntarelle themselves) are harvested by cutting just above the root crown. In warm-climate gardens (zones 8–11), puntarelle is an outstanding cool-season crop that fills the winter vegetable gap when few other greens are available.

subcategory: Clumping culm and edible shoot bamboo
plant_note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in zone 8–11; Punting Pole Bamboo is a medium-sized, non-invasive clumping bamboo native to Taiwan and southeastern China, producing dense clusters of straight, thin-walled, lightweight culms historically used as punting poles in Chinese rivers — and an excellent culinary bamboo with large, edible, sweet spring shoots.
directions: Plant in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Bambusa tuldoides is a clumping bamboo that does not run — safe to plant in most garden settings without rhizome barriers; water deeply in establishment and regularly during shooting season for maximum edible shoot production. Bambusa tuldoides (Punting Pole Bamboo, Canton Bamboo, or Greenstripe Bamboo) is a medium to large, fast-growing, non-invasive clumping bamboo native to Taiwan and southeastern China (Guangdong, Fujian), widely cultivated across subtropical Asia and naturalized in many tropical regions. The culms are straight, thin-walled, and lightweight — traditionally harvested as punting poles for river transport in Guangdong and as construction material, scaffolding, and utility poles — yet flexible and strong. The spring shoots are among the most commercially important edible bamboo shoots in China, produced in large quantities as an important culinary ingredient. Bambusa tuldoides performs reliably as an ornamental landscape bamboo in zones 8–11, forming dense, attractive clumps 15–35 feet tall with glossy, dark-green foliage. Considerably smaller and more garden-appropriate than B. oldhamii while still producing excellent edible shoots. Excellent as privacy screen, windbreak, and edible bamboo grove plant for Gulf Coast and similar warm subtropical gardens.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after nights stay warm.
directions: Purple Beauty is a striking heirloom bell pepper with thick-walled, four-inch fruits that ripen from green to a deep glossy purple, then to red if left longer. The crisp, mild flesh is as ornamental as it is tasty. Start seed indoors well before the last frost and transplant into full sun once nights are warm. The compact plants suit containers; harvest at the purple stage for color or leave to sweeten fully.

common_name: Purple Beauty Bell Pepper (AAS-Winning Dark Purple Blocky Sweet Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Purple Beauty is a compact, early-maturing bell pepper suited to zone 9 where the long warm season allows plenty of time for full purple maturity. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The purple color at harvest is a fully mature stage — not an intermediate green-to-red stage. If left on the plant beyond the purple stage, Purple Beauty peppers will turn red, but the ornamental and culinary purpose of this variety is the purple color, which should be harvested at full purple development. The anthocyanin pigment in Purple Beauty's skin makes the fruit mildly antioxidant-rich. Purple color fades to brown-green when cooked.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 78–85°F; transplant after last frost. Compact plants do not require staking. Harvest peppers at full purple color for best appearance. Purple Beauty is a 1990 All-America Selections-winning bell pepper — a fully blocky, 4-lobed, medium-large sweet bell pepper that matures to a deep purple-violet color rather than the standard red, yellow, or orange of typical bell pepper types. The purple coloration comes from anthocyanin pigments produced in the skin (not the flesh, which remains pale green-white), and the purple color intensifies as the pepper approaches maturity, creating one of the most striking visual effects in the summer garden among vegetables. Purple Beauty is frequently planted in ornamental-edible garden designs and kitchen garden borders where the dark purple fruits contrast dramatically with the green plant and with neighboring yellow and orange peppers. The flavor is standard sweet bell pepper — no heat, with a clean, slightly grassy-sweet taste similar to green bell peppers (purple bell peppers are harvested at the same maturity stage as green bells in terms of flavor development). Purple Beauty's compact plants (18–24 inch) set fruit heavily and are among the earlier-maturing bell peppers, making them well-suited to short-season gardens and zone 9 spring plantings before summer heat affects fruit set.

plant_note: Start indoors early; transplant after frost when soil warms.
directions: This bell pepper shifts from creamy lime to deep purple and finally red, with a contrasting lime-green interior that is both ornamental and tasty. The compact, very early plants adapt to many climates. Start seeds indoors and transplant into warm soil in full sun. Pick peppers at the purple stage for color or let them redden for sweetness, and water evenly to prevent blossom-end rot.

plant_note: Keep seedbed constantly moist during slow germination.
directions: These anthocyanin-rich carrots range from purple skin with orange cores to solid purple throughout. Sow the fine seed a quarter inch deep in deep, loose, stone-free soil and never let the surface dry during germination. Thin seedlings to 2 to 3 inches so roots develop without forking or crowding. Purple pigment intensifies in cool weather, so fall crops often show the deepest color. Harvest when shoulders reach three-quarters of an inch and store in cool, humid conditions.

common_name: Purple Carrot (Cosmic Purple Carrot, Anthocyanin Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow fall through early winter (September–November in zone 9) in deeply tilled, loose, stone-free, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cosmic Purple carrot has deep purple-skinned roots with orange and yellow interior flesh — the purple color from anthocyanin pigments intensifies in cool weather and makes this one of the most nutritionally rich carrot varieties available to home growers.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly (1/4 inch deep) in deeply tilled, loose, stone-free, lean soil in full sun; thin to 2–3 inches; harvest at 6–8 inches for best color and flavor. Daucus carota 'Cosmic Purple' (purple carrot or anthocyanin carrot) is an open-pollinated purple-rooted carrot variety developed by the USDA Agricultural Research Service — one of the most richly pigmented and nutritionally dense carrot varieties available to home growers. The root has deep purple to nearly black outer skin from very high anthocyanin concentrations (the same antioxidant pigments found in blueberries and red cabbage) with orange interior flesh, creating a dramatic color contrast when sliced. The flavor is significantly different from standard orange carrots: 'Cosmic Purple' is notably sweeter, with a mild, distinctive flavor complexity from both sugars and secondary compounds. Anthocyanins in the skin are heat-labile and can fade during cooking — roasting at high heat preserves them better than boiling or steaming. Eating purple carrots raw in salads or quick-pickling with vinegar (which intensifies the purple to fuchsia-red) are excellent ways to enjoy both flavor and color. In zone 9, purple carrots are planted in fall for winter harvest when cool temperatures concentrate sugars; spring-planted carrots in warm areas tend to be less sweet and may bolt before fully sizing. A beautiful addition to diverse carrot sowings alongside orange, yellow, and white types.

plant_note: Consistent cool weather prevents buttoning; avoid heat stress.
directions: The vivid purple curds come from anthocyanins and do not require blanching like white types. Start seed indoors five to six weeks before transplanting and set plants out in rich, moisture-retentive soil. Keep growth steady and unchecked, since any stress from heat, drought, or transplant shock can cause premature small heads. Harvest while the head is still tight and dome-shaped, before the curds begin to separate. The color softens somewhat when cooked but stays vibrant if steamed briefly.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in loose, deep, stone-free soil; Purple Dragon develops its deepest, most vivid color when harvested in cool conditions — fall-sown roots grown into winter have significantly more intense purple pigmentation than spring-sown roots harvested in warming temperatures.
