directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Purple Dragon is among the darkest-colored purple carrots available, producing 6–7 inch Chantenay-type roots with an almost purple-black exterior of extraordinary depth — the highest anthocyanin content of the major purple carrot varieties on the market, with the deep pigment extending well into the shoulder of the carrot. The interior flesh is vivid orange, creating a dramatic two-toned cross-section when sliced that makes Purple Dragon the most visually striking carrot in a rainbow mix. The flavor is earthy and subtly spicy with good sweetness, distinctly more complex than standard orange carrots. Raw eating shows the anthocyanin benefits and full visual impact; cooking at high heat fades the exterior purple toward brown, but moderate-heat roasting preserves considerable color. Outstanding raw in salads, crudités, and juicing where the deep purple color makes an impression.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; purple color develops best in cool conditions — fall-harvested roots have deeper color than spring-harvested ones.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Purple Haze is an All-America Selection Edible Vegetable winner with striking purple-skinned, orange-fleshed 10-inch carrots that turn purple skin orange when cooked (the purple color fades with heat), with slightly higher anthocyanin content than orange carrots. When eaten raw, the purple exterior provides both visual drama and a hint of earthiness that complements the sweet orange interior. Excellent for rainbow carrot mixes, farmers markets, and home gardens looking for an unusual and conversation-starting variety with genuinely good flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 this is typically February–March for spring and again August–September for a productive fall crop. Purple hull peas thrive in high heat and humidity and are the classic summer legume of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; purple hull peas are exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and require no added fertilizer on moderately fertile ground since they fix atmospheric nitrogen. The distinctive purple-hull pods flush violet-pink to purple at maturity, making them easy to spot at harvest time — pick pods when the hull is fully colored but before it begins to dry and yellow. Fresh-shelled purple hull peas cook faster than dried beans and have a richer, earthier flavor than black-eyed peas; they are a staple of Southern cooking, particularly New Year's Day hoppin' john and summer side dishes. The vines sprawl moderately — plant in wide rows or support with short stakes for easier harvest.

plant_note: Sprout indoors year-round in a jar or tray; no field planting needed.
directions: These purple kohlrabi sprouts add eye-popping color and crunch to salads and sandwiches with a classic brassica flavor and spicy note. Sprout the seeds indoors in a jar or shallow tray, rinsing and draining two to three times daily. They are ready to eat in four to seven days once the shoots stand an inch or so tall with tiny leaves. Keep them moist but drained to avoid mold.

common_name: Purple Majesty Potato (Deep Purple Skin and Flesh Specialty Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.8–6.5) soil in full sun; Purple Majesty retains its vivid purple color best when steamed or microwaved rather than boiled — water-cooking leaches anthocyanins and dilutes the distinctive purple color in the finished dish.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Purple Majesty is a Colorado State University potato introduction producing tubers with dramatic deep-purple skin and equally vivid deep-purple flesh throughout — not a surface tint or partial coloring but consistently, intensely purple from skin to center in every tuber. The purple coloration comes from high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments that are the same class of antioxidants found in blueberries and acai — Purple Majesty has among the highest anthocyanin levels of any potato variety tested, providing both the extraordinary visual quality and the health-attributed benefits associated with anthocyanin-rich foods. The color partially survives light cooking — steamed or microwaved Purple Majesty retains much of its striking purple appearance, while hard-boiled or oven-roasted preparations create dramatic visual presentations unlike any other potato. The flavor is mild and pleasant — comparable to other specialty potatoes — with the skin adding a slightly earthy complexity. Purple Majesty is oblong-shaped with smooth skin and produces well under typical potato growing conditions. In zone 9, plant in January–February for spring harvest. The vivid color makes Purple Majesty outstanding in mixed potato salads where the purple tubers contrast dramatically with red, gold, and white varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall for fall/winter harvest in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple mustard greens are among the fastest cool-season crops, producing harvestable baby leaves in 3–4 weeks from sowing and full-sized leaves in 5–7 weeks. Bolts in heat and long days.
directions: Direct sow in late summer for fall harvest or very early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; purple mustard greens (varieties include 'Red Giant', 'Osaka Purple', and 'Crimson Forest') produce large, crinkled or frilly, deep burgundy-red to purple-red leaves with a pleasant, pungent, spicy mustard flavor. The purple color is most intense in cool temperatures and fades slightly in warm weather. Extremely fast to harvest — baby leaves ready in 3–4 weeks, full size in 5–7 weeks. The flavor is spicier than milder Asian greens but milder than mature yellow mustard plants. Use in salad mixes for color and spice, stir-fry when young and tender, or braise the mature leaves Southern-style with pot liquor. Overwintering plants in zones 7–9 produce early spring regrowth before bolting. A staple of Asian-American vegetable gardens and increasingly popular in American farmers markets for its dramatic color and quick harvest.

plant_note: Plant 1-year crowns in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for winter establishment before spring emergence. Allow plants to establish for two full seasons without harvesting before taking a full crop in the third year. In zone 9 asparagus goes dormant in summer heat and re-emerges in fall; harvest timing differs from northern gardens and is primarily a spring vegetable.
directions: Plant 1-year crowns 6–8 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil amended with compost in full sun; Purple Passion is a New Zealand-bred asparagus cultivar that produces vivid deep-purple spears with 25–40% higher sugar content and significantly lower fiber than standard green varieties — the purple color comes from anthocyanins concentrated in the outer tissues. The raw spears are noticeably sweeter and more tender than green asparagus and can be eaten raw in salads and crudités where the color is preserved; cooking turns the spears green as the anthocyanins break down under heat. Flavor is superior to most green varieties whether raw or cooked. Established beds are productive for 15–25 years. In zone 9 the plant benefits from a sandy, well-drained location and may require supplemental irrigation in the long, dry spring. Skip the first two seasons' harvest to allow crown development; thereafter harvest only the first 4–6 weeks of the spring flush.

common_name: Purple Peruvian Fingerling Potato (Andean Purple Heritage Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Purple Peruvian is an Andean heirloom fingerling potato originating in the Andes of Peru and Bolivia where hundreds of diverse potato varieties developed over 8,000+ years of indigenous cultivation — it produces long, slender, finger-shaped tubers with deep purple skin and deep purple flesh, representing one of the many colorful heritage potato types from the center of potato genetic diversity.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces (whole small tubers work best for fingerlings) 10–12 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; fingerling potatoes produce many small, elongated tubers that benefit from slightly closer planting than large-tuber varieties. Purple Peruvian fingerling potatoes come from the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, the center of origin of the domestic potato (Solanum tuberosum), where indigenous Quechua and Aymara peoples developed thousands of diverse potato cultivars over 8,000+ years — the wild ancestral diversity of potatoes in this region dwarfs the few dozen varieties commonly grown in North America. Purple Peruvian produces long (2–4 inch), slender, finger-shaped tubers with intensely dark purple to near-black skin and uniformly deep purple to violet flesh throughout; the color comes from the same anthocyanin pigments found in Adirondack Blue and All Blue but at high concentrations. The texture is waxy and the flavor is earthy, slightly nutty, and distinctly more complex than commercial potato varieties — reflecting centuries of selection in high-altitude Andean environments. The fingerling shape makes them visually dramatic on the plate and ideal for roasting whole (the skin caramelizes beautifully), potato salads, and presentations where the purple color adds visual impact. High in antioxidants.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–March for fall through spring harvest. Purple Plum is one of the fastest-maturing radish varieties — ready in as little as 25 days. Sow in succession every 7–10 days for continuous harvest through the cool season. In zone 9 fall sowings in October–November produce the best radish quality; spring radishes may bolt quickly as temperatures rise. Thin to 2 inches apart for proper round shape development. Harvest promptly when roots reach 1 inch diameter — oversize radishes become pithy and unpleasantly hot.
directions: Plant in full sun in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Purple Plum is a round, globe-shaped spring radish with uniformly deep violet-purple skin — a dramatic and attractive departure from the familiar red-and-white Cherry Belle type, with the rich purple skin creating an unusual ornamental effect in the radish row and on vegetable platters. When sliced, Purple Plum reveals clean white flesh with only the thin purple skin providing color — the interior is typical crisp, juicy, peppery radish with the same satisfying bite as standard spring radishes. The flavor is classic spring radish: pungent, peppery, slightly sweet when very fresh, and progressively hotter as the root ages or the weather warms. The round, smooth shape and uniform size make Purple Plum excellent for sliced vegetable platters, salads, and garnishes where the deep purple skin creates visual contrast with other vegetables. As one of the fastest-maturing vegetables available, radishes including Purple Plum are often direct-sown between slow-growing transplants (tomatoes, peppers, squash) to use the space productively while the main crop establishes.

plant_note: Sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; succession sow every 1-2 weeks.
directions: Direct sow 'Purple Plum' seeds 1/2 inch deep and thin seedlings to about 1-2 inches apart for well-formed, violet-skinned roots. This fast-maturing radish is ready in roughly a month and stays crisp and mild even as bulbs enlarge. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent pithiness and cracking, and harvest promptly once roots reach about 1 inch across. Tolerant of cool weather and containers, it thrives in full sun to partial shade.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost and provide a trellis or pole support; Purple Podded Pole bean is one of the most visually dramatic vegetable plants available — producing vines covered in deep purple pods that stand out brilliantly against the green foliage, though the pods turn standard green when cooked; a beautiful edible ornamental for trellises and arbors.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost at base of a trellis, poles, or fence that will support 6–8 foot vines; thin to 4–6 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Purple Podded Pole bean is an old American heirloom snap bean with the dramatic characteristic of deep purple pods that develop against the green foliage — a striking visual contrast in the garden that makes this one of the most ornamentally interesting of all vegetable plants. The long (6–8 inch), round-sectioned pods are deep maroon-purple when raw and suitable for fresh eating or canning; however, the anthocyanin purple pigment is water-soluble and the pods turn standard green when cooked in water, a characteristic that surprises many gardeners. The flavor is excellent, similar to other pole snap beans; the raw purple pods are also edible in salads where the color can be appreciated. Very productive and continuous bearing through summer; the purple color also makes the beans somewhat easier to spot for harvesting against the green foliage.

plant_note: Detach pads and callous the cut end for 3–5 days before planting in very well-drained, alkaline to neutral, dry, rocky to sandy soil in full sun; purple prickly pear is distinctive for the brilliant reddish-purple color that develops on its pads in cold weather and drought stress, providing outstanding winter ornamental color.
directions: Plant callused pads in very well-drained, dry, rocky to sandy, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun — purple prickly pear is one of the most ornamentally striking native cacti of the Chihuahuan Desert and Texas prairies, valued for the brilliant reddish-purple to wine-red coloration that develops on its blue-green pads during cold weather and drought stress, providing some of the most vivid winter color of any cactus or succulent in cultivation. The yellow flowers with red centers in spring are beautiful; the edible purple-red fruits (tunas) follow in late summer and fall. Long, 3–4 inch white to gray spines give the plant a dramatic, bold texture. The distinctive purple winter color is the result of anthocyanin pigments produced as a cold-stress response — pads return to blue-green in summer warmth. An outstanding xeriscape and dry garden plant for hot, dry, alkaline soils of the southern Gulf Coast and Texas. Edible pads and fruit used as other prickly pears.

plant_note: Overwintering type; sow midsummer for spring harvest in mild zones.
directions: This hardy overwintering broccoli produces many small purple spears in early spring rather than a single central head. Start seed indoors in mid to late summer and transplant in early fall so plants establish before cold sets in. Provide steady moisture and rich soil, and mulch heavily to protect crowns through winter in zones 6 and 7. Harvest spears when buds are tight and cut regularly to encourage continued side-shoot production. Exposure to winter chill is what triggers the abundant spring flush.

plant_note: Plant slips (rooted cuttings from sprouted tubers) 2–3 weeks after last frost in full sun in loose, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in zone 8–12; Purple Sweet Potato varieties (Okinawan, Japanese, Stokes) produce deeply purple-fleshed tubers with exceptional levels of anthocyanin antioxidants — 2–3 times higher than blueberries — distinct from the orange-flesh sweet potatoes, with a slightly drier, nuttier, less sweet flavor profile valued in Asian-American cooking and superfood markets.
directions: Plant slips 2–3 weeks after last frost in loose, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Purple Sweet Potato produces better tubers in slightly poor, loose soil rather than heavily amended rich soil — excess nitrogen encourages vine growth at the expense of tuber development; harvest 90–120 days after transplanting when the vines begin to yellow. Ipomoea batatas 'Purple' (Purple Sweet Potato, Okinawan Sweet Potato, or Stokes Purple Sweet Potato) encompasses a group of purple-fleshed sweet potato varieties — including 'Okinawan,' 'Japanese Purple' (Satsumaimo), and 'Stokes Purple' — sharing the characteristic of producing tubers with deep violet-purple flesh caused by exceptionally high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments (cyanidin and peonidin glycosides). These anthocyanins give purple sweet potatoes one of the highest antioxidant levels of any commonly eaten vegetable — ORAC values 2–3 times higher than blueberries — and have generated significant interest in functional food and nutraceutical research. Purple-fleshed sweet potatoes retain their vibrant purple color when baked or boiled (better than in acidic cooking), are somewhat drier and nuttier in texture than orange sweet potatoes, and are traditional in Okinawan Japanese cuisine (where they are called 'beni imo'), Hawaiian cuisine (Okinawan sweet potato poi), Filipino cuisine, and increasingly in American superfood markets. Grow exactly like standard sweet potato: loose, sandy soil, full sun, long warm season. Slips (not tubers or seeds) are the standard planting material.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Start purple tomatillo seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil in full sun. Plant at least two seedlings to ensure cross-pollination, since tomatillos are largely self-incompatible. The sprawling plants benefit from staking or caging; harvest fruit when the papery husk splits open and the berry turns deep violet for the sweetest flavor. Keep watering consistent through fruit set to encourage a heavy crop.

plant_note: Sow in mid summer for a fall harvest; flavor sweetens after frost.
directions: American Purple Top rutabaga produces large five- to six-inch roots with purple shoulders and smooth ivory flesh that is sweet, mild, and fine-textured. Grown as a fall crop, it stores exceptionally well for winter use in mashes and stews. Direct sow in mid summer so roots mature in cool weather, and thin generously to size up. A light frost sweetens the roots; harvest before the ground hard-freezes and store in a cool, humid place.

plant_note: Sow in late summer for fall roots, or early spring for a quick crop.
directions: Purple Top is the classic heirloom turnip, forming smooth white roots with bright purple shoulders plus tender, nutritious greens. Both roots and tops are edible, giving a dual harvest from one planting. Direct sow in early spring for a fast crop or in late summer for sweeter fall roots, thinning to give roots room. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest roots young at two to three inches for the mildest flavor.

scientific_name: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa 'Purple Top White Globe'
plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; in zone 9 sow September–February for a fall through spring harvest — fall planting produces the finest quality turnips as cool temperatures sweeten the roots and reduce bitterness. Sow thickly and thin to 4–6 inches after seedlings establish; thinnings at 3–4 inches tall are edible as turnip greens. Harvest roots at 2–3 inches diameter for the most tender, mildest flavor — oversize roots become pithy and bitter. Both roots and greens are productive throughout the zone 9 cool season.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of stones and compaction; Purple Top White Globe is the definitive American turnip variety — the standard against which all other turnip cultivars are measured, with over a century of continuous cultivation making it the most widely recognized turnip appearance in North America. The smooth, round roots develop their characteristic two-tone coloration from the soil surface: the shoulder (exposed to light above ground) develops a rich, vivid purple-violet pigmentation while the buried portion stays clean creamy white, creating the immediately recognizable bicolor that defines the visual identity of a turnip. Both the roots and the large, hairy, dark green leaves (turnip greens) are edible — the mild, slightly sweet, pleasantly peppery roots can be eaten raw at small size or cooked in soups, stews, and roasted vegetable preparations, while the greens are a classic Southern potherb simmered with smoked pork and eaten alongside collards and mustard. Fall-planted turnips develop the finest flavor in zone 9 as cool temperatures concentrate sugars and reduce any harshness in the roots.

plant_note: Sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow 'Purple Top White Globe' 1/2 inch deep and thin to 3-4 inches apart for smooth, globe-shaped roots with purple shoulders and white bottoms. This classic heirloom is dual-purpose: harvest young greens for cooking and pull roots at about 3 inches across before they turn woody. Keep soil consistently moist for tender, sweet roots, and grow in cool spring or fall weather. Turnips store well in a cool, humid place through winter.

common_name: Purple Top White Globe Turnip (Standard American Turnip)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile, loose soil in full sun; Purple Top White Globe is the standard fall turnip for Gulf South gardens — sow every 3 weeks from August through October for a continuous harvest from October through February.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Purple Top White Globe is the classic American turnip — an old open-pollinated variety that has been the standard American garden turnip for generations and remains by far the most widely grown turnip variety in both home gardens and commercial production. The medium-large globe roots (3–4 inches diameter at ideal harvest size) have a distinctive two-tone appearance: the upper portion (exposed above the soil line) turns vivid purple to purple-red in sunlight, while the lower portion remains white. The firm, crisp, sweet-peppery flesh is mild when harvested young (under 3 inches) and becomes stronger and more pungent as roots age and enlarge — harvest promptly at desired size for best quality. The tender, nutritious greens (tops) are equally valuable: they are among the best-flavored of all Southern cooking greens, prized in traditional Gulf South cooking simmered with pork and seasonings. In zone 9, Purple Top White Globe is strictly a fall and winter crop — heat above 75°F causes the roots to become pithy, bitter, and tough. Sow from August through early October and harvest from October through February. Turnips are extremely fast-maturing and exceptionally cold-hardy — they tolerate freezes to the mid-20s°F without damage and flavor actually improves after frost exposure.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall and January–February for spring. Purple Vienna has slightly better heat tolerance than white-stemmed types and can hold at harvest size slightly longer without becoming pithy. Harvest when stems are 2–3 inches across for the best texture — over-mature kohlrabi become fibrous and woody regardless of variety.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Purple Vienna Kohlrabi is the standard purple-skinned kohlrabi, identical in flavor and culture to white-stemmed types but with a striking deep purple-red skin color that makes it visually distinctive in the garden and at market. The interior flesh is white, mild, and sweet — identical to white kohlrabi in texture and taste despite the purple exterior. The purple color, from anthocyanin pigments, is present only in the skin and does not penetrate the flesh; peeled Purple Vienna looks and tastes exactly like White Vienna. The visual contrast between the purple skin and white interior makes it popular for raw preparations like kohlrabi slaws, crudités, and salads where slicing reveals the striking bicolor cross-section. In zone 9 kohlrabi is primarily a fall vegetable transplanted in September–October; it withstands light frosts and can be harvested from November through February. Remove leaves and store harvested kohlrabi in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer for fall.
directions: Purple Vienna is a cool-season heirloom kohlrabi forming deep purple bulbs above the soil with crisp, tender, mildly sweet flesh similar to a turnip. Direct sow in early spring and again in late summer, thinning to give the swelling stems room. Keep growth steady with even moisture, since stress can make the bulbs woody. Harvest when bulbs reach two to three inches across for the best texture, before they turn fibrous.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or in mid to late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow 'Purple Vienna' kohlrabi 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart so the purple, edible swollen stems develop cleanly. The bulbs are best harvested at 2-3 inches in diameter while crisp and sweet; larger bulbs turn tough and fibrous. Grow in the cool weather of spring or fall in full sun, keeping moisture even to avoid cracking. Both the bulb and young leaves are edible raw or cooked.

common_name: Purple Viking Potato (Purple-Skinned White-Flesh Storage Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Purple Viking produces large, oval tubers with striking purple-splashed pink skin over dense, moist, pure white flesh that holds together well when boiled, making it a favorite for potato salad as well as roasting and mashing. The vigorous plants are heavy yielders and the thick skin gives the tubers good storage life compared to thinner-skinned varieties. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to keep developing tubers covered and prevent greening, and harvest after the vines die back for the best storage tubers.

common_name: Purple Yam (Ube, Water Yam, Winged Yam)
plant_note: Plant tuber sections (3–4 oz, each with at least one eye) 4–6 inches deep after last frost when soil has warmed to 70°F; provide a sturdy trellis or fence at least 6 feet tall — the vigorous vines twine counterclockwise and can reach 15–20 feet; aerial bulbils produced in the leaf axils can also be planted and will produce harvestable tubers in their second season.
directions: Plant tuber sections in loose, deep (18–24 inches), well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with strong trellis support; purple yam (ube) is the most widely cultivated yam species in the world and a treasured ingredient in Filipino cuisine, where its vivid violet-purple flesh and sweet, mildly nutty flavor are used in ube halaya (jam), halo-halo, ice cream, pastries, and a growing global trend in purple foods. Originating in Southeast Asia and now grown pantropically, D. alata produces large (up to 20 lb), winged-stemmed vines that require a full 9–12 month season for maximum tuber development; in frost-prone zones grow in the longest available frost-free window and harvest after vine dieback. The distinctive purple color comes from anthocyanins and deepens with cooking; unlike taro, the flesh is not irritating raw. Tubers store well for several months in cool, dry conditions.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Purple de Milpa is a traditional small-fruited tomatillo of the Mexican milpa system, highly prized by Mexican cooks for its richer, more complex flavor and purple-green to deep purple color compared to the standard large-fruited green tomatillos used in commercial salsa verde production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide staking or caging as plants become sprawling. Purple de Milpa is a traditional Mexican tomatillo variety grown in the traditional milpa polyculture system; it produces small (1–1.5 inch diameter), round fruits with papery husks that burst and split when ripe, ripening to purple-green to deep purple-green rather than the standard yellow-green of commercial tomatillos. The flavor is more concentrated, fruitier, and tangier than standard green tomatillos, with a more complex background of citrus, herbs, and earthiness that many Mexican cooks and chefs consider superior for salsa verde, enchiladas verdes, and mole verde when an authentic deep flavor is desired. Plant in pairs or groups as tomatillos need cross-pollination for best fruit set; highly productive in warm weather.

plant_note: Sow direct 2–4 weeks after last frost in warm soil in full sun; purslane thrives in heat and poor, dry soil — it is one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-resistant summer greens available, ideal for the Gulf Coast summer when other greens fail.
directions: Sow direct 2–4 weeks after last frost in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; purslane requires warm, loose soil (70°F+) to germinate and thrives in heat and drought that would wilt most salad greens. Portulaca oleracea is one of the world's most widespread wild plants, a succulent, mat-forming annual with thick, water-storing, paddle-shaped leaves and reddish stems; in the Middle East, Mexico, and much of Europe and Asia it is cultivated as a valued summer vegetable — snipped stems and leaves are eaten fresh in salads (particularly Greek salads and Mexican ensalada), lightly sautéed, pickled, or added to soups and stews for a mild, slightly lemony, slightly mucilaginous texture. Purslane is extraordinarily rich in omega-3 fatty acids for a leafy green, and is one of the highest plant sources of ALA. It naturalizes aggressively in warm climates — harvest regularly to prevent unwanted spreading.

common_name: Queensland Blue Pumpkin (Australian Heirloom Blue-Gray Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Queensland Blue is a classic 19th-century Australian heirloom pumpkin prized for its deeply ribbed, hard, blue-gray rind, dense sweet orange flesh, and outstanding storage life of six months or longer.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the vigorous vines. Queensland Blue is a classic Australian heirloom pumpkin, developed in the 19th century and still one of the most widely grown pumpkin varieties in Australia, valued for its distinctive, deeply ribbed, slate-blue-gray rind — a color that stands out dramatically against typical orange pumpkins in a fall display — and its dense, dry, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and pies. The hard rind, while tough to cut into, is also the reason for the variety's outstanding keeping quality; well-cured fruit routinely stores for six months or longer in a cool, dry location, among the best storage life of any winter squash. Fruits typically run 8-12 pounds with a flattened, ribbed shape. Vines are vigorous and productive given full sun, fertile soil, and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and resists a fingernail, and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to sweeten over the following months.

plant_note: Start indoors or sow directly once soil is warm; well suited to indoor container growing year-round.
directions: 'Quick Snack' is a compact, parthenocarpic cucumber bred for 6-8 inch pots on a sunny windowsill, counter, or balcony. Because it sets fruit without pollination, it produces well indoors with no bees needed; keep it in bright light and evenly moist soil. Harvest the smooth, dark green fruits young at 1.5-2.5 inches long for the best sweet, crisp flavor and to keep the plant producing. Feed lightly and provide a small trellis or let vines trail over the pot rim.

plant_note: Sow around the last frost date in spring; quinoa bolts in midsummer heat, so timing for a cool finish is critical in most climates.
directions: Broadcast or sow seed 1/4 in deep in firm, well-drained soil and thin to 12–18 in when seedlings are 3–4 in tall; quinoa is highly drought-tolerant once established and prefers cool, dry weather through seed fill. The colorful seed heads (red, orange, or cream) are ready to harvest when the seed falls easily from the panicle when rubbed — typically after the first light fall frost has dried the plant. Cut the seed heads into paper bags, dry for 1–2 weeks in a warm airy space, then thresh by rubbing heads between hands and winnow away the chaff outdoors in a breeze. Rinse seed thoroughly before eating to remove bitter saponins from the seed coat.

plant_note: For tight, colorful heads, sow in midsummer so radicchio heads up during cool fall weather, 10–14 weeks before first frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep and thin to 10–14 in; radicchio produces loose, green summer foliage before forming its characteristic red and white tight head as days shorten and temperatures fall. Cut back summer foliage to about 1 in when plants look tired and cool temperatures arrive; new heads will form from the crown within 3–4 weeks. Harvest compact heads by cutting at the base once they feel firm and the color is deep burgundy. Hard frost may damage outer leaves but the inner head often survives.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 direct sow or transplant August–September for a November–February harvest. Radicchio intensifies in color and flavor after light frosts — temperatures of 25–32°F trigger the characteristic deepening of the red-purple color and the development of the bittersweet flavor. In zone 9, the mild winters allow radicchio to head up and be harvested through February without protection.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rossa di Verona is the classic round-headed radicchio from the Verona region of Italy and the dominant variety in world commerce — the compact, baseball-sized heads of deep red-purple leaves with white midribs are the defining image of radicchio. The bitter, slightly sweet flavor is characteristically Italian and develops most fully after light frost exposure, which converts some starches to sugars and intensifies the red-purple anthocyanin pigmentation. In zone 9 plant in August–September for a fall-through-winter crop; the heads form and mature in cool weather from October through February. For sweeter flavor, blanch heads by loosely tying outer leaves over the center 1–2 weeks before harvest, reducing bitterness 30–40%. Rossa di Verona is excellent grilled (the bitterness mellows dramatically under high heat), used in risotto bianco, or eaten raw in Gorgonzola and walnut salads where the bitter note is a feature rather than a flaw.

plant_note: Sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; succession sow every 10 days for continuous harvest, stopping when summer heat sets in.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 in deep in cool, well-drained soil at 10-day intervals for a steady supply. Radishes bolt quickly in heat or long days, so spring and fall are the prime windows. Thin to 2 in as soon as seedlings are up to prevent overcrowding, which causes lanky tops and small or misshapen roots. Pull spring types at 3/4 to 1 in diameter before they become hot and pithy.

plant_note: Among the fastest microgreens; sow densely and blackout only one to two days.
directions: Radish is one of the fastest and most forgiving microgreens, germinating within a day or two of dense sowing on a moist tray. Keep the blackout period short, then give bright light to develop sturdy stems and, in some varieties, a pink or purple blush. Mist regularly and provide airflow to keep the vigorous growth clean. Harvest the crisp, boldly peppery shoots in about a week at the cotyledon stage.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after frost danger passes.
directions: This color-coded blend produces cherry tomatoes in orange, yellow, brown, red, and green, mixing mostly indeterminate pole types with one determinate. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm soil in full sun. Provide sturdy stakes or tall cages for the vining plants and pinch suckers to keep them manageable. Harvest the sweet, bite-sized fruits as each color ripens for a colorful, all-summer supply.

plant_note: Sow directly in loose, deep soil; carrots resent transplanting.
directions: This F1 hybrid produces white, yellow, orange, and coral roots from a single sowing, each 7-9 inches long, uniform and conical. Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and keep the surface consistently moist during the slow germination period. Thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart so roots size up evenly, and harvest this early-season Nantes x Imperator type once shoulders reach full color. Cool weather sweetens the flavor.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March for fall through spring harvest. Rainbow chard includes red, yellow, orange, white, and pink-stalked plants in each packet — plant thickly and thin, saving the thinnings for salads. Harvest outer leaves as needed starting when plants are 6–8 inches tall; this 'cut and come again' approach keeps plants productive for months. In zone 9 the cool season from fall through early spring is prime time; plants may bolt in spring heat but often resprout and produce again in fall.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Rainbow Chard is a mixture of Swiss chard varieties with stalks in multiple vivid colors — red, yellow, orange, gold, pink, white, and bicolors — creating one of the most visually striking vegetable plantings possible in a kitchen or ornamental garden. The broad, crinkled, dark green leaves and brilliantly colored stalks make Rainbow Chard simultaneously one of the most productive and most ornamental vegetables available. Nutritionally, Swiss chard is among the most nutrient-dense vegetables: extremely high in vitamins K, A, and C, iron, calcium, and magnesium. The mild, spinach-like flavor of young leaves is pleasant raw in salads; older leaves and the colorful stalks are best sautéed, stir-fried, or added to soups where the color partially fades but the substantial flavor and nutrition remain. The partial shade tolerance makes Rainbow Chard one of the best vegetables for gardens with limited full-sun exposure.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow again in late summer for fall crop; rainbow chard is biennial but grown as an annual; one of the most ornamental edible garden plants suitable for flower borders as well as vegetable beds.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil, thinning to 6–12 inches; rainbow chard is a mixture of white, yellow, orange, red, and vivid pink-stemmed chard varieties grown together, producing an exceptional display of color in the garden while providing the same mild, earthy leaves as single-colored chard. The stems of different colors have slightly different flavor intensities (red-stemmed are earthier, white-stemmed milder) but all are equally nutritious and versatile in cooking. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep plants productive for months. An outstanding cut-and-come-again green for the productive ornamental garden.

plant_note: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; a second sowing in late summer extends fall harvests.
directions: Soak the corky seed clusters overnight to speed germination, then sow half an inch deep directly in the garden. Thin seedlings to 6-12 inches, since each cluster can produce several plants. The vivid red, pink, yellow, orange, and white stems hold their color best in full sun with steady moisture. Harvest outer leaves regularly on a cut-and-come-again basis and the plant will keep pushing new growth well into fall.

plant_note: Plant small bulbs (sets) in late summer to fall in well-drained, fertile soil; rakkyo grows through the cool season and is harvested in late spring. In mild climates (zone 8–11) it naturalizes as a perennial bulb and spreads freely. Space bulbs 3–4 inches apart to allow for multiplication.
directions: Plant small bulbs in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; rakkyo (Allium chinense) is a small, perennial allium grown throughout Japan, China, and Southeast Asia specifically for pickling — one of Japan's most beloved preserved foods, pickled rakkyo (rakkyo no su-zuke) are the sweet-tart, crispy pickled bulbs served as a condiment alongside curry rice, bento boxes, and traditional Japanese meals. The small, elongated bulbs are harvested in early summer, cleaned, and pickled in vinegar with sugar and salt. They have a milder, more delicate onion flavor than regular onions, with a distinctive crispy texture retained through the pickling process. The plant itself is an attractive ornamental — the purple-pink flowers appear in fall on upright stems and are followed by the edible bulbs that multiply underground like shallots. In mild climates it naturalizes readily and provides bulbs year after year with minimal care.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer on the soil surface in a prepared seedbed (rampion requires light for germination and should not be covered); rampion is the edible plant at the center of the Brothers Grimm fairy tale 'Rapunzel' — a European biennial with a parsnip-like edible root and edible young leaves that was widely grown in kitchen gardens throughout Europe from the Middle Ages through the 19th century before largely disappearing from cultivation.
directions: Press seeds onto the soil surface without covering (light required for germination); keep the seedbed consistently moist until germination; thin to 4–6 inches apart; harvest roots in fall of the first year or early spring of the second year by digging carefully with a fork; the slender white roots are eaten raw or cooked, and the young leaves and shoots are used in salads. Rampion (Campanula rapunculus) is a European biennial wildflower and traditional kitchen garden vegetable that is best known as the plant at the center of the Brothers Grimm fairy tale 'Rapunzel': the story's plot hinges on a pregnant woman's craving for the rampion growing in the enchanted garden next door, her husband's theft of the plant to satisfy the craving, and the consequence of giving up their daughter as payment — 'Rapunzel' is simply the German and Italian name for Campanula rapunculus. The real rampion is a slender-rooted biennial native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, whose edible taproot (resembling a small, white parsnip or radish) was eaten raw in salads (with a mild, slightly nutty, turnip-like flavor) or cooked in soups and stews in French, Italian, and German kitchen gardens from medieval times through the 1800s. The young leaves are also edible — mildly sweet and tender — and were used in spring salads. Rampion largely disappeared from cultivation as more productive root vegetables (parsnips, turnips, carrots) displaced it, but the plant is still grown by kitchen garden historians and edible plant collectors. In its second year it sends up 2–4 foot spikes of pale violet-blue, bell-shaped flowers typical of the bellflower family.

plant_note: Plant bulbs or transplant divisions with intact roots in early fall in moist, very rich, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; ramps require cold-stratification and are very slow from seed — planting bulb divisions is much faster, yielding harvestable plants in 2–3 years.
directions: Plant bulb divisions in early fall in moist, very rich, leaf-mold-enriched, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in partial to full shade under deciduous hardwoods — the classic habitat is slopes with sugar maple, beech, and tulip poplar; ramps are a celebrated foraged edible of eastern North American forests with broad, smooth, rich-green leaves (like lily of the valley) and a small, white, garlic-like bulb with an intense, complex garlic-wild onion flavor that has become a culinary phenomenon. Both leaves and bulbs are edible; leaves emerge in early spring before the canopy closes and die back by June. Harvest no more than one leaf per plant per year, and never take more than a third of any colony to ensure sustainable harvest. Slow-growing: colonies planted from bulb divisions become harvestable in 3–5 years and persist indefinitely in suitable shaded conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rapini bolts rapidly in heat — timing is critical. Sow in late summer for fall harvest, or in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring harvest. Does not transplant well; direct sow only. Use successive sowings 2 weeks apart for extended harvest.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; rapini (broccoli raab, cime di rapa) is an Italian-heritage cool-season brassica grown for its tender stem tips, leaves, and immature flower bud clusters harvested before the yellow flowers fully open. Harvest the central stem with 6 inches of stem, leaves, and tight bud cluster when buds are still green and closed — this is the prime eating stage. The characteristic pleasantly bitter flavor (due to glucosinolates) intensifies in heat and with age. Rapini is a staple of southern Italian cooking — used in pasta, sautéed with garlic and olive oil, and in sausage dishes throughout Campania, Apulia, and Calabria. Succession sow every 2 weeks from late summer into fall for a continuous harvest through October–November in zone 7+. After the main head is cut, side shoots continue to produce smaller edible buds for several additional weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; rapini is not a true broccoli but a turnip-family vegetable grown for its tender stems, buds, and leaves with a distinctive pleasantly bitter flavor that is essential in Italian cuisine — harvest before the flower buds open for the most tender and flavorful results.
directions: Direct sow thinly in early spring or late summer in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; thin to 6 inches. Rapini (broccoli rabe, cime di rapa, or in dialect rabé) is a fast-growing cool-season vegetable in the Brassica rapa family, more closely related to turnips than to true broccoli; the tender stems, small leaves, and unopened flower buds are harvested together as a bundle when the buds are still tightly closed (40–60 days from seed). The flavor is distinctive — pleasantly bitter, peppery, and slightly nutty — and is considered an essential element of Italian-American and southern Italian cooking: rapini sautéed with garlic, olive oil, and red pepper flakes is the classic accompaniment to sausage, pasta, and orecchiette in Pugliese and Neapolitan traditions. In warmer climates (zones 8–11) it is an outstanding cool-season crop for fall-through-spring production, bolting quickly in heat.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; heat causes premature bolting.
directions: Rapini, or broccoli raab, is grown for its tender stems, leaves, and small budding florets with a pleasantly bitter, peppery flavor. Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart, growing in the cool weather of spring or fall to avoid rapid bolting. Harvest the whole plant or cut budding shoots just before the small yellow flowers open, when flavor is best. Fast to mature, it can be succession sown for repeat harvests.

common_name: Rat Tail Radish (Edible-Pod Radish, Podding Radish)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in spring or summer; Rat Tail Radish is an unusual radish grown NOT for its root (which is tough and pithy) but for its edible seed pods — long (4–8 inch), slender, purple to green, crunchy pods that taste like radish with a snappy, peppery bite — and it tolerates the heat that causes standard radishes to bolt, making it productive throughout summer when root radishes fail.
directions: Sow directly 1/2 inch deep after last frost; allow plants to grow and bolt (flower); harvest pods when 3–6 inches long and still crisp and tender — before the seeds inside develop fully; harvest daily once production begins as pods become fibrous when overripe. Rat Tail Radish (Raphanus sativus var. caudatus) is a Southeast Asian and South Asian radish cultivated specifically for the edible seed pods it produces after bolting, rather than for the root — a striking reversal of the usual reason for growing radishes. When most radishes bolt, the gardener curses the heat and pulls the plant; with Rat Tail Radish, bolting is the point. The plants grow to 24–36 inches tall, produce small flowers (white or pale violet), and then develop long, slender, arching or pendant seed pods typically 4–8 inches long with a characteristic curved tip that gives the variety its common name. The pods are harvested young and tender (before full seed development) and have a crunchy, snappy texture and peppery, radish-flavored taste that is excellent raw in salads, pickled, stir-fried in Asian cooking, or used in Indian chutneys and curries where the peppery pod flavor is prized. The purple-podded forms (the most commonly grown) are visually dramatic and the pods are mildly ornamental on the plant. A practical advantage: Rat Tail Radish tolerates summer heat that destroys root radish production, providing fresh radish flavor throughout summer months.

plant_note: Sow after the last frost; tolerates summer heat better than root radishes.
directions: Unlike ordinary radishes, 'Rat's Tail' is grown for its abundant slender, edible seed pods borne above ground on tall 2-5 foot plants. Direct sow 1/2 inch deep, thin to 6-12 inches apart, and give the plants room and support as they grow large. Harvest the crisp, spicy pods young at 3-5 inches long while still tender, picking often to keep new pods forming. Heat tolerant, it produces through summer when other radishes bolt.

common_name: Rattlesnake Pole Bean (Purple-Streaked Heirloom Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Rattlesnake is a vigorous pole bean that needs a sturdy 6-foot trellis or pole support. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer harvest; a late summer planting in August–September can produce well in the cooler fall. Rattlesnake shows excellent heat and drought tolerance, making it one of the most reliable pole beans for the Gulf South summer. The pods turn fully green at maturity but are streaked with purple while developing.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost; install a 6-foot trellis or pole support before or at planting. Harvest pods when 5–7 inches long and pods are still tender — before seeds inside begin to bulge prominently. Rattlesnake (also known as Preacher Bean or Streaked Cranberry) is a Southern heirloom pole bean with a documented history stretching back at least 200 years in Appalachian and Gulf South gardens, where its combination of heat tolerance, productivity, and exceptional flavor made it a staple of traditional kitchen gardens. The name comes from the pods' appearance: pale to medium green pods with distinctive purple-brown streaks and mottling that resemble rattlesnake skin — a striking visual character that makes the variety easy to identify in the garden and interesting as a fresh or dried bean. The flavor is particularly noteworthy — Rattlesnake has a richer, fuller, more complex bean flavor than most modern bush bean varieties, with a slightly nutty, almost buttery quality when cooked as a snap bean. The beans also mature into excellent shell beans (harvested when seeds are plump but before pods dry) and dry beans (harvested when pods are fully dry and papery), making Rattlesnake a versatile three-stage bean. The pole habit — 5–7 feet tall — requires support but produces over a longer season than bush types and handles the heat and drought of Gulf South summers better than most bush bean varieties.

common_name: Raven Zucchini (AAS-Winning Dark-Green Disease-Tolerant Compact Zucchini)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raven's compact, open plant habit improves air circulation around the crown — a practical advantage in the humid Gulf South where powdery mildew is a consistent challenge for summer squash.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raven is an All-America Selections-winning zucchini hybrid notable for its very dark green to nearly black-green skin color, compact open plant habit, excellent flavor, and improved disease tolerance. The extremely dark skin — darker than standard dark-green zucchini — is the most visually distinctive quality: Raven zucchini are nearly black-green at harvest size, creating a visually striking contrast with yellow and light-green squash in market displays and mixed vegetable presentations. The compact, open plant habit (non-vining, upright-spreading, with good air circulation through the plant canopy) reduces powdery mildew pressure in Gulf South humid conditions where powdery mildew often devastates standard bush-type zucchini by mid-season. The earlier maturity (48–55 days) compared to many other zucchini allows faster first harvest and more production within the spring window before summer heat. In zone 9, plant in February–March for spring production and again in August–September for fall production. Harvest Raven at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture — the dark skin makes it slightly harder to judge size at a glance, so check plants frequently during peak production. An outstanding choice for Gulf South summer gardens where disease pressure is the primary limitation of zucchini production.

common_name: Red & Yellow Pear Blend Pole Cherry Tomato
plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: This heirloom blend combines 'Red Pear' and 'Yellow Pear', indeterminate vines bearing small, firm, pear-shaped fruit with sweet, mild, low-acid flavor. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, full-sun beds. The vigorous vines need tall stakes or cages and regular pinching of suckers. Harvest the bite-sized fruits all summer for snacking, salads, pickling, or preserves.

common_name: Red Ace Beet (Early Disease-Tolerant Hybrid Globe Beet)
plant_note: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in well-tilled, fertile soil; thin to 4–6 inches for best root development. Red Ace germinates reliably across a wide soil temperature range and is particularly valued for its tolerance of Cercospora leaf spot — the main disease limiting beet production in humid regions. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter harvest; Red Ace holds well in the ground after reaching maturity without becoming pithy or woody.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-amended, fertile soil with consistent moisture; thin to 4–6 inch spacing. Red Ace is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid beet that has become one of the most widely recommended standard beet varieties for home gardens and commercial production alike — a globe-shaped, smooth, uniformly sized hybrid that consistently produces high-quality roots with reliable stand establishment, uniform maturity, and excellent disease tolerance (particularly for Cercospora leaf spot, the fungal disease that causes disfiguring brown leaf spots in humid regions). The roots are uniformly round to slightly oval, medium-large (2.5–3 inches diameter), with very smooth, deep red-purple skin, excellent internal uniformity and color (consistently dark red throughout with minimal zoning), and a tender, sweet, earthy-sweet flavor that compares favorably with the best heirloom types while delivering the hybrid advantages of uniformity, consistency, and disease resistance. Red Ace is an all-season variety that performs reliably in spring, fall, and winter production, holds well in cold storage, and has excellent greens quality for dual-purpose use (root plus cooking greens). One of the most practically reliable and consistently productive beet varieties available, recommended by university extension services across North America as a benchmark hybrid against which other beets are evaluated.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 start seeds in September and transplant October for fall through winter maturity. Red Acre reaches full maturity in 75–85 days from transplant — plant timing to ensure heads mature before summer heat. Heads split if left too long after maturity; harvest when heads are firm and solid. In zone 9 the fall planting is preferred, with heads maturing December–February when cool weather develops the fullest red-purple color and sweetest flavor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Acre is a classic open-pollinated red cabbage variety producing firm, round, 5–7 inch heads with deep red-purple to burgundy outer leaves and a bright magenta-red interior — the characteristic vivid color that makes red cabbage one of the most ornamental vegetables and the most visually distinctive cole crop. The red-purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that are pH-sensitive: the same compound that makes red cabbage turn blue when cooked with alkaline water is stabilized and brightened by adding acid (vinegar, apple juice) during cooking — a useful culinary fact for maintaining the vivid color in braised preparations. Red Acre's flavor is slightly stronger and more peppery than green cabbage, with a firmer texture that holds up extremely well to long braising, pickling, and fermentation. Braised red cabbage with apples, vinegar, and spices (the classic German Rotkohl) and quick-pickled red cabbage for tacos and grain bowls represent the two most common culinary applications, both of which take advantage of the vivid color and firm texture that make Red Acre specifically valuable.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant a few weeks before the last frost; also sows well in mid-summer for a fall crop.
directions: Start seeds indoors six weeks before setting out, then transplant hardened seedlings into rich, well-drained soil. This compact heirloom forms dense, deep-purple heads around 3-4 pounds and tolerates cold well, making it a good choice for tight spaces and raised beds. Keep moisture even to prevent the round heads from splitting as they firm up. Harvest when heads feel solid, and enjoy the crisp, colorful leaves fresh, in slaws, or lightly cooked.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant a few weeks before the last frost, or sow in summer for fall.
directions: 'Red Acre' forms solid, deep-red heads early on compact plants, making it a strong pick for small gardens and containers. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before setting out, then transplant into rich, full-sun soil spaced 12-18 inches apart. Keep moisture steady to prevent splitting and harvest heads once firm and about 5-7 inches across. This cool-season variety offers good storage and resistance to yellows.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 12–18 inches and sidedress with nitrogen at 30 days for best grain production.
directions: Direct sow after last frost (or start indoors 3–4 weeks before) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 12–18 inches and sidedress with nitrogen at 30 days for best grain production. Amaranthus cruentus is a remarkable dual-purpose annual producing enormous, showy, red-purple to magenta flower plumes from midsummer through fall while simultaneously growing highly nutritious seeds (up to 20% protein with a complete amino acid profile including lysine) that can be harvested as a pseudo-grain and popped, ground into flour, or cooked like porridge; the young leaves and shoots are also edible as a nutritious cooking green high in iron and calcium. The bold, often dark-red to bronze-red foliage is highly ornamental; selected grain varieties include 'Burgundy', 'Hot Biscuits', and 'Hopi Red Dye'. Young leaves are an excellent spinach substitute in hot weather when true spinach bolts.

plant_note: Tiny warmth-loving seed; do not presoak, sow on the surface of moist medium.
directions: Scatter the very fine amaranth seed on the surface of a moist tray without burying it, and keep the medium warm to trigger germination. It grows more slowly than brassicas and prefers extra heat, so be patient during the first week. Mist gently to keep the delicate seedlings from drying out while avoiding standing water. Harvest the vivid crimson, mild-sweet microgreens once the cotyledons color up, usually around two weeks, for an elegant gourmet garnish.

plant_note: Start indoors early; this is an intermediate-day onion best for mid latitudes.
directions: 'Red Amposta' is an intermediate-day onion producing large, reddish-purple globes with sweet, snappy flavor and attractive red-and-white rings. Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings 3-4 inches apart in fertile, full-sun soil. Keep the shallow-rooted plants weed-free and evenly watered until the tops begin to fall over. Cure bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storing.

plant_note: Start indoors well before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm.
directions: Sow seeds indoors about six weeks before your last frost, then transplant deeply, burying much of the stem to encourage strong roots. These indeterminate Amish heirloom vines are large and sprawling, so provide tall stakes or heavy cages for support. The rosy-red, deeply lobed beefsteak fruits are sweet, low-acid, and best eaten fresh in slices. Water consistently and mulch to reduce cracking and blossom-end rot on the big fruits.

plant_note: Time transplants so sprouts mature in cool fall weather; a light frost sweetens the flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into firm, fertile soil, giving each plant plenty of room and support in windy sites. This striking heirloom produces purple-red sprouts along tall stalks with a nutty-sweet flavor that deepens after frost. The long season means patience is required, so plan the planting date backward from your first fall frost. Harvest sprouts from the bottom up as they firm to about an inch, and the color intensifies with cold weather.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun; soak seeds 12–24 hours in warm water before planting to speed germination; Red Burgundy is an AAS award-winning heirloom okra variety producing deeply colored deep-red to burgundy-purple pods that are as ornamental as they are edible — the pods maintain their color fresh but turn green when cooked.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms to 70°F+ in full sun, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; harvest pods at 3–4 inches for best tenderness; Red Burgundy produces excellent fresh pods and makes a very beautiful ornamental edible garden plant. Abelmoschus esculentus 'Red Burgundy' is an All-America Selections award-winning heirloom okra variety selected for its striking deep red-burgundy to near-black pod color — one of the most visually dramatic okra varieties available. The compact, 4–5-foot plants produce deep-red stems, leaf veins, and pods that create a stunning ornamental effect in the edible garden or mixed border. The pods are tender, flavorful, and productive at 3–4 inches; they have the same culinary properties as green okra but with the added visual appeal of the deep color. The color is caused by anthocyanin pigments, the same antioxidant compounds found in red cabbage and purple sweet potatoes; like other anthocyanin-rich vegetables, Red Burgundy okra pods lose most of their red color and turn green when cooked, though the anthocyanins are still consumed. The flavor and texture are essentially identical to high-quality green okra. Red Burgundy is productive in the long, hot Gulf Coast summer and was a 1988 AAS winner — one of the most enduringly popular colored okra varieties in American seed catalogs.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil a few weeks after the last frost; soaking seed overnight speeds sprouting.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and sow one inch deep only after soil is thoroughly warm, since okra hates cold. This 1988 All-America Selections winner grows into tall five-foot plants with deep-red stems and burgundy pods that add ornamental appeal. Harvest pods young, at about three to four inches, snipping every day or two to keep the plants productive and the pods tender. The rich color can fade with cooking but the plants remain handsome all season.

plant_note: Short-day type best for southern gardeners; start early and transplant while cool.
directions: Start seeds indoors two to three months before transplanting, as onions need a long lead time. This short-day variety forms bulbs when days reach 10-12 hours, so it suits southern and mild-winter gardens best. Set transplants a few inches apart in loose, fertile soil and keep them weed-free and evenly watered. The glossy red bulbs reach about four inches with sweet, mild white flesh ringed in pink, and are best used fresh rather than for long storage.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest November–February. Red Choi can also be sown January–February for a spring crop. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide continuous harvest. Cool temperatures intensify the red-purple color; heat causes plants to revert toward green and bolt quickly. Baby leaves are harvestable 25–30 days from sowing.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil; Red Choi is a red-leafed bok choy (pak choi) selection producing compact rosette plants with deep burgundy-red to purple-red leaves with contrasting white or pale pink midribs — visually striking in both the garden and on the plate. The flavor is identical to standard green bok choy — mild, slightly mustardy, very tender — but the anthocyanin pigments in the red leaves indicate additional antioxidant content. Red Choi performs best and shows the deepest color in cool weather; warm temperatures cause the plants to green up and bolt quickly. The compact size and partial-shade tolerance make it ideal for intercropping under taller crops, growing in containers, or filling shady corners of the fall garden where other vegetables would fail. Harvest the whole head at 45–55 days or cut outer leaves for continuous baby green harvest. Stir-fry briefly to preserve some color, or use raw in salads where the red color provides striking visual contrast.

plant_note: Small legume seed grown like alfalfa; sow densely on moist trays or as sprouts.
directions: Sow the small clover seed densely and evenly across a moist tray, or grow it in a sprouting jar with regular rinsing. It germinates quickly and grows fine, upright stems, so uncover early and provide bright light. Mist frequently to keep the delicate mat hydrated without souring. Harvest the mild, fresh-tasting green shoots after about a week to ten days at the cotyledon stage.

plant_note: Grown indoors as sprouts in a jar year-round, not planted in the garden.
directions: Red clover sprouts are grown indoors in a jar or sprouting tray, offering a crisp, mild flavor and easy-to-hull seed coats similar to alfalfa. Soak seeds several hours, then rinse and drain two to three times daily in indirect light. Harvest in about 5-7 days once the sprouts show tiny green leaves, then refrigerate. They add crunch and nutrition to sandwiches, salads, and green drinks.

plant_note: Direct sow; well suited to heavy or shallow soils where longer carrots fail.
directions: 'Red Cored Chantenay' produces thick, blunt, 6-inch roots that reliably size up even in heavy or shallow soils where longer carrots struggle. Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and keep the seedbed moist through the slow germination, then thin to 2-3 inches apart. The heavy-yielding, split-resistant roots are excellent for juicing, canning, freezing, and cooking, and they store well. Cool weather deepens their sweetness.

plant_note: In zone 9, sow seeds or set transplants in October–November for harvest in March–April; Red Creole is a short-day onion (requires about 12–13 hours of daylight to bulb) well-matched to the Gulf South's winter day length. Direct sow or set transplants 4 inches apart.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Creole C-5 is the predominant short-day red onion of the Gulf South, widely grown in Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and Alabama and a staple of Gulf Coast kitchen gardens for generations. Unlike the mild, low-pungency sweet onions prized in other regions, Red Creole is a distinctly pungent, storage-type red onion — strongly flavored, with a sharp, assertive onion bite that makes it preferred for Creole and Cajun cooking where onion flavor needs to stand up through long cooking in jambalayas, étouffées, and red beans. The medium-sized, somewhat flattened bulbs cure well and keep for several months in a dry, well-ventilated location. Red Creole bolts in long days, so it MUST be grown on the short-day winter schedule in zone 9 (planted October–December, harvested March–April). It is heat-tolerant once past the bulbing stage and handles the warming temperatures of spring well. A foundational vegetable of Louisiana foodways alongside celery and bell pepper in the Cajun 'holy trinity.'

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or start in midsummer for fall harvest 90–105 days before first frost; Red Drumhead is a traditional European heirloom red cabbage producing large, flat to slightly rounded, very densely packed deep red-purple heads of excellent quality for fresh eating, braising, pickling, and long-term storage.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 3–4 weeks before last frost (cabbage tolerates light frost); space 18–24 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Red Drumhead is a traditional European heirloom red cabbage with a distinctive flattened or slightly convex head shape — broader and flatter than the round heads of varieties like Red Acre or Mammoth Red Rock — that packs very tightly with dense, waxy, deep red-purple leaves. The name 'Drumhead' refers to this characteristically wide, flat shape reminiscent of a drum (a category designation historically used for flat-headed cabbages in both red and green forms). The flavor is bold, earthy, and slightly peppery when raw — excellent for traditional German red cabbage dishes (braised with apples and vinegar), pickling, sauerkraut, and coleslaw; the purple pigment (from anthocyanins) is water-soluble and will turn the cooking liquid blue-purple, traditionally corrected by adding vinegar or apple to keep the red color. Individual heads weigh 4–8 lbs at full maturity; the dense heads resist splitting and store well in cool conditions (35–40°F) for 3–4 months after harvest. Excellent cold hardiness — can withstand frosts to 20°F, making it suitable for overwintering in mild climates.

common_name: Red Express Cabbage (Early Small Red Cabbage for Fall Production)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Express is particularly well-suited to fall production — the cool temperatures of fall intensify the anthocyanin red-purple color and sweeten the flavor. In zone 9, transplant mid-August through September for October–December harvest. The small, compact heads (1.5–3 lbs) reach maturity in just 63–72 days from transplant and hold in the garden without splitting for several weeks after reaching maturity.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Red Express is an early-maturing red cabbage that matures 2–3 weeks faster than standard red varieties like Red Acre or Ruby Ball, producing small to medium (1.5–3 lb), nicely rounded, deep purple-red heads in just 63–72 days from transplant. Red cabbages in general contain significantly more anthocyanin antioxidants than green types and have a characteristic slightly sharper, more peppery flavor profile; Red Express delivers these attributes in an early-maturing, compact form well-suited to small gardens and fall production windows where there may not be time for the standard 80–85 day maturity of most red cabbage varieties. The red-purple pigmentation intensifies with cool fall temperatures — heads started in late summer and maturing in fall have dramatically deeper, more saturated color than spring-grown heads. Red Express holds well in the garden after reaching maturity and stores very well in refrigeration (4–6 months at 32°F), making it an excellent variety for gardeners who want to put up a supply of red cabbage for winter coleslaw and braised preparations.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, sow September through January for fall and winter production; the striking purple foliage makes Red Giant ornamentally valuable in cool-season beds alongside kale and Swiss chard.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season; Red Giant is the most widely grown purple mustard green — a Japanese mustard variety with large, deeply frilled to semi-smooth leaves in a striking deep burgundy-purple to reddish-purple color that makes it simultaneously ornamental and edible. The bold purple color intensifies with cool temperatures and frost exposure, making Red Giant one of the most visually dramatic cool-season vegetables for the Gulf South garden — combining beautifully with green kale, white cauliflower, and orange-flowered pansies in the fall edible landscape. The flavor is distinctly pungent and spicy with a mustard heat that develops more fully in mature leaves; young leaves at 4–6 inches are milder and excellent for salads and slaws. In hot weather, the plant bolts and the leaves become extremely pungent and bitter — in zone 9, grow strictly as a fall/winter/spring crop. The purple color partially transfers to cooking liquid and mixed dishes, giving cooked dishes a beautiful purple-tinted sauce. The combination of culinary value and ornamental purple foliage makes Red Giant an excellent choice for edible landscape plantings where vegetables serve double duty as ornamentals.

plant_note: Start indoors with bottom heat well ahead of the last frost; this crop needs a long warm season.
directions: Start seeds indoors early with consistent warmth, since habaneros germinate slowly and need a long, hot season to ripen. As tender perennials they can be grown year-round outdoors only in frost-free zones. Transplant into full sun after nights stay warm, and support the branching plants as the crimson pods develop. These are among the hottest habaneros with a fruity flavor, so handle the ripe red pods with gloves when harvesting for salsa and hot sauce.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors with heat mats; transplant only when soil and nights are warm.
directions: Sow seeds indoors eight or more weeks before transplanting, using bottom heat to coax the slow-germinating seeds along. This heirloom Capsicum chinense produces bright red, extremely hot, fruity pods perfect for salsas and Caribbean cooking. Move plants outdoors only after the weather is settled and warm, spacing them for good air circulation. Ripen fruits fully to deep red for maximum heat and flavor, wearing gloves whenever you handle them.

common_name: Red Hubbard Squash (Large Traditional Orange-Red Winter Storage Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Red Hubbard requires a long season (92–105 days) and is harvested as a storage squash in fall. In zone 9, plant March–April for September–October harvest. Cure harvested fruits at 80–85°F for 2 weeks to harden the skin before moving to cool, dry storage (50–55°F) where they keep 3–5 months. The very hard shell and warty skin require a heavy, sharp knife or cleaver to cut — many cooks bake the whole squash before cutting.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants. Cure harvested fruits 2 weeks at warm temperature before cool storage. Red Hubbard is a classic large Cucurbita maxima winter squash — one of the largest commonly grown winter squash types, producing fruits typically weighing 10–15 lbs with distinctive warty, orange-red to brick-red-orange skin and a teardrop to large, irregular form with a knobby, pointed blossom end. The Hubbard class of squash has a long American horticultural history, dating to the mid-19th century when the Blue Hubbard type was brought to New England and became a regional storage squash staple. Red Hubbard is a warmer-colored variant with orange-red skin rather than the Blue Hubbard's steel-blue-gray. The very thick, hard shell provides exceptional storage capability (stored roots keep 4–6 months) and was important in pre-refrigeration households where squash served as an important carbohydrate source through winter. The deep orange flesh is very dense, dry, and sweet — the classic winter squash flavor in concentrated form, excellent for pies, soups, and roasted preparations where the flavor holds up to extended cooking.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March for fall through spring harvest. Red Kingdom produces baby salad leaves in as little as 21 days and reaches full size by 35–40 days — one of the fastest-growing cool-season greens available. Harvest as baby leaves for mild salad use or allow to reach full size for a more pronounced peppery flavor. In zone 9 successive sowings every 2–3 weeks maintain continuous supply through the cool season. The vibrant red-purple color makes Red Kingdom an excellent cut-and-come-again salad green that persists beautifully through zone 9 winters.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Kingdom is a red-leaved selection of mizuna (Brassica rapa var. japonica) that combines the deeply cut, feathery leaf shape of traditional green mizuna with vivid deep ruby-red to burgundy-purple leaf color — creating one of the most ornamental salad greens available for kitchen garden beds and mixed containers.
