Mizuna is a Japanese mustard green with a mild, slightly peppery, pleasantly tangy flavor that is substantially less harsh than red mustard or arugula, making Red Kingdom one of the most approachable and versatile peppery greens for fresh salads. Baby leaves harvested at 2–3 inches have a particularly mild and delicate flavor that works well in mixed salad blends; mature leaves develop more pronounced peppery notes similar to mild arugula. The vivid red-purple color is most intense in cool weather and fades somewhat as temperatures rise in spring — a cool autumn or winter planting in zone 9 produces the most visually striking, deeply colored leaves. Red Kingdom's partial shade tolerance makes it a productive salad green for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun space.

common_name: Red Knight Bell Pepper (Hybrid Thick-Walled Red Bell Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Red Knight is harvested green at 65 days from transplant or left to ripen red at 80–85 days. The red-ripe stage has much higher vitamin C and sweetness than the green stage. In zone 9, transplant March–April for June–August harvest. Red Knight shows excellent resistance to Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), which helps maintain productivity in summer stress conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun, well-drained soil after last frost. Red Knight is a premium F1 hybrid bell pepper from PanAmerican Seed that has become one of the most consistently recommended thick-walled, high-quality bell peppers for both home gardens and commercial production in the eastern United States — a large (4 x 4 inch), blocky, 4-lobed bell pepper with very thick walls (0.3–0.35 inch) that set it apart from thinner-walled standard bell types. The thick walls are the key eating-quality trait: they provide a satisfying crunch, substantial texture for stuffing (the walls hold up to heat without collapsing), and a longer postharvest shelf life than thin-walled types that wilt rapidly after picking. Red Knight ripens from deep, dark green to a uniformly rich red with clean, complete color change. The fruit flavor at the red stage is noticeably sweeter and more complex than at the green stage — the extended ripening time converts starches and develops sugars, creating a pepper that many cooks use specifically in the red stage for roasted red pepper, jarred pimento-style preparations, and raw salads. Disease resistance includes Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), which can devastate pepper plantings in summer heat — a practical advantage in zone 8–10 summer production.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for summer harvest. Red Kuri stores remarkably well — properly cured fruits (2 weeks at 85°F, then cool dry storage) keep 5–6 months, providing winter squash into late winter. The medium-size fruits (5–8 lbs) are manageable for home cooking. In zone 9 the long, warm season allows the fruit to cure fully on the vine — leave until the vine withers and the skin is hard before harvesting.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Red Kuri (also known as Red Hokkaido, Orange Hokkaido, or Uchiki Kuri) is a Japanese heirloom winter squash producing distinctive, medium-sized, pear-to-teardrop-shaped fruits with deep reddish-orange skin and bright orange, dry, starchy flesh. The flavor is described as a rich chestnut-like sweetness with buttery, nutty notes and an exceptionally dense, dry texture that distinguishes it from the moister, stringier flesh of butternut and acorn squash. The dry, starchy texture makes Red Kuri outstanding for soups and purees (where it thickens naturally), Japanese-style simmered preparations (kabocha), and stuffed squash presentations where watery flesh would dilute the flavor. The medium size (5–8 pounds) is more practical for home cooking than very large winter squash. Red Kuri has been popular in French and Japanese cuisine for decades and is now widely grown in American specialty gardens and farmers markets.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil warms to 65°F; in short-season areas, start indoors 3 weeks before transplanting.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds 1 inch deep per hill in compost-enriched soil and thin to one or two vines per hill once established. Red Kuri is a teardrop-shaped Cucurbita maxima with vivid orange-red skin and nutty, chestnut-flavored, dry flesh that is among the finest of all winter squash. Harvest when skin is deep orange-red and hard; the stems will be beginning to dry and the skin will resist a thumbnail. Cure for 10–14 days at room temperature before storing; fruits keep well for three to four months under cool, dry conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow once soil is warm, or start indoors 3 weeks early.
directions: 'Red Kuri', also called Orange Hokkaido, yields teardrop-shaped 3-4 pound fruits with smooth, sweet, chestnut-like flesh. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and give the vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl in full sun. Keep watering steady while fruit develops, then cure harvested squash to build sweetness and storage life. Cut fruit once the rind hardens and the stem dries, leaving a stub of stem attached.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces January–February in zone 9 for May–June harvest; Red LaSoda is specifically adapted to the Gulf South's winter planting schedule and performs better in warm, humid climates than most northern potato varieties. It tolerates slightly warmer soil temperatures than white potatoes and handles the transition into warm spring weather better.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil; Red LaSoda is a red-skin, white-flesh potato variety developed at Louisiana State University specifically for Gulf Coast and Southern growing conditions — it is one of the few potato varieties bred with the hot, humid Deep South in mind rather than the cool Pacific Northwest or Northeast where most commercial varieties originate. The round, attractively smooth, deep-red skinned tubers have firm, white, waxy flesh excellent for boiling, potato salads, and roasting — the waxy texture holds shape during cooking rather than falling apart. Red LaSoda shows better tolerance of warm temperatures, clay soils, and the wet winters common to the Gulf South than most commercial varieties. It is the most widely recommended red potato for Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Texas Gulf Coast gardens, and is a staple offering at Southern feed-and-seed stores each January. Harvest as new potatoes when plants bloom; for storage potatoes, harvest after vines begin yellowing and dying back.

plant_note: Direct sow at or just after last frost once soil is consistently warm; the heat-season replacement for spinach in tropical and subtropical gardens.
directions: Scatter seeds thinly on the soil surface — they need light to germinate — then press gently and keep moist; thin seedlings to 6 inches apart, using thinnings as baby greens. Leaves are brilliantly colored in shades of red, purple, and green and are mildly flavored, used in stir-fries, soups, and as a cooked green throughout South and Southeast Asia. Harvest outer leaves or cut entire young plants at 6–8 inches tall to encourage regrowth; plants that are allowed to flower and set seed will readily self-sow for the following year. This species thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that cause true spinach to bolt immediately.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; red leaf lettuces are loose-head types harvested as cut-and-come-again crops by removing outer leaves as needed, or as whole heads — heat bolts them quickly so sow again in early fall for best flavor.
directions: Sow seed thinly on the surface and press in gently; lettuce seeds need light to germinate and should not be covered more than 1/8 inch deep; keep moist until germination. Red leaf lettuce encompasses looseleaf types with varying degrees of red-to-burgundy pigmentation in the leaves, including classics like 'Lollo Rossa,' 'New Red Fire,' 'Red Sails,' and 'Oak Red' — the anthocyanin pigmentation develops best in cool temperatures and direct sunlight, with heat causing color to fade and bitterness to increase. Red leaf lettuces are the most commonly grown looseleaf types in American home gardens, valued for their visual appeal, nutritional density (the red pigment is anthocyanins with antioxidant value), and ease of growing as cut-and-come-again salad plants. Harvest outer leaves when 4–6 inches long, leaving the center to continue growing; provide shade cloth (30%) in warm climates to extend the season. Interplant with taller vegetables for natural afternoon shade.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start August–September and transplant October–November. Red Long of Tropea is a long-day onion adapted to the short winter days and mild temperatures of coastal Mediterranean and Gulf South climates. In zone 9 it produces a winter-to-spring crop, bulbing up in January–March as day length increases. Unlike short-day bulbing onions, Red Long of Tropea can be pulled young as a sweet salad onion before full bulb development.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Long of Tropea (Cipolla Rossa di Tropea) is the iconic long, elongated red onion of the Calabrian coast town of Tropea in southern Italy, with IGP protected status as a geographic-origin food product. The bulbs are strikingly elongated — cylindrical to torpedo-shaped rather than globe-shaped — with brilliant deep-magenta-red skin and white-to-light-pink flesh with exceptionally low pungency and high natural sweetness. The Tropea onion is the standard for Italian raw onion preparations — sliced thin on bruschetta, dressed with olive oil and herbs, or pickled in vinegar — where the mild, almost sweet flavor allows the onion to be eaten raw without the harsh bite of standard globe onions. The visual appeal of the deep red, elongated shape makes it a striking addition to salads and charcuterie boards. In zone 9 it bulbs up reliably through the mild winter and produces excellent results in the sandy loam soils typical of Gulf Coast gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Red Malabar Spinach thrives in zone 9's hot, humid summers when traditional spinach bolts within weeks — it is at its most productive in conditions (heat and humidity) that make conventional cool-season greens impossible. Provide a trellis, fence, or string support — the vines reach 6–10 feet in a full season. Harvest regularly by cutting stem tips 4–6 inches long, which stimulates branching and more production.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil — Red Malabar Spinach tolerates partial shade better than most warm-season vegetables and grows productively in dappled light; Red Malabar Spinach is the magenta-stemmed ornamental form of Malabar spinach (Basella), a tropical Asian climbing vine whose thick, succulent leaves and stems provide a heat-tolerant alternative to true spinach (Spinacia) for hot-summer gardens. While true spinach bolts and becomes unusably bitter within days of warm weather arriving, Red Malabar Spinach actively thrives in the heat and humidity of zone 9 summers, producing increasingly large quantities of glossy, thick, mild-flavored leaves through the entire warm season. The mild, slightly mucilaginous, neutral flavor of the leaves works well in stir-fries, soups, green smoothies, and anywhere true spinach would be used — the slight mucilage (similar to okra) actually serves as a natural thickening agent in soups and stews. The striking red-purple stems and glossy dark green leaves make the vine ornamentally attractive climbing a fence or trellis.

common_name: Red Malabar Spinach (Red Vine Spinach, Malabar Nightshade Red)
plant_note: Direct sow or plant stem cuttings after last frost in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Red Malabar spinach is the red-stemmed form of Malabar spinach — a vining tropical Asian leafy green that produces abundantly through summer heat when true spinach (Spinacia oleracea) bolts and fails, with beautiful crimson stems contrasting the glossy dark-green leaves.
directions: Direct sow seeds or plant rooted stem cuttings in moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; provide trellis or fence for the vining stems. Basella rubra (red Malabar spinach or red vine spinach) is the red-stemmed form of Malabar spinach, with strikingly beautiful deep-crimson to purplish-red stems and petioles contrasting with glossy, dark green, somewhat succulent, heart-shaped leaves. Botanically, red (B. rubra) and green (B. alba) Malabar spinach are sometimes treated as separate species, sometimes as forms of the same species — both are grown identically and used the same way. The ornamental value of red Malabar spinach is substantial: the crimson stems winding up a trellis create a dramatic tropical display throughout the warm season. The leaves are cooked like spinach — slightly mucilaginous (slippery) in texture, mild in flavor, wilting quickly in heat — used in stir-fries, soups, curries, and as a spinach substitute throughout South and Southeast Asia. In zone 9–12, it grows as a perennial vine; in colder zones, a summer annual. It is one of the very few spinach-type leafy greens that performs well in high heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast summer, bridging the gap when cool-season greens have failed. Stem cuttings root easily.

common_name: Red Marconi Frying Pepper (Italian Open-Pollinated Sweet Roasting Pepper)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Marconi is an open-pollinated Italian frying pepper that can be seed-saved year to year — select the best-shaped, most productive fruits from the healthiest plants. In zone 9, transplant March–April. Harvest green for frying (sweeter and more delicate) or let ripen to full deep red for roasting — the red-ripe stage has dramatically more sweetness and vitamin C than the green stage.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Red Marconi is the classic Italian open-pollinated sweet frying/roasting pepper — a traditional heirloom variety that produces long (6–8 inch), moderately tapered, thick-walled, slightly ridged fruits of the Italian frying type, ripening from medium green to deep, vivid red. Unlike the Giant Marconi hybrid (AAS 1997), Red Marconi is open-pollinated, allowing seed to be saved and maintained from year to year — the preservation choice for gardeners who want a self-sustaining seed supply. The traditional Italian frying pepper form is distinctive: longer and more tapered than bell peppers, with a slightly irregular, ridged exterior and relatively thick, meaty walls. At the green stage, the flavor is mild, fresh, and subtly sweet — the standard for Italian sautéed peppers (peperoni fritti) where the pepper is sliced and cooked in olive oil until tender. At the red stage, the flavor concentrates into a sweet, rich, complex character ideal for roasting, peeling, and incorporating into antipasto, stuffed preparations, or the classic Italian peperonata. Red Marconi plants are tall (30–42 inches), productive, and require staking when loaded with fruit.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost for spring; sow again 6–8 weeks before first fall frost for the best-flavored autumn harvest.
directions: Scatter seeds thinly and cover with 1/4 inch of soil in a cool, moist seedbed; germination is rapid in cool conditions. Red mizuna has the same deeply-cut, feathery leaf form as green mizuna but with vivid burgundy-red stems and leaf coloring that intensifies in cool weather, making it as ornamental as it is edible. Harvest outer leaves continuously once plants reach 4 inches, or cut the entire plant 1 inch above the base to allow regrowth; flavor is peppery and nutty, similar to green mizuna but with slightly more bite. Fall sowings consistently outperform spring plantings in flavor and color intensity as frost sweetens the leaves.

plant_note: Sow only after soil has warmed thoroughly; cold soil rots seed.
directions: Provide a sturdy 7-8 ft trellis before sowing, as vines climb aggressively and produce deep burgundy pods up to 18 inches long. Direct sow two weeks after last frost when soil reaches at least 70 F, planting seeds 1 inch deep. Harvest pods young and tender at pencil thickness for best flavor and to keep plants productive. Pick every two to three days during peak season to prevent pods from becoming fibrous. Feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer since heavy nitrogen reduces pod set.

common_name: Red Noodle Yard-Long Bean (Striking Deep-Red Extra-Long Asian Pole Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 70°F in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence at least 5 feet tall — Red Noodle vines grow vigorously to 10+ feet and require substantial support for the trailing bean clusters.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Red Noodle is a striking red-podded yard-long bean (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis) producing deep burgundy-red to dark red pods 18–24 inches long — the dramatic red color and extraordinary length combine to make this one of the most visually spectacular edible climbing plants available for Gulf South summer gardens. Yard-long beans (also called asparagus beans or Chinese long beans) are a tropical subspecies of cowpea adapted to hot, humid conditions that make them particularly suitable for Gulf South summer production when standard snap beans decline. The pods should be harvested at 12–18 inches for best tenderness and flavor — they become tough and fibrous when allowed to develop past 20 inches. Red Noodle maintains its red color when raw and in raw preparations but turns greenish-brown when cooked — similar to the color loss in Burgundy snap beans and Red Russian kale. The cooking texture is similar to standard yard-long beans: slightly firmer and less watery than snap beans, holding texture well in stir-fries and sautés. The vines grow vigorously to 8–12 feet in Gulf South heat and require substantial trellis support (minimum 5–6 foot fence or trellis height) — the trailing red bean clusters hanging from overhead structures create a dramatic ornamental and productive display simultaneously.

common_name: Red Noodle Yardlong Bean (Burgundy Asparagus Bean, Red Long Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost (yardlong beans are more heat-loving than Phaseolus beans and benefit from warmer soil, 70°F+); provide a trellis 6–8 feet tall; Red Noodle is the most visually dramatic yardlong bean variety, producing 18–24 inch pods of an extraordinary deep burgundy-crimson color that fade to purple-gray when cooked — the intensely colored pods are the most striking visual feature of any long bean grown in American gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after the soil reaches 70°F or more (1–3 weeks after last frost) at the base of a sturdy trellis 6–8 feet tall; Red Noodle bean is extremely heat-tolerant and actually performs best in the hottest summer conditions — it continues producing during summer heat that stops most beans from setting pods. Red Noodle is a cultivar of the yardlong bean (also called asparagus bean, long bean, or snake bean), which is the same species as the cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) but selected for long pod production — the typical yardlong bean produces green pods 18–24 inches long; Red Noodle produces pods of the same length but in a spectacular deep burgundy to crimson-red color that is unique among commonly grown beans and makes the loaded trellis a visual centerpiece of the summer garden. The flavor is similar to standard green yardlong beans — somewhat starchier and with more umami than fresh Phaseolus beans — and is excellent stir-fried in Chinese cooking (the primary culinary tradition that uses yardlong beans), in pad thai, in Southeast Asian salads and pickles, or simply sautéed with garlic and soy. The dark color fades significantly when cooked, but remains visually interesting as a dark grayish-purple. Yardlong beans including Red Noodle are far more heat-tolerant than any Phaseolus bean variety and are ideal for Gulf Coast gardeners in zones 8b–10 who want continuous summer bean production through July and August when other beans fail.

common_name: Red Norland Potato (Very Early Smooth Red-Skinned White-Flesh Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed potato pieces (each with at least one eye) 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.8–6.5) soil in full sun; Red Norland is one of the earliest-maturing potato varieties (70–80 days) making it well-suited to the short cool season in zone 9 before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Red Norland is one of the finest early-maturing red potato varieties for home garden production — producing attractive, smooth, bright-red-skinned, white-fleshed tubers that mature in only 70–80 days from planting, making it the best choice for Zone 9 gardeners whose spring potato window closes when summer heat arrives. The smooth red skin (without the russeting or rough texture of some red varieties) and excellent appearance make Red Norland outstanding for presentation at harvest — new Red Norland potatoes dug fresh from the garden have bright color and clean appearance. The white flesh is excellent for boiling, steaming, and potato salad — waxy enough to hold its shape when cooked, with a moist, creamy texture and mild potato flavor that excels in salads, soups, and boiled presentations. In zone 9, plant seed potatoes in January–February for a May–June harvest before summer heat makes potato production impractical. Hill soil over the developing plants 2–3 times as they grow to ensure tubers do not green from light exposure. Red Norland has been one of the most widely grown early red potato varieties in American home gardens since its introduction in the 1950s — a reliable, consistent producer of high-quality fresh-eating potatoes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Red Oak Leaf is exceptionally heat-tolerant for a red lettuce and holds quality longer than most red types before bolting. Succession sow every 3 weeks through fall for continuous harvest. Harvest outer leaves for cut-and-come-again or pull entire plants.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Red Oak Leaf is the red-leafed counterpart to the classic green Oak Leaf lettuce — producing deeply lobed, sinuate leaves with an outline resembling the characteristic deeply-indented silhouette of an oak leaf, in deep burgundy-red to bronze-red coloring. The deeply-indented, non-frilly leaf form distinguishes Oak Leaf types immediately from the more common looseleaf lettuces with wavy or ruffled edges. The flavor is mild, tender, and slightly nutty — one of the better-flavored looseleaf lettuces with a soft, non-bitter quality. Red Oak Leaf lettuce is notably heat-tolerant and slow-to-bolt compared to most red lettuces, making it particularly valuable for extending the spring harvest season in zone 9 and for reliable color retention in warm fall conditions when other red varieties revert to green. The striking leaf form and consistent deep-red color make it one of the most popular lettuces for mesclun mixes and specialty salad blends.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before outdoor transplant date in late winter, or plant red onion sets outdoors as soon as soil is workable in spring; select long-day varieties for northern gardens (zone 3–6) and short-day or intermediate varieties for southern gardens (zone 7–10).
directions: Grow identically to yellow onions, starting seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting or planting sets as early as soil can be worked in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; red onions get their distinctive color from anthocyanin pigments concentrated in the outer layers and are the premier choice for fresh use in salads, salsas, pickles, and raw preparations where their mild, slightly sweet flavor and dramatic purple-red color provide visual impact alongside their culinary role. The color fades when cooked, making them less suitable for long-cooked dishes than yellow onions. Popular varieties include 'Red Burgundy' (short-day, for zone 7–10), 'Red Wethersfield' (long-day, for zone 3–6), and 'Redwing' (intermediate-day). Quick-pickled red onion in lime juice or vinegar is one of the most versatile condiments in modern cooking.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest. Autumn sowing also works well in mild climates. Plants bolt in heat, so focus on spring and fall crops.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in early spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; red orach is a striking annual with wine-red to burgundy foliage that makes it as ornamental as it is edible. The arrow-shaped leaves have a flavor similar to spinach — mild, slightly salty, and earthy — and are excellent raw in salads when young or lightly cooked when larger. Unlike spinach, orach is more heat-tolerant and slightly less cold-tolerant. The upright habit and vivid red color make it an excellent backdrop plant in the kitchen garden. Self-sows freely where happy, so either deadhead before seeds ripen or allow to naturalize. Young seedlings that sprout the following spring can be transplanted to preferred locations.

plant_note: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in any reasonably fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; orache germinates in cool soil and is one of the fastest-growing cool-season greens.
directions: Sow direct 4–6 weeks before last frost in any reasonably fertile, well-drained to moist, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; orache germinates and grows extremely rapidly in cool conditions and can be harvested as baby leaf greens in 3 weeks or as full plants at 40–60 days. Atriplex hortensis is a large, fast-growing cool-season annual producing striking red, gold, or green arrow-shaped to triangular leaves with a mild, slightly salty, spinach-like flavor excellent for salads, stir-fries, and as a spinach substitute; the red form ('Rubra') is especially ornamental, growing to 3–6 feet tall and making a dramatic statement in the potager. It self-seeds prolifically and can naturalize in gardens; in the Gulf South it is best grown in fall, winter, and spring as a cool-season crop. Related to quinoa and lamb's quarters; all parts including the young seed heads are edible.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Red Pear is the red-fruited counterpart to the Yellow Pear tomato, with the same diminutive, pear-shaped fruit and prolific production of sweet, bite-sized cherry tomatoes but ripening to brilliant red rather than yellow — excellent for snacking, salads, and garnishing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide sturdy caging or staking as Red Pear is an indeterminate vine that reaches 5–7 feet and produces abundant clusters of small fruit through the season. Red Pear is the red-fruited version of the classic pear tomato type, producing small (1–1.5 inch), distinctively pear-shaped, bright red fruits in prolific hanging clusters from midsummer through frost; the flavor is sweet and mild, slightly less complex than larger tomatoes but ideal for snacking directly from the vine, halved in salads, and as a colorful contrast to yellow or orange cherry types. Like Yellow Pear, Red Pear is indeterminate and extremely vigorous, producing continuously until frost and sometimes overloading cages with fruit weight; the plants may need supplemental tying. Resistant to cracking even in wet conditions. Popular in children's gardens for the playful shape and snacking appeal.

common_name: Red Pontiac Potato (Red Skin Waxy Potato)
plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January–February for May harvest. Red Pontiac is a late-season potato that performs well in the South's cool winter window, producing large, round tubers that are harvested before summer heat terminates the season.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 2–3 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost, after cutting to egg size with 1–2 eyes and allowing cut surfaces to cure for 1–2 days. Red Pontiac is the most widely grown red-skinned potato in the United States for over 50 years — a late-season, round, medium to large potato with smooth, dark red skin and white, waxy to slightly waxy flesh with moderate moisture content that holds its shape when boiled (making it excellent for potato salad, boiled potatoes, and roasting) while also mashing reasonably well. The bright red skin is attractive when left on for roasted preparations, and the firm texture keeps it together in soups and stews. Red Pontiac produces large, impressive tubers and is very productive in a wide range of soils, making it a reliable choice for home gardeners who want attractive, versatile red potatoes with a genuine all-purpose cooking character. In zone 9, plant in late January or early February and harvest in late April through May before summer heat causes plant decline.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant near the last frost, or sow in summer for a fall crop.
directions: 'Red Power' forms uniform, 1.5-2 pound pointed heads of tightly wrapped magenta leaves on a compact, upright plant ideal for small gardens. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before setting out and transplant into rich, full-sun soil. Keep moisture even to prevent splitting and harvest once heads feel firm. The sweet, mild flavor and striking color make it excellent raw in salads, stir-fried, or braised.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: 'Red Pride' is a determinate bush tomato that yields a heavy set of firm, 10-ounce red fruits on vigorous, compact plants. Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm, full-sun soil. Its strong disease-resistance package covers Alternaria stem canker, gray leaf spot, Fusarium wilt, and Verticillium wilt, making it low-fuss. A short cage or stake supports the concentrated fruit load; harvest when fully red.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F, in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; give the vigorous vining plants a trellis, fence, or plenty of ground to sprawl, and expect a long production season lasting until frost.
directions: Direct sow in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving with minimal irrigation through the hottest, driest part of the Gulf South summer. Red Ripper is a vigorous, long-vining heirloom cowpea grown across the South since the 19th century both as a food crop and as a dependable summer cover crop and livestock forage, valued for its toughness in poor soil and drought that would fail most other legumes. The sprawling vines carry deep red-brown, kidney-shaped seeds in long pods over an extended late-summer season, continuing to set new pods until the first frost, which makes it one of the longer-producing Southern peas for a continuous late-season harvest. Beyond the table, Red Ripper is prized as a nitrogen-fixing green manure and grazing forage crop, tilled or turned under at the end of the season to build soil fertility for the following year. A dual-purpose, low-input heirloom well suited to the toughest garden conditions, zone 5–11.

common_name: Red Ripper Southern Pea (Red Ripper Cowpea, Old Timer Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Red Ripper is an heirloom Southern pea variety with distinctive reddish-tan to red-brown seeds with darker mottling — one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant of all Southern pea types, widely used as both a summer vegetable and a warm-season cover crop for building organic matter in hot, dry conditions where other cover crops struggle.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; Red Ripper is semi-vining and may need minimal support or can be left to sprawl; for cover crop use broadcast at 5–10 lbs per 1000 sq ft; harvest pods at green-shell stage for fresh eating or allow to fully dry for storage as dry peas. Red Ripper is one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant Southern pea varieties available, valued for both its role as a food crop and its exceptional performance as a summer cover crop in the hot, dry conditions of the Southern Plains and Gulf Coast. The plants are semi-vining (not quite as bushy as modern varieties, not as long-vining as pole types) and produce prolifically under conditions that would reduce the yield of more refined modern varieties — poor, sandy soil, minimal rain, and sustained heat above 95°F. The seeds are distinctive: larger than many Southern peas, reddish-tan to brown with darker mottling, with a hearty, earthy cowpea flavor when cooked. As a cover crop, Red Ripper builds nitrogen at high rates (80–120 lbs N/acre under good conditions), suppresses summer weeds aggressively with its spreading canopy, and its large biomass decomposes quickly in the warm soil to build organic matter. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and LSU AgCenter recommend Red Ripper as one of the top summer cover crops for the Gulf South. For food production, Red Ripper is an old heirloom with deep roots in Southern and Texan food traditions — used as fresh shelled peas, dried peas, and as the source of pot likker in traditional Southern cooking.

common_name: Red Robin Micro Tomato (Patio Container Micro-Dwarf Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Robin's extremely compact size (8–12 inches) makes it suitable for growing in 6–8 inch pots, hanging baskets, or window boxes — one of the few tomatoes practical for small apartment balconies and windowsills. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The determinate habit means all fruits ripen over a relatively short window (2–3 weeks); start 2–3 pots in succession for continuous harvest.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; grow in 6–8 inch containers or hanging baskets. Red Robin is a micro-dwarf determinate tomato — one of the smallest tomato plants available to gardeners, typically reaching only 8–14 inches tall and 8–12 inches wide at maturity. The extreme compact size distinguishes Red Robin from standard 'patio' tomatoes (which reach 24–36 inches) and makes it the tomato of choice for situations where space is extremely limited: kitchen windowsills, apartment balcony pots of any size, children's garden projects, hanging baskets, and window box plantings. Despite its tiny size, Red Robin produces red, round, 1-inch cherry tomatoes of acceptable sweet-tangy flavor in small but meaningful quantities — a single plant might produce 30–50 fruits over its harvest period, sufficient for salads and snacking. The determinate habit means the plant stops growing at its genetic maximum size and sets a crop over a 2–3 week window, making it ideal for succession planting (start a new plant every 3 weeks from late winter through late summer for continuous small harvests). Red Robin requires no staking, no pruning, and no trellising — it simply grows into a self-supporting mound and fruits.

plant_note: Sow in early spring and again in late summer; hot weather encourages bolting.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. This Cos-type heirloom forms upright heads of sturdy, crisp leaves in a rich burgundy that fades to pale green at the heart. Keep the soil evenly moist and provide some afternoon shade in warm regions to delay bolting. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut whole heads once they are full and firm.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Red Russian is the most tender and mildest-flavored kale — young leaves harvested before 4 inches are excellent raw in salads without any massage or marinating required. In zone 9 fall planting in September–October produces beautiful leaves through the cool season; the red-purple color intensifies with cold temperatures, making fall-harvested Red Russian particularly attractive.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Russian Kale is widely considered the most versatile and palatable kale variety for fresh and minimally processed use — the flat, deeply indented, gray-green leaves with red-purple stems and leaf margins have a tenderness and mild sweetness that allows them to be eaten raw in salads (particularly baby leaves) without the fibrous toughness and bitterness that makes many kale varieties unpleasant uncooked. Unlike the curly kales that require extensive massage to soften for salad use, Red Russian baby leaves can be used directly in mixed green salads, smoothies, and fresh preparations. The flavor is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than curly kale, with a mild earthiness and peppery undertone that becomes even more pleasant after frost — cold temperatures convert starches to sugars, dramatically improving the sweetness of all kale but especially Red Russian. The partial shade tolerance makes Red Russian one of the better kale choices for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun space.

plant_note: Tender enough for baby-leaf salad harvest as well as mature use.
directions: This oleracea-type kale has flat, frilly gray-green leaves with purple stems and is notably tender and sweet. Direct sow half an inch deep and thin to 12 inches, or harvest thinnings as baby greens. It tolerates both heat and cold better than curly kale, making it a good four-season crop. Snap off outer leaves as needed and the plant will keep pushing new growth from the center. A light frost improves its mild, sweet flavor.

plant_note: Sow thickly for cut-and-come-again baby greens; grows indoors year-round.
directions: Grown as baby greens, 'Red Russian' kale delivers tender, flat, purple-veined leaves loaded with vitamins A and C plus calcium and iron. Sow seeds thickly in shallow rows or trays and harvest by cutting leaves at about 3-4 inches tall, allowing regrowth for repeat cuttings. It grows quickly indoors any season or outdoors in cool weather, tolerating light frost. Snip young for salads or a quick saute.

plant_note: Sow in succession from early spring; heat tolerant enough to extend into warm weather.
directions: 'Red Sails' is a loose-leaf lettuce with soft, buttery, bronze-red leaves that resist bitterness even in warm weather. Sow seeds shallowly, barely covering them since light aids germination, and thin to 8-12 inches for full heads. Harvest baby greens in 2-3 weeks or full heads in about 6 weeks, or pick outer leaves for a continuous supply. Its heat tolerance and slow bolting make it a reliable choice for extended harvest.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather, barely covering seeds with soil; Red Sails tolerates heat somewhat better than many lettuces and is slower to bolt, making it a good choice for extending the spring lettuce season. In zone 9, direct sow September–February for fall and winter production, or February–March for a brief spring window before summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; Red Sails is a 1985 All-America Selections winner red leaf lettuce that has remained one of the most widely grown and recommended loose-leaf lettuces for over 40 years, valued for its combination of attractive deep burgundy-red to bronze coloring, excellent flavor, and — most practically — its slow bolting characteristic that gives it several weeks longer in the garden before going to seed than most lettuces under warming spring conditions. The large, ruffled, wavy leaves are moderately to deeply red throughout, with a mild, sweet lettuce flavor that is pleasant and non-bitter even in moderate heat. As a loose-leaf type, Red Sails can be harvested by removing outer leaves continuously (cut-and-come-again), or the entire plant can be cut at once. Red Sails is excellent for mixed salad bowls and provides visual contrast when grown alongside green lettuce varieties. In zone 9, it excels in the fall-through-winter season (September–February) when temperatures are cool enough for crisp lettuce production.

plant_note: Sow successively from early spring; this heat-tolerant type resists bolting better than most.
directions: Scatter seeds thinly and press lightly into the soil surface, as they germinate best with light. This loose-leaf heirloom forms large open rosettes of frilly burgundy-red leaves with a crisp, mild flavor. It is notably heat-tolerant, so it holds longer than many lettuces before bolting in warm weather. Harvest leaves individually on a cut-and-come-again basis for a steady supply of baby or full-size greens.

common_name: Red Samurai Carrot (Scarlet Japanese Nantes-Type Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow in a deeply tilled, well-amended bed free of rocks and clods; thin seedlings to 2–3 inches apart when plants reach 2 inches tall. In zone 9, sow September through October for December–February harvest; the cool fall/winter season produces the sweetest roots. Red Samurai develops best color and sweetness when grown in cool weather — summer production produces paler, less sweet roots.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly, 0.25 inch deep, in deeply tilled, loose, rock-free soil; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall, keeping thinnings for salads. Red Samurai is a Japanese-bred Nantes-type carrot (developed by Takii Seeds of Kyoto) that stands apart from most modern carrot varieties through its extraordinary deep scarlet-red to crimson skin and pinkish-red interior flesh, coloration that comes from lycopene — the same red pigment in tomatoes — rather than from the beta-carotene responsible for orange carrot color. The rich red color makes Red Samurai visually striking in the garden (the feathery tops are standard-green, revealing nothing of the flamboyant root below), stunning when sliced for salads and crudités, and exceptionally nutritious from a lycopene perspective. The roots are long (7–8 inches), slender, tapered in the classic Nantes style, with excellent sweet, mild flavor that compares favorably to the best orange Nantes varieties — the red pigmentation does not negatively affect flavor. Red Samurai is one of the most ornamentally distinctive of all carrot varieties and serves as an outstanding conversation piece in CSA boxes and farmers market displays where its unusual color draws immediate attention. Grows best in cool weather when the roots develop their deepest color; summer-grown roots are paler and somewhat less flavorful. An excellent addition to rainbow carrot mixes or grown on its own for maximum visual impact.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 8–10 weeks before last frost; Red Savina is a selected strain of habanero developed by Frank Garcia of GNS Spices that held the Guinness World Record for hottest pepper from 1994 to 2006, reaching 350,000–580,000 Scoville units — significantly hotter than standard habaneros.
directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 85°F and grow under strong grow lights until transplanting outdoors after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Red Savina grows as a compact, bushy plant and does best with consistent moisture and fertilization in full sun. Red Savina was developed by Frank Garcia in Walnut, California as a selected sport of the standard orange habanero and registered with the US Plant Variety Protection office; from 1994 until 2006 it held the Guinness World Record for hottest pepper at 350,000–580,000 Scoville Heat Units — since surpassed by even hotter superhot varieties but still among the most intensely hot widely available peppers. The fruits are classic habanero-shaped, medium-sized, bright red at maturity, with the characteristic fruity, apricot-like habanero aroma and overwhelming heat. Often grown by heat enthusiasts who want a genuinely hot habanero with well-established provenance and consistent heat levels.

plant_note: Long-day Italian type; best where summers have long daylight.
directions: This elongated torpedo-shaped Italian onion has a mild, sweet flavor ideal for fresh eating and grilling. Start indoors and transplant early, giving each bulb room to elongate in loose, fertile soil. Maintain even moisture through bulbing to develop full size, then taper off as tops lodge. Because it is a fresh-use onion, it stores only a few weeks compared with storage types. Harvest when most tops have fallen and cure briefly before use.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–February harvest. Rossa di Treviso is the elongated, pointed-head variety of Treviso radicchio — distinct from the round-head Rossa di Verona and from the forced Tardivo type. It heads naturally in cool weather without the forcing process required for Tardivo, making it the more accessible Treviso-type for home growers. In zone 9 light frosts intensify the red-purple color and reduce bitterness.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rossa di Treviso (Red Treviso Radicchio) is the elongated, cone-to-torpedo-shaped Treviso type of radicchio, producing pointed heads of 10–14 inches long with deep wine-red to burgundy leaves with prominent white midribs — visually distinct from the round, compact Rossa di Verona radicchio. The naturally-heading (non-forced) Treviso type forms its distinctive elongated shape through the cool-weather growing process without requiring the dark forcing period of Tardivo, making it accessible to home growers who want Treviso-type radicchio without the complexity of forcing. The flavor is bittersweet and complex — similar to Rossa di Verona but with the elongated form lending itself to halving and grilling (the standard preparation for Treviso-type radicchio) where the heads can be placed directly on the grill without splitting apart. In zone 9 it is planted in fall and harvested November through February, with color and flavor improving with each frost.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Red Velvet is an ornamental-edible okra with stunning deep burgundy-red to velvet-red pods, stems, and veins that make it one of the most visually striking plants in the summer vegetable garden while producing tender, flavorful pods identical in taste to standard green okra.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Red Velvet is well-suited to the edible landscape as both a productive vegetable and ornamental plant with dramatic color. Red Velvet okra is one of the most ornamentally striking of all vegetable plants, producing intensely pigmented deep burgundy-red to crimson-velvet pods, stems, leaf veins, and even young leaves that make it outstanding as an edible ornamental in landscape plantings and containers; the yellow hibiscus flowers with purple-red centers add additional ornamental value. The pods are edible and flavorful at 3–4 inches, with a taste and texture identical to standard green okra; when cooked they unfortunately lose much of their dramatic red coloring (it leaches into the cooking water, which turns bright pink — interesting for certain preparations like red okra pickles). Plants are more compact than many okra varieties (4–6 feet), making them practical for smaller gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after the soil warms; needs a long, warm season.
directions: 'Red Warty Thing', descended from the 1897 heirloom 'Victor', bears bumpy, thick, red-orange 10-20 pound pumpkins with fine-textured, flavorful flesh. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil and give the sprawling vines ample space in full sun. Water deeply and feed the heavy-feeding plants through the long season. The thick rind lets these fruits store for many months and doubles as striking fall decor.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Red Wethersfield is one of the oldest documented American onion varieties, originating in Wethersfield, Connecticut, where it was the commercial engine of an extraordinarily productive onion trade with the West Indies and Eastern Seaboard ports that began in the late 1600s and made the town famous throughout Colonial and Federal-era America.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost when seedlings are 6–8 inches tall; direct seed outdoors can also be attempted in early spring when soil is workable. Red Wethersfield (also called 'Large Red Wethersfield') is perhaps the oldest onion variety with documented continuous American cultivation, grown commercially in Wethersfield, Connecticut since the late 17th century; colonial-era records describe the Wethersfield onion trade as one of the most profitable agricultural enterprises of early New England, with flat-bottomed boats (called 'onion sloops') carrying Wethersfield red onions to New York, Boston, and West Indies markets. The medium to large (3–4 inch), flattened-globe bulbs have deep red-purple to dark crimson skin and white-to-pinkish flesh with a moderately pungent flavor that mellows to mild sweetness when cooked. A long-day variety suited to zones 3–7 northern growing conditions where summer day length exceeds 14–16 hours; the thick skin provides excellent storage quality with bulbs keeping 4–6 months when properly cured in a warm, dry location before transferring to cool storage.

common_name: Red and Yellow Blend Biquinho Chile Pepper
plant_note: Start indoors early with bottom heat; transplant well after frost.
directions: These small, teardrop 'little beak' Brazilian peppers are tangy, sweet, and smoky with only a whisper of heat, ripening from green to red or yellow. Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before the last frost with warm soil, as germination is slow, and transplant only when nights stay warm. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and light feeding; the compact plants do well in containers. Harvest fully colored pods for fresh eating, pickling, or drying.

plant_note: Start indoors or direct sow; also excellent as a fall crop for cold-sweetened leaves.
directions: 'Redbor' is a strikingly ruffled, deep purple kale that is both ornamental and delicious, with color and curl intensifying as temperatures drop. Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost or direct sow, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Extremely cold hardy, plants sweeten in fall and can survive hard freezes for late-season harvest. Pick outer leaves as needed, letting the center keep producing.

plant_note: Plant divisions of the rhizomatous rootstock in fall or early spring in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in deep shade; redwood sorrel requires cool, moist conditions and will not survive in dry or exposed sites.
directions: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade in zones 7–9; redwood sorrel is native to the floor of coastal conifer forests from the California redwoods north to British Columbia, where it forms dense, lush carpets of clover-like trifoliate leaves in one of the deepest shade environments in North America. The leaves close and fold downward in bright light — a nyctinastic response also seen in clover — and reopen in shade or at night. Small white to pale pink flowers bloom from spring through early summer. The foliage is edible in small quantities as a salad ingredient or garnish, with a bright, lemony flavor from oxalic acid; consume in moderation as large quantities can interfere with calcium absorption. Provides one of the best groundcovers for deep, moist shade under mature conifers or where dense tree canopy suppresses most other plants.

plant_note: In zones 8-10, sow in autumn for winter and spring harvests; in cooler zones, sow in early spring as temperatures warm above 55°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in full sun into well-drained, moderately fertile soil; plants thrive in the same rocky or sandy conditions that challenge most vegetables. Once established, reichardia is remarkably drought-tolerant and requires minimal irrigation, making it an excellent choice for dry summer gardens in the Mediterranean climate zone. Harvest basal leaves as needed throughout the cooler months, cutting back to encourage fresh, tender regrowth; the plant is perennial in frost-free zones and will produce for several years from a single sowing. Young leaves are mild enough for raw salads, while older leaves are better cooked briefly as a spinach substitute.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January–March for spring or September–October for fall. Rezista's primary value is extreme heat tolerance that allows it to produce harvestable lettuce through zone 9 warm springs when standard varieties have bolted. Provide shade cloth (30%) in late spring to extend the season further.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Rezista is a heat-tolerant, slow-bolting European butterhead lettuce selected specifically for warm-climate production — it remains productive 2–3 weeks longer than standard butterhead varieties under heat stress before bolting, providing a meaningfully extended spring harvest window in zone 9 and making it one of the most useful warm-season lettuces for Gulf Coast gardeners. The medium-sized butterhead heads have soft, mild, tender leaves typical of the butterhead type, with a flavor and texture that are difficult to distinguish from standard butterhead when grown in cool weather. Rezista's key value is in the warm-spring transition period (March–May in zone 9) when most lettuces have given up but cool-season crops are still preferred over summer alternatives. Partial shade from established transplants or shade cloth reduces heat stress further during this critical period. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through winter maximize the productive season.

plant_note: Plant divisions as soon as soil is workable in early spring; each division should have at least one large bud.
directions: Plant root divisions 3–4 in deep in deeply dug, compost-enriched soil, setting buds just at the soil surface. Do not harvest any stalks in the first year, and take only a few in year two so the crown can establish a deep root system. From year three onward, harvest stalks when they are 12–18 in long and 3/4 in thick by pulling and twisting at the base; remove any flower stalks that appear immediately to prevent weakening the crown. Note that only the stalks are edible—the leaves contain high concentrations of oxalic acid and are toxic.

common_name: Rhubarb Chard (Ruby Red Swiss Chard, Classic Red-Stemmed Chard)
plant_note: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fertile, well-amended soil; chard seeds are multi-germ clusters (1–4 seedlings emerge per seed), so thin after germination to 6–9 inches for full-sized leaves. Harvest outer leaves from about 30 days for baby greens, or wait for full-size at 55–65 days. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest; spring sowing in February–March provides excellent spring production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in fertile, moist, well-amended soil; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued growth — leaving some inner leaves promotes sustained production. Rhubarb Chard (also called Ruby Red Swiss Chard or simply Red Chard) is the classic red-stemmed form of Swiss chard, grown for centuries for both its striking ornamental appearance and excellent culinary value. The deep, vivid crimson-red to ruby-red stems and ribs contrast dramatically against the dark green, deeply crinkled leaves, creating one of the most visually attractive vegetables in the edible garden and making Rhubarb Chard a staple in ornamental kitchen gardens and edible landscape plantings. The name references the stems' resemblance in color (but not flavor) to rhubarb. The red pigmentation comes from betalain pigments — the same compounds in red beets — which are vibrant raw but bleed into cooking water, giving a pinkish tint to any cooking liquid and fading the stems somewhat when cooked. The leaves are excellent cooked like spinach or kale (sauté with garlic and olive oil is the classic preparation), and young leaves are delicious raw in salads. Rhubarb Chard is more heat-tolerant than spinach and more cold-tolerant than basil, occupying a useful niche as a year-round leaf vegetable in zone 8–9 gardens where it often grows through the winter as an important fresh green when other vegetables are unavailable.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant when soil temperature reaches 70°F. In warm climates (zones 9–11) direct sow in flooded beds after last frost.
directions: Start seeds in shallow flats of moist potting mix at 70–80°F, then transplant 6–9-inch seedlings to flooded paddies, water gardens, or large containers filled with heavy garden soil and submerged under 2–4 inches of standing water; upland (dry-land) varieties can be grown in moist garden beds without flooding but require consistently wet soil throughout the season. Rice matures in 90–150 days depending on variety — grain is ready when the panicle droops and grains turn golden-yellow. Drain standing water 3–4 weeks before harvest and allow the plant to dry on the stalk before cutting. Threshing by hand is practical for small plots.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; rice bean is adapted to hot, humid conditions and is extremely productive in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast summer. It can be trellised for pod harvest or left bushy.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil; rice bean is a heat-tolerant tropical legume widely grown across Southeast and South Asia, where it is often intercropped with rice and maize. The small, oval seeds range from yellow to red to brownish-red and are cooked in the same ways as adzuki beans — in soups, dals, sweet red bean paste, and as a dried bean staple. The plant is semi-vining or bushy and fixes atmospheric nitrogen. It is one of the more underutilized warm-season legumes for Gulf Coast and tropical climates where cowpeas and yard-long beans already perform well. Nutritionally the seeds are high in protein (20–25%) and iron. Young pods may also be eaten as snap beans.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August for fall. Richmond Green Apple is harvested when the skin has turned from green to pale ivory-green with a slight yellowish tint — at this stage the flavor is at its sweetest and most apple-like. Do not allow fruits to turn fully yellow, which indicates over-maturity. The vines are vigorous and productive; provide a trellis for best air circulation.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Richmond Green Apple is an Australian heirloom cucumber producing small, round, apple-shaped fruits of 2–3 inches diameter with smooth, pale green to ivory-green skin and crisp, exceptionally sweet, very mild, lightly perfumed white flesh with minimal seeds. The round shape and pale coloration are genuinely apple-like, and the name is descriptive — the flesh has a fresh, delicate sweetness with a faint floral note unlike the somewhat vegetal flavor of standard slicing cucumbers. The skin is thin and does not require peeling; the whole fruit can be eaten like an apple or sliced into salads where its elegant shape makes for attractive presentation. Richmond Green Apple has a reputation for very low bitterness and is considered by some cucumber enthusiasts the sweetest and most refined of the heirloom cucumber types. In zone 9 it performs well in the spring and fall cucumber seasons; the small fruit size and productive vines make it excellent for container growing on a small trellis.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 75°F; requires sustained heat to produce well.
directions: Sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in warm soil after last frost and provide a trellis or fence immediately, as vines climb vigorously by tendrils. Ridge gourd differs from smooth luffa in having ten prominent sharp ridges running the length of the fruit and slightly more tender flesh when young. Harvest fruits at 6–9 inches long while skin is still soft and the ridges are firm and green — the young flesh is mild, slightly sweet, and commonly used in Indian dal, stir-fries, and curries. Like smooth luffa, fruits left to fully mature develop a tough fiber skeleton and can serve as a scrubbing sponge.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; ridged luffa is faster-maturing and milder-flavored than smooth luffa and is the preferred luffa for eating — it should be harvested at 6–8 inches when young and tender, as it becomes bitter and fibrous if allowed to mature.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide strong trellis — ridged luffa is a vigorous climber. Luffa acutangula (ridged luffa or angled loofah) is the more tender, edible species of luffa — a tropical Asian cucurbit vine grown throughout South and Southeast Asia as a primary vegetable crop. Ridged luffa is distinguished from smooth luffa (L. aegyptiaca) by its deeply ridged, angled, dark-green fruits (hence 'ridged' and 'angled' in the name) and by being significantly milder, more tender, and less bitter when eaten young. At 6–8 inches, young ridged luffa fruits have a mild, delicate flavor similar to mild zucchini with a slightly slippery texture — excellent stir-fried, in curries, soups, and Indian sabzi. It is an extremely productive vine in the Gulf Coast heat, producing continuous fruit through summer. The vine also produces attractive, bright-yellow flowers. If fruits are allowed to mature fully and dry, they produce a natural fiber loofah (the vascular skeleton of the mature fruit) — both varieties produce usable loofahs, but ridged luffa fibers are softer. In Indian, Filipino, and Southeast Asian cuisines, ridged luffa is preferred over smooth for vegetable use.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Riesentraube (German for 'giant bunch of grapes') is a 19th-century German heirloom cherry tomato that produces the most spectacular, enormous hanging clusters of small red fruits of any heirloom variety — clusters of 20–40 or more fruits per stem that cascade down the vine in a grape-like arrangement of extraordinary visual impact.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide substantial staking, caging, or trellis support as plants grow vigorously to 6–8 feet; Riesentraube benefits from pruning to 1–2 leaders for best cluster development and air circulation. Riesentraube is a German heirloom cherry tomato documented in American seed catalogs by the 1850s and one of the oldest cherry tomato varieties maintained in continuous cultivation; the name 'Riesentraube' translates as 'giant bunch of grapes,' which perfectly describes the plant's most distinctive characteristic — enormous, pendulous clusters of 20, 30, or even 40+ small (1–1.5 oz) round, red fruits hanging in tight, cascade-like grape formations from the indeterminate vines. Each individual fruit has a pointed blossom end, which together with the cluster arrangement gives the plant an unmistakable profile compared to modern cherry tomatoes. The flavor is rich, tangy, and well-balanced with classic cherry tomato sweetness; the pointed fruits with thicker skin crack less than many cherry types and hold on the cluster longer after ripening. Riesentraube is both ornamentally spectacular in the garden (the cascading clusters are genuinely striking) and extremely productive, with harvests continuing from midsummer through first frost.

common_name: Ring of Fire Cayenne Pepper (AAS Early Compact Cayenne)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Ring of Fire is an All-America Selections award-winning cayenne pepper developed by Park Seed — earlier-maturing and more compact than standard Long Red Cayenne, with upward-pointing fruits that ripen earlier (60–75 days) and can be dried in clusters on the compact plant for ornamental as well as culinary use; heat is typical cayenne range (70,000–85,000 SHU).
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost into warm, well-drained soil; Ring of Fire is compact enough for containers (5-gallon minimum) and makes an excellent patio pepper both for culinary use and as an ornamental with upright clusters of ripening red fruits. Ring of Fire is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning cayenne pepper introduced by Park Seed that distinguished itself in AAS trials for its early maturity and compact plant habit compared to standard Long Red Cayenne types. Where standard Long Red Cayenne reaches 24–36 inches and takes 70–80 days from transplant, Ring of Fire is more compact (18–24 inches) and earlier (60–75 days), making it better suited for containers, shorter growing seasons, and gardeners who want cayenne peppers without managing large, sprawling plants. The fruits are classic cayenne in form — pencil-thin, 4–5 inches long, tapering to a point — and ripen from green through yellow to red in an attractive cluster that gives the variety its name; fruits remain attached to the plant well through ripening, making the loaded plant highly ornamental. Heat level is typical cayenne range (70,000–85,000 SHU) — significantly hotter than jalapeños and suitable for use in all traditional cayenne applications: fresh salsa, hot sauce, cayenne powder, drying into ristras, and as a heat element in cooking. Ring of Fire is particularly well-suited to Gulf Coast home gardeners who want a reliable cayenne producer through the long warm season.

common_name: Rio Zape Bean (Hopi Purple String Bean, Ancient Aztec Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; a pole bean requiring 5–6 feet of support; drought-adapted from its desert Southwest origins, requiring less water than many beans once established.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost at the base of sturdy poles or trellises in full sun; Rio Zape is an ancient bean of Aztec and Hopi origin with distinctive dark purple-brown seeds streaked and spotted with maroon or lavender markings that fade to a deep chocolate color on cooking. It has an exceptional rich, chocolatey-earthy flavor with complex undertones — often called the best-tasting dry bean by chefs who discover it — and a creamy texture excellent in tacos, soups, and refried beans. Drought-adapted from its desert Southwest heritage; it performs well in hot, dry conditions where other beans struggle. A prized heirloom for serious bean enthusiasts.

plant_note: Sow in early spring and again in late summer; bred for baby-size harvest.
directions: 'Robin' was bred for harvesting at baby size, delivering well-rounded, tender, sweet 1 to 1.5 inch roots with high bolt resistance. Direct sow the seed clusters 1/2 inch deep and thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart, since each cluster can produce several plants. Keep moisture even for crisp, crack-free roots, and harvest young for the best texture. The tender baby greens are also excellent raw or cooked.

plant_note: Direct sow in blocks after frost for good pollination; isolate from other corn.
directions: 'Robust Pop R400MR' produces large, round popped kernels sturdy enough to hold coatings, unlike the more common butterfly popcorn. Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil in blocks of at least four short rows to ensure good wind pollination. Give plants full sun, steady moisture, and rich soil through the long season. Let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvesting, then cure the kernels further before popping. Isolate from sweet corn to keep quality true.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2–3 inches deep in October–November; Rocambole requires 6–8 weeks of vernalization below 40°F for proper bulb formation, making it best suited to zone 4–7. In zone 9, pre-chill cloves in the refrigerator for 6–8 weeks before planting to compensate for mild winters — or choose Creole garlic instead, which requires no pre-chilling.
directions: Plant pre-chilled cloves 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Rocambole is considered by most garlic connoisseurs to be the finest-flavored garlic group — rich, complex, deeply savory, and mellow with a characteristic lingering warmth and almost chocolate-like earthiness that no other garlic group fully matches. Named varieties include 'Spanish Roja,' 'German Red,' 'Killarney Red,' and 'Music.' The medium-sized, brownish-purple skinned bulbs contain 8–12 cloves per head arranged in a single layer. The paper wrapping is loose, almost shaggy, and the inner skins of individual cloves are characteristically streaked with purple-brown. Rocambole is a hardneck garlic producing a central flower stalk (scape) that should be removed in June to direct energy into bulb formation; scapes are edible and delicious in stir-fries and pestos. In zone 9, Rocambole requires refrigerator pre-chilling of cloves for 6–8 weeks before October planting, or better yet, substitute Creole garlic, which is naturally adapted to mild winters without chilling. Rocambole stores only 3–5 months.

plant_note: Sow in spring or fall; perennial in mild zones 6-10.
directions: 'Rocky' is a fast-growing wild-type arugula forming a compact rosette with a stronger, more complex, nutty-peppery flavor than salad arugula. Direct sow shallowly and thin to 4-6 inches, harvesting leaves young and often for the mildest taste. It tolerates cold well and behaves as a short-lived perennial in USDA zones 6-10, resprouting after cutting. Grow in cool weather and shear back before flowering to prolong tender leaf production.

common_name: Rocky Ford Cantaloupe (Colorado Classic Heirloom Cantaloupe)
plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Rocky Ford reaches peak flavor in dry, hot summer conditions and performs best in climates with hot days, warm nights, and low humidity — it is excellent in the arid Southwest and Mountain West but somewhat prone to fungal diseases in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; harvest when stem slips easily from the vine ('slip' stage) and the blossom end is slightly soft. Rocky Ford is the historic heirloom cantaloupe variety that made the Arkansas River Valley around Rocky Ford, Colorado famous for melon production in the late 19th century — producing medium-sized, netted, round to slightly oval fruits with bright green skin under tan netting and pale green to orange flesh with exceptional sweetness and classic old-fashioned cantaloupe flavor. The variety was so famous that 'Rocky Ford' became synonymous with high-quality cantaloupe across America in the early 20th century, and special rail cars shipped Rocky Ford melons to Chicago, New York, and other major cities during the peak season. Rocky Ford performs best in dry climates with hot days and cool nights (like the high-altitude semi-arid conditions of Colorado) where low humidity reduces fungal disease and water-stressed plants concentrate sugars at maturity. In humid Gulf Coast conditions it requires careful disease management, but dedicated heirloom melon enthusiasts appreciate its distinctive flavor, which has a more complex, old-fashioned character than modern hybrids.

plant_note: Start on a heat mat 6–8 weeks before last frost; Rocotillo is a traditional Caribbean seasoning pepper related to the habanero but with minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU), prized entirely for its intensely tropical, fruity habanero aroma and flavor with none of the fire — a favorite seasoning pepper in Cuban, Puerto Rican, and Dominican cooking.
directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 80°F; transplant outdoors after frost when soil is warm and nights are above 60°F. Rocotillo is a Capsicum chinense seasoning pepper of Caribbean origin that looks remarkably like a miniature, squashed habanero with its distinctive ribbed, round, flattened form — but carries minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) while retaining the intensely fruity, tropical, citrusy habanero aroma that makes this species unique; it is used in Cuban, Puerto Rican, Dominican, and Venezuelan cooking wherever the habanero flavor without the fire is desired. The small, round, ribbed fruits ripen from green through yellow to orange or red and are used fresh in sofrito, salsas, sauces, and seasoning blends. Related to and sometimes confused with the aji dulce (sweet habanero) and cachucha peppers of the Caribbean. Highly productive in hot weather; perennial in zone 9b–12.

plant_note: Start indoors 12–14 weeks before last frost; unlike most peppers, rocoto prefers cool nights and actually performs poorly in intense summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep at a cooler 65–70°F — unlike other peppers, Capsicum pubescens actually germinates better in cooler soil and is damaged by excessive heat. This Andean species is unique among cultivated peppers for its purple flowers and distinctive black seeds; it tolerates light frost better than any other pepper species. Transplant to a position with afternoon shade in hot climates, as rocoto stops setting fruit when temperatures exceed 90°F — coastal or mountain gardens suit it best. Fruits resemble small apples (hence 'manzano') and ripen to yellow, orange, or red with thick, sweet flesh and intense, burning heat.

plant_note: Direct sow after all frost danger once soil is warm.
directions: 'Roma II' is a bush-type Italian flat snap bean with a rich, nutty flavor rarely found in stores, borne on compact plants that need no support. Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil, spacing them 3-4 inches apart in full sun. The 4-5 inch pods stay tender and slow to develop fiber, so harvest regularly to keep plants producing. Excellent fresh, frozen, or canned; good in containers.

plant_note: Start indoors about six weeks before the last frost, then transplant once nights are warm.
directions: Sow indoors six weeks ahead of transplanting and set plants deep to build strong roots. Roma is a compact, determinate paste tomato producing firm, meaty three-inch fruits with few seeds, ideal for sauces and canning. A single stake or small cage supports the tidy vines, which set most of their fruit in a concentrated window. Water evenly and mulch to prevent blossom-end rot, and expect a heavy flush of fruit that ripens over a few weeks.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant 2–4 weeks before last frost; for fall, sow 8–10 weeks before first frost.
directions: Sow seed at 1/8 in depth in cool soil and thin to 8–12 in; romaine forms an upright, elongated head that needs slightly more space than loose-leaf types. Keep soil evenly moist to prevent tip burn, which appears as brown leaf edges due to calcium deficiency from moisture stress. Harvest by cutting the whole head at soil level when it is 8–10 in tall and the inner leaves feel firm. Outer leaves can be removed individually as the head develops to extend the harvest period.

common_name: Romance Nantes Carrot (Very Sweet Crack-Resistant Bejo Hybrid Carrot)
plant_note: Direct sow thinly; carrot seed is tiny and needs consistent moisture for the 10–21 day germination period. In zone 9, sow August–November for fall and winter harvest when carrots are at their best; spring planting (February–March) is possible but quality diminishes as temperatures rise. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid: 7–8 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical, uniform roots. Thin to 2–3 inches after seedlings establish (3 weeks after germination); crowded roots become forked and deformed. Romance is noted for excellent crack resistance — roots hold in the ground without splitting even when mature, which extends the harvest window.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in loose, deep, well-worked soil free of rocks and clods; thin to 2–3 inches. Keep soil consistently moist until germination. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid carrot from Bejo Seeds, a Dutch vegetable breeding company with a long history of Nantes-type carrot refinement. The Nantes type — originating in the Nantes region of western France — defines a carrot form that differs fundamentally from the long Imperator types common in grocery stores: Nantes carrots are shorter (6–8 inches vs. 9–11 inches), blunt-tipped rather than tapering to a point, rounder in cross-section, and notably sweeter with more tender, less fibrous flesh. Romance carries Nantes-type characteristics to a high standard: the roots are uniformly 7–8 inches long with a clean, blunt Nantes tip, bright orange interior color throughout (no pale core), very high sugar content, and notably fine-textured, tender flesh that makes Romance excellent for eating raw as well as cooked. The crack resistance that gives Romance particular value means that unlike some other sweet, high-sugar varieties that develop radial cracks if left in ground too long, Romance holds well after reaching maturity — a practical advantage for home gardeners harvesting over weeks rather than in a single commercial harvest. Fall-grown carrots in zone 9 achieve maximum sweetness as cold nights concentrate sugars in the roots.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant so heads mature in cool fall weather; aim to transplant about 16 weeks before first frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant date; romanesco demands consistent temperatures between 60–65°F during head formation or it fails to produce proper fractal spirals. Transplant into deeply amended soil and water evenly throughout the season, as any moisture stress affects head quality. Harvest the single central head when the spiral turrets are sharp and well-defined but before any yellowing begins. Unlike broccoli, romanesco rarely produces usable side shoots after the main head is cut.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before desired transplant date (July–August in zone 9 for a fall transplant); plant out in September–October in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Romanesco produces its characteristic spiraling, lime-green fractal heads (a naturally occurring example of a logarithmic spiral and Fibonacci sequence) and has a milder, nuttier flavor than either standard broccoli or cauliflower.
