directions: Sow seeds direct in early spring in deep, sandy to gravelly, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; sea kale has a very long taproot and deeply resents transplanting — choose its permanent location carefully. Crambe maritima is a spectacular, ornamental-as-well-as-edible native of European coastal shingle beaches, producing large, blue-gray, crinkled, cabbage-like leaves and billowing clouds of tiny, honey-scented white flowers on 24–36-inch stems in early summer that are outstanding in the border; the young, blanched shoots are the edible crop, harvested in early spring by covering the dormant crown with a forcing pot or dark bucket 4–6 weeks before harvest, producing pale, sweetly nutty, asparagus-like shoots. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, and long-lived, thriving in poor, well-drained soils in coastal and hot, dry inland gardens.

plant_note: Root stem cuttings in moist sand or soil after last frost; the plant establishes quickly and can be planted directly into saline or sandy coastal soils.
directions: Plant stem cuttings in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this remarkable halophyte naturally colonizes tidal flats, beach margins, and coastal dunes where few other edibles survive, tolerating periodic saltwater flooding and saline spray. The succulent, bright-green to purplish leaves and stems have a pleasantly salty, crisp flavor — rinse before eating to reduce saltiness — and are excellent raw in salads, briefly stir-fried, or used as a sea-vegetable garnish. The plant forms a dense, prostrate mat that suppresses weeds and helps stabilize sandy soils against erosion. In zone 9–11 it is a reliable perennial that can be harvested throughout the year.

plant_note: Sow in early spring directly into sandy, free-draining soil; tolerates saline conditions and coastal exposure where most vegetables struggle.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, directly into sandy or well-drained soil in a sunny position in early spring. Sea rocket is exceptionally tolerant of salt spray, coastal winds, and drought once established, requiring very little supplemental water. Harvest young, succulent leaves and stems regularly for use raw in salads where they contribute a pleasant peppery bite; young seed pods are also edible and can be added to salads or pickled. Allow some plants to set seed for reliable self-seeding in subsequent years.

common_name: Sea of Red Lettuce (Deep Red Frilly Oakleaf Lettuce)
plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Sea of Red is a deeply colored, frilly-leaved oakleaf lettuce that holds its intense burgundy-red color and resists bolting and bitterness longer than many other red lettuce varieties, making it a reliable performer through a wider harvest window.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Sea of Red is an oakleaf-type lettuce prized for deeply lobed, ruffled, deep burgundy-red leaves that stay glossy and appetizing-looking even as outer leaves are repeatedly harvested, making it a favorite for cut-and-come-again baby leaf production as well as full-head harvest. It holds its rich color and resists premature bolting and the bitterness that develops in many red lettuces once temperatures climb, giving it a somewhat longer productive window than more heat-sensitive varieties, though it still performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons in zone 9. Harvest outer leaves as needed for continuous production, or cut the whole loose head at once for a single larger harvest. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings to further delay bolting as the weather warms.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained soil; in zone 9–10 an excellent late summer/fall planting (August–September) allows the long vines to run through fall when powdery mildew pressure is lower. The Seminole pumpkin is the most heat-tolerant, disease-resistant winter squash for Gulf Coast and Florida gardens and should be a standard in zone 8–10 gardens where other pumpkins and squash struggle in summer humidity.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; Seminole pumpkin is a historic Native American heirloom cultivated by the Seminole people of Florida for generations and is exceptionally well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate where most pumpkins and butternut squash struggle with vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat collapse. It produces tan-buff, round to pear-shaped fruits weighing 5–10 pounds on very vigorous vines that can reach 15–20 feet — the vines are traditionally trained up trees or fences in Florida to keep the fruits off the moist ground. The buff-orange flesh has excellent butternut-like flavor, keeping quality of months, and outstanding resistance to diseases and insects that devastate other squash. Once established, vines are genuinely drought-tolerant. One of the most important heirloom vegetables for sustainable subtropical gardening.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for fall/winter/spring production in zones 7–11; Senposai is a Japanese hybrid leafy green that is significantly more heat-tolerant than standard cabbages and brassicas, making it one of the better cool-season leafy greens for the Gulf South where the heat ends conventional brassica production early — it continues producing into warmer temperatures than kale, collards, or Chinese cabbage.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 8–14 inches apart; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again from about 30 days; Senposai is mild enough to eat raw as well as cooked; spring plantings should go in very early since it bolts in sustained heat. Senposai is a hybrid leafy green developed in Japan by crossing common cabbage (Brassica oleracea) with komatsuna or Japanese mustard spinach (Brassica rapa var. perviridis), producing a vigorous, fast-growing green that combines characteristics of both parents — the large, smooth, broadly oval leaves of cabbage with the faster maturity, milder flavor, and somewhat greater heat tolerance of komatsuna. The resulting hybrid fills a useful niche in both Japanese home gardens and warm-climate gardens worldwide: it is ready for harvest significantly faster than heading cabbages (40–60 days versus 80–120), produces continuously as a cut-and-come-again crop rather than requiring a single heading harvest, and tolerates heat better than most brassicas while retaining the mild, slightly sweet, cabbage-family flavor without the sharpness of mustard greens. Senposai is versatile in the kitchen — the large, smooth leaves are excellent raw in salads, quickly stir-fried or sautéed, braised in Japanese-style dashimono or miso soup, or used like savoy cabbage leaves for wrapping. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Senposai is most valuable as a fall-through-spring cool-season green, sown from September through February for harvest from October through April. Available from Kitazawa Seed Company and other Asian vegetable seed specialists.

plant_note: Start indoors and set out after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Start seed indoors about six to eight weeks ahead of transplanting and provide bright light and warmth for sturdy seedlings. Move plants outdoors once the soil warms and frost danger has passed, spacing them about a foot and a half apart. These prolific plants set many slender, spicy peppers used green for salsas and pico de gallo. Pick fruits green for the classic sharp heat, or leave them to ripen red for a slightly sweeter kick. Steady moisture and full sun keep production high through the season.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth and transplant only after the soil has warmed.
directions: Start seeds indoors with warm soil about eight weeks before transplanting, since peppers need heat to germinate. Move seedlings outdoors only after nights are reliably warm, spacing plants for good airflow. This heirloom produces slender 3-4 inch peppers with medium heat around 10,000 to 25,000 Scoville units and a bright, crisp flavor. Harvest green for classic salsa heat, or let the pods ripen to red for a slightly sweeter, hotter bite.

plant_note: Sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; sesame demands heat for germination and will rot in cool, wet soil.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in rows 18–24 in apart after soil reaches at least 70°F; sesame seed is very small, so mixing with dry sand aids even distribution and prevents clumping. Thin to 6–12 in once plants are 3 in tall and keep well-weeded until the canopy closes. The upright plants produce attractive tubular flowers along the stem that develop into rectangular seed capsules; the key challenge is timing harvest before 'shattering' — when ripe capsules split and scatter seed spontaneously. Cut entire stalks when the bottom capsules begin to yellow, invert plants into large paper bags, and allow to dry for a week indoors; the capsules then split easily and seed falls into the bag when shaken.

common_name: Seven Top Turnip (Leafy Greens Turnip for Gulf South)
plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top can be sown thickly and harvested by cutting young, regrowing from the base for multiple cuttings over the cool season.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top is a turnip variety grown exclusively for its prolific, tender, flavorful greens (tops) rather than its roots — the roots of Seven Top are small, tough, and not typically eaten, but the plant produces an extremely vigorous canopy of large, lush, tender, deeply flavored greens that are among the most productive and flavorful of all Southern cooking greens. The variety's name describes its characteristic of producing an exceptionally dense canopy of seven or more vigorous shoots per plant — creating a tall, productive leafy mass that yields far more greens per plant than Purple Top or other root-type turnips when grown for tops. Seven Top is a staple of traditional Gulf South fall and winter gardening — it's the turnip greens variety most commonly grown for pot greens in Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama, and Georgia gardens where a large quantity of flavorful cooking greens from a small space is the primary objective. The greens are best harvested young and tender (6–10 inches tall) and become progressively more robust in flavor as they mature — a quality that appeals to those who prefer the traditional strong, minerally flavor of Southern cooking greens. Seven Top tolerates temperatures well into the teens once established. Cut-and-come-again harvesting (cutting to 4 inches, allowing regrowth) produces multiple flushes through the cool season.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost when soil is warm; provide a tall trellis.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is warm, planting alongside a sturdy trellis or pole seven to nine feet tall. This All-America Selections winner bears clusters of tender four-to-six-inch pods well ahead of many standard pole beans. Pick pods young and often to keep the vines producing over a long season. Even, moderate watering during flowering and pod set gives the best yields. Avoid handling the plants when wet to reduce the spread of disease.

plant_note: Plant cloves 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; in mild climates, an autumn planting produces larger bulbs.
directions: Separate shallot clusters into individual cloves and plant each with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, 1 in deep, in fertile, well-drained soil. Each clove multiplies into a cluster of 6–12 new bulbs by season's end, so generous spacing pays off. Harvest when most of the green tops have toppled and turned papery. Dry clusters on screens in good airflow for 2–3 weeks and store in a cool, airy spot; well-cured shallots keep for 6 months or more.

plant_note: Plant cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes.
directions: Break bulbs into individual cloves and plant them pointed end up about two inches deep in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes. This early-maturing Turban-type hardneck yields white bulbs with six to eight cloves and matures noticeably faster than most hardnecks. Mulch after planting to protect the cloves through winter and conserve moisture. Cut the curling scapes in early summer to direct energy into bulb sizing. Harvest when the lower leaves brown, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer/early fall for a fall crop; Shanghai pak choi bolts quickly in long, hot days, so in zone 8–9 it performs best as a fast fall-through-winter and very early spring green rather than a summer crop.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; keep evenly watered, since any dry stress speeds bolting. Shanghai pak choi is a compact, fast-maturing bok choy type with pale jade-green, spoon-shaped petioles and glossy dark green leaves that form a tidy, vase-shaped rosette — smaller and quicker to mature than standard white-stemmed bok choy varieties, and prized for its exceptionally tender, mild, sweet stems that need no peeling or trimming before cooking. Its speed and compact size make it ideal for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season, providing a steady supply of baby greens for stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. In warm-winter climates like the Gulf South it can be grown nearly through the whole cool season, from fall through early spring, before rising temperatures push it to bolt. Zone 2–10.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring or fall in lean, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; sheep sorrel self-sows freely and may spread aggressively in garden beds. In many gardens it is managed as a foraged weed rather than intentionally sown.
directions: Direct sow in lean, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; sheep sorrel is a diminutive native of Eurasia, now naturalized as a common weed across North America in sandy, acidic, infertile soils. The small, arrowhead-shaped leaves with backward-pointing lobes are more strongly acidic and citrusy than common sorrel (R. acetosa), with a bright lemon-sour flavor from oxalic acid. Young leaves are excellent in salads, soups, and sauces — the same culinary uses as garden sorrel — and the plant has a long history of use in traditional medicine as a spring tonic herb. Consume in moderation as with all oxalic-acid-containing plants. The plant spreads by both seed and underground rhizomes and becomes a persistent presence once established in appropriate acidic, lean soil; treat it as a semi-wild foraged herb rather than a crop requiring intensive management.

plant_note: Sow as early as the ground is workable, typically 4–6 weeks before the last frost date.
directions: Sow seeds 1 in deep in rows 18 in apart and provide support for tall types. Consistent moisture from flowering through pod fill is critical; drought during this window sharply reduces yield. Harvest when pods are well rounded and the peas inside feel firm through the pod wall; sugar converts rapidly to starch after picking, so chill or eat immediately. Shell and freeze any surplus the same day for best sweetness.

plant_note: Heat-tolerant, so it can be sown into late spring and summer.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in loose, deep soil and keep the surface moist during the slow germination. Unlike many carrots, this heat-tolerant Kuroda type can be sown well into late spring and summer for fall harvests. Thin seedlings to about two inches so the tapered five-inch roots with broad shoulders can size up. Steady moisture prevents cracking and keeps the roots sweet and tender. Harvest before roots become oversized for the best texture.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out after the soil warms. This popular Japanese frying pepper produces heavy sets of slender two-to-four-inch fruits with a mild, citrusy, slightly smoky flavor. Harvest peppers green and small for the best flavor when blistered in a hot pan or on the grill. Roughly one in ten pods surprises with mild heat, adding to the fun. Pick frequently to keep the highly productive plants setting new fruit.

plant_note: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay consistently above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant in February–March and expect harvests from May through October. The plants tolerate heat well and remain productive through the Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; shishito peppers are a slender, thin-walled Japanese variety harvested green at 3–4 inches long, when they are mild and sweet with an occasional — roughly 1 in 10 — surprisingly hot fruit that keeps diners guessing. Plants produce prolifically once they begin fruiting and require consistent moisture and monthly fertilization with a balanced vegetable fertilizer to maintain production. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive; once fruits redden they become hotter and the plant redirects energy away from new fruit. The standard preparation is to blister whole fruits in a dry or lightly oiled cast-iron skillet over high heat until charred and softened, then finish with sea salt and a squeeze of lemon.

plant_note: Sow direct around last frost date or lightly earlier indoors; seeds require light to germinate — press them onto the soil surface rather than burying them — and the seedlings tolerate mild frost but are killed by a hard freeze.
directions: Surface-sow seeds (they need light to germinate) directly in the garden around last frost or start indoors 3–4 weeks earlier in trays, transplanting after frost danger has passed into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Perilla frutescens (green shiso) is an annual herb used as a vegetable throughout East Asian cooking — the large, ruffled, vivid green, anise-and-clove-scented leaves are used to wrap sashimi, roll rice and pickles in, scatter over noodles and salads, and deep-fry as tempura; it is a fundamental ingredient in Japanese cuisine. Shiso self-seeds prolifically and often becomes a welcome recurring presence in the garden without any replanting effort; deadhead promptly if you do not want it to naturalize. Harvest individual leaves as needed from the outside of the plant, or snip whole stem tips to encourage bushier growth.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is an excellent dual-purpose turnip — the mild, sweet roots are outstanding for fresh eating and the tender tops are milder-flavored than most American turnip greens.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is a Japanese heirloom turnip cultivar that is outstanding in two distinct ways: it produces unusually mild, sweet, tender-fleshed white roots appropriate for fresh eating and light cooking, and simultaneously produces exceptionally mild, tender, palatable greens that are significantly less pungent than the traditional American turnip greens grown for Southern cooking. This dual mildness — both roots and tops — makes Shogoin the turnip of choice for those who find standard American turnips too strongly flavored but want to grow a dual-purpose root vegetable for fall and winter. The pure-white, globe-shaped roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter at ideal harvest size — smaller and more tender than Purple Top White Globe when harvested young. The roots are outstanding raw in salads and slaws, steamed or roasted with light seasoning, and pickled (Shogoin is commonly used for Japanese-style pickled turnips). The tender greens can be used raw in salads when young, stir-fried, or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, Shogoin is a fall and winter crop — sow from August through October for harvest from October through February. The mild flavor makes Shogoin an outstanding variety for introducing turnips to gardeners and cooks unfamiliar with or averse to the pungency of traditional varieties.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; make a second sowing 6–8 weeks before first fall frost. In zones 8–11 sow in fall for a winter crop. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks.
directions: Broadcast seed or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches; shungiku is a cool-season Asian vegetable in the chrysanthemum family grown for its highly aromatic, slightly bitter leaves that are fundamental to Japanese hot pot (nabe), sukiyaki, and Korean soups. The flavor is herbal, slightly medicinal, and distinctly chrysanthemum-like — beloved in East Asian cooking, particularly in winter one-pot dishes where the leaves add fragrance as well as nutrition. Harvest outer leaves when plants reach 6–8 inches; or cut whole plants at soil level for a cut-and-come-again crop. It bolts quickly in heat, producing bright yellow daisy-like flowers — these are also edible as a garnish. Sow in succession for continuous harvest through cool seasons.

common_name: Siberian Hardneck Garlic (Marbled Purple Stripe, Cold-Climate Heritage)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost; Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic of Russian origin, known for exceptional cold hardiness that makes it one of the most reliable varieties in zones 3–4 — it produces large, 5–9 clove bulbs with a rich, full-bodied flavor and an attractive purple-striped outer wrapper typical of its garlic group.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch heavily after the ground cools (especially important in zones 3–4); keep consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl and straighten; harvest in early to midsummer when lower leaves yellow. Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic originating in Russia and introduced to North American garlic culture through seed-saver networks and specialist garlic growers in the 20th century; it is particularly valued for its exceptional cold hardiness, with reliable performance in zones 3–4 where many garlic varieties struggle with winterkill or produce reduced bulb size. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) and typically contain just 5–9 large, easy-to-peel cloves — fewer than most garlic types but each clove is substantial in size, making them easy to use in cooking. The outer skins are cream-colored with distinctive purple-violet streaking and spotting characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe group; the flavor is rich, moderately pungent, and earthy with good complexity — similar in character to Persian Star and other Marbled Purple Stripe types. Siberian is an excellent choice for northern gardeners in zones 3–5 who struggle with hardneck variety performance, and for seed-saving gardens that want geographic diversity in their garlic collection. Storage life of 5–7 months under good conditions.

common_name: Sibley Squash (Pike's Peak Heirloom Winter Squash)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Sibley, also known as Pike's Peak squash, is an 1880s heirloom prized for its distinctive teardrop shape, thin blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-grained orange flesh that many heirloom growers consider among the best-flavored of all winter squash.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the long, vigorous vines. Sibley squash, introduced in the 1880s and also sold as Pike's Peak squash, is an American heirloom valued by generations of gardeners for its unusual teardrop or pear shape, thin, smooth, blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-textured deep orange flesh with almost no fiber, a texture and flavor that many long-time growers rank above modern hybrid winter squash. Fruits typically run 6-10 pounds, large enough to serve a crowd, and the thin rind, while making the squash slightly more vulnerable to handling damage than thick-shelled types, also makes it easier to peel and cook than harder-shelled Hubbard-type squash. Vines are long and productive given full sun and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before storing in a cool, dry spot, where well-cured fruit keeps for several months while its sweetness continues to improve.

plant_note: Fall-plant cloves; softnecks also do well in milder winter regions.
directions: Separate bulbs into cloves and plant them pointed end up about two inches deep in fall. This Artichoke-type softneck forms twelve to twenty cloves per bulb with classic pearl-white papery skin sometimes streaked purple. Softnecks store especially well and are ideal for braiding, and they perform reliably in milder-winter regions. Mulch for winter protection and keep the bed weed-free and evenly moist through spring. Harvest when the lower leaves yellow, then cure in a dry, ventilated spot before storing.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; Sierra's exceptional heat and bolt resistance makes it valuable for extending the lettuce season into early summer; an excellent choice for warm-climate gardeners.
directions: Sow seed on or just below the soil surface in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sierra is a batavian-type lettuce combining the crisp texture of a crisphead with the loose, outer-leaf harvest convenience of a loose-leaf type — producing green, ruffled, tender-crisp heads with outstanding bolt and heat resistance that extends the spring lettuce season significantly later than butterhead or loose-leaf types. An excellent choice for zone 8–10 gardeners where spring heat arrives quickly, giving a several-week extension window before quality declines. Harvest heads when firm but before any heat stress causes bitterness.

common_name: Sieva Bean (Baby Lima Bean, Carolina Lima Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, warm soil in full sun; sieva beans (baby limas) are the small-seeded lima bean type traditional to the southeastern United States — faster-maturing, more heat-tolerant, and less prone to poor pod set in hot weather than large-seeded Fordhook-type lima beans, making them far superior for the Gulf Coast summer garden.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; provide support for pole types; pick pods when full and plump but still green. Phaseolus lunatus var. sieva (sieva bean or baby lima bean) is the small-seeded form of lima bean — traditionally called 'butter beans' across the South — that has been cultivated in the southeastern United States for centuries, adapted to the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast and Deep South where the large-seeded Fordhook-type limas are far less reliable. Sieva beans are smaller (1/3 to 1/2 the seed size of Fordhook), have thinner seed coats, cook more quickly, and are more heat-tolerant at pollination — a critical advantage in Gulf Coast summers where high night temperatures (above 70°F) cause heavy-seeded limas to drop flowers and fail to set pods. Heritage varieties like 'Florida Speckled' (with beautiful purple-speckled green seeds), 'Henderson Bush,' and 'Christmas Butter Bean' are treasured in Southern heirloom seed collections. Fresh sieva beans (butter beans) are a beloved Southern side dish — simmered with fatback or butter until creamy-tender, they have a rich, buttery, starchy flavor distinct from Northern-style green limas. Also excellent dried and shelled for winter use.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Siletz is an Oregon State University development bred specifically for cool, short-season growing in the Pacific Northwest, setting fruit at temperatures below 55°F when standard varieties fail, and producing large red beefsteak-style fruits in as few as 52 days from transplant — ideal for cloudy coastal gardens where summers are cool and brief.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Siletz can be transplanted 1–2 weeks before last frost in mild climates due to its cold tolerance for a tomato; it is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage helps manage the heavy fruit load. Siletz was developed by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University as part of the Pacific Northwest vegetable breeding program, named for the Siletz River in Oregon's Coast Range; it was released specifically to address the challenge of growing tomatoes in the cool, overcast summers of the Pacific Coast where nighttime temperatures regularly fall below the fruit-set threshold of standard varieties. The large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flattened, bright red fruits have good meaty texture and pleasant, balanced sweet-acid flavor — not the most complex among heirloom varieties, but reliably excellent given its exceptional earliness and cold tolerance. In Gulf Coast gardens, Siletz makes an outstanding early-season variety when planted in February–March, producing ripe fruit well before the onset of summer heat that terminates most tomato production. Its determinate growth habit allows clean harvest before the hot season, with plants ripening a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks.

common_name: Silver Queen Okra (Pale Ivory-Green Ornamental Okra)
plant_note: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Silver Queen is an heirloom okra valued for its pale, silvery ivory-green pods and foliage, a striking, almost ghostly color that sets it apart from the deep green of most okra varieties and makes it as much an ornamental curiosity as a productive vegetable. The tender pods have the classic okra flavor and texture, well suited to frying, gumbo, and pickling, and the plant produces reliably through the heat of a Gulf South summer. Harvest young, at three to four inches, for the best tenderness, and pick regularly to keep the plant producing over a long season.

common_name: Silver Queen Sweet Corn (Classic White Sweet Corn Standard)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks (at least 4 rows wide) for adequate wind pollination; Silver Queen is a late-season variety at 88–94 days, making it the last corn of the season for most gardeners. In zone 9, plant March–April for a June–July harvest, or plant again in August for a fall harvest. Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil amended with balanced fertilizer; side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer when plants reach knee height.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Silver Queen is perhaps the most historically influential and recognizable white sweet corn variety in American horticulture — an su (standard sugar) white hybrid introduced around 1955 that rapidly became the benchmark white sweet corn against which all others were measured for decades. The large, 8–9 inch ears carry 14–16 rows of pure white, tender, milky kernels with the classic, unmistakable sweet corn flavor that made Silver Queen famous across the mid-Atlantic and southeastern states, where roadside stands and home gardens grew Silver Queen as the late-summer corn of choice for multiple generations of cooks who planned their summer around it. At 88–94 days, Silver Queen is a late-season variety that reaches peak quality in the hottest part of summer, a timing that traditionally marked the height of summer corn season in the South and Midwest. The flavor at peak maturity — kernels plump, skins tender, sugar at maximum before starch conversion begins — is the standard by which many older gardeners still evaluate all corn. Silver Queen must be harvested and consumed or preserved within a narrow window (1–3 days after peak) as the su type converts sugar to starch more rapidly than modern se or sh2 types. In the Gulf South, Silver Queen is a classic late-spring-to-early-summer variety with a dedicated following among gardeners who grew up eating it.

plant_note: Fall-plant cloves; adaptable to cold, hot, humid, and coastal climates.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed end up about two inches deep in the fall. This California-bred silverskin softneck yields ten to twelve cloves per bulb and is prized for consistent performance and high yields. It adapts well across cold, hot, humid, and coastal climates and offers excellent long-term storage. Mulch after planting, then keep the bed evenly moist through the spring growing period. Harvest when lower leaves brown and cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place for months of storage.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, deeply dug soil in zone 7–12; Silver-seed Gourd (Cushaw Squash, Striped Cushaw, Mixta Gourd) is an ancient Mexican heritage cucurbit — the fourth domesticated Cucurbita species — cultivated for at least 7,000 years in Mesoamerica and the traditional base for Mexican pepita (pumpkin seed) oil, tamale fillings, and pumpkin candies; bearing large, distinctively curved-neck or round-and-striped fruits with flat, silvery-white seeds.
directions: Direct sow Cucurbita argyrosperma seeds in hills 4–6 inches apart after soil warms to 70°F in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil; provide ample space as vines spread 10–15 feet; water deeply once or twice weekly and side-dress with compost at vine set; harvest when rinds are hard and stems begin to cork. Silver-seed Gourd is the least-known of the four domesticated Cucurbita species but arguably the most heat-tolerant — better adapted to hot, dry summers of the US Southwest, Mexico, and Central America than C. pepo or C. maxima. It encompasses the familiar Cushaw squash (large, curved-neck, striped with light and dark green) and many traditional Mexican varieties grown specifically for their large, flat, silverish seeds (pepitas) used in the classic Mexican mole negro, pepita oil production, and traditional candies (dulce de pepita). The flesh of the large fruits is mild and sweet, excellent for pies and tamale fillings; the seeds are dried, shelled, and used as a significant protein and oil source in Mexican cuisine. Cushaw squash resists vine borers and powdery mildew better than many other Cucurbita species and performs excellently in zone 8–12 heat. Several named heirloom varieties are available including 'Green Striped Cushaw', 'White Cushaw', and 'Jonathan' (round-fruited).

plant_note: Plant runners or divisions in spring in moist, sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; silverweed spreads aggressively by runners in moist, open sites and should be contained in garden settings. It naturally colonizes coastal beaches, estuary margins, and disturbed moist ground.
directions: Plant in moist, sandy or gravelly, open soil in full sun along coastal margins, wet meadows, and disturbed open ground; silverweed is a cosmopolitan coastal and temperate wildflower with distinctive pinnate leaves that are silver-silky on the underside — providing a striking two-toned effect as the wind turns the leaves. The bright yellow five-petaled flowers in summer attract numerous small native bees. The starchy taproots were historically an important famine food in coastal Scotland, Ireland, and in Indigenous communities across the Pacific Northwest, where they were boiled, roasted, or dried for winter storage. The roasted roots have a pleasant, slightly sweet, parsnip-like flavor. Spreads rapidly by runners and can become a weed in garden settings — best planted where it can naturalize on moist, open disturbed ground. Also listed as Argentina anserina in some taxonomic systems.

common_name: Silvery Fir Tree Tomato (Russian Heirloom with Distinctive Ferny Silver-Green Foliage)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Silvery Fir Tree is determinate and compact (24–30 inches), making it well-suited for containers and small gardens. In zone 9, transplant February–March for the earliest spring tomato harvest (May–June); as a determinate variety, the plant ripens most of its fruit within a concentrated 3–4 week window. A second planting in late July or August can produce a fall crop. The variety's very early maturity (58–65 days from transplant) is a significant advantage in zone 9 where the spring tomato window is narrow before summer heat limits production — Silvery Fir Tree can begin producing in late April to May when planted on schedule, before most standard varieties set their first ripe fruits.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. No staking needed for compact plants. Harvest when fruits are uniformly red and slightly soft. Silvery Fir Tree is a Russian heirloom tomato of exceptional visual distinction — the variety is immediately recognizable in the garden by its foliage, which is finely dissected and ferny in appearance, closely resembling carrot leaves or fir tree needles rather than the broad, palmately lobed leaves of standard tomato types. The silvery-green color of the leaves (more gray-green than the typical bright green of most tomato foliage) reinforces the fir tree visual impression and gives the variety its English common name. Botanically, the finely cut leaf form is a recessive mutation in leaf architecture that has been maintained in this Russian variety through traditional seed saving — the same mutation appears occasionally in other tomato varieties but rarely becomes the defining characteristic of a named variety. The plants are determinate and compact (24–30 inches), producing clusters of small-medium red round fruits (2–3 oz each) that ripen in a concentrated season-appropriate window. The flavor is excellent for an early determinate — sweet, well-balanced, genuine tomato character without the flatness that sometimes characterizes early-season determinate types. Silvery Fir Tree has become popular in North American heirloom tomato cultivation not only for its early production and good flavor but also as an ornamental garden plant: the unusual ferny foliage makes it visually striking in container plantings, edible landscapes, and kitchen gardens where visual diversity among plants adds character.

plant_note: Start indoors in early to midsummer for a fall harvest sweetened by frost.
directions: Start seed indoors in early to midsummer and transplant sturdy seedlings for a long-season fall crop. Brussels sprouts need a lengthy, cool finish, and a light frost actually sweetens the tight little sprouts. Space plants generously and stake tall stalks in windy sites to keep them upright. Remove yellowing lower leaves as sprouts form to improve air flow and size. Harvest from the bottom of the stalk upward once sprouts are firm and about an inch across.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Sioux is one of the most heat-tolerant tomatoes available, originally developed by the University of Nebraska in the 1940s specifically for hot, humid Midwestern conditions and still treasured by Gulf Coast and Southern gardeners for its ability to set fruit through summer heat that defeats most other varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and stake or cage early — Sioux is an indeterminate variety that sets fruit continuously through the season. Sioux was introduced by the University of Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station in 1944, bred specifically for heat tolerance and disease resistance in hot, humid, continental climates; it remains one of the most reliably productive tomatoes for hot Southern summers and Gulf Coast conditions where other varieties drop blossoms during heat waves — Sioux continues setting medium-sized (6–8 oz), round, bright red fruits even when nighttime temperatures stay above 75°F. The flavor is classic, balanced, and mildly acidic — a dependable slicer with good disease resistance and continuous production from early summer until frost. Highly recommended for gardeners in zones 8–11 who struggle to keep tomatoes producing through midsummer.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the very short 6-week maturity makes this an excellent choice for succession planting through the whole Gulf South growing season, from spring through a final late-summer sowing.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and one of the fastest-maturing Southern peas available, ready to pick as fresh shell peas in as little as six weeks. Six Weeks Purple Hull is a classic, widely grown heirloom cowpea prized above all for its speed — the compact, semi-bush plants set pods and fill out quickly, making it the go-to variety for gardeners who want an early first picking or need to squeeze in extra succession plantings between other summer crops. The pods mature to a deep purple that makes ripe pods easy to spot against the green foliage, and the cream-colored peas inside have the classic mild, earthy purple hull flavor, excellent fresh-shelled and cooked down Southern-style with a bit of pork or simmered as a simple pot of field peas. Reliable, heat-tolerant, and fast, it is a Gulf South garden staple for a quick, dependable pea crop, zone 5–11.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost or start indoors 6 weeks early; established clumps can also be divided in spring.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in well-prepared, deeply cultivated soil; skirret produces a cluster of multiple sweet, carrot-like roots that need loose ground to develop well. Keep well-watered through summer as drought stress causes woody, fibrous roots with an unpleasant core. Harvest in autumn after frost, washing and separating the finger-sized roots; any woody central strings are removed before eating. Divide clumps in early spring to propagate, replanting the outer sections and discarding the old center.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in groups of 2–3 seeds per hill after last frost when soil is above 65°F; cucumbers can be started indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost in individual peat pots to minimize root disturbance at transplanting, but they resent transplanting and direct sowing is preferred.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; slicing cucumbers are bred for fresh eating with smooth, glossy, dark-green skins, mild flavor, and few seeds compared to pickling types. Provide a trellis for vining varieties to keep fruits straight and clean and improve air circulation; bush types are more compact and work well in raised beds. Water deeply and consistently — inconsistent moisture causes bitter fruit and misshapen cucumbers. Harvest when fruits are 7–9 inches long before the skin yellows or seeds harden. Pick frequently — leaving overripe fruits on the vine signals the plant to stop producing. Cucumber beetles are the primary pest; row covers until flowering provide effective protection.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring and fall; more heat tolerant than standard arugula.
directions: Direct sow seed shallowly in cool weather and keep the bed moist for quick, even germination. As the name suggests, this variety resists bolting longer than standard arugula and tolerates a bit more heat. Harvest young leaves for microgreens or baby greens, or let plants reach full size for peppery salad leaves. Cut outer leaves and let the center regrow for repeated harvests. Successive sowings every couple of weeks keep a steady supply of tender greens.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; needs a long, warm season to ripen fully.
directions: Sow seeds one inch deep in warm, fertile soil, planting in hills and thinning to the strongest plants. This classic heirloom pie pumpkin produces compact, deep-orange fruits with sweet, fine-grained flesh perfect for baking. Give the vines plenty of room to run and keep them well watered as fruits develop. Harvest in fall when the rind is hard and fully colored, then cure the pumpkins for a week or two to improve storage and flavor.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; surface sow as seeds need light to germinate. In zones 8–11 it can be direct sown in early fall for a winter and spring harvest.
directions: Surface sow seed on moist starting mix at 65°F and provide bright light; smallage is the ancient, semi-wild form of celery with thin, hollow stems and very intensely flavored leaves — flavor is perhaps 10 times stronger than modern celery and reminiscent of the finest celery seed spice. It is grown primarily for its leaves, not its stalks, and a small amount goes a long way in soups, stews, and sauces. Unlike stalk celery, smallage is relatively easy to grow, tolerates partial shade, and does not require blanching. It is the celery of most historical European recipes before hybridization for thick stalks. A biennial or short-lived perennial that self-sows readily to establish a permanent presence in the herb garden.

plant_note: Direct sow 4-2 weeks before the last frost; the tiny seeds germinate quickly in cool soil and rosettes develop fast in early spring light.
directions: Surface-sow or barely cover seeds in full sun in early spring, thinning to 6-10 inches once seedlings are established; smooth hawk's beard germinates quickly and is ready to harvest within a month of sowing. Cut young rosette leaves when they are 3-4 inches long for the mildest flavor, using them raw in salads or wilting briefly in a pan with olive oil and garlic. Plants can be cut back to within an inch of the crown and will regrow for additional harvests before bolting triggers the small yellow flower heads. Self-seeding is prolific in disturbed ground, making smooth hawk's beard a low-maintenance, cut-and-come-again addition to the productive garden.

common_name: Smooth Luffa (Loofah, Sponge Gourd, Vegetable Sponge)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9, start in February–March for April transplanting; luffa requires a very long, warm growing season (90–120 days of warm weather) to produce mature fibrous sponges — in zone 9, this is easily achieved, and it is one of the best climates in the continental US for productive luffa growing.
directions: Start seeds indoors in peat pots 2–4 weeks before last frost; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained, deeply cultivated, moist, fertile soil on a very sturdy trellis or fence — luffa vines become heavy and must have strong support. Luffa aegyptiaca (smooth luffa or vegetable sponge) produces dual crops: the immature fruits (3–5 inches long) are eaten as a vegetable throughout Asia and Africa — tasting like a mild, slightly sweet zucchini — while the fully mature, dried fruits are harvested for their fibrous interior skeleton, which dries into the familiar luffa or loofah bath sponge. The vine produces large, bright-yellow flowers (4–5 inches, excellent for pollinators) and cylindrical fruits 18–24 inches long that must be allowed to ripen fully on the vine until the skin yellows and shrivels before harvesting for sponges. To process sponges: cure dried gourds in the sun, peel off the papery skin, shake out seeds (save for next year), wash, and bleach lightly if desired. Zone 9 provides the long, hot season luffa requires to complete its full lifecycle and produce dry, mature sponges.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 75°F; a truly tropical vine requiring a long, hot summer.
directions: Nick the seed coat or soak seeds 24 hours before sowing 1/2 inch deep to improve germination rates in this heat-demanding tropical. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis or overhead structure — vines can exceed 12 feet and produce pendulous fruits that must hang freely to grow straight, reaching 1–3 feet in length. Harvest young fruits at 12–18 inches while skin is still soft and pale green-striped white; the tender young fruit is used like summer squash in South and Southeast Asian cooking. Overripe fruits develop an unpleasant bitter compound and turn orange-red, signaling they should be discarded rather than eaten.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; a fall planting 8 weeks before first frost is equally productive in many climates.
directions: Sow seed 1 in deep as soon as the ground can be worked and provide twiggy brush or mesh netting for vines to climb. Pre-soaking seeds overnight can improve germination in cold soil. Harvest when pods are plump, fully filled, and glossy; snap peas pass their peak quickly in warm weather. Powdery mildew is common late in the season — choose resistant varieties when available.

plant_note: Sow 4–6 weeks before the last spring frost or in early autumn; cool weather produces the crispest, sweetest pods.
directions: Press seeds 1 in deep into cool, well-drained soil and erect support netting before the vines need it. Snow peas are harvested when pods are flat, bright green, and the seeds inside are barely visible; even slight bulging means the pod is overripe for stir-fry use. Keep pods picked daily during peak production to sustain cropping. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush foliage at the expense of pods.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant before the last frost, or sow in summer for a fall crop.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into rich, evenly moist soil, since cauliflower needs steady growth without checks. This early-maturing heirloom forms uniform, snow-white heads with excellent flavor. When the curds reach the size of an egg, tie or fold the outer leaves over them to blanch and protect the head from yellowing. Harvest while the heads are firm and tight, before the curds begin to loosen or separate.

plant_note: Sow in early spring and again in late summer for a fall crop; turnips prefer cool weather.
directions: Direct sow seeds a quarter to half an inch deep and thin seedlings so roots have room to round out. This reliable heirloom produces smooth, round white roots with a mild, sweet flavor, and its tender greens are edible too. Keep the soil evenly moist for fast, crack-free growth in the cool seasons. Harvest roots young, at about two to three inches, when they are sweetest and most tender.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; this cool-season root matures quickly.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly directly in the garden and thin the seedlings to a few inches apart for well-formed roots. This timeless heirloom yields smooth, round white roots with a mild, sweet taste, and both roots and greens are good eating. Provide steady moisture so the roots stay crisp and do not turn woody in warm spells. Pull turnips while young and tender for the best flavor and texture.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 start in August–September and transplant September–October for fall through winter harvest. Blanching is required for white curds: when the central head begins to form, gather the outer leaves over the developing curd and secure with a rubber band or clothespin to exclude sunlight — cauliflower exposed to sun develops yellow color and may lose some quality. Self-blanching varieties with overlapping leaves reduce this labor requirement. Harvest before heads loosen or develop a rice-like granular texture.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — cauliflower requires more nitrogen and consistent moisture than any other Brassica; Snowball Y is one of the classic open-pollinated white cauliflower varieties — an improved selection from the Snowball strain that has defined the white-headed cauliflower in American horticulture for a century. The compact, round, pure white heads (when properly blanched) represent the culmination of cauliflower development — the plant's edible curd is composed of densely packed, malformed (fasciated) flower buds arrested before they develop, creating the characteristic curded texture of cauliflower. Unlike broccoli, where the flower buds are visible and intact, cauliflower's curd represents a complete developmental halt before budding — a botanical curiosity that produces one of the most unusual vegetable textures available, simultaneously firm and mealy, dense and delicate. Cauliflower's reputation for difficulty is warranted — it requires the most specific temperature range (50–70°F) of any commonly grown vegetable, failing in heat or extreme cold. In zone 9 this restricts successful cauliflower to a narrow fall window of September–December planting.

plant_note: Start indoors; good for short-season areas thanks to its early maturity.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant sturdy seedlings into rich, evenly moist soil for a spring or fall crop. This dependable variety forms flavorful six-inch snow-white heads in about seventy to eighty days, making it well suited to short-season gardens. The leaves naturally curl around the head for self-blanching and protection from sun scald. Keep water and nutrients steady, since stress can trigger loose or off-color curds. Mature heads hold well in the garden, so they need not all be cut at once.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Snowcap is a compact bush bean with strikingly beautiful seeds — white with maroon-red markings concentrated around the hilum — and outstanding flavor as both a shell bean and dried bean, with a creamy texture and rich taste that earned it wide popularity among heirloom bean enthusiasts.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Snowcap is a bush-type bean that needs no support and can be direct-seeded in rows 18 inches apart. Snowcap is an heirloom bush dry bean producing attractive, round-to-oval seeds that are white with a distinctive cap of maroon-red coloring concentrated around the seed scar (hilum) — the 'snowcap' pattern from which it takes its name. The flavor is rich, buttery, and creamy when cooked, with a thin skin that doesn't need pre-soaking for most applications; it is outstanding in soups, chilis, and bean salads where its firm-yet-creamy texture holds up well. An attractive plant for the vegetable garden with modest height and compact habit; the ornamental seeds are a bonus when drying for seed saving. One of the most beautiful and best-flavored heirloom dry beans in the Seed Savers Exchange collection.

plant_note: Start indoors with warmth and transplant only after nights are reliably warm.
directions: Start seeds indoors with bottom heat about eight weeks before transplanting, as eggplant loves warmth. Set plants out only after the weather is settled and warm, spacing them for good air movement. This variety produces firm, sweet white eggplants up to eight inches long with meaty flesh that holds up to grilling and roasting. Harvest fruits while the skin is glossy and the flesh is firm, cutting rather than pulling to avoid damaging the plant.

plant_note: Transplant into sandy, well-drained soil at or just after the last frost date; protect from late cold snaps as young transplants are sensitive to frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant to a full-sun site with sandy or gravelly, well-drained soil after frost danger has passed. Native to the southeastern coastal plain from Virginia to Florida and Texas, this softly hairy perennial ground cherry produces papery-husked yellow berries from late summer through fall that are sweet and pleasant when fully ripe. Plants require excellent drainage and tolerate drought well once established, making them well-suited to xeric southern food gardens. They spread by rhizomes to form loose colonies over time and may die back to the roots in cooler parts of zone 7.

common_name: Solar Fire Tomato (AAS-Winning Heat-Adapted Gulf South Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Solar Fire's All-America Selections recognition reflects outstanding performance across multiple growing regions, including the hot, humid Gulf South.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Solar Fire is an All-America Selections-recognized tomato hybrid developed at the University of Florida for superior performance in hot climates — combining good heat tolerance for extended fruit set with excellent fresh-eating flavor, disease resistance, and attractive fruit appearance. The medium-large (8–10 oz), round, firm, bright-red fruits are well-suited to Gulf South conditions — they hold well on the vine and in post-harvest storage better than some softer hybrid types. Solar Fire carries resistance to the major tomato diseases of the humid Gulf South including Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), Alternaria stem canker, Gray leaf spot, and Nematodes — a disease package that significantly reduces the fungicide and nematicide inputs required for production. The determinate to semi-determinate growth habit reaches 4–6 feet with moderate staking requirements. Solar Fire typically performs well for zone 9 gardeners in both spring (February–June) and fall (August–November) planting windows. The spring crop produces the largest volume of fruit before summer heat; the fall crop frequently produces the best-quality fruit as temperatures cool. An excellent choice for Gulf South gardeners seeking a reliable, productive, disease-resistant red tomato with better heat tolerance than standard commercial varieties.

common_name: Solar Set Tomato (UF Heat-Setting Gulf South Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring harvest and August for fall. Solar Set was specifically developed to set fruit at higher temperatures than standard varieties — the key trait for Gulf South spring production where nighttime temperatures frequently exceed 75°F before the crop is finished. Unlike most tomatoes, which fail to pollinate when nights stay above 70–75°F, Solar Set continues fruit set during warm spells.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Solar Set is a determinate hybrid tomato developed by the University of Florida specifically to address the most critical failure point in Gulf Coast tomato production — the inability of most varieties to set fruit when nighttime temperatures exceed 70–75°F. In standard tomatoes, high night temperatures destroy pollen viability and prevent fruit set even when flowering is abundant, causing the characteristic 'drop-out' where plants flower profusely but set no fruit as spring transitions to summer. Solar Set was bred to maintain viable pollen and fruit set at higher temperatures than standard varieties, extending the productive window by 2–4 weeks in warm spring conditions — a significant advantage in zone 8–11 where the spring growing window is narrow. The medium-large (6–10 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have good flavor and adequate disease resistance including Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, and gray leaf spot. Solar Set is not as widely known as Solar Fire or Heatmaster but performs a similar heat-set function and has been a reliable variety in UF variety trials for Gulf Coast spring production. Best suited to spring and fall production in zone 8b–11 where heat-setting capacity provides measurable yield advantages.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; yellow carrots retain their color both raw and cooked, making them visually distinctive in soups, roasted vegetable dishes, and salads.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Solar Yellow is a bright lemon-yellow carrot with Nantes-type cylindrical shape and excellent flavor — somewhat milder and less earthy than orange carrots with a clean, slightly sweet taste and better carotene stability (it holds its yellow color both raw and when cooked, unlike purple carrots that fade to orange). Rich in xanthophylls rather than beta-carotene, with distinct nutritional benefits associated with yellow pigments. An excellent variety for multicolored carrot mixes alongside orange, purple, red, and white types for maximum visual and nutritional diversity.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; can also be started indoors for transplants.
directions: Direct sow seed thickly in shallow rows in early spring and keep the bed evenly moist. This specialty bunching onion forms uniform, sweet, tender stalks with only a small bulb at the base, prized for grilled cebollitas asadas. Vigorous and easy to grow, it can also be started indoors and transplanted in clumps. Hill a little soil around the stalks to lengthen and blanch the white bases. Harvest whenever stalks reach usable size, pulling entire plants as needed.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; Soldier bean is a New England heirloom dry bean with large, white seeds marked with a distinctive red figure near the hilum that resembles a standing soldier or musketeer — one of the most visually striking and historically significant New England heirloom beans.
directions: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; soldier bean is a bush type that performs best in cool to moderate summer climates (zones 3–7) but is grown across a wide range. Soldier bean is a New England heirloom dry bean with a long history in Maine and New England, documented in American seed catalogs for well over a century; the seeds are large, kidney-shaped, and pure white with a striking red figure near the hilum that — with some imagination — resembles a soldier or musketeer with a distinctive hat and cloak, making it one of the most visually interesting of all heirloom beans. The cooked flavor is mild, creamy, and rich, similar to navy beans but larger; soldier beans are the traditional bean of New England baked beans, Boston baked beans, and bean soups and make excellent succotash. An outstanding heirloom for seed saving, showing true and breeding reliably from year to year.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: Start seed indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once frost danger passes. This F1 hybrid produces extra-large, dark green, thick-walled four-inch jalapenos with a slightly above-average heat around 6,500 Scoville units. The disease-resistant plants are high yielding and the fruit has an exceptional shelf life. Pick peppers green and firm for classic use, or let some ripen red for added sweetness. Steady water and full sun keep the heavy sets coming all season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; do not cover seeds — they require light to germinate. Set transplants out in moist, fertile soil up to 4 weeks before last frost; soup celery is far more tolerant of heat, drought, and poor growing conditions than standard stalk celery and will produce in gardens where regular celery fails.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting (seeds need light — do not cover); set transplants in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; soup celery (cutting celery, leaf celery, smallage) is the ancestral form of cultivated celery, grown for its intensely flavored, aromatic leaves and slender stems used as an herb rather than a stalk vegetable. Plants produce dense, bushy clumps of dark-green, deeply cut celery-flavored leaves throughout the growing season, cut repeatedly like parsley. A single plant provides an essentially unlimited supply of celery flavor for soups, stews, salads, and stocks without the exacting cultural demands of stalk celery — no blanching is needed, and the plant tolerates some heat, drought, and partial shade that would devastate standard celery. Can be grown year-round in mild-winter climates (zones 8–10) and will self-sow in suitable conditions. 'Afina' and 'Amsterdam Cutting' are reliable selections.

plant_note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist to wet soil or in shallow water (2–12 inches deep) at pond margins, rain gardens, or wet ditches in full sun; southern cattail is a warm-climate native cattail adapted to the Gulf Coastal Plain and is the dominant cattail species of southern marshes, ditches, and shorelines.
directions: Plant rhizome divisions in moist to wet soil or shallow water at pond or wetland margins in full sun; southern cattail spreads aggressively by rhizome and may be invasive in small water features — best for large ponds or natural wetland restoration. Typha domingensis (southern cattail) is the dominant native cattail of the Gulf Coastal Plain, replacing common cattail (T. latifolia) in warm-climate marshes and ditches from the Carolinas through Florida and Texas. It is distinguished from common cattail by its narrower leaves (hence 'narrow-leaf cattail') and the characteristic gap between the female and male portions of the cigar-shaped flower spike — the two sections are separated by a visible gap in T. domingensis, while they are contiguous in T. latifolia. Cattails are among the most important edible wild plants of temperate and subtropical North America: the young shoots (peeled) are eaten like asparagus in spring; the green flower spikes are boiled and eaten like corn on the cob; the pollen is collected as a golden flour rich in protein; the starchy rhizomes can be processed into flour. They also provide outstanding wildlife habitat — nesting material and cover for numerous marsh bird species, seeds for waterfowl, and dense stands shelter fish.

plant_note: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for the superior fall crop. Southern Giant Curled is cold-hardy to about 20°F when established and thrives in the cool, mild winters of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Broadcast seeds and rake in lightly, or sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–15 inches; Southern Giant Curled is the classic all-purpose mustard green of the American South, grown for over a century in Gulf Coast and Southeastern gardens and still the standard by which other mustard greens are judged for traditional Southern cooking. The large, heavily ruffled and curled, bright yellow-green leaves are pungent and mustardy, with a characteristic bite that is best tamed by long, slow cooking with pork (a smoked ham hock or fatback) in the traditional Southern style. The big, broad leaves are also excellent braised in olive oil with garlic for a more Mediterranean preparation, or wilted into beans and soups. Flavor improves dramatically after a frost — the cold converts starches to sugars and mellows the pungency, making fall mustard greens distinctly better than spring. In zone 9, plants sown in October are typically at their peak in December–January. Harvest outer leaves for continuous production; entire heads can also be cut at once for batch cooking. An exceptionally easy, productive, nutritious cool-season crop.

plant_note: Sow in early spring or late summer; fast-growing and heat-tolerant for warm regions.
directions: Direct sow seeds a quarter inch deep and thin seedlings so the large plants have room to spread. This heirloom produces giant, frilled green leaves with a bold, spicy flavor and good heat tolerance for warm climates. It grows quickly, so harvest outer leaves young for milder taste or let them mature for a stronger bite. Keep the soil moist to slow bolting, and sow in succession for a continuing supply of spicy greens.

common_name: Southern Pea (Cowpea, Black-eyed Pea, Field Pea)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Southern peas are one of the most important and widely grown summer vegetables in the Gulf South, thriving in heat and humidity while fixing atmospheric nitrogen — a dual-purpose food and cover crop.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; thin to 4–6 inches. Vigna unguiculata (southern pea, cowpea, or black-eyed pea) is the most heat-tolerant major legume in North American horticulture and an absolute staple of Southern gardens and cuisine — encompassing black-eyed peas, crowder peas, cream peas, pink-eye purple hull peas, lady peas, and Iron-and-Clay peas in a single species with hundreds of named varieties grouped by pod color, seed markings, and intended use. All share the capacity to fix atmospheric nitrogen (greatly enriching soil when the crop residue is turned under), exceptional heat and drought tolerance, and thrive in the humid, hot conditions of Gulf Coast summers when other legumes fail. Fresh 'green' (immature) southern peas are shelled and cooked like shell beans; dry peas are stored for long-term use. 'California Black-eye' (classic black-eyed pea), 'Pinkeye Purple Hull,' 'Iron-and-Clay' (cover crop type), 'Mississippi Silver,' and 'Texas Cream' are widely grown named varieties. In zone 9, southern peas can be planted from April through August for continuous production.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Southport Red Globe is a classic American heirloom red storage onion from Southport, Connecticut — where it was the foundation of a thriving 19th-century commercial onion trade — producing medium to large, globe-shaped, deep red-purple bulbs with white, mildly pungent flesh and excellent long storage quality.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost when seedlings are 6–8 inches tall and pencil-width. Southport Red Globe is a long-day heirloom red onion from Southport (now part of Fairfield), Connecticut, where it was the commercial foundation of one of the most important onion-growing regions of 19th-century America — the Connecticut shoreline towns of Southport, Wethersfield, and Granby exported enormous quantities of dried storage onions to markets up and down the Eastern Seaboard and into the Caribbean. The medium to large (3–4 inch diameter), globe-shaped bulbs have deep red-purple skin and white flesh lightly tinged with red at the outer rings; the flavor is moderately pungent when raw, milder when cooked, with a typical red onion character. As a long-day type, Southport Red Globe performs best in northern gardens (zones 3–7) where the long summer days trigger good bulb development; in Gulf Coast gardens (short-day conditions), use short-day red onion varieties instead. Excellent storage quality — properly cured bulbs keep 4–6 months.

plant_note: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–February for fall through early spring harvest. Space is an F1 hybrid with outstanding downy mildew resistance — particularly important in zone 9 where the warm, humid fall climate creates conditions favorable for mildew. The smooth, upright leaves are easy to harvest and clean, with less dirt trapping than savoy-type spinach. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest; even heat-tolerant spinach will bolt in zone 9's rising spring temperatures. Partial shade extends the season slightly.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — spinach benefits from afternoon shade protection in warmer climates to delay bolting; Space is an F1 hybrid spinach developed specifically for exceptional downy mildew (Peronospora spinaciae) resistance — the most significant disease of fresh-market spinach. The smooth, slightly cupped, dark green, upright leaves are the commercial fresh spinach leaf type: uniformly sized, easy to wash without the texture trapping of savoy (crinkled) types, and attractive in fresh salads and smoothies. Unlike savoy-type spinach that requires multiple washings to remove soil from the heavily crinkled leaves, Space's smooth, upright leaves release dirt easily and drain well in salad spinners. The F1 hybrid vigor produces noticeably more uniform and productive plants than open-pollinated varieties. Space's disease resistance makes it the practical choice for zone 9 fall spinach where warm, humid conditions can destroy less resistant varieties; the resistance ratings cover multiple races of downy mildew, providing durable protection across multiple seasons.

plant_note: Direct sow in cool weather; good bolt tolerance for spring and fall.
directions: Direct sow seed in cool soil in early spring or late summer and keep the bed consistently moist. This upright, compact spinach produces smooth to lightly savoyed, medium-green leaves that are excellent fresh or sauteed. High resistance to downy mildew and good bolting tolerance make it dependable across seasons. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut whole plants at the base for a full crop. Successive sowings extend the harvest before summer heat triggers bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; compact vines suit containers.
directions: Direct sow seed after the last frost once the soil is thoroughly warm, or start indoors in peat pots for an early start. This compact variety carries full-sized slicing cucumbers on short two-to-three-foot vines, making it ideal for small beds and containers. Keep plants evenly watered, especially during flowering and fruiting, to avoid bitter or misshapen cucumbers. Harvest fruits young and often to keep the vines productive. A little support keeps fruit clean and straight even in tight spaces.

plant_note: Direct sow into warm soil after frost; compact habit suits containers and small beds.
directions: Sow seeds one inch deep in warm soil, and take advantage of the compact, bush-type habit that thrives in containers and small spaces. Despite their short vines, the plants produce full-size 7-8 inch cucumbers with crisp, mild flesh. Keep the soil evenly moist to prevent bitterness and misshapen fruits during the warm season. Harvest cucumbers regularly while they are firm and dark green to encourage continued production.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil temperature reaches 65°F.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, compost-enriched hills, placing 3 seeds per hill and thinning to 1–2 plants. Give vines ample room to spread, or train onto a strong trellis and support heavy fruits with a sling. The rind turns from pale green to golden yellow when mature and will feel hard when pressed. Allow picked fruits to cure in a warm spot for 1–2 weeks before using or storing; they keep for several months in a cool, dry room.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. The cream-colored, football-shaped fruits should be left on the vine until the skin is hard and turns from yellow-green to deep golden-yellow. Cure harvested fruit at room temperature for 2 weeks, then store in a cool, dry place for up to 3 months. In zone 9 the long warm season allows fruits to cure fully on the vine before harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Spaghetti Squash (also called Vegetable Spaghetti) is a unique winter squash whose cooked flesh separates naturally into long, thin strands closely resembling spaghetti pasta — when halved and baked cut-side down, the flesh is scraped out with a fork to produce a pile of mildly sweet, slightly crunchy, pasta-like strands. The mild, neutral flavor serves as an effective low-carbohydrate substitute for pasta under tomato sauces, pesto, or any pasta topping, and has become one of the most popular low-carb vegetables for health-conscious cooks since the 1970s. The oblong, cream-to-golden fruits (4–8 pounds) are a Cucurbita pepo type with the same excellent disease resistance and productivity as other C. pepo squash. In zone 9 the long warm season is ideal for spaghetti squash, which requires the full warm season to develop and cure properly on the vine.

plant_note: Direct sow seeds in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Spanish oyster plant requires a long, cool growing season (cool fall and winter for root development) before roots are harvested in late spring. The roots become milky-white and soft when cooked and have a mild, oyster-like or artichoke-like flavor. The stems and leaves are covered with strong spines — handle with care.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Spanish oyster plant is a Mediterranean native chicory-family perennial that has been grown as an edible root vegetable since at least medieval times throughout Spain, Italy, and southern France, where its long, white, deeply growing taproot is harvested in late spring and cooked like salsify or parsnip — boiled, roasted, or sautéed in olive oil. The cooked root has a pleasant, mild, artichoke-like or oyster-like flavor that makes it an interesting, underused culinary vegetable. The plant in the garden is a bold, deep-green, heavily spined thistle-like perennial with golden-yellow, star-shaped composite flowers in summer that are attractive to pollinators. The spines on stems and leaf margins are sharp and require careful handling. A drought-tolerant, deep-rooted perennial for Mediterranean-climate and Gulf Coast gardens where its cool-season root-development period suits the mild winter conditions. Once harvested, it is generally treated as an annual or biennial. Grown in Spain and southern Europe as an artisan market vegetable.

common_name: Spanish Roja Garlic (Classic Rocambole with Superior Flavor)
plant_note: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Spanish Roja is a rocambole-type hardneck with a strong cold requirement for good bulb formation, best suited to zone 3-7 with a real winter chill.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Spanish Roja is a classic rocambole-type hardneck garlic, brought to the Pacific Northwest by Spanish settlers generations ago, and widely considered by garlic growers and chefs to have some of the finest, most complex flavor of any garlic variety — rich, hot, and full without being harsh. Bulbs have a distinctive rich reddish-brown skin over 8-12 large, very easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it produces a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. The main tradeoff for its superior flavor is shorter storage life than porcelain or softneck types, typically only 4-5 months, so plan to use Spanish Roja earlier in the storage season.
