directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into a hanging basket, window box, or large container with rich, well-draining potting mix. Water consistently (containers dry out faster than in-ground plantings) and fertilize every 2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer for best production. Tumbling Tom is a compact, pendulous-stemmed cherry tomato developed specifically for container and hanging basket growing — the first cherry tomato variety widely distributed with 'tumbling' in the name to describe its characteristic cascading habit, where the naturally trailing stems drape over pot edges and hang 18–24 inches below the rim, making it one of the most dramatic edible container plants available. Unlike most cherry tomatoes, which require staking and training on indeterminate vines that climb 5–8 feet, Tumbling Tom is a bushy, pendent type that requires no staking, no caging, and no training — just water, light, and fertilizer. The plants produce abundant clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), round, bright red cherry tomatoes with good sweet tomato flavor on the pendulous stems; a large hanging basket with a well-established Tumbling Tom plant loaded with red fruits is a genuinely beautiful and productive edible ornamental display. Available in both red and yellow strains ('Tumbling Tom Red' and 'Tumbling Tom Yellow'). Ideal for balconies, patios, decks, and any space where in-ground gardening is not possible.

plant_note: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Turban squash is both an ornamental and edible winter squash producing the most architecturally dramatic fruits in the cucurbit family — a protruding 'cap' or acorn-like secondary lobe emerges from the top of the main squash creating the distinctive turban shape in brilliant orange and cream and green swirling patterns.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in rich, well-amended soil in full sun; provide 6–8 feet of space for sprawling vines. Turban squash (also called Turk's Cap, Turk's Turban, or French Turban) is one of the most visually distinctive of all winter squash, producing medium to large (5–10 lb) fruits with a dramatic secondary lobe or 'cap' protruding from the blossom end in a shape resembling a Turkish turban or Ottoman fez — this unusual morphology is a Cucurbita maxima trait that occasionally appears in several varieties but is most pronounced and reliable in this dedicated 'Turban' selection. The skin is spectacularly patterned in orange, cream, and green with mottled, swirling patterns that vary between fruits; the ornamental quality makes Turban squash one of the most popular fall decorative squashes alongside regular pumpkins. The flesh is edible with a mild, somewhat dry, floury texture and pleasant squash flavor well-suited to stuffing — the cap portion is often removed and used as a natural serving bowl for soups or stuffings.

common_name: Turk's Turban Squash (Turban Squash, French Turban, Giraumon Turban)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Turk's Turban is grown as much for ornament as for eating — the extraordinary multi-colored fruits with their protruding turban-shaped secondary lobe are among the most visually dramatic of any squash, making them a centerpiece of autumn decorations and farmers' market displays as well as a rich-flavored eating squash.
directions: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after last frost in a fertile, well-drained bed; Turk's Turban produces medium-length vines of 6–8 feet; harvest when the skin is fully hard and the color has developed to its mature orange-red with green and white swirling markings; cure at room temperature for 2–3 weeks to harden the rind and improve flavor. Turk's Turban is one of the most visually spectacular squashes in cultivation — an heirloom Cucurbita maxima variety that has been grown in American and European gardens since the 19th century, renowned for the extraordinary shape of its fruits: a squat, flattened orange-red primary body topped by a rounded, turban-like secondary lobe that protrudes from the blossom end, often striped or mottled in contrasting shades of green, cream, and orange. The distinctive shape comes from an unusual growth pattern in which the secondary floral section of the fruit expands outward from the blossom end, creating the appearance of a hat or turban imposed on top of the primary fruit body. No two Turk's Turban fruits are exactly alike in their color patterning — each shows a unique arrangement of orange, green, cream, and white in swirls and stripes that makes them natural art objects. The flesh beneath is the dense, sweet, orange type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties; at full maturity after curing, the flavor is rich and sweet with a dry, starchy texture excellent for baking, soups, and puréeing. While widely grown as a purely ornamental squash for autumn display, Turk's Turban is fully edible and good-flavored — it deserves to be eaten rather than simply displayed.

plant_note: Start from seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or purchase transplants; turkey berry grows as a woody perennial shrub in zones 9–11 and may be used as a rootstock for grafting eggplant in commercial production.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; turkey berry is a sprawling tropical nightshade shrub producing prolific clusters of small (marble-sized) green berries that are an essential ingredient in Thai green curry — they add a distinctive bitter, slightly crunchy texture and are used whole or halved. In Caribbean and West African cooking the cooked berries appear in stews and salt fish dishes, including the Jamaican classic susumber in salt fish. Unlike many nightshades, the berries are always cooked before eating. In zone 9–11 the shrub becomes a large multi-stemmed perennial that produces year-round; in zone 8 it may dieback and resprout from the roots. The stems have scattered spines — wear gloves when harvesting.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained soil; Turkey Craw is a half-runner or semi-vining type requiring 2–3 feet of support. It is heat-tolerant once established and produces prolifically through Gulf Coast summer conditions that discourage northern bean varieties.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing low supports of 2–3 feet for the semi-vining plants; Turkey Craw is an Appalachian heirloom snap bean dating back at least to the 19th century, named for seeds reportedly found in the crop (craw) of a wild turkey shot by a hunter — the story illustrating how food plants spread naturally through the American South via birds and early farmers. It is a cutshort type, meaning the seeds are crowded together in the pod and shortened in length to accommodate more seeds — the characteristic shape that identifies many traditional Southern snap beans. The pods are tender and flavorful when harvested young as snap beans, or the plants can be allowed to mature for dry bean use. Excellent heat tolerance and prolific production make it a dependable Southern garden bean; the seeds' tan and brown mottling is distinctive and appealing.

common_name: Turkish Orange Eggplant (Round Heirloom Orange-Fruited Eggplant)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Turkish Orange can be harvested at two stages — green (immature, mildest) or orange (ripe, slightly sweeter and more complex). Harvest at the orange stage for the full Turkish Orange experience; at this stage the skin may show some streaking or mottling. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The plants are ornamental as well as edible — the clusters of round, orange, tomato-like fruits are visually striking in the garden.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun. Harvest at the orange stage when fruits are 2–3 inches in diameter for full flavor development. Turkish Orange is an heirloom eggplant from Turkey that produces compact, round fruits 2–3 inches in diameter that ripen from green to a deep, vibrant orange-red — a color completely unlike any other common eggplant and more reminiscent of a small tomato or tomatillo than a traditional eggplant. This color difference signals a different flavor profile: Turkish Orange eggplants are slightly sweeter than standard purple types, with less bitterness and a slightly more complex, slightly acidic note at the ripe orange stage. The plants are productive and ornamental — clusters of round, orange fruits hanging from attractive, somewhat spiny plants create a striking garden display that frequently prompts questions from visitors unfamiliar with the variety. The flesh is firm, white to cream-colored, and suitable for all standard eggplant preparations; the round shape makes them particularly interesting for stuffing whole, hollowing and filling with rice-and-meat preparations in the Turkish culinary tradition from which the variety originates.

plant_note: Direct sow seed in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, deeply cultivated soil in full sun to partial shade; Turkish rocket has a taproot and dislikes transplanting — sow in its permanent location. Once established it is extremely long-lived and drought tolerant. A perennial vegetable that will produce for decades in the right site.
directions: Direct sow in fall or early spring in well-drained, slightly alkaline, deeply cultivated soil in full sun to partial shade; Turkish rocket is one of the most productive and versatile perennial vegetables for the four-season food garden — a member of the mustard family (Brassicaceae) with an edible flavor profile that shifts through the season. The young spring leaves are used raw in salads with a mild, arugula-like flavor; as they age and before flowering they develop a stronger, mustardy bite better suited to cooking as a potherb. The young flower buds and flowers are eaten like broccoli raab. After flowers open, the distinctive warty, corky, two-seeded pods are produced. The plant is extremely long-lived, drought tolerant, and cold hardy once established, and produces earlier in spring than almost any other perennial vegetable. Self-seeds freely — deadhead after flowering if spread is unwanted. An outstanding low-maintenance perennial vegetable for the permaculture food garden.

plant_note: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring; fall plantings 6–8 weeks before first frost often produce the sweetest, most tender roots.
directions: Direct-sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun as early as 2–3 weeks before last frost in spring, or 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; turnips are among the fastest-maturing root vegetables available, producing edible roots in 40–60 days and providing both edible roots and edible greens from a single planting. The roots are sweetest and most tender when harvested at 2–3 inches in diameter — larger roots become pithy and bitter. In zone 7–10 fall-planted turnips can overwinter in the ground and are sweetened by frost exposure. The greens of varieties like 'Seven Top' and 'Purple Top White Globe' are prized in Southern cooking and highly nutritious. Turnips also function as a quick-maturing catch crop, cover crop, and forage plant.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring; sow again in early fall for a second crop of sweet greens.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 in deep in fertile soil; turnips are among the fastest-germinating brassicas and begin producing harvestable greens within a month. Thin to 4–6 in if growing for both greens and roots, or leave closer together for greens-only production. Begin harvesting outer leaves when plants are 6–8 in tall, leaving the crown to continue growing. Fall-harvested greens are noticeably sweeter than spring greens due to the conversion of starches to sugars in cool temperatures.

common_name: Turnip Tops (Turnip Greens, Cima di Rapa)
plant_note: For the finest flavor, sow in late summer to early fall for a late-fall through winter harvest; turnip greens are among the best fall garden crops in zones 8–10, growing through mild winters and improving in sweetness and tenderness after repeated frost exposure. Spring sowing works in cooler climates but is secondary to fall production in the Gulf Coast.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seeds thinly and cover with 1/4 inch of soil, thinning to 4–8 inches for greens production; when grown specifically for greens rather than root turnips, dense spacing produces tender young leaves more quickly and the roots remain small and edible as a bonus harvest. Turnip greens are one of the most nutritious and productive winter vegetables for the Southern garden — far superior in flavor after frost than when cut in warm weather. The traditional Southern pot of turnip greens slow-cooked with a smoked hock concentrates their earthy, slightly bitter, mineral richness into a deeply savory dish. Whole young plants can be harvested, roots and all, or cut repeatedly above the crown for ongoing regrowth. Italian cima di rapa strains are grown specifically for the tender florets and top leaves and are harvested before the flower buds fully open.

subcategory: European heirloom root vegetable cool season
plant_note: Sow seeds in fall — they require cold stratification and germinate in early spring — in partial shade in moist, deep, well-drained, fertile, sandy loam in zone 5–9; Turnip-rooted Chervil (Bulbous Chervil) is a rare heirloom root vegetable of European origin bearing small, turnip-shaped tubers with grey-brown skin and creamy-white, nutty, chestnut-flavored flesh — once popular in 19th-century French and German kitchen gardens but nearly lost to cultivation, now enjoying renewed interest among heirloom vegetable enthusiasts and gourmet chefs.
directions: Sow Chaerophyllum bulbosum seeds fresh in fall directly where they are to grow — seeds lose viability quickly and are best sown immediately after harvest; thin seedlings to 4–6 inches apart and keep soil moist but not waterlogged throughout the cool growing season; harvest roots in early to midsummer as foliage yellows and dies back. Turnip-rooted Chervil is among the rarest and most intriguing of all heirloom root vegetables — an annual or biennial carrot-family plant with delicate, ferny foliage and small, grey-skinned tubers with exceptionally delicate, nutty, chesnut-sweet flavor. It requires cold stratification to germinate (hence fall sowing is essential) and tolerates partial shade well — performing in spots where carrots or parsnips would not thrive. The roots are at their best when small, around an inch in diameter; larger roots can become pithy. Their flavor has been compared to a cross between chestnut, sweet potato, and parsley root — distinctive and prized by those lucky enough to taste them. Auguste Escoffier featured turnip-rooted chervil in classic French cuisine; it fell from fashion in the 20th century as it does not store or ship well and demands specific growing conditions. Fresh seeds from specialty heirloom seed suppliers are essential as germination rates drop sharply after a few months. The feathery foliage is also edible and mildly anise-flavored, usable as a garnish like regular chervil.

common_name: Tuxedo Sweet Corn (Bicolor Supersweet Sh2 Hybrid Corn)
plant_note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows wide for wind pollination; Tuxedo is a supersweet (sh2) type that requires isolation of at least 250 feet from su, se, or other sh2 varieties with different genetics to prevent starchy cross-pollination. Sh2 varieties also require warmer soil temperatures for reliable germination (65°F minimum, ideally 70°F) and should not be planted as early as su or se types. In zone 9, plant March–April when soils have warmed adequately.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil (65°F minimum) in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen at knee height. Isolate from other corn varieties (including other sh2 types) by 250+ feet or stagger planting dates by 2+ weeks. Tuxedo is a bicolor (white and yellow kernel) supersweet (sh2) hybrid that has become one of the most popular bicolor fresh-market and roadside stand corns in the eastern United States — a Syngenta/Rogers Brothers variety that delivers the maximum sweetness possible from the sh2 gene type combined with a visually appealing bicolor kernel appearance that many consumers associate with premium sweet corn. The sh2 (shrunken-2) mutation creates corn with up to 4 times the sugar content of standard su types at harvest, and unlike se types, sh2 varieties retain their sweetness for 5–7 days after picking under refrigeration — a major commercial advantage that has made sh2 types dominant in the fresh sweet corn market. Tuxedo produces large (7.5–9 inch), well-filled ears with 16–18 rows of alternating white and yellow kernels; the kernels are very tender with thin skins and intensely sweet flavor when harvested at peak. The bicolor appearance in uniform, well-filled ears of Tuxedo is particularly attractive for roadside stand and farmers market sales where visual appeal drives purchasing decisions. One of the most commercially successful bicolor sh2 varieties of the past two decades.

plant_note: Start indoors and transplant for spring or fall; a self-blanching type.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant seedlings for a spring or fall crop, keeping plants evenly watered and never letting them check from stress. This self-blanching variety has well-wrapping leaves that curl over the developing curd, shielding the snowy-white heads from sun scald and rain discoloration. It reliably produces uniform, dense, medium-large heads and tolerates heat, so in mild climates it can even be grown nearly year-round.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production and again in early August for a fall crop. Tycoon is a heat-tolerant determinate hybrid bred specifically for the Southern United States with strong resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1–2, and nematodes.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a cage or stake; Tycoon is a determinate, heat-tolerant hybrid tomato that produces concentrated harvests of large, smooth, firm red globe tomatoes averaging 10–12 ounces. Its compact determinate habit keeps the plant manageable in the garden while still delivering excellent yields suited to canning, slicing, and fresh eating. Bred for Southern growing conditions, Tycoon sets fruit reliably when temperatures climb into the upper 80s and maintains production longer than many other large-fruited varieties. Strong disease resistance package including resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), and root-knot nematodes makes it especially valuable in zone 9 soils where these pathogens are widespread.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall for cool-season production; Tyee is particularly valued for fall and overwinter production where its disease resistance and cold tolerance are most advantageous. In zone 9, sow September–November for harvest November–February. For spring production, sow February–March as soon as soil can be worked. Germination occurs in very cool soils (35°F) but is slowest below 45°F; optimal germination is at 50–65°F.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; thin to 2–4 inch spacing as seedlings develop and use thinnings in salads. Tyee is a 1987 All-America Selections-winning spinach that has maintained its status as one of the most recommended disease-resistant spinach varieties for over 35 years — a semi-savoy (slightly crinkled leaf) hybrid that combines excellent productivity with broad disease resistance. The 'semi-savoy' designation means the leaves have moderate crinkle — more texture and surface area than flat leaf types but less crinkle than fully savoy varieties, striking a balance between the ornamental quality of savoy and the easy washing of flat types. Tyee's most important attributes are its comprehensive disease resistance: it carries resistance to five races of downy mildew (Peronospora farinosa), the primary fungal disease that terminates spinach crops early in humid and wet conditions. This resistance profile extends the productive season dramatically compared to susceptible varieties that collapse when mildew strikes. The dark green, upright, medium-large leaves are tender and mild-flavored with the classic, clean spinach taste. Tyee remains the benchmark spinach variety against which others are evaluated in university trials, consistently placing at or near the top for yield, disease resistance, and leaf quality.

common_name: UC 157 Asparagus (Classic California Commercial Hybrid Asparagus)
plant_note: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; UC 157 is a classic hybrid asparagus bred at the University of California, valued for concentrated, uniform spear emergence that suits both machine and hand harvesting.
directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. UC 157 is a long-standing, widely planted hybrid asparagus developed by the University of California, prized for producing spears in a more concentrated, uniform flush than many older varieties, along with good heat tolerance that suits warmer growing regions better than some Northeastern-bred cultivars. It has been a mainstay of commercial asparagus production for decades and performs well in home gardens too, given deep, well-drained soil and full sun. As with other asparagus, avoid harvesting the first year and harvest lightly the second year to let the crown establish a strong root system for many years of future spring harvests.

plant_note: Divide established crowns in early spring before growth begins, or plant container-grown plants in moist, rich, humus-heavy soil in part to full shade; udo is a deep-shade forest plant that tolerates very low light levels. It dies completely back to the crown in winter. For edible use, force blanched shoots by covering the emerging crown with a bucket or mounding soil to exclude light — producing tender, white, asparagus-like shoots.
directions: Plant in moist, rich, humus-heavy soil in part to full shade; udo is a large, bold Japanese perennial vegetable native to shaded mountain valleys and forests of Japan, Korea, and China — one of the few perennial vegetables that genuinely thrives in deep shade and also functions as a dramatic ornamental. The emerging spring shoots — harvested when 6–12 inches tall by covering the crown to force blanched growth — are prepared in Japanese cuisine as a crisp, pleasantly bitter vegetable resembling white asparagus in texture, eaten raw in salads, pickled, or lightly cooked. When not harvested for food, the plant develops into an enormous, deeply tropical-looking perennial 6–10 feet tall with compound leaves nearly 3 feet across and clusters of small cream flowers in summer, followed by small black berries. The dramatic architectural scale makes it a remarkable ornamental for shaded woodland gardens. An ancient Japanese vegetable with no close Western analog, combining edible usefulness with the visual impact of a large tropical foliage plant in deep shade.

plant_note: Plant small whole tubers or large tuber sections 3–4 inches deep in cool, moist soil after last frost; ulluco is highly photoperiod-sensitive and, like oca, will not form tubers until autumn day lengths shorten — it performs best where summers are cool (below 75°F) and the frost-free period extends into November.
directions: Plant tubers 3–4 inches deep in loose, moist, well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; ulluco is a creeping, succulent-stemmed Andean tuber crop in the family Basellaceae, domesticated in the Andes over 5,000 years ago and second only to potato in importance across Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, and Colombia where it is called 'papa lisa' (smooth potato). The tubers are waxy, colorful (yellow, orange, pink, red, purple), and retain their shape when cooked, making them excellent for stews such as the Bolivian dish 'soltero de ulluco'. Unlike potato, ulluco has never suffered a catastrophic blight and is rich in protein, calcium, and carotenoids. Harvest after first light frost kills back the vines; plants are almost entirely propagated vegetatively as fertile seed is rare.

plant_note: Sow densely in trays indoors year-round; harvest at the first true-leaf stage.
directions: Sow the seed densely across a shallow tray of moist growing mix and keep it evenly moist under bright light. This Asian blend of savory and spicy brassica-type greens is harvested very young, when the first true leaves appear, roughly one to three weeks after sowing. Snip the tender shoots at soil level with scissors and use the complex, umami-rich mix as a garnish for Asian dishes; sow in succession for a steady supply indoors year-round.

plant_note: Sow in trays indoors, or direct sow outdoors in cool weather as a leafy green.
directions: Sow seed densely in a tray for microgreens or thinly outdoors in cool soil to grow as a peppery leafy green. Also called creasy greens, upland cress is high in vitamins A and C and delivers a sharp, watercress-like bite without needing running water. Keep it consistently moist, since dryness makes it more pungent and prone to bolting; harvest microgreens at the true-leaf stage or pick mature outer leaves for sandwiches and salads.

plant_note: Direct sow in late summer or fall for winter harvest in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; upland cress is more tender and milder than Barbarea vulgaris and has been cultivated as a garden salad green in Britain for centuries as a watercress substitute for gardens without streams.
directions: Direct sow in late summer or fall for winter harvest in well-drained, average to fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; upland cress (early yellowrocket) is a European biennial grown as a cool-season salad green, long cultivated in British kitchen gardens as a dry-land substitute for watercress in gardens without access to streams. The dark green, round-lobed leaves are similar to watercress in appearance and have a pleasant, mild peppery flavor when young and harvested before flowering — less bitter and more refined than winter cress (B. vulgaris). Produces pickable leaves very quickly in cool weather, from fall through early spring. Allowed to bolt, the spring flower buds can be harvested like tender broccoli. An old and underappreciated cool-season salad green that thrives when other salad crops fail in cold weather. Well-suited to fall and winter salad gardening in zones 5–9 where it overwinters reliably.

plant_note: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start July–August and transplant September–October for a December–March harvest. Celery germination is slow and requires light — sow on the surface and keep evenly moist at 60–65°F. In zone 9 celery is a winter crop; the Gulf Coast's mild winters allow consistent production from November through March without protection. Consistent irrigation is critical — celery is among the most water-demanding vegetables.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into very fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Utah 52-70 is the standard commercial and home garden celery in North America — an improved Utah-type celery producing tall, upright stalks of thick, crisp, rounded (not hollow) pale-green to cream-colored ribs with a classic, full celery flavor. The '52-70' designation refers to the original development period. Utah-type celery has largely replaced older Pascal types in commercial production because of superior rib thickness, crunchiness, and reduced stringiness compared to older varieties. Celery is among the most demanding vegetables in terms of water and fertility requirements; it grows naturally in moist, fertile wetland soils and demands consistent irrigation and rich soil throughout its long growing period. Blanch by earthing up or wrapping paper around the stalks 2 weeks before harvest to lighten the color and reduce bitterness. In zone 9 celery is exclusively a cool-season vegetable, transplanted in fall and harvested through winter.

plant_note: Start indoors early; celery needs a long, mild, moist growing season.
directions: Start the tiny seed indoors 10 to 12 weeks before transplanting, pressing it into the surface since it needs light to germinate and is slow to sprout. Celery grows best in climates with long, mild-temperature seasons and demands consistently rich, moist soil to develop tender stalks. Harvest individual stalks when they reach about 6 inches, or wait for the full bunch to mature; keep the plants well watered throughout to avoid stringy, bitter stems.

common_name: Valencia Tomato (Bright Orange Sweet Low-Acid Open-Pollinated Heirloom)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Valencia is an open-pollinated heirloom — seeds can be saved from the best fruits for successive seasons to maintain a low-acid orange tomato supply.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Valencia is one of the finest and most widely grown orange-fruited heirloom tomatoes — an open-pollinated variety producing medium-large (6–8 oz), round to slightly oblate, smooth, vivid orange fruits with meaty, dense flesh in an orange-gold color and characteristically low acid content combined with fruity sweetness that creates a very clean, mild, sweet flavor quite different from the sharper acid quality of standard red tomatoes. The vivid orange exterior color is striking in the garden and at market — Valencia's clear, bright-orange skin lacks the russet or reddish tones of some orange varieties and produces a consistent, pure-orange appearance across the crop. The low-acid quality makes Valencia particularly appealing to people sensitive to tomato acidity, and the sweet, fruity flavor is excellent in fresh eating, mixed tomato salads (where the orange color provides contrast to red and yellow types), and in light cooking where the low-acid character is preserved. As an open-pollinated heirloom, Valencia produces reliable seed that comes true to type, allowing gardeners to maintain a permanent seed supply. Valencia is an indeterminate variety requiring staking and producing consistently through the season rather than in a single concentrated flush. In zone 9, Valencia performs best in spring (February–May) before summer heat reduces fruit quality.

plant_note: Plant slips in warm soil after last frost; Vardaman is an exceptionally compact sweet potato whose naturally short vines (24–30 inches) make it the best choice for small beds, containers, and home gardens with limited space.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Vardaman is a compact, short-vined sweet potato (24–30 inch vines versus 6–10 feet for standard varieties) developed at Mississippi State University specifically for the home garden, where its restrained spread and ornamental purple foliage make it an attractive edible landscape plant. The orange-flesh tubers are typically smaller than commercial varieties but have excellent rich, sweet flavor and moist texture. An outstanding choice for container growing, raised beds, and small garden spaces where standard sweet potatoes would overwhelm their neighbors. Keeps well in storage and is the most popular sweet potato for the home garden in the southeastern United States.

plant_note: For fall planting in zone 9, start transplants in late August–September and set out October–November; in the Gulf South, collards are primarily a fall through spring vegetable — the mild winters allow nearly year-round harvests. In zone 9 summer heat, plants often go to seed; replant fresh transplants each fall for the best quality greens.
directions: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 9 plant fall transplants October–November for harvest December through March; Vates is the classic Southern collard variety developed at the Virginia Truck Experiment Station in the 1950s and for decades was the standard garden collard of the South — compact, slow to bolt, very cold hardy (surviving temperatures well below 20°F with frost actually improving the flavor by converting starches to sugars), and producing thick, blue-green leaves of the authentic Southern collard flavor. The name 'Vates' (meaning 'prophet' in Latin) was chosen by the Virginia researchers. Harvest outer leaves regularly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving the growing tip to continue producing; plants that are allowed to keep their lower leaves become leggy and produce smaller, tougher leaves. The slow-bolt characteristic makes Vates substantially more useful in cool-season gardens than older varieties that rush to flower.

common_name: Vates Collards (Compact Slow-Bolt Virginia Station Collard)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Vates is a compact collard (18–24 inch plants) appropriate for small gardens where the 3–4 foot Georgia types would be too large. In zone 9, transplant August–September for fall and winter harvest. Vates shows excellent cold hardiness and slow bolting in spring, which extends the harvest into early spring when other types bolt prematurely.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Vates is an open-pollinated collard developed at the Virginia Agricultural and Experiment Station (the acronym 'VATES' gives the variety its name) specifically for compact size, dark color, and improved cold tolerance compared to the taller, more open Georgia types. Vates produces distinctly compact plants (18–24 inches tall vs. the 36–48 inches of Georgia Southern), with upright, heavy, dark blue-green leaves that are more tightly held on the stem than the open habit of older types. The compact habit makes Vates practical for smaller garden spaces and easier to manage in the fall garden without the sprawling character of the traditional large types. The dark blue-green color is visually attractive and indicates high chlorophyll content. Vates shows better cold hardiness than Georgia types — surviving temperatures to 15–18°F rather than the 20–23°F limit of less cold-hardy types — and is notably slow to bolt in spring. This slow-bolting character extends the productive leaf harvest into late spring, 2–4 weeks beyond when other varieties have bolted and become bitter. Vates is consistently recommended by eastern U.S. extension services as one of the most reliable all-purpose collard varieties.

plant_note: Surface sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 direct sow from March through August for a continuous supply of summer greens. Vegetable amaranth grows explosively in heat and humidity and is ready for first harvest in as little as 3 weeks after germination.
directions: Scatter seeds on the surface of fertile, moist soil in full sun; thin or transplant to final spacing, using thinnings as baby greens. Vegetable amaranth thrives in conditions that defeat spinach, lettuce, and other cool-season greens, making it the premier summer leafy vegetable for hot, humid climates. Harvest entire young plants thinly, or cut growing tips regularly from larger plants to stimulate bushy regrowth; the tricolor varieties also produce striking ornamental foliage in red, yellow, and green. Young leaves and tips are cooked as a spinach substitute in Asian, Caribbean, and West African cuisines — they cook down dramatically and benefit from high heat in a wok. Remove plants before seed heads shatter if naturalizing is not desired.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in full sun in well-drained to poorly drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Sesbania grandiflora grows with remarkable speed (4–6 feet per month in warm conditions) and begins flowering within 3–6 months of planting — it is treated as a warm-season annual in zones 8–9 or a short-lived perennial in zone 10–11.
directions: Sow seeds (scarify or nick seed coat to improve germination) directly in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun after last frost; plants grow very rapidly and begin producing edible flowers within 3–6 months. Sesbania grandiflora (vegetable hummingbird or agati) is a fast-growing tropical tree or large shrub grown throughout South and Southeast Asia as one of the most productive edible-flowering plants — producing spectacular, orchid-like flowers 2–4 inches long in white (the typical form) or red, that are harvested and cooked as a vegetable throughout Southeast Asian and Indian cuisines. The flowers are slightly bitter, nutritious (high in calcium, iron, and vitamin C), and used stir-fried, in curries, in salads, and in soups; they are a common street food ingredient in Thailand, India, and the Philippines. All parts of the plant are edible: young leaves are used like spinach, young seed pods like string beans, and the flowers are the most prized part. Sesbania fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodules, improving soil fertility. The tree is native to tropical Asia and grows with such speed that it can produce harvestable crops within its first growing season as an annual in temperate climates.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; give vines room to run.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, giving the vines plenty of room to spread. This heirloom is unique among winter squashes: when cooked, the flesh separates into spaghetti-like strands that stay tender yet al dente. Let fruits fully ripen to a hard, golden rind and cure them before storing; the mild, low-calorie flesh is delicious with a bit of butter or a favorite sauce.

common_name: Vermont Cranberry Bean (New England Heirloom Shell Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Vermont Cranberry is an heirloom bush shell bean from New England with a centuries-long tradition of cultivation in Vermont and New Hampshire — the round, red-and-cream speckled beans were the traditional baked bean of New England cooking and remain one of the finest-flavored shell beans for baking, soups, and traditional New England bean dishes.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; can be harvested as a shell bean at 55–65 days (when pods are plump and mottled red-cream) or allowed to dry fully for 75–90 days for a dry-bean crop; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous shell bean harvest. Vermont Cranberry is a heirloom bush bean with deep New England roots — the speckled red-and-cream oval seeds are the traditional 'cranberry bean' of Vermont and New Hampshire, where they have been grown for baked beans since at least the 1700s. The name 'cranberry bean' (also applied to other speckled beans throughout New England) refers to the red cranberry-like speckled coloration of the pods and seeds at the shell bean stage, not to any relationship with cranberries. The shell beans have a rich, creamy, full flavor that is considered by many cooks superior to navy beans or Great Northern beans for traditional New England baked beans — the beans hold their shape well under long, slow baking while developing a creamy, dense interior texture that absorbs the sweet-savory baked bean flavors. At the dry bean stage the seeds turn darker and lose their red mottling; still excellent for winter cooking. Adapted to short New England growing seasons; performs equally well in Gulf Coast fall gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Vert de Massy is the classic French cornichon pickling cucumber used to produce the tiny, intensely flavored gherkins traditional in French charcuterie and cuisine, harvested at just 1–2 inches long for the smallest and finest quality, or at 2–3 inches for a slightly larger cornichon.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants productive, picking at 1–3 inches long. Vert de Massy (Green of Massy) is the traditional French cornichon gherkin, a small, bumpy-skinned pickling cucumber prized in France for the production of cornichons — the tiny, intensely flavored pickles that accompany pâté, charcuterie, and raclette throughout French cuisine. The fruits are small, cylindrical to slightly tapered, dark green with small warts and spines, and have firm, crisp flesh with excellent flavor even when very small (1–2 inches). Harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants productive — if fruits are allowed to mature they divert energy from new production. Pickled in white wine vinegar with tarragon, chervil, and pearl onions in the traditional French method; also excellent as fresh gherkins. The vines are compact and productive.

plant_note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring; in zone 7–8 plant January–February while dormant. Rhubarb requires 500+ hours below 40°F to break dormancy and produce vigorously — it performs best in zones 3–7 where cold winters are reliable. In zone 8 rhubarb is possible with adequate winter cooling but may decline after a few years. In zone 9 rhubarb is very challenging as insufficient chilling produces poor growth; gardeners in zone 9 should consider growing rhubarb in containers that can be refrigerated in winter. Do not harvest stalks in the first year — allow the plant to establish.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with high organic matter content; Victoria is the oldest and most widely grown named rhubarb variety, introduced in the 1830s in Britain and remaining the standard variety against which others are compared — it has an exceptionally long cultivation record of nearly 200 years as a garden and commercial vegetable. The thick, large, greenish-pink to light red stalks are produced in large quantities and have the classic, sharp, tart-sour rhubarb flavor used in pies, crumbles, jams, and sauces — the pairing of rhubarb's tartness with strawberry sweetness in strawberry-rhubarb pie is one of the iconic spring desserts of North American and British cooking. Victoria produces primarily green to light pink stalks rather than the deep red of ornamental varieties like Crimson Red; the color is purely cosmetic with no effect on flavor. As a cool-climate perennial, Victoria thrives best where winters are cold and long (zones 3–6) but performs adequately through zone 8 with attention to soil improvement and consistent watering.

plant_note: Start indoors, then transplant into a permanent bed after frost.
directions: Start Victoria rhubarb seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before setting plants into a permanent, fertile bed spaced 3 to 4 feet apart. This cold-hardy heirloom perennial develops deep crimson-tinged stalks with a rich sweet-tart flavor and returns for many years. Do not harvest the first year and take only a few stalks the second, letting the crown establish. Never eat the leaves, which are toxic, and remove flower stalks to keep energy in the roots.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; an Appalachian family heirloom from West Virginia producing extraordinarily large and meaty orange beefsteak fruits — a lesser-known gem introduced through Seed Savers Exchange that rivals better-known orange types in flavor and productivity.
directions: Sow seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed and stake or cage firmly from the start. Vinson Watts is a West Virginia Appalachian family heirloom that arrived at Seed Savers Exchange through Vinson Watts, who grew it for many years before contributing it to the seed exchange; it produces very large, 1–2 pound orange beefsteak fruits with deep, meaty, mostly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, low-acid flavor that rivals the better-known Kellogg's Breakfast and Dr. Wyche's Orange. The vigorous indeterminate vines are productive and the fruits have a pleasing globe shape and smooth skin that resists cracking better than some large heirlooms. An excellent choice for anyone building a collection of orange heirloom beefsteak tomatoes.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; violet mustard is a cool-season biennial that germinates in fall, overwinters, and produces edible leaves through winter and beautiful violet flowers in early spring before setting seed.
directions: Direct sow in fall in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; violet mustard is a Chinese brassica grown both as a winter vegetable and as a spring ornamental — the young leaves through winter have a mild, pleasant flavor used fresh in salads or cooked, and the plant concludes its season with a spectacular display of pale to bright violet flowers in spring that are edible as garnish and highly attractive to early pollinators. The winter foliage often develops attractive purple-violet tints in cold weather. In zone 9, it self-sows to naturalize, returning each fall for a winter vegetable and spring flower display with no replanting. An excellent edible-ornamental for the winter garden.

plant_note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting; Violetta requires vernalization, a period of cool temperatures around 50 degrees F for about 10 days, once seedlings have several true leaves, to trigger flower bud formation in the first year.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after vernalization. Violetta is a classic Italian heirloom artichoke producing smaller, tender, purple-tinged buds traditionally harvested young and eaten whole, including the tender inner leaves and heart, either braised, fried, or grilled in traditional Italian preparations like carciofi alla romana. The striking violet-purple coloring on the bud scales, especially pronounced in cooler weather, makes it as ornamental as it is productive. Like other seed-grown artichokes it can flower and produce a harvest the first year if properly vernalized as a young seedling, and in mild-winter zones it may persist as a short-lived perennial for a second season of harvest.

common_name: Violetta di Firenze Eggplant (Florentine Purple-White Striped Italian Heirloom)
plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms to at least 70°F and nights are reliably above 55°F; Violetta di Firenze is an Italian heirloom eggplant from the Florence area of Tuscany, producing large, round to slightly oval, deeply ribbed fruits with dramatic lavender-purple and white vertical striping — one of the most visually stunning and historically important eggplant varieties in Italian kitchen garden tradition.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; Violetta di Firenze produces fewer, larger fruits than Asian types — typically 2–4 fruits per plant at a time — harvest when fruits reach 4–6 inches across and the skin is still glossy; do not allow to over-ripen (seeds enlarge and flesh becomes bitter). Violetta di Firenze (Florentine Violet) is a traditional Italian heirloom eggplant from the Florence area of Tuscany, where it has been grown for generations as the quintessential garden eggplant of the region — so important locally that it appears in Florentine recipe traditions and Renaissance-era botanical descriptions of the kitchen garden. The variety is immediately recognized by its dramatic appearance: very large (6–10 inches across), round to pear-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with beautiful vertical striping in shades of lavender-violet and white; no other commonly grown eggplant has the same combination of large round shape, deep ribbing, and purple-white striping. The flesh is creamy-white with a mild, sweet, slightly nutty flavor with less bitterness than many eggplant varieties — the large cavity and abundant flesh make it particularly suited for stuffing (ripieno), slicing and grilling, or layering in the classic Italian Parmigiana di Melanzane. The plant is robust and tall (30–48 inches) and requires staking; it is adapted to long, warm Mediterranean summers and performs well in Gulf Coast zone 8b–10 conditions with the hot summers they provide.

plant_note: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Violette di Firenze is an Italian market type that performs well in zone 9 heat. A second planting in July extends production into fall. The plants are larger and more vigorous than most eggplants; provide generous spacing and heavy staking to support the large fruits.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Violette di Firenze (Violet of Florence) is a striking Italian heirloom eggplant from the Tuscany region, producing large, squat, round to pear-shaped fruits with distinctive lavender-to-violet skin streaked with white — a bicolor pattern that is dramatically different from the solid-purple standard eggplant. The large fruits (6–8 inches across, up to 2 pounds) have flesh that is notably sweeter, milder, and less bitter than standard globe eggplant types, with fewer seeds and a creamier texture when cooked. The Italian tradition of grilling, broiling, or pan-frying Violette di Firenze without salting (a technique used to reduce bitterness in standard eggplant) reflects the naturally mild, sweet character of this variety. The striking bicolor appearance makes it a showstopper in the garden and at market. Cut fruits at their most beautiful stage — when lavender-violet with white streaks and still firm — rather than allowing them to develop the dull, fully-mature purple that indicates over-ripeness.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant; in zone 9 plant February–March. Violetto produces smaller, more numerous buds than Green Globe — harvest the central bud first when tightly closed, which stimulates production of side-shoot buds for a longer season of smaller edible heads. In Italian and French cuisine, these smaller side buds (carciofini) are the prized preparation stage for pickling in olive oil, braising whole, and raw artichoke salads where tender, non-fibrous bracts are required.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Violetto is an Italian artichoke type producing elongated, conical to teardrop-shaped heads with striking purple-green bracts that deepen to rich violet as the buds develop — the ornamental purple coloration makes Violetto one of the most attractive artichokes for kitchen garden displays and edible landscape design. The heads are smaller than American Green Globe types (typically 2–3 inches across) but considerably more tender in the bract meat and heart, with a milder, slightly more nutty flavor that is less assertive than the large green varieties. Smaller Violetto heads can be eaten raw when very young and tender — an important distinction from large artichokes that require cooking. In Italian cooking, Violetto di Romagna and similar purple artichoke types are specifically selected for preparations requiring tenderness: carciofi alla giudea (deep-fried), carciofi sott'olio (preserved in olive oil), and raw shaved artichoke salads. The purple color is heat-sensitive and fades during cooking, but the ornamental value in the growing plant is substantial.

plant_note: Direct sow on the soil surface in fall; seeds will overwinter and germinate in early spring as soon as temperatures begin to rise. For an edible leaf crop, thin to 4-6 inches and harvest young basal leaves before the flower stalk rises.
directions: Virginia Peppergrass is a native annual or biennial of open, disturbed ground, roadsides, and garden edges throughout eastern North America, producing a basal rosette of toothed, peppery-flavored leaves followed by upright racemes of tiny white flowers and distinctive round, notched, flattened seed pods that rattle pleasingly in the breeze. The young basal leaves are edible raw in salads, contributing a sharp, peppery, radish-like heat, and the ripe seed pods can be ground or crushed as a mild pepper substitute in cooking. Sow directly in fall in thin, well-drained, even nutrient-poor soil in full sun; it germinates readily in disturbed or compacted ground where other plants struggle. Once established it self-sows freely, naturalizing open areas with minimal effort.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a large bicolor beefsteak that needs staking; the striking yellow and red coloring of the flesh and exterior make it a showstopper at market and on the table.
directions: Sow seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to rich, deeply prepared soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem and staking firmly to support the large fruits. Virginia Sweet is a stunning American heirloom bicolor beefsteak tomato with large, 1–2 pound fruits that are golden-yellow with dramatic red streaking on the skin and brilliant pink-red and golden-yellow marbled flesh that is as beautiful to look at as it is flavorful — sweet, rich, and low-acid. It is related to other bicolor heirlooms like Big Rainbow and striped varieties that are prized both for taste and visual appeal; the swirling interior color pattern is most pronounced in cool weather. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the yellow shoulder transitions fully from green.

plant_note: Direct sow in early spring or again in late summer for fall.
directions: Sow Viroflay seeds half an inch deep in cool soil, thinning to 4 to 6 inches apart for full-size plants. This vigorous French heirloom produces large, tender leaves up to 10 inches long with a mild, sweet taste. Harvest baby leaves early or let plants mature for hearty cooking greens, and keep the soil evenly moist. Grow it in the cool weather of spring, fall, or winter, since heat and long days trigger bolting.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–March for spring. Vitamin Green is one of the fastest-maturing Asian brassicas — baby leaves are harvestable in 20–25 days for baby green mixes. It is more heat-tolerant than most Asian brassicas and can extend into early summer in zone 9 before bolting. Successive sowings every 2 weeks provide a continuous harvest of tender young greens.
directions: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Vitamin Green is a non-heading Asian brassica green selected for extremely rapid growth, mild flavor, and excellent nutritional value — the name reflects its high vitamin content (particularly vitamins A, C, and K) relative to other leafy greens. The smooth, round to slightly oval, bright medium-green leaves are strikingly mild in flavor — among the mildest of all Asian brassica types, with a clean, grassy-vegetable taste more like spinach or mild bok choy than the mustardy pungency of standard Asian mustard greens. This mildness makes Vitamin Green accessible to people who find other Asian greens too strongly flavored. In the kitchen it is interchangeable with bok choy or baby spinach in virtually any preparation — stir-fries, soups, braising, steaming, and raw use in salads and baby green mixes. The combination of very rapid growth (30–45 days to full size, 20–25 days to baby green stage), mild flavor, and excellent nutritional content makes it one of the most practical cool-season greens for zone 9.

common_name: Viva Italia Tomato (Hybrid Roma Paste Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Viva Italia is a determinate paste tomato that ripens a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for sauce-making; in zone 9 aim for spring harvest in May–June before summer heat.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Viva Italia is an improved hybrid roma-type paste tomato that addresses the main weakness of heirloom Roma — its susceptibility to disease. An AAS (All-America Selections) winner, Viva Italia combines the thick-walled, low-moisture flesh and rich, concentrated paste-tomato flavor of traditional Roma with VFFNTA disease resistance (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and Alternaria), making it far more reliable in humid climates and typical garden soils than open-pollinated Roma varieties. The determinate, compact (3–3.5 foot) plants produce large, concentrated sets of uniform, thick-skinned, 2–4 oz, elongated-oval, bright red fruits with very low moisture content and dense, meaty flesh — exactly what's needed for sauce, paste, sun-dried tomatoes, and canning. Because of the dense flesh and concentrated flavor, Viva Italia produces much higher yields of usable sauce per pound of fruit than wet, beefsteak-type tomatoes. An outstanding choice for serious sauce-makers who want disease resistance and reliability.

plant_note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; IMPORTANT: Install a high-density polyethylene rhizome barrier (30 mil or thicker) at least 24–36 inches deep around all running bamboos before planting to prevent invasive spreading.
directions: Plant in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, contained within a rhizome barrier; vivax bamboo is one of the tallest, fastest-growing temperate bamboos, with culms reaching 25–45 feet and diameters of 2–3.5 inches — making it among the most productive timber bamboos available in zones 5–10. The spring shoots are edible and moderately sweet; the culms are strong and used for construction, fencing, and crafts. Its extreme cold hardiness (to about –10°F / USDA zone 5) makes it one of the few large-statured bamboos reliable in cold climates. CAUTION: Like all Phyllostachys species, vivax is a spreading 'running' bamboo with invasive potential — rhizome barriers are mandatory in all garden settings. The cultivar 'Aureocaulis' has yellow culms with green stripes.

plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather; bolt resistant for later sowing.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool weather, keeping the soil moist and cool for good germination, and make succession sowings for continuous salads. This emerald-green romaine forms tight heads that reach a striking 12 to 16 inches tall and 4 to 6 inches across, giving large, sturdy leaves ideal for salads and lettuce wraps. Its bolt resistance and vigorous growth let it hold longer into warm weather than many romaines.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. The deep purple-blue exterior color of Vorlon develops most intensely with sun exposure on the skin — fruits shaded by foliage will be less colorful. In zone 9 fall planting in August for October–November harvest often produces the best fruit quality. Support with cages or stakes as the large, indeterminate vines require substantial support.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy cage or stake support; Vorlon is a large beefsteak tomato bred by Tom Wagner, the Washington State plant breeder also responsible for Green Zebra, known for developing novel tomato colors and flavors. Vorlon produces large (often 12–20 ounce) fruits with a distinctive deep purple-to-near-black exterior that develops from sun exposure on the skin — the dark color comes from anthocyanin pigments (the same blue-purple compounds in blueberries and purple cabbage) that accumulate in the skin when exposed to sunlight. When sliced, Vorlon reveals a complex interior with dark-streaked red flesh and a rich, full-bodied, complex tomato flavor with earthy, wine-like undertones that distinguish dark tomato varieties from standard red types. The anthocyanin content in dark tomatoes like Vorlon represents significantly higher antioxidant levels than red-only tomatoes — a characteristic that has made dark-skinned tomatoes of interest in nutritional research. The dramatic appearance of the purple-black exterior with rich red interior when sliced makes Vorlon outstanding in salads and fresh presentations.

common_name: Walking Stick Collard (Tall Perennial Heirloom Collard from the Carolina and Gulf South Tradition)
plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, start seeds in August for September transplanting ahead of fall. Walking Stick Collard is a truly perennial (or at minimum biennial) collard that develops an upright, thick stem over multiple years of growth — eventually reaching 4–8 feet in height with a distinctive woody stem that in the South was historically harvested for use as a walking stick, giving the variety its name. Unlike annual collard varieties grown as single-season crops, Walking Stick Collard can remain productive for 2–5 years in zone 9's mild winters, producing new growth from the upper portion of the plant as it elongates. Individual leaves are harvested from the lower portion of the stem as new growth continues from the top. In zone 9, the plants perform well through winter (tolerating multiple frosts and brief freezes) and may slow in summer heat but rarely die entirely, giving them a distinctly perennial character that sets them apart from annual collard varieties. Space widely (24–36 inches) to allow each plant to develop its multi-year structure.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant to permanent location and allow to develop over multiple seasons. Harvest outer lower leaves as needed year-round. Walking Stick Collard is one of the most historically distinctive vegetables of the American South — a tall, perennial collard type that was maintained for generations in family gardens across the Carolinas, Georgia, and the Gulf South as a semi-permanent garden plant rather than an annual crop. The 'walking stick' in the name refers to the thick, woody stems that develop as the plant grows upward over multiple years: historical accounts describe Southern farmers and homesteaders harvesting old Walking Stick Collard stems, drying them, and using them as walking sticks, canes, and tool handles — a practical byproduct of a plant grown primarily for its edible leaves. The leaves are classic collard — large, blue-green, thick, and of the rich, mild-bitter flavor that defines Southern greens cuisine — harvested continuously from the lower stem as the plant elongates upward. A well-established Walking Stick Collard plant can produce leaves continuously for 3–5 years in zone 9's mild climate, making it a true perennial food plant for gardens where winter rarely kills brassicas completely. The variety is maintained by seed savers and small heirloom seed companies as a Southern heritage vegetable; it is not available in commercial mass-market seed catalogs but has been preserved through the living tradition of Southern kitchen gardens and organizations like Seed Savers Exchange and Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Walking Stick Collard's extraordinary height (sometimes reaching 6–8 feet) and its multi-year productive life make it one of the most distinctive and visually arresting vegetables possible in zone 9 gardens, forming a structural element with year-round productivity that no annual collard variety can match.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep soil in full sun; walking stick kale is biennial, producing a thick, very tall central stem in its second year that can reach 6–10 feet — the dried stems were traditionally harvested in the Channel Islands and Cornwall for use as walking sticks and umbrella handles.
directions: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost, transplant after last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; walking stick kale (Jersey kale) is a traditional biennial brassica of the Channel Islands and Cornwall, where it was grown for the extraordinary height its main stem achieves in the second year — up to 6–10 feet tall — with stems so strong and straight that they were traditionally dried, lacquered, and sold as walking sticks, canes, and umbrella handles, a traditional cottage industry on the Isle of Jersey. The large, dark green, curled leaves produced at the top of the tall stem are edible (though tough) throughout the growing season, and the plant is also fed to livestock. Primarily a curiosity and heritage vegetable today, prized by collectors of unusual brassicas. Requires staking as it grows taller. Harvest leaves from the base upward as needed, leaving the growing tip intact for continued height.

plant_note: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; wall rocket tolerates light freezes without damage and is best as a spring or autumn crop. It self-seeds so freely that once established in a garden it rarely needs replanting.
directions: Broadcast seeds lightly over prepared soil and press in gently without covering, as the tiny seeds need light to germinate well; thin to 4-6 inches apart once seedlings are established and harvest the outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production. Wall rocket is a wilder, more pungent relative of common arugula, with deeply lobed, almost dandelion-like leaves that carry a sharper, more sulfurous edge and pair especially well with cured meats, strong cheeses, and dressed lentils. It thrives in poor, dry, even gravelly soils where most salad greens would fail, making it useful for difficult spots in the garden. Allow a few plants to flower and set seed each season and they will self-sow prolifically, often producing volunteers in cracks in paving, at wall bases, and in disturbed soil across the garden.

plant_note: Start indoors or overwinter in mild areas; a long-day type that matures early.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant out once the soil is workable, or sow in fall to overwinter in mild-winter regions. This famous long-day onion traveled from Italy to Walla Walla, Washington, and produces enormous, juicy, sweet bulbs that are one of the best for eating fresh. It matures early enough to grow as an intermediate-day type; these sweet onions do not store long, so enjoy them soon after harvest.

plant_note: Start indoors in late winter and transplant in early spring.
directions: Start Walla Walla seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before your last frost and transplant seedlings 4 to 6 inches apart. This long-day heirloom produces exceptionally sweet, crisp, juicy yellow bulbs and performs best in northern gardens. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and keep the bed weeded while the large bulbs form. These onions are sweet but do not store long, so use them fresh soon after the tops fall and dry.

plant_note: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Walter is an outstanding spring and fall tomato with excellent disease resistance for humid Gulf Coast conditions. Determinate habit means a concentrated, predictable harvest good for canning large batches.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set determinate plants 2–3 feet apart in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Walter tomato was released by the University of Florida in 1963, the same year as Tropic, and quickly became a commercial and home garden staple in the Southeast for its reliable production, disease resistance, and compact determinate growth habit. It produces medium-large (6–8 oz), red, round fruits with smooth skin, firm flesh, and good canning and fresh-eating quality, with resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. Walter's determinate habit (which concentrates flowering and ripening into a defined period rather than producing continuously like indeterminate types) makes it efficient for gardeners who want a single large harvest for preserving and canning. Once the standard commercial processing tomato in Florida, it remains an important heirloom for Gulf Coast gardeners who need a reliably productive, disease-resistant, compact-season tomato.

plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or sow in midsummer for a fall crop; Waltham 29 is a classic American open-pollinated broccoli developed by the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 — long the standard garden broccoli before modern hybrids and still prized for heat tolerance, blue-green color, and reliable production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after hardening off when temperatures are consistently below 80°F during the day. Waltham 29 broccoli was developed by the Waltham Field Station of the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 as an improvement over earlier open-pollinated varieties; for decades before hybrid broccoli varieties became dominant in the 1970s and 80s, Waltham 29 was the standard home garden and market broccoli. It produces a large, domed, blue-green to grey-green central head of excellent flavor and tight bead formation, followed by adequate sideshot production; it is notably more tolerant of fall frost than many varieties and holds well in the field without yellowing. Still widely grown for its reliable open-pollinated nature (seed-saveable), cold tolerance, and classic blue-green broccoli flavor. Excellent for fall production in zones 5–11.

plant_note: Start for a fall crop, or in early spring for a spring harvest.
directions: Start Waltham 29 seeds indoors 5 to 6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants 18 to 24 inches apart in rich soil. This cold-tolerant heirloom is bred for fall harvests, producing large blue-green central heads followed by side shoots. Keep the plants well watered and feed with nitrogen to encourage big, tight heads. Cut the central head while the buds are still firm and closed, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks.

plant_note: Start indoors for spring, or sow in summer for a fall crop; adapted to fall.
directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. This heirloom is specially adapted to fall growing and produces 4 to 6 inch blue-green central heads followed by a prolific flush of side shoots. Cut the central head while the buds are still tight, then keep harvesting the smaller side shoots for weeks; the plants tolerate frost well.

common_name: Waltham Butternut Squash (Classic Long-Storing Winter Squash Heirloom)
plant_note: Direct sow in late summer (July in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; Waltham Butternut is a Cucurbita moschata variety with better heat and humidity tolerance than pepo-type winter squash — an important practical advantage for Gulf South production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Waltham Butternut is the standard commercial and home garden butternut squash — developed by Robert Young at the Waltham Experiment Station in Massachusetts and recognized with an All-America Selections award for its exceptional production, uniformity, and storage quality. The classic cylindrical fruits with tan skin, small seed cavity, and large neck of deep-orange flesh represent the butternut ideal: consistent shape, excellent flavor, and long storage life (3–6 months at cool room temperature). The Cucurbita moschata species provides better heat and humidity tolerance than C. pepo winter squash types — allowing Waltham Butternut to succeed in Gulf South conditions where pepo types (acorn, Delicata) often struggle with disease and heat in late-season production. In zone 9, the most reliable production method is a late-summer planting (July–August direct sow) for a fall harvest (October–November) — the fall planting avoids peak summer heat during vulnerable early growth and produces during the cooler fall weather that improves storage quality. Cure harvested fruits for 10 days at 80–85°F to harden the skin and develop the characteristic butterscotch sweetness that distinguishes fully cured butternut from freshly harvested green fruit. Waltham Butternut vines spread extensively (6–10 feet) and require substantial garden space.

plant_note: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; give vines plenty of space to run.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the long vines room to spread. This classic butternut yields four to five tan, richly sweet fruits per plant, and its solid stems help resist squash vine borers. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind and cure it in a warm, dry spot; properly cured butternut stores for months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–6 weeks before last frost in spring or in fall 8–10 weeks before first frost; Wando is the most heat-tolerant commonly available shelling pea, developed by USDA for Southern gardens — it sets pods in warmer conditions that cause bloom drop in all other pea varieties, making it the recommended choice for Gulf Coast and Southern spring pea planting.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep 2–6 weeks before last frost; Wando tolerates both cool and moderately warm conditions and is particularly valuable for later-season spring planting in Southern zones. Wando pea was developed by USDA and named for the Wando River in the Charleston, South Carolina area, reflecting its adaptation to warm Southern conditions. Unlike most shelling peas that drop flowers and fail to set pods when temperatures rise above 75°F, Wando continues producing pods at temperatures 5–10°F warmer than other varieties, extending the harvest window in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 24–30 inch plants produce smooth-seeded peas (less sweet than wrinkled but better adapted to warm-soil planting) in pods with 6–8 peas; the flavor is good. Exceptionally valuable for fall pea production in zones 7–10 when planted in late August–September.

plant_note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked; more heat tolerant than most peas.
directions: Direct sow seed as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, since peas germinate and grow best in cool soil. Introduced in 1943 as a cross between Laxton's Progress and Perfection, this heirloom is both cold tolerant for early sowing and more heat tolerant than most peas, extending the season on both ends. The sturdy 24 to 30 inch plants carry seven to nine medium peas per pod; provide light support and pick regularly to keep them producing.

common_name: Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato (Iowa Heirloom Peach-Yellow Sweet Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Wapsipinicon Peach is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato producing 1–1.5-inch round fruits with a distinctive pale peach-yellow color and a slightly fuzzy-looking surface texture that inspired the 'peach' descriptor. Named for the Wapsipinicon River in northeastern Iowa where it originated, this variety has been maintained by seed-savers as an example of mid-American heirloom tomato diversity. In zone 9, transplant March–April and stake or cage to 6 feet; indeterminate growth continues until frost. The pale coloration indicates low lycopene (the pigment responsible for red color) and high carotenoid content of a different type, contributing to the notably sweet, low-acid flavor profile that has made this variety a favorite among cherry tomato enthusiasts seeking flavor over color.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield gently to pressure and separate easily from the calyx. Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato is an Iowa heritage cherry tomato distinguished by its pale peach-yellow coloration and the exceptionally sweet, low-acid flavor that develops as fruits ripen fully. The name refers to both the peach-like appearance of the ripe fruit (the pale skin with a subtle blushed tinge on the sunny side closely resembles a small yellow peach) and the Wapsipinicon River region of northeastern Iowa where the variety was grown and saved by farm families through the twentieth century. The variety reached national seed-saver networks through the Seed Savers Exchange network and has been grown in trial gardens across the country where it consistently earns high marks for flavor complexity — a balance of sweetness with sufficient acid to provide depth, rather than the flat sweetness of some low-acid cherry types. As an indeterminate variety, Wapsipinicon Peach continues to grow and produce throughout a long warm season, which is particularly advantageous in zone 9 where the long frost-free period extends production well into fall. Fruits cluster in modest-sized trusses and are best harvested when fully colored and just soft; they have a thinner skin than many modern cherry types, which is prized for fresh eating but means they are more susceptible to cracking after rain or irrigation following dry periods. Cage or stake firmly and prune suckers selectively to manage plant size and improve air circulation in humid conditions.

plant_note: Direct sow in spring; cold hardy and can overwinter in many areas.
directions: Direct sow seed in spring for summer harvests, thinning to about an inch apart, or leave clumps to overwinter. This 2016 All-America Selections winner is a cold-hardy bunching onion with crisp texture and a strong, pungent flavor, and it resists pink root rot. Harvest by pulling whole clusters of upright green stalks, or cut individual stems and let the plants regrow for repeated cut-and-come-again picking.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, deeply amended soil; needs a long season of 100–115 days; this is the classic 'True Hubbard' type with heavily warted, dark blue-green skin and exceptional 6-month storage life.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, in hills enriched with compost, spacing 5–7 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill and provide consistent moisture through the long growing season. True Hubbard is the heavily warted, dark blue-green Hubbard squash that was a staple of 19th-century New England kitchens; fruits weigh 10–20 pounds and have extremely hard, deeply ribbed and warted blue-green skin and dense, dry, bright orange flesh with outstanding sweet, nutty flavor. The exceptional storage quality — fruits in good condition can last 6 months or more at cool temperatures — made it the premier cellar squash before canning became widespread. Harvest only after the vine has fully died back and the rind cannot be dented with a thumbnail; cure for 2 weeks in a warm, airy spot before moving to cold storage.
