directions: Start seed indoors in winter and transplant to the garden while still cool, since this is a short-day onion that bulbs best in southern regions. For really sweet, mild bulbs, grow it in soil that is low in sulfur; this pink-root-resistant type is among the few approved to be sold as a Vidalia onion. Keep plants weed-free and evenly watered, and cure the harvested bulbs before use, as sweet onions do not store long.

plant_note: Start indoors early; germination is slow and needs warmth.
directions: Start Yellow Habanero seeds indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil around 85F since this species germinates slowly. Transplant the plants 18 to 24 inches apart into a warm, sunny bed. The lantern-shaped fruits ripen golden-yellow with intense heat around 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville units and a sweet, tropical, fruity flavor. Handle the ripe pods with gloves, and harvest steadily to keep the productive plants setting fruit through the warm season.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before outdoor transplant date in late winter, or plant onion sets (small bulbs) outdoors as soon as soil is workable in spring; choose long-day varieties for zone 3–6 and short-day varieties for zone 7–10 for best bulb development.
directions: Start seeds or transplant pencil-thick seedlings in full sun in well-drained, fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil early in spring; yellow onions are the most versatile and widely grown culinary onion, with their characteristic balance of sulfurous pungency and underlying sweetness that mellows to a rich sweetness when cooked, making them essential in virtually every cuisine worldwide. Long-day varieties (required for zone 3–6 where summer days exceed 14 hours) include 'Copra' and 'Patterson'; short-day varieties (zone 7–10) include 'Texas 1015', 'Candy', and 'Georgia Sweet'. Harvest when most tops have fallen over naturally; cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for 2–4 weeks. Well-cured yellow onions store for 3–6 months.

plant_note: Start indoors 6 to 4 weeks before the last frost and transplant after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: This indeterminate heirloom produces heavy clusters of small, bright yellow pear-shaped fruits with a mild, tangy flavor. Provide sturdy caging or staking, since vines sprawl vigorously all season. Pinch suckers if you want a more manageable plant and pick fruit regularly to keep production going. Water consistently at the base to avoid cracking and blossom-end rot.

common_name: Yellow Pear Tomato (Heirloom Yellow Cherry Tomato)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cultivar with true-to-type seed that can be saved from year to year.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cherry tomato with a history extending back to at least the 1800s — producing clusters of small, bright-yellow, pear-shaped fruits with a distinctive teardrop shape and mild, low-acid, sweet flavor. The fruit shape and bright yellow color make Yellow Pear one of the most visually distinctive tomatoes in the garden, and it is a consistent favorite at farmers markets and in mixed salads where its cheerful yellow color and unusual shape create visual interest. The low-acid flavor profile makes it approachable for children and adults who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The indeterminate vine grows vigorously to 5–8 feet and sets fruit prolifically throughout the growing season — an established Yellow Pear plant produces hundreds of fruits over the course of the season. Seed can be saved from non-hybrid heirloom Yellow Pear true-to-type for future seasons — select fruit from the most vigorous and productive plants. In zone 9, Yellow Pear performs well in the spring window (February–June) and fall window (September–frost) but stalls during the peak summer heat above 95°F. The low-acid taste makes it excellent for children's snacking, fresh salads, and pasta dishes where a mild tomato flavor is preferred.

plant_note: Direct sow 1 to 2 weeks after the last frost once soil is thoroughly warm.
directions: This compact, early-maturing heirloom yields round 5 to 7 pound melons with sweet yellow flesh, ideal for small gardens and containers. Sow in warm soil and give vines room to run along the ground or a low trellis with fruit support. Water deeply but reduce moisture as fruits ripen to concentrate sweetness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy.

plant_note: Start indoors 10 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant while weather is still cool.
directions: This heirloom long-day variety forms large, golden globe bulbs with a mild, sweet flavor, best suited to northern gardens with long summer days. Start seed early indoors and transplant seedlings while cool weather encourages leafy growth before bulbing. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist, then taper off water as tops fall over. Cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot before storage.

common_name: Yellow Sweet Spanish Utah Bulb Onion
plant_note: Start indoors and transplant out; a long-day type for northern gardens.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant out as soon as the soil can be worked, spacing plants four to six inches apart. This long-day heirloom, grown in the U.S. since at least 1916, forms large 3 to 6 inch globe-shaped bulbs with mild, sweet flavor and grows best in states north of the 37th parallel. Keep the soil evenly moist during bulbing, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy place before storing.

common_name: Yellow Tomatillo (Sweet Yellow-Ripening Tomatillo, Fruitier and Milder Alternative to Green)
plant_note: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; yellow tomatillo is grown identically to green tomatillo (Physalis ixocarpa) but ripens to yellow or golden rather than green, with a notably sweeter and less acidic flavor profile. In zone 9, transplant March–April; like all tomatillos, two plants are required for good fruit set (cross-pollination). Harvest when the papery husk is fully filled and just beginning to split — at this stage the fruit inside is plump, fully yellow, and at peak flavor. Overripe yellow tomatillo (husk fully split, fruit exposed) becomes starchy and flavor declines. Zone 9's long warm season allows multiple plantings from March through July; a July planting produces fall tomatillos in October–November when cooler temperatures improve flavor development.
directions: Start indoors; plant two or more for cross-pollination. Harvest when husk just fills completely and turns yellow-gold. Yellow Tomatillo (sometimes called 'miltomate amarillo' in its native Mexican context) is a color variant of the tomatillo (Physalis ixocarpa) that ripens to golden-yellow rather than the standard green, with a fundamentally different flavor profile: sweeter, less acidic, more fruity, and less pungent than the standard green tomatillo. The standard green tomatillo has an assertive, somewhat tart flavor with herbaceous, citrus-like notes that characterize the classic salsa verde (green sauce) of Mexican cuisine; the tartness and acidity are fundamental to the sauce's role of cutting through rich meats and cheeses. Yellow tomatillo has less of this characteristic tartness and more fruit-forward sweetness — a flavor profile that lends itself to milder, sweeter sauces and preparations where the aggressive acid of green tomatillo would be too dominant. Yellow tomatillo salsas tend to be used in different culinary contexts than green tomatillo salsas: they pair well with fish, light meats, and as a condiment where a sweeter, less assertive sauce is preferred. The plants grow identically to standard green tomatillo varieties — vigorous, spreading, 3–5 feet tall, requiring two plants for pollination — and have the same growing requirements. The papery husk that encloses the developing fruit is similar in color to green tomatillo husks (tan-brown with green veining) and turns slightly yellow-tan as the fruit inside ripens; the fully ripe fruit inside is a clear lemon-yellow to golden color.

common_name: Yellow Yam (Twelve-Month Yam, Yellow Guinea Yam)
plant_note: Plant tuber sections (2–3 oz minimum) 4–6 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; this tropical vine needs 6–8 feet of strong trellis support; do not confuse with sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) which is unrelated.
directions: Plant tuber pieces with at least one eye 4–6 inches deep in loose, deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; the yellow guinea yam is a major food staple in West and Central Africa, producing large (up to 10 lb) elongated tubers with yellow-orange flesh and a pleasant earthy flavor quite different from sweet potato — the starchy tubers are boiled, roasted, fried, or pounded into fufu and other traditional preparations. Grows as a perennial tropical vine requiring sturdy staking; in frost-free zones it can remain in the ground year-round, multiplying year after year. Requires a long frost-free growing season of 8–9 months for full tuber development. Harvest when vine begins to die back.

common_name: Yellow Yam (Yellow Guinea Yam, Cayenne Yam, Yellow Cocoyam)
plant_note: Plant cut tuber sections ('setts') or small tubers in full sun after last frost in well-drained, deep, fertile, loamy to sandy soil; provide a sturdy vertical support (trellis, fence, or pole) as the vine will climb vigorously to 10–20 feet. Harvest when the vine dies back in late fall or early winter (240–300 days from planting). The distinctive yellow to deep-orange flesh (the 'yellow yam' characteristic) distinguishes D. cayennensis from white-fleshed yam species. Tubers must be cooked before eating (raw tubers contain toxic alkaloids). Cured tubers store for months. Zone 9-12 outdoor culture.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, loamy to sandy soil with a tall climbing support — Yellow Yam vines climb vigorously (10–20 feet) and require sturdy support throughout the growing season; deep, loose, well-worked soil allows the tubers to expand to their full size without impediment. Dioscorea cayennensis is a tuberous, annual to perennial twining vine native to West Africa and naturalized throughout the tropical world in the Dioscoreaceae family, one of the most important yam species in West African cuisine — the principal yam of the 'yam belt' that stretches across Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, and Togo where yams are a dietary staple, ceremonially important, and economically critical. The distinctive feature of D. cayennensis is the yellow to deep orange-yellow flesh of the tubers — in contrast to the white-fleshed D. rotundata (white guinea yam), D. cayennensis tubers have the appearance of cooked sweet potato inside after cooking. The large (5–15 pound per tuber), cylindrical to irregularly shaped tubers are smooth-skinned and store well after curing. In zone 9-12 gardens, the vine grows vigorously through the warm months before dying back as days shorten, signaling tuber maturity. Raw tubers contain dioscorine and other toxic alkaloids — always cook before eating. One of the finest true yam species for Gulf Coast tropical food gardens.

plant_note: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in loose, well-prepared soil; Yellowstone is one of the best yellow carrots, with a bright, true yellow exterior and interior and a distinctly sweet, mild, fruity flavor that stands out from standard orange carrots.
directions: Sow seed thinly 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, friable, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Yellowstone is one of the top-performing yellow carrots for home gardens, producing uniform, 7–9 inch, Nantes-type cylindrical roots with vivid yellow skin and flesh throughout and a notably mild, sweet, slightly fruity flavor that some tasters prefer to standard orange carrots; it lacks the beta-carotene of orange types but is rich in lutein, a carotenoid beneficial to eye health. Excellent for fresh eating, roasting (where it holds its color beautifully), and for adding visual variety to rainbow carrot mixes. The flavor improves after mild frost. Direct sow works best as the taproot does not transplant well.

plant_note: Grown mainly as a dry bean; needs full season to mature seed.
directions: Also called orca or calypso bean, this dry bush bean bears striking black-and-white seeds resembling the yin-yang symbol. Direct sow 1 inch deep after frost danger passes, spacing 4 inches apart in rows. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant until they rattle before harvesting. Pull whole plants and cure them in a dry, airy spot if wet weather threatens the maturing crop. Reduce watering as pods fill to encourage even drying and prevent mold.

common_name: Yolo Wonder Bell Pepper (Virus-Resistant Open-Pollinated Sweet Pepper)
plant_note: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Yolo Wonder's virus resistance is a practical advantage in zone 9 where tobacco mosaic virus and pepper mosaic virus persist in soil and infect peppers through insect vectors.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Yolo Wonder is one of the most important open-pollinated bell pepper varieties in American horticulture — developed at the University of California, Davis, from California Wonder breeding stock specifically to incorporate resistance to tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), a common disease that devastates susceptible bell pepper varieties throughout warm-season gardens. Yolo Wonder produces large, four-lobed, blocky, thick-walled fruits in the classic California Wonder mold — essentially identical in fruit character to California Wonder but with the added practical advantage of TMV resistance that makes it significantly more reliable in gardens where the virus is endemic in the soil. The fruits ripen from green to red and have full, sweet bell pepper flavor at both stages. Yolo Wonder is the virus-resistant standard for open-pollinated bell pepper production that replaced California Wonder in many commercial plantings when TMV was recognized as a major production challenge. As an open-pollinated variety, seeds can be saved reliably from season to season. The practical combination of virus resistance, large fruit size, thick walls, and excellent flavor has kept Yolo Wonder among the most commonly recommended open-pollinated bell peppers for home gardeners in disease-prone environments throughout the Gulf South.

plant_note: Harvest flowering stems just as buds open for best flavor.
directions: Grown for its tender flowering stems, yu choy is a fast staple of Cantonese cooking with a mild, sweet flavor. Direct sow and thin to about 4 inches, keeping the soil consistently moist for quick, succulent growth. Harvest the main stem with a few leaves and a cluster of yellow buds when the first flowers just begin to open. Cutting the central stalk encourages tender side shoots for a second picking. Grow in cool weather to avoid the bitterness and toughness that come with heat.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Yugoslavian Red is notable for maintaining red coloration even in warm fall conditions when many red lettuces revert to green, making it the most reliably red butterhead for zone 9 fall planting. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through fall extend the harvest window. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for continuous production.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Yugoslavian Red Butter Lettuce is a large-headed butterhead type from the former Yugoslavia, producing open, loose heads of deeply wine-red outer leaves that contrast dramatically with the pale green-to-yellow interior heart — one of the most visually striking red butterhead lettuce varieties. The large heads weigh 8–12 ounces at maturity with a buttery, tender, mild flavor characteristic of the butterhead type. Yugoslavian Red maintains its deep red color even during the warmer stretches of fall in zone 9, when most red lettuces revert to green with heat — this color stability is a primary reason it is favored for warm-climate fall gardens. The loose, open head structure forms quickly and is ready for harvest at 50–60 days. The deep red outer leaves are high in anthocyanin antioxidants; the green interior provides visual contrast when the head is split or leaves are separated in a salad.

plant_note: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall-winter harvest. Can also be sown January–February for a spring crop before heat causes bolting. Yukina Savoy is more heat-tolerant than most brassica greens and can extend into early summer in zone 9 before bolting. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest season through the cool months.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Yukina Savoy is a distinctive Asian brassica with dark green, heavily blistered (savoy-textured), crinkled leaves on upright rosette plants — a texture entirely unlike the smooth leaves of tatsoi, pak choi, or komatsuna. The savoy-type leaf surface catches dressings and sauces in cooking and stands up to heat and wilting better than smooth-leaved types. The flavor is mild and slightly mustardy, similar to komatsuna but with a hint of sweetness, making it suitable for stir-fries, soups, steaming, and raw use as a baby green. Yukina Savoy is notably cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures below 20°F with light mulch) and heat-tolerant for a brassica, making it one of the most adaptable fall-through-spring greens for zone 9 gardens. Cut outer leaves for continuous harvest or cut the whole head at once for cooking.

common_name: Yukina Savoy Brassica (Japanese Savoyed Brassica Green, Gulf South Winter Leafy Green)
plant_note: Direct sow or transplant in fall; Yukina Savoy is a vigorous, cold-tolerant brassica green that produces abundantly in zone 9's fall and winter gardens. In zone 9, sow August–November for harvest beginning October and continuing through February or March. The deeply puckered, savoyed leaves are distinctive among Asian brassica greens — the surface texture creates an unusual visual character and traps seasonings in the leaf folds when cooking. Very cold-hardy: survives temperatures into the low 20s°F once established. Harvest outer leaves and the plant will continue producing from the center for an extended season.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves from 40 days or cut whole plant. Yukina Savoy (Brassica rapa var. narinosa 'Yukina Savoy') is a Japanese brassica green that occupies an unusual position in the Asian brassica spectrum: it is not clearly tatsoi (which is also var. narinosa but with very different flat-rosette form), not bok choy, not komatsuna, and not napa cabbage, but shares characteristics with all of these while maintaining its own distinctive identity primarily defined by the heavily savoyed (puckered, crinkled, blistered) texture of the leaves. The savoy texture in Yukina produces a leaf that is visually striking — deep green, heavily textured, with bold surface relief — and practically advantageous in cooking because the crinkled surface texture holds oils, sauces, and seasonings in a way that smooth-leaved brassicas cannot. The flavor is mild and versatile, somewhat between spinach and bok choy — appealing to gardeners who find other Asian brassicas too strongly flavored but want more character than spinach. Yukina Savoy is extremely productive in cool weather, producing large rosettes of leaves over an extended harvest season. It is widely used in restaurant and specialty market salad mixes in the American Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, where its striking appearance makes it a valuable visual element in mixed greens.

plant_note: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January–February for May harvest before summer heat. Yukon Gold is a mid-season variety (70–90 days) well-suited to the Gulf Coast's cool winter growing window. Cut seed pieces to egg size, each with 1–2 eyes; allow cut surfaces to cure 1–2 days before planting.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun; Yukon Gold is a Canadian-bred variety introduced in 1980 that transformed the North American potato market by demonstrating that consumers would pay a premium for a potato with inherently golden flesh and superior flavor. The medium-large, round to oval tubers have smooth, thin, slightly golden skin and deep butter-yellow flesh with a naturally buttery, slightly sweet flavor that requires no added butter to taste rich and satisfying. Yukon Gold is equally excellent baked, mashed, roasted, and sautéed — its lower starch content than russets makes it a smooth masher that doesn't become gluey. It is now the most widely planted 'specialty' potato in North America and has spawned an entire category of yellow-flesh varieties. In zone 9, plant January–February in loose, well-drained soil; hill soil around stems as they emerge. Harvest new potatoes when plants flower (60–70 days); for cured storage, harvest after vines die back. Cure at 60–70°F for one week before storing in a cool, dark location.

plant_note: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March for an early spring crop before peak summer heat. In zone 9 a fall planting in August for harvest in October–November often produces higher-quality fruits than the spring crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and stake or cage the indeterminate vines; Zapotec Pleated is a Mexican heirloom tomato from the Zapotec people of Oaxaca, producing large (8–16 ounce), deeply ridged and pleated, hollow, orange-red fruits unlike any standard tomato — the characteristic heavy ribbing creates a natural cavity in the hollow center that makes Zapotec Pleated the ideal stuffing tomato for chiles-rellenos-style preparations, baked stuffed tomatoes, and presentations where the natural hollow serves as an edible container. The thick, meaty, sweet-acidic flesh has excellent flavor and the hollow structure minimizes the gel and seeds that make most large tomatoes watery when sliced. The unusual appearance — rustic, ridged, and slightly irregular — reflects the traditional Mesoamerican approach to tomato selection where utility (hollow stuffing structure, thick walls) was prioritized alongside flavor. In zone 9 the fall planting often produces the most attractive, well-colored fruits as cooler October temperatures enhance both color development and flavor concentration.

plant_note: Start indoors from seed in late winter and transplant out in early spring.
directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out in early spring, spacing them several inches apart. This eschalion, or banana-type shallot, produces large, elongated, easy-to-peel bulbs with coppery-pink skin and a sweet, mild flavor prized by chefs. Grow it much like an onion with steady moisture and weed control, then cure the harvested bulbs in a dry, airy spot; they store well for months.

plant_note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; an All-America Selections winner with striking bicolor fruits — yellow with a green tip — and exceptional flavor; bush habit suits small gardens and container growing.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost; Zephyr is a bush-type summer squash that requires no staking and produces heavily from a compact plant. Zephyr is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid summer squash with a visually striking bicolor pattern — straight, yellow upper portion with a distinctive lime-green tip — and very nutty, firm flesh with a noticeably drier texture than standard yellow squash that holds up well to sautéing, grilling, and roasting without becoming waterlogged. Harvest at 4–6 inches for peak tenderness and flavor; the compact bush plants are excellent for small gardens where the large rambling vines of traditional squash would be impractical. Powdery mildew tolerance and prolific production make it a reliable summer standby.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; Zipper Cream is adapted to Gulf Coast and Deep South conditions and performs well in the summer heat. Multiple plantings 3–4 weeks apart extend the harvest season; in zone 9 plant from April through August for successive harvests into fall.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; Zipper Cream is one of the most popular Southern peas in home gardens and small farms of the Gulf Coast for its exceptionally easy shelling — the pods split along a natural 'zipper' seam that allows the cream-colored peas to fall out with almost no effort, a practical advantage that makes large harvests much faster to process. The peas themselves are plump, cream-white, and have a mild, sweet, buttery flavor prized in Southern pea dishes, boiled fresh with ham or bacon, or frozen for winter use. A bush-type plant that produces heavily over a long season; heat and drought tolerant once established. One of the most recommended varieties for first-time Southern pea growers because of the easy harvest and reliable production.

common_name: Zolfino Bean (Italian Pratomagno Yellow Heirloom Bean)
plant_note: Direct sow after last frost; Zolfino is an Italian heirloom bean from the Pratomagno area of Arezzo province in Tuscany, recognized and protected as a Slow Food Presidium — it produces small, round, pale yellow beans with exceptionally thin skin and a uniquely dense, creamy, buttery texture when cooked, considered by many Italian food experts the finest cooking bean in Italy.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Zolfino beans are bush type and do not require staking; harvest when pods are dry and papery. Zolfino is an Italian heirloom bean from the Pratomagno hills of Arezzo province in Tuscany, where it has been grown for centuries at elevations between 1,300 and 2,600 feet on the slopes of the Pratomagno massif — the specific local environment (poor, well-drained, slightly acidic volcanic soil with cool nights) contributes to the bean's exceptional quality. Zolfino (the name likely derives from 'zolfo,' Italian for sulfur, referring to the pale yellow color) is a Slow Food Presidium product, meaning it is recognized as an endangered, culturally important food requiring preservation support; only farmers in the Pratomagno area using traditional methods are technically authorized to use the Zolfino denomination. The small (thumbnail-sized), round, pale yellow beans have extraordinarily thin skins — almost imperceptible when eaten — and cook to a dense, creamy, buttery texture entirely different from the grainy or mealy texture of common dried beans; the flavor is rich, earthy, and complex with sweet undertones. Outstanding in simple Italian preparations: olio e fagioli (beans with olive oil), in ribollita soup, or simply simmered with sage, garlic, and good olive oil.

plant_note: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil is warm; can also start indoors 2–3 weeks before transplanting.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, compost-enriched soil arranged in hills of 2–3 seeds, then thin to the strongest plant. Water at the soil level rather than overhead to reduce the risk of powdery mildew, which is the most common problem. Check plants daily once fruiting begins, as zucchini grows very rapidly. Harvest fruits at 6–8 inches for the best texture, leaving a short stem attached.
